Before we could clean ourselves up.
Before we could repair our own brokenness.
Before we could earn anything.
Christ died for us.
And now, through repentance and faith in Him, we are invited to receive the forgiveness and new life that only He can give.
So perhaps the question is no longer merely:
“Lord, when will You remove these waters?”
Perhaps it is also:
“Lord, what does faithfulness look like while I am here?”
“Where do I need to repent?”
“Who do I need to forgive?”
“Whose help do I need to receive?”
“What truth have I forgotten?”
“How can I honor You even when life is not going the way I planned?”
Because the Gospel does not simply change what we expect from God.
It changes how we live before Him.
And that brings me to something deeply important.
If this message has reached you during a difficult season, please do not let it become another article you read, feel emotional about for a moment, and then forget.
Take it to prayer.
Open Isaiah 43 and read the whole chapter.
Read Mark 4:35–41.
Read Romans 8.
Let Scripture shape your understanding of God more deeply than fear shapes your understanding of your circumstances.
And if you have been silently struggling, consider telling a trusted believer what you are going through.
You were never meant to live the Christian life in isolation.
The body of Christ is called to bear one another's burdens.
That means your tears do not have to remain a secret simply because you are afraid of appearing weak.
And if you are reading this while carrying something that feels impossible to explain, I want to invite you into an honest moment.
Not a performance.
Not a religious slogan.
Just truth.
If you are still holding on to Jesus even though your faith has been tested, you can comment, “I'm still fighting.”
And if the Holy Spirit has brought something into the light that you need to surrender, you can simply write, “Lord, lead me to repentance.”
You do not have to share private details publicly.
God knows the story behind your words.
And perhaps someone else reading the comments will realize that they are not the only believer struggling to remain faithful.
Perhaps someone will stop hiding.
Perhaps someone will ask for prayer.
Perhaps someone who has been away from church will take the first step toward returning.
And perhaps someone who has never truly understood the Gospel will begin to see that Christianity is not about pretending to be strong.
It is about coming to the Savior who is mighty to save.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Not because a social media algorithm can measure spiritual fruit.
But because a simple act of encouragement can reach a person at a moment when they desperately need biblical truth.
You may never know which exhausted friend, struggling parent, grieving spouse, discouraged believer, or searching soul will encounter it because you made it visible.
Not because these words possess power in themselves.
But because the Scriptures we have considered are worth returning to when fear becomes loud again.
There may come another night when your heart feels heavy and you need to remember the truth.
God did not promise that the Christian life would be painless.
Jesus did promise His continuing presence with His disciples.
“And, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.” — Matthew 28:20, KJV
What a promise.
Not merely for the days when the prayers are answered quickly.
Not merely for the seasons when everything seems to make sense.
But for every day of faithful discipleship, until the end of the age.
And if you are looking for a place to keep growing in that truth, I want to personally invite you to stay connected with Gospel Warrior.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has grown weary.
Invite the person who has drifted from church.
Invite the person who is curious about Christianity but has never truly understood grace.
We want to keep pointing people beyond temporary inspiration and toward the unchanging truth of God's Word.
I want to speak about that invitation with the same biblical honesty we have tried to bring to this entire article.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, purposeful, and cheerful, not pressured or compelled.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Some believers may choose to include such support within their personal giving budget, while continuing to honor their responsibilities to their local church, families, and others in need.

But voluntary generosity can help sustain the work of sharing biblical teaching, encouraging struggling believers, developing discipleship resources, and reaching people who might otherwise never encounter this message.
And there is something beautiful about that.
You may be walking through your own difficult waters, yet God can still use your generosity to encourage someone else who is struggling.
We want people to have access to biblical nourishment, not merely another moment of inspiration that disappears when they close their phones.
These products can be useful reminders, gifts, and resources, but they are never a substitute for Scripture, prayer, fellowship, or genuine obedience to Christ.
And while the discount is a practical way of saying thank you, it is not the heart of this invitation.
The heart is discipleship.
The heart is the Gospel.
The heart is helping people move beyond merely surviving their spiritual struggles toward growing in the knowledge, grace, and truth of Jesus Christ.
Read.
Pray.
Learn.
Encourage someone.
Grow in Christ.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God or your place among those who seek Him.
Every thoughtful share can create an opportunity for someone to hear the truth.
Every sincere conversation can become an opportunity to encourage a struggling soul.
And every act of service done in faith and love can honor the Lord.
But above all, remember this.
The mission is not to build a following around a page. It is to point people to Jesus Christ.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save anyone.
A library cannot give eternal life.
A powerful article cannot regenerate the human heart.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
Only His blood cleanses from sin.
Only His resurrection gives us living hope.
Only His grace can transform a sinner into a new creation.
And if everything we do does not ultimately lead people back to Him, then we have missed the very reason this ministry exists.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to the person who began reading this article.
The person who is tired.
The person who has been holding back tears.
The person who wondered whether God had forgotten them.
The person who has been carrying a burden so long that it has begun to feel like part of their identity.
I cannot promise you that tomorrow will be easy.
I cannot promise that the doctor will deliver the news you want.
I cannot promise that the person who left will return.
I cannot promise that every financial problem will disappear.
And I will not tell you that enough faith will guarantee the outcome you desire.
That would not be faithful to Scripture.
But I can point you to the One who has already entered our suffering, borne our sin, conquered death, and promised never to forsake those who belong to Him.
I can remind you that the cross was not the end of Jesus' story.
And because He rose again, death will not be the end of the story for those who are His.
So bring Him your exhausted heart.
Bring Him your fear.
Bring Him your questions.
Bring Him the sin you have been hiding.
Bring Him the grief you cannot explain.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
And if you have already trusted Him, keep turning toward Him.
Not because you are strong enough to hold everything together.
But because He is faithful.
Maybe tonight your prayer is not eloquent.
Maybe all you can whisper is:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Then pray it.
And if you want, pray this with me.

“Lord Jesus, You know the waters I am facing. You know the fears I have hidden, the tears I have cried, and the burdens I have tried to carry alone. Forgive me for the times I have measured Your love by my circumstances instead of remembering Your cross. Forgive my sins and lead me in repentance. Teach me to trust Your Word, even when I cannot understand Your ways. Give me courage to take the next faithful step, humility to receive help, and strength to endure what I cannot change. Keep my heart close to You. And above all, remind me that my greatest hope is not an easier life, but eternal life through Your death and resurrection. In Your holy name, Jesus, Amen.”
And now, one final thought.
When Israel stood before the sea, the waters looked like the end.
When the disciples faced the storm, the waves looked stronger than their little boat.
When Jesus hung upon the cross, His enemies thought they had witnessed His defeat.
But the sea opened.
The storm obeyed.
And on the third day, the tomb was empty.
Not every storm ends with an immediate miracle.
Not every earthly loss is restored in this lifetime.
But the resurrection assures us that God's redemptive purpose will not fail.
So if you are standing before waters you never expected to face, do not mistake the difficulty of the crossing for the absence of your Savior.
Keep praying.
Keep trusting.
Keep repenting.
Keep following Christ.
And when you cannot see the other side, remember the One who has already conquered the grave.
The waters may be deeper than you ever imagined, but they will never be deeper than the faithfulness of the Savior who holds your eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR WIFE STILL LOVES YOU… SO WHY DOES SHE NO LONGER WANT YOU TO TOUCH HER?
paragraphs: YOUR WIFE STILL LOVES YOU… SO WHY DOES SHE NO LONGER WANT YOU TO TOUCH HER?
The Silent Heartbreak of a Christian Husband Who Feels Rejected in His Own Marriage—and the Biblical Truth That Could Save What Both of You Are Slowly Losing.
There is a kind of loneliness that only a married man understands.
It is not the loneliness of coming home to an empty house.
It is coming home to a house where the woman you love is still there.
Her clothes are beside yours. Her toothbrush is next to yours. Her name is still joined to yours before God.
She still asks whether you have eaten. She still reminds you to take your medicine. She still worries when you come home late.
She says she loves you.
And you believe her.
But somewhere along the way, something changed.
The kisses became shorter.
The embraces became less frequent.
The nights became quieter.
And the woman who once reached for you now seems uncomfortable whenever you reach for her.
You lie beside your wife, staring into the darkness, wondering how two people can share the same bed and still feel thousands of miles apart.
You begin asking questions you are almost ashamed to admit.
Am I no longer attractive to her?
Did I do something wrong?
Is there someone else?
Does she still see me as her husband—or have I become nothing more than a provider, a roommate, and the father of her children?
Sometimes you try to initiate intimacy.
She says she is tired.
Another night, she has a headache.
Another night, she turns away.
And eventually, something inside you begins to change.
You stop asking.
Not because you no longer desire her.
But because rejection has started to hurt more than loneliness.
Then comes the temptation to become cold.
To withdraw affection.
To stop helping.
To punish her with silence.
To look for validation somewhere else.
And perhaps the most dangerous thought of all begins whispering in your heart:
If she really loved me, she would never make me feel this way.

Christian husband, before that thought becomes bitterness, before bitterness becomes distance, and before distance opens a door that neither of you intended to open, there is something you need to understand.
Your wife can genuinely love you and still struggle with physical intimacy.
And the way you respond to that struggle may either help rebuild the safety your marriage desperately needs—or deepen the wound neither of you knows how to explain.
Because this is not simply a story about sex.
It is a story about two hearts that may be hurting in different languages.
And Jesus Christ cares about both.
The Bible does not treat physical intimacy in marriage as dirty, shameful, or unspiritual.
In fact, Scripture speaks of it with remarkable tenderness.
Genesis 2:24 says:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." (KJV)
The original Hebrew expression for "one flesh" is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad).
Basar means flesh, and echad means one.
This union includes bodily intimacy, but it is not limited to the physical act. Marriage joins two people in a covenant of shared life, faithfulness, belonging, and responsibility.
God did not design marriage to be merely two individuals occupying the same address.
He intended a union where love is lived, not merely announced.
Where affection is expressed.
Where burdens are shared.
Where the body is honored and the soul is cherished.
So if you are a husband grieving the loss of physical closeness, your pain should not automatically be dismissed as selfishness.
Wanting to feel desired by your wife is not inherently sinful.
Longing for her embrace does not make you less spiritual.
Feeling hurt by prolonged distance does not make you a bad Christian.
Your longing deserves to be heard.
But there is a truth that must stand beside it.
Your longing is real. Your wife's dignity is equally real.
Marriage gives neither spouse permission to disregard the other's humanity.
And this is where some husbands have been taught an incomplete understanding of Scripture.
They have heard 1 Corinthians 7:3–5 quoted as though it gives a husband the right to demand intimacy whenever he desires it.
But listen carefully to what the apostle Paul actually says.
"Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband." (1 Corinthians 7:3, KJV)
The Greek expression τὴν ὀφειλήν (tēn opheilēn) refers to what is owed or due.
Paul is describing a mutual marital responsibility.
Notice the word mutual.
The husband has responsibilities toward his wife.
The wife has responsibilities toward her husband.
Neither is presented as the sole beneficiary of the other's body.
Paul continues:
"The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife." (1 Corinthians 7:4, KJV)
The Greek verb behind "hath power" is ἐξουσιάζει (exousiazei), meaning to exercise authority.
But look at the extraordinary balance of the passage.
Paul applies the same principle to both spouses.
The husband is not given unlimited authority over his wife while remaining independent of her.
His own body is also described in relation to her.
The passage confronts selfishness, not just sexual distance.
It calls married believers toward mutual consideration, fidelity, and care.
And it must never be twisted into permission for coercion, intimidation, threats, or unwanted sexual contact.
A wedding vow is not permanent consent to every sexual act.
A marriage covenant is not a license to violate someone's boundaries.
Biblical intimacy is not strengthened by fear.
It is nurtured through love, trust, mutual willingness, and honor.
A husband who uses Scripture to pressure his wife may obtain outward compliance while destroying the very closeness he longs to recover.
And a wife who feels she cannot safely say no may eventually find it difficult to say yes with genuine joy.
That is not the kind of marital relationship Christian husbands should be seeking.
Because Jesus did not teach us to use power to satisfy ourselves at another person's expense.
He showed us what love looks like when it has the power to serve.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
The Greek verb translated "love" is ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate), from agapaō, calling husbands to love their wives.
And Paul does not leave the meaning of that love to the husband's imagination.
He points directly to Christ.
Christ gave Himself.
Christ sacrificed.
Christ served.
Christ sought the good of those He loved.
He did not treat love as a transaction in which affection was offered only after His demands were satisfied.
Husband, here is a question that may be uncomfortable.
When your wife refuses intimacy, does she still experience your tenderness?
Or does your kindness disappear the moment you realize sex is not going to happen?
Do you still hold her hand?
Do you still speak gently?
Do you still help with the children?
Do you still ask how her day went?
Do you still make her feel beautiful without expecting the compliment to lead somewhere?
Or has every embrace become a negotiation?
Every kiss, an invitation she is afraid to decline?
Every act of kindness, something she worries she must repay?
This is not an accusation against every hurting husband.
Some men have spent years showing genuine patience, affection, and care while their wives remain unwilling or unable to discuss the distance.
Their grief is real, too.
But every husband should be willing to examine his own heart before God.
Because sometimes what a wife misses most is not physical desire.
It is the freedom to receive affection without feeling that she owes something in return.
Imagine a woman who has spent the entire day working, cleaning, preparing meals, managing appointments, caring for children, and carrying concerns she has not spoken aloud.
By evening, her body is exhausted.
Her mind is crowded.
She has been needed by everyone.
The children needed her.
Her employer needed her.
Her parents needed her.
The household needed her.
Then her husband reaches for her.
He may be reaching for connection, comfort, and reassurance.
But she may experience that same gesture as one more request from a person who needs something she has no energy left to give.
He thinks, She doesn't want me.
She thinks, I have nothing left.
Two people.
One bed.
Two completely different experiences.
Neither may understand the other.
And unless they begin speaking honestly, both may quietly interpret the other's behavior as rejection.
But exhaustion is only one possible explanation.
Sometimes a wife avoids physical intimacy because sex has become painful.
Sometimes childbirth has changed her body.
Sometimes breastfeeding, hormonal changes, perimenopause, menopause, medications, illness, depression, anxiety, or chronic fatigue have affected her desire.
Sometimes she carries unresolved trauma.
Sometimes she feels emotionally disconnected.
Sometimes conflict has been buried rather than resolved.
Sometimes she is struggling with body image.
Sometimes she has never experienced intimacy as something mutually pleasurable.
Sometimes there are concerns about pregnancy, privacy, or feeling rushed.
And sometimes she herself does not understand why her desire has changed.
There is also something many couples do not realize.
Not everyone experiences desire as an immediate, spontaneous urge.
For some people, desire emerges only after they feel relaxed, emotionally connected, and comfortable with affectionate touch.
This is sometimes called responsive desire.
It is not a universal explanation, and it does not mean a person should engage in unwanted intimacy hoping desire will eventually appear.
But understanding different patterns of desire can help couples stop assuming that a lack of immediate sexual interest always means a lack of love.
Christian husband, what if the problem you have been interpreting as rejection is actually something your wife has been silently struggling to explain?
What if she needs medical attention?
What if she needs rest?
What if she needs emotional healing?
What if she needs to feel heard before she can feel close?
And what if your marriage needs more than another argument about how often you have sex?
This is why one of the most important things a husband can do is also one of the hardest.
Ask without accusing. Listen without preparing your defense.
Not in the middle of another painful rejection.
Not when emotions are already burning.
Not while either of you feels cornered.
Choose a peaceful moment.
Sit beside her.
And say something like this:

"I love you. I miss being close to you, and sometimes I feel lonely in this part of our marriage. But I don't want you to feel pressured or afraid of disappointing me. I want to understand what intimacy has been like for you. Is something hurting? Is something missing between us? Is there anything I have done that makes closeness difficult? I want us to work through this together."
Then listen.
Even if the answer is difficult.
Even if she tells you something you never expected.
Even if she says she has felt unseen, overwhelmed, pressured, or emotionally alone.
And if she cannot explain it immediately, do not force an answer.
You may need several conversations.
You may need help from a qualified marriage counselor.
You may need to learn how to discuss intimacy without turning every conversation into a confrontation.
James 1:19 says:
"Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." (KJV)
The Greek word ταχὺς (tachys) means quick or swift.
The instruction is simple, but its application can be profoundly difficult.
Be quick to listen.
Not quick to accuse.
Not quick to compare your wife with other women.
Not quick to threaten separation.
Not quick to quote Scripture as a weapon.
Listen.
Because the answer you need may be hidden behind the pain you have not yet made room to hear.
But there is another side to this conversation that must not be ignored.
A husband can become so afraid of being labeled selfish that he stops acknowledging his own emotional needs altogether.
He tells himself that being a godly man means never expressing disappointment.
Never asking for closeness.
Never admitting that he feels unwanted.
He serves.
He provides.
He prays.
He remains faithful.
Yet behind his smile, he is grieving.
And perhaps nobody knows.
Brother, Scripture does not command you to pretend that your heart is made of stone.
Psalm 62:8 says:
"Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us." (KJV)
Pour out your heart.
Not only your respectable feelings.
Not only your carefully edited prayers.
Tell God about the loneliness.
Tell Him about the temptation.
Tell Him about the nights you have felt invisible.
Tell Him about the resentment you are afraid is growing inside you.
Then bring those feelings into honest, respectful conversation with your wife.

You can say, "I understand that you may not feel ready for physical intimacy, and I will respect that. But I need you to understand that the distance has been painful for me. I don't want us to ignore it. Can we seek help together?"
That is not coercion.
That is vulnerability.
There is a difference between expressing a need and demanding that another person satisfy it.
A godly marriage must make room for both spouses to speak truthfully.
And if your wife has consistently avoided the subject, it is reasonable to ask whether she would be willing to explore the issue with a qualified professional.
If intimacy is painful or desire has changed significantly, a medical evaluation may help identify treatable causes.
If there are deep emotional wounds, trauma-informed counseling may be appropriate.
If there is longstanding conflict, a qualified couples therapist who respects both spouses' faith and autonomy may help.
And where abuse, threats, or coercion are present, safety and appropriate individual support must come before attempts to restore sexual intimacy.
Prayer is essential to Christian life.
But seeking competent care is not a failure of faith.
Sometimes God answers prayers through wisdom, treatment, counseling, repentance, and the difficult work of rebuilding trust.
Now there is something else we need to discuss.
Something that has destroyed marriages far more quickly than the original intimacy problem.
The temptation to look elsewhere.
At first, it may seem harmless.
A conversation with a coworker.
A message from an old friend.
A woman online who laughs at your jokes.
Someone who notices you.
Someone who makes you feel desirable again.
And suddenly, after months or years of feeling unwanted, you experience something you have desperately missed.
Attention.
Admiration.
Excitement.
You tell yourself, It's only conversation.
But slowly, you begin sharing with another woman the emotional intimacy you have stopped trying to build with your wife.
Then comes secrecy.
Then comparison.
Then fantasy.
And sometimes, betrayal.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
"Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." (KJV)
Husband, your loneliness deserves compassion.
But loneliness does not make adultery righteous.
Rejection does not justify pornography.
Pain does not authorize revenge.
And your wife's struggles do not release you from your covenant commitment.
Jesus speaks seriously about the direction of our desires in Matthew 5:27–28.
He does not treat lust as harmless simply because no physical act has occurred.
If your heart has begun looking outside your marriage for sexual or romantic fulfillment, do not wait until the damage becomes irreversible.
Bring the temptation into the light.
Seek wise accountability.
Establish boundaries.
Repent where repentance is needed.
But understand this, too.
Repentance is not merely saying, I'm sorry.
The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, a turning or change of mind and direction.
Biblical repentance involves a genuine turning away from sin and toward God.
It produces a changed response.
If you have been punishing your wife with silence, repent.
If you have been using Scripture to pressure her, repent.
If you have been nurturing lust or an emotional affair, repent.
If you have spoken cruelly because you felt rejected, repent.
And if your wife has been dismissive, dishonest, or unwilling to acknowledge the pain in your relationship, those patterns also deserve truthful, loving attention.
Marriage is not healed by pretending only one person matters.
It is healed when truth and grace are welcomed by both.
But please hear this carefully.
Repentance is not a technique for making your wife want sex again.
You do not repent so God will reward you with physical intimacy.
You repent because Jesus Christ is Lord, because sin harms people, and because obedience is right even when the outcome remains uncertain.
That distinction matters.
Because a husband can appear patient while secretly keeping score.
He helps with the dishes for three days.
He buys flowers.
He speaks kindly.
He leads family prayer.
Then he becomes angry when intimacy does not immediately return.
And his wife realizes that what looked like transformation was actually another transaction.
Brother, do not make love a performance designed to secure a reward.
Love her because she is your wife.
Love her because she bears God's image.
Love her because you made a covenant.
And above all, love in response to the grace Christ has shown you.
Colossians 3:19 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them." (KJV)
The Greek expression μὴ πικραίνεσθε (mē pikrainesthe) carries the prohibition against becoming embittered toward one's wife.
Think about that.
God's Word speaks directly to the bitterness that can quietly poison marriage.
Not just explosive anger.
Not just shouting.
Bitterness.
That coldness that grows when disappointment is rehearsed over and over.
That habit of interpreting everything your wife does through the lens of your unmet expectations.
That resentment that makes you stop noticing her goodness because you are focused entirely on what is missing.
You can become so consumed by the intimacy you are not receiving that you forget the person standing in front of you.
The woman who may have carried your children.
The woman who has stood beside you during financial struggles.
The woman who has prayed for you.
The woman who may be fighting battles you do not fully see.
Or perhaps your marriage has endured wounds much deeper than ordinary exhaustion.
Perhaps there has been betrayal.
Perhaps there have been harsh words.
Perhaps there has been emotional neglect.
Perhaps she has spent years feeling unsafe opening her heart.
And now you are wondering why opening her body feels difficult.
Physical intimacy cannot be separated entirely from the condition of a relationship.
It does not mean every marital disagreement must be solved before spouses can enjoy closeness.
But it does mean that persistent hurt, fear, resentment, and broken trust deserve serious attention.
First Peter 3:7 instructs husbands to dwell with their wives according to knowledge and to give them honor.
The Greek phrase κατὰ γνῶσιν (kata gnōsin) means "according to knowledge."
In context, Peter calls husbands to considerate, honorable conduct toward their wives, recognizing their shared standing as heirs of God's grace.
That is a remarkable standard.
Not merely live with your wife.
Seek to understand her.
Learn what burdens her.
Learn what brings her peace.
Learn what makes her feel respected.
Learn how she experiences affection.
Learn how your words affect her.
And allow her to know you, too.
Your fears.
Your disappointments.
Your hopes.
Your need for companionship.
Because marriage is not a competition over whose pain deserves more sympathy.
It is a covenant in which two imperfect people are called to care for one another.
And sometimes the beginning of healing looks surprisingly ordinary.
It looks like putting your phone down when she speaks.
It looks like sharing household responsibilities without treating them as favors.
It looks like spending time together without a hidden sexual expectation.
It looks like holding hands during a walk.
It looks like laughing again.
It looks like apologizing without adding, "But you also..."
It looks like asking whether a hug would feel welcome.
It looks like planning time together that both of you genuinely enjoy.
It looks like remembering that friendship is not a lesser form of marital intimacy.
It is one of the foundations that helps a marriage endure.
And sometimes it looks like a husband saying:
"I miss you. Not just sexually. I miss us."
Imagine the difference those words might make.
Not, "Why won't you give me what I need?"
But, "I miss us."
Not, "The Bible says you owe me."
But, "I want us both to experience the closeness God intended."
Not, "You never want me anymore."
But, "Help me understand what has changed."
Not, "If you loved me, you would."
But, "I love you, and I want us to find a way forward that honors both of us."
That kind of conversation does not guarantee immediate restoration.
But it opens a door that accusation often closes.
And there may be husbands reading this who have already tried.
You have listened.
You have apologized.
You have sought counseling.
You have shown patience.
And still, nothing has changed.
You may be asking, How long am I supposed to keep trying?
Scripture does not provide a universal deadline for the restoration of sexual intimacy.
Nor does it promise that every marriage will recover in the way either spouse hopes.
That uncertainty can be painful.
But it does not mean you are powerless.
You can continue to pursue honest communication.
You can seek wise pastoral guidance and professional support.
You can establish appropriate boundaries against contempt, dishonesty, and harmful behavior.
You can refuse to make another person's choices the measure of your worth.
And you can entrust your deepest identity to Christ rather than to the frequency of physical affection in your marriage.
Your wife cannot carry the burden of being your savior.
And you cannot be hers.
Only Jesus can bear that weight.
This is where the Gospel enters a marriage in a way that reaches deeper than techniques and communication strategies.
Because the Gospel is not merely advice for becoming a better husband.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Christ did not wait until we had made ourselves worthy of His love.
He came in mercy.
He gave Himself.
He bore sin.
He died.
And He rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
That grace does not erase the consequences of our actions.
It does not excuse abuse.
It does not remove the need for truth, accountability, or patient rebuilding.
But it means our failures do not have to be the final word.
A husband who has been bitter can repent.
A wife who has been emotionally distant can begin speaking honestly.
A couple who has misunderstood each other for years can learn new ways to communicate.
A marriage wounded by selfishness can seek restoration.
And even where the relationship remains difficult, both spouses can grow in faithfulness to Christ.
Jesus can transform a marriage without turning either spouse into the other's possession.
That is the beauty of grace.
It changes not only what we want from people.
It changes how we treat them.
And perhaps the most powerful picture of this is found in the way Jesus washed His disciples' feet.
John 13:14 records His words:
"If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." (KJV)
The Lord of glory took the posture of a servant.
Not because He lacked authority.
But because His love was expressed through humility.
Christian husband, imagine what might happen if you approached your marriage with that kind of heart.
Not as a man demanding that his wife prove her love.
But as a man asking how he can love faithfully while also speaking honestly about his needs.
Not as a man trying to win a battle.
But as a husband seeking the good of the woman he promised to cherish.
And wives who may be reading this, your voice matters here, too.
If you love your husband but struggle with physical intimacy, you are not automatically a failure as a wife.
You are not spiritually defective because your desire is different from his.
But if your relationship is safe enough for honest conversation, please do not assume your husband can understand your silence.
He may be interpreting your exhaustion as rejection.
Your pain as indifference.
Your fear as a lack of love.
Tell him what you can.
Tell him when something hurts.
Tell him when you feel overwhelmed.
Tell him when you need medical help, emotional support, or more time.
And when you do not know the answer, it is okay to say, "I don't fully understand what is happening, but I want us to understand it together."
Neither spouse should be expected to solve this alone.
The goal is not to decide who is guilty for the absence of sex.
The goal is to pursue a marriage where truth, affection, safety, and mutual care can grow.
And now, husband, I want you to imagine one final scene.
It is late.
The children are asleep.
The house is quiet.
Your wife is beside you.
You feel that familiar ache.
The temptation to withdraw.
The temptation to become angry.
The temptation to turn away and silently rehearse every rejection you have experienced.
But this time, something changes.
You do not pretend that you are fine.
You do not demand that she fix your pain.
You simply reach for honesty.
"Can we talk? I don't want us to keep drifting apart."
Maybe she turns toward you.
Maybe she begins to cry.
Maybe she tells you she has been struggling with something you never knew.
Maybe you both discover how much pain has accumulated between you.
Maybe the conversation is awkward.
Maybe you need help to continue it.
Maybe there is no immediate breakthrough at all.
But you have chosen something important.
You have chosen truth over silent resentment.
You have chosen understanding over accusation.
You have chosen faithfulness over temptation.
You have chosen to seek Christ's way rather than allow disappointment to rule your heart.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, your wife realizes that your desire for intimacy is not merely about what you want from her.
It is also about the relationship you long to rebuild with her.
And perhaps you begin to realize that her struggle is not necessarily a verdict on your worth.
That moment may not end with sex.
It may end with tears.
It may end with an apology.
It may end with an agreement to seek counseling.
It may end with nothing more than two people holding hands.
But sometimes a marriage begins healing long before physical intimacy returns.
Sometimes it begins when two people finally stop fighting each other's pain.
And start facing the problem together.
Dear husband, do not let a season of sexual distance become an excuse for spiritual destruction.
Do not let rejection turn you into someone you never wanted to become.
Do not let bitterness rob you of tenderness.
Do not let temptation persuade you that faithfulness is foolish.
And do not allow shame to convince you that seeking help is weakness.
Your pain matters.
Your wife's pain matters.
Your covenant matters.
But above all, your relationship with Jesus Christ matters.
If you have sinned, come to Him in repentance.
If you are exhausted, come to Him for strength.
If your heart has become hard, ask Him to soften it.
If your marriage needs help, seek it.
If your wife needs care, honor her.
If you need to be heard, speak truthfully.
And if you are both willing to begin again, do not despise the smallest step toward restoration.
Because the story of redemption is not about pretending that nothing was ever broken.
It is about what the grace of God can do in the midst of brokenness.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
This verse speaks of the new creation found in Christ. It is not a guarantee that every troubled marriage will be restored or that every sexual difficulty will disappear.
But it is a powerful reminder that the person you have been does not have to determine the person you become through God's grace.
Your bitterness does not have to rule you.
Your past mistakes do not have to define you.
Your loneliness does not have to lead you into sin.
And your marriage does not have to be approached without hope.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
From secrecy to honesty.
From resentment to repentance.
From selfishness to sacrificial love.
From spiritual exhaustion to renewed dependence on Jesus.
Because Jesus rewrites everything—not by promising that every circumstance will become easy, but by offering forgiveness, new life, and the grace to walk faithfully through what is hard.
If this article exposed something you have been carrying silently, please do not bury it again.
Maybe you are the husband who feels unwanted.
Maybe you are the wife who feels misunderstood.
Maybe you are the couple who still loves each other but no longer knows how to reach each other.
You do not have to share intimate details publicly. Your marriage deserves privacy and dignity. But your words may remind another struggling believer that seeking help is not shameful.
And if you have experienced healing, consider sharing a testimony of what helped you rebuild trust, communicate honestly, or grow in Christ.
Someone reading the comments may be looking for a reason not to give up on doing what is right.
Not because every sentence will be easy to hear.
But because there may come another night when disappointment tempts you to forget what love requires.

Not merely to increase its reach, but because somewhere among your friends may be a husband suffering in silence, a wife carrying hidden pain, or a couple who desperately needs a conversation rooted in biblical truth rather than blame.
If someone comes to mind, consider tagging them only when it would be welcome and respectful. You can also send this privately. Some messages are best shared gently rather than publicly.
Here, we want to keep pointing people beyond temporary inspiration and toward the living Christ—through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, and genuine discipleship.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is more than a place to read an occasional article.
Our desire is to build a growing community where believers are continually nourished by God's Word, challenged to live faithfully, and encouraged to follow Jesus when life becomes complicated.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and grow in spiritual maturity.
Some believers choose to support ministries through regular giving as an expression of gratitude and stewardship.
But we want to be biblically clear.
Scripture says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
The Greek word ἀνάγκης (anankēs) in this verse refers to necessity or compulsion.
Christian generosity should not be manipulated through guilt.
And you cannot buy His favor.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, not a reward for financial support.
But if you believe in this mission and have the means to help sustain it, your partnership can make a meaningful difference in the work we are seeking to do.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for personal reflection, or thoughtful gifts that encourage others in their walk with Christ.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Grow.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Our hope is that every person who encounters Gospel Warrior will be pointed toward Jesus Christ, whether they ever spend a single cent or not.
It is to proclaim the Savior who gave Himself for sinners and calls us into a transformed life.
And if you have stayed with this article until now, perhaps there is one last thing you need to hear.
Husband, your wife may still love you even when physical intimacy has become difficult.
Wife, your husband may be deeply hurting even when he struggles to express that pain without frustration.
Neither of you can heal a marriage by denying the other's humanity.
And neither of you can force the other person to become whole.
But you can seek truth.
You can practice kindness.
You can pursue understanding.
You can repent where you have sinned.
You can ask for help.
You can pray.
You can choose faithfulness.
And you can trust Jesus Christ with what you cannot control.
Tonight, before you turn away from each other again, perhaps the most important question is not:
"Why don't you want me anymore?"
Perhaps it is:
"What has been hurting between us that we have been too afraid to talk about?"
And perhaps the first prayer is not:
"Lord, change my wife."
But:

"Lord, search my heart. Teach me to love faithfully, speak truthfully, listen humbly, and honor the person You have entrusted to my care. Give us wisdom to face what is broken without hurting each other further. And whatever happens, keep us close to You."
Because sometimes the deepest tragedy in a marriage is not that two people have stopped touching.
It is that they have stopped believing they can safely tell each other the truth.
And sometimes the first sign of grace is not a passionate embrace.
It is a trembling voice in the darkness saying:
"I still love you. I don't know how we got here. But I want us to find our way forward."
The most heartbreaking distance in marriage is not the space between two bodies—it is the silence between two hearts that still long to be loved.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU WERE TOLD YOU ARE NO LONGER UNDER THE LAW… BUT DOES THAT MEAN YOU CAN LIVE HOWEVER YOU WANT?
paragraphs: YOU WERE TOLD YOU ARE NO LONGER UNDER THE LAW… BUT DOES THAT MEAN YOU CAN LIVE HOWEVER YOU WANT?
Jesus fulfilled the Law. Paul said we are under grace. Yet Jesus warned against setting aside God's commandments. So which commands still apply to Christians—and what happens when we get this wrong?
There is a sentence in the Bible that has set countless people free.
And that very same sentence has been used by others to justify the very sins Jesus died to save them from.
“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.” — Romans 6:14 (KJV)
Read those words again.
Not under the Law.
Under grace.
Beautiful words. Liberating words. Words that can make a guilty soul weep with relief.
If you are no longer under the Law, does that mean God no longer cares how you live?
Can you lie because you are under grace?
Can you commit adultery because Jesus fulfilled the Law?
Can you hate your neighbor, worship money, refuse forgiveness, indulge your flesh, and dismiss conviction because salvation is not earned by obedience?
And if the answer is no, then which commandments still apply?
The Ten Commandments?
The Sabbath?
The dietary laws?
The sacrifices?
The commands about clothing, circumcision, purity, and worship?
Who decides?
Paul?
Moses?
Your pastor?
Your denomination?
Or Jesus Christ Himself?
Because somewhere between the words “Jesus paid it all” and “God expects holiness,” many sincere believers have become deeply confused.
Some are terrified that one failure will cost them their salvation.
Others have been taught that because Jesus fulfilled the Law, obedience is practically optional.
One group lives as though the cross accomplished too little.
The other risks living as though the cross demands nothing.
And both desperately need to hear what Scripture actually says.
Because the truth is more beautiful, more demanding, and more liberating than either extreme.
Jesus did not die to make sin acceptable. He died to make sinners new.
And to understand why that matters, we need to go back to a hillside in Galilee.
Imagine standing among the crowds.
The air is warm. People have traveled from surrounding villages. Some are sick. Some are exhausted. Some have spent their entire lives trying to satisfy religious expectations.
Then Jesus begins teaching.
And He says something that should settle one of the greatest misunderstandings about Christianity.
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.” — Matthew 5:17 (KJV)
In the Greek text, the word translated “destroy” is καταλῦσαι (katalysai), from katalyō, meaning to tear down, dismantle, or abolish.
The word translated “fulfil” is πληρῶσαι (plērōsai), from plēroō, meaning to fulfill, complete, or bring to fullness.
Jesus was not announcing that God's previous revelation had been a mistake.
He was declaring that it was reaching its intended fulfillment in Him.
That distinction changes everything.
The Law was never a collection of random religious restrictions that God later regretted.
It revealed His holiness.
It exposed human sin.
It governed Israel's covenant life.
It established patterns of worship, sacrifice, justice, purity, and community.
And throughout its ceremonies, promises, and prophetic expectations, it pointed forward to something greater.
Someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “law” is תּוֹרָה (torah), meaning instruction, teaching, or law.
It was God's covenant instruction to Israel, not merely a list of penalties.
But even that understanding is incomplete without recognizing where the story was heading.
Because the Law could identify sin.
It could command righteousness.
It could prescribe sacrifices.
But it could not, through human obedience, transform guilty sinners into righteous people.
And that is where the scandal begins.
The God who gave the Law entered human history in the person of His Son.
The One who never sinned stood among sinners.
The One who perfectly obeyed was condemned by lawless men.
And the One who deserved no judgment voluntarily bore the judgment our sins deserved.
At Calvary, grace did not declare sin harmless.
Grace revealed just how serious sin was—and how far God's love would go to redeem us.
But wait.
If Jesus fulfilled the Law, why did He continue by saying:
“Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 5:19 (KJV)
That sounds very different from saying commandments no longer matter.
And it is.
Jesus was warning His listeners not to treat God's revelation as disposable.
Matthew 5:18–20 makes clear that He regarded the Law and the Prophets as enduringly significant in God's redemptive purpose.
But the rest of the New Testament also teaches that Christ's fulfillment changes how believers relate to the Mosaic covenant.
That is not a contradiction.
It is the difference between abolishing God's revelation and fulfilling the covenant to which that revelation belonged.
Consider what happened when Jesus continued His sermon.
He did not say, “You have heard that murder is wrong, but now murder is acceptable.”
Instead, He confronted the anger and contempt that grow inside the human heart.
He did not say, “Adultery no longer matters.”
He exposed the lust that can corrupt a person long before an outward act occurs.
He did not lower the moral seriousness of God's commands.
He carried their implications deeper.
Beyond appearances.
Beyond public reputation.
Beyond the carefully managed religious image.
Straight into the places we hide from everyone else.
And suddenly, the question is no longer merely whether you have broken a visible commandment.
It becomes whether your heart truly loves what God loves.
That is uncomfortable.
Because you can avoid murder while quietly nurturing hatred.
You can avoid physical adultery while feeding lust in secret.
You can appear generous while being ruled by greed.
You can attend church every Sunday while refusing to forgive someone you claim to love.
You can quote Scripture publicly while manipulating people privately.
And you can defend biblical morality while remaining completely indifferent to the suffering of your neighbor.
Jesus exposes all of it.
Not because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
But because superficial religion cannot heal what we refuse to acknowledge.
The Law can expose the wound. Only Christ can save and transform the wounded sinner.
Now return to Paul's words.
“For ye are not under the law, but under grace.”
The Greek expression in Romans 6:14 is:
οὐ γάρ ἐστε ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ χάριν
ou gar este hypo nomon alla hypo charin
A close translation is:
“For you are not under law, but under grace.”
The word νόμον (nomon) means law.
The word χάριν (charin) comes from charis, meaning grace or favor.
Paul is describing a decisive change in the believer's relationship to sin, the Law, and God's saving grace.
But what does he mean?
Thankfully, Paul answers the question himself.
In the very next verse.
“What then? shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid.” — Romans 6:15 (KJV)
There it is.
The question people are still asking two thousand years later.
And Paul's answer could hardly be stronger.
The Greek expression is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
An emphatic rejection.
“Absolutely not!”
“May it never be!”
Paul anticipated the possibility that someone would turn grace into permission for sin.
And he rejected it immediately.
Why?
Because Romans 6 is not primarily about receiving permission to ignore God's will.
It is about being united with Jesus Christ in His death and resurrection.
Paul teaches that believers have died to sin's old dominion and are called to walk in newness of life.
That does not mean Christians become incapable of sinning.
It means sin no longer has the rightful claim of mastery it once exercised over them.
Grace does not simply pardon.
Grace also begins to transform.
This is where many of us need to confront an uncomfortable possibility.
We may have been asking the wrong question.
Instead of asking, “How much sin can I commit and still be saved?”
Perhaps we should ask, “If Jesus rescued me from sin, why am I trying to make peace with it?”
Because salvation is not a loophole.
It is a rescue.
Imagine a man drowning in deep water.
Someone dives in, reaches him, and carries him toward shore.
The man survives because another person saved him.
He did not earn that rescue.
He did not accomplish it through his own strength.
But imagine that after being rescued, he turns around and says:
“Since you saved me for free, I suppose I should jump back into the water and stay there.”
Something is terribly wrong with that understanding of rescue.
The rescuer did not save him because drowning was harmless.
He saved him because drowning was destroying him.
And Jesus did not come to make us comfortable in the very bondage from which He came to deliver us.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved. It is God's power at work in those He has redeemed.
But this raises another difficult question.
If Christians must obey God, are we still required to keep every commandment in the Old Testament?
Here is where careful biblical interpretation matters.
And where simplistic answers can cause real spiritual damage.
The Mosaic Law was given to Israel as part of God's covenant with that nation.
It included commands concerning worship, sacrifices, priesthood, food, purity, civil justice, festivals, moral conduct, and community life.
Christians often speak of moral, ceremonial, and civil laws.
Those categories can be useful for explaining different functions of the Mosaic commandments.
But we should be careful.
The Bible does not present them as three formally separated legal codes with those exact labels.
They are theological distinctions used to help readers understand the Law's varied purposes.
And sincere Christians have differed about precisely how those distinctions should be applied.
What the New Testament clearly teaches is that Jesus Christ fulfilled the sacrificial system and inaugurated the new covenant.
Hebrews 10:1 describes the Law as having a shadow of the good things to come.
Hebrews 10:10–14 teaches that Christ's once-for-all offering accomplishes what repeated animal sacrifices could not.
Think about what that means.
You do not need to bring a lamb to an altar to obtain forgiveness.
Not because sin has become less serious.
But because the Lamb of God has come.
You do not need a succession of Levitical priests to offer sacrifices for your sins.
Not because mediation no longer matters.
But because Jesus is our great High Priest.
You do not need to repeat the old sacrificial system.
Because the sacrifice to which it pointed has been offered.
The shadow was never meant to replace the Savior.
Hebrews 8:6–13 presents Jesus as the mediator of a better covenant and describes the former covenant as becoming obsolete.
That is why Christians are not required to reconstruct ancient Israel's sacrificial and priestly system.
The new covenant is not merely the old covenant with a different name.
Something decisive has happened in Christ.
And the apostles had to confront the practical consequences.
In Acts 15, the early church faced a serious controversy.
Did Gentile believers need to be circumcised and required to keep the Law of Moses in order to belong to God's people?
The apostles and elders gathered in Jerusalem.
The question was not theoretical.
It concerned the very identity of the Gospel.
Would Gentiles be accepted through the grace of Jesus Christ?
Or would they first have to enter the Mosaic covenant through circumcision and its obligations?
Peter declared:
“But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.” — Acts 15:11 (KJV)
The council did not require Gentile Christians to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic Law as a condition of salvation.
Instead, it gave specific instructions concerning idolatry, sexual immorality, blood, and things strangled (Acts 15:19–29).
Those instructions arose in the setting of Gentile conversion, holiness, and fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers.
Christians have debated aspects of their continuing application, particularly the food-related restrictions.
But the council's central conclusion is unmistakable.
Gentiles do not become God's people by first becoming Jews under the Mosaic covenant. They are received through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
That same truth appears in Paul's letter to the Galatians.
He strongly opposed requiring circumcision as a condition of justification.
He warned that seeking to be justified by the Law abandons reliance upon Christ's grace (Galatians 5:2–4).
But notice what he said only a few verses later.
“For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.” — Galatians 5:13 (KJV)
And then:
“For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” — Galatians 5:14 (KJV)
This is extraordinary.
Paul defends freedom from the Mosaic Law as a covenantal system.
Then he immediately insists that Christian freedom must express itself through love.
Not selfishness.
Not exploitation.
Not indulgence.
Love.
The Greek word translated “serve” in Galatians 5:13 is δουλεύετε (douleuete), from douleuō, meaning to serve as a slave or be in service.
Do you see the beautiful reversal?
We are freed from sin's slavery and from the Law as the means of obtaining righteousness.
Yet we willingly serve one another in love.
Freedom in Christ is not the absence of responsibility.
It is the liberation of the heart to love God and others rightly.
And that brings us to the question many Christians have been waiting for.
So which commandments still apply?
The New Testament does not hand Christians a single replacement list that simply labels every Mosaic command “active” or “canceled.”
Instead, it teaches us to understand God's commands through Jesus Christ, His completed work, His apostles' teaching, and the new covenant.
Commands against murder, adultery, theft, lying, idolatry, and covetousness are reaffirmed as part of Christian moral life.
Jesus condemns murder, adultery, and falsehood.
Paul condemns sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, and dishonesty.
Romans 13:8–10 explicitly recalls commandments against adultery, murder, stealing, and coveting, and shows how love fulfills their righteous intent.
Ephesians 4–5 calls believers to truthfulness, forgiveness, sexual purity, kindness, and holiness.
Galatians 5:19–23 contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit.
These are not optional religious preferences.
They are expressions of the life to which Christ calls His people.
But there is a crucial distinction.
Christians do not obey these commands to purchase salvation. They obey because they belong to the Savior.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
And the very next verse says that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do not separate what Scripture holds together.
Good works are not the price of redemption.
They are part of the purpose for which the redeemed have been made new.
The same grace that saves us also teaches us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–14).
This is why a Christian cannot reasonably say, “Since I am under grace, I have no obligation to love my neighbor.”
Love is not a minor addition to Christianity.
It is central to the life of Christ's disciples.
Jesus said:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.” — John 14:15 (KJV)
He also commanded His disciples to love one another as He had loved them (John 13:34–35).
And after His resurrection, He commissioned them to make disciples, teaching them to observe all that He had commanded (Matthew 28:18–20).
Grace does not erase discipleship.
Grace makes genuine discipleship possible.
Now, what about the Sabbath?
This is one of the places where Christians should be especially careful not to claim more certainty than the biblical discussion permits.
The Sabbath command appears in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8–11), and it was also a distinctive covenant sign between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13–17).
Jesus affirmed His authority as Lord of the Sabbath and challenged interpretations that turned it into a burden rather than a gift (Mark 2:27–28).
Yet the New Testament also records differences over the observance of particular days.
Romans 14:5–6 speaks of believers esteeming days differently while seeking to honor the Lord.
Colossians 2:16–17 warns against allowing others to judge believers concerning food, festivals, new moons, or sabbaths, describing these as shadows whose substance belongs to Christ.
Christian traditions understand the continuing Sabbath obligation differently.
Some hold that the fourth commandment remains binding as a weekly day of rest and worship, often observed on Sunday.
Others maintain that the seventh-day Sabbath remains the proper observance.
Still others understand Sabbath observance as fulfilled in Christ and do not regard a particular day as universally binding under the new covenant.
These differences deserve serious biblical study, not careless accusations against fellow believers.
What Christians should not do is use their convictions about days as an excuse to neglect worship, despise other believers, or ignore the rest and devotion that honor God.
And what about food?
Jesus' teaching in Mark 7:14–23 places profound emphasis on the uncleanness that proceeds from the human heart.
Mark 7:19 is commonly understood, particularly in many modern translations, as indicating that Jesus declared all foods clean, although the passage's wording and interpretation have been discussed.

Acts 10 uses Peter's vision involving clean and unclean animals to confront the exclusion of Gentiles, with Peter himself emphasizing that God had taught him not to call any person common or unclean (Acts 10:28).
Romans 14 addresses differences over food and urges believers not to destroy one another over disputed matters.
Colossians 2:16 likewise warns against judgment concerning food and drink.
For these reasons, most Christian traditions do not regard Israel's dietary regulations as binding covenant requirements for Christians.
But this freedom must never become an excuse for gluttony, disregard for health, or contempt toward someone whose conscience leads them to abstain.
Paul's concern is not merely what a Christian has the right to do.
It is whether that freedom is exercised in love.
And what about circumcision?
Galatians 5:6 gives a remarkably clear answer concerning its spiritual status in Christ:
“For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love.” — Galatians 5:6 (KJV)
Circumcision is not required for justification or membership in Christ's people.
The decisive issue is not an external covenant marker.
It is faith in Jesus Christ expressing itself through love.
And what about the laws governing ancient Israel's civil penalties, land arrangements, and national institutions?
Those belonged to Israel's historical covenant administration.
Christians can still learn enduring truths about God's justice, concern for the vulnerable, honesty, fairness, and the seriousness of evil from those laws.
But the New Testament does not command the church to establish itself as a replacement nation-state and enforce the entire Mosaic civil code.
The church is called to bear witness to Christ among the nations.
To proclaim the Gospel.
To practice holiness.
To love its neighbors.
To seek justice and mercy.
To make disciples.
Not to confuse the mission of the church with the political institutions of ancient Israel.
And what about the Ten Commandments as a whole?
Christians broadly affirm their profound importance as a revelation of God's moral character and covenant instruction.
Yet traditions differ over how the Decalogue functions within the new covenant, particularly regarding the Sabbath.

It is therefore more accurate to say that Christian obedience is governed by God's will as revealed and fulfilled in Jesus Christ and taught by His apostles than to pretend that every Christian tradition agrees on one simple classification of every Old Testament command.
But do not mistake that nuance for uncertainty about the heart of Christian living.
Jesus was asked which commandment was greatest.
He answered:
“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.” — Matthew 22:37 (KJV)
And then:
“Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” — Matthew 22:39 (KJV)
He declared that all the Law and the Prophets hang upon these two commandments.
This is not permission to redefine love according to our feelings.
Biblical love is shaped by God's truth.
Love refuses to exploit.
Love refuses to betray.
Love refuses to celebrate evil.
Love seeks the good of another person.
Love speaks truth without cruelty.
Love practices mercy without pretending sin is harmless.
And love begins with wholehearted devotion to God.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” — Galatians 6:2 (KJV)
There is the phrase worth remembering.
The law of Christ.
Christians are not lawless.
They belong to Jesus.
They live under His lordship.
They follow His teaching.
They are led by His Spirit.
They are called to love as He loved.
And that kind of love is far more demanding than merely checking off religious requirements.
Because a checklist can sometimes be completed without compassion.
But Christlike love asks what happens when nobody is watching.
It asks how you treat the person who cannot repay you.
It asks whether you tell the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
It asks whether you forgive when resentment feels justified.
It asks whether you repent when the Holy Spirit exposes your pride.
It asks whether the Jesus you praise on Sunday is the same Jesus you obey on Monday.
And now the conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps you have spent years trying to be good enough for God.
You pray.
You attend church.
You give.
You serve.
You avoid certain sins.
But deep inside, you are exhausted.
Every mistake feels like proof that God must be disappointed in you.
Every spiritual failure sends you back into fear.
You read Romans 6:14 and desperately want to believe that grace is real.
But part of you still thinks God's love rises and falls with your performance.
If that is you, listen carefully.
Your obedience did not put Jesus on the cross, and your obedience cannot replace what He accomplished there.
You cannot earn what Christ purchased by His blood.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
Not to those who have achieved sinless perfection.
Not to those who have never struggled.
Not to those who have never needed to repent.
To those who belong to Him.
But perhaps your struggle is different.
Perhaps you have been using grace to silence conviction.
You know the relationship is sinful.
You know the habit is destroying you.
You know the dishonesty needs to stop.
You know you have been mistreating someone.
You know you have been neglecting prayer, feeding resentment, or hiding behind a public Christian identity while privately surrendering to something you refuse to confront.
And whenever conviction rises, you tell yourself:
“I'm not under the Law. I'm under grace.”
Friend, do not turn the kindness of God into an argument against the holiness of God.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
First John 1:9 assures believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
And 1 John 2:1 reminds us that if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
The Gospel gives no encouragement to despair.
But neither does it encourage us to defend the sins for which Christ died.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is power to begin walking differently.
Not because you are strong enough to save yourself.
But because Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior.
Maybe you are reading this after failing again.
The same temptation.
The same secret compromise.
The same promise you made to God last week.
And now you feel ashamed even to pray.
You wonder whether you have exhausted His patience.
You wonder whether someone like you can still be changed.
Look at Peter.
He boldly promised loyalty.
Then denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the weight of that failure.
The sound of his own voice.
The memory of his denial.
The knowledge that he had abandoned the Lord he claimed to love.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
In John 21, the risen Jesus met him again.
And three times Jesus asked Peter about his love.
The encounter was painful.
But it was restorative.
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never failed.
Nor did He declare Peter beyond redemption.
He recommissioned him.
“Feed my sheep.”
What a Savior.
The One Peter denied became the One who restored him.
And that is why the Gospel is so much more than a system of rules.
It is the announcement that the crucified and risen Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners and makes them His own.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because obedience has been abolished.
But because Jesus rewrites what sin and shame seemed determined to make final.

The woman caught in adultery in John 8 provides another powerful picture, though the passage's manuscript history deserves an important note: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is marked or discussed in many modern Bibles.
In the traditional account, Jesus refuses to join the woman's accusers in condemning her.
But He does not tell her that adultery is acceptable.
He says:
“Go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11 (KJV)
Mercy and holiness stand together.
Forgiveness and transformation belong together.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
It says, “Your sin is serious, but Christ's mercy is greater than your guilt, and His grace calls you into a new life.”
This is what happens when we stop treating Law and grace as though they are competing gods.
God is not divided against Himself.
The God who revealed His holiness through the Law is the God who revealed His saving mercy through Jesus Christ.
His moral character has not changed.
His redemptive plan has reached its fulfillment in His Son.
And the new covenant promises something astonishing.
Jeremiah 31:33 says:
“I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.” — Jeremiah 31:33 (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the phrase is:
נָתַתִּי אֶת־תּוֹרָתִי בְּקִרְבָּם
natatti et-torati beqirbam
“I will put my law within them.”
And:
וְעַל־לִבָּם אֶכְתֲּבֶנָּה
ve'al-libbam ekhtavennah
“And on their heart I will write it.”
The promise is not simply that God would issue another external list.
It is that His covenant people would know Him through a transformed relationship.
Ezekiel 36:26–27 develops the same hope through the promise of a new heart and God's Spirit, who moves His people to walk in His ways.
Hebrews 8:8–12 applies Jeremiah's new-covenant promise to the work of Christ.
Do you see the wonder?
The goal of redemption is not merely to change your religious status while leaving your heart untouched.
God intends to make a people who know Him, love Him, and walk in His ways.
That transformation is not completed by human willpower.
It is the work of divine grace.
And it continues as believers repent, trust, obey, struggle, grow, and depend upon the Holy Spirit.
So when someone asks, “Are Christians still under the Law?” the biblical answer needs to be more careful than a simple slogan.

Christians are not under the Mosaic Law as the covenantal system by which they must obtain righteousness or establish their standing among God's people. They are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But Christians are not free from God's moral will.
They are called to obey Christ, walk by the Spirit, love God and neighbor, and pursue the holiness that belongs to their new life.
The sacrificial and priestly system finds its fulfillment in Jesus.
Circumcision is not required for salvation.
The Mosaic food laws are not generally regarded as binding new-covenant obligations, though conscience and love remain important.
The civil institutions of ancient Israel are not simply transferred wholesale to the church.
Questions such as Sabbath observance require careful interpretation and charitable engagement across Christian traditions.
And the moral commands reaffirmed and deepened through Christ and His apostles remain essential to Christian discipleship.
Not as a ladder by which sinners climb into heaven.
But as part of the life of those whom grace has rescued.
This is the balance we must never lose.
We are not saved because we obey. But saving grace does not leave us indifferent to obedience.
And even that sentence needs one more truth.
Our obedience will never become the foundation of our confidence before God.
Jesus Christ remains that foundation.
On your strongest spiritual day, you still need His grace.
On your weakest spiritual day, His invitation to repent and trust Him still matters.
You never graduate beyond the cross.
You never outgrow your need for mercy.
And you never become so spiritually mature that you can safely ignore His commands.
The Christian life is not a choice between grace and holiness.
It is a life in which grace produces the desire and strength to pursue holiness.
And perhaps this is where the real question finally emerges.
Not, “Which commands can I stop obeying?”
But, “Lord Jesus, what would it look like for every part of my life to belong to You?”
My thoughts.
My marriage.
My sexuality.
My money.
My conversations.
My private habits.
My ambitions.
My bitterness.
My worship.
My relationships.
My treatment of strangers.
My response when I am wrong.
My willingness to forgive.
My willingness to tell the truth.
My willingness to surrender what I have been defending.
Because Christianity is not simply agreeing with a doctrine about grace.
It is trusting the Savior who gives that grace.
And when His Word confronts something in us, we do not need to run away.
We can come into the light.
We can confess.
We can repent.
We can ask for help.
We can begin again.
Not by pretending we are already perfect.
But by trusting the One who is.
If this message exposed a place where you have been confusing grace with permission, or obedience with earning God's love, do not bury that conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
“Lord Jesus, teach me to walk in Your grace and truth.”
You do not need to share private details. Sometimes a few honest words are enough to invite another believer to stand with you in prayer.
And if you have experienced Christ's forgiveness after a season of rebellion, your testimony may encourage someone who believes restoration is no longer possible.
Tell us what Jesus has been teaching you.
Because somewhere in this community, another person may be facing the same battle you thought you were fighting alone.
If you know a believer who is exhausted from trying to earn salvation, send this article to them.
One thoughtful share may place the Gospel before someone who would never search for a sermon, open a Christian book, or enter a church building.
Return to Romans 6, Matthew 5, Galatians 5, Acts 15, and Hebrews 8–10. Read them in their full context. Test what you have read against Scripture.
Never allow even a moving Christian article to replace your own faithful study of God's Word.
Because discipleship is not meant to be a single emotional moment.
It is a lifelong journey of learning to follow Jesus.
Not because a monthly payment earns God's favor.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life shaped by love, truth, worship, generosity, and obedience.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
So please hear the invitation in that spirit.

If this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you to repent, strengthened your faith, or pointed you back to Jesus when your heart was growing cold, consider helping us carry that message further.
Not under pressure.
Not out of guilt.
But from a willing heart.
Those resources and products can be meaningful reminders of biblical truth, but they are never the measure of someone's faith.
It is about pointing people to the One who saves.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who fulfilled the Law.
The Redeemer who bore our sins.
The risen Lord who calls us to follow Him.
The One who does not ask us to purchase grace, but to receive it through faith.
And the One whose grace never gives us permission to abandon Him.
Before you leave, remember this.
When Jesus died on the cross, He did not cry, “You must finish paying for your salvation.”
He cried:
“It is finished.” — John 19:30 (KJV)
The Greek word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai), from teleō, meaning to finish, accomplish, or bring to completion.
In John's account, Jesus' cry declares the completion of the work He came to accomplish.
It does not mean that repentance, discipleship, and obedience no longer matter.
It means that His saving work is sufficient and cannot be improved upon by our attempts to earn redemption.
And because He rose again, those who belong to Him are called to walk in newness of life.
Not to return to bondage.
Not to live under condemnation.
Not to disguise rebellion as freedom.
But to follow Him.
So come to Christ if you have never truly trusted Him.
Return to Him if you have wandered.
Confess what you have hidden.
Receive the forgiveness He offers.
And learn to walk by His Spirit, one day at a time.
Because the final question is not whether you can find a commandment that permits you to keep your favorite sin.
The question is whether you have encountered the Savior whose grace is powerful enough to change what you once believed could never change.
The Law exposed the guilt you could not erase. Grace brought you to the Savior who could—and the hands that bore your judgment are the same hands inviting you into a new life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS COULD HAVE SENT THEM ALONE. SO WHY DID HE SEND THEM TWO BY TWO?
paragraphs: JESUS COULD HAVE SENT THEM ALONE. SO WHY DID HE SEND THEM TWO BY TWO?
The Hidden Lesson in Mark 6:7–13 That Exposes Our Loneliness, Confronts Our Pride, and Reveals Why Some of Our Greatest Spiritual Battles Were Never Meant to Be Fought Alone.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
You can spend the entire day smiling, encouraging people, quoting Scripture, telling everyone that God is good, and still go home feeling like you are barely holding yourself together.
You pray for other people while secretly wondering who is praying for you.
You remind everyone else to trust God while quietly fighting doubts you are ashamed to admit.
You show up at church. You serve. You give. You tell people you are fine.
But somewhere beneath the worship songs and the Sunday smiles, something is breaking.
And perhaps the most painful part is that nobody knows.
Because you have become so good at appearing strong that people have stopped asking whether you are struggling.
Now imagine something.
Jesus stands before twelve ordinary men.
Men who will misunderstand Him. Men who will argue about greatness. Men who will eventually run when the darkness becomes unbearable.
One of them will deny knowing Him.
Another will betray Him.
And yet Jesus is about to entrust these imperfect men with an extraordinary mission.
He could have sent twelve individuals into twelve different directions.
