If this article exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
Someone reading may need to know that grief and faith can coexist, and that the grace of Christ is sufficient to sustain His people.
You do not need to share private details you are not ready to reveal.
But do not underestimate what one sincere testimony can mean to another hurting believer.
And please, think about the person who needs to read this.
Not the person who will give you the most reactions.
The person who is exhausted.
The person who feels forgotten.
The person who has spent years caring for others.
The person who is quietly grieving.
Not because you need to remember every sentence.
But because there may come a day when you feel unseen, when grief returns unexpectedly, or when you need to be reminded that your worth is not determined by the world's attention.
And when that day comes, return to the Scriptures.
Return to the God who sees.
Return to the Savior who saves.
Invite your family, your friends, those who are struggling in their faith, those who have grown spiritually indifferent, and even those who are still searching for truth.

We want this community to be a place where people are not merely entertained by religious content but encouraged to open their Bibles, examine their hearts, repent of sin, and grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has been helping you grow, I want to speak to you about something important.

Every article, biblical study, discipleship resource, and Gospel-centered message represents an opportunity to reach another person who may be hurting, confused, spiritually hungry, or searching for answers.
Continuing and expanding that work requires time, resources, and the support of people who believe in the mission.
Not because giving money makes someone more spiritual.
Not because you must support this particular ministry to prove that you love Jesus.
The Gospel is never for sale.
Salvation is a gift of grace.
And no monthly payment can replace repentance, faith, obedience, or generosity toward your local church and people in need.
But Scripture does teach that believers may freely and joyfully support those who faithfully labor in sharing God's Word.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly. Not of necessity.
Christian generosity is not supposed to be manufactured through guilt or fear.
It should arise from a willing heart.
And in Philippians 4:15–18, Paul acknowledges the material support believers provided for his ministry, describing their generosity as an offering pleasing to God.
That gives us a biblical foundation for inviting voluntary partnership in Gospel work.
We want your partnership to come from conviction, not pressure.
From love, not fear.
From a genuine desire to help more people encounter the truth of Scripture.
These products can be reminders of biblical truth, conversation starters, and resources for personal encouragement, but the heart of this ministry will always be Jesus Christ, not merchandise.
That free library is part of the mission we want to continue developing and sharing.
If this work has blessed you, and you are willing and financially able to partner with us, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside the mission.
And our gratitude for you is not dependent upon a payment.
There is still something beautiful you can do right now without spending anything.
And pray that the Word of God will reach hearts far beyond our own.
Because the goal is not simply to build an audience.
It is to see people turn to Jesus.
To see sinners repent.
To see believers grow.
To see wounded people encounter biblical hope.
To see families strengthened through truth.
To see the forgotten reminded that the God of Scripture is neither indifferent nor unjust.
And to see the name of Jesus Christ exalted above every human platform, personality, or ministry.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to that oak tree one final time.
Somewhere near Bethel, a woman named Deborah was buried.
We do not know the words spoken at her funeral.
We do not know how long the people mourned.
We do not know the complete story of her service.
And we do not know whether the physical tree survived for generations.
But we know her name.
We know she was Rebekah's nurse.
We know she died.
And we know that her burial place was called the Oak of Weeping.
Thousands of years have passed.
Kingdoms have risen and fallen.
Empires have disappeared.
The people who once walked those roads are long gone.
And still, when someone opens Genesis 35, Deborah's name is there.
A woman who never occupied the center of the story has not disappeared from its pages.
What a powerful reminder that the world does not always recognize the people who help hold it together.
But there is an even greater reminder.
Your deepest hope is not that your name will survive in a book.
Your deepest hope is that you belong to Jesus Christ, the crucified and risen Savior.
Because the day is coming when earthly applause will mean nothing.
When every platform will be silent.
When wealth and reputation will no longer protect anyone.
And what will matter eternally is whether we have been reconciled to God through His Son.
So live faithfully.
Love deeply.
Repent quickly.
Forgive as you have been forgiven.
Serve without demanding applause.
Grieve with hope.
And never confuse being overlooked by people with being beyond the knowledge and care of God.
Deborah's grave reminds us that even quiet lives can leave a profound absence.
But Christ's empty tomb reminds us that, for those who belong to Him, death does not have the final word.

One day, the last tear will fall, the last grave will lose its power, and everyone who belongs to Jesus will discover that the Savior who saw their sorrow was carrying them toward a world where sorrow could never follow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS LIKE EAGLES” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISUNDERSTANDING GOD’S PROMISE ALL ALONG?
paragraphs: “THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS LIKE EAGLES” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISUNDERSTANDING GOD’S PROMISE ALL ALONG?

Isaiah 40:31 was never mainly about becoming successful, achieving your dreams, or rising above everyone else. It was spoken to exhausted people who wondered whether God had forgotten them. And once you understand what God was actually promising, you may never read this verse the same way again.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
You wake up tired. You smile because people expect you to. You answer, “I’m okay,” because explaining what is happening inside your heart would take more strength than you have left.
You still believe in God.
You still pray.
You still open your Bible, even if some days you stare at the words without feeling anything.

But somewhere between the prayers that seem unanswered, the responsibilities that never stop, the disappointments you never expected, and the battles nobody knows you are fighting, a question has quietly settled into your soul.
Lord, how much longer can I keep going?
And perhaps the hardest part is that you have heard Christians quote Isaiah 40:31 countless times.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles.”

You have seen those words printed beneath pictures of majestic birds flying over mountains. You have heard them preached as encouragement to dream bigger, reach higher, break limitations, and achieve extraordinary things.
And perhaps you have wondered why, if God promised you wings, you still feel like you are crawling.
Why does everyone else seem to be soaring while you are struggling just to survive?
Why does the person who barely acknowledges God appear to be prospering while you, who have been trying to remain faithful, can hardly catch your breath?
What if the problem is not that God has failed to fulfill His promise?
What if we have been asking this promise to mean something God never intended it to mean?
Because Isaiah 40:31 is not primarily a motivational speech for ambitious people.
It is a divine word of comfort for weary people.
And to understand its beauty, we must return to the people who first received it.
Before God spoke about eagle's wings, He spoke to people who believed their suffering had become invisible to Him.
Listen to the complaint recorded in Isaiah 40:27:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?” (KJV)
Do you hear the heartbreak?
God's people were not simply asking how to become more successful.
They were asking whether God still saw them.
Their circumstances had become so painful that they began to wonder whether their lives mattered to the One who had made a covenant with them.

Isaiah 40 speaks comfort into the shadow of exile. The preceding chapter announces the coming Babylonian crisis, while Isaiah 40 addresses God's people with hope beyond judgment, anticipating their restoration.
Jerusalem would suffer. The people would experience displacement and humiliation. Their national security, religious confidence, and familiar way of life would be shaken.
And beneath their suffering was a terrifying question.
Has the God who chose us abandoned us?
Perhaps you have never experienced exile from your homeland.
But you may know what it feels like to become a stranger to the life you once recognized.
You had plans.
You thought your marriage would be different.
You thought your family would remain together.
You thought the business would survive.
You thought the diagnosis would be better.
You thought the person you trusted would never betray you.
You thought that by this stage of your life, you would be somewhere else.
Instead, you find yourself standing among the ruins of expectations you once carried with confidence.
And although you would never say it publicly, sometimes your prayers sound painfully similar to Israel's complaint.
God, have You overlooked me?
This is where the promise of eagle's wings begins.
Not with achievement.
With abandonment fears.
Not with a guarantee of prosperity.
With God's answer to people who believe they have been forgotten.
And His answer is more magnificent than a promise to make them rich, famous, influential, or admired.
He reminds them who He is.
Isaiah 40:28 declares:
“Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.” (KJV)
Notice what God does not say.
He does not tell His people that their suffering is imaginary.
He does not accuse them of being worthless because they are exhausted.
He does not promise that their circumstances will immediately become comfortable.
He directs their attention away from the limits of their strength and toward the limitless strength of their Creator.
The God who made the ends of the earth does not become exhausted.
The God who governs history does not run out of wisdom.
The God who sustains creation does not lose track of His people.
And that means something extraordinary.
Your strength may be running out, but God's strength is not.
There is a difference between those two realities, and confusing them has wounded many sincere believers.
Some Christians have been taught to treat exhaustion as proof of spiritual failure.
If you were really faithful, you would never feel overwhelmed.
If you prayed enough, you would never struggle.
If your faith were strong enough, you would always be victorious, energetic, confident, and emotionally unshakable.
But that is not what Isaiah says.
In fact, Isaiah 40:29 declares:
“He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.” (KJV)
Read that again.
He gives power to the faint.
Not merely to the impressive.
Not only to the influential.
Not exclusively to those whose lives look victorious.
To the faint.
The Hebrew word translated “faint” here comes from יָעֵף (yaʿef), associated with being weary or exhausted.
God knows what weariness is.
He knows the difference between rebellion and human limitation.
He knows when His children are carrying burdens they cannot sustain by their own power.
And His promise is not that genuine believers will never become weak.
His promise is that He is able to strengthen those who are weak.
That distinction matters.
Because some of you have been ashamed of the very weakness that should have driven you toward the Lord.
You have been pretending to be strong because you thought weakness would disappoint Him.
You have been hiding your tears because you assumed mature Christians were supposed to have everything under control.
You have been measuring your spiritual life by how productive, cheerful, successful, and emotionally stable you appear.
But Isaiah does not tell exhausted people to manufacture an impressive appearance.
He tells them to look to the everlasting God.
And then comes the verse so many of us have memorized.
Isaiah 40:31:
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.” (KJV)
Beautiful.
Familiar.
Often quoted.
But the meaning becomes even richer when we examine the Hebrew.
The expression translated “wait upon the LORD” is:
וְקוֹיֵ יְהוָה — veqovey YHWH
It refers to those who wait for, hope in, or look expectantly to the LORD.
The verb is related to the Hebrew root קוה (q-w-h), commonly associated with waiting and hoping.
This is not simply waiting for circumstances to improve while doing nothing.
Nor is it a formula for forcing God to deliver whatever outcome we desire.
It is expectant dependence upon the LORD Himself.
It is the posture of someone who says:
God, I do not understand everything You are doing, but I will not abandon my hope in You.
I cannot see the entire road, but I will trust the One who can.
I do not possess enough strength for everything ahead, but I believe You remain faithful.
This kind of waiting is not spiritual laziness.
It is trust that continues when immediate answers do not come.
It is obedience when obedience is costly.
It is prayer when words are difficult.
It is refusing to make despair the final authority over your life.
And sometimes it looks remarkably ordinary.
Getting out of bed.
Opening Scripture.
Asking forgiveness.
Choosing not to retaliate.
Showing up for your family.
Seeking help when the burden becomes too heavy.
Taking the next faithful step without knowing how the entire journey will unfold.
That may not look like soaring.
But heaven does not measure faithfulness by how impressive it appears to other people.
Now consider another Hebrew expression:
יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ — yaḥalifu koaḥ
The phrase is translated in the KJV as “shall renew their strength.”
The verb comes from חלף (ḥ-l-f), which can carry the sense of changing, replacing, or renewing, depending on its context.
Here, the idea is that those who hope in the LORD receive renewed strength.
It is not a promise that human beings become limitless.
It is not a guarantee that every faithful person will possess extraordinary physical energy.
It is not a declaration that Christians will never experience illness, emotional distress, financial hardship, or suffering.
It is God's assurance that His people are not ultimately left to depend upon their own inadequate resources.
The strength they need comes from Him.
And this is where the eagle imagery becomes so powerful.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles.”
The Hebrew expression is:
יַעֲלוּ אֵבֶר כַּנְּשָׁרִים — yaʿalu ever kannešarim
The image is of rising or ascending with wings like eagles.
The Hebrew word נֶשֶׁר (nešer) refers to a great bird of prey, often translated “eagle,” though its usage may include birds such as vultures in some contexts.
The image communicates remarkable strength and elevation.
But we must be careful not to build doctrines upon popular stories about eagles that Scripture itself never teaches.
You may have heard claims that an eagle must break off its beak, remove its talons, or pluck out its feathers to be reborn into a stronger life.
Those dramatic stories are not reliable descriptions of eagle biology.
And Isaiah does not teach them.
The power of God's Word does not need a fabricated nature story to make it more inspiring.
The image is already glorious.
God promises renewed strength to those who wait upon Him.
And notice something that often disappears when this verse becomes a slogan about success.
The promise does not end with flying.
It continues:
“They shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.”
Flying.
Running.
Walking.
Three images.
One divine assurance.
God is able to sustain His people.
And perhaps the final image is the one some of us need most.
Because sometimes the greatest evidence of God's sustaining grace is not that you are flying above your problems. It is that you are still walking with Him through them.
Think about that.
There are seasons when life seems full of extraordinary spiritual encouragement.
You feel energized.
You see answers to prayer.
Doors open.
Your heart overflows with gratitude.
You feel as though you could run for miles.
But there are other seasons.
Seasons when you have to fight just to remain faithful.
When you cannot see the next breakthrough.
When the same temptation returns.
When grief interrupts ordinary moments.
When you are caring for someone who cannot care for themselves.
When the bills are waiting.
When the marriage requires another difficult conversation.
When the children need patience you barely have.
When your body hurts.
When your mind is overwhelmed.
When your prayers are shorter because your tears are longer.
And you wonder whether God is disappointed that you are no longer soaring.
But the promise includes walking.
Not every season will feel spectacular.
Not every victory will attract attention.
Not every act of faithfulness will produce a dramatic testimony that thousands of people share.
Sometimes faithfulness is simply continuing to trust God when the road is long.
And that is not insignificant.
It is precious.
Yet we must go even deeper.
Because Isaiah 40:31 is not an isolated promise floating in a collection of inspirational sayings.
It belongs to the larger story of God's redemption.
Isaiah 40 begins with words of extraordinary tenderness:
“Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.” (Isaiah 40:1, KJV)
The chapter announces comfort for God's people and speaks of the LORD coming to rescue and restore.
Then Isaiah 40:3 declares:
“The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.” (KJV)
Centuries later, the New Testament identifies John the Baptist's ministry with this wilderness proclamation.
Matthew 3:3 explicitly connects John's message to Isaiah's words.
John came preparing the way for Jesus Christ.
And suddenly the horizon becomes even greater.
The God who promised comfort to weary Israel was unfolding a redemptive plan that would reach its fulfillment in Jesus.
The New Testament does not reduce Isaiah's original message to a prediction of personal success.
It shows that God's promised salvation reaches its climactic revelation in Christ.
And here is something that should stop us in our tracks.
The One who gives strength to the weary entered our weary world and experienced genuine human exhaustion.
John 4:6 tells us that Jesus, wearied by His journey, sat beside Jacob's well.
The eternal Son of God truly became human.
He knew hunger.
He knew thirst.
He knew grief.
He knew what it meant to be rejected.
He knew the pain of betrayal.
He knew the weight of sorrow.
And in the Garden of Gethsemane, He faced suffering of a depth we cannot fully comprehend.
Jesus did not come into this world merely to teach exhausted people how to become more productive.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins upon the cross.
He came to defeat death through His resurrection.
He came to accomplish what no amount of human determination, ambition, or religious performance could ever accomplish.
Our redemption.
And this is where the Gospel confronts a misunderstanding that can quietly poison the Christian life.
We sometimes approach God as though Christianity were a transaction.
We give Him our prayers, our service, our offerings, and our obedience.
And in return, we expect uninterrupted success.
We assume that faithfulness should guarantee financial abundance, physical health, public recognition, and protection from disappointment.
But the cross tells a different story.
The perfectly obedient Son of God suffered.
The sinless Savior was rejected.
The Lord of glory was crucified.
And His suffering was not evidence that the Father had lost control.
It was central to God's saving purpose.
If our definition of divine favor cannot make sense of the cross, our definition needs to change.
Because Jesus did not redeem us by avoiding suffering.
He redeemed us through His obedient suffering, death, and victorious resurrection.
That does not mean every tragedy has an explanation we can identify.
It does not mean suffering is good in itself.
It does not mean Christians should remain in abusive situations, neglect medical care, or refuse necessary help because they believe endurance requires silence.
It means suffering cannot automatically be interpreted as evidence that God has abandoned His children.
And that truth changes how we read Isaiah 40:31.
The promise of renewed strength is not permission to worship achievement.
It is an invitation to depend upon the God who saves.
And Jesus gives that invitation a deeply personal voice.
In Matthew 11:28, He says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (KJV)
In the Greek New Testament, the invitation begins:
Δεῦτε πρός με — Deute pros me
“Come to me.”
Not merely, “Come to a better strategy.”
Not, “Come to a more successful version of yourself.”
Not, “Come once you have fixed your life.”
Come to Me.
The word translated “heavy laden” is πεφορτισμένοι (pephortismenoi), describing those who have been burdened or loaded down.
Jesus is addressing the weary and burdened, offering rest under His gracious lordship.
He does not invite us to a life without obedience.
In the following verses, He calls us to take His yoke and learn from Him.
But His yoke is not the crushing burden of trying to earn acceptance before God through our own righteousness.
He is gentle and lowly in heart.
He offers rest for our souls.
And that rest is not merely the relief of getting everything we want.
It is the blessing of belonging to Him.
Perhaps that is what you have been missing.
You have been asking Jesus to give you wings so you can escape your circumstances.
But He is calling you to Himself so you can learn to trust Him in every circumstance.
You have been praying for enough success to finally feel secure.
But your deepest security is not found in your achievements.
It is found in the Savior who gave Himself for you.
You have been asking God to prove His love by making your road easier.
But the greatest demonstration of His love has already been revealed at Calvary.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we achieved financial stability.
Not after we developed a perfect reputation.
Not after we conquered every weakness.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
This is grace.
And grace is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Maybe your story contains things you wish you could erase.
A relationship you destroyed.
A lie you told.
A habit you kept hidden.
A season of rebellion.
A betrayal.
A secret sin.
A decision that still makes you uncomfortable when you remember it.
Maybe people know your worst chapter and have decided it is the only chapter worth remembering.
Maybe you have even begun to believe them.
But the Gospel announces something astonishing.
Your sin is serious.
Your need for repentance is real.
And the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than your ability to save yourself.
He does not offer forgiveness by pretending sin does not matter.
He bore sin's judgment at the cross.
He does not call us to repentance because He enjoys humiliating broken people.
He calls us to turn from sin and trust Him because life is found in Him.
The grace that forgives also begins to transform.
And the Christ who receives repentant sinners does not leave them without hope.
From scandal to grace is not the story of people who finally became good enough for God. It is the story of a Savior whose mercy reaches people who could never rescue themselves.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He insisted that even if others abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denials.
Three times Peter denied knowing the Lord.
And when the rooster crowed, his failure became unbearable.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The man who had walked with Jesus.
The man who had witnessed miracles.
The man who had spoken boldly about faithfulness.
Now broken by the memory of his own words.
If Peter's story ended there, it would be a devastating account of human failure.
But it did not end there.
The risen Jesus restored Peter, as recorded in John 21.
He confronted him with love, called him again to shepherd His sheep, and gave him a future of faithful service.
Peter's restoration did not erase the seriousness of his denial.
It demonstrated the mercy and authority of the risen Christ.
That is the Gospel's power.
Not that our failures are harmless.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
Not that every earthly consequence disappears.
But that Jesus Christ is able to forgive, restore, and transform those who return to Him.
Perhaps you are reading this with a heart that feels more like Peter's courtyard than an eagle soaring over mountains.
You remember what you promised God.
You remember what you did instead.
You remember the compromises.
The excuses.
The moments when fear mattered more to you than faithfulness.
And you wonder whether you have disqualified yourself from ever being useful again.
Do not confuse conviction with a declaration that Christ cannot forgive you.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing sin, do not hide it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Seek reconciliation where possible.
Receive the mercy that is found in Jesus.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
The answer to spiritual failure is not pretending you never fell.
It is returning to the Savior who died and rose again.
And perhaps your greatest need today is not another motivational message about reaching the top.
Perhaps you need to kneel before the Lord and say:
Jesus, I have spent so much time trying to build a life that looks successful that I have neglected the life of faithfulness You are calling me to live.
I have compared myself to others.
I have confused comfort with blessing.
I have treated unanswered prayers as evidence that You do not care.
I have tried to appear strong while my soul was becoming exhausted.
Forgive me.
Teach me to wait upon You.
Teach me to trust You.
Teach me to walk with You, even when I cannot see the road ahead.
And if those words expose something you have been carrying, you do not have to pretend otherwise.
You can be honest before God.
You can be honest with a trusted brother or sister in Christ.
Not to prove your faith to strangers.
Not because typing a phrase earns God's favor.
But because sometimes an honest confession becomes the beginning of a conversation another weary believer desperately needs.
Someone else may read your words and realize they are not the only person struggling to trust God.
Someone may find courage to admit that their own spiritual life has become exhausted.
The Christian life was never intended to be lived entirely alone.
We need the Word.
We need prayer.
We need the fellowship of believers.
We need the local church.
We need brothers and sisters who will tell us the truth with love.
And above all, we need Christ.
Because there is another danger hidden inside the popular interpretation of Isaiah 40:31.
When we turn eagle's wings into a guarantee of worldly success, we can unintentionally make struggling believers feel condemned.
The business owner whose company failed may wonder whether he lacked faith.
The mother whose child remains seriously ill may wonder whether she prayed incorrectly.
The faithful worker who never receives a promotion may wonder whether God favors everyone else.
The believer living with chronic pain may wonder whether the promise of renewed strength somehow excludes them.
But Isaiah 40:31 is not a weapon to use against the weary.
It is a word of hope for them.
And the New Testament confirms that God's sustaining grace does not always appear as the removal of weakness.
The apostle Paul pleaded with the Lord concerning a painful affliction he called a thorn in the flesh.
The Lord's answer was not immediate removal.
In 2 Corinthians 12:9, Jesus told him:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” (KJV)
Paul did not conclude that God's grace had failed because the affliction remained.
He learned to depend more deeply upon Christ.
That is not a command to enjoy suffering.
It is an assurance that weakness does not place us beyond the reach of divine grace.
And one day, God's people will experience a restoration far greater than anything this present world can offer.
The resurrection of Jesus guarantees that death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
The Christian hope is not limited to improved circumstances before we die.
It reaches toward the resurrection, the renewal of creation, and eternal fellowship with God.
Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear and that death, sorrow, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
That future is not a reward for people who achieved the most impressive earthly success.
It is the inheritance of those redeemed by the Lamb.
So yes, God may open doors for you.
He may bless your work.
He may grant healing.
He may restore relationships.
He may provide opportunities beyond anything you imagined.
Receive such gifts with gratitude.
But do not make them the foundation of your faith.
Because if your confidence in God depends entirely upon favorable circumstances, every storm will threaten to destroy it.
Build your hope upon Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who remains faithful when circumstances change.
The One who is worthy of worship when prayers are answered as we hoped, and still worthy when the answers are difficult to understand.
The One who holds His people even when their hands are trembling.
And now, perhaps, we can hear Isaiah 40:31 differently.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles.”
Not necessarily because they will become famous.
Not because they will always have money.
Not because they will never suffer.
Not because everyone who opposes them will watch them achieve spectacular success.
But because the everlasting God is able to renew and sustain those who place their hope in Him.
“They shall run, and not be weary.”
Not because human strength is infinite.
But because God's power is not exhausted.
“And they shall walk, and not faint.”
Even when the road is long.
Even when progress is slow.
Even when the next step requires courage.
Even when nobody applauds.
Even when the testimony is still being written.
And perhaps this is the part that makes the promise so deeply personal.
You may not be where you expected to be.
You may still be waiting for an answer.
You may still be grieving.
You may still be recovering from something that changed your life.
You may still be learning how to pray again after a season of disappointment.
You may be carrying responsibilities that seem heavier every morning.
But your present exhaustion does not mean that God has ceased to be faithful.
You are not required to manufacture the strength of the everlasting God.
You are invited to trust Him.
And sometimes that trust will feel courageous.
Sometimes it will feel quiet.
Sometimes it will look like worship.
Sometimes it will look like repentance.
Sometimes it will look like reaching out for help.
Sometimes it will look like taking one more step in obedience to Christ.
Do not despise that step.
The world celebrates people who appear to be soaring.
But the Lord sees the believer who keeps walking with Him when the journey is painful.
And He knows every tear.
He knows every prayer.
He knows every act of obedience that nobody else notices.
He knows the burdens you have never found words to explain.
And His invitation remains:
Come to Christ.
Hope in the LORD.
Receive His grace.
Walk in His truth.
And keep your eyes fixed upon the Savior who has already conquered sin and death.
If this message has helped you understand Isaiah 40:31 more faithfully, consider saving it.

Not because every difficult day can be solved by rereading an article, but because the Scriptures explored here may help you return your attention to Christ when weariness begins to distort your perspective.
There may be someone among your family, friends, or acquaintances who has been silently wondering whether God has forgotten them.
They may never tell you what they are going through.
But a Scripture-centered message shared at the right moment can open a door to encouragement, prayer, and a deeper conversation about Jesus.
Not to put their private struggles on display.
Simply to remind them that the Christian hope is greater than the pressure to appear successful.
And if you know someone who has drifted from faith, or someone who has never understood the Gospel, invite them to read and consider the claims of Jesus for themselves.
We are not trying to gather people around a personality.
We want to direct hearts toward Christ.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your Bible.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to replace faithful pastors, Christian fellowship, or personal discipleship.
But to serve as another place where people can encounter Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, calls to repentance, and reminders of the grace of Jesus Christ.
A friend who is exhausted.
A family member who is searching.
A believer who needs encouragement.
Someone who has been wounded by shallow teaching.
Someone who needs to hear that Christianity is not a promise of effortless success, but the good news of salvation through Jesus Christ.
And if you want to help us continue and expand this work, I want to speak to you about something important.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes clear that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
But Scripture also teaches that believers may voluntarily support those who labor in Gospel ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It can be one meaningful expression of Christian generosity and stewardship.
But it is not a spiritual obligation, a replacement for faithful giving to your local church, or a requirement for glorifying God.
You are no less welcome here.
You can still pray for the ministry.
You can still invite someone to read Scripture.
You can still encourage a struggling believer.
Your worth before God has never depended upon your ability to give money.
These products are not the reason to follow Jesus, and they do not make anyone more spiritual.
They are simply a tangible expression of appreciation for those who choose to help sustain the work.

These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, develop habits of prayer and discipleship, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
The library's free resources remain a way for people to learn and grow without making financial support a condition of access.
A thoughtful comment may begin a conversation about faith.
A personal invitation may encourage someone to return to prayer, seek Christian fellowship, or open the Bible again.
The goal is that more people would come to know, love, trust, and follow Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, I want to return to the question that began this conversation.
What if you have been wondering why God promised you eagle's wings when you can barely walk?
What if the verse was never meant to shame you for not flying high enough?
What if it was meant to remind you that the everlasting God has not exhausted His strength?
What if you have been measuring your life by the height of your achievements while God has been calling you to the depth of your trust?
What if the most important thing about your story is not whether the world considers you successful?
What if the most important thing is whether you belong to Jesus Christ?
Because one day, the applause will stop.
The achievements will fade.
The possessions will pass away.
The titles will no longer matter.
The numbers on our screens will mean nothing.
But the salvation accomplished by Jesus Christ will remain.
And those who belong to Him will discover that their hope was never misplaced.
So if you are tired tonight, come to Him.
If you have sinned, repent and seek His forgiveness.
If you are grieving, bring Him your sorrow.
If you are confused, seek His wisdom in Scripture.
If you are struggling, do not be ashamed to ask for prayer and help.
If you are waiting, do not assume waiting means you have been abandoned.
And if all you can do today is take one faithful step, take it with your eyes upon Christ.
You do not need to impress Him with a performance of strength.
You need the grace of the Savior.
Are you in a season of soaring, running, or simply trying to keep walking with God?
You can share your testimony, your struggle, a prayer request, or simply write “I'm still walking with Jesus.”
There is no need to disclose anything you would rather keep private.
But perhaps your honest words will encourage another believer who has been quietly wondering whether they are the only one still struggling.
Because Isaiah 40:31 was never mainly about how high you could rise in the eyes of the world.
It was about the faithfulness of the God who gives strength to the weary.
And the greatest gift He has given us is not worldly success.
It is His Son.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Calling the weary to Himself.
Worthy of our trust.
Worthy of our repentance.
Worthy of our worship.
Worthy of our lives.
And when the world sees only how slowly you are walking, remember this: the Savior who carried your sin to the cross has not stopped being faithful to you on the road.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD CHRISTIAN PARENTS CUT OFF AN ADULT CHILD WHO REJECTS THEIR FAITH? WHAT IF THE CHILD YOU RAISED TO LOVE JESUS NO LONGER WANTS HIM?
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIAN PARENTS CUT OFF AN ADULT CHILD WHO REJECTS THEIR FAITH? WHAT IF THE CHILD YOU RAISED TO LOVE JESUS NO LONGER WANTS HIM?

When your child walks away from the faith, should you close the door to protect your convictions—or leave the light on because you remember the Savior who never stopped calling sinners home? The biblical answer may challenge both the parents who want to hold on and those who are ready to let go.
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that doesn't come with a funeral.
Your child is still alive.
Still breathing. Still posting pictures. Still laughing with friends. Still making plans for tomorrow.
But the little boy who once folded his hands beside his bed and whispered, "Dear Jesus, thank You for Mommy and Daddy," now says he doesn't believe in God.
The little girl who used to sing worship songs in the back seat of your car now tells you she wants nothing to do with Christianity.
And suddenly, the house that once echoed with bedtime prayers feels painfully quiet.
You remember dedicating that child to the Lord.
You remember the Sunday school lessons, the Bible stories, the prayers before examinations, the whispered blessings over a sleeping forehead.
You remember begging God to protect that child from the world.
But you never imagined that one day, the world would seem more believable to your child than the God you taught them to love.
Then comes the conversation you have been dreading.
"Mom, Dad... I don't believe what you believe anymore."
Perhaps they say Christianity is too restrictive.
Perhaps they have questions you cannot answer.
Perhaps they have been wounded by Christians.
Perhaps they have chosen a lifestyle that conflicts with your understanding of Scripture.
Or perhaps they simply look you in the eyes and say something that makes your stomach drop.
"Please stop trying to make me believe."
And now you are standing at a crossroads no parenting book prepared you for.
Do you keep calling?
Do you invite them home for Christmas?
Do you allow them around the younger children?
Do you tell them they are welcome at your table even when they openly reject the faith that built your home?
Or do you cut them off, hoping the pain of separation will finally bring them to repentance?
Before you answer, there is something you need to understand.
You can refuse to compromise the truth without refusing to love the person who rejects it.
And if that sentence makes you uncomfortable, stay with me.

Because Jesus told a story about a father, a rebellious son, a broken relationship, and a road that would eventually become the setting for one of the most extraordinary pictures of grace in all of Scripture.
But the detail that changes everything is not simply that the son came home.
It is what the father did when he saw him.
In Luke 15, Jesus tells us about a younger son who demanded his inheritance while his father was still alive.
In the cultural setting of the story, the demand was profoundly dishonoring. The son wanted the benefits of his father's estate without remaining under his father's household.
He wanted the gifts.
Not the relationship.
He wanted freedom.
Not responsibility.
He wanted the inheritance.
Not the father.
And the father let him go.
Read that again.
The father let him go.
He did not chain him to the house.
He did not manufacture a false confession.
He did not demand that the son pretend to love what he had already rejected.
The son left, squandered his wealth, and eventually found himself desperate and hungry.
Then Jesus gives us these remarkable words in Luke 15:17:
"And when he came to himself..."
The Greek expression is εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν (eis heauton de elthōn).
Literally, the phrase conveys the idea of coming to himself, or coming to his senses.
The son began to recognize the reality of his condition.
But notice something.
The father did not travel to the distant country to force his son into repentance.
He did not pretend the rebellion was harmless.
He did not finance the son's destructive living indefinitely.
Yet nothing in the story suggests that the father had stopped loving him.
And when the son finally returned, Scripture says:
"But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." — Luke 15:20, KJV
The Greek word translated "had compassion" is ἐσπλαγχνίσθη (esplanchnisthē), from a verb expressing deep, inward compassion.
This was not a father casually tolerating his son's return.
This was compassion that moved him to action.
He ran.
In a culture where the dignified behavior of an older household patriarch mattered, that image is striking.
The father moved toward the son who had dishonored him.
Not because rebellion had suddenly become righteousness.
Not because truth no longer mattered.
But because the lost son had returned.
And here is where many Christian parents need to hear something difficult.
The father did not have to approve of the distant country to welcome his son home.
But we must also read the parable carefully.

The son in Luke 15 returned acknowledging his sin. Jesus was describing the joy of repentance and restoration, not giving a blanket command that parents must accept every behavior or remove every boundary.
The father represents God's gracious welcome of the repentant sinner. He is not a complete instruction manual for every difficult family situation.
Still, the story reveals something precious about the heart of God.
His mercy is not reluctant.
His compassion is not cold.
And His grace does not require Him to call evil good.
So what does that mean when your adult child rejects Christianity?
It means you must learn the difference between loving your child and affirming everything your child believes.
Those are not the same thing.
You can say, "I believe Jesus Christ is the only way to the Father," because Jesus Himself said so in John 14:6.
You can say, "I cannot call something righteous when Scripture calls it sin."
You can refuse to participate in actions that violate your conscience.
You can remain faithful to the Gospel without rewriting biblical teaching to avoid an uncomfortable conversation.
But you can also say:
"You are still my child."
"I still love you."
"You are welcome to speak honestly with me."
"I will not pretend we agree, but I will not treat you as worthless because we disagree."
And perhaps the most difficult sentence of all:
"I cannot make you believe. But I will continue praying for you."
Some parents are afraid that this kind of love will communicate approval.
But the Bible never teaches that kindness automatically equals compromise.
Romans 2:4 speaks of the kindness of God leading toward repentance.
The Greek word χρηστότης (chrēstotēs) refers to kindness or goodness.
God's kindness does not erase His holiness.
It reveals His patience toward sinners.
And if God's kindness can serve His purpose of leading people toward repentance, why should Christian parents assume that cruelty is a better instrument of spiritual restoration?
Think about that.
When did humiliation become a fruit of the Spirit?
When did emotional punishment become a substitute for discipleship?
When did refusing to answer your child's phone calls become proof of biblical courage?
Galatians 5:22–23 identifies the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, and temperance.
It does not list manipulation.
It does not list contempt.
It does not list using affection as a weapon.
And yet some Christian parents, out of genuine fear for their children's souls, begin doing exactly that.
They turn every dinner into a debate.
Every phone call into a sermon.
Every family gathering into an interrogation.
They begin treating their adult child's spiritual condition as a problem that must be solved before a relationship can exist.
And slowly, the child stops visiting.
Stops calling.
Stops sharing.
Not necessarily because the child has stopped loving the parents.
Sometimes because every interaction has become another opportunity to feel condemned, cornered, or unheard.
Now, this does not mean every accusation of judgment is fair. Faithful biblical correction can be painful, and people sometimes reject truth precisely because it challenges them.
But Christian parents must be willing to examine their own conduct.
Because there is a difference between someone being offended by the Gospel and someone being wounded by our pride.
Do not confuse your child's rejection of Christ with your child's rejection of the way you have represented Christ.
Those two things may overlap.
But they are not always identical.
And this is where the story becomes even more uncomfortable.
What if your child did not walk away from Christianity because they never heard the Gospel?
What if they heard plenty of religious language but rarely experienced confession, humility, or forgiveness at home?
What if they watched you worship on Sunday and tear people apart on Monday?
What if they saw you quote Scripture to correct them but never heard you use Scripture to correct yourself?
What if they learned that admitting doubt brought punishment rather than patient conversation?
What if the wounds they associate with Christianity came from the very people who were supposed to demonstrate Christlike love?
That possibility does not excuse unbelief.
Parents are not responsible for every decision an adult child makes.
And even faithful, loving parents can have children who reject the faith.
But if we want our children to take repentance seriously, we must be willing to practice it ourselves.
Imagine the power of a father looking his adult son in the eyes and saying:
"I still believe the Bible is true. But I also realize that I have sometimes used my anger in ways that dishonored the Lord. I was wrong. Will you forgive me?"
Imagine a mother saying:
"I cannot change what Scripture teaches. But I can change how I speak to you. I want to listen better."
That is not surrendering biblical authority.
That is submitting to it.
Because the same Bible that commands children to honor their parents also warns fathers not to provoke their children to wrath (Ephesians 6:4).
The same Scriptures that call believers to speak the truth also command them to speak it in love (Ephesians 4:15).
And James 1:19 calls us to be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to wrath.
Sometimes the most powerful Gospel conversation begins when a parent stops preparing a rebuttal long enough to hear the pain behind the question.
But perhaps you are thinking:
"Doesn't the Bible command Christians to separate from unbelievers?"
That question deserves an honest answer.
Scripture does command believers to reject idolatry, refuse participation in sin, and exercise appropriate church discipline.

Second Corinthians 6:14 warns believers against being unequally yoked with unbelievers. Its surrounding context concerns partnerships that compromise loyalty to God, not a universal prohibition against maintaining family relationships with nonbelievers.
First Corinthians 5 discusses church discipline for a person who claims to belong to the Christian community while persisting in serious, unrepentant sin.
But Paul makes an important distinction in verses 9–13.
He explains that his instruction is not a command to avoid all immoral people outside the church.
Otherwise, believers would have to leave the world altogether.
The church has a responsibility to address serious sin among those who profess membership in the believing community.
That is not the same as ordering Christian parents to abandon an adult child simply because that child does not profess faith.
And consider 1 Corinthians 7:12–16.
Paul instructs a Christian married to an unbelieving spouse not to initiate separation merely because the spouse does not share the faith, provided the unbelieving spouse is willing to remain.
Marriage and parenthood are different relationships, and that passage cannot be transferred mechanically to every parent-child situation.
But it demonstrates an important principle.
The presence of unbelief in a close family relationship does not automatically make separation a Christian duty.
Then there are Jesus' words in Matthew 10:34–37, where He warns that allegiance to Him may divide households.
These words are serious.
Christ must come before every earthly relationship.
A parent must never deny Jesus to preserve family approval.
A child must never be treated as more authoritative than God.
But Jesus' warning that discipleship may bring division is not permission to manufacture division unnecessarily.
Sometimes faithfulness to Christ will cost you the approval of your family.
That is painful.
But it is very different from deliberately withholding love in order to pressure someone into religious conformity.
Christ calls us to love Him above our families. He does not call us to use our families as targets for spiritual coercion.
There is another passage that deserves attention.
In 2 Timothy 2:24–25, Paul writes:
The Greek phrase ἐν πραΰτητι (en prautēti) means "in gentleness" or "with meekness."
Gentleness is not weakness.
It is strength governed by humility.
And Paul continues by recognizing that repentance is something God may grant.
That should humble every parent who thinks enough arguments, enough pressure, or enough emotional punishment can manufacture genuine conversion.
You can teach.
You can explain.
You can warn.
You can testify.
You can pray.
But you cannot regenerate a human heart.
Jesus told Nicodemus that a person must be born again (John 3:3).
Spiritual rebirth is not something parents can accomplish through control.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
And perhaps that is the part that hurts most.
Because when your child was small, you could hold their hand while crossing the street.
You could tell them when to sleep.
You could decide which school they attended.
You could bring them to church.
You could teach them Scripture.
But adulthood arrives.
And suddenly you discover that the child whose hand you once held has a conscience, a will, and decisions you cannot control.
You can still influence.
You can still witness.
You can still love.
But you cannot believe on their behalf.
There is a grief in that realization that only a praying parent truly understands.
You can raise a child in a Christian home without being able to guarantee that the child will become a Christian.
Proverbs 22:6 gives wisdom about training a child in the right way. It should not be treated as an unconditional promise that every properly raised child will remain faithful.
The Bible itself contains examples of godly people with unfaithful children and unfaithful parents with godly children.
Every person remains accountable before God.
And that means a child's unbelief is not automatic proof that their parents failed.
Some of you need to hear that.
You have been replaying twenty years of memories, searching for the exact moment you ruined everything.
You wonder whether you should have prayed more.
Been stricter.
Been gentler.
Chosen another church.
Answered that question differently.
Not lost your temper that afternoon.
And while honest self-examination is good, endless self-condemnation is not the same as repentance.
If you sinned, confess it.
If you wounded your child, seek reconciliation.
If you neglected your responsibility, acknowledge it.
But do not appoint yourself the savior of a soul that only Jesus can redeem.
There is only one Christ.
And you are not Him.
Now we must address something equally important.
Does loving an unbelieving adult child mean allowing anything and everything?
Absolutely not.
Christian love does not require parents to surrender their homes to abuse, threats, violence, theft, manipulation, or destructive behavior.
You may need to say:
"I love you, but you cannot threaten people in this house."
"I care about you, but I will not provide money that I know will support destructive behavior."
"You are welcome to talk with me when we can speak respectfully."
"I want a relationship with you, but I cannot continue conversations where you insult or intimidate me."
Those are boundaries.
They are not necessarily rejection.
And in situations involving violence or serious danger, physical separation and professional or legal protection may be necessary.
Forgiveness does not eliminate the need for safety.
Reconciliation does not always mean immediate restoration of trust.
And maintaining love does not mean granting unlimited access to your home, money, or personal life.
Sometimes loving someone requires saying no.
Sometimes it requires allowing an adult child to experience the consequences of their decisions.
Sometimes it means keeping a safe line of communication open while refusing to enable harmful behavior.
But the crucial question is this:
Are you establishing a boundary because something is genuinely harmful, or are you withholding your relationship simply to punish unbelief?
Those motives are not interchangeable.
A boundary protects what is good.
Punishment intended to force faith may produce outward compliance without inward conversion.
And a child who says "I believe" merely to regain parental affection has not necessarily come to saving faith.
God is not glorified by counterfeit repentance.
He desires truth in the inward being, as Psalm 51:6 teaches.
This brings us to another scene in Scripture.
In John 4, Jesus encounters a Samaritan woman at a well.
She belongs to a community marked by deep religious division from the Jews.
Her personal history also becomes part of their conversation.
Jesus does not pretend that theological differences are insignificant.
He tells her plainly that salvation is from the Jews.
He speaks about true worship.
He reveals truth about her life.
Yet He begins by speaking with her.
He treats her as someone worth engaging.
And through that encounter, she becomes a witness to others in her community.
Jesus did not need to compromise truth to cross a social barrier.
He crossed it because truth and grace were not enemies in Him.
John 1:14 describes Jesus as full of grace and truth.
In Greek, χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (charitos kai alētheias).
Grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And this is where Christian parenting becomes a living testimony.
Your adult child may reject your interpretation of Scripture.
They may reject your church.
They may reject your invitations to worship.
They may even reject the very existence of God.
But when they encounter you, what do they see?
Do they see someone whose love disappears whenever they disagree?
Or someone whose convictions remain firm while their conduct remains marked by patience, humility, and compassion?
Do they see a parent more interested in winning arguments than understanding questions?
Or someone who loves Jesus enough to obey Him even when obedience requires restraint?
You do not have to pretend the distance between your beliefs is small.
Sometimes it is enormous.
But your child should not have to wonder whether you still recognize their humanity.
And now I want to speak to the adult child who may be reading this.
Perhaps you are the one who walked away.
Perhaps your parents sent you this article.
Perhaps you have already decided that Christianity has nothing left to say to you.
I am not asking you to pretend you believe something you do not believe.
And I am not asking you to excuse mistreatment because someone claims to speak for God.
But I want to ask you something.
Have you rejected Jesus Christ Himself, or have you rejected a version of Christianity that was never faithful to His character?
Those are not necessarily the same thing.
Christians can be hypocritical.
Churches can fail.
Parents can sin.
Religious institutions can misuse authority.
None of those failures should be minimized.
But the failures of Christians do not, by themselves, settle the question of whether Jesus is who He claimed to be.
Consider Him.
Read the Gospels.
Examine His words.
Look at His compassion toward the broken, His confrontation of hypocrisy, His call to repentance, His death on the cross, and the testimony of His resurrection.
Do not build your entire conclusion about Christ on the worst behavior of people who claim His name.
And please understand this.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your family's reputation.
He came to save sinners.
That includes religious sinners.
Rebellious sinners.
Self-righteous sinners.
Wounded sinners.
People who have hidden behind church attendance.
And people who have run as far away from church as they possibly could.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — KJV
The Gospel is not the announcement that good families produce good children.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Christ lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Forgiveness is not earned by having Christian parents.
And it is not received by attending church merely to keep the peace.
It is received through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
No family heritage can replace that.
No religious performance can manufacture that.
And no parent's tears can purchase what Christ alone has accomplished.
But His grace is sufficient to save.
And His invitation to repent and believe the Gospel is real.
Now, parent, I want you to imagine something.
It is late at night.
Your phone lights up.
You see your child's name.
The child you have barely spoken to in months.
Perhaps years.
Your heart begins racing.
You answer.
And on the other end, there is silence.
Then a familiar voice whispers:
"Mom?"
Or perhaps:
"Dad?"
And then:
"Can we talk?"
What will that moment find in you?
A speech you have rehearsed for years?
A list of accusations?
A demand for immediate agreement?
Or a heart prepared to listen?
You may not hear the words "I want to come back to Jesus."
Perhaps your child simply needs help.
Perhaps they want to apologize.
Perhaps they want to ask a question.
Perhaps they are lonely.
Perhaps they are still completely unconvinced about Christianity.
And perhaps that phone call is not the moment of conversion you have been praying for.
But it may be a moment when your response can bear witness to the character of Christ.
Do not waste it by trying to control the outcome.
Listen.
Speak truth when appropriate.
Show compassion.
And remember that genuine faith cannot be forced.
There is one more person in Luke 15 we cannot ignore.
The older brother.
While the father rejoiced over the younger son's return, the older brother became angry.
He had remained at home.
He had worked.
He had obeyed.
And now he struggled to celebrate mercy shown to someone who had behaved so disgracefully.
The father came out and pleaded with him too.
What a revealing detail.
The father showed compassion toward the rebellious son.
And patience toward the resentful son.
Jesus told this parable in a setting where religious leaders were complaining that He welcomed sinners.
The story exposes not only rebellion but also self-righteousness.
And that should make every Christian parent examine their heart.
Because sometimes we become so offended by our children's rebellion that we forget how much mercy we ourselves have received.
We begin speaking as though our obedience makes us deserving of God's love.
As though our church attendance has erased our need for grace.
As though the only lost person in the family is the one who stopped attending worship.
But the cross leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and come short of the glory of God.
The parent needs grace.
The child needs grace.
The preacher needs grace.
The person writing these words needs grace.
And the person reading them needs grace.
Nobody stands at the foot of the cross as a self-made saint.
We stand there as people who need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
So should Christian parents cut off an adult child who rejects their faith?
Not merely because the child no longer believes.
There is no general biblical command requiring parents to sever their relationship with an adult son or daughter simply for rejecting Christianity.
Faithfulness may require difficult boundaries.
It may require refusing to participate in sin.
It may require accepting that your child does not want religious conversations.
It may require distance when a relationship becomes abusive or unsafe.
And in some circumstances, an adult child may choose to end contact despite a parent's willingness to remain connected.
You cannot control that either.
But when a safe and respectful relationship remains possible, Christian parents have strong biblical reasons to pursue love, patience, truthfulness, prayer, and an open door to reconciliation.
Not because unbelief is harmless.
Not because salvation is optional.
Not because every belief leads to God.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of being represented faithfully.
You are not being asked to surrender the Gospel.
You are being called to live in a manner consistent with it.
And if your child has already been gone for years?
If the messages remain unanswered?
If the holidays have become painful reminders of an empty chair?
If you have prayed until you no longer know what words to use?
Then hear this carefully.
You do not know how your child's story will end.
I cannot promise that every wandering child will return to the faith.
Scripture does not authorize that guarantee.
I cannot promise that every broken family will be reconciled in this lifetime.
And I will not use the pain of a praying parent to manufacture a comforting promise God has not made.
But I can tell you what Scripture does reveal.
God is patient.
God is merciful.
God calls sinners to repentance.
God hears the prayers of His people.
And the Gospel remains the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes (Romans 1:16).
So keep praying.
Not as though prayer gives you control over another person's will.
But because you trust the Lord who is wiser, holier, and more merciful than you.
Keep living faithfully.
Keep examining your own heart.
Keep telling the truth without cruelty.
Keep extending appropriate kindness without surrendering necessary boundaries.
And if a conversation opens, do not treat it as a courtroom where your child must first lose an argument before receiving your love.
Let it be a conversation.
A real one.
Between two human beings who both need grace.
Perhaps tonight, before you sleep, you need to stop rehearsing what your child has done wrong and ask God to search your own heart.
Perhaps you need to send a simple message.
Not a sermon.
Not a warning disguised as a greeting.
Just something honest.
"I know we disagree about faith. I still love you. I would like to hear how you are doing. If I have hurt you, I am willing to listen."
Perhaps you need to apologize.
Perhaps you need to establish a boundary you have been afraid to establish.
Perhaps you need to stop financing destruction.
Perhaps you need to stop confusing your anxiety with the voice of the Holy Spirit.
Or perhaps you need to release the burden of trying to accomplish what only God can do.
Because there is a difference between carrying your child in prayer and trying to carry the weight of your child's salvation.
One is an expression of faith.
The other is a burden no parent was created to bear.
And if this article has reached you while your relationship with your child is breaking apart, I want to ask you something personal.
Have you been trying to protect your faith by closing a door that God never commanded you to close?
Or have you been afraid to establish a necessary boundary because you thought love meant accepting everything?
Be honest before the Lord.
Sometimes repentance begins not with a dramatic public confession but with a quiet recognition that we have allowed fear, anger, or pride to govern our responses.
And sometimes the most Christlike thing a parent can say is:
"Lord, I cannot change my child's heart. But please change whatever is wrong in mine."

And if you are the adult child who has been hurt, confused, or distant, you are welcome in this conversation too. Tell us what you wish Christian parents understood about listening, honesty, and love.
Let this be a place where people speak truthfully, without cruelty.
Because there may be another parent reading the comments at two in the morning, wondering whether anyone else understands the ache of loving a child who no longer shares their faith.
Your words may remind that parent they are not alone.
And if this article brought someone to mind, consider tagging them with sensitivity, especially if doing so will encourage rather than publicly embarrass them.

Better still, send it privately to a mother who has been crying in silence, a father who does not know how to reconnect, or an adult child who needs to know that following Jesus should never be an excuse for cruelty.
Not to expose your family's struggles.
Not to win an argument.
But because there are families quietly breaking apart over questions they have never learned to discuss with both biblical conviction and Christlike compassion.
One thoughtful share may help someone reconsider a painful decision.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown cold in their faith, and even those who are not yet Christians to follow along.
Not because we have every answer.
But because the Word of God deserves careful attention, and every human soul deserves to hear the Gospel faithfully proclaimed.
This is also why Gospel Warrior continues creating biblical articles, devotionals, discipleship materials, and resources that address the real struggles people carry behind their smiles.
And I want to speak for a moment to those who have been spiritually nourished by this ministry.
It is a practical way to help sustain and expand this work so that more people can encounter biblical teaching, encouragement, and resources centered on Jesus Christ.
But I want to make something absolutely clear.
Christian giving is to be willing and cheerful, not pressured or manipulated.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share the Gospel in everyday life.
But the greater purpose of this ministry will always be spiritual, not commercial.
We want people to open their Bibles.
To understand the Gospel.
To repent of sin.
To receive Christ by faith.
To grow in grace.
To forgive.
To be restored.
To become faithful disciples of Jesus.
The ministry is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Christ crucified and risen is.
Our calling is to point people toward Him, not to make people dependent upon us.
And that brings us back to the parent sitting alone tonight.
Perhaps the dinner table is set for fewer people than it used to be.
Perhaps your child's old bedroom remains untouched.
Perhaps you still remember the sound of their little voice reciting John 3:16.
Perhaps you wonder whether you will ever hear them pray again.
I cannot tell you when that pain will end.
But I can remind you of something greater than your ability to control the future.
The Lord is still God.
His truth has not changed.
His mercy has not run out.
And your responsibility is not to write the final chapter of another person's soul.
Your responsibility is to remain faithful to Jesus Christ.
To love what He loves.
To reject what He calls sin.
To practice the humility He commands.
To extend the mercy you yourself have received.
To trust Him with what you cannot control.
Because the greatest scandal in the Gospel is not that rebellious children can come home.
It is that a holy God welcomes repentant sinners through the sacrifice of His own Son.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse our sin.
He bore its judgment.
He did not pretend we were righteous.
He gave Himself so that sinners could be justified through faith in Him.
He did not offer cheap forgiveness.
He purchased redemption with His blood.
And when He rose from the dead, He proved that sin and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is the Gospel.
That is our hope.
That is why we pray.
That is why we speak truth.
That is why we keep loving.
And that is why, when it is safe and right to do so, we leave room for the conversation we thought would never happen.
Not every child will return.
Not every relationship will be restored.
But no parent needs to become cruel to remain faithful.
And no child needs to pretend to believe in order to be treated with human dignity.
So if your son or daughter has walked away from the faith, do not throw away your convictions.
Do not throw away your compassion either.
Hold fast to Christ.
Keep your heart tender.
Let your words be truthful.
Let your boundaries be wise.
Let your prayers be sincere.
And let your life testify that the grace of Jesus Christ is not merely something you preach to strangers.
It is something you are learning to live before the people who know you best.
You may not be able to bring your child back to faith, but you can refuse to let your fear turn your love into another reason they run.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SOLOMON HAD 700 WIVES, 300 CONCUBINES… AND WISDOM FROM GOD. SO HOW DID THE WISEST KING BECOME A FOOL?
paragraphs: SOLOMON HAD 700 WIVES, 300 CONCUBINES… AND WISDOM FROM GOD. SO HOW DID THE WISEST KING BECOME A FOOL?

Did Solomon's Many Wives Destroy His Wisdom… or Reveal That He Wasn't Following It? The heartbreaking story of a man who knew God's truth, ignored God's warnings, and discovered that even extraordinary wisdom cannot protect a heart that refuses to obey.
He knew better.
That's what makes his story so terrifying.
Solomon wasn't an ordinary man who stumbled into sin because nobody had taught him the truth.

He was the king who asked God for wisdom instead of wealth. The man whose understanding astonished nations. The ruler who spoke about righteousness, warned against temptation, and understood the devastating consequences of a divided heart.
He knew what sin could do.
He knew where compromise could lead.
He knew the difference between loving God and merely speaking about Him.
And yet, somewhere between the throne God gave him and the desires he refused to surrender, Solomon began living as though the warnings he understood were meant for everyone except himself.
Seven hundred wives.
Three hundred concubines.
One thousand women in his royal household.
And eventually, a heart turned away from the God who had given him everything.
But here is the question that should disturb every Christian reading this:
Did Solomon lose his wisdom because he had so many women… or did his many women expose the terrifying truth that a person can possess extraordinary wisdom and still refuse to live by it?

Because if Solomon could know so much about God and still drift so far from Him, what does that mean for those of us who know Scripture, attend church, share Bible verses, recognize sin, and yet secretly negotiate with the very things God has told us to surrender?
Stay with me.
This is not merely the story of a king who loved too many women.
It is the story of what happens when the heart stops obeying what the mind already knows.
And before we reach the end, Solomon's tragedy may reveal something about our own lives that we have been avoiding for years.
The story begins with something beautiful.
In 1 Kings 3, God appeared to Solomon in a dream and invited him to ask for what he desired.
Solomon could have asked for longer life. He could have requested the destruction of his enemies. He could have pursued riches beyond imagination.
Instead, he recognized the enormous responsibility of governing God's people.
He asked for understanding.
The Hebrew expression in 1 Kings 3:9 is לֵב שֹׁמֵעַ — lev shomea, meaning literally a hearing heart or listening heart.
What an extraordinary request.
Solomon wasn't simply asking to become intellectually brilliant.
He wanted a heart capable of listening, discerning, and judging rightly.
In biblical thought, the heart is not merely the seat of emotion. It is deeply connected with thought, intention, understanding, and moral decision-making.
Solomon wanted to govern with discernment.
And God was pleased.
The Lord granted him remarkable wisdom, along with riches and honor.
But there was something else in God's response that people sometimes overlook.
In 1 Kings 3:14, God told Solomon that if he walked in God's ways, keeping His statutes and commandments as David had walked, God would lengthen his days.
Do you see it?
Even at the beginning, the gift of wisdom did not eliminate the necessity of obedience.
God gave Solomon wisdom.
But Solomon still had to choose whether to walk in it.
And that distinction would eventually become the dividing line between his glory and his downfall.
Soon, the world began witnessing his extraordinary discernment.
Two women came before the king, each claiming to be the mother of the same living child.
Solomon proposed dividing the child, exposing the true mother's compassion when she pleaded for the baby to be spared.
The king's judgment revealed an astonishing understanding of human motives.
Israel stood in awe.
The wisdom of God was evident in him.
Later, Scripture describes his extraordinary knowledge, his proverbs, his songs, and the international reputation of his understanding.
Kings and dignitaries wanted to hear him.
The queen of Sheba traveled to test him with difficult questions.
Solomon answered.
His wealth was immense. His palace was magnificent. His kingdom enjoyed extraordinary prominence.
From the outside, he appeared to have everything.
And perhaps that was part of the danger.
Because success can make disobedience look harmless when the consequences have not yet arrived.
A person can be admired publicly while becoming spiritually careless privately.
A ministry can grow while its leader neglects repentance.
A family can look beautiful in photographs while its relationships quietly fracture.
A Christian can know exactly how to explain temptation while secretly feeding it.
And the frightening thing is that none of these contradictions necessarily become visible overnight.
Sometimes the collapse begins long before anyone notices the cracks.
Long before Solomon's first wife entered the palace, God had already spoken about what Israel's kings must not do.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
"Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away."
That is the wording of the King James Version.
The Hebrew warning is remarkably direct:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim, ve-lo yasur levavo.
A close translation is:
"And he shall not multiply wives for himself, so that his heart does not turn aside."
Notice what God identified as the danger.
Not merely public embarrassment.
Not simply political complications.
Not even the financial burden of maintaining an enormous household.
His heart.
God warned that multiplying wives could turn the king's heart away.
And that is precisely what the biblical narrative later records.
This was not an obscure command hidden in some forgotten corner of Israel's history.
Deuteronomy 17:18–20 also instructed the king to make a copy of God's law, keep it with him, and read it throughout his life so that he would learn to fear the Lord and obey His commandments.
The king was never supposed to become too powerful to be corrected by Scripture.
His throne was subject to God's Word.
His desires were subject to God's Word.
His decisions were subject to God's Word.
And his heart was supposed to remain teachable.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us whether Solomon personally copied and regularly read that royal manuscript.
We should not pretend to know what the Bible does not reveal.
But the command itself is unmistakable.
The king was supposed to live under the authority of the God who established his kingdom.
And Solomon's later conduct stood in direct contradiction to that command.
Here is the tragedy.
Solomon did not need another revelation to know that multiplying wives was dangerous. God had already spoken.
And how often is that our problem?
We ask God to reveal His will while resisting what He has already revealed.
We pray for clarity while avoiding obedience.
We want confirmation that a relationship is right even when we know it is pulling us away from Christ.
We ask God to bless decisions we have not honestly submitted to Him.
