We keep searching for a spiritual answer that will allow us to keep the thing He is asking us to surrender.
And sometimes the most painful truth is this:
We are not confused.
We are conflicted.
We know what Scripture says.
We simply wish it said something else.
Then comes one of the saddest chapters in the Old Testament.
First Kings 11 begins by describing Solomon's love for many foreign women, including women from nations associated with the very religious influences Israel had been warned against.
The passage specifically emphasizes the danger of being drawn toward other gods.

The issue was not that women from other nations were inherently incapable of worshiping the Lord. Ruth, a Moabite woman, had faithfully embraced Israel's God and became part of the family line leading to David and ultimately to Jesus.
The issue in Solomon's story was covenant unfaithfulness, prohibited royal accumulation of wives, and the embrace of idolatrous worship.
Scripture says Solomon held fast to these women in love.
And then the numbers arrive.
Seven hundred wives, described as princesses.
Three hundred concubines.
The scale is almost impossible to imagine.
These relationships likely included royal and political alliances, but the biblical account does not reduce them to diplomacy.
It describes Solomon's attachment to these women and the spiritual consequences that followed.
First Kings 11:3 delivers the devastating conclusion:
"And his wives turned away his heart."
The Hebrew reads:
וַיַּטּוּ נָשָׁיו אֶת־לִבּוֹ
Vayyattu nashav et-libbo.
Literally, the phrase communicates that his wives turned or inclined his heart away.
But be careful here.
It would be easy to read those words and place all the blame on the women.
That would miss the moral responsibility Scripture places upon Solomon himself.
He was the king.
He had received God's warnings.
He made the choices.
He multiplied the relationships.
And he permitted the religious compromise that followed.
The women were involved in the turning of his heart, but Solomon was not an innocent victim of circumstances beyond his control.
He was accountable for his own disobedience.
And this is where the story becomes especially unsettling.
Solomon's downfall was not merely sexual excess.
It was spiritual betrayal.
First Kings 11:4 says that when Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly devoted to the Lord his God.
He followed Ashtoreth and Milcom.
He built high places associated with Chemosh and Molech.
The king who had built a magnificent temple for the worship of the Lord was now facilitating worship that dishonored the Lord.
Imagine that contradiction.
The same hands that had overseen the construction of God's temple were now involved in establishing places of idolatry.
The same king who once prayed that the nations would know the Lord was now participating in practices that violated God's covenant.
The same man who had asked for a listening heart had become a man whose heart was turning away.
What happened?
Did his intelligence disappear?
Did he suddenly forget everything he knew?
Did the wisdom God had given him evaporate?
The Bible does not say that Solomon lost his intellectual capacity or that God removed his entire gift of wisdom.
What it does say is far more disturbing.
Solomon's heart turned away from God despite the extraordinary wisdom he had received.
That is the distinction we must not miss.
His downfall was not proof that he had never been wise.
It was proof that possessing wisdom does not automatically mean practicing it.
And that should make us examine ourselves.
Because you can know that forgiveness is right and still nurse bitterness for years.
You can understand the danger of pornography and still keep returning to it.
You can preach about humility while secretly craving applause.
You can quote verses about generosity while allowing money to become your master.
You can teach about marriage while neglecting the person you promised to love.
You can explain the Gospel beautifully and still resist the repentance that Gospel demands.
Knowledge can identify the right road.
But knowledge alone does not make your feet walk it.
And there is a terrible kind of spiritual self-deception that begins when we mistake our ability to explain God's truth for our willingness to obey it.
Maybe that is why Solomon's story hurts.
Because some of us have been living with that contradiction for a long time.
We know the verses.
We know the sermons.
We know the language of faith.
We know how to say, "God is good," even when our private lives are becoming increasingly distant from Him.
We have learned how to sound spiritually healthy while avoiding the questions that would expose our condition.
And if we are not careful, we can become more concerned about appearing wise than actually walking with God.
There is another Hebrew word worth examining.
In 1 Kings 11:4, Solomon's heart is described as not being שָׁלֵם — shalem toward the Lord.
The word carries the sense of being whole, complete, or undivided in this context.
It is related to the Hebrew word family associated with wholeness and peace.
Solomon's problem was not simply that he had too many responsibilities or too many competing interests.
His devotion had become divided.
He was no longer wholly faithful to the Lord.
And divided devotion is not always obvious at first.
Sometimes it begins with a small exception.
Just one relationship we refuse to examine.
Just one habit we refuse to confess.
Just one compromise we excuse because everybody else seems to be doing it.
Just one ambition that gradually becomes more important than faithfulness.
Just one private indulgence we insist we can control.
Until one day we discover that what we once called a harmless exception has become a governing influence.
We still believe in God.
We still know His name.
We may even continue religious activity.
But our deepest loyalties have shifted.
And the most dangerous idols are not always the ones we bow before physically.
Sometimes they are the things we cannot imagine surrendering.
The approval of people.
The pursuit of pleasure.
The hunger for power.
The fear of being alone.
The desperate need to be admired.
The comfort of a secret sin.
Whatever occupies the place of ultimate loyalty in our hearts is competing with the worship that belongs to God.
And Solomon's story forces us to ask a question we would rather avoid.
What have I allowed to become so important that I am willing to disobey God to keep it?
Not what has somebody else done.
Not what is wrong with the church.
Not what society has become.
What am I protecting?
What am I defending?
What am I unwilling to place before Jesus?
Because Solomon's thousand women may look like an extreme example that has nothing to do with our lives.
But the spiritual mechanism is painfully familiar.
We want what we want.
God has spoken.
And we try to find a way to keep both our desires and the appearance of obedience.
Eventually, something has to give.
For Solomon, Scripture tells us what gave way.
His wholehearted devotion to the Lord.
And the consequences were enormous.
In 1 Kings 11:9–13, the Lord expressed His anger because Solomon's heart had turned away, even though God had appeared to him twice and had commanded him concerning other gods.
God declared that the kingdom would be torn away from Solomon's dynasty, though the full judgment would not occur during Solomon's lifetime, for David's sake.
The kingdom would not be completely removed from David's line.
God's covenant purposes would continue.
But Solomon's disobedience would have consequences beyond his own lifetime.
That is another truth we do not like discussing.
Sin can be forgiven without every earthly consequence being erased.
Grace is not permission to treat God's warnings as meaningless.
And the choices we make today can wound people who never participated in making them.
A parent's compromise can destabilize a home.
A leader's hidden sin can damage a community.
A spouse's unfaithfulness can leave scars that take years to heal.
A believer's persistent hypocrisy can cause others to question whether the faith being proclaimed is genuinely transforming the life of the person proclaiming it.
This is not because every suffering person is being punished for personal sin.
Scripture rejects that simplistic assumption.
It is because our decisions are rarely isolated.
We live in relationships.
We influence others.
And disobedience can carry consequences far beyond the moment in which it seemed attractive.
Now here is something that makes Solomon's story even more heartbreaking.
He was associated with the very wisdom literature that warns against the patterns that destroyed him.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
"Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life."
What a devastating sentence to read beside 1 Kings 11.
Guard your heart.
Yet Solomon's heart was turned away.
Proverbs 3:5–6 teaches trust in the Lord rather than dependence on one's own understanding.
Yet Solomon's life reveals the danger of allowing extraordinary understanding to coexist with disobedience.
Proverbs 9:10 declares:
"The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom."
And that brings us to the deepest issue.
Biblical wisdom is not merely the possession of correct information.
It is inseparably connected to reverence for God and the moral response that reverence requires.
The Hebrew word חָכְמָה — chokhmah, commonly translated wisdom, can describe skill, discernment, and the capacity to act wisely.
But in the biblical wisdom tradition, the fear of the Lord is foundational.
Wisdom is not simply knowing what works.
It is learning to live rightly before God.
And Solomon's story exposes the terrible gap that can exist between wisdom received and wisdom practiced.

We should also be careful not to assume that Solomon personally composed every line in the final biblical books associated with his name. Proverbs contains collections and editorial material, and the precise authorship and dating of Ecclesiastes are debated.
But the canonical portrait remains striking.
The king celebrated for wisdom becomes the king whose life warns us against ignoring wisdom.
And perhaps that is why this account still speaks so powerfully after thousands of years.
It does not allow us to hide behind our gifts.
It does not allow us to say, "But God has used me."
It does not allow us to assume that public success proves private faithfulness.
God can give a person remarkable ability.
That person can accomplish remarkable things.
And that same person can still make devastating moral choices.
A spiritual gift is not a substitute for spiritual maturity.
A platform is not proof of holiness.
An impressive ministry is not a license to ignore accountability.
And knowing the Bible is not the same as surrendering to the God who speaks through it.
James 1:22 gives the New Testament warning with piercing clarity:
"But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."
The Greek expression is:
γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγου καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταί
Ginesthe de poiētai logou kai mē monon akroatai.
The command is to become doers of the word, not merely hearers.
James identifies the danger as self-deception.
Not simply ignorance.
Not a lack of access to teaching.
Self-deception.
The frightening possibility that we can hear truth repeatedly and become skilled at agreeing with it without allowing it to change us.
We can say amen to a sermon about forgiveness and go home determined to remain bitter.
We can cry during worship and return to a sin we have already decided not to surrender.
We can post a powerful Scripture passage on Facebook while privately refusing to obey its message.
And yes, we can read an article like this, feel deeply convicted, and still close the screen without changing anything.
That may be the most uncomfortable sentence in this entire story.
Because emotional conviction is not the same as repentance.
Tears can accompany repentance.
But tears alone are not repentance.
Feeling guilty is not the same as turning toward God.
Being moved by a message is not the same as obeying its truth.
And Jesus did not come merely to make us feel religious emotions.
He came to save sinners, reconcile us to God, and transform our lives through His grace.
Which brings us to the question that matters more than Solomon's thousand relationships.
What happens when we realize that we have been living against the truth we already know?
What happens when we recognize that we have been protecting something that is slowly pulling our hearts away from Christ?
What happens when we have failed so badly that we are afraid to face God honestly?
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a beautiful religious idea.
It becomes our only hope.
Because if this story ended with Solomon's failure, it would leave us with a warning but no Savior.
And Scripture does not end with Solomon.
It points us toward someone greater.
Centuries later, Jesus spoke about Solomon's glory.
In Matthew 6:29, He said that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of the lilies of the field.
And in Matthew 12:42, Jesus declared:
"Behold, a greater than Solomon is here."
Those words change everything.
Solomon was a king blessed with extraordinary wisdom.
Jesus Christ is greater than Solomon.
Solomon received wisdom from God.
Christ is described in 1 Corinthians 1:24 as the power of God and the wisdom of God.
Solomon built a temple.
Jesus spoke of His own body as the temple that would be raised after His death.
Solomon's kingdom was marked by division after his reign.
Jesus is the promised Son of David whose kingdom will have no end.
Solomon's heart was turned away by disordered loves.
Jesus remained faithful to the Father even through suffering and death.
Solomon's disobedience brought judgment upon his kingdom.
Jesus, the sinless King, willingly bore the judgment deserved by sinners so that all who trust in Him may receive forgiveness and eternal life.
Do not miss the contrast.
The answer to Solomon's failure is not simply, "Try harder to be wiser."
The answer is to come to the greater King.
Jesus Christ.
The One who never surrendered to sin.
The One who perfectly obeyed where humanity has failed.
The One who died for sinners and rose again.
The One who calls us not to hide our failures, but to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek word commonly translated repent is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It conveys a change of mind or understanding that, in the biblical call to repentance, involves turning away from sin and toward God.
Repentance is not an attempt to purchase forgiveness through good behavior.
It is the appropriate response to God's mercy and truth.
We do not earn salvation by becoming impressive enough for God.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works.
And the very next verse, Ephesians 2:10, reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not make obedience unnecessary.
Grace rescues us from the hopeless attempt to save ourselves and begins transforming the way we live.
That is why the Gospel is such good news for the person who has known better and still done wrong.
Jesus does not require you to pretend that your compromise was harmless.
He does not ask you to rewrite your past.
He does not call evil good.
He calls you to bring your sin into the light, confess it, turn from it, and trust His mercy.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
What a promise.
Not that sin does not matter.
Not that consequences always disappear.
But that forgiveness and cleansing are available through the faithfulness and righteousness of God.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying something you have never told anyone.
A hidden addiction.
A relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ.
A habit you keep promising to abandon.
A bitterness you have carried for years.
A spiritual double life that is exhausting you.
Or perhaps your struggle is quieter.
You have not openly rejected God.
You have simply become comfortable living without seriously listening to Him.
You still believe.
You still pray occasionally.
You still know what is right.
But your heart is no longer as tender toward His Word as it once was.
And somewhere deep inside, you know it.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
You do not have to wait until your life collapses to return to Jesus.
You do not have to lose your marriage before taking repentance seriously.
You do not have to destroy your testimony before confessing what is wrong.
You do not have to become another cautionary story before choosing obedience.
The fact that God is confronting your heart through His Word today is not a reason to despair.
It is a reason to respond.
Do not turn conviction into another moment of temporary emotion.
Bring your life before the Lord.
Name the sin honestly.
Stop defending it.
Seek forgiveness.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Ask for help from trustworthy, mature believers when the struggle requires accountability.
And when you stumble, do not make hiding your refuge.
Return to Christ.
Again and again, not with a casual attitude toward sin, but with genuine faith in the Savior whose mercy is greater than your failures.
There is one question people often ask about Solomon.
Did he eventually repent?
Some readers interpret Ecclesiastes as evidence of Solomon's later disillusionment and return to the fear of God, especially its concluding call to fear God and keep His commandments.
Others question whether Ecclesiastes should be read as Solomon's personal autobiography.
The biblical narrative in 1 Kings does not explicitly record a final repentance by Solomon.
We should not claim certainty where Scripture remains silent.
We know he sinned grievously.
We know God judged his disobedience.
We know the biblical account does not give us a clear final scene of his repentance.
And perhaps that silence makes the warning even more urgent.
Do not build your spiritual life on the assumption that you can postpone repentance indefinitely.
Do not presume upon tomorrow.
Do not tell yourself that you will surrender once you have enjoyed the thing God has forbidden.
Do not wait until the consequences become unbearable before taking His Word seriously.
Second Corinthians 6:2 says:
"Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation."
Now.
Not after one more secret indulgence.
Not after one more year of pretending.
Not after the relationship finally breaks your heart.
Not after you have exhausted every other possibility.
Now.
And if you are wondering whether God can truly receive someone who has wandered far from Him, remember the father in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son.
The son had squandered his inheritance and dishonored his father.
Yet when he returned, the father received him with compassion.
That parable is not permission to squander our lives.
It is a revelation of the mercy awaiting the repentant.
The Father's compassion does not make sin beautiful.
It makes grace astonishing.
And that is the heartbeat of everything we proclaim at Gospel Warrior.
Not because every consequence vanishes.
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ redeems sinners, restores fellowship with God, and transforms lives that once seemed beyond hope.
A scandal does not have to become your eternal identity.
Your worst decision does not have to be the final word over your life.
Your secret struggle does not have to remain your master.
Through Christ, the guilty can be forgiven.
The proud can be humbled.
The broken can be restored.
The wandering can return.
And the spiritually exhausted can discover that their hope rests not in their own perfection, but in the faithfulness of their Savior.
If this story has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply reacting to another Facebook post.
Be honest before God.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing those words earns forgiveness.
But as a simple testimony that you do not want to remain merely a hearer of God's Word.
You do not have to explain private details publicly.
God knows what you are carrying.
Your story may remind someone else that repentance is possible and that grace is real.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who desperately needs this message.
Someone who looks successful but is spiritually exhausted.
Someone who knows the Bible but has quietly drifted from the Lord.
Someone who believes they have gone too far to return.
Someone who has mistaken God's patience for permission to continue in sin.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because the truth of God's Word deserves to travel farther than our own circles.
Because temptation has a way of making yesterday's conviction feel inconvenient tomorrow.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown lukewarm, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ to follow along and encounter the truth of the Gospel.
But I also want to speak to those who believe this ministry should continue reaching more people.
Every article takes work.
Every resource requires time and effort.
Every opportunity to teach, encourage, and proclaim Jesus Christ is a stewardship we want to take seriously.
Our desire is to keep biblical nourishment accessible while expanding the resources available to believers who are hungry for truth.
And that is where your partnership can make a difference.
For believers who choose to give from their worshipful gratitude to God, supporting sound Gospel ministry can be one expression of Christian generosity.
Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers participating in Gospel ministry through material support, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not reluctant or compelled.
That distinction matters.
It is a voluntary monthly ministry contribution that you may prayerfully consider as part of your personal giving and stewardship.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply additional ways to encourage believers and express our gratitude to those who help sustain the ministry.
The heart of the invitation is deeper than merchandise.
It is about helping more people open their Bibles.
Helping someone who has fallen rediscover the mercy of Jesus.
Helping a young believer understand Scripture.
Helping a weary Christian find encouragement grounded in truth.
Helping a searching soul hear the Gospel clearly.
And helping build a community that is not satisfied with merely knowing about Jesus, but longs to follow Him faithfully.
The message of salvation is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus cannot be purchased.
Because the goal has never been to gather supporters around a personality.
It is to point souls toward the Savior.
Now, before you leave, I want to bring you back to Solomon one final time.
Picture the old king.
The throne.
The wealth.
The magnificent buildings.
The international reputation.
The extraordinary wisdom.
Everything that once made the world marvel at his life.
And yet the biblical account tells us that his heart had turned away from the Lord.
What a devastating contrast.
A man could possess so much and still lose sight of what mattered most.
A man could understand so deeply and still disobey so tragically.
A man could be celebrated by nations and yet stand under the rebuke of God.
And somewhere in that story is a warning for every one of us.
Your greatest danger may not be that you do not know enough.
It may be that you have become comfortable ignoring what you already know.
You may not need another sermon to identify the compromise.
You may not need another book to explain the command.
You may not need another sign to tell you that your heart is drifting.
You may need to stop running.
Stop excusing.
Stop negotiating.
And surrender.
Not because your obedience can purchase salvation.
But because the Savior who gave Himself for you is worthy of your trust, your love, and your allegiance.
Solomon teaches us that extraordinary wisdom without faithful obedience can coexist with extraordinary failure.
Jesus shows us something greater.
That sinners who have failed can find forgiveness and new life in the One who perfectly obeyed.
And if your heart has wandered, you can come to Him today.
No performance.
No pretending.
No hiding behind how much Scripture you know.
Just an honest sinner coming to a gracious Savior.
Perhaps your prayer tonight needs to be as simple as this:

"Lord Jesus, I have known Your truth and still chosen my own way. Forgive me. Expose what I have been defending. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. Give me a heart that listens, faith that obeys, and humility that keeps returning to You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. My hope is not in my wisdom, but in Your grace. Amen."

If you prayed those words sincerely, remember that the power is not in the wording of a prayer. Our hope rests in Jesus Christ, His finished work, and His promise to save those who come to Him in faith.
And if this message reached a place in your heart you have been avoiding, don't let the moment pass unnoticed.
And keep walking with Christ.
Because the most important question is not whether you can impress others with how much you know about God.
It is whether you are willing to trust and obey the God you know.
Solomon's tragedy was not that he lacked enough wisdom to recognize the wrong road. It was that he kept walking down it.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking thing you could ever say at the end of your life is not, "I never knew."
But, "I knew… and I would not listen."
Don't wait until your life becomes the warning you were once wise enough to understand.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE WE GIVING SATAN THE ATTENTION THAT BELONGS TO JESUS?
paragraphs: ARE WE GIVING SATAN THE ATTENTION THAT BELONGS TO JESUS?
The Devil May Be Real, but He Is Not the Center of Your Story. And Some Christians Have Become So Busy Watching the Enemy That They Have Forgotten to Look at Their Savior.
What if one of the most dangerous distractions in your Christian life isn't something obviously sinful?
What if it's something that sounds spiritual, feels urgent, and even uses the language of warfare?
What if you've spent so much time talking about what Satan is doing that you've barely noticed what Jesus has already done?
Read that again.

Because somewhere between our prayers against the enemy, our warnings about demonic attacks, our fear of curses, and our endless conversations about spiritual warfare, a troubling question deserves an honest answer.
When did the defeated enemy become the main character in a story that was supposed to be about the victorious Christ?
And before you dismiss this as another article telling Christians to ignore spiritual warfare, stay with me.
Satan is real. Demonic opposition is real. Temptation is real. Spiritual warfare is biblical.
But so is the empty tomb.
And if our understanding of spiritual warfare leaves us more conscious of Satan's activity than Christ's authority, something has gone terribly wrong.
Because the Gospel was never meant to produce Christians who are constantly terrified of the devil.
It was meant to produce disciples who trust the risen Jesus.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of this conversation is that some of us have unintentionally made the enemy seem more powerful than the Savior we claim to worship.
Imagine a Christian woman sitting on the edge of her bed at two in the morning.

She has prayed. She has cried. She has listened to sermons about spiritual attacks. She has watched videos warning about hidden curses, generational strongholds, demonic doors, and the enemy's plans against her family.
Every disappointment has become an attack.
Every delay has become opposition.
Every nightmare has become a warning.
Every difficult relationship has become a battlefield.
She loves Jesus. She genuinely does.
But she is exhausted.
Not because Christ has abandoned her.
Not necessarily because a demon is attacking her.
But because she has learned to interpret almost everything through the possibility of Satan's involvement.
And somewhere along the way, her faith became a constant search for danger instead of a growing relationship with her Redeemer.
Perhaps you know someone like her.
Perhaps, painfully, you recognize yourself.
You wake up wondering what the enemy might do today instead of remembering whose mercy has carried you into another morning.
You spend more time investigating darkness than meditating on the light.
You can describe the enemy's strategies in astonishing detail, yet struggle to remember the promises of God when anxiety comes knocking.
You know how to rebuke.
But have you learned how to rest?
You know how to identify a battle.
But do you know how to abide in Christ?
You know the language of spiritual warfare.
But is your heart becoming more like Jesus?
Those questions are not meant to shame you.
They are meant to lead you back to the One who never stopped calling you closer.
Because Scripture does not command believers to become obsessed with Satan.
It commands us to be sober-minded, watchful, faithful, prayerful, and firmly rooted in Christ.
And there is an enormous difference.
The apostle Peter wrote:
“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: Whom resist stedfast in the faith.” — 1 Peter 5:8–9, KJV
Notice something remarkable.
Peter acknowledges the danger without making the danger the center of Christian existence.
He does not tell believers to spend their lives studying every movement of the devil.
He tells them to resist him, steadfast in the faith.
The Greek word translated “resist” is ἀντίστητε (antistēte), from a verb meaning to stand against or oppose.
It is a call to firm resistance, not frantic obsession.
And the phrase “steadfast in the faith” matters.
Our resistance is not rooted in how loudly we shout, how dramatically we pray, or how much secret knowledge we believe we possess about the kingdom of darkness.
It is rooted in faithful dependence upon God.
Peter's warning is serious.
But Peter's letter does not end with Satan.
It points suffering believers toward the God of all grace, who will restore, strengthen, and establish them (1 Peter 5:10).
Even when Peter talks about the devil, his destination is the faithfulness of God.
That should tell us something.
The enemy deserves vigilance. Jesus deserves worship.
Those are not the same thing.
And confusing them can quietly deform our spiritual lives.
Think about how Jesus Himself handled the temptation in the wilderness.
Matthew 4 tells us that the devil approached Jesus after forty days of fasting.
The temptations were deliberate.
Turn stones into bread.
Throw Yourself down and force a demonstration of divine protection.
Bow down and receive the kingdoms of the world.
Jesus did not respond by delivering a long speech about Satan's power.
He answered with Scripture.
“It is written.”
Again.
“It is written.”
And again.
“It is written.”
Then came the decisive command:
“Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.” — Matthew 4:10, KJV
Jesus refused to let the tempter redefine His mission.
He would not exchange obedience for immediate satisfaction.
He would not turn trust into presumption.
He would not accept a crown by bowing before evil.
And the words He quoted came from Deuteronomy 6:13, where Israel was commanded to fear the LORD and serve Him.
In the Hebrew text, the phrase יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא וְאֹתוֹ תַעֲבֹד (YHWH elohekha tira ve'oto ta'avod) means, in context, “You shall fear the LORD your God, and Him you shall serve.”
The word tira comes from the Hebrew verb associated with fearing or revering.
This is not an invitation to live in terror of Satan.
It is a summons to give God the reverence and allegiance that belong to Him alone.
Jesus demonstrated the very priority that some believers are in danger of losing.
Worship belongs to God.
Obedience belongs to God.
Our deepest attention, ultimate allegiance, and lasting confidence belong to God.
Not to the enemy.
Not to the fear of the enemy.
Not even to our fascination with defeating the enemy.
To God.
And perhaps that is why some of the most powerful words Jesus ever spoke about spiritual authority were not the words many Christians emphasize.
In Luke 10, the seventy returned rejoicing that demons were subject to them through Jesus' name.
Imagine their excitement.
They had witnessed something extraordinary.
They had seen the authority of Christ demonstrated in their ministry.
Jesus affirmed the reality of that authority.
But then He redirected their joy.
“Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.” — Luke 10:20, KJV
Let those words settle into your heart.
Jesus did not deny the significance of spiritual authority.
He taught His disciples that something greater deserved their joy.
Their relationship with God.
Their place in His saving purposes.
The grace that had brought them into His kingdom.
The miracle was not merely that demons submitted to them.
The greater reason for rejoicing was that they belonged to God.
And this raises a question worth sitting with.
If Jesus told His disciples not to make authority over demons their greatest reason for rejoicing, why have some of us made demonic activity the subject of nearly every spiritual conversation?
We talk about attacks.
We talk about curses.
We talk about enemies.
We talk about hidden forces.
But how often do we talk about the holiness of God?
The beauty of repentance?
The cost of the cross?
The wonder of forgiveness?
The transforming work of the Holy Spirit?
The quiet miracle of a hardened heart becoming tender again?
The beauty of a father apologizing to his children?
The courage of a wife choosing truth instead of pretending her marriage is healthy?
The repentance of a man who finally confesses the sin he has hidden for years?
The grace of Jesus meeting someone in the ruins of decisions they can never undo?
These are not small things.
These are places where the Gospel changes actual human lives.
And sometimes, while we are searching for dramatic evidence of the enemy, we overlook the ordinary, costly, beautiful work of Christ.
A man loses his temper and wounds his family.
Instead of admitting that he has allowed anger to govern his words, he says the enemy attacked his home.
A woman becomes consumed by jealousy.
Instead of confessing envy and learning contentment, she assumes someone has placed a spiritual curse upon her happiness.
A believer refuses to forgive.
Instead of confronting bitterness, he spends months praying against every perceived enemy.
Now, spiritual opposition can be real.
But Scripture never teaches us to attribute every sinful choice, painful circumstance, or personal failure directly to Satan.
James writes:
That verse should sober us.
Sometimes the problem is not a demon hiding behind the door.
Sometimes it is pride sitting openly in the heart.
Sometimes it is greed.
Sometimes it is unforgiveness.
Sometimes it is an appetite we refuse to discipline.
Sometimes it is a lie we keep telling ourselves because the truth would require repentance.
And blaming Satan for everything can become a convenient way of avoiding the responsibility God calls us to embrace.
It is easier to say, “The enemy is attacking my marriage,” than to admit, “I have been selfish, dishonest, or cruel.”
It is easier to say, “The devil is stealing my peace,” than to examine whether we have been feeding our minds with fear and refusing to bring our anxieties to God.
It is easier to search for an invisible enemy than to confront a visible pattern of disobedience.
But Jesus did not come merely to help us identify evil outside ourselves.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive us.
To cleanse us.
To give us new hearts.
To call us away from darkness and into His marvelous light.
And genuine spiritual maturity requires us to recognize both the reality of external temptation and the responsibility of personal repentance.
That is not condemnation.
That is grace telling the truth.
Because the Savior who exposes sin is also the Savior who offers forgiveness.
Consider the man in Mark 5 who lived among the tombs.
His life had become a portrait of torment.
He cried out.
He wounded himself.
He lived isolated among the dead.
The Gospel account describes him as possessed by unclean spirits.
People tried to restrain him with chains, but they could not restore him.
Then Jesus arrived.
And the story changed.
The demons were real.
Their destructive influence was real.
The man's suffering was real.
But the central revelation of that encounter was not the greatness of the demonic powers.
It was the authority and compassion of Jesus Christ.
The man who had lived among the tombs was later seen sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
And when he wanted to accompany Jesus, the Lord gave him an astonishing assignment.
“Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.” — Mark 5:19, KJV
Do you see it?
Jesus did not commission him to build his identity around the demons that once tormented him.
He told him to testify about the mercy he had received.
Not, “Go and make everyone fascinated by your darkness.”
But, “Tell them what the Lord has done for you.”
The man had a history of torment.
But his future would be marked by testimony.
His past was not denied.
It was no longer the center of his identity.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that.
You may have a past filled with shame.
You may have been trapped in addictions, destructive relationships, bitterness, sexual sin, spiritual confusion, or years of rebellion.
You may have spent so long describing what went wrong that you have forgotten to celebrate what Christ is making new.
But if you belong to Jesus, your deepest identity is not your worst chapter.
Your story is not ultimately about the darkness that held you.
It is about the Redeemer who came for you.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin harmless.
Not by removing the need for repentance or accountability.
But by meeting guilty and broken people with a mercy that neither excuses evil nor abandons the sinner who turns to Him.
That is the scandalous beauty of grace.
Jesus does not merely change the language of our story.
He changes its direction.
And nowhere is that truth clearer than at the cross.
Colossians 2:13–15 describes God's saving work in Christ.
Paul speaks of forgiveness, the cancellation of the record of debt against us, and Christ's triumph over hostile spiritual powers.
Verse 15 declares:
“And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.” — Colossians 2:15, KJV
The Greek verb ἀπεκδυσάμενος (apekdysamenos) is commonly understood here in the sense of stripping off or disarming.
The language of triumph presents Christ's decisive victory over hostile powers.
Scholars discuss certain details of the Greek construction, but Paul's central emphasis is unmistakable: the crucified Christ is victorious.
The cross was not Satan's ultimate success.
It was the place where God accomplished redemption through His Son.
What looked like humiliation became the revelation of divine wisdom and saving power.
What looked like defeat was followed by resurrection.
And the enemy who seeks to accuse God's people does not possess the final verdict over those who are in Christ.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
That does not mean Christians will never experience temptation, suffering, accusation, or spiritual conflict.
It means that condemnation does not have the final word over those united to Christ.
Jesus does.
So why do we sometimes speak as though the devil has more authority over a redeemed believer than the Savior who purchased that believer with His blood?
Why do we act as though every setback proves Satan is winning?
Why do we sometimes live as though the cross is merely a symbol of hope rather than the decisive saving act of God?
Perhaps because fear is loud.
And faith often grows in quiet places.
Fear demands immediate attention.
Faith learns to trust what God has said even when emotions are unsettled.
Fear makes us desperate to know every possible threat.
Faith teaches us to know the Shepherd's voice.
Fear keeps asking, “What if Satan attacks?”
Faith asks, “How can I remain faithful to Jesus whatever comes?”
And there is something profoundly freeing about that change of focus.
Not because we suddenly become invulnerable.
Not because suffering disappears.
But because our security is no longer built upon our ability to predict or control every danger.
It rests upon the character and promises of God.
This is why James 4:7 is so important.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — KJV
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
The Greek word ὑποτάγητε (hypotagēte) means “submit” or “place yourselves under” authority.
And ἀντίστητε (antistēte), again, means “resist” or “stand against.”
The command begins with our relationship to God.
It does not begin with fascination about Satan.
Submission is not a decorative introduction to spiritual warfare.
It is essential to the Christian life.
You cannot substitute dramatic declarations against darkness for ordinary obedience to God.
You cannot nurture secret sin all week and assume a few shouted words will replace genuine repentance.
You cannot continually reject the teachings of Jesus and expect spiritual maturity to emerge from religious intensity alone.
James is addressing a community troubled by worldliness, conflict, and divided loyalties.
His call is not merely to confront the devil.
It is to draw near to God, cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, humble themselves, and repent.
And that is where some of us need to return.
Not to another endless search for hidden enemies.
But to honest surrender.
To prayer without performance.
To Scripture without sensationalism.
To worship without fear-driven obsession.
To repentance without excuses.
To the daily, sometimes difficult work of following Jesus.
Paul teaches spiritual warfare in Ephesians 6.
He tells believers to put on the whole armor of God.
He speaks of the devil's schemes and of spiritual forces of evil.
He does not minimize the battle.
But look at the armor.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The readiness that comes from the Gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The Word of God.
Prayer.
This is not a costume for spiritual theatrics.
It is a picture of believers standing firm through God's provision.
And the passage begins with a command that should never be forgotten:
“Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.” — Ephesians 6:10, KJV
Not strong in your ability to frighten demons.
Not strong in your knowledge of occult terminology.
Not strong in your confidence that you can identify every spiritual attack.
Strong in the Lord.
The Greek expression ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν κυρίῳ (endynamousthe en kyriō) communicates being strengthened in the Lord.
The source of strength is not the believer's independent power.
It is the Lord Himself.
And that changes everything.
Because Christian courage is not pretending that evil is powerless in every present circumstance.
It is trusting that evil does not possess ultimate authority over Christ.
The New Testament still warns believers against the devil.
It still commands resistance.
It still speaks of spiritual conflict.
But it never invites us to build a Christian identity around fear of darkness.
Our life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3).
Our minds are to be set on things above (Colossians 3:1–2).
Our eyes are to be fixed upon Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2).
The Greek expression in Hebrews 12:2 begins with ἀφορῶντες εἰς Ἰησοῦν (aphorōntes eis Iēsoun).
It conveys the idea of looking toward Jesus with focused attention.
That is a beautiful picture of Christian perseverance.
The surrounding passage describes believers running the race set before them, laying aside sin and every hindrance, and enduring through hardship.
Where are their eyes directed?
Toward Jesus.
Not because the obstacles are imaginary.
Not because suffering is unimportant.
But because the One who endured the cross and is seated at God's right hand is worthy of their unwavering trust.
And maybe that is the correction our generation needs.
We have become skilled at spotting darkness.
But are we becoming skilled at recognizing Christlike character?
We can spend hours debating demonic influences.
But can we spend ten minutes confessing our own pride?
We can identify spiritual warfare in everyone else's life.
But can we admit when our own words have wounded someone?
We can declare that Satan is defeated.
But do we live as though Jesus is Lord?
That last question is the one that reaches beneath the surface.
Because saying “Jesus is Lord” is more than making a religious statement.
It is a confession that calls for allegiance.
The Greek phrase Κύριος Ἰησοῦς (Kyrios Iēsous) means “Jesus is Lord.”
It is central to the New Testament's proclamation of Christ's authority.
And if He is Lord, then He has authority over our decisions.
Our relationships.
Our hidden habits.
Our money.
Our words.
Our ambitions.
Our fears.
Our worship.
Our treatment of people who cannot benefit us.
Our willingness to forgive.
Our response when nobody is watching.
The enemy may tempt us.
But Jesus calls us to follow Him.
And following Him is where faith becomes more than religious vocabulary.
It becomes a transformed life.
There is a particularly sobering warning in Acts 19.
Some itinerant Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name of Jesus over an evil spirit, using the authority associated with the Jesus whom Paul preached.
But the encounter exposed the danger of treating Jesus' name as a formula detached from genuine submission to Him.
The episode ended in humiliation and fear.
And the larger narrative resulted in the name of the Lord Jesus being magnified, with people confessing their practices and turning away from magic.
The point is not that Christians must discover a more powerful verbal technique.
It is that Jesus is not a magical instrument to be used for personal control.
He is Lord.
And no religious phrase can replace a real relationship of faith and obedience.
Some people want the authority associated with Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
They want victory without repentance.
Power without holiness.
Deliverance without discipleship.
The benefits of the kingdom without the King.
But Christ never offered Himself as an accessory to our existing lives.
He calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
And that call is far deeper than a moment of emotional excitement.
It is a lifetime of grace-fueled transformation.
Perhaps you are reading this after years of living under spiritual fear.
Maybe you have been taught that every family difficulty is a curse.
That every illness is demonic.
That every financial struggle is evidence of an attack.
That every anxious thought means the enemy has gained control.
Please hear this carefully.
Scripture does not authorize us to make those assumptions.
The Bible recognizes spiritual evil, but it also recognizes sickness, human weakness, ordinary suffering, injustice, consequences of human choices, and the brokenness of creation.
Jesus Himself rejected a simplistic connection between personal sin and a man's blindness in John 9:1–3.
And when Elijah was exhausted and overwhelmed in 1 Kings 19, God's care included rest, food, and gentle direction.
Not every hardship has a single explanation.
Not every struggle requires a dramatic spiritual diagnosis.
Sometimes you need to repent.
Sometimes you need to forgive.
Sometimes you need wise counsel.
Sometimes you need rest.
Sometimes you need medical care.
Sometimes you need help from mature believers who will walk with you in truth and love.
And in every circumstance, you need the grace and wisdom of God.
There is no shame in receiving appropriate help.
Faithfulness does not require us to deny the ordinary means through which God can care for people.
The Lord who made us knows that we are dust.
He is not glorified by our pretending to be stronger than we are.
He is glorified when we trust Him enough to walk in truth.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking consequence of excessive attention to Satan is not simply that it produces fear.
It is that it can steal our attention from the beauty of Jesus.
We become so concerned with what the enemy might be doing that we fail to marvel at what the Savior has done.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He welcomed sinners.
He touched lepers.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He fed the hungry.
He wept beside a tomb.
He forgave those who came to Him in repentance and faith.
He gave His life as a ransom for many.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us into a new life shaped by His love and truth.
There is enough glory in Christ to occupy the Christian heart for a lifetime.
Yet sometimes we give more emotional energy to a frightening story about demons than to the resurrection of Jesus.
More attention to alleged curses than to the promises of God.
More fascination to the enemy's supposed plans than to the mission Christ entrusted to His Church.
And somewhere in the noise, the simple invitation of Jesus waits to be heard again.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
He did not say, “Come to Me only after you have identified every hidden attack.”
He did not say, “Come to Me when you have mastered every spiritual warfare formula.”
He said, “Come unto me.”
To Him.
The Person.
The Savior.
The Lord.
The One who knows every secret and still calls sinners to repentance and grace.
And maybe tonight, that is the invitation your soul has been waiting for.
Not another terrifying warning.
Not another explanation of why your life feels like a battlefield.
But a return to Jesus Himself.
The Jesus who is holy enough to confront your sin and merciful enough to forgive it.
The Jesus who will not flatter your pride but will receive the humble.
The Jesus who does not promise a painless life but promises His presence with His people.
The Jesus who can be trusted even when you do not understand what is happening around you.
You do not have to understand every strategy of the enemy to obey the Word of God.
You do not have to identify every spiritual force to pray with confidence in your Father.
You do not have to turn every disappointment into a supernatural conspiracy to believe that God is sovereign.
You can acknowledge the reality of spiritual warfare without making Satan the center of your spiritual imagination.
You can be watchful without becoming consumed by suspicion.
You can resist evil without living in terror.
You can take sin seriously without despairing of grace.
And you can pursue holiness without losing the joy of salvation.
Because the Christian life is not ultimately about becoming an expert on the devil.
It is about knowing, loving, trusting, obeying, and becoming more like Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the prayer we need tonight is not the loudest prayer we have ever prayed.
Perhaps it is the most honest.

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have allowed fear to become louder than Your promises. Forgive me for giving darkness more attention than Your Word. Teach me to resist evil without becoming obsessed with it. Expose the sins I have excused. Heal what is wounded in me. Give me discernment without suspicion, courage without pride, and peace rooted in Your truth. Let my life be known not for how much I talk about Satan, but for how faithfully I follow You. Amen.”
And if that prayer uncovered something you have been carrying, do not bury the moment beneath another scroll.
Let it become a turning point.
Maybe you have been afraid for so long that you have forgotten what it feels like to pray with confidence in God's love.
Maybe you have blamed the enemy for choices that require your repentance.
Maybe you have spent years fighting battles in your imagination while neglecting the simple obedience Christ has placed before you.
Maybe your faith has become loud on the outside but weary on the inside.
You are invited to come back.
Not to a shallow version of Christianity that ignores evil.
But to a Christ-centered faith that puts evil in its proper place.
A faith where the devil is resisted, sin is confessed, truth is loved, Scripture is treasured, the Church is strengthened, and Jesus is worshiped above all.
Or, if you have been spiritually exhausted and need prayer, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to disclose private struggles to strangers. A few honest words can be enough to invite encouragement from brothers and sisters in Christ.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture fear.
Not to make believers dependent on dramatic spiritual content.
Not to build a community around fascination with darkness.
But to keep pointing people toward the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Toward Scripture.
Toward repentance and grace.
Toward biblical discipleship.
Toward a faith that does not disappear when emotions settle.
And if this message helped you see Jesus more clearly, would you consider helping it reach someone else?
Someone may be exhausted from treating every difficulty as an attack.
Someone may be longing for a Christianity that is both spiritually serious and deeply rooted in the peace of Christ.

Invite your family, your friends, believers who have grown weary, people who are seeking truth, and even those who are unsure what they believe. They do not have to pretend to have everything figured out to begin hearing the Gospel.
There is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Scripture teaches that supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of generosity and partnership.
Paul wrote:
“For we are labourers together with God.” — 1 Corinthians 3:9, KJV
But the broader New Testament does affirm voluntary, generous support for Gospel ministry.
In Philippians 4:15–18, Paul thanks believers for sharing in his ministry through their gifts.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not pressured:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That distinction matters.
Your standing before God rests upon His grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a monthly payment.

You may choose to include it in your personal budget for ministry giving, alongside your commitments to your local church and other responsibilities. Whether you regard such support as an offering is a matter to consider prayerfully within your own Christian convictions; it should not automatically replace the giving and stewardship responsibilities you have already embraced.
These items are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and support the ongoing work.
That free library reflects something important about the heart of this mission.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And those who are unable to give financially can still make a meaningful difference by praying, sharing biblical teaching, encouraging others, and inviting people to grow in the Word of God.
Give freely if you choose to give.
Share faithfully if you choose to share.
And above everything, glorify Jesus in the way you live.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that admires a ministry.
The goal is to serve people who will love and follow Christ.
And that brings us back to the question that began this entire conversation.
Are Christians giving Satan too much attention and Jesus too little?
Sometimes, yes.
Not every Christian.
Not every discussion of spiritual warfare.
Not every warning about the enemy.
But whenever fear of Satan becomes more prominent in our hearts than confidence in Christ, we need to return to the biblical center.
Whenever our conversations about demons outnumber our conversations about discipleship, we should examine our priorities.
Whenever we become more excited about spiritual confrontation than about repentance, love, holiness, and the Gospel, we should ask what is shaping our imagination.
And whenever we make Satan seem like the controlling force in our story, we need to remember the authority of the risen Lord.
Jesus said:
“All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.” — Matthew 28:18, KJV
The Greek text uses πᾶσα ἐξουσία (pasa exousia), meaning “all authority.”
That is the authority from which the Great Commission flows.
Jesus did not announce His authority so that His followers would spend their lives obsessing over Satan.
He sent them to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching people to obey everything He had commanded.
And He promised to be with them.
That is our mission.
Not endless speculation about darkness.
But faithful witness to the Light.
Not making the devil famous.
But proclaiming Jesus Christ.
Not denying the battle.
But remembering who holds ultimate authority.
One day, the final defeat of Satan and evil will be fully manifested, as Revelation 20:10 declares.
Until then, believers remain called to vigilance, endurance, faith, and obedience.
We do not pretend the battle has disappeared.
We simply refuse to make the enemy the object of our devotion.
Because the cross is not a footnote in Satan's story.
Satan is a defeated enemy in the larger story of God's redeeming purpose through Jesus Christ.
And if you have spent years looking over your shoulder in fear, perhaps today is the day to look again toward your Savior.
Open the Scriptures.
Return to prayer.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is required.
Stand firm in the faith.
Love your neighbor.
Serve your church.
Tell someone what Jesus has done for you.
And when the enemy comes to mind, do not allow fear to become the center of your worship.
Remember the One who died.
Remember the One who rose.
Remember the One who reigns.
Remember the One who is coming again.
And let your life become a testimony not to the greatness of the darkness you once feared, but to the greater glory of the Savior who called you into His light.
Because the most tragic thing would not be that you spent your life knowing the enemy was real, but that you became so consumed with the enemy that you neglected to know your Savior more deeply.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THOMAS REFUSED TO BELIEVE WITHOUT EVIDENCE—BUT WHAT JESUS DID NEXT SHOULD SHAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO HAS EVER DOUBTED
paragraphs: THOMAS REFUSED TO BELIEVE WITHOUT EVIDENCE—BUT WHAT JESUS DID NEXT SHOULD SHAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO HAS EVER DOUBTED

He missed the moment everyone else witnessed. He questioned the testimony everyone else believed. And when the risen Jesus finally stood before him, Thomas discovered something far greater than the evidence he demanded: the Savior he struggled to believe in had not abandoned him.
There is a kind of pain that makes you question everything you once believed about God.
Not because you hate Him.
Not because you have decided to walk away.
But because you prayed until your voice trembled, waited until your strength disappeared, and watched something happen that you never imagined a loving God would allow.
You believed He could heal.
But someone you loved still died.
You believed He could restore your marriage.
But the papers were signed anyway.
You believed He would open a door.
But another rejection arrived.
And somewhere between the prayers that seemed unanswered and the nights nobody knew you were crying, a question began forming inside your heart.
Lord, are You really there?
Perhaps you have never spoken those words aloud.
Perhaps you are afraid to.
Because somewhere along the way, you were taught that strong Christians never question, faithful believers never struggle, and genuine disciples never wrestle with uncertainty.
But there is a man in Scripture whose story challenges that assumption.
His name was Thomas.
And before you dismiss him as the disciple who doubted, you need to understand something.
Thomas was not an outsider mocking Christianity.
He was one of the Twelve.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had listened to His teaching.
He had witnessed His ministry.
And yet, when the most extraordinary news in human history reached him, Thomas could not bring himself to believe it.
Jesus was alive.
The tomb was empty.
Death had been defeated.
But Thomas wanted evidence.
And what happened next reveals something extraordinary about the patience of Christ, the nature of genuine faith, and the mercy of a Savior who knows exactly how fragile the human heart can become.
Because the story of Thomas is not merely about a man who doubted.
It is about a risen King who confronted his unbelief and called him into worship.
And somewhere in this encounter, you may recognize your own heart.
The Gospel of John introduces Thomas with a detail many readers overlook.
Before Thomas ever demanded evidence of the resurrection, he had already demonstrated remarkable courage.
In John 11, Jesus announced His intention to return to Judea after receiving news concerning Lazarus.
The disciples understood the danger.
Religious leaders had recently attempted to stone Jesus there.
Returning could mean death.
Yet Thomas spoke words that hardly sound like those of a coward.
“Let us also go, that we may die with him.” — John 11:16, KJV
Read that again.
The disciple remembered primarily for doubting once declared his willingness to die alongside Jesus.
Thomas was not necessarily a man without courage.
He was a man whose courage did not make him immune to confusion, grief, or unbelief.
And that distinction matters.
Because you can sincerely love Jesus and still struggle to understand what He is doing.
You can possess genuine courage and still experience fear.
You can have a history of obedience and still face a moment when your expectations collapse.
Thomas had been willing to follow Jesus toward danger.
But then came the crucifixion.
The One he had followed was arrested.
The One he had trusted was condemned.
The One he had called Master was nailed to a Roman cross.
Imagine what that did to the disciples.
The sound of accusations.
The brutality of the execution.
The public humiliation.
The horrifying finality of death.
Their Teacher was gone.
Their hopes appeared shattered.
And although Jesus had foretold His death and resurrection, the disciples had not yet grasped the full meaning of His words.
Thomas had not simply lost a religious teacher.
He had witnessed the apparent destruction of the future he thought he understood.
Have you ever experienced something like that?
Not necessarily a crucifixion, but the death of an expectation.
A future you thought God had promised.
A relationship you believed would survive.
A prayer you were certain would be answered differently.
Sometimes the most painful spiritual struggles begin when God does not act according to the story we had already written for Him.
And that is where Thomas's story becomes painfully familiar.
On the evening of the first day of the week, the risen Jesus appeared to His disciples.
John 20:19 tells us that the doors were shut where they had gathered because they feared the Jewish authorities.
They were frightened.
They were uncertain.
And suddenly Jesus stood among them.
“Peace be unto you.”
He showed them His hands and His side.
And the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
But one disciple was absent.
Thomas.
John 20:24 states plainly that Thomas, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.
Scripture does not tell us why.
Perhaps he was grieving alone.
Perhaps he was elsewhere for an ordinary reason.
Perhaps he was struggling with emotions we can only imagine.
We must not invent a motive the Bible does not provide.
But we do know the consequence.
Thomas missed that appearance of the risen Christ.
And when the others told him what they had seen, he refused to accept their testimony.
“We have seen the Lord.”
Imagine hearing those words from people you knew.
People who had walked beside you.
People who had experienced the same terrible loss.
They were telling Thomas that the crucified Jesus was alive.
But Thomas responded with a demand that has echoed through centuries.
“Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.” — John 20:25, KJV
There it is.
The statement that earned him the enduring nickname Doubting Thomas.
But notice something important.
Thomas was not asking whether an ordinary event had happened.
He was being told that a man who had been publicly executed had risen bodily from the dead.
That is an extraordinary claim.
And Thomas wanted personal verification.
His mistake was not that he understood resurrection to be extraordinary.
His mistake was making his own direct physical examination the condition for accepting the testimony of those who had seen Jesus.
There is a difference between asking sincere questions and declaring that no testimony will be enough unless God meets our personal demands.
And that distinction should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we do something similar.
Lord, I will trust You when You fix this.
I will believe You are good when You explain why this happened.
I will surrender when You show me exactly where this road leads.
We may not demand to touch the wounds in His hands.
But we sometimes demand that God submit His wisdom to our expectations before we will obey Him.
And yet the Christian faith does not ask us to pretend that evidence is irrelevant.
John's Gospel itself was written to bear witness to Jesus through His words, works, death, and resurrection.
The issue is not whether faith has a foundation.
The issue is whether we will receive the trustworthy witness God has given.
Then comes one of the most moving details in the entire account.
Eight days later, the disciples were gathered again.
And this time, Thomas was with them.
Eight days.
Scripture does not describe everything Thomas thought or felt during that interval.
We do not know how many conversations took place.
We do not know whether he wrestled privately with hope or stubbornly defended his refusal.
But we know this.
The other disciples had testified that Jesus was alive.
Thomas had not believed them.
And eight days later, Jesus came.
The doors were shut.
The disciples were inside.
And the risen Christ stood among them.
Again, His greeting was peace.
Then Jesus turned directly to Thomas.
“Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.” — John 20:27, KJV
Stop there.
Do not rush past this moment.
Thomas had spoken his demands to the other disciples.
Now Jesus addressed those very demands.
The Lord knew.
He knew what Thomas had said.
He knew the condition Thomas had placed upon belief.
And instead of pretending the problem did not exist, Jesus confronted it directly.
But notice how He did it.
He did not deny the reality of His wounds.
He did not offer a vague spiritual message detached from what had happened at Calvary.
He invited Thomas to examine the marks of His crucifixion.
The wounds were not evidence that Jesus had failed.
They belonged to the victorious Savior who had truly died and truly risen.
The scars of the cross were now inseparable from the triumph of the resurrection.
And the same Jesus who had been crucified stood alive before Thomas.
This is where the original Greek helps us hear the force of Christ's words.
John 20:27 includes the command:
μὴ γίνου ἄπιστος ἀλλὰ πιστός
Transliterated: mē ginou apistos alla pistos.
A close translation is:
“Do not become unbelieving, but believing.”
The Greek word apistos can mean unbelieving or lacking faith, while pistos describes one who believes or is faithful.
Jesus was not merely offering Thomas a comforting emotional experience.
He was calling him away from unbelief and toward faith.
There was tenderness in the encounter, but there was also a command.
Christ did not celebrate Thomas's refusal to believe.
He challenged it.
And that is something our generation desperately needs to recover.
Jesus is patient with struggling people.
But His patience is not permission to remain in unbelief forever.
His mercy invites us to come closer to the truth, not to make peace with whatever keeps us from trusting Him.
Sometimes the most loving thing Christ does is confront the very condition we have placed upon our obedience.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
You have been waiting for every question to disappear before surrendering your life to Jesus.
You have been waiting for the pain to make sense.
Waiting for the perfect sign.
Waiting for the certainty that nothing difficult will ever happen again.
But the risen Christ does not promise a life without unanswered questions.
He calls us to trust the One who has conquered death.
And then Thomas speaks.
Not a long explanation.
Not a defense of his earlier position.
Not a carefully worded theological essay.
Just five English words that contain one of the most extraordinary confessions in the New Testament.
“My Lord and my God.” — John 20:28, KJV
In Greek:
Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου
Transliterated: Ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou.
Literally:
“The Lord of me and the God of me.”
In natural English:
“My Lord and my God.”
Notice what Thomas did not say.
He did not merely say, “Now I believe something supernatural happened.”
He did not say, “You must be a remarkable prophet.”
He did not simply acknowledge that Jesus was alive.
He addressed the risen Jesus as his Lord and his God.
And John records no correction from Jesus.
Instead, Jesus responded by speaking about belief and the blessing of those who would believe without having seen Him.
Thomas's confession is therefore not a minor emotional outburst.
It is one of the clearest declarations of Jesus' divine identity in John's Gospel.
The Gospel that begins by declaring, “the Word was God” in John 1:1 brings us to a disciple standing before the risen Christ and confessing, “My Lord and my God.”
The movement is breathtaking.
The man who demanded to see the wounds now recognizes the Lord who bears them.
And there is another detail we must not overlook.
John never explicitly says Thomas actually touched Jesus.
Jesus invited him to do so.
But the recorded response is Thomas's confession.
We should not claim as a biblical fact that Thomas placed his fingers into the wounds.
The text does not say that he did.
What it does show is that the encounter with the risen Jesus brought Thomas from his stated refusal to a profound confession of faith.
And perhaps that is the deepest turning point in the story.
Thomas had demanded evidence.
But the climax was not an examination of wounds.
It was worship.
Because the ultimate purpose of encountering the truth about Jesus is not simply to win an argument.
It is to recognize who He is.
And once you truly recognize Him, the question changes.
It is no longer merely, Can I prove that Jesus is real?
It becomes, If Jesus is truly my Lord and my God, what part of my life am I still refusing to surrender?
That question reaches far beyond Thomas.
It reaches into our private habits.
Our hidden compromises.
Our bitterness.
Our pride.
Our relationships.
Our secret sins.
Our desire to follow Jesus only when following Him does not cost us anything.
It is possible to defend Christian doctrine publicly while resisting Christ's authority privately.
It is possible to argue about the resurrection while living as though Jesus never rose.
And it is possible to know the correct words about Jesus without honestly calling Him my Lord.
Thomas's confession was personal.
My Lord.
My God.
Not merely the God of his family.
Not merely the Lord his fellow disciples believed in.
His own Lord.
His own God.
And this is where the story stops being about a man from the first century and starts confronting the person holding this article.
Who is Jesus to you?
A comforting religious figure?
A name you mention when life becomes frightening?
Someone whose teachings you admire but whose authority you resist?
Or the crucified and risen Son of God, worthy of your trust, repentance, worship, and obedience?
Because Thomas's story does not end with the importance of asking questions.
It ends with the necessity of answering the greatest question of all.
Who is Jesus Christ?
Then Jesus speaks words that reach beyond that locked room, beyond the first disciples, beyond the centuries, and directly into our lives.
“Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.” — John 20:29, KJV
In Greek, the central blessing reads:
μακάριοι οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες καὶ πιστεύσαντες
Transliterated: makarioi hoi mē idontes kai pisteusantes.
Meaning:
“Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”
The word makarioi means blessed or fortunate in the sense of enjoying God's favor.
Jesus was not declaring that ignorance is holy.
He was not telling future generations to believe whatever anyone says without discernment.
And He was not dismissing the importance of evidence.
In fact, immediately after this account, John explains why he recorded the signs of Jesus.
“But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.” — John 20:31, KJV
Think about that.
Jesus blesses those who believe without personally seeing His risen body.
And John explains that his written testimony exists so that readers may believe.
Christian faith is not founded on the idea that evidence does not matter.
It is grounded in the testimony concerning what God has done in Jesus Christ.
The apostles proclaimed that Jesus had been crucified and raised.
Paul likewise appealed to resurrection witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8.
The New Testament presents the resurrection as an event in history, not merely a symbol of hope.
And it calls us to respond to that testimony with faith.
This does not mean every historical or philosophical question is simple.
It does not mean every person who investigates Christianity will immediately become convinced.
But it does mean biblical faith is not the same thing as pretending to know something without any reason to believe it.
The disciples were not merely proclaiming that Jesus lived on in their memories.
They proclaimed that God had raised Him from the dead.
And Thomas's encounter became part of that testimony.
Here is what makes the words of Jesus so astonishing.
Thomas saw.
But generations of believers would not have that same experience.
They would hear the Gospel.
They would encounter the apostolic witness preserved in Scripture.
They would be called to trust the risen Christ without placing their hands into His wounds.
And Jesus called such believers blessed.
That includes ordinary Christians who wake up exhausted and still pray.
Believers who face persecution and refuse to deny Him.
People who repent after falling into sin.
Mothers and fathers teaching their children about a Savior they have never physically seen.
Men and women who open their Bibles with trembling hands because life has become unbearably heavy.
It includes the person reading this who has been struggling to believe that Christ is still worthy of trust.
But we must be careful not to turn this passage into a promise Jesus never made.
Being blessed does not mean every prayer will be answered according to our wishes.
It does not mean we will escape grief, illness, poverty, rejection, or suffering.
The cross itself destroys the idea that God's favor always looks like worldly comfort.
Jesus was perfectly loved by the Father, yet He suffered.
The apostles faithfully proclaimed Christ, yet many endured persecution.
Faith is not a guarantee that life will become painless.
Faith rests in the Savior who has overcome sin and death.
And that changes how we understand our own unanswered questions.
Some of us have spent years asking why God allowed something terrible to happen.
We want an explanation.
We want the missing pieces.
We want the story to finally make sense.
And sometimes, even after years of prayer, the answers remain incomplete.
But the resurrection tells us something greater than the promise of immediate explanations.
It tells us that death did not have the final word over Jesus.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have a living hope.
Not a hope built on wishful thinking.
Not a hope dependent on our circumstances.
But a hope rooted in the death and resurrection of Christ.
That is why the wounds matter so much.
The risen Jesus did not appear as someone who had never suffered.
He appeared as the One who had suffered and conquered.
He was not untouched by human cruelty.
He had endured it.
He was not unfamiliar with betrayal.
He had experienced it.
He was not ignorant of death.
He had entered it.
And He had risen victorious.
So when you bring your grief to Jesus, you are not approaching a Savior who has never encountered suffering.
You are approaching the crucified and risen Lord.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One who was raised for our justification, as Romans 4:25 declares.
And here is the scandal at the center of the Gospel.
The holy Son of God was rejected by the world He came to save.
He was mocked.
Condemned.
Crucified.
Yet through His sacrificial death and resurrection, God accomplished the salvation of sinners who could never rescue themselves.
The cross looked like defeat.
But it became the place where God's justice, mercy, and redeeming love were revealed with astonishing clarity.
And the resurrection publicly vindicated the crucified Christ.
This is why our message is not simply that broken people can become stronger.
It is that guilty sinners can be forgiven.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The rebellious can be reconciled to God.
The ashamed can find mercy.
And the person whose past seems impossible to redeem can be transformed through Jesus Christ.
Not because our sins were insignificant.
Not because God simply overlooked evil.
But because Jesus bore the judgment sinners deserved, and salvation is received by grace through faith in Him.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is God's gift, not something we purchase or earn through our works.
And Romans 5:8 declares that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is grace.
Undeserved.
Unpurchased.
Unimaginably costly to the Savior who gave Himself for us.
And available to all who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Perhaps the most dangerous misunderstanding of Thomas's story is the idea that Jesus simply wants us to feel comfortable with doubt.
He does not.
He wants us to come to the truth.
He wants us to believe.
He wants us to recognize Him as Lord.
He wants us to have life in His name.
Doubt may be a struggle we experience, but it is not meant to become the throne from which we judge every command of Christ.
Questions should lead us to seek the truth, not become an excuse to avoid it.
And if you are struggling today, that does not mean you must pretend your questions are gone.
