That is why our message remains:
Not because Jesus changes the facts of what happened.
Not because repentance removes every earthly consequence.
Not because believers never suffer again.
But because the crucified and risen Christ can redeem people whose histories seem beyond repair.
And if this story has uncovered something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe there is a conversation you need to have.
A wrong you need to confess.
A person you need to stop controlling.
A wound for which you need wise, trustworthy help.
A child you need to listen to.
A truth you need to stop hiding.
Or a Savior you have been keeping at a distance.
Do not mistake religious activity for surrender.
Do not mistake a respected reputation for a transformed heart.
David had a crown, a palace, military victories, and a place in Israel’s history.
But none of those things exempted him from the need for repentance.
And neither does our church attendance, our Bible knowledge, our ministry involvement, or the Christian image we present online.
The question is not whether people think we belong to God.
The question is whether we are actually surrendering our lives to Jesus Christ.
If you have never trusted Him, you can turn to Him today.
Confess your sin.
Believe that Jesus died for sinners and rose again.
Call upon Him for mercy.
And if you have followed Him for years but know you have been hiding something, bring it into His light.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive our sins and cleanse us from unrighteousness when we confess them.
You do not have to pretend before the One who already knows the truth.
And you do not have to earn His forgiveness through a public performance.
Come to Christ sincerely.
Come in repentance.
Come in faith.
Come because He is worthy of your trust.
And if you are carrying the consequences of someone else’s wrongdoing, remember that your healing is not measured by how quickly you can make the pain disappear.
Seek the Lord.
Seek safety where needed.
Seek wise counsel and trustworthy support.
Your suffering deserves to be taken seriously.
There may be someone reading this right now who has never told another person how deeply their family history has wounded them.
Someone who has spent years trying to be strong.
Someone who has been smiling in church while silently grieving at home.
Someone who is afraid that the brokenness they inherited will become the brokenness they pass on.
If that is you, there is room for your honesty here.
And if you have witnessed God’s grace changing your family, your testimony may encourage someone who has almost stopped hoping.
Tell us what the Lord has taught you.
Not to impress anyone.
But to remind another weary soul that God is still at work.
Because spiritual growth should not end when we finish reading an article.
It should continue when we open our Bibles.
When we pray.
When we repent.
When we obey.
When we learn to love others in truth.
And when we begin helping other people discover the hope we have found in Jesus.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning, encouragement, and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
But we want to be biblically clear about something important.
Your salvation cannot be bought.
Your spiritual worth is not measured by a monthly payment.
And no one should ever feel that giving money to this ministry is a condition for receiving God’s favor.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful—not reluctant or compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary support can certainly be an expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel work.
If you are not able to give financially, you are still welcome here. Your prayers, encouragement, and thoughtful sharing can also make a meaningful difference.
These items are not what makes this ministry valuable.
Jesus Christ is the center.
The products are simply another way to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and support the continuing work.
It will be the lives directed toward Jesus Christ, the truth of Scripture, genuine repentance, enduring faith, and love for God and neighbor.
And now, before you leave, remember the father we met at the beginning of this story.
David.
The shepherd who became a king.
The giant-slayer who could not keep his own household from becoming a battlefield.
The father who wept over a son he could not save.
The man who experienced the bitter consequences of his own sin.
Yet God’s promise did not end in David’s grave.
Generations later, another Son of David entered Jerusalem.
Not to steal hearts through deception.
Not to seize a throne through rebellion.
Not to exploit the weak.
But to lay down His life for sinners.
And when He rose from the dead, He revealed the victory no earthly dynasty could ever achieve.
A kingdom that death itself could not overthrow.
So when you read about David’s broken family, do not stop at the brokenness.
Look beyond the palace.
Beyond the conspiracies.
Beyond the graves of fallen princes.
Look toward Calvary.
Look toward the empty tomb.
Look toward the King who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His finished work.
Because the most important question in this story is no longer which of David’s sons deserved the throne.
It is whether you have surrendered to the Son of David who reigns forever.
David’s sons fought to inherit a crown. Jesus wore a crown of thorns so that broken sinners could inherit grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE GOSPEL THAT PROMISES YOU EVERYTHING—EXCEPT THE CROSS
paragraphs: THE GOSPEL THAT PROMISES YOU EVERYTHING—EXCEPT THE CROSS
Is the Prosperity Gospel Simply Misunderstood Scripture, or Has It Become the Very Different Gospel the Apostle Paul Warned Us About?
There is a kind of preaching that can make a struggling person feel like heaven is finally about to open.
The mother who has been praying over unpaid bills hears that her financial breakthrough is coming.
The father who has been unemployed for months is told that his season of supernatural abundance is just around the corner.
The woman fighting cancer hears that if she believes strongly enough, healing is guaranteed.
The young believer who has given everything he can afford is promised that God will multiply his offering a hundredfold.
And for one beautiful moment, everyone feels hopeful.
Then the bills remain unpaid.
The cancer progresses.
The job never comes.
The promised breakthrough doesn't arrive.
And the same person who was told that faith would change everything begins wondering whether the problem is not the preacher, not the promise, not the interpretation of Scripture...
But himself.
Maybe I didn't believe enough.
Maybe I didn't give enough.
Maybe God is disappointed in me.
And somewhere in that terrible silence, a wounded Christian begins confusing unanswered expectations with the absence of God's love.
That is where this conversation becomes more than a theological disagreement.
Because when someone changes what God has promised, people can end up blaming themselves for promises God never made.
And the question we must face is not whether God can bless His children financially.
Of course He can.
The question is far more serious.

When wealth becomes evidence of God's favor, poverty becomes evidence of spiritual failure, and giving becomes a transaction to secure divine rewards, are we still preaching the Gospel Jesus Christ gave His Church?
Or have we placed the name of Jesus over a message that He never taught?
Stay with me, because the answer is not as simple as condemning every wealthy Christian or criticizing every church that speaks about blessings.
Scripture is more beautiful, more demanding, and far more liberating than either extreme.
And there is something about the cross that exposes the entire issue.
Something we cannot afford to miss.
The apostle Paul once wrote words so severe that they should make every preacher, ministry leader, and Christian content creator examine the message they proclaim.

In Galatians 1:6–9, Paul expressed astonishment that believers were turning toward a different gospel. He warned that even if an angel from heaven proclaimed a gospel contrary to the one the apostles had preached, that message was to be rejected.
The Greek wording matters.
Paul used the expression ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον (heteron euangelion), meaning "a different gospel."
He immediately clarified that it was not truly another gospel at all.
His concern was not that Christians disagreed about secondary matters.
His concern was that people were distorting the message of Christ.

In its original context, Galatians confronted teachers who were making observance of the Mosaic Law, particularly circumcision, necessary for full inclusion among God's covenant people. Paul defended justification through faith in Jesus Christ rather than through works of the Law.
That historical context must not be erased.
Paul was not specifically writing about modern prosperity preaching.
But his warning establishes a principle that reaches far beyond first-century Galatia.
When something other than the saving work of Jesus Christ becomes essential to the message of salvation, the Gospel itself is being altered.
And when the Gospel is altered, the consequences are eternal.
So what exactly is the prosperity gospel?
We need to be careful here, because not every sermon about God's provision is prosperity theology.
Not every Christian who becomes financially successful has compromised the faith.
Not every prayer for healing is an expression of unbelief or greed.
And not every preacher who encourages generosity is exploiting people.
The Bible openly acknowledges that material blessings can come from God.

Abraham possessed great wealth. Job experienced prosperity before his suffering and restoration afterward. Lydia was a merchant who opened her home to believers. Joseph of Arimathea was wealthy and honored Jesus in His burial.
The problem is not possessing resources.

The problem begins when resources become the measure of righteousness, when material success is presented as the normal and guaranteed outcome of sufficient faith, and when giving money is portrayed as a reliable spiritual mechanism for obtaining wealth, healing, or personal success.
That is the crucial distinction.
Biblical Christianity teaches that God is a generous Father who provides for His people according to His wisdom.

Prosperity theology, in its more extreme forms, teaches that believers can expect or claim material abundance and physical health as guaranteed benefits of faith, sometimes activated through positive declarations or financial giving.
Those are not identical messages.
One trusts God's character.
The other risks treating God's promises as a system that produces predictable material results.
And there is a devastating difference between trusting God for provision and demanding that God provide according to our expectations.
Consider one of the most frequently quoted passages in discussions about prosperity.
Third John, verse 2.
In the King James Version, the apostle writes:
At first glance, it sounds like a sweeping divine promise of wealth and health.
But look closer.
The Greek begins:
Ἀγαπητέ, περὶ πάντων εὔχομαί σε εὐοδοῦσθαι καὶ ὑγιαίνειν
Agapēte, peri pantōn euchomai se euodousthai kai hygiainein.
A careful translation is:
"Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health."
The verb εὔχομαι (euchomai) expresses a wish or prayer.
And εὐοδοῦσθαι (euodousthai) conveys the idea of things going well or succeeding.
This is a personal greeting from John to Gaius, a beloved Christian whose faithfulness and hospitality are commended in the letter.
It is not a universal guarantee that every Christian who possesses enough faith will become wealthy.
It is a prayer.
A beautiful prayer.
But a prayer is not automatically an unconditional promise.
And when we turn a personal apostolic greeting into a guaranteed financial formula, we have moved beyond what the text actually says.
Now consider another passage.
Jeremiah 29:11.
The verse has comforted countless believers, and rightly so when understood within its biblical setting.
God speaks of His plans for the welfare and future of His people.
The Hebrew includes the words:
מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה
Machshevot shalom velo lera'ah.
Meaning:
"Plans for peace/well-being and not for harm."
The word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) carries the rich sense of peace, wholeness, and well-being.
But who originally received this promise?
Jewish exiles living in Babylon.
And what did God tell them immediately before this?
That their exile would last seventy years.
Seventy years.
Imagine hearing that God's good plan included decades of waiting in a foreign land.
Imagine realizing that some who first heard the promise might never personally witness the full restoration of their nation.
Yet God remained faithful.
His promise was not false because the fulfillment did not arrive immediately.
His goodness was not absent because His people were experiencing hardship.

Jeremiah 29:11 reveals God's faithfulness to His covenant purposes in a specific historical situation. Christians may draw comfort from God's character and His ultimate redemptive purposes, but the verse does not promise every individual immediate prosperity, a successful business, or freedom from suffering.
Sometimes the most dangerous misuse of Scripture is not an outright denial of God's Word.
It is taking something God truly said and making it mean something He never intended.
And nowhere is that more apparent than in the way some people handle the words of Jesus about giving.
Luke 6:38 is often quoted:
"Give, and it shall be given unto you."
The verse continues with the picture of a generous measure being poured into one's lap.
But read the surrounding verses.
Jesus is teaching about mercy, forgiveness, generosity, and the way His disciples treat others.
He commands His followers to love their enemies, refuse vindictiveness, forgive, and give generously.
The passage is not a fundraising formula promising that a financial donation will generate a predetermined monetary return.
Jesus is forming a people who reflect the generosity of their heavenly Father.
The difference matters.
One message says, "Give because God has been generous to you."
The distorted version says, "Give because this is how you make God enrich you."
One produces worship.
The other can produce spiritualized greed.
And greed does not become holy simply because someone places a Bible verse beside it.
Now someone may ask, "But doesn't the Bible teach sowing and reaping?"
Absolutely.
Second Corinthians 9:6 teaches that whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, while whoever sows generously will also reap generously.
But Paul continues.
He says each person should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Then Paul explains that God's provision enables believers to abound in good works, increases the harvest of righteousness, and produces thanksgiving to God.
The entire discussion concerns generosity, God's sufficiency, and the needs of His people.
It is not a guarantee that every monetary gift will return as a larger cash payment.
In fact, Paul's emphasis is profoundly different.
God enriches His people in ways that equip them for generosity.
He does not instruct them to use generosity as a technique for enriching themselves.
And here is a question worth asking.
If someone gives only because they have been promised more money in return, is that truly the selfless generosity Jesus taught?
Or has giving quietly become an investment strategy dressed in religious language?
This is why motive matters.
This is why context matters.
And this is why those who teach Scripture carry such serious responsibility.
But perhaps the most revealing passage of all comes from the apostle Paul himself.
In Philippians 4:12–13, Paul explains that he knows what it means to have little and what it means to have plenty.
He has learned the secret of facing hunger and abundance, need and provision.
Then he declares:
"I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me."
How often have we heard that verse used as a promise that Christians can achieve any ambition?
A bigger house.
A successful business.
A dream career.
Financial independence.
Yet Paul was not writing from a luxury residence while celebrating his latest breakthrough.
He was writing as a man acquainted with imprisonment, hardship, and dependence upon Christ.
The Greek expression in Philippians 4:13 is:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με
Panta ischyō en tō endynamounti me.
A faithful rendering is:
"I have strength for all things through the one who strengthens me."
In context, those "all things" refer to the circumstances Paul has just described, including both plenty and hunger.
Paul was not claiming that Christ guaranteed him unlimited achievement.
He was declaring that Christ strengthened him to remain faithful regardless of his circumstances.
Read that again.
The promise was not that Paul would never experience lack. The promise was that Christ would sustain him even when he did.
That is not a smaller Gospel.
That is a deeper one.
Because a faith that survives only when the bank account is full has not yet learned the secret Paul was describing.
A faith that worships only when the diagnosis is favorable is vulnerable to collapse when suffering arrives.
But a faith anchored in the crucified and risen Christ can say through tears, "Lord, I do not understand what is happening, but I still belong to You."
And this brings us to a man whose life should make every prosperity preacher reconsider any promise of guaranteed comfort.
Jesus Christ Himself.
The Son of God entered the world in humility.
He lived without the kind of earthly security that many people today associate with divine favor.
In Luke 9:58, Jesus said that foxes have holes and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.
He was rejected.
Misunderstood.
Betrayed.
Falsely accused.
Beaten.
And crucified.
Now ask yourself something.
If material prosperity is the necessary evidence of God's approval, what do we do with the earthly life of Jesus?
If suffering always proves a lack of faith, what do we do with Gethsemane?
If opposition means someone has failed to activate divine favor, what do we do with Calvary?
And if God's greatest blessing must look like visible success, how do we explain the cross?
The cross looked like defeat.
The crowd mocked.
The disciples scattered.
The religious leaders believed they had won.
But what looked like humiliation became the place where God's redemptive purpose was accomplished.
Jesus bore our sins.
He suffered in our place.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, sinners are offered forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
The center of Christianity is not a promise that believers will never experience suffering.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death, and that everyone who turns to Him in faith receives a treasure this world cannot manufacture or destroy.
That is the Gospel.
And no earthly prosperity can compare with it.
The apostle Paul understood this.
In Second Corinthians 12, he describes a painful affliction he calls a thorn in the flesh.
Three times he pleaded with the Lord to remove it.
Three times.
This was not a spiritually immature believer who had forgotten how to pray.
This was an apostle of Jesus Christ.
A man who had seen extraordinary revelations.
A man through whom God had performed remarkable works.
Yet the affliction remained.
And God's answer was not, "Paul, your faith is too weak."
It was:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
Second Corinthians 12:9.
Those words should change how we speak to suffering Christians.
Because sometimes God delivers His people from suffering.
And sometimes He sustains them through it.
Both can display His faithfulness.
Neither gives us permission to condemn a suffering believer as spiritually defective.
Think of the Christian mother who prays for healing but still has to attend chemotherapy.
Think of the father who faithfully gives to his church yet struggles to buy groceries.
Think of the elderly widow who loves Jesus deeply but lives on a small pension.
Think of believers in places where following Christ may cost them employment, freedom, or even their lives.
Are we prepared to tell them that their hardships prove they have not believed enough?
Are we prepared to say that persecuted Christians are missing the blessings of God because they have not discovered the right financial principles?
Or might it be that the Church has sometimes confused the comforts of a prosperous society with the promises of the eternal Kingdom?
Hebrews 11 gives us a startling answer.
The chapter celebrates people who conquered kingdoms, escaped danger, and witnessed extraordinary deliverance through faith.
But then the narrative changes.
Others were tortured.
Some suffered mockery, imprisonment, and violence.
Others wandered in poverty and affliction.
And Scripture says that the world was not worthy of them.
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not divide the faithful into those who believed enough to become prosperous and those who failed.
It presents both deliverance and suffering within the testimony of faith.
Some believers escaped the sword.
Others died by it.
And both could belong to God.
That truth is not comfortable.
But it is liberating.
Because it means your circumstances do not have the final authority to define your relationship with Jesus.
Your financial situation is not your spiritual identity.
Your medical condition is not a verdict on your worth before God.
Your unanswered prayer is not proof that Christ has abandoned you.
And your suffering does not cancel the promises of the resurrection.
Now, does that mean Christians should never pray for prosperity, provision, or healing?
No.
Jesus taught His disciples to ask the Father for daily bread.
James instructed the sick to seek prayer.
Paul encouraged believers to work, share, and care for those in need.
Scripture celebrates honest labor, wise stewardship, generosity, and gratitude for God's gifts.
There is nothing inherently unspiritual about asking God to provide a job, restore health, rescue a family from debt, or bless a business.
The difference lies in whether we approach God as our Father or attempt to control Him through a formula.
A child can ask a loving father for help without believing that the father is obligated to grant every request exactly as desired.
Prayer is an expression of dependence.
It is not a contract that places God under our command.
And genuine faith does not mean believing that we can dictate the outcome.
It means trusting the Lord whose wisdom exceeds our own.
But now we must confront something even more uncomfortable.
Because the danger of prosperity theology does not end with misunderstood Bible verses.
Sometimes it becomes a system of spiritual pressure.
A struggling believer hears that a special offering will unlock a miracle.
A desperate parent is encouraged to give beyond their means to demonstrate faith.
A person awaiting medical results is told that a financial seed will release supernatural healing.
And when the promised result fails to arrive, the explanation shifts.
Perhaps the person doubted.
Perhaps they spoke negatively.
Perhaps they failed to give enough.
The burden returns to the wounded believer.
That is not how shepherds are called to care for Christ's flock.
First Peter 5:2–3 instructs elders to shepherd God's people willingly and not for shameful gain or through domineering leadership.
And First Timothy 6 speaks with extraordinary clarity.
Paul warns about people who imagine that godliness is a means of financial gain.
Then he writes:
First Timothy 6:6.
The Greek phrase is:
ἔστιν δὲ πορισμὸς μέγας ἡ εὐσέβεια μετὰ αὐταρκείας
Estin de porismos megas hē eusebeia meta autarkeias.
Meaning:
"Godliness with contentment is great gain."
The word αὐτάρκεια (autarkeia) refers to contentment or sufficiency.
And the irony is powerful.
Paul uses the language of gain to redefine what true gain looks like.
Not godliness as a tool for accumulating wealth.
Godliness accompanied by contentment.
He continues by warning that those who desire to be rich can fall into temptation and destructive desires.
He does not say money itself is the root of every evil.
He warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.
That distinction matters.
Wealth is not automatically wicked.
Poverty is not automatically holy.
But the craving for wealth can become an idol, and religious language does not make that craving harmless.
In Matthew 6:24, Jesus declared that no one can serve two masters.
He specifically named God and mammon, a term referring to wealth or riches.
He did not merely warn that money might become distracting.
He described a conflict of allegiance.
And perhaps that is where this discussion becomes painfully personal.
Because it is easy to criticize a preacher who promises luxury cars and enormous houses.
It is harder to recognize the same desire in our own hearts.
Have we ever treated prayer as a way of getting what we want rather than drawing near to God?
Have we ever measured God's love by whether life was going well?
Have we ever felt more grateful for the blessing than for the One who gave it?
Have we ever wanted Jesus to improve our circumstances while resisting His authority over our lives?
The prosperity gospel is not merely a problem somewhere on a television screen.
Its underlying temptation can whisper inside any human heart.
I will follow You, Lord, as long as You make my life work.
I will trust You, as long as You protect everything I love.
I will obey You, as long as obedience brings visible rewards.
And then Jesus speaks words that cut through every condition we try to attach to discipleship.
In Luke 9:23, He says that anyone who would follow Him must deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow Him.
Not take up his guaranteed financial breakthrough.
Not take up his promise of an effortless life.
His cross.
The cross represents surrender.
It represents dying to the illusion that we belong to ourselves.
It represents following Jesus even when obedience is costly.
And that is where the prosperity gospel, when preached as a guarantee of earthly success, collides with the teachings of Christ.
Because Jesus never concealed the cost of following Him.
He told His disciples that they would face trouble.
He warned that the world would hate them.
He called them to seek first God's Kingdom and righteousness.
He taught them to store up treasures in heaven.
And He promised something infinitely greater than uninterrupted earthly comfort.
He promised Himself.
Now we can answer the question we began with.
Is the prosperity gospel simply a misunderstanding of Scripture, or is it a different gospel altogether?
The answer requires both discernment and precision.

Some prosperity-oriented teachings arise from sincere but mistaken interpretations of biblical passages. A believer may genuinely love Jesus while misunderstanding texts about blessing, healing, giving, or provision.
Such errors should be corrected patiently, carefully, and biblically.

But when a message systematically replaces repentance with self-improvement, substitutes guaranteed wealth for the hope of eternal life, treats financial giving as a mechanism for purchasing divine favor, or makes material success the central proof of saving faith, the problem becomes far more serious.
At that point, we are not merely dealing with an overemphasis on blessing.
We are confronting a distortion of the Gospel's center.

And if the message of Christ crucified and risen is displaced by a message that fundamentally makes God the means to our material ambitions, then the warning about a different gospel becomes profoundly relevant.
We should not claim to know every preacher's motives or every listener's spiritual condition.
But we must examine what is actually being taught.
Because sincerity does not make a false promise true.
Popularity does not establish biblical authority.
And a crowded church does not automatically prove that its message faithfully represents Jesus.
The Gospel must be tested by Scripture, not by applause.
And here is the part that may surprise you.
The answer to prosperity theology is not a gospel of misery.
It is not teaching that God enjoys watching His children suffer.
It is not glorifying poverty or telling believers to refuse every earthly blessing.
It is recovering the incomparable riches of Christ.
In Ephesians 1:3, Paul praises God for blessing believers in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
He then speaks of election in Christ, adoption, redemption through His blood, forgiveness of sins, and the riches of divine grace.
These blessings are not imaginary.
They are not consolation prizes for people who failed to become wealthy.
They are the deepest realities of Christian salvation.
A person can own a mansion and still be spiritually lost.
Another can live in a small rented room and possess eternal life in Christ.
A person can have perfect health and remain unreconciled to God.
Another can be physically weak yet belong forever to the risen Savior.
The question is not whether you have enough money to be considered blessed.
The question is whether you have been reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Because if you gain the whole world and lose your soul, you have gained nothing that can save you.
But if you belong to Christ, then even death cannot separate you from His love.
Romans 8:35–39 makes that truth unmistakable.
Tribulation cannot separate us from Christ.
Distress cannot separate us.
Persecution cannot separate us.
Famine cannot separate us.
Nakedness, danger, and the sword cannot separate us.
Notice something extraordinary.
Paul does not say these things will never happen to believers.
He says they cannot separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
That is a promise strong enough to carry a suffering Christian through the darkest night.
And it is a promise no prosperity formula can improve.
Maybe you are reading this while facing financial hardship.
Maybe you once believed that a certain offering would change your circumstances.
Maybe you gave sincerely, prayed desperately, and waited for a miracle that never came.
Maybe someone told you that your suffering was evidence of weak faith.
And perhaps, after enough disappointment, you quietly stopped praying.
Not because you stopped wanting God.
But because you began wondering whether God wanted you.
Hear what Scripture actually teaches.
The Father does not sell His love.
Christ does not auction His mercy.
The Holy Spirit is not a reward purchased by the highest donor.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And God's grace cannot be purchased through an offering.
You do not have to make yourself wealthy enough, successful enough, or impressive enough to come to Jesus.
Come with your sins.
Come with your doubts.
Come with your disappointments.
Come with your repentance.
Come with the truth about who you are.
Jesus did not die to make you a more successful consumer.
He died to redeem sinners and bring them to God.
And the resurrection announces that sin and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is where the story turns.
The scandal of human greed, religious exploitation, misplaced trust, and our desperate attempts to control God meets the astonishing grace of a Savior who gives Himself freely.
And perhaps the greatest miracle you need today is not the sudden arrival of wealth.
Perhaps it is the restoration of your confidence in the Jesus who was always enough, even when life was not.
Not because your needs are insignificant.
They matter deeply.
Not because God is indifferent to your pain.
He invites you to bring your burdens to Him.
But because the greatest gift of the Gospel is not something Christ places in your hands.
It is Christ Himself.
And when you finally see that, something changes.
You can work diligently without worshiping success.
You can enjoy blessings without building your identity upon them.
You can give generously without trying to purchase a miracle.
You can pray boldly while surrendering the outcome to your Father's wisdom.
You can grieve without concluding that God has abandoned you.
And you can rejoice in Christ even when the world gives you little reason to celebrate.
That is not defeat.
That is freedom.
And it is the kind of freedom the Church desperately needs to recover.
There is another responsibility that comes with this truth.
Those of us who teach, write, preach, publish, or share Christian content must be willing to apply these same principles to ourselves.
But it must remain voluntary, transparent, and free from spiritual coercion.
Paul himself thanked the Philippian believers for supporting his ministry, describing their generosity as participation in his work and as an offering pleasing to God (Philippians 4:10–18).
Their giving mattered.
It helped sustain Gospel ministry.
But Paul's confidence was ultimately in Christ, not in the size of their gifts.

If these articles have helped you understand Scripture more faithfully, return to Jesus more deeply, or recognize teachings that once confused you, I invite you to become part of the work that makes this ministry possible.
It can be a voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in ministry, much like the support believers offered to those serving the early Church.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, and the faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
But because Gospel work requires people willing to serve, give, teach, and share.
That benefit is simply our way of saying thank you.
It is not a spiritual reward, and it does not measure anyone's standing before God.
Your worth to Christ has never depended on your financial capacity.
You are welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep growing.
And please keep testing everything, including what we publish, against the Word of God.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that depends unquestioningly on Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people toward Jesus Christ and help them become rooted in Scripture, faithful in discipleship, and discerning in a world filled with competing messages.
And sometimes the simplest way to participate in that mission costs nothing.
Not merely to increase a page's reach, but because someone in your circle may be carrying guilt from a religious promise that never came true.
Someone may have been told that poverty proves God's displeasure.
Someone may be grieving an unanswered prayer.
Someone may have walked away from church because they were promised a version of Christianity that collapsed under the weight of real suffering.
And perhaps a careful, compassionate explanation of Scripture could help that person see Jesus clearly again.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, spiritual seekers, and even those who no longer believe to follow along.
There is room for honest questions here.
There is room for people who have been hurt.
There is room for those who are learning how to distinguish the voice of Christ from the promises people have made in His name.
And I want to ask you something personally.
Not as a test of your spirituality.
Not as a way to measure your faith.
But because your experience may help someone else feel less alone.
Have you ever been made to feel that God was disappointed in you because you were struggling financially, physically, or emotionally?
Or have you ever confused God's blessing with material success, only to discover through hardship that His grace was greater than you understood?
You can simply comment, "Jesus, teach me to treasure You above everything."
Or comment, "Christ is still healing me," if you are recovering from spiritual disappointment.
And if your faith has been exhausted lately, you can comment, "Pray for me."
You do not need to share details you would rather keep private.
But your honest testimony might become the encouragement another person needs.
Because this is not just a debate about theology.
This is about the woman who thinks God rejected her because her prayers for healing were not answered as she expected.
This is about the father who believes he has failed spiritually because he cannot provide everything his children need.
This is about the young believer who gave money he could not afford because someone promised him a miracle.
This is about the person who has quietly wondered whether Christianity itself was false, when what failed was a human promise that Scripture never made.
And this is about the Church remembering the Savior at the center of everything.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for our sins.
Risen from the dead.
Calling sinners to repentance.
Offering forgiveness through grace.
Giving eternal life to those who trust in Him.
The Gospel does not promise that following Jesus will make every chapter of your earthly life comfortable.
It promises that those who belong to Him have a living hope that reaches beyond suffering, beyond poverty, beyond sickness, and even beyond the grave.
And when the final chapter comes, the Christian's greatest joy will not be discovering how much wealth was accumulated on earth.
It will be seeing the Savior whose grace was sufficient all along.
So pray for provision.
Work faithfully.
Give generously.
Receive God's blessings with gratitude.
Seek healing.
Care for the poor.
Support faithful Gospel ministry as you are able.
And never apologize for thanking God when He answers your prayers in wonderful and unexpected ways.
But do not allow anyone to convince you that Jesus is valuable only because of what He can give you.
He is worthy when the harvest is abundant.
He is worthy when the fields are empty.
He is worthy when healing comes.
He is worthy when the struggle continues.
He is worthy when the door opens.
He is worthy when you must wait.
And He is worthy because He is the crucified and risen Lord, not because He has agreed to fulfill every earthly dream.
The prosperity gospel, at its most distorted, asks what you can gain by having Jesus.
The true Gospel announces what God has already given through Jesus—and calls you to surrender your life to Him.
And that changes everything.
You may have lost the prosperity you were promised, but in Jesus Christ you can discover the grace you were never able to buy.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “OBEY YOUR LEADERS AND SUBMIT TO THEM” — BUT WHAT IF YOUR LEADER IS LEADING YOU AWAY FROM CHRIST?
paragraphs: “OBEY YOUR LEADERS AND SUBMIT TO THEM” — BUT WHAT IF YOUR LEADER IS LEADING YOU AWAY FROM CHRIST?

Hebrews 13:17 has been used to silence questions, demand loyalty, and frighten wounded believers into submission. But what did the Holy Spirit actually mean? The answer may confront abusive leadership, challenge rebellious hearts, and set exhausted Christians free to follow Jesus without abandoning His Church.
There is a kind of pain that only happens inside a church.
It is the pain of trusting someone who taught you about Jesus… only to discover that the same person could use the name of Jesus to control you.
It is the confusion of sitting beneath a pulpit, hearing the Word of God preached, while quietly wondering why asking an honest question suddenly makes you rebellious.
It is the fear of being called disobedient when all you wanted was to understand Scripture.

And sometimes, it is the loneliness of realizing that the people who taught you to recognize the voice of the Good Shepherd are now demanding that you stop questioning the voice of the shepherd standing in front of you.
Perhaps you have been there.
Perhaps you were told, “Touch not the Lord's anointed.”
Perhaps someone warned you that questioning your pastor was equivalent to questioning God.
Perhaps you were pressured to give money you could not afford, remain silent about something you knew was wrong, or accept decisions that wounded your conscience.
And when you finally found the courage to speak, someone opened a Bible and read Hebrews 13:17.
“Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account…” (Hebrews 13:17, KJV).
Then came the sentence that broke something inside you.
“God said you must obey.”
But here is the question that deserves an answer from Scripture, not intimidation:
Does God command Christians to obey spiritual leaders even when those leaders are wrong?
And here is an equally important question:
What happens when a Christian uses the failures of church leaders as an excuse to reject every form of spiritual accountability?
Because this passage confronts both dangers.
The leader who wants unquestioned power.
And the believer who refuses godly correction.
One can turn the church into a place of control.
The other can turn Christian freedom into spiritual isolation.
Neither reflects the heart of Jesus Christ.
And if we are going to understand Hebrews 13:17, we must allow Scripture to speak even when its answer challenges the people we admire, the traditions we inherited, and the wounds we carry.
The truth is more beautiful, more demanding, and more liberating than either blind obedience or complete independence.
It begins with a Greek word.
The New Testament was written in Koine Greek, and Hebrews 13:17 opens with a command:
Πείθεσθε τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ὑμῶν καὶ ὑπείκετε.
Peithesthe tois hēgoumenois hymōn kai hypeikete.
The traditional English rendering is:
“Obey your leaders and submit to them.”
But the Greek deserves careful attention.
The word translated “obey” is πείθεσθε (peithesthe), from the verb πείθω (peithō).
This verb can carry meanings connected with persuading, convincing, trusting, and obeying. In this grammatical form and context, it is appropriately translated “obey,” “be persuaded by,” or “heed.”
That does not mean the command is optional.
It does mean we should not automatically imagine the kind of obedience demanded by a dictator who forbids questions.
The verse addresses believers who are expected to respond to legitimate spiritual leadership, receive sound instruction, and cooperate with those entrusted with caring for them.
Then comes the second command.
Ὑπείκετε (hypeikete).
It means to yield, give way, or submit.
The writer is calling Christians to a genuine willingness to cooperate with their spiritual leaders.
Not merely to listen when the sermon feels encouraging.
Not merely to respect leaders when every decision agrees with personal preferences.
Real submission involves humility.
It sometimes requires accepting correction.
It sometimes means setting aside personal pride for the good of the church.
But notice something important.
Neither Greek word makes a human leader infallible.
And neither command erases the authority of Jesus Christ.
The verse continues:
αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἀγρυπνοῦσιν ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν
Autoi gar agrypnousin hyper tōn psychōn hymōn.
“For they keep watch over your souls.”
The word ἀγρυπνοῦσιν (agrypnousin) describes keeping awake, remaining watchful, or maintaining vigilance.
Think about that.
The picture is not of a king sitting comfortably on a throne, demanding that everyone bow.
It is of someone remaining awake because others have been entrusted to their care.
A faithful shepherd notices when a sheep is wandering.
A faithful shepherd warns when danger approaches.
A faithful shepherd does not celebrate having power over vulnerable people.
He understands the weight of being responsible for their spiritual well-being.
And the verse adds something that should make every pastor, elder, ministry leader, and spiritual mentor tremble:
ὡς λόγον ἀποδώσοντες
Hōs logon apodōsontes.
“As those who will give an account.”
An account to whom?
Ultimately, to God.
That changes everything.
Hebrews 13:17 is not simply a command directed toward church members.
It is also a solemn reminder that spiritual leaders are accountable for the way they exercise their responsibilities.
The pastor is not the owner of the sheep.
The elder is not the savior of the congregation.
The ministry leader is not the final authority over another person's conscience.
Jesus Christ is the Chief Shepherd.
And every under-shepherd must answer to Him.
Peter understood this.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, he instructed elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for dishonest gain, and not as those who dominate the people entrusted to them, but as examples.
The Greek expression translated “being lords over” is connected with κατακυριεύω (katakyrieuō), meaning to exercise mastery or dominion over others.
Peter explicitly warns against that kind of leadership.
And he does not stop there.
In 1 Peter 5:4, he points to the appearing of the Chief Shepherd.
The message is unmistakable.
The flock belongs to God.
Leadership is stewardship.
Authority is responsibility.
And spiritual oversight is never permission to dominate the people Jesus purchased with His blood.
Imagine a pastor standing before Christ.
Not standing before a congregation that applauds every sermon.
Not standing before a social media audience impressed by his influence.
Not standing before a ministry board that measures success only by attendance, donations, and buildings.
Standing before Jesus.
The One who sees what happened behind closed doors.
The One who heard the conversations nobody recorded.
The One who knows whether a struggling believer was gently restored or publicly humiliated.
The One who knows whether church money was handled honestly.
The One who knows whether Scripture was taught faithfully or twisted to protect a reputation.
The One who knows whether leadership was exercised through love or fear.
Suddenly, Hebrews 13:17 becomes far more serious than a convenient verse for demanding obedience.
It becomes a warning against the abuse of spiritual trust.
But we must be equally careful not to turn that truth into an excuse for rejecting all authority.
Because the same Bible that condemns domineering leadership commands believers to respect faithful leaders.
Hebrews 13:7 tells Christians to remember those who spoke the Word of God to them, consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
Notice the emphasis.
Their teaching.
Their conduct.
Their faith.
Not merely their title.
Not merely their popularity.
Not merely their ability to speak powerfully.
Their lives must demonstrate the truth they proclaim.
And Hebrews 13:9 warns believers not to be carried away by strange teachings.
These surrounding verses matter.
Hebrews 13:17 was not written as an isolated slogan that leaders could use whenever someone disagreed with them.
It belongs to a chapter concerned with faithful teaching, Christian perseverance, worship, holiness, and the unchanging identity of Jesus Christ.
Just a few verses earlier, Hebrews 13:8 declares:
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.”
That is the center.
Not the personality of a pastor.
Not the prestige of a denomination.
Not the survival of a ministry brand.
Jesus Christ.
The same Savior who forgives sinners also calls His people to holiness.
The same Lord who commands humility also opposes oppression.
The same Christ who appoints leaders also holds them accountable.
And His authority never becomes less important because a human leader has been given a position in the church.
Consider what happened in Acts 5.
The apostles were commanded by the religious authorities to stop preaching in the name of Jesus.
These were not insignificant people.
They held recognized religious positions.
They possessed institutional authority.
They could impose serious consequences.
Yet Peter and the apostles answered:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” (Acts 5:29, KJV).
The Greek is striking:
Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.
Peitharchein dei theō mallon ē anthrōpois.
“We must obey God rather than human beings.”
The principle is clear.
When human authority commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, obedience to God takes precedence.
This is not permission to disregard every inconvenient instruction from a church leader.
It is a necessary boundary.
No pastor can authorize sin.
No elder can command dishonesty.
No spiritual mentor can require someone to conceal abuse.
No ministry can demand loyalty that belongs to Christ alone.
And no leader can make disobedience to God's Word righteous simply by calling it submission.
But there is another biblical scene we desperately need to remember.
In Acts 17:11, the Bereans received Paul's message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether his teaching was true.
Paul was an apostle.
His calling was extraordinary.
Yet the Bereans were commended for testing what they heard against Scripture.
They did not reject teaching simply because it came from a person in authority.
They listened.
They investigated.
They searched the Scriptures.
Their eagerness and discernment belonged together.
Biblical submission does not require switching off your discernment.
It requires bringing your heart, your questions, and your convictions beneath the authority of God's Word.
That distinction can save a person from years of spiritual confusion.
Because there is a difference between a pastor who says, “Let us examine what Scripture teaches,” and one who says, “You must agree because I am your pastor.”
There is a difference between correction that seeks restoration and humiliation that demands compliance.
There is a difference between protecting the unity of the church and protecting the reputation of someone who has done wrong.
There is a difference between respecting spiritual authority and treating a human being as though he cannot be questioned.
And there is a difference between being difficult to lead and refusing to participate in something sinful.
Sometimes those differences become painfully clear only after trust has been broken.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
You once served gladly.
You volunteered when nobody else would.
You gave generously.
You defended your church when others criticized it.
You believed the best about your leaders.
Then something happened.
Maybe you witnessed favoritism.
Maybe you discovered dishonesty.
Maybe you were pressured to remain silent about harmful behavior.
Maybe your private struggles became material for public embarrassment.
Maybe you asked a sincere question and suddenly found yourself treated like an enemy.
And now even hearing the word “submission” makes your chest tighten.
You still love Jesus.
But trusting a church leader again feels frightening.
If that describes you, hear this carefully.
Jesus does not ask you to pretend that evil is good.
He does not require you to deny the truth in order to preserve a leader's image.
And He does not confuse silence with holiness.
The Bible itself contains warnings against corrupt shepherds.
In Ezekiel 34, God rebukes the shepherds of Israel who cared for themselves while neglecting the flock.
They failed to strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, bring back the straying, and seek the lost.
Instead, they ruled harshly.
God did not congratulate them for maintaining authority.
He confronted them.
And He declared His intention to care for His sheep.
In Ezekiel 34:11, the Lord says:
“Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out.” (KJV).
That promise reaches its beautiful fulfillment in the revelation of Jesus as the Good Shepherd.
In John 10:11, Jesus declares:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
Read that slowly.
The Good Shepherd gives His life for the sheep.
He does not treat the sheep as disposable sacrifices for his personal ambition.
He sacrifices Himself for them.
That is the difference between the heart of Christ and the spirit of domination.

And when Jesus taught His disciples about leadership in Mark 10:42–45, He contrasted the rulers of the nations, who exercised power over others, with the servant-hearted leadership expected among His followers.
“Whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister.” (Mark 10:43, KJV).
Then He pointed to Himself.
The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Christian leadership must be measured against that cross-shaped standard.
Not celebrity.
Not wealth.
Not the number of followers.
Not the ability to command a room.
Service.
Sacrifice.
Faithfulness.
Truth.
Love.
And accountability before God.
Yet here is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable for another reason.
Some people have genuinely suffered under unhealthy leadership.
Others have never been abused by their pastors, but they call every correction “spiritual abuse” because they do not want anyone confronting their sin.
A pastor lovingly challenges sexual immorality, and someone calls him controlling.
An elder addresses divisive gossip, and someone calls it persecution.
A church insists that its teachers uphold sound doctrine, and someone calls it oppression.
A spiritual mentor urges repentance, and someone accuses that mentor of being judgmental.
We must not confuse biblical correction with abuse.
The same Jesus who protects His sheep also calls them to repent.
The same grace that welcomes sinners teaches them to turn away from ungodliness.
And the same Scripture that restrains abusive leaders calls believers to receive godly instruction with humility.
Hebrews 13:17 still says what it says.
Believers are commanded to obey and submit to their leaders.
That command cannot simply be erased because some leaders have misused it.

When a leader faithfully teaches Scripture, exercises appropriate pastoral oversight, and makes legitimate decisions for the good of the congregation, believers should not automatically resist because of pride, personal preference, or discomfort.
A healthy church cannot function when everyone insists on being accountable only to themselves.
There are times when humility means admitting, “I was wrong.”
There are times when spiritual maturity means receiving correction without becoming defensive.
There are times when love for the body of Christ means accepting a decision that was not your preferred choice.
And there are times when a faithful pastor sees a danger that you have not yet recognized.
That is why godly leadership is a gift.
Not because leaders are perfect.
But because Christ cares for His people through the ministry of faithful servants.
First Thessalonians 5:12–13 urges believers to recognize those who labor among them, lead them in the Lord, and admonish them, and to esteem them highly in love because of their work.
Their work matters.
Their faithfulness matters.
Their spiritual labor matters.
But faithful leaders must also be open to biblical accountability.
In Galatians 2:11–14, Paul publicly confronted Peter when Peter's conduct was not consistent with the truth of the Gospel.
Peter was an apostle.
Yet his position did not make his behavior immune from correction.
This should humble every leader who thinks accountability is disrespect.
And every believer who thinks spiritual authority is inherently evil.
The biblical pattern is neither authoritarianism nor anarchy.
It is a church under the lordship of Jesus Christ, governed by His Word, where leaders serve faithfully and believers respond with humility and discernment.
And when serious allegations arise, the church must respond with truth and justice.
First Timothy 5:19–20 teaches that accusations against elders must be handled with proper evidentiary care and that elders who persist in sin must be rebuked appropriately.
The passage protects against reckless accusations without giving leaders immunity from accountability.
It must never be used to prevent someone from reporting abuse, threats, or criminal conduct to appropriate authorities.
Biblical accountability and lawful protection are not enemies.
And protecting vulnerable people is not rebellion against God.
Now consider another verse frequently used to silence people.
“Touch not mine anointed.” (Psalm 105:15, KJV).
This statement appears in a passage recounting God's protection of His covenant people as they journeyed among nations.
It is not a universal prohibition against questioning pastors, examining doctrine, reporting wrongdoing, or holding church leaders accountable.
To turn it into such a prohibition is to pull the words away from their context.
Anointing does not mean moral perfection.
Calling does not mean immunity.
Spiritual gifting does not cancel the need for integrity.
And a person can speak eloquently about God while behaving in ways that contradict God's commands.
Jesus Himself warned that false prophets could appear in sheep's clothing while inwardly being ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15).
That warning would make little sense if Christians were forbidden from examining those who claim spiritual authority.
In 1 John 4:1, believers are instructed to test the spirits because many false prophets have gone into the world.
And in Matthew 7:16, Jesus teaches that people can be recognized by their fruits.
Discernment is not the enemy of faith.
It is part of faithful obedience.
But discernment must also be honest.
It cannot be driven merely by rumors, resentment, personality conflicts, or the assumption that every imperfect leader is a false shepherd.
Truth requires evidence.
Love refuses slander.
Justice refuses cover-ups.
And holiness refuses to excuse sin simply because the sinner has a microphone.
There is one more detail in Hebrews 13:17 that is often overlooked.
The verse concludes by urging believers to cooperate so that their leaders may carry out their work with joy rather than grief, because grief in that work would be unprofitable for the congregation.
That matters.
Godly pastoral ministry can be exhausting.
A faithful leader may spend years praying for people who never know how much he has carried.
He may visit the sick, counsel struggling marriages, teach Scripture, comfort grieving families, and confront destructive behavior.
He may sacrifice time, energy, and personal comfort because he loves the people entrusted to his care.
Believers should not make that work unnecessarily painful through constant hostility, gossip, selfishness, or refusal to receive sound instruction.
The church should be a place where faithful shepherds can serve with joy.
But the joy of a leader is not purchased by silencing wounded people.
And the grief of a pastor is not automatically proof that the congregation has sinned.
Sometimes leaders grieve because believers resist truth.
Sometimes believers grieve because leaders have betrayed trust.
Both realities deserve biblical honesty.
This is why the Gospel must remain at the center of the conversation.
Because the deepest answer to abusive authority is not simply finding a nicer leader.
And the deepest answer to rebellious independence is not merely finding a stricter church.
We need hearts transformed by Jesus Christ.
We need leaders who have been humbled by the cross.
We need believers who have been softened by grace.
We need churches where repentance is not a slogan preached only to the congregation while the leadership remains untouchable.
We need churches where confession is not weaponized against the vulnerable.
We need churches where forgiveness is never used to pressure people into unsafe situations or to eliminate appropriate consequences.
And we need churches where the Word of God is not treated as a tool for protecting power.
Because Jesus did not shed His blood to create religious empires centered on human personalities.
He came to redeem sinners and gather a people who belong to Him.
Think about Peter.
The disciple who once boldly promised that he would never deny Jesus.
The disciple who failed three times.
The disciple who wept bitterly after his betrayal.
The disciple who knew the shame of discovering that his confidence was greater than his courage.
Yet after the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
In John 21, the risen Christ repeatedly asked Peter whether he loved Him.
And He entrusted Peter with a responsibility.
“Feed my sheep.”
Not “Build your kingdom.”
Not “Make them fear you.”
Not “Protect your image at all costs.”
Feed My sheep.
The sheep still belonged to Jesus.
And the man entrusted with feeding them was himself a forgiven failure.
What a picture of grace.
A fallen disciple restored to service.
A broken man given responsibility.
A shepherd who must never forget that he, too, survives only because of mercy.
That is what spiritual leadership should remember every single day.
The people sitting in the pews are not trophies.
They are souls.
Some arrived carrying grief.
Some are recovering from addiction.
Some are fighting temptations they are ashamed to name.
Some are struggling to believe that God could still love them.
Some are trying to rebuild their faith after religious betrayal.
Some are barely holding on.
And the pastor standing before them is not called to exploit their vulnerability.
He is called to point them to Christ.
But if you are the believer who has been hurt, there is something else you must hear.
Do not allow the failure of a human shepherd to convince you that the Chief Shepherd has abandoned you.
The person who misrepresented Jesus is not Jesus.
The leader who betrayed your trust is not the measure of God's faithfulness.
The church that wounded you does not have the authority to rewrite the character of Christ.
And the pain you experienced does not mean your spiritual future is over.
You may need time to heal.
You may need trustworthy counsel.
You may need to establish boundaries.
You may need to leave an unsafe congregation and find a healthier one.
You may need to report serious wrongdoing.
You may need to relearn what faithful spiritual leadership looks like.
None of those steps automatically means you have rejected Jesus.
But do not mistake healing for permanently closing your heart to every Christian community.
Christ calls His people into fellowship, mutual encouragement, and loving accountability.
There are still faithful pastors.
There are still humble elders.
There are still congregations where Scripture is opened carefully, where questions are welcomed sincerely, where sin is confronted consistently, and where wounded people are treated with dignity.
There are still shepherds who would rather lose their reputation than compromise the truth.
There are still leaders who apologize when they are wrong.
There are still churches where Christ is more important than the person behind the pulpit.
Do not let one person's betrayal become the final chapter of your faith.
And if you are a church leader reading this, perhaps the Holy Spirit is confronting something in you.
Perhaps you have demanded respect without cultivating trust.
Perhaps you have mistaken disagreement for disloyalty.
Perhaps you have used biblical authority to win arguments rather than shepherd hearts.
Perhaps you have been more concerned about protecting your ministry than listening to someone you wounded.
There is grace for repentance.
But repentance must be more than tears in a public statement.
It means acknowledging wrongdoing.
It means turning away from sinful patterns.
It means accepting appropriate accountability.
It means making restitution where possible.
It means recognizing that forgiveness does not automatically restore someone to a position of leadership or remove the consequences of harm.
And sometimes, true repentance means stepping away from authority because the safety of the flock matters more than preserving a title.
That is not the destruction of ministry.
That may be the beginning of genuine obedience to Christ.
Because the Gospel does not exist to preserve our carefully constructed images.
It exposes our sin so that we may come into the light of God's mercy.
The cross tells us two truths we desperately need.
Our sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
And God's love is great enough that Christ willingly came to save sinners.
At Calvary, Jesus did not manipulate people into surrendering their lives for His personal comfort.
He gave Himself for our redemption.
He bore our sins.
He conquered death.
And through His resurrection, He offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why Hebrews 13:17 must never become a weapon that obscures Jesus.
The purpose of faithful spiritual leadership is to help people grow in Christ.
The purpose of biblical submission is not to make believers dependent on a human personality.
It is to encourage humble, orderly, accountable Christian life under the authority of God's Word.
A good shepherd does not become threatened when the sheep learn to recognize the voice of Jesus.
He rejoices.
Because the goal was never to make them follow him instead of Christ.
It was to help them follow Christ more faithfully.
So what should you do when a pastor teaches something you believe is wrong?
Begin with Scripture.
Read the passage in context.
Consider the whole counsel of God.
Ask sincere questions.
Avoid rushing to accusations based on fragments or rumors.
Seek wise counsel from mature believers who are not merely interested in defending a personality.
If the disagreement concerns a legitimate matter of church order or personal preference, practice humility and seek peace.
If it concerns false doctrine, coercion, serious misconduct, or a command to sin, do not surrender your conscience to human authority.
Respond truthfully and wisely.
And where safety is at risk, prioritize protection and appropriate help.
You do not have to choose between honoring God's Word and refusing wrongdoing.
The Bible itself requires both.
Perhaps the most searching question is not simply, “Must I obey my pastor?”
Perhaps it is this:
Am I truly submitted to Jesus Christ?
Because a pastor can demand too much.
And a believer can resist too much.
A leader can become intoxicated with authority.
And a church member can become intoxicated with independence.
Both must kneel before the same Savior.
Both must repent where they have sinned.
Both must receive the same grace.
And both must remember that the Church belongs to Jesus.
Not to the loudest preacher.
Not to the wealthiest donor.
Not to the most influential family.
Not to the most offended member.
Not to the most popular online personality.
To Jesus.
The One who purchased His people with His own blood.
The One who searches hearts.
The One who knows every hidden wound.
The One who sees every secret compromise.
The One who restores the repentant and calls His people to walk in truth.
If this message has touched something you have kept buried, you do not need to pretend that everything is fine.
Perhaps you have been afraid to speak.
Perhaps you have been afraid to trust.
Perhaps you have been resisting correction because of pride.
Perhaps you are a leader who needs to apologize.
Perhaps you are simply tired of seeing Scripture used to divide people who desperately need Jesus.
Whatever your story, bring it honestly before the Lord.
You do not owe strangers the details of your wounds.
God already knows.
And there may be someone reading your simple words who will stop, pray, and remember that they are not the only one struggling.
Not to start another religious argument.
Not to embarrass anyone.
But because someone may be silently wondering whether following Jesus requires surrendering their God-given responsibility to discern truth.
Someone needs to know that the Bible calls us to respect faithful leaders without making them idols.
Someone needs to know that spiritual abuse is not the voice of the Good Shepherd.
And someone needs to know that being corrected by a faithful pastor is not the same thing as being controlled.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown cold, the person searching for answers, and even the skeptic who believes Christianity is nothing more than religious control.
Let them encounter the Jesus who calls sinners to repentance, exposes hypocrisy, forgives the guilty, and restores broken lives.
And if this ministry has helped you understand God's Word more deeply, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.
Not because God withholds His love from those who cannot afford to give.
It is not.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 encourages those who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–18 describes the generosity of believers who partnered with Paul in Gospel ministry.
Financial support can be a meaningful expression of worship when it flows from gratitude, love, wisdom, and a sincere desire to serve Christ.
A voluntary, recurring ministry offering that helps sustain and expand the creation of biblical articles, devotional teaching, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered encouragement.
For those who wish to set aside a monthly amount as an offering toward this ministry, that support can be a beautiful act of generosity.
It should not, however, be confused with a compulsory biblical tithe or presented as a replacement for responsibilities to your local church, your family, or those in genuine need.
And when many believers each contribute what they can, the ministry can be strengthened to reach more people with the truth of Scripture.
There is also something we want every serious student of God's Word to know.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, prayer, Christian character, spiritual discernment, and a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
They are not reserved only for those who can pay.
They are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible.
It is partnership.

It is the opportunity to help strengthen a ministry committed to teaching Scripture, encouraging repentance, proclaiming grace, and reminding broken people that their story is not beyond the redeeming power of Jesus.
You can still participate meaningfully.
Pray for this ministry.
Read and study the Scriptures.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
And above all, remain faithful to Christ.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build a following that replaces the Church, and certainly not to create another authority that people are afraid to question.
It is to point people to the One whose authority is perfectly righteous, whose mercy is immeasurable, and whose truth can withstand every honest question.
Jesus Christ.
So the next time someone opens Hebrews 13:17 and says, “Obey your leaders and submit to them,” do not dismiss the verse.
Receive its instruction.
Respect faithful shepherds.
Value spiritual accountability.
Remain teachable.
Refuse the arrogance that makes correction impossible.
But also remember the rest of Scripture.
Test teaching by God's Word.
Refuse commands that contradict God's will.
Protect the vulnerable.
Hold leaders to biblical standards.
And never give to a human shepherd the absolute allegiance that belongs to the Chief Shepherd alone.
Because one day, every pastor will lay down his title.
Every elder will surrender his position.
Every congregation will stand before the Lord.
Every hidden motive will be known.
Every act of faithful service will be seen.
And every person who belongs to Christ will discover that the safest place was never beneath the unquestioned authority of a human being.
It was always in the hands of Jesus.
The hands that washed His disciples' feet.
The hands that touched the unclean.
The hands that welcomed the broken.
The hands that were pierced for sinners.
The hands of the Shepherd who did not abandon His sheep when saving them required His own blood.
And perhaps that is what your wounded heart has needed to hear all along.
You can honor faithful leaders without worshiping them.
You can reject spiritual manipulation without rejecting the Church of Jesus Christ.
You can repent of rebellion without surrendering your discernment.
You can forgive without pretending that harm never happened.
And you can begin again, not because people have always represented Christ faithfully, but because Christ Himself remains faithful.
The shepherd who failed you does not get to write the ending of the story that Jesus died to redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LET YOUR CURSE FALL ON ME.” — THE MOTHER WHO HELPED HER SON STEAL A BLESSING… AND THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO LET DECEPTION HAVE THE FINAL WORD
paragraphs: “LET YOUR CURSE FALL ON ME.” — THE MOTHER WHO HELPED HER SON STEAL A BLESSING… AND THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO LET DECEPTION HAVE THE FINAL WORD

She knew her husband was about to bless the wrong son. She knew her plan was a lie. And when her frightened son warned her about the consequences, she spoke seven terrifying words: “Let your curse be on me.” What happened inside that family would tear a household apart, send a son running for his life, and reveal a truth many Christians still struggle to accept: God’s promises never need our sins to make them come true.
There are things a mother will do for her child that nobody else would dare to do.
She will sacrifice her sleep. Give away her last meal. Carry burdens she never speaks about. Pray through nights when everybody else has stopped believing.
But there is a dangerous moment when a mother's love becomes tangled with fear.
When protecting a child becomes controlling his future.
When believing God's promise turns into trying to force God's hand.
And when the desire to secure a blessing becomes so overwhelming that a person begins justifying the very sin that could destroy the family.
That is where we find Rebekah.
Not standing in a temple.
Not kneeling beside an altar.
Not offering a beautiful prayer.
She was listening to a conversation she was never meant to hear.
Her elderly husband, Isaac, was preparing to bless their older son, Esau.
And Rebekah was about to do something that would change her family forever.
She would help her younger son, Jacob, deceive his own father.
But what makes this story so disturbing is not simply that a mother encouraged deception.
It is what she said when her son became afraid.
“Upon me be thy curse, my son: only obey my voice.” — Genesis 27:13, KJV
Read that again.
She was willing to speak of bearing a curse rather than allow her preferred outcome to slip away.
And perhaps the most unsettling part of this story is that Rebekah was not a woman who knew nothing about God.
She had heard from Him.
She knew something about His promise.
Yet she still chose deception.
And before we condemn her too quickly, we need to ask a question that might expose something uncomfortable in our own hearts.
Have you ever believed God for something so deeply that you became willing to disobey Him to make it happen?
Maybe you never dressed your child in another person's clothes.
Maybe you never deceived a dying father.
But perhaps you manipulated a situation because you were afraid of losing someone.
Perhaps you hid the truth because you believed the truth would destroy what you were trying to protect.
Perhaps you prayed for God's will while quietly arranging everything to ensure your own will prevailed.
That is why Genesis 27 is not merely an ancient family scandal.
It is a mirror.
And sometimes the hardest part of reading Scripture is discovering that the person we are most disappointed in looks disturbingly like us.
Long before the deception, Rebekah had received a remarkable revelation.
During her pregnancy, when the children struggled within her, she inquired of the LORD.
God answered:

“Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.” — Genesis 25:23, KJV
The Hebrew conclusion is especially important:
וְרַב יַעֲבֹד צָעִיר
Ve-rav ya'avod tsa'ir.
Commonly understood in this context as:
“And the older shall serve the younger.”
This was extraordinary.
In the ancient world, the firstborn son ordinarily enjoyed special privileges of inheritance and family standing.
But God had revealed that the expected order would be overturned.
Jacob, the younger twin, would have a significant place in God's covenant purposes.
Rebekah did not have to invent that promise.
God had spoken before either child was born.
But knowing what God has promised and trusting how God will accomplish it are two very different things.
And that distinction would become the fracture running through her entire household.
Years passed.
The boys grew.
Esau became a skilled hunter, a man of the field.
Jacob was described as a quiet man dwelling in tents.
Isaac loved Esau, particularly enjoying the food he brought from hunting.
Rebekah loved Jacob.
Genesis 25:28 does not hide the division.
This was a family where parental favoritism had taken root.
And favoritism rarely stays confined to the heart.
Eventually, it finds a way into conversations, decisions, alliances, and wounds that children carry for years.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You grew up in a house where one child was celebrated and another was compared.
Where affection seemed easier for one sibling to receive.
Where approval had to be earned.
Where love was real, perhaps, but painfully unequal.
You may be an adult now, with children of your own, yet a sentence spoken at the dinner table decades ago still echoes inside you.
Genesis does not romanticize this family.
The patriarchs were not flawless heroes.
They were human beings living under the mercy of a faithful God.
And one day, their divided affections would collide with a divine promise.
Isaac was old, and his eyesight had become poor.
Believing his death might be approaching, he called Esau and asked him to hunt game and prepare the food he loved so that he might bless him.
Rebekah overheard.
She understood what was at stake.
And instead of seeking a truthful resolution, she moved immediately into action.
She summoned Jacob.
She instructed him to bring two young goats from the flock.
She would prepare the food Isaac enjoyed.
Jacob would carry it to his father.
And Isaac, unable to see clearly, would be led to believe that Jacob was Esau.
The plan was calculated.
The food.
The clothing.
The timing.
The disguise.
Every detail was designed to make a lie believable.
But Jacob noticed a problem.
His brother was hairy.
He was not.
What if Isaac touched him?
What if the deception was discovered?
Listen carefully to Jacob's objection.
“My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver; and I shall bring a curse upon me, and not a blessing.” — Genesis 27:12, KJV
Jacob was afraid.
But the text does not present his initial objection as a courageous refusal to lie.
He was concerned about being discovered and cursed.
That is an important distinction.
Sometimes we resist sin not because we hate what it is, but because we fear what will happen if somebody finds out.
We are afraid of exposure more than disobedience.
Afraid of consequences more than corruption.
Afraid of losing our reputation more than grieving the God who sees what is hidden.
Then Rebekah answered.
In Hebrew, Genesis 27:13 reads:
עָלַי קִלְלָתְךָ בְּנִי אַךְ שְׁמַע בְּקֹלִי
Alai qilelatekha beni, akh shema beqoli.
A close translation is:
“Upon me be your curse, my son; only listen to my voice.”
