Not a desperate bargain made in the darkness.
But the promise of God Himself.
Hebrews 6 tells us that when God made His promise to Abraham, He confirmed it with an oath.
And Hebrews 6:18 speaks of:
“Two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie.” (KJV)
Impossible for God to lie.
Think about that.
We make promises because we are uncertain, afraid, hopeful, or desperate.
God's promises arise from His unchanging character.
We sometimes promise what we cannot accomplish.
God is never surprised by the limits of His power.
We sometimes speak confidently and then discover our weakness.
God never discovers a weakness He did not know He had.
And at the center of His redemptive purpose stands Jesus Christ.
Second Corinthians 1:20 says:
“For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us.” (KJV)
In Christ, God's redemptive promises find their fulfillment.
The Gospel is not the announcement that human beings finally learned how to keep every promise.
It is the announcement that God has acted decisively in His Son to save sinners.
Jesus lived in perfect obedience.
Jesus went to the cross.
Jesus bore our sins.
Jesus rose from the dead.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and new life.
This is why we must never confuse grace with permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus did not die so that we could make peace with our sin.
He died to redeem us from it.
Romans 6:1–2 rejects the idea that we should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
And Titus 2:14 declares that Christ gave Himself to redeem and purify a people zealous for good works.
The Gospel does not merely comfort the guilty.
It calls the guilty to repentance.
It does not merely tell the ashamed that forgiveness exists.
It invites them to come to the Savior who forgives and transforms.
So if you are reading this while carrying the weight of a broken vow, listen carefully.
You do not need to invent a more dramatic promise to make Jesus receive a repentant sinner.
You need to come to Him truthfully.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have lied, confess.
If you have wounded someone, seek to make it right.
If you are trapped in repeated temptation, stop hiding and seek prayer, accountability, and practical help.
If you are struggling with a compulsive pattern, do not assume that shame alone will make you holy.
Bring the struggle into the light with trusted, mature believers and appropriate professional support where necessary.
And if you are afraid to pray because you have disappointed God again, remember the invitation of Hebrews 4:16:
“Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.” (KJV)
The throne of grace.
Not the throne of negotiation.
Not the throne where you present a list of impossible promises as payment for forgiveness.
The throne of grace.
Approached through our great High Priest, Jesus Christ.
That is where the broken believer belongs.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because Christ is merciful.
Perhaps you need to pray something like this today:

“Lord Jesus, I have made promises I could not keep. Sometimes I spoke out of love, sometimes out of fear, and sometimes because I wanted You to give me what I desperately desired. Forgive me for treating holy things carelessly. Forgive my sins and my attempts to bargain with You. Teach me to speak truthfully, obey sincerely, and trust Your wisdom when Your answers are not what I expected. I do not want a faith built on emotional promises that disappear when life becomes difficult. I want a life rooted in Your Word, strengthened by Your Spirit, and transformed by Your grace. Help me follow You today. And when I stumble, lead me back to repentance rather than hiding. In Your name, amen.”
Maybe those words describe exactly where you are.
Maybe you have spent years measuring God's love by your ability to keep the promises you made in your weakest moments.
Maybe you have confused the conviction of the Holy Spirit with a hopeless condemnation that tells you there is no way back.
But Scripture gives us a better foundation.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That promise does not belong to everyone regardless of their relationship to Christ.
It belongs to those who are in Him.
And if you have not yet turned to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith, the invitation is open.
Do not merely promise to become a better person someday.
Come to the Savior today.
Acknowledge your sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the crucified and risen Christ.
And begin following Him.
For those already in Christ, stop measuring the certainty of your salvation by the emotional intensity of your last promise.
Look to Jesus.
Examine your life honestly, yes.
Pursue holiness, absolutely.
But remember where salvation begins and where your hope rests.
Not in your flawless record.
In the finished work of Christ.
And before you leave this article, I want to ask you something.
Not for appearances.
Not because you need to prove your faith to strangers.
But because someone else may be silently carrying the same burden.
Have you ever made a promise to God in desperation and then struggled with the guilt of failing to keep it?
If you are comfortable, share what Scripture is teaching you about repentance, grace, and honest obedience.
You do not need to disclose private sins or painful details.
Even a simple, sincere response may encourage someone who thought they were the only one struggling.
Return to Matthew 5:33–37.
Read Numbers 30, Deuteronomy 23, Ecclesiastes 5, James 5, and John 21 in their full contexts.
Do not settle for an emotional moment when Scripture invites you into lasting understanding.
That simple act may introduce a struggling friend, a discouraged family member, a confused believer, or even someone who does not yet know Christ to biblical truth they desperately need to hear.
You are not being asked to make a vow.
You are being invited to consider a meaningful act of partnership.
Because at the end of the day, the most important thing is not how loudly we promise to serve Jesus.
It is whether we truly belong to Him, trust His Word, repent when we sin, and follow Him in the ordinary moments when no one is watching.
The Christian life is not a contest to see who can make the grandest declaration.
It is a life of faith in the Savior who calls us to take up our cross and follow Him.
A life where yes means yes.
Where no means no.
Where worship is not bargaining.
Where generosity is not coercion.
Where repentance is not performance.
Where grace is not an excuse for sin.
And where obedience grows from a heart being transformed by Jesus Christ.
So the next time you find yourself on your knees, frightened, ashamed, or desperate, remember this.
You do not have to begin with another impossible promise.
You can begin with the truth.
“Lord, I need You.”
And if you belong to Christ, you can keep coming to Him, trusting that the Savior who calls you to repentance is also the Savior who supplies mercy and grace for the journey.
You may still remember the promise you broke, but the cross calls you to remember the Savior who did not abandon His mission to redeem sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FOOD ON YOUR PLATE COULD BE REVEALING SOMETHING ABOUT YOUR FAITH—BUT NOT WHAT YOU THINK
paragraphs: THE FOOD ON YOUR PLATE COULD BE REVEALING SOMETHING ABOUT YOUR FAITH—BUT NOT WHAT YOU THINK

Should Christians Still Obey the Old Testament Dietary Laws? What Jesus, Moses, Peter, and Paul Actually Taught—and Why Getting This Wrong Could Turn a Gift of Grace Into a Burden God Never Asked You to Carry.
There is a Christian somewhere right now who loves Jesus with all their heart… but is terrified that the food they ate yesterday might have offended God.
Maybe it was pork at a family gathering.
Maybe it was shrimp at a restaurant.
Maybe someone sent them a video claiming that eating unclean animals is rebellion against the commandments of the Almighty.
And suddenly, something that once seemed ordinary becomes a spiritual crisis.
What if I've been sinning without knowing it?
What if my pastor never told me the whole truth?
What if Jesus expects me to follow dietary laws that my church has ignored for generations?
And perhaps the most frightening question of all…
What if I think I'm walking in grace, but I'm actually living in disobedience?
If you've ever wrestled with those questions, stay with me.
Because this conversation is not ultimately about bacon, shrimp, or what ends up on your dinner table.
It's about the cross.
It's about the covenant.
It's about whether Jesus Christ truly accomplished what He came to accomplish.

And somewhere between the laws given to Israel, the words spoken by Jesus, and the blood shed at Calvary, there is a truth that can either liberate your conscience or expose the religious pride you've been carrying without realizing it.
But we cannot discover that truth by grabbing one Bible verse and ignoring the rest.
We must allow Scripture to speak in its own context.
Even when it challenges what we have always believed.
Even when it confronts what we have been taught.
And especially when it exposes how easily we confuse personal conviction with the commandments of God.
Imagine standing among the Israelites thousands of years ago.

The wilderness stretches endlessly before you. The memory of Egyptian slavery is still painfully fresh. Your people have witnessed the sea part, the power of Pharaoh collapse, and the presence of God descend upon Mount Sinai.
You are no longer slaves.
You are a people rescued by God.
And now the Lord is teaching you what it means to live as His covenant nation.
Among His instructions are commands concerning food.

Leviticus 11 distinguishes between animals Israel may eat and animals Israel must avoid. Land animals generally must both chew the cud and have divided hooves. Creatures living in water must have fins and scales.
And then comes the command concerning the pig.
Leviticus 11:7–8 identifies the swine as unclean for Israel because it has divided hooves but does not chew the cud. Israel is forbidden to eat its flesh.
This was not an invention of religious leaders.
It was not a cultural preference disguised as Scripture.
It was a genuine commandment given by God under the Mosaic covenant.
And that matters.
Because anyone who teaches that the Old Testament dietary laws were never commanded by God is already mishandling the Bible.
But there is another question we must ask.
To whom was this command given, under which covenant, and how does the coming of Jesus Christ affect its application today?
That is where the discussion becomes more profound.
In Leviticus 11:44, God declares:
"For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy."
The Hebrew word for holy is קָדוֹשׁ (qādôsh), carrying the sense of holiness, sacredness, and being set apart.
Israel's food distinctions were part of a much larger covenant system that shaped the nation's worship, identity, and separation from surrounding peoples.
The dietary commands were not merely about nutrition.
They belonged to Israel's holy calling under the law of Moses.
Leviticus 20:25–26 connects the distinction between clean and unclean animals with God's separation of Israel from the nations.
And here is something we must not miss.
Israel did not earn its rescue from Egypt by first obeying dietary laws.
God delivered His people, and then He gave them covenant instructions.
Redemption came before Sinai.
Yet the commandments given at Sinai were real obligations for those living under that covenant.
So when someone says, "God commanded His people not to eat pork," they are quoting a genuine biblical reality.
But when someone immediately concludes, "Therefore every Christian must obey the same dietary restrictions today," they have made a theological leap that must be examined through the New Testament.
Because something happened after Sinai.
Something the prophets anticipated.
Something the apostles proclaimed.
Something that changed the history of redemption forever.
Jesus came.
And He did not come merely to give Israel another collection of religious instructions.
He came to fulfill the Scriptures.
In Matthew 5:17, Jesus declares:
"Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."
The Greek verb translated "fulfil" is πληρῶσαι (plērōsai), from plēroō, meaning to fulfill, complete, or bring to fullness.
Jesus was not announcing that God's previous revelation had been a mistake.
He was declaring that His mission brought the law and the prophets toward their intended fulfillment.
But notice something important.
Fulfillment does not mean that every commandment continues to function in precisely the same covenantal way.
Christians do not continue offering animal sacrifices at the Jerusalem temple.
We do not seek forgiveness through the Levitical priesthood.
We do not regard circumcision as a requirement for belonging to God's covenant people.
Why?
Because the New Testament teaches that Christ's sacrifice, priesthood, and covenant work have transformed how God's people relate to those institutions.
Hebrews 10:1–14 explains that the repeated sacrifices of the law could never perfect worshipers, but Christ offered Himself once for all.
Hebrews 8:6–13 presents Jesus as mediator of a better covenant and describes the former covenant as becoming obsolete.
This does not mean God's holiness disappeared.
It means that God's redemptive plan reached its decisive fulfillment in His Son.
And that brings us to a moment in the ministry of Jesus that should make every Christian pay close attention.
In Mark 7, the Pharisees and scribes confront Jesus because some of His disciples eat with hands considered ceremonially defiled.
The immediate controversy concerns traditional handwashing practices, not a direct dispute over whether pork should be eaten.
That distinction matters.

Jesus rebukes the tendency to elevate human traditions above God's commandments. He then teaches that what enters a person from outside does not defile the heart in the way evil desires and actions do.
Mark 7:20–23 identifies the deeper source of moral defilement: the human heart.
And in Mark 7:19, many modern translations include an explanatory statement that Jesus was declaring all foods clean.
The Greek expression commonly discussed is:
καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα
Katharizōn panta ta brōmata.
Literally, the phrase concerns "cleansing all foods."
Many contemporary translators understand it as Mark's explanation of the implications of Jesus' teaching: that Jesus declared all foods clean.
Other interpreters argue that the immediate context concerns digestion, ritual washing, and the foods already recognized as edible under Jewish law.
We should acknowledge that interpretive discussion rather than pretending every detail is uncontested.
Nevertheless, the broader New Testament gives us additional evidence that the old covenant food distinctions are not binding requirements for Christians under the new covenant.
And that evidence becomes impossible to ignore when we arrive at a rooftop in Joppa.
The apostle Peter is hungry.
He goes up to pray.
Then he sees something extraordinary.
A vessel resembling a great sheet descends from heaven, containing various animals.
A voice commands him to rise, kill, and eat.
Peter objects.
In Acts 10:14, he says:
"Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean."
Think about that.
Peter had walked with Jesus.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed His death and resurrection.
And yet Peter still resisted eating what he considered unclean.
Then the voice responds in Acts 10:15:
"What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common."
The Greek statement is:
ἃ ὁ θεὸς ἐκαθάρισεν, σὺ μὴ κοίνου
Ha ho Theos ekatharisen, sy mē koinou.
"What God has cleansed, do not call common."
Now here is where careful Bible reading becomes essential.
Peter himself explains the vision's immediate meaning in Acts 10:28.
God had shown him that he must not call any person common or unclean.
The vision prepared Peter to enter the home of Cornelius, a Gentile, and proclaim the Gospel without treating Gentiles as spiritually untouchable.
Therefore, it would be careless to claim that Acts 10 is simply a story about God giving Peter permission to eat pork.
Its central purpose concerns the acceptance of Gentiles.
But it would also be careless to ignore the way God used the imagery of clean and unclean animals to confront Peter's assumptions about covenant boundaries.
The vision belongs to the larger New Testament revelation that Gentiles are welcomed into God's people through faith in Jesus Christ.
Not by first becoming Jews.
Not by earning acceptance through the Mosaic law.
Not by adopting Israel's entire covenant identity.
But through Christ.
And then came a controversy that threatened to divide the early Church.
Some believers insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and commanded to keep the law of Moses.
The issue was serious enough to bring the apostles and elders together in Jerusalem.
You can read the account in Acts 15.
Imagine the tension.
Jewish believers had grown up honoring the Torah.
Gentile believers were now receiving the Holy Spirit and coming to faith in the Messiah.
Would they have to adopt the full Mosaic covenant to be accepted as God's people?
Peter spoke of God's grace.
He warned against placing a yoke upon the disciples that Israel itself had not been able to bear.
Then James gave his judgment concerning Gentile believers.
The resulting letter instructed them to abstain from things associated with idols, from blood, from what had been strangled, and from sexual immorality (Acts 15:19–29).
Notice what the council did not do.
It did not command Gentile Christians to observe the complete dietary regulations of Leviticus 11.
It did not declare that eating pork would prevent salvation.
It did not make the Mosaic food distinctions a condition of justification.
At the same time, the council did give certain food-related instructions, so it would be equally inaccurate to say that food behavior never mattered to the early Church.
The precise relationship between those instructions, idolatry, table fellowship, and later Christian practice has been discussed throughout Christian history.
But the central conclusion is clear.
The apostles refused to make full observance of the Mosaic law a requirement for Gentiles to belong to Christ.
And then the apostle Paul takes us even deeper.
In Romans 14, believers disagree about food and religious observances.
Some eat broadly.
Others restrict their diets because of conscience.
Paul does not command every Christian to eat everything.
Neither does he permit believers to condemn one another over disputable food practices.
Romans 14:3 says:
"Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him."
Read that again.
The one who eats must not despise.
The one who abstains must not judge.
Why?
Because God has received them.
In Romans 14:14, Paul writes:
The Greek word κοινόν (koinon) here refers to something considered common or defiled.
Paul is addressing how believers regard food in relation to conscience and fellowship.
And then comes Romans 14:17:
"For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost."
This does not mean obedience is unimportant.
It means the kingdom of God cannot be reduced to dietary regulations.
And suddenly the conversation is no longer just about food.
It's about how you treat the Christian sitting across from you.
The brother who does not eat pork.
The sister who eats shrimp without hesitation.
The believer whose conscience is troubled.
The believer who has studied the Scriptures and believes these foods are permitted.
Can they sit together at the Lord's table without treating one another as enemies?
Can they love each other without turning dinner into a courtroom?
Can they remember that the blood of Jesus Christ is infinitely more important than the contents of their plates?
Because Paul continues with a warning that should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Romans 14:20 says:
"For meat destroy not the work of God."
Imagine being so determined to win an argument about food that you wound someone Christ died to redeem.
Imagine proving your dietary knowledge while failing to demonstrate Christian love.
Imagine having the correct menu and the wrong spirit.
That is a tragedy.
And it is not the holiness Jesus calls us to pursue.
But perhaps you are still wondering:
Doesn't the Bible say God never changes?
Yes.
Malachi 3:6 declares that the Lord does not change.
But God's unchanging character does not mean every covenant administration remains identical throughout redemptive history.
The same God who commanded animal sacrifices under the Mosaic covenant also provided Jesus Christ as the final and sufficient sacrifice.
The same God who established the Levitical priesthood has appointed Christ as our eternal High Priest.
The same God who separated Israel from the nations has brought believing Jews and Gentiles together in one body through Christ (Ephesians 2:11–22).
God did not become less holy.
His promises were being fulfilled.
And the new covenant does not make sin acceptable.
It makes the saving work of Jesus central.
This distinction is especially important when people quote 1 Peter 1:15–16:
"Be ye holy; for I am holy."
Peter is drawing from the holiness language of Leviticus.
But he does not use it to command the Church to reinstate every dietary distinction of the Mosaic covenant.
Instead, he calls believers to holiness in all their conduct.
That means Christians must still take holiness seriously.
We must repent of sexual immorality, dishonesty, greed, bitterness, idolatry, cruelty, and every other sin Scripture condemns.
Grace does not give us permission to rebel against God.
Titus 2:11–14 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
But holiness must be defined through the revelation of God fulfilled in Jesus Christ, not through selectively importing old covenant regulations while ignoring the covenantal context.
And this brings us to one of the clearest passages on the question.
Colossians 2:16–17 says:
"Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."
The Greek word translated "shadow" is σκιὰ (skia).
A shadow points beyond itself.
It is not the final substance.
Paul's point is that these observances must be understood in relation to Christ, to whom they point.
And here is a picture I want you to remember.
Imagine waiting years for someone you love to return home.
You have a photograph of them.
You hold it close.
You treasure it.
You look at it when the nights are lonely.
But then, one evening, the door opens.
The person you have been waiting for is standing right in front of you.
Would you turn away from the living person and insist that you must keep staring at the photograph?
Of course not.
The photograph was precious.
But the person is greater.
In a similar way, the Old Testament covenant institutions pointed forward to the fulfillment of God's redemptive promises in Jesus.
We do not dishonor the shadow by rejoicing in the One to whom it pointed.
We honor God's purpose by recognizing Christ.
That is why Paul warns against allowing others to judge believers over food and calendar observances.
Not because God never gave those instructions.
But because Christ has come.
And if you are a Christian who chooses to avoid pork or shellfish, hear this carefully.
You are not wrong simply because you abstain.
There may be personal, cultural, health-related, or religious reasons for your decision.
You may regard abstaining as a way of honoring God with your body.
You may find it spiritually meaningful.
You are free to make that choice in good conscience.
But there is a difference between saying, "I choose not to eat this before the Lord," and saying, "Every Christian who eats this is sinning against God."
The first may be a sincere personal conviction.
The second requires a binding command under the new covenant that the New Testament does not establish.
Likewise, if you believe you are free to eat pork or shellfish, your freedom is not a license for arrogance.
You do not need to mock Christians who abstain.
You do not need to deliberately offend someone's conscience.
You do not need to turn Christian liberty into an excuse for gluttony or disregard for your health.
First Corinthians 10:31 reminds us:
"Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God."
Notice the scope.
Whatever you do.
Eating.
Drinking.
Speaking.
Serving.
Giving.
Living.
All to the glory of God.
That means your relationship with food should reflect gratitude, wisdom, self-control, and love.
But it does not mean every believer must return to the dietary restrictions given to Israel under Moses.
And perhaps the most decisive theological statement comes from the same apostle who once fiercely defended the traditions of his ancestors.
Paul writes in Galatians 2:16 that a person is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.
The Greek word for justification comes from the δικαιόω (dikaioō) word family, referring in this context to being declared righteous or vindicated before God.
And in Ephesians 2:8–9, Paul says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
This is the center of the matter.
You are not made righteous before God by eating the right animal.
You are not justified by avoiding the wrong animal.
You are not cleansed from sin by designing a flawless religious menu.
You are justified through faith in Jesus Christ, whose saving work is sufficient.
And that should humble both sides of this discussion.
Because the Christian who abstains from pork cannot boast that their diet makes them more worthy of salvation.
And the Christian who eats pork cannot boast that their freedom makes them more spiritually mature.
Neither person can stand before God and say, "Look at my plate. This is why You must accept me."
Our only hope is Christ.
His perfect obedience.
His atoning death.
His victorious resurrection.
His grace.
But there is another passage we cannot ignore.

In 1 Timothy 4:1–5, Paul warns about false teaching that includes forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
He explains that what God has created is good and is to be received with thanksgiving, being sanctified by God's word and prayer.
The passage does not mean that everything physically edible is automatically wise, safe, or appropriate to consume.
Nor does it mean all food-related restrictions are sinful.
It addresses religious prohibitions that conflict with the truth of God's creation and the Gospel.
The point is not reckless consumption.
It is grateful reception of God's gifts without turning human restrictions into conditions of spiritual acceptance.
Now, some readers may be thinking about Isaiah 66:17, where the prophet speaks of judgment involving people who eat swine's flesh and other abominations.
This is a serious text, and it should not be dismissed.

Isaiah's prophecy addresses rebellion and corrupt worship within its prophetic context, and interpreters differ about how its final-judgment imagery relates to dietary practices in the age of the new covenant.
But Christians must interpret prophetic passages alongside the clearer apostolic teaching about Gentile inclusion, justification, conscience, and food.
We cannot simply quote Isaiah 66, bypass Acts 15, Romans 14, Colossians 2, and the teaching of Jesus, and announce that every pork-eating Christian stands condemned.
That would not be careful biblical interpretation.
It would be selective interpretation.
And the same caution applies to those who quote Mark 7 and then act as though the Old Testament no longer matters.
Every part of Scripture deserves to be read faithfully.
The law reveals God's holiness.
The prophets reveal His promises.
The Gospels reveal the Messiah.
The apostolic writings explain the significance of His death, resurrection, and new covenant.
Together, they lead us toward Christ.
So what is the answer?
Christians are not required to observe the Old Testament clean-and-unclean animal distinctions as binding covenant law in order to obey God or be accepted by Him.
Believers may voluntarily observe dietary restrictions, but they must not make those restrictions a universal condition of salvation or Christian faithfulness.

At the same time, Christians must honor the food-related moral responsibilities that remain relevant under the new covenant, including avoiding idolatry, practicing self-control, caring for others, and refusing to violate their own conscience.
That conclusion is not based on a single isolated verse.
It emerges from the movement of Scripture from Moses to Christ, from Israel's covenant institutions to the new covenant, and from the Jerusalem council to the teaching of the apostles.
But now I want to speak to the person who came into this article afraid.
The person who has been losing sleep because someone told you that eating a certain food means Jesus will reject you.
The person who watched a frightening sermon and began questioning whether your entire Christian life has been a lie.
The person who desperately wants to obey God but no longer knows whom to trust.
Please hear this.
Jesus Christ is not a fragile Savior whose finished work collapses because you ate a piece of bacon.
The cross was not an incomplete transaction waiting for your dietary performance to finish the payment.
When Jesus cried, "It is finished" in John 19:30, He declared the completion of His earthly redemptive mission at the cross.
The Greek word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai), from teleō, meaning to finish, accomplish, or bring to completion.
That word should never be reduced to a slogan that makes obedience irrelevant.
But neither should we treat Christ's sacrifice as though it were insufficient to save those who trust in Him.
He did not come to make salvation possible only for people who can perfectly navigate every disputed religious regulation.
He came to save sinners.

And if you have been trying to earn peace with God through dietary perfection, religious performance, or constant fear of accidentally breaking a rule, the Gospel invites you to place your confidence somewhere infinitely stronger.
In Jesus Christ.
Not in your menu.
Not in your religious résumé.
Not in the approval of people who measure holiness by outward appearances.
In Christ.
And to the person who has been using grace as an excuse to live carelessly, the Gospel speaks to you too.
Freedom in Christ is not freedom from loving God.
It is freedom to serve Him from a transformed heart.
If you celebrate being allowed to eat certain foods but refuse to forgive someone who wounded you, something is wrong.
If you defend Christian liberty while nourishing hatred, lust, greed, or dishonesty, something is wrong.
If you can debate Leviticus for hours but cannot humble yourself enough to apologize to your spouse, your child, or your brother in Christ, something is wrong.
Because the deepest uncleanness Jesus exposed was not hiding inside a particular animal.
It was hiding inside the human heart.
And that is why we all need a Savior.
Not merely better habits.
Not merely better religious knowledge.
Not merely a more disciplined lifestyle.
We need forgiveness.
We need repentance.
We need new hearts.
We need the mercy of God.
And that is exactly what Jesus offers.
The Gospel is not that you were already clean enough for God to accept you.
The Gospel is that Jesus came for sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds a Savior who is able to save.
Maybe you have spent years carrying religious fear.
Maybe you have spent years judging other Christians.
Maybe you have been secretly proud of how much Scripture you know.
Maybe you have confused winning theological arguments with actually becoming more like Jesus.
This may be the moment to surrender something deeper than a dietary preference.
Your pride.
Your fear.
Your need to prove yourself.
Your tendency to condemn people whom God has welcomed through His Son.
Because at the foot of the cross, the self-righteous and the ashamed stand on the same ground.
Both need mercy.
Both need forgiveness.
Both need Jesus.
And both can be transformed by His grace.
If this has exposed something in your heart, don't hide behind another theological debate.
Be honest before God.
Not as a formula to earn His favor.
Not as proof that you are saved.
But as a simple expression of your desire to follow Him faithfully.

And if you have studied these passages and understand them differently, you are welcome in the conversation too. Share the Scripture and the reasoning behind your view with humility. We can disagree seriously without treating one another as enemies.
Because biblical truth does not need cruelty to defend it.
And Christian love does not require us to abandon biblical truth.
I also want you to think about someone you know.
Perhaps a family member who has been frightened by religious teaching.
A friend who left church because Christians kept fighting over secondary issues.
A believer who has become harsh and judgmental without noticing.
Or someone who thinks Christianity is nothing more than a thousand complicated rules designed to make ordinary people feel guilty.
Not because sharing a post earns spiritual favor.
But because a single Scripture-grounded conversation might help someone examine the Gospel more carefully.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, people who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still searching for the truth.
They do not need to pretend to have everything figured out before they can begin listening to the Word of God.
And if these teachings are helping you grow, I want to extend a deeper invitation.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to be a place where people merely consume inspiring words, react emotionally for a moment, and return unchanged to their old lives.
Our desire is to keep pointing people to the Scriptures, to the cross, to repentance, and to the daily transformation that comes through knowing Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to more people, including those who may not have the means to purchase Christian learning materials.
And this is where your partnership can make a meaningful difference.
That distinction matters deeply to us.
God's grace is not for sale.
And your spiritual worth is never measured by what you can afford.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
So if you choose to partner with us, let it be because you believe in the mission and genuinely desire to help us continue.
Those products are simply another way to encourage faith, share Scripture, and keep meaningful reminders of Christ in everyday life.
It is the opportunity to help make Christ-centered resources available to people who need them.
Somewhere, someone may be reading Scripture for the first time.
Someone may be quietly wrestling with doubt.
Someone may be ashamed to return to church.
Someone may be wondering whether Jesus could possibly forgive what they have done.
We cannot promise what every article, resource, or shared message will accomplish.
But we can faithfully plant seeds, speak the truth, and trust God with the results.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who needs the Word of God.
Speak about Jesus with kindness and courage.
Those acts of faithfulness matter too.
Because the goal was never to build a community of people who simply agree with every article we publish.
The goal is to point people toward the living Christ.
To help believers open their Bibles.
To encourage honest repentance.
To remind the weary that grace is real.
To proclaim that forgiveness is found in Jesus.
And to show a watching world that biblical truth and genuine love belong together.
Now return with me to the question that brought us here.
Should Christians follow Old Testament dietary laws today?
You have seen that the dietary commands were real, holy-covenant instructions given to Israel.
You have seen that Jesus came not to dismiss God's revelation but to fulfill it.
You have seen that the apostles did not impose the full Mosaic dietary code upon Gentile believers.
You have seen that Paul instructed Christians not to judge or despise one another over food and conscience.
And you have seen that the foundation of our acceptance before God is not what we eat, but Jesus Christ.
So the next time you sit down at a table, remember this.
Give thanks.
Honor your conscience.
Respect your brother or sister.
Exercise wisdom.
Do not use your freedom to wound someone else.
Do not use your convictions to condemn someone whom Christ has received.
And never confuse the outward appearance of religious discipline with the inward transformation of the Holy Spirit.
Because a person can avoid every unclean animal mentioned in Leviticus and still harbor a heart filled with hatred.
And a person can enjoy a meal that would have been forbidden under the Mosaic covenant while walking humbly before God through faith in Jesus Christ.
The food does not save either one.
Christ alone saves.
The real question is not simply whether your plate is clean according to the old covenant dietary code.
The deeper question is whether your heart has been surrendered to the Savior.
Have you repented of your sin?
Are you trusting in Jesus rather than your own righteousness?
Are you growing in love?
Are you becoming more truthful, merciful, patient, and obedient to Christ?
Are you learning to recognize the difference between the commandments of God and the traditions or convictions of human beings?
Because one day, you will not stand before Jesus holding a menu as the evidence that you deserve eternal life.
You will stand before the One who knows every secret of your heart.
And your only sufficient hope will be His mercy.
So don't make food your savior.
Don't make religious performance your righteousness.
Don't make your personal convictions the cross upon which you crucify your brothers and sisters.
Look to Jesus.
The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
The fulfillment of God's promises.
The mediator of the new covenant.
The risen Lord.
The Savior who does not merely change what is permitted on a plate, but transforms the hearts of those who belong to Him.
And if you remember nothing else from this article, remember this:
The greatest danger was never that you might eat something unclean—it was that you might spend your life trying to make yourself clean while overlooking the only Savior who can wash away your sins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The frightening difference between fighting for biblical truth online and actually surrendering to it in real life—and why the greatest threat to your Christian witness may not be the unbeliever arguing against your faith, but the person you become when nobody is watching.
paragraphs: The frightening difference between fighting for biblical truth online and actually surrendering to it in real life—and why the greatest threat to your Christian witness may not be the unbeliever arguing against your faith, but the person you become when nobody is watching.

There is something deeply unsettling about a Christian who can defend the holiness of God in a comment section… and then go home and treat the people they love as though God's holiness has nothing to do with them.
Someone needs to talk about this.
Not to embarrass the Church. Not to give unbelievers another reason to mock Christianity. And certainly not because biblical truth should be watered down to make everyone comfortable.
But because there is a kind of Christianity that has become dangerously good at winning arguments while quietly losing its resemblance to Jesus.
And the most frightening part?
You can become that Christian without ever realizing it.
You can quote Scripture accurately, recognize false teaching immediately, defend biblical marriage, confront cultural compromise, and passionately declare that Jesus Christ is Lord.
You can receive hundreds of likes from believers who admire your courage.
You can be called bold. Faithful. Uncompromising. A defender of the Gospel.
And still have a spouse who is afraid to speak honestly around you.
Children who know your religious convictions but rarely experience your gentleness.
Parents you have neglected.
People you have wounded without apologizing.
A private life you would never allow anyone to examine as closely as you examine someone else's theology.
Then, when another controversial post appears on your screen, you are suddenly ready to fight for Jesus again.
But what if Jesus is asking you to put down the phone and obey Him in the room you're sitting in?
What if the battle you keep avoiding is the very battle where your faith is supposed to become visible?
And what if the truth you so passionately defend has been trying to confront you all along?
This is not a call to stop defending Scripture.
It is a call to stop using the defense of Scripture as a substitute for surrendering to its Author.
Because Jesus never commanded His disciples merely to be correct.
He commanded them to follow Him.
And following Him costs considerably more than posting about Him.
Think about the last time you witnessed a heated theological argument online.
Someone posted an opinion about sin, repentance, marriage, salvation, or Christian living.
Within minutes, believers were quoting verses, correcting one another, challenging interpretations, and declaring what God approves or condemns.
Some were genuinely trying to protect biblical truth.
Others seemed more interested in humiliating whoever disagreed.
The conversation became increasingly hostile.
People who claimed to represent the Prince of Peace began speaking with contempt.
Those defending the command to love God appeared to forget the command to love their neighbor.
And somewhere beneath the noise, an uncomfortable question remained unanswered.
If we are defending the truth of Jesus, why do we sometimes abandon the character of Jesus while doing it?
The Apostle James addressed this contradiction long before social media existed.
In James 1:22, the Greek text says:
Γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγου καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταί
Ginesthe de poiētai logou kai mē monon akroatai.
A faithful translation is:
“But be doers of the word, and not hearers only.”
James continues by warning against deceiving ourselves.
That final warning matters.
Because the danger is not simply that someone knows the Bible but refuses to obey it.
The danger is that the person may genuinely believe their familiarity with biblical truth proves their spiritual faithfulness.
The Greek word ποιηταί (poiētai) refers to doers—people who put something into practice.
James is not contrasting biblical knowledge with ignorance.
He is contrasting hearing God's Word with responding to it through obedience.
A Christian can understand the correct interpretation of a passage and still resist the very obedience that passage demands.
That is spiritual self-deception.
And self-deception is terrifying precisely because it rarely announces itself.
It often sounds like confidence.
It looks like conviction.
Sometimes it even receives applause.
You may be defending the Bible while the Bible is exposing you.
You may be correcting someone else's sin while refusing to confess your own.
You may be explaining the importance of forgiveness while carrying resentment you have no intention of releasing.
And because your public convictions are so visible, you may never notice how much your private obedience has disappeared.
Jesus confronted something remarkably similar in the religious culture of His own day.
In Matthew 23:3, speaking about the scribes and Pharisees, He said:
“For they preach, but do not practice.” (ESV)
Those words are devastating.
Not because every religious teacher was equally hypocritical, or because teaching God's commandments was wrong.
But because knowing what should be done is not the same as doing it.
Jesus was exposing the contradiction between religious instruction and personal conduct.
The people who could explain God's requirements were sometimes unwilling to submit to those requirements themselves.
They knew how to place burdens on others.
But they did not consistently practice what they taught.
Now imagine that sentence being spoken over your own life.
You preach, but do not practice.
You teach forgiveness, but refuse to forgive.
You defend purity, but secretly entertain impurity.
You condemn dishonesty, but manipulate people when the truth becomes inconvenient.
You insist that Christians must demonstrate love, but your family knows you primarily through anger.
You demand repentance from strangers while treating your own apologies as optional.
You can identify compromise in everyone else, but you have become remarkably skilled at explaining away your own.
And perhaps the most painful contradiction of all…
You speak beautifully about the grace of Jesus while making it almost impossible for the people closest to you to experience grace through your behavior.
That should trouble us.
Not because we must become perfect before we can speak about God.
We cannot.
But because genuine faith should produce a growing willingness to be corrected by the very truth we proclaim.
There is a difference between a Christian who struggles against sin and a Christian who has made peace with hypocrisy.
One falls and returns to Christ in repentance.
The other builds a religious explanation for why repentance is always someone else's responsibility.
One grieves the distance between their profession and their conduct.
The other hides that distance behind louder professions.
And if we are not careful, online Christianity can make the second kind of life feel remarkably successful.
Because the internet rewards visibility.
It can reward outrage, certainty, speed, and confrontation.
It cannot reliably measure the patience you showed your exhausted spouse last night.
It cannot see whether you apologized to your child after losing your temper.
It cannot verify whether you paid your employee fairly, kept your promise, resisted temptation, or helped someone who had nothing to offer you in return.
It can count reactions.
But it cannot measure holiness.
It can amplify your declarations.
But it cannot confirm your discipleship.
And that creates a dangerous temptation: to invest more energy in appearing faithful than in becoming faithful.
Not every outspoken Christian falls into that trap. Many believers faithfully defend Scripture online and quietly live it with integrity offline.
But every one of us needs to recognize that the trap exists.
Because public religious approval can become a counterfeit form of spiritual assurance.
People begin affirming your theology.
Your followers increase.
Your comments receive praise.
And gradually, without a conscious decision, you start confusing being recognized as a Christian with becoming more like Christ.
Then comes the moment that reveals what public approval cannot.
Your wife says something that frustrates you.
Your husband disappoints you.
Your child interrupts you when you are exhausted.
A coworker takes credit for something you accomplished.
Someone speaks disrespectfully to you.
Nobody is recording.
Nobody is watching.
There are no likes to receive.
No Christian audience to impress.
No comment section where you can demonstrate your biblical knowledge.
Only a choice.
Will you respond according to the flesh, or will you submit to the Spirit?
Will you demand your rights, or practice humility?
Will you retaliate, or exercise self-control?
Will you justify your anger, or admit where you have sinned?
This is where biblical truth becomes painfully personal.
Because the real test of our discipleship is not limited to what we say when people are listening.
It also includes who we become when obedience is costly and applause is impossible.
Paul wrote in Galatians 5:22–23 that the fruit of the Spirit includes love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
Notice what is not on that list.
Winning theological debates.
Humiliating opponents.
Having the final word.
Receiving public recognition for defending Christianity.
These things are not the Spirit's fruit.
And yet we sometimes evaluate spiritual maturity by how aggressively someone confronts error rather than by whether their life increasingly demonstrates the character produced by the Holy Spirit.
That does not mean doctrinal accuracy is unimportant.
Paul himself defended the Gospel against serious distortions.
He corrected false teaching.
He instructed believers to hold firmly to sound doctrine.
But he also wrote in Ephesians 4:15 about speaking the truth in love.
The Greek expression is:
ἀληθεύοντες δὲ ἐν ἀγάπῃ
Alētheuontes de en agapē.
The phrase conveys the idea of being truthful, or speaking and living truthfully, in love.
The surrounding passage concerns the Church growing toward maturity in Christ.
Truth and love are not competing virtues.
They belong together in Christian maturity.
Love without truth can become sentimental compromise.
Truth spoken without love can become a weapon of pride.
Biblical faithfulness refuses both distortions.
You do not have to abandon conviction to demonstrate compassion.
You do not have to insult someone to confront sin.
You do not have to become cruel to prove you are courageous.
Jesus was never morally indifferent.
He called people to repentance.
He exposed religious hypocrisy.
He warned about judgment.
He spoke with divine authority.
Yet He also welcomed repentant sinners, showed compassion to the broken, touched the unclean, and gave His life for people who could never save themselves.
His holiness was not compromised by His mercy.
His mercy did not erase His holiness.
And His followers have no permission to separate what He held together.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
The religious leaders wanted to use her situation as a test against Him.
They placed her in the center of public accusation.
Her sin was being discussed.
Her shame was exposed.
And the crowd was waiting for a verdict.
Jesus responded in a way that confronted the accusers' self-righteousness without declaring sin acceptable.
When the accusers departed, He told the woman that He did not condemn her and instructed her to leave her life of sin.

There is an important textual detail here: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is marked as textually disputed in many modern Bibles. It should therefore be handled with appropriate caution rather than used as the sole foundation for a doctrine.
Nevertheless, the broader New Testament clearly establishes both truths: Christ calls sinners to repentance, and salvation is received through His grace.
The Gospel does not say that sin is harmless.
It says sin is so serious that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
And grace is so astonishing that those who repent and believe in Christ can receive forgiveness instead of the condemnation they deserve.
That is why the cross should make Christians both courageous and humble.
Courageous, because truth matters.
Humble, because none of us stands before God as a self-made example of righteousness.
We stand in need of mercy.
Every one of us.
The person who has been a Christian for thirty years.
The pastor who teaches every Sunday.
The believer who posts Scripture every morning.
The new convert still learning how to walk with Jesus.
And the person who has been secretly struggling while everyone assumes their spiritual life is strong.
Nobody graduates beyond the need for grace.
Nobody becomes too spiritually important to repent.
Nobody defends the Gospel so successfully that they are exempt from obeying it.
And perhaps that is why Jesus' words in Luke 6:46 are so piercing:
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?” (ESV)
Read that again.
Not because it is complicated.
But because it is not.
Jesus connects calling Him Lord with obeying what He says.
He does not teach that our obedience purchases salvation.
Scripture is clear that salvation is God's gift, received by grace through faith, not earned by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the very next verse teaches that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Good works are not the price of redemption.
They are part of the life for which the redeemed have been created.
Obedience does not make Jesus our Savior.
Jesus saves us by grace.
And His saving grace does not leave us indifferent to His commands.
That distinction matters.
Because an article about hypocrisy can easily become another instrument of hypocrisy if it merely encourages us to condemn everyone else.
It is easy to read these words and immediately think of someone you know.
A pastor who preached holiness while living dishonestly.
A Christian influencer who spoke about humility while treating others with contempt.
A family member who quoted Scripture but wounded you deeply.
A church leader who defended morality while concealing misconduct.
Perhaps you have legitimate reasons to feel hurt.
Perhaps you have seen hypocrisy so destructive that it made you question whether the Christian faith itself was trustworthy.
That pain should not be dismissed.

Religious hypocrisy can inflict lasting wounds, particularly when authority, manipulation, or abuse are involved. Forgiveness does not require concealing wrongdoing, abandoning appropriate boundaries, or refusing to seek justice.
But before you use this article as evidence against someone else, consider one uncomfortable possibility.
What if God also wants to speak to you?
Not to deny what others have done.
Not to excuse their behavior.
But to reveal the places in your own life where knowing the truth has become easier than living it.
Because it is possible to be right about another person's sin and still be resisting God's correction of your own heart.
Jesus asked in Matthew 7:3 why someone notices the speck in another person's eye while overlooking the log in their own.
He did not forbid all moral discernment.
In Matthew 7:5, He instructed the hypocrite to remove the log first, so that they could see clearly to help their brother.
The point was not that sin should never be addressed.
The point was that correction must begin with honest self-examination.
And sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do after reading a controversial post is not write a response.
It is close the app.
Sit quietly.
And ask God a question you have been avoiding.
“Lord, where am I demanding from others what I refuse to practice myself?”
That prayer can change the direction of a life.
Because suddenly, the issue is no longer merely what is wrong with the Church.
It becomes what Christ is calling you to surrender.
Perhaps you have defended biblical marriage online while neglecting the tenderness, faithfulness, and sacrificial love your own marriage needs.
Perhaps you have written passionately about honoring parents while carrying bitterness you refuse to address.
Perhaps you have preached generosity while being unwilling to help someone in genuine need.
Perhaps you have demanded purity from others while hiding habits that are slowly hardening your conscience.
Perhaps you have defended the authority of Scripture while selectively ignoring the verses that confront your pride.
And perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you know exactly what has happened.
You still believe the Bible.
You still love the idea of following Jesus.
But somewhere along the way, you became more committed to protecting your Christian reputation than exposing your heart to God's transforming grace.
You learned how to sound spiritually strong while becoming spiritually exhausted.
You learned how to correct people while avoiding correction.
You learned how to defend the light while keeping certain rooms of your life locked in darkness.
And now you are tired.
Tired of performing.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of having an answer for everyone else while secretly struggling with questions about your own walk with God.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The answer is not to abandon Jesus because you have failed to resemble Him. The answer is to return to Jesus, who alone can forgive and transform you.
The Gospel is not merely good news for the unbeliever who has never entered a church.
It remains good news for the believer who has drifted into pride, compromise, resentment, or hypocrisy.
The same Savior who calls you to repentance is the Savior who welcomes those who come to Him in faith.
First John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from a verb commonly used for acknowledging or confessing.
In this context, confession means honestly acknowledging our sins before God rather than denying them.
Not dressing them up.
Not blaming everyone else.
Not turning every correction into an argument.
Not using religious language to protect what God is calling us to forsake.
Just coming into the light.
“Lord, I have been proud.”
“Lord, I have been cruel.”
“Lord, I have spoken about forgiveness while refusing to forgive.”
“Lord, I have wanted people to admire my faith more than I have wanted You to change my heart.”
“Lord, I know what Your Word says. Please help me obey it.”
There is no need to perform before the One who already knows you completely.
He knows the conversations you regret.
The promises you broke.
The resentment you carry.
The habits you conceal.
The times you defended righteousness publicly while privately choosing what you knew was wrong.
And He also knows the full cost of redemption.
The cross was not an empty religious symbol.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for sinners.
He died and rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed.
That is the foundation of our hope.
Not our reputation.
Not our online influence.
Not our ability to answer difficult theological questions.
Christ Himself.
And when His grace takes hold of a life, something begins to change.
Not always instantly.
Not without struggle.
Not without painful confession, restitution where appropriate, difficult conversations, or the daily discipline of obedience.
But genuinely.
The person who once needed to win every argument begins learning how to listen.
The person who once hid behind spiritual language begins telling the truth about their failures.
The parent who once demanded respect without showing gentleness begins apologizing when wrong.
The spouse who once used Scripture to control begins learning what sacrificial love actually requires.
The believer who once treated repentance as something other people needed begins practicing it personally.
And the Christian who once saw every disagreement as an opportunity to defeat someone begins recognizing an opportunity to bear witness to Christ.
That is transformation.
Not merely changing what you post.
Changing how you live.
Romans 12:2 calls believers not to be conformed to this world but to be transformed through the renewal of the mind.
The Greek verb μεταμορφοῦσθε (metamorphousthe) means “be transformed.”
It describes transformation, not merely the adoption of a religious appearance.
Christian discipleship involves a life increasingly shaped by God's truth.
And sometimes that transformation begins with something as ordinary and difficult as saying:
“I was wrong.”
No excuses.
No theological speech to make yourself sound better.
No reminder of how much worse someone else's behavior was.
Just an honest acknowledgment.
“I hurt you. I sinned. Will you forgive me?”
Imagine how different our Christian witness would become if we practiced that kind of humility as passionately as we defended doctrine.
Imagine fathers who could explain Scripture and also admit when they had failed their children.
Mothers who taught biblical truth and modeled patient, truthful love.
Husbands and wives who stopped using religious correctness as ammunition against one another.
Church leaders who welcomed accountability instead of fearing it.
Believers who corrected false teaching without delighting in the humiliation of those who were mistaken.
Christians who were as concerned about the integrity of their private lives as they were about the accuracy of their public statements.
Not a Church without conviction.
A Church whose convictions are visible in its conduct.
Not a Church that refuses to confront sin.
A Church willing to confront its own sin first.
Not a Church that replaces truth with kindness.
A Church that understands why truth and love must walk together.
Because the world does not need Christians who merely know how to describe holiness.
It needs the witness of Christians who are actually being made holy by the grace of God.
And yes, that process will expose our failures.
There will be days when we speak too quickly.
Days when pride gets the better of us.
Days when our patience disappears.
Days when we discover that we have not grown as much as we imagined.
But the evidence of God's work is not that a believer never struggles.
It is that the believer does not make permanent peace with the sin Christ calls them to forsake.
A repentant Christian does not need to pretend to be flawless.
They need to keep coming honestly to the Savior who is faithful.
And that brings us to a question that cannot be answered with a comment-section victory.
If the people closest to you described your Christianity without mentioning anything you post online, what would they say?
Would they describe someone who listens?
Someone who apologizes?
Someone who keeps promises?
Someone who tells the truth even when lying would be easier?
Someone who is patient with the weak?
Someone who shows compassion without compromising conviction?
Someone who can be corrected?
Someone whose faith becomes most visible when life becomes most difficult?
Or would they describe a person who knows many verses but has not learned how to live beside other people with grace?
This is not an invitation to obsess over whether everyone approves of you. Even faithful obedience can be misunderstood, and no human relationship provides a perfect measure of spiritual maturity.
But it is an invitation to examine whether our closest relationships reveal patterns we have been unwilling to confront.
Because those who live with us often encounter the version of our faith that the internet never sees.
And sometimes their pain reveals a contradiction that our public reputation has concealed.
So before you write another passionate defense of biblical truth, consider the possibility that the Holy Spirit is inviting you into a quieter, harder act of obedience.
Make the apology.
Tell the truth.
Confess the hidden sin.
Seek accountability.
Honor the commitment.
Practice generosity.
Show patience.
Refuse the cruel reply.
Listen before condemning.
Forgive without pretending wrongdoing was acceptable.
Take appropriate action to repair what you have damaged.
And when you fail, return to Christ instead of constructing another excuse.
None of these acts will make you famous.
Some may never be noticed.
But faithfulness does not become less meaningful because nobody applauds it.
Colossians 3:23 teaches believers to work heartily as for the Lord rather than merely for people.
The God who sees what is done in secret is not limited by the world's measurements of success.
Your private obedience matters.
Your unseen repentance matters.
Your quiet acts of mercy matter.
Your decision to honor Christ when nobody is watching matters.
And your willingness to be changed by the truth you defend matters far more than the number of strangers who agree with you.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create a louder religious audience.
Not to manufacture outrage.
Not to turn biblical conviction into entertainment.
But to call people back to Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and genuine discipleship.
Because the goal is not simply to help people recognize what is wrong with the world.
The goal is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and respond with lives increasingly surrendered to Christ.
That kind of work requires more than a viral post.
It requires consistent biblical teaching, resources for spiritual growth, encouragement for struggling believers, and a community willing to pursue truth even when truth confronts us personally.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration toward consistent engagement with Scripture.
Because a powerful message may stir your heart for a moment.
But discipleship calls for a lifetime of following Jesus.
If this article has challenged you, do not let the conviction disappear when the next notification arrives.
Not as another inspirational post to collect, but as something to revisit when you are tempted to confuse defending truth with practicing it.
And think of one person who needs encouragement rather than condemnation.
Perhaps someone you love has been wounded by Christian hypocrisy.
Perhaps a friend has become discouraged by the hostility they see among believers.
Perhaps a family member knows Scripture well but is struggling to live it.
Perhaps an unbeliever has concluded that Christianity is nothing more than religious people judging one another.
Let them encounter a message that does not excuse hypocrisy but points beyond human failure to the grace and transforming power of Jesus Christ.
Not because following a page makes someone a disciple.
But because consistent exposure to biblical teaching can become one helpful part of a much deeper journey of learning, repentance, prayer, fellowship, and obedience.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this ministry, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Supporting Gospel ministry can be one meaningful way to glorify God through stewardship and generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not the suggestion that you must pay to receive God's favor.
The greatest gift we can share is still the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
And your worth before Him is not measured by your financial contribution to any ministry.
If you are able to support, thank you.
If you cannot, you are still welcome here.
What matters most is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that people are encouraged to know Him, trust Him, and follow Him.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something more personal than whether you agree with this article.
I want to ask whether it has revealed something you need to bring before God.
Not someone else's hypocrisy.
Yours.
Not someone else's failure.
The place where your own heart needs repentance, healing, courage, or renewed surrender.
You do not have to expose private details publicly. Some confessions belong in prayer, in appropriate pastoral care, or in safe and accountable conversations with people directly affected.
You do not need an impressive testimony.
You do not need polished religious language.
You do not need to pretend you have everything together.
Sometimes the beginning of genuine spiritual growth is an honest admission that something needs to change.
Because there is still hope for the Christian who has become proud.
There is still grace for the believer who has been living inconsistently.
There is still forgiveness for the person who has been hiding.
There is still restoration to pursue where relationships have been damaged.
There is still transformation through Jesus Christ.
Consider Peter.
He boldly declared that he was ready to follow Jesus even to prison and death.
Yet when the pressure came, he denied knowing Him three times.
His public confidence collapsed under the weight of fear.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61–62 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The disciple who had spoken so confidently now confronted the terrible reality of his own weakness.
He had said one thing.
And done another.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.

After His resurrection, Jesus met with Peter, and John 21 records a deeply personal conversation in which Peter was repeatedly asked about his love for Christ and entrusted with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
Peter was not restored because his denial was insignificant.
He was restored through the grace of the risen Lord.
And the same Peter who once failed so publicly later became a courageous witness to Christ.
That is not permission to treat sin lightly.
It is evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter for someone who returns to Jesus.
The Lord does not call us to manufacture an impressive religious image.
He calls us to follow Him.
Peter's story reminds us that a person can fail terribly and still be transformed by the grace of Christ.
And perhaps that is the message you needed most today.
You do not need to win another argument to prove you love Jesus.
You need to answer His call to follow Him.
You do not need to pretend your private life is perfect.
You need to bring it honestly into His light.
You do not need to silence every critic.
You need to listen when God's Word corrects you.
And you do not need to spend the rest of your life trapped inside the contradiction between the faith you proclaim and the life you actually live.
Through Jesus Christ, repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is real.
Grace is sufficient.
And transformation is not an empty religious slogan.
It is the work of God in people who belong to Christ.
So defend biblical truth.
Do not be ashamed of the Gospel.
Do not compromise what Scripture teaches simply because the culture disagrees.
Speak courageously when courage is required.
But remember this.
The same Bible that calls you to contend for the faith also calls you to humility, self-control, gentleness, forgiveness, holiness, and love.
The same Jesus you proclaim publicly is Lord over your private life.
The same cross you point others toward is the place where your own pride must surrender.
And the same grace you want the world to receive is the grace you must never stop needing yourself.
One day, the arguments will end.
The comment sections will fall silent.
The applause will fade.
The online reputation you worked so hard to build will no longer be the question.
What will matter is whether you truly belong to Jesus Christ—the Savior who knows your heart, whose grace alone saves, and whose transforming work bears fruit in the lives of those who follow Him.
So the next time you feel compelled to defend Jesus in public, remember to honor Him in private.
Let your words be truthful.
Let your conduct be faithful.
Let your repentance be genuine.
Let your love be visible.
And let the people who know you beyond the screen encounter something more than your ability to quote Scripture.
Let them see the evidence of a life being changed by the Savior Scripture reveals.
Because the greatest testimony is not that you have never fallen.
It is that, by God's grace, you no longer want to remain where you fell.
The world may remember what you said about Jesus, but the people closest to you will remember whether your life helped them see Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE PERSON WHO PROMISED TO LOVE YOU FOREVER LOOKS YOU IN THE EYES AND SAYS, “I DON'T FIND YOU SEXUALLY ATTRACTIVE ANYMORE”?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE PERSON WHO PROMISED TO LOVE YOU FOREVER LOOKS YOU IN THE EYES AND SAYS, “I DON'T FIND YOU SEXUALLY ATTRACTIVE ANYMORE”?

The confession that can shatter a marriage without ending it—and the heartbreaking truth about desire, rejection, covenant love, and the God who sees you when the person beside you no longer seems to.
There are sentences that hurt when you hear them.
And then there are sentences that move into your chest, rearrange everything you believed about yourself, and refuse to leave.
“I don't find you sexually attractive anymore.”
Seven words, depending on how they're spoken. But the damage they can do?
Sometimes years.

Imagine sitting across from the person who once couldn't wait to hold you. The person who used to reach for your hand without thinking. The person who once looked at you as though the rest of the world had disappeared.
And now they're looking at you differently.
Maybe they said it gently. Maybe they were frustrated. Maybe it came during an argument. Maybe you asked the question because you'd been feeling the distance for months.
“Do you still find me attractive?”
And for one terrible moment, they hesitated.
That hesitation told you something before their mouth ever did.
Then came the confession.
And suddenly, you weren't thinking about marriage counseling, communication, or rebuilding intimacy.
You were thinking about your stomach.
Your wrinkles.
Your weight.
Your hair.
The scars from childbirth. The changes from aging. The exhaustion that has settled into your face after years of carrying responsibilities nobody else sees.
You remembered the younger version of yourself.
The one who stood at the altar.
The one who believed that being chosen meant never having to wonder whether you were enough.
And somewhere in the silence, a question began forming that you were almost too ashamed to say aloud.
“If my own spouse doesn't want me anymore, what does that say about me?”
Stay with me, because what happens after that question can either begin the slow destruction of your marriage—or expose wounds that Jesus wants to bring into the light.
And the answer is not as simple as telling you to pray harder, lose weight, dress better, or accept that attraction disappears with age.
The Bible has something far more honest to say.
Something both confronting and healing.
Because the tragedy is not merely that your spouse's desire may have changed.
The deeper tragedy would be allowing another person's changing desire to become the final authority over your God-given worth.
And that is where we must begin.
Not with the mirror.
Not with your spouse.
But with the God who knew you before anyone ever found you beautiful.
Genesis 1:27 declares:
“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” (KJV)
The Hebrew expression בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים (be-tselem Elohim) means “in the image of God.”
Think about what that means.
Before your wedding photographs.
Before your first kiss.
Before anyone complimented your appearance.
Before someone desired your body.
Before age, pregnancy, illness, disability, stress, or the passing years changed anything about you...
You already possessed a dignity no human being had the authority to give you.
And therefore, no human being has the authority to take it away.
You were made in God's image.
Not in the image of your spouse's preferences.
Not in the image of cultural beauty standards.
Not in the image of who you used to be twenty years ago.
Your spouse may struggle to desire you. But their struggle does not cancel your dignity.
Read that again.
Because somebody has been standing in front of a mirror, silently apologizing to themselves for growing older.
Somebody has been avoiding intimacy because rejection feels unbearable.
Somebody has been pretending not to care because admitting how much it hurts would make the pain feel even more real.
And somebody has been crying beside a sleeping spouse, wondering how two people can share the same bed and still feel so terribly alone.
Jesus sees that person.
He sees you.
But Scripture does not stop at comforting the wounded spouse.
It also confronts the person whose attraction has changed.
Because marriage was never meant to be a lifelong arrangement dependent upon the permanent preservation of youthful appearance.
When you stood before God and made your vows, you were not promising that your spouse would remain physically unchanged.
You were promising faithfulness to a real human being who would inevitably change.
Aging was always coming.
Sickness was always possible.
Exhaustion, disappointment, and seasons of emotional distance were never outside the possibilities of married life.
And if your understanding of marriage was built entirely upon physical excitement, you may have entered a covenant with the expectations of a temporary romance.
That is a dangerous foundation.
Malachi 2:14 describes marriage in striking language:
“Yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.” (KJV)
The Hebrew word בְּרִית (berit) means “covenant.”
A covenant is not simply a passing emotional preference.
It is a binding commitment involving faithfulness and responsibility.

In Malachi's context, God confronts men who have acted treacherously toward their wives. The passage is not teaching that spouses must manufacture sexual desire on command. It is confronting marital unfaithfulness.
And that distinction matters.
Because love and attraction are related, but they are not identical.
A person may genuinely love their spouse while experiencing a painful decline in sexual desire.
Hormonal changes can affect desire.
Depression can affect desire.
Certain medications can affect desire.
Chronic pain, unresolved conflict, emotional disconnection, trauma, exhaustion, and ongoing resentment can affect desire.
Sometimes the issue is physical.
Sometimes it is relational.
Sometimes it is psychological.
Sometimes it is a combination of several things.
And sometimes the person experiencing the change does not fully understand it themselves.
That is why the confession “I don't find you attractive anymore” should not automatically become a verdict on the marriage.
It should become the beginning of a deeper, truthful conversation.
Not an excuse for cruelty.
Not permission for infidelity.
Not an invitation to humiliate the other person.
A conversation.
Because there is an enormous difference between saying:
“You are no longer desirable.”
And saying:
“Something has changed in how I experience desire, and I don't understand it yet. I love you, and I want us to face this together.”
One statement can crush a person's sense of worth.
The other acknowledges a serious problem while protecting the dignity of the person who shares your life.
Words matter.
Especially when spoken by the person whose words carry the most weight in your heart.
Proverbs 18:21 says:
“Death and life are in the power of the tongue...” (KJV)
This is wisdom literature emphasizing the profound consequences of speech, not a claim that words possess magical power.
But anyone who has been wounded by a spouse's careless confession understands its truth.
Some sentences can remain in a marriage long after the argument ends.
And if you are the spouse who said those devastating words, please hear this.
