Honesty is important.
But honesty without tenderness can become cruelty.
You are not required to pretend you feel something you do not feel.
You are responsible for how you treat the person entrusted to your care.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak “the truth in love.”
Not truth instead of love.
Not love that avoids truth.
Truth in love.
Because your spouse is not a product whose value expires when your preferences change.
Your spouse is a person.
A fellow image-bearer.
Someone with fears, vulnerabilities, memories, and a heart that may still be reaching for you even after your desire has weakened.
And before you make their body the explanation for everything that has changed, ask yourself something uncomfortable.
Have you stopped finding your spouse attractive—or have you stopped truly seeing your spouse?
There is a difference.
When was the last time you looked at them without criticizing something?
When was the last time you listened without waiting for your turn to speak?
When was the last time you noticed their sacrifices?
The hands that worked to provide.
The body that carried your children, if that is part of your story.
The shoulders that carried grief.
The eyes that stayed awake when the family was struggling.
The face that has aged beside yours.
Have you become so accustomed to their presence that you no longer recognize the extraordinary gift of being known by someone who has seen your worst days and still remains willing to walk with you?
That question may be painful.
But sometimes repentance begins with realizing that we have been treating a gift as though it were an inconvenience.
Still, we must be careful.
Not every loss of attraction is evidence of selfishness.
Not every sexually distant spouse is unloving.
And not every struggling marriage can be healed by simply deciding to appreciate one another more.
Real problems deserve real attention.
A spouse experiencing persistent loss of desire may need medical assessment, emotional support, counseling, or help addressing unresolved relational wounds.
A couple may need to rebuild trust before sexual closeness feels safe.
And if there has been coercion, betrayal, humiliation, or abuse, the solution is not to demand more physical intimacy from the wounded person.
Safety, accountability, and appropriate support matter.
Biblical faithfulness never requires someone to surrender their bodily autonomy or remain exposed to abuse.
The God who commands love does not authorize cruelty in its name.
Now consider something that many Christian couples rarely discuss honestly.
The Bible does not portray sexual desire within marriage as something dirty or unspiritual.
It recognizes its goodness.
Song of Solomon contains vivid expressions of affection, admiration, longing, and mutual delight.
In Song of Solomon 4:7, the beloved declares:
“Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.” (KJV)
This is poetic language of delighted admiration, not a theological assertion that a spouse is literally flawless.
The lover is expressing the beauty he sees in the beloved.
And perhaps that is something many marriages have forgotten.
Physical intimacy was never meant to be reduced to mechanical obligation.
It involves being welcomed.
Being cherished.
Being emotionally safe.
Being desired rather than merely tolerated.
For the spouse who has been rejected, that distinction can be heartbreaking.
Because sometimes what you miss most is not sex itself.
It's being wanted.
It's the spontaneous embrace.
The affectionate glance.
The hand resting gently on your shoulder.
The feeling that the person who knows you most intimately still delights in being near you.
And when those things disappear, the wound can reach far deeper than physical frustration.
You begin wondering whether affection has become something you must earn.
Whether you need to become thinner, younger, stronger, prettier, more successful, or more sexually adventurous just to deserve attention.
But please listen carefully.
You may work on your health. You may grow in confidence. You may address habits that affect your relationship. But you must never confuse personal growth with purchasing the right to be loved.
You are not a renovation project whose completion determines whether you deserve tenderness.
You are a human being.
And in Christ, you are called to live from grace—not from the terror of never being enough.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
The Greek expression ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν (eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn) conveys “while we were still sinners.”
Paul's point is not about sexual attractiveness or marriage.
It is about the astonishing initiative of God's love in Christ toward people who had not earned His favor.
And that truth speaks powerfully to the person who has begun measuring their entire worth by whether another human being wants them.
God's saving love was never purchased by your appearance.
Christ did not go to the cross because humanity was impressive enough to deserve Him.
He came in mercy.
He died for sinners.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered by grace.
That does not mean human rejection stops hurting.
It means human rejection is not the final word about who you are.
And if you are reading this while carrying a wound your spouse does not even realize is still bleeding, I want you to understand something.
You do not have to pretend the confession didn't hurt.
You do not have to call emotional devastation a lack of faith.
You do not have to smile through rejection to prove that you are spiritually mature.
You can grieve.
You can speak honestly.
You can say, “When you told me that, something inside me broke, and I need you to understand why.”
You can ask for patience.
You can ask for counseling.
You can ask whether your spouse is willing to work with you toward rebuilding closeness.
And you can acknowledge that healing may take time.
But there is another side of this story that must not be ignored.
What if you are the one who no longer feels attracted?
What if you still care deeply for your husband or wife, but the physical longing you once experienced has faded?
What if you are ashamed to admit it?
What if you are afraid that telling the truth will destroy the person you love?
You need more than condemnation.
You need wisdom.
Because feelings cannot always be commanded into existence.
But our responses to those feelings are moral choices.
You can choose honesty instead of deception.
Kindness instead of contempt.
Faithfulness instead of betrayal.
Curiosity instead of blame.
You can investigate what has changed without treating your spouse as defective.
You can refuse to compare them with carefully edited images, fantasies, or unrealistic expectations.
You can examine whether pornography, secret relationships, or habitual comparison have influenced your desires, without assuming those are the cause in every marriage.
You can ask whether unresolved anger has gradually poisoned affection.
You can seek qualified help.
And you can pray not merely, “Lord, make my spouse attractive to me again,” but also:
“Lord, search my heart. Show me where I have become selfish, resentful, dishonest, or unkind. Help me see my spouse truthfully and love them faithfully.”
That is a different prayer.
And it may lead to a different kind of transformation.
Psalm 139:23–24 says:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” (KJV)
Notice the posture.
Not, “God, expose everything wrong with my spouse.”
But, “Search me.”
There is something profoundly humbling about inviting God to examine the heart we have spent years defending.

And sometimes, the most important change in a marriage begins when someone stops asking, “Why aren't you enough for me?” and starts asking, “What has happened inside us—and what responsibility must I take?”
That does not guarantee restored attraction.
It does open the door to truth.
And truth is where genuine restoration must begin.
Consider 1 Corinthians 7:3–5.
Paul speaks about mutual marital responsibilities and warns spouses against unilateral, prolonged sexual deprivation, while recognizing mutual agreement and seasons of abstinence.
The Greek phrase ἐκ συμφώνου (ek symphōnou) in verse 5 means “by agreement” or “by mutual consent.”
That is significant.
Paul addresses husbands and wives with reciprocal responsibilities. The passage must not be twisted into permission for forced sex, intimidation, or the dismissal of a spouse's pain.
Sexual intimacy should never be weaponized.
Not as punishment.
Not as leverage.
Not as proof that someone is spiritually obedient.
A marriage may have genuine obligations of mutual care, but physical intimacy cannot be made loving through coercion.
And if the relationship has become a place of fear, the immediate priority is not increasing sexual frequency.
It is addressing the fear.
This is where some marriages need a very different kind of courage.
The courage to stop pretending.
The courage to admit that resentment has accumulated.
That trust has eroded.
That exhaustion has replaced tenderness.
That a husband or wife has been silently lonely for years.
And perhaps the courage to say:
“I don't know how to fix this. But I don't want us to keep hurting each other while pretending nothing is wrong.”
That sentence may not sound romantic.
But it can be the beginning of something deeply meaningful.
Because marriage restoration is not always cinematic.
Sometimes it looks like two tired people sitting in a counselor's office.
Sometimes it looks like a difficult medical appointment.
Sometimes it looks like learning to communicate without attacking.
Sometimes it looks like a spouse finally apologizing without adding excuses.
Sometimes it looks like rebuilding affectionate touch without making every embrace a demand for sex.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving a careless statement while still allowing time for trust to recover.
And sometimes it looks like acknowledging that the relationship has serious problems requiring boundaries, accountability, and outside help.
There is no biblical promise that every struggling marriage will recover its former sexual attraction.
We must not promise what Scripture does not promise.
But there is a biblical call to faithfulness, truthfulness, repentance, patience, and love.
And those things matter whether restoration happens quickly, slowly, or not in the way we hoped.
Ephesians 5:25 commands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
The Greek verb ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is a command to love.
Paul grounds the husband's responsibility in Christ's sacrificial love.
He does not say, “Love your wife as long as she looks the way she did when you married her.”
He points to Jesus.
And Jesus did not demonstrate love by exploiting weakness.
He gave Himself.
The passage also calls marriage toward reverence, holiness, and profound unity, not domination or self-serving demands.
Christ's love is not a justification for mistreatment.
It is the standard that exposes it.
And for the spouse who has been wounded, there is another essential truth.
Christlike love does not mean you must silently absorb repeated humiliation.
Forgiveness is not pretending something never happened.
Reconciliation requires truth and, where wrongdoing has occurred, meaningful repentance.
Trust is rebuilt through consistent actions.
You can forgive someone while still acknowledging that their words caused serious harm.
You can desire restoration while insisting that cruelty stop.
You can remain committed to biblical marriage while seeking protection and wise counsel when necessary.
Grace does not require denial.
And repentance is more than saying, “I'm sorry you felt that way.”
It sounds more like:
“I wounded you. I spoke carelessly. I made you feel unwanted and ashamed. I understand why that hurt, and I want to take responsibility for what I said.”
For some readers, hearing those words from a spouse would feel like rain falling on ground that has been dry for years.
But maybe your spouse has not said them.
Maybe they don't even know how.
Maybe you're still waiting.
And that brings us to one of the hardest truths in this entire conversation.
You cannot force another person to desire you, repent, or participate in rebuilding the marriage.
You can communicate.
You can pray.
You can pursue wise help.
You can take responsibility for your own behavior.
You can offer reconciliation where it is safe and appropriate.
But you cannot carry a marriage alone.
And you were never meant to make another person's response the measure of your relationship with God.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that comes from loving someone who no longer reaches for you.
It can make you question everything.
Your attractiveness.
Your identity.
Your future.
Even your faith.
But remember the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus met a Samaritan woman whose relational history was complicated. He knew the truth about her life, including her history of multiple husbands and her current relationship.
Yet He did not treat her as invisible.
He spoke to her.
He revealed Himself to her.
He offered living water.
We must not impose a story of sexual rejection onto this woman that the text never tells.
But we can recognize something unmistakable in the passage.
Jesus encountered a person with a complicated relational life and did not reduce her to that history.
He led the conversation toward truth and worship.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that.
You are more than the most painful thing that has happened in your marriage.
More than your spouse's opinion.
More than your body.
More than your sexual history.
More than your fear of being replaced.
You are a person whom God calls to Himself through Jesus Christ.
And even when your marriage feels uncertain, the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come into the light.
Bring the grief.
Bring the anger.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the insecurity.
Bring the bitterness you have been too ashamed to confess.
Bring the secret comparisons.
Bring the unspoken resentment.
Bring the fear that you will never be desired again.
Do not pretend those things are not there.
Bring them to Christ.
Because the Gospel is not a demand that wounded people act as though they are fine.
It is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven, the brokenhearted can find comfort in God, and people can be transformed through the grace of Jesus Christ.
Not every consequence disappears.
Not every relationship is restored.
But no person who turns to Christ in faith and repentance is beyond the reach of His mercy.
And now, I want to speak to the person who has quietly been blaming themselves for everything.
Maybe your spouse's confession sent you into a desperate attempt to become desirable again.
You changed your clothes.
You changed your diet.
You changed your hairstyle.
You tried to become more affectionate.
You tried to become less demanding.
You studied every expression on their face.
You started measuring yourself against strangers.
And every time they failed to respond the way you hoped, another piece of your confidence disappeared.
Please hear this.
There is nothing wrong with caring for your body.
There is nothing wrong with pursuing physical health.
There is nothing wrong with wanting to nurture romance and attraction within marriage.
But you are not required to destroy yourself in the attempt to control another person's desires.
Your body is not your enemy.
Your age is not a moral failure.
Your scars are not evidence that you have become unworthy of tenderness.
And your spouse's loss of attraction, painful as it may be, does not prove that you have failed as a husband or wife.
You may have areas where you need to grow.
So may your spouse.
But growth should be pursued in truth, not in terror.
And if you are the spouse who has withdrawn affection, consider what your partner may be experiencing.
They may be lying awake beside you, wondering whether you regret marrying them.
They may have stopped initiating affection because they cannot bear another rejection.
They may smile in public and cry in private.
They may have begun believing that their body has become a burden to you.
You may not have intended all of that.
But if your words or behavior have contributed to that pain, love calls you to take it seriously.
Not with false promises.
Not with forced intimacy.
But with compassion, accountability, and a willingness to seek understanding together.
Because one of the cruelest things that can happen in a marriage is for one spouse to experience a wound while the other insists there is nothing to discuss.
And one of the most hopeful things that can happen is for both people to admit that something is broken without immediately deciding that the other person is the enemy.
Your spouse is not your enemy simply because desire has changed.
And you are not worthless simply because your spouse is struggling.
There may still be a path forward.
But it will require more than pretending.
It will require truth spoken with kindness.
It may require professional help.
It will require each person to take responsibility for what belongs to them.
And for Christians, it should include bringing the marriage before God with humility rather than using Scripture to win arguments.
Because Jesus Christ is not a weapon to use against your spouse.
He is Lord.
And His Word calls both of you to truth.
Perhaps tonight, the most meaningful thing you can do is sit beside your spouse and say:
“I need to talk about what happened between us. Not to attack you. Not to pressure you. But because I miss feeling close to you, and I don't want us to keep living like strangers.”
And perhaps the other person will finally answer:
“I miss us too.”
Or perhaps the conversation will reveal deeper problems.
Either way, you will have begun replacing silence with truth.
And that matters.
If you are not safe having that conversation alone, seek support from a qualified professional or a trusted person who can help you protect your well-being.
No article can diagnose your marriage from a distance.
But Scripture gives us a direction.
Love truthfully.
Repent where necessary.
Refuse cruelty.
Honor one another's dignity.
Seek wisdom.
And keep Christ at the center.
Because here is what makes the Gospel so different from the world's obsession with desirability.
The world often asks, “Are you still attractive enough to be chosen?”
The Gospel asks us to behold the Savior who came to redeem sinners who could never earn His grace.
The world says, “Stay impressive, or risk being discarded.”
Christ calls us away from building our identity upon the unstable approval of human beings.
The world can turn love into a competition of appearances.
Jesus calls His people toward sacrificial love, holiness, faithfulness, and truth.
And the cross exposes the poverty of every version of love that exists only to serve itself.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our romantic relationships.
He came to save sinners.
Through His death and resurrection, He accomplished what no human relationship could ever accomplish: reconciliation with God for those who trust in Him.
That is the foundation.
Marriage is precious.
But marriage is not your savior.
Sexual attraction is a meaningful gift.
But attraction is not your god.
Your spouse's affection matters.
But it cannot carry the full weight of your identity.
Only Christ belongs at the center of that place.
And when He is there, you can face painful truths without surrendering your entire worth to them.
You can grieve without believing you are worthless.
You can repent without believing you are beyond redemption.
You can pursue restoration without pretending that restoration is guaranteed.
You can love faithfully without calling abuse love.
You can hope without lying to yourself.
And you can trust that the Lord remains worthy of worship even when your marriage is passing through a season you never imagined.
That is not shallow optimism.
That is faith learning to stand in the middle of uncertainty.
And perhaps that is the message someone in your family needs tonight.
Not another perfect photograph of a smiling couple.
Not another Christian slogan that ignores complicated pain.
But an honest reminder that marriages involve real people, real bodies, real wounds, real choices, and a real need for the grace of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to reveal intimate details about your spouse or expose private conversations.
You can simply comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Or if you are struggling to find the courage to have an honest conversation, comment, “Pray for our marriage.”

And if God has helped you and your spouse rebuild closeness after a painful season, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading your words may need the encouragement that change is possible, even when it takes time and hard work.
Not because every marriage can be repaired with a few paragraphs, but because you may need to return to these truths on a night when rejection feels louder than faith.
You may never know which married couple is silently struggling behind a beautiful family picture.
Which husband has stopped believing he is wanted.
Which wife has been crying over the changes in her body.
Which spouse is carrying guilt over a confession they wish they had expressed differently.
A thoughtful share may help someone find the courage to seek a healthier conversation, professional support, or renewed dependence upon Christ.
Sometimes sending an article privately is the kinder act.
We are here to speak about the realities people often hide behind their Sunday smiles.
Marriage.
Shame.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Temptation.
Loneliness.
Healing.
And above all, the redeeming grace of Jesus Christ.
Because we believe discipleship should not end when the church service is over.
It should reach the kitchen table.
The hospital room.
The exhausted parent.
The struggling marriage.
The person quietly wondering whether God still sees them.
Not out of guilt.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
But because supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful way to serve others for His glory.
Scripture teaches that believers may generously support those who minister the Word. Philippians 4:15–18 records Paul's gratitude for the Philippians' financial partnership in his ministry.
Paul describes their gift as an offering pleasing to God.
That gives us a beautiful picture of voluntary generosity.
These free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter Scripture, hear the Gospel, and be pointed toward Jesus Christ.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still make a difference.
Pray for this ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Speak truth with love.
And keep pointing people to Christ.
Because the mission is bigger than a platform.
Bigger than any one article.
It is about Jesus being known, His Word being heard, and wounded people discovering that grace is not merely a beautiful religious word.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners, revealed supremely through Jesus Christ.
And when that grace takes hold of a life, it changes how we confess, forgive, love, endure, and begin again.
So, to the spouse who no longer feels attractive...
To the husband who misses being desired...
To the wife who no longer recognizes herself in the mirror...
To the person whose heart sank when their spouse finally told the truth...
And to the spouse who wants to find a way back but does not know where to begin...
Do not allow this painful chapter to become the entire definition of your story.
Seek truth.
Seek wisdom.
Seek help when you need it.
Repent where you have sinned.
Extend grace without abandoning necessary boundaries.
And bring your broken places to Jesus.
Because He is not frightened by the conversations you are afraid to have.
He is not surprised by the weakness you have been hiding.
And He does not ask you to pretend that your wounds are healed when they are not.
He calls you to Himself.
Maybe your marriage will find renewed tenderness.
Maybe rebuilding trust will take longer than you hoped.
Maybe you will need to confront realities you have spent years avoiding.
But whatever happens next, do not forget the truth that existed before your spouse ever chose you.
You were created in God's image.
And the invitation to find forgiveness, new life, and lasting hope in Jesus Christ remains open.
The person you love may no longer look at you the way they once did—but the cross still declares that your deepest worth was never theirs to decide.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A PERSON BE SAVED, LOVE JESUS, AND STILL END UP LOST FOREVER?
paragraphs: CAN A PERSON BE SAVED, LOVE JESUS, AND STILL END UP LOST FOREVER?
Jesus Said No One Can Snatch His Sheep Away. Hebrews Warns That Some Can Fall Away. And John Says Some Who Left Were Never Truly His. What Happens When All Three Scriptures Confront the Same Soul?
There is a kind of silence that falls over a Christian's heart when someone who once loved Jesus suddenly says, "I don't believe anymore."
Not someone who merely attended church.
Not someone who only knew how to quote Bible verses.
Someone who prayed with tears in their eyes. Someone who worshiped with their hands lifted. Someone who spoke about the cross as though they had personally stood beneath it.
Someone who once told you, "Jesus changed my life."
And now?
They want nothing to do with Him.
Their Bible sits unopened. Their prayers have stopped. The faith they once defended is now something they question, reject, or even ridicule.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you remember how sincere they seemed.
You remember their testimony.
You remember their tears.
You remember the way they spoke about heaven.
So a question begins to disturb you.
Can someone truly belong to Jesus Christ, receive salvation, and later lose everything by walking away?
Or is something even more unsettling possible?
Were they never truly saved at all?
And then another question quietly rises.
What if that person is me someday?
What if the faith I feel so strongly today grows cold tomorrow?
What if I stumble badly enough?
What if I become exhausted, distracted, deceived, or spiritually numb?
What if I wake up one morning and discover that the Jesus I once pursued has become a stranger to my heart?
This is not merely a theological argument.
For some people, it is the question that keeps them awake at night.
For others, it is the question they refuse to ask because they are terrified of the answer.
And for someone reading this right now, it may be the very question God will use to expose a dangerous false assurance—or bring a frightened, struggling believer back to the security of Christ.
Because the Bible contains three passages that refuse to let us settle for a shallow answer.
Jesus says His sheep will never perish.
Hebrews warns about people who fall away after experiencing extraordinary spiritual privileges.
And John says some who departed from the Christian community revealed that they never truly belonged.
All three are Scripture.
All three must be taken seriously.
And none should be silenced simply because another makes us uncomfortable.
Listen carefully to the words of Jesus.
In John 10:27–29, He declares:

"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand." (KJV)
Read those words again.
"They shall never perish."
Jesus does not say, "I will try to keep them."
He does not say, "They will be secure as long as the enemy is not too powerful."
He does not say, "I will protect them unless the forces of darkness overwhelm My strength."
He says they will never perish.
The Greek text makes His promise especially forceful.
The expression is οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (ou mē apolōntai eis ton aiōna).
It communicates an emphatic denial: they will certainly never perish, forever.
The double negative οὐ μή is a powerful way of denying a future possibility in this construction.
Jesus is not offering His sheep a fragile hope.
He is announcing the strength of His saving care.
And notice something extraordinary.
He says, "I know them."
Before He speaks about their following Him, He speaks about His knowledge of them.
Their security is not grounded in the perfection of their grip upon Him.
It is grounded in the power of the Shepherd who holds them.
But do not overlook the other words.
"My sheep hear my voice ... and they follow me."
The Greek verbs ἀκούουσιν (akouousin, "they hear") and ἀκολουθοῦσίν (akolouthousin, "they follow") are present-tense forms describing the sheep's characteristic response to their Shepherd.
This does not mean genuine Christians never struggle, stumble, doubt, or disobey.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Thomas struggled to believe the resurrection.
The disciples themselves fled when Jesus was arrested.
Yet the sheep of Christ are not defined by a settled, final rejection of their Shepherd.
They are people who belong to Him and respond to His voice.
This distinction matters.
Because there is a tremendous difference between a sheep that has fallen into a pit and a person who has never belonged to the flock.
And there is a difference between struggling to follow Jesus and deliberately declaring that you want no part of Him.
A wounded sheep still needs its Shepherd.
A wandering sheep still needs to be brought home.
And the Good Shepherd is not indifferent to either.
Remember what Jesus said in Luke 15 about the shepherd who went after the lost sheep until he found it.
He did not celebrate the sheep's wandering.
He went looking for it.
That is the heart of Christ.
But just when we begin to rest comfortably in John 10, another passage confronts us.
And it is impossible to read it thoughtfully without feeling the weight of its warning.

Hebrews 6:4–6 describes people who were once enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, became partakers of the Holy Ghost, tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come, and then fell away.
The passage says that renewing such people again to repentance is impossible, describing their apostasy in terms of crucifying the Son of God afresh and exposing Him to shame.
These are not casual words.
They are among the most solemn warnings in the New Testament.
The Greek word translated "fall away" is παραπεσόντας (parapesontas), from parapiptō.
In this context, it refers to a grave departure or apostasy, not simply an ordinary moment of weakness.
The author is not describing a believer who became distracted during prayer.
He is not describing someone who struggled with temptation and later repented.
He is not describing a Christian who went through depression, spiritual dryness, or a painful season of unanswered questions.
The warning concerns something far more serious: a decisive turning away from Christ after profound exposure to the realities of the Christian faith.
But here is where faithful Christians have disagreed for centuries.
And we must be careful not to pretend that the debate is easier than Scripture allows.

Some Christians understand Hebrews 6 as a warning that genuine believers can finally abandon Christ and forfeit salvation. They point to the extraordinary descriptions of the people involved, especially their participation in the Holy Spirit.

Others understand the passage as describing people who experienced the blessings and power of the Christian community without ever possessing genuine saving faith. They point out that exposure to spiritual realities does not necessarily prove regeneration.
Still others understand these warnings as one of the means God uses to preserve His people: genuine believers hear the warning, take it seriously, and persevere through God's grace.
These interpretations differ significantly.
They cannot all be correct in exactly the same sense.
But each seeks to account for biblical language that deserves careful attention.
And the author of Hebrews himself gives us an important clue.
Immediately after this severe warning, he says:
"But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things that accompany salvation, though we thus speak." (Hebrews 6:9, KJV)
Do you see the significance?
The author distinguishes the frightening scenario he has described from the "things that accompany salvation" which he expects to see among his readers.
That observation is especially important to interpretations that distinguish profound spiritual exposure from genuine conversion.
Yet the warning remains real.
It is not a decorative threat.
It is not permission to say, "I once prayed a prayer, so nothing about my life matters anymore."
Hebrews repeatedly calls believers to hold fast to Christ.
Hebrews 3:14 says:
"For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end." (KJV)
The passage does not invite us to purchase salvation through endurance.
It shows how seriously the New Testament treats persevering faith.
And now we come to the third passage.
The one that may be the most unsettling of all.
First John 2:19 says:

"They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us." (KJV)
Imagine hearing that about someone you once considered a brother or sister in Christ.
Someone who knew the songs.
Someone who knew the language.
Someone who served alongside you.
Someone who looked like they belonged.
John says that the departure of certain people revealed something that had been hidden.
Their outward association with the church was not the same as truly belonging to the apostolic fellowship.
In its original context, John is addressing people who departed from the community and were associated with false teaching about Christ.
He is not declaring that every person who changes churches, experiences spiritual confusion, or temporarily stops attending worship was never saved.
That would be a serious misuse of the passage.
But his central warning remains piercing.
It is possible to appear to belong to Christ's people without truly belonging to Christ.
The Greek phrase οὐκ ἦσαν ἐξ ἡμῶν (ouk ēsan ex hēmōn) means "they were not of us."
And John's explanation is that genuine belonging would have been expressed in continuing with them.
This is the biblical foundation for a sobering distinction.
A person can experience religious excitement without spiritual regeneration.
A person can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
A person can enjoy worship music without worshiping God in spirit and truth.
A person can become deeply involved in ministry while remaining spiritually unconverted.
Jesus Himself warned about people who would call Him "Lord, Lord" and appeal to their religious works, only to hear His devastating declaration:
"I never knew you." (Matthew 7:23, KJV)
Not, "I knew you once, but I forgot you."
"I never knew you."
That statement should make every religious performer uncomfortable.
Because the most dangerous place to be spiritually is not always outside a church building.
Sometimes it is inside one, surrounded by Christian language, applauded for Christian activity, and completely unfamiliar with genuine repentance.
You can know how to behave like a Christian without having surrendered your life to Christ.
You can be admired by a congregation and still be hiding from God.
You can become so skilled at looking spiritually alive that you stop noticing the emptiness within.
And perhaps that is why this question hurts so much.
Because we want salvation to be something we can verify by looking backward at one emotional moment.
One altar call.
One prayer.
One baptism.
One powerful experience.
But the New Testament repeatedly directs our attention to the person and work of Jesus Christ and to the reality of living faith.
Not merely to a memory of religious excitement.
And that brings us to a man whose story should give every struggling Christian reason to keep reading.
His name was Peter.
Peter was not a distant observer of Jesus.
He walked with Him.
He heard His teaching.
He witnessed miracles.
He confessed that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of the living God.
And when the pressure became unbearable, Peter denied that he even knew Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine turning and seeing the face of the Savior you had just denied.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that the Lord turned and looked upon Peter.
Then Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
There are tears that come from embarrassment.
There are tears that come from being caught.
And there are tears that come when a human being realizes how deeply they have betrayed someone they love.
Peter wept bitterly.
But his story did not end beside that fire.
Before Peter ever denied Him, Jesus had already said:
"But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." (Luke 22:32, KJV)
Jesus knew Peter would fall.
He knew the denial was coming.
He knew how ugly that night would become.
And still, He prayed for him.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The man who had denied his Shepherd was not beyond the Shepherd's restoring grace.
Now listen carefully.
Peter's restoration does not prove that apostasy is harmless.
It does not erase the warnings of Hebrews.
It does not mean that everyone who rejects Christ will necessarily return.
But it proves something precious.
A terrible failure is not automatically the same as final apostasy.
And a believer's darkest chapter does not have to be the final chapter.
Perhaps you need to hear that.
Because you have fallen.
You made promises to God and broke them.
You returned to a sin you thought you had conquered.
You stopped praying because you felt ashamed.
You avoided Scripture because every verse seemed to expose you.
And somewhere in that darkness, you began wondering whether you had crossed a line from which there could be no return.
You read Hebrews 6 and felt your stomach tighten.
You wondered whether your failure meant you were beyond repentance.
But the very warning that should make us take sin seriously must never be twisted into a command for repentant sinners to stay away from Jesus.
Christ says:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (John 6:37, KJV)
That is not a promise to people who boast that they no longer need Him.
It is an invitation of extraordinary comfort to those who come to Him.
If you are grieving over sin, do not turn your grief into a reason to avoid Christ.
Bring it to Him.
If your faith feels weak, do not pretend it is strong.
Cry out as the father in Mark 9:24 did:
"Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." (KJV)
If you have wandered, do not make your wandering your permanent home.
Return.
Not because your tears purchase forgiveness.
Not because your repentance earns the cross.
But because Jesus Christ is the Savior of sinners, and His mercy is greater than the false image of a Savior who refuses every broken person who approaches Him.
Yet there is another side to this truth.
And it is dangerous to ignore it.
Imagine someone saying:
"I accepted Jesus when I was twelve. I know I am going to heaven. It doesn't matter that I now reject everything He taught."
They have no desire to repent.
No interest in following Christ.
No concern about their deliberate rebellion.
They treat the grace of God as permission to remain in sin.
And when anyone challenges them, they answer:
"Once saved, always saved."
But that slogan, used carelessly, can become a hiding place for spiritual presumption.

The doctrine commonly called eternal security, in its historic perseverance-of-the-saints form, does not teach that an empty profession of faith guarantees heaven regardless of a person's settled rejection of Christ.
It teaches that those whom God truly saves will be kept by His grace and brought to persevering faith.
And Christians who believe genuine salvation can be forfeited also warn against presumption, emphasizing the necessity of continuing in faith.

Despite their serious disagreement about whether a genuinely regenerate person can finally fall away, both perspectives have biblical reasons to reject the idea that deliberate unbelief should be treated as spiritually safe.
Paul wrote:
"Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." (Romans 6:1–2, KJV)
Grace is not God's permission slip for rebellion.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves sinners and teaches them to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
That does not mean genuine Christians become sinlessly perfect.
First John 1:8 warns against claiming that we have no sin.
And First John 1:9 promises God's faithfulness and justice in forgiving and cleansing those who confess their sins.
But it does mean that we must stop confusing forgiveness with indifference.
Christ did not die so that we could become comfortable with the chains He came to break.
He died and rose again to reconcile us to God and bring us into new life.
So what is the answer?
Can someone truly be saved and later walk away?
Or were they never saved in the first place?
The most responsible answer is that Christians who affirm the authority of Scripture have reached different conclusions about whether genuine salvation can finally be lost.

Those who hold to the perseverance of the saints understand John 10 as teaching that Christ will certainly preserve all who truly belong to Him. They interpret final apostasy as revealing that a person's earlier profession was not genuine saving faith, consistent with their understanding of First John 2:19.

Those who hold to conditional security understand John 10 as a magnificent promise of Christ's protecting power, while maintaining that the warnings against apostasy describe a genuine danger for believers who later abandon faith. They do not see Jesus' promise against being snatched away as necessarily answering every question about a person's own subsequent rejection of Him.
Both positions must wrestle seriously with the entire biblical witness.
Neither should be defended by pretending that the difficult passages do not exist.
And we should be especially cautious about declaring with absolute certainty what was happening inside another person's soul.
We can recognize a person's present confession.
We can observe patterns of life.
We can respond to persistent unbelief and disobedience with biblical seriousness.
But we are not omniscient.
God knows the heart perfectly.
We do not.
Here is what the passages make unmistakably clear.
Jesus is a mighty Savior.
A profession of faith is not the same thing as possessing saving faith.
Apostasy is a dreadful matter, not something to celebrate or dismiss.
And Scripture repeatedly calls people to continue trusting, following, and abiding in Christ.
So perhaps the question that should consume us is not simply:
"Was that person really saved ten years ago?"
Perhaps the more urgent question is:
"Am I trusting Jesus Christ today, or am I trusting a religious memory while refusing His voice?"
Because there is a difference.
A person can spend years arguing about whether salvation can be lost while never seriously examining whether they have come to Christ in repentance and faith.
They can memorize theological terminology while ignoring the Savior those doctrines are meant to honor.
They can become experts at debating assurance and apostasy while slowly becoming strangers to prayer.
And that would be tragic.
Not because theology is unimportant.
Sound doctrine matters deeply.
But sound doctrine should lead us toward Christ, not merely toward winning arguments about Christ.
The purpose of studying eternal security is not to become careless.
The purpose of studying apostasy is not to live in constant terror.
The purpose is to understand God's Word faithfully, to take His warnings seriously, and to rest our hope in the Savior Scripture reveals.
Philippians 2:12–13 holds together two truths that we often try to separate.
Believers are commanded to work out their salvation with fear and trembling.
And the very next verse explains that God is working in them both to will and to do His good pleasure.
Human responsibility.
Divine grace.
Serious obedience.
God's sustaining work.
Not enemies.
Not contradictions to be casually discarded.
Truths that should humble us before the Lord.
And if you are wondering whether your faith is real, do not begin by measuring how emotional you feel.
Emotions change.
Some mornings you wake up with a heart overflowing in worship.
Other mornings you can barely whisper a prayer.
Some seasons are filled with spiritual joy.
Others are marked by grief, confusion, and exhaustion.
The presence of struggle does not automatically mean the absence of faith.
Ask instead whether you are willing to come honestly before Christ.
Do you recognize your need for His mercy?
Are you trusting His death and resurrection rather than your own goodness?
When Scripture exposes sin, are you willing to repent, even when repentance is painful?
Do you desire to know Him, even when your feelings are weak?
Do not turn these questions into a demand for flawless performance.
The ground of salvation is not the quality of your spiritual résumé.
It is Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
And verse 10 immediately teaches that believers are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
We are not saved because we produce good works.
We are saved by grace for a life in which God's transforming work bears fruit.
Fruit does not purchase the tree's life.
It reveals something about the life within.
And even here, we must remember that spiritual growth can be uneven.
A bruised reed is not necessarily a dead one.
A struggling Christian is not necessarily a false Christian.
But a person who deliberately rejects Christ should never be encouraged to find assurance in a past religious experience while remaining unwilling to return to Him.
That would not be love.
It would be spiritual negligence.
And perhaps you are not the person who walked away.
Perhaps you are the one who watched someone leave.
A husband.
A wife.
A son.
A daughter.
A parent.
A friend who once knelt beside you in prayer.
You have replayed their testimony in your mind.
You have wondered whether every tear was false.
You have questioned whether every moment of worship was meaningless.
You have asked God why someone who seemed so close to Him now speaks as though He does not exist.
And perhaps, beneath all those questions, there is grief you have never allowed yourself to express.
You miss the person they used to be.
You miss praying together.
You miss talking about Scripture.
You miss the confidence that you would both continue walking with Christ.
Please hear this.
You do not have to pretend their departure is harmless.
And you do not have to pretend you know the final verdict on their soul.
You can grieve.
You can pray.
You can speak truth with gentleness.
You can refuse to manipulate them while still refusing to abandon the hope that God can bring a wandering person to repentance.
The father in Luke 15 did not call the far country a good place for his son.
But when the son returned, he received him with extraordinary joy.
The parable does not settle every theological dispute about whether salvation can be lost.
It does reveal the astonishing welcome of the father toward the repentant prodigal.
And that matters.
Because someone reading this may have spent years in the far country.
Not geographically.
Spiritually.
You have tried to silence the conviction.
You have buried yourself in distractions.
You have told yourself that the Christian life was only a phase.
You have laughed at the things that once brought you to tears.
But something about the name of Jesus still unsettles you.
Something about the cross still breaks through your defenses.
And maybe, even now, you are tired of running.
Then stop treating your past as a reason to remain away.
Do not wait until you feel worthy.
You will never make yourself worthy of grace.
Come to Christ because He is worthy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting the crucified and risen Savior.
Confess your sins.
Turn away from what you know is destroying your soul.
Seek the fellowship of faithful believers who will teach you Scripture, pray with you, and help you walk in truth.
And if you have never genuinely trusted Christ, do not settle for merely returning to religious activity.
Come to Him for salvation.
Romans 10:9 connects salvation with confessing Jesus as Lord and believing that God raised Him from the dead.
First Corinthians 15:3–4 proclaims that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that you can save yourself by holding on tightly enough.
Not that you can earn eternal life by maintaining a flawless record.
Not that a prayer spoken years ago gives you permission to reject the Lord today.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sinners and rose victorious over death.
He is the Savior.
He is the Shepherd.
He is the One to whom the weary must come.
And He is the One whom every professing believer must take seriously.
Perhaps this article has exposed something you have been hiding.
Perhaps you have been trusting a Christian identity more than Christ Himself.
Perhaps you have been terrified that one failure means God has abandoned you.
Perhaps you have been watching someone you love drift farther from faith, and you have not known how to pray anymore.
Or perhaps you have been caught between two voices.
One telling you that your sin does not matter.
The other telling you that your sin is too great for forgiveness.
Neither voice faithfully represents the full Gospel.
The Gospel tells us that sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross.
And grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly went there for sinners.
That is why we cannot make light of apostasy.
And that is why we must never make light of mercy.
Jesus is not a temporary religious accessory.
He is Lord.
He is not merely an emotional experience from your past.
He is the living Savior who calls people to repent, believe, and follow Him.
And whether you have been a Christian for fifty years or you are considering the claims of Christ for the first time, the invitation remains centered on Him.
Not on your reputation.
Not on your spiritual achievements.
Not on the applause of other believers.
On Jesus.
The One who said His sheep hear His voice.
The One who warned against false discipleship.
The One who restored Peter after his denial.
The One who died for our sins and rose again.
The One who is worthy of our trust, obedience, worship, and love.
So when the question returns—"Can someone truly be saved and later walk away, or were they never saved?"—remember that Scripture gives us both extraordinary promises and terrifying warnings.
Do not erase either.
Do not use assurance to excuse rebellion.
Do not use warnings to crush the repentant.
Do not declare yourself the final judge of another person's eternal destiny.
And do not spend so much time analyzing someone else's departure that you neglect your own relationship with Christ.
Hear His voice. Trust His grace. Take His warnings seriously. And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because this is not merely a debate about who once stood near the Shepherd.
It is a matter of eternal importance.
And I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Have you ever experienced a season when your faith almost collapsed?
Have you ever walked away from God—or watched someone you love abandon the faith?
Have you ever wondered whether you were truly saved?
You do not have to tell the world every detail of your private struggle.
But your honest response might encourage someone who believes they are the only person fighting this battle.
Your story may remind another reader that repentance is possible and that the mercy of Christ is not a small thing.
Please keep the conversation gracious. Christians who disagree about eternal security can still listen carefully, open their Bibles together, and treat one another with dignity.
And if a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article with them privately or tagging them if that would be welcome.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win an argument.
But because sometimes a difficult question becomes the beginning of an honest conversation about Jesus.
And invite your family, your friends, the struggling believer, the person who has grown spiritually indifferent, and even the person who does not yet believe in Jesus to follow along.
Because we are not here merely to collect religious opinions.
We want people to encounter the truth of God's Word and be pointed toward Jesus Christ.

If these writings have helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you to return to prayer, or strengthened you during a difficult season, I also want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Not because paying money proves that you are saved.
Not because you must support this particular ministry to glorify God.
The Gospel cannot be bought, and salvation is never for sale.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers participating financially in Paul's ministry.
And Third John 5–8 commends faithful support for those who labor in the truth.
You may choose to make it part of your planned Christian giving, alongside your responsibilities to your local church, your family, and others in need.
But it should never replace faithful participation in your local church or be presented as a mandatory tithe owed to Gospel Warrior.
Your generosity should come from love for Christ, not fear, guilt, or pressure.
The mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Jesus Christ known.
Our only Savior is Jesus Christ.
And that is precisely why every resource, every article, every act of generosity, and every invitation should ultimately point back to Him.
To the cross.
To the empty tomb.
To repentance.
To grace.
To forgiveness.
To the new life that only He can give.
Can someone truly be saved and later walk away?
Christians may continue to wrestle with how the biblical promises and warnings fit together.
But there is something you do not have to postpone until every theological question has been answered.
You can come to Jesus Christ today.
You can confess what you have been hiding.
You can stop treating yesterday's religious experience as a substitute for today's faith.
You can stop imagining that your weakness makes the Savior unwilling to receive you.
You can open your Bible again.
You can pray again.
You can seek help again.
You can take one honest step toward Christ.
And if you are already walking with Him, you can continue by His grace, not boasting in your own strength but depending upon His.
Because the greatest hope of the Christian is not that we have never fallen.
It is that Jesus Christ died and rose again, and that His saving grace is sufficient for all who truly come to Him.

The most frightening tragedy is not that someone once stumbled on the road of faith—it is that someone might spend a lifetime standing near the cross without ever surrendering to the Savior who hung upon it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: RACHEL GAVE HER HUSBAND ANOTHER WOMAN… BUT THE REAL REASON WILL BREAK YOUR HEART
paragraphs: RACHEL GAVE HER HUSBAND ANOTHER WOMAN… BUT THE REAL REASON WILL BREAK YOUR HEART

Behind the birth of Israel’s twelve tribes was a household filled with jealousy, rejection, infertility, wounded marriages, and desperate attempts to earn love. Yet through one of the Bible’s most complicated family scandals, God was preparing a story of redemption that would ultimately lead to Jesus Christ.
There is a kind of pain that makes you question everything.
You can smile in front of people, celebrate their blessings, congratulate them on their victories, and still go home wondering why God seems to be answering everyone’s prayers except yours.
You love God. You believe His promises. You know He is good.
But somewhere deep inside, a question keeps returning.
“Lord, when will it finally be my turn?”
Now imagine watching your own sister receive the very thing you have been begging God to give you.
Not once.
Not twice.
But again and again.
And every time she receives another blessing, you are reminded of what is missing from your life.
That was part of Rachel’s story.
But what happened next was far more disturbing than ordinary sibling rivalry.
Rachel became so desperate to have children that she gave her own servant, Bilhah, to her husband Jacob so that Bilhah could bear children within their household.
Read that again.
A woman who desperately wanted to become a mother brought another woman into her marriage.
Why?
Was it faith?
Was it jealousy?
Was it an ancient custom?
Was it desperation disguised as a solution?
The answer takes us into one of the most emotionally complicated families in Scripture.
And before we finish, we will discover something extraordinary.
The family from which God raised the twelve tribes of Israel was not built upon flawless relationships, perfect decisions, or people who always trusted Him.

It was a family marked by deception, rivalry, favoritism, sexual exploitation within unequal power structures, wounded hearts, and the astonishing faithfulness of a God who refused to abandon His covenant.
And somewhere inside that ancient household, we may recognize uncomfortable pieces of ourselves.
Because sometimes the greatest battle is not against someone who hates us.
Sometimes it is against the fear that God has forgotten us.
Jacob’s story began long before Bilhah entered the picture.
He had fallen in love with Rachel, the daughter of Laban.
Genesis 29:18 tells us that Jacob loved Rachel and offered to serve Laban seven years for the privilege of marrying her.
Seven years.
Eighty-four months of labor.
And Scripture describes those years with remarkable tenderness:
“And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.” — Genesis 29:20, KJV
Imagine being loved so deeply that seven years felt like a few days.
Rachel was the woman Jacob wanted.
The woman he had worked for.
The woman he expected to marry.
But on the wedding night, Laban deceived him.
Instead of Rachel, Laban gave Jacob his older daughter, Leah.
The following morning, Jacob discovered the deception.
The deceiver had been deceived.
The man who had previously participated in deceiving his own father now experienced betrayal at the hands of his future father-in-law.
There is a painful irony here, although Scripture does not explicitly identify Laban’s deception as a divine punishment for Jacob’s earlier conduct.
Jacob confronted Laban.
Laban appealed to a local marriage custom regarding the older daughter and arranged for Rachel also to become Jacob’s wife after Leah’s bridal week, in exchange for another seven years of service.
And suddenly, two sisters were married to the same man.
One was loved more.
The other lived beneath the shadow of that preference.
Genesis 29:30 says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Then comes one of the saddest verses in the entire narrative.
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.” — Genesis 29:31, KJV
The Hebrew word translated “hated” is שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah).
In this context, it describes Leah as the less-loved or rejected wife, particularly in comparison with Rachel. It does not require us to conclude that Jacob felt nothing but active hatred toward her.
Yet the emotional reality was devastating.
Leah had a husband, but she longed for his affection.
Rachel had Jacob’s greater affection, but she longed for children.
One woman wanted to be loved.
The other wanted to become a mother.
And both were living in the painful belief that something essential was missing.
Have you ever noticed how easily we assume someone else has the life we need?
We look at another person’s marriage, family, ministry, career, finances, or opportunities and imagine that possessing what they have would finally quiet the ache inside us.
But we rarely see what happens behind their closed doors.
Rachel might have envied Leah’s children.
Leah might have envied Rachel’s place in Jacob’s heart.
Both had something the other desperately wanted.
Neither had everything.
And comparison was slowly poisoning their home.
Leah gave birth to Reuben.
Then Simeon.
Then Levi.
Then Judah.
Each birth carried its own emotional significance.
When Reuben was born, Leah hoped her husband would love her.
When Simeon arrived, she spoke of the Lord hearing that she was unloved.
When Levi was born, she hoped Jacob would become attached to her.
But with Judah, something in her words changed.
Genesis 29:35 records her declaration:
“Now will I praise the LORD.”
The Hebrew text says:
הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
Ha-pa'am odeh et-YHWH.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
The verb אוֹדֶה (odeh) comes from the Hebrew root ידה (y-d-h), associated here with giving thanks or praise.
It is a beautiful moment.
But we should not turn it into an exaggerated claim that Leah never struggled again. Her later actions show that the family’s rivalry continued.
Still, her words offer a glimpse of worship rising from a wounded heart.
She had spent years longing for Jacob’s love.
Now, at least in this moment, she was directing her praise toward the Lord.
And there is something deeply moving about the name of that fourth son.
Judah.
Because generations later, the Messiah would come through Judah’s line.
Not through the family member everyone admired most.
Not through a household untouched by scandal.
But through a son born to the woman who knew what rejection felt like.
Hold on to that.
We will return to it.
Meanwhile, Rachel was watching her sister become the mother of four sons.
Four children.
Four reminders of her own infertility.
Genesis 30:1 says:
“And when Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister; and said unto Jacob, Give me children, or else I die.”
There it is.
The sentence that exposes the desperation beneath the rivalry.
“Give me children, or else I die.”
The Hebrew is striking:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, ve'im-ayin metah anokhi.
“Give me sons, and if not, I am dying.”
This is the language of anguish.
Rachel was not calmly discussing family planning.
She was expressing the depth of her distress.

In the ancient world, children carried enormous social, economic, and familial significance. Infertility could bring profound shame and insecurity, especially for women whose social standing was closely connected to motherhood.
But Scripture does not teach that an infertile woman is less valuable before God.
Nor does it teach that every faithful person will eventually have biological children.
Rachel’s suffering was real.
Her worth was never dependent upon her fertility.
Yet pain can become so consuming that we begin measuring our entire identity by the one thing we cannot obtain.
Perhaps your longing is not for a child.
Perhaps it is for a spouse who has not come.
A marriage that has not healed.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
A ministry that has not grown.
A financial breakthrough that has not arrived.
A loved one who has not returned to Christ.
You keep watching other people celebrate the very things you are still waiting for.
And you wonder whether heaven has somehow overlooked your address.
Rachel turned toward Jacob.
But Jacob was not God.
And when she demanded children from him, he responded angrily:
“Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” — Genesis 30:2, KJV
Jacob’s response was harsh.
Yet his question exposed an important truth.
He did not possess the power to give Rachel what only God could ultimately grant.
And this is where the story takes its most troubling turn.
Instead of waiting, Rachel proposed another arrangement.
Genesis 30:3 records her words:
“Behold my maid Bilhah, go in unto her; and she shall bear upon my knees, that I may also have children by her.”
The Hebrew begins:
הִנֵּה אֲמָתִי בִלְהָה
Hinneh amati Bilhah.
“Behold, my female servant Bilhah.”
Rachel was offering Bilhah as a means of obtaining children within her household.

The expression about bearing “upon my knees” is generally understood in relation to the recognition or incorporation of the child into Rachel’s family position, although the exact customary practice behind the phrase is debated.
In that ancient social setting, a wife could sometimes arrange for a female servant to bear children who would be associated with the wife’s household.
We encounter a similar arrangement earlier in Genesis when Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
But there is something we must understand.
The Bible’s description of a practice is not automatically God's approval of that practice.
Genesis tells us what Rachel did.
It does not command Christian wives to imitate her.
It does not present the treatment of Bilhah as a model for marriage.
And it does not erase the enormous imbalance of power between a mistress and an enslaved servant.
Bilhah was not an equal participant in this household.
She was a woman whose life was shaped by the authority of others.
Scripture does not record her personal consent, desires, fears, or reflections concerning the arrangement.
We must not invent her thoughts.
But neither should we romanticize her vulnerability.
Rachel's suffering mattered.
Leah's suffering mattered.
And Bilhah's humanity mattered too.
One of the most dangerous ways to read Scripture is to become so fascinated by the ambitions of powerful people that we forget those with little power at all.
Bilhah was not merely a solution to Rachel’s problem.
She was a person.
And God’s Word never gives us permission to treat people as instruments for satisfying our desperation.
Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob, and Bilhah bore a son.
Rachel named him Dan.
Genesis 30:6 records Rachel saying:
“God hath judged me, and hath also heard my voice, and hath given me a son.”
The name Dan is connected to the Hebrew root דין (din), meaning to judge or vindicate.
Rachel interpreted the birth as an answer from God.
Then Bilhah conceived again and gave birth to another son.
Rachel named him Naphtali.
Her explanation was revealing:
“With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed.” — Genesis 30:8, KJV
The Hebrew expression includes:
נַפְתּוּלֵי אֱלֹהִים
Naftulei Elohim.
An idiom often understood as “mighty wrestlings” or “great struggles,” rendered literally in some translations as “wrestlings of God.”
The language communicates the intensity of Rachel’s struggle.
And notice whom she identified as her opponent.
Her sister.
Not merely infertility.
Not simply social expectations.
Her sister.
What began as a longing for motherhood had become entangled with a contest for significance.
Rachel was counting children as though they were victories.
And that is what comparison does when it takes control of the heart.
It turns blessings into scoreboards.
It turns relationships into competitions.
It makes someone else’s joy feel like our defeat.
It whispers that another person must lose before we can finally feel valuable.
Have you ever caught yourself doing that?
Not necessarily with children.
Maybe with followers.
Money.
Recognition.
Marriage.
Physical appearance.
Career advancement.
Even ministry.
Someone else receives an opportunity, and instead of celebrating, something inside you tightens.
You know you should rejoice.
But you feel threatened.
And suddenly, another person’s blessing exposes an insecurity you thought you had conquered.
That is not a reason to pretend you are spiritually fine.
It is a reason to bring your heart honestly before God.
Because envy rarely heals when we hide it.
It grows in secrecy.
And it becomes even more dangerous when we begin justifying harmful decisions because our pain feels unbearable.
The rivalry did not end with Bilhah.
When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, she gave her own servant, Zilpah, to Jacob.
Zilpah bore Gad and Asher.
Now the household had become even more complicated.
Four women were involved in bearing Jacob’s children.
Two sisters were competing.
Two servants were living within the consequences of decisions made by their mistresses.
And the children were being born into a family already fractured by favoritism and resentment.
Later came the strange episode involving mandrakes.
Reuben found mandrakes in the field and brought them to Leah.
Rachel wanted some.
In the ancient Near East, mandrakes were associated with fertility, although Genesis does not establish that they were medically effective.
Leah responded bitterly, accusing Rachel of taking her husband and now wanting her son’s mandrakes as well.
Rachel then arranged for Leah to spend the night with Jacob in exchange for the mandrakes.
Think about the emotional condition of this home.
A husband’s companionship had become something to negotiate.
Sisters were bargaining over access to him.
The longing for children had become intertwined with jealousy, resentment, and attempts to gain control.
Yet the narrator does not attribute the next conception to the mandrakes.
Genesis 30:17 says:
“And God hearkened unto Leah, and she conceived, and bare Jacob the fifth son.”
Leah later bore Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter named Dinah.
Then comes the verse Rachel had been waiting for.
Genesis 30:22.
“And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb.”
Stop there.
God remembered Rachel.
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayyizkor Elohim et-Rachel.
“And God remembered Rachel.”
The Hebrew verb זָכַר (zakhar) means “to remember.”
When Scripture speaks of God remembering someone, it does not imply that He previously forgot that person.
God does not suffer lapses of memory.
In biblical narrative, divine remembrance often signals God’s attention expressed through action in keeping with His purposes.
Rachel had been waiting.
Rachel had been grieving.
Rachel had tried to obtain children through Bilhah.
Rachel had struggled with her sister.
But the decisive turning point in her own conception was not a mandrake.
It was not her ability to manipulate circumstances.
It was God’s action.
And she gave birth to Joseph.
Genesis 30:23 records her saying:
“God hath taken away my reproach.”
For a woman who had lived beneath the crushing weight of infertility in her social world, this was a moment of immense relief.
But Joseph’s name also carried a further longing.
Rachel said:
“The LORD shall add to me another son.” — Genesis 30:24, KJV
Joseph’s name is associated with the Hebrew verb יָסַף (yasaf), meaning “to add.”
Even after receiving Joseph, Rachel expressed hope for another son.
And eventually, another son did come.
Benjamin.
But the story did not unfold as a simple happily-ever-after ending.
Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin.
Genesis 35:16–20 records her difficult labor and death.
The woman who once cried, “Give me children, or else I die,” eventually died in childbirth.
The narrative is heartbreaking.
We should not turn that tragic connection into a claim that God punished Rachel for her earlier words. Scripture does not say that.
Nor should we treat her death as a warning that desperate prayers cause tragedy.
That would go beyond what the text teaches.
Instead, her story reminds us that life in a fallen world can hold both answered prayers and profound sorrow.
Faith does not guarantee an easy ending to every earthly chapter.
And God's faithfulness cannot be measured simply by whether our circumstances unfold as we hoped.
Now consider the family that emerged from all this turmoil.
The twelve sons of Jacob, who became the ancestral heads of Israel’s twelve tribes, came through four mothers.
Leah bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
Rachel bore Joseph and Benjamin.
Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali.
Zilpah bore Gad and Asher.
Twelve sons.
Four mothers.
One deeply divided household.
And one covenant God who remained faithful.
There is something important here that we must not miss.
The twelve tribes did not emerge because the family’s sins were good.
They emerged because God remained faithful to His covenant purposes despite human sin.
That distinction matters.
God's ability to bring redemption out of brokenness does not make betrayal righteous.
It does not make jealousy holy.
It does not justify treating vulnerable people as possessions.
It does not mean every destructive decision was secretly God’s preferred plan.
It means human failure could not ultimately overthrow what God had promised.
Long before Rachel and Leah, God had promised Abraham that his descendants would become a great nation and that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him.
That covenant promise continued through Isaac and Jacob.
And through Jacob’s descendants, Israel’s history unfolded.
But the family’s wounds did not magically disappear.
Jacob later showed special affection toward Joseph.
Joseph’s brothers grew jealous.
Their resentment became so severe that they sold him into slavery.
The pattern continued.
Favoritism.
Comparison.
Rejection.
Jealousy.
Betrayal.
The pain of one generation echoing into the next.
Does that sound familiar?
Perhaps your family has its own history of broken trust.
A parent who loved one child more openly than another.
A sibling who always seemed to receive the praise.
A marriage wounded by betrayal.
A household where everyone learned to survive, but nobody learned how to heal.
Maybe you promised yourself that you would never repeat what hurt you.
Yet under pressure, you hear yourself speaking the same words.
Reacting with the same anger.
Protecting yourself with the same silence.
Passing along wounds you never intended to pass along.
That is why this story is more than an ancient account of family conflict.
It confronts a question many people are afraid to ask.
Can God still work through a family that has made a terrible mess of itself?
The answer is yes.
But not because sin does not matter.
And not because broken relationships should be ignored.
God’s grace does not excuse evil.
It exposes our need for redemption.
Look at Joseph.
The son Rachel had longed to hold eventually became the brother his siblings betrayed.
He was carried into Egypt.
He suffered injustice.
He endured imprisonment.
Yet God worked through his suffering to preserve many lives during famine.
Years later, when Joseph stood before the brothers who had sold him, he declared:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.” — Genesis 50:20, KJV
Joseph did not pretend their actions were harmless.
He called their intention evil.
But he also recognized God's providence working toward the preservation of life.
That is biblical redemption.
Not pretending the wound never happened.
Not renaming evil as good.
But recognizing that evil does not possess ultimate authority over God’s purposes.
And even Joseph’s story was pointing toward something greater.
Because among Jacob’s sons was Judah.
Judah, whose birth prompted Leah’s words of praise.
Judah, whose own life included serious moral failure.
Judah, whose descendants would eventually include King David.
And through David’s royal line, according to the flesh, came Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1 traces the Messiah’s genealogy through Judah’s family line.
Revelation 5:5 calls Jesus:
“The Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David.”
Think about that.
The promised Savior entered human history through a family tree filled with imperfect people.
The Bible does not conceal their failures.
It records them.
Not to entertain us with scandal.
But to show us why humanity desperately needs a Savior.
Jesus did not come because human families had finally become righteous enough to deserve Him.
He came because sinners needed redemption.
He came to save those who could not save themselves.
He came to bear sin.
To conquer death.
To reconcile sinners to God.
To call people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And unlike Jacob, whose divided affections helped wound his household, Jesus loves His people with perfect covenant faithfulness.
Unlike Rachel and Leah, who struggled to secure their place through competition, believers are called to receive their identity through grace.
Unlike the household arrangements that left vulnerable servants with little control, Christ teaches His followers that greatness is found in humble service rather than domination.
He does not treat His people as disposable instruments.
He gave Himself for them.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
There is the difference.
Human love often asks, “What can you give me?”
Christ’s sacrificial love reveals what He has given for us.
And this is where Rachel’s story becomes painfully personal.
How many times have we tried to obtain through control what we were supposed to entrust to God?
We force conversations.
Manipulate outcomes.
Compete for attention.
Measure our worth through other people’s approval.
We become resentful when someone else advances.
We call our impatience determination.
We call our jealousy discernment.
We call our fear wisdom.
And sometimes we call our attempts to control everything faith.
But faith is not the ability to make God follow our preferred timetable.
Faith is trusting His character even when we do not understand His timing.
That does not mean doing nothing.
It does not mean refusing wise medical care, counseling, responsible planning, or practical action.
It means refusing to make desperation our moral compass.
It means we do not get permission to wound other people simply because we are wounded ourselves.
It means we can bring our desires before God without turning those desires into idols.
And perhaps that is the word someone needs tonight.
You are allowed to grieve.
You are allowed to admit that waiting hurts.
You are allowed to tell God that your heart is exhausted.
The Psalms are filled with honest lament.
But do not let your unanswered prayer become an excuse to abandon obedience.
Do not sacrifice your integrity to obtain something you are afraid of losing.
Do not destroy a relationship because someone else appears to be more blessed.
Do not confuse God's silence with His absence.
And do not believe that your worth depends on achieving the life you imagined.
For those who belong to Christ, their deepest identity is not found in marital status, parenthood, wealth, popularity, or visible success.
It is found in Him.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
And Romans 8:32 reminds us that God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us.
That is where the believer must look for the strongest assurance of God's love.
