Someone who needs to hear that the Lord Jesus Christ does not despise the brokenhearted.
We cannot promise that every share will change a life.
But we can faithfully offer truth and trust God with what happens next.
And now, before you leave, I want to speak to the husband and wife who have made it this far.
Perhaps you are reading separately.
Perhaps your spouse has no idea how much this subject hurts you.
Perhaps you are sitting beside each other, realizing for the first time that you have both been carrying pain.
Do not let this article become another thing you read, agree with, and forget.
If it is safe to do so, turn toward one another.
Ask a question you may have avoided for years.
"What has been hardest for you?"
And then listen.
Do not prepare your defense.
Do not interrupt to explain why you have suffered more.
Do not turn vulnerability into an argument.
Listen.
You may discover that beneath the rejection you felt was fear you never understood.
Beneath the silence was shame.
Beneath the frustration was loneliness.
Beneath the distance was someone who still wanted to be loved but did not know how to ask for help.
And perhaps, by God's grace, you will begin to see your spouse not as the source of all your disappointment, but as another human being in need of compassion, truth, and care.
That does not erase responsibility.
It does not excuse cruelty.
It does not replace medical treatment or professional counseling.
But it can change the way you begin to face the struggle.
Together.
You stood before God and promised to love one another.
You may have imagined that the hardest part of honoring Him would be waiting until marriage.
But perhaps one of the deeper lessons of your marriage will be learning how to love faithfully when the experience is not what you expected.
Learning to be patient when you are disappointed.
Learning to be truthful when you are ashamed.
Learning to ask forgiveness when you have wounded one another.
Learning to receive help without believing you have failed.
Learning that Christian love is not merely a feeling that appears when everything is easy.
It is a commitment shaped by the self-giving love of Jesus Christ.
And above all, learning that your deepest hope is not in the perfection of your marriage.
It is in the perfection of your Savior.
Your marriage cannot save you.
Your virginity cannot save you.
Your sexual fulfillment cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
He died for our sins and rose again, and through Him there is forgiveness and reconciliation with God for all who repent and believe.
That is the foundation beneath every other hope we carry.
So if your marriage has been difficult, do not confuse difficulty with defeat.
Seek the truth.
Pursue wise care.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Extend grace without abandoning healthy boundaries.
And keep bringing your lives before the Lord who is faithful even when the road ahead is uncertain.
You may have entered marriage believing that the wedding night would be the beginning of effortless intimacy.
Instead, you discovered how much there was to learn about vulnerability, patience, and love.
But the story does not have to end in that disappointment.
And perhaps the next chapter will begin not with a perfect romantic moment, but with two people finally telling each other the truth.
Not every wound heals quickly.
Not every marriage is safe.
Not every difficulty has a simple solution.
But no painful beginning has the authority to declare that God is finished working in your life.

You thought the tragedy was that you waited for each other and still found pain. But perhaps the deeper tragedy would be letting that pain convince you that tenderness, truth, and grace are no longer worth pursuing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU DEFEND THE SANCTITY OF LIFE AND STILL SUPPORT THE DEATH PENALTY? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT MAY CHALLENGE BOTH SIDES
paragraphs: CAN YOU DEFEND THE SANCTITY OF LIFE AND STILL SUPPORT THE DEATH PENALTY? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT MAY CHALLENGE BOTH SIDES

If every human life bears the image of God, why does Scripture permit the taking of life as punishment? And if Jesus died to save sinners, how should Christians respond when a sinner deserves the severest judgment? This is not merely a debate about criminals and punishment. It is a confrontation with justice, mercy, the Cross, and the uncomfortable truth about our own hearts.
Imagine receiving a phone call that changes your life forever.
Someone you love has been murdered.
Not in an accident. Not through an unfortunate mistake. Someone deliberately took their life.
Your knees weaken. Your mind refuses to accept what you have heard. You reach for your phone, hoping someone will tell you it isn't true.
But it is.
Yesterday, that person had a voice. A smile. Plans for tomorrow. Perhaps a child waiting at home. Perhaps a mother who had been praying for their safety.
Today, there is an empty chair.
And somewhere, the person responsible is still breathing.
Now imagine standing in a courtroom, listening as the evidence reveals exactly what happened.
The cruelty. The suffering. The final moments.
The judge announces that the crime is punishable by death.
Would you support that sentence?
Before you answer, consider another scene.
A condemned prisoner sits alone in a cell. He has committed a terrible crime. He cannot undo what he did. His victim will never return to their family.
But one night, he opens a Bible.
For the first time in years, he begins to weep.
Not because he has been caught.
Because he finally understands the weight of his sin.
He falls to his knees and cries out to Jesus Christ for mercy.
And the Gospel declares that even a murderer who truly repents is not beyond the saving power of the blood of Jesus.
Now the question becomes painfully complicated.
If God can forgive him, should the government still execute him?
If we believe every human being bears God's image, can we support capital punishment?
And if we oppose capital punishment, are we ignoring the justice God Himself established?
Here is what makes this question so difficult: Scripture confronts both the person who demands punishment without mercy and the person who speaks of mercy while overlooking the seriousness of evil.
We cannot settle it with a slogan.
We must open the Word of God.
And we must be willing to let Scripture correct us, even when it challenges what we already believe.
The first truth we must establish is that human life is sacred.
Not because people are innocent.
Not because people are useful.
Not because people have earned the right to exist through good behavior.
Human life has extraordinary dignity because human beings are created in the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 declares:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — be-tselem Elohim, meaning "in the image of God."
This is not a declaration that human beings are divine. It means that humanity possesses a God-given dignity and calling unlike anything else in creation.
And here is something we cannot afford to miss.
The image of God is not erased simply because someone commits a terrible crime.
A murderer remains morally accountable before God precisely because he is a human being responsible for his actions.
His sin does not make him innocent.
But neither does it make him something less than human.
That distinction matters.
Because the moment we begin treating human beings as worthless objects, even when they are guilty, we risk forgetting whose image they bear.
Yet the very next biblical passage many Christians cite in defense of capital punishment is rooted in that same sacredness of human life.
Genesis 9:6 declares:
"Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man." (KJV)
Read that again.
The verse does not present human life as cheap.
It presents human life as so valuable that the deliberate shedding of innocent blood calls for the gravest accountability.
The Hebrew reads:
שֹׁפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם דָּמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ
Shofekh dam ha-adam, ba-adam damo yishafekh.
A close rendering is:
"Whoever sheds human blood, by a human shall his blood be shed."
The wording is part of God's covenantal instructions to Noah after the flood, before the establishment of Israel's Mosaic law.
This is one reason many Christians believe capital punishment can be consistent with the sanctity of life.
Their reasoning is not necessarily that criminals have no value.
It is that murder is such a profound violation of human dignity that the state may impose the ultimate penalty.
But notice something important.

Genesis 9:6 establishes the seriousness of bloodshed. It does not provide a complete modern criminal justice system. It does not explain contemporary standards of evidence, wrongful convictions, appeals, corruption, or whether every government should exercise the maximum punishment available to it.
Those questions require further biblical and moral reasoning.
And Scripture gives us more to consider.
Under the law given to ancient Israel, certain offenses were punishable by death.
Exodus 21:12 states that a person who strikes another so that he dies is subject to death.
But the same chapter distinguishes intentional murder from an unintentional killing, providing for refuge in appropriate circumstances (Exodus 21:12–14).
Numbers 35:30 also requires multiple witnesses before a murderer may be put to death.
And Deuteronomy 17:6 rejects execution on the testimony of a single witness.
These provisions reveal something deeply significant.
Even where Scripture authorized capital punishment, it did not treat the taking of life as something to be done carelessly.
There were distinctions.
There were evidentiary requirements.
There was a recognition that guilt had to be established rather than assumed.

We must also remember that ancient Israel's covenant laws were given to a particular nation under a particular divine arrangement. Christians disagree about which judicial principles carry forward directly into modern civil government.
We cannot simply lift every penalty from the Mosaic law and demand its implementation today while ignoring the broader covenantal context.
Then we arrive at the New Testament.
And the discussion becomes even more searching.
Romans 13:1–4 describes governing authorities as accountable to God for maintaining public order and punishing wrongdoing.
Paul writes that the ruler "beareth not the sword in vain" (Romans 13:4, KJV).
The Greek expression is:
οὐ γὰρ εἰκῇ τὴν μάχαιραν φορεῖ
Ou gar eikē tēn machairan phorei.
A close translation is:
"For he does not bear the sword without purpose."
The Greek word μάχαιρα — machaira refers to a sword or large knife, a weapon that could symbolize coercive authority and the ability to use deadly force.
Many Christian interpreters understand this passage as recognizing the state's authority to impose severe punishment, potentially including capital punishment.
But we must be careful.
Paul does not explicitly command every government to execute murderers. Nor does the mere mention of the sword establish that every use of state power is just.
Romans 13 recognizes legitimate governing authority. It does not declare that governments are incapable of corruption.
The same Bible that calls believers to respect lawful authority also records rulers who murdered the innocent, abused their power, and condemned righteous people.
And that brings us to a scene that should make every Christian tremble before speaking too confidently about the death penalty.
Jesus Christ Himself was sentenced to death by human authorities.
Think about that.
The only perfectly innocent human being who ever lived was condemned through a profoundly unjust process.
Religious leaders pursued His destruction.
Political authority failed to protect the innocent.
The crowd demanded His death.
And the Roman governor, despite recognizing the weakness of the accusations, handed Him over to be crucified.
Luke 23:4 records Pilate saying:
"I find no fault in this man." (KJV)
Yet Jesus was still executed.
The Cross exposes the terrifying possibility that a legal system can possess the power to kill without possessing the justice to use that power rightly.
A government can issue a sentence.
A court can announce a verdict.
A crowd can applaud.
And an innocent person can still die.
That does not automatically prove that all capital punishment is immoral.
But it permanently destroys the illusion that human institutions are incapable of catastrophic error.
And unlike imprisonment, execution cannot be reversed.
An innocent prisoner may one day walk free.
An executed innocent person cannot be restored to earthly life by a corrected verdict.
This is one of the strongest reasons Christians who affirm the sanctity of life may oppose the death penalty, even while believing that murder deserves severe punishment.
They are not necessarily denying justice.
They are asking whether fallible governments should possess an irreversible power when their judgments can be wrong.
And that question becomes even more serious in societies where wealth, influence, discrimination, inadequate legal representation, unreliable evidence, or corruption can affect criminal proceedings.
If the powerful can escape punishment while the poor face execution, are we witnessing biblical justice?
Or are we witnessing something Scripture repeatedly condemns?
Proverbs 17:15 declares:
"He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD." (KJV)
God condemns both failures.
Acquitting the guilty.
And condemning the innocent.
Biblical justice cannot be reduced to punishment alone.
It must also concern truth, impartiality, integrity, and protection against wrongful judgment.
But there is another side of this conversation that deserves equal seriousness.
What about the victims?
What about the families whose lives have been shattered?
What about the child who will never see her father again?
What about the mother who must bury her son because someone deliberately murdered him?
Christians must never use the language of grace to silence the suffering of victims.
Forgiveness does not mean that murder was a minor offense.
Mercy does not require pretending that evil was harmless.
And compassion for a convicted murderer must never become indifference toward the people whose lives were destroyed.
The God of Scripture hears the cries of the oppressed.
He cares about the vulnerable.
He hates injustice.
Psalm 9:9 describes the Lord as a refuge for the oppressed.
And Revelation 6:10 portrays the martyrs crying out for God's righteous judgment.
The desire for justice is not inherently sinful.
Sometimes it is a response to something genuinely evil.
But there is a line between seeking justice and surrendering our hearts to vengeance.
And Scripture warns us not to cross it.
Romans 12:19 declares:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord." (KJV)
Interestingly, this instruction appears immediately before Paul's discussion of governing authority in Romans 13.
That context matters.
Paul distinguishes personal retaliation from the public responsibility of civil government.
A Christian may believe that the state has authority to punish while also believing that private vengeance is forbidden.
Yet a Christian may also conclude that the state should exercise its authority through secure imprisonment rather than execution.
These positions differ on the proper exercise of civil power, but neither should be caricatured as automatically rejecting biblical justice.
Now consider the moment when Jesus was confronted with people demanding a woman's death.
In John 8:1–11, the account of the woman caught in adultery presents an extraordinary confrontation between accusation, sin, and mercy.
Jesus says:
"He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." (John 8:7, KJV)
One by one, the accusers depart.
Then Jesus tells her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)

We should note that this passage has a well-known textual history: the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John do not contain it, and many modern Bibles mark it accordingly. Its message should therefore be considered alongside the wider, securely attested teaching of Scripture.
We must also avoid misusing the account.
It is not a straightforward judicial ruling abolishing every form of capital punishment.
The situation concerns adultery, not murder, and involves serious questions about the accusers and their application of the law.
But the account powerfully illustrates a truth consistent with Jesus' wider ministry.
He did not minimize sin.
He confronted it.
Yet He also exposed self-righteousness and extended mercy.
"Go, and sin no more."
Not, "Your sin never mattered."
Not, "There is no such thing as accountability."
But an invitation to leave sin behind.
Grace is not permission to continue in evil.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that calls sinners into a transformed life.
And nowhere is that truth more startling than at Calvary.
There were three men hanging on crosses that day.
Two were criminals.
One was the sinless Son of God.
One criminal joined in the mockery.
But the other came to recognize something that changed everything.
He acknowledged his own guilt.
He admitted that his punishment was deserved.
And he recognized the innocence of Jesus.
Luke 23:41 records his words:
"And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss." (KJV)
Then he turned toward Jesus.
Not with an impressive religious record.
Not with years of good works.
Not with the opportunity to repair everything he had broken.
He had nothing left to offer.
Only a dying confession.
And a desperate plea.
"Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." (Luke 23:42, KJV)
Jesus answered:
"Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." (Luke 23:43, KJV)
Do not miss what happened.
The criminal was not rescued from earthly execution.
He was rescued from condemnation before God.
His repentance did not erase the earthly consequences of his actions.
But the mercy of Christ reached him even in his final hours.
The Cross reveals that forgiveness before God and consequences under human law are not the same thing.
A person can be genuinely forgiven by God and still face imprisonment.
A murderer can truly repent and still owe restitution wherever restitution is possible.
A criminal can receive eternal life through Jesus Christ without becoming innocent of the earthly crime committed.
And yes, a person facing execution can be saved by grace through faith.
That is not an endorsement of every death sentence.
It is a declaration that no human punishment possesses the power to cancel the saving promise of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is greater than a prison cell.
Greater than a courtroom verdict.
Greater than a criminal record.
Greater even than the approaching hour of death.
But here is the question that should haunt every one of us.
If the thief on the cross had been your child's murderer, would you still rejoice that Jesus offered him paradise?
That is not an easy question.
It is not meant to shame grieving families.
No one should demand that a victim's loved ones instantly feel forgiveness or abandon their pursuit of lawful justice.
But it confronts something deep within the human heart.
We love the idea of grace when we are the ones who need it.
We sometimes struggle with grace when it reaches someone who has wounded us.
And yet the Gospel does not belong to us.
We do not decide who is beyond the reach of Christ.
Consider the apostle Paul.
Before he became a missionary, he persecuted the church.
Acts 8:1 records his approval of Stephen's killing.
Acts 9:1 describes him breathing out threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord.
Later, Paul remembered his former life with deep humility.
In 1 Timothy 1:15, he wrote:
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." (KJV)
God did not excuse Paul's persecution.
He confronted him.
He transformed him.
And He used the very man who had once terrorized Christians to proclaim the Gospel of grace.
This does not mean every criminal will repent.
It does not mean every profession of faith is genuine.
And it does not mean a dangerous offender should automatically be released.
But it does mean that no Christian should casually declare another person spiritually irredeemable.
We do not possess God's perfect knowledge of a human heart.
Only God can judge repentance without error.
And that leads to a distinction too often forgotten in public debates.
The question of whether the death penalty is morally permissible is not identical to the question of whether it is wise, just, or necessary for a particular government to use it.
A Christian may believe Genesis 9 and Romans 13 establish the moral legitimacy of capital punishment in principle, while opposing its use in a country with unreliable courts.

Another Christian may believe the sanctity of life, the possibility of repentance, the example of Jesus, and the danger of wrongful execution provide compelling reasons to reject the practice altogether.
Another may support its use only for the most extreme cases of intentional murder, with exceptionally strong safeguards.
These positions cannot simply be declared equally correct on every point.
They involve real disagreements about biblical interpretation, moral responsibility, the authority of the state, and the application of justice.
But Christians should recognize that thoughtful believers who submit to Scripture have reached different conclusions.
The Bible explicitly condemns murder.
It explicitly affirms human dignity.
It explicitly recognizes a role for civil authorities in punishing wrongdoing.
It explicitly forbids personal vengeance.
It explicitly calls God's people to justice and mercy.
And it explicitly proclaims forgiveness through Jesus Christ to repentant sinners.
What it does not provide is a single detailed New Testament policy prescribing how every modern nation must legislate capital punishment.
We should therefore be cautious about claiming more certainty than Scripture itself establishes.
And we should be especially cautious about declaring that anyone who disagrees with us on the death penalty must be an unfaithful Christian.
Our convictions should be strong enough to withstand honest examination.
And our humility should be deep enough to recognize where faithful interpretation requires careful judgment.
But perhaps the most dangerous thing in this entire debate is not the disagreement itself.
Perhaps it is what the disagreement can reveal about our hearts.
Because it is possible to support the death penalty while secretly enjoying the thought of another person's suffering.
And that is not justice.
It is possible to oppose the death penalty while showing little concern for victims and their families.
And that is not biblical compassion.
It is possible to quote Romans 13 while ignoring governmental corruption.
It is possible to quote John 8 while refusing to acknowledge the seriousness of sin.
It is possible to defend the sanctity of life in public while speaking of certain human beings as though they were disposable.
And it is possible to speak passionately about mercy while withholding it from the people closest to us.
The problem is not always that we lack Bible verses.
Sometimes the problem is that we have learned to use Bible verses to defend conclusions without allowing God's Word to examine our motives.
So before asking whether a Christian can support the death penalty, perhaps we should ask something more personal.
When you imagine a murderer standing before a judge, what do you want most?
Justice?
Protection for the innocent?
Truth?
Repentance?
Or simply the satisfaction of watching someone suffer?
There is a difference.
God is just.
But He is not cruel.
God is merciful.
But He is not indifferent to evil.
Exodus 34:6–7 reveals the Lord as merciful and gracious, while also declaring that He does not simply leave guilt unaddressed.
The God of the Bible is not divided between an angry Old Testament and a loving New Testament.
He is the same holy God.
His justice and mercy are not competing personalities.
They are revealed together in His righteous character.
And nowhere do we see that more clearly than at the Cross of Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
He did not announce that evil no longer mattered.
The Son of God bore our sins.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." (KJV)
Romans 3:25–26 presents Christ's sacrifice as the demonstration of God's righteousness, showing how God can be just and the justifier of the one who believes in Jesus.
The Cross is not a picture of justice being abandoned.
It is the place where God's holiness, love, righteousness, and mercy are revealed through the saving work of Christ.
Jesus was not an unwilling victim of the Father's cruelty.
He willingly gave His life in obedience to the Father for the redemption of sinners.
John 10:18 records Jesus saying:
"No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself." (KJV)
And the resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
This is why Christians must be careful not to confuse the Cross with an ordinary criminal execution.
Jesus' death was a unique, voluntary, redemptive sacrifice by the sinless Savior.
No modern government can reproduce it.
No condemned criminal can atone for the sins of humanity.
And no execution carried out by the state possesses the power to save a soul.
Only Jesus saves.
So where does that leave us?
Can a Christian support the death penalty while believing in the sanctity of life?

Yes, a Christian can hold those convictions together, if the support for capital punishment is grounded in a serious understanding of human dignity, legitimate civil authority, proportionate justice, and the protection of the innocent—not hatred, cruelty, or revenge.
That position has biblical arguments deserving careful consideration.

But a Christian can also oppose the death penalty precisely because human life is sacred, governments are fallible, wrongful execution is irreversible, and the state may be able to protect society through other severe penalties.
That position also has substantial biblical and moral arguments deserving careful consideration.
The more important question is whether our convictions have been shaped by the whole counsel of Scripture or merely by the verses most convenient to our position.
Do we care about innocent lives before a crime happens?
Do we care about victims after a crime happens?
Do we care about fair trials?
Do we care about prisoners who may truly repent?
Do we care about the families of those who are executed?
Do we care about the possibility that an innocent person may be condemned?
Do we care about protecting society without allowing hatred to shape our hearts?
And above all, do we care about honoring Jesus Christ more than winning an argument?
Because the Christian calling is not merely to take a position.
It is to become more like Christ.
Micah 6:8 declares:
"He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" (KJV)
Justice.
Mercy.
Humility.
Not justice without mercy.
Not mercy without truth.
Not moral confidence without humility.
And not religious language without love.
Perhaps you are reading this as someone who has lost a loved one to violence.
You may be carrying grief that other people cannot comprehend.
You may be angry.
You may be exhausted by a justice system that seems painfully slow.
You may have heard Christians tell you to forgive before anyone has even acknowledged the depth of what happened.
Please hear this.
Your loved one's life mattered.
Their death matters.
Your grief matters.
The Lord does not command you to call evil good.
And seeking lawful accountability does not make you less Christian.
Healing may be long and difficult. Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation, and it does not eliminate the need for safety, boundaries, or justice.
Jesus sees the pain that other people cannot see.
Psalm 34:18 reminds us:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." (KJV)
And perhaps you are reading this from the other side.
Maybe you have done something terrible.
Maybe you have harmed someone.
Maybe you have destroyed relationships, betrayed trust, or committed a sin you cannot undo.
You cannot escape responsibility by simply saying that God forgives.
True repentance turns away from sin, tells the truth, and accepts the responsibility that follows.
But do not believe the lie that you are beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
The same Savior who heard the dying thief can hear you.
The same Lord who confronted Paul can transform you.
The same grace that rescued sinners throughout Scripture is still sufficient for everyone who comes to Christ in genuine repentance and faith.
Your past may carry consequences.
But it does not have to remain the master of your soul.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
From Scandal to Grace. Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because grace makes evil acceptable.
Not because forgiveness erases every earthly consequence.
But because the risen Christ can take a life ruined by sin and begin a transformation no human court could ever accomplish.
And now, I want to ask you something that requires more than a quick reaction.
After reading the Scriptures, where do you stand?
Do you believe capital punishment can be a legitimate expression of justice?
Do you believe the sanctity of life calls Christians to oppose it?
Or are you still wrestling with the tension between justice, mercy, and the possibility of wrongful judgment?
You do not have to pretend to have every answer.
If you are still wrestling, you can simply comment, "Lord, teach me justice and mercy."
If this article has exposed bitterness, a desire for revenge, or a lack of compassion in your own heart, you can pray, "Jesus, change my heart."
You do not owe anyone the details of your suffering.
Let the conversation become a place where people seek truth without cruelty and practice compassion without compromising conviction.
Because perhaps someone reading the comments is a grieving parent.
Perhaps someone is a prison chaplain.
Perhaps someone has a loved one serving a life sentence.
Perhaps someone is struggling to believe that God could ever forgive what they have done.
Your words, spoken with humility and truth, may help someone take one more step toward Jesus.
Not to provoke an argument.
Not to embarrass people who disagree.
But because our world desperately needs conversations about justice that do not forget mercy, and conversations about mercy that do not abandon truth.
One thoughtful share may reach someone who would never enter a church or open a Bible on their own.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who are still searching for God to follow along.
Because spiritual growth does not happen merely by collecting inspirational quotes.
It happens as the Holy Spirit works through God's Word, calling us to repentance, faith, obedience, and deeper communion with Jesus Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped strengthen your faith, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.

It is a practical way of standing alongside a ministry committed to proclaiming Jesus Christ, teaching Scripture, encouraging wounded hearts, calling sinners to repentance, and helping believers grow in biblical understanding.
It should not be confused with a required biblical tithe to a local church, nor should it replace your responsibilities to your family or your faithful support of your local congregation.

But if you believe this work is bearing good fruit, and God has given you the ability and desire to support it, your generosity can help make more Scripture-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to others.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the kind of support we value.
Not pressured giving.
Not guilt-driven giving.
But cheerful, voluntary partnership in Gospel ministry.
These items are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
They are simply an additional way of expressing gratitude to those who help sustain the work.
That commitment matters.
Because the Gospel must never be placed behind a price tag.
Pray for the ministry.
A faithful prayer, a compassionate conversation, or a shared Gospel message can be a meaningful act of service.
Because the goal has never been to build a following for its own sake.
The goal is to point people to Jesus Christ.
And as we close, return with me one final time to Calvary.
Three crosses.
Two guilty men.
One innocent Savior.
One criminal mocked Him.
The other asked for mercy.
And Jesus made a promise that death itself could not cancel.
That scene does not answer every legal question surrounding capital punishment.
But it answers something infinitely more important.
It tells us that even when earthly justice has reached its final sentence, the saving mercy of Jesus Christ is still powerful enough to reach a repentant sinner.
It tells us that human guilt is real.
That God's judgment is righteous.
That grace is undeserved.
And that the crucified and risen Savior is mighty to save.
So whether you support or oppose the death penalty, never forget the truth that stands above the debate.
The murderer is accountable before God.
The victim is precious before God.
The judge is accountable before God.
The government is accountable before God.
And every one of us will ultimately stand before the One who judges with perfect righteousness.
That should make us humble.
That should make us careful.
That should make us merciful.
And that should drive us to the Cross.
Because when we look at Calvary, we discover something none of us should ever forget.
The most important question is not simply whether a guilty person deserves to die, but whether any of us could stand before a holy God without the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The answer is no.
And the hope of the Gospel is that we do not have to.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And everyone who truly turns to Him in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness and eternal life.
Justice matters.
Life matters.
Truth matters.
Mercy matters.
But above everything else, Jesus Christ is Lord.
And when the arguments are over, when the courtroom has emptied, when the headlines have disappeared, and when every earthly verdict has become part of history, one truth will remain:
The Cross reminds us that the only perfectly innocent Man ever executed willingly gave His life so that guilty people like us could be forgiven.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT SEX, BREASTS, LUST, ADULTERY, PROSTITUTION, AND BROKEN FAMILIES—AND THE REASON WHY MAY BRING YOU TO YOUR KNEES.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT SEX, BREASTS, LUST, ADULTERY, PROSTITUTION, AND BROKEN FAMILIES—AND THE REASON WHY MAY BRING YOU TO YOUR KNEES.

The Scriptures expose what religion often tries to hide. But Hebrews 4:12–16 reveals something even more astonishing: the God who sees your deepest secrets is the very God who invites you to come closer.
There are things people will never admit in church.
Not because they don't believe in God.
But because they're terrified of what people might think if they knew the truth.
The married man who worships on Sunday but secretly struggles with pornography.
The woman who smiles during fellowship while carrying the shame of an affair nobody knows about.
The young believer who loves Jesus but keeps falling into sexual temptation and wonders whether God has finally grown tired of forgiving them.
The husband and wife sleeping in the same bed but living like strangers.
The person who was sexually violated and has spent years feeling dirty because of something someone else did to them.
The single mother who still hears the judgment in people's voices.
The former prostitute who wonders whether anyone will ever see her as more than her past.
And the person reading this right now who has never told another living soul what happened behind closed doors.
Some of these people are guilty of choices they need to repent of.
Others are carrying wounds they never deserved.
Some are carrying both.
And that distinction matters enormously to God.
Because the Bible does not treat every broken person as though they committed the same sin.
But it does reveal a Savior who knows every story.
And here is what might surprise you.
The Bible is far more willing to discuss the uncomfortable realities of human sexuality than many Christians are.
It talks about breasts.
It talks about sexual desire.
It talks about prostitution.
It talks about adultery, incest, rape, lust, betrayal, pregnancy outside marriage, and families shattered by human decisions.
It even contains an entire poetic book celebrating the beauty of marital love and physical affection.
Why?
Because God is not embarrassed by the human body He created.
He is not confused by the desires He designed.
And He is certainly not surprised by the ways sin has distorted what He originally declared good.
But there is something even deeper happening in Scripture.
God already knows the part of your story you are most afraid to tell Him.
And Hebrews tells us exactly what happens when that hidden place meets the living Word of God.
Hebrews 4:12 declares:

"For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." (KJV)
Read that last phrase again.
The thoughts and intents of the heart.
Not merely what you did.
Not merely what someone saw.
Not merely what appeared on the screen.
Not merely what you confessed.
The thoughts.
The intentions.
The motives.
The desires you entertained.
The bitterness you protected.
The secret compromises you justified.
The wounds you covered with a convincing smile.
God's Word reaches beneath the behavior and exposes what is happening in the heart.
The original Greek makes this even more piercing.
Hebrews describes God's Word as ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐνεργής (zōn gar ho logos tou theou kai energēs).
Literally, "For the word of God is living and active."
The word ἐνεργής (energēs) carries the sense of being active or effective.
This is not a dead religious document sitting quietly on a shelf.
God's Word is living and active, accomplishing His purposes and confronting us with His truth.
And then comes a remarkable expression.
κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας
Kritikos enthymēseōn kai ennoiōn kardias.
A discerner or judge of the heart's thoughts and intentions.
The Greek word kritikos describes the capacity to evaluate or judge.
Scripture does not merely identify what happened.
It confronts why.
And that is where things become uncomfortable.
Because we can sometimes hide our behavior from other people.
But we cannot hide our hearts from God.
A person can delete their browsing history.
They cannot delete God's knowledge of what happened.
A person can conceal an affair.
They cannot conceal it from the One who sees all things.
A person can pretend their marriage is healthy.
God knows about the tears that fall after the lights go out.
And a wounded person can spend decades pretending that the abuse never happened.
But the Lord has never been ignorant of their suffering.
Being fully known by God is terrifying when we want to protect our sin. But it becomes a profound comfort when we realize He also sees the wounds nobody else understands.
That is why Hebrews 4 cannot be reduced to a warning about sexual immorality.
The passage is bigger than that.
It reveals the searching power of God's Word, the impossibility of hiding from His sight, and the astonishing mercy available through Jesus Christ.
Listen to verse 13:
"Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do." (KJV)
All things.
Naked.
Opened.
Nothing hidden.
The Greek text says:
πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα
Panta de gymna kai tetrachēlismena.
"All things are naked and exposed."
The word gymna means naked or uncovered.
The unusual word tetrachēlismena conveys being laid bare or exposed.
The precise background of the expression is debated, but its meaning in the passage is unmistakable.
Nothing is concealed from God's sight.
And notice something important.
Hebrews is not using nakedness here to create sexual imagery.
It is describing our complete exposure before the God to whom we must give account.
No costume.
No performance.
No carefully edited testimony.
No religious reputation strong enough to conceal the truth.
Just us.
Before Him.
And perhaps that is exactly what frightens us.
Because many of us have spent our lives trying to control what others know about us.
We show them the wedding photographs.
Not the screaming arguments.
We show them the Bible verses.
Not the private messages.
We show them the ministry involvement.
Not the secret addiction.
We show them the happy family portrait.
Not the child who cries because the house no longer feels safe.
And yet the Bible keeps opening doors that respectable society would rather leave closed.
Consider the very beginning.
Genesis 2:25 says Adam and Eve were both naked and were not ashamed.
Before sin entered the world, nakedness itself was not presented as something evil.
The human body was part of God's good creation.
Then Genesis 3 records humanity's rebellion, and shame enters the story.
Suddenly, the man and woman who once stood unashamed begin covering themselves and hiding from God.
The problem was not that their bodies had suddenly become wicked.
The problem was that sin had fractured their relationship with God, with each other, and even with themselves.
And humanity has been hiding ever since.
Hiding behind success.
Hiding behind pleasure.
Hiding behind religion.
Hiding behind relationships.
Hiding behind another secret encounter that promises comfort but leaves the soul emptier than before.
And still the question of Genesis echoes through the centuries.
"Where art thou?" (Genesis 3:9, KJV)
God was not asking because He had lost Adam.
He was confronting a man who was hiding.
And perhaps that question has followed you into this very moment.
Where are you?
Not geographically.
Spiritually.
Where are you in your marriage?
Where are you in your private life?
Where are you in the struggle you keep promising to surrender?
Where are you in the grief you refuse to speak about?
Where are you in your relationship with Jesus?
Because the God who sees everything is not interested in maintaining the illusion that everything is fine.
He calls us into truth.
And Scripture refuses to pretend that sexuality exists outside that truth.
Read the Song of Songs.
You will discover poetic celebrations of attraction, longing, affection, and the beauty of the beloved.
Song of Songs 4:5 uses the imagery of two young gazelles to describe the woman's breasts.
Song of Songs 7:7–8 also contains intimate poetic language.

These passages belong to ancient Hebrew love poetry. Their imagery should be understood within the book's literary and cultural setting rather than treated as a modern anatomical description or a license for voyeurism.
But their presence in Scripture still teaches something important.
The Bible does not teach that sexual attraction within God's design is inherently filthy.
The Hebrew word דּוֹדִים (dodim) can refer to expressions of love or lovemaking, depending on context.
And the Song celebrates the delight of love without pretending that physical affection is absent from human relationships.
The God who created marriage did not accidentally create desire.
Genesis 2:24 presents the union of husband and wife as becoming "one flesh."
Sexual intimacy within marriage is not something Christians need to describe as shameful in order to defend holiness.
It is a good gift that requires faithfulness, mutual honor, and love.
But the same Bible that celebrates marital intimacy also confronts sexual sin.
Jesus makes that unmistakable.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He moves beyond the outward act of adultery and confronts lustful intention in the heart.
He does not condemn the mere recognition that another person is attractive.
He confronts the deliberate cultivation of desire that treats someone as an object of illicit sexual possession.
And that distinction matters.
Because temptation itself is not identical to surrendering to temptation.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
The issue is not whether a person ever experiences an unwanted thought or attraction.
The issue is what they choose to welcome, nurture, pursue, and obey.
God does not call us to pretend we have no bodies.
He calls us to honor Him with them.
And the consequences of refusing that call can be devastating.
Think about David.
A king.
A worshiper.
A man who knew the language of prayer.
Yet 2 Samuel 11 records his adultery with Bathsheba and the terrible abuse of royal power that followed.
Bathsheba was summoned by the king, and the text does not give us grounds to assume she enjoyed equal power or freedom in that encounter.
David then arranged for her husband Uriah to be placed in a deadly military situation.
The biblical account does not romanticize David's actions.
It exposes them.
And when the prophet Nathan confronts him, the king finally says:
"I have sinned against the LORD." (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
No more pretending.
No more manipulating appearances.
No more hiding behind a crown.
David's repentance did not erase the harm or the consequences of what he had done.
But it marked a necessary turning toward the God he had offended.
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a broken man pleading for mercy.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
The Hebrew is beautiful and searching.
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create for me a clean heart, O God."
The verb bera comes from בָּרָא (bara), "to create."
David does not merely ask God to help him manage his reputation.
He asks for inward renewal.
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have avoided.
We want God to remove the consequences.
But we hesitate to ask Him to transform the desires that led us there.
We want peace without confession.
Healing without honesty.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Restoration without change.
Yet biblical grace is not permission to keep destroying ourselves and others.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy that receives repentant sinners and begins transforming the very lives sin has damaged.
And the Bible makes this clear through stories that many religious communities would rather soften.
Rahab was identified as a prostitute.
Yet Joshua 2 records her response of faith in the God of Israel, and Hebrews 11:31 remembers her among those who acted by faith.
Matthew 1:5 even places Rahab in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A woman remembered for prostitution appears in the family history of the Messiah.
Not because prostitution was righteous.
Not because her past did not matter.
But because her past did not have the final word over her future.
And then there is the woman at the well.
John 4 records Jesus speaking with a Samaritan woman whose marital history was complicated.
She had had five husbands, and the man she was then living with was not her husband.
Jesus knew.
He did not need someone to whisper the details to Him.
But notice what the passage does not tell us.
It does not explain how each marriage ended.
It does not say that she caused every separation.
It does not justify labeling her a prostitute.
Those assumptions are often added to the story, but they are not stated by the text.
What Scripture actually shows is even more powerful.
Jesus knew her history and still spoke to her about living water.
He revealed truth without treating her as beyond the reach of God.
And she went back to her community saying:
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" (John 4:29, KJV)
The woman who had been fully known became a witness.
The encounter she could not have anticipated became a doorway through which others came to hear Jesus.
Isn't that extraordinary?
The very knowledge that could have made her want to run became part of her testimony.
Because Jesus did not reveal Himself merely to expose her past.
He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
And then there is another woman.
One caught in adultery.
John 7:53–8:11 preserves the famous account of a woman brought before Jesus by religious accusers.

An important textual note belongs here: this passage is absent from many of the earliest Greek manuscripts of John and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions. Christians should be aware of that textual history rather than conceal it.
The account nevertheless illustrates themes clearly taught elsewhere in Scripture: the danger of hypocritical condemnation, the reality of sin, and the call to turn away from it.
The accusers wanted a spectacle.
Jesus refused to make her humiliation their entertainment.
And in the familiar words of John 8:11, He said:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (KJV)
Mercy.
And a command to change.
Neither one canceled the other.
That is the beauty of biblical grace.
Jesus does not need to pretend sin is harmless in order to show mercy to sinners.
And He does not need to humiliate sinners in order to call them to holiness.
But now consider the other side of these stories.
What about the person who did not choose what happened?
What about the girl whose innocence was stolen?
What about the boy who was abused and grew into a man who cannot explain why he feels so much shame?
What about the wife whose husband repeatedly betrayed her?
What about the child caught between two parents who have turned their home into a battlefield?
The Bible does not ignore them.
In 2 Samuel 13, Tamar suffers sexual violence at the hands of her half-brother Amnon.
It is one of Scripture's most heartbreaking accounts.
The text does not present Amnon's violence as love.
It reveals the destruction caused by selfish desire, abuse of power, and injustice.
Tamar protests.
Her suffering matters.
Her voice matters.
And the tragedy is not that she failed to remain pure.
The guilt belongs to the person who violated her.
That is a truth some wounded people desperately need to hear.
What someone did to you is not proof that you are dirty, worthless, or rejected by God.
You do not need to repent for another person's abuse.
You deserve safety, compassion, and appropriate support.
And if someone is currently harming you, seeking protection and help is not a betrayal of faith.
The Lord's compassion is not reserved only for people whose suffering fits neatly into a church testimony.
He sees the wounded.
He sees the betrayed.
He sees the children who learned fear before they learned trust.
He sees the person who still freezes when certain memories return.
And He does not confuse the victim with the offender.
This is why we must read the whole Bible, not merely collect verses that make powerful captions.
Scripture tells the truth about both human sin and human suffering.
It tells us that desire can be beautiful.
It tells us that lust can become destructive.
It tells us that marriage is honorable.
It tells us that families can become places of deep betrayal.
It tells us that people are responsible for their choices.
And it tells us that the wounded must not be crushed beneath the guilt of those who hurt them.
But now we arrive at the moment that changes everything.
Return to Hebrews 4.
Because if we stop at verse 13, we are left standing exposed before a holy God.
Every secret known.
Every motive uncovered.
Every false excuse stripped away.
And the terrifying question becomes:
Who can stand before Him?
Who can survive the truth about themselves?
Who can approach the God who sees what nobody else has seen?
The answer comes immediately.
Hebrews 4:14:
"Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession." (KJV)
There He is.
Jesus.
Not an indifferent observer.
Not a religious celebrity.
Not a Savior who looks away when our stories become uncomfortable.
Our great High Priest.
The One who has entered heaven.
The Son of God.
The One who represents His people before the Father.
And Hebrews continues:
"For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." (Hebrews 4:15, KJV)
That final phrase is everything.
Yet without sin.
Jesus understands human weakness without being guilty of human rebellion.
He knows temptation without surrendering to it.
He knows rejection without becoming cruel.
He knows suffering without becoming corrupt.
He is not merely another broken person telling us to try harder.
He is the sinless Savior who can actually rescue sinners.
The Greek word συμπαθῆσαι (sympathēsai) in Hebrews 4:15 means to sympathize or share in the feeling of another's weakness.
This does not mean Jesus personally committed every sin or experienced every possible human circumstance.
It means His real humanity and sinless endurance make Him a compassionate High Priest who understands the weakness and testing of His people.
And then comes one of the most astonishing invitations in the entire New Testament.
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." (Hebrews 4:16, KJV)
Wait.
Read that again.
The same passage that says everything is naked and exposed before God tells us to approach His throne with confidence.
How can that be?
Because between our exposure and our invitation stands Jesus Christ.
Our High Priest.
Our mediator.
Our hope.
The Greek expression μετὰ παρρησίας (meta parrēsias) means "with confidence" or "with boldness."
And θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος (thronō tēs charitos) means "throne of grace."
Not a throne where sin is declared insignificant.
Not a throne where victims are told their suffering does not matter.
Not a throne where repentance is unnecessary.
A throne of grace.
A place where God's mercy is available through Jesus Christ.
And this is the great surprise of Hebrews 4.
The God whose Word exposes everything is the God who invites us to seek mercy through His Son.
You do not have to clean up your entire life before you can cry out to Christ.
You do not have to manufacture a spotless history.
You do not have to convince God that you are better than you really are.
But you must not mistake His invitation for permission to remain comfortably in sin.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
Come ready to surrender what has been ruling you.
And if you have been wounded, come knowing that His mercy is not another accusation against you.
It is an invitation to bring your pain into His care.
Maybe you are reading this after another failure.
You promised you would never open that website again.
But you did.
You promised the affair was over.
But you kept the conversation alive.
You promised you would stop flirting with what was destroying your marriage.
But part of you still wanted the attention.
You promised you would tell the truth.
But the fear of losing your reputation felt stronger than the conviction in your heart.
And now you are exhausted.
Not merely from the sin.
From the hiding.
From pretending.
From living two different lives.
One that people applaud.
And another that keeps you awake at night.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not another secret promise made in a moment of panic.
It is genuine repentance, faith in Jesus Christ, and a willingness to walk in the light.
That may mean confessing what you have hidden.
Ending an immoral relationship.
Seeking pastoral accountability from someone trustworthy.
Getting professional help for compulsive behavior.
Accepting the consequences of your actions.
Making restitution where appropriate.
Or taking the difficult first steps toward rebuilding trust without demanding immediate forgiveness from the people you harmed.
Grace is free to us because of Christ.
But grace is not cheap.
The cross reveals just how seriously God takes sin.
Jesus did not die because our rebellion was harmless.
He died because sin is serious, judgment is real, and humanity cannot save itself.
And the resurrection declares that death does not have the final victory.
This is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
Not shame management.
Not a motivational speech about becoming the best version of yourself.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners, reconcile us to God, and make us new.
And perhaps the most painful thing about your story is that you have begun to believe your worst chapter is your permanent identity.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Failure.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Unwanted.
Damaged.
Unworthy.
Some of those words may describe real choices or circumstances.
But none of them has the authority to replace what God says about those who belong to Christ.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about people whose former lives had been marked by various sins, including sexual immorality.
Then he said:
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
Such were some of you.
Not because their past never happened.
Not because repentance made consequences disappear.
But because God's saving work had changed their standing and begun changing their lives.
And 2 Corinthians 5:17 announces:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
That does not promise that every relationship will be restored.
It does not guarantee that every marriage will survive betrayal.
It does not mean trauma disappears overnight.
It does not erase legal responsibility or remove the need for patient healing.
But it does mean that through Christ, a person's past need not determine their ultimate future.
And that is why we keep proclaiming this message.
Not because scandal is glamorous.
Not because sin makes a better testimony.
Not because brokenness should be celebrated.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the darkness that brought us to our knees.
He can forgive the guilty.
He can comfort the wounded.
He can humble the proud.
He can strengthen the tempted.
He can restore people who have forgotten what hope feels like.
And He can teach those who have received mercy to become people who extend mercy without compromising truth.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious controversy.
Not to turn someone's suffering into a spectacle.
But to bring the truth of Scripture into the places where people are silently struggling.
To remind the ashamed that repentance is possible.
To remind the wounded that God has not forgotten them.
To remind families that Christ is worthy of their trust even when life is painfully complicated.
To help believers move beyond inspirational posts into actual discipleship.
Because the world does not need another Christian page that knows how to attract attention but never leads people deeper into the Word.
We need hearts rooted in Scripture.
Minds renewed by truth.
Homes shaped by prayer.
Lives marked by holiness.
And believers who understand that following Jesus is not merely something we do when someone posts a beautiful verse.
It is a daily surrender.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Bible, understand the Gospel, strengthen their prayer lives, grow in spiritual maturity, and remain anchored in Jesus Christ.
And keeping that work going requires real time, effort, resources, and faithful support.
If these messages have helped you return to Scripture, confront a hidden struggle, or remember the mercy of Christ, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading.
It doesn't.
Not because you owe a monthly payment to prove that you love Jesus.
You don't.
It shouldn't.
But because voluntary, generous support for faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful way to honor God and help His Word reach more people.
Scripture teaches that those who receive spiritual instruction may share good things with those who teach (Galatians 6:6), and that giving should be willing rather than compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is the possibility that another person might encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Someone battling an addiction.
Someone quietly considering abandoning their faith.
Someone sitting alone after discovering their spouse's betrayal.
Someone who believes their sexual past makes them permanently unworthy.
Someone who needs to discover that God calls sinners to repentance and offers mercy through His Son.
You can still help this mission.
Not merely to increase its reach.
Someone may be one honest conversation away from seeking help.
Someone may need to hear that holiness and compassion belong together.
Someone may need to discover that the Bible does not hide from the realities that have shattered their life.
Because there may come a night when the battle feels louder than your prayers.
A night when shame returns.
A night when you need to remember that Hebrews 4 does not end with exposure.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
And I want to ask you something before you leave.
Not a question designed to make you reveal private details that could endanger you or someone else.
Not an invitation to confess another person's sins publicly.
Just one honest question between your heart and God.
What have you been afraid to bring into the light?
Is it a sin you need to turn away from?
A wound you need help healing?
A marriage that needs truth?
A hidden struggle that needs accountability?
Or a season of exhaustion in which you can barely find the strength to pray?
God already knows.
And the people of God should be a community where truth is spoken with compassion, prayer is offered without spectacle, and struggling people are encouraged to seek wise and trustworthy help.
Before we finish, I want you to imagine something.
Imagine standing before God.
No audience.
No social media profile.
No church title.
No impressive achievements.
No carefully rehearsed explanation.
Everything known.
Every hidden decision.
Every wound.
Every secret.
Every motive.
And imagine understanding, perhaps more clearly than ever before, why you could never save yourself.
Now remember the invitation of Hebrews 4.
There is a great High Priest.
Jesus Christ.
He is holy.
He is sinless.
He is merciful.
He is risen.
And through Him, those who trust in Him may approach the throne of grace.
Not because they have successfully hidden their worst moments.
But because their hope rests in the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, you can call upon Him today.
A prayer does not save by the mere repetition of its words. Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Christ, and genuine faith turns toward Him in repentance.
But you can speak honestly to Him right now.

"Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know my sins, my fears, my wounds, and the things I have tried to hide. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to turn away from sin and follow You. Heal what is wounded, correct what is wrong, and make my life a testimony to Your grace. I surrender myself to You. Amen."
And if you have already trusted Christ but wandered far from Him, hear the call of Scripture again.
Return.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help where you need it.
Walk in the light.
Do not let shame persuade you that hiding is safer than the mercy of God.
Do not let pride convince you that your reputation matters more than your soul.
And do not let the cruelty of others convince you that Jesus shares their contempt.
The Bible talks about sex because God created human beings as embodied people.
It talks about lust because our desires can become disordered.
It talks about adultery because covenant betrayal matters.
It talks about prostitution because people are more than the sins and circumstances by which society labels them.
It talks about sexual violence because injustice must not be disguised as love.
It talks about broken families because Scripture tells the truth about a fallen world.
And Hebrews 4:12–16 reminds us that the God who knows all these realities also provides a compassionate High Priest.
That is the heart of this message.
Not that God is fascinated by scandal.
But that no scandal is too hidden for His knowledge, no sinner is beyond the reach of His call to repentance, and no wound is beneath His compassion.
The cross does not make evil good.
It reveals the righteousness and mercy of God.
And the empty tomb declares that Jesus Christ is alive.
So stop believing that your only choices are to keep pretending or to give up completely.
There is another way.
The way of truth.
The way of repentance.
The way of grace.
The way of Jesus Christ.

The most frightening thing about coming into the light is discovering that God already knows everything. The most beautiful thing is discovering that, through Jesus Christ, He still invites you to His throne of grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD WE BAPTIZE BABIES… OR ARE WE PUTTING WATER BEFORE FAITH?
paragraphs: SHOULD WE BAPTIZE BABIES… OR ARE WE PUTTING WATER BEFORE FAITH?
One of Christianity’s Most Emotional Disagreements—And the Uncomfortable Question Every Parent, Pastor, and Believer Must Face About Baptism, Salvation, and What Jesus Actually Commanded.
A mother stands at the front of a church, holding her newborn baby.
The child is barely old enough to recognize her voice. Tiny fingers curl around hers. The congregation watches quietly as a minister approaches with water.
A prayer is spoken.
Water touches the baby's forehead.
And somewhere in that sanctuary, a grandmother begins to cry.
Not because she is sad.
Because she believes something holy has just happened.
She believes her grandchild has been welcomed into God's covenant family.
She believes this moment matters for eternity.
Now travel to another church, perhaps just a few streets away.
A seventeen-year-old boy stands trembling in a baptismal pool.
His past is complicated.
He has lied to his parents. Hidden addictions. Questioned whether God was real. Spent nights feeling so ashamed of himself that he wondered whether Jesus could possibly want someone like him.
But something changed.
He heard the Gospel.
He repented.
He believed.
And now, with tears running down his face, he declares that Jesus Christ is his Lord.
The pastor lowers him beneath the water.
When he rises, the congregation erupts in praise.
Two churches.
Two baptisms.
Two families convinced they are honoring Jesus.
But here is the question that can make even devoted Christians uncomfortable:
Did Jesus command us to baptize people before they believe, or to baptize those who have personally responded to the Gospel?
And if Christians have disagreed about this for centuries, how do we know which understanding is faithful to Scripture?
Before you answer, consider something.
The mother holding that baby may love Jesus with all her heart.
The teenager entering that baptismal pool may genuinely have been transformed by grace.
And neither family's sincerity, by itself, settles the biblical question.
Because love does not eliminate our responsibility to examine Scripture.
Tradition does not become truth merely because it is old.
And something does not become false simply because it is practiced by a church different from ours.
We must go deeper.
Not to win an argument.
Not to humiliate another denomination.
Not to turn the sacred name of Jesus into ammunition for religious superiority.
But because baptism matters.
The Gospel matters.
And the difference between trusting Christ and trusting a religious ceremony matters more than many people realize.
Perhaps you were baptized as a baby.
Perhaps you were baptized as an adult.
Perhaps you have never been baptized at all.
Or perhaps you are a parent who genuinely wants to do what is right before God, but you are afraid of making the wrong decision for your child.
Stay with this question.
Because somewhere beneath the centuries of theological debate lies something far more personal:
When God looks at you, is He looking for water on your skin—or faith in His Son?
The answer begins with Jesus.
After His resurrection, Christ gave His disciples a command that would carry the Gospel across generations and nations.
Matthew 28:19–20 records His commission to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything He commanded.
The original Greek begins with a crucial expression:
μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη
mathēteusate panta ta ethnē
“Make disciples of all the nations.”
The central imperative is mathēteusate—make disciples.
The passage then uses the participles baptizontes and didaskontes, describing baptizing and teaching as activities involved in making disciples.
That matters.
Jesus did not present baptism as an isolated religious performance disconnected from discipleship.
He placed baptism inside the mission of bringing people under His lordship.
But we must be careful.

Matthew 28 does not explicitly state the minimum age of a baptismal candidate. Christians who baptize infants understand the command as including the children of believers within the covenant community, with lifelong instruction following baptism.
Christians who practice believer's baptism understand the command as directing the church to baptize people who have become disciples through faith.
Both appeal to the passage.
The disagreement is not whether Jesus commanded baptism.
He did.
The disagreement concerns who should receive it, what it signifies, and how it relates to faith.
And that is why we cannot stop at one verse.
We must follow the testimony of Scripture.
Travel with me to Jerusalem.
It is Pentecost.
The apostle Peter is preaching.
The crowd hears that the Jesus they crucified has been raised from the dead and exalted as Lord and Messiah.
Suddenly, the message becomes personal.
These are not spectators listening to an interesting religious lecture.
They are people confronted by the reality of their sin.
Acts 2:37 says they were pierced to the heart.
Imagine the silence.
Imagine realizing that the One you rejected was the very Savior God had sent.
They ask:
“What shall we do?”
Peter answers in Acts 2:38:
Μετανοήσατε ... καὶ βαπτισθήτω ἕκαστος ὑμῶν
Metanoēsate ... kai baptisthētō hekastos hymōn
“Repent ... and let each of you be baptized.”
The first word, metanoēsate, is a command to repent.
The verb baptisthētō calls for baptism.
Peter joins repentance and baptism in his response to people who have heard the Gospel.
Then Acts 2:41 describes those who received his message being baptized.
Read that again.
They heard.
They received the message.
They were baptized.
For advocates of believer's baptism, this is a powerful example of the New Testament pattern.
The Gospel is proclaimed.
People respond.
Baptism follows.
But Peter also says something that Christians must not overlook.
In Acts 2:39, he declares that the promise is for his hearers, their children, and those far away—everyone whom the Lord calls.
Those who baptize infants see significant covenantal implications in that mention of children.

Those who advocate believer's baptism emphasize the concluding qualification: the promise extends to those whom God calls, and the immediate narrative describes people receiving the apostolic message.
The verse deserves more than a slogan.
It demands careful interpretation.
Now consider the Ethiopian official in Acts 8.
He is traveling along a desert road, reading from the prophet Isaiah.
He does not understand whom the prophet is describing.
God sends Philip to him.
Philip begins with the Scripture and announces the good news about Jesus.
Then they come upon water.
The Ethiopian asks what prevents him from being baptized.
And the narrative tells us that Philip baptizes him.
The central movement is unmistakable.
Scripture is explained.
Christ is proclaimed.
Baptism follows.
Some Bible translations include an additional statement in Acts 8:37 in which Philip requires belief with all the heart and the Ethiopian confesses Jesus as the Son of God.
But there is an important textual detail.
Acts 8:37 is absent from several of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is generally treated by modern textual scholars as a later addition.
That means we should not build an entire doctrine on that disputed verse as though its textual status were beyond question.
The surrounding account, however, still describes an adult hearing the Gospel and requesting baptism.
And the wider book of Acts repeatedly connects baptism with the spread of the Gospel.
In Acts 10, Cornelius and those gathered with him hear Peter preach. The Holy Spirit comes upon the hearers, and Peter orders them to be baptized.
In Acts 16, the Philippian jailer hears the message of the Lord and is baptized with his household.
In Acts 18:8, many Corinthians hear, believe, and are baptized.
These accounts provide substantial support for the practice of baptizing professing believers.
But then comes the question that has divided Christians for generations.
What about the households?
The New Testament records household baptisms, including Lydia's household in Acts 16, the jailer's household in the same chapter, and the household of Stephanas in 1 Corinthians 1.
Those who support infant baptism argue that the household language fits the ancient biblical pattern in which God's covenant dealings extend to families.
Those who support believer's baptism respond that none of these accounts explicitly identifies an infant being baptized.
And they are correct about that specific observation.
The New Testament does not give us an unambiguous narrative saying, “An infant was baptized.”
But the opposite claim also requires caution.
The household accounts do not always specify the age and spiritual response of every person involved.
The jailer's household is associated with hearing the word of the Lord and rejoicing over faith in God, although interpreters debate precisely how the language applies to each household member.
Lydia's household is baptized, but the narrative does not tell us the ages of its members.
Therefore, the household passages are important evidence in the debate, but they do not settle it by themselves.
We cannot honestly make the Bible say more than it says.
And perhaps that is where some of our arguments have gone wrong.
We become so determined to defend our position that we stop distinguishing between what Scripture explicitly teaches and what our theological conclusions infer.
But God does not need us to exaggerate His Word to defend it.
Now we must enter the deepest part of the discussion.
The covenant.
Because Christians who baptize infants are not necessarily claiming that babies have personally repented or consciously professed faith.
Many are making a different argument altogether.
They are asking whether the children of believers should receive the covenant sign because they belong to a household set apart within God's visible covenant community.
In Genesis 17, God commands Abraham to circumcise the males of his household, including infant sons on the eighth day.
The Hebrew word for covenant is:
בְּרִית
berit — “covenant.”
A covenant is not merely a casual promise.
It establishes a binding relationship, with obligations and promises defined by God.
Under the Abrahamic covenant, infant boys received circumcision before they could personally understand or articulate faith.
For many Presbyterian and Reformed Christians who practice infant baptism, this is a foundational part of the argument.
They see baptism as the new-covenant sign that corresponds to circumcision, with Colossians 2:11–12 forming part of their biblical reasoning.
They also appeal to the continuity of God's covenant purposes across generations.

Other traditions that baptize infants, including Catholic, Orthodox, and some Lutheran and Anglican churches, emphasize different combinations of covenant theology, sacramental grace, regeneration, and the faith of the Church.
These traditions should not be treated as though they all teach precisely the same theology of baptism.
Some regard baptism as a means through which God ordinarily gives regenerating grace.
Others emphasize incorporation into the visible covenant community while distinguishing that outward membership from inward salvation.
But here is the question believer's-baptism advocates raise.
Does the New Testament actually command the church to apply baptism to infants because circumcision was applied to infants?
Colossians 2:11–12 connects circumcision made without hands, burial with Christ in baptism, and resurrection with Him through faith in the working of God.
Believer's-baptism advocates emphasize that Paul speaks of spiritual circumcision and faith, not an explicit command to baptize infants.
Infant-baptism advocates see continuity between covenant signs and God's covenant dealings with families.
This is a genuine interpretive disagreement.
It cannot be resolved responsibly by pretending that one side has no biblical argument.
But neither should we pretend that the New Testament explicitly commands infant baptism.
It does not.
And that observation carries weight.
Especially when the clearest narrative examples of baptism repeatedly involve people who hear and respond to the Gospel.
Now listen to what Paul writes in Romans 6:3–4.
He describes believers being baptized into Christ Jesus and into His death, buried with Him through baptism, so that they might walk in newness of life.
The Greek expression is beautiful:
ἐν καινότητι ζωῆς
en kainotēti zōēs
“In newness of life.”
Not merely a new religious label.
Not merely a family tradition.
A new life.
A life shaped by the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
This is why baptism is so powerful.
It points beyond itself.
It declares the saving work of Another.
The water is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
The ceremony is not the crucified and risen Lord.
Jesus is.
And baptism must never be presented as a substitute for the grace that comes through Christ.
Yet we should also resist the opposite error of treating baptism as meaningless.
The New Testament speaks of baptism with remarkable seriousness.
Acts 22:16 connects baptism with calling upon the Lord's name and the washing away of sins.
