Because one careless answer could make biblical truth seem optional.
And another could make salvation seem impossible for anyone who has not mastered every disputed doctrine in Christianity.
Neither answer does justice to the Gospel.
And somewhere between arrogant certainty and careless compromise, Scripture gives us something far more glorious.
Grace that never abandons truth.
Truth that never makes grace unnecessary.
And a Savior who does not need imperfect people to become omniscient before He can redeem them.
THE MAN DYING BESIDE JESUS DID NOT HAVE TIME TO BECOME A THEOLOGIAN.
Picture Calvary.
Three crosses.
A dying criminal.
A bleeding Savior.
No comfortable church building. No theological library. No opportunity to attend years of discipleship classes.
Only a man confronting the wreckage of his life while death approached.
Luke 23:40–43 records something extraordinary.
One criminal rebuked the other, acknowledged that they were receiving the consequences of their crimes, and confessed that Jesus had done nothing wrong.
Then he turned toward Christ.
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, ESV)
And Jesus answered:
“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, ESV)
Read that again.
Jesus did not say, “First, explain your position on the millennium.”
He did not demand that the man settle every disputed question concerning church government, spiritual gifts, or the precise sequence of future events.
He did not require a theological examination before extending mercy.
The dying criminal recognized his guilt, acknowledged Jesus' innocence and kingship, and appealed to Him for mercy.
And Jesus promised him paradise.
Now, we must not twist this passage.

The thief's experience does not prove that baptism, discipleship, obedience, and sound doctrine are unimportant. Jesus commanded His disciples to baptize and teach believers to obey everything He commanded (Matthew 28:19–20).
The extraordinary circumstances of a dying criminal do not cancel the ordinary responsibilities of Christian discipleship.
But they reveal something breathtaking about salvation.
The criminal was not saved by possessing complete theological knowledge. He was saved by the mercy of the King in whom he placed his hope.
And perhaps that should make every one of us a little slower to pronounce judgment on the eternal destiny of a fellow believer over a disputed secondary doctrine.
Because the Savior who welcomed that dying criminal is the same Savior who receives repentant sinners today.
But does that mean doctrine does not matter?
Absolutely not.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
NOT EVERY THEOLOGICAL ERROR IS A SECONDARY ISSUE.
There is a difference between misunderstanding a biblical teaching and rejecting the Gospel itself.
The apostle Paul did not treat every doctrinal disagreement as equally serious.
In Galatians 1:8–9, he pronounced a severe warning against proclaiming a gospel contrary to the one the apostles had preached.
In 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Paul summarized matters of first importance: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day.
These are not optional decorations around Christianity.
They concern the very foundation of the Christian faith.
Jesus Christ is not merely a moral teacher who offered helpful religious advice.
He is the eternal Son of God who became flesh (John 1:1, 14).
He died for sinners.
He rose bodily from the dead.
He is Lord.
And salvation comes through Him, not through our ability to earn God's acceptance.
Paul writes:
The original Greek makes this especially meaningful.
The expression χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι — chariti este sesōsmenoi means, in context, “by grace you have been saved.”
The construction emphasizes salvation as a reality brought about by God's gracious action, with continuing significance for those who have been saved.
The word χάρις — charis means grace, favor, or gift-like generosity.
And the verb behind σεσῳσμένοι — sesōsmenoi comes from σῴζω — sōzō, meaning to save, rescue, or deliver.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “By flawless theological precision you have been saved.”
He does not say, “By winning every doctrinal debate you have been saved.”
He says salvation is by grace through faith.
But that faith is not faith in faith itself.
It is faith in Jesus Christ.
The object of saving faith matters.
The identity of the Savior matters.
The Gospel matters.
A person cannot simply redefine Jesus, reject His saving work, and assume that every religious belief leads to the same salvation.
Scripture does not permit that conclusion.
Yet Scripture also never teaches that a believer must achieve perfect understanding of every biblical subject before Christ can save them.
That distinction changes everything.
YOU CAN BE WRONG ABOUT SOMETHING IMPORTANT WITHOUT BEING WRONG ABOUT THE ONE WHO SAVES YOU.
Consider two sincere Christians.
One believes that Christ will return before a future thousand-year reign described in Revelation 20.
Another understands that passage differently.
Both confess that Jesus Christ will return, judge the living and the dead, defeat evil, and bring God's redemptive purposes to completion.
Their disagreement is meaningful.
They should study Scripture carefully.
They should not pretend the difference is imaginary.
But must one automatically be unsaved because their interpretation of the millennium is mistaken?
Scripture gives us no warrant to make that declaration.
Or consider believers who disagree about whether certain miraculous spiritual gifts continue in the church today.
One is a continuationist.
Another is a cessationist.
Both may genuinely confess Christ, trust His saving work, submit to Scripture, and seek to live holy lives.
Their interpretations cannot both be correct in every respect.
But theological disagreement does not automatically prove that one has never belonged to Jesus.
The same principle can apply to certain disagreements about worship practices, church governance, the timing of end-times events, and other disputed questions.
However, we must be precise.
Christians do not universally agree on which doctrines should be classified as secondary.

For example, baptism is commanded by Christ, and Christians disagree not only about its mode and subjects but also about its relationship to salvation. Those disagreements can have serious implications for church membership and fellowship.
Calling a doctrine secondary does not mean it is insignificant.
It means that an error concerning that doctrine does not necessarily amount to a denial of the saving Gospel.
That is an important distinction.
Because there is a dangerous difference between saying, “This doctrine matters,” and saying, “Anyone who disagrees with me about it is going to hell.”
One statement can express biblical conviction.
The other may claim authority over another person's eternal destiny that God has not given us.
PAUL ALREADY CONFRONTED THIS PROBLEM INSIDE THE EARLY CHURCH.
Imagine a Christian community divided over food.
Some believers were convinced that certain foods could be eaten freely.
Others abstained because of conscience.
To modern ears, that may sound insignificant.
But in the early church, these questions could touch religious identity, holiness, fellowship, and deeply held convictions.
The disagreement was real.
And Paul did not respond by pretending that truth was unknowable.
He addressed the issue while commanding believers to stop despising and condemning one another.
Romans 14:3 says:
“Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.” (ESV)
Then comes a question that should silence much of our spiritual arrogance.
“Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another?” (Romans 14:4, ESV)
Think about that.
A servant belongs to his master.
And a Christian belongs to Christ.
Paul was not saying that Christians should never evaluate teaching or confront sin.
Elsewhere, he explicitly commanded believers to guard sound doctrine and correct serious error.
He was addressing disputes in which believers were tempted to treat their own conscience and convictions as grounds for rejecting those whom God had received.
And Romans 14:17 gives us the wider perspective:
“For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” (ESV)
That does not make biblical obedience irrelevant.
It reminds us that the kingdom is larger than the particular controversy consuming our attention.
Some Christians are so busy defending the boundaries of their theological position that they forget the Lord of the kingdom.
They can identify another person's doctrinal mistakes in seconds.
But they struggle to recognize pride in their own hearts.
They can explain the Greek tense of a verb.
But they cannot apologize to their spouse.
They can defend the doctrine of grace.
But they refuse to extend grace to a brother or sister.
And the tragedy is not that they care too much about truth.
The tragedy is that they have separated their defense of truth from the character of the Christ who is Truth.
KNOWING MORE ABOUT JESUS IS NOT ALWAYS THE SAME AS BECOMING MORE LIKE JESUS.
That sentence should trouble us.
Especially those of us who love theology.
Because theological knowledge is a gift.
Studying the Bible deeply is good.
Learning biblical languages can be valuable.
Understanding church history can protect us from repeating old errors.
Defending sound doctrine is necessary.
But knowledge can become dangerous when it feeds pride instead of worship.
Paul wrote:
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1, ESV)
The Greek expression ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ — hē gnōsis physioi conveys the idea that knowledge can inflate or puff someone up.
Paul was not condemning knowledge itself.
He was confronting knowledge used without love.
And there is a painful irony here.
A person can accurately explain the doctrine of justification while treating other believers with a spirit that contradicts the humility that justification should produce.
Someone can correctly defend the sovereignty of God while behaving as though God's throne needs their personal arrogance to remain secure.
Someone can preach the sufficiency of Christ while acting as though Christ's finished work must be supplemented by agreement with every one of their secondary interpretations.
But the Gospel leaves no room for boasting.
If salvation is grace, then nobody gets to stand before God and say:
“I deserved to be here because I understood everything.”
No.
The redeemed will praise the Lamb who was slain.
Not the brilliance of their own theological systems.
AND YET, GRACE IS NEVER PERMISSION TO REMAIN CARELESS ABOUT TRUTH.
Perhaps someone reading this has been wounded by harsh, argumentative Christians.
Maybe you were publicly embarrassed because you asked a sincere question.
Maybe somebody questioned your salvation because you did not share their interpretation of a disputed passage.
Maybe you were made to feel that you could never belong to Jesus unless you understood every theological term.
If that happened, I want you to hear something clearly.
You do not need to pretend you know what you do not know.
You are allowed to ask questions.
You are allowed to study.
You are allowed to admit that a passage is difficult.
And you are allowed to change your mind when Scripture corrects you.
But do not let the cruelty of an argumentative believer convince you that doctrine itself is the enemy.
Truth is not your enemy.
Jesus prayed:
“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” (John 17:17, ESV)
The answer to spiritual arrogance is not biblical ignorance.
The answer is humble submission to God's Word.
A teachable heart does not say, “Doctrine doesn't matter.”
It says, “Lord, Your truth matters so much that I am willing to be corrected.”
There is a profound difference between being mistaken and being unteachable.
A sincere believer may misunderstand a secondary doctrine while genuinely desiring to obey Christ.
Another person may cling to error because admitting the truth would threaten their reputation, influence, or pride.
God sees what we cannot fully see.
And that is why theological humility must never become theological indifference.
We should hold our convictions seriously.
But we should hold ourselves humbly.
PETER WAS TRULY CHRIST'S DISCIPLE—AND HE STILL NEEDED TO BE CORRECTED.
Think about Peter.
He confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16).
Yet soon afterward, he resisted Jesus' announcement of His coming suffering and death.
Jesus rebuked him sharply (Matthew 16:21–23).
Later, Peter denied knowing Jesus three times.
And after the resurrection, Christ graciously restored him (John 21:15–19).
Still later, Paul publicly confronted Peter because his conduct toward Gentile believers was not consistent with the truth of the Gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).
Peter was not a model of perfect understanding or flawless behavior.
He was a man transformed by a faithful Savior who corrected him, restored him, and continued to use him.
Now, Peter's mistakes were not harmless.
His conduct in Galatians threatened the practical expression of Gospel truth.
Paul confronted him because the Gospel mattered.
But the account also shows that even a genuine apostle could act inconsistently with what he knew.
Correction was necessary.
Grace was still real.
That is not an excuse for sin.
It is a testimony to the patience of Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear it.
You may be wrong about something today.
You may discover next year that a position you defended with great confidence was mistaken.
You may need to repent of the way you treated people who disagreed with you.
You may need to revisit passages you thought you had completely understood.
But discovering your own limitations does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
It may be part of how He is teaching you to depend more deeply on Him.
THERE IS A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN GROWING IN TRUTH AND MAKING YOUR OWN UNDERSTANDING THE SAVIOR.
Paul described Christian maturity as something believers grow toward.
In Philippians 3:12, he openly acknowledged that he had not already obtained perfection.
And in Philippians 3:15–16, he spoke of believers continuing forward, trusting God to clarify what they did not yet understand.
That is remarkable.
The apostle who wrote so much of the New Testament recognized that spiritual growth was not complete.
Now consider the implications.
If Christian maturity involves growth, then immaturity cannot automatically mean the absence of salvation.
If believers are commanded to grow in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ (2 Peter 3:18), then growth necessarily involves moving from less understanding toward greater understanding.
A new Christian may not know the meaning of eschatology.
A struggling believer may not understand the distinctions between various interpretations of Revelation.
A faithful elderly Christian may never have studied biblical Greek.
A poor believer with limited access to theological education may know little about historic doctrinal controversies.
Does that mean Christ cannot save them?
No.
The Gospel was never reserved for the intellectually privileged.
The same Jesus who welcomes scholars also welcomes children.
The same grace that reaches trained theologians reaches repentant sinners who can barely find words to pray.
The decisive issue is not whether someone can explain every dimension of Christian theology.
It is whether they truly belong to Jesus Christ.
And belonging to Christ is not a license to ignore His teaching.
It is the beginning of a life in which we learn to follow Him.
BUT WHAT ABOUT THE CHRISTIAN WHO IS SINCERELY WRONG?
This is where we need to be especially careful.
Sincerity alone does not save.
People can sincerely believe things that are false.
The Bible never teaches that every sincere religious belief leads to eternal life.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” (John 14:6, ESV)
Salvation is found in Christ.
Not sincerity detached from Christ.
Not moral effort.
Not religious identity.
Not theological achievement.
Christ.
But a Christian can sincerely trust the true Christ while misunderstanding some of His teachings.
That is different from rejecting who Christ is or denying the Gospel that saves.
We must also distinguish between ignorance, confusion, honest disagreement, deliberate distortion, and persistent rebellion against clearly understood truth.
These are not spiritually identical.
Only God perfectly knows the heart.
We can evaluate a person's confession, teaching, and conduct according to Scripture.
We can identify false doctrine.
We can warn against dangerous teaching.
Churches can establish doctrinal boundaries for membership, leadership, and ministry.
But we should be extremely cautious about claiming to know with certainty the eternal state of every person who disagrees with us on a disputed secondary issue.
Jesus did not appoint us as omniscient judges of the human soul.
He commanded us to make disciples.
To teach His Word.
To love one another.
To proclaim repentance and forgiveness in His name.
And to remain faithful until He comes.
THE MOST DANGEROUS QUESTION MAY NOT BE, “WHAT IF MY BROTHER IS WRONG?”
It may be:
“What if I am the one who needs correction?”
That question takes courage.
Because pride loves certainty more than truth.
Pride wants to win.
Humility wants to understand.
Pride asks, “How can I prove this person wrong?”
Humility asks, “Lord, what does Your Word actually say?”
Pride treats correction as humiliation.
Humility receives correction as an opportunity to grow.
And the truly frightening thing about pride is that it can hide behind correct theology.
You can defend a true doctrine with a sinful spirit.
You can win an argument and wound a brother.
You can be right about a passage while being terribly wrong about how you treat the person standing in front of you.
James 3:17 describes wisdom from above as pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, and sincere.
That is not weak Christianity.
That is biblical maturity.
Truth without love can become a weapon of self-exaltation.
Love without truth can become sentimental compromise.
But truth and love together reflect the character of Jesus Christ.
John 1:14 describes Him as full of grace and truth.
Not half grace and half truth.
Not grace at the expense of truth.
Not truth stripped of grace.
Full of both.
And every Christian who claims to follow Him should desire the same.
SOMEONE YOU DISAGREE WITH MAY BE YOUR BROTHER OR SISTER IN ETERNITY.
Think about that for a moment.
The believer whose interpretation frustrates you.
The Christian whose denominational background is different from yours.
The person who worships with a style you find unfamiliar.
The brother who has not reached your conclusion about a disputed theological issue.
If that person truly belongs to Jesus Christ, you may spend eternity worshiping the same Savior together.
Not because truth did not matter.
Not because all doctrinal disagreements were equally harmless.
But because both of you were redeemed by the same blood.
Revelation 7:9 portrays a multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the throne and before the Lamb.
The redeemed are united in worship.
Their salvation is centered on God and the Lamb.
And when that day comes, none of us will boast about the theological arguments we won.
We will worship the Christ who saved us.
Perhaps we will finally understand just how much we misunderstood.
Scripture does not give us a detailed account of every correction that may occur in eternity, so we should not invent one.
But it does promise that our present knowledge is partial.
Paul writes:
Our understanding is real.
But it is not exhaustive.
Our knowledge can be true.
But it is not infinite.
We know enough through God's revelation to trust Christ, obey His commands, and proclaim His Gospel.
Yet we still await the fullness of what God will reveal.
That should not make us uncertain about Jesus.
It should make us humble about ourselves.
SO CAN A CHRISTIAN BE SAVED WHILE HOLDING INCORRECT BELIEFS ABOUT SECONDARY DOCTRINES?
Yes.
A genuine Christian can be saved while holding mistaken beliefs about secondary doctrines.
Because salvation is grounded in the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ, not in perfect mastery of every theological question.
But that answer comes with important biblical qualifications.
The Gospel itself cannot be treated as optional.
Not every disputed doctrine is automatically secondary.
Not every claim of faith is genuine.
Not every error is harmless.
And grace never removes our responsibility to seek truth, receive correction, repent of sin, and grow in obedience.
A Christian who is mistaken should be taught patiently.
A Christian who is confused should be helped compassionately.
A Christian who is proud should be corrected lovingly.
A Christian who distorts the Gospel should be warned seriously.
And every Christian, regardless of knowledge or maturity, should be pointed continually back to Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not merely about having the correct answers.
It is about being reconciled to the living God through His Son.
And the more deeply we understand that Gospel, the less room we should have for spiritual arrogance.
THIS IS WHERE SCANDAL MEETS GRACE.
The scandal is that sinners who do not deserve eternal life can be welcomed into God's family.
The scandal is that people with broken histories, incomplete understanding, embarrassing failures, and painful regrets can receive forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
The scandal is that the proud religious expert and the trembling new believer must enter through the same door.
Grace.
Not earned.
Not purchased.
Not achieved through intellectual superiority.
Received through faith in the crucified and risen Savior.
But grace does not leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace corrects.
Grace transforms.
And the Jesus who saves us also calls us to follow Him.
Maybe your scandal was not a public moral failure.
Maybe it was pride.
Maybe you used theology to feel superior.
Maybe you mocked Christians who had not studied as much as you.
Maybe you confused your denomination's distinctives with the boundaries of salvation itself.
Or maybe your scandal was fear.
You spent years wondering whether Jesus would reject you because you could not understand every difficult passage.
You quietly worried that one mistaken interpretation might erase your hope of eternal life.
You loved Christ.
You wanted to obey Him.
But you were terrified that your imperfect understanding made you unacceptable to God.
If that is you, hear the invitation of Jesus.
“Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.” (John 6:37, ESV)
Do not turn that promise into permission to ignore Scripture.
Let it become the reason you run toward Him.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come willing to learn.
Come ready to surrender what Scripture exposes.
And trust the Savior who is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).
You do not need to pretend that you have all the answers.
You need the One who is the Truth.
AND IF YOU HAVE NEVER TRULY SURRENDERED YOUR LIFE TO CHRIST, THIS IS MORE THAN A THEOLOGICAL DISCUSSION.
You can spend your entire life debating salvation without ever personally trusting the Savior.
You can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
You can memorize doctrines while refusing to repent.
You can defend the Bible publicly while resisting its authority privately.
And you can be surrounded by religious activity while remaining spiritually far from God.
That is why the central question is not merely whether you hold an incorrect secondary doctrine.
The deeper question is whether you have truly placed your faith in Jesus Christ.
Have you acknowledged your sin before God?
Have you trusted in Christ's death and resurrection as your only hope of salvation?
Are you willing to turn from sin and follow Him as Lord?
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
But sincerely.
Because saving faith is not merely agreeing that certain religious statements are true.
It is trusting in the living Christ whom those truths reveal.
Romans 10:9 connects confessing Jesus as Lord and believing that God raised Him from the dead with salvation.
And Romans 10:13 declares:
“For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” (ESV)
That invitation remains open.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus is sufficient.
Not because truth is optional.
But because the Truth Himself came to rescue sinners.
If you need to return to Him, you can pray in your own words.

“Lord Jesus, I confess that I am a sinner who needs Your mercy. Forgive my pride, my unbelief, and my rebellion. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to trust Your Word above my opinions, to love others without compromising truth, and to follow You with a humble and obedient heart. I cannot save myself. My hope is in You alone. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula.
Christ saves, not the mere repetition of words.
But if those words express the sincere cry of your heart, do not delay in turning to Him.
And do not try to walk alone.
Find a faithful, Bible-teaching local church where you can be discipled, baptized if you have not been, encouraged, corrected, and equipped to grow in Christ.
BEFORE YOU LEAVE, THERE IS SOMETHING I WANT TO ASK YOU.
Have you ever been made to feel that you were not a real Christian because you disagreed with someone about a secondary doctrine?
Or have you ever realized that you were the person who treated another believer harshly because of a theological disagreement?
Be honest.
Not to win another argument.
Not to embarrass anyone.
But because spiritual healing often begins when we stop pretending we have nothing left to learn.
If this message exposed pride in your heart, you can comment, “Lord, teach me humility.”
If you have been wounded by harsh religious judgment and are learning to trust Jesus again, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
You may need to return to it the next time a theological argument begins to harden your heart.
You may need its reminder when somebody challenges a conviction you have held for years.
Or when you discover that you were wrong.
Because spiritual maturity is not demonstrated only by how strongly we defend what we believe.
Sometimes it is demonstrated by how humbly we respond when God's Word corrects us.
AND MAYBE SOMEONE YOU LOVE NEEDS TO READ THIS TODAY.
There may be a friend on your Facebook feed who has quietly walked away from Christian fellowship after being wounded by needless condemnation.
There may be a young believer who is afraid to ask questions.
There may be a family member who has mistaken religious arguments for the heart of Christianity.
There may even be someone who has never understood that salvation is a gift of grace through Jesus Christ.
Not merely to increase its reach.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you grow in your faith, I want to invite you into something deeper.
HELP US KEEP BRINGING THE GOSPEL TO PEOPLE WHO NEED IT.
Every article written, every biblical resource shared, and every message of encouragement is part of a larger mission: to point people away from themselves and toward Jesus Christ.
We want those resources to continue reaching people who may never be able to purchase a Christian book, attend a conference, or afford a discipleship program.
That work requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful—not forced by guilt or spiritual pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And your responsibility to support your local church and care for those entrusted to you should never be displaced by pressure from an online ministry.
Those products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
You can pray for the ministry.
You can use the free resources and continue growing in God's Word.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
What matters is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully, His Word is handled truthfully, and people are invited to know and follow Him.
BECAUSE ONE DAY, EVERY ARGUMENT WILL END.
The comment sections will go silent.
The debates will be over.
The theological disagreements that consumed so much of our time will finally be placed beneath the perfect knowledge and righteous judgment of God.
And every person will stand before the Lord.
On that day, the only Savior who can redeem us will not be our theological intelligence.
It will be Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The Lamb of God.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who conquered the grave.
The One who calls His people to truth, holiness, humility, and love.
So study deeply.
Defend the Gospel faithfully.
Reject false teaching.
Receive correction.
Love the brethren.
Never confuse humility with compromise.
Never confuse conviction with cruelty.
And never forget that the same grace you desperately need is the grace you should never be ashamed to celebrate when Christ extends it to another repentant sinner.
Because the question is not whether you will ever discover that you were wrong about something.
You almost certainly will.
The question is whether you will allow God's Word to correct you—and whether your confidence rests in your own understanding or in the finished work of Jesus Christ.

You may reach heaven having misunderstood some things about God, but you will never reach heaven apart from the mercy of the God who understood everything about you—and loved you enough to send His Son to save you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID, “I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.” SO WHY ARE THERE SO MANY? THE QUESTION CHRISTIANS CAN NO LONGER AFFORD TO IGNORE.
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.” SO WHY ARE THERE SO MANY? THE QUESTION CHRISTIANS CAN NO LONGER AFFORD TO IGNORE.

One Savior. One Cross. One Body. Thousands of Denominational Labels. Did Jesus Establish One Visible Church, or Can Different Denominations Truly Belong to Him? The Answer May Challenge Your Loyalty, Expose Our Divisions, and Change How You See the Family of God Forever.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.

Not before your pastor. Not before your bishop. Not before your denomination's founders. Not before a church council, a theological professor, or the people who taught you everything you believe about Christianity.
Just you.
And Jesus.
The One whose hands still bear the scars of the price He paid to redeem sinners.
Now imagine Him asking you a question.
“Did you love My Church as I commanded you to love her? Or did you spend your life defending your group while forgetting the people I died to save?”
That is not a quotation from Scripture. But it is a question worth allowing Scripture to examine.
Because somewhere between the empty tomb and the thousands of church signs scattered across our cities, something happened that should make every follower of Jesus stop and think.
We became very good at explaining why we are different.
But have we become equally good at demonstrating why we belong to the same Lord?
A Catholic walks into a Protestant church and wonders whether the worship is legitimate.
A Protestant enters a Catholic church and wonders whether the Gospel is being obscured.
An Orthodox Christian looks at both and asks what happened to the ancient faith.

A Baptist questions infant baptism. A Pentecostal questions why some Christians seem uncomfortable with spiritual gifts. A Reformed believer challenges teachings about salvation. A non-denominational Christian says, “I just follow Jesus,” while often inheriting theological traditions without realizing it.
And somewhere in the middle of all these arguments sits a person who has never truly known Christ.
Watching.
Listening.
Wondering.
“If Jesus is the Prince of Peace, why does His family seem so divided?”
That question should trouble us.
Not because every disagreement is sinful.
Not because truth does not matter.
But because Jesus Himself prayed for the unity of those who would believe in Him.
And His prayer was not casual.
It was spoken on the night before His crucifixion.
“That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.” — John 17:21, KJV
Read those final words again.
That the world may believe.
Jesus connected the visible love and unity of His followers to the world's recognition of His divine mission.
And that means our divisions are not merely an internal family problem.
They affect our witness.

But before we rush to condemn denominations, before we declare that only one institution can possibly be the true Church, or that all denominations are equally faithful simply because they use the name of Jesus, we need to return to a place where our arguments must become quiet.
The Word of God.
Because the Church does not belong to the loudest defender of tradition.
The Church belongs to Jesus Christ.
And He has already told us something extraordinary about it.
In Matthew 16, Jesus asks His disciples who they believe He is.
Peter answers:
“Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.” — Matthew 16:16, KJV
Jesus then declares:
“And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” — Matthew 16:18, KJV
There is something powerful here that is easy to overlook.
Jesus did not say, “You will build your church.”
He did not say, “The strongest religious institution will build My church.”
He said:
“I will build my church.”
The Builder is Christ.
The ownership is Christ's.
The promise is Christ's.
And the victory belongs to Christ.
But the original Greek text reveals something important about the question we are asking.
Jesus says:
κἀγὼ δέ σοι λέγω ὅτι σὺ εἶ Πέτρος, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν.
Kagō de soi legō hoti sy ei Petros, kai epi tautē tē petra oikodomēsō mou tēn ekklēsian.
“And I also say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build My church.”
The word ἐκκλησίαν (ekklēsian) is the accusative form of ekklēsia, commonly translated “church” or “assembly.”
In this context, Jesus is speaking of the community that belongs to Him.
Not merely a building.
Not merely a religious brand.
Not merely a collection of individuals who privately believe in God.
A people called together under His authority.
The singular matters.
Jesus says μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν — mou tēn ekklēsian — “My church.”
But we must be careful.
The singular word “church” establishes the unity of Christ's people. By itself, it does not settle every historical dispute about how that unity must be institutionally expressed.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because sincere Christians have disagreed for centuries about the meaning of the rock upon which Jesus promised to build His Church.
Catholic theology understands Peter's role and the authority entrusted to him as foundational to the continuing visible structure of the Church, including the papacy.
Eastern Orthodox theology affirms the apostolic foundations and visible continuity of the Church while rejecting the Catholic understanding of universal papal jurisdiction.

Protestant interpreters have commonly emphasized Peter's confession of Christ, Christ Himself as the ultimate foundation, or Peter's foundational role without accepting the later Catholic claims concerning the papacy.
And these are not trivial differences.

The Greek distinction between Πέτρος (Petros) and πέτρα (petra) has often been discussed in these debates. Yet it would be misleading to claim that the difference alone conclusively proves one interpretation. Jesus may have originally spoken these words in Aramaic, where kepha could serve for both Peter's name and “rock.” The precise original Aramaic wording of this exchange has not been preserved independently.
Whatever interpretation one holds, no faithful reading should remove Jesus from the center of the passage.
Peter is not the Savior.
The Church is not the Savior.
No succession of human leaders can replace the crucified and risen Lord.
Jesus Christ is the One who builds and preserves His Church.
And when we turn to the apostle Paul, the mystery becomes even more profound.

“There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.” — Ephesians 4:4–6, KJV
In the Greek, Paul begins with a declaration:
ἓν σῶμα καὶ ἓν πνεῦμα.
Hen sōma kai hen pneuma.
“One body and one Spirit.”
Not many competing bodies belonging to different saviors.
One body.
And the word ἕν (hen) means “one.”
Paul continues with a rhythm that leaves no room for divided ultimate allegiance.
One Lord.
One faith.
One baptism.
One God and Father.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say that every disagreement between Christians is meaningless.
He does not say that doctrine can be sacrificed for the appearance of peace.
He does not say that every religious organization claiming Christ necessarily teaches His Gospel faithfully.
But neither does he give Christians permission to turn their secondary identities into rival kingdoms.
The unity of the Church is rooted in the unity of the God we worship.
And this brings us to a question that is more personal than denominational statistics.
What if some of us have become more loyal to the name on our church sign than to the Lord whose name we confess?
That question is not an accusation against every denominational Christian.
Many believers deeply love Jesus and faithfully serve Him within their traditions.
But all of us need to examine our hearts.
Because denominational pride can become a form of spiritual blindness.
And spiritual blindness is particularly dangerous when it disguises itself as faithfulness.
Think about the church in Corinth.
The believers were already forming factions around respected leaders.
Some claimed Paul.
Others claimed Apollos.
Others claimed Cephas.
Paul confronted them with a question that still pierces the Church today.
“Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?” — 1 Corinthians 1:13, KJV
Imagine replacing those names with our modern identities.
Was your denomination crucified for you?
Did your favorite preacher carry your sins to Calvary?
Did your theological tradition rise from the dead on the third day?
Did your church founder conquer death?
No.
Jesus did.
And if that truth does not humble us, we have not yet allowed the Cross to confront our pride.
But here is where we must resist an easy answer.
Some people respond to Christian division by saying, “Denominations do not matter. All that matters is Jesus.”
It sounds beautiful.
And it contains an important truth: no denominational label can save a soul.
But it can also conceal a serious problem.
The Jesus we claim to follow has revealed truths that matter.
The identity of Christ matters.
His bodily resurrection matters.
His saving work matters.
The authority of Scripture matters.
The meaning of the Gospel matters.
Baptism, the Lord's Supper, church leadership, worship, and the nature of the Church itself matter enough to deserve serious biblical examination.
Love does not require us to pretend that contradictions are agreements.
And unity is not strengthened by hiding theological differences beneath emotional language.
Paul urged believers to speak “the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15).
Both words are necessary.
Truth without love can become a weapon.
Love without truth can become an excuse to avoid obedience.
But truth spoken in love builds up the body of Christ.
So can different denominations faithfully represent His body?
The answer requires an important distinction.
Christ has one body. Christians disagree about the visible boundaries and proper structure of that body.
Catholic teaching identifies the Church of Christ as subsisting in the Catholic Church, while recognizing elements of sanctification and truth outside its visible structure.
Eastern Orthodox Christians understand the fullness of the apostolic Church to be preserved in the Orthodox communion, with its sacramental and episcopal continuity.
Many Protestants understand the one universal Church as encompassing all who truly belong to Christ through faith, while local congregations and denominations may express that unity imperfectly.
These positions cannot simply be declared identical.
They make different claims about authority, sacraments, apostolic succession, and the Church's visible identity.
And it would be dishonest to suggest that Matthew 16:18 and Ephesians 4:4–6 alone resolve every one of those disputes.
But they do establish something no Christian should evade.
Jesus intended His people to belong to one body under one Lord.
And the New Testament gives that unity visible expression.
The first believers devoted themselves to apostolic teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayers (Acts 2:42).
They shared life.
They cared for the needy.
They gathered for worship.
They submitted to spiritual oversight.
They were not simply isolated believers connected by a private spiritual feeling.
They were a recognizable community.
At the same time, the New Testament describes churches in Jerusalem, Antioch, Corinth, Ephesus, Philippi, and other places.
There were many local congregations.
But not many Christs.
There were different communities.
But not different Gospels that could all be equally true.
And when serious doctrinal disputes arose, the apostles did not simply shrug and say, “Everyone has their own interpretation.”
Acts 15 records a gathering in Jerusalem to address a controversy that threatened the unity and faithfulness of the early Church.
They examined the matter together.
They listened.
They appealed to God's work and the Scriptures.
They sought a faithful judgment.
That should tell us something.
Biblical unity is not the absence of conviction.
It is the pursuit of faithfulness to Christ together.
And now comes the part that may hurt.
Because it is easier to debate which Church has the strongest historical claim than to ask whether our own lives resemble the Church Jesus calls us to be.
We can defend apostolic succession while refusing to forgive someone who wounded us.
We can quote sola Scriptura while neglecting the Scriptures we claim to honor.
We can celebrate spiritual gifts while lacking the fruit of the Spirit.
We can insist that our worship is biblical while treating fellow believers with contempt.
We can explain justification, sanctification, and ecclesiology with impressive precision while our families are starving for patience, kindness, humility, and love.
We can be correct about a doctrine and still sin in the way we defend it.
And we can be sincere about our faith while still needing correction.
That is why the question of the true Church must never become an excuse to avoid the deeper question.
Am I truly following the Head of the Church?
Paul writes:
The Head is Jesus.
Not our preferred institution considered apart from Him.
Not our favorite theological personality.
Not our spiritual reputation.
Jesus.
The One who touched lepers when others withdrew.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners when respectable people were offended.
The One who confronted religious hypocrisy without surrendering truth.
The One who wept over Jerusalem.
The One who washed His disciples' feet.
The One who went willingly to the Cross.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking irony in all our divisions is this:
We sometimes fight over who represents the crucified Christ while refusing to demonstrate the humility of the crucified Christ.
We defend the Church He purchased with His blood while speaking about other people He loves as though they are beneath our compassion.
And somewhere, a wounded believer walks away from a congregation.
Not because Jesus failed.
But because the people claiming His name failed to reflect His character.
Perhaps that person is you.
Perhaps you were raised in a tradition where questions were treated as rebellion.
Perhaps you entered a different church and were made to feel that your entire spiritual history was worthless.
Perhaps you watched leaders protect reputations instead of wounded people.
Perhaps you were taught to fear every Christian outside your denomination.
Or perhaps you have become so exhausted by arguments about religion that you have quietly wondered whether following Jesus is even possible without becoming trapped in another conflict.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The sins of Christians do not make the holiness of Christ disappear.
The failures of churches do not invalidate the resurrection.
And the existence of division does not mean Jesus has abandoned His people.
But neither should those truths be used to excuse abuse, silence legitimate questions, or demand loyalty to leaders who refuse accountability.
Jesus does not ask us to confuse institutional self-protection with faithfulness.
He calls His people to truth, repentance, justice, holiness, and love.
And sometimes that means confronting sin inside our own community before criticizing anyone else's.
Remember what Jesus said:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” — John 13:35, KJV
He did not say the world would recognize His disciples by the complexity of their arguments alone.
Or by the age of their institutions alone.
Or by the emotional intensity of their worship alone.
Or by the number of people attending their services.
He pointed to love.
Not sentimental love that ignores sin.
Not counterfeit love that abandons truth.
But the kind of love that bears burdens, seeks reconciliation, practices forgiveness, serves the vulnerable, and remains faithful to Christ.
And we need to be clear about something else.
Not every division is equally blameworthy, and not every separation can be healed by pretending that truth is negotiable.
Some Christians have separated over serious doctrinal convictions.
Others have separated because of corruption, coercion, abuse, or failures of leadership.
Some divisions involve questions of authority that centuries of theological dialogue have not resolved.
Some reflect human pride that should have been crucified long ago.
It would be simplistic to declare that every denomination exists because someone rebelled against God.
It would be equally simplistic to insist that the existence of thousands of Christian groups is exactly what Jesus intended.
Scripture calls us toward unity, not complacency about division.
And yet the unity we seek must be unity in Christ and His truth.
This is why the words of Ephesians 4 become even more demanding when we read what comes before the famous declaration of one body.
“With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love; Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” — Ephesians 4:2–3, KJV
Do you see it?
Before Paul speaks of one body, he speaks of humility.
Gentleness.
Patience.
Bearing with one another in love.
Why?
Because Christian unity is not merely a theological proposition to defend.
It is a spiritual responsibility to practice.
And nobody practices humility by constantly announcing their superiority.
Nobody practices patience by refusing to listen.
Nobody practices love by delighting in another believer's humiliation.
We must be willing to ask hard questions about doctrine.
But we must also be willing to ask hard questions about ourselves.
Have I mistaken inherited tradition for personal conviction?
Have I ever studied the strongest biblical arguments of Christians who disagree with me?
Have I used the word “heretic” carelessly?
Have I confused disagreement with hatred?
Have I treated another believer as an enemy simply because we differ on church government, baptism, or worship?
Have I allowed my desire to win arguments to become greater than my desire to honor Jesus?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question:
If Jesus examined the way I defend His Church, would He recognize His own character in me?
That question does not belong only to Catholics.
Or Orthodox Christians.
Or Protestants.
Or non-denominational believers.
It belongs to all of us.
Because all of us need grace.
And grace does not mean that truth becomes unimportant.
Grace means that sinners who cannot save themselves are invited to come to the Savior who can.
This is where our theme becomes more than a phrase.
The scandal is not merely that Christians disagree.
The scandal is that people redeemed by undeserved mercy can sometimes become merciless toward one another.
The scandal is that we can preach reconciliation with God while resisting reconciliation with our brothers and sisters.
The scandal is that we can celebrate the Cross while protecting the pride that the Cross exposes.
But grace speaks another word.
Grace says that repentance is still possible.
Grace says that hardened hearts can soften.
Grace says that truth can be defended without cruelty.
Grace says that a wounded believer can find healing without pretending the wound never happened.
Grace says that people divided by history can still speak honestly, listen carefully, and pursue peace without denying their convictions.
And above all, grace declares that Jesus Christ remains faithful even when His followers fail.
He is not waiting helplessly for human institutions to rescue His mission.
He is the risen Lord.
The Shepherd who knows His sheep.
The Savior who gave Himself for His people.
Paul writes:
There is the measure of His commitment.
Not a slogan.
Not a denominational manifesto.
His blood.
And if Christ loved the Church enough to give Himself for her, how can we claim to love Him while treating His people carelessly?
This does not require us to surrender discernment.
Jesus warned about false prophets.
The apostles warned about false teaching.
The New Testament repeatedly calls believers to guard the Gospel.
But the same Scriptures command us to pursue peace, correct with gentleness, and love one another sincerely.
The faithful Christian must hold these commands together.
Never sacrificing truth to purchase a superficial peace.
Never sacrificing love to satisfy religious pride.
So what should you do if you are wondering whether your own denomination faithfully represents the body of Christ?
Do not begin with fear.
Begin with Jesus.
Read the Gospels carefully.
Study the apostolic teaching.
Examine what your church teaches about Christ, salvation, the Scriptures, worship, holiness, and the nature of the Church.
Learn the history of your tradition.
Listen fairly to serious Christians who disagree.
Ask whether the claims of your community can withstand honest biblical and historical examination.
Seek leaders who welcome sincere questions and demonstrate integrity.
Look for a congregation where Christ is faithfully proclaimed, Scripture is taken seriously, worship is reverent, discipleship is practiced, and love is more than a word painted on the wall.
And remember that visible beauty, ancient continuity, passionate worship, intellectual sophistication, or impressive growth, considered alone, cannot settle every question of faithfulness.
Do not choose a church merely because it makes you comfortable.
But do not remain in a spiritually harmful environment merely because someone tells you that leaving would mean abandoning God.
Seek truth.
Seek wisdom.
Seek the Lord.
And do so with the humility of someone who knows that only Christ is infallible.
Perhaps you are reading this as a Catholic.
You do not need to abandon your convictions to recognize that contempt for other Christians is contrary to Christ's command to love.
Perhaps you are Orthodox.
You can take the historical and sacramental claims of your Church seriously while remembering that humility is not optional.
Perhaps you are Protestant.
You can remain deeply committed to the authority of Scripture and the Gospel of grace while refusing to treat every Christian outside your tradition as an enemy.
Perhaps you belong to a non-denominational congregation.
You can love the simplicity of identifying as a follower of Jesus while recognizing that your church still has interpretations, practices, and theological commitments that deserve examination.
And perhaps you do not belong to any church at all.
Perhaps you have been watching Christianity from a distance because you cannot understand why people who claim to follow one Savior disagree so fiercely.
Please do not judge Jesus solely by the worst behavior of those who claim His name.
Read His words.
Examine His life.
Consider His death and resurrection.
Listen to His invitation.
Because the center of Christianity is not the claim that Christians have always behaved faithfully.
The center is the good news that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Salvation is not purchased through denominational membership.
It is not earned by winning theological debates.
It is not secured by financial contributions.
It is God's gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us into a transformed life.
A life of repentance.
A life of obedience.
A life of love.
A life in which our loyalty to Jesus becomes greater than our desire to be admired, applauded, or proven superior.
If you have spent years attacking other Christians without love, repent.
If you have dismissed biblical truth merely to avoid uncomfortable conversations, repent.
If you have treated your church as a substitute for a living relationship with Christ, repent.
If you have walked away from Jesus because people wounded you, consider again the Savior who never promised that His followers would be sinless, but who gave His own life to reconcile sinners to God.
And if you are carrying wounds caused by religious people, healing does not require you to deny what happened.
Bring the truth of those wounds into the light.
Seek trustworthy support.
Remember that forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical, and rebuilding trust requires genuine repentance and accountability.
Christ does not call His sheep to celebrate the behavior of wolves.
He calls them to know His voice.
And His voice still speaks.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27, KJV
That is where the question becomes personal again.
Not simply, “Which church is right?”
But, “Am I listening to Jesus?”
Am I following Him when He calls me to forgive?
Am I following Him when He calls me to examine my beliefs?
Am I following Him when He calls me to love the difficult person sitting across the aisle?
Am I following Him when He calls me to stand for truth even when it costs me?
Am I following Him when He calls me to repent of the pride I have disguised as spiritual maturity?
Because the Lord who builds His Church is also the Lord who transforms His people.
And perhaps that is what some of us have been missing.
We have spent so much time asking whether our church has the correct name that we have forgotten to ask whether our lives are bearing His name faithfully.
We have argued over the boundaries of the body while neglecting the commands of its Head.
We have searched for the perfect religious community while resisting the personal holiness to which Jesus calls us.
And still, He has not abandoned His promise.
“I will build my church.”
Not “I might.”
Not “I will try.”
“I will.”
The gates of Hades will not overcome what belongs to Him.
Human pride will not ultimately defeat His purposes.
Historical controversy will not erase His resurrection.
The failures of His followers will not dethrone the King.
But His promise is not permission for complacency.
It is a summons to faithfulness.
And the question of one visible Church versus many denominations must ultimately drive us toward deeper biblical study, not shallow slogans.
The New Testament clearly teaches one body, one Lord, and a unity meant to be expressed in the real life of believers.
It does not provide a simple modern denominational directory.
Christians disagree about which present-day communion most faithfully preserves the visible structure and fullness of the apostolic Church.
Those disagreements deserve serious examination rather than dismissal.
Yet no Christian has permission to make division a virtue, pride a sacrament, or hostility a substitute for holiness.
The Church is called to bear witness to Jesus Christ.
And our responsibility is not merely to defend our understanding of that Church.
It is to obey the Lord who purchased her.
Maybe today you need to stop fighting a brother or sister over an issue you have never seriously studied.
Maybe you need to stop avoiding a difficult truth because it challenges your upbringing.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you humiliated in the name of defending doctrine.
Maybe you need to return to faithful Christian fellowship after years of isolation.
Maybe you need to ask your pastor a question you have been afraid to ask.
Or maybe, for the first time, you need to surrender your life to Jesus Christ instead of merely inheriting a religious identity.
Whatever the case, do not waste this moment.
Because eternity is too serious for spiritual arrogance.
The Gospel is too precious to be reduced to tribal competition.
And the people Christ calls us to love are too valuable to be treated as disposable.
If this article has challenged something you have believed for years, I would genuinely like to hear from you.
You do not need to pretend you have resolved every theological question.
And you do not need to disclose private wounds to strangers.
You can simply tell us what Scripture has challenged you to reconsider.
If you disagree with this article, you are welcome to explain why with biblical reasoning and respect. Serious discussion is more valuable than empty agreement.
And if you have witnessed genuine Christian love across denominational lines without compromising your convictions, share that testimony.
Someone reading your words may desperately need to know that humility and faithfulness can still exist together.
Not to win an argument.
Not to embarrass another denomination.
But to invite people to examine what Jesus actually said.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who have become skeptical of Christianity to follow along.
There are people who need more than another religious argument.
They need to encounter the truth and mercy of Jesus Christ.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter Scripture, grow in discipleship, wrestle honestly with difficult questions, and discover the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Our desire is to continue this work and expand its reach.
To help more struggling believers.
To encourage people returning to faith.
To reach families searching for biblical guidance.
To make meaningful Christian resources accessible to those who may not otherwise be able to afford them.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That matters.
Your giving should never be driven by fear, guilt, or the idea that you must pay to glorify God.
You can glorify God through prayer, obedience, generosity, service, sharing biblical truth, and loving your neighbor.
Every sustainable ministry needs people willing to serve, pray, share, create, encourage, and, when possible, give.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to provide useful resources and express appreciation to those helping sustain the ministry.
One thoughtful conversation can open a door.
One Scripture can confront a hardened heart.
One testimony can encourage someone who was ready to give up.
And one person turning to Jesus Christ matters more than any social media metric ever could.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not building a kingdom around a personality.
Not creating another tribe that despises everyone outside it.
But continually pointing people toward the King who gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus Christ.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The Head of His Church.
The One who calls His people to repentance, truth, forgiveness, holiness, and love.
And when the noise of religious controversy finally fades, one truth will remain.
The Church was never meant to be a monument to our superiority.
It was meant to bear witness to His glory.
So study deeply.
Ask courageously.
Love faithfully.
Repent sincerely.
And never forget whose Church it is.
Because one day, the arguments that consumed so much of our attention will be measured against the holiness of the Lord we claimed to defend.
And on that day, the question will not be whether we were impressive enough to win every debate.
The question of whether we truly belonged to Christ will matter infinitely more.
The hands that built the Church are the same hands that were pierced to save the people we are so quick to divide.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HUSBANDS, LOVE YOUR WIVES”—FOUR WORDS THAT COULD DESTROY THE MAN YOU PRETEND TO BE
paragraphs: “HUSBANDS, LOVE YOUR WIVES”—FOUR WORDS THAT COULD DESTROY THE MAN YOU PRETEND TO BE

God never commanded a husband merely to provide a house, pay the bills, or demand respect. He commanded him to love his wife like Christ loved the Church. And when you discover what that actually means, you may never look at your marriage—or yourself—the same way again.
There is a woman somewhere tonight lying beside a man who would fight a stranger for disrespecting her…
But will not apologize for the way he spoke to her.
A man who would work twelve hours to make sure she has food on the table…
But cannot give her twelve uninterrupted minutes to explain why her heart is hurting.
A man who would never allow another man to put his hands on her…
But has learned to wound her with words, silence, contempt, and indifference.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part?
He genuinely believes he is a good husband.
Because he provides.
Because he stays.
Because he has never cheated.
Because he comes home every night.
And those things matter. Faithfulness matters. Provision matters. Commitment matters.
But somewhere between the wedding vows and the weight of everyday life, he has forgotten something terrifying.
A man can be physically present in his marriage while being emotionally absent from his wife.
He can sleep beside her every night and still leave her feeling painfully alone.
He can know her favorite meal, her birthday, and her clothing size…
And no longer know what makes her cry.
Then one Sunday morning, he opens his Bible and reads a verse he has probably heard a hundred times.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Ephesians 5:25, KJV
And suddenly, those familiar words begin to sound less like a wedding decoration…
And more like a summons to repentance.
Because Paul did not say, “Husbands, love your wives when they deserve it.”
He did not say, “Love them when they are agreeable, affectionate, beautiful, peaceful, or easy to understand.”
He said something infinitely more demanding.
Love your wives as Christ loved the Church.
And brother, before you say you already do…
You need to look at what happened to Jesus.
Because the standard for a Christian husband is not the strongest man in the room.
It is the Savior who laid down His life.
And that changes everything.
The apostle Paul wrote these words in Greek:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
Ephesians 5:25
A close English rendering is:
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
Notice the word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate).
It comes from the Greek verb agapaō, meaning “to love.”
Here it is a present active imperative, second-person plural.
In plain language, Paul is commanding husbands to love.
This is not merely a suggestion to feel something romantic.
It is a command that calls for deliberate, ongoing action.
The grammatical form does not mean a husband must experience the same emotional intensity every moment. It means love is not optional simply because emotions fluctuate.
There will be mornings when your wife is exhausted.
There will be seasons when the children consume nearly every ounce of her attention.

There will be financial pressure, illness, disagreements, disappointment, aging, grief, and ordinary days when marriage feels less like a beautiful photograph and more like two tired people trying to survive another week.
And still, the command remains.
Love her.
Not because every day is easy.
But because Christ is your example.
Now look at another word in the same verse.
παρέδωκεν (paredōken).
It comes from paradidōmi, a verb that can mean “to hand over,” “deliver,” or “give up.”
Paul says Christ gave Himself up for the Church.
The verb points to the historical reality of Christ's self-giving sacrifice.
Jesus did not merely announce His love from a safe distance.
He demonstrated it.
He entered suffering.
He bore rejection.
He endured the cross.
And He willingly gave Himself for the people He came to redeem.
This does not mean a husband's suffering can atone for his wife's sins. Only Jesus Christ is the Savior.
It means a husband's love must be shaped by the self-giving character of the Savior's love.
And here is where the verse becomes deeply uncomfortable.
If your understanding of marriage always places your comfort first, you have not yet understood the love Paul is describing.
You may have understood authority.
You may have understood responsibility.
You may have understood the cultural expectations of being a husband.
But have you understood the cross?
Because the cross confronts the selfishness that quietly destroys marriages.
It confronts the husband who believes an apology makes him weak.
The husband who uses financial provision to excuse emotional neglect.
The husband who quotes Scripture when he wants obedience but ignores Scripture when it demands tenderness.
The husband who expects his wife to understand his stress but dismisses hers as complaining.
The husband who wants admiration without accountability.
And the husband who knows how to lead a meeting, manage a business, or command respect in public…
But does not know how to speak gently to the woman he promised to cherish.
This is not written to humiliate men.
It is written because the Gospel is too precious to be reduced to religious language that never transforms our homes.
And because some husbands desperately need to hear a truth that nobody has loved them enough to say.
You cannot use the Bible to demand honor while refusing to let the Bible confront your own heart.
Read Ephesians 5 carefully.
Before Paul addresses husbands and wives, he writes about being filled with the Spirit and about believers submitting to one another in reverence for Christ.
Ephesians 5:18–21 establishes a larger context of Spirit-shaped Christian living.
Then Paul addresses marriage.
Yes, the passage speaks about the husband as head of the wife.
Yes, Christians have differed over precisely how marital headship and submission should be understood and practiced.
But one thing cannot be honestly removed from Paul's instruction.
Whatever a husband believes about his role, he is commanded to love his wife in the pattern of Christ's sacrificial care.
And Jesus did not use His authority as an excuse for selfishness.
He said:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
Mark 10:45, KJV
Do you see the difference?
The world often teaches men to ask, “How much respect am I receiving?”
Christ teaches His followers to consider how faithfully they are serving.
The world admires the man who can control everyone around him.
Jesus reveals greatness through humble service.
The world celebrates the man who always wins the argument.
But a Christian husband must sometimes ask whether winning the argument has become more important to him than loving his wife.
Imagine this.
Your wife has been quiet all evening.
You ask what is wrong.
She says, “Nothing.”
But you know something is wrong.
Finally, she tells you.
She feels invisible.
She feels like every conversation becomes a competition.
She feels that you listen only long enough to defend yourself.
And before she finishes speaking, you interrupt.
“I work hard for this family. What more do you want from me?”
Silence.
She looks down.
And something inside her closes.
You think the argument is over because she stopped talking.
But silence does not always mean peace.
Sometimes it means someone has become too exhausted to keep explaining their pain.
Now imagine a different response.
You sit beside her.
You put your phone down.
You listen without preparing your defense.
And you say something that pride has been resisting for years.
“I didn't realize how alone you've been feeling. I want to understand. I'm sorry for the ways I've hurt you.”
No dramatic music.
No audience.
No applause.
Just a husband allowing humility to enter a room where pride has lived for too long.
That is not weakness.
That is a small but meaningful expression of repentance.
And repentance is not simply saying, “I'm sorry.”
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, a change of mind and direction that involves turning away from sin.
In the Christian life, genuine repentance bears fruit.
It changes behavior.
It does not demand immediate forgiveness as payment for an apology.
It does not say, “I apologized yesterday. Why are you still hurt?”
It does not use tears to escape accountability.
It takes responsibility.
It makes room for the consequences of wrongdoing.
And where trust has been damaged, it patiently participates in rebuilding what was broken.
Some marriages do not need another expensive anniversary dinner as much as they need a sincere confession.
Some wives do not need another public declaration of love as much as they need private evidence of change.
Some husbands do not need another sermon about their position in the household.
They need to kneel before Christ and ask Him to expose the pride they have mistaken for strength.
And perhaps that husband is reading these words right now.
Perhaps you have been faithful with your paycheck but careless with your tongue.
Perhaps you have never committed adultery, yet you have allowed your heart to grow cold.
Perhaps you have been so determined to be respected that you have forgotten how to be gentle.
Perhaps your wife has been asking for the same change for years.
And perhaps, deep down, you know she has not been asking for perfection.
She has been asking to be heard.
Brother, do not turn this moment into another opportunity to defend yourself.
Bring it before God.
Because the Holy Spirit does not expose sin merely to leave us drowning in shame.
He convicts us and directs us toward Christ, in whom forgiveness and transformation are found.
And there is more.
Paul continues:
“So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself.”
Ephesians 5:28, KJV
Think about that.
Paul connects a husband's treatment of his wife with the care he gives his own body.
When your body is hungry, you feed it.
When you are injured, you seek relief.
When you are exhausted, you recognize your need for rest.
Yet how easily can a man become attentive to his own discomfort while remaining indifferent to his wife's?
You notice immediately when your phone battery is low.
But have you noticed when her emotional strength is running low?
You recognize when the car needs maintenance.
But do you recognize when your marriage needs intentional attention?
You know when work is becoming overwhelming.
But do you know what has been overwhelming her?
This does not mean a husband must become a mind reader.
Marriage requires honest communication from both spouses.
But love does require attention.
It requires the willingness to learn.
It requires caring enough to ask and remaining present long enough to hear the answer.
And then Paul uses two beautiful verbs in Ephesians 5:29.
ἐκτρέφει (ektrephei) — “nourishes.”
θάλπει (thalpei) — “cherishes” or “cares for tenderly.”
These words describe the care a person gives his own body, which Paul connects to Christ's care for the Church.
Nourishing is not merely keeping someone alive.
It is contributing to their well-being.
Cherishing is not merely tolerating someone's presence.
It is treating that person as precious.

A husband who loves biblically should therefore be concerned not only with whether his wife has food, shelter, and clothing, but also with whether his conduct reflects patience, kindness, faithfulness, and care.
Does she feel safe telling you the truth?
Can she disagree without being threatened?
Can she express hurt without being mocked?
Does she know that her dignity matters even when you are angry?
Can she trust that your private behavior will reflect the faith you profess in public?
These are not small questions.
They reach into the heart of Christian discipleship.
And Scripture becomes even more direct.
“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.”
Colossians 3:19, KJV
The Greek says:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς.
The verb pikrainesthe is related to bitterness and harshness.
Paul does not merely command husbands to love.
He also warns them against becoming embittered toward their wives.
That matters because bitterness rarely announces itself as bitterness.
Sometimes it sounds like sarcasm.
Sometimes it looks like contempt.
Sometimes it hides behind cold silence.
Sometimes it becomes a pattern of cutting remarks disguised as jokes.
Sometimes it turns every disagreement into a record of old offenses.
And sometimes a man becomes so accustomed to his harshness that he no longer recognizes it.
But Christ calls His people to something different.
Consider 1 Peter 3:7.
Peter instructs husbands to live with their wives according to knowledge and to show them honor as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
That phrase is extraordinary.
Fellow heirs of the grace of life.
Your wife is not a lesser soul.
She is not your servant.
She is not a possession you purchased with a wedding ring.
She is a person made in God's image.
And if she belongs to Christ, she is your fellow heir of His grace.
The same Savior who died for you is the Savior who died for her.
The same grace you desperately need is the grace she desperately needs.
The same Lord before whom you will stand is the Lord before whom she will stand.
How, then, can you treat lightly someone whom God commands you to honor?
And Peter adds a sobering warning about husbands' prayers being hindered.
That does not mean every unanswered prayer is punishment for marital failure.
But it does mean that how a husband treats his wife is spiritually significant.
A man cannot simply separate his worship from his conduct at home.
He cannot assume that public religious activity makes private cruelty irrelevant.
He cannot sing loudly about God's mercy while refusing to show mercy to those closest to him.
And he cannot excuse abuse by appealing to biblical authority.
Let this be unmistakably clear.
Sacrificial love is never permission for violence, coercion, intimidation, sexual abuse, or controlling behavior.
Christlike leadership cannot be used to justify sin against another person.
A wife is not commanded to remain in immediate danger to prove her faith.
Where abuse exists, safety, appropriate outside support, and genuine accountability matter. Forgiveness does not eliminate the need for protection or automatically restore trust.
And where a husband has harmed his wife, repentance requires more than religious promises. It requires ending the harmful behavior and accepting accountability.
Because the Jesus who calls us to love is also the Lord who loves righteousness.
Now perhaps another man is reading this, and his heart is breaking for a different reason.
He has tried.
He has worked.
He has prayed.
He has sought reconciliation.
He has admitted his failures.
And still, his marriage is painful.
He wonders whether being a godly husband means silently accepting every wrong done to him.
It does not.
Christlike love is not the abandonment of truth, wisdom, or appropriate boundaries.
A husband can be gentle without becoming passive.
He can forgive without pretending that sin has no consequences.
He can pursue peace without denying reality.
He can seek wise pastoral care, counseling, and other appropriate help when his marriage is struggling.
And he must remember that he cannot force another person's heart to change.
His calling is to be faithful to Christ in what belongs to his own responsibility.
The Gospel never promises that one person's obedience will automatically produce a perfect marriage.
But it does call every believer to walk in the light.
And that brings us to the part of this passage that may be the most beautiful of all.
Paul does not stop with husbands.
He points beyond marriage itself.
In Ephesians 5:31–32, he recalls the biblical truth that a man and woman become one flesh, then says that he is speaking of a profound mystery concerning Christ and the Church.
Marriage, in Paul's teaching, is connected to a reality greater than itself.
It points toward the covenant love of Christ for His people.
And that means a Christian husband's love is not ultimately about displaying how impressive he is.
It is about reflecting, however imperfectly, the character of Jesus.
A husband is not the savior of his wife.
He cannot cleanse her from sin.
He cannot replace the Holy Spirit.
He cannot carry the divine responsibilities that belong to Christ alone.
But he can reflect something of Christ's love through faithfulness, tenderness, truthfulness, humility, and sacrificial care.
And perhaps this is why the command is so demanding.
Because it does not merely ask, “Do you love your wife?”
It asks something deeper.
Does the way you love your wife increasingly resemble the love you have received from Jesus?
That question reaches beyond flowers.
Beyond anniversaries.
Beyond romantic photographs.
Beyond the public image of a happy Christian family.
It reaches the moment when you are tired and she needs you to listen.
The moment when you are angry and must choose your words.
The moment when you have sinned and must confess without excuses.
The moment when she is weak and needs compassion.
The moment when you disagree and must remember that she is not your enemy.
The moment when no one is watching.
Especially then.
Because Christian character is not measured only by what people see on Sunday.
It is also revealed in how we behave on an ordinary Tuesday evening when we are frustrated, disappointed, and nobody is applauding.
Stay here for a moment.
Not because you should drown in guilt.
But because there is hope for the man who is willing to repent.
Maybe your father never taught you how to love gently.
Maybe you grew up in a home where affection was rare and anger was normal.
Maybe the men around you taught you that admitting wrong was weakness.
Maybe you learned to survive by hiding your emotions.
