"Do I need to stop condemning myself for something Your Word has not clearly condemned?"
"Do I need to tell my husband how lonely I have become?"
Those questions may not produce a convenient one-sentence answer.
But they can lead to something better.
Spiritual maturity.
And maturity does not always mean having fewer questions.
Sometimes it means finally learning to ask the right ones.
So let us answer the original question as clearly as Scripture allows.
Does masturbation while your husband is away automatically constitute adultery or betrayal of your marriage?
The Bible does not explicitly classify every act of masturbation as adultery.
It does, however, clearly call Christians to sexual holiness, faithfulness, self-control, purity of heart, and love within marriage.
Whether a particular act involves lustful fantasy, pornography, dishonesty, compulsive behavior, or violation of marital commitments can affect its moral significance.
Christian traditions also differ on whether masturbation itself is permissible, even without those additional concerns.
For that reason, it would be irresponsible to announce either that every instance is necessarily marital betrayal or that every instance is unquestionably acceptable to God.
The faithful response is not careless permission.
It is not automatic condemnation.
It is serious biblical discernment, prayerful conscience, honest marital communication, and a willingness to obey Christ even when obedience is difficult.
And please remember this.
You are not less of a Christian woman because you miss your husband's touch.
You are not less devoted because prolonged separation is painful.
You are not spiritually inferior because you need affection, reassurance, or closeness.
But neither should you allow legitimate desires to become the unquestioned authority over your decisions.
Jesus remains Lord over the whole of life.
Including the parts we rarely discuss in church.
Especially those parts.
If this article has brought a question into the light that you have carried in silence, I want to invite you into a conversation that is honest without being humiliating.
You do not need to reveal private sexual experiences in a public comment.
But perhaps you can share what this discussion has taught you about grace, faithfulness, or the importance of talking honestly with your spouse.
And if you have walked through years of separation and found ways to protect your marriage, your testimony may encourage another couple who is struggling tonight.
What helped you remain emotionally connected?
What conversations do you wish you had started sooner?
How has your faith sustained you through loneliness?
Your answer may remind someone that they are not alone.

If you know a wife whose husband is working overseas, a military spouse waiting for a reunion, or a couple trying to keep their marriage strong across thousands of miles, consider sharing this article privately with them.
Not to expose anyone.
Not to embarrass anyone.
But because silence sometimes leaves struggling believers with only shame, confusion, and misinformation.
A difficult conversation may become the beginning of a healthier season.
Because the church does not need more people pretending they never struggle.
It needs people who are learning to bring their struggles honestly before Christ.
Not because a payment makes someone more faithful than another believer.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and lives increasingly transformed by His grace.
One way you may freely choose to express that generosity is by helping sustain and expand Gospel Warrior.
Biblically, giving should be willing, not coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver." (ESV)
It is an additional, voluntary way to help a ministry continue reaching people.
If you are able and willing to help sustain this work, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
You do not have to pay to belong among people who are seeking Christ.
You do not have to purchase anything to receive the grace of God.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Our calling is to proclaim it faithfully.
And perhaps that is the most important reminder to carry away from this entire conversation.

Whether you are the lonely wife staring at an empty pillow, the husband working far from home, or the believer quietly wrestling with questions nobody taught you how to answer, your deepest hope is not found in winning an argument about a difficult sexual question.
Your deepest hope is Jesus.
The One who calls us to holiness without denying our humanity.
The One who exposes sin without taking pleasure in our humiliation.
The One who offers forgiveness without pretending sin does not matter.
The One who restores what shame tells us can never be restored.
So protect your marriage.
Guard your heart.
Speak the truth.
Seek wisdom.
Repent wherever repentance is needed.
Receive grace where grace is offered.
And remember that the distance between you and your husband does not have to become a distance between you and God.
Tonight, that empty side of the bed may still be empty.
The longing may still be real.
The reunion may still be months away.
But you can bring your questions, your loneliness, your conscience, and your entire heart before the Savior who knows you completely.
And the most beautiful thing about being fully known by Jesus is that you no longer have to hide in order to come home to His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WAY UP IS DOWN: THE DANGEROUS PRAYER THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING ABOUT YOUR LIFE
paragraphs: THE WAY UP IS DOWN: THE DANGEROUS PRAYER THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING ABOUT YOUR LIFE

“Humble Yourselves Before the Lord, and He Will Exalt You” — Why God Sometimes Allows Your Pride to Break Before His Grace Can Lift You, and Why the Lowest Place in Your Story May Become the Place Where You Finally Encounter Jesus.
There is a kind of falling that feels like the end of your life.

You lose the position you worked so hard to earn. Someone you trusted walks away. The people who once applauded you suddenly have nothing to say. Your prayers seem to hit the ceiling. Your confidence disappears. And the version of yourself you spent years building begins to collapse right in front of you.
You smile when people ask how you're doing.
You say, “I'm fine.”
But late at night, when nobody is watching, you stare into the darkness and wonder why God has allowed you to become so small.
And perhaps the most painful part isn't what you've lost.
It's the possibility that God is allowing you to see something about yourself you never wanted to confront.
Your pride.
Your need to be recognized.
Your desperate desire to control everything.
Your habit of measuring your worth by how important other people think you are.
What if the greatest obstacle between you and a deeper walk with Jesus isn't the enemy standing against you, but the throne you've quietly built for yourself?
And what if the very thing you're begging God to restore is something He is asking you to surrender?
There is a sentence in Scripture that turns the world's understanding of greatness completely upside down.
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.” — James 4:10 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not promote yourselves.
Not prove yourselves.
Not make everyone regret underestimating you.
Humble yourselves.
And He shall lift you up.
But before you imagine a promotion, a bigger platform, a financial breakthrough, or the public humiliation of everyone who ever doubted you, we need to talk about what that promise actually means.
Because biblical exaltation is far more beautiful—and far more demanding—than the version often preached to people who simply want their circumstances to improve.
The original Greek of James 4:10 reads:
Ταπεινώθητε ἐνώπιον Κυρίου, καὶ ὑψώσει ὑμᾶς.
Tapeinōthēte enōpion Kyriou, kai hypsōsei hymas.
A faithful translation is:
“Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.”
The Greek verb tapeinōthēte comes from tapeinoō, meaning to humble, lower, or bring low. Here it is an imperative calling for a genuine posture of humility before God.
The verb hypsōsei, from hypsoō, means “He will lift up” or “He will exalt.”
Notice who does the lifting.
God.
Not your connections.
Not your reputation.
Not your carefully managed public image.
God.
But the surrounding verses reveal something we cannot afford to ignore.
James is not giving ambitious people a secret technique for becoming successful.
He is confronting spiritual pride, selfish desires, quarrels, divided loyalties, and friendship with the world.
Just before this promise, James declares:
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.” — James 4:6 (KJV)
And then he calls believers to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, mourn over sin, and humble themselves before the Lord.
This is not a motivational speech about climbing higher.
It is a call to repentance.
A call to stop pretending.
A call to come back to God.
And that changes everything.
Because the promise is not that humility will make you famous.
The promise is that the God who gives grace to the humble will not abandon those who bow before Him.
Some of us have spent years asking God to lift us into places our character was not ready to occupy.
We prayed for influence while secretly craving applause.
We prayed for authority while resisting correction.
We prayed for blessings while treating obedience as optional.
We wanted God to open doors, but we didn't want Him to examine what was hiding behind our hearts.
And sometimes the most revealing question isn't, “Why hasn't God promoted me?”
It's this:
“If God gave me everything I've been asking for, would I use it to glorify Jesus—or to make people finally notice me?”
That question is uncomfortable.
It is supposed to be.
Because pride rarely introduces itself by saying, “I am pride.”
Sometimes pride sounds like, “I deserve better than this.”
Sometimes it sounds like, “After everything I've done, how dare they overlook me?”
Sometimes it hides inside ministry.
Inside generosity.
Inside biblical knowledge.
Inside the need to win every argument.
Even inside the desire to appear humble.
You can serve in church and still hunger for recognition.
You can quote Scripture and still refuse to apologize.
You can preach about forgiveness while privately enjoying the thought of someone else's downfall.
You can lift your hands during worship while refusing to surrender the bitterness in your heart.
And yes, you can be publicly admired for your Christianity while privately becoming less and less like Christ.
That is why humility is not a small subject.
It reaches into the places where our religious appearance and our actual obedience no longer agree.
Jesus once told a story about two men who went to the temple to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
The other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and thanked God that he was not like other sinners. He rehearsed his religious achievements, his fasting, and his giving.
He looked impressive.
Disciplined.
Respectable.
The kind of person others might have assumed was spiritually secure.
The tax collector stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He struck his chest and prayed:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13 (KJV)
That was it.
No spiritual résumé.
No comparison with someone worse.
No explanation about why his sins should be overlooked.
Just a guilty man asking for mercy.
Then Jesus delivered a verdict that must have shocked His listeners.
The tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee.
And Jesus said:
“For every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.” — Luke 18:14 (KJV)
Think about that.
The man who appeared righteous went home without the justification he assumed he possessed.
The man who knew he needed mercy went home justified before God.
One man trusted his goodness.
The other cried out for grace.
One stood tall in his own eyes.
The other bowed low before God.
And the one who bowed low was the one Jesus said went home justified.
Perhaps you've been exhausting yourself trying to prove that you are good enough, strong enough, holy enough, successful enough.
Perhaps you have been carrying the crushing weight of needing to be better than everyone else.
But the Gospel does not begin with you proving your worthiness.
It begins with the truth that you are a sinner who needs a Savior—and that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
You cannot earn your way into God's acceptance through impressive religious performance.
You cannot purchase forgiveness through good works.
You cannot build a staircase tall enough to reach heaven.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
And that is where the scandal becomes grace.
Because the sinner who stops pretending and turns to Christ discovers that God's mercy is greater than the reputation he has ruined.
But there is another side to humility that deserves to be spoken about with great care.
Not everyone who has been brought low has been brought low because of personal pride.
Some people are suffering because they were betrayed.
Some have been abused.
Some are grieving.
Some have lost their jobs through no wrongdoing of their own.
Some are battling illnesses they never chose.
And some have spent years being humiliated by people who claimed to speak for God.
If that is you, please hear this.
Being mistreated is not the same thing as being humbled by God.
Humility does not require you to remain in an abusive situation.
It does not mean allowing someone to destroy your dignity.
It does not mean accepting lies about your worth.
And it certainly does not mean that every tragedy in your life is punishment for hidden arrogance.
Biblical humility is not self-hatred.
It is seeing yourself truthfully before God.
It is refusing both the lie that you are greater than everyone else and the lie that you are worthless.
You are a human being created in God's image.
You are not God.
You need grace.
And through Jesus Christ, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
That is humility rooted in truth.
And nowhere do we see that truth more clearly than in the life of Jesus Himself.
Before the cross, before the empty tomb, before the resurrection proclamation shook the world, there was a room.
A meal.
A table.
A group of disciples who still had so much to learn about greatness.
And their Lord did something extraordinary.
He rose from supper, laid aside His outer garments, took a towel, and began washing His disciples' feet.
Imagine that room.
The Teacher kneeling.
The Master serving.
The One through whom all things were made taking the position of a servant.
The hands that would soon be pierced by nails were washing dust from human feet.
And among those gathered was Judas, whose betrayal Jesus already knew was coming.
John 13 records Jesus washing the disciples' feet, although it does not narrate each washing individually.
This was not a performance designed to impress an audience.
It was an act of love.
Jesus was showing His followers that greatness in His kingdom does not look like the world's obsession with status.
He said:
“For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.” — John 13:15 (KJV)
And then, beyond that room, beyond the towel and basin, the road led toward something infinitely more costly.
The cross.
Philippians 2:5–11 tells us to have the mind of Christ Jesus.

Though He existed in the form of God, He did not treat equality with God as something to exploit for His own advantage. Instead, He took the form of a servant, became truly human, and humbled Himself in obedience to death—even death on a cross.
The apostle Paul writes:
The Greek expression is:
ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτόν
etapeinōsen heauton
“He humbled Himself.”
Jesus did not cease to be divine when He became human.
He did not become less holy by serving.
He did not surrender His righteousness by taking the lowest place.
He willingly humbled Himself in obedience to the Father.
And the cross was not merely an inspiring illustration of humility.
It was the place where the sinless Son of God gave His life for sinners.
He bore our sins.
He suffered for our salvation.
He accomplished what no amount of human humility could ever accomplish.
Then comes one of the most astonishing declarations in the New Testament.
“Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name.” — Philippians 2:9 (KJV)
The Greek uses the remarkable verb:
ὑπερύψωσεν
hyperypsōsen
“He highly exalted.”
This speaks of the Father's supreme exaltation of Christ, the crucified and risen Lord.
And here we must make an essential distinction.
Jesus was not exalted because He needed to repent of pride.
He was sinless.
His humiliation was His willing obedience and sacrificial service.
Our humility, by contrast, includes acknowledging our sin, abandoning self-righteousness, and submitting ourselves to His lordship.
We do not become saviors by imitating His humility.
We bow before the Savior who has already accomplished our redemption.
And because He is exalted, every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
Do you see it now?
The kingdom of God overturns our assumptions.
The world says, “Make yourself important.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
The world says, “Never let anyone see your weakness.”
Jesus says, “My grace is sufficient for thee,” as He told Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:9.
The world says, “Climb over others to get ahead.”
Jesus says that whoever desires to be great among His followers must become a servant (Mark 10:43).
And the world says, “Protect your image at all costs.”
The Gospel says, “Confess your sin and come into the light.”
That is where the real battle begins.
Not always in public.
Sometimes in a kitchen after an argument.
You know you spoke cruelly.
You know your words wounded someone who loves you.
You know the apology should come from you.
But something inside whispers, “Why should I be the first one to say sorry?”
And suddenly your pride becomes more important than peace.
Sometimes the battle happens when another person's ministry grows while yours remains unnoticed.
You congratulate them publicly.
But privately, envy begins to grow.
Sometimes it happens when your child points out something inconsistent in your behavior.
You could listen.
You could admit your mistake.
But instead, you use your authority to silence the conversation.
Sometimes it happens when someone confronts you with a sin you've carefully concealed.
Your first instinct is not repentance.
It's damage control.
Who knows?
What will they think?
Can I explain my way out of this?
Can I preserve my reputation?
And beneath all those questions is the one we are terrified to ask:
“Am I more concerned about being seen as righteous than actually turning back to God?”
David knew what it meant to be confronted with that question.
After his sin involving Bathsheba and the arranged death of Uriah, the prophet Nathan confronted him.
David had abused his power.
He had sinned grievously against God and against other people.
His position as king did not make his actions less wicked.
His public achievements did not erase his guilt.
And when Nathan exposed his sin, David said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13 (KJV)
Those words did not undo the damage.
His repentance did not remove every earthly consequence.
And the Bible does not ask us to overlook the people harmed by his actions.
But David's confession mattered.
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a sinner who understands that no religious performance can substitute for a repentant heart.
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” — Psalm 51:17 (KJV)
The Hebrew expression for a broken and contrite heart includes:
לֵב־נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה
lev-nishbar ve-nidkeh
A heart that is broken and crushed.
Not a heart that enjoys suffering.
Not a heart that believes God's love must be purchased through misery.
But a heart that has stopped defending its sin and is genuinely turning toward the Lord.
God does not despise such repentance.
Perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
You have spent so long defending yourself that you've forgotten how to confess.
You have spent so long hiding that honesty feels dangerous.
You have spent so long trying to look spiritually strong that you've forgotten how to cry out for mercy.
But Jesus did not come to save people who have successfully maintained the appearance of perfection.
He came to call sinners to repentance.
And the invitation still stands.
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Turn away from the sin.
Trust the Savior.
Because grace is not God's permission to continue destroying your life.
Grace is His undeserved favor that brings forgiveness and teaches us to renounce ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
And humility is not a performance you put on to manipulate God into giving you what you want.
It is the posture of someone who finally recognizes that Jesus is Lord.
There is another promise closely connected to James 4:10.
Peter writes:
In due time.
Those three words can be difficult to live with.
Because we want the restoration immediately.
We want the answer today.
We want the people who misunderstood us to discover the truth by tomorrow morning.
We want God to vindicate us in front of everyone who ever questioned our worth.
But Peter does not give us a deadline.
And he does not promise that every humble Christian will become wealthy, famous, influential, or publicly celebrated.
The passage calls suffering believers to trust God's mighty hand.
It continues by inviting them to cast their cares upon Him because He cares for them.
And later, in 1 Peter 5:10, Peter points to God's eternal glory in Christ and His work of restoring and strengthening His people after suffering.
That is a much deeper hope than worldly promotion.
God's exaltation is not a guarantee of a higher social position. It is the assurance that those who belong to Christ are not forgotten by God and that His purposes will ultimately prevail.
Sometimes He restores a relationship.
Sometimes He opens an unexpected opportunity.
Sometimes He changes circumstances we thought would never change.
And sometimes His faithful people suffer without receiving public vindication in this life.
Yet their hope remains secure in Jesus Christ.
The resurrection is our great assurance that suffering and death do not have the final word for those who belong to Him.
That is why humility can wait.
Not because waiting is easy.
But because the One holding our future is faithful.
And maybe someone reading this has been waiting for years.
Waiting for an apology.
Waiting for reconciliation.
Waiting for a prayer to be answered.
Waiting for someone to notice how hard you've tried to do what is right.
You are tired.
You have wondered whether obedience is worth it.
You have watched people who seem arrogant prosper while your own life remains painfully ordinary.
And a quiet temptation has begun to grow inside you.
“If pride gets people ahead, why should I keep choosing humility?”
Because Jesus is worthy of your obedience even when obedience costs you.
Because the approval of God matters more than the applause of people.
Because the goal of the Christian life is not to become the most admired person in the room.
It is to become more like Christ.
And because the final measure of your life will not be the size of your audience, your bank account, or the number of people who remember your name.
It will be whether you belong to the Lord Jesus Christ.
Think about the thief crucified beside Jesus.
He had no opportunity to build a respectable Christian reputation.
No years of ministry accomplishments to present.
No chance to repair his public image.
He acknowledged his guilt, recognized Jesus' innocence, and pleaded:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42 (KJV)
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43 (KJV)
What a staggering picture of grace.
A condemned man.
A dying Savior.
A desperate plea.
And a promise of paradise.
The thief did not earn salvation by suffering.
His suffering did not pay for his sins.
Jesus was the Savior.
And the man turned to Him in faith.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not self-improvement as a substitute for redemption.
Not humility as a currency for buying heaven.
But a sinner placing his hope in Jesus Christ.
From guilt to mercy.
From condemnation to the promise of life with Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending our sins never happened.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.
Not by declaring evil harmless.
But by forgiving sinners who turn to Him, reconciling them to God, and beginning the transforming work of His Spirit.
And that means your story does not have to end where your pride led you.
The person who refused to apologize can learn to say, “I was wrong.”
The believer who secretly envied others can learn to rejoice when God blesses them.
The father who ruled his home through intimidation can repent and begin learning Christlike gentleness.
The mother who measured her worth by everyone else's approval can rest in the love of God.
The church leader who has confused influence with spiritual maturity can return to the humility of a servant.
The Christian who has been hiding a secret sin can stop making excuses, seek help, make appropriate amends, and walk in the light.
And the wounded person who has been told that humility means remaining silent under mistreatment can learn that submitting to God does not mean surrendering to abuse.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the repentant.
There is mercy for the guilty.
There is strength for the weary.
There is hope for those who feel forgotten.
But there is no room for the illusion that we can save ourselves.
We need Christ.
All of us.
The proud preacher.
The struggling believer.
The person who has walked away from church.
The religious person who knows every verse but has forgotten how to love.
The sinner who believes forgiveness is impossible.
We all come to God on the same basis.
Not our greatness.
His grace.
Not our righteousness.
Christ's saving work.
Not our ability to lift ourselves.
His power to save.
What are you still holding onto because you're afraid that surrendering it to Jesus will make you look small?
Is it your reputation?
Your resentment?
Your secret sin?
Your need to be right?
Your demand to be recognized?
Your refusal to forgive?
Your fear of admitting you need help?
You don't have to confess your private sins publicly in a comment section.
But you do need to be truthful before God.
And where your actions have harmed others, genuine repentance may also require confession, accountability, restitution where possible, and a willingness to face consequences.
Because humility is not just something we feel during a moving sermon.
It changes how we live when the sermon is over.
It changes how we speak to our families.
How we treat people who cannot benefit us.
How we respond when corrected.
How we handle money.
How we use influence.
How we treat those who disagree with us.
How we serve when nobody notices.
How we love when nobody applauds.
And perhaps the most beautiful evidence of humility is this:
You become less interested in making your own name great and more interested in making Jesus known.
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior.
Not building a throne for a personality.
Not selling spiritual status.
Not suggesting that a monthly payment makes anyone more acceptable to God.
But proclaiming the Gospel of Jesus Christ, encouraging repentance, strengthening believers through Scripture, and helping people grow in a faith that survives beyond emotional moments.
And if this message has confronted something in your heart, I want to invite you to respond.
Not with a polished religious answer.
With honesty.
You don't owe strangers the details of your pain. But your honest response may remind someone else that they are not alone in their struggle.
And if this article made you think of a friend, a brother, a sister, a spouse, or someone who has quietly been wrestling with pride, shame, or spiritual exhaustion, consider sharing it with them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
But because a message rooted in Scripture can reach someone you may never have the opportunity to speak to personally.
You may never know who reads it in the middle of a sleepless night.
Who finds the courage to repent.
Who decides to ask for prayer.
Who opens a Bible again after years of neglect.
Who realizes that the mercy of Jesus is still being proclaimed.
There is also something deeply practical I want to share with those who believe in this mission.
These resources are part of our desire to help people read Scripture, understand the Gospel, and continue growing long after they finish an article.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry like this requires time, resources, consistent work, and the willing support of people who believe that biblical teaching should continue reaching others.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, generously, and cheerfully—not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It also affirms the legitimacy of supporting those who labor in Gospel ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6).
If you are already faithfully supporting your local church, caring for your household, and meeting your responsibilities, I do not want you to neglect those commitments.
Your local church matters.
Your family matters.
Your financial responsibilities matter.

You might choose to make it part of your personal giving budget. Whether you call that support an offering or a ministry contribution, its value is not determined by the amount but by the willingness and faithfulness of the heart.
These are simply expressions of appreciation—not spiritual rewards, and certainly not a measure of anyone's standing before God.
You can still pray for this ministry.
You can still invite people to read the Scriptures.
You can still encourage someone who is struggling.
You can still make a difference without spending a single cent.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is not a product.
We support Gospel ministry because we love the Savior who first loved us—not because we can buy His approval.
That distinction matters.
Especially in a world where people have sometimes been taught to confuse financial giving with guaranteed divine favor.
Genuine Christian generosity flows from grace.
It is never a transaction that obligates God to make us rich, successful, or publicly exalted.
And perhaps that is one more way humility changes us.
We stop asking, “What will I get if I give?”
And begin asking, “How can I faithfully use what God has entrusted to me?”
Some will serve through financial support.
Some through prayer.
Some through sharing.
Some through teaching, hospitality, encouragement, or quiet acts of love that never appear on a screen.
Every faithful act matters when it is offered to the Lord.
Not because your salvation depends on it.
Not because you are less faithful if you don't.
But because you genuinely want to help this work continue.
Now I want to return to the person we met at the beginning of this story.
The person staring into the darkness.
The one who feels overlooked.
The one who has lost something important.
The one who wonders whether God has forgotten them.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe your life does not look anything like you imagined it would.
Maybe the doors you wanted never opened.
Maybe someone else received the recognition you hoped for.
Maybe your pride has cost you relationships you desperately wish you could repair.
Maybe your secret sins have left you exhausted from pretending.
Or maybe you have been faithfully following Jesus through suffering that nobody else understands.
Wherever you are, the invitation of James 4:10 still stands.
Humble yourself before the Lord.
Not so you can force Him to promote you.
Not so you can become more impressive than the people who rejected you.
Not so you can use humility as another strategy for personal advancement.
But because He is God.
Because you need His grace.
Because Jesus Christ is worthy of your surrender.
Because there is freedom in no longer needing to pretend you are the center of the universe.
And because the One who calls you to humility is the same Savior who humbled Himself to the point of death on a cross.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And He is Lord.
The Christian's ultimate hope is not that every humiliation will end in public applause.
It is that the crucified and risen Jesus will keep His promises, finish His work in His people, and bring those who belong to Him into His eternal glory.
That is exaltation worth waiting for.
So tonight, if you can, find a quiet place.
Put down the phone for a moment.
Stop rehearsing the arguments you wish you had won.
Stop comparing your life with someone else's.
Stop trying to convince God that you deserve a higher position.
And pray something like this:

“Lord Jesus, You know me completely. You see the pride I hide, the sins I excuse, the wounds I carry, and the approval I keep chasing. Forgive me for the times I have wanted Your gifts more than I have wanted You. Teach me to repent sincerely, to love without demanding recognition, to serve without needing applause, and to trust You when I cannot understand Your timing. Protect me from confusing humility with worthlessness, and from confusing worldly success with Your favor. Thank You for humbling Yourself for sinners, dying for our sins, and rising again. Let my life belong to You. Make me more like You. Amen.”
And when you rise from that prayer, don't measure its value by whether you feel an emotional rush.
Look for the next act of obedience.
Make the apology.
Tell the truth.
Seek accountability.
Forgive where you can, without denying the need for justice or healthy boundaries.
Serve someone quietly.
Open your Bible.
Return to prayer.
Give thanks when someone else succeeds.
And when your pride rises again tomorrow, humble yourself before the Lord again.
This is not a one-time performance.
It is part of the daily life of following Jesus.
The world may never understand why you stopped fighting for the highest seat.
People may never applaud the battles you win in secret.
They may never know how much courage it took to confess, surrender, forgive, or begin again.
But the Lord sees.
And in Christ, your hope is not in being noticed by the world.
It is in being known by the Savior.
So don't despise the humble place.
Don't confuse surrender with defeat.
Don't mistake the absence of applause for the absence of God.
And never forget that the highest name in heaven belongs to the One who willingly took the lowest place for our salvation.
You may spend your whole life trying to rise above everyone else, only to discover that the place you most needed to reach was on your knees before Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS TOLD ONE RICH MAN TO SELL EVERYTHING… BUT WELCOMED ANOTHER INTO SALVATION. WHY?
paragraphs: JESUS TOLD ONE RICH MAN TO SELL EVERYTHING… BUT WELCOMED ANOTHER INTO SALVATION. WHY?

Two wealthy men. Two encounters with Jesus. One walked away grieving. The other welcomed Him with joy. The difference exposes a truth about money, salvation, and the hidden idols of the human heart that many Christians would rather not confront.
There is something unsettling about the way Jesus treated two wealthy men in the Gospels.
One came running toward Him.
The other was sitting in a tree.
One appeared morally upright, religiously disciplined, and genuinely interested in eternal life.
The other was a notorious tax collector, a man whose wealth was associated with a system of exploitation and whose reputation had made him an outcast among his own people.
Yet the respectable man walked away sorrowful.
And the despised man heard Jesus declare that salvation had come to his house.
Read that again.
The man who looked closest to the kingdom walked away.
The man everyone thought was hopeless welcomed the King.
And somewhere between those two encounters is a truth that could change the way you understand your money, your obedience, your generosity, and perhaps even your relationship with Jesus Christ.
Because the question is not simply why Jesus told one man to sell everything while allowing another to retain some of his possessions.
The more disturbing question is this:
What did Jesus see in their hearts that nobody else could see?
And what might He see in ours?
In Mark 10:17–27, a man approaches Jesus with an urgency that should make every religious person pay attention.
He runs.
He kneels.
And he asks, "Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?" (Mark 10:17, KJV).
He is not mocking Jesus. He is not openly trying to trap Him. Mark presents a man seriously concerned about eternal life.
He seems to have everything people spend their lives chasing.
Money. Position. Respectability. Religious knowledge.
Matthew identifies him as young, and Luke calls him a ruler. When the Gospel accounts are read together, we understand why Christians traditionally call him the rich young ruler.
But beneath his achievements is an unanswered question.
What must I do to inherit eternal life?
There is something painfully familiar about that question.
You can have a respectable career and still lie awake wondering whether your life means anything.
You can own a beautiful home and still feel like a stranger inside it.
You can provide for your family, attend church, give offerings, avoid public scandal, and still carry a quiet fear that something essential is missing.
You can know how to succeed in this world without knowing whether your soul has truly surrendered to Christ.
The young ruler had possessions.
But he wanted assurance about eternity.
And Jesus was about to show him that those are two very different things.
Jesus begins by directing his attention to God's commandments.
The man responds that he has observed them from his youth.
Then Mark records a detail so beautiful, so easily overlooked, that it changes the emotional atmosphere of the entire encounter.
"Then Jesus beholding him loved him" (Mark 10:21, KJV).
Before Jesus confronts him, Jesus loves him.
Before exposing his deepest attachment, Jesus looks upon him with love.
This matters.
Because what follows is not an act of cruelty.
It is not Jesus humiliating a wealthy man for being successful.
It is not Christ declaring that financial prosperity automatically makes someone wicked.
It is the loving Savior identifying the one thing this particular man cannot imagine surrendering.
Jesus says:
"One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me." (Mark 10:21, KJV).
One thing.
Not ten things.
Not a complicated religious performance.
One thing standing between this man's professed desire for eternal life and the costly reality of following Jesus.
His possessions had become more than possessions.
They had become something he could not bear to release.
And Jesus knew it.
The Greek text of Mark 10:21 includes the words:
ἕν σε ὑστερεῖ — hen se hysterei
Literally, "One thing is lacking to you," or more naturally, "You lack one thing."
The verb hystereō communicates lacking or falling short.
Jesus is not teaching that the man can purchase eternal life by liquidating his assets.
He is exposing the contradiction between the man's desire to follow God and his unwillingness to relinquish what competes with God's authority.
And then comes the invitation that gives the entire command its meaning:
δεῦρο ἀκολούθει μοι — deuro akolouthei moi
"Come, follow me."
That is the center of the encounter.
Not merely selling.
Not merely donating.
Not merely becoming poor.
Following Jesus.
The command to sell his possessions was the particular surrender Jesus placed before him. The destination was discipleship.
And the man could not bring himself to take that step.
Mark 10:22 tells us:
"And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions."
Imagine that moment.
The dust beneath his sandals.
The crowd watching.
The Teacher standing before him.
The possibility of an entirely different future opening before his eyes.
And the unbearable weight of what obedience would cost.
Perhaps he thought about his estates.
His accounts.
His inherited security.
His reputation.
The comfort of knowing that whatever happened tomorrow, his wealth could protect him from many of life's uncertainties.
Scripture does not tell us his private thoughts, so we cannot know precisely what he imagined.
But we know his decision.
He walked away.
And here is the tragedy.
He came asking about eternal life.
He stood before the One who gives eternal life.
Yet he departed because the cost of following Him touched something he valued too deeply.
He was willing to approach Jesus.
He was willing to kneel before Jesus.
He was willing to discuss obedience with Jesus.
But when Jesus required the surrender of his ruling attachment, he chose to leave.
How many people still do something similar?
We want Jesus to forgive our sins, but not confront our secret compromises.
We want Him to bless our relationships, but not challenge the ones pulling us away from holiness.
We want Him to protect our finances, but not question the greed, dishonesty, or fear governing our financial decisions.
We want peace without repentance.
Comfort without surrender.
A Savior who rescues us, but not a Lord who has authority over us.
And sometimes the most dangerous thing in our lives is not something obviously sinful.
Sometimes it is something legitimate that has quietly become ultimate.
A career.
A relationship.
A reputation.
A bank account.
A dream.
Even a ministry.
Something good can become an idol when we refuse to obey God because we fear losing it.
The young ruler's wealth was not merely something he owned.
In that decisive moment, it was something he would not surrender.
But now the story becomes even more uncomfortable.
Because if Jesus commanded this man to sell everything, why did He not give the same explicit command to every wealthy person He encountered?
Why did Jesus enter the home of Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector, without first demanding that he dispose of every possession?
Why did Scripture portray wealthy people among those who supported His ministry?
Was Jesus applying different standards?
Was one man being treated more harshly?
Was Zacchaeus receiving an easier version of discipleship?
Not at all.
And to understand why, we must travel from the road where the rich ruler walked away to the crowded streets of Jericho.
In Luke 19, another wealthy man is about to encounter Jesus.
His name is Zacchaeus.
Luke does not soften his background.
He was a chief tax collector.
And he was rich.
Tax collectors in Roman-occupied Judea were often despised because they worked within an oppressive revenue system, and some enriched themselves through dishonest collection.
Zacchaeus was not introduced as a respected spiritual leader.
He was not presented as the kind of person religious society would naturally celebrate.
He was a wealthy man whose occupation carried a deeply damaged reputation.
And yet he wanted to see Jesus.
There was one problem.
He was short, and the crowd blocked his view.
So he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree.
Pause there.
A wealthy chief tax collector, a man accustomed to status and financial power, climbs a tree simply to catch a glimpse of Jesus.
He risks looking ridiculous.
He leaves behind the dignity that people in positions of authority often work so hard to preserve.
And then something astonishing happens.
Jesus stops.
Looks up.
And calls him by name.
"Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." (Luke 19:5, KJV).
Notice the difference.
The rich young ruler approaches Jesus with a question about what he must do.
Jesus approaches Zacchaeus with an announcement of His intention to visit.
The rich ruler is confronted with the cost of discipleship.
Zacchaeus is confronted with the astonishing grace of being welcomed by the very One he wanted to see.
And the crowd does not celebrate.
They complain.
Jesus is going to be the guest of a sinner.
The religiously respectable people see a scandal.
Jesus sees a man He has come to seek.
This is where the Gospel begins overturning our assumptions.
Because grace is not reserved for people whose reputations are clean.
And salvation is not distributed according to how impressive someone appears from the outside.
Jesus enters the life of a man whom society has already condemned.
Not because Zacchaeus's sins are insignificant.
Not because dishonesty suddenly becomes acceptable.
Not because wealth excuses exploitation.
But because Christ came to save sinners.
And when grace truly enters a person's life, something begins to change.
Zacchaeus stands and says:
"Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." (Luke 19:8, KJV).
Half his possessions.
And fourfold restitution where he has wrongfully taken from others.
Now ask yourself something.
Why does Jesus not interrupt him?
Why does He not say, "Half is insufficient. I told another wealthy man to sell everything. You must do exactly the same"?
Instead, Jesus declares:
"This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham." (Luke 19:9, KJV).
And then Jesus gives the explanation that illuminates both encounters.
"For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." (Luke 19:10, KJV).
There it is.
The heart of the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to reorganize people's finances.
He came to seek and save the lost.
And genuine salvation does not leave the human heart unchanged.
Consider what happened to Zacchaeus.
A man associated with taking money from others begins speaking about giving.
A man connected to an exploitative system begins committing himself to restitution.
A man whose wealth had helped define his public identity openly acknowledges responsibility toward the poor and those he has wronged.
His words do not prove that he was already a perfect man.
Nor does Luke provide a later financial audit confirming every payment.
But the narrative presents his declaration as the visible expression of a profound change, and Jesus announces salvation in connection with this encounter.
The contrast is extraordinary.
One wealthy man hears a command to release his possessions and walks away grieving.
Another wealthy man welcomes Jesus and voluntarily declares a generosity that would dramatically change his financial life.
One cannot imagine surrendering his wealth.
The other begins relinquishing wealth in response to Christ.
And the difference is not that Jesus has two different standards of salvation.
The difference is that Jesus knows exactly what the human heart is clinging to, and His grace produces a new relationship with whatever once controlled us.
But we must be careful here.
It would be a mistake to claim that Zacchaeus earned salvation by giving away half his possessions.
That would contradict the larger teaching of Scripture.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
The Greek expression χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι — chariti este sesōsmenoi means, "By grace you have been saved."
The form sesōsmenoi emphasizes the state of having been saved, while chariti identifies grace as the basis.
Salvation is God's gift, not a transaction we negotiate through charitable contributions.
And Ephesians does not stop at verse 9.
Verse 10 explains that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Good works do not purchase our salvation.
They are the fruit of God's transforming grace.
That distinction is everything.
If you give money to make God love you, you have misunderstood grace.
If you give money to erase your sins, you have misunderstood the cross.

But if you have received the mercy of Jesus Christ, and that mercy begins loosening the grip of greed, selfishness, and indifference in your heart, your generosity can become a beautiful expression of gratitude and obedience.
We do not give so that Jesus will save us. We learn to give because the Savior is changing us.
And the two wealthy men illustrate that distinction in unforgettable ways.
Yet there is another detail we cannot ignore.
After the rich young ruler walks away, Jesus tells His disciples how difficult it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God.
They are astonished.
And Jesus gives the famous picture of a camel passing through the eye of a needle.
This is not a lesson about a supposed small Jerusalem gate through which a camel could squeeze by kneeling and unloading its baggage. That popular explanation lacks reliable historical support.
Jesus is using a shocking image of impossibility.
The disciples understand the force of His words.
"Who then can be saved?" they ask.
Jesus answers:
"With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible." (Mark 10:27, KJV).
This changes everything.
The answer to the rich young ruler's problem was never simply better financial management.
His deepest need was the saving power of God.
And the answer to Zacchaeus's problem was not simply a more generous budget.
His deepest need was the saving grace of Christ.
Money was the visible issue.
The human heart was the battlefield.
Salvation was the miracle.
The Hebrew Scriptures had already warned God's people about this danger.
Deuteronomy 8:17 describes the temptation to say:
"My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth."
The Hebrew phrase כֹּחִי וְעֹצֶם יָדִי — kochi ve'otsem yadi means "my power and the strength of my hand."
The danger is not merely possessing resources.
It is forgetting the God from whom our ability, opportunities, and provisions ultimately come.
We begin by thanking God for what we have.
Then, if we are not careful, we begin trusting what we have more than the God who provided it.
We stop seeing money as a responsibility and begin treating it as our security.
We stop asking how our resources can serve God and neighbor and begin asking how to protect ourselves from ever needing to trust Him.
And slowly, without noticing, our possessions become our refuge.
That is why Jesus teaches in Matthew 6:24:
"Ye cannot serve God and mammon."
The Greek word μαμωνᾷ — mamōna refers to wealth or riches, pictured here as a rival master.
Jesus is not saying every wealthy person is automatically enslaved to money.
He is warning that wealth can demand the loyalty that belongs to God alone.
And no human being can ultimately serve two competing masters.
This is where the story stops being about two ancient men.
And starts being about us.
Because not everyone reading this article is rich.
Some are struggling to pay rent.
Some are wondering how to buy groceries.
Some are carrying debts they are ashamed to discuss.
Some have worked honestly for years and still feel financially trapped.
Others have been blessed with businesses, homes, savings, investments, and comfortable lives.
But every one of us can be tempted to find our identity or security in something other than Christ.
The person with millions can worship money.
And the person with almost nothing can become consumed by the desire for it.
The person with abundance can be generous.
And the person with little can also be extraordinarily generous.
Jesus sees beyond the amount.
He sees the allegiance.
He sees whether we are using our resources to serve love or using people to protect our resources.
He sees whether our financial decisions reflect integrity, compassion, responsibility, and trust.
And He sees the sacrifices nobody else notices.
The parent who refuses dishonest income even when money is desperately needed.
The business owner who chooses fair treatment of employees over additional profit.
The believer who quietly helps a struggling family without posting the act online.
The person who returns money obtained dishonestly.
The Christian who gives faithfully while also honoring responsibilities to children, aging parents, creditors, and others entrusted to their care.
None of these actions buys salvation.
But each can express a heart learning to live under the lordship of Christ.
And Scripture gives us further evidence that Jesus did not impose an identical liquidation requirement on every wealthy disciple.
Luke 8:1–3 describes women who supported Jesus and His disciples from their resources.
Among them was Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward.
The text does not tell us her personal net worth, but it does show that material resources could be used to sustain Jesus' ministry.
Joseph of Arimathea, described in Matthew 27:57 as a rich man and a disciple of Jesus, provided his own new tomb for the burial of Christ.
Scripture does not record Jesus commanding Joseph to sell every possession before he could be His disciple.
In Acts 4:36–37, Barnabas sells a field and lays the proceeds at the apostles' feet.

And in Acts 5:4, Peter's words to Ananias show that the property had been his to control before its sale and that the proceeds remained under his authority afterward. The sin was not failing to donate a required amount. It was deceit.
Later, Paul instructs wealthy Christians in 1 Timothy 6:17–19 not to be arrogant or trust in uncertain riches, but to trust God, do good, be rich in good works, and be generous and ready to share.
He does not tell every wealthy Christian to become penniless.
He tells them how wealth must be regarded and used under God's authority.
These passages do not make the rich ruler's command irrelevant.
They help us understand its particular application.
Jesus' call to discipleship is universal.
His specific instructions can expose different attachments in different people.
For the rich ruler, obedience required selling his possessions and giving to the poor.
For Zacchaeus, repentance was visibly expressed through substantial generosity and restitution.
For other believers, faithfulness involved using resources for hospitality, ministry, justice, and the needs of others.
But none of them received permission to place wealth above Christ.
That is the unchanging standard.
Everything we possess must remain subordinate to the One who gave Himself for us.
And perhaps this is the question we have been avoiding.
If Jesus asked you to surrender the thing you are most afraid to lose, would you still follow Him?
Not theoretically.
Not in a Sunday morning song.
Not in a beautifully written social media comment.
In real life.
If following Jesus cost you a dishonest source of income, would you obey?
If repentance required returning money you wrongfully took, would you make restitution?
If generosity meant sacrificing a luxury so someone else could eat, would compassion overcome comfort?
If obedience threatened your reputation, would you choose Christ over applause?
And if God called you to serve Him faithfully without public recognition, would His approval be enough?
These questions are uncomfortable.
They should be.
But they are not invitations to despair.
They are invitations to surrender.
Remember the words Mark recorded before Jesus confronted the rich ruler.
Jesus loved him.
Christ's call to repentance is not the opposite of His love.
It is an expression of His love.
He does not expose our idols because He enjoys watching us suffer.
He exposes them because false gods cannot save us.
Money cannot forgive sin.
Status cannot conquer death.
A successful career cannot reconcile us to the Father.
An impressive reputation cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
And even the most generous donation cannot accomplish what Jesus accomplished on the cross.
Only Christ can save.
The One who confronted the rich ruler would Himself go to Jerusalem, be rejected, suffer, die, and rise again.
He would bear the burden of sin that no human being could remove through wealth, morality, or religious achievement.
The rich ruler was invited to surrender his treasures and follow Jesus.
Jesus Himself would give His life for sinners.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more beautiful than either man's financial story.
We are not saved because we finally manage to release everything perfectly.
We are saved by the grace of the crucified and risen Savior, received through faith.
And the Christ who saves us begins teaching us to release whatever has held our hearts captive.
For some, that means abandoning greed.
For others, confessing dishonesty.
For others, learning generosity after years of fear.
For others, accepting that they cannot purchase God's acceptance through endless religious activity.
And for some, it means admitting that they have spent years using Christian language while keeping Jesus at a safe distance from their actual decisions.
Perhaps you recognize yourself in the rich young ruler.
You love hearing about Jesus.
You respect His teachings.
You want eternal life.
But there is something you have quietly declared untouchable.
A hidden sin.
An unhealthy relationship.
A financial compromise.
An ambition that has swallowed your integrity.
A bitterness you refuse to release.
You keep telling yourself you will surrender it later.
When life is more stable.
When you have enough money.
When you are older.
When obedience becomes less expensive.
But the rich ruler's story leaves us with a sobering picture of what happens when the invitation to follow Jesus is met with grief instead of surrender.
And perhaps you recognize yourself in Zacchaeus.
Your past is complicated.
People remember what you did.
Maybe you have hurt others.
Maybe you built parts of your life through choices you now regret.
Maybe you have become so accustomed to being judged that you no longer believe anyone could look at you with hope.
Listen carefully.
The same Jesus who stopped beneath Zacchaeus's tree still receives repentant sinners.
Your reputation is not stronger than His mercy.
Your past is not beyond His power to redeem.
Your failures are not a reason to hide from the Savior who came to seek and save the lost.
But grace does not merely comfort us while leaving our wrongdoing untouched.
It calls us into truth.
Where we have deceived, we must turn toward honesty.
Where we have exploited, we must turn toward justice.
Where restitution is possible and appropriate, repentance should move us toward making things right.
Where selfishness has ruled, love must begin taking root.
And where wealth has become our master, Christ calls us back to freedom.
Not because we can repair our souls through our own efforts.
But because the Savior who forgives also transforms.
That is the beauty of Zacchaeus's story.
Jesus did not wait for Zacchaeus to become respectable before approaching him.
Yet the encounter did not leave Zacchaeus content with his old ways.
Grace welcomed him.
And grace began changing the direction of his life.
From taking to giving.
From hiding above the crowd to standing openly before the Lord.
From a reputation shaped by sin to a new life marked by repentance and generosity.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But there is one more truth we must carry into our own generation.
If Jesus is Lord over our possessions, then our resources can become instruments of mercy, truth, and Gospel ministry.
The early Christians understood this.
They shared with those in need.
They supported ministry.
They practiced hospitality.
They gave willingly and sacrificially.
Paul taught in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
Not because someone has frightened you into believing God will reject you if you refuse.
Christian generosity is not spiritual extortion.
It is a willing response to God's grace.
And that matters deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
Our mission is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ through Scripture, discipleship, biblical encouragement, repentance, healing, and the transforming truth of the Gospel.
Every article, every devotional, every resource, and every message of hope is an opportunity to place the truth of God's Word before someone who may be quietly fighting a battle nobody else can see.
Someone who has stopped praying.
Someone who feels too ashamed to return to church.
Someone who thinks God has forgotten them.
Someone who is one difficult night away from giving up.
We cannot know how God will use every message.
But we can faithfully make His Word available.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture more deeply, return to prayer, confront a hidden struggle, or remember the mercy of Christ, we invite you to become part of sustaining and expanding this work.

These products can be meaningful reminders of biblical truth and useful tools for encouragement, study, and conversation. They are not substitutes for Scripture, prayer, fellowship, or obedience to Christ.
It is the opportunity to participate in making Christ-centered encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
That free library is part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible beyond the limits of someone's financial circumstances.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Think about the people in your life.
The successful friend who seems to have everything but never appears at peace.
The relative whose pursuit of money has slowly consumed their relationships.
The Christian who has confused financial prosperity with spiritual maturity.
The person drowning in guilt over financial mistakes.
The believer who wants to give but fears that God will be displeased because they cannot afford to support every ministry asking for help.
This message may speak to each of them differently.
And if you are willing, leave something more meaningful than a quick reaction.
What is harder for you to surrender to Jesus: your possessions, your need for security, your reputation, or your desire to remain in control?
You do not need to expose private details or confess something you are not ready to share publicly.
Or, if you are walking through a difficult season and would welcome prayer, write:
Perhaps your testimony will encourage another believer who thought they were fighting alone.
Perhaps your honesty will help someone discover that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is the beginning of returning to the Savior.
And now, before you leave, consider the two men one final time.
One ran toward Jesus.
One climbed a tree to see Him.
One appeared righteous.
One was publicly despised.
One was confronted with the demand to surrender his wealth.
One responded to grace with an extraordinary commitment to generosity and restitution.
One walked away grieving.
One welcomed Jesus with joy.
But the ultimate hero of neither story is the man.
It is Jesus.
The Savior who loved the rich ruler enough to tell him the truth.
The Savior who welcomed Zacchaeus without excusing his wrongdoing.
The Savior who warned against the slavery of riches.
The Savior who taught that salvation is impossible by human power but possible with God.
The Savior who gave Himself to redeem sinners who could never buy their way into heaven.
And this is why the two encounters do not contradict each other.
They reveal the same Lord.
A Lord who refuses to be reduced to a formula.
A Lord who cannot be bribed with donations.
A Lord who is not impressed by religious appearances.
A Lord who knows exactly where our hearts are imprisoned.
And a Lord whose grace is powerful enough to set us free.
The question was never whether every Christian must have the same bank balance.
The question is whether every Christian must surrender to the same Savior.
And the answer is yes.
So do not leave this story merely wondering how much money Jesus wants you to give.
Ask whether He has your heart.
Do not measure your standing with God by the size of your offering.
Look to Christ, who alone can save you.
Do not confuse financial abundance with divine approval or financial hardship with divine rejection.
And do not assume that because you have never stolen like a corrupt tax collector, there is nothing in your heart that needs repentance.
Come to Jesus.
Bring Him your ambition.
Your fear.
Your shame.
Your unfinished obedience.
Your hidden attachments.
Your past.
Your future.
Your wealth, if you have it.
Your poverty, if that is your present reality.
Bring Him the part of your life you have been most afraid to place in His hands.
And trust the Savior who died and rose again to accomplish what no amount of human effort could achieve.
Because the richest person in the story is not necessarily the one who walks away with the most possessions.
It is the one who receives the grace of Christ and discovers that nothing in this world can replace Him.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility is not that Jesus might ask us to surrender something precious.
It is that we might spend our lives protecting something temporary while turning away from the One who offers eternal life.
The greatest tragedy is not losing what you hold in your hands, but walking away from Jesus because you cannot bear to open them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MUST YOU CONFESS YOUR SINS TO A PRIEST BEFORE GOD WILL FORGIVE YOU? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU APPROACH JESUS FOREVER
paragraphs: MUST YOU CONFESS YOUR SINS TO A PRIEST BEFORE GOD WILL FORGIVE YOU? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU APPROACH JESUS FOREVER

What if the shame you've been carrying has convinced you that God is farther away than He really is? A journey through Scripture, the original Greek and Hebrew, the authority Jesus gave His Church, and the extraordinary grace that opens the way to the Father.
There is a kind of guilt that follows you into the night.
You can laugh with your family. You can attend church. You can sing worship songs, raise your hands, and tell everyone you're doing fine.
But when the noise disappears, something inside you begins whispering.
You know what you did.
And perhaps the most painful question isn't whether you've sinned.
You already know you have.
The question is whether God will still receive you.

Maybe you've wondered whether you need to find a priest before God will listen. Maybe you've been taught that confessing your sins directly to Jesus is enough. Maybe you've heard Christians passionately defending both positions, each opening the same Bible and insisting the other has misunderstood it.
And somewhere between those arguments stands a person who simply wants to be forgiven.
Someone like you.
Someone like me.
Someone who doesn't need another religious shouting match.
Someone who needs to know what Jesus actually said.
So before we answer whether confession to a priest is necessary, we need to travel somewhere uncomfortable.
Not to a modern church building.
Not to a confessional booth.
But to a courtyard in Jerusalem, where a man who loved Jesus had just committed the betrayal he swore he would never commit.
Peter.
The disciple who declared that he would follow Jesus even to death.
The man who walked on water, witnessed miracles, and heard the voice of the Son of God.
And yet, when a servant girl questioned him, his courage collapsed.
He denied Jesus.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 records something devastating:
"And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." (KJV)
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of Jesus meeting the eyes of the man who had just denied knowing Him.
No sermon.
No public humiliation.
Just a look.
And Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Have you ever had a moment like that?
A moment when you realized that the person you had become was not the person you promised God you would be?

A secret relationship. A hidden addiction. A lie that became another lie. A marriage wounded by betrayal. An angry outburst that shattered someone's trust. A private habit you keep promising to abandon.
And then comes the question.
How do I get back to God?
That question is where our journey begins.
Because the Bible doesn't treat sin as a minor mistake that disappears when we feel better about ourselves.
Sin is serious.
The Hebrew word חָטָא (chata) commonly carries the meaning of sinning or missing the mark. In the Greek New Testament, ἁμαρτία (hamartia) is the ordinary word for sin.
But biblical sin is more than simply failing to achieve our personal potential.
It is rebellion against the holy God who created us. It includes what we do, what we desire, what we neglect, and the ways we refuse His rightful authority.
Romans 3:23 declares:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (KJV)
All.
The pastor.
The priest.
The church volunteer.
The person reading Scripture every morning.
The person who hasn't entered a church in twenty years.
And yes, the person writing these words.
None of us stands before God on the strength of our own goodness.
Which makes the next question incredibly important.
If every human being is a sinner, who has the authority to bring us back to God?
The answer begins with a word that once shaped Israel's entire worship.
כֹּהֵן — kohen.
Priest.
Under the old covenant, God appointed priests to serve in Israel's sacrificial worship. The high priest had a particularly solemn responsibility connected with the Day of Atonement.
Leviticus 16 describes the sacred rituals through which atonement was made for Israel.
The priest did not invent forgiveness.
He served within the covenantal system God had established.
And the sacrifices pointed beyond themselves.
Hebrews 10:4 declares:
"For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins." (KJV)
Those sacrifices could not accomplish the final, complete removal of sin that humanity desperately needed.
Something greater was coming.
Or rather...
Someone.
When Jesus entered the world, He did not arrive merely to improve religious behavior.
He came to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He lived without sin.
He willingly offered Himself.
He died for our sins.
He rose from the dead.
And the book of Hebrews identifies Him as our great High Priest.
The Greek word is ἀρχιερεύς — archiereus.
Hebrews 4:14–16 says:
"Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." (KJV)
Read that final sentence again.
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace."
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because we have earned an audience with heaven.
But because Jesus is our High Priest.
The Greek word translated "boldly" is παρρησία (parrēsia), conveying openness, confidence, or freedom of speech.
It does not mean approaching God arrogantly.
It means approaching Him with confidence grounded in Christ.
And the invitation is extraordinary.
The throne of the holy God is called a throne of grace.
Not because God's holiness has diminished.
But because Jesus has opened the way.

Hebrews 10:19–22 develops this truth further, describing believers as having confidence to enter the holy place through the blood of Jesus and calling them to draw near with sincere hearts and full assurance of faith.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We do not approach God by pretending our sins are small.
We approach Him because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
And this brings us to one of the clearest declarations in the entire New Testament.
First Timothy 2:5:
"For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." (KJV)
In Greek, the central phrase reads:
εἷς γὰρ θεός, εἷς καὶ μεσίτης θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἄνθρωπος Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς
Heis gar Theos, heis kai mesitēs Theou kai anthrōpōn, anthrōpos Christos Iēsous.
A faithful rendering is:
"For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus."
The crucial word is μεσίτης — mesitēs.
Mediator.
Someone who stands between parties to bring about reconciliation.
And Paul identifies one ultimate mediator between God and humanity.
Jesus Christ.
Not because pastors have no purpose.
Not because priests are automatically dishonest.
Not because the Church is unnecessary.
But because no human minister can replace the saving work of the crucified and risen Son of God.
Christ alone is the mediator whose sacrificial work reconciles sinners to the Father.
That truth is affirmed across historic Christian traditions, including Catholicism, Orthodoxy, and Protestantism.
But here is where the conversation becomes more complicated.
Because although Christians agree that Jesus is the one saving mediator, they disagree about how He has appointed His Church to minister forgiveness.
And if we want the truth, we must be willing to examine the passages that challenge our assumptions.
After His resurrection, Jesus appeared to His disciples.
John 20:21–23 records:
"Then said Jesus to them again, Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.
And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost:
Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained." (KJV)
Those words cannot simply be ignored.
Jesus truly gave His disciples a commission involving the forgiveness and retention of sins.
The Greek text of John 20:23 includes:
ἄν τινων ἀφῆτε τὰς ἁμαρτίας
An tinōn aphēte tas hamartias.
"If you forgive the sins of any..."
The verb ἀφῆτε (aphēte) comes from ἀφίημι (aphiēmi), which can mean to release, remit, or forgive.
The passage speaks of genuine authority entrusted by the risen Christ.
The disagreement concerns how that authority continues to operate in the Church.

Catholic teaching understands this commission as foundational to the sacrament of Penance or Reconciliation, through which bishops and priests exercise a ministry of absolution received through apostolic succession.
Eastern Orthodox Christians also practice sacramental confession to a priest, understanding forgiveness as God's gift and the priest as a minister and witness within the Church's healing ministry.

Many Protestant Christians understand John 20:23 primarily as authority to proclaim the Gospel, declare forgiveness to the repentant, and exercise church discipline according to Christ's Word. Some Protestant traditions also retain private confession and pastoral absolution.
These differences matter.
It would be unfair to claim that Catholics believe priests independently manufacture forgiveness.
Official Catholic teaching identifies God as the source of forgiveness and Christ as the one who reconciles sinners. The priest acts sacramentally in Christ's name, not as a competing savior.
It would also be unfair to claim that Protestants who confess directly to God necessarily reject the importance of the Church, pastoral care, or accountability.

The real theological question is whether Christ instituted individual priestly confession as an ordinarily necessary sacramental means of reconciliation for grave sins committed after baptism, or whether the believer may seek and receive God's forgiveness directly through Christ without such a requirement.
And to answer responsibly, we must examine more Scripture.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
The Greek verb translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen.
It comes from ὁμολογέω (homologeō), meaning to confess, acknowledge, or agree.
In this context, it refers to acknowledging our sins truthfully before God rather than denying or concealing them.
Notice the promise.
"He is faithful and just to forgive us."
God is the one who forgives.
And the verse does not explicitly require the presence of a priest.
That observation is important.
But we should also be careful.

The absence of an explicit priestly requirement in this verse does not, by itself, settle every question about the sacrament of reconciliation. Catholic and Orthodox interpreters read this passage alongside John 20 and the Church's sacramental life.
Nevertheless, 1 John 1:9 unmistakably teaches that forgiveness comes from God and that genuine confession involves truthfulness about our sin.
You cannot heal a wound you insist does not exist.
You cannot honestly repent of a sin you continually defend.
And you cannot build a life of spiritual integrity while maintaining a secret agreement with darkness.
Confession is not an attempt to inform an uninformed God.
He already knows.
It is the surrender of our excuses.
It is when we stop saying, "I had no choice," and begin saying, "Lord, I sinned."
It is when blame finally gives way to repentance.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years confusing feeling guilty with actually turning away from sin.
Those are not the same thing.
Guilt can make you cry.
Repentance changes the direction of your life.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia — means repentance, a change of mind or disposition that, in biblical usage, involves turning toward God and away from sin.
It is not merely regret over consequences.
It is a transformed response to God's truth.
And Scripture shows us what that looks like through another man who committed terrible sin.
King David.
A man described as one after God's own heart.
A man who worshiped, prayed, and wrote psalms.
Yet David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged circumstances that led to her husband Uriah's death.
His position did not excuse him.
His spiritual history did not protect him from accountability.
And his public reputation could not erase what he had done.
When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David finally spoke words that broke through his self-deception.
"I have sinned against the LORD." (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
Nathan replied:
"The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die." (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
Notice the beauty and seriousness of that moment.
David confessed his sin before a prophet who confronted him with God's Word.
But Nathan identified the LORD as the one who had put away David's sin.
And forgiveness did not mean that every earthly consequence disappeared.
David's story refuses to let us cheapen grace.
God forgives.
But sin can still wound families, destroy trust, and leave consequences that require humility, restitution, and long obedience.
Psalm 51 gives us a window into David's repentance.
"Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight." (Psalm 51:4, KJV)
David was not denying the terrible harm he had done to other people.
He was acknowledging that every sin is ultimately an offense against God.
Later he prayed:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create for me a clean heart, O God."
