“Lord, I have been selective with Your Word.”
“Lord, I have justified things You have called me to surrender.”
“Lord, I have mistaken emotional comfort for spiritual growth.”
“Lord, I need Your mercy.”
And if you are genuinely struggling, remember that repentance is not the same as instant perfection.
The Christian life involves ongoing growth, confession, dependence, and perseverance.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness when we confess them.
Do not let the reality of your struggle convince you that returning to Jesus is pointless.
Return to Him.
Again, with genuine repentance.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because Christ is merciful.
And because His mercy is powerful enough to transform lives.
Your story may encourage someone who believes their worst chapter must be their final chapter.
You do not have to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss. A sincere prayer or a few words of testimony can be enough.
Because behind every comment is a real person.
Someone carrying a burden.
Someone fighting temptation.
Someone searching for answers.
Someone who needs to know that the grace of Jesus Christ is not merely a theological idea.
It is living hope.
Not to prove that you are more spiritual than anyone else.
Not to attack a pastor or embarrass another believer.
But because someone in your circle may be confusing a comfortable message with a faithful one.
Someone may be drifting from Scripture without realizing it.
Someone may be wounded by harsh religion and need to discover that biblical truth and genuine compassion belong together.
Someone may have abandoned hope because they believe their failures have placed them beyond the mercy of God.
Invite your family, fellow believers, those who are questioning Christianity, and even those who have walked away from church to examine the claims of Christ for themselves.
Not because every sentence here deserves to be remembered, but because the Scriptures behind it deserve to be revisited.
Return to 2 Timothy 4.
Read the entire chapter.
Read 2 Timothy 3.
Read the Gospels.
Study how Jesus treated sinners, challenged hypocrisy, comforted the brokenhearted, and called people to follow Him.
Let God's Word—not the emotional force of any article—be the foundation of your convictions.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to be a place where people simply consume emotional Christian content and move on.
Our desire is to build a community where believers are nourished by Scripture, challenged toward spiritual maturity, encouraged in their struggles, and continually directed back to Jesus Christ.
Those free resources are part of our commitment to make biblical learning and spiritual encouragement more accessible.
And maintaining and expanding that work requires real time, resources, and support.
It is an opportunity to help sustain the work of creating and sharing Christ-centered resources, strengthening discipleship, and reaching more people with biblical truth.
But we also want to be biblically clear.
The Bible teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”

We also recognize that Christians understand and practice tithing differently, and that financial support for a digital ministry should not automatically be equated with a biblical tithe or replace responsibilities to one's local church, family, or those in genuine need.
Your generosity should flow from love for God, not pressure, guilt, or fear.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, personal encouragement, or meaningful gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to participate in a mission that seeks to point people toward Jesus Christ.
To help someone encounter Scripture.
To encourage someone who is close to giving up.
To provide resources for someone who wants to grow in faith but does not know where to begin.
To remind someone burdened by shame that repentance and forgiveness are possible through the cross.
And to keep proclaiming that our hope is not found in religious performance, human popularity, or messages designed to satisfy itching ears.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
You are still welcome here.
A person who cannot give financially is no less precious to Christ than someone who can.
The Gospel is not for sale.
We want to serve people with the truth of God's Word, while inviting those who are able to help us continue serving others.
Because the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be proclaimed faithfully.
Not edited to please an audience.
Not softened to protect a platform.
Not exaggerated to attract attention.
And not turned into a business transaction that promises God's blessings in exchange for money.
It must remain the Gospel.
The good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The good news that forgiveness is available through Him.
The good news that sinners can be reconciled to God.
The good news that repentance is not the end of hope, but the turning of a heart toward the Savior who alone can save.
And now, before you leave, remember how this entire conversation began.
Paul warned that people would no longer endure sound teaching.
They would seek teachers who satisfied their desires.
They would turn away from truth.
And they would embrace what their itching ears wanted to hear.
But you do not have to become that person.
You can choose to love the truth even when it corrects you.
You can choose to remain teachable.
You can choose to study Scripture rather than merely collecting favorite verses.
You can choose to listen carefully, test what you hear, and follow Jesus rather than personalities.
And when the Word of God exposes something you have been hiding, you can come into the light instead of running from it.
Because the Savior who calls you to repentance is the same Savior who stretched out His arms upon the cross.
The One who knows the worst truth about your sin is the One who gave His life to save sinners.
And the One who calls you to follow Him is the risen Lord who can sustain you by His grace.
So here is the question I hope you carry long after you close this article:
If Jesus told you the truth you least wanted to hear today, would you still follow Him tomorrow?
Do not answer too quickly.
Take that question into prayer.
Let it examine your loyalties.
Let it expose your excuses.
Let it remind you that genuine discipleship is not about finding a version of Jesus who agrees with everything you want.
It is about surrendering to the real Jesus, who is infinitely more worthy of your trust than your own desires.
Not as a performance for other people.
But as a simple expression of your desire to remain faithful to Christ.
Because one day, the applause will fade.
The trends will disappear.
The viral sermons will be forgotten.
The platforms will change.
But the Word of the Lord will endure forever.
And when everything else falls silent, what will matter is not how many voices told you what you wanted to hear.
It will be whether you listened to the One who spoke the truth that could save your soul.
The most loving voice in your life may be the one that refuses to bless the chains Jesus died to break.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD COULD HAVE DESTROYED THE TOWER OF BABEL IN ONE SECOND. SO WHY DID HE ATTACK THEIR WORDS INSTEAD?
paragraphs: GOD COULD HAVE DESTROYED THE TOWER OF BABEL IN ONE SECOND. SO WHY DID HE ATTACK THEIR WORDS INSTEAD?

The terrifying truth behind Genesis 11:1–9—and why God's decision to confuse humanity's language may reveal something about pride, mercy, judgment, and the desperate human desire to build a life without Him.
What if the most dangerous thing about the Tower of Babel was never its height—but the condition of the human heart that built it?
Imagine waking up tomorrow morning and discovering that the people you love can no longer understand a single word you say.
Your wife looks at you, frightened. You try to reassure her, but every sentence makes her more afraid.
Your children are crying. Your neighbors are shouting. The people you worked beside yesterday suddenly sound like strangers.
You know exactly what you want to say.
But nobody understands you anymore.
Now imagine that happening across an entire city.
Construction stops. Orders become meaningless. Cooperation collapses. Families and communities struggle to communicate.
And somewhere above the confusion stands an unfinished tower—a monument to humanity's ambition, suddenly powerless to unite the very people who built it.
The astonishing part?
God did not need to send fire from heaven.
He did not need to split the earth beneath their feet.
He did not need to crush their tower into dust.
He simply confused their language.
And the project fell apart.
Why?
Why would the Almighty God, who had already judged the ancient world through the Flood, choose such an unusual judgment?
Why attack communication instead of construction?
Why scatter the builders instead of destroying the building?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all:
Could the same spiritual disease that infected Babel still be hiding inside our churches, our ambitions, our families, and even our prayers?
Because the Tower of Babel is not merely an ancient story about why people speak different languages.
It is a warning about what happens when human beings become so impressed with what they can accomplish together that they forget the God who gave them life.
And buried inside that warning is a glimpse of mercy that many readers overlook.
Genesis 11 begins with a remarkable statement:
"And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech." — Genesis 11:1, KJV
Humanity shared a common language. Communication was easy. Cooperation was possible on an extraordinary scale.
They migrated, settled in the land of Shinar, and discovered a way to manufacture bricks and use bitumen for mortar.
It was technological progress.
It was human ingenuity.
It was civilization developing the ability to accomplish something impressive.
And Scripture does not condemn brickmaking.
There is nothing inherently sinful about architecture, engineering, innovation, cooperation, or building a city.
That matters.
Because if we misunderstand the sin of Babel, we may end up condemning the very gifts God has given humanity to cultivate and steward His creation.
The problem was not that human beings had become capable of building.
The problem was what they intended their building to accomplish.
Listen carefully to their words:

"And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth." — Genesis 11:4, KJV
There it is.
Not merely a tower.
A declaration of independence.
"Let us make us a name."
In Hebrew, the expression is:
וְנַעֲשֶׂה־לָּנוּ שֵׁם
Ve-na'aseh lanu shem.
Literally, "And let us make a name for ourselves."
The Hebrew word שֵׁם (shem) means "name," but in this context it carries the significance of reputation, recognition, and lasting renown.
They wanted to become somebody.
They wanted their achievements to establish their importance.
They wanted a civilization impressive enough to preserve their identity and prevent their scattering.
And suddenly, an ancient story begins sounding painfully modern.
Because how many of us are still trying to make a name for ourselves?
We work until our bodies are exhausted because we are terrified of being insignificant.
We measure our worth through money, recognition, followers, accomplishments, titles, and the approval of people who may forget us tomorrow.
We build careers that consume our families.
We build public images that conceal private wounds.
We build ministries that sometimes become more concerned with reputation than repentance.
We build carefully managed versions of ourselves, hoping nobody discovers the fear underneath.
And sometimes we even use the language of faith to disguise our hunger for recognition.
We say, "I just want to do something great for God."
But deep inside, another voice whispers:
I hope they notice me.
That is where Babel becomes personal.
Not because every ambition is sinful.
Not because success is evil.
But because a good gift becomes spiritually dangerous when it replaces the Giver.
A career can become a tower.
A bank account can become a tower.
A social media platform can become a tower.
Even a church building, a ministry, or a religious reputation can become a tower when the glory of Christ is displaced by the glory of human beings.
And the frightening thing about towers is that we can spend years building them without noticing what they are doing to our souls.
We call it progress.
We call it security.
We call it legacy.
But God sees the heart.
Now notice another phrase in Genesis 11:4.
"Lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth."
They were not simply pursuing recognition.
They were resisting dispersion.
Earlier in Genesis, God blessed humanity with the calling to be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth (Genesis 1:28; 9:1).
Babel's builders wanted to remain together in one concentrated center.
Their fear of scattering stood in tension with God's purpose for humanity to fill the earth.
There is a profound irony here.
They believed their unity would secure their future.
But their unity was being organized around a purpose that resisted God's design.
And unity, however impressive, is not automatically holy.
People can unite around compassion.
They can unite around justice.
They can unite around worship.
But they can also unite around exploitation, idolatry, oppression, and rebellion.
A thousand people agreeing on something does not make it righteous.
A million people celebrating something does not make it true.
Even an entire civilization can move together in the wrong direction.
And that is why the next verse should make us stop.
"And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded." — Genesis 11:5, KJV
Read that again.
The LORD came down.
The builders were constructing something intended to reach the heavens.
Yet the biblical narrator describes God as coming down to inspect it.
The irony is devastating.
Humanity believed its tower was magnificent.
But the God who created the heavens and the earth was not threatened by its height.
The Hebrew says:
וַיֵּרֶד יְהוָה
Vayyered YHWH.
"And the LORD came down."
This does not mean God lacked knowledge or needed to travel somewhere to discover what was happening.
Scripture consistently presents God as knowing all things (Psalm 139:1–12).
The language is a vivid narrative portrayal of divine examination and judgment.
The builders were reaching upward.
God was looking downward.
And in that contrast, the story quietly exposes the absurdity of human pride.
We can become so impressed with the things we have built that we forget how small they are before the One who made the universe.
The tower may have looked enormous from the ground.
But it was never a threat to God's throne.
And this brings us to the central mystery.
If God was not threatened by the tower, why intervene at all?
Genesis 11:6 records His assessment:

"And the LORD said, Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do: and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do." — Genesis 11:6, KJV
This is not God confessing that human beings might eventually become powerful enough to defeat Him.
The Creator cannot be overthrown by His creatures.
Rather, the passage highlights the extraordinary capacity of unified humanity to carry out its intentions.
The concern is not that human beings have become divine.
It is that their shared language and coordinated determination can enable them to pursue their chosen purposes without the restraint that division would introduce.
The Hebrew phrase לֹא־יִבָּצֵר מֵהֶם (lo-yibbatser mehem) communicates that what they plan will not be withheld or beyond their ability to accomplish.
In context, the emphasis falls on the dangerous potential of coordinated human intention—not on any weakness in God's sovereignty.
And here is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Sometimes the most dangerous thing God can allow a human being to experience is uninterrupted success in a destructive direction.
Because success can convince us that our motives are pure.
Achievement can make us believe we no longer need correction.
Applause can drown out conviction.
And the longer we succeed without examining our hearts, the easier it becomes to confuse God's patience with His approval.
Think about it.
Have you ever received something you desperately wanted, only to discover that it was slowly pulling you away from the Lord?
Have you ever fought to keep a relationship that was destroying your peace and compromising your obedience?
Have you ever begged God to open a door, only to realize later that walking through it would have taken you somewhere your soul was not prepared to go?
Have you ever watched a carefully constructed plan collapse and wondered why God did not stop the collapse?
Babel does not give us permission to declare that every disappointment is a divine intervention.
Scripture does not teach that every failed business, broken relationship, lost opportunity, or painful setback is God personally dismantling our pride.
But Babel does teach something essential:
God's judgment can sometimes take the form of interrupting what humanity is determined to accomplish.
And in the larger biblical story, divine judgment and divine mercy are not always as far apart as we imagine.
Now listen to God's decision.
"Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech." — Genesis 11:7, KJV
The Hebrew expression for confusing their language includes:
וְנָבְלָה שָׁם שְׂפָתָם
Ve-navlah sham sefatam.
"And let us confuse their language there."
The verb comes from בָּלַל (balal), meaning to mix or confuse.
The word שָׂפָה (safah) literally means "lip" and is used here for language or speech.
This is not an arbitrary punishment disconnected from their sin.
Their project depended upon coordinated communication.
God disrupted the very means by which they intended to preserve their self-directed unity.
They had said, "Let us build."
God said, "Let us go down."
They had said, "Let us make a name."
God acted so that their intended achievement would not define humanity's future.
They had said, "Lest we be scattered."
And the result?
"So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city." — Genesis 11:8, KJV
The outcome they feared became the outcome they experienced.
They wanted to avoid scattering.
They were scattered.
They wanted to preserve their unified project.
Their project stopped.
And notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say God destroyed the tower with lightning.
It does not say the tower collapsed in an earthquake.
It does not say the builders were all killed.
It does not even explicitly tell us what eventually happened to the unfinished structure.
The text focuses on the disruption of language, the scattering of the people, and the cessation of construction.
That distinction matters because we should never add dramatic details to Scripture and then present them as if God revealed them.
The biblical account is already powerful enough.
So why did God confuse their languages instead of destroying their tower?
Because the central problem was not a dangerous structure that needed demolition.
It was a united human project organized around self-exaltation and resistance to dispersion.
Destroying the building alone would not necessarily have addressed the shared intention behind it.
Confusing their language directly disrupted the cooperation that sustained the project and brought about the scattering they had tried to prevent.
That is what Genesis explicitly shows.
And there is another dimension worth considering.
God's intervention was a real judgment.
We should not soften that truth.
Human communication was disrupted. Human plans were frustrated. Human communities were scattered.
Yet the narrative does not describe the total destruction of those people.
The judgment restrained their project while leaving humanity alive to continue its history.
Within the wider biblical story, this makes it reasonable to recognize a merciful dimension to God's restraint.
Not because Genesis 11 explicitly says, "God confused them to spare their lives."
It does not.
But because the God who judges rebellion is also the God who continues His purposes through a sinful human race.
The story does not end with humanity's extinction.
And this becomes even more remarkable when we remember what happened earlier in Genesis.
After the Flood, God established His covenant with Noah and his descendants.
He promised that never again would all flesh be destroyed by the waters of a flood (Genesis 9:11).
That covenant did not mean God would never judge human sin again.
It meant His promise concerning another universal flood would stand.
Babel belongs to a world still living under the patience and faithfulness of God.
A world where human rebellion remains serious.
A world where judgment remains real.
And a world where God's redemptive purpose has not been abandoned.
But there is something even more astonishing waiting immediately after Babel.
Something many readers miss because they stop at Genesis 11:9.
The next movement of Genesis takes us through a genealogy toward a man named Abram.
And in Genesis 12, God makes a promise that changes everything.
"I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing." — Genesis 12:2, KJV
Did you catch it?
At Babel, humanity said:
"Let us make us a name."
To Abram, God said:
"I will... make thy name great."
At Babel, people attempted to secure greatness through their own collective ambition.
With Abram, greatness was presented as a gift within God's covenant purpose.
The contrast is breathtaking.
And the promise does not stop with Abram's personal reputation.
God says:
"And in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed." — Genesis 12:3, KJV
All families.
The same world whose peoples had been scattered now stands within the horizon of God's promised blessing.
Babel shows humanity attempting to establish its own greatness.
Abraham's calling shows God beginning to unfold a promise of blessing for the nations.
And that promise ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
Not merely to a better civilization.
Not merely to a more impressive human achievement.
Not merely to a new religious movement.
But to the Savior through whom the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations.
Galatians 3:8 connects God's promise to Abraham with the Gospel.
Galatians 3:14 declares that the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ.
And suddenly Babel is no longer an isolated story about ancient architecture.
It becomes part of the biblical account of humanity's rebellion and God's unfolding plan of redemption.
Now travel forward to the New Testament.
To Jerusalem.
To the day of Pentecost.
The disciples are gathered.
The Holy Spirit comes upon them.
And people from many nations hear the mighty works of God proclaimed in their own languages.
Acts 2:6 says:
"Every man heard them speak in his own language." — KJV
The Greek text uses the expression:
τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ
Tē idia dialektō.
"In his own language" or "in his own dialect."
Notice the beauty.
At Babel, confused language interrupted a project centered on human ambition.
At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit enabled people from different linguistic communities to hear the proclamation of God's mighty works.
At Babel, language became a barrier to their common undertaking.
At Pentecost, God enabled His message to cross language barriers.
But we must be precise.
Pentecost did not abolish the world's languages.
It did not make every nation speak one earthly language again.
Nor does Acts explicitly call Pentecost a complete reversal of Babel.
Rather, the two accounts create a powerful biblical contrast.
God did not need to erase human diversity to make His saving message understood.
He empowered witnesses to proclaim His works across that diversity.
And the center of that proclamation was not a tower.
It was Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Exalted.
Lord and Messiah.
The people of Babel wanted to establish a name for themselves.
The apostles proclaimed the name through which salvation is given.
Acts 4:12 declares:
"Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved." — KJV
Not the name of a civilization.
Not the name of a king.
Not the name of a religious institution.
Not the name of a preacher.
The name of Jesus Christ.
And that is where the story stops being merely fascinating and becomes deeply personal.
Because the real question is no longer simply why God confused the languages at Babel.
The question is:
Whose name are you living to make great?
There is a kind of exhaustion that comes from trying to prove you matter.
You wake up feeling behind.
You compare your life to people who appear more successful.
You wonder whether you have accomplished enough.
You fear being forgotten.
You chase the next achievement because the last one never satisfied you for very long.
And sometimes you bring that same desperation into your relationship with God.
You try to become impressive enough to deserve His love.
You promise to pray more.
You promise to stop sinning.
You promise to become someone He can finally be proud of.
Then you fail.
Again.
And the shame returns.
You begin to wonder whether God is tired of you.
Whether He has already given up.
Whether your failures have become too many.
But hear the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity had finally built something worthy of heaven. He came because sinners could never save themselves.
The builders of Babel wanted to reach upward and establish their own greatness.
But the Gospel announces something radically different.
The eternal Son of God came down.
Not as a confused or powerless visitor.
Not as a rival competing for human recognition.
But as the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He died.
He rose again.
And He calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Philippians 2:8–9 says:

"And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name." — KJV
Do you see the contrast?
At Babel, sinful humanity sought self-exaltation.
In Christ, the sinless Son humbled Himself in obedience to the Father.
At Babel, people attempted to secure their name through human accomplishment.
In Christ, God exalted the obedient Savior.
At Babel, humanity struggled to preserve its greatness.
At Calvary, Jesus willingly endured humiliation to redeem sinners.
And because of His resurrection, His name will not fade like the names carved into ancient ruins.
He is alive.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately about climbing high enough to impress God.
It is about receiving, through repentance and faith, the salvation accomplished by Jesus Christ.
You cannot build a tower tall enough to erase your guilt.
You cannot accumulate enough achievements to purchase forgiveness.
You cannot become famous enough to conquer death.
You cannot manufacture righteousness through human determination.
But Christ can forgive sinners.
Christ can reconcile us to God.
Christ can transform hearts.
Christ can give eternal life.
And perhaps someone reading this has been building a tower for years.
Not with bricks.
With secrets.
With pride.
With bitterness.
With carefully hidden compromises.
With the desperate need to appear strong.
You smile in public.
You struggle in private.
You know how to quote Scripture.
You know how to sound spiritually mature.
But when the room becomes quiet, you know there are places in your heart you have refused to surrender.
Maybe you have been protecting an addiction.
Maybe you have been nurturing resentment.
Maybe you have been chasing applause while neglecting prayer.
Maybe you have been building an image of holiness while resisting the very repentance that holiness requires.
And perhaps this article has reached you at a moment when the Lord is confronting something you would rather not examine.
Do not mistake conviction for hopelessness.
God's Word exposes sin so that we may turn from it and find mercy in Christ.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — KJV
That promise does not make sin harmless.
It reveals the faithfulness of the God who forgives through Jesus Christ.
You do not need to pretend your tower is standing when the foundation is already cracking.
You do not need to defend the pride that is slowly destroying your peace.
You do not need to continue hiding from the Savior who calls sinners into the light.
Repent.
Not because your tears can purchase forgiveness.
Not because your promises can earn salvation.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust, your obedience, and your surrendered life.
And if you are wondering whether grace can reach someone who has failed as often as you have, remember the thief beside Jesus on the cross.
He had no lifetime left to build a religious reputation.
No opportunity to establish an impressive record of good works.
No grand achievement to offer.
He turned to Jesus.
And Jesus promised him paradise (Luke 23:39–43).
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that God ignores sin.
But that the sinless Savior bore sin's penalty so that guilty people could be forgiven.
The cross does not celebrate our rebellion.
It reveals how seriously God takes it.
And the resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
Now consider where the biblical story is going.
Revelation 7:9 describes a multitude from every nation, kindred, people, and tongue standing before the throne and before the Lamb.
Every nation.
Every people.
Every tongue.
The nations are not absent from God's eternal purpose.
Their diversity is represented in worship before the Lamb.
The final hope of God's people is not a rebuilt Babel.
It is the redeemed worshiping Jesus Christ.
The Bible begins with humanity seeking to establish its own greatness.
It leads us through the promise to Abraham, the coming of Christ, the proclamation of the Gospel, and the gathering of people from the nations.
And it gives us a vision of a multitude worshiping the Lamb.
The answer to Babel's pride is not simply better human cooperation.
It is redemption in Jesus Christ.
A people brought near to God through His blood.
A people who no longer need to manufacture their worth through self-exaltation.
A people who can serve one another because their identity is rooted in Christ.
A people who can use their gifts, resources, talents, and voices for God's glory instead of their own.
And this is where the message must reach beyond our private emotions.
Because if we truly believe that Jesus Christ is the only Savior, we cannot be indifferent to whether others hear His Gospel.
Someone in your family may be silently losing hope.
Someone you work beside may have spent years believing that Christianity is only for people who have already cleaned up their lives.
Someone may be one honest conversation away from opening a Bible for the first time.
We cannot save them.
Only Christ saves.
But we can speak the truth.
We can pray.
We can encourage.
We can share Scripture.
We can point them to the Savior.
Not every person will read it.
Not every person will agree.
But you do not know whose heart may be searching for an answer.
Not to promote a personality.
Not to make a ministry famous.
But to help place the message of Jesus Christ before people who need to hear it.
And if you are the one who has been exhausted by the need to appear strong, you do not have to perform here.
You can be honest.
If you are struggling and would appreciate prayer, you can simply comment, "Pray for me."
You do not need to disclose private details to be welcomed into a conversation about faith.
Sometimes the first step toward honest fellowship is admitting that we still need the grace of God every day.

Not because a saved post has spiritual power, but because the next time pride, comparison, fear, or disappointment begins to dominate your thoughts, you may need to return to the Scriptures we have considered.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers, sincere seekers, people who have become spiritually complacent, and even those who do not yet believe.
They do not need to pretend to agree with everything before they can begin reading the Bible and considering the claims of Jesus Christ.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep pointing people back to Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and transformation through the Gospel.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another way to participate in this work.
These resources are intended to encourage biblical learning, spiritual maturity, and a life increasingly shaped by God's Word.
Making Christian resources accessible requires ongoing effort.
Preparing articles, organizing materials, developing resources, and reaching more readers takes time, work, and practical support.
It can be a voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in a ministry you believe is faithfully serving others.
Scripture teaches the importance of generosity in supporting Gospel ministry.
Paul wrote:
"Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." — 1 Corinthians 9:14, KJV
And in 2 Corinthians 9:7, he also taught:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — KJV
Both truths matter.
Supporting faithful Gospel work is a worthy expression of Christian stewardship.
But generosity must never be manipulated.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It is not a substitute for repentance, faith, worship, obedience, or responsibility toward your local church.
The Gospel is free.
God's grace cannot be purchased.

But if this ministry has helped you grow, encouraged you through Scripture, or equipped you to share Christ with others, consider whether supporting its continuation is one meaningful way you can steward the resources God has entrusted to you.
You are not buying God's favor.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus Christ is.
The resources are simply additional ways to encourage learning, remembrance, conversation, and the sharing of biblical truth.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share a biblical message matters.
Your commitment to live faithfully before the people around you matters.
Not because any of these things earn God's love, but because a life transformed by grace should increasingly reflect the Savior who gave Himself for us.
And before you leave, I want you to return to the image where this story began.
An unfinished tower.
A scattered people.
A dream of human greatness interrupted.
We do not know the names of the individual builders.
We do not know what became of every brick.
We do not know how long their abandoned construction remained standing.
But we know what God wanted us to remember.
They said, "Let us make us a name."
And their story became a lasting warning against self-exalting pride.
Then God called Abram.
He promised blessing to the nations.
And through the unfolding history of redemption came Jesus Christ.
The Savior who did not cling to earthly prestige.
The King who wore a crown of thorns.
The Lord who humbled Himself to the point of death.
The risen Christ whose name is above every name.
So here is the question I hope stays with you long after you close this article:
When your accomplishments are forgotten, when your possessions belong to someone else, when your titles no longer matter, and when every earthly monument to your existence has faded...
Will your life have been spent trying to make your own name great, or trusting and glorifying the name of Jesus?
There is still time to repent.
There is still time to surrender what pride has been protecting.
There is still time to stop treating earthly recognition as the measure of your worth.
There is still time to turn to Christ in faith.
And if you already belong to Him, there is still time to examine your motives, renew your obedience, love your neighbor, and use what He has entrusted to you for His glory.
Babel reminds us that God can interrupt humanity's proudest plans.
The cross reminds us that He has provided the only Savior sinners need.
And the empty tomb reminds us that the hope of those who trust in Christ does not end in ruins.
So build faithfully.
Work diligently.
Use your gifts.
Serve your family.
Love your neighbor.
Support sound Gospel ministry as you are able.
But never confuse the greatness of what you are building with the greatness of the One you are called to worship.
Because one day, every earthly tower will lose its significance.
And only what is truly rooted in Christ will have eternal value.
The greatest tragedy is not watching your tower fall—it is spending your whole life building a name while neglecting the Savior whose name alone can save you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MAN WHO WROTE GOD’S WARNING WHILE A KING TRIED TO SILENCE IT
paragraphs: THE MAN WHO WROTE GOD’S WARNING WHILE A KING TRIED TO SILENCE IT
His name was Baruch. He wasn't the prophet. He wasn't the king. But when God's Word was rejected, his trembling hands helped preserve a message that would outlive the throne.
What if the greatest thing God ever asks you to do is something the world will never applaud?
What if your name never appears on a stage?
What if nobody remembers the sacrifices you made, the tears you cried, the nights you stayed awake, or the battles you fought just to remain faithful?
What if you spend your life helping someone else fulfill the calling God placed upon them?
Would you still obey?
Before you answer, I want you to meet a man whose story is buried in one of the most heartbreaking confrontations between God's mercy and human rebellion.
His name was Baruch.
And his story begins with a scroll, a prophet under restriction, a nation approaching disaster, and a king who would eventually take a knife to the very words God had sent to save his people.
But here is what makes this story so unsettling.
The king had the power to destroy the scroll.
He did not have the power to destroy the truth.
And the man holding the pen would discover that faithfulness to God does not always protect you from suffering.
Sometimes, it leads you directly into it.
If you have ever served God while feeling invisible, exhausted, unappreciated, or afraid, stay with this story.
Because Baruch's life may reveal something about your own that you have never considered.
And before we reach the end, we will encounter a promise God gave this overlooked servant—a promise that may change the way you understand success, survival, and the cost of following Jesus.
It was the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, around 605 BC.
Jerusalem was living on borrowed time.
The people still had their religious institutions. The temple still stood. Religious activity continued.
But beneath the appearance of spiritual security, the nation was drifting toward judgment.
For years, Jeremiah had warned Judah to turn from evil, abandon false confidence, and return to the Lord.
His warnings were not popular.
Truth rarely feels comforting when it confronts the sins we have learned to excuse.
Then God gave Jeremiah an extraordinary command.
In Jeremiah 36:2–3, the Lord instructed him to take a scroll and write the words He had spoken concerning Israel, Judah, and the nations. The purpose was not merely to announce punishment.
God declared that perhaps the people of Judah would hear of the disaster He intended, turn from their evil ways, and receive His forgiveness.
Read that carefully.
God sent a warning because He was still calling people to repentance.
The message of judgment was also an expression of mercy.
The Hebrew of Jeremiah 36:3 contains a phrase worth remembering:
וְשָׁבוּ אִישׁ מִדַּרְכּוֹ הָרָעָה
Ve-shavu ish mi-darko ha-ra'ah.
Meaning, in context, “and each one may turn from his evil way.”
The verb shuv (שׁוּב) carries the sense of turning or returning. In prophetic passages such as this, it describes a moral and spiritual turning away from evil.
Repentance was not presented as a religious performance.
It meant changing direction.
And the verse continued with God's promise to forgive their iniquity and sin.
There it was.
Judgment was approaching, but mercy was still being offered.
God was not telling Judah that rebellion did not matter.
He was telling them that their rebellion did matter—and that they needed to turn before destruction came.
That is the context in which Baruch entered the story.
Jeremiah 36:4 records that Jeremiah called Baruch, the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll the words the Lord had spoken to Jeremiah, as Jeremiah dictated them.
His name in Hebrew was:
בָּרוּךְ בֶּן־נֵרִיָּה
Barukh ben-Neriyyah.
Baruch, son of Neriah.
The name Baruch means “blessed.”
But being blessed by God did not mean his life would be easy.
Baruch was a scribe—a man capable of recording written documents. In the ancient world, scribal work required literacy and training, skills not universally possessed.
He was also associated with Jeremiah's prophetic ministry.
Jeremiah received the prophetic message from the Lord.
Baruch wrote it down as Jeremiah dictated.
That distinction matters.
Baruch was not inventing prophecies, speaking on his own authority, or secretly rewriting Jeremiah's message.
He was serving as the prophet's scribe.
And sometimes the most sacred responsibility God entrusts to someone is not creating a message of their own, but faithfully preserving the message He has already given.
Imagine the scene.
Jeremiah speaks.
Baruch listens.
The writing instrument moves across the scroll.
Sentence after sentence.
Warning after warning.
The sins of the nation are exposed. The consequences of rebellion are announced. The call to repentance remains.
And Baruch keeps writing.
He cannot soften the message simply because people may dislike it.
He cannot remove the uncomfortable passages.
He cannot make the warning more fashionable.
He must be faithful to what he has been given.
There is a lesson here for every Christian living in an age when biblical truth is sometimes reshaped to gain acceptance.
We are not authorized to change God's Word to make obedience more convenient.
But neither are we authorized to use God's Word as an excuse for cruelty.
The same Scripture that exposes sin reveals the mercy of the God who calls sinners to return.
Truth and grace are not enemies.
They meet perfectly in Jesus Christ.
And Baruch's story helps us understand why the written Word matters.
Because the message was never supposed to end with the person who first heard it.
Jeremiah could not personally enter the house of the Lord at that time. Jeremiah 36:5 describes him as restricted, although the passage does not specify the precise nature of that restriction.
So he gave Baruch another assignment.
He was to take the scroll into the temple and read the words publicly.
Not quietly to a trusted friend.
Not privately to a sympathetic audience.
But openly, before people who desperately needed to hear the truth.
Jeremiah 36:6 instructed Baruch to read the words from the scroll in the Lord's house on a day of fasting.
Then Jeremiah explained the hope behind the assignment.
Perhaps the people would bring their plea before the Lord.
Perhaps they would turn from their evil ways.
The anger and wrath pronounced against them were great.
But the call to repentance remained.
Think about what Baruch was being asked to do.
He was not simply copying religious literature.
He was becoming the public voice of a message that challenged the spiritual condition of his nation.
He would be associated with a prophet whose warnings had provoked resistance.
And he was entering a situation where obedience could become dangerous.
Would you have gone?
Would I?
It is easy to say we would stand for biblical truth when we imagine ourselves surrounded by people who agree with us.
It becomes harder when telling the truth might cost us relationships, opportunities, comfort, or security.
Sometimes we are willing to follow Jesus as long as obedience does not disturb the life we have carefully built.
But the Gospel never promised a comfortable path.
Jesus said in Luke 9:23 that anyone who would come after Him must deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow Him.
That does not mean every difficulty we experience is persecution.
It does mean discipleship cannot be reduced to seeking personal convenience.
Baruch's obedience was not glamorous.
It was costly service.
And Jeremiah 36:8 gives us one of the simplest and most powerful descriptions of his character.
Baruch did everything Jeremiah commanded him concerning the reading of the Lord's words in the temple.
No dramatic speech about his own greatness.
No record of demanding recognition.
No insistence that his name receive equal prominence.
He obeyed.
And sometimes obedience is the most powerful testimony a person can give.
But the story did not end at verse eight.
And if we stop there, we miss the terrifying moment that reveals why Baruch's faithfulness mattered so much.
In the following events of Jeremiah 36, Baruch publicly read the scroll, and its contents eventually reached the royal court.
Officials heard the message and recognized its seriousness.
They questioned Baruch about how the words had been written.
He explained that Jeremiah had dictated them and he had written them with ink on the scroll.
The officials then told Baruch and Jeremiah to hide.
Why?
Because the message was moving toward the king.
And the king was not a man who welcomed correction.
Jehoiakim eventually heard the scroll read.
It was winter.
He was sitting in his winter house, with a fire burning before him.
And as portions of the scroll were read, the king cut them off with a scribe's knife and threw them into the fire.
Again.
And again.
Until the scroll was consumed.
Jeremiah 36:23 describes the destruction.
Imagine that moment.
The words of warning had reached the highest authority in the land.
The king had an opportunity to humble himself.
He could have listened.
He could have repented.
He could have acknowledged the seriousness of Judah's rebellion.
Instead, he destroyed the written message.
Jeremiah 36:24 adds a devastating detail.
Neither the king nor the servants who heard the words were afraid, nor did they tear their garments.
The scroll burned.
But the greater tragedy was not the destruction of parchment.
It was the hardness of the hearts listening.
A person can hear God's warning clearly and still refuse to surrender.
That is frightening.
Because spiritual danger does not always look like open hatred of God.
Sometimes it looks like hearing His Word repeatedly while refusing to let it change us.
We know what Scripture says about forgiveness, yet we continue nurturing bitterness.
We know what Jesus teaches about honesty, yet we keep protecting our secret compromises.
We know the call to repentance, yet we tell ourselves we will change someday.
We may never take a knife to a biblical manuscript.
But we can resist the authority of Scripture by refusing to obey what we understand.
The king destroyed the scroll because he did not want to submit to its message.
And the question reaches across the centuries.
What are we doing with the truth God has already placed before us?
Are we receiving it?
Or are we quietly cutting away the parts that confront us?
The story grows even more remarkable.
Jehoiakim commanded that Baruch and Jeremiah be seized.
But Jeremiah 36:26 records that the Lord hid them.
Scripture does not explain every detail of how God protected them.
It simply tells us that He did.
And then something happened that the king could not prevent.
God instructed Jeremiah to take another scroll and write again the words that had been on the first.
Jeremiah called Baruch.
Baruch wrote the words once more.
Jeremiah 36:32 tells us that many similar words were also added.
The first scroll was destroyed.
The prophetic message was not silenced.
The king's fire could consume the material on which the words were written.
It could not cancel the authority of the God who had spoken.
There is something deeply moving about Baruch returning to his work.
We are not told every emotion he experienced.
We cannot honestly claim to know whether his hands trembled, whether he wept, or whether he questioned what would happen next.
The biblical account does not describe those details.
But we know this.
He wrote again.
After the danger.
After the rejection.
After the king burned the scroll.
He wrote again.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear what that kind of faithfulness can teach us.
You may have tried to do what was right and watched everything fall apart.
You may have poured your heart into serving others and received little gratitude.
You may have spoken truth with love and still been rejected.
You may have prayed for someone who continued walking away from God.
You may be exhausted from trying to remain faithful when the results seem painfully small.
Baruch's story does not promise that every lost opportunity will return or that every earthly dream will be restored.
But it does remind us that the visible response to our obedience is not the final measure of its value.
Faithfulness belongs to us.
The outcome belongs to God.
And Baruch himself would need to learn that lesson in a deeply personal way.
Because there was another side to his story.
One that reveals he was not merely a courageous servant untouched by fear or disappointment.
He was human.
In Jeremiah 45, God addressed Baruch personally.
The chapter is dated to the same fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Baruch had written Jeremiah's words on a scroll.
And what we discover is startling.
Baruch was hurting.
Jeremiah 45:3 records his lament, including the words:
“Woe is me now!”
He spoke of sorrow, groaning, and finding no rest.
This is the man who faithfully wrote the prophetic message.
The man who served beside Jeremiah.
The man whose obedience placed him in the middle of a national spiritual crisis.
And he was weary.
Not every faithful servant feels strong.
Not every believer who speaks courageously in public feels courageous in private.
Some people carry the Word of God to others while struggling under burdens nobody sees.
They encourage their families while privately grieving.
They serve in ministry while fighting discouragement.
They remind others of God's promises while wondering how they themselves will make it through another difficult season.
If that describes you, Baruch's story is not permission to abandon obedience.
But it is evidence that Scripture does not hide the emotional struggles of God's servants.
God knew Baruch's distress.
And God spoke to him.
But His response was not merely the reassurance Baruch might have expected.
Jeremiah 45:5 records a piercing question:
“And seekest thou great things for thyself? seek them not.” (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
וְאַתָּה תְבַקֶּשׁ־לְךָ גְדֹלוֹת
Ve-attah tevaqqesh-lekha gedolot.
“And you, are you seeking great things for yourself?”
The Hebrew emphasizes the personal nature of the question.
God was confronting Baruch's pursuit of greatness for himself in a time when judgment was coming upon the land.
We are not told precisely what those great things were.
We should not invent ambitions the passage does not identify.
But the warning is clear.
Baruch needed to reconsider what he was seeking.
God was about to bring disaster upon the land, and Baruch was not to measure his future by the pursuit of personal greatness.
Instead, God promised that wherever Baruch went, He would give him his life as a prize of war.
It was a promise of preservation amid catastrophe.
Not a guarantee of wealth.
Not a promise of public recognition.
Not an assurance that suffering would disappear.
His life would be spared.
And that was a gift.
What a difficult but necessary lesson.
Sometimes we ask God to make our names great when He is calling us to make His name known.
Sometimes we want the platform more than the obedience.
The recognition more than the responsibility.
The blessing more than the One who blesses.
And sometimes God, in His mercy, confronts the ambitions that are quietly taking possession of our hearts.
Baruch was called blessed by name.
Yet the blessing God promised him was not the kind of greatness people normally celebrate.
It was life preserved through judgment.
That should challenge the way we define success.
Because in the kingdom of God, being known by the Lord matters more than being admired by the world.
And this is where Baruch's story begins to point us toward someone infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ.
Baruch was a faithful scribe who recorded a prophetic warning.
Jesus is the eternal Word who became flesh.
John 1:1 declares:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “Word” is:
λόγος — Logos.
And John 1:14 declares that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
Baruch wrote words entrusted to Jeremiah.
Jesus did not merely write or carry a message from God.
He is God the Son, who entered human history to reveal the Father and accomplish our redemption.
We must not confuse their roles.
Baruch was a servant.
Jesus is the Savior.
Baruch helped preserve a warning that called Judah to repentance.
Jesus came to accomplish the salvation to which the Scriptures ultimately bear witness.
And the contrast is breathtaking.
A king in Jeremiah's day rejected God's warning and burned the scroll.
Centuries later, the promised Messiah would also face rejection from human authorities.
But Jesus would not simply survive His enemies.
He would willingly go to the cross.
He would bear the sins of His people.
He would die.
And on the third day, He would rise again.
The resurrection was not merely a recovery from defeat.
It was the decisive victory of the crucified and risen Lord over sin and death.
And here is where the message becomes painfully personal.
The greatest danger in your life is not that someone might reject your achievements.
It is that you might reject the Savior who came to rescue you.
Because the Gospel does not tell us that we are basically good people who only need a little encouragement.
It tells us that we are sinners who need forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works, so no one may boast.
Do you see the beauty?
The answer to our guilt is not pretending we have never sinned.
The answer is not hiding our failures beneath religious appearances.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
His sacrifice.
His mercy.
His righteousness.
His resurrection.
And the invitation to repent and believe.
The Hebrew call to turn from evil in Jeremiah 36 finds a profound Gospel resonance in the preaching of Jesus.
Mark 1:15 records His proclamation:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
The Greek verb translated “repent” is:
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite.
It calls for repentance—a change of mind and heart that turns away from sin toward God.
It is not merely feeling sorry after being caught.
It is not making promises to God while deliberately planning to continue in rebellion.
True repentance involves a changed orientation toward sin and toward the Lord.
And even repentance is not a way to purchase forgiveness.
We come to Christ empty-handed, depending on His mercy.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin is insignificant.
But that the holy Son of God willingly gave Himself to redeem sinners who could never save themselves.
And grace does not leave those who receive it unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
This is why our message has always been:
Not because Jesus erases every consequence of our past.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored.
Not because Christians never struggle again.
But because the risen Christ forgives sinners, gives them new life, and brings them into a future defined by His redeeming mercy rather than by the final authority of their past failures.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to be the master of your future.
Your sin must be confessed, not defended.
Your shame can be brought into the light of Christ.
Your failures do not make you beyond the reach of His mercy.
And your life, however ordinary it may appear, can become an instrument of faithfulness in His hands.
Baruch did not need a throne to matter.
He needed to obey the Lord.
And perhaps that is the word your heart has been avoiding.
You keep waiting for a greater opportunity before becoming faithful with the one already in front of you.
You keep comparing your assignment with someone else's calling.
You keep wondering whether your service matters because nobody seems to notice.
But the kingdom of God is not built only through the people whose names are remembered.
It is also served by those who pray when nobody is watching.
Those who teach children the Scriptures.
Those who care for aging parents.
Those who refuse dishonest gain.
Those who forgive when bitterness would be easier.
Those who share the Gospel with one frightened soul.
Those who give generously without demanding recognition.
Those who quietly keep showing up.
And those who, like Baruch, continue doing what God has entrusted to them even when the world seems determined not to listen.
Maybe your assignment is not to stand before thousands.
Maybe it is to speak truth gently to one person who is drifting away from Jesus.
Maybe it is to return to prayer after months of spiritual dryness.
Maybe it is to confess a hidden sin.
Maybe it is to reconcile with someone you have wounded.
Maybe it is to stop seeking admiration and begin seeking faithfulness.
Whatever the Lord is calling you to do, do not despise obedience simply because it looks small.
The God who saw Baruch sees His servants today.
And He does not need the world's applause to know whether we have been faithful.
There is another reason this story matters in our generation.
We live in a world overflowing with messages.
Millions of words are written, posted, shared, and forgotten.
People are surrounded by information while often starving for wisdom.
A person can spend hours consuming content and still go to sleep spiritually empty.
We can know the latest controversy, recognize every celebrity, and remember every argument on social media while struggling to recall the words of Jesus.
But the Word of God is not disposable content.
It is not merely another opinion competing for attention.
Second Timothy 3:16–17 teaches that Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, equipping God's servant for good works.
And Hebrews 4:12 describes the Word of God as living and active.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture religious excitement.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to build a personality around human applause.
But to help place Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, discipleship resources, and the message of Jesus Christ before people who desperately need the truth.
Some are believers growing weary.
Some are Christians who have become spiritually distracted.
Some are struggling with secret sin.
Some have been wounded by others and are trying to understand the difference between human failure and the faithfulness of God.
Some have never truly understood the Gospel.
And some may be one honest conversation away from opening the Bible again.
This is why sharing a Christ-centered message can matter.
You do not know what someone is carrying behind the photograph they posted today.
You do not know which friend is questioning whether God could forgive them.
You do not know which family member is silently wrestling with shame.
You do not know who needs to be reminded that repentance is still possible and that Christ's mercy is greater than their ability to repair themselves.
Not to impress anyone with your spirituality.
Not to prove you are a better Christian.
But because truth worth receiving is often worth passing along.
Send this to someone who has grown tired of doing good.
And if Baruch's struggle exposed something in your own heart, I want to invite you to do something more personal.
You do not need to reveal private details publicly.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to let fellow believers know that someone needs prayer.
Someone else may need the encouragement your story can provide.
Not because every sentence is something you must remember.
But because the biblical passages behind this story are worth returning to when faithfulness feels difficult.
Read Jeremiah 36 for yourself.
Then read Jeremiah 45.
Read them slowly.
Notice the mercy in God's warning.
Notice the courage required of His servants.
Notice the danger of rejecting correction.
And notice how God addressed the hidden struggles of a man whose work helped preserve His message.
Let Scripture speak more loudly than the article that introduced you to it.
And if you have been blessed by this ministry, there is another way you can participate in helping its work continue.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical encouragement and discipleship resources accessible to people who need them.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and become better equipped to follow Christ.
Maintaining, developing, and expanding ministry resources takes time, effort, and practical support.
It can be a voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in a work you believe is worth sustaining.
But I want to be especially clear about something important.
Christians should give thoughtfully, freely, and responsibly, including honoring their commitments to their local churches and those in genuine need.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not a payment for God's favor.
Not a purchase of spiritual blessing.
Not a requirement for becoming a faithful Christian.
And certainly not a substitute for repentance, faith, prayer, Scripture, fellowship, or the life of the local church.
The Gospel is free because Jesus paid the price we could never pay.
Our financial support does not make us more worthy of His love.
We give because we have received grace, not because we are trying to buy it.
And whether or not you are able to contribute financially, you can still make a meaningful difference.
Invite someone to read Jeremiah 36.
Pray that the message of Jesus Christ would reach people whose hearts are ready to hear it.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth in God's kingdom.
The invitation to receive the Gospel is not behind a payment wall.
The invitation to help sustain this ministry is simply an opportunity for those who are willing and able.
And perhaps that is a fitting lesson from Baruch.
Not everyone is called to the same assignment.
Not everyone has the same resources.
Not everyone serves in the same way.
But every believer can seek to honor Christ with what has been entrusted to them.
A voice.
A prayer.
A gift.
A word of encouragement.
A quiet act of obedience.
A willingness to share truth.
A life surrendered to Jesus.
Now, before you leave this story, I want to bring you back to that winter room in Jerusalem.
A king sits beside a fire.
A scroll is read.
The warning of God reaches his ears.
He takes a knife.
He cuts.
He burns.
And for a moment, it might appear that the king has won.
The message is reduced to ashes.
The servants of God are threatened.
The voice of warning seems silenced.
But somewhere beyond the reach of that royal fire, the Lord's purpose continues.
Another scroll will be written.
Another opportunity to preserve the prophetic words will be given.
And Baruch, the overlooked scribe, will take up his work again.
The king's name remains in Scripture as a warning.
Baruch's name remains as the record of a servant who faithfully wrote what he was given.
Yet even Baruch's faithfulness is not the center of the Christian story.
Jesus is.
Because our hope is not that we can become strong enough to save ourselves through obedience.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ has done what we could never do.
He lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
So perhaps the most important question is not whether you will ever be remembered like Baruch.
Perhaps it is whether you have surrendered your life to the Savior to whom all Scripture ultimately directs us.
Have you been resisting God's correction?
Have you been hiding behind religious activity while avoiding repentance?
Have you been seeking great things for yourself while neglecting the One who gave Himself for you?
Have you allowed disappointment to convince you that quiet faithfulness is worthless?
Then hear the invitation of Christ.
Come to Him.
Not with a performance.
Not with a carefully edited version of your past.
Not with the illusion that you can earn your way into His favor.
Come confessing your need for mercy.
Come trusting His finished work.
Come ready to follow Him.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive confessed sins and cleanse from unrighteousness.
And John 6:37 records Jesus' promise that the one who comes to Him He will never cast out.
There is room for the repentant sinner at the feet of Jesus.
There is forgiveness for those who turn to Him in faith.
There is grace for the weary servant.
And there is a calling for the believer who has forgotten that obedience matters even when nobody applauds.
Baruch's pen reminds us that one faithful act can become part of a story far greater than the servant can see.
But Christ's cross reminds us of something greater still.
Our salvation rests not in the greatness of our service, but in the greatness of our Savior.
So do not merely admire Baruch.
Learn from him.
Do not merely fear Jehoiakim's hard heart.
Examine your own.
Do not merely celebrate that God's message survived the fire.
Receive the truth it proclaims.
And above everything else, look to Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy is not being forgotten by the world.
It is hearing the call of Christ and refusing the grace He offers.
Surrender to Jesus.
Trust His grace.
Follow His Word.
And remember this:
The world may never remember the hands that served in secret, but the Savior who bore the scars of your redemption will never overlook a life surrendered to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS COMMUNION REALLY THE BODY AND BLOOD OF JESUS—OR HAVE WE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT HAPPENS AT THE LORD’S TABLE?
paragraphs: IS COMMUNION REALLY THE BODY AND BLOOD OF JESUS—OR HAVE WE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT HAPPENS AT THE LORD’S TABLE?
Symbolic, spiritual, or literally Christ Himself? The shocking words of Jesus, the warning that made the Corinthian church tremble, and the sacred truth we cannot afford to treat casually.
There is something deeply unsettling about the night Jesus broke the bread.
He knew who would betray Him.
He knew who would deny Him.
He knew His disciples would scatter when the darkness came.
And He knew that before another day had passed, His body would be wounded, His blood would be shed, and the very people He came to save would watch Him die.
Yet in those final hours, Jesus did something extraordinary.
He took bread.
He gave thanks.
He broke it.
And then He spoke words that Christians have been wrestling with for nearly two thousand years.
“This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.” — Luke 22:19 (KJV)
Then He took the cup.
“This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.” — Luke 22:20 (KJV)
Not merely, “Think about Me.”
Not simply, “Remember that I was a good teacher.”
He spoke of His body. His blood. His sacrifice.
And what He commanded that night became one of Christianity's most sacred practices.
But here is the question that still divides sincere, Bible-believing Christians:
When we receive Communion, are we simply eating bread and drinking wine as symbols? Are we encountering Christ spiritually? Or do the bread and wine truly become His body and blood?
And perhaps an even more uncomfortable question follows.
What if we have spent so much time arguing about what is happening to the bread that we have forgotten what Jesus intended to happen in our hearts?
Before you answer, stay with me.
Because the Scriptures contain a warning about Communion that should make every Christian examine the way they approach the Lord's Table.
And they also contain a promise of grace that no struggling sinner should overlook.
Imagine yourself in that upper room.
The air is heavy. The disciples do not fully understand what is coming. The Teacher they have followed, loved, and trusted is speaking about betrayal, suffering, and departure.
Then Jesus takes ordinary bread and gives it extraordinary significance.
The Greek text of Luke 22:19 records His words:
Τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ σῶμά μου τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον.
Touto estin to sōma mou to hyper hymōn didomenon.
“This is my body, which is given for you.”
Notice the phrase ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν (hyper hymōn).
It means “for you” or “on your behalf.”
Those two words carry the weight of the Gospel.
Jesus was not merely announcing that suffering was approaching.
He was identifying His coming death as a sacrifice given on behalf of others.
For the disciples who would fail Him.
For Peter, who would deny knowing Him.
For the fearful followers who would abandon Him.
And for sinners like us, who desperately need the mercy of God.
This is where Communion begins.
Not with a debate about religious terminology.
Not with a contest over which Christian tradition has the most convincing explanation.
It begins with Jesus Christ giving Himself for sinners.
But we must not pretend that the theological question is unimportant.
It matters because Jesus' words matter.
And faithful Christians have reached different conclusions precisely because they take those words seriously.
Some understand Communion primarily as a memorial ordinance.
Others believe Christ is truly present and received spiritually by faith.
Still others confess that the consecrated bread and wine are truly His body and blood, although they explain that mystery in different ways.
These are not trivial differences.
They concern the meaning of Christ's words, the nature of His presence, and the way His people participate in the sacred meal.
So what does Scripture actually say?
We must begin by allowing each passage to speak in its own context.
In Luke 22:19, Jesus commands:
“This do in remembrance of me.”
The Greek word translated “remembrance” is ἀνάμνησις (anamnēsis).
It refers to remembrance or recollection.
But we should not automatically reduce biblical remembrance to a passing mental thought.
Jesus established this meal in the context of Passover, when Israel remembered God's mighty deliverance from slavery in Egypt.
In Exodus 12, the Passover meal was closely connected to God's saving action and His covenant relationship with His people.
The Hebrew word זִכָּרוֹן (zikkārôn) means “memorial” or “remembrance.”
The connection is significant, although the Hebrew and Greek words do not by themselves settle every question about the nature of Christ's presence in Communion.
Biblical remembrance can involve much more than recalling historical information.
It can involve worship, thanksgiving, covenant identity, and the proclamation of God's saving works.
And now Jesus stands before His disciples as the fulfillment toward which the Passover story points.
The lambs of Israel's ancient deliverance anticipated a greater redemption.
Paul later writes:
At the Lord's Table, believers remember not merely that a man died, but that the Son of God willingly gave Himself for their salvation.
Yet does remembering Christ mean that the bread and cup are only symbols?
That conclusion cannot be established from the word anamnēsis alone.
A memorial can be profoundly meaningful without requiring a change in the substance of the elements.
But remembrance also does not automatically exclude a real participation in Christ.
The word itself does not resolve the entire debate.
And this is where we need to be careful.
Because the moment we make one Greek word carry more theological weight than it can bear, we risk confusing our interpretation with the authority of Scripture itself.
Now consider something even more startling.
Long before the Last Supper, Jesus spoke words that caused some of His listeners to recoil.
In John 6:53, He declared:
“Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.” (KJV)
Imagine hearing those words as a first-century Jewish listener.
The Law of Moses strictly prohibited consuming blood.
Leviticus 17:11 explained that the life of the flesh is in the blood and connected blood with atonement.
The Hebrew word דָּם (dam) means “blood.”
Against that biblical background, Jesus' language would have sounded astonishing.
Eat His flesh?
Drink His blood?
What could He possibly mean?
Jesus continued:
“Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.” — John 6:54 (KJV)
Then came another extraordinary statement:
“For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.” — John 6:55 (KJV)
The Greek reads:
ἡ γὰρ σάρξ μου ἀληθής ἐστιν βρῶσις, καὶ τὸ αἷμά μου ἀληθής ἐστιν πόσις.
Hē gar sarx mou alēthēs estin brōsis, kai to haima mou alēthēs estin posis.
The expression ἀληθής (alēthēs) means “true” or “genuine.”
Jesus was speaking about something of ultimate spiritual reality.
But we must ask what He meant by eating and drinking.
Was He speaking directly about the future Lord's Supper?
Was He using vivid language to describe believing in Him and receiving the saving benefits of His death?
Or does the passage illuminate both faith in Christ and sacramental participation in Him?
Christians disagree.
And the context deserves careful attention.
Earlier in the same chapter, Jesus said:
“He that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.” — John 6:35 (KJV)
Notice the parallel.
Coming to Jesus answers hunger.
Believing in Jesus answers thirst.
That is a major reason many Protestant interpreters understand eating His flesh and drinking His blood as powerful imagery for receiving Christ through faith.
John 6:47 also declares that the one who believes in Christ has everlasting life.
This interpretation takes seriously the chapter's repeated emphasis on faith.
But Christians who understand John 6 eucharistically point to the increasingly explicit language of flesh, blood, eating, drinking, and abiding in Christ.
They argue that these words reach beyond a purely mental act of remembrance and illuminate the mystery of Communion.
Both approaches must reckon with the whole passage.
And both must acknowledge something essential.
Jesus is not teaching that salvation comes through a physical act detached from faith in Him.
His entire discourse centers on Himself as the bread of life, the One sent from heaven, the One who gives life to the world.
Later, in John 6:63, He says:
“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing.” (KJV)
This does not mean that His incarnation or sacrificial flesh is worthless. That would contradict His earlier declaration that He gives His flesh for the life of the world.
Rather, His words warn us against understanding His teaching in merely fleshly, unaided human terms.
Life comes through the Spirit.
And the saving work of Christ must be received according to the truth He reveals.
John 6 does not explicitly narrate the institution of the Lord's Supper.
That historical and literary fact matters.
The discourse certainly has profound connections with the themes Christians celebrate in Communion, but whether it directly teaches a particular doctrine of Eucharistic presence remains debated.
We should not erase that distinction merely because one interpretation feels emotionally compelling.
Scripture deserves more than our strongest feelings.
It deserves our careful attention.
But now we come to a passage that should disturb anyone who thinks Communion can be treated as an empty religious routine.
The apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians about the Lord's Supper.
And he was not congratulating them.
Their gatherings had become marked by division, selfishness, humiliation, and disregard for poorer believers.
Some were eating while others went hungry.
Some were drinking excessively while others were left with nothing.
They had turned a meal meant to proclaim Christ's self-giving love into an occasion for displaying their own lack of love.
And Paul confronted them.
He reminded them of the words Jesus spoke on the night He was betrayed.
Then he declared:
“For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.” — 1 Corinthians 11:26 (KJV)
Do not miss that.
Communion looks backward to the cross.
It looks inward toward the condition of our hearts.
It looks outward toward the unity of Christ's people.
And it looks forward to His return.
Every time the church faithfully observes the Lord's Supper, it announces that Jesus died, that His sacrifice matters, and that the crucified Savior is coming again.
But Paul does not stop there.
He writes:
Then:
“But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.” — 1 Corinthians 11:28 (KJV)
And finally:
“For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.” — 1 Corinthians 11:29 (KJV)
The KJV's word “damnation” here translates κρίμα (krima), which means “judgment.”
In this context, Paul is warning about divine judgment or discipline, not declaring that every unworthy participant is automatically condemned eternally.
That distinction is crucial.
Because someone reading this right now may be carrying a terrible memory.
Perhaps you took Communion while secretly struggling with sin.
Perhaps you received the bread and cup while your marriage was collapsing.
Perhaps you were sitting in church with a smile on your face while bitterness was eating away at your heart.
Perhaps you knew you had been living a double life.
And now you are wondering whether God rejected you at the table.
Listen carefully.
Paul does not say that only sinless people may receive Communion.
If sinless perfection were required, no ordinary believer could approach.
