So the next time someone asks you, “If God opposes polygamy, why did Exodus 21:10 tell men how to treat multiple wives?” don't run from the question.
Open the Bible.
Read the context.
Tell the truth about the ancient world.
Explain the distinction between regulation and divine ideal.
Listen to Jesus.
And remember the woman whose rights the passage was written to protect.
Because sometimes the most revealing thing about a difficult Bible passage is not what it permits powerful people to do.
It is what it refuses to let them take away from someone who has almost nothing.
The world may remember the man who took another wife. But God made sure His Law also spoke about the woman who must not be forgotten.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID THE KINGDOM BELONGS TO PEOPLE LIKE CHILDREN. BUT WHAT IF WE'VE MISUNDERSTOOD HIM OUR ENTIRE LIVES?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID THE KINGDOM BELONGS TO PEOPLE LIKE CHILDREN. BUT WHAT IF WE'VE MISUNDERSTOOD HIM OUR ENTIRE LIVES?

The shocking truth behind Mark 10:13–16: Why the people everyone considered insignificant became the very people Jesus held up as examples of how to enter God's Kingdom—and why this changes everything about grace, salvation, and the way we come to Christ.
There is something heartbreaking about watching a child apologize for something they never did.
Maybe you've seen it.

A little boy standing in a doorway, afraid to speak because the adults are angry. A little girl trying desperately to be good enough to earn a hug. A child learning, far too early, that love sometimes feels like something you have to deserve.
And then that child grows up.
He learns to hide his tears.
She learns to disguise her wounds.
They learn to smile when they're falling apart, say they're fine when they're not, and work themselves to exhaustion trying to prove they are worthy of being loved.
Eventually, they walk into church carrying the same fear.
What if God is disappointed in me?
What if I've sinned too many times?
What if I pray and He doesn't want to hear me?
What if I have to become someone better before Jesus will welcome me?
And somewhere in the middle of all that striving, they encounter one of the most beautiful—and most misunderstood—statements Jesus ever made.
“Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.” — Mark 10:14, ESV
Read that again.
Not because the words are difficult.
But because we have spent so much of our lives believing the exact opposite.

We assume God's Kingdom belongs to the spiritually impressive. The disciplined. The knowledgeable. The people whose prayers sound beautiful, whose families look perfect, whose pasts are respectable, and whose faith never seems to tremble.
But Jesus looked at children—people with little social standing, no impressive achievements, and no ability to claim special importance—and said something that must have startled everyone listening.
The Kingdom belongs to such as these.
And if we understand what He meant, we may never approach God the same way again.
The scene begins in Mark 10:13.
Parents and caregivers were bringing little children to Jesus so He might touch them. It was a simple act, overflowing with hope. They wanted their children to receive His blessing.
But the disciples rebuked them.
Imagine that moment.
A mother approaches with her child, perhaps nervous, perhaps excited, perhaps believing that one touch from Jesus would be worth the entire journey.
And suddenly someone tells her to stop.
Not now.
Don't bother the Teacher.
He has more important things to do.
The Bible does not record their exact words, but their actions were clear enough.
The disciples tried to turn the children away.
And then something extraordinary happened.
Jesus became indignant.
Mark 10:14 uses the Greek verb ἠγανάκτησεν (ēganaktēsen), from aganakteō, expressing strong displeasure or indignation.
This wasn't merely a gentle correction.
Jesus was deeply displeased by what His disciples were doing.
Think about that.
The same Jesus who patiently explained difficult truths, who endured misunderstanding, who welcomed broken sinners, was indignant when His own followers placed barriers between children and Himself.
Why?
Because they were treating as unimportant the very people He wanted to welcome.
They were standing at the doorway of grace, deciding who deserved access.
And Jesus would not allow it.
How many people have experienced something similar?
Maybe nobody physically stopped you from entering a church.
But someone made you feel unwelcome.
Someone looked at your past and decided you weren't spiritual enough.
Someone treated your questions as rebellion, your weakness as failure, or your brokenness as an inconvenience.
Maybe the person who discouraged you was someone who claimed to represent God.
And slowly, without realizing it, you began confusing people's rejection with God's rejection.
But listen carefully.
The disciples tried to keep the children away. Jesus commanded that they be allowed to come.
Never confuse the barriers people build with the heart of the Savior who calls you to Himself.
And Jesus didn't stop there.
He said:
“Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” — Mark 10:15, ESV
There it is.
The statement that turns our assumptions upside down.
Jesus did not merely say that children were welcome in His Kingdom.
He said that everyone who enters must receive it like a child.
But what does that actually mean?
Does it mean Christians should be childish?
Does it mean we should stop thinking critically?
Does it mean children are naturally sinless, spiritually perfect, or incapable of wrongdoing?
No.

Scripture does not teach that children are morally perfect. Nor does Jesus command His followers to abandon wisdom or discernment. In fact, 1 Corinthians 14:20 tells believers not to be children in their thinking, but to be mature.
Jesus was not praising immaturity.
He was revealing something about the posture of those who receive God's Kingdom.
The Greek text of Mark 10:15 reads:
ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὃς ἂν μὴ δέξηται τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ὡς παιδίον, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς αὐτήν.
A close English rendering is:
“Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a child certainly will not enter it.”
Pay attention to one word.
δέξηται (dexētai).
It comes from the Greek verb dechomai, meaning to receive, welcome, or accept.
Jesus speaks of receiving the Kingdom.
Not purchasing it.
Not achieving it.
Not bargaining for it.
Receiving it.
That distinction matters enormously.
A child in the ancient world generally possessed little independent power or social authority. Children were dependent upon others for protection, provision, and care.
Jesus used children to challenge the human obsession with status, self-importance, and deservingness.
He was not saying that every child is automatically humble in every situation.
He was teaching His hearers that God's reign must be welcomed rather than approached as something earned through human greatness.
And here is where the Gospel begins to confront our pride.
Because most of us would rather achieve something than receive something.
We like being able to say, I worked for this.
I deserved this.
I made myself worthy.
But grace does not give us that opportunity.
Grace requires us to acknowledge something our pride desperately resists.
We cannot save ourselves.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — KJV
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis), referring in this context to God's gracious favor.
And the word translated “gift” is δῶρον (dōron).
Paul's message is unmistakable: salvation is God's gift, not a human achievement that gives us grounds for boasting.
This does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean obedience is irrelevant.
It does not mean Jesus came to make sin comfortable.

It means salvation begins with God's mercy, not our merit. Genuine faith turns toward Christ and produces a transformed life, but that transformation is the fruit of grace—not the price we pay to purchase it.
And perhaps that is why Jesus' words are so difficult for us.
Because some of us have spent years trying to impress a Father who is calling us to trust Him.
We have turned prayer into a performance.
Repentance into an attempt to negotiate.
Church attendance into proof that we deserve acceptance.
Bible knowledge into a measure of superiority.
And obedience into an exhausting attempt to make God love us.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became spiritually impressive.
Not after we finally managed thirty consecutive days without failure.
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That does not minimize the seriousness of sin.
It reveals the astonishing greatness of divine mercy.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity had become worthy.
He went because humanity needed redemption.
And the love revealed at Calvary is not permission to remain in darkness.
It is the grace that calls us out of it.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying a sin nobody knows about.
Perhaps you have promised God a hundred times that you would change, only to find yourself crying over the same failure again.
Perhaps you are ashamed of what you watched, what you said, what you did, what you became, or the people you hurt.
You want to return to Jesus.
But shame keeps whispering:
You cannot come back like this.
And now you can hear the echo of the disciples.
Don't come closer.
You're not worthy.
You're a disappointment.
But the voice of Jesus in the Gospel is different.
“Let the children come to me; do not hinder them.”
Do not misunderstand this invitation.
Jesus does not welcome sinners by pretending sin is harmless.
He welcomes sinners as the Savior who calls them to repentance, forgiveness, and new life.
The hands that welcomed children would later be pierced for our sins.
The Savior who embraced the powerless would give His life for the ungodly.
And the One who calls us to come is also the One who calls us to follow.
That is grace.
Not God lowering His holiness to accommodate our rebellion.
But God, in Christ, providing the mercy and redemption we could never provide for ourselves.
There is another detail in this passage that many readers overlook.
Immediately after Jesus welcomes the children, Mark tells us about a wealthy man who approaches Jesus and asks what he must do to inherit eternal life.
The placement is striking.
First, children are welcomed—people without impressive status or accomplishments to offer.
Then comes a man with wealth, religious seriousness, and an apparently respectable moral record.
Yet when Jesus confronts him with the demand to surrender what possesses his heart, he walks away sorrowful.
Why?
Because he has great possessions.
The contrast is powerful.
The children are brought to Jesus with empty hands.
The wealthy man comes with many things, yet struggles to let go.
The issue is not that possessing money automatically excludes someone from God's Kingdom. Scripture does not teach that.
The issue is what happens when our possessions, achievements, or self-confidence become more precious to us than surrendering to Christ.
And Jesus' disciples are astonished by how difficult it is for the rich to enter the Kingdom.
Jesus answers:
“With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible.” — Mark 10:27, KJV
There is the heart of salvation.
What human effort cannot accomplish, God can.
What human righteousness cannot purchase, God's grace provides through Christ.
The Kingdom cannot be conquered by spiritual ambition.
It must be received through humble dependence upon the Lord.
And now we need to confront a painful possibility.
What if the greatest obstacle between you and a deeper relationship with Jesus is not merely your weakness, but your refusal to admit how much you need Him?
What if your carefully maintained religious image has become a hiding place?
What if you know how to sound Christian but have forgotten how to come before God with an honest heart?
You can memorize verses while refusing to forgive.
You can lead worship while secretly nurturing bitterness.
You can post Scripture every morning while privately living a double life.
You can know the language of repentance without ever surrendering the sin you keep defending.
And you can spend years appearing spiritually mature while remaining terrified of being truly known.
Jesus was not calling His disciples to perform innocence.
He was calling them away from self-importance and toward humble reception of God's reign.
In Matthew 18, a related teaching makes this even clearer.
The disciples ask Jesus:
“Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” — Matthew 18:1, KJV
Jesus calls a little child and places the child among them.
Then He says:
“Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 18:3, KJV
The Greek word translated “be converted” is στραφῆτε (straphēte), from strephō, meaning to turn.
In this context, Jesus is demanding a fundamental change of direction.
His disciples are thinking about greatness.
Jesus confronts them with the necessity of turning from that way of thinking.
Then He says:
“Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 18:4, KJV
There is no ambiguity about the humility Jesus is emphasizing in Matthew's account.
Kingdom greatness does not operate according to the world's hierarchy of prestige and self-promotion.
The way of Jesus turns human ambition upside down.
And that should trouble every one of us who has ever wanted to be admired for appearing holy.
Because sometimes we do not want to become more like Christ.
We want people to think we are more like Christ.
Those are not the same thing.
One seeks transformation.
The other seeks applause.
One kneels before the Savior.
The other quietly builds a throne for the self.
And the tragedy is that religious pride can become so polished that we stop recognizing it as pride.
We compare our prayers.
We compare our ministries.
We compare our knowledge.
We compare our sacrifices.
We look at the sins of other people and congratulate ourselves for not being like them.
Until one day, without realizing it, we begin resembling the Pharisee in Jesus' parable in Luke 18:9–14.
The Pharisee stands and speaks confidently of his religious practices.
The tax collector stands at a distance, unwilling even to lift his eyes toward heaven.
He cries:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13, KJV
And Jesus says the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee.
Not because sin was unimportant.
Not because religious devotion was inherently wrong.
But because the tax collector recognized his need for mercy, while the Pharisee trusted in his own righteousness.
Do you see how closely these passages belong together?
The children receive a welcome they cannot earn.
The tax collector pleads for mercy he cannot manufacture.
The wealthy man struggles to surrender what gives him security.
And the disciples must learn that Kingdom greatness looks nothing like worldly greatness.
Different scenes.
The same devastating confrontation with human pride.
We cannot come to Jesus clutching our self-righteousness and expecting to receive grace as though it were a reward for being superior.
We come as sinners in need of a Savior.
And there is something else we must understand.
Being like a child does not mean pretending that every childhood was safe.
For some readers, the word father brings comfort.
For others, it brings memories of abandonment, fear, violence, neglect, or promises that were never kept.
Some of you learned early that dependence could be dangerous.
You trusted someone who should have protected you.
And that trust was betrayed.
So when someone tells you to trust God like a child, your heart tightens.
Because the last time you trusted like that, somebody hurt you.
If that describes you, please hear this carefully.
Jesus was not commanding you to return to unsafe relationships, ignore abuse, abandon discernment, or surrender yourself to people who misuse spiritual authority.
Childlike faith is not blind obedience to human beings.
It is humble trust in the character of God revealed through Jesus Christ.
And the character of Christ is not revealed by those who exploit the vulnerable.
It is revealed by the Savior who became indignant when vulnerable children were pushed away.
The Savior who warned against causing little ones to stumble.
The Savior who laid down His life for His sheep.
The Savior who does not need manipulation to establish His authority.
Psalm 27:10 offers a deeply comforting truth:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.” — KJV
God's faithfulness is not limited by the failures of earthly parents.
And learning to trust Him may be a journey.
A trembling prayer can still be sincere.
A wounded person can come to Christ while still learning what safety means.
A believer can seek wise counsel, establish healthy boundaries, receive appropriate help, and grow in faith without pretending the past never happened.
You do not need to manufacture a cheerful childhood you never had.
You need the real Jesus.
The One Scripture reveals.
And He is worthy of your trust.
Perhaps the most tender moment in Mark 10 comes at the end.
After Jesus corrects the disciples, after He teaches about receiving the Kingdom, Mark records:
“And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them.” — Mark 10:16, KJV
Don't rush past that.
He took them in His arms.
The Greek expression includes ἐναγκαλισάμενος (enankalisamenos), a participle conveying the act of taking into one's arms or embracing.
Mark does not leave us with a Savior who merely tolerates children.
He shows us a Savior who embraces them.
Jesus did not simply allow them to remain nearby.
He welcomed them personally and blessed them.
Picture the scene.
The same children the disciples considered an interruption are now in the arms of the Messiah.
The people who tried to keep them away must stand and watch.
And the children who had no social greatness to present receive the attention of the King.
What a beautiful reversal.
Those who appeared insignificant were not insignificant to Jesus.
Those who could not claim importance were not overlooked.
And those who were treated as interruptions became the living illustration of His teaching.
This is not a promise that every believer will experience constant emotional comfort or an easy life.
It is a revelation of the gracious character of Christ.
The One who welcomes the lowly is not embarrassed by our need.
And that brings us to the deepest truth of this entire passage.
The Kingdom belongs to those who receive it like children because nobody enters God's Kingdom by being impressive enough to deserve it.
We enter through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
His sinless life.
His sacrificial death.
His victorious resurrection.
His gracious call to repent and believe the Gospel.
Mark 1:15 records Jesus proclaiming:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — KJV
Notice that childlike reception of the Kingdom and repentance are not competing messages.
They belong together.
To receive God's Kingdom is not to insist that God approve everything about us.
It is to bow before the King.
To acknowledge our sin.
To abandon the illusion that we can save ourselves.
To trust the crucified and risen Christ.
And to follow Him in the new life His grace makes possible.
The Greek word μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) in Mark 1:15 is a command to repent—to change one's mind and direction in response to God's message.
True repentance is more than feeling guilty.
It involves turning from sin toward God.
And faith is more than admiring Jesus from a distance.
It is trusting Him.
A childlike posture before God does not make discipleship shallow.
It makes discipleship possible.
Because the Christian life never outgrows dependence upon Christ.
We mature in understanding.
We grow in obedience.
We develop discernment.
We learn to endure suffering.
We become increasingly grounded in Scripture.
But we never graduate from needing grace.
Not after ten years of following Jesus.
Not after thirty.
Not after becoming a pastor, teacher, missionary, or ministry leader.
Not after memorizing entire books of the Bible.
The most mature Christian in the room is still a person whose hope rests entirely upon Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is what you needed to remember today.
You have been trying so hard to hold everything together.
Trying to be strong for your family.
Trying to overcome the same temptation.
Trying to forgive someone who never apologized.
Trying to rebuild after a failure.
Trying to believe that God has not abandoned you.
You have prayed with tears.
You have worshiped while exhausted.
You have opened your Bible while your mind was filled with fear.
And somewhere along the way, you started believing that your weakness made you unwelcome.
But your weakness is not a reason to run from the Savior.
It is a reason to recognize how desperately you need Him.
You may be too exhausted to impress anyone.
You may have no beautiful words left.
You may have nothing to offer except an honest confession:
Jesus, I need You.
And that is not a meaningless prayer.
It is the cry of a heart turning toward the only Savior who can redeem it.
Remember the father in Mark 9:24 who cried:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.” — KJV
What a startling confession.
Faith and struggle in the same sentence.
Belief and need.
Trust and trembling.
And he brought it all to Jesus.
Maybe your prayer today sounds similar.
Lord, I believe, but I'm struggling.
Lord, I want to obey, but I'm afraid.
Lord, I know Your Word is true, but my heart is hurting.
Lord, I want to surrender, but I keep reaching for control.
Bring that struggle into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn from what needs to be abandoned.
Seek reconciliation where it is possible and right.
Ask for help where you need help.
And trust the Savior whose grace is greater than your ability to rescue yourself.
Because the goal of childlike faith is not to remain spiritually helpless forever.
It is to remain humbly dependent upon God while growing into mature obedience.
And that is a beautiful difference.
The world tells you to become so powerful that you need nobody.
Jesus calls you to recognize your need for Him.
The world tells you to build an identity nobody can question.
Jesus calls you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him.
The world tells you to hide your failures until you can repair your reputation.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His blood.
The world tells you that greatness is measured by how many people serve you.
Jesus teaches that greatness in His Kingdom is expressed through humility and service.
And the world tells you that your story is defined by what happened to you, what you achieved, or how badly you failed.
But the Gospel declares that those who belong to Christ are made new.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
This is why we keep returning to the message:
Not because the past never happened.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance erases every earthly wound overnight.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, restore their relationship with God, transform their lives, and give them a future that sin and shame could never create.
He does not merely improve our public image.
He makes us new in Him.
And if you're reading this with tears in your eyes, perhaps this is the moment to stop pretending.
You don't have to announce your private struggles to the world.
But you can be honest before God.
You can pray:

Father, I have spent so much time trying to prove myself. I have hidden my weakness, defended my pride, and sometimes treated Your grace as though I could earn it. Forgive me. Thank You for sending Jesus Christ to save sinners like me. Teach me to repent sincerely, trust You humbly, and obey You faithfully. Heal what is wounded in me. Expose what needs to change. Give me the courage to surrender what I have been holding back. Help me grow in wisdom without losing my dependence upon You. I come not because I am worthy, but because Jesus is my Savior. In His name, amen.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not for appearances.
Not to measure how spiritual you are.
But because sometimes an honest response is the beginning of a conversation someone desperately needs.
When was the last time you approached God without trying to hide anything?
You never know who might recognize their own story in yours and find the courage to seek Jesus.
And if you're not ready to say anything publicly, that's okay too.
God hears prayers that never appear in a comment section.
Return to it when shame tells you that God only welcomes impressive people.
Read Mark 10:13–16 again.
Remember the children.
Remember the disciples.
Remember the indignation of Jesus.
And remember the arms that welcomed those whom others were trying to turn away.
A single share may place this Scripture before someone who would never think to search for it.
Because there are people who don't need another reminder that the world is cruel.
They need to hear what Jesus actually said.
They need to know that grace is real.
That repentance is possible.
That forgiveness is found in Christ.
That spiritual growth is not reserved for people with perfect histories.
And that the Kingdom of God is not an exclusive club for those who have learned how to look religious.
It is God's reign, received through humble faith in the Savior.
That is also why the work of Gospel Warrior matters to us.
We want to keep putting Scripture-centered messages, biblical teaching, and discipleship resources into the hands of people who need them.
These resources are meant to help people move beyond a moment of inspiration into a life of learning, prayer, repentance, spiritual discernment, and faithful obedience.
And if Gospel Warrior has encouraged you, strengthened your understanding of Scripture, or helped you draw closer to Jesus, we would be grateful for your partnership.
But we want to be biblically clear about something important.
Scripture teaches that Christians glorify God through faith, obedience, worship, love, service, generosity, and lives surrendered to Christ.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not pressured or reluctant.
That would contradict the very grace this article proclaims.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for reflection, or thoughtful gifts that encourage conversations about faith.
And while not everyone can contribute financially, everyone who wishes to participate can help in other ways.
Pray for this ministry.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Speak about Jesus with someone who has lost hope.
And when possible, help us continue making Gospel-centered resources accessible.

We would be honored to walk alongside you as we keep learning to follow Jesus—not as people who have already arrived, but as disciples who continually need His Word, His grace, and His transforming power.
Because that is what this entire passage has been teaching us.
We never become so mature that we no longer need the Father.
We never become so knowledgeable that we no longer need His wisdom.
We never become so strong that we no longer need His sustaining grace.
And we never become so accomplished that the cross becomes less necessary.
The little children in Mark 10 had no idea how profoundly their encounter with Jesus would speak to generations yet unborn.
They came to Him.
Others tried to stop them.
Jesus defended their welcome.
And then He held them in His arms.
One day, those children would grow older.
They would encounter suffering.
They would face temptation.
They would make choices.
They would need forgiveness, wisdom, and faith, just as we do.
The passage does not tell us what became of them.
But it tells us something enduring about Jesus.
He welcomed those who had nothing impressive to offer.
And He called everyone listening to receive God's Kingdom in the same humble way.
Maybe you have spent your entire life trying to become somebody the world would admire.
Maybe you have built your identity around achievement, approval, wealth, influence, ministry success, or appearing strong.
Maybe you're terrified that if people saw the real you, they would walk away.
But here is the question you cannot afford to ignore.

What if the thing you need most is not another achievement, another title, another compliment, or another opportunity to prove yourself—but the humility to come to Jesus as someone who desperately needs His grace?
Not with excuses for your sin.
Not with demands that God submit to your plans.
Not with a religious performance.
But with repentance.
With faith.
With open hands.
With a heart willing to be changed.
Because the Kingdom of God is not received by those who convince themselves they have no need of mercy.
It is received by those who turn to the King.
And that King is Jesus Christ.
The One who welcomed the children.
The One who confronted the proud.
The One who touched the untouchable.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who carried our sins to the cross.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who still calls people to follow Him.
So come to Him.
Not tomorrow, when you've finally managed to become the person you think you should be.
Not someday, when your past feels less shameful.
Not after you have found the perfect words.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
And let His grace begin changing the parts of your life you could never transform on your own.
You may have spent years trying to become worthy of His embrace, while the Gospel has been calling you to surrender to the Savior who opens His arms to sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES GOD REALLY LOVE EVERYONE THE SAME? THE BIBLE'S ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS IT.
paragraphs: DOES GOD REALLY LOVE EVERYONE THE SAME? THE BIBLE'S ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS IT.

John 3:16 says God loved the world. Romans 9 says He loved Jacob but not Esau. Ephesians 5 says Christ loved the Church and gave Himself for her. So does God love every person equally—or have we misunderstood what divine love actually means?
There is a question that can quietly torment a believer for years.
Not because they have stopped believing in God.
But because they are terrified of what the answer might reveal about Him.
“Does God love me the same way He loves everyone else?”
Maybe you have never dared to ask it out loud.

You have watched someone else receive the breakthrough you have begged God for. You have seen prayers answered in other people's lives while yours seemed to disappear into the ceiling. You have watched people who barely acknowledge God prosper while you struggle to remain faithful through another exhausting night.
And somewhere between the unanswered prayers and the Scriptures you cannot fully explain, a frightening thought enters your heart.
What if God loves them more than He loves me?
Then you open your Bible.
You read that God so loved the world that He gave His only Son.
And you feel relief.
Until you turn a few pages and encounter words that seem to tell a different story.
“Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.” (Romans 9:13, KJV)
Suddenly, the God you thought you understood seems harder to understand.
How can God love the world and yet speak of loving Jacob and hating Esau?
How can Jesus command us to love our enemies while Scripture describes God's particular love for His people?
And if Christ loved the Church and gave Himself for her, does that mean His love for the Church is different from His love for the world?
These are not small questions.
They reach into the character of God, the mystery of salvation, the meaning of grace, and the deepest fears of the human heart.
And the answer is more beautiful, more sobering, and more personally challenging than simply saying, “God loves everybody exactly the same.”
Because Scripture reveals something extraordinary.
God's love is never less than holy. But His love is not described in exactly the same relationship, purpose, or expression toward every person.
And understanding that distinction might change the way you see the cross forever.
Before we go any further, we need to begin where the Bible begins—with God's own revelation of His character, rather than with our assumptions about what love must mean.
John 3:16 declares:
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” (KJV)
We have heard this verse so often that familiarity can steal its wonder.
But listen carefully.
The verse does not say God loved the world because the world was lovable.
It does not say humanity deserved a Savior.
It does not say God looked down upon a civilization filled with righteousness and decided to reward its goodness.
The world John describes is a world that needs saving.
A world where people love darkness rather than light because their deeds are evil (John 3:19).
A world broken by rebellion, stained by sin, and unable to rescue itself.
And yet—
God loved.
The original Greek says:
Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον
Houtōs gar ēgapēsen ho Theos ton kosmon.
“For in this way God loved the world.”
The word οὕτως (houtōs) is important.
It does not merely communicate how intensely God loved. In context, it points especially to the manner in which His love was demonstrated.
God loved the world in this way: He gave His Son.
Love was not merely announced.
Love acted.
Love entered human history.
Love came into a world of betrayal, hypocrisy, violence, pride, lust, greed, and spiritual blindness.
And love did not arrive carrying a sword to destroy every sinner.
Love came in the person of Jesus Christ.
The sinless Son of God walked among people who would eventually demand His crucifixion.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He wept beside a grave.
He ate with people respectable society preferred to avoid.
And He willingly went to the cross.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because sin was so serious that forgiveness required something far greater than sentimental reassurance.
It required the sacrifice of the Lamb of God.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Notice those words.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we proved our worth.
Not after we finally became the kind of people who deserved to be loved.
While we were still sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
God did not wait for sinners to become beautiful before revealing the beauty of His mercy.
But John 3:16 also says something we must never remove.
“Whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.”
The promise of everlasting life is given to those who believe in Christ.
John continues by explaining that the one who believes is not condemned, while the one who refuses to believe remains under condemnation (John 3:18).
This means God's love for the world cannot honestly be interpreted as a promise that every human being will be saved regardless of faith or repentance.
The invitation is genuine.
The gift is glorious.
The Savior is sufficient.
But Scripture does not erase the distinction between those who receive Christ and those who reject Him.
And that brings us to the passage many Christians quietly wish were not in their Bibles.
Romans 9.
Paul writes about Rebecca's twin sons, Jacob and Esau.
Before they were born, before either had performed good or evil, God declared that the older would serve the younger.
Paul explains that this was so God's purpose according to election would stand, not because of works, but because of Him who calls.
Then comes the statement:
“As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.” (Romans 9:13, KJV)
Read that again.
It is uncomfortable.
It challenges our instincts.
And we must resist the temptation to make it say either less or more than Scripture intends.
The underlying Hebrew text comes from Malachi 1:2–3:
וָאֹהַב אֶת־יַעֲקֹב׃ וְאֶת־עֵשָׂו שָׂנֵאתִי
Va'ohav et-Ya'aqov, ve'et-Esav sane'ti.
“I have loved Jacob, but Esau I have hated.”

In Malachi, the Lord speaks of Jacob and Esau in connection with Israel and Edom, the nations descended from these brothers. The passage emphasizes God's covenant dealings and His judgment in history.

When Paul brings this language into Romans 9, he uses it within his argument about God's sovereign purpose, His calling, and the fact that His saving plan does not depend upon human ancestry or achievement.
The Hebrew verb שָׂנֵא (sane') can express hatred, rejection, or a contrasting preference depending on context.

Scripture sometimes uses strong love-and-hate language to describe comparative allegiance. Jesus, for example, uses such language in Luke 14:26 to demand that devotion to Him take precedence even over family relationships.
But we should not simply erase the force of Romans 9 by pretending that “hated” means nothing more than a mild preference.
Paul's argument is stronger than that.
He is confronting the assumption that God must distribute His covenant privileges and mercy according to human expectations.
And then Paul asks the question we might be afraid to ask.
“What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid.” (Romans 9:14, KJV)
Paul knows how disturbing this can sound.
He does not avoid the objection.
He answers it by pointing to God's words to Moses:
“I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.” (Romans 9:15, KJV)
The Greek word for mercy here comes from ἐλεέω (eleeō), meaning to show mercy or compassion.
And here is where something important becomes clear.
Mercy is not something God owes. Mercy is something God freely gives.
If God were obligated to grant mercy as a debt, it would no longer be mercy in the fullest sense.
Justice gives what is deserved.
Mercy withholds deserved judgment.
Grace gives undeserved favor.
Every human being stands in need of God's mercy because, as Romans 3:23 declares, all have sinned and fall short of His glory.
Nobody approaches the throne of God carrying a résumé impressive enough to demand salvation.
Not the preacher.
Not the worship leader.
Not the generous donor.
Not the person who has attended church since childhood.
Not the one whose public reputation appears spotless.
And certainly not the person who secretly believes that everyone else's sins are worse than their own.
We come as sinners.
And if any of us are saved, it is by grace.
But there is a theological distinction worth understanding.

Faithful Christians who affirm the authority of Scripture have differed over precisely how Romans 9 relates to individual election, corporate election, human response, and God's sovereign administration of salvation.
Reformed interpreters generally see this chapter as teaching God's sovereign election of individuals unto salvation, with His mercy ultimately grounded in His own gracious purpose.

Many Arminian and other non-Reformed interpreters emphasize the historical and corporate dimensions of Paul's argument, particularly God's freedom in choosing the people and means through which His covenant promises are fulfilled, while understanding salvation in relation to faith in Christ.
Both approaches must reckon seriously with Paul's language about divine mercy, hardening, and God's purposes.
And neither should be misrepresented as simply ignoring Scripture.
The central truth we cannot escape is this:
God is not unjust because His mercy is sovereign, and no sinner can claim salvation as something God owes them.
Romans 9 also speaks of Pharaoh, whose heart was hardened.
The biblical account includes both Pharaoh's own resistance and God's judicial hardening. Paul emphasizes God's sovereignty even over the opposition of rulers.
This is not an invitation to imagine God as cruel or arbitrary.
Nor does it authorize us to decide which particular people are beyond His mercy.
It is a warning against treating God as though He were answerable to human pride.
The Creator is not a defendant standing trial before His creation.
Yet the same apostle who wrote Romans 9 also expressed profound sorrow over his unbelieving fellow Israelites.
He did not respond to the mystery of election with cold indifference.
He grieved.
He prayed.
He proclaimed Christ.
In Romans 10:1, Paul says his heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is that they might be saved.
And in Romans 10:13, he declares:
“For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”
Do you see the balance?
God's sovereignty did not silence Paul's compassion.
Divine election did not extinguish his evangelistic urgency.
The mystery of mercy did not make him stop pleading with people to come to Christ.
If your understanding of God's sovereignty makes you less compassionate toward sinners, you have missed something essential about the heart of the apostle who taught it.
And if your understanding of God's love makes repentance unnecessary, you have also missed something essential about the Gospel.
God's love is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
His grace is not an endorsement of rebellion.
His mercy is not a denial of His holiness.
The God who welcomes sinners is the same God who calls them to repentance.
Now consider another passage.
Ephesians 5:25.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
The original Greek says:
Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς
Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian kai heauton paredōken hyper autēs.
“Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Notice how personal this language becomes.
John 3:16 speaks of God's love for the world.
Ephesians 5:25 speaks of Christ's love for the Church.
And Paul does not describe that love merely as a general kindness toward humanity.
He describes it through the imagery of a husband giving himself for his bride.
The Church is not simply a crowd that Jesus happens to tolerate.
She is His beloved people.
His body.
His bride.
Those united to Him by faith.
Ephesians continues by explaining that Christ gave Himself to sanctify and cleanse the Church, presenting her to Himself in splendor.
This is covenantal love.
Redeeming love.
Sanctifying love.
A love that does not merely observe suffering from a distance but enters into a binding relationship with those Christ has redeemed.
And there is something deeply personal here.
A man may genuinely love his neighbors, show compassion to strangers, and seek the good of his enemies.
But the covenant love he owes his wife has a particular character.
That does not make every other human being worthless.
It means love can be genuinely expressed in different relationships without becoming false or contradictory.
Similarly, Scripture describes God's love through different dimensions.
There is His benevolent goodness toward creation.
Jesus says the Father causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous (Matthew 5:45).
There is His compassionate disposition toward a rebellious world, seen in His call to repentance and His patience.
Ezekiel 33:11 records God's declaration that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but calls them to turn and live.
There is His covenant love, expressed in His faithfulness to His people.
And there is the particular, self-giving love of Christ for His Church.
These distinctions are not a mathematical formula for measuring how much affection God possesses for different individuals.
They are biblical descriptions of different ways God's love is revealed and experienced.

God's love is not divided into smaller portions as though He might run out. But Scripture does describe different relationships to His love, different purposes of His love, and different gifts flowing from His love.
This is why we should be careful with the question, “Does God love everyone equally?”
If by equally we mean that every person has dignity as God's image-bearer and must be treated with genuine love and compassion, Scripture gives us strong grounds to affirm that dignity.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that humanity was created in God's image.
James 3:9 warns against cursing people made in God's likeness.
Jesus commands us to love even our enemies.
No human being is disposable.
No sinner is beneath our compassion.
No person should be treated as though their suffering does not matter.
But if equally means that God relates to every person in precisely the same covenantal and saving way, Scripture does not speak that way.
The Bible distinguishes between the world and the Church, between unbelief and faith, between condemnation and justification, between rebellion and reconciliation.
John 1:12 says that those who receive Christ, believing in His name, are given the right to become children of God.
Romans 8 speaks of believers receiving the Spirit of adoption.
There is a real difference between being created by God and being reconciled to Him through Jesus Christ.
And that difference matters eternally.
But now I want to speak to the person who has been reading all of this with a wound that theology alone has not yet touched.
Perhaps you are thinking:
What if I am not among those God loves with saving love?
What if I want Him, but He does not want me?
What if I have sinned too much?
What if I am the person He will reject?
Listen carefully.
Do not use the hidden counsels of God as an excuse to ignore His revealed invitation.
Jesus said:
“All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV)
Did you hear that last part?
Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
Jesus does not instruct the trembling sinner to discover the secret decree of election before approaching Him.
He calls people to come.
He calls the weary.
He calls the burdened.
He calls sinners to repentance.
And He promises not to cast out the one who comes to Him.
You may not understand every mystery of Romans 9.
You may not be able to resolve centuries of theological disagreement.
You may have questions about providence, election, suffering, and why your life has unfolded as it has.
But you do not need to solve every mystery before trusting the Savior who openly calls you.
The secret things belong to God. The call to repent and believe has been revealed to you.
And there is a difference between reverently acknowledging mystery and using mystery to remain distant from Christ.
Think about the prodigal son.
He squandered his inheritance.
He disgraced his family.
He reached a place so desperate that he longed to eat the food given to pigs.
And when he finally came to his senses, he did not return home with a persuasive argument about why he deserved restoration.
He returned with a confession.
“Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee.” (Luke 15:18, KJV)
He expected to be treated as a hired servant.
But while he was still a great way off, his father saw him, had compassion, ran toward him, embraced him, and kissed him.
What a picture of mercy.
The son brought no achievement worthy of celebration.
He brought repentance.
And the father welcomed him.
Jesus told this parable in the context of religious people grumbling because He welcomed sinners.
The story reveals the joy of restoration, not a secret formula for identifying the elect.
And that matters.
Because some people are so consumed with asking whether God loves them that they refuse to respond to the love He has revealed in Christ.
They stand outside the Father's house arguing about whether the door could possibly be open.
While the Gospel calls them to come home.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe your scandal is not something the world knows about.
Maybe nobody knows what you did when the door was locked.
Nobody knows what you watched.
Nobody knows whom you betrayed.
Nobody knows the lie you have maintained for years.
Nobody knows how much bitterness you carry toward someone you claim to have forgiven.
Nobody knows how exhausted you are from appearing spiritually strong while privately wondering whether God has abandoned you.
But the Lord knows.
And the Gospel does not tell you to hide your sin behind religious performance.
It calls you into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because tears earn salvation.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior whose atoning work is the foundation of forgiveness.
There is no need to pretend that sin is harmless.
It cost the Son of God His life.
There is no need to pretend that repentance is optional.
Jesus Himself proclaimed it.
And there is no need to pretend that grace is too weak to reach a genuinely repentant sinner.
The cross declares otherwise.
This is where the question about God's love becomes more than a theological debate.
Because the most important question is not whether you can arrange every biblical passage into a perfectly comfortable explanation.
It is whether you have personally responded to Jesus Christ.
Have you trusted Him?
Have you repented of your sin?
Are you resting in His finished work, or are you still trying to convince God that you are worthy enough to be saved?
Are you following Christ, or merely admiring Christian language?
Are you surrendering to His Lordship, or asking Him to bless the life you refuse to surrender?
These questions matter because Jesus did not die merely to improve our emotional well-being.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to destroy the works of the devil.
He came to redeem a people who would belong to Him.
And He rose from the dead.
The empty tomb is not a sentimental metaphor.
It is the proclamation that the crucified Christ is alive.
That sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That forgiveness is not wishful thinking.
That redemption is real.
And that the sinner who comes to Christ does not have to remain defined by yesterday's disgrace.
Perhaps that is why the words of Romans 8 are so precious.
Paul asks:
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8:35, KJV)
Then he names tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, and sword.
And he concludes that neither death nor life, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Notice what Paul does not promise.
He does not promise that Christians will never suffer.
He does not promise that faithful people will always prosper.
He does not promise that the redeemed will never experience loneliness, persecution, grief, or disappointment.
He promises something deeper.
For those who are in Christ, suffering cannot sever the bond of God's saving love.
That means an unanswered prayer is not proof that God has stopped loving you.
A painful season is not proof that someone else is more precious to Him.
Your bank account is not a reliable measurement of His affection.
Your social status is not a spiritual scoreboard.
And another believer's visible blessings are not evidence that you have been forgotten.
The cross—not your circumstances—is the supreme demonstration of God's redeeming love.
And if you are in Christ, you belong to the One who gave Himself for His people.
So when you ask, “Does God love everyone in the same way?” remember the full biblical picture.
God genuinely shows goodness to all His creatures.
He commands love toward every neighbor, including enemies.
He reveals His love for the world through the giving of His Son.
He freely exercises mercy according to His righteous purposes.
He loves His Church with the particular, self-giving, covenantal love of the Bridegroom.
And He calls sinners everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
We must not flatten these truths until every distinction disappears.
But neither must we distort them until God appears reluctant to receive the repentant sinner.
The Bible gives us no permission to become arrogant about grace.
If you are saved, you have nothing to boast about except the Lord.
And it gives us no permission to become cruel toward those who do not yet believe.
The very people you are tempted to dismiss may be the people God is calling you to love, pray for, and reach with the Gospel.
Imagine standing before someone who has spent their entire life running from God.
They have ruined relationships.
They have betrayed trust.
They have made decisions they cannot undo.
And now, trembling, they ask you:
“Could Jesus really forgive someone like me?”
What would you say?
Would you begin by speculating about the hidden decree of election?
Would you tell them to determine whether they belong to the right theological category before they are allowed to seek mercy?
Or would you open the Scriptures and tell them about the crucified and risen Savior who calls sinners to repent and believe?
Would you tell them that Christ receives those who come to Him?
Would you tell them that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works?
Would you tell them that there is forgiveness in His name?
That is the Gospel we are entrusted to proclaim.
Not a Gospel that hides God's holiness.
Not a Gospel that makes light of sin.
Not a Gospel that promises universal salvation apart from Christ.
But a Gospel that announces the sufficient Savior and calls the world to Him.
And perhaps someone reading these words right now needs to stop running.
You have spent years believing that your worst moment permanently disqualified you from God's mercy.
You have allowed shame to preach louder than Scripture.
You have confused conviction with hopelessness.
You have mistaken the pain of your circumstances for a verdict on God's love.
But listen to what the cross announces.
Sin is serious.
Judgment is real.
Grace is costly.
Christ is sufficient.
And the invitation to come to Him is not a cruel illusion.
You do not have to make yourself worthy before you repent.
You must come to Christ as the sinner you are, trusting the Savior He is.
Not because you are strong.
But because He is mighty to save.
Not because your past is innocent.
But because His blood is sufficient to cleanse.
Not because your future will be painless.
But because His resurrection guarantees that death will not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
If these words have exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn that conviction into another performance for people to applaud.
Bring it to Jesus.
Perhaps your testimony of Christ's mercy will encourage someone who is one disappointment away from walking away from the faith.
Send this article privately to someone who needs hope.
Our desire is not simply to create content people admire for a moment.
It is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and live in obedience to Christ.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible to people who genuinely desire to grow deeper in Jesus Christ, including those who cannot afford to purchase books or paid resources.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding a ministry like this involves real work and real expenses.
And this is where I want to extend a personal invitation.

For those who already practice giving as an act of worship, supporting a trustworthy Gospel ministry can be one expression of generosity. Scripture encourages believers to support those who labor in teaching the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Timothy 5:17–18) and to give willingly, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And please understand this clearly.
God's favor cannot be purchased.
Salvation is not a membership benefit.
And glorifying Christ is never restricted to those who can afford a monthly payment.
If you are able and willing to help, however, your recurring support can become a meaningful part of sustaining and expanding this work.
Think of the person who cannot afford a devotional but finds one in our free library.
The young believer who is trying to understand the Bible.
The exhausted parent searching for spiritual encouragement after everyone else has gone to sleep.
The person who has never entered a church but encounters the message of the cross through an article shared by a friend.
We cannot promise that every resource will change a life.
Only God can bring spiritual life and transformation.
But we can faithfully plant, teach, share, and serve, trusting Him with the results.
These products are not the reason to give.
They are simply one way of thanking those who choose to walk alongside the ministry.
Read the Scriptures.
Use the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
Share Gospel-centered teaching when it can genuinely serve someone.
And remain rooted in a faithful local church where you can worship, grow, serve, and be accountable alongside other believers.
The Gospel was never meant to be locked behind a payment.
We offer this invitation because we believe the work of discipleship matters, and we are grateful for every person who freely helps make it possible.
But before you leave, return with me to the question that began everything.
Does God love every person in exactly the same way?
Scripture does not give us a simplistic answer that erases His holiness, sovereignty, covenant faithfulness, or saving purposes.

It reveals a God whose goodness reaches His creation, whose mercy is freely given, whose love for the world is demonstrated in the gift of His Son, and whose covenant love for His redeemed people is secure in Jesus Christ.
And when we encounter truths we cannot fully explain, our response should not be to invent an easier God.
It should be to worship the God who has revealed Himself.
The God who is perfectly just.
The God who is rich in mercy.
The God who does not excuse sin.
The God who gave His Son.
The God who raises the dead.
The God who welcomes those who come to Christ.
And the God who will one day make all things new.
So perhaps tonight, instead of asking whether someone else has received more love than you, ask a question Scripture places directly before your heart.
Have I come to Jesus Christ?
Not merely admired Him.
Not merely quoted Him.
Not merely posted about Him.
But come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because the deepest tragedy would not be failing to solve every mystery of divine love.
It would be spending your life discussing the Savior while refusing His call to follow Him.
And the greatest miracle is not that you finally become someone the world considers worthy.
It is that the holy Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners who could never save themselves.
That is where shame meets mercy.
Where pride bows before grace.
Where the lost are called home.
Where the guilty discover forgiveness.
Where the spiritually dead are made alive in Christ.
And where a life once defined by scandal can become a testimony to the redeeming power of Jesus.
You may never understand every mystery of why God loved—but you can come to the cross where He has shown what His love has done.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOST TERRIFYING WORDS JESUS COULD EVER SAY TO SOMEONE WHO THOUGHT THEY BELONGED TO HIM
paragraphs: THE MOST TERRIFYING WORDS JESUS COULD EVER SAY TO SOMEONE WHO THOUGHT THEY BELONGED TO HIM
You can know His name, quote His Word, defend His truth, attend His church, and even do things in His name… yet still miss the one thing that matters most: actually belonging to Jesus Christ.
There is a moment coming that should make every person who calls themselves a Christian stop and examine their heart.
Not because God wants you living in terror.
Not because salvation is impossible to know.
But because Jesus once described people standing before Him who were absolutely convinced they belonged to Him.
They weren't strangers to Christianity.
They knew what to call Him.
They knew how to speak about Him.
They had apparently done remarkable things in His name.
And when the moment came to stand before the Lord, they expected to be welcomed.
But then Jesus spoke words that must have shattered everything they thought they knew.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Read those words again.
Not, “I used to know you.”
Not, “You weren't religious enough.”
Not, “You failed to impress Me.”
“I never knew you.”
Imagine spending your life believing you were walking toward heaven, only to discover that you had been walking around Jesus instead of walking with Him.
Imagine knowing the songs but never surrendering your heart.
Knowing the Scriptures but resisting the Savior those Scriptures reveal.
Knowing how to appear Christian while secretly living as though Christ had no authority over your life.
And here is the question that makes this personal.
What if the greatest spiritual danger isn't that you don't know who Jesus is… but that you have mistaken knowing about Him for belonging to Him?
Because those two things are not the same.
And Jesus loved people enough to tell them the difference.
There is something painfully familiar about the person who knows exactly how to behave when other Christians are watching.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which Bible verses to post when life becomes difficult.
You know how to write “God is good” beneath a photograph.
You know how to encourage somebody else to trust the Lord.
But then the phone goes quiet.
The church service ends.
The worship music stops.
And you find yourself alone with the thoughts, desires, habits, resentments, and compromises you have learned to keep hidden.
Nobody sees the conversation you keep returning to.
Nobody hears the bitterness you rehearse in your mind.
Nobody knows how many times you have promised God you would stop something, only to find yourself doing it again.
Maybe you genuinely love Jesus, yet you are struggling.
Or maybe, if you are painfully honest, you have spent years loving the idea of being Christian without ever surrendering yourself to Christ.
Those are not necessarily the same spiritual condition.
And that distinction matters.
Because a struggling believer who keeps turning toward Jesus is not the same as a person who has made peace with rejecting His authority.
One is fighting a battle.
The other may have stopped recognizing that there is a battle at all.
And Scripture calls us to examine ourselves, not to manufacture despair, but to bring our lives into the light of truth.
Paul wrote:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” — 2 Corinthians 13:5, KJV
That examination is not an invitation to obsess endlessly over every imperfection.
It is an invitation to ask whether our confidence rests in Jesus Christ or merely in the religious identity we have constructed around Him.
Because you can be surrounded by Christian things and still be spiritually far from Christ.
You can own a Bible without allowing its truth to confront you.
You can sit beneath preaching without receiving the Word with faith.
You can be respected in a congregation while quietly refusing to repent.
And you can be so busy maintaining the appearance of a relationship with Jesus that you never stop to ask whether you are actually trusting and following Him.
This is where the original language of Scripture makes Jesus' warning even more piercing.
In Matthew 7:21, Jesus says:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” — KJV
In the Greek text, the repeated address is:
Κύριε κύριε — Kyrie, Kyrie
“Lord, Lord.”
They weren't refusing to acknowledge His title.
They were calling Him Lord.
The problem was not that they lacked religious vocabulary.
The problem was that their confession was contradicted by their lives.
And when Jesus says, “I never knew you,” the Greek reads:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς — oudepote egnōn hymas
“I never knew you.”
The verb egnōn comes from ginōskō, meaning “to know.” Depending on context, the Greek verb can describe knowledge, recognition, or personal acquaintance.
Here, Jesus is not suggesting that He lacked information about these people.
The One who knows the human heart was not surprised by their existence.
His words communicate a devastating rejection of their claim to belong to Him.
He did not recognize them as His own.
And the warning becomes even more serious when we remember that these people appealed to impressive religious activities.
They spoke of prophecy.
They spoke of casting out demons.
They spoke of mighty works.
But Jesus did not accept those claims as proof of a saving relationship with Him.
Think about that.
Religious activity can never substitute for genuine faith in Christ.
And neither can an emotional worship experience, a ministry title, a Christian family background, a public testimony, or a social media profile filled with Bible verses.
None of those things can save you.
Only Jesus saves.
That does not mean good works are meaningless.
It means good works cannot become your substitute savior.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works, and that those who belong to Christ are created for good works.
The order matters.
We do not obey Jesus to purchase salvation.
We obey because His saving grace is transforming us.
We do not repent to convince God that we are worthy of His love.
We repent because the God who loved us while we were sinners is calling us away from the sin that destroys us.
And we do not become children of God by learning how to look like children of God.
We receive Christ through faith.
John 1:12 says:
“But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.” — KJV
The Greek speaks of those who received Him:
ἔλαβον αὐτόν — elabon auton
Those who received Him.
Not merely those who heard His name.
Not merely those who admired His teachings.
Not merely those who knew religious facts about Him.
Those who received Him.
And that changes the entire conversation.
Because Christianity is not merely agreement that Jesus existed, died, and rose again.
It is trusting the crucified and risen Lord, receiving Him as Savior, and acknowledging His rightful authority over your life.
Even demons possess accurate knowledge about God.
James 2:19 reminds us:
“Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.” — KJV
James is confronting the idea that intellectual agreement alone is sufficient evidence of living faith.
The demons know truths about God.
But they do not love Him, trust Him in saving faith, or submit to Him as redeemed children.
So knowing the right answers is not the same as having a heart reconciled to God.
And suddenly, a question emerges that is much harder than asking whether you believe Jesus is real.
Has what you believe about Jesus changed the way you respond to Jesus?
When He confronts your pride, do you defend it or bring it before Him?
When His Word exposes your dishonesty, do you excuse it or confess it?
When He calls you to forgive, do you at least begin wrestling honestly with obedience, even when the wounds are deep?
When you fall into sin, do you run toward His mercy or settle comfortably into hiding?
Not perfectly.
No genuine Christian obeys perfectly in this life.
But is there repentance?
Is there faith?
Is there a growing willingness to let Christ correct what you once insisted on protecting?
Because belonging to Jesus does not mean you never stumble.
It means that your failures are no longer something you want to defend against Him.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that distinction more than anything else.
You have been fighting a private battle for months.
Maybe years.
You have prayed through tears.
You have confessed the same sin so many times that you are ashamed to open your mouth again.
You have wondered whether God is tired of hearing from you.
You have looked at other Christians and imagined that everyone else is stronger, cleaner, more faithful, more deserving.
And now, after reading Jesus' warning, you are frightened that perhaps He will say those terrible words to you.
But listen carefully.
Jesus' warning against false assurance must never be twisted into a denial of His mercy toward repentant sinners.
The same Savior who warned about empty religious professions also promised:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Do not overlook that promise.
The Greek phrase includes:
οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω — ou mē ekbalō exō
A strongly emphatic denial, expressing that He will certainly not cast out the one who comes to Him.
The invitation is not reserved for people with spotless histories.
It is for sinners who come to Christ.
The exhausted.
The ashamed.
The person who has made terrible decisions and cannot undo them.
The believer who is learning to hate what once controlled them.
The person who has been pretending for so long that they no longer know how to tell the truth about their own soul.
Come to Jesus.
Not because your tears are payment.
Not because your remorse makes you worthy.
But because His mercy is real, His sacrifice is sufficient, and His invitation is sincere.
And if you want to understand how completely Jesus can rewrite a human story, remember a man whose life became a public scandal.
Peter.
He walked with Jesus.
He heard His teachings.
He witnessed His miracles.
He confessed that Jesus was the Christ.
And then, on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had boldly declared his loyalty suddenly insisted that he did not know the One he had promised to follow.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The courtyard.
The firelight.
The fear.
The sound of his own denial still hanging in the air.
And then the eyes of Jesus.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
There are moments when a person does not need anyone to explain how badly they have failed.
They already know.
The weight is crushing enough.
Maybe you understand that kind of moment.
You said something you cannot take back.
You betrayed somebody's trust.
You crossed a boundary you once swore you would never cross.
You abandoned a conviction when keeping it became costly.
You failed publicly.
Or perhaps you failed privately, and the secrecy made the shame even heavier.
Peter knew what it meant to collapse beneath the weight of his own weakness.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After His resurrection, Jesus met His disciples again.
And in John 21, He addressed Peter personally.
Three times, Jesus asked Peter about his love.
And He entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
The man who had denied Him was not beyond the reach of restoring grace.
But notice something important.
Jesus did not restore Peter by pretending his denial never happened.
He brought Peter into a renewed encounter with the truth.
Grace did not make sin harmless.
Grace made restoration possible.
And this is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus does not save us by calling our darkness light. He saves us by entering our darkness, bearing our sin, and bringing us into His light.
The cross was not God overlooking evil.
It was Christ bearing the judgment our sin deserved.
Isaiah 53:6 declares:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” — KJV
The Hebrew phrase for “we have gone astray” is:
תָּעִינוּ — ta'inu
We have wandered.
We have strayed.
That is not merely the story of openly rebellious people.
It is the story of humanity.
The religious person who trusts in personal goodness.
The successful person who believes they need nothing.
The broken person who thinks they have gone too far.
The respectable person hiding a second life.
The person who knows the right theology but refuses to surrender.
All of us need the Shepherd.
And the astonishing announcement of the Gospel is that the Shepherd came for the sheep.
Jesus said:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” — John 10:11, KJV
Then, a few verses later, He described those who belong to Him:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27, KJV
Hear that.
“I know them.”
The very thing missing from the frightening declaration in Matthew 7 is beautifully present here.
Jesus knows His sheep.
They hear His voice.
They follow Him.
Not because they have become incapable of weakness.
But because they belong to the Shepherd who gave His life for them.
And in John 10:28, Jesus promises them eternal life and declares that they will never perish.
That is not fragile hope.
That is the assurance Christ gives to those who are His.
So the answer to spiritual uncertainty is not to become obsessed with proving how religious you are.
The answer is to look to Jesus Christ, trust His finished work, receive His Word, and follow Him in the grace He supplies.
You cannot earn your place in His flock.
But you cannot honestly claim to follow the Shepherd while deliberately treating His voice as irrelevant.
Jesus Himself asked in Luke 6:46:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — KJV
That question reaches into places we would rather keep untouched.
It reaches into our marriages.
Our friendships.
Our finances.
Our private habits.
Our treatment of strangers.
Our unforgiveness.
Our secret ambitions.
Our words when we are angry.
Our behavior when nobody will ever find out.
It reaches into the difference between the Jesus we publicly celebrate and the Jesus we privately obey.
And it asks us to stop using His name as decoration while resisting His lordship.
Maybe the most dangerous spiritual deception is not a dramatic rejection of Christianity.
Maybe it is a comfortable version of Christianity that allows us to keep everything except surrender.
A Christianity that gives us inspirational quotes without repentance.
Community without accountability.
Blessings without obedience.
Religious identity without a changed heart.
A cross we admire but never allow to confront our pride.
A Savior we want to rescue us from consequences while we refuse to acknowledge the sin itself.
But Jesus did not come merely to improve the appearance of our old lives.
He came to save us and make us new.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
Notice those words.
“In Christ.”
Not simply near Christian people.
Not simply familiar with Christian ideas.
Not simply emotionally moved by Christian music.
In Christ.
United to Him by faith.
Belonging to Him.
Being transformed through His grace.
And transformation is not always loud.
Sometimes it looks like a husband finally admitting he was wrong.
A wife choosing truth instead of pretending everything is fine.
A young person closing a screen because the Holy Spirit has convicted their conscience.
A father asking his child for forgiveness.
A mother praying through exhaustion instead of surrendering to bitterness.
A believer returning to Scripture after months of spiritual dryness.
A person making restitution where possible.
Someone walking away from a relationship that keeps drawing them into sin.
Someone seeking help instead of hiding an addiction.
Someone who has been wounded learning, slowly and with appropriate boundaries, to release vengeance into God's hands.
Sometimes transformation is a dramatic testimony.
Sometimes it is a thousand quiet acts of repentance that nobody applauds.
But Christ is at work.
And the evidence of His work is not that we become impressive.
It is that we increasingly recognize how desperately we need Him.
There is another scene in Scripture that exposes the difference between religious confidence and genuine dependence upon God's mercy.
In Luke 18:9–14, Jesus tells a parable about two men who went to the temple to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
Religiously disciplined.
Confident in his own righteousness.
He thanked God that he was not like other sinners.
The other was a tax collector.
A man associated with a profession notorious for corruption and betrayal.
He stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
Instead, he struck his chest and prayed:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13, KJV
The Greek reads:
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ — Ho Theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
The verb hilasthēti carries the idea of mercifully dealing with sin, with an association to atonement.
The tax collector was not presenting a résumé of religious accomplishments.
He was pleading for mercy.
And Jesus said that this man, rather than the other, went home justified.
Think about the reversal.
The man who thought he had enough righteousness went away without the justification he presumed.
The man who knew he needed mercy received it.
That is why the Gospel is such devastating news for pride and such glorious news for repentant sinners.
You do not come to Jesus boasting that you are good enough.
You come because He is the Savior you need.
And when His grace reaches you, it does not leave you celebrating the chains from which He came to free you.
It teaches you to walk in a new way.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us and trains us to live differently.
And this brings us to the question you cannot afford to answer merely with your lips.
If Jesus were to confront the one area of your life you have worked hardest to protect from His authority, would you surrender it to Him?
Maybe you already know what that area is.
You don't need me to name it.
Perhaps your conscience has been bringing it to mind throughout this entire article.
The dishonesty.
The resentment.
The hidden relationship.
The secret habit.
The spiritual performance.
The pride that cannot admit fault.
The refusal to forgive.
The belief that because you have been Christian for years, you no longer need correction.
Or perhaps it is the fear that you are too ruined to be loved.
Even that fear must be brought to the truth of Christ's promises.
Because the Gospel confronts both the self-righteous person who thinks they need no mercy and the despairing person who thinks mercy could never reach them.
Neither pride nor despair should have the final word.
Jesus Christ should.
And what does He say?
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
Repentance is not simply feeling terrible about yourself.
It is a turning of mind and heart toward God that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Faith is not simply acknowledging a historical fact.
It is trusting Jesus Christ, the crucified and risen Savior.
And salvation is not the reward for becoming flawless.
It is God's gift of grace to sinners who trust in His Son.
