We can challenge wrongdoing without despising human beings.
We can submit to legitimate authority without surrendering obedience to God.
We can pursue justice without abandoning grace.
And we can suffer loss without believing that Christ has lost His throne.
The apostle Peter captures this balance with extraordinary clarity.
In 1 Peter 2:13–17, he instructs believers to submit to human authorities for the Lord's sake.
Yet in verse 17, he writes:
Notice the distinction.
Honor the king.
Fear God.
Peter does not use the same command for both.
The ruler deserves appropriate honor.
God alone deserves ultimate reverence.
And this is the Peter who later declared before the council that God must be obeyed rather than men.
There is no necessary contradiction.
The apostles understood something we desperately need to recover.
Submission to government is part of Christian obedience. But government is never the final authority over Christian obedience.
And perhaps that truth is reaching someone right now who has been wrestling with fear.
You know something is wrong.
You have witnessed dishonesty.
You have been pressured to compromise.
You have watched someone vulnerable suffer while powerful people looked away.
You want to do what is right.
But you are afraid.
Afraid of losing your job.
Afraid of retaliation.
Afraid of being misunderstood.
Afraid that speaking the truth will cost more than you can afford.
God does not ask you to pretend those fears are imaginary.
Courage is not the absence of fear.
Courage is faithfulness to what is right even when fear is real.
And faithfulness does not always mean making the loudest public statement.
Sometimes wisdom requires careful documentation, trustworthy counsel, lawful reporting, protecting those at risk, and choosing the right time and manner to act.
If you are facing threats or abuse, seeking safety and appropriate help is not a failure of faith.
God does not command you to manufacture danger to prove your devotion.
But neither should fear become the master of your conscience.
There is a difference between acting wisely and surrendering what is right.
And Jesus knows the difference.
Remember the apostles.
Remember the Hebrew midwives.
Remember Daniel.
Remember the three men before the furnace.
Above all, remember Christ.
The One who stood before Pilate is the One who rose from the dead.
The One condemned by human authorities is the One to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given (Matthew 28:18).
The One who suffered injustice is the One who will judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31).
No corrupt official will escape His final judgment merely because of political influence.
No act of cruelty will become righteous because a government legalized it.
No hidden compromise will remain hidden forever.
And no act of faithfulness done for Christ is forgotten by Him.
But before we turn this message into an accusation against unjust leaders, we need to allow the Gospel to confront our own hearts.
Because the scandal of sin is not confined to government offices.
It lives in the human heart.
We have all been tempted to protect ourselves through dishonesty.
We have all been tempted to remain silent when truth was inconvenient.
We have all been tempted to excuse wrongdoing when it benefited us.
We have all fallen short of God's glory (Romans 3:23).
That means our greatest need is not merely better laws, better leaders, or better political institutions.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need new hearts.
We need Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story turns from scandal to grace.
Jesus did not enter our broken world merely to expose corrupt systems.
He came to save sinners.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And through repentance and faith in Him, guilty people can receive forgiveness and new life.
The cross does not excuse our sin.
It reveals how serious sin truly is.
But the resurrection declares that sin, death, and human injustice do not have the final word.
Perhaps you have been complicit in something you now regret.
Perhaps you signed what you knew was false.
Perhaps you stayed silent when you should have spoken.
Perhaps you used authority to hurt someone.
Perhaps you defended a leader's wrongdoing because admitting it would have cost you something.
Do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Gospel calls you to repentance, not despair.
Confess what you have done.
Turn away from it.
Where possible and appropriate, make restitution and seek to repair the harm.
Receive the mercy of Christ, and begin walking in truth.
Grace is not permission to continue in corruption.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy that calls and empowers us to live differently.
And if you have suffered under injustice, hear this too.
You do not need to pretend the harm was good in order to trust that God can bring good out of evil.
You do not need to call abuse holy.
You do not need to surrender your right to seek protection or justice in order to forgive.
Forgiveness is not the same as declaring an offender innocent, restoring unsafe access, or abandoning accountability.
The Lord who commands mercy also loves righteousness.
You can place your pain before Him without denying what happened.
You can pursue justice without surrendering your heart to vengeance.
And you can hope in Christ even when earthly justice is delayed.
Maybe that is the message someone in your family needs today.
Maybe a friend has been struggling with whether faith requires silence.
Maybe someone you know has become so consumed by political anger that they have forgotten the gentleness and truth of Jesus.
Have you ever faced a moment when doing what was right could have cost you something important?
You do not need to share private details or put yourself at risk.
Or, if you have a testimony of God's faithfulness through an unjust situation, share what you are comfortable sharing. Someone else may need the encouragement you once needed.
Because the church should be a place where difficult questions can be brought into the light of God's Word, not buried beneath fear or partisan loyalty.
And if you have been reading Gospel Warrior for some time, I want to share something close to the heart of this ministry.
Messages like this are not meant to be consumed for a moment and forgotten.
They are meant to send us back to Scripture.
To make us examine our hearts.
To strengthen our love for Christ.
To help us become believers who can discern truth from deception, courage from recklessness, and genuine faithfulness from mere religious performance.
That is why we continue building Gospel Warrior as a place for biblical teaching, encouragement, discipleship, repentance, restoration, and spiritual growth.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word.
And certainly not because a financial contribution can purchase His favor.
Salvation is the gift of God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for giving money (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But Scripture does teach the value of willingly supporting faithful ministry.
Galatians 6:6 encourages those who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not reluctant or forced, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You may prayerfully consider it part of your personal giving toward Christian ministry, while continuing to honor your responsibilities to your local church, family, and those in need.
It is a voluntary act of generosity.
And that voluntary generosity matters.
It helps support the ongoing creation and sharing of Christ-centered articles, biblical teaching, devotional materials, and discipleship resources.
It is the opportunity to help keep biblical encouragement and discipleship available to people who may be searching for hope, struggling with their faith, or beginning to discover who Jesus truly is.
Your prayers matter.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
There is no price attached to the Gospel.
The invitation to repent and believe in Jesus is freely extended to all.
Because we are not trying to build a community that merely agrees on every political question.
We want to grow into a community that takes God's Word seriously and places Christ above every earthly allegiance.
And that brings us back to the question that began this entire conversation.
Does the Bible require Christians to obey government authorities even when those authorities act unjustly?
The biblical answer requires a distinction.

Christians are generally called to submit to governing authorities, even when those authorities are imperfect or unjust. But Christians must not obey a particular command that requires them to disobey God.
An authority's wrongdoing does not automatically cancel every legitimate obligation owed to that authority.
And an authority's legitimate office does not make every command morally binding.
Romans 13 teaches us to respect the governing order.
Acts 5:29 teaches us that obedience to God takes priority when human commands conflict with His will.
Together, they call us away from both lawless rebellion and unquestioning compliance.
They call us to faithful discernment.
And the example of Jesus teaches us how that faithfulness must be shaped.
With truth.
With humility.
With courage.
With love.
With a willingness to suffer rather than commit evil.
With confidence that God's kingdom will outlast every earthly throne.
So when the world demands that you choose between popularity and truth, remember Christ.
When fear tempts you to compromise your conscience, remember Christ.
When anger tempts you to repay injustice with injustice, remember Christ.
When earthly leaders disappoint you, remember Christ.
And when the cost of faithfulness feels unbearable, remember the Savior who carried the cross and conquered the grave.
He does not promise that every act of obedience will make your life easier.
He promises that He will be with His people, and that those who belong to Him have a hope no earthly ruler can destroy.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, do not leave this message thinking the greatest question is which government deserves your loyalty.
The greatest question is whether you have been reconciled to God through His Son.
Turn to Christ.
Confess your sins.
Believe the Gospel of His death and resurrection.
Trust Him as Savior and Lord.
And let His grace begin transforming the way you live, the way you treat others, the way you respond to injustice, and the way you exercise whatever authority has been entrusted to you.
Because the final measure of Christian faithfulness is not how loudly we condemn the sins of those in power.
It is whether we ourselves are becoming more like Jesus.
And when the day comes that obedience to Christ costs you something, may your faith be rooted deeply enough in His grace to remain steadfast.
Not because you are naturally fearless.
Not because you are stronger than everyone else.
But because the Lord who saved you is worthy of your trust.
An earthly ruler may have the power to silence your voice, but no earthly throne has the authority to replace the King who redeemed your soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS OBSERVE LENT? THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH ABOUT A TRADITION JESUS NEVER COMMANDED
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS OBSERVE LENT? THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH ABOUT A TRADITION JESUS NEVER COMMANDED

Forty days of fasting. Ashes on foreheads. Sacrifices made in God's name. But what if the greatest danger isn't observing Lent—or refusing to observe it—but missing the very Savior it is supposed to honor?
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ and telling Him everything you gave up for Lent.
The coffee you stopped drinking.
The meat you refused to eat.
The social media accounts you temporarily abandoned.
The sweets you pushed away, the meals you skipped, the religious services you attended.
And then imagine hearing a question that reaches far deeper than your sacrifices.
"But did you give Me your heart?"
That question should disturb us.
Not because fasting is wrong. Not because Lent is necessarily sinful. And certainly not because every Christian who observes Lent is merely performing empty religious rituals.
But because there is something frightening about the possibility of doing religious things for the right God while allowing our hearts to remain far from Him.
A person can spend forty days abstaining from chocolate while continuing to feed bitterness.
Someone can walk into church with ashes on their forehead while carrying unforgiveness they refuse to surrender.
A believer can faithfully observe a religious season while neglecting prayer, repentance, mercy, and obedience throughout the rest of the year.
And someone who proudly refuses to observe Lent can be just as spiritually blind, mistaking contempt for tradition as proof of biblical faithfulness.
That is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because the real question isn't simply whether Lent is biblical.
The deeper question is whether our religious practices are leading us closer to Jesus—or quietly replacing the surrender He actually requires.
And before you decide which side of this debate you're on, there is something in Scripture you need to see.
Something about forty days.
Something about fasting.
Something about human traditions.
And something about the difference between remembering the cross and actually following the One who died upon it.
Because this isn't merely a debate about a religious calendar.
It is a question about the condition of the human heart.
And that includes yours.
The word Lent comes through Old English lencten, associated with springtime. It is not a biblical Hebrew or Greek term, nor does the word itself appear in the original text of Scripture.

Lent developed within the history of the Christian Church as a season of preparation before Easter, commonly emphasizing prayer, fasting, repentance, generosity, and reflection on Christ's suffering, death, and resurrection.

In many Western Christian traditions, Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and extends toward Easter, with forty fasting days traditionally counted by excluding Sundays. Eastern Christian traditions have related but distinct fasting calendars and practices.

Its historical development was gradual. Early Christians practiced fasting in preparation for Easter, but the duration and form varied. By the fourth century, a forty-day preparation was becoming well established in various Christian communities.
That distinction matters.
Lent is an ecclesiastical tradition, not a forty-day observance directly commanded by Jesus or the apostles.
But does that automatically make it wrong?
Not necessarily.
And does its widespread acceptance automatically make it right?
Absolutely not.
Scripture—not popularity, antiquity, denominational loyalty, or personal preference—must guide our evaluation.
Consider what happened immediately after Jesus was baptized.
Matthew 4:1–2 records that the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, where He fasted for forty days and forty nights before facing temptation.
The Greek text of Matthew 4:2 says:
καὶ νηστεύσας ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα, ὕστερον ἐπείνασεν.
Kaì nēsteúsas hēméras tesserákonta kaì nýktas tesserákonta, hýsteron epeínasen.
A faithful translation is:
"And having fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward He was hungry."
The Greek participle νηστεύσας (nēsteúsas) comes from nēsteuō, meaning "to fast" or "to abstain from food."
Jesus truly fasted.
His hunger was real.
His physical weakness was real.
And the temptation that followed was real.
But notice what Matthew does not say.
Matthew does not command every Christian to repeat Jesus' forty-day fast annually.
Matthew does not establish Lent.
Matthew does not instruct the Church to mark its members with ashes or to observe a particular pre-Easter calendar.
The passage describes a decisive event in the earthly ministry of Jesus Christ.
And its meaning reaches far beyond an example of personal discipline.
Where Israel had failed during its wilderness testing, Jesus remained faithful.
Where humanity repeatedly surrendered to temptation, Christ obeyed.
When Satan tempted Him to turn stones into bread, Jesus answered with Scripture.
Matthew 4:4 records His response:
"Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God." (KJV)
Jesus was quoting Deuteronomy 8:3.
The Hebrew expression at the heart of that passage is:
כִּי עַל־כָּל־מוֹצָא פִי־יְהוָה יִחְיֶה הָאָדָם
Ki al-kol motza fi-YHWH yichyeh ha-adam.
Meaning:
"But by everything that comes from the mouth of the LORD shall man live."
The message is not that food is evil.
It is that human beings depend ultimately upon God.
And here is the beautiful truth that must never be lost in our discussion of Lent:
Jesus did not fast forty days to establish a religious competition. He stood faithful where sinners had failed, fulfilling His mission as the obedient Son.
His wilderness victory points toward the greater victory He would accomplish through His death and resurrection.
We are not saved because we successfully imitate forty days of fasting.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
And this is where some Christians become deeply concerned about Lent.
They remember the warning Jesus gave about human traditions.
In Mark 7:8, Jesus declared:
"For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men..." (KJV)
The Greek text begins:
ἀφέντες τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ κρατεῖτε τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων
Aphéntes tēn entolēn tou Theou krateîte tēn parádosin tōn anthrōpōn.
In context, Jesus was confronting religious leaders who elevated certain inherited practices in ways that undermined God's commandments.
The Greek word παράδοσις (parádosis) means "tradition" or "that which is handed down."
But we must be careful.
The word itself is not automatically negative.
In 2 Thessalonians 2:15, Paul tells believers to hold firmly to the traditions they had been taught through apostolic teaching, whether spoken or written.
Therefore, the biblical issue is not simply whether something is called a tradition.
The issue is its source, content, authority, and relationship to God's revealed will.
A tradition becomes spiritually dangerous when it contradicts Scripture, displaces God's commandments, claims authority God has not given it, or becomes a false measure of righteousness.
That principle should humble Christians on every side.
Someone who observes Lent must never teach that participation earns forgiveness or makes a person more deserving of salvation.
Someone who does not observe Lent must never assume that every believer who practices it is worshiping God in vain.
And no Christian should turn a disputed calendar observance into a substitute for the Gospel.
Because the cross was not an invitation to build a ladder of religious achievements toward heaven.
It was the place where the sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners who could never climb high enough.
Now consider another passage.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:16:
"Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance..." (KJV)
Notice His wording.
When you fast.
Not simply "if you fast."
Jesus anticipated that fasting would have a place in the spiritual lives of His disciples.
But He immediately confronted the temptation to turn fasting into a public performance.
In Matthew 6:17–18, He instructed His followers to anoint their heads and wash their faces so their fasting would not be displayed for human applause.
This does not mean every publicly known fast is automatically sinful. Scripture also records communal fasts, including the worshiping and fasting of believers in Acts 13:2–3.
The issue is motive.
Who are you trying to impress?
God?
Or the people watching you?
That question reaches into places we would rather leave untouched.
Because sometimes we want others to know how spiritual we are.
We want people to notice the sacrifices.
We want our religious seriousness to become visible.
We want to be recognized as disciplined, devoted, and holy.
But the Father sees what happens when nobody is watching.
He sees the words you type and delete.
He sees how you treat your family after church.
He sees the resentment you keep rehearsing.
He sees the private compromise you have learned to excuse.
He sees whether your fasting is accompanied by love, humility, repentance, and justice.
And He sees the person who quietly prays through tears without ever announcing it online.
God is not impressed by the appearance of surrender when the heart is determined to remain in control.
That truth becomes even sharper in Isaiah 58.
The people of Israel were fasting, yet God confronted their oppression, quarrels, and injustice.
In Isaiah 58:6, God asks:
"Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens..." (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase begins:
הֲלוֹא זֶה צוֹם אֶבְחָרֵהוּ
Halo zeh tzom evcharehu.
Meaning:
"Is not this the fast that I choose?"
The Hebrew word צוֹם (tzom) means "fast."
The passage does not abolish fasting.
It exposes fasting separated from righteousness and compassion.
God was confronting people who practiced religious self-denial while continuing to harm others.
And that warning is painfully relevant today.
What good is giving up meat while feeding cruelty?
What good is avoiding sweets while refusing to forgive?
What good is fasting from entertainment while neglecting your children?
What good is abstaining from food while withholding generosity from someone who is hungry?
What good is observing a season of repentance while refusing to acknowledge the sin you already know God is confronting?
These questions are not arguments against fasting.
They are arguments against hypocrisy.
And they should challenge those who observe Lent and those who never have.
Because we can reject a religious tradition and still cling to the very sins that tradition was intended to confront.
We can defend biblical truth in public while refusing to obey it in private.
We can win arguments about Lent and still lose sight of love.
And perhaps that is the tragedy.
We become so busy debating the practice that we stop examining the person practicing it.
Us.
Our hearts.
Our motives.
Our desperate need for grace.
But there is another passage we must consider if we want to be faithful to the whole counsel of Scripture.
Romans 14.
Paul addresses believers who differed over food and the observance of particular days.
Romans 14:5–6 says:
"One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord..." (KJV)
The Greek expression in Romans 14:5 is:
ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω
Hékastos en tō idíō noḯ plērophoreísthō.
A faithful translation is:
"Let each person be fully convinced in his own mind."
Paul's immediate discussion concerns differences of conscience among believers. He was not specifically discussing Lent, which developed later in Christian history.
Nevertheless, the passage gives an important principle for evaluating disputable observances.
Believers should act with sincere conviction before the Lord rather than condemning one another over matters Scripture has not universally commanded.
This does not mean every religious practice is acceptable.
Paul elsewhere strongly rejects practices that compromise the Gospel or place believers under false spiritual obligations.

Galatians 4:9–11 warns against returning to bondage through religious observances. Colossians 2:16–23 warns against being judged over food and festivals and against self-imposed religion that lacks power to overcome sinful desires.
These passages must be considered together.

The New Testament leaves room for sincere differences over certain days and practices, while firmly rejecting attempts to make human observances necessary for salvation, spiritual superiority, or acceptance before God.
So can a Christian observe Lent with a clear conscience?
Yes, provided the observance does not contradict Scripture, replace obedience, or become a condition of salvation or righteousness before God.
Can a Christian refuse to observe Lent with a clear conscience?
Yes.
Christians are not commanded in the New Testament to keep a forty-day pre-Easter fast.
Observing Lent does not make someone a better Christian. Refusing Lent does not automatically make someone a more biblical Christian. Faithfulness to Jesus is the issue.
And there is something else we should understand.
In Mark 2:19–20, Jesus described Himself as the bridegroom and spoke of a time when His disciples would fast after the bridegroom was taken away.
The passage establishes a place for fasting among His followers.
But it does not establish Lent as a required annual observance.
The Church may organize times for prayer, teaching, fasting, and remembrance, but such practices must remain servants of the Gospel, never its masters.
A church calendar can remind believers of Christ.
It cannot replace Christ.
A season of fasting can help someone devote attention to prayer.
It cannot purchase God's favor.
An ash cross can symbolize human mortality and repentance.
It cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His resurrection secures the hope of eternal life.
And that brings us to one of the most moving moments in the entire Bible.
David had committed terrible sins.
Adultery.
Deception.
The orchestration of another man's death.
He was a king with power, influence, and religious knowledge.
Yet none of those things could erase what he had done.
When confronted by the prophet Nathan, David could no longer hide behind his position.
He confessed.
And Psalm 51 gives us a window into his brokenness.
Psalm 51:17 declares:
"The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is:
לֵב־נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה
Lev-nishbar venidkeh.
"A broken and crushed heart."
The Hebrew words communicate a heart shattered and humbled before God.
David was not suggesting that repentance could be reduced to emotion or that God's commands no longer mattered.
He was acknowledging that religious offerings could not substitute for genuine contrition.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have attended services.
You have sung worship songs.
You have posted Bible verses.
You have tried to look strong.
But somewhere beneath the religious language is a heart carrying guilt.
Something you did.
Something you said.
Someone you wounded.
A habit you keep returning to.
A secret you are terrified someone will discover.
And perhaps every time you hear a message about repentance, you wonder whether God could still receive someone like you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not that your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The cross does not minimize sin.
It reveals how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's grace truly is.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after forty days of perfect discipline.
Not after we had finally repaired our reputations.
Not after we had managed to appear holy enough.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
And this is why our Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8:1–11.
She was brought before Jesus in humiliation.
Her accusers were ready to condemn her.
Her sin was being used as a public spectacle.
Jesus did not pretend that sin was harmless.
Nor did He join the crowd in treating her as though her failure was the end of her story.
He told her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Grace.
And transformation.
That is the beauty of Christ.
He does not offer forgiveness so we can comfortably remain enslaved to the sins destroying us.
He calls us out of darkness and into newness of life.

And although the account of the woman caught in adultery has a well-known textual history—being absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts—the mercy and holiness it portrays are consistent with the broader New Testament witness to Jesus.
Consider Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had declared his loyalty crumbled under pressure.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Peter wept bitterly.
But failure was not the final word over his life.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Or consider Saul of Tarsus.
A persecutor of the Church.
A man associated with violence against believers.
Yet Christ confronted him, showed him mercy, and transformed his life.
The persecutor became an apostle proclaiming the Savior he once opposed.
Not because his past was imaginary.
Not because his actions were harmless.
But because the risen Jesus is powerful enough to redeem the undeserving.
This is the Gospel.
And this is why Lent, if observed, must point beyond itself.
Beyond ashes.
Beyond fasting schedules.
Beyond religious customs.
Beyond forty days.
Toward the crucified and risen Christ.
Because a religious season cannot rewrite your story.
Jesus can.
Now imagine a different kind of Lent.
Not one where someone gives up a favorite drink simply to prove they can endure forty days without it.

But one where a believer uses the season to confront an addiction, seek accountability, pray faithfully, reconcile with someone they have wronged, care for the poor, and meditate deeply on the suffering and resurrection of Christ.
Would those actions be wrong simply because they occurred during Lent?
Of course not.
Those are good responses to biblical truth, though their value does not depend on the calendar.
Now imagine someone who chooses not to observe Lent.
Instead, that believer practices prayer, fasting, generosity, repentance, and Scripture meditation throughout the year without adopting a particular liturgical season.
Would that believer be disobedient for not participating in Lent?
No.
The New Testament does not impose Lent as a requirement.
The question is not whether every Christian must follow the same devotional calendar.
The question is whether we are walking in obedience to the same Lord.
And here is where the discussion becomes even more personal.
What happens after Lent ends?
What happens when the fasting season is over?
When the foods return?
When the regular routines resume?
When the religious excitement fades?
Does your pursuit of holiness disappear with the calendar?
Does your prayer life go silent?
Does your generosity stop?
Does your repentance become something you postpone until the next religious season?
Because Jesus did not say:
He said:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." (Luke 9:23, KJV)
Daily.
The Greek word is:
καθ᾽ ἡμέραν
Kath' hēméran.
"Day by day."
That expression appears in Luke's account and emphasizes the ongoing nature of discipleship.
Following Christ is not a seasonal performance.
It is a lifelong response to grace.
Not a means of earning salvation, but the fruit of belonging to the Savior.
And perhaps this is the truth we have been avoiding.
We are often willing to give up something temporarily.
But surrendering ourselves completely?
That is harder.
Giving up sugar for forty days may be uncomfortable.
Giving up the pride that keeps destroying your relationships may be agonizing.
Skipping a meal can be difficult.
Confessing a hidden sin can feel terrifying.
Turning off social media may require discipline.
Turning away from a cherished idol may require the painful honesty of admitting how much control it has over your heart.
But Christ does not call us merely to temporary inconvenience.
He calls us to repentance and faith.
And He gives grace to those who come to Him.
The Greek word often translated "repentance" is μετάνοια (metánoia), referring to a change of mind or heart that involves turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling bad because you were exposed.
It involves acknowledging sin, turning toward God, and seeking to walk in obedience through His grace.
It is not a payment for forgiveness.
It is a proper response to the God who calls sinners to Himself.
And that is why the words of Joel 2:13 are so powerful:
"And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God..." (KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
וְקִרְעוּ לְבַבְכֶם וְאַל־בִּגְדֵיכֶם
Veqir'u levavkhem ve'al-bigdeikhem.
"Rend your hearts, and not your garments."
In ancient Israel, tearing garments could express grief, distress, or repentance.
But God was calling His people beyond the outward sign.
He wanted genuine turning.
Not merely torn clothing.
Torn hearts.
Not merely visible sorrow.
True repentance.
And this is the passage I wish every Christian would remember whenever Lent becomes a source of pride, division, or religious performance.
God is not looking for the most impressive outward display of repentance. He calls for the heart to turn back to Him.
Whether you observe Lent or not, that call remains.
Whether your church practices Ash Wednesday or not, that call remains.
Whether you fast before Easter or at another time, that call remains.
The same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance also promises rest to those who come to Him.
And if you are exhausted from trying to prove yourself worthy of God's love, you need to hear this.
You cannot earn the cross.
You cannot purchase the resurrection.
You cannot make yourself worthy of grace through the number of meals you skip or the number of religious services you attend.
Jesus Christ accomplished what we could never accomplish.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for sins.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to turn from sin and trust in Him.
This does not make spiritual discipline meaningless.
It gives spiritual discipline its proper place.
We pray because we depend upon God.
We fast to humble ourselves and devote attention to Him.
We give because His generosity transforms our hearts.
We obey because we love the One who first loved us.
We do not do these things to force God to save us.
We do them as people responding to His grace.
And if Lent helps you remember those truths, practice it with humility, biblical discernment, and a clear conscience before God.
If you choose not to observe Lent, do not despise those who sincerely seek Christ through that season.
But if Lent has become a substitute for daily discipleship, you need more than another religious routine.
You need to return to Jesus.
And if rejecting Lent has become a badge of spiritual superiority, you also need to examine your heart.
Because pride can wear ashes.
And pride can also boast about never wearing them.
Both need the same Savior.
Perhaps you have been reading this article while quietly carrying something nobody knows about.
A marriage that is breaking.
A child you desperately want to see return to God.
A faith that feels weaker than it once did.
A secret struggle that has lasted longer than you ever imagined.
A painful memory that still makes you question whether you can be forgiven.
Maybe you have spent years looking religious while privately feeling spiritually empty.
Or perhaps you have avoided church because you assumed Christianity was nothing more than rules, rituals, and people judging one another.
Please do not confuse the failures of religious people with the character of Jesus Christ.
Look at Him.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the Savior who welcomed repentant sinners, confronted hypocrisy, cared for the broken, and gave His life to redeem His people.
He is not merely the subject of a religious season.
He is Lord.
He is Savior.
He is worthy of your whole life.
And His invitation is not limited to forty days.
It is for today.
Right now.
If you have been hiding, you can stop pretending before God.
If you have sinned, confess it and turn to Christ.
If you have wandered, return to Him.
If you have grown proud of your religious knowledge, ask Him to restore humility.
If you have grown cold, seek Him again in His Word and prayer.
And if you are not yet a believer, do not imagine that Christianity begins with mastering religious customs.
It begins with the good news of Jesus Christ—His death for sinners, His resurrection, and His call to repentance and faith.
You do not need a perfect religious record to come to Him.
You need the Savior.
Maybe your prayer today is simple.

"Lord Jesus, I have been more concerned about looking faithful than being faithful. Forgive my pride. Forgive my hypocrisy. Forgive the sins I have tried to hide. Teach me to trust Your grace, love Your truth, and follow You every day. Whether I observe Lent or not, let my life belong to You. Amen."
And if this message uncovered something you have been avoiding, I want to invite you to be honest.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly. God knows your circumstances, and Christian community should be a place where people are treated with compassion rather than shame.
Someone reading silently may need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and no sinner is beyond the saving power of Jesus.
Not to win a religious argument.
Not to embarrass someone who observes Lent differently from you.

But because there may be a friend, a relative, a struggling believer, or someone who has walked away from church who needs to encounter the Gospel rather than another fight about religious traditions.
Not because following a page makes someone a disciple.
But because the truth of God's Word deserves to be heard, examined, and lived.
There is also something important I want to share with those who have been blessed by this ministry.

Behind every Gospel-centered article, every biblical resource, and every message of encouragement is a continuing commitment to help people encounter the truth of Scripture and grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
Our desire is not simply to attract readers.
It is to help nurture disciples.
People who know the Word.
People who recognize false teaching.
People who understand grace without treating sin lightly.
People who can explain the Gospel to their children.
People who continue trusting Christ when life becomes painful.
And people who learn to love God not only with emotion, but with truth, obedience, and perseverance.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But a genuine opportunity to participate in work that seeks to glorify Jesus Christ and serve others through His Word.
These products can serve as personal reminders of biblical truth, thoughtful gifts, or practical resources for faith-centered living.
It is the opportunity to help more people hear the Gospel and gain access to biblical encouragement and discipleship resources.
Others cannot.
Both are welcome.
That no religious ritual can replace the Savior.
That no amount of human effort can earn redemption.
That repentance is not merely an annual event.
That grace is never permission to remain in sin.
And that Jesus Christ is still transforming lives through the power of His Gospel.
So, should Christians observe Lent?
Here is the answer.

Christians may observe Lent as a voluntary season of prayer, fasting, repentance, and reflection upon Christ, provided they do so in a way that honors Scripture and does not treat the observance as necessary for salvation or as a measure of spiritual superiority.
Christians may also choose not to observe Lent, because the New Testament does not command the Church to keep this particular forty-day season.
Neither position gives us permission to judge another believer's standing before God merely on the basis of the observance.
The danger is not simply tradition.
It is tradition that replaces truth.
It is fasting that replaces repentance.
It is ritual that replaces relationship with Christ.
It is religious confidence that replaces humble dependence upon grace.
And it is the arrogance of believing that our preferred practice—or rejection of a practice—makes us righteous before God.
The cross destroys that illusion.
At Calvary, nobody could boast of having earned redemption.
The Savior was crucified for sinners.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That is our hope.
Not forty days of perfect fasting.
Not ashes.
Not religious superiority.
Not the absence of tradition.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
If you remember only one thing from this article, remember this:
You can give up something for Lent and still refuse to surrender to Christ.
You can refuse Lent and still refuse to surrender to Christ.
But when you truly come to Jesus in repentance and faith, you discover that salvation was never something you could achieve through religious performance.
It is God's gift of grace, received through faith in the Savior.
And a life transformed by that grace is called to follow Him—not merely for a season, but every day.
Because the deepest question has never been simply what you gave up for forty days.
It is whether you have entrusted your life to the One who gave Himself for you.
The tragedy would not be reaching Easter without observing Lent; it would be spending your life surrounded by reminders of the cross while never surrendering to the Savior who died upon it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID'S OWN SON TOOK HIS FATHER'S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP—AND ALL ISRAEL WAS MEANT TO KNOW
paragraphs: DAVID'S OWN SON TOOK HIS FATHER'S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP—AND ALL ISRAEL WAS MEANT TO KNOW

The son wanted his father's throne. He chose public sexual humiliation to prove he had taken it. But behind this horrifying betrayal was an older sin, a shattered family, and a warning about what happens when the wounds we refuse to confront become the weapons that destroy us.
There are betrayals that break your heart.
And then there are betrayals so cruel that you wonder whether the person who committed them ever loved you at all.
Imagine being a father.

You have made terrible mistakes. You have sinned against God. You have hurt people you should have protected. You have repented, but the consequences of your choices have continued to haunt your family.
Then one day, your own son turns against you.
He steals the loyalty of people you once led. He forces you out of your home. He takes the throne you occupied.
And as though taking your kingdom were not enough, he does something so humiliating, so calculated, and so publicly degrading that the entire nation is meant to hear about it.
He takes the women you left behind.
He goes up onto the roof of your palace.
And there, in a tent deliberately erected for public notice, he has sexual relations with your concubines.
Your own son.
Your own house.
Your own roof.
The same rooftop from which your own disastrous sin had once begun.
This is not a fictional tragedy written to shock an audience.
This is Scripture.
And what makes it even more disturbing is that the Bible had already warned David that something terrible would happen inside his own household.
But before we go any further, understand something important.
This story is not simply about a wicked son and a broken father.

It is about the devastating consequences of sin, the abuse of power, the suffering of people caught in someone else's rebellion, and the difference between being forgiven by God and being spared every earthly consequence.
And eventually, it will bring us face-to-face with a greater Son of David.
A King who did not seize His Father's throne through humiliation.
A King who willingly endured humiliation to rescue sinners.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And to understand why that matters, we must return to the rooftop.
Second Samuel 16:20–22 records the horrifying scene:
"Then said Absalom to Ahithophel, Give counsel among you what we shall do.

And Ahithophel said unto Absalom, Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.
So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel."
— 2 Samuel 16:20–22, King James Version
Read that last sentence again.
"In the sight of all Israel."
The Hebrew text makes the public nature of this act unmistakable.
The phrase is:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
Le'einei kol-Yisra'el.
Literally, "before the eyes of all Israel."
This was not a private affair driven merely by lust.
It was a political declaration.
Absalom was announcing that he had taken his father's royal position and was prepared to break with him beyond reconciliation.

In the ancient royal world, taking possession of a king's women could carry a claim to his authority. We see related tensions elsewhere in Scripture, including the accusations involving Abner and Saul's concubine in 2 Samuel 3:7–8 and Adonijah's request concerning Abishag in 1 Kings 2:13–25.
But there is a crucial detail many readers miss.
Scripture says a tent was pitched on the rooftop and that the act occurred "in the sight of all Israel." It does not require us to imagine every intimate detail being visibly exposed to the crowd.
The point is that Absalom made the act publicly known.
He wanted the nation to understand what he had done.
He wanted his father to be disgraced.
And he wanted his followers to believe there was no turning back.
This was rebellion turned into spectacle.
A son publicly dishonoring his father to strengthen his own claim to power.
And behind that spectacle were ten women whose suffering must not be forgotten.
They were not trophies.
They were not political decorations.
They were human beings.
David had left these ten concubines to care for the palace when he fled Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:16). Absalom then used them as instruments of his political rebellion.
The biblical text does not record their consent. Given the circumstances and the severe imbalance of power, we must not romanticize what happened or treat these women as willing participants.
Their bodies became the ground on which powerful men fought for control.
And their suffering did not end when Absalom died.

Second Samuel 20:3 tells us that when David returned, he provided for these women but did not resume marital relations with them. They lived in confinement, described as living in widowhood until their deaths.
Think about that.
Absalom pursued a throne.
David endured humiliation.
But these women carried lifelong consequences from a conflict they did not create.
Sometimes the people who suffer most from a family's sin are the ones whose names history barely remembers.
And if you have ever been wounded by someone else's selfishness, someone else's appetite, someone else's ambition, or someone else's abuse of authority, there is something you need to hear.
God did not overlook those women simply because the narrative does not tell us their names.
Their suffering is preserved in His Word.
And the fact that Scripture records an evil act does not mean Scripture approves of it.
But how did David's family reach such a horrifying moment?
To understand the rooftop of Absalom's rebellion, we must return to another rooftop.
Years earlier, David had been walking on the roof of his palace when he saw Bathsheba bathing.
Second Samuel 11 describes what followed.

David sent for her. He slept with her. She became pregnant. And when his attempts to conceal the pregnancy failed, David arranged for her husband, Uriah, to be placed in a deadly position during battle.
Uriah died.
David had taken another man's wife and arranged the death of a loyal soldier.
The king who had once confronted giants was now hiding monstrous wrongdoing behind royal authority.
But God saw everything.
Second Samuel 11:27 delivers a devastating verdict:
"But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD."
There is no royal exemption from holiness.
No spiritual reputation powerful enough to erase God's moral standards.
No title, ministry, following, wealth, or public success that can make hidden evil righteous.
David was God's anointed king.
And David had sinned grievously.
Then the prophet Nathan confronted him.
Through a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's beloved lamb, Nathan exposed the king's wrongdoing.
When David condemned the guilty man in Nathan's story, the prophet answered:
"Thou art the man."
— 2 Samuel 12:7
Four words.
And the walls of David's self-deception came crashing down.
Have you ever noticed how easily we recognize sin when someone else commits it?
We can identify another person's pride.
Another person's dishonesty.
Another person's lust.
Another person's cruelty.
But when the Holy Spirit begins exposing our own hearts, suddenly we have explanations.
We were lonely.
We were hurt.
We were under pressure.
We were misunderstood.
We did not mean for things to go that far.
And sometimes those explanations contain real pain.
But pain does not automatically make our choices righteous.
David could not blame the pressure of kingship.
He could not blame Bathsheba.
He could not blame Uriah.
He could not blame his circumstances.
When Nathan confronted him, David finally said:
"I have sinned against the LORD."
— 2 Samuel 12:13
No elaborate defense.
No attempt to negotiate innocence.
Just confession.
And Nathan answered:
"The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die."
Here is the astonishing mercy of God.
David was guilty.
David deserved judgment.
Yet God extended forgiveness.
But forgiveness did not mean that every consequence disappeared.
Nathan had already declared in 2 Samuel 12:11–12 that calamity would arise from David's own household and that what David had done secretly would be answered by public disgrace.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 sharpens the contrast:
אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ בַסָּתֶר
Attah asita vasater.
"You did it in secret."
And then:
וְאֶעֱשֶׂה אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
Ve'e'eseh et-haddavar hazzeh neged kol-Yisra'el.
"But I will do this thing before all Israel."
Secret sin.
Public disgrace.
A palace rooftop.
And years later, another palace rooftop.
The connection is horrifying.
But we must understand it carefully.

God's prophetic announcement of judgment does not make Absalom's actions morally acceptable. God can sovereignly bring judgment through events involving sinful human choices without approving those choices.
Absalom remained responsible for his rebellion and the harm he inflicted.
And David's concubines were not guilty merely because they suffered its consequences.
That distinction matters.
Because there are people who have been told that every terrible thing done to them must somehow be punishment for their own sin.
That is not what Scripture teaches.
Jesus Himself rejected the assumption that every individual tragedy can be traced to the victim's personal wrongdoing (John 9:1–3).
Do not take the consequences of another person's evil and turn them into an accusation against the wounded.
But the story grows darker still.
Because Absalom's rebellion did not appear out of nowhere.
Before the rooftop, there was a family already torn apart.
David's son Amnon had sexually violated his half-sister Tamar.
Second Samuel 13 records her anguish and the devastating injustice she endured.
Absalom, Tamar's brother, became furious.
And David, though angry, is not recorded in that chapter as bringing Amnon to justice.
For two years, Absalom carried his anger.
Then he arranged Amnon's murder.
Afterward, Absalom fled.
Later, he returned to Jerusalem, but his relationship with David remained deeply fractured.
Eventually, Absalom began cultivating public support, presenting himself as someone who would give the people the justice they sought.
Second Samuel 15:6 says that Absalom "stole the hearts of the men of Israel."
Notice the tragedy.
A family had experienced sexual violence, grief, anger, murder, estrangement, and unresolved conflict.
And out of that brokenness grew a rebellion that threatened an entire kingdom.
We should not pretend the Bible explicitly tells us every motive in Absalom's heart.
It does not.
But it does show us how a history of grave wrongdoing and fractured relationships preceded his revolt.
And there is a warning here for every family.
Unaddressed evil does not become harmless simply because people stop talking about it.
Silence is not always peace.
Distance is not always healing.
And pretending that nothing happened does not restore what was broken.
Some families are sitting at dinner tables where everyone knows something is wrong, but nobody dares speak.
Some children have grown into adulthood carrying wounds that were never acknowledged.
Some parents want reconciliation without confession.
Some relatives demand forgiveness while refusing accountability.
Some churches want the appearance of unity without confronting the wrongdoing that shattered it.
But biblical restoration is not built on denial.
It requires truth.
It requires repentance where sin has occurred.
It requires justice and protection for those who have been harmed.
And sometimes it requires boundaries even when forgiveness is sincerely offered.
Absalom's story does not excuse revenge.
His pain did not give him permission to abuse others.
But neither should his rebellion make us overlook the earlier injustices that helped shape the tragedy.
Hurt people are still morally responsible for what they do with their hurt.
And wounded people deserve care before their pain becomes another chapter of destruction.
Then came the day David fled Jerusalem.
The king who once entered the city in triumph now walked away from it in grief.
Second Samuel 15:30 describes David ascending the Mount of Olives, weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare.
Imagine that scene.
The king is crying.
His servants are crying.
The city is behind him.
His son is coming for his throne.
And David does not know how the story will end.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of heartbreak.
Not because your child seized a kingdom.
But because someone you loved became someone you no longer recognized.
A son who will not speak to you.
A daughter who carries years of anger.
A marriage destroyed by betrayal.
A friendship poisoned by jealousy.
A family inheritance turned into a battlefield.
A person you helped who now speaks against you.
A reputation damaged by someone who once knew your most vulnerable moments.
You may have experienced the terrible loneliness of realizing that the person who knows where you are weakest has decided to strike there.
David knew that pain.
And he knew something else.
He was not innocent of everything that had brought his household into crisis.
That is part of what makes his grief so complicated.
He was a sinner who had been forgiven.
A father who had failed.
A king suffering the consequences of his own wrongdoing.
And a man genuinely wounded by his son's evil.
All those realities could exist together.
That is often how real life works.
People are rarely as simple as the labels we attach to them.
A person can be responsible for terrible choices and still suffer genuine betrayal.
A person can repent sincerely and still have relationships that remain damaged.
A person can be forgiven by God and still have difficult responsibilities to face.
And a person can be deeply wounded without being permitted to wound others in return.
The Gospel does not ask us to lie about any of these realities.
It brings them into the light.
But here is where the story takes another devastating turn.
The adviser who encouraged Absalom's public violation of David's concubines was Ahithophel.
He had once been David's counselor.
Second Samuel 16:23 says his counsel was highly regarded, as though someone had consulted the word of God.
Now his wisdom was being used to strengthen rebellion.
He advised Absalom to make the break with David unmistakable.
To turn private family betrayal into a national political statement.
And Absalom listened.
This is what happens when intelligence becomes detached from righteousness.
A person can be brilliant and morally corrupt.
Strategic and spiritually blind.
Persuasive and destructive.
Not every voice that sounds wise is leading you toward God.
Some counsel will strengthen your pride while weakening your soul.
Some people will tell you exactly what your wounded ego wants to hear.
Some will encourage you to expose, humiliate, retaliate, and destroy, then call it strength.
But James 3:17 describes wisdom from above as pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.
Ahithophel's advice was politically calculated.
But it was not holy.
And Absalom's decision showed what kind of king he was becoming.
He wanted power badly enough to turn vulnerable women into instruments of humiliation.
He wanted the throne without the character required to rule it.
And this is where the story stops being merely ancient history.
Because Absalom's temptation still lives in the human heart.
We may not be standing on palace rooftops.
But we still want to win arguments by humiliating people.
We still want to expose those who embarrassed us.
We still want to prove that we have moved on by making someone else suffer.
We still want to answer rejection with revenge.
We still want to use our pain as permission to become cruel.
And sometimes, the most frightening question is not what someone has done to us.
It is what we are becoming because of what they did.
Are we healing?
Or are we rehearsing revenge?
Are we pursuing justice?
Or are we beginning to enjoy the thought of another person's destruction?
Are we surrendering our wounds to Christ?
Or are we building an identity around them?
There is a difference between seeking accountability and seeking humiliation.
There is a difference between telling the truth and weaponizing the truth.
There is a difference between refusing to tolerate evil and allowing evil to transform your own heart.
Romans 12:19 calls believers away from personal vengeance and toward trust in God's justice.
That does not mean refusing lawful protection or accountability.
It means we do not have to become instruments of cruelty to prove that cruelty was wrong.
And now comes one of the most heartbreaking details in this entire account.
Absalom's rebellion ultimately failed.
David's forces defeated the rebels.
And Absalom died.
When David received the news, he did not celebrate the death of the son who had betrayed him.
He wept.
Second Samuel 18:33 records his cry:
"O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
Those words are almost unbearable.
The son had stolen his father's throne.
Humiliated his father.
Threatened his life.
And still, David cried out in grief.
"O my son."
Not "my enemy."
Not "the traitor."
"My son."
The text does not tell us that David was an exemplary father in every respect. Far from it.
It does not erase the injustice that had unfolded under his roof.
But it does show a father whose grief survived his son's betrayal.
And there is something deeply human in that.
You can love someone and be devastated by what they have done.
You can grieve a relationship that became unsafe.
You can mourn someone who rejected you.
You can recognize wrongdoing without pretending your love never existed.
Sometimes the hardest grief is not for someone who never loved you.
It is for someone you loved who chose a path you could not follow.
David's cry is heartbreaking.
But it also points us toward a greater question.
What if there were a King who could do more than wish He had died in another person's place?
What if there were a King who actually gave His life to save His enemies?
This is where the story must lead us.
Not merely to David.
Not merely to Absalom.
But to Jesus.
The New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the promised Son of David.
In Luke 1:32–33, the angel announces that He will receive the throne of His father David and reign over a kingdom without end.
But Jesus is not another Absalom.
Absalom sought a throne through betrayal.
Jesus, the rightful King, humbled Himself in obedience to the Father.
Absalom used other people's bodies to strengthen his political power.
Jesus gave His own body for the salvation of sinners.
Absalom made humiliation a weapon against his father.
Jesus endured humiliation from sinful men while accomplishing His Father's saving purpose.
Absalom's path led to rebellion and death.
Jesus passed through death and rose again in victory.
Philippians 2:8–9 declares:
"And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name."
Consider the contrast.
Absalom wanted to be exalted, so he brought disgrace upon others.
Jesus humbled Himself, and the Father exalted Him.
Absalom tried to secure a kingdom by demonstrating that he could take what belonged to another.
Jesus established His saving reign through perfect obedience and sacrificial love.
And there is another connection worth remembering.
David crossed the Mount of Olives in tears while fleeing betrayal.
Centuries later, Jesus also approached His suffering through the Mount of Olives, knowing that betrayal and arrest were near.
These events are not identical, and we should not force every detail into a symbolic prediction.
But the contrast is spiritually powerful.
David was a flawed king suffering in a world scarred by his own sins and the sins of others.
Jesus was the sinless King who willingly suffered for sinners.
David cried that he wished he could have died in Absalom's place.
Jesus actually died for the ungodly.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that God ignores sin.
Not that betrayal does not matter.
Not that victims must pretend their wounds are insignificant.
Not that repentance is optional.
But that Jesus Christ entered a world filled with guilt, injustice, rebellion, shame, and suffering, and gave Himself as the atoning sacrifice for sinners.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
The Greek word often translated "repentance" is μετάνοια, metanoia.
It refers to a change of mind and heart that turns a person away from sin and toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed after being exposed.
It is more than regretting that consequences arrived.
It is a genuine turning toward God, expressed in a changed direction of life.
David's confession in Psalm 51 helps us see that kind of repentance.
He prayed:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me."
— Psalm 51:10
In Hebrew:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create for me a clean heart, O God."
Not merely a repaired reputation.
Not a better excuse.
Not a way to escape embarrassment.
A clean heart.
David needed something deeper than image restoration.
And so do we.
Because the deepest problem in our lives is not always what other people know about us.
Sometimes it is what God knows about us that we keep refusing to face.
The envy.
The bitterness.
The secret dishonesty.
The unforgiveness we are nurturing.
The sexual sin we keep justifying.
The pride that makes confession feel unbearable.
The anger we have begun to enjoy.
The way we have used people to satisfy our desires.
The way we have avoided responsibility because admitting the truth would cost us something.
Jesus did not come simply to make our public image more respectable.
He came to save sinners and transform hearts.
And perhaps that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
Because somewhere in it, we recognize ourselves.
Sometimes we are like David, desperately needing to stop hiding and confess.
Sometimes we are tempted to become like Absalom, allowing wounded pride to turn into destructive choices.
Sometimes we are like those ten women, suffering because someone with power treated us as though our dignity did not matter.
And sometimes we are simply standing among the broken pieces of a family, wondering whether anything good can ever grow there again.
But hear this carefully.
You are not required to pretend that evil was good in order to receive God's healing.
You do not have to excuse an abuser to honor Christ.
You do not have to return to an unsafe relationship to prove that you have forgiven.
And you do not have to deny your own wrongdoing in order to believe that grace is possible.
The cross tells the truth about both sin and mercy.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God gave His life to save us.
Grace is so extraordinary that even guilty sinners may come to Him for forgiveness.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
But that promise is not permission to continue harming others.
True repentance bears fruit.
Where restitution is possible, we should pursue it.
Where accountability is required, we should accept it.
Where someone has been harmed, their safety and dignity must matter.
And where reconciliation is not presently possible, we can still seek to walk faithfully before God.
This is what makes grace so different from denial.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace brings sinners into the light so they can be changed.
And if you have reached this point with tears in your eyes, anger in your chest, or a memory you have never fully spoken about, perhaps this is the moment to be honest with God.
Not with a performance.
Not with polished religious language.
Just honesty.
"Lord, I am hurt."
"Lord, I have sinned."
"Lord, I am angry."
"Lord, I have been hiding."
"Lord, I do not know how to forgive."
"Lord, I need help."
He already knows.
And He invites you to come.
You do not owe the internet the details of your pain. You do not have to reveal a traumatic experience publicly to prove your sincerity.
But if you want prayer, let this be a place where brothers and sisters in Christ can respond with compassion rather than condemnation.

And if you have a testimony of how Jesus has led you from shame toward repentance, from bitterness toward forgiveness, or from spiritual exhaustion toward renewed faith, your words may encourage someone who has almost given up.
Someone reading may be one prayer away from asking for help.
One honest confession away from beginning the process of restoration.
One act of courage away from refusing to repeat the sins that wounded their family.
That is why stories like this matter.
Not because scandal is entertaining.
But because Scripture refuses to hide the reality of human brokenness.
And because Jesus Christ is greater than the darkness that brokenness reveals.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
Not because consequences vanish.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored in this lifetime.
But because the risen Christ offers forgiveness, new life, and a future that does not have to be ruled by the sins of yesterday.
And if this message has strengthened your faith, please do not let it end with you.
Send it privately to a person who needs encouragement.
There is also a deeper way to stand with this ministry.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical teaching, Christian literature, and discipleship resources accessible to more people.

The mission is to keep nourishing believers, helping people understand Scripture, and reaching those who may never enter a church building but are willing to read a message about Jesus on their phone.
That work requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Scripture encourages generous, willing giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That means no one should be pressured into giving.
You do not have to pay for God's favor.
And your standing before God is never measured by a monthly payment.
Salvation is the gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not something purchased through financial support.
But if you believe in the work Gospel Warrior is doing, your monthly contribution can be a meaningful way to help sustain and expand it.
These items are not the reason to give.
They are simply a small expression of gratitude for those who choose to stand alongside the ministry.
You can still be part of this mission.
Read the Word.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Speak the truth in love.
Your prayers, your witness, and your willingness to point another person toward Jesus matter deeply.
Because the goal has never been merely to grow a page.
It is to make Christ known.
To call sinners to repentance.
To remind wounded people that their suffering is seen.
To help believers grow in the truth.
And to proclaim that no human scandal is beyond the reach of the Gospel's invitation to repentance and grace.
Now return with me, one final time, to that rooftop in Jerusalem.
A son wanted to prove that he had conquered his father.
He used humiliation to announce his power.
He believed that taking what belonged to another man would make him king.
But his kingdom did not last.
His rebellion ended.
His life ended.
And his father was left weeping.
Then look toward another hill, centuries later.
There stands Jesus Christ.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Stripped of His garments.
Crowned with thorns.
Crucified beneath a public accusation.
He did not climb a throne by disgracing the helpless.
He went to the cross to redeem the guilty.
He did not need to steal a kingdom.
He was the rightful King.
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated a victory no earthly rebellion could ever achieve.
Victory over sin and death.
So perhaps the most important question is not what Absalom did on the rooftop.
Perhaps the most important question is what you will do with the Savior who went to the cross.
Will you continue hiding?
Will you keep defending what God is calling you to confess?
Will you let the people who hurt you determine the kind of person you become?
Or will you bring your guilt, your grief, your anger, and your brokenness to Jesus Christ?
You cannot change what happened yesterday.
But by God's grace, you can turn toward Christ today.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek help where you have been harmed.
Choose truth over appearances.
Choose obedience over revenge.
And trust the Savior whose mercy is greater than the shame you thought would define you forever.
Because the rooftop revealed how far human rebellion can fall.
But the cross revealed how far divine love was willing to go to save sinners.
The scandal may be part of your history, but through Jesus Christ, it does not have to be the final word over your eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF JEREMIAH 29:11 WAS NEVER GOD’S PROMISE TO MAKE YOUR DREAMS COME TRUE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF JEREMIAH 29:11 WAS NEVER GOD’S PROMISE TO MAKE YOUR DREAMS COME TRUE?
The Shocking Truth Behind One of Christianity’s Most Beloved Verses—and Why Its Original Meaning May Give You a Deeper Hope Than the Promise You Thought You Had
There is a Bible verse hanging on bedroom walls, printed on coffee mugs, written inside graduation cards, and whispered through trembling lips when life begins falling apart.
“For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.” — Jeremiah 29:11 (KJV)
You have probably heard it.
You may have claimed it.

You may have held onto it when the doctor delivered frightening news, when your marriage was falling apart, when your business collapsed, when someone you loved walked away, or when you were begging God to open a door that seemed permanently shut.
And perhaps someone told you, “Don't worry. God has a wonderful plan for your life. Jeremiah 29:11 says so.”
But what happens when the door never opens?
What happens when the person you prayed for still dies?
What happens when the healing doesn't come, the marriage isn't restored, the financial breakthrough never arrives, and the future you imagined disappears before your eyes?
Did God break His promise?
Did you lack enough faith?
Or is it possible that we have been holding onto a beautiful verse while missing the very story that makes it so powerful?
Because here is something many Christians have never been told.
Jeremiah 29:11 was not originally spoken to someone about to receive an immediate breakthrough. It was written to people who were being told they would have to wait seventy years.
Seventy years.
Not seven days.
Not seven weeks.
Not even seven months.
And some of the people who first heard those words would never live to see the promised homecoming.
Read that again.
Because what we are about to discover may dismantle a comfortable interpretation of Scripture while revealing a far more durable hope.
A hope that does not collapse when life refuses to cooperate.
A hope that can survive the hospital room, the funeral, the rejection, the unanswered prayer, and the years when heaven seems painfully silent.
And strangely enough, the truth begins not with prosperity, but with judgment.
Not with a breakthrough, but with exile.
Not with people getting everything they wanted, but with God refusing to abandon people who had repeatedly turned away from Him.
That is where Jeremiah 29:11 actually lives.
And that is where we must begin.
Imagine being torn away from your homeland.
Your familiar streets are gone. Your community is scattered. The temple that represented the center of your nation's worship is far away. You are living under the authority of a foreign empire.
You wake up in Babylon.
You remember Jerusalem.
And every day, you wonder whether you will ever go home.
This was the world of the Jewish exiles who received Jeremiah's letter.

In 597 BC, Babylon's King Nebuchadnezzar deported King Jehoiachin and many others from Judah to Babylon. Jerusalem had not yet suffered its final destruction in 586 BC, but the nation's crisis was already devastating.
These people were not simply experiencing an unfortunate season.
They were living through the consequences of covenant unfaithfulness, national rebellion, and divine judgment, just as the prophets had warned.
And while they struggled to understand their suffering, false prophets were offering a message that sounded wonderfully encouraging.
The exile would end soon.
The painful season would be brief.
Everything would return to normal.
It was exactly the kind of message frightened people wanted to hear.
But it was not what God had said.
Through Jeremiah, the Lord confronted that false reassurance.

Instead of promising an immediate return, He told the exiles to build houses and live in them, plant gardens and eat their produce, marry, raise families, and seek the welfare of the city where they had been carried away.
Jeremiah 29:5–7.
Can you imagine how that sounded?
They wanted deliverance.
God told them to build.
They wanted escape.
God told them to plant.
They wanted Babylon to disappear.
God told them to pray for its welfare.
And then came the words that must be read before anyone claims Jeremiah 29:11.
“For thus saith the LORD, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.” — Jeremiah 29:10 (KJV)
Only after that comes the famous promise.
“For I know the thoughts that I think toward you…”
Do you see what happened?
We often begin reading at verse 11 because it feels comforting.
But God began His message much earlier, with instructions for faithfulness during a long and painful exile.
The promise was not an announcement that suffering would end tomorrow.
It was God's assurance that Babylon would not have the final word over His covenant purposes.
And the distinction changes everything.
Because sometimes the most dangerous misunderstanding of God's Word is not an obvious lie.
Sometimes it is a true sentence detached from the story that gives it meaning.
Consider the Hebrew.
The phrase commonly translated “thoughts” or “plans” comes from the Hebrew word מַחֲשָׁבוֹת (maḥăšāḇôṯ), the plural of maḥăšāḇâ, which can refer to thoughts, intentions, designs, or plans.
The word translated “peace” is שָׁלוֹם (shalom).
And shalom is richer than our everyday idea of feeling peaceful.
Depending on context, it can describe peace, well-being, welfare, completeness, and wholeness.
But there is something else.
God contrasts shalom with רָעָה (ra‘ah), a Hebrew word that can refer to evil, harm, calamity, or disaster, depending on its context.
In Jeremiah 29:11, the contrast concerns God's intended welfare for His people rather than their ultimate destruction.
And the final expression is especially significant.
אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה (aḥărîṯ wəṯiqwâ).
It speaks of a future or outcome and hope.
The King James Version renders it “an expected end.”
Modern translations often express the sense as “a future and a hope.”
This was not a secret Hebrew formula promising every individual believer financial success, career advancement, physical healing, or the fulfillment of personal ambitions.
It was God's assurance to an exiled people that His covenant purposes for them had not been extinguished.
The Lord had not forgotten them.
Their present humiliation was not the end of their national story.
His word would stand even when their circumstances seemed to contradict it.
And perhaps the most unsettling part is this.
God's promise of a hopeful future did not cancel the seventy-year wait.
He did not pretend the exile was painless.
He did not tell them that judgment was imaginary.
He did not encourage them to deny reality in the name of faith.
He told them the truth.
Then He gave them a reason to hope.

And that is where this passage begins speaking to our own hearts—not because we are the original recipients of the same national promise, but because we are learning what the God of Scripture is like.
He is truthful.
He is faithful.
He is not defeated by human failure.
And His purposes cannot be measured simply by how quickly our circumstances improve.
Somebody reading this has been silently measuring God's love by the speed of an answered prayer.
You prayed for the relationship.
It ended.
You prayed for the job.
Someone else got it.
You prayed for healing.
The medical report remained unchanged.
You prayed for your child to return to the Lord.
Years have passed, and the distance feels greater than ever.
You have tried to remain strong because everyone expects Christians to be strong.
You have smiled in church while carrying questions you are afraid to say out loud.
And maybe the question beneath all your questions is painfully simple.
“God, if You have good plans, why does my life hurt this much?”
That question deserves more than a slogan.
It deserves the whole counsel of Scripture.
Because Jeremiah 29:11 does not teach that faithful people will always experience comfortable circumstances.
It teaches, in its original setting, that God's declared purpose for the exiles' future was not erased by their present suffering.
