“Lord Jesus, You know what is in my heart. You know the jealousy I have hidden, the pride I have justified, the words I regret, and the people I have struggled to love. Forgive me. Teach me to celebrate what You are doing in others without despising what You are doing in me. Give me humility to confess my sin, courage to make things right where I can, and grace to forgive those who have wounded me. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. I surrender my heart to You. Change me, Lord. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects where you are today, I would love to hear from you.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Your story may encourage someone who has begun to believe that restoration is impossible.
Not because every sentence is easy to hear.
But because some truths need to be revisited when our hearts are tempted to compare, complain, or condemn.
And consider tagging someone who would genuinely appreciate this reminder of God's mercy. Let it be an invitation to hope, not a public accusation about their struggles.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
But to help people open the Bible, understand its meaning, confront the truth about sin, discover the grace of Jesus Christ, and grow into lives shaped by His Word.
There are people who are spiritually exhausted.
People who are curious about Jesus but afraid to ask questions.
People who have drifted from their faith.
People who need biblical truth without manipulation, encouragement without compromise, and reminders that repentance and grace belong together.
Your sharing and encouragement can help bring these messages to them.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment accessible to more people.
There is also a meaningful way to help sustain and expand this work.
It can be part of your personal giving in support of Christian ministry.
But it is important to understand this biblically.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
God is glorified by sincere generosity, not pressured giving.
And if you cannot contribute financially, you are no less valuable to God or to this community.
Your prayers, comments, encouragement, and willingness to share biblical truth are meaningful ways to participate in this mission.
These products are simply an added expression of appreciation. They are not the reason we preach Christ, and they are not a measure of anyone's spiritual maturity.
The heart of this invitation is discipleship.
More Scripture.
More encouragement.
More resources to help people grow.
More opportunities to place the message of repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and new life in Jesus before people who desperately need to hear it.
It is what happens between you and Jesus when you close this page.
Will you continue protecting the pride He is exposing?
Will you continue comparing your calling with someone else's?
Will you continue carrying bitterness that is slowly hardening your heart?
Or will you surrender?
Miriam's story began with words spoken against her brother.
It moved through the terrifying reality of divine judgment.
It brought a guilty brother to confession and a wounded brother to intercession.
And it ended with a woman being received again among her people.
But the greater story of Scripture takes us beyond the wilderness.
To a cross.
To an empty tomb.
To a risen Savior who calls sinners to come to Him.
The question that brought us here was why Miriam suffered a visible judgment while Aaron did not.
Scripture does not reveal every reason behind that difference.
But it reveals enough to leave us with something far more important than speculation.
God takes sin seriously.
God sees the heart.
God calls His people to humility.
And God's mercy is not exhausted by human failure.
So before you leave, ask yourself one final question.
If Jesus exposed the hidden condition of my heart today, would I spend my energy defending myself… or would I finally ask Him to heal me?
Because sometimes the most frightening thing is not being exposed.
It is becoming so comfortable with what is hidden that we no longer want to be changed.
And sometimes the beginning of restoration is a simple, trembling prayer:
“Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.”
The deepest tragedy is not that God sees the sin we have hidden. It is that we could walk away from His mercy still determined to hide it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HANNAH WAS LOVED BY HER HUSBAND… SO WHY DID GOD ALLOW ANOTHER WOMAN TO BREAK HER HEART?
paragraphs: HANNAH WAS LOVED BY HER HUSBAND… SO WHY DID GOD ALLOW ANOTHER WOMAN TO BREAK HER HEART?

The painful marriage story behind 1 Samuel 1 reveals what happens when love cannot heal your deepest wound, your rival knows exactly where to hurt you, and heaven seems silent while your tears keep falling.
Imagine being loved by someone who cannot understand why you are still crying.
Imagine sitting at a family table where everyone else seems to have what you have spent years begging God to give you.
Imagine watching another woman enjoy the very blessing you desperately desire.
Now imagine that woman knows your pain.
And instead of showing compassion, she uses it against you.
Not once.
Not accidentally.
Year after year.
And the hardest part?
The man who loves you sees your tears, tries to comfort you, and still cannot understand the depth of what is happening inside your heart.
That was Hannah's world.
Before she became the mother of Samuel, one of Israel's great prophets, she was a wounded woman living inside a complicated marriage.
Before her prayer became famous, her pain was familiar.
Before Scripture recorded her song of victory, it recorded her tears.
And hidden inside this ancient household is a truth that may confront everything you believe about unanswered prayer, marriage, jealousy, suffering, and the silence of God.
Because Hannah's story is not simply about a woman who wanted a baby.
It is about a woman who was loved but still hurting.
A woman who worshiped while wounded.
A woman whose rival could reach places her husband could not heal.
And a God who heard a prayer that no human being could even hear.
But to understand why Hannah suffered so deeply, we must first enter the marriage that made her suffering so complicated.
There were two women in one household. One had children. The other had her husband's special affection. Neither possessed everything she wanted.
First Samuel 1:2 introduces a man named Elkanah:
"He had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children." (1 Samuel 1:2, KJV)
Read that carefully.
The Bible introduces the women through a painful contrast.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah had none.
Later, Scripture reveals that Elkanah loved Hannah and gave her a special portion of the sacrificial meal.
The household contained two forms of blessing, but neither blessing guaranteed peace.
One woman possessed the motherhood Hannah longed for.
The other possessed a special place in Elkanah's affections.
And somewhere between those unequal circumstances, a rivalry grew.
We must be careful here. Scripture never explicitly says Peninnah was jealous of Elkanah's love for Hannah. It also does not tell us which woman Elkanah married first or why he married two women.
Those details are often supplied by preachers, dramatizations, and imagined backstories.
But they are not stated in 1 Samuel 1.
What Scripture does reveal is already heartbreaking enough.
Elkanah's polygamous household became the setting for deep relational suffering.
Polygamy existed in ancient Israel, and the Old Testament records its presence without portraying every recorded practice as God's ideal.
Jesus later directed attention back to God's creation design for marriage, where a man and woman become one flesh (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6).
The Bible does not ask us to romanticize the brokenness inside Elkanah's home.
It invites us to see what happened there.
Because a family can be religious and still be wounded.
A husband can be affectionate and still be unable to meet every emotional need.
A household can participate in worship while carrying years of unresolved cruelty.
And someone can sit beside you in a sacred place while silently fighting a battle you cannot see.
Peninnah had what Hannah wanted. But instead of becoming a source of compassion, she became a source of torment.
First Samuel 1:6 says:
"And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the LORD had shut up her womb." (KJV)
The Hebrew language makes the hostility especially striking.
The word translated "adversary" is צָרָתָהּ (tsaratah), referring to her rival or female adversary.
The verse also uses the Hebrew expression כַּעַס (ka'as), associated with vexation, irritation, and distress.
The text describes deliberate provocation.
Peninnah was not merely celebrating her own children.
She was intentionally distressing Hannah over her childlessness.
Think about the cruelty of that.
Hannah did not need anyone to remind her that she had no children.
She knew.
She knew when she woke up.
She knew when she saw other mothers.
She knew when another year passed.
She knew when she returned to worship carrying the same unanswered longing.
And Peninnah knew too.
Sometimes the deepest wounds are inflicted by people who know exactly where we are vulnerable.
Not every painful word comes from an enemy.
Sometimes it comes from someone sharing your home, your family gatherings, or your place of worship.
Someone who knows your history.
Someone who knows what you have been praying about.
Someone who knows what makes your voice tremble.
And instead of protecting that vulnerable place, they press against it.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
You have been asked why you are still single.
Why you have not had a child.
Why your marriage has not improved.
Why you are still struggling financially.
Why you have not recovered.
Why you are not as successful as someone else.
And the question sounds innocent to everyone listening.
But you know what it does to you.
You know the nights you have cried about it.
You know how many times you have already brought it before God.
You know how much strength it takes not to break down in front of everyone.
Hannah knew that pain.
But here is something important.
Peninnah's cruelty was her own moral responsibility. Hannah's suffering was not evidence that she deserved it.
Scripture says the Lord had closed Hannah's womb. That is part of the biblical narrative, and we should not erase it.
But the passage does not tell us why God permitted Hannah's childlessness for those years.
It does not say Hannah had committed some secret sin.
It does not say she lacked faith.
It does not say her suffering was punishment.
And it certainly does not say Peninnah was authorized to torment her.
The Bible distinguishes God's sovereignty from human cruelty.
God's authority over Hannah's circumstances did not make Peninnah's behavior righteous.
That distinction matters.
Because some wounded believers have been taught to interpret every painful circumstance as evidence that God is angry with them.
But Hannah's story does not support that conclusion.
Neither does the Gospel.
When Jesus encountered a man born blind, He rejected the assumption that the man's condition must have resulted from his own sin or his parents' sin (John 9:1–3).
Suffering is not a reliable measurement of someone's spiritual standing.
And infertility is never a measure of a woman's worth.
Hannah was not less valuable because she had no child.
Her dignity did not begin when Samuel was born.
She was already a person worthy of compassion before her circumstances changed.
Please hear that.
You do not have to receive the blessing you are waiting for before your life becomes precious to God.
Now consider the timing of Peninnah's provocation.
First Samuel 1:7 says this continued year after year, especially as the family went up to the house of the Lord.
The place where Hannah came to worship was also a place where her grief intensified.
Imagine preparing for a sacred journey.
Perhaps hoping this year would be different.
Perhaps telling yourself you would remain strong.
Perhaps believing you could get through the gathering without crying.
Then the familiar hostility begins.
A remark.
A comparison.
A reminder.
And suddenly the pain you tried to contain rises to the surface.
Scripture tells us Hannah wept and would not eat.
Her suffering affected her appetite.
It affected her participation in a family celebration.
It affected the way she experienced what should have been a joyful occasion.
This was not a passing disappointment.
It was persistent grief.
And then Elkanah spoke.
His words are among the most revealing sentences in the entire story.
"Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?" (1 Samuel 1:8, KJV)
There is tenderness in his concern.
He notices her tears.
He wants her to eat.
He wants her to recognize his love.
But there is also a painful limitation in his question.
Elkanah seems to believe that his affection should be enough to comfort her.
He cannot fully understand why the love he offers does not remove the grief she carries.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Have you ever been loved and still felt lonely?
Have you ever had people tell you how blessed you were while you were silently grieving something they could not replace?
Have you ever heard someone say, "But you have so much to be thankful for," when you were trying to explain the one thing that kept breaking your heart?
Gratitude and grief can exist together.
Love and longing can exist together.
Faith and tears can exist together.
Hannah could appreciate her husband without pretending her desire for a child had disappeared.
And Elkanah's love, however genuine, could not solve everything.
There are wounds a spouse cannot heal.
There are burdens a friend cannot remove.
There are questions no human reassurance can fully answer.
That does not make human love worthless.
It simply reminds us that human love is limited.
Only God can occupy the place that belongs to God.
But even that truth must be handled carefully.
We should never use spiritual language to dismiss another person's pain.
Telling someone to trust God is not a substitute for listening.
Quoting Scripture is not permission to ignore cruelty.
And encouraging prayer does not excuse a family from its responsibility to protect someone who is being mistreated.
Elkanah's household needed more than religious activity.
It needed compassion and righteousness.
Then Hannah did something that changed the direction of her story.
She got up.
First Samuel 1:9 records that after the meal at Shiloh, Hannah rose.
It is a small movement in the narrative.
But it leads to one of the most moving prayers in Scripture.
She went before the Lord.
Not because the problem had been resolved.
Not because Peninnah had apologized.
Not because Elkanah finally understood everything.
Not because she had received a promise that she would conceive.
She went while she was still hurting.
First Samuel 1:10 says:
"And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is מָרַת נָפֶשׁ (marat nefesh), describing a person deeply embittered or distressed in soul.
It does not mean Hannah was necessarily bitter against God.
It describes the anguish of her condition.
This was not a polished prayer.
It was not a performance.
It was not a carefully rehearsed speech designed to impress religious people.
It was the cry of a wounded woman.
And something extraordinary happened.
Her lips moved.
But her voice was not heard.
Eli, the priest, watched her and wrongly assumed she was drunk.
Think about that.
Hannah had been misunderstood at home.
Now she was misunderstood at the sanctuary.
The woman who came to pour out her heart before God was accused of behaving shamefully.
Even in a sacred place, someone misread her suffering.
Perhaps you have experienced something similar.
You finally gathered enough courage to speak.
And someone judged your tears.
You tried to explain your exhaustion.
And someone called you dramatic.
You admitted that you were struggling.
And someone questioned your faith.
Hannah could have withdrawn.
She could have allowed Eli's accusation to silence her.
Instead, she answered with dignity.
"No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD." (1 Samuel 1:15, KJV)
"I have poured out my soul before the LORD."
The Hebrew wording includes וָאֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת־נַפְשִׁי (va'eshpokh et-nafshi).
The verb conveys pouring out.
Her nefesh—her soul, her very self—was being poured before God.
What an image.
Not hiding the pain.
Not disguising the disappointment.
Not pretending everything was fine.
Pouring it out.
Some of us have become experts at appearing strong.
We know how to smile at church.
We know how to answer, "I'm blessed."
We know how to encourage everyone else.
We know how to post Bible verses while carrying private grief.
But there comes a moment when the soul grows tired of pretending.
Hannah teaches us that reverence does not require emotional dishonesty.
You can approach God with trembling faith.
You can pray while crying.
You can worship without understanding.
You can bring Him questions you do not know how to answer.
The Psalms repeatedly demonstrate that faithful prayer can include lament, confusion, sorrow, and desperate appeals for help.
God does not require you to manufacture happiness before coming to Him.
He calls you to come truthfully.
And here is the detail that should stop us.
Hannah's circumstances had not yet changed when her countenance changed.
After Eli spoke a blessing over her, Scripture says:
"So the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad." (1 Samuel 1:18, KJV)
She had not yet conceived.
She had not yet held Samuel.
She had not yet watched Peninnah's provocation lose its power.
She had prayed.
She had received a word of blessing.
And she went away able to eat again.
We should not pretend this means every believer will immediately feel better after praying.
The Bible does not promise that every episode of grief will disappear in one moment.
But Hannah's experience shows something beautiful.
Her circumstances remained unresolved, yet she was no longer carrying her sorrow in exactly the same way.
Prayer had become the place where her anguish was brought into God's presence.
Sometimes God's people experience peace before they receive an answer.
Sometimes they must continue trusting while the pain remains.
And sometimes the faithful thing is to seek help, receive comfort, and keep walking one day at a time.
None of those experiences makes a believer less loved.
Now we must confront one of the most difficult questions in Hannah's story.
Why did God allow the suffering to continue for so long?
The text does not give us a complete explanation.
And we must resist the temptation to invent one.
It would be easy to declare that God allowed Peninnah to torment Hannah specifically to make her pray harder.
But Scripture never says that.
It would be easy to claim that every painful rival is secretly assigned by God to push someone toward destiny.
But the Bible does not teach that as a universal principle.
It would also be dangerous to suggest that abuse or cruelty should simply be endured because God might use it.
God can work redemptively through suffering without approving the evil that causes it.
What we can say is that the Lord heard Hannah.
First Samuel 1:19 records that the Lord remembered her.
In biblical language, divine remembrance does not imply that God had forgotten her existence.
It expresses His purposeful attention and action.
The Hebrew verb זָכַר (zakhar) means to remember, and in this context it introduces God's gracious response to Hannah.
The narrative continues:

"Wherefore it came to pass, when the time was come about after Hannah had conceived, that she bare a son, and called his name Samuel, saying, Because I have asked him of the LORD." (1 Samuel 1:20, KJV)
Hannah received the child for whom she had prayed.
But notice what Scripture does not teach.
It does not teach that every woman who prays like Hannah will conceive.
It does not teach that childlessness is always temporary.
It does not teach that enough tears, faith, or vows can compel God to grant a specific request.
Hannah's experience is a true account of God's action in her life, not a formula that guarantees identical outcomes for everyone.
And that matters profoundly for those who have prayed for years and are still waiting.
For the woman who has endured another disappointing medical appointment.
For the couple who has quietly grieved pregnancy loss.
For the person whose marriage did not survive.
For the believer who prayed for healing and still lives with illness.
For the parent whose child has not returned home.
For the person who prayed for a loved one who nevertheless died.
Hannah's story should never become another Peninnah-like weapon against someone who is suffering.
We must not use her answered prayer to shame those whose prayers remain unanswered.
The Christian hope is greater than the promise of receiving every earthly blessing we desire.
It is the promise that God has acted decisively for our salvation through Jesus Christ and will ultimately make all things new.
And this is where Hannah's story opens into something much larger than one household.
Hannah's son Samuel would become a prophet and judge in Israel.
He would later anoint David as king.
And from David's royal line, according to the Scriptures, the Messiah would come.
Hannah could not have seen the full historical significance of the child she held.
She knew she had prayed.
She knew God had answered.
She knew the boy belonged ultimately to the Lord.
And she honored her vow by bringing Samuel to serve at the sanctuary under Eli's care.
Her prayer had begun with a request for a son.
Her response to God's answer became an act of dedication.
Then, in 1 Samuel 2, Hannah sang.
The woman introduced through weeping became a woman whose words proclaimed the holiness, sovereignty, and saving power of God.
Her song declares:
"There is none holy as the LORD: for there is none beside thee: neither is there any rock like our God." (1 Samuel 2:2, KJV)
And later:
"He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory." (1 Samuel 2:8, KJV)
Her song celebrates the God who overturns human pride and lifts the lowly.
Centuries later, Mary's song in Luke 1 would echo strikingly similar themes.
Mary rejoiced in the God who regards the humble and reverses human expectations.
Through Mary, Jesus Christ entered the world.
And in Jesus, we encounter the deepest fulfillment of the hope that runs through Scripture.
Not merely that God can reverse earthly circumstances.
But that God has come to rescue sinners.
That grace reaches people who cannot save themselves.
That the proud are called to repentance.
That the broken are invited to come.
That forgiveness is available through the crucified and risen Savior.
And that death itself will not have the final word.
Hannah's story is not a direct prophecy that every wounded person will receive a Samuel.
But it belongs to the biblical story that ultimately leads us to Christ.
And there is another connection we dare not miss.
Hannah was misunderstood by a priest who thought her distress was drunkenness.
Jesus, our great High Priest, is not ignorant of human weakness.
Hebrews 4:15–16 teaches that Christ can sympathize with our weaknesses and invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence.
Hannah came to the sanctuary with a burden that human beings struggled to understand.
Through Christ, believers have access to the Father, whose mercy does not depend on our ability to explain our pain perfectly.
And Jesus knows suffering from the inside.
He was rejected.
He was falsely accused.
He was mocked.
He was betrayed.
He wept.
He endured the cross.
Not because He was powerless, but because He willingly gave Himself to accomplish our redemption.
The cross tells us something Hannah's story alone cannot fully reveal.
God's love is not measured by how quickly He removes our suffering. It is revealed supremely in the Savior who gave Himself for us.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Before you were healed.
Before you understood.
Before your life became orderly.
Before you knew how to pray properly.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not that Jesus exists to fulfill every desire we bring to Him.
But that through His death and resurrection, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life to all who repent and believe.
This is why our theme is more than a memorable phrase.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending our wounds never happened.
He redeems sinners.
He restores our relationship with God.
He transforms lives through His Spirit.
And He promises a future in which sorrow and death will finally be defeated.
Hannah's marriage story also contains a warning we must not overlook.
Do not become Peninnah in someone else's story.
Do not turn another person's unanswered prayer into a comparison.
Do not use your marriage to shame someone who is single.
Do not use your children to diminish someone struggling with infertility.
Do not use your financial success to humiliate someone who is poor.
Do not use your ministry, knowledge, or spiritual experiences to make another believer feel worthless.
And do not assume that because God has blessed you in one area, you are spiritually superior to someone who has not received the same blessing.
Peninnah had children.
That was a blessing.
But possessing a blessing did not justify her cruelty.
A gift from God should never become a weapon against another human being.
And if you recognize yourself in Peninnah's behavior, the answer is not to hide behind excuses.
Repent.
Confess the wrong.
Stop the cruelty.
Where appropriate and safe, seek to make things right with those you have hurt.
The Gospel does not merely comfort victims of sin.
It also calls those who commit sin to turn from it.
Perhaps you identify more with Elkanah.
You genuinely love someone.
You want to help.
You cannot understand why your affection has not fixed their sadness.
Then learn from his limitations.
Sometimes the most loving response is not another explanation.
It is listening.
It is refusing to minimize grief.
It is taking mistreatment seriously.
It is acknowledging that someone's pain may be real even when you cannot personally experience it.
And perhaps you are Hannah.
You are tired.
You have been faithful in ways nobody notices.
You have prayed prayers nobody has heard.
You have watched other people celebrate blessings you are still waiting for.
You have tried to rejoice with those who rejoice, even when their joy reminds you of your own grief.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you feel guilty for hurting.
You think a stronger Christian would not cry so much.
You think a more faithful believer would have stopped asking questions.
You think your sadness means you have disappointed God.
But remember Hannah.
She wept.
She could not eat.
She prayed out of anguish.
And Scripture did not erase her tears to make her faith look impressive.
Her tears are part of the testimony.
Your tears are not proof that you have abandoned God.
The question is what you will do with your pain.
Will you allow it to become bitterness toward others?
Will you let comparison determine your worth?
Will you begin believing that God owes you the exact life someone else has received?
Or will you bring your wounded heart honestly before the Lord?
Not with a demand that He follow your timetable.
Not with a bargain that tries to purchase His favor.
But with faith that says:
"Lord, You know what I desire. You know what I have endured. You know what I cannot explain. Teach me to trust You, even when I do not understand."
That is not a weak prayer.
It is a deeply human prayer of surrender.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not mistake Christianity for a promise that your circumstances will immediately improve.
Jesus calls us to something greater and more costly.
Repent of sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Him.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And learn to live under His lordship, whether the season brings abundance or loss.
Because the greatest miracle in Hannah's story was not that human worth could finally be established through childbirth.
Her worth was never dependent on childbirth.
The extraordinary gift was that God acted graciously in her circumstances and incorporated her family into His unfolding purposes for Israel.
And the greater miracle offered through Christ is that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
That is the grace worth proclaiming.
That is the truth worth carrying into a wounded world.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with emotional religious content that disappears when they close their phones.
But to keep directing hearts back to Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, biblical discipleship, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who look completely fine.
But privately, they are Hannah.
Their marriages are struggling.
Their prayers seem unanswered.
Their families do not understand them.
Their faith is exhausted.
And sometimes one biblically faithful message reaches them at the moment they are ready to give up.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
But because truth shared with love can reach someone who might never walk into a church or ask openly for prayer.
You do not have to share private details.

And if God has carried you through a season of grief, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading silently may need to know that faithful people can struggle, weep, seek help, and still find strength in the Lord.
And if these messages have helped you grow in faith, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
It can help keep Scripture-centered encouragement reaching people who need it.
It can support the development of teaching materials.
It can help make discipleship resources more accessible.
And it can allow you to participate in a shared effort to proclaim Christ faithfully.
Those free resources remain an important part of our mission.
These products are simply resources and reminders. They are not measures of spiritual maturity, and purchasing them is never a condition of receiving God's grace.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share the truth matters.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
And the purpose of every faithful Christian ministry should be to point people toward Him, not make people dependent on the ministry itself.
Now, before you leave, return with me to Hannah.
Picture her one more time.
Not holding Samuel.
Not singing her song.
Not standing in the moment of answered prayer.
Picture her earlier.
In the sanctuary.
Her lips moving.
Her eyes wet.
Her heart aching.
A priest misunderstanding her.
A rival tormenting her.
A husband unable to remove her grief.
And no child yet in her arms.
She did not know what the next chapter would contain.
She did not know how her story would be remembered.
She did not know that generations of wounded believers would someday read about her tears and find courage to pray.
All she knew was that she needed God.
And she came.
That may be the most important part of her story for you today.
Not the moment she received what she wanted.
But the moment she brought her broken heart before the Lord without knowing what He would do next.
Because some of you are still living in that moment.
You have not received the answer.
The relationship has not been restored.
The diagnosis has not changed.
The grief has not disappeared.
The person who hurt you has not apologized.
And you are wondering whether God still sees you.
The Gospel does not authorize me to promise that tomorrow everything will change.
But it gives me every reason to point you toward Jesus Christ.
The Savior who knows suffering.
The Lord who welcomes the weary.
The Redeemer who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness.
The risen King who will one day make all things new.
So come to Him.
Not because your tears guarantee a particular outcome.
But because He is worthy of your trust even when the outcome is unknown.
Come with your questions.
Come with your repentance.
Come with your exhaustion.
Come with your longing.
Come with the parts of your story you are afraid to say aloud.
And remember this:
Hannah's unanswered years did not mean she was unseen, and your unfinished story does not mean Christ has abandoned you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU CAN SPEAK IN TONGUES, PROPHESY, UNDERSTAND THE MYSTERIES OF GOD—AND STILL HEAR JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
paragraphs: YOU CAN SPEAK IN TONGUES, PROPHESY, UNDERSTAND THE MYSTERIES OF GOD—AND STILL HEAR JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
The most terrifying spiritual tragedy is not having no gifts from God. It is becoming so impressed with what happens through you that you stop examining what is happening inside you.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.

Not before your pastor. Not before the people who admired your ministry. Not before the thousands who shared your sermons, listened to your prophecies, or testified that your prayers changed their lives.
Before Jesus.
The One who sees what nobody else could see.
And for the first time, there is no microphone to hold. No spiritual language to impress anyone. No ministry title to introduce yourself with. No crowd to confirm how anointed you were.
Only you.
And the Lord who knows you completely.
You begin remembering everything you did in His name.
The prayers. The prophecies. The fasting. The spiritual encounters. The people who called you a mighty man or woman of God.
Surely all of that must mean something.
Then you remember the words Jesus spoke in Matthew 7:22–23.
“Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?”
And His answer:
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Read those words again.
“I never knew you.”
Not, “You never preached.”
Not, “You never performed impressive works.”
Not even, “You never used My name.”
The warning is far more devastating.
You can be surrounded by religious activity and still be spiritually lost.
You can become familiar with the language of heaven while remaining unwilling to surrender the hidden chambers of your heart.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you might not realize it until everything you trusted to prove your spirituality is exposed as insufficient.
But before you assume this article is about some famous preacher who fell into scandal, some arrogant prophet, or some religious person you know, consider something.
What if the Holy Spirit is asking you to examine yourself?
Not because Jesus wants to destroy you.
But because He loves you too much to let you confuse spiritual performance with a living relationship with Him.
Because there is something more important than being gifted.
Being known by Christ—and belonging to Him.
The apostle Paul understood this danger.
He wrote to a church overflowing with spiritual activity, theological disputes, impressive gifts, and competing claims of spiritual maturity.
The church in Corinth.
These were not people unfamiliar with spiritual gifts.
Paul acknowledged that they were not lacking in any spiritual gift as they waited for Christ's revelation (1 Corinthians 1:7).

Yet this same congregation struggled with division, jealousy, pride, sexual immorality, lawsuits among believers, disorder in worship, and humiliating treatment of poorer members during the Lord's Supper.
They had spiritual gifts.
But their conduct often contradicted the character of the Savior they claimed to follow.
And into that contradiction, Paul spoke words that should still shake the modern church.
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.”
—1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV
The Greek word translated “charity” in the King James Version is ἀγάπη (agápē).
Love.
But not merely sentimental affection.
Not simply being polite, agreeable, or emotionally warm.
In Paul's argument, this love expresses itself through patience, kindness, humility, truthfulness, endurance, and concern for the good of others.
It reflects the character of the God who loved us while we were still sinners.
Paul continues:
“And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
—1 Corinthians 13:2, KJV
Nothing.
The Greek expression is οὐθέν εἰμι (outhén eimi).
“I am nothing.”
Paul does not say spiritual gifts are evil.
He does not say prophecy is worthless or that speaking in tongues should be despised.
In fact, he explicitly instructs believers to pursue love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 14:1).
His warning is that gifts without love cannot establish genuine spiritual greatness.
The most impressive manifestation cannot substitute for the character of Christ.
You can speak eloquently about God's holiness while secretly enjoying another person's humiliation.
You can explain the mysteries of Scripture while refusing to forgive someone who wounded your pride.
You can preach repentance to a congregation and spend the evening defending the very sin God has been confronting in your private life.
You can pray loudly in public while refusing to apologize quietly at home.
You can call fire down in your prayers and still have a heart that has grown cold toward the people nearest to you.
And perhaps you have never stood behind a pulpit.
But when someone disagrees with you, something ugly rises inside.
Contempt.
Cruelty.
The satisfaction of making another person look foolish.
And suddenly, the question is no longer whether you know the right verses.
The question is whether those verses have been allowed to confront you.
Because knowing what the Bible says and submitting to what the Bible says are not the same thing.
James warned believers against becoming hearers of the Word without becoming doers (James 1:22).
And Jesus asked a question that still reaches beyond church buildings, denominations, and generations:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
—Luke 6:46, KJV
That question is uncomfortable.
Because it does not allow us to hide behind religious vocabulary.
Jesus is not impressed by the title “Lord” on our lips when our lives persistently refuse His authority.
And this is where we need to be careful.
We must not confuse spiritual gifts with spiritual fruit.
The gifts of the Spirit are discussed in passages such as 1 Corinthians 12.
The fruit of the Spirit is described in Galatians 5:22–23.
Love. Joy. Peace. Longsuffering. Gentleness. Goodness. Faithfulness. Meekness. Temperance.
Gifts are graciously given for service and the building up of Christ's body.
Fruit reflects the Spirit's transforming work in the believer's character.
They are not enemies.
They are not interchangeable.
And neither should be used to replace Jesus Himself.
A person may possess remarkable speaking ability and still be immature.
Someone may demonstrate extraordinary biblical knowledge and still struggle with pride.
A person may be publicly admired for ministry while privately resisting correction.
This does not mean every gifted believer is secretly hypocritical.
It means no believer should mistake giftedness for permission to stop growing in holiness.
The same God who calls us to serve also calls us to repent.
The same Spirit who empowers ministry produces love.
And the same Jesus who sends His people into the world commands them to abide in Him.
Jesus said:
“Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.”
—John 15:4, KJV
The Greek verb translated “abide” is μένω (ménō).
It carries the sense of remaining, continuing, or staying.
Jesus was not describing a momentary emotional experience.
He was describing ongoing dependence upon Him.
A branch does not produce life by announcing how closely connected it is to the vine.
It bears fruit because it remains connected.
And that is where many of us need to examine our hearts.
We have become very good at appearing connected.
We know how to sound spiritual.
We know which Bible verses to post.
We know when to say “Amen.”
We know how to lift our hands when the music reaches its most emotional moment.
But when the music stops, when nobody is watching, when obedience becomes costly, when forgiveness feels unfair, when temptation offers something our flesh desperately wants—
Who are we then?
Not who do we pretend to be.
Who are we becoming?
There is a kind of religious life that can become an elaborate hiding place.
A man may lead powerful prayers at church while his wife quietly cries because he refuses to listen to her.
A woman may encourage hundreds of strangers online while carrying bitterness she refuses to bring before God.
A ministry leader may preach against greed while privately measuring every relationship by what it can contribute to his platform.
A Bible teacher may explain grace beautifully while showing none to the person who made an honest mistake.
And someone reading this may be thinking:
“I used to be different.”
You remember when you first encountered the mercy of Jesus.
You did not care whether anyone noticed your prayers.
You were simply grateful that God heard them.
You did not need a title.
You were amazed to be forgiven.
You did not measure your spiritual life by influence.
You measured your days by how desperately you needed the Savior.
Somewhere along the way, perhaps the work of ministry became louder than the voice of the Master.
You started protecting an image instead of confessing your struggles.
You learned how to speak about brokenness without admitting your own.
You became afraid that if people saw your weakness, they would stop respecting you.
So you kept serving.
Kept posting.
Kept preaching.
Kept smiling.
While something inside you was quietly starving.
And now the question you are afraid to ask is rising again.
Have I been doing things for Jesus while drifting away from Jesus?
There is a moment in Luke 10 that speaks powerfully to this fear.
Jesus sent out seventy disciples, according to the traditional Greek text reflected in the King James Version. Some ancient manuscripts read seventy-two.
They returned rejoicing that even demons were subject to them through His name.
Imagine their excitement.
They had witnessed extraordinary spiritual authority.
But Jesus redirected their joy.
“Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.”
—Luke 10:20, KJV
What a correction.
Jesus did not deny the reality of what they had experienced.
He redirected them toward a greater reason for rejoicing.
Not spiritual power.
Not public success.
Not supernatural experiences.
But their standing before God.
Your deepest joy must never rest in how much spiritual power people believe you possess.
It must rest in the saving grace of God.
And if that truth does not humble us, we have not understood it deeply enough.
Because salvation is not an achievement we present to Jesus.
It is mercy we receive through Him.
Paul wrote:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
—Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (cháris).
God's gracious favor and gift.
We are not saved because our sermons were powerful.
Not because our prayers sounded impressive.
Not because we accumulated enough spiritual accomplishments.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the very next verse teaches that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Good works matter.
Obedience matters.
Holiness matters.
Love matters.
But they are not the price by which we purchase salvation.
They are part of the life God creates in those who belong to Christ.
This distinction is everything.
Because without it, a message about love can become another exhausting attempt to earn God's acceptance.
You begin thinking you must become perfectly patient before Jesus will receive you.
Perfectly gentle before you can approach Him.
Perfectly pure before you can ask for forgiveness.
But the Gospel does not tell sinners to repair themselves and then approach the Savior.
It calls sinners to repent and believe in the Savior who died and rose again.
And His grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live in a way that honors Him (Titus 2:11–14).
Consider Peter.
He was bold.
Passionate.
Quick to speak.
He confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16).
He witnessed the transfiguration.
He walked on water toward Jesus.
He promised loyalty even unto death.
And then, on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Luke records that after Peter's third denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.”
—Luke 22:62, KJV
Imagine that moment.
The man who had spoken so confidently about his devotion was suddenly confronted with his own weakness.
His words had collapsed.
His courage had failed.
And the Savior he had promised never to abandon was being led toward suffering.
What could Peter possibly say?
What explanation would make his denial acceptable?
There was none.
Only tears.
Only failure.
Only the terrible realization that he was not as strong as he believed.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus met His disciples beside the Sea of Tiberias.
And in John 21, Jesus asked Peter a question.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
Not, “Peter, how many people will follow your ministry?”
Not, “Peter, can you explain every mystery?”
Not, “Peter, can you prove how powerful you are?”
“Lovest thou me?”
Three times, Jesus questioned Peter about his love, and three times Peter responded.

The exchange is rich with meaning, but we should avoid a popular oversimplification: although the Greek text uses both ἀγαπάω (agapáō) and φιλέω (philéō), John's Gospel sometimes uses these verbs interchangeably. We cannot confidently build the entire meaning of Peter's restoration upon a supposed sharp contrast between two different levels of love.
What the passage clearly reveals is more than enough.
The risen Christ confronted the disciple who had denied Him.
And He restored Peter to the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
“Feed my sheep.”
—John 21:17, KJV
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
Christ's mercy was greater.
And the restoration did not end with a comforting conversation.
Jesus called Peter to follow Him, even along a path that would involve suffering.
Grace was not permission to return to self-confidence.
Grace was an invitation into renewed obedience.
That is the Gospel.
Not the denial of sin.
Not the celebration of scandal.
Not the claim that consequences never matter.
But the breathtaking truth that Jesus Christ can redeem sinners who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
You may have been spiritually proud.
You may have confused ministry success with intimacy with God.
You may have wounded people while claiming to defend the truth.
You may have used your knowledge of Scripture to win arguments rather than love your neighbor.
You may have been hiding behind your reputation because admitting your sin feels unbearable.
But if the Lord is exposing your heart through His Word, do not waste that mercy by defending yourself.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek forgiveness from those you have wronged.
Make restitution where it is appropriate and possible.
Accept accountability.
Turn away from what is destroying your fellowship with God and harming others.
And come to Jesus.
Not with a résumé.
Not with a list of spiritual achievements.
Not with a carefully prepared explanation of why your behavior was understandable.
Come with empty hands.
Because the hands that were pierced for sinners are more than sufficient to receive those who turn to Him.
The apostle John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
The Greek verb translated “confess,” ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), is a form of ὁμολογέω (homologéō), meaning to acknowledge or confess.
Confession is not merely feeling embarrassed that we were caught.
It is agreeing with the truth about our sin before God.
No more disguising pride as discernment.
No more calling cruelty boldness.
No more confusing attention with anointing.
No more treating ministry activity as a substitute for private obedience.
No more pretending that because God has used us, He must approve of everything we do.
And no more believing that our failures are beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
There is room at the cross for repentant sinners.
But there is no room at the cross for boasting.
And this is why 1 Corinthians 13 is so much more than a beautiful passage read at weddings.
It is a confrontation.
A mirror.
A summons to become more like Jesus.
“Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up.”
—1 Corinthians 13:4, KJV
Read that slowly.
Love is patient.
When someone disappoints you.
Love is kind.
When you have enough information to humiliate someone but choose to speak truth without cruelty.
Love does not envy.
When another person's ministry grows faster than yours.
Love does not boast.
When God gives you opportunities others may never receive.
Love is not arrogant.
When you know more Scripture than the person asking a sincere question.
Love rejoices in the truth.
Even when the truth exposes your own sin.
Love does not excuse evil or demand silence from those who have been harmed. Biblical love stands with truth, protects the vulnerable, and refuses to use spiritual language to conceal wrongdoing.
And above all, biblical love is not merely an ideal we admire.
It is displayed supremely in Jesus Christ.
The One who washed His disciples' feet.
The One who touched the unclean.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who spoke with uncompromising truth to religious hypocrites.
The One who willingly laid down His life.
Paul declared:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
That is the love we are called to reflect.
Not a manufactured sweetness that refuses to confront sin.
Not a performative kindness designed to earn applause.
Not an emotional experience that disappears when obedience becomes difficult.
Christlike love is grounded in truth, shaped by holiness, and sustained by grace.
It costs something.
Sometimes it costs your pride.
Sometimes it costs your reputation.
Sometimes it costs the satisfaction of winning an argument.
Sometimes it requires you to say three words your ego has been resisting for years.
“I was wrong.”
Or four words that might begin a long-overdue healing process.
“Will you forgive me?”
Perhaps the person who needs to hear those words is sitting in the same house as you.
Perhaps your children know how passionately you worship but rarely experience your gentleness.
Perhaps your spouse has heard you speak beautifully about grace while waiting years to receive an apology.
Perhaps someone left the church wounded by the way you treated them, and you have been calling their departure rebellion because admitting your responsibility would be painful.
If this is exposing something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Sit with the question.
What is the Holy Spirit calling you to surrender?
Not to impress anyone with a public confession.
Not to reveal private sins that should be addressed safely and appropriately.
But as a simple acknowledgment that you want the truth of Christ to reach beyond your outward appearance.
There are believers who need to know they are not the only ones struggling.
And sometimes a humble request for prayer is the beginning of a conversation someone has been afraid to start.
But do not stop at a comment.
Let the conviction become obedience.
Let the prayer become repentance.
Let the repentance produce fruit.
Because Jesus is not calling us to perform vulnerability for an audience.
He is calling us to follow Him.
There is another warning in Paul's words that we cannot afford to ignore.
“And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.”
—1 Corinthians 13:3, KJV
Even extraordinary sacrifice can be corrupted by the wrong motives.
A person may give generously and still crave admiration.
A ministry may accomplish visible good while its leaders neglect humility and accountability.
A Christian may sacrifice time, money, and comfort while secretly believing those sacrifices make them superior to others.
And it is why financial generosity must never be presented as a way to purchase God's favor.
Jesus does not sell salvation.
The Holy Spirit is not a reward for financial contributions.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not coerced.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The Greek word ἀνάγκη (anánkē), translated “necessity,” can convey compulsion or constraint.
Paul's instruction protects the freedom and sincerity of Christian generosity.

So if Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, recognize hidden sin, rediscover the mercy of Jesus, or grow in your walk with Christ, there is a meaningful opportunity to help carry that work further.
Not because financial support guarantees spiritual blessing.
But because you freely believe that Scripture-centered encouragement, Gospel proclamation, and discipleship resources are worth helping others receive.
What matters is that the decision comes from faith, wisdom, genuine willingness, and love.
And there is something beautiful about knowing that a resource which strengthened you today might reach someone tomorrow who is quietly losing hope.
Someone sitting alone after a terrible mistake.
Someone afraid to return to church.
Someone convinced that their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has never truly understood why Jesus died on the cross.
Someone who needs to discover that repentance is not the end of their story.
Christ is.
These resources are part of a wider mission to make biblical encouragement and spiritual nourishment accessible, including to people who cannot afford paid materials.
These are expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards or promises of divine favor.
The greater purpose remains the same.
To make much of Jesus.
To help people encounter the truth of Scripture.
To encourage genuine repentance, lasting discipleship, and lives increasingly transformed by the grace of God.
You can still help.
Not merely to increase a page's reach, but because someone among your friends may need its message.
A person who has spent years mistaking religious activity for a relationship with Jesus.
A believer who has grown weary of pretending.
A ministry worker who needs to rediscover the joy of simply belonging to Christ.
A friend who has wandered far from God and no longer believes restoration is possible.
But never forget this.
The mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Jesus Christ known.
If a ministry becomes more concerned with its own influence than with faithfulness to Christ, it has lost sight of its calling.
If a Christian becomes more interested in being admired than in being transformed, something is terribly wrong.
And if we preach grace to the world but refuse to extend grace to repentant people, we contradict the very Gospel we claim to defend.
The church does not need more spiritual celebrities.
It needs disciples who love Jesus.
It needs believers who will speak truth without arrogance.
People who will serve when nobody applauds.
People who will confess sin without manufacturing excuses.
People who will protect the vulnerable rather than defend wrongdoing for the sake of a ministry's reputation.
People who will open their Bibles not merely to prepare another post, but to hear and obey the Lord.
People who understand that the purpose of spiritual gifts is not self-exaltation but service.
People who remember that the greatest commandment is to love God with all their heart, soul, and mind, and the second is to love their neighbor as themselves (Matthew 22:37–39).
And above all, people who understand that their hope rests not in their own greatness but in the crucified and risen Christ.
There is a reason Paul could write so powerfully about love.
His own life had been radically interrupted by grace.
Before becoming an apostle, Paul persecuted the church of God.
He knew what it meant to be religiously zealous and tragically wrong.
He knew Scripture.
He had convictions.
He believed he was defending what was holy.
Yet he was opposing the very Messiah whom the Scriptures proclaimed.
Then the risen Jesus confronted him.
And the persecutor became a servant of the One he had persecuted.
Paul would later write:
—1 Corinthians 15:10, KJV
Not by his intellectual brilliance.
Not by his religious credentials.
Not by his impressive accomplishments.
By the grace of God.
That is the confession every believer must return to.
The preacher.
The worship leader.
The prophet.
The teacher.
The new Christian.
The exhausted parent.
The person who has served faithfully for decades.
The person who has just returned to church after years of running.
We stand in need of the same Savior.
And the Gospel is not that spiritually impressive people finally become worthy of God's attention.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He is not merely a moral example.
He is the Savior and Lord.
And through Him, sinners are called to repent, believe, receive forgiveness, and walk in newness of life.
That is why the words “I never knew you” should not drive us toward frantic attempts to manufacture spiritual achievements.
They should drive us toward Jesus Himself.
Toward genuine faith.
Toward repentance.
Toward obedience that flows from grace.
Toward the love that the Spirit produces in those who belong to Christ.
Because on the day we stand before Him, no number of followers can save us.
No ministry title can justify us.
No record of religious accomplishments can take the place of His righteousness.
Our only sufficient hope is Jesus Christ.
And those who truly belong to Him are called to follow Him.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one final question.
Not whether people think you are spiritual.
Not whether you can quote more verses than someone else.
Not whether your prayers move a congregation.
Not whether your posts receive thousands of reactions.
Ask yourself:
Am I trusting in Jesus Christ, and is His grace changing the way I live and love?
If the answer exposes something painful, do not despair.
The purpose of conviction is not to leave the repentant sinner hopeless.
It is to bring what is hidden into the light of God's truth.
You can turn to Christ today.
You can ask Him for mercy.
You can begin making things right.
You can stop defending the sin that has been destroying you.
You can ask trusted believers to walk with you in accountability and prayer.
And if you have fallen, you do not have to pretend that the fall never happened in order to seek restoration.
Jesus knows the truth already.
Come to Him with it.
“Christ is still healing me.”
And if you are struggling to believe that restoration is possible, write:
Not as a declaration of confidence in your own strength, but as a prayerful acknowledgment that you are looking to Christ and refusing to abandon the hope of His Gospel.
Let others pray with you.
Let the Word confront you.
Let grace humble you.
And let love become more than something you preach.
Let it become something people experience when they encounter your life.
Because the world has heard enough Christians proclaim that God is love while treating people as though love were optional.
May they see something different in us.
May they see truth with compassion.
Conviction with humility.
Holiness without hypocrisy.
Courage without cruelty.
Repentance without excuses.
Grace without compromise.
And through all of it, may they see Jesus.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Lord who calls His people to obedience.
The Shepherd who restores the wandering.
The King who will one day make all things new.
You may speak in tongues.
You may prophesy.
You may understand mysteries.
You may have faith that astonishes people.
But do not let the extraordinary things you do distract you from the extraordinary Savior you need.
Paul ends his great chapter on love with these words:
“And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.”
—1 Corinthians 13:13, KJV
Faith.
Hope.
Love.
And the greatest is love.
Not because love replaces the Gospel.
But because the Gospel reveals the love of God in Jesus Christ and calls His redeemed people to live in that love.
When the applause fades, when the platform disappears, when every hidden motive stands exposed before the Lord, may our hope be found in Christ alone.
And may the love He has shown us be visible in the lives we have surrendered to Him.

The greatest tragedy is not reaching the end of your life without the world knowing your name—it is spending your life making a name for yourself while never truly surrendering to the One who died to save you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD COULD HAVE FED ISRAEL FOR AN ENTIRE MONTH… SO WHY DID HE MAKE THEM COME BACK EVERY MORNING?
paragraphs: GOD COULD HAVE FED ISRAEL FOR AN ENTIRE MONTH… SO WHY DID HE MAKE THEM COME BACK EVERY MORNING?

The heartbreaking, life-changing truth hidden in Exodus 16:4–21 about fear, provision, obedience, and the God who sometimes gives you only enough for today—not because He has forgotten tomorrow, but because He wants you to discover who holds it.
What if the very thing you keep begging God to give you is the thing He knows could eventually make you forget Him?
Read that again.

Because somewhere tonight, someone is staring at an unpaid bill. Someone is wondering how to feed their children next week. Someone is exhausted from praying the same prayer, fighting the same fear, and waking up to the same uncertainty.
And perhaps that someone is you.
You believe God can provide.
You've seen Him do it before.
But there's a question you hardly dare to say aloud.
"Lord, if You already know what I'm going to need tomorrow… why don't You just give it to me today?"
Why must provision sometimes arrive at the last possible moment?
Why does peace seem to last only until the next problem?
Why does God sometimes give enough strength to survive the day, but not enough certainty to stop worrying about the next thirty?
There is a story buried in the wilderness of Exodus that speaks directly to that question.
And the most unsettling part is this:
God could have given Israel an entire month's worth of food in a single morning.
He chose not to.
Not because heaven was running out.
Not because God was calculating how much He could afford.
Not because His people were unimportant.
He was teaching former slaves something they had never truly learned.
How to live free without being ruled by fear.
And what happened in that wilderness may explain something about the wilderness you're walking through right now.
Imagine the scene.
Thousands upon thousands of Israelites have escaped Egypt. Behind them lies a land of slavery, humiliation, forced labor, and generations of suffering.
They have witnessed plagues that shook an empire.
They have walked through the sea on dry ground.
They have seen the power of God overthrow the army that pursued them.
They are free.
But freedom has brought them into a wilderness where there are no fields ready for harvest, no overflowing markets, and no reliable supply of bread.
And hungry people can begin to remember even a cruel past differently.
In Exodus 16:3, the Israelites speak longingly of Egypt, remembering the meat pots and bread they believed they had enjoyed there.
Think about that.
They were remembering food in the very land where they had been enslaved.
They were looking backward at captivity because the uncertainty of freedom frightened them.
Sometimes the familiar chains of yesterday can begin to look safer than the unfamiliar promises of tomorrow.
And isn't that painfully human?
A person can leave a destructive relationship and still miss the familiarity.
Someone can turn away from a sinful habit and still remember the temporary comfort it offered.
A believer can experience God's deliverance and still panic when the next crisis arrives.
Israel had left Egypt.
But the fear Egypt cultivated had not yet left Israel.
Then God spoke.
In Exodus 16:4, the Lord declared:
"Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you."
— Exodus 16:4, KJV
Pause there.
Bread. From. Heaven.
Not bread earned through slavery.
Not bread purchased from Pharaoh.
Not bread secured by returning to Egypt.
Bread descending from the God who had already brought them out.
And yet the next part of God's instruction is where the deeper lesson begins.
The people were to go out and gather a daily portion, with a special arrangement for the sixth day.
Why?
God Himself explained that this would test whether they would walk in His instruction.
The Hebrew text gives us a remarkable window into the meaning.
Exodus 16:4 uses the expression:
דְּבַר־יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ
Devar-yom beyomo.
Literally, the idea is "the matter of a day in its day," expressing what was needed or assigned for each day.
A daily portion.
A daily responsibility.
A daily opportunity to obey.
The text does not say that God was unable to provide more.
It says He deliberately established a pattern that would reveal whether His people would trust and obey Him.
And that changes how we understand the miracle.
Because the miracle was not merely that bread appeared.
The miracle was also that God was teaching a frightened people to live under His faithful care.
They had spent generations under Pharaoh, whose system demanded labor and offered no dependable mercy.
Now the Lord was showing them a different kind of authority.
Pharaoh had used their hunger and labor to sustain his kingdom.
God was feeding them by grace.
Pharaoh's rule had made them slaves.
God's provision was teaching them to live as His covenant people.
And every morning, when they opened their eyes, they faced a choice.
Would they trust the God who had provided yesterday?
Or would they let fear convince them that tomorrow was already lost?
That question did not remain theoretical for long.
When the Israelites first saw the mysterious substance on the ground, they asked one another what it was.
Exodus 16:15 records their bewilderment.
The Hebrew expression associated with the name manna is traditionally connected to:
מָן הוּא
Man hu.
Commonly understood in the narrative as "What is it?"
They did not recognize what God had placed before them.
And perhaps there is a lesson even in their surprise.
Sometimes God's answer does not look like the answer we imagined.
Sometimes we pray for one form of provision, and God provides another.
Sometimes help arrives through an unexpected person, an unfamiliar opportunity, or a door we never considered.
But we must be careful here.
Exodus does not promise that every unexpected opportunity is a message from God.
It shows us that the Lord was faithful to provide for Israel in a way they had never experienced.
And His faithfulness did not depend on their ability to recognize the provision immediately.
Moses explained that this was the bread the Lord had given them to eat.
Then came the instruction.
Each household was to gather according to its need.
Exodus 16:18 records something beautiful: those who gathered much had nothing left over, and those who gathered little had no lack.
There was enough.
Not an invitation to greed.
Not a reward for hoarding.
Enough according to God's provision and command.
But then something happened.
Some of the people refused to leave the future in God's hands.
Moses had instructed them not to keep any of the manna until morning.
Yet some kept part of it overnight.
Perhaps they were thinking about their children.
Perhaps they were afraid the miracle would stop.
Perhaps they simply wanted the reassurance of having something stored away.
Scripture does not tell us their private motives.
What it does tell us is that they disobeyed the command.
And by morning, the manna they had kept had bred worms and become foul.
Imagine waking up, uncovering the food you secretly saved, and discovering that the very thing you kept for security had spoiled.
The problem was not that planning ahead is sinful.
The Bible repeatedly commends wisdom, diligence, and prudent preparation. Proverbs 6:6–8 even praises the ant for preparing its food.
And Exodus 16 itself commands Israel to gather twice as much on the sixth day so they can rest on the seventh.
The problem was not storing food in every circumstance.
The problem was disobeying God's specific instruction because they wanted security on their own terms.
That distinction matters.
Because Scripture does not teach that believers must empty their savings accounts, refuse to prepare for emergencies, or neglect tomorrow's responsibilities to prove their faith.
It teaches us that even the wisest preparation must never become a substitute for trust in God.
You can have money saved and still be terrified.
You can own a house and still feel homeless inside.
You can have a full refrigerator and still live with a heart convinced that everything will be taken away.
And you can have very little, yet know the deep peace of belonging to the Lord.
The amount you possess does not automatically determine the condition of your trust.
That is why the wilderness lesson reaches far beyond food.
God was confronting the illusion that life becomes secure only when we can control everything that comes next.
And perhaps this is where the story begins to touch something you've been hiding.
You don't necessarily want to be rich.
You just want to stop being afraid.
You want to know your children will be okay.
You want to know the medical results will be good.
You want to know the job will still be there.
You want to know the marriage can survive.
You want to know you won't have to endure another season that nearly broke you.
You want tomorrow to send you a guarantee.
And when it doesn't, you begin to wonder whether God is listening.
But consider what Israel experienced.
They woke up one morning and found manna.
Then another morning.
Then another.
For forty years, the Lord sustained His people in the wilderness, as Exodus 16:35 records.
Not because they deserved forty years of miracles.
Not because they never complained.
Not because their faith was always strong.
They complained.
They doubted.
They disobeyed.
They repeatedly struggled to trust the One who had delivered them.
Yet God's covenant faithfulness was greater than their instability.
And this is where the story becomes more than a lesson about daily dependence.
It becomes a window into grace.
Because if God provided only for people who never struggled, how many of us would have eaten this morning?
If His mercy were reserved for those who never doubted, who among us could stand?
If His faithfulness depended entirely on the steadiness of our emotions, how often would we find ourselves abandoned?
But the God of Scripture is not a reflection of our changing feelings.
He is faithful to His word.
That does not mean rebellion is harmless or that disobedience has no consequences.
Israel's wilderness history makes the opposite unmistakably clear.
It means that God's character remains steadfast even when human hearts are inconsistent.
And then, centuries later, Jesus Christ took this wilderness story and revealed its deepest significance.
In John 6, after feeding a multitude, Jesus encountered people who wanted more bread.
They remembered the manna their ancestors had eaten.
They spoke of bread from heaven.
And Jesus redirected their attention.
He declared:
"I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst."
— John 6:35, KJV
There it is.
The wilderness was never the end of the story.
The manna was real food, given by a real God to sustain real people in a real desert.
But it also belonged to a greater biblical story that finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The Greek words in John 6:35 are:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς
Egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs.
"I am the bread of life."
Not merely, "I can give you bread."
Not merely, "I know where to find bread."
I am the bread of life.
Jesus was not offering a temporary solution to an empty stomach.
He was revealing Himself as the One who gives eternal life.
And in John 6:49–51, He drew the contrast unmistakably.
Israel's ancestors ate manna in the wilderness, and they died.
But Jesus identified Himself as the living bread that came down from heaven, the One through whom those who believe receive life that death cannot finally destroy.
The manna sustained physical life for a time.
Christ gives eternal life.
The manna had to be gathered again.
Christ's saving sacrifice does not need to be repeated.
The manna could not remove sin.
Jesus, through His death and resurrection, accomplished the redemption sinners could never secure for themselves.
And now the question changes.
What if your deepest hunger was never going to be satisfied by having thirty days of provision?
What if you received every financial answer you've been praying for, yet still carried the same emptiness inside?
What if the bills were paid, the future looked predictable, and your plans finally worked out…
But your soul remained far from God?
Would you truly be satisfied?
Jesus did not come merely to improve the conditions of our temporary lives.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He came to bear our sins.
He came to die in the place of the guilty and rise again in victory.
He came to give life to people who could never save themselves.
That is why this story must lead us to the cross.
Because our greatest problem is not simply that we don't know what tomorrow holds.
Our greatest problem is that sin has separated humanity from the holy God who holds tomorrow.
And our greatest hope is not that every difficulty will disappear.
It is that Jesus Christ has opened the way for sinners to be forgiven, reconciled, and made new.
Think of the scandal of grace.
Israel complained while God was preparing to feed them.
Humanity rebelled while God, in His mercy, was unfolding His plan of redemption.
We have all sinned and fallen short of God's glory, as Romans 3:23 declares.
Yet Romans 5:8 tells us that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we cleaned up every failure.
Not after we proved we could survive without Him.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
And this is the heart of Gospel Warrior's message:
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The rebellious can repent.
The spiritually dead can receive life in Christ.
The person who has wasted years running from God can turn to Him today.
Not because their past was insignificant.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
But because the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than the power of sin to condemn those who belong to Him.
And perhaps you're reading this with a history you wish you could erase.
A secret habit.
A broken promise.
A betrayal.
A season of unbelief.
A prayer life that has nearly disappeared.
You still know the right Christian words.
You still know how to smile when someone asks how you're doing.
But underneath the surface, you're exhausted.
And the hardest thing to admit is that you may have spent more time worrying about what God hasn't given you than remembering what He has already given you in Christ.
Don't rush past that.
The greatest gift God has given His people is not the promise of a painless life.
It is His Son.
And if you belong to Jesus, you are not spiritually abandoned simply because your circumstances remain uncertain.
That does not make your suffering imaginary.
It does not mean financial hardship is easy.
It does not mean every unanswered prayer will resolve the way you hope.
But it means your suffering does not have the final authority to define God's love for you.
The cross has already revealed the depth of that love.
Now listen to how Jesus taught His disciples to pray.
In Matthew 6:11, He said:
"Give us this day our daily bread."
The Greek text reads:
Τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον δὸς ἡμῖν σήμερον
Ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion dos hēmin sēmeron.
The traditional translation is "Give us this day our daily bread."
The Greek word epiousion is unusually rare, and scholars have discussed its precise meaning, including senses connected with daily need or what is needed for the coming day.
We should not pretend every linguistic question has been settled.
But the prayer's practical emphasis is clear.
Jesus taught His followers to bring their needs to their Father.
Today.
Not because tomorrow is outside God's knowledge.
Not because believers are forbidden to think ahead.
But because dependence on the Father belongs to the daily life of faith.
And a few verses later, in Matthew 6:34, Jesus taught His disciples not to be consumed by anxiety about tomorrow.
He did not deny that tomorrow would have troubles.
He acknowledged them.
He taught us not to carry tomorrow's anxieties as though God had ceased to be our Father today.
That is a profoundly different way of living.
It is possible to prepare responsibly for the future without surrendering your peace to fear.
It is possible to work diligently, save wisely, seek counsel, and make careful decisions while still confessing that your ultimate security is in the Lord.
It is possible to pray for a month's provision and remain thankful when God provides today's necessities.
