And it is possible to experience genuine lack without concluding that God has rejected you.
Because the Bible does not promise that every faithful Christian will always have a full bank account or never experience hunger.
The apostle Paul knew both abundance and need.
He learned contentment in circumstances he would not have chosen.
And when he wrote that he could do all things through Christ who strengthened him in Philippians 4:13, he was speaking within that very context.
Christ strengthened him to endure both plenty and want.
That is not a promise that every desire will be fulfilled.
It is a testimony that Christ is sufficient to sustain His people through changing circumstances.
And that brings us to something easy to miss in Exodus 16.
On the sixth day, God commanded Israel to gather twice the normal amount.
This time, the food did not spoil as it had when people kept it against His instruction.
Why?
Because the Lord was preparing them for the Sabbath.
The seventh day was to be a day of rest.
Do you see the beauty?
The same God who taught His people to gather daily also taught them when to stop gathering.
Their lives were not supposed to revolve around endless striving.
God did not deliver them from Pharaoh so that they could become slaves to their own fear of scarcity.
He was teaching them obedience.
Dependence.
And rest.
Not laziness.
Not irresponsibility.
Rest rooted in His provision and His command.
And for Christians, this truth finds an even deeper resonance in Jesus, who invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest in Matthew 11:28–30.
Some of you are not merely tired because you have too much work.
You are tired because your mind never stops rehearsing disasters that haven't happened.
You lie down, but you don't rest.
You close your eyes, but your thoughts keep running.
You finish one crisis and immediately begin preparing emotionally for the next.
Even your prayers sometimes feel like desperate attempts to make sure God hasn't forgotten you.
And perhaps today you need to hear something simple.
You are not the one holding the universe together.
God is.
You are responsible for the obedience He has placed before you.
You are called to work, pray, love, repent, forgive, act wisely, and trust Him.
But you were never commanded to become sovereign over tomorrow.
That throne is already occupied.
And the One who occupies it is not indifferent to the cries of His children.
He is the Father Jesus taught us to trust.
This does not mean you will never cry again.
It does not mean you will never feel afraid.
Faith is not the complete absence of trembling.
Sometimes faith looks like a frightened person praying, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," as the father cried in Mark 9:24.
Sometimes it looks like opening Scripture when your emotions are telling you to give up.
Sometimes it looks like admitting to another believer that you need prayer.
Sometimes it looks like taking the next responsible step even when you cannot see the whole road.
And sometimes it looks like waking up tomorrow and remembering that the God who met you yesterday has not changed.
Perhaps that is one reason the manna came in the morning.
Exodus 16:21 tells us that the people gathered it morning by morning.
The text does not say that God intended every sunrise to produce a particular emotional experience.
But it does show a repeated pattern of provision and obedience.
Every morning presented another opportunity to receive what God had given.
And there is something profoundly moving about that.
Yesterday's obedience could not replace today's.
Yesterday's meal could not eliminate today's hunger.
Yesterday's experience of provision did not remove the need to trust God again.
And in our walk with Christ, yesterday's spiritual encouragement cannot replace today's need to abide in Him.
You cannot build a living relationship with Jesus entirely on what you experienced years ago.
You need His Word.
You need prayer.
You need fellowship with His people.
You need repentance when sin is exposed.
You need the continual reminder that your standing before God rests on Christ's finished work, not on your ability to manufacture perfect emotions.
Not to earn salvation.
Not to make Jesus love you more.
But because the Savior who has redeemed you is worthy of your daily devotion.
And maybe that's where the real question of this story finally lands.
Not simply, "Why didn't God give Israel thirty days of manna?"
But, "What was God teaching Israel about Himself through the way He provided?"
He was showing them that He could be trusted.
That His word mattered.
That His provision was not controlled by Pharaoh.
That obedience mattered more than fearful hoarding.
That rest was part of His design.
And that life with Him required more than escaping Egypt.
It required learning to walk with Him.

Deuteronomy 8:3 later reflects on the wilderness and explains that God humbled Israel, allowed them to hunger, and fed them with manna so they would learn that human life depends on more than bread alone, but on what proceeds from the mouth of the Lord.
That is the Bible's own explanation of the deeper lesson.
The manna was never just about manna.
It was about the Lord who spoke, provided, instructed, and sustained.
And when Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He quoted that very passage in Matthew 4:4.
Where Israel had struggled in the wilderness, Jesus remained obedient to the Father's word.
He would not turn stones into bread at Satan's command to prove His identity or satisfy hunger apart from His Father's will.
The faithful Son stood firm.
And that matters because our salvation ultimately rests not on our flawless wilderness performance, but on the obedience, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
He is the Savior we need when our faith has faltered.
He is the Bread of Life we need when our souls are empty.
He is the Lord to whom we must turn when sin has taken us farther than we ever intended to go.
And He is worthy of our trust even when tomorrow remains hidden.
So tonight, if you are anxious about the future, bring that anxiety to Him.
Tell Him the truth.
Tell Him you're afraid.
Tell Him you're tired.
Tell Him you don't understand why the answer hasn't come.
You do not need to impress God with polished religious language.
Come humbly.
Come honestly.
Come in repentance and faith.
Ask Him for the wisdom to do what is right today and the grace to trust Him with what you cannot control.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, don't mistake this story for a motivational lesson about positive thinking.
You need more than encouragement.
You need the Savior.
Turn from sin and trust in the crucified and risen Christ.
Receive the forgiveness and new life that only He can give.
Because one day every bank account will be irrelevant.
Every earthly possession will be left behind.
Every human guarantee will reach its limit.
But those who belong to Jesus have a hope that reaches beyond the grave.
And that is why this message matters too much to keep to ourselves.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who looks completely fine but is quietly wondering how to survive another day.
Maybe it's a parent.
Maybe it's a friend who has stopped attending church.
Maybe it's someone who has money but no peace.
Maybe it's someone who no longer believes God cares.

You don't have to explain everything publicly. You don't owe strangers the details of your struggle. But sometimes a small, honest confession opens the door to prayer, fellowship, and the reminder that you are not walking alone.
Because sometimes we need to hear the same biblical truth more than once before it begins to shape the way we respond.

Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown spiritually cold, the seeker who is asking difficult questions, and even the person who does not yet believe. The Gospel is not a private treasure to be hidden away. It is good news to be proclaimed.
And if this ministry has helped you draw closer to Christ, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources available to people who may never walk through the doors of a church or purchase a Christian book.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, understand the Gospel, strengthen their faith, and develop a more deeply rooted walk with the Lord.
And if you believe this work is worth sustaining, you can help make it possible.
The Bible teaches generous, willing giving—not giving driven by guilt or spiritual pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, God loves a cheerful giver.
It does not replace repentance, faith, or obedience.
It is not a guarantee of financial blessing.
The deeper invitation is to participate in helping more people encounter Scripture and the Gospel.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, pray, share, invite others, and make use of the free resources available.
The Gospel must never become a product available only to those who can afford it.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
And His invitation to repent and believe is not hidden behind a payment.
And perhaps that brings us back to the very place where this story began.
A wilderness.
A frightened people.
An uncertain tomorrow.
And a God who had already decided to provide.
Picture an Israelite father standing outside his tent at dawn.
His children are hungry.
His family has no field to harvest.
He cannot point to a month's supply of bread.
But as the morning light spreads across the wilderness, he looks down.
There it is again.
Manna.
Enough to gather according to God's command.
Not because he controlled tomorrow.
Not because he had mastered every possibility.
But because the Lord had kept His word.
Now imagine him kneeling to gather the food.
Yesterday, he had been afraid.
Today, he is being fed.
Tomorrow is still unknown to him.
But it is not unknown to God.
And perhaps that is the truth you need to carry into your own uncertain morning.
You may not know how every bill will be paid.
You may not know how every relationship will be restored.
You may not know when the waiting will end.
You may not know why some prayers remain unanswered.
And I will not promise you that every painful circumstance will change by sunrise.
Scripture gives us something deeper than a guarantee of immediate relief.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who bore our sin.
The One who conquered death.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness and eternal life.
The One who will never fail to accomplish what He has promised.
So make your plans.
Do your work.
Care for your family.
Seek help when you need it.
Give generously as you are able.
Obey what God has clearly revealed.
And when fear starts demanding guarantees that no human being can give, remember the wilderness.
Remember the manna.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
And remember that the greatest Bread from Heaven was not something Israel could collect in a basket.
He was Someone who would one day give His life for the world.
Jesus Christ.
You may not receive everything you want for the next thirty days.
But today, you can turn to the Savior who gives eternal life.
And if you already belong to Him, you can bring your fears, your needs, and your uncertain future to the Father who knows you.
Before you close this article, ask yourself one final question:
Am I seeking God's hand only because I want Him to secure my tomorrow, or am I learning to love and trust His heart today?
Because the greatest tragedy would not be waking up without thirty days of bread.
It would be spending your entire life chasing the bread that perishes while rejecting the Bread of Life standing before you.
The manna was on the ground every morning, but the greatest miracle was always the God who refused to stop being faithful.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU’RE 40, STILL SINGLE, AND STILL A VIRGIN. BUT NOBODY WARNED YOU THAT WAITING FOR MARRIAGE COULD HURT THIS MUCH.
paragraphs: YOU’RE 40, STILL SINGLE, AND STILL A VIRGIN. BUT NOBODY WARNED YOU THAT WAITING FOR MARRIAGE COULD HURT THIS MUCH.

You kept your body for a marriage that never came. You watched other people fall in love, build families, and move forward while you kept praying, hoping, and growing older. Now you're wondering something you're almost ashamed to ask: “God, did I obey You only to end up alone?”
There is a kind of loneliness that doesn't announce itself in public.
It waits until you get home.
Until you've taken off your shoes, finished dinner, and checked your phone for a message that never came.
Until another wedding invitation appears.
Another engagement announcement.
Another baby shower.
Another photograph of someone younger than you holding the life you once imagined would be yours by now.
You smile. You congratulate them. You genuinely want them to be happy.
And then you close the app.
The room becomes quiet.
And somewhere between folding your laundry and turning off the lights, a question rises from a place you've tried so hard to keep surrendered.
“Lord, what about me?”
You're forty.
Still single.
Still a virgin.
Not because you've never wanted intimacy.
Not because you don't understand desire.
Not because you've never had opportunities, temptations, or nights when your convictions felt heavier than your loneliness.
But because somewhere along the way, you became convinced that your body was not something to give away casually.
You believed sexual intimacy belonged within marriage.
You wanted to honor Jesus.
And perhaps you imagined that by forty, obedience would have led you somewhere different.
A wedding ring.
A familiar voice calling from the kitchen.
Someone reaching for your hand during Sunday worship.
Someone beside you when life becomes frightening.
Someone who chooses you.
Not just for a season.
For a lifetime.
But here you are.
And what nobody told you about waiting until marriage is that sometimes the hardest part isn't resisting sexual temptation.
It's resisting the temptation to believe that God has forgotten you.
Because sexual desire is one thing.
But the desire to be known, held, cherished, and chosen?
That reaches into places no sermon about purity ever fully explained.
And if you've ever cried yourself to sleep while wondering whether your obedience has cost you the very love you longed for, please keep reading.
There is something Jesus wants you to understand that may change how you see your entire life.
Not by promising you a wedding.
But by revealing something even more important about your worth.
Let's begin with a truth that many Christians need to hear.
Your virginity is not your righteousness. Jesus Christ is.
Read that again.
Because somewhere in Christian culture, a beautiful biblical conviction became tangled with a dangerous misunderstanding.
We began speaking as though people who remained sexually inexperienced were somehow more valuable than those whose stories included sexual sin.
As though virginity were a spiritual trophy.
As though marriage were God's reward for good behavior.
As though those who waited long enough would eventually receive a spouse as payment for their faithfulness.
But Scripture never teaches that God owes us marriage because we have obeyed His commands concerning sexuality.
And Scripture never teaches that a person's worth before God is determined by sexual history.
The apostle Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9:
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of grace, favor, and gift.
Not wages earned through perfect performance.
Not compensation for years of sexual restraint.
Not a reward purchased through personal sacrifice.
Grace is God's undeserved favor, given through Jesus Christ.
This matters enormously.
Because if you have remained sexually abstinent until forty, you have not purchased a husband or wife through obedience.
You have sought to honor God with your body.
And that obedience matters.
But it is not a transaction.
God is not a vending machine into which you deposit holiness until a marriage certificate comes out.
He is your Father.
And your Father has never asked you to earn His love by becoming someone's spouse.
Perhaps the most painful thing about Christian singleness isn't simply waiting.
Perhaps it's discovering that some of the promises people attached to waiting were never promises God actually made.
“Just keep yourself pure. God will send the right person.”
“Your future husband is being prepared.”
“Your wife is coming. Just be patient.”
“You'll understand why you had to wait when you finally meet the one.”
Sometimes those words are spoken with sincere love.
But they can quietly become a burden.
Because what happens when forty arrives?
What happens when fifty arrives?
What happens when the person you've prayed for still hasn't appeared?
Were you insufficiently faithful?
Did you miss God's timing?
Did you ruin His plan?
Were your prayers somehow less powerful?
No.
A delayed marriage is not evidence of defective faith. And a marriage that never happens is not proof of divine rejection.
The Bible gives us a far more honest picture of singleness.
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul speaks about marriage and unmarried life without treating either as a spiritual failure.
In verse 7, he writes:
The Greek word for “gift” is χάρισμα (charisma).
It refers to a gracious gift.
Paul's point is not that every unmarried person must enjoy being alone, never experience sexual desire, or possess some extraordinary ability to endure loneliness.
He recognizes different gifts and circumstances among believers.
And later, in 1 Corinthians 7:28, he makes something clear:
“But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned.” (KJV)
Marriage is good.
And faithful singleness is not a lesser form of Christian existence.
Both must be understood under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That means you can desire marriage without idolizing it.
You can pursue marriage without being desperate.
You can grieve your unmarried circumstances without being ungrateful to God.
You can experience sexual desire without automatically being guilty of sexual sin.
And you can remain unmarried without being spiritually incomplete.
Because your completeness is not found in another human being.
It is found in Christ.
Colossians 2:10 declares:
“And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power.” (KJV)
The Greek expression ἐστὲ ἐν αὐτῷ πεπληρωμένοι (este en autō peplērōmenoi) carries the sense that believers have been brought into fullness in Christ.
In context, Paul is speaking of the spiritual sufficiency believers possess through union with Jesus, not promising that every emotional longing will disappear.
You may still ache for companionship.
You may still want someone to hold you.
You may still pray for marriage.
But your standing before God is not incomplete because your left hand has no wedding ring.
You are not half a person waiting for another half to make you whole.
You are a human being created in God's image, invited into the fullness of life found in His Son.
And that truth becomes especially important when the world begins treating your age like an expiration date.
Because people can be cruel without realizing it.
They ask questions that sound innocent.
“Why are you still single?”
“Are you too picky?”
“Don't you want children?”
“Are you sure you're not afraid of intimacy?”
And sometimes the most painful questions come from people sitting beside you in church.
People who mean well.
People who pray for you.
People who still make you feel as though you are a problem waiting to be solved.
They celebrate marriages, anniversaries, pregnancies, and growing families.
And those things deserve celebration.
But somehow, the forty-year-old believer who has spent decades serving, working, resisting temptation, caring for aging parents, and walking faithfully with Jesus can become almost invisible.
No ceremony.
No special announcement.
No recognition of the sacrifices nobody saw.
Just another Sunday.
Another prayer.
Another year.
And perhaps you're wondering whether anyone understands how much strength it has taken to remain faithful in a world that often laughs at restraint.
Jesus understands more than you may realize.
Because Jesus Christ Himself lived an unmarried earthly life.
He never needed a wedding ring to possess perfect humanity.
He never needed sexual experience to become fully mature.
He never needed romantic validation to establish His identity.
He was fully human, yet without sin.
Hebrews 4:15 says:
“For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.” (KJV)
This does not mean Jesus experienced every exact circumstance or personal history that you have experienced.
It means our Savior truly entered human weakness and temptation without surrendering to sin.
He understands rejection.
He understands grief.
He understands being misunderstood.
He understands what it means to obey the Father when obedience is costly.
And when you come to Him with loneliness, you are not approaching a distant religious figure who has no understanding of human suffering.
You are approaching the crucified and risen Lord.
The One who knows what tears feel like.
The One who knows what abandonment feels like.
The One who endured the cross for sinners.
And here's something worth considering.
If Jesus lived a perfectly holy unmarried life, then marriage cannot be the ultimate measurement of a successful human life.
It simply cannot.
Marriage is a beautiful covenant established by God.
But marriage is not the gospel.
Jesus is.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because some of us have been waiting for marriage while quietly postponing our lives.
We've told ourselves that real happiness will begin when someone chooses us.
That meaningful adventures will begin after the wedding.
That ministry will become significant once we have a spouse.
That our homes will feel valuable once someone else lives inside them.
That our stories will finally matter when another person becomes part of them.
But what if you've been waiting for a wedding while Jesus has been calling you to live faithfully today?
Not to abandon your desire for marriage.
Not to pretend you don't care.
Not to stop praying.
But to stop treating your present life as though it were merely a waiting room.
Because your life is happening right now.
The people who need your encouragement are alive right now.
The family members who need your love are here right now.
The opportunities to serve, learn, grow, create, and share the gospel exist right now.
And you don't need a spouse's permission to become the person God is calling you to be.
You can build meaningful friendships.
You can develop a community.
You can pursue godly relationships intentionally.
You can seek wise counsel.
You can serve your church.
You can build a home filled with hospitality.
You can experience joy without betraying your hope for marriage.
You can be lonely and still deeply loved.
You can be disappointed and still deeply faithful.
You can be waiting and still fully alive.
But there is another part of this story that deserves honesty.
The sexual struggle.
The part many believers are afraid to discuss openly.
Because being forty and a virgin doesn't necessarily mean your body has stopped longing for intimacy.
You may know exactly what it feels like to wake up with desires you cannot simply switch off.
You may have wrestled with fantasies.
You may have struggled with pornography.
You may have crossed boundaries you regret.
You may have found yourself emotionally attached to someone who could never become your spouse.
You may have almost surrendered your convictions because you were tired of feeling unwanted.
And perhaps you've wondered:
“Is something wrong with me because I still want sex?”
No.
Sexual desire itself is not automatically sin.
God created human beings as embodied creatures.
Genesis 2:24 describes the covenant union of husband and wife, who become “one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad), meaning “one flesh.”
It describes a profound union that includes bodily intimacy but is not reducible to the sexual act alone.
The biblical vision of marriage is not merely two people satisfying physical urges.
It is a covenant relationship involving faithfulness, mutual belonging, and shared life.
And within that covenant, sexual intimacy has a rightful place.
The Bible does not teach that sexual desire is dirty.
It teaches that our desires must be governed by holiness and love.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5, Paul calls believers to abstain from sexual immorality and to live with holiness and honor.
The Greek term πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to sexual immorality.
It is not a word that means sexual desire itself.
There is a difference between experiencing temptation and choosing to indulge sin.
There is a difference between longing for marriage and demanding that God provide it on your schedule.
And there is a difference between being sexually inexperienced and being spiritually mature.
You can be a virgin and still struggle with lust, pride, bitterness, selfishness, or unbelief.
You can also have a sinful sexual past and be genuinely forgiven, cleansed, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
That is why we must never turn virginity into an idol.
Because purity is not simply about what your body has never done. It is also about whom your heart belongs to and how you live before God.
And even then, none of us can stand before God claiming that our own purity is sufficient to save us.
We need the righteousness of Jesus.
Every one of us.
The person who has never had sex.
The divorced believer.
The widow or widower.
The person who regrets past relationships.
The person who has fallen repeatedly and is learning to repent.
The person who waited until marriage.
And the person who didn't.
All of us need grace.
In 1 Corinthians 6:11, after describing serious patterns of sin, Paul tells believers:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” (KJV)
Notice the power of those words.
“And such were some of you.”
Their past was real.
Their sin was real.
But their past was not the final word over their identity.
Jesus Christ had changed their standing before God.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists around a message we refuse to compromise:
Not because Jesus pretends sin never happened.
Not because grace makes repentance unnecessary.
But because the blood of Jesus is sufficient to forgive repentant sinners and His Spirit is powerful enough to transform lives.
And perhaps the scandal in your story isn't a sexual mistake.
Perhaps it's the secret resentment you've been carrying toward God.
You obeyed.
You waited.
You watched.
You cried.
And somewhere along the way, you began to feel cheated.
You never said it aloud because it sounded disrespectful.
But in the privacy of your heart, you wondered whether the people who ignored God's commands somehow ended up happier than you.
They found relationships.
They got married.
They built families.
Some even seem to be thriving.
And you're still alone.
It's painful to admit.
But if that thought has ever crossed your mind, Scripture gives you a place to bring it.
Psalm 73 records the struggle of Asaph, who became troubled when he observed the apparent prosperity of the wicked.
In verse 13, he cried:
“Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency.” (KJV)
Do you hear the ache?
What was the point of remaining faithful?
What did obedience accomplish?
Why does righteousness sometimes appear to cost more than rebellion?
Asaph's struggle was not resolved by receiving everything he wanted.
His perspective changed as he came before God and recognized the deeper reality of God's presence and eternal purposes.
Later, in Psalm 73:25–26, he declares:
“Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.” (KJV)
God Himself is the psalmist's enduring portion.
Not a consolation prize.
Not a substitute handed to someone who lost the opportunity for a better life.
His ultimate treasure.
This does not make human relationships meaningless.
It puts them in their proper place.
A spouse can love you deeply.
A spouse cannot become your Savior.
A husband can comfort you.
He cannot redeem your soul.
A wife can walk beside you.
She cannot carry the weight of being your god.
Even the most beautiful Christian marriage remains a relationship between two imperfect human beings who both need Jesus.
And sometimes the greatest mercy God gives us is exposing the false belief that another person could finally make us secure forever.
That doesn't mean marriage is bad.
It means marriage was never designed to bear the weight of eternity.
Only Christ can do that.
Now, perhaps you're asking the question that has been haunting you for years.
“But what if I never get married?”
I won't insult your pain by promising that your wedding day is just around the corner.
I won't tell you that God is secretly preparing someone and that you'll understand everything soon.
I don't know whether you will marry.
No human writer has the authority to guarantee that outcome in God's name.
And pretending otherwise would be cruel.
But I can tell you what Scripture actually promises.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
Romans 8:38–39 declares that neither death nor life, nor anything else in creation, can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him.
And Matthew 28:20 records the risen Savior's promise to His disciples:
“...lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.” (KJV)
These promises are not wedding predictions.
They are better than that.
They are assurances of Christ's faithful presence, saving love, and enduring commitment to His people.
Marriage may or may not be part of your earthly story.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, abandonment by your Savior will never be the ending.
And perhaps that is the truth your exhausted heart needs to hear today.
You are not behind in God's kingdom because you are unmarried at forty.
You are not spiritually disqualified because you have never experienced sexual intimacy.
You are not automatically more holy than someone who has a sexual past.
You are not required to stop wanting marriage.
And you are not required to pretend that waiting has been easy.
You are called to follow Jesus.
Today.
In the life you actually have.
With the desires you actually feel.
With the questions you still carry.
With the tears you haven't told anyone about.
With the future you cannot control.
And if you have fallen into sexual sin along the way, the invitation is not to hide behind shame.
It is to repent and come to Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
The Greek verb ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), translated “confess,” comes from a verb meaning to acknowledge or confess.
The verse does not portray forgiveness as something earned by dramatic displays of guilt.
It points to God's faithfulness and righteousness in forgiving and cleansing those who confess their sins.
The gospel is not an invitation to maintain a perfect public image.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
So if you're forty and still a virgin, please don't build your identity around a label.
Don't make sexual inexperience your crown.
Don't make singleness your shame.
Don't let another person's marriage become the measurement of God's love for you.
And don't let disappointment turn your heart cold toward the One who gave His life to save you.
Because the cross tells you something no dating app, wedding invitation, or relationship status ever could.
You were loved by Christ before anyone on earth chose you romantically.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
He did not wait for you to become desirable by the world's standards.
He did not wait for you to become married.
He did not wait for you to establish a flawless record of sexual purity.
Christ died for sinners.
And through His death and resurrection, those who repent and trust in Him receive forgiveness and new life.
That is the center of the Christian story.
Not the ring.
Not the wedding.
Not the honeymoon.
Not even the waiting.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
And I want to speak to the person reading this with tears gathering in their eyes.
The person who has spent years being strong.
The person who laughs when relatives joke about being single forever.
The person who has prayed over an empty pillow.
The person who has watched friends become grandparents while still wondering what it would feel like to be someone's husband or wife.
The person who has secretly feared that being unwanted romantically means being unwanted altogether.
Please hear this.
You are allowed to grieve what you hoped your life would look like.
You are allowed to bring that grief to God.
You are allowed to ask Him for marriage.
You are allowed to seek a godly spouse actively, thoughtfully, and courageously.
You do not have to sit motionless and call it faith.
You can meet people.
You can accept introductions.
You can build healthy friendships.
You can pursue someone whose faith and character are consistent with your convictions.
You can seek pastoral counsel and wise accountability.
And if marriage becomes part of your story, receive it with gratitude rather than treating it as overdue compensation.
But if marriage does not come, your life is still capable of bearing fruit that matters eternally.
There is no biblical requirement to become someone's spouse before you can become a faithful disciple.
And there is no biblical reason for the church to treat unmarried believers as permanent adolescents waiting to graduate into adulthood.
You belong in the body of Christ.
Your gifts matter.
Your service matters.
Your spiritual maturity matters.
Your friendship matters.
Your prayers matter.
Your life matters.
Not someday.
Now.
And maybe this article isn't only for the forty-year-old virgin.
Maybe it's for the thirty-year-old who is terrified of becoming one.
The fifty-year-old who has stopped explaining why they're single.
The divorced believer who feels disqualified from a new beginning.
The person who gave away their virginity and believes God can never make them clean again.
The married Christian who has never understood the quiet grief of unmarried friends.
Or the parent who keeps asking their adult child when they're finally going to settle down.
You don't need to reveal anything private.
You don't need to explain your entire story.
But perhaps you could write:
Or simply:
“I'm still trusting Jesus.”
Let this become a place where believers encourage one another instead of competing over who reached life's milestones first.
Because those nights may come again.
And when they do, you may need to remember that your circumstances have not canceled the gospel.
We want to keep pointing people back to the Word of God.
Not shallow promises.
Not emotional manipulation.
Not religious performances.
Jesus Christ.
His truth.
His grace.
His call to repentance.
His power to restore.
It doesn't.
And not because your faithfulness to Jesus is measured by how much money you give.
It never has been.
But because the gospel is worth sharing, and faithful ministry requires people who are willing to help carry the work.
The New Testament encourages believers to support gospel ministry while emphasizing that giving should be willing rather than compelled.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
The Greek word ἱλαρόν (hilaron) means cheerful or glad.
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say to give because someone made you feel guilty.
It does not say that giving guarantees marriage, prosperity, healing, or special blessings.
And it does not say that supporting an online ministry replaces your responsibilities to your local church, family, or people in genuine need.
It is a voluntary contribution you may choose to make as part of your generosity toward gospel work.
If you already practice tithing or giving through your local congregation, continue to honor those commitments with prayerful discernment.
Your presence matters.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
One thoughtful comment may encourage someone who feels invisible.
One invitation may introduce a searching soul to the truth of Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, develop spiritual discernment, strengthen their faith, and become more rooted in Jesus Christ.
Because following Jesus was never meant to be reduced to watching inspirational posts.
It is a daily life of repentance, prayer, obedience, learning, worship, fellowship, and transformation by His grace.
We need believers who will pray for one another.
Believers who will tell the truth with compassion.
Believers who will stop shaming people for being single.
Believers who will stop glorifying virginity as though it were salvation.
Believers who will honor marriage without worshiping it.
Believers who will extend grace to those who have fallen and encourage those who are struggling to remain faithful.
Believers who understand that the Christian life is not a contest to see who gets married first.
It is a call to follow the crucified and risen Christ.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that began this entire conversation.
“God, did I obey You only to end up alone?”
Perhaps the most important thing I can tell you is this:
You were never called to obey God in exchange for a spouse. You were called to follow the Savior who gave Himself for you.
That truth may not erase the ache of an empty bed.
It may not silence the longing for children.
It may not make the next wedding invitation easier to open.
But it can free you from believing that your faithfulness has been meaningless simply because your story unfolded differently from what you imagined.
And one day, whether your earthly life includes marriage or not, the ultimate hope of every Christian will be fulfilled not in a romantic relationship, but in the presence of Jesus Christ.
Revelation 21:4 describes the glorious future God promises His redeemed people:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.” (KJV)
Think about that.
A day when grief will not follow you into another year.
A day when loneliness will no longer wound you.
A day when disappointment will no longer haunt your prayers.
Not because every earthly desire was fulfilled exactly as you planned.
But because God's people will dwell with Him in a renewed creation where sorrow and death are no more.
Until then, you may still have questions.
You may still want to be held.
You may still hope for a wedding.
And you may still cry sometimes.
But you can bring all of that to Jesus.
You do not have to become emotionally numb to become spiritually faithful.
You do not have to pretend your heart is satisfied with every circumstance.
You only need to keep coming to the One who welcomes sinners, comforts the brokenhearted, and calls His people to trust Him.
So tonight, if you find yourself alone again, don't look at your empty ring finger as proof that God has withheld your worth.
Look to the cross.
Remember the Savior who loved you while you were still a sinner.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that your future rests in the hands of the risen Christ.
And if you pray through tears, let your prayer be something like this:

“Lord Jesus, You know how long I've waited. You know the desires I struggle to explain. You know the disappointment I've carried and the questions I've been afraid to ask. Forgive me where I've made marriage an idol. Forgive me where I've grown bitter or doubted Your goodness. Teach me to honor You with my body, my thoughts, my relationships, and my choices. Give me courage to pursue what is good without trying to control the future. If marriage is part of my life, help me receive it with humility and gratitude. If it is not, help me live faithfully and fruitfully in You. Surround me with godly friendships and a church family that truly cares. And above everything else, teach my heart to treasure You. Amen.”
Because perhaps the most important message they need today is not that marriage is coming soon.
Perhaps they need to know that Jesus Christ is worthy of their trust even when the future remains uncertain.
You may reach forty without ever hearing someone say, “I do”—but at the cross, you can know the love of the Savior who gave Himself for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF GOD KNEW THEY WOULD EAT THE FORBIDDEN FRUIT, WHY DID HE PUT THE TREE THERE?
paragraphs: IF GOD KNEW THEY WOULD EAT THE FORBIDDEN FRUIT, WHY DID HE PUT THE TREE THERE?
The heartbreaking mystery of Eden, the freedom God gave humanity, the lie that shattered paradise, and the Savior who walked into our ruin to bring us home.
There is a question buried in the opening pages of the Bible that has troubled believers, fascinated theologians, and quietly haunted people who have never dared to ask it inside a church.
If God already knew Adam and Eve would eat from the forbidden tree, why did He put it there in the first place?
Think about that.

God knew the serpent would deceive. He knew Eve would reach for the fruit. He knew Adam would eat. He knew shame would enter the human experience, that the ground would be cursed, that death would become humanity's enemy, and that generations yet unborn would inherit a world fractured by sin.
He knew there would be graves.
He knew there would be wars.

He knew there would be children crying beside hospital beds, marriages collapsing under betrayal, mothers burying sons, and people lying awake at three in the morning wondering why life hurts so much.
And still, in the middle of Eden, stood the tree.
Why?
Was it a trap?
Was God testing humanity with a test He already knew they would fail?
And if He knew everything that would happen, why didn't He simply create a garden without the possibility of disobedience?
Perhaps you've asked that question before. Perhaps someone told you to stop questioning God and just have faith.
But Scripture does not require us to pretend difficult questions are easy.
And the answer is far more profound than the familiar explanation that God simply wanted people to have free will.
Because when we examine Genesis carefully, something extraordinary begins to emerge.
The story of the forbidden tree is not merely about why humanity fell. It is also the beginning of the biblical story that leads us to the cross where Jesus Christ came to rescue the fallen.
But to understand that, we must return to the garden.
Before the shame.
Before the hiding.
Before the first human being ever learned what it meant to be afraid of the God who loved him.

Genesis 2:9 tells us that the LORD God caused trees to grow from the ground, trees that were beautiful to look at and good for food. Among them were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
Notice something easily overlooked.
God did not create a barren prison and place one tempting fruit in front of two starving people.
He created abundance.
There were trees everywhere. Food everywhere. Beauty everywhere. Provision everywhere.
And then God gave a command.
In Genesis 2:16–17, the LORD told the man that he could freely eat from every tree of the garden except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Eating from that tree would bring death.
The original Hebrew contains a detail worth noticing.
The words translated "you may surely eat" are:
אָכֹל תֹּאכֵל — ʾākōl tōʾkēl
This construction repeats the Hebrew verb for eating to emphasize the certainty or freedom of the permission.
In natural English, the sense is, "You may freely eat."
Before God spoke about the one forbidden tree, He spoke about the many trees they could enjoy.
The first emphasis was generosity, not restriction.
That matters.
Because the serpent's strategy would be to make Adam and Eve forget the abundance and obsess over the boundary.
And isn't that still how temptation works?
You can have a hundred reasons to be grateful, yet one thing you cannot have begins consuming your thoughts.
You can have a loving family, yet someone else's attention starts feeling irresistible.
You can have blessings you once prayed for, yet comparison whispers that God has withheld the one thing that would finally make you happy.
Suddenly, everything God has given looks smaller than the thing He has forbidden.
The garden begins to feel like a prison.
And the boundary begins to look like cruelty.
But was the tree itself evil?
No.
Genesis calls it the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. It does not say the tree was inherently wicked, nor does it describe its fruit as poisonous.
In fact, Genesis 3:6 describes the tree as good for food, pleasing to the eyes, and desirable for gaining wisdom.
The danger was not that God had created an evil substance.
The danger was that human beings would cross a boundary God had established, choosing disobedience over trust.
The Hebrew name of the tree is especially important:
עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע — ʿēṣ haddaʿat ṭôḇ wā-rāʿ
Literally, "the tree of the knowledge of good and evil."
The word דַּעַת — daʿat means knowledge.
But what exactly does "knowledge of good and evil" mean?

Christians have offered several interpretations. Some emphasize moral discernment, others the pursuit of wisdom apart from God's instruction, and others the human desire to claim authority over what is good and evil.
The phrase also appears elsewhere in the Old Testament in contexts involving discernment and maturity.
Genesis does not provide a complete philosophical definition.
But the serpent's promise reveals something central to the temptation.
"You will be like God," he tells the woman, "knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:5).
The temptation was not simply to taste something delicious.
It was to reach for a godlike status on the serpent's terms.
To distrust the Creator.
To believe that God's command stood between humanity and something better.
To treat independence from God's word as the pathway to fullness of life.
And suddenly the question changes.
It is no longer only, "Why did God put the tree there?"
It becomes, "Why did humanity believe that disobeying the God who gave them everything would somehow give them more?"
That question is painfully personal.
Because we have been repeating the same tragedy ever since.
We know what Scripture says about forgiveness, but bitterness feels safer.
We know what Jesus teaches about truth, but a lie seems more convenient.
We know that sexual immorality damages lives, but desire promises satisfaction without consequences.
We know that greed cannot save us, but we keep believing one more possession will finally bring peace.
We know that pride destroys relationships, yet admitting we were wrong feels unbearable.
And then, when the consequences arrive, we ask why God allowed us to make the choice.
There is a little Eden in every human heart.
Not because we are personally responsible for Adam's individual decision, but because we recognize the same struggle between trusting God and believing we know better.
Yet the original question remains.
Why allow such a choice at all?
Here we must be careful.
A popular Christian answer says God placed the tree in Eden because genuine love requires free will.
There is something meaningful in that explanation. Scripture portrays Adam and Eve as morally responsible creatures who received a real command and were accountable for their disobedience.
But Genesis never explicitly says, "God planted this tree because love requires free will."
That is a theological inference, not a direct quotation from Scripture.
And thoughtful Christians have differed about how human freedom, divine sovereignty, and God's foreknowledge fit together.
What we can say with confidence is that God created humanity good, gave humanity a meaningful command, and did not portray disobedience as something He approved.
The tree marked a real distinction between the Creator and His creatures.
Adam and Eve were made in God's image, but they were not God.
They were given dignity, responsibility, fellowship, and extraordinary freedom.
Yet they were still called to trust the One who made them.
Being made in God's image never meant being entitled to take God's place.
And that is where the serpent attacked.
Genesis 3:1 records his opening question:
"Did God really say...?"
Those words should disturb us.
Because the first recorded temptation in Scripture begins by casting suspicion on what God has spoken.
The serpent did not begin by openly declaring war against heaven.
He began with a question designed to unsettle trust.
Then he contradicted God's warning.
"You will not surely die" (Genesis 3:4).
The Hebrew is emphatic:
לֹא־מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן — lōʾ-môt tĕmutûn
The serpent was directly denying the certainty of death.
God had warned that disobedience would bring death.
The serpent insisted it would not.
And the woman listened.
She saw that the tree was good for food, pleasing to the eyes, and desirable for wisdom.
She took.
She ate.
She gave some to her husband, who was with her.
And he ate.
No lightning is described striking the garden.
No dramatic explosion is recorded.
Just an act of disobedience.
A moment in which the word of the serpent was trusted above the word of God.
And then everything changed.
Genesis 3:7 says their eyes were opened, and they realized they were naked.
Before the fall, Genesis 2:25 says they were naked and unashamed.
Afterward, they covered themselves.
The people who had lived without shame were suddenly trying to hide their vulnerability.
And then came one of the most heartbreaking moments in the entire Bible.
They heard the LORD God in the garden.
And they hid.
Imagine that.
The very presence that should have been their greatest comfort had become the presence they feared.
Adam, formed from the dust by God's own creative power, was now hiding among the trees God had made.
And God called to him.
אַיֶּכָּה — ʾayyekkāh
"Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9).
Read those words slowly.
Where are you?
The text does not explain God's inner reason for asking, but the question clearly draws Adam into an encounter with the truth about what has happened.
The God who knows His creation calls the hiding man to answer.
And Adam replies that he was afraid because he was naked, so he hid.
There it is.
Fear.
Shame.
Concealment.
The human heart learning to run from God.
And if we're willing to be truthful, this is where Genesis stops feeling like ancient history.
Because some of us have been hiding for years.
Not behind fig leaves.
Behind a smile.
Behind church attendance.
Behind ministry involvement.
Behind carefully selected Bible verses posted online while our private lives are falling apart.
Behind the words, "I'm fine," when we know we are not.
Maybe you love Jesus, but there is a sin you keep returning to.
Maybe you have been wounded by someone who claimed to represent God.
Maybe your prayers have become shorter because guilt has convinced you that heaven is tired of hearing your voice.
Maybe you still attend worship, but something inside you feels distant.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you remember a time when being close to God felt easier.
Now you hide.
You distract yourself.
You promise to change.
You fail.
You feel ashamed.
And you hide again.
But listen carefully.
The God who confronted Adam's sin did not leave Adam hidden among the trees.
He called him into the open.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because hiding was never going to heal what disobedience had broken.
You can simply write, "No more hiding," or "Pray for me."
You do not need to expose private details to strangers. But you do not have to keep pretending that the battle is not real.
Now comes the difficult part.
God had warned that eating from the tree would bring death.
And death did enter the human story.
Adam and Eve did not physically collapse the moment they ate. Genesis goes on to describe their continued lives outside Eden.
But the sentence of mortality was pronounced, and their access to the tree of life was barred.
Genesis 3:19 declares that humanity would return to the ground, for from dust human beings were taken, and to dust they would return.
Romans 5:12 later connects the entrance of sin and death into the human world with Adam's transgression.
The Bible does not treat the fall as a harmless mistake.
It treats it as a catastrophe.
The relationship between humanity and God was ruptured.
Human relationships were distorted.
The ground became a place of painful toil.
Death cast its shadow over human existence.
And the garden was lost.
So we must ask the question again.
If God knew this would happen, why did He not prevent it?
The most faithful answer begins with an admission that many of us find uncomfortable.
Scripture does not reveal every reason God permitted the fall.
It reveals enough for us to know that God is holy, that His creation was good, that human disobedience was real, and that He was not surprised or defeated by sin.
But it does not give us permission to invent a complete explanation of every mystery in God's eternal purposes.
Deuteronomy 29:29 reminds us that the secret things belong to the LORD, while what He has revealed belongs to His people.
That is not an invitation to abandon thought.
It is a reminder that there is a difference between trusting what God has revealed and claiming to know what He has not.
We must not say that God needed Adam and Eve to sin.
We must not say that evil is good because God can bring good from it.
We must not say that suffering is merely a tool God uses without regard for the people experiencing it.
And we must never suggest that the horrors of human history are somehow insignificant because redemption is possible.
Sin is evil.
Death is an enemy.
Suffering is real.
The tears matter.
But here is the astonishing testimony of Scripture.
God is able to bring redemption out of a rebellion He never commands us to commit.
The cross itself demonstrates this.
Acts 2:23 speaks of Jesus being delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, while also holding those who crucified Him responsible for their wicked actions.
God's sovereign purpose did not turn human evil into righteousness.
And human evil did not overthrow God's saving purpose.
That distinction is essential.
Because otherwise we risk portraying God as the author of the very wickedness Scripture condemns.
But the biblical story shows something far greater.
A holy God who judges sin and, in astonishing mercy, acts to save sinners.
And the first glimpse of that mercy appears before Adam and Eve ever leave Eden.

In Genesis 3:15, God speaks to the serpent about enmity between the serpent's offspring and the woman's offspring, and about the conflict in which the serpent's head will be struck and the offspring's heel will be struck.
Christians have long recognized this passage as the first anticipation of the Gospel, often calling it the protoevangelium, or "first Gospel."
The Hebrew word for offspring is:
זֶרַע — zeraʿ
It can refer to seed, descendants, or offspring.
In its immediate context, Genesis 3:15 announces conflict between the serpent and the woman's offspring.
Read within the whole Christian canon, the promise finds its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the victorious offspring who defeats the works of the devil.
We should not pretend Adam and Eve necessarily understood every future detail of Christ's crucifixion.
The verse does not explicitly name Jesus or describe the nails of Calvary.
But the New Testament reveals the larger story into which this promise fits.
First John 3:8 declares that the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
Hebrews 2:14–15 explains that through death Jesus defeated the one who held the power of death and delivered those enslaved by its fear.
And Romans 16:20 promises that the God of peace will crush Satan under the feet of His people.
What began in Eden was not going to have the final word.
The serpent would not reign forever.
Sin would not triumph forever.
Death would not hold God's redeemed people forever.
And the answer would not come through humanity somehow climbing its way back to innocence.
It would come through a Savior.
Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed.
That is not merely a poetic comparison.
It is apostolic teaching.
Romans 5:19 declares that through the disobedience of the one man, many were made sinners, and through the obedience of the One, many will be made righteous.
First Corinthians 15:22 says that as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive, a statement Paul develops in the context of resurrection and belonging to Christ.
And First Corinthians 15:45 calls Jesus the last Adam.
Think about what that means.
The first Adam stood in a garden surrounded by provision and chose disobedience.
Jesus, the last Adam, entered a garden of anguish and submitted Himself to the Father's will.
In Gethsemane, with the suffering of the cross before Him, Jesus prayed:
"Not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:42).
Adam grasped at what God had forbidden.
Christ surrendered Himself in obedience to the Father.
Adam's sin brought condemnation and death.
Christ's obedience, culminating in His sacrificial death and victorious resurrection, brings justification and life to those who belong to Him.
The contrast is breathtaking.
But do not miss the cost.
Jesus did not restore sinners by pretending sin did not matter.
He carried our sins.
He endured the cross.
He suffered under the weight of human cruelty and the judgment associated with our sin.
First Peter 2:24 says that He bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sins and live for righteousness.
The Greek word used there for tree or wood is:
ξύλον — xylon
The word can refer to wood, a tree, or a wooden instrument.
Peter uses it for the cross.
And the connection is deeply moving.
Humanity's rebellion involved a forbidden tree.
Our redemption was accomplished through the obedience of Christ, who bore our sins upon the wood of the cross.
This is a theological contrast drawn from the wider biblical story, not a claim that Genesis explicitly identifies the two trees as identical symbols.
But the connection calls us to worship.
The first Adam reached out his hand in disobedience.
Jesus stretched out His hands in sacrificial love.
And what humanity could never repair by its own righteousness, Christ accomplished through His death and resurrection.
The scandal of Eden was answered by the grace of Calvary.
This is why the Gospel is not merely advice for becoming a better person.
It is good news about what Jesus Christ has done for people who cannot save themselves.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes most personal.
Because the question, "Why did God put the tree there?" can sometimes conceal a second question.
One we are almost afraid to speak.
"Why did God allow me to become the person I am today?"
Why did He allow me to make those choices?
Why did He let me walk into that relationship?
Why didn't He stop me before I destroyed something precious?
Why didn't He intervene before my life became so complicated?
Those are painful questions.
And not every tragedy in your life is the result of your own sin. Scripture itself rejects simplistic explanations that blame every sufferer for the suffering they endure (John 9:1–3).
Some wounds were inflicted on you.
Some losses came without your choosing.
Some sorrows remain mysteries this side of eternity.
But where you have sinned, the Gospel offers something greater than excuses.
It offers forgiveness.
Where you have been wounded, it offers the presence and hope of the risen Christ, even when healing is slow.
Where you are ashamed, it calls you out of hiding.
Where you are enslaved by sin, it calls you to repentance and new life through the power of the Holy Spirit.
And where you have convinced yourself that your story is beyond repair, it points you to a crucified and risen Savior.
Not every consequence disappears when you repent.
Not every broken relationship is restored immediately.
Not every wound closes overnight.
But in Jesus Christ, sin does not have to remain your master.
And shame does not have to become your identity.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
Not a person who never had a past.
A new creation.
Someone whose past no longer has the authority to define their standing before God.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue in sin.
Not denial of the damage sin causes.
Grace is God's undeserved favor in Christ, which forgives and transforms.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
The same grace that welcomes the repentant sinner also teaches that sinner to walk away from the sin.
And that is why Jesus did not die merely to make us feel better about ourselves.
He died to reconcile us to God.
He rose again so that death would not be the end of the story.
And He calls us to follow Him.
Now look at the Bible's ending.
Because the story that begins with a tree in Genesis does not conclude with humanity permanently banished from God's presence.
In Revelation 22, the tree of life appears again.
Revelation 22:2 describes the tree of life in the New Jerusalem, and Revelation 22:3 declares that there will no longer be any curse.
Do you see the movement of the biblical story?
Genesis begins with humanity enjoying God's provision in a garden.
Sin brings exile, suffering, and death.
Christ comes, dies, and rises again.
And Revelation ends with God's redeemed people dwelling in His presence, with the curse removed.
The Bible does not end with Adam hiding.
It ends with God's servants seeing His face (Revelation 22:4).
The Hebrew Bible begins with the tragedy of humanity turning away from the Creator.
The Christian Scriptures conclude with the glorious hope of redeemed humanity living in the presence of God and the Lamb.
The tree of life, once inaccessible to fallen humanity, appears in the final vision of God's restored creation.
That is not a small ending.
That is cosmic redemption.
And the center of it all is Jesus.
Not human goodness.
Not religious performance.
Not an impressive ministry.
Not the ability to quote enough Bible verses to hide a wounded conscience.
Jesus Christ.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Savior who rose.
The King who will make all things new.
So what is the answer to our original question?
Why did God place the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in Eden when He knew Adam and Eve would eat from it?
Scripture shows that God created a good world, gave humanity abundant provision and a genuine command, and held humanity responsible for choosing disobedience.
It also shows that God's foreknowledge did not mean the fall took Him by surprise, and that His saving purpose in Christ would overcome the devastation of sin.
But Scripture does not reveal an exhaustive explanation of why God permitted this particular history rather than a different one.
We should be humble enough to admit that.
What Scripture does reveal is the character of the God who entered our broken history to redeem us.
We may not understand every reason He permitted the fall.
But we can look at the cross and see that He did not remain distant from the suffering of this fallen world.
In Jesus Christ, God the Son took on human nature and entered the world of grief, temptation, rejection, betrayal, suffering, and death.
Yet He was without sin.
He did not merely observe humanity's misery from heaven.
He came to save.
And the empty tomb declares that death itself will not have the final word.
Perhaps the deepest question is no longer why the tree was there.
Perhaps it is this:
Now that Christ has come to rescue sinners, what will you do with Him?
Will you continue hiding?
Will you keep telling yourself that you will repent when life becomes less complicated?
Will you wait until your habits improve before coming to the Savior who calls sinners to Himself?
Or will you finally admit that you need the mercy of God?
You do not need to manufacture a perfect testimony before you come to Jesus.
You need to turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Confess your sins.
Trust in His finished work, not your own righteousness.
Believe that He died for sins and rose again.
Follow Him.
And when you stumble, do not make hiding your home.
Return to the Savior.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive confessed sins and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That promise is not an excuse to cherish sin.
It is a reason to stop running from the One who saves.
And if you have been reading this with tears in your eyes because you recognize yourself in Adam's hiding, please hear this:
Your sin is serious.
But the mercy of Christ is greater than the hope you could ever build on your own goodness.
Your wounds are real.
But they do not place you beyond the compassion of the Savior.
Your past may contain chapters you wish you could erase.
But through Jesus Christ, your future does not have to be ruled by them.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because consequences never matter.
But because redemption is real.
Because the cross is sufficient.
Because the tomb is empty.
Because Jesus Christ is alive.
And because the God who called to Adam in the garden still calls sinners through His Gospel to come out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Write "No more hiding" if you are ready to stop running from God.
Write "Jesus, forgive me" if this has brought you to honest repentance.
Or write "Christ is still healing me" if you are learning to trust His grace in the middle of a difficult journey.
You can also share a testimony or ask for prayer without revealing anything you need to keep private.
Sometimes the courage to speak one honest sentence encourages another struggling believer to seek help, confess sin, and return to Christ.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
Someone may be angry with God.
Someone may be quietly questioning their faith.
Someone may be drowning in shame while pretending everything is fine.
Someone may have never understood why Jesus came.
We want to help people open their Bibles, ask honest questions, grow in discernment, and keep their eyes on Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers go deeper into Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has blessed you, there is another way you can help carry the work forward.
But we want to be biblically clear about something important.
Scripture calls believers to give willingly, not under pressure or guilt.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that each person should give what they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your prayers, thoughtful comments, sharing of Gospel-centered content, and encouragement to others also matter.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, conversation starters, or thoughtful gifts. But the greatest gift we could ever point you toward is not something sold in a store.
It is the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
We would be grateful to walk alongside you as we continue studying Scripture, confronting difficult questions, and encouraging one another to follow Jesus faithfully.
It is not to build a kingdom around a page.
It is to point people to the Kingdom of God.
It is not to make a name for ourselves.
It is to proclaim the name of Jesus Christ.
It is not to sell the appearance of spiritual transformation.
It is to bear witness to the Savior who truly transforms lives.
And now, before you go, I want you to picture something.
A man hiding among the trees in Eden.
Ashamed.
Afraid.
Unable to undo what he had done.
Then picture another scene.
A Savior hanging upon the wood of a cross.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Bearing sins that were not His own.
The first scene shows humanity's desperate need.
The second reveals God's astonishing answer.
And beyond the cross stands an empty tomb.
Beyond the tomb stands the promise of resurrection.
Beyond this broken age stands the hope of a new creation where the curse will be no more.
We began with a question about why God allowed a tree to stand in Eden.
We end with a Savior who willingly endured the cross to bring sinners back to God.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth is not that Adam reached for what God had forbidden.
It is that, after humanity fell, God did not abandon His purpose to redeem.
The first Adam hid among the trees in shame. The last Adam bore our shame upon a tree, so that those who belong to Him could come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY NAMED HIM PAIN… BUT GOD REFUSED TO LET PAIN WRITE HIS FINAL CHAPTER
paragraphs: THEY NAMED HIM PAIN… BUT GOD REFUSED TO LET PAIN WRITE HIS FINAL CHAPTER
Who Was Jabez, the Man Whose Prayer Interrupted a Genealogy? — The forgotten man in 1 Chronicles 4:9–10 whose two-verse story reveals what happens when a wounded life reaches for the living God.
Some people are born into a family name.
Others are born into a family wound.
And sometimes, before you are old enough to understand what happened to you, somebody has already decided what your life is going to mean.
Maybe they called you a disappointment.
Maybe you grew up hearing that you were a mistake.
Maybe nobody actually said those words, but the way they treated you made the message painfully clear.
You were the difficult child. The unwanted pregnancy. The one who never measured up. The person who always seemed to bring trouble into the room.
And somewhere along the way, you stopped questioning the label.
You started living inside it.
But buried in one of the most easily skipped sections of the Bible is a man whose name carried the memory of pain.
His name was Jabez.
And what Scripture says about him takes only two verses.
Two verses.
No dramatic account of armies falling. No record of a sea splitting open. No detailed biography explaining his childhood, his failures, his relationships, or his accomplishments.
Just a name.
A wound.
A prayer.
And an answer from God.
Yet there is something extraordinary about where his story appears.
The writer of 1 Chronicles is tracing generations. Names follow names. Families follow families. The record moves forward through the history of God's covenant people.
Then, suddenly, the narrative slows.
A man named Jabez steps into view.
And for two remarkable verses, the genealogy becomes a testimony.

If you have ever wondered whether God sees you when your life feels ordinary, whether your painful beginning has already determined your ending, or whether your prayers still matter after years of disappointment, stay with this story.
Because the most important thing about Jabez was not the pain attached to his name.
It was the God he called upon.
And the difference between those two truths may change the way you understand your own life.
The Bible introduces him this way:
“Jabez was more honourable than his brethren: and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, Because I bare him with sorrow.”
— 1 Chronicles 4:9, KJV
Read that again.
His mother named him Jabez because she bore him in sorrow.
In Hebrew, the name appears as יַעְבֵּץ (Yaʿbēṣ), commonly transliterated Jabez.
The verse connects his name with the Hebrew word עֹצֶב (ʿōṣeb), meaning pain or sorrow, through a deliberate wordplay.
His name became associated with the suffering surrounding his birth.
But notice something important.
Scripture does not tell us exactly why his mother suffered.
Perhaps it involved a difficult delivery. Perhaps there were painful circumstances surrounding his birth. The text does not explain.
We must not turn possibilities into biblical facts.
What we do know is that his name preserved the memory of sorrow.
Imagine growing up carrying a name that reminded people of pain.
Imagine hearing it called across the courtyard.
At the family table.
Among relatives.
Every time someone said his name, the association remained.
Pain.
Sorrow.
Distress.
Some of us understand that more deeply than we want to admit.
Our names may not literally mean pain, but we carry memories that have become identities.
The marriage that collapsed.
The addiction that nearly destroyed us.
The child we lost.
The betrayal we never saw coming.
The mistake everyone remembers.
The season when we walked away from God and wondered whether we could ever come home.
And the terrible thing about shame is that it does not merely remind you of what happened.
It tries to convince you that what happened is who you are.
But the Bible does something fascinating before recording Jabez's prayer.
It tells us that he was more honorable than his brothers.
Not more famous.
Not necessarily wealthier.
Not more powerful.
More honorable.
The Hebrew word translated “honourable” is נִכְבָּד (nikhbād), related to the root כבד (k-b-d), which carries ideas of weight, honor, and significance.
The writer does not give us enough information to explain every reason for that description.
But the contrast is unmistakable.
His name was associated with pain.
His character was associated with honor.
And that distinction matters.
Because the circumstances surrounding your beginning do not automatically determine the character of your life.
Your parents' failures do not have to become your convictions.
The cruelty you experienced does not have to become the cruelty you practice.
The darkness you inherited does not have to be the darkness you pass down.
By God's grace, a different way of living is possible.
Jabez was not introduced as a man without pain.
He was introduced as a man whose life could not be reduced to it.
And then came the prayer.

“And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.”
— 1 Chronicles 4:10, KJV
There it is.
One prayer.
Four closely connected requests.
And a final sentence so simple that we might miss its significance.
“God granted him that which he requested.”
But before we rush to turn this prayer into a formula for financial success, we need to understand what Jabez was actually saying.
Because this is where a beautiful biblical passage has sometimes been reduced to something much smaller than its original meaning.
Jabez was not handing God a business plan.
He was calling upon the God of Israel.
That distinction changes everything.
The Hebrew begins:
וַיִּקְרָא יַעְבֵּץ לֵאלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayyiqrāʾ Yaʿbēṣ lēʾlōhê Yiśrāʾēl.
“And Jabez called upon the God of Israel.”
He did not address an anonymous force.
He did not appeal to the universe.
He did not attempt to manipulate supernatural power through the correct combination of words.
He called upon the God who had made covenant promises to Israel.
The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
The God who had delivered His people from slavery.
The God whose faithfulness was greater than the failures of those who belonged to Him.
And that is where his prayer begins.
Not with confidence in himself.
But with dependence upon God.
“Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed…”
The Hebrew expression includes:
אִם־בָּרֵךְ תְּבָרֲכֵנִי
ʾIm-bārēkh təvā­răkhēnî.
The repetition of the Hebrew verb for blessing gives the request emphasis.
Jabez is earnestly asking God to bless him.
But blessing in Scripture cannot be reduced to having more money, acquiring a larger house, or enjoying a trouble-free life.
God's blessing can include material provision. Scripture does not deny that.
Yet the biblical understanding of blessing is far richer.
It includes God's favor, His provision, His covenant faithfulness, and the good He gives according to His wisdom.
Sometimes God's blessing comes through an open door.
Sometimes it comes through the strength to remain faithful when the door stays closed.
Sometimes it comes through provision.
Sometimes through correction.
Sometimes through an answered request.
And sometimes through a grace that teaches us to endure what we desperately wanted removed.
The apostle Paul prayed three times for his thorn in the flesh to be taken away.
The Lord's answer was:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Think about that.
Jabez received what he requested.
Paul did not receive the removal he requested.
Yet both accounts reveal the goodness of God.
One demonstrates God's generosity in granting a petition.
The other demonstrates God's sustaining grace when a petition is not granted in the way we desire.
That is why we must never tell a suffering believer that an unanswered prayer automatically proves a lack of faith.
Some of the most faithful people in Scripture suffered deeply.
And the most important blessing God gives us is not a life in which nothing hurts.
It is the gift of belonging to Him.
Jabez continued:
“...and enlarge my coast…”
The Hebrew expression is:
וְהִרְבִּיתָ אֶת־גְּבוּלִי
Vəhirbîtā ʾet-gəvûlî.
It refers to increasing or enlarging his border or territory.
In the historical setting of ancient Israel, land and boundaries were concrete realities, connected with inheritance, livelihood, and the life of the covenant community.
Jabez was asking for an enlargement of his territory.
We should not pretend the verse originally meant increasing social media followers, expanding a ministry platform, or multiplying a business.
Those may be modern applications people consider, but they are not the literal meaning of the Hebrew text.
And yet the passage does invite us to examine something deeply personal.
What are we asking God to enlarge?
Our influence?
Our possessions?
Our opportunities?
Or our capacity to honor Him with whatever He entrusts to us?
Because there is a dangerous kind of expansion.
A person can gain a larger platform and lose their integrity.
Build a successful business and neglect their family.
Acquire more possessions and become less generous.
Receive greater influence and slowly begin loving applause more than truth.
Not everything that grows is becoming spiritually healthy.
Jesus asked a question that should disturb every heart chasing success without surrender:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
— Mark 8:36, KJV
Jabez asked for more territory.
But the Christian reading his prayer today must remember that our greatest calling is not territorial expansion.
It is faithfulness to Jesus Christ.
We can ask God to enlarge our opportunities to serve, our generosity, our usefulness, and our witness.
But we must submit those desires to His will.
Because a bigger life is not necessarily a better life.
A life surrendered to Christ is.
