Then Jabez prayed something that deserves more attention than it often receives.
“...and that thine hand might be with me…”
Not simply, “Give me more.”
But, “Let Your hand be with me.”
In the Old Testament, God's hand can signify His power and active involvement, including His help, protection, and judgment according to the context.
Here, Jabez is asking for God's sustaining presence and assistance.
And suddenly the prayer becomes more than a request for changed circumstances.
It becomes a confession of dependence.
What good would larger territory be if he lived apart from the God who gave it?
What good would a blessing be if it became an excuse to forget the Blesser?
What good would an answered prayer be if the answer eventually became an idol?
There are people who have everything they once begged God to give them.
And they are still empty.
They have the promotion.
The house.
The recognition.
The relationships.
The money.
Yet somewhere between receiving the gift and enjoying the gift, they stopped seeking the Giver.
That is why the presence of God matters more than the size of the territory.
Moses understood something similar when he told the Lord:
“If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence.”
— Exodus 33:15, KJV
Moses did not want to move forward without God's presence.
And Jabez's prayer gives us a reason to examine our own ambitions.
Are we asking God to accompany us in obedience?
Or are we asking Him to endorse plans we have never surrendered to Him?
Those are not the same thing.
You can pray over an opportunity without ever asking whether it honors Christ.
You can ask God to bless a relationship while refusing to obey His Word within it.
You can ask Him to prosper your work while ignoring dishonesty in the way you conduct it.
But the hand of God is not a religious decoration we place over our personal desires.
We are called to trust Him, obey Him, and seek His will.
And sometimes the most merciful thing God does is stop us from going somewhere we were convinced we needed to go.
Then comes the final request.
“...and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me!”
This part of the prayer carries an especially moving connection with Jabez's name.
The Hebrew includes:
וְעָשִׂיתָ מֵּרָעָה לְבִלְתִּי עָצְבִּי
Vəʿāśîtā mē­rāʿāh ləviltî ʿāṣbî.
The wording is compact and has been translated in different ways.
It expresses a request involving protection from evil or harm, so that pain or distress will not overtake him.
The final Hebrew word, ʿāṣbî, echoes the language of pain associated with his name.
Do you see the literary connection?
The man whose name was tied to sorrow asks God to protect him from sorrow.
The man whose birth was remembered through pain calls upon the Lord concerning the pain that might lie ahead.
It is as though the story brings his name and his prayer face-to-face.
But we must be careful.
The Bible does not say Jabez was trying to break a generational curse.
It does not say his name carried supernatural power to condemn him.
It does not tell us that his mother had spoken a spiritual sentence over his future.
Those ideas may sound dramatic, but they go beyond what Scripture reveals.
What the text actually gives us is already powerful enough.
A man associated with sorrow turned to God in prayer.
And God heard him.
That is not a magical formula.
It is a testimony of divine mercy.
And perhaps this is where the story touches the places we normally hide.
Because some of us are not afraid of failure anymore.
We are afraid of being hurt again.
We have survived things we never expected to survive.
We have buried dreams.
Trusted people who betrayed us.
Prayed beside hospital beds.
Stared at unanswered messages.
Sat in church while quietly wondering why God seemed so distant.
And after enough disappointment, the heart begins protecting itself.
You stop hoping too much.
Stop trusting too quickly.
Stop telling people what you are carrying.
Sometimes you even stop praying honestly.
Not because you have stopped believing God exists.
But because you are exhausted from feeling disappointed.
Jabez reminds us that we do not have to pretend pain is insignificant before bringing it to God.
We can ask for protection.
We can ask for help.
We can ask for blessing.
We can admit that we are afraid.
We can bring the very thing that hurts us into the presence of the One who knows us completely.
And still, we must remember that God has not promised every believer freedom from earthly suffering.
Jesus told His disciples:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
— John 16:33, KJV
Not you might have tribulation.
“You shall have tribulation.”
The Christian hope is not that suffering becomes impossible.
It is that suffering does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And now we arrive at the sentence that closes Jabez's entire recorded story.
“And God granted him that which he requested.”
That is all.
The writer does not describe the celebration.
He does not tell us how much land Jabez received.
He does not explain how the blessing unfolded or what happened afterward.
He simply records that God granted his request.
Then the genealogy continues.
And this is where the story becomes unforgettable.
For two verses, we encounter a man whose name was associated with pain, whose character was described as honorable, and whose prayer was answered by God.
Then he disappears from the biblical narrative.
No monument is described.
No extended biography follows.
No detailed list of achievements is preserved.
Yet thousands of years later, believers are still reading his prayer.
Not because Jabez became the center of the biblical story.
But because his brief appearance directs our attention toward the God who hears.
And perhaps that is precisely the perspective we need.
You do not need to become famous for your life to matter before God.
You do not need a massive audience.
A recognizable name.
An impressive title.
A perfect family history.
You can live an ordinary life, pray in an ordinary room, obey God in ordinary circumstances, and still have a life of extraordinary significance in His sight.
But there is an even greater truth waiting beyond the story of Jabez.
Because if we stop with Jabez, we have not yet reached the heart of the Gospel.
Jabez prayed that God would keep him from pain.
Jesus Christ entered a world of pain willingly.
Jabez asked for God's hand to be with him.
Jesus, the eternal Son of God, came in the flesh to accomplish the Father's saving purpose.
Jabez asked for blessing.
Christ became the source of the greatest blessing sinners could ever receive: reconciliation with God.
And here is where the contrast becomes deeply personal.
Jabez's name was associated with sorrow surrounding his birth.
Jesus was described by the prophet Isaiah as:
“...a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief...”
— Isaiah 53:3, KJV
But Jesus did not merely experience human sorrow.
He bore our sins.
Isaiah declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
— Isaiah 53:5, KJV
This prophecy finds its fulfillment in the suffering and saving work of Jesus Christ, who bore our sins and secured our reconciliation with God.
And consider the difference.
Jabez cried out because he wanted to be spared from harm.
Jesus prayed in Gethsemane:
“...nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
— Matthew 26:39, KJV
Jesus did not escape the cross.
He obeyed the Father through it.
He was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
He endured the judgment our sins deserved, not because He had sinned, but because He came to save sinners.
And on the third day, He rose from the dead.
That is the center of our hope.
Not that every earthly request will be granted.
Not that every painful memory will disappear.
Not that our bank accounts will always increase.
But that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Through Him, forgiveness is offered to sinners.
Through Him, the guilty can be justified by faith.
Through Him, those who were far from God can be brought near.
And through Him, the final destiny of everyone who belongs to Him is not condemnation, but eternal life.
This is what makes the Gospel more glorious than a story about personal improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to help wounded people become more successful.
He came to save sinners.
Including the ones who have learned to hide their sins behind religious language.
Including the ones who know how to raise their hands in worship but cannot remember the last time they truly surrendered their hearts.
Including the ones who have hurt others and spent years pretending they were only victims.
Including the ones who feel so ashamed of their past that they cannot imagine being forgiven.
The Gospel does not tell us that our sin is harmless.
It tells us that God's grace is greater than the debt we could never repay.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
It calls us to repentance.
To turn away from sin.
To abandon our self-righteousness.
To trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
To follow Him.
There is a difference between wanting Jesus to improve your circumstances and surrendering to Jesus as Lord.
One asks, “Lord, will You give me what I want?”
The other asks, “Lord, teach me to want what honors You.”
One is interested in His gifts.
The other is learning to treasure Him.
And perhaps that is the question this ancient prayer is placing before us.
If God enlarged your territory tomorrow, would your heart become more devoted to Christ?
If He increased your income, would you become more generous?
If He gave you influence, would you speak the truth with greater courage and humility?
If He opened the door you have been praying about, would you walk through it in obedience?
And if He did not grant the request, would you still trust His goodness?
That last question may be the hardest.
Because faith is not proven only when prayers are answered the way we hoped.
Sometimes faith is revealed when we continue clinging to Christ while tears are still falling.
Maybe you are reading this from a hospital room.
Maybe you are waiting for a child to come home.
Maybe your marriage is quietly falling apart.
Maybe you have been battling a private sin for years, promising God that this would be the last time.
Maybe you are carrying a grief nobody knows about because you have become the person everyone else depends on.
Or maybe your life looks completely normal from the outside.
You smile.
You work.
You serve.
You post encouraging verses.
You tell people you are blessed.
But there is a part of you that has been spiritually exhausted for a very long time.
And the question you are afraid to ask is whether God still wants to hear from you.
Listen carefully.
You do not have to become impressive before you come to Jesus.
You do not have to manufacture a beautiful prayer.
You do not have to hide the ugliness of your sin or the depth of your grief.
Come to Him truthfully.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent of what needs to be abandoned.
Ask for the mercy you cannot earn.
Trust the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
And remember His promise:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
— John 6:37, KJV
Those words are not a guarantee that every circumstance will immediately change.
They are an invitation to come to the One who can save you.
And there is no greater transformation than being brought from spiritual death into life through Jesus Christ.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
— 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
Not because our past never happened.
Not because the consequences of sin automatically disappear.
Not because every earthly relationship will be restored.
But because in Christ, the past no longer has the authority to define our standing before God.
The sinner can be forgiven.
The proud can be humbled.
The brokenhearted can find comfort.
The wandering can repent and return.
The believer can be renewed in faith and obedience.
And the life that once seemed entirely defined by shame can become a testimony to the mercy of Jesus Christ.
That is not positive thinking.
That is the transforming power of the Gospel.
And if something in this story has touched a place you rarely talk about, I want to invite you to do something simple.
Be honest before God.
Not performative.
Not dramatic.
Just honest.
Or, if you are comfortable, share a few words of your testimony.
Not because a comment earns God's attention.
Not because public confession is required for forgiveness.
And certainly not because you owe strangers the details of your wounds.
But because your words may encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
Someone may read your testimony tonight and find the courage to pray again.
Someone may discover that repentance is possible.
Someone may be reminded that God's mercy has not run out.
Send it privately to a family member who needs the reminder that Christ is greater than their past.
You may never know what God does through a Scripture-filled message placed before someone at the right moment.
Not as a lucky charm.
Not as a formula for obtaining blessings.
But as a reminder to return to Scripture when your prayers feel weak and your circumstances seem louder than God's promises.
Because one emotional moment is not the same as lifelong discipleship.
We need Scripture when life is beautiful.
And we need Scripture when life is unbearable.
We need truth that corrects us, grace that humbles us, and fellow believers who encourage us to remain faithful.
We want these resources to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel more clearly, strengthen their faith, and develop habits of spiritual growth.

Some believers choose to support Gospel-centered ministries as part of their regular giving and offerings. If you choose to do that here, we receive it with gratitude and a commitment to steward that support responsibly.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is the kind of support we desire.
Willing.
Thoughtful.
Cheerful.
Free from pressure.
God is not selling His grace.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Salvation is the free gift of God through Jesus Christ.
These products are simply another way to keep Scripture, encouragement, and meaningful reminders of faith close in everyday life.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, and grow.
You can still explore the free resources.
You can still encourage this ministry by inviting others to follow.
It is good news to be proclaimed freely.
Perhaps it is by opening your Bible tonight.
Reading 1 Chronicles 4:9–10 for yourself.
Then turning to the Gospels.
Looking at the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus.
And asking the question that matters more than whether your territory becomes larger:
“Lord Jesus, does my life truly belong to You?”
Because one day, the possessions we accumulated will no longer matter.
The applause will fade.
The online numbers will disappear.
The titles we worked so hard to earn will lose their importance.
And what will matter eternally is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
Jabez had only two verses recorded about him.
Yet his prayer still speaks.
Your life may never be recorded in a history book.
Your name may never be known by thousands.
But the God who heard Jabez is not limited by the obscurity of the person praying.
And through Jesus Christ, we have an even greater reason to approach God with confidence.
Hebrews 4:16 tells believers to come boldly to the throne of grace, to obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
So come.
Come with your fear.
Come with your repentance.
Come with the questions you cannot answer.
Come with the wounds you are tired of hiding.
Come with your hopes, but surrender them to God's wisdom.
Come asking not merely for a larger life, but for a heart that belongs wholly to Christ.
And if you cannot find the words tonight, perhaps begin here:
“Father, I have carried things that have shaped the way I see myself. Some were done to me. Others were the result of my own sinful choices. You know the truth about all of them.
Forgive my sins through Jesus Christ. Teach me to repent where I have rebelled against You. Heal what is wounded according to Your wisdom, and help me obey You even where healing takes time.
Bless me in the ways that truly honor You. Give me opportunities to serve others faithfully. Let Your hand guide me, protect me from evil, and keep my heart from wandering away from Your Word.
And if my circumstances do not change as quickly as I hope, remind me that Your grace is still sufficient.
Let my life tell the truth about Jesus, not merely about what I have survived.
In His holy name, amen.”
And now, before you leave this story behind, remember the man whose name meant so much more to the people around him than we can fully reconstruct.
Jabez did not get to choose the circumstances of his birth.
He did not get to erase the sorrow associated with his name.
But the Bible remembers him as honorable, as a man who called upon God, and as someone whose request God granted.
We should not add to his story what Scripture has not revealed.
And we should not miss what Scripture has made clear.
The Lord heard him.
And the same Scriptures lead us beyond Jabez to Jesus Christ, whose cross and resurrection provide a hope no painful history can cancel for those who trust in Him.
So do not make your wound your savior.
Do not make your success your identity.
Do not make an answered prayer the foundation of your faith.
Build your life on Jesus.
He is greater than the pain you remember.
Greater than the shame you carry.
Greater than the sin you must repent of.
Greater than the future you fear.
And when you find yourself tempted to believe that the worst chapter of your life is the only chapter that matters, remember the Gospel.
The world may remember the name they gave your pain, but in Christ, your pain does not get to pronounce the final word over your eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU STILL LOVE YOUR SPOUSE… SO WHY DOES YOUR HEART FEEL LIKE IT HAS ALREADY LEFT THE MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: YOU STILL LOVE YOUR SPOUSE… SO WHY DOES YOUR HEART FEEL LIKE IT HAS ALREADY LEFT THE MARRIAGE?

When the butterflies disappear, the conversations grow cold, and the person you once couldn't live without becomes someone you barely know—does God expect you to stay in a marriage where love no longer feels alive?
There is a kind of heartbreak nobody prepares you for.
It doesn't begin with an affair.
It doesn't always involve shouting, slammed doors, or divorce papers.
Sometimes, it begins with two people sitting on the same couch, staring at different screens, silently wondering how they became strangers.
You still care about your spouse.
You would be devastated if something terrible happened to them.
You remember the sacrifices you've made together. The bills you've paid. The children you've raised. The storms you've survived.
You don't hate them.
You don't necessarily want someone else.
But somewhere between the wedding vows and the weight of everyday life, something changed.
The excitement disappeared.
The affection became mechanical.
The conversations became logistical.
"Did you pay the electricity bill?"
"What time are you coming home?"
"Have the kids eaten?"
"Don't forget the groceries."
And the person whose voice once made your heart race now speaks to you mostly about responsibilities.
Then comes the thought you feel almost ashamed to admit.
"I love my spouse… but I don't think I'm in love anymore."
And perhaps the most frightening part isn't that you feel this way.
It's that you don't know whether those feelings will ever come back.
You look at your wedding pictures and wonder what happened to those two people.
They looked so certain.
So hopeful.
So convinced that love would always feel the way it did that day.
And now?
You sometimes lie beside the person you promised to love forever, feeling lonelier than you ever felt when you were single.
If that sentence describes something you've been afraid to say aloud, please keep reading.
Because what you're experiencing deserves more than a shallow Christian answer.

And what Scripture actually teaches about love, covenant, suffering, repentance, and restoration may challenge both the person desperate to leave and the person desperately trying to make their spouse stay.
But first, we need to confront something many marriages never survive long enough to understand.
The disappearance of romantic feelings is not automatically the death of love. But neither is a wedding vow permission to ignore a wounded heart.
Those two truths must remain together.
Because when we separate them, we can turn marriage into either an idol of personal happiness or a prison disguised as holiness.
And Jesus calls us to something more truthful than either.
Think back to the beginning.
Remember when you couldn't wait to see each other?
When ordinary conversations lasted until midnight?
When a simple message could change your entire day?
When holding hands felt like the most natural thing in the world?
You weren't imagining those feelings.
They were real.
But feelings, even beautiful ones, were never designed to carry the entire weight of a lifelong covenant.
Infatuation often thrives on discovery, anticipation, novelty, and desire.
Marriage eventually introduces repetition, exhaustion, disappointment, financial pressure, parenting, aging, illness, and the painful discovery that the person you married is as imperfect as you are.
The person who once seemed incapable of hurting you eventually says something that cuts deeply.
And you discover something unsettling.
You can genuinely love someone and still feel disappointed by them.
You can remain committed and still feel emotionally disconnected.
You can be faithful and still feel lonely.
You can even be a devoted Christian and find yourself wondering whether you made a terrible mistake.
That doesn't automatically make you a hypocrite.
It makes your situation serious enough to deserve honesty.
And honesty is where healing often begins.
In Revelation 2:4, Jesus confronts the church in Ephesus:
"Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love." (KJV)
The original Greek contains the words:
τὴν ἀγάπην σου τὴν πρώτην ἀφῆκες
tēn agapēn sou tēn prōtēn aphēkes
A close translation is:
"You have abandoned your first love."
The verb aphēkes, from aphiēmi, carries the sense of leaving, releasing, or abandoning.
Notice something important.
Jesus was addressing a church, not teaching a marriage seminar. We must not pretend this passage was originally written about romantic relationships.
But the spiritual principle is worth considering.
A relationship can retain its outward activity while losing something essential in its inward devotion.
The Ephesian church had works, perseverance, and discernment.
Yet Jesus called attention to love.
And His instruction in Revelation 2:5 was not merely to manufacture an emotion.
It was to remember, repent, and return to the works they had done at first.
That is not a formula guaranteeing marital reconciliation.
But it confronts a question worth asking.
What if part of what has disappeared from your marriage is not merely a feeling you lost, but a way of loving you both gradually stopped practicing?
Perhaps you stopped asking questions because you assumed you already knew the answers.
Perhaps you stopped expressing appreciation because sacrifice became expected.
Perhaps tenderness disappeared beneath criticism.
Perhaps every attempt at conversation became an argument, until silence felt safer than honesty.
Perhaps your spouse tried to explain their loneliness years ago, but you were too defensive to listen.
Or perhaps you were the one pleading for connection while your spouse repeatedly dismissed your pain.
Those situations are not identical.
And they should not be treated as though both people always bear equal responsibility.
Sometimes disconnection develops through mutual neglect.
Sometimes one person has been carrying the relationship almost alone.
Sometimes emotional distance is a response to betrayal, intimidation, cruelty, or repeated broken promises.
The Gospel does not require us to erase those distinctions.
Love rejoices in truth, not denial.
And before asking whether the romance can return, we must be willing to ask what actually happened.
Was it exhaustion?
Unresolved resentment?
Years of emotional neglect?
A betrayal that was never properly addressed?
Unspoken grief?
A pattern of contempt?
A life so consumed by survival that you forgot how to enjoy each other?
Or has the marriage become unsafe?
These questions matter because a marriage suffering from routine is not the same as a marriage suffering from abuse.
And a spouse who feels emotionally numb after years of mistreatment does not need to be shamed into pretending that everything is fine.
God sees what happens behind closed doors.
Including what nobody at church knows.
Including what the smiling anniversary photographs conceal.
Including the tears you wiped away before Sunday worship.
Including the prayers you whispered when you didn't know whether you could endure another year.
Psalm 34:18 says:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." (KJV)
God's nearness to the brokenhearted is not reserved for people whose pain fits neatly into someone else's expectations.
He sees the spouse who longs to be loved.
He sees the spouse who has become emotionally exhausted.
He sees the person who regrets what they have done.
And He sees the person who has been harmed.
But there is another truth we must confront.
Sometimes we confuse the end of infatuation with the end of marriage because we were taught to recognize love primarily by how it makes us feel.
Scripture presents a deeper vision.
In 1 Corinthians 13:4, Paul writes:
The Greek word translated "charity" in the King James Version is:
ἀγάπη — agapē
It means love.
In this chapter, Paul describes love through its character and conduct: patience, kindness, humility, truthfulness, perseverance.
He does not define it as a constant state of romantic excitement.
Yet we must understand the context correctly.
First Corinthians 13 addresses Christian love within the wider life of the church. It is not exclusively a marriage passage.
Nevertheless, its teaching applies powerfully to how Christians should treat their spouses.
Love is not merely something we experience.
It is also something we practice.
But please don't misunderstand this.
Biblical love is not simply enduring anything another person chooses to do.
First Corinthians 13:6 says love "rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth."
Real love cannot be separated from truth.
It does not demand that a wounded spouse conceal abuse.
It does not excuse adultery.
It does not baptize manipulation.
It does not require someone to surrender their safety to prove their faithfulness.
And it does not allow a neglectful spouse to quote Scripture while refusing to change.
Covenant love is not the freedom to stop trying because the other person promised to stay.
Read that again.
Some people have mistaken their spouse's faithfulness for permission to become careless.
They stopped listening.
Stopped apologizing.
Stopped showing affection.
Stopped being considerate.
Stopped protecting the emotional intimacy of the marriage.
And when their spouse finally said, "I don't feel anything anymore," they acted shocked.
But a heart can become exhausted from reaching toward someone who continually refuses to reach back.
This is why Ephesians 5:25 is so confronting:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
The Greek command begins:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas
"Husbands, love your wives."
The word agapate is a command to love.
And the model Paul gives is astonishing.
Christ's self-giving love.
Not domination.
Not selfish entitlement.
Not spiritual intimidation.
Not using the Bible to demand obedience while refusing responsibility.
Christ gave Himself.
And throughout Ephesians 5, marriage is placed within a vision of holiness, sacrificial care, and the profound mystery of Christ and His church.
The passage also calls wives to respond within this covenant relationship, and Ephesians 5:21 frames the discussion with reverence for Christ.
Whatever differences Christians may have about the precise application of marital roles, no faithful reading should turn Christlike love into an excuse for cruelty or coercion.
Jesus did not love His church by exploiting its vulnerability.
He gave Himself for her good.
So if you say you love your spouse, ask yourself something uncomfortable.
When was the last time your spouse actually experienced that love?
Not merely heard you claim it.
Experienced it.
When did they last feel heard without being interrupted?
When did you last apologize without explaining why your behavior was really their fault?
When did you last notice their exhaustion and offer help without expecting praise?
When did you last touch them with tenderness that wasn't a demand for sex?
When did you last pray for their spiritual well-being without using prayer to criticize them?
And when did you last ask:
"Have I made it difficult for you to feel safe, valued, and loved beside me?"
That question can hurt.
Especially when the answer is yes.
But sometimes the most important turning point in a marriage begins when someone stops saying, "You aren't making me happy," and begins asking, "What have I done with the heart that trusted me?"
And sometimes it begins when a wounded spouse finally says, "I cannot keep pretending that this is acceptable."
Both moments can be acts of truth.
There is a beautiful word in the Hebrew Scriptures that helps us understand the seriousness of covenant commitment.
חֶסֶד — ḥesed
The word can communicate steadfast love, covenant loyalty, mercy, or faithful kindness, depending on its context.
It is frequently used to describe God's faithful love toward His people.
Psalm 136 repeatedly celebrates the enduring nature of God's ḥesed.
We should not flatten the word into a simple synonym for romantic affection or claim that every biblical marriage passage uses it.
But it reveals something extraordinary about the biblical understanding of faithful love.
Love can possess a steadfastness deeper than changing circumstances.
And that challenges a culture in which the loss of excitement is sometimes treated as sufficient proof that a relationship has no future.
Yet God's covenant faithfulness must never be used to demand unlimited tolerance of human wrongdoing.
God's love is holy.
His mercy does not make evil good.
His patience does not make injustice righteous.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because there may be someone reading this who is not simply bored.
You have been betrayed.
You have been humiliated.
You have been threatened.
You have been controlled financially, emotionally, physically, or sexually.
And someone has told you that if you really loved Jesus, you would just endure it quietly.
Please hear this clearly.
Being faithful to Christ does not require you to remain in immediate danger.

Seek safety and qualified help when abuse is present. In situations of violence, threats, or coercive control, safety planning and appropriate professional support should come before joint counseling, which can sometimes increase danger.
Christians hold different interpretations of divorce and remarriage, and Scripture's teaching on marriage must be handled carefully rather than reduced to slogans.
Jesus addresses sexual immorality and divorce in Matthew 19:3–9. Paul addresses marital separation, reconciliation, and abandonment in 1 Corinthians 7.
These are serious passages, deserving careful study and wise pastoral counsel.
No one should casually promise that every marriage can be restored, or condemn someone for protecting themselves and their children.
But for those whose marriages are not unsafe, whose love has become buried beneath disappointment and distance, another question remains.
What if you are not standing at the end of your marriage?
What if you are standing at the end of the version of your marriage that could no longer continue?
Because sometimes the old patterns need to die before something healthier can grow.
The contempt needs to stop.
The secrecy needs to end.
The defensiveness needs to be confronted.
The emotional neglect needs to be acknowledged.
The pride needs to surrender.
And both people, where both are willing and able, need to learn how to love each other with greater maturity than they possessed on their wedding day.
Not by pretending to become the same two people they once were.
But by learning how to meet each other honestly as the people they have become.
Consider what Scripture says in Colossians 3:13:
"Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye." (KJV)
Forgiveness is central to Christian discipleship.
But forgiveness is not the same as restored trust.
Forgiveness does not eliminate consequences.
And reconciliation cannot be manufactured by one person's willingness alone.
A spouse who has betrayed trust must do more than say, "I'm sorry."
Repentance should bear fruit.
Jesus says in Luke 3:8, through John the Baptist's call to repentance, that people must "bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance."
The principle is clear.
Genuine repentance should become visible.
If you have repeatedly wounded your spouse, don't demand that they immediately feel close to you because you've finally admitted wrongdoing.
Become trustworthy.
Tell the truth.
Accept accountability.
Respect boundaries.
Seek help where needed.
Be patient with the healing you cannot control.
And if you are the wounded spouse, you are not required to manufacture romantic feelings to prove you have forgiven someone.
Trust may take time.
Some relationships may not be safely or wisely restored.
The goal is not to preserve appearances at any cost.
The goal is to walk in truth before God.
Now imagine a different scene.
It's late.
The house is quiet.
The children are asleep.
You and your spouse are sitting at the kitchen table.
There is no dramatic music.
No perfect speech.
No sudden flood of romantic feelings.
Just two tired people.
And for once, neither is trying to win.
One of you finally says:
"I miss us."
The other looks down.
Silence.
Then perhaps:
"I didn't know you still did."
And instead of launching into another argument, you begin telling the truth.
Not every truth at once.
Not every accusation you've been collecting for years.
Just enough honesty to open a door.
"I've felt alone."
"I know I've hurt you."
"I stopped trying because I thought you didn't care."
"I was afraid you would reject me."
"I don't know how to fix this."
And perhaps the most courageous sentence of all:
"I don't know whether my feelings will come back, but I'm willing to explore whether we can rebuild something honest and good."
That is not a guarantee.
But it is a beginning.
And beginnings do not always feel romantic.
Sometimes they feel terrifying.
Sometimes they sound like an apology.
Sometimes they look like making a counseling appointment.
Sometimes they mean learning to listen without preparing a defense.
Sometimes they mean confronting depression, burnout, trauma, or other struggles that have affected emotional connection.
Sometimes they mean making space for rest, friendship, laughter, and affection again.
Sometimes they mean admitting that you cannot repair a marriage through prayer alone while refusing the practical obedience, accountability, and help that love requires.
Prayer matters.
Deeply.
But prayer is not an excuse to avoid responsibility.
James 2:17 says:
"Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." (KJV)
James is teaching about living faith, not presenting a specialized marriage-repair technique.
Still, his warning should challenge anyone who prays for transformation while refusing to take an honest step toward it.
Don't only pray for your spouse to change.
Ask God to expose what needs repentance in you.
Don't only pray for affection to return.
Consider whether your daily behavior creates conditions in which trust and tenderness can grow.
Don't only ask God to heal what is broken.
Be willing to stop doing what keeps breaking it.
And please remember this.
You cannot repent on behalf of your spouse.
You cannot force someone to love faithfully.
You cannot make another person tell the truth.
You cannot single-handedly create mutual intimacy.
You can take responsibility for your own conduct, seek wise support, establish healthy boundaries, and invite honest change.
But you are not the Holy Spirit.
And the salvation of your marriage is not a burden God has commanded you to carry alone.
This brings us to the deepest truth of all.
Your spouse was never meant to be your savior.
And neither were you meant to be theirs.
Marriage can be a beautiful gift from God.
But it is a terrible substitute for God.
When we expect another human being to satisfy every longing, heal every wound, and guarantee our happiness, we place a weight upon them that no imperfect person can carry.
Your spouse may be your companion.
Your friend.
Your covenant partner.
Your closest earthly confidant.
But they cannot redeem your soul.
Only Jesus can do that.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Notice where the Gospel begins.
Not with people who have finally become lovable enough.
Not with people who have perfected their relationships.
But with sinners who need grace.
Jesus Christ entered a broken world.
He lived without sin.
He bore our sins upon the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That is the foundation of Christian hope.
Not the promise that every broken marriage will be restored.
Not the promise that every romantic feeling will return.
But the certainty that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior, even when earthly relationships are painfully uncertain.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
Paul is speaking about the new creation reality of belonging to Christ.
We must not misuse this verse as a guarantee that every damaged marriage will become happy again.
But it does tell us something glorious.
Your past does not have to be the final definition of who you are in Christ.
The person who has sinned can repent.
The person who has been wounded can receive grace and pursue healing.
The person whose marriage has failed is not beyond God's mercy.
The person whose marriage is struggling is not automatically a spiritual failure.
And the person whose marriage is being rebuilt can learn a kind of love that goes deeper than the excitement that first brought two people together.
Perhaps this is why the words of Lamentations 3:22–23 are so precious:
"It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." (KJV)
These words arise from a context of profound suffering, not a promise of easy circumstances.
And that makes them even more meaningful.
God's faithfulness is not dependent upon life feeling beautiful.
His mercies are not exhausted by the darkest chapter.
So perhaps tomorrow morning, instead of asking only, "Do I still feel in love?" you might begin with a different prayer.
"Lord Jesus, show me what is true."
"Show me where I have become selfish."
"Show me where I have been wounded."
"Give me courage to repent where I have sinned."
"Give me wisdom to recognize what is healthy and what is harmful."
"Teach me to love without pretending."
"Teach me to forgive without denying the truth."
"And whatever happens in my marriage, keep my heart anchored in You."
Because sometimes God restores a marriage through the slow rebuilding of trust, affection, and friendship.
Sometimes the path involves painful boundaries, separation, or decisions that require wise counsel.
And sometimes the outcome is not the one a person prayed for.
But no outcome can make the cross of Christ meaningless.
No marital status can determine your worth before God.
No broken human relationship can cancel the invitation to receive His grace.
And if you are reading this while your spouse sleeps beside you, unaware of how close you've come to giving up, I want to leave you with something practical.
Don't make a lifelong decision based solely on a season of emotional numbness.
But don't ignore years of serious harm simply because you fear disappointing others.
Tell the truth.
Seek wise, trustworthy counsel.
If it is safe, speak with your spouse honestly about what has changed.
Consider a qualified marriage counselor who respects both your faith and your safety.
Give meaningful change the time it deserves, without pretending that time alone heals anything.
And if you are both willing to rebuild, start with something small and real.
A conversation without phones.
A sincere apology.
A shared prayer.
A walk together.
A question you haven't asked in years.
"What has life felt like for you lately?"
Then listen.
Really listen.
You might discover a pain you never understood.
You might discover a longing your spouse was afraid to express.
You might discover that the person you thought you knew has been silently grieving the same distance you have.
Or you might discover that deeper intervention is necessary.
Either way, truth is better than pretending.

And if both of you are willing to practice patient, accountable, sacrificial love, you may find that intimacy can grow again—not as a perfect repetition of your first romance, but as something tested, wiser, and more deeply rooted.
A love that knows the cost of forgiveness.
A love that no longer takes kindness for granted.
A love that has learned the difference between being right and being reconciled.
A love that does not need every day to feel like a honeymoon in order to remain meaningful.
A love that reflects, however imperfectly, the grace of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps one day, you will look across the table at the person you nearly gave up on and realize something unexpected.
You are not the same people who stood at the altar.
You have both changed.
You have both suffered.
You have both learned things the younger versions of yourselves could never have understood.
But by God's grace, where repentance, safety, truth, and mutual willingness have made rebuilding possible, you have learned how to choose each other with open eyes.
Not because you are afraid to be alone.
Not because everyone expects you to stay.
Not because your marriage is your identity.
But because love has become more than a feeling you wait to receive.
It has become a faithful way of treating someone whose humanity you have finally learned to see.
And maybe, somewhere in that patient work, affection begins to return.
A laugh you haven't heard in months.
A hand reaching for yours.
A conversation that doesn't end in resentment.
A smile that reminds you of the beginning.
Not every marriage will experience that ending.
But some will.
And if yours can, don't underestimate the significance of the first honest step.
There may be someone reading this who has already begun crying.
Someone who has been silently asking God whether their marriage is worth fighting for.
Someone who has made terrible mistakes and wants to repent.
Someone who is exhausted from trying alone.
Someone who needs permission to seek safety.
Someone who still loves their spouse but no longer knows how to reach them.
If that person is you, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply reacting to another post.
Tell the truth before God.
You might write, "Lord, teach us to love again."
Or "Pray for my marriage."
Or "Jesus, heal what I cannot fix."
If you are carrying a story too private to explain, you don't owe strangers the details. Even a simple "I need prayer" can invite others to stand with you.
Not to promise everyone the same outcome.
But to remind someone that change is possible.
Someone reading your words may be sitting at the very kitchen table where you once cried.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is real, that counseling can help, that trust takes time, and that God's grace is not exhausted by human failure.
That simple act can help the message reach people who would never openly search for marriage advice.
Invite your spouse, your friends, your family, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who have drifted from the faith to follow along.
Because discipleship is not merely about learning what the Bible says.
It is about allowing the truth of God's Word to transform the way we live, forgive, repent, speak, and love.
And if these messages have helped you, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by purchasing anything.

Scripture teaches that believers may freely support those who labor in sharing the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled.
What matters is a willing heart, wise stewardship, and genuine love for Christ.
And please remember that discipleship resources are not reserved only for paying supporters.
A single article may reach someone in a season of despair.
A devotional may help someone open Scripture again.
A message about repentance may lead someone to confess a hidden sin.
A reflection about grace may remind a wounded believer that Jesus has not abandoned them.
We cannot control the outcome of every message.
But we can faithfully plant seeds and trust God with the increase.
Because this work is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing people toward the Savior.
The One who forgives sinners.
The One who calls us to repentance.
The One who never confuses love with deception.
The One who meets the brokenhearted with truth and mercy.
The One who is still worthy of our trust when the future of a marriage remains uncertain.
So before you close this article, return to the question that brought you here.
"I love my spouse, but I'm no longer in love. Is my marriage over?"
Not necessarily.
The fading of romantic feelings alone does not determine the future of a marriage.
But neither can the future be decided by feelings alone, by pressure from others, or by one spouse's efforts while the other refuses accountability.
Look honestly at the relationship.
Consider whether it is safe.
Seek wisdom.
Make room for repentance.
Invite real change.
And remember that the greatest love story in Scripture is not about two flawless people who never disappointed each other.
It is about the holy Son of God who came to redeem sinners through His death and resurrection.
That is where our hope begins.
That is where grace becomes more than a beautiful word.
And that is where broken people discover that their failures do not have to be the final word over their lives.
Perhaps your marriage needs restoration.
Perhaps your heart needs healing.
Perhaps you need to repent.
Perhaps you need the courage to establish boundaries.
Perhaps you need to stop trying to save your marriage through your own strength and begin seeking Christ's wisdom one faithful step at a time.
Whatever your situation, do not mistake the silence of your emotions for the silence of God.
The wedding photograph may remind you of the love you once felt—but the cross reminds you of the Savior whose love remains when everything else feels uncertain.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING WENT TO SLEEP WITH ANOTHER MAN’S WIFE UNDER HIS ROOF… THEN GOD TOLD HIM HE WAS A DEAD MAN.
paragraphs: THE KING WENT TO SLEEP WITH ANOTHER MAN’S WIFE UNDER HIS ROOF… THEN GOD TOLD HIM HE WAS A DEAD MAN.

He thought he was innocent. He thought nobody had been harmed. But one terrifying dream exposed a dangerous deception—and revealed a God who confronts sin, protects the vulnerable, and offers mercy before judgment falls.
“But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night, and said to him, Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man's wife.” — Genesis 20:3 (KJV)
Imagine going to bed believing everything in your kingdom is under control.
Your servants obey you. Your reputation is secure. Your authority is unquestioned.
Then, somewhere between midnight and morning, the God of heaven interrupts your sleep.
And the first thing you hear is that you are a dead man.
Not because an enemy army has surrounded your palace.
Not because someone has poisoned your food.
Not because your throne has been stolen.
But because of a woman sleeping under your roof.
A woman you believed was available.
A woman whose husband had allowed you to believe she was his sister.
And now the God you cannot command, bribe, or silence is telling you that your life is in danger.
What would you do?
Would you defend yourself?
Would you blame the man who deceived you?
Would you argue that you never intended to do anything wrong?
Or would you discover, perhaps for the first time, that being powerful enough to take something does not mean you have the right to possess it?
Because this story is not merely about an ancient king who nearly lost his life.
It is about the terrifying difference between what we believe about ourselves and what God knows to be true.

And before this story ends, the man who appears most spiritually respectable will be exposed, the pagan king will plead his innocence, and the mercy of God will become the only reason a terrible tragedy does not unfold.
But there is one detail you must not miss.
The woman had not yet been touched.
That single fact changes how we understand the entire story.
And it reveals something extraordinary about the God who sometimes intervenes before the damage we are about to cause becomes irreversible.
Abraham had journeyed into the region of the Negev and settled for a time in Gerar.
He was not an ordinary traveler.
He was the man God had called out of his homeland. The man who had received extraordinary promises. The man through whom God had promised blessing to the nations.
Yet even people who have encountered God can make decisions that reveal how deeply fear still controls them.
When Abraham arrived in Gerar, he said of Sarah, his wife, “She is my sister.”
There was a partial truth behind the statement. Genesis 20:12 later reveals that Sarah was Abraham's half-sister.
But a partial truth deliberately used to conceal a crucial fact can become a powerful instrument of deception.
Sarah was also his wife.
And that was the truth Abraham withheld.
He feared that the men of the land might kill him because of Sarah.
So he tried to protect himself by placing her in a vulnerable position.
Read that again.
The man who had received God's promise was afraid of what human beings might do to him.
And instead of trusting the God who had promised to preserve his future, he reached for an old strategy of self-preservation.
This was not the first time Abraham had done something like this.
Genesis 12 records a similar incident in Egypt.
Years had passed. God had been faithful. Abraham had witnessed divine intervention.
Yet the same fear had resurfaced.
Isn't that painfully familiar?
You can survive one season of spiritual failure, experience God's forgiveness, and still find yourself struggling with the same fear years later.
The same insecurity.
The same temptation to control the outcome.
The same habit of hiding behind carefully chosen words.
You may know the promises of God and still panic when circumstances threaten your security.
You may genuinely love the Lord and still make decisions that hurt people you were supposed to protect.
That does not make the wrongdoing harmless.
It makes the need for repentance undeniable.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because Abraham's fear did not remain a private struggle inside his heart.
It reached into someone else's life.
Sarah was taken into the household of Abimelech, king of Gerar.
Scripture does not describe every conversation or every emotion Sarah experienced, and we should not pretend to know what the text does not reveal.
But the danger was real.
She was a married woman in another man's royal household.
And the king had been led to believe she was unmarried.
Then came the dream.
Not a vague feeling.
Not a disturbing coincidence.
Not a nightmare Abimelech could dismiss as an overactive imagination.
Genesis 20 explicitly tells us that God came to him in a dream.
And the message was devastating.
In the Hebrew text of Genesis 20:3, God says:
הִנְּךָ מֵת
Hinnekh met.
“Behold, you are a dead man.”
The expression carries the force of a divine death warning. It does not mean Abimelech had already physically died. God was confronting him with the mortal danger of the situation.
And the reason follows:
כִּי־בְעֻלַת בָּעַל הִוא
Ki-ve'ulat ba'al hi.
“Because she is a married woman.”
The Hebrew expression identifies Sarah as a woman bound in marriage to a husband.
She was not simply another beautiful woman who had entered a king's household.
She belonged to a marriage covenant that Abimelech had no right to violate.
And God was not treating that covenant as a small matter.
Think about that.
The king possessed political authority.
He could command servants.
He could make decisions affecting an entire kingdom.
But his authority ended where God's moral authority began.
A crown could not make adultery righteous.
A palace could not make deception harmless.
And royal power could not erase the sanctity of another person's marriage.
This is a truth our generation desperately needs.
We live in a world where people sometimes confuse opportunity with permission.
Where the ability to pursue someone becomes an excuse for disregarding commitments.
Where attraction is treated as destiny.
Where secret conversations are defended because nothing physical has happened yet.
Where emotional betrayal is minimized because someone insists, “We haven't crossed that line.”
But the God of Genesis 20 does not wait until every consequence has unfolded before revealing that something is wrong.
He sees the danger before the king acts.
And in this particular case, He intervenes.
Not because Abimelech is morally perfect.
Not because Abraham has behaved faithfully.
But because God is both holy and merciful.
Abimelech responds with a question that almost sounds like a desperate cry from a man standing at the edge of judgment.
“Lord, wilt thou slay also a righteous nation?” — Genesis 20:4 (KJV)
Then he explains himself.
Abraham had told him Sarah was his sister.
Sarah had also said Abraham was her brother.
Abimelech had acted without knowing the truth about their marriage.
He says:
“In the integrity of my heart and innocency of my hands have I done this.” — Genesis 20:5 (KJV)
And then comes one of the most astonishing moments in the passage.
God acknowledges the king's lack of knowledge.
“Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart.” — Genesis 20:6 (KJV)
God knew.
He knew what Abraham had concealed.
He knew what Sarah had said.
He knew what Abimelech believed.
He knew what had happened.
And He knew what had not happened.
There is something deeply sobering about serving a God who cannot be deceived by appearances.
He knows when we are pretending.
But He also knows when we have genuinely been misled.
He sees the intentions behind our decisions, the information available to us, and the actions we have actually taken.
This does not mean that sincerity automatically makes every action right.
Abimelech's situation still required correction.
But it means that the judgment of God is never based on ignorance.
He knows the truth completely.
And here is the line that should make every reader stop.
God tells Abimelech:
“For I also withheld thee from sinning against me: therefore suffered I thee not to touch her.” — Genesis 20:6 (KJV)
Did you catch that?
“I also withheld thee.”
In Hebrew:
וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ גַּם־אָנֹכִי אוֹתְךָ
Va'echsokh gam-anokhi otkha.
The sense is, “I myself also kept you back.”
Abimelech had not committed adultery with Sarah.
But God revealed that His own intervention had prevented that sin.
The king's innocence regarding physical relations was real, yet he had also been protected from crossing a boundary he did not fully understand.
And suddenly this story becomes much more than a warning about wrongdoing.
It becomes a testimony to divine restraint.
How many times have we thanked God for the doors He opened but never considered the doors He kept closed?
How many times have we praised Him for opportunities He gave us but complained about opportunities He refused to allow?
We remember the prayers He answered.
We rarely think about the consequences His providence may have spared us from.
Sometimes a relationship does not develop.
Sometimes a secret is exposed.
Sometimes a plan collapses.
Sometimes a conversation ends before it becomes something far more destructive.
We cannot automatically claim that every disappointment is a supernatural intervention like the dream recorded in Genesis 20.
Scripture does not give us permission to explain every closed door that way.
But this passage does teach us that God is capable of restraining evil before it reaches its intended outcome.
And that should humble us.
Because not every disaster avoided is evidence of our own wisdom.
Not every temptation resisted is an achievement for which we should congratulate ourselves.
Sometimes we have been more dependent on God's mercy than we realized.
And perhaps one of the most dangerous sentences a human being can say is:
“I would never do something like that.”
Peter believed he would never deny Jesus.
Yet before the rooster crowed, he denied knowing Him three times.
Abraham had witnessed God's faithfulness.
Yet fear still led him into deception.
Abimelech believed he was acting with integrity.
Yet he was standing dangerously close to violating another man's marriage.
The lesson is not that nobody can ever be trusted.
The lesson is that no human heart is so strong that it no longer needs the grace of God.
And this is where the Gospel begins to shine through the shadows of the story.
Not because Genesis 20 directly narrates the cross.
It does not.
But because the same Scriptures that expose human sin ultimately lead us to the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
Abraham was God's chosen servant, but he was not the sinless Savior.
He was a man of faith who still needed correction.
He was a recipient of God's promises who still needed mercy.
And the promise given to Abraham would ultimately reach its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Galatians 3:16 identifies Christ as the promised offspring through whom God's covenant purposes find their fulfillment.
The Bible is not ultimately the story of impressive people who never fail.
It is the unfolding revelation of a faithful God who keeps His redemptive promises despite the failures of human beings.
And that distinction matters.
Because if your hope depends on never failing, your hope will eventually collapse.
But if your hope rests in Jesus Christ, you have a Savior whose righteousness does not collapse when yours does.
Abraham's deception was real.
Abimelech's danger was real.
Sarah's vulnerability was real.
And God's intervention was real.
Grace did not make the deception acceptable.
Grace prevented the situation from becoming worse and opened the way for restoration.
Then God commanded Abimelech to return Sarah to Abraham.
“Now therefore restore the man his wife; for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live.” — Genesis 20:7 (KJV)
Notice the command.
Restore the man's wife.
Not merely regret what happened.
Not simply explain the misunderstanding.
Not promise to be more careful next time.
Return her.
Make the situation right.
God also warned that refusing to restore Sarah would bring death upon Abimelech and those belonging to him.
This was not an empty threat.
It was a divine warning accompanied by a clear path of obedience.
And there is a lesson here that modern Christianity must not soften.
Repentance is more than feeling emotional about sin.
When possible, genuine repentance seeks to correct the wrong.
If you have stolen, repentance should move you toward restitution.
If you have deceived, repentance should move you toward truth.
If you have harmed someone, repentance should move you toward accountability and appropriate repair.
If you are pursuing someone else's spouse, repentance means ending that sinful pursuit, not merely asking God to bless your feelings.
And if you are using religious language to justify something Scripture condemns, you do not need a more convincing excuse.
You need to surrender.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance.
It conveys a change of mind or heart that, in biblical teaching, is expressed in a changed direction of life.
Jesus proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15 (KJV)
Repentance is not the price by which we purchase forgiveness.
Forgiveness is God's gift of grace through Christ.
But the grace that saves us does not teach us to remain comfortable with the sins from which Christ came to deliver us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
And the Gospel never asks us to pretend our failures were insignificant.
It calls us to bring them into the light of the One who died for sinners.
Abimelech obeyed the warning.
Genesis 20:8 tells us that he rose early, called his servants, and explained what had happened.
The men were afraid.
Then Abimelech confronted Abraham.
And what he asked should disturb anyone who has ever used fear to justify dishonesty.
“What hast thou done unto us?” — Genesis 20:9 (KJV)
In other words:
What have you brought upon us?
How could your decisions have exposed other people to such danger?
Abraham had been afraid of losing his life.
Yet his attempt to protect himself had placed others at risk.
This is one of the most painful realities of sin.
It rarely stays as private as we imagine.
The lie you tell to protect your image may damage someone else's reputation.
The secret you keep to preserve your comfort may destroy someone else's trust.
The compromise you excuse as personal may wound the people who depend on you.
And sometimes the person confronting you with the truth is not someone you expected to have greater moral clarity.
In this story, a foreign king challenges the behavior of God's covenant servant.
That should make every believer deeply humble.
Being familiar with Scripture does not make our actions automatically righteous.
Having a ministry does not excuse dishonesty.
Holding a spiritual title does not exempt us from accountability.
And knowing the right words about faith does not mean we are actually trusting God.
Abraham explained that he believed there was no fear of God in that place and that people might kill him because of Sarah.
Yet the narrative reveals that Abraham's assumption about the people of Gerar was dangerously incomplete.
The king had responded seriously to God's warning.
The servants feared.
And Abraham, the man who should have trusted the Lord, had allowed fear to govern his choices.
What a reversal.
Sometimes we spend so much time worrying about the darkness around us that we fail to confront the compromise within us.
We fear what unbelievers might do.
We fear what people might say.
We fear rejection, embarrassment, financial loss, and humiliation.
And in trying to control those fears, we sometimes become the very people whose behavior dishonors the God we claim to represent.
That is not a reason to abandon faith.
It is a reason to return to Christ with humility.
Because Christianity is not a performance of moral superiority.
It is a life of repentance, trust, obedience, and transformation under the lordship of Jesus.
The story continues with an extraordinary act of restoration.
Abimelech returned Sarah.
He gave Abraham sheep, cattle, and servants.
He offered him freedom to settle in his land.
And he provided silver, described in Genesis 20:16 as a public vindication concerning Sarah.
The king who had been warned of death now took concrete steps to correct the situation.
Then Abraham prayed.
And God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants so that they could bear children.
Genesis 20:17–18 explains that the Lord had closed the wombs of Abimelech's household because of Sarah.
The story that began with a royal household under divine warning ends with restoration and healing.
But do not overlook the strange beauty of what happened.
God instructed Abraham to pray for the very household endangered by Abraham's own deception.
The man who had failed was still called to serve within God's purposes.
Not because his failure did not matter.
Not because his conduct was beyond correction.
But because God's covenant faithfulness was greater than Abraham's inconsistency.
And if that does not give you hope, perhaps you have been carrying your own failures for so long that you have forgotten what grace can do.
Maybe you are reading this with a memory you wish you could erase.
A conversation you should never have started.
A lie that became easier to repeat than to confess.
A relationship you knew was wrong.
A marriage you damaged.
A trust you betrayed.
A season when fear made your decisions for you.
Or perhaps you were the one hurt by someone else's deception.
You were the person whose trust was sacrificed so somebody else could feel safe.
You were the one who suffered because another person refused to tell the truth.
Hear this carefully.
God's mercy toward the person who sinned does not mean He has forgotten the person who was harmed.
Sarah's marriage mattered to God.
The danger to her mattered.
The truth mattered.
And restoration mattered.
The Gospel does not require wounded people to pretend that betrayal was harmless.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust, remove consequences, or require someone to remain in an unsafe situation.
God's grace is not permission for another person to continue hurting you.
The Lord who calls sinners to repentance also calls His people to walk in truth, justice, and love.
And this is why the story of Abimelech still speaks with such force.
It exposes the illusion that we can control the moral consequences of our choices.
It reveals the danger of fear-driven deception.
It reminds us that marriage is sacred before God.
It shows that ignorance and intention matter, while also demonstrating the necessity of correcting a wrong once it is revealed.
And it confronts us with the reality that God's mercy can intervene before catastrophe becomes complete.
But there is a greater King we must look toward.
Not Abimelech, who nearly committed a terrible wrong without knowing it.
Not Abraham, who tried to preserve his life through deception.
But Jesus Christ.
The King who never lied to protect Himself.
The King who never betrayed His Father's will.
The King who did not sacrifice the vulnerable to preserve His own comfort.
The King who willingly laid down His life for His people.
Where Abraham's fear endangered others, Christ's obedience brought salvation to sinners.
Where Abimelech needed a warning to avoid sin, Jesus remained without sin.
Where the ancient story shows mercy interrupting danger, the cross reveals the astonishing depth of God's mercy toward the guilty.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we made ourselves respectable.
Not after we cleaned up every hidden corner of our lives.
Not after we became worthy of His sacrifice.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
But do not mistake grace for indifference toward sin.
The cross does not announce that sin is unimportant.
It reveals how serious sin is and how extraordinary God's love is.
Jesus did not die so that we could comfortably remain enslaved to the very things destroying us.
He died and rose again so that sinners might be reconciled to God and receive new life in Him.
And perhaps this is the question that should follow you long after you finish reading.
What if the thing you keep defending is the very thing God is calling you to surrender?
What if you have spent years explaining why your compromise is understandable, when the Lord is calling you to walk in truth?
What if the relationship you refuse to release is pulling you away from obedience?
What if the lie you call protection is quietly damaging someone you love?
What if the pride you call strength is keeping you from admitting that you need forgiveness?
What if the warning you resent is actually an expression of mercy?
Abimelech could have dismissed the dream.
He could have appealed to his authority.
He could have insisted that his intentions made obedience unnecessary.
But once God revealed the truth, he had a decision to make.
And so do we.
We cannot rewrite yesterday.
We cannot undo every consequence.
We cannot recover every opportunity we wasted.
But by God's grace, we can repent today.
We can stop hiding.
We can confess what is true.
We can make restitution where possible.
We can seek forgiveness without demanding that other people immediately trust us again.
And above all, we can come to Jesus Christ, whose mercy is sufficient for every sinner who truly turns to Him.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
The forgiveness Christ offers is not a shallow reassurance that nothing was wrong.
It is cleansing purchased through His saving work.
The Savior who knows the worst about us is also the Savior who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
So do not build your future around defending your past.
Bring your past to the cross.
Do not make a home inside your shame.
Bring your shame to the One who bore sin and disgrace for our redemption.
Do not confuse another day of life with permission to continue in rebellion.
Receive today as another opportunity to turn toward God.
And if this story has exposed something you have been hiding, do not silence that conviction with another excuse.
Talk to the Lord.
Tell Him the truth.
You do not need an impressive speech.
You need a surrendered heart.

“Lord Jesus, I have tried to protect myself in ways that have dishonored You. I have defended things I should have confessed. I have allowed fear, pride, and desire to influence my decisions. Forgive me. Teach me to walk in truth. Give me courage to correct what I can, humility to accept the consequences of my actions, and faith to trust Your grace. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I surrender myself to You. Lead me into a life that honors Your name. Amen.”
And if you prayed those words sincerely, remember that the power is not in repeating a particular prayer.
Our hope is in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Keep turning to Him.
Keep learning His Word.
Keep walking in obedience.
And when you stumble, do not run farther into darkness.
Return to the light.
Because the story of Genesis 20 is not an invitation to admire human perfection.
It is an invitation to stand in awe of divine holiness, mercy, and faithfulness.
A king went to sleep believing he was safe.
God awakened him to the truth.
A prophet tried to protect himself through deception.
God exposed the danger.
A woman was caught in a situation she should never have been placed in.
God intervened to protect the marriage covenant.
And a household that had come under judgment experienced restoration.
All of it reminds us that the Lord is not indifferent to the decisions we make.
He sees.
He knows.
He warns.
He calls us to obedience.
And in Jesus Christ, He offers the grace that sinners could never earn.
Perhaps someone you know is standing at a crossroads right now.
Someone who has convinced themselves that a secret relationship is harmless.
Someone whose fear has made dishonesty seem necessary.
Someone who thinks their past has disqualified them from ever coming back to God.
Someone whose heart is exhausted from carrying guilt.
Or someone who has been wounded by another person's betrayal and desperately needs to know that God sees the truth.
Not simply to fill a newsfeed with another religious post, but because the Word of God deserves to be heard beyond the walls of our churches and the boundaries of our familiar circles.
A single Scripture-centered message may become the beginning of an important conversation, a needed confession, or someone's renewed search for Christ.
And I want to ask you something.
Not for a polished religious answer.
Not for something that makes you appear spiritually strong.
But for an honest response.
Has God ever stopped you from going down a road you later realized could have destroyed something precious?
If you are comfortable sharing, tell us what you learned.
You do not need to reveal private details to be welcomed into a conversation about grace.
Come back to Genesis 20 when fear tempts you to compromise, when shame tempts you to hide, or when pride tempts you to believe you no longer need correction.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, seekers, and even those who have not yet placed their faith in Christ to follow along.
The Gospel is too precious to keep inside the circle of people who already agree with us.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and reach farther, there is another meaningful way to participate.
Some believers may prayerfully choose to include this kind of support within their broader Christian giving, alongside their responsibilities to their local church, family, and others in need.
Scripture teaches that Christian generosity should come from a willing heart.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
We never purchase grace through a monthly payment.
Christ has already paid the price for our salvation.
But when believers freely support sound biblical teaching and Gospel-centered ministry, their generosity can become a practical expression of love for God and neighbor.
These are not the reason we follow Jesus.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
To help people open their Bibles again.
To encourage the believer who has grown weary.
To strengthen those learning to walk in obedience.
To proclaim the hope of Christ to people who may never enter a church building but will pause long enough to read a message on their phone.
The free resources remain an important part of the mission because biblical nourishment should not be treated as something available only to paying supporters.
Your prayer matters.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to speak the truth in love matters.
And your faithful witness matters far beyond what a social media number can measure.
Because ultimately, this ministry is not about building a name for ourselves.
It is about making much of the name above every name.
Jesus Christ.
The One who forgives sinners.
The One who calls us to repentance.
The One who restores what His wisdom determines can be restored.
The One who never compromises holiness to offer mercy.
The One whose blood is sufficient to cleanse the guilty.
And the One whose resurrection declares that sin and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
So tonight, when you lay your head down, remember the king of Gerar.
Remember the dream.
Remember the warning.
Remember the marriage God protected.
Remember the deception that was exposed.
Remember the mercy that made restoration possible.
And remember that the God who knows every hidden part of your story is the same God who calls you to come into the light through Jesus Christ.
You may not receive a dream like Abimelech.
But you have something precious in your hands right now.
The written Word of God.
And through that Word, you have heard the warning, the call to repentance, and the promise of grace.
Do not ignore them.
Because the most important question is not whether you have ever made a terrible mistake.
It is whether you will turn to the Savior who alone can forgive your sin and transform your life.
The king was warned that he could die because of another man's wife—but the King of kings willingly died to save sinners who could never save themselves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID YOU MUST HATE YOUR OWN FAMILY TO FOLLOW HIM. DID WE MISUNDERSTAND THE MOST SHOCKING WORDS HE EVER SPOKE?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID YOU MUST HATE YOUR OWN FAMILY TO FOLLOW HIM. DID WE MISUNDERSTAND THE MOST SHOCKING WORDS HE EVER SPOKE?

Luke 14:26 reveals a terrifying question about love, loyalty, and the cost of discipleship. But when we uncover the original Greek, the Jewish context, and the heart of Jesus, we discover something far more powerful than hatred: a love so surrendered that nothing—not even the people we cherish most—can take the place of God.
Imagine standing in a crowd, listening to Jesus.
You have heard about His miracles. The blind receiving sight. The broken finding hope. Sinners discovering that their past does not have to be their future.
You have heard Him speak about the love of the Father. About mercy. Forgiveness. Eternal life.
Perhaps you came because you were desperate for something to change.
And then Jesus turns around.
He looks at the people following Him.
And says something that makes your stomach tighten.
“If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.” — Luke 14:26 (KJV)
Wait.
What?
Hate your father?
Hate your mother?
Hate your wife? Your husband? Your children?
Hate even your own life?
Is this really the same Jesus who commanded us to love our enemies?
The same Jesus who taught us to honor our parents?
The same Jesus who, while suffering on the cross, made sure His mother would be cared for?
Something feels almost impossible to reconcile.
And maybe that is precisely why we need to stop treating this verse like a frightening sentence we would rather skip.
Because Jesus was not contradicting love.
He was exposing what happens when even our deepest human love becomes greater than our devotion to God.
And the truth hidden in this passage may reach into places of your heart you have never allowed anyone to touch.
Especially if you have ever had to choose between pleasing the people you love and obeying the Savior who died for you.
Before we go any further, we need to understand something important.
Jesus was not speaking these words in the middle of a private argument with His family.
Luke tells us that great multitudes were traveling with Him (Luke 14:25).
Large crowds.
People drawn by His teaching, His authority, and the extraordinary things happening around Him.
But Jesus knew something that crowds often forget.
Being fascinated by Jesus is not the same as following Jesus.
It is possible to admire His miracles without surrendering to His authority.
