Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those struggling with their faith, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, hard questions are not feared, repentance is welcomed, and Jesus Christ remains at the center.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who genuinely want to grow.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, there is another way you can help us continue.
For those who are able and freely willing to give, it can be a meaningful expression of generosity and partnership in the Gospel.

Scripture teaches that those who receive spiritual instruction may share good things with those who teach, as Galatians 6:6 explains. Philippians 4:15–18 also shows believers participating in Gospel ministry through financial support.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"God loveth a cheerful giver."
That means giving should never be driven by fear, pressure, or the belief that God's favor can be purchased.

Some believers may prayerfully regard such regular giving as part of their broader Christian generosity. Others may reserve their tithes and offerings for their local church while choosing to support ministries separately.
Either way, what matters is that generosity flows from faith and love, not compulsion.
But if you believe in this mission, have been nourished by these teachings, and want to help us reach more people with the Gospel, your monthly partnership can make a real difference.
It helps turn encouragement into continued ministry.
It helps sustain the work behind the words.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for study, and opportunities to share your faith with others.
It is the opportunity to participate in the continued work of a ministry devoted to Scripture, discipleship, and the transforming Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Not to build a platform greater than the message.
Not to make people dependent upon a ministry.
But to direct hearts toward the Savior who alone can forgive sins, restore sinners, and make all things new.
Because the neglected woman in Exodus was never merely an ancient legal problem.
She was a human being whose welfare mattered.
And the law that protected her reminds us that power does not erase responsibility.
But Jesus Christ brings us to something greater still.
He calls us not merely to avoid neglecting others, but to love with a heart shaped by His own sacrificial grace.
So before you leave, ask yourself one final question.
Who in my life needs to experience the faithfulness, justice, humility, and compassion that I claim to have received from Jesus?
Maybe the answer will require an apology.
Maybe a difficult conversation.
Maybe a change in behavior.
Maybe the courage to seek help.
Maybe a prayer of surrender you have postponed for years.
Whatever it is, do not settle for admiring the truth.
Walk in it.
Because the same Gospel that comforts the wounded also confronts the one who wounds.
And the same Savior who forgives our sins calls us to turn away from them.
You may have been treated as someone's second choice, but your worth was never theirs to decide—and at the cross, Jesus proved that broken people are not beyond the reach of redeeming grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LOST BOOK THE BIBLE MENTIONS… BUT NEVER LETS YOU READ
paragraphs: THE LOST BOOK THE BIBLE MENTIONS… BUT NEVER LETS YOU READ

Twice, Scripture names a mysterious book called Jashar. Once, when the sun stood still over a battlefield. Again, when a broken king mourned the death of his closest friend. What was inside this ancient book? Why did it disappear? And what does its disappearance reveal about the difference between the stories humanity remembers and the Word God has preserved?
There is something unsettling about discovering that the Bible mentions a book you cannot open.
Not because someone has necessarily hidden it from you.
Not because a secret council buried it.
But because, for thousands of years, two passages of Scripture have quietly pointed toward an ancient collection of writings that we no longer possess with certainty.
And most Christians have read straight past its name.
The first mention appears in the middle of one of the most astonishing battles in the Old Testament.
The second appears beside the bodies of a fallen king and his son.
One is surrounded by victory.
The other is soaked in grief.
One speaks of a day when the sun appeared to stop moving.
The other preserves the memory of a man whose heart was shattered by loss.
And both point to the same mysterious source.
The Book of Jashar.
But here is the question that should stop every serious Bible reader:
If the Holy Spirit inspired Scripture to mention this book, why don't we have it?
And perhaps an even deeper question…
Does the Bible's reference to an ancient book mean that everything written in that book was inspired by God?
Stay with me, because the answer is more important than the mystery itself.

And before we are finished, we will discover something about Joshua, David, forgotten human stories, and the faithfulness of Jesus Christ that may change how you think about the Scriptures sitting in your hands.
It begins on a battlefield.

Joshua was leading Israel against a coalition of Amorite kings. The battle was fierce. The enemy was retreating. The Lord had already thrown their forces into confusion, and great hailstones had fallen upon them.
Then Joshua spoke.
Not merely to his soldiers.
Not merely to the enemy.
He addressed the sun and the moon.
Joshua 10:12 records his words:
“Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.” (KJV)
And the next verse declares:
“And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher?” (Joshua 10:13, KJV)
There it is.
Almost hidden inside the account of an extraordinary divine intervention.
The Book of Jasher.
Or, as many modern translations render the name, the Book of Jashar.
Imagine being an ancient Israelite hearing that account.
The enemy is fleeing. The daylight is precious. The battle has not yet ended. Joshua calls upon the Lord, and Scripture describes a day unlike any other.
Then the biblical writer directs the reader toward another written source.
Why?
The most natural explanation is that the Book of Jashar contained a poetic or historical remembrance of the event, one that was familiar enough to be cited.
The Hebrew wording is particularly revealing.
The phrase is:
סֵפֶר הַיָּשָׁר
Sefer ha-Yashar.
Literally, “Book of the Upright” or “Book of the Just.”
The Hebrew word yashar (יָשָׁר) carries the sense of uprightness, straightness, or what is right.
That matters.
Because “Jashar” may not have been the name of a mysterious prophet or forgotten author at all.
It may have described the character or subject of the collection.
A book associated with the upright.
A collection celebrating noble deeds, heroic acts, or significant events in Israel's memory.

We cannot establish its complete contents or original form with certainty. But the biblical references strongly suggest that it preserved material connected with Israel's history, possibly in poetic form.
And the second reference makes that possibility even more compelling.
Because centuries later, we find David standing in the ruins of a different kind of battlefield.
This time, there is no triumphant celebration.
No great military victory to rejoice over.
No sunlight stretching across the horizon as Israel pursues its enemies.
There is only death.
King Saul is gone.
Jonathan is gone.
And David, the man who had spent years running from Saul's hostility, does something that reveals the complicated beauty of a heart shaped by God's grace.
He mourns.
Not only Jonathan, the friend he loved.
He mourns Saul, the king who had repeatedly sought his life.
Think about that.
David could have celebrated Saul's death as the end of his suffering.
He could have announced that the man who hunted him was finally gone.
He could have turned the moment into a speech about vindication.
Instead, he wrote a lament.
A song of sorrow.
A remembrance of fallen men.
And 2 Samuel 1:17–18 tells us:
“And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son: (Also he bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow: behold, it is written in the book of Jasher.)” (KJV)
The Hebrew text calls the lament qinah (קִינָה), a song of mourning.
And the passage again refers to Sefer ha-Yashar.

The words translated in the KJV as “the use of the bow” are more literally connected with “the bow,” which may be the title or subject of the lament or the instruction David wanted Judah to learn. Scholars differ on the precise interpretation.
But the larger picture is unmistakable.
The Book of Jashar was associated not only with the memory of a miraculous victory but also with the preservation of a national tragedy.
The book appears where Israel remembers both triumph and tears.
And there is something deeply human about that.
Because isn't that how we remember our own lives?
We remember the day God brought us through something we thought would destroy us.
And we remember the day we lost someone we thought we could never live without.
We remember prayers answered in ways that left us speechless.
And we remember gravesides where all we could whisper was, “Lord, why?”
Victory and grief.
Deliverance and loss.
Songs of celebration and songs that can barely be sung through tears.
Both belong to the story of a fallen world in which God is still working.
Perhaps that is part of what makes the Book of Jashar so fascinating.
It reminds us that the people of Scripture were not cardboard figures living in religious illustrations.
They were real people.
They fought.
They wept.
They remembered.
They composed poetry.
They preserved accounts of events that mattered to them.
And they lived in a world where written collections existed alongside the writings that would become part of the biblical canon.
But now we reach the question that has fueled centuries of curiosity.
Where is the original Book of Jashar today?
The careful answer is that no surviving manuscript can be securely identified as the original book cited in Joshua 10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18.
That is not the same as proving that no copy could ever be discovered.
It means that, based on the evidence currently available, its original text is not known.
And this distinction is important because there are books circulating today under the title Book of Jasher.
Some readers encounter one online, see its biblical-sounding name, and immediately assume they have found the ancient work mentioned by Joshua and Samuel.
But a familiar title does not establish an ancient identity.

One well-known work, often called Sefer ha-Yashar, is a later Hebrew narrative that retells and expands stories from Genesis and the early history of Israel. A version was printed in Venice in 1625, and the work later became widely available in English.
Its stories may interest readers studying Jewish interpretive traditions, but it has not been demonstrated to be the lost ancient source referenced in the Bible.

Another work published in the eighteenth century under the name Book of Jasher claimed a much more ancient origin, but it is generally recognized as a modern literary fabrication rather than an authentic biblical-era document.
So when someone tells you, “They finally found the lost Book of Jashar, and it reveals what the Bible left out,” do not surrender your discernment to the excitement of the claim.
Ask a better question.
Where is the manuscript evidence?
What is the text's documented history?
What do its language, literary features, and historical context actually establish?
Does the evidence support the claimed date?
And does the person presenting it distinguish ancient evidence from later religious imagination?
Christians should not be afraid of serious historical questions.
Truth does not become less true because someone examines the evidence carefully.
But neither should we baptize speculation as revelation simply because it sounds spiritual.
And this brings us to one of the most important lessons in the entire discussion.
Being mentioned in the Bible is not the same thing as being a book of the Bible.
Read that again.
The biblical writers sometimes refer to other writings, records, poems, and sources.
Numbers 21:14 mentions the Book of the Wars of the LORD.
First Kings refers to royal chronicles.
First Chronicles refers to historical records associated with prophets and seers.
The apostle Paul even quotes nonbiblical Greek poetry in Acts 17:28.
Yet the presence of a quotation or reference does not automatically establish the divine inspiration of the entire source from which it came.
God can inspire a biblical writer to record a true statement from a source without thereby declaring every sentence of that source to be Holy Scripture.
Consider Paul's words in Acts 17.
He uses language familiar to his Greek audience while proclaiming the true God.
He does not thereby endorse every religious belief held by the poets whose words he draws upon.
In the same way, Joshua and Samuel can refer to the Book of Jashar without requiring us to conclude that the entire lost collection possessed the same authority as the inspired Scriptures.
Second Timothy 3:16 declares:
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.” (KJV)
The Greek expression translated “given by inspiration of God” is:
θεόπνευστος
Theopneustos.
Literally, “God-breathed.”
That is a remarkable word.
It speaks of Scripture's divine origin.
Not merely human religious reflection.
Not simply ancient literature that people happened to find meaningful.
But Scripture given through God's sovereign work.
The question, then, is not whether a text is old, interesting, mysterious, or mentioned by an inspired author.
The question is whether it belongs to the writings received as Holy Scripture.

The historical recognition of the biblical canon involved real processes, debates, and distinctions among Jewish and Christian communities. Those complexities deserve honest study rather than oversimplified stories.
But the Book of Jashar itself is not included in the established biblical canons of the major Jewish and Christian traditions.
Its mention in Scripture does not make it a missing chapter of the Bible.
And its absence does not mean that the Bible is incomplete in everything God intended it to teach for salvation and faithful living.
That distinction can protect us from a very old temptation.
The temptation to believe that the truth we most desperately need must be hidden somewhere beyond the Word God has already given us.
Some people spend years chasing secret manuscripts while neglecting the Gospel of John.
They become fascinated with lost books but rarely open Romans.
They can discuss obscure ancient traditions for hours, yet have never sat quietly with Jesus' words:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28, KJV)
Please understand.
Studying ancient texts is not wrong.
Historical investigation is not a threat to faith.
The original Book of Jashar, if ever recovered and authenticated, would be an extraordinary discovery for biblical scholarship.
It could illuminate ancient Israelite poetry, historical memory, and the literary world of the Old Testament.
But it would not become the Savior of the world.
And it would not replace the Gospel.
Because there is a difference between wanting to understand an ancient mystery and believing that your spiritual life depends on uncovering one.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Some of us are fascinated by what God has not revealed because we are struggling to obey what He already has.
We want another sign.
Another explanation.
Another discovery.
Another confirmation.
Meanwhile, the command to forgive is still sitting in front of us.
The call to repent is still waiting.
The invitation to pray remains open.
The neighbor who needs mercy is still next door.
And the Savior who calls us to follow Him has not changed.
The mystery of Jashar can stir our curiosity.
But the words of Jesus confront our hearts.
And sometimes confrontation is exactly what grace looks like before it begins to heal us.
There is another detail in David's lament that deserves our attention.
After Saul and Jonathan die, David cries:
“How are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle!” (2 Samuel 1:25, KJV)
And concerning Jonathan, he says:
“I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women.” (2 Samuel 1:26, KJV)
These are words of deep personal grief and covenant friendship.
David is not pretending that loss is painless.
He is not hiding his tears behind the language of religious strength.
He is grieving someone he loved.
And this matters because some believers have been taught, directly or indirectly, that strong faith means never falling apart.
That if you really trust God, you should stop crying quickly.
That if you believe in heaven, grief should somehow become easy.
But David's lament stands against that shallow understanding of faith.
He was a man who trusted the Lord.
And he wept.
He was anointed for kingship.
And he wept.
He knew God's promises.
And he wept.
Faith did not erase his humanity.
It gave him a place to bring it.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ Himself stood outside the tomb of Lazarus.
John 11:35 gives us two words:
“Jesus wept.”
The Greek text reads:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
“Jesus wept.”
The verb describes the shedding of tears.
The Son of God stood in the presence of human sorrow and did not treat it as something beneath Him.
He entered it.
He knew that Lazarus would be raised.
And still, He wept.
That should tell us something about the heart of our Savior.
Christian hope does not require pretending that death is harmless.
The resurrection does not make every funeral painless.
And trusting God does not mean you must deny the ache in your chest when someone you love is gone.
Jesus meets His people in their grief.
He does not always explain every loss.
But He has entered death itself, defeated its ultimate power through His resurrection, and promised that those who belong to Him will share in His victory.
That is not sentimental optimism.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
And suddenly, the two biblical references to Jashar stand beside something even greater.
Joshua's battlefield reminds us that God is sovereign over creation and the affairs of nations.
David's lament reminds us that even the mighty fall and that human love feels the wound of death.
But Jesus Christ brings both realities into focus.
He is the Lord through whom all things were created.
And He is the suffering Savior who entered our broken world.
At Calvary, the Gospel accounts describe darkness falling over the land during the crucifixion.
Matthew 27:45 says:
“Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.” (KJV)
Joshua's account describes extraordinary daylight in the midst of battle.
Matthew describes extraordinary darkness as Jesus suffers upon the cross.
These are distinct events, and Scripture does not explicitly identify one as a prophecy or direct parallel of the other.
Yet the contrast invites reverent reflection.
In Joshua, God gives His people victory over their enemies.
At the cross, Christ achieves the decisive victory over sin and death through His sacrificial death and resurrection.
In David's lament, the mighty have fallen.
At Calvary, the One who possessed all authority willingly laid down His life.
And unlike Saul and Jonathan, whose deaths David could only mourn, Jesus rose again.
The grave could not hold Him.
Acts 2:24 declares that God raised Him up, having loosed the pains of death.
This is where the Christian story becomes more than a record of ancient battles and national tragedies.
It becomes the announcement that God has acted to rescue sinners.
Not because we were upright enough to deserve Him.
Not because our lives were clean enough to impress Him.
Not because our spiritual achievements earned us a place in His kingdom.
But because of His mercy.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
And here, the title Book of the Upright offers a striking contrast.
Whatever the ancient collection contained, its Hebrew title speaks of uprightness.
But when we look honestly into our own hearts, who among us can claim perfect uprightness before God?
Who has never lied?
Never envied?
Never cherished bitterness?
Never used words to wound someone?
Never loved comfort more than obedience?
Never hidden sin behind a respectable appearance?
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
That includes the religious.
The skeptical.
The outwardly successful.
The quietly broken.
The person who has served in church for thirty years.
And the person who is reading a Christian article for the first time, wondering whether God could possibly welcome someone with their past.
Here is the scandal of grace.
The perfectly righteous Son of God came to save people who could never make themselves perfectly righteous.
Jesus lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Not to purchase forgiveness.
Not to earn His attention.
But to receive the salvation that only He can give.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” (KJV)
That is the heart of the message.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because God simply overlooks evil.
But because Jesus bore sin's judgment and opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by declaring every consequence meaningless.
But by giving forgiven sinners a new standing before God and a new life through His Spirit.
And maybe that is what you needed to hear today.
Maybe you opened this article because you were curious about a missing book.
But somewhere along the way, another kind of missing story came to mind.
Your own.
The years you cannot recover.
The choices you wish you could reverse.
The relationship you damaged.
The prayer you stopped praying.
The faith you once carried with confidence but now struggle to hold.
The private battle nobody knows about.
The shame that returns when the room becomes quiet.
You may feel as though the best chapters of your life have already been lost.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly loss will be reversed in this lifetime.
It does not guarantee that every relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
It does not mean every consequence of sin will disappear.
But it does promise something greater than the illusion of a painless past.
In Christ, forgiveness is real.
Reconciliation with God is possible.
The Holy Spirit transforms those who belong to Jesus.
And no failure is beyond the power of His mercy when a sinner turns to Him in repentance and faith.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to build an impressive religious record.
He could not undo his crimes.
He could not spend decades proving himself worthy.
But he turned to Christ.
And Jesus told him:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
Grace did not make his wrongdoing good.
Grace brought a guilty man to the Savior who could forgive him.
That is why the Gospel remains greater than every lost manuscript.
A forgotten ancient book may tell us more about Israel's past.
But the Scriptures we possess already bear witness to the One who can save us from our sins.
John 20:30–31 acknowledges that Jesus performed many other signs not written in John's Gospel, then explains why the selected signs were recorded:
“But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.” (John 20:31, KJV)
Notice the purpose.
Not to satisfy every possible historical curiosity.
Not to answer every question humanity might ever ask.
But to bear witness to Jesus Christ so that people might believe and have life in His name.
That is why we must never confuse curiosity with discipleship.
Knowledge of ancient manuscripts can be valuable.
But knowing facts about biblical history is not the same as trusting Christ.
You can recognize Hebrew letters and still refuse to forgive.
You can explain Greek verbs and still be consumed by pride.
You can know the names of lost books and still neglect the living Word.
Jesus said in John 5:39–40 that the Scriptures testify of Him, yet His hearers were unwilling to come to Him for life.
What a terrifying possibility.
To study the testimony and reject the Person to whom it points.
To admire the pages while resisting the Savior.
To pursue the mystery while avoiding repentance.
Please do not let that become your story.
Open the Bible.
Ask hard questions.
Study history.
Learn the original languages when you can.
Examine claims carefully.
But above all, come to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest treasure of Scripture is not an undiscovered document.
It is the revelation of God's saving work through His Son.
And if this message has uncovered something in your own heart, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
Not with a polished religious performance.
Not with words designed to impress strangers.
But with the kind of truth you might whisper to God when nobody else is listening.
If God has been teaching you to trust His Word instead of chasing every sensational claim, share what you have learned.
And if you have a question about Jashar, biblical history, or the reliability of Scripture, ask it. Serious questions deserve thoughtful, respectful answers.
You do not have to disclose private wounds publicly to prove your faith. The Lord hears prayers that never appear in a comment section.
But your honest testimony may encourage someone else who thought they were the only one struggling.
And perhaps that is why this kind of biblical teaching matters so much.
We live in a world where spiritual misinformation can travel around the globe before anyone stops to examine a source.
A dramatic headline can reach millions.
A misleading claim about a “forbidden book” can attract attention overnight.
A distorted interpretation can leave sincere believers confused about the Bible they once trusted.
And while curiosity spreads quickly, careful discipleship requires patience, prayer, study, and people willing to keep showing up.
That is part of the mission of Gospel Warrior.

We want to keep bringing Scripture-centered teaching to people who are hungry for truth, including those who are wounded, questioning, returning to faith, or beginning to discover who Jesus really is.
And I want to speak plainly about something important.
If this ministry has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or encouraged you to return to Christ, would you prayerfully consider helping us continue?
For those who choose to give from a heart of worship, that support can be part of their Christian generosity and stewardship.
But I want to be careful with the language of giving because God's Word deserves better than financial pressure dressed up as spiritual authority.
It does not replace your responsibility to support your local church, care for your household, or respond to the needs of people around you.
And it certainly does not purchase God's blessing, forgiveness, favor, or salvation.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not out of guilt.
Not because you must pay to glorify God.
But because supporting faithful biblical teaching can be one practical way to serve others and honor the Lord.
You can still pray for the ministry.
You can still share the Gospel.
You can still encourage another believer.
You can still grow in Christ.
Because discipleship is not a membership fee.
It is a life of following Jesus.
These are small ways of saying thank you for standing with a mission that seeks to point people back to Christ.

These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their prayer lives, understand biblical truth, and continue following Jesus beyond the moment they finish reading an article.
Because the goal is not simply to collect followers.
The goal is to help people become faithful followers of Christ.
Not because every post must go viral.
Not because numbers are the measure of spiritual fruit.
But because someone in your circle may be wrestling with the very questions we have discussed.
Perhaps a friend has been confused by claims about missing books of the Bible.
Perhaps a family member has begun doubting the reliability of Scripture.
Perhaps someone who has not opened a Bible in years will see the title and become curious enough to read.
And perhaps, somewhere between Joshua's battlefield and David's tears, that person will encounter the message of Jesus Christ.
Come for the questions.
Stay for the Scriptures.
And above all, seek the Christ to whom the Scriptures testify.
Because long after this article disappears from your feed, the questions it raises will still matter.
What do we actually know?
What are we merely assuming?
Whose authority are we trusting?
And what are we doing with the truth God has already placed before us?
The Book of Jashar remains a fascinating historical mystery.
Its two biblical references invite us to imagine an ancient literary world filled with remembered battles, songs of grief, and accounts of Israel's past.
We should not pretend to know everything about it.
We should not dismiss the value of studying it.
And we should never manufacture certainty where the evidence does not provide it.
But neither should we allow the mystery of a lost book to eclipse the clarity of the Gospel.
Joshua's victory reminds us that the Lord is mighty.
David's lament reminds us that even the mighty are mortal.
The cross reminds us that our sin is serious.
And the empty tomb announces that Jesus Christ has conquered death.
That is the story worth carrying into every generation.
Not a promise that every earthly mystery will be solved.
But the proclamation that God has made Himself known through His Son.
And when the final page of our earthly lives is written, the question that matters most will not be whether we discovered every ancient manuscript.
It will be whether we have turned from our sin and placed our trust in Jesus Christ.
So study faithfully.
Question carefully.
Grieve honestly.
Repent sincerely.
Love deeply.
Give freely.
And follow Jesus.
Because there is one final thought I want to leave with you.
The ancient Book of Jashar may be lost to history.
But the Lord has not lost sight of those who belong to Him.
He knows their names.
He knows their tears.
He knows their battles.
He knows the wounds they have never been able to explain.
And through Jesus Christ, He offers forgiveness, new life, and the hope of resurrection.
The world may forget your story.
People may misunderstand it.
Some chapters may remain painful until the day you see your Savior face to face.
But the grace of God is not limited by the pages of your past.
The greatest tragedy is not that an ancient book has been lost. It is that a person can hold the Gospel in their hands and never come to the Savior who gave His life to bring them home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE KILLED THE ROYAL CHILDREN TO STEAL THE THRONE… BUT SHE NEVER KNEW ONE BABY WAS STILL ALIVE.
paragraphs: SHE KILLED THE ROYAL CHILDREN TO STEAL THE THRONE… BUT SHE NEVER KNEW ONE BABY WAS STILL ALIVE.

For six years, a ruthless queen ruled Judah while a little boy remained hidden behind the walls of God's house. She thought the royal bloodline was finished. But what she could not see would one day bring her kingdom crashing down. And buried inside this terrifying story is a truth every wounded believer needs to hear: God's promises do not die just because evil appears to be winning.

“But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain.” — 2 Kings 11:2, KJV
Imagine being a little boy whose own grandmother wanted him dead.
Not because he had committed a crime.
Not because he had betrayed his family.
But because his very existence threatened the throne she wanted for herself.
Now imagine that same child growing up behind closed doors, unaware of the full weight of the danger outside.
Six years.
Six years of silence.
Six years of secrecy.
Six years while the woman who wanted him eliminated sat on the throne of Judah.
And somewhere inside the house of the Lord, a child was breathing who was never supposed to survive.
His name was Joash.
And his story begins with a massacre.
But it does not end there.

Because there is something about this story that reaches far beyond ancient Jerusalem. It reaches into the life of the person who has ever wondered why God seems silent while wickedness prospers, why the innocent suffer, why the powerful appear untouchable, or why a promise from God can seem buried beneath years of disappointment.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to be forgotten.
To watch someone who hurt you move forward while you are still trying to recover.
To pray for something that seems to grow farther away instead of closer.
To wonder whether God has seen what happened.
If that is you, stay with this story.
Because the most important person in the kingdom was not the woman everyone could see sitting on the throne.
It was the child almost nobody knew was alive.
And the difference between those two lives reveals something extraordinary about the faithfulness of God.
The year was a dark one for Judah.
King Ahaziah was dead.
His mother, Athaliah, saw an opportunity to seize royal power. According to 2 Kings 11:1, when she realized her son was dead, she arose and destroyed the royal offspring.
The Hebrew describes the horror with chilling directness:
וַתְּאַבֵּד אֵת כָּל־זֶרַע הַמַּמְלָכָה
Vatte'abbed et kol-zera hammamlakhah.
The phrase means, in context, “she destroyed all the royal offspring.”
The Hebrew word zera (זֶרַע) literally means “seed” and can refer to descendants or offspring.
That detail matters.
Athaliah was not simply removing political opponents. She was attempting to eliminate the royal descendants who might challenge her rule.
The biblical text does not tell us every thought in her mind, nor does it give us permission to invent conversations that never happened. But her actions are unmistakable.
She was prepared to destroy her own family to secure the throne.
Think about the horror of that.
A grandmother.
A palace.
Children belonging to the royal household.
And a ruthless struggle for power that left lives shattered.
The Bible does not soften this evil.
It does not ask us to pretend that every family relationship is safe, that every person in authority is righteous, or that every person with power deserves our trust.
Sometimes the people who should protect others become the very people from whom protection is needed.
Some readers understand that sentence more personally than they wish they did.
Maybe the betrayal in your life did not involve a palace.
Maybe it happened in your own home.
Maybe someone who was supposed to love you became the source of your deepest wounds.
Maybe the person who should have defended you remained silent.
Maybe you were forced to become strong long before you should have needed strength.
The story of Joash does not trivialize that kind of suffering.
It shows us a world in which evil can be terrifyingly real.
But it also shows us that evil does not possess unlimited authority over God's purposes.
Because while Athaliah was destroying the royal household, another woman was making a very different decision.
Her name was Jehosheba.
She was the daughter of King Jehoram and the sister of Ahaziah.
And when destruction threatened the royal children, she took Joash, the son of Ahaziah, and rescued him.
The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 22:11 identifies her as the wife of Jehoiada the priest.
This was not a small act of kindness.
This was an act of extraordinary courage.
She took a child who was marked for death and hid him with his nurse.
Then she kept him concealed from Athaliah.
And Scripture records the result with remarkable simplicity:
“And he was with her hid in the house of the LORD six years. And Athaliah did reign over the land.” — 2 Kings 11:3, KJV
Read those two sentences again.
The child was hidden in the house of the Lord.
Athaliah ruled the land.
Both realities existed at the same time.
A wicked ruler held visible political power.
A vulnerable child remained alive in secret.
The throne appeared to belong to Athaliah.
But the Davidic royal line had not been extinguished.
And that is where this story becomes more than palace history.
Centuries earlier, God had made a covenant with David concerning his royal house and kingdom (2 Samuel 7:12–16).
That covenant did not mean every descendant of David would be faithful. Judah's history proves otherwise. It did not mean the nation would never experience judgment, disaster, or exile.
But God's covenant purposes would not be defeated by Athaliah's violence.
She could seize a throne.
She could terrorize a kingdom.
She could attempt to eliminate the royal family.
But she could not make God unfaithful to His word.
The promise was still alive, even when almost everyone thought the royal line had been destroyed.
Not because Joash was powerful.
He was a child.
Not because Jehosheba commanded an army.
Scripture gives no indication that she did.
Not because Judah was experiencing a season of national righteousness.
It was not.
The child survived through a courageous rescue, careful concealment, and the unfolding providence of God.
The promise was preserved in a place the reigning queen did not control.
For six years, Joash remained hidden.

The Bible does not tell us what he thought during those years. It does not describe his childhood prayers, his daily conversations, or whether he understood why he could not live openly as other children did.
We must not pretend to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But we do know that six years passed.
And for those six years, Athaliah remained on the throne.
That is a difficult detail.
Because we often want God's deliverance to happen immediately.
We want evil exposed today.
We want the truth revealed tomorrow.
We want the door opened before the week ends.
We want God to explain why He has allowed a painful situation to continue.
But the biblical story does not rush past the six years.
It makes us face them.
God's covenant had not failed.
Yet the wicked ruler still reigned.
The child had survived.
Yet he was still hidden.
The future king was alive.
Yet the kingdom had not been restored.
And perhaps that tension sounds familiar.
You believe God is faithful, but you are still waiting.
You believe Jesus heals, but the wound still hurts.
You believe the Lord hears prayer, but the answer has not arrived in the form you hoped for.
You believe the truth matters, but the person who lied about you seems to be doing just fine.
There is a kind of spiritual exhaustion that comes from trying to reconcile what you believe about God with what you are experiencing in life.
And sometimes the most honest prayer is not eloquent.
It is simply, “Lord, how much longer?”
Scripture makes room for that cry.
“How long, O LORD? wilt thou forget me for ever?” David asked in Psalm 13:1.
Those words are in the Bible because faithful people can experience seasons when God seems distant.
But feeling forgotten is not proof that God has abandoned you.
And a delayed outcome is not, by itself, evidence that His word has failed.
We must be careful here.

Joash's rescue does not promise that every child will escape danger, that every injustice will be corrected within six years, or that every believer will eventually receive a position of earthly influence.
The Bible never gives us permission to turn one historical deliverance into a guarantee that all our circumstances will unfold the same way.
But it does give us something stronger than a prediction about our circumstances.
It reveals the character of the God whose redemptive purposes cannot ultimately be defeated.
And sometimes that truth is what keeps faith alive when everything else feels uncertain.
Then came the seventh year.
And everything changed.
Jehoiada the priest began to act.
According to 2 Kings 11:4–12, he gathered commanders, made a covenant with them, organized the guards, and arranged for the young king to be brought out.
The secrecy was ending.
The child who had been hidden was about to stand before the people.
Imagine the astonishment of those who had believed the royal line was gone.
There was a surviving son of Ahaziah.
There was an heir.
The child had been alive all along.
Jehoiada brought him forward, placed the crown upon him, gave him the testimony, and the people proclaimed him king.
Then came the sound Athaliah had not expected.
Clapping.
Celebration.
A kingdom shouting:
“God save the king.” — 2 Kings 11:12, KJV
The boy who had been hidden was now publicly crowned.
The woman who had ruled through violence heard the commotion and came to see what was happening.
And when Athaliah saw the young king standing by the pillar, surrounded by the officers and the people rejoicing, she tore her clothes and cried:
“Treason, Treason.” — 2 Kings 11:14, KJV
There is a terrible irony in that moment.
The woman who had seized power after destroying the royal offspring now accused others of treason when the surviving rightful heir was crowned.
Her accusation did not change the truth.
Her authority was coming to an end.
Athaliah was taken outside the temple precincts and executed, as recorded in 2 Kings 11:15–16.

The text does not invite us to celebrate cruelty or imitate political violence. It records a particular event in Judah's royal history, not a license for Christians to take vengeance against their enemies.
The larger biblical witness is clear:
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” — Romans 12:19, KJV
For those who have suffered injustice, this distinction matters.
God's justice is real.
But personal revenge is not the Gospel.
You do not need to become like the person who wounded you in order to prove that what happened was wrong.
You can seek safety, tell the truth, pursue lawful justice, establish boundaries, and refuse to excuse evil without surrendering your heart to hatred.
And you can entrust ultimate judgment to God.
But the most important thing about the seventh year was not merely that Athaliah fell.
It was what happened next.
Jehoiada made a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people, that they should be the Lord's people (2 Kings 11:17).
The people destroyed the temple of Baal.
Worship and covenant loyalty became central to the nation's renewal.
This was not simply a political replacement.
It was a call back to the Lord.
And that is where the story begins pointing toward something greater than Joash.
Because Joash was a real king in the line of David.
But he was not the final answer to Judah's spiritual problem.
He began his reign as a child.
Under Jehoiada's influence, he did what was right in the sight of the Lord, as 2 Kings 12:2 records.
Yet the fuller account in 2 Chronicles 24 reveals a tragic development.
After Jehoiada died, Joash listened to corrupt leaders, abandoned faithful worship, and eventually ordered the death of Zechariah, Jehoiada's son, who had confronted the nation's unfaithfulness.
Think about the sorrow of that.
A child who had once been rescued through the courage of Jehoiada's household later turned against the family connected to his preservation.
Being rescued from death did not automatically make Joash a righteous man for the rest of his life.
Receiving a crown did not transform his heart permanently.
And this is one of the most sobering truths in the entire account.
You can survive the danger around you and still need deliverance from the sin within you.
You can escape a terrible childhood and still need God's grace to address the bitterness that grows afterward.
You can receive opportunities you never expected and still misuse them.
You can know the right religious language and still wander far from the Lord.
You can be surrounded by godly people and still need personal repentance and genuine faith.
That is why this story cannot end with a rescued child wearing a crown.
It must take us to Jesus Christ.
Because Judah did not merely need another descendant of David.
Humanity needed a Savior.
A King who would not simply inherit a throne but fulfill God's redemptive promises.
A King whose righteousness would not collapse when a faithful mentor died.
A King who would not need to be rescued from His own sin.
A King who would rescue sinners through His own sacrifice.
And His name is Jesus.
The Gospel of Matthew opens by identifying Jesus Christ as the son of David and the son of Abraham (Matthew 1:1).
That is not an incidental detail.
It places Jesus within the history of God's covenant promises.
The line of David matters because the Messiah's identity matters.
The preservation of Joash was one chapter in the much larger history through which God brought His promised King into the world.
And when Jesus came, the story of a threatened royal child found a striking, though not identical, historical parallel.
In Matthew 2, King Herod sought to kill the young Jesus.
Joseph was warned in a dream, and he took Mary and the child into Egypt.
Once again, a ruler's fear of losing power became a threat to a child.
Once again, the child was preserved.
But Jesus was not merely another Joash.
Joash was a flawed king who needed mercy.
Jesus is the sinless King who brings mercy.
Joash was hidden from someone who wanted him dead.
Jesus would eventually surrender Himself to death according to the Father's saving purpose.
Joash received a crown of earthly royalty.
Jesus endured a crown of thorns.
And the contrast is overwhelming.
The King of kings stood before men who mocked His authority.
They struck Him.
They spat upon Him.
They placed thorns upon His head.
They led Him to the cross.
And for a moment, to those who did not understand what God was accomplishing, it must have appeared that evil had won.
The religious leaders had secured His condemnation.
Roman soldiers carried out the execution.
His followers were scattered and afraid.
His body was placed in a tomb.
But the cross was not the collapse of God's plan.
It was central to its fulfillment.
Jesus was not an unwilling victim overtaken by circumstances beyond His control.
He willingly laid down His life.
As He said in John 10:18:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.” — KJV
And then came the resurrection.
Death did not hold Him.
The grave did not defeat Him.
The risen Christ appeared to His followers, and the apostles proclaimed that God had raised Him from the dead.
Peter declared in Acts 2:24 that God raised Jesus, “having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.”
The Greek New Testament uses the word ἀνέστησεν (anestēsen) in Acts 2:24, meaning “raised up.”
The resurrection is not merely a poetic metaphor for finding hope after disappointment.

It is the historical and theological claim at the center of apostolic Christianity: Jesus Christ truly died, was buried, and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And because He lives, the Gospel is not a message of wishful thinking.
It is the announcement that sin and death do not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
Now return for a moment to that little boy in the temple.
Six years hidden.
Six years while Athaliah ruled.
Six years before the people saw the child who had survived.
And consider how different his story looks when you know the ending.
The hidden years were not evidence that the royal line had ceased to exist.
The queen's public power was not proof that her rule would endure.
What was visible was not the whole story.
But there is a difference between knowing Joash's ending and knowing yours.
You and I cannot see every chapter ahead.
We do not know how long certain struggles will last.
We do not know whether every relationship will be restored, every illness healed in this life, or every earthly opportunity recovered.
But Christians have been given something far greater than the ability to predict tomorrow.
We have been given Jesus Christ.
And in Him, we have the assurance that our deepest need—reconciliation with God—has been answered through His death and resurrection.
The Gospel does not say, “Trust Jesus, and nothing painful will happen to you.”
It says that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
It does not say that every hidden season will end with public applause.
It says that nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him (Romans 8:38–39).
It does not say that every earthly enemy will fall before our eyes.
It says that Jesus will reign until every enemy is placed beneath His feet, and that death itself will finally be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).
That is a hope strong enough to survive disappointment.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear a difficult but liberating truth.
You do not have to turn your suffering into a spectacular success story to prove that God loves you.
You do not have to become famous.
You do not have to make everyone who rejected you regret it.
You do not have to win every argument or recover every opportunity.
You do not have to convince the world that you were worth protecting.
Your worth is not determined by the cruelty you survived.
And your standing before God is not purchased through achievement.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
The same grace that forgives also begins to transform.
It teaches us to turn away from sin, to forgive as we have been forgiven, to pursue holiness, and to walk in the good works God has prepared for His people.
That is why repentance matters.
Not because we can earn the love of God by punishing ourselves.
But because Christ did not die merely to make us feel better about the darkness.
He came to save us from our sins.
And maybe the darkness you need to confront today is not only what someone else did to you.
Maybe it is what you have been allowing to grow inside your own heart.
The resentment you keep feeding.
The secret compromise you keep defending.
The dishonesty you keep explaining away.
The bitterness that has slowly become part of your identity.
The religious appearance you maintain while your private life drifts farther from Jesus.
Do not mistake outward survival for inward surrender.
Joash survived Athaliah.
Yet his later choices still exposed the danger of a heart that turns away from God.
You can make it through the crisis and still lose your way spiritually.
You can experience remarkable protection and still need repentance.
You can be familiar with the house of God and still need to know the God of the house.
And that should humble every one of us.
Because the question is not merely, “Will God bring me out of this?”
The deeper question is, “Lord, who am I becoming while I am in it?”
Am I growing in truth?
Am I learning obedience?
Am I allowing the Word of God to correct me?
Am I becoming more like Christ?
Or am I allowing the pain of yesterday to determine the person I become tomorrow?
The grace of Jesus does not erase the reality of what happened.
But it opens a way for the past not to have the final authority over your future.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not that Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not that He calls evil good.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
Not that every consequence disappears.
But that sin, shame, betrayal, and human failure do not have to be the final chapter for a person who turns to Him.
The cross confronts our guilt.
The resurrection announces His victory.
And the grace of God calls us into a new life.
The apostle Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:17:
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means “new creation.”
This is more than cosmetic improvement.
It is the reality of a new identity and life in Christ.
Not instant perfection.
Not the absence of struggle.
But a genuine beginning made possible by God's grace.
And if you are reading this while carrying something you have never told anyone, I want you to understand something.
You do not have to keep pretending that everything is fine.
You can bring your sin into the light through confession and repentance.
You can bring your grief to the Father who sees.
You can ask for help.
You can seek wise counsel.
You can tell the truth about what happened to you.
And you can come to Jesus without first manufacturing a perfect version of yourself.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He receives those who come to Him in faith.
He is not impressed by a polished religious performance that hides an unrepentant heart.
He is worthy of the truth.
Perhaps your prayer tonight needs to be simple.

“Lord Jesus, I have spent so much time asking You to change what is happening around me that I have neglected what needs to change within me. Forgive my sins. Heal what is wounded. Correct what is wrong. Teach me to trust You without demanding that You explain everything first. Help me follow You faithfully, whether my circumstances change quickly or not. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I need Your grace. Make my life Yours. Amen.”
If those words express the cry of your heart, do not let this become another emotional moment that fades as soon as you close the page.
Open your Bible.
Read 2 Kings 11 and 12 alongside 2 Chronicles 22–24.
Then read Matthew 1–2 and the Gospel accounts of Jesus' death and resurrection.
See how the story of God's faithfulness stretches across generations, through human failure, until it reaches its fulfillment in Christ.
You can write “Christ is still healing me” if you are learning to trust Jesus through a painful season.
You do not need to reveal private details or explain wounds you are not ready to discuss.
Sometimes a simple prayer request is enough to remind another believer that they are not alone.
Your experience may help someone else persevere—not because every story unfolds the same way, but because God's faithfulness deserves to be remembered.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who needs to encounter this message.
Someone who has stopped praying because they think God has forgotten them.
Someone whose family history is full of pain.
Someone who is beginning to believe that their past has made redemption impossible.
Someone who knows the language of Christianity but has drifted from the living Christ.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who need strengthening, and seekers who are beginning to ask serious questions about Jesus to follow as well.
Because discipleship is not supposed to end when an article ends.
We need the Word of God when we are encouraged.
We need it when we are exhausted.
We need it when temptation comes.
We need it when life is ordinary and nobody is watching.
And we need it when the Lord lovingly exposes areas of our lives that still require repentance.
This is also why the mission of Gospel Warrior matters to us.
Our desire is not merely to create content that moves people for a few minutes.
It is to encourage a life of Scripture, prayer, repentance, obedience, and genuine spiritual growth.

Scripture encourages believers to support faithful ministry. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
We want to honor both truths.
And please remember this:
The free Gospel resources are not reserved for people who can afford to give.
The message of Jesus Christ must never become a privilege sold to the highest bidder.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your value before God.
The Gospel is received by grace.
Our response is worship, gratitude, obedience, love, and willing generosity.
That is the kind of partnership we want to build.
Not a community held together by guilt.
A community growing together in Christ.
Not people chasing emotional experiences while neglecting Scripture.
People learning to test every message against the Word of God.
Not followers who depend on a ministry more than they depend on Jesus.
Disciples whose deepest loyalty belongs to the Savior.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the King.
Jesus is.
And that brings us back to the palace in Jerusalem.
Back to a frightened kingdom.
Back to a woman who seized a throne.
Back to a courageous woman who rescued a child.
Back to six years of concealment.
Back to a seventh year when the hidden heir was finally revealed.
Athaliah had power for a season.
But she did not have the final word over the Davidic royal line.
Joash received the crown.
But even Joash was not the King who could save humanity from sin.
The story was still moving toward someone greater.
Toward the Son of David.
Toward the promised Messiah.
Toward the One who would carry a cross before receiving the open recognition of His everlasting reign.
Toward Jesus Christ, crucified and risen.
And one day, every knee will bow and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11).
Until then, we live by faith.
We repent when we sin.
We endure when life is hard.
We love when hatred seems easier.
We seek truth when lies appear stronger.
We trust God's Word even when we cannot see how the next chapter will unfold.
And we remember that the visible triumph of evil is never proof that God has surrendered His throne.
If you take only one truth away from this story, let it be this:
The world may not see what God is preserving, but the world cannot overturn what God has promised in Christ.
So do not place your ultimate hope in a change of circumstances.
Place it in the Savior who died and rose again.
Do not build your identity around the person who hurt you.
Build your life upon the One who gave Himself to redeem you.
And do not confuse a season of silence with the absence of God's faithfulness.
The God who kept His covenant promises through the darkest chapters of Judah's history is the same God who has spoken His final saving word through His Son.
Above all, open your heart to Christ.
Because the greatest miracle in this story is not simply that a hidden child survived a murderous queen.
It is that God's faithfulness continued through generations of human sin and failure until the promised Savior came.
And that Savior is still calling sinners to repentance, still offering forgiveness through His finished work, and still transforming lives by His grace.
The throne Athaliah stole could not destroy God's promise—and the grave that received Jesus could not hold the King who fulfilled it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMEN AT GOD’S DOOR: THE SHOCKING CONNECTION BETWEEN A SACRED MIRROR, A CORRUPT PRIESTHOOD, AND THE JESUS WHO SEES THE FORGOTTEN
paragraphs: THE WOMEN AT GOD’S DOOR: THE SHOCKING CONNECTION BETWEEN A SACRED MIRROR, A CORRUPT PRIESTHOOD, AND THE JESUS WHO SEES THE FORGOTTEN

Why does the Bible mention women serving at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting in Exodus 38:8 and 1 Samuel 2:22? Behind these easily overlooked verses lies a story of worship, betrayal, sacred service, and the Savior who refuses to let human corruption have the final word.
There are some Bible verses we read without stopping.
A name. A measurement. A strange detail about an ancient building.
We turn the page, assuming there is nothing there for us.
But sometimes, buried in a sentence we almost skipped, is a truth that will make us put the Bible down for a moment and examine our own hearts.
And this is one of those moments.
Because the Bible tells us something unusual about women standing at the entrance of God's sacred dwelling.
In one passage, their mirrors become part of a holy vessel.
In another, women associated with that same sacred entrance appear in a devastating account of priestly corruption.
Two passages.
One sacred location.
Two very different pictures of what happens when human beings approach the presence of God.

And somewhere between those pictures is a question that should disturb every person who has ever trusted a spiritual leader, served in a church, been wounded by religious hypocrisy, or wondered whether God still sees the people everyone else overlooks.
What happens when the place where people come to meet God becomes the place where they are mistreated?
And perhaps even more personally...
What does Jesus do with the people who have been wounded near the very place they came looking for Him?
To understand the answer, we have to return to the wilderness.
Before the corruption.
Before the scandal.
Before the priesthood became a warning.
We have to meet the women whose mirrors became part of Israel's worship.
Exodus 38:8 records:
"He made the laver of brass, and the foot of it of brass, of the lookingglasses of the women assembling, which assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation." (KJV)
It sounds like a small construction detail.
But slow down.

Moses is describing the making of the bronze basin, a vessel placed between the altar and the entrance to the sanctuary, where the priests would wash their hands and feet before ministering (Exodus 30:17–21; 40:30–32).
And where did the bronze come from?
The mirrors belonging to women who assembled at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
In the ancient world, mirrors were not the glass objects we use today. They were made from polished metal, often bronze, which could reflect a person's appearance.
These women possessed objects associated with looking at themselves.
And those objects became material for a basin associated with priestly cleansing.
That is what the text actually tells us.
But the Hebrew takes us somewhere even more interesting.
The phrase describing these women includes the words:
הַצֹּבְאֹת אֲשֶׁר צָבְאוּ
Hatsov'ot asher tsav'u.
The wording comes from the Hebrew root צבא (tsava'), which can carry the sense of assembling, being organized for service, or performing an assigned duty.
The same root is used in contexts involving organized groups and service, including certain Levitical responsibilities (Numbers 4:23).
This is why Bible translations differ in how they describe these women.
Some emphasize their assembling or gathering.
Others describe them as women who served or ministered at the entrance.
The Hebrew wording suggests an organized activity associated with the sanctuary, but the passage does not give us a complete description of their responsibilities.
We are not told that these women were priestesses.
We are not told that they performed sacrifices.
We are not told exactly what their daily duties involved.
And we must not invent details simply because a mysterious verse captures our imagination.
But one thing is unmistakable.
These women were not invisible to God.
Their presence was remembered.
Their contribution was recorded.
And the materials they provided became part of the sacred furnishings used in Israel's worship.
Think about that.
The book of Exodus contains astonishing details about the tabernacle.
Gold.
Silver.
Bronze.
Curtains.
Precious stones.
Priestly garments.
Exact measurements.
Specific instructions.
And right there, among the sacred construction records, Scripture pauses to acknowledge women whose mirrors were used to make the basin.
God did not need to mention that detail for us to understand the dimensions of the basin.
Yet the detail is there.
And perhaps that should challenge the way we measure significance.
Because human beings tend to remember the people standing in front.
The speakers.
The leaders.
The people whose names appear on buildings.
But God also sees the people whose names never appear on the program.
The person who cleans after everyone leaves.
The widow who gives quietly.
The exhausted mother who prays when nobody is watching.
The believer who serves without applause.
The woman who has spent years wondering whether her contribution mattered.
The man who thinks his small act of obedience will never make a difference.
The women in Exodus 38:8 are unnamed.
Yet their contribution is preserved in Scripture.
And there is something deeply comforting about serving a God who does not need the world to recognize you before He sees you.
But we must be careful with one popular interpretation.
You may have heard someone preach that these women surrendered their mirrors because they were giving up vanity, pride, or an obsession with outward beauty.
It is a memorable sermon illustration.
But Exodus does not explicitly say that.
The passage does not accuse the women of vanity.
It does not describe their mirrors as sinful.
It does not say that possessing a mirror was spiritually wrong.
What it does say is that the mirrors became material for the bronze basin.
We can draw a meaningful spiritual reflection from that transformation, but we must distinguish reflection from what Scripture directly teaches.
A mirror shows us our outward appearance.
The basin was used for ceremonial washing.
That contrast can remind us that God cares about something deeper than what other people see.
But the deeper biblical teaching comes from passages such as 1 Samuel 16:7, where God declares that human beings look at outward appearance while the LORD looks at the heart.
And from James 1:23–25, where God's Word is compared to a mirror that exposes what a person must not merely observe but respond to.
The problem is not that we have mirrors.
The problem is that we can spend our lives examining our faces while refusing to examine our hearts.
We can look presentable and remain spiritually exhausted.
We can wear the right clothes, speak the right religious language, and know exactly when to raise our hands during worship...
While hiding bitterness.
Unconfessed sin.
Jealousy.
Secret compromise.
Or a wound so deep that we have learned to smile over it.
And this is where the bronze basin becomes a powerful reminder.
The priests were commanded to wash before approaching their sacred duties.
Their position did not exempt them from God's requirements.
Their religious clothing did not make cleansing unnecessary.
Their public ministry did not remove their responsibility to approach God reverently.
And that matters because the next passage reveals what happens when religious position becomes an excuse for moral corruption.
Years later, the scene shifts to Shiloh.
The tabernacle is associated with Israel's worship there.
Eli is the priest.
His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, hold priestly positions.
And something is terribly wrong.
First Samuel 2 describes men who abused their sacred responsibilities.
They treated the LORD's offerings with contempt.
They took portions of sacrifices unlawfully.
They used their authority to satisfy their appetites rather than honor God.
Then we reach verse 22.
"Now Eli was very old, and heard all that his sons did unto all Israel; and how they lay with the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation." (1 Samuel 2:22, KJV)
Read that carefully.
The women are again described in connection with the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
The Hebrew uses the same verbal root found in Exodus 38:8, creating a striking linguistic connection between the two passages.
But there is an important distinction.
The Bible does not say these were the same individual women.
The events are separated by generations.
The repeated wording points to women associated with the sanctuary entrance, not to a single group of women living across both periods.
And the text does not give us enough information to establish every detail of their role.
What it does give us is a devastating report concerning the conduct of Eli's sons.
The Hebrew expression in 1 Samuel 2:22 is:
יִשְׁכְּבוּן אֶת־הַנָּשִׁים
Yishkevun et-hannashim.
It refers to lying with the women and, in this context, describes sexual relations.
The surrounding narrative presents the conduct of Eli's sons as part of their serious wickedness.
But we must not claim more than the text reveals.
Scripture does not explicitly explain whether these sexual encounters involved coercion, threats, manipulation, or some other circumstance.
Given the men's priestly authority and the narrative's condemnation of their conduct, the possibility of exploitation is a serious concern. Yet the precise circumstances are not specified.
The women should not automatically be blamed for what the text presents as the corruption of the priests.
Nor should we turn this verse into a sensational story about supposed temple prostitution.
There is no sufficient basis in these passages to conclude that the women were cult prostitutes or that their presence at the sanctuary entrance was inherently immoral.
The biblical emphasis falls on the wickedness of Hophni and Phinehas.
And the tragedy is severe enough without adding details God did not reveal.
These were men entrusted with sacred responsibilities.
They were supposed to help preserve reverence for the LORD.
Instead, their conduct dishonored Him.
And there is something particularly disturbing about sin committed by people who occupy positions of spiritual trust.
Because when someone who claims to represent God acts wickedly, the damage can reach far beyond the immediate wrongdoing.
People can begin to associate the character of God with the character of the person who misrepresented Him.
A believer can lose confidence in spiritual leadership.
A young person can become disillusioned with the church.
A wounded person can begin to wonder whether the God they were taught to trust is anything like the people who claimed to serve Him.
And if you have ever experienced that kind of betrayal, this part of Scripture may feel painfully personal.
Maybe someone used Bible verses to silence your questions.
Maybe a person who spoke publicly about holiness lived privately in hypocrisy.
Maybe you trusted a spiritual authority who later violated that trust.
Maybe you were told to protect a ministry's reputation instead of speaking truthfully about wrongdoing.
Or maybe you simply watched people use God's name to excuse behavior that contradicted His Word.
There is something you need to see in this passage.
God did not call the wickedness of Eli's sons holy simply because they were priests.
Their position did not change the moral nature of their actions.
Their religious responsibilities did not shield them from accountability.
And their connection to the sanctuary did not make their behavior acceptable.
First Samuel 2:12 describes Eli's sons as wicked men who did not know the LORD.
Imagine that.
Men who worked around sacred things.
Men who handled religious responsibilities.
Men who belonged to a priestly family.
Yet Scripture says they did not know the LORD.
That should make every Christian examine something uncomfortable.
It is possible to become familiar with religious activity without truly walking with God.
You can know the language of worship without possessing a worshipful heart.
You can be recognized in a congregation and still resist repentance.
You can hold a title and remain spiritually rebellious.
You can teach people about holiness while secretly protecting the very sins you condemn.
And no amount of public ministry can substitute for genuine faith, obedience, and repentance.
Jesus would later issue a sobering warning in Matthew 7:21–23 about people who appealed to impressive religious works while lacking a true relationship with Him.
That warning is not an invitation to live in constant terror that every imperfect believer is secretly rejected.
It is a call to stop confusing religious performance with genuine surrender to Christ.
Because the Gospel does not merely invite us to appear righteous.
It calls us to come honestly before the only One who can save us.
And here is another detail we cannot afford to miss.
Eli knew that his sons were behaving wickedly.
He confronted them verbally.
But the biblical account shows that he failed to restrain them as he should have.
In 1 Samuel 3:13, God declares judgment against Eli's house because of the evil involving his sons and Eli's failure to restrain them.
This is not a small warning.
It means spiritual responsibility includes more than privately disapproving of wrongdoing.
It requires taking evil seriously.
Especially when people under someone's authority are being harmed or placed at risk.
A ministry does not become faithful by hiding scandal.
A church does not glorify Jesus by protecting unrepentant wrongdoing.
A leader does not honor God by preserving an image of holiness while refusing necessary accountability.
The name of Christ is not protected by concealing evil committed in His name.
It is honored when His truth is obeyed.
And that truth includes justice, repentance, care for the vulnerable, and the refusal to treat people as expendable.
If wrongdoing is happening in a spiritual community, seeking safety, reporting abuse to appropriate authorities, and pursuing responsible accountability are not acts of rebellion against God.
They can be necessary acts of truth and protection.
Forgiveness does not require silence.
Grace does not eliminate consequences.
And repentance is not a substitute for protecting people from further harm.
Now return, for a moment, to those two scenes.
In Exodus, women associated with the entrance of the Tent of Meeting contribute mirrors that become part of a basin for priestly washing.
In Samuel, women associated with the sanctuary entrance appear in a report exposing the wicked conduct of priests.
The biblical writers do not explicitly present these two accounts as a deliberate symbolic contrast.
We should not pretend that they do.
But reading them together confronts us with a meaningful theological question.
What happens when those entrusted with sacred service refuse the moral seriousness their calling demands?
The basin was a reminder that priests were not above God's requirements.
Hophni and Phinehas demonstrate the danger of behaving as though sacred office places someone beyond correction.
And that contrast points us toward a much greater need.
Because Israel did not merely need better religious appearances.
It needed faithful mediation between a holy God and sinful humanity.
And so do we.
This is where the story becomes more than a lesson about ancient women, bronze mirrors, or corrupt priests.
This is where it leads us to Jesus Christ.
The New Testament presents Jesus as the great High Priest who is fundamentally different from the sinful priests of old.
Hebrews 4:15 says:
"For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." (KJV)
Do you see the difference?
Hophni and Phinehas used sacred responsibility while living wickedly.
Jesus exercised His ministry in perfect obedience to the Father.
Corrupt religious leaders can use authority for selfish gain.
Jesus gave Himself for the salvation of sinners.
Human priests needed cleansing.
Jesus, the sinless Son of God, became the source of the cleansing we could never accomplish through our own righteousness.
Hebrews 7:26 describes Him as holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners.
Hebrews 9 explains that Christ entered the greater heavenly sanctuary through His own blood, securing eternal redemption.
And Hebrews 10:22 speaks of drawing near to God with hearts cleansed and bodies washed with pure water.
The bronze basin did not save Israel.
It belonged to the system of worship God established under the old covenant.
Its washing was part of priestly ceremonial preparation.
But those cleansing requirements help us appreciate the holiness of God and the greater purification accomplished through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not that we must polish ourselves until God finally finds us acceptable.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ, who was without sin, died for sinners and rose again, and that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
We do not earn salvation by becoming impressive.
We receive God's grace through faith in Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us away from sin and into a transformed life.
That is why the message of the Gospel is so much greater than religious self-improvement.
It is redemption.
It is forgiveness.
It is reconciliation.
It is a new beginning grounded in the finished work of Jesus.
And perhaps the most beautiful part is how Jesus treated women in a world where they could so easily be dismissed.
Consider the woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years.
In Mark 5:25–34, she approached Jesus believing that touching His clothing would bring healing.
She had suffered for years.
She had spent her resources seeking help.
And her condition had left her desperate.
When she touched His garment, she was healed.
But Jesus did not simply allow her to disappear into the crowd.
He stopped.
He called attention to what had happened.
He listened to her truth.
And He addressed her with tenderness.
"Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague." (Mark 5:34, KJV)
Daughter.
Not an inconvenience.
Not a distraction.
Not an anonymous problem.
Daughter.
Now think of the Samaritan woman in John 4.
Jesus met her at a well and spoke openly about her life.
He did not pretend her past was irrelevant.
But neither did He reduce her entire identity to her history.
He revealed Himself as the Messiah, and her encounter with Him became part of the testimony that brought others to hear His words.
And consider the woman caught in adultery in John 7:53–8:11, a passage with a significant textual-history question because the earliest surviving manuscripts of John do not contain it.
In the traditional account, Jesus refuses to join the crowd's condemnation while also calling the woman to leave her sin.
The broader New Testament teaching is clear regardless of that passage's textual status.
Jesus does not make peace with sin.
But neither does He treat broken people as disposable.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He welcomes those who come to Him.
He restores people through grace and truth.
And this is the heart of our theme:
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because evil should be forgotten.
Not because repentance is optional.
And certainly not because every wound disappears the moment someone says a prayer.
Jesus rewrites lives because His death and resurrection accomplish what human religion cannot.
He forgives the repentant sinner.
He brings the spiritually dead to life.
He gives hope to the wounded.
He calls the proud to humility.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He establishes a new identity for those who belong to Him.
