And He promises a final restoration in which evil will not have the last word.
But notice something.
Jesus does not rewrite the past by pretending it never happened.
The Bible itself preserves the scandal of Eli's sons.
Their wickedness is not erased from Scripture.
It is exposed.
Why?
Because grace is not the same thing as denial.
The Gospel is powerful precisely because it tells the truth about sin and then reveals a Savior powerful enough to redeem sinners.
There is no need to minimize darkness to magnify the light.
And that brings us to a question that is no longer about ancient Israel.
It is about you.
What are you carrying into the presence of God today?
Is it guilt?
Is it shame?
Is it anger toward someone who misused spiritual authority?
Is it a secret you have been too afraid to confess?
Is it disappointment because people who claimed to represent Jesus failed to reflect His character?
Or is it the quiet exhaustion of serving God while wondering whether anybody notices?
Perhaps you recognize yourself in the unnamed women of Exodus.
You have given.
You have served.
You have sacrificed.
You have shown up when nobody applauded.
And you have wondered whether your obedience matters.
Remember that Scripture preserved the contribution of women whose individual names were not recorded.
The God who sees in secret is not indifferent to faithful service.
Or perhaps you recognize the pain that can surround 1 Samuel 2.
You came near a religious community hoping to encounter truth, only to discover hypocrisy.
You trusted someone who should have acted responsibly.
You heard people speak about holiness while refusing to confront wrongdoing.
If that is part of your story, do not confuse the failures of sinful people with the character of the sinless Christ.
Jesus is not another Hophni.
Jesus is not another Phinehas.
He is the faithful High Priest.
He does not need to exploit people to preserve His position.
He does not use spiritual authority to satisfy selfish appetites.
He does not excuse evil because the offender holds an impressive title.
He is righteous.
He is holy.
He is merciful.
And He is worthy of your trust.
That does not mean you must immediately trust every religious institution or leader again.
Trust can require time, demonstrated integrity, and accountability.
But the failures of human beings do not cancel the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this is not primarily wounded by another person's sin.
Perhaps you are confronted by your own.
You have become very good at looking spiritually presentable.
You know how to answer, "How are you?"
You know how to smile.
You know how to post Scripture.
You know how to appear strong.
But behind closed doors, you know there are things that need to change.
And you are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of promising yourself that tomorrow will be different.
Then hear the invitation of the Gospel.
You do not have to protect your image before Jesus.
He already knows the truth.
And the One who knows the truth is the very One who calls sinners to come to Him.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because we have finally become worthy.
But because God's forgiveness rests on the righteous and sufficient work of Jesus Christ.
So stop confusing concealment with safety.
Stop calling spiritual exhaustion normal.
Stop defending the sin that is destroying your peace.
And stop believing that your worst chapter must become your final identity.
Turn to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Repent of what needs repentance.
Seek help where help is needed.
Make restitution where it is possible and appropriate.
And receive the grace that cannot be purchased with good behavior.
You may not be able to undo yesterday.
But in Christ, yesterday does not have to rule tomorrow.
That is not permission to escape responsibility.
It is hope for genuine transformation.
And if you have witnessed God's mercy in a season when you thought your life was beyond repair, share a little of your testimony.
You do not have to reveal private details or painful experiences publicly.
God hears prayers that never appear in a comment section.
But your willingness to speak honestly, even in a few simple words, may encourage another person who thought they were struggling alone.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
Not because an algorithm measures your faithfulness.
But because someone in your circle may desperately need to understand that religious hypocrisy is not the same as the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Someone may be ready to abandon faith because of what a human leader did.
Someone may be carrying shame they have never told anyone about.
Someone may be faithfully serving in obscurity and wondering whether God sees.
Or send this privately to a family member who needs to remember that Christ remains faithful even when people fail.
Come back to the passages.
Read Exodus 38.
Read 1 Samuel 2 and 3.
Read Hebrews 4, 7, 9, and 10.
Do not build your understanding of Scripture on a single emotional message, including this one.
Open the Bible for yourself.
Examine the context.
Ask questions.
Grow in discernment.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, Christians who have grown spiritually complacent, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
There is room for honest questions.
There is room to learn.
There is room to be challenged by Scripture.
And there is room to discover that the Gospel is far more beautiful than the religious performances people sometimes mistake for Christianity.
These resources are intended to help believers become more grounded in Scripture, more discerning about biblical truth, and more mature in their walk with Jesus Christ.
And there is another invitation I want to extend with sincerity.
Not because you must pay to receive God's grace.
And not because anyone should feel guilty if they cannot afford to give.
The Gospel is not for sale.
But sharing biblical teaching, developing discipleship resources, preparing books, and expanding outreach can involve real costs.
It is a practical way to participate in the mission of making Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, not under compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
But it can be a meaningful voluntary offering toward Christian teaching and outreach.
They are not spiritual rewards.
The greatest gift is still the Gospel itself.
And that gift cannot be bought.
That Jesus Christ would be known.
That His Word would be understood faithfully.
That people would turn from sin and find forgiveness in Him.
That wounded hearts would encounter truth and compassion.
And that believers would grow beyond religious appearances into genuine discipleship.
Because when everything else is stripped away, this is what matters.
Not how impressive our ministry looks.
Not how many people applaud.
Not how many religious titles we accumulate.
Not how polished our public image becomes.
But whether we truly know Jesus Christ and are being transformed by His grace.
Remember the women at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
Remember the mirrors that became part of a vessel used for priestly washing.
Remember the wickedness of priests who dishonored their sacred calling.
And remember the faithful High Priest who came to accomplish what no sinful priest could ever accomplish.
The women of Exodus remind us that seemingly overlooked service can matter.
The scandal in Samuel reminds us that religious authority must never be confused with righteousness.
And Jesus reminds us that our ultimate hope is not in the perfection of human leaders but in the perfection of our Savior.
One day, every earthly title will lose its importance.
Every carefully managed reputation will be exposed to the truth.
Every hidden thing will stand before the righteous judgment of God.
And the only righteousness sufficient to save sinners will be the righteousness found in Jesus Christ.
So do not spend your entire life polishing the mirror while neglecting the condition of your soul.
Do not spend your entire life admiring religious appearances while refusing the cleansing only Christ can give.
And do not allow the failures of those who misrepresented Him to make you forget the One who never failed.
The story began with women whose mirrors were used in a sacred basin.
It passed through a painful account of men who corrupted their sacred responsibilities.
But it brings us, finally, to a Savior who is holy, compassionate, and faithful forever.
And perhaps that is the truth someone reading this has been waiting to hear.
You are not saved by looking clean.
You are saved by Jesus Christ.
You are not healed by pretending the wound never happened.
You can bring the truth of your suffering before the Savior who sees.
You are not made righteous by standing near holy things.
You need the grace of the Holy One Himself.
And your past, however painful, does not have to be the final chapter of your life.
The hands that were pierced for your redemption are still more trustworthy than every hand that ever failed you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE BURIED THE TREASURE BENEATH HIS TENT… AND 36 MEN NEVER CAME HOME
paragraphs: HE BURIED THE TREASURE BENEATH HIS TENT… AND 36 MEN NEVER CAME HOME
The Terrifying Truth About Achan’s Hidden Sin, the Disaster at Ai, and the God Who Can Turn Your Valley of Trouble Into a Door of Hope — Joshua 7:1–26
There was a secret buried beneath the floor of a tent.
Nobody outside that tent knew it was there.
Not Joshua. Not the elders. Not the soldiers preparing for their next battle.
And thirty-six men were about to die.

Their wives would wait for footsteps that would never return. Their children would lose fathers. An entire nation would discover that the victory they had celebrated at Jericho did not mean they could disregard the holiness of the God who had given it.
And the man responsible?
He was living among them.
Worshiping among them.
Looking like everybody else.
With stolen treasure hidden beneath his feet.
But here is what should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Achan's story is not merely about a man who stole something he should never have touched. It is about the terrifying distance that can exist between what people see and what God knows.
And before you decide this story has nothing to do with you, consider one question.
What if the thing you keep convincing yourself is harmless is quietly damaging the very life you have been asking God to bless?
Stay with this story.
Because it begins with buried treasure and ends in a valley of judgment.
But centuries later, that same valley will become the setting of one of Scripture's most astonishing promises of hope.
And that is where the Gospel will meet us.
Not where we are pretending to be.
Where we actually are.
Israel had just experienced something extraordinary.
Jericho had fallen.
Not because Israel possessed superior weapons. Not because Joshua had discovered some brilliant military strategy. Not because the walls had been weakened by human engineering.
The Lord had given Jericho into their hands.
For six days, the Israelites marched around the city according to God's instructions. On the seventh day, they marched seven times. The priests blew their trumpets. The people shouted.
And the walls fell.
Imagine standing there.
The dust rising. The impossible becoming visible. The unmistakable realization that the God who had brought Israel through the Jordan was still fighting for His people.
But before Jericho fell, God had given a command.

The city and its contents were devoted to the Lord under the ban of destruction, with specific exceptions. Rahab and those sheltered with her were to be spared. Silver, gold, bronze, and iron were to be placed in the treasury of the Lord.
The people were not free to treat the devoted things as personal spoils.
Joshua 6:18–19 had made that unmistakably clear.
This was not an ordinary opportunity to enrich themselves.
It was a moment demanding obedience.
And somewhere among the ruins of Jericho, one man saw something that captured his heart.
His name was Achan.
He belonged to the tribe of Judah.
And when he saw the beautiful garment, the silver, and the gold, something happened inside him before anything was buried beneath his tent.
He wanted what God had forbidden him to take.
Perhaps he looked around.
Perhaps he calculated the risk.
Perhaps he reasoned that one garment and a little precious metal could hardly matter after such an enormous victory.
Scripture does not tell us his private thoughts.
But it tells us exactly what he did.
He took the devoted things.
He carried them home.
He concealed them in the earth inside his tent.
And he apparently expected life to continue.
That is one of the most dangerous assumptions a human being can make.
That because judgment has not arrived, the secret must be safe.
That because nobody has confronted us, God must not be concerned.
That because yesterday was victorious, tomorrow is guaranteed.
But the opening sentence of Joshua 7 tells us something Achan could not see.
Israel had acted unfaithfully concerning the devoted things.
And the anger of the Lord burned against Israel.
Notice the disturbing detail.
The text identifies one man as the offender, yet describes the breach in terms of the covenant community.
In Hebrew, Joshua 7:1 uses the expression:
וַיִּמְעֲלוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל מַעַל
Vayyimʿalu vene-Yisra'el maʿal.
The expression communicates that the children of Israel committed an act of unfaithfulness or trespass.
The Hebrew root מעל (maʿal) conveys treachery or a breach of trust, especially in matters involving what belongs to God.
This was more than ordinary theft.
Achan had violated something sacred.
And the narrative deliberately makes us feel the weight of that violation within the whole community.
It does not mean every Israelite personally committed Achan's sin. Nor does it mean we should automatically blame someone else's hidden wrongdoing whenever tragedy strikes.
It means that within Israel's particular covenant situation, the rebellion of one member had consequences beyond himself.
That distinction matters.
Because the Bible is not inviting us to become suspicious detectives searching for secret sinners whenever something goes wrong.
It is warning us that sin is rarely as isolated as we imagine.
A husband's dishonesty can wound his family.
A leader's corruption can devastate a congregation.
A parent's destructive choices can leave scars on children who never chose them.
A believer's concealed compromise can damage relationships built on trust.
And sometimes the people paying the emotional price are not the people who committed the offense.
That is why the story of Achan should make us sober rather than self-righteous.
Because the question is not simply, "Who is hiding something?"
The question is, "Lord, is there anything in me that I have refused to bring into Your light?"
Then came Ai.
Compared with Jericho, Ai appeared manageable.
Joshua sent men to investigate. They returned with confidence. Only a few thousand soldiers would be necessary, they said.
Why exhaust the entire army over such a small city?
So about three thousand men went up.
And Israel was defeated.
The men of Ai struck down about thirty-six Israelites and pursued the others.
The soldiers who had watched Jericho's walls collapse were now running for their lives.
The confidence of the nation dissolved.
Joshua 7:5 describes the people's hearts as melting and becoming like water.
The imagery is devastating.
The people who had once caused their enemies to tremble were now trembling themselves.
And Joshua fell facedown before the ark of the Lord.
He tore his clothes.
The elders joined him.
Dust covered their heads.
Joshua cried out, distressed that Israel had crossed the Jordan only to face destruction.
He feared what would happen when the surrounding nations heard of their defeat.
And he asked what would become of God's great name.
Then God answered.
Not with the reassurance Joshua might have expected.
Not by telling him that the defeat was merely an unfortunate military setback.
God said:
"Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?" — Joshua 7:10, ESV
And then the accusation came.
Israel had sinned.
They had transgressed His covenant.
They had taken devoted things, stolen, deceived, and placed the stolen objects among their own possessions.
There was a reason Israel had been unable to stand before its enemies.
And until the covenant violation was dealt with, they could not expect God's continued help in battle.
Here is the painful truth.
Sometimes we are asking God to bless the very life we are refusing to surrender to Him.
We want peace while protecting dishonesty.
We want restoration while refusing repentance.
We want spiritual intimacy while nurturing something that is pulling our hearts away from Him.
We want the comfort of God's presence without allowing His Word to confront our choices.
And yet we must be careful.
Not every unanswered prayer is evidence of hidden sin.
Not every financial struggle is divine punishment.
Not every sickness, disappointment, or painful season means God has withdrawn His favor.
Jesus Himself rejected simplistic assumptions connecting personal suffering to personal wrongdoing in John 9:1–3.
The faithful can suffer deeply.
The innocent can endure terrible losses.
The righteous can experience hardship.
But Joshua 7 describes a particular situation in which God explicitly revealed that covenant disobedience was behind Israel's defeat.
And within that specific story, the warning is unmistakable.
What we conceal from people is never concealed from God.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
You smile when people ask how you are doing.
You still attend church.
You still share Bible verses.
You still know how to say, "God is good."
But somewhere in your private life, something has become difficult to surrender.
Maybe it is a relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ.
Maybe it is dishonesty that began with something small.
Maybe it is bitterness you have quietly fed for years.
Maybe it is an addiction you keep promising to confront tomorrow.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe it is greed.
Maybe it is a secret habit that has slowly reshaped your desires.
Or perhaps it is simply the exhausting effort of pretending you are spiritually healthy when you desperately need help.
The point is not that your struggles make you another Achan.
The point is that hiding can become its own prison.
And the longer something remains buried, the more frightening it can feel to bring it into the light.
God instructed Joshua to consecrate the people.
The following morning, Israel would come forward tribe by tribe, clan by clan, household by household, and man by man.
The Lord would identify the offender.
Imagine the tension.
Thousands of people gathered.
A nation still grieving its dead.
Families standing together.
And somewhere in that assembly stood Achan.
The tribe of Judah was selected.
Then the clan of the Zerahites.
Then the household of Zabdi.
Then Achan.
The hidden man was no longer hidden.
Joshua spoke to him, urging him to give glory to the Lord God of Israel, make confession, and tell what he had done.
And Achan finally admitted it.
Joshua 7:20–21 records his confession.
He had sinned against the Lord.
He had seen a beautiful cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels.
He had coveted them.
He had taken them.
And there they were, hidden in the ground inside his tent, with the silver underneath.
There is a sequence here worth remembering.
He saw. He coveted. He took. He hid.
That is the anatomy of temptation in this account.
And it resembles the pattern James describes centuries later:
"But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire." — James 1:14, ESV
Temptation does not always announce itself as rebellion.
Sometimes it arrives dressed as opportunity.
Sometimes it whispers, "You deserve this."
Sometimes it says, "Nobody will ever know."
Sometimes it promises that obedience can wait until tomorrow.
But the things we repeatedly entertain in our hearts can eventually become the things we act upon with our hands.
Achan's confession also reveals something deeply unsettling.
He could describe his sin accurately.
He knew what he had done.
He acknowledged that he had sinned against God.
But his confession came after he had been exposed.
The text does not tell us enough about his inner condition to determine everything he felt or whether he experienced genuine inward repentance.
And that is important.
We must not claim to know what Scripture does not reveal.
What we do know is that his admission did not remove the earthly judgment announced in this particular covenant setting.
Men were sent to the tent.
They found the stolen objects exactly where Achan had said they would be.
The treasures were brought before Joshua and the Israelites and laid out before the Lord.
The evidence was no longer underground.
What had been concealed was now exposed.
Then came one of the hardest scenes in the book of Joshua.
Achan, the stolen objects, and the people and possessions associated with his household were taken to the Valley of Achor.
Joshua pronounced the judgment.
And the narrative records the destruction of Achan and his household, followed by the raising of a great heap of stones.
The details of the passage are severe, and interpreters have discussed the precise sequence of the executions and burning described in Joshua 7:24–25.
But we should not soften the horror.
This is not a scene to celebrate casually.
It is not permission for religious people to punish suspected sinners.
It is not a model for churches to imitate.
It is an account of divine judgment within Israel's ancient covenant history, in a setting involving a direct command from God and a particular judicial process.
We must read it with reverence, moral seriousness, and attention to its historical context.
Scripture elsewhere insists that children must not be executed merely for their parents' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16), and Ezekiel 18 emphasizes individual moral responsibility.
Joshua 7 does not give us enough information to establish the individual culpability of every member of Achan's household.
We should not invent details to make the passage easier.
We should allow the difficult questions to remain difficult.
And we should resist turning a tragedy into a simplistic slogan.
Because thirty-six men had already died.
A family was destroyed.
A nation had suffered.
And the treasure that seemed so valuable was powerless to save its owner.
Think about that.
Achan had risked everything for objects that would never be able to love him, forgive him, rescue him, or give him life.
A garment.
Silver.
Gold.
Things that glittered in the ruins of Jericho.
Things that looked worth possessing.
Things that ultimately could not deliver what his heart had imagined.
And there is something painfully familiar about that.
How many people have traded their peace for something that promised pleasure?
How many have damaged a marriage for a moment of attention?
How many have sacrificed integrity for money they could not keep?
How many have lost years of spiritual joy trying to protect a secret that never truly satisfied them?
Not every compromise ends in the same earthly catastrophe as Achan's.
But every sin makes promises it cannot ultimately fulfill.
And this is why repentance is not God trying to rob us of happiness.
Repentance is turning away from what destroys and returning to the One who gives life.
The Greek word commonly translated "repent" in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō).

It carries the sense of changing one's mind or turning in repentance. In biblical context, genuine repentance is more than feeling embarrassed or regretting consequences. It involves a reorientation toward God that bears fruit in how we live.
Jesus proclaimed:
"Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." — Matthew 4:17, ESV
He did not preach repentance because He enjoyed condemning broken people.
He proclaimed the arrival of God's kingdom and called people to turn toward Him.
And this is where Achan's story becomes more than an ancient warning.
Because if the story ended with the stones in the valley, we would be left staring at the terrible consequences of sin.
But the Bible does not end in Joshua 7.
And the Valley of Achor does not disappear from Scripture.
Its name becomes part of a much larger story.
The Hebrew name עָכוֹר (ʿAkhor) is associated with trouble.
Joshua 7:26 explains why the place was called the Valley of Achor.
It was a place marked by judgment.
A place whose very name carried the memory of disaster.
But generations later, God spoke through the prophet Hosea.
And He said something astonishing.
"And there I will give her her vineyards and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope." — Hosea 2:15, ESV
Read that again.
The Valley of Achor.
The valley of trouble.
The place associated with shame, judgment, and devastating consequences.
God declared that He would make it a door of hope.
In Hebrew, the phrase is:
לְפֶתַח תִּקְוָה
Lefetach tiqvah.
"A doorway of hope."
The Hebrew פֶּתַח (petach) means an opening or doorway, while תִּקְוָה (tiqvah) means hope or expectation.
In Hosea's immediate context, God is speaking of restoring His unfaithful covenant people, using the language of renewed relationship after judgment.
This is not a promise that every consequence of our wrongdoing will disappear.
It is not a guarantee that every lost opportunity will return.
And it does not mean Achan's judgment was reversed.
But it reveals something magnificent about the character of God.
The Lord who judges sin is also the Lord who promises restoration.
The place that remembered trouble would become an image of renewed hope.
And when we read that promise in light of the full biblical story, we are led toward Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest human problem is not merely that we have made bad decisions.
It is that we have sinned against a holy God.
We have loved created things more than the Creator.
We have failed to obey perfectly.
We have broken trust.
We have hidden what should have been confessed.
And no amount of religious performance can erase our guilt.
But Jesus Christ came into a world full of guilty people.
Not to approve their sin.
Not to pretend evil was harmless.
Not to tell them that holiness no longer mattered.
He came to save sinners.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." — 1 Timothy 1:15, ESV
And this is the breathtaking difference between Achan's story and the Gospel's saving announcement.
Achan took what was forbidden and brought guilt upon himself.
Jesus committed no sin, yet willingly gave Himself to bear the sins of others.
Achan concealed stolen treasure beneath the earth.
Jesus was laid in a tomb after openly giving His life for the world.
Achan's sin brought devastating consequences.
Christ's obedience unto death opened the way for forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life.
And unlike Achan, Jesus did not remain in the grave.
He rose again.
The resurrection is God's declaration that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:21 that God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
That does not mean Jesus became morally corrupt.
It means He bore the burden of sin in His saving work, so that sinners could be reconciled to God through Him.
This is grace.
Not God ignoring evil.
Not God lowering His holiness.
But God providing redemption through the death and resurrection of His Son.
And if you are reading this with something hidden in your life, please understand the invitation.
You do not have to keep defending what is destroying you.
You do not have to keep calling darkness light.
You do not have to keep building your identity around your worst decision.
You can come to Christ.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can ask for help.
You can begin walking in truth.
The apostle John writes:
What a promise.
Not that confession makes us worthy.
Not that our tears purchase salvation.
But that God is faithful to forgive and cleanse those who come to Him through Christ.
And perhaps the most beautiful part is this.
Jesus already knows what you are afraid to tell Him.
You are not informing Him of something He overlooked.
You are coming out of hiding before the One who sees everything and still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
You may need to tell the truth to someone you have hurt.
You may need to make restitution.
You may need to seek pastoral guidance or professional help.
You may need to end a destructive relationship or remove access to something that repeatedly leads you into sin.
You may have consequences to face.
Grace does not make every consequence disappear.
But grace means your future does not have to be governed by the lie that change is impossible.
Through Christ, there is forgiveness.
Through the Holy Spirit, there is power to pursue holiness.
Through the fellowship of believers, there can be accountability, encouragement, and help for the long road of restoration.
And if you have already confessed your sin and turned toward Jesus, do not keep treating yourself as though His mercy is unavailable to you.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." — ESV
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It does not excuse continuing rebellion.
It announces the saving security of those united to the Savior.
You may still remember what happened.
Others may still remember.
Some wounds may take years to heal.
Some relationships may not return to what they once were.
But the blood of Jesus is not weaker than the guilt of a repentant sinner.
And the resurrection of Jesus is not a small promise.
It is the foundation of a new life.
Maybe you came into this article thinking about Achan.
A man who hid a beautiful garment, silver, and gold.
But now you are thinking about something else.
Something you have not told anyone.
Something you have been avoiding in prayer.
Something you keep justifying because facing it would require a painful decision.
Or maybe you are not the one who committed the wrong.
Maybe you are one of the people who suffered because somebody else refused to tell the truth.
Maybe someone else's betrayal broke your trust.
Maybe somebody else's choices shattered the safety of your home.
Maybe you are still grieving the damage caused by a secret you never knew existed.
Then hear this too.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend that betrayal was harmless.
Forgiveness does not automatically require immediate reconciliation, the removal of wise boundaries, or the restoration of trust without evidence of change.
God sees the wounded as well as the guilty.
Jesus is not indifferent to injustice.
And the God who calls sinners to repentance also calls His people to protect the vulnerable, pursue truth, and love one another faithfully.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the ashamed.
And there is room for the wounded.
There is room for the person who needs to confess.
And there is room for the person who needs time to heal.
Because the Savior we proclaim is not merely interested in making people feel better for a moment.
He came to redeem.
To reconcile.
To transform.
To make people new.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with dramatic Bible stories while leaving their hearts untouched.
Not to collect religious applause.
But to keep bringing people back to Scripture, to the truth about sin, to the beauty of grace, and above all to Jesus Christ.
Some people reading these words are fighting battles nobody around them can see.
Some are struggling to pray.
Some are returning to church after years away.
Some are trying to rebuild their families.
Some are searching for God but do not know where to begin.
And some simply need a faithful reminder that the Lord has not abandoned those who sincerely seek Him.
That is why we keep writing.
Why we keep sharing the Word.
Why we keep building resources for discipleship.
And why your participation matters.
If this message has challenged you, please do not let the conversation end when you close this article.
You do not have to expose private details publicly to prove your sincerity.
And if God has already carried you through a season of repentance and renewal, consider sharing a testimony that may strengthen someone who believes change is impossible.
Your words may remind another believer that they are not alone.
Your testimony may help someone find the courage to seek help.
Your prayer may encourage a person you have never met.
And if someone came to mind while reading, consider tagging them with kindness and discretion. Do not publicly expose another person's private struggles. Simply invite them into a message of hope.
Not because an algorithm can measure faithfulness.
But because biblical truth is worth passing along, and someone in your circle may need to hear that repentance is possible and Jesus still receives sinners.
Conviction calls us out of sin and toward Christ.
Condemnation tells us there is no hope.
The Gospel tells repentant sinners to look to the crucified and risen Savior.
There is also a deeper way to stand with this mission.
Scripture teaches that believers may freely and joyfully support Gospel work. Paul speaks of partnership in the Gospel in Philippians 1:5, and of generous giving in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
But it is important to say this clearly.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your faithful sharing of biblical truth matters.
Your commitment to following Christ matters far more than any financial contribution.
But the deepest value of this community is not merchandise.
It is the opportunity to keep growing in the Word of God.
These resources are meant to help you study Scripture, strengthen your prayer life, understand the Gospel, grow in spiritual maturity, and encourage others in their walk with the Lord.
We want to help believers move beyond simply reading an inspiring post and toward a life increasingly shaped by God's Word.
Because discipleship is not a moment of emotional excitement.
It is a lifelong journey of following Jesus.
And if this ministry has helped you, consider helping it reach someone else.
The glory belongs to Jesus.
The salvation belongs to Jesus.
The power to transform lives belongs to Jesus.
And every faithful act of service should point people toward Him.
Now return with me, one final time, to that tent.
The treasure is still beneath the ground.
The garment still looks beautiful.
The silver still has value.
The gold still glitters.
But none of it can give Achan what he truly needs.
He has possessions he cannot safely enjoy.
A secret he cannot escape.
And a judgment he cannot purchase his way out of.
Then look beyond the tent.
Beyond Ai.
Beyond the Valley of Achor.
Look toward Calvary.
There stands another man from the tribe of Judah.
Jesus Christ.
The Lion of Judah.
The One who never stole what belonged to God.
The One who never broke His Father's will.
The One who never needed to hide a single sin.
And yet He willingly endured the cross to save sinners.
There is no stolen gold beneath His feet.
There is a crown of thorns upon His head.
There is no hidden garment to protect.
His clothing is divided among the soldiers.
There is no desperate attempt to escape the consequences of His own wrongdoing.
He has done no wrong.
And still, He gives His life.
For people who have.
For people like us.
And three days later, the grave cannot hold Him.
This is the Gospel.
Not that our sins are small.
But that our Savior is great.
Not that holiness no longer matters.
But that grace brings us into a new life where holiness becomes our calling.
Not that yesterday's wounds were imaginary.
But that Jesus Christ can bring redemption into lives that seemed beyond repair.
So before you leave, ask yourself one last question.
What am I still holding beneath the floor of my heart that I need to surrender to Jesus?
Do not answer for somebody else.
Do not use Achan's story to condemn a person you dislike.
Bring the question before God.
Ask Him to search you.
Ask Him to reveal what needs repentance.
Ask Him for the courage to tell the truth.
And ask Him to teach you how to walk in the freedom of obedience.
Because the most valuable treasure you can possess is not silver hidden beneath the earth.
It is Christ Himself.
And the greatest miracle is not that God can uncover what we have buried.
It is that through Jesus Christ, God can forgive, cleanse, and transform those who turn to Him in faith.
The Valley of Achor was once remembered as a place of trouble.
But God spoke of making it a door of hope.
That does not erase the seriousness of Joshua 7.
It magnifies the wonder of the redemption Scripture reveals.
And perhaps today, you are standing at a doorway of your own.
Not knowing what confession will cost.
Not knowing how long healing will take.
Not knowing what restoration may look like.
But knowing that Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
So come into the light.
Not because you have nothing to be ashamed of.
But because you have a Savior who is able to forgive.
The treasure Achan buried could never save him—but the Savior who was buried and rose again can save everyone who comes to Him in faith.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE LOOKED AT HER BREASTS AND COMPARED THEM TO TWO YOUNG GAZELLES. WHY IS THIS IN THE HOLY BIBLE?
paragraphs: HE LOOKED AT HER BREASTS AND COMPARED THEM TO TWO YOUNG GAZELLES. WHY IS THIS IN THE HOLY BIBLE?
Song of Songs 4:5 — The Scripture That Makes Some Christians Uncomfortable, the Beauty God Never Called Dirty, and the Gospel That Restores What Shame Has Stolen.
There is a verse in your Bible that some Christians would be embarrassed to read aloud in church.
Not because it contains profanity.
Not because it celebrates sin.
But because a man looks at the woman he loves, admires her breasts, and describes them with astonishing tenderness.
And the Holy Spirit allowed those words to remain in Scripture.
For thousands of years.
Think about that.
The same Bible that commands us to flee sexual immorality contains a love poem in which a man openly delights in the physical beauty of his beloved.
The same God who calls His people to holiness preserved a passage that many religious people would rather skip.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question isn't why God allowed such language into His Word.
Perhaps it's why so many of us have learned to feel ashamed of something God originally created good.
Because somewhere between Eden and our broken world, something happened to the human heart.
Love became confused with lust.
Beauty became confused with temptation.
Intimacy became confused with exploitation.
And shame began speaking so loudly that even God's beautiful design could sound scandalous.
But what if this verse is not an embarrassment to explain away?
What if it is an invitation to recover something we have almost forgotten?
Something about love.
Something about the body.
Something about holiness.
And ultimately, something about the grace of Jesus Christ.
Stay with me, because the deeper we enter this passage, the more clearly we will see why the Bible refuses to surrender the beauty of love to the ugliness of sin.
Song of Songs 4:5 says:
“Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies.” — Song of Solomon 4:5, KJV
Yes.
That is actually in the Bible.
And no, we do not need to apologize for it.
But we do need to understand it.
Because Scripture deserves more than a nervous laugh, a provocative headline, or a shallow interpretation.
It deserves reverence.
And the people whose hearts have been wounded by distorted ideas of love deserve to hear what God actually says.
In the original Hebrew, the verse reads:
שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים תְּאוֹמֵי צְבִיָּה הָרוֹעִים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים
Shenei shadayikh kishnei ofarim, te'omei tseviyyah, haro'im bashoshanim.
A close English rendering is:
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.”
The Hebrew word שָׁדַיִךְ (shadayikh) means “your breasts.”
The word עֳפָרִים (ofarim) refers to young deer or fawns.
תְּאוֹמֵי (te'omei) means “twins of,” emphasizing the paired imagery.
And צְבִיָּה (tseviyyah) refers to a female gazelle.
The final image, הָרוֹעִים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים (haro'im bashoshanim), describes them grazing among lilies, though the precise botanical identity of the Hebrew shoshanim is debated.
The picture is pastoral, gentle, graceful, and alive.
In the ancient poetic world of the Song, gazelles evoke beauty, elegance, tenderness, and graceful movement.
The lover is not giving an anatomical lecture.
He is writing poetry.
He sees beauty in the woman he loves, and he reaches into the natural world for language worthy of his admiration.
And here is something important.
He is not speaking about a nameless body.
He is addressing his beloved.
The surrounding verses describe her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, temples, and neck through a series of imaginative comparisons.
Her beauty is celebrated through the language of an intimate relationship.
This is not a stranger being reduced to a collection of body parts.
It is the voice of a lover expressing delight.
And the distinction matters.
Because the Bible does not teach that sexual desire is inherently sinful. It teaches that desire must be governed by love, faithfulness, and holiness.
That truth may challenge the person who has spent years believing that any acknowledgment of physical beauty is automatically impure.
But it also challenges the person who uses physical attraction as an excuse to objectify, manipulate, or consume another human being.
Scripture refuses both distortions.
And that is where this ancient poem begins to speak with startling relevance to our modern lives.
We live in a world where bodies are displayed everywhere, yet people are increasingly afraid they are not beautiful enough.
A world where intimacy is advertised constantly, yet genuine tenderness can feel painfully rare.
A world where someone can receive a thousand compliments about their appearance and still go to bed wondering whether anyone truly loves them.
Perhaps you know that feeling.
Perhaps someone once told you that you were beautiful, but their actions eventually revealed that they only wanted access to your body.
Perhaps you trusted someone who promised love but left you carrying shame.
Perhaps you gave your affection to someone who treated your vulnerability like an opportunity.
Or perhaps you have been on the other side.
You have looked at people without honoring their humanity.
You have confused attraction with entitlement.
You have allowed pornography, fantasy, comparison, or selfish desire to shape the way you see another person.
And now, when you encounter a verse like Song of Songs 4:5, you are forced to confront a question that goes deeper than the verse itself.
Have I learned to see another human being as someone to cherish, or merely someone to desire?
Because those are not the same thing.
And the difference can change a life.
Long before the Song of Songs was written, the opening chapters of Genesis described a world where the human body was not an object of shame.
Genesis 1:27 declares that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
Genesis 1:31 tells us that God saw everything He had made, and it was very good.
Then Genesis 2:25 gives us an extraordinary picture:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Read that slowly.
Naked.
And not ashamed.
There was no need to pretend.
No fear of being used.
No suspicion that vulnerability would become a weapon.
No comparison with another person's body.
No anxiety that love would disappear when physical beauty changed.
The man and woman stood before each other without the fear that now haunts so many relationships.
But then sin entered the story.
And one of the first things Adam and Eve experienced was shame.
Genesis 3:7 says their eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and they made coverings for themselves.
Their bodies had not suddenly become evil.
What had changed was their condition before God and one another.
Innocence had been shattered.
Trust had been wounded.
Sin had introduced fear, alienation, and hiding.
And humanity has been struggling with those consequences ever since.
We cover more than our bodies.
We cover our disappointments.
Our insecurities.
Our secret addictions.
Our memories.
Our regrets.
Our desperate longing to be loved without being rejected.
Some people hide behind religious performance.
Some hide behind sexual attention.
Some hide behind emotional distance.
Some hide behind the appearance of a perfect marriage.
And some have become so accustomed to being treated carelessly that genuine affection feels suspicious.
This is why the Song of Songs matters.
It reminds us that sin did not erase God's original goodness from creation.
The beauty of faithful love is still worth celebrating.
The body is still part of God's good creation.
Tenderness is still possible.
Delight is not automatically defilement.
And holiness does not require us to despise what God has made.
Yet we must also understand what the Song is, and what it is not.
Song of Songs is Hebrew love poetry.
It contains intimate dialogue, longing, admiration, separation, reunion, and rich imagery drawn from nature.
Jewish and Christian interpreters have long discussed its meaning.
Some have emphasized its celebration of human love and marriage.
Others have also understood it allegorically or spiritually, seeing in the lovers' relationship a reflection of God's covenant love for His people or Christ's love for the Church.
These interpretations have a long history, but they should not be confused with the direct literary meaning of every image.
Song of Songs 4:5 is, in its immediate context, a lover's poetic description of his beloved's physical beauty.
It does not directly say that the two breasts symbolize the Old and New Testaments, the two covenants, or any other specific spiritual pair.
Such interpretations may appear in historical allegorical readings, but the Hebrew text itself does not establish them.
We honor Scripture by refusing to make it say what it does not say.
And we honor Christ by recognizing how the whole biblical story ultimately reveals the goodness of creation, the devastation of sin, and the hope of redemption.
The beauty of the Song does not need to be erased in order for us to discover its place in the larger story of God's love.
Consider another remarkable statement from this same biblical book.
Song of Songs 8:7 declares:
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.”
That is not a description of disposable affection.
It is a poetic celebration of love's extraordinary strength.
And Song of Songs 8:6 speaks of love as strong as death, with a flame-like intensity that cannot be treated casually.
This is a very different vision from the one our culture frequently sells.
Our world often says, “I want you because of what you can give me.”
Faithful love says, “Your well-being matters to me.”
Lust without love asks, “How can I satisfy myself?”
Love shaped by holiness asks, “How can I honor you before God?”
And that distinction becomes even clearer when we turn to Jesus.
Think about the way Christ treated people whom society had reduced to their failures.
In John 4, Jesus met a Samaritan woman at a well.
He knew the complicated history of her relationships.
He did not pretend her story was irrelevant.
But neither did He treat her as someone unworthy of conversation, truth, or grace.
He spoke to her about living water.
He revealed that He was the Messiah.
And the woman who came to the well carrying a complicated personal history went back to her community speaking about the One who knew her.
She said:
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?” — John 4:29, KJV
There is something deeply moving about that moment.
Jesus knew.
And He still spoke to her.
He knew her history.
And He still offered living water.
He did not need to exploit her vulnerability to demonstrate His authority.
He met her with truth.
And with grace.
Maybe that is the part of the Gospel you need to hear today.
Because some people have been told they are no longer worthy of love because of what happened to them.
Some carry guilt over sexual sins they committed willingly.
Others carry shame for violations committed against them, even though the wrongdoing was never theirs.
Those are not the same experiences.
And Scripture must never be used to place the guilt of an abuser upon the person who was harmed.
If someone violated your dignity, their sin does not make you spiritually dirty.
And if you have sinned, your failure does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's forgiveness.
The Gospel speaks truthfully to both woundedness and guilt without confusing them.
Jesus does not call evil good.
But He also does not declare that every broken person must remain broken forever.
This is why the cross matters.
Not because Jesus came merely to improve our self-esteem.
Not because He came to reassure us that our choices have no consequences.
But because our sin is real, our need for reconciliation with God is real, and His mercy is greater than we could ever deserve.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we fixed every habit.
Not after we learned how to appear holy in public.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is the difference between a temporary emotional experience and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Jesus does not simply tell us that we are loved.
He calls us to repent, believe, follow Him, and receive new life through His grace.
And that new life changes how we see other people.
It changes how we treat their bodies.
It changes how we understand intimacy.
It changes what we do when temptation comes.
It changes the way we love someone who has trusted us with their heart.
Consider the words of 1 Corinthians 6:19–20:

“What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.”
The Apostle Paul is addressing believers and calling them to honor God with their bodies.
He does not describe the body as worthless.
He teaches that it matters profoundly.
So much so that our physical conduct belongs within our worship.
And suddenly the supposed contradiction begins to disappear.
Song of Songs celebrates the beauty of embodied love.
First Corinthians calls believers to embodied holiness.
These truths are not enemies.
They belong together.
God's design for sexual intimacy is not that people should feel nothing.
It is that desire should not become a master that destroys love, faithfulness, and obedience.
The Bible's vision is neither prudish contempt for the body nor unrestricted indulgence of every impulse.
It is something richer.
A love that can delight without degrading.
A desire that can honor boundaries.
An intimacy that is not separated from covenant faithfulness.
A tenderness that refuses to turn another person's vulnerability into a transaction.
And this matters whether you are married, single, widowed, divorced, or carrying the pain of a relationship that did not survive.
Your worth before God is not determined by whether someone finds you sexually attractive.
You do not become less human because you are unmarried.
You do not become less deserving of dignity because your body has aged.
You do not lose the image of God because of scars, disability, illness, infertility, or changes in appearance.
And you do not need another person's desire to prove that your life has meaning.
Physical beauty has a place in the Song of Songs.
But it is not the foundation of human worth.
That foundation is deeper.
You were made in the image of God.
And the call of Christ is not to worship beauty, but to worship the Creator.
For married couples, this passage offers a particular challenge.
When was the last time you looked at your spouse with genuine appreciation rather than silent criticism?
When was the last time your words made them feel cherished rather than evaluated?
When was the last time affection was given freely, without manipulation or pressure?
Perhaps the person beside you has changed since the day you first met.
There are new wrinkles.
New scars.
New responsibilities.
Perhaps childbirth, sickness, exhaustion, financial hardship, or years of sacrifice have altered the body you once knew.
And perhaps the world keeps whispering that beauty belongs only to the young, the flawless, and the endlessly desirable.
But faithful love learns to recognize beauty that cannot be captured by a photograph.
It sees the hands that worked when the family had little.
The face that stayed awake beside a hospital bed.
The body that carried burdens nobody else noticed.
The person who remained when life became difficult.
Song of Songs 4:5 celebrates physical beauty, and we should not pretend otherwise.
But the broader biblical call to covenant love challenges us to cherish the whole person through every season of life.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Notice the standard.
Not domination.
Not entitlement.
Not self-centered pleasure.
Sacrificial love.
Christ gave Himself.
And although human marriage can never perfectly reproduce the love of Christ, Christian husbands are called to reflect His self-giving care.
That means tenderness without coercion.
Affection without humiliation.
Faithfulness without double lives.
Repentance when wrong has been done.
And a willingness to serve rather than merely demand.
For anyone who has used Scripture to excuse control, abuse, or sexual entitlement, this is a necessary correction.
The Bible's celebration of marital intimacy never gives permission to disregard another person's dignity, safety, or consent.
Love does not become holy simply because someone attaches God's name to it.
Its character must agree with God's commands.
And perhaps, as you read this, you realize the deepest problem is not what someone else has done.
Perhaps you recognize your own sin.
Maybe you have been feeding desires that are destroying your ability to love faithfully.
Maybe pornography has trained your eyes to see people as images rather than neighbors.
Maybe you have been flirting with betrayal while telling yourself that nothing serious has happened.
Maybe you have been comparing your spouse to strangers.
Maybe you have convinced yourself that because temptation is common, surrender is inevitable.
But temptation does not have to become obedience to sin.
And shame does not have to become your permanent identity.
The Gospel does not invite you to hide more skillfully.
It invites you to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not permission to continue carelessly.
It is an invitation to genuine confession and repentance.
And sometimes repentance will require difficult, practical steps.
Ending a secret relationship.
Seeking accountability.
Removing access to material that feeds destructive habits.
Confessing wrongdoing to someone you have harmed.
Seeking wise pastoral guidance or professional help when necessary.
Accepting consequences instead of demanding immediate trust.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes a new beginning possible.
And perhaps the most powerful transformation is not simply that you stop looking at something sinful.
Perhaps it is that, through the work of God's Spirit, you begin learning how to see people rightly.
Not as possessions.
Not as trophies.
Not as objects created to satisfy you.
But as human beings bearing the image of their Creator.
That is a beautiful kind of freedom.
And it brings us back to the verse that started everything.
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.”
What an unexpected place to begin a conversation about holiness.
Yet that is part of the beauty of Scripture.
God's Word does not require us to pretend that physical attraction does not exist.
It teaches us to understand it within the larger purposes of creation, covenant, and obedience.
The lover's admiration is not a command for every reader to speak in the same metaphors.
Nor is it permission to direct intimate language toward anyone we happen to find attractive.
It is a poetic moment within a biblical love song.
And when we respect its context, we can appreciate its beauty without turning it into either scandal or spectacle.
There is another line in this same chapter that deserves our attention.
Song of Songs 4:7 says:
“Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.”
Within the poem, these are words of affectionate admiration spoken by the lover.
They should not be turned into a claim that his beloved was literally sinless.
Nor should we pretend that the verse directly describes Christ declaring sinners righteous.
But within the whole Christian story, those words can awaken a longing for something that human romance alone cannot give us.
To be fully known.
To be received without deception.
To be freed from the guilt we cannot remove by ourselves.
To stand before God, not because we have manufactured our own perfection, but because Jesus Christ has become our Savior.
And that hope is not found in a romantic partner.
It is found in Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:21 declares:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Here is the greater wonder.
The sinless Savior took upon Himself the judgment our sins deserved.
He died.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith is offered forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
Not because sin was harmless.
But because His sacrifice was sufficient.
That is the grace that can reach into the most complicated human story.
The woman who has been told she is undesirable.
The husband who knows he has neglected his wife.
The single believer struggling with loneliness.
The person fighting a secret addiction.
The survivor learning that another person's cruelty does not define their worth.
The Christian who has become more skilled at hiding sin than confessing it.
The person who wonders whether God could possibly receive them after everything they have done.
The Gospel does not promise that every relationship will be restored.
It does not promise that every wound will disappear overnight.
And it does not promise that repentance will erase every earthly consequence.
But it does proclaim that forgiveness is available through Jesus Christ, and that His Spirit is able to transform those who belong to Him.
That is not a small promise.
That is resurrection hope.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not for the sake of religious performance.
Not because a comment section can measure the condition of your soul.
But because sometimes putting a struggle into words helps us stop pretending it does not exist.
What has been harder for you: believing that your body is part of God's good creation, learning to honor other people with purity, or accepting that Christ can forgive your past?
You do not have to share private details or disclose wounds you are not ready to discuss.
And if this passage has changed the way you understand biblical love, tell us what stood out to you.
Your reflection may help another person realize they are not alone in seeking truth, healing, and obedience.
Because this is not merely about one surprising verse.
It is about the way we read the Bible.
The way we see people.
The way we approach marriage.
The way we respond to temptation.
The way we carry shame.
And the way we understand the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.
There are people who have abandoned Scripture because they thought Christianity could offer only condemnation for their brokenness.
There are others who have embraced a distorted version of Christianity that excuses whatever their desires demand.
Both need the truth.
God's grace is not contempt for human weakness.
And God's holiness is not permission to redefine sin.
In Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
John 1:14 describes the incarnate Word as “full of grace and truth.”
We need both.
Truth without grace can be used to crush the wounded.
A counterfeit grace without truth can leave people trapped in the very sins destroying them.
But Christ calls us into the light where sin can be confessed, forgiveness received, and lives transformed.
That is the message Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim.
Not to sensationalize Scripture.
Not to build a following around controversy.
But to help people encounter the living Christ through the faithful teaching of His Word.
And if this article has helped you understand a passage you once found confusing, uncomfortable, or embarrassing, consider what might happen if it reached someone else.
Someone who believes their body is disgusting.
Someone who thinks holiness means despising physical affection.
Someone who has confused lust with love.
Someone who is afraid their past has disqualified them from grace.
Someone who has never heard that Jesus receives repentant sinners.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
But because a simple act of sharing can place biblical truth before someone who might never intentionally search for it.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who feel spiritually exhausted, seekers who have difficult questions, and even people who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along.
They do not need to pretend they have everything figured out before they can begin reading God's Word.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, worship, obedience, generosity, service, and love—not through a mandatory payment to any ministry.
But freely chosen financial support can be a genuine expression of Christian generosity.
Just as believers have supported the work of Gospel ministry throughout history, you can choose to help sustain the creation and distribution of Scripture-centered teaching today.
If you already give to your local church, this invitation is not meant to replace your responsibilities there.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit of this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not fear.
But willing partnership in a mission you believe is worth supporting.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and spiritual encouragement accessible.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
A deeper commitment to Scripture.
A growing hunger for Christ.
A community of believers seeking to become more faithful, more discerning, more prayerful, and more willing to live what they profess.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
The invitation to repent and believe is freely proclaimed to everyone.
And that is precisely why we want this message to reach farther.
Because someone is still hiding.
Someone is still ashamed.
Someone is still mistaking attention for love.
Someone is still trying to become worthy of a grace that can never be earned.
Someone is still reading the Bible through the lens of wounds that have never healed.
And perhaps that someone is you.
A man looks at his beloved.
He sees her beauty.
And he describes it with the language of young gazelles among the lilies.
What once sounded scandalous becomes something different when we understand its place in Scripture.
It becomes a reminder that God created the human body good.
That sin corrupts what God made beautiful.
That holiness protects rather than despises God's design.
That love is more than appetite.
That faithfulness is more than a feeling.
And that the deepest restoration we need is found not in being desired by another human being, but in being reconciled to the God who made us.
The Song of Songs does not tell the whole story of redemption.
But it belongs to the Bible that does.
And that Bible leads us to Jesus Christ.
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who never sinned.
The One who loved with perfect holiness.
The One who gave His life for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls us to turn from sin and follow Him.
So if you have been using desire to fill a spiritual emptiness, come to Christ.
If you have been hiding behind shame, bring your burdens to Him.
If you have harmed someone, repent and take responsibility.
If you have been wounded, remember that what happened to you does not erase your God-given dignity.
If your marriage has grown cold, ask God to teach you how to love with renewed tenderness and faithfulness.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, do not mistake admiration for Christian teaching with saving faith.
Come to the Savior Himself.
Trust His finished work.
Turn from sin.
Receive His mercy.
And follow Him.
Because the greatest love story in Scripture is not merely about a man admiring the beauty of a woman.
It is about the holy God who did not abandon His saving purpose when humanity fell into sin.
It is about the Son of God who came to redeem sinners at the cost of His own blood.
And it is about the hope that those who belong to Christ will one day dwell with Him in a creation where sin, death, and shame are no more.
If this truth has reached your heart, do not let it remain only a passing emotion.
Respond to God in prayer.
Open His Word again.
And remember the difference between being admired and being redeemed.
A human lover may see beauty in you for a season, but only Jesus Christ can save your soul for eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID HE CAME TO DIVIDE FAMILIES—AND THE REASON IS MORE HEARTBREAKING THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: JESUS SAID HE CAME TO DIVIDE FAMILIES—AND THE REASON IS MORE HEARTBREAKING THAN YOU THINK

He is the Prince of Peace. So why did He say He came to bring fire, division, and even conflict between parents and children? The answer may change how you understand your family, your suffering, and what it truly costs to follow Jesus.
There is a kind of pain that doesn't come from strangers.
It comes from the people whose voices once made you feel safe.
The mother who taught you to pray but now questions why you're taking your faith so seriously.
The father who raised you to respect God but cannot understand why you've stopped compromising.
The spouse who once shared everything with you but now seems uncomfortable whenever you mention Jesus.
The people who know your childhood, your mistakes, your weaknesses, and your history.
And somehow, the closer you try to walk with Christ, the farther away some of them seem to become.
You didn't ask for a war.
You didn't want to lose anyone.
You simply wanted to follow Jesus.

But now family gatherings feel different. Certain conversations end in silence. You find yourself choosing your words carefully because you already know what will happen if you speak openly about your faith.
And sometimes, when nobody is watching, you ask God a question you're almost ashamed to admit.
"Lord, if following You is supposed to bring peace, why does everything feel like it's falling apart?"
What if I told you that Jesus spoke about this exact kind of pain nearly two thousand years ago?
And what if His words were so shocking that even today, many Christians would rather explain them away than face what they actually mean?

Because one day, the same Jesus who blessed the peacemakers, commanded us to love our enemies, and promised His followers peace said something that seems almost impossible to reconcile with everything else we know about Him.
"Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division." — Luke 12:51, KJV
Read that again.
Not peace.
Division.
And He wasn't finished.

He went on to describe households torn apart, fathers and sons standing on opposite sides, mothers and daughters divided, and relationships strained by the most consequential decision a human being can make.
How could the Savior who came to reconcile sinners to God speak so plainly about division?
Was Jesus contradicting Himself?
Was He telling believers to abandon their families?
Was He giving religious people permission to become harsh, intolerant, and unloving?
No.
And understanding why may rescue you from two dangerous mistakes: compromising your faith to keep everyone happy, or mistaking your own unkindness for persecution.
Because Jesus was not teaching His disciples how to start a fight.
He was preparing them for what happens when the truth of the Gospel enters a world that does not always want to receive it.
And the first thing we need to understand is that Jesus did not begin this conversation with division.
He began it with fire.
"I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled!" — Luke 12:49, KJV.
In the original Greek, the opening words are:
Πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν
Pyr ēlthon balein epi tēn gēn.
Literally, "Fire I came to cast upon the earth."
The word πῦρ (pyr) means fire.
And throughout Scripture, fire can signify God's holy presence, His judgment, His purifying work, or the testing of what is genuine.
Think of the burning bush before Moses.
The fire of God's presence on Mount Sinai.
The refining fire described by the prophets.
The coming judgment proclaimed by John the Baptist.
But we must be careful here. Luke 12:49 does not explicitly say that this fire means the Holy Spirit, a worldwide revival, or one particular form of purification.

In its immediate context, the imagery is serious and urgent. Jesus is speaking about the decisive crisis His mission will bring, including judgment, the suffering awaiting Him, and the divided responses to His coming.
The fire is not permission for believers to burn relationships down in the name of righteousness.
It is a warning that the arrival of God's kingdom confronts the world with a decision that cannot remain neutral forever.
Then Jesus says something even more revealing.
"But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!" — Luke 12:50, KJV.
The Greek reads:
βάπτισμα δὲ ἔχω βαπτισθῆναι
Baptisma de echō baptisthēnai.
"But I have a baptism to undergo."
Jesus had already been baptized in water by John.
This was something else.
He was speaking of the overwhelming suffering He would endure as His earthly mission moved toward the cross.
The same image appears in Mark 10:38–39, where Jesus speaks of the cup He must drink and the baptism He must undergo.
And here is what makes this passage so deeply moving.
Before Jesus described the division His followers might experience, He spoke about the suffering He Himself would face.
He wasn't standing at a safe distance, demanding sacrifices He would never understand.
He was walking toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward rejection.
Toward false accusations.
Toward the scourging.
Toward nails driven through His hands and feet.
Toward the cross.
And He knew.
He knew what was coming.
The One who warned His followers that faithfulness could cost them relationships was preparing to give His own life for sinners.
Jesus did not come to divide people because He hated them. He came to save sinners, knowing that not everyone would welcome the salvation He offered.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because if we misunderstand this passage, we can turn a warning about the cost of discipleship into an excuse for cruelty.
Jesus never commanded His disciples to despise their families.
In fact, He condemned religious traditions that allowed people to neglect their responsibility to honor their parents (Mark 7:9–13).
He commanded His followers to love one another (John 13:34–35).
He taught them to love their enemies and pray for those who persecuted them (Matthew 5:44).
Even while suffering on the cross, He entrusted His mother to the care of the beloved disciple (John 19:26–27).
This is not the behavior of a Savior who considers family love worthless.
But He did teach that even the most precious earthly relationships cannot take the place of God.
And that is where His words become painfully personal.
Because sometimes the hardest idol to surrender isn't money.
It isn't success.
It isn't popularity.
Sometimes it is the approval of someone you love.
You know what Scripture says.
You know what obedience requires.
But you also know how disappointed someone will be if you follow through.
So you begin negotiating.
Not openly.
Quietly.
You tell yourself that maybe obedience can wait.
Maybe repentance can wait.
Maybe you can keep that secret compromise a little longer.
Maybe you can follow Jesus without anyone noticing that your life has changed.
And little by little, the desire to avoid conflict begins making decisions that should belong to your loyalty to Christ.
Not because you stopped believing in Jesus.
But because you became afraid of what believing Him might cost.
And this is where Luke 12 becomes a mirror.
Jesus continues:
"For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three." — Luke 12:52, KJV.
Then He describes father against son, son against father, mother against daughter, daughter against mother, and conflict between mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law.
The Greek word translated "divided" in verse 52 is διαμεμερισμένοι (diamemerismenoi), from a verb meaning to divide or separate.
Jesus was describing real relational fractures.
Not merely differences of opinion.
Not harmless disagreements about religious customs.
But the possibility that allegiance to Him would place people who once shared a home on opposite sides of the most important question in life.
Who is Jesus Christ?
Is He simply a teacher whose advice we can accept when convenient?
Or is He the crucified and risen Lord who calls us to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him?
The consequences of that question can reach into the closest relationships we have.
And Jesus knew it.
His words also echo Micah 7:6, where the prophet describes the breakdown of trust and faithfulness within society, even among members of the same household.
Jesus was not inventing a new commandment to divide families.
He was drawing on prophetic language to explain the painful opposition that could accompany His mission.
And if you have ever been misunderstood because you decided to take Christ seriously, you may recognize something of that pain.
Perhaps you stopped participating in something you once knew was wrong.
Perhaps you confessed a sin you had hidden for years.
Perhaps you began setting boundaries against dishonesty, exploitation, or destructive behavior.
Perhaps you chose forgiveness when everyone expected revenge.
Or perhaps you became a Christian in a family where your new faith was unwelcome.
You didn't become perfect.
You still struggle.
You still need grace every morning.
But something changed.
And not everyone celebrated.
Some people may have accused you of thinking you're better than them.
Others may have treated your convictions as a personal attack.
And suddenly you were carrying a grief you didn't know how to explain.
You loved them.
You still loved them.
But you could no longer pretend that your loyalty to Jesus meant nothing.
If that is where you are, hear this carefully.
Being rejected for faithfully following Christ is painful. But being rejected does not automatically prove that you are faithfully following Christ.
That second sentence matters.
Because not every argument about religion is persecution.
Not every offended family member is resisting the Gospel.
Sometimes people are reacting to our pride.
Sometimes our words have been unnecessarily sharp.
Sometimes we have confused biblical conviction with the desire to win every argument.
Sometimes we have spoken the truth without the love that Scripture commands.
And if that describes us, repentance is not compromise.
It is obedience.
Peter writes that believers should be prepared to explain their hope with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).
Paul tells us, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (Romans 12:18, KJV).
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
Scripture acknowledges that peace is not always within our control.
But it also places responsibility on us to pursue peace wherever faithfulness allows.
You cannot force someone to accept Christ.
You cannot make another person respect your convictions.
You cannot guarantee that every relationship will remain unchanged when you obey God.
But you can refuse to become bitter.
You can refuse to humiliate people who disagree with you.
You can apologize when you have sinned.
You can speak truth without cruelty.
You can pray for those who misunderstand you.
You can continue showing genuine love even when that love is not returned.
And sometimes, that quiet faithfulness will preach more clearly than a thousand angry arguments.
Because Jesus did not call us to become people who enjoy division.
He called us to become people who love Him more than we love the approval of the world.
There is a difference.
A life centered on Christ may provoke opposition.
But opposition is not the goal.
Christ is.
And now we must confront the question that makes this entire passage so difficult.
If Jesus came to bring division, why does Isaiah call Him the Prince of Peace?
Why did the angels announce peace at His birth?
Why did Jesus say, "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you" (John 14:27, KJV)?
And why does Ephesians 2:14 declare, "For he is our peace"?
The answer is not that Scripture contradicts itself.
The answer is that the peace Jesus gives is deeper than the absence of conflict.
In John 14:27, the Greek word for peace is εἰρήνη (eirēnē).
It refers to peace and is closely related in meaning to the rich biblical idea of shalom—wholeness, well-being, and right relationship.
The Hebrew word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) carries a range of meanings that can include peace, welfare, and completeness.
But biblical peace is not simply everyone agreeing with us.
It is not pretending sin is harmless.
It is not keeping a relationship comfortable at the expense of truth.
And most importantly, the peace Christ secured through His death and resurrection begins with reconciliation to God.
Romans 5:1 declares:
"Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." — KJV.
That is the peace we desperately need.
Because before we worry about whether everyone around us approves of our faith, we must face a more serious reality.
Apart from Christ, our greatest problem is not that other people misunderstand us.
Our greatest problem is sin.
We have all fallen short of God's glory (Romans 3:23).
We have loved created things more than our Creator.
We have excused what God calls evil.
