We have hidden behind religious appearances.
We have wounded people, resisted truth, and tried to justify ourselves.
And no amount of family harmony, public admiration, or religious activity can erase our guilt before a holy God.
But the Gospel announces something astonishing.
The Son of God came into the world not to congratulate sinners for their righteousness, but to rescue people who could never save themselves.
He lived the life of obedience we failed to live.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Through Him, forgiveness is proclaimed.
Through Him, sinners can be reconciled to God.
Through Him, people who once lived in rebellion can become children of God.
This is why the cross stands at the center of the Christian faith.
Not because suffering is beautiful in itself.
Not because conflict is holy in itself.
But because Jesus willingly entered the suffering our salvation required.
And here is the heartbreaking irony.
The One who came to make peace between sinners and God was Himself rejected by many of the people He came to save.
John 1:11 says:
"He came unto his own, and his own received him not." — KJV.
The Savior knew rejection.
He knew what it meant to be misunderstood.
He knew what it meant to be abandoned.
He knew the pain of betrayal by someone who had shared His table.
And yet He did not stop loving.
He did not abandon His mission.
He did not turn away from the cross.
His love was not dependent on being welcomed.
His obedience was not dependent on being applauded.
And His willingness to suffer was not proof that the Father had forgotten Him.
It was part of the mission through which our redemption would be accomplished.
Now imagine the disciple who hears Jesus describe a divided household.
Perhaps that disciple thinks of a father whose approval means everything.
Perhaps a mother whose tears would be unbearable.
Perhaps a spouse who might never understand.
The disciple is not being asked to stop loving those people.
The disciple is being confronted with a deeper question.
If loving Jesus costs you the approval of someone you love, will Jesus still be worthy of your obedience?
That is not an easy question.
And anyone who answers it casually may not have understood its weight.
Because the Gospel does not ask us to pretend that losing a relationship is painless.
It does not ask us to celebrate estrangement.
It does not command us to seek unnecessary conflict or remain in harmful situations to prove our faith.
It calls us to trust Christ above every competing allegiance while continuing to love others in the ways Scripture commands.
And there may be tears along the way.
There may be lonely evenings.
There may be conversations that end without resolution.
There may be prayers whispered for a family member who has not yet come to faith.
But those tears are not wasted simply because the relationship has not yet changed.
God sees.
And He calls you to faithfulness, not to control the outcome.
Perhaps the most difficult part of following Jesus is discovering that you cannot make everyone happy and remain obedient to Him in every circumstance.
You can love people deeply.
You can honor them sincerely.
You can listen patiently.
You can serve generously.
But you cannot surrender the lordship of Christ to purchase their approval.
Jesus says in Matthew 10:37:
"He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me: and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me." — KJV.
Those are demanding words.
But notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, "Do not love your father or mother."
He does not say, "Stop caring about your children."
He says that no earthly love can rightly occupy the place that belongs to Him.
And that is not because Jesus is competing with our families like an insecure human being.
It is because He is Lord.
The Creator.
The Redeemer.
The One through whom all things were made and in whom all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17).
To love Him supremely is not to diminish genuine love for others.
It is to bring our love under the authority of the One who teaches us what love truly is.
Sometimes that means staying and patiently serving.
Sometimes it means refusing to participate in sin.
Sometimes it means setting necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it means confessing that our own behavior has caused harm.
And sometimes it means continuing to pray for someone who has shut the door on every conversation about faith.
But in all these situations, we are called to reflect the character of Christ.
Not self-righteousness.
Not spiritual arrogance.
Not cruelty disguised as courage.
Christ.
And this brings us to something we need to say with great tenderness.
If your family is divided right now, please do not assume that God has promised every relationship will be restored in this lifetime.
Scripture gives us reason to pray, to hope, to forgive, and to pursue reconciliation.
But it does not guarantee that every person we love will respond as we desire.
We must not make promises God has not made.
What we can say is that Christ is faithful.
He is present with His people.
He gives grace to endure.
And He is able to sustain believers even through painful rejection.
If someone you love has walked away from you because of your faith, pray for them.
But also examine your heart.
Have you treated them with kindness?
Have you listened?
Have you admitted your own failures?
Have you made the Gospel visible through humility, patience, honesty, and love?
Because it is possible to defend the truth while behaving in ways that obscure the beauty of the Savior we proclaim.
And sometimes the bravest Christian response is not another argument.
Sometimes it is an apology.
Sometimes it is a meal prepared without expecting thanks.
Sometimes it is a gentle answer.
Sometimes it is refusing to retaliate.
Sometimes it is remaining faithful to Christ while allowing another person the freedom to disagree.
And sometimes it is quietly saying:
"Lord, I cannot change their heart. But please keep mine from becoming hard."
That prayer may be one of the most important prayers you ever pray.
Because division can tempt us toward bitterness.
Rejection can tempt us toward pride.
Suffering can tempt us to imagine that we are always the innocent party.
But the cross does not give us permission to become superior to others.
It reminds us that we are sinners saved by grace.
And that truth should make us both courageous and humble.
Courageous enough to refuse compromise.
Humble enough to repent when we are wrong.
Courageous enough to confess Christ.
Humble enough to listen.
Courageous enough to stand firm.
Humble enough to keep loving.
That is the kind of discipleship that reveals the power of the Gospel.
And perhaps someone reading this is not struggling with rejection at all.
Perhaps your struggle is the opposite.
You have been keeping your faith hidden because you are afraid of what might happen if people discover that you truly want to follow Jesus.
You know you need to repent of something.
You know a relationship, habit, or dishonest practice is drawing you away from God.
You know you have been choosing comfort over obedience.
But you keep postponing the decision.
Tomorrow.
Next week.
When life settles down.
When people understand.
When following Jesus becomes less costly.
But what if that perfect moment never comes?
What if the approval you are waiting for is approval that only Christ can give you?
Jesus did not conceal the cost of discipleship.
In Luke 9:23, He said:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." — KJV.
Not because suffering earns salvation.
It does not.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith, not a reward for human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the grace that saves us also begins to transform us.
It teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
It teaches us to follow Christ.
It teaches us that obedience matters, even when it is difficult.
And if you have been living with one foot in the world and one foot in the church, perhaps the most loving thing anyone can tell you today is this:
You cannot make Jesus Lord of your life only in the places where His lordship costs you nothing.
He is not asking you to manufacture conflict.
He is calling you to surrender.
And surrender may begin with a simple, honest prayer.

"Jesus, I have been afraid of losing people. I have been afraid of being misunderstood. I have been more concerned about keeping everyone pleased than about obeying You. Forgive me. Teach me to love people without making their approval my god. Give me courage to follow You, humility to recognize my own sins, and grace to remain faithful without becoming hardhearted."
If those words describe your struggle, you are not alone.
And you do not need to pretend otherwise.
There is room for honest faith here.
Room for people who are still learning.
Room for believers who have stumbled and need to repent.
Room for those who have been wounded by religious harshness and need to rediscover the gentleness of Jesus.
Room for those who are asking difficult questions.
Because Gospel Warrior is not about pretending that every Christian has already arrived.
It is about continually pointing one another back to the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And that is why our message has always been:
Consider what that means.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
The man who boldly promised loyalty collapsed under the pressure of fear.
But after His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Peter's failure was real.
His denial was serious.
But his story did not end in the courtyard where he wept.
Grace met him again.
And the same Lord who restored Peter is able to forgive and transform sinners today.
Perhaps you have denied Christ, not with your lips, but through years of compromise.
Perhaps you have kept silent when you should have spoken.
Perhaps you have spoken harshly when you should have listened.
Perhaps you have caused division through pride and called it boldness.
Perhaps you have loved someone's approval more than the truth.
The answer is not to despair.
The answer is to repent and return to Christ.
Because forgiveness is not found in pretending we never failed.
It is found in the Savior who died for our sins and rose again.
And the Gospel does not end with a divided household.
It points us toward the day when Christ will make all things new.
Revelation 21:4 describes the future God has promised His redeemed people: a day when death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That does not mean every present relationship will unfold exactly as we wish.
It means that the final hope of the Christian is greater than anything this broken world can guarantee.
The Prince of Peace will not leave His people forever surrounded by the effects of sin.
His kingdom will be fully revealed.
His righteousness will prevail.
And those who belong to Him will know the fullness of the peace He has promised.
Until then, we follow.
Sometimes with joy.
Sometimes through tears.
Sometimes surrounded by people who understand.
Sometimes misunderstood by the people we love most.
But always with our eyes fixed on Jesus.
Not to prove that you're more spiritual than anyone else.
Not to send a hidden accusation to a family member.
But because someone you know may be silently struggling with the same question.
Someone may be considering abandoning their faith because following Christ has become difficult.
Someone may be using this passage to justify cruelty and desperately need to see the love of Jesus.
Someone may need to discover that the Gospel offers more than temporary comfort—it offers reconciliation with God.

If you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, we invite you to stay connected. Invite a friend, a struggling believer, a searching family member, or even someone who does not yet believe to follow along for Scripture, biblical teaching, encouragement, repentance, restoration, and a growing understanding of Jesus Christ.
This is not about purchasing God's favor.
It is not about paying for a blessing.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful way to participate in the work of teaching and encouraging others.

Scripture recognizes the value of materially supporting those who labor in teaching the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), while also teaching that giving should be voluntary and cheerful, never compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Rather, it is an opportunity to help us continue creating Christ-centered articles, biblical encouragement, discipleship materials, and resources that can reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
And we want to give something meaningful back.
Not because the Gospel is for sale.
It never has been.
But because we appreciate those who freely choose to help sustain this work.
You are welcome here whether you give financially or not.
But before you leave this article, I want you to return to the question we began with.
Why did Jesus say He came to bring division instead of peace?
Because His coming confronts humanity with a decision.
And when people respond differently to Him, even the closest relationships may feel the consequences.
But division is not His ultimate purpose.
His mission is the salvation of sinners, the reconciliation of people to God, and the gathering of a redeemed people who belong to Him.
He does not command you to destroy your family to prove your devotion.
He calls you to follow Him faithfully, love others sincerely, and refuse to exchange truth for approval.
And perhaps tonight, somewhere, a believer will sit quietly at the edge of a bed, carrying the grief of being misunderstood.
Perhaps their Bible will be open to Luke 12.
Perhaps they will read the words "but rather division" and finally understand that Jesus was not surprised by the cost of following Him.
Perhaps they will cry.
Perhaps they will pray.
Perhaps they will finally stop blaming themselves for every response they cannot control, while still taking responsibility for their own conduct.
And perhaps they will find the courage to wake up tomorrow and keep loving the people who disagree with them.
Not with resentment.
Not with superiority.
But with the steady, costly love of someone who belongs to Jesus.
Because following Christ does not always mean everyone will stand beside you.
It means that even when others walk away, your hope remains anchored in the One who went to the cross for you.
So if this message has reached something deep within you, don't rush past it.
Pray over it.
Examine your heart.
Read Luke 12:49–53 for yourself.
Ask the Holy Spirit to show you where you need courage, where you need humility, and where you need repentance.
"Jesus, help me choose You without ceasing to love them."
Because that is the heart of faithful discipleship.
Not choosing between truth and love.
But following the One who is full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
And when the cost of that faithfulness feels unbearable, remember this:
The hands that were pierced to make peace with God are the same hands that will hold you when following Him costs you the peace you once knew.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS IT WRONG FOR A PASTOR TO OWN A PRIVATE JET? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING FAR MORE DANGEROUS THAN WEALTH.
paragraphs: IS IT WRONG FOR A PASTOR TO OWN A PRIVATE JET? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING FAR MORE DANGEROUS THAN WEALTH.

When a preacher flies above the clouds while struggling believers can barely afford their next meal, is it God's blessing, a betrayal of the Gospel, or a question the Church has been too afraid to answer honestly?
Imagine this.
A single mother sits in the back row of a church, holding an offering envelope between trembling fingers.
Inside is money she could have used for groceries.
Her electricity bill is overdue. Her children need school supplies. She has been praying for a financial breakthrough that hasn't come.
But she loves Jesus.
She believes in the work of the Church. She wants people to hear the Gospel. She wants to give, even when giving costs her something.
So she places the envelope into the offering basket.
That same week, she sees a video of a famous pastor stepping onto a multimillion-dollar private jet.
The aircraft is beautiful. The leather seats are immaculate. The preacher smiles as cameras capture another journey across the world.
This is what divine favor looks like."
Another responds, "Jesus rode a donkey. Why does His servant need a private jet?"
And somewhere between those two voices, the single mother asks a question she almost feels guilty for thinking.
"Lord, is this really what my sacrifice was for?"
That question deserves more than an angry argument.
It deserves Scripture.
It deserves compassion.
It deserves the courage to examine what happens when the name of Jesus becomes associated with a lifestyle that ordinary believers could never imagine.
And before we finish, we need to confront something even more uncomfortable.
The greatest danger may not be the private jet.
It may be what happens to a human heart when wealth, spiritual authority, and the applause of thousands begin to occupy the same throne.
Because this is not merely a story about expensive airplanes.
It is a story about stewardship, sacrifice, temptation, power, trust, and the terrifying possibility of using the language of heaven to protect the appetites of earth.
And somewhere in this story, every one of us may discover something about our own heart.
Jesus never told His followers that holiness could be measured by the price of their possessions.
But He never told them that wealth was spiritually harmless, either.
In Luke 12:15, Jesus warned:
"Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "covetousness" is πλεονεξία (pleonexia), describing greed or an insatiable desire to possess more.
Notice something important.
Jesus was not speaking only to people who had already become rich.
He was warning human beings about the power of wanting more.
More security.
More recognition.
More comfort.
More possessions.
More evidence that we have finally become somebody.
And that temptation can enter a pastor's heart just as easily as it can enter the heart of a businessman, a politician, or a person struggling to survive.
A private jet does not automatically prove that a pastor is corrupt.
But neither does a private jet automatically prove that God is pleased with him.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
There is no biblical command that says, "A pastor shall never own an aircraft."
Airplanes did not exist in the world of the apostles.
The Bible does not address private jets directly.
But Scripture does give us principles by which every possession, every financial decision, and every ministry expense must be examined.
And those principles are demanding.
Consider the apostle Paul.
In 1 Corinthians 9:14, he acknowledged that those who proclaim the Gospel have a legitimate right to receive their living from Gospel ministry.
Pastors are not required to live in poverty.
Their families need food. Their children need education. They need housing, transportation, medical care, rest, and reasonable provision.
The Church should not expect faithful shepherds to neglect their households or suffer unnecessarily merely to demonstrate humility.
Paul also wrote:
"Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine." (1 Timothy 5:17, KJV)
The surrounding passage connects this honor with appropriate material support.
A congregation that benefits from faithful pastoral labor should not be ashamed to provide for its shepherds.
But here is where the conversation becomes difficult.
The biblical right to receive support is not an unlimited right to pursue luxury at the expense of those being shepherded.
Paul understood that distinction.
Although he possessed legitimate rights, he sometimes voluntarily refused financial support when accepting it could hinder the Gospel.
He wrote in 1 Corinthians 9:12:
"...nevertheless we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ." (KJV)
Read that again.
Paul was willing to surrender something he was entitled to receive because the credibility and advancement of the Gospel mattered more to him than exercising his personal rights.
That should disturb anyone who believes ministry exists to maximize a preacher's comfort.
Paul did not ask only, "Am I allowed to have this?"
He also asked, "Will this help or hinder the Gospel?"
And perhaps that is the question we have been missing.
Not simply whether a pastor can legally purchase a private jet.
Not simply whether wealthy donors can afford to provide one.
Not even whether the aircraft makes international travel easier.
But whether the decision reflects faithful stewardship, transparent accountability, and genuine love for the people entrusted to that pastor's care.
Because something can be lawful without being wise.
Something can be affordable without being necessary.
And something can be impressive to the world while becoming a stumbling block to the people of God.
Now imagine another scene.

A missionary has spent years traveling to remote communities. Commercial connections are unreliable. Medical emergencies are common. Certain destinations are difficult to reach. The ministry has carefully examined transportation options, and an aircraft may genuinely serve its mission.
Would Scripture automatically condemn such a ministry for using private aviation?
No.
We should not pretend that every aircraft serves the same purpose or that every ministry has identical circumstances.
There can be legitimate operational reasons for specialized transportation.
But legitimate possibilities do not eliminate the need for evidence.
A pastor claiming that a private jet is necessary should be willing to explain why.
How often is it used for ministry?
What does it cost to purchase, maintain, insure, staff, and operate?
Would commercial flights or occasional chartering accomplish the same purpose at substantially lower cost?
Who owns the aircraft?
Who approves its use?
Are personal trips separated from ministry expenses?
Is there independent financial oversight?
Are donors given truthful information about how their contributions are used?
These are not necessarily questions of rebellion.
They can be questions of faithful stewardship.
In fact, Paul demonstrated concern for financial accountability when discussing the collection for believers in need.
In 2 Corinthians 8:20–21, he explained that care was being taken in administering a generous gift so that the work would be honorable not only before God but also before people.
Biblical ministry does not have to fear honest examination.
Transparency is not the enemy of spiritual authority.
Sometimes it is one of the ways spiritual authority demonstrates integrity.
And this brings us to a verse that should make every pastor examine his heart.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, church elders are instructed to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for shameful gain, and not as domineering rulers over those entrusted to them, but as examples.
The Greek expression αἰσχροκερδῶς (aischrokerdōs) carries the sense of seeking shameful or dishonest gain.
It does not mean that receiving compensation for ministry is shameful.
It warns against a corrupt motive in which personal gain becomes a driving force behind spiritual service.
And the word τύποι (typoi), translated "examples," points to patterns worthy of imitation.
That is the weight of pastoral leadership.
A pastor is not merely someone who delivers sermons.
He is someone whose life teaches even when his microphone is turned off.
His financial decisions preach.
His treatment of employees preaches.
His response to criticism preaches.
His willingness to be accountable preaches.
His compassion for the poor preaches.
And yes, even his relationship with luxury can communicate something about the Jesus he claims to represent.
This is why the issue cannot be reduced to envy.
Certainly, envy exists.
Some people resent anyone who possesses more than they do.
A Christian must repent of that kind of bitterness.
But not every question about a pastor's wealth comes from jealousy.
Sometimes it comes from a wounded believer who has watched generosity become a fundraising strategy while accountability remains painfully absent.
Sometimes it comes from a family that gave sacrificially because they were promised that their own financial miracle would follow.
Sometimes it comes from someone who no longer knows whether the offering basket represents worship or pressure.
And those people should not automatically be dismissed as enemies of God.
They deserve to be heard.
Especially when they have been hurt in the name of Jesus.
The Bible contains a sobering warning about religious leaders who exploit the vulnerable.
In Mark 12:40, Jesus condemned scribes who "devour widows' houses" while making long prayers for appearance.
Think about that.
Their public religion looked impressive.
Their prayers sounded spiritual.
But beneath the performance was exploitation.
Jesus did not defend them because they occupied respected religious positions.
He exposed them.
And immediately afterward, Mark records the account of a poor widow placing two small coins into the temple treasury.
Jesus recognized the extraordinary cost of her gift.
But we must be careful not to twist that account into a command that struggling people must give away their necessities to enrich religious leaders.
Mark 12:41–44 describes the widow's costly offering; it does not authorize coercive fundraising or guarantee that impoverished donors will become wealthy.
The preceding warning about exploitation makes careless appeals to that passage especially troubling.
God sees the sacrifice of the giver.
And leaders must never treat that sacrifice as permission to manipulate.
Remember the single mother holding the envelope?
Her offering is not a business transaction through which she purchases God's favor.
She does not need to prove her faith by surrendering money she cannot responsibly spare.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
The Greek word ἀνάγκης (anankēs), translated "necessity" in this verse, carries the sense of compulsion or constraint.
Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through spiritual intimidation.
A person should not be told that refusing to fund a preacher's luxury means refusing to honor God.
That is not the Gospel.
And if someone has made you feel that your salvation, healing, or acceptance before God depends upon financing a ministry, you need to hear this clearly.
Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
His forgiveness is not for sale.
His mercy does not come with a premium membership.
His love is not reserved for the people who can afford the largest offering.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not something earned through human works.
And 1 Peter 1:18–19 reminds believers that redemption comes through the precious blood of Christ, not through silver or gold.
The Cross is not a fundraising mechanism.
It is the place where the Son of God gave Himself for sinners who could never pay the price of their own redemption.
Now consider the most important person in this entire conversation.
Jesus.
He was not opposed to every form of material provision.
Luke 8:1–3 tells us that women who followed Jesus supported Him and His disciples from their own resources.
Some of His followers had significant means.
Joseph of Arimathea, described in Matthew 27:57 as a rich man and disciple of Jesus, provided the tomb in which Christ was buried.
Scripture does not teach that every wealthy person is automatically wicked.
Nor does it teach that poverty itself makes someone righteous.
Abraham possessed substantial wealth.
Job was prosperous, endured devastating loss, and later received restored blessings.
Yet these narratives do not establish a universal promise that faithful Christians will become materially wealthy.
And they certainly do not provide a blank check for religious extravagance.
The central question is never simply how much a person owns.
It is whether possessions have begun to own the person.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:24:
"Ye cannot serve God and mammon." (KJV)
The Greek text uses μαμωνᾷ (mamōna), a term referring to wealth or riches.
Jesus was not saying that possessing money is identical to worshiping money.
He was warning that wealth can become a competing master.
And when wealth becomes master, even religious language can be recruited to serve it.
A preacher can speak passionately about heaven while quietly building an earthly kingdom around himself.
A congregation can begin measuring spiritual authority by visible prosperity.
A ministry can become so dependent upon maintaining an expensive image that honest questions feel like existential threats.
And eventually, people may become afraid to challenge anything because they have been taught that questioning a leader is the same as questioning God.
But no pastor is Jesus.
No ministry is the Kingdom of God in its entirety.
No leader stands above Scripture.
And no amount of spiritual influence removes the need for repentance.
Even Peter, an apostle, was publicly confronted by Paul when his conduct contradicted the truth of the Gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).
Accountability is not automatically persecution.
Correction is not automatically betrayal.
And asking where the money goes is not automatically an attack against the Holy Spirit.
A faithful pastor should be able to distinguish genuine hostility from sincere concern.
But the congregation must also examine itself.
Because we sometimes create the very culture we later condemn.
We celebrate wealth as though it were proof of divine approval.
We treat expensive clothing, enormous buildings, luxury vehicles, and celebrity associations as signs of exceptional anointing.
We become fascinated with spiritual celebrities.
And then we wonder why some leaders begin behaving like celebrities.
James 2 warns believers against showing favoritism to the wealthy.
The Church was never meant to become a place where rich people receive special honor while poor people feel invisible.
In the Kingdom of God, the widow is not worth less than the millionaire.
The struggling father is not spiritually inferior because he takes the bus.
The elderly woman who quietly prays for her neighbors is not less significant than a preacher whose sermons reach millions.
God's measure of greatness is not the world's measure.
Jesus said in Mark 10:43:
"...whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister." (KJV)
The Greek word διάκονος (diakonos) means servant or minister.
And in Mark 10:45, Jesus explains the pattern of His own life:
"For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." (KJV)
That is the center of Christian leadership.
Not the throne.
The towel.
Not personal elevation.
Self-giving love.
Not the constant question, "How much more can I receive?"
But the searching question, "How faithfully am I serving those Christ has entrusted to me?"
Jesus washed His disciples' feet.
He welcomed children.
He touched lepers.
He noticed the overlooked.
He wept with the grieving.
He ate with sinners without celebrating their sin.
He confronted religious hypocrisy without abandoning the possibility of repentance.
And when the hour came, He did not demand that others suffer so He could remain comfortable.
He gave Himself.
The King of glory wore a crown of thorns.
That does not mean every pastor must reject comfortable transportation or live without ordinary conveniences.
But it does mean that Christian leadership must remain recognizably shaped by the character of Christ.
Imagine standing before Jesus and explaining every major ministry expenditure.
Not before a hostile internet audience.
Not before a group of critics.
Before Jesus Himself.
Would you be able to explain why that aircraft was purchased?
Would you be able to show that it served the mission responsibly?
Would you be able to account for the donors who trusted you?
Would you be able to say that the decision was made with humility, independent oversight, and love?
Or would the explanations begin to collapse when the applause disappeared?
This is not a question only for pastors.
It is a question for all of us.
What would happen if Jesus examined the things we justify because we can afford them?
The habits we defend because they make us comfortable?
The purchases we make because we want people to admire us?
The compromises we excuse because everyone around us is doing the same?
It is easy to criticize a preacher's multimillion-dollar aircraft while refusing to examine our own greed.
The scale may be different.
The temptation can be painfully similar.
First Timothy 6:9 warns about those who desire to be rich falling into temptation and destructive desires.
And verse 10 is often misquoted.
It does not say that money itself is the root of all evil.
The KJV says:
"For the love of money is the root of all evil..."
The Greek expression φιλαργυρία (philargyria) refers to love of money.
The Greek wording describes the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils, rather than claiming that every evil act originates in money.
That distinction matters.
Money can feed the hungry.
Money can fund Bible translation.
Money can provide shelter, medical treatment, education, and disaster relief.
Money can also finance vanity, manipulation, exploitation, and an endless hunger for more.
The moral issue is not resolved by the mere presence or absence of wealth.
It is revealed in the heart's allegiance and in the way resources are acquired, managed, and used.
So is it wrong for a pastor to own a private jet?
Here is the answer that may disappoint people on both sides.
Not necessarily. But it can be profoundly wrong.
If an aircraft is genuinely needed, responsibly financed, transparently governed, and demonstrably serves the Gospel better than reasonable alternatives, ownership or use is not automatically sinful.

But if a pastor acquires one through deception, coercion, misuse of restricted donations, exploitation of vulnerable believers, or a desire for personal prestige, the issue becomes far more serious than an expensive purchase.
It becomes a matter of sin, integrity, and spiritual responsibility.
And even when no explicit wrongdoing is established, the decision can still be unwise or harmful.
A ministry may possess the legal right to make an expenditure and yet fail to demonstrate that the expenditure is the best stewardship of entrusted resources.
That is why Christians should neither condemn every pastor with a private jet nor defend every pastor who claims to need one.
We should examine the evidence.
We should refuse gossip and unsupported accusations.
We should insist upon accountability.
We should pray for leaders.
And we should remember that biblical love does not require us to abandon discernment.

But perhaps the most heartbreaking part of this conversation is what happens when people who have been spiritually wounded begin turning away from Jesus because of what someone did while representing Him.
Maybe you know that pain.
Maybe you gave faithfully for years.
You served.
You volunteered.
You trusted.
You believed every testimony.
You defended your pastor when others raised questions.
Then something happened.
A financial scandal.
A hidden lifestyle.
An abuse of authority.
A promise that was never fulfilled.
And suddenly the sanctuary that once felt safe became a place of confusion.
You started wondering whether everything you believed was a lie.
You stopped praying as often.
You struggled to open your Bible.
You heard another preacher ask for money, and something inside you shut down.
If that is you, please hear this.
The failure of a pastor does not cancel the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
A shepherd may betray his calling.
The Good Shepherd does not betray His sheep.
In John 10:11, Jesus says:
"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." (KJV)
The Greek expression ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός (ho poimēn ho kalos) identifies Jesus as the good shepherd.
The word kalos conveys goodness, nobility, and excellence in the shepherd's character.
Jesus is not merely a better version of a religious celebrity.
He is the Shepherd who lays down His life for His sheep.
Human leaders can fail.
Jesus remains worthy of trust.
Human institutions can become corrupted.
The Gospel remains true.
People may misuse God's name.
But their misuse does not change who God is.
And if you have been wounded by religious manipulation, you do not need to pretend the wound is small.
You do not need to call exploitation a blessing.
You do not need to silence your conscience to prove your loyalty to Christ.
You can seek truth.
You can pursue appropriate accountability.
You can grieve.
You can heal.
And you can come back to Jesus without returning to an environment that harmed you.
There is room for wounded people at the feet of Christ.
There is also room for repentance among leaders who have fallen into greed.
The Gospel does not merely expose sin.
It announces that sinners can be forgiven and transformed through Jesus Christ.
Think about Zacchaeus.
He was a wealthy chief tax collector whose life had been shaped by a system associated with financial exploitation.
Then Jesus entered his story.
And something changed.
In Luke 19:8, Zacchaeus declared that he would give half of his possessions to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had defrauded.
His encounter with Jesus produced visible repentance.
He did not simply announce that he had received a new spiritual revelation.
He addressed the financial wrongs connected to his life.
He demonstrated that grace had reached beyond his words into his conduct.
And Jesus declared that salvation had come to his house.
That is a picture the modern Church desperately needs.
Not public relations disguised as repentance.
Not emotional speeches without accountability.
Not spiritual language used to avoid restitution.
But the kind of transformation that makes people willing to surrender what sin once convinced them they could never live without.
A pastor who has misused ministry resources does not need a more impressive defense of his lifestyle.
He needs truth, repentance, accountability, and, where appropriate, restitution and the consequences required by justice.
And a believer consumed by jealousy does not need another reason to despise the wealthy.
That believer needs the same transforming grace.
Because the Gospel confronts the greedy pastor and the bitter critic alike.
It calls both to the Cross.
It tells the wealthy that their riches cannot save them.
It tells the poor that their poverty does not make them worthless.
It tells the wounded that healing is possible.
It tells the proud that repentance is necessary.
And it tells every sinner that the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse those who turn to Him in faith.
This is where scandal can become a testimony of grace.
Not because scandal is good.
Not because wrongdoing should be hidden.
Not because forgiveness eliminates consequences.
But because Jesus Christ is powerful enough to redeem lives that sin has damaged.
From scandal to grace does not mean pretending the scandal never happened. It means allowing the truth and mercy of Christ to begin writing a different ending.
And now I want to speak to the pastor reading this.
Maybe you do not own a private jet.
Maybe your church is small.
Maybe you are exhausted from working another job while preparing sermons late at night.
Maybe people assume you are wealthy because you are a pastor, when the truth is that you are struggling to provide for your own family.
This article is not an accusation against you.
Faithful pastors deserve prayer, encouragement, reasonable financial support, and genuine appreciation.
Your work matters.
Your unseen sacrifices matter.
Your integrity matters.
And if God has entrusted you with substantial resources, the call is not to feel guilty merely for possessing them.
The call is to remain faithful.
Hold your possessions with open hands.
Welcome accountability.
Resist the temptation to turn spiritual authority into personal entitlement.
Remember the poor.
Protect the vulnerable.
Tell the truth about money.
And never allow the ministry of Christ to become a monument to yourself.
Now to the church member reading this.
Do not make poverty your definition of holiness.
Do not make wealth your definition of blessing.
Do not turn suspicion into a substitute for discernment.
And do not surrender your conscience to anyone who claims that spiritual authority places them beyond biblical examination.
Support faithful ministry generously and voluntarily, according to your means and convictions.
Ask reasonable questions.
Seek trustworthy leadership.
Care for those in need.
And remember that your ultimate loyalty belongs to Jesus Christ.
Not to a personality.
Not to a platform.
Not to a building.
Not to a brand.
To Christ.
Because one day the private jets will stop flying.
The luxury vehicles will lose their shine.
The expensive watches will stop ticking.
The enormous auditoriums will empty.
The cameras will turn off.
The applause will fade.
And every person, whether famous preacher or anonymous believer, will stand before the Lord.
Second Corinthians 5:10 teaches that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
What will matter then is not how impressive our earthly image appeared.
What will matter is the truth of our lives before the One who sees every motive and every deed.
And if you are reading this while wondering whether your own heart has become too attached to money, comfort, recognition, or spiritual appearances, there is still an invitation.
Come to Jesus.
Not with an impressive reputation.
Not with a carefully managed public image.
Not with excuses.
Come honestly.
Confess your sin.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Receive His grace.
And allow His Word to reshape the way you live.
Because the deepest miracle is not when God places a person inside a luxurious aircraft.
The deepest miracle is when Christ takes a heart enslaved by sin and makes it new.
That is the transformation worth celebrating.
That is the Gospel worth proclaiming.
And that is the message Gospel Warrior exists to keep bringing into homes, timelines, conversations, and hearts.
If this article challenged you, please do not allow it to disappear beneath tomorrow's newsfeed.
A single share may reach someone who has been quietly wrestling with spiritual disappointment.
Someone who needs to know that asking sincere questions does not make them an enemy of God.
Someone who needs to discover that Jesus is still worthy of trust, even after a religious leader has failed them.
Do you believe a pastor can own a private jet and still faithfully represent Jesus? What biblical principle most strongly shapes your answer?
Please share your perspective respectfully, even if you disagree with this article or with another reader.
And if you have been wounded by financial manipulation in a religious setting, you can simply comment, "Christ is still healing me."
You do not owe anyone the details of your pain.
But perhaps your honest words will remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And if you believe this kind of Gospel-centered work should continue reaching more people, I want to invite you into something deeper.
And certainly not because a monthly payment can purchase divine favor.

Some Christians may prayerfully regard that support as part of their giving. But it should not be presented as a mandatory biblical tithe, a replacement for responsibilities to one's local church, or a condition for God's blessing.
Scripture teaches willing, thoughtful generosity, not giving under pressure.
And there is more to discover.
The library's free resources are part of our desire to make Christian learning and spiritual nourishment accessible, not something reserved only for those who can pay.
Every prayer matters.
Every thoughtful comment can strengthen the conversation.
Every share can place biblical truth before someone who might never have encountered Gospel Warrior otherwise.
And every life genuinely changed by Jesus Christ is worth more than all the wealth this world could ever display.
That is why we must never confuse the appearance of success with the fruit of faithfulness.
A private jet may carry a preacher across continents.
But it cannot carry a sinner into the Kingdom of God.
Only Jesus saves.
And whether we have millions in the bank or barely enough for tomorrow, we all come to the same Cross with the same desperate need for grace.
When the applause of this world finally falls silent, the only treasure that will matter forever is the Christ we trusted, not the kingdom we built for ourselves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BECAUSE YOU ARE LUKEWARM, I WILL SPIT YOU OUT” — THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT
paragraphs: “BECAUSE YOU ARE LUKEWARM, I WILL SPIT YOU OUT” — THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT

You may have heard this verse preached your entire life. But what if the most frightening part isn't that Jesus threatens to spit the lukewarm out of His mouth… but that the very people He was warning believed they were spiritually rich, perfectly fine, and needed absolutely nothing?
There is something more dangerous than a sinner who knows he is lost.
It is a person who believes he is close to God simply because he has learned how to look like a Christian.
Someone who knows when to say “Amen.”
Someone who shares Bible verses, attends church, listens to worship music, and knows exactly how to sound spiritual when other believers are listening.
But behind closed doors…
Prayer has become an occasional emergency call.
Repentance has become something other people need.
The Bible remains unopened for days.
And Jesus has slowly become someone they acknowledge rather than someone they follow.
The frightening part?
They may not even realize anything is wrong.
Because the most dangerous spiritual condition is not always rebellion that announces itself.
Sometimes it is self-sufficiency dressed in religion.
And nearly two thousand years ago, Jesus spoke directly to a church living in that condition.
Not to pagans in the marketplace.
Not to Roman soldiers.
Not to people who had never heard His name.
To a church.
And His words were so disturbing that generations of Christians have repeated them with trembling:
“So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.” — Revelation 3:16, KJV
But here is the question we desperately need to ask.
What did Jesus actually mean by lukewarm?
Was He saying that God prefers someone who openly rejects Him over someone who follows Him imperfectly?
Was He condemning Christians who struggle with temptation, spiritual exhaustion, depression, unanswered prayers, or seasons of weakness?
Was He teaching that unless your emotions burn with spiritual excitement every moment of every day, you are in danger of being rejected?
Or have we sometimes reduced a devastatingly specific warning into a slogan that misses the deeper wound Jesus was exposing?
Because when you understand the city receiving this message, the original Greek words, and the astonishing invitation Jesus gives immediately afterward…
This passage becomes more than a warning.
It becomes a mirror.
And perhaps, for someone reading this right now, it will become the moment they finally stop pretending.
The words appear in Revelation 3:14–22, in a message addressed to the church in Laodicea.
Laodicea was a prosperous city in Roman Asia Minor, in what is now Türkiye.
It was known for its wealth, commercial activity, textile production, and connections to medicine, including eye treatments.
After a devastating earthquake in the first century, ancient accounts describe the city's ability to recover using its own resources.
That detail matters.
Laodicea had money.
Laodicea had influence.
Laodicea had the confidence that comes from being able to provide for itself.
And the church living in that environment was confronted by Jesus with words that exposed the spiritual danger beneath its prosperity.
“Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing…” — Revelation 3:17, KJV
Read that slowly.
I have need of nothing.
Not merely, “I have enough money.”
Not merely, “My business is doing well.”
But a posture of self-sufficiency so deep that the people could no longer recognize their spiritual poverty.
Jesus continued:
“…and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.” — Revelation 3:17, KJV
Imagine hearing those words.
You believe you are wealthy.
Jesus says you are poor.
You believe you can see clearly.
Jesus says you are blind.
You believe you are properly clothed.
Jesus says you are naked.
You believe you need nothing.
Jesus says you do not even recognize your deepest need.
The tragedy of Laodicea was not simply that the church had problems.
Every church has problems.
Every believer is still being sanctified.
The tragedy was that its self-assessment had become almost completely disconnected from Christ's assessment.
And that is where the warning begins to reach into our lives.
Because it is possible to become financially successful while spiritually impoverished.
It is possible to know Christian vocabulary without knowing the Shepherd's voice.
It is possible to defend biblical truth in arguments while resisting that same truth in private.
It is possible to become so comfortable with the appearance of Christianity that we stop asking whether our hearts are actually surrendered to Christ.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question is not whether we can identify lukewarm Christians around us.
It is whether we have become too confident in our own spiritual condition to recognize what Jesus might be correcting in us.
Now consider the original language.
The Greek word translated lukewarm in Revelation 3:16 is χλιαρός (chliaros).
It means lukewarm or tepid.
Jesus says:
“οὔτε ψυχρὸς εἶ οὔτε ζεστός”
Oute psychros ei oute zestos.
“You are neither cold nor hot.”
And then:
“μέλλω σε ἐμέσαι ἐκ τοῦ στόματός μου”
Mellō se emesai ek tou stomatos mou.
“I am about to vomit you out of My mouth.”
The verb ἐμέσαι (emesai) comes from the Greek verb meaning to vomit.
This is stronger than the polite English word spit might suggest.
Jesus deliberately uses a disturbing physical image.
Something is so objectionable that the response is expulsion from the mouth.
But what makes the image especially interesting is the geography surrounding Laodicea.
Nearby Hierapolis was famous for its hot mineral springs, while Colossae was associated with cold, refreshing water.
Laodicea depended on water brought into the city through an engineered supply system, and ancient water infrastructure and mineral deposits remain part of its archaeological history.
This has led many interpreters to suggest that Jesus was drawing on the familiar contrast between useful hot water, refreshing cold water, and unpleasant tepid water.
Under this interpretation, hot water could serve beneficial purposes, cold water could refresh, and lukewarm water represented something distasteful or ineffective.
That is a compelling explanation.
But biblical honesty requires an important distinction.
The text itself does not explicitly say that Jesus was comparing the water supplies of Hierapolis, Colossae, and Laodicea.
The geographical explanation is a plausible historical interpretation, not a detail directly stated in Revelation.
Scholars have debated how much weight it should carry.
What the passage clearly establishes is that Jesus found the church's present condition unacceptable and that its confident claim to need nothing was profoundly false.
And this corrects a common misunderstanding.
You may have heard someone say:
“God would rather you be completely cold toward Him than halfway committed.”
But we should be careful.

Revelation 3:15 says Jesus wishes the church were either cold or hot. It does not explicitly define cold as hatred of God, nor does it teach that outright unbelief is spiritually preferable to imperfect discipleship.
If the water imagery is intended, both hot and cold can represent something beneficial, while lukewarm represents something objectionable.
Even if someone understands the temperatures differently, the central rebuke remains unmistakable.
Jesus is confronting a church whose spiritual reality contradicts its confidence.
And that should stop us from turning this verse into a weapon against every struggling Christian.
Because there is a difference between a believer who is fighting sin and a person who has made peace with sin.
There is a difference between someone who cries, “Lord, help my unbelief,” and someone who believes they no longer need correction.
There is a difference between spiritual weariness and spiritual complacency.
A Christian who feels exhausted but keeps reaching for Christ is not automatically the lukewarm person Revelation condemns.
A believer who falls, repents, and returns to Jesus is not the same as someone who uses grace as permission to remain unchanged.
The person who whispers through tears, “Jesus, I want to love You more, but I am struggling,” should not hear Revelation 3 as proof that Christ has abandoned them.
Remember the father in Mark 9:24 who cried:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
Jesus did not respond by demanding that the man manufacture perfect confidence before receiving help.
And remember Peter.
Peter promised extraordinary loyalty.
Then, when fear took hold, he denied Jesus three times.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
He stood near a fire, warming himself, while the Savior he claimed to love was being rejected.
Imagine the shame when the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering every promise.
Imagine realizing that the courage you believed you possessed had collapsed when it mattered most.
Yet after the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Christ confronted him with a deeply personal question:
“Lovest thou me?”
And then entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
But his failure was not the final chapter of his story.
That is the difference grace makes.
Grace does not tell us that denying Jesus is harmless.
Grace tells us that failure does not have to be the end when we return to the risen Savior.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying a failure that still feels impossible to escape.
You once prayed with conviction.
You once read Scripture with hunger.
You once believed that you would never compromise certain things.
But life became complicated.
A relationship pulled you away.
A disappointment hardened your heart.
An unanswered prayer left you confused.
A secret habit became a repeated surrender.
You stopped confessing because you were tired of promising to change.
And slowly, without a dramatic announcement, your spiritual life became something you maintained in public while neglecting in private.
You still believe in Jesus.
But you know there are rooms in your heart where you have resisted His authority.
And this is where Revelation refuses to let us hide behind either religious performance or hopeless shame.
Because the same Jesus who says, “I will spit you out,” also says something astonishing.
“As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.” — Revelation 3:19, KJV
Do not rush past those first words.
As many as I love.
The warning is severe.
The call to repentance is urgent.
But Jesus explicitly connects His rebuke to His love.
The Greek text says:
“ἐγὼ ὅσους ἐὰν φιλῶ ἐλέγχω καὶ παιδεύω”
Egō hosous ean philō elenchō kai paideuō.
“Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline.”
The verb φιλῶ (philō) expresses love or affection.
The verb ἐλέγχω (elenchō) concerns exposing, reproving, or correcting.
And παιδεύω (paideuō) carries the sense of discipline, training, or correction.
Jesus is not describing a sentimental love that refuses to confront what destroys us.
He is describing love that tells the truth.
Love that exposes deception.
Love that calls people away from self-destruction.
Love that refuses to affirm spiritual blindness simply because honesty might feel uncomfortable.
Sometimes the most merciful thing Jesus can do is disturb the peace we have made with sin.
Not because He delights in humiliating us.
But because a comfortable lie can keep us from seeking the only One who can save us.
And notice what Jesus commands next.
“Be zealous therefore, and repent.”
The Greek word translated repent is μετανόησον (metanoēson), an imperative form of metanoeō.
It calls for repentance—a genuine change of mind and heart that turns a person away from sin and toward God.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling guilty after being exposed.
It is not crying for a few minutes and then deliberately returning to the same rebellion without concern.
It is not posting a spiritual quote to compensate for a private life we refuse to surrender.
Repentance involves turning toward Christ in faith and allowing His truth to confront the direction of our lives.
And genuine repentance bears fruit.
Not because good works purchase salvation.
But because saving grace does not leave us indifferent to the Savior.
Ephesians 2:8–10 makes the relationship clear.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
Yet we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The works do not buy the grace.
The grace produces a transformed life.
And this matters enormously.
Because if you read Revelation 3 and conclude, “I must become impressive enough for Jesus to accept me,” you have misunderstood the Gospel.
Jesus is not selling salvation to the most emotionally passionate Christians.
He is calling self-sufficient sinners to recognize their need and receive from Him what they cannot provide for themselves.
Listen to what He tells Laodicea:

“I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed… and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.” — Revelation 3:18, KJV
Think about the tenderness and precision of this invitation.
To a wealthy city, Jesus offers true riches.
To a city associated with textiles, He offers garments that cover spiritual nakedness.
To a place connected with eye treatments, He offers the sight its people desperately lack.
Their greatest strengths had become illustrations of their deepest needs.
They had resources.
But they needed Christ.
They had clothing.
But they needed His righteousness.
They had remedies for physical eyes.
But they needed spiritual sight.
And here is the uncomfortable question.
What if the very thing that makes you feel secure is the thing that has helped you forget your dependence on God?
Your income?
Your reputation?
Your ministry?
Your biblical knowledge?
Your years of church attendance?
Your ability to quote Scripture faster than someone else?
Your position in a Christian community?
None of these things is inherently evil.
But none of them can replace Jesus.
You can be surrounded by religious activity and still need to repent.
You can serve in a ministry while secretly neglecting communion with Christ.
You can become skilled at explaining grace while struggling to receive it with humility.
And you can spend so much time examining everyone else's spiritual temperature that you never allow the Word of God to examine your own heart.
Perhaps that is why the message to Laodicea is so enduring.
It dismantles the illusion that spiritual health can be measured by outward success.
But now we reach the verse that makes this entire passage almost unbearable in its beauty.
After the rebuke…
After the exposure…
After Jesus describes a church that makes Him want to vomit…
He says:
“Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.” — Revelation 3:20, KJV
Stop there.
Read it again.
Jesus is knocking.
The One who knows their condition.
The One who has exposed their poverty.
The One who has called them to repentance.
He is still inviting them to fellowship.
The Greek begins:
“Ἰδοὺ ἕστηκα ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν καὶ κρούω”
Idou hestēka epi tēn thyran kai krouō.
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock.”
The verb ἕστηκα (hestēka) is a perfect-tense form of the verb meaning to stand, conveying a present standing condition.
And κρούω (krouō) means I knock.
The picture is vivid.
Christ stands at the door and calls for a response.
Importantly, this verse was originally addressed to a church, not written primarily as a generic formula for inviting Jesus into one's heart.
Its immediate context is Christ's call for a compromised congregation to repent and be restored to fellowship with Him.
Yet the invitation is deeply personal.
“If any man hear my voice…”
Not merely if the congregation changes its reputation.
Not merely if the church becomes more impressive.
If anyone hears.
One person.
One responding heart.
And the promise is fellowship.
“I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.”
In the ancient world, sharing a meal was an expression of hospitality, relationship, and communion.
Jesus is offering more than an improved religious image.
He is offering restored fellowship with Himself.
The Savior who exposes the truth also extends the invitation.
And that should break something open inside us.
Because we often imagine that if Jesus saw everything, He would immediately turn away.
But He already sees everything.
The envy you never confessed.
The bitterness you keep defending.
The private compromise.
The spiritual pride.
The prayerlessness.
The fear.
The exhaustion.
The ways you have tried to satisfy your soul with things that cannot save it.
He sees it all.
And His call is not, “Pretend you are better.”
It is, “Repent.”
Come into the light.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Stop confusing religious appearances with spiritual life.
Stop trying to purchase with performance what only grace can provide.
And come to Christ.
Because the Gospel is not the story of morally impressive people climbing their way into God's acceptance.
It is the story of Jesus Christ coming to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
His resurrection is not merely an inspirational ending to a tragic story.
It is the victory of the living Savior over sin and death.
And everyone who truly turns to Him in repentance and faith finds mercy that cannot be earned by religious performance.
That does not make holiness optional.
It makes holiness the fruit of belonging to Him.
Jesus does not save us so we can comfortably worship the sins that nailed Him to the cross.
He saves us to reconcile us to God and transform us into His likeness.
And transformation is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like opening the Bible again after months of neglect.
Sometimes it looks like confessing a hidden sin to God and seeking accountable, trustworthy help.
Sometimes it looks like apologizing without defending yourself.
Sometimes it looks like deleting what repeatedly leads you into temptation.
Sometimes it looks like choosing integrity when nobody would discover the compromise.
Sometimes it looks like praying through tears when you have no idea what to say.
And sometimes it looks like admitting the sentence your pride has avoided for years:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Not just for heaven someday.
Not just when life becomes unbearable.
Today.
In my decisions.
In my relationships.
In my finances.
In my ambitions.
In my habits.
In the places where I have resisted Your Word.
I need You.
That is not weakness to be ashamed of.
That is the beginning of spiritual honesty.
And perhaps you have spent years believing that the opposite of lukewarm Christianity is constant emotional intensity.
You thought you needed louder worship.
More tears.
More religious activity.
More visible enthusiasm.
But emotional intensity alone is not the measure of faithfulness.
A person can shout during worship and still refuse to forgive.
A person can cry at the altar and still deliberately nurture dishonesty.
A person can speak passionately about Jesus while treating people with cruelty.
And a person can quietly care for a sick parent, resist temptation, pray faithfully, love difficult neighbors, and obey Christ without ever becoming publicly impressive.
The question is not simply, “How excited do I feel?”
The deeper question is, “Am I trusting Christ, listening to His Word, repenting when confronted, and learning to obey Him?”
Because spiritual life is not measured by how convincing we look to an audience.
It is measured by our relationship to the living Christ, whose grace bears fruit in our lives.
You do not need to describe your private sins publicly.
But perhaps you can make a simple, honest declaration.
Not because a comment saves you.
Not because public engagement proves repentance.
But because sometimes the first visible step toward renewed fellowship is admitting that we need prayer, truth, and the encouragement of the body of Christ.
And if you are reading this while feeling deeply convicted, remember something essential.
Conviction should lead you toward repentance and Christ, not into endless despair.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
This is not permission to remain unrepentant.
It is the assurance that those who belong to Christ are not required to live under the hopeless verdict of their past.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is grace.
Not cheap grace that pretends sin is harmless.
Costly grace, purchased through the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that teaches.
Grace that disciplines.
Grace that restores.
Grace that transforms.
And perhaps this is where the words “From Scandal to Grace” become more than a beautiful phrase.
Because Peter's denial was scandalous.
The woman caught in adultery in John 8 stood publicly exposed, and Jesus confronted both her accusers and the reality of her sin.
The prodigal son disgraced himself in a distant country, only to discover that his father was ready to receive his return.
And Paul, once a persecutor of Christians, became a witness to the grace of the risen Christ.
Their stories were not identical.
Their circumstances were different.
But each reminds us that sin, shame, and failure do not have to possess the final word when God's redeeming grace intervenes.
Jesus does not rewrite our history by pretending our sins never happened.
He rewrites the future of those He redeems by forgiving their guilt, reconciling them to God, and transforming the direction of their lives.
Not because scandal was beautiful.
But because the Savior is merciful.
And if Christ can restore Peter, forgive sinners, and transform persecutors into servants of the Gospel, then do not assume your own story is beyond His reach.
But do not use His mercy as an excuse to delay repentance.
The invitation is precious precisely because it must be taken seriously.
Revelation 3 does not end with Jesus merely knocking.
It ends with a promise to the one who overcomes, followed by a call to listen:
“He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.” — Revelation 3:22, KJV
That includes us.
Not because we are ancient Laodiceans.
But because the Word of God still confronts the human heart.
And our generation has its own forms of spiritual self-sufficiency.
We can accumulate information without wisdom.
Followers without discipleship.
Religious content without prayer.
Online arguments without love.
Christian merchandise without Christian character.
Public declarations without private obedience.
We can build an entire digital identity around Jesus while neglecting the actual teachings of Jesus.
And that possibility should sober every Christian content creator, every ministry leader, and every believer—including us at Gospel Warrior.
Because this warning is not something we get to preach at everyone else while placing ourselves above it.
We need it too.
We need the Word to correct us.
We need accountability.
We need humility.
We need the Holy Spirit's work in our lives.
We need the Gospel we proclaim.
And we never want Gospel Warrior to become another place where people merely consume emotional religious content and then walk away unchanged.
We want these words to send you back to Scripture.
Back to prayer.
Back to your local church and faithful Christian fellowship.
Back to the hard, beautiful work of discipleship.
Back to Jesus.
That is why sharing this message matters.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who still appears spiritually strong but is quietly drifting.
Someone who has not prayed honestly in months.
Someone who feels ashamed of how far they have wandered.
Someone who believes God could never receive them again.
Someone who has confused religious activity with a surrendered life.
And someone who has been wounded by the careless misuse of this very passage.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to announce that your friends are lukewarm.
But to place a biblically grounded invitation to repentance, grace, and restoration where someone might encounter it at the moment they need it.
His invitation matters too.
Invite your family, your Christian friends, those who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still exploring who Jesus really is.
Because the goal is not merely to gather an audience.
It is to help people encounter the truth of the Gospel and grow in faithful discipleship.
And if these articles have strengthened your walk with Christ, there is another meaningful way to participate in this mission.
For believers who choose to give as an expression of generosity and stewardship, that support can be a meaningful part of their Christian giving.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
We will never tell you that you must pay us to glorify God.
You can glorify Him through obedience, prayer, generosity, service, faithful stewardship, and love for your neighbor.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
The resources are simply tools that can help keep biblical encouragement, learning, and discipleship present in everyday life.
We want the Word of God to remain accessible.
We want struggling Christians to find biblical encouragement.
We want new believers to have resources for spiritual growth.
We want families to discover materials that help them talk about Jesus together.
And we want the message of repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Christ to travel far beyond the reach of any single article.
Not out of fear.
Not because God needs your money.
But because, if this mission reflects your convictions and you are able to give, your generosity can help make more biblical discipleship resources available to others.
Pray for the people these messages reach.
Invite others to read the Bible for themselves.
Speak about Jesus with patience and truth.
And live the Gospel you profess.
Because in the end, the most important thing about this article is not how many people read it.
It is whether we hear what Christ is saying.
Perhaps tonight, after the phone is placed on the table and the noise of the day finally disappears, you will sit quietly with an open Bible.
Perhaps you will read Revelation 3:14–22 for yourself.
Perhaps you will notice the words you have heard so many times and suddenly understand them differently.
Not as an invitation to panic every time your emotions feel weak.
Not as permission to condemn struggling believers.
Not as a threat that can be escaped through religious performance.
But as a solemn warning against self-sufficient, unrepentant Christianity—and a gracious invitation to return to the One who alone can make us spiritually rich.
Maybe your prayer will not be eloquent.
Maybe it will be only a few words.
“Lord Jesus, show me what I cannot see about myself.”
“Forgive me for the ways I have trusted my own righteousness.”
“Teach me to repent without making excuses.”
“Restore my hunger for Your Word.”
“Help me follow You when no one is watching.”
“Make my life a reflection of Your grace.”
That prayer will not make you impressive in the eyes of the world.
But spiritual renewal has never depended on impressing the world.
It begins with the mercy of God and a heart that responds to His truth.
And before you leave this article, there is one final question worth carrying into the silence.
When Jesus says, “You do not know that you are poor, blind, and naked,” are you willing to let Him reveal the things you have been unwilling to see?
Because the real danger is not discovering that you need repentance.
The danger is becoming so satisfied with yourself that you no longer believe you need it.
And the real hope is not that you can somehow manufacture enough spiritual heat to make yourself acceptable to God.
The hope is Jesus Christ Himself.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who exposes our sin without being deceived by our appearances.
The One who calls us to repent.
The One who offers forgiveness and fellowship.
The One who is worthy of our trust, our obedience, our worship, and our lives.
And if all you can say today is “Christ is still healing me,” that is a meaningful place to begin a conversation and ask for prayer.
But whatever you do, do not let the comment become a substitute for the conversation you need to have with God.
The screen will go dark.
The notifications will stop.
The world will move on to another story.
But the words of Jesus will remain.
The most frightening thing about being lukewarm is believing you need nothing. The most beautiful thing about grace is discovering that Jesus is everything you need.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU CAN MOVE MOUNTAINS WITH YOUR FAITH… AND STILL BE NOTHING BEFORE GOD
paragraphs: YOU CAN MOVE MOUNTAINS WITH YOUR FAITH… AND STILL BE NOTHING BEFORE GOD

The terrifying truth behind 1 Corinthians 13:2: You can possess extraordinary spiritual gifts, speak with breathtaking conviction, and accomplish things people call miraculous—yet still be missing the very thing that makes you look like Jesus.
What if the most frightening words you could ever hear from God are not, “You didn't have enough faith,” but something far more devastating?
“You had faith. You had knowledge. You had power. You had influence. But where was your love?”
Imagine standing before Jesus.
Not as an atheist. Not as someone who openly rejected Christianity. But as someone who spent years doing what appeared to be the work of God.

You prayed for people. You defended biblical truth. You shared Scripture. You served in ministry. You attended worship services. You spoke boldly about holiness. Perhaps people even admired your spiritual strength.
And yet, somewhere along the way, you became so occupied with doing things for Jesus that you stopped treating people the way Jesus would.
You could recognize false teaching from a distance, but you couldn't recognize the pain in your own spouse's eyes.
You could spend hours studying the Bible, but you couldn't spare five minutes to listen to someone who was breaking.
You could publicly defend the Gospel, yet privately destroy someone with your words.
You could rebuke sin with extraordinary confidence, yet refuse to acknowledge the pride growing quietly inside your own heart.
And the most dangerous part?
You might not even realize something is terribly wrong.
Because spiritual activity can become so loud that it drowns out the quiet examination of the heart.
And that is precisely why the apostle Paul wrote one of the most unsettling statements in the entire New Testament.

“And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.” — 1 Corinthians 13:2 (KJV)
Read those final words again.
Not “I am less effective.”
Not “I need additional training.”
Not “I am spiritually underdeveloped.”
“I am nothing.”
Paul was not speaking about someone who lacked spiritual ability.
He was describing someone who appeared to possess an extraordinary abundance of it.
And that should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Because the question is not merely whether you believe in God.
The question is whether your faith is making you more like Jesus Christ.
The original Greek makes Paul's warning even more striking.
He writes:
Kan echō pasan tēn pistin hōste orē methistanein, agapēn de mē echō, outhen eimi.
A faithful rendering of this portion is:
“Even if I have all faith so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.”
Notice the Greek expression οὐθέν εἰμι — outhen eimi.
It means, “I am nothing.”
Paul does not merely say that his extraordinary abilities would become useless. He places the devastating conclusion upon himself.
Without love, he is nothing.
This is not a declaration that human beings have no worth. Scripture teaches that human beings are created in God's image (Genesis 1:26–27).
Rather, Paul is exposing the emptiness of spiritual accomplishments when they are divorced from the love that ought to govern them.
And the word he uses for love is ἀγάπη — agapē.
In this passage, agapē is not simply an emotional attachment, romantic affection, or pleasant feeling.
Paul describes it through patient, kind, humble, truthful, enduring conduct.
Love is not merely something we claim to feel.
It is something that becomes visible in how we treat people.
That is where this passage stops being a beautiful verse for weddings and becomes a mirror that can expose the condition of a Christian's heart.
Because it is possible to know the language of heaven while refusing to practice the character of Christ.
And if that sounds uncomfortable, perhaps we need to ask why.
There is something deeply revealing about the church in Corinth.
The Corinthians were not strangers to spiritual gifts.
Paul had already acknowledged that they were not lacking in any spiritual gift as they awaited the revelation of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:7).
Yet this same church struggled with divisions, jealousy, arrogance, lawsuits, disorder, and shameful treatment of fellow believers.
They possessed gifts.
But their conduct repeatedly demonstrated how desperately they needed to grow in love.
In 1 Corinthians 11, Paul confronted the humiliating divisions surrounding their gatherings, where some had plenty while others went hungry.
Then, in chapters 12 through 14, he addressed spiritual gifts and their proper exercise.
And right in the middle of that discussion, he placed 1 Corinthians 13.
Not as an unrelated poetic interruption.
But as a necessary correction.
The Corinthians needed to understand that spiritual gifts were never intended to become substitutes for spiritual character.
The Holy Spirit distributes gifts according to His will (1 Corinthians 12:11).
But the fruit of the Spirit reveals the kind of character His work produces in believers.
