Not a medieval legend.
Not a sentimental invention designed to make a sermon more dramatic.
Matthew names Rahab in the genealogy that leads to Jesus Christ.
According to Matthew's account, Rahab was the mother of Boaz.
Boaz became the father of Obed through Ruth.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And through the royal line of David, Matthew traces the ancestry of Jesus, the promised Messiah.
Pause and consider the staggering beauty of that.
Rahab had once been a woman living behind the walls of Jericho.
Now her name stood inside the family history of Israel's greatest King and, ultimately, the Messiah.
The woman once associated with prostitution was remembered in Scripture as an ancestor of Jesus.
And Matthew did not hide her.
He named her.
Why?
Because the genealogy of Jesus is not a public-relations campaign designed to make His human ancestry look impressive.
It is a testimony to the faithfulness of God across generations of deeply imperfect human beings.
Matthew includes Tamar.
He includes Rahab.
He includes Ruth.
He refers to the wife of Uriah, Bathsheba, in a way that recalls David's grievous sin.
These women have different stories, and we should not pretend their circumstances or moral responsibilities were identical.
Ruth, for example, is presented as a woman of remarkable loyalty and faithfulness, not as someone with Rahab's former occupation.
But their presence together reveals something significant.
God's redemptive purposes were not restricted to the socially powerful, the ethnically privileged, or those whose family histories appeared uncomplicated.
The promised Messiah entered human history through a family line that included outsiders, broken situations, grievous sins, courageous faith, and astonishing mercy.
Jesus did not inherit personal sin from His ancestors.
Scripture is clear that Christ Himself was without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
His holiness was not compromised by the moral failures found in His earthly genealogy.
Rather, His genealogy shows the extraordinary faithfulness of God in bringing the sinless Savior into a sinful world.
And this is where Rahab's story begins to confront us personally.
Because we often assume God works the way human beings do.
We think He looks for impressive résumés.
We think He prefers spotless backgrounds.
We think He must be reluctant to associate Himself with people who have embarrassing histories.
We imagine that our past has the final authority to determine our future.
But Rahab's story dismantles that assumption.
She was not rescued because prostitution was harmless.
She was not included in the Messiah's genealogy because sin does not matter.
She was not honored because repentance is unnecessary.
She was spared in the context of a genuine response of faith, and the New Testament holds her up as an example of faith that acted.
Hebrews 11:31 declares:
"By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace." (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη
Pistei Rhaab hē pornē.
"By faith, Rahab the prostitute..."
That opening is extraordinary.
The Greek word πίστει (pistei) means "by faith."
The writer of Hebrews does not pretend her past never existed.
He places her among the examples of faith.
And James 2:25 points to her actions as evidence of that faith.
This is crucial.
Rahab was not saved by an impressive record of good works.
Nor was her faith merely a private opinion that changed nothing about her behavior.
She believed, and her allegiance became visible in what she did.
James uses her example to demonstrate that living faith is not empty religious talk.
True faith bears fruit.
And that leads us to a question more important than whether people still remember your past.
Has your faith in Jesus Christ begun to change the direction of your life?
Not whether you have become perfect.
Not whether you have erased every consequence of yesterday.
Not whether everyone has forgiven you.
But whether you have truly turned toward Christ.
Because grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us and begins transforming us.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Forgiveness is not something we purchase through moral improvement.
Obedience is not the price we pay to make Jesus love us.
But when His grace truly takes hold of a life, it does not leave that life untouched.
Somebody needs to hear that.
Especially the person who has been using shame as an excuse to stay away from God.
You tell yourself that you will pray when you become better.
You will return to church when you feel worthy.
You will open your Bible when your habits are under control.
You will surrender when you have finally cleaned up the mess.
But if you could cleanse your own soul, you would not need a Savior.
Jesus did not come because humanity needed a little religious encouragement.
He came because sinners needed redemption.
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The cross is not a decorative symbol for people who have already made themselves acceptable.
It is the place where the holy Son of God gave Himself for sinners who could never save themselves.
And the resurrection is the declaration that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why Rahab's story matters.
Not because everyone with a painful past will become famous.
Not because faith guarantees that every damaged relationship will be repaired immediately.
Not because following God removes all earthly consequences.
And certainly not because God owes us an impressive future if we make one courageous decision.
Rahab's place in Jesus' genealogy was a particular gift within God's unfolding plan of redemption.
We should not turn it into a universal promise that every believer will receive public recognition or extraordinary earthly success.
The deeper promise is better.
Through Jesus Christ, sinners can receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a new life that their past cannot purchase or prevent.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired everything.
Not after everyone approved of us.
Not after our reputations became respectable.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That truth should break the pride of the religious and lift the eyes of the ashamed.
Because there are two ways to misunderstand Rahab.
One is to despise her because of her former life.
The other is to romanticize her former life as though sin itself were the reason she was honored.
Neither understands grace.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace reveals a Savior whose mercy is greater than the guilt of those who turn to Him.
And perhaps that is why this genealogy feels so personal.
Some of us have lived through our own Jericho.
Not a literal Canaanite fortress, but a life surrounded by walls of secrecy, regret, fear, addiction, bitterness, compromise, or spiritual rebellion.
We built those walls to protect ourselves.
We learned how to smile while hiding the truth.
We became skilled at looking normal.
We posted the family pictures.
We attended the worship services.
We said, "I'm blessed," while quietly fighting battles nobody knew existed.
And somewhere inside, we wondered whether God could see the person behind the performance.
He can.
He sees the hidden sin that needs repentance.
He sees the wounds that need healing.
He sees the pride that needs surrender.
He sees the fear beneath the anger.
He sees the exhaustion behind the smile.
And He calls us not to manufacture a better disguise, but to come into the light.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Notice that the promise does not say we should pretend we never sinned.
It calls us to confess.
To stop defending what God calls evil.
To stop making peace with what is destroying us.
To come honestly before the Lord.
Perhaps your first step today is not to write a long explanation of why you became the person you are.
Perhaps it is simply to say:
"Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. I believe You died and rose again. Have mercy on me. Teach me to follow You."
That prayer is not a magical formula.
The saving power belongs to Jesus Christ, not to the precise arrangement of our words.
But genuine repentance and faith are never wasted on Him.
And if you are already a believer who has stumbled badly, do not mistake the pain of conviction for proof that God has no more mercy for you.
Come back to the truth.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Make restitution where it is appropriate and possible.
Seek wise pastoral counsel and accountability when needed.
Turn away from the sin that has been consuming your life.
Do not use grace to hide from responsibility.
Let grace give you the courage to face it.
And remember Rahab.
Not as permission to keep living in Jericho.
But as a witness that God can receive someone who turns to Him in faith.
There is another detail in her story that deserves our attention.
Rahab did not simply escape a burning chapter of her past.
She became part of a community.
Joshua 6:25 says she lived among Israel.
Her story moved from separation to belonging.
And that is one reason Christianity was never meant to be lived as an isolated private experience.
We need Scripture.
We need prayer.
We need sound teaching.
We need fellowship.
We need believers who will encourage us when we are weary and lovingly confront us when we are drifting.
We need a community that does not confuse holiness with pretending.
A community where repentance is taken seriously, forgiveness is celebrated, and Jesus remains at the center.
That is also the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not to build a following around human personalities.
Not to sell people the illusion that spiritual growth can be purchased.
Not to replace the local church or the shepherding of faithful Christian leaders.
But to help place biblical truth, Christian encouragement, and discipleship resources within reach of people who need to hear about Jesus Christ.
These resources are offered to encourage deeper study, spiritual growth, and a more faithful walk with the Lord.
Perhaps there is a struggling believer who has almost stopped praying.
Perhaps there is a young person who has never been taught how to read Scripture carefully.
Perhaps there is someone who feels too ashamed to walk into a church building but is willing to read one article about the mercy of Jesus.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—an expression of generosity that helps continue and expand this work.
Your money does not purchase God's favor.
But supporting faithful Christian ministry can be one meaningful way to honor Him, serve others, and participate in the work of making the Gospel known.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you grow closer to Christ, and you believe in the mission, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
Those products are simply an additional expression of appreciation.
The greater purpose is the ministry itself.
More Scripture shared.
More discipleship resources made available.
More people encouraged to seek Christ.
More opportunities to point weary hearts toward the Savior.
Keep reading.
Keep studying.
Keep praying.
Keep growing.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And neither is the love of Jesus.
There is another powerful way you can help.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
But because somebody in your circle may be carrying a shame they have never spoken aloud.
Somebody may be convinced that the worst thing they ever did is the only thing God sees when He looks at them.
Somebody may have abandoned prayer because they think heaven has stopped listening.
And perhaps, through a simple act of sharing, they will encounter the biblical testimony of a woman named Rahab and discover that the door of mercy is not closed to repentant sinners.
And if this story has touched a place in your heart that you usually keep hidden, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss publicly.
And if you need prayer, simply write:
Let the comments become a place where people encourage one another with Scripture, compassion, truth, and prayer rather than judgment or spectacle.
For the nights when your past seems louder than God's promises.
For the moments when you need to remember that biblical grace does not deny sin, but points sinners to the Savior.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually cold, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to join us.
Because the goal is not merely to collect followers.
It is to help people become faithful followers of Jesus.
But before you leave, I want you to return to that ancient city one final time.
Picture Rahab at her window.
The scarlet cord is there.
The city is facing judgment.
She has heard what the LORD has done.
She has confessed who He is.
She has acted in faith.
She does not know the full story of what her life will become.
She does not know that generations later, a Jewish tax collector named Matthew will write a Gospel account tracing the ancestry of the Messiah.
She does not know that her name will be read by believers across nations and centuries.
She does not know that people wrestling with shame thousands of years later will find encouragement in her testimony.
All she knows is that the God of Israel is truly God, and she has sought mercy from Him.
Then the walls fall.
But Rahab lives.
Years pass.
Generations come and go.
A son named Boaz enters the family story.
Then Obed.
Then Jesse.
Then David.
And much later, in Bethlehem, Jesus Christ is born.
The promised Son of David.
The Son of Abraham.
The Savior who would bear the sins of many.
The One who would welcome repentant sinners, confront the proud, heal the broken, call people out of darkness, and give His life as a ransom for many.
The One who would rise from the grave.
The One before whom every knee will bow.
And there, in the opening chapter of Matthew's Gospel, is Rahab's name.
Not because her past was righteous.
Not because her faith made her worthy of every blessing.
Not because her story was free from complications.
But because God, in His sovereign faithfulness, chose to include this woman of faith in the earthly ancestry of His Son.
The scandal did not become the center of her story.
God's grace did.
And now we can answer the question that brought us here.
Why did Rahab, a Canaanite woman with a troubled reputation, become part of Jesus' genealogy?
Because God was accomplishing His redemptive purposes through real human history, showing that His mercy reaches beyond the boundaries people often assume are permanent.
Because Rahab responded to the revelation of the LORD with faith that became visible through her actions.
Because she was received among Israel, and Matthew records her place in the family line leading to the Messiah.
And because her inclusion helps us see something essential about the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come into a world of morally spotless people who had no need of salvation.
He came into our world.
A world of sin and sorrow.
Of pride and betrayal.
Of broken families and wounded hearts.
Of people who need more than advice.
People who need redemption.
And through His sinless life, sacrificial death, and victorious resurrection, He provides the salvation no human ancestry, reputation, religious achievement, or personal effort could ever secure.
That is why the story of Rahab is not ultimately about celebrating Rahab.
It is about magnifying the God who showed her mercy and fulfilled His promises through Jesus Christ.
And that is why your story does not have to end where your sin began.
You may not be able to change what happened yesterday.
You may not be able to make everyone forget.
You may still have consequences to face, relationships to repair, and difficult steps of obedience ahead.
But if you turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith, you are not asking a reluctant Savior to consider helping you.
You are coming to the One who gave Himself to save sinners.
The One whose grace is not fragile.
The One whose forgiveness is not earned.
The One who does not need to falsify your history in order to redeem your life.
So come to Him.
Not with excuses.
Not with a carefully edited version of yourself.
Not with the belief that you must first become worthy.
Come with the truth.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
And let the Savior who died and rose again have the final word over your eternal future.
Because the most extraordinary thing about Rahab is not that a woman with a scandalous past appeared in the genealogy of Jesus.
It is that Jesus, the holy Son of God, came to save people with scandalous pasts—and people with respectable appearances who are just as desperately in need of grace.
The world may remember the name they gave you in your darkest chapter, but in Christ, that chapter does not have to be the ending of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF GOD ALREADY KNOWS WHO WILL BE SAVED, WHY ARE WE STILL BEGGING PEOPLE TO COME TO JESUS?
paragraphs: IF GOD ALREADY KNOWS WHO WILL BE SAVED, WHY ARE WE STILL BEGGING PEOPLE TO COME TO JESUS?

If Heaven Already Knows Their Names, Why Does Jesus Still Command Us to Go? The Uncomfortable Truth About God's Sovereignty, Human Responsibility, and the Souls We May Never Reach Because We Chose Silence.
Imagine standing in heaven one day, looking into the face of Jesus Christ.
The One who carried your sins. The One who endured the cross. The One who knew every shameful chapter of your life and still extended His mercy toward you.
And somewhere in that overwhelming moment, a question crosses your mind.
What about the people I never told?
Your brother who laughed whenever you mentioned God.
Your coworker who quietly battled depression while you assumed everything was fine.
Your childhood friend who slowly disappeared from church.
Your father who grew older without ever hearing you personally explain why Jesus mattered so much to you.
The stranger sitting beside you on a bus who looked perfectly normal but was silently wondering whether life was worth living.
You had opportunities.
You had the Gospel.
You knew the name of Jesus.
But you kept telling yourself there would be another day.
And perhaps the most unsettling part is that you had a theological explanation for your silence.
"If God already knows who will be saved, why should I evangelize? Won't His will happen anyway?"
It sounds intelligent.
It sounds spiritual.
It even sounds like confidence in God's sovereignty.
But what if the question we have been using to defend our silence is actually exposing how little we understand the heart of the God who saved us?
Because there is something astonishing in Scripture that changes the entire conversation.
The God who knows the end from the beginning is the very God who commands His people to go into the world and preach the Gospel.
And He never treated those two truths as contradictions.
We do.
God doesn't.
Consider what happened when the apostle Paul arrived in Corinth.
He entered a city known for idolatry, immorality, commercial ambition, and competing philosophies. He preached Christ in a place where the Gospel encountered both resistance and remarkable openness.
Then, one night, the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision.
"Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace: For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee: for I have much people in this city."
— Acts 18:9–10, KJV
Read that final sentence again.
"For I have much people in this city."
God already knew what Paul could not see.
There were people in Corinth who would belong to Christ.
But notice what God did not say.
He did not tell Paul to stop preaching because the outcome was already known.
He did not tell him to rest because divine sovereignty made human obedience unnecessary.
He said the exact opposite.
Speak. Do not be silent.
And Paul remained there for a year and six months, teaching the Word of God among them (Acts 18:11).
Do you see it?
God's knowledge did not cancel Paul's mission.
It strengthened it.
The Lord's assurance became a reason for Paul to continue speaking, not an excuse to withdraw.
This is where many of us have misunderstood the relationship between God's sovereignty and evangelism.
We imagine that if God knows the outcome, our actions cannot matter.
But Scripture never teaches that conclusion.
God not only knows what He will accomplish; He also works through the means by which His purposes unfold.
And one of those means is the proclamation of the Gospel.
Paul explains this with breathtaking clarity in Romans 10.
"For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved."
Then he asks:
"How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"
— Romans 10:13–14, KJV
The Greek text of Romans 10:14 contains this piercing question:
πῶς δὲ ἀκούσωσιν χωρὶς κηρύσσοντος;
Pōs de akousōsin chōris kēryssontos?
A faithful translation is:
"And how will they hear without someone preaching?"
The word κηρύσσοντος (kēryssontos) comes from the verb kēryssō, meaning to proclaim or announce publicly, as a herald announces a message.
Paul is not describing someone inventing a religious opinion.
He is describing someone delivering a message entrusted to them.
A herald does not create the king's decree.
He announces it.
And the Christian does not invent the Gospel.
We proclaim what God has accomplished through Jesus Christ.
This changes everything.
You are not being asked to manufacture salvation.
You are being commanded to bear witness to the Savior.
You cannot open a spiritually blind heart by your own power.
You cannot forgive another person's sins.
You cannot force repentance.
You cannot produce the new birth.
But you can speak the truth about Jesus.
You can explain the cross.
You can testify to His mercy.
You can answer questions patiently.
You can pray.
You can invite.
You can love someone enough to tell them what Christ has done.
And God can work through that witness in ways you may never fully understand.
Perhaps someone reading this has carried a quiet burden for years.
You have prayed for a son who no longer believes.
You have watched a daughter slowly drift from the faith.
You have tried to reach a spouse who becomes uncomfortable whenever Jesus enters the conversation.
And after so many unanswered prayers, you have started wondering whether your words matter anymore.
Please hear this.
Your inability to change someone's heart does not mean your faithful witness is meaningless.
The responsibility to save belongs to God.
The responsibility to bear witness belongs to His people.
Those are not competing responsibilities.
They are beautifully connected in Scripture.
And there is another distinction we must understand.
God's foreknowledge is not the same thing as our knowledge.
The Lord declares in Isaiah 46:9–10:
"I am God, and there is none like me, Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done."
God's knowledge is not limited by time as ours is.
Nothing surprises Him.
No conversion catches Him unprepared.
No act of rebellion forces Him to revise His understanding.
But we are not God.
We do not possess His exhaustive knowledge.
We do not know who will repent tomorrow.
We do not know who will reject Christ today but surrender to Him years later.
We do not know which hardened atheist may become a missionary.
We do not know which exhausted mother may encounter the Gospel through one unexpected conversation.
We do not know which prisoner may become a faithful servant of Christ.
And we certainly do not possess a list of those who will ultimately be saved.
God has not given us permission to treat people as hopeless simply because we cannot see what He sees.
That is why our task is not to identify the elect.
Our task is to proclaim Christ.
Christians have long disagreed about how divine election, foreknowledge, grace, and human freedom fit together.
Some understand election as God's unconditional choice of those He will save.
Others understand God's election in relation to His foreknowledge and His gracious purposes in Christ, while emphasizing the genuine human response to the Gospel.
These differences deserve careful biblical study, humility, and serious theological discussion.
But notice what faithful Christians across these traditions can affirm together.
Jesus commands the Gospel to be proclaimed.
Salvation is found in Him.
Human beings are called to repent and believe.
And no Christian has the authority to use God's sovereignty as an excuse for disobedience.
The mystery of God's eternal knowledge does not erase the clarity of Christ's command.
In Matthew 28:19–20, the risen Jesus tells His disciples:
"Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you."
The Greek expression at the heart of this commission is:
μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη
Mathēteusate panta ta ethnē.
"Make disciples of all the nations."
The verb μαθητεύσατε (mathēteusate) is an imperative.
It is a command.
And the command is not merely to collect religious decisions.
It is to make disciples.
People who learn from Jesus.
People who follow Him.
People who are baptized into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
People who are taught to obey what Christ commanded.
Evangelism is therefore not about winning arguments, accumulating impressive numbers, or pressuring people into emotional responses.
It is about faithfully announcing the crucified and risen Savior and calling people to the life of discipleship that flows from genuine faith.
And this is where the question becomes painfully personal.
If Jesus has commanded us to make disciples, why are we so comfortable remaining silent?
Sometimes the answer is fear.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of embarrassment.
Fear of losing friendships.
Fear of being called judgmental.
Fear that someone will ask a question we cannot answer.
Sometimes the answer is exhaustion.
We are struggling with our own problems, our own temptations, our own responsibilities, and we feel we have nothing left to give.
And sometimes, if we are willing to be painfully honest, the answer is that our love has grown cold.
We can spend hours discussing politics, entertainment, business, and other people's mistakes.
But when an opportunity comes to speak of the One who died for us, suddenly we cannot find the words.
That should trouble us.
Not because every conversation must become a sermon.
Not because every Christian must possess the personality of a public evangelist.
Not because we should manipulate vulnerable people or treat friendships as evangelistic projects.
But because the love of Christ should make His Gospel too precious for us to deliberately bury.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:14:
The Greek verb is συνέχει (synechei).
In this context, it communicates the idea of being compelled, controlled, or held under the compelling influence of something.
Paul is explaining why Christ's love governs his ministry.
He continues by declaring that Christ died and rose again, and that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for Him (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).
Then he describes believers as ambassadors for Christ.
Imagine that.
Not salespeople trying to sell God.
Not performers attempting to build personal fame.
Ambassadors representing a King who has already acted to reconcile sinners to Himself through Jesus Christ.
And the message entrusted to us is extraordinary.
"Be ye reconciled to God."
— 2 Corinthians 5:20, KJV
We do not announce that human beings can save themselves through religious improvement.
We announce that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Because the central problem of humanity is not merely emotional emptiness.
It is sin.
We have rebelled against our Creator.
We have loved darkness.
We have violated His righteous standards.
We have attempted to live independently of the One who gave us life.
And no amount of good behavior can erase our guilt before a holy God.
Yet the Gospel does not end with our rebellion.
It announces God's astonishing mercy.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered our broken world.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He loved the rejected.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He exposed the darkness people preferred to hide.
And then He went to the cross.
Not because He had committed sin.
But because He came to save sinners.
Paul summarizes the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4:
"Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures."
This is the message we proclaim.
Not that Jesus merely improves difficult lives.
Not that Christianity guarantees financial prosperity.
Not that following Christ removes every earthly struggle.
But that Jesus died for our sins, was buried, and rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness is proclaimed.
Through Him, sinners are called to repentance and faith.
Through Him, those who were spiritually dead can receive new life.
And no human being is too respectable to need that grace.
No human being is too scandalous to be beyond the reach of Christ's power to save.
Remember the apostle Paul himself.
Before he became a missionary, he persecuted the church.
He approved of violence against believers.
He entered houses and dragged Christians away.
He was not merely uninterested in Jesus.
He was actively opposing His people.
If you had encountered Saul before his conversion, would you have considered him a promising candidate for Christian ministry?
Probably not.
You might have avoided him.
You might have feared him.
You might have assumed he would never change.
But on the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus confronted him.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy of the church became a servant of Christ.
And the man who once sought to silence the Gospel spent his life proclaiming it.
Paul later wrote:
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief."
— 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
That is grace.
Not the denial of his scandalous past.
Not the claim that his sins never mattered.
But the astonishing truth that Jesus could forgive and transform a man whose past was stained by persecution.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now think about the person you have almost given up on.
The one who mocks your faith.
The one who drinks to numb the pain.
The one whose marriage is falling apart.
The one who says Christianity is nothing but hypocrisy.
The one who seems spiritually unreachable.
What if you are looking at someone whose story is not finished?
You do not know what God may do.
You do not know how deeply the Holy Spirit may be working beyond what you can observe.
You do not know whether a conversation, a Scripture passage, an invitation, or an act of Christian love may become part of that person's journey toward Christ.
This does not mean every person you speak to will be converted.
Jesus Himself encountered rejection.
The apostles encountered rejection.
The Scriptures never promise that every evangelistic conversation will produce visible fruit.
But rejection does not prove that faithful witness was worthless.
And a delayed response does not mean the Gospel was powerless.
Sometimes the seed is planted long before the harvest becomes visible.
Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 3:6:
"I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase."
There it is again.
Human responsibility.
Divine power.
Not enemies.
Not contradictions.
God working through His servants.
One person plants.
Another waters.
God gives the growth.
And because God gives the growth, no evangelist has the right to boast as though salvation were a human achievement.
But because planting and watering matter, no believer should dismiss faithful ministry as unnecessary.
This is why we evangelize even though God already knows who will be saved.

Because God commands it. Because Christ deserves to be proclaimed. Because people need to hear the Gospel. Because God works through the message of His Son. And because we love our neighbors enough to tell them the truth.
But there is another question that deserves attention.
If God knows who will be saved, does that mean our prayers for unbelievers are pointless?
Absolutely not.
Paul, who taught extensively about God's sovereignty, also prayed passionately for the salvation of others.
In Romans 10:1, he writes:
Notice the tenderness.
This is not cold theological speculation.
This is a man who understands God's greatness and still carries a burden for people.
He prays.
He reasons.
He persuades.
He suffers.
He preaches.
And he trusts God with the outcome.
The same Paul who writes about God's gracious purposes also says in 2 Timothy 2:10:
"Therefore I endure all things for the elect's sakes, that they may also obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory."
That verse is especially important.
Paul does not conclude that election makes ministry unnecessary.
He endures suffering so that others may obtain salvation in Christ.
His confidence in God's purpose fuels perseverance.
It does not produce indifference.
And perhaps this is the correction some of us need.
We have turned mysteries that should inspire worship into arguments that excuse inactivity.
We have become skilled at discussing sovereignty while neglecting compassion.
We can debate election for hours, yet struggle to spend five minutes praying for an unbelieving friend.
We can explain theological systems, but cannot remember the last time we gently and clearly shared the Gospel with someone who needed to hear it.
Knowledge of Scripture is a precious gift.
Sound doctrine matters.
Truth matters.
But theology that never produces love, humility, worship, obedience, or compassion has been tragically misunderstood.
Jesus did not command His disciples to solve every mystery of eternity before making disciples.
He commanded them to go.
And He promised His presence.
"Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world."
— Matthew 28:20, KJV
What a promise.
The One who sends us does not abandon us.
The One who commands us also sustains us.
And when we are afraid, we can remember that evangelism does not depend upon our brilliance.
Some Christians can speak before thousands.
Others can barely manage a conversation with one person.
Some can answer complicated theological questions.
Others can simply say, "I was lost, and Jesus showed me mercy."
God can use both.
Consider the Samaritan woman in John 4.
She came to a well carrying a complicated personal history.
Jesus knew the truth about her life.
He did not flatter her.
He did not pretend her situation was righteous.
Yet He engaged her with remarkable dignity and revealed Himself to her.
And after encountering Him, she went back to her community and said:
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?"
— John 4:29, KJV
She did not possess a seminary degree.
She did not have decades of ministry experience.
She had encountered Jesus.
And she invited others to come and see.
John 4:39 tells us that many Samaritans believed in Him because of the woman's testimony.
Then, after hearing Jesus themselves, more believed because of His word.
That distinction matters.
Her testimony pointed people toward Christ.
Christ Himself became the center of their faith.
That is the purpose of authentic evangelism.
Not to make people dependent on our personalities.
Not to make our ministry indispensable.
Not to gather admirers around ourselves.
But to point people beyond us to the Savior.
And perhaps you are reading this while secretly wondering whether you have any right to tell others about Jesus.
Because you know your own failures.
You remember the temptation you surrendered to last week.
You remember the prayer you neglected.
You remember the bitterness you still struggle to release.
You remember the person you hurt.
You know there are areas of your life where repentance is still urgently needed.
And a voice whispers:
Who are you to talk about Jesus?
Listen carefully.
Unrepentant hypocrisy must never be excused.
If you are living in deliberate rebellion while publicly pretending to be holy, the answer is not to polish your religious image.
The answer is repentance.
Come into the light.
Confess your sins.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Seek forgiveness and, where appropriate, make restitution.
But do not confuse genuine humility with the lie that only flawless Christians can testify about a flawless Savior.
If perfection were the qualification for evangelism, no human messenger would ever qualify.
We proclaim Jesus precisely because we need Him.
We are not witnesses to our own moral greatness.
We are witnesses to His grace.
And this is why the theme of Gospel Warrior matters so deeply.
Not because every painful consequence disappears.
Not because repentance rewrites historical facts.
Not because forgiveness means sin was harmless.
But because the grace of God in Jesus Christ can give a repentant sinner a new identity, a new direction, and a living hope.
Your past may explain where you have been.
It does not have the authority to overrule what Christ can make of your future.
And that is a message worth sharing.
Before you continue scrolling today, think of one person.
Just one.
Someone whose name has been sitting quietly in your heart.
Maybe you have not spoken to them in months.
Maybe you have been avoiding a difficult conversation.
Maybe you have assumed they would never listen.
You do not need to force a religious argument.
You do not need to corner them with fear.
You do not need to pretend you have answers to every question.
Begin with prayer.
Ask God to give you genuine love for that person.
Ask for wisdom.
Ask for courage.
Ask for an opportunity to listen before speaking.
And when the opportunity comes, tell them about Jesus.
Tell them that sin is real, but so is mercy.
Tell them that the cross is not merely a religious symbol.
Tell them that Jesus died and rose again.
Tell them that forgiveness is offered through Him.
Tell them that repentance is not a performance to earn God's love but a genuine turning from sin to God.
Tell them that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for religious achievements (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And remember that you are not responsible for controlling their response.
Faithfulness is not measured only by immediate visible results.
Sometimes love speaks.
Sometimes love listens.
Sometimes love waits patiently.
Sometimes love continues praying through years of uncertainty.
But love does not become indifferent to the eternal good of another human being.
And if you are the person who needs to respond to the Gospel today, this message is also for you.
Maybe you have been hiding behind theological questions because you are afraid of what surrendering to Jesus would require.
You ask about predestination.
You ask about foreknowledge.
You ask about election.
Those are serious questions, and they deserve serious answers.
But do not allow questions about God's hidden knowledge to distract you from the invitation clearly revealed in His Word.
Jesus said:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."
— John 6:37, KJV
You are not being commanded to discover whether your name appears in a hidden heavenly register before coming to Christ.
You are called to repent and believe the Gospel.
Come to Him.
Bring your sin into the light.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Stop pretending you can rescue yourself.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose from the grave.
The Greek word often translated "repent" in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It means to repent, involving a change of mind or understanding that, in biblical calls to repentance, is expressed in turning away from sin toward God.
It is not merely feeling guilty for a few minutes.
It is not crying during a worship song and returning unchanged to deliberate rebellion.
Biblical repentance involves a genuine turning to God, with a transformed life bearing fruit over time.
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live in a way that honors Christ (Titus 2:11–12).
That transformation does not happen because we purchase God's favor.
It happens because God's grace is powerful.
This is also why supporting faithful Gospel ministry matters.
Someone has to prepare biblical teaching.
Someone has to teach new believers.
Someone has to make discipleship resources available.
Someone has to spend time answering difficult questions, encouraging the weary, and pointing people back to Scripture.
And while the Gospel itself must never be sold, those who freely and faithfully support its proclamation participate in something meaningful.
Paul thanked the Philippian believers for their partnership in the Gospel and their material support of his ministry (Philippians 1:5; 4:15–18).
He described their generosity as an offering pleasing to God.
Their gifts were not payments for salvation.
They were expressions of love, partnership, and worship.
That distinction is essential.
What matters is the heart behind the gift.
Paul writes:
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The same passage teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion.
So this is not a demand.
It is an invitation to partnership.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
The greater purpose is to help more people encounter Scripture, grow in sound doctrine, understand the Gospel, and become faithful disciples of Jesus.
If money is tight, take care of your family and essential responsibilities.
You can still participate meaningfully.
Pray for this work.
Add a few honest words about why it mattered to you.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to pressure them.
But to open a door for a thoughtful conversation about Jesus.
And if this article has challenged your heart, please do not leave without responding.
You do not need to share private details.
Sometimes a few honest words can remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Someone may need to hear that their prayers and patient conversations are not necessarily in vain.
We want people to read.
To study.
To test every teaching against Scripture.
To grow in discernment.
To become rooted in Christ rather than dependent on personalities.
Because genuine Christian ministry should never make itself the center.
Jesus is the center.
Always.
And now we return to the question that began this conversation.
If God already knows who will be saved, why evangelize?
Because the God who knows the future has commanded us to proclaim His Son.
Because the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes (Romans 1:16).
Because faith comes by hearing the message concerning Christ (Romans 10:17).
Because God's sovereignty does not make obedience meaningless.
Because we do not know whom God will save.
Because Jesus Christ is worthy of being known, loved, trusted, and worshiped among the nations.
And because somewhere, someone may be closer to hearing the Gospel than you realize.
Perhaps it is the friend who keeps asking questions.
Perhaps it is the husband who has quietly started reading Scripture.
Perhaps it is the teenager who acts uninterested but remembers every conversation.
Perhaps it is the person who hurt you.
Perhaps it is someone you have already written off.
Do not claim to know the end of a story that God has not revealed to you.
Do not confuse someone's present resistance with an unchangeable future.
And do not allow your inability to understand every mystery of divine sovereignty to become an excuse for neglecting a command that Jesus has made clear.
One day, every opportunity to speak in this present life will be behind us.
That is not a reason to live in panic or crippling guilt.
Christ is a merciful Savior, not a cruel taskmaster demanding that you personally convert everyone you meet.
But it is a reason to live with purpose.
A reason to love more deeply.
A reason to pray more earnestly.
A reason to speak more courageously.
A reason to stop treating the Gospel as something we merely admire and start living as people entrusted with its proclamation.
The results belong to God.
The message belongs to Christ.
The mission has been entrusted to His church.
And the time to obey is now.
So when you see that person's face again, perhaps your prayer will be different.
Not, "Lord, prove to me that this person will be saved before I speak."
But, "Lord, help me love this person faithfully. Open a door for Your Word. Give me wisdom, humility, and courage. And let Jesus Christ be glorified, whatever the outcome."
Because in the end, evangelism is not an attempt to surprise an all-knowing God.
It is an act of obedience to the risen King.
It is love carrying good news.
It is a forgiven sinner pointing another sinner toward the only Savior.
And it is the church participating in the mission of the Lord who died, rose again, and promised to remain with His people until the end of the age.
You do not have to know whose name is written in heaven to faithfully speak the name of Jesus on earth.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WOULD JESUS RECOGNIZE HIS CHURCH… OR WOULD HE BE ASKED TO SIT IN THE BACK WHILE THE PASTOR GETS THE VIP TREATMENT?
paragraphs: WOULD JESUS RECOGNIZE HIS CHURCH… OR WOULD HE BE ASKED TO SIT IN THE BACK WHILE THE PASTOR GETS THE VIP TREATMENT?
When shepherds become celebrities, the altar becomes a stage, and the people who came looking for Jesus begin wondering whose kingdom they are actually building.
Imagine Jesus walking into a modern megachurch on a Sunday morning.
Not as the honored guest.
Not with an entourage.
Not wearing expensive designer clothing.
Just Jesus.

The same Jesus who touched lepers when everyone else stepped away. The same Jesus who washed dirty feet while His disciples argued about greatness. The same Jesus who had nowhere to lay His head, yet carried the riches of heaven in His presence.
He approaches the entrance.

Security personnel are standing nearby. Reserved parking spaces await important guests. A special lounge has been prepared for the pastor. The lighting is spectacular. The music is powerful. Thousands are gathered.
And somewhere inside, a single mother is wondering whether the little money left in her purse should buy groceries or become an offering.
An elderly man is sitting alone, hoping someone will notice him.
A young believer is silently battling depression, desperate to hear that God has not abandoned him.
Then the pastor arrives.
The cameras turn.
The crowd rises.
The applause begins.
And here is the question that should make every Christian uncomfortable:
If Jesus walked into that church unnoticed, would anyone recognize the most important Person in the building?
Before anyone becomes defensive, understand something.
This is not an attack on every wealthy pastor.
This is not an accusation against every large church.
This is not a declaration that successful ministries are automatically corrupt.
And some ministers who appear ordinary publicly may still be consumed by pride privately.
The issue is not simply how expensive a pastor's clothes are.
The issue is whose glory the ministry exists to display.
Because there is a difference between being known because you preach Jesus and using Jesus to become known.
And Scripture does not leave us guessing about that difference.
Jesus once looked at religious leaders who loved recognition, public honor, and privileged seats.
He said:
“They love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others.” (Matthew 23:6–7, ESV)
Then He exposed the deeper problem.
“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12, ESV)
The original Greek gives us something worth examining.
In Matthew 23:12, the word translated “exalts” comes from ὑψόω (hypsoō), meaning to lift up or exalt.
The word translated “humbles” comes from ταπεινόω (tapeinoō), meaning to humble or bring low.
Jesus was confronting more than an unfortunate personality trait.
He was confronting the spiritual danger of making oneself great in the eyes of others.
And that danger has not disappeared.
It has simply learned how to use microphones, television cameras, expensive stages, social media algorithms, and carefully managed public images.
A pastor can now become a brand.
A sermon can become a product.
A congregation can become an audience.
And without anyone announcing the change, a ministry that began by lifting up Jesus can slowly become organized around protecting the reputation, comfort, and influence of one human being.
But the Gospel was never meant to be a platform for manufacturing Christian celebrities.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
And nobody gets to replace Him at the center.
There is a moment in Scripture that should haunt every Christian leader who secretly enjoys being treated as spiritually untouchable.
Jesus was eating with His disciples on the night before His crucifixion.
He knew betrayal was approaching.
He knew suffering was coming.
He knew the cross awaited Him.
And what did He do?
He rose from supper.
He took a towel.
He poured water into a basin.
And He began washing His disciples' feet.
Think about that.
The One whom John describes as having come from God and returning to God knelt before imperfect men and performed the work of a servant.
The hands that would soon be pierced by nails were washing the dirt from human feet.
The King of glory was not demanding special treatment.
He was demonstrating sacrificial love.
Jesus said:
“If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet.” (John 13:14, ESV)
He was not merely teaching politeness.
He was overturning the world's understanding of greatness.
And if the Lord of heaven could kneel before His followers, how can any pastor believe that leadership places him above the people he is called to serve?
Imagine the difference between a pastor who expects everyone to carry his belongings and a pastor who notices the exhausted volunteer stacking chairs after everyone else has gone home.
Imagine the difference between a leader who demands unquestioning loyalty and one who welcomes biblical accountability.
Imagine a pastor who knows the names of wealthy donors but cannot remember the widow who has faithfully attended for twenty years.
Now imagine Jesus standing beside that widow.
Whom would He notice?
The answer becomes even more uncomfortable when we read Mark 10.
James and John wanted places of honor in Christ's kingdom.
The other disciples became indignant.
Jesus gathered them and explained that the rulers of the Gentiles exercised authority over others, but His followers were to live differently.
“Whoever would be great among you must be your servant.” (Mark 10:43, ESV)
The Greek word translated “servant” is διάκονος (diakonos).
It describes someone who serves or ministers to others.
Jesus then said:
“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45, ESV)
Read that again.
The Son of Man did not come to be served.
He came to serve.
And He gave His life.
That is the standard.
Not popularity.
Not luxury.
Not the size of a building.
Not the number of followers.
Not how many people stand when a pastor enters the room.
The standard is Jesus Christ.
But we must be careful not to replace biblical discernment with resentment.
Because Scripture does not teach that every wealthy believer is wicked or that every pastor must live in poverty.
Jesus also received material support during His earthly ministry, as Luke 8:1–3 records.
And Paul explicitly taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14).
First Timothy 5:17–18 recognizes appropriate honor and material provision for faithful elders, especially those laboring in preaching and teaching.
So receiving financial support is not automatically wrong.
Having a comfortable home is not automatically wrong.
Owning a vehicle is not automatically wrong.
A church providing reasonable protection for a pastor facing genuine security threats is not automatically wrong.
Even having a large audience is not evidence of unfaithfulness.
Jesus Himself attracted crowds.
The problem begins when possessions become objects of devotion, privilege becomes entitlement, and ministry resources are treated as though they exist primarily to elevate the leader.
Paul warned Timothy:
“But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare.” (1 Timothy 6:9, ESV)
Notice what Paul identifies.
The desire to be rich.
Not merely the possession of money.
He continued:
“For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils.” (1 Timothy 6:10, ESV)
The Greek expression φιλαργυρία (philargyria) refers to the love of money.
Paul did not say money itself is the root of every evil.
He identified a disordered affection that can pull the human heart away from faithfulness.
And that warning applies to pastors and congregations alike.
A poor man can worship money he does not possess.
A rich man can use money faithfully without worshiping it.
The real question is whether money has become a servant or a master.
Jesus was unmistakable:
“You cannot serve God and money.” (Matthew 6:24, ESV)
Not because earning money is sinful.
But because the human heart cannot ultimately bow before two competing masters.
And this is where the conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because celebrity Christianity does not survive on celebrity pastors alone.
It also survives on people who want them.
People who equate visible wealth with divine approval.
People who assume an expensive lifestyle proves extraordinary faith.
People who believe that being close to a famous minister somehow brings them closer to God.
People who defend a preacher's every action because admitting that a spiritual hero might be wrong feels like losing part of their own identity.
Sometimes we have helped build the very pedestals that later disappoint us.
We have confused charisma with character.
Confidence with conviction.
Influence with anointing.
A beautiful sermon with a beautiful life.
But a person can preach about humility without practicing it.
A person can speak passionately about generosity while privately living in greed.
A person can fill a stadium and still neglect the wounded people entrusted to their care.
And a person can have a small congregation, a modest salary, and no public recognition while faithfully shepherding souls in a way that deeply honors Christ.
Heaven's measurements are not the same as ours.
Consider the apostle Peter.
He had seen Jesus transfigured.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard the risen Lord speak.
Yet when Peter instructed church elders, he did not tell them to become spiritual royalty.
He wrote:
“Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly.” (1 Peter 5:2, ESV)
And then:
“Not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.” (1 Peter 5:3, ESV)
The Greek verb ποιμάνατε (poimanate), translated “shepherd,” carries the sense of tending or caring for a flock.
It is a command to shepherd God's people.
Not to own them.
Not to exploit them.
Not to build a personal empire upon their sacrifices.
Not to make them afraid of questioning financial decisions or reporting misconduct.
A pastor is an under-shepherd.
Christ is the Chief Shepherd.
That distinction matters because sheep do not exist to make the shepherd famous.
A shepherd exists to care for the sheep.
And there are wounded believers who know exactly why this conversation matters.
Perhaps you once trusted a pastor deeply.
You believed his sermons.
You volunteered in his ministry.
You sacrificed financially because you wanted the Gospel to reach more people.
You prayed for him.
You defended him when others criticized him.
Then something happened.
Maybe you discovered that money was being handled without transparency.
Maybe serious allegations were dismissed without proper investigation.
Maybe ordinary members were struggling while leaders appeared to live without restraint.
Maybe questions were labeled rebellion.
Maybe spiritual authority was used to silence people who were already hurting.
And suddenly, something inside you began to fracture.
Not merely your trust in a pastor.
Your understanding of God.
You wondered whether the Gospel itself had been used against you.
You wondered whether your prayers had been wasted.
You wondered whether your generosity had been foolish.
And perhaps the most painful question was one you barely dared to say aloud:
If the people who preached Jesus to me could behave this way, how can I trust Jesus Himself?
Please hear this carefully.
A pastor's betrayal does not make Jesus unfaithful.
A minister's hypocrisy does not make the cross powerless.
A church's failure does not erase the resurrection.
And the sins of someone who claimed to represent Christ must never be mistaken for the character of Christ Himself.
Jesus warned against false prophets (Matthew 7:15–20).
He confronted religious hypocrisy (Matthew 23).
He spoke severely about causing vulnerable believers to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
He did not ask wounded people to pretend evil was good.
And He did not teach that accountability is rebellion.
If a pastor has abused spiritual authority, misused church funds, or harmed people, the answer is not gossip, mob judgment, or automatic assumptions of guilt.
The answer is truth.
Evidence.
Fair investigation.
Appropriate reporting to civil authorities when laws have been broken.
Protection for vulnerable people.
Repentance where wrongdoing is established.
And accountability that does not disappear simply because someone is gifted at preaching.
First Timothy 5:19–20 establishes both safeguards against unsupported accusations and accountability for elders who persist in sin.
Biblical honor is not the same as unquestioning obedience.
And biblical forgiveness does not automatically restore someone to a position of trust.
But this article is not only for those who have been hurt by celebrity Christianity.
It is also for the pastor who may be reading this privately.
Perhaps your ministry began with tears.
You remember the first person you led to Christ.
You remember preaching to a handful of people in a borrowed room.
You remember praying over empty chairs.
You remember trusting God when there was barely enough money to pay the bills.
You never imagined that one day people would recognize you in public.
You never planned to become obsessed with influence.
But success came.
Then invitations.
Then honorariums.
Then followers.
Then people who praised everything you said.
And slowly, perhaps without noticing, you began to need the applause.
You began measuring your worth by attendance figures.
You became uncomfortable around people who challenged you.
You started protecting your image more carefully than you protected your private prayer life.
And now, when the room becomes quiet, you sometimes wonder whether you still love Jesus as simply as you did in the beginning.
Pastor, if that is you, the invitation is not to despair.
It is to repent and return.
Jesus has not run out of mercy.
But His mercy is not permission to continue in pride.
He calls you back to the towel.
Back to the basin.
Back to the secret place.
Back to the Scriptures.
Back to loving people who cannot advance your reputation.
Back to remembering that the Church was purchased with Christ's blood, not your achievements.
Acts 20:28 reminds overseers that the church belongs to God and was obtained at the cost of blood.
That is holy ground.
You are handling people for whom Christ died.
Do not treat them as instruments for building your name.
And if you are a Christian who has become overly attached to a famous preacher, there is grace for you too.
You do not have to hate your pastor to stop idolizing him.
You do not have to reject every sermon he has preached to examine his conduct biblically.
You do not have to abandon the Church because you discovered that leaders are human.
You can honor faithful pastors, pray for them, support them appropriately, and still remember that only Jesus deserves your ultimate allegiance.
Paul once confronted divisions among believers who were attaching themselves to different Christian leaders.
Some identified with Paul.
Others with Apollos.
Others with Cephas.
Paul asked:
“Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1 Corinthians 1:13, ESV)
That question still cuts through our modern celebrity culture.
Was your favorite preacher crucified for you?
Did your favorite pastor rise from the grave?
Can any minister forgive your sins by his own authority?
Can any celebrity Christian carry the weight of your eternal hope?
No.
Only Jesus.
The Hebrew Scriptures offer a remarkable picture of what God expects from spiritual shepherds.
In Ezekiel 34, God confronts Israel's shepherds for feeding themselves instead of caring for the flock.
The Hebrew word רֹעִים (ro'im) means “shepherds.”
In the chapter, the shepherd imagery describes leaders who were responsible for God's people but had neglected and exploited them.
God condemns their failure to strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the injured, bring back the straying, and seek the lost.
Then comes the breathtaking promise:
“Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out.” (Ezekiel 34:11, ESV)
Centuries later, Jesus declared:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11, ESV)
Do you see the contrast?
Faithless shepherds consume the flock.
The Good Shepherd gives Himself for the flock.
Faithless shepherds use authority to protect themselves.
The Good Shepherd sacrifices Himself to save others.
Faithless shepherds abandon the vulnerable.
The Good Shepherd seeks the lost.
And at Calvary, Jesus demonstrated what His shepherding love truly costs.
He did not climb onto a golden throne while sinners suffered beneath Him.
He carried a wooden cross.
He was mocked.
He was stripped.
He was wounded.
He was crucified.
And there, bearing the judgment sinners deserve, He accomplished what no pastor, no ministry, no church building, and no religious celebrity could ever accomplish.
Redemption.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
The One who possessed all authority willingly humbled Himself, becoming obedient to death on a cross (Philippians 2:5–11).
And God highly exalted Him.
This is the astonishing reversal at the heart of Christianity.
The world says greatness means being served.
Jesus says greatness is revealed through service.
The world says protect your status.
Jesus says deny yourself and follow Me.
The world says accumulate glory.
Jesus says glorify the Father.
And the cross exposes the emptiness of every spiritual empire built around human pride.
There is something deeply tragic about using the name of a crucified Savior to justify a life that refuses His example.
But there is also something deeply beautiful about a pastor who genuinely follows Him.
The pastor who quietly visits the hospital after a long Sunday.
The pastor who refuses to manipulate struggling families into giving beyond their means.
The pastor who allows financial oversight and independent accountability.
The pastor who admits when he is wrong.
The pastor who rejoices when someone grows closer to Jesus, even if that person never becomes a fan of his ministry.
The pastor who has opportunities to become famous but remains determined to be faithful.
Those shepherds exist.
Some serve enormous congregations.
Some serve tiny churches.
Some receive generous compensation.
Others work additional jobs to support their families.
Their circumstances differ, but their calling is the same.
Point people to Jesus.
And if you have a faithful pastor, do not let the failures of others prevent you from appreciating him.
Pray for him.
Encourage him.
Support his family.
Help create a church culture where leaders can be honest, accountable, and cared for without being idolized.
Because pastors are not machines.
They get tired.
They experience grief.
They face temptation.
They need friendship, correction, prayer, and grace just like the people they serve.
The goal is not to humiliate pastors.
The goal is to honor Christ.
And sometimes honoring Christ means confronting what has become normal in His name.
So would Jesus approve of pastors living like celebrities?
The most biblically faithful answer is this:

Jesus does not condemn a pastor merely for being well-known, financially provided for, or entrusted with a large ministry. But He unmistakably condemns pride, greed, exploitation, hypocrisy, self-exaltation, and leadership that seeks privilege instead of serving God's people.
We cannot claim to know His judgment about every pastor's bank account, home, vehicle, or personal circumstances.
We can, however, examine the standards He has already revealed in Scripture.
Does the pastor preach the Gospel faithfully?
Does his conduct reflect Christlike character?
Are finances handled honestly and transparently?
Are vulnerable people protected?
Is correction possible?
Are generosity and service evident?
Is the congregation being discipled to follow Jesus or conditioned to depend upon a personality?
And perhaps the question that reveals the most:
If the pastor's name disappeared from every advertisement tomorrow, would the ministry still have a reason to exist?
Because a truly Christ-centered ministry does not collapse spiritually when a human personality steps out of the spotlight.
Its foundation is not a celebrity.
Its foundation is Jesus Christ.
Now I want to speak to the person who has been reading this with a heavy heart.
Maybe you are not a pastor.
Maybe you are not wealthy.
Maybe nobody knows your name outside your family, workplace, or neighborhood.
You have been serving God quietly for years.
You have given what you could.
You have prayed when nobody noticed.
You have cared for people who never thanked you.
You have wondered whether your small acts of obedience matter in a world obsessed with visibility.
They do.
Jesus sees what human applause overlooks.
He knows the widow's generosity.
He knows the exhausted father's prayers.
He knows the believer who chooses integrity when compromise would be profitable.
He knows the church volunteer who cleans the floor after the crowd has gone home.
He knows the pastor who refuses to exploit people even when doing so could make him rich.
And the God who sees in secret is not confused about what faithfulness looks like.
You do not have to become famous to become fruitful.
You do not have to become wealthy to become generous.
You do not have to be publicly celebrated to be deeply loved by God.
And you do not have to impress Jesus to receive His grace.
You need Him.
We all do.
Because the temptation to seek glory is not confined to celebrity pastors.
It lives in ordinary hearts too.
We want to be noticed.
We want to be admired.
We want people to recognize our sacrifices.
Sometimes even our acts of service become opportunities to seek praise.
That is why this conversation must end not with pointing fingers, but with examining ourselves before God.
Lord, where have I loved recognition more than obedience?
Where have I confused worldly success with spiritual maturity?
Where have I placed a human leader on a pedestal that belongs only to You?
Where have I failed to love the people You placed in front of me?
And where do I need to repent?
The answer is not simply to become less impressed with famous pastors.
The answer is to become more captivated by Jesus.
His holiness.
His humility.
His compassion.
His sacrifice.
His resurrection.
His grace toward repentant sinners.
That is the Gospel worth proclaiming.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture another Christian celebrity.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to sell you access to God.
But to keep pointing people back to the Word of God and the Savior who changes lives.
If this message exposed something you have been struggling to express, I would love to hear from you.
Let the conversation become a place for honest reflection, prayer, biblical encouragement, and testimony rather than personal attacks or unverified accusations.
Because the Church needs discernment.
But it also needs healing.
And perhaps someone on your Facebook friends list desperately needs this reminder.
Someone who has walked away from church after being hurt.
Someone who has mistaken a pastor's failure for God's failure.
Someone who loves Jesus but has become confused by Christian celebrity culture.
Someone who needs to know that Christ has not abandoned His people.
Not merely to create engagement, but because biblical truth is worth passing on.
There is also a deeper way to walk alongside this mission.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
Those resources matter because spiritual growth should not depend on a person's ability to purchase expensive materials.
A struggling believer deserves access to biblical encouragement.
A young Christian deserves opportunities to study Scripture.
A family seeking to grow in faith deserves resources that point them toward Christ.
That is why the free resources remain an important part of the mission.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding a ministry also involves real costs.
Writing, editing, preparing resources, maintaining a library, developing new discipleship materials, and reaching more people all require time, effort, and financial support.
Not because God needs your money.
And certainly not because giving to Gospel Warrior guarantees financial blessings.
Support should never be purchased through guilt, fear, or spiritual pressure.
It should come from a willing heart.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your first responsibility is to steward what God has entrusted to you faithfully, care for your household, and honor your commitments, including appropriate support for your local church.
But it can be a voluntary monthly ministry offering—a practical way to help sustain and expand Gospel-centered work beyond your local church.
And that distinction matters.
Because this very article has warned against ministries that manipulate generosity.
We cannot call others to biblical integrity while using spiritual pressure to raise support ourselves.
Let your contribution become an expression of generosity, partnership, and stewardship.
Not an attempt to purchase God's approval.
These products are not the Gospel.
They cannot make anyone holier.
They are simply practical resources and reminders that can accompany a life of faith.
If that is a mission you believe in and you are financially able to participate, you are warmly invited to join us.
You can still pray.
You can still encourage someone who is struggling.
You can still use the free resources to grow in your faith.
Your worth before God is not measured by a monthly payment.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by purchasing religious access, accumulating spiritual achievements, or contributing to a particular organization (Ephesians 2:8–9).
That truth must remain nonnegotiable.
Because if Gospel Warrior ever becomes more interested in building its own name than proclaiming the name of Jesus, it will have forgotten the very message it was created to share.
And that brings us back to the beginning.
Jesus entering the church.
The cameras.
The lights.
The reserved seats.
The applause.
The pastor.
The struggling mother.
The lonely elderly man.
The wounded believer.
But imagine a different ending.
Imagine that the pastor notices the struggling mother and quietly makes sure she receives help.
Imagine the elderly man being welcomed as someone precious rather than overlooked as someone unimportant.
Imagine the wounded believer being treated with patience, compassion, and truth.
Imagine the pastor refusing to be treated as a spiritual celebrity because he understands that his calling is to serve.
Imagine a congregation so captivated by Christ that the loudest celebration is not reserved for a famous preacher's arrival, but for the grace of God that brings a sinner to repentance.
Imagine a church where success is measured not only by attendance and income, but by faithfulness, discipleship, generosity, integrity, and love.
A church where the wealthy are welcomed without favoritism.
Where the poor are honored without being used as publicity.
Where pastors are supported without being worshiped.
Where accountability is normal.
Where the wounded are heard.
Where the Gospel is proclaimed without compromise.
And where Jesus is not merely mentioned during the service.
He is the reason for everything.
That kind of church will never be perfect on this side of eternity.
But it can be faithful.
It can repent when it fails.
It can turn away from pride.
It can reject exploitation.
It can return to the Word.
It can remember whose blood purchased the flock.
And it can become a living witness that the kingdom of God operates differently from the kingdoms of this world.
So the next time you see a pastor surrounded by celebrity treatment, do not immediately condemn him based on appearances.
But do not automatically defend everything either.
Open your Bible.
Examine the fruit.
Ask honest questions.
Remember the vulnerable.
Pray for discernment.
And refuse to give any human being the devotion that belongs to Christ.

Because when the final applause fades, when the cameras turn off, when the buildings age, when the crowds disperse, and when every earthly title loses its importance, only one name will remain worthy of ultimate worship.
Jesus.
The One who washed feet.
The One who welcomed sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls proud hearts to repentance and broken hearts to grace.
And the One who can rewrite even the ugliest story of spiritual pride, betrayal, and failure through genuine repentance, forgiveness, truth, and transformation.
The greatest tragedy is not that a pastor might become famous—it is that Jesus could become a stranger in a church built in His name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EVEN THE DEMONS BELIEVE—AND SHUDDER: THE TERRIFYING DIFFERENCE BETWEEN KNOWING JESUS AND BELONGING TO HIM
paragraphs: EVEN THE DEMONS BELIEVE—AND SHUDDER: THE TERRIFYING DIFFERENCE BETWEEN KNOWING JESUS AND BELONGING TO HIM

You can believe that God exists, know the Bible, attend church, defend Christianity, and still miss the very Savior you claim to follow. James 2:19 exposes a truth that should awaken every comfortable Christian: saving faith is more than knowing who Jesus is.
There is a terrifying possibility that many people sitting in church every Sunday have never seriously considered.
You could spend your entire life believing the right things about Jesus… and still never surrender your life to Him.
You could know the worship songs.
You could quote Scripture when someone needs encouragement.
You could defend the resurrection, believe in heaven and hell, and confidently tell people that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
You could even be the person everyone calls when they need prayer.
And yet, beneath the religious vocabulary, the Christian reputation, and the familiar Sunday routine, there could be a question you have spent years avoiding.
Do I actually belong to the Jesus I say I believe in?
Because there is a verse in the Bible that tears through the illusion that knowing religious truth is the same as possessing saving faith.
It is short.
Uncomfortably short.
And once you understand what it actually says, you may never read your own profession of faith quite the same way again.
James 2:19 declares:
“Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.” — James 2:19, KJV
Read that again.
The demons believe.
And they tremble.
They are not atheists.
They are not confused about whether God exists.
They do not need another philosophical argument proving that the supernatural is real.
They know.
And still, they remain enemies of God.
That should disturb every person who has quietly confused agreement with the truth for surrender to the Truth Himself.
But before you turn this verse into a weapon against somebody else's spiritual life, allow it to do something far more necessary.
Allow it to examine yours.
Because the most dangerous deception is not always the lie that says God does not exist.
Sometimes it is the lie that whispers, Because I believe God exists, everything must be right between us.
And that is precisely where James refuses to let us hide.
In the original Greek, James 2:19 reads:
“σὺ πιστεύεις ὅτι εἷς ἐστιν ὁ θεός· καλῶς ποιεῖς· καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιστεύουσιν καὶ φρίσσουσιν.”
A close translation is:
“You believe that God is one. You do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder.”
Notice what James is actually addressing.
He is not criticizing the doctrine that God is one.
He is affirming its truth while exposing the inadequacy of mere intellectual agreement.
The phrase “εἷς ἐστιν ὁ θεός” means “God is one,” echoing Israel's foundational confession in Deuteronomy 6:4:
“שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד”
Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai Echad.
“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.” — Deuteronomy 6:4, KJV
This was no insignificant religious statement.
It was central to Israel's covenant identity.
Yet James confronts a devastating possibility: someone can affirm a profoundly true doctrine without responding to God in genuine, living faith.
The Greek verb πιστεύουσιν (pisteuousin) means “they believe.”
James deliberately uses the language of belief for the demons, making his argument impossible to dismiss.
The verb φρίσσουσιν (phrissousin) means “they shudder” or “they tremble,” expressing a reaction of dread.
The demons possess knowledge.
They recognize divine authority.
They experience terror.
But none of that constitutes the repentant, trusting allegiance to God that James is defending.
And here is what makes the passage so searching.
It is possible to react emotionally to the truth of God without being reconciled to God.
You can cry during worship and still refuse to forgive someone.
You can feel convicted by a sermon and still cling to the sin God is calling you to confess.
You can be frightened by the thought of judgment and still refuse the mercy offered in Jesus Christ.
You can even feel deeply moved by this article and return to the very life you were being called to leave behind.
Tears are not necessarily repentance.
Fear is not necessarily faith.
Religious knowledge is not necessarily spiritual life.
And emotional intensity is not necessarily surrender.
