It is the story of God taking sin with such seriousness, and loving sinners with such astonishing grace, that Christ gave Himself for our redemption.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we had cleaned up every failure.
Not after we had finally made ourselves worthy.
Christ died for sinners.
And this is where the Gospel confronts us with a truth that is both humbling and beautiful.
Before we ask how God could command us to pray for our enemies, we must remember that His grace reached us when we ourselves needed reconciliation.
Romans 5:10 speaks of being reconciled to God through the death of His Son while we were enemies.
That does not make your abuser's actions acceptable.
It does not equate every human offense with every other offense.
It does not minimize your suffering.
But it does remind every Christian that the mercy we have received in Christ is the mercy we are called to reflect.
Not perfectly.
Not effortlessly.
Not by pretending.
But by the power of the Holy Spirit working within us.
And perhaps that is where you are struggling tonight.
You want to obey Jesus.
But you are exhausted.
You want to forgive.
But the memories keep returning.
You want to pray.
But every time you try, you remember another lie, another betrayal, another moment when you needed someone to protect you and nobody came.
So your prayer gets stuck somewhere between your heart and your lips.
And you wonder whether God is disappointed in you.
Listen carefully.
The Psalms give God's people language for grief, anger, fear, and cries for justice.
Psalm 13 begins with David asking how long the Lord will seem to forget him.
Psalm 55 describes the agony of betrayal by someone who had been a close companion.
Psalm 10 cries out against the arrogance and violence of the wicked.
Scripture does not require wounded people to pretend they are emotionally untouched.
It teaches them to bring their pain honestly before God.
You do not have to manufacture feelings you do not possess.
You can begin with the truth.
Jesus, I know what You commanded.
But I am struggling.
I don't want to pray for this person.
I am angry.
I am tired.
I am afraid of being hurt again.
Please help me obey You without pretending the evil was acceptable.
Protect me.
Protect others.
Bring what is hidden into the light.
Lead this person to genuine repentance.
And heal the places in me that still ache.
That is a meaningful beginning.
Not because the prayer is eloquent.
But because it is honest.
And honest surrender is better than religious performance.
There is a difference between saying, "Lord, I surrender my right to revenge," and saying, "Lord, I will allow this person to keep hurting me."
The first can be an act of faith.
The second may be a dangerous misunderstanding of faith.
There is also a difference between forgiveness and reconciliation.
Forgiveness concerns our response to wrongdoing and our refusal to nurture personal vengeance.
Reconciliation concerns the restoration of a relationship.
And healthy reconciliation requires truth.
Where trust has been broken, rebuilding it normally requires accountability, changed behavior, and time.
Luke 17:3 says:
"Take heed to yourselves: If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him." (KJV)
Notice that Jesus explicitly includes rebuke.
He does not treat confronting sin as incompatible with love.
And He does not portray repentance as meaningless.

Christians understand the relationship between forgiveness and repentance in different ways, especially regarding inward forgiveness before an offender repents. Yet Scripture clearly distinguishes the command to love enemies from the restoration of trust and fellowship.
You can maintain a forgiving disposition and pray for someone without declaring a damaged relationship safe.
You can refuse revenge while refusing renewed access.
You can hope for repentance while recognizing that repentance has not yet occurred.
And if genuine repentance does come, wisdom still matters.
A spoken apology does not automatically undo years of destructive behavior.
Trust should not be demanded as proof of forgiveness.
It must be rebuilt through truthfulness and consistent change.
Think of Joseph.
Betrayed by his brothers.
Sold into slavery.
Separated from his father.
Forced to live with consequences he never deserved.
Years later, when those brothers stood before him in Egypt, Joseph possessed extraordinary power over their lives.
He could have destroyed them.
Instead, he ultimately extended mercy.
But the account in Genesis 42–45 also shows that Joseph did not immediately reveal himself or restore the relationship without examining how his brothers would respond.
The story is not a universal formula for every broken relationship.
It is a profound witness that mercy, wisdom, and accountability can coexist.
And later, in Genesis 50:20, Joseph told his brothers:
"But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." (KJV)
Joseph did not say their intentions were good.
He named their intentions as evil.
Yet he recognized that God had worked through the suffering to preserve many lives.
This is one of the most powerful truths in the entire Bible.
God's ability to redeem what happened does not mean He approved of what happened.
The betrayal was evil.
The injustice was real.
The suffering mattered.
And God was still able to bring good out of it.
Perhaps someone needs that truth today.
Because you've been looking at the wreckage of your life and wondering whether the damage is too deep for God to restore anything beautiful.
Perhaps a marriage has collapsed.
Perhaps a friendship has become a battlefield.
Perhaps family members have turned against you.
Perhaps someone used the language of Christianity to manipulate you into silence.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to earn love from someone who keeps using your compassion against you.
And now you're afraid that setting a boundary means you've stopped being Christlike.
But Jesus did not die to make you a prisoner of another person's unrepentant sin.
He came to save sinners, reconcile us to God, and make us new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
This promise is not a guarantee that every earthly relationship will be repaired.
It is the glorious announcement that those who belong to Christ receive new life in Him.
And that new life changes how we respond to suffering.
We no longer need to become the very thing that wounded us.
We no longer need to repay cruelty with cruelty.
We no longer need to let another person's sin determine the condition of our souls.
We can pursue justice without worshiping revenge.
We can seek safety without surrendering compassion.
We can pray for repentance without pretending repentance has occurred.
We can grieve honestly and still trust God.
And when our strength is insufficient, we can ask the Holy Spirit to produce what we cannot manufacture on our own.
Because loving an enemy is not a performance designed to prove that you are spiritually superior.
It is a costly expression of obedience to the Savior who first loved us.
And sometimes it begins with the smallest prayer imaginable.
Lord, I cannot change their heart.
But please don't let them destroy mine.
There may be someone reading this who needs to hear something else.
Perhaps you are not the wounded person in this story.
Perhaps you are the one who has been doing the wounding.
Perhaps you have been excusing your cruelty because the people around you keep forgiving you.
Perhaps you have used the patience of a spouse, the loyalty of a friend, the trust of a child, or the kindness of a fellow believer as permission to continue behaving in ways that dishonor Christ.
If that is you, do not mistake another person's mercy for God's approval of your conduct.
Do not demand forgiveness while refusing accountability.
Do not quote Scripture to silence the person you harmed.
Do not call their boundaries bitterness simply because those boundaries prevent you from continuing the same behavior.
The Gospel does not invite you to hide behind religious language.
It calls you to repentance.

The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," refers to a change of mind or turning, and in the New Testament its meaning includes a changed response to God that bears fruit in life.
Jesus said in Luke 3:8:
"Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance." (KJV)
Real repentance is not merely being sorry that consequences arrived.
It involves turning away from sin.
Confessing truthfully.
Accepting responsibility.
Making appropriate restitution where possible.
And demonstrating change rather than demanding instant trust.
The same grace that welcomes sinners also teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that connection unmistakable.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is God's gift that brings salvation and trains us toward godliness.
That is the heart of our message.
Not because the scandal never happened.
Not because the wounds were imaginary.
Not because accountability is unnecessary.
But because the finished work of Jesus Christ means sin and suffering do not have to write the final chapter of a redeemed life.
The cross speaks forgiveness.
The resurrection declares victory.
And the Gospel calls both the wounded and the guilty to come to Jesus, though the response required of each may be very different.
To the wounded, Christ offers His presence, His compassion, His truth, and the hope of healing.
To the unrepentant, Christ calls for confession, surrender, and a genuine turning away from sin.
To every sinner who comes to Him in faith, the Gospel announces forgiveness and new life through His death and resurrection.
And to all of us, Jesus says:
Not your bitterness.
Not your fear.
Not your desire for revenge.
Not the pressure of people who misunderstand your pain.
Maybe that means you need to stop rehearsing imaginary arguments and begin praying for God to guard your heart.
Maybe it means you need to tell someone trustworthy what has been happening behind closed doors.
Maybe it means reporting a serious wrong instead of covering it up.
Maybe it means apologizing to someone you have harmed.
Maybe it means accepting that you cannot force another person to repent.
Maybe it means finally understanding that you are not responsible for rescuing someone from every consequence of their choices.
Or maybe it means kneeling beside your bed tonight and whispering the hardest words you have ever prayed:
Father, I place this person in Your hands.
I do not excuse what they have done.
I do not ask You to bless their wrongdoing.
I ask You to stop the evil, protect the innocent, and bring genuine repentance.
And I surrender my desire to take revenge.
Heal me, Lord.
Not so I can pretend nothing happened.
But so that what happened does not become the ruler of my life.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, you will begin to understand the difference between peace and denial.
Peace does not require you to rewrite the past.
It invites you to entrust your future to Christ.
Now, before you leave this message, I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Who is harder for you to pray for: the person who hurt you and walked away, or the person who continues hurting you while expecting you to forgive them?
You don't have to expose anyone's identity or reveal details that could put you at risk.
But perhaps your honest answer could help another believer realize they are not alone in this struggle.
These aren't magic words.
They are simply opportunities to speak honestly, ask for prayer, and encourage one another to keep looking to Christ.
And perhaps your testimony of God's faithfulness will remind them that healing is possible even when circumstances have not yet changed.
Not because you need another article in your collection.
But because there may come a night when anger returns, when an old memory opens, or when someone tries to convince you that biblical forgiveness requires you to tolerate continued harm.
On that night, remember what Scripture actually says.
Love your enemies.
Pray for those who persecute you.
Do not repay evil with evil.
Leave ultimate vengeance to God.
Seek what is right.
Protect the vulnerable.
Walk in truth.
And follow Jesus.
Because faith was never meant to be reduced to an occasional inspirational quote.
We need to be rooted in the Word.
We need to understand Scripture in context.
We need to recognize the difference between biblical truth and religious manipulation.
We need the courage to confront sin, the humility to repent, the wisdom to establish righteous boundaries, and the grace to love people without approving of their wrongdoing.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God's favor can be purchased.
But because faithful Gospel ministry requires people who are willing, able, and joyful in supporting its work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from the heart, not from compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It can be one meaningful expression of generosity and stewardship.
These items are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage biblical reflection, spiritual growth, and conversations about faith.
And there is more.
The invitation to grow in God's Word is open.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone to read the Scriptures for themselves.
Because the goal is not merely to grow an audience.
It is to point people to Jesus Christ.
The Savior who forgives sinners.
The Lord who calls us to repentance.
The Shepherd who does not abandon His people.
The risen King who will one day judge evil with perfect righteousness and make all things new.
And as we wait for that day, we are called to reflect His character in a world where hatred often seems easier than holiness.
So let me leave you with one final picture.
Imagine standing before Jesus with every wound you've carried.
Every betrayal.
Every false accusation.
Every night you cried where nobody could hear you.
Every prayer you struggled to pray.
Every moment you wanted revenge but chose to entrust judgment to God.
And imagine discovering that none of those tears were invisible to Him.
Psalm 56:8 speaks poetically of God taking account of David's wanderings and tears.
The Lord is not indifferent to the suffering of His people.
He knows.
He sees.
He judges rightly.
And through Christ, He gives hope beyond what human cruelty can destroy.
You may never receive the apology you deserved.
You may never see the repentance you prayed for.
You may never regain everything that was taken from you in this life.
But the person who wounded you does not have authority to determine the final meaning of your story.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And His grace is greater than the power of your past to define who you are in Him.
So yes, pray for your enemies.
Even the ones who continue doing harm.
Pray that God will stop their evil.
Pray that truth will be revealed.
Pray that justice will be done.
Pray that they will repent and find mercy in Christ.
Pray that the innocent will be protected.
And pray that your own heart will remain anchored in the Savior who loved you first.
Because the deepest victory is not watching the person who hurt you finally break. It is watching Jesus keep your heart from becoming what hurt you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS KNEW JUDAS WOULD BETRAY HIM. SO WHY DID HE LET HIM STAY?
paragraphs: JESUS KNEW JUDAS WOULD BETRAY HIM. SO WHY DID HE LET HIM STAY?

He knew who would sell Him. He knew the price. He knew the kiss was coming. Yet Jesus still washed Judas’ feet, shared His table, and allowed him to remain among the Twelve. The reason is more heartbreaking—and more revealing about the heart of Christ—than most people realize.
There is something deeply unsettling about the story of Judas Iscariot.
Not simply that a man betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver.
Not simply that someone who witnessed miracles, heard the greatest Teacher who ever lived, and walked beside the Son of God could eventually hand Him over to His enemies.
It is something even more disturbing.
Jesus knew.
Before the betrayal.
Before the secret negotiations.
Before the silver changed hands.
Before Judas entered the garden with armed men.
Jesus already knew what was living inside the heart of the man sitting at His table.
And still, He let Judas stay.
Think about that for a moment.

If you knew someone close to you would eventually destroy your reputation, expose you to your enemies, and participate in a plot that would cost you your life, would you continue inviting that person into your home?
Would you share your food?
Would you let that person travel with you, listen to your private conversations, and remain among your closest companions?
Most of us would begin creating distance the moment we discovered the truth.
We would protect ourselves.
We would close the door.
We might even tell everyone what that person was planning.
But Jesus did something that confronts nearly everything we understand about betrayal, patience, love, and divine mercy.
He allowed Judas to remain close enough to betray Him.
And if we misunderstand why, we may misunderstand something essential about the Gospel itself.
Because the story of Judas is not merely about a traitor who sold Jesus.
It is also about the terrifying possibility of being physically close to Christ while remaining spiritually far from Him.
And it raises a question that should make every believer examine their own heart:
What if the most dangerous place to be is not outside the church, but inside it—close enough to know the language of faith, yet unwilling to surrender to the Lord of faith?
The Gospel of John gives us an extraordinary detail.
Jesus said:
“Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:70, KJV).
John immediately explains that Jesus was speaking about Judas Iscariot, the one who would betray Him.
This was not a sudden discovery on the night of the Last Supper.
John 6:64 tells us that Jesus knew from the beginning who did not believe and who would betray Him.
The Greek text says:
ᾔδει γὰρ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Ēdei gar ex archēs ho Iēsous.
“For Jesus knew from the beginning.”

The phrase ex archēs means “from the beginning.” In this context, it emphasizes that Judas’ unbelief and future betrayal were not hidden from Jesus. It does not require us to assume that every event in Judas’ life had already been described in detail to the other disciples.
Jesus was not deceived into choosing Judas.
He was not blindsided by a trusted companion.
He did not discover the betrayal when Judas finally walked into Gethsemane.
He knew.
But knowing that Judas would betray Him did not mean Jesus Himself caused Judas to become a betrayer.
That distinction matters.
God's foreknowledge does not make Him the author of human evil. Scripture holds Judas accountable for his actions even while showing that Christ's suffering fulfilled God's redemptive purpose.
In Acts 2:23, Peter declares that Jesus was delivered up according to God's determined counsel and foreknowledge, yet those responsible for crucifying Him remained morally accountable.
Divine sovereignty did not turn human wickedness into innocence.
And God's ability to accomplish redemption through betrayal did not make betrayal righteous.
This is where the story begins to become painfully personal.
Because many of us have quietly asked God questions we are almost ashamed to speak aloud.
“Lord, if You knew that person would hurt me, why did You allow them into my life?”
“If You knew that friendship would end in betrayal, why did You let me trust them?”
“If You knew that relationship would break my heart, why didn't You stop it before it began?”
Those questions are real.
And the story of Judas does not give us permission to pretend that every betrayal has a simple explanation.

It certainly does not mean Christians should knowingly remain in abusive or dangerous relationships. Jesus' voluntary journey toward the cross was a unique act of redemption, not a command for victims to abandon healthy boundaries or personal safety.
But it does reveal something astonishing.
Jesus was never helpless before the betrayal that would lead Him to the cross.
He willingly moved toward the suffering He had come to bear.
In John 10:18, Jesus says of His life:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.”
Judas would betray Him.
Religious leaders would condemn Him.
Roman authorities would crucify Him.
Yet none of these events meant that Jesus had lost control of His mission.
The cross was not an emergency solution to a plan that had gone wrong.
It was central to the saving purpose of God.
And Judas, despite his wicked intentions, could not overturn that purpose.
But here is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Jesus did not merely tolerate Judas from a distance.
He gave him a place among the Twelve.
Judas traveled with the disciples.
He heard Jesus teach about forgiveness, hypocrisy, repentance, the kingdom of God, and the danger of loving money.
He witnessed the ministry of the One whom he would eventually betray.
He was even entrusted with the group's moneybag.
John 12:6 tells us that Judas was a thief who used to take what was put into it.
Consider the contradiction.
The man entrusted with the money was secretly stealing.
The man traveling with the Truth was living a lie.
The man who heard Jesus warn against serving both God and money was allowing greed to occupy his heart.
And somehow, outward religious participation continued.
That should disturb us.
Because Judas did not begin his public life as a man standing outside the circle of discipleship shouting against Jesus.
He was inside.
He belonged to the visible company of the Twelve.
He could speak the language.
He knew the routines.
He had access to the ministry.
And when Jesus announced that one of them would betray Him, the disciples did not immediately point to Judas.
They began questioning who it could be.
A person can become so familiar with the activities of Christianity that everyone assumes their heart belongs to Christ.
But familiarity is not the same as faith.
Ministry is not the same as surrender.
Religious responsibility is not the same as spiritual transformation.
You can carry a Bible and still refuse its authority.
You can sing about the cross and still resist the One who died upon it.
You can defend Christian truth in public while secretly protecting sin in private.
And this is why the story of Judas must never become an opportunity for us to feel superior to him.
It should drive us toward honest self-examination.
Not because every struggling Christian is secretly Judas.
Not because every temptation proves someone has never truly believed.
But because the human heart is capable of astonishing self-deception.
The question is not merely whether we have spent time around Jesus.
The question is whether we have truly come to Him in repentance and faith.
And then comes one of the most emotionally powerful scenes in all of Scripture.
The night before the crucifixion.
A room.
A meal.
Twelve disciples.
And Jesus, knowing that His hour had come, rose from supper.
He laid aside His outer garments.
He took a towel.
He poured water into a basin.
And He began washing the disciples' feet.
Try to picture the room.
The Lord of glory kneeling before ordinary men.
The hands that had touched lepers now touching dusty feet.
The One through whom all things were made taking the position of a servant.
And Judas was there.
John 13:2 tells us that the devil had already put betrayal into Judas' heart. John then describes Jesus washing the disciples' feet before identifying Judas as the betrayer later in the chapter.

The natural reading is that Judas was present for the foot washing and was included in this astonishing act of humility, although John does not narrate a separate moment in which Jesus specifically washes Judas' feet.
That distinction is worth preserving.
We do not need to invent details to make Scripture powerful.
What John actually tells us is already overwhelming.
Jesus knew what was coming.
And Jesus served.
He did not stop being the perfect Servant because a betrayer was present.
He did not abandon His character because someone else had abandoned faithfulness.
His humility was not dependent upon the worthiness of the people around Him.
This does not mean Jesus approved of Judas' betrayal.
It means the coming betrayal did not change who Jesus was.
And perhaps that is one of the most beautiful truths hidden in this terrible night.
The sinfulness of the people around Jesus never made Jesus less holy, less truthful, or less faithful to the Father's will.
But we must be careful here.
The foot washing was not merely a sentimental gesture.
Jesus was teaching His disciples the nature of humble service and the cleansing they needed from Him.
When Peter resisted, Jesus answered:
“If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.” (John 13:8, KJV).
And then Jesus said something chilling:
“Ye are clean, but not all.” (John 13:10, KJV).
John explains that Jesus said this because He knew who would betray Him.
In other words, a man could be present while Jesus washed feet and still remain spiritually unclean.
Physical proximity did not guarantee inward cleansing.
Participation in a sacred moment did not automatically produce saving faith.
And this is where the story reaches beyond Judas and into our own lives.
There are people who know how to look devoted while privately drifting away.
People who still attend worship but have stopped praying honestly.
People who serve in ministry while carrying secret bitterness.
People who can encourage everyone else while slowly losing their own hunger for God.
Some are fighting sin and desperately longing to return.
Others have learned to protect sin while maintaining a religious appearance.
Those are not the same spiritual condition.
And Jesus knows the difference.
He does not despise the broken believer who comes confessing sin.
First John 1:9 assures us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
But Scripture also warns against hardening our hearts through the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13).
The danger is not that a wounded Christian struggles.
The danger is learning to live comfortably with rebellion while refusing the mercy that calls us to repent.
Judas heard the warnings.
He saw the example.
He remained among the disciples.
Yet Scripture never portrays him as a repentant follower who entrusted himself to Christ for salvation.
And the darkness continued growing.
Then came the moment when betrayal took a definite price.
Matthew 26:14–16 records Judas approaching the chief priests and asking what they would give him to deliver Jesus into their hands.
They weighed out thirty pieces of silver.
Thirty pieces.
The exact purchasing power of that payment is difficult to translate into modern currency, and the Gospels do not specify the precise denomination of each coin.
But the spiritual horror does not depend on calculating its modern value.
Judas was willing to hand over his Master for money.
The tragedy was not that Jesus had suddenly become worth only thirty pieces of silver.
The tragedy was that Judas was willing to betray the priceless Son of God for something that could be counted.
And isn't that how sin often works?
It offers something measurable in exchange for something immeasurably precious.
A moment of pleasure in exchange for faithfulness.
A dishonest advantage in exchange for integrity.
A secret indulgence in exchange for a clear conscience.
A temporary reward in exchange for obedience to God.
Not every sinful compromise is equivalent to Judas' betrayal.
But the warning is unmistakable.
When we begin treating Christ as negotiable, we are walking into dangerous territory.
And still, Jesus moved toward the cross.
At the Last Supper, He announced that one of those eating with Him would betray Him.
Matthew 26:24 records His solemn warning:
“The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed!”
Do not miss the tension.
Jesus said His suffering would unfold as Scripture had foretold.
And in the same breath, He declared judgment upon the betrayer.
The betrayal was known.
The betrayal was wicked.
The betrayer was responsible.
Jesus' foreknowledge did not remove Judas' guilt.
And the fulfillment of Scripture did not excuse his choices.
In John 13:18, Jesus also invokes Psalm 41:9:
“He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.”
The Hebrew of Psalm 41:9 includes the expression:
הִגְדִּיל עָלַי עָקֵב
Higdil ʿalay ʿaqev.
Literally, the imagery concerns someone magnifying or raising a heel against another.
The language communicates treachery by someone once trusted.
In its original setting, Psalm 41 describes the pain of betrayal by a close companion. Jesus applies this Scripture to the betrayal He is about to experience.
This matters because the Bible does not treat betrayal as an insignificant inconvenience.
It recognizes the wound.
The pain of betrayal is not simply that an enemy opposed you.
It is that someone close enough to share your table became an instrument of harm.
Someone who knew your voice.
Someone who had seen your kindness.
Someone who had been welcomed into your confidence.
And perhaps that is why betrayal can hurt so deeply.
It attacks not only what happened, but what you believed was true about the relationship.
If you have ever been betrayed, you may know that peculiar grief.
You replay conversations.
You remember moments that once seemed genuine.
You wonder which smiles were sincere.
You begin questioning whether your own trust was foolish.
And sometimes the wound follows you into relationships with people who never harmed you.
But the Gospel gives us a Savior who is not unfamiliar with betrayal.
Hebrews 4:15 teaches that Jesus is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
He knows what it is to be rejected.
He knows what it is to be abandoned.
He knows what it is to be betrayed by someone who shared His table.
And He remained without sin.
That means you can bring your wounded heart to Him without having to explain why betrayal hurts.
He knows.
But there is another question we cannot avoid.
If Jesus knew Judas would betray Him, why didn't He remove him before the betrayal happened?
Scripture does not give us a private conversation in which Jesus explains every reason for allowing Judas to remain.
We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But Scripture does reveal enough to understand several essential truths.
Jesus' choice of the Twelve was made with full knowledge of Judas' future betrayal.
Jesus' death fulfilled the saving purpose of God.
The betrayal fulfilled Scripture without making Judas innocent.
And Jesus' continued ministry among the disciples revealed the consistency of His own righteousness, humility, and obedience.
Most importantly, Judas' betrayal did not create the Gospel.
Jesus' sacrificial death and victorious resurrection are the heart of the Gospel.
Judas was not the hero of redemption.
His sin was not a virtue.
And Christians should never praise betrayal as though wickedness were necessary goodness.
Rather, we worship a God so sovereign and holy that human evil cannot defeat His saving purpose.
What Judas intended for betrayal, God incorporated into the events through which Christ would accomplish redemption.
That does not make God the author of Judas' greed.
It makes the triumph of Christ all the more astonishing.
But the story does not end at the table.
It moves into the darkness of Gethsemane.
Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs.
And he has arranged a sign.
A kiss.
The ordinary gesture of greeting and affection becomes the signal of betrayal.
Matthew 26:49 records Judas approaching Jesus, greeting Him as Rabbi, and kissing Him.
Then Jesus says:
“Friend, wherefore art thou come?” (Matthew 26:50, KJV).
The Greek word translated “Friend” here is:
ἑταῖρε
Hetaire.
It is a form of address that can mean “companion,” “comrade,” or “friend,” depending on context.
It is not the same word as philos, the familiar Greek term often associated with personal affection.
That matters because we should not build an entire doctrine on the assumption that Jesus was expressing intimate friendship through this particular word.
Yet the scene remains extraordinary.
Jesus does not respond with uncontrolled rage.
He does not pretend the betrayal is harmless.
In Luke 22:48, He confronts Judas directly:
“Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?”
There is a terrible contrast in that question.
A kiss should communicate affection.
Judas used it to conceal treachery.
An outward expression of closeness became the instrument of surrendering Jesus to His enemies.
And the question almost seems to echo through the centuries.
How often do people offer God the outward signs of devotion while withholding their hearts?
How often do we speak lovingly about Jesus while resisting His commands?
How often do we want the reputation of being Christian without the surrender that following Christ requires?
This is not a call to become suspicious of every believer.
It is a call to stop confusing religious performance with genuine discipleship.
Jesus is not looking for a flawless performance.
He calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
He calls the weary to come to Him.
He calls the broken to receive His mercy.
But He also calls us to follow Him.
And following Him means we cannot make peace with the very sin He came to save us from.
Then comes another devastating part of Judas' story.
After Jesus was condemned, Matthew 27:3 says Judas experienced remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver.
The Greek verb used is:
μεταμεληθείς
Metamelētheis.
It conveys regret, remorse, or a change of feeling.
The New Testament also uses the word metanoia for repentance, a turning of mind and life toward God.
We should not oversimplify these words as though one always means false sorrow and the other always means genuine salvation. Their meanings can overlap depending on context.
But Matthew's account shows Judas' remorse ending in despair and death rather than describing a return to Jesus in trusting repentance.
Judas confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood.
He returned the money.
Yet he did not find the restoration that the Gospel later shows so powerfully in Peter.
And here is the comparison that should break our hearts.
Judas betrayed Jesus.
Peter denied Jesus.
Judas handed Jesus over to His enemies.
Peter publicly insisted that he did not know Him.
Both men sinned grievously.
Both experienced the crushing reality of what they had done.
But their stories moved in different directions.
Judas' story ends in tragedy.
Peter wept bitterly, and after the resurrection Jesus restored him.
In John 21, the risen Christ questioned Peter three times about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter's restoration was not because his sin had been small.
His denial was serious.
His restoration testified to the grace of the risen Savior.
And this contrast brings us to one of the most important truths in the entire story.
Your greatest hope is not that you have never failed Jesus. Your greatest hope is that Jesus saves sinners who turn to Him.
The answer to sin is not hiding.
It is not religious acting.
It is not trying to purchase forgiveness through good works.
It is repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Christ.
Second Corinthians 7:10 speaks of godly sorrow producing repentance leading to salvation, while worldly sorrow produces death.
The difference is not merely how intensely someone feels guilty.
The question is where that sorrow leads.
Does it drive us into hopelessness?
Or does it bring us honestly before the mercy of God?
Maybe you are reading this with something hidden in your life.
A habit nobody knows about.
A compromise you keep promising to abandon.
A prayer life that has quietly disappeared.
A relationship with God that looks healthy to everyone else but feels frighteningly distant to you.
Perhaps you still post Bible verses.
Perhaps you still attend church.
Perhaps you still encourage others.
But deep inside, you know there is something you have refused to surrender.
Please hear this carefully.
Do not confuse the patience of God with His approval of your sin.
Second Peter 3:9 teaches that the Lord is patient, not wishing that any should perish but that all should reach repentance.
His patience is not permission to remain in rebellion.
It is a reason to turn to Him while the call to repentance is before you.
And do not allow the story of Judas to convince you that your sin has placed you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
Judas' story is a warning.
It is not a declaration that every person who has failed terribly must share his end.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
That is a promise worth holding onto.
If you come to Christ, you are not approaching a Savior who reluctantly tolerates repentant sinners.
You are coming to the One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One who carried our sins in His body on the tree.
The One who shed His blood for the forgiveness of sins.
The One who rose again and lives forever.
And perhaps you need to hear this tonight:
You do not have to keep pretending.
You do not have to polish your spiritual appearance before coming to Jesus.
You do not have to wait until your life looks impressive.
Come honestly.
Confess what is wrong.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally earned their way into God's presence.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And that changes everything.
Someone reading silently may need to know that repentance, forgiveness, and a new beginning are real.
Because the story of Judas does not simply ask us to look backward at one man's betrayal.
It asks us to look inward.
And then upward.
Toward the Savior who was betrayed, condemned, crucified, buried, and raised in victory.
The cross tells us that our sin is more serious than we want to admit.
But it also tells us that God's grace in Jesus Christ is greater than we could ever deserve.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse sin.
He bore sin.
He did not declare evil harmless.
He suffered to redeem sinners from its guilt and power.
He did not come merely to improve our religious appearance.
He came to reconcile us to God.
And that is why this story belongs to the Gospel rather than merely to the history of betrayal.
Judas shows us the tragedy of remaining close to holy things without surrendering to the Holy One. Jesus shows us the mercy of God reaching toward sinners through the cross.
One warns us.
The Other saves us.
And the invitation remains open to everyone who hears His voice and comes to Him in faith.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious stories that disappear from memory by tomorrow.
Not to build a community that confuses emotional reactions with spiritual transformation.
But to keep placing the truth of Scripture before real people facing real battles.
People struggling with temptation.
People rebuilding their faith.
People carrying wounds from betrayal.
People who have been away from God for years.
People who need more than another inspirational sentence.
They need the Word of God.
They need the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
They need encouragement that leads toward obedience, repentance, forgiveness, and genuine discipleship.
And if these messages have helped you understand Scripture, confront sin, or find courage to return to Christ, I want to invite you to help us continue.
But let us be biblically clear.
It does not purchase His favor.
It does not replace your responsibility to care for your family, give faithfully according to your convictions, or support your local church.
And it should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
We want support that flows from love for Christ and a genuine desire to help others grow in Him—not guilt, fear, or pressure.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, personal discipleship tools, or meaningful gifts for people you love.
It is participating in the work of making Christ known.
We want the Word of God to remain accessible to people who are hungry for truth, including those who cannot afford to give financially.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Think of the friend who quietly stopped attending church.
The brother who is losing hope.
The sister who has been wounded by betrayal.
The parent praying for a wandering child.
The person who appears strong but is secretly struggling with sin.
Someone in your circle may need to hear that Jesus knows the truth about the human heart—and still calls sinners to come to Him.
Because we do not want people merely to read about Jesus.
We want people to know Him.
To repent.
To believe.
To grow.
To endure.
To experience the transforming grace of God.
And now, before you leave this story, return with me to that upper room one final time.
Jesus is at the table.
The disciples are gathered.
Judas is still there.
The cross is approaching.
Jesus knows the betrayal is coming.
And He continues toward the Father's will.
Not because Judas is stronger than Him.
Not because the darkness has won.
Not because God has lost control.
But because Jesus has come to accomplish a redemption no betrayal can defeat.
In a matter of hours, Judas will hand Him over.
The disciples will scatter.
Peter will deny Him.
Jesus will be condemned.
And the One who never sinned will bear the sins of many.
But three days after His burial, the tomb will be empty.
Death will not hold Him.
The betrayal will not have the final word.
The cross will not be the end.
Jesus Christ will rise.
And the risen Savior will continue calling sinners out of darkness into His marvelous light.
So perhaps the most important question tonight is not simply why Jesus allowed Judas to stay among the Twelve.
Perhaps it is this:
Now that you know Jesus sees the truth about your heart, what will you do with His call to repentance and faith?
Will you continue hiding behind appearances?
Will you keep negotiating with the sin that is pulling you away from Him?
Or will you come honestly to the One who gave His life to save sinners?
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every failure.
You cannot return to the moments before your worst decisions.
But through Jesus Christ, forgiveness is real.
Redemption is real.
A transformed life is possible.
And your past does not have to be the final chapter of your story.
Judas stood close enough to kiss the face of Jesus and still walked into darkness. Today, don't settle for being close to the things of Christ when Christ Himself is calling you to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WAS TAKEN INTO A KING’S HAREM, PREPARED FOR TWELVE MONTHS, AND GIVEN ONE NIGHT TO BE CHOSEN—BUT GOD WAS WRITING A STORY NO KING COULD CONTROL
paragraphs: SHE WAS TAKEN INTO A KING’S HAREM, PREPARED FOR TWELVE MONTHS, AND GIVEN ONE NIGHT TO BE CHOSEN—BUT GOD WAS WRITING A STORY NO KING COULD CONTROL

Before Esther ever wore a crown, she entered a palace where young women were evaluated by their beauty and their future depended on a king’s approval. But behind the perfume, the luxury, and the royal doors was a story about power, vulnerability, hidden providence, and a God who can bring redemption out of circumstances nobody would have chosen.
Imagine being taken from the only life you knew.
Not because you committed a crime.
Not because you volunteered for an opportunity.
But because someone more powerful than you decided that your appearance made you suitable for a king.
You are young. Your future is uncertain. Your family cannot simply walk through the palace gates and bring you home.
And now strangers are preparing your body for a man whose decision could change the rest of your life.
For twelve months.
Oil. Perfume. Cosmetics. Instructions. Expectations.
Every detail carefully arranged.
But almost nobody asks what is happening inside your heart.
Were you afraid?
Did you miss home?
Did you cry when nobody was watching?
Did you wonder whether God could still see you behind those palace walls?
The Bible does not tell us everything Esther felt. And we must be careful not to invent her private thoughts as though Scripture recorded them.
But the circumstances Scripture does describe are unsettling enough.
Because this was not simply a glamorous beauty competition.
And Esther was not merely a beautiful young woman waiting for her fairy-tale ending.
She was a Jewish orphan living under a foreign empire, caught inside a royal system where the king possessed extraordinary power and the women possessed far less.
And somehow, in that very place, a story of deliverance began unfolding.
Perhaps that is why Esther's story still reaches people who have lived through circumstances they never asked for.
People who were judged by their appearance.
People whose choices were restricted by someone else's power.
People who learned to smile while carrying fear.
People who were placed in situations they could not control and later wondered whether God had abandoned them.
If you have ever looked at your life and whispered, "Lord, how could anything good come from this?" stay with Esther's story.
Because the most important thing happening inside that palace was not the beauty preparation.
It was something the palace could not manufacture.
Something the king could not purchase.
Something no human being could completely see.
The providence of God was moving through a story where His name was never explicitly mentioned.
Esther 2:8 tells us:

"So it came to pass, when the king's commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought also unto the king's house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women." — Esther 2:8, KJV
Notice the language.
The young women were gathered under a royal decree.
Esther was brought into the king's house.
The text does not describe Esther enthusiastically applying for a royal opportunity. Neither does it tell us precisely how she responded when she was taken into the system.
What it does show is a powerful monarchy gathering young women into a process controlled by royal authority.
That distinction matters.
Because when we romanticize every detail of Esther's journey, we risk overlooking the vulnerability of the women involved.
The palace was magnificent.
The power imbalance was real.
And beauty did not make that imbalance disappear.
Esther 2:12 reveals the extraordinary preparation required before each young woman approached the king:

"Now when every maid's turn was come to go in to king Ahasuerus, after that she had been twelve months, according to the manner of the women, (for so were the days of their purifications accomplished, to wit, six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours, and with other things for the purifying of the women;)" — Esther 2:12, KJV
Twelve months.
Six months with oil of myrrh.
Six months with fragrant substances and other preparations.
A full year devoted to preparing a woman for royal presentation.
The Hebrew text contains an expression worth examining:
שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ
Shenem asar chodesh — twelve months.
And another significant expression:
יְמֵי מְרוּקֵיהֶן
Yeme meruqeihen — the days of their beauty treatments or cosmetic preparations.
The Hebrew term comes from a root associated with polishing, cleansing, or refining. In this setting, it refers to the prescribed treatment of the young women before they were presented to the king.
This is important because the KJV uses the word "purifications," which modern readers might mistakenly interpret as a spiritual cleansing ritual.
But Esther 2 is describing royal cosmetic preparation, not the forgiveness of sins or purification before God.
The young women were being prepared according to palace customs.
Not sanctified by the Holy Spirit.
Not spiritually transformed by expensive perfume.
Not made more valuable before their Creator.
Their appearance was being cultivated for the king's approval.
And there is something deeply revealing about that.
The palace could spend twelve months preparing a woman's appearance.
But it could not determine her worth.
It could control the schedule.
But it could not create her soul.
It could cover her with costly fragrance.
But it could not give her the peace that comes from knowing the living God.
And suddenly this ancient story begins to sound painfully modern.
Because our world still has its own versions of the palace.
We may not have Persian attendants distributing myrrh, but we have industries selling perfection.
We have screens teaching young women that beauty is their greatest currency.
We have algorithms rewarding appearance while overlooking character.
We have men who feel they must prove their worth through wealth, status, strength, and achievement.
We have people spending years preparing themselves to be accepted by someone who may never truly love them.
Change your face.
Change your body.
Change your personality.
Hide your weakness.
Become more desirable.
Become more impressive.
Become whatever the people with power want you to become.
And perhaps the saddest part is that some people become so skilled at being admired that they forget what it feels like to be known.
You can be surrounded by compliments and still feel invisible.
You can receive attention and still hunger for genuine love.
You can be chosen by someone and still wonder whether you are safe.
You can look beautiful in public and feel completely broken in private.
That is why we must never confuse being desired with being valued.
Human approval can change overnight. Your worth before God is not created by the people who approve of you.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that human beings are created in the image of God.
That dignity belongs to women and men alike.
It does not begin when someone finds you attractive.
It does not increase when someone wealthy chooses you.
It does not disappear when someone rejects you.
And it cannot be purchased with cosmetics, clothing, status, or royal favor.
But Esther's story becomes even more complicated.
Because Scripture tells us that Esther had already experienced profound loss before she entered the palace.
Esther 2:7 explains that she had neither father nor mother and that Mordecai had taken her as his own daughter.
Her Hebrew name was Hadassah.
The text introduces her not merely as beautiful, but as a young woman whose parents had died and whose older relative had cared for her.
Before the crown, there was bereavement.
Before the palace, there was displacement.
Before the royal favor, there was a life shaped by loss.
And that matters.
Because the people we admire from a distance often carry histories we know nothing about.
Sometimes the woman who appears strongest has survived the deepest grief.
Sometimes the person who seems most composed has learned how to endure uncertainty because life never gave them another option.
Sometimes the people who encourage everybody else are still trying to understand their own suffering.
Esther's beauty was visible.
Her entire history was not.
And we should remember that before making assumptions about anyone whose life appears enviable.
Then something remarkable happens.
Esther finds favor with Hegai, the official responsible for the women.
She receives special provisions and attendants.
Later, Esther 2:15 tells us that when her turn came to approach the king, she requested nothing beyond what Hegai advised.
And Esther 2:17 records that the king loved Esther above the other women, placed the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti.
It is tempting to stop here.
The orphan becomes queen.
The overlooked girl receives a crown.
The beautiful woman is chosen.
End of story.
But if we stop there, we miss the very heart of Esther.
Because the crown was not the conclusion.
It was the beginning of a much more dangerous chapter.
The palace that elevated Esther would soon become the place where she had to risk everything.
And the position that appeared to promise security would place her before a terrifying decision.
When Haman's plot threatened the destruction of the Jewish people, Esther faced the possibility that approaching the king without being summoned could cost her life.
The royal system had not suddenly become safe simply because she wore a crown.
She still had to reckon with the limits of her power.
Mordecai challenged her with words that have echoed across generations:
"And who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" — Esther 4:14, KJV
Who knows?
Those two words are important.
Mordecai did not claim to possess a complete explanation of God's hidden purposes.
He recognized that Esther's position might become an instrument of deliverance.
But he also understood that deliverance did not ultimately depend on Esther's beauty, status, or personal comfort.
In the same verse, he warned that relief and deliverance for the Jews would arise from another place if Esther remained silent.
Esther was being called to courageous responsibility, not to believe she was the savior of her people.
And that distinction points us toward a truth we desperately need.
God can work through human beings without making human beings the center of redemption.
He can use a position without endorsing everything about the system that created it.
He can bring good out of suffering without declaring the suffering itself good.
He can accomplish His purposes in the midst of human wrongdoing without becoming the author of that wrongdoing.
That is why Romans 8:28 must be handled with reverence.
The apostle Paul teaches that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
It does not say all things are good.
Betrayal is not good.
Exploitation is not good.
Abuse is not good.
Grief is not good simply because God can bring redemption into a grieving life.
The God who brings light into darkness does not require us to call darkness light.
And if someone has ever used the words "God has a plan" to dismiss your pain, hear this carefully.
The Bible does not require you to pretend that what happened to you was harmless.
The Lord is able to redeem what is broken.
That is very different from saying the breaking was righteous.
Esther's story never asks us to celebrate the unequal power of the Persian harem.
It invites us to see that imperial power was not ultimate.
The king was powerful.
But he was not God.
Haman was dangerous.
But he was not sovereign.
The royal decree seemed irreversible.
But it was not beyond God's providential rule.
And the young Jewish woman who appeared to have so little control would become a courageous participant in the preservation of her people.
When Esther finally chose to act, she did not rush forward in arrogant self-confidence.
She called for a fast.
Esther 4:16 records her instruction that the Jews in Susa gather and fast for her for three days, and that she and her attendants would do likewise.
Then she declared:
"And if I perish, I perish." — Esther 4:16, KJV
There is no cheap optimism in those words.
No promise that courage eliminates danger.
No guarantee that obedience will preserve earthly comfort.
Esther understood that the risk was real.
And still she moved forward.
This is not the language of someone who believed the crown made her untouchable.
It is the language of someone who recognized that there are moments when doing what is right may cost more than remaining silent.
And perhaps that is where this story confronts us most deeply.
Not in the beauty treatments.
Not in the crown.
Not even in the palace.
But in the moment when a woman who had been brought into a system of power decided to use the influence she possessed to help save others.
There are moments when God calls us to speak even when silence would be easier.
To defend someone who cannot defend themselves.
To refuse the approval of people when that approval requires disobedience to God.
To stand for truth when doing so threatens our reputation.
To confess sin when pretending would be more comfortable.
To seek reconciliation when pride tells us to remain distant.
To walk away from a relationship that demands the surrender of our conscience.
And sometimes, to admit that we have been chasing a crown that was never meant to save us.
Because there is another truth hidden beneath the glittering surface of Esther's story.
You can receive everything the world told you to desire and still discover that your deepest need remains unanswered.
A crown cannot forgive sin.
A palace cannot reconcile a soul to God.
Beauty cannot defeat death.
Influence cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
And the approval of an earthly king cannot give eternal life.
This is where Esther's story leads us toward something greater than Esther.
Toward Jesus Christ.
We must be careful here.
Esther is not Jesus.
Her experience is not identical to His.
And the twelve months of beauty preparation are not a secret biblical formula for spiritual purification or salvation.
But when we read Esther within the whole testimony of Scripture, we can see a meaningful contrast.
Esther approached an earthly king knowing that entering his presence without permission might cost her life.
Through Jesus Christ, sinners are invited to approach the throne of grace with confidence.
Hebrews 4:16 declares:
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." — KJV
Think about that.
Esther faced a throne where access depended on royal permission.
Believers in Christ are invited to a throne where mercy is available because of the finished work of their great High Priest.
Esther risked her life to intercede for her people.
Jesus willingly laid down His life to save sinners.
Esther's courage was extraordinary.
Christ's saving work is incomparable.
He did not merely enter a dangerous throne room.
He went to the cross.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
He did not purchase our redemption with perfume, gold, or political influence.
He purchased it through His sacrificial death.
First Peter 1:18–19 teaches that believers were not redeemed with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
And this is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Because some of us have spent years trying to make ourselves acceptable.
We polish our public image.
We hide our private failures.
We carefully manage what people know about us.
We tell ourselves that once we become beautiful enough, successful enough, disciplined enough, religious enough, or respectable enough, we will finally be worthy of love.
But the Gospel does not say that Jesus died for people who had already perfected themselves.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after twelve months of spiritual cosmetics.
Not after we had erased every shameful memory.
Not after we had convinced the world that we were good.
Christ died for sinners.
And the grace that receives repentant sinners is the same grace that begins transforming their lives.
The Greek New Testament uses the word χάρις — charis, commonly translated "grace."
It speaks of favor and gift, and in the saving work of Christ it directs us to God's undeserved generosity toward those who cannot rescue themselves.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." — KJV
There is a freedom in those words that no earthly palace could ever provide.
You cannot buy the grace of God.
You cannot earn salvation by becoming more attractive.
And you do not have to compete with another person to receive Christ's mercy.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And genuine faith is not merely admiration from a distance.
It calls us to repentance.
To turn from sin.
To abandon the illusion that we can save ourselves.
To trust the crucified and risen Savior.
To follow Him in a life increasingly shaped by His truth.
Perhaps you have been living behind a carefully maintained image.
Everybody thinks you are fine.
You know the right Christian language.
You can quote Scripture.
You know when to smile.
You know how to say, "God is good."
But when the room becomes quiet, you are exhausted.
You are tired of pretending.
Tired of comparing.
Tired of trying to be chosen.
Tired of carrying guilt you have never confessed.
Tired of returning to the same sin and calling it a small weakness when you know it is slowly hardening your heart.
Or perhaps your struggle is different.
You were mistreated.
You were rejected.
You were abandoned.
You were made to feel that your body was more valuable than your personhood.
And now you find it difficult to believe that anyone could know your whole story and still love you.
Hear what the Gospel actually says.
Jesus Christ does not excuse sin.
He calls sinners to repentance.
But He also does not turn away the brokenhearted who come to Him.
He is not impressed by the masks that impress other people.
He knows the truth about us.
And His invitation is not to remain hidden behind appearances.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — KJV
There is no need to pretend before the One who already knows.
No need to manufacture a royal appearance before the Savior who sees the heart.
No need to call your wounds imaginary.
No need to call your sin harmless.
Bring the truth to Him.
Your guilt.
Your grief.
Your fear.
Your resentment.
Your compromise.
Your exhaustion.
And if you have been harmed by someone else's sin, remember that another person's wrongdoing is not your guilt to confess.
You can seek God's healing, wise support, and safety without accepting blame for what someone else chose to do.
Christ is not asking you to make evil look beautiful.
He is inviting you to trust Him with what is true.
And there is something else about Esther that makes her story unforgettable.
The book never explicitly names God.
Not once in its Hebrew narrative.
Yet the sequence of events repeatedly invites readers to consider the hidden workings of providence.
A young woman becomes queen.
A plot against the king is discovered.
A faithful act is recorded.
A sleepless night leads to the reading of royal records.
A murderous scheme is overturned.
And a threatened people are preserved.
The narrative does not explain every event through a direct divine announcement.
Instead, it shows how circumstances that seem disconnected become part of an extraordinary deliverance.
For believers, this is a profound reminder that God's faithfulness is not limited to the moments when His activity is obvious to us.
But we must not turn that truth into a promise that every painful situation will end with a crown.
Some faithful people never receive public recognition.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Some losses remain painful for the rest of our earthly lives.
Some courageous acts cost more than we imagined.
The Christian hope is not that every story becomes comfortable before the final page.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death, that He remains faithful, and that His promised restoration extends beyond the limits of this present life.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of the day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is a greater hope than becoming queen of Persia.
That is the hope of the resurrection.
That is the hope secured by Jesus Christ.
And now I want to ask you something that may be more personal than you expected when you began reading.
Whose approval has been ruling your life?
Who has the power to make you feel worthless with one sentence?
What are you still trying to prove?
What part of your past have you allowed to become the final definition of your identity?
And what would change if you began believing that the verdict of Jesus Christ matters more than the shifting approval of the world?
You may never walk through a royal palace.
You may never wear a golden crown.
You may never have your name recorded in a history book.
But you can belong to the King of kings.
Not because you impressed Him.
Not because you were more desirable than someone else.
Not because you endured enough suffering to earn His attention.
But because Jesus Christ came to save sinners, and His mercy is sufficient for all who turn to Him in faith.
If you are struggling, you do not have to pretend that you are strong.
If you have sinned, you do not have to defend what God is calling you to forsake.
If you have been wounded, you do not have to pretend the wound never existed.
And if you have wandered from Christ, today is a good day to turn toward Him.
Not toward a more polished version of yourself.
Toward the Savior.
Perhaps your prayer today is simple:

"Lord Jesus, I have spent too much of my life seeking approval in places that could never save me. Forgive my sins. Heal what is broken. Teach me to live in Your truth. Give me courage to obey You, humility to repent, and faith to trust Your grace. I surrender my life to You. Amen."
If this message has reached something you have been carrying quietly, I would love to hear from you.
You do not have to explain private details publicly. A sincere request is enough.

And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from shame into forgiveness, from fear into courage, or from spiritual darkness into new life, consider sharing it. Your story may encourage someone who believes their own life is beyond redemption.
Please do not let this message end with you.
One thoughtful share can place Scripture before a person who would never have searched for it.
If this ministry has helped you grow closer to the Lord, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing emotional stories.

Our desire is to point people toward the Word of God, proclaim Jesus Christ faithfully, encourage repentance and genuine faith, and help believers continue growing after the emotion of a single article has faded.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, develop spiritual discipline, and remain rooted in biblical truth.
And the library's free resources are an important part of our mission.
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
And nobody should have to pay to hear that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
But sharing biblical resources, maintaining ministry platforms, producing new materials, and reaching more people can require ongoing practical support.
It can be part of your planned Christian giving, alongside your other responsibilities and commitments.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — KJV
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
And not because a monthly payment can replace every believer's responsibility to steward their resources faithfully, including their commitment to a local church.
Rather, it is one opportunity to give generously and voluntarily toward a ministry whose mission you believe is worth supporting.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your value in the Kingdom of God.
More importantly, your ongoing support can help us continue developing resources, sharing Scripture, and making Christ-centered messages available to people who need them.
Your prayer may strengthen a work whose impact you may never fully see.
Your invitation may lead a friend to open the Bible again.
Your testimony may remind someone that repentance and restoration are still possible through Jesus Christ.
We do not know every person who will read these words.
We do not know which heart is close to surrender.
We do not know who has been silently asking God for a reason to keep trusting Him.
But we know the message worth carrying.
Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.
And in Him there is forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the hope of eternal life.
That is the message we want to keep proclaiming.
Not the greatness of Gospel Warrior.
Not the greatness of any writer.
Not the greatness of a platform.
The greatness of Jesus Christ.
Because Esther's story was never ultimately about perfume.
It was not ultimately about physical beauty.
And it was not simply about a young woman becoming queen.
It was about the preservation of a threatened people in a world where earthly rulers seemed to hold all the power.
And as Christians read that story within the wider biblical narrative, we are reminded of the greater salvation God has accomplished through His Son.
Esther's courage helped preserve her people from destruction.
Jesus Christ, the righteous Savior, gave Himself to redeem sinners from every nation who trust in Him.
Esther received a crown from an earthly king.
Jesus, who endured a crown of thorns, is now exalted as Lord.
And unlike the changing favor of earthly rulers, the saving grace of Christ rests upon His finished work.
So the next time you read about the twelve months of preparation in Esther's palace, remember what the perfume could never accomplish.
It could make a woman ready for royal presentation.
It could not make her righteous before God.
It could prepare her appearance for a king.
It could not purchase eternal life.
And the next time the world tells you that you must become more beautiful, more impressive, more successful, or more acceptable before you can matter, remember the cross.
The Savior did not wait for sinners to make themselves worthy of His sacrifice.
He loved us while we were still sinners.
He calls us to repent and believe.
And He transforms those who belong to Him by His grace.
If you remember only one thing from Esther's story, remember this:
The palace may have determined how Esther was presented, but it did not possess ultimate authority over the purposes of God.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, neither your past shame, your present struggle, nor the judgment of this world has the authority to cancel the redemption He has accomplished.
The world may spend a lifetime teaching you how to be chosen, but Jesus Christ gave His life to save those who could never earn His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE HOLIDAY JESUS NEVER COMMANDED: ARE WE HONORING GOD… OR DEFENDING TRADITIONS HE NEVER ASKED FOR?
paragraphs: THE HOLIDAY JESUS NEVER COMMANDED: ARE WE HONORING GOD… OR DEFENDING TRADITIONS HE NEVER ASKED FOR?

Christmas. Easter. Holy Week. Religious celebrations passed down through generations. But what happens when a sincere Christian opens the Bible and discovers that some of the holidays they have celebrated all their lives were never explicitly commanded by Jesus? Is celebrating them an act of worship—or could refusing them become another form of religious pride? The answer may expose something far deeper than the dates on our calendars.
There is a kind of spiritual discomfort that begins with one innocent question.
“Where does the Bible actually command Christians to celebrate this?”
At first, the room becomes quiet.
Someone says, “We have always celebrated it.”
Another answers, “But it is about Jesus.”
Someone else becomes defensive. “Are you saying our parents and grandparents were wrong?”
And suddenly, a question about a holiday becomes a question about faith, family, obedience, and whether we have been honoring God or merely repeating what we inherited.
Perhaps you have been there.

Perhaps you grew up waiting for Christmas morning, singing hymns about the birth of Christ, attending Easter services, remembering the crucifixion during Holy Week, and believing that these celebrations were simply part of being a Christian.
Then one day, someone challenged you.
“Show me where Jesus commanded Christmas.”
You searched.
“Show me where the apostles commanded an annual Easter celebration.”
You searched again.
And the silence between the verses began to trouble you.

But before you throw away your decorations, condemn your church, accuse your family of paganism, or defend every tradition simply because it carries the name of Jesus, there is something we desperately need to understand.
The Bible does not command Christians to celebrate every religious holiday. But neither does it teach that every religious observance not explicitly commanded is automatically sinful.
And if we miss that distinction, we may end up fighting for biblical faithfulness while violating the very Scriptures we claim to defend.
This is not merely about Christmas.
This is not merely about Easter.
This is about who has the authority to bind your conscience.
And whether Jesus Christ is truly Lord over your worship.
Because sometimes the most dangerous tradition is not the one hanging on your calendar.
It is the one sitting unnoticed on the throne of your heart.
Consider the words of the apostle Paul.
In Romans 14:5–6, he writes:
Read that again.
One believer regards a particular day.
Another regards every day alike.
And Paul does not immediately pronounce one faithful and the other rebellious.
Instead, he directs attention toward the Lord.
In the original Greek, Romans 14:5 includes the expression:
ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω
Hekastos en tō idiō noi plērophoreisthō.
A careful translation is:
“Let each one be fully convinced in his own mind.”
The Greek verb plērophoreisthō communicates being fully assured or convinced.
Paul is not encouraging careless religious individualism. He is not saying that every practice becomes acceptable simply because someone sincerely believes in it.
He is addressing a matter where believers differed over the observance of days and urging them to act with conviction before God rather than contempt toward one another.
The immediate context concerns disputable matters, including food and the observance of days. Paul is not specifically discussing modern Christmas or Easter celebrations.
Nevertheless, the passage gives us a principle that matters profoundly when evaluating religious observances Scripture has not commanded.
A Christian must not turn a matter of conscience into a universal command that God Himself has not given.
That truth cuts in both directions.
The believer who celebrates must not automatically condemn the believer who abstains.
And the believer who abstains must not automatically condemn the believer who celebrates.
Because Paul had already asked a piercing question in Romans 14:4:
“Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?”
Imagine standing before Jesus and discovering that you spent years attacking a brother who sincerely honored Christ on a particular day, while ignoring the pride growing inside your own heart.
Or imagine discovering that you pressured another believer to participate in a celebration that troubled their conscience, simply because you could not tolerate their refusal.
Both situations should make us uncomfortable.
Because Jesus never gave us permission to replace His authority with our preferences.
But there is another passage we cannot afford to ignore.
In Mark 7:6–8, Jesus confronts religious leaders whose traditions had begun to displace God's commandments.
He quotes Isaiah:
“This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” (Mark 7:6–7, KJV)
Then He declares:
“For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men.” (Mark 7:8, KJV)
Those words should stop us.
Jesus was not impressed merely because a practice was old.
He was not impressed merely because respected religious leaders approved it.
He was not impressed merely because people called it worship.
The question was whether human tradition had displaced divine authority.
And that is where every Christian celebration must face an honest examination.
Not simply, “Did my family practice this?”
Not simply, “Does my church approve of it?”
Not even simply, “Does this make me feel close to God?”
But, “Does this practice honor Christ in a way consistent with His Word, or am I treating human customs as though God commanded them?”
There is a difference between remembering Jesus' birth and declaring that God requires every Christian to celebrate Christmas.
There is a difference between rejoicing in Christ's resurrection and insisting that every faithful believer must observe a particular annual holiday.
There is a difference between participating in a church tradition voluntarily and teaching that refusal to participate makes someone spiritually inferior.
And there is a difference between questioning a tradition and condemning everyone who practices it.
The distinction matters because the Gospel is not a religious calendar.
The Gospel is the good news of Jesus Christ—His incarnation, sinless life, atoning death, bodily resurrection, and saving grace received through faith.
Our salvation rests upon Christ, not upon our holiday observance.
Now consider Christmas.
Scripture clearly teaches that Jesus Christ was born.
Matthew and Luke record the extraordinary circumstances surrounding His birth. Luke 2:11 announces:
“For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.” (KJV)
That is glorious truth.
The eternal Son entered human history.
The promised Messiah came.
The Savior was born.
But the New Testament does not command Christians to establish an annual celebration of His birth on December 25.
Nor does Scripture identify December 25 as His actual birthday.
The date became associated with Christian observance through later historical developments, and historians continue to discuss the factors behind its adoption.

Some popular claims about Christmas origins are much more confident than the historical evidence allows. It is inaccurate to assume that every Christmas custom has one simple pagan origin or that all Christian celebrations of December 25 arose through a single deliberate act of borrowing.
Historical questions deserve historical evidence.
Biblical questions deserve careful biblical interpretation.
And spiritual accusations deserve more than viral slogans.
The absence of a biblical command for Christmas does not, by itself, prove that remembering Christ's birth on a chosen day is sinful.
But neither does the importance of Christ's birth justify every activity associated with the holiday.

A celebration centered on generosity, thanksgiving, worship, and the truth of the incarnation is not spiritually identical to a celebration dominated by drunkenness, greed, deception, or neglect of the needy.
The name attached to a celebration does not sanctify everything done in it.
