Which raises an uncomfortable question.
What if someone celebrates Christmas every year but rarely thinks about Christ outside December?
What if the decorations are magnificent, the gifts are expensive, the photographs are beautiful—but the family has no time for prayer, forgiveness, or Scripture?
What if we become furious when someone questions Christmas traditions, yet remain strangely calm when the commands of Jesus are neglected?
Perhaps the greater danger is not the calendar.
Perhaps it is a heart that knows how to celebrate Jesus without actually following Him.
Now consider Easter.
The resurrection of Jesus Christ is not an optional doctrine.
It stands at the center of Christianity.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:17:
Without the resurrection, Christianity collapses.
But Christ has risen.
The tomb was empty.
Death did not have the final word.
And every Christian has reason to rejoice.
Yet the New Testament does not issue a universal command requiring all Christians to observe an annual Easter Sunday according to a particular ecclesiastical calendar.

The history of Christian Pascha, often called Easter in English, is closely connected with the biblical Passover and early Christian remembrance of Christ's death and resurrection. Early Christians also differed over the timing of annual observances.
That history is more complicated than the popular claim that Easter is simply a pagan festival with a Christian label.
The English word Easter has its own linguistic history, while many Christian traditions use words derived from Pascha, connected to Passover.
The word's history alone cannot establish the spiritual meaning of every celebration bearing its name.
What matters is whether the actual practices are faithful to Christ.
A church may gather on an annual day to proclaim the resurrection without claiming that the date is a divine command.
Another believer may decline that annual observance while celebrating the risen Lord throughout the year.
Neither position, by itself, proves greater holiness.
But what about the holidays God actually commanded in Scripture?
This is where the discussion becomes even more important.
Leviticus 23 records appointed times given to Israel, including Passover, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles.
The Hebrew expression used for appointed times is:
מוֹעֲדֵי יְהוָה
Mo'adei YHWH.
It means “the appointed times of the LORD.”
These were not merely cultural inventions. They were covenantal observances established by God for Israel.
Their significance should never be dismissed.
They reveal God's holiness, redemption, provision, and faithfulness. They also provide profound biblical context for understanding the ministry of Jesus Christ.
Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 5:7:
“For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν ἐτύθη Χριστός
To pascha hēmōn etythē Christos.
A close rendering is:
“For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.”
Paul identifies Jesus as the fulfillment of the Passover sacrifice's redemptive significance.
And Hebrews explains how Christ's priestly work and once-for-all sacrifice surpass the repeated sacrifices of the old covenant.
This does not make Israel's appointed feasts meaningless.
It means Christians must understand them through the finished work of Christ.
Under the new covenant, believers are not justified by observing Israel's ceremonial calendar.
Paul warns in Colossians 2:16–17:
“Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” (KJV)
The Greek phrase:
τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ
To de sōma tou Christou.
Can be rendered, in this context, “but the substance belongs to Christ,” or more literally, “but the body is of Christ.”
The contrast is between shadow and the reality to which the shadow points.
Christ is the center.
Christ is the fulfillment.
Christ is not an accessory to religious observance.
He is the One toward whom the redemptive story moves.
Christians differ over how particular biblical festivals and Sabbath principles should be practiced today. Those differences deserve careful study rather than caricature.
But one truth is unmistakable: no holiday observance can replace the saving work of Jesus.
And no celebration can accomplish what His blood has already accomplished.
Yet someone may ask, “Doesn't Deuteronomy warn against adopting pagan worship?”
Yes.
And we must take that warning seriously.
Deuteronomy 12:30–31 warns Israel not to imitate the detestable worship practices of the nations in serving the LORD.
The passage addresses real idolatrous practices, including horrific acts God condemned.
Christians must not worship idols, participate in occult rituals, or assume that an idolatrous act becomes acceptable merely because someone attaches Jesus' name to it.
Paul is equally clear in 1 Corinthians 10:14:
“Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry.” (KJV)
But we must be careful in applying these texts.
A historical resemblance between two customs does not automatically prove that everyone practicing a modern custom is worshiping a pagan deity.
The origin of a practice, its present meaning, the actions involved, and the participant's intentions all deserve examination.
Even good intentions cannot justify genuine idolatry.
But neither should uncertain historical associations be treated as conclusive proof of idolatry.
We cannot defend biblical truth by making claims the evidence cannot support.
And we cannot honor the God of truth by becoming careless with the truth.
There is another biblical event worth considering.
In John 10:22–23, Jesus is present in Jerusalem during the Feast of Dedication.
The Greek calls it:
τὰ ἐγκαίνια
Ta enkainia.
It refers to the Feast of Dedication, known today as Hanukkah.
This commemoration developed after the events recorded in the Hebrew Bible's Torah and commemorated the rededication of the Jerusalem temple.
John tells us that Jesus was at the temple during this festival.
That detail matters.
It demonstrates that a later religious commemoration could exist within the Jewish world in which Jesus ministered.
However, the passage does not explicitly say that Jesus endorsed every practice associated with the festival, nor does it command Christians to celebrate religious holidays of their own choosing.
It would be an overstatement to use His presence as blanket approval for every later Christian holiday.
But it would also be an overstatement to claim that Scripture presents every religious commemoration established after Moses as inherently sinful.
The biblical evidence calls for discernment, not simplistic slogans.
And perhaps that is what makes this subject so uncomfortable.
It refuses to give us an easy weapon against everyone who disagrees.
Some Christians want a verse that condemns every uncommanded holiday.
Others want a verse that blesses every cherished tradition.
But Scripture calls us to something more demanding.
Faithfulness.
Humility.
Truth.
Love.
A conscience shaped by God's Word.
And worship centered on Jesus Christ.
Now imagine two believers sitting in the same church.
One is a young mother who grew up in a home filled with anger.
Every December, her family gathers to read Luke 2, pray together, prepare meals for struggling neighbors, and remember the coming of Christ.
For her, the occasion has become an opportunity to teach her children about God's mercy.
Across the aisle sits a man who once practiced idolatrous religious rituals.
Certain seasonal customs remind him of the worship he abandoned when he surrendered his life to Jesus.
His conscience will not allow him to participate.
He does not want to return to anything that resembles his former bondage.
Both love Jesus.
Both want to obey Scripture.
Both are trying to act faithfully.
Now imagine the mother accusing the man of being legalistic because he abstains.
Imagine the man accusing the mother of being an idolater simply because she observes the day.
And imagine the grief of watching two people redeemed by the same Savior wound one another over a matter that requires careful discernment.
Romans 14:13 says:
“Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way.” (KJV)
This is not permission to compromise with sin.
It is a command to exercise love where Scripture allows differences of conscience.
And that command is not optional.
We must distinguish between what God has forbidden, what God has commanded, and what God has left to responsible Christian judgment.
Because confusion between those categories has wounded families, divided churches, and turned sincere believers into enemies.
There is a special danger in religious pride.
It can wear the clothing of strictness.
And it can wear the clothing of freedom.
The strict believer may begin to think, “I am more faithful because I refuse what others celebrate.”
The permissive believer may begin to think, “I am more mature because I participate without guilt.”
Both can begin trusting their own position more than the grace of God.
And suddenly, the argument is no longer about honoring Jesus.
It is about winning.
Being right.
Feeling superior.
Proving that our group understands what everyone else has missed.
But the cross leaves no room for spiritual boasting.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
You are not saved because you celebrate Christmas.
You are not saved because you refuse Christmas.
You are not saved because you observe Easter.
You are not saved because you reject Easter.
You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And genuine saving faith bears fruit in a life increasingly shaped by obedience, repentance, love, and holiness.
That does not mean our choices are irrelevant.
It means our choices must flow from belonging to Christ rather than become substitutes for belonging to Him.
There is something deeply sobering about the way religious disputes can distract us from the commands we already understand.
Jesus commanded His disciples to love one another.
Have we obeyed?
He taught us to forgive.
Have we forgiven?
He told us to make disciples.
Are we making them?
He called us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
Are we following?
He commanded us to remember Him in the breaking of bread.
Do we approach His sacrifice with reverence?
He taught us to care for those in need.
Are we caring?
He warned against hypocrisy.
Have we examined our own hearts?
We can spend hours debating whether a Christian should put up a Christmas tree while refusing to reconcile with someone we have wounded.
We can condemn commercialized holidays while allowing greed to control our everyday decisions.
We can insist that the resurrection should be celebrated every day while living as though the risen Christ has no authority over our speech, relationships, or secret habits.
And we can defend a beautiful church tradition while forgetting the Savior it was supposed to honor.
That is the tragedy.
We become experts at discussing the calendar while neglecting the Christ who rules over every day.
What would happen if we asked a different question?
Not merely, “Am I allowed to celebrate this?”
But, “Can I genuinely do this for the glory of God?”
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:31:
That principle reaches into every part of Christian life.
If you choose to observe a religious holiday, can you do so with gratitude to God, faithfulness to Scripture, integrity, and love?
Can you explain to your children the difference between biblical truth and human tradition?
Can you avoid treating customs as commands?
Can you refuse practices that involve sin or idolatry?
Can you celebrate without placing unnecessary burdens on your family or looking down on those who abstain?
And if you choose not to observe a religious holiday, can you abstain without pride?
Can you respect fellow believers whose consciences differ?
Can you explain your convictions without spreading unsupported accusations?
Can you remain gentle while holding firmly to Scripture?
Can you refuse to make your personal practice a test of salvation?
These questions are harder than simply declaring everyone else wrong.
Because they require us to examine ourselves.
And sometimes self-examination is more painful than argument.
Perhaps you are reading this while remembering a family disagreement.
A parent who felt rejected when you stopped participating in a celebration.
A child who felt condemned because you insisted on a tradition.
A spouse who became frustrated when your convictions changed.
A church friend who stopped speaking to you because you asked a sincere biblical question.
Perhaps words were spoken that cannot be taken back.
Perhaps you were called rebellious.
Perhaps you called someone deceived.
Perhaps what began as a desire to honor God became a battle that wounded people you love.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
You do not have to abandon biblical conviction to pursue reconciliation.
And you do not have to win every argument to remain faithful to Jesus.
You can say, “I still believe what I believe, but I am sorry for the way I treated you.”
You can say, “I cannot participate because of my conscience, but I do not want to condemn you unfairly.”
You can say, “I choose to observe this day, but I will not pressure you to join me.”
You can say, “I want us to open the Bible together instead of attacking each other.”
Sometimes repentance begins not with changing your conclusion, but with confessing the pride, harshness, or dishonesty that accompanied it.
And that kind of repentance is not weakness.
It is evidence that Christ is still transforming you.
Remember the thief on the cross.
He had no opportunity to build a religious calendar.
No years of holiday observances.
No impressive record of ceremonial faithfulness.
He turned to the crucified Jesus and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
What saved that man?
Not a feast.
Not a festival.
Not a tradition.
Not his ability to settle every religious controversy.
His hope rested in the mercy and authority of the Savior beside him.
That does not make obedience unnecessary.
It reveals the foundation upon which all true obedience stands.
Grace.
The undeserved mercy of God in Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who welcomed that dying sinner is the Jesus who calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
He does not invite us to replace obedience with religious sentiment.
And He does not invite us to replace grace with religious performance.
He calls us to Himself.
That is why the answer to our original question must remain anchored in Scripture.

Christians are not universally required to celebrate religious holidays that Scripture does not command. Yet the mere absence of an explicit command does not automatically make every voluntary religious commemoration sinful.
Such observances must be evaluated according to biblical teaching, the nature of the practices involved, the conscience of the believer, the good of others, and the glory of God.

A tradition becomes spiritually dangerous when it contradicts Scripture, encourages sin, displaces God's commandments, promotes idolatry, or is imposed as a divine requirement without biblical authority.
Likewise, rejecting a tradition becomes spiritually dangerous when abstinence turns into pride, false accusation, contempt, or a self-made standard of righteousness.
The issue is not whether we can invent a religious celebration and expect God to approve it automatically.
We cannot.
The issue is whether Scripture permits a particular voluntary remembrance without violating God's commands or binding the consciences of others.

Faithful Christians may reach different conclusions about particular observances, especially when they understand the historical background, associated practices, or relevant biblical principles differently.
Those differences should lead us deeper into Scripture, not further away from love.
And where a practice genuinely involves sin, we must refuse it, no matter how popular or traditional it becomes.
Jesus must have the final word.
Not nostalgia.
Not cultural pressure.
Not internet controversy.
Not denominational pride.
Not fear of disappointing people.
Jesus.
The One who was born in humility.
The One who lived without sin.
The One who was betrayed, mocked, beaten, and crucified.
The One who carried the judgment sinners deserved.
The One who rose bodily from the grave.
The One who will return in glory.
He is worthy of more than an annual celebration.
He is worthy of our lives.
And perhaps this is the question that should stay with us long after this article ends:
If every religious holiday disappeared tomorrow, would your devotion to Jesus remain?
Would you still open your Bible?
Would you still pray?
Would you still love your enemies?
Would you still forgive?
Would you still proclaim the Gospel?
Would you still worship when no special music was playing and no decorations were hanging?
Would you still follow Christ when obedience became costly?
Because the strongest evidence of genuine discipleship is not how passionately we defend a religious date.
It is whether our lives increasingly reflect the Lord we claim to honor.
There is room for sincere disagreement over certain observances.
There is no room for replacing Jesus with them.
And there is no excuse for forgetting the Gospel while arguing about how to remember it.

If this message has challenged something you have always believed, do not rush to defend yourself. Open the Scriptures. Read Romans 14, Mark 7, Colossians 2, 1 Corinthians 8–10, and Galatians 4 in their contexts. Ask God for wisdom. Examine your practices and your motives.
And if this exposed pride, fear, judgment, or confusion in your heart, you do not need to hide it.
Bring it to Jesus.
His grace is sufficient to forgive sinners, and His Word is sufficient to guide His people.
I want to invite you into an honest conversation, not a fight.

Or share your conviction respectfully: Do you celebrate religious holidays not explicitly commanded in Scripture, or do you choose to abstain? Which biblical passages have most shaped your understanding?
Your testimony may help someone who has been struggling silently with the same question.
There may be someone in your family who needs this conversation before another holiday becomes another argument.
There is also something personal I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people encounter the truth of Scripture, grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ, and move beyond surface-level religion into genuine discipleship.
That work requires prayer, faithful service, time, resources, and people who believe biblical encouragement should continue reaching hearts beyond their own.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the heart of this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that financial support purchases God's favor.
But an opportunity to participate willingly in a work you believe is helping people grow closer to Jesus.
Others can pray, share, encourage, or introduce someone to the Gospel.
All of those contributions matter.
That commitment to making biblical resources accessible remains an important part of the mission.
Keep growing in the Word.
Keep praying.
Keep sharing truth.
Keep pointing people to Jesus.
Because the goal has never been to build a community of people who merely agree about holidays.
The goal is to see lives transformed by the Gospel.
To see sinners repent.
To see the wounded find hope in Christ.
To see families reconciled.
To see believers become mature in Scripture.
To see people move from inherited religion to a living, obedient faith in the Savior.
And to see Jesus glorified—not merely on selected dates, but through lives surrendered to Him.
One day, the calendars we argued over will be forgotten.
The decorations will be packed away for the final time.
The songs of another season will fade.
The debates that seemed so enormous will fall silent.
And what will matter eternally is not whether we successfully defended every human tradition, but whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
So celebrate with a clear conscience where Scripture permits.
Abstain with a clear conscience where conviction requires.
Never excuse what God calls sin.
Never command what God has not commanded.
Never let your freedom become an excuse for selfishness.
Never let your conviction become an excuse for pride.
And never forget the Savior while defending the celebration.
Because a holiday can remind you of Jesus.
But only Jesus can save you.
The tragedy would not be discovering that you celebrated the wrong day—it would be spending your life defending a day while never surrendering your heart to the Lord of every day.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY MEANT TO DESTROY YOU. GOD WAS NOT FINISHED WRITING YOUR STORY.
paragraphs: THEY MEANT TO DESTROY YOU. GOD WAS NOT FINISHED WRITING YOUR STORY.
If God Is Good, Why Did He Allow What They Did to You? The Disturbing Truth Behind Genesis 50:20 and Acts 2:23 That Leads From Betrayal to the Cross.
What if the worst thing someone ever did to you was not the final chapter of your story?

What if the betrayal that shattered your trust, the injustice that stole your peace, the rejection that made you question your worth, and the suffering that brought you to your knees were not beyond God's power to redeem?
But before you answer, there is something we need to confront.
Something uncomfortable.
Something that has caused believers to wrestle with God through sleepless nights, unanswered prayers, and tears nobody else ever saw.
Can God use an evil action to accomplish His good purposes without ever approving of the evil itself?
Because if He can, that changes how we understand suffering.
And if we misunderstand that truth, we may end up blaming God for the very wickedness He condemns.
Somewhere, someone is reading this while carrying a wound that still has a name.
A father who abandoned them.
A spouse who betrayed them.
A friend who exposed their secrets.
A leader who abused their trust.
A person who smiled in their face while quietly working against them.
And perhaps the most painful part was not simply what happened.
It was what happened afterward.
You prayed.
You waited.
You wondered why God did not stop it.
You watched people who hurt you continue with their lives while you struggled to put yours back together.
And somewhere in the silence, a question began forming that you were almost afraid to ask:
Lord, if You knew what they were going to do, why did You allow it?
The Bible does not mock that question.
It does not demand that wounded people pretend evil was good.
And it does not offer the shallow comfort of telling every suffering person that everything happened because God wanted them to be hurt.
Instead, Scripture takes us into two of the darkest scenes in human history.
One involves a young man betrayed by his own brothers.
The other involves the Son of God betrayed, condemned, and crucified.
And in both stories, we discover a truth so astonishing that it forces us to reconsider what evil can accomplish when it encounters the sovereign purposes of God.
Human beings can intend evil. God can accomplish good through the very event they intended for evil. And their evil remains evil.
That distinction matters more than most people realize.
Joseph knew what betrayal felt like long before he understood what God would do through it.
He was seventeen when his brothers' jealousy turned into hatred.
They resented their father's favoritism. They hated Joseph's dreams. They could not stand the thought that the younger brother might one day stand above them.
And when an opportunity came, they acted.
They stripped him of his special robe.
They threw him into a pit.
Then, instead of rescuing him, they sold him into slavery.
Imagine the scene.
Joseph looking upward from the pit.
The faces of his brothers disappearing above him.
The sound of their voices continuing while his future collapsed.
Genesis 42:21 later reveals that Joseph had pleaded with them in anguish, but they refused to listen.
He begged.
They heard him.
And they did it anyway.
That detail matters.
Because some wounds are not caused by misunderstanding.
Sometimes people know they are hurting you.
Sometimes they see the tears.
Sometimes they hear the pleading.
And they still choose to continue.
Joseph was carried away from his home into Egypt, separated from his father and everything familiar.
And his suffering did not end there.
He served in Potiphar's household, resisted the sexual advances of Potiphar's wife, and was falsely accused after refusing her.
His integrity did not protect him from imprisonment.
His obedience did not produce immediate deliverance.
He did what was right and still suffered for it.
Think about that.
There are people who believe that if they obey God faithfully enough, they will never experience injustice.
Joseph's life destroys that illusion.
Sometimes faithfulness leads you through a prison before you ever see the palace.
Sometimes doing the right thing costs you something precious.
Sometimes you can be exactly where obedience has led you and still find yourself surrounded by circumstances you never would have chosen.
Yet Genesis repeatedly tells us something remarkable.
The LORD was with Joseph.
Not merely when he became powerful.
Not merely when his circumstances improved.
God was with him in the house where he served and in the prison where he suffered.
The presence of God was not proved by the absence of hardship.
And Joseph's imprisonment was not evidence that God had abandoned him.
Years passed.
Joseph eventually interpreted Pharaoh's dreams, was elevated to authority in Egypt, and administered preparations that preserved food through a devastating famine.
The same brothers who sold him eventually stood before him, desperate for grain.
They did not recognize him.
But Joseph recognized them.
Imagine that moment.
The people who once controlled his suffering were now standing before a man who possessed the power to punish them.
He could have used his authority to destroy them.
He could have made them experience the helplessness he once experienced.
Instead, after testing their character and seeing evidence of change, Joseph eventually revealed himself.
And later, after their father's death, the brothers feared that Joseph would finally take revenge.
That is when Joseph spoke words that have echoed through generations.
Genesis 50:20, in the King James Version, declares:
"But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."
Read that carefully.
Joseph did not say, "What you did was not evil."
He did not say, "You were secretly doing the right thing."
He did not excuse their cruelty or pretend the betrayal never happened.
He named their intention.
Evil.
Then he revealed something about God's purpose.
Good.
The original Hebrew makes the contrast especially striking.
אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה וֵאלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Attem chashavtem alai ra'ah, ve'Elohim chashavah letovah.
A close rendering is:
"You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good."
The Hebrew verb chashav (חָשַׁב) appears in both clauses. In this context, it carries the sense of planning, devising, or intending.
Joseph's brothers planned evil.
God planned good.
The same historical event stood within two radically different intentions.
Their purpose was betrayal and removal.
God's purpose was preservation of life.
And here is the extraordinary part.
God did not need to approve of their wicked motives in order to accomplish His righteous purpose.
Their hatred belonged to them.
Their guilt belonged to them.
God's wisdom and goodness belonged to Him.

The text does not portray God as the author of their moral evil. Nor does it portray Him as helplessly improvising after their sin. It presents a sovereign God accomplishing a good purpose through events in which human beings were genuinely responsible for their wicked choices.
That does not answer every philosophical question about divine sovereignty and human freedom.
Faithful Christians have debated those questions for centuries.
But it establishes something the text refuses to let us ignore.
God's sovereignty does not make evil morally good.
And human wickedness does not place events beyond God's power.
Now consider something else.
Joseph could see a particular purpose because God had brought him to a place where that purpose became visible.
He saw that many lives had been preserved during the famine.
But Scripture does not promise that every believer will discover a similarly identifiable explanation for every tragedy.
Some suffering remains mysterious in this life.
Some losses are not reversed.
Some relationships are not restored.
Some people die without seeing earthly justice.
We must never use Joseph's story to promise that every victim will become wealthy, powerful, publicly vindicated, or reunited with those who hurt them.
That is not the Gospel.
And we must never tell an abused person to remain in danger because God might use their suffering.
God's ability to redeem evil does not excuse the person committing it.
Forgiveness does not require denying what happened.
Reconciliation requires more than words; where serious harm has occurred, safety, truth, accountability, and genuine repentance matter.
Joseph's story gives us hope without requiring us to pretend that pain is harmless.
But there is another story.
One that goes deeper.
One that takes us beyond a pit in Canaan and a prison in Egypt.
It takes us to a hill outside Jerusalem.
And there, the question becomes almost unbearable.
If God can use evil without approving of evil, what do we do with the crucifixion of Jesus Christ?
Because the cross was not merely a tragedy.
It was an injustice of staggering proportions.
Jesus Christ was sinless.
He healed the sick.
He welcomed sinners to repentance.
He showed mercy to the broken.
He exposed religious hypocrisy.
He spoke the truth about the Father.
Yet He was betrayed, falsely accused, mocked, beaten, and handed over for execution.
The religious authorities who opposed Him were accountable for their actions.
Judas was accountable for his betrayal.
The Roman authorities and soldiers were accountable for their injustice and cruelty.
And still, when the apostle Peter stood before the crowd at Pentecost, he declared something that should make every reader stop.
Acts 2:23, in the King James Version, says:
"Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain."
Notice the two truths standing together.
Jesus was delivered according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge.
And the people who crucified Him acted wickedly.
Peter did not erase human guilt because God's purpose was being fulfilled.
He did not suggest that crucifixion became righteous simply because salvation would come through it.
He proclaimed divine sovereignty and human responsibility in the same breath.
The Greek text begins with a remarkable expression:
τοῦτον τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βουλῇ καὶ προγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ ἔκδοτον
Touton tē hōrismenē boulē kai prognōsei tou theou ekdoton.
A close translation is:
"This one, handed over by the determined plan and foreknowledge of God."
The word boulē (βουλή) refers here to counsel, purpose, or plan.
The participle hōrismenē (ὡρισμένῃ) communicates something determined or appointed.
And prognōsis (πρόγνωσις) means foreknowledge.
Peter is not describing a God who was surprised by the cross.
The crucifixion was not an emergency that forced heaven to invent a rescue plan.
Yet the same verse attributes the killing of Jesus to lawless human action.
The cross was within God's redemptive purpose.
The crucifiers were still guilty of their sin.
And Acts 4:27–28 reinforces this truth when the early believers pray about the opposition of Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel against Jesus.
Their prayer acknowledges that these opponents acted in ways encompassed by God's predetermined purpose.
The Bible does not explain away their responsibility.
It holds both truths together.
Now we reach the heart of the matter.
God did not call the murder of His Son good. God accomplished the greatest good through the greatest injustice ever committed.
The distinction is everything.
The betrayal was evil.
The false accusations were evil.
The mockery was evil.
The cruelty was evil.
The unjust condemnation was evil.
But the saving purpose of God was holy.
Jesus was not merely a helpless victim caught in circumstances beyond divine control.
He willingly gave His life.
In John 10:18, Jesus explains that no one takes His life from Him in the ultimate sense; He lays it down of His own accord.
And in the garden of Gethsemane, He submitted Himself to the Father's will.
This was not the Father approving human cruelty.
This was the Son willingly entering human suffering to accomplish redemption.
The crucifixion reveals both the wickedness of human sin and the immeasurable love of God.
At the cross, justice was not dismissed as unimportant.
Sin was not redefined as harmless.
Rather, Christ bore our sins, fulfilling the saving purpose described in passages such as Isaiah 53, Romans 3:25–26, and 1 Peter 2:24.
And on the third day, He rose from the dead.
Death did not have the final word.
The tomb did not have the final word.
The wicked intentions of those who condemned Him did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ rose victorious.
That is why the cross cannot be reduced to a motivational slogan about turning bad days into good ones.
The Gospel is far greater than that.
It announces that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and given new life through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And here is where this truth becomes deeply personal.
Because perhaps you have spent years believing that what happened to you has permanently disqualified you from being loved, useful, or restored.
Maybe you have replayed the betrayal so many times that it has become part of how you see yourself.
You no longer say, "Someone betrayed me."
You say, "I am someone nobody stays for."
You no longer say, "I experienced injustice."
You say, "My life is ruined."
You no longer say, "I made a terrible mistake."
You say, "I am beyond forgiveness."
But the Gospel confronts those conclusions.
Your suffering may have shaped parts of your story.
It does not have the authority to determine your ultimate worth before God.
And your sin, however serious, need not be the final word if you turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
There is a difference between acknowledging what happened and allowing it to become your identity.
There is a difference between remembering your wounds and believing that your wounds are all you are.
And there is a difference between trusting God's power to redeem and pretending that every terrible event was secretly wonderful.
God does not ask you to celebrate evil.
He calls you to trust Him in a world where evil is real, justice matters, and redemption is possible.
Perhaps you are still in the part of the story that feels like Joseph's prison.
You have not seen the outcome.
You cannot explain the delay.
You are trying to remain faithful while everything around you feels uncertain.
Then hear this carefully.
You do not need to invent a beautiful explanation for your suffering to be loved by God.
You do not need to call your trauma a blessing.
You do not need to smile while your heart is breaking.
The Psalms contain cries of anguish.
Job wrestled with devastating loss.
Jeremiah lamented.
Even Jesus wept.
Biblical faith is not emotional dishonesty.
It is bringing the truth of our pain before the God who sees.
And when you cannot trace His purposes, you can still look to the character of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
The cross tells us that God is not indifferent to suffering.
The resurrection tells us that suffering and death will not ultimately defeat His saving purpose.
But there is a warning here too.
God's ability to bring good from evil must never become permission for us to do evil.
Romans 3:8 explicitly rejects the reasoning that we should do evil so that good may result.
James 1:13 teaches that God does not tempt anyone with evil.
And James 1:17 describes God as the giver of good gifts.
We cannot defend our cruelty by saying God will use it.
We cannot excuse dishonesty because someone might learn from it.
We cannot justify abuse because a victim might eventually grow stronger.
The possibility of redemption does not erase moral responsibility.
If you are the person who caused the wound, Joseph's story is not your permission slip.
It is your invitation to repent.
Stop hiding behind God's sovereignty.
Confess what you did.
Turn away from the sin.
Make restitution where possible.
Accept accountability.
Seek forgiveness without demanding it.
And understand that another person's healing does not automatically cancel your responsibility for the harm you caused.
Grace does not require pretending that justice is unnecessary.
True repentance bears fruit.
But perhaps the evil you are struggling with today is not something another person did.
Perhaps it is something you did.
A decision you regret.
A betrayal you committed.
A lie you told.
A relationship you destroyed.
A season of rebellion you cannot undo.
And you wonder whether God could possibly receive you after everything.
Then remember who stood at the cross.
There was a criminal dying beside Jesus.
He could not travel backward in time.
He could not erase his crimes.
He could not rebuild his reputation.
He could only turn toward the Savior and ask to be remembered.
And Jesus gave him a promise of paradise (Luke 23:39–43).
That man was not saved because his past suddenly became righteous.
He was saved by the mercy of Christ.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue in sin.
Not denial of guilt.
Not an excuse to avoid repentance.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners through Jesus Christ, a mercy that forgives and begins to transform those who come to Him.
This is why our message is not simply that God can turn your pain into a platform.
Our message is that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
He restores people who could never restore themselves.
He gives hope to the ashamed.
He calls the wandering home.
He gives new life to those who trust Him.
And He is able to sustain His people even when the explanation for their suffering remains hidden.
Not because every scandal ends in public success.
Not because every wound disappears.
Not because every person who betrayed you returns with an apology.
But because the risen Christ has the authority to redeem sinners, sustain the suffering, and bring His people into a future that evil cannot finally destroy.
Romans 8:28 promises that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And the following verse helps us understand that good.
Romans 8:29 speaks of being conformed to the image of God's Son.
God's ultimate purpose is not merely our comfort, prosperity, or public vindication.
It is our conformity to Christ and our final redemption in Him.
That matters when life does not improve according to our preferred schedule.
Because God's faithfulness cannot be measured only by how quickly circumstances change.
Sometimes His sustaining grace is seen in the strength to endure another day.
Sometimes it is seen in the courage to tell the truth.
Sometimes it is seen in repentance after years of running.
Sometimes it is seen in the willingness to seek help, establish boundaries, or walk away from danger.
Sometimes it is seen in forgiveness that grows slowly, without denying the need for justice.
And sometimes it is seen in a wounded believer whispering a prayer when there are no words left for anything else.
You may not know what God will do with every broken piece of your life.
Joseph did not know while he was in the pit.
He did not know while he was being sold.
He did not know while he was imprisoned.
But we know something Joseph's story points us toward and the resurrection of Jesus confirms.
Evil is not sovereign.
God is.
And the God who raised Jesus from the dead has not surrendered His purposes to the darkness of this world.
That does not mean every outcome will make sense today.
It means our hope rests in someone greater than our ability to understand.
So perhaps the question you need to ask tonight is not simply, "Why did God allow this?"
Perhaps another question belongs beside it.
"Lord, how do I remain faithful to You while I am still hurting?"
"How do I seek justice without surrendering my heart to hatred?"
"How do I forgive without pretending the wrong was acceptable?"
"How do I repent of my own sins without believing I am beyond Your mercy?"
"How do I trust You when I cannot see what You are doing?"
These are not questions for people who have mastered faith.
They are questions for people who desperately need Jesus.
And that is precisely where the Gospel meets us.
Not at the moment we become impressive.
Not when we finally learn to hide our weakness.
Not when we have a perfect testimony with a beautiful ending.
But when we come honestly before the Savior and acknowledge our need for Him.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe you have been attending church while quietly losing hope.
Maybe you have been encouraging everybody else while struggling to pray for yourself.
Maybe you have been posting Scripture while privately wrestling with resentment.
Maybe you have been calling yourself a Christian while resisting the repentance Christ has been calling you toward.
Or maybe you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus at all.
Wherever you are, the invitation is not to manufacture a dramatic spiritual experience.
It is to come to Christ in truth.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Turn toward Him.
Receive the mercy that you could never earn.
And begin walking in obedience, supported by His grace.
If you need words for that surrender, you can pray:

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I need Your mercy. I have sinned against You, and I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You. Where I have been wounded, help me seek healing without embracing bitterness. Where I have done wrong, give me the courage to repent and make things right. Teach me to trust Your goodness even when I do not understand my circumstances. My hope is in You alone. Amen."
A prayer is not a formula that saves by its wording.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by the performance of a religious ritual (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But if that prayer expresses the genuine turning of your heart toward Him, do not dismiss the importance of that moment.
And do not walk alone.
Find a faithful, Bible-teaching local church where you can grow, be discipled, and learn to follow Christ alongside other believers.
Because following Jesus is not meant to be a lonely performance.
It is a life of grace, truth, repentance, love, and growing obedience.
And perhaps this is where you can help someone else.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who has quietly concluded that their life is too broken for God to use.
Someone is carrying shame over a past they cannot change.
Someone has been betrayed and is beginning to believe that God must have abandoned them.
Someone has confused God's sovereignty with God's approval of evil.
Someone desperately needs to hear that the cross was not heaven's defeat and that resurrection is real.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page.
You may never know who reads it in the middle of a sleepless night.
You may never know who needed that reminder to seek help, return to prayer, repent of sin, or open the Bible again.

And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with kindness and sensitivity. If their struggle is private, send the article directly instead of exposing their pain in a public comment.
Do not make their suffering a spectacle.
Make your encouragement personal.
You can simply write "Christ is still healing me" if you are learning to trust Him through wounds that have not fully healed.
Write "I'm still fighting" if you are weary but determined to keep following Jesus.
Or write "Jesus, forgive me" if the Holy Spirit has brought you face to face with something you need to confess and turn away from.
You do not owe strangers the details of your suffering. You can share only what is safe and appropriate.
But your honest testimony may help another person realize that they are not the only one wrestling with faith in the middle of pain.
And invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have drifted from their faith, and even people who do not yet know Jesus to follow along.
We are not building a community around the illusion that Christians never suffer.
We want to build a community that keeps pointing suffering people, repentant sinners, and searching hearts toward the risen Christ.
That is also why we are committed to making biblical resources accessible.
These resources are offered to encourage serious study, spiritual maturity, and continued growth in the Gospel.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, there is another meaningful way you can help us continue.
For those who choose to make this part of their regular Christian giving, it can be an expression of generosity toward ministry work.
But we want to be clear about something important.
Scripture calls believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Christians also have responsibilities toward their local churches, families, and people in need.
We would never want anyone to neglect those responsibilities or give beyond their means because they feel spiritually pressured.
For those who can, it is a practical way to help us continue producing and sharing Christ-centered teaching, strengthening discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the message of Jesus.
These products are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
They are simply another way to encourage believers, share biblical messages, and express our appreciation to those who help sustain the ministry.
It is about Jesus Christ.
His Word.
His Gospel.
His grace toward sinners.
His power to transform lives.
And His promise to complete the good work He has begun in His people (Philippians 1:6).
Before you leave, I want you to return to the question that brought us here.
Can God use evil actions to accomplish His purposes without approving of evil?
Joseph's testimony says yes.
Peter's preaching at Pentecost says yes.
The cross of Jesus Christ gives us the clearest and greatest demonstration.
But that truth should never make us careless about evil.

It should make us more serious about holiness, more courageous in seeking justice, more compassionate toward the wounded, more humble about what we do not understand, and more grateful for the grace that comes through Christ.
The brothers meant evil.
God accomplished good.
The crucifiers acted wickedly.
God accomplished redemption through the willing sacrifice of His Son.
And the risen Jesus now calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is where our confidence belongs.
Not in the promise that every betrayal will make us successful.
Not in the assumption that every tragedy will be explained before we die.
Not in the fantasy that faithful Christians never suffer.
But in the crucified and risen Savior who has overcome sin and death.
So if you are still in the pit, do not mistake the darkness for proof that God has disappeared.
If you are still in the prison, do not assume that your suffering makes your obedience meaningless.
If you are struggling with guilt, do not use God's sovereignty to excuse your sin.
And if you are longing for forgiveness, do not imagine that your past is stronger than the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Bring your pain into the light.
Bring your sin into the light.
Bring your unanswered questions to the Lord.
And remember that the One who suffered unjustly, died for sinners, and rose victorious is worthy of your trust.
Because the greatest hope of the Christian faith is not that God will make every chapter of our earthly lives pleasant.
It is that Jesus Christ has opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God, and that those who belong to Him have a living hope that even death cannot extinguish.
And when the final chapter is written, the victory will belong to Him.
The hands that nailed Jesus to the cross could not stop the hands that would rise from the grave—and the evil that wounded your story will never have the authority to rewrite His Gospel.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE DREAM YOU CALLED GOD’S VOICE WAS NEVER FROM GOD? AND WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN IGNORING THE VOICE HE HAS ALREADY GIVEN YOU?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE DREAM YOU CALLED GOD’S VOICE WAS NEVER FROM GOD? AND WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN IGNORING THE VOICE HE HAS ALREADY GIVEN YOU?

God promised dreams and visions in the last days. But Scripture also warns us about spiritual deception. Between supernatural encounters, unanswered prayers, and the desperate longing to hear heaven speak, there is a truth every Christian needs to understand before trusting the next dream.

There is something deeply unsettling about waking up at three in the morning with your heart pounding, your eyes filled with tears, and a dream so vivid that you cannot shake the feeling that heaven just visited your bedroom.
You remember the faces.
The words.
The warning.
Maybe someone you love appeared in that dream. Maybe you saw something frightening. Maybe you heard a voice telling you to make a decision that could change your life.
And now you are lying in the darkness, staring at the ceiling, asking a question that millions of Christians have quietly wrestled with:
“Lord… was that You?”
But there is another person reading this who has never experienced anything like that.
You have prayed for years.
You have begged God for direction.
You have watched other believers testify about prophetic dreams, angelic encounters, and visions of Jesus while your own nights have remained painfully ordinary.
And somewhere along the way, a terrible suspicion entered your heart.
Maybe God speaks to everyone except me.
Maybe your faith is too weak.
Maybe you are not spiritual enough.
Maybe heaven has gone silent because something is wrong with you.
If that sounds familiar, please keep reading.
Because the Bible contains a truth that can both humble the person who claims to hear God in every dream and comfort the person who has never experienced a supernatural vision.
And it begins with two passages that some Christians have mistakenly treated as enemies.
One says God will pour out His Spirit and people will dream dreams.
The other says God has spoken to us through His Son.
Both are true.
And when we understand them together, something extraordinary happens.
We stop chasing spiritual experiences as though Jesus were insufficient.
And we begin discovering just how gloriously sufficient He really is.
In Acts 2:17, Peter declares:

“And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.” — Acts 2:17, KJV
Read that again.
God did not say that every dream would be divine.
He did not say that every Christian would receive a vision.
He did not command believers to seek dreams as proof of spiritual maturity.
He announced the extraordinary outpouring of His Spirit in the last days.
And Peter declared that this promise was being fulfilled as the Holy Spirit descended upon the believers at Pentecost.
The original Greek contains a beautiful expression:
ἐνυπνίοις ἐνυπνιασθήσονται
enypniois enypniasthēsontai
“They shall dream dreams.”
This expression emphasizes the reality of dreaming within the prophetic promise. It does not, by itself, establish that every dream experienced by a believer carries a message from God.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because the moment we confuse the possibility of divine revelation with the certainty that our personal experiences are divine, we become vulnerable to something Scripture repeatedly warns against.
Deception.
And sometimes the most dangerous deception is not the obvious lie whispered by an enemy.
Sometimes it is the religious certainty we attach to something God never actually said.
Consider the person who announces, “God showed me in a dream that you must marry me.”
Or the preacher who claims a vision has revealed a secret doctrine that no one else understands.
Or the frightened believer who wakes from a nightmare convinced that a family member is about to die.
Or the struggling Christian who begins making major decisions based on symbols, numbers, and mysterious impressions rather than biblical wisdom.
These experiences can feel overwhelmingly real.
But emotional intensity is not the same as divine authority.
A racing heartbeat does not authenticate a revelation.
Tears do not establish that a message came from heaven.
And the fact that something happened while you were sleeping does not make it spiritually trustworthy.
A dream can be unforgettable and still be unreliable.
That is not unbelief.
That is discernment.
And biblical discernment does not insult the Holy Spirit.
It honors the God who commanded us to test what claims to come from Him.
First John 4:1 says:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.” — KJV
Notice what John did not say.
He did not tell believers to accept every supernatural claim because questioning it might offend God.
He commanded examination.
Testing.
Discernment.
Because not everything that sounds spiritual is holy.
Not everything that feels supernatural is divine.
And not every person who says, “The Lord told me,” has actually heard from the Lord.
This is where the story becomes even more serious.
Because the Bible does not merely acknowledge that God has communicated through dreams.
It also records people who used dreams to spread falsehood.
In Jeremiah 23:25, God says:
“I have heard what the prophets said, that prophesy lies in my name, saying, I have dreamed, I have dreamed.” — KJV
Imagine the weight of those words.
People were invoking God's name.
Claiming spiritual experiences.
Speaking with religious confidence.
Yet God Himself exposed their claims as lies.
The problem was not that dreaming was inherently wrong.
The problem was that people were attaching divine authority to messages God had not given.
And that danger did not disappear when the New Testament began.
It followed humanity into every generation.
Including ours.
Especially ours.
Today, a dramatic dream can become a viral video before anyone opens a Bible.
Someone announces that God revealed a date, a catastrophe, a political outcome, or a hidden conspiracy.
People panic.
Families become frightened.
Believers begin questioning their salvation.
And sometimes, when the prediction fails, the person who made it simply announces another revelation.
But Scripture does not teach us to measure truth by views, followers, confidence, or emotional impact.
Truth is not established by popularity.
The voice that claims to come from God must never be allowed to contradict the Word God has already given.
Now, before anyone concludes that this means God cannot speak through dreams today, we need to return to Scripture with humility.
Because the Bible contains genuine accounts of God using dreams and visions.
Joseph received dreams that became significant in God's providential purposes (Genesis 37).
Daniel received visions revealing matters far beyond ordinary human knowledge (Daniel 7).
Joseph, the earthly husband of Mary, was warned in a dream to protect the child Jesus (Matthew 2:13).
Peter received a vision that contributed to his understanding of God's acceptance of Gentiles (Acts 10).
Paul received a vision concerning Macedonia (Acts 16:9–10).
These events are not embarrassing details that Christians need to explain away.
They are part of God's inspired Word.
God has used dreams.
God has used visions.
And Scripture does not explicitly declare that God has become incapable of doing so.
But here is the crucial question:
Does the fact that God did something in biblical history mean every believer should expect Him to do it in the same way today?
Not necessarily.
God parted the Red Sea.
That does not mean every Christian should expect an ocean to divide whenever a journey becomes difficult.
God fed Elijah through ravens.
That does not mean every hungry believer should wait for birds to deliver dinner.
God spoke to Moses from a burning bush.
That does not mean spiritual maturity requires finding a shrub that talks.
The Bible records what God has done.
It also teaches us what God has promised, commanded, and provided for His people.
Those categories must not be confused.
And that brings us to one of the most breathtaking statements in the entire New Testament.
Hebrews 1:1–2 declares:

“God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds.” — KJV
The original Greek begins:
Πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως πάλαι ὁ θεὸς λαλήσας
Polymerōs kai polytropōs palai ho theos lalēsas
“In many portions and in many ways, long ago, God having spoken…”
Then comes the magnificent contrast:
ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ
elalēsen hēmin en huiō
“He has spoken to us in a Son.”
The Greek expression emphasizes the climactic significance of God's revelation in His Son.
The point is not merely that God changed His preferred communication method.
The point is that God's revelation has reached its decisive fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The prophets pointed forward.
The promises anticipated Him.
The sacrifices foreshadowed Him.
The covenant story moved toward Him.
And then, in the fullness of time, the eternal Son entered human history.
God did not merely send another message.
He sent His Son.
The Word became flesh.
The invisible God was made known through Jesus Christ.
The promised Messiah came to reveal the Father, bear our sins, conquer death, and reconcile sinners to God.
And suddenly, the question is no longer simply, “Can God speak through dreams?”
The deeper question becomes:
Why would I treat a dream as the center of my spiritual life when God has already revealed His glory in Jesus Christ?
Please understand the distinction.
Hebrews 1 does not explicitly say that every dream or vision after the coming of Christ is impossible. The New Testament itself records visions after Jesus' resurrection and ascension.
But Hebrews does establish something that no Christian should surrender.
Jesus Christ is God's supreme and climactic revelation.
No dream can improve upon His identity.
No vision can replace His Gospel.
No private revelation can become a rival authority to the truth God has revealed through His Son and preserved for us in Scripture.
And no experience can make Jesus more Savior than He already is.
This is where the conversation often becomes uncomfortable.
Because some Christians have begun to measure closeness to God by the unusual things they experience.
They do not merely desire to know Jesus.
They desire to see something extraordinary.
They want a supernatural confirmation.
A mysterious sign.
A heavenly voice.
A dream that tells them they are chosen.
And without realizing it, they begin treating ordinary faithfulness as spiritually disappointing.
Reading Scripture feels too simple.
Prayer feels too quiet.
Repentance feels too ordinary.
Serving others feels too small.
They want fire from heaven while overlooking the light already shining from the Word of God.
But think about the disciples on the road to Emmaus.
They were confused.
Grieving.
Disappointed.
Their hopes seemed buried.
And the risen Jesus walked beside them.
Yet instead of beginning by giving them a spectacular display of supernatural power, Luke 24:27 tells us that Jesus explained the Scriptures concerning Himself.
Later, they said:
“Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?” — Luke 24:32, KJV
Their hearts burned as Christ opened the Scriptures.
Not because they had decoded a mysterious dream.
Not because they had discovered a hidden spiritual formula.
But because Jesus revealed the truth of God's redemptive plan.
And perhaps that is what some of us desperately need to recover.
The wonder of an open Bible.
The miracle of understanding the Gospel.
The astonishing privilege of knowing the Savior who died for us.
Because there is something heartbreaking about a believer who keeps begging God for a message while neglecting the Scriptures that testify about His Son.
You may be asking heaven to tell you that you are loved.
Meanwhile, Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love through Christ's death for sinners.
You may be begging for proof that forgiveness is possible.
Meanwhile, 1 John 1:9 promises forgiveness and cleansing to those who confess their sins.
You may be desperately searching for confirmation that God has not abandoned His people.
Meanwhile, Hebrews 13:5 reminds believers of His promise never to leave or forsake them.
You may be asking for a sign that salvation is available to someone with your past.
Meanwhile, Romans 10:9–13 announces salvation through faith in the risen Lord Jesus.
Please do not misunderstand.
Scripture does not provide the name of the person you should marry, the exact job you should accept, or the date every difficulty will end.
But it gives us something far more foundational.
It reveals the character of God.
The truth about sin.
The sufficiency of Christ.
The promises of the Gospel.
And the wisdom by which we learn to walk faithfully when the future remains hidden.
Sometimes the answer to your prayer is not a secret message about tomorrow.
Sometimes God is calling you to obey what He has already made clear today.
Forgive.
Repent.
Tell the truth.
Love your neighbor.
Flee sexual immorality.
Seek wisdom.
Care for the vulnerable.
Trust Christ.
And when you do not know what comes next, walk by faith rather than pretending you possess knowledge God has not given.
But what about the Christian who genuinely believes God has spoken through a dream?
Must that person automatically dismiss the experience?
No.
A humble, biblically responsible response does not require us to deny that God can work in extraordinary ways.
Christians differ on whether revelatory gifts such as prophecy and visions continue today.

Some believe such gifts ceased with the foundational apostolic era. Others believe God may still grant them, while insisting that any contemporary impression or experience must remain subordinate to Scripture and cannot add to the faith once delivered to the saints.
These are serious theological differences, and faithful Christians have debated them.
But both perspectives should be able to affirm this:
No claimed dream or vision has the right to overturn the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Galatians 1:8 warns against accepting a contrary gospel even if an angel from heaven were to proclaim it.
That is an astonishing standard.
Even an apparently heavenly messenger must not be trusted if the message contradicts the Gospel.
How much more carefully should we evaluate our dreams?
So if you experience a dream that seems spiritually significant, do not panic.
Do not immediately announce it as a prophecy.
Do not build your theology around it.
Do not demand that other people obey it.
Pray.
Examine its content in light of Scripture.
Consider whether ordinary circumstances, fears, memories, stress, or desires may explain it.
Seek wise counsel from mature believers who know the Bible and are willing to question your interpretation.
And remember that a dream's emotional power does not make its interpretation infallible.
Ecclesiastes 5:3 acknowledges that dreams can arise amid much activity and concern.
That observation should encourage humility.
Sometimes a dream is simply a dream.
Sometimes it reflects grief.
Sometimes it reveals what has occupied our thoughts.
And if God, in His wisdom, chooses to use an extraordinary experience for His purposes, He does not need us to exaggerate it, sensationalize it, or turn it into a new commandment.
We can acknowledge the experience without pretending to know more than we do.
We can remain open to God's power while remaining anchored in His Word.
And we can refuse the false choice between believing in the supernatural and practicing biblical discernment.
But there is another wound hidden inside this conversation.
And it belongs to the Christian who feels forgotten.
The one who has listened to testimonies about visions of heaven and wondered why nothing extraordinary ever happens to them.
The one who has fasted, prayed, wept, and waited.
The one who secretly fears that the absence of dreams means the absence of God.
If that is you, listen carefully.
Your relationship with Jesus is not measured by the number of supernatural experiences you can describe.
Your salvation does not rest upon whether you have heard an audible voice.
Your adoption into God's family is not validated by prophetic dreams.
Your standing before the Father is grounded in Jesus Christ.
His righteousness.
His sacrifice.
His resurrection.
His grace.
Not your ability to produce an extraordinary testimony.
Remember Thomas.
He struggled to believe the testimony that Jesus had risen.
And when the risen Christ appeared to him, Thomas confessed:
“My Lord and my God.” — John 20:28, KJV
Jesus then declared:
“Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.” — John 20:29, KJV
Those words do not condemn people who have experienced something unusual.
They bless those who believe in Christ without requiring personal sight of the risen Savior.
There is a quiet, beautiful courage in trusting Jesus when there is no spectacle.
When the room is silent.
When prayers seem unanswered.
When grief remains.
When your circumstances do not change overnight.
When you open your Bible with trembling hands and whisper, “Lord, I still believe You.”
That faith is not second-class Christianity.
It is precious.
And the Savior who gave Himself for His people has not forgotten you simply because you have never had a vision.
Now consider something even more personal.
What if your greatest spiritual danger is not that you will miss a dream from God?
What if it is that you will become so fascinated with extraordinary experiences that you overlook the ordinary ways your heart is drifting from Christ?
You can spend hours discussing prophetic dreams while refusing to forgive someone.
You can search for hidden meanings in visions while hiding a secret addiction.
You can become obsessed with supernatural warnings while neglecting your family.
You can claim to hear God's voice while refusing to obey His clear commands.
And that is a tragedy.
Because Jesus did not shed His blood merely to give us fascinating spiritual stories.
He came to save sinners.
To reconcile us to the Father.
To free us from sin's dominion.
To make us new.
To call us into a life of love, holiness, truth, and obedience.
He did not say that the world would recognize His disciples by the number of visions they reported.
He said:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” — John 13:35, KJV
And in John 14:15, He said:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.” — KJV
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Because we are often eager to hear something new from God while resisting what He has already told us.
We want a dream about our destiny.
But we do not want to surrender our pride.
We want a vision about our future.
But we do not want to confess our sin.
We want supernatural reassurance that God is pleased with us.
But we do not want to examine whether our lives reflect repentance and faith.
And still, in astonishing mercy, Jesus calls us back.
Not to a life of fear.
Not to spiritual performance.
Not to endless uncertainty about whether we have experienced enough.
But to Himself.
To the cross.
To the empty tomb.
To grace that forgives.
To truth that transforms.
To the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Maybe your scandal is that you once claimed God told you something He never said.
Maybe you used spiritual language to justify a decision you already wanted to make.
Maybe you trusted a prophecy more than Scripture.
Maybe you followed someone who manipulated your fears with supposed revelations.
Maybe you were wounded by a religious leader who claimed divine authority over your life.
Or maybe your scandal is quieter.
You have spent years feeling spiritually inferior because other people seem to have extraordinary encounters and you do not.
You have confused God's silence in your dreams with His absence from your life.
And you are exhausted.
Here is the good news.
Jesus Christ is not waiting for you to produce a supernatural experience before you can come to Him.
He calls sinners to repentance and faith.
He welcomes the weary.
He forgives those who turn to Him.
And He is able to restore what spiritual confusion, deception, pride, and fear have damaged.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because every dream becomes reality.
Not because every vision proves authentic.
Not because every question receives an immediate answer.
But because the crucified and risen Jesus can redeem people whose lives have been marked by sin, confusion, failure, and spiritual brokenness.
And when Christ rewrites a life, the greatest miracle is not necessarily what happens during the night.
It is what His grace produces when that person wakes up.
A proud heart begins to humble itself.
A liar begins to tell the truth.
A bitter soul begins learning forgiveness.
A sinner turns from darkness toward Christ.
A frightened believer learns to rest in God's promises.
A person who once chased experiences begins treasuring the Savior Himself.
That is transformation worth celebrating.
That is grace worth proclaiming.
And that is why this message matters far beyond a theological debate about dreams.
There are people right now who are terrified because someone told them a nightmare was a prophecy.
There are believers who have been spiritually controlled by people claiming private revelations.
There are Christians who think they are abandoned because they have never heard an audible voice.
And there are others who have become so dependent upon supernatural excitement that the simple reading of Scripture no longer satisfies them.
They need to hear that Jesus is enough.
Not that God is powerless.
Not that the Holy Spirit is absent.
Not that extraordinary things can never happen.
But that the center of Christian faith is not the extraordinary experience.
The center is the extraordinary Savior.
And if you are wondering what to do the next time you wake from a dream that seems significant, remember this:
You do not have to be afraid.
You do not have to rush to interpret every detail.
You do not have to announce something before you understand it.
You can pray.
You can open Scripture.
You can seek wisdom.
You can refuse fear.
You can acknowledge uncertainty.
And above all, you can cling to Jesus Christ.
Because the God who revealed Himself in His Son has not left His people without truth.
Second Timothy 3:16–17 teaches that Scripture is God-breathed and equips the servant of God for every good work.
That does not mean the Bible answers every speculative question or reveals every future circumstance.
It means God's Word is sufficient for its God-given purpose of teaching, correcting, training, and equipping His people.
You do not need a secret revelation to know that Jesus died for sinners.
You do not need a vision to know that He rose from the dead.
You do not need a dream to discover that repentance and forgiveness are proclaimed in His name.
And you do not need to become a famous prophet to live a faithful Christian life.
Perhaps the most important question tonight is not whether God will speak to you in a dream.
Perhaps it is whether you are willing to listen to what He has already revealed about His Son.
Because one day, the question will not be how many supernatural experiences impressed us.
The question of eternal importance is whether we truly belong to Jesus Christ.
Have we turned from sin and trusted Him?
Have we received His grace through faith?
Are we learning to follow Him in truth?
Are we loving what He loves and turning away from what He condemns?
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
But sincerely, by His grace.
And if you realize today that you have been pursuing spiritual experiences more passionately than you have pursued Christ, you can turn to Him now.
You do not need to manufacture an emotional encounter.
You do not need to wait for a dream.
You can confess your sin.
You can ask for mercy.
You can trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And you can begin walking in the light of His Word.
Maybe your prayer is, “Jesus, teach me to recognize Your truth.”
Maybe it is, “Lord, forgive me for chasing signs more than seeking You.”
I have been confused and afraid.”
You do not need to reveal private details or share an experience you are not ready to discuss. But your honest words may help another believer realize they are not alone.

And if you have a testimony of how Scripture helped you discern a troubling dream or recover from spiritual confusion, consider sharing it with humility. Your experience does not have to become someone else's doctrine to become a source of encouragement.
Please also think of the person in your life who needs this message.
The friend who is frightened by a dream.
The family member who is being misled by sensational prophecies.
The Christian who feels spiritually inadequate.
The seeker who has questions about God's voice.
One thoughtful share can place biblical encouragement in front of someone who would never have known to search for it.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond momentary inspiration into sustained engagement with Scripture, prayer, and Christian discipleship.
It is a voluntary act of generosity that can help sustain this ministry's work.
Scripture teaches the importance of cheerful, willing giving. Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
But if you believe this ministry is faithfully serving Christ and helping people understand His Word, supporting it can be one practical way to participate in that work for God's glory.
The products are simply a gesture of appreciation.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
Not buying a blessing.
Not purchasing spiritual status.
Not earning God's approval.
But freely helping more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Use the free resources.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage another believer.
Your worth before God is not measured by what you can contribute financially.
We want this ministry to point people toward Christ, never toward the idea that grace can be purchased.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus already paid the price of our redemption with His own blood.
And that brings us back to the person lying awake at three in the morning.
The room is dark.
The dream is still vivid.
The questions have not completely disappeared.
You still do not know whether the experience meant anything.
But perhaps tonight you can rest without forcing an answer.
You can entrust your unanswered questions to the Lord.
You can refuse to be ruled by fear.
You can remember that the God who spoke through the prophets has revealed Himself supremely in His Son.
And you can open the Scriptures without feeling that you have settled for something less than God's voice.
Because the Bible does not lead you away from the living Christ.
It bears witness to Him.
The One who was betrayed.
The One who was mocked.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose victorious from the grave.
The One who will return in glory.
That is the Jesus you need.
Not a Jesus invented by someone's dream.
Not a Jesus reshaped by a sensational prophecy.
Not a Jesus who can only be encountered through extraordinary experiences.
But the real Jesus Christ revealed in the Gospel.
And whether you dream tonight or sleep without remembering a single image, whether tomorrow brings an extraordinary experience or another ordinary day, His truth remains.
The Savior does not become less glorious when the room is quiet.
His cross does not become less powerful when heaven gives you no new sign.
His resurrection does not become less certain because you have never seen a vision.
And His grace does not become less sufficient because your testimony sounds ordinary.
You may never receive the dream you have been asking for, but in Jesus Christ, God has already given a revelation far greater than any dream could contain.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BABYLON SAID, “I WILL NEVER BE A WIDOW.” THEN GOD SPOKE—AND HER THRONE BECAME HER GRAVE.
paragraphs: BABYLON SAID, “I WILL NEVER BE A WIDOW.” THEN GOD SPOKE—AND HER THRONE BECAME HER GRAVE.

She had wealth. She had power. She had everything the world could offer. But she made one terrifying mistake: she believed she could never fall. And the warning God gave Babylon thousands of years ago may be closer to your own life than you realize.
There is something frightening about a person who has become so comfortable in their success that they no longer believe they need God.
Not because they are rich.
Not because they are influential.
Not even because they have sinned.
But because somewhere between their blessings and their ambitions, they have quietly convinced themselves that nothing can touch them.
No judgment. No consequences. No collapse.
They have mistaken God's patience for His approval.
And perhaps the most terrifying thing about that kind of spiritual blindness is that you can be living in it without even realizing it.
You can still wake up every morning. Still earn money. Still laugh with friends. Still make plans for next year. Still post pictures of a beautiful life.
And all the while, something inside your soul is moving farther and farther away from the One who gave you breath.
That was Babylon.
A kingdom that looked untouchable.
A civilization that appeared unstoppable.
A queen who believed she would never have to mourn.
Until God spoke.
And everything she trusted began to tremble.
Listen carefully to the words recorded in Isaiah 47:7–9:

“And thou saidst, I shall be a lady for ever: so that thou didst not lay these things to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it.
