Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow, neither shall I know the loss of children: But these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood: they shall come upon thee in their perfection for the multitude of thy sorceries, and for the great abundance of thine enchantments.”
— Isaiah 47:7–9, King James Version
Read those words again.
Especially this part.
“I shall not sit as a widow.”
Can you hear the arrogance?
Can you sense the confidence?
Babylon was not asking whether she would survive.
She was declaring that she could never be brought down.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because Babylon's greatest danger was not simply the enemies gathering beyond her walls.
It was the pride growing within them.
The Hebrew text exposes something extraordinary.
In Isaiah 47:8, Babylon declares:
אֲנִי וְאַפְסִי עוֹד
Ani ve'afsi od.
In context, the expression means, “I am, and there is none besides me.”
This was not merely the confidence of a successful empire. It was a claim of unrivaled importance and self-sufficiency.
And there is a devastating irony here.
In Isaiah 45:5, the LORD declares:
אֲנִי יְהוָה וְאֵין עוֹד
Ani YHWH ve'ein od.
“I am the LORD, and there is none else.”
These Hebrew expressions are not identical, but their resemblance is theologically striking.
God alone is sovereign.
Babylon spoke as though she were beyond every rival, every consequence, and every power capable of bringing her low.
The Creator declares His unique deity.
The creature imagines herself untouchable.
And this is the ancient temptation that still lives in the modern human heart.
We may never say, “I am, and there is none besides me.”
But we say something dangerously close.
“I built this life myself.”
“I don't need anyone.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“Nobody can tell me what to do.”
“I have plenty of time to get right with God.”
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence of all:
“Nothing bad will happen to me.”
Until something does.
Until the doctor calls.
Until the marriage begins to unravel.
Until the money disappears.
Until the secret comes into the light.
Until the person who promised never to leave walks out the door.

Not every tragedy is God's punishment. Scripture does not permit us to treat every illness, loss, or broken relationship as evidence of divine judgment. Jesus Himself rejected that simplistic way of thinking in John 9:1–3.
But moments of vulnerability can reveal how fragile the things are that we have mistaken for permanent security.
Babylon's fall was not an ordinary misfortune.
It was a specific judgment announced by God against an arrogant and oppressive empire.
And the warning beneath that judgment remains deeply relevant.
Whatever takes God's place in your heart will eventually prove incapable of being God.
Babylon was magnificent by human standards.
Its walls, wealth, military strength, royal power, and cultural achievements made it one of the great imperial centers of the ancient world.
But beneath that splendor was a history of domination.
Babylon had conquered Jerusalem, destroyed the temple, and carried many of God's people into exile.
The suffering was real.
The humiliation was real.
The tears of displaced families were real.
Imagine a father watching his children grow up in a foreign land.
Imagine a mother trying to explain why they could no longer return to the streets where she had played as a little girl.
Imagine worshipers remembering Zion while surrounded by the power of the empire that had shattered their city.
Psalm 137 preserves the grief of those exiles:
“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.”
— Psalm 137:1, KJV
Babylon saw conquest.
God saw the captives.
Babylon saw political victory.
God heard the weeping.
Babylon imagined her throne would endure forever.
God had already declared that her glory would not last.
There is a lesson here for anyone who has ever been crushed by someone more powerful than themselves.
God's silence is not proof that He has forgotten you.
The people of Judah had experienced judgment for their own covenant unfaithfulness, but Babylon's cruelty and arrogance were not therefore beyond God's accountability.
God can use nations within His sovereign purposes without approving everything those nations do.
And He had not abandoned His promises.
In Isaiah 47:6, God tells Babylon that she showed His people no mercy and placed a particularly heavy yoke upon the elderly.
Then comes the accusation in verse 7:
“Thou didst not lay these things to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it.”
That sentence should disturb us.
Babylon's problem was not merely that she had done evil.
It was that she had stopped taking evil seriously.
She had become comfortable with what should have broken her conscience.
And isn't that how spiritual numbness begins?
The first lie troubles you.
The second becomes easier.
The third barely registers.
The first betrayal keeps you awake at night.
The next one becomes something you know how to explain.
The first compromise brings conviction.
Eventually, you learn how to silence the conviction.
Until the thing you once prayed God would deliver you from becomes the very thing you defend.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You remember when your heart was softer.
When Scripture could bring you to tears.
When you couldn't go very long without praying.
When worship wasn't merely music playing in the background, but a genuine encounter with the truth of who God is.
And now?
You still know the language of faith.
You still know the right verses.
You may even know how to encourage everyone else.
But privately, something has changed.
You have learned how to look spiritually alive while feeling spiritually distant.
And the frightening part is that you have almost become accustomed to it.
Friend, do not confuse becoming accustomed to darkness with being safe inside it.
Babylon did.
Isaiah 47:8 describes her as one who dwells carelessly, or securely, given to pleasures.
The Hebrew word בֶּטַח (betach) carries the sense of security or confidence.
Security itself is not evil. Scripture repeatedly presents genuine security in the LORD as a blessing.
The problem is security placed in the wrong foundation.
Babylon rested in her own power while disregarding the God who rules over kingdoms.
She trusted her position.
Her pleasures.
Her wealth.
Her supposed ability to control what came next.
And God announced that what she considered impossible would come upon her.
Widowhood.
Loss of children.
The collapse of the security she had taken for granted.

These images are part of the prophetic portrayal of Babylon as a royal woman brought low. They symbolize devastating national loss and humiliation; they are not a declaration that every bereaved woman is under divine judgment.
That distinction matters.
Because the Bible is not mocking the suffering of widows or grieving mothers.
It is exposing the arrogance of an empire that believed itself exempt from loss.
And there is another detail we cannot afford to miss.
Isaiah 47:9 connects Babylon's judgment with her sorceries and enchantments.
The empire did not merely trust political strength.
It also sought security through forbidden spiritual practices.
Babylon wanted knowledge and control over the future without humble submission to the LORD.
That temptation has never disappeared.
People still search desperately for ways to control what tomorrow will bring.
Some look to spiritual practices that God forbids.
Others make money, influence, relationships, or personal ambition into functional saviors.
Different methods.
The same human longing.
We want assurance without surrender.
Protection without obedience.
Peace without repentance.
A future we can control without trusting the God who holds it.
But the future has never belonged to us.
And here is where the prophecy becomes even more haunting.
In Isaiah 47:11, God declares that disaster will come upon Babylon in a way she cannot ward off.
All her calculations, resources, and spiritual advisers would be unable to rescue her from the judgment God had announced.
The empire had experts.
It had systems.
It had accumulated wisdom.
But it did not possess the power to overrule God.
Centuries after Isaiah's prophetic ministry, Babylon fell to the Persian forces of Cyrus in 539 BC.
That historical conquest did not instantly erase the city from existence. Babylon continued to be inhabited afterward.
But its imperial supremacy was broken.
The kingdom that had seemed so secure passed under another ruler.
The historical fall and the prophetic imagery should not be flattened into a claim that every poetic detail occurred literally in one twenty-four-hour period.
Yet the central message stands.
The power Babylon believed would endure did not endure.
Her claim to permanence was exposed.
And her fall became a lasting biblical warning against human arrogance.
But if we stop here, we have not yet reached the deepest part of the Gospel.
Because this story is not merely about the downfall of an ancient empire.
It is also about the kind of pride from which Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And that includes us.
Perhaps you have never ruled a kingdom.
Perhaps you do not possess great wealth.
Perhaps you are simply trying to survive another difficult week.
But pride does not always wear a crown.
Sometimes pride wears the face of someone who refuses to apologize.
Sometimes it sounds like a husband who would rather lose his marriage than admit he was wrong.
Sometimes it looks like a wife carrying bitterness for years because forgiveness feels too costly.
Sometimes it hides behind religious activity, where someone is more concerned with appearing holy than actually surrendering to Christ.
Sometimes it whispers into the heart of a wounded person:
“Never trust anyone again. Never become vulnerable. Never let God touch that part of your life.”
Not every protective boundary is pride. Wisdom and safety matter, especially after abuse or betrayal.
But even our wounds can become places where we struggle to trust God.
And sometimes our deepest spiritual battle is not against a visible enemy.
It is against the part of us that keeps saying:
“Lord, You can have everything except this.”
That secret habit.
That bitterness.
That relationship you know is leading you away from Him.
That hunger for admiration.
That resentment you keep feeding.
That sin you have learned to rename so you no longer have to confront it.
What if the most dangerous Babylon in your life is not something surrounding you?
What if it is the throne you have built inside your own heart?
That question is uncomfortable.
It should be.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
And this is where the story takes a turn that Babylon's pride could never have imagined.
The God who brings down the proud is also the God who welcomes the repentant.
The God who judges evil is the God who offers mercy through His Son.
The God who exposes false thrones is the God who sent the true King to save people who had rebelled against Him.
Look at Jesus.
Babylon said, “I shall be a lady for ever.”
Jesus, though truly Lord, humbled Himself.
Babylon exalted herself.
Jesus took the form of a servant.
Babylon used power to dominate.
Jesus used His power to serve, heal, and ultimately lay down His life.
Philippians 2:6–8 tells us that Christ, being in the form of God, humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
And here is the difference that changes everything.
Babylon grasped at a glory she could not preserve.
Jesus possessed divine glory and willingly entered our suffering to redeem us.
The King of kings wore a crown of thorns.
The One before whom every knee will bow allowed Himself to be mocked.
The sinless Savior was nailed to a Roman cross.
And while human pride keeps insisting, “I deserve the throne,” the Gospel confronts us with a Savior who endured the cross for sinners.
Babylon wanted to rise so high that nothing could bring her down. Jesus humbled Himself so deeply that sinners could be lifted up by grace.
Do not miss that.
The answer to Babylon's arrogance is not merely becoming a more modest version of yourself.
It is being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Because the problem is deeper than an inflated ego.
Scripture teaches that all have sinned and come short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23).
Our rebellion is not simply a series of unfortunate decisions.
It is sin against the holy God who made us.
And no amount of self-improvement can erase that guilt.
But the Gospel announces something extraordinary.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were sinners.
Not after we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we had become impressive.
Not after we had convinced everyone we were spiritually mature.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
And on the third day, He rose again.
His resurrection declares that death did not defeat Him and that His saving work is not an empty promise.
The One who calls sinners to repentance is alive.
The One who offers forgiveness has conquered the grave.
The One who warns us against pride is the same Savior who receives the brokenhearted who come to Him in faith.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain in sin.
Not a religious excuse for refusing to change.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us through Christ and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that clear.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You have spent so much time hiding what is wrong that you have forgotten what it feels like to be honest before God.
You are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of the secret compromises.
Tired of the guilt that returns when the room becomes quiet.
Tired of saying you will change tomorrow.
And you are afraid that if you finally bring everything into the light, God will turn away from you.
But listen to Jesus.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
— John 6:37, KJV
What a promise.
Not a promise that sin does not matter.
Not a promise that repentance is unnecessary.
But a promise that those who come to Christ will not find a Savior unwilling to receive them.
You do not have to defend your sin before Him.
You do not have to pretend that you have been faithful when you have wandered.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect testimony.
You can come with the truth.
“Lord, I have been proud.”
“Lord, I have been running.”
“Lord, I have loved things more than I have loved You.”
“Lord, I need Your mercy.”
And if that is where you are today, please understand something.
The fact that you are being confronted by Scripture is an invitation to respond, not a reason to run farther away.
God's Word is not given merely to make you feel exposed.
It calls you to the Savior who can forgive, restore, and transform.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not an excuse to cherish sin.
It is encouragement to stop hiding it.
And James 4:6 says:
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.”
Perhaps those are the words you need to carry with you tonight.
He gives grace unto the humble.
Not because humility earns salvation.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But because a heart that stops defending itself is finally acknowledging its need for mercy.
And mercy is exactly what Christ offers.
There is something else about Isaiah 47 that makes this prophecy unforgettable.
Babylon called herself a queen.
But Scripture ultimately points us toward a far greater picture of security and belonging.

In Revelation 18, Babylon appears again as a symbol of arrogant, corrupt worldly power standing under God's judgment. Its imagery echoes Isaiah's description of a self-confident woman who denies that mourning will come.
The message is larger than one ancient empire.
Human systems built upon pride, exploitation, idolatry, and rebellion against God will not reign forever.
But Revelation does not end with Babylon.
It moves toward the victory of Christ, the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the New Jerusalem.
Revelation 21:2 describes the holy city as a bride adorned for her husband.
Do you see the contrast?
One city represents arrogant self-sufficiency and rebellion.
The other represents the people of God dwelling with Him through His redeeming grace.
Babylon says, “I need no one.”
The redeemed belong to the Lamb.
Babylon trusts her own splendor.
The New Jerusalem is filled with the glory of God.
Babylon's confidence collapses.
Christ's kingdom endures forever.
And this is the question that matters more than your reputation, your possessions, or the approval of the world.
Where is your ultimate hope?
In something you can lose?
In something death can take?
In something that requires you to keep pretending you are stronger than you really are?
Or in Jesus Christ, who died and rose again?
Because one day every earthly title will become irrelevant.
Every account balance will lose its power to impress.
Every carefully constructed public image will be stripped of its ability to protect.
And every human being will stand accountable before God.
That truth is not meant to produce despair in those who trust Christ.
It is meant to awaken us to what matters eternally.
The Gospel does not say that you can make yourself worthy of heaven by being frightened enough, generous enough, or religious enough.
It says that Jesus Christ is the sufficient Savior of sinners.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
Let His Word confront what needs to change.
Let His grace heal what sin has damaged.
Let His truth reshape how you live.
And do not wait until everything around you collapses before you admit that you need Him.
Babylon said she would never mourn.
But her confidence was misplaced.
You do not have to repeat her mistake.
You can humble yourself before God today.
You can confess the sin you have been excusing.
You can ask forgiveness from the person you have wounded.
You can turn away from the path that is destroying your integrity.
You can return to prayer, not as a performance, but as honest communion with your Father.
You can open Scripture again, not merely searching for words that make you feel better, but receiving the truth that makes you more like Christ.
And if you have never truly placed your faith in Jesus, you can call upon Him today.
Not with a magical formula.
Not with an attempt to purchase His favor.
But with genuine repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Savior.
You might pray:

“Lord Jesus, I have trusted myself more than I have trusted You. I have sinned against You, and I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Turn my heart away from sin and teach me to follow You. I surrender the throne I was never meant to occupy. Be the Lord of my life. Amen.”
The prayer itself does not save by the mere repetition of words. Christ saves those who come to Him in genuine faith.
And when He saves, He begins a work of transformation that reaches far beyond one emotional moment.
That is why discipleship matters.
That is why sound biblical teaching matters.
That is why we need Christian fellowship, prayer, repentance, encouragement, and a steady diet of God's Word.
Because the Christian life is not merely about being moved by a powerful message.
It is about following Jesus when the emotion fades.
When Monday arrives.
When temptation returns.
When obedience becomes costly.
When nobody is watching.
And when the old voice inside you begins whispering that you can live perfectly well without surrendering everything to Christ.
This is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior.
Not simply to produce another article that people read and forget.
But to help people return to Scripture, recognize the beauty of the Gospel, grow in discernment, and take their next faithful step toward Jesus.

These resources are offered freely because we believe the truth of God's Word should be accessible to people who are hungry to learn, including those who may not have the means to purchase books or study materials.
And if this ministry has encouraged you, challenged you, or helped you understand Scripture more clearly, I want to invite you into something deeper than simply reading another post.
But it is important to say this clearly.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Those items can serve as reminders of faith, encouragement, and opportunities for conversations about Jesus.
It is the opportunity to help make faithful, Scripture-centered encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
You are no less welcome here.
Your spiritual worth is not measured by financial support.
The Gospel is not for sale.
You can still help this mission in a deeply meaningful way.
Not because every post needs more views.
But because somewhere among your friends and family may be a person quietly living behind a wall of pride, shame, or spiritual exhaustion.
Someone who has stopped praying.
Someone who feels too far gone.
Someone who thinks repentance means God has already rejected them.
Someone who has been trusting everything except Christ.
Your simple act of sharing may put a biblical message in front of someone who genuinely needs to hear it.
And if a particular person comes to mind as you read this, consider tagging them with kindness or sending this privately with a personal word of encouragement.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to publicly expose their struggles.
But to remind them that the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than the life they have been trying to hold together without Him.
There may come a day when you need to return to Isaiah 47 and remember that no earthly security can take the place of God.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not for a polished religious answer.
Not for a performance.
But for an honest moment before God.
What is one thing in your life that you have been struggling to surrender to Jesus?
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe it is fear.
Maybe it is unforgiveness.
Maybe it is a secret battle that has exhausted you.
Maybe you have been distant from God for so long that you are not even sure how to begin coming back.
You do not have to share private details.
Or simply write:
And if God has already brought you through a season when everything you trusted was shaken, your testimony may encourage someone else who is walking through that darkness today.
Tell us what Christ has taught you about trusting Him.
Let the comments become a place of sincere encouragement, Scripture, prayer, and testimony rather than a place where people feel pressured to pretend they have everything together.
Because there is no shame in admitting you need the Savior.
There is danger in insisting that you do not.
And now, before this article ends, return with me one last time to the woman sitting upon her throne in Isaiah 47.
Imagine the royal confidence.
The magnificent city.
The treasures.
The celebrations.
The servants moving through the palace.
The sound of a kingdom that believes tomorrow belongs to it.
And somewhere in the middle of that splendor, the declaration:
“I shall be a lady for ever.”
“I shall not sit as a widow.”
No fear.
No humility.
No thought of the end.
Then the prophetic Word of the LORD interrupts her confidence.
What she thought could never happen would happen.
What she believed would never be lost would be taken away.
What she trusted could not save her.
And the throne she treated as permanent would not remain hers.
Now look at another King.
Not seated in Babylon's palace.
But hanging upon a cross outside Jerusalem.
His enemies mock Him.
His followers are scattered.
His body is wounded.
And to the watching world, it looks as though His kingdom has ended before it has even begun.
But the cross is not the defeat of Jesus.
It is the place where the sinless Son of God gives His life for sinners.
And the tomb is not His final resting place.
On the third day, He rises.
Babylon's kingdom could not escape history.
Christ's kingdom cannot be overthrown.
Babylon's glory faded.
Christ's glory endures.
Babylon trusted herself and fell.
Those who trust in Christ receive a hope that death itself cannot destroy.
That is the difference between the pride of this world and the grace of the Gospel.
And perhaps, after everything you have read, the question is no longer whether Babylon deserved to fall.
Perhaps the question is whether you will surrender before the things you have made into gods fail you.
You do not have to wait for a disaster to humble yourself.
You do not have to lose everything to discover that Jesus is enough.
You do not have to keep defending a life that is quietly pulling you away from Him.
Today, you can turn.
Today, you can repent.
Today, you can trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Because the greatest miracle is not that an arrogant empire was brought down.
It is that a holy God would extend mercy to rebellious sinners through His beloved Son.
And that mercy is still being proclaimed.
To the proud.
To the broken.
To the ashamed.
To the exhausted.
To the person who thought they had gone too far.
To the person who has been pretending for years.
To you.
Babylon lost the throne she thought she could never lose. But at Calvary, Jesus opened the way for sinners to receive a grace they could never earn.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE CHURCH CALLED YOU TO SERVE JESUS… SO WHY DID YOU END UP FEELING USED?
paragraphs: THE CHURCH CALLED YOU TO SERVE JESUS… SO WHY DID YOU END UP FEELING USED?

When sacred service becomes unpaid labor, exhausted volunteers begin disappearing quietly—and the Church must confront a painful question: Are we making disciples of Jesus Christ, or simply finding people to keep our ministries running?
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.

It happens when you have spent years giving your time, sacrificing your weekends, missing family gatherings, spending your own money, and showing up for church responsibilities even when your personal life is falling apart.
You keep smiling.
You keep saying, “Yes, Pastor.”
You keep telling everyone, “It's all for the Lord.”
But somewhere between another late-night ministry meeting and another Sunday when nobody even asked how you were doing, something inside you began to break.
And the worst part?
You feel guilty for being tired.
Because how do you tell people you are exhausted from serving God without sounding like you no longer love Him?
How do you explain that you still love Jesus, still believe in the Church, still want people to be saved…
But you are beginning to dread the very ministry that once made your heart come alive?
Maybe you are the worship team member who has not experienced a Sunday simply sitting in God's presence for months.
Maybe you are the children's ministry teacher who spends every service caring for other people's children while quietly wondering who is discipling your own.
Maybe you are the media volunteer who arrives before everyone else, leaves after everyone else, and only hears from leadership when something goes wrong.
Maybe you are the usher, cleaner, driver, administrator, sound technician, prayer worker, or ministry assistant whose absence is noticed faster than your suffering.
And maybe the sentence you are most afraid to say is this:
“I don't think they care about me anymore. I think they only care about what I can do for them.”
If those words hurt, stay with me.
Because what Jesus teaches about serving, leadership, and the value of His people may change how you see your ministry forever.
And if you are a pastor or ministry leader reading this, please don't leave.
This is not an attack against faithful shepherds.
It is an invitation to examine whether the people entrusted to our care are being loved as disciples or managed as resources.
Because a church can have a full ministry calendar and still have volunteers with empty hearts.
It can celebrate tremendous attendance while overlooking the quiet suffering of the people who made those gatherings possible.
It can preach the love of Christ from a beautifully decorated platform while failing to practice that same love toward the exhausted people who decorated it.
And Scripture gives us no permission to ignore that contradiction.
Consider a moment in the Gospel of Mark that we sometimes read too quickly.
Jesus had sent His apostles into ministry. They had preached, served, and carried out the work entrusted to them.
When they returned, they gathered around Him and reported what they had done and taught.
And what did Jesus say?
Did He immediately assign them another project?
Did He rebuke them for needing rest?
Did He remind them how many people still needed ministry?
No.
He said:
“Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while.” — Mark 6:31, KJV
The Gospel explains that so many people were coming and going that the apostles did not even have leisure to eat.
Read that again.
They were serving.
The needs were real.
The crowds were waiting.
Yet Jesus recognized their need for rest.
The Greek wording is striking:
ἀναπαύσασθε ὀλίγον — anapausasthe oligon
“Rest a little.”
The verb anapauō, from which anapausasthe comes, means to rest, refresh, or find relief.
Jesus was not dismissing the needs of the crowds. In the very next verses, He would respond compassionately to the multitude.
But He did not treat the exhaustion of His disciples as irrelevant.
He cared about the workers, not merely the work.
And that distinction matters more than many churches realize.
Because somewhere along the way, some Christian communities have confused faithfulness with unlimited availability.
They have confused sacrifice with the inability to say no.
They have confused commitment with constant attendance.
And sometimes, without realizing it, they have created environments where volunteers feel more valued for their productivity than for their spiritual growth.
But a disciple is not a machine.
A brother in Christ is not a staffing solution.
A sister in Christ is not a ministry department's permanent emergency backup.
These are people purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ.
They have families.
They have responsibilities.
They have private battles.
They have prayers nobody hears.
And sometimes the person operating the sound system is silently begging God to save his marriage.
Sometimes the woman teaching children about God's faithfulness is struggling to believe God has not forgotten her.
Sometimes the smiling greeter at the church entrance is battling depression, grief, or financial hardship.
Yet everyone assumes they are fine because they keep showing up.
Until one Sunday…
They don't.
And suddenly the messages begin.
“Where are you?”
“Why weren't you at your post?”
“Who will cover your schedule?”
“We really need committed people.”
But the question that should have been asked long before they disappeared was much simpler.
“How is your soul?”
That is the question ministry leadership cannot afford to forget.
Jesus never taught that greatness in His Kingdom meant acquiring the most people to serve our ambitions.
He taught the opposite.
In Mark 10, James and John approached Jesus seeking positions of honor.
The other disciples became indignant.
Jesus gathered them together and confronted the world's understanding of authority.
He explained that worldly rulers often exercise power over those beneath them.
Then He declared:
“But so shall it not be among you.” — Mark 10:43, KJV
In the Greek text, the contrast is unmistakable:
οὐχ οὕτως δέ ἐστιν ἐν ὑμῖν — ouch houtōs de estin en hymin
“But it is not so among you.”
Jesus was establishing a radically different pattern for His followers.
Leadership in His Kingdom was not supposed to imitate the domination and status-seeking of worldly power.
He continued:
“But whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister.” — Mark 10:43, KJV
The Greek word translated “minister” is διάκονος — diakonos, meaning a servant or one who ministers to others.
And then Jesus gave the ultimate reason:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45, KJV
This is where the Gospel exposes every leadership model built on self-importance.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, did not enter this world demanding that everyone organize themselves around His personal comfort.
He came to serve.
He came to give.
He came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And His service was not a publicity strategy.
It led Him all the way to the cross.
Think about that.
The One who deserved all worship willingly took the position of a servant.
And yet some who claim to represent Him can become offended when volunteers ask for a weekend with their families.
Something is deeply wrong when ministry leaders expect sacrifices from others that they would never willingly make themselves.
Something is wrong when a volunteer's legitimate need for rest is automatically labeled rebellion.
Something is wrong when people are praised publicly for their faithfulness but privately pressured through guilt, fear, or spiritual intimidation.
And something is wrong when “Do it for Jesus” becomes a convenient way to avoid treating people with dignity.
Those words should never be used to silence someone who is being mistreated.
Because Jesus is not honored by using His name to justify behavior that contradicts His character.
Now, we need to be careful here.
The Bible absolutely calls Christians to serve.
It calls us to sacrifice.
It calls us to bear one another's burdens, to use our gifts for the good of the body, and to remain faithful even when ministry becomes difficult.
Galatians 5:13 tells believers to serve one another through love.
First Peter 4:10 teaches that we should minister our gifts to one another as stewards of God's grace.
And Galatians 6:9 encourages us not to grow weary in doing good.
Christian service is not supposed to revolve around personal convenience.
Sometimes love really does cost us something.
Sometimes faithfulness requires staying when leaving would be easier.
Sometimes we must serve without applause, appreciation, or immediate reward.
But none of those truths gives a leader permission to exploit another believer.
There is a difference between choosing sacrifice out of love and being pressured into sacrifice through fear.
There is a difference between carrying your cross and being forced to carry responsibilities that someone else refuses to share.
There is a difference between serving Christ faithfully and believing your worth to the Church depends on how much work you can perform.
Jesus calls His disciples to self-denial.
He does not command church leaders to deny the humanity of the people they lead.
And Scripture is remarkably direct about the spirit in which Christian leadership must operate.
Peter wrote to the elders:

“Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.” — 1 Peter 5:2–3, KJV
Notice that phrase.
“God's heritage.”
The people do not belong to the pastor.
They do not belong to the ministry director.
They do not belong to the institution.
They belong to God.
And the Greek expression behind the warning against domineering leadership is particularly revealing:
μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων — mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes tōn klērōn
“Not as domineering over those entrusted to you.”
The verb katakyrieuō carries the sense of exercising mastery or domination.
Peter is not forbidding leadership, accountability, correction, or appropriate authority.
He is forbidding the kind of leadership that treats God's people as possessions to control.
A shepherd does not own the sheep.
A shepherd is accountable to the Chief Shepherd.
And one day, every Christian leader will answer to the Lord Jesus Christ for how the people under their care were treated.
Not merely for how many programs succeeded.
Not merely for how impressive the attendance figures looked.
Not merely for how much money was raised.
But for whether they shepherded the flock faithfully.
Hebrews 13:17 reminds believers that leaders watch over souls as those who must give an account.
Souls.
Not merely schedules.
Not merely departments.
Not merely performance reports.
Souls.
There is another scene in Scripture that makes this even more personal.
In John 13, Jesus knew that His hour had come.
The cross was approaching.
His betrayal was near.
And during the meal, He rose, laid aside His outer garments, took a towel, and began washing His disciples' feet.
The Master knelt before His followers.
The Lord of glory performed a task associated with humble service.
Then He said:
“For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.” — John 13:15, KJV
Imagine how different some churches would become if leaders genuinely lived that verse.
What if the pastor occasionally helped clean the building alongside the volunteers?
What if ministry directors learned the names of volunteers' children and asked about their families?
What if leadership meetings included honest conversations about whether ministry schedules were sustainable?
What if people were encouraged to attend Bible studies, receive pastoral care, and grow spiritually rather than being perpetually assigned to another duty?
What if volunteers were allowed to say, “I need help,” without being made to feel spiritually inferior?
What if a struggling member could step away from a ministry role temporarily and still know they were loved, welcomed, and valued?
That would not weaken the Church.
It could help the Church become healthier.
Because people who are genuinely discipled are not merely more effective servants.
They are being formed into the likeness of Jesus Christ.
And that is the purpose.
Not simply filling positions.
Making disciples.
Jesus commanded His followers in Matthew 28:19–20 to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to observe His commands.
He did not commission His Church merely to create religious events that require an endless supply of exhausted volunteers.
The mission is to proclaim the Gospel and nurture people into faithful obedience to Christ.
Ministries are meant to serve that mission.
People are not meant to be consumed by the machinery of ministry.
And this is where some of us need to examine our own hearts as well.
Because not every exhausted volunteer has been exploited.
Sometimes we say yes when we should prayerfully say no.
Sometimes we want to be needed so badly that we take on responsibilities God never assigned us.
Sometimes we fear disappointing people more than we fear neglecting our own spiritual health.
Sometimes we quietly resent responsibilities we voluntarily accepted but never communicated that we could no longer sustain.
And sometimes we have confused being indispensable to a ministry with being faithful to Christ.
That is a dangerous confusion.
Because you were never meant to be anyone's savior.
There is already a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
And the Church does not stand because you never miss a Sunday.
It stands because Jesus Christ is its Head.
Colossians 1:18 declares that Christ is the Head of the body, the Church.
He is the One who holds His people together.
He is the One who builds His Church.
He is the One who saves.
You can be faithful without being constantly available.
You can love your church while establishing wise boundaries.
You can honor your leaders while respectfully communicating concerns.
You can serve sacrificially without pretending you have unlimited strength.
And you can acknowledge genuine mistreatment without abandoning your faith in Jesus Christ.
But please hear this, especially if you are wounded.
Do not allow the failures of imperfect Christians to become your final definition of Christ.
People may have misrepresented Him.
Leaders may have disappointed you.
A ministry may have taken more than it should have.
But Jesus is not the sum of the failures of those who claim His name.
He is the sinless Savior who died for sinners, rose again, and calls His people to repentance, reconciliation, and new life.
And if you have been deeply hurt, healing does not require pretending the harm never happened.
Forgiveness does not mean declaring sinful behavior acceptable.
Reconciliation may require truth, repentance, accountability, and restored trust.
Sometimes wise boundaries are necessary.
Sometimes a conversation with responsible church leadership can lead to meaningful change.
And when abuse, threats, or serious misconduct are involved, seeking appropriate outside help and protection is not a betrayal of Christ.
The Gospel does not ask us to protect appearances at the expense of truth.
It calls us to walk in the light.
First John 1:7 speaks of walking in the light as God is in the light.
And Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Both matter.
Truth without love can become cruelty.
But love without truth can become an excuse for allowing harm to continue.
The Church needs both.
There is a beautiful lesson in Acts 6 that we cannot overlook.
As the number of disciples increased, a complaint arose because certain widows were being neglected in the daily distribution.
This was not a minor inconvenience.
Real people were being overlooked.
And the apostles did not simply tell everyone to stop complaining and work harder.
They addressed the problem by establishing an appropriate distribution of responsibility, appointing qualified men to oversee the need.
The passage shows the importance of recognizing practical ministry problems and responding with wise organization.
Not every problem is solved by another sermon about commitment.
Sometimes the schedule needs to change.
Sometimes more people need to be trained.
Sometimes responsibilities need to be shared.
Sometimes a ministry needs to become smaller until it can operate without continually exhausting the same few people.
And sometimes a leader needs to say something that is surprisingly difficult:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Those words can become the beginning of restoration.
Because repentance is not only for people sitting in the congregation.
It is also for those standing behind the pulpit.
It is for ministry directors.
It is for volunteers.
It is for every believer who has allowed pride, resentment, control, selfish ambition, or fear to distort the way we love one another.
The cross leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
We all come to Jesus in need of mercy.
And the same grace that forgives us also teaches us to change.
Titus 2:11–12 describes God's grace as bringing salvation and instructing believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not permission to continue harmful patterns.
Grace calls us into transformation.
Now imagine a church where volunteers are not simply recruited but discipled.
Where a young man joins the media ministry and someone cares enough to teach him how to study the Bible, pray, and grow in character.
Where a single mother serving in children's ministry receives practical support rather than constant pressure.
Where an elderly usher is celebrated not merely for decades of attendance but for his testimony of faithfulness to Christ.
Where young volunteers are trained, encouraged, corrected lovingly, and given room to mature.
Where leaders notice when people are struggling before their ministry performance begins to decline.
Where serving is a joyful expression of belonging to Christ rather than a desperate attempt to prove one's worth.
And where rest is not interpreted as spiritual laziness.
Wouldn't that be a beautiful testimony to the world?
Not a perfect church.
There is no perfect congregation on this side of eternity.
But a repentant church.
A humble church.
A church where leaders and members alike are willing to be corrected by Scripture.
A church that remembers the people in the pews, on the platforms, behind the cameras, in the classrooms, and outside directing traffic are not disposable workers.
They are brothers and sisters for whom Christ died.
Paul wrote:
“And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.” — 1 Corinthians 12:26, KJV
The Church is a body.
Not a factory.
And when one part of the body is hurting, the answer is not to demand that it keep functioning until it collapses.
The answer is to care.
To listen.
To pray.
To support.
To restore.
To share burdens.
To remember that we belong to one another in Christ.
Galatians 6:2 says:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”
One another.
Those words matter.
Burden-bearing is not supposed to flow permanently in only one direction.
The volunteer who serves others also needs care.
The leader who carries responsibility also needs encouragement and accountability.
The pastor who ministers to the wounded also needs fellow believers who will pray for him and speak truth to him.
We need each other.
And above all, we need Jesus.
Perhaps you have been reading this with tears in your eyes because nobody knew how close you were to giving up.
You have not told anyone how much it hurts to feel invisible.
You have wondered whether your years of service mattered.
You have questioned whether God noticed the sacrifices nobody else remembered.
Let me remind you of Hebrews 6:10:
“For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister.” — KJV
God sees the labor of love done in His name.
Not every unnoticed act of service was wasted.
Not every difficult season was meaningless.
But this promise is not a command to remain indefinitely in a harmful situation.
It is a reminder that the Lord is just and faithful, even when human recognition is absent.
Your value was never created by your ministry position.
Your salvation was never earned by your volunteer hours.
And your place in Christ is not secured by how many responsibilities you can carry.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Notice the order.
Grace comes first.
Good works follow.
We do not serve to purchase God's acceptance.
We serve because of the grace He has given us.
That is the Gospel.

And if your ministry has quietly become an attempt to earn love, prove your worth, or escape the fear of disappointing others, perhaps Jesus is inviting you to remember where your identity truly begins.
Not in your title.
Not in your schedule.
Not in your achievements.
In Him.
There is a passage in Matthew 11 that feels especially tender here.
Jesus says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
In Greek, the invitation begins:
Δεῦτε πρός με — Deute pros me
“Come to me.”
And His promise includes:
κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς — kagō anapausō hymas
“And I will give you rest.”
In context, Jesus is calling the burdened to Himself and inviting them to take His yoke and learn from Him.
This is not a promise that discipleship will never involve suffering or demanding work.
It is an invitation into life under the gentle and humble Lord, whose way is fundamentally different from oppressive religious burden-bearing.
He does not invite us to become spiritually independent.
He invites us to come to Him.
And maybe that is exactly what you need today.
Not another assignment.
Not another demand.
Not another lecture about commitment.
But a renewed encounter with the Savior you began serving in the first place.
The One who knows your name.
The One who sees your tears.
The One who knows the motives of every heart, including yours.
The One who can expose what needs repentance, heal what has been wounded, and give wisdom for what must change.
And to the pastors and ministry leaders reading this, consider one question before your next volunteer meeting.
If every volunteer in your church stopped performing their assigned tasks for one Sunday, would you still know how to love them as members of Christ's body?
Would you know their struggles?
Would you know their spiritual needs?
Would you know whether they were growing in their relationship with Jesus?
Would they still feel welcomed and valued if they had nothing left to contribute?
These are not questions designed to humiliate leaders.
They are questions worth bringing before the Lord.
Because the greatest achievement of a church is not producing a flawless weekly program.
It is faithfully proclaiming Christ and nurturing people who know Him, love Him, and follow Him.
And to every volunteer who feels weary, I want to encourage you to do something courageous.
Speak honestly.
Not with bitterness.
Not with a desire to destroy.
But with truth and humility.
Ask for help where help is needed.
Seek wise counsel.
Make room for prayer, Scripture, family responsibilities, and genuine rest.
Examine your own motives.
Forgive where forgiveness is needed.
Pursue appropriate accountability where wrong has occurred.
And do not let your exhaustion convince you that Jesus has abandoned you.
If you have been serving out of fear rather than love, bring that fear to Him.
If you have become resentful, confess it to Him.
If you have used your authority to pressure or control others, repent before Him and seek to make things right.
If you have been wounded, ask Him for wisdom, courage, and healing.
Because this is where our story must always return.
Not merely to better volunteer management.
Not merely to healthier church systems.
Not merely to stronger leadership practices.
But to Jesus Christ.
Crucified for our sins.
Risen from the dead.
The Good Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.
The Lord who washes feet.
The Savior who restores sinners.
The Head of the Church who calls every one of us to follow Him.
This is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Even the story of a church volunteer who has forgotten what it feels like to be loved.
Even the story of a leader who must face the painful truth that good intentions do not excuse harmful actions.
Even the story of a congregation learning to replace pressure with discipleship, pride with humility, and appearances with genuine Christian love.
Jesus can rewrite those stories.
Not by pretending the damage never happened.
But through truth, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and transformed lives.
And if this article has exposed something in your own heart, please don't rush past that conviction.
Bring it to the Lord.
You do not need to disclose painful details to prove that your struggle is real.
Someone who is close to walking away may need to hear how the Lord helped you find wisdom, healing, and renewed faith.
Not to embarrass a church.
Not to attack a pastor.
But because there may be someone among your friends who has been silently asking whether anybody sees what they are going through.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow along.
Because our desire is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you draw closer to Him, I want to invite you into something more personal.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life of loving obedience, including generosity freely offered according to your ability and conviction.
But one meaningful way you can help glorify God is by supporting the faithful sharing of His Word.
We never want financial pressure to become another burden placed on the people of God.
The very message you have just read should remind us why that matters.
Support should flow from love, conviction, and willingness.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not manipulation.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
And discipleship should never be reduced to a transaction.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build a brand that people admire.
It is to point people toward the Savior who alone can redeem them.
Before you leave, I want to return to the person who started reading this article with a heavy heart.
The volunteer who is exhausted.
The pastor who is convicted.
The leader who knows something must change.
The believer who has been silently carrying resentment.
The person who loves the Church but has been deeply hurt by what happened inside it.
You are not beyond the reach of God's grace.
You can repent where you have sinned.
You can seek help where you have been harmed.
You can begin difficult conversations.
You can pursue restoration without denying the truth.
And you can return to Jesus, not because you have finally done enough for Him, but because He is the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
The Church belongs to Him.
The ministry belongs to Him.
Your life belongs to Him.
And His invitation still stands.
“Come unto me.”
So come.
Bring the exhaustion.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the questions.
Bring the guilt.
Bring the bitterness you need to surrender.
Bring the wounds you cannot heal by yourself.
Come to the One whose hands still bear the marks of His love.
And remember this:
Jesus did not shed His blood to turn you into disposable labor for His Church. He shed His blood to redeem you, make you His own, and teach you how to love and serve as someone who belongs to Him.
Never let the people who only noticed your empty ministry position make you forget the Savior who sees your entire soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE GOT OFF HER DONKEY AND ASKED FOR WATER—BUT WHAT ACHSAH UNDERSTOOD COULD CHANGE THE WAY YOU PRAY FOREVER
paragraphs: SHE GOT OFF HER DONKEY AND ASKED FOR WATER—BUT WHAT ACHSAH UNDERSTOOD COULD CHANGE THE WAY YOU PRAY FOREVER

Her father had already given her land. But she knew something was missing. One courageous request in Judges 1:14–15 reveals a forgotten lesson about faith, spiritual thirst, and the difference between receiving a blessing and having what you need to flourish.
There is a kind of suffering that comes from having nothing.
But there is another kind that is harder to explain.
It is the suffering of having something you once prayed for… and still feeling like something essential is missing.
You finally got the opportunity. The relationship. The home. The responsibility. The answer you begged God for.
And yet, somewhere beneath the gratitude, there is a quiet ache.
You have the land.
But where is the water?

You have the responsibilities of a family, but sometimes you feel emotionally empty. You have a Bible beside your bed, but your prayer life has become a whisper. You attend church, smile at people, serve when you can, and tell everyone you are blessed.
But when the room gets quiet, you know how thirsty your soul has become.
And perhaps the most painful part is that you feel guilty for admitting it.
Because shouldn't you be grateful?
Shouldn't what you already have be enough?
Somewhere in the ancient hills of Judah, a woman faced a question that still reaches into our lives thousands of years later.
Her name was Achsah.
She had received land.
But she understood that land without sufficient water could become a burden instead of a flourishing inheritance.
And what she did next was so significant that Scripture preserved her story not once, but twice.
In Judges 1:14–15, we read:
"And it came to pass, when she came to him, that she moved him to ask of her father a field: and she lighted from off her ass; and Caleb said unto her, What wilt thou?
And she said unto him, Give me a blessing: for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs." — Judges 1:14–15, KJV
Read that again.
She had land.
She asked for springs.
And her father gave her both the upper and the lower springs.
At first glance, this may seem like a small family conversation buried inside the history of Israel's conquest of Canaan.
But it is not a meaningless detail.
It is a glimpse into the life of a woman who understood her circumstances, recognized what was lacking, and was willing to speak.
And the deeper you look, the more remarkable her story becomes.
Achsah was the daughter of Caleb.
Yes, that Caleb.
The man who, alongside Joshua, had trusted God's promise when the majority of Israel's spies were overwhelmed by fear.
The man who, decades later, could still declare that he was ready to take possession of the hill country God had promised him (Joshua 14:6–12).
Caleb knew what it meant to trust God when circumstances looked impossible.
But now the story turns toward his daughter.
Before Achsah made her request, Caleb had promised her in marriage to the man who captured Kiriath-sepher, also known as Debir.
Othniel accomplished the conquest, and Caleb gave Achsah to him as his wife (Judges 1:12–13).
This was an ancient marriage arrangement within a historical setting very different from our own. Scripture records the arrangement without asking modern readers to imitate its customs.
And then comes the moment that makes Achsah unforgettable.
She did not remain silent about the land's needs.

The passage describes a conversation involving Achsah and Othniel about asking her father for a field. The Hebrew wording in verse 14 has a pronoun ambiguity, reflected in differences among English translations about who urged whom to make the request.
But the central event is unmistakable.
Achsah herself spoke to Caleb.
And she asked for water.
Something about that moment deserves our attention.
Because Achsah was not simply asking for something beautiful.
She was asking for something necessary.
The land was in the Negev, the southern region associated with dry conditions and limited rainfall.
In such a place, water was not a luxury.
Water meant life.
Water meant agriculture.
Water meant animals could survive, households could be sustained, and land could become genuinely useful.
A field could be legally yours and still be difficult to cultivate.
An inheritance could be valuable and still need resources to sustain the people living on it.
Achsah recognized the difference.
And instead of pretending the land had no limitations, she addressed them.
That is where her story begins to confront us.
Because how many people are quietly struggling under blessings they do not know how to steward?
How many parents love their children deeply but are exhausted beyond words?
How many husbands and wives have a home but are starving for honest communication?
How many believers have responsibilities in ministry but have neglected the private fellowship with Christ that sustains their service?
How many people have become so accustomed to surviving that they no longer remember what spiritual nourishment feels like?
Achsah did not deny the value of the land.
She recognized what the land required.
And there is wisdom in that distinction.
Gratitude does not require pretending that every need has already been met.
You can thank God for your family and still ask Him for wisdom to love them well.
You can thank God for your work and still ask for strength when the pressure becomes overwhelming.
You can thank God for the ministry He has entrusted to you and still admit that you need rest, correction, encouragement, and renewed dependence upon Him.
Sometimes the most faithful prayer is not an elaborate declaration.
Sometimes it is simply:
"Father, I am grateful for what You have given me. But I need Your help to live faithfully with it."
And then there is that extraordinary detail.
She got off her donkey.
The King James Version says she "lighted from off her ass."
The Hebrew verb used here is וַתִּצְנַח — wattitsnaḥ, from a verb describing her movement down from the animal.
It is a physical action in the narrative.
We should be careful not to invent a hidden spiritual meaning and claim that the Hebrew secretly commands every believer to "come down from pride."
The text does not say that.
But the scene is still powerful.
A woman approaches her father.
He notices her.
And he asks a question that changes the conversation.
"What wilt thou?"
What do you want?
What is it that you need?
Imagine standing in that moment.
You have already been given something valuable.
You know your father has been generous.
But you also know that the land will need water.
Would you speak?
Or would you remain silent because you were afraid of appearing ungrateful?
Achsah spoke.
And her words are worth examining carefully.
In Hebrew, her request begins:
תְּנָה־לִּי בְרָכָה — tenah-li verakhah.
"Give me a blessing."
The word בְּרָכָה — berakhah means "blessing" and can also refer to a gift or benefit in contexts like this one.
Achsah was not asking her father to make her spiritually superior.
She was requesting a tangible provision connected to the land.
She continued:
כִּי אֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב נְתַתָּנִי — ki erets ha-negev netattani.
"For you have given me land in the Negev."
Then came the heart of her request:
וְנָתַתָּה לִי גֻּלֹּת מָיִם — ve-natattah li gullot mayim.
"Give me also springs of water."
The Hebrew expression גֻּלֹּת מָיִם — gullot mayim refers to water sources or springs.
This was not a vague demand for more possessions.
It was a specific request grounded in a real need.
And Caleb's response was remarkable.
He gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
The text does not tell us the exact volume of water those springs supplied, or the precise location of every source.
It does tell us that her father responded by granting the resources she requested.
The gift of land was accompanied by the gift of water.
And that detail is so important that the account appears again in Joshua 15:16–19.
Two passages.
One request.
One unforgettable lesson about recognizing need and speaking honestly.
But we must be careful here.
Achsah's story is not a promise that God will give every Christian whatever they ask for.
Caleb was a human father distributing land and water resources within Israel's history.
God is not simply a larger version of Caleb, obligated to approve every request we bring.
And this account is not a secret formula for wealth, prosperity, property ownership, or guaranteed success.
The Bible never gives us permission to turn every narrative into a promise of personal abundance.
Sometimes faithful believers pray for healing and still endure illness.
Sometimes they pray for financial relief and continue through hardship.
Sometimes they ask God to remove a burden, and the answer is not removal but sustaining grace.
The apostle Paul knew this.
He pleaded with the Lord three times concerning his thorn in the flesh.
And the answer he received was:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Not every prayer ends with the circumstances changing.
Sometimes the miracle is that Christ sustains us while the circumstances remain difficult.
And that brings us to something even deeper than Achsah's springs.
Because there is another woman in Scripture who had a conversation about water.
She was not standing before Caleb.
She was standing beside a well.
And the Man speaking to her was Jesus Christ.
In John 4, Jesus met a Samaritan woman who had come to draw water.
She had a complicated personal history, and the conversation exposed truths about her life that Jesus already knew.
But He did not approach her merely to shame her.
He spoke to her about a gift she could never draw from that well.
Living water.
Jesus told her:

"But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life." — John 4:14, KJV
The Greek phrase translated "living water" is ὕδωρ ζῶν — hydōr zōn.
In ordinary usage, the expression could describe fresh, flowing water.
But Jesus used it to reveal a spiritual reality far greater than the physical water the woman came to collect.
He was offering the life that comes through Him.
Not a temporary improvement in her circumstances.
Not an escape from every earthly difficulty.
Eternal life.
And in John 7:37–39, Jesus again spoke of living water, with John explicitly connecting His words to the Holy Spirit who would be given to believers.
Now we begin to see an important biblical connection.
Achsah needed actual springs to sustain life on her land.
The Samaritan woman needed more than the water in Jacob's well.
And every human being needs more than earthly provision to be reconciled to God.
We need Jesus Christ.
The connection is a meaningful comparison between passages, not a claim that Judges secretly identifies Achsah's springs as Christ or the Holy Spirit.
The original story concerns a real woman and real water.
But read alongside the fuller testimony of Scripture, it reminds us how deeply dependent human life is upon provision—and how much more deeply our souls depend upon God.
You can own land and still need water.
You can possess wealth and still lack peace.
You can have thousands of followers and still feel unseen.
You can know religious language and still have never truly surrendered to Jesus.
You can serve in a church and still be hiding sin that is slowly hardening your heart.
And no amount of public admiration can substitute for private repentance.
That is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we are not simply thirsty.
Sometimes we have been drinking from the wrong places.
We turn to applause to feel valuable.
We turn to possessions to feel secure.
We turn to relationships expecting another human being to heal wounds only God can fully address.
We turn to entertainment to escape conviction.
We turn to religious activity to avoid the harder work of confession.
We learn how to look spiritually alive without being honest about what is happening inside.
And eventually, the noise fades.
The distractions stop working.
The applause grows quiet.
And we discover that the thirst is still there.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our religious appearance.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins through His death on the cross and rise again in victory over death.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not to pretend we have never failed.
It is to repent and believe in Him.
That is the scandal of grace.
The holy Son of God gave Himself for people who could never earn their own salvation.
He does not call sin harmless.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He does not excuse our rebellion.
He offers forgiveness through His sacrifice.
He does not leave those who trust Him where they were.
He begins transforming them by His grace.
Think of the people Jesus welcomed.
The tax collector despised by his neighbors.
The woman whose life had become a public disgrace.
The disciple who denied Him.
The dying criminal who had nothing left to offer but a desperate appeal for mercy.
Jesus was never impressed by a polished reputation.
He came to seek and save the lost.
And perhaps that is the word someone reading this needs tonight.
You do not need to manufacture a beautiful spiritual performance before you come to Christ.
You need to come truthfully.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have wandered, turn back.
If you have become spiritually cold, do not call your indifference maturity.
If you are carrying grief, bring it before the Lord.
If you have been exhausted by trying to prove your worth, remember that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for impressive religious performance (Ephesians 2:8–10).
And if you have never trusted Jesus as Savior and Lord, do not confuse knowing Christian stories with belonging to Christ.
Hear His call to repent and believe the Gospel.
Because the deepest thirst of the human soul cannot be healed by simply receiving more earthly blessings.
It is answered in the One who said:
"If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink." — John 7:37, KJV
Notice where Jesus directs the thirsty.
Not to a personality.
Not to a religious brand.
Not to a building.
To Himself.
That distinction matters deeply.
Christian ministries can teach, encourage, equip, and help believers grow.
Books can deepen understanding.
Devotionals can nurture daily discipline.
A community of believers can pray together and strengthen one another.
But none of these can replace Jesus.
They are useful only when they lead us toward Him and remain faithful to His Word.
And that is why the story of Achsah should not end with a shallow message about demanding more blessings.
Its historical lesson is richer.
She understood what had been entrusted to her.
She recognized a genuine need.
She spoke plainly.
And her father responded generously.
For us, that scene can become an invitation to examine our lives with the same seriousness.
What has God entrusted to you?
And what do you need in order to steward it faithfully?
Maybe you need wisdom more than another opportunity.
Maybe you need reconciliation more than another public victory.
Maybe you need to return to Scripture instead of endlessly consuming religious content that leaves you entertained but unchanged.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you wounded.
Maybe you need to stop hiding an addiction and seek real accountability.
Maybe you need to forgive someone—not by pretending the harm never happened, but by entrusting justice to God and refusing to let bitterness rule your heart.
Maybe you need rest.
Maybe you need to ask your church family for help.
Maybe you need to admit that you have spent years teaching others about Christ while neglecting your own fellowship with Him.
And maybe the words you have been afraid to pray are the very words you need to say.
"Lord, I need You."
Not because those words force heaven to obey you.
But because they acknowledge the truth.
Apart from Christ, we can do nothing of lasting spiritual fruitfulness (John 15:5).
There is no shame in depending on the One who made us.
There is no disgrace in admitting that we are not self-sufficient.
And there is no spiritual maturity in pretending to be strong when we are quietly falling apart.
Achsah asked for springs because she understood the land.
We should ask God for wisdom because we understand our limitations.
James 1:5 encourages believers who lack wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.
And Hebrews 4:16 calls us to approach the throne of grace with confidence so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
These promises do not guarantee that life will become effortless.
They assure us that those who belong to Christ may draw near to God through Him.
That is better than a formula.
That is relationship.
And it changes how we pray.
Instead of treating God as someone whose generosity must be manipulated, we learn to trust Him as our heavenly Father.
Instead of demanding that every earthly desire be fulfilled, we seek His will.
Instead of assuming unanswered prayer means we have been abandoned, we remember that His wisdom exceeds ours.
And instead of measuring His love by the comfort of our circumstances, we look to the cross.
Because the cross is where the love of God has been revealed with a clarity no earthly success can surpass.
If you ever doubt whether God takes sin seriously, look at the cross.
If you ever doubt whether His grace can reach the undeserving, look at the cross.
If you ever wonder whether broken people can be restored, remember the empty tomb.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose again.
And everyone who truly comes to Him in faith is offered forgiveness and new life—not because they have earned it, but because of what He has accomplished.
This is why we keep returning to the Gospel.
Not because every story in the Old Testament is secretly about our personal success.
But because the whole testimony of Scripture ultimately directs us toward God's redemptive purposes fulfilled in Christ (Luke 24:44–47).
Achsah's story teaches us something about wise requests and the practical needs of an inheritance.
Jesus reveals the greater gift that no earthly inheritance can provide.
And when we understand that difference, the story becomes more beautiful, not less.
Because we no longer have to force Achsah to say something she never said.
We can honor her actual story.
And we can honor Christ as the Savior Scripture truly proclaims.
Now imagine Achsah returning to the land.
The Bible does not describe her private emotions or tell us what she said afterward.
We should not invent a conversation Scripture never records.
But we do know this:
She had asked for water.
And she received the upper and lower springs.
The land that needed water now had water sources.
The request mattered.
And Scripture considered it worth remembering.
Perhaps your next step will not look dramatic to anyone watching.
It may be opening your Bible after months of neglect.
It may be getting on your knees beside your bed.
It may be confessing the truth to someone who can help you.
It may be reaching out to a pastor.
It may be returning to a church community after a painful season.
It may be asking your spouse to pray with you.
It may be telling God, with no impressive words and no attempt to hide:
"Father, I have been trying to survive without depending on You. Forgive me. Teach me to walk with You again."
And if that is where you are, remember this:
Your weakness does not disqualify you from coming to Christ.
Your past does not place you beyond the reach of His mercy.
But His grace is not an invitation to remain comfortable in sin.
It is an invitation to turn from sin and follow Him.
Repentance is not merely feeling emotional for a few moments.
It is a change of heart and direction, brought about through God's grace, that bears fruit in a transformed life.
Some changes happen immediately.
Others require patient obedience, support, confession, and perseverance over time.
And through it all, the believer's hope rests not in the perfection of personal effort but in the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
That is the kind of faith we want to nurture at Gospel Warrior.
Not a faith built on sensational claims.
Not a faith that promises everyone will become wealthy.
Not a faith that confuses buying religious products with being close to God.
But a faith anchored in Scripture, grounded in the Gospel, honest about suffering, serious about repentance, and overflowing with gratitude for the grace of Jesus.
Because people do not simply need more inspirational words.
They need biblical truth that can withstand a difficult Tuesday.
They need the courage to keep trusting God when the medical report is frightening.
They need the strength to remain faithful when a marriage is strained.
They need wisdom to raise children in a confusing world.
They need discipleship that continues after the emotional moment has passed.
And they need to know that following Christ is not about pretending life is easy.
It is about belonging to the Savior who is faithful even when life is hard.
That is why your participation matters.
If this article has helped you see Scripture more clearly, please do not let it end as something you read and forget.

Not because saving a post makes someone spiritually mature, but because there may come a day when you need to revisit this reminder: you can be grateful for what God has given you and still humbly ask for His help.

Somewhere among your friends may be a mother who feels depleted, a father carrying silent pressure, a young believer struggling with doubt, or someone who has been afraid to admit that their spiritual life has grown dry.
You cannot know every burden people carry.
But you can help place a Scripture-centered message within their reach.
Not to embarrass them or publicly expose their struggles.
You do not need to reveal private details or tell strangers everything you are going through.
But perhaps you can simply write:
And if you have seen the Lord sustain you through a season when you felt spiritually empty, consider sharing a short testimony.
Someone reading your words may need that encouragement.
Your testimony does not have to be dramatic to glorify God.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony is simply:
"I was struggling, but Christ has been faithful."
Our desire is to make biblical truth accessible, to encourage genuine discipleship, and to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, deepen their understanding of the Christian faith, strengthen their prayer lives, and grow in obedience to Christ.
And they remain free because we believe biblical encouragement and opportunities for spiritual learning should not depend on someone's ability to pay.
But continuing and expanding this work requires practical support.
Writing, preparing, organizing, maintaining, and sharing discipleship resources takes time, effort, and financial resources.
This is where those who believe in the mission can make a meaningful difference.
For believers who are prayerfully deciding how to give, this support can be considered part of their voluntary Christian generosity and stewardship.
But an important biblical distinction must remain clear.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the heart behind this invitation.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
But an opportunity to participate voluntarily in a ministry whose purpose is to proclaim Christ and help people grow in His Word.
If you are able to support, your contribution can help make those resources available to others who cannot.
The greater mission remains the same.
Jesus Christ proclaimed.
Scripture faithfully taught.
Believers encouraged.
Sinners called to repentance.
The broken invited to find forgiveness and new life in Christ.
A single shared article may reach someone who would never walk into a church building on their own.
A sincere comment may encourage someone who thought they were the only person struggling.
A conversation started by a Scripture passage may become an opportunity to speak about Jesus.
We cannot manufacture spiritual transformation.
Only God can change the human heart.
But we can faithfully proclaim His Word, serve others, and trust Him with the fruit.
And that brings us back to the woman on the donkey.
Achsah.
A daughter who understood the land she had been given.
A woman who recognized the need for water.
A woman whose request became part of the biblical record.
Her story is not about the power of demanding whatever we desire.
It is about a real need, a thoughtful request, and a generous response.
And as we close, there is one question worth carrying into your own life.
What are you trying to sustain without the help you genuinely need?
Is it your family?
Your faith?
Your emotional well-being?
Your responsibilities?
Your ministry?
Your walk with Christ?
Perhaps you have become so skilled at carrying everything that no one knows how tired you are.
Perhaps people admire your strength while you quietly wonder how much longer you can keep going.
