Perhaps you have spent so much time trying to appear spiritually mature that you have forgotten how to pray with the honesty of a child who needs his Father.
You do not need to impress God with your ability to survive without Him.
You need to trust Him.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, the invitation is greater than asking for relief from your circumstances.
Come to the Savior Himself.
Turn from sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the forgiveness and new life that only He can give.
For those who already belong to Him, return to His Word, remain in fellowship with His people, and continue learning to depend upon His grace.
The springs in Achsah's story sustained an earthly inheritance.
The living water Jesus gives points to eternal life in Him.
And no earthly possession, no public success, and no human approval can take His place.
So tonight, before you close this article, perhaps your prayer can be simple.

"Lord Jesus, forgive me for the ways I have tried to live without depending on You. Expose what needs to change. Give me wisdom for what You have entrusted to me. Teach me to be grateful without pretending I have no needs. Help me repent where I have sinned, trust You where I am afraid, and follow You even when the road is difficult. Let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen."
And when you remember Achsah, remember what Scripture actually tells us.
She did not pretend the dry land had everything it needed.
She asked for water.
But when you remember Jesus, remember something infinitely greater.
He does not merely offer to improve the landscape of your life.
He offers Himself as Savior.
And the greatest gift of grace is not that we receive everything we have ever wanted.
It is that, through Jesus Christ, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
You can spend your whole life trying to make dry ground look beautiful—or you can finally admit your thirst and come to the One who gives living water.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LOVE CHAPTER WAS NEVER MEANT TO MAKE YOU FEEL ROMANTIC. IT WAS MEANT TO MAKE THE CHURCH REPENT.
paragraphs: THE LOVE CHAPTER WAS NEVER MEANT TO MAKE YOU FEEL ROMANTIC. IT WAS MEANT TO MAKE THE CHURCH REPENT.

We quote 1 Corinthians 13 at weddings, print it on beautiful pictures, and call it the greatest description of love ever written. But when Paul first wrote those words, he was confronting Christians who had spiritual gifts, biblical knowledge, and religious confidence—yet were hurting the very people they claimed to love.
What if the chapter you've always found comforting was actually written to expose something dangerous in your own heart?
There is something deeply unsettling about the possibility that you can speak about Jesus beautifully and still treat people terribly.
You can know Scripture and still wound someone with your words.
You can pray with passion and still carry bitterness.
You can worship with tears streaming down your face, then walk out of church and destroy someone's reputation.
You can defend sound doctrine while becoming arrogant toward the people Christ died to save.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility of all...
You can become so impressed with what God has given you that you forget why He gave it to you.
That is the uncomfortable world behind one of the most beloved chapters in the entire Bible.
First Corinthians 13.
The famous love chapter.
The passage people read while brides walk down aisles, couples exchange vows, and families celebrate the beauty of commitment.
And there is nothing wrong with applying its truth to marriage. Every Christian marriage desperately needs the kind of love Paul describes.
But Paul was not originally writing wedding vows.
He was confronting a troubled church.
A church with spiritual gifts.
A church with knowledge.
A church that had experienced remarkable manifestations of the Spirit.
And a church that was being torn apart by pride, rivalry, selfishness, and spiritual immaturity.

Imagine receiving a letter from an apostle of Jesus Christ, gathering with your congregation to hear it read aloud, and discovering that the very spiritual abilities you celebrated had become evidence of how badly you misunderstood the heart of God.
That was the confrontation awaiting Corinth.
And before we point our fingers at them, we should recognize something.
The modern church is not nearly as different as we might wish.
Somewhere right now, a believer is being humiliated by someone who knows more Bible verses than they do.
Someone is leaving a congregation because the people who preached grace refused to extend it.
Someone is being treated as insignificant because they do not possess the gifts, influence, wealth, or visibility that others admire.
Someone is using spiritual language to disguise an unrepentant heart.
And someone is quietly asking a devastating question:
"If these people belong to Jesus, why do they treat me like this?"
Paul's answer reaches across nearly two thousand years.
And it begins with a warning that should make every spiritually confident Christian tremble.
You can have extraordinary gifts and still be spiritually bankrupt in love.
Paul writes:
— 1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV
Read that again.
Paul does not say the person cannot speak.
He does not say the person lacks impressive abilities.
He says the person can possess extraordinary speech and still amount to nothing more than noise when love is absent.
The Greek word translated "charity" in the King James Version is ἀγάπη (agapē).
In contemporary English, "love" communicates Paul's meaning more clearly than the modern sense of "charity" as financial giving.
But this is not merely romantic affection, emotional warmth, or the ability to say something kind when everyone is watching.
Paul is describing love that expresses itself in patience, humility, truthfulness, endurance, and genuine concern for another person's good.
It is love that refuses to turn God's gifts into weapons of self-importance.
It is love shaped by the character of the God who first loved us.
And the Corinthians desperately needed to hear about it.
Because their problem was not a complete absence of religion.
Their problem was that religion had become a stage upon which human pride could perform.
Earlier in the letter, Paul confronted divisions among believers who were identifying themselves with different Christian leaders.
Some claimed allegiance to Paul.
Others to Apollos.
Others to Cephas.
Still others said they belonged to Christ.
Instead of celebrating the one Savior who had redeemed them, they were allowing human loyalties to divide the body.
Paul confronted their jealousy and strife in 1 Corinthians 3:3.
He challenged their arrogance.
He rebuked their tolerance of serious sexual immorality.
He addressed lawsuits between believers, abuses of Christian freedom, and behavior at the Lord's Supper that humiliated poorer members of the congregation.
In 1 Corinthians 11:21, some were eating abundantly while others went hungry.
Think about that.
They were gathering around a meal meant to proclaim the Lord's death, yet their conduct exposed painful divisions among the very people His death had brought together.
They knew how to participate in a religious gathering.
But they were failing to recognize the dignity of their brothers and sisters.
Then came the disputes surrounding spiritual gifts.
Some gifts appeared more impressive than others.
Some believers seemed to consider themselves more important because of what they could do.
And Paul had to remind them that the body of Christ does not consist of one member, but many.
The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of thee."
The head cannot say to the feet, "I have no need of you."
Those words from 1 Corinthians 12:21 were not merely an inspirational lesson about teamwork.
They were a direct challenge to spiritual superiority.
The church was treating some members as though they mattered less.
And Paul was saying, in effect:
You cannot honor the Head while despising His body.
Then, at the end of chapter 12, Paul introduces "a more excellent way."
Not a replacement for every spiritual gift.
Not a rejection of the Holy Spirit's work.
But the indispensable way in which every gift must be exercised.
Love.
That is where chapter 13 begins.
And suddenly, the beautiful passage we thought we knew becomes far more searching.
Paul continues:
"And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing."
— 1 Corinthians 13:2, KJV
Not merely less effective.
Not simply immature in one area.
"I am nothing."
The Greek is striking:
οὐθέν εἰμι (outhen eimi)
"I am nothing."
Paul is using sweeping, hypothetical language to expose the complete inadequacy of spiritual greatness without love.
He is not declaring that spiritual gifts are evil.
He is declaring that gifts cannot substitute for Christlike character.
And that distinction matters.
Because there are Christians who can explain complex doctrines but cannot apologize.
Christians who can recognize errors in other people's theology but cannot recognize cruelty in their own tone.
Christians who will argue passionately about the authority of Scripture while ignoring its commands to be gentle, patient, forgiving, and humble.
Perhaps you have encountered someone like that.
Perhaps you have been wounded by someone like that.
Or perhaps, if you are willing to be painfully honest before God, you have sometimes been that person.
I know that is not easy to consider.
It is far more comfortable to examine Corinth than to examine ourselves.
It is easier to condemn a proud preacher than to acknowledge the pride hiding inside our own desire to be right.
It is easier to criticize an unloving church than to remember the family member we have refused to forgive.
It is easier to quote a chapter about love than to obey it when love becomes costly.
And Paul is not finished.
He writes:
— 1 Corinthians 13:3, KJV
Even radical generosity cannot compensate for the absence of love.
Even an outwardly extraordinary sacrifice can be emptied of its proper spiritual purpose when driven by pride, self-exaltation, or some motive other than genuine love.

There is an important textual detail here. Some ancient Greek manuscripts read, in effect, "that I may boast," where the King James tradition reads "to be burned." The textual question does not change Paul's central argument: even the most dramatic acts of sacrifice are spiritually deficient without love.
And that should confront something deeply human in all of us.
Because sometimes we do good things for complicated reasons.
We serve because we want to be noticed.
We give because we want to be admired.
We help because we want someone to feel indebted to us.
We sacrifice, but quietly keep a record of what everyone owes us.
We speak about ministry, yet become resentful when someone else receives recognition.
And suddenly, Paul's words are no longer aimed at an ancient congregation.
They are standing in our living room.
Sitting beside us in church.
Following us into our private thoughts.
Asking us a question we cannot escape:
Are you loving people, or are you using people to feel spiritually important?
That question can hurt.
Especially when you have spent years serving God.
Especially when you have sacrificed time, money, comfort, and opportunities for ministry.
Especially when you genuinely believe you are doing the right thing.
But the Lord who loves us does not flatter our self-deception.
He exposes what needs healing.
And Paul moves from the spectacular to the painfully ordinary.
"Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up."
— 1 Corinthians 13:4, KJV
Here is where the passage becomes almost unbearably personal.
Love is patient.
Not merely when the other person is easy to love.
Love is kind.
Not only when kindness earns appreciation.
Love does not envy.
Not even when someone else receives the opportunity, blessing, or recognition you wanted.
Love does not boast.
Not even when you actually know more, have accomplished more, or possess a gift someone else does not.
Love is not arrogant.
Even when you are correct.
In Greek, Paul's description begins:
Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται ἡ ἀγάπη.
Hē agapē makrothymei, chrēsteuetai hē agapē.
"Love is patient; love is kind."
The verb μακροθυμεῖ (makrothymei) conveys patience or long-suffering, particularly the willingness to endure provocation without quickly retaliating.
The verb χρηστεύεται (chrēsteuetai) expresses kindness.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not define love primarily by emotional intensity.
He describes what love does.
How love behaves.
How love responds when the other person disappoints us.
How love restrains pride when we are tempted to elevate ourselves.
How love treats someone who cannot offer us anything in return.
This is not sentimental poetry.
It is a mirror.
And sometimes the reflection is painful.
Consider the Christian who speaks gently to strangers at church but harshly to a spouse at home.
The ministry leader who encourages an audience but humiliates volunteers behind closed doors.
The parent who teaches children about God's mercy but rarely admits when they have been wrong.
The believer who publicly celebrates forgiveness while privately enjoying another person's downfall.
The person who can spend hours discussing spiritual warfare but cannot endure a minor disagreement without becoming cruel.
These are not imaginary temptations.
They are recognizable human struggles.
And no amount of religious vocabulary makes them holy.
Paul continues by saying love does not behave disgracefully, does not insist on its own way, is not easily provoked, and does not keep an account of wrongs.
The Greek phrase in verse 5, οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακόν (ou logizetai to kakon), communicates that love does not calculate or keep a ledger of wrongs in the spirit of resentment.
That does not mean pretending abuse never happened.
It does not mean abandoning accountability, refusing necessary boundaries, or allowing an unrepentant person to continue harming others.
Biblical love is not moral blindness.
In fact, verse 6 says love does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth.
Love and truth are not enemies.
Real love does not protect sin merely to preserve appearances.
Real love does not call evil good.
Real love can confront, correct, establish boundaries, seek justice, and protect the vulnerable.
But it does not delight in humiliation.
It does not weaponize truth to satisfy pride.
It does not turn another person's failure into entertainment.
And that is a message the church urgently needs.
Because we live in a world where outrage travels quickly.
Where public humiliation can attract attention.
Where arguments become performances.
Where someone can gain an audience by exposing another person's failures.
And where even Christians can confuse the ability to win an argument with the ability to represent Jesus.
But a person can win an argument and still fail to love.
A person can expose someone else's sin while refusing to repent of their own.
A person can defend truth with such arrogance that the manner of their defense contradicts the very Savior they claim to represent.
The Gospel never requires us to compromise truth.
It requires us to speak and live truth in a way that reflects the character of Christ.
And this is where the story becomes even more beautiful.
Because 1 Corinthians 13 does not simply reveal what is wrong with us.
It directs us toward the One who can make us new.
Jesus Christ.
Consider how Jesus treated people.
He confronted religious hypocrisy without hesitation.
He exposed sin without calling sin righteousness.
He warned of judgment.
He commanded repentance.
Yet He also welcomed sinners who came to Him in need.
He touched the unclean.
He showed compassion to the suffering.
He received the brokenhearted.
He called sinners to leave their sin behind, while offering mercy they could never earn.
He was neither weak in truth nor cruel in righteousness.
He embodied perfect holiness and perfect love.
And when we look at the cross, we discover something even more astonishing.
God did not wait for us to become lovable before demonstrating His love.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had mastered patience.
Not after we had conquered pride.
Not after we had repaired every relationship.
Not after we had learned to love as we should.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
The cross does not excuse our lack of love.
It exposes the seriousness of our sin while revealing the greatness of God's grace.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
That is the difference between moral improvement and Gospel transformation.
Paul was not merely telling the Corinthians to become nicer people.
He was addressing believers whose lives needed to reflect the crucified and risen Lord.
Because the Christian life is not simply about displaying spiritual ability.
It is about belonging to Jesus and being transformed into His likeness.
And that transformation begins with grace.
Not performance.
Not spiritual competition.
Not the desperate attempt to prove we deserve God's acceptance.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
And the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave us unchanged.
Grace produces a new direction.
The Holy Spirit forms in believers the fruit of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control, as Galatians 5:22–23 teaches.
Notice that love is first in that list.
Not because the other virtues are unimportant, but because love is central to the life God calls us to live.
And the love Paul describes is not something we can manufacture through religious performance alone.
We need the Spirit of God to transform our hearts.
We need repentance when pride rises.
We need forgiveness when we fail.
We need humility to recognize that knowing the right answer does not mean we have always responded in the right spirit.
We need Jesus.
Not merely as the subject of our sermons.
Not merely as the name attached to our ministries.
Not merely as the One we mention in our testimonies.
We need Him as Savior, Lord, and the living center of everything we are becoming.
And perhaps that is why Paul's rebuke is so merciful.
He could have allowed the Corinthians to remain impressed with themselves.
He could have let them confuse extraordinary gifts with extraordinary maturity.
Instead, he confronted them.
Because a loving correction can rescue someone from a dangerous illusion.
Sometimes God's mercy comes through comfort.
Sometimes it comes through conviction.
Sometimes it comes through a passage we have read a hundred times, suddenly revealing a sin we have refused to acknowledge.
And if this chapter has exposed something uncomfortable in you, do not run from the Lord.
Run toward Him.
The same Jesus who exposes our sin is the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The same Gospel that humbles our pride announces forgiveness through His blood.
The same grace that saves us also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
You do not have to pretend you have always loved well.
You do not have to defend every harsh word you have spoken.
You do not have to keep calling stubbornness conviction when God is calling you to humility.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can seek forgiveness from someone you wounded.
You can begin rebuilding trust through changed behavior.
And where reconciliation is safe and appropriate, you can pursue peace without pretending that repentance removes every consequence.
Because genuine repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
It is turning toward God and away from sin.
It bears fruit.
And sometimes the first evidence of transformation is not a dramatic public testimony.
Sometimes it is a quiet apology.
A restrained tongue.
A decision not to retaliate.
A willingness to listen.
A refusal to gossip.
An act of kindness nobody sees.
A prayer for someone you once envied.
A choice to tell the truth without destroying the person who needs to hear it.
Small moments.
Unseen moments.
Holy moments in which the character of Christ begins to become visible.
And perhaps those moments reveal more about spiritual maturity than the applause we receive in public.
Paul goes on to say that prophecies will cease, tongues will cease, and knowledge will pass away.
He is contrasting the partial and temporary nature of present spiritual gifts and understanding with the enduring reality of love.
Christians have differing interpretations of precisely when certain gifts cease, but Paul's central argument is unmistakable.
The Corinthians were boasting in things that were never meant to become the ultimate measure of spiritual greatness.
He tells them that now we know in part.
Now we see through a glass, darkly.
But a day is coming when what is partial will give way to fullness.
And then he reaches the magnificent conclusion:
"And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."
— 1 Corinthians 13:13, KJV
The greatest is love.
Not because faith is unnecessary.
Not because hope is insignificant.
But because love holds an extraordinary place in God's purpose for His people.
And here is something we must not miss.
Paul does not end his discussion by telling believers to abandon spiritual gifts.
In 1 Corinthians 14:1, he writes:
Love is not an excuse to neglect the Spirit's work.
It is the essential way we must pursue and exercise that work.
A spiritually gifted church should also be a loving church.
A biblically knowledgeable Christian should also be a humble Christian.
A bold defender of truth should also be someone whose conduct honors the Lord of truth.
And when these things are separated, something has gone terribly wrong.
Now consider the most uncomfortable possibility of all.
What if the person who most needs to hear this message is not the preacher who hurt you?
Not the Christian who disappointed you?
Not the church member who offended you?
What if it is you?
What if there is someone who still remembers the words you spoke when you were angry?
Someone who stopped opening up because you made them feel small?
Someone whose weakness became the subject of your conversation?
Someone you dismissed because they did not seem as spiritually mature as you?
Someone who needed compassion but received condemnation without gentleness?
It is possible to have been genuinely wronged and still need to repent of how we responded.
It is possible to have defended a true principle with an unloving heart.
And it is possible to spend so much time identifying everyone else's spiritual failures that we stop allowing Scripture to examine our own.
That is why this chapter must never become merely another weapon to use against people we dislike.
Paul's words should first lead us into honest self-examination before God.
Not despair.
Not self-hatred.
Repentance.
The kind that leads us back to the mercy of Jesus.
Maybe your prayer today needs to be very simple.

"Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have been more concerned about being right than being loving. Forgive my pride, my bitterness, and the ways I have hurt people while claiming to honor You. Teach me to love without compromising truth. Change my heart. Help me become more like You."
You do not need impressive language to come before God.
You need an honest heart.
And if this message has reached a place you have been hiding, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
Or, if you are struggling with wounds caused by other believers, you can simply comment, "Pray for me."
You do not have to explain private details publicly.
Sometimes those few words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Someone reading may desperately need to know that genuine transformation is possible.
Because this message is not meant to end with conviction.
It is meant to lead us to Christ.
And perhaps someone on your Facebook friends list needs that reminder right now.
Someone who has walked away from church because they were wounded by religious pride.
Someone who loves Jesus but is exhausted by spiritual competition.
Someone who has mistaken biblical knowledge for spiritual maturity.
Someone who is struggling to forgive.
Someone who has been hiding behind ministry activity while quietly growing distant from God.
Not merely because it might reach more people, but because the truth of Scripture is worth placing where someone else can encounter it.
Not as another piece of religious content to collect, but as a reminder to revisit 1 Corinthians 12–14 and examine the way you are living.
Because the temptation to substitute spiritual performance for genuine love does not disappear after reading one powerful message.
We need to keep returning to God's Word.
We need fellowship.
We need discipleship.
We need correction.
We need encouragement.
And above all, we need to keep our eyes on Jesus Christ.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a platform around a personality.
Not to turn conviction into entertainment.
Not to make people dependent on a ministry instead of dependent on Christ.
But to keep pointing people back to Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Through Gospel Warrior, we want to help believers grow beyond occasional inspiration into a deeper, steadier walk with Jesus.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who cannot afford to pay.
And certainly not because your standing before Jesus depends on a financial contribution.
But Scripture does teach that believers can honor God by freely and generously supporting faithful Gospel work.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
That matters deeply.
Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through fear, guilt, or spiritual pressure.
It is meant to flow from a willing heart.
Some believers can support through financial giving.
Others can support by praying, sharing, encouraging, and faithfully pointing people toward Christ.
Every sincere act of service has value before God, even when it is unseen by the world.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Christ is.

Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who feel spiritually lukewarm, those who have been wounded by religious hypocrisy, and even those who are still searching for the truth about Jesus.
Not everyone who encounters this ministry will agree with every word.
Not everyone is ready to believe.
But everyone deserves to hear the Gospel clearly, without manipulation, and to be treated with the dignity owed to someone made in the image of God.
And that brings us back to Corinth.
Back to a congregation with remarkable gifts and painful divisions.
Back to an apostle who loved the church enough to confront its pride.
Back to a chapter that has been recited at countless weddings but was originally written to correct a congregation that had forgotten how to love.
Perhaps we have spent too many years admiring the beauty of 1 Corinthians 13 without allowing its truth to disturb us.
Perhaps we have memorized its words while resisting its demands.
Perhaps we have been asking God for greater gifts when we should also be asking Him for deeper humility.
And perhaps the most powerful thing that could happen in our churches is not another impressive performance, another public recognition, or another moment of religious excitement.
Perhaps it is a proud believer finally admitting they were wrong.
A wounded person finding the courage to seek help and healing.
A family beginning to practice forgiveness.
A ministry leader learning to serve without needing applause.
A Christian choosing gentleness when anger would have been easier.
A congregation learning to honor its weakest members.
A sinner falling before Jesus and discovering that His grace is greater than the shame they have been carrying.
That is not weakness.
That is the beauty of the Gospel bearing fruit in human lives.
The world does not need Christians who merely sound impressive.
It needs to encounter the truth about Jesus through believers who refuse to separate their confession of faith from the way they live.
Jesus Himself said:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another."
— John 13:35, KJV
Not if you have the largest audience.
Not if you win every theological debate.
Not if everyone recognizes your gifts.
But if you have love for one another.
And no, that love does not save us.
Christ saves us.
But genuine love is one of the ways His transforming grace becomes visible in the lives of His people.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one final question.
Not, "Who do I know who needs to read this?"
That question may have its place later.
First ask:
"Lord, where have I been using my spiritual knowledge, my gifts, or my religious activity to avoid confronting the condition of my own heart?"
Then listen.
Open the Scriptures.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Make right what you can.
Seek wise help where wounds are deep.
Receive the forgiveness Christ offers to those who come to Him.
And walk forward in the grace that teaches us to love.
Because Paul did not write 1 Corinthians 13 so that spiritually gifted Christians could admire a beautiful description of love.
He wrote it so that they would recognize how desperately they needed to practice it.
And nearly two thousand years later, the same Word is still calling the church away from pride and back toward the heart of Christ.
If this message convicted you, let that conviction lead to repentance rather than shame.
If it comforted you, let that comfort lead to gratitude.
If it challenged you, let that challenge produce action.
But do not forget the person who must hear it first.
You.
Me.
All of us who still need the Lord to transform our hearts.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that the church might lack impressive gifts—it is that people could hear us speak about the love of Jesus and never experience that love in the way we treat them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD KEPT USING SAMSON… EVEN WHILE SAMSON KEPT DESTROYING HIMSELF. WHY?
paragraphs: GOD KEPT USING SAMSON… EVEN WHILE SAMSON KEPT DESTROYING HIMSELF. WHY?
The terrifying truth behind a man who broke his vows, surrendered to his desires, lost his strength, and discovered that God's mercy could reach him even in the wreckage of his own choices.
What if the most frightening thing about Samson's story isn't that he lost his strength… but that he had been losing himself long before he realized God had departed from him?
Not because it describes a demon.
Not because it announces judgment upon an entire nation.
But because it describes a man who once carried the power of God.
A man who had torn apart a lion with his bare hands.
A man who had defeated enemies that ordinary soldiers feared.
A man whose birth had been announced by an angel.
And yet, one morning, he woke up believing everything was still the same.
He thought he could rise.
He thought he could fight.
He thought the power would come again.
But Scripture records something devastating.
“And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.” — Judges 16:20 (KJV)
Read that again.
He did not know.
Samson had become so accustomed to living with compromise that he failed to recognize the moment his spiritual condition had reached a catastrophic turning point.
And perhaps that is why his story is not merely about a strong man who fell.
It is about the terrifying possibility of becoming comfortable with what is destroying us.
Still attending church.
Still knowing the worship songs.
Still quoting Scripture.
Still speaking about God.
Still remembering the victories of yesterday.
While quietly making peace with the very things we once begged God to deliver us from.
And the question becomes almost unbearable.
Why did God permit Samson to remain a judge over Israel despite his repeated moral failures?
Why did God continue working through a man who repeatedly demonstrated such poor judgment?
Why wasn't Samson immediately replaced?
Why did a holy God accomplish His purposes through someone whose personal life was so deeply compromised?
And perhaps the question beneath all those questions is even more personal.
If God knew everything Samson would become, why did He call him in the first place?
The answer takes us into one of the most uncomfortable and hope-filled accounts in the Old Testament.
Because Samson's story reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing sovereignty of God.
And when we finally understand what happened between his miraculous birth and his final prayer, we discover something that points beyond Samson himself.
We discover why even the strongest human deliverer was never enough.
We discover why Israel needed Jesus.
And why we still do.
Before Samson ever opened his eyes, Israel was already in trouble.
Judges 13:1 tells us that the Israelites had again done evil in the sight of the LORD, and God had delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.
Forty years.
An entire generation growing up beneath foreign domination.
Children learning to live under oppression.
Families adjusting to conditions that should never have become normal.
And unlike some earlier accounts in Judges, chapter 13 records no national cry for deliverance before God announces Samson's birth.
That detail matters.
God initiates the deliverance.
Not because Israel has suddenly become righteous.
Not because its people have demonstrated extraordinary faithfulness.
But because the LORD remains sovereign over His covenant purposes.
Then an angel appears to a woman who has been unable to conceive.
Her barrenness is about to become the setting for an extraordinary act of God.
The angel announces that she will bear a son who must be set apart to God from the womb.
And then comes the declaration that defines Samson's calling.
“And he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.” — Judges 13:5 (KJV)
Notice one word.
Begin.
Not complete.
Not permanently liberate.
Begin.
In the Hebrew text, the verb is יָחֵל (yāḥēl), meaning “he will begin.”
Samson was not promised the complete overthrow of Philistine domination.
His calling was to initiate a work of deliverance within God's larger purpose.
That means Samson's mission was never dependent upon his becoming a flawless national hero.
But neither did God's purpose give Samson permission to live carelessly.
There is a profound difference between God's ability to accomplish His purposes through imperfect people and God's approval of their imperfections.
God's sovereignty is not the same as God's endorsement.
And if we miss that distinction, we will misunderstand everything that follows.
Samson was to be a Nazirite, a person specially consecrated to God.
The Hebrew term נָזִיר (nāzîr) carries the idea of someone separated or consecrated.
Numbers 6 describes the ordinary Nazirite regulations, including abstaining from products of the vine, not cutting one's hair, and avoiding contact with the dead.
Samson's consecration was unusual because it was announced before his birth and intended to last throughout his life.
His uncut hair was an outward sign of that consecration.
It was not a magical source of supernatural energy.
God Himself was the source of Samson's strength.
Judges 13:25 tells us that the Spirit of the LORD began to move him.
Judges 14:6, 14:19, and 15:14 describe extraordinary moments when the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him.
This is essential to understanding the story.
Samson's power was a divine gift connected to his God-given calling.
It was not proof that every decision he made was pleasing to God.
And this is where the account begins to confront us.
Because it is possible to possess remarkable gifts while displaying deeply troubling character.
It is possible to have a genuine calling and still make destructive choices.
It is possible for God to accomplish something through a person without approving of everything that person does.
The presence of a gift is not a certificate of personal holiness.
A powerful ministry does not excuse a private pattern of sin.
A public victory does not automatically mean a private life is healthy.
And yesterday's usefulness does not give anyone permission to disregard God's Word today.
Samson's tragedy begins with something that seems almost ordinary.
He sees a woman.
And he wants her.
In Judges 14, Samson goes down to Timnah, sees a Philistine woman, and demands that his parents arrange the marriage.
His parents object, asking why he must seek a wife among the uncircumcised Philistines.
But Samson insists.
“Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well.” — Judges 14:3 (KJV)
The Hebrew expression כִּי־הִיא יָשְׁרָה בְעֵינָי (kî-hîʾ yāšərāh bəʿênāy) communicates that she is right or pleasing in his eyes.
In the wider book of Judges, that language becomes especially significant.
The book eventually describes Israel's spiritual disorder with the repeated observation that everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
Samson's personal desires reflect something of the spiritual confusion surrounding him.
He sees.
He wants.
He insists.
And what makes this passage particularly challenging is Judges 14:4.
Scripture explains that Samson's parents did not know that the matter was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines.
Does that mean God approved of Samson's attitude, every aspect of his romantic pursuit, or the destructive decisions that followed?
No.
The passage reveals God's sovereign purpose in bringing confrontation against the Philistines.
It does not turn every human motive involved into a righteous one.
God can govern events involving sinful human choices without becoming the author or moral approver of those sins.
This is not an excuse for Samson.
It is a revelation about God.
Human failure cannot overthrow divine sovereignty.
But divine sovereignty never makes human failure harmless.
And Samson would learn that through pain.
His wedding arrangements collapse into betrayal, anger, violence, and retaliation.
A riddle becomes a conflict.
A marriage becomes a disaster.
A cycle of revenge begins.
And with every escalation, Samson's extraordinary strength becomes more visible while his personal instability becomes harder to ignore.
He can defeat enemies.
But he struggles to govern his impulses.
He can break physical restraints.
But he repeatedly allows his desires to lead him into danger.
He can carry the gates of Gaza on his shoulders.
But he cannot seem to recognize how vulnerable he has become to his own appetites.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because some of us know what it means to appear strong while quietly losing battles nobody else can see.
You can be the person everyone calls for advice and still need someone to confront you.
You can encourage an entire room and return home to a temptation you have stopped resisting.
You can be gifted, respected, needed, and exhausted.
You can know exactly what Scripture says and still find yourself negotiating with something you know is wrong.
The danger is not merely that we are weak.
The danger is that we may begin treating God's patience as permission.
And that brings us back to the question.
Why did God allow Samson to continue?
First, because Samson's judgeship was not a modern public office with a recorded process of election, removal, and replacement.
The judges in Israel were deliverers and leaders raised up in particular circumstances.
Judges 15:20 and 16:31 report that Samson judged Israel for twenty years during the days of the Philistines.
The text does not record a formal hearing in which God repeatedly considered removing Samson from office and decided to retain him.
We must not invent one.

What Scripture does show is that God had announced a purpose for Samson before his birth, empowered him at decisive moments, and used his conflict with the Philistines as part of Israel's deliverance.
Yet Scripture also shows that Samson's moral failures brought terrible consequences.
God's patience was not indifference.
God's continued sovereignty was not moral approval.
And the fact that Samson remained a judge did not mean he escaped accountability.
In fact, his story demonstrates the opposite.
A person can continue to occupy a position while already moving toward the consequences of unrepented sin.
That should sober every leader.
Every preacher.
Every parent.
Every Christian who has mistaken God's delay in judgment for His approval of hidden compromise.
Samson's story does not teach us to celebrate gifted people regardless of their character.
It warns us against confusing visible effectiveness with spiritual maturity.
And then Delilah enters the story.
By Judges 16, Samson has already demonstrated a dangerous pattern of sexual recklessness.
The chapter first records his visit to a prostitute in Gaza.
Later, he loves a woman in the Valley of Sorek named Delilah.
The Philistine rulers offer Delilah silver to discover the secret of his strength.
She repeatedly asks him how he can be subdued.
Again and again, Samson gives misleading answers.
Again and again, she tests what he tells her.
And again and again, the warning signs become unmistakable.
This is what makes the narrative so painful.
Samson is not simply deceived by one unexpected betrayal.
He repeatedly exposes himself to a danger that is becoming increasingly obvious.
Eventually, under persistent pressure, he reveals the truth about his uncut hair and his consecration from birth.
While he sleeps, his hair is cut.
Then comes the cry.
“The Philistines be upon thee, Samson.”
And he awakens.
Confident.
Familiar with victory.
Expecting strength to return.
“I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself.” — Judges 16:20 (KJV)
But this time, something is different.
The LORD has departed from him.
The Philistines seize him.
They gouge out his eyes.
They bring him down to Gaza.
They bind him with bronze shackles.
And they force him to grind grain in prison.
The man who once moved with terrifying strength is now blind, restrained, and humiliated.
The man who had so often followed what pleased his eyes has lost his sight.
The man who had broken ropes is now bound.
The man who had defeated Philistines is now their captive.
And the Bible does not soften the tragedy.
Sin has consequences.
Sometimes devastating ones.
Not every consequence is immediate.
Not every warning is dramatic.
Sometimes the collapse comes after a long season of assuming we can keep living as before.
And I wonder how many people reading this are standing somewhere in that dangerous space.
Not yet exposed.
Not yet confronted.
Not yet experiencing the full consequences of a choice they know is wrong.
Perhaps nobody knows about the messages.
The dishonesty.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The secret relationship.
The compromises you keep promising to end.
And because life has continued, you have begun to believe everything must be fine.
But Samson's story refuses to let us confuse delay with safety.
It asks a question that deserves more than a quick religious answer.
What are you continuing to entertain because you have not yet experienced its full cost?
If that question touches something you have been hiding, you do not need to explain the details publicly.
But you do need to bring them honestly before God.
Repentance is not merely feeling frightened by consequences.
It is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy we desperately need.
And there is a difference between being sorry that we were caught and grieving that we have sinned against the Lord.
Samson's account does not give us permission to postpone that turning.
It urges us to take God's warnings seriously while there is still time.
Yet just when the story seems to have reached its darkest point, Scripture gives us one quiet sentence.
One sentence that feels almost impossible to ignore.
“Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven.” — Judges 16:22 (KJV)
His hair began to grow again.
Not his eyesight.
Not his freedom.
Not his reputation.
His hair.
The text does not say that growing hair automatically restored God's power.
It does not announce that all consequences had been reversed.
It simply tells us that the outward sign of his consecration began to return.
And within the unfolding story, that detail prepares us for what comes next.
There is something profoundly moving about the way Scripture places this sentence between Samson's humiliation and his final prayer.
The Philistines believe they have finished him.
His enemies celebrate.
His strength appears gone.
His life seems reduced to a spectacle.
But the story is not over.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to understand that the consequences of your past do not place you beyond the reach of God's mercy.
That does not mean every relationship will be restored.
It does not mean every lost opportunity will return.
It does not mean repentance erases earthly consequences.
It means that failure does not have to be the final word about your relationship with God.
You may have damaged something precious.
You may have ignored warnings.
You may be carrying regret that still hurts when the room becomes quiet.
But while you have breath, you can turn to the Lord.
Not because you deserve another opportunity.
But because God's mercy is greater than our ability to earn it.
Then comes Samson's final scene.
The Philistine rulers gather to celebrate their god Dagon, claiming that their god has delivered Samson into their hands.
They bring Samson out to entertain them.
The once-feared deliverer stands between the pillars of the building.
Blind.
Humiliated.
Dependent upon a young servant to guide him.
And there, in the middle of enemy celebration, Samson prays.
“O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God.” — Judges 16:28 (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה זָכְרֵנִי נָא
ʾĂdōnāy YHWH, zokhrēnî nāʾ.
“O Lord GOD, please remember me.”
The verb זָכְרֵנִי (zokhrēnî) means “remember me.”
In biblical prayer, asking God to remember someone is not suggesting that God has forgotten their existence.
It is an appeal for God to turn His attention toward them in mercy or action.
But we must be careful not to romanticize Samson's final prayer.
He also asks to be avenged for his eyes.
His words contain a personal desire for vengeance.
The passage does not explicitly describe a complete confession of every sin or a fully purified motive.
We should not claim more than Scripture reveals.
What we can say is that Samson finally appeals to the LORD for strength.
He no longer speaks as though he can simply rise and exercise power at will.
He asks.
And God grants him strength for one final act against the Philistine rulers.
Samson pushes against the supporting pillars.
The building collapses.
He dies along with those inside.
Judges 16:30 records that he killed more Philistines in his death than during his life.
His final act advances the conflict against Israel's oppressors, but it is also tragic and fatal.
This is not a model for Christians to imitate through violence or self-destruction.
It is a historical account of God's dealings with Israel during a particular period of redemptive history.
And it leaves us with a complicated man.
A divinely called deliverer.
A deeply flawed sinner.
A man whose failures were real.
A man whose strength was never truly his own.
A man whose final appeal to God was heard.
And then, centuries later, Scripture does something extraordinary.
In Hebrews 11, among the names associated with faith, we find Samson.
“And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae…” — Hebrews 11:32 (KJV)
Samson.
The man who compromised.
The man who fell.
The man who lost his eyes.
The man who died beneath the ruins of a Philistine temple.
His name appears in a chapter celebrating faith.
Does that mean Hebrews approves of his moral failures?
Absolutely not.
Hebrews 11 does not declare Samson sinless.
It does not erase the warnings of Judges 13–16.
It does not turn his recklessness into righteousness.
It recognizes him among those whose stories testify to faith and God's work through human weakness.
The Greek word translated “faith” in Hebrews 11:1 is πίστις (pistis), a word associated with faith, trust, and confidence.
And the great surprise of Hebrews 11 is not that God found a collection of morally perfect people.
He did not.
It is that the biblical record of faith includes people whose lives reveal just how deeply human beings need God's grace.
Samson's inclusion reminds us that a person's worst failure does not necessarily exhaust everything God has done in their life.
But that truth must never become an excuse to keep sinning.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts that distortion directly.
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Grace does not invite us to become comfortable with the chains Christ came to break.
Grace calls us to repentance.
Grace teaches us to deny ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes a transformed life possible.
And this is where Samson's story becomes much bigger than Samson.
Because if we finish the account merely saying, “God can still use broken people,” we have not yet reached its deepest significance.
The entire book of Judges exposes the insufficiency of human deliverers.
Israel repeatedly falls into evil.
Oppression follows.
God raises up deliverers.
Relief comes.
And the cycle returns.
Even the judges themselves are often deeply flawed.
Samson may be extraordinarily strong, but he cannot rescue Israel from the deepest problem afflicting the nation.
Sin.
And he cannot rescue himself from it either.
Israel needs more than a stronger warrior.
It needs a righteous King.
It needs a Deliverer whose obedience will not collapse beneath temptation.
A Savior who will not confuse personal desire with the will of God.
Someone who can confront evil without becoming enslaved to it.
Someone who can deal not merely with outward oppression but with the guilt and power of sin.
Israel needed Jesus Christ.
And so do we.
Consider the contrast.
Samson was set apart before birth for a particular mission.
Jesus was sent by the Father to accomplish the salvation of His people.
Samson repeatedly yielded to temptation.
Jesus was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
Samson's strength was a gift he could not command independently of God.
Jesus, the eternal Son, willingly humbled Himself in obedience to the Father (Philippians 2:5–8).
Samson's final act brought judgment upon his enemies and cost him his life.
Jesus willingly gave His life for sinners, bearing our sins and securing redemption through His death and resurrection (1 Peter 2:24; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
These are not identical deaths.
Samson's death involved vengeance and the destruction of Philistine rulers.
Christ's death was the once-for-all sacrifice for sins, accomplished by the sinless Savior.
The difference matters.
Samson was a temporary, imperfect deliverer.
Jesus is the perfect and sufficient Savior.
Samson could begin a deliverance from Philistine oppression.
Jesus came to save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).
And where Samson's story ends beneath the wreckage of a fallen building, the Gospel announces an empty tomb.
Jesus Christ is risen.
Death did not hold Him.
Sin did not defeat Him.
And everyone who repents and believes in Him receives forgiveness and the promise of eternal life.
This is the Gospel.
Not that God overlooks sin because people are talented.
Not that God rewards us for being religious.
Not that our good deeds outweigh our failures.
But that Jesus Christ, the righteous One, died for the unrighteous to bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18).
That is why the answer to Samson's story is not greater confidence in our own strength.
It is surrender to Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to prove that you are still strong.
Strong enough to hide the struggle.
Strong enough to control the temptation.
Strong enough to maintain the image.
Strong enough to keep everyone believing you are fine.
But the Christian life was never meant to be built upon pretending we do not need grace.
It is built upon the crucified and risen Christ.
The One who knows the truth about us.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who receives those who come to Him in faith.
The One who does not merely cover our shame with religious language but begins transforming us from within.
And perhaps the prayer you need tonight is not complicated.

“Lord Jesus, I have trusted my own strength for too long. I have excused things You have called me to surrender. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to walk in truth. Help me turn away from what is destroying me. I do not want to hide behind my gifts, my reputation, or my past. I need Your grace. I need You.”
There is no magic in repeating those words.
Salvation is not earned by reciting a prayer.
But a heart that truly turns to Christ in repentance and faith will not find Him unwilling to save.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
That promise is stronger than your shame.
And it is more trustworthy than your feelings.
Now I want to ask you something.
Not as someone trying to judge your past.
But as a fellow human being who understands how easy it is to look strong while carrying an invisible battle.
What part of Samson's story feels uncomfortably familiar?
Is it the repeated compromise?
The ignored warnings?
The temptation to mistake God's patience for approval?
The painful consequences?
Or the desperate realization that you need the Lord more than you ever admitted?
You do not have to disclose private sins or painful details to strangers.
Someone reading may need to know that a life surrendered to Jesus can truly change.
Not every testimony begins with a dramatic miracle.
Sometimes it begins with a quiet confession.
Sometimes it begins with an apology.
Sometimes it begins with deleting a number, telling the truth, seeking pastoral counsel, making restitution, or finally asking for help.
Sometimes it begins when a person stops defending what God is calling them to forsake.
And if this message has helped you see Scripture more clearly, please don't let it disappear into your feed.
Not because every word here is more important than Scripture, but because you may want to return to Judges 13–16 and examine these truths for yourself.
Perhaps there is a friend who has walked away from church because they believe their failures have disqualified them from ever coming back to God.
Perhaps there is a Christian leader quietly confusing ministry success with spiritual health.
Perhaps there is a son, a daughter, a spouse, or a friend who needs both the warning of Samson's collapse and the hope of Christ's mercy.

We want this community to be a place where biblical truth is taken seriously, where difficult passages are examined honestly, where sin is never celebrated, and where the grace of Jesus Christ is never treated as a small thing.
That is also why I want to share something personal about the mission behind Gospel Warrior.
Writing, researching, preparing, and distributing Christ-centered biblical teaching takes time, effort, and resources.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
God's forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver, not one pressured into giving.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a promise that money will purchase God's blessing.
But a shared desire to make Christ known.
These free resources are part of our desire to make spiritual nourishment and Christian learning more accessible.
These items are simply a way to support and identify with the ministry's mission. They are not substitutes for prayer, Scripture, fellowship, or faithful obedience to Christ.
Because the goal is not to build a community impressed with Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to build a community increasingly devoted to Christ.
And that brings us to the question we began with.
Why did God permit Samson to remain a judge despite his repeated moral failures?
Because God had appointed Samson to begin a particular work of deliverance, and Scripture shows that His sovereign purposes continued even through Samson's deeply flawed life.
But God did not approve of Samson's sins.
He did not shield Samson from the consequences.
He did not present Samson as the perfect deliverer Israel needed.
Instead, the account exposes the weakness of human strength, the danger of compromise, the seriousness of sin, and the necessity of depending upon the LORD.
Samson's life was a warning.
His final appeal to God was a reminder that divine mercy is not exhausted by human failure.
And his inadequacy as a deliverer directs our attention toward the One who would never fail.
Jesus Christ.
So do not leave this story merely impressed by a man who tore down pillars.
Leave it asking whether you have been building your life upon a strength that cannot save you.
Do not wait until your world collapses before taking repentance seriously.
Do not mistake the gifts God has given you for permission to disregard His commands.
Do not confuse a platform with holiness.
Do not assume that because nobody sees your struggle, it is not shaping your soul.
And do not believe the lie that your past is stronger than the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
Tell the truth.
Turn from sin.
Receive His forgiveness through faith.
And walk with Him, one day at a time.
Because the greatest miracle in this story is not that Samson could bring down a building.
It is that the God who worked through such a flawed deliverer would ultimately send His own sinless Son to accomplish a salvation no human judge could ever achieve.
Samson's strength could defeat enemies.
Only Jesus can save sinners.
And when you finally stop pretending you can rescue yourself, you may discover that the Savior you desperately need has been calling you to come to Him all along.
The tragedy is not that Samson finally discovered his weakness; it is that he spent so much of his life believing his strength was enough.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BY THEIR FRUIT YOU WILL KNOW THEM” — JESUS SAID FRUIT, NOT GIFTS
paragraphs: “BY THEIR FRUIT YOU WILL KNOW THEM” — JESUS SAID FRUIT, NOT GIFTS
The Most Dangerous Spiritual Deception Is Not Always Found in Someone Who Denies Jesus. Sometimes It Is Found in Someone Who Speaks His Name Beautifully but Refuses to Live Under His Lordship.
What if the person who taught you how to pray was secretly destroying someone else's faith?
What if the voice that moved you to tears during worship belonged to someone who went home and treated their family with cruelty?
What if the person who could quote entire chapters of Scripture could not bring themselves to say three simple words?
“I was wrong.”
And here is the question that should make every one of us uncomfortable.
What if that person is not somebody else?
What if it is you?
What if it is me?
Because somewhere between the applause of a congregation and the silence of a locked bedroom, there is a truth we desperately need to confront.
A person can know the language of Christianity without displaying the character of Christ.
A person can be admired publicly and remain spiritually unhealthy privately.
A person can have extraordinary gifts and still desperately need repentance.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that we can become so fascinated with what God allows someone to do that we stop examining who that person is becoming.
Jesus knew this danger long before Christianity had microphones, television ministries, viral sermons, or millions of followers.
He warned us about it in words so simple that even a child could remember them.
And so piercing that even the most celebrated religious leader should tremble before them.
“Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.” — Matthew 7:20, KJV
Not by their popularity.
Not by their eloquence.
Not by the number of people who admire them.
Not even by the extraordinary things they claim to have accomplished in His name.
By their fruits.
But before we turn those words into another weapon against people who have disappointed us, we need to understand something.
Jesus did not give us this warning merely so we could examine everyone else.
He gave it so that truth could expose deception, including the deception hiding inside our own hearts.
And what He said immediately afterward may be one of the most sobering warnings in the entire New Testament.
Imagine standing in a crowded church.
The worship is powerful. Hands are lifted. Tears are falling. The preacher speaks with extraordinary confidence.
People testify that lives have changed through the ministry.
Everything appears blessed.
Then imagine that the service ends.
The music stops.
The congregation leaves.
The preacher walks into a private room, and the person who seemed so gentle behind the pulpit becomes someone entirely different.
The kindness disappears.
The humility evaporates.
The words become sharp.
The people closest to that person know a version of them that the congregation has never seen.
This is not an accusation against every gifted minister. Many faithful servants of Christ demonstrate genuine humility, integrity, and love both publicly and privately.
But the possibility of a divided life is precisely why Jesus told His followers to exercise discernment.
In Matthew 7:15, He warned:
“Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
Notice the imagery.
The danger does not always announce itself with obvious wickedness.
Sometimes it comes dressed in familiarity.
Sometimes it knows the right words.
Sometimes it looks exactly like what we expected a spiritual leader to look like.
And that is why Jesus directs our attention away from appearance and toward fruit.
The original Greek of Matthew 7:20 reads:
ἄρα γε ἀπὸ τῶν καρπῶν αὐτῶν ἐπιγνώσεσθε αὐτούς.
Ara ge apo tōn karpōn autōn epignōsesthe autous.
A close translation is:
“So then, from their fruits you will recognize them.”
The word καρπῶν (karpōn) means “fruits,” the plural form of karpos, a word used for literal fruit and, figuratively, for the results or products of a life.
The verb ἐπιγνώσεσθε (epignōsesthe) means “you will recognize” or “you will know.”
Jesus is describing discernment based on what a life produces.
Not merely what a person claims.
Not merely what others say about them.
Not merely what appears impressive from a distance.
He uses an illustration that is almost impossible to misunderstand.
A good tree produces good fruit.
A bad tree produces bad fruit.
The nature of the tree is revealed through what grows from it.
And here is where the warning becomes painfully personal.
A microphone can amplify a voice, but it cannot manufacture holiness.
A title can establish a position, but it cannot create integrity.
A spiritual gift can benefit others, but it is not, by itself, proof of spiritual maturity.
This distinction matters because the Bible never teaches that spiritual gifts are evil or unimportant.
They are gifts of grace.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 12:7:
Spiritual gifts are given for the common good.
Teaching matters.
Prophecy must be tested.
Service matters.
Encouragement matters.
God's people are called to steward what He has entrusted to them.
But gifts and fruit are not interchangeable.
A gift concerns what God graciously enables a person to contribute.
Spiritual fruit concerns the character produced through the Holy Spirit's work in a life that belongs to Christ.
And Scripture gives us a devastating example of what happens when giftedness is mistaken for godliness.
The church in Corinth was not lacking in spiritual gifts.
Paul acknowledged this in 1 Corinthians 1:7.
Yet the same congregation struggled with jealousy, divisions, pride, sexual immorality, disorder, and a failure to love one another.
They had spiritual gifts.
But their conduct exposed serious spiritual immaturity.
And when Paul addressed the problem, he did not tell them to pursue more impressive performances as the solution.
He placed love at the center.
In 1 Corinthians 13:1, he wrote:
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.”
The Greek word translated “charity” in the King James Version is ἀγάπη (agapē), meaning love.
Not merely emotional affection.
Not religious excitement.
But the kind of love Paul describes as patient, kind, not boastful, not arrogant, not self-seeking, and unwilling to rejoice in wrongdoing.
Then he goes further.
In 1 Corinthians 13:2, Paul explains that even extraordinary spiritual knowledge, prophetic ability, and faith capable of moving mountains leave him as nothing if he lacks love.
Think about that.
A person could astonish a crowd and still fail the test of love.
Someone could speak about God's mercy and refuse to extend mercy.
Someone could teach forgiveness and nourish bitterness.
Someone could preach repentance and become furious whenever confronted about their own sin.
And suddenly the question is no longer, “How gifted are they?”
It becomes:
“Where is the love of Christ in the way they live?”
This is not a call to despise gifts.
It is a call to stop using gifts as an excuse to ignore character.
Because the Bible does not present spiritual ability as a substitute for obedience.
And Jesus makes that terrifyingly clear only a few verses after His warning about fruit.
In Matthew 7:22–23, He says:
“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
These are not people claiming they openly rejected Jesus.
They are people appealing to religious activity performed in His name.
They point to prophecy.
They point to deliverance.
They point to mighty works.
But Jesus points to something they cannot overcome with a religious résumé.
“I never knew you.”
The Greek text of Matthew 7:23 includes these words:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”
And the warning concludes:
οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν
Hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian.
“You who practice lawlessness.”
The word ἀνομία (anomia) refers to lawlessness, a disregard for what is right before God.
Jesus is not teaching that believers earn salvation by producing an impressive record of moral achievements.
He is exposing the danger of claiming allegiance to Him while remaining committed to lawlessness.
That distinction is everything.
Because salvation is not purchased through good behavior.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
But the very next verse tells us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not mean that transformation is unnecessary.
Grace is the very reason transformation becomes possible.
We are not saved because we bear fruit. We bear fruit because God's saving grace is at work in us.
And when genuine faith takes root, it does not remain permanently indifferent to the character of the Savior.
This brings us to the passage that reveals what spiritual fruit actually looks like.
Galatians 5:22–23:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.”
The Greek begins:
Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἀγάπη
Ho de karpos tou pneumatos estin agapē.
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love...”
Notice something beautiful.
Paul uses the singular καρπός (karpos) — fruit.
He describes the Spirit's fruit through a connected series of qualities that reflect the Spirit's transforming work.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Patience.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Gentleness.
Self-control.
The King James Version uses “longsuffering,” “faith,” and “temperance,” where many modern translations use “patience,” “faithfulness,” and “self-control.”
These are not competing messages. They are translation choices that help express the meaning of the Greek terms in context.
And none of these qualities requires a stage.
You do not need a microphone to be patient.
You do not need a congregation to be gentle.
You do not need a ministry title to practice self-control.
You do not need an audience to tell the truth.
You do not need applause to forgive someone.
In fact, some of the clearest evidence of spiritual growth appears in places where nobody is watching.
When you are exhausted and still choose not to humiliate your spouse.
When your child makes a mistake and you correct them without cruelty.
When you have the opportunity to retaliate and instead entrust justice to God.
When you admit that your words wounded someone.
When you refuse to exploit the vulnerability of a person who trusts you.
When you turn away from a temptation that nobody else would have discovered.
When you stop defending a sin simply because admitting it would cost you your reputation.
These moments may never become testimonies shared before thousands.
But they matter to God.
And perhaps someone reading this knows the pain of discovering that the person who taught them about God's love did not practice that love at home.
Perhaps you were raised in a house where Scripture was quoted loudly but apologies were almost never spoken.
Perhaps your father prayed publicly but frightened everyone privately.
Perhaps your mother served faithfully at church while your deepest emotional wounds remained unacknowledged.
Perhaps a spiritual leader demanded loyalty while refusing accountability.
Perhaps you were told that questioning harmful behavior meant you were rebelling against God.
And perhaps, after everything you experienced, you began wondering whether Christianity itself was the problem.
Please hear this carefully.
The hypocrisy of someone who speaks for Jesus does not erase the truth of Jesus.
Christ never commanded you to call cruelty holiness.
He never taught that spiritual authority gives someone permission to abuse others.
He never told His followers to confuse religious performance with genuine righteousness.
Jesus confronted religious hypocrisy directly.
In Matthew 23, He condemned leaders who emphasized outward religious appearance while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
He did not defend their hypocrisy because they possessed religious status.
He exposed it.
And if you have been wounded by someone who used the name of Jesus while behaving in ways contrary to His teaching, your pain should not be dismissed.
You are not required to pretend the harm was harmless.
Forgiveness does not mean denying the truth.
Reconciliation does not mean abandoning wisdom or safety.
And spiritual discernment does not require surrendering your conscience to someone simply because they possess a title.
Jesus remains worthy of your trust even when someone who claimed to represent Him has betrayed it.
But there is another side to this message.
And it may be harder to hear.
Because it is possible to spend so much time identifying bad fruit in others that we forget to examine the fruit growing in our own lives.
It is easy to criticize an arrogant preacher.
But what happens when someone corrects us?
It is easy to condemn a dishonest leader.
But are we honest when telling the truth costs us something?
It is easy to expose someone else's hypocrisy.
But what happens when our private behavior contradicts our public testimony?
We can share Christian content every day and still refuse to forgive.
We can post Bible verses and still entertain cruelty in our conversations.
We can defend sound doctrine online and still neglect compassion toward the people living under our roof.
We can speak passionately about holiness while secretly protecting habits we know dishonor God.
And the uncomfortable truth is this:
A person can be right in an argument and still be wrong in spirit.
That does not mean truth should be sacrificed for politeness.
Jesus Himself spoke difficult truths.
It means that the truth we defend should increasingly shape the character with which we defend it.
So before we use Matthew 7 to examine every preacher, teacher, worship leader, or Christian influencer, perhaps we should sit quietly with God and ask:
“Lord, what is growing in me?”
Not, “How many people agree with me?”
Not, “How many people shared my testimony?”
Not, “How many people admire my faith?”
But:
“Am I becoming more loving?”
“Am I becoming more truthful?”
“Am I more willing to repent?”
“Am I gentler with those who cannot offer me anything?”
“Am I learning to obey You when obedience is costly?”
And if those questions expose something painful, do not run from the light.
Run toward Jesus.
Because the purpose of conviction is not to leave a repentant sinner hopeless.
It is to bring what is hidden into the presence of the Savior who forgives and transforms.

There is a difference between a struggling believer who hates their sin and keeps returning to Christ in repentance, and a person who deliberately protects wrongdoing while demanding spiritual admiration.
There is a difference between immaturity and calculated deception.
There is a difference between falling into sin and making peace with it.
Christians are not sinless people.
Even sincere believers struggle, fail, and require ongoing correction.
First John 1:8 warns that claiming to have no sin is self-deception.
And 1 John 1:9 offers this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
This is why spiritual fruit must never become a tool for demanding instant perfection from ourselves or others.
Fruit grows.
It develops over time.
It is nourished.
It can be hindered by neglect.
And it is recognized through the ongoing direction and pattern of a life, not by a single impressive moment or one isolated failure.
A young believer may still struggle with impatience.
A mature believer may experience a season of profound grief.
A faithful Christian may be exhausted, wounded, or battling temptation.
None of these experiences automatically proves the absence of the Holy Spirit.
But when the Spirit is at work, He leads us toward repentance, truth, love, and obedience rather than teaching us to celebrate or conceal sin.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus did not merely command His followers to produce fruit and then leave them alone to accomplish the impossible.
He told them where the life required for fruitfulness comes from.
In John 15:5, Jesus declares:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.”
In the Greek, Jesus says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος, ὑμεῖς τὰ κλήματα
Egō eimi hē ampelos, hymeis ta klēmata.
“I am the vine; you are the branches.”
Then comes the essential truth:
χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν
Chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden.
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
There it is.
The secret is not trying to look more fruitful than the person beside you.
The secret is abiding in Christ.
Remaining dependent on Him.
Receiving His Word.
Walking in His truth.
Turning from sin.
Seeking His help.
Allowing His Spirit to transform what human willpower alone cannot heal.
A branch does not produce grapes by painting grapes onto itself.
It bears fruit because it remains connected to the vine.
And this is the tragedy of performance-driven Christianity.
We can become so busy trying to appear spiritually impressive that we neglect the very relationship through which spiritual transformation takes place.
We learn how to sound holy before we learn how to surrender.
We learn how to build a platform before we learn how to carry a cross.
We learn how to impress Christians before we learn how to love people.
And sometimes God, in His mercy, allows our carefully constructed image to crack.
Not because He delights in humiliating us.
But because what is hidden must sometimes be confronted before genuine healing can begin.
Consider Peter.
He was bold.
Passionate.
Certain of his devotion.
He declared that even if others fell away, he would remain faithful.
Yet when fear overtook him, he denied knowing Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame.
The man who had spoken so confidently about loyalty could not withstand the pressure of a courtyard confrontation.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that after Peter's denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
What did Peter have left to boast about?
Not his courage.
Not his consistency.
Not his flawless devotion.
His failure had exposed him.
But his failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in a deeply personal encounter recorded in John 21.
Three times Jesus asked Peter about his love.
And He entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
The man who had denied Him was not beyond the reach of His restoring grace.
Peter's restoration was not permission to treat denial casually.
It was evidence that repentance and grace can open a future that failure seemed to have destroyed.
That is the difference Jesus makes.
He does not merely improve our religious image.
He confronts the truth about us and offers redemption.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear today.
You have spent years trying to appear stronger than you really are.
You have smiled through spiritual exhaustion.
You have hidden resentment behind religious language.
You have spoken about forgiveness while carrying wounds you never brought honestly before God.
You have tried to convince everyone that you are doing well.
But privately, you know there are things that need to change.
Perhaps you are not the person who wounded others.
Perhaps you are the person who has been wounded and is struggling not to become bitter.
Perhaps you are both.
Perhaps you have harmed someone and been harmed yourself.
And now you are afraid that admitting the truth will destroy the identity you have spent years protecting.
But listen.
Jesus did not go to the cross to rescue a fictional, polished version of you.
He came to save sinners.
Real sinners.
People with regrets.
People with shame.
People who have failed.
People who cannot repair their own hearts.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we built a spotless reputation.
Not after we learned how to hide every weakness.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
The sinless Son of God bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that sinners can become excellent religious performers.
But that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not merely change the ending of our story.
It changes who we are becoming.
From pride to humility.
From deception to truth.
From bitterness to forgiveness.
From spiritual performance to sincere devotion.
