Not because the scandal was insignificant.
Not because wrongdoing should be excused.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem lives that sin has devastated.
And there is one more truth we must not overlook.
In Matthew 7, Jesus tells us to recognize people by their fruit.
But He never authorizes us to pretend that we can see every secret of the human heart.
Final judgment belongs to God.
Discernment belongs to the responsibilities He has given us.
We can evaluate teaching against Scripture.
We can examine patterns of behavior.
We can refuse to excuse manipulation, exploitation, and persistent unrepentant wrongdoing.
We can protect vulnerable people.
We can seek accountability.
We can test spiritual claims.
But we must resist the temptation to appoint ourselves as infallible judges of another person's eternal destiny.
The same Jesus who warned against false prophets also warned against hypocritical judgment earlier in Matthew 7.
Biblical discernment is not gossip dressed in religious language.
It is not envy disguised as righteousness.
It is not destroying someone's reputation because we dislike their personality.
And it is certainly not treating every weakness as proof that someone is a false Christian.
True discernment requires truth, humility, patience, evidence, and obedience to God's Word.
It recognizes that fruit matters.
And it remembers that we, too, stand in need of grace.
So here is the question I want to leave in your heart.
When the applause disappears...
When nobody is watching...
When your title no longer impresses anyone...
When your social media account is silent...
When the sermon is over and the worship music fades...
Who are you becoming in the presence of Jesus?
Because one day, every platform will be silent.
Every earthly title will lose its power to impress.
Every reputation will stand beneath the perfect knowledge of God.
And the question will not be whether we successfully convinced people that we belonged to Christ.
What matters is whether we truly belong to Him.
Do we know Him?
Have we trusted Him?
Are we abiding in Him?
Is His grace changing the direction of our lives?
Do not mistake religious visibility for intimacy with God.
Do not mistake talent for holiness.
Do not mistake emotional excitement for spiritual maturity.
And do not mistake a public gift for private obedience.
If you have been trusting in your religious accomplishments instead of Christ, come back to the Gospel.
If you have been using your gifts to avoid confronting your character, repent.
If you have been wounded by hypocrisy, do not let the failures of people keep you from the Savior who condemned hypocrisy.
If you have fallen, do not remain on the ground pretending that you cannot rise.
Come to Jesus.
Confess what is true.
Receive His mercy.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Accept accountability.
And walk forward in the newness of life that His grace makes possible.
Because the most beautiful testimony is not always the person who can command the attention of thousands.
Sometimes it is the father who finally apologizes to his child.
The husband who stops using Scripture to win arguments and begins practicing sacrificial love.
The wife who chooses truth over appearances.
The ministry leader who welcomes correction instead of silencing it.
The believer who breaks a destructive habit and seeks help.
The wounded soul who begins learning to trust Christ again.
The person who once loved being admired but now longs to become more like Jesus.
No spotlight.
No applause.
No extraordinary public performance.
Just grace quietly producing fruit.
And heaven is not confused about the difference.
If this message has exposed something you have been avoiding, please do not bury that conviction beneath another religious performance.
Bring it to the Lord.
You do not need to reveal private details to be honest before God.
And if you have witnessed Christ change your character, your testimony may encourage someone who believes they will never change.
There may also be someone in your life who desperately needs this message.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Not because you want to win an argument.
But because you love them enough to point them toward Jesus.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow as well.
Because the Gospel is not meant to remain trapped inside the walls of our own comfort.
It is good news worth sharing.
And if this ministry has been helping you grow in God's Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.

Not merely as someone who enjoys Christian articles, but as someone who wants to help sustain and expand the work of sharing Scripture, encouraging believers, reaching seekers, and pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Every monthly contribution helps provide ongoing support for the creation and sharing of biblical teaching, Gospel-centered articles, encouragement, and discipleship resources.
You never know whose life may be reached through one faithful act of sharing.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and Christian growth more accessible.
The greater invitation is to participate in something that points beyond merchandise, beyond content, and beyond any individual ministry.
A continuing mission to make Jesus Christ known.
Gospel Warrior is not the vine.
No ministry is.
No preacher is.
No Christian platform is.
Jesus Christ alone is the true Vine.
Our purpose is not to make people dependent on a ministry.
It is to continually point people toward the Savior who gives life.
Spend a moment alone with Jesus.
Ask Him to examine your heart.
Ask Him to expose what is false.
Ask Him to heal what is wounded.
Ask Him to forgive what is sinful.
Ask Him to strengthen what is weak.
And ask Him to produce in you the kind of fruit that cannot be manufactured by applause.
Because you may forget the sermon that made you cry.
You may forget the voice that gave you goosebumps.
You may forget the name of the person who impressed you most.
But you will remember the person who loved you when you were difficult to love.
The person who told the truth when lying would have been easier.
The person who apologized when pride demanded silence.
The person who showed you something of Jesus without needing to announce how spiritual they were.
And perhaps, through the grace of God, you can become that person for someone else.
Not perfect.
Not famous.
Not always strong.
But repentant.
Faithful.
Growing.
Abiding in Christ.
Bearing fruit that points beyond yourself to the Savior.
Because when Jesus said, “By their fruits ye shall know them,” He gave us more than a warning about deceptive religious leaders.
He gave us a reason to examine what our lives are revealing about the One we claim to follow.
When the world forgets the sound of your voice, may someone still remember the love of Jesus they encountered through your life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU SAY JESUS CHANGED YOUR LIFE… BUT WHY DO PEOPLE STILL HAVE TO SURVIVE THE WAY YOU TREAT THEM?
paragraphs: YOU SAY JESUS CHANGED YOUR LIFE… BUT WHY DO PEOPLE STILL HAVE TO SURVIVE THE WAY YOU TREAT THEM?

You can worship with tears in your eyes, quote Scripture with confidence, and tell the world how Jesus rescued you. But the person who disappointed you last week may know something about your Christianity that your Sunday testimony never reveals.
There is someone in your life who has seen a version of you that the people at church have never met.
They have heard the tone you use when your patience runs out.
They have felt the silence you use when you want someone to suffer for disappointing you.
They have watched your face change when their name comes up.
And perhaps the most painful part is that they know how passionately you speak about the mercy of Jesus.
They have heard you say, "God has been so good to me."
They just wish some of that goodness would reach them.
That sentence may sting.
But please don't leave yet.
Because this is not a story about how terrible you are.
It is about how deeply Jesus wants to transform the parts of you that nobody sees when the worship music is playing.
And before this is over, you may discover that the person you have been waiting for God to change is not the only person He has been trying to reach.
You remember what happened.
The promise they broke.
The message they never answered.
The moment they embarrassed you.
The friend who disappeared when you needed someone.
The family member who should have known better.
The person you helped repeatedly who somehow made you feel like you were the problem.
You remember the exact words.
You remember where you were standing.
You remember how your stomach tightened when you realized that someone you trusted had disappointed you again.
And perhaps you made a decision that day.
"Never again."
Never again would you be that vulnerable.
Never again would you let them get that close.
Never again would you give them the satisfaction of seeing you hurt.
You did not necessarily stop believing in Jesus.
You still prayed.
You still worshiped.
You still posted Bible verses.
But something inside you quietly hardened.
And you began calling that hardness wisdom.
Sometimes it was wisdom. Sometimes distance really was necessary. Sometimes the safest, most loving decision was to establish boundaries and refuse further mistreatment.
But sometimes...
What you called a boundary was actually a punishment.
What you called discernment was resentment.
What you called protecting your peace was your refusal to surrender the right to make someone pay.
And there is a difference.
A difference Jesus loves us too much to ignore.
Because the Gospel does not merely change where we hope to spend eternity. It changes how we are called to treat people while we are still here.
Listen to the words of Jesus in John 13:34–35:

"A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (KJV)
In the original Greek, Jesus says:
καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς
kathōs ēgapēsa hymas
"Just as I have loved you."
Those words change everything.
Jesus did not simply command His disciples to be pleasant.
He did not tell them to love only the people who understood them, agreed with them, respected them, or never let them down.
He placed His own love before them as the pattern.
As I have loved you.
And where was Jesus when He said those words?
He was in the upper room, on the night before His crucifixion.
He had washed His disciples' feet.
He knew betrayal was approaching.
He knew Peter would deny Him.
He knew the disciples would scatter.
Yet He spoke of love.
Not because betrayal was harmless.
Not because sin did not matter.
Not because everyone around Him was trustworthy.
But because His love was never dependent upon human perfection.
Now think about that person who disappointed you.
Not the imaginary version of them that you wish existed.
The actual person.
With their failures.
Their selfishness.
Their limitations.
Their wounds.
Their responsibility for what they did.
Can you still see them as a human being made in God's image?
Or have you reduced their entire existence to the worst thing they ever did to you?
That is a question worth sitting with.
Because sometimes the most frightening thing about resentment is not how much we remember.
It is how much we stop seeing.
We stop seeing the person.
We see only the offense.
We stop praying for their restoration.
We rehearse their failure.
We stop hoping they will grow.
We secretly feel satisfied when they struggle.
And all the while, we may continue asking God to show us mercy for the very things we have not yet overcome.
Then Jesus tells a story that feels almost unbearably personal.
In Matthew 18:21–35, Peter asks how often he should forgive someone who sins against him.
Seven times?
Jesus answers with a number that points far beyond Peter's proposed limit, and then He tells the parable of an unforgiving servant.
A servant owes his king an enormous debt.
A debt he cannot repay.
Judgment is approaching.
The servant falls down and begs for patience.
But the king does something extraordinary.
He forgives the debt.
Not a fraction of it.
Not a small installment.
The debt.
Gone.
Imagine the servant walking out of that room.
Imagine his trembling hands.
His breath returning.
His family spared.
His future restored.
He has just experienced mercy that he could never have purchased.
And then he sees another servant.
Someone who owes him a comparatively small amount.
Suddenly the forgiven man becomes merciless.
He grabs his fellow servant.
He demands payment.
He refuses the plea for patience.
He has received compassion, yet refuses to extend it.
And that is where the story becomes dangerous for anyone who loves talking about grace but struggles to practice it.
Because the question is no longer whether God has been merciful to us.
The question is whether His mercy is changing us.
The king confronts the unforgiving servant:
"Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" (Matthew 18:33, KJV)
Read that slowly.
Even as I had pity on thee.
The king was not saying the second debt was imaginary.
The debt was real.
The obligation existed.
The wrong mattered.
But the mercy the first servant had received should have transformed the way he treated someone else.
That is the point.
Forgiveness does not require pretending the offense never happened. It requires surrendering our claim to personal vengeance.
And please hear this carefully.
Forgiveness is not the same as immediate reconciliation.
It does not automatically restore trust.
It does not mean giving an abusive person continued access to your life.
It does not cancel accountability, erase consequences, or forbid you from seeking protection and justice.
Romans 12:18 acknowledges that peace with others is not always fully within our control: "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men." (KJV)
Those words matter.
If it be possible.
You can forgive someone who remains unrepentant without pretending the relationship is safe.
You can release vengeance without removing boundaries.
You can pray for someone's repentance while refusing to enable their sin.
Biblical love is not moral blindness.
Jesus Himself confronted evil, exposed hypocrisy, and spoke truth without compromise.
But here is the question we cannot escape.
When you establish a boundary, are you seeking what is right and safe?
Or are you secretly hoping the other person will hurt as much as you did?
Only God sees the heart perfectly.
And sometimes, when we are finally quiet enough to listen, His Word exposes motives we have spent years defending.
Perhaps you are thinking, "But you don't understand what they did."
You're right.
I may not know.
I do not know the betrayal you carried into adulthood.
I do not know the childhood wounds that still surface when someone raises their voice.
I do not know how many times you forgave someone who promised to change and never did.
And I would never ask you to call evil good.
But I want you to look at Jesus.
Not at a sentimental picture of Jesus.
Not at the comfortable version who never confronts us.
Look at Him on the cross.
The nails.
The mockery.
The public humiliation.
The soldiers dividing His garments.
The religious leaders ridiculing Him.
And listen to Luke 23:34:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς
Pater, aphes autois
"Father, forgive them."

There is an important textual detail here. This saying appears in many ancient manuscripts and has been cherished throughout Christian history, though some early manuscripts omit it. Faithful translations may therefore include a textual note.
Yet the mercy displayed in Christ's crucifixion is not dependent upon this one textual question.
The entire New Testament bears witness to it.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we learned to pray beautifully.
Not after we stopped struggling.
Christ died for us while we were still in need of His mercy.
And now the Gospel confronts us with an uncomfortable truth.
We love being the person Jesus forgives.
But we struggle when He calls us to become people who forgive.
We rejoice that He does not define us by our worst moments.
Then we define others by theirs.
We ask God to be patient with our growth.
Then become furious when someone else's growth is slow.
We want the Lord to understand the wounds behind our reactions.
Then refuse to consider the wounds behind another person's behavior.
No, another person's wounds do not excuse their sin.
But neither do our wounds excuse ours.
That is why grace is so extraordinary.
It tells the truth about sin without abandoning the hope of redemption.
And perhaps the most unsettling example of this is Peter.
Peter loved Jesus.
He truly did.
He was passionate, outspoken, courageous at times, and painfully overconfident at others.
He promised loyalty.
He insisted he would never deny the Lord.
But when fear surrounded him, his courage collapsed.
Three times he denied knowing Jesus.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The realization.
The memory of his own promises.
The eyes of Jesus.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Now imagine what might have happened if Peter's failure had been the final word about his identity.
Imagine if every future conversation began with, "Remember what you did?"
Imagine if the other disciples refused to see anything beyond his denial.
Imagine if his worst night became the only name anyone would ever give him.
But John 21 shows us something remarkable.
After His resurrection, Jesus meets Peter beside the Sea of Tiberias.
There is a charcoal fire.
There is breakfast.
There is a conversation Peter cannot avoid.
Three times Jesus asks Peter about his love.
Three times Peter answers.
And Jesus commissions him to care for His sheep.
The restoration is not cheap.
Jesus does not pretend the denial was insignificant.
He brings Peter face-to-face with the question of love and calls him into faithful service.
Peter's failure was real.
But it was not the end of his story.
And somewhere in that scene is a truth that could change the way you look at the people who have disappointed you.
You may know the chapter where someone failed. But you do not know every chapter Jesus may yet write.
That does not mean you must place them back in a position of trust.
Peter's restoration was accompanied by a renewed call to follow Jesus, not a declaration that failure has no consequences.
But it does mean you should be careful about treating someone's worst chapter as though it were their final one.
Because what if Jesus had treated you that way?
What if your worst decision had become your permanent identity?
What if the sins you repented of were the only things heaven ever remembered about you?
The Gospel announces something better.
In Christ there is forgiveness.
In Christ there is a new beginning.
In Christ there is power for real transformation.
Not the kind of transformation that merely improves our religious vocabulary.
The kind that reaches our mouths when we are angry.
Our fingers when we are about to send a cruel message.
Our thoughts when we hear someone else's name.
Our behavior when nobody is watching.
Our willingness to apologize without adding ten excuses.
Our capacity to speak truth without enjoying the pain it causes.
And yes, even our response when someone disappoints us again.
Paul writes in Ephesians 4:31–32:
The original Greek includes a beautiful word:
εὔσπλαγχνοι
eusplanchnoi
Often translated "tenderhearted" or "compassionate."
It communicates deep compassion, not merely outward politeness.
Paul is calling believers to something deeper than controlling appearances.
A heart increasingly shaped by the mercy of God.
Notice also the foundation of his command.
"Even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."
Christian forgiveness is not a performance designed to earn God's acceptance.
It is a response to the grace received through Jesus Christ.
We do not purchase salvation by being kind enough.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the very next verse reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace saves us.
And grace begins changing us.
This is why we must never confuse spiritual activity with spiritual maturity.
You can know the lyrics of every worship song and still need to repent of the way you speak to your spouse.
You can teach a Bible study and still owe your child an apology.
You can lead a ministry and still be cruel to someone who challenges you.
You can be absolutely correct about what someone did wrong and still be wrong about how you responded.
That last sentence deserves another moment.
Because some of us have spent years defending our reactions by pointing to someone else's offense.
"But they started it."
"But they deserved it."
"But I was only telling the truth."
"But you should have heard what they said."
Perhaps they really were wrong.
Perhaps you were genuinely mistreated.
But another person's sin does not give us permission to abandon Christlike character.
James 1:20 tells us:
"For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God." (KJV)
Not every expression of anger is sinful. Scripture itself speaks of anger without sin (Ephesians 4:26).
But anger becomes spiritually dangerous when it takes control of our words, our judgments, and our desire to retaliate.
Sometimes the most powerful evidence of the Holy Spirit's work is not that you never feel angry.
It is that you no longer let anger become your master.
You feel the heat rising.
You recognize the old reaction.
You want to strike back.
But something interrupts you.
A remembered Scripture.
A conviction.
A quiet awareness that Jesus is Lord even over this moment.
And instead of saying the cruel thing, you choose restraint.
Instead of humiliating someone publicly, you address the matter honestly and appropriately.
Instead of spreading their failure, you refuse to turn their pain into entertainment.
Instead of pretending you did nothing wrong, you say words that pride hates.
"I'm sorry."
"I was hurt, but I should not have spoken to you that way."
"What you did was wrong, but my reaction was wrong too."
"I forgive you, but rebuilding trust will take time."
"I love you, but I cannot continue allowing this behavior."
That is not weakness.
That is the difficult, beautiful work of discipleship.
And sometimes it is harder than delivering an inspiring sermon.
Because a sermon can end with applause.
An apology may begin with tears.
A public testimony can make people admire you.
Private repentance requires you to stop protecting the version of yourself you want everyone to believe.
And here is where this becomes deeply personal.
There may be someone in your life who is not waiting for another Bible verse from you.
They are waiting for you to live the one you already know.
A child who needs you to stop using harshness as discipline.
A spouse who needs you to listen instead of winning every argument.
A parent you need to address with both honesty and respect.
A friend who needs you to stop bringing up an offense you said you forgave.
A church member you have quietly judged without ever hearing their full story.
Or perhaps someone you have hurt is waiting for you to acknowledge what happened without turning the conversation back to their mistakes.
You may have been praying, "Lord, change this relationship."
And perhaps one of the first answers to that prayer is the Holy Spirit revealing something in you.
Not because every broken relationship is your responsibility.
Not because the other person is innocent.
But because following Jesus means allowing Him to examine our hearts even when we have legitimate grievances.
Psalm 139:23–24 gives us words for that kind of prayer:
"Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting." (KJV)
In the Hebrew, the opening words are:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל
ḥoqreni ʾEl
"Search me, O God."
It is an invitation for God to examine what we cannot always recognize clearly in ourselves.
And that may be one of the bravest prayers a believer can pray.
Not "Lord, show me everything wrong with them."
But "Lord, show me what still needs to change in me."
Because the danger is not merely that we might be disappointed by people.
The danger is that disappointment might become the excuse we use to stop loving like Christ.
And if you are reading this with a heavy heart because you recognize yourself in these words, do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
The same Savior who exposes our sin is the Savior who died and rose again to redeem sinners.
You do not need to pretend.
You do not need to manufacture an impressive spiritual image.
You can confess what is true.
You can repent.
You can ask for forgiveness.
You can begin making things right where possible.
And when you fail again, you can return to Christ rather than hiding behind religious appearances.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
The Christian life is not the story of people who never need correction.
It is the story of people being transformed by the grace of a Savior who will not abandon His work in them.
That is why the words From Scandal to Grace mean so much to us at Gospel Warrior.
Scandal is not always a headline.
Sometimes it is the contradiction between what we profess and how we live.
Sometimes it is the secret bitterness behind a smiling church photograph.
Sometimes it is the damage caused by someone who knows the Bible but has forgotten how to be gentle.
And grace is not pretending those things do not matter.
Grace is Jesus meeting us in the truth, calling us to repentance, forgiving us through His finished work, and teaching us to walk differently.
Because Jesus does not simply rewrite the story we tell about our past. He transforms the people we are becoming.
And that transformation has consequences far beyond ourselves.
Imagine what could happen if more Christian homes became places where apologies were normal.
Where parents could admit they were wrong.
Where children were corrected without being crushed.
Where husbands and wives stopped using silence as a weapon.
Where forgiveness was practiced without excusing abuse.
Where truth was spoken without cruelty.
Imagine churches where people were accountable without being treated as disposable.
Where repentance mattered.
Where victims were protected.
Where restored relationships were pursued wisely rather than forced.
Where no one confused being spiritually gifted with being spiritually mature.
Imagine a world where the people who encountered Christians could say:
"They told me the truth, but they did not humiliate me."
"They held me accountable, but they did not enjoy my downfall."
"They could not trust me again, but they still treated me with dignity."
"They showed me something of the mercy they said they had received from Jesus."
That would not make the Gospel true.
The Gospel is already true because of who Jesus is and what He has accomplished.
But it would make our witness more consistent with the Lord we proclaim.
And perhaps someone watching your life would begin asking a question they had never seriously considered before.
"What kind of Savior can change a person like that?"
That is the kind of witness we want Gospel Warrior to encourage.
Not religious performance.
Not manufactured perfection.
Not a community where everyone agrees and nobody struggles.
But believers who keep returning to Scripture, keep confessing sin, keep learning obedience, keep receiving grace, and keep pointing one another to Jesus Christ.
If this message has exposed something you have been carrying, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than leaving a casual reaction.
Be honest before God.
Not because a comment proves your repentance.
Not because public confession is required for forgiveness.
But because your honesty may help someone else realize they are not the only believer struggling to let go of bitterness.
You do not have to reveal their name or disclose private details.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to invite a community of believers to pray with you.
Someone else may need to know that real change is possible.
Perhaps this article brought a particular person to mind.
Before you send it to them, ask yourself something important.
Am I sharing this because I want them to be convicted?
Or am I sharing it because I genuinely want both of us to become more like Jesus?
That question matters.
Because even a message about grace can become a weapon in the hands of resentment.
But shared with humility, Scripture-centered encouragement can become an invitation to healing.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page.
But because someone among your friends may be struggling with a family conflict, a broken friendship, or a heart slowly hardening under the weight of disappointment.
Because the next time someone disappoints you, you may need to return to these Scriptures before responding.
Not out of guilt.
And certainly not because financial support is a condition of glorifying God.
We glorify God through faith in Jesus Christ and lives of grateful obedience, including generosity expressed in many different ways.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful expression of Christian generosity.
In Philippians 4:15–18, Paul speaks appreciatively of believers who shared in supporting his ministry. He describes their generosity as an offering pleasing to God.
That gives us a beautiful biblical picture of partnership.
Some believers serve by writing.
Some teach.
Some pray.
Some encourage.
Some give.
And together, under Christ, they participate in making the truth known.
Give freely, thoughtfully, and according to your ability.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver, not one pressured into giving.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share the Gospel matters.
These items are simply practical resources and reminders. They are not measures of spiritual maturity, and purchasing them does not make anyone more faithful to Christ.
The deeper invitation is to grow in the Word together.
Because a ministry is never the Savior.
Jesus is.
And He is the One who changes hearts.
Go back in your mind to the person who disappointed you.
The one whose name still changes your mood.
The one you have been avoiding.
The one whose apology never came.
The one who has not yet earned your trust.
You do not have to call them tonight.
You do not have to reopen a dangerous relationship.
You do not have to pretend that healing has already happened.
But perhaps you can begin here.
You can stop asking God to punish them merely to satisfy your wounded pride.
You can pray for justice without craving revenge.
You can ask the Lord to protect you without allowing hatred to rule you.
You can admit where you were wrong, even if they never admit where they were wrong.
You can ask Jesus to help you see them truthfully, without minimizing their sin or denying their humanity.
And perhaps, when the time is right and wisdom permits, you can take one small step toward peace.
Maybe that step is an apology.
Maybe it is an honest conversation.
Maybe it is a boundary spoken without contempt.
Maybe it is choosing not to repeat a story that would unnecessarily shame someone.
Maybe it is simply praying, through tears:

"Lord Jesus, I am still hurt. I do not know how to let this go. I cannot pretend what happened was acceptable. But I do not want bitterness to become the ruler of my heart. Teach me to forgive as You have forgiven me. Give me wisdom to recognize what is safe, courage to speak the truth, and humility to repent where I have sinned. Heal what has been wounded. Change what has become hardened. And let the way I treat people bear witness to Your grace. Amen."
You may not feel different immediately.
Some wounds require time, wise counsel, protection, and patient healing.
But the Lord is not limited to the emotions you feel in this moment.
He calls you to follow Him.
One surrendered decision at a time.
One truthful conversation at a time.
One refusal to retaliate at a time.
One act of obedience at a time.
Until the people who know you best begin to notice something.
Not that you have become easy to mistreat.
Not that you never feel disappointed.
Not that you have stopped caring about truth.
But that you no longer respond to every wound the way you once did.
That you can be firm without being cruel.
That you can be honest without being hateful.
That you can forgive without pretending.
That you can love without abandoning wisdom.
And that the grace you speak about is becoming visible in the life you live.
That is the kind of change no amount of religious performance can manufacture.
It is the fruit of a life increasingly surrendered to Jesus Christ.
So yes, tell people that Jesus changed your life.
Tell them how He rescued you.
Tell them how He forgave you.
Tell them how He brought you out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
But when someone disappoints you...
When your patience is tested...
When your pride is wounded...
When you have every opportunity to answer cruelty with cruelty...
May they see something of Jesus in the way you respond.
Not perfectly.
But increasingly.
Because the Savior who forgave you is also teaching you how to forgive.
And the Lord who has been patient with you is teaching you how to extend patience without compromising truth.
The Gospel is not only good news for the person you used to be.
It is good news for the person you are still becoming.

One day, someone may forget every Scripture you posted, every sermon you shared, and every testimony you gave—but they may never forget the moment you had every reason to hurt them back, and chose to honor Jesus instead.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF JESUS IS GOD, WHO WAS HE PRAYING TO? THE QUESTION THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING YOU BELIEVE ABOUT CHRIST
paragraphs: IF JESUS IS GOD, WHO WAS HE PRAYING TO? THE QUESTION THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING YOU BELIEVE ABOUT CHRIST

Jesus said, “I and my Father are one.” Yet He lifted His eyes toward heaven and prayed. Was He talking to Himself? Was He less than God? Or does this moment reveal something so extraordinary about the Father, the Son, and the love that carried Jesus to the cross that we cannot afford to misunderstand it?
There is a question that has troubled sincere believers, confused new Christians, and given skeptics something to challenge for centuries.
And perhaps, somewhere deep inside, you have wondered about it too.
If Jesus is God, why did He pray to God?
Think about that for a moment.
Jesus commanded storms to be still, and the winds obeyed Him.
He called Lazarus out of a tomb, and a dead man walked into the daylight.
He forgave sins, received worship, and declared that before Abraham existed, He already was.
Then, on another occasion, this same Jesus looked toward heaven and began speaking to His Father.
Not performing for a crowd.
Not pretending to pray.
Actually praying.
And suddenly, the question becomes impossible to ignore.
If Jesus and the Father are one, why would Jesus need to speak to the Father at all?
Was He talking to Himself?
Was He somehow less than the One He called Father?
Did His prayers prove He was not truly God?
Or have we misunderstood what Jesus meant when He said they were one?
Because here is what makes this question so important.
If we misunderstand who Jesus is, we risk misunderstanding the very One who came to save us.
And the answer is not found by avoiding the difficult verses.
It is found by opening them.
By listening carefully.
By allowing Scripture to explain Scripture.
And by discovering that the prayers of Jesus do not weaken His divine identity.
They reveal something breathtaking about it.
In John 10:30, Jesus makes one of the most astonishing declarations recorded in the Gospels:
“I and my Father are one.” — John 10:30, KJV
The original Greek reads:
ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν
Egō kai ho patēr hen esmen.
Literally:
“I and the Father are one.”
Now look carefully at two words.
ἕν — hen.
ἐσμεν — esmen.
The word hen means “one.” It is grammatically neuter, rather than the masculine form that would more naturally suggest one individual person.
And esmen means “we are.”
Not “I am.”
“We are.”
That distinction matters.
Jesus did not say that He and the Father were the same person.
He spoke of Himself and the Father distinctly while declaring their oneness.
The grammar alone does not explain the entire doctrine of the Trinity. But it fits the distinction Scripture repeatedly makes between the Father and the Son.
They are not one person wearing different masks.
Nor are they two competing gods.
The historic Christian confession is that the Father and the Son are distinct persons who share the one undivided divine being.
And the immediate context makes it clear that Jesus was claiming something extraordinary.
The people listening understood that His words carried tremendous weight.
John 10:33 records their accusation:
“Thou, being a man, makest thyself God.” — KJV
They picked up stones.
Why?
Because they believed He was making a blasphemous claim.
Jesus did not respond by saying that He was merely a religious teacher who had been misunderstood.
Instead, He continued speaking of His unique relationship with the Father, saying in John 10:38 that the Father was in Him and He in the Father.
But now we arrive at the question that changes the entire conversation.
If Jesus truly shared the divine nature, why do we find Him praying?
To understand that, we need to enter one of the most sacred moments in the Gospel of John.
Not the scene where Jesus silenced a storm.
Not the scene where He multiplied bread.
Not even the scene where Lazarus emerged from his grave.
We need to stand, in our imagination, near Jesus as the shadow of the cross draws closer.
His betrayal is approaching.
His disciples are about to be scattered.
The suffering of Calvary is near.
And Jesus lifts His eyes toward heaven.
John 17:1 records:
“Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee.” — KJV
Stop there.
Read it again.
“Father, the hour is come.”
He knows what is coming.
He knows the betrayal.
The rejection.
The humiliation.
The nails.
The cross.
And instead of running from the Father's purpose, He prays.
This is not a confused man desperately trying to discover His identity.
This is the eternal Son, having taken on genuine human nature, speaking to the Father with whom He has eternally shared divine glory.
And what He says next is astonishing.
In John 17:5, Jesus prays:
“And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.” — KJV
Before the world was.
Before Bethlehem.
Before Abraham.
Before Adam drew his first breath.
Before there was a mountain, an ocean, a star, or a human heartbeat.
Jesus speaks of glory He already possessed with the Father.
The Greek expression is especially significant:
πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι
Pro tou ton kosmon einai.
“Before the world existed.”
Jesus was not merely asking to become glorious for the first time.
He was speaking of glory He had with the Father before creation.
And notice the relational language.
“With thee.”
With the Father.
Not simply as the Father.
With the Father.
This is where the answer begins to unfold.
Jesus prayed to the Father because the Son is not the Father.
And Jesus could pray as a man because the eternal Son had truly become human.
Two truths.
Both essential.
Neither can be discarded without distorting the biblical picture.
Christianity does not teach that Jesus is the Father.
It teaches that Jesus is God the Son.
The Father is God.
The Son is God.
The Holy Spirit is God.
Yet there are not three gods, but one God.
The Father is not the Son. The Son is not the Spirit. The Spirit is not the Father.
The three persons are distinct, yet share the one divine essence.
This is what Christians mean by the Trinity.
Not three separate divine beings.
Not one person changing costumes.
One God, eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
And while the word Trinity is not written in the Bible, the doctrine seeks to faithfully express the truths Scripture reveals together.
The opening of John's Gospel gives us a remarkable foundation.
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” — John 1:1, KJV
In Greek:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
En archē ēn ho logos, kai ho logos ēn pros ton theon, kai theos ēn ho logos.
The Word was with God.
And the Word was God.
John holds both truths together.
Personal distinction.
Full deity.

The Greek expression pros ton theon speaks of the Word being with God, while theos ēn ho logos affirms the divine identity of the Word. The grammar does not mean that the Word was merely one lesser god among others.
Then John 1:14 tells us:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” — KJV
That is the miracle of the incarnation.
The eternal Son did not stop being God.
He became truly human.
He did not exchange divinity for humanity.
He took humanity to Himself.
And this matters more than we often realize.
Because when Jesus prayed, He was not demonstrating that He lacked deity.
He was living a genuinely human life of communion, obedience, and dependence upon His Father.
Philippians 2:6–8 describes Christ as existing in the form of God, yet humbling Himself, taking the form of a servant, and becoming obedient unto death.
The Greek of Philippians 2:7 includes the words:
μορφὴν δούλου λαβών
Morphēn doulou labōn.
“Taking the form of a servant.”
Notice the word taking.
The Son's humility involved taking the servant's condition, not ceasing to possess the divine nature.
Jesus became what He had not previously been—truly human—without ceasing to be who He eternally is.
The historic Christian understanding is that Jesus Christ is one person with two natures: fully God and fully man.
Not half God and half man.
Not a divine person temporarily pretending to be human.
Not an ordinary man who later earned divine status.
The eternal Son truly entered our humanity.
And that means His human life was real.
His hunger was real.
His exhaustion was real.
His tears were real.
His suffering was real.
His prayers were real.
When Jesus prayed, He was not staging a conversation for an audience.
The Son was genuinely addressing the Father.
And as the incarnate Son, He lived the perfect human obedience that we have failed to live.
Think about what that means for your own life.
Have you ever been so exhausted that you could barely form a prayer?
Have you ever knelt beside your bed, trying to find words, while everything inside you felt heavy?
Have you ever whispered, “Father, I don't know what to do anymore”?
Jesus knows what it means to pray in human weakness.
Not because He was sinful.
He was without sin.
But because He truly entered the conditions of our human existence, including suffering, sorrow, and temptation.
Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted as we are, yet without sin.
And Hebrews 5:7 describes Him offering prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears.
The One who created the human voice used a human voice to pray.
The One who sustains creation entered a human life in which He experienced weariness and suffering.
The One who knew the glory of heaven willingly walked the road to Calvary.
Not because He had lost His divine identity.
But because He came to save people who could never save themselves.
And perhaps that is where this question stops being merely theological.
Because behind the question, “Why did Jesus pray?” is another question.
Why would the eternal Son willingly come this close to our brokenness?
Why enter a world filled with betrayal?
Why experience rejection?
Why accept humiliation?
Why submit to death on a cross?
Scripture gives us the answer.
Love.
Not sentimental love that ignores evil.
Not shallow love that pretends sin does not matter.
Holy love.
Sacrificial love.
Redeeming love.
The kind of love that confronts our rebellion while opening the way for our forgiveness.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we conquered every temptation.
Not after we convinced everyone that we were spiritually strong.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And suddenly, the prayer of Jesus in John 17 becomes even more beautiful.
He is not merely speaking about glory.
He is approaching the hour through which the Father's saving purpose will be accomplished.
John 17:4 records Jesus saying:
“I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.” — KJV
These words anticipate the completion of His earthly mission, which will reach its climax in His death and resurrection.
And later, from the cross, Jesus will cry:
“It is finished.” — John 19:30, KJV
In Greek:
Τετέλεσται
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
The word communicates completion.
In its immediate Gospel context, Jesus is declaring the fulfillment of the work leading to His death, not offering a vague promise that earthly suffering has ended for everyone who believes.
His sacrifice was not an accident.
The cross was not God's emergency response to a failed plan.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
John 10:18 makes that clear.
And this is why we must never separate the identity of Jesus from the mission of Jesus.
If He were merely another religious teacher, His death could inspire us, but it could not accomplish what the New Testament says His sacrifice accomplished.
If He were not truly human, He would not have entered our condition as the representative and mediator of His people.
But Scripture presents Him as the incarnate Son, fully divine and fully human, the one mediator between God and humanity.
First Timothy 2:5 says:
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” — KJV
The same Jesus who shares divine glory with the Father is the mediator who gave Himself for us.
This is not a contradiction.
It is the wonder of the incarnation.
And now consider another objection.
Someone may say, “But Jesus said the Father is greater than He is.”
Yes.
John 14:28 records those words.
We should never hide them.
We should understand them alongside the rest of Scripture.
Jesus was speaking as the Son who had entered the humble condition of the incarnation and was returning to the Father.
His submission in His earthly mission does not require us to conclude that He possesses an inferior divine nature.
Philippians 2 explains His willing humiliation.
John 17:5 reveals His glory with the Father before the world existed.
And John 5:23 teaches that the Son is to be honored just as the Father is honored.
We cannot faithfully interpret one verse by silencing the others.
Someone else may ask, “But if Jesus is God, how could He say that He did not know the day or hour?”
Mark 13:32 does indeed record Jesus saying that the Son did not know the day or hour.
That verse deserves careful attention, not dismissal.
The incarnation is not an illusion. Jesus possessed a genuine human mind and underwent genuine human development, as Luke 2:52 describes.
Christian theologians have explained the relationship between Christ's divine knowledge and His human knowledge in different ways. The precise mechanics remain mysterious.
But the New Testament does not treat His real human limitations as proof that the eternal Word was not divine.
It presents the incarnate Christ as truly human while also affirming His divine identity.
We must be humble enough to acknowledge what Scripture reveals without pretending to explain every mystery beyond it.
And perhaps the most emotionally difficult objection comes from the cross itself.
When Jesus cried:
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” — Matthew 27:46, KJV
Was the Trinity broken?
Did the Son cease to be God?
Did the Father stop loving the Son?
No.
Jesus was quoting the opening of Psalm 22, a psalm that begins with the anguish of apparent abandonment and moves toward vindication and praise.
His cry expressed the real horror of His suffering.
The New Testament also teaches that Christ bore our sins and endured the judgment associated with them.
Yet Scripture does not teach that the divine nature was torn apart or that the eternal Trinity ceased to exist.
The Son's suffering was real.
His sacrifice was real.
His cry was real.
But God's eternal being was not shattered at Calvary.
The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit did not become enemies or separate gods.
The cross reveals the terrible seriousness of sin and the astonishing depth of God's saving love.
And this brings us back to John 17.
Because there is something in that chapter that many people overlook.
Jesus did not pray only about Himself.
He prayed for His disciples.
And then He prayed for those who would believe through their message.
That includes believers who came centuries later.
John 17:20 records:
“Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word.” — KJV
Think about that.
Before the nails.
Before the crown of thorns.
Before the darkness of Calvary.
Jesus prayed for those who would come to believe in Him.
For the church that would be formed through the apostolic witness.
For people who had not yet been born.
For believers who would struggle.
For disciples who would stumble.
For Christians who would need grace every single day.
And if you belong to Christ, this prayer concerns you.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret battle.
Maybe your family sees someone strong, but your private life tells another story.
Maybe you have become skilled at saying, “I'm fine,” while your heart is quietly falling apart.
Maybe you have spent years attending church while struggling to believe that God could still welcome someone with your history.
Or maybe you have never truly surrendered to Jesus at all.
You know the language.
You know the songs.
You know when to say amen.
But somewhere between religious activity and daily life, your heart has grown distant.
And now you are wondering whether there is still a way back.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not that your sins are insignificant.
They are not.
The answer is not that repentance is unnecessary.
It is necessary.
The answer is that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
He does not invite you to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
He calls you to turn from it and trust Him.
He offers forgiveness and a new life grounded in His death and resurrection.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
And Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
Not because sin has become harmless.
But because Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
This is the Gospel.
This is the grace that confronts scandal.
This is the redemption that reaches into ruined stories.
And this is why the words “From Scandal to Grace” are more than a memorable phrase.
They describe the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
The person who lied can repent and learn to walk in truth.
The person who betrayed trust can confess, seek reconciliation, and begin the difficult work of rebuilding what was damaged.
The person trapped in bitterness can learn forgiveness.
The person ashamed of yesterday can discover that yesterday does not have to govern tomorrow.
Not every earthly consequence disappears.
Not every relationship is instantly restored.
Not every wound heals overnight.
But in Christ, guilt does not have to be the final word.
Sin does not have to remain your master.
And your past does not have to become your identity.
Because Jesus does not merely improve the appearance of a broken life.
He reconciles sinners to God and begins transforming them from the inside out.
Now return to the original question.
If Jesus and the Father are one, why did Jesus pray to the Father?
Because their oneness is not the erasure of their personal distinction.
Because the eternal Son truly became human.
Because His prayers expressed genuine communion with His Father and perfect obedience in His earthly mission.
Because He came not merely to teach us about prayer, but to accomplish our salvation.
And because the Father and the Son have never been two rival gods struggling for control.
Jesus was not talking to Himself.
He was speaking to His Father.
The Son who was with the Father before creation had entered human history to fulfill the Father's saving purpose.
And His prayers reveal both the reality of His humanity and the eternal relationship that the incarnation did not destroy.
This is not something we should reduce to a clever argument for winning debates.
It is truth that should lead us toward worship.
Because the One who prayed in John 17 is the same One who went to the cross.
The same One who rose from the dead.
The same One whom Scripture presents as our risen Lord and intercessor.
Romans 8:34 declares that Christ is risen, is at the right hand of God, and makes intercession for us.
Hebrews 7:25 teaches that He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them.
Consider the comfort in that.
Your salvation does not rest on your ability to produce perfect prayers.
It rests on the finished work and continuing priestly ministry of Jesus Christ.
When you cannot find the words, He has not stopped being your Savior.
When you are confronted by your sin, His grace does not become permission to hide.
It becomes the reason to come into the light.
When you stumble, you do not need to pretend you never fell.
You need to return to Christ in repentance and faith.
And when someone tells you that Jesus cannot be God because He prayed, you do not need to panic.
Open John 10.
Open John 17.
Open John 1.
Read Philippians 2.
Read Hebrews.
Let the whole witness of Scripture speak.
The same Bible that records Jesus praying also declares His eternal glory.
The same Bible that reveals His obedience also reveals His divine identity.
The same Bible that describes His tears also tells us that all things were made through Him.
And the same Bible that takes us to His cross leads us to His empty tomb.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy would be to spend our lives arguing about whether Jesus could pray while never personally responding to the One who came to save us.
Because this question is not merely asking what you think about Jesus.
Eventually, it confronts you with what you will do with Him.
Will you keep Him at a safe intellectual distance?
Will you admire His teachings while refusing His lordship?
Will you continue hiding behind religious familiarity?
Or will you surrender?
Not to an institution.
Not to a personality.
Not to a ministry.
To Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The eternal Son who became man.
The Savior who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
If this truth has exposed something in your heart, don't rush past it.
You can begin with a simple, sincere prayer:

“Lord Jesus, I believe You are the Son of God who came in the flesh, died for sinners, and rose again. I confess that I have sinned against You. Forgive me. Teach me to turn away from what dishonors You. Help me trust Your Word, follow Your truth, and live for Your glory. I do not want merely to know facts about You. I want to know You, obey You, and belong to You. Amen.”

The words themselves are not a magic formula. Salvation is not earned by repeating a prayer. It is God's gracious gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ, and genuine faith bears fruit in repentance and a transformed life.
And if you are already a believer, perhaps today is the day to stop treating prayer as a last resort.
Jesus prayed.
The sinless Son, living a genuinely human life, prayed.
How much more should we, who are weak and dependent upon grace, seek the Father through Him?
Pray when you are grateful.
Pray when you are confused.
Pray when you are tempted.
Pray when you have fallen and need to repent.
Pray when you are afraid.
Pray when you have no impressive words left.
Prayer does not make God aware of something He previously overlooked.
It is one of the gracious ways He draws His children into fellowship with Himself.
And you do not have to pretend to be stronger than you are.
God already knows.
Now I want to ask you something personal.
Not to test your theology.
Not to judge your spiritual maturity.
But because the truth about Jesus deserves more than a passing reaction.
Has this helped you understand why Jesus prayed to the Father, or is there still a question you have been afraid to ask?
If you have been wrestling with doubt, you can write, “Lord, help my unbelief.”
And if this teaching has strengthened your faith, share what Scripture helped you understand.
Your testimony might encourage someone who has been silently asking the same question for years.
You never know who is reading the comments while searching for hope.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
Not because sharing a post earns God's approval.
But because someone among your family, friends, coworkers, or acquaintances may be struggling with this very question.
Someone may have heard that the prayers of Jesus disprove His deity.
Someone may be close to abandoning faith because nobody has patiently opened the Scriptures with them.
Someone may be carrying shame and desperately need to hear that forgiveness is found in Christ.
And if someone you love is not yet following Jesus, consider sharing this with a personal message rather than turning their spiritual journey into a public spectacle.
Return to it when questions arise.
Read the passages again.
Examine the Greek words in their context.
And allow the Scriptures to deepen your understanding rather than relying on a single sentence pulled away from its chapter.
We want this community to be a place where difficult questions are welcomed, Scripture is handled responsibly, repentance is taken seriously, and the grace of Jesus Christ remains central.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another way to walk with us.
These resources are meant to help you study, reflect, pray, and mature in faith.
But creating and sharing biblical content, maintaining resources, and expanding Gospel-centered outreach also require ongoing support.
It is a practical way to partner with a ministry seeking to proclaim Christ, encourage believers, answer difficult questions, and make discipleship resources more accessible.
And there is an important distinction we want to honor.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
God's grace is not for sale.
The Gospel is not a product.
But when believers freely support sound biblical teaching and Gospel outreach, their generosity can become a meaningful expression of love and stewardship.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
Pray for this ministry.
Invite others into thoughtful conversations about Christ.
Encourage someone to open the Bible.
Support your local church.
Help a struggling neighbor.
Live the Gospel you profess.
It is the calling of an entire life surrendered to Jesus.
And now, before you leave, remember the scene where we began.
Jesus lifting His eyes toward heaven.
The cross approaching.
The Father hearing the Son.
The eternal glory of Christ revealed through words spoken in the shadow of suffering.
The prayer was not proof that Jesus was less than God.
It was part of the revelation of who He is.
The eternal Son.
The incarnate Savior.
The obedient servant.
The risen Lord.
The One who came from glory, entered our broken world, bore our sins, conquered death, and opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
So the next time someone asks, “If Jesus is God, why did He pray?” remember this:
He prayed because He is the Son, not the Father.
He prayed because He truly became human.
He prayed in perfect communion with the Father as He fulfilled the mission of redemption.
And His prayers invite us to behold not a contradiction, but the majesty of the incarnate Christ.
Do not let the mystery drive you away from Him.
Let the truth draw you nearer.
Because the most important question is no longer simply whether you understand why Jesus prayed.
It is whether you have placed your trust in the Jesus who prayed, suffered, died, and rose again to save sinners.
The One who lifted His eyes toward heaven before the cross is the same Savior who can lift a repentant sinner out of shame and into the grace of God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE APOSTLES HAD THE POWER OF GOD. TODAY’S FALSE APOSTLES WANT THE POWER OVER YOU.
paragraphs: THE APOSTLES HAD THE POWER OF GOD. TODAY’S FALSE APOSTLES WANT THE POWER OVER YOU.

Acts 2:42–43 reveals what genuine apostolic authority looked like. And the difference between the first-century Church and some of today's self-appointed spiritual authorities should make every Christian open their Bible again.

There is something deeply disturbing about a man standing behind a pulpit, demanding that people recognize his apostolic authority, while the very Scripture he uses to defend himself exposes everything wrong with his ministry.
He quotes Acts 2.
He speaks about signs and wonders.
He reminds everyone that God appointed apostles to lead His Church.
And somewhere in the congregation sits a struggling mother who has barely enough money to feed her children, wondering whether refusing to give another offering means she is resisting God.
A young believer is afraid to ask questions because he has been taught that questioning the apostle is rebellion.
A wounded Christian has watched leaders escape accountability while ordinary members are publicly humiliated for much smaller failures.
And someone who genuinely loves Jesus is beginning to wonder whether following Christ means surrendering their conscience to a man who claims to speak for Him.
But here is the question that changes everything.
When Luke wrote Acts 2:42–43, was he describing men who demanded unquestioning loyalty, financial privilege, and spiritual superiority? Or was he describing something entirely different?
Because if we misunderstand these two verses, we may mistake religious control for spiritual authority.
And if we understand them correctly, we may finally recognize the difference between shepherds who serve Christ and wolves who use His name.
Listen carefully.
The greatest danger is not always someone openly denying Jesus.
Sometimes it is someone speaking constantly about Jesus while quietly placing himself where only Jesus belongs.
And Acts 2:42–43 gives us a remarkable place to begin examining that danger.
The King James Version records:
“And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
And fear came upon every soul: and many wonders and signs were done by the apostles.”
— Acts 2:42–43, KJV
At first glance, these verses appear simple.
The believers followed the apostles' teaching. They lived in fellowship. They broke bread. They prayed. God worked signs and wonders through the apostles.
But underneath those familiar words is a truth that challenges both religious deception and our own tendency to put human personalities on pedestals.
The early Church was not built around the celebrity of the apostles.
It was built around the risen Jesus Christ whom the apostles proclaimed.
That distinction is everything.
Look at the original Greek of Acts 2:42.
“Ἦσαν δὲ προσκαρτεροῦντες τῇ διδαχῇ τῶν ἀποστόλων”
Ēsan de proskarterountes tē didachē tōn apostolōn.
A faithful rendering is:
“And they were devoting themselves to the teaching of the apostles.”
The word προσκαρτεροῦντες (proskarterountes) communicates steadfast devotion, perseverance, and continued commitment.
These believers were not casually listening to religious speeches whenever they felt inspired.
They were devoted to the teaching handed down by the apostles.
But notice what the verse actually says.
It does not say they devoted themselves to the apostles' personal ambitions.
It does not say they surrendered their ability to discern truth.
It does not say they were required to finance luxurious lifestyles.
And it certainly does not say that anyone claiming the title of apostle automatically deserves unquestioning obedience.
They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching.
And what was the center of that teaching?
Jesus Christ.
Just before these verses, Peter had stood before the crowd at Pentecost and proclaimed Jesus' death, resurrection, exaltation, and lordship.
He declared:
“Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.”
— Acts 2:36, KJV
Peter did not stand before the people announcing, “God has made me your supreme spiritual authority. Submit to me.”
He announced Jesus.
The crucified Jesus.
The resurrected Jesus.
The exalted Jesus.
The Jesus whom sinners had rejected, but whom God had vindicated.
And when the people were pierced to the heart and asked what they should do, Peter did not tell them to purchase a blessing or prove their loyalty through financial sacrifice to his ministry.
He told them:
“Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins...”
— Acts 2:38, KJV
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Jesus Christ.
The gift of the Holy Spirit.
That was the message surrounding the birth of the Church.
And it raises an uncomfortable question.
If the apostles' ministry was centered on bringing sinners to Jesus, why do some modern ministries seem centered on bringing believers into permanent dependence upon their leaders?
There is a difference between honoring spiritual leadership and giving a human being authority that belongs to God alone.
There is a difference between receiving biblical correction and being spiritually intimidated.
There is a difference between supporting Gospel ministry and being manipulated into believing that God's love, favor, or blessing is for sale.
And if you have ever been wounded by someone who claimed to represent Jesus, you need to hear this.
A leader's misuse of Scripture does not make Scripture false. And a leader's betrayal of Christ does not make Christ unfaithful.
Now look at the next verse.
Acts 2:43 begins:
“ἐγίνετο δὲ πάσῃ ψυχῇ φόβος”
Egineto de pasē psychē phobos.
A natural translation is:
“And awe was coming upon every soul.”
The Greek word φόβος (phobos) can refer to fear, reverence, or awe, depending on context.
Here, the surrounding description of God's extraordinary activity gives the word a strong sense of reverent awe.
The people were witnessing something beyond ordinary human achievement.
God was working among them.
But notice what Luke does not say.
He does not say the apostles terrified the congregation into submission.
He does not say the believers were afraid to question their leaders.
He does not say spiritual authority was measured by how effectively a minister could intimidate people.
The awe arose in the context of God's work.
And the second half of the verse says:
“πολλά τε τέρατα καὶ σημεῖα διὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐγίνετο”
Polla te terata kai sēmeia dia tōn apostolōn egineto.
“And many wonders and signs were taking place through the apostles.”
Pay attention to one small Greek word.
διά (dia).
In this construction, it means “through.”
The wonders and signs were happening through the apostles.
They were instruments, not the ultimate source.
God was the One at work.
This is consistent with Acts 3, where Peter and John encounter a man who had been unable to walk.
After the man is healed, the crowd looks at the apostles in astonishment.
Peter immediately redirects their attention:
“Why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk?”
— Acts 3:12, KJV
Read that again.
Peter refuses to take credit for the miracle.
He refuses to let the crowd believe that the healing came from his personal greatness.
He refuses to become the center of the story.
He points them to Jesus.
Now imagine how different some religious platforms would look if every leader responded to admiration the way Peter did.
Imagine a minister refusing to make himself indispensable.
Imagine someone praying for the sick without turning their desperation into a fundraising opportunity.
Imagine a leader who was more concerned about people knowing Christ than people knowing his title.
That is not weakness.
That is a servant understanding who the Master is.
And this brings us to the question many Christians are afraid to ask.
Are the apostles in Acts 2:42–43 the same as the people today who claim apostolic authority?
The direct historical answer is no.
Luke was describing the actual apostles ministering in the earliest Jerusalem Church after Pentecost.
These were identifiable people within a particular moment of redemptive history, including the apostles whom Jesus had chosen and commissioned.
The passage is not a blanket endorsement of everyone throughout history who adopts the title “apostle.”
But we must be careful here.
The Greek word ἀπόστολος (apostolos) broadly means a messenger or one who is sent.
The New Testament uses the term in more than one context.

The Twelve held a foundational and distinctive place in Jesus' ministry. Paul also identified himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ, called by God and a witness of the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8–9; Galatians 1:1).
Other passages use apostolic language for individuals serving in particular missionary or representative capacities.
Christians today disagree about whether an apostolic ministry or office continues and, if so, in what sense.
Some believe the foundational apostolic office ended with the first generation of authoritative witnesses to the risen Christ.
Others believe certain apostolic functions, particularly church planting, missionary leadership, and oversight, continue under the authority of Scripture.
Those differences deserve careful biblical discussion.
But one truth does not depend on which position you hold.
No modern claim to apostolic authority gives a person permission to contradict the Gospel, escape accountability, exploit believers, or place himself above the Word of God.
Not one.
And Scripture does not leave us defenseless.
In 2 Corinthians 11:13, Paul writes:
The Greek phrase is striking:
“ψευδαπόστολοι, ἐργάται δόλιοι”
Pseudapostoloi, ergatai dolioi.
“False apostles, deceitful workers.”
Paul was not warning the Church only about people who openly rejected Christianity.
He was warning about people who presented themselves as representatives of Christ while operating deceptively.
That means a title is not proof.
A platform is not proof.
A large congregation is not proof.
A dramatic testimony is not proof.
Even a claim to supernatural power is not sufficient proof.
Jesus Himself warned in Matthew 7:22–23 that some would appeal to prophecy, exorcisms, and mighty works done in His name, yet hear Him reject their claims to belong to Him.
The point is not that every reported miracle is false.
The point is that impressive religious activity cannot replace genuine submission to Christ.
Deuteronomy 13:1–3 had already established that even an apparently extraordinary sign could not justify leading God's people away from Him.
And in the New Testament, believers are explicitly told to test spiritual claims.
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.”
— 1 John 4:1, KJV
Notice what Scripture commands.
Test.
Discern.
Examine.
That is not rebellion against God.
That is obedience to God.
And the risen Jesus commended the church at Ephesus because they had tested those who claimed to be apostles and had found some of them false (Revelation 2:2).
Think about that.
Jesus did not condemn them for examining apostolic claims.
He praised their discernment.
So when someone tells you that questioning his doctrine is equivalent to questioning God, remember the words of Christ.
When someone claims that his title places him beyond correction, remember the apostles who themselves taught the Church to test claims.
And when someone insists that genuine submission means silence in the face of wrongdoing, remember that the New Testament never makes a minister's reputation more sacred than the truth.
But there is another side to this conversation that we must not ignore.
Not every leader who makes a mistake is a wolf.
Not every pastor who receives financial support is corrupt.
Not every church that believes spiritual gifts continue is deceptive.
And not everyone who uses the word “apostle” is automatically a false teacher.
Careless accusations can destroy reputations, divide churches, and wound innocent people.
Scripture requires discernment, not suspicion without evidence.

Paul instructed Timothy not to receive an accusation against an elder except on the testimony of two or three witnesses, while also requiring appropriate public rebuke when established sin persisted (1 Timothy 5:19–20).
Truth matters.
Evidence matters.
Justice matters.
And the same Bible that warns us about false leaders also commands us to honor faithful ones.
The question is not simply what someone calls himself.
The question is whether his teaching, conduct, and use of authority withstand biblical examination.
Does he proclaim the biblical Jesus?
Does he faithfully teach the Gospel of grace?
Does he welcome accountability?
Does he demonstrate humility?
Does he handle money honestly?
Does he protect the vulnerable?
Does he serve the flock rather than use the flock to serve himself?
Does he point people toward Christ or make them dependent on his personal approval?
Jesus gave us an unforgettable picture of spiritual leadership in Mark 10:42–45.
The rulers of the nations exercise power over others.
But Jesus tells His disciples that greatness among them must look different.
The great must become servants.
The first must become the servant of all.
And then Jesus points to Himself.
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
— Mark 10:45, KJV
There it is.
The pattern.
The standard.
The King of glory did not come to exploit His people.
He came to give His life for them.
How can anyone claim the authority of Christ while despising the servant-hearted character of Christ?
How can a leader demand sacrifices from struggling believers while refusing to sacrifice his own pride?
How can someone preach about the cross while treating ministry as a throne?
The apostle Peter later wrote to church elders:
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.”
— 1 Peter 5:3, KJV
The original Greek includes the expression:
“μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων”
Mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes tōn klērōn.
The verb κατακυριεύω (katakyrieuō) conveys the idea of exercising mastery or domineering over others.
Peter explicitly forbids that kind of leadership over God's people.
The same Peter associated with the apostles in Acts 2 later warned elders not to dominate the flock.
That should settle at least one thing.
Apostolic authority was never a license for spiritual tyranny.
And the wider context of Acts 2 makes this even clearer.
Continue reading beyond verse 43.
Acts 2:44–45 describes believers sharing their possessions and distributing resources according to people's needs.
The passage is not describing apostles accumulating wealth through pressure while the congregation suffers.
It describes a community marked by generosity and practical care.
Acts 4:34–35 further describes gifts being distributed according to need.
And in Acts 5:4, Peter acknowledges that property belonged to its owner before it was sold and that the proceeds remained under the owner's authority.
The early believers' generosity was real.
But Scripture does not present it as a system in which religious leaders owned the consciences and possessions of everyone in the congregation.
This matters because financial manipulation often hides behind biblical language.
Someone may tell you that if you truly honor God, you must give a particular amount to a particular leader.
Someone may imply that refusing an offering means rejecting a blessing.
Someone may even use the language of tithes, firstfruits, and sacrifice to make you feel that your financial hardship is proof of spiritual failure.
But listen to Paul.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The Greek expression μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης means “not out of sorrow or compulsion.”
Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through fear.
The New Testament does teach that those who minister the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).
Faithful ministry requires resources, and supporting it can be a meaningful act of worship and partnership.
Your obedience to Jesus cannot be reduced to a payment.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
And God's grace is not a premium membership.
That is precisely why any Christian ministry asking for support must be willing to say something that manipulative leaders rarely say:
If you cannot afford to give, you are not less loved by God.
The widow who gave two small coins in Mark 12:41–44 reminds us that Jesus sees the heart and the sacrifice behind a gift, not merely its monetary value.
And Christians must also remember that Scripture calls us to care responsibly for those entrusted to us, especially our households (1 Timothy 5:8).
No faithful ministry should use guilt to force a family to neglect essential needs.
That truth does not weaken Gospel generosity.
It protects it.
Because giving becomes beautiful when love, gratitude, freedom, and sound judgment replace fear.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Maybe you have never encountered a self-appointed apostle.
Maybe you have never been pressured into giving money.
Maybe your pastor is a humble servant who loves the Scriptures and faithfully cares for the congregation.
Thank God for such leaders.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Support them as you are able.
But perhaps your story is different.
Perhaps you once trusted someone who spoke about Jesus with such confidence that you assumed every word he said carried divine authority.
You believed him.
You defended him.
You brought your family to his church.
