Your body matters so much that God calls you to glorify Him through it.
And the Christian hope goes even further.
In 1 Corinthians 6:14, Paul reminds the church that God raised the Lord and will also raise believers by His power.
That means the body is not disposable.
It has an eternal future in God's redemptive purpose.
Christian holiness is therefore not hatred of the body.
It is reverence for the God who created it, redeemed His people, and promises resurrection.
And this is why Paul's quotation of Genesis matters so profoundly.
He began with the reality of bodily union.
He moved to the believer's union with Christ.
He commanded believers to flee sexual immorality.
And he concluded by reminding them that their bodies belong to God.
Everything points toward one central truth.
You cannot fully understand Christian sexual holiness until you understand Christian belonging.
We do not pursue purity to make Jesus willing to love us.
We pursue holiness because His grace has called us to belong to Him.
And when we fail, we do not need to invent excuses or surrender to despair.
We confess our sins.
We turn back to Christ.
We trust His mercy.
And we take the next step of obedience.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not an invitation to manipulate grace.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is hope for the person who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from being loved by God.
And there is a call to repentance for the person who has been using God's patience as permission to continue in deliberate rebellion.
Both need the same Savior.
Both need the same cross.
Both need the same grace.
Perhaps the most tragic thing about sexual sin is not simply that it violates God's design.
It is that people sometimes trade something precious for something that cannot ultimately satisfy.
They exchange truth for secrecy.
Faithfulness for excitement.
Peace for temporary pleasure.
And sometimes they discover too late that what promised freedom has become a form of bondage.
But Jesus Christ is not powerless before the chains we have forged through our own choices.
He came to save sinners.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day.
That is the Gospel Paul preached in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And that is the Gospel at the center of this warning.
Not merely, “Stop sinning.”
But, “You belong to the One who died and rose again. Therefore, live in a way that honors Him.”
What would happen if you began to see your body through that truth?
What would change in your private decisions?
What would happen to the relationship you know is leading you away from obedience?
What would happen to the habits you have been defending?
What would happen if, instead of asking how close you could remain to temptation, you began asking how faithfully you could follow Jesus?
And what would happen if the person drowning in shame finally understood that repentance and forgiveness are not empty religious words?
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you have read this far because there is something in your life you know God has been confronting.
Not through an audible voice.
Not through some mysterious sign.
But through the plain truth of His Word.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, you are ready to stop making excuses.
You do not need to make a public spectacle of your repentance.
But you can be honest before God right now.
You can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have treated Your gifts carelessly and allowed desires to lead me away from Your truth. I cannot cleanse my own heart. I need Your forgiveness. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to turn from what dishonors You and to walk in obedience through the power of Your Spirit. Help me remember that my body and my life belong to You. Amen.”
You do not have to explain the details. You do not have to expose your personal history. And you do not have to prove your sincerity to strangers.
But sometimes a simple request for prayer becomes the beginning of an honest conversation with people who will encourage you toward Christ.
Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that change is impossible.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be living with shame over something they have never told anyone.
Someone may be quietly justifying a relationship that is pulling them away from Christ.
Someone may have stopped attending church because they believe their past makes them unworthy of walking through its doors.
Return to 1 Corinthians 6 when temptation begins to sound reasonable, when shame begins to sound final, or when you need to remember why your body matters to God.
Because this passage is not merely about the danger of sexual immorality.
It is about the dignity of belonging to Christ.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious content that disappears after a few seconds of scrolling.
Not to build a following around human personalities.
But to keep bringing people back to the Scriptures, to repentance, to the cross, and to the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
We want more people to encounter the Gospel, understand God's Word in its proper context, and discover that following Jesus is not merely a Sunday activity.
It is a life of discipleship.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this work, there is another meaningful way to participate.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It is not a substitute for repentance, prayer, obedience, or faithful participation in a local church.
And it should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe owed to Gospel Warrior.
But it can be a voluntary, prayerful expression of generosity—a recurring gift of support, offered to the Lord as you help make ongoing Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship resources possible.
In 1 Corinthians 9:14, Paul affirms the principle that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive support from that ministry.
In Philippians 4:15–18, he gratefully acknowledges the financial partnership of believers who helped sustain his work.
And in 2 Corinthians 9:7, he teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctance or compulsion.
That matters.
Because God is not glorified by manipulating people into giving. He is honored by generosity flowing from faith, love, and a willing heart.
It can help sustain the work behind messages like this one and make it possible to reach more readers with biblical truth.
These products are not the Gospel itself, and purchasing them does not make anyone more spiritual.
Those free resources reflect something important about our mission.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And nobody should ever feel that their inability to contribute financially makes them less welcome in this community.
Pray about it.
Give willingly.
Support according to your ability.
And let your generosity be an expression of gratitude to God, not an attempt to earn anything from Him.
A thoughtful share may introduce someone to a biblical truth they have never understood.
A personal invitation may bring a struggling believer into a community where Scripture is taken seriously.
And a simple comment may remind another person that they are not alone in their desire to follow Christ faithfully.
Jesus Christ.
Not an organization.
Not a platform.
Jesus.
He is the One who saves.
He is the One who forgives.
He is the One who calls sinners to repentance.
He is the One who gives new life.
And He is the One to whom every Christian ministry must ultimately point.
So return with me one final time to Paul's question.
Why did he quote, “The two shall become one flesh,” while warning against prostitution?

Because he wanted believers to recognize that sexual intimacy involves a genuine bodily union, that God's design for that union must not be treated casually, and that those who belong to Christ must honor Him with their bodies.
Paul reached back to Genesis because God's original design still mattered.
He spoke of union with Christ because redemption had changed the Corinthians' identity.
He commanded them to flee sexual immorality because grace never makes sin harmless.
And he reminded them that they were bought with a price because the cross gives the believer's life a new purpose.
There is warning here.
Real warning.
But there is also extraordinary hope.
The Corinthians were not told that their past made redemption impossible.
They were reminded that some of them had already been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
And that same Gospel still calls sinners to turn from darkness and come to the Savior.
Perhaps you cannot undo yesterday.
Perhaps there are consequences you must still face.
Perhaps rebuilding trust will take time.
Perhaps obedience will require painful decisions.
But if you come to Christ in repentance and faith, your past does not have to be the final word over your life.
His grace is sufficient to forgive.
His Word is sufficient to guide.
His Spirit is able to strengthen.
And His resurrection is the guarantee that sin and death do not have the final victory.
The most beautiful thing about redemption is not that Jesus pretends your scars never existed, but that He can make a life once marked by sin become a testimony to His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING WHO WAS SHOT THROUGH THE HEART… AND THROWN INTO A FIELD WHERE GOD HAD BEEN WAITING FOR HIM
paragraphs: THE KING WHO WAS SHOT THROUGH THE HEART… AND THROWN INTO A FIELD WHERE GOD HAD BEEN WAITING FOR HIM

He wore a crown. He commanded an army. He thought he was chasing an enemy. But one arrow exposed a judgment that had been waiting for years. And what happened to his body reveals a terrifying truth about sin, a breathtaking truth about God's justice, and the only hope any of us have in Jesus Christ.
“And Jehu drew a bow with his full strength, and smote Jehoram between his arms, and the arrow went out at his heart, and he sunk down in his chariot.” — 2 Kings 9:24, KJV
There are some places you can leave behind without ever really escaping what happened there.
A house where someone betrayed you.
A room where your innocence was taken.
A family table where everybody pretended nothing was wrong.
A field where an innocent man lost everything because someone powerful wanted what belonged to him.
Years pass. People die. New rulers take their places. The world moves on.
And eventually, someone begins to believe that what happened has been forgotten.
But there is something terrifying about the story you are about to read.
A king was riding through the countryside, completely unaware that the ground beneath him was connected to a crime committed by his own family.
He had horses. Soldiers. Authority. A throne waiting for him.
But he was about to discover that a crown cannot protect a man from the judgment of God.
An arrow would enter his body.
His chariot would become the place of his death.
And his corpse would be thrown into a field.
Not just any field.
The very field connected to the blood his father had shed.
And the most chilling part?
God had spoken about that field years before the king ever arrived there.
Stay with this story, because the arrow is not the deepest part.
The field is.
And beyond that field is a question every human heart must eventually answer.
What happens when the sins we thought were buried finally come into the light?
His name was Joram, also called Jehoram, king of Israel.
He was the son of Ahab.
And if you know anything about Ahab and Jezebel, you know this family carried a terrible history.
But to understand why Joram's body ended up in a field, we must return to a moment when another man was still alive.
His name was Naboth.
Naboth owned a vineyard in Jezreel.
It was not merely a piece of real estate. It was his ancestral inheritance, something deeply connected to the covenant life of Israel and the land passed down through generations.
King Ahab wanted it.
He offered Naboth money or another vineyard in exchange.
But Naboth refused.
“The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.” — 1 Kings 21:3, KJV
Naboth was not being disrespectful.
He was honoring an inheritance that mattered before God.
But Ahab did not like being told no.
Imagine that.
A king who possessed enormous wealth, servants, influence, and military power became miserable because one ordinary man would not surrender a small piece of land.
Ahab went home, lay on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat.
Then Jezebel entered the story.
She saw her husband's disappointment and decided that the problem could be solved.
Not through negotiation.
Not through justice.
Through murder disguised as righteousness.
She arranged for false witnesses to accuse Naboth of blaspheming God and the king.
A fast was proclaimed. A public proceeding was staged. Religious language became a weapon against an innocent man.
And Naboth was taken outside the city and stoned to death.
Read that slowly.
An innocent man was murdered through a conspiracy that pretended to defend the honor of God.
And afterward, Ahab went down to take possession of the vineyard.
The man was dead.
The property was available.
The powerful had won.
At least, that is how it looked.
But heaven had witnessed everything.
The false testimony.
The abuse of authority.
The bloodshed.
The theft.
The terrible silence after the crowd went home.
And God sent Elijah with a message.
“Thus saith the LORD, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?” — 1 Kings 21:19, KJV
What a question.
You killed him.
And now you are taking what belonged to him?
God was not confused about the transaction.
He saw the murder behind the ownership.
He saw the injustice behind the royal privilege.
And He announced judgment against Ahab's house.
But something unexpected happened.
Ahab humbled himself.
He tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, and walked in mourning.
And God took notice.
In 1 Kings 21:29, the Lord declared that because Ahab had humbled himself, the announced disaster against his house would not come during Ahab's lifetime but during his son's days.
Do not miss this.
Even in a story filled with corruption, God noticed an act of humility.
That did not erase the consequences of Ahab's evil.
It did not make Naboth's murder acceptable.
But it revealed something about the God of Scripture.
He is not indifferent to repentance.
And He is never obligated to ignore justice.
Years passed.
Ahab died.
His son Joram eventually became king.
And the old prophecy continued moving toward fulfillment.
By the time we reach 2 Kings 9, Joram had been wounded in battle against the Arameans and was recovering at Jezreel.
Meanwhile, Jehu, a military commander, had been anointed king through a messenger sent by the prophet Elisha.
Jehu was commissioned to execute judgment against Ahab's dynasty.
Then came the ride toward Jezreel.
A watchman saw Jehu's company approaching.
Messengers were sent to ask whether he came in peace.
They did not return.
Finally, Joram ordered his chariot prepared.
He rode out to meet Jehu.
Ahaziah, king of Judah, went with him.
And then Scripture includes one detail that should make the reader stop.
“And they went out against him, and met him in the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite.” — 2 Kings 9:21, KJV
There it was.
Naboth's land.
The ground associated with the injustice of Ahab's house.
The place where a man had lost his inheritance because powerful people had decided his life was expendable.
Joram did not know how the encounter would end.
But the reader has already been told enough to recognize the significance of the location.
He asked Jehu a question.
“Is it peace, Jehu?” — 2 Kings 9:22, KJV
And Jehu answered:
“What peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many?”
The language is severe because the confrontation is severe.

In the biblical context, Jezebel's influence included idolatry and practices condemned under Israel's covenant with God. The accusation concerns a kingdom corrupted by persistent rebellion against the Lord.
Joram understood the danger.
He turned his chariot and fled, warning Ahaziah:
“There is treachery, O Ahaziah.”
Then Jehu drew his bow.
Scripture says he drew it with his full strength.
The Hebrew expression in 2 Kings 9:24 is:
מִלֵּא יָדוֹ בַקֶּשֶׁת
Millēʾ yādô baqqešet.
Literally, the expression describes filling his hand with the bow, an idiom understood in context as drawing or handling the bow with full force.
It emphasizes the deliberate action of the archer.
This was not a stray arrow in the confusion of battle.
Jehu aimed.
He released.
And the arrow struck Joram between the shoulders, passing through his heart.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיֵּצֵא הַחֵצִי מִלִּבּוֹ
Vayyēṣēʾ haḥēṣî millibbô.
“And the arrow came out from his heart.”
The king collapsed in his chariot.
The man who had ridden out demanding to know whether there was peace was dead.
His horses could still move.
His chariot still existed.
His title had not vanished from the historical record.
But none of those things could give him another heartbeat.
And then came the command that makes this account unforgettable.
Jehu turned to Bidkar, his officer, and ordered him to take Joram's body and throw it into the portion of Naboth's field.
Why?
Because Jehu remembered the word of the Lord spoken against Ahab.
He recalled that he and Bidkar had been riding behind Ahab when the prophetic judgment was pronounced.
Then Jehu quoted the divine declaration:
“Surely I have seen yesterday the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons, saith the LORD; and I will requite thee in this plat, saith the LORD.” — 2 Kings 9:26, KJV
Notice those words.
“I have seen.”
The Hebrew reads:
אִם־לֹא אֶת־דְּמֵי נָבוֹת וְאֶת־דְּמֵי בָנָיו רָאִיתִי אֶמֶשׁ
ʾIm-lōʾ ʾet-demê Nābôt weʾet-demê bānāyw rāʾîtî ʾemeš.
The force of the oath is that the Lord had certainly seen the blood of Naboth and his sons.
The Hebrew word רָאִיתִי (rāʾîtî) means “I saw” or “I have seen.”
And דְּמֵי (demê) is the plural construct form of “blood,” used here in the expression referring to bloodshed.

There is a textual detail worth understanding: 2 Kings 9:26 mentions Naboth's sons, while the account in 1 Kings 21 focuses on Naboth's murder without narrating the deaths of his sons. The later passage supplies that additional detail without explaining the circumstances.
The Bible does not invite us to invent a scene that it does not describe.
But it does tell us that God saw the blood.
The crime had not disappeared simply because the people who committed it had moved on.
The field had not forgotten its history in the eyes of the Lord.
And the royal family could not erase God's testimony.
Joram's body was thrown into Naboth's portion of land.
A king ended up lifeless in the place associated with a man his family had wronged.
No royal ceremony is described.
No magnificent procession.
No final speech.
Just a dead king.
A field.
And the fulfillment of a divine word.
Now consider something that makes this story more uncomfortable than many of us want to admit.
Joram was not Ahab.
He did not personally arrange the conspiracy against Naboth in the account of 1 Kings 21.
Yet he belonged to the dynasty under judgment, and Scripture also describes him as continuing in evil, though not in precisely the same manner as his father and mother (2 Kings 3:2–3).
This is not permission for us to punish children for their parents' crimes.
Deuteronomy 24:16 explicitly rejects that practice in Israel's human courts, and Ezekiel 18 teaches personal responsibility before God.
The judgment in 2 Kings 9 belongs to a particular prophetic and covenantal history, not a general rule that descendants should suffer violence for ancestral wrongdoing.
But it does confront us with a truth we cannot escape.
Sin does not always stop hurting people when the person who began it is gone.
A father's cruelty can leave wounds in his children.
A mother's deception can become a pattern repeated in the family.
A leader's corruption can poison a community long after that leader dies.
And what one generation excuses, another generation may learn to normalize.
Perhaps that is why this ancient story can feel painfully modern.
Because not every stolen vineyard looks like a vineyard.
Sometimes it is a reputation destroyed by a lie.
Sometimes it is an inheritance taken through manipulation.
Sometimes it is a worker cheated by someone who knows that the worker cannot afford to fight back.
Sometimes it is a child silenced to protect the image of an adult.
Sometimes it is a church member wounded by a leader who knows how to quote Scripture but refuses to practice justice.
And sometimes the hardest part is not what happened.
It is watching the people responsible continue living as though nothing happened at all.
You wonder whether God noticed.
You wonder whether your tears mattered.
You wonder whether truth will ever come out.
Naboth's story reminds us that God is not blind to injustice.
But we must be careful here.
It does not promise that every wrong will be publicly exposed during our lifetime.
It does not promise that every abuser will fall in a dramatic confrontation.
And it certainly does not authorize us to become Jehu, take vengeance into our own hands, or treat our anger as a divine commission.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
God's justice is not a license for our cruelty.
It is a reason to entrust ultimate judgment to Him while pursuing truth, protection, accountability, and lawful justice where we can.
And there is another danger in this story.
It is easy to read about Ahab and Jezebel and think only about the people who hurt us.
It is easy to see ourselves as Naboth.
The wounded one.
The betrayed one.
The one who lost something.
But what happens when the Holy Spirit turns the light toward us?
What if there are moments when we have been Ahab?
Wanting something so badly that we resented the person who stood in our way.
What if there are moments when we have been Jezebel?
Using pressure, manipulation, falsehood, or spiritual language to control an outcome.
What if we have been Joram?
Comfortable inside patterns of sin that we inherited, defended, or refused to confront.
Not every sin is murder.
Not every failure is equivalent in seriousness.
But every one of us has reason to examine our own heart before the holiness of God.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
That includes the person who wounded you.
And it includes you.
It includes me.
And suddenly, the field becomes more than the location of a king's death.
It becomes a mirror.
Because the question is no longer simply whether God saw what someone else did.
The question is what God has seen in us.
The private compromises.
The jealousy we dressed up as concern.
The bitterness we fed in silence.
The apology we never offered.
The truth we twisted because honesty would have cost us something.
The sin we kept calling a struggle while secretly making room for it.
God sees.
Not because He delights in humiliating sinners.
But because nothing is hidden from the One who is perfectly holy.
Hebrews 4:13 says that all things are naked and opened before the eyes of Him with whom we have to do.
And if the story ended there, we would have reason to tremble.
Because Joram's story reminds us that judgment is real.
But the Gospel announces something Joram's field could never accomplish.
There is a King who did not come to escape judgment, but to bear the judgment His people deserved.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story takes a turn no human imagination could have earned.
Joram was a king whose heart was pierced by an arrow.
Jesus was the King whose side was pierced after His death on the cross.
John 19:34 tells us that a soldier pierced His side with a spear, and blood and water came out.
These are different events, with different meanings. Scripture does not explicitly identify Joram's death as a prophecy of Christ's crucifixion.
But the contrast is worth contemplating.
Joram's death was part of the judgment against a corrupt royal house.
Jesus, the sinless Son of God, willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
Joram could not save himself from the arrow.
Jesus did not save Himself from the cross, though He had the authority to lay down His life and take it up again (John 10:17–18).
Joram's body was cast into a field associated with injustice.
Jesus' body was laid in a new tomb in a garden, according to John 19:41–42.
And unlike Joram, Jesus did not remain dead.
On the third day, He rose again.
The resurrection is not a poetic way of saying that His influence survived.
It is the Christian proclamation that the crucified Christ truly conquered death.
And that changes everything.
Because the same God who sees the blood of the innocent also sees the blood of His Son.
The blood of Naboth cried out as evidence of injustice.
The blood of Jesus is the blood of the new covenant, shed for the forgiveness of sins.
Hebrews 12:24 speaks of Jesus as the mediator of the new covenant and of His sprinkled blood, which speaks better things than the blood of Abel.
The point is not that God stopped caring about justice.
The point is that, through Jesus Christ, God provides a righteous way to forgive sinners without pretending that sin is harmless.
Romans 3:25–26 presents Christ as the One through whom God demonstrates His righteousness, so that He is both just and the justifier of the person who has faith in Jesus.
Think about that.
God does not look at your sin and call it beautiful.
He does not call betrayal faithfulness.
He does not call abuse love.
He does not call pride humility.
He does not pretend that darkness is light.
But in Christ, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and a new life to people who could never make themselves righteous.
That is grace.
Not God ignoring evil.
Not God lowering His holiness.
Not God declaring that the damage we caused never mattered.
Grace is the undeserved mercy of God given through the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And repentance is not an attempt to purchase that mercy.
It is the fitting response of a heart turning away from sin and toward the Savior.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō), meaning to repent or change one's mind.
Biblical repentance is more than an emotional moment.
It involves a changed orientation toward God and sin, with a life that increasingly bears fruit consistent with that change.
Jesus proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
Notice that He did not say, “Hide your past until you become acceptable.”
He called people to turn and believe.
The cross is where the guilty can find forgiveness.
The resurrection is where the hopeless can find living hope.
And the Holy Spirit begins the work of transformation in those who belong to Christ.
That is why the Gospel is not merely a message for people who have never entered a church.
It is for the father who knows he has wounded his family.
The mother who is exhausted from pretending to be strong.
The young person carrying shame over a secret.
The church leader who needs to stop defending an image and start telling the truth.
The believer who has become cold, distracted, proud, or spiritually numb.
And the wounded person who wonders whether God has forgotten the injustice done to them.
Jesus does not ask the wounded to pretend their wounds are imaginary.
And He does not invite the guilty to hide behind religious performance.
He calls us into truth.
For some, that means repentance and confession.
For others, it means receiving comfort, seeking safety, and beginning the difficult journey of healing.
For those who have harmed others, genuine repentance may require restitution, accountability, and accepting consequences.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust or remove the need for justice.
But no life is beyond the reach of Christ's transforming power simply because its story contains scandal.
And perhaps that is the part you needed to hear.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The shame you carry does not have to be your permanent identity.
The sin you have confessed does not have to remain your master.
The wound someone gave you does not have to define the whole of your future.
Because Jesus Christ does more than offer a new public image.
He gives new life.
“If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
Not a better disguise.
Not a more religious mask.
A new creation.
And if you are reading this with something heavy on your conscience, perhaps you already know what needs to change.
There is a conversation you have been avoiding.
A sin you have been rationalizing.
A relationship where you need to tell the truth.
A hidden habit that is slowly stealing your peace.
A wound you need help carrying rather than continuing to bury.
Do not confuse God's patience with His approval.
Second Peter 3:9 describes His patience as connected to His desire that people come to repentance.
Today is not an invitation to panic.
It is an invitation to return.
You do not need to wait until an arrow strikes your life before you take God's Word seriously.
You do not need to reach the end of yourself before admitting that you need a Savior.
You can come to Jesus now.
Not with a perfect speech.
Not with an impressive religious résumé.
But with faith, repentance, and a heart willing to surrender.
You can pray:

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have done, what I have hidden, what I have suffered, and what I have become. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me. Teach me to turn away from sin and trust You. Heal what is broken in me. Give me courage to tell the truth, make right what I can, and follow You even when obedience costs me something. I surrender my life to You. Amen.”
Open your Bible.
Read the Gospel of John.
Find a faithful, Scripture-teaching local church.
Speak with a mature Christian who can help you grow in the faith.
If you need to confess a wrong, seek wise and appropriate accountability.
If you have been harmed, reach out to trustworthy people who can help protect and support you.
And keep walking with Christ.
Because discipleship is not one dramatic moment followed by a lifetime of spiritual neglect.
It is a daily life of abiding in the One who saved us.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish stories that make people feel something for a few minutes.
But to help people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, examine their lives honestly, and grow in Jesus Christ.
We want the person who feels too ashamed to enter a church to know that the invitation of Christ is real.
We want the exhausted believer to find encouragement rooted in God's Word.
We want families to open the Bible together.
We want those who have grown spiritually cold to rediscover the seriousness and beauty of following Jesus.
And we want people who have been wounded by sin to know that the Gospel offers more than condemnation or empty reassurance.
It offers the living Savior.
You do not need to reveal private details or tell strangers something that would put you at risk.
But perhaps you can simply write:
Or if you are weary but still holding on to faith:
“I'm still fighting. Pray for me.”
And if Christ has already begun restoring something you once thought was beyond repair, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness.
Someone reading the comments may be struggling to believe that change is possible.
Your words may remind them to turn toward Jesus rather than away from Him.
And think about one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to attack with a Bible verse.
Someone you genuinely love.
Maybe a brother who has drifted from God.
A sister who is carrying silent grief.
A friend who has stopped praying.
A parent who has been burdened by regret.
Or someone who thinks their past is too dark for Christ to redeem.
One sincere share can place Scripture before someone who might never search for a Christian article on their own.
Read 1 Kings 21 and 2 Kings 9:21–26 together when you have time.
Then read Romans 3, Luke 15, and John 19–20.
Let Scripture itself deepen what this story has stirred in you.
We want this community to be a place where God's Word is taken seriously, Jesus Christ is exalted, and people are encouraged to grow beyond a momentary emotional response into faithful discipleship.
And for those who have been wondering how to help this ministry continue, there is another meaningful way to stand with us.
Scripture affirms the value of supporting faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 teaches that those who receive instruction in the Word should share good things with those who teach.
First Corinthians 9:14 recognizes the legitimacy of Gospel workers receiving support through Gospel ministry.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That matters deeply.
Your salvation cannot be purchased, and your generosity is not a payment for grace.
Your local church and the responsibilities God has entrusted to you should not be neglected.

You may choose to treat it as part of your voluntary giving toward Gospel work, while recognizing that biblical tithing and financial stewardship are matters Christians understand and practice within their church traditions and convictions.
No guilt.
No spiritual pressure.
Just an opportunity to participate in something you believe is worth supporting.
These items can become practical reminders of faith, encouragement for daily life, or thoughtful gifts that open conversations about Jesus.
It is ministry.
It is helping us continue to write, teach, share Scripture, and make Christian discipleship resources available.
That is important.
God's Word is not a luxury product.
And no one should ever feel excluded from spiritual encouragement because they cannot afford a monthly commitment.
But those who can and willingly choose to support make it easier for this work to continue and grow.
Pray for the people who will encounter these messages.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Tell someone what Jesus has done in your life.
Support faithful Gospel work in whatever responsible way God has enabled you.
Because the mission has never been to make a platform famous.
The mission is to make Christ known.
And now, before you leave, return with me one final time to that field.
Picture the road to Jezreel.
The approaching chariots.
The king asking whether there is peace.
The sudden realization that danger is coming.
The bow drawn tight.
The arrow released.
The king collapsing.
And the body carried into Naboth's field.
Years earlier, a man had been murdered because a king wanted what was not his.
Now another king lay dead on the ground connected to that injustice.
The Lord had not forgotten.
But remember, that field is not the final destination of the biblical story.
The story of Scripture moves toward another place.
A hill outside Jerusalem.
A cross.
A Savior crowned with thorns.
A body laid in a tomb.
And an empty grave.
At Naboth's field, we see the seriousness of God's judgment.
At Calvary, we see the astonishing cost of our redemption.
At the empty tomb, we see the victory of the risen Christ.
The warning is real.
The mercy is real.
And the invitation is still open.
So do not spend your life trying to protect a crown that cannot save you.
Do not build your identity on power, reputation, possessions, or the appearance of being righteous.
Do not let the fear of exposure keep you from the freedom of confession and repentance.
Come to Jesus.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him your guilt.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him the pieces of your life that you cannot repair by yourself.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And let His grace begin writing what sin could never write for you.
Because the most terrifying thing is not that God remembers the sins we try to bury. It is to stand before Him still refusing the Savior who came to forgive them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF GOD ALREADY KNOWS YOUR TOMORROW, DID YOU EVER REALLY HAVE A CHOICE?
paragraphs: IF GOD ALREADY KNOWS YOUR TOMORROW, DID YOU EVER REALLY HAVE A CHOICE?
The terrifying question about free will, the God who knows every secret, and the extraordinary truth that your future is known to Heaven without making your decisions meaningless.
What if I told you that God already knows the worst decision you will ever make?
He knows the words you haven't spoken. The temptation you haven't faced. The person you haven't met. The tears you haven't cried.
He knows whether you will stand firm when your faith is tested—or fall so hard that you wonder whether you were ever truly His.
And He knows something else.
What you will choose when nobody is watching.
Now here is the question that has kept philosophers awake, divided theologians, unsettled believers, and quietly haunted Christians who are afraid to say it aloud:
If God already knows exactly what I will do tomorrow, can I genuinely choose to do something different?
Think carefully.
If God knows you will make a particular decision next Tuesday, and God's knowledge cannot be wrong, then how could you possibly choose otherwise?
If you cannot choose otherwise, are you truly free?
And if you are not truly free, why would God hold you responsible?
Why command repentance?
Why warn us about sin?
Why plead with humanity to choose life?
Why would Jesus weep over people who refused Him if their refusal was already known?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all:
If God knew every sin you would commit before He created you, why did He create you anyway?
Don't rush past that.
Because beneath this theological question is something painfully human.
A young man kneeling beside his bed after falling into the same sin for the hundredth time.
A mother staring at the ceiling, wondering whether one terrible decision ruined her family's future.
A believer who prayed for years, made a choice that seemed right, and watched everything collapse.
Someone who whispers, "God, if You knew I would become this person, why didn't You stop me?"
Maybe that someone is you.
And maybe the answer you need is not a clever philosophical argument.
Maybe you need to discover what Scripture actually says about the God who knows your future—and the responsibility you still carry for your choices.
Because one thing must be clear from the beginning.
God's perfect knowledge does not make Him the author of your sin. And your responsibility does not make God less sovereign.
The Bible refuses to sacrifice either truth.
And what happens when we hold both together may change the way you understand your past, your future, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
David understood something about being completely known.
In Psalm 139, he begins with a confession that is almost frightening in its intimacy:
"O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me." — Psalm 139:1, KJV
The original Hebrew says:
יְהוָה חֲקַרְתַּנִי וַתֵּדָע
YHWH, ḥaqartani vattedaʿ.
The verb חָקַר (ḥāqar) carries the sense of searching, examining, or investigating thoroughly.
David is not describing a God who casually notices people from a distance.
He is describing a God whose knowledge penetrates beyond appearances.
God knows the person beneath the performance.
The struggle beneath the smile.
The motives beneath the religious language.
The resentment you hide while telling everyone you have forgiven.
The fear you disguise as wisdom.
The pride you rename confidence.
The temptation you keep promising to abandon.
And the prayers you cannot finish because your heart is too exhausted to find the words.
David continues:
"Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off." — Psalm 139:2, KJV
Then comes an extraordinary statement:
"For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether." — Psalm 139:4, KJV
Before David speaks, God already knows.
Before a sentence leaves his mouth, its meaning is no mystery to Heaven.
And David's response?
"Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it." — Psalm 139:6, KJV
Notice what David does not say.
He does not claim to have solved the mechanics of divine omniscience.
He does not pretend that the infinite mind of God fits neatly inside human reasoning.
He worships.
Because there comes a point when faithful theology must recognize the limits of human understanding.
God is not simply a more intelligent version of us. He is the eternal Creator, and we are His creatures.
Isaiah 46:9–10 portrays God as declaring the end from the beginning and accomplishing His purpose.
Psalm 139:16 speaks of God's knowledge of David's days before they unfolded.
Scripture presents a God whose knowledge is not limited by our uncertainty.
But knowing that God knows everything raises another question.
Does knowing something will happen mean causing it to happen?
Not necessarily.
Imagine watching a recorded football match.
You already know which team wins.
You know who scores.
You know the exact moment someone makes a disastrous mistake.
But your knowledge of the recording is not what caused the players to make their decisions.
They acted within the match itself.
Now, this illustration has limits. God is not merely a spectator watching a recording, and His relationship to time and providence is far greater than ours.
Still, it helps us recognize an important distinction:
Knowledge and causation are not identical.
Yet we must be careful.
That distinction does not completely settle the philosophical problem.
If God's foreknowledge is infallible, then what He knows will happen cannot turn out differently from what He knows.
Christians have wrestled with what this means for freedom for centuries.
Some understand human freedom primarily as acting voluntarily according to one's desires, even within God's sovereign providence.
Others emphasize a person's genuine ability to choose among alternatives, while maintaining that God's foreknowledge does not cause those choices.
Still others have proposed different accounts of how God's knowledge and human decisions relate.
These are serious theological discussions, not questions that can be dismissed with one analogy.
But amid those disagreements, Scripture gives us truths we cannot afford to overlook.
God knows.
God reigns.
Human beings make meaningful choices.
Human beings are accountable.
And God genuinely calls people to repent, believe, and obey.
That brings us to a scene in the Old Testament.
Israel stands at a crossroads.
Moses has reminded the people of God's covenant, His commandments, His mercy, and the consequences of turning away.
Then he speaks words that should make every person who has ever wondered about free will pay attention:

"I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live." — Deuteronomy 30:19, KJV
In Hebrew, the central command is:
וּבָחַרְתָּ בַּחַיִּים
Uvaḥarta baḥayyim.
"And you shall choose life."
The verb comes from בָּחַר (bāḥar), meaning "to choose" or "to select."
This is not an imaginary invitation.
Moses is calling Israel to covenant faithfulness.
The surrounding passage explains what choosing life involves: loving the LORD, obeying His voice, and holding fast to Him (Deuteronomy 30:20).
The choice is not merely about personal happiness or selecting whichever future feels most attractive.
It is a call to turn toward the living God.
And here is the tension.
The God who knows the end from the beginning is the same God who commands His people to choose.
He does not treat their response as meaningless.
He does not say, "Your obedience is irrelevant because I already know what happens."
He calls them to faithfulness.
He warns them.
He holds them accountable.
Divine foreknowledge never becomes an excuse for human disobedience in Scripture.
And that matters when we confront our own choices.
Because sometimes the question "If God knows everything, am I really free?" is a sincere search for truth.
But sometimes, hidden beneath it, is another question.
"Can I blame God for what I have done?"
That is where theology becomes painfully personal.
We want God to be sovereign enough to protect us from disaster.
But sometimes we want Him to be responsible for the decisions we regret.
We want freedom when choosing what we desire.
But when consequences arrive, we wish the responsibility belonged to someone else.
Think about Adam.
After eating the forbidden fruit, he did not simply confess.
He said:
"The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat." — Genesis 3:12, KJV
The woman.
Whom You gave me.
Even in humanity's earliest account of disobedience, blame begins shifting.
And we have been repeating that pattern ever since.
"My upbringing made me do it."
"My circumstances left me no choice."
"My anger was justified."
"My loneliness was unbearable."
"My temptation was too strong."
"My future must already have been decided."

Some circumstances truly do wound us deeply. Trauma, coercion, deprivation, and suffering can constrain human choices in profound ways. Scripture does not require us to pretend that every person acts under identical conditions.
But neither does Scripture allow us to use God's foreknowledge as permission to embrace sin.
James 1:13 teaches that God does not tempt anyone with evil.
And James 1:14 describes temptation arising as a person is drawn away by desire.
God's holiness remains intact.
Human moral responsibility remains real.
And God's mercy remains available.
That last truth is essential.
Because if this conversation ends only with responsibility, we will miss the Gospel.
And without the Gospel, the knowledge that God sees everything would be unbearable.
Imagine if every hidden thought, every shameful memory, every selfish motive, and every failure were displayed before the people whose respect you value most.
How many of us would still feel comfortable?
How many carefully constructed reputations would survive?
How many people who look spiritually strong on Sunday would feel exposed by Monday morning?
Now consider this.
Jesus Christ knew what Peter would do before Peter did it.
He knew Peter would deny Him.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
In Luke 22:34, Jesus foretold Peter's denial before the rooster crowed.
And Peter, full of confidence, had just insisted that he was ready to go with Jesus to prison and death.
Can you imagine that moment?
Peter looks at Jesus and believes his loyalty is unbreakable.
Jesus looks at Peter and knows the night is coming when fear will unravel that confidence.
He knows the courtyard.
He knows the accusations.
He knows the denials.
He knows the rooster will crow.
He knows Peter will remember.
He knows Peter will weep bitterly.
But listen to what Jesus says before predicting Peter's failure:
"But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." — Luke 22:32, KJV
Do you see it?
Jesus knows the failure.
And He is already speaking about restoration.
He does not approve of Peter's denial.
He does not remove Peter's responsibility.
He does not pretend that betrayal is harmless.
But He prays for him.
And He speaks of a future beyond his collapse.
Christ's foreknowledge of Peter's sin did not cancel Christ's mercy toward Peter.
That should reach somebody who has been living under the weight of yesterday.
Because you may have believed that your worst moment permanently disqualified you.
You may have convinced yourself that God was surprised by your weakness.
That Jesus looked at your failure and decided you were no longer worth loving.
But Peter's story tells us something extraordinary.
Jesus knew.
And Jesus still loved him.
After the resurrection, in John 21, the risen Christ restores Peter through a searching conversation about love and a renewed call to follow Him.
The man who denied knowing Jesus would go on to proclaim Him publicly.
Not because denial was insignificant.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
But because the grace of Christ is greater than the disgrace of a repentant sinner.
This is where our theme becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing the consequences of every decision.
But by redeeming sinners and giving them a future they could never manufacture through their own righteousness.
And Peter was not the only one.
Consider Judas.
Jesus knew betrayal was coming.
John 13:21 records Jesus declaring that one of His disciples would betray Him.
Judas was not an anonymous figure in the crowd.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had heard the teaching.
He had witnessed the miracles.
He had been near the Light of the world.
And still, he betrayed Him.
Acts 1:16 presents Judas's betrayal within the fulfillment of Scripture, while Matthew 26:24 holds the betrayer morally accountable.
This confronts us with a mystery we should not simplify.
God's sovereign purpose was not defeated by Judas's betrayal.
Yet Judas was not treated as morally innocent.
And this tension becomes even clearer at the cross.
In Acts 2:23, Peter declares that Jesus was delivered up according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge, yet was crucified by lawless hands.
Later, Acts 4:27–28 describes the opposition against Jesus as occurring within what God's hand and purpose had determined beforehand.
Think about that.
The crucifixion was not an accident that caught Heaven unprepared.
Neither were the people who committed injustice excused simply because God accomplished His redemptive purpose through those events.
The greatest evil human beings ever committed became the occasion of God's greatest revelation of saving grace.
The innocent Son of God was condemned.
The Holy One was mocked.
The hands that healed the sick were pierced.
The One who gave life entered death.
And what looked like the triumph of darkness became the place where Christ bore sin and accomplished redemption.
God did not become evil because He sovereignly accomplished salvation through the wicked actions of human beings.
And the people involved did not become innocent merely because God used those actions within His plan.
The cross shows us that divine sovereignty and human accountability are not enemies in the biblical story.
They stand together in the very event through which sinners are offered forgiveness.
And here is where the question changes.
Instead of asking only, "If God knows my future, am I free?"
We must also ask:
"If God already knew the depth of human sin, why did Jesus willingly go to the cross?"
The answer is not that human beings were secretly innocent.
The answer is love.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had conquered every temptation.
Not after we had accumulated enough good decisions to deserve mercy.
Christ died for sinners.
And the Gospel does not stop at the cross.
Jesus rose bodily from the dead.
Sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
The resurrection declares that the crucified Savior is Lord and that His saving work is not a failed promise.
Now return to the question that may have brought you here.
If God already knows your future, why pray?
Why repent?
Why fight temptation?
Why evangelize?
Why make difficult decisions?
Why bother trying to live faithfully?
Because Scripture never teaches that God's knowledge makes the means of His work irrelevant.
God commands prayer.
God calls sinners to repentance.
God works through the preaching of the Gospel.
God calls believers to perseverance.
And God uses ordinary acts of obedience in the unfolding of His purposes.
Your prayers are not meaningless because God already knows what you need.
Jesus says in Matthew 6:8 that the Father knows what His children need before they ask Him.
Yet only a few verses later, Jesus teaches them to pray.
God's knowledge does not eliminate prayer.
It gives prayer a foundation of trust.
You are not informing an ignorant God.
You are approaching a Father who already knows your need.
Likewise, the call to repentance is not meaningless because God knows the outcome.
Repentance is the fitting response to God's truth and grace.
And the fact that God knows your future does not give you permission to treat tomorrow carelessly.
You do not know what tomorrow holds.
You do not know which opportunities will return.
You do not know whether the conversation you keep postponing will still be possible next month.
You do not know how long you will have to make peace with someone you have hurt.
You do not know how many more times your conscience will warn you before your heart becomes hardened.
That is why Scripture speaks urgently.
"To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts." — Hebrews 3:15, KJV
Today.
Not when life becomes convenient.
Not when temptation becomes less attractive.
Not when everyone you have disappointed finally approves of you.
Today.
And perhaps that is the most important distinction in this entire conversation.
God knows your tomorrow. You are responsible for how you respond to Him today.
You do not have to understand every mystery of eternity before you obey the truth God has revealed.
You do not have to solve every debate about freedom before you confess your sin.
You do not have to comprehend the infinite mind of God before you trust the crucified and risen Christ.
But you must not confuse intellectual uncertainty with spiritual permission to remain unchanged.
There are people who have spent years debating whether their choices are free while refusing to confront the choices they are actually making.
They know they need to forgive.
They know they need to confess.
They know they need to turn away from a destructive habit.
They know they need to stop living two different lives.
Yet they keep postponing obedience while waiting for a certainty Scripture never promises to provide.
And I wonder whether someone reading this has been doing exactly that.
Not because you are incapable of asking sincere theological questions.
Ask them.
Study deeply.
Think carefully.
Test every teaching against Scripture.
But do not let the mysteries you cannot resolve become excuses to neglect the commands you can understand.
Because while you are wondering whether God knows your next decision, you already know something about the decision standing in front of you.
You know whether you are nurturing bitterness.
You know whether you are hiding dishonesty.
You know whether you are feeding temptation.
You know whether you are resisting the conviction that keeps returning to your heart.
And you know whether you have been treating the mercy of Jesus as an invitation to repentance—or as an excuse to delay it.
That is uncomfortable.
It is supposed to be.
Not because God delights in crushing sinners.
But because the truth that exposes our sin can also lead us to the Savior who forgives it.
And we must say something else clearly.
You cannot save yourself through the sheer power of making better decisions.
The Bible does not teach salvation by moral determination.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works, so no one can boast.
Jesus says in John 6:44 that no one can come to Him unless the Father draws that person.
And in John 6:37, He promises not to cast out the one who comes to Him.
Whatever differences Christians hold about the precise relationship between divine grace and human response, salvation is never something sinners can boast of earning.
We are saved because of Jesus Christ.
His righteousness.
His sacrifice.
His resurrection.
His grace.
And genuine saving faith does not leave a person content to make peace with sin.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for God, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
The Gospel does not say, "Your choices do not matter."
It says that your choices cannot purchase salvation, but the grace that saves you also begins transforming how you live.
And that brings us to one more truth that should change how you look at your life.
Being completely known by God is terrifying only if we forget what Christ has done for sinners.
Without grace, the knowledge that God sees everything exposes our guilt.
But through Christ, the believer can approach the throne of grace to obtain mercy and find help in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).
The same God who knows your hidden battles invites you to bring them into His light.
You do not have to impress Him with a polished testimony.
You do not have to pretend your faith has never trembled.
You do not have to conceal the sins you need to confess.
You do not have to explain away every tear.
And you do not have to invent a version of yourself that is more worthy of His attention.
He already knows.
And the Gospel calls you to come to Him in truth.
Not because every person who hears the Gospel will automatically be saved regardless of response.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior, and everyone who truly comes to Him is received.
Romans 10:9–13 connects salvation with faith in the risen Lord Jesus and calls upon people to call on His name.
That invitation is not reserved for people with spotless histories.
It reaches the guilty.
The ashamed.
The religious hypocrite who finally admits the truth.
The exhausted believer who needs to return to the Lord.
The person who has been running from God while secretly longing to come home.
And yes, the person who has spent years wondering whether the future is already written.
Here is what I want you to remember.
You are not God.
You cannot see the end from the beginning.
You cannot carry the weight of knowing every possible consequence of every decision.
And you were never commanded to.
You were called to trust the Lord, obey His revealed Word, and walk by faith.
Proverbs 3:5–6 tells us to trust in the LORD with all our heart rather than lean on our own understanding, acknowledging Him in our ways.
That is not a command to stop thinking.
It is a command to stop treating our limited understanding as the final authority over God's wisdom.
Some questions remain difficult.
Some mysteries remain unresolved.
And Christians who love Scripture may still disagree about how divine foreknowledge and human freedom fit together philosophically.
But none of that changes the clarity of the Gospel.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.
And the call to repent and believe is real.
So perhaps tonight you need to stop trying to see your entire future.
Perhaps you need to make the phone call.
Confess the lie.
End the deception.
Seek forgiveness.
Ask for help.
Open the Bible again.
Pray even when the words feel weak.
Return to the church community you have been avoiding.
Or, for the first time, turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
Not to earn His love.
Not to manipulate His plans.
But because the God who knows the end from the beginning has revealed the Savior in whom sinners can find mercy.
And if you have been waiting for a sign that you should take your relationship with Christ seriously, consider the words already before you.
"Choose life."
Not as a slogan promising that every earthly decision will lead to comfort.
But as a biblical call to love the Lord, heed His voice, and hold fast to Him.
Because He is your life.
There is one more thing I want to ask you.
Not as a theological examination.
As a question for your heart.
If Jesus already knew every failure of Peter and still called him to follow, what makes you think your own failure must be the end of your story?
Maybe you have fallen.
Maybe you have made a decision that changed everything.
Maybe you have spent years living with consequences that cannot simply be reversed.
The Gospel does not promise to erase every earthly consequence.
But it does proclaim forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life through Jesus Christ.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to become the lord of your future.
Christ is Lord.
And for those who belong to Him, even suffering and regret do not have the authority to separate them from His love (Romans 8:38–39).
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish words that stir emotion for a moment.
Not to collect applause from people who agree with us.
But to keep pointing wounded, searching, struggling, and growing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, discipleship, and biblical truth.
Return to it when fear about the future begins speaking louder than the promises of God.
And please, don't leave without joining the conversation.
You do not have to tell strangers every private detail of your life. But sometimes a simple, honest request for prayer becomes the beginning of meaningful encouragement and fellowship.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is possible, that forgiveness is real, and that God is still at work in the lives of imperfect people.
And if you believe this ministry is helping people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ, I want to invite you to consider something deeper than simply reading another article.

Giving to support Gospel ministry is a biblical practice. Philippians 4:15–18 describes believers partnering materially in the work of the Gospel, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled.
So I want to be careful about something important.
It does not replace your responsibility to your local church.
It is not a required tithe, a condition of salvation, or a measure of how much you love Jesus.
But it can be a meaningful, prayerfully chosen ministry offering—an opportunity to help support biblical content and discipleship beyond your immediate community.
Those products can serve as reminders of Scripture, tools for reflection, or simple opportunities to begin conversations about faith.
It is the opportunity to participate in a ministry devoted to making Christ known.
Our desire is to keep biblical nourishment accessible while inviting those who are able and willing to help sustain the work.
Invite someone into the conversation.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Pray for those who are searching.
And above all, point people to Jesus—not to a personality, a platform, or a ministry name.
Because the goal is not simply to build a larger audience.
It is to see more people hear the Gospel, grow in the truth, and follow Jesus Christ.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to where we began.
God knows your tomorrow.
He knows the questions you will ask.
He knows the battles you will face.
He knows the tears that have not yet fallen.
He knows the decisions whose consequences you cannot yet imagine.
And the same Scriptures that reveal His perfect knowledge also call you to trust Him, repent, obey, and believe.
You do not need to know everything God knows to take the next faithful step.
You need the Savior God has revealed.
The One who knew Peter would deny Him.
The One who went willingly to the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls sinners to repent and follow Him.
So do not surrender to fatalism.
Do not pretend your choices are meaningless.
Do not imagine that your mistakes are stronger than the mercy of Christ.
And do not mistake the mystery of God's knowledge for the absence of God's love.
The God who knew your darkest chapter before it was written is the same God who sent His Son to make redemption possible.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LETTER THAT DISAPPEARED: DID PAUL WRITE TO CORINTH BEFORE FIRST CORINTHIANS?
paragraphs: THE LETTER THAT DISAPPEARED: DID PAUL WRITE TO CORINTH BEFORE FIRST CORINTHIANS?

One overlooked sentence in your Bible reveals a forgotten letter, a struggling church, and a warning Christians today desperately need to hear. But the most astonishing part isn't the letter that disappeared. It's the Gospel truth that survived.
There is a sentence in your Bible that most Christians have read without realizing what they just discovered.

A sentence so ordinary that you could pass over it during your morning devotion, close your Bible, drink your coffee, and never realize you had stumbled upon one of the most fascinating mysteries in the New Testament.
But once you see it, you cannot unsee it.
Because buried in Paul's first canonical letter to the Corinthians is a reference to another letter.
A letter he had already written.
A letter we do not possess.
And the unsettling question is this:
If Paul wrote a letter to the Corinthians before First Corinthians, what happened to it?
Was it lost?
Was it deliberately excluded from Scripture?
Did the early Christians know something we don't?
And perhaps the most important question of all: If an apostle's letter could disappear from history, does that mean something is missing from the Word of God?
Stay with me, because the answer takes us somewhere far deeper than ancient manuscripts.
It takes us into a church that looked spiritual on the outside while tolerating sin on the inside.
It takes us into the heart of an apostle who loved people enough to confront what was destroying them.
And ultimately, it takes us to Jesus Christ, who never promised that His people would be without struggles, but who gave His life to rescue sinners from the very darkness they sometimes try to hide.
The mystery begins with one verse.
"I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators." — 1 Corinthians 5:9 (KJV)
Read those words again.
"I wrote unto you..."
Not, "I am writing to you."
Not, "I will write to you."
Paul is referring to something he had already written.
And this is where the story changes.
The book we call First Corinthians was not necessarily Paul's first communication with the Corinthian church.
In fact, this verse provides strong evidence that it wasn't.
And if that surprises you, imagine how much more there is to discover when we stop treating the Bible like a collection of familiar quotations and begin listening carefully to what it actually says.
The original Greek makes the point even clearer.
Paul writes:
Ἔγραψα ὑμῖν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι πόρνοις.
Transliteration:
Egrapsa hymin en tē epistolē mē synanamignysthai pornois.
A close translation is:
"I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with sexually immoral people."
Notice the opening word.
Ἔγραψα — Egrapsa.
It means "I wrote."
It is the aorist form of the Greek verb graphō, meaning "to write."
By itself, the aorist does not automatically prove that Paul is referring to a different document. Greek writers could sometimes use this tense while referring to the letter being composed.
But context matters.
And in 1 Corinthians 5:9–11, Paul appears to be clarifying instructions that his readers had already received and possibly misunderstood.
That is why the prevailing scholarly understanding is that Paul is referring to an earlier letter sent to Corinth.
A letter written before the document now known as First Corinthians.
Think about that.
The title "First Corinthians" identifies the first Corinthian letter preserved in the New Testament canon.
It does not guarantee that it was the first letter Paul ever sent to that congregation.
And Scripture itself gives us the clue.
There is something profoundly important about this discovery.
The Bible is not hiding the existence of Paul's earlier correspondence. The Bible is the very source that tells us about it.
That distinction matters more than you might realize.
Because in an age when sensational claims about "missing books" and "suppressed Scriptures" spread across social media, Christians need something stronger than fear.
We need truth.
Not manufactured mysteries.
Not dramatic conspiracy theories.
Truth that can withstand honest questions.
And sometimes the truth is already sitting in the verse we almost skipped.
But why was Paul writing to Corinth in the first place?
To understand that, you need to see the city behind the letter.

Corinth was a prosperous and influential Roman city, positioned along important commercial routes. It attracted merchants, travelers, workers, wealthy patrons, and people from different cultural and religious backgrounds.
It was a place where opportunity and temptation lived side by side.
A place where social status mattered.
Where wealth could create influence.
Where competing philosophies, religious practices, and moral expectations shaped everyday life.
And right there, in the middle of that complicated world, God established a church.
Not a church filled with people who had always lived holy lives.
Not a church whose members had never made terrible decisions.
A church made up of people who needed the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
People with histories.
People with habits.
People with wounds.
People whose old ways of living did not disappear automatically the moment they heard the Gospel.
Does that sound familiar?
Because if we're willing to be honest, the distance between ancient Corinth and the modern church may not be as great as we imagine.
We have better technology.
Different clothing.
Different languages.
But the human heart?
It still knows how to worship God publicly while hiding compromises privately.
It still knows how to justify what Scripture confronts.
It still knows how to become offended when someone lovingly challenges what we have decided to tolerate.
And that is precisely why Paul's words still matter.
In Acts 18, we learn that Paul ministered in Corinth and spent approximately eighteen months teaching the Word of God there.
He worked alongside Aquila and Priscilla.
He preached Christ.
He faced opposition.
And the Lord encouraged him in a vision, saying:
"Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace: For I am with thee." — Acts 18:9–10 (KJV)
Imagine the emotional weight of those words.
Paul was not building a religious brand.
He was not gathering followers to admire his personality.
He was proclaiming a crucified and risen Savior in a city that desperately needed Him.
And people believed.
Lives began changing.
A Christian community took shape.
But becoming a church did not mean becoming immune to sin.
The same congregation that received spiritual gifts also struggled with division, pride, sexual immorality, lawsuits, disorderly worship, and confusion about Christian freedom.
The church had experienced grace.
But some were beginning to confuse grace with permission.
And Paul loved them too much to remain silent.
Somewhere before the writing of First Corinthians, Paul sent a letter warning believers about associating with sexually immoral people.
We know this because he later refers to that correspondence in 1 Corinthians 5:9.
But the earlier letter itself has not survived as an independently identifiable document.
We do not know its complete wording.
We do not know its precise length.
We do not know every subject it addressed.
And we do not know exactly when or how it ceased to circulate.

Some scholars have explored whether fragments of earlier Corinthian correspondence might be embedded within surviving letters, including proposals involving 2 Corinthians. Those reconstructions remain debated and cannot be presented as established fact.
The responsible conclusion is simple:
Paul almost certainly wrote an earlier letter to Corinth, but we do not possess a securely identifiable copy of it today.
And this is where some believers begin to feel uncomfortable.
Because the next question is understandable.
If Paul wrote something inspired by God, shouldn't we still have it?
But notice the assumption hidden inside that question.
It assumes that every letter an apostle wrote was necessarily intended by God to become part of the permanent biblical canon.
Scripture never teaches that.
The apostles lived real lives.
They traveled.
They spoke.
They taught.
They answered questions.
They corresponded with churches and individuals.
Not every sentence they spoke was preserved in Scripture.
Not every conversation was recorded.
And not every piece of correspondence was necessarily intended to become canonical Scripture.
The inspiration of Scripture, as affirmed in 2 Timothy 3:16, does not require us to conclude that every written communication from an apostle was inspired Scripture.
We must distinguish between Paul's apostolic authority and the specific writings God has preserved for the church as Scripture.
That distinction protects us from making claims the Bible itself does not make.
The missing Corinthian letter does not prove that God lost control of His Word.
Neither does it give us permission to invent its contents.
It reminds us that the biblical writings emerged within real historical relationships, where letters were written, delivered, read, answered, and sometimes lost.
And here is something beautiful.
Even though we do not have that earlier letter, we do have Paul's inspired clarification of its instruction.
Listen carefully to what he says next.
"Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world." — 1 Corinthians 5:10 (KJV)
Paul was correcting a potentially devastating misunderstanding.
He was not telling Christians to withdraw from every person who lived in sin.
He was not commanding believers to avoid all unbelievers.
He was not teaching the church to build walls so high that broken people could no longer hear about Jesus.
If Christians refused all ordinary contact with sinners outside the church, Paul explains, they would have to leave the world entirely.
And that would contradict the very mission of the Gospel.
Jesus Himself ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He entered the homes of people religious society despised.
He spoke with the rejected.
He touched the unclean.
He offered mercy to people whose reputations were already ruined.
But never confuse His compassion with approval of sin.
Jesus came close to sinners because He came to save them.
He did not need to become like their sin to demonstrate His love.
And He did not abandon holiness to make people feel comfortable.
This is the balance the church desperately needs to recover.
We are called to love sinners without celebrating sin, and to pursue holiness without becoming self-righteous.
Paul then makes the distinction unmistakable.

"But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat." — 1 Corinthians 5:11 (KJV)
This was not a command to abandon every Christian who struggles, falls, or sincerely seeks repentance.

Paul was addressing a serious situation involving a person identified with the church whose conduct contradicted the faith he professed, and a congregation that was tolerating the situation rather than confronting it.
The immediate context is shocking.
In 1 Corinthians 5:1, Paul reports sexual immorality among them of a kind that even the surrounding Gentile world regarded as scandalous: a man had his father's wife.
And instead of mourning, the congregation had become arrogant.
Imagine that.
A church with spiritual knowledge.
A church with impressive gifts.
A church that knew how to speak about God.
Yet somehow, it had learned to live comfortably beside a sin that should have brought it to tears.
Paul's concern was not merely the reputation of the congregation.
It was the spiritual destruction that unrepentant sin could bring.
And it was the danger of a church losing its moral witness while continuing to congratulate itself on being spiritual.
Read that again, because it is possible to be religiously active while spiritually asleep.
You can know the language of worship and still resist the Lord of worship.
You can defend biblical doctrine online and refuse to obey it at home.
You can post verses about holiness while privately feeding the very desires that are hardening your heart.
You can look spiritually alive to everybody watching and be quietly drifting away from Christ.
And the most frightening part is that, after enough compromises, conviction can begin to feel like an inconvenience rather than a gift.
But Paul does not confront Corinth because he hates the church.
He confronts Corinth because he loves it.
This is something our generation struggles to understand.
We have sometimes confused love with endless affirmation.
We have treated correction as rejection.
We have assumed that anyone who challenges our behavior must be against us.
Yet Scripture presents a more demanding and more beautiful vision.
Love tells the truth.
Love seeks restoration.
Love refuses to call darkness light.
And love never forgets that the sinner being confronted is a human being whose soul matters to God.
That is why Paul can speak firmly about church discipline while still keeping salvation in view.
In 1 Corinthians 5:5, he expresses the purpose of severe corrective action in terms of the person's ultimate spiritual good.
And in 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul urges the church to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love toward a disciplined individual.
We should not confidently assume that the individual in 2 Corinthians 2 is the same man described in 1 Corinthians 5; scholars disagree about that identification.
But the broader pastoral principle is unmistakable.
Church discipline must never become an excuse for cruelty.
The goal is not to enjoy another person's humiliation.
The goal is repentance, protection of the congregation, and restoration wherever repentance makes that possible.
Because the church is not a museum displaying people who have never sinned.
It is a community of people called to follow the Savior who died for sinners.
And that brings us to the most important part of this entire story.
The real scandal in Corinth was not simply that sin existed.
Sin exists wherever fallen human beings gather.
The scandal was that the church had begun treating serious, unrepentant sin as something it could accommodate without grief.
But the greater wonder is that God had not stopped speaking to them.
He sent correction.
He exposed what was hidden.
He called them to repentance.
And He reminded them of the Savior whose sacrifice made their cleansing possible.
Listen to Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 5:7:
"For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." (KJV)
There it is.
The center of the whole passage.
Not Paul.
Not the lost letter.
Not the controversy.
Christ.
Paul reaches for the imagery of Passover, when Israel remembered God's deliverance from Egypt and the blood of the lamb associated with that deliverance.
He identifies Jesus as our Passover sacrifice.
The One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One whose blood secures redemption.
The One whose death makes reconciliation with God possible.
The One who did not merely come to improve our public image, but to deal with the guilt and power of sin.
And suddenly the entire chapter looks different.
Paul's call to holiness is not a demand that Christians save themselves through moral performance.
It is a call to live consistently with the redemption Christ has accomplished.
