The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who will make all things new.
That is why the answer to our original question is yes—anointing sick believers with oil remains a biblically grounded practice for Christians today.
James gives the church no indication that his instruction was intended to expire after the apostolic generation.
We should therefore take it seriously, while recognizing that faithful Christians may differ over the precise theological meaning of the oil.
But anointing is never a substitute for the gospel.
It is never permission to exploit the desperate.
And it is never a guarantee that every illness will disappear.
The church must not turn an act of compassion into a spectacle, a business transaction, or a test of whether someone deserves God's mercy.
The sick need prayer.
They need truth.
They need care.
And above all, they need Jesus.
Maybe you began reading this article because you wanted to know whether Christians should still use anointing oil.
But perhaps somewhere along the way, another question surfaced.
Have you been seeking God's hand while keeping your heart closed to His grace?
It is possible to want a miracle without wanting the Savior.
It is possible to ask Jesus to remove pain while refusing to surrender the sin that is destroying us.
And it is possible to know religious language while remaining far from Christ.
The greatest need of the human soul is not merely to escape physical suffering.
It is to be reconciled to God.
We have all sinned (Romans 3:23).
We cannot save ourselves through rituals, offerings, church attendance, or religious performance.
But Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again.
And the call of the gospel is to repent and believe in Him.
Not to purchase His mercy.
Not to earn His forgiveness.
But to receive the grace that only He can give.
If you have been running from God, you do not have to keep running.
If you have been hiding behind religious appearances, you can come into the light.
If you have been wounded by someone who used God's name to manipulate your desperation, do not confuse that person's wrongdoing with the character of Jesus.
Come to Christ.
Bring Him the sin you have concealed.
Bring Him the grief you cannot explain.
Bring Him the fears that return when the lights go out.
And trust the Savior who receives those who come to Him in faith.
You may pray something like this:

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I am a sinner in need of Your mercy. Forgive me for trusting in myself more than in You. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to repent, to trust Your Word, and to follow You. Whether I am healed quickly, slowly, or must endure suffering, help me remain faithful. Let my hope rest in You and not in any ritual. Amen."
There is no magical power in repeating these words. Salvation is not produced by a formula. It is God's gracious gift received through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And if you are already a believer who is suffering, remember this.
Your illness has not made you less valuable to God.
Your weakness has not placed you beyond the reach of His grace.
Your unanswered questions do not surprise Him.
You may not know what tomorrow's medical report will say.
But the resurrection of Jesus gives you a hope that reaches beyond tomorrow.
And that truth deserves to be carried beyond this article.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be sitting in a hospital waiting room right now, wondering whether God has abandoned them.
Someone may be afraid to ask for prayer because they have been told their sickness is proof of hidden sin.
Someone may be spending money they cannot afford on so-called miracle products because nobody has explained what James 5 actually teaches.
But before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Have you ever prayed for healing and received an answer you did not expect?
Have you witnessed God restore someone?
Or are you still waiting, still trusting, still fighting to believe while the suffering continues?
And if God has brought you through a season of suffering, consider sharing a brief testimony. Not every testimony needs to end with a dramatic physical miracle. Sometimes a testimony is simply this:
"I was hurting, but Jesus did not abandon me."
Your words may help another believer persevere.
And if this kind of Scripture-grounded teaching has helped you, I invite you to stay connected with Gospel Warrior.

These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment more accessible, especially to people who need encouragement and teaching but may not have the means to purchase books and study materials.
And for those who believe in this mission and are able to help sustain it, there is another way to participate.
Scripture says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Giving that honors God is not produced by guilt or pressure.
It flows from love, gratitude, and a willing heart.
The gospel is not for sale.
The free resources are not a reward reserved for people who pay.
And God's love cannot be purchased through monthly payments.
Your decision to follow may help you stay connected with teaching that points you back to Scripture.
And your prayers for this ministry matter deeply.
Because the purpose is not to build a following around a human personality.
It is to point people toward Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who welcomed the broken.
The same Jesus who called sinners to repentance.
The same Jesus who died for the ungodly.
The same Jesus who rose from the grave.
And the same Jesus who promises that one day, for those who belong to Him, death itself will be swallowed up in victory.
So yes, bring the oil when Scripture calls for it.
Call the elders.
Pray with faith.
Seek wise medical care.
Confess your sins.
Care for the suffering.
Trust the Lord.
But never mistake the sign for the Savior.

Because when the oil has been wiped away, when the prayers have ended, when the hospital room grows quiet again, and when you are left facing everything you cannot control, there is still Someone worthy of your trust.
His name is Jesus.
And if you belong to Him, even death will not have the final word over your story.
The oil may touch your skin for a moment, but only Jesus can redeem your soul for eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS PERFORMED MIRACLES FOR SINNERS… SO WHY DID HE REFUSE TO GIVE PROOF TO RELIGIOUS PEOPLE?
paragraphs: JESUS PERFORMED MIRACLES FOR SINNERS… SO WHY DID HE REFUSE TO GIVE PROOF TO RELIGIOUS PEOPLE?
The terrifying difference between a heart searching for God and a heart demanding that God prove Himself—and why the only sign Jesus promised still confronts every one of us today.
There is something deeply unsettling about Jesus that many people never notice.
He opened blind eyes.
He cleansed lepers.
He made the paralyzed walk.
He fed thousands with a little boy's lunch.
He even stood outside a tomb where a dead man had been buried for four days and called him back to life.
Yet when certain religious leaders approached Him and demanded a miraculous sign, Jesus refused.
Think about that.
The same Jesus who showed extraordinary compassion to broken people would not perform a miracle merely because powerful religious men demanded one.
Why?
Was He offended?
Was He unwilling to answer difficult questions?
Was He afraid of being examined?
Or was something happening beneath their demand that exposed a dangerous condition of the human heart?
Because the answer is not simply about the Pharisees.
It is about the person who keeps telling God, "If You really love me, prove it."
It is about the believer who has witnessed God's faithfulness before but still struggles to trust Him today.
It is about the wounded soul who wants to believe but is afraid of being disappointed again.
And perhaps most uncomfortably, it is about those of us who have quietly decided that God must meet our conditions before we will surrender to His.
There is a difference between asking God an honest question and putting God on trial.
Jesus knew that difference.
And what He said about it should make every one of us examine our hearts.
In Matthew 12:38, some scribes and Pharisees approached Jesus with a request:
"Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you." (ESV)
At first, that sounds reasonable.
After all, Scripture contains accounts of God confirming His messengers through extraordinary works.
Moses was given signs before confronting Pharaoh.
Elijah called upon the Lord on Mount Carmel.
The prophets proclaimed that God would act powerfully among His people.
So why would Jesus object to someone asking for evidence?
Here is the detail we must not overlook.
The problem was not that they wanted truth. The problem was what they were doing with the truth already standing in front of them.
Read the surrounding verses.
Earlier in Matthew 12, Jesus healed a man whose hand was withered.
Instead of celebrating the man's restoration, the Pharisees began conspiring against Jesus (Matthew 12:9–14).
Later, Jesus delivered a demon-oppressed man who had been blind and unable to speak.
The crowd was astonished.
But the Pharisees attributed His power to Beelzebul, the ruler of demons (Matthew 12:22–24).
Let that sink in.
A suffering man had been delivered.
A life had been changed.
The power of God was being displayed before their eyes.
And rather than rejoicing, they attempted to discredit the One who had brought freedom.
Then they asked for another sign.
Another miracle.
Another demonstration.
As though the previous ones had never happened.
Jesus was not dealing with a simple shortage of evidence.
He was confronting hardened opposition to the evidence they had already received.
And that distinction changes everything.
In Matthew 12:39, Jesus answered:
"An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah." (ESV)
Those words are severe.
But we must understand them correctly.
Jesus was not declaring that every person who asks for evidence is evil.
He was addressing a particular kind of unbelief—a generation represented by leaders who had repeatedly witnessed His works yet continued resisting Him.
The Greek expression translated "seeks for a sign" includes the word sēmeion (σημεῖον), meaning a sign, a distinguishing indication, or a miraculous event pointing beyond itself.
That matters.
In the Gospel accounts, Jesus' miracles were never meant to be entertainment.
They were signs revealing something about His identity, authority, compassion, and the arrival of God's kingdom.
The miracle was not supposed to become the final destination.
It was supposed to direct people toward the Messiah.
Imagine standing beside a road sign that clearly points toward home.
Instead of following it, you demand that someone build another sign.
Then another.
Then another.
Eventually, the issue is no longer whether the road has been marked.
The issue is whether you are willing to travel it.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
How many times have we prayed, "Lord, if You do this one thing, I will finally trust You"?
"If You heal this sickness, I will surrender."
"If You restore this relationship, I will obey."
"If You rescue my finances, I will believe You care."
"If You answer this prayer exactly the way I want, I will stop doubting."
And when the answer comes differently—or does not come when we expect—we quietly withdraw our trust.
Not every prayer like this comes from rebellion. Some are cries of genuine pain. God knows the difference between a wounded heart and a defiant one.
But we must be willing to ask ourselves something uncomfortable.
Have I been seeking God Himself, or have I been seeking a God who will agree to my terms?
Because faith does not mean we never struggle.
Faith means that even in our struggle, we are learning to trust the character of God rather than demanding control over His actions.
And there is another detail in Jesus' response that is easy to miss.
He called that generation "adulterous."
The Greek word is moichalis (μοιχαλίς).
In this context, the language recalls the Old Testament prophets, who frequently portrayed Israel's covenant unfaithfulness to God as spiritual adultery.
This was not merely an insult.
It was a covenant accusation.
The people who claimed to belong to God were resisting the One God had sent.
Their lips could speak religious language while their hearts remained far from Him.
And suddenly the question becomes frightening.
Can someone know Scripture, attend worship, defend religious traditions, and still resist Jesus?
According to the Gospels, yes.
The Pharisees in these encounters were not people who had never heard about God.
They were people deeply familiar with religious life.
They knew the commandments.
They studied the sacred writings.
They recognized the language of holiness.
Yet some of them stood face-to-face with the fulfillment of God's promises and opposed Him.
Religious knowledge had not automatically produced spiritual surrender.
That should humble every Christian.
Because knowing the right words is not the same as loving the Lord.
Posting Bible verses is not the same as obeying them.
Being able to explain repentance is not the same as repenting.
And defending the truth in public does not excuse refusing to let that truth examine us in private.
There is a kind of religion that wants Jesus as a subject to debate but not as Lord to obey.
And Jesus will not be reduced to a spectacle for people determined to remain their own masters.
But before anyone concludes that Jesus rejected honest doubt, we need to look at another man.
A father.
A desperate father whose son was suffering terribly.
In Mark 9, this father brought his child to Jesus after the disciples had been unable to deliver him.
The man's words were filled with both hope and uncertainty.
"If you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us." (Mark 9:22, ESV)
Jesus responded by directing him toward faith.
And the father cried out:
"I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24, ESV)
What a confession.
Not polished.
Not impressive.
Not the kind of statement someone makes when trying to appear spiritually strong.
Just a father standing before Jesus with a breaking heart.
"I believe."
"Help my unbelief."
And Jesus delivered his son.
Do you see the difference?
One group demanded a sign while resisting the One who performed the signs.
One father confessed his weakness and brought it directly to Jesus.
The father was not pretending that his faith was perfect.
He was asking Jesus to help him where it was not.
That is extraordinarily good news for anyone struggling to believe.
You do not need to manufacture certainty before coming to Christ.
You can bring your questions.
You can bring your fear.
You can bring the grief that makes prayer difficult.
You can confess that you are exhausted from waiting.
You can admit that certain passages confuse you.
You can tell Him that you want to believe but do not know how to move forward.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend that your wounds are not real.
It calls you to bring your real self to the real Savior.
And Scripture gives us another powerful example.
After the resurrection, Thomas struggled to accept the testimony that Jesus was alive.
He wanted to see the wounds.
He wanted physical confirmation.
When Jesus appeared again, He graciously invited Thomas to examine the evidence.
Thomas responded:
"My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28, ESV)
Jesus then pronounced a blessing upon those who would believe without having seen Him physically (John 20:29).
Notice the balance.
Jesus did not treat evidence as inherently sinful.
Nor did He suggest that faith must be blind or disconnected from truth.
John explicitly says that the signs recorded in his Gospel were written so that readers might believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name (John 20:30–31).
That is crucial.
Christianity is not a command to believe without any reason.
It is a call to respond to the revelation God has given, supremely in Jesus Christ.
The problem arises when someone continually moves the conditions of belief because surrender is the one outcome they are unwilling to consider.
And this brings us back to the religious leaders.
Jesus said that no sign would be given to that generation except the sign of Jonah.
What did He mean?
Matthew 12:40 explains:
"For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth." (ESV)
Jesus was pointing ahead to His death, burial, and resurrection.
The sign of Jonah was not merely another miracle added to a growing collection.
It pointed to the central event of the Gospel.
The crucified Messiah would rise.
The One they rejected would be vindicated by God.
The One they condemned would conquer death.
In the original Greek, Jesus' words include the phrase ho huios tou anthrōpou (ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου), "the Son of Man."
This title carries profound biblical significance, including its connection with Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives dominion and an everlasting kingdom.
Jesus was not merely claiming to be another teacher with extraordinary abilities.
He was revealing Himself as the promised Messiah whose mission would reach its decisive fulfillment through suffering, death, and resurrection.
And there is something astonishing about the way He answered their demand.
They wanted a sign that would satisfy their conditions.
Jesus pointed to the event that would expose humanity's sin and reveal God's saving grace.
They wanted a demonstration of power.
Jesus pointed toward a cross.
They wanted Him to prove Himself on their terms.
He would accomplish redemption according to the Father's will.
And this is where the entire story turns.
Because the greatest sign Jesus gave was not designed to flatter human pride.
It was designed to save sinners.
The cross tells us something about ourselves that we often do not want to hear.
Our deepest problem is not simply that life is difficult.
It is not merely that we need better circumstances.
It is not even that we lack enough miraculous experiences.
Our deepest problem is sin.
The rebellion, selfishness, unbelief, pride, and disobedience that separate us from the holy God who made us.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
Not just the Pharisees.
Not just the people we consider worse than ourselves.
All of us.
And Romans 6:23 tells us that the wages of sin is death, but God's gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is why Jesus came.
Not merely to impress crowds.
Not merely to improve circumstances.
Not merely to provide extraordinary experiences.
He came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10).
He came to give His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
And the cross is where the scandal of human sin meets the astonishing grace of God.
Think about the irony.
Human beings demanded that Jesus prove who He was.
Then human beings crucified Him.
They mocked Him.
They challenged Him to come down from the cross.
Matthew 27:42 records their taunt:
"He saved others; he cannot save himself." (ESV)
They misunderstood what was happening.
Jesus was not powerless because He remained on the cross.
He was giving His life in obedience to the Father's saving purpose.
He did not need to abandon His mission to establish His authority.
His death was part of that mission.
And three days later, the tomb was empty.
The resurrection was not a public-relations stunt.
It was God's decisive vindication of His Son and the foundation of the apostolic proclamation that Jesus is Lord.
Paul writes that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The same chapter records testimony concerning His appearances to Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred brothers at one time, James, and the apostles.
Paul did not present the resurrection as a comforting metaphor.
He proclaimed it as an event on which Christian faith stands or falls.
And here is the part that should leave us speechless.
The people who rejected Jesus did not stop God's redemptive purpose.
Their opposition became part of the history through which the saving work of Christ unfolded.

Acts 2:23–24 holds together both human responsibility and God's sovereign purpose: Jesus was delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, was crucified by lawless men, and was raised by God.
The worst act of human injustice did not defeat the plan of redemption.
God raised His Son from the dead.
The cross looked like the end of the story. The resurrection revealed that God was writing something greater.
From condemnation to forgiveness.
From death to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But we must be careful with that beautiful truth.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending sin never happened.
He does not call evil good.
He does not offer forgiveness by ignoring justice.
He bears our sins, fulfills His saving mission, and calls us to repentance and faith.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us and begins transforming the way we live.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
And 2 Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
That means the Gospel is not simply about receiving a better ending to the life we already wanted.
It is about receiving new life in Christ.
And perhaps that is why the demand for signs can become so spiritually dangerous.
A person may want Jesus to change everything around them while refusing to let Him change anything within them.
We want Him to remove the consequences but not confront the compromise.
We want Him to heal the relationship but not expose our pride.
We want Him to restore our peace but not address the sin we keep protecting.
We want the comfort of His promises without the authority of His commands.
Yet the Savior who loves us too much to abandon us also loves us too much to affirm what is destroying us.
His call to repentance is not cruelty.
It is mercy.
His commands are not an invitation to earn salvation.
They are the rightful authority of the Lord who saves by grace.
And when Jesus confronts our hearts, He does so as the One who gave Himself for sinners.
Maybe this is touching a place in your life you have kept hidden.
Maybe you have spent years waiting for a dramatic experience before taking the next step of obedience.
Maybe you keep asking God to prove His love while overlooking what Christ has already accomplished at Calvary.
Or maybe you are genuinely hurting, and you are afraid this message means you are wrong for asking God why.
Please hear this carefully.
The Bible does not condemn every cry of confusion.
The Psalms are filled with lament.
Habakkuk brought troubling questions before God.
Job wrestled with suffering.
Even Jesus, in His agony on the cross, cried out with the opening words of Psalm 22.
There is a difference between wrestling with God because you desperately want to hold on to Him and challenging God because you have decided you will never bow.
God is not threatened by honest questions.
And the Christian response to sincere inquiry should not be contempt, shame, or fear.
First Peter 3:15 calls believers to give a reason for their hope with gentleness and respect.
So if you are searching, keep seeking the truth.
Read the Gospels.
Examine the claims of Christ.
Ask difficult questions.
Speak to faithful Christians who will take your questions seriously.
But also examine your own heart.
Because there comes a moment when the question is no longer merely, "Has God given me a reason to believe?"
It becomes, "Am I willing to follow the truth wherever it leads?"
And if that truth leads to Jesus Christ, are you willing to surrender?
There is another sobering detail in Matthew 12.
Jesus spoke about the people of Nineveh, who repented at Jonah's preaching.
He also spoke about the queen of the South, who traveled to hear Solomon's wisdom.
Then He declared that something greater than Jonah and greater than Solomon was present (Matthew 12:41–42).
Think about the contrast.
Nineveh responded to the warning of a reluctant prophet.
The queen of the South made a difficult journey to hear the wisdom of a king.
Yet some of the religious leaders were standing before One greater than both and still refused to respond.
The tragedy was not that God had remained silent.
The tragedy was that God had spoken, and they were resisting His voice.
Could that happen to us?
Could we become so accustomed to hearing about Jesus that we stop being moved by Him?
Could the cross become a familiar symbol rather than the place where we remember the terrible cost of our redemption?
Could we sing about grace on Sunday while withholding forgiveness on Monday?
Could we pray for revival in public while refusing repentance in private?
Could we ask for another word from God while neglecting the Word He has already given?
These are not questions meant to crush a sincere believer.
They are questions meant to awaken us.
Because spiritual familiarity can become dangerous when it replaces genuine devotion.
We can become experts at discussing the Gospel while forgetting to live as people who have been changed by it.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility is this:
We might spend our lives asking Jesus to show us something extraordinary while overlooking the extraordinary mercy that has already been revealed in Him.
If this has exposed something in your own heart, you do not have to pretend.
You do not need to write a polished testimony.
You do not need to make yourself look spiritually impressive.
You do not have to explain private wounds publicly.
And if God has already brought you through a season of doubt, your testimony may encourage someone who is still struggling.
Because sometimes another believer does not need to hear that you have never doubted.
They need to hear how Jesus sustained you when you did.
Now consider something else.
What if the answer you have been waiting for is not another sign?
What if the next faithful step is to respond to the truth you already know?
To forgive the person you have been resenting.
To confess the sin you have been hiding.
To return to prayer after months of silence.
To open the Bible again.
To seek reconciliation where it is wise and safe.
To ask for help with a destructive habit.
To stop treating obedience as something you will consider only after God improves your circumstances.
None of these actions purchases God's love.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But genuine faith does not leave us indifferent to the One who saved us.
We follow Jesus because He is Lord.
We obey because we belong to Him.
We repent because His grace has opened the way home.
And if you have wandered far from Him, hear the invitation of the Gospel.
You are not beyond the reach of His mercy.
The same Christ who confronted religious hypocrisy also welcomed repentant sinners.
He ate with tax collectors.
He received the broken.
He forgave those who came to Him in faith.
He restored Peter after Peter denied Him.
He saved a dying criminal who turned to Him in his final hours.
And He continues to call sinners to repentance and faith.
Your past does not have to be your final identity.
Your shame does not have to be your permanent home.
Your failure does not have to be the last word.
But your hope is not that you can rewrite your own story through sheer determination.
Your hope is Jesus Christ—crucified, risen, and able to save those who come to God through Him.
That is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not collecting emotional reactions that disappear by tomorrow.
But continually pointing people back to the Scriptures, back to repentance, back to the sufficiency of Christ, and back to the transforming power of His Gospel.
You never know who may be silently wrestling with the same questions.
Someone in your family may be waiting for a reason to open the Bible again.
A friend may be carrying disappointment with God that they have never admitted.
A believer may be confusing a season of unanswered prayer with abandonment.
Someone who does not yet believe may be willing to consider Jesus if the conversation is approached with truth, compassion, and humility.
There is also a practical way to help this ministry continue.
It does not earn salvation.
It does not make you more valuable to Jesus.
And it should never replace your responsibility to care for your family or give faithfully according to your convictions and the needs of your local church.

But it can be a meaningful, voluntary expression of generosity—a ministry offering that helps sustain and expand the work of sharing Scripture, creating discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the Gospel.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that each person should give as they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not pressure.
Not spiritual fear.
Simply an opportunity to participate in work you believe is worth supporting, as the Lord leads and as your circumstances allow.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in everyday life, and conversation starters about the hope we have in Jesus.
It is the opportunity to help make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources more accessible to others.
These resources are intended to encourage biblical understanding, prayer, spiritual maturity, and a closer walk with the Lord.
Pray for the ministry.
Share Scripture faithfully.
Encourage someone who is suffering.
Invite someone to read the Gospels.
Help a new believer learn to follow Jesus.
Christ is the center.
The Gospel is the message.
And transformed lives—not financial transactions—are the fruit we long to see.
But before you leave, I want you to return to the question that began this entire conversation.
Why did Jesus refuse to perform signs for people who demanded proof?
Because in those encounters, their demands were not simply expressions of sincere searching.
They were part of a pattern of resisting the revelation already given.
Jesus would not submit His divine mission to the conditions imposed by hardened unbelief.
Instead, He pointed them toward the greatest sign of all.
His death.
His burial.
His resurrection.
And that sign still confronts the human heart today.
Not as an invitation to abandon reason.
Not as a demand to suppress every question.
But as a call to face the claims of Jesus Christ and consider what our response reveals about us.
You may never witness the Red Sea part before your eyes.
You may never see fire descend from heaven.
You may never receive the particular miracle you have been asking for.
And that can be painful.
Deeply painful.
But the Christian hope does not rest on receiving every earthly outcome we desire.
It rests on the crucified and risen Savior.
The One who entered our suffering.
The One who bore our sin.
The One who defeated death.
The One who promises to be with His people even when the road ahead is dark.
And if you are waiting for God to prove that He loves you, look again at the cross.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." (ESV)
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we solved every doubt.
Not after we earned His approval.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is grace.
And grace calls for a response.
If you have never turned to Christ in repentance and faith, you can call upon Him today.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive His forgiveness.
Follow Him as Lord.
And if you already belong to Jesus but have been living in fear, spiritual exhaustion, or hidden compromise, return to Him.
Do not wait until your prayers sound beautiful.
Do not wait until your emotions feel strong.
Do not wait until you can explain everything that has happened to you.
Come to Him in truth.
The father in Mark 9 did not bring perfect faith.
He brought the faith he had and asked Jesus to help what was lacking.
Perhaps that is where your prayer begins tonight.
"Lord, I believe. Help my unbelief."
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, instead of demanding that Jesus prove Himself on your terms, you will open your heart to the Savior who has already given Himself for you.
Because the greatest tragedy is not having questions about God.
The greatest tragedy is refusing to recognize the Savior while demanding that He keep proving He is worthy of your attention.
And the greatest mercy is that the Gospel still calls us to turn to Him.
If Jesus never performed another miracle on your terms, would His cross and resurrection still be enough to make you trust Him as Lord?
You do not have to answer that publicly.
Let the conversation be marked by honesty, humility, and grace.
Because somewhere, someone else may be asking the same question.
And your willingness to point them toward Jesus may help them begin seeking Him.
The sign they demanded could never replace the Savior they refused to receive—and the Savior they crucified is the One who rose to offer sinners life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE CALLED HIMSELF A MAN OF GOD… UNTIL HIS EMPLOYEES BEGAN TALKING ABOUT HOW HE TREATED THEM.
paragraphs: HE CALLED HIMSELF A MAN OF GOD… UNTIL HIS EMPLOYEES BEGAN TALKING ABOUT HOW HE TREATED THEM.

He raised his hands in worship on Sunday. By Monday, the people working under him were praying just to survive another day. And the most frightening part of this story isn't what his employees said about him. It's what Jesus might say.
Nobody questioned his Christianity.
Not at first.

He posted Bible verses almost every morning. His social media profile proudly declared, “Jesus is Lord.” He donated to church projects, spoke passionately about faith, and never missed an opportunity to tell people how God had blessed his business.
When someone complimented his success, he smiled.
“All glory to God.”
And people believed him.
Why wouldn't they?
He knew Scripture. He spoke confidently about prayer. He could explain the importance of obedience, generosity, and Christian leadership.
But there was something the congregation never saw.
Something his employees knew all too well.
Because behind the office doors, the same man who spoke about God's love could make another human being feel utterly worthless.
And eventually, the people who worked for him began talking.
Not because they wanted to destroy his reputation.
But because they were exhausted from trying to survive it.
And here is the question that should make every Christian uncomfortable:
What if the people who know us outside the church are telling a completely different story about the Jesus we claim to represent?
Before you decide this story is about someone else, keep reading.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual blindness is not failing to recognize sin in another person.
It is becoming so familiar with our own religious appearance that we stop examining the condition of our hearts.
The following workplace story is an illustrative composite, not an accusation against an identifiable individual. But the spiritual problem it exposes is painfully real.
One employee had been working there for years.
She was dependable. Rarely complained. Often stayed late when deadlines became impossible.

At home, she had responsibilities no one in the office fully understood. Bills waiting. Family members depending on her. Nights when she calculated how much money would remain after groceries and electricity.
She needed that job.
And her employer knew it.
One morning, she made a mistake.
Not a dishonest mistake. Not an act of rebellion.
A human mistake.
The kind almost everyone makes when overwhelmed.
But instead of correcting her privately and helping her understand what went wrong, her employer humiliated her in front of her coworkers.
His voice grew louder.
His words became sharper.
She tried to explain.
He interrupted.
She apologized.
He continued.
By the time it ended, she was fighting tears.
And the man who had publicly thanked God for his company's success returned to his office as though nothing unusual had happened.
That evening, she sat in her car before driving home.
Her hands were still trembling.
She looked at her reflection in the rearview mirror and whispered something heartbreaking.
“Lord, am I really that useless?”
Think about that.
A woman who had spent the day trying to earn a living was now asking God whether she had any worth.
Not because God had rejected her.
But because someone claiming to represent Him had treated her as though she were disposable.
And somewhere else, her employer was preparing another inspirational Christian post.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
Perhaps you've worked for someone who spoke beautifully about God but treated people cruelly when no one important was watching.
Perhaps you were the employee who cried in the restroom, wiped your face, and returned to work because your family needed the paycheck.
Or perhaps you are reading this with an uncomfortable realization.
You have never been that employee.
You have been the employer.
The supervisor.
The manager.
The parent.
The ministry leader.
The person whose words carried enough authority to make someone afraid.
And you have called your behavior “discipline,” “high standards,” or “leadership,” when deep down you knew some of it was anger, pride, impatience, or the need to control.
If that possibility makes you uncomfortable, don't run from it.
Sometimes conviction is the beginning of mercy.
Because Scripture has something to say about the distance between a person's religious reputation and the way they treat people.
And it is far more serious than most of us realize.
In Colossians 4:1, the apostle Paul writes:
The original Greek contains the expression:
τὸ δίκαιον καὶ τὴν ἰσότητα
to dikaion kai tēn isotēta
Meaning, in context, what is just and fair.
Paul was addressing masters and enslaved people within the social world of the Roman Empire. We should not pretend that ancient slavery was identical to modern employment. It was not.
But the moral force of Paul's command remains unmistakable.
People who possess authority are accountable to the Lord for how they exercise it.
Power does not cancel justice.
Position does not excuse cruelty.
And claiming to serve God does not give anyone permission to mistreat those under their authority.
Notice something else.
Paul does not merely tell those with power to be religious.
He commands them to practice justice and fairness.
Then he reminds them that they, too, have a Master.
A heavenly Master.
Someone whose authority is infinitely greater than theirs.
Imagine how differently a workplace would operate if every Christian employer remembered that the people beneath their organizational authority are never beneath their human dignity.
Imagine a supervisor pausing before shouting because he remembers that Christ hears his words.
Imagine a business owner examining wages, workloads, and working conditions because he understands that profitability does not erase accountability.
Imagine a manager realizing that the employee standing nervously in front of his desk is someone made in the image of God.
Because that is exactly what Scripture teaches.
Genesis 1:27 declares that God created humanity in His image.
In Hebrew, the expression is:
בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים
b'tselem Elohim
“In the image of God.”
That truth does not disappear when someone puts on a uniform.
It does not disappear when someone earns minimum wage.
It does not disappear when someone makes a mistake.
It does not disappear because an employer pays their salary.
A person's dignity is not a benefit granted by a company.
It is rooted in the God who created them.
And when we forget that, something spiritually dangerous begins happening.
We start treating people as instruments of our ambitions instead of neighbors we are commanded to love.
We begin measuring their worth by productivity.
We demand patience when we make mistakes but offer little mercy when they do.
We expect loyalty without practicing fairness.
We call ourselves blessed while the people helping us build our success quietly suffer.
And then we wonder why the world sometimes struggles to believe our testimony.
But Jesus already warned us about this kind of contradiction.
In Matthew 23:27, He rebuked religious leaders who appeared righteous outwardly while concealing corruption within.
He compared them to whitewashed tombs.
Beautiful on the outside.
But inwardly filled with death and uncleanness.
Those words were spoken in a particular confrontation with religious hypocrisy. They were not a blanket condemnation of every religious leader.
Still, the warning reaches into every generation.
Because religious appearances can become dangerously convincing.
A person can learn the vocabulary of holiness without surrendering the habits of pride.
A person can give money publicly while withholding compassion privately.
A person can defend biblical truth in an argument while refusing to practice biblical love in a relationship.
A person can know exactly when to say “Praise the Lord” and still refuse to say “I was wrong.”
And that last sentence may expose more than we want to admit.
Because repentance is not proven by how passionately we condemn the sins of other people.
It is revealed in what we do when God confronts our own.
James 3:9–10 describes the contradiction of using the tongue to bless God while cursing human beings made in God's likeness.
James concludes:
“My brethren, these things ought not so to be.” (KJV)
Not “these things are understandable because leadership is stressful.”
Not “these things are acceptable because the business is profitable.”
Not “these things are excusable because the person is generous at church.”
They ought not so to be.
That is the uncomfortable clarity of Scripture.
And perhaps the most devastating detail in our story is this:
The employees were not asking their employer to become perfect.
They were asking him to become humane.
They wanted correction without humiliation.
Accountability without intimidation.
Expectations without constant fear.
A workplace where honesty was not punished and exhaustion was not mistaken for laziness.
Some wanted fair compensation.
Others wanted reasonable workloads.
Some simply wanted to be spoken to with dignity.
And several had stopped believing that bringing their concerns forward would change anything.
Then one day, an employee finally spoke.
Not loudly.
Not disrespectfully.
Just honestly.
“Sir, you always tell us you're a man of God. But sometimes we're afraid to come to work because of how you treat us.”
The room became quiet.
And for the first time, the employer had to face a question his success had helped him avoid.
What if the people who worked closest to him were seeing something his church friends never saw?
What if his employees knew his temper better than his congregation knew his testimony?
What if the people he paid were suffering under behavior that contradicted the Lord he praised?
He could have defended himself.
He could have reminded them that he owned the business.
He could have listed everything he had done for them.
He could have accused them of being ungrateful.
He could have reached for a Bible verse about obedience while ignoring the verses about his own responsibilities.
And that is where this story becomes about more than one employer.
Because every one of us eventually encounters a moment when the truth threatens the version of ourselves we prefer to believe.
The question is not whether we have ever failed.
Romans 3:23 tells us that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
The question is what we do when our failure is exposed.
Do we become defensive?
Do we punish the messenger?
Do we hide behind religious language?
Or do we allow the truth to lead us toward repentance?
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It speaks of a change of mind or heart, a reorientation that, in biblical repentance, bears fruit in changed conduct.
It is not simply embarrassment because someone discovered what we did.
It is not regret because our reputation suffered.
And it is certainly not an emotional apology designed to end an uncomfortable conversation.
Biblical repentance turns away from sin and toward God.
It takes responsibility.
It seeks to repair what can be repaired.
And it stops demanding that wounded people pretend the wounds never happened.
That distinction matters.
Because an employer can apologize on Friday and resume humiliating employees on Monday.
A pastor can preach about humility and still refuse correction.
A husband can ask forgiveness without abandoning controlling behavior.
A Christian can cry during worship without allowing the Holy Spirit to change how they treat their family.
Tears can accompany repentance.
But tears alone do not prove it.
John the Baptist said in Luke 3:8:
“Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance.” (KJV)
And when people asked him what that meant, his answers became remarkably practical.
Share with those in need.
Do not collect more than you are authorized to collect.
Do not extort.
Be content with your wages.
In other words, repentance was never intended to remain an invisible religious feeling.
It was meant to change how people lived.
How they handled money.
How they exercised authority.
How they treated their neighbors.
How they behaved when personal advantage tempted them to do wrong.
And if that was true in the days of John the Baptist, why would it be less true in a modern workplace?
Consider another passage.
James 5:4 says:

“Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
κυρίου σαβαώθ
kyriou sabaōth
“Lord of hosts.”
The title invokes God's sovereign power, drawing on the Hebrew יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH tseva'ot), often rendered “LORD of hosts.”
James was specifically condemning wealthy oppressors who fraudulently withheld wages from laborers.
That context matters.
We should not use the passage to claim that every disagreement over compensation is automatically wage theft.
But where wages are deliberately withheld through fraud, Scripture does not treat the matter as a minor business inconvenience.
It declares that the cries of exploited workers reach the Lord of hosts.
Think about that.
The employee whose wages were withheld may have no influence.
The worker who fears retaliation may have no powerful connections.
The laborer who cannot afford legal representation may feel completely invisible.
But Scripture refuses to call that person invisible to God.
The Lord hears.
And the same God who hears prayers offered in beautiful sanctuaries also hears the cries of people suffering injustice.
That should comfort the oppressed.
And sober anyone entrusted with authority.
But now we must go deeper.
Because the Gospel is not merely a warning against becoming a cruel employer.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners and transform human hearts.
Including hearts corrupted by pride.
Including hearts hardened by success.
Including hearts that have used religion as a shield against accountability.
Including yours.
Including mine.
And this is where the story changes.
Because if all we do is expose hypocrisy, we may leave people feeling condemned without showing them the Savior.
And Jesus did not come merely to expose the darkness.
He came as the Light of the world.
In Luke 19, we meet Zacchaeus.
A wealthy chief tax collector.
A man associated with a system in which tax collectors could exploit others for personal gain.
He was not presented as someone whose social standing automatically proved righteousness.
Yet Jesus stopped beneath the tree where Zacchaeus had climbed and called him by name.
Jesus entered his home.
And grace began confronting the life he had been living.
Then something remarkable happened.
Zacchaeus declared:
“Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.” (Luke 19:8, KJV)
Do not miss the beauty of that moment.
He did not simply announce that he had become more religious.
He did not ask the crowd to forget his past because he had met Jesus.
He did not use grace as permission to keep whatever he had unjustly gained.
His response included generosity and restitution.
He was willing to confront the financial consequences of wrongdoing.
And Jesus declared that salvation had come to his house.
Then came one of the most beautiful statements in all of Scripture:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” (Luke 19:10, KJV)
There it is.
The heart of the Gospel.
Jesus seeks the lost.
Not merely the respectable.
Not merely the publicly admired.
Not merely the people whose reputations remain spotless.
He seeks sinners.
And when His saving grace takes hold of a life, it does not teach us to celebrate the sins from which He came to redeem us.
It teaches us to turn from them.
Zacchaeus did not purchase salvation through restitution.
His response demonstrated the transforming power of grace.
That distinction is essential.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
Yet the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not a transaction in which we earn God's acceptance by becoming morally impressive.
Grace is God's undeserved favor in Christ, bringing forgiveness and new life that produces the fruit of obedience.
So what would repentance look like for the employer in our story?
Perhaps it would begin with a sentence he had never learned to say sincerely.
“I have sinned against God in how I treated you.”
No excuses.
No “I'm sorry if you were offended.”
No blaming stress, business pressure, or difficult personalities.
Just responsibility.
Perhaps he would invite employees to speak without fear of punishment.
Perhaps he would discover that some had endured far more than he realized.
Perhaps he would have to repay withheld wages, correct unfair practices, establish meaningful protections against retaliation, or seek independent accountability.
Perhaps some employees would decide to leave anyway.
And he would have to accept that.
Because repentance does not entitle us to immediate forgiveness from those we have wounded.
Nor does forgiveness automatically restore trust.
Trust may require time, consistent conduct, and accountability.
And some relationships cannot safely return to what they were.
That does not mean grace has failed.
It means grace is not the same as pretending harm never happened.
Sometimes the most honest evidence of repentance is accepting consequences without resentment.
Sometimes it is listening without defending yourself.
Sometimes it is making restitution even when nobody is watching.
Sometimes it is stepping away from authority until you have demonstrated that you can exercise it responsibly.
And sometimes it is finally understanding that the people you hurt were never obstacles to your success.
They were human beings you were commanded to love.

Jesus said in Mark 10:43–45 that greatness among His followers must be expressed through service, pointing to His own mission as the Son of Man who came not to be served but to serve and give His life as a ransom for many.
The cross overturns our worldly understanding of power.
The King of kings did not come demanding that suffering humanity make Him comfortable.
He humbled Himself.
He served.
He gave Himself.
He bore sin.
And through His death and resurrection, He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
That is the Lord Christian leaders claim to follow.
Not a Savior who used authority to crush the vulnerable.
But the Savior who laid down His life.
Now imagine the employer standing at the foot of that cross.
Not holding his business awards.
Not displaying his donation receipts.
Not rehearsing his religious accomplishments.
Just standing there.
A sinner in need of mercy.
The same mercy his employees needed him to show.
And imagine finally understanding that the greatest testimony he could offer was not another carefully written Christian caption.
It was a changed life.
A gentler answer.
A fairer workplace.
An honest apology.
A corrected injustice.
A willingness to serve.
A heart no longer desperate to be admired.
Because Jesus does not merely improve our public image.
He makes us new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
This does not promise instant moral perfection.
Christians continue to battle sin and need ongoing repentance.
But it does proclaim the reality of new life in Christ.
And new life must eventually touch the places where our old ways have caused pain.
For the employer, that includes the office.
For the pastor, the congregation.
For the parent, the home.
For the spouse, the marriage.
For the Christian business owner, the people who help keep the business alive.
And for every believer, the people who encounter us when there is no audience to impress.
Maybe you are reading this as someone who has been hurt by a person claiming to be godly.
Please hear this carefully.
Their cruelty does not define Jesus.
Their hypocrisy does not invalidate the Gospel.
And their misuse of Scripture does not mean God approves of what happened to you.
You are not required to remain in an abusive workplace to prove your faith.
You are not disobeying Christ by documenting mistreatment, seeking appropriate help, reporting unlawful conduct, or establishing necessary boundaries.
Forgiveness is not permission for someone to keep harming you.
And Christian humility does not require surrendering your God-given dignity.
The Jesus who calls sinners to repentance is also the Jesus who cares for the wounded.
He sees what others overlook.
He knows the prayers you whispered after difficult days.
He knows how hard it was to keep showing up when you felt small.
And though healing may take time, His grace is not beyond your reach.
But perhaps you are on the other side of this story.
Perhaps you have been the one whose words wounded people.
Perhaps you recognize the impatience, the pride, the need to dominate, the tendency to excuse harshness because you carry responsibility.
Then hear the invitation of Christ.
You do not have to keep hiding behind the image of a good Christian.
You can confess your sin.
You can turn away from it.
You can seek forgiveness from God through Jesus Christ.
You can take responsibility for the people you have harmed.
You can begin making things right.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
His sacrifice is greater than the shame you have been hiding.
His mercy is greater than your carefully protected reputation.
And His transforming grace is powerful enough to confront the habits you thought would never change.
But do not confuse being forgiven with being excused from obedience.
If you have wronged someone, do what is right.
If you have withheld what belongs to them, restore it.
If you have used your position to intimidate, stop.
If you have cultivated a workplace of fear, begin the difficult work of changing it.
If you have spoken about Christ while refusing to resemble His humility, repent.
Not to earn salvation.
But because the Savior who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
And if you're wondering whether this message is meant for you, consider one final question.
If the people who experience you at your worst were asked what kind of Christian you are, would their answer resemble the testimony you give about yourself?
That question is not meant to destroy you.
It is meant to invite honest examination before God.
Because sometimes the most important testimony is not the one we give with a microphone.
It is the one other people experience through our conduct.
The employee who is corrected with patience.
The cleaner greeted with respect.
The struggling worker treated with compassion.
The person who receives the wages they are owed.
The exhausted mother who is allowed to speak without being humiliated.
The colleague whose dignity is protected even when they make a mistake.
These things may never go viral.
They may never earn applause.
They may never appear in a church testimony video.
But they matter to God.
And when we fail, the answer is not to abandon the name of Jesus.
It is to return to Jesus in repentance and faith.
Because Christianity is not a performance for people who have mastered the appearance of holiness.
It is a life of following the crucified and risen Savior who calls sinners out of darkness into His marvelous light.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people who merely know how to sound Christian.
But to keep pointing hearts toward Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, discipleship, and genuine transformation through Jesus Christ.
If this story reminded you of something you have endured, or something you need to change, you do not have to pretend it did not touch you.
You do not need to explain your private pain publicly.
But you are welcome to share your testimony or a lesson God has been teaching you. Your words may encourage someone who has been suffering in silence.
Not to embarrass or accuse a particular person.
But because someone in your circle may need the courage to seek help, the humility to repent, or the reminder that Jesus has not abandoned them.
These resources are intended to help believers become more rooted in Scripture, more discerning in faith, and more faithful in everyday life.
And if this ministry has been spiritually helpful to you, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Not because paying a ministry earns forgiveness, salvation, favor, or spiritual blessing.
And not because you are obligated to give money to prove you love Jesus.
You are not.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ.
But Scripture does encourage voluntary, cheerful generosity in support of faithful ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
But the deeper invitation is not about merchandise.
It is about participating in the work of putting Christ-centered truth before people who desperately need it.
Some are struggling to pray.
Some have been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Some are drifting from their faith.
Some have never understood the Gospel clearly.
Some are outwardly successful but inwardly exhausted.
And some are one honest encounter with Scripture away from beginning a life-changing journey of repentance and faith.
We cannot manufacture conversion.
Only God can change the heart.
But we can faithfully proclaim His Word, make biblical resources accessible, and encourage one another to keep following Jesus.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your faithfulness to Jesus matters.
The Gospel is not for sale.
So before you close this article, return to that employee sitting alone in her car.
Remember her trembling hands.
Remember the question she whispered.
“Lord, am I really that useless?”
Now imagine what could have happened if her employer had understood the Gospel not merely as something to proclaim, but as truth that should transform the way he exercised authority.
Perhaps he would have corrected her mistake without crushing her spirit.
Perhaps he would have recognized the burdens she was carrying.
Perhaps he would have remembered that the woman sitting across from him was made in God's image.
Perhaps he would have spoken to her the way he hoped his own family would be treated.
And perhaps she would have driven home that evening without wondering whether she mattered.
That is not a small thing.
Because the way we treat people can leave wounds that outlast our words.
And the way we follow Christ can become a living witness to the grace we proclaim.
The employer in this story began with a reputation for being a man of God.
But the question that mattered was whether he would allow God to change the man behind the reputation.
That question belongs to all of us.
We can protect the image.
Or we can surrender the heart.
We can keep defending the old life.
Or we can follow the Savior who makes all things new.
And when we fail, we can come back to the cross, where the holiness of God confronts our sin and the mercy of God meets repentant sinners through Jesus Christ.
Because no amount of religious applause can replace genuine obedience.
And no scandal is beyond the redeeming power of Christ when a sinner truly turns to Him.
The people you wounded may never remember your favorite Bible verse, but they will remember whether your life gave them a reason to believe you took Jesus seriously.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE DIDN’T HAVE THE PULPIT. BUT SHE KNEW THE TRUTH HE WAS MISSING.
paragraphs: SHE DIDN’T HAVE THE PULPIT. BUT SHE KNEW THE TRUTH HE WAS MISSING.

The untold power of Priscilla, the woman who helped a gifted preacher understand the way of God more accurately—and why her story still confronts every Christian who thinks knowing Scripture is the same as knowing Christ.
He could preach.

He could reason from the Scriptures. He could hold the attention of a room. He had the education, the eloquence, the confidence, and the kind of passion that made people stop what they were doing and listen.
There was just one problem.
He didn't know everything he needed to know.
And somewhere in the congregation sat a woman who recognized what was missing.
She could have embarrassed him.
She could have publicly challenged him, made an example of his incomplete understanding, or quietly dismissed him as another confident religious voice who needed correcting.
But she didn't.
Instead, she and her husband did something so beautiful, so humble, and so spiritually mature that the Holy Spirit preserved it in Scripture for generations to read.
They took him aside.
And they explained the way of God more accurately.
Her name was Priscilla.

And if you have ever felt that your contribution to God's kingdom was too small, your voice too ordinary, your past too complicated, or your place too insignificant to matter, you need to understand what happened in Acts 18.
Because this story is not simply about a woman who knew her Bible.
It is about what happens when truth meets humility, when knowledge becomes discipleship, and when God uses people who are more interested in building His kingdom than building their own reputation.
But there is something else here.
Something uncomfortable.
Something that might expose the difference between the Christianity we display and the Christianity we actually live.
And it begins with a man named Apollos.
Acts 18:24–25 introduces him as a Jewish man from Alexandria who arrived in Ephesus. He was eloquent, competent in the Scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord, and fervent in spirit.
He spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus.
Read that carefully.
Accurately.
Luke does not describe Apollos as a fraud, an enemy of Christ, or a man deliberately deceiving people.
He was sincere. He was knowledgeable. He was passionate. He had received genuine instruction.
But his understanding was incomplete.
Acts 18:25 says he knew only the baptism of John.
John the Baptist had preached repentance and prepared Israel for the coming Messiah. His baptism pointed people toward the One who was coming after him.
But the Christian proclamation could not stop at preparation.
Jesus Christ had come.
He had been crucified for sins. He had risen from the dead. He had been exalted as Lord. And the promised Holy Spirit had been poured out upon His people.
Luke does not tell us precisely which details Apollos had yet to understand. We must not pretend to know what Scripture does not reveal.
What we do know is that Apollos needed a fuller explanation of God's way.
And God placed Priscilla and Aquila in his path.
Not to destroy him.
To help him grow.
That distinction matters more than many of us realize.
Because somewhere along the way, some Christians began confusing correction with humiliation.
We learned how to win arguments but forgot how to restore people.
We learned how to identify theological mistakes but sometimes neglected the gentleness required to help someone understand the truth.
We became skilled at exposing what others did not know while becoming strangely resistant to anyone exposing what we ourselves still needed to learn.
And then we encounter Priscilla.
A woman whose quiet act of discipleship asks every one of us a question:
Do you love the truth enough to receive correction—and do you love people enough to correct them without crushing them?
Before we go further, we need to know who this woman actually was.
Priscilla, also called Prisca, was a Jewish Christian woman married to Aquila, a Jewish man originally from Pontus.

Acts 18:2–3 tells us that Aquila and Priscilla had come from Italy after Emperor Claudius ordered Jews to leave Rome. Paul encountered them in Corinth and stayed and worked with them because they shared the same trade: tentmaking.
Imagine that for a moment.
A husband and wife uprooted from their home.
Their ordinary life interrupted by an imperial decree.
The uncertainty of relocation. The need to rebuild. The exhausting work of making a living somewhere else.
Scripture does not tell us everything they felt, what they lost, or how they processed that disruption.
But it tells us enough to see that their story included displacement and a new beginning.
And in Corinth, their path crossed with the apostle Paul.
What looked like an unwanted relocation became part of a remarkable story of Christian fellowship and ministry.
That does not mean every painful displacement is secretly a blessing in disguise, or that God approves of the injustice that causes suffering.
It means that suffering does not place a person beyond God's ability to work.
Some of you know what it feels like to have your plans overturned.
You worked for stability, and everything changed.
You prayed for one door to open, and instead another closed.
You thought your life was finally becoming predictable, and suddenly you were rebuilding from the beginning.
Priscilla's story does not promise that every disruption will end in visible success.
It reminds us that a changed address does not cancel our calling to faithfulness.
You can lose your familiar surroundings without losing your place in God's purposes.
And Priscilla did not need a public platform to become useful in those purposes.
She worked.
She traveled.
She served alongside her husband.
She participated in the life and mission of the early church.
And when the moment came to help Apollos, she was ready.
Acts 18:26 records the encounter.
In the Greek text, the crucial phrase reads:
ἀκριβέστερον αὐτῷ ἐξέθεντο τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ θεοῦ
akribesteron autō exethento tēn hodon tou theou
A faithful translation is:
“They explained to him the way of God more accurately.”
That word, ἀκριβέστερον (akribesteron), is the comparative form of a word expressing accuracy or precision.
More accurately.
Not more aggressively.
Not more dramatically.
Not more impressively.
More accurately.
The Greek verb ἐξέθεντο (exethento) communicates the act of explaining or setting something forth.
And notice the plural verb.
They explained.
Priscilla and Aquila.
Together.
Luke explicitly includes both husband and wife in this work of helping Apollos understand God's way.
The text does not tell us exactly which words Priscilla spoke or how much of the explanation came from either spouse. It would be dishonest to invent a conversation that Scripture does not record.
But it would be equally dishonest to erase her participation.
She was there.
She was named.
She helped explain.
And the Holy Spirit, who inspired Scripture, did not consider her contribution unworthy of remembrance.
There is another detail that deserves attention.
Luke names her before Aquila in Acts 18:26.
In several other passages, including Romans 16:3 and 2 Timothy 4:19, her name also appears first.

Scholars have suggested several possible reasons for this ordering, including her prominence or recognized contribution to ministry. But the text does not explicitly explain why her name sometimes comes first.
We should not build more upon the order than Scripture allows.
What we can say with confidence is that Priscilla was a respected Christian coworker who actively participated in teaching Apollos.
And that alone should make us think.
How many people have we overlooked because they did not look like our idea of a significant servant of God?
How many faithful believers have served quietly while everyone watched the person holding the microphone?
How many men and women have strengthened churches through hospitality, patient instruction, prayer, encouragement, generosity, and years of unseen sacrifice?
Not everyone is called to the same role.
Christians also differ in how they understand the relationship between this passage and other New Testament teachings about church leadership and teaching authority.
But those discussions must not obscure what Acts 18 plainly says.
Priscilla, alongside Aquila, helped a gifted man understand God's way more accurately.
Her contribution mattered.
And the way she made that contribution is just as important as the fact that she made it.
Acts 18:26 says Apollos began to speak boldly in the synagogue.
Priscilla and Aquila heard him.
Then they took him aside.
The Greek expression προσελάβοντο αὐτόν (proselabonto auton) conveys taking him to themselves or receiving him into their company.
Luke does not describe a public confrontation or a spectacle.
He describes a personal encounter.
Think about how different that is from the culture many of us have learned to accept.
Someone says something incomplete.
Someone else notices.
Within minutes, the disagreement becomes a performance.
Screenshots.
Accusations.
Mockery.
An audience gathering to watch someone be dismantled.
And somehow we convince ourselves that because we are defending truth, every method we use must be justified.
But biblical truth never gives us permission to abandon biblical love.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Galatians 6:1 teaches that those who are spiritual should restore someone caught in transgression with a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves.
And 2 Timothy 2:24–25 describes the Lord's servant as someone who must not be quarrelsome, but kind, able to teach, and patient, correcting opponents with gentleness.
These passages do not forbid necessary public correction. Scripture itself sometimes requires public rebuke, especially when public wrongdoing or harmful teaching demands it.
But Acts 18 shows us something precious.
A situation where personal instruction served the truth without making humiliation the goal.
Priscilla and Aquila did not need to make Apollos look small in order to make God's truth clear.
And there is a second lesson here that may be even harder to receive.
Apollos listened.
At least, the narrative presents him continuing in ministry after their instruction, without describing resistance or rejection.
Imagine his position.
He was educated.
He was eloquent.
He knew the Scriptures.
He was already speaking boldly in the synagogue.
And then two fellow believers took him aside to explain what he had not yet fully understood.
He could have treated the conversation as an insult.
He could have allowed pride to protect his ignorance.
He could have insisted that his knowledge was sufficient because his ministry was already attracting attention.
But the story moves forward with Apollos continuing to serve.
Acts 18:27–28 tells us that when he wished to go to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him.
When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed.
He powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
Do you see the beauty?
The man who needed further instruction became a great help to others.
The correction did not end his usefulness.
It became part of the story of his continued service.
And this is where the passage stops being a distant account of first-century Christians and begins speaking directly to us.
Because there is an Apollos in many of us.
We know enough Scripture to sound convincing.
We have been Christians long enough to recognize familiar verses.
We can explain doctrines, debate interpretations, and identify errors in other people's beliefs.
But can we still be taught?
Can we admit when our understanding is incomplete?
Can we receive correction from someone we did not expect God to use?
Can we say, without defensiveness, “I need to study that more carefully”?
Or have we become so attached to appearing spiritually mature that we are afraid to admit we are still growing?
There is a dangerous kind of pride that hides behind biblical knowledge.
It does not always look arrogant.
Sometimes it looks like certainty that refuses examination.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to apologize because we believe our intentions were good.
Sometimes it looks like quoting Scripture to silence someone whose correction we do not want to hear.
And sometimes it looks like knowing the language of grace while treating other people with contempt.
That is not the maturity Christ calls us to.
First Corinthians 8:1 warns that knowledge can puff up, while love builds up.
Knowledge matters. Doctrine matters. Accuracy matters.
Priscilla and Aquila did not dismiss Apollos's incomplete understanding as unimportant.
They helped him understand more accurately precisely because the truth mattered.
But truth was not a trophy to display.
It was a gift to steward faithfully.
And Apollos was not an enemy to defeat.
He was a fellow servant to strengthen.
The goal of Christian correction is not to prove that we are superior. It is to serve the truth of Christ and the good of His people.
Perhaps you are reading this while remembering a time someone corrected you.
Maybe they were right, but the way they spoke wounded you.
Maybe they embarrassed you in front of people you respected.
Maybe you stopped asking questions because you were afraid of being made to feel foolish.
If that happened, the wound deserves to be acknowledged.
But do not allow someone's unkindness to convince you that growing in biblical understanding is dangerous.
The answer to harsh correction is not refusing all correction.
The answer is learning to recognize truth, receive it humbly, and practice it with love.
Or perhaps you are remembering someone you corrected.
A child.
A spouse.
A fellow believer.
A new Christian who was still learning.
You knew the answer.
But now, remembering the conversation, you realize that your words may have communicated superiority more than love.
You wanted them to recognize the truth.
But did you help them recognize the heart of Christ?
That question is worth sitting with.
Because we can be factually correct and relationally careless.
We can defend a biblical position while failing to display the patience Scripture commands.
And we can become so focused on exposing error that we forget the person standing in front of us is someone God calls us to love.
Priscilla's example invites us to something better.
Not compromise.
Not silence.
Not pretending that every interpretation is equally faithful to Scripture.
But courage joined with gentleness.
Conviction joined with humility.
Accuracy joined with love.
And all of it submitted to Jesus Christ.
There is one more detail about Priscilla that makes her story even richer.
Her service did not end with Apollos.
In Romans 16:3–4, Paul calls Prisca and Aquila his fellow workers in Christ Jesus and says they risked their necks for his life.
He expresses gratitude to them, adding that the churches of the Gentiles also give thanks.
The exact circumstances of that danger are not recorded.
We cannot responsibly invent a dramatic rescue scene or claim to know how they risked their lives.
But Paul's words are unmistakable.
Their commitment to Christ and His people had cost them something.
And in Romans 16:5, Paul also greets the church meeting in their house.
First Corinthians 16:19 likewise refers to Aquila and Prisca and the church in their house.
Their home was not merely a private refuge from the world.
It became a place where believers gathered.
Think about that.
The same couple who shared ordinary work with Paul also opened their home for Christian fellowship and helped instruct a gifted teacher.
They served through labor, hospitality, instruction, partnership, and costly faithfulness.
Their ministry was not confined to a single moment.
It was woven into the ordinary fabric of their lives.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You may never preach before thousands.
You may never write a bestselling Christian book.
You may never have a public ministry, a recognizable name, or an audience applauding your faithfulness.
But you can open your home.
You can explain a passage of Scripture to someone who is confused.
You can encourage a believer who is ready to give up.
You can teach your children the Gospel.
You can help a friend recognize a misunderstanding.
You can pray with someone who has run out of words.
You can support faithful Christian work without needing public recognition.
You can remain steady when no one is watching.
And none of that is insignificant simply because it is unseen.
Jesus taught in Matthew 6 that our Father sees what is done in secret.
That does not mean every private act of service will produce visible success.
It means our faithfulness is not measured by public attention.
And the story of Priscilla reminds us that a quiet act of instruction can have consequences beyond what the people involved could have imagined.
Yet we must be careful about where we place the glory.
Priscilla was not the Savior.
Aquila was not the Savior.
Apollos was not the Savior.
Paul was not the Savior.
Jesus Christ was—and is—the Savior.
That is the center of this story.
The way of God that Apollos needed to understand more accurately ultimately leads us to the person and work of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not merely a call to become more educated, more eloquent, or more morally impressive.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, died for our sins and was raised from the dead.
As Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.
That is not a minor detail in Christian teaching.
It is the heart of the message.
And if we speak beautifully about faith while neglecting the crucified and risen Christ, our message has lost its center.
If we teach repentance without pointing people to the grace of Christ, we leave them staring at their guilt without showing them the Savior.
If we speak about grace while refusing Christ's call to repentance, we distort the very grace we claim to celebrate.
