The Bible does not give us access to all of them.
But his words and actions reveal something extraordinary.
He chose to use his authority to sustain the very family that had once rejected him.
He provided for his brothers.
He sent for his father.
He made arrangements for them to live in Egypt during the remaining years of famine.
The story that began with a brother being separated from his family moved toward a family being preserved through the brother they had rejected.
And that is where the account begins pointing our eyes beyond Joseph.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Not because Joseph and Jesus are identical.
They are not.
Joseph was a sinful human being in need of God's grace, just like every other descendant of Adam.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Son of God.
Joseph's suffering was not the atoning sacrifice that saves humanity.
Christ's death and resurrection stand uniquely at the center of our salvation.
Yet Joseph's story belongs to the larger biblical account of God's faithfulness to His covenant promises, ultimately fulfilled in Christ.
Through the preservation of Jacob's family, God preserved the family line through which the Messiah would come.
And there is a meaningful resemblance in the way a rejected one becomes an instrument of deliverance.
Joseph's brothers rejected him.
Jesus was rejected by many of His own people.
Joseph was humbled and later exalted to a position through which lives were preserved.
Jesus humbled Himself, even to death on a cross, and God highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:5–11).
Joseph offered food during a famine.
Jesus declared Himself the Bread of Life (John 6:35).
Joseph could provide temporary preservation from starvation.
Jesus gives eternal life to those who believe in Him.
And while Joseph's story shows a brother forgiving those who betrayed him, the Gospel reveals something even greater.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Jesus did not wait for humanity to become worthy before demonstrating His love.
He came into a world ruined by sin.
He bore the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Think about that.
Joseph's brothers stood before the one they had wronged, terrified of what he might do.
And every one of us must face the reality that we have sinned before a holy God.
We have loved things more than Him.
We have hidden what should have been confessed.
We have justified attitudes that His Word condemns.
We have wounded others.
We have sometimes called our pride strength and our bitterness wisdom.
Yet the Gospel is not that God overlooks sin.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ has dealt with sin through His sacrificial death and victorious resurrection, so that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
The Greek New Testament uses the word χάρις (charis) for grace.
Grace is not permission to continue in rebellion.
It is God's undeserved favor, freely given, that saves us and teaches us to live differently.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
And verse 10 reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave a surrendered life untouched.
It changes what we love.
It changes how we respond.
It changes how we treat people who cannot repay us.
It teaches us to tell the truth.
To confess.
To forgive.
To make restitution where possible.
To establish wise boundaries where necessary.
To love without pretending that evil is harmless.
And sometimes, by God's mercy, it makes possible a reconciliation we once thought could never happen.
But not every relationship will end like Joseph's.
Some people remain dangerous.
Some refuse responsibility.
Some continue to abuse the trust they have been given.
Forgiveness does not require returning to unsafe circumstances, concealing wrongdoing, or abandoning appropriate protection and accountability.
The command to forgive must never be twisted into a demand that victims expose themselves to further harm.
Joseph's account is not a command to trust every person who says, "I've changed."
It is a testimony to God's providence, the importance of genuine repentance, and the possibility of mercy.
And there is a final detail that makes this story almost unbearably tender.
After Joseph reveals himself, he tells his brothers to bring their father to Egypt.
Then Genesis 45:14–15 says he fell upon Benjamin's neck and wept.
Benjamin wept too.
And Joseph kissed all his brothers and wept over them.
Afterward, his brothers talked with him.
Earlier, they could not answer him.
Now they could speak.
Fear had silenced them.
Mercy had opened the door to conversation.
What a picture.
The brothers who once could not speak peaceably to Joseph (Genesis 37:4) were now speaking with him after his tears and embrace.
The story does not tell us that every memory vanished.
It does not say that the past became painless.
It shows something more believable.
A family once fractured by envy, cruelty, and deception was being brought into a new chapter through truth, responsibility, and mercy.
And perhaps that is what makes this account so unforgettable.
Joseph's greatest moment was not when Pharaoh placed authority in his hands.
It was not when he wore fine linen.
It was not when Egypt bowed before him.
It was the moment when the people who had once made him powerless stood helpless before him, and he chose not to destroy them.
But we must be careful here too.
Joseph's mercy was not the source of his salvation.
God's faithfulness was the foundation of his story.
And every beautiful act of human forgiveness should lead us to marvel at the far greater mercy revealed in Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest scandal is not simply that Joseph's brothers betrayed him.
It is that sinful human beings have rebelled against the God who made them.
And the greatest grace is not simply that Joseph embraced his brothers.
It is that God, through Jesus Christ, opens the way for sinners to be reconciled to Himself.
Not because Jesus erases history.
Not because He promises an easy life.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored on our preferred timetable.
But because through His death and resurrection, sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
The cross tells us how seriously God takes sin.
The empty tomb tells us how completely Christ has conquered death.
And the invitation of the Gospel tells us that no sinner who truly comes to Christ in repentance and faith must remain separated from God's mercy.
So now I want to ask you something personal.
Are you Joseph, still carrying a wound that people around you cannot see?
Are you one of the brothers, haunted by something you have never confessed?
Are you Judah, standing at a moment when you finally have the opportunity to do the opposite of what you once did?
Or are you someone who has spent years trying to convince yourself that the past is too ugly for grace?
Wherever you recognize yourself, don't stop at identifying with the characters.
Look to Christ.
If you have sinned, confess it to God.
If you have harmed someone, take responsibility and seek to make things right where appropriate.
If you have been wounded, bring your pain to the Lord without pretending it was insignificant.
If bitterness has been ruling your heart, ask the Holy Spirit to teach you the freedom of forgiveness.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, hear His call to repent and believe the Gospel.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect testimony before coming to Him.
You need the Savior.
And if this story has exposed something in your heart, don't rush away from that conviction.
Sit with it.
Pray about it.
Open Genesis 42–45 for yourself.
Let Scripture speak more deeply than any article ever could.
Maybe your prayer today is as simple as:

"Lord Jesus, You know what happened to me, and You know what I have done. Forgive my sins. Heal what is wounded. Expose what I have hidden. Teach me to repent where I have been wrong and to forgive without surrendering wisdom or truth. Help me trust Your faithfulness when I cannot understand my circumstances. Make my life a testimony to Your grace. Amen."
You don't need to share private details or expose anyone else's story. Even a few sincere words can encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
Someone reading may need the courage to believe that change is possible through Christ.
A family member carrying regret.
A friend who has been betrayed.
A believer struggling with forgiveness.
Someone who feels too ashamed to return to God.
Even someone who does not yet believe in Jesus but needs to hear what the Gospel actually says.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen, but because God's Word is worth sharing, and a story of grace may reach someone who would never have searched for it.
We want this community to be more than a place where people read inspiring words.
We want it to be a place where people are continually pointed back to the Bible, challenged to follow Jesus, encouraged to pray, and equipped to grow in their faith.
Every article, every biblical resource, every effort to reach another person with the Gospel is part of work we hope to continue and expand.
And it is never a condition for glorifying God.
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that financial support purchases God's favor.
But a voluntary opportunity to participate in work you believe is bearing good fruit.
These resources are intended to encourage serious biblical study, spiritual growth, and a life increasingly shaped by the truth of God's Word.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
And the value of a believer is never measured by how much money they give.
We simply want to keep pointing people toward Jesus, and we welcome those who freely choose to help us do that.
Because somewhere, there may be a person who is living in the same kind of darkness Joseph once knew.
Somewhere, there may be a brother carrying guilt he has never confessed.
Somewhere, there may be a family that desperately needs truth, repentance, and mercy.
And somewhere, there may be someone who has mistaken the worst thing that ever happened to them for the final chapter of their life.
Joseph's story reminds us that the chapter written by betrayal was not the end.
And the Gospel tells us something infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ has opened the way for sinners to receive forgiveness, new life, and everlasting hope.
The brothers who once rejected Joseph eventually heard him say, "I am Joseph."
And one day, every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10–11).
Do not wait until you have everything figured out before turning to Him.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Him.
And let His grace begin changing the way you live today.
The wound may still be part of your story, but in Christ, it does not have to be the name of your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS MASTURBATION REALLY A SIN—OR HAVE CHRISTIANS BEEN CONDEMNING PEOPLE FOR SOMETHING THE BIBLE NEVER ACTUALLY SAYS?
paragraphs: IS MASTURBATION REALLY A SIN—OR HAVE CHRISTIANS BEEN CONDEMNING PEOPLE FOR SOMETHING THE BIBLE NEVER ACTUALLY SAYS?

What if the sin you've been taught to fear isn't as clearly defined in Scripture as you thought? And what if the real battle isn't simply about what your hands are doing—but what is happening in your heart, your desires, your conscience, and your relationship with Jesus Christ?
There is a prayer some Christians have whispered more times than they can count.
“Lord, forgive me. I did it again.”
Sometimes it comes at two in the morning.
Sometimes after a stressful day. Sometimes after loneliness has settled into the room so heavily that silence feels unbearable.
And sometimes, strangely enough, after doing something they aren't even certain the Bible explicitly forbids.
They bow their heads.
Promise God they'll never do it again.
Feel clean for a little while.
Then the cycle repeats.
Desire. Resistance. Surrender. Shame. Repentance. Another promise.
And somewhere in that exhausting cycle, a terrifying question begins to form.
“Does God still love me?”
But there is another question many Christians are afraid to ask aloud.
“Is masturbation actually a sin according to Scripture, or have we sometimes confused Christian tradition with God's commandments?”
That question deserves more than an angry sermon.
More than an embarrassing conversation.
More than a frightening warning about hell.
It deserves an open Bible, careful interpretation, an honest examination of human sexuality, and the courage to distinguish what God has actually said from what people have assumed He meant.
Because when we call something a sin, we are making a serious claim about God's authority.
And when we declare something permissible, we are also making a serious claim.
Neither should be done carelessly.
Especially when real people are carrying real wounds from what they've been taught.
So before anyone rushes to defend masturbation or condemn everyone who has ever practiced it, there is something we must establish.
The Bible never explicitly names masturbation as a sin.
Read that again.
Not because this automatically makes every instance morally acceptable.
It doesn't.
But because the difference between an explicit biblical prohibition and a moral conclusion drawn from broader biblical principles matters enormously.
And if we love the truth, we must be willing to acknowledge that difference.
Even when it complicates the answers we grew up hearing.
Consider one of the most frequently misunderstood passages in this entire conversation.
Genesis 38 tells the disturbing story of Onan.
Onan was instructed to fulfill his family obligation toward Tamar, his deceased brother's widow, so that his brother's family line could continue.
Instead, he deliberately prevented conception while taking advantage of the sexual relationship.
Scripture says:
“And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also.”
— Genesis 38:10, KJV
For generations, some Christians have used this account to argue that masturbation is condemned by God.
But there is a serious problem with that interpretation.
Onan was not masturbating.
The passage describes intercourse with Tamar and Onan's deliberate refusal to fulfill his obligation to provide offspring for his deceased brother.
His wrongdoing involved selfishness, disobedience, and injustice toward Tamar within the specific family obligations of that time.
The Hebrew expression in Genesis 38:9, וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה (wəšiḥēt ʾarṣāh), describes his wasting or spilling semen on the ground.
But describing that physical action is not the same as establishing a universal prohibition against masturbation.
The context matters.
The person matters.
The injustice matters.
And the reason the action was condemned matters.
We cannot responsibly take a passage about one man's betrayal of his family obligation and turn it into a direct command about an act the passage never addresses.
That is not defending biblical authority.
That is asking Scripture to say more than it actually says.
And Christians should be deeply concerned whenever human assumptions are presented as divine commandments.
Jesus Himself warned against this danger.
In Mark 7:8, He confronted religious leaders who elevated human traditions above God's commandments.
The Greek word παράδοσις (paradosis) means tradition—something handed down.
Not every tradition is wrong.
But a tradition becomes spiritually dangerous when people give it the authority of God's own Word without sufficient biblical justification.
Think about that.
A person can spend years feeling condemned by something their church taught, while never being shown a passage that explicitly establishes the claim.
And that possibility should make every pastor, parent, teacher, and Christian communicator more careful.
But before anyone concludes that masturbation must therefore be morally harmless, we need to confront the other side of the question.
Because the absence of an explicit prohibition is not the same as unconditional moral approval.
The Bible does not give a separate command addressing every conceivable human behavior.
Instead, Scripture also teaches principles about holiness, love, self-control, the body, the conscience, and the direction of our desires.
And those principles matter.
Deeply.
Jesus said something in Matthew 5:28 that forces us to look beneath outward behavior.
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
The Greek phrase πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) expresses looking at someone with lustful intent.
The verb ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō) means to desire or long for something. Its moral meaning depends on context; desire itself is not always sinful.
In Matthew 5, however, Jesus is addressing desire directed toward another person in a way that violates the moral demands of faithfulness.
He is not saying that every experience of sexual arousal is adultery.
He is exposing the reality that sexual wrongdoing can begin in the heart before it becomes an outward act.
That distinction changes the conversation.
Because masturbation and lust are not identical concepts.
They may occur together.
They often do.
But they are not automatically interchangeable.
A person may engage in masturbation while deliberately entertaining fantasies that objectify someone, involve infidelity, or cultivate desires contrary to Christian sexual ethics.
Those accompanying thoughts raise genuine moral concerns under Jesus' teaching.
But does Matthew 5:28 explicitly say that every act of masturbation, under every circumstance, is adultery?
No.
And intellectual honesty requires us to say so.
Otherwise, we risk placing words in Jesus' mouth that He did not speak.
Yet there is something else we cannot ignore.
Pornography.
For many people, masturbation has become closely connected with pornography, and pornography introduces moral issues that go far beyond the physical act.
It can train a person to view human beings primarily as objects of sexual gratification.
It may involve exploitation, coercion, or abuse.
It can encourage secrecy, distorted expectations, and patterns of desire that undermine intimacy and faithfulness.
Not everyone who masturbates uses pornography, and those behaviors should not be treated as identical.
But when pornography is involved, the Christian concern is not merely whether a particular physical movement is forbidden.
It is whether our desires are being shaped by love or by consumption.
Whether we are honoring people as image-bearers of God or reducing them to instruments of pleasure.
Whether our private choices are helping us become more truthful, faithful, and loving.
And sometimes the answer is painful.
Because it is possible to tell ourselves that something is harmless while quietly watching it reshape our character.
Paul wrote:
“All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:12, KJV
The Greek expression οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος (ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos) means, in context, that Paul refuses to be mastered or dominated by anything.
This is especially important because Paul is responding to claims about freedom in a passage that goes on to address sexual immorality and the significance of the body.
He is not explicitly discussing masturbation.
But his principle raises a legitimate question.
Is this something you freely choose, or something that increasingly feels as though it controls you?
Can you walk away from it?
Can you make decisions without feeling compelled?
Has it become your primary escape from loneliness, anxiety, disappointment, or emotional pain?
Are you hiding patterns that are damaging your marriage, responsibilities, or relationships?
Not every repeated behavior is an addiction.
Not every strong sexual desire is evidence of spiritual bondage.
And not every person who struggles with sexual self-control is living in rebellion against God.
But when a behavior becomes compulsive, harmful, or destructive, it deserves attention rather than denial.
Sometimes the deepest issue is not simply sexual desire.
Sometimes it is grief.
Sometimes rejection.
Sometimes the unbearable ache of wanting to be held, wanted, understood, or loved.
And that brings us to something the church has not always handled well.
Shame is not the same thing as repentance.

There are people who have spent years believing that their bodies are disgusting, that ordinary sexual feelings make them spiritually filthy, or that God turns His face away whenever they experience arousal.
Some have even been taught that nocturnal emissions, involuntary bodily responses, or the arrival of sexual thoughts automatically mean they have sinned.
But Scripture makes distinctions that such teachings often overlook.
Leviticus 15:16–18 addresses emissions of semen and the ceremonial washing associated with them under Israel's ritual purity laws.
The Hebrew term טָמֵא (ṭāmēʾ) means ritually unclean.
Ritual uncleanness under the Mosaic law was not automatically equivalent to moral guilt.
The text does not declare that every emission of semen is a sinful act.
Nor does it provide an explicit moral ruling on masturbation.
We must also remember that Christians understand these ceremonial laws in light of Christ and the New Covenant, rather than simply transferring every ritual requirement into Christian moral law.
This is why context is not an academic luxury.
It protects people from misunderstanding God.
Imagine a teenager who wakes up frightened because of an involuntary sexual dream.
Imagine a young believer who has been told that the mere experience of arousal makes them impure.
Imagine someone who desperately wants to follow Jesus but has never been taught the difference between temptation, involuntary experience, deliberate fantasy, and conscious action.
Now imagine telling that person that God is disgusted with them.
Where did Jesus say that?
Where does Scripture teach that an involuntary bodily response is itself a deliberate moral offense?
We must be careful not to manufacture guilt where Scripture has not established it.
Because manufactured guilt can produce real spiritual harm.
It can make people afraid to pray.
Afraid to confess.
Afraid to ask honest questions.
Afraid to believe that grace could still reach them.
And perhaps the saddest consequence is this:
Some people eventually stop running toward God because they have become convinced He is waiting only to condemn them.
But that is not the whole story of the Gospel.
John 3:17 says:
“For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved.”
Jesus did not come to make sin seem harmless.
He came to save sinners.
He did not deny the need for repentance.
He called people to repentance while revealing the mercy of God.
He did not offer cheap reassurance that nothing matters.
He offered redemption powerful enough to transform what matters most.
And there is a difference between the Holy Spirit convicting us of genuine sin and a conscience crushed beneath teachings that may go beyond Scripture.
Paul understood the importance of conscience.
Romans 14:23 teaches that acting against one's conviction of faith can itself become sinful.
The immediate context concerns disputed practices involving food, not masturbation.
We should not pretend otherwise.
Nevertheless, the passage establishes that conscience and faith matter in moral decision-making.
That does not mean every guilty feeling is an infallible message from God.
A conscience can be informed by truth, but it can also be confused, overly burdened, or insufficiently trained.
The goal is neither to silence conscience nor to obey every fear unquestioningly.
The goal is to bring conscience under the light of Scripture, wisdom, prayer, and sincere devotion to Christ.
And this is where sincere Christians sometimes reach different conclusions.
Some believe masturbation is inherently inconsistent with the biblical vision of sexuality because sexual pleasure belongs within the covenantal union of marriage.

Others believe Scripture does not establish that every solitary sexual act is sinful and therefore evaluate it according to lust, self-control, conscience, relational faithfulness, and other biblical principles.
These are real disagreements among Christians who may share a serious commitment to biblical authority.
They should not be dismissed by pretending that one explicit verse settles a question the Bible never directly names.
At the same time, we should not pretend that all Christian traditions have reached the same conclusion.

For example, the Catholic Church explicitly teaches that masturbation is morally wrong, while also recognizing that personal culpability may be affected by factors such as habit, anxiety, or psychological circumstances.
Other Christian communities approach the issue differently.
Understanding these distinctions does not require abandoning conviction.
It requires humility about the difference between direct biblical statements and theological reasoning.
And humility is not weakness.
Sometimes humility is what faithfulness looks like when Scripture has not answered our question in precisely the form we wish it had.
Consider another passage.
“Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:18, KJV
The Greek command is φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν (pheugete tēn porneian).
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The word πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to illicit sexual conduct, with its application understood within biblical sexual ethics.
It is not simply a Greek synonym for masturbation.
We cannot honestly claim that Paul explicitly named masturbation by using this word.
But neither can we ignore his wider teaching about the body.
A few verses later, Paul writes:
— 1 Corinthians 6:20, KJV
There is the deeper question.
Not merely, “How close can I get to the boundary without crossing it?”
But, “How can I honor the Lord with the body He has given me?”
That question is bigger than masturbation.
It reaches into our entertainment, our relationships, our habits, our private thoughts, our treatment of other people, and the things we allow to shape our hearts.
It calls us away from using grace as an excuse for selfishness.
But it also calls us away from using holiness as an excuse for cruelty.
Because Christian holiness is not built on hatred of the human body.
The body is God's creation.
Sexual desire is not automatically sinful.
Marriage and sexual intimacy are treated as good gifts within Scripture.
And the Christian hope is not escape from embodiment but resurrection and redemption through Jesus Christ.
That means the body should neither be worshiped nor despised.
It should be honored.
And honoring it requires wisdom.
There may be someone reading this who needs to confront a pornography habit that has been destroying their relationships.
Someone else may need to recognize that they have been using sexual gratification to numb emotional wounds that need genuine care.
Another person may need to stop condemning themselves for involuntary experiences or for having a body that experiences ordinary desire.
And someone else may need to examine whether their religious guilt is grounded in Scripture or in years of fear-based teaching.
Different people may need different forms of correction, encouragement, and support.
The Gospel is not served by treating all these situations as identical.
And here is a truth that might be difficult for both sides of this debate.
You can be wrong by declaring something sinful without sufficient biblical warrant. And you can also be wrong by defending a behavior without honestly examining its consequences.
Both errors matter.
Both can distort discipleship.
Both can distract us from Jesus.
So what should a Christian actually do?
Bring the question into the light.
Not into a room filled with humiliation.
Into the light of God's Word.
Ask whether lustful fantasy is involved.
Ask whether pornography is involved.
Ask whether the behavior is harming your relationships, integrity, responsibilities, or spiritual life.
Ask whether you are acting against your sincerely held convictions.
Ask whether you are becoming mastered by a habit.
Ask whether fear, loneliness, or emotional pain needs attention.
Ask whether your conclusions come from Scripture itself or from assumptions you have inherited.
And ask whether your response to the issue is making you more loving, honest, self-controlled, and dependent upon Christ.
If your conscience remains troubled, do not force yourself to act against it.
If you recognize genuine sin, repent.
If you recognize compulsive behavior, seek wise and compassionate help.
If you discover that you have carried unnecessary shame, allow Scripture to correct that burden too.
And if you are uncertain, it is permissible to admit that you are still studying, praying, and seeking understanding.
Faith does not require pretending to know what you do not know.
Now consider the words of Romans 8:1:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is not permission to celebrate sin.
It is the announcement that our standing before God rests upon Jesus Christ, not upon our ability to manufacture a flawless record through human effort.
Christians are called to repentance and holiness.
But salvation is not earned through a perfect streak of sexual self-control.
It is received through the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And verse 10 reminds us that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not make transformation unnecessary.
Grace makes genuine transformation possible.
That is why the person who has fallen into pornography can repent and seek restoration.
The person trapped in compulsive behavior can pursue freedom without surrendering to despair.
The person burdened by religious misinformation can rediscover the difference between God's commandments and human traditions.
And the person who has spent years believing that Jesus is disgusted with them can begin to understand that His call to holiness comes from the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
Not from a cruel judge inventing new reasons to reject them.
Think about Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
Not because his body experienced an ordinary desire.
Not because he misunderstood a disputed theological question.
He openly denied knowing the Lord he had promised to follow.
And yet, after the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
In John 21, the risen Christ confronted Peter with love, calling him again into faithful service.
Peter's failure was real.
So was his restoration.
The same Jesus who called Peter back is the Savior Christians are invited to trust today.
That does not mean every struggle is the same as Peter's denial.
It means failure does not have to be the final word for someone who turns to Christ.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this most desperately needs to hear.
You are not saved because you have never struggled.
You are not loved because you have never experienced sexual temptation.
You are not made righteous because you managed to avoid every uncomfortable question about your body.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
His truth.
His power to forgive and transform.
And if there is sin in your life, His grace is not an invitation to hide it.
It is an invitation to bring it into the light.
First John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice what this verse does not require.
It does not require you to invent sins God has not identified.
It does not require you to pretend that genuine sin is harmless.
It calls you to honesty before the God who forgives and cleanses.
That is the balance we desperately need.
Truth without unnecessary condemnation.
Grace without moral compromise.
Conviction without manipulation.
Repentance without hopelessness.
And biblical teaching without pretending that every traditional interpretation is an explicit command from God.
So, is masturbation really a sin?

The most biblically careful answer is that Scripture does not explicitly prohibit masturbation by name, and Christians disagree about whether broader biblical principles prohibit every instance of it.

Certain things associated with it—such as deliberately cultivated lust, pornography, betrayal of relational commitments, or behavior that becomes destructive and controlling—can raise serious moral concerns.
But we should not collapse all these distinct questions into one sweeping declaration that the Bible never explicitly makes.
Nor should we use the Bible's silence on the specific act as an excuse to disregard its wider teaching on sexual holiness.
A faithful answer requires more discernment than a slogan.
And perhaps that is exactly why this conversation matters.
Because somewhere there is a Christian who has been terrified to ask this question.
Someone who has silently wondered whether God hates them.
Someone who has been taught to measure their entire spiritual worth by one private struggle.
Someone who has genuinely sinned and needs repentance.
Someone who has been burdened with guilt that Scripture does not clearly justify.
Someone who needs accountability.
Someone who needs compassion.
Someone who needs sound biblical teaching.
And someone who simply needs to hear that Jesus Christ is greater than the shame they have been carrying.
If that someone is you, please hear this.
You do not have to choose between biblical truth and the mercy of God.
In Jesus Christ, truth and grace meet.
John 1:14 describes Him as “full of grace and truth.”
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And when we separate what Christ holds together, we wound people who desperately need the fullness of His Gospel.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community where people are frightened into religious performance.
Not to tell struggling believers whatever they want to hear.

But to keep opening Scripture, confronting difficult questions, correcting misunderstandings, calling people to repentance where repentance is needed, and pointing wounded hearts back to Jesus Christ.
Because the world does not need more Christians who know how to shame people.
It needs disciples who know how to speak the truth in love.
And the church does not need to become less biblical to become more compassionate.
It needs to become more faithful to the whole counsel of God.
If this article challenged something you have believed for years, don't rush past that discomfort.
Sit with Scripture.
Read the passages in context.
Pray for wisdom.
If you have a testimony of how Jesus helped you move from shame into honest repentance, healing, or deeper biblical understanding, your words may encourage someone who has been suffering in silence.
You do not need to disclose intimate personal experiences to be part of this conversation.
And please, let the comments be a place of humility rather than humiliation.
Someone reading may be a teenager with unanswered questions.
Someone may be a married believer carrying a private struggle.
Someone may be a pastor reconsidering how they have taught this subject.
Someone may not even believe in Jesus yet, but may be discovering that Christianity is more thoughtful, compassionate, and rooted in grace than they imagined.
Treat them with the dignity of people made in God's image.
Not because every reader must agree with every conclusion.
But because honest biblical conversations deserve to reach beyond the walls of our own communities.
You may have a friend who has silently carried unnecessary shame for years.
You may know someone who has used biblical silence to excuse genuinely harmful choices.
You may know a parent, youth leader, pastor, or struggling believer who needs a more careful conversation about this subject.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, curious seekers, and even those who have walked away from church to follow along.
Not every question can be answered in a single article.
But every sincere question deserves to be approached with humility before God.
There is also something deeply practical I want to share with those who believe in this ministry's mission.
Gospel Warrior is working to provide ongoing biblical teaching, encouragement, discipleship, and Christian resources for people who want to grow deeper in their relationship with Jesus Christ.
Those resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, grow in spiritual maturity, strengthen their faith, and keep Christ at the center of their lives.
And maintaining and expanding that kind of ministry takes time, work, and financial support.
It is a voluntary way of supporting the continued creation and sharing of Christ-centered resources.
For those who choose to give from their regular budget for Christian ministry, that support can be an expression of generosity and an offering of thanksgiving to God.
Biblical giving must never be driven by spiritual pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Freely.
Prayerfully.
With joy rather than obligation.
It is the Gospel itself.
And that Gospel must never be sold.
You are still welcome here.
Your value before God has never depended on your ability to pay.
What matters most is that Jesus is proclaimed faithfully, Scripture is handled responsibly, and people are invited into genuine repentance, forgiveness, and transformation.
Because one day, the debates will end.
The arguments about what Christians should or should not have taught will become part of history.
Our hidden struggles will no longer be hidden.
And what will matter eternally is not whether we won an online argument about a disputed question.
It will be whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
Whether we trusted His grace.
Whether we responded to His truth.
Whether we allowed His Word to correct us.
Whether we loved others as people He created.
Whether our lives bore the fruit of genuine faith.
So don't leave this conversation merely asking whether masturbation is sinful.
Leave asking something far more important.
“Lord Jesus, what is true? What in my life needs repentance? What shame have I carried that You never asked me to carry? And how can I honor You with my whole life?”
Then open your Bible.
Seek wise counsel when needed.
Be honest about your desires.
Take genuine sin seriously.
Refuse unnecessary condemnation.
And remember that the Savior who calls you to holiness is also the Savior who gave His life to redeem you.
Because the goal of Christian discipleship has never been to make people terrified of their humanity.
It is to bring redeemed human beings into deeper communion with their Creator through Jesus Christ.
And that is where the real transformation begins.
Not when you learn to hide your struggles more successfully.
Not when you win an argument by making Scripture say more than it says.
Not when you convince yourself that holiness no longer matters.
But when you stand before Jesus with nothing to pretend, nothing to defend dishonestly, and nothing to offer as the price of His mercy.
Only a heart willing to hear His truth.
Only a sinner in need of grace.
Only a life surrendered to the One who makes all things new.
The most dangerous thing about shame is not that it reminds you of your past—it is that it can make you forget the Savior who came to give you a future.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU HAVEN’T HAD SEX IN TEN YEARS. DOES GOD UNDERSTAND YOUR FRUSTRATION?
paragraphs: YOU HAVEN’T HAD SEX IN TEN YEARS. DOES GOD UNDERSTAND YOUR FRUSTRATION?
When Your Body Is Crying for Intimacy, Your Heart Is Tired of Waiting, and Your Faith Is Being Tested in Places Nobody Sees.
Ten years. No sex. No intimacy. No one reaching for you in the middle of the night. And somehow, you're still expected to smile in church and act like nothing inside you is aching.
But what if the battle you're ashamed to talk about is the very place where Jesus wants to meet you?
Read this carefully, because we're going somewhere most churches rarely dare to go.
It's 11:47 at night.
Your phone is beside you. The lights are off. The room is quiet.
And there it is again.
That feeling.
Not just sexual desire.
Something deeper.
The longing to be touched. To be chosen. To have somebody look at you and genuinely want you. To know what it feels like to be held without having to ask.
You turn to the other side of the bed.
Empty.
Again.

Maybe you've been single for ten years. Maybe you're divorced. Maybe you lost your spouse. Maybe you're married, but physical intimacy disappeared so long ago that you feel more like roommates than lovers.
Maybe your situation is even harder to explain.
You love Jesus.
You pray. You read Scripture. You worship on Sundays. You genuinely want to honor God.
But there are nights when your body seems to be fighting against everything your spirit believes.
And sometimes, in the privacy of your own thoughts, you whisper something you would never dare say in a Bible study.
"Lord, how much longer?"
"Do You even understand what this feels like?"
"Am I supposed to pretend I don't have these desires?"
And perhaps the most frightening question of all:
"Does God get disappointed in me simply because I want sex?"
Before we answer that, you need to hear something that may change the way you see this entire struggle.
Your desire for intimacy does not automatically mean your heart is sinful.
And your frustration does not make you a failure as a Christian.
But what you choose to do with that frustration matters deeply.
Because the God who created your body is also the God who calls you to holiness.
And He is not confused about either one.
In Genesis 2:18, before sin entered the world, God declared:
"It is not good that the man should be alone." (KJV)
Notice something extraordinary.
God said this before the fall.
Before shame.
Before rebellion.
Before human brokenness.
Human companionship was part of God's good design from the beginning.
The Hebrew phrase is לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ (lo-tov heyot ha'adam levado).
It means, in context, "It is not good for the man to be alone."
God was addressing Adam's need for a suitable counterpart, ultimately fulfilled in the creation of the woman.
This verse is not a promise that every person will marry, nor does it teach that single people are incomplete.
But it reveals something important.
God never designed human beings to be indifferent to relationship.
And when He established marriage, He did not treat sexual intimacy as something dirty.
Genesis 2:24 describes a husband and wife becoming "one flesh."
Sexual union within marriage belongs to God's good creation.
It was not invented by Satan.
It was not an unfortunate consequence of sin.
And it was never something Christians needed to pretend did not exist.
So why does something God created as good sometimes become one of the most painful struggles in a believer's life?
Because we live in a fallen world where good desires do not always find immediate, righteous fulfillment.
And sometimes, the waiting hurts.
Terribly.
You may have watched people around you get married.
You attended their weddings. Smiled for their photographs. Celebrated their anniversaries.
Then you went home.
Alone.
You watched couples hold hands at church.
You saw another pregnancy announcement.
Another engagement.
Another person saying, "God finally answered my prayers."
And you were genuinely happy for them.
But somewhere beneath that happiness was a question you felt guilty for asking.
"Jesus, when will it be my turn?"
You don't necessarily resent their blessings.
You're simply exhausted from wondering whether yours will ever come.
And perhaps you've been told, "Just be patient."
As though patience switches off hormones.
As though quoting a Bible verse instantly removes loneliness.
As though a person can simply decide never to long for affection again.
But Scripture is more honest about human struggle than some religious conversations are.
Consider the apostle Paul.
In 1 Corinthians 7:9, he writes:
The Greek phrase behind "to burn" is πυροῦσθαι (pyrousthai), meaning "to burn" or "to be inflamed."
In this context, Paul is speaking about strong sexual passion and the wisdom of marriage for those who lack self-control.
He is not declaring that every unmarried person must marry.
He is not promising marriage to everyone who experiences sexual frustration.
And he is certainly not giving permission to enter a destructive relationship merely to satisfy desire.
But he does acknowledge something Christians sometimes avoid discussing.
Sexual desire can be powerful.
Even for believers.
Even for people who love God sincerely.
Even for people who are trying to live holy lives.
Paul did not pretend the struggle was imaginary.
He addressed it.
And that matters.
Because acknowledging a desire is not the same thing as surrendering to it.
You can feel something intensely without allowing it to become your master.
Now perhaps you're thinking:
"That's easy to say. But you don't understand what ten years feels like."
You're right about something.
Ten years is not a small thing.
Ten years can contain thousands of lonely evenings.
Thousands of moments when you wish someone were beside you.
Years of unanswered questions.
Years of temptation.
Years of wondering whether your body will ever experience intimacy again.
And if you've been sexually active before, the memories may make the longing even more complicated.
You remember what closeness felt like.
You remember being desired.
You remember the warmth of another person.
And sometimes your memories become their own kind of temptation.
You know what Scripture teaches.
But knowing what is right does not always make obedience emotionally painless.
And this is where the Gospel becomes extraordinarily personal.
Hebrews 4:15 says:
"For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." (KJV)
Read that again.
The Greek describes Jesus as one who can συμπαθῆσαι (sympathēsai)—to sympathize with, or share understanding of, our weaknesses.
The passage does not teach that Jesus experienced every individual human circumstance, including sexual relationships or every particular sexual temptation.
Scripture makes no such claim.
But it does teach that Jesus truly entered human life, experienced real testing and suffering, and remains a compassionate High Priest.
He understands human weakness without being conquered by sin.
He knows what it means to be tired.
To be misunderstood.
To experience rejection.
To suffer.
To obey the Father when obedience is costly.
Jesus was fully human and fully divine.
And His compassion is not theoretical.
He is not standing in heaven looking at your struggle with cold indifference.
He is the Savior who invites struggling people to approach the throne of grace.
Hebrews 4:16 continues:
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." (KJV)
Not the throne of humiliation.
Not the throne of mockery.
The throne of grace.
That means you can bring this struggle to Jesus.
Not dressed up in religious language.
Not pretending you're unaffected.
Not pretending you haven't cried about it.
You can tell Him the truth.
"Lord, I miss being touched."
"Lord, I'm frustrated."
"Lord, I'm tempted."
"Lord, I don't want to disobey You, but this is becoming difficult."
And you can ask Him for help.
Because temptation is not automatically sin, and struggling is not the same as surrendering.
But we must also be careful.
The Bible does not say that every desire should be fulfilled simply because it is powerful.
And this is where the message becomes uncomfortable.
Because the same God who understands your frustration also calls you to surrender your sexuality to Him.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5, Paul writes:
The Greek word ἁγιασμός (hagiasmos) means sanctification or holiness.
God's desire is not merely that we avoid scandal.
He desires that we become holy.
In our thoughts.
In our decisions.
In our relationships.
And yes, in our sexuality.
But holiness is not the destruction of everything human about you.
Holiness means belonging to God.
It means allowing Him to shape how you respond to desires that are real, sometimes intense, and not always immediately fulfilled.
And sometimes holiness looks less like a dramatic public victory and more like a private decision nobody applauds.
Closing the website.
Putting down the phone.
Refusing to contact the person you know would pull you into compromise.
Walking away from an affair before it begins.
Ending a relationship that keeps demanding what God has not permitted.
Choosing honesty rather than secretly building a second life.
Nobody sees those moments.
There is no audience.
No applause.
No inspirational music.
Just you.
Your temptation.
And the decision to honor Jesus.
But heaven does not measure faithfulness by the number of people watching.
And God sees what happens in secret.
Now I need to speak to someone who has already fallen.
Someone who is reading this with a heavy heart.
Maybe the loneliness became unbearable.
Maybe you went back to pornography.
Maybe you slept with someone you knew you shouldn't.
Maybe you returned to a relationship that keeps wounding you.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you would never cross.
And now you're sitting there wondering whether you have ruined your testimony.
Whether God is disgusted with you.
Whether your years of trying to live faithfully have become meaningless.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious. But Jesus Christ is a greater Savior than your sin is a master.
That is not permission to keep sinning.
That is an invitation to repent.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
The Greek word ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), translated "confess," carries the sense of acknowledging or admitting.
Confession means we stop disguising sin.
We stop defending what God calls wrong.
We stop treating our wounds as an excuse to harm ourselves or others.
We bring the truth into His light.
And through Jesus Christ, forgiveness is available.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because His sacrifice was sufficient.
At the cross, Jesus did not merely offer encouragement to people who had made mistakes.
He bore sin.
He died for sinners.
And He rose again.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that you can save yourself through perfect self-control.
But that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
And if you have fallen, your next step is not to hide from Him.
It is to return.
Repentance is not pretending you never wanted what you wanted.
It is turning away from sin and turning toward Christ.
There is a difference.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear another difficult truth.
Sometimes what you call sexual frustration is also grief.
Grief over a marriage that ended.
Grief over a spouse who died.
Grief over years of rejection.
Grief over a relationship where affection disappeared.
Grief over being betrayed by someone you trusted.
Grief over a future you thought you would have by now.
And sex has become the language through which that grief speaks.
You say, "I need intimacy."
But underneath that sentence may be another one.
"I want to feel loved again."
"I want to know I still matter."
"I want someone to choose me."
"I am tired of feeling invisible."
And while sexual intimacy can be a beautiful expression of marital love, it cannot carry the entire weight of your identity.
A spouse cannot become your savior.
A relationship cannot become your righteousness.
And sex cannot heal every wound that loneliness exposes.
Only Jesus can reconcile you to God and give you an identity that does not depend on whether another human being desires you.
This does not mean human affection is unnecessary.
It does not mean marriage is unimportant.
It does not mean you should stop praying for companionship.
It means you must not confuse a beautiful gift with the God who gives gifts.
Because gifts can change.
Relationships can end.
Bodies grow older.
Circumstances shift.
But Jesus Christ remains faithful.
And perhaps this is the part that hurts the most.
God has not promised every believer marriage.
He has not promised every married couple a satisfying sexual relationship.
He has not promised that every season of loneliness will end on our preferred timetable.
That may be painful to read.
But Christian hope must be built on what God has actually promised, not on assurances we wish Scripture had made.
Paul himself spoke positively about singleness in 1 Corinthians 7.
Jesus spoke about those who remain unmarried for the sake of the kingdom in Matthew 19:12.
Neither taught that unmarried believers are second-class Christians.
Neither presented sexual experience as a requirement for a meaningful life.
And Jesus Himself lived without marriage.
His life was not incomplete.
His humanity was not defective.
His obedience was not wasted.
So please hear this.
You are not less valuable because nobody is sleeping beside you.
You are not less masculine.
You are not less feminine.
You are not less worthy of respect.
You are not spiritually inferior to the married couple sitting in front of you at church.
And your life is not on hold until somebody puts a ring on your finger.
If you belong to Christ, your identity is already anchored in something greater than your relationship status.
But perhaps you're married.
And this conversation feels different for you.
Because you're not waiting for a spouse.
You already have one.
You just haven't experienced physical intimacy in years.
And every time someone speaks about purity, you feel an ache nobody seems to understand.
You made vows.
You stayed.
You tried.
And somewhere along the way, affection disappeared.
Maybe because of illness.
Maybe because of trauma.
Maybe because of unresolved conflict.
Maybe because of emotional distance.
Maybe because your spouse is struggling in ways you don't fully understand.
And now you feel trapped between your longing for marital closeness and your commitment to faithfulness.
First Corinthians 7:3–5 teaches that marriage includes mutual responsibilities of affection and intimacy and warns against unilateral deprivation.
But that passage must never be twisted into permission for sexual coercion.
Marriage does not erase consent.
It does not authorize pressure, threats, manipulation, or abuse.
Biblical marital intimacy belongs within mutual love, dignity, care, and willing participation.
If your marriage is suffering, the answer is not to silently accumulate resentment until it explodes.
Speak honestly.
Listen carefully.
Seek appropriate medical care when health issues are involved.
Consider trustworthy pastoral support and qualified marriage counseling.
Address wounds that cannot be repaired merely by demanding physical access.
And if there is abuse or danger, seek safety and appropriate professional help.
God's design for marriage is not domination.
It is covenant love.
The kind of love that seeks another person's good.
The kind of love Christ demonstrated through sacrifice.
Now let me ask you something.
What if the greatest danger of these ten years is not that you haven't had sex?
What if it is that frustration has slowly convinced you that God has forgotten you?
Because that's where temptation becomes especially dangerous.
Not merely in the body.
But in the story you begin believing about God.
"He doesn't care."
"He blesses everyone else."
"Obedience is pointless."
"I've waited long enough."
"I deserve to take matters into my own hands."
And suddenly, the temptation is no longer simply about sexual gratification.
It is about whether you trust God's character when His timing is painful.
That is a spiritual battle.
And it deserves more than shallow advice.
James 1:13–15 reminds us that God does not tempt anyone to evil and warns how desire, when it is allowed to entice and conceive sin, leads toward death.
Notice the progression.
Desire.
Enticement.
Sin.
Destruction.
The passage does not declare every natural desire sinful.
It warns us about desire becoming a doorway into disobedience.
And if you've been living in that dangerous space, where frustration is slowly turning into justification, this may be your moment to stop.
Not because God hates you.
But because He loves you too much to call destruction freedom.
You do not have to surrender your future to a moment of temporary relief.
You do not have to sacrifice your conscience to prove that you are still desirable.
You do not have to return to someone who treats your body as valuable but your soul as disposable.
You do not have to turn loneliness into a secret prison.
You can seek support.
You can build meaningful friendships.
You can pursue healthy community.
You can receive wise counsel.
You can pray honestly.
You can take practical steps to avoid situations that repeatedly lead you toward sin.
And when you stumble, you can repent and return to Christ.
Not once as a religious performance.
But as a genuine pattern of surrender.
Because Christian maturity is not measured by how convincingly you pretend you have no struggles.
It is revealed in how faithfully you bring those struggles under the lordship of Jesus.
And if you're still reading, perhaps something in these words has reached a place you've kept hidden for years.
Maybe you've cried over this.
Maybe you've been ashamed of your own body.
Maybe you've wondered why your prayers seem unanswered.
Maybe you've felt guilty for longing for something Scripture itself recognizes as good within marriage.
Or maybe you've been using that legitimate longing to excuse choices that are slowly pulling you away from God.
Whatever your situation, I want you to remember one encounter from the Gospel.
In John 4, Jesus met a Samaritan woman at a well.
A woman whose relationship history was complicated.
Jesus knew she had had five husbands and that the man she was currently living with was not her husband.
He did not pretend her situation was irrelevant.
He spoke truthfully about it.
But He also offered her living water.
He did not reduce her entire identity to her relational history.
He engaged her as a person capable of hearing the truth about God.
And that conversation became a turning point.
The woman went back to her community and spoke about Jesus.
Her story did not end with the exposure of her past.
It moved toward the revelation of the Messiah.
That is grace.
Not grace that denies truth.
Grace that meets people truthfully and calls them toward something greater.
Perhaps your story is different from hers.
Perhaps your struggle is ten years of abstinence.
Perhaps it is ten years of marital distance.
Perhaps it is a decade of loneliness, broken relationships, or hidden compromise.
But the same Jesus who spoke to that woman is the Savior proclaimed in the Gospel today.
And His invitation is not limited to people whose lives already look respectable.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He welcomes the weary.
He forgives those who come to Him in faith.
And He transforms lives.
Not because Jesus promises to erase every consequence of our choices.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored.
Not because every lonely person will eventually marry.
But because the Gospel changes the deepest truth about those who belong to Christ.
Our past no longer has the final word over our standing before God.
Our shame does not have the final word.
Our failures do not have the final word.
Jesus Christ does.
And His resurrection is the foundation of that hope.
So what do you do tomorrow morning if you wake up and the bed is still empty?
You do not have to pretend the longing has disappeared.
You bring it to God again.
You ask Him for the grace to be faithful today.
Not for imaginary strength to survive every possible future at once.
For today.
You open Scripture.
You guard your heart.
You make room for genuine Christian fellowship rather than withdrawing into isolation.
You pursue healing where you have been wounded.
You seek wise help when the struggle becomes overwhelming.
You refuse to make a desperate decision simply because you are exhausted from waiting.
And you remember that a season without sex is not a season without purpose.
Your body matters.
Your desires matter.
Your choices matter.
Your obedience matters.
But none of those things can replace the Savior who loved you and gave Himself for you.
Romans 8:32 asks:
"He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?" (KJV)
This verse does not guarantee marriage or sexual intimacy.
It points us toward the extraordinary generosity of God in giving His Son and assuring believers of everything necessary for His saving purposes.
That is where Christian confidence belongs.
Not in the certainty that life will unfold exactly as we hoped.
But in the certainty that God has demonstrated His love through Jesus Christ.
And sometimes the most courageous prayer is not:
"Lord, give me what I want."
Sometimes it is:
"Lord, I still want it. I still ache. I still don't understand. But please do not let my disappointment become disobedience. Teach me to trust You here."
That prayer may be whispered through tears.
It may come from someone who has been waiting ten years.
Or twenty.
Or someone who fears the waiting may never end.
And the beauty of the Gospel is that you do not need to manufacture emotional perfection before coming to Christ.
You come because you need Him.
You come weak.
You come honest.
You come repentant.
You come trusting His mercy.
And you keep walking with Him.

If this article has described something you've never been brave enough to say aloud, you are not required to reveal private details publicly. But you do not have to carry the struggle in isolation either.
Someone reading may desperately need to know that repentance and restoration are possible.
Your story might help someone stop hiding and begin seeking Jesus.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
Not to display how spiritual you are, but because there may be someone silently fighting this exact battle who will never admit it publicly.
Someone in your church.
Someone in your family.
Someone who has been divorced.
Someone grieving a spouse.
Someone struggling to remain sexually faithful.
Someone whose marriage is hurting.
Someone who loves God but has begun to wonder whether God understands their pain.
One thoughtful share may place biblical encouragement in front of someone who would never ask for it.
Because there may come a moment when you need to remember that God understands your weakness, calls you to holiness, and welcomes you to His throne of grace.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ to follow as well.
Our mission is to keep pointing people toward Jesus through biblical truth, repentance, grace, healing, forgiveness, and discipleship.
Not merely to inspire people for a few minutes.
But to help them grow deeper in the Word of God.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their faith, develop spiritual discipline, and grow in their relationship with Jesus Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you draw closer to Jesus, I want to invite you into something more personal.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
And certainly not because the Gospel should ever be sold.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith.
But Scripture does encourage believers to support faithful ministry voluntarily and generously.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
Cheerfully.
Supporting Gospel ministry should come from willing love, never spiritual pressure.

If you are already committed to giving tithes or offerings through your local church, please continue honoring those responsibilities. Gospel Warrior is not asking you to abandon your church or replace your local congregation.
It can help sustain the work of sharing Scripture with people who are hurting, searching, struggling, and longing for truth.
People who may never walk into a church building before encountering a message about Jesus on their phone.
These products are simply an added expression of appreciation.
The deeper purpose is to help make continued biblical encouragement and discipleship possible.
If you believe in this mission, and you have the financial freedom to participate, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep growing in Christ.
Use the free resources.
Pray for this ministry.
Share the Gospel.
Your value in God's kingdom is not determined by your ability to contribute financially.
It is to point people toward the Savior who paid the price for our redemption.
And now, before you leave, I want to speak to that person who has been waiting ten years.
The one who started reading because of the word "sex" but kept reading because something in your soul felt understood.
You may still be alone tonight.
You may still have unanswered questions.
Your body may still ache for intimacy.
Your marriage may still need healing.
Your future may still look uncertain.
And I cannot promise that tomorrow will bring the relationship, affection, or physical intimacy you've been longing for.
But I can tell you what Scripture promises.
Jesus Christ is a merciful High Priest.
God's grace is available to those who come to Him through Christ.
There is forgiveness for repentant sinners.
There is strength to pursue holiness.
And there is a hope that does not depend on your relationship status.
You have not been forgotten simply because you have been waiting.
You are not disqualified from a meaningful life because you have not had sex.
And you do not have to surrender your convictions to prove that you are still human.
So tonight, if the loneliness comes again, speak honestly to Jesus.
If temptation comes, seek His help and choose what honors Him.
If you have fallen, repent and return.
If your heart is broken, allow trusted people to help you carry the burden.
And if tomorrow arrives without the answer you wanted, remember that God's faithfulness is not measured by the speed at which He fulfills your desires.
It was revealed most clearly at the cross.
Where Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
Where mercy met justice.
Where redemption was purchased.
And where the foundation of our hope was established.
Ten years without sex may be part of your story.
But it does not have to become the definition of your life.
The empty space beside you does not mean there is an empty space in the heart of God where His love for you should have been.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE “PROPHETIC WARNING” YOU RECEIVED WAS ACTUALLY SOMEONE TRYING TO CONTROL YOU?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE “PROPHETIC WARNING” YOU RECEIVED WAS ACTUALLY SOMEONE TRYING TO CONTROL YOU?

When someone says, “God told me,” but leaves you terrified, confused, and afraid to disobey them, you need to know the difference between the voice of the Shepherd and the voice of someone using His name.
There is a particular kind of fear that only someone who has been spiritually manipulated can understand.
It is the fear of disappointing God when you are not even sure God was the One speaking.
You remember the conversation.
Perhaps it happened after a church service. Maybe it came through a private message, a prayer meeting, or a person you deeply respected.
They looked you in the eyes and said something that immediately made your stomach tighten.
“God showed me something about you.”
And suddenly, everything changed.

They told you that the relationship you were pursuing was dangerous. That the opportunity you were considering was outside God's will. That something terrible might happen if you did not obey their warning.
Perhaps they even told you that questioning their message was questioning God Himself.
You wanted to be faithful.
You wanted to honor Jesus.
You were not trying to rebel. You were trying to understand.
But every time you asked a question, the pressure increased.
Every time you hesitated, they called it disobedience.
Every time you considered seeking another perspective, they warned you against listening to other voices.
And eventually, something happened inside you that you could barely explain.
You stopped asking, “Lord, what are You teaching me?”
You started asking, “What will this person do if I don't obey?”
Read that again.
Because somewhere between your desire to honor God and your fear of disappointing another human being, someone may have crossed a boundary that never belonged to them.
And the most heartbreaking part?
You may have called that fear reverence.
You may have called that anxiety conviction.
You may have called that surrendering your conscience to another person obedience to God.
But what if the warning was not from God?
What if someone had discovered that the easiest way to control a sincere Christian was to make disagreement feel like rebellion against heaven?
Before we go any further, understand something important.
Not every uncomfortable prophetic warning is manipulation. And not every comforting message comes from God.
Scripture contains genuine warnings that confronted sin, exposed deception, called people to repentance, and demanded costly obedience.
Nathan confronted David about adultery and murder. John the Baptist confronted Herod. Agabus warned Paul about suffering ahead.
God's truth does not always make us comfortable.
But the fact that a message makes you uncomfortable does not automatically make it divine, either.
That distinction could protect your faith.
Because the Bible never commands you to surrender your discernment merely because someone claims to speak for God.
In fact, it commands the opposite.
The apostle John wrote:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.” — 1 John 4:1, KJV
The Greek expression translated “try the spirits” is δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα (dokimazete ta pneumata).
The verb dokimazete carries the sense of testing, examining, or discerning whether something is genuine.
Notice what John did not say.
He did not say, “Believe every person who sounds spiritual.”
He did not say, “Accept every warning delivered with confidence.”
He did not say, “If someone claims divine authority, silence your questions.”
He commanded believers to test.
And the command was not given to people who hated God.
It was given to people who loved Him.
Testing a claimed revelation is not necessarily a rejection of the Holy Spirit. It may be an act of obedience to the Holy Spirit's written Word.
Think about that.
The very person accusing you of rebellion for asking questions may be discouraging you from practicing discernment that Scripture explicitly commands.
And that should make you pay attention.
Perhaps you have encountered someone who regularly begins sentences with, “The Lord told me…”
At first, you admired their confidence.
They seemed spiritually sensitive. They spoke passionately. They prayed with intensity. They appeared to know things you did not know.
You trusted them.
Then the messages became more personal.
“God told me you shouldn't marry that person.”
“God revealed that your family is blocking your destiny.”
“The Lord said you must stay under my spiritual covering.”
“If you leave this ministry, you will lose your blessing.”
“God showed me that you need to give this offering before your breakthrough comes.”
And when you asked how they knew, they offered no meaningful biblical explanation.
Only greater certainty.
Only stronger warnings.
Only the terrifying suggestion that something bad would happen if you refused.
That is when discernment becomes urgent.
Because a person may speak with spiritual vocabulary while exercising very human control.
And the Bible gives us a sobering picture of what happens when people claim divine authority for messages God has not given.
In Jeremiah 23:21, the Lord declares:
“I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied.” — KJV
Let those words settle.
They were speaking.
They were moving.
They were claiming authority.
But God said He had not sent them.
In Jeremiah 23:16, the people are warned about prophets who speak visions arising from their own hearts rather than from the mouth of the Lord.
The Hebrew phrase חֲזוֹן לִבָּם (chazon libbam) means “a vision of their own heart.”
It is a devastating distinction.
A message can come from someone's own imagination, desires, fears, or ambitions while being presented as a message from heaven.

That does not mean every mistaken person is deliberately lying. Some people sincerely misinterpret their impressions. Others may be influenced by their own anxieties, assumptions, or personal interests.
But sincerity does not establish divine authority.
And confidence does not turn a human opinion into God's command.
You may have spent months blaming yourself for resisting a warning that was never God's instruction in the first place.
You may have cried yourself to sleep, wondering whether heaven was angry with you.
You may have abandoned an opportunity, damaged a relationship, or remained in an unhealthy situation because someone insisted that leaving would invite judgment.
And perhaps the most painful part was this:
You were not afraid of losing that person's approval.
You were afraid of losing God.
That is why spiritual manipulation can wound so deeply.
It attaches a human demand to your deepest love.
It takes your desire to please Jesus and makes another person the gatekeeper of that relationship.
But Jesus never appointed a human being to replace Himself as the Shepherd of your soul.
In John 10:27, He says:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — KJV
The Greek reads:
Τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούει, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι.
The central truth is unmistakable: Christ's sheep belong to Him, are known by Him, and follow Him.
This verse is not a promise that every inward impression you experience is God's voice. Christians still need Scripture, wisdom, prayer, and the counsel of mature believers.
But it does establish whose sheep you are.
You belong to Jesus.
Not to the most intimidating person in the prayer meeting.
Not to the individual who insists that obedience to them is the measure of your loyalty to Christ.
You are Christ's.
And that changes everything.
Consider how Paul instructed the church concerning prophetic messages.
“Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge.” — 1 Corinthians 14:29, KJV
The Greek phrase οἱ ἄλλοι διακρινέτωσαν (hoi alloi diakrinetosan) calls for the others to evaluate or discern what has been spoken.
Even in a congregation where prophetic speech was being exercised, the message was not exempt from examination.
It was to be weighed.
Not automatically believed.
Not weaponized against the listener.
Not placed beyond accountability.
And in 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21, Paul holds two truths together:
“Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” — KJV
That is biblical balance.
Do not automatically dismiss everything claimed to be prophetic.
But do not automatically embrace it, either.
Test it.
Hold on to what is good.
Reject what does not withstand examination.
Some Christians have been taught that discernment means believing the strongest spiritual personality in the room.
But biblical discernment requires something far more demanding.
It requires us to love truth more than impressive delivery.
To love Christ more than religious reputation.
And sometimes, to ask difficult questions even when the person speaking is someone we admire.
Imagine a young woman sitting across from a respected church leader.
She has been praying about accepting a job in another city.
The opportunity appears legitimate. Her family supports her. She has sought counsel, considered her responsibilities, and prayed carefully.
Then the leader tells her, “God revealed that if you leave, your life will fall apart.”
She becomes frightened.
When she asks for biblical guidance, he repeats that God has spoken.
When she asks to discuss the matter with other mature Christians, he accuses her of seeking people who will tell her what she wants to hear.
When she decides to take more time, he says her hesitation proves she is spiritually immature.
Notice what is happening.
The issue is no longer simply whether the job is wise.
The issue has become whether she will surrender her decision-making to someone claiming unquestionable authority.
A genuinely concerned leader could have discussed practical risks, offered biblical principles, prayed with her, and respected the need for careful discernment.
Instead, the alleged revelation has become a means of shutting down examination.
And this is one of the clearest warning signs of spiritual coercion:
The person delivering the message makes their own authority impossible to question.
That is not how the apostles instructed the church to handle claims of spiritual revelation.
It is also not how faithful shepherds are commanded to lead.
Peter writes to church elders:
The Greek word κατακυριεύοντες (katakyrieuontes) refers to exercising domineering authority or lording it over others.
Peter specifically forbids that posture.
Spiritual leadership is not ownership.
Pastoral care is not domination.
Accountability is not captivity.
A faithful shepherd can correct you without making you dependent on his personal approval for your relationship with God.
A faithful mentor can disagree with your decision without threatening you with divine punishment.
A faithful Christian friend can share a concern without demanding that you treat it as infallible revelation.
And a genuine warning, even when difficult, should remain open to biblical examination.
Now perhaps someone reading this is thinking:
“But what if the person really did hear from God? What if I ignore the warning and something terrible happens?”
That fear deserves a careful answer.
You are not required to pretend that God cannot warn His people.
Scripture clearly records occasions when He did.
But you are also not required to treat another person's unverified claim as though it carries the same authority as Scripture.
Deuteronomy 18:20–22 addresses the seriousness of falsely speaking in God's name, including the case of a prediction that fails to occur.
