Deuteronomy 13:1–4 goes even further: even an impressive sign does not justify following a message that leads people away from faithfulness to the true God.
The standard is not simply whether a speaker seems supernatural.
The standard includes faithfulness to God and His revealed truth.
And Christians must never forget that Jesus Christ is the decisive revelation of God.
Hebrews 1:1–2 tells us that God, who spoke through the prophets in former times, has spoken to us in His Son.
That does not settle every disagreement among Christians about contemporary spiritual gifts.
Faithful believers differ on how certain gifts operate today.
But Christians across those differences can affirm this:
No claimed revelation has permission to contradict the gospel of Jesus Christ or overturn the authority of Scripture.
No prophetic warning can make salvation dependent on obeying a particular leader.
No private message can cancel the truth that we are saved by grace through faith, not by purchasing favor or earning acceptance.
No spiritual authority can rightfully demand that you participate in sin.
And no human messenger becomes infallible simply by attaching the words “God told me” to a personal demand.
Perhaps you need to hear something else.
Not every experience of fear means you are being manipulated.
Godly conviction can be painful.
Repentance can be uncomfortable.
The Holy Spirit may expose a sin you desperately want to protect.
When Nathan confronted David, David could not excuse his actions by saying the message made him feel ashamed.
His sin was real.
He had abused power, committed adultery, and arranged the death of Uriah.
Nathan's rebuke was not manipulation. It was truthful confrontation.
And David responded:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
That is the difference we must preserve.
A biblical warning may confront real wrongdoing and call for repentance.
Manipulation, by contrast, may exploit fear, distort Scripture, invent divine threats, or demand personal submission that God has not commanded.
The distinction is not merely whether the message hurts.
It is whether the message is truthful, biblically accountable, and rightly directed toward obedience to God rather than control by another person.
And this matters because the gospel itself contains a warning.
Sin is serious.
Judgment is real.
Repentance is necessary.
But the gospel does not leave the sinner trapped beneath the power of a human religious authority.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
The One who carried our sins.
The One who was crucified.
The One who rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repent and believe.
The One who does not need a manipulator to make His grace effective.
Paul writes:
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα (Ouden ara nyn katakrima).
“No condemnation, therefore, now…”
That declaration is not permission to continue in sin.
It is the glorious announcement that those who belong to Christ are no longer under sin's condemning verdict.
So when someone tells a believer that questioning their private revelation will automatically bring divine condemnation, that claim deserves serious scrutiny.
God's children are called to holiness.
But they are not called to live beneath invented threats.
And perhaps that is where this article has become painfully personal.
Because you remember the person who said you were cursed if you left.
You remember the warning that made you afraid to marry.
You remember the offering you felt pressured to give.
You remember being told that your suffering proved you had failed to obey someone's prophetic instruction.
You remember how small you became.
How anxious.
How suspicious of your own judgment.
How afraid to pray without wondering whether God was angry.
And eventually, you stopped feeling safe even when reading Scripture.
Not because Scripture had failed you.
But because someone had repeatedly used religious language to frighten you.
If that describes your experience, please hear this carefully.
You do not have to settle the question of someone's motives before recognizing that a demand was inappropriate.
You do not have to prove that a person intentionally deceived you before setting a healthy boundary.
You do not have to accuse every spiritual leader of abuse in order to acknowledge that some leaders misuse their authority.
And you do not have to abandon Christianity to reject the misuse of Christ's name.
You can return to Scripture.
You can seek wise, independent counsel.
You can ask questions.
You can take time to examine a claimed revelation without surrendering to artificial urgency.

If a situation involves threats, financial exploitation, sexual pressure, intimidation, or isolation from trusted relationships, seek help from safe people outside the controlling relationship. Where appropriate, contact qualified safeguarding professionals or relevant authorities.
God's Word does not require you to remain exposed to abuse in order to prove that you are submissive.
And if you are a pastor, prophet, mentor, or ministry leader reading this, there is a necessary warning here for you as well.
Be careful with the words “God told me.”
Those words are not a shortcut around accountability.
They are not a substitute for sound biblical teaching.
They are not a tool for winning arguments.
They are not a way to secure loyalty, money, influence, or emotional dependence.
If you have presented your personal preference as a command from God, repent.
If you have frightened people into obeying you, repent.
If you have used claims of revelation to silence legitimate questions, repent.
If you have made believers feel that leaving your ministry means leaving Jesus, repent.
There is mercy in Christ for the leader who genuinely turns away from sin.
But genuine repentance includes acknowledging wrongdoing, accepting accountability, and making appropriate changes. It must not become another demand that wounded people immediately restore trust.
Jesus did not call His shepherds to build personal kingdoms out of frightened sheep.
He called them to care for people who belong to Him.
And now I want to speak to the person who still feels guilty for walking away.
Maybe you left that church.
Maybe you stopped answering those messages.
Maybe you finally told someone, “I need time to pray and think.”
And ever since, a question has followed you:
“What if I disobeyed God?”
Do not answer that question by blindly trusting your feelings.
But do not answer it by blindly trusting the person who frightened you, either.
Bring the claim into the light of Scripture.
Ask whether it contradicts God's revealed commands.
Examine whether the messenger had something to gain from your compliance.
Consider whether the message could be questioned without retaliation.
Seek counsel from mature Christians who are not dependent on the person making the claim.
Pray for wisdom.
James 1:5 says that those who lack wisdom may ask God, who gives generously.
And remember the believers in Berea.
Acts 17:11 commends them for examining the Scriptures daily to see whether the things they heard were true.
They were examining the teaching of the apostle Paul.
Think about that.
If the Bereans were commended for examining apostolic preaching against Scripture, why should any contemporary spiritual personality demand immunity from biblical examination?
The truth does not become less true when examined.
And falsehood does not become holy when delivered from a pulpit.
Some of you have spent years believing that your deepest spiritual problem was disobedience.
But perhaps one of the things you need to repent of is not asking questions.
Perhaps you need to repent of allowing human approval to become more important than God's Word.
Perhaps you need to confess that fear has sometimes governed your decisions more than faith.
And perhaps you need to receive the grace of Jesus for the ways you were confused, pressured, or led astray.
Not every wounded person is guilty of the wrongdoing committed against them.
And not every wrong decision was made with full understanding or freedom.
Christ knows the difference.
He sees the whole story.
He sees the person who was sincerely trying to obey Him.
He sees the tears no one else witnessed.
He sees the prayers whispered in fear.
He sees the longing to do what is right.
And He is not a cruel Master waiting to punish His children for failing to obey every human claim made in His name.
Look at Jesus in the Gospels.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He exposed those who loved status and public recognition.
He rebuked leaders who placed heavy burdens on others while failing to practice what they taught.
In Matthew 23:4, He described religious leaders who bound heavy burdens and placed them on people's shoulders.
Yet in Matthew 11:28, He extended an invitation:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — KJV
Notice the invitation.
“Come unto me.”
Not, “Come to the person who claims to control access to Me.”
Not, “Earn your place by obeying every spiritual threat.”
Not, “Pay for your freedom.”
Come to Jesus.
The Savior who tells the truth about sin.
The Savior who calls us to take up our cross.
The Savior who demands our ultimate allegiance.
And the Savior who gives rest to those who come to Him.
His call to discipleship is costly.
But His grace is not for sale.
His forgiveness cannot be purchased.
His lordship cannot be transferred to a religious personality.
And His finished work cannot be improved by human manipulation.
This is where the story turns.
Because the deepest scandal is not merely that some people misuse God's name.
The deeper scandal is that sinful human beings, including religious people, are capable of turning even sacred things into instruments of selfish ambition.
And the greater wonder is that Jesus came to redeem sinners from the very darkness we have created.
He did not die so that we could replace one form of bondage with another.
He died and rose again so that those who trust in Him might be reconciled to God, forgiven, transformed, and brought under His gracious lordship.
This is why our message has always been:
Not because every painful chapter instantly disappears.
Not because every person who hurt you will apologize.
Not because every consequence will be reversed.
But because your story does not have to end where someone else's misuse of spiritual authority left you.
In Christ, there is forgiveness for sin.
There is grace for the repentant.
There is wisdom for the confused.
There is hope for the wounded.
There is a new way to live.
And you do not have to pretend that everything was acceptable in order to move forward with Jesus.
Perhaps today your first act of courage is not making a dramatic announcement.
Perhaps it is opening your Bible without hearing that person's threats in your head.
Perhaps it is praying, “Lord, teach me to know You through Your Word.”
Perhaps it is admitting to a trusted believer, “I think I was spiritually manipulated, and I need help understanding what happened.”
Perhaps it is finally recognizing that humility before God and unquestioning obedience to another person are not the same thing.
And perhaps, for someone else, this article is not about escaping manipulation.
It is about recognizing that you have participated in it.
Maybe you have spoken too confidently about impressions you could not verify.
Maybe you have used fear to influence someone you claimed to love.
Maybe you have treated disagreement as rebellion because you could not bear losing control.
Jesus calls you to repentance, too.
Not performative sorrow.
Not excuses.
Not another spiritual explanation that protects your reputation.
Real repentance.
The kind that admits the truth.
The kind that stops doing harm.
The kind that accepts correction.
The kind that seeks restoration without demanding that others erase the consequences.
Because grace does not require us to deny what happened.
Grace calls us to bring the truth into the light.
And the light belongs to Christ.
Before you leave this article, I want you to consider one question.
Have you ever been more afraid of disappointing a spiritual leader than you were concerned about understanding what Scripture actually teaches?
You do not have to share the details publicly.
You do not have to name anyone.
If you are recovering from spiritual pressure, you can simply comment, “Christ is still healing me.”

And if God has brought you through a season of confusion into a deeper trust in His Word, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Your experience may help another believer realize that asking biblical questions is not the same as abandoning faith.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who is quietly struggling with this exact fear.
Someone who still believes that disagreeing with a religious leader means disagreeing with God.
Someone who has stopped praying because they feel condemned.
Someone who needs to know that Scripture itself commands discernment.
Not to create suspicion toward every church or spiritual leader.
Not to encourage rebellion against godly correction.
But to help people distinguish biblical shepherding from spiritual domination, and to lead them back to Jesus.
Because the next time someone speaks a frightening claim over your life, you may need to return to the Scriptures we have examined together.
We want to keep pointing people beyond religious performance, spiritual confusion, and fear toward the Person and finished work of Jesus Christ.
Not because a payment can purchase His blessing.
Scripture gives us the right foundation.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
The Greek word ἀνάγκης (anankēs), translated “necessity” in this verse, conveys compulsion or constraint.
Paul's instruction is clear: Christian generosity should not be extracted through pressure.
That is especially important in an article about spiritual manipulation.
We will tell you what your voluntary support can mean.
It can help us continue reaching people who need biblical encouragement, gospel clarity, and a reminder that Jesus Christ remains the only Savior.
We simply invite you to become a willing partner in this mission.
Those products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are an additional way to encourage believers, share meaningful messages, and support the continuing work.
Those free resources matter deeply to us.
Because spiritual nourishment should never be presented as something that only paying supporters deserve.
You can read Scripture without paying us.
You can receive God's grace without purchasing anything.

But if this ministry has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, encouraged your family, or given you something meaningful to share with another soul, we would be grateful for your voluntary support.
Not a manufactured version of Jesus.
Not a Jesus used to frighten people into obedience to a human personality.
But the Jesus revealed in Scripture.
Holy.
Merciful.
Truthful.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Worthy of repentance, worship, trust, and lifelong obedience.
And if you have spent years living under a so-called prophetic warning that made you afraid to breathe, I want to leave you with this.
You do not have to reject the supernatural to reject manipulation.
You do not have to despise prophecy to test a claimed prophecy.
You do not have to hate the church to hold church leaders accountable.
You do not have to abandon submission to Christ to refuse ungodly control.
You do not have to pretend the wound never happened to believe that Jesus can bring healing.
And you do not have to know every answer today.
Begin with what God has already revealed.
Open the Scriptures.
Seek wise counsel.
Pray for discernment.
Repent wherever the Word exposes your own sin.
Refuse to make another human being the final authority over your conscience.
And trust the Savior who knows His sheep by name.
Because one day, you may look back on the warning that terrified you and recognize that the most important question was never whether that person sounded powerful.
It was whether their message was faithful to the God revealed in Jesus Christ.
And if the answer is no, you are not required to call darkness light simply because someone used the language of heaven.
Jesus is still Lord.
His Word is still true.
His grace is still sufficient.
And His sheep still belong to Him.
The voice that once made you afraid to question a human being does not deserve to drown out the Word of the Savior who gave His life to redeem you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY HAD MANY WIVES. SO WHY CAN’T CHRISTIANS TODAY? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: THEY HAD MANY WIVES. SO WHY CAN’T CHRISTIANS TODAY? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING

Abraham had Sarah and Hagar. Jacob had Leah and Rachel. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. But when Jesus spoke about marriage, He took His listeners somewhere they never expected—back before the kings, before the patriarchs, before the heartbreak. And what He revealed should make every Christian reconsider the difference between what God permitted in a fallen world and what God intended from the beginning.
There is a question that can make an entire church uncomfortable.
Not because the Bible refuses to answer it.
But because the Bible contains stories that seem, at first glance, to support the very thing many Christians condemn.
If Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon had multiple wives, why do Christians insist that marriage should be between one man and one woman?
Think about that.
These were not obscure men hiding in the shadows of biblical history.
Abraham was called God's friend.
Jacob became the father of the twelve tribes of Israel.
David was described as a man after God's own heart.
Solomon was given extraordinary wisdom.
And yet their households included multiple wives, concubines, rivalry, jealousy, and complicated family relationships.
So here is the uncomfortable question.
If God worked through these men, does that mean He approved of everything they did?
And if the Old Testament records polygamy without always explicitly condemning it, can a Christian today point to those examples and declare, "God allowed it then, so He must allow it now"?
Before you answer, consider something that might change the way you read your Bible forever.
Not everything Scripture records is something Scripture recommends.
The Bible tells us that David committed adultery and arranged a man's death. It does not invite us to imitate him.
It tells us that Abraham lied about Sarah. It does not turn dishonesty into righteousness.
It tells us that Peter denied Jesus three times. It does not make denying Christ acceptable.
And it tells us that men had multiple wives.
But does the existence of those marriages establish God's original design?
That is where this story becomes far more personal than a debate about ancient households.
Because underneath the question about polygamy lies a question every Christian must eventually face.
Are we searching Scripture to discover what God desires?
Or are we searching Scripture for someone whose behavior can justify what we already want?
That question does not belong only to people defending polygamy.
It belongs to the person excusing bitterness because someone in the Bible became angry.
To the person justifying dishonesty because a biblical hero once lied.
To the believer who keeps returning to a destructive relationship because they can find a verse that seems to make it acceptable.
And to every one of us who has ever whispered, "But Lord, someone else did it."
The Gospel does not call us to imitate every failure of the people God used.
It calls us to follow the Savior who came to redeem people like them.
And people like us.
To understand this, we have to return to a place older than Abraham.
Older than Jacob.
Older than David.
Older than the entire nation of Israel.
We have to return to the garden.
Before sin fractured human relationships, before jealousy entered marriage, before powerful men accumulated wives as signs of wealth or status, Scripture introduces a man and a woman.
Adam and Eve.
Not Adam and several wives.
Not Eve competing with another woman for her husband's attention.
One man.
One woman.
One covenantal union.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." (KJV)
The Hebrew text contains the expression:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
"And they shall become one flesh."
The word echad means "one."
In this context, the phrase describes the profound union established through marriage.
It is not merely about physical intimacy.
It is about two lives joined in a covenantal bond.
We should be careful not to claim that the Hebrew word echad, by itself, proves monogamy. Hebrew can use this word in several ways, and the meaning must be determined by context.
But the context matters enormously.
Genesis presents one man joined to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He deliberately returned to this passage.
That should get our attention.
Because when people challenged Jesus about the boundaries of marriage, He did not begin with Solomon's household.
He did not point to Jacob's arrangements.
He did not make David's royal marriages the controlling example.
He went back to creation.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus said:
"Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." (KJV)
Notice His words.
"At the beginning."
Jesus was addressing divorce, not answering a direct question about polygamy. We must not pretend otherwise.
But His answer establishes something important about how Christians should understand marriage.
He grounds its meaning in God's creative intention rather than simply treating every arrangement tolerated in Israel's history as the ideal.
In the Greek text of Matthew 19:5, we find:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
Hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
"The two into one flesh."
The word dyo means "two."
Jesus is quoting the creation account and affirming the union of the two.
This does not mean that a single Greek word settles every historical and theological question surrounding polygamy.
But it does mean that the marriage pattern Jesus chose to uphold was the creation pattern of two becoming one flesh.
And suddenly, the question changes.
Instead of asking, "How many wives did Solomon have?"
We begin asking, "What kind of marriage did Jesus hold before His followers?"
That distinction is everything.
Now imagine Sarah.
Not as a stained-glass figure.
Not as a character in a children's Bible lesson.
Imagine her as a woman.
A woman who had waited years for a child.
A woman who knew the ache of unanswered prayers.
A woman who watched time pass while God's promise seemed impossible.
Then came a decision that would fracture her household.
In Genesis 16, Sarah, then called Sarai, gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham in an attempt to obtain a child through her.
It was a decision shaped by desperation, social customs, and the painful reality of infertility in the ancient world.
But when Hagar conceived, the household became a place of conflict.
Genesis 16:4 describes tension between Hagar and Sarai.
Genesis 16:6 tells us that Sarai dealt harshly with Hagar, who fled.
Read that again.
The arrangement did not simply produce another child.
It produced suffering.
And Hagar, a vulnerable servant caught in decisions made by people with power over her, found herself alone in the wilderness.
Yet there, God saw her.
She called Him:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Ro'i.
A Hebrew expression commonly understood as "God who sees me," or "God of seeing" (Genesis 16:13).
What a moment.
In a story often used to debate whether a man may have more than one wife, Scripture draws our attention to a suffering woman whom God does not overlook.
Hagar was not invisible to Him.
Her pain mattered.
Her child mattered.
Her future mattered.
And if we use Abraham's household merely to defend a marriage arrangement while ignoring Hagar's suffering, we have missed something deeply important in the narrative.
God's mercy toward Hagar does not establish that every decision leading to her suffering was righteous.
Neither does Abraham's place in salvation history mean that every action he took reflected God's perfect will.
God's faithfulness is often revealed not through human perfection, but in spite of human failure.
And that should give hope to every reader who carries regrets.
Because perhaps you, too, have made a decision in desperation.
Perhaps you tried to force an answer that God had not yet given.
Perhaps you wounded someone while trying to protect yourself.
Perhaps your family still carries the consequences.
The God who saw Hagar still sees people in pain.
And the God who remained faithful to His promise to Abraham is not defeated by human failure.
But His mercy should never become our excuse to repeat that failure.
Then there was Jacob.
Two sisters.
One husband.
A household full of longing.
Leah wanted to be loved.
Rachel wanted children.
Jacob favored Rachel.
And the competition between the women intensified.
Genesis 29–30 records the heartbreak, rivalry, and painful struggle for affection and motherhood within this family.
Listen to Leah's words after the birth of Reuben:
"Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." (Genesis 29:32, KJV)
"Now therefore my husband will love me."
Can you hear the ache?
A woman holding her newborn child, hoping that perhaps this time she will finally receive the love she has been longing for.
This is not a romantic advertisement for polygamy.
It is the account of a family through whom God worked while deep emotional wounds remained.
God brought the twelve tribes of Israel out of Jacob's complicated household.
But divine providence does not mean divine approval of every human choice within that household.
That distinction is crucial.
God can bring redemption out of a broken situation without declaring the brokenness His ideal.
And if you have ever wondered whether your family is too complicated for God's grace, remember Jacob's household.
The Lord's redemptive purposes were not destroyed by their dysfunction.
But neither did their dysfunction become the standard for everyone else.
Now consider David.
A man who worshiped.
A man who repented.
A man who wrote psalms that still comfort wounded souls.
A man whose household also became a place of devastating conflict.
Some defenders of polygamy appeal to 2 Samuel 12:8, where God, through Nathan, speaks of having given David his master's house and wives.
This is one of the more difficult passages in the discussion, and it deserves an honest response.
The verse appears within Nathan's confrontation of David over his adultery with Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah.
The language emphasizes what God had granted David in contrast to David's sinful grasping for what was not his.
It is a serious mistake to ignore this text.
But it is also a mistake to treat the verse as an unrestricted command or universal endorsement of polygamy.
The passage does not instruct Christians to take multiple wives. Nor does it overturn the creation pattern to which Jesus later appealed.
We must allow the text to say what it says, without forcing it to say more.
The Old Testament does contain laws regulating marriages involving multiple wives.
Exodus 21:10 protects a wife's food, clothing, and marital rights if another wife is taken.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives, one loved and one unloved.
These laws are real.
They cannot simply be erased.
But regulation is not the same thing as a declaration that a practice represents God's highest intention.
Biblical law sometimes addresses the realities of a fallen society and places limits on injustice within those realities.
Jesus Himself made a related distinction when explaining that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of human hearts, while directing His hearers back to the beginning (Matthew 19:8).
That does not automatically prove every Old Testament allowance functioned identically to the divorce concession.
It does, however, warn us against assuming that every practice addressed by Mosaic law must therefore be God's ideal for all times.
Even Israel's kings were warned.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says of the king:
"Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away." (KJV)
The warning is especially striking when we reach Solomon.
Solomon.
The king renowned for wisdom.
The man who built the temple.
The ruler whose name became associated with extraordinary wealth and splendor.
First Kings 11:3 records that he had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
But the biblical account does not present this as a glorious achievement.
It says his wives turned away his heart.
First Kings 11:4 declares:
"For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father." (KJV)
We must be precise here.
The passage particularly condemns Solomon's disobedience and idolatry, including the influence of his foreign wives who worshiped other gods.
It should not be reduced to the simplistic claim that every polygamous household inevitably experiences Solomon's exact downfall.
But neither can Solomon's marriages honestly be presented as an uncomplicated biblical endorsement of modern polygamy.
His story is a warning.
And perhaps the most haunting part is this:
A man may possess extraordinary knowledge of God and still fail to obey Him.
A person can quote Scripture and still use it to defend the desires of the heart.
A believer can be admired publicly while privately drifting away from the Lord.
That should humble every one of us.
Because the danger is not merely having the wrong answer to a marriage debate.
The danger is becoming so determined to defend ourselves that we stop allowing Scripture to correct us.
Now we come to the New Testament.
And the question becomes sharper.
What did the apostles teach the churches?
In 1 Corinthians 7:2, Paul writes:
The Greek reads:
ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω
Hekastos tēn heautou gynaika echetō, kai hekastē ton idion andra echetō.
The sense is:
"Let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband."
Paul describes marriage in reciprocal terms.
The husband belongs in covenantal faithfulness to his wife, and the wife to her husband.
The surrounding verses emphasize mutual responsibility, mutual consideration, and the shared obligations of marriage.
Paul is not describing a husband collecting wives.
He is instructing husbands and wives in a relationship of mutual marital faithfulness.
In 1 Timothy 3:2, an overseer is required to be:
"the husband of one wife." (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
Mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, "a man of one woman," commonly expressed as "husband of one wife."
The same expression appears in Titus 1:6, while 1 Timothy 3:12 uses comparable language for deacons.
Scholars discuss whether this phrase primarily emphasizes marital faithfulness, excludes polygamy, addresses remarriage, or combines several concerns.
We should acknowledge that debate rather than pretend every detail is uncontested.
These qualifications directly concern church leaders, so they should not be presented as though they are, by themselves, an explicit universal prohibition addressed to every married Christian.
Yet they fit naturally with the wider New Testament portrayal of marriage as an exclusive covenant between husband and wife.
Then Paul gives us something even deeper.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
And in Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul returns to Genesis 2:24 and describes the marriage union as a profound mystery related to Christ and the church.
Here the conversation moves beyond ancient kings and household arrangements.
Marriage is held up as a picture of covenantal, self-giving love.
Christ does not exploit His bride.
He does not abandon her.
He gives Himself for her.
And the Christian husband's calling is not to pursue the greatest number of relationships he can justify.
It is to love with the sacrificial faithfulness modeled by Jesus.
This is why the historic mainstream Christian understanding of marriage is monogamous.
Not because Christians are embarrassed by the Old Testament.
Not because the patriarchs have been erased.
But because the Bible's creation account, Jesus' teaching, and the apostolic vision of marriage together provide a compelling foundation for the covenantal union of one man and one woman.

To be fair, some contemporary defenders of polygamy argue that the Old Testament's regulation of plural marriages, the absence of a single explicit New Testament sentence saying "all polygamy is forbidden," and certain difficult passages leave room for plural marriage.
Those arguments deserve to be examined seriously rather than mocked.
But the absence of one particular prohibition is not sufficient to establish positive Christian authorization.
Christian ethics are not formed merely by searching for everything Scripture does not forbid in one sentence.
They are formed by reading the whole biblical witness in its context, with Jesus Christ at the center.
And that is where the argument for adopting modern polygamy as a Christian ideal becomes deeply unpersuasive.
The Old Testament shows that polygamy existed among God's people. It does not establish that Christians should practice it.
Still, there is another question that deserves compassion.
What about people already living in polygamous families?
What about women and children who would suffer if a husband suddenly abandoned them?
What about converts to Christianity whose family circumstances were established before they came to faith?
These are not abstract theological puzzles.
These are human lives.
Real mothers.
Real children.
Real responsibilities.
Real consequences.
And the church must not answer complex family situations with careless commands that create new injustices.
Repentance never gives someone permission to abandon vulnerable dependents.
The New Testament takes family provision seriously (1 Timothy 5:8), and the Old Testament itself demonstrates concern for the rights of women within existing plural marriages.

How an existing polygamous household should be pastorally addressed can involve difficult questions of civil law, covenantal obligations, protection of women, provision for children, and church membership or leadership.
Faithful Christian communities may differ in their pastoral handling of such circumstances.
But one thing should be clear.
People must never become disposable in the name of defending a theological position.
Jesus calls us to truth.
And He calls us to love.
Not truth without compassion.
Not compassion that refuses truth.
Both.
Always both.
And perhaps you have read this far thinking, "This has nothing to do with me. I am not considering polygamy."
But stay with me.
Because the deepest issue has been following us from the first paragraph.
What do we do when God's Word confronts something we want?
Maybe your struggle is not multiple marriages.
Maybe it is a secret relationship you know dishonors Christ.
Maybe it is pornography that you keep promising to leave behind.
Maybe it is resentment toward your spouse.
Maybe it is emotional unfaithfulness that you have convinced yourself is harmless because nothing physical has happened.
Maybe you have used the failures of biblical characters to excuse your own.
"David sinned."
"Solomon had many wives."
"Abraham made mistakes."
"God still used them."
Yes.
God still used them.
But their stories were never written to make sin comfortable.
They reveal the extraordinary mercy of God toward imperfect people.
And the same grace that forgives us also calls us to change.
Romans 6:1–2 asks:
"What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?" (KJV)
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners, received through faith in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection accomplish the salvation we could never earn.
And that grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
Not because obedience purchases God's love.
But because the love of Christ transforms those who belong to Him.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to win theological arguments.
He came to save sinners.
He came for the ashamed.
For the compromised.
For the self-righteous.
For the wounded.
For the people who know the Bible but have forgotten how to surrender.
For the person whose marriage is falling apart.
For the person whose family history is complicated.
For the believer who has been using Scripture as a shield against conviction.
He came for people who need more than a better argument.
People who need a new heart.
And He gave His life on the cross, bearing our sins, and rose again so that all who repent and trust in Him may receive forgiveness and eternal life.
That is why our message is not simply "Defend monogamy."
Our message is Jesus Christ.
The faithful Bridegroom.
The Savior who keeps His covenant.
The Lord whose mercy is greater than our past and whose authority is greater than our preferences.
Maybe today you need to stop asking, "Can I find a biblical example that makes this acceptable?"
And begin asking, "Lord Jesus, what would faithfulness look like in my life?"
That is a much more difficult prayer.
Because sometimes the truth does not simply correct our theology.
It confronts our desires.
Our relationships.
Our pride.
Our excuses.
But the same Savior who calls us to surrender also welcomes those who come to Him.
He does not promise that repentance will erase every earthly consequence.
He does promise that those who come to Him in faith will not be cast out (John 6:37).
And if your heart is being convicted right now, do not run from Him.
Run to Him.
Tell Him the truth.
Tell Him where you have compromised.
Tell Him where you have been confused.
Tell Him where you have hurt someone.
Tell Him where you need wisdom to make things right.

And if you are already carrying the consequences of complicated relationships, seek wise, biblically grounded pastoral counsel that takes seriously the safety, dignity, and responsibilities owed to everyone involved.
There is grace for the repentant.
There is wisdom for the confused.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
And there is hope for families that desperately need His mercy.
Perhaps this is why the words "From Scandal to Grace" matter so deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
The Bible is filled with people whose stories could have ended in shame.
Abraham's failures did not cancel God's promise.
Jacob's broken family did not prevent God from forming a nation.
David's terrible sin did not place him beyond the possibility of repentance.
Peter's denial did not become the final chapter of his life.
And Saul the persecutor became Paul the apostle through the astonishing grace of Jesus Christ.
None of these stories make wrongdoing righteous.
They make God's mercy magnificent.
That is the difference.
We do not glorify the scandal.
We glorify the Savior who redeems sinners.
And if this article has challenged something you believed, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
Not an argument fueled by anger.
Not a contest to see who can quote the most verses.
A conversation that honors Scripture and the people affected by our conclusions.

If you are wrestling with this question, share the passage that troubles you most. If you have a sincere disagreement, explain it with Scripture and humility. If your own family has been affected by complicated marital circumstances, you are welcome to share only what you feel safe sharing.
And if this article has exposed a deeper struggle in your own heart, you can simply comment, "Pray for me."
You do not owe strangers the details of your pain.
But you do not have to pretend that you have everything figured out.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who has heard someone use Abraham, David, or Solomon to justify modern polygamy.
Someone who has been confused by the difference between biblical description and biblical approval.
Someone who thinks the Bible contradicts itself.
Someone who may have walked away from Christianity because they believed Christians were hiding difficult passages.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to attack another family.
But to open a door for thoughtful, Christ-centered discussion.
Because the next time someone says, "But Solomon had seven hundred wives," you may want to return to the passages we examined and consider the whole biblical picture.
There are too many people forming their understanding of Christianity from isolated verses, viral arguments, and confident voices that have never taken the time to read the surrounding passage.
We want to help change that.
One Scripture.
One honest question.
One wounded heart.
One Gospel-centered conversation at a time.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, there is another meaningful way you can stand with us.
Christ has already paid the price for our redemption.
But Scripture does teach that believers may freely and generously support faithful Gospel ministry.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
A willing heart.
It should not replace the responsibility to provide for your family, and it should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe to a local church.
We encourage believers to remain faithful in supporting their local congregations and the needs of their communities.
But if God has placed Gospel Warrior on your heart as another ministry you would like to support, your partnership would mean a great deal.
To keep pointing people back to Scripture.
To keep proclaiming Jesus Christ.
To keep addressing difficult questions without compromising biblical truth or abandoning compassion.
To keep creating resources for people who are hungry to grow deeper in the faith.
We want these resources to keep reaching people who need them.
It is a small way of expressing gratitude for those who choose to help sustain and expand the work.
You are not less valuable to this ministry.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your decision to share a biblical message with one person who needs it matters.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And God's grace cannot be purchased.
We simply want to build a community where believers are nourished by Scripture, sharpened in truth, strengthened through prayer, and continually directed toward Jesus Christ.
Because in the end, the question is not whether we can find a famous biblical man who did something we want to do.
The question is whether we are willing to follow the Lord who came to make us new.
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
And so do we.
Not grace that excuses every desire.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that restores.
Grace that teaches us to surrender.
Grace that changes the direction of a life.
The Bible does not invite us to build our convictions on the worst decisions of its greatest heroes.
It invites us to place our faith in the one perfect Savior to whom its story ultimately points.
Jesus Christ.
The One who never sinned.
The One who loved sacrificially.
The One who gave Himself for His people.
The One who still calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
So when someone asks you again, "If the men of the Old Testament had many wives, why can't Christians today?"
Do not be afraid of the question.
Open the Bible.
Read the stories honestly.
Acknowledge the difficult passages.
Listen to Jesus.
And remember that the greatest example in Scripture is not Abraham, Jacob, David, or Solomon.
It is Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy is not discovering that the heroes of the Bible were broken—it is using their brokenness as an excuse to refuse the healing offered by Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DRAW NEAR TO GOD, AND HE WILL DRAW NEAR TO YOU” — BUT THE VERY NEXT WORDS ARE THE ONES WE KEEP AVOIDING
paragraphs: “DRAW NEAR TO GOD, AND HE WILL DRAW NEAR TO YOU” — BUT THE VERY NEXT WORDS ARE THE ONES WE KEEP AVOIDING

We love the promise of God's presence. But James 4:8 doesn't end with an invitation to feel closer to heaven. It continues with a command that confronts the sin we've learned to hide. And what comes after that may change the way you understand repentance, brokenness, and the grace of Jesus Christ forever.
There is something deeply unsettling about reading a Bible verse you've loved for years… and suddenly realizing you stopped reading right before it confronted you.
You highlighted the promise.
You memorized it.
You whispered it during sleepless nights when heaven felt silent and your prayers seemed to hit the ceiling.
“Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.”
Beautiful words.
Comforting words.

Words that have carried exhausted Christians through hospital corridors, broken marriages, financial disasters, unanswered prayers, and seasons when faith felt like the last fragile thread holding their lives together.
But what if I told you that the very next words are not the comforting embrace many people expect?
What if the same verse that invites you closer to God also exposes the very things keeping your heart divided?
And what if that exposure is not God pushing you away…
…but His mercy calling you home?
Because James did not stop where our favorite inspirational graphics usually stop.
He continued.
And what he wrote next should make every one of us examine our hearts.
James 4:8 says:
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Slowly.
The same verse that says God will draw near also says, “Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.”
There it is.
The part that doesn't fit neatly on a coffee mug.
The part that interrupts our carefully managed religious image.
The part that confronts the person who wants God's comfort without surrendering the sin that is destroying them.
And before you think this is about somebody else…
Remember how easy it is to recognize another person's compromise while defending our own.
We can condemn dishonesty while hiding the truth.
We can sing about forgiveness while secretly feeding resentment.
We can pray for purity while protecting habits we know are poisoning our minds.
We can ask God to bless our relationships while refusing to apologize to the people we've wounded.
We can raise our hands in worship on Sunday and use those same hands to tear someone apart with our words on Monday.
And sometimes the most frightening spiritual condition is not that we have stopped believing in God.
It is that we have learned how to speak His language while resisting His authority.
James is writing to people who know the language of faith.
People who understand religious practices.
People who have heard about God.
And yet their communities are being damaged by envy, selfish ambition, quarrels, and desires that have become more important than obedience.
In James 4:1, he asks where their conflicts come from.
His answer is painfully personal.
The battle outside is connected to desires waging war inside.
By James 4:4, he uses the shocking language of spiritual adultery to confront friendship with the world.
He is not saying that loving people outside the church is wrong. Jesus Himself ate with sinners and came to seek and save the lost.
James is confronting allegiance to a system of desires that opposes God.
A heart that wants God's name attached to a life still governed by pride, envy, and selfish ambition.
Then comes the breathtaking promise of James 4:6:
“But he giveth more grace.”
More grace.
Not less grace.
Not a declaration that every struggling believer is beyond hope.
More grace.
But James immediately reminds us that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.
Then he calls us to submit to God, resist the devil, and draw near.
Do you see the movement?
The invitation to intimacy is surrounded by the call to surrender.
And that changes everything.
Because the biblical invitation is not simply, “Come closer so you can feel better.”
It is, “Come to the God whose grace is greater than your sin, and stop pretending your sin is harmless.”
There is a difference between wanting God to comfort your conscience and allowing God to transform your heart.
And that difference can be painful.
Especially when the thing God is confronting is the thing you have spent years justifying.
Maybe it's the bitterness you call discernment.
Maybe it's the pride you call confidence.
Maybe it's the relationship you keep defending even though you know it is pulling you away from obedience.
Maybe it's the secret habit that has slowly become your refuge whenever life hurts.
Maybe it's the dishonesty you excuse because you're afraid of what the truth might cost you.
Or maybe it's something quieter.
You have become so busy doing things associated with God that you barely spend time with God Himself.
You know how to post Scripture.
You know how to encourage others.
You know how to appear spiritually strong.
But behind the screen…
Behind the smile…
Behind the familiar “I'm blessed”…
You are tired of pretending.
And somewhere deep inside, you wonder whether the Lord would still welcome you if everything hidden were brought into the light.
Listen carefully.
The answer to that question is found not in your ability to manufacture a spotless past, but in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Yet to understand the invitation properly, we need to listen to what James actually wrote.
In the original Greek, the opening command of James 4:8 is:
ἐγγίσατε τῷ θεῷ, καὶ ἐγγιεῖ ὑμῖν
Engisate tō Theō, kai engiei hymin.
“Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.”
The verb ἐγγίσατε (engisate) is an imperative from the Greek verb engizō, meaning to approach or come near.
James is issuing a command.
He is calling his readers to respond.
And the following verb, ἐγγιεῖ (engiei), expresses the promise that God will draw near to them.
But the next two commands are just as important:
καθαρίσατε χεῖρας, ἁμαρτωλοί, καὶ ἁγνίσατε καρδίας, δίψυχοι.
Katharisate cheiras, hamartōloi, kai hagnisate kardias, dipsychoi.
“Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.”
James is drawing on the biblical language of cleansing and purity.
The hands point naturally toward conduct—what we do.
The heart points toward our inward life—our desires, motives, and loyalties.
And the word δίψυχοι (dipsychoi) is especially revealing.
It literally combines the ideas of “two” and “soul” or “inner life.”
It describes someone divided in allegiance, unstable in devotion.
James also uses this word in James 1:8 when speaking of a double-minded person.
This does not mean that every Christian who experiences doubt, anxiety, temptation, or emotional struggle is automatically living in deliberate rebellion.
James is confronting divided loyalty.
The heart that tries to hold on to God while refusing to release what stands against Him.
And perhaps that is why this verse cuts so deeply.
Because we know what it feels like to be divided.
To love Jesus and still wrestle with temptation.
To desire holiness and still fall.
To long for peace while repeatedly returning to things that steal it.
To want God's will until His will challenges something we desperately want to keep.
But here is where we must be careful.
James is not teaching that sinners must make themselves morally perfect before God will receive them.
If that were the message, none of us could approach Him.
The very passage begins with the declaration that God gives more grace.
The call to cleanse our hands and purify our hearts is a call to genuine repentance, not a demand to purchase God's acceptance through flawless behavior.
Scripture is clear that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And that same grace does not leave us unchanged (Ephesians 2:10; Titus 2:11–12).
We do not repent to make Jesus willing to save us.
We repent because the Savior calls sinners to turn to Him.
We do not earn cleansing through religious performance.
We come to the One whose blood cleanses us from sin.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Notice who is faithful to forgive.
God.
Notice who cleanses.
God.
And notice what we are called to do.
Confess.
Stop hiding.
Stop defending the darkness.
Bring it into the light.
That is why the next verse in James is so uncomfortable.
James 4:9 says:
“Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness.” (KJV)
Those are not words designed to make a casual reader comfortable.
But neither are they a command for Christians to live in perpetual misery.
James is addressing people who have treated serious sin with spiritual carelessness.
He calls them to recognize the weight of what they have been doing.
There is a kind of laughter that comes from genuine joy in the Lord.
And there is a kind of laughter that comes from refusing to take evil seriously.
James is confronting the second.
He is not condemning happiness.
He is confronting unrepentance.
Because sometimes the first evidence that a heart is awakening is that it can no longer laugh at what once seemed harmless.
The joke stops being funny.
The excuse stops sounding convincing.
The secret stops feeling safe.
And suddenly the person who has spent years saying, “It's not that serious,” begins to whisper…
“Lord, what have I done?”
That moment can be terrifying.
But it can also become the beginning of restoration.
Second Corinthians 7:10 distinguishes godly sorrow, which produces repentance leading to salvation, from worldly sorrow, which produces death.
Not every tear is repentance.
And repentance does not always arrive with tears.
The issue is not how dramatic our emotions become.
The issue is whether sorrow turns us toward God.
Worldly sorrow may grieve over consequences, embarrassment, or exposure.
Godly sorrow recognizes sin for what it is and turns toward the mercy of God.
One can leave a person trapped in shame.
The other leads toward the Savior.
And perhaps nowhere is that distinction more beautifully illustrated than in one of the most heartbreaking stories Jesus ever told.
A young man demanded his inheritance from his father.
Then he left home.
He wanted the father's gifts without the father's presence.
He wanted freedom without accountability.
He wanted the pleasures of a distant country without considering what would happen when the money ran out.
And for a while, everything probably seemed wonderful.
Until it didn't.
The inheritance disappeared.
A famine came.
The friends, the pleasures, the illusion of control…
None of them could save him.
Eventually he found himself feeding pigs, so hungry that he longed for their food.
And then Luke 15:17 records a remarkable turning point:
“And when he came to himself…” (KJV)
What a phrase.
He came to himself.
The illusion broke.
He finally saw the truth.
He had traded the security of his father's house for a freedom that left him starving.
And he decided to return.
Not with a speech about how unfair life had been.
Not with excuses.
But with a confession.
He had sinned against heaven and before his father.
Yet while he was still a great way off, his father saw him.
And ran.
And embraced him.
And kissed him.
The son had prepared to ask for the place of a servant.
But the father called for a robe, a ring, sandals, and a celebration.
Do not miss the beauty of this.
The son did not return because he had already repaired everything he had broken.
He returned because he finally stopped running.
And the father's welcome revealed a mercy greater than the son's shame.
That parable is not a promise that every earthly relationship will be restored immediately, or that repentance removes every consequence.
It is a revelation of God's joy over the sinner who repents.
Jesus Himself says there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7).
And this is why James 4:8 must never be preached without the Gospel.
Because if all we hear is “Cleanse your hands,” we may begin to imagine that Christianity is simply a desperate attempt to scrub ourselves clean enough to deserve God's love.
But the cross tells a different story.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, came into a world of sinners.
He did not merely deliver moral advice from a safe distance.
He entered our brokenness.
He endured rejection.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He was crucified.
And on that cross, He bore our sins, accomplishing what our religious effort could never accomplish.
First Peter 3:18 says:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God…” (KJV)
Read those final words again.
“That he might bring us to God.”
There is the heart of the invitation.
Jesus did not die merely so that we could feel spiritual during a worship song.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
The way back is not paved with our perfection.
It is opened through His sacrifice.
Hebrews 10:19–22 connects our confidence to enter God's presence with the blood of Jesus and calls believers to draw near with sincere hearts and the assurance of faith.
And the Greek verb used for drawing near in Hebrews 10:22, προσερχώμεθα (proserchōmetha), is not the same verb James uses.
Yet the passages beautifully complement each other.
James calls us away from divided loyalty and toward humble repentance.
Hebrews reminds us that our confidence in approaching God rests upon the priestly work of Christ.
Together they protect us from two dangerous distortions.
Grace without repentance becomes permission to remain unchanged.
Repentance without grace becomes an exhausting attempt to save ourselves.
But biblical Christianity offers something infinitely better.
A Savior who forgives sinners and transforms them.
A Lord who welcomes the repentant and teaches them to walk in holiness.
A Redeemer who does not excuse our sin, yet does not abandon those who come to Him in faith.
And that brings us to the words immediately after James 4:9.
Words so beautiful that they should never be separated from the hard ones before them.
James 4:10 says:
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.” (KJV)
There it is.
The destination of the passage.
Not humiliation without hope.
Not endless condemnation.
Not spiritual despair.
Humility before the Lord.
And His promise to lift up the humble.
The Greek says:
ταπεινώθητε ἐνώπιον κυρίου, καὶ ὑψώσει ὑμᾶς.
Tapeinōthēte enōpion Kyriou, kai hypsōsei hymas.
“Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.”
The word ταπεινώθητε (tapeinōthēte) calls for humbling oneself.
The promise ὑψώσει (hypsōsei) means that He will lift up or exalt.
This is not a guarantee of immediate financial success, public recognition, or the disappearance of earthly suffering.
James is not offering a formula for worldly advancement.
He is declaring that God honors humility rather than pride.
And what a breathtaking reversal that is.
The world tells you to protect your image.
Jesus calls you to walk in truth.
The world tells you never to admit weakness.
The Gospel teaches you to depend upon grace.
The world tells you that being exposed is the end of your story.
But in Christ, confession and repentance can become the beginning of a new chapter.
Maybe the most dangerous thing you have been doing is not the sin itself alone.
Maybe it is the exhausting effort to keep that sin hidden while maintaining the appearance that everything is fine.
Because secrecy can become a prison.
And pride can make the prison feel like protection.
You learn to smile at church.
You learn which Bible verses to post.
You learn how to say “God is good” while avoiding the conversation you know you need to have.
You become skilled at managing what people see.
But when the room grows quiet and the phone screen goes dark…
You know.
You know the thing you keep returning to.
You know the apology you keep postponing.
You know the forgiveness you keep resisting.
You know the truth you have been afraid to face.
And perhaps tonight, the Holy Spirit is using these ancient words to confront something you have kept buried.
Not so that you will despair.
But so that you will stop running from the One who can forgive and restore you.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is not permission to make peace with sin.
It is freedom from the crushing verdict that sin deserves, because Christ has borne it for those who belong to Him.
And Romans 8 continues by describing life through the Spirit.
The Gospel does not merely change our standing before God.
It begins changing the way we live.
So what does drawing near to God actually look like when you have failed?
Sometimes it looks like closing the app that keeps feeding your temptation.
Sometimes it looks like finally telling the truth.
Sometimes it looks like ending a pattern of deception and accepting the consequences.
Sometimes it looks like asking forgiveness without adding a long explanation of why you were justified.
Sometimes it looks like seeking help from a mature Christian, pastor, or trusted counselor because you know the battle has become too heavy to fight in isolation.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible again after months of avoidance.
And sometimes it looks like kneeling beside your bed with no eloquent prayer left.
Only these words:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There is no magic in the length of the prayer.
No special power in the volume of your voice.
The power belongs to the Savior to whom you are praying.
The tax collector in Luke 18:13 could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
He pleaded:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” (KJV)
And Jesus said that man went home justified rather than the self-righteous Pharisee who trusted in his own goodness.
Why?
Because the way to God is not self-exaltation.
It is humble dependence upon His mercy.
And if you are reading this while carrying years of regret, there is something else you need to hear.
Your past may have consequences.
Some relationships may need time to heal.
Some trust may need to be rebuilt.
Some wounds may require patient care, accountability, and difficult conversations.
Grace does not erase the need for responsibility.
But your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity.
The apostle Paul once persecuted the church.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
David committed grievous sins and faced painful consequences.
Their stories are not identical, and Scripture does not minimize what they did.
But each reveals, in different ways, that human failure is not greater than God's power to show mercy and accomplish His purposes.
And above every human testimony stands the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
The One who makes redemption possible.
The One who turns enemies into reconciled children of God.
The One who calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
That is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because the past never matters.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the sin that brought us down.
He is able to forgive.
He is able to restore.
He is able to transform.
And He is worthy of the life we once tried to live without Him.
Maybe that is why you needed to read beyond the first half of James 4:8.
You came looking for a promise that God would come near.
And you found a call to surrender.
But hidden inside that confrontation was a mercy you might have missed.
God does not invite you to keep pretending.
He invites you to come into the light.
Not because the light will flatter you.
But because the light reveals the truth.
And Jesus Christ is the Savior who meets repentant sinners with grace.
Not as a test of how spiritual you appear.
Not because a public comment can prove the condition of your soul.
But because sometimes an honest conversation begins when someone finally admits they are struggling.
What is harder for you right now: trusting that God will forgive you, or surrendering the thing you know He is calling you to release?
You don't have to expose private details.
You don't have to tell strangers what belongs in a confidential conversation with a trusted person.
Someone else may need to hear that repentance and restoration are possible.
Let this become more than another article people read and forget.
Let it become a place where struggling believers can encourage one another to return to Christ.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't ignore that thought.
Perhaps it is a brother who has quietly withdrawn from fellowship.
A sister who feels disqualified because of her past.
A friend who has stopped praying because shame convinced them that God no longer wants to hear their voice.
Or someone who has never understood why Christians speak so passionately about the grace of Jesus.
You never know who is silently searching for a reason to believe that coming home to God is still possible.
Not because the article itself has power.
But because the Word of God deserves to be revisited long after an emotional moment has passed.
Return to James 4:1–10.
Read the entire passage.
Examine your heart.
Pray over it.
And let Scripture, not merely an inspirational quotation, shape your understanding of repentance and grace.
This is also why we continue building Gospel Warrior.
Not simply to produce more Christian content.
But to keep placing Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources within reach of people who desperately need the truth of Jesus Christ.
Some are new believers trying to understand the Bible.
Some are parents searching for resources to strengthen their families.
Some are exhausted Christians trying to rebuild neglected spiritual habits.
Some are people who have been wounded, confused, or discouraged and are looking for trustworthy biblical encouragement.
And some are still standing at the edge of faith, wondering whether the Gospel could truly change a life like theirs.
We want those resources to remain accessible.
Because biblical nourishment should not become a privilege reserved only for people who can afford to pay.
And if this ministry has encouraged you, strengthened your understanding of Scripture, or helped you return to the Lord in a difficult season, I want to invite you to consider something meaningful.
Not because a financial contribution proves your faith.
God's grace cannot be purchased, and no Christian should be made to feel that paying a ministry is a condition of glorifying Him.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a sincere act of generosity and partnership in the work of making biblical truth available to others.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully—not under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is a voluntary ministry contribution, not a substitute for every biblical responsibility connected with tithes, offerings, or supporting your local church.
There are real costs involved in maintaining, developing, and expanding ministry resources.
It is the opportunity to stand alongside a ministry seeking to point people toward Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, spiritual growth, and the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
If you are financially able, believe in this mission, and want to help it continue reaching more people, prayerfully consider becoming a monthly supporter here:
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Use the free resources.
A sincere prayer, a thoughtful comment, a personal invitation, or a Facebook share can help bring biblical encouragement to someone who might otherwise never encounter it.
And your generosity, whatever form it takes, should flow from love rather than fear.
Because the message we are carrying is not that people can buy their way closer to God.
It is that Jesus Christ has opened the way for sinners to draw near through His grace.
That is the message worth protecting.
That is the Gospel worth sharing.
And that is why we keep pointing people back to the cross.
But before this ends, I want to return to the verse where we began.
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.”
Perhaps you have been reading those words for years while imagining that God was waiting for you to become impressive enough to approach Him.
Perhaps you thought you needed to fix every weakness, defeat every temptation, and silence every painful memory before you could pray with confidence.
But the Gospel says our hope rests in Christ.
Come honestly.
Come humbly.
Come ready to turn from sin.
Come trusting in the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not confuse admiration for Christian teaching with saving faith.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
He is not merely an example to admire.
He is the Lord to whom we must surrender and the Savior in whom we must trust.
And if you already belong to Him but have wandered, do not let pride keep you in the distant country.
Return.
Confess.
Seek His forgiveness.
Take the next faithful step.
There is no promise that obedience will be painless.
But there is a Savior who is faithful.
A High Priest who understands our weakness.
A Lord whose mercy is greater than the darkness we are finally willing to confess.
Maybe tonight there will be no dramatic music.
No extraordinary sign.
No sudden emotional rush.
Maybe there will only be a quiet room, an open Bible, and a tired heart finally telling the truth.

“Lord Jesus, I have been divided. I have defended things I should have surrendered. I have sought comfort while resisting Your correction. Forgive me. Cleanse me. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. I place my trust in You. Lead me in the truth. Amen.”
And tomorrow, keep walking.
Keep reading.
Keep praying.
Keep obeying.
Keep depending on grace.
Because drawing near to God is not a technique for producing a momentary feeling.
It is a life of faith and repentance, made possible through Jesus Christ.
James began by exposing the conflict within the human heart.
He confronted pride.
He called for surrender.
He commanded repentance.
And then he left us with a promise:
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.”
So don't stop reading at the comforting half of the verse.
Read the confrontation.
Read the call to repentance.
Read the promise of grace.
And above all, look to the Savior who makes reconciliation with God possible.
Because sometimes the words that wound our pride are the very words God uses to awaken our hearts.
The door you were afraid to approach was opened by the Savior who gave His life to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID PAUL SAY TO STOP ASSOCIATING WITH SOMEONE WHO CLAIMS TO FOLLOW JESUS BUT REFUSES TO TURN AWAY FROM SEXUAL SIN?
paragraphs: WHY DID PAUL SAY TO STOP ASSOCIATING WITH SOMEONE WHO CLAIMS TO FOLLOW JESUS BUT REFUSES TO TURN AWAY FROM SEXUAL SIN?
The Warning Most Churches Are Afraid to Preach, the Truth Many Christians Misunderstand, and the Heartbreaking Reason Biblical Love Sometimes Requires Walking Away.
“I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators.” — 1 Corinthians 5:9 (KJV)
Imagine sitting across from someone you love.
Someone who knows the Scriptures. Someone who raises their hands during worship. Someone who says, “Jesus is Lord,” and perhaps has said those words for years.
But there is something you cannot ignore anymore.
They are openly living in sexual sin.
Not because they stumbled once and are desperately trying to get back up.
Not because they are struggling with temptation and crying out to God for deliverance.
But because they have decided that what Scripture calls sin is no longer something they need to repent of.
And when someone lovingly confronts them, they respond:
“Only God can judge me.”
“Jesus ate with sinners.”
“Stop being so religious.”
“God knows my heart.”
Then comes the question that can tear a Christian friendship, a family, or even an entire church apart.
What does love require you to do when someone claims to belong to Jesus but refuses to listen to Jesus?
Do you stay silent because you are afraid of losing them?
Do you keep affirming their choices because you do not want to appear judgmental?
Or is there a moment when continuing to act as though nothing is wrong becomes a form of spiritual dishonesty?
The Apostle Paul answered that question in one of the most uncomfortable passages in the New Testament.
And before you decide his words sound too harsh, you need to understand something.
Paul was not writing because he hated sinners.
He was writing because he understood what unrepentant sin could do to a soul, to a church, and to the credibility of the Gospel.
But there is another truth hidden in the context that makes this passage even more powerful.
The same Paul who commanded the church to remove an unrepentant person also taught that a repentant sinner must be welcomed back with love.
That changes how we read everything.
Because this is not ultimately a story about who deserves to be thrown away.
It is about what happens when a church stops taking sin seriously—and what grace looks like when someone finally comes home.
To understand Paul's warning, we must return to Corinth.
The church in Corinth was surrounded by a culture where sexual immorality was widespread. Yet Paul was not primarily concerned that sinful behavior existed outside the church.
He was confronting something far more disturbing.
Inside the Christian community, a man was involved in a sexual relationship with his father's wife.
Paul described the situation in 1 Corinthians 5:1, using the Greek expression γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν (gynaika tina tou patros echein), meaning that someone had his father's wife.
The wording does not establish every detail of the relationship, but it clearly describes a grave sexual violation.
And the church's response?
Instead of mourning, they were arrogant.
Paul writes:
Think about that.
The scandal was not only what one man was doing.
The scandal was that the church had become comfortable with it.
They had confused tolerance with maturity.
They had mistaken the absence of correction for the presence of love.
And Paul was telling them that their spiritual pride had blinded them to the danger.
There is something terrifying about a church that can still sing about holiness while refusing to confront serious, unrepentant sin within its own fellowship.
Not because the church is supposed to be filled with perfect people.
It never was.
But because the church is supposed to be a community where sinners are being transformed by the grace of Jesus Christ.
And transformation becomes impossible to celebrate honestly when repentance is treated as optional.
Then Paul writes the words that many Christians struggle to understand.
“I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators.” — 1 Corinthians 5:9 (KJV)
The Greek expression translated “to company with” is συναναμίγνυσθαι (synanamignysthai).
It carries the sense of associating or mixing together with others.
But here is the crucial detail.
Paul immediately explains that he does not mean Christians must stop associating with every sexually immoral person in the world.
He writes:
Read that again.
Paul is explicitly rejecting the idea that Christians should isolate themselves from unbelievers who live contrary to biblical morality.
If that were the standard, Christians would have to leave the world entirely.
How could we evangelize?
How could we show compassion?
How could we serve our neighbors?
How could we follow Jesus, who was criticized for welcoming tax collectors and sinners?
Jesus did not avoid people because their lives were broken.
He came to seek and save the lost.
And His church must never forget that.
But then Paul makes a distinction.

“But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.” — 1 Corinthians 5:11 (KJV)
The Greek expression ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος (adelphos onomazomenos) refers to someone who is called or identified as a brother.
In this context, Paul is speaking about a person who professes membership in the Christian community.
And the distinction matters enormously.
Paul is not saying:
“Reject anyone who struggles with sexual temptation.”
He is not saying:
“Abandon every believer who has fallen.”
He is not saying:
“Treat everyone with a painful past as spiritually contaminated.”

He is confronting the serious problem of someone claiming Christian identity while continuing in conduct plainly contrary to the Gospel, without repentance, and while the church treats the situation as acceptable.
The issue is not simply that a sinner exists among sinners.
The issue is that someone is claiming the authority of Christ while refusing His call to repentance.
And before anyone uses this passage as permission to become cruel, we need to remember something.
Paul did not limit his warning to sexual immorality.
He also named greed, idolatry, abusive speech, drunkenness, and exploitation.
The Greek word πλεονέκτης (pleonektēs) refers to a greedy or covetous person.
The word λοίδορος (loidoros) refers to someone who reviles or abuses others verbally.
The word ἅρπαξ (harpax) describes someone who takes advantage of others through robbery or extortion.
This should make every self-righteous reader uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to condemn sexual sin while excusing greed.
Easy to expose adultery while overlooking cruelty.
Easy to confront another person's immoral relationship while ignoring our own dishonest business practices, abusive words, or exploitation of vulnerable people.
Paul did not give the church permission to choose a favorite category of sinner to condemn.
He called the church to integrity.
And integrity begins when we allow Scripture to examine us before we use it to examine someone else.
Jesus Himself warned against trying to remove a speck from another person's eye while ignoring the plank in our own (Matthew 7:3–5).
That does not mean Christians must never correct anyone.
It means correction must begin with humility.
Because there is a difference between someone who is broken over sin and someone who is determined to defend it.
Imagine two believers.
One has fallen into sexual sin.
They are ashamed. They know they have disobeyed God. They are not proud of what happened.
They confess it.
They ask for prayer.
They seek accountability.
They may still be struggling, and the road to restoration may be difficult.
But their heart is turning toward Christ.
Now imagine another person.
They openly continue in sexual immorality.
They refuse biblical correction.
They insist that repentance is unnecessary.
