Because if the point of the parable were simply to accumulate as much financial wealth as possible, the servant who produced ten talents would appear twice as successful as the servant who produced four.
But Jesus gives them the same commendation.
The measure of faithfulness is not the size of the fortune.
It is the servant's response to the master.
And that brings us to the third servant.
The one who buried his talent.
The one whose story makes this parable so unsettling.
He approaches the master and says:

"Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed: And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine." (Matthew 25:24–25, KJV)
"I was afraid."
Four words.
And suddenly the parable becomes painfully personal.
Because not everyone who buries what God has entrusted to them is openly rebellious.
Sometimes people bury things because they are terrified.
Terrified of failure.
Terrified of rejection.
Terrified of being criticized.
Terrified of losing what little they have.
Terrified of stepping into a calling that might cost them their comfort.
Sometimes fear dresses itself as responsibility.
Sometimes disobedience hides behind the language of caution.
Sometimes we call it waiting for the right moment when, deep inside, we know we are refusing to move.
And sometimes we become so concerned about preserving what belongs to God that we never actually use it for His purposes.
But we must be careful here.
Jesus is not condemning every cautious person, every failed entrepreneur, or every believer who has suffered financial loss.
The third servant's problem is not simply that he failed to generate a profit.
His words reveal a deeply distorted relationship with his master.
He describes the master as harsh, acts from fear, and refuses the responsibility entrusted to him.
The master's reply exposes the inconsistency of the servant's excuse. If he truly believed what he claimed, he could at least have placed the money with bankers.
The issue is not that every Christian must invest money in a bank or start a business.
The issue is that the servant's professed understanding of his master produced no faithful response at all.
And the ending is severe.
The talent is taken from him.
He is cast into outer darkness.
There is weeping and gnashing of teeth.
This is not a harmless motivational story about improving your financial habits.
It is a warning about accountability before the returning Lord.
To understand why, we must remember where Jesus placed the parable.
Matthew 24–25 contains Jesus' teaching about His coming, the need for watchfulness, and the judgment that follows.
Immediately before the talents, Jesus tells the parable of the ten virgins.
Immediately afterward, He describes the Son of Man coming in glory and separating the sheep from the goats.
The setting is not a business seminar.
It is the kingdom of heaven.
The returning master, within this larger context, points us toward the return of Christ and the reality that His servants must answer for how they have lived during His apparent absence.
That is why reducing this parable to "God wants you to become rich" misses its central force.
Yes, the story uses real money.
Yes, it commends productive action rather than passive neglect.
Yes, it teaches that what is entrusted to us carries responsibility.
But a story that uses financial investment as its imagery does not automatically establish financial enrichment as its ultimate spiritual command.
Jesus regularly used familiar earthly situations to reveal eternal realities.
He spoke of farmers and seeds.
Shepherds and sheep.
Fathers and sons.
Debtors and creditors.
Kings and servants.
And here, He speaks of entrusted wealth.
The financial details are important to the story, but the greater question is what faithfulness to the Master looks like while we await His return.
And Scripture refuses to let us confuse that faithfulness with the pursuit of riches.
In fact, Jesus gives a warning so direct that it should make every prosperity-centered interpretation tremble.
"No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon." (Matthew 6:24, KJV)
The Greek word translated "mammon" is μαμωνᾶς (mamōnas), referring to wealth or riches, treated here as a rival master.
Jesus does not say money is inherently evil.
He says wealth can become something you serve.
Something that claims your loyalty.
Something that commands your decisions.
Something that slowly takes the place in your heart that belongs to God alone.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you can speak constantly about God while quietly organizing your entire life around money.
You can quote Scripture over your investments.
You can pray over your business.
You can give generously in public.
And still have a heart that trusts wealth more than Christ.
Jesus says in Luke 12:15:
"Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." (KJV)
Not the abundance.
Not the house.
Not the car.
Not the investment portfolio.
Not the number of zeros in your savings account.
Your life is worth more than what you own.
And if that sounds obvious, remember how easily we forget it.
We admire people because they are wealthy.
We assume someone is blessed because their business is expanding.
We call expensive possessions "favor."
We look at someone struggling financially and sometimes wonder what they did wrong.
But consider the apostle Paul.
He knew abundance.
He knew hunger.
He knew comfort.
He knew deprivation.
In Philippians 4:12, he writes:
Then he explains the secret of his contentment.
"I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." (Philippians 4:13, KJV)
That famous verse is not originally a promise that every Christian can become financially successful.
It is Paul's testimony that Christ strengthens him to remain faithful through changing circumstances, including poverty and plenty.
The strength is in Christ.
Not in the balance of the account.
Not in the certainty of the next paycheck.
Not in the guarantee that everything will work out financially.
Christ Himself is enough to sustain His servant.
And that should bring comfort to someone reading this who has been silently ashamed of struggling.
Your unpaid bills do not automatically mean God has abandoned you.
Your modest income does not make you a second-class Christian.
Your inability to afford what others possess is not evidence that Jesus loves you less.
The Son of God entered our world without the earthly wealth people so often associate with success.
He was laid in a manger.
He lived without the security of worldly riches.
He had nowhere to lay His head (Luke 9:58).
And He died on a cross while soldiers divided His garments.
Yet no life has ever been more faithful.
No life has ever glorified the Father more perfectly.
No life has ever produced greater eternal fruit.
If financial wealth were the supreme evidence of divine approval, how would we explain the earthly life of Jesus Christ?
We couldn't.
Because the Gospel does not teach that the richest person is the most righteous.
It teaches that the perfectly righteous One gave Himself for sinners.
And that is where the parable begins to reach beyond financial stewardship into the deepest question of our existence.
What have we done with what belongs to God?
Not merely our money.
Our time.
Our opportunities.
Our influence.
Our strength.
Our relationships.
Our knowledge of the truth.
Our access to Scripture.
Our ability to encourage someone who is close to giving up.
Our willingness to forgive.
Our courage to speak about Christ.
Our capacity to serve.
The parable itself speaks specifically of entrusted money, but the broader biblical principle of stewardship reaches into every area of life.
First Peter 4:10 tells believers:
"As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God." (KJV)
The Greek word οἰκονόμοι (oikonomoi) means stewards or managers—people entrusted with responsibilities that ultimately belong to another.
A steward is not the owner.
And that is a truth we desperately need to recover.
Your possessions are not your ultimate identity.
Your abilities are not grounds for self-worship.
Your opportunities are not simply tools for building your own kingdom.
Whatever God has entrusted to you should be handled with gratitude, wisdom, and a heart willing to honor Him.
And sometimes the most faithful use of what God gives you will not make you richer.
Sometimes it will cost you.
Sometimes faithfulness means giving when you would rather keep.
Sometimes it means refusing a profitable opportunity because it requires dishonesty.
Sometimes it means paying your employees fairly when exploiting them would increase your margins.
Sometimes it means closing a corrupt deal even though you desperately need the money.
Sometimes it means spending your evening with a grieving friend instead of working another hour.
Sometimes it means raising your children in the truth when nobody outside your home sees the sacrifice.
Sometimes it means caring for an aging parent.
Sometimes it means supporting a struggling family.
Sometimes it means speaking the Gospel to someone who may reject you.
And sometimes it means remaining faithful through a season in which you have very little to show the world.
No applause.
No impressive financial breakthrough.
No public recognition.
Just obedience.
Quiet.
Costly.
Beautiful obedience.
Do not misunderstand.
Scripture does not condemn earning money honestly, building a business, practicing wise financial management, or increasing resources through diligent work.
Proverbs commends diligence and prudence.
The apostle Paul instructs believers to work responsibly and provide for their households.
First Timothy 5:8 speaks seriously about providing for one's own family.
Money can feed the hungry.
Provide shelter.
Fund Bible translations.
Help churches serve their communities.
Support Christian teaching.
Care for widows and orphans.
And relieve genuine suffering.
Wealth, when handled faithfully, can become an instrument of extraordinary generosity.
But there is a difference between possessing wealth and being possessed by wealth.
There is a difference between building a business to serve people and using people to build an empire around yourself.
There is a difference between asking God to bless your work and treating God as a means of obtaining riches.
Paul writes:
Notice the warning.
It concerns those determined to become rich.
Then comes the verse so frequently misquoted.
"For the love of money is the root of all evil..." (1 Timothy 6:10, KJV)
The underlying Greek describes the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils; the verse is not teaching that money itself is the source of every evil act.
The Greek word φιλαργυρία (philargyria) means love of money or avarice.
Not money.
The love of it.
The craving.
The devotion.
The appetite that is never satisfied.
The willingness to compromise whatever must be compromised to obtain more.
And then Paul tells Timothy what the wealthy should actually do.
"That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate." (1 Timothy 6:18, KJV)
Rich in good works.
Imagine if that became our definition of a prosperous Christian life.
Not simply how much we accumulated.
But how much love our resources expressed.
How much suffering our generosity relieved.
How faithfully we served.
How honestly we worked.
How freely we gave.
How completely we surrendered our hearts to Jesus.
And before someone uses this article to condemn every wealthy believer, remember that Scripture also contains faithful people who possessed considerable resources.
Abraham had great wealth.
Job possessed substantial resources, suffered devastating loss, and later received restoration.
Joseph of Arimathea was a rich man who honored Jesus by providing his tomb.
Lydia, a dealer in purple goods, responded to the Gospel and opened her household to believers.
Wealth is not automatic evidence of wickedness.
Poverty is not automatic evidence of holiness.
The heart matters.
The source of the wealth matters.
The use of the wealth matters.
And above all, the Lordship of Jesus Christ matters.
But there is another danger here.
One that can enter even Christian ministries.
We must never turn the Parable of the Talents into a weapon for pressuring people to give money.
And we must be particularly careful with the sacred language of tithes and offerings.
In the Old Testament, tithing belonged to Israel's covenant life and supported the Levites and other prescribed needs.
In the New Testament, believers are called to generous, willing, purposeful giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
The Greek word ἱλαρόν (hilaron) means cheerful or glad.
Not manipulated.
Not threatened.
Not shamed.
Not forced by fear that God will withdraw His favor.
Cheerful.
It can support the creation of biblical resources, discipleship materials, teaching, outreach, and encouragement.
It can become one expression of a believer's generosity.
But it cannot purchase spiritual favor.
It cannot replace responsibility to one's family or local church.
It cannot guarantee financial blessings.
And it must never be confused with the price of God's grace.
Because grace has already been purchased.
Not by your monthly contribution.
But by the blood of Jesus Christ.
And that brings us to the scandal at the center of Christianity.
We have been talking about servants and their accountability.
About faithfulness and failure.
About responsibility and judgment.
But what happens when we examine our own lives honestly?
What happens when we realize how often we have wasted time, misused opportunities, withheld generosity, and pursued things that could never satisfy our souls?
What happens when we discover that we are not as faithful as we imagined?
Because if we are honest, every one of us has buried something.
Perhaps you buried a calling because you were afraid.
Perhaps you buried your compassion beneath years of disappointment.
Perhaps you buried your integrity for financial gain.
Perhaps you buried your generosity because you became obsessed with security.
Perhaps you buried your faith beneath a mountain of religious appearances.
Perhaps you buried the truth because speaking it might cost you something.
Or perhaps you have spent years building a life that looks successful to everyone except the One who knows your heart.
And here is the question that should make us tremble.
If Jesus returned today, what would He find?
Would He find a heart surrendered to Him?
Or would He find a person who had learned how to speak the language of Christianity while living for another master?
The Parable of the Talents does not give us permission to dismiss judgment.
Jesus' warning is real.
The accountability is real.
The danger of false discipleship is real.
But the Gospel also tells us something the parable must not be separated from.
The very Lord who will return as Judge first came as Savior.
The One who calls His servants to faithfulness is the One who lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
And where sinners have failed, Jesus Christ did not fail.
He obeyed where we rebelled.
He loved where we acted selfishly.
He remained faithful where we were faithless.
He carried our sins to the cross.
And He rose from the dead, conquering sin and death.
This is not a message that our works can earn salvation.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
And the very next verse says:
"For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." (Ephesians 2:10, KJV)
Do you see the order?
Grace first.
Then the transformed life.
We do not work faithfully so that Jesus will finally agree to save us.
We are saved by grace through faith, and God's grace begins transforming how we live.
Good works are not the purchase price of salvation.
They are the fruit of a life being renewed by Christ.
This is why the Parable of the Talents must never be preached as though salvation belongs to those who generate the highest financial return.
Its warning belongs within Jesus' larger call to genuine, watchful, obedient discipleship.
And its promise points toward something money could never buy.
"Enter thou into the joy of thy lord."
Not merely into greater wealth.
Not into a luxury mansion purchased by superior investment decisions.
Into the joy of the Lord.
Imagine that moment.
Not the applause of the world.
Not the admiration of people who once underestimated you.
Not the satisfaction of proving you were financially successful.
But the joy of belonging to Christ.
The joy of being received by the Savior.
The joy of a life that was not lived in vain.
And perhaps that changes what you need to do today.
Perhaps you do need to become more diligent with your finances.
Perhaps you need to stop wasting money.
Perhaps you need to learn how to save, plan, invest wisely, and provide responsibly for your family.
Those can be faithful decisions.
But perhaps your greatest need is something far deeper.
Perhaps you need to repent of loving money more than God.
Perhaps you need to stop measuring your worth by your income.
Perhaps you need to forgive yourself for a financial failure and bring your shame to Christ.
Perhaps you need to stop envying people whose lives you only see through photographs.
Perhaps you need to give something away.
Perhaps you need to apologize to someone you neglected while chasing success.
Perhaps you need to open your Bible again.
Perhaps you need to pray for the first time in months without asking God for anything material.
Just to be near Him.
Just to remember who He is.
Just to say, "Lord Jesus, my life belongs to You."
Because one day, everything you have accumulated will pass out of your hands.
Every possession.
Every account.
Every title.
Every earthly achievement.
And what will matter most is not whether the world considered you successful.
It will be whether you truly belonged to Christ.
Whether your faith was genuine.
Whether His grace had transformed your life.
Whether you lived as a servant awaiting your Master.
And whether the resources entrusted to you were handled in ways that honored Him.
If this truth has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past it.
You do not need to perform spirituality for the people reading the comments.
And if Jesus has been teaching you that your worth is not measured by money, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Someone else may desperately need that encouragement.
Not because every word here is easy.
But because when fear, comparison, ambition, or financial pressure begins speaking louder than Scripture, you may need to return to these truths.
There may be a friend who has spent years believing that financial struggle means spiritual failure.
There may be someone who has confused greed with faith.
There may be a believer who has buried their God-given responsibilities beneath fear.
There may even be someone who has never understood that Jesus offers something infinitely greater than wealth.

And if this message has helped you see Scripture more clearly, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow along.

We want this community to be a place where Scripture is opened carefully, where difficult questions are answered honestly, where the wounded find encouragement, and where every message ultimately points to Jesus Christ.
That is also why your voluntary support matters.
Behind every article, biblical reflection, discipleship resource, and effort to reach another struggling soul is the ongoing work of creating and sharing Gospel-centered content.
Our desire is not simply to attract readers for a moment.
It is to help people continue growing in the Word, learning the Gospel, and following Christ in everyday life.
These products can serve as personal reminders of biblical truth or thoughtful gifts that open conversations about faith.
But please understand this clearly.
You do not need to purchase anything to prove your faithfulness.
And if your family is facing financial hardship, caring for their essential needs is not a failure to support God's work.
Because the goal is not to build an audience impressed by Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people toward Jesus Christ.
The One who forgives sinners.
The One who restores the broken.
The One who calls us out of darkness.
The One who transforms hearts.
The One who teaches us that our lives are not our own.
And the One who is coming again.
So return to the question we began with.
Does the Parable of the Talents really teach Christians to pursue financial wealth?
No—not as the central command or measure of faithfulness.
It teaches, through a story involving substantial entrusted wealth, that the Master's servants must respond faithfully to what He has entrusted to them as they await His return.
It warns against fearful, unfaithful neglect.
It honors responsible action.
And within the larger teaching of Jesus and the apostles, it calls us to stewardship that is governed by faith, obedience, generosity, and love for God rather than the pursuit of riches.
You may become wealthy while living faithfully.
You may remain financially poor while living faithfully.
You may experience extraordinary success.
You may endure devastating loss.
But neither your prosperity nor your poverty can replace the question that matters most.
Does Jesus Christ have your heart?
Because the tragedy would not be reaching the end of your life without becoming a millionaire.
The tragedy would be reaching the end of your life having gained everything you wanted, only to discover that you never truly surrendered to the Savior you claimed to follow.
And the beauty of the Gospel is that even now, before that final day arrives, the door of repentance is open.
You can turn to Christ.
You can confess your sins.
You can trust His finished work.
You can stop trying to purchase the approval that only grace can give.
You can begin again—not because yesterday's failures were imaginary, but because the mercy of Jesus Christ is real.
The world may remember your financial failures.
People may remember your mistakes.
You may still carry the consequences of decisions you wish you could undo.
But in Christ, failure does not have to be the final chapter.
The Savior who redeems sinners can transform what comes next.
And when your earthly story finally closes, may your greatest treasure never have been something you could deposit, purchase, inherit, or lose.
May your greatest treasure be Christ Himself.
Because the greatest tragedy is not burying a talent in the ground—it is burying your heart beneath everything you were afraid to surrender to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WAS A KING’S CONCUBINE. ONE ACCUSATION ABOUT HER NEARLY TORE A KINGDOM APART.
paragraphs: SHE WAS A KING’S CONCUBINE. ONE ACCUSATION ABOUT HER NEARLY TORE A KINGDOM APART.

Her name was Rizpah. The Bible records no words from her in this scandal. Yet the accusation involving her exposed a dangerous struggle for power—and her later story would reveal a mother's grief that refused to disappear. This is the forgotten story of a woman caught between powerful men, and the Gospel truth that no human being is invisible to God.
“And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” — 2 Samuel 3:7, KJV
Imagine waking up one morning and discovering that your name has become the center of a national crisis.
Not because you led a rebellion.
Not because you commanded an army.
Not because you stood before a throne and demanded anything.
But because two powerful men were fighting over something that involved you.
Your reputation. Your body. Your place in a royal household.
And the frightening part?
The Bible never tells us that anyone stopped to ask for your side of the story.
Her name was Rizpah.
And if you think this is merely an ancient scandal about a king's concubine, stay with me.
Because buried beneath this political confrontation is a painful question that reaches into our homes, churches, relationships, and private wounds today.
What happens when people with power turn another human being into a weapon in their struggle for control?
And what happens when the person caught in the middle has no recorded voice?
The answer begins in the broken kingdom of Israel.
King Saul was dead.
His son Jonathan was dead.
The nation was divided.

David had been anointed to become king, but he was ruling from Hebron over Judah. Meanwhile, Saul's surviving son Ish-bosheth had been established as king over Israel, with the powerful military commander Abner standing behind his throne.
The situation was fragile.
And the Bible tells us something important before the scandal even erupts.
“Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.” — 2 Samuel 3:1, KJV
One dynasty was fading.
Another was rising.
And in the middle of that transition stood a woman named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.
She had been Saul's concubine.
That description may sound distant to modern readers, but it matters enormously.

A concubine in the ancient royal household was a woman in a recognized but generally lower-status union than a principal wife. Her relationship to the king could carry dynastic and political significance, while her social position often left her especially vulnerable to decisions made by powerful men.
We should not pretend that Scripture tells us whether Rizpah entered this relationship willingly, what she experienced inside Saul's household, or what she thought of the events that followed.
It does not.
And that silence should make us careful.
Because sometimes the most faithful way to read the Bible is to refuse to invent the testimony of someone whose testimony was never recorded.
Then came the accusation.
Ish-bosheth confronted Abner.
“Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?”
In modern language:
Why have you slept with my father's concubine?
That was not an ordinary question.
In the political world of ancient Israel, sexual access to a former king's concubines could carry implications of claiming royal authority.
We see the significance of royal concubines elsewhere in Scripture.
In 2 Samuel 16:21–22, Absalom publicly took possession of David's concubines as part of his rebellion against his father.

In 1 Kings 2:13–25, Adonijah's request to marry Abishag was treated by Solomon as politically threatening, although Abishag herself is not identified as David's concubine in the same manner as Rizpah.
These passages do not prove what happened between Abner and Rizpah.
But they help us understand why Ish-bosheth's accusation was politically explosive.
If Abner had taken Saul's concubine, it could have been interpreted as an attempt to assert authority associated with Saul's throne.
Yet we must notice what Scripture does not say.
It never independently confirms that Abner slept with Rizpah.
It records Ish-bosheth's accusation and Abner's furious response.
It does not establish Rizpah's consent, involvement, motives, or even her knowledge of the confrontation.
And this distinction matters.
An accusation recorded in Scripture is not automatically an accusation proven by Scripture.
How many people today need to hear that?
How many reputations have been destroyed because someone repeated a suspicion as though it were a verified fact?
How many families have fractured because one angry voice became more influential than the truth?
How many people have been forced to defend themselves against stories they never created?
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
To walk into a room and sense that people have already made their decision about you.
To discover that your name has traveled farther than your explanation.
To realize that people are discussing your life without ever speaking to you.
Rizpah's story does not give us permission to claim she experienced all those things.
But it certainly gives us reason to examine the damage that power, suspicion, and unverified accusations can cause.
And the crisis was about to become even more dangerous.
The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 3:8 says:
וַיִּחַר לְאַבְנֵר מְאֹד עַל־דִּבְרֵי אִישׁ־בֹּשֶׁת
Vayyíḥar le-Avnēr me'od 'al-divrê Ish-boshet.
A close translation is:
“And Abner became exceedingly angry over the words of Ish-bosheth.”
The Hebrew expression conveys intense anger.
Abner was not mildly offended.
He was furious.
He responded by reminding Ish-bosheth of his loyalty to Saul's household and his protection of Ish-bosheth's position.
Then he declared that he would transfer the kingdom from Saul's house and establish David's throne over Israel and Judah, according to what the LORD had sworn concerning David.
Read that carefully.
The man who had been sustaining Ish-bosheth's rule was now threatening to help dismantle it.
And the confrontation that triggered his declaration involved Rizpah.
One accusation.
One furious response.
One threatened reversal of political allegiance.
A kingdom already divided was moving toward another dramatic shift.
But the text reveals something even more unsettling.
In 2 Samuel 3:11, we read:
“And he could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him.” — KJV
Ish-bosheth was king.
Yet he was afraid of his own commander.
The crown was on his head, but Abner possessed enormous practical influence.
What a frightening picture of leadership.
A man occupying the throne while fearing the man who helped keep him there.
And isn't that how power can work even today?
Someone holds the title.
Someone else controls the decisions.
Someone appears to be in charge.
Someone else determines what can and cannot be said.
Families can function this way.
Organizations can function this way.
Even religious communities can fall into this pattern when accountability disappears and influence becomes more important than truth.
The lesson is not that every disagreement is a conspiracy or that every leader is corrupt.
The lesson is that authority without humility becomes dangerous, and influence without accountability can wound the vulnerable.
Jesus taught His disciples a radically different understanding of greatness.
In Mark 10:42–45, He contrasted rulers who exercise domination with the servant-hearted leadership expected among His followers.
And then He pointed to Himself.
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45, KJV
Do you see the contrast?
Earthly rulers may use people to protect their position.
Jesus gave Himself to rescue people who could never repay Him.
Earthly power can turn human beings into instruments.
Christ came as the Servant who gave His life for sinners.
Earthly ambition asks, “How can this person strengthen my kingdom?”
The Gospel asks us to behold the King who laid down His life to bring undeserving sinners into His kingdom.
That is not a small difference.
That changes everything.
And before we go further, there is something else we must confront.
We often read the Bible through the eyes of the people who speak the loudest.
The kings.
The generals.
The prophets.
The people whose decisions move armies and shape nations.
But Scripture also preserves the names of people who stood within those events without controlling them.
Rizpah was one of them.
The narrator tells us her name.
He tells us her father's name.
He identifies her connection to Saul.
But in this confrontation, he records no speech from her.
And we must resist the temptation to fill that silence with invented guilt or invented innocence concerning an event the text does not fully explain.
Her silence in the narrative is not evidence that she agreed with anything.
Nor is it proof of exactly what happened to her.
It is a reminder that the historical record is incomplete.
Yet her story does not end in 2 Samuel 3.
And what happens later is so devastating that it changes the way many readers remember her.
Years afterward, in 2 Samuel 21, Rizpah appears again.
This time, the issue is not an accusation involving a military commander.
It is the death of her sons.

During David's reign, Israel suffered a famine lasting three years. David sought the LORD, and the narrative connected the crisis to Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites, a people Israel had sworn to protect.
The Gibeonites demanded seven male descendants of Saul, and David handed them over.
Among those put to death were Rizpah's two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth.
This Mephibosheth was not Jonathan's son whom David had previously welcomed and protected.
He was a son of Saul and Rizpah.
Imagine the weight of that moment.
Rizpah had already lived through the collapse of Saul's dynasty.
Her name had appeared in a confrontation between powerful men.
Now two of her sons were dead.
And the biblical narrative gives us one of the most haunting pictures of maternal grief in the Old Testament.

“And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.” — 2 Samuel 21:10, KJV
Can you picture it?
A woman on a rock.
Sackcloth beneath her.
The bodies of her sons exposed.
Birds circling by day.
Wild animals threatening by night.
And a mother who would not leave.
Day after day.
Night after night.
Through a prolonged season of grief.
The passage does not give us an exact number of days.
But it tells us enough.
She remained until rain fell.
She could not restore their lives.
She could not reverse the execution.
She could not erase the decisions that brought her to that rock.
But she could remain.
She could guard their bodies from scavengers.
She could refuse to let their remains be abandoned without care.
The text does not tell us every thought in her heart.
It does not record a prayer from her lips.
But it records her actions.
And sometimes actions reveal a depth of sorrow that words cannot carry.
Perhaps this is why her story hurts so much.
Because many people know what it means to remain beside something they cannot fix.
A hospital bed.
A graveside.
An empty bedroom.
A broken marriage.
A child who has wandered far from home.
A future that collapsed despite years of prayer.
You keep showing up.
Not because you have all the answers.
Not because you are strong every morning.
But because love does not simply disappear when life becomes unbearable.
And perhaps someone reading this right now is exhausted from carrying grief that nobody else can see.
You smile when people ask how you are.
You say you are managing.
You keep serving.
You keep working.
You keep taking care of everybody else.
But when the room becomes quiet, the ache returns.
Rizpah's story does not promise that every earthly tragedy will be reversed.
It does not offer a formula for getting everything back.
And we should never use her suffering to guarantee outcomes God has not promised.
But it does remind us that suffering is not insignificant simply because the sufferer lacks political power or public recognition.
Something remarkable happens next.
David hears what Rizpah has done.
He then takes action to gather the remains of Saul and Jonathan, along with those who had been executed, and arranges for their burial in the family tomb of Kish.
The narrative moves from exposed bodies toward burial and public recognition of the dead.
It would go beyond the text to claim that Rizpah single-handedly changed every royal decision.
But the passage deliberately places the report of her vigil immediately before David's action.
Her grief was not left entirely outside the royal story.
The king heard.
And this is where we must be careful not to rush into a sentimental conclusion.
Because 2 Samuel 21 is a difficult passage.
It raises serious questions about judgment, covenant obligations, responsibility, violence, and the suffering of descendants for the sins of previous generations.
Faithful readers should wrestle with those questions rather than pretend they are simple.
The Bible itself elsewhere emphasizes that individuals must not be treated as automatically guilty merely because of their parents' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20).
We should not use Rizpah's tragedy to teach that God casually punishes innocent children for their parents' wrongdoing.
Nor should we present every action recorded in a historical narrative as an action God commands believers to imitate.
Scripture sometimes describes events that expose the brokenness of human history without asking us to celebrate every human decision within them.
And this matters deeply.
Because biblical faith is not strengthened by pretending that painful passages are painless.
It is strengthened when we bring our hardest questions before the God whose character is ultimately revealed in Jesus Christ.
And Jesus is where this story must lead us.
Not because Rizpah is secretly a coded prophecy of Christ.
Not because every detail of her vigil directly symbolizes the crucifixion.
But because her story exposes a world desperately in need of the kind of King Jesus came to be.
A world where political ambition can overshadow human dignity.
A world where accusations can reshape lives.
A world where families carry the consequences of decisions made by powerful people.
A world where grief sits on a rock while the machinery of government continues moving.
Into that broken world came Jesus.
Not as another Abner fighting to secure influence.
Not as another insecure ruler terrified of losing control.
But as the promised Son of David, the righteous King whose kingdom is not established through selfish ambition.
He came in humility.
He welcomed the overlooked.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He touched those others avoided.
He defended the dignity of people whom society treated as disposable.
And He went to the cross.
There, the innocent Son of God suffered at the hands of sinful humanity.
Yet His death was not merely another tragedy.
According to the Gospel, He willingly gave Himself as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
The apostle Peter wrote:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God...” — 1 Peter 3:18, KJV
The Greek phrase is:
δίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων
Dikaios hyper adikōn.
“The righteous one for the unrighteous.”
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus, the righteous One, suffered on behalf of unrighteous people to bring us to God.
He did not come merely to inspire us to endure suffering.
He came to save us from sin and reconcile us to the Father.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
And because He lives, the final word over those who belong to Him is not condemnation, abandonment, or death.
It is life in Him.
That does not mean every earthly wound immediately disappears.
It means the resurrection of Jesus has opened a hope stronger than the grave.
And suddenly the story of Rizpah presses a question into our hearts.
If Jesus has treated us with such costly mercy, how can we continue treating other people as disposable?
How can we claim to follow Christ while destroying reputations through gossip?
How can we celebrate grace while refusing to acknowledge the suffering of those harmed by our decisions?
How can we speak of biblical leadership while using authority to intimidate rather than serve?
How can we proclaim the Gospel of reconciliation while refusing to repent when we have wronged someone?
Perhaps the scandal you need to confront today is not a scandal involving a throne.
Perhaps it is something happening inside your own heart.
The resentment you have been feeding.
The accusation you repeated without checking the facts.
The person you quietly dismissed because their story made you uncomfortable.
The authority you used to control instead of protect.
The apology you keep postponing.
The bitterness you have begun to mistake for strength.
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
You are the person who has been misrepresented.
The person who was never asked to explain.
The person whose suffering was ignored because someone more influential controlled the conversation.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to call evil good.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending injustice never happened.
Repentance is not the same as public image management.
And reconciliation, where possible, requires truth, responsibility, and wisdom.
You can forgive someone without immediately restoring unsafe access to your life.
You can seek peace without surrendering the boundaries necessary to protect yourself or others.
And you can entrust your ultimate vindication to God while still pursuing appropriate justice.
Jesus never asked His followers to confuse holiness with silence in the face of wrongdoing.
He calls us to truth and love.
To mercy and righteousness.
To humility and repentance.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because there are times when we resemble the wounded.
And there are times when we resemble the people doing the wounding.
We may be quick to recognize the Abner in somebody else.
But slower to recognize the pride in ourselves.
We may condemn the misuse of power in ancient Israel while excusing the smaller ways we manipulate people today.
We may grieve over Rizpah's suffering while ignoring someone sitting quietly in the back of our own church.
The Gospel does not allow us to remain comfortable with that contradiction.
Jesus calls us to turn from sin.
To stop defending what we know is wrong.
To confess what we have hidden.
To seek forgiveness.
To make things right where we can.
And to trust not in our moral performance, but in His finished work.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It means to repent, involving a change of mind and direction.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling bad because our actions were exposed.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And that turning is inseparable from the grace that calls us home.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect life before coming to Jesus.
You need to come honestly.
With your sin.
With your grief.
With your questions.
With your failures.
With the parts of your story you would rather nobody knew.
The same Christ who calls sinners to repentance also welcomes those who come to Him in faith.
He does not offer permission to remain enslaved to sin.
He offers forgiveness and new life.
And maybe that is the most important moment in this entire article.
Not the accusation.
Not Abner's anger.
Not the political realignment.
Not even the heartbreaking image of Rizpah guarding her sons.
But this moment.
Right here.
Where you decide what you will do with the truth you have heard.
Will you keep treating repentance as something other people need?
Will you keep waiting for a less inconvenient time to surrender?
Will you keep allowing the opinions of people to define you more deeply than the Word of God?
Or will you finally come to Jesus without the performance?
No religious mask.
No carefully rehearsed excuses.
No pretending that your heart is healthier than it is.
Just you before the Savior.
Because the scandal of human sin is real.
But the grace of Jesus Christ is greater than any sinner can earn.
And grace is not God pretending our sins do not matter.
Grace is God providing, through Christ, the salvation we could never achieve ourselves.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always been more than a memorable phrase.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because faith guarantees that every earthly relationship will be restored.
But because Jesus can redeem sinners, transform hearts, and give an eternal future to people who thought their story was over.
And this is also why we continue sharing these stories.
There are people who will never walk into a church building but will read a testimony on their phone.
There are exhausted believers who need to be reminded of Scripture before they face another difficult day.
There are people trapped in shame who have confused their worst moment with their entire identity.
There are seekers who have heard plenty about religion but very little about the grace and truth of Jesus Christ.
And there are families who desperately need conversations grounded in God's Word.
If this article reached something deep inside you, please do not let it end as another post you scrolled past.
Not because every sentence is equally important, but because the Scriptures behind this story deserve another careful reading.
Return to 2 Samuel 3:7–11 and 2 Samuel 21:1–14.
Read the surrounding chapters.
Examine what the text actually says.
Let the Word of God correct what needs correcting and comfort what needs comforting.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Maybe it is a friend who has been falsely accused.
Maybe it is a mother carrying an unbearable grief.
Maybe it is someone who has been hurt by spiritual or family authority.
Maybe it is a believer who has become so distracted by human conflicts that they have forgotten the beauty of Christ.
Or send the article privately if their struggle is not something they want displayed in public.
A single share may bring Scripture into the life of someone we could never reach ourselves.
We cannot control what that person will do with the message.
But we can faithfully make the truth available.
If you have been following Gospel Warrior quietly, I also want to invite you to become part of this growing community.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite believers who are growing weary.
Invite people who have questions about Christianity.
Invite those who are struggling spiritually and those who have not yet come to faith.
Not to build a crowd around a personality.
But to direct more hearts toward Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not fear.
Not the suggestion that you must pay money to prove you love God.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, never a reward for financial support.
These resources are not substitutes for Scripture, a local church, or personal fellowship with Christ. They are simply additional tools and reminders that may encourage a life centered on God's Word.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Christ whether they can give financially or not.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Encourage someone.
Your presence and sincere engagement matter, too.
Before you leave, I want to ask you something.
Not as a performance for strangers.
Not because your pain needs to become public property.
But because sometimes one honest sentence can become the beginning of a meaningful conversation.
Which part of this story spoke most deeply to you?
Was it the danger of accusations?
The misuse of power?
The silence surrounding Rizpah?
The grief of a mother who would not abandon her sons?
Or the reminder that Jesus is a very different kind of King?
If you are weary and would welcome prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
If you are learning to surrender bitterness, guilt, or hidden sin to Christ, you can comment, “Jesus, keep changing my heart.”
If God has brought you through a painful season and you want to encourage someone else, share as much of your testimony as you feel comfortable sharing.
You do not have to reveal private wounds to prove your faith.
But your words may remind another person that they are not the only one seeking the Lord through difficult circumstances.
Not every comment needs a debate.
Sometimes a fellow believer needs compassion, Scripture, and someone willing to listen.
Now return with me, one final time, to the rock.
Rizpah is there.
The biblical narrative tells us that she guarded the bodies of her sons until rain came.
We do not know everything she thought.
We do not know everything she prayed, or whether she spoke aloud at all.
But we know her name.
We know her grief was recorded.
And we know the story did not end with the bodies left exposed.
Yet the Christian hope reaches beyond even that moment.
Because there is another place in Scripture where grieving people stood near death.
Another place where a body was laid in a tomb.
Another place where it seemed that violence and human power had won.
But on the third day, the tomb of Jesus Christ was empty.
The risen Lord had conquered death.
And because of Him, those who belong to Christ do not grieve as people without hope.
We still grieve.
We still face injustice.
We still carry wounds.
But we look toward the promised resurrection and the day when God will make all things new.
Revelation 21:4 declares:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.” — KJV
That is not a promise that this world will never hurt us.
It is a promise about the glorious future God will bring to His redeemed people.
And it is secured not by human kings, military commanders, or political alliances.
But by Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen King.

So whether you are carrying the shame of something you did, the wound of something done to you, or the grief of something you lost, do not let the darkness convince you that Christ has no place in your story.
Come to Him.
Trust Him.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive His grace through faith.
Walk in His truth.
And remember that the King who gave His life for sinners is worthy of your whole heart.
Rizpah could not bring her sons back from the dead—but Jesus walked out of His own grave, and in Him, death will not have the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE WAS AN EGYPTIAN SERVANT. THEN HIS MASTER GAVE HIM HIS DAUGHTER—AND HIS NAME ENTERED A FAMILY LINE NOBODY EXPECTED.
paragraphs: HE WAS AN EGYPTIAN SERVANT. THEN HIS MASTER GAVE HIM HIS DAUGHTER—AND HIS NAME ENTERED A FAMILY LINE NOBODY EXPECTED.

Buried inside a genealogy most Christians skip is the astonishing story of Sheshan and Jarha—a foreign servant, a daughter whose name Scripture never reveals, and a family line that challenges everything we assume about status, belonging, inheritance, and the grace of God.

“Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters. And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha. Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant as wife; and she bore him Attai.” — 1 Chronicles 2:34–35 (WEB)
Imagine spending your entire life being known by what you do for somebody else.
Not by your dreams.
Not by your potential.
Not by the person you might become.
Just your position.
Your background.
Your limitations.
The name people use when they need something from you.

Now imagine somebody opening the family records generations later and discovering that the person everyone would have expected to remain on the margins had become part of the family's continuing story.
His name was Jarha.
He was Egyptian.
He was a servant.
And somehow, in the middle of a genealogy that most Bible readers rush past, his name survived.
But before we go any further, there's something we need to understand.
The Bible does not explicitly say that Jarha inherited Sheshan's entire estate or became his legal heir.

What it tells us is remarkable enough without adding something God did not reveal: Sheshan had no sons, he gave his daughter in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha, and the children of that marriage continued the genealogical line recorded under Sheshan's name.
That distinction matters.
Because the real story is not about inventing a spectacular inheritance.
It is about recognizing the extraordinary significance of the family line Scripture actually records.
And perhaps the most haunting detail is this:
We know the servant's name.
We know the father's name.
We know the son's name.
But we are never told the daughter's name.
Yet without that unnamed woman, the next generation in this account would not exist.
Sometimes the people whose names history overlooks are the very people through whom history continues.
And if you have ever felt invisible, underestimated, or reduced to what others think you are worth, there is something in these ancient verses worth hearing.
Not because Jarha's story promises that every overlooked person will become wealthy or powerful.
But because the Bible refuses to erase this Egyptian servant from the record.
Think about where this account appears.
First Chronicles opens with genealogies.
Names upon names.
Fathers and sons.
Families and generations.
The kind of biblical reading where even committed Christians sometimes begin to lose concentration.
And suddenly, in 1 Chronicles 2:34–35, the pattern changes.
Sheshan has no sons.
He has daughters.
He also has an Egyptian servant named Jarha.
And he gives his daughter to Jarha as his wife.
She bears a son named Attai.
Then the record continues.
“Attai became the father of Nathan, and Nathan became the father of Zabad.” — 1 Chronicles 2:36 (WEB)
It does not stop there.
The genealogy traces successive generations until it reaches Elishama in verse 41.
A family line that might have appeared to reach an obstacle because Sheshan had no sons is recorded as continuing through his daughter and Jarha.
And there is something deeply significant about the fact that Jarha's Egyptian identity is mentioned at all.
The Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles 2:34 says:
וּלְשֵׁשָׁן עֶבֶד מִצְרִי וּשְׁמוֹ יַרְחָע
Ule-Sheshan eved Mitsri u-shemo Yarcha.
“And Sheshan had an Egyptian servant, and his name was Jarha.”
The Hebrew word עֶבֶד (eved) means servant or slave, depending on the setting.
It is a word associated with service and subordination, and we should not soften its meaning merely to make the story more comfortable.
The text does not tell us whether Jarha was enslaved, how he entered Sheshan's household, what freedom he possessed, or whether he could have refused the marriage.
Those unanswered questions matter.
Ancient servitude was not the same as modern employment. There were serious inequalities of power, and we must not romanticize them.
Yet the writer does something striking.
He names Jarha.
וּשְׁמוֹ יַרְחָע — u-shemo Yarcha.
“And his name was Jarha.”
Not merely an Egyptian.
Not merely a servant.
Jarha.
A real man with a name.
A man whose life was significant enough to be preserved in Israel's family records.
We are not told his private thoughts.
We are not told whether he was respected or despised.
We are not told whether he ever imagined becoming part of this family.
So we should not pretend to know.
But we do know that his name was not discarded.
And perhaps that is where this ancient passage begins to speak to the people who feel forgotten today.
Because there are people reading this who know what it means to be valued for their usefulness but rarely appreciated for their humanity.
The mother who gives everything and wonders whether anybody notices.
The father working exhausting hours to keep food on the table.
The employee who serves faithfully but remains overlooked.
The believer who sits quietly in church while carrying a private battle nobody sees.
The person who has spent years being reminded of where they came from, what they lack, or what they once did wrong.
And somewhere in the middle of all that, a dangerous thought begins to grow.
Maybe this is all I will ever be.
But a person's social position is not the measure of their worth before God.
That truth does not depend on turning Jarha into a hero the Bible never claims he was.
It rests on something much older and much stronger.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that human beings are created in God's image.
And the New Testament reveals the astonishing worth of people through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Your dignity does not begin when someone important finally recognizes you.
It begins with the God who made you.
Now look again at Sheshan.
The text says he had no sons, but daughters.
In the genealogical world of ancient Israel, sons were commonly the means through which family lines and inherited property were recorded.
But daughters were not without legal significance.
Numbers 27 tells us about the daughters of Zelophehad, who approached Moses because their father had died without sons.
They asked why their father's name should disappear from his clan simply because he had no son.
And God answered.
“The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.” — Numbers 27:7 (WEB)
The Lord instructed Moses that a daughter could receive an inheritance when her father had no son.
That does not mean every inheritance question in ancient Israel was simple.
Numbers 36 later addresses marriage and the preservation of tribal inheritances.
But it does show that Scripture had already recognized daughters as legitimate heirs under specified circumstances.
This matters when we read about Sheshan.
His decision to give his daughter in marriage to Jarha is unusual enough to be recorded.
Yet we must distinguish the marriage itself from the inheritance arrangements we might imagine surrounding it.
First Chronicles does not explain the legal terms of the marriage.
It does not tell us what property changed hands.
It does not say Jarha received all of Sheshan's possessions.
What it does show is that Sheshan's line continued through the marriage of his daughter and an Egyptian servant.
And that is where the story becomes more intriguing.
Because Jarha was not simply a man of lower status within the household.
He was Egyptian.
For anyone familiar with Israel's history, that word carries enormous historical weight.
Egypt was the land where the descendants of Jacob multiplied.
It was also the land where Israel suffered oppression.
Egypt was the setting of Pharaoh's cruelty, Moses' confrontation, the Passover, and the Exodus.
But Scripture never teaches that every Egyptian individual was personally guilty of Pharaoh's sins.
In fact, Deuteronomy 23:7 gives Israel this command:
“You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land.” (WEB)
And verse 8 makes provision for descendants of Egyptians to enter the assembly of the Lord in the third generation.
The biblical story is more complex than a simple division between one favored ethnicity and every other people.
The God of Israel is also the Creator of the nations.
And His redemptive purposes were never intended to end with one people keeping His blessing to themselves.
Long before the birth of Jesus, God promised Abraham:
“All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” — Genesis 12:3 (WEB)
All the families.
Not merely the powerful.
Not merely the wealthy.
Not merely those with impressive family histories.
All the families of the earth.
Jarha's appearance in a Judahite genealogy does not prove that he personally understood the full meaning of that promise.
The text tells us nothing about his faith.
But his inclusion reminds us that the Old Testament's family histories were never as ethnically isolated or socially predictable as some people imagine.
And that should prepare us for an even greater revelation.
Because when the Gospel of Jesus Christ arrives, the question of belonging becomes impossible to ignore.
Who is welcomed?
Who can be forgiven?
Who can become part of God's household?
Who gets to call God Father?
And what happens to people whose histories are filled with shame?
The apostle Paul answers with words that should shake every person who has ever believed their past makes them permanently unacceptable.
In Ephesians 2:12, Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were once strangers to the covenants of promise.
They were without hope and without God in the world.
Then comes verse 13.
“But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ.” (WEB)
Read that again.
You who once were far off are made near.
The original Greek says:
ὑμεῖς οἵ ποτε ὄντες μακρὰν ἐγενήθητε ἐγγὺς ἐν τῷ αἵματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ
Hymeis hoi pote ontes makran egenēthēte engys en tō haimati tou Christou.
“You who once were far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ.”
The contrast is breathtaking.
μακράν (makran) — far away.
ἐγγύς (engys) — near.
Paul is speaking about the reconciliation accomplished through Christ, particularly the inclusion of Gentile believers in God's people.
He is not discussing Jarha directly.
We must not pretend that he is.
But the theological truth is glorious.
Through Jesus, people who were once separated from the covenant community are brought near to God.
Not through superior ancestry.
Not through money.
Not through social achievement.
Not through an impressive religious reputation.
Through the blood of Jesus Christ.
And if you understand what that means, you begin to realize how astonishing the Gospel really is.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the public image of respectable people.
He came to save sinners.
People who had lied.
People who had failed.
People who had worshiped false gods.
People who had hurt others.
People who had ruined relationships.
People whose outward appearance looked religious while their hearts were far from God.
People who were ashamed to tell the truth about what they had become.
And that includes every one of us.
Because the deepest problem in the human heart is not that we lack recognition.
It is that we need reconciliation with God.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.” (WEB)
All.
The master and the servant.
The wealthy and the poor.
The admired and the ignored.
The person with a celebrated family name and the person whose history is full of disgrace.
All have sinned.
And all need the mercy that only Christ can provide.
This is where we must be careful not to confuse an inspiring family story with the saving Gospel.
Jarha's marriage was not the cross.
His place in a genealogy was not salvation.
And his social advancement, whatever its exact extent, was not proof that he had been spiritually redeemed.
But his story can make us stop long enough to consider something that the New Testament reveals unmistakably.
In Jesus Christ, belonging to God's family is not earned through social position. It is received through grace by faith.
John 1:12 declares:
“But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God's children, to those who believe in his name.” (WEB)
Imagine that.
Not simply being allowed into a household.
Not merely having your name included in a family record.
But being welcomed as a child of God.
And unlike an earthly inheritance, this promise does not depend on the decisions of an ancient patriarch.
It depends on Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who entered our broken world.
The Savior who lived without sin.
The Lamb who carried our guilt.
The crucified Redeemer who rose again.
The Lord who calls sinners to repent and believe.
The One who does not excuse sin, but forgives those who come to Him in faith.
That is the difference between sentimental encouragement and the Gospel.
The Gospel does not simply say, “You deserve a better life.”
It says that although we are sinners, Christ died for the ungodly.
It does not merely promise that people will finally appreciate us.
It offers reconciliation with the God against whom we have sinned.
It does not promise every servant will become an heir to earthly wealth.
It promises that those who belong to Christ are heirs of God.
Romans 8:17 speaks of believers as children and heirs of God, fellow heirs with Christ.
And Galatians 3:29 declares:
“If you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise.” (WEB)
Notice the condition.
If you are Christ's.
Not if you have a perfect history.
Not if your family has always been religious.
Not if you have never fallen.
If you belong to Christ.
And that brings us to the part of this story that may be the hardest to face.
Because some people are desperate to have their names remembered by the world while neglecting the question of whether they truly belong to Jesus.
We spend our lives building reputations.
Defending appearances.
Collecting approval.
Trying to make sure people know we matter.
But what happens when the applause stops?
What happens when the people who admired us move on?
What happens when the achievements we built our identity around can no longer save us from grief, sickness, aging, or death?
And what happens when we stand before the holy God who knows everything about us?
There will be no impressive résumé capable of erasing sin.
No family reputation strong enough to purchase forgiveness.
No religious performance sufficient to replace the righteousness of Christ.
That is why the cross matters.
Jesus did not die because our sins were small.
He died because our need was desperate and His love was immeasurable.
He bore the judgment sinners deserved.
He rose from the grave.
And He calls us to turn away from sin and trust Him.
Perhaps you have spent years thinking your greatest need is for someone to finally see your worth.
But what if your greatest need is to surrender your life to the Savior who already sees your heart?
The parts you display.
The parts you conceal.
The wounds you carry.
The sins you justify.
The bitterness you have protected.
The habits you have promised to abandon a hundred times.
He knows.
And still the invitation of the Gospel stands.
“Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (WEB)
Not an invitation to continue pretending.
An invitation to come.
To confess.
To repent.
To believe.
To receive the mercy of Christ.
And to begin walking in the new life that His grace makes possible.
Perhaps that is why the story of Jarha feels so unexpectedly personal.
Not because we know everything about his life.
We do not.
But because we know what it means to live in a world that categorizes people.
Servant.
Foreigner.
Failure.
Outsider.
Unworthy.
Forgotten.
And then we encounter a genealogy where an Egyptian servant is named, his marriage is recorded, and the family line continues through his son.
It is a small window into a much larger biblical world.
A world in which the people God records are not always the people society would expect.
Think of Rahab, the woman of Jericho whose past was associated with prostitution, yet who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.
Think of Ruth, the Moabite widow who clung to Naomi and placed her trust in the God of Israel, later becoming an ancestor of David.
Think of Matthew, the tax collector whom Jesus called.
Think of Peter, who denied his Lord and was later restored.
Think of Paul, who persecuted the church before Christ confronted him.
Their stories are not identical.
Their circumstances are not interchangeable.
But together they testify that the Bible is not a museum of flawless people.
It is the testimony of God's work in a fallen world.
And at the center stands Jesus.
The One whose grace is never permission to remain in rebellion.
The One whose forgiveness is not a denial of justice.
The One who welcomes repentant sinners and transforms lives.
From scandal to grace does not mean that sin stops mattering. It means that Jesus Christ is mighty enough to redeem sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And now I want you to think about the unnamed daughter of Sheshan one more time.
We know that she bore Attai.
We know that her marriage is essential to the continuation of the recorded line.
But Scripture does not give us her name.
That silence should make us humble.
We cannot tell her story in full.
We cannot know whether she welcomed the marriage or how she experienced her life with Jarha.
We cannot turn her into a symbol of happiness, suffering, romance, or rebellion without evidence.
Yet her presence is undeniable.
The family line passed through her.
And maybe someone reading this understands that kind of hidden significance.
You have served for years without being celebrated.
You have prayed for people who never knew.
You have cared for children, elderly parents, or struggling relatives while your own dreams waited.
You have tried to live faithfully in places where nobody applauds obedience.
And sometimes you wonder whether any of it matters.
Please hear this carefully.
Your worth is not determined by whether a human genealogy records your name.
Your faithful service is not worthless because it is unseen.
And your salvation is not dependent on becoming historically important.
Jesus taught that the Father sees what is done in secret.
Hebrews 6:10 reminds believers that God is not unjust to forget their work and the love they have shown for His name.
You may be overlooked by people.
You are not beyond the knowledge of God.
But knowing that God sees you should lead to something deeper than simply feeling appreciated.
It should lead you to ask whether your life is truly surrendered to Him.
Because being noticed is not the same as being saved.
Being included is not the same as being converted.
And having a remarkable personal story is not the same as having a living relationship with Jesus Christ.
That relationship begins with repentance and faith.
And if you have never truly turned to Christ, this moment can become more important than anything you have read about Sheshan or Jarha.
You do not need to invent a religious performance.
You need to come honestly before God.
Confess your sin.
Stop defending what He calls evil.
Believe that Jesus died for sinners and rose again.
Ask Him for mercy.
And entrust your life to Him.
You may pray something like this, not because these exact words possess saving power, but because they express the repentance and faith to which Scripture calls us:

“Lord Jesus, You know the truth about me. You know the sins I have hidden, the ways I have resisted You, and the places where I have trusted myself more than Your Word. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to follow You in truth. I surrender my life to You. Amen.”
And if you have already trusted Christ but have grown cold, distracted, or spiritually exhausted, perhaps this is your reminder to return to the One who first loved you.
Not merely to recover an emotional feeling.
But to return to prayer.
To return to Scripture.
To confess what needs confessing.
To seek reconciliation where possible.
To worship with the church.
To walk in obedience.
To remember that grace does not merely comfort us in our old ways.
Grace trains us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and instructs us to reject ungodliness and worldly desires.
Real grace transforms.
Real faith bears fruit.
Real discipleship costs something.
And real Christian hope rests on the finished work of Christ, not on our ability to create an impressive testimony.
So here is a question I hope you will not rush past.
What label have you allowed to become louder than what God says in His Word?
Is it the name of a past failure?
A broken marriage?
A family scandal?
An addiction you are fighting?
A season of spiritual compromise?
A mistake you cannot undo?
Or perhaps it is the opposite.
Maybe the label you are holding onto is your success.
Your position.
Your reputation.
Your religious image.
And maybe you have become so comfortable being admired by people that you have stopped examining your heart before God.
The Gospel confronts both kinds of people.
Those crushed by shame.
And those blinded by pride.
Because neither shame nor pride can save us.
Only Jesus can.
Not as a public performance.
Not because a comment proves your faith.
But as a simple expression of hope, if those words genuinely reflect where you are.
Sometimes an honest request for prayer is the beginning of a much-needed conversation.
And perhaps someone else reading the comments will discover they are not the only one struggling to keep their eyes on Jesus.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to make Christianity look like a collection of dramatic stories.
Not to promise prosperity whenever someone demonstrates enough faith.
Not to replace the local church, faithful pastors, or the fellowship of believers.
But to keep pointing people back to the Word of God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
To help people encounter passages they might otherwise skip.
To explain Scripture carefully.
To challenge comfortable assumptions.
To encourage repentance, prayer, obedience, and spiritual growth.
And to remind those who are weary that the Gospel remains good news.
You never know who among your family, friends, or followers has been quietly wrestling with feelings of rejection, shame, or spiritual distance.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, people who have drifted from church, and even those who are still searching for answers about Jesus.
Not everyone will agree with everything immediately.
That is all right.
Our responsibility is not to manipulate people into a response.
It is to speak the truth in love and point them to Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior's ministry has helped strengthen your walk with God, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.

Your tithe and your offerings are matters of biblical stewardship, worship, and conscience. Supporting an online ministry should not be presented as an automatic replacement for your responsibility to support your local church and the work of the Gospel.
It helps make it possible to keep showing up for the person who opens Facebook late at night looking for encouragement.
For the believer who is beginning to study Scripture seriously.
For the parent who wants to share biblical truth with their children.
For the person who has been away from church and is quietly asking whether God would welcome them back.
And for the reader who encounters a passage like 1 Chronicles 2 and realizes that even a genealogy can open a door to a deeper understanding of Scripture.
Those free resources are part of the mission.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, or thoughtful gifts that open conversations about faith.
It is the opportunity to participate voluntarily in a ministry you believe is worth sustaining.
Your financial situation does not determine your worth before God.
Even one thoughtful share can begin a conversation.
Because this has never been about building a platform that makes people admire us.
It must always be about pointing people to the Savior.
Now, before you leave, return with me one final time to the ancient record.
Sheshan.
An Egyptian servant named Jarha.
An unnamed daughter.
A son named Attai.
Generations following generations.
No elaborate description of a wedding.
No dramatic account of a servant receiving an estate.
No explanation of what every person felt.
Just a few lines in a genealogy.
Yet those lines are still being read thousands of years later.
And there is something deeply moving about that.
A man once identified as an Egyptian servant is remembered by name in Scripture.
A woman whose name was not preserved nevertheless occupies an essential place in the recorded family line.
A father without sons sees his descendants traced through his daughter.
And a reader living centuries later is invited to look more carefully at a passage that could so easily have been ignored.
But the greatest hope of the Christian life is not that someone will remember our names centuries from now.
It is that we belong to Jesus Christ.
Because earthly family records can be lost.
Reputations can disappear.
Property can pass into other hands.
Generations can forget the people who came before them.
But the hope offered through Christ is greater than an earthly legacy.
In Luke 10:20, Jesus told His disciples to rejoice that their names were written in heaven.
And that is where this story leaves us with a question more important than the inheritance we might have imagined Jarha receiving.
Not whether your name will become famous.
Not whether people will finally recognize everything you have done.
Not whether you will leave behind wealth, influence, or a remarkable reputation.
But whether you have placed your faith in the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
Whether you have turned from sin.
Whether you belong to Jesus.
Because the greatest inheritance is not the house you leave behind, the money someone gives you, or the family name you carry.
It is the eternal life God gives through His Son.
And the greatest transformation is not from servant to wealthy heir.
It is from condemnation to forgiveness.
From alienation to reconciliation.
From spiritual death to life in Christ.
From a life ruled by sin to a life being transformed by grace.
That is the Gospel.
That is our hope.
And that is why the name of Jesus must remain greater than every story we tell.
The world may never remember your name—but the question that matters forever is whether you belong to the Savior who knows it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR HUSBAND DOESN’T WANT SEX ANYMORE. IS IT A SIN TO SATISFY YOURSELF?
paragraphs: YOUR HUSBAND DOESN’T WANT SEX ANYMORE. IS IT A SIN TO SATISFY YOURSELF?

When the man who promised to love you stops reaching for you, what does God say about the desires that refuse to disappear? A deeply personal conversation about sexual loneliness, marriage, temptation, biblical truth, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
There is a kind of rejection that doesn't leave bruises.
It leaves an empty space in the bed.
You lie beside the man you married. You can hear him breathing. You can feel the warmth of his body. His wedding ring is still on his finger.
But you cannot remember the last time he reached for you like he wanted you.
And perhaps the hardest part isn't even the absence of sex.
It's the questions that come afterward.
Am I still beautiful?
Is there something wrong with me?
Does he still love me?
Is there someone else?
And then comes the question you would probably never ask out loud in church.
"If my husband no longer wants to have sex with me, is it wrong for me to satisfy myself?"
You have prayed about it.
You have tried to be understanding.
You have told yourself that marriage is about more than physical intimacy. And you know that is true.
But knowing something is true doesn't automatically make the loneliness disappear.
You are a Christian woman. You love Jesus. You want to honor your marriage.
Yet you still have a body that longs for affection, a heart that aches for connection, and desires that didn't suddenly die because your husband's interest changed.
So what are you supposed to do?
Pretend you don't feel anything?
Silently suffer?
Or find relief on your own and hope God understands?

Before anyone throws a Bible verse at you, before anyone rushes to condemn you, and before anyone gives you permission that Scripture itself has not clearly given, there is something we need to understand.
God sees more than the question you are asking. He sees the pain that brought you to ask it.
And the answer deserves more than a careless yes or no.
Because sometimes the deepest wound in a marriage isn't that two people have stopped having sex.
