It's that one of them has started believing they are no longer worth wanting.
And that is where this conversation must begin.
The Bible does not treat sexual intimacy within marriage as something dirty, embarrassing, or unspiritual.
Quite the opposite.
In Genesis 2:24, Scripture describes a husband and wife becoming one flesh.
The Hebrew expression is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad), meaning "one flesh."
This is more than a reference to sexual intercourse. It describes a profound covenant union in which two people establish a shared life, belonging, and intimacy.
But physical union is not excluded from that beautiful picture.
God created marriage with room for tenderness, affection, delight, and sexual desire.
And that matters.
Because some Christian women have been made to feel guilty simply for wanting their husbands.
They have been taught to suppress every longing until they begin confusing holiness with emotional numbness.
But wanting sexual intimacy with your own husband does not make you impure.
It makes you human.
The Song of Songs openly celebrates romantic longing and mutual delight between lovers.
In Song of Songs 7:10, the woman declares:
"I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me." (KJV)
Imagine that.
A woman in Scripture rejoicing in being desired.
Not apologizing for it.
Not treating it as shameful.
Not pretending physical attraction has no place in a godly relationship.
She celebrates it.
So when a wife longs to be touched, kissed, held, and desired by her husband, that longing is not automatically sinful.
But there is another truth that must be spoken with equal compassion.
Your husband's lack of sexual desire does not automatically mean he has stopped loving you.
And assuming otherwise can turn a painful situation into an even deeper wound.

Sometimes a husband withdraws sexually because of exhaustion, depression, anxiety, chronic illness, medication, hormonal changes, erectile difficulties, unresolved conflict, past trauma, or the emotional weight of responsibilities he doesn't know how to explain.
Sometimes shame keeps him silent.
Sometimes he is struggling with something he is afraid to admit.
Sometimes pornography, secrecy, or another relationship may be involved.
But those possibilities must not become accusations without evidence.
And sometimes, quite simply, two spouses experience different levels of sexual desire.
That difference can be painful without either person being the villain.
A wife may interpret her husband's withdrawal as rejection.
A husband may interpret her repeated attempts at intimacy as pressure.
She feels unwanted.
He feels inadequate.
She stops asking because she cannot bear another rejection.
He stops initiating because he fears disappointing her.
And slowly, two people who once promised to share everything begin protecting themselves from each other.
They still live in the same house.
They still discuss groceries, bills, children, and schedules.
They may even attend church together.
But somewhere between surviving life and managing responsibilities, they have forgotten how to reach each other's hearts.
Then comes the private struggle.
The loneliness grows.
The physical tension remains.
And the thought enters her mind:
What if I simply take care of this myself?
No affair.
No other man.
No secret relationship.
Just a private moment of physical relief.
Would that be sin?
Here is where we must be careful not to claim more biblical certainty than God has actually revealed.
The Bible does not explicitly name or directly prohibit masturbation.
That statement may surprise some readers.
But biblical faithfulness requires us to distinguish what Scripture clearly says from what Christians conclude through broader moral reasoning.
Some people point to the story of Onan in Genesis 38:8–10.
But that passage is not a direct teaching about masturbation.

Onan refused to fulfill his obligation concerning his deceased brother's widow and deliberately prevented offspring in that particular covenant and family context. His wrongdoing involved serious disobedience and exploitation of the situation.
To present that account as a straightforward prohibition of every act of self-stimulation goes beyond what the text itself establishes.
That does not mean the Bible has nothing relevant to say.
It means we need to examine the question more honestly.
Jesus teaches in Matthew 5:28 that looking at another person with lustful intent is a matter of the heart, not merely outward behavior.
The Greek expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) communicates looking at a woman with the purpose or intent of lusting after her.
In context, Jesus is confronting adulterous desire and the inner attitudes that violate covenant faithfulness.
He is not saying that every experience of sexual desire is itself adultery.
That distinction is essential.
Sexual desire is not identical to lust.
Attraction is not automatically betrayal.
And experiencing physical arousal does not mean a Christian has already sinned.
Yet the way desire is cultivated, directed, and acted upon matters deeply.
If private sexual stimulation depends upon pornography, fantasizing about someone outside the marriage, or deliberately nurturing adulterous desires, then serious biblical concerns arise.
But what if none of those things is involved?
What if a wife is thinking only about her husband?
What if she is not consuming pornography, imagining another man, or seeking to betray her marriage?
What if she is simply trying to manage sexual frustration in a marriage where intimacy has become rare or nonexistent?
Faithful Christians disagree about that situation.
Some believe masturbation is inherently inconsistent with God's design for sexual intimacy as a shared marital expression.

Others believe Scripture does not establish an absolute prohibition against every instance of solitary sexual stimulation, particularly when it is free from lustful fantasy, pornography, compulsive behavior, and marital dishonesty.
Those differences should not be erased by pretending that one disputed interpretation is a direct quotation from God.

Romans 14:23 teaches an important principle about acting contrary to one's conviction before God, although the chapter originally addresses disputes over food and observances rather than masturbation.
Its broader lesson calls believers to act in faith rather than knowingly violate conscience.
And 1 Corinthians 6:12 reminds us that not everything permissible is beneficial, and that we should not allow ourselves to be mastered by anything.
The Greek verb ἐξουσιασθήσομαι (exousiasthēsomai) carries the idea of being brought under another's authority or control.
Paul's concern is not simply whether something offers temporary satisfaction.
It is whether something begins to exercise mastery over us.
That gives us a more searching question.
Not merely, Can I do this?
But, What is this doing to my heart, my conscience, my marriage, and my relationship with Christ?
Does it become an occasional response to physical tension, or a pattern of emotional escape?
Does it leave you at peace before God, or does it deepen a cycle of secrecy and distress?
Is it replacing conversations that desperately need to happen?
Are you using it to avoid the pain of feeling unwanted?
Are you gradually withdrawing from your husband because private relief feels safer than the possibility of another rejection?
These questions are not intended to humiliate you.
They are intended to help you see the whole picture.
Because something can offer physical relief without addressing the wound beneath it.
And sometimes the wound beneath sexual frustration is the quiet grief of feeling abandoned while still married.
You may not merely miss sex.
You may miss the way your husband used to look at you.
You may miss being pursued.
You may miss the playful affection, the unplanned kisses, the feeling that he couldn't wait to be near you.
You may miss the woman you used to be when you felt secure in his love.
And when that affection disappears, it is easy to start blaming your body.
Maybe you are older now.
Maybe childbirth changed you.
Maybe illness, stress, or years of caring for everyone else have left you feeling unfamiliar to yourself.
Maybe you look in the mirror and wonder whether the woman staring back is still someone worth desiring.
Please hear this.
Your worth did not begin with your husband's attraction, and it does not end with his lack of desire.
You were made in the image of God before you ever became someone's wife.
You were known by God before you ever wore a wedding ring.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, your identity is not ultimately determined by how frequently someone reaches for you.
Your marriage matters.
Your pain matters.
Your sexual needs deserve compassionate attention.
But your value is not measured by another person's libido.
The Gospel speaks directly to the temptation to make human acceptance the foundation of our worth.
Romans 5:8 tells us:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Jesus did not wait until you were beautiful enough, desirable enough, emotionally strong enough, or spiritually impressive enough to love you.
He came while humanity was still lost in sin.
He gave Himself to reconcile sinners to God.
That is grace.
Not a promise that your husband will suddenly become affectionate tomorrow.
Not a guarantee that every marriage will be restored exactly as you imagine.
But the assurance that your deepest identity rests in the Savior who gave Himself for you.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable for husbands, too.
Because Scripture does not place the entire burden of marital intimacy on wives.
In 1 Corinthians 7:3, Paul writes:
The Greek wording includes τὴν ὀφειλήν (tēn opheilēn), referring to what is owed or due within the relationship.
The passage emphasizes mutuality.
Husbands are called to consider their wives.
Wives are called to consider their husbands.
Neither spouse is presented as the only person whose needs matter.
And in 1 Corinthians 7:5, Paul speaks against unilateral sexual deprivation, apart from mutual agreement for a limited time of prayer.
But this passage must never be twisted into a weapon.
Marriage does not eliminate the need for consent.
A husband's or wife's body is not property to be seized.
Scripture's call to mutual care is not permission to pressure, threaten, manipulate, or force sexual activity.
Sexual intimacy should never be extracted through fear.
A spouse may have legitimate reasons for declining sex, including illness, pain, trauma, exhaustion, or emotional distress.
Those reasons deserve compassion, not condemnation.
At the same time, a persistent lack of intimacy should not automatically be dismissed as insignificant.
When one spouse is suffering, love calls both people to listen.
The biblical vision is not one spouse demanding and the other surrendering under pressure.
It is two people seeking each other's good.
That is why Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
The Greek word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is a command to love.
And the model of that love is Jesus Christ.
Sacrificial.
Attentive.
Faithful.
Concerned for the beloved's good.
Christlike love does not mean a husband must always feel sexual desire or consent to sex whenever his wife asks.
But it does mean he should not treat her suffering with indifference.
And a wife who loves Christ is likewise called to respond with honesty, patience, respect, and compassion rather than coercion or retaliation.
This is where healing may begin.
Not with an accusation.
Not with, "You never want me anymore."
Not with, "A real husband would satisfy his wife."
But perhaps with a trembling voice and words that have been buried for months.
"I miss you."
"I don't just miss sex. I miss feeling close to you."
"I know you may be going through something I don't understand, but this distance is hurting me."
"Can we talk about what has changed between us?"
There may be tears.
There may be awkward silence.
He may not have an immediate answer.
And perhaps you will discover that he has been struggling, too.
Maybe he feels ashamed of a physical problem.
Maybe he is afraid of failing you.
Maybe he is carrying stress that has affected his desire.
Maybe there is an unresolved hurt between you that neither of you has known how to name.
Or maybe the conversation will reveal a deeper problem requiring counseling, medical care, repentance, or rebuilding trust.
Whatever emerges, truth gives you something to work with.
Silence only leaves you guessing.

And if your husband repeatedly refuses to discuss the problem, you do not have to pretend the situation is healthy. Seeking support from a qualified marriage counselor, an appropriate healthcare professional, or a trustworthy pastor who respects both spouses' dignity may be a wise next step.
If there is coercion, intimidation, or abuse, safety and specialized support must take priority.
But there is another person who may need healing in this story.
You.
Not because your longing is shameful.
But because prolonged rejection can slowly turn longing into bitterness.
And bitterness can change the way you see everything.
A small disagreement becomes evidence that he doesn't care.
A forgotten compliment becomes proof that you are unattractive.
A night when he falls asleep early becomes another silent verdict against your worth.
Eventually, you may stop seeing your husband as a struggling human being and start seeing him only as the source of your pain.
That is a dangerous place for any marriage.
Hebrews 12:15 warns believers against allowing a root of bitterness to grow and cause trouble.
That warning does not mean you must deny your pain.
It means you must be careful about what your pain is becoming.
You can acknowledge rejection without turning it into hatred.
You can ask for change without humiliating your spouse.
You can seek help without exposing intimate details to people who will only gossip.
And you can bring your sexual frustration before God without pretending He is too holy to hear about it.
The Lord who created the human body is not embarrassed by the fact that you have one.
Psalm 62:8 says:
"Pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us." (KJV)
Pour it out.
The disappointment.
The frustration.
The longing.
The jealousy you feel when other couples seem affectionate.
The fear that you are growing older beside someone who no longer desires you.
Even the questions you are ashamed to ask.
God is not asking you to impress Him with a carefully edited prayer.
He calls you to come to Him truthfully.
And when your conscience is troubled, remember that the answer is not to hide from Christ.
The answer is to draw near to Him.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
This promise must not be misused to label every disputed sexual behavior as sin.
But wherever there is actual sin—whether lust, dishonesty, cruelty, pornography, selfishness, or bitterness—the Gospel offers forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the blood of Christ is sufficient.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to understand.
You may have already crossed a boundary that troubles your conscience.
You may have been secretly using pornography.
You may have started fantasizing about another man.
You may have developed an emotional attachment to someone who makes you feel noticed.
Or perhaps you have been carrying guilt about masturbation without ever knowing whether your church's teaching on the subject accurately reflects Scripture.
Whatever your situation, do not confuse spiritual conviction with hopelessness.
Conviction calls us toward repentance and truth.
Despair tells us there is no way home.
Jesus Christ did not die so that repentant sinners would spend the rest of their lives believing they are beyond His mercy.
Romans 8:1 says:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." (KJV)
That promise is not permission to disregard God's commands.
It is the glorious announcement that those who belong to Christ are not condemned.
The same Savior who calls us to holiness also receives those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
And holiness is not merely the absence of certain behaviors.
It is a life increasingly shaped by love, truth, self-control, humility, and communion with God.
So where does that leave the wife who still wants to know whether satisfying herself is wrong?
It leaves her with an honest biblical answer.
Scripture does not directly settle every circumstance of masturbation, and Christians should be cautious about declaring an absolute rule where the biblical text does not explicitly provide one.
That is not the same as saying every form of masturbation is spiritually harmless.
Pornography, adulterous fantasy, compulsive behavior, dishonesty, and the neglect of marital reconciliation raise genuine moral concerns.
But neither should a woman be condemned merely because she experiences sexual desire or asks an honest question about her body.
She should examine her motives and conscience before God, seek wisdom through Scripture, and consider whether her choices support or undermine the health of her marriage.
She should also remember that physical relief is not a substitute for the mutual affection, communication, and companionship that a struggling marriage may need.
And she should not have to navigate all of this alone.
Perhaps tonight, the most courageous thing you can do is not make another private promise that you will somehow stop feeling lonely.
Perhaps it is to tell the truth.
To God.
To yourself.
And, when it is safe and appropriate, to your husband.
"Something between us is hurting, and I don't want us to keep pretending it isn't."
That sentence may not solve everything.
But it may open a door.
And if your husband responds with compassion, there is room to rebuild.
Slowly.
Without pressure.
Without demanding that every affectionate gesture lead to sex.
Perhaps you begin by talking again.
Taking walks.
Holding hands.
Making space for tenderness that doesn't come with an expectation.
Addressing medical or emotional difficulties where necessary.
Learning how to be vulnerable without immediately becoming defensive.
And remembering that sexual intimacy is not a performance that proves your marriage is successful.
It is one possible expression of a deeper covenant relationship that needs care in many dimensions.
There may be setbacks.
There may be difficult discoveries.
Some marriages may require extensive help, and some painful circumstances may not resolve as hoped.
But your story is not reduced to this one struggle.
And your future is not defined by the emptiness of one season.
This is why the message of the Gospel matters so deeply.
Jesus Christ is not merely a religious figure who gives us rules for managing our behavior.
He is the crucified and risen Savior who reconciles us to God and calls us into new life.
He meets sinners with both truth and mercy.
He exposes what destroys us and offers forgiveness.
He calls us away from darkness and toward Himself.
He teaches us to love in ways that confront selfishness and cultivate faithfulness.
And His grace reaches into places where human relationships have left us wounded.
Grace does not guarantee that every husband will change.
Grace does not mean every marriage will be repaired.
Grace does not make painful conversations unnecessary.
But grace means your failures and wounds do not have to be the final word about who you are.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by denying the wounds.
Not by calling sin righteousness or turning legitimate desire into shame.
But by bringing what is broken into the light of His truth and mercy.
Maybe the scandal in your story is betrayal.
Maybe it is years of silence.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is a marriage where two people have forgotten how to love one another well.
Or maybe the scandal is simply that you have been suffering quietly because you believed good Christian women were never supposed to talk about sexual loneliness.
Whatever the struggle, Jesus invites you to come to Him.
And that invitation is more important than winning an argument about one sexual behavior.
Because the ultimate goal of Christian discipleship is not merely to find the outer limit of what we can do without sinning.
It is to know Christ, trust Him, and increasingly reflect His character.
So, dear wife, if you are reading this with tears in your eyes, hear these words.
You are not dirty because you long for intimacy.
You are not worthless because your husband struggles to desire you.
You are not a failure because your marriage has entered a painful season.
You are not required to ignore your emotional and physical well-being to prove that you are faithful.
And you are not beyond the reach of God's wisdom, comfort, or grace.
Bring your desires to Christ.
Bring your questions to Scripture.
Bring your pain into honest conversation.
And refuse to let shame become the voice that tells you who you are.
If this article has touched something you have been afraid to admit, I would love for this conversation to become a place of compassion rather than judgment.
You do not have to disclose intimate details or expose your spouse publicly.
And if you have experienced restoration in your marriage, consider sharing a testimony that protects your family's privacy while giving someone else hope.
There may be a woman reading the comments tonight who needs to know that she is not the only one struggling.
There may also be a husband who needs to realize that his wife's silence does not necessarily mean she is okay.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to create arguments.
But because churches and Christian families need more conversations where biblical truth and genuine compassion can exist together.

You may want to return to these Scriptures when the emotions are less overwhelming, when you are preparing for a difficult conversation, or when you need to remember that God's Word deserves more careful attention than quick, condemning answers.
If you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, I invite you to join us.
Invite your husband, your wife, your family, your Christian friends, and even those who are still searching for faith.
We want to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
And if this ministry has helped you, I want to extend a more personal invitation.
It is a voluntary way to support the ongoing work of this ministry.
For those who choose to give regularly, it can become part of their personal generosity and offering to the Lord, expressed through support for Christian teaching, discipleship, and outreach.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
But because the Gospel is worth sharing, and Christian ministry requires people willing to help carry the work forward.
We want these resources to keep helping people study the Bible, understand the Christian faith, and develop a closer walk with Jesus.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for personal reflection, and meaningful ways to share faith with others.
You can pray for this ministry.
You can encourage a struggling believer.
Every sincere act of service matters, even when it involves no money.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
The One who receives the weary.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who offers forgiveness through His cross.
The One whose resurrection declares that death and darkness do not have the final word.
And to the wife who started reading this because she was desperate for an answer about her sexual frustration, I want to leave you with something more important than an argument.
You deserve an honest conversation about your marriage.
Your husband deserves compassion and the opportunity to explain what he is experiencing.
Both of you deserve to be treated as human beings, not as problems to be solved or obligations to be fulfilled.
And above all, both of you need the grace and truth of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you will close this article and still have unanswered questions.
Perhaps your husband will still be asleep beside you tonight.
Perhaps the conversation you need to have will be difficult.
But do not let the absence of his touch convince you of the absence of God's love.
The Lord has not promised that you will never experience loneliness.
He has promised that His people can bring their burdens to Him.
So bring Him yours.
Not the polished version.
Not the church-friendly version.
The real one.
The woman who is tired of being rejected.
The woman who is confused about her desires.
The woman who loves her husband but misses being loved in ways she can feel.
The woman who wants to honor God but doesn't always know what faithfulness should look like in a painful marriage.
Bring that woman to Jesus.
And ask Him for wisdom, courage, holiness, compassion, and the grace to take the next faithful step.
Because even when your marriage feels painfully quiet, your story is not finished.
The empty space beside you may be painfully real, but it is not the measure of your worth—and it will never be the final word of your Redeemer.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY LOOKED AT HIS CLOTHES. GOD LOOKED AT HIS HEART. AND THE CHURCH ALMOST MISSED HIM.
paragraphs: THEY LOOKED AT HIS CLOTHES. GOD LOOKED AT HIS HEART. AND THE CHURCH ALMOST MISSED HIM.
When appearance becomes the measure of holiness, wealth becomes the language of worth, and the people Jesus came to save begin feeling unwelcome in the very place they should encounter His grace.
What if the person your church quietly looks down on is the very person God is preparing to use?
Read that again.
Because somewhere this Sunday, a man will walk into a church wearing an expensive suit, and people will assume he is blessed.
Another man will walk into the same church wearing faded jeans, worn-out shoes, and a shirt that has seen better days.
And before either man opens his Bible, bows his head, or whispers a single prayer, some people will have already decided which one looks more spiritual.
One will receive smiles, handshakes, and invitations.
The other may receive a few uncomfortable glances.
And perhaps nobody will say anything cruel.
That is what makes it so heartbreaking.
Sometimes rejection doesn't announce itself with hateful words.
Sometimes it is simply the empty seat nobody invites you to occupy.
The conversation that stops when you approach.
The eyes that travel from your face to your shoes.
The warmth that suddenly disappears when someone discovers you have no impressive job title, no influential family, and no money to contribute.
And the saddest part?
All of this can happen beneath a cross that represents a Savior who was rejected by men.
How did we become so impressed by the things Jesus never told us to worship?
How did clothing become a measure of holiness?
How did financial success become evidence of spiritual maturity?
How did social influence become more convincing than humility, repentance, compassion, and obedience?
And how many people have walked away from a church gathering, not because they rejected Jesus Christ, but because they felt rejected by people claiming to represent Him?
Before we answer, we need to return to a moment in Scripture when God confronted this very human tendency.
Because this problem did not begin with modern Christianity.
It was already present in the days of Samuel.
And God had something unforgettable to say about it.
When the prophet Samuel arrived at Jesse's house to anoint the next king of Israel, he saw Eliab, a man whose appearance apparently suggested leadership.
Samuel was impressed.
Surely this must be the one.
But God interrupted his judgment.
In 1 Samuel 16:7, the Lord declared:
“For man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.” — 1 Samuel 16:7, KJV
The original Hebrew makes this contrast especially striking.
כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וַיהוָה יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב
Ki ha'adam yir'eh la'enayim, va-YHWH yir'eh lalevav.
The phrase לַלֵּבָב (lalevav) refers to the heart, the inner person.
In biblical Hebrew, the heart is not merely the place where emotions are felt. It is closely associated with thought, intention, desire, will, and moral character.
God was not telling Samuel that physical appearance was always meaningless.
He was correcting Samuel's assumption that outward impressiveness revealed the person God had chosen.
Samuel could see Eliab's appearance.
God knew what Samuel could not see.
And that distinction matters.
Because we can observe someone's clothing.
We can notice someone's financial circumstances.
We can recognize someone's position in society.
But we cannot look into another human being and possess God's complete knowledge of the heart.
We are not omniscient.
We are not qualified to make final judgments about someone's standing before God based on appearances.
And when we act as though we are, we begin occupying a position that belongs to the Lord alone.
The next king was not the impressive son Samuel initially expected.
It was David.
The young shepherd who had not even been brought into the initial gathering.
Imagine that.
The one overlooked by the people in the room was the one God had chosen.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what it feels like to be overlooked.
You know what it feels like to be the person nobody expects much from.
The one without the education others admire.
The one whose family name opens no doors.
The one who cannot afford the clothes that seem to make everyone else look respectable.
The one who loves Jesus deeply but sometimes feels painfully out of place among people who appear to have everything together.
You may have wondered whether your life matters less because you have less.
But listen carefully.
Your financial condition is not the measurement of your value before God.
Your wardrobe cannot purchase His acceptance.
Your family background cannot disqualify you from receiving His mercy.
And your social status cannot make the blood of Jesus more powerful for you than for someone else.
At the cross, the ground is level.
Every sinner needs the same Savior.
Every believer is saved by the same grace.
And nobody enters the kingdom of God through an expensive entrance reserved for the socially impressive.
But there is another passage that brings this truth painfully close to the modern church.
And it is so direct that we cannot honestly read it without examining ourselves.
James chapter 2.
Picture the scene.
Two visitors enter a Christian assembly.
One is wealthy.
He wears fine clothing and a gold ring.
The other is poor.
His clothing is shabby.
The wealthy man receives special attention and a desirable seat.
The poor man is told to stand aside or sit in a humiliating place.
Then James asks a devastating question:
“Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?” — James 2:4, KJV
The original Greek uses the word προσωπολημψίαις (prosōpolēmpsiais) in James 2:1, referring to acts of favoritism or partiality.
The expression is connected with the idea of judging or treating people according to their outward standing.
James begins with a command:
“My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.” — James 2:1, KJV
In other words, faith in the glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not be practiced alongside discriminatory favoritism.
Notice what James does not say.
He does not say wealthy people are automatically evil.
He does not say fine clothing is sinful.
He does not command Christians to despise successful people.
He condemns the act of assigning unequal honor and treatment because one person appears wealthy and another appears poor.
That is the sin.
And it is astonishing how easily the same thing can happen today.
A successful businessman visits a congregation, and suddenly people want to know his name.
A struggling laborer visits, and hardly anyone asks whether he needs prayer.
A wealthy family arrives, and someone quickly introduces them to church leadership.
A single mother arrives with tired eyes, restless children, and clothes she could barely afford, and someone notices only that her children are making noise.
A well-known personality shares a Bible verse online, and thousands celebrate.
An unknown believer quietly cares for the sick, feeds a hungry neighbor, and prays through the night, and almost nobody notices.
Yet which one is more spiritually mature?
We cannot answer that question merely by looking at their public image.
God knows the truth.
And Scripture calls us to examine the fruit of a person's life rather than assume spiritual superiority from outward status.
Jesus Himself taught:
“Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.” — Matthew 7:20, KJV
That means the Bible does not prohibit all moral discernment.
Christians are called to recognize truth, reject hypocrisy, and examine conduct according to God's Word.
But biblical discernment is not the same as superficial prejudice.
A person wearing modest clothing is not automatically humble.
A person wearing expensive clothing is not automatically proud.
A poor person is not automatically righteous.
A rich person is not automatically corrupt.
A person with tattoos, scars, unconventional hair, or a difficult past is not automatically rebellious against God.
And a person carrying a Bible, wearing a cross, and speaking fluent Christian language is not automatically surrendered to Jesus.
The question is deeper.
What is happening in the heart?
What does the person's life reveal over time?
Is there repentance?
Is there love?
Is there truthfulness?
Is there obedience to Christ?
Is there the fruit of the Holy Spirit?
Because it is possible to look religious while remaining spiritually far from God.
Jesus confronted this very danger.
In Matthew 23:27–28, He rebuked religious leaders who appeared righteous outwardly while harboring hypocrisy and lawlessness within.
Think about the weight of that warning.
You can look holy and still need repentance.
You can appear successful and still be spiritually empty.
You can receive admiration from an entire congregation and still be hiding a heart that has not surrendered to Christ.
And you can be the person sitting quietly at the back, wearing worn-out clothes, carrying invisible grief, yet sincerely trusting the Savior who sees you.
That should change the way we look at people.
But perhaps the hardest part of this message is not recognizing how others have judged us.
Perhaps it is admitting how we have judged others.
Because prejudice rarely feels like prejudice when we are the ones practicing it.
We call it discernment.
We call it maintaining standards.
We call it protecting the church's image.
We call it being careful about the company we keep.
And sometimes genuine wisdom and appropriate standards really are necessary.
But sometimes those explanations become respectable disguises for pride.
We notice someone's appearance and invent an entire story about their character.
We hear that someone is unemployed and assume they are irresponsible.
We see someone living in poverty and quietly wonder whether they have failed to earn God's blessing.
We see someone financially successful and assume they must have extraordinary faith.
We see a person struggling with addiction, broken relationships, or a shameful past, and forget that the Gospel was never intended only for people whose lives already looked presentable.
And here is the question that should disturb us:
If Jesus welcomed repentant sinners, why are we sometimes uncomfortable when sinners come close enough to encounter Him?
In Luke 7:36–50, a woman known in her city as sinful approached Jesus while He was dining in the house of Simon the Pharisee.
She wept at His feet.
She wet His feet with her tears.
She wiped them with her hair.
She kissed His feet and anointed them.
Simon looked at her reputation.
Jesus addressed the reality of her love, faith, and need for forgiveness.
Simon saw a scandal.
Jesus revealed the power of grace.
But do not miss the heart of the passage.
Jesus did not declare that sin was harmless.
He spoke of forgiveness.
He exposed Simon's failure to love.
And He told the woman:
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” — Luke 7:50, KJV
That is the Gospel we must never lose.
Jesus does not save us by pretending our sins do not matter.
He saves sinners through His grace, calling us to repentance and faith, and transforming us through His redeeming work.
He does not merely improve our public reputation.
He reconciles us to God.
And sometimes the people who most clearly understand the beauty of forgiveness are the people who know how desperately they needed it.
Perhaps you have been that person.
The one who entered church carrying a past you wished you could erase.
The one who sat through worship wondering whether anyone would still welcome you if they knew your story.
The one who wanted to pray but could barely lift your head because shame had become so heavy.
The one who heard people talk about holiness and wondered whether there was still room for someone like you.
There is something you need to hear.
You do not have to make your past look respectable before you come to Jesus Christ.
You come to Him as a sinner in need of mercy.
You confess.
You repent.
You believe.
And you learn to walk in the new life that His grace makes possible.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had repaired every broken piece.
Not after we had earned society's approval.
Not after we could afford better clothing.
Not after we had become impressive enough to deserve attention.
Christ died for sinners.
That truth should produce extraordinary humility in every Christian heart.
Because nobody who truly understands grace can honestly boast that they saved themselves.
But we must also address another uncomfortable question.
Does this mean Christians should never care about clothing, modesty, or respectful presentation?
No.
That would be another misunderstanding of Scripture.
The Bible does teach modesty, self-control, humility, and godliness.
In 1 Timothy 2:9–10, Paul speaks about appropriate dress and the greater importance of good works.
In 1 Peter 3:3–4, Peter directs attention away from merely external adornment toward the lasting beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit.
These passages are not permission to humiliate someone who cannot afford expensive clothing.
Neither do they mean every form of dress is morally irrelevant.
They teach us to place outward presentation beneath the greater priorities of godliness and the heart.
There is a difference between lovingly teaching biblical modesty and making someone feel spiritually inferior because their clothes are inexpensive.
There is a difference between maintaining appropriate standards for a particular ministry responsibility and judging someone's worth by their appearance.
There is a difference between encouraging reverence in worship and turning the church into a place where people feel they must dress like the wealthy to be treated with dignity.
And there is a difference between honoring God with our resources and assuming financial prosperity proves divine approval.
Remember Job.
He lost his possessions, his children, and his health.
His suffering did not mean he had suddenly become worthless to God.
Remember the poor widow in Mark 12:41–44.
Others gave larger amounts.
She gave two small coins.
Jesus drew attention to the significance of her sacrificial gift.
Her offering was not impressive by worldly financial standards.
But Jesus saw something deeper than the amount.
He saw what the gift cost her.
That is why we must be careful whenever money becomes a measure of spiritual worth.
A large donation does not automatically prove great faith.
A small donation does not automatically reveal weak faith.
And someone who cannot give financially may still serve Christ faithfully through prayer, encouragement, hospitality, mercy, and countless unseen acts of love.
God's people should never be treated as spiritual customers whose dignity increases with their spending power.
The church belongs to Jesus Christ.
And the people He purchased with His blood are not merchandise.
Giving can be a beautiful expression of worship, gratitude, generosity, and partnership in the Gospel.
Paul encouraged believers to support Gospel work.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, he wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
Giving should arise from a willing heart.
It should never be presented as a purchase of salvation, a guarantee of financial prosperity, or a payment required to prove that someone truly loves God.
And that matters deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
Because our mission is not to build a community where those who can pay are treated as more valuable than those who cannot.
Our mission is to proclaim Jesus Christ, teach Scripture faithfully, encourage repentance, strengthen struggling believers, and help people grow in the grace and knowledge of the Lord.
We believe Christian teaching should reach the person who can afford to support it and the person who cannot.

These resources are intended to help believers study the Word of God, deepen their prayer lives, strengthen their understanding of Scripture, and continue following Jesus beyond a single inspirational moment.
Not because God loves paying supporters more.
But because freely choosing to support Gospel-centered ministry can be one meaningful way to glorify God through generosity and help make biblical encouragement available to others.
It can help us keep creating, teaching, sharing, and developing resources for people who may never be able to contribute financially themselves.
Those products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, opportunities for conversation, and practical encouragement in daily life.
It is the opportunity to participate in work that seeks to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
You are still welcome here.
You are still invited to learn.
You are still invited to grow.
You can still access our free resources, pray for this ministry, encourage someone with Scripture, and help the message reach others.
Your value before God is not determined by whether you can contribute financially.
Perhaps there is a friend who stopped attending church because they felt judged.
Perhaps there is a family member who believes God must be disappointed with them because their life does not look successful.
Perhaps there is a struggling believer who has confused poverty with spiritual failure.
Or perhaps there is someone who has spent years pretending to be spiritually strong because they are terrified of what people might think if they told the truth.
Because the message of the Gospel is too important to be confined to people who already look acceptable to society.
But there is something even more important than sharing this article.
There is something God may be asking us to confront in ourselves.
Think about the last person you quietly judged.
Not the person you openly criticized.
The person you silently dismissed.
Maybe their clothes seemed inappropriate.
Maybe their appearance made you uncomfortable.
Maybe their financial struggles made you assume they were irresponsible.
Maybe their social background made you feel superior.
Maybe you knew something about their past and decided they could never become a serious follower of Christ.
Now imagine that person standing before the cross.
Imagine Jesus looking upon a sinner who desperately needs mercy.
And remember that you and I stand before that same cross with exactly the same fundamental need.
Forgiveness.
Grace.
Redemption.
A new heart.
We cannot save ourselves.
And the more clearly we see the holiness of God, the less room we have to boast about our own appearance of righteousness.
This is why James does not treat favoritism as a minor social mistake.
In James 2:8–9, he connects it directly to the command to love our neighbor as ourselves and identifies partiality as sin.
That is serious.
When we honor people according to their wealth while humiliating those who are poor, we are not merely violating good manners.
We are acting against the royal law of love.
And love is not simply an emotion we feel toward people who resemble us.
It is a command that reaches across differences in income, education, appearance, social standing, and personal history.
It calls us to treat others with dignity because they are human beings made in God's image.
It calls believers to honor one another as members of Christ's body.
It calls us to resist pride.
And sometimes it calls us to apologize.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you treated differently because they had less.
Maybe you need to stop laughing when others mock someone's appearance.
Maybe you need to invite the person who always sits alone to sit beside you.
Maybe you need to learn the name of the church visitor nobody else seems interested in meeting.
Maybe you need to stop confusing someone's polished public image with genuine spiritual maturity.
Or perhaps your next act of obedience is not directed toward someone else.
Perhaps it is time to stop believing the cruel judgment you have placed upon yourself.
You have spent so long comparing your life with others.
Their careers.
Their homes.
Their clothes.
Their beautiful family photographs.
Their accomplishments.
Their confidence.
Their apparently effortless success.
And somewhere along the way, you began believing that because your life looks smaller, your faith must be smaller too.
But Scripture never teaches that God measures His children's spiritual maturity by the price of their possessions.
The Lord calls us to faithfulness.
To humility.
To love.
To holiness.
To perseverance.
To repentance.
To trust in Jesus Christ.
Some of the most faithful believers in history have suffered poverty, rejection, persecution, and obscurity.
And the greatest example is our Savior Himself.
Isaiah 53:2–3 describes the promised Servant as lacking the outward majesty people would naturally admire and as being despised and rejected.
The Gospel accounts show Jesus mocked, beaten, and crucified.
The One through whom all things were created entered the deepest humiliation.
The Lord of glory was treated as though He had no glory.
The sinless Savior was condemned by sinful men.
And at Calvary, human judgment appeared to have delivered its final verdict.
Rejected.
Humiliated.
Defeated.
But the resurrection revealed the truth.
Jesus Christ was not defeated.
He rose from the dead.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and eternal life are proclaimed to those who repent and believe in Him.
That is why our theme is more than an inspiring slogan.
The scandal of our sin is real.
The shame we carry can be devastating.
The judgments people make can leave wounds that remain for years.
But the grace of God in Jesus Christ reaches deeper than human reputation.
He does not merely teach us to appear better.
He gives new life.
He calls sinners out of darkness.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
And He teaches His people to see one another through the lens of truth and love rather than the distorted lens of pride and worldly status.
This does not mean we suddenly possess God's ability to know every heart.
We do not.
It means we become humbler about what we cannot know and more faithful in how we treat the people standing before us.
It means the wealthy visitor receives genuine love without flattery.
The poor visitor receives genuine love without humiliation.
The wounded visitor receives compassion without the abandonment of truth.
The repentant sinner receives encouragement without the denial of sin.
And the person who seems outwardly impressive is reminded that spiritual life is about far more than appearance.
Imagine what could happen if our churches lived this way.
Imagine a congregation where a businessman and a janitor could worship side by side without either being considered more valuable.
Imagine a church where a struggling single mother was welcomed with practical compassion rather than suspicious glances.
Imagine a fellowship where people did not have to pretend they were financially successful to feel respected.
Imagine a community where holiness was taught faithfully but human dignity was never reserved for the well-dressed.
Imagine the person who once felt too ashamed to enter a church finally finding believers who spoke truth, extended mercy, and pointed them to Jesus.
And imagine the testimony that could emerge from that encounter.
Not because the church became a place where sin was ignored.
But because it became a place where the Gospel was believed.
Where truth and grace were not treated as enemies.
Where repentance was welcomed.
Where pride was confronted.
Where mercy was practiced.
Where Jesus Christ was honored above social status.
Perhaps this article has brought back a painful memory.
A time someone judged you because of what you wore.
A moment you were treated differently because you had less.
A season when you felt invisible among people who claimed to love God.
Or perhaps it has exposed something you would rather not admit.
You have been the person doing the judging.
If so, do not waste this moment defending yourself.
Bring it before the Lord.
Ask Him to search your heart.
Ask Him to expose pride, prejudice, bitterness, and resentment.
Ask Him to teach you to love people without pretending that outward appearances reveal everything about their souls.
And if you have been wounded by the hypocrisy of Christians, remember that the failures of Christ's followers do not change the character of Christ Himself.
Do not let someone else's prejudice convince you that Jesus shares their prejudice.
Look at Him in the Scriptures.
Listen to His words.
Consider His cross.
Remember His resurrection.
And bring your pain to the One who knows the heart perfectly.
If you need words to begin, perhaps your prayer could be as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have judged others by appearances. Forgive me for the pride I have hidden behind religious language. Heal the wounds left by rejection, and teach me to treat others with the mercy and truth You have shown me. Help me see people as human beings who need Your grace, not as social rankings to admire or dismiss. Change my heart. Make me more like You. Amen.”
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not for a perfect answer.
Not for a religious performance.
Just for honesty.
Have you ever felt judged in a church because of your appearance, clothing, poverty, or social status? Or has God convicted you that you once treated someone else that way?
Your testimony may help another believer realize they are not alone.
And your willingness to admit where you need to grow may encourage someone else to repent.
You do not need to reveal private details or reopen wounds you are not ready to discuss.
But if God has used this message to bring conviction, comfort, or clarity, do not let that truth disappear when you close your screen.
Jesus Christ must remain the center.
Not our clothing.
Not our reputation.
Not our financial success.
Not our religious performance.
Not even the ministry that shares His message.
Christ alone is the Savior.
And the same Jesus who calls us to repentance also offers mercy to those who come to Him in faith.
So the next time someone enters your church, do not begin by examining their shoes.
Do not calculate their value from their profession.
Do not measure their spiritual worth by their possessions.
Remember David.
Remember James.
Remember the woman who wept at Jesus' feet.
Remember the poor widow.
Remember the cross.
And remember how much grace you yourself have needed.
Because one day, the clothes we were so impressed by will be gone.
The titles will be gone.
The applause will be silent.
The money we used to measure people's importance will no longer impress anyone.
And every human being will stand before the Lord who judges with perfect righteousness.
What will matter then is not whether we looked impressive to the world, but whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
So here is the question I pray will stay with you long after this article ends:
How many people have we failed to love because we were too busy judging what they wore, what they owned, or where they came from?
May God forgive us.
May He change us.
And may our churches become places where the truth of the Gospel is not merely preached from the pulpit but demonstrated in the way we treat the people standing at the door.
The person you almost refused to sit beside may be the person whose prayers God will one day use to help carry you through your darkest hour.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Because this story did not begin with Abishag.
paragraphs: Because this story did not begin with Abishag.
It did not begin with Adonijah.
And it certainly did not begin with Solomon's anger.
It began long before that, when a king looked from his rooftop and made a decision that would leave scars across generations.
His name was David.
And the woman at the center of that earlier scandal was Bathsheba.
The same Bathsheba who would one day walk into Solomon's throne room.
The same Bathsheba whose life had been shattered by royal power.
The same Bathsheba whose son now sat upon Israel's throne.
And the same Bathsheba who was about to discover that even a mother's request could carry consequences she never anticipated.
Stay with this story.
Because somewhere between David's rooftop, Solomon's throne, and the cross of Jesus Christ, Scripture confronts a question we would rather avoid.
What happens when something we desperately want begins to matter more to us than what God has already made clear?
Bathsheba knew what it meant to live beneath the weight of another person's desire.

Second Samuel 11 tells us that David saw her bathing, sent messengers, and took her. The biblical account places responsibility upon David, the king who possessed the power and initiated the encounter.
Bathsheba was married to Uriah, a soldier serving David's kingdom.
When she became pregnant, David attempted to conceal what had happened.
When his attempts failed, he arranged for Uriah to be placed in a deadly military position and abandoned in battle.
Uriah died.
Bathsheba mourned her husband.
And David took her into his house.
For a season, the scandal may have appeared buried beneath the authority of a royal throne.
But God had seen everything.
Second Samuel 11:27 declares:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” (KJV)
That sentence should terrify anyone who believes that successfully hiding sin means escaping God's attention.
David could manipulate military orders.
He could command messengers.
He could control appearances.
But he could not control the holiness of God.
When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
And Nathan announced that the LORD had put away his sin.
Yet forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence.
The child born from that first pregnancy died. Violence and betrayal would trouble David's household. His family would experience devastating conflict.
We must be careful here. Scripture does not permit us to blame Bathsheba for David's abuse of royal power, nor does it teach that every suffering person is being punished for a particular sin.
But it does reveal something deeply sobering.
Sin can be forgiven without becoming harmless.
And choices made in secret can leave consequences that outlive the moment.
Still, the story did not end in disgrace.
Bathsheba later bore Solomon.
Second Samuel 12:24 says that the LORD loved him.
Think about that.
Out of a family history marked by grief and moral failure, God continued His redemptive purposes.
Not because David's wrongdoing was acceptable.
Not because Bathsheba's suffering was insignificant.
But because human sin does not possess the final authority over God's mercy.
Grace does not rename evil as good. Grace reveals that evil does not have the power to defeat God's ultimate purpose.
Years passed.
David grew old.
And the question of who would inherit his throne became increasingly urgent.
Adonijah, another son of David, decided to make himself king.
First Kings 1:5 records his declaration:
“I will be king.” (KJV)
Notice those words.
Not, “Has the LORD appointed me?”
Not, “What is my father's instruction?”
Not, “How can I serve God's people?”
Simply:
“I will be king.”
Adonijah gathered supporters, including Joab and Abiathar. He arranged a royal celebration and acted as though the kingdom already belonged to him.
But David had designated Solomon as his successor.
Through the intervention of Nathan and Bathsheba, David publicly confirmed Solomon's kingship.
Adonijah's attempted seizure of the throne collapsed.
And for a moment, it appeared that mercy might prevail.
Adonijah feared Solomon and sought refuge by grasping the horns of the altar.
Solomon did not immediately execute him.
Instead, he granted conditional mercy.
First Kings 1:52 records Solomon's warning:
“If he will shew himself a worthy man, there shall not an hair of him fall to the earth: but if wickedness shall be found in him, he shall die.” (KJV)
Adonijah had been given an opportunity to live peacefully under the king God had appointed.
That detail matters.
Because when we reach the next chapter, we are not watching an innocent man encounter a king who has never shown him mercy.
We are watching a previously defeated claimant approach the boundaries of that mercy.
And what he does next changes everything.
Adonijah approaches Bathsheba.
Imagine the tension.
She is the mother of Solomon.
He is Solomon's older half brother.
They belong to the same fractured royal family.
And Adonijah has already attempted to take the throne now occupied by her son.
When Bathsheba sees him, she asks a revealing question:
“Comest thou peaceably?” (1 Kings 2:13, KJV)
He answers:
“Peaceably.”
Then he begins speaking about the kingdom.
He tells her that the throne had been his expectation and that Israel had looked toward him as king.
But he acknowledges that the kingdom has become Solomon's, saying:
“For it was his from the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:15, KJV)
Read that carefully.
Adonijah acknowledges that Solomon's kingship came from the LORD.
Yet he is about to request something Solomon will interpret as another attempt to claim royal standing.
There is a dangerous contradiction here.
A person can acknowledge God's decision with his lips while still pursuing something that challenges it.
We cannot see every hidden thought in Adonijah's heart. Scripture does not give us permission to claim that we know every private motive.
But it does show us his previous rebellion, his present request, and Solomon's interpretation of its political meaning.
Then Adonijah says:
“Ask on my behalf for Abishag the Shunammite to be given to me as my wife.” (1 Kings 2:17, translated from the Hebrew)
Abishag.
A name that might seem insignificant to a modern reader.
But in the royal household of ancient Israel, this was no ordinary marriage proposal.
Abishag had been brought to care for the elderly David during his final days.
First Kings 1:4 explicitly states that David did not have sexual relations with her.
She was not described as David's wife in that passage, and we should not invent a marriage the text does not establish.
Nevertheless, she had occupied an intimate position within the former king's household.
In the political world of ancient monarchy, relationships involving women associated with a previous king could carry implications of succession and royal authority.
Second Samuel 16:21–22 had already demonstrated how publicly taking possession of a king's concubines could serve as a claim to his royal position.
Adonijah's request therefore carried implications far beyond romance.
Whether he personally understood every consequence or not, Solomon certainly recognized the danger.
And Bathsheba agreed to carry the request.
First Kings 2:18 records her answer:
“Well; I will speak for thee unto the king.” (KJV)
That single sentence changed the direction of the story.
Bathsheba went to Solomon.
And what happened next is one of the most striking scenes in the chapter.
When Solomon saw his mother, he rose to meet her.
He bowed before her.
Then he sat upon his throne and ordered another seat to be placed for her at his right hand.
Imagine that scene.
The most powerful man in Israel standing in honor of his mother.
The king bowing before the woman who had once endured terrible suffering under the power of another king.
Bathsheba was no longer standing at the margins of royal life.
She was seated beside her son.
Honored.
Heard.
Given a place of dignity.
And Solomon invited her to speak.
She said:
“I desire one small petition of thee; I pray thee, say me not nay.” (1 Kings 2:20, KJV)
One small petition.
That is how she described it.
Solomon answered:
“Ask on, my mother: for I will not say thee nay.”
Then Bathsheba presented the request.
Give Abishag the Shunammite to Adonijah as his wife.
And suddenly the atmosphere changed.
The king who had risen to honor his mother now responded with unmistakable alarm.
“And why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also.” (1 Kings 2:22, KJV)
There it is.
The sentence that reveals why Solomon considered the request so dangerous.
In his judgment, asking for Abishag was not merely asking for a marriage.
It was effectively asking for the kingdom.
Solomon explicitly connected Adonijah's request with his status as the older brother and with the political influence of Abiathar and Joab.
To Solomon, this was a threat to the established throne.
And he refused it.
Now consider the Hebrew wording behind the confrontation.
In 1 Kings 2:22, Solomon says:
וְלָמָּה אַתְּ שֹׁאֶלֶת אֶת־אֲבִישַׁג הַשֻּׁנַמִּית לַאֲדֹנִיָּהוּ
Ve-lammah att sho'elet et-Avishag ha-Shunammit la-Adoniyyahu?
A close translation is:
“And why are you asking for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah?”
Then comes the piercing command:
וְשַׁאֲלִי־לוֹ אֶת־הַמְּלוּכָה
Ve-sha'ali lo et-ha-melukhah.
“Ask for him the kingdom also.”
The Hebrew word מְלוּכָה (melukhah) refers to kingship or royal rule.
Solomon was identifying what he believed stood behind the marriage request: a renewed challenge to royal authority.
Bathsheba had described her request as small.
Solomon understood its implications as enormous.
And here is where this ancient account begins pressing into our modern lives.
How many things have we called small because we did not want to confront what they might become?
A conversation we should never have continued.
A secret attachment we insisted was innocent.
A compromise we excused because nobody seemed hurt.
A bitterness we protected because we felt justified.
A desire we refused to surrender because we had already decided we deserved it.
Not every request hides an evil intention. Not every desire is rebellion.
But Scripture repeatedly warns that our hearts require examination.
Jeremiah 17:9 speaks of the heart's capacity for deceit.
James 1:14–15 describes how desire, when it gives birth to sin, can ultimately lead to death.
And Jesus teaches that evil actions emerge from within the human heart (Mark 7:20–23).
The danger is not merely that other people may deceive us.
It is that we can become remarkably skilled at deceiving ourselves.
We can call pride conviction.
We can call jealousy discernment.
We can call revenge justice.
We can call disobedience freedom.
We can even call our refusal to surrender “waiting for God's timing.”
And sometimes, while our mouths are saying, “Lord, Your will be done,” our decisions are quietly saying, “But I still want my throne.”
That is a terrifying place to live.
Because the human heart does not need a crown to struggle with the desire to rule.
Sometimes the throne we refuse to surrender is simply control over our own lives.
Solomon's response was immediate.
He swore by the LORD that Adonijah would die because of the request.
First Kings 2:24 says:
“Adonijah shall be put to death this day.” (KJV)
Then Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada.
And Adonijah was executed.
The chapter states the outcome without softening it.
No extended farewell.
No dramatic final speech.
No invented last-minute confession.
Just the stark conclusion of a political struggle inside Israel's royal household.
We must resist the temptation to turn this into a simplistic lesson that every harsh action taken by a biblical king automatically reflects God's moral ideal.
The narrative reports Solomon's judgment and the execution. It also places these events within the establishment of his kingdom.
But the passage does not explicitly record a fresh divine command ordering this particular execution.
The Bible's historical descriptions must be interpreted carefully. Reporting an action is not always the same as commanding believers to imitate it.
Christians are not authorized by this passage to punish personal rivals, destroy those who threaten their influence, or confuse human anger with divine justice.
The deeper warning is not that we should behave like absolute monarchs.
It is that the pursuit of power, the consequences of rebellion, and the vulnerability of human hearts are profoundly serious matters.
And there is another person in this story we should not overlook.
Abishag.
The woman whose name was spoken.
The woman whose marriage was requested.
The woman whose future became entangled with royal ambition.
She is not recorded speaking in this scene.
We are not told what she wanted.
We are not told whether anyone sought her consent.
The silence of the narrative should make us cautious about romanticizing Adonijah's proposal.
Behind the political struggle was a real woman whose wishes are not preserved in the account.
And behind many human struggles for control are people who become instruments in someone else's ambitions.
That, too, is a warning.
Whenever our desires become so important that we stop seeing the dignity of others, something has gone terribly wrong.
Jesus Christ calls His followers to a different understanding of greatness.
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus contrasts rulers who exercise power over others with the servant-hearted leadership He requires of His disciples.
Then He declares:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45, KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Adonijah reached toward a throne.
Jesus willingly humbled Himself.
Human kings struggled to preserve their power.
The eternal Son of God took the form of a servant.
Earthly rulers could sentence others to death.
Jesus went to the cross to save sinners.
And this is where the story becomes more than a palace tragedy.
Because Solomon, for all his wisdom and royal authority, was not the final answer to humanity's brokenness.
He was a flawed human king.
His reign would eventually reveal serious spiritual failures of its own.
First Kings 11 records how Solomon's heart turned away from wholehearted devotion to the LORD.
Even the king who could recognize danger in another man's ambition would not remain immune to the temptations of his own heart.
That should humble every one of us.
It is possible to recognize someone else's compromise while overlooking our own.
It is possible to speak wisely and still live foolishly.
It is possible to begin with extraordinary privilege and finish with devastating disobedience.
Knowledge alone cannot redeem the human heart.
Position cannot redeem it.
Religious heritage cannot redeem it.
Even a throne connected to God's covenant promises cannot make a sinful human being righteous.
We need a greater King.
And Scripture points us to Him.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The righteous King.
The One who came not to seize what did not belong to Him, but to fulfill the Father's will.
The One who did not manipulate His way into power but humbled Himself in obedience, even to death on a cross.
Philippians 2:8 declares:
“He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” (KJV)
Consider the difference.
Adonijah said, “I will be king.”
Jesus prayed:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” (Luke 22:42, KJV)
One statement reveals the danger of self-exaltation.
The other reveals the beauty of perfect surrender.
And only one of these men could save us.
Not Adonijah.
Not Solomon.
Not David.
Only Jesus.
Because the deepest problem in this story is not simply a disputed marriage request.
It is the fallen human heart.
The heart that wants authority without submission.
Blessing without obedience.
Forgiveness without repentance.
A crown without a cross.
And if we are willing to be spiritually honest, we have all wrestled with that heart in one form or another.
Perhaps you have never tried to take a kingdom.
But have you ever tried to take control away from God?
Have you ever prayed for His guidance while secretly deciding you would only obey if His answer matched your desires?
Have you ever justified something you knew was wrong because giving it up would hurt?
Have you ever mistaken an open opportunity for divine permission?
Or have you been so wounded by what someone else did that you now struggle to believe God can write anything beautiful from your life?
That last question matters especially when we remember Bathsheba.
Her story was not simply about the sins and ambitions of kings.
It was also about a woman who experienced loss, lived through the consequences of royal wrongdoing, and later became the mother of a king.
We should never use her later position to minimize her earlier suffering.
Nor should we suggest that suffering automatically produces earthly promotion.
But her story does remind us that a person's painful past need not be the final description of their life.
And the New Testament gives us a remarkable reminder.
In Matthew 1:6, the genealogy of Jesus identifies Solomon's mother as the woman who had been Uriah's wife.
Matthew does not erase Uriah from the story.
The Gospel does not pretend the scandal never happened.
It preserves the uncomfortable history within the family line through which the Messiah came.
Why is that so powerful?
Because God's redemptive work does not depend upon rewriting the past as though sin never existed.
He tells the truth about human failure.
And then He reveals a Savior greater than that failure.
The Gospel is not that our scandals were secretly harmless. The Gospel is that Jesus Christ is mighty enough to redeem sinners without ever calling sin righteous.
That is the grace we need.
Not a religious performance.
Not a carefully edited testimony.
Not a public image designed to conceal private wounds.
We need forgiveness.
We need repentance.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need a new heart.
And Jesus does not invite us to save ourselves by becoming impressive enough.
He calls us to turn from sin and believe the Gospel.
Mark 1:15 records His words:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what we did.
It is turning toward God with a changed understanding of sin and a willingness to surrender to His authority.
And grace is not permission to remain enslaved to the very things Christ came to save us from.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace also trains us to reject ungodliness and live in a manner that honors Him.
The grace of Jesus forgives.
And the grace of Jesus transforms.
Perhaps that is the message someone reading this needs most tonight.
You have been hiding.
Not necessarily from other people.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing well.
You still attend church.
You still share Bible verses.
You still say “God is good.”
But privately, you are exhausted from negotiating with the very things God has been calling you to surrender.
There is a habit you keep defending.
A resentment you keep feeding.
A relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ.
A secret you are afraid to confess.
Or a wound you have mistaken for your permanent identity.
And the hardest part is that you know enough Scripture to recognize the truth.
You just do not know whether you have the courage to face it.
Listen carefully.
The same Jesus who exposes sin is the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
You do not have to pretend before Him.
You do not have to manufacture a beautiful testimony.
You do not have to convince Him that your failures were smaller than they were.
Come into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not an invitation to manipulate God with empty words.
It is an invitation to genuine confession grounded in the faithfulness and righteousness of God.
And if you are in Christ, your past does not get to overrule His saving work.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
What a breathtaking contrast.
In Solomon's court, Adonijah's request ended in an execution.
At Calvary, Jesus willingly endured death so that guilty sinners who trust in Him might receive forgiveness and life.
We must not pretend those two events are morally or theologically identical.
But the contrast directs our attention to the glory of Christ.
The final hope of the Christian faith is not that we find a human king powerful enough to eliminate every rival.
It is that God has given us a Savior righteous enough to defeat sin and death.
Jesus was crucified.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
His resurrection declares that death does not possess the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why the message of Gospel Warrior is not merely about surviving scandals.
It is about redemption through the crucified and risen Christ.
Not because our mistakes were insignificant.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored in this life.
But because Jesus Christ can forgive sin, transform lives, restore fellowship with God, and give eternal hope to those who trust Him.
And sometimes that transformation begins with the most difficult prayer a human heart can offer.
“Lord, I wanted my own way more than I wanted Yours.”
No impressive speech.
No spiritual performance.
Just surrender.
Maybe you need to pray that tonight.
Maybe you need to stop calling something harmless when your conscience has been warning you for months.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you wounded.
Maybe you need to seek help for a destructive pattern.
Maybe you need to return to Scripture instead of listening only to voices that affirm what you already want.
Maybe you need to believe that repentance is not the end of your story.
It can be the beginning of a life increasingly shaped by Christ.
And maybe someone you love is standing at that same crossroads.
A son who has drifted from faith.
A daughter who believes she has gone too far.
A husband carrying silent shame.
A wife whose heart has been crushed.
A friend who keeps smiling while privately losing hope.
Someone who has confused religious activity with actually knowing Jesus.
Someone who needs to hear that God is holy, sin is serious, and the mercy offered through Jesus Christ is real.
Do not let this message end with you.
You can simply write “No more hiding” if you are ready to bring something into the light before God.
You do not have to expose private details or explain wounds you are not ready to share.
And if you have experienced the forgiveness and restoring mercy of Jesus, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that change is impossible.
Not as a substitute for reading Scripture, but as a reminder to return to 1 Kings 2:13–25 and examine the passage carefully for yourself.
Read the chapter.
Read what came before it.
Ask God for wisdom to distinguish your desires from His revealed will.
Because the goal is not merely to feel moved by a powerful story.
The goal is to become a faithful disciple of Jesus Christ.
And that is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
We are not here simply to produce content that stirs emotion for a few minutes before disappearing into another social media feed.
Our desire is to help people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in biblical truth, pursue repentance, and continue following Christ when the emotional moment has passed.
Through Gospel Warrior, we want to keep bringing Scripture-centered teaching, devotionals, encouragement, discipleship resources, and honest conversations about faith to people who need them.
These resources are part of our commitment to making biblical nourishment accessible, including to those who cannot afford paid materials.
Think of it as an opportunity for ongoing ministry support—an offering of generosity, not a payment for God's favor.

Scripture teaches that believers may freely and willingly support Gospel ministry. First Corinthians 9:14 recognizes the legitimacy of supporting those who proclaim the Gospel, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not arise from pressure or compulsion.
“For God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
That matters.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and faithful service in the life He has entrusted to you.
These products are simply expressions of encouragement and ministry identity. They are not the Gospel, and buying them is not a measure of anyone's faith.
You can still be part of this mission.
Read the Word.
Pray for those who are struggling.
You can help a message travel farther without spending anything.
Sometimes a simple share becomes the doorway to a conversation about eternity.
Sometimes a thoughtful comment gives another struggling believer the courage to admit that they need prayer.
Sometimes a saved article becomes a reminder, weeks later, to open the Bible again.
We cannot promise what God will do through any particular post.
But we can be faithful with the truth we have been entrusted to share.
And that brings us back to Bathsheba.
The mother who entered a throne room.
The king who honored her.
The request that seemed small.
The danger Solomon recognized.
The execution that followed.
And the haunting question left for every reader.
What are you asking for that you have not first surrendered to God?
What desire has become so precious that you are afraid to let Scripture examine it?
What part of your life are you still trying to rule?
Because there is a King greater than Solomon.
A King who sees the heart completely.
A King who cannot be manipulated by appearances.
A King who does not need to seize a throne because all authority in heaven and on earth belongs to Him.
And that King is Jesus Christ.
He does not invite you to pretend that sin is harmless.
He invites you to repent and believe.
He does not promise that every earthly consequence will vanish.
