He promises eternal life to those who believe in Him.
He does not ask you to build a throne beside His.
He calls you to follow Him.
So before you close this article, before you scroll to the next story, before another distraction fills the silence, ask yourself one final question.
Am I truly surrendering my life to Jesus, or am I still asking Him to bless the kingdom I have built for myself?
Do not answer quickly.
Let Scripture search your heart.
Let the Holy Spirit bring conviction where repentance is needed.
Let the mercy of Christ give you courage to come into the light.

And remember that the same Bible that tells the truth about David's sin, Bathsheba's suffering, Adonijah's ambition, and Solomon's judgment also reveals the coming of the Savior through David's family line.
The scandal was not erased from the record.
But neither was God's promise defeated by it.
And for every repentant sinner who places their faith in Jesus Christ, that is hope worth holding onto.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but it does not have to become the throne from which your future is ruled—Jesus Christ is a greater King than your greatest failure.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID, “ASK AND IT WILL BE GIVEN TO YOU.” SO WHY DID GOD SAY NO WHEN YOU NEEDED HIM MOST?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “ASK AND IT WILL BE GIVEN TO YOU.” SO WHY DID GOD SAY NO WHEN YOU NEEDED HIM MOST?
The heartbreaking truth about Matthew 7:7 that many Christians misunderstand—and the extraordinary promise Jesus was actually making when He told us to ask, seek, and knock.
There is a kind of silence that can shake your faith more than any storm.
It happens when you've prayed until you have no words left.
When you've begged God to heal someone you love.
When you've asked Him to save your marriage, rescue your child, open a door, provide enough money to survive another month, or remove the pain you've carried for years.
And nothing seems to happen.
You remember what Jesus said.
“Ask, and it shall be given you.”
So you asked.
You believed.
You waited.
And still, the hospital called. The marriage collapsed. The application was rejected. The bills kept coming. The person you prayed for never came home.
Now there's a question buried beneath your worship songs, your Sunday smiles, and every “God is good” you've whispered while trying not to cry.
“Jesus, You told me to ask. So why didn't You give me what I asked for?”
Perhaps you've been afraid to say that out loud.
Perhaps you think questioning what happened means your faith is weak.
But what if the problem isn't that you failed to believe enough?
What if you've been carrying a misunderstanding of one of Jesus' most beautiful promises?
And what if the words that once made you feel abandoned were actually spoken by a Savior who was inviting you into something far deeper than getting everything you wanted?
Because when Jesus said, “Ask, and it will be given to you,” He wasn't handing humanity a blank check.
He was revealing the heart of a Father.
And that changes everything.
Before we go any further, we need to hear what Jesus actually said—not merely the sentence printed on inspirational posters, but His words in their biblical context.
In Matthew 7:7–8, the King James Version records:
“Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:
For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.”
Beautiful words.
Powerful words.
But also words that can become deeply painful when we separate them from everything Jesus said around them.

The Gospel of Matthew was written in Koine Greek, the common Greek language of the New Testament world. Although Jesus likely taught much of His earthly ministry in Aramaic, Matthew preserves this teaching in Greek. We do not possess an original Aramaic transcript of this sermon.
The Greek text of Matthew 7:7 reads:
Αἰτεῖτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν· ζητεῖτε, καὶ εὑρήσετε· κρούετε, καὶ ἀνοιγήσεται ὑμῖν.
Transliteration:
Aiteite, kai dothēsetai hymin; zēteite, kai heurēsete; krouete, kai anoigēsetai hymin.
A faithful English rendering is:
“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”
Now notice something important.
The Greek verbs αἰτεῖτε (aiteite), ζητεῖτε (zēteite), and κρούετε (krouete) are present-tense imperatives.
They command asking, seeking, and knocking as ongoing practices.
That's why some teachers explain the sense as “keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking.”
This is a reasonable way to communicate the ongoing force of the commands, although the Greek tense alone does not guarantee that every repeated request will eventually be granted.
Jesus is teaching His disciples to live in persistent dependence upon God.
Not to treat prayer as a magic formula.
Not to use repetition to manipulate heaven.
Not to assume that enough emotional intensity can force the Father's hand.
He is teaching them to come.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Even when life hurts.
Even when the answer is not what they expected.
Even when the waiting becomes unbearable.
But here's where the passage becomes astonishing.
Jesus doesn't stop at verse 8.
He continues:
“Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?
Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent?”
—Matthew 7:9–10, KJV
Picture that.
A hungry child approaches his father.
His stomach aches. His hands are empty. He asks for bread.
Would a loving father place a stone in those little hands and watch him try to eat it?
Of course not.
Jesus continues in Matthew 7:11:
“If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?”
There it is.
The heart of the promise.
Jesus wasn't saying that the Father will give you absolutely anything you desire. He was saying that you can trust the Father's goodness when you ask.
That distinction may sound small.
Until you're the one who prayed for bread and received something you couldn't understand.
Until you're the one standing beside a hospital bed.
Until you're the one holding divorce papers.
Until you're the one watching other people celebrate answers to prayers that sound painfully similar to yours.
And suddenly you're asking, “If God is good, why didn't He stop this?”
Scripture does not answer every particular tragedy by telling us exactly why God allowed it.
We must be careful here.
Not every loss is a hidden blessing waiting to be discovered.
Not every death is something we should explain away with a cheerful sentence.
Not every closed door is proof that something materially better is coming next month.
Sometimes suffering remains mysterious.
Sometimes we grieve without understanding.
Sometimes faith means refusing to call evil good while still trusting that evil will not have the final word.
And Jesus never asks His followers to pretend that suffering doesn't hurt.
He wept at the tomb of Lazarus.
He grieved in Gethsemane.
He knows what tears feel like.
But there is another part of this passage that changes how we understand the promise.
In Matthew 6, just before Jesus teaches about asking, seeking, and knocking, He tells His disciples not to be consumed by anxiety over food, clothing, and tomorrow.
Then He says:
“But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.”
—Matthew 6:33, KJV
Do you see the connection?
Before Jesus says, “Seek, and ye shall find,” He has already taught His disciples what should come first in their seeking.
The kingdom of God.
His righteousness.
His will.
His presence.
This doesn't mean that asking for food, employment, healing, marriage, or financial provision is wrong.
Jesus explicitly teaches us to pray for daily bread.
But it does mean that prayer is not ultimately about making God serve our personal kingdom.
It is about learning to live under His.
And that truth confronts something uncomfortable inside every human heart.
Sometimes we don't merely want God to answer our prayers.
We want God to approve our plans.
We want His power without surrendering our pride.
His blessings without His correction.
His provision without His lordship.
His forgiveness without repentance.
We want Him to open doors we've already decided to walk through, even if those doors lead us away from Him.
But Jesus loves us too much to reduce His Father to a servant of our desires.
Consider the apostle James.
He writes:
—James 4:3, KJV
The Greek expression translated “ask amiss” includes κακῶς αἰτεῖσθε (kakōs aiteisthe)—asking wrongly or with improper motives.
James is addressing prayers corrupted by selfish desires.
That doesn't mean every unanswered prayer is selfish.
Please don't turn this verse into a weapon against grieving people.
A mother begging God to heal her child is not necessarily asking wrongly.
A father pleading for work to feed his family is not necessarily being greedy.
A wounded believer asking for relief is not necessarily lacking faith.
James is exposing one real danger, not explaining every unanswered prayer.
And there is an even more startling example in Scripture.
A man prayed repeatedly for his suffering to be removed.
He wasn't spiritually immature.
He wasn't an unbeliever.
He wasn't a stranger to miracles.
He was the apostle Paul.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7–9, Paul describes a painful affliction he calls a “thorn in the flesh.”
He says:
“For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.”
Three times.
Paul pleaded.
And the Lord's response?
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
Paul asked for the thorn to leave.
God answered by promising sustaining grace rather than removing the affliction.
And here's what we must understand.
Paul's unanswered request was not evidence that Christ had abandoned him.
The Lord's presence remained with him in his weakness.
The thorn was painful.
The grace was sufficient.
Both realities were true.
Maybe you've been waiting for God to remove something.
And maybe, in the middle of that waiting, you've begun to believe your pain means you are forgotten.
But Paul reminds us that God's faithfulness cannot be measured solely by whether suffering disappears.
Sometimes grace is not the removal of the burden.
Sometimes grace is the strength to endure while the burden remains.
And yet even that is not the deepest revelation in this story.
Because there was Someone greater than Paul who prayed for something He did not receive in the form He requested.
Jesus Himself.
In the garden of Gethsemane, with the shadow of the cross approaching, Jesus prayed:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
—Matthew 26:39, KJV
Read that again.
The sinless Son of God asked His Father whether the cup could pass from Him.
And the cup did not pass.
Jesus went to the cross.
Now we must be precise.
The Father did not reject the Son because the Son lacked faith.
Jesus was not praying selfishly.
And the cross was not evidence that the Father's love had failed.
Christ willingly submitted to the Father's redemptive purpose.
The cup He faced was bound up with the suffering and judgment He would bear in accomplishing our salvation.
And through that obedience, the greatest rescue in human history unfolded.
The Son of God was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And buried.
For a moment, to human eyes, it looked as though evil had won.
But on the third day, the tomb was empty.
The resurrection did not make the suffering imaginary.
It declared that suffering and death would not have the final victory over Christ.
And this is where Matthew 7:7 becomes more than a promise about prayer.
It becomes an invitation to trust the Father whom Jesus has made known.
Because the One who tells you to ask is the very One who gave Himself to reconcile sinners to God.
Think about that.
We often measure God's love by what He has not yet given us.
But the Gospel points us toward what He has already given in Jesus Christ.
Romans 8:32 says:
“He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?”
Paul is not promising every earthly luxury.
He is assuring believers that the God who gave His Son will not fail to accomplish His saving purpose for those who belong to Christ.
And sometimes we forget what our greatest need actually was.
It wasn't a bigger house.
It wasn't a perfect marriage.
It wasn't another promotion.
It wasn't public recognition.
Those things may be good gifts, but none could save us from sin.
Our greatest need was reconciliation with the holy God against whom we had sinned.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed mercy.
We needed a Savior.
And Jesus came.
Not because we earned Him.
Not because we prayed with flawless words.
Not because our faith was impressive.
But because God is rich in mercy.
This is the scandal of grace.
That sinners who could never purchase their own redemption are invited to come to God through the blood of Jesus Christ.
That the guilty can be forgiven.
That the ashamed can be cleansed.
That the rebellious can repent and return.
That the spiritually dead can be made alive in Christ.
And that the invitation to ask is spoken by a Savior who knows exactly what it costs to redeem us.
But perhaps you're wondering something.
“If Jesus loves me, can I still ask Him for the thing that breaks my heart?”
Yes.
Absolutely.
Ask for healing.
Ask for provision.
Ask for reconciliation.
Ask for freedom from addiction.
Ask for the salvation of someone you love.
Ask for wisdom.
Ask for courage.
Ask for help when you can barely get out of bed.
You do not have to disguise your needs behind religious language.
The Father already knows them.
But learn to pray with open hands.
Because Christian prayer is not a battle to make God's will surrender to ours.
It is communion with the Father through the Son, in the Holy Spirit, in which we bring our real desires before Him and learn to trust His wisdom.
First John 5:14 says:
“And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us.”
Notice those words.
According to His will.
Not because He is reluctant to love us.
Not because prayer is pointless.
But because His will is wiser than ours.
And we need to remember that this truth is not permission to become passive.
We still pray earnestly.
We still seek medical care when we're sick.
We still apply for jobs when we need employment.
We still seek counsel when relationships are broken.
We still take responsibility for the choices before us.
Trusting God does not mean refusing the ordinary means through which He may provide help.
Prayer and faithful action belong together.
And sometimes the answer to our prayer includes the courage to take the next step.
There is another detail in Luke's parallel account that is too beautiful to overlook.
In Luke 11:9–13, Jesus also teaches His disciples to ask, seek, and knock.
But when He describes what the Father gives, He says:
“If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?”
—Luke 11:13, KJV
Matthew emphasizes the Father's good gifts.
Luke specifically emphasizes the Holy Spirit.
These accounts are complementary, not contradictory.
And Luke's emphasis reveals something profound.
God's generosity is not merely about giving us things.
It includes giving His people the Holy Spirit—God's own presence and power at work in their lives.
We ask for help.
And the Father gives what is truly good.
We seek His kingdom.
And He draws us into life with Him.
We knock.
And we discover that the greatest gift is not merely access to a better circumstance.
It is access to God Himself through Jesus Christ.
That does not erase our earthly needs.
But it transforms the center of our hope.
Because money can disappear.
Health can change.
Relationships can fracture.
Careers can end.
The things we celebrate today may be gone tomorrow.
But Christ remains.
And for those who belong to Him, His promise stands:
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
—Hebrews 13:5, KJV
Now I want to speak to the person who has been quietly blaming themselves for an unanswered prayer.
The one who thinks:
“Maybe I didn't fast enough.”
“Maybe I didn't pray long enough.”
“Maybe I didn't believe hard enough.”
“Maybe God is punishing me.”
Listen carefully.
Scripture does teach that sin, motives, faith, and obedience matter in prayer.
But Scripture does not teach that every tragedy proves personal spiritual failure.
Jesus rejected that simplistic way of judging suffering in John 9:1–3, when His disciples assumed a man's blindness must have resulted from someone's particular sin.
And in Romans 8, Paul describes believers experiencing distress, persecution, hunger, danger, and even death—yet insists that none of these can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
You can be loved by God and still suffer.
You can be faithful and still grieve.
You can pray sincerely and still hear an answer you never wanted.
And you can bring your confusion to the Lord without pretending that you understand everything.
The Psalms are filled with cries like that.
Psalm 13 begins:
“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?”
That is Scripture.
Not the language of someone pretending everything is fine.
The language of someone hurting in the presence of God.
And the same psalm eventually says:
“But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation.”
The pain did not have to be denied for trust to emerge.
Perhaps that is where you are today.
Somewhere between “How long, Lord?” and “I will trust You.”
And perhaps your next prayer doesn't need to sound impressive.
Perhaps it can be as simple as:

“Father, I don't understand. I am hurting. I still need Your help. Please don't let my suffering drive me away from You. Teach me to trust You. And if there is anything in my heart that needs to change, give me the grace to surrender it.”
That is a prayer you can pray without pretending.
And if you're struggling to pray at all, remember Romans 8:26: the Spirit helps us in our weakness.
You are not required to manufacture perfect sentences before you come to God.
But there is something else we cannot overlook.
Some people have turned Matthew 7:7 into a promise that God will give wealth, success, and comfort to anyone who asks with sufficient confidence.
That teaching can sound exciting.
It can fill auditoriums.
It can make people feel powerful.
But it is not a faithful reading of Jesus' words.
The same Jesus who taught us to ask also told His followers to take up their cross.
The same Jesus who promised the Father's care warned that His disciples would face persecution.
The same Jesus who taught us to seek the kingdom said that earthly treasures can be destroyed or stolen.
The Gospel is not a technique for obtaining everything we desire.
The Gospel is the good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, so that all who repent and believe in Him may be reconciled to God.
And that is infinitely greater than a promise of temporary prosperity.
We should never turn Jesus into a means of acquiring things while treating the things as more precious than Jesus.
That is not discipleship.
That is idolatry dressed in religious language.
And if that truth stings, perhaps it is worth asking why.
Because the deepest question may not be, “Why hasn't God given me what I want?”
It may be, “Would I still want God if He never gave me that particular thing?”
That's a difficult question.
I know.
Especially when what you want is not selfish or sinful, but something genuinely good.
A restored family.
A healthy child.
A peaceful home.
A chance to start again.
God does not ask you to stop caring about those things.
He invites you to bring them to Him without making them the foundation of your faith.
And this is where surrender begins.
Not when you stop wanting.
But when you place even your most precious desires before the Father and say:
“Your will be done.”
Not because you no longer hurt.
But because you believe the One who holds your life is worthy of trust.
And if you've fallen into sin while struggling with disappointment, hear this too.
You do not have to hide.
You do not have to pretend you are spiritually strong.
You do not have to clean yourself up before turning to Christ.
Come in repentance.
Confess what is true.
Ask for mercy.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because His sacrifice is sufficient.
There is hope for the person who has wandered.
Hope for the person who has doubted.
Hope for the person who has mistaken God for a wish-granting servant and now wants to know Him as Father.
And hope for the person whose life has become a scandal they are ashamed to tell anyone about.
Because grace does not mean your past never happened.
Grace means your past does not have to be the final chapter of your story.
This is why we say:
Not because every broken relationship will be restored in this lifetime.
Not because every illness will disappear.
Not because every earthly consequence will be reversed.
But because through Christ, sinners can be forgiven, hearts can be transformed, and lives can be redirected toward the glory of God.
And because the risen Jesus has promised a future in which death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally be no more.
Revelation 21:4 does not promise that believers will never weep now.
It promises that God Himself will one day wipe away every tear.
What a difference.
We do not have to deny today's tears to believe in tomorrow's resurrection hope.
And perhaps this is the answer your weary soul needed to hear.
When Jesus said, “Ask, and it will be given to you,” He was not promising a life in which every request would be fulfilled exactly as you imagined.
He was calling you into persistent, trusting prayer before a good heavenly Father.
A Father who hears.
A Father who knows.
A Father who gives good gifts.
A Father whose wisdom is greater than ours.
And a Father who has made the way for us to come to Him through His Son.
So keep asking.
Keep seeking.
Keep knocking.
But above all, keep coming to Jesus.
When the answer is yes, thank Him.
When the answer is wait, trust Him.
When the answer is no, grieve honestly before Him and ask for grace to continue.
And when you cannot understand what He is doing, remember the cross and the empty tomb.
Because Christianity does not rest on the claim that life will always make sense.
It rests on the crucified and risen Christ.
Maybe you've reached this point with tears in your eyes.
Maybe you've been angry at God for months.
Maybe you've carried guilt because someone told you that your loved one would have survived if you had only prayed harder.
Maybe you stopped praying because you couldn't bear another disappointment.
If that's you, I want to invite you to do something simple.
Not to prove your faith to strangers.
Not to impress anyone.
But to speak honestly.
You don't have to explain your private pain publicly. A few honest words are enough.
Someone else may need to know that they are not the only one walking through that valley.
Perhaps there's someone in your life who has quietly stopped praying.
A friend who lost a child.
A sister whose marriage ended.
A brother struggling to provide.
A believer who feels ashamed because the miracle they hoped for never came.
Send this article to them with compassion, not as a correction to their grief.
Because those are the days when we especially need to remember what Scripture actually says.

We want this community to be a place where people are not merely inspired for a moment but are continually pointed back to Jesus Christ, biblical truth, repentance, forgiveness, and faithful discipleship.
These resources are intended to nourish faith, encourage spiritual maturity, and make biblical learning more accessible.
And there is another way you can help us continue this work.
For those who are able and willing, this can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity and stewardship.

Scripture teaches that believers may support those who labor in teaching and sharing the Gospel. In 1 Corinthians 9:14, Paul explains that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support through that ministry.
And in 2 Corinthians 9:7, he reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That matters deeply to us.
They are not the reason we preach Christ.
Jesus is.
Tell a friend about the free resources.
Pray that the Word of God would be proclaimed faithfully and received with open hearts.
Because the goal is not merely to grow a page.
It is to point people to Christ.
One person reading Scripture again.
One exhausted believer finding courage to pray.
One wandering soul returning in repentance.
One family beginning to talk about Jesus.
One person discovering that salvation is not something they can earn, but a gift of grace received through faith in Christ.
That is worth laboring for.
And before you leave, I want you to return to the question that brought you here.
“Why didn't God give me what I asked for?”
I cannot tell you why every particular prayer has gone unanswered.
I will not pretend to know the secret purposes of God in your suffering.
But I can tell you what Jesus has revealed.
Your heavenly Father is good.
You are invited to come to Him.
His wisdom is trustworthy.
His grace is sufficient.
His Son has conquered the grave.
And everyone who turns to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith finds in Him a Savior who is able to save.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, consider praying again.
Not because you've finally discovered a formula that guarantees the outcome you want.
But because prayer was never meant to be a formula.
It is an invitation to draw near to God.
Maybe all you can manage is:
“Jesus, I still don't understand. But I'm here.”
That is a place to begin.
And perhaps the greatest change will not be that every circumstance suddenly becomes easy.
Perhaps it will be that, through the Gospel, you begin to know and trust the Father more deeply, even in the circumstances you would never have chosen.
The door Jesus calls you to knock upon is not the door of a vending machine filled with earthly rewards.
It is an invitation to seek the Father who gives what is good.
And the way to the Father is Jesus Christ.
Don't confuse a delayed answer with a Savior who has stopped loving you.
Don't confuse a painful season with proof that God has abandoned you.
Don't confuse the absence of the miracle you wanted with the absence of grace.
Come to Christ.
Bring your questions.
Bring your grief.
Bring your sin in repentance.
Bring your empty hands.
And keep seeking the kingdom of God.
Because even when you cannot see what lies beyond tomorrow, the Gospel gives you a reason to hope beyond the grave.
The prayer you cried over may still be unanswered in the way you hoped—but the cross and the empty tomb have already shown you how far Jesus went to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE SHARED HIS BED… BUT NEVER HELD THE TITLE OF WIFE. WHY DID THE OLD TESTAMENT ALLOW THIS?
paragraphs: SHE SHARED HIS BED… BUT NEVER HELD THE TITLE OF WIFE. WHY DID THE OLD TESTAMENT ALLOW THIS?
The disturbing truth about concubines, the women history often overlooked, and the God who never confused human permission with His perfect design.
There is a woman in the Bible whose story should make every Christian uncomfortable.
We do not know her name.
We do not know what she dreamed about when she was younger. We do not know whether she ever imagined being loved, protected, cherished, or growing old beside someone who would never abandon her.
But we know how her story ended.
Her body lay at the doorway of a house.
Her hands were stretched toward the threshold.
And the man who had been traveling with her said, “Up, and let us be going.”
There was no answer.
Judges 19:27–28.
Read those words again.
Because this was not a stranger.
She was his concubine.
And before you turn away from this disturbing passage, there is something you need to understand.
The Bible records things that God never approved.
Some of Scripture's darkest stories are not instructions for how God's people should live. They are warnings about what happens when human beings abandon His ways.
That distinction matters.
Because somewhere between the wives, the concubines, the kings, the patriarchs, and the laws of ancient Israel, a question emerges that Christians cannot afford to answer carelessly.
Why were concubines treated differently from wives in the Old Testament?
Did God consider some women less valuable than others?
Did having a concubine mean a man could enjoy the privileges of marriage without accepting its full responsibilities?
And if God created marriage between one man and one woman, why do we repeatedly encounter men in Scripture who had multiple wives and concubines?
The answer is not as simple as saying, “That was just their culture.”
Because culture explains some of what happened.
It does not automatically justify it.
And the deeper we go into Scripture, the more we discover something remarkable.
The Bible is not hiding the failures of its heroes. It is exposing humanity's desperate need for a Savior.
To understand concubinage, we must begin before Abraham, before Jacob, before David, and before Solomon.
We must return to a garden.
Before sin entered the world, there were no royal harems, no concubines competing for security, and no women being divided into categories according to their place within a man's household.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was a covenantal union established by God.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the final expression is:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
“And they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew word echad means “one.”
Here, the expression describes a profound union, not merely a physical encounter.
The man and woman are joined in a relationship that creates a new family bond.
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not say a man shall accumulate women according to his wealth.
It does not establish one category of women for covenantal dignity and another for convenient companionship.
It presents a foundational picture of marriage.
One man.
One woman.
One flesh.
And when Jesus later addressed marriage in Matthew 19:4–6, He returned to this very beginning.
Not to Solomon's palace.
Not to Jacob's household.
Not to the customs of ancient kings.
To creation.
That is significant.
Because when Jesus wanted to explain God's intention for marriage, He pointed His listeners back to what God established before human rebellion distorted relationships.
But the world outside Eden was different.
Sin entered.
Power became corrupted.
Human relationships became tangled in pride, jealousy, exploitation, insecurity, and the desire to control.
And eventually, Scripture introduces a man named Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 records that Lamech took two wives.
The Bible does not pause to celebrate his decision.
It simply records it.
That is one of the most important principles for interpreting Old Testament narratives:
Description is not the same as divine endorsement.
Just because a biblical character did something does not mean God commanded it, celebrated it, or intended everyone else to imitate it.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
David committed adultery and arranged a man's death.
Solomon pursued relationships that turned his heart away from the Lord.
Their inclusion in Scripture does not make their sins holy.
It demonstrates how deeply humanity needs grace.
And this brings us to the concubines.
In the Hebrew Bible, one of the primary words translated “concubine” is:
פִּילֶגֶשׁ
Pilegesh.
The precise historical origin of this Hebrew word is uncertain, but its biblical usage generally identifies a woman in a recognized secondary marital or household relationship.
A concubine was not simply the ancient equivalent of a modern girlfriend.
Nor was she necessarily a prostitute or a woman involved in a casual relationship.
Concubinage was a socially recognized institution in parts of the ancient Near East.
A concubine could belong to a man's household, bear his children, and have a continuing relationship with him.
But her status was generally lower than that of a principal wife.
The exact legal arrangements varied across periods, regions, and households.
And that last detail is important.
The Old Testament does not present one comprehensive, uniform legal definition governing every concubine in every generation.
Sometimes a concubine had previously been enslaved.
Sometimes she was connected to a household through a secondary union.
Sometimes her position was closely tied to inheritance, family arrangements, or royal power.
And sometimes the Bible uses marital language in ways that overlap with the language of concubinage.
For example, Genesis 25:1 calls Keturah Abraham's wife, while 1 Chronicles 1:32 identifies her as Abraham's concubine.
This reminds us that ancient household categories cannot always be forced neatly into modern definitions.
Nevertheless, a broad distinction remains.
A principal wife generally occupied a more established and socially prominent marital position.
A concubine generally held a secondary position, often with fewer recognized privileges and less security.
Her children could be acknowledged as the father's children, but their inheritance prospects might differ.
Genesis 25:5–6 gives us a striking example.
Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac, while also giving gifts to the sons of his concubines and sending them away from Isaac.
The passage demonstrates a real distinction in inheritance arrangements.
But it does not prove that every concubine's child was automatically excluded from every inheritance in ancient Israel.
The circumstances varied.
And here is where the question becomes painfully human.
Imagine living in a household where your security depended heavily on the favor of a powerful man.
Imagine bearing children who might never enjoy the same position as another woman's children.
Imagine knowing you belonged to the family, yet not possessing the same standing within it.
Now imagine being told that because this arrangement appears in the Bible, God must have considered it ideal.
That would be a serious misunderstanding of Scripture.
Because God's willingness to deal with people inside a broken social system does not mean He created that brokenness or approved every part of it.
Consider Hagar.
Her story begins in Genesis 16.
She was an Egyptian servant belonging to Sarai, Abraham's wife.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
But the years passed.
The waiting became painful.
And Sarai decided to take matters into her own hands.
She gave Hagar to Abraham.
Genesis 16:3 says Sarai gave Hagar to Abram “to be his wife” (KJV).
Yet Hagar's position remained deeply unequal.
She was still a servant.
She did not suddenly gain Sarai's authority.
And when Hagar conceived, conflict erupted.
Sarai treated her harshly.
Hagar fled.
Think about that.
A woman was drawn into a family arrangement shaped by someone else's desperation.
She became pregnant.
Then she found herself running into the wilderness.
And there, far from the security of the household, the angel of the LORD encountered her.
Genesis 16:13 records Hagar's response:
“Thou God seest me.” (KJV)
In Hebrew, the passage includes the expression:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Ro'i.
Commonly understood as “God who sees me,” though the precise rendering of the expression is discussed by translators.
The meaning within the story is extraordinary.
Hagar had been overlooked by powerful people.
But she had not escaped God's attention.
She was a servant.
A foreigner.
A woman whose life had become entangled in the failures of Abraham and Sarai.
Yet God addressed her personally.
He heard her suffering.
He spoke concerning her son.
And later, when Hagar and Ishmael were sent away, God again heard the boy and provided for them in the wilderness (Genesis 21:17–19).
Do not misunderstand this.
God's care for Hagar does not mean He approved every decision that brought her into that situation.
Nor does His command to her in Genesis 16:9 erase the hardship or moral complexity of her circumstances.
But the narrative makes something unmistakable.
Hagar's social status did not determine whether God would see her.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what it feels like to be treated as secondary.
Not necessarily as a concubine.
But as an afterthought.
The person contacted only when someone needs something.
The spouse who gives everything yet feels invisible.
The child who grew up wondering why another sibling received more affection.
The believer who smiles in church while quietly carrying the wound of being unwanted.
People may rank human beings according to usefulness, wealth, beauty, reputation, or status.
But Scripture repeatedly confronts the arrogance of treating another person as though their dignity depends on human approval.
Genesis 1:27 establishes that humanity was created in God's image.
That truth is older than every royal household and every ancient inheritance custom.
And it belongs to women as surely as it belongs to men.
Now consider Jacob.
He loved Rachel.
But through Laban's deception, he first married Leah.
Then he married Rachel.
And eventually, the household included Bilhah and Zilpah, the servants of Rachel and Leah, who bore children to Jacob.
Genesis 30 records these arrangements.
Genesis 35:22 explicitly identifies Bilhah as Jacob's concubine.
But what does this household reveal?
Peace?
Contentment?
A beautiful example of covenantal harmony?
No.
It reveals rivalry.
Jealousy.
Pain.
Competition.
A desperate struggle for love and recognition.
Leah longed for Jacob's affection.
Rachel struggled with infertility.
Children became entangled in the emotional conflicts of adults.
And the household that would produce the twelve tribes of Israel was far from an example of perfect family relationships.
Yet God continued working through this deeply imperfect family.
That is grace.
But grace must never be confused with approval.
God's faithfulness to His promises does not mean every human decision within the story was righteous.
Sometimes the Bible shows us God accomplishing His purposes despite people's failures, not because those failures were good.
And then we arrive at the laws of Moses.
This is where some readers become confused.
Because the Law contains provisions addressing relationships involving enslaved women, multiple wives, and unequal household arrangements.
Exodus 21:7–11, for example, deals with a female servant in circumstances involving marriage arrangements.
The passage places obligations on the household and addresses her rights if certain provisions are not fulfilled.
Exodus 21:10 specifically mentions food, clothing, and marital rights in a situation where a man takes another wife.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives and favors one over the other.
These passages show that the Law sometimes regulated social situations that already existed.
But regulating an existing practice is not necessarily the same as declaring it God's highest ideal.
Jesus Himself provides an important interpretive principle in Matthew 19:8.
Speaking about divorce, He says:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” (KJV)
Jesus was speaking specifically about divorce.
We should not pretend that this statement directly explains every law concerning concubines.
Nevertheless, it demonstrates that Scripture itself distinguishes between certain accommodations within a fallen society and God's intention from creation.
This is why we must read the Old Testament carefully.
We cannot simply collect everything that happened under the old covenant and announce that every recorded arrangement represents God's timeless moral ideal.
And we cannot ignore the protective intent of certain laws merely because the social world they addressed was deeply unequal.
The Law sometimes restrained harm within conditions that were far from Eden.
But the presence of regulation did not magically transform every unequal relationship into a model for Christian marriage.
In fact, the Old Testament itself repeatedly exposes the dangers of multiplying wives.
Deuteronomy 17:17 warns Israel's future king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.” (KJV)
Now think about Solomon.
A man associated with extraordinary wisdom.
A king who possessed wealth, influence, power, and international prestige.
Yet 1 Kings 11:3 records that he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
And Scripture does not describe this as the triumph of biblical masculinity.
It tells us that his wives turned away his heart.
The man who possessed extraordinary wisdom still failed to guard his devotion to God.
That should humble every believer.
Because knowledge of God is not the same as obedience to God.
Religious privilege is not the same as faithfulness.
And having access to Scripture does not mean someone is automatically living according to it.
Solomon's relationships were not merely private romantic arrangements.
Royal marriages could involve political alliances, wealth, succession, and power.
Concubines in royal households could also be connected to the public demonstration of a king's status and authority.
That helps explain why royal concubines sometimes appear in political conflicts.
In 2 Samuel 16:21–22, Absalom publicly took his father's concubines in an act connected to his rebellion against David.
The women were caught in a violent struggle for royal power.
Then 2 Samuel 20:3 tells us David provided for the ten concubines involved but did not resume sexual relations with them. They remained confined to a form of widowhood while he was still alive.
Pause there.
These women were not merely symbols in a political drama.
They were human beings whose lives were permanently affected by the actions of powerful men.
The text does not tell us everything they thought or felt.
We must not invent details Scripture does not provide.
But it tells us enough to recognize the tragic consequences of a household system in which women's lives could become entangled with royal ambition.
And then there is the unnamed concubine in Judges 19.
One of the most horrifying accounts in the Old Testament.
The woman is sexually assaulted by a mob after being handed over to them.
The next morning, she is found at the doorway.
Her death is strongly implied by the narrative, and Judges 20:5 later reports that she died.
Her body is subsequently dismembered and sent throughout Israel.
There is no responsible way to turn this passage into comfortable religious entertainment.
The account is meant to horrify us.
And the wider book of Judges repeatedly describes a society collapsing into moral chaos.
Judges 21:25 concludes:
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.” (KJV)
The repeated refrain exposes the disorder of Israel's life in that period.
But we should also be careful not to reduce this woman's suffering to a simple illustration about political leadership.
The narrative exposes violence, failed protection, collective wickedness, and profound moral breakdown.
And it forces us to confront a difficult reality.
A society can possess religious language and still become terrifyingly cruel to vulnerable people.
The existence of a biblical covenant community did not mean everyone within it acted faithfully.
The existence of religious customs did not mean women were always treated justly.
And the existence of a man with social authority did not make his decisions righteous.
If anything, this story should make us more serious about protecting the vulnerable, condemning sexual violence, and refusing to use Scripture to excuse abuse.
Because no woman becomes less human because she lacks social power.
No person becomes disposable because another person has greater authority.
And no amount of religious language can transform cruelty into holiness.
Perhaps this is where the question becomes even more personal.
Because we live in a different century, but human hearts have not changed nearly as much as we imagine.
We may no longer use the word pilegesh in ordinary conversation.
But we still see people wanting the benefits of intimacy without accepting the responsibilities of faithful love.
We still see relationships built on unequal power.
We still see people treated as replaceable.
We still see men and women wounded by promises that were never meant to be kept.
We still see people using religious language to defend selfish desires.
And we still see wounded souls wondering whether God notices what others have done to them.
That is why this subject matters.
It is not merely an ancient historical curiosity.
It exposes questions about power, commitment, dignity, justice, and the human tendency to turn another person into something useful rather than someone to love.
But the Bible does not end with the failures of patriarchs and kings.
It moves toward Jesus Christ.
And when Jesus enters the story, something remarkable happens.
He does not treat women as spiritually insignificant.
He speaks with the Samaritan woman at the well in John 4.
He receives the devotion of Mary, who sits at His feet as a disciple in Luke 10:38–42.
He defends the woman who anoints Him in Luke 7:36–50.
He heals women, listens to them, and receives them among His followers.
And when Mary Magdalene encounters the risen Christ, John 20 records her role in announcing His resurrection to the disciples.
These encounters do not mean that every social injustice instantly disappeared from the ancient world.
They reveal the character of the Savior.
Jesus does not measure a person's worth by the social hierarchy that surrounds them.
He calls people to repentance.
He extends mercy.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He restores dignity.
And He reveals what love looks like when it is not corrupted by the desire to dominate.
Consider what Paul later writes in Ephesians 5:25:
In the Greek text, the command begins:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
The verb agapate comes from agapaō, meaning “to love.”
The passage does not leave the meaning of that love to a husband's selfish imagination.
It provides a model.
Christ.
And what did Christ do?
He gave Himself.
He sacrificed.
He did not exploit His bride.
He did not abandon her when loving her became costly.
He gave Himself for her good.
That is the standard Paul places before Christian husbands.
Not Solomon's accumulation of women.
Not the competition inside Jacob's household.
Not the political arrangements of ancient kings.
Christ's sacrificial love.
And this is where the entire discussion changes.
Because the ultimate Christian model for marriage is not the most powerful man in the Old Testament.
It is Jesus Christ.
The One who loved sacrificially.
The One who remained faithful.
The One who laid down His life.
The One whose love cannot be purchased with beauty, status, wealth, or social influence.
The One who came to redeem sinners rather than use them.
Now, we must be careful.
Jesus did not come merely to provide a better example of human relationships.
He came to save sinners.
The deepest problem in humanity is not simply that people have constructed unjust social arrangements.
It is that sin has corrupted our relationship with God and with one another.
We have rebelled against our Creator.
We have pursued selfish desires.
We have harmed others.
We have failed to love as we should.
And none of us can make ourselves righteous by comparing our behavior with someone else's failures.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
That includes kings.
Patriarchs.
Religious leaders.
Husbands.
Wives.
And every person reading these words.
But the Gospel does not leave us under condemnation without hope.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
There it is.
The difference between human exploitation and divine redemption.
Sinful humanity often asks, “What can I get from this person?”
Christ demonstrated a love that gave Himself to rescue those who could never earn their salvation.
At the cross, Jesus bore the penalty of sin.
Through His resurrection, He conquered death.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
This is not permission to continue harming others.
Grace does not excuse cruelty.
Forgiveness does not erase the need for repentance.
And Christian love never requires victims to remain in dangerous or abusive situations.
The Gospel calls those who have sinned to turn from their sin.
It calls those who have abused power to abandon exploitation and accept responsibility.
It calls believers to pursue holiness, justice, mercy, and truth.
And it reminds the wounded that another person's wrongdoing does not determine their worth before God.
Maybe you have never thought much about concubines before today.
Maybe the subject sounded strange, uncomfortable, or irrelevant.
But perhaps you kept reading because something deeper began to stir.
Perhaps you recognized the pain of being treated as less important.
Perhaps you remembered a relationship where someone wanted your loyalty but refused to give you theirs.
Perhaps you have watched someone misuse the Bible to justify behavior that contradicted the character of Christ.
Or perhaps you are confronting something in your own heart.
A tendency to control.
A desire to be served without serving.
A willingness to excuse selfishness because someone in Scripture once behaved similarly.
If that is you, do not run from conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is grace for the humbled.
There is healing for the wounded.
There is transformation for those who surrender to Christ.
And there is a better way to love.
Not because human beings suddenly become perfect.
But because the Holy Spirit works in those who belong to Jesus, teaching them to turn away from sin and walk in obedience.
The story of concubines in the Old Testament is therefore not a story about God creating different grades of human worth.
It is a story unfolding within ancient societies where marriage, slavery, inheritance, fertility, political power, and household status were often deeply intertwined.
Some concubines occupied recognized secondary marital positions.
Some were enslaved women whose choices were severely constrained.
Some bore children who became important figures in Israel's history.
Some suffered profoundly.
And Scripture does not portray every such relationship in exactly the same way.
We should resist both extremes.
We must not claim that every concubine was identical to a modern sex slave, because the historical evidence does not support such a sweeping statement.
But neither should we romanticize concubinage as though unequal status, constrained freedom, and diminished security were unimportant.
The biblical accounts demand more honesty than either simplification allows.

And when we ask why concubines were treated differently from wives, the historical answer is that ancient household systems distinguished between principal and secondary unions, with differences in status, legal protection, social recognition, and sometimes inheritance.
The theological answer requires us to go further.
Those distinctions arose within human societies marked by sin and inequality.
They were not a declaration that women possessed different levels of value before their Creator.
The Bible's larger story moves from God's good creation, through humanity's rebellion, toward redemption in Jesus Christ and the promised restoration of all things.
That is why we must never build our understanding of God's heart on an isolated ancient custom while ignoring the whole counsel of Scripture.
And that is why we must never use the failures of biblical figures as permission to repeat them.
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
And we need grace too.
Not cheap grace that tells us our sins do not matter.
But the costly grace purchased through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that restores.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that teaches us to love people as people, not possessions.
If this article has exposed something you have struggled to understand, I want to invite you into the conversation.
You do not have to pretend that every passage is easy.
Faithful Bible study makes room for difficult questions while remaining committed to the truth of God's Word.
Not to reopen their pain.
But to remind them that the Lord sees what human beings overlook.
You never know which friend is silently questioning whether God cares about people who have been mistreated.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who have not yet come to faith in Jesus.
Because understanding the Bible should not be reserved for people who have already learned all the religious language.
The Word of God deserves to be opened, studied, understood, and shared.
And there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
It is not a requirement for glorifying God.
And it is not a replacement for the biblical responsibilities of generosity, worship, and care for your local church.
We never want financial pressure to replace cheerful generosity.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These resources can serve as daily reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share your faith.
The Library is a resource for spiritual nourishment and study, not a substitute for Scripture, prayer, fellowship, or faithful participation in a local church.
You can still help.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage a friend to open the Bible.
But Jesus Christ is the reason the mission exists.
And that distinction must never be forgotten.
Because one day, our lives will not be measured by how impressive our religious platforms became, how many followers we gained, or how much money we collected.
We will stand before the Lord who knows every heart.
The same Lord who saw Hagar in the wilderness.
The same Lord who condemned injustice through His prophets.
The same Lord who called sinners to repentance.
The same Lord who gave Himself on the cross.
The same Lord who rose again.
And the same Lord who is coming again.
So when you think about the concubines of the Old Testament, do not merely remember the complicated laws or the households of ancient kings.
Remember the human beings inside those stories.
Remember the difference between what Scripture records and what God commands.
Remember that no social title can increase or decrease the worth of someone created in God's image.
Remember that the sins of biblical heroes are not instructions for our lives.
And above all, remember Jesus.
Because the answer to humanity's brokenness is not found in defending every custom of the past.
It is found in surrendering to the Savior who came to redeem sinners and make all things new.
The world may remember the position someone gave you, but the God who saw Hagar in the wilderness knows your name—and no human rejection can erase the dignity He gave you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID, “BE PERFECT.” BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN TERRIFIED OF WHAT HE ACTUALLY MEANT?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “BE PERFECT.” BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN TERRIFIED OF WHAT HE ACTUALLY MEANT?

The command that has haunted struggling Christians for centuries may be one of the most misunderstood invitations in the Sermon on the Mount. And when you discover what Jesus was really saying in the original Greek, you may never look at your failures, your enemies, or your Heavenly Father the same way again.
There is a particular kind of exhaustion that only a struggling Christian understands.
It is the exhaustion of loving Jesus while knowing you still have things in your heart that do not look like Him.
You pray. You repent. You promise yourself that this time will be different.
And then it happens again.
The anger you thought you had conquered returns. The temptation you swore you would never entertain finds another opening. The bitterness you buried begins speaking through your words.
You look at your Bible.
You remember everything God has done for you.
And somewhere between your disappointment and your shame, a verse comes back to haunt you.
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.” — Matthew 5:48 (KJV)
Perfect?
Not better?
Not improving?
Not trying your best?
Perfect?
You stare at that word, and suddenly the Christian life feels like a mountain you were commanded to climb without ever being given the strength to reach the summit.
You begin wondering whether God is disappointed every time He looks at you.
Whether your repeated failures mean your repentance was never sincere.
Whether the fact that you are still struggling proves you were never truly changed.
And perhaps the most painful question of all begins forming in your heart.
What if I love Jesus, but I will never become the kind of person He commanded me to be?
If you have ever felt that fear, please do not rush past what comes next.
Because Jesus really did command His followers to be perfect.
We must not erase His words to make ourselves comfortable.
But we must also never separate His words from the conversation in which He spoke them.
And that conversation changes everything.
Jesus was standing before people who lived under the weight of religious expectations, social divisions, personal enemies, and the constant temptation to measure righteousness by outward appearances.
In Matthew 5, He was not offering a motivational speech about becoming the best version of yourself.
He was revealing the righteousness of the kingdom of heaven.
He confronted anger that grows into contempt.
Lust that begins before an outward act.
Promises made carelessly.
Retaliation disguised as justice.
And finally, He confronted something so deeply rooted in the human heart that even religious people could easily defend it.
The belief that love should be reserved for people who deserve it.
Listen carefully to what Jesus said immediately before the command to be perfect.
“Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy.” — Matthew 5:43 (KJV)
Here is an important distinction.
The command to love one's neighbor came from Scripture, particularly Leviticus 19:18.
But the command to hate one's enemy was not part of that verse.
Jesus was confronting a distorted understanding of love, one that allowed people to divide humanity into those worthy of compassion and those worthy of contempt.
And then He said something that must have stunned His listeners.
“But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” — Matthew 5:44 (KJV)
Imagine hearing that while remembering someone who had deliberately humiliated you.
Someone who betrayed your trust.
Someone who spread lies about you.
Someone who walked away when you needed them most.
Jesus did not say that their actions were acceptable.
He did not say that evil should be ignored, that abuse should be tolerated, or that boundaries should disappear.
He said something far more challenging.
Do not allow another person's evil to become the pattern for your own heart.
And then Jesus pointed toward heaven.
He explained that the Father causes His sun to rise on both the evil and the good and sends rain on both the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).
Think about that.
The same sunlight warms the home of the person who praises God and the person who curses His name.
The same rain falls upon the fields of those who worship Him and those who refuse to acknowledge Him.
God's ordinary kindness extends beyond the circle of those who love Him.
This does not mean God approves of wickedness. Scripture consistently teaches His holiness, justice, and coming judgment.
It means that even a rebellious world continues to receive undeserved gifts from its Creator.
And Jesus was saying that the children of this Father should increasingly reflect His character.
Then came the sentence that has frightened so many sincere believers.
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.”
Notice the word therefore.
It matters.
Jesus was drawing a conclusion from everything He had just taught about love, mercy, and the Father's generous kindness.
He was not suddenly abandoning the subject to demand flawless performance in every imaginable human activity.
He was bringing His teaching about kingdom righteousness to its breathtaking conclusion.
To understand this, we need to look at the original language.
Matthew's Gospel preserves this teaching in Greek.
The word translated “perfect” is τέλειος (teleios).
In Matthew 5:48, the plural form is τέλειοι (teleioi), describing what Jesus commands His followers to be.
The word can mean perfect, complete, mature, or fully developed, depending on its context.
It is related to the Greek word telos, meaning an end, goal, or intended purpose.
But here is where careful interpretation matters.
It would be misleading to claim that teleios never means moral perfection or that Jesus was merely saying, “Just be a little more mature.”
The command is far too serious for that.
God Himself is the standard.
Yet the surrounding verses show us a particular expression of the perfection Jesus requires.
A love that does not stop at the boundaries of personal affection.
A love that refuses to become selective merely because someone is difficult, hostile, or undeserving.
A love that reflects the Father's generous character.
The point is not that the word teleios secretly means something entirely different from perfection.
The point is that Jesus defines the shape of this perfection through the Father's character and the radical love He has just commanded.
And there is another passage that makes this even clearer.
In Luke 6:36, within a closely related teaching about loving enemies, Jesus says:
“Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.” (KJV)
Matthew emphasizes being perfect as the Father is perfect.
Luke emphasizes being merciful as the Father is merciful.
These statements should not be flattened into identical definitions. They appear in distinct Gospel presentations, and each carries its own emphasis.
But together, they help us see the profound connection between the Father's character and the life Jesus calls His disciples to imitate.
The perfection Jesus commands cannot be separated from mercy.
And Christian maturity cannot be separated from love.
Suddenly, the question becomes much more uncomfortable.
Not merely, Have I avoided every mistake today?
But...
Am I becoming more like my Father in the way I treat people who cannot repay me?
Can I pray for someone who has wounded me without secretly hoping they will suffer?
Can I refuse revenge even when I have every opportunity to take it?
Can I speak truth without cruelty?
Can I love without pretending that sin is harmless?
Because sometimes the person who appears most religious is the very person whose heart has become hardest toward others.
And sometimes the person who knows how desperately they need mercy is the one most ready to extend it.
But there is still a problem.
A massive one.
Even when we understand the context, Jesus' command remains beyond our natural ability.
We cannot simply decide to become perfectly loving.
We cannot manufacture the holiness of God through stronger resolutions.
We cannot transform a sinful heart by promising harder.
And Scripture does not pretend otherwise.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Not merely the visibly rebellious.
Not merely the people whose scandals became public.
All.
The respected church leader.
The faithful volunteer.
The exhausted mother.
The young believer battling temptation.
The person reading this article while quietly carrying a secret they have never told another soul.
All have sinned.
And if God's perfect righteousness is the standard, none of us can stand before Him boasting that we have reached it.
That is why the command of Jesus should never lead us into self-righteousness.
It should expose our need for a Savior.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The One who commanded perfect righteousness is the very One who came to rescue people who could never establish their own.
Jesus Christ did not merely preach the Sermon on the Mount.
He lived the righteousness it reveals.
He loved without hypocrisy.
He obeyed the Father without rebellion.
He spoke truth without sin.
He showed compassion without compromising holiness.
And when His enemies mocked Him, rejected Him, and nailed Him to a cross, He demonstrated the very enemy-love He had commanded.
Luke 23:34 records His prayer:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
The hands that had healed the sick were pierced.
The mouth that had spoken life was surrounded by insults.
The One who deserved worship received cruelty.
And still, He prayed.
Do you see it?
The command to love your enemies was not merely a beautiful teaching delivered by someone safely removed from suffering.
Jesus embodied it in the midst of unimaginable suffering.
At Calvary, the perfect love of God was displayed in the sacrifice of His Son.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we conquered every temptation.
Not after we proved we could become respectable religious people.
While we were still sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One died for the guilty.
The Righteous One gave Himself for the unrighteous.
And the sinners who could never earn salvation are invited to receive forgiveness through the crucified and risen Christ.
This is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the beginning of a transformation we could never accomplish by ourselves.
The Gospel does not say that holiness no longer matters because Jesus died.
The Gospel says that because Jesus died and rose again, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed by His grace.
Listen to the difference.
Religion without grace says, “Become perfect so God will finally accept you.”
The Gospel announces that those who repent and trust in Jesus Christ are received through Him, not through the perfection of their personal record.
And the grace that saves them also begins teaching them to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 describes God's grace as bringing salvation and teaching us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires.
Grace is not merely pardon for yesterday.
It is also God's powerful work in the believer's life today.
That distinction matters because someone reading this is exhausted from confusing spiritual growth with earning God's love.
You have been measuring your relationship with Jesus by whether you managed to have a flawless week.
If you prayed consistently, resisted temptation, and controlled your temper, you felt worthy to approach Him.
But if you stumbled, you hid.
You delayed prayer.
You avoided Scripture.
You felt ashamed to worship.
As though the blood of Christ was sufficient for your conversion but somehow insufficient for your continued need of mercy.
Friend, hear this carefully.
Your failures must never become excuses for sin, but neither should they become reasons to run away from the only Savior who can cleanse you.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Confession is not pretending sin was small.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible because you were caught.
True repentance involves turning toward God, agreeing with His judgment about sin, and seeking to walk in obedience through His grace.
Sometimes it also requires confession to people we have harmed, restitution where possible, accountability, and difficult changes in our daily lives.
But repentance is not the purchase price of God's mercy.
Forgiveness is grounded in Jesus Christ and His saving work.
And the believer who has stumbled is not instructed to manufacture a perfect past.
They are called to come into the light.
This is where the original language of another passage gives us a beautiful perspective.
In Philippians 3:12, Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “perfect” in this verse is τετελείωμαι (teteleiōmai), a form of the verb teleioō, which is related to teleios.
Paul openly acknowledges that he has not already reached the final state of perfection.
Yet he does not use that admission as an excuse to stop pursuing Christ.
He presses forward.
Later, in Philippians 3:15, Paul uses τέλειοι (teleioi), often translated “perfect” or “mature,” when addressing believers who should share this Christ-centered outlook.
There is a meaningful distinction here.
Paul can speak of spiritual maturity while admitting that he has not yet reached the ultimate goal.
Christian maturity does not mean pretending you have already arrived.
It means pressing toward Christ with increasing humility, obedience, and dependence upon His grace.
And this is deeply important for understanding Matthew 5:48.
We must preserve the full seriousness of Jesus' command without confusing the believer's present growth with the final perfection God promises.
Hebrews 10:14 says:
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.”
The verse holds together Christ's decisive sacrifice and the people who are being sanctified.
There is a finished work of Christ that believers must trust.
And there is an ongoing work of holiness that believers must not neglect.
These are not competing truths.
They belong together.
The Christian life is not a desperate attempt to become worthy of a Savior.
It is a life of faith and obedience flowing from the grace of the Savior who has already given Himself for us.
But perhaps you are thinking about something more personal.
You are not merely struggling with your own failures.
You are struggling with someone else's.
Someone who hurt you.
Someone who never apologized.
Someone who betrayed you and then behaved as though nothing happened.
You know Jesus commanded you to love your enemies.
But every time you remember what happened, something inside you tightens.
You want to forgive.
Then you remember the humiliation.
You want to pray.
Then you remember the lies.
You want to move forward.
Then the pain returns.
And suddenly Matthew 5:48 feels impossible again.
But consider what loving an enemy actually means.
It does not mean calling evil good.
It does not mean denying the damage someone caused.
It does not mean immediately restoring trust to someone who continues to violate it.
It does not require remaining in an abusive or dangerous situation.
Love can seek another person's ultimate good while maintaining wise boundaries and pursuing justice.
Forgiveness does not erase the need for accountability.
Jesus Himself confronted wrongdoing, exposed hypocrisy, and refused to entrust Himself indiscriminately to others (John 2:24).
So perhaps the first expression of enemy-love in your life will not be a dramatic reconciliation.
Perhaps it will be a quiet prayer.
“Father, I am still hurting. I do not know how to love this person rightly. But I do not want hatred to become my home. Teach me to respond in a way that honors You.”
That prayer may not instantly remove the pain.
But it can be an honest beginning.
And perhaps that is where God is confronting some of us today.
We have been asking Him to make us stronger while resisting His invitation to make us more merciful.
We have been asking for spiritual maturity while protecting bitterness.
We have been praying for a deeper relationship with Jesus while refusing to release our desire for revenge.
We want the comfort of being forgiven.
But we struggle with the cost of forgiving.
And the words of Jesus expose us.
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.”
Not because He is indifferent to our weakness.
Not because He expects us to save ourselves.
But because the life of His kingdom is meant to reflect the character of our Heavenly Father.
This command does not become meaningless because we need grace to obey it.
It becomes a reason to depend upon grace more deeply.
And here is another truth we cannot overlook.
The perfection of God is not merely the perfection of His kindness toward enemies.
God is perfectly holy.
Perfectly righteous.
Perfectly truthful.
Perfectly just.
His love is never corrupt, and His mercy never requires Him to deny His holiness.
Therefore, becoming more like our Heavenly Father cannot mean becoming tolerant of everything or treating repentance as unnecessary.
Jesus calls us to love our enemies, and the same Jesus calls sinners to repent.
He offers mercy, and He warns of judgment.
He welcomes the broken, and He commands those who follow Him to deny themselves and take up their cross.
Biblical love and biblical holiness belong together.
That is why we must resist two dangerous distortions of Matthew 5:48.
One distortion says, “If you are not flawless, God has no place for you.”
The other says, “Since nobody is flawless, holiness does not matter.”
Both miss the Gospel.
The first forgets the sufficiency of Christ.
The second forgets the transforming purpose of His grace.
Jesus did not come to leave sinners trapped in condemnation.
And He did not come to leave them comfortably enslaved to sin.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To redeem.
To transform.
To make a people who increasingly reflect His character.
Second Corinthians 3:18 describes believers being changed into the Lord's image from glory to glory by the Spirit.
That transformation is real.
It may be gradual.
It may involve painful correction.
It may require repeatedly surrendering attitudes you once defended.
But it is not imaginary.
The Holy Spirit does not merely teach Christians to sound more religious.
He produces fruit.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Gentleness.
Goodness.
Faith.
Meekness.
Temperance.
These qualities, described in Galatians 5:22–23, are not decorations added to an otherwise unchanged life.
They are evidence of the Spirit's work.
And sometimes the clearest evidence of spiritual growth is not that you never feel anger.
It is that you no longer surrender to anger as easily.
Not that you never experience temptation.
But that you increasingly learn to resist it and flee toward Christ.
Not that you never feel wounded.
But that you are learning to bring your wounds before God instead of allowing them to become weapons against other people.
Not that you never need forgiveness.
But that you are becoming quicker to confess, quicker to repent, and less willing to hide.
And one day, the work God has begun will reach its promised completion.
First John 3:2 says:
“Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.”
What a promise.
We are not yet what we shall be.
But those who belong to Christ have a future that is not defined by the permanence of their present weaknesses.
The hope of Christian perfection is not ultimately confidence in our ability to improve ourselves.
It is confidence in the Savior who redeems His people and will complete His work.
Philippians 1:6 reminds believers that the One who began a good work in them will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
So when Jesus says, “Be perfect,” we must neither soften His standard nor despair as though He has offered no salvation.
We must look to the Father whose character He commands us to reflect.
We must look honestly at the sin that still lives in us.
And above all, we must look to Jesus Christ.
The One who fulfilled righteousness.
The One who loved His enemies.
The One who carried our sins.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who calls us to repentance and faith.
The One who gives His Spirit to those who belong to Him.
And the One who will not abandon His saving purpose.
Maybe you have spent years believing that your greatest problem was that you were not perfect enough for Jesus.
But the deeper problem was never something you could solve by trying harder without Him.
You needed redemption.
You needed forgiveness.
You needed a new heart.
You needed grace.
And you still need Him today.
Not less than you did when you first believed.
Every single day.
So here is a question I want you to sit with.
If someone examined the way you treat the people who have hurt you, would they see anything of your Heavenly Father's mercy?
If someone watched the way you respond after you sin, would they see genuine repentance or a cycle of hiding and excuses?
If someone listened to the way you speak about people you dislike, would they hear the voice of someone being transformed by Jesus?
These are not questions meant to crush the repentant believer.
They are invitations to examine our hearts in the light of God's Word.
Because sometimes we spend so much time asking whether God has forgiven our past that we forget to ask what He wants to transform in our present.
And perhaps the most important response you can make today is not to promise Jesus that you will never fail again.
Perhaps it is to stop defending what He has been calling you to surrender.
The bitterness.
The secret sin.
The pride.
The spiritual performance.
The resentment.
The belief that you must hide your weakness before you can approach Him.
Bring it into the light.
Call sin what Scripture calls it.
Trust the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Ask the Holy Spirit to change what your own strength has failed to change.
And then walk in obedience, one faithful step at a time.
Not to purchase the Father's love.
But because, through Christ, you have encountered a love that changes people.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to reveal private details to strangers. Sometimes a simple confession of dependence on God can encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
And if you have a testimony about how Christ helped you release bitterness, repent of sin, or grow in mercy, consider sharing it.
Someone reading the comments may need to be reminded that transformation through Jesus Christ is possible.
There is also someone in your circle who needs this message.
Perhaps a believer who has become exhausted by perfectionism.
A friend who believes one terrible mistake has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
A family member who has quietly drifted away from faith.
Or someone who has never understood why Christians speak so passionately about grace.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because someone you know may be asking the very question this article addresses.
Because the struggle between shame and grace is not always settled by reading one message.
