Sometimes we need to return to Scripture again and again until the truth begins shaping the way we think, pray, repent, forgive, and live.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish emotionally moving articles, but to help people encounter biblical truth, grow in discipleship, and continually return to Jesus Christ.

We want this community to become a place where Scripture is taken seriously, where sin is not excused, where wounded people are treated with compassion, and where Jesus Christ remains at the center of everything.
And for those who want to help us continue and expand this mission, there is another meaningful way to participate.
Scripture teaches that believers may support those who labor in teaching the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), and that giving should be willing rather than pressured (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And we want to express our appreciation in a practical way.
It is participating in an ongoing effort to make Christ-centered encouragement and biblical discipleship more accessible.
We want people to grow in their understanding of Scripture, deepen their relationship with Christ, and become equipped to share the Gospel with others.
Pray for this ministry.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Tell someone what Jesus Christ has done for you.
These are meaningful ways to serve the Gospel.
Because the mission is not ultimately about building a platform.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
And before you leave, I want to bring you back to the question that started this entire conversation.
What did Jesus mean when He said we must be perfect as our Heavenly Father is perfect?
He was calling His disciples to the complete, holy, wholehearted love that reflects the character of their Father, especially a love that reaches beyond friends and extends even toward enemies.
He was not giving us permission to settle for sin.
Nor was He teaching that we could earn salvation through flawless performance.
He was revealing the righteousness of God's kingdom, a standard that exposes our need for grace and a way of life into which Christ calls those who follow Him.
The standard is not lowered.
The Savior is exalted.
And through the grace of Jesus Christ and the work of the Holy Spirit, those who belong to Him are being transformed toward the likeness of the One who saved them.
So do not walk away from Matthew 5:48 believing that Jesus has simply demanded the impossible and left you alone to accomplish it.
Walk away humbled by the holiness of God.
Convicted by the depth of His command.
Grateful for the cross.
Dependent upon His Spirit.
And ready to take your next step of obedience.
Because the same Jesus who said, “Be ye therefore perfect,” also said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
He never invited us to make peace with our sin.
But He did invite weary sinners to come to Him.
And that invitation still stands.
So come.
Not pretending you have already arrived.
Not demanding that God accept the sins you refuse to surrender.
Not trusting your religious achievements.
Come in repentance and faith.
Come to the crucified and risen Christ.
Come to the Savior whose mercy is greater than anything you could ever deserve.
And let His grace begin changing the places in your heart that you once believed could never change.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but in Christ, it does not have to write the final sentence of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN CALLING SOMETHING FAITH THAT JESUS NEVER CALLED ALIVE?
paragraphs: “FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN CALLING SOMETHING FAITH THAT JESUS NEVER CALLED ALIVE?

James Wasn't Teaching You How to Earn Salvation. He Was Exposing Something Far More Terrifying: A Person Can Know the Truth About Jesus, Speak Like a Believer, and Still Refuse to Live Like Someone Who Has Been Changed by Him.
There is a kind of Christianity that knows exactly what to say when someone asks about Jesus.
It knows the worship songs. It knows when to say “Amen.” It knows how to quote Scripture, post Bible verses, defend Christian beliefs, and tell everyone that God is good.
But there is one question it desperately hopes nobody will ask.
If Jesus has truly changed your heart, where is the evidence?
Not the cross around your neck.
Not the number of years you have attended church.
Not even how passionately you can explain the Gospel.
Where is the evidence when someone hurts you?
When a hungry person stands in front of you?
When telling the truth could cost you something?
When nobody is watching?
When obedience becomes inconvenient?
Because somewhere between knowing about Jesus and actually following Him, a frightening thing can happen.
We can become so comfortable discussing the Christian life that we forget to live it.
And James, the brother of the Lord Jesus, wrote something that cuts straight through that comfortable illusion.
“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” — James 2:17, KJV
Dead.
Not weak.
Not temporarily unpopular.
Dead.
That is a devastating word to find in a letter written to people who professed faith in God.
But before you panic, before you begin questioning whether you have done enough good deeds to make heaven, you need to understand something absolutely essential.
James was not telling sinners to work their way into salvation. He was warning professing believers against confusing an empty profession with living faith.
And once you understand the difference, this passage becomes both deeply uncomfortable and extraordinarily beautiful.
Because the same Gospel that refuses to let us earn salvation also refuses to leave us unchanged.
Consider the original Greek.
James 2:17 reads:
οὕτως καὶ ἡ πίστις, ἐὰν μὴ ἔχῃ ἔργα, νεκρά ἐστιν καθ’ ἑαυτήν.
Transliteration: houtōs kai hē pistis, ean mē echē erga, nekra estin kath’ heautēn.
A close translation is:
“So also faith, if it does not have works, is dead by itself.”
The word πίστις (pistis) means faith, trust, or belief, depending on context.
The word ἔργα (erga) means works, deeds, or actions.
And the word νεκρά (nekra) means dead.
James was not using a complicated expression that secretly means something harmless.
He meant what he said.
A claimed faith that produces no corresponding action is lifeless.
But what actions was he talking about?
Was he demanding that Christians donate large amounts of money?
Was he talking about keeping the ceremonial regulations of the Mosaic Law?
Was he saying you must preach publicly, lead a ministry, perform miracles, or accomplish impressive religious achievements before God will accept you?
No.
In fact, the example James chose is so ordinary that it becomes impossible to hide behind religious accomplishments.
He described someone who was hungry.
Someone who was cold.
Someone who needed help.
And another person who had the right religious words but refused to do anything.
James 2:15–16 says:

“If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?”
Imagine that scene.
A sister in Christ stands before you.
Her clothes are inadequate. She has not eaten properly. She is struggling to survive.
You look into her eyes.
You smile.
You tell her, “God bless you. Stay warm. I’ll pray that the Lord provides.”
And then you walk away, although you could have helped.
James asks a question that leaves almost no room for excuses.
What good was that?
Your words sounded spiritual.
Your concern sounded sincere.
But the person was still hungry.
Still cold.
Still abandoned.
And suddenly we understand what kind of works James was talking about.
Not religious performances designed to purchase God's approval, but acts of obedience and love that demonstrate the reality of faith.
Compassion that moves beyond sentiment.
Generosity that costs something.
Mercy that refuses to remain theoretical.
Integrity when dishonesty would be easier.
Forgiveness when resentment feels justified.
Care for people who cannot repay you.
A willingness to obey Christ even when obedience disrupts your comfort.
These are not substitutes for the Gospel.
They are among the fruits of a life being transformed by the Gospel.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because someone reading this right now may be carrying a terrible fear.
Perhaps you have failed God repeatedly.
Perhaps your past is full of decisions you wish you could erase.
Perhaps you have been told that unless you do enough good things, give enough money, serve enough hours, or prove yourself sufficiently worthy, God will eventually reject you.
Listen carefully.
You cannot purchase with good works what Jesus purchased with His blood.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
There it is.
Salvation is a gift.
Not a paycheck.
Not a trophy.
Not a reward for religious productivity.
A gift.
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis), describing favor given rather than wages earned.
And Paul is unmistakably clear.
We are not saved because our works have made us worthy.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
So was James contradicting Paul?
Absolutely not.
And the next verse in Ephesians reveals why.
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” — Ephesians 2:10, KJV
Read that again.
Not saved by good works.
Created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
The order matters.
Grace comes first.
New life comes from Christ.
Good works follow as the fruit of that new life.
Paul was confronting the idea that human works could establish our standing before God.
James was confronting the idea that someone could claim to have faith while remaining indifferent to the obedience and love that faith calls for.
They were addressing different errors, not preaching different saviors.
Paul explains why works cannot be the foundation of salvation. James explains why living faith cannot remain fruitless.
And if you miss that distinction, you may fall into one of two spiritual traps.
You may spend your entire life trying to earn the love of a God who calls sinners to receive His grace.
Or you may claim the grace of Jesus while refusing to take His commands seriously.
Neither is the freedom of the Gospel.
Now James goes even deeper.
He writes:
That verse should make every religious heart uncomfortable.
Because James is exposing the difference between accepting true information about God and personally trusting Him.
The demons are not atheists.
They know God exists.
They recognize spiritual realities.
They tremble.
But their knowledge is not saving faith.
Their recognition of truth does not amount to loving submission to Christ.
Which means it is possible to believe correct things about God without trusting Him as Lord and Savior.
You can know that Jesus died on the cross.
You can know that He rose from the dead.
You can know that judgment is real.
You can know the language of salvation.
And still resist the One you claim to believe in.
That is why James refuses to treat a verbal profession as sufficient evidence of living faith.
He is not demanding perfection.
He is challenging the dangerous assumption that agreement with religious facts is the same thing as genuine trust in God.
And now the question becomes personal.
When you say you believe in Jesus, do you mean merely that you believe He exists?
Or do you mean that you are entrusting yourself to Him?
Because trust changes how we respond.
A person who trusts a physician does not merely admire the prescription while refusing the treatment.
A person who trusts a rescuer does not insist on remaining in the burning building.
And a person who trusts Jesus does not regard His voice as irrelevant to daily life.
That does not mean obedience is always easy.
It does not mean Christians never stumble.
It means genuine faith has a living relationship with the Savior it confesses.
And sometimes that relationship leads us into places we never expected.
James gives two astonishing examples.
Abraham.
And Rahab.
One was a revered patriarch.
The other was a woman known in Scripture for prostitution.
One stood near the beginning of Israel's covenant history.
The other lived in Jericho, a city facing judgment.
Yet James placed them in the same discussion about faith.
Why?
Because both demonstrated their trust in God through costly action.
Abraham believed God, and Genesis 15:6 says that his faith was counted to him for righteousness.
Later, when God tested Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, Abraham obeyed, trusting God even when he could not understand how the promise would be fulfilled.
James writes:
The Greek verb translated “was made perfect,” ἐτελειώθη (eteleiōthē), carries the sense of being brought to completion or maturity.
James is describing faith reaching its intended expression through action.
Abraham's obedience did not mean he had earned God's earlier promise.
His obedience demonstrated the reality and maturity of the faith he professed.
And then there was Rahab.
A woman whose past could easily have become the only thing anyone remembered about her.
A woman living inside a city that was about to fall.
A woman who had every reason to protect herself by siding with the powers around her.
But when the Israelite spies came, Rahab recognized what God was doing.
She confessed that the LORD was God in heaven above and earth beneath.
Then she acted.
She received the messengers and helped them escape.
Her faith became visible through a dangerous decision.
James 2:25 refers to her receiving the messengers and sending them out another way.
And Hebrews 11:31 remembers her faith.
Think about that.
The woman known as Rahab the prostitute became a testimony to the mercy and power of God.
Her former identity did not have the final word.
God's grace reached into a life marked by scandal and brought her into His unfolding redemptive story.
Matthew 1:5 even places Rahab in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
What a breathtaking reminder.
The Gospel does not require you to have a spotless past. It calls you to trust the spotless Savior.
Rahab was not saved because she had successfully constructed a respectable religious image.
She trusted the God whose power and mercy she had come to recognize, and her actions revealed that trust.
And that is where this passage becomes more than a theological debate.
Because some of us are still living as though our past disqualifies us from ever becoming useful to God.
We remember the addiction.
The betrayal.
The dishonesty.
The sexual sin.
The years of pretending.
The people we wounded.
The promises we broke.
The secret decisions we hope nobody discovers.
We look at those memories and wonder whether God could ever produce anything beautiful from such a damaged story.
But look at Rahab.
And then look at Jesus.
The Savior who welcomed sinners did not come to congratulate the self-righteous.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He did not die because humanity needed a little moral improvement.
He died because sin is serious, judgment is real, and we could not rescue ourselves.
And He rose again because death could not hold Him.
His resurrection is not merely a hopeful metaphor.
It is the heart of the Christian proclamation that the crucified Jesus is alive.
So when Christ calls you to repent, He is not inviting you to manufacture a flawless history.
He is calling you to turn from sin and come to Him.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind or heart that involves turning toward God.
Real repentance does not mean you can undo yesterday.
It means you stop defending the sin that is destroying you and turn to the Savior who can forgive and transform you.
And yes, that transformation should eventually become visible.
Not always in spectacular ways.
Sometimes the work of faith looks like a father apologizing to the child he has repeatedly hurt.
Sometimes it looks like a wife or husband telling the truth after years of hiding.
Sometimes it looks like returning money that was dishonestly taken.
Sometimes it looks like visiting a lonely person nobody remembers.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to join in gossip.
Sometimes it looks like feeding someone who cannot afford a meal.
Sometimes it looks like walking away from temptation when nobody would have known.
Sometimes it looks like seeking help to break a destructive pattern.
Sometimes it looks like praying through tears and choosing to obey Christ again after another painful failure.
None of those actions purchases salvation.
But each can become an expression of faith working through love.
Paul himself used that beautiful phrase in Galatians 5:6:
“Faith which worketh by love.”
The Greek expression is πίστις δι’ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη (pistis di’ agapēs energoumenē).
Faith expressing itself through love.
Not faith performing for applause.
Not faith competing for religious status.
Not faith trying to make God indebted to us.
Faith working through love.
And suddenly the person who serves quietly, unnoticed by everyone except God, begins to look very different from the person who collects religious attention but refuses to love.
Jesus Himself warned about doing righteous deeds merely to be seen by others in Matthew 6:1.
That means even impressive religious activities can be corrupted by selfish motives.
You can give money to impress people.
You can serve to build your reputation.
You can publish Christian content to gain attention.
You can speak about compassion without genuinely caring for the suffering.
You can even turn ministry into a monument to yourself.
James does not give us permission to replace one kind of empty religion with another.
The works he describes belong to a faith that takes God seriously and responds to people with genuine love.
And this matters especially in a world where religious visibility is easier than ever.
A Christian message can reach thousands of people in seconds.
A Bible verse can be shared with one tap.
A sermon can be watched while preparing breakfast.
These can be wonderful gifts.
But none of them should become substitutes for following Jesus.
You can post about generosity while ignoring a person you could help.
You can write “God is love” while treating people with contempt.
You can defend biblical truth online while refusing to practice biblical humility offline.
And you can become so busy appearing faithful that you never confront what is happening inside your own heart.
That is why James's warning is still so necessary.
Not because every Christian must accomplish something extraordinary.
But because ordinary obedience matters to God.
And yet there is another danger here.
A tenderhearted believer may read this and become overwhelmed.
“What if my works are not enough?”
“What if I still struggle with anger?”
“What if I am trying to forgive but the pain is still there?”
“What if I keep failing?”
“What if my faith feels weak?”
Please hear this distinction.
Struggling faith is not automatically dead faith.
The father in Mark 9:24 cried:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
That was not the language of a man who possessed perfect confidence.
It was the cry of someone bringing his weakness to Jesus.
Peter denied the Lord three times.
Yet the risen Christ restored him and entrusted him with responsibility to care for His sheep.
The Christian life is not a straight line of uninterrupted victories.
Believers still wrestle with sin, weakness, fear, and immaturity.
James is not teaching that every failure proves someone was never saved.
He is confronting a claim of faith that remains detached from obedience and love.
There is a profound difference between someone who falls into sin and grieves it, and someone who deliberately embraces sin while insisting that faith makes repentance unnecessary.
There is a difference between a believer who struggles to forgive and a person who proudly refuses even to consider Christ's command to forgive.
There is a difference between a person who has little to give and a person who has the means to help but chooses indifference.
God sees what people cannot.
He knows our limitations.
He knows our motives.
He knows the hidden battles.
And the fruit of genuine faith is not measured by wealth, public recognition, or the size of a person's ministry.
Remember the widow in Mark 12:41–44.
Her offering was small in monetary value, but Jesus recognized the extraordinary sacrifice behind it.
The point was never that everyone must give a particular amount to prove their faith.
The point was that God sees beyond appearances.
Which brings us to something that must be said clearly, especially wherever money and ministry are involved.
Financial giving can be a beautiful work of faith, but no Christian ministry has the authority to sell salvation, forgiveness, spiritual status, or God's favor.
It is not a substitute for repentance.
And it is not a biblical requirement for proving that your faith is alive.
In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word מַעֲשֵׂר (ma'aser) means “tenth” and is associated with the tithing practices of ancient Israel.
In the New Testament, Christians are instructed to give generously, willingly, and without coercion.
Paul writes:
The New Testament also supports material provision for those who labor in Gospel ministry, as seen in 1 Corinthians 9:14 and Galatians 6:6.
So supporting trustworthy Christian teaching and discipleship is a legitimate and potentially fruitful expression of generosity.
But it must remain an offering of willing support, not a spiritual transaction.
Why does this matter?
Because the very passage we are studying warns us against religious appearances that do not reflect the heart of God.
We cannot preach grace with one hand and use guilt to sell spiritual acceptance with the other.
The Gospel is too precious for that.
And if Gospel Warrior is going to proclaim the truth that Jesus rewrites everything, then even the way this ministry invites support must reflect the character of Christ.
That means transparency.
Freedom.
Gratitude.
Accountability.
And a sincere desire to serve people, whether they can financially contribute or not.

If Gospel Warrior has encouraged you, strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or reminded you that your story is not beyond the reach of Jesus, there is a meaningful way to help this ministry continue.

Your voluntary support can help sustain the ongoing work of creating and sharing Christ-centered articles, biblical encouragement, discipleship materials, and resources intended to reach people who may never walk into a church but might stop long enough to read a message about Jesus.
Somewhere there is a man who has not opened his Bible in years.
Somewhere there is a woman who believes her past makes her unworthy of forgiveness.
Somewhere there is a young believer quietly questioning whether God has abandoned them.
Somewhere there is a family member you have been praying for who would never willingly sit through a sermon but might read a story shared by someone they trust.
Not because God needs our money to accomplish His purposes.
But because He graciously allows His people to participate in the work of making the Gospel known.
And that participation is not limited to financial support.
Sharing the truth is also a meaningful act of love when it is done with sincerity.
Not to prove how spiritual you are.
Not to collect approval.
But because someone connected to you may be carrying questions they have never dared to ask.
Someone may be exhausted from trying to earn God's acceptance.
Someone may have mistaken religious knowledge for a relationship with Jesus.
Someone may need to understand that genuine faith is not a performance, but it is never meant to remain merely theoretical.
And someone may need to hear that their scandal does not have to be the final chapter of their life.
You never know what conversation may begin with one sincere act of sharing.
And if this passage has confronted something personal in your life, do not rush past that conviction.
Perhaps you have been using Christian language to avoid Christian obedience.
Perhaps you have been postponing an apology.
Perhaps you have been refusing to help someone when you have the ability.
Perhaps you have been confusing ministry activity with intimacy with God.
Perhaps you have been trying so desperately to earn salvation that you have forgotten to rest in the finished work of Jesus.
Or perhaps you are simply tired.
Tired of failing.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of wondering whether God could ever make something beautiful from your life.
Then bring that honestly to Him.
You do not need to pretend.
You do not need to impress Him.
You need Jesus.
Not as a ritual that earns favor with God.
Not as a public test of your salvation.
But as a simple expression of the prayer forming in your heart.
You do not have to disclose private details.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to invite a community of believers to pray with you.
Your story may encourage someone who thinks transformation is impossible.
Because the beauty of Christian community is not that everyone has already arrived.
It is that we point one another toward the Savior who is still at work.
Return to it when you begin confusing good works with the price of salvation.
Return to it when your faith becomes comfortable but your compassion becomes cold.
Return to it when you feel tempted to measure your standing with God by your religious accomplishments.
Return to it when your failures make you question whether grace is real.
Remember the order.
Jesus saves.
Jesus changes.
Jesus teaches us to walk in love.
The goal is not merely to gather an audience.
It is to help people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, ask honest questions, and grow toward a life centered on Jesus Christ.
Those products are not instruments of salvation, and purchasing them is not a measure of spiritual maturity.
They are simply another way to encourage, equip, and support the continuing work of this ministry.
Your monthly contribution can become part of your intentional, voluntary Christian giving toward the work of Gospel proclamation and discipleship.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Grow.
The grace of Jesus Christ is not reserved for paying supporters.
And the message of the cross must never become something people are required to purchase.
Now return with me to James.
Because there is one final image in his letter that we cannot afford to overlook.
He writes:
A body can retain its outward shape after life has departed.
Its features may still be recognizable.
Its appearance may still remind people of the person who once lived.
But something essential is missing.
Life.
That is the comparison James chooses.
A profession of faith may retain the outward shape of Christianity.
It may have the vocabulary.
The traditions.
The religious knowledge.
The public identity.
But where genuine trust in Christ is absent, religious appearance cannot manufacture spiritual life.
And here is the most important truth of all.
James is not telling dead faith to decorate itself with religious activity. He is exposing the emptiness of faith that exists only as a claim.
The answer is not to glue a few good deeds onto a lifeless profession and hope God will be impressed.
The answer is to come to Jesus Christ in genuine repentance and faith.
Because only Christ can give the life that our religious performances cannot produce.
He is the One who lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He is the One who loved sinners without excusing sin.
He is the One who carried our sins to the cross.
He is the One who rose from the grave.
And He is the One who calls us to follow Him.
Not to purchase His love.
But because His grace is powerful enough to change the direction of a human life.
Maybe today your first act of obedience is not something dramatic.
Maybe it is closing the door on a secret sin.
Maybe it is admitting that you need help.
Maybe it is forgiving someone while still working through the pain.
Maybe it is opening your Bible again.
Maybe it is reaching out to someone you have ignored.
Maybe it is giving quietly to someone in need.
Maybe it is finally surrendering your life to Jesus rather than merely agreeing with facts about Him.
Whatever that next faithful step looks like, do not confuse it with earning your rescue.
You are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
You are not the source of grace.
Jesus is.
You are not the author of redemption.
Jesus is.
And the Christian life begins and continues by depending on Him.
One day, the things we accumulated will no longer matter.
The applause will fade.
The social media numbers will disappear.
The impressive titles will lose their shine.
But what was done in sincere love for Christ will not have been meaningless.
The hungry person who was fed.
The wounded person who was treated with mercy.
The truth that was spoken with gentleness.
The secret temptation that was resisted.
The apology that was finally offered.
The gift that was given without seeking recognition.
The Gospel that was shared without shame.
These are not payments made toward the purchase of heaven.
They are glimpses of what the grace of God can produce in ordinary human lives.
And perhaps that is the most unforgettable lesson James leaves us.
God is not asking you to prove that you deserve Jesus.
He is calling you to stop treating Jesus as though knowing His name is the same thing as following Him.
So ask yourself tonight, when the noise fades and nobody is there to applaud your answer:
Does my faith exist only in what I say?
Or is the grace of Jesus teaching me how to love?
Do not answer too quickly.
Let the Holy Spirit search your heart through the truth of Scripture.
Where there is sin, repent.
Where there is unbelief, ask Christ for help.
Where there is selfishness, seek His grace to love.
Where there is failure, return to the Savior rather than hiding from Him.
And where there is genuine spiritual fruit, give God the glory.
Because the evidence of living faith is not that you have become your own savior.
It is that you belong to the Savior who is changing you.
The greatest tragedy is not having a past stained by sin; it is standing before the Savior who can give you new life and choosing to remain satisfied with merely knowing His name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD HARDENED PHARAOH’S HEART… THEN PUNISHED HIM FOR IT. HOW IS THAT JUST?
paragraphs: GOD HARDENED PHARAOH’S HEART… THEN PUNISHED HIM FOR IT. HOW IS THAT JUST?
The terrifying truth behind Exodus 4:21, Exodus 9:12, and Romans 9:17–18—and why the story of a stubborn king may reveal something about your own heart that you never expected.
What if the most frightening thing God could do to a rebellious person is allow that person to become exactly what they have insisted on being?
Read that again.

Because buried inside one of the most disturbing stories in the Old Testament is a question that has troubled sincere believers, confused Bible students, and given skeptics a reason to challenge the justice of God.
God told Moses that He would harden Pharaoh's heart.
Then Pharaoh refused to release the Israelites.
Then God judged Pharaoh for refusing.
Wait.
If God hardened his heart, how could Pharaoh be responsible for what he did?
Was Pharaoh merely a puppet in a divine drama? Was he condemned for a decision God had already determined? And if God is perfectly righteous, how can He judge someone whose heart He Himself hardened?
These are not foolish questions.
They are questions worth asking carefully, with an open Bible and a humble heart.
Because the answer is far more profound than the popular explanation that Pharaoh was simply a bad man who deserved punishment.
And it is more complicated than saying God merely watched Pharaoh make bad choices.
Scripture says something stronger.
Something that should make every one of us pay attention.
God hardened Pharaoh's heart.
Pharaoh hardened his own heart.
And the Bible deliberately tells us both.
But before we understand what happened inside Pharaoh, we need to remember what was happening outside his palace.
There were people crying.
Families suffering.
Children growing up under oppression.
Generations of Israelites living beneath the crushing weight of Egyptian slavery.
Exodus 2:23 tells us that the Israelites groaned because of their bondage, and their cry rose to God.
Imagine a mother holding her exhausted child after another day of forced labor.
Imagine a father who cannot promise his family that tomorrow will be better.
Imagine people praying for deliverance year after year, wondering whether heaven has heard a single word.
And then God speaks.
He tells Moses:
"I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows."
—Exodus 3:7, KJV
Before the Bible introduces us to the mystery of Pharaoh's hardened heart, it introduces us to the compassion of the God who hears the oppressed.
That matters.
Because this story is not primarily about a ruler being denied the freedom to make choices.
It is about the living God confronting an oppressive king who believed he had the authority to hold an entire people captive.
And Pharaoh's first recorded response to God's demand reveals something devastating.
"Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the LORD, neither will I let Israel go."
—Exodus 5:2, KJV
Can you hear the arrogance?
Who is the LORD?
Why should I obey Him?
Why should His command interrupt my kingdom?
Pharaoh did not merely reject a religious suggestion.
He rejected the authority of the God who had come to deliver His people.
And his response was not harmless disbelief.
He increased Israel's burdens.
He commanded that the people continue producing bricks without being supplied with straw (Exodus 5:6–9).
His rebellion had victims.
Real people.
Real suffering.
Real tears.
And suddenly the question becomes more personal.
How many times have we heard what God says and quietly answered, "But I want things my way"?
Perhaps not from a golden throne.
Perhaps from a bedroom where nobody knows what we are watching.
Perhaps from a relationship we know is pulling us away from Christ.
Perhaps from an apology we refuse to make.
Perhaps from a sin we have renamed so that we no longer have to confront it.
Pharaoh had a kingdom to protect.
We have our own little kingdoms, too.
And sometimes the throne we defend most fiercely is the one inside our hearts.
But here is where the mystery deepens.
Before Moses ever confronted Pharaoh, God had already declared:

"And the LORD said unto Moses, When thou goest to return into Egypt, see that thou do all those wonders before Pharaoh, which I have put in thine hand: but I will harden his heart, that he shall not let the people go."
—Exodus 4:21, KJV
Notice the timing.
God announced His intention before the confrontation unfolded.
That means we cannot simply explain away the passage by saying that God only reacted after Pharaoh had already resisted several plagues.
The text will not allow us to make it that simple.
God knew what would happen.
God declared what He would do.
And God remained sovereign throughout the confrontation.
But the same book also records Pharaoh's responsibility.
Exodus 8:15 says that when Pharaoh saw relief from the plague of frogs, he hardened his heart.
Exodus 8:32 says Pharaoh hardened his heart again.
Exodus 9:34 records that Pharaoh and his servants continued in sin and hardened their hearts after the hail stopped.
Then Exodus 9:12 declares:
"And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had spoken unto Moses."
—Exodus 9:12, KJV
So which was it?
Did Pharaoh harden his heart?
Or did God?
According to Scripture, both.
And understanding that requires us to pay attention to the language God chose.
The Hebrew Scriptures use several expressions to describe the hardening of Pharaoh's heart.
One important verb is חָזַק (chazaq), which can communicate strength, firmness, or becoming strong. In the hardening narrative, it describes a heart becoming firm or unyielding.
Another is כָּבֵד (kaved), associated with heaviness or weight. When applied to Pharaoh's heart, it conveys stubbornness or unresponsiveness.
A third is קָשָׁה (qashah), meaning to be hard, severe, or difficult, and in this context, to make stubborn.
These words help us understand the picture.
Pharaoh's heart was not described as a physical organ turning into stone.
His heart represented his inner will, disposition, and response to God's authority.
He was becoming increasingly resistant.
Unyielding.
Unwilling to bow.
And there is a crucial distinction we must preserve.
The Bible does not portray Pharaoh as an innocent man desperately wanting to obey God while God forced him to become evil against his will.
Pharaoh was already an oppressive ruler.
He repeatedly rejected God's command.
He chose cruelty.
He clung to his power.
And yet Scripture also insists that God's hardening was a real divine action, not merely a poetic way of describing Pharaoh's choices.
How those two truths fit together has been debated by faithful Christian interpreters for centuries.
Some understand God's hardening as judicial: God gives a rebellious person over to the stubbornness that person has embraced, withdrawing restraint and allowing rebellion to become more entrenched.
Others emphasize that God actively and sovereignly confirmed Pharaoh in his resistance to accomplish His righteous purposes, while Pharaoh still acted willingly and remained accountable.
These explanations differ in how they understand divine causation and human freedom.
But neither requires us to imagine Pharaoh as morally innocent.
And neither gives us permission to pretend that God's sovereignty is absent from the story.
The Bible does not erase either truth.
God rules.
Human beings are accountable.
We may not fully comprehend how divine sovereignty and human responsibility meet, but we must not solve the mystery by deleting one side of Scripture.
And there is something else we cannot afford to overlook.
God did not send Moses to Pharaoh without warning.
Again and again, Pharaoh heard God's command.
Again and again, he witnessed God's power.
Again and again, he had evidence that the God of Israel was not an imaginary rival to Egypt's gods.
Even some of Pharaoh's own servants began to recognize the danger.
Before the plague of hail, Exodus 9:20 tells us that those among Pharaoh's servants who feared the word of the LORD brought their servants and livestock into shelter.
Others refused to heed the warning.
Think about that.
Within the same confrontation, people responded differently to the word of God.
Some took warning.
Others dismissed it.
Pharaoh, however, continued to resist.
And the consequences were devastating.
Not because God was entertained by suffering.
Not because the Israelites were disposable pieces in a heavenly contest.
But because Pharaoh's oppressive kingdom was being confronted by a God who would not abandon His covenant people.
This is where we need to understand the purpose God Himself declared.
In Exodus 9:16, God tells Pharaoh:
"And in very deed for this cause have I raised thee up, for to shew in thee my power; and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth."
The Hebrew expression translated "raised thee up" includes the verb הֶעֱמַדְתִּיךָ (he'emadtikha), from a root meaning to stand or establish.
The statement emphasizes that Pharaoh's position and continued existence served God's declared purpose of displaying His power.
It does not require us to conclude that Pharaoh was created solely for damnation.
Nor does it suggest that Pharaoh's evil became morally good because God used it.
God can sovereignly accomplish His purposes through the actions of wicked rulers without becoming wicked Himself.
The distinction matters.
A person may intend evil.
God may overrule that evil for His righteous purpose.
The human intention remains accountable.
The divine purpose remains holy.
We see a similar distinction later in Genesis 50:20, when Joseph tells his brothers that they intended evil against him, but God intended it for good.
The same event can involve sinful human intentions and God's righteous providence.
And then, centuries after the Exodus, the apostle Paul returns to Pharaoh's story.
He writes:
Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth."
—Romans 9:17–18, KJV
There it is.
The statement that makes some readers uncomfortable.
God has mercy on whom He wills.
And He hardens whom He wills.
The Greek verb translated "hardens" is σκληρύνει (sklērynei), from σκληρύνω (sklērynō), meaning to make hard or stubborn.
Paul does not soften the statement.
He emphasizes God's sovereign freedom.
Romans 9 is not simply an essay about human psychology or the dangers of repeatedly rejecting conviction.
Paul is discussing God's purposes, His mercy, His promises, and the question of His righteousness in relation to Israel and the nations.
And immediately after discussing God's mercy and hardening, Paul anticipates an objection:
"Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will?"
—Romans 9:19, KJV
In other words:
If God's purpose stands, how can He still hold human beings accountable?
Does that sound familiar?
It is almost exactly the question we began with.
Paul does not pretend the objection is ridiculous.
He anticipates it.
But his answer is not a complete philosophical explanation of how every aspect of divine sovereignty and human responsibility fits together.
Instead, he confronts the arrogance of placing the Creator on trial as though the creature possessed authority over Him.
He uses the image of a potter and clay.
God is not one moral agent among many, competing for authority inside a universe He did not create.
He is the Creator.
His wisdom exceeds ours.
His purposes are not subject to our permission.
But this does not mean every human interpretation of God's actions is automatically correct.
Nor does it mean we should silence sincere questions with the phrase, "God can do whatever He wants."
Scripture itself teaches that God is righteous in all His ways (Psalm 145:17), that He does not act wickedly (Job 34:12), and that He does not tempt anyone to evil (James 1:13).
We must hold those truths together with Romans 9.
God's sovereignty is not an excuse to attribute moral evil to His character.
And God's righteousness is not an excuse to deny what Scripture says about His sovereign judgments.
The mystery is real.
But so is the revelation.
And perhaps the most sobering part of Pharaoh's story is not that his heart became hard.
It is that he repeatedly experienced relief without experiencing lasting repentance.
When the pressure increased, Pharaoh sometimes sounded willing to negotiate.
When the suffering eased, he returned to resistance.
He wanted the consequences removed.
But he did not want to surrender his authority.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
A crisis comes.
We pray.
We cry.
We promise God things will change.
"Lord, if You get me through this, I will never go back."
Then the danger passes.
The tears dry.
The fear fades.
And the same temptation begins to whisper again.
We return to the very thing we begged God to rescue us from.
Not always because our earlier tears were fake.
Sometimes because fear of consequences is not the same thing as repentance.
A person can hate the pain that sin produces while still loving the sin itself.
A person can want deliverance from judgment without wanting the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
A person can be deeply religious and still resist the God they claim to worship.
And this is where Pharaoh stops being merely an ancient Egyptian king.
His story becomes a mirror.
Not because every struggling Christian is Pharaoh.
Not because every repeated sin proves that God has hardened someone's heart.
And certainly not because a wounded believer who feels spiritually numb should assume God has abandoned them.
The Bible does not authorize those conclusions.
But Pharaoh's story does warn us against treating repeated rebellion as harmless.
Hebrews 3:13 warns believers about becoming hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Notice that phrase.
The deceitfulness of sin.
Sin rarely begins by announcing what it will eventually destroy.
It whispers.
Just this once.
Nobody will know.
You deserve this.
You can repent later.
You are not hurting anyone.
God understands.
And yes, God understands our weakness.
But His grace was never intended to become permission to cherish the very sin from which Christ came to save us.
The danger is not that God is unwilling to forgive a repentant sinner.
The danger is that sin can train us to stop wanting repentance.
That is terrifying.
Because a hardened heart does not always look angry.
Sometimes it looks comfortable.
Sometimes it looks successful.
Sometimes it sings worship songs.
Sometimes it knows the right theological answers.
Sometimes it can quote Scripture while refusing to obey the Scripture it quotes.
And sometimes the most dangerous words a person can say are not, "I don't believe in God."
Sometimes they are:
"I'll deal with this later."
Later.
When life settles down.
When the relationship ends.
When the money is better.
When the temptation becomes easier to resist.
When obedience no longer costs so much.
But Scripture never promises that tomorrow will be more convenient for repentance.
Hebrews 3:15 says:
"To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts."
Today.
Not because God is cruel.
But because the invitation to turn to Him is too precious to treat casually.
And now we come to the most beautiful contrast in this entire story.
Pharaoh was a king who hardened his heart to preserve his throne.
Jesus Christ is the King who humbled Himself and went to the cross to save sinners.
Pharaoh held people in bondage.
Jesus came to set captives free.
Pharaoh resisted the word of God.
Jesus perfectly obeyed His Father.
Pharaoh used power to protect himself.
Jesus willingly laid down His life for others.
Philippians 2:8 says that Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
The Greek word translated "humbled" is ἐταπείνωσεν (etapeinōsen), from ταπεινόω (tapeinoō), meaning to humble or bring low.
Consider the contrast.
One king would not bow.
The true King humbled Himself.
One king clung to earthly power.
The King of kings accepted a crown of thorns.
One king brought suffering upon others through his rebellion.
Jesus willingly bore suffering to redeem those who had rebelled against God.
And at Calvary, we encounter another profound mystery of divine sovereignty and human responsibility.
Acts 2:23 declares that Jesus was delivered according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge, yet was crucified by lawless human hands.
God's saving purpose was being accomplished.
The human beings who committed evil were still responsible.
The cross did not make their wrongdoing righteous.
But their wrongdoing could not defeat God's redemptive plan.
Do you see it?
The same Bible that refuses to remove God's sovereignty from Pharaoh's story refuses to remove God's sovereignty from the crucifixion.
And the same Bible that holds Pharaoh accountable also holds those who crucified Jesus accountable.
Yet the cross reveals something Pharaoh's story alone cannot fully show us.
The God who judges evil is also the God who has provided salvation for sinners through His Son.
He is not indifferent to injustice.
He is not indifferent to rebellion.
And He is not indifferent to the brokenhearted sinner who cries out for mercy.
At the cross, God's holiness and love are not enemies.
His justice and mercy are not competing personalities.
Romans 3:26 presents God as both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin never mattered.
Not that God stopped being holy.
Not that judgment was imaginary.
But that Jesus Christ gave Himself for sinners, died, and rose again, so that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Maybe you have been fighting the same sin for years.
Maybe you have ignored conviction so many times that you are frightened by how little you feel.
Maybe you once wept during worship, but now you sit through sermons without being moved.
Maybe your Bible has been closed for months.
Maybe you have learned how to appear spiritually healthy while privately feeling exhausted, ashamed, or distant from God.
Listen carefully.
Do not confuse the warning about a hardened heart with a declaration that you are beyond grace.
Pharaoh's story was written to reveal God's power and purposes, not to give every struggling believer a reason to despair.
The very Scriptures that warn us against hardening our hearts also call us to turn to the Lord.
God says in Ezekiel 36:26:
"A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh."
In Hebrew, the phrase for "heart of stone" is לֵב הָאֶבֶן (lev ha'even), contrasted with לֵב בָּשָׂר (lev basar), a "heart of flesh."
The picture is extraordinary.
A heart that is unresponsive.
A heart that has become spiritually resistant.
A heart that cannot make itself alive by merely pretending to feel something.
And God promises renewal.

In its original setting, Ezekiel's promise concerns God's restoration of His people and the transforming work of His Spirit. Christians understand this promised renewal in light of the new covenant accomplished through Jesus Christ.
It is not a promise that every stubborn person will automatically repent without faith.
But it is a glorious declaration that the God who commands repentance is also the God who can transform the human heart.
You cannot purchase that transformation.
You cannot earn it through religious performance.
You cannot manufacture it by crying hard enough.
You come to Christ in repentance and faith.
You confess your sin.
You stop defending what God calls evil.
You trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And you ask Him to do what you cannot do for yourself.
Make my heart tender again.
Teach me to love what is holy.
Help me surrender what I have been protecting.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
"...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."
What an extraordinary promise.
The Savior does not tell the repentant sinner to return after becoming worthy.
He welcomes those who come to Him.
That does not make repentance optional.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
Because grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings us to Christ and teaches us to turn from ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
And if you are reading this while carrying shame over your past, remember something.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The Gospel does not say your choices have no consequences.
It says your past does not have to be the final word over your future in Christ.
The Gospel does not say that repentance is painless.
It says the mercy of God is worth surrendering everything for.
And maybe that is why this story has reached you today.
Not so you can spend another hour speculating about Pharaoh while avoiding the condition of your own heart.
But so you can ask a question that matters more personally than any theological debate.
Where am I resisting God?
What have I continued defending even though His Word has exposed it?
Whose forgiveness have I refused to seek?
What secret sin have I made peace with?
What part of my life still carries a sign that says, "Jesus, You may enter everywhere except here"?
Be careful with that last room.
Not because Christ is powerless.
But because surrendering to Him is not supposed to be a ceremonial gesture.
He is Lord.
Not merely an emergency contact.
Not merely a source of comfort when life collapses.
Not merely someone whose name we mention while continuing to govern ourselves.
He is the crucified and risen Savior, worthy of our faith, love, worship, and obedience.
And here is a truth we should never forget.
God's judgment on Pharaoh was not proof that God had forgotten mercy.
It was part of His deliverance of an oppressed people.
And God's mercy toward sinners today is not proof that He has forgotten justice.
It is a call to receive the salvation provided in Jesus Christ.
The Exodus points forward to a greater redemption.
At Passover, Israel's households were marked by the blood of the lamb, according to God's instructions.
In the New Testament, Paul declares:
"For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us."
—1 Corinthians 5:7, KJV
The connection is not accidental.
The Exodus revealed God's power to deliver His people from slavery.
The death and resurrection of Christ accomplish the greater redemption from sin and its condemnation.
And in Christ, the invitation extends beyond one nation.
People from every tribe, language, and nation are called to repent and believe the Gospel.
So when you look at Pharaoh, do not merely ask why God hardened a king's heart.
Ask what the Lord is teaching us about the seriousness of rebellion, the certainty of His purposes, the justice of His judgments, and the greatness of His mercy.
And when you look at Jesus, remember that the final answer to your need for salvation is not found in your ability to explain every mystery.
It is found in the One who died and rose again.
There are mysteries in Scripture we must approach with humility.
There are truths we must proclaim with confidence.
And there are commands we must not postpone.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Jesus.
Don't underestimate what God can do through a sincere testimony.
Someone may be reading in silence.
Someone may have wandered from the faith.
Someone may be one difficult night away from giving up on prayer.
Someone may be wrestling with the same questions about God's justice that brought you to this article.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown lukewarm, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along.
There is room here for sincere questions.
There is room for biblical correction.
There is room for testimony.
And there is always a reason to point one another back to Christ.
Not merely to publish articles that people read once and forget.
But to help people develop a deeper love for Scripture, a stronger understanding of the Gospel, and a more faithful walk with Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment accessible to more people.
It is a voluntary way to help sustain and expand the work of sharing biblical teaching, developing discipleship resources, and reaching people who may never otherwise encounter these messages.
But we want to be clear about something important.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"...for God loveth a cheerful giver."
We would never want anyone to feel that God's favor can be purchased through a monthly payment.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not through financial support of any ministry.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus Christ is.
Your soul is not a sales opportunity.
You are someone Christ calls to repentance, faith, and new life.
A sincere share can reach a person we may never meet.
A thoughtful comment can begin a conversation that someone has been afraid to start.
A faithful testimony can remind another believer that the grace of Jesus Christ is still transforming lives.
And a prayer offered in secret is never insignificant to the God who sees.
But before you leave, return with me to Egypt one final time.
Picture Pharaoh standing in his palace.
He has witnessed warnings.
He has seen signs.
He has experienced the consequences of his rebellion.
He has heard the command of the living God.
And still he refuses to bow.
Now picture another King.
Not surrounded by Egyptian wealth.
Not demanding that the suffering serve His comfort.
But hanging on a Roman cross.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Rejected.
Giving Himself for sinners.
The contrast is almost unbearable.
One king would rather see his kingdom suffer than surrender his pride.
The other King willingly suffered to redeem those who could never save themselves.
And that is where the story leaves us.
Not with a complete explanation of every hidden purpose of God.
But with a revelation of the kind of Savior we have been given.
The question is no longer only, "Why did God harden Pharaoh's heart?"
It is also, "What am I doing with the mercy God has revealed in Jesus Christ?"
Because the most important response to the mystery of Pharaoh is not arrogance toward God.
It is humility before Him.
It is repentance.
It is faith.
It is worship.
It is surrender.
And perhaps, for someone reading this right now, it is finally time to stop running.
You do not need to pretend your sin is small.
You do not need to pretend your wounds are healed.
You do not need to pretend you understand everything.
Come to Jesus Christ.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the guilt.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the heart you have been afraid to examine.
And trust the Savior who receives repentant sinners and makes all things new.
Pharaoh's tragedy was a heart that would not bow before God; your hope is the Savior who humbled Himself to bring sinners home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID JESUS REALLY DECLARE ALL FOODS CLEAN? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU SEE GOD, HOLINESS, AND GRACE
paragraphs: DID JESUS REALLY DECLARE ALL FOODS CLEAN? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU SEE GOD, HOLINESS, AND GRACE

For centuries, Christians have wrestled with one uncomfortable question: If God once called certain foods unclean, why do millions of believers eat them today? Did God's standards change? Did Jesus abolish His Father's commandments? Or have we been missing something far greater than what is on our plates? The answer takes us from the holiness laws of ancient Israel to a rooftop vision, a divided dinner table, and the bloodstained cross where Jesus changed everything.
There is a question that can turn an ordinary Christian dinner into a theological battlefield.
Someone reaches for a piece of pork.
Another believer quietly shakes his head.
“You know the Bible says that's unclean, right?”
The first Christian smiles.
“But Jesus made all foods clean.”
Then comes the question neither of them expected.
“So was God wrong when He forbade it in the first place?”
Suddenly, nobody is talking about dinner anymore.
They're talking about the character of God.
The authority of Scripture.
The meaning of obedience.
And whether Christians have misunderstood something that God took seriously enough to put into His written Law.
Perhaps you've been there.
Maybe you grew up believing that eating pork, shrimp, or shellfish was sinful. Maybe someone warned you that Christians who eat those things are deliberately disobeying God.
Or perhaps you were taught that the Old Testament dietary laws no longer apply, but nobody ever explained why.
You simply heard, “We're under grace now.”
And somewhere inside, a question remained.
Does grace mean God stopped caring about holiness?
Before you answer, consider something that might challenge both sides of this debate.
The God who gave Leviticus 11 is the same God who sent Jesus Christ.
He did not become wiser.
He did not discover a mistake in His earlier commandments.
He did not change from a strict Father into a forgiving Son.
And Jesus did not come to rescue humanity from a Father whose laws were unreasonable.
The Father and the Son are united in holiness, truth, and love.
So if we want to understand whether Christians should follow the Old Testament dietary laws today, we cannot begin with our appetites, traditions, or denominational loyalties.
We must begin with Scripture.
And we must be willing to follow the truth even when it challenges what we've always believed.
Because the real question is not merely what a Christian is permitted to eat.
The deeper question is whether we understand what Jesus accomplished.
Travel back thousands of years.
Imagine standing among the Israelites after their deliverance from Egypt.
These were not ordinary circumstances.
They were a people whom God had rescued from slavery, brought into covenant with Himself, and called to live differently from the surrounding nations.
Their worship was different.
Their sacrifices were different.
Their calendar was different.
Even their meals were different.
In Leviticus 11, God identified animals that Israel could eat and animals that were to be regarded as unclean.
Land animals generally needed to both chew the cud and have divided hooves. Aquatic creatures needed fins and scales. Other categories of animals were addressed through additional distinctions.
The pig, for example, had a divided hoof but did not chew the cud.
Therefore, Israel was forbidden to eat it.
Leviticus 11:7–8 identifies the pig as unclean and commands Israel not to eat its flesh.
But notice something important.
God did not present these instructions as arbitrary culinary preferences.
He connected them to His holiness.
In Leviticus 11:44, the Hebrew text declares:
כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אָנִי
Ki ani Adonai Eloheikhem, vehitqaddishtem vihyitem qedoshim ki qadosh ani.
“For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy.” — Leviticus 11:44, KJV
The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh) means holy, carrying the idea of being set apart.
And that changes how we understand the passage.
Israel's dietary laws were part of a larger covenant life in which God's people were taught to distinguish between holy and common, clean and unclean.
Even ordinary activities became reminders that they belonged to the LORD.
Their food was not merely food.
It was part of their covenant identity.
And we should never mock that.
We should never speak as though God's commandments were foolish or meaningless.
The Law was holy, righteous, and good, as Paul affirms in Romans 7:12.
But now comes the question that changes the entire conversation.
If these commandments were good, why don't most Christians observe them today?
To understand that, we must distinguish between God's unchanging holiness and the particular covenant obligations He gave to Israel.
Not every command God gave to a particular person or people was intended to function as an identical obligation for every believer in every era.
God commanded Noah to build an ark.
That command was righteous.
But faithfulness to God today does not require every Christian to construct a wooden vessel.
God commanded Israel to offer sacrifices through the priestly system.
Those commands were divinely given.
Yet Christians do not continue offering animals for the forgiveness of sins because Jesus Christ fulfilled what those sacrifices anticipated.
Hebrews 10 explains that the sacrifices under the Law pointed toward the once-for-all offering of Christ.
The issue is not whether God was right to command something.
The issue is how that command functions within the unfolding story of redemption.
And that story leads directly to Jesus.
Picture Him surrounded by religious leaders.
They are watching His disciples.
Not because the disciples have committed some spectacular crime.
But because they are eating with hands that have not undergone the customary ritual washing.
This is the setting of Mark 7.
The immediate controversy is not about someone eating pork.
It concerns ritual purity traditions and the accusation that Jesus' disciples were eating with defiled hands.
That distinction matters enormously.
Jesus confronts religious hypocrisy, exposing how human traditions can be elevated above God's commandments.
Then He teaches something that reaches deeper than the controversy itself.
In Mark 7:18–19, Jesus explains that what enters a person from outside does not enter the heart but the stomach and then passes out.
Mark adds a significant explanatory statement.
The Greek reads:
καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα
Katharizōn panta ta brōmata.
Commonly understood in context as:
“Thus he declared all foods clean.” — Mark 7:19, ESV
The Greek word katharizōn comes from a verb meaning to cleanse or make clean.
The phrase panta ta brōmata means “all foods.”
This passage deserves careful handling.
The original Greek does not contain a separate verb meaning “declared” in this phrase. The ESV's wording expresses an interpretive understanding of Mark's grammatical construction.
Many modern translations understand Mark to be explaining the implications of Jesus' teaching: that all foods are clean.
Other interpreters understand the phrase differently, including as a reference to the digestive process.

And because Jesus' immediate dispute concerned ritual handwashing rather than a direct challenge about pork, Christians should acknowledge the contextual question instead of pretending there is no debate.
Nevertheless, Mark's Gospel presents a profound teaching about defilement.
Jesus redirects attention from external contamination to the moral corruption that proceeds from the human heart.
He says in Mark 7:21–23 that evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, envy, slander, pride, and foolishness come from within.
These things defile a person.
Read that again.
Jesus is not minimizing sin.
He is exposing its true depth.
A man can refuse every forbidden food and still destroy his marriage through adultery.
A woman can carefully observe dietary restrictions while secretly nurturing bitterness and hatred.
A religious leader can maintain an immaculate table while exploiting the poor.
Someone can spend years inspecting ingredients and never once seriously examine the cruelty coming out of their mouth.
And suddenly the question becomes painfully personal.
What good is a carefully guarded plate if the heart remains surrendered to sin?
Jesus is not teaching that outward obedience never matters.
He is teaching that external religious observance cannot substitute for a heart transformed by God.
And this is where the story begins to move beyond the dinner table.
Because there was another man who had spent his entire life honoring the dietary boundaries of Israel.
His name was Peter.
And one day, God interrupted everything he thought he understood.
Acts 10 tells us that Peter went onto a rooftop to pray.
He became hungry.
While food was being prepared, he fell into a trance and saw heaven opened.
Something like a large sheet descended, containing various kinds of animals.
Then came a command.
“Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” — Acts 10:13, KJV
Peter resisted.
“Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” — Acts 10:14, KJV
Imagine that moment.
Peter had walked with Jesus.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed the resurrection.
Yet he still regarded the eating of common or unclean things as unacceptable.
This detail reminds us that the early church's understanding of the implications of Christ's work developed as God revealed His purposes more fully.
Then the voice spoke again.
“What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” — Acts 10:15, KJV
The event occurred three times.
But before anyone uses this passage as a quick answer to every dietary question, we must listen to Peter's own explanation.
Because Acts 10 is not primarily a story about Peter discovering a new menu.
It is about God breaking through a barrier between Jews and Gentiles.
The Holy Spirit was preparing Peter to enter the home of Cornelius, a Gentile.
In Acts 10:28, Peter explains the meaning he had come to understand:
“God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.” — KJV
There it is.
The vision's explicit application concerns people.
Gentiles were not to be treated as spiritually untouchable outsiders whom God could never welcome.
Through Jesus Christ, God was bringing the good news to the nations.
Peter later witnessed the Holy Spirit fall upon Gentile believers.
And the Jewish believers who accompanied him were astonished.
Why?
Because God's saving grace was reaching people they had not expected to receive it in this way.
The sheet was not merely a lesson about animals.
It was part of a revelation about the expanding family of God.
This means we should not claim that Acts 10, by itself, is a straightforward announcement abolishing every dietary restriction.
That goes beyond Peter's stated interpretation.
But neither should we ignore the wider New Testament teaching about food, covenant identity, and the inclusion of Gentiles.
And that brings us to a moment when the early church faced an explosive question.
Must Gentile believers come under the Law of Moses to belong fully to God's people?
The disagreement was so serious that the apostles and elders gathered in Jerusalem.
Acts 15 records their deliberation.
Some argued that Gentile believers should be circumcised and commanded to keep the Law of Moses.
But Peter reminded the assembly that salvation comes through the grace of the Lord Jesus.
Then the church issued instructions to Gentile believers.
They were to abstain from things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, what had been strangled, and blood.
Notice what the apostles did not do.
They did not command Gentile converts to adopt the entire dietary system of Leviticus 11.
That omission is significant.
Yet we must also be accurate.

Acts 15 does not mean the apostles believed food-related conduct was entirely irrelevant. The instructions concerning blood, strangled animals, and idol-related food show that the church still addressed dietary practices in its communal life.
Christians differ on how those instructions apply today, particularly regarding their continuing force and their relationship to Jewish-Gentile fellowship.
But the central conclusion is unmistakable.
Gentile believers were not required to become Jewish proselytes and observe the whole Mosaic Law in order to be saved or accepted as God's people.
Salvation was not obtained through a change of diet.
It was received through the grace of Jesus Christ.
And Paul would later make this truth even clearer.
In Romans 14, he addresses believers who differ over food and special days.
Some eat freely.
Others abstain because of conscience.
Paul does not tell the stronger believer to mock the weaker.
He does not tell the abstaining believer to condemn the one who eats.
Instead, he calls both to honor the Lord.
Romans 14:3 says:
“Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him.” — KJV
That last phrase is extraordinary.
For God hath received him.
Not because his plate satisfied the judgment of every Christian around him.
Not because he successfully defended his position in a theological argument.
But because he belonged to the Lord.
Romans 14:14 records Paul's conviction that nothing is unclean in itself, while recognizing that a person who regards something as unclean must take that conscience seriously.
Romans 14:20 likewise says that all things are indeed pure, while warning against using food in a way that causes another believer to stumble.
The passage is not permission to disregard conscience.
It is a call to let love govern liberty.
And in Romans 14:17, Paul gives us a sentence that deserves to be written across every Christian argument about food:
“For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.” — KJV
Think about how much unnecessary pain might have been avoided if Christians had remembered that.
Families divided over food.
Believers accusing one another of rebellion.
New converts frightened into thinking they could lose God's acceptance through an unfamiliar meal.
Others arrogantly ridiculing Christians whose consciences remain sensitive about what they eat.
And all the while, Scripture is calling us to something higher.
Righteousness.
Peace.
Joy in the Holy Spirit.
The same apostle writes in Colossians 2:16–17:
Paul's language of shadow and substance points us toward the fulfillment found in Christ.
This does not make the Old Testament worthless.
Quite the opposite.
A shadow can reveal something about the reality toward which it points.
But when the reality arrives, we must not confuse the shadow with the Savior.
The Law reveals God's holiness.
The sacrificial system anticipates redemption.
Israel's covenant distinctions help us understand the extraordinary significance of God bringing the nations together in Christ.
And Jesus stands at the center of the entire story.
He said in Matthew 5:17:
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.” — KJV
That word fulfil matters.
The Greek verb is πληρόω (plēroō), which can mean to fill, complete, or bring to fulfillment.
Jesus did not come to treat the Scriptures as meaningless.
He came to bring God's redemptive purposes to their intended fulfillment.
And the New Testament explains that Christ's work establishes a new covenant.
Hebrews 8:13 speaks of the first covenant becoming obsolete in light of the new.
Ephesians 2:14–16 describes Christ breaking down the dividing wall of hostility and creating one new humanity through His cross.
The question, therefore, is not whether Christians should despise the Law.
Never.
The question is whether the Mosaic covenant's dietary restrictions remain binding requirements for Christians living under the new covenant.

The mainstream Christian understanding, supported by Mark 7, Acts 15, Romans 14, Colossians 2, and the New Testament's teaching about the new covenant, is that Christians are not required to observe the clean-and-unclean animal distinctions of Leviticus 11.
That conclusion does not mean every Christian tradition agrees.

Some Seventh-day Adventists, Messianic Jewish believers, and other Torah-observant Christians continue to abstain from foods classified as unclean in Leviticus 11, though their theological reasons and interpretations differ.
Some understand the distinctions as continuing divine instructions.
Others emphasize health, identity, tradition, or conscience.
Their convictions should be represented fairly.
And Christians who disagree should still treat one another with dignity.
But no Christian should confuse dietary observance with the saving work of Jesus Christ.
We are not justified by what we eat or refuse to eat.
We are justified through faith in Christ, not through works of the Law, as Paul teaches in Galatians 2:16.
And now, perhaps, we are ready to answer the question that brought us here.
Should Christians follow the Old Testament dietary laws today?
Christians may choose to observe those dietary restrictions as a matter of conscience, personal discipline, cultural practice, or religious conviction.
But under the New Testament's teaching about Christ and the new covenant, observance of Leviticus 11 is not a universal requirement for Christian salvation or holiness.
A Christian who abstains from pork out of sincere conviction should not be mocked.
A Christian who eats pork with thanksgiving to God should not automatically be condemned as disobedient.
Both are accountable to Christ.
Both must act in faith.
Both must love their neighbors.
And neither may use food as a substitute for the righteousness that comes through Jesus.
There are, of course, other legitimate reasons to avoid particular foods.
Medical conditions.
Allergies.
Health concerns.
Personal discipline.
Cultural sensitivities.
Concern for another believer's conscience.
Christian freedom is not a command to eat everything.
Nor is it permission to act selfishly.
Paul reminds us in 1 Corinthians 10:31:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.” — KJV
And that is where the matter becomes deeply personal.
Because some of us have spent years asking whether our food is acceptable to God while avoiding questions about our conduct.
We want to know whether shrimp is forbidden.
But are we willing to confront the gossip we spread?
We debate whether pork is unclean.
But what about the pornography we keep returning to?
We inspect the ingredients of our meals.
But when was the last time we inspected the bitterness we carry toward someone who hurt us?
We argue over religious traditions.
But do we forgive?
Do we tell the truth when lying would benefit us?
Do we love people who cannot repay us?
Do we care about the poor?
Do we repent when the Holy Spirit convicts us?
These questions do not make dietary convictions meaningless.
They expose the danger of using external observance to hide internal rebellion.
And Jesus knows the difference.
He knows when obedience comes from love.
He knows when religion becomes a performance.
He knows when we are more interested in winning an argument than surrendering our hearts.
And He knows the sins we have managed to conceal behind a respectable Christian appearance.
Maybe that's the uncomfortable part of this article.
You came expecting an answer about food.
But Scripture has brought you face-to-face with your own heart.
And perhaps the most important question is no longer whether you should eat something.
Perhaps it is whether you have truly surrendered everything to Christ.
Because the tragedy of religious pride is that it can make us feel clean while leaving us spiritually empty.
You can know Hebrew.
You can quote Greek.
You can defend your doctrine.
You can avoid every forbidden ingredient.
And still desperately need the mercy of Jesus.
So can the Christian who proudly celebrates freedom while secretly living in sin.
Both need the same Savior.
Both need the same cross.
Both need the same grace.
And this is why the Gospel is so much greater than a religious food debate.
We were not saved because we finally learned the correct dietary interpretation.
We were saved because the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The cross did not make sin acceptable.
It revealed how serious sin truly is.
And the resurrection declared that death would not have the final word.
Through repentance and faith in Christ, guilty people can receive forgiveness.
The spiritually dead can receive new life.
The ashamed can find mercy.
The rebellious can be reconciled to God.
The outsider can be welcomed into God's family.
And the person who has spent years trying to earn divine acceptance can finally discover that salvation is God's gift of grace.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — KJV
But don't stop at verse 9.
Verse 10 reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave us unchanged.
It transforms the way we live.
It teaches us to reject ungodliness.
It moves us toward holiness.
It produces gratitude, obedience, humility, generosity, and love.
We do not obey to purchase salvation.
