It is refusing to claim more certainty than Scripture itself provides on a disputed question.
And here is another truth that deserves to be heard.
Not all evolution-related claims carry the same scientific meaning.
Changes within populations, adaptation, genetic inheritance, speciation, and large-scale common ancestry are connected but distinguishable subjects.
Evolutionary biology is a mature scientific field supported by extensive evidence from genetics, comparative anatomy, biogeography, observed evolutionary change, and the fossil record.
Scientists continue investigating its details, mechanisms, rates, and historical pathways.
But ongoing scientific debate about details should not be confused with the claim that the entire field lacks evidence.
Likewise, questions about the first origin of life are not identical to questions about evolution after life exists.
A Christian should be free to examine the evidence without feeling compelled to misrepresent it.
Truth does not become the enemy of faith simply because it challenges an inherited interpretation.

Yet scientific explanations should also be examined without assuming that methodological descriptions of natural processes establish philosophical naturalism—the belief that nature is all that exists.
Science investigates the natural world through testable explanations.
It does not possess a laboratory instrument capable of measuring God's existence or nonexistence.
The Christian conviction that God is Creator is a theological and metaphysical claim grounded in divine revelation, not a competing laboratory measurement.
This is why Christians have developed several approaches to Genesis and biological origins.
Some hold to young-earth creationism, understanding the creation days as ordinary days and the earth as relatively young.
Others affirm an ancient earth while rejecting universal common ancestry or maintaining special creation of particular kinds of organisms.
Others accept evolutionary creation, sometimes called theistic evolution, believing God providentially created through evolutionary processes.
These perspectives involve important differences in biblical interpretation and scientific judgment.
They cannot all be correct in every detail.
But we should evaluate them fairly rather than relying on caricatures.
And we must remember that Christians have wrestled with the literary and theological interpretation of Genesis long before Darwin.

Augustine, for example, did not simply treat the creation days as an ordinary sequence of twenty-four-hour periods. His interpretation was not modern evolutionary theory, and it would be misleading to claim that he anticipated Darwin.
Nevertheless, his writings demonstrate that Christian reflection on Genesis has never been confined to only one interpretive approach.
The historical Christian tradition contains both conviction and interpretive diversity.
So can a Christian believe in evolution while affirming God as Creator?
Yes—if by evolution we mean the scientific account of biological development, rather than a worldview that denies God, divine purpose, human dignity, sin, or the necessity of Christ.

There are Christians who sincerely accept evolutionary biology while affirming the authority of Scripture, the doctrine of creation, the image of God, humanity's sinfulness, the deity of Christ, His atoning death, and His bodily resurrection.
That does not mean every evolutionary interpretation is biblically sound.
Nor does it mean all Christian traditions agree that evolutionary creation is compatible with their doctrinal commitments.
Some Christian churches and theologians maintain that certain evolutionary accounts conflict fundamentally with the historical teaching of Genesis and Paul.
Those objections deserve serious engagement.
And Christians who accept evolution still bear the responsibility of explaining how their understanding coheres with the full testimony of Scripture.
The Christian answer cannot be, "Science has spoken, so the Bible must be silenced."
Neither should it be, "My interpretation cannot possibly be questioned, so evidence must be ignored."
The better response is humility before God's revelation and honesty before God's creation.
And if you are struggling with this, I want you to hear something.
You do not have to pretend that difficult questions are easy.
You do not have to manufacture certainty where you have not yet reached conviction.
You do not have to insult scientists to defend Christ.
You do not have to mock sincere believers who interpret Genesis differently.
And you do not have to abandon Jesus because a scientific discovery challenges something you were once taught about the Bible.
But you must also be willing to let Scripture correct you.
You must distinguish the authority of God's Word from the authority of your own interpretation.
And you must never allow intellectual curiosity to become an excuse for spiritual indifference.
Because the danger is not simply believing the wrong thing about biological origins.
The danger is knowing about the Creator without knowing Him.
It is possible to win an argument about creation and lose sight of the cross.
It is possible to possess impressive knowledge and remain spiritually empty.
It is possible to defend Genesis 1 while refusing to obey the Lord revealed in John 1.
And it is possible to spend a lifetime studying the history of life while never surrendering your own life to Jesus Christ.
What a tragedy that would be.
To know so much about creation.
And remain a stranger to the Creator.
Perhaps you came into this article expecting a fight.
Perhaps you wanted ammunition against evolution.
Perhaps you wanted permission to dismiss Genesis.
Perhaps you hoped someone would finally tell you that your questions do not automatically disqualify you from being a Christian.
But the Gospel brings us to something deeper than winning an argument.
It brings us to a cross.
There, the sinless Son of God suffered for sinners.
There, human rebellion met divine mercy.
There, the One through whom all things were created gave Himself for the redemption of His people.
And three days later, the tomb was empty.
Not because humanity had finally discovered the perfect philosophy.
Not because we had solved every mystery of the natural world.
But because Jesus Christ conquered death.
And now the risen Lord calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek word often translated "repent" is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), as found in Mark 1:15.
It is a call to turn—to change one's mind and direction in response to God's reign and truth.
Biblical repentance is more than intellectual reconsideration.
It involves turning away from sin and turning toward God.
So whether you believe the earth is thousands of years old or billions...
Whether you understand the creation days as ordinary days or through another literary framework...
Whether you reject common ancestry or believe God providentially worked through evolutionary processes...
The call of Jesus remains.
Repent.
Believe.
Your view of evolution cannot wash away your sins.
Your knowledge of Hebrew cannot make you righteous.
Your ability to defend Genesis cannot purchase eternal life.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith, not by our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 declares.
And the Savior who offers that grace is the same Lord through whom all things were made.
That is the wonder of Christianity.
The Creator did not merely give us existence.
In Christ, He offers us redemption.
And perhaps that is the truth you needed most today.
Not an excuse to stop asking questions.
But a reason to keep seeking truth without running away from Jesus.

If this article has exposed an assumption you have never examined, challenged a fear you have carried quietly, or reminded you that Christ must remain at the center of your faith, I would love to hear from you.

And if you disagree with the conclusion, you are welcome here too. Tell us which passage of Scripture you believe is most important to this discussion and why. Let's reason together with humility, biblical conviction, and love.
Because the Church needs more than people who know how to win arguments.
We need disciples who know how to love the truth.
And one of the greatest gifts you can give another believer is permission to ask sincere questions without being humiliated for asking them.
Think about the Christian teenager who is afraid to speak in church because of what they learned in biology class.
Think about the university student who believes their only choices are intellectual dishonesty or abandoning Jesus.
Think about the parent who wants to raise children with both a deep love for Scripture and the courage to investigate God's world.
Think about the skeptic who has never heard a Christian discuss evolution without anger.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be living through that very struggle.
Because discipleship should never stop at the moment someone clicks "follow."
It should lead us deeper into God's Word.
Deeper into prayer.
Deeper into obedience.
Deeper into the kind of faith that remains anchored in Christ even when our understanding is tested.
That is why we are building Gospel Warrior as more than a place for inspirational posts.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for truth, including those who may not have the means to purchase books or study materials.
And if this ministry has helped you, there is another way you can participate in that mission.
Not because God needs your money.
Not because a payment can replace repentance, worship, generosity to your local church, or a life of obedience.
And certainly not because salvation or spiritual maturity can be purchased.
But because freely chosen generosity can be one meaningful way to glorify God by helping others hear and understand His Word.
Paul reminds believers in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not come from pressure or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.

You may consider that support part of your personal Christian giving, but it should not be confused with a biblically mandated tithe or treated as a replacement for your responsibilities to your local church.
The deeper reason is the mission.
More people encountering biblical truth.
More struggling believers receiving encouragement.
More seekers being invited to consider Jesus.
More disciples being equipped to stand firmly in Scripture.
And more opportunities for conversations like this one to reach people who may otherwise never hear them.
And please remember this.
The goal of Gospel Warrior is not to gather an audience around a personality.
It is to point people toward a Person.
Jesus Christ.
The One who was there before the beginning.
The One through whom creation exists.
The One who entered human history.
The One who carried our sins.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And the One who will remain Lord long after every scientific theory has been refined, every human argument has fallen silent, and every hidden thing has been brought into the light.
One day, you will no longer need to ask how everything began.
You will stand before the One in whom all things hold together.
And on that day, the most important question will not be whether you understood every mystery of creation.
It will be whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
So study carefully.
Ask courageously.
Read Scripture faithfully.
Listen humbly.
Repent sincerely.
Love generously.
And keep your eyes fixed upon Christ.
Because the greatest miracle is not merely that God brought life into existence.
It is that the holy Creator came to redeem sinners who had turned away from Him.
You may spend your whole life searching for the beginning of everything—but do not miss the Savior who can give your broken life a new beginning.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU'RE MARRIED… SO WHY ARE YOU STILL ATTRACTED TO SOMEONE ELSE? IS IT ALREADY SIN?
paragraphs: YOU'RE MARRIED… SO WHY ARE YOU STILL ATTRACTED TO SOMEONE ELSE? IS IT ALREADY SIN?

The uncomfortable truth about sexual attraction, secret desires, emotional affairs, and the battle between temptation and faithfulness. What Jesus actually taught may convict you more deeply than you expect—but it may also free you from guilt you were never meant to carry.
There is a kind of guilt that doesn't begin in a bedroom.
It begins with a glance.
Someone walks into the room. Maybe it's a coworker. Someone at church. An old friend you haven't seen in years. Someone who listens a little more carefully than your spouse has lately.
You notice their face.
Their smile.
Their voice.
And suddenly, something happens inside you that you never intended to happen.
You feel attracted.
Not just impressed by their appearance.
Sexually attracted.
And almost immediately, another thought follows.
I'm married. Why am I feeling this?
You look away.
You remember your wedding vows.
You remember standing before God, promising faithfulness to one person for the rest of your life.
And now you're wondering whether something has already gone terribly wrong in your heart.
Perhaps you've even whispered a prayer that sounded more like an apology.
"Lord, I'm sorry. I don't know why I felt that."
But here's where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
What if I told you that feeling sexual attraction toward someone other than your spouse is not automatically the same thing as committing sexual sin?
And what if I also told you that something which begins without sin can become spiritually destructive if you choose to entertain it?
Because there is a difference between noticing someone is attractive and deliberately turning that attraction into a private world of desire.
A difference between temptation and surrender.
A difference between an unwanted thought and a welcomed fantasy.
And a difference between being human and allowing your heart to become unfaithful.
Jesus spoke directly to this territory.
And His words are far more searching than most of us realize.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus says:
"You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart." (ESV)
Read that carefully.
Jesus didn't merely address the physical act of adultery.
He went deeper.
Into the place nobody else can see.
Into the imagination.
Into the hidden intentions of the heart.
Into the private decisions we make long before our bodies ever cross a boundary.
And this is where understanding the original language matters.
The Greek text of Matthew 5:28 includes these words:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn
The phrase conveys looking at a woman with the purpose of desiring or lusting after her.
The verb epithymeō means to desire or long for something. Depending on its context, that desire may be good or sinful.
For example, Jesus uses the same Greek verb when He says that He has earnestly desired to eat the Passover with His disciples in Luke 22:15.
So the word itself does not automatically mean sexual sin.
Context matters.
In Matthew 5, Jesus is confronting desire that violates the moral boundaries of faithfulness.
He is not teaching that every involuntary awareness of another person's attractiveness is equivalent to adultery.
He is exposing the deliberate, lustful intention that turns another human being into the object of forbidden sexual desire.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because some Christians are living under crushing guilt over feelings they never invited, while others are excusing desires they have deliberately cultivated.
And both need to hear the truth.
You may not be responsible for the first spark of attraction, but you are responsible for what you choose to do with it.
Imagine a married man who notices an attractive woman at work.
He recognizes that she's beautiful.
A moment of attraction passes through his mind.
He doesn't pursue it. He doesn't feed it. He doesn't begin imagining intimacy with her.
He returns his attention to his responsibilities.
Has he necessarily sinned simply because he experienced that initial attraction?
No.
Now imagine the same man beginning to look forward to seeing her.
He deliberately watches her.
He replays conversations.
He imagines what it would be like to kiss her.
He begins comparing her to his wife.
He tells himself that nothing is wrong because he hasn't physically touched anyone.
But slowly, privately, he is nurturing a relationship that exists inside his imagination.
The situation has changed.
The initial attraction may have been uninvited.
The cultivated lust is not.
And Jesus cares about that difference.
Because sin doesn't become harmless simply because it remains invisible.
Perhaps the most frightening affairs are the ones that begin long before two people ever touch.
They begin when someone starts protecting a desire that should have been surrendered.
They begin when an innocent conversation becomes a secret anticipation.
When an ordinary friendship becomes emotionally exclusive.
When you start sharing things with another person that you have stopped sharing with your spouse.
When you delete a message, not because it contains anything explicitly sexual, but because you know your spouse would be wounded by its meaning.
When you begin dressing differently because you hope one particular person will notice.
When their attention starts affecting your mood more than your spouse's affection.
And then comes the sentence that has excused countless dangerous situations:
"But nothing happened."
Nothing physical, perhaps.
But something may already be happening to your heart.
James 1:14–15 describes the progression with unsettling clarity:
"But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death." (ESV)
The original Greek uses the imagery of conception and birth.
Desire conceives.
Sin is born.
And sin, when fully grown, produces death.
James is not saying that every experience of temptation is itself a completed sin.
He is showing how sinful desire, when embraced and allowed to develop, becomes destructive.
Think about that.
Something can begin as a momentary attraction and eventually become a decision that devastates a marriage.
Not because attraction is irresistibly powerful.
But because what we repeatedly entertain can gradually reshape what we want.
And what we want can begin influencing what we choose.
This is why Scripture does not simply tell believers to avoid committing adultery.
It teaches us to guard the heart.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
"Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life." (ESV)
In Hebrew, the command begins with:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
Mikkol-mishmar netsor libbekha.
A natural rendering is, "Above all guarding, guard your heart."
The Hebrew verb natsar carries the sense of watching over, keeping, or preserving.
This isn't an invitation to live terrified of every thought that enters your mind.
It is a call to spiritual vigilance.
Because your heart is not a playground where every desire deserves permission to stay.
Some desires need to be confronted.
Some fantasies need to be abandoned.
Some conversations need boundaries.
And some relationships need distance—not because the other person is evil, but because you recognize the weakness of your own heart.
That isn't cowardice.
Sometimes that is wisdom.
But now I want to speak to the person who is quietly struggling with something deeper.
You love your spouse.
You really do.
You don't want an affair.
You don't want to destroy your family.
You don't want to dishonor Christ.
But lately, someone else has been making you feel something you haven't felt in a long time.
Seen.
Wanted.
Interesting.
Alive.
And the frightening part isn't merely that you find them attractive.
It's that you like how you feel when they're around.
Maybe your marriage has become painfully routine.
Maybe affection has diminished.
Maybe the two of you have been arguing for months.
Maybe your spouse is emotionally distant.
Maybe you are carrying loneliness that nobody knows about.
And then someone comes along who seems to notice everything your spouse has stopped noticing.
They laugh at your jokes.
They remember small details.
They ask how you're doing and actually wait for an answer.
And suddenly, you feel something stirring.
Please understand this.
Your loneliness may be real.
Your emotional needs may be legitimate.
Your marital pain may deserve serious attention.
But real pain does not make every possible response to that pain righteous.
You can be genuinely neglected and still be responsible for remaining faithful.
You can be deeply wounded and still be called to holiness.
You can need tenderness without seeking it through a relationship that violates your marriage covenant.
And you can acknowledge that your marriage needs help without making another person your emotional escape.

This doesn't mean every struggling marriage can be repaired by one spouse trying harder. Both spouses have responsibilities, and situations involving abuse require protection and appropriate support, not pressure to remain in danger.
But when the issue is emotional disconnection, the answer is not to secretly build intimacy somewhere else.
It is to bring the truth into the light and seek help where it is needed.
Sometimes the most courageous words a married person can speak are not romantic words to someone new.
They are difficult words to the person they already promised to love.
"I'm lonely."
"I miss us."
"We need help."
"I don't want us to keep drifting apart."
Those conversations may feel uncomfortable.
But uncomfortable honesty can protect a marriage from devastating secrecy.
And before you conclude that this teaching applies only to husbands, understand something important.
Jesus' teaching on the heart is not permission for men to police women while ignoring their own desires.
Nor does it excuse women from faithfulness.
The call to sexual holiness belongs to both husband and wife.
A woman can cultivate lust.
A man can cultivate lust.
Either spouse can begin an emotional affair.
Either spouse can justify secrecy.
And either spouse can repent.
God's standard is not based on gender.
It is rooted in covenant faithfulness.
But perhaps you're wondering about something else.
What if you're attracted to someone and the thought keeps returning even though you don't want it?
What if you try to dismiss the thought, but it comes back?
Does that mean you secretly want to sin?
Not necessarily.
An unwanted thought is not automatically an embraced desire.
A temptation that returns is not proof that you have surrendered to it.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
That doesn't mean Jesus experienced every specific temptation in precisely the same way every person does.
It means He truly faced temptation while remaining completely sinless.
And this establishes a crucial truth.
Temptation and sin are not identical.
Jesus never sinned.
Yet Jesus was tempted.
So a believer should not automatically treat the mere experience of temptation as evidence of moral failure.
What matters is how you respond.
Do you resist?
Do you deliberately feed the thought?
Do you seek opportunities to intensify the attraction?
Do you surrender it to God?
Or do you begin building your private life around it?
You may not control every thought that appears.
But you can learn, through the Spirit's help, to redirect your attention rather than repeatedly nourishing what you know is wrong.

And if unwanted thoughts become persistent and distressing, remember that repeatedly examining yourself for proof of sin can sometimes deepen anxiety rather than produce holiness. A trusted pastor or qualified mental health professional can help you distinguish genuine moral choices from intrusive thoughts.
God does not call His children to endless self-accusation.
He calls them to truth, repentance where repentance is needed, and freedom in Christ.
First Corinthians 10:13 reminds believers that God is faithful and provides a way to endure temptation.
But don't misunderstand that promise.
It doesn't mean temptation will always disappear immediately.
It means you are not required to surrender to it.
Sometimes the way of escape is looking away.
Sometimes it's ending a conversation.
Sometimes it's refusing to send the message.
Sometimes it's admitting to a trusted, mature believer that you're struggling.
Sometimes it's deleting an inappropriate connection.
Sometimes it's finally addressing the wounds inside your marriage.
And sometimes it's doing the painful, unglamorous work of rebuilding intimacy with the spouse you already have.
Because faithfulness is not simply the absence of adultery.
It is the continuing practice of honoring your covenant.
And that brings us to something we rarely discuss honestly.
Marriage does not magically eliminate your ability to recognize beauty in other people.
Your wedding vows did not erase your humanity.
They established a covenant governing what you do with your desires.
Genesis 2:24 describes marriage as a man leaving his father and mother, holding fast to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
The Hebrew expression:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
Vedavaq be'ishto
means "and he shall cling to" or "hold fast to his wife."
The verb davaq expresses attachment, holding fast, or cleaving.
Marriage is not merely a legal arrangement that restricts sexual activity.
It is a covenantal union that calls for enduring attachment and loyalty.
And loyalty becomes especially meaningful when alternatives appear attractive.
Think about it.
Faithfulness isn't proven only when nobody else interests you.
Faithfulness is demonstrated when you choose to honor your covenant even when temptation offers another direction.
Not because your spouse is the only attractive person in the world.
But because your spouse is the person to whom you have pledged marital faithfulness.
And those vows were never meant to be sustained by fleeting emotions alone.
They require love expressed through decisions.
Patience.
Sacrifice.
Forgiveness.
Self-control.
And sometimes the deliberate rejection of a desire that promises pleasure but threatens what is sacred.
Galatians 5:22–23 identifies self-control as part of the fruit of the Spirit.
The Greek word is:
ἐγκράτεια
Enkrateia.
It refers to self-mastery or self-control.
Not a cold, emotionless existence.
Not pretending temptation doesn't exist.
But a life increasingly shaped by the Holy Spirit rather than ruled by uncontrolled impulses.
This is important because the Christian answer to sexual temptation is not simply, "Try harder."
The Gospel calls us to something deeper.
A transformed life.
A renewed mind.
A heart increasingly surrendered to Christ.
You don't defeat sin merely by becoming more skilled at hiding it.
You confront sin by bringing it into the light and walking in the truth.
And now, perhaps, the most difficult question of all.
What if you've already crossed the line?
What if you've been fantasizing about someone for months?
What if you've been flirting?
What if you've exchanged messages you would never want your spouse to read?
What if an emotional attachment has already formed?
What if you've committed adultery?
Is there still hope?
Listen carefully.
Yes.
There is hope.
But hope is not the same as pretending nothing happened.
Grace is not permission to continue what Christ calls you to leave behind.
Forgiveness does not make deception righteous.
And repentance is more than feeling terrible after enjoying something you knew was wrong.
The Greek word commonly translated "repent" is:
μετανοέω
Metanoeō.
It means to repent, to change one's mind or thinking in a way that involves turning from sin.
Biblical repentance is not merely emotional regret.
It is a turning toward God that bears fruit in changed conduct.
And sometimes that turning requires painful decisions.
Ending an inappropriate relationship.
Stopping secret communication.
Seeking wise pastoral accountability.
Taking responsibility without blaming your spouse.
Addressing the damage caused by deception.
Accepting that rebuilding trust may take time.
If sexual infidelity has occurred, seeking appropriate professional and pastoral guidance can help you navigate truthful disclosure, health considerations, and the consequences responsibly.
Repentance cannot demand immediate forgiveness from the person you have wounded.
It cannot force trust to return on your preferred schedule.
And it cannot erase consequences simply because you are sorry.
But it can mark the beginning of a different life.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to make guilty people feel better.
He came to save sinners.
And the cross is where the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's mercy meet.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was publicly accused of adultery.
The crowd wanted condemnation.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of her accusers.
And when they departed, He said:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more." (John 8:11, ESV)

There is an important textual detail here: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, and many modern Bibles identify the passage as a later textual addition. For that reason, we should not build a doctrine on this account alone.
Yet the themes of mercy and repentance are firmly established elsewhere in Scripture.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
And 1 John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Grace does not deny sin.
Grace meets repentant sinners with the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
And that is where the Gospel becomes more than religious language.
Because maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret.
Maybe your marriage looks respectable from the outside.
Your children are doing well.
Your family photographs are beautiful.
You attend church.
You know the worship songs.
You smile when people ask how everything is going.
But privately, your heart has been divided.
You haven't told anyone.
You keep promising yourself you'll stop thinking about that person.
But you keep returning to the same conversations, the same fantasies, the same emotional escape.
And you're exhausted from pretending.
Or perhaps your struggle is the opposite.
You've been condemning yourself over every passing attraction, convinced that your marriage is already dishonored because you noticed someone beautiful.
You've confused being tempted with having surrendered.
And the guilt has become unbearable.
Whichever person you are, the answer begins in the same place.
Jesus Christ.
Not because every struggle is identical.
Not because every action carries the same guilt.
But because only Christ can give us the truth and grace we desperately need.
To the person living under unnecessary shame, He offers freedom from condemnation that Scripture does not require you to carry.
To the person deliberately cultivating lust, He calls you to repent.
To the person whose marriage is wounded, He calls you toward truth, wisdom, and whatever faithful steps are possible.
To the person who has fallen, He offers forgiveness through His finished work, not through denial or excuses.
And to every believer, He offers the transforming power of His Spirit.
You are not saved by having a flawless history of sexual thoughts.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
But the grace that saves us also trains us to reject ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 reminds us of that.
Grace does not merely pardon the past.
It teaches us how to live differently.
And perhaps this is what somebody needed to hear today.
Your attraction does not have to become your direction.
You can notice beauty without pursuing possession.
You can experience temptation without embracing lust.
You can acknowledge loneliness without betraying your covenant.
You can confront hidden sin without believing that your life is beyond redemption.
And you can choose faithfulness today, even if yesterday was a struggle.
Not because you're stronger than everyone else.
But because Jesus is worthy of your obedience.
Your spouse may never know every temptation you resisted.
Nobody may applaud the message you chose not to send.
Nobody may see you closing the application, walking away from the conversation, or praying through a moment of weakness.
There may be no audience.
No recognition.
No public testimony.
But those private choices matter.
And there is something profoundly beautiful about a person who chooses to honor God when nobody else is watching.
Perhaps you need to stop asking only, "How far can I go before it becomes sin?"
And begin asking, "How can I honor Christ with my heart, my body, my marriage, and my choices?"
That question changes everything.
Because the goal of Christian marriage is not merely to avoid a scandal.
It is to reflect covenant love through faithfulness, forgiveness, sacrifice, and truth.
Ephesians 5:25 calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.
That is not a call to self-centered desire.
It is a call to sacrificial love.
And the broader passage calls believers to a life shaped by reverence for Christ.
Imagine what might change if married believers stopped treating fidelity as merely a rule against cheating and began seeing it as a daily expression of worship.
Imagine husbands who guard their hearts not because they fear being caught, but because they love Christ and their wives.
Imagine wives who pursue faithfulness not merely because society expects it, but because their covenant matters before God.
Imagine couples who admit when something is wrong before resentment becomes secrecy.
Who seek help before distance becomes betrayal.
Who pray together when they can.
Who learn to listen again.
Who stop measuring love only by emotional intensity and begin practicing the difficult, beautiful discipline of remaining present.
No marriage is perfect.
No spouse can meet every emotional need.
And marriage itself cannot replace the place that belongs to God.
But a marriage can become a place where two imperfect people learn, through grace, to love with increasing honesty and faithfulness.
That kind of love may not always feel cinematic.
Sometimes it looks like turning your phone off.
Sometimes it looks like apologizing.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth.
Sometimes it looks like counseling.
Sometimes it looks like holding your spouse's hand after a season of distance.
Sometimes it looks like choosing the person beside you instead of pursuing the fantasy in your mind.
And sometimes it looks like falling on your knees and saying:
"Jesus, my heart is not where it should be. I need You to change me."
That prayer is not weakness.
It may be the beginning of repentance.
And repentance is not the end of your story.
Through Jesus Christ, it can be the beginning of restoration.
If this article has exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to confess intimate details publicly to prove your sincerity. But you can take an honest first step.
Your words might encourage someone who thinks change is impossible.
There may be a husband reading this who needs to recognize the danger of a seemingly harmless attachment.
There may be a wife who needs reassurance that an unwanted attraction does not automatically make her an adulterer.
There may be a couple quietly drifting apart who need to begin an honest conversation tonight.
And there may be someone already caught in sin who needs to hear that Jesus still calls sinners to repentance and offers genuine forgiveness.
Not merely to spread a post.
But because biblical truth about temptation, marriage, repentance, and grace deserves to reach people who may never ask these questions out loud.
Not because every word needs to be remembered, but because the Scriptures discussed here may be worth returning to when your heart needs clarity.
And if you've been walking with Gospel Warrior for some time, I want to invite you into something deeper than reading another post and moving on.
Invite your spouse, family, friends, struggling believers, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow along.
Because discipleship should not end when an article ends.
It should continue in the ordinary decisions of everyday life.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their faith, understand the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Christ.
And I want to speak directly to those who believe this ministry is worth supporting.
Every article takes effort.
Every resource requires work.
Every effort to reach another struggling soul requires people who are willing to help carry the mission forward.

It is a voluntary act of support that can help sustain and expand this ministry's work of sharing Scripture, developing discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
But we must be clear about something important.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, not coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says that each person should give as they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You do not need to give money to earn His approval.
And your financial circumstances do not determine your value in God's Kingdom.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of faith and opportunities to encourage conversations about Jesus.
Christ is.
The mission is to point people toward His Word, His cross, His resurrection, His grace, and the transformation He brings.
Pray for this ministry.
Send it to someone who needs encouragement.
Make use of the free resources.
Your prayers, encouragement, and willingness to share biblical truth are genuinely valuable.
Thank you for helping us keep Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to those who need them.
And before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought you here.
Is it sinful to feel sexually attracted to someone other than your spouse?
Not automatically.
An initial, uninvited experience of attraction is not necessarily lust or adultery.
But deliberately nurturing forbidden sexual desire, pursuing an inappropriate relationship, or choosing to violate your marriage covenant is another matter entirely.
Jesus calls us beyond outward appearances into faithfulness of the heart.
And He does not leave us to pursue that faithfulness without His grace.
Maybe tonight, you need to stop entertaining a fantasy.
Maybe you need to establish a boundary.
Maybe you need to have a difficult conversation with your spouse.
Maybe you need to confess a sin and seek wise accountability.
Or maybe you need to stop condemning yourself for a temptation you resisted.
Whatever your situation, bring it honestly before Christ.
Don't hide behind religious appearances.
Don't excuse what Scripture calls sin.
Don't invent guilt where Scripture does not place it.
And don't believe that your failures are greater than the saving power of Jesus.
Because the cross tells us that sin is serious enough to require the death of our Savior.
And the empty tomb tells us that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Your marriage may have painful chapters.
Your heart may have battles nobody knows about.
Your past may contain decisions you wish you could undo.
But in Christ, repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is real.
Transformation is not an empty promise.
And while restoration in human relationships may be difficult, incomplete, or sometimes impossible, no repentant sinner is beyond the reach of God's mercy.
So guard your heart.
Honor your covenant.
Walk in the light.
And when you stumble, don't run farther into darkness.
Run to Jesus.
Because the temptation you refuse to feed today may become the testimony of faithfulness you thank God for tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE SOULMATE YOU'VE BEEN PRAYING FOR IS A PROMISE GOD NEVER MADE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE SOULMATE YOU'VE BEEN PRAYING FOR IS A PROMISE GOD NEVER MADE?
The heartbreaking truth about “the one,” unanswered prayers, waiting for love, and why Jesus never promised you a perfect soulmate—but offered you something infinitely greater.
There is a prayer that has been whispered into pillows soaked with tears.
“Lord, where is my person?”
Not a stranger. Not just someone to hold hands with on Sunday. Not another relationship that begins with beautiful promises and ends with another broken piece of your heart.
Someone who stays.

Someone who understands your silence. Someone who sees the scars you have spent years hiding and doesn't turn away. Someone who chooses you when life becomes difficult, when beauty fades, when money runs out, when the excitement of falling in love becomes the ordinary responsibility of remaining faithful.
Maybe you've prayed for that person for years.
You've watched friends get engaged. You've attended weddings where you smiled for photographs, congratulated the newlyweds, and returned home to an apartment that suddenly felt painfully quiet.
You've heard testimonies about how God brought two people together.
And somewhere between another wedding invitation and another unanswered prayer, a frightening question entered your heart.
“God, did You forget about me?”
But what if the deepest problem isn't that God has failed to send your soulmate?
What if someone taught you to expect a promise that Scripture never actually made?
And what if believing that promise has quietly caused you to question God's goodness, overlook warning signs, idolize marriage, or measure your worth by whether someone chooses you?
Stay with me, because what the Bible actually says about love may disappoint the fantasy you've been carrying.
But it could also set your heart free.
The Bible never promises that every Christian will discover one perfect soulmate.
Read that again.
Not because marriage is unimportant. Not because romance is sinful. Not because your longing to be loved is foolish.
But because there is a difference between something God calls good and something God promises to give every believer.
And confusing those two things can leave a sincere Christian heartbroken over an expectation God never placed upon it.
Genesis 2:18 records the Lord saying:
“It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.” (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the phrase translated “an help meet for him” is עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ — ʿezer kenegdô.
The word ʿezer means help or helper. It does not imply inferiority; the same Hebrew word is used elsewhere for the help God provides His people.
The expression kenegdô conveys the idea of someone corresponding to him, suitable for him, or standing as his counterpart.
God created Eve as a fitting partner for Adam.
This is a beautiful foundation for marriage.
But notice something essential.

Genesis 2 describes God's provision for the first man and establishes the goodness of human companionship and marriage. It does not declare that every person throughout history has one predetermined romantic counterpart whom they are guaranteed to find.
The passage gives us a theology of companionship.
It does not give us a universal promise of a soulmate.
And that distinction matters.
Because when you believe that God has promised you one perfect person, every failed relationship can begin to feel like a spiritual disaster.
Every rejection becomes a crisis of identity.
Every year of singleness becomes evidence that heaven is withholding something you were supposedly guaranteed.
You stop asking, “How can I faithfully follow Jesus in this season?”
And begin asking, “What is wrong with me that God hasn't given me what everyone else seems to have?”
That question can slowly poison your relationship with the very Savior who loves you.
But Scripture tells a different story.
Consider the apostle Paul.
Paul did not write about singleness as a shameful waiting room where incomplete Christians sit until marriage finally makes their lives meaningful.
He wrote:
“For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.” (1 Corinthians 7:7, KJV)
In the Greek text, the word translated “gift” is χάρισμα — charisma.
It refers to a gracious gift.
Paul recognized that believers receive different gifts and callings. He affirmed marriage as good while also recognizing the genuine value of remaining unmarried.
He continued:
“He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord.” (1 Corinthians 7:32, KJV)
Paul was not declaring married Christians less spiritual.
He was explaining that unmarried believers can experience particular freedoms for undivided service to Christ.
Think about that.
A man whose writings helped shape Christian understanding for centuries did not teach that every believer must find a spouse to fulfill God's purpose.
And Jesus Himself lived an unmarried earthly life.
The sinless Son of God.
Perfect in obedience. Perfect in love. Perfect in His humanity.
Yet never married.
If marriage were necessary to become a complete human being, what would that imply about Jesus?
The thought itself exposes the weakness of the soulmate myth.
Marriage is a good gift, but it is not the measure of a complete life.
Jesus is.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else tonight.
You are not half a person waiting for another half to arrive.
You are not spiritually defective because your wedding day hasn't come.
You are not less loved by God because nobody has placed a ring on your finger.
Your relationship status is not heaven's report card on your worth.
The cross has already revealed the immeasurable value of the grace God has extended to you.
But there is another side to this conversation, and it may be even more uncomfortable.
Some Christians are not merely waiting for a soulmate.
They are waiting for someone who will function like a savior.
Someone who will finally silence their insecurity.
Someone whose affection will erase childhood wounds.
Someone who will make them feel beautiful, chosen, protected, significant, and permanently safe.
And those desires often grow out of very real pain.
Maybe you grew up watching love disappear.
Maybe someone promised forever and abandoned you.
Maybe you were cheated on, manipulated, humiliated, or made to believe you were difficult to love.
So now you dream of meeting someone whose love will undo everything another person destroyed.
But even a faithful spouse cannot carry the weight of being your redeemer.
A husband cannot forgive your sins.
A wife cannot reconcile your soul to God.
A romantic relationship cannot provide the ultimate security that belongs to Christ alone.
Human love is precious.
But human love was never designed to replace divine love.
This is why Colossians 2:10 is so important:
“And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is ἐστὲ ἐν αὐτῷ πεπληρωμένοι — este en autō peplērōmenoi.
In context, Paul is declaring the spiritual fullness believers possess in Christ, not promising that Christians will never experience loneliness or emotional need.
That matters.
Being complete in Christ does not mean you never desire marriage.
It means marriage is not the source of your standing before God.
You can long for a spouse without making that spouse your god.
You can pray for companionship without treating singleness as a curse.
You can grieve a broken relationship without believing your future has been destroyed.
And you can be deeply loved by Jesus while still experiencing the very human ache of an empty chair beside you.
Faith does not require pretending loneliness never hurts.
Sometimes the most faithful prayer is simply:
“Lord, I trust You. But this is hard.”
And God is not offended by honest lament.
The Psalms are filled with people bringing their anguish before Him.
You do not have to disguise your tears to qualify for His compassion.
Now consider another phrase Christians often repeat:
“When you meet the one, you'll just know.”
Really?
Where does Scripture promise that?

The Bible certainly describes remarkable marriages and providential encounters. Isaac and Rebekah's story in Genesis 24 is one example of God's guidance within a particular family and covenant history.
But a descriptive biblical narrative is not automatically a promise that every Christian will experience the same circumstances.
Ruth and Boaz also have a beautiful story.
Yet Ruth's account includes widowhood, poverty, courage, loyalty, and difficult decisions. It is not simply a romantic formula for obtaining a spouse.
And neither story teaches that a person should ignore wisdom, character, or warning signs because a relationship feels destined.
In fact, one of the most dangerous consequences of the soulmate myth is how easily it can be used to excuse unhealthy relationships.
“He's my soulmate, so I have to endure whatever he does.”
“God showed me she's the one, so the warning signs don't matter.”
“We have such a powerful spiritual connection. Surely that means we're supposed to be together.”
But intensity is not the same as intimacy.
Chemistry is not character.
And a strong feeling is not automatically the voice of the Holy Spirit.
A person may know how to speak Christian language while refusing to practice Christian love.
They may quote Scripture while manipulating your conscience.
They may pray beautifully in public while treating you cruelly in private.
Please hear this.
God does not require you to surrender biblical wisdom in order to prove your faith in a romantic relationship.
First Corinthians 13:4–5 says:

“Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “charity” is ἀγάπη — agapē.
It means love, and in this passage Paul describes the character and conduct of love.

This passage is not exclusively about marriage. Its original context concerns love within the Christian community. Nevertheless, its teaching provides a powerful standard for how Christians should treat one another, including within marriage.
Love is patient.
Love is kind.
Love does not rejoice in wrongdoing.
And love does not become godly merely because someone attaches the phrase “God told me” to it.
If someone continually humiliates you, controls you, threatens you, or uses Scripture to silence you, do not confuse that behavior with biblical love.
Forgiveness is Christian.
But forgiveness does not require remaining in danger, pretending abuse is acceptable, or restoring trust without repentance and meaningful change.
The Gospel calls sinners to repentance.
It does not call victims to sanctify cruelty.
And perhaps that is the freedom someone needs today.
Not the freedom to find a soulmate.
But the freedom to stop calling a destructive relationship God's will.
Because sometimes the relationship you're afraid to lose is the very relationship that has taught you to forget who you are in Christ.
And still, Scripture does not ask us to become cynical about marriage.
Marriage is beautiful.
It is God's creation, not humanity's invention.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar ʾeḥad means “one flesh.”
This is covenantal union, not a claim that two people were previously incomplete fragments of one soul.
And in Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul connects marriage to a profound mystery concerning Christ and the Church.
Christian marriage is meant to reflect something beyond romantic fulfillment.
It points toward covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, and the relationship between Christ and His people.
That means the most important question in choosing a spouse is not simply:
“Does this person give me butterflies?”
But also:
“Can we honor Christ together?”
“Is there honesty when nobody is watching?”
“Does this person demonstrate humility and repentance?”
“Are we willing to forgive, serve, grow, and remain faithful through ordinary and difficult seasons?”
“Are we both pursuing Jesus rather than expecting each other to become Jesus?”
The Bible gives us principles for wise and godly relationships, not a guaranteed method for identifying one flawless romantic destiny.
And here is another truth that may challenge what you've been taught.
Even if you marry a wonderful Christian, you will not marry a perfect person.
Two redeemed sinners can build a beautiful covenant.
But they will still need grace.
There will be misunderstandings.
Exhausting days.
Unspoken expectations.
Disagreements about money.
Moments when affection feels easier than patience.
Seasons when love looks less like a romantic movie and more like choosing kindness when both people are tired.
A healthy marriage is not the discovery of someone who never disappoints you.
It is the faithful cultivation of covenant love between imperfect people who continue to need God's mercy.
And this is why the fantasy of a perfect soulmate can actually damage a good marriage.
If you believe your spouse was created to satisfy every emotional longing, normal disappointments may begin to feel like proof that you married the wrong person.
But perhaps you did not marry the wrong person.
Perhaps you married a human being.
Someone who needs the same grace you do.
Someone who cannot read your mind.
Someone whose sanctification, like yours, is still unfolding.
Christian marriage is not sustained by perfection.
It requires faithfulness, repentance, forgiveness, wisdom, and the continuing grace of God.

That does not mean every marriage is healthy or that every broken marriage can be repaired by one person's effort. Scripture recognizes serious covenant violations, and situations involving abuse require safety and wise intervention.
But it does mean that ordinary imperfection is not evidence that love has failed.
Sometimes real love begins to mature precisely when fantasy ends.
And now we come to a question that has broken many hearts.
“What if I never get married?”
Not everyone will.
Scripture does not hide that possibility.
In Matthew 19:12, Jesus speaks about those who remain unmarried for different reasons, including those who choose celibacy for the kingdom of heaven.
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul explicitly recognizes both marriage and singleness within Christian life.
There is no biblical promise that every believer who prays faithfully, waits patiently, and maintains sexual purity will eventually receive a spouse.
Purity is not a payment for marriage.
Prayer is not a transaction.
Obedience is not a vending machine where you insert faithfulness and receive a wedding ring.
And God is not indebted to us because we have waited.
That may be painful to hear.
Especially if you have been told, “Just keep believing. Your husband is coming.”
Or, “God wouldn't put the desire for marriage in your heart unless He planned to fulfill it.”
Those statements may be intended as encouragement.
But neither is a universal promise found in Scripture.
Psalm 37:4 says:
“Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.” (KJV)
Yet this verse belongs to a psalm about trusting God, refusing envy, committing one's way to Him, and waiting faithfully amid injustice.
It is not a blank check guaranteeing every personal desire exactly as imagined.
Delighting in the Lord changes our relationship with our desires. It does not make God a servant of our preferred timeline.
And Jeremiah 29:11, so often quoted as proof that a desired marriage must be coming, was originally spoken to God's people in exile concerning His purposes for their future restoration.
Its original context must not be erased to turn it into a personalized guarantee of romance.
God is faithful.
But we honor His faithfulness by trusting what He has actually promised.
Not by inventing promises and becoming angry when they are not fulfilled.
So what has He promised?
Jesus said:
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” (Hebrews 13:5, KJV)
Romans 8:38–39 declares that nothing in all creation can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
And John 6:37 records Jesus saying:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
These promises are not small consolation prizes for people who never find romantic love.
They are the foundation of eternal hope.
A spouse may walk beside you for decades.
Christ is your Savior forever.
A marriage may be a beautiful earthly covenant.
But the Gospel offers reconciliation with God Himself.
And this is where the story becomes even more astonishing.
Because the Bible does contain a love story greater than the search for a soulmate.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing sinners through the saving work of His Son.
Not because we were flawless.
Not because we were desirable by worldly standards.
Not because we had earned His affection.
But because of His mercy and grace.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
The Greek word συνίστησιν — synistēsin, translated here as “commendeth,” carries the sense of demonstrating or showing.
God demonstrates His love through Christ's death for sinners.
This is not romantic love.
It is something infinitely more consequential.
It is redemptive love.
Love that confronts sin rather than pretending it does not exist.
Love that does not abandon justice but satisfies it through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Love that calls us to repentance, faith, and new life.
And perhaps this is the most important correction we can make to the soulmate narrative.
The greatest love story in Scripture is not about finding the perfect person. It is about the perfect Savior redeeming imperfect people.
You may have a scandal in your past.
A relationship you regret.
A sexual sin you have tried to bury.
A divorce that still hurts.
A betrayal that left you questioning whether love can ever be trusted again.
Perhaps you stayed where you should have left.
Perhaps you wounded someone who trusted you.
Perhaps you crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you would never cross.
And now shame whispers:
“Who would want someone like you?”
But shame does not get the final word over a repentant sinner who comes to Jesus.
The cross does.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
And 2 Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
This does not erase every earthly consequence of our choices.
But it does announce the extraordinary reality of new life in Christ.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have authority to cancel the grace of God.
And the person who has been rejected by people can still be welcomed by Christ.
The person who has sinned can repent and be forgiven.
The person who has been abandoned can still discover that the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
The person who never marries can still live a life overflowing with purpose, friendship, service, holiness, and joy.
Because from scandal to grace is not merely the story of a broken romance becoming a happy marriage.
It is the story of a sinner being brought from death to life through Jesus Christ.
And that story does not require a wedding ring.
It requires a Savior.
Maybe you will marry someday.
Maybe the person God providentially brings into your life will be someone whose faithfulness, humility, kindness, and love make you thank Him every morning.
If so, receive that gift with gratitude.
But do not worship the gift.
Maybe you are already married and have spent years comparing your spouse to an imaginary perfect person.
If so, perhaps today is the day to repent of unrealistic expectations and begin practicing the patient, truthful, sacrificial love Scripture commands.
And maybe you are single, tired, and frightened that the years are passing too quickly.
You do not need another shallow assurance that your wedding is just around the corner.
You need something stronger than a prediction.
You need truth sturdy enough to hold you even if your circumstances do not change.
Here it is.
God's goodness is not measured by whether you get married.
Christ's sufficiency is not disproved by your loneliness.
And your usefulness in the kingdom of God is not postponed until someone chooses you.
You can serve now.
Grow now.
Love your neighbors now.
Build meaningful friendships now.
Pursue holiness now.
Participate in the life of the Church now.
Seek wise counsel, develop character, and remain open to marriage if that is your desire.
You do not have to choose between contentment and hope.
You can desire marriage deeply while refusing to make it the condition of your joy in Christ.
You can pray boldly without pretending you know God's answer.
And you can grieve honestly without surrendering your trust in Him.

There is a profound difference between saying, “Jesus, I will follow You once You give me the person I want,” and saying, “Jesus, I will follow You because You are worthy, whether or not that person ever comes.”
The second prayer is not easy.
Sometimes it must be prayed through tears.
But it is the prayer of a heart learning that Jesus is not merely the means to a better life.
He is life itself.
And one day, earthly marriage will no longer be the center of anyone's hope.
Jesus teaches in Matthew 22:30 that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage.
And Revelation 19:7–9 presents the glorious imagery of the marriage supper of the Lamb.
The ultimate fulfillment toward which Christian marriage points is not an endless earthly romance.
It is the consummation of Christ's relationship with His redeemed people.
The Church is described as the bride of Christ.
Not because Jesus is a romantic replacement for a human spouse, but because Scripture uses covenant marriage imagery to reveal His faithful, saving love for His people.
That is the greater story.
And it changes how we understand every lesser love.
So tonight, if you are still waiting, I want to leave you with something more valuable than the promise of a soulmate.
You are invited to trust a Savior who has already given Himself for sinners.
You are invited to surrender your fears, desires, regrets, and future to Him.
You are invited to stop measuring your life against engagement announcements and wedding photographs.
You are invited to believe that the God who raised Jesus from the dead is not powerless to sustain you in a season you never expected.
And if you have made romance an idol, you can repent.
If you have made marriage the condition of your obedience, you can surrender.
If you have placed unbearable expectations upon another human being, you can ask God to reshape your understanding of love.
If you have believed your singleness makes you worthless, you can reject that lie in light of the Gospel.
Not because everything will suddenly become easy.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust even in the unanswered places.
Perhaps the most courageous thing you will do after reading this is not download another dating app, search for another sign, or beg God to reveal the name of your future spouse.
Perhaps it will be to sit quietly before Him and say:

“Lord Jesus, I still desire to be loved by someone. I still hope for marriage. I still struggle when I see other people receiving what I have prayed for. But forgive me for treating a relationship as though it could save me. Teach me to seek You first. Give me wisdom if marriage comes, contentment and faithful purpose in every season, and courage to trust You with what I cannot control. Heal what has been wounded. Expose what needs repentance. And make my life a testimony of Your grace, whether I walk through it married or single. Amen.”
And if that prayer touched a place you have kept hidden, please don't feel pressured to pretend you're fine.
You don't need to reveal private details. Even a few honest words can open the door for another believer to encourage you, pray with you, and remind you that you are not alone in the body of Christ.

And if you are married, consider sharing what God has taught you about the difference between romantic expectations and faithful covenant love. Your testimony may help someone entering marriage with unrealistic expectations.
Not everyone who needs it will admit they are struggling.
Someone scrolling tonight may be questioning God's goodness because another relationship ended.
Someone may be preparing to marry a person whose character they have ignored because they believe they have found their destined soulmate.
Someone may be quietly wondering whether their unmarried life has any purpose at all.

Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those wrestling with their faith, and even those who do not yet know Christ to follow along. The Gospel is too important to keep confined to people who already agree with us.
There is also another way you can help this ministry continue.
Rather, it is one voluntary way to glorify Him through generosity by helping support the creation, continuation, and expansion of Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship resources.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, not coerced:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
Monthly supporters help sustain this work and make it possible to reach more people with biblical teaching, encouragement, and resources rooted in the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
We want the truth of Scripture to remain accessible, because the grace of God is not for sale.
The goal has never been merely to grow a page.
It is to see people come to know Jesus, turn from sin, receive His grace, grow in His Word, and walk faithfully with Him.
That is what matters.
And before you leave, remember the question that brought you here.
Does the Bible promise that every Christian will discover a perfect soulmate?
No.
But it reveals something far greater than the soulmate fantasy.
A perfect Savior who receives repentant sinners.
A faithful Lord who never abandons His people.
A Redeemer whose love is not dependent on your relationship status.
A King whose kingdom gives purpose to both marriage and singleness.
And a Gospel powerful enough to transform even the most painful chapters of your story.
You may never know what tomorrow will bring.
You may still desire marriage.
You may still cry over what has not happened.
But you do not have to wait for another human being to make your life worth living.
Because your deepest need was never a perfect soulmate.
It was reconciliation with God.
And Jesus Christ came to accomplish what no human relationship ever could.
You may spend years waiting for someone to choose you, but never let that waiting blind you to the Savior who gave His life to redeem you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID, “CALL NO MAN YOUR FATHER.” SO WHY DID PAUL CALL HIMSELF A SPIRITUAL FATHER?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “CALL NO MAN YOUR FATHER.” SO WHY DID PAUL CALL HIMSELF A SPIRITUAL FATHER?
One command from Jesus. One startling statement from Paul. And a question that could expose whether we are honoring spiritual leadership—or giving a human being the place that belongs to God alone.
There is a kind of spiritual danger that doesn't begin with rebellion.
Sometimes, it begins with respect.

A young believer walks into a church carrying wounds nobody can see. Perhaps his earthly father abandoned him. Perhaps he grew up without guidance, without affection, without anyone who cared enough to tell him the truth.
Then someone comes along.
A pastor who listens. A mentor who prays. A spiritual leader who opens the Scriptures and helps him understand the Gospel for the first time.
For the first time in years, he feels seen.
He feels protected.
He feels like he belongs.
And one day, with tears in his eyes, he says something that comes straight from his heart.
“You have been like a father to me.”
Beautiful words.
But then someone opens the Bible and reads what Jesus said.
“And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.” — Matthew 23:9 (KJV)
Suddenly, the room becomes quiet.
Was that young believer wrong?
Was his gratitude misplaced?
Should Christians never call a pastor, priest, mentor, or spiritual guide their father?
And if Jesus clearly said not to do it, why would the apostle Paul write something that seems to say the opposite?
“For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel.” — 1 Corinthians 4:15 (KJV)
Read those verses again.
Jesus said, “Call no man your father.”
Paul said, in effect, “I became your father through the Gospel.”
Two statements.
One Bible.
And a question that cannot be answered faithfully by pretending either passage does not exist.
Because this is about far more than a religious title.
It is about authority.
It is about spiritual dependence.
It is about the difference between a shepherd who leads you to Jesus and a leader who slowly teaches you that you cannot reach Jesus without him.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question is not whether you call someone your spiritual father.
Perhaps it is this:

Has someone who was supposed to lead you closer to Christ quietly become the person you are afraid to question, afraid to disappoint, and afraid to leave—even when Scripture tells you something is wrong?
That question deserves an answer.
Not from denominational pride.
Not from tradition alone.
Not from personal resentment toward religious leaders.
But from the Word of God.
To understand what Jesus meant, we must return to the moment He spoke those words.
In Matthew 23, Jesus was confronting the scribes and Pharisees.
He was not delivering a casual lesson about family vocabulary.
He was exposing a religious culture in which outward holiness could conceal inward pride.
He described leaders who loved prominent seats, public recognition, and impressive greetings.
People who wanted to be noticed.
People who enjoyed being treated as spiritually superior.
People who placed burdens on others while failing to practice what they preached.
Then Jesus spoke these piercing words:
“But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.” — Matthew 23:8 (KJV)
And immediately afterward:
“And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.” — Matthew 23:9 (KJV)
Then:
“Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ.” — Matthew 23:10 (KJV)
And finally, the words that reveal the heart of the entire warning:
“But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant.” — Matthew 23:11 (KJV)
Do you see the movement?
Jesus was confronting the human appetite for spiritual importance.
The desire to stand above others.
The temptation to receive honor that belongs ultimately to God.
He was not merely asking His followers to replace one title with another.
He was dismantling the pride that makes titles dangerous.
And the original Greek helps us see why this matters.
In Matthew 23:9, the word translated “father” is πατέρα (patera), an accusative form of πατήρ (patēr), meaning “father.”
The Greek expression is:
καὶ πατέρα μὴ καλέσητε ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
Kai patera mē kalesēte hymōn epi tēs gēs.
A close translation is:
“And do not call anyone on earth your father.”
Jesus continues:
εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῶν ὁ πατὴρ ὁ οὐράνιος
Heis gar estin hymōn ho patēr ho ouranios.
“For one is your Father, the heavenly One.”
Notice something important.
The Greek word itself does not carry a special hidden meaning that magically resolves the difficulty.
Patēr is an ordinary Greek word for father. Its meaning must be understood within the sentence, the surrounding passage, and the wider teaching of Scripture.
And that wider teaching gives us something remarkable.
Jesus Himself used the language of earthly fatherhood.
In Matthew 15:4, He affirmed God's command to honor one's father and mother.
In Matthew 19:19, He repeated the commandment.
In Luke 15, He told the unforgettable parable of a son returning to his father.
And in Matthew 23:30, within the very chapter containing His warning, Jesus referred to the ancestors of His opponents as their fathers.
Therefore, Matthew 23:9 cannot reasonably mean that every use of the word “father” for a human being is sinful.
If it did, the Scriptures themselves would repeatedly violate the supposed rule.
But this does not mean we can dismiss Jesus' command.
Quite the opposite.
Jesus was forbidding something deeper than a word: the elevation of human religious authority into a position that competes with the unique fatherhood of God.
That is the heart of the warning.
And that warning is terrifyingly relevant.
Because spiritual authority can become an idol without ever looking like one.
It may begin with admiration.
Then admiration becomes unquestioning loyalty.
Then loyalty becomes fear.
Then fear becomes silence.
A believer notices something wrong but refuses to speak.
A leader teaches something questionable, but nobody dares examine it.
Someone is wounded, manipulated, or humiliated, yet is told that questioning the leader means dishonoring God.
Eventually, the name of Jesus is still spoken.
The Bible is still opened.
Worship songs are still sung.
But the practical center of the community has shifted.
Everything revolves around one human personality.
And the people are no longer being taught to stand firmly in Christ.
They are being taught to stand only as long as that leader approves.
Friend, that is not spiritual fatherhood as the New Testament presents it.
That is spiritual control.
And Jesus did not shed His blood to rescue sinners from bondage only for religious leaders to place them under another form of bondage.
But now we must face Paul's words.
Because Paul did not simply tolerate spiritual fatherhood as a metaphor.
He used the language personally.
“For in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel.” — 1 Corinthians 4:15 (KJV)
In the original Greek, Paul writes:
ἐν γὰρ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ διὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου ἐγὼ ὑμᾶς ἐγέννησα
En gar Christō Iēsou dia tou euangeliou egō hymas egennēsa.
A close translation is:
“For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I became your father.”
The verb ἐγέννησα (egennēsa) comes from γεννάω (gennaō), meaning to beget, give birth to, or become the parent of someone.
Paul was describing a genuine spiritual relationship.
He had preached the Gospel to the Corinthians.
Through that Gospel ministry, they had come to faith in Christ.
He had labored for their spiritual formation.
He had corrected them.
He had warned them.
He had loved them enough to confront their sins.
But notice the two expressions Paul placed around his claim.
“In Christ Jesus.”
“Through the gospel.”
Those words change everything.
Paul did not claim that he possessed independent spiritual power to produce eternal life.
He did not claim to replace God as their heavenly Father.
He did not claim that the Corinthians belonged to him as personal property.
Their new life came through Christ and the Gospel.
Paul was the human servant through whom that message reached them.
In fact, Paul had already explained this distinction earlier in the same letter.
“Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?” — 1 Corinthians 3:5 (KJV)
Then he declared:
“I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.” — 1 Corinthians 3:6 (KJV)
And listen to this:
“So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.” — 1 Corinthians 3:7 (KJV)
There it is.
The same apostle who described himself as a spiritual father also insisted that the human minister is nothing in comparison with the God who gives growth.
Paul did not build his ministry around making people dependent on Paul.
He wanted people rooted in Jesus.
That distinction is not small.
It is everything.
Because a true spiritual father does not compete with the heavenly Father.
He serves under Him.
A true spiritual mentor does not replace the Savior.
He points to Him.
A faithful pastor does not make himself the source of grace.
He proclaims the grace that comes through Jesus Christ.
And Paul demonstrated that distinction even when it cost him personal influence.
When believers began dividing themselves around favorite leaders, saying, “I am of Paul” or “I am of Apollos,” Paul confronted their factionalism.
He asked:
“Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?” — 1 Corinthians 1:13 (KJV)
Think about that.
Paul refused to allow the people he had helped bring to Christ to turn his name into the center of their faith.
He could acknowledge a fatherlike relationship without accepting the worshipful loyalty that belongs to Jesus.
That is what healthy spiritual leadership looks like.
And it is why a careful reading of Matthew 23:9 and 1 Corinthians 4:15 does not require us to accuse either Jesus or Paul of contradiction.
Jesus condemns the pride and spiritual supremacy that displace God.
Paul describes a Gospel-centered, fatherlike ministry that remains entirely dependent upon God.
Still, we should not pretend every Christian tradition reaches exactly the same conclusion about religious titles.

Some Christians, including many Catholics and Orthodox believers, understand Paul's words and the broader biblical use of fatherhood language as permitting respectful spiritual titles such as “Father,” provided those titles never rival God's authority.

Other Christians, especially within certain Protestant traditions, avoid addressing ministers as “Father” because they believe the most faithful application of Matthew 23:9 is to reserve that religious form of address for God.
Both positions must take Jesus' warning seriously.
And both should be examined with Scripture rather than caricature.

The New Testament clearly uses fatherhood language for human relationships, including spiritual ones. But that does not, by itself, settle every question about formal clerical titles, institutional authority, or church tradition.
A description of Paul's relationship to the Corinthians is not automatically a command requiring every Christian to address a minister as “Father.”
And Jesus' warning cannot simply be erased because Paul used a fatherhood metaphor.
Faithfulness requires us to hold both truths together.
The Bible recognizes fatherlike spiritual care while warning against the exaltation of human religious authority.
But there is another passage that makes this even more personal.
Paul wrote to the Thessalonians:
“As ye know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children.” — 1 Thessalonians 2:11 (KJV)
What did fatherlike ministry look like to Paul?
Exhortation.
Comfort.
Encouragement.
Personal care.
A call to walk worthy of God.
And in the same chapter, Paul also described his ministry using the tenderness of a nursing mother caring for her children.
His point was not status.
His point was sacrificial love.
