He was willing to give not only the Gospel but his own life in service to those he loved.
Now compare that with the kind of leadership Jesus condemned.
One seeks the highest seat.
The other bends down to serve.
One wants people to notice his greatness.
The other wants people to know the greatness of Christ.
One uses spiritual authority to make people smaller.
The other uses spiritual responsibility to help believers grow into maturity.
And perhaps this is where the question stops being theological theory and begins touching the hidden places of our lives.
Because some of us know what it means to long for a father.
Maybe your earthly father was present physically but absent emotionally.
Maybe he provided food but never affection.
Maybe he gave correction without encouragement.
Maybe the word “father” does not bring comfort to your mind.
It brings pain.
And when a pastor or mentor finally showed you patience, compassion, and consistent care, something inside you began to heal.
There is nothing shameful about being grateful for someone God used to help you.
Spiritual mentorship can be a beautiful gift.
But even the most loving spiritual mentor is still human.
He can become tired.
He can misunderstand.
He can sin.
He can fail.
He may even disappoint you deeply.
And if your entire faith rests upon his perfection, what happens when his humanity becomes impossible to ignore?
What happens when the voice you trusted says something that contradicts Scripture?
What happens when the person who taught you about grace fails to show grace?
What happens when the shepherd himself needs repentance?
This is why your relationship with God must never be reduced to your relationship with a religious leader.
The man who introduced you to Jesus is not the Jesus who saved you.
Read that again.
The person who prayed with you did not die for your sins.
The person who baptized you did not rise from the grave for your justification.
The person who taught you the Bible is not the eternal Word made flesh.
And the person who helped you find your way home is not the Father waiting to receive you.
There is only one Savior.
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 2:5 (KJV)
One mediator.
Jesus Christ.
This does not eliminate the importance of pastors, teachers, elders, or spiritual mentors.
Ephesians 4:11–13 describes Christ giving ministry leaders to equip the saints and build up the body of Christ.
Hebrews 13:17 teaches believers to take spiritual leadership seriously, while reminding us that leaders must give an account.
And 1 Peter 5:2–3 commands elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not as domineering rulers, but as examples.
Biblical leadership is real.
Biblical accountability is real.
Biblical submission has a place.
But none of those truths gives any leader permission to demand unquestioning obedience, conceal wrongdoing, or claim the authority that belongs to Christ alone.
Even the apostle Peter, when writing to fellow elders, did not present himself as a supreme personality beyond correction.
He directed attention to the Chief Shepherd.
And that title belongs to Jesus.
So how can you recognize a spiritually healthy mentor?
Watch what happens when you ask a sincere biblical question.
Does he patiently open the Scriptures, or does he treat your question as personal betrayal?
Watch what happens when he makes a mistake.
Does he repent, or does he insist that his position places him beyond accountability?
Watch what happens when you begin growing spiritually.
Does he rejoice as you become more grounded in Christ, or does he become threatened when you no longer depend on his approval?
Watch what happens when people praise him.
Does he receive gratitude with humility and direct glory toward God, or does he cultivate an atmosphere where his name matters more than the name of Jesus?
These are not perfect tests of a person's heart.
Only God sees the heart completely.
But they are important questions about observable fruit.
Jesus said:
“Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.” — Matthew 7:20 (KJV)
And the fruit of faithful ministry should not be spiritual captivity.
It should be growing faith, truth, holiness, love, humility, and maturity in Christ.
That is why the apostle John could write:
Notice what brings joy.
Not that his spiritual children repeat his name.
Not that they defend his reputation at any cost.
Not that they become incapable of thinking without his permission.
But that they walk in truth.
And Jesus Christ is the truth.
Now, before anyone uses this article as an excuse to despise pastors, mock priests, reject spiritual counsel, or become unteachable, we need to confront another danger.
Pride does not exist only in religious leaders.
It can also live in the hearts of those who refuse to be led.
Some people say, “I follow Jesus, not men,” but use those words to escape every form of correction.
They reject accountability.
They dismiss faithful teaching.
They confuse independence with spiritual maturity.
That is not what Jesus taught either.
The same Lord who warned against religious pride also gave His Church shepherds and teachers.
The same New Testament that warns against domineering leaders calls believers to humility, mutual service, and fellowship.
The answer to abusive authority is not the rejection of all authority.
The answer is authority submitted to Christ.
The answer to spiritual manipulation is not spiritual isolation.
The answer is truth, accountability, and relationships shaped by the Gospel.
And the answer to a leader who has taken too much space in your heart is not necessarily hatred toward that leader.
It may begin with repentance.
Not only his.
Yours, too, if you have given a human being the trust, fear, or devotion that belongs to God.
Because idolatry is not always a statue.
Sometimes it is a person whose approval we fear losing more than we fear disobeying God.
Sometimes it is a ministry we refuse to examine.
Sometimes it is a religious title we treat as proof of holiness.
Sometimes it is our own reputation as a loyal follower.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave those idols untouched.
He did not come to create a new class of untouchable religious celebrities.
He came to reconcile sinners to the Father.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He came to expose hypocrisy and offer mercy to the repentant.
He came to bear the sins of people who had trusted the wrong things, followed the wrong voices, and wandered far from God.
At the cross, the Son of God did not merely teach us humility.
He demonstrated it.
The One who possessed all authority allowed Himself to be mocked.
The One who deserved every crown wore a crown of thorns.
The One before whom every knee will bow knelt in service and gave Himself for sinners.
And when He rose from the grave, He did not become one spiritual guide among many.
He stood revealed as the victorious Lord and Savior.
That is the difference between Christianity and a personality cult.
Christianity does not end with a human leader.
It begins and ends with Jesus Christ.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior theme becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Think of Peter.
He had promised loyalty.
He had declared that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
But when the pressure came, he denied knowing the Lord.
Three times.
The man who had spoken so boldly broke under fear.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering the sound of your own voice denying the Savior you loved.
Imagine wondering whether your failure had permanently destroyed your calling.
But after the resurrection, Jesus met Peter in his brokenness.
In John 21, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with a responsibility:
“Feed my sheep.” — John 21:17 (KJV)
Not “Build a kingdom around your personality.”
Not “Make people dependent on your greatness.”
Not “Convince everyone that you are incapable of failure.”
Feed My sheep.
Whose sheep?
Jesus' sheep.
That one word matters.
My.
The flock belongs to Christ.
The Church belongs to Christ.
The redeemed belong to Christ.
Even the most faithful shepherd is only a servant caring for what belongs to Another.
And perhaps that is the word some leaders desperately need to hear.
You do not have to pretend you are the source of everyone's spiritual life.
You do not have to be the answer to every question.
You do not have to control every decision.
You do not have to make people afraid of leaving your ministry.
You are called to serve faithfully, teach truthfully, love sacrificially, and point people to the Chief Shepherd.
And perhaps that is also the word some wounded believers need to hear.
You can honor the person who helped you without surrendering your conscience.
You can appreciate a mentor without making him infallible.
You can receive correction without accepting manipulation.
You can forgive someone without pretending that harm never happened.
You can seek wise pastoral care while remembering that your ultimate hope rests in Christ.
And if a leader has wounded you, that wound does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
Human shepherds can fail.
The Chief Shepherd remains faithful.
Now return to the original question.
Should Christians call anyone on earth their spiritual father when Jesus said, “Call no man your father”?
Here is the most biblically responsible answer I can give.

Scripture permits fatherhood language to describe genuine spiritual care, as Paul himself demonstrates. But Scripture never permits a human spiritual father to take the unique place of God, claim unquestionable spiritual supremacy, or become a rival to Christ.

Whether a Christian should use “Father” as a formal religious title remains a matter on which traditions disagree. Those who use it must not empty Matthew 23:9 of its force. Those who avoid it must not ignore Paul's fatherhood language.
No one should be pressured to violate a sincerely held, Scripture-informed conviction about such a title.
And every Christian, regardless of denomination, must face the warning Jesus gave.
Because a person can refuse the title “Father” and still idolize a pastor.
A person can use the title “Father” respectfully while genuinely recognizing God as the supreme Father.
The title alone does not reveal the whole condition of the heart.
But the way authority is exercised, the way Scripture is handled, and the way Christ is honored reveal a great deal.
And that brings us to something we cannot afford to overlook.
The most dangerous spiritual father is not necessarily the one who accepts the title. It is the one who demands the place that belongs to God.
And the safest spiritual mentor is not necessarily the one who refuses every title.
It is the one who continually leads you away from dependence on himself and toward deeper dependence on Jesus.
That is the kind of discipleship worth building.
That is the kind of truth worth defending.
That is the kind of Gospel-centered community Gospel Warrior exists to encourage.
Not a community where people worship a personality.
Not a community where questions are silenced.
Not a community where religious titles become weapons.

But a community where Scripture is examined carefully, Christ is exalted faithfully, sinners are called to repentance, wounded believers find biblical encouragement, and spiritual growth becomes a lifelong pursuit.
And if this message has challenged you, please do not simply move on to the next post.
Ask yourself one question.
Am I following Jesus through the help of faithful spiritual leaders, or have I allowed a human leader to become the center of my faith?
That question may reveal something painful.
But the grace of God is not afraid of exposing what needs to change.
You do not need to reveal private wounds publicly to prove your faith. A simple prayer, an honest question, or a testimony of God's faithfulness can become a blessing to someone else.
Not to win an argument.
Not to attack a denomination.
Not to embarrass a pastor or priest.
But because someone in your circle may be silently wrestling with this very question.
Someone may be confusing spiritual loyalty with spiritual bondage.
Someone may be rejecting every form of Christian mentorship because one leader betrayed their trust.
Someone may need to discover that honoring faithful spiritual care and worshiping God alone are not enemies.
There is also a deeper way to help this ministry continue.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical teaching, Christian reading, and discipleship resources more accessible to people who are hungry for the Word of God.
And here is something important.
We believe the Gospel should never be treated as merchandise.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is not reserved for paying supporters.
The Word of God is not a luxury that belongs only to those who can afford it.
That is precisely why freely accessible Christian resources matter.
Scripture says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Not guilt.
Not fear.
But a willing heart that wants to help good work continue.
These items are not the reason we preach Christ.
You are no less valuable.
Your prayers matter.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your sharing matters.
Your willingness to help another person understand the Gospel matters.
We want them to encounter more than religious content.
We want them to encounter the truth of Scripture and the saving message of Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, remember the words of Jesus:
“And all ye are brethren.” — Matthew 23:8 (KJV)
What a beautiful reminder.
In a world obsessed with titles, positions, recognition, and power, Jesus called His followers to remember their shared dependence on God.
The pastor needs grace.
The priest needs grace.
The teacher needs grace.
The mentor needs grace.
The new believer needs grace.
The person who has failed needs grace.
And the person who thinks he has never failed needs grace more than he realizes.
None of us stands before God because a human spiritual father has made us worthy.
We stand only through the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who conquered the grave.
The One who calls us to repentance and faith.
The One who gives us access to the Father.
So honor those who have faithfully taught you.
Pray for those entrusted with spiritual responsibility.
Be willing to receive biblical correction.
Refuse to turn human servants into spiritual idols.
And never forget whose blood purchased your redemption.
Because when every earthly title fades, when every human reputation is forgotten, and when every earthly ministry has completed its work, one name will remain above every name.
Jesus Christ.
And if your spiritual father truly loves you, he will want you to remember that long after you have forgotten his own name.
The hands that helped lead you to Jesus may one day let you down—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus will never lose their power to save.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DEMONS HAVE BETTER THEOLOGY THAN SOME PEOPLE—AND THEY’RE STILL DEMONS
paragraphs: DEMONS HAVE BETTER THEOLOGY THAN SOME PEOPLE—AND THEY’RE STILL DEMONS

They know Jesus is the Son of God. They recognize His authority. They tremble at His name. Yet they remain enemies of God. What if the most terrifying spiritual deception isn't denying that Jesus exists—but knowing exactly who He is while refusing to surrender to Him?
There is a verse in the Bible that should make every churchgoer uncomfortable.
Not because it questions the existence of God.
Not because it attacks Christianity.
But because it exposes something that can hide beneath years of sermons, Bible studies, worship services, ministry involvement, and religious activity.
You can believe everything true about Jesus Christ and still refuse to belong to Him.
And Scripture gives us a disturbing example.
Demons.
Yes. Demons.
They are not atheists.
They do not need archaeological discoveries to convince them Jesus existed.
They do not debate whether He has supernatural authority.
They know.
They recognize Him.
They fear Him.
And they are still demons.
James wrote something that should silence every person who has ever confused religious knowledge with saving faith:
“You believe that God is one. You do well. The demons also believe—and shudder.”
—James 2:19, translated from the Greek
Read that again.
The demons believe.
And they shudder.
But their belief is not repentance. Their recognition is not worshipful surrender. Their knowledge is not reconciliation with God.
Now comes the question that makes this passage painfully personal.
If demons can possess correct theology without possessing saving faith, what makes us think knowing the right answers automatically means our hearts belong to Jesus?
That question is not meant to destroy your assurance in Christ.
It is meant to expose the counterfeit assurance that can keep a person from ever coming to Him.
Because the greatest tragedy is not simply that someone could spend an entire lifetime rejecting Jesus openly.
It is that someone could spend an entire lifetime talking about Jesus, defending Jesus, singing about Jesus, and never truly surrendering to Jesus.
And one day discover that being familiar with the Savior was never the same as being reconciled to Him.
There is something extraordinary buried inside the original Greek of James 2:19.
James begins with the words:
Σὺ πιστεύεις ὅτι εἷς ἐστιν ὁ θεός.
Sy pisteueis hoti heis estin ho theos.
“You believe that God is one.”
This echoes the great confession of Israel found in Deuteronomy 6:4:
שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
Shema Yisra'el, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad.
“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.”
This confession was foundational to Israel's worship of the one true God.
James is not mocking that truth. He affirms it.
Believing in the one true God is right.
But then he delivers the devastating comparison.
καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιστεύουσιν καὶ φρίσσουσιν.
Kai ta daimonia pisteuousin kai phrissousin.
“And the demons believe—and shudder.”
The Greek verb φρίσσουσιν (phrissousin) conveys trembling or shuddering in fear.
James is making a piercing argument: correct belief about God, by itself, is not proof of a living, obedient faith.
He is not saying demons have complete or superior theology in every respect.
They do not.
Their understanding is corrupted by rebellion, and their response to God is not the trusting love of redeemed children.
But they know certain truths that many people deny.
And that makes the comparison so frightening.
Because there are people who recognize the existence of God without ever submitting to His authority.
People who can explain salvation while resisting the Savior.
People who know the language of repentance but have spent years defending the very sins they refuse to abandon.
People who can identify false teaching in someone else's life while refusing to confront the pride growing inside their own.
And before you imagine somebody else while reading those words, consider the possibility that Scripture is inviting you to examine yourself.
Not your pastor.
Not the person who offended you.
Not the Christian who disappointed you.
You.
Because religious deception becomes most dangerous when we are certain it could never happen to us.
Consider what happened when Jesus encountered a man tormented by demons in the region of the Gerasenes.
The man was living among tombs.
His life had become a picture of isolation, torment, and destruction.
People had tried to restrain him.
Chains could not hold him.
Human strength could not restore him.
He lived surrounded by death, crying out and injuring himself.
Then Jesus arrived.
And the spiritual powers tormenting that man immediately recognized the One standing before them.
In Mark 5:7, the cry comes:
“What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?”
They knew His identity.
They recognized His authority.
They understood that they could not treat Him as an ordinary man.
And yet they were not His disciples.
They were His enemies.
Do you see the distinction?
Recognizing the authority of Jesus is not the same as lovingly submitting to Jesus.
The demons knew who stood before them.
But they did not love Him.
They did not repent.
They did not become obedient followers.
And the man they had tormented desperately needed something they could never give him.
Deliverance.
Restoration.
A new life.
That is exactly what Jesus brought.
Later in the same account, the formerly tormented man is found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
The man who had lived among the tombs was no longer defined by the place where everyone expected him to remain.
Jesus had stepped into his devastation and rewritten the story.
And here is something worth remembering.
The demons recognized Jesus.
But the delivered man wanted to follow Him.
One response was terror before authority.
The other was the beginning of a transformed life.
That difference matters.
Because Christianity is not merely the ability to make accurate statements about Christ.
It is being brought to God through Christ.
It is receiving His grace through faith.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
It is the beginning of a new life that His Spirit continues to transform.
Not perfection.
Not sinlessness.
Not an impressive religious résumé.
A genuine relationship with the living Lord that bears fruit because His grace is at work.
And that brings us to one of the most sobering statements Jesus ever made.
In Matthew 7:21–23, Jesus warns that not everyone who calls Him “Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven.
Some will point to astonishing religious activity performed in His name.
They will appeal to what they said.
What they did.
What appeared to happen through their ministry.
But Jesus describes a terrible reality.
There can be outward religious activity without a genuine relationship with Him.
And the words at the center of His warning are devastating:
“I never knew you.”
—Matthew 7:23
Notice what He does not say.
He does not say, “You never attended enough services.”
He does not say, “You never collected enough Bible knowledge.”
He does not say, “You failed to build an impressive ministry.”
His warning exposes the absence of a genuine relationship with Him, alongside a life characterized by lawlessness.
That should sober us.
But we must read this passage carefully.
Jesus is not teaching that genuine believers earn salvation through flawless obedience.
He is not saying a struggling Christian who sincerely trusts Him will be rejected because of weakness, tears, or repeated battles with sin.
Scripture teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the very next verse says that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
The order matters.
We are not saved because we have successfully transformed ourselves.
We are saved by Christ, and His grace begins transforming us.
Good works are not the purchase price of salvation.
They are the fruit of a faith made alive by God's grace.
James is confronting a faith that exists only as a claim, never expressing itself in mercy or obedience.
Paul is confronting the idea that sinners can earn justification through their works.
They are not contradicting one another.
They are exposing two different errors.
Paul tells us that we cannot save ourselves.
James tells us that living faith is not merely an empty profession.
And both point us away from self-reliance and toward Jesus Christ.
But perhaps this is where the article stops being theological and starts becoming personal.
Because some of us have learned how to sound spiritually healthy while quietly falling apart.
We know which Bible verses to post.
We know how to say “God is good” when somebody asks how we are doing.
We know how to encourage other people.
We know how to pray in public.
But behind closed doors, there are battles nobody sees.
The resentment we keep feeding.
The secret habit we keep excusing.
The bitterness we call discernment.
The pride we disguise as spiritual maturity.
The dishonesty we justify because telling the truth might cost us something.
The unforgiveness we have allowed to become part of our identity.
And sometimes the most exhausting part is not the struggle itself.
It is the effort of maintaining an image that says we have no struggle at all.
You can know the Greek word for repentance and still be terrified to confess your sin.
You can explain grace beautifully while believing that God could never forgive what you have done.
You can defend the authority of Scripture while quietly resisting the very command God is bringing to your attention.
You can tell everyone that Jesus changes lives while secretly wondering whether He can still change yours.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Not because you need another argument about demons.
But because something inside you is tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of knowing the right words without experiencing the honesty those words require.
Tired of carrying guilt into worship and taking it home again.
Tired of promising God that tomorrow will be different, only to discover that willpower alone cannot rescue the human heart.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to make you better at appearing religious. He came to save sinners.
That is the Gospel.
Not that you are good enough to impress God.
Not that you can repair your past through religious activity.
Not that your public reputation can compensate for your private rebellion.
Christ came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).
He lived the righteous life we could not live.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And because He lives, forgiveness is not an empty religious slogan.
Redemption is not wishful thinking.
New life is not reserved for people whose past looks respectable.
The cross tells us that sin is far more serious than we wanted to admit.
The resurrection tells us that Jesus is far more powerful than our sin.
And grace tells us that the door of mercy is opened by the Savior, not by our ability to deserve Him.
Think about Peter.
Peter knew Jesus personally.
He heard His teaching.
He witnessed His miracles.
He declared that Jesus was the Christ.
And then, on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The third denial was followed by the crowing of a rooster.
And Luke tells us that Peter went outside and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).
Imagine that moment.
The man who had promised loyalty now carried the memory of his own cowardice.
The disciple who had spoken so confidently had discovered how weak he really was.
He had the right confession.
But he had failed terribly when faithfulness became costly.
And yet his failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ asked him three times whether he loved Him.
Three questions.
Three opportunities to answer.
And with those questions came a renewed commission to care for Christ's sheep.
Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial never happened.
He restored a fallen disciple and entrusted him with responsibility.
That is grace.
Not grace that declares betrayal harmless.
Grace that confronts failure and restores the repentant.
Grace that does not leave a broken person chained forever to the worst night of his life.
Peter's story was not rewritten because Peter suddenly became impressive.
It was rewritten because the risen Jesus was merciful.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the most extraordinary part is that Jesus is still doing the work of redemption.
Not by excusing sin.
Not by celebrating rebellion.
Not by lowering the holiness of God.
But by calling sinners to repentance and offering the forgiveness He purchased through His blood.
There is another Greek word worth understanding.
μετάνοια — metanoia.
Repentance.
The word refers to a change of mind, and in biblical usage it involves a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because somebody discovered what you did.
It is not merely crying because consequences have arrived.
It is not negotiating with God so that you can keep the sin and escape the judgment.
Repentance is turning to God with a changed heart and mind, acknowledging that His ways are right and that we need His mercy.
And even here, we depend upon grace.
We cannot manufacture spiritual life by sheer determination.
God calls us to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15), and His kindness leads us toward repentance (Romans 2:4).
Which means that the conviction you feel while reading Scripture should not automatically be mistaken for God pushing you away.
His Word may be exposing what needs to be brought into the light.
And the answer is not to hide more carefully.
It is to come to Christ.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe people know what happened.
Maybe your name became attached to a mistake, a betrayal, an addiction, or a decision that shattered relationships.
Or maybe your scandal is invisible.
Nobody knows how cold your heart has become.
Nobody knows how long you have carried jealousy.
Nobody knows how much you have compromised.
Nobody knows how often you have smiled while feeling spiritually empty.
But Jesus knows.
And this is where the Gospel becomes astonishing.
The One who knows the truth about your sin is the very One who calls sinners to come to Him for mercy.
He is not deceived by religious performance.
He cannot be manipulated by impressive words.
He does not need your carefully edited testimony.
He calls you to come truthfully.
Confess what is wrong.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Trust what He accomplished through His death and resurrection.
And follow Him.
Not because following Him will always be comfortable.
But because no other Savior can give eternal life.
In John 6:68, Peter asked Jesus:
“Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
That is the question every exhausted soul eventually has to face.
Where else will you go?
Back to the sin that promised freedom and produced bondage?
Back to the approval of people who cannot cleanse your conscience?
Back to religious activity that helps you avoid dealing honestly with God?
Back to the belief that one more achievement will finally make you worthy?
Or will you come to Jesus?
The Jesus who welcomed the repentant tax collector.
The Jesus who restored Peter.
The Jesus who promised paradise to a dying criminal who turned to Him in faith.
The Jesus who bore our sins and rose victorious over death.
The Jesus who still calls the weary to Himself.
And here is the distinction that changes everything.
Demons believe Jesus is powerful.
Saving faith entrusts itself to Jesus as Savior and Lord.
Demons recognize His identity.
Believers are called to love Him, trust Him, and follow Him.
Demons tremble before His authority.
Those reconciled to God can approach Him through Christ with confidence in His mercy.
Not because they are stronger than demons.
Not because their knowledge is more impressive.
But because Jesus saves.
This is why the Christian life cannot be reduced to winning theological arguments.
Sound doctrine matters deeply.
Truth matters.
The deity of Christ matters.
His bodily resurrection matters.
The Gospel must not be distorted.
But doctrine was never meant to become a trophy that allows us to admire our knowledge while neglecting the God who revealed Himself.
Theology should lead us toward worship, humility, love, repentance, and obedience.
If studying Scripture makes us increasingly arrogant, cruel, dishonest, and unteachable, something is wrong with the way we are responding to what we know.
First Corinthians 8:1 warns that knowledge can puff up, while love builds up.
That does not make knowledge unnecessary.
It means knowledge without love can become a weapon in the hands of pride.
And perhaps one of the saddest sights in Christianity is a person who can dismantle somebody else's doctrinal error in minutes but cannot bring themselves to say three simple words.
“I was wrong.”
Or two even harder words.
“Forgive me.”
Some people can explain the doctrine of grace but refuse to extend grace.
Some can preach about holiness while secretly making peace with sin.
Some can quote the words of Jesus while treating people in ways that contradict His commands.
And every one of us needs to remain humble enough to ask whether that contradiction has found a home in our own hearts.
Not because every inconsistency proves someone is unsaved.
Christians still struggle.
Christians still stumble.
Christians still need correction, confession, and forgiveness.
But there is a profound difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
Between falling and refusing to get up.
Between confessing wrongdoing and continually defending it.
The evidence of grace is not that a Christian never needs repentance.
It is that the Christian life becomes one of continually returning to Christ in faith and repentance.
And if you are reading this while feeling deeply convicted, please do not turn this article into another reason to despair.
Look at the Savior.
First John 1:9 tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive and cleanse us.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
And John 6:37 contains a promise that should be precious to every person afraid of being rejected:
“The one who comes to me, I will in no way throw out.”
Jesus does not promise that following Him will require no change.
He promises that those who come to Him will not be cast away.
That is where your hope belongs.
Not in the intensity of your emotions.
Not in the number of tears you cry.
Not in how convincingly you can describe your spiritual experiences.
In Christ.
His finished work.
His resurrection.
His faithfulness.
His mercy.
And His power to make all things new.
Maybe tonight you need to stop asking whether you know enough about Jesus and start asking whether you are actually trusting Him.
Maybe you need to confess something.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you wounded.
Maybe you need to walk away from a compromise you have been protecting.
Maybe you need to stop performing spiritual strength and finally tell a trusted believer that you need prayer.
Or maybe you have been avoiding Jesus because you believe your past has placed you beyond His reach.
Remember Peter.
Remember the criminal beside the cross.
Remember the man who once lived among the tombs.
Remember that the Gospel is not a story about flawless people finding a religion that congratulates them.
It is the announcement that the holy Son of God came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And that rescue is not something we purchase with money, religious service, or moral accomplishments.
It is the gift of God's grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
So if you have never truly turned to Him, do not settle for knowing facts about Him.
Come to Him.
And if you already belong to Him but have been hiding in shame, return to the light.
Tell Him the truth.
You do not need a theatrical prayer.
You need an honest heart before the living God.
You can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I believe You are the Son of God, that You died for my sins, and that You rose again. I confess that I have sinned against You. I have sometimes been more concerned with appearing faithful than actually obeying You. Forgive me. Teach me genuine repentance. I cannot save myself. I place my trust in Your grace and Your finished work. Change my heart. Lead me in Your truth. Help me love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. Let my life bear witness that You are not merely someone I know about, but the Savior and Lord I trust. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects what is happening in your heart, do not let the moment disappear beneath another scroll.
Take the next faithful step.
Open your Bible.
Speak to a mature Christian who can walk alongside you.
Become part of a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and believers care for one another.
Seek reconciliation where possible.
And remember that spiritual growth is not measured by how impressive you appear tomorrow.
It is measured over time by a life increasingly shaped by the grace and truth of Jesus Christ.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell access to God.
But to keep bringing biblical truth into a world filled with distraction, confusion, spiritual exhaustion, and countless voices competing for the human heart.
There are people who will never walk into a church building but may read a Scripture-centered article shared by a friend.
There are believers who are struggling quietly and need to be reminded of the promises of God.
There are families who need encouragement to open the Bible together.
There are people whose understanding of Christianity has been shaped by hypocrisy, disappointment, or misinformation, who deserve to hear the actual Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And there are Christians who are hungry to grow beyond inspirational quotations into deeper biblical understanding.
We want those resources to remain accessible to people who need them.
We want to keep creating Christ-centered articles, biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship materials that help people return to Scripture and grow in their walk with Jesus.
But meaningful ministry takes time, work, and resources.
Not because a monthly payment earns His favor.
You glorify God by trusting and obeying Christ. Supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one voluntary expression of that love.
Scripture encourages believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And it recognizes the value of supporting those who faithfully labor in Gospel ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6).
If you already give to your local church, please continue to honor those responsibilities as you prayerfully discern your generosity.
It is simply an opportunity to help sustain and expand the work.
To help more people encounter biblical truth.
To help more struggling believers find encouragement rooted in Scripture.
To help make discipleship resources more accessible.
To stand alongside a mission that seeks to point people beyond personalities, platforms, and religious performance to Jesus Christ Himself.
They are a small expression of gratitude to those who choose to help carry it forward.

If Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you through a difficult season, or reminded you that Jesus has not finished His work in your life, consider joining us as a monthly supporter.
Not merely to increase numbers.
Somebody may be attending church while privately wondering whether God could ever forgive them.
Somebody may be defending Christianity publicly while slowly drifting away from Christ privately.
And somebody may be one honest conversation away from admitting that they need the Savior they have spent years talking about.
And if this message exposed something in your heart, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly. A simple request is enough for fellow believers to know you would welcome prayer.
And if God has restored you after a season of failure, consider sharing a brief testimony that honors Christ. Your story may encourage someone who believes their own failure must be the end.
Because the world does not need more Christians who are merely impressive at sounding Christian.
It needs the faithful witness of people who have encountered the mercy of Jesus and are learning to live in His truth.
People who know that salvation is by grace.
People who take sin seriously without pretending to be sinless.
People who speak truth without abandoning love.
People who can say, “I was wrong,” because they no longer need to build their identity on being right about everything.
People who can extend forgiveness because they know how much they have been forgiven.
People whose lives make the Gospel visible, not because they are perfect, but because they keep pointing back to the perfect Savior.
And now, one final thought.
The demons in the Gospels recognized Jesus when He stood before them.
They knew His authority.
They feared His power.
They could not deny who He was.
But their knowledge did not make them His followers.
So do not let your confidence rest merely in the fact that you know the right religious answers.
Ask yourself what you are doing with the truth you know.
Is it leading you toward Jesus?
Is it humbling you?
Is it awakening love for God and others?
Is it calling you to repent where you have compromised?
Is it teaching you to depend more deeply upon His grace?
Because one day, your theological vocabulary will not be your Savior.
Your ministry achievements will not be your Savior.
Your reputation will not be your Savior.
Your social media following will not be your Savior.
Your financial contributions will not be your Savior.
Jesus Christ alone is the Savior.
And the good news is that He does not merely offer you information about Himself.
He offers Himself.
His mercy.
His forgiveness.
His righteousness.
His life.
The One who died and rose again is worthy of more than our acknowledgment.
He is worthy of our trust, our love, our worship, and our lives.
And if your story is filled with things you wish you could undo, remember that the risen Christ is not limited by the chapter you are ashamed to remember.
He does not call evil good.
He does something infinitely more wonderful.
He saves sinners.
He restores the repentant.
He makes the dead alive.
And He writes grace into stories that once seemed hopeless.
The most terrifying thing is to know who Jesus is and never come to Him. The most beautiful thing is that, even now, He calls sinners to come.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM LAUGHED. SARAH LAUGHED. BUT GOD WASN’T JOKING.
paragraphs: ABRAHAM LAUGHED. SARAH LAUGHED. BUT GOD WASN’T JOKING.

Two people laughed at an impossible promise. One laughed before God. The other laughed behind a tent door. But what God did next reveals something breathtaking about doubt, disappointment, divine timing, and the grace that refuses to let human weakness have the final word.
There is a kind of laughter that comes from happiness.
And then there is another kind.
The kind that escapes when somebody promises you something you stopped believing could ever happen.
You don't laugh because it's funny.
You laugh because you've cried about it too many times.
Because you've prayed about it for too many years.
Because you've learned how to smile when people ask questions that reopen wounds you've spent decades trying to close.
And sometimes, when hope has disappointed you enough, laughter becomes the only way to keep your heart from breaking again.
Now imagine hearing God Himself promise you the very thing you've spent most of your life waiting for.
Would you believe Him?
Or would you laugh?
Because in Genesis, two people did exactly that.
Abraham laughed.
Sarah laughed.
And somehow, the child God promised them would eventually carry a name that meant...
He laughs.
But there is something hidden in these two moments that many readers overlook.
Something about the difference between believing God's power and struggling to believe His timing.
Something about a woman who laughed privately, only to discover that heaven had heard her.
And something about a God who could have named their unbelief as the end of their story, but instead made laughter part of the miracle.
Stay with this story.
Because by the time we reach the birth of Isaac, you may realize that the question was never simply why Abraham and Sarah laughed.
The deeper question is what happens when God speaks life into the very place where your hope has almost died.
Abraham was ninety-nine years old when the Lord spoke to him in Genesis 17.
Ninety-nine.
Not twenty-nine, when possibilities still seem endless.
Not forty-nine, when there might still be time to rearrange your plans.
Ninety-nine.
His wife, Sarah, was approaching ninety.
And their marriage had carried a particular sorrow for decades.
No child together.
No son born to Sarah.
No visible fulfillment of the promise God had made about their descendants.
To understand the weight of this moment, you have to remember what had already happened.
God had called Abram to leave his homeland and promised to make him into a great nation (Genesis 12:1–3).
Later, God brought him outside and told him to look toward the heavens.
Count the stars.
If you can.
That is how numerous your offspring will be.
And Genesis 15:6 tells us something extraordinary:
"And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." (KJV)
Abraham believed.
But believing a promise does not mean you immediately understand how it will happen.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
And eventually, they attempted to secure a family through Hagar, Sarah's Egyptian servant, following an arrangement Sarah herself proposed.
Ishmael was born.
But the consequences were painful.
Tension entered the household. Hagar suffered mistreatment. Relationships became strained.
Genesis 16 does not give us a neat story about faithless villains and flawless heroes.
It gives us something painfully human.
People who had heard God's promise but still struggled to live patiently inside the waiting.
And isn't that where many of us find ourselves?
We believe God can provide.
But when the bills keep arriving, we panic.
We believe God can restore.
But when the relationship remains broken, we start controlling what we cannot heal.
We believe God hears prayer.
But when the answer takes longer than expected, we quietly begin constructing alternatives.
Sometimes our greatest struggle is not believing that God exists.
It is trusting Him when obedience offers no immediate evidence that things are changing.
Then Genesis 17 arrives.
God establishes His covenant with Abraham, changes Abram's name to Abraham, and declares that Sarah herself will bear a son.
Not merely that Abraham will have descendants.
Not merely that Ishmael will become a great nation.
But that Sarah, the woman who had waited so long, would give birth.
Listen carefully to the words of Genesis 17:16:
"And I will bless her, and give thee a son also of her: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations; kings of people shall be of her." (KJV)
The promise was specific.
The woman was named.
The future was declared.
And Abraham's response?
He fell on his face.
And laughed.
Genesis 17:17 says:
"Then Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?" (KJV)
Now here is where we need to read Scripture carefully.
Because it would be easy to say Abraham laughed entirely from joyful faith while Sarah later laughed entirely from sinful unbelief.
But the biblical text deserves more honesty than that.
The Hebrew verb used for Abraham's laughter comes from the root צָחַק — tsachaq, meaning to laugh, and in different contexts it can carry senses of laughter, amusement, or mockery.
Genesis 17:17 uses the form וַיִּצְחָק — vayitschaq.
"And he laughed."
The Hebrew word itself does not tell us every emotion Abraham experienced.
And the text does not explicitly explain whether his laughter was pure joy, astonishment, incredulity, or some mixture of those responses.
What it does tell us is that Abraham immediately questioned how such a birth could happen at their ages.
And then he said something revealing.
"O that Ishmael might live before thee!" (Genesis 17:18, KJV)
In other words, Abraham brought before God the son he already had.
Perhaps, from his human perspective, Ishmael seemed the more understandable path forward.
But God answered with unmistakable clarity.
"Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son indeed; and thou shalt call his name Isaac." (Genesis 17:19, KJV)
Not an alternative plan.
Not a revised promise.
Sarah.
A son.
Isaac.
And the name Isaac comes from the same Hebrew root associated with laughter.
יִצְחָק — Yitschaq.
"He laughs" or "he will laugh."
Imagine that.
God chose a name that would forever recall the astonishing laughter surrounding this promise.
Every time Abraham called his son's name, the sound of laughter would return.
Every time Sarah called him home, she would speak a name connected to the moment when the impossible seemed almost absurd.
But notice something crucial.
God did not reject Ishmael as worthless.
He explicitly promised to bless him and make him fruitful (Genesis 17:20).
Yet He also distinguished His covenant promise concerning Isaac.
"But my covenant will I establish with Isaac." (Genesis 17:21, KJV)
God's faithfulness to one promise did not require Him to abandon compassion toward another child.
And His decision to work through Sarah was not an admission that human circumstances had finally become manageable.
They had not.
The circumstances were still impossible by ordinary human expectation.
That was the point.
God was not asking Abraham to believe that old age had somehow become youth.
He was asking Abraham to trust the One whose promise was not limited by human capacity.
And then, in Genesis 18, the story becomes even more intimate.
Abraham was sitting near the entrance of his tent by the oaks of Mamre.
Three visitors appeared.
Abraham welcomed them with hospitality.
Food was prepared.
A meal was served.
And in the conversation that followed, the Lord's promise concerning Sarah was repeated.
"I will certainly return unto thee according to the time of life; and, lo, Sarah thy wife shall have a son." (Genesis 18:10, KJV)
But Sarah was listening.
Behind the tent door.
Picture her for a moment.
An elderly woman standing where she could hear the conversation but was not its center.
A woman whose body had already passed through the ordinary years of childbearing.
A woman who had probably endured more questions, expectations, disappointments, and private grief than the narrative pauses to describe.
The Bible does not record every tear she shed.
It does not tell us how many times she watched another mother hold a newborn.
It does not reveal every thought that crossed her mind as the years went by.
We should not pretend to know those unrecorded details.
But we do know what Scripture says about her circumstances.
Genesis 18:11 tells us that Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years, and that Sarah had passed the ordinary time of childbearing.
And when Sarah heard the promise...
She laughed.
Not loudly before the visitors.
Not publicly in the courtyard.
She laughed within herself.
Genesis 18:12 records her thoughts:
"After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?" (KJV)
The Hebrew again uses the root צחק — tsachaq.
But Sarah's laughter is followed by a question that exposes the apparent impossibility of what she has heard.
She knows her age.
She knows her husband's age.
She knows the limitations of their bodies.
She knows the difference between a beautiful promise and the biological reality she has lived with for years.
And she laughs.
Perhaps you understand that more than you wish you did.
Maybe you once prayed with complete confidence for your marriage.
But now you barely know how to speak to each other.
Maybe you once believed your family would be restored.
But another Christmas passed with an empty chair.
Maybe you prayed for a child.
Maybe you prayed for healing.
Maybe you begged God to change something that still has not changed.
And now, when someone tells you to keep trusting God, you smile politely.
But inside, something whispers...
You don't understand how long I've been waiting.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because the Lord heard Sarah's laughter.
Even though she laughed within herself.
Even though she was behind the tent door.
Even though the question had never been spoken aloud to the visitors.
The Lord asked Abraham:
"Wherefore did Sarah laugh, saying, Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old?" (Genesis 18:13, KJV)
Then came one of the most powerful questions in the entire Old Testament.
"Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" (Genesis 18:14, KJV)
In Hebrew:
הֲיִפָּלֵא מֵיְהוָה דָּבָר
Hayippale me-YHWH davar?
A faithful rendering is:
"Is anything too difficult or extraordinary for the LORD?"
The Hebrew verb comes from the root פלא — pala, associated with what is wonderful, extraordinary, or beyond ordinary human ability.
This is more than a question about whether God possesses enough strength.
It confronts the assumption that what exceeds human possibility must also exceed divine ability.
Sarah looked at her circumstances and saw impossibility.
The Lord pointed her toward His own power and faithfulness.
And here is the detail that should stop us.
God did not ask whether the situation was difficult for Sarah.
It was.
He did not deny her age.
He did not pretend her body was functioning as though she were young.
He did not suggest that decades of disappointment had been imaginary.
He asked whether anything was too difficult for the LORD.
That changes the center of the question.
Because faith does not require us to deny reality.
Faith requires us to recognize that reality is not greater than God.
But we must be careful here.
This passage does not promise that every Christian will conceive a child, recover from every illness, or receive every specific outcome they desire.
God had made Abraham and Sarah a particular covenant promise.
And He was declaring His faithfulness to that promise.
We must not turn their unique calling into a guarantee God has not given to every believer.
The truth is still glorious without making promises Scripture never makes.
God is able.
God is faithful.
God can accomplish everything He has actually promised.
And even when His providence does not unfold according to our expectations, His character remains trustworthy.
Then Sarah did something else.
Something painfully recognizable.
She denied laughing.
Genesis 18:15 says:
"Then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not; for she was afraid. And he said, Nay; but thou didst laugh." (KJV)
Read those words slowly.
"For she was afraid."
The Bible tells us the reason for her denial.
Fear.
She had been exposed.
The laughter she thought was private had been brought into the light.
And suddenly she was no longer simply the woman who struggled to believe.
She was the woman trying to hide her struggle.
How often do we do the same?
We tell people we are fine when our hearts are exhausted.
We say we trust God while secretly wrestling with resentment.
We sing about His faithfulness while wondering why our own prayers seem unanswered.
We conceal disappointment because we think admitting it will make us appear spiritually weak.
And sometimes we even try to hide our doubts from God.
As though He does not already know.
But listen to the Lord's answer.
"Nay; but thou didst laugh."
He corrected her.
He did not pretend the denial was true.
Grace is not the same thing as ignoring dishonesty.
God's mercy does not require Him to call darkness light.
He exposed the truth.
And yet the promised son would still come.
That is what makes this scene so extraordinary.
Sarah's fear did not make God forget His word.
Her denial did not erase His covenant.
Her inward laughter did not prevent Him from accomplishing what He had promised.
And before we turn that into an excuse for unbelief, remember that Scripture does not celebrate dishonesty or encourage us to remain in doubt.
It calls us toward truth, repentance, and faith.
But it also reveals that God's faithfulness is greater than the instability of human emotions.
Somebody needs to hear that distinction.
Your feelings are not the foundation of God's character.
Your perfect performance is not what makes Him truthful.
And your struggle to understand His timing does not give you permission to rewrite what He has said.
There is room to bring your questions into His presence.
But there is also a call to let His truth correct you.
Then comes another remarkable detail.
In Genesis 21, the narrative finally moves from promise to fulfillment.
"And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken." (Genesis 21:1, KJV)
Do you see the emphasis?
As He had said.
As He had spoken.
The miracle is not presented as a lucky reversal of circumstances.
It is the fulfillment of God's word.
Sarah conceived.
She bore Abraham a son.
And the child was born at the appointed time God had spoken of.
Not according to their preferred schedule.
Not because they finally discovered a way to force the promise into existence.
But according to the time God had declared.
Abraham was one hundred years old.
Sarah held the son she had once considered impossible.
And they named him Isaac.
Laughter.
But now listen to Sarah.
"God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me." (Genesis 21:6, KJV)
There it is.
The same Hebrew root.
The same sound that once accompanied astonishment and uncertainty now appears in a declaration of joy.
Earlier, Sarah laughed within herself.
Now she speaks of laughter shared with others.
Earlier, the promise sounded impossible.
Now the promised child is in her arms.
Earlier, she was afraid to admit she had laughed.
Now she openly declares what God has done.
The story has come full circle.
Not because Sarah became the hero of her own miracle.
But because God remained faithful.
And there is something even deeper.
The New Testament does not leave Abraham and Sarah's story behind.
Hebrews 11:11 speaks of Sarah in connection with faith and the faithfulness of the One who promised.
Romans 4:19–21 describes Abraham's faith in God's promise despite the apparent lifelessness of his and Sarah's reproductive circumstances.
This does not mean their earlier moments of uncertainty never happened.
Genesis records those moments plainly.
Rather, Scripture presents a fuller picture of faith.
Faith is not always the absence of an initial struggle.
It is ultimately resting in the trustworthiness of God.
Abraham's story includes questions, mistakes, obedience, and perseverance.
Sarah's story includes laughter, fear, correction, and the fulfillment of God's word.
Neither person is presented as a flawless savior.
And that is important.
Because the Bible is not ultimately a collection of stories about perfect people who earned miracles.
It is the unfolding revelation of a faithful God who accomplishes His redemptive purposes through deeply imperfect human beings.
And this is where Isaac's birth begins pointing us toward something far greater than Isaac.
God had promised Abraham that through his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed.
That promise would reach its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Galatians 3:16 draws our attention to Christ as the promised offspring.
And Galatians 3:29 tells believers who belong to Christ that they are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise.
Think about the beauty of that.
The story of an elderly couple and their impossible child is connected to the unfolding history of salvation.
Isaac was not the Savior.
He needed God's grace like everyone else.
But through the covenant line that followed, God's plan moved toward the coming of Jesus Christ.
And when Christ came, He did something no merely human descendant of Abraham could ever accomplish.
He lived without sin.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God through faith in Him.
Abraham and Sarah needed God to accomplish what they could not accomplish for themselves.
And we need something even greater.
We need forgiveness that we cannot earn.
Righteousness that we cannot manufacture.
Resurrection life that we cannot produce.
We need Jesus.
Romans 4 connects Abraham's faith with the Gospel and concludes by speaking of Jesus our Lord:
"Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification." (Romans 4:25, KJV)
There is the center of our hope.
Not merely that God can change circumstances.
But that God has acted decisively in Jesus Christ to save sinners.
The greatest miracle is not simply that an elderly woman held a newborn son.
It is that the holy God of heaven made a way for guilty people to be forgiven and brought into His family.
And that means the Gospel speaks even to the person whose circumstances never resolve the way Abraham and Sarah's did.
The believer who prayed for a child and never conceived.
The widow whose husband did not recover.
The parent still grieving.
The person whose earthly story contains questions that have not been answered.
Jesus Christ is not less faithful to you because your life does not end with the particular miracle you requested.
His resurrection is our assurance that death, sin, and suffering do not have the final word.
The Gospel gives us something greater than a guarantee of comfortable circumstances.
It gives us Christ Himself.
And through Him, the hope of eternal life.
That is why the laughter of Abraham and Sarah matters.
Because underneath their story is the question every generation must face.
Will you measure God's faithfulness only by what you can currently see?
Or will you trust the God who has revealed Himself in His Word and ultimately in His Son?
Perhaps you are reading this with a promise you believe God has made, but you are unsure whether you understood it correctly.
Bring it before Scripture.
Test what you believe.
Do not confuse your desires with God's declarations.
And do not let someone pressure you into claiming a miracle that God has not specifically promised.
But where God has spoken clearly, hold fast.
He has promised forgiveness to those who repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
He has promised never to abandon those who belong to Him.
He has promised resurrection and eternal life in Christ.
He has promised that nothing can separate His people from His love in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:38–39).
Those promises are not fragile.
They are anchored in the character of God.
And perhaps tonight, your most important response is not to demand an answer about tomorrow.
Perhaps it is to stop hiding what is happening inside your heart today.
Sarah laughed in secret.
Then she denied it because she was afraid.
But the Lord already knew.
He knew the laughter.
He knew the fear.
He knew the years.
And He knew exactly what He had promised.
You do not need to manufacture a religious smile before coming to Jesus.
You can confess the bitterness.
The impatience.
The envy.
The exhaustion.
The unbelief.
The sins you have been hiding beneath spiritual language.
He already knows the truth.
And He calls you to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not because sin is harmless.
But because Jesus Christ has paid the price for our redemption.
That is grace.
Not pretending the failure never happened.
But meeting sinners with forgiveness through the finished work of Christ and calling them into a transformed life.
Not because scandal becomes beautiful.
Not because disobedience suddenly becomes righteous.
But because Jesus can redeem people whose histories are marked by sin, shame, regret, and brokenness.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing the truth about our past.
But by changing our standing before God and giving us a new future in Him.
Maybe you once laughed at the thought that your life could change.
Maybe you have whispered, Someone like me could never be forgiven.
Maybe you think your sins have already decided your ending.
Look to the cross.
Look to the empty tomb.
The blood of Christ is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Your past is not stronger than His saving power.
Your shame is not a greater authority than His Word.
And your final chapter does not have to be written by the worst thing you have ever done.
But do not delay surrender while assuming you will always have another opportunity.
Turn to Christ today.
Confess your sins.
Trust His death and resurrection.
Follow Him.
And if you have been a believer for years but have grown spiritually cold, return to the truth you once treasured.
Open your Bible again.
Pray honestly again.
Walk in obedience again.
Seek the fellowship and accountability of a faithful local church.
You do not have to pretend that the waiting has been easy.
But you also do not have to let disappointment become the god that governs your heart.
The Lord who asked Sarah, "Is anything too hard for the LORD?" is worthy of your trust.
And the Christ who rose from the grave is worthy of your entire life.
What is the one area of your life where disappointment has made it difficult to trust God?
You do not need to share details you are not ready to make public.
Those words echo the prayer of a desperate father in Mark 9:24.
You may discover that someone reading your words is carrying a similar burden.
And perhaps your willingness to be honest will encourage another believer to stop pretending.
Not to expose their pain, but to remind them that they have not been forgotten.
You never know who is silently wrestling with disappointment, spiritual exhaustion, or the fear that God has abandoned them.
Someone in your family.
An old friend.
A believer who has stopped attending church.
A person who has never truly understood the Gospel.
And there is something more I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to be a place where people simply read something emotional, react for a moment, and move on unchanged.
Our desire is to help people grow deeper in Scripture, understand the Gospel more faithfully, and develop a life of genuine discipleship.
These resources are intended to help believers study God's Word, grow in spiritual maturity, and become better equipped to encourage others in Christ.
It is a practical way of helping sustain and expand the work of creating biblical teaching, sharing Gospel-centered resources, and reaching more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
For believers who desire to honor God through generosity, supporting faithful Christian ministry can be one meaningful expression of stewardship and service.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers may share good things with those who teach them the Word (Galatians 6:6).
But we also need to be clear about something important.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to encourage meaningful conversations about faith.
It is helping make Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of God cannot be purchased.
Your generosity can help the work continue.
But only Christ can save a soul.
That is why everything we do must ultimately lead back to Him.
Not to a platform.
Not to a personality.
Not to a product.
To Jesus.
The One who died for our sins and rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who gives forgiveness freely to those who trust in Him.
The One who can take a life marked by shame and make it a testimony of redeeming grace.
And now, before we finish, return with me to that tent.
An elderly woman stands behind the doorway.
She hears a promise that seems impossible.
She laughs within herself.
She is afraid when her laughter is exposed.
But years of waiting have not made God unfaithful.
Her weakness has not made His word powerless.
And when the appointed time arrives, she holds Isaac.
The child whose name means laughter.
The child whose birth testifies that God did exactly what He said.
But beyond Isaac stands a greater Son.
Jesus Christ.
And because He has conquered sin and death, our hope rests on something stronger than changing circumstances.
It rests on a risen Savior.
So when your heart is weary, remember Abraham.
When your faith is trembling, remember Sarah.
When your sins accuse you, remember the cross.
And when death itself seems to have the final word, remember the empty tomb.
The laughter of Genesis was never the end of the story.
God's faithfulness was.
And for everyone who belongs to Jesus Christ, His faithfulness still is.

The God who heard Sarah laughing behind a tent door also hears the prayers you are afraid to speak aloud—and in Jesus Christ, He has already given you a hope greater than anything this broken world can take away.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU KNOW THE BIBLE. BUT IS THE BIBLE CHANGING YOU? THE TRUTH THAT SHOULD SHAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN AWAKE.
paragraphs: YOU KNOW THE BIBLE. BUT IS THE BIBLE CHANGING YOU? THE TRUTH THAT SHOULD SHAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN AWAKE.

You can memorize Scripture, defend sound doctrine, attend church for decades, and still be dangerously unprepared for the battles happening inside your own heart. Because God never gave you His Word merely to fill your mind. He gave it to equip you for a life transformed by Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply unsettling about a person who knows exactly what the Bible says about forgiveness but refuses to forgive.
Someone who can explain the love of Christ with remarkable accuracy but treats the people closest to them with cruelty.
Someone who can quote Scripture about trusting God, yet secretly lives as though everything depends on their own control.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this.
Sometimes, that person is us.
Not the stranger arguing about religion on Facebook.
Not the hypocrite we quietly criticize.
Not the church member whose failures everyone seems to know.
Us.
The ones who highlight Bible verses but sometimes ignore the very truth we highlight.
The ones who say, “God is good,” while privately wondering whether He has forgotten us.
The ones who know that Jesus commands us to love our enemies, yet still rehearse conversations in our heads about how we would finally put someone in their place.
The ones who have learned how to sound spiritually mature while carrying wounds, bitterness, pride, secret compromises, and unanswered questions that nobody sees.
And before you dismiss this as another message about trying harder to become a better Christian, understand something.
The answer is not simply more religious effort. The answer is a deeper surrender to the Jesus Christ whom the Scriptures reveal.
Because the Bible was never given merely to make you informed.
It was given to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus and to equip you for the life God calls you to live.
And if we miss that, we can spend years studying the Book while resisting the very Lord to whom the Book points.
The apostle Paul wrote something to Timothy that every believer should read slowly, especially those of us who have become comfortable with our spiritual routines.

“All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.” — 2 Timothy 3:16–17, KJV
Read those final words again.
“Throughly furnished unto all good works.”
Paul was not describing a Christian who merely possesses religious information.
He was describing someone being prepared for faithful living.
And the original Greek makes this even more powerful.
The word translated “given by inspiration of God” is θεόπνευστος (theopneustos).
It combines theos, meaning God, and a form associated with breathing or blowing. The word communicates that Scripture is God-breathed—that its ultimate source is God Himself.
Paul was not saying that the Bible is simply an impressive collection of human reflections about God.
He was affirming its divine origin.
Then comes another extraordinary word.
ἐξηρτισμένος (exērtismenos).
It means equipped, furnished, or thoroughly prepared.
It is connected to the verb exartizō, conveying the idea of being fully equipped for a purpose.
The preceding word, ἄρτιος (artios), carries the sense of being capable, complete, or fitted for a task.
Together, these expressions emphasize readiness.
Not sinless perfection achieved by human effort.
Not intellectual superiority.
Not the ability to win every theological argument.
But a life being furnished for the good works God has prepared for His people.
And here is what makes this passage even more beautiful.
Just one verse earlier, Paul reminds Timothy that the sacred writings are able to make him “wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15, KJV).
That is the foundation.
Scripture does not equip us apart from Christ. It leads us to Christ, teaches us His truth, and shapes our lives as we trust and obey Him.
This changes everything.
Because you can know the biblical definition of grace and still live like you must earn God's acceptance.
You can understand the doctrine of forgiveness and still be imprisoned by shame over something Jesus has already called you to bring into the light.
You can recognize every piece of the armor of God in Ephesians 6 and still walk into temptation without prayer, without vigilance, and without dependence on the Lord.
You can know where the verses are.
But when the darkness comes, do you know where to turn?
Think about that for a moment.
What happens when the doctor delivers news you were not prepared to hear?
When the marriage you thought was secure begins falling apart?
When the child you raised in church no longer wants anything to do with God?
When the bills arrive and your bank account cannot carry the weight?
When temptation finds you alone, exhausted, and emotionally vulnerable?
When someone you trusted betrays you?
When you are lying awake at two in the morning, staring at the ceiling, wondering how you can encourage everyone else while your own faith feels painfully fragile?
Suddenly, Bible knowledge is no longer an abstract discussion.
Suddenly, you need the truth you have been reading to steady your soul.
You need to remember that the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
You need to believe that Christ's grace is sufficient in weakness.
You need the wisdom to recognize temptation, the humility to confess sin, and the courage to obey when obedience costs something.
You need more than a verse that looks beautiful on a background image.
You need the God who speaks through His Word.
And that is precisely why biblical discipleship matters.
Not because studying more earns us salvation.
It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10).
Do you see the order?
Good works are not the price of salvation. They are the fruit of God's saving grace.
And Scripture helps train and equip us to walk in that grace.
There is a scene in the Gospels that should make every serious Bible reader uncomfortable.
Jesus is speaking to people who diligently search the Scriptures.
They are not ignorant of religious texts.
They are not strangers to theological discussion.
They know the sacred writings.
Yet Jesus says:
“Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.” — John 5:39–40, KJV
Imagine hearing those words from the very Messiah the Scriptures reveal.
They had studied the testimony.
But they were refusing the One to whom it testified.
They knew the words.
But they would not come to the Word made flesh.
And that raises a question that deserves more than a quick religious answer.
Are we studying Scripture to encounter God's truth and submit to Christ—or merely to become more confident in what we already think we know?
Because it is possible to use Bible knowledge to feed the very pride that Scripture condemns.
It is possible to quote truth without walking in love.
It is possible to correct other people's theology while refusing correction in our own character.
It is possible to become so accustomed to discussing repentance that we forget what it feels like to repent.
And Jesus never called us merely to become experts at describing discipleship.
He called us to follow Him.
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Remember Peter?
The disciple who boldly declared that he was ready to go with Jesus to prison and even to death.
Peter was not unfamiliar with the teachings of Jesus.
He had walked beside Him.
He had heard His voice.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had seen the impossible happen before his eyes.
And yet, on the night of Jesus' arrest, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had spoken with such confidence was suddenly overwhelmed by fear.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
What passed through Peter's heart in that moment, Scripture does not fully describe.
But it tells us what happened next.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.” — Luke 22:62, KJV
There are tears that come from physical pain.
And there are tears that come when the person you thought you were collapses under the weight of what you have done.
Peter knew the truth.
But that night exposed how desperately he still needed grace.
And maybe you understand that feeling.
Maybe you promised God you would never return to that sin.
Then you did.
Maybe you told yourself you had finally overcome that anger.
Then one conversation exposed how much bitterness remained.
Maybe you publicly encouraged people to trust God while privately struggling to believe His promises for yourself.
Maybe you have been so ashamed of your failures that opening your Bible feels less like coming home and more like standing before a mirror you are afraid to face.
But listen carefully.
The same Jesus whom Peter denied was the Jesus who later restored him.
In John 21, after the resurrection, Jesus met Peter beside the Sea of Tiberias.
Three times, Jesus questioned Peter about his love.
And He entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
His need for repentance was real.
But his failure was not stronger than the mercy of the risen Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Not that our sins are harmless.
Not that repentance is optional.
Not that grace excuses continued rebellion.
But that Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose from the dead, and receives those who turn to Him in faith.
He does not merely provide information about forgiveness.
He is the Savior through whom forgiveness comes.
And the Scriptures reveal Him.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the consequences of every wrong decision.
But by bringing forgiveness, restoration, and new life to people who could never rescue themselves.
This is why you must never separate Bible study from the Gospel.
Without Christ at the center, we can turn Scripture into little more than a collection of moral instructions.
Be stronger.
Try harder.
Do better.
Stop failing.
Become impressive.
But the Bible tells a far greater story.
It reveals the holiness of God, the reality of human sin, the promises of redemption, and the fulfillment of those promises in Jesus Christ.
It tells us that our greatest problem is not a lack of motivation.
It is our need for reconciliation with God.
And our greatest hope is not self-improvement.
