It is the crucified and risen Savior.
When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He answered the devil with Scripture.
Matthew 4 records Him repeatedly saying, “It is written.”
He did not treat God's Word as an ornament.
He responded with it in faithful obedience to His Father.
And when Jesus quoted Deuteronomy 8:3, He declared:
“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.” — Matthew 4:4, KJV
The Hebrew text behind the passage in Deuteronomy includes this profound expression:
כִּי עַל־כָּל־מוֹצָא פִי־יְהוָה יִחְיֶה הָאָדָם
Ki al-kol motza fi-YHWH yichyeh ha-adam.
Its sense is:
“But by everything that comes from the mouth of the LORD shall man live.”
The context is Israel's wilderness experience, where God humbled His people, allowed them to hunger, and fed them with manna so they would learn their dependence on Him.
Jesus applies that truth during His own wilderness testing.
Physical bread sustains the body.
But human life cannot be rightly understood or faithfully lived apart from dependence on God.
And there is something deeply revealing about that.
Jesus did not quote Scripture as a magical formula.
He answered temptation by remaining faithful to the Father's will.
That distinction matters.
The Bible is not a collection of spiritual spells we recite to force circumstances to change.
Its power is not in our ability to pronounce certain words with enough intensity.
Its authority comes from the God who speaks.
And its teaching equips us to know His will, resist deception, endure trials, and walk in faithful obedience.
Sometimes that means standing firm when the world pressures you to compromise.
Sometimes it means confessing a sin you have worked hard to conceal.
Sometimes it means refusing revenge.
Sometimes it means telling the truth when a lie would protect your reputation.
Sometimes it means staying faithful when obedience is costly and no one is applauding.
And sometimes it means admitting, with tears in your eyes, that you cannot carry your burdens without God's help.
That is not spiritual weakness to be despised.
That is dependence on the Lord.
James gives us another picture that is impossible to ignore.
He describes a person who hears God's Word but does not act upon it as someone who looks at his natural face in a mirror, walks away, and immediately forgets what he saw (James 1:22–24).
Think about how absurd that is.
Imagine looking into a mirror before leaving the house.
Your face is covered in dirt.
Your hair is a mess.
There is something plainly wrong.
You see it.
You recognize it.
Then you walk away without doing anything.
The mirror did its job.
You simply refused to respond.
And that is what can happen when we read Scripture.
The Word exposes our pride.
We agree.
It confronts our dishonesty.
We underline the verse.
It reveals our unforgiveness.
We share a devotional about it.
It warns us against loving money.
We comment, “Amen.”
Then we close the Bible and return to the very patterns the Word has confronted.
James does not say that hearing is worthless.
He warns against hearing without obedience.
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” — James 1:22, KJV
There is a frightening phrase in that verse.
“Deceiving your own selves.”
Not deceiving the pastor.
Not deceiving the congregation.
Not deceiving your Facebook friends.
Your own selves.
Because religious activity can create the appearance of spiritual progress even when our hearts are resisting God's correction.
We can mistake familiarity for maturity.
We can mistake emotional excitement for repentance.
We can mistake biblical vocabulary for Christlike character.
And we can mistake the ability to explain God's Word for the willingness to obey it.
But Scripture does not call us to become merely impressive hearers.
It calls us to receive God's truth with humility and respond in faith.
That does not mean every struggle disappears after one Bible study.
Some battles are long.
Some habits require patient, repeated repentance.
Some wounds require time, wise counsel, prayer, and the support of other believers.
Some circumstances remain painful even when we are walking faithfully.
The Bible never promises that obedience will eliminate every difficulty.
Jesus Himself told His disciples that they would experience tribulation in the world (John 16:33).
But He also told them to take courage because He had overcome the world.
And that is where genuine spiritual strength begins.
Not in pretending that you are never afraid.
But in learning where to turn when fear comes.
Not in claiming that you have no weaknesses.
But in bringing your weaknesses to Christ.
Not in announcing that you have mastered every temptation.
But in remaining watchful, praying, fleeing sin, and relying on God's grace.
The apostle Paul knew what it meant to live with weakness.
He pleaded with the Lord concerning the thorn in his flesh.
And the answer he received was not the immediate removal of his suffering.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Notice what God did not say.
He did not say, “Paul, you should have memorized more verses.”
He did not say, “If your faith were impressive enough, you would never suffer.”
He pointed Paul to the sufficiency of divine grace.
And Paul's response was to boast in his weaknesses so that the power of Christ might rest upon him.
This is why being equipped by Scripture must never be confused with becoming self-sufficient.
The more deeply God's Word shapes us, the more clearly we recognize our dependence on Jesus.
A spiritually equipped believer is not someone who never needs help.
It is someone who increasingly knows where true help is found.
And perhaps this is the part that someone reading today needs most.
You do not have to pretend that you are doing well when you are not.
You do not have to hide behind a perfect Christian image.
You do not have to make your testimony sound cleaner than your actual journey.
Bring your sins into the light.
Confess them to God.
Seek forgiveness where you have wronged others.
Ask for help when you need it.
Return to Scripture, not to prove that you deserve God's love, but to hear the truth of the Savior who loved us while we were yet sinners.
And remember that the goal of discipleship is not to create a more impressive version of your old self.
It is to become more like Jesus.
To love what He loves.
To hate what is evil.
To grow in holiness.
To serve without demanding recognition.
To speak truth with compassion.
To endure with hope.
To forgive as one who has been forgiven.
To recognize that the person sitting beside you in church may be fighting a battle you know nothing about.
And to remember that the Gospel you desperately need is the same Gospel your neighbor desperately needs.
Maybe this article has been uncomfortable to read.
Maybe you expected encouragement and instead found yourself remembering something you have been avoiding.
A conversation you need to have.
An apology you need to make.
A secret sin you need to confess.
A relationship that needs honesty.
A habit that has slowly been drawing your heart away from God.
Or perhaps you have been exhausted from trying to appear strong.
You have read the verses.
You have attended the services.
You have served others.
You have smiled when people asked how you were doing.
But somewhere along the way, you stopped allowing yourself to be honest about your own need for grace.
If that is you, hear this.
The invitation of Jesus is not to become flawless before approaching Him.
It is to come to Him.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
Those are not the words of a Savior who delights in crushing the weary.
They are the words of the One who calls burdened people to Himself.
And the same Christ who welcomes the weary also calls sinners to repentance and disciples to obedience.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace brings us to the Savior who changes us.
And His Word continually calls us back to that truth.
So perhaps the next time you open your Bible, instead of asking only, “What new information can I learn today?” you might also pray:
“Lord, what are You teaching me about Yourself?”
“What does this passage reveal about Jesus?”
“Where have I been resisting Your truth?”
“What must I believe, confess, surrender, or obey?”
“How can I love others more faithfully because of what I have read?”
And when you finish reading, do not rush away as though completing a chapter were the entire purpose.
Pray.
Reflect.
Respond.
If the passage reveals sin, repent.
If it reveals a promise, trust the God who made it, understanding that promise in its biblical context.
If it commands obedience, ask for grace to obey.
If it reveals the beauty of Christ, worship Him.
If it reminds you of someone who is suffering, consider how you might serve that person.
Because the Word that equips you is not meant to stop with you.
It should bear fruit in your home, your relationships, your work, your church, and your witness to the world.
And this is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community that simply collects inspiring Christian quotations.
Not to produce believers who can repeat spiritual phrases without understanding their meaning.
But to keep pointing people back to the Scriptures, to the Gospel, and to the Lord Jesus Christ.
To encourage serious Bible study.
To strengthen weary believers.
To call wandering hearts to repentance.
To remind the ashamed that forgiveness is found in Christ.
To help people move beyond merely knowing about the Christian faith toward faithfully living as disciples of Jesus.
And that kind of work deserves more than a passing glance.
There may come a day when you need to remember that spiritual maturity is not measured by how many verses you can quote, but by how faithfully you are learning to trust and follow Christ.
Not because sharing a post makes someone spiritually superior.
Not because a social media reaction is the same as discipleship.
But because someone in your circle may be struggling with exactly what we have discussed.
Someone may be tired of pretending.
Someone may be drowning in shame.
Someone may know the Bible but have forgotten the mercy of the Savior it reveals.
Someone may need to be reminded that the Christian life is not about earning grace but responding to the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
And when you share, consider adding a few words of your own.
Tell people why this message matters to you.
A sincere testimony can reach a heart that a polished message alone might never reach.
Or send this privately to a person who needs gentleness more than public attention.
And if you are reading this while carrying a struggle you have not known how to express, I want to invite you to do something simple but meaningful.
If you are exhausted and need prayer, you can comment, “Pray for me.”
If you have been wrestling with repentance, you can simply say, “Jesus, help me surrender.”
You do not need to reveal private details to strangers.
But you may discover that you are not the only person who is still learning how to trust God in the middle of the struggle.
Your story may encourage someone who has almost given up.
There is room here for honest questions, biblical learning, spiritual encouragement, and the continuing call to follow Jesus.
But I also want to speak about something practical, because Gospel ministry and discipleship resources require real work, real time, and real support.
These resources are part of a larger desire to make biblical teaching and Christian encouragement more accessible.
And if you believe this work is worth continuing, you can help sustain and expand it.
It is not a purchase of salvation.
It does not make you more loved by Jesus than someone who cannot afford to give.
And it should never replace the responsibilities you already have to your family, your local church, or those in genuine need.
But it can be a meaningful, voluntary act of generosity and stewardship.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not under compulsion.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
It helps sustain the work of creating and sharing Scripture-centered articles, devotionals, Christian resources, and discipleship materials.
It can help us continue reaching people who may never be able to pay for the resources they need.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
Because the goal is not to fill homes with Christian merchandise while leaving hearts spiritually hungry.
The goal is to encourage people to open the Scriptures, understand the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Jesus.
You can pray for the work.
You can invite others to read the Scriptures.
And you can encourage a struggling believer with a simple message of hope.
There is no shame in being unable to give financially.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Christ's grace cannot be purchased.
What matters is that Jesus Christ is proclaimed faithfully, that His Word is handled truthfully, and that people are encouraged to follow Him.
And I want you to remember one final thing.
One day, the number of Bible verses you posted on Facebook will not be the measure of your faithfulness.
Neither will the number of arguments you won, the number of Christian books on your shelf, or the number of people who admired your spiritual knowledge.
The question that should concern us now is whether we are truly hearing the voice of our Shepherd and following Him.
Did the truth you learned lead you to repentance?
Did the grace you received make you more gracious?
Did the forgiveness you celebrated teach you to forgive?
Did the Scriptures you studied make you more attentive to the suffering of others?
Did your growing knowledge of Christ lead you to love Him more deeply?
And when you failed, did you run from Him in shame, or return to Him in repentance and faith?
Because the Christian life is not a performance in which we prove ourselves worthy of Jesus.
It is a life of faith in the One who gave Himself for us.
The Bible equips us by directing our hearts toward His truth, correcting our errors, exposing our sins, strengthening our hope, and teaching us to live as people who belong to Him.
And through it all, we must never forget who stands at the center of the story.
Not us.
Not our achievements.
Not our religious reputation.
Jesus Christ.
The One who was crucified for our sins.
The One who rose again.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who restores the fallen.
The One who calls His people to take up their cross and follow Him.
The One whose grace does not merely comfort us in our brokenness, but begins transforming the way we live.
So open your Bible again.
Not as someone trying to impress God with how much you know.
Not as someone attempting to earn the forgiveness Christ purchased at the cross.
But as a disciple who desperately needs the truth of God.
Read with humility.
Study with care.
Pray with honesty.
Repent when convicted.
Trust when afraid.
Obey when challenged.
Love when it costs you something.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be reaching the end of your life without knowing every detail of Scripture.
It would be spending your life surrounded by biblical truth while continually refusing the Savior to whom that truth points.
Do not become so familiar with the words about Jesus that you forget to fall at the feet of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE TOLD HIS WORKERS TO DROP THE GRAIN ON PURPOSE… BUT THE POOR WIDOW HAD NO IDEA WHO WAS WATCHING HER.
paragraphs: HE TOLD HIS WORKERS TO DROP THE GRAIN ON PURPOSE… BUT THE POOR WIDOW HAD NO IDEA WHO WAS WATCHING HER.
She thought she was gathering leftovers just to survive another day. But in a field belonging to a wealthy stranger, God was quietly writing a story that would lead all the way to Jesus Christ.
“And let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave them, that she may glean them, and rebuke her not.” — Ruth 2:16 (KJV)
There is a kind of poverty that doesn't just empty your pockets.
It empties your confidence.

It makes you rehearse what you're going to say before asking for help. It makes you pretend you're not hungry. It teaches you to smile when someone asks how you're doing because explaining the truth would take more strength than you have left.
And sometimes, the hardest part isn't having nothing.
It's remembering when you had something.
A home. A family. A future you could almost touch.
Then something happened.
A death. A betrayal. A financial collapse. A diagnosis. A season so cruel that you stopped making plans and started praying only for enough strength to survive tomorrow.
If you've ever been there, you need to meet a woman named Ruth.
Because one morning, she walked into a field looking for leftover grain.
She had no idea that the owner of that field had already noticed her.
And she certainly didn't know that her ordinary struggle to survive would become part of one of the most extraordinary redemption stories in Scripture.
But before we reach the moment when a wealthy landowner tells his workers to deliberately leave food behind for her, you need to understand something.
Ruth wasn't walking into that field with a beautiful testimony. She was walking in carrying a broken life.
Her husband was dead.
Her father-in-law was dead.
Her brother-in-law was dead.
The family she had married into had been devastated by loss.
Her mother-in-law, Naomi, was returning to Bethlehem after years in Moab. Naomi had left Judah with a husband and two sons. Now she was returning without them.
The grief was so deep that when people recognized her, she said something almost unbearable.
“Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.” — Ruth 1:20 (KJV)
Naomi means pleasant. Mara means bitter.
She was essentially saying, “Don't call me by the name I had before life broke my heart.”
Have you ever felt that?
When the person you used to be feels like a stranger?
When people remember your old smile, but they don't know what it costs you to produce one now?
Naomi was grieving.
And Ruth, her Moabite daughter-in-law, was grieving too.
Yet Ruth made an astonishing decision.
She refused to abandon Naomi.
She left her homeland, her familiar surroundings, and the possibility of rebuilding her life among her own people.
Instead, she spoke words that would echo across generations.
“Whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” — Ruth 1:16 (KJV)
Those weren't the words of a woman who knew everything would work out.
They were the words of a woman choosing faithfulness without a guarantee of comfort.
And that matters.
Because sometimes obedience doesn't immediately lead you into abundance.
Sometimes it leads you into a field where you still have to pick up grain from the ground.
Ruth and Naomi arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
That detail sounds small.
It wasn't.

In ancient Israel, God had commanded landowners not to harvest every last corner of their fields or gather every remaining stalk. The leftovers were to be available for the poor, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19 establish this principle.
God's law made room for people whose lives had become painfully vulnerable.
The poor were not supposed to be invisible.
The foreigner was not supposed to be forgotten.
The widow was not supposed to be treated as disposable.
And Ruth was both a foreigner and a widow.
So she went out to glean.
Not to collect a salary.
Not to negotiate a business deal.
Not to demand luxury.
She went to gather what the harvesters left behind.
Imagine her that morning.
The sun rising over Bethlehem.
Workers already moving through the fields.
The sound of stalks being cut.
Dust clinging to her clothes.
The uncertainty of whether she would return home carrying enough food for herself and Naomi.
She didn't know how the day would unfold.
She only knew that two women needed to eat.
And then Scripture gives us a sentence so ordinary that we could easily miss its beauty.
“And her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz.” — Ruth 2:3 (KJV)
Her hap.
In the Hebrew text, the expression is וַיִּקֶר מִקְרֶהָ (vayyiqer miqrehā), an emphatic way of describing what happened to her as a chance occurrence.
From Ruth's limited perspective, she simply happened upon that field.
The narrator does not describe an audible voice from heaven directing her steps. There is no angel standing at the entrance. No miraculous sign floating above the barley.
She simply arrived.
But as the story unfolds, the reader begins to recognize something deeper.
What looked ordinary would become extraordinarily significant.
And isn't that how much of life feels?
We want God to explain the entire journey.
Instead, we often receive enough light for the next step.
We want to know how the story ends.
But all we can see is the field in front of us.
Ruth didn't know that the landowner was a man named Boaz.
She didn't know that he was a relative of her deceased father-in-law's family.
She didn't know how important that relationship would eventually become.
She was simply trying to survive.
Then Boaz arrived.
And he noticed her.
“Whose damsel is this?” — Ruth 2:5 (KJV)
It's a brief question.
But think about what it means.
In a field full of people, a wealthy man noticed a poor foreign widow working behind the harvesters.
He asked about her.
His overseer explained who she was and described her diligence.
Boaz had already heard about Ruth's extraordinary loyalty to Naomi.
He knew that she had left her homeland and had come to live among people she had not previously known.
And rather than treating her as an inconvenience, he spoke to her with kindness.
He told her to remain in his fields, to stay near the women working there, and to drink from the water his workers had drawn.
He had also instructed the young men not to touch her.
In a world where a foreign widow could face serious vulnerability, those instructions mattered.
Boaz wasn't merely offering grain.
He was providing access, protection, and dignity.
Ruth was astonished.
She fell on her face and asked why she had found favor in his sight, since she was a foreigner.
And Boaz answered with one of the most beautiful blessings in the book.
“The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.” — Ruth 2:12 (KJV)
Under whose wings.
The Hebrew word translated wings is כָּנָף (kānāf), which can mean a wing or the edge of a garment, depending on its context.
Here it evokes the shelter and protection found in the Lord.
Ruth had come to seek refuge under the wings of Israel's God.
And now, standing before her, was a man whose generosity would become one of the means through which that refuge was experienced.
Please don't miss this.
Boaz prayed for Ruth to experience God's protection, and then he acted in ways that helped protect her.
Sometimes we pray for hungry people while refusing to share our bread.
We pray for lonely people while ignoring their messages.
We pray for struggling families while pretending we don't see their needs.
Boaz reminds us that genuine faith can become visible through practical mercy.
And then came the meal.
The moment that makes this story even more tender.
Ruth 2:14 says:
“And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar.”
He invited her to eat.
Not merely to stand nearby while everyone else enjoyed their food.
Not to wait until the workers were finished.
He invited her to the meal.
Scripture says she sat beside the reapers, and Boaz passed her roasted grain.
She ate until she was satisfied.
And she had some left over.
Stop there for a moment.
A woman who had entered the field uncertain of what she would eat was now sitting down with enough food to satisfy her hunger.
There is something profoundly moving about that.
Not because the meal solved every problem in her life.
It didn't.
Naomi was still a widow.
Ruth was still grieving.
Their future was still uncertain.
But for that moment, hunger gave way to fullness.
And kindness interrupted hardship.
Some of you know exactly how much that can mean.
When someone unexpectedly paid for your groceries.
When a friend brought food without making you explain why you needed it.
When a stranger helped you while you were trying desperately not to cry.
When someone treated you with dignity during a season when life had made you feel small.
You may have forgotten the date.
But you remember the kindness.
Because mercy has a way of staying with us.
And Boaz wasn't finished.
After Ruth rose to continue gleaning, he gave his workers a remarkable instruction.
“Let her glean even among the sheaves, and reproach her not.” — Ruth 2:15 (KJV)
Then came the command that makes this entire scene unforgettable.
“And let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave them, that she may glean them, and rebuke her not.” — Ruth 2:16 (KJV)
Leave some grain behind. Deliberately. For her.
The Hebrew is especially vivid.
וְגַם שֹׁל־תָּשֹׁלּוּ לָהּ מִן־הַצְּבָתִים
Vegām shōl-tāshōllū lāh min-hatstsevātīm.
The wording emphasizes that the workers were to pull out or drop grain from the gathered bundles for Ruth.
The familiar KJV expression “handfuls of purpose” means this was intentional.
Not an accident.
Not carelessness.
Not grain dropped because the workers were incompetent.
Boaz deliberately instructed them to leave extra for her.
And they were not to rebuke or humiliate her for gathering it.
Imagine that scene.
Ruth bends down.
Picks up grain.
Moves forward.
Bends down again.
More grain.
She continues working.
More provision.
What she could not see was the instruction that had been given on her behalf.
The grain didn't fall by accident.
Someone had decided to be generous.
And the beautiful thing is that Boaz did not need to make a public spectacle of his kindness.
He didn't demand that Ruth announce his generosity to the entire village.
He didn't make her perform gratitude before she could receive help.
He simply made sure she could gather more.
That is a picture of human generosity shaped by reverence for God.
But we must be careful with this story.

Ruth 2 does not promise that every Christian will receive unexpected money, that every financial hardship will suddenly disappear, or that God has secretly instructed someone wealthy to make us prosperous.
That would place a promise in the passage that Scripture itself does not make.
The real message is both humbler and more powerful.
God's providence can be at work in ordinary circumstances.
God cares about vulnerable people.
And those who have resources are called to use them with justice, compassion, and generosity.
Sometimes God's provision comes through the obedience of another person.
And sometimes you are the person God is calling to leave extra grain.
That may be the part of this story we would rather avoid.
Because it's comforting to imagine ourselves as Ruth.
The struggling person.
The one who needs help.
The one waiting for someone to notice.
And there are seasons when that is exactly where we are.
But what if, today, God is calling you to act like Boaz?
What if someone around you is trying to survive a season you've already come through?
What if the single mother beside you isn't asking for luxury, but breathing room?
What if the exhausted father at church doesn't need another lecture about faith, but someone willing to help him carry a burden?
What if the widow living quietly down the street has been praying that somebody would remember her?
What if the person who always says “I'm fine” is one conversation away from admitting they're not?
The question isn't merely whether we believe God provides.
The question is whether we're willing to become generous with what He has entrusted to us.
Because the same Bible that tells us about Boaz also tells us:
“But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?” — 1 John 3:17 (KJV)
That verse doesn't allow us to admire compassion from a distance.
It calls us to practice it.
And the Gospel takes this even deeper.
Because Ruth's story doesn't end with extra barley.
When Ruth returned home, Naomi was astonished by what she had gathered.
Ruth had gleaned about an ephah of barley that day, a substantial amount for one day's work.
She also brought Naomi the food she had saved from her meal.
Even in her own hunger, she had remembered someone else.
Then Naomi asked where she had worked.
And Ruth told her the name.
Boaz.
Suddenly, Naomi recognized something Ruth had not fully understood.
Boaz was a close relative.
One of the family's potential redeemers.
In the Hebrew, the word is גֹּאֵל (gōʾēl).
A goel was a family redeemer, someone who could fulfill particular responsibilities to protect or restore family interests under Israel's laws and customs.
The concept is richer and more specific than simply being a kind wealthy man.
And as the narrative continues, Boaz acts honorably to redeem family property and marry Ruth, following the legal process described in Ruth 4.
Their story involves more than romantic attraction.
It involves faithfulness.
Responsibility.
Public integrity.
The restoration of a family line threatened by death and loss.
And something extraordinary happens.
Ruth, the foreign widow who once gathered leftovers behind harvesters, becomes the wife of Boaz.
They have a son named Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And generations later, from David's royal line, comes Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:5 specifically includes Boaz and Ruth in the genealogy leading to Jesus.
Think about that.
The woman who entered Bethlehem with grief and uncertainty became part of the family history of the Messiah.
The field where she gathered barley was not merely the setting of a beautiful love story.
It was part of a much larger account of redemption.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Boaz was a generous and honorable redeemer within his family's circumstances.
But Boaz was not sinless.
He was not the Savior of the world.
And we should not force every detail of his actions into a hidden prophecy about Jesus.
Instead, his story helps us appreciate the biblical theme of redemption that finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ.
Boaz could help restore Ruth and Naomi's family circumstances.
Jesus Christ came to redeem sinners from sin and death.
Boaz provided grain.
Jesus declared Himself the Bread of Life.
Boaz welcomed a vulnerable foreigner.
Jesus receives all who come to Him in faith.
Boaz acted at personal cost to fulfill his family responsibility.
Jesus gave Himself as the sacrifice for our sins.
The difference is immeasurable.
Because our deepest poverty is not merely financial.
It is spiritual.
We have all sinned.
We have all fallen short of God's glory.
No amount of money, religious performance, social status, or outward respectability can erase our guilt before a holy God.
And yet Scripture declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
The Greek word translated grace is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor and gift, and in this passage it identifies salvation as God's gracious work rather than something we earn.
We cannot purchase it.
We cannot deserve it.
We cannot make ourselves righteous by collecting enough good deeds.
Christ died for our sins and rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe the Gospel.
And that means your past does not have to be the final word over your future.
Not because your past was harmless.
Not because your sins didn't matter.
Not because every earthly consequence will disappear.
But because Jesus Christ is a greater Savior than you are a sinner.
Maybe your story contains things you wish you could erase.
Maybe you've hurt people.
Maybe you've wasted years chasing things that left you emptier than before.
Maybe you once walked closely with God, but somewhere along the way, compromise became comfortable and prayer became unfamiliar.
Maybe you've learned how to look spiritually healthy while quietly falling apart.
You can fool a crowd.
You can hide behind religious language.
You can even convince yourself that you're fine.
But you cannot heal a heart by pretending it isn't wounded.
And you cannot be reconciled to God by hiding the sin Christ calls you to confess and forsake.
The invitation of Jesus is not to polish your reputation.
It is to repent and come to Him.
Not after you've made yourself worthy.
Not after you've repaired every broken thing.
Come in faith, acknowledging your sin and trusting the crucified and risen Savior.
Because the Gospel is not about a good person becoming slightly better.
It is about the dead being made alive through Christ.
And that brings us back to Ruth.
There is something else we should remember.
Ruth did not stop being faithful while she waited for her circumstances to change.
She worked.
She cared for Naomi.
She responded with humility.
She listened to wise counsel.
She lived faithfully through a season when the ending was still hidden from her.
And perhaps that is the word someone needs tonight.
You may not know what God will do with the next chapter of your life.
You may still be grieving.
Still rebuilding.
Still searching for work.
Still waiting for reconciliation.
Still trying to understand why something you prayed desperately to keep was taken away.
I will not tell you that every loss will be reversed in this lifetime.
Scripture doesn't promise that.
I will not tell you that every widow will marry again, every debt will disappear, or every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But I can tell you that the God revealed in Scripture has not ceased to be faithful.
His character is not measured by the ease of our circumstances.
His love is revealed supremely at the cross of Jesus Christ.
And His promise to those who belong to Christ reaches beyond even death itself.
That is a hope stronger than a temporary change of fortune.
So if you're in a difficult season, don't despise the ordinary steps of faithfulness available to you today.
Pray.
Tell the truth.
Seek help when you need it.
Work honestly where you can.
Receive kindness without shame.
Offer kindness without demanding applause.
Remain near the people who will point you toward Christ.
And remember that Ruth's story was not ultimately about a woman becoming rich.
It was about the faithfulness of God working through ordinary people, real suffering, and costly acts of love.
Now, I want to ask you something personal.
Not for the sake of a religious performance.
Not because you owe strangers an explanation of your pain.
But because sometimes an honest sentence can help another person realize they are not alone.
Have you been living in a season where you're just trying to gather enough strength for one more day?
You don't have to share details you're not ready to share.
But perhaps your honest response will become an encouragement to someone else who has been suffering in silence.
Not to glorify the person above God.
But to remind others that compassion is still possible in a world that can feel painfully indifferent.
There may be someone reading your words who is beginning to believe nobody cares.
Your testimony could encourage them to keep going.
And if this story has brought someone to mind, don't ignore that thought.
Send this article privately to someone who needs comfort.
A person who appears successful may be grieving privately.
A friend who jokes constantly may be struggling with loneliness.
A family member who has stopped attending church may be carrying questions they've been afraid to ask.
And someone who doesn't yet believe in Jesus may need to hear the Gospel explained with compassion rather than condemnation.
You cannot force someone to believe.
But you can lovingly point them to the One who saves.
Not because these words possess special power, but because the Scriptures behind them are worth returning to.
Come back to Ruth 2 when you're tempted to believe your ordinary faithfulness doesn't matter.
Come back to Ruth 4 when you need to remember that God can work through generations in ways we cannot foresee.
Come back to Ephesians 2 when you need to remember that salvation is a gift of grace, not a reward for religious achievement.
And come back to the cross whenever your heart begins to confuse God's love with your circumstances.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish emotional stories.
Not merely to collect reactions, shares, or followers.
But to keep directing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, discipleship, and the hope of the Gospel.
There is room here for people who are learning, struggling, questioning, repenting, and growing.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, strengthen their faith, and develop a more consistent walk with Jesus Christ.
We want the message of Scripture to remain accessible, including to those who cannot afford to purchase Christian books or study materials.
That mission takes time, work, and resources.
And this is where Ruth's story becomes more than something we admire.
It becomes something we can practice.
Boaz had resources, and he chose to use some of them to help someone else.
He didn't give because Ruth could repay him.
He gave because mercy mattered.
For those who are able, it can be one expression of Christian generosity and a voluntary offering toward ministry work.
But I want to be clear about something important.
Your giving does not purchase God's favor.
Biblical tithes and offerings should never be reduced to a commercial transaction, and your responsibilities to your local church, family, and those in need deserve prayerful consideration.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not compelled.
God loves a cheerful giver.
So this invitation is not meant to pressure anyone who is struggling financially.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The free resources remain an important part of this mission.
A small, consistent contribution can help a ministry plan, create, publish, and continue serving people over time.
Those items are simply an added expression of appreciation.
It may reach someone who is struggling.
Someone who needs to hear about repentance and forgiveness.
Someone who has been away from church for years.
Someone who has never understood what Jesus Christ accomplished through His death and resurrection.
If even one person is encouraged to open the Bible, seek the Lord, or take a serious step toward faith in Christ, that is worth caring about.
We are not trying to build a kingdom around a Facebook page.
We want to point people toward the Kingdom of God.
Now, before you leave, I want you to picture Ruth one last time.
Not at her wedding.
Not holding her son.
Not standing in the family line that would eventually lead to David.
Picture her at the beginning.
A grieving widow.
A foreigner in Bethlehem.
Bent over in a field.
Picking up grain from the ground.
She could not see the generations ahead.
She did not know her name would be preserved in Scripture.
She did not know that centuries later, people across the world would read about her faithfulness.
She was simply living the day in front of her.
And somewhere nearby, a man had instructed his workers to leave extra grain for her.
There was kindness she hadn't arranged.
There was help she hadn't demanded.
There was a larger story she could not yet understand.
But the greatest beauty of Ruth's story isn't that she eventually found a husband.
It's that her story points us toward the God whose redemptive purposes would culminate in Jesus Christ.
The Savior who came not merely to improve our circumstances, but to rescue us from sin.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Savior whose blood was shed for our forgiveness.
The Savior who rose from the grave.
The Savior who can take a life marked by shame, failure, and rebellion and make it a testimony of grace.
So if you're Ruth today, weary and uncertain, keep looking to Christ.
If you're Naomi today, grieving what you've lost, bring your bitterness honestly before the Lord.
If you're in a position like Boaz, with something to share, don't wait until generosity becomes convenient.
And if you've been running from God, don't confuse another day of delay with another day of safety.
Turn to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the grace you could never earn.
And begin walking in the new life He gives.
Because the most important question isn't whether someone has noticed you in a field.
It's whether you have responded to the Savior who calls sinners to Himself.
“I'm still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Lord, make me willing.”
Or share what God has been teaching you through this passage.
Your story may help someone else find the courage to open theirs.
Because Gospel ministry is never supposed to make people feel that grace has a price tag.
Jesus has already paid the price for our redemption.
And that is why this story will always be bigger than a wealthy landowner and a poor widow.
It is a reminder that the God who worked through an ordinary barley field was carrying forward a redemptive story that would lead to the cross, the empty tomb, and the hope of eternal life.
Ruth bent down to gather what others left behind, never knowing that her name would one day stand in the earthly family history of the Redeemer who came to rescue the lost.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LET THE ONE WITHOUT SIN CAST THE FIRST STONE”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN HOLDING A STONE ALL ALONG?
paragraphs: “LET THE ONE WITHOUT SIN CAST THE FIRST STONE”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN HOLDING A STONE ALL ALONG?

They dragged a guilty woman before Jesus, expecting Him to condemn her. But what happened next exposed the hearts of her accusers, revealed the holiness of God, and showed a kind of mercy that never makes peace with sin. This is the part of John 8:1–11 we cannot afford to misunderstand.
There is something terrifying about being exposed.
Not simply being caught doing something wrong.
Being exposed.
When the thing you prayed nobody would discover suddenly becomes the thing everybody is talking about.
When your worst decision becomes your reputation.
When people stop seeing your humanity and start seeing only your failure.
Imagine standing in front of a crowd that already knows your sin.
No opportunity to explain.
No one stepping forward to defend you.
Every face looking at you as though your entire life can be summarized by the worst thing you have ever done.
And then someone picks up a stone.
Now imagine something even more uncomfortable.
What if you are not the woman standing in the middle?
What if you are the person holding the stone?
Because the story of the woman caught in adultery is not merely about a sinner who needed mercy.
It is also about religious people who needed to discover how desperately they needed mercy themselves.
And before we finish this story, we need to confront one question:
Are we more interested in seeing sinners restored—or seeing them punished?
The answer may reveal more about our relationship with Jesus than we are prepared to admit.
The scene unfolds in John 8:1–11.
But before entering it, there is an important truth we must acknowledge if we want to handle Scripture faithfully.

The account commonly called the woman caught in adultery, traditionally located in John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel. Other manuscripts preserve it, sometimes in different locations. For this reason, many modern Bible translations place the passage in brackets or include a textual note.

That does not mean we should pretend the account has no history or spiritual significance. It means we should be honest about its textual status. We cannot establish with certainty that John originally wrote these verses, and we should not build a doctrine upon this disputed passage alone.
Yet the mercy, holiness, repentance, and forgiveness reflected in this account can be examined alongside teachings firmly established throughout the New Testament.
And with that understanding, consider the scene the passage places before us.
Jesus is teaching in the temple.
People have gathered around Him.
Then suddenly, the atmosphere changes.
The scribes and Pharisees bring forward a woman caught in adultery.
They place her in the middle of the crowd.
Not quietly.
Not privately.
Publicly.
Her sin is now everybody's business.
Her shame has become a spectacle.
And her accusers have a question.
“Teacher, this woman was caught in adultery, in the very act.”
They appeal to the Law of Moses, then ask Jesus what He says should happen to her.
At first glance, it sounds like a question about righteousness.
But the passage exposes their actual intention.
They are testing Jesus, seeking grounds to accuse Him.
The woman is not their ultimate target.
Jesus is.
And suddenly the cruelty of the moment becomes even clearer.
A human being has been turned into a weapon in a religious confrontation.
Her humiliation is useful to them.
Her suffering is secondary.
Her future hardly seems to matter.
They want an answer that will trap Jesus.
And they are willing to destroy a woman in the process.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
Have you ever watched someone else's failure become entertainment?
A marriage collapses, and people rush to discuss the details.
A church leader falls into sin, and some people seem more excited about the scandal than grieved by the damage.
Someone confesses a struggle, and instead of receiving wise, truthful, compassionate help, they become the subject of whispered conversations.
A person's past resurfaces online, and strangers who know almost nothing about their life compete to deliver the harshest judgment.
Sometimes even Christians participate.
We call it defending righteousness.
We call it exposing darkness.
We call it standing for truth.
And sometimes exposing wrongdoing really is necessary, especially to protect victims, confront abuse, and pursue justice.
But there is a difference between confronting evil because we love what is right and enjoying another person's humiliation because it makes us feel superior.
You can speak the language of holiness while secretly feeding the appetite of pride.
That is what makes this account so disturbing.
The accusers know the Law.
But their hearts are being exposed by the very One they are attempting to trap.
There is another detail that should trouble us.
Where is the man?
The woman has been caught in adultery, yet only she is presented.

Under Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22, the law concerning adultery addressed both parties. The precise legal circumstances matter, and the passage does not tell us everything that happened before this confrontation.
We cannot claim to know why the man is absent.
But his absence raises an unavoidable question about the consistency and motives of those bringing the accusation.
If this is truly about faithful obedience to God's Law, why is only one accused person standing there?
Selective outrage is not the same as biblical justice.
And religious hypocrisy becomes especially dangerous when it uses genuine moral truth as cover for dishonest motives.
Then Jesus does something nobody seems to expect.
He bends down.
And writes on the ground.
The Greek text uses the verb κατέγραφεν (kategraphen), describing His act of writing.
For centuries, readers have wondered what Jesus wrote.
The names of the accusers?
Their secret sins?
A passage from Scripture?
A warning?
Perhaps something connected to Jeremiah 17:13?
We do not know.
The passage never tells us.
And we should resist the temptation to turn an imaginative possibility into a biblical fact.
What matters is what Jesus actually says.
As the questioning continues, He straightens and declares:
“Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” — John 8:7, ESV
In Greek, the central expression is:
Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν
Ho anamartētos hymōn.
“The one without sin among you.”
The word ἀναμάρτητος (anamartētos) means “without sin” or “sinless.”
But we need to be careful.
Jesus is not teaching that human courts must release every guilty person because judges and witnesses are sinners.
Nor is He teaching that Christians must never identify wrongdoing, confront sin, practice church discipline, or protect those who have been harmed.
That interpretation would contradict other clear biblical teachings, including Matthew 18:15–17, Galatians 6:1, and Romans 13:1–4.
The point is not that sin no longer matters.
The point is that these particular accusers cannot escape the examination of their own hearts.
They are attempting to use the Law against Jesus while their own motives are compromised.
And Jesus turns the moment of accusation into a moment of moral accountability.
Think about that.
They arrived expecting to examine a woman's guilt.
Instead, they found themselves standing before someone who could see through their performance of righteousness.
There are moments when Scripture does this to us.
We open the Bible looking for a verse that proves somebody else is wrong.
And suddenly, the Word confronts something we have been hiding.
Our bitterness.
Our dishonesty.
Our secret lust.
Our envy.
Our unforgiveness.
Our appetite for gossip.
Our habit of treating people as permanently disqualified because of failures we would desperately want forgiven if they were our own.
We are quick to recognize the sin that disgusts us.
Slower to recognize the pride that pleases us.
We condemn the person whose failure became public while protecting the sins that remain private.
And sometimes our greatest spiritual danger is not that we have stopped believing in God.
It is that we have become comfortable using God's truth without allowing it to transform our own hearts.
Jesus warned about this elsewhere.
In Matthew 7:3–5, He describes the absurdity of noticing a speck in another person's eye while ignoring a plank in our own.
Notice what He actually teaches.
Remove the plank first.
Then you can see clearly to help your brother.
He does not say the speck should remain forever.
He calls for repentance and clarity before correction.
That is the difference between self-righteous condemnation and humble restoration.
One wants to stand above another sinner.
The other remembers that every sinner needs grace.
And now the stones begin to fall.
Not because the woman has been declared morally innocent.
Not because adultery has become acceptable.
Not because God's holiness has changed.
But because the accusers begin leaving.
One by one.
The older ones first, according to the account.
We are not told exactly what each person thought or felt. We should not pretend to know their private reasons.
But the narrative makes the outcome unmistakable.
The public accusation collapses.
The crowd of accusers disappears.
And the woman remains before Jesus.
Imagine that moment.
The voices that had demanded her punishment are gone.
The people who treated her as an object lesson have walked away.
The woman who had been placed in the middle of a hostile crowd now stands before the One who has not joined their condemnation.
Then Jesus asks:
“Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?”
She answers:
“No one, Lord.”
And Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” — John 8:11, ESV
Do not rush past those words.
Because if we misunderstand them, we misunderstand the very heart of this story.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
And:
“Sin no more.”
Mercy.
And holiness.
Compassion.
And a call to change.
Not one without the other.
Jesus does not say, “Your adultery was never wrong.”
He does not say, “Continue living however you please.”
He does not announce that sin is an outdated concept invented by religious people.
He refuses to condemn her in this confrontation, and He calls her away from sin.
That distinction matters.
In the Greek text, the final instruction reads:
πορεύου, ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
Poreuou, apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
The command calls for a decisive departure from sinful living.
It is not a promise that she will never struggle again.
Nor does the passage tell us what happened afterward.
We are not given her name, her later testimony, or the story of her remaining years.
And that silence matters.
Because sometimes preachers tell this story as though Scripture describes her becoming a disciple, rebuilding her life, or following Jesus for decades.
Those may be moving possibilities.
But they are not recorded facts.
We must not add details simply because they make the ending more emotionally satisfying.
The words Jesus speaks are already powerful enough.
Mercy does not give sin permission to remain. Mercy opens the door to a life no longer ruled by it.
And here is where this story begins to reach beyond the temple courtyard.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be the woman.
Not necessarily because of adultery.
Maybe your marriage broke apart after decisions you deeply regret.
Maybe you betrayed someone's trust.
Maybe you fell into a pattern of sexual sin that left you feeling divided between the person you present publicly and the person you are privately.
Maybe you have spent years carrying the shame of addiction, dishonesty, bitterness, or a secret nobody knows.
Maybe you once served God with joy, but now you avoid prayer because you feel ashamed to approach Him.
You still believe in Jesus.
You still know the worship songs.
You still recognize the Bible verses.
But somewhere along the way, you began believing that your failure had become your identity.
And the hardest person to face is no longer the one who discovered your sin.
It is yourself.
You remember what you did.
You remember who was hurt.
You remember the opportunities you wasted.
You remember the promises you made to God and then broke.
And sometimes, even after you have confessed your sin, your memory continues acting like a courtroom.
The evidence is presented again.
The accusations return.
And you feel as though you must keep paying for something you cannot undo.
But hear this carefully.
The Christian Gospel does not teach that forgiveness makes consequences disappear.
Some relationships may need time to heal.
Some trust may never be fully restored.
Some actions require restitution, accountability, legal consequences, or long-term changes.
If you harmed someone, grace does not erase your responsibility toward them.
And if someone harmed you, forgiveness does not require you to deny what happened, abandon appropriate boundaries, or remain in danger.
Biblical mercy never requires us to pretend evil is harmless.
But neither does the Gospel teach that a repentant sinner must remain forever imprisoned beneath the identity of their worst failure.
Listen to the apostle Paul.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, ESV
That is not a declaration that everybody is automatically forgiven regardless of their response to Christ.
It is a glorious promise concerning those who are in Him.
And Paul explains why.
God has acted through His Son to deal with sin.
The forgiveness Christians proclaim is not based on God pretending sin does not matter.
It is grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
At the cross, the seriousness of sin and the depth of divine love meet.
Jesus, the sinless Savior, bears sin's judgment on behalf of His people.
He dies.
He is buried.
And He rises again.
That is the Gospel proclaimed in passages such as 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Romans 3:23–26, and 1 Peter 2:24.
We must not flatten the distinction between the disputed account in John 8 and the full doctrine of salvation taught elsewhere in Scripture.
The passage itself does not narrate the cross or explain every dimension of justification.
But read in the light of the New Testament's wider testimony, it directs our attention toward a Savior whose mercy never requires Him to abandon righteousness.
And that changes everything.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that sin is imaginary.
It is the announcement that sin is so serious that we cannot save ourselves, and God's grace is so great that He sent His Son to save sinners.
The Greek word commonly translated “grace” is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor, gift, and gracious generosity.
In Ephesians 2:8–9, Paul teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not something earned by our works.
And verse 10 continues by describing believers as created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not purchased by our obedience.
Obedience is the fruit of a life being transformed by grace.
This is why the words “go, and sin no more” must never be separated from the mercy that precedes them.
Jesus does not offer forgiveness as a reward for becoming perfect first.
Nor does He call people to remain comfortable in rebellion.
He calls sinners to turn toward Him.
The biblical word for repentance, μετάνοια (metanoia), refers to repentance, a change of mind and direction involving a turning away from sin and toward God.
It is more than feeling embarrassed after getting caught.
More than crying because people found out.
More than promising to improve because consequences have become painful.
True repentance begins when we stop defending what God calls sin and turn toward the Savior who can forgive and change us.
Sometimes repentance is accompanied by tears.
Sometimes by confession.
Sometimes by the painful decision to end a relationship that dishonors God.
Sometimes by admitting that we need help with an addiction.
Sometimes by returning what we stole.
Sometimes by telling the truth after years of deception.
Sometimes by apologizing without demanding immediate forgiveness.
Sometimes by finally seeking accountability instead of making another private promise we have no plan to keep.
And sometimes repentance begins with a trembling prayer:
“Lord Jesus, I have been hiding. I have made excuses. I have called my sin a weakness when I knew I was choosing it. Please forgive me. Teach me to walk in Your truth.”
That is not weakness.
That is surrender.
But perhaps you have been reading this story and feeling strangely uncomfortable for a different reason.
You have not been imagining yourself as the accused woman.
You have been remembering the people you condemned.
The person whose failure you shared with others.
The friend whose confession became gossip.
The family member you quietly decided would never change.
The Christian who fell and whom you treated as though the grace of God had finally reached its limit.
Maybe you were technically correct about their wrongdoing.
But your attitude was wrong.
You wanted them exposed.
You wanted people to know.
You wanted the satisfaction of being proven right.
And deep down, their humiliation made you feel morally superior.
If that is you, the Gospel has something to say to you too.
You do not need to pretend your judgmental spirit was righteousness.
You can repent.
You can stop spreading the story.
You can apologize where appropriate.
You can make room for genuine restoration without minimizing harm or abandoning discernment.
Galatians 6:1 instructs those who are spiritual to restore someone caught in transgression in a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
That is not moral indifference.
That is Christian maturity.
A mature believer does not celebrate sin.
But neither does a mature believer celebrate the destruction of a sinner.
And sometimes the person who most needs to hear “go, and sin no more” is not the one everybody is talking about.
It is the person who cannot stop talking about them.
There is a sentence worth carrying into every church conversation, every family conflict, and every social media controversy:
The truth of someone's sin never gives us permission to sin against them.
Let that settle.
Because it is possible to defend a biblical standard while violating biblical love.
It is possible to confront an actual wrong with an arrogant spirit.
It is possible to expose hypocrisy while being blind to our own.
And it is possible to become so fascinated with somebody else's scandal that we forget the reason Jesus came.
He came to save sinners.
Paul understood this personally.
In 1 Timothy 1:15, he calls himself the foremost of sinners while proclaiming that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.
This was a man who had persecuted the church.
He could not erase his past.
But his past was no longer the final authority over his identity.
The risen Christ had met him.
Grace had changed his direction.
And the man who once persecuted believers became a servant of the Gospel he had opposed.
That is why our theme at Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Not because every painful chapter disappears.
Not because the people we hurt automatically forget.
Not because repentance guarantees a trouble-free future.
But because Jesus can give a new direction to a life that seemed defined by sin, shame, and spiritual ruin.
He does not rewrite history by declaring evil good.
He changes people through truth, forgiveness, repentance, and His transforming grace.
Consider Peter.
He denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
And after the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with responsibility to care for His sheep, as recorded in John 21.
Consider the tax collector in Luke 18:9–14.
He did not approach God boasting about his righteousness.
He pleaded for mercy.
And Jesus said that he, rather than the self-righteous Pharisee, went home justified.
Consider the believers Paul addresses in 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.
After naming serious sins, Paul reminds them that some of them had once lived in those ways.
Then he speaks of their washing, sanctification, and justification in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is not the message of a Savior who merely tells guilty people to feel better.
It is the message of a Savior who truly saves.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because your past is ugly.
You are not beyond His mercy because your struggle has lasted longer than you expected.
You are not disqualified from approaching Him because you are ashamed.
But you must not confuse His patience with permission to remain unchanged.
Come into the light.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Seek help where you need it.
Make things right where you can.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And keep walking with Him.
First John 1:9 teaches that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
First John 2:1 also reminds believers that if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
Those promises are not invitations to careless living.
They are reasons not to surrender to despair.
The enemy would love for you to believe there are only two possibilities.
Hide your sin.
Or be destroyed by your shame.
But the Gospel calls you to something better.
Bring your sin into the light of Christ.
Receive His forgiveness through faith.
And begin walking in repentance.
Not because you have become strong enough to rescue yourself.
But because the risen Jesus is a greater Savior than your sin is a master.
Not as a test of how religious you are.
Not as an invitation to reveal private details that belong in a safe conversation with a trusted pastor, counselor, or mature believer.
But as an opportunity for spiritual honesty.
Which person in this story do you recognize in yourself today?
The woman carrying shame?
The accuser holding a stone?
Or someone who knows that, in different seasons of life, you have been both?
You do not owe strangers your private story.
But you may discover that honest words of faith and repentance can encourage someone else who thought they were struggling alone.
And if this article brought someone to mind, please do not treat that thought as meaningless.
Perhaps you know a believer who has stopped attending church because shame has convinced them they are no longer welcome.
Perhaps you know someone who has become harsh, bitter, or quick to condemn.
Perhaps a friend has confused God's grace with permission to continue in sin.
Send it privately if that would be kinder.
And consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ to follow along.
Not because following a page makes anyone more spiritual.
But because regular exposure to Scripture, faithful teaching, prayer, and Christian encouragement can help us keep our attention on the One who truly changes lives.
We want to do more than publish words that stir emotions for a moment.
We want to help people return to Scripture.
Understand the Gospel.
Recognize false ideas about God.
Grow in prayer.
Practice repentance.
Recover from spiritual discouragement.
And mature in their walk with Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
And keeping a ministry of teaching, publishing, outreach, and resource development active requires real work, time, and financial support.
But I want to be clear about something important.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
God is glorified through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and sincere service—not through the size of a monthly payment.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Inviting a friend to read Scripture matters.
The Gospel is not for sale.
These products are not what makes the ministry valuable.
Jesus Christ is the reason the ministry exists.
The products are simply another way to carry encouraging messages into ordinary life, while supporting the continued work of Gospel Warrior.
Because the goal is not merely to build a larger audience.
It is to see more people know Jesus Christ, understand His Gospel, repent of sin, receive His grace, and grow into lives that reflect His truth and love.
Now return with me, one last time, to that temple courtyard.
The crowd has dispersed.
The accusers have gone.
The stones were not thrown.
And the woman has heard words that confront both her shame and her sin.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Two truths that must remain together.
If we preach holiness without mercy, we may crush people beneath shame while forgetting our own desperate need for forgiveness.
If we preach mercy without repentance, we may comfort people in the very sin from which Christ calls them to turn.
But the Gospel of Jesus Christ gives us neither cruelty disguised as righteousness nor permissiveness disguised as love.
It gives us the crucified and risen Savior.
The One who calls us to repent.
The One who receives sinners who come to Him.
The One who forgives.
The One who transforms.
The One who teaches His people to speak truth without abandoning love.
And perhaps the most searching question is not whether you have ever committed a sin worthy of public shame.
Romans 3:23 already tells us that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
The question is what you will do when the truth of your own sin confronts you.
Will you hide?
Will you excuse it?
Will you point to someone worse?
Will you keep holding a stone so nobody notices the condition of your own heart?
Or will you come to Jesus?
You can put down the stone.
You can stop pretending.
You can confess what is wrong.
You can seek forgiveness and begin making things right.
You can turn from the sin that has been destroying you.
And you can trust the Savior who did not remain in the grave.
Do not mistake the silence of the accusers for the end of the story.
The deepest question is what happens when a sinner encounters the truth and mercy of Jesus Christ.
Because the goal of grace is not simply to leave you feeling less ashamed.
It is to lead you into a restored relationship with God and a transformed life.
So before you leave this article, remember this:
The hands that once held stones can be opened in repentance, and the heart that once hid in shame can be brought into the light of Christ.
And if you remember only one thing, let it be this:
Your sin must never be defended, your wounds must never be dismissed, and your story does not have to end where your shame began—because Jesus Christ is still mighty to save.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY CAST OUT DEMONS IN JESUS’ NAME… SO WHY DID JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?
paragraphs: THEY CAST OUT DEMONS IN JESUS’ NAME… SO WHY DID JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?

The terrifying warning of Matthew 7:21–23 isn't about people who rejected Jesus openly. It's about people who called Him Lord, claimed to perform miracles in His name, and believed they belonged to Him—until the moment they heard words no soul would ever want to hear.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.
Not in a church service. Not during an altar call. Not while worship music plays and everyone around you has their hands raised.
But before the King Himself.

The One whose eyes see beyond every religious performance. The One who knows what you did when nobody was watching. The One who knows every secret you buried beneath a smile, every prayer you whispered through tears, every sin you justified, and every moment you chose either to surrender or to walk away.
And you are confident.
You remember the ministry you served in. The prayers you prayed. The people you helped. The demons you commanded to leave. The miracles you witnessed. The times you spoke His name with authority.
You have evidence.
You have stories.
You have spiritual accomplishments that would impress an entire congregation.
Then Jesus looks at you.
And instead of welcoming you, He says something that shatters every assumption you ever made about your relationship with God.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Not, “I knew you once.”
Not, “You were Mine until you made one terrible mistake.”
Not, “You failed to perform enough miracles.”
“I never knew you.”
How can someone speak the name of Jesus, perform extraordinary works, and still be rejected by Him?
And perhaps the question that should trouble us even more is this:
Could someone spend an entire lifetime doing things for Jesus without ever truly belonging to Jesus?
Because what Christ reveals in this passage is not merely a warning to false prophets somewhere out there.
It is a warning that reaches into the human heart.
Including yours.
Including mine.
And if we misunderstand it, we may spend our lives measuring spiritual success by things Jesus never promised would prove that we knew Him.
Jesus spoke these words near the conclusion of the Sermon on the Mount.

He had already exposed the danger of religious hypocrisy. He had warned against practicing righteousness merely to be noticed by others. He had taught His listeners that genuine obedience reaches deeper than outward appearances, into anger, lust, truthfulness, mercy, forgiveness, and the secret motives of the heart.
Then came this astonishing declaration:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” — Matthew 7:21, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say that everyone who uses His name belongs to Him.
He did not say that religious enthusiasm guarantees salvation.
He did not say that spiritual activity automatically proves spiritual life.
He said that not everyone who calls Him Lord will enter the kingdom.
And then He revealed what some of those people would say.
“Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?” — Matthew 7:22, KJV
Read that again.
These are not people presenting a lifetime of atheism as their defense.
They are appealing to religious accomplishments.
They are saying, in effect, “Jesus, look at everything we did in Your name.”
And the frightening part is that they seem genuinely surprised by His response.
They expected recognition.
They received rejection.
They expected their works to establish their relationship with Him.
Jesus exposed the absence of that relationship.
But to understand why, we need to look carefully at what the Scripture actually says.
In the original Greek of Matthew 7:23, Jesus declares:
“Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
Transliterated: Oudépote égnōn hymâs.
The meaning is:
“I never knew you.”
The Greek word οὐδέποτε (oudepote) means “never” or “not ever.”
The verb ἔγνων (egnōn) comes from γινώσκω (ginōskō), meaning “to know.”
But here is something important.
Jesus is not saying He lacked information about these people.
That would contradict the biblical testimony concerning His knowledge of human hearts.
John 2:24–25 tells us that Jesus knew what was in humanity. Hebrews 4:13 declares that no creature is hidden from God's sight.
So when Jesus says, “I never knew you,” He is not confessing ignorance.
He is denying that they ever belonged to Him in the saving relationship they claimed.
This is the language of recognition, belonging, and relationship—not merely the possession of information.
Paul gives us a remarkable parallel:
“But if any man love God, the same is known of him.” — 1 Corinthians 8:3, KJV
And again:
“The Lord knoweth them that are his.” — 2 Timothy 2:19, KJV
The issue is not whether Jesus knows that a person exists.
The issue is whether that person is truly His.
That distinction changes everything.
Because you can know biblical facts without knowing Christ.
You can memorize sermons without surrendering your heart.
You can recognize the sound of worship music without worshiping God in spirit and truth.
You can become familiar with Christian language while remaining a stranger to Christian repentance.
And you can learn how to impress religious people without ever being transformed by the grace of Jesus Christ.
There is a difference between being recognized by a congregation and being known by the Savior.
A difference between having a ministry and having genuine fellowship with Christ.
A difference between carrying His name publicly and submitting to His lordship privately.
And Jesus knows the difference.
Perhaps that is why this passage feels so uncomfortable.
Because many of us have learned to evaluate our spiritual condition by visible things.
We ask whether we attend church.
Whether we serve.
Whether we give.
Whether people respect our faith.
Whether our prayers sound powerful.
Whether our posts receive encouragement.
Whether others consider us spiritually mature.
Those things may have value in their proper place.
But none of them can substitute for saving faith in Jesus Christ.
A person can become highly skilled at Christian activity while remaining deeply resistant to Christ Himself.
And that resistance does not always look like open rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like a person who can quote Scripture but refuses to forgive.
A worship leader who sings about surrender but secretly treasures an unrepentant life.
A preacher who speaks passionately about holiness while exploiting the people who trust him.
A believer who publicly defends biblical truth but privately refuses to let that truth confront his own pride.
A person who loves being associated with Jesus but resents being corrected by Jesus.
And before we point toward someone else, we should remember how easily the human heart deceives itself.
We can become experts at identifying hypocrisy in others while explaining away our own.
We can condemn another person's visible sins while protecting the hidden sins that have become comfortable to us.
We can mistake emotional experiences for spiritual maturity.
We can confuse being busy in ministry with being close to God.
And sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not knowing that we are spiritually empty.
It is being convinced that we are full.
But there is another question that demands an answer.
Were these people actually performing miracles?
Jesus says they will claim to have prophesied, cast out demons, and performed mighty works in His name.
The passage records their claims, but it does not explicitly verify that every claimed miracle genuinely occurred.
That distinction matters.
We should not build a doctrine on an assumption Jesus did not state.
Nevertheless, Scripture makes something equally sobering clear: extraordinary spiritual phenomena are not, by themselves, conclusive proof that a person is approved by God.
Consider Judas Iscariot.
Jesus chose twelve apostles and sent them out with authority over unclean spirits and diseases, as Matthew 10:1–8 records.
Judas was among the Twelve, according to Matthew 10:4.
Yet Judas later betrayed Christ.
The text does not tell us whether Judas personally performed a particular miracle during that mission. We should not pretend it does.
But his inclusion among those commissioned with spiritual authority reminds us that participation in extraordinary ministry does not, by itself, establish the final condition of someone's heart.
Or consider the warning Jesus gave in Matthew 24:24:
“For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.” — KJV
Signs can be misused to deceive.
Claims of supernatural power can become instruments of manipulation.
And even when God genuinely works through a situation, the person involved cannot claim that divine power as personal proof of holiness.
The power belongs to God.
The glory belongs to God.
The authority belongs to Jesus Christ.
No preacher owns a miracle.
No ministry owns the Holy Spirit.
No spiritual leader becomes exempt from repentance because people admire the results of his work.
That is why Jesus directs our attention away from spectacular accomplishments and toward something far more searching.
He says:
“Depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
The Greek expression is:
“οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν”
Transliterated: hoi ergazómenoi tēn anomían.
It describes those who practice or work lawlessness.
The word ἀνομία (anomia) refers to lawlessness, wrongdoing, or disregard for God's law.
And the wording portrays people characterized by such practice.
Jesus is not describing someone who hates their sin, falls into temptation, confesses, repents, and returns to Him seeking mercy.
He is exposing people whose religious claims coexist with a life fundamentally opposed to God's will.
They invoke His authority while disregarding His commands.
They appeal to His name while refusing His rule.
They present their accomplishments as a defense while the reality of their lives testifies against them.
And here is where we must be especially careful.
Jesus is not teaching that salvation must be earned through perfect obedience.
That would contradict the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — KJV
We are not saved because we have performed enough good deeds.
