Scripture repeatedly teaches that obedience matters.
Jesus Himself said, "If ye love me, keep my commandments" (John 14:15, KJV).
The tragedy is when obedience becomes a substitute for intimacy with God.
When we know how to work in the Father's field but no longer know how to rejoice in the Father's presence.
When our hands remain busy with religious responsibilities while our hearts become increasingly bitter.
When we are physically close to the house but spiritually unwilling to enter its joy.
And then the older brother said something even more revealing.
"But as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf." (Luke 15:30, KJV)
"This thy son."
Not my brother.
Your son.
Notice how resentment changes the language of relationship.
The older brother no longer speaks of the returning man as his brother.
He distances himself from him.
He reduces him to his disgrace.
He brings up the worst of his past as though that past should permanently determine how he is treated.
And there is an important detail here.
Earlier in the parable, Jesus describes the younger son as wasting his substance through reckless living. It is the older brother who specifically accuses him of spending the money on prostitutes.
The narrative does not independently establish every detail of that accusation.
But it certainly reveals how the older brother now sees him.
Not as someone who has returned in repentance.
Not as someone who was lost and has been found.
But as the man who squandered everything.
Have you ever done that?
Have you remembered someone's worst season more vividly than their repentance?
Have you quietly believed that certain people should remain ashamed a little longer before being welcomed?
Have you struggled to accept that God could forgive someone who hurt you, betrayed you, or destroyed something precious?
These are not easy questions.
And they are not meant to minimize real wounds.
Forgiving someone does not always mean restoring immediate trust, removing healthy boundaries, or ignoring the need for accountability.
But the Gospel confronts the desire to make another person's past their permanent identity.
Because if our hope rests in Jesus Christ, none of us stands before God on the strength of a spotless personal record.
We stand in need of mercy.
All of us.
The one who wandered publicly.
And the one who struggled privately.
The one whose sins became a scandal.
And the one whose pride remained hidden beneath respectable behavior.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (KJV)
That includes the person whose failures everyone knows.
And the person whose failures are concealed beneath years of religious activity.
Then comes perhaps the most tender moment in the entire parable.
The father does not abandon the older brother outside.
He comes out to him.
Think about that.
Earlier, the father ran toward the younger son who was returning from rebellion.
Now, the father goes out to the older son who is refusing to celebrate.
Two sons.
Two different expressions of lostness.
And a father who moves toward both.
The Greek of Luke 15:28 says the father παρεκάλει αὐτόν (parekalei auton), meaning that he was appealing to, urging, or entreating him.
The verb form portrays an ongoing appeal.
The father was not merely issuing a command from the doorway.
He was pleading with his son.
And when the father finally answered, he began with a word overflowing with tenderness.
"Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine." (Luke 15:31, KJV)
The Greek word translated "Son" here is τέκνον (teknon), an affectionate term for a child.
It is not a word of rejection.
The father is speaking to a son he still loves.
In effect, the father is reminding him:
You have not been forgotten.
Your place in this family has not disappeared.
Your brother's restoration has not erased your relationship with me.
The father does not tell the older brother that his years of service were meaningless.
He does not deny his place in the household.
Instead, he invites him to see something greater than the comparison that has consumed him.
His father's presence was already his privilege.
"Thou art ever with me."
What a sentence.
And what a searching question it raises.
What if the greatest blessing we keep overlooking is the God who has been with us all along?
Some of us are so focused on the blessing we have not received that we have stopped recognizing the grace already surrounding us.
We want the answered prayer.
The recognition.
The breakthrough.
The restoration.
The moment when everything finally makes sense.
And those desires are not automatically wrong.
But there is a danger when our hearts become unable to say, even in seasons of waiting:
Lord, You are still good.
Your presence is still precious.
Your mercy toward someone else is not a rejection of me.
Then the father says:
"It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found." (Luke 15:32, KJV)
Notice the father's correction.
The older brother had said, this thy son.
The father answers, "this thy brother."
He restores the language of relationship.
He reminds the older son that the returning man is not merely an offender with a shameful history.
He is family.
And the father explains why the celebration is appropriate.
The lost has been found.
The dead is alive again.
The Greek expression ἔδει δὲ εὐφρανθῆναι (edei de euphranthēnai) carries the sense that celebrating was fitting or necessary.
Not because sin was being rewarded.
Not because rebellion was admirable.
But because restoration is worthy of joy.
The father was not celebrating the younger son's reckless living.
He was celebrating his return.
That difference changes everything.
God does not rejoice in the destruction sin causes.
But heaven rejoices when sinners repent.
Jesus had already declared in Luke 15:7 that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
And now the older brother is being invited to participate in that joy.
But here is the detail many readers overlook.
Jesus never tells us whether the older brother entered the house.
The story ends with the father's invitation.
No recorded apology.
No final embrace between the brothers.
No description of the older son joining the feast.
Just an open doorway.
And a decision left unanswered.
Why would Jesus end the story like that?
Remember who was listening.
The Pharisees and scribes were criticizing Him for receiving sinners.
The older brother's refusal to celebrate reflects the very attitude Jesus was confronting.
The parable ends without revealing the older brother's response, leaving the original listeners—and every reader since—with a question.
Will you enter the Father's joy?
Or will you remain outside, clinging to your resentment?
That is the question this story brings into our churches, our families, our ministries, and our private prayers.
Can we rejoice when a person we once judged comes to Christ?
Can we welcome genuine repentance without demanding that someone remain forever trapped in the humiliation of their past?
Can we faithfully pursue justice and accountability while still hoping for redemption?
Can we celebrate God's mercy toward others even when our own lives are painful?
And perhaps most difficult of all…
Can we admit that we sometimes resemble the older brother more than we want to believe?
Maybe you have spent years serving in church.
You have given when it was difficult.
You have prayed when your faith felt weak.
You have encouraged others while carrying your own burdens.
And lately, something has changed.
You still attend.
You still serve.
You still know the right words.
But the joy has become harder to find.
You see someone else being blessed, and instead of rejoicing, you feel an ache.
You hear a testimony of restoration, and your first thought is about what that person once did.
You watch people celebrate a new believer, and a small voice inside you asks why your quiet faithfulness seems invisible.
You haven't abandoned the Father's house.
But perhaps resentment has been keeping part of your heart outside.
If that describes you, please hear this carefully.
Jesus is not telling this story to convince you that your faithful service has been worthless.
He is inviting you to examine what has happened to your heart.
He is calling you away from the exhausting belief that love must always be earned through performance.
He is reminding you that grace is not a limited supply that becomes smaller whenever someone else receives it.
And He is inviting you to repent—not merely of visible wrongdoing, but also of the pride, envy, and self-righteousness that can grow quietly within a religious life.
That repentance may be painful.
It may require confessing attitudes you have hidden even from yourself.
It may mean asking God to soften your heart toward someone you would rather avoid.
It may mean releasing the belief that your years of obedience entitle you to control how generously God treats others.
But repentance is not the enemy of your spiritual life.
It is part of the way God restores us.
And there is something even more beautiful here.
The father in Jesus' parable points us toward the mercy of God, but the full Gospel reveals how that mercy reaches sinners without compromising God's righteousness.
We are not forgiven because sin does not matter.
We are forgiven through Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for sinners.
The cross declares both the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's love.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Jesus did not wait for us to become impressive enough to deserve His sacrifice.
He came to save the lost.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
This is why the Gospel leaves no room for spiritual boasting.
The younger son cannot boast about his rebellion.
The older son cannot boast about his record.
Neither can purchase the Father's love.
And neither can claim that another person's need for mercy makes his own need disappear.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
Grace does not make obedience unnecessary.
Grace makes grateful obedience possible.
It does not excuse continuing in sin.
It transforms the sinner's relationship with God.
And when we truly understand what Christ has done for us, we begin to see other people differently.
Not as competitors for divine affection.
Not as permanently defined by their worst mistakes.
Not as people whose restoration threatens our significance.
But as human beings who desperately need the same Savior we do.
There is another kind of older brother worth remembering.
Not the resentful brother in the parable, but Jesus Christ Himself.
Scripture calls the risen Christ "the firstborn among many brethren" (Romans 8:29, KJV).
He is the righteous Son who does not resent the rescue of sinners.
He is the Savior who gave Himself to bring us to God.
Where the older brother in the parable refused to enter the celebration, Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before Him (Hebrews 12:2).
Where human pride says, Why should that person receive mercy?
The Gospel points us to Christ, whose sacrifice makes forgiveness possible.
And that is why the story must never end with our admiration for a forgiving father or our criticism of a bitter brother.
It must bring us to Jesus.
Because without Him, we are all lost.
Some of us are lost in obvious rebellion.
Others are lost in the illusion that religious performance makes us righteous.
But the answer to both is not greater self-confidence.
It is surrender to Christ.
Perhaps today you need to return like the younger son.
You have wandered far.
You have compromised.
You have made decisions you wish you could erase.
You wonder whether there is still room for you in the Father's house.
Hear the Gospel.
Turn from your sin.
Come to Jesus Christ in faith.
His mercy is greater than your ability to repair your past.
Or perhaps today you need to repent like the older brother.
You have remained outwardly faithful, but inwardly you have become angry.
You have compared.
You have judged.
You have kept records of offenses long after God began calling you to release your bitterness.
You have mistaken spiritual activity for spiritual health.
And now, standing in the quiet of your own heart, you realize something frightening.
You know how to work for God.
But you have forgotten how to delight in Him.
The invitation is still before you.
Come inside.
Not because your hurt was imaginary.
Not because injustice should be ignored.
Not because repentance and accountability no longer matter.
But because the Father's joy is not your enemy.
And another person's restoration does not diminish the love of God for you.
Maybe the most painful realization is that we can spend years criticizing the younger brother while failing to recognize our own desperate need for grace.
We can condemn the person who wasted an inheritance while wasting our own years in bitterness.
We can resent someone else's second chance while overlooking the countless mercies that have carried us through our own failures.
We can demand that others demonstrate repentance while refusing to confess the hardness of our own hearts.
And all the while, Jesus continues calling sinners to Himself.
The scandal is that people who have failed terribly can be forgiven.
The greater wonder is that people who have hidden behind their own righteousness can be forgiven too.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by erasing responsibility.
Not by declaring sin harmless.
But by redeeming lives through His death and resurrection, forgiving the repentant, and transforming hearts that once seemed beyond hope.
And maybe that is the moment you are standing in right now.
Not in a distant country.
Not among pigs.
Not surrounded by the wreckage of a visibly rebellious life.
But outside a house filled with joy.
Holding years of disappointment.
Remembering everything you have done.
Wondering why the Father's kindness toward someone else has stirred so much pain inside you.
And perhaps, for the first time, you are ready to stop arguing about who deserves the celebration.
Perhaps you are ready to ask God for a heart that can celebrate what heaven celebrates.
A heart that still values holiness.
Still honors truth.
Still takes sin seriously.
But no longer confuses bitterness with righteousness.
If this story has exposed something in you, don't rush past it.
You do not have to pretend that you have never struggled with jealousy, resentment, or spiritual exhaustion.
You can bring those things into the light before Christ.
You can pray:

Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have measured Your goodness by what others receive. Forgive me for the moments I have allowed resentment to replace compassion. Heal the wounds I have carried, and teach me to pursue truth without losing love. Give me a heart that rejoices when sinners repent. Remind me that I am saved by grace, not by my ability to outperform anyone else. Restore my joy in You. I surrender my pride, my bitterness, and my need to keep score. Make my heart more like Yours. In Jesus' name, amen.
And if that prayer describes something you are wrestling with, I would love to hear from you.
There is no shame in admitting that your heart needs healing.
Sometimes the most meaningful testimony begins not with Look how strong I am, but with Lord, I still need You.
And perhaps someone reading the comments will discover they are not alone in the struggle they have been too afraid to confess.
Before you leave this story, think of one person who needs to hear it.
Maybe a family member who has been struggling with bitterness.
Maybe a friend who has wandered from Christ and wonders whether forgiveness is possible.
Maybe a believer who has served for years but quietly feels overlooked.
Maybe someone who believes church is only for people who have never made serious mistakes.
Because there may come a day when you hear about someone else's breakthrough while still waiting for your own, and you will need to remember that God's goodness is not a competition.
Our desire is not merely to produce content that moves people for a moment.
It is to keep pointing hearts toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and daily discipleship.
We want biblical nourishment and resources for spiritual growth to reach people who might otherwise never seek them out.
Scripture encourages believers to give willingly, not because they are pressured.
"God loveth a cheerful giver." (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
And we want to honor that principle.
If you are financially able and believe in this mission, your monthly partnership can help us keep going and reach further.
It is the opportunity to participate in a mission that continually points people back to Jesus.
Pray for the people who read it.
Speak about Jesus with someone who needs hope.
Live out the mercy you have received.
Because the goal is not simply to build a larger community around a page.
The goal is to see more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ and grow as His disciples.
And now, one last thought.
The younger son came home with a confession.
The older son stood outside with a complaint.
Both needed their father's mercy.
One had to surrender his rebellion.
The other had to surrender his self-righteousness.
And Jesus leaves us standing at that same doorway, facing the same question.
Will we humble ourselves enough to receive grace—and rejoice when others receive it too?
The Father in the parable had not forgotten the son who stayed.
He had not stopped loving the son who wandered.
And the joy of restoration was an invitation, not a threat.
So if you have been the younger son, come to Christ.
If you have been the older brother, come to Christ.
If you are carrying shame, come to Christ.
If you are carrying resentment, come to Christ.
Because the deepest need of both brothers is the deepest need of every human heart.
Not merely a better circumstance.
Not merely a fairer reward.
Not merely the approval of others.
But reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.

The younger brother nearly lost his life by leaving home. The older brother nearly missed the joy of home by refusing to open his heart. Don't spend your whole life standing outside the grace you desperately need.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE TORE A LION APART WITH HIS BARE HANDS… BUT WHAT HE FOUND INSIDE ITS DEAD BODY WAS EVEN MORE SHOCKING.
paragraphs: HE TORE A LION APART WITH HIS BARE HANDS… BUT WHAT HE FOUND INSIDE ITS DEAD BODY WAS EVEN MORE SHOCKING.

The lion was dead. The honey was real. But the greatest revelation in Samson’s story isn't about strength or sweetness. It's about the danger of a powerful man who could defeat what attacked him but struggled to defeat what was destroying him from within.

“And he took thereof in his hands, and went on eating, and came to his father and mother, and he gave them, and they did eat: but he told not them that he had taken the honey out of the carcase of the lion.” — Judges 14:9 (KJV)
There is something deeply unsettling about a man reaching into the remains of something that once tried to kill him… and pulling out something sweet.
A lion had roared against him.
Its jaws were powerful enough to crush bone. Its claws were sharp enough to tear flesh. Its attack could have ended his life in seconds.
But the lion died.
And sometime later, when the man returned to the place where the animal had fallen, he discovered something he never expected.
Honey.
Not beside the lion.
Not hanging from a nearby tree.
Inside the carcass of the very beast that had tried to destroy him.
But before you turn this into a beautiful little message about how God brings sweetness out of suffering, there is something you need to know.
The man who killed that lion would eventually lose his freedom, his eyesight, and his life.
And the same man who was strong enough to tear apart a lion would later become helpless in the hands of his enemies.
How?
How does someone experience the supernatural power of God and still walk toward personal destruction?
How does a man defeat a lion with his bare hands yet fail to recognize the danger growing inside his own heart?
And what does any of this have to do with the secret battles you are fighting right now?
Stay with this story.
Because the honey is not the most disturbing part.
The silence is.
And somewhere between that dead lion, that hidden honey, and a Savior who would come centuries later, there is a truth about grace that every struggling believer needs to hear.
Samson was not an ordinary man.

Before he was born, an angel of the LORD announced that he would be set apart to God from the womb. His mother was instructed concerning his consecration, and the child was to begin delivering Israel from the Philistines (Judges 13:3–5).
His calling began before his first breath.
But having a calling does not automatically mean a person will always make wise choices.
That distinction matters.
Because some of the most heartbreaking stories in Scripture belong to people who were genuinely used by God yet made decisions that brought terrible consequences.
Samson was one of them.
Judges 14 opens with Samson going down to Timnah, where he saw a Philistine woman and wanted to marry her.
His parents questioned the decision.
Samson insisted.
He wanted what he wanted.

And although Judges 14:4 reveals that God was working through these events to confront the Philistines, that divine purpose does not mean every desire, attitude, or decision Samson displayed was morally right.
God's sovereignty is not the same thing as God's approval.
That is an important truth for anyone who has ever confused an open door with divine permission.
Sometimes we become so determined to pursue something that we stop asking whether our hearts are aligned with the Lord.
We want the relationship.
We want the opportunity.
We want the pleasure.
We want the outcome.
And when someone who loves us raises a concern, we call it interference.
When Scripture challenges our desires, we search for a more comfortable interpretation.
When conviction interrupts us, we convince ourselves that everything will work out.
But not everything we can pursue is something we should pursue.
And not every path that appears exciting leads somewhere safe.
As Samson traveled toward Timnah with his parents, he encountered something terrifying.
Judges 14:5 says that a young lion came roaring against him near the vineyards of Timnah.
Imagine that moment.
The sudden movement.
The violent sound.
The terrible realization that a predator was charging toward him.
No sword is mentioned in Samson's hand.
No spear.
No shield.
No army standing behind him.
And then Scripture records something extraordinary.
“And the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and he rent him as he would have rent a kid, and he had nothing in his hand.” — Judges 14:6 (KJV)
The Hebrew text begins its description of the Spirit's action with the words:
וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה
Vattitslach alav ruach YHWH.
The phrase communicates that the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon Samson.
The Hebrew verb used here, from tsalach (צָלַח), describes the Spirit's powerful action upon him in this context.
This was not merely an impressive demonstration of physical strength.
The biblical writer deliberately identifies the source of Samson's extraordinary ability.
The Spirit of the LORD empowered him.
Samson tore the lion apart.
And then something surprising happened.
He kept the incident from his parents.
Judges 14:6 says he did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us why he remained silent, and we should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But the detail becomes significant as the story unfolds.
Because this will not be the last time Samson keeps something important from the people closest to him.
Some time later, Samson returned to marry the woman.
And as he traveled, he turned aside to look at the lion's remains.
There, in the carcass, he discovered a swarm of bees and honey.
The Hebrew of Judges 14:8 describes the discovery with the words:
עֲדַת דְּבֹרִים בִּגְוִיַּת הָאַרְיֵה וּדְבָשׁ
Adat devorim bigviyat ha'aryeh udevash.
A swarm or colony of bees in the lion's carcass, and honey.
It was an extraordinary sight.
Something associated with death had become the location of something sweet.
But we need to be careful here.
The Bible does not explicitly say that God placed the honey there as a promise that every painful experience will eventually produce a pleasant outcome.
Nor does the passage teach that the lion represents Satan or that the honey represents the Gospel.
Those may sound like compelling sermon illustrations, but they are not explanations the text itself gives us.
The honey becomes central to the riddle Samson later tells at his wedding feast.
And the circumstances surrounding its discovery raise serious questions about Samson's conduct.

As someone set apart under a Nazirite calling, Samson was connected to the consecration instructions of Numbers 6, which included restrictions concerning contact with the dead. Judges does not explicitly explain whether he touched the carcass itself, so we should not claim a proven violation on that detail alone.
What the passage does tell us is that Samson took the honey, ate it, gave some to his parents, and concealed where it came from.
He enjoyed the sweetness.
He shared the sweetness.
But he withheld the truth about its source.
And this is where the story begins to reach beyond ancient Timnah and into the uncomfortable realities of our own lives.
Because it is possible to enjoy something while refusing to examine what surrounds it.
It is possible to receive something that feels good without asking whether the way we obtained it was wise.
It is possible to look strong in public while privately entertaining choices that threaten our integrity.
And it is possible to tell people enough of our story to appear transparent while carefully hiding the details we do not want questioned.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe you have become skilled at saying, “I'm fine,” while quietly struggling with something you are afraid to confess.
Maybe people admire your faith because they see you serving, praying, posting Scripture, encouraging others, and showing up at church.
But they do not see what happens when the room is empty.
They do not know about the temptation you keep revisiting.
The resentment you keep feeding.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The bitterness you have learned to disguise as discernment.
The secret habit you promised God you would abandon.
The exhaustion you hide because everyone expects you to be strong.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you have become so accustomed to carrying these things that you no longer recognize how heavy they are.
You can still smile.
Still worship.
Still encourage somebody else.
Still quote the right verses.
Still appear spiritually alive.
While something inside you is quietly falling apart.
Listen carefully.
Being used by God is not permission to ignore the condition of your heart.
That truth should humble every one of us.
Samson's strength was extraordinary.
But his strength did not make him immune to temptation.
His calling was real.
But his calling did not remove his responsibility to obey.
God's Spirit empowered him for particular acts of deliverance.
But that empowerment was not a guarantee that Samson would always exercise self-control.
And the rest of his story makes that painfully clear.
The man who tore apart a lion would eventually be betrayed through his relationship with Delilah.
The man whose enemies could not easily overpower him would be bound.
The man who once moved with astonishing strength would be forced to grind grain in prison.
And the man who had seen so much would have his eyes gouged out by the Philistines.
Judges 16:20 records one of the most devastating statements in Samson's life.
“And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.” (KJV)
He did not know.
Those words should disturb us.
Not because every struggling Christian should fear that one failure means God has abandoned them. That is not what this passage teaches.
Samson lived in a particular period of Israel's history and experienced a particular Spirit-given empowerment connected to his calling.
The New Testament gives believers in Christ the assurance of God's faithfulness and the sealing of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13–14).
But Samson's experience still warns us about the danger of spiritual presumption.
We can become so familiar with God's gifts that we begin to neglect God's commands.
So accustomed to yesterday's victories that we stop examining today's compromises.
So confident in our ability to withstand temptation that we ignore the first steps leading toward it.
And sometimes the most dangerous sentence a believer can speak is not “I am struggling.”
It is “I can handle this.”
Because confession recognizes a need for grace.
Pride denies the danger.
The apostle Paul would later write:
Perhaps you have been fighting a lion everyone can see while ignoring a temptation nobody knows about.
You have been battling financial pressure, family problems, grief, rejection, betrayal, or disappointment.
And those battles are real.
They hurt.
They exhaust you.
They sometimes make it difficult to get out of bed and face another day.
But while you are trying to survive what is happening around you, have you paid attention to what is happening within you?
Has suffering made you more dependent on Christ, or have you begun using your pain to justify choices you once knew were wrong?
Has disappointment brought you into honest prayer, or has it slowly hardened your heart?
Has loneliness drawn you toward healthy Christian community, or toward secrecy?
These are not questions meant to condemn the wounded.
They are invitations to bring our whole lives into the light of Christ.
Because Jesus does not merely care about the battles that threaten us from the outside.
He cares about the sins, wounds, fears, and desires shaping us on the inside.
And He is not afraid of what He finds there.
There is another detail in Samson's story that makes the lion and the honey even more significant.
At the wedding feast, Samson turned the discovery into a riddle.
“Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness.” — Judges 14:14 (KJV)
In the language of the King James Version, “meat” here means food.
The Hebrew says:
מֵהָאֹכֵל יָצָא מַאֲכָל וּמֵעַז יָצָא מָתוֹק
Meha'okhel yatza ma'akhal, ume'az yatza matok.
“Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came sweetness.”
The riddle depends on the unusual reversal Samson witnessed.
The predator had become the location of food.
The powerful beast had become associated with sweetness.
But the riddle also became part of a deeply troubled wedding celebration marked by threats, manipulation, anger, and violence.
The story is not a simple inspirational account of a strong man discovering a blessing.
It is part of a larger narrative about a gifted, complicated, frequently impulsive man through whom God nevertheless advanced His purposes against Israel's oppressors.
And that complexity matters.
Because the Bible is not interested in protecting the reputations of its human heroes by hiding their failures.
It tells us the truth.
Abraham believed God, yet he also acted out of fear.
David was a man after God's own heart, yet he committed grievous sin.
Peter loved Jesus, yet denied knowing Him.
Samson was empowered by the Spirit, yet repeatedly made destructive choices.
Scripture does not present these men as flawless saviors.
It reveals how desperately humanity needs the One who is.
Jesus Christ.
And here is where the story becomes greater than the lion.
Greater than the honey.
Greater than Samson's strength.
Because Samson's life ultimately forces us to confront the limits of human deliverers.
He could tear apart a lion.
But he could not save himself from his own sin.
He could defeat enemies.
But he could not become the sinless Redeemer Israel truly needed.
He could begin delivering Israel from the Philistines.
But he could not deliver humanity from the power and penalty of sin.
For that, we needed someone greater.
We needed Jesus.
And the difference between Samson and Jesus is breathtaking.
Samson was empowered by God's Spirit, yet morally imperfect.
Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
Samson's strength was used in violent confrontations with Israel's enemies.
Jesus demonstrated His authority over sin, death, demons, disease, and the grave.
Samson's story ends with his death in the collapse of a Philistine temple.
Jesus willingly gave His life on the cross, rose bodily from the dead on the third day, and lives forever.
Samson's final act brought judgment upon his enemies.
Christ's saving work provides forgiveness and reconciliation to all who repent and believe in Him.
And while Samson's riddle speaks of sweetness coming from the remains of a dead lion, the Gospel announces something infinitely greater.
Life came through the death and resurrection of the sinless Son of God.
Not because the honey in Judges 14 was secretly a prediction of the cross.
But because the whole biblical story directs our attention beyond imperfect deliverers toward the perfect Savior.
Jesus did not simply survive death.
He conquered it.
He did not merely escape the power of sin.
He bore the penalty of sin for His people.
He did not simply give us a temporary victory over an earthly enemy.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And what He accomplished cannot be reduced to a motivational saying about turning pain into purpose.
It is redemption.
It is grace.
It is the Gospel.
The Greek New Testament uses a beautiful word for grace:
χάρις — charis.
Grace.
God's undeserved favor.
In Ephesians 2:8–9, Paul declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
The Greek phrase τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως expresses the truth that salvation is by grace through faith.
Not by our strength.
Not by our religious reputation.
Not by the number of battles we have won.
Not by our ability to conceal our weaknesses.
Not by our giving.
Not by our achievements.
By grace.
Through faith.
Because of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps this is what you most need to hear today.
You do not have to pretend you are stronger than you really are.
You do not have to perform spiritual perfection to approach the Savior.
You do not have to hide your failures behind religious language.
You do not have to wait until you have repaired every broken part of your life before crying out for mercy.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
And His grace is sufficient for those who come to Him in faith.
That does not mean repentance is optional.
It does not mean sin is harmless.
It does not mean grace gives us permission to continue embracing what Christ died to save us from.
Romans 6:1–2 rejects that very idea.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness that saves us and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that clear.
And 1 John 1:9 gives struggling believers a promise worth holding onto:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Not “If we successfully hide our sins.”
Not “If we convince everyone we are doing well.”
Not “If we promise never to struggle again.”
If we confess our sins.
There is a kind of freedom that begins when we stop defending what God is calling us to surrender.
When we stop pretending.
When we finally say, “Lord, I need You here too.”
In the anger.
In the addiction.
In the jealousy.
In the bitterness.
In the shame.
In the secret grief.
In the temptation we have been too embarrassed to name.
Jesus is not impressed by a polished version of us that refuses to tell the truth.
He calls us to come into His light.
And His light does not merely expose what is wrong.
It leads us toward the forgiveness, cleansing, and transformation we cannot manufacture ourselves.
Maybe your life has become a collection of contradictions.
You love God, yet you struggle.
You believe His Word, yet sometimes disobey it.
You want to forgive, yet the memory still hurts.
You want to trust Him, yet fear keeps returning.
You want to be faithful, yet you know how often your heart wanders.
Do not confuse those struggles with permission to surrender to sin.
But do not confuse them with proof that Christ cannot restore you either.
The answer is not to become better at hiding.
The answer is to bring the truth before God.
To repent where repentance is needed.
To seek help where help is needed.
To confess to trustworthy believers when secrecy has become a prison.
To return again and again to the Scriptures.
To remember that sanctification is not the achievement of self-sufficient people.
It is the work of God in those who belong to Christ.
And this is why the end of Samson's story matters so much.
In Judges 16, after his humiliation and imprisonment, Samson cried out to the LORD.
He asked God to remember him and strengthen him once more.
God granted him strength for his final act against the Philistines, although that act also cost Samson his life.
The passage is sobering.
It is not a promise that every consequence of sin will disappear when we pray.
Samson's eyes were not restored.
His imprisonment was not erased.
His life did not return to what it had been.
But even at the end of a deeply troubled life, Scripture records him calling upon the LORD.
And Hebrews 11:32 later includes Samson among those remembered in the testimony of faith.
That does not excuse his sins.
It reminds us that God's dealings with imperfect people are more profound than a simple division between impressive heroes and hopeless failures.
And if you are reading this with regret in your heart, please understand something.
Your past may have consequences.
Some relationships may require patient rebuilding.
Some wounds may take time to heal.
Some wrongs may require confession, restitution, or difficult changes.
And not every earthly loss can be reversed.
But your failure does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
The cross is not a reward for people who never fell.
It is the place where the sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners.
And His resurrection is the declaration that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why our message is not simply that broken people can become successful.
It is something far greater.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the truth.
But by redeeming sinners who repent and believe, forgiving what they could never cleanse themselves, and transforming lives through the power of His Gospel.
Maybe the lion in your life has already fallen.
Maybe you survived something you thought would destroy you.
Maybe you are still standing after betrayal, grief, abandonment, or a season that nearly crushed your faith.
Give God thanks for sustaining you.
But do not assume that surviving one battle means you no longer need to guard your heart.
And maybe you are still in the middle of the fight.
Still praying through tears.
Still resisting temptation.
Still waiting for healing.
Still wondering why obedience feels so costly.
Do not measure God's love by how quickly your circumstances become sweet.
Measure His love by the cross of Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
There is your assurance.
Not a lion's carcass.
Not a handful of honey.
Not a temporary victory.
The crucified and risen Christ.
The One who loved sinners enough to die for them.
The One who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The One who does not merely make our stories more inspiring.
He makes the spiritually dead alive by grace through faith.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not for the sake of appearances.
Not so anyone can judge your answer.
But because somebody reading this may have been silently fighting a battle for months.
What is harder for you right now?
The lion attacking your life from the outside?
Or the struggle you have been hiding on the inside?
Let those words become a reminder of a real decision to seek God honestly, not a substitute for repentance or the help you may need.
Because somewhere in this community is another person who thinks they are the only one struggling.
And your simple act of honesty may encourage them to stop suffering in silence.
There is another way you can help this message reach someone who needs it.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
It doesn't.
But because someone in your circle may never open a Bible study, attend a church gathering, or ask for prayer publicly.
They may still read a message shared by someone they trust.
Someone you love may be losing hope.
Someone you know may be struggling with secret sin.
Someone in your family may have drifted away from Christ.
Someone who has never believed may be searching for answers.
And perhaps this article can become an invitation for them to open the Scriptures and discover Jesus for themselves.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who are uncertain about Christianity to join us.
Because this ministry is not about building a personality.
It is about making the truth of Jesus Christ known.
And if these messages have helped strengthen your faith, I want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, encourage faithful discipleship, and help people become more firmly rooted in God's Word.
The Gospel is a gift of grace.
And that is what makes generous support meaningful.
It can be given freely, prayerfully, and joyfully.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Christ is.
But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, opportunities for conversation, and practical expressions of encouragement.
The free Gospel resources are not reserved for those who can afford to give.
Your worth before God is not measured by your financial contribution.
A faithful ministry should never make someone feel that they must pay to be loved by God.
We give because He first loved us.
We serve because Christ has served us.
We share because the Gospel is too precious to keep to ourselves.
And as we come to the end of Samson's story, I want you to remember one final thing.
The lion was strong.
Samson was stronger than the lion because the Spirit of the LORD empowered him.
But Samson was never strong enough to become his own savior.
Neither are we.
And that is not the end of our hope.
It is the beginning of understanding why we need Jesus.
You may have conquered things that once terrified you.
You may have survived circumstances that nearly broke you.
You may have discovered unexpected kindness in seasons of terrible pain.
But none of those victories can take the place of the cross.
And none of your failures can make Christ's saving power insufficient for those who truly turn to Him.
So if you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have been wandering, repent and return.
If you have been proud, humble yourself before God.
If you have been wounded, bring your pain to the Savior.
If you have been trying to save yourself through your own strength, put your trust in the One who died and rose again.
And if you are tired of pretending to be the strongest person in the room, remember that you were never meant to be your own redeemer.
You need Jesus.
We all do.
The lion and the honey may be what first captured your attention.
But I pray that when you close this article, the image you carry will not be a dead animal filled with honey.
It will be an empty tomb.
Because a lion's death became the setting for Samson's strange discovery.
But Christ's death and resurrection accomplished something no human strength could ever achieve.
The salvation of sinners.
And that is a sweetness greater than anything Samson ever tasted.
You may have survived the lion that came to destroy you—but only Jesus can save the soul you were never strong enough to rescue.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS DIDN’T TELL THEM TO FILL THE JARS HALFWAY—AND THE REASON MAY CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR EMPTY LIFE
paragraphs: JESUS DIDN’T TELL THEM TO FILL THE JARS HALFWAY—AND THE REASON MAY CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR EMPTY LIFE
Six stone jars. A wedding on the edge of embarrassment. One impossible command. And a Savior who was about to reveal that what human effort could never produce, His glory could provide.
“Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.” — John 2:7 (KJV)
Have you ever wondered why Jesus told the servants to fill those water jars all the way to the brim?
Not halfway.
Not almost full.
Not just enough to get through the wedding.
To the brim.
It sounds like such a small detail that most people read right past it.
But what if I told you that this little detail sits inside one of the most extraordinary revelations of who Jesus Christ really is?
And what if the part of this miracle that speaks most deeply to your life isn't even the moment the water became wine?
It's what happened before anybody tasted it.
Before the celebration was rescued.
Before the master of the feast knew anything had happened.
Before anyone realized that the ordinary water they had carried was about to become a testimony to the glory of God.
There were servants.
There were empty vessels.
And there was a command from Jesus that probably didn't make much sense.
Perhaps that sounds familiar.
Because sometimes the hardest part of following Jesus isn't believing that He can do miracles.
It's obeying Him when what He's asking you to do seems completely unrelated to the miracle you desperately need.
And if you've ever found yourself praying for one thing while God seems to be leading you through something entirely different, stay with me.
There is something at Cana worth seeing.
Something beautiful.
Something that points far beyond a wedding.
And ultimately, something that leads us straight to the cross.
The wedding was already underway in Cana of Galilee.
People were celebrating. Families were gathered. A bride and groom were beginning their life together.
Then a problem arose.
The wine ran out.
To modern readers, that might sound like a minor inconvenience. Someone could simply apologize and serve something else.

But in the social world of a first-century Jewish wedding, hospitality carried tremendous importance. Running out of wine could bring embarrassment upon the hosts and cast a shadow over what should have been a joyful occasion.
And here's what makes the scene so human.
The guests were there to celebrate.
But somewhere behind the celebration, somebody knew there was a problem.
Doesn't life sometimes feel exactly like that?
Everybody sees the wedding.
Nobody sees the shortage.
Everybody sees your smiling profile picture.
Nobody sees the tears you wiped away before taking it.
Everybody hears you say, "I'm doing fine."
Nobody hears the prayer you whisper when the house is finally quiet.
There are people reading this who have mastered the art of looking full while feeling empty.
Your marriage looks fine.
Your ministry looks fine.
Your family thinks you're strong.
Your friends believe you're managing.
But you know how exhausted you've become trying to keep everything together.
And then you encounter two of the most quietly devastating words in John's account.
“They have no wine.” — John 2:3 (KJV)
Mary brought the problem to Jesus.
No elaborate speech.
No impressive explanation.
Just the truth about what was missing.
And sometimes that's where genuine prayer begins.
Not with polished religious language.
Not with pretending to be stronger than you are.
But with finally telling the Lord the truth.
"Jesus, I don't have the strength I used to have."
"Lord, my marriage is struggling."
"Father, I've been hiding a sin I need to confess."
"Jesus, I know the right things to say, but my heart has grown cold."
"Lord, I cannot save myself."
The miracle at Cana is not a promise that every shortage in our lives will disappear immediately. John records it for a far greater purpose.
But it does introduce us to a Savior whose glory was revealed in the middle of an ordinary human need.
And the story becomes even more remarkable when we notice what Jesus said next.
Mary told the servants:
“Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.” — John 2:5 (KJV)
Read that again.
She didn't tell them to understand everything first.
She didn't tell them to negotiate.
She didn't tell them to wait until the instructions made perfect sense.
She directed their attention to Jesus.
Whatever He says.
Do it.
That is not a call to follow every religious voice that claims to speak for God. It is a call to listen to Christ Himself, whose words are trustworthy.
And what Jesus said next must have sounded unusual.
John tells us that six stone water jars were standing there, used for the Jewish rites of purification.
These were not ordinary wine containers.
They were vessels associated with ceremonial washing.
John 2:6 describes them as holding two or three metrētai each, a Greek unit of liquid measure. Depending on the conversion used, each jar could hold roughly 75 to 115 liters.
Six substantial stone vessels.
A remarkable quantity of water.
And Jesus said:
“Fill the waterpots with water.”
Then John adds the detail that refuses to leave my heart alone.
“And they filled them up to the brim.”
In the original Greek of John 2:7, the phrase is:
καὶ ἐγέμισαν αὐτὰς ἕως ἄνω
Kai egemisan autas heōs anō.
Literally, the sense is:
“And they filled them up to the top.”
The word ἐγέμισαν (egemisan) means "they filled."
The expression ἕως ἄνω (heōs anō) communicates the uppermost extent, or all the way to the top.
John did not merely say that the servants put water into the jars.
He specifically recorded how fully they filled them.
Why?
We need to be careful here.

Scripture does not explicitly tell us that Jesus demanded the jars be filled to the brim because He was testing their faith, measuring their obedience, or promising that complete surrender would automatically produce a miracle.
Those might sound like powerful sermon statements, but we must never make the Bible say more than it actually says.
The text tells us that Jesus commanded the servants to fill the jars and that they filled them completely.
And within John's account, that detail matters.
The vessels were genuinely filled with water before the servants drew anything out.
There was no mention of adding wine.
No secret ingredient.
No human technique that could explain the transformation.
The water was there.
The servants knew it.
And what followed would reveal the power of Jesus.
The servants could fill the jars. Only Jesus could turn the water into wine.
Don't miss that distinction.
Because it exposes something about the human heart.
We love the idea of being useful to God.
But sometimes we quietly begin to believe that our usefulness makes us powerful.
We pray longer.
We serve harder.
We give more.
We attend church.
We read Scripture.
And all those things can be beautiful expressions of faith.
But none of them can accomplish what only Jesus can do.
You can clean up your appearance without cleansing your heart.
You can learn Christian language without being born again.
You can become religiously active while remaining spiritually distant.
You can carry the water.
But you cannot manufacture the miracle.
And that is precisely why the Gospel is such good news.
Salvation is not a spiritual achievement awarded to people who have finally become impressive enough.
It is God's gift of grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to become good enough for God to love.
You keep promising that you'll never fall again.
Then you fall.
You keep telling yourself this will be the last time.
Then the temptation returns.
You keep carrying the shame of things nobody else knows.
And eventually you start wondering whether Jesus is tired of hearing your name.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you to transform yourself into someone worthy of being rescued.
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Repentance is necessary. Faith is necessary. A transformed life matters.
But our transformation flows from God's grace; it is not the price we pay to purchase that grace.
The servants did not create the wine by filling the jars. And you cannot create a new heart by trying harder without Christ.
That is why you need a Savior.
Not merely an inspirational teacher.
Not merely a religious example.
A Savior.
Now imagine standing beside those servants.
You've just carried water into enormous stone vessels.
You know exactly what went into them.
You know what water looks like.
You know what water smells like.
And then Jesus gives another instruction.
“Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast.” — John 2:8 (KJV)
And they did.
John does not describe the precise instant the transformation occurred.
There is no detailed account of the color changing.
No description of the chemistry.
No dramatic announcement from Jesus.
The servants obeyed, and when the master of the feast tasted what was brought to him, the water had become wine.
Then something astonishing happened.
The master of the feast praised the quality of the wine.
He told the bridegroom that people ordinarily served the good wine first and brought out the inferior wine after the guests had drunk freely.
But this wedding was different.
“Thou hast kept the good wine until now.” — John 2:10 (KJV)
The master of the feast did not know where it had come from.
But the servants knew.
John 2:9 makes that distinction explicit.
And there's something deeply moving about that.
The people who carried the water knew something about the miracle that the honored guest did not.
They had witnessed the ordinary work that preceded an extraordinary revelation.
No applause was recorded for them.
No special seats.
No names preserved in the passage.
Just servants who listened to Jesus and did what He said.
How many faithful Christians are living like that right now?
The mother who keeps praying for her children even though she sees little change.
The father who quietly chooses integrity when dishonesty would be easier.
The believer who refuses to abandon Christ while walking through grief.
The person who finally confesses a hidden sin and begins the difficult journey of repentance and restoration.
The Christian who serves without recognition.
No spotlight.
No audience.
No guarantee that tomorrow will be easy.
Just faithfulness to Jesus.
And I want to say something to the person who feels invisible.
Your worth before God is not determined by how many people notice your obedience.
Christ sees what others overlook.
But there is an even deeper truth here.
The servants were not the center of the story.
Jesus was.
And if we make this passage only about how hard the servants worked, we miss the very reason John recorded the miracle.
Because John tells us plainly what it meant.
“This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him.” — John 2:11 (KJV)
There it is.
The purpose of the sign.
Jesus manifested His glory.
And His disciples believed in Him.
The Greek word John uses for these miraculous signs is σημεῖα (sēmeia).
A sign points beyond itself.
The wedding miracle was real, but John wants us to see more than an extraordinary supply of wine.
He wants us to see Jesus.
The One through whom all things were made.
The One whose presence brings the fulfillment toward which the Scriptures point.
The One who does not merely improve religious ceremonies but brings the saving reality that human purification rituals could never accomplish by themselves.
Notice what kind of vessels Jesus used.
Stone jars associated with Jewish purification.
That detail is not accidental background decoration.
John deliberately identifies their purpose.
In the biblical story, ritual washing had a place within Israel's religious life. But outward washing could never, by itself, remove the guilt of sin or give a person a new heart.
The prophets had already spoken of a deeper cleansing God Himself would provide.
Through Ezekiel, the Lord promised:
“Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean.” — Ezekiel 36:25 (KJV)
And then:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.” — Ezekiel 36:26 (KJV)
The Hebrew expression for "a new heart" is:
לֵב חָדָשׁ
Lev chadash.
A new heart.
Not merely a better reputation.
Not merely a more convincing religious appearance.
A heart made new by God's gracious work.
We should not pretend that John explicitly identifies each jar with a separate spiritual meaning or that every measurement contains a hidden code.
He doesn't.
But the broader biblical connection is profound.
The God who promised cleansing and renewal has sent His Son.
And the first sign in John's Gospel begins revealing the glory of that Son.
Jesus came to accomplish something deeper than rescuing a wedding celebration.
He came to rescue sinners.
He came to confront the evil we cannot excuse.
He came to bear the judgment we deserve.
He came to reconcile us to God through His death and resurrection.
And that brings us to a detail from the beginning of the story that is easy to overlook.
When Mary first spoke to Jesus about the wine, He responded:
“Mine hour is not yet come.” — John 2:4 (KJV)
That word "hour" matters in John's Gospel.
As the Gospel unfolds, Jesus repeatedly speaks of His appointed hour.
And later, as the cross approaches, He declares:
“The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified.” — John 12:23 (KJV)
Then in John 17:1, Jesus prays:
“Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee.”
Do you see where John's Gospel is taking us?
From a wedding in Cana to the suffering and glory of the cross.
From a temporary shortage to humanity's deepest need.
From water transformed into wine to the Savior who would shed His blood for the forgiveness of sins.
This does not mean the water in John 2 literally represents Jesus' blood. John does not make that identification.
But the Gospel's unfolding narrative unmistakably leads us from the first revelation of Christ's glory toward His death, resurrection, and the full revelation of His saving mission.
And suddenly, the miracle at Cana becomes part of a much greater story.
At Cana, Jesus rescued a celebration from shame.
At Calvary, Jesus bore shame for sinners.
At Cana, He provided what the wedding hosts could not provide.
At Calvary, He accomplished the salvation humanity could never accomplish.
At Cana, the servants carried water.
At Calvary, the Savior carried the cross.
And when Jesus cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30), He was not announcing that He had merely made salvation possible through human religious effort.
He was declaring the completion of His appointed work of suffering and obedience.
His resurrection would vindicate His victory.
And all who truly trust in Him receive forgiveness and life.
This is why the Christian message is not simply, "Fill your jars and wait for your miracle."
That may sound encouraging, but it is not the central message of John 2.
The message is far more glorious.
Look at Jesus.
Look at His authority.
Look at His glory.
Look at His compassion.
Look at His power.
Look at the Savior who entered our broken world and accomplished what we could never do for ourselves.
And then ask yourself a question that no amount of religious activity can answer for you.
Do I actually know Him?
Not just know about Him.
Not just recognize His name.
Not just attend church.
Do I know Jesus Christ as my Lord and Savior?
Because there is a kind of emptiness that a successful career cannot fill.
A kind of guilt that public applause cannot silence.
A kind of loneliness that thousands of online followers cannot cure.
A kind of spiritual death that moral improvement cannot reverse.
You can have everything people admire and still be separated from the God who made you.
And you can have very little in this world yet possess eternal life through Jesus Christ.
That is not a motivational slogan.
That is the difference between religion that merely decorates the outside and redemption that reaches the heart.
Perhaps this is why the detail about the jars has stayed with me.
They were filled completely.
But even completely filled jars contained only water until Jesus acted.
Think about that.
Full vessels were still dependent on Christ.
And so are we.
You may have years of Bible knowledge.
You may have decades of church attendance.
You may have a respected ministry.
You may have served faithfully for a lifetime.
But none of us ever outgrows our need for Jesus.
We do not begin by grace and then graduate into self-sufficiency.
We remain dependent on Him.
Every day.
Every breath.
Every act of repentance.
Every step of sanctification.
Every moment of perseverance.
It is Christ who saves.
It is Christ who sustains.
It is Christ who deserves the glory.
And if you've been running from Him, perhaps this is the moment to stop.
Not because an article has somehow earned the right to manipulate your emotions.
But because the truth of the Gospel deserves your response.
You cannot undo yesterday.
You cannot rewrite your past by sheer determination.
You cannot make your sins disappear by pretending they never happened.
But you can come to Jesus in repentance and faith.
You can confess what you've been hiding.
You can turn away from the sin you've been defending.
You can stop trying to negotiate your way into God's favor.
And you can trust the Savior who died and rose again.
The apostle John later wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
That promise does not make sin harmless.
It makes God's mercy astonishing.
Grace is not permission to remain in darkness.
Grace calls us into the light.
Grace does not excuse the destruction sin causes.
Grace brings forgiveness and begins the work of making us new.
And that is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always centered on this truth:
Not because the consequences of our past magically vanish.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored.
Not because believers never struggle again.
But because in Jesus Christ, guilt does not have to be the final word.
Shame does not have to define your identity.
Your worst failure does not have to be the whole story.
The crucified and risen Savior offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a new life of following Him.
Some of you have been carrying a secret for so long that you've forgotten what it feels like to be honest.
Some of you are exhausted from trying to look spiritually strong.
Some of you love Jesus but have been fighting a battle you are afraid to tell anyone about.
And some of you are still standing outside the faith, wondering whether there is really room for someone with your history.
Hear the invitation of Christ.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
Come to Him.
Not with excuses.
Not with a carefully edited version of your life.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting His mercy.
And if your heart is ready, you can pray something like this:

"Lord Jesus, You know the truth about me. You know my sins, my failures, my hidden struggles, and everything I have tried to cover. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I turn from my sin and place my trust in You. Forgive me, cleanse me, and teach me to follow You. Give me a heart that loves Your truth more than the approval of people. Let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen."
The prayer itself is not a magical formula.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ, not in the perfection of our words.
And if you have prayed sincerely, don't stop at an emotional moment.
Open the Scriptures.
Find a faithful local church.
Seek biblical discipleship.
Bring hidden sin into the light with wise, trustworthy Christian support.
Learn to follow Jesus when the emotions of this moment have passed.
Because genuine discipleship is not merely being moved by a message.
It is being transformed through a growing relationship with Christ.
And that is exactly why Gospel Warrior exists.
We do not want to create content that simply makes people cry for a few minutes before returning unchanged to the same spiritual emptiness.
We want to keep pointing people back to Scripture.
Back to repentance.
Back to the cross.
Back to the empty tomb.
Back to the daily reality of walking with Jesus.
These resources are meant to encourage serious Bible study, spiritual maturity, healing grounded in biblical truth, and a life increasingly shaped by the Gospel.
Not because you can buy God's favor.
You cannot.
It doesn't.
And certainly not because a monthly payment can replace the faithful stewardship, generosity, and responsibilities you already have toward your local church, your family, and those in need.
The Gospel is free. Salvation cannot be purchased.
But Gospel ministry does require real resources, faithful labor, and people willing to help carry the work forward.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may rightly receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), while also calling believers to give willingly rather than under pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But for those who are able and genuinely desire to partner with us, it can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
Helping someone discover the Gospel.
Helping a struggling believer return to Scripture.
Helping a family find trustworthy Christian reading material.
Helping a person who has been quietly drowning in shame hear that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
You can still help.
You can pray.
You can read.
You can grow.
You can encourage someone.
You never know who is reading silently.
The friend who has stopped attending church.
The relative who is questioning whether God still loves them.
The believer who has fallen into a familiar sin and feels too ashamed to return.
The person who seems happy in every photograph but cries alone at night.
Sharing this article doesn't guarantee a changed life.
Only God can change the heart.
But it may place biblical truth in front of someone who needs to hear it.
And if a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with kindness or sending this privately if that would better respect their circumstances.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to publicly expose their struggles.
But to remind them that they are not beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
Not because every line here is perfect, but because the Scriptures it points to deserve to be revisited, studied, and tested carefully.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually indifferent, and even those who are still searching for the truth.
Everyone needs the Gospel.
Before you leave, though, I want to ask you something.
Not as a social media trick.
Not to collect a meaningless response.
But because sometimes writing a few honest words can become the beginning of a much-needed conversation.
What part of your life are you still trying to change without fully depending on Jesus?
Is it a hidden habit?
A wound you refuse to acknowledge?
A bitterness you've carried for years?
A spiritual exhaustion you've been afraid to admit?
A fear that God could never forgive what you've done?
You don't have to disclose anything private or unsafe.
You don't have to pretend.
And if God has already brought you through a season of repentance and restoration, consider sharing a testimony that gives Christ the glory rather than drawing attention to yourself.
Your testimony might encourage someone who is beginning to believe that change is impossible.
Because that person may be closer than you think.
Maybe they're reading these very words.
Maybe they're remembering the last time they prayed sincerely.
Maybe they're realizing that the life they've built around appearances is no longer enough.
Maybe they're finally ready to stop hiding.
And perhaps that brings us back to the wedding at Cana.
Back to those six stone jars.
Back to the servants carrying water.
Back to the quiet obedience that preceded a public revelation of Christ's glory.
Why did Jesus ask them to fill the water jars to the brim?
John does not explicitly explain why Jesus chose that precise level, and we should not invent a secret commandment about it.
But the complete filling makes the account strikingly clear.
The vessels were filled with water.
The servants knew what had been placed inside them.
And when the water became wine, the glory belonged to Jesus.
Not to the jars.
Not to the servants.
Not to the water.
To Jesus.
That's the truth I don't want you to forget.
You can obey Him.
You can serve Him.
You can bring your needs before Him.
You can faithfully do what His Word commands.
But never confuse your obedience with His saving power.
Never make your spiritual effort the hero of your testimony.
Never turn a miracle that reveals Jesus into a story that ultimately glorifies human achievement.
The servants filled the jars.
Jesus changed what was inside.
And the greatest hope for your life is not that you can somehow become impressive enough to deserve God's attention.
It is that Jesus Christ, who revealed His glory at Cana and accomplished redemption through His cross and resurrection, is worthy of your trust.
So bring Him your honest confession.
Bring Him your repentance.
Bring Him your faith.
Bring Him your broken story.
And follow Him.
Because the miracle at Cana was never merely about having enough wine for a wedding.
It was a sign pointing to the glory of the Savior.
And the Savior is still the One we need most.
You may spend your whole life trying to fill what is empty, only to discover that the deepest thing you needed was never something you could pour into yourself—it was the grace of Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY CAN CAST OUT DEMONS… BUT CAN THEY CAST OUT THE HATRED IN THEIR OWN HEARTS?
paragraphs: THEY CAN CAST OUT DEMONS… BUT CAN THEY CAST OUT THE HATRED IN THEIR OWN HEARTS?

Why are some Christians fearless when confronting darkness in the spiritual realm, yet strangely silent when racism, greed, and injustice are standing right in front of them? Jesus warned us about a kind of religion that looks powerful in public while quietly resisting the very transformation He came to bring.
There is something deeply unsettling happening in parts of modern Christianity.
A person can spend three hours discussing demonic oppression, spiritual warfare, generational curses, and the schemes of Satan…
Yet become visibly uncomfortable when someone mentions racism.
They can passionately rebuke the spirit of poverty while refusing to question the greed that exploits the poor.
They can identify supposed demonic influences in music, movies, clothing, and culture, but struggle to recognize the cruelty in their own words.
They can pray against darkness in a city while remaining silent when the vulnerable are mistreated in that very same city.
And perhaps the most disturbing possibility is this:
Sometimes the darkness we are most eager to confront is the darkness that requires the least repentance from us personally.
Read that again.
Because this is not an attack on spiritual warfare.
The Bible is unmistakably clear that spiritual evil is real. Jesus confronted demons. The apostles encountered demonic opposition. Paul instructed believers to stand against the schemes of the devil.
But something has gone terribly wrong when Christians become more fascinated with identifying demons in other people than recognizing sin in themselves.
And before anyone starts thinking about that one pastor, that one denomination, that one political movement, or that one Christian who desperately needs to read this…
There is a question we need to answer first.
What if Jesus is speaking to us?
What if the problem is not merely what the Church refuses to confront?
What if the problem is what we have learned to excuse?
Because a person can know the vocabulary of spiritual warfare and still be spiritually immature.
A person can speak passionately about holiness and still harbor prejudice.
A person can preach against the devil and still worship money.
And a person can appear deeply religious while repeatedly walking past the very people Jesus commanded them to love.
That is not a new problem.
Jesus confronted it two thousand years ago.
And His words are still capable of shaking the foundations of our comfortable Christianity.
In Matthew 23:23, Jesus confronted religious leaders who were meticulous about giving a tenth of even their herbs while neglecting what He called the weightier matters of the law.
Justice.
Mercy.
Faithfulness.
The Greek text uses the expression τὰ βαρύτερα τοῦ νόμου (ta barytera tou nomou).
Literally, the weightier matters of the law.
Jesus was not telling them to abandon obedience in smaller things. He explicitly said they should practice the weightier matters without neglecting the others.
His accusation was far more devastating.
They were carefully practicing visible religious duties while neglecting the moral responsibilities that revealed the condition of their hearts.
Imagine standing before Jesus with a record of religious activity.
You attended worship.
You fasted.
You prayed.
You gave offerings.
You defended biblical doctrine.
You argued passionately against spiritual darkness.
And then Jesus asks about the people you mistreated.
The worker whose wages you withheld.
The stranger you despised because of their ethnicity.
The poor family whose suffering you dismissed.
The person you humiliated because they looked different, spoke differently, or came from another social class.
The neighbor whose pain you refused to acknowledge because doing so would have made your life uncomfortable.
Suddenly, religious activity no longer feels like a hiding place.
Because Jesus is not impressed by the appearance of holiness when the heart remains unwilling to love.
And here is where this becomes painfully personal.
Sometimes it is easier to pray against an invisible enemy than apologize to someone we have visibly wounded.
It is easier to shout, "I rebuke you, Satan!" than whisper, "I was wrong. Please forgive me."
It is easier to discuss demonic strongholds than admit that prejudice has become a stronghold in our own thinking.
It is easier to condemn the greed of billionaires than examine our own dishonesty, selfish ambition, or unwillingness to share.
It is easier to demand justice for people we agree with than extend fairness to people we dislike.
And it is easier to call ourselves defenders of truth than allow the truth to defend someone we would rather ignore.

Not every Christian who discusses demons is avoiding justice. Many believers faithfully pursue both spiritual discernment and practical righteousness. Nor is every disagreement about a social issue evidence of racism or hatred.
But whenever our religious convictions consistently protect us from examining our own sin, we should be concerned.
Because biblical discernment does not merely identify what is wrong with the world.
It allows God's Word to expose what is wrong within us.
Hebrews 4:12 describes the Word of God as living and active, able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
Not just somebody else's heart.
Ours.
And sometimes the most frightening thing about opening Scripture is discovering that the passage we wanted to use against someone else was meant to confront us first.
Consider the story Jesus told in Luke 10.
A man was traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho when robbers attacked him, stripped him, beat him, and left him half dead.
A priest came down the road.
He saw the wounded man.
And passed by on the other side.
Then a Levite approached.
He also saw him.
And passed by.
These were men associated with religious life.
They were not strangers to sacred responsibilities.
Yet the wounded man remained abandoned.
Then came a Samaritan.
To appreciate the force of this story, we must remember that serious ethnic and religious tensions existed between Jews and Samaritans.
Jesus deliberately made the compassionate outsider the moral example.
The Samaritan approached the wounded man, treated his injuries, transported him to an inn, and paid for his care.
The story is not merely about having sympathetic feelings.
Compassion cost him something.
Time.
Money.
Convenience.
Personal involvement.
Jesus then asked which traveler had proved to be a neighbor to the wounded man.
The answer was the one who showed mercy.
And Jesus commanded, "Go, and do thou likewise" (Luke 10:37, KJV).
Now imagine the priest had stopped to pray against the demons responsible for the robbery.
Imagine the Levite had delivered a passionate sermon about the spiritual darkness affecting the road to Jericho.
Imagine both men had spoken with perfect theological vocabulary.
But neither had helped the bleeding man.
Would their words have changed the condition of the person lying in the dust?
Prayer matters.
Spiritual warfare matters.
But Jesus did not tell the lawyer in Luke 10 to admire the Samaritan's religious language.
He commanded him to imitate his mercy.
A wounded neighbor does not become less wounded because we have correctly identified the existence of evil.
And some of us need to hear that.
Because we have become skilled at explaining darkness while remaining reluctant to carry light into the places where people are suffering.
We speak about spiritual bondage but ignore human trafficking.
We condemn wickedness but remain indifferent to exploitation.
We denounce the devil's hatred while allowing ethnic hostility to remain unchallenged among us.
We preach generosity while quietly treating financial success as evidence of spiritual superiority.
And when someone raises these contradictions, we sometimes accuse them of being divisive.
But is it always division to expose injustice?
Or can it be an act of faithfulness?
The prophet Isaiah addressed a religious community that practiced fasting while simultaneously exploiting workers and engaging in conflict.
In Isaiah 58:6, God described the kind of fasting He desired as one that loosens the bonds of wickedness, releases oppressive burdens, and lets the oppressed go free.
The Hebrew text includes the expression פַּתֵּחַ חַרְצֻבּוֹת רֶשַׁע (patteakh chartsubbot resha).
It speaks of loosening the bonds or restraints of wickedness.
The passage continues by calling God's people to share bread with the hungry, provide shelter for the poor, and clothe the naked.
Notice what God was confronting.
