Not the absence of religious activity.
The contradiction between religious activity and unrighteous conduct.
They were fasting.
But their treatment of others contradicted the purpose of their worship.
They were seeking God.
But refusing to practice the justice and mercy His character required.
And this is where the modern Church must be extraordinarily careful.
Because we can create impressive worship experiences while neglecting the suffering beyond our walls.
We can organize conferences about spiritual breakthrough while overlooking the people whose lives are being broken by exploitation.
We can raise our hands during worship while refusing to extend those same hands toward someone we have been taught to fear.
And we can become so preoccupied with what demons might be doing that we stop asking what the Holy Spirit is commanding us to do.
The Holy Spirit does not lead believers into indifference toward the image-bearers of God.
He produces love.
Galatians 5:22 identifies love as the first characteristic in the fruit of the Spirit.
Not spectacle.
Not popularity.
Not spiritual intimidation.
Love.
And biblical love is not sentimental approval of everything another person believes or does.
It is a Christ-shaped commitment to seek their good in truth, humility, and righteousness.
That includes people whose backgrounds are different from ours.
People whose politics we dislike.
People whose suffering challenges our assumptions.
People whose stories expose injustices we would rather believe do not exist.
And people who cannot offer us anything in return.
In Acts 17:26, Paul declares that God made the nations from one, emphasizing humanity's common origin under the Creator.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that human beings are created in God's image.
James 2 condemns favoritism within the Christian assembly, particularly the preference shown to the wealthy over the poor.
And Revelation 7:9 presents a vision of a redeemed multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before God's throne and the Lamb.
Think about that.
The eternal worship of Jesus Christ includes people from every nation.
Yet some Christians struggle to treat people of another ethnicity with dignity in the present.
How can we celebrate a multiethnic multitude in heaven while defending racial contempt on earth?
How can we rejoice that Christ has purchased people from every people group while behaving as though certain people are less worthy of respect?
How can we preach reconciliation with God while refusing to pursue reconciliation with the people we have wronged?
Racism is not merely an unfortunate personality flaw when it expresses contempt for people because of their ancestry or ethnicity.
It contradicts the biblical dignity of human beings made in God's image.
And when racial prejudice becomes embedded in institutions, practices, or systems, Christians should be willing to examine the evidence and seek what is just.
That does not require accepting every political slogan, theory, or proposed solution.
Christians may disagree about policies and the causes of particular inequalities.
But we cannot use those disagreements as permission to abandon truthfulness, impartiality, compassion, or justice.
Our loyalty to Jesus must be greater than our loyalty to any tribe, party, culture, or ideology.
And sometimes faithfulness means admitting that people on our own side have done wrong.
That kind of honesty is uncomfortable.
But repentance was never meant to be a comfortable performance.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," speaks of a change of mind or turning that, in biblical usage, is inseparable from a transformed response to God.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed after being exposed.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is admitting what is wrong without dressing it in religious excuses.
It is making restitution when appropriate and possible.
It is learning to love where we once despised.
It is surrendering the pride that keeps insisting we have nothing to confess.
And perhaps that is why confronting racism, greed, and injustice can feel more threatening than discussing demons.
Because it may require us to change.
It may cost us approval.
It may expose our hypocrisy.
It may challenge our financial habits.
It may force us to confront the ways we have benefited from unfairness or contributed to someone else's suffering.
It may require a difficult conversation with a family member.
It may mean refusing to laugh at a racist joke.
It may mean paying workers fairly when underpaying them would be more profitable.
It may mean listening to someone's experience before dismissing it.
It may mean admitting that our favorite preacher, political leader, or Christian organization was wrong.
And none of those things can be accomplished merely by shouting at the devil.
They require humility before God.
They require obedience.
They require the kind of discipleship that follows Jesus even when following Him costs us something.
But we must also confront another temptation.
The temptation to turn justice itself into a substitute for the Gospel.
Because activism cannot save us.
Moral outrage cannot forgive our sins.
Political reform, however necessary or beneficial, cannot regenerate the human heart.
Only Jesus Christ can reconcile sinners to God.
Only His death and resurrection provide the foundation of our salvation.
Only His grace can transform the deepest roots of human rebellion.
We must never reduce Christianity to social activism.
But neither should we reduce Christianity to religious language that leaves our treatment of others unchanged.
The Gospel is not less than forgiveness of sins.
And the forgiveness of sins produces a new life.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
We do not earn salvation by fighting injustice.
We pursue righteousness and mercy because God's grace has begun transforming us.
We do not love our neighbor to purchase God's acceptance.
We love because we have first been loved.
We do not repent to prove we are worthy of Jesus.
We repent because Jesus is worthy of our surrender.
And if we forget that order, we will eventually turn even good causes into opportunities for self-righteousness.
The answer to hypocrisy is not another kind of hypocrisy.
The answer is Christ.
Look at Zacchaeus.
Luke 19 tells us that he was a chief tax collector and a wealthy man.
Tax collection under Roman rule was associated with opportunities for financial exploitation, and Zacchaeus himself acknowledged the possibility of having defrauded others.
When Jesus entered his life, something remarkable happened.
Zacchaeus declared that he would give half his possessions to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
Jesus responded by declaring that salvation had come to his house.
Notice what changed.
His encounter with Jesus did not end with an emotional religious experience.
It reached his wallet.
His treatment of others.
His willingness to make wrongs right.
His relationship with wealth.
He did not merely announce that he had been spiritually delivered.
He demonstrated a changed direction through concrete acts of repentance.
And that should make every one of us uncomfortable in the healthiest possible way.
Because sometimes the most convincing evidence of spiritual transformation is not how loudly someone speaks about demons.
It is how differently they treat people after meeting Jesus.
The dishonest employer begins paying fairly.
The prejudiced believer begins confronting the hatred they once defended.
The greedy person becomes generous.
The proud person learns to apologize.
The indifferent Christian begins noticing the suffering they previously walked past.
The person who once used Scripture to justify contempt begins reading Scripture with humility and fear of God.
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
Not without failures that require fresh confession and repentance.
But genuinely.
Because grace does not merely offer us a new religious vocabulary.
Grace begins making us new.
And there is one passage that should silence every attempt to separate impressive spiritual activity from obedience to Christ.
Matthew 7:22–23.
Jesus warns that many will appeal to extraordinary religious works done in His name, including prophecy, casting out demons, and mighty works.
Yet He says that He will declare to some of them that He never knew them, calling them workers of lawlessness.
Consider the seriousness of that warning.
Jesus does not say that the ability to speak about demons proves someone belongs to Him.
He does not say that public spiritual activity automatically reveals a surrendered heart.
He warns against trusting religious achievements while living in disobedience.
This passage is not permission for us to pronounce judgment on the salvation of particular people.
It is a warning that should lead each of us to examine ourselves.
Because the most dangerous spiritual deception may not be believing that demons exist.
It may be believing that our religious performance makes repentance unnecessary.
And before we go any further, I want to speak to someone who has been wounded by this contradiction.
Perhaps you experienced racism from people who called themselves Christians.
Perhaps you were exploited by someone who quoted Scripture while withholding what they owed you.
Perhaps you watched a church defend a powerful person while ignoring those who had been harmed.
Perhaps you were told to remain silent because speaking about injustice would damage the reputation of a ministry.
Perhaps the people who should have protected you used religious language to dismiss your pain.
I cannot tell you that every person who claims to represent Jesus has represented Him faithfully.
Scripture itself warns us otherwise.
But I can tell you this:
The hypocrisy of those who misuse His name does not define the character of Christ.
Jesus did not overlook religious hypocrisy.
He exposed it.
Jesus did not praise those who devoured the vulnerable while performing impressive acts of devotion.
He condemned such behavior.
Jesus did not treat the wounded as disposable inconveniences.
He moved toward people who were suffering.
And at the cross, He did something none of us could do for ourselves.
He bore sin.
The sin of the proud.
The sin of the prejudiced.
The sin of the greedy.
The sin of the cruel.
The sin of the self-righteous.
And the sin of those who know exactly what righteousness requires but repeatedly refuse to practice it.
Isaiah 53:6 declares that all of us have gone astray and that the Lord laid upon His suffering servant the iniquity of us all.
The cross is not a place where we gather to congratulate ourselves for being morally superior to other sinners.
It is where our pride is exposed and our desperate need for mercy becomes undeniable.
The same Jesus who commands repentance offers forgiveness to those who turn to Him in faith.
The same Savior who confronts hypocrisy welcomes the repentant sinner.
The same Lord who demands love for our neighbors gives His Spirit to transform hearts that have been shaped by hatred.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word.
This is the scandal of grace.
Not that God pretends our sins do not matter.
But that the sinless Son of God gave Himself to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And those whom He rescues are called to follow Him into a new way of living.
From prejudice to love.
From greed to generosity.
From indifference to mercy.
From self-righteousness to repentance.
From religious performance to genuine surrender.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
But by bringing forgiveness, truth, accountability, reconciliation, and transformation into places we once believed were beyond redemption.
Now imagine what would happen if the Church took both spiritual warfare and biblical justice seriously.
Imagine believers praying fervently against evil while also refusing to participate in it.
Imagine pastors preaching repentance with the same conviction whether the sin involved sexual immorality, racism, greed, dishonesty, or oppression.
Imagine Christian employers treating their workers with dignity.
Imagine churches becoming places where the wealthy are not automatically honored above the poor.
Imagine people from different ethnic backgrounds worshiping together without being pressured to ignore genuine wounds.
Imagine Christians disagreeing about politics without abandoning their obligation to love one another.
Imagine a generation of believers who understood that fighting the good fight of faith includes resisting the devil and refusing to surrender their character to hatred.
Ephesians 6:12 reminds us that our struggle is not against flesh and blood.
That truth should make us more careful about how we treat human beings, not less.
People are not the ultimate enemy.
Our neighbors are not demons.
Someone from another race is not our enemy because of their ancestry.
A person who challenges our assumptions is not automatically an instrument of Satan.
And someone who has suffered injustice is not being unspiritual merely because they ask Christians to respond with integrity.
We can confront falsehood without dehumanizing people.
We can resist wickedness without becoming cruel.
We can uphold biblical convictions without abandoning biblical compassion.
And we can proclaim the power of Christ over darkness while recognizing that one of the places His light must shine is inside our own hearts.
So here is the question I want to leave with you.
Not whether you believe demons exist.
Not whether you know how to quote Ephesians 6.
Not whether you have ever attended a deliverance service.
But this:
What sin are you willing to confront in someone else that you are still unwilling to surrender in yourself?
Think about it.
Is it prejudice?
Is it greed?
Is it pride?
Is it indifference toward suffering?
Is it a habit of defending injustice when it benefits someone you admire?
Is it the need to appear righteous while secretly resisting the changes God is calling you to make?
You do not have to announce every private struggle to the world.
But you do need to bring it honestly before the Lord.
And perhaps your next act of spiritual warfare will not look dramatic at all.
Perhaps it will look like a sincere apology.
Perhaps it will look like returning money that was never yours.
Perhaps it will look like defending someone being mistreated.
Perhaps it will look like asking God to expose the prejudice you inherited but never questioned.
Perhaps it will look like choosing mercy when bitterness feels easier.
Perhaps it will look like opening your Bible, falling to your knees, and praying:

"Lord Jesus, I have spent so much time recognizing what is wrong with others that I have neglected what You are confronting in me. Forgive my pride. Expose my hypocrisy. Remove the hatred I have excused, the greed I have defended, and the indifference I have disguised as wisdom. Teach me to love what You love, hate what is evil, and walk humbly before You. I cannot transform my own heart. I need Your grace. Make me more like You. Amen."
Not as a performance.
Not because strangers need to know your private sins.
But as a simple expression of your willingness to be corrected and transformed by Jesus.
You do not owe anyone the details of your pain.
There may be someone reading those words who realizes they are not alone in their struggle.
There may be another believer who finally finds the courage to acknowledge a wrong.
There may be someone who has almost abandoned Christianity because of religious hypocrisy and begins to understand that Jesus Himself condemned the very behavior that wounded them.
Not to win an argument.
Not to shame people.
But because conversations about biblical justice, repentance, mercy, and the transforming power of Christ belong within the Church, not outside its concern.
Someone in your family may need to read this.
A friend may be quietly wrestling with prejudice they have never acknowledged.
A church leader may need a reminder that spiritual authority must never become an excuse for moral blindness.
A struggling believer may need to discover that Jesus is not calling them to pretend everything is fine.
And someone who does not yet believe may need to see that Christianity, faithfully understood, does not require defending hypocrisy.
Our desire is not to build an audience addicted to religious controversy.
It is to help build disciples whose lives increasingly reflect Jesus Christ.
Gospel-centered discipleship requires more than one powerful article.
It requires returning to Scripture when emotions fade, confronting difficult truths when conviction becomes uncomfortable, and receiving encouragement when the journey of obedience feels exhausting.

Through Gospel Warrior, we want to continue producing Christ-centered teaching, devotional encouragement, biblical reflections, and resources that point people toward repentance, forgiveness, spiritual maturity, and genuine transformation.
Scripture calls believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and without compulsion. As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver.
You are not less valuable to God.
You are not less welcome in this community.
Your prayers, your thoughtful comments, your willingness to share biblical truth, and your personal obedience to Jesus matter.
What matters most is that Christ is honored, Scripture is handled faithfully, and people are pointed toward Him rather than toward a personality, platform, or brand.
It is a growing community of people who love Jesus enough to let His Word change them.
And now, one final thought.
One day, every mask will fall.
Every carefully constructed religious reputation will lose its power to impress.
Every hidden motive will be known to the Lord who sees the heart.
On that day, our public image will not be able to replace a genuine relationship with Christ.
The question will not be how many arguments we won about demons.
Or how many people admired our spiritual vocabulary.
Or how convincingly we appeared righteous in front of others.
The question that should concern us now is whether we truly know Jesus and are responding to His grace with repentant faith.
Because the Savior who commands us to love our neighbors is the same Savior who died for our sins.
And the Lord who exposes our hypocrisy is the same Lord who welcomes sinners who turn to Him.
Do not run from His conviction.
Do not confuse His correction with rejection.
Do not protect the very sin He is calling you to surrender.
Come to Him.
Bring your pride.
Bring your prejudice.
Bring your greed.
Bring your indifference.
Bring the wounds inflicted by others.
Bring the shame of your own failures.
Come honestly, trusting not in your ability to make yourself righteous but in the crucified and risen Christ, who alone can save.
And then follow Him.
Not just into conversations about spiritual warfare.
But into the costly, beautiful obedience of loving God and loving your neighbor.
Because the darkness you keep rebuking in the world must never become the darkness you refuse to surrender in your own heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD CALLED JERUSALEM AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE… BUT WHAT HE SAID NEXT SHOULD BRING EVERY SINNER TO TEARS
paragraphs: GOD CALLED JERUSALEM AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE… BUT WHAT HE SAID NEXT SHOULD BRING EVERY SINNER TO TEARS

The shocking prophecy of Ezekiel 16 exposes the spiritual betrayal of an entire city, the terrifying consequences of forgetting God, and the covenant mercy that points us toward Jesus Christ—the Savior who can rewrite even the most scandalous story.
There are chapters in the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that strengthen you.
And then there are chapters that make you uncomfortable enough to wonder whether God is speaking about someone else… or exposing something inside you.
Ezekiel 16 is one of those chapters.
It is not a gentle bedtime story. It is not a collection of inspirational sayings meant to make everyone feel better about themselves.
It is a devastating portrait of betrayal.
A city rescued from death. A people loved beyond anything they deserved. A covenant established by the living God.
And then…
The very people God rescued turned the gifts of His kindness into instruments of rebellion.
But here is what makes this chapter almost unbearable.
God does not describe Jerusalem's idolatry merely as breaking a religious rule.
He describes it as the betrayal of a marriage.
The God who rescued her becomes the Husband she abandons.
The blessings He gives become the treasures she carries into the arms of false gods.
And the city that once lay helpless, with nobody willing to save her, begins living as though she never needed Him at all.
Before this story ends, however, God will speak words that seem almost impossible after everything Jerusalem has done.
Words about remembering His covenant.
Words about atonement.
Words that make the coming of Jesus Christ shine with extraordinary beauty.
And perhaps the most disturbing question in this entire prophecy is not what Jerusalem did thousands of years ago.
Perhaps it is this:
What have we done with the blessings God placed in our hands?
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual betrayal begins not when someone openly declares war against God…
But when someone slowly learns to enjoy His gifts while forgetting His presence.
The prophet Ezekiel was living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon when the word of the LORD came to him.

Jerusalem was facing the consequences of generations of covenant rebellion. Its leaders had repeatedly embraced injustice, idolatry, and false security. The city that carried God's name had become deeply corrupted.
And God commanded Ezekiel to confront her with her abominations.
In Ezekiel 16:2, the prophet is told:
"Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations." (KJV)
Notice something important.
God was not exposing Jerusalem because He lacked knowledge of her sin.
He was exposing Jerusalem because she had become dangerously comfortable with it.
There is a frightening condition of the human heart in which wrongdoing no longer feels wrong.
The conscience grows quiet.
The excuses grow louder.
The things that once brought conviction become normal.
And eventually, a person can become so accustomed to spiritual compromise that correction begins to sound like cruelty.
That was Jerusalem's condition.
But instead of beginning with her crimes, God begins with her history.
He takes her back to the place where everything started.
And what He reveals is heartbreaking.
Jerusalem is portrayed as an abandoned newborn.
Unwashed.
Unprotected.
Unwanted.
Left exposed in a field, with no one showing compassion.
Ezekiel 16:5 describes a child cast into the open field because nobody pitied her.
This is prophetic imagery, not a literal account of one infant's biography. God is describing Jerusalem's helpless beginnings and the grace by which He established her.
Then comes one of the most astonishing declarations in the chapter.
In Ezekiel 16:6, God says:
"Yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is:
בְּדָמַיִךְ חֲיִי
Bĕdamayikh ḥăyî.
Literally, the expression means, "In your blood, live!"
The image is startling.
The child has no ability to rescue herself.
She has no beauty or achievement with which to negotiate her survival.
She cannot promise future loyalty.
She cannot offer anything in return.
Yet God commands life where abandonment seemed to have pronounced death.
Live.
One word changes everything.
And although Ezekiel is speaking specifically about Jerusalem, the imagery reminds Christians of a greater truth found throughout Scripture.
Salvation begins with God's mercy, not human merit.
Ephesians 2:4–5 declares that God, rich in mercy and great love, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in sins.
Think about that.
Before you knew how to pray properly.
Before you understood theology.
Before you knew how to explain grace.
God was already the kind of Savior who shows mercy to the helpless.
Some of you reading this remember seasons when your life seemed beyond repair.
Perhaps addiction had taken more than you wanted to admit.
Perhaps pride destroyed a relationship you thought would last forever.
Perhaps you betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps your public life looked respectable while your private life was collapsing.
Or perhaps you have carried shame so long that you have forgotten what it feels like to stand before God without hiding.
Ezekiel 16 does not tell you that sin is harmless.
It tells you something more profound.
The God who exposes sin is also the God whose mercy gives life.
And Jerusalem's story does not end in the field.
God describes her growth, His covering of her nakedness, His covenant with her, and the extraordinary beauty He bestows upon her.
In Ezekiel 16:8, God declares:
"I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine." (KJV)
There is a beautiful Hebrew expression here:
וַתִּהְיִי לִי
Vattihyî lî.
"And you became mine."
These words belong to the covenant-marriage imagery of the prophecy.
God is portraying Jerusalem as someone He rescued, clothed, adorned, and bound to Himself by covenant.
Her beauty was not independent of Him.
Her honor was not self-created.
Her prosperity was not proof that she had outgrown her need for God.
Ezekiel 16:14 explains that her beauty was perfect through the splendor God had placed upon her.
And then comes the turning point.
One of the saddest sentences in the entire chapter.
"But thou didst trust in thine own beauty..." (Ezekiel 16:15, KJV)
Read that again.
She trusted in her own beauty.
The beauty God had given her.
The gifts that should have awakened gratitude became the foundation of her pride.
The blessing became more important than the Blesser.
And the heart that should have said, "Everything I have came from You," began behaving as though God were no longer necessary.
This is where the prophecy stops feeling like ancient history.
Because how many of us have done something similar?
We prayed for employment, and when God provided, our work consumed the time we once devoted to Him.
We prayed for financial stability, and when our circumstances improved, generosity became harder.
We prayed for relationships, but once those relationships entered our lives, we allowed them to determine our obedience.
We prayed for opportunities, recognition, influence, or success.
And somewhere along the way, we began measuring our worth by the very things we once begged God to provide.
Not every blessing leads to idolatry.
Not every success is evidence of pride.
But any good gift can become spiritually dangerous when we begin trusting it more than the Giver.
Jerusalem did not merely forget God.
She used what God had given her to pursue other gods.
Ezekiel describes the city taking her beautiful garments, jewelry, gold, silver, oil, incense, and food—gifts associated with God's provision—and directing them toward idolatrous worship.
The language becomes deliberately graphic.
God portrays Jerusalem as a wife pursuing other lovers.
The Hebrew verb used in Ezekiel 16:15 comes from the root:
זנה
Z-N-H, commonly represented as zanah.
The verb can describe prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness. In prophetic contexts, it is also used figuratively for religious infidelity, especially idolatry and covenant betrayal.
This distinction matters.
Ezekiel is not inviting readers to indulge in sexual scandal.
He is using shocking marriage imagery to reveal the seriousness of spiritual betrayal.
The metaphor is severe because the covenant relationship is sacred.

And the chapter's explicit language should not be softened into something harmless, nor used to shame victims of sexual abuse or betrayal. Jerusalem is the prophetic subject, and the accusations concern the city's covenant rebellion.
God is exposing the ugliness of idolatry, not treating wounded people as objects of disgust.
The accusation becomes even more devastating when Ezekiel describes the sacrifice of children.
In Ezekiel 16:20–21, Jerusalem is condemned for offering her sons and daughters in connection with idolatrous worship.
This was not merely a matter of personal preference or cultural difference.
It involved the destruction of vulnerable human lives.
The chapter also exposes the wider moral corruption of Jerusalem, including her failure to care for the poor and needy.
Ezekiel 16:49 identifies pride, abundance, complacency, and neglect of the vulnerable among the sins associated with Sodom.
That is an uncomfortable combination.
Religious rebellion.
Social injustice.
Pride.
Cruelty.
Indifference toward suffering.
All appearing within a people who claimed a covenant relationship with God.
And suddenly, we are confronted with a truth that modern Christianity cannot afford to ignore.
You can possess religious language and still be spiritually unfaithful.
You can know worship songs and still mistreat people.
You can defend biblical morality publicly while privately excusing your own cruelty.
You can condemn another person's sins while refusing to repent of your own pride.
You can appear deeply religious and still withhold compassion from someone God commands you to love.
Jesus Himself confronted this kind of hypocrisy.
In Matthew 23:23, He rebuked religious leaders who were meticulous about certain religious duties while neglecting weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith.
God has never been impressed by outward religion that refuses inward surrender.
And Ezekiel's message becomes even more piercing when God repeatedly reminds Jerusalem of something she had forgotten.
Her beginning.
Her helplessness.
Her rescue.
Her covenant.
Her dependence.
Ezekiel 16:22 declares:
"And in all thine abominations and thy whoredoms thou hast not remembered the days of thy youth..." (KJV)
She forgot.
Not because the past had ceased to exist.
But because gratitude had disappeared from her heart.
There is a kind of spiritual forgetfulness that destroys people quietly.
You forget the prayers you once prayed through tears.
You forget how desperately you once needed forgiveness.
You forget the people who carried you when you could barely stand.
You forget the mercy that met you when your life was falling apart.
And eventually, you begin treating grace as though it were something you earned.
That is a dangerous place to live.
Because when gratitude disappears, entitlement often takes its place.
And when entitlement takes over, repentance begins to feel unnecessary.
Perhaps someone reading this remembers when prayer was not a religious routine but a desperate cry.
When worship was not merely music but a response to mercy.
You remember who you were.
You remember what God brought you through.
But somewhere between surviving the storm and enjoying the sunshine, your heart drifted.
You still believe in God.
You still know the right words.
You might even still attend church.
But the closeness is gone.
The hunger has faded.
And you have become skilled at living a Christian-looking life without surrendering the places Jesus keeps asking you to open.
If that describes you, do not turn this into another opportunity to condemn yourself without returning to God.
Let the conviction do what godly conviction is meant to do.
Lead you toward repentance.
Because the purpose of biblical correction is not to make repentance seem impossible.
It is to expose what must be forsaken so that a sinner may return to the Lord.
But we must not rush past the judgment in Ezekiel 16.
Jerusalem's betrayal had consequences.
God declares that He will expose her shame and bring judgment upon her unfaithfulness.
The imagery is disturbing, including public humiliation and violence within the prophetic judgment scene.

It reflects the terrifying consequences of covenant rebellion and the historical catastrophe facing Jerusalem. It must never be used to justify domestic abuse, sexual violence, public humiliation, or cruelty toward people accused of sin.
God's judgment is not a license for human vengeance.
The chapter confronts us with the holiness of God and the seriousness of sin.
Grace does not mean evil is imaginary.
Forgiveness does not mean injustice is unimportant.
And repentance is not simply feeling emotional for a few minutes before returning to the same deliberate rebellion.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly connect genuine turning to God with a changed direction of life.
Ezekiel himself records God's appeal in Ezekiel 18:32:
"For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye." (KJV)
Turn.
And live.
The God who pronounced life over Jerusalem's helpless beginning also calls sinners to turn from the path of destruction.
And then…
Just when Ezekiel 16 seems to have exhausted every possibility of hope…
The chapter changes.
After the accusations.
After the shame.
After the announcement of judgment.
God speaks of His covenant again.
Ezekiel 16:60 says:
"Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with thee in the days of thy youth, and I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant." (KJV)
Nevertheless.
What an extraordinary word.
Not because Jerusalem's sins were insignificant.
Not because her betrayal deserved to be overlooked.
Not because repentance and justice no longer mattered.
But because God's covenant purposes were not exhausted by Jerusalem's failure.
The Hebrew text begins with:
וְזָכַרְתִּי אֲנִי
Vĕzakhartî ʾănî.
"But I myself will remember…"
The verb comes from the Hebrew root zakhar, meaning "to remember."
In this context, God's remembering is not the recovery of information He had forgotten.
It is His covenant faithfulness coming into focus.
Jerusalem had forgotten her beginnings.
But God declares that He will remember His covenant.
Do you see the contrast?
The people forgot.
God remembered.
The people betrayed.
God declared His purpose to establish an everlasting covenant.
This is not cheap grace.
The chapter still speaks of shame, remembrance, and the silencing of self-justification.
Yet its conclusion reveals that divine judgment is not the final word in God's covenant purposes.
Then Ezekiel 16:63 gives us one of the most important statements in the chapter:
"When I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord GOD." (KJV)
The underlying Hebrew expression is:
בְּכַפְּרִי־לָךְ
Bĕkhapperî-lakh.
It comes from the Hebrew root kaphar, associated with making atonement.
A more direct rendering of the phrase is, "When I make atonement for you."
This is crucial.
The KJV's older English expression "when I am pacified" can obscure the atonement language present in the Hebrew.
The chapter does not conclude with Jerusalem successfully purchasing God's forgiveness through her own achievements.
God Himself speaks of making atonement.
And for Christians reading Ezekiel within the whole biblical story, this opens a profound connection to Jesus Christ.
We must be careful here.
Ezekiel 16 was first spoken concerning Jerusalem and God's covenant dealings with His people. It should not be treated as though every verse were a direct prediction of the crucifixion.
Yet the themes of covenant, judgment, mercy, restoration, and atonement find their fullest Christian significance in the person and saving work of Jesus.
Ezekiel later speaks of a new heart and a new spirit in Ezekiel 36:26.
Jeremiah 31:31–34 promises a new covenant in which God forgives iniquity and remembers sin no more.
And at the Last Supper, Jesus declares:
"This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." (Luke 22:20, KJV)
The Greek expression is:
ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη
Hē kainē diathēkē.
"The new covenant."
Jesus does not merely offer religious inspiration.
He gives Himself.
His blood is shed.
His body is offered.
His resurrection announces that sin and death do not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
And the apostle Paul declares in Ephesians 5:25:
"Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
There is something deeply moving about placing this beside Ezekiel 16.
In Ezekiel, the covenant wife is exposed as unfaithful.
In Ephesians, Christ is revealed as the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His church.
The church is not saved because she can claim a flawless history.
She is saved by the grace of the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
That does not mean every person is automatically forgiven regardless of their response to Christ.
The Gospel calls us to repentance and faith.
But it means that the door of salvation is opened through Christ's finished work, not through our ability to manufacture a spotless past.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we learned how to hide our failures.
Not after we finally convinced everyone that we had always been faithful.
Christ died for sinners.
And that is where this ancient prophecy begins to reach into the deepest places of a modern heart.
Because perhaps your greatest fear is not that people will discover what you have done.
Perhaps your greatest fear is that if they knew everything, they would never look at you the same way again.
You know the secret.
The compromise.
The repeated failure.
The relationship you damaged.
The truth you avoided.
The bitterness you have protected.
The person you became when nobody was watching.
And maybe you have spent years trying to outrun the memory of it.
But the Gospel does not ask you to pretend that darkness was light.
It calls you to bring your sin into the light of Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue sinning without repentance.
It is an invitation to stop hiding from the One who alone can cleanse you.
And there is another important distinction.
If someone has sinned against you, their wrongdoing is not your shame to carry.
God's call to forgive does not require you to remain in danger, conceal abuse, or abandon the pursuit of justice.
The Gospel confronts perpetrators with repentance and protects the dignity of those who have been harmed.
Christ's mercy never makes evil good.
It makes redemption possible.
That is why the theme of this ministry is more than a beautiful phrase.
Not because Jesus erases historical facts.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because wounds instantly stop hurting.
But because through His death and resurrection, Jesus gives sinners a future that their past could never create.
A proud person can become humble.
A dishonest person can learn to walk in truth.
A bitter heart can begin to forgive.
A person enslaved by sin can discover freedom through the Son of God.
A believer who has wandered can return in repentance.
And a life once defined by rebellion can become a testimony of mercy.
That is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
That is transformation through the Gospel.
And now, I want to ask you something.
Not as a preacher standing above you.
But as one sinner speaking to another about the mercy of Jesus Christ.
What blessing has become more important to you than the God who gave it?
Is it money?
A relationship?
A reputation?
A position?
A habit?
An ambition?
An online identity?
The approval of people who cannot save your soul?
Or perhaps it is your own religious image—the exhausting need to appear spiritually strong even when you desperately need prayer.
You do not have to answer publicly with details that could expose you to harm or violate someone else's privacy.
But do not avoid answering God.
Because Ezekiel 16 is not merely about a city that committed spiritual adultery.
It is about what happens when a heart receives mercy but refuses to remember the One who gave it.
And it is about the astonishing covenant faithfulness of God, who speaks of atonement even after exposing devastating betrayal.
Maybe today is the day you stop defending the sin you know Christ is calling you to forsake.
Maybe today is the day you apologize.
The day you confess.
The day you ask for help.
The day you reopen your Bible, not to collect another religious quotation, but to hear the voice of God through His Word.
The day you stop pretending that spiritual exhaustion is the same as spiritual maturity.
The day you come back to Jesus.
Not with excuses.
Not with performances.
Not with a carefully edited version of your story.
Just with the truth.
"Lord, I have sinned. I have wandered. I have loved things more than I have loved You. Have mercy on me through Jesus Christ. Teach me to walk in Your ways again."
That is a prayer a broken heart can pray.
And the promise of Christ is not that He turns away everyone who comes carrying shame.
He says in John 6:37:
"...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
What a Savior.
The One who knows the truth about our sin is the very One who calls us to come to Him.
Not to prove your salvation to strangers.
Not to turn your pain into a performance.
But as a simple, honest expression of your desire to draw near to Christ.
You do not have to explain everything.
Sometimes those three words are all a weary person can manage.
Your story may help another person believe that change is possible through Christ.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sending this article to them privately with compassion rather than accusation.
Not every person who needs this message will ever walk into a church building.
Some are sitting alone with their phones, wondering whether God still receives people who have made terrible decisions.
Some are quietly battling temptation.
Some are carrying grief.
Some are Christians who have drifted farther than they ever intended.
And some have never truly understood why Jesus died on the cross.
A simple share may place Scripture before someone who would otherwise never encounter this message.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are growing, Christians who have grown weary, and even those who are still asking questions about faith.
We are not trying to build an audience that admires religious content while remaining unchanged.
We want to point people to Jesus.
To His Word.
To repentance.
To forgiveness.
To grace.
To the kind of discipleship that shapes how we live when nobody is watching.
And if this ministry has helped you grow closer to Christ, there is another way you can participate in its work.

Some believers may prayerfully choose to give from their regular charitable-giving budget. But Scripture does not require anyone to redirect their tithe to an online ministry, and we would never want you to neglect your family's needs or your responsibilities to your church.
The apostle Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Cheerfully.
Not under pressure.
Not out of guilt.
But out of a sincere desire to help sound biblical teaching reach more people.
These products are not the Gospel itself. They are simply additional resources and everyday reminders that can encourage biblical reflection and conversations about faith.
Our desire is that people would not merely read one powerful article and move on.
We want them to open Scripture.
To test what they read against God's Word.
To know Christ more deeply.
To grow in prayer.
To turn away from sin.
To become more compassionate, more truthful, more faithful, and more grounded in the Gospel.
You can still help by sharing biblical resources, praying for the ministry, inviting others to follow, and making good use of the free materials available.
And every genuine act of service should ultimately point people toward Him.
Now, before you leave, return with me to that abandoned child in Ezekiel 16.
Unwanted.
Helpless.
Lying in the open field.
Then the voice of God speaks.
"Live."
Years pass.
The child becomes a beautiful city.
Blessings multiply.
Pride enters.
The heart wanders.
Covenant betrayal follows.
Judgment comes.
And yet, near the end of the prophecy, God says:
"I will remember my covenant."
That is the emotional weight of Ezekiel 16.
The chapter does not minimize the scandal.
It exposes it.
It does not flatter the sinner.
It confronts the sinner.
And it does not teach that forgiveness is cheap.
It speaks of atonement.
For those of us reading this chapter on the other side of the cross, the call is clear.
Do not trust in your own beauty.
Do not worship your blessings.
Do not mistake religious appearance for covenant faithfulness.
Do not presume upon grace while refusing repentance.
And do not believe that your shame is a greater savior than Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
The crucified and risen Lord is able to forgive, cleanse, and transform those who repent and believe.
Your past may still have consequences.
Some relationships may still need repair.
Some wrongs may still require restitution.
Some wounds may need time, wise counsel, and patient healing.
But your sin does not have to remain your master.
Jesus Christ is greater.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth of Ezekiel 16 is this:

Jerusalem forgot the God who gave her life, but God spoke of a covenant mercy that her betrayal could not earn—and in Jesus Christ, sinners are called to discover the grace that only His sacrifice can provide.
If God placed every blessing He has given you on one side, and asked whether you would still love Him without those blessings…
What would your heart reveal?
Do not answer quickly.
Let that question follow you into prayer.
Let it follow you into the decisions nobody else sees.
Let it follow you into the way you treat your family, handle your money, speak to the wounded, resist temptation, and worship when life is difficult.
And when the truth about your heart hurts, remember where the Gospel directs you.
Not toward a better disguise.
Toward the Savior.
Because the greatest tragedy is not simply that Jerusalem forgot her first love.
It is that any of us could read her story, recognize ourselves, and still refuse to return.
The most heartbreaking betrayal is to receive everything from God's hand, then live as though His heart means nothing—and the greatest mercy is that Jesus still calls sinners to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD DIDN’T ASK ADAM, “WHY ARE YOU NAKED?” HE ASKED, “WHO TOLD YOU?”
paragraphs: GOD DIDN’T ASK ADAM, “WHY ARE YOU NAKED?” HE ASKED, “WHO TOLD YOU?”
The First Time Humanity Hid in Shame—and the Heartbreaking Reason God Came Looking Anyway | Genesis 3:7–11
Before Adam ever learned how to hide from God, he had already forgotten what it felt like to stand before Him without shame.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of the story isn't that Adam was hiding.
It's that the God who knew exactly what Adam had done still came looking for him.
Imagine it.
The garden is quiet.
The leaves are moving gently in the breeze. The trees are standing where they have always stood. Everything looks familiar.
But something has changed.
Two human beings who once walked in the presence of their Creator without fear are now crouching among the trees, trying desperately not to be seen.
Their hearts are racing.
Their innocence is gone.
Their hands have been busy sewing leaves together, trying to cover something they have never felt the need to cover before.
And then comes a voice.
The same voice that gave them life.
The same God whose presence had once been their delight.
But now, instead of running toward Him, they hide.
And God asks a question that has echoed through the centuries.
“Who told thee that thou wast naked?” — Genesis 3:11, KJV
Read that again.
Who told you?
Not simply, "Why are you naked?"
Not, "How could you disappoint Me?"
But, "Who told you that you were naked?"
And buried inside that question is a truth that reaches far beyond the Garden of Eden.
Because some of us are still hiding behind leaves we stitched together years ago.
Some of us are still living under the weight of what happened, what we did, what someone said, or what we have become convinced we can never escape.
And the God who called to Adam is still the God before whom nothing is hidden.
But before we turn His question into a comforting slogan, we need to understand what Scripture actually says.
Because this story is more serious, more devastating, and ultimately more hopeful than we sometimes realize.
In Genesis 2:25, before the serpent's deception and before the forbidden fruit, Scripture tells us:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
The original Hebrew says:
וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ
Velo yitboshashu.
“And they were not ashamed.”
That last word comes from the Hebrew root בושׁ (bôsh), associated with shame, disgrace, or being put to shame.
Adam and Eve were naked.
Completely exposed.
Nothing concealed.
Yet there was no shame.
Their nakedness was not a defect. Their bodies were not something sinful. They were God's creation, living in the goodness of what He had made.
There was no guilt to conceal, no disobedience to excuse, no broken trust to fear.
And then Genesis 3 happens.
The serpent questions God's word. Eve sees that the forbidden tree is desirable. She takes its fruit and eats. Adam, who is with her, also eats.
And immediately, something changes.
Genesis 3:7 records:
“And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.” — KJV
The Hebrew begins:
וַתִּפָּקַחְנָה עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם
Vattippaqachnah einei sheneihem.
“Then the eyes of both of them were opened.”
But notice the terrible irony.
They had been promised something greater.
The serpent had told Eve that eating would open their eyes and make them like God, knowing good and evil (Genesis 3:5).
Their eyes did open.
But the first thing Scripture tells us they recognized was their nakedness.
The knowledge they sought did not make them sovereign.
It left them painfully aware of their vulnerability.
The text does not say their bodies suddenly became evil. It does not say that nakedness itself was sin.
It says they recognized their nakedness and immediately tried to cover themselves.
And that is where the first human attempt to conceal shame begins.
They reached for fig leaves before they ever answered to God.
Can you picture it?
Adam gathering leaves.
Eve trying to fasten them together.
Two people who had known perfect fellowship with their Creator now desperately attempting to make themselves presentable.
The leaves were real.
The covering was real.
But the deeper problem remained.
They had disobeyed the God who gave them everything.
They could cover their bodies.
They could not undo their rebellion.
And if that doesn't sound painfully familiar, consider how often we do the same thing.
We make a terrible decision and then work harder to appear respectable.
We wound someone and then become defensive rather than confess.
We struggle with secret sin while carefully maintaining a public image of spiritual strength.
We smile in church, say we are blessed, share Bible verses, and make sure no one suspects what has been happening behind closed doors.
Sometimes the leaves look like religious activity.
Sometimes they look like perfectionism.
Sometimes they look like excuses.
Sometimes they look like a carefully edited life on social media.
And sometimes they look like the words:
"I'm fine."
Even when we are not.
There is a difference, of course, between wise privacy and sinful concealment. Not every private struggle belongs before a public audience.
But we know when we are no longer simply protecting something personal.
We are protecting a lie.
We are avoiding repentance.
We are afraid that if the truth comes out, everything will fall apart.
And that fear can become a prison.
You can be surrounded by people and still feel profoundly alone.
You can receive compliments while privately wondering what those same people would think if they knew everything.
You can sing about God's mercy while struggling to believe that mercy could reach you.
And eventually, you can become so accustomed to hiding that you forget what it means to be honest before God.
That is why the next scene in Genesis is so devastating.
Genesis 3:8 says Adam and Eve heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden, and they hid themselves among the trees.
Think about that.
The trees God created became the hiding place of people who had sinned against Him.
The gifts of creation were being used as cover from the Creator.
And then God called to the man:
“Where art thou?” — Genesis 3:9, KJV
The Hebrew is only one word:
אַיֶּכָּה
Ayyekkah.
“Where are you?”
Now we must be careful here.
God was not searching because He lacked information.
Scripture teaches that nothing is hidden from His sight (Hebrews 4:13).
He knew where Adam was.
He knew what had happened.
He knew what they had eaten.
The question was not evidence of divine ignorance.
It was the beginning of a divine confrontation.
God was summoning Adam to answer.
And notice what Adam said.
“I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.” — Genesis 3:10, KJV
There it is.
"I was afraid."
Three words that tell us something had gone terribly wrong.
The man who once enjoyed God's presence now feared it.
The one who had nothing to conceal now hid.
The one who had been unashamed now felt exposed.
Sin had not made God less holy.
It had changed humanity's relationship to Him.
And then comes the question.
The one we cannot afford to rush past.
“Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” — Genesis 3:11, KJV
The Hebrew reads:
מִי הִגִּיד לְךָ כִּי עֵירֹם אָתָּה
Mi higgid lekha ki eirom attah?
“Who told you that you were naked?”
The verb הִגִּיד (higgid) comes from a Hebrew root meaning to tell, declare, or make known.
But here is an important distinction.
God was not necessarily asking Adam to identify a person who had spoken a negative message over him.
The verse does not say Satan whispered, "You are worthless."
It does not say Eve insulted Adam.
And it does not teach that Adam's problem was merely poor self-esteem.
God's next question explains the direction of His interrogation:
"Have you eaten of the tree?"
In other words, Adam's new awareness of nakedness was connected to his disobedience.
God was confronting the sin behind the hiding.
And that makes the passage far more searching than a simple message about ignoring negative opinions.
Because sometimes the voice we need to confront is not someone else's criticism.
Sometimes it is our own conscience, troubled because we have genuinely done wrong.
Sometimes our shame is tangled together with guilt that needs confession.
Sometimes the answer is not simply, "Stop feeling bad about yourself."
Sometimes the answer is, "Come into the light. Tell the truth. Turn back to God."
And that is where grace becomes so beautiful.
Because the God who confronted Adam did not cease to be holy.
And the God who is holy did not cease to be merciful.
Both truths matter.
We cannot appreciate the Gospel if we minimize sin.
And we cannot understand the heart of God if we forget His mercy.
But there is another heartbreaking detail in this story.
When God asks Adam about the forbidden fruit, Adam does not simply confess.
He says:
“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.” — Genesis 3:12, KJV
Do you hear it?
"The woman..."
And then:
"Whom Thou gavest..."
Adam acknowledges eating, but he also points toward Eve and, indirectly, toward God.
The man who should have taken responsibility begins shifting blame.
Eve, when questioned, points to the serpent's deception.
And suddenly the garden is filled with something humanity still knows too well.
Excuses.
Accusations.
Fear.
Broken trust.
Sin does not merely produce shame.
It damages relationships.
It teaches us to protect ourselves at someone else's expense.
It makes confession difficult because confession requires us to stop defending the image we have constructed.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Not hiding behind a tree.
But hiding behind an explanation.
You know you were wrong, but you keep replaying what someone else did first.
You know you need to apologize, but pride keeps telling you to wait.
You know the relationship needs honesty, but fear keeps you silent.
You know the habit is destroying your peace, but you have become skilled at explaining why you cannot stop.
You know God is calling you to repentance, but you are still gathering leaves.
And perhaps the hardest thing to admit is that you have become exhausted trying to maintain a version of yourself that cannot survive the truth.
But listen carefully.
The answer to the shame of Eden was never going to be better fig leaves.
It had to be something only God could provide.
Genesis 3 does not end with Adam and Eve successfully repairing what they broke.
There are real consequences.
The serpent is cursed.
Human life becomes marked by pain, conflict, toil, and death.
Adam and Eve are eventually sent out of Eden.
God's mercy does not erase the seriousness of rebellion.
Yet right there, in the middle of judgment, Scripture gives us a promise that Christians have long understood as pointing toward the coming victory of Christ.
In Genesis 3:15, God speaks of the offspring of the woman and the conflict with the serpent.
The Hebrew uses the word:
זֶרַע
Zera.
“Seed” or “offspring.”
God announces that the woman's offspring will strike the serpent's head, while the serpent strikes his heel.
Within the unfolding story of Scripture, this promise points us toward Jesus Christ, the One who came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8).
It is not a promise that human beings will save themselves by becoming stronger.
It points toward God's answer to the ruin of sin.
And then Genesis 3:21 gives us another remarkable moment:
“Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.” — KJV
Read that slowly.
God clothed them.
The very people who had disobeyed Him.
The very people who had hidden from Him.
The very people who had tried to cover themselves.
God made garments for them.
We should not claim more than the text reveals. Genesis does not explicitly describe an animal sacrifice here, nor does it directly call these garments an act of atonement.
But it does show something beautiful and unmistakable.
God provided clothing for the people who had failed to cover their situation adequately on their own.
Even in judgment, He acted with care.
And when we follow the whole biblical story forward, we discover that God's provision reaches its fullness in someone far greater than a garment.
Jesus Christ.
The second Adam.
The One who came to do what the first Adam failed to do.
Romans 5:19 declares:
“For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” — KJV
The contrast is breathtaking.
Adam disobeyed in a garden.
Jesus submitted to the Father's will in Gethsemane.
Adam reached for what God had forbidden.
Jesus refused to abandon the obedience the Father required.
Adam hid after sinning.
Jesus, who had no sin, willingly stepped forward to suffer for sinners.
And at Calvary, something happened that should stop every one of us in our tracks.
The Son of God was stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Exposed to public humiliation.
Soldiers divided His garments.
The sinless Savior endured the shame of crucifixion.
Not because He had committed some secret wrong.
Not because He deserved condemnation.
But because He had come to save the guilty.
Hebrews 12:2 says that Jesus endured the cross, “despising the shame,” and is seated at the right hand of God's throne.
The Greek expression is:
αἰσχύνης καταφρονήσας
Aischynēs kataphronēsas.
“Despising the shame,” or regarding its disgrace as something not worthy of turning Him away from His mission.
Jesus did not pretend the cross was painless.
He did not deny its humiliation.
He endured it.
For the joy set before Him.
And this is where Eden and Calvary meet in a way that should bring us to our knees.
In Eden, guilty humanity tried to cover its shame. At Calvary, the innocent Christ endured shame to redeem the guilty.
That is the Gospel.
Not that our sins were insignificant.
Not that shame can simply be wished away.
Not that God lowered His standards because He felt sorry for us.
But that Jesus Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He did what no amount of human effort could accomplish.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And this is why you must not confuse conviction with hopeless condemnation.
The Holy Spirit convicts us of sin and points us toward the truth of Christ (John 16:8–14).
But the Gospel does not leave repentant believers trapped under an endless sentence of rejection.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
In the Greek, the word for condemnation is:
κατάκριμα
Katakrima.
A judicial sentence of condemnation.
Paul is not saying believers never feel regret.
He is not saying Christians no longer need to repent.
He is not saying consequences magically disappear.
He is announcing that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict their sins deserve.
That is not cheap comfort.
That is costly grace.
Grace purchased through the blood of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps you need to hear that distinction today.
Because some of you are carrying shame for sins you have already confessed and turned away from.
You keep returning to the same memory.
The same failure.
The same terrible decision.
You have asked God for forgiveness, but you still punish yourself as though suffering long enough might finally make you worthy of mercy.
You keep rehearsing what happened.
You keep imagining what your life would have been if you had chosen differently.
You keep calling yourself by the name of your worst mistake.
And while repentance is necessary, endless self-condemnation is not the same as holiness.
If you are in Christ, your identity is not exhausted by your history.
Your sin was real.
The damage may have been real.
The consequences may still require responsibility, restitution, difficult conversations, and patient rebuilding.
But the cross is real too.
And the resurrection is real.
And the mercy of God is not imaginary.
Consider Peter.
He boldly declared his loyalty to Jesus.
Then, when the pressure came, he denied knowing Him three times.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Can you imagine that moment?
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of his own promises.
The crushing realization that he had denied the Lord he loved.
Peter could not blame someone else for the words that came out of his mouth.
He had failed.
Publicly.
Painfully.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The Lord did not pretend the denial never happened.
He confronted Peter with a searching question about love and called him forward into faithful service.
That is what grace does.
It does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
It rewrites the future by redeeming sinners who could never save themselves.
And perhaps that is why you are still reading.
Because somewhere beneath the responsibilities, the routines, the carefully maintained smile, and the words you use to reassure everyone else, there is a part of you that is tired.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of remembering.
Tired of wondering whether God could possibly use someone with your history.
Maybe you are the believer who fell back into the very sin you promised you would never commit again.
Maybe you are the parent carrying regret over words you cannot take back.
Maybe you are the husband or wife who knows an apology is overdue.
Maybe you are the young person who has allowed a secret struggle to convince you that God must be disgusted with you.
Maybe you were deeply wounded by someone else's sin, and shame has attached itself to you even though you were not responsible for what happened.
If that last sentence describes you, hear this clearly: another person's wrongdoing is not your guilt to carry. What was done to you does not make you less valuable before God.
And if you are the one who sinned, hear this too: the way forward is not denial, but repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
There is room at the cross for truth.
For tears.
For confession.
For wounded people who need healing.
For guilty people who need forgiveness.
For believers who need to return to the Lord.
For those who have spent years assuming they are beyond redemption.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Notice what John does not say.
He does not say, "If we hide our sins successfully."
He does not say, "If we convince everyone we are righteous."
He does not say, "If we punish ourselves enough."
He says:
"If we confess."
The Greek word is:
ὁμολογῶμεν
Homologōmen.
“If we confess” or “acknowledge.”
It carries the idea of openly acknowledging what is true.
God is not asking us to perform a more convincing version of righteousness.
He calls us to come into the light.
And because of Jesus Christ, confession is not the end of hope.
It is part of walking in the truth before the God who forgives.
You do not need to expose every intimate detail of your life to strangers to prove you are repentant. But you do need to stop treating concealment as a substitute for obedience.
If you have wronged someone, take responsibility.
If you need help overcoming destructive patterns, seek wise, trustworthy support.
If you have been living in deliberate disobedience, turn from it.
If you have wandered from Christ, return to Him.
If you have never trusted Jesus as Savior and Lord, come to Him in repentance and faith.
Not because you have finally made yourself clean.
But because He is the Savior who cleanses sinners.
And here is the question I want you to sit with tonight.
When Adam said, "I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself," he was describing more than an embarrassing moment.
He was revealing what sin had done to his fellowship with God.
Now ask yourself:
What have I been hiding?
What truth am I afraid to acknowledge?
What excuse have I repeated so often that I have begun to believe it?
What shame have I allowed to define me more deeply than the promises of God?
And what would obedience look like if I stopped hiding today?
Maybe it begins with a quiet prayer.
Not a polished prayer.
Not a performance.
Just the truth.

"Lord Jesus, I have been hiding. I have tried to cover things I should have confessed. I have carried shame that I do not know how to release. Forgive my sins. Teach me to repent sincerely. Heal what is wounded. Give me courage to make right what I can. Help me trust what You accomplished through Your death and resurrection. I do not want to keep running from the One who came to save me. Amen."
And if this message has exposed something in your heart, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You do not have to explain the details of your pain publicly.
A simple request for prayer is enough.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that the mercy of Jesus Christ is not just a theological idea.
It is the hope by which real sinners are saved and changed.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to accuse.
Someone you genuinely love.
Someone who has been unusually quiet.
Someone who has drifted away from church.
Someone who is struggling to believe that forgiveness is possible.
Someone who has spent years wearing a smile while carrying a hidden burden.
Because there may come a night when an old memory returns, when guilt feels overwhelming, or when you are tempted to run back into hiding.
On that night, return to the Scriptures.
Return to the truth.
Return to the cross.
And remember that Jesus Christ did not come to congratulate the self-righteous.
He came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32).
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish words that stir emotion for a few minutes.
Not to collect religious reactions and then leave people spiritually hungry.
But to keep pointing people toward the Word of God, the person and work of Jesus Christ, genuine repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the kind of transformation that only God can accomplish.
There are people who will never walk into a church building simply because someone invited them.
But they may read a Scripture-centered message shared by someone they trust.
And that message may become one of the ways God draws them to hear the Gospel.
These resources are meant to help people move beyond momentary inspiration into a deeper, more consistent relationship with the Lord.
It is a practical way to stand behind the ongoing work of creating, sharing, and expanding Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources.
We believe that giving generously to support faithful Christian ministry can be an act of worship and stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully, and with the desire to honor God.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver—not one who gives under compulsion.
You can pray.
You can share.
You can encourage someone who is struggling.
You can help put the truth of God's Word in front of someone who desperately needs to hear it.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus Christ is.
The products are simply another way to encourage faith-centered living, share meaningful reminders of Scripture, and support the ongoing work.
Because we are not trying to build a following that admires Gospel Warrior more than it loves Jesus.
We want to help build a community that knows His Word, treasures His grace, takes sin seriously, and follows Him faithfully.
And now, before this message ends, I want to return to the garden one final time.
Adam is standing before God.
His makeshift covering cannot undo his disobedience.
His excuses cannot change what happened.
The trees cannot protect him from the One who sees everything.
And the question still hangs in the air.
"Who told you that you were naked?"
For Adam, the answer leads directly to the sin he committed.
For us, the question invites serious examination of what we have done, what we have believed, and what we are trying to conceal.
But thank God the biblical story does not end with a frightened man among the trees.
It leads us to another Man.
Jesus Christ.
The sinless Savior who hung upon a tree.
The risen Lord who conquered death.
The Redeemer who calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And the day is coming when all who belong to Christ will stand before Him, not because they managed to hide their failures, but because His righteousness and saving grace are sufficient.
Revelation 7:14 speaks of those whose robes have been washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb.
What a beautiful picture of redemption.
Humanity began trying to cover its shame with leaves.
The redeemed stand clothed in garments made white through the Lamb's blood.
Not through their own perfection.
Not through their ability to conceal the past.
But through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
So stop running from the truth.
Stop calling darkness your home.
Stop allowing your worst chapter to become the final definition of your life.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy of Christ by faith.
And walk forward in the light.
Because the most important question is no longer whether you can make yourself look righteous enough to be accepted.
It is whether you will trust the Savior who alone can make sinners right with God.
Adam hid among the trees because of his sin. Jesus hung upon a tree to save sinners like Adam—and sinners like us.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BE STILL AND KNOW THAT I AM GOD”—WHAT IF WE’VE BEEN MISSING THE MOST POWERFUL PART OF THIS VERSE?
paragraphs: “BE STILL AND KNOW THAT I AM GOD”—WHAT IF WE’VE BEEN MISSING THE MOST POWERFUL PART OF THIS VERSE?

We turned it into a comforting whisper for anxious hearts. But in its original Hebrew context, these words carry a breathtaking command that can change how you face fear, fight your battles, surrender control, and recognize the God who has never lost a war.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
You can spend eight hours in bed and still wake up feeling like you've been fighting all night.
Your body is tired. Your thoughts are louder than ever. Your prayers seem to hit the ceiling and fall back into your lap.

And somewhere between another unpaid bill, another strained relationship, another unanswered prayer, and another private battle nobody knows you're fighting, you whisper something you've heard Christians say a thousand times:
“Be still and know that I am God.”
You try to calm down.
You close your eyes.
You breathe.
You tell yourself that God is in control.
But five minutes later, you're worrying again.
And now, on top of everything else, you feel guilty because you can't even seem to be still.
What if I told you that the verse you've been using to quiet your emotions was originally spoken in a setting of nations raging, kingdoms collapsing, and God confronting the chaos of a world at war?
What if the command was never simply about sitting quietly until your anxiety disappears?
What if God was saying something far more confronting?
Something that doesn't merely comfort your troubled heart.
Something that challenges the throne you've been trying to occupy.
Because sometimes the greatest battle isn't happening around you.
It's happening inside you, where fear keeps convincing you that everything will fall apart unless you personally hold it together.
And Psalm 46:10 has something to say about that.
Something we desperately need to hear.
But to understand it, we have to go back to the words God actually gave us.
The familiar King James Version reads:
“Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.” — Psalm 46:10 (KJV)
Beautiful words.
But notice something.
The verse doesn't end with your peace.
It ends with God's exaltation.
That matters more than we realize.
Because the center of this Scripture is not our ability to become calm.
The center is God's absolute supremacy.
And the original Hebrew helps us see why.
The opening command is:
הַרְפּוּ וּדְעוּ כִּי־אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהִים
Harpû ûdeʿû kî-ʾānōkî ʾĕlōhîm.
A close rendering is:
“Cease, and know that I am God.”
The first word, הַרְפּוּ (harpû), comes from the Hebrew verb רָפָה (raphah), which can carry the sense of letting go, relaxing one's grip, ceasing, or desisting, depending on its context.
This is where the passage becomes especially powerful.
The word is not primarily an instruction to practice a breathing exercise or empty your mind.
In Psalm 46, it belongs to a declaration about God's authority over violent nations and human conflict.
Some translations therefore render the command “Stop fighting” or “Cease striving.”
The Hebrew does not mean that every personal struggle is automatically a sin, nor does it command us to abandon responsibility.
But it does confront something deeply human.
Our stubborn belief that we must control what only God can govern.
And the more you understand the surrounding verses, the more astonishing the command becomes.
Because Psalm 46 doesn't begin in a peaceful garden.
It begins with catastrophe.
“God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.” — Psalm 46:1 (KJV)
Then the psalmist describes the earth being removed, mountains falling into the sea, waters roaring, and mountains shaking.
Imagine that.
The world beneath your feet is no longer stable.
The things you thought were immovable are collapsing.
Everything familiar feels threatened.
And yet the psalmist says:
“Therefore will not we fear.” — Psalm 46:2 (KJV)
Not because nothing frightening is happening.
Not because the people of God are naturally fearless.
Not because they have mastered their emotions.
But because God is their refuge.
Do you see the difference?
Biblical confidence isn't pretending the mountains aren't shaking.
It's knowing who remains sovereign when they do.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction right now.
Because you've been measuring God's faithfulness by how peaceful your circumstances feel.
When the bills are paid, you feel blessed.
When your family is getting along, you feel secure.
When your health is good, your faith feels strong.
When prayers are answered quickly, you tell everyone God is good.
But when the diagnosis comes...
When the marriage begins to fracture...
When your child stops listening...
When the person you trusted betrays you...
When the opportunity disappears...
When the prayer remains unanswered...
Suddenly you wonder whether God has moved.
Psalm 46 gives a different picture.
The mountains move.
The waters roar.
The nations rage.
The kingdoms shake.
But God remains God.
And that changes everything.
The psalm continues:
“The heathen raged, the kingdoms were moved: he uttered his voice, the earth melted.” — Psalm 46:6 (KJV)
Notice the contrast.
Human beings make noise.
God speaks.
Nations rage.
God reigns.
Kingdoms tremble.
God remains enthroned.
And then comes a remarkable invitation:

“Come, behold the works of the LORD, what desolations he hath made in the earth. He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.” — Psalm 46:8–9 (KJV)
Only after this description of God's power to end warfare do we hear:
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
This is not a random inspirational sentence inserted into a peaceful devotional.
It is the declaration of the Lord who can silence the instruments of war.
The nations may resist Him, but they cannot overthrow Him.
The powers of the earth may boast, but they cannot remove Him from His throne.
The command addresses a world that must recognize His supremacy.
And because God's people are listening to this psalm, they too are invited to rest their confidence in His reign.
Here is the crucial distinction.

The original context is about God's sovereignty over the nations and their conflicts. The personal application is that His people can stop treating fear, striving, and control as though those things were their saviors.
We should not erase the first meaning to make room for the second.
The second becomes stronger when we honor the first.
Because the God who rules over raging nations is not powerless before the trouble in your home.
The God who can break the bow and shatter the spear is not intimidated by the situation that has brought you to tears.
And the God who will be exalted in the earth has not surrendered His throne because your life has become complicated.
But there is another truth we need to confront.
Sometimes the thing we call “faith” is actually fear wearing religious clothing.
We pray, but immediately begin planning how to force the outcome.
We say we trust God, but we cannot tolerate waiting.
We ask for His will, but become angry when His answer threatens our preferred future.
