We sing about surrender on Sunday, then spend Monday desperately trying to control everyone around us.
And when things don't go our way, we call it spiritual warfare without first asking whether our own pride, impatience, or disobedience might be part of the struggle.
That is uncomfortable.
I know.
Because surrender sounds beautiful until God touches the thing we've been refusing to release.
It's easy to surrender a problem after it's already solved.
It's another matter to surrender while the outcome remains unknown.
It's easy to trust God when the door is opening.
It's harder when you've prayed for months and the door remains closed.
It's easy to say, “Jesus, take control,” when His direction agrees with your plans.
But what happens when following Him requires an apology you don't want to make?
A relationship you need to leave?
A sin you need to confess?
A habit you need to abandon?
A person you need to forgive?
A financial decision that requires honesty rather than appearances?
A season of waiting you cannot accelerate?
That is where surrender stops being a Christian slogan and becomes an act of worship.
And perhaps the most revealing question isn't whether you believe God exists.
Perhaps it's whether you're willing to let Him be God.
Because there is a difference between acknowledging God's authority and yielding to it.
You can believe He is sovereign while living as though the universe depends on your next decision.
You can know the words of Psalm 46:10 while refusing to release the illusion of control.
You can speak about peace while secretly worshiping predictability.
And you can attend church every week while carrying a burden Christ never asked you to carry alone.
But don't misunderstand this.
God is not demanding that you become emotionally numb.
Being still before God does not mean you must stop crying.
It does not mean you cannot ask difficult questions.
It does not mean depression disappears through stronger willpower.
It does not mean a frightened believer has automatically failed in faith.
And it certainly does not mean you should remain passive in the face of abuse, injustice, or danger.
Scripture calls us to pray, act wisely, seek justice, bear one another's burdens, and obey God.
Surrender is not the abandonment of responsibility.
It is the abandonment of the claim that we are ultimately sovereign.
Sometimes obedience means waiting.
Sometimes it means speaking.
Sometimes it means leaving.
Sometimes it means seeking help.
Sometimes it means taking the next faithful step while your hands are still trembling.
And sometimes it means admitting, with tears running down your face:
“Lord, I cannot fix this. But I know You are God.”
That prayer may be more honest than a thousand confident religious statements.
And God is not offended by honest dependence.
Look at Jesus.
In the Garden of Gethsemane, He did not pretend that suffering was painless.
He said:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.” — Matthew 26:38 (KJV)
Then He prayed:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39 (KJV)
Read that again.
The sinless Son of God expressed profound sorrow.
He prayed honestly about the suffering before Him.
Yet He submitted Himself completely to the Father's will.
And we need to understand this carefully.
Jesus wasn't surrendering a sinful desire or repenting of rebellion. He was the perfectly obedient Son, willingly embracing the Father's saving purpose.
His prayer shows us that submission to God and deep emotional anguish are not opposites.
You can be sorrowful and obedient.
You can be afraid of suffering and still entrust yourself to the Father.
You can weep and worship.
You can tremble and trust.
You can feel the weight of tomorrow without pretending to know how tomorrow will unfold.
The question is not whether your heart ever shakes.
The question is where you turn when it does.
And this is where Psalm 46 begins to point us toward the fullness of the Gospel.
The psalm celebrates the Lord as the refuge of His people.
It repeats the magnificent declaration:
“The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge.” — Psalm 46:7, 11 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the phrase “LORD of hosts” is:
יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת
YHWH tsevaʾot.
It speaks of the LORD of hosts, the sovereign God whose authority extends over the heavenly armies and all creation.
The expression “God of Jacob” is equally remarkable.
Jacob was not a man whose story began with spotless perfection.
His life included deception, conflict, fear, and painful consequences.
Yet God remained faithful to His covenant promises.
And the psalm doesn't say, “The God of people who have never failed is our refuge.”
It says:
“The God of Jacob is our refuge.”
Think about that.
The God who showed mercy to Jacob is the refuge of His people.
Not because human failure is insignificant.
Not because sin has no consequences.
But because God's covenant faithfulness is greater than the unworthiness of those He calls.
And when we read the whole Bible, we discover how that faithfulness reaches its glorious fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The One who came into our broken world did not merely give us another technique for managing stress.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear the judgment our sins deserved.
He came to do what no amount of religious effort, self-improvement, or emotional discipline could accomplish.
And He did it through a cross.
Consider the scene.
The Son of God is betrayed.
False witnesses accuse Him.
Religious leaders condemn Him.
Roman soldiers mock Him.
A crown of thorns is pressed upon His head.
His body is wounded.
His hands and feet are nailed to the wood.
And to the watching world, it looks like evil has won.
The Messiah appears defeated.
The disciples are scattered.
Hope seems buried beneath public shame.
But the cross was not an accident that caught God by surprise.
It was the place where the innocent Savior willingly gave Himself for the guilty.
The apostle Peter declared that Jesus was delivered according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge, while also holding those who crucified Him accountable for their wickedness (Acts 2:23).
Human evil was real.
Divine sovereignty was real.
And God's saving purpose was not defeated.
Then came the resurrection.
The stone was rolled away.
The crucified Christ rose bodily from the dead.
Sin and death did not have the final word.
Jesus did.
And this is why the Gospel is so much greater than the advice to “just relax.”
We don't merely need relief from anxiety.
We need reconciliation with God.
We don't merely need our circumstances rearranged.
We need our hearts redeemed.
We don't merely need someone to tell us everything will be fine.
We need a Savior who has conquered sin and death.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
This is the scandal of grace.
The guilty are invited to come to the Holy One.
The ashamed are offered forgiveness.
The spiritually exhausted are called to receive mercy.
The sinner who cannot repair the past is offered a new beginning through repentance and faith in Christ.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
But because Jesus paid a price we could never pay.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
Notice what salvation is not.
It is not a reward for becoming perfectly calm.
It is not payment for attending enough church services.
It is not earned through donations.
It is not achieved by sharing Christian content.
It is God's gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And genuine faith produces a transformed life, as Ephesians 2:10 goes on to explain.
That is why the call to surrender is so serious.
Jesus does not simply want to become another comforting voice in a life where we remain our own masters.
He calls us to repent, believe the Gospel, deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
And yes, following Him may cost us something.
But nothing we surrender for His sake can compare with the worth of knowing Him.
Perhaps you're reading this while carrying a private scandal.
Something you regret.
Something you've hidden.
Something that still makes your stomach tighten whenever you remember it.
Maybe nobody knows the whole story.
Maybe people see your smile, your church attendance, your Bible posts, your family photographs.
But they don't see the guilt you carry into the night.
They don't know about the addiction you keep promising to quit.
The bitterness you've been feeding.
The lie you've been maintaining.
The secret compromise.
The betrayal.
The years you've spent running from God while convincing everyone you're doing fine.
And now you're wondering whether you have gone too far.
Listen carefully.
The invitation of the Gospel is not that your sin was harmless.
It is that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior for sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
You do not have to defend what God is calling you to confess.
You do not have to pretend that your wounds are healed when they are still bleeding.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony that sounds impressive.
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Turn from sin.
Trust the Savior.
Receive His grace.
And begin walking in obedience, one step at a time.
Because Christ doesn't rewrite everything by pretending the past never happened.
He redeems sinners, changes their relationship with God, and gives them a new direction through His death and resurrection.
Sometimes the consequences of yesterday remain.
Sometimes trust must be rebuilt.
Sometimes healing takes years.
Sometimes reconciliation requires more than one person's willingness.
But even when the earthly story remains complicated, forgiveness and new life in Christ are real.
That is not shallow inspiration.
That is redemption.
And maybe now we can return to Psalm 46:10 with different ears.
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
What if the Lord is calling you to stop making your fear the final authority?
What if He's calling you to stop using endless activity to avoid repentance?
What if He's calling you to stop confusing control with faithfulness?
What if He's calling you to obey the truth you already know instead of demanding another sign?
What if your greatest need today isn't another explanation of why everything went wrong?
What if your greatest need is to remember who God is?
Not a distant force.
Not a servant of your personal plans.
Not a guarantee that every earthly desire will be fulfilled.
But the holy, faithful, sovereign Lord who has revealed His saving love in Jesus Christ.
And if you're wondering whether the New Testament actually teaches believers to entrust their anxieties to God, it does.
“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.” — 1 Peter 5:7 (KJV)
And Jesus Himself said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
That is the beauty of reading Scripture in context.
We don't have to force Psalm 46:10 to say everything we need to hear.
We can let it declare God's sovereignty over the earth, and then listen as the rest of Scripture reveals His compassion toward weary people.
His sovereignty is not cold.
His mercy is not weak.
His holiness is not negotiable.
His grace is not for sale.
And His Son is not merely one possible source of comfort among many.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
There may be someone reading these words who has spent years trying to be strong for everybody.
The parent who cries only after the children fall asleep.
The husband who doesn't know how to admit he's frightened.
The wife who has prayed for change so long that hope itself feels exhausting.
The young person who seems confident online but secretly feels lost.
The pastor who encourages everyone else while quietly battling discouragement.
The believer who loves Jesus but feels ashamed to admit that anxiety still comes.
The person who once walked closely with God but has slowly drifted into compromise.
If that's you, hear this.
You do not need to pretend that you are the Almighty.
You are a human being.
You have limits.
You need grace.
You need wisdom.
You need other believers.
You need the Word of God.
And above all, you need Jesus.
Your weakness is not evidence that God's throne is empty.
Your tears are not proof that His promises have failed.
Your unanswered questions do not cancel His resurrection.
And the battle you're facing is not permission to forget who holds ultimate authority over heaven and earth.
But neither is God's sovereignty a promise that you will escape every hardship.
Christians suffer.
Faithful people experience loss.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hope.
Some earthly wounds do not fully heal in this life.
Jesus never promised His followers an existence without tribulation.
He said:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33 (KJV)
There it is.
Not the absence of trouble.
The victory of Christ.
And because He has overcome, our hope reaches beyond what we can presently see.
So perhaps tonight, instead of trying to force yourself into a feeling of perfect peace, you can pray something simpler.
“Father, I confess that I have tried to control what belongs to You. I have let fear speak louder than Your Word. I have held tightly to things I cannot save, change, or guarantee.
Forgive my pride, my unbelief, and the sins I have excused.
Teach me to recognize what You have entrusted to my responsibility and what I must leave in Your hands.
Give me courage to obey, humility to repent, wisdom to seek help when I need it, and patience to wait when I cannot see the outcome.
Lord Jesus, thank You for the cross. Thank You for Your resurrection. Thank You that forgiveness is found in You.
I surrender my claim to be in control.
You are God.
And I am Yours.
Amen.”
If that prayer describes the battle you've been fighting, don't rush past it.
Be honest before God.
Not because a comment proves your faith.
Not because public confession is required for God to hear you.
But because someone else reading may be carrying the same struggle, and your honest words might remind them they are not alone.

And if Christ has brought you through a season when everything seemed to collapse, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Someone may need to hear that God's faithfulness does not depend on a trouble-free life.
There is another way you can help this message reach people who may never enter a church building or open a Bible on their own.
Not as a performance of spirituality.
Not to collect approval.
But because someone scrolling in silence may be asking questions they've never dared to speak aloud.
Someone may be mistaking their anxiety for spiritual failure.
Someone may be trying to earn forgiveness.
Someone may be one conversation away from opening the Scriptures and discovering the hope of the Gospel.
A thoughtful share can begin that conversation.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown weary, the person who has wandered, and even the seeker who isn't sure what to believe.
Let them know there is a place where difficult questions can be explored under the authority of Scripture and where the good news of Jesus Christ remains central.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Bible, strengthen their faith, understand Christian teaching, and grow in their walk with Jesus.
And there is something important I want to share with those who believe in this mission.
Behind every article, every resource, every message of encouragement, and every effort to reach another soul, there is work that requires time, commitment, and practical support.
The Gospel itself is free.
The forgiveness of God cannot be bought.
But producing and distributing sound biblical resources still involves real costs.
The New Testament teaches us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Those words matter.
God-honoring generosity is not manufactured through guilt.
It is not measured by whether someone can afford a monthly payment.
It is not proof that one Christian loves Jesus more than another.
It is a willing response to grace.
It is the opportunity to help sustain a mission that continually points people back to Jesus Christ.
You are still welcome here.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your value before God or your place among those who seek Him.
It is about proclaiming the Savior who came to redeem sinners and make disciples.
And now, before you leave, I want to bring you back to the verse that started everything.
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
Maybe you first heard those words as a child.
Maybe you've seen them printed on coffee mugs, framed above living room couches, or written beneath beautiful pictures of mountains and sunsets.
Maybe you've repeated them during some of the hardest nights of your life.
There is nothing wrong with finding comfort in those words.
But never forget the God who spoke them.
He is not merely offering you a peaceful moment.
He is declaring His unmatched authority.
He is the God before whom nations must cease their raging.
The God whose voice is greater than the noise of kingdoms.
The God whose purposes cannot be overthrown by human arrogance.
The God who is the refuge of His people.
And through Jesus Christ, we come to know the saving mercy of this sovereign Lord.
So when you face tomorrow, don't imagine that faith requires you to know everything that will happen.
It doesn't.
You may still have difficult conversations.
You may still need to seek counsel.
You may still need to work, repent, forgive, set boundaries, or take a courageous step you've been avoiding.
You may still have to live with unanswered questions.
But you can do those things without pretending to be God.
You can be faithful without being all-powerful.
You can be responsible without being sovereign.
You can grieve without surrendering your hope.
You can wait without abandoning your trust.
And you can place your life in the hands of the risen Christ, whose grace is sufficient for every sinner who comes to Him.
Because the most important truth in Psalm 46:10 is not that you have finally learned how to make your heart perfectly still.
It is that God is God, even when your world is anything but still.
And the Gospel tells us that this sovereign God has acted decisively to save through His Son.
So stop trying to earn what Christ freely offers.
Stop hiding what needs to be brought into His light.
Stop treating your past as though it has more authority than His grace.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
And when the mountains shake again, remember whose throne has never moved.
The world may still be shaking beneath your feet, but the nail-scarred hands of your risen Savior have never lost their power to hold you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE LOVED DAVID. HER FATHER SAW A WAY TO KILL HIM.
paragraphs: SHE LOVED DAVID. HER FATHER SAW A WAY TO KILL HIM.

Michal gave her heart to a man marked for death—and King Saul turned his own daughter’s love into a weapon. But behind this royal betrayal lies a devastating truth about manipulation, wounded hearts, and the grace of Jesus Christ that can reach us even when the people who should have protected us become the ones who hurt us.

“And Michal Saul's daughter loved David: and they told Saul, and the thing pleased him. And Saul said, I will give him her, that she may be a snare to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” — 1 Samuel 18:20–21, KJV
Imagine discovering that the person who celebrated your love was secretly hoping it would lead to the death of the person you loved.
Imagine your own father smiling at the news that you had fallen in love—not because he cared about your happiness, but because he had finally found something he could use.
Your heart.
Your feelings.
Your future.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part?
You had no idea.
This is not the plot of a modern psychological thriller.
This happened in the household of Israel's first king.
Her name was Michal.
She was a princess. The daughter of King Saul. A woman whose name appears in one of Scripture's most disturbing accounts of love, jealousy, manipulation, and betrayal.
And the Bible tells us something remarkable about her.
She loved David.
But when her father learned about that love, Scripture says something that should make every reader stop.
“The thing pleased him.”
Not because Saul wanted his daughter to be happy.
Not because he admired David's character.
Not because he saw a beautiful future for the two of them.
Saul was pleased because he saw an opportunity to destroy David.
Think about that.
What Michal experienced as love, Saul intended to turn into a trap.

And if you have ever loved someone while another person tried to control your relationship, used your vulnerability against you, or treated your happiness as something to exploit, there is something painfully familiar about this story.
But stay with me.
Because what happened to Michal and David is not merely a warning about manipulative people.
It is also a window into the brokenness of the human heart—and why we desperately need a King who is nothing like Saul.
Before we go further, we need to understand what was happening in Israel.
David was rising.
The young shepherd who had defeated Goliath was becoming a celebrated warrior. His victories brought admiration, and the people began singing about his success.
“Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” (1 Samuel 18:7, KJV)
That song became a turning point.
Saul heard praise for David and interpreted it as a threat to his throne.
Scripture says Saul became angry, and from that time forward he watched David with suspicion.
The king who should have been grateful for a courageous servant began treating that servant as an enemy.
David had not seized Saul's throne.
He had not organized a rebellion.
He had served the king and fought Israel's enemies.
Yet Saul's jealousy was consuming him.
This is what envy can do when it is allowed to grow unchecked.
Someone else's blessing begins to feel like your humiliation.
Someone else's success becomes your personal defeat.
And instead of asking God to heal what is happening inside you, you begin searching for ways to bring the other person down.
Saul had already attempted to kill David with a spear (1 Samuel 18:10–11).
When violence failed, he tried something more calculated.
He would place David in danger through the very thing that should have brought joy.
Marriage.
Love.
Family.
The Bible records the plan with frightening clarity.
In the original Hebrew of 1 Samuel 18:20, we read:
וַתֶּאֱהַב מִיכַל בַּת־שָׁאוּל אֶת־דָּוִד
Vatte'ehav Mikhal bat-Sha'ul et-David.
“And Michal, Saul's daughter, loved David.”
The verb וַתֶּאֱהַב (vatte'ehav) comes from the Hebrew root אהב (ʾ-h-b), meaning “to love.”
The text does not tell us every detail of Michal's emotions, how their relationship developed, or everything David felt in return.
But it does plainly tell us that Michal loved him.
And that detail matters.
Because Scripture does not present her affection as an invention of Saul.
Her love was real enough to be reported to the king.
Saul's response was the corruption.
The following verse contains the Hebrew expression:
לְמוֹקֵשׁ
Lemoqesh.
Meaning “as a snare” or “as a trap.”
The word moqesh refers to something that ensnares or catches.
Saul was not simply arranging a royal wedding.
He was planning to use his daughter's marriage as the means of drawing David into mortal danger.
His intention was that the Philistines would kill David.
And here is the detail that makes the betrayal even darker.
Saul wanted David dead without appearing to be the one who killed him.
He wanted someone else's hands to accomplish what his own murderous attempts had failed to achieve.
How often does sin work that way?
It hides behind respectable appearances.
It disguises selfishness as concern.
It calls manipulation wisdom.
It calls jealousy discernment.
It calls control protection.
And sometimes the people being used do not even realize they have become part of someone else's agenda.
Michal was Saul's daughter.
David was the man she loved.
But to Saul, their relationship was an opportunity.
There is a terrible difference between loving a person and loving what that person can do for you.
One protects.
The other consumes.
One seeks the other's good.
The other calculates how the other can be used.
And when the human heart becomes ruled by jealousy, even family relationships can become instruments of harm.
Saul's next move exposed his intention.
He demanded a dangerous bride-price from David: one hundred Philistine foreskins.
This was not an ordinary romantic gesture. It was a violent military demand tied to the warfare of that time.
The biblical narrator tells us exactly what Saul expected.
He intended David to fall by the hand of the Philistines (1 Samuel 18:25).
In other words, Saul designed the requirement to expose David to lethal danger.
But the plan failed.
David went with his men and killed two hundred Philistines, bringing back the required proof.
Saul gave Michal to David as his wife.
The king's trap had not destroyed the young warrior.
Instead, Saul became even more afraid.
Why?
Because Scripture says he saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that Michal loved him (1 Samuel 18:28).
Notice the contrast.
Saul saw the LORD's favor upon David.
And instead of humbling himself before God, he became more determined to oppose him.
That is one of the most frightening conditions of the human heart.
To recognize that God is at work—and still choose jealousy over surrender.
To see another person's life bearing evidence of God's blessing—and still resent them.
To know something is wrong inside you—and protect your pride instead of repenting.
Friend, that is not merely Saul's problem.
It is a warning to every one of us.
Because jealousy does not always announce itself with a spear.
Sometimes it appears in a quiet comparison.
A bitter thought.
A secret pleasure when someone fails.
A refusal to celebrate another person's blessing.
A need to control someone because you are afraid of losing influence.
And unless we bring those things into the light before God, they can become more destructive than we ever imagined.
But Michal's story does not end with the wedding.
Later, Saul sent men to David's house to watch him and kill him in the morning.
This time, Michal intervened.
She warned her husband:
“If thou save not thy life to night, to morrow thou shalt be slain.” (1 Samuel 19:11, KJV)
Then she helped David escape through a window.
Think about the courage and conflict in that moment.
Her father was the king.
Her husband was the target.
The danger was real.
And Michal chose to warn David and help him escape.
The woman whose love had been used as part of a murderous scheme became instrumental in preserving the very life her father wanted destroyed.
That is extraordinary.
Yet Scripture refuses to turn this into a simple fairy tale.
Michal also used deception in the escape, including a household image placed in the bed and a false explanation to Saul's messengers (1 Samuel 19:13–17).
The biblical account reports these actions without requiring us to approve every method she used.
And what followed was not an uncomplicated happily-ever-after.
David fled.
Michal remained caught in the consequences of Saul's hostility.
Later, Saul gave her to another man, Palti, son of Laish (1 Samuel 25:44).
Still later, David demanded her return, and 2 Samuel 3:15–16 records Palti following her, weeping, until he was ordered to turn back.
Scripture does not fully reveal Michal's inner thoughts during those years.
We should not pretend it does.
But we can recognize the painful reality the narrative places before us.
Her marriage became entangled with royal power, political rivalry, separation, and decisions made by others.
The woman who loved David was living in a world where kings could make decisions that reshaped her life.
And then comes another heartbreaking scene.
Years later, when David brought the ark of the LORD into Jerusalem, he danced before the LORD in celebration.
Michal saw him from a window.
And the Bible says she despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:16).
The woman who once loved David is now described as despising him.
Scripture does not give us permission to claim we know every reason for that change.
We cannot confidently say it was entirely caused by her father's manipulation, her marital history, David's conduct, or any single event.
The text does not tell us that.
But the contrast is unmistakable.
In 1 Samuel 18, Michal loved David.
In 2 Samuel 6, she despised him.
And between those two statements lies a history marked by fear, danger, separation, political conflict, and deep relational complexity.
What a sobering reminder that a person's story cannot always be understood from one moment of their life.
We see an angry person and assume anger is all they have ever known.
We see a bitter person and forget that bitterness may have developed across years of conflict.
We see someone whose relationships are broken and assume we understand how everything happened.
But God sees what we cannot.
He knows the whole story.
He knows the choices people made, the wrongs they suffered, the sins they committed, and the circumstances we will never fully understand.
And that should make us slower to condemn and quicker to examine our own hearts.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to have your trust exploited.
Perhaps someone used your love to keep you under control.
Perhaps a parent treated your choices as a threat to their authority.
Perhaps you were caught between people you cared about, pressured to prove loyalty at the expense of your own conscience.
Or perhaps the most uncomfortable possibility is this:
You recognize something of Saul in yourself.
You have been jealous.
You have wanted control.
You have resented someone who seemed more favored, more successful, more loved, or more recognized than you.
You have smiled outwardly while something ugly was growing inwardly.
If that is you, do not rush past the conviction.
Because the Gospel does not only speak to people who have been wounded.
It also speaks to people who have wounded others.
And every one of us needs that Gospel.
Here is where this ancient royal tragedy begins pointing us toward something greater.
Saul was Israel's first king.
But he was not the king Israel ultimately needed.
He was fearful of losing power.
He used others to protect himself.
He allowed jealousy to corrupt his judgment.
He treated David's life as expendable.
And he turned his daughter's affection into part of a deadly plan.
Now look at Jesus Christ.
Saul sought to preserve his throne at another man's expense.
Jesus, though truly Lord, humbled Himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–8).
Saul wanted another man's blood shed to protect his position.
Jesus willingly shed His own blood to redeem sinners.
Saul used someone else's love as a weapon.
Jesus demonstrated His love through sacrifice.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Read that again.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we became emotionally healthy.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Not after we cleaned up every hidden motive.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is grace.
And the difference between Saul and Jesus is not merely that one was a bad king and the other was a better king.
Jesus is the righteous King and Savior whose reign reveals the holy, self-giving love that sinful human rulers cannot perfectly embody.
His kingdom is not established through jealousy, manipulation, or the destruction of innocent rivals.
He gave Himself for His people.
And through His death and resurrection, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life to everyone who comes to Him in faith.
The Greek New Testament gives us a beautiful word that helps us understand this love.
ἀγάπη — agapē.
It is the noun commonly translated “love” in passages such as Romans 5:8 and 1 John 4:9–10.
The word does not automatically mean divine or unconditional love in every context. Its meaning is shaped by how Scripture uses it.
But when the New Testament describes God's love demonstrated through the sending and sacrifice of His Son, we see the extraordinary depth of that love.
First John 4:10 says:
“Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.”
Do you see the difference?
Saul's love of power made other people expendable.
God's love was revealed in the costly gift of His Son for undeserving sinners.
And this matters because some of us have learned the wrong definition of love from the people closest to us.
We learned that love means walking on eggshells.
That love means never disappointing someone.
That love means accepting manipulation.
That love means sacrificing truth to keep the peace.
That love means someone gets to control us because they claim to care.
But the love of Christ exposes those distortions.
Love is not permission to dominate.
Love is not a license to use someone.
Love does not rejoice in evil.
First Corinthians 13:6 says that love “rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth.”
Jesus does not call us to confuse manipulation with holiness.
Nor does forgiveness mean pretending evil never happened.
You can forgive someone while recognizing that what they did was wrong.
You can pray for someone without surrendering yourself to their control.
You can seek peace while maintaining wise and necessary boundaries.
And you can acknowledge your own sin without accepting responsibility for the sinful choices of another person.
The Gospel calls us to repentance, truth, forgiveness, and love—not denial.
And for someone reading this right now, that distinction may be deeply important.
Because you have been carrying guilt for something another person chose to do.
You have been asking whether you should have loved harder, stayed quieter, surrendered more, or endured longer.
But Michal's story reminds us that one person's genuine affection can be exploited by another person's wicked intentions.
Her love did not make Saul's plan righteous.
And your sincerity does not make another person's manipulation acceptable.
Yet we must also hear the other side.
Being wounded does not make every response we choose righteous.
Pain can explain why certain temptations feel powerful, but it cannot automatically justify bitterness, cruelty, deception, or revenge.
That is why we all need more than sympathy.
We need redemption.
We need the Holy Spirit to search the places we have hidden from others and sometimes even from ourselves.
We need the courage to say:
“Lord, show me where I have been sinned against, but also show me where I have sinned.”
“Teach me to forgive without calling evil good.”
“Teach me to love without surrendering truth.”
“Teach me to repent without drowning in shame.”
“Teach me to trust You even when people have made trust difficult.”
And perhaps most of all:
“Jesus, do not let what happened to me become an excuse for what I become.”
Because the tragedy is not only that Saul tried to destroy David.
The tragedy is also that Saul repeatedly resisted opportunities to humble himself.
He saw David's faithfulness.
He saw evidence that the LORD was with David.
He experienced fear and jealousy.
But instead of turning from his destructive path, he continued pursuing the man he regarded as a rival.
There is a warning here for anyone who keeps postponing repentance.
You can be close to sacred things and still resist God.
You can know religious language and still be ruled by pride.
You can occupy a position of authority and still desperately need a transformed heart.
Saul wore a crown.
But a crown cannot cure jealousy.
A title cannot cleanse the conscience.
Religious appearance cannot replace surrender.
And being admired by people cannot make us right with God.
Only God's grace can rescue sinners.
And that grace calls us to turn from sin and come to Jesus Christ.
Maybe this story has exposed a wound you thought you had buried.
Maybe it has exposed jealousy you have been excusing.
Maybe it has reminded you of someone you have not been able to forgive.
Or maybe you have simply realized how exhausted you are from trying to earn love from people who keep changing the conditions.
Whatever brought you here, hear the invitation of Jesus.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28, KJV)
He is not promising that every earthly relationship will be restored exactly as you desire.
He is not promising that every person who hurt you will apologize.
He is not promising that following Him will remove every painful consequence of this broken world.
He is offering something deeper.
Rest for the soul that comes to Him.
Forgiveness for the sinner who repents and believes.
A new relationship with God through His finished work.
And the transforming presence of the Holy Spirit in those who belong to Him.
That is why we keep returning to the message:
Not because the Bible promises every painful story will receive a perfect earthly ending.
Michal's story itself warns us against that assumption.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, restore our relationship with God, transform our hearts, and give eternal hope even when parts of our earthly stories remain unresolved.
The Gospel does not erase history.
It announces that sin, shame, and death do not have the final word over those who are in Christ.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes, you do not need to manufacture a perfect prayer.
You can begin with the truth.
“Lord Jesus, I need You.”
If you have been hiding sin, confess it.
If you have been resisting repentance, turn to Him.
If you have been carrying bitterness, ask Him to teach you the long and sometimes difficult work of forgiveness.
If you have been confusing human approval with your worth, remember that salvation is received by grace through faith, not earned by pleasing people (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ as your Savior, today you can turn to Him in repentance and faith.
He died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He is not merely a comforting idea for wounded people.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
And He is worthy of your trust, obedience, and worship.
Before you leave this story, I want to ask you something.
Not a question designed to make you look spiritual.
A question that requires honesty.
Which part of this story found you?
Was it Michal, loving sincerely while someone else tried to exploit that love?
Was it David, discovering that faithfulness does not always protect you from another person's jealousy?
Was it Saul, allowing insecurity and pride to become something dangerous?
Or was it the contrast between a broken earthly king and Jesus, the King who laid down His life to save His people?
And if you are comfortable, share what Scripture is teaching you. Your testimony may encourage someone who has been struggling in silence.
You do not have to reveal private wounds publicly to prove your faith. God hears the prayers that never become comments, too.
But sometimes a few honest words can remind another believer that they are not alone.
And that is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with dramatic Bible stories and leave them unchanged.
Not to replace the local church, pastoral care, or the personal study of Scripture.
But to keep pointing people toward the Word of God, the truth of the Gospel, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who look perfectly fine.
They are smiling in photographs.
Working.
Caring for their families.
Replying to messages.
Going through ordinary routines.
Yet privately, they are fighting battles nobody sees.
Some are carrying betrayal.
Some are trapped in bitterness.
Some are losing hope.
Some have been wounded by people they trusted.
Some have never truly understood what Jesus Christ accomplished on the cross.
And perhaps one Scripture-centered article shared at the right moment could become the beginning of an important conversation about faith, repentance, and grace.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
But to help place biblical truth in front of someone who might never intentionally search for it.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from their faith, and those who are still searching for answers to follow as well.
Because the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be heard beyond the walls of our familiar circles.
And if Gospel Warrior has become a meaningful part of your spiritual growth, I want to invite you into something deeper.
It does not purchase forgiveness.
It does not replace repentance, faith, prayer, fellowship, or obedience to Christ.
And it should not automatically replace the giving you prayerfully commit to your local church.
Scripture teaches us that Christian generosity should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”

If you are already setting aside resources for Christian giving, you may prayerfully consider Gospel Warrior among the ministries you choose to support, while honoring your existing responsibilities and commitments.
It is not the amount that determines your worth before God.
It is not a spiritual test.
It is an invitation to participate in work you believe is worth supporting.
But beyond the products, our hope is that your connection with Gospel Warrior will encourage a deeper hunger for Scripture, prayer, spiritual growth, and faithful Christian living.
These free resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual encouragement more accessible.
You do not have to pay to hear the Gospel.
Those actions matter, too.
We want support that comes from sincere conviction and love—not guilt or fear.
Because the One we preach did not come to exploit wounded hearts.
He came to save sinners.
And that brings us back to Michal.
A young woman loved David.
Her father saw an opportunity for death.
The same love that should have been treated with care became part of a dangerous scheme.
Yet Saul's plan did not succeed in destroying David.
And through the larger story of Scripture, we eventually arrive at the promised Son of David, Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:1 identifies Jesus as the son of David.
But Jesus came to do what no earthly king could accomplish.
To bear the sins of His people.
To defeat death through His resurrection.
To bring sinners back to God.
To reign as the righteous King forever.
And perhaps that is the most powerful contrast of all.
Saul feared losing his kingdom, so he tried to sacrifice someone else.
Jesus willingly sacrificed Himself to bring sinners into His kingdom.
One king turned love into a trap.
The true King demonstrated love through the cross.
One king's jealousy threatened innocent life.
The risen King's grace offers eternal life to repentant sinners who believe in Him.
And now the question is no longer simply what Saul did, what Michal suffered, or what David survived.
The question is what you will do with Jesus Christ.
Will you continue hiding what needs to be confessed?
Will you keep protecting bitterness that is poisoning your heart?
Will you continue seeking your worth in the approval of people who cannot save you?
Or will you come to the Savior who knows the truth about you and still calls you to repentance and faith?
Because there is a love that manipulates.
There is a love that demands control.
There is a love that takes and takes until nothing seems left.
But there is also the holy love of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
A love that does not excuse sin, but provides the only sufficient Savior from sin.
A love that does not promise a painless life, but gives an unshakable hope.
A love that does not need to destroy someone else to prove its power.
A love that was displayed when the Son of God gave Himself upon the cross.
So before you close this article, remember the woman who loved David.
Remember the father who tried to use that love.
Remember the danger of jealousy left unrepented.
And above all, remember Jesus.
Come to Christ.
Not when you are perfect.
Not when every wound has healed.
Not when you have figured out every chapter of your story.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because your deepest need is not merely for your circumstances to change.
Your deepest need is to be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
And the Savior who died and rose again is able to save those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).
The people who were supposed to protect your heart may have broken it—but the King who died to redeem you will never use your wounds as a weapon against you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN WRONG ABOUT WHO GOD CHOOSES TO SAVE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN WRONG ABOUT WHO GOD CHOOSES TO SAVE?

If God chooses who will be saved, why does He command everyone to repent? And if everyone can choose Him, why did Jesus say, “You did not choose Me, but I chose you”? The answer may challenge what you believe about grace, free will, and the heart of God.
There is a question that has divided theologians, troubled sincere believers, and kept searching souls awake at night.
Does God choose who will be saved, or does every person have the freedom to accept or reject His grace?
But beneath that theological question lies something painfully personal.
What if I want to be saved, but God hasn't chosen me?
What if I pray, repent, cry, and reach toward heaven, only to discover that salvation was never meant for someone like me?
Or perhaps the opposite question haunts you.
If God truly wants everyone to be saved, why doesn't everyone come to Him?
Why does one person fall to their knees in repentance while another hears the same Gospel and walks away?
Why does one hardened sinner become a passionate follower of Jesus while another spends a lifetime resisting Him?
And if salvation is entirely God's work, why does Scripture repeatedly tell human beings to believe, repent, come, and receive?
These are not small questions.
They touch the character of God, the meaning of the Cross, the responsibility of humanity, and the very nature of grace.
And somewhere in the middle of this centuries-old debate is a person who doesn't care about winning an argument.
A person who just wants to know whether Jesus will receive them.
Maybe that person is you.
So before we begin arguing about election, predestination, sovereignty, and free will, we need to remember something.
The Bible was not given merely to make us experts in salvation. It was given to lead us to the Savior.
And the Savior has a name.
Jesus Christ.
But to understand what Scripture actually teaches, we must be willing to examine passages that seem to pull in different directions without silencing any of them.
Because a theology that must hide certain Bible verses to survive is not a theology we should trust.
Consider one of the most breathtaking declarations in all of Scripture.
John 3:16 says:
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” (KJV)
In the original Greek, we encounter the expression:
πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν
Pas ho pisteuōn eis auton.
Literally, “everyone who believes in Him.”
Notice what Jesus emphasizes.
The promise is attached to believing in the Son.
It does not say that only morally impressive people may come.
It does not say that those with spotless histories may receive eternal life.
It does not say that only people who have never struggled, doubted, fallen, or failed are invited.
Everyone who believes in Christ has the promise of eternal life.
But we must be careful.
This Greek expression identifies those who believe; by itself, it does not settle the theological question of why one person believes and another does not.
That distinction matters.
Because Christians who affirm unconditional election and Christians who affirm resistible grace both believe that everyone who truly believes in Jesus will be saved.
Their disagreement concerns how God's saving grace brings a sinner to faith.
And that brings us to one of the most difficult chapters in the New Testament.
Romans 9.
Paul writes:
The original Greek reads:
Ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ, καὶ οἰκτιρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτίρω.
Eleēsō hon an eleō, kai oiktirēsō hon an oiktirō.
“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”
Then comes a statement that unsettles our instinct for control.
“So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.” (Romans 9:16, KJV)
Read that again.
Not of the one who wills.
Not of the one who runs.
But of God who shows mercy.
Paul is dismantling the idea that human determination, religious performance, ancestry, or effort can force God to grant salvation.
Mercy is not a salary.
Grace is not a trophy.
And salvation is not something God owes humanity.
If you have ever believed that enough religious activity could make God indebted to you, Romans 9 confronts that illusion.
You cannot purchase divine mercy with your obedience.
You cannot manipulate God with your tears.
You cannot make the Cross unnecessary by becoming a better person.
Salvation begins with a merciful God, not a deserving sinner.
But does Romans 9 mean that God arbitrarily creates some people for heaven and others for hell, regardless of anything else?
That question requires more than one isolated verse.
Paul's argument begins with anguish over Israel.
He is grieving because many of his fellow Israelites have not embraced their Messiah, despite receiving extraordinary covenant privileges.
He discusses Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Pharaoh, and the potter's authority over the clay.
The chapter teaches unmistakably that God is sovereign and that His saving purpose cannot be controlled by human ancestry or effort.
Yet Christians have historically disagreed about how its examples relate to individual eternal salvation.
In the Reformed understanding, Romans 9 strongly supports God's unconditional election of individuals to salvation, grounded in His sovereign mercy rather than foreseen human faith.

In Arminian and other non-Calvinist interpretations, Paul's central concern is often understood in relation to God's covenant purposes, the identity of His people, and His freedom to extend mercy beyond ethnic Israel, while human response to grace remains significant.
Neither interpretation should be dismissed with a careless slogan.
And neither should be presented as though sincere, Bible-believing Christians have never wrestled with the passage.
Because the same apostle who wrote Romans 9 also wrote Romans 10.
And there he declares:
“For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” (Romans 10:13, KJV)
The Greek expression is:
πᾶς γὰρ ὃς ἂν ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου σωθήσεται.
Pas gar hos an epikalesētai to onoma kyriou sōthēsetai.
“For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”
Paul did not forget what he had written one chapter earlier.
He was not confused.
He proclaimed God's sovereignty in Romans 9 and the necessity of faith and the universal Gospel invitation in Romans 10.
Then, in Romans 11, he continued explaining God's purposes concerning Israel and the Gentiles, warning against arrogance and emphasizing both divine kindness and severity.
These chapters belong together.
And perhaps one of our greatest mistakes is trying to make one chapter erase another.
Now consider something equally astonishing.
Paul writes to Timothy:
The Greek says:
ὃς πάντας ἀνθρώπους θέλει σωθῆναι καὶ εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἐλθεῖν.
Hos pantas anthrōpous thelei sōthēnai kai eis epignōsin alētheias elthein.
The natural sense is:
“Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”
The word πάντας (pantas) means “all,” and ἀνθρώπους (anthrōpous) means “human beings” or “people.”
The immediate context calls believers to pray for all people, including kings and those in authority.
This matters because the early Church was not supposed to imagine that God's saving concern belonged only to one social class, ethnicity, or political group.
The Gospel crosses human boundaries.
Yet the theological discussion does not end with the word “all.”
Some Christians understand this verse as expressing God's genuine desire for the salvation of every individual, even though people can resist His grace.
Others understand it as emphasizing all kinds of people, or distinguish between God's revealed desire that people repent and His sovereign decree concerning what ultimately occurs.
Those are serious interpretive differences.
But whatever position we hold, the passage gives us no permission to treat anyone as beyond the reach of Gospel proclamation.
The Church is commanded to pray broadly.
The Church is commanded to preach Christ.
And the Church is never authorized to inspect someone's supposed eternal election before offering them the Gospel.
Imagine how devastating it would be if we began looking at broken people and deciding that they were probably not chosen.
The addicted father.
The woman ashamed of her past.
The teenager secretly battling despair.
The husband who has betrayed his family.
The prisoner who has done something terrible.
The religious person who has spent decades pretending to be righteous.
What if we stopped preaching to them because we assumed their story was already beyond redemption?
That would be a betrayal of the mission Christ entrusted to His Church.
Because we are not given access to God's hidden counsel.
We are given the Gospel.
And we are commanded to proclaim it.
But there is another side of Scripture we cannot ignore.
Jesus says:
“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.” (John 6:44, KJV)
The Greek word translated “draw” is ἑλκύσῃ (helkysē), from the verb helkō.
It communicates drawing or pulling.
The verse establishes that coming to Christ requires the Father's action.
It does not portray fallen humanity as spiritually self-sufficient.
And the wider New Testament agrees.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works.
Jesus says in John 15:16:
“Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you.”

In context, He is speaking to His disciples about their appointment to bear fruit. The verse reveals His initiative, though its immediate setting should be considered before treating it as a complete explanation of individual predestination.
Ephesians 1:4–5 also speaks of believers being chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world and predestined for adoption.
These passages cannot simply be explained away.
God is not a helpless observer waiting anxiously to see whether humanity will allow Him to accomplish His purposes.
He is Lord.
His grace comes first.
His mercy is indispensable.
His purpose is not fragile.
But then we encounter Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.
In Matthew 23:37, He says:

“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” (KJV)
Those last words are painful.
“And ye would not.”
The Greek is:
καὶ οὐκ ἠθελήσατε
Kai ouk ēthelēsate.
“And you were not willing.”
Here we see Christ's expressed desire to gather Jerusalem's children and the unwillingness of those He addresses.
Christians differ on how this relates to the doctrine of irresistible or resistible saving grace. The verse is not, by itself, a complete philosophical account of free will.
But it unmistakably portrays the tragedy of resistance to God's gracious dealings.
And it should make every complacent heart tremble.
Because it is possible to be surrounded by religious language and remain resistant to the One to whom that language points.
You can know Bible verses and refuse to repent.
You can attend worship and resist the truth.
You can defend a doctrine of grace while showing little evidence that grace has humbled you.
You can argue about who is chosen while neglecting the command to love your neighbor.
And you can become so consumed with explaining salvation that you forget to worship the Savior.
This is where the debate becomes painfully personal.
Perhaps you have spent years blaming God for your spiritual distance.
You tell yourself that if God wants you, He will somehow change you.
So you postpone repentance.
You continue hiding the sin that is slowly destroying your peace.
You refuse to seek forgiveness.
You resist the truth you already understand.
And you call your delay a theological mystery.
But Scripture never gives us permission to use divine sovereignty as an excuse for unbelief.
Acts 17:30 declares that God commands all people everywhere to repent.
And perhaps you are on the opposite side.
You believe salvation depends so heavily on your own decision that you have begun treating faith as an achievement.
You remember the moment you responded to the Gospel, and somewhere along the way, gratitude quietly became pride.
You look at those who still struggle and wonder why they cannot simply make the right choice.
But Scripture never gives us permission to boast as though we rescued ourselves.
First Corinthians 4:7 asks:
“What hast thou that thou didst not receive?”
Whether you emphasize God's sovereign election or humanity's responsibility to respond, there is one truth that must remain standing.
Nobody will enter heaven boasting that Jesus was unnecessary.
The redeemed will not gather around the throne congratulating themselves for being spiritually superior.
They will worship the Lamb.
Because the foundation of salvation is not the brilliance of our theology.
It is the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And this is where we must return to the Cross.
Picture the scene.
A condemned criminal hangs beside Jesus.
His life has been marked by wrongdoing.
His opportunities are almost gone.
He has no time to build a reputation for holiness.
No years remain for impressive religious accomplishments.
He cannot undo the harm of his past.
He cannot climb down from the cross and prove himself through decades of obedience.
He is dying.
And yet, in the middle of his suffering, he turns toward the crucified Christ.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
Jesus answers:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
Think about that.
The man had no righteousness of his own that could purchase paradise.
He had no opportunity to repair his entire history.
His hope rested in the mercy and authority of the King dying beside him.
And Jesus received him.
The passage does not tell us precisely how divine election and human willing relate in that moment.
But it shows us something gloriously clear.
A guilty sinner who turns to Jesus in faith is not turned away.
That truth is not theoretical.
It is the difference between despair and hope.
Maybe you have done things you cannot bear to remember.
Maybe your family knows one version of you while God knows the secrets you have buried.
Maybe you have promised to change so many times that even your own promises sound empty.
Maybe you are afraid that your repeated failures prove you were never loved by God.
Listen carefully.
Your past is not more powerful than the blood of Christ.
Your shame is not greater than His mercy.
Your sin is serious. Serious enough that the Son of God went to the Cross.
But His sacrifice is sufficient to save those who come to Him.
Jesus says:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV)
Do not overlook that promise.
The same chapter that emphasizes the Father's sovereign work also contains Christ's assurance that the one who comes to Him will not be rejected.
You do not need to discover a secret list in heaven before approaching Jesus.
You do not need to solve every theological dispute before repenting.
You do not need to become worthy before seeking mercy.
You need Christ.
And Christ is not a reluctant Savior.
He came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).
He died for our sins and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He is the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).
And salvation is found in no other name (Acts 4:12).
But perhaps you are still asking the central question.
Does God choose us, or do we choose Him?
Here is what we can say with confidence from Scripture.
God takes the initiative in salvation.
Human beings are commanded to repent and believe.
Salvation is by grace, not earned by works.
Those who come to Christ in faith are received.
Those who persist in unbelief are warned of judgment.
God's sovereign purpose is real.
Human accountability is real.
And the relationship between God's sovereignty and human freedom has been understood differently by faithful Christians throughout Church history.
The Reformed tradition generally teaches that God's effectual grace brings His elect to saving faith.
The classical Arminian tradition generally teaches that God's prevenient grace enables sinners to respond freely, while allowing that grace to be resisted.
Both traditions seek to explain biblical passages about divine initiative and human responsibility.
Both affirm that salvation is possible only through Jesus Christ.
Both reject the idea that sinners can earn salvation through good works.
Their differences are meaningful, and they should be examined honestly.
We should not pretend they are identical.
But neither should we make our preferred theological system more central than the crucified and risen Lord.
Romans 9 must be read.
John 3:16 must be read.
First Timothy 2:4 must be read.
John 6 must be read.
Ephesians 1 and 2 must be read.
Romans 10 must be read.
And we must allow Scripture to challenge us, even when it refuses to fit neatly inside our favorite explanations.
Because there is something deeply dangerous about becoming more passionate about defending Calvinism or Arminianism than proclaiming Christ.
We can win an argument and wound a brother.
We can memorize theological terminology and neglect prayer.
We can discuss election for hours while ignoring the neighbor who has never heard a clear explanation of the Gospel.
We can defend grace with our mouths while refusing to extend grace through our lives.
And that should convict us.
Not because doctrine is unimportant.
Doctrine matters enormously.
What we believe about God shapes how we worship, pray, evangelize, and live.
But sound doctrine should produce humility, not arrogance.
It should lead us toward holiness, not hostility.
It should deepen our gratitude for mercy, not give us a reason to despise those who disagree.
And above all, it should lead us to Jesus.
The One who was betrayed.
The One who was mocked.
The One who carried the Cross.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
So here is a question more urgent than whether you can explain every mystery of election.
Have you personally turned to Jesus Christ?
Not merely to a religious institution.
Not merely to a theological position.
Not merely to a childhood tradition.
To Jesus.
Have you acknowledged your sin?
Have you stopped trying to justify what God calls evil?
Have you placed your trust in Christ's death and resurrection rather than your own goodness?
Are you willing to follow Him as Lord?
Because the Gospel is not an invitation to remain comfortably enslaved to sin while borrowing the language of grace.
Jesus calls us to repentance.
And repentance is not simply feeling guilty because we were caught.
It is a turning of the heart toward God, inseparable from genuine faith.
It does not mean we become instantly flawless.
It means we no longer want to make peace with the very sin from which Christ came to rescue us.
And when we fall, we do not make excuses.
We confess.
We return to Him.
We learn obedience.
We keep depending on His grace.
This is the beauty of redemption.
Not that God overlooks evil as though it never mattered.
But that Christ bore sin's judgment and opened the way for guilty people to be forgiven and transformed.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is:
Not because every consequence of sin disappears.
Not because every broken relationship is immediately restored.
Not because becoming a Christian guarantees an easy life.
But because Jesus can redeem people whose stories seemed hopeless.
The scandal of our rebellion does not have to be the final word.
The grace of Christ can write a new chapter.
And that brings us to something we rarely discuss when debating salvation.
If we truly believe that the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation, what are we doing to make it known?
There are people scrolling through Facebook tonight who will never enter a church voluntarily.
Some are carrying secret grief.
Some are spiritually exhausted.
Some have been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Some are convinced that God could never forgive them.
Some have never heard the Gospel explained with both biblical truth and genuine compassion.
And sometimes an article shared by an ordinary believer becomes the beginning of an extraordinary conversation.
Not because an algorithm can save a soul.
Only Christ saves.
But God uses ordinary people, faithful words, and unexpected encounters to make His truth known.
That is why I want to ask something personal.
If this message helped you understand God's grace more clearly, please don't let it end with you.
Not to collect attention.
Not to prove how religious you are.
But because someone who trusts you may be willing to read a message about Jesus that they would otherwise ignore.
And if you know someone who has been running from God, share this gently. Let love, not pressure, guide the conversation.
There may come a day when you hear someone say, “What if God never chose me?”
And you will want to remember the Scriptures that point them toward Christ.
Not with insults.
Not with theological arrogance.
Not with a desire to humiliate believers who understand these passages differently.
But with honesty.
Do you believe God's grace can be resisted, or do you believe His saving grace unfailingly brings His chosen people to faith? Which Scripture has most shaped your understanding?
And if you are not ready for that theological discussion, perhaps you can simply write:
You do not need to reveal private details publicly. But you are welcome to ask for prayer, share a testimony, or describe how the Lord has been working in your life.
Because this community should be more than a place where people consume religious content.
It should be a place where believers encourage one another, seekers can ask sincere questions, and Scripture continually brings us back to Jesus.
And if you believe that kind of Gospel-centered ministry is worth strengthening, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim biblical truth, encourage repentance, strengthen struggling believers, and help people grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, grow in prayer, understand Christian doctrine, and become more deeply rooted in Christ.
We want these resources to remain accessible.
We want more people to discover them.
And we want to expand the reach of this ministry so that people searching for answers can encounter the message of Jesus.
That takes time, effort, resources, and the faithful support of people who believe in the mission.
You may choose to regard that support as part of your Christian giving, alongside the other responsibilities and commitments you prayerfully honor.
But I want to be very clear about something important.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
God's favor is not sold through a monthly membership.
And Scripture never teaches that financially supporting a particular online ministry is a condition of being a faithful Christian.
Giving should be willing, thoughtful, and joyful, not compelled by guilt.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
If you already support your local church and other ministries, honor those commitments wisely.
You can still help by praying, sharing these articles, inviting others to follow, and encouraging people to study God's Word.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, tools for personal growth, or meaningful gifts that encourage conversations about Jesus.
It is the opportunity to help sustain a ministry committed to making Christ known.
To support continued biblical teaching.
To help keep free discipleship resources available.
To encourage the creation of more Gospel-centered content.
And to become part of a community that wants to grow deeper in God's Word rather than remain satisfied with surface-level Christianity.
There is room here for honest questions.
There is room for biblical correction.
There is room for repentance.
There is room for people who are learning how to walk faithfully with Jesus.
And every resource, every article, every invitation must ultimately point beyond this ministry to the One who alone deserves our worship.
Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be failing to understand every mystery of predestination.
The greatest tragedy would be hearing about the Savior again and again while continuing to refuse His call to repent and believe.
So if you have been postponing your response to the Gospel, do not hide behind the debate.
Do not tell yourself that you must first discover whether your name appears in some hidden decree.
Listen instead to what Christ has openly promised.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
Come to Him.
Bring your sin into the light.
Confess what you have tried to excuse.
Trust in the Savior who died and rose again.
Ask Him for mercy.
Follow Him.
And if you are already His, stop treating salvation as a reason for superiority.
Let it become the reason you worship more deeply, love more generously, pray more faithfully, and proclaim the Gospel more courageously.
We may not agree on every detail of how divine sovereignty and human responsibility fit together.
But we must never lose sight of the One who stands at the center of salvation.
The Father who sent His Son.
The Son who gave Himself for sinners.
The Holy Spirit who brings conviction and life.
And the Gospel that announces forgiveness and reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
One day, the arguments that once consumed so much of our attention will seem very different in the light of eternity.
And those who belong to Christ will not be praising their theological cleverness.
They will be praising the Lamb who was slain.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself one final question.
Not merely, “Did God choose me?”
But:
“Am I listening to the Christ who calls me to repent, believe, and follow Him?”
Because the Gospel does not tell a broken sinner to climb into heaven and uncover God's secret counsel.
It points that sinner to the crucified and risen Savior.
And His promise remains.
The one who comes to Him will not be cast out.
You may not know every mystery behind God's saving grace, but you can know the Savior who stretched out His arms on the Cross—and promised not to turn away the one who comes to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD DIDN’T BRING THEM TO MARAH TO DESTROY THEM—HE WAS ABOUT TO REVEAL SOMETHING THEY COULD NEVER LEARN AT THE RED SEA
paragraphs: GOD DIDN’T BRING THEM TO MARAH TO DESTROY THEM—HE WAS ABOUT TO REVEAL SOMETHING THEY COULD NEVER LEARN AT THE RED SEA

They had just witnessed one of the greatest miracles in human history. Three days later, they were thirsty, disappointed, and questioning the God who had rescued them. What happened at the bitter waters of Marah reveals a truth about suffering, obedience, healing, and Jesus Christ that every wounded believer needs to understand.
Imagine watching an entire sea split open before your eyes.
Not in a dream. Not in a story someone told you. You were standing there when it happened.
Behind you, an army was coming to kill you. Before you, an ocean stood between you and freedom. There was nowhere to run, nowhere to hide, and absolutely nothing you could do to save yourself.
Then God made a way.
You walked between walls of water on dry ground. Your children crossed safely. Your enemies followed, but the waters returned, and the army that had terrified you was swallowed by the sea.
You were free.
You sang. You worshiped. You celebrated the God who had done what no human being could accomplish.
And then, just three days later...
You were wondering whether you were going to die of thirst.
That is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to praise God on Sunday and struggle to trust Him by Wednesday.
We know what it means to testify about His goodness while secretly wondering why He has allowed our lives to become so difficult.
We remember the prayers He answered, the doors He opened, the disasters He carried us through.
Yet one new disappointment can make yesterday's miracles feel strangely distant.
And perhaps the most unsettling detail in the entire story is this:
The Israelites did not arrive at Marah because they had escaped God's leadership. They arrived there while following the path He had appointed for them.
Think about that.
Sometimes the road of obedience leads through places we would never have chosen.
And sometimes the place where our faith is most severely tested becomes the place where God teaches us something we could never have learned in comfort.
But before we call every painful experience a divine test, we need to understand what Scripture actually says.
Because the bitter waters of Marah were not merely about water.
They were about the hearts of a newly redeemed people learning to trust the God who had delivered them.
And ultimately, they point us toward the greater redemption that would come through Jesus Christ.
Exodus 15:22 tells us that Moses led Israel away from the Red Sea into the wilderness of Shur. They traveled three days without finding water.
Three days.
In the wilderness.
With families, livestock, children, and elderly people.
This was not a minor inconvenience. Water was essential to their survival.
Then, finally, they reached a place where water was available.
Imagine the relief.
Someone sees it first. A cry goes up. Exhausted parents hurry forward. Children run toward the water. People who have spent days fighting thirst suddenly believe their suffering is about to end.
But when they try to drink...
They cannot.
The water is bitter.
Exodus 15:23 records:
"When they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah." (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated "bitter" is מָרִים — marim, from the root מרר — m-r-r, associated with bitterness.
The place was called מָרָה — Marah, a name connected to that same idea.
The text does not tell us the precise chemical composition of the water or why it was undrinkable. It tells us what mattered to the people standing there.
They had found water.
But they could not drink it.
And isn't that sometimes the most heartbreaking kind of disappointment?
Not when there is no hope in sight.
But when hope appears, comes close enough to touch, and then collapses in your hands.
You thought the relationship would finally become healthy.
You thought the medical results would bring relief.
You thought the job would provide stability.
You thought the apology would come.
You thought that after everything you had survived, this season would finally be different.
Instead, you found yourself standing before something that looked like an answer but tasted like another wound.
And somewhere inside you, a question began to form.
"Lord, after everything You've brought me through, why am I here?"
The Israelites asked their question in a far less patient way.
Exodus 15:24 says:
"And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink?" (KJV)
Their thirst was real.
Their need was legitimate.
Their suffering was not imaginary.
But their response revealed something troubling.
They grumbled against Moses rather than turning to the Lord in trust.
The Hebrew verb behind "murmured" is וַיִּלֹּנוּ — vayillonu, from a root associated with grumbling or complaining.
This was more than acknowledging a problem. The narrative presents their response as a failure of trust in the midst of a genuine crisis.
And this distinction matters.
God does not require His people to pretend that pain does not hurt.
The Bible is filled with faithful lament. The Psalms contain desperate questions, tears, confusion, and cries for help.
Even Jesus, in His suffering, prayed to the Father with profound anguish.
There is a difference between bringing your wounded heart honestly before God and allowing bitterness to harden your heart against Him.
One says, "Lord, I am hurting. Help me trust You."
The other begins to say, "Lord, because I am hurting, I no longer believe You are good."
The difference may sound small.
But spiritually, it can change everything.
Because bitterness is not always born from rebellion.
Sometimes it begins with disappointment that was never surrendered.
A prayer that seemed unanswered.
A betrayal that was never addressed.
A loss that still makes no sense.
A wound that everyone else expects you to have healed from by now.
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, what happened to you begins to shape how you see God.
You stop praying with expectation.
You continue attending church, but worship feels mechanical.
You smile when people ask how you are doing, because explaining the truth would take more strength than you have left.
You still believe God exists.
You are simply struggling to believe that He sees you.
If that describes your heart, please do not rush past this next moment.
Because the story does not end with Israel's complaint.
It turns on one man's response.
While the people murmured, Moses cried out to the Lord.
Exodus 15:25 says:
"And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet..." (KJV)
Notice the movement.
The people complained.
Moses prayed.
And God responded.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיִּצְעַק אֶל־יְהוָה
Vayyits'aq el-YHWH.
"And he cried out to the LORD."
The verb conveys a cry for help, not a polished religious performance.
Moses did not have an engineering solution.
He did not possess a technique for purifying the water.
He did not command the people to manufacture enough faith to change their circumstances.
He cried out to God.
And God showed him what to do.
There is something deeply comforting about that.
You do not need to understand every detail of your crisis before you can pray.
You do not need to have the right words.
You do not need to feel spiritually impressive.
Sometimes faith sounds like nothing more than:
"Jesus, help me."
"Lord, I don't understand."
"Father, I am afraid."
"God, please don't let this suffering turn my heart away from You."
