“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And verse 10 immediately reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
That order matters.
Good works are the fruit of salvation, not the price we pay to purchase it.
We do not obey to make Jesus owe us eternal life.
We obey because the One who saved us is worthy of our love, trust, and surrender.
And this changes everything.
Because some of you reading this have been the early workers.
You have served faithfully while others disappeared.
You have prayed through painful seasons.
You have given when money was tight.
You have cared for people who never thanked you.
You have remained in ministry when your heart was exhausted.
And perhaps, deep down, you are wondering whether God has noticed.
He has.
Scripture says God is not unjust to forget the work and love shown in service to His people (Hebrews 6:10).
Jesus did not condemn the early workers for working all day.
Their labor was real.
Their burden was real.
Their agreed payment was real.
The warning came when they allowed comparison to poison their hearts.
Please hear this carefully.
You do not need to minimize your sacrifice to celebrate someone else's restoration.
You do not need to deny your suffering to rejoice when another sinner receives mercy.
And you do not need to become bitter because God has been generous to someone whose journey looks different from yours.
His goodness toward another person does not diminish His goodness toward you.
But perhaps you are not the early worker.
Perhaps you are the person who feels like you arrived too late.
You spent years running from God.
You broke promises.
You damaged relationships.
You made decisions that still keep you awake at night.
You carry memories you wish you could erase.
You see other believers with years of testimony, Scripture knowledge, and faithful service, and you wonder whether there is still a place for someone like you.
You hear them talk about their spiritual victories while you are still trying to find the courage to confess what happened yesterday.
And sometimes you whisper:
Jesus, would You still receive me?
Listen.
The vineyard parable does not promise that everyone can postpone repentance without consequence. Life is uncertain, and Scripture calls us to respond to God today.
But it does destroy the lie that your late arrival makes Christ unwilling to receive you.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV).
That promise is not reserved for people with respectable histories.
It is spoken by the Savior who receives those who come to Him.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because His grace is greater than our ability to save ourselves.
And here is where the Gospel becomes even more astonishing.
The One who told the story of the vineyard workers was Himself walking toward the cross.
In Matthew's Gospel, shortly after this parable, Jesus again foretells His betrayal, condemnation, crucifixion, and resurrection (Matthew 20:17–19).
Then He declares why He came:
“Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28, KJV).
Do you see the beauty of that connection?
The King who overturns our obsession with being first came not to be served, but to serve.
The Lord of glory humbled Himself.
The sinless Savior took the place of sinners.
The One worthy of all honor endured the shame of the cross.
And through His death and resurrection, He opened the way for undeserving people to be reconciled to God.
The Gospel is not the announcement that God has decided sin does not matter.
The cross announces just how seriously sin matters.
And just how far divine love went to rescue sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every consequence.
Not after we proved we were better than everyone else.
Christ died for sinners.
And that is why no redeemed person has the right to boast as though salvation were a trophy earned through personal superiority.
There is room for gratitude.
There is room for worship.
There is room for faithful obedience.
But there is no room for spiritual arrogance at the foot of the cross.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all is this:
Would you still rejoice in God's grace if He gave it generously to someone you secretly believe deserves it less than you?
The person who betrayed your trust.
The person whose scandal embarrassed your family.
The person who once ridiculed your faith.
The person who hurt you and never fully understood the damage.
This does not mean their actions were harmless.
It does not mean repentance removes every earthly consequence.
It does not mean you must restore unsafe relationships, abandon wise boundaries, or pretend justice no longer matters.
Forgiveness, reconciliation, accountability, and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
Yet it does mean that no sinner is beyond God's power to redeem.
And if that person genuinely turns to Christ, can you acknowledge the goodness of God without denying the seriousness of what happened?
That is not an easy question.
Sometimes the most difficult evidence of spiritual maturity is not how loudly we worship when God blesses us.
It is whether we can worship when He shows mercy to someone we would have preferred to see rejected.
Remember the older brother in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son.
He remained at home.
He worked.
He obeyed.
But when his younger brother returned after squandering his inheritance, the older brother became angry and refused to join the celebration (Luke 15:25–30).
His father went out and pleaded with him.
And the father said:
“It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.” (Luke 15:32, KJV).
The older brother was so focused on what his brother had received that he struggled to celebrate what his father had restored.
He was near the father's house.
But in that moment, his heart was far from the father's joy.
That is the danger Jesus is exposing.
You can be near religious activity and still resist the heart of grace.
You can know the language of righteousness and still be controlled by envy.
You can spend years doing outwardly good things while quietly turning your obedience into a reason to despise others.
And when that happens, the answer is not to stop obeying.
The answer is to repent.
To return to Christ.
To ask Him to cleanse not only our visible behavior but also our hidden motives.
Because grace does not merely welcome the scandalous sinner.
It also confronts the proud saint.
It humbles both.
And it invites both to find their hope in Jesus alone.
Maybe that is why these words are so unforgettable.
“The last shall be first, and the first last.”
They are not simply a comforting slogan for people who feel overlooked.
They are a warning against presumption.
A rebuke to envy.
A challenge to spiritual pride.
And a beautiful reminder that God's Kingdom does not operate according to the status games we play on earth.
The person everyone applauds may desperately need repentance.
The person everyone has written off may be turning toward Jesus with genuine faith.
The believer with decades of service must still depend on grace.
The new convert has no reason to despair because of a late beginning.
And every one of us must remember that Christ, not our religious résumé, is our only Savior.
So do not use this parable to delay your surrender.
Do not say, I will come to Jesus when I am old. I will live however I want and seek forgiveness at the eleventh hour.
The thief on the cross received mercy, but Scripture never promises you another hour.
Today is the day to turn to Christ.
And do not use your years of service as permission to become proud.
If you have followed Jesus for decades, praise God for His sustaining grace.
If you have only recently come to Him, praise God for His receiving grace.
If you have wandered and need to return, do not make peace with the darkness.
Come back to the Savior.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust in His finished work.
Follow Him.
Because the purpose of grace is not to leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Real grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Real grace leads us toward the One who transforms us.
And that brings us to the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because consequences automatically disappear.
Not because the past becomes acceptable simply because someone has found religion.
But because Jesus can redeem what sin has devastated.
He can forgive the guilty.
Humble the proud.
Restore the repentant.
Give hope to the ashamed.
And create a new life where there was once spiritual death.
That is the Gospel we want to keep proclaiming.
Not a Gospel that flatters the religious.
Not a Gospel that excuses rebellion.
Not a Gospel that sells blessings to the highest bidder.
But the biblical Gospel of Jesus Christ—crucified, risen, reigning, and mighty to save.
And if these words have exposed something in you, please do not rush past that conviction.
Maybe you have been comparing your journey with someone else's.
Maybe you have secretly resented another person's restoration.
Maybe you have been trying to earn God's acceptance through endless religious activity.
Or maybe you have spent so long believing you are too late that you have almost stopped hoping.
Bring that honestly before Jesus.
And if this message has challenged you to surrender the pride, comparison, or hidden sin you have been carrying, you can simply write “no more hiding.”
Let it become a moment of honest reflection before God.
And please, think of someone who needs this message.
Someone who has given up on church because they feel judged.
Someone who believes their past has disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has faithfully served for years but is quietly becoming bitter.
Someone whose family is still praying for their return to Christ.
A simple share can put a Gospel message before someone who would never have searched for it.
Not as a spiritual good-luck charm, but as a reminder to return to Matthew 19 and 20 whenever comparison, discouragement, or pride begins to distort your understanding of grace.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people grow beyond the emotional moment of reading an article.
We want to help believers open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, examine their hearts, and become more faithful disciples of Jesus Christ.
We believe biblical nourishment should be accessible, especially to people who are hungry for truth but may not have the means to purchase every resource they need.
And that ongoing work requires real support.
Writing, publishing, developing resources, maintaining a growing library, and expanding Gospel-centered outreach all involve time, labor, and practical expenses.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).
And no amount of money can purchase salvation, forgiveness, spiritual maturity, or a special place in His Kingdom.
But generous, willing support can be a beautiful expression of Christian partnership.
Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers participating in the work of Gospel ministry through material generosity.
The greatest purpose is not merchandise.
It is the message.
It is the possibility of another person encountering the Gospel.
Another struggling believer being encouraged to return to Scripture.
Another ashamed sinner discovering that repentance and forgiveness are possible through Jesus Christ.
Another family receiving resources that help them grow in faith.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone.
Use the free resources.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God or your place in this community.
And perhaps that is one more way this very parable should shape our ministry.
We must never preach the generosity of God's grace while treating people as though their financial contributions determine their spiritual importance.
The longtime believer is welcome.
The new believer is welcome.
The wounded seeker who is still asking questions is welcome to listen, learn, and explore the claims of Jesus Christ.
Because the vineyard belongs to the Master.
The Gospel belongs to Christ.
And the glory belongs to God.
One day, the applause of this world will fade.
The titles will disappear.
The numbers on our screens will no longer matter.
The arguments about who was more important, more impressive, or more deserving will sound painfully small in the presence of the Lord.
What will matter is whether we truly belong to Jesus Christ.
Whether our hope was in His grace rather than our own righteousness.
Whether our faith bore the fruit of love and obedience.
Whether we learned to rejoice in the mercy that rescued us instead of resenting the mercy that rescued someone else.
And perhaps the person standing beside you in God's Kingdom will have a story you never expected to hear.
A former enemy.
A notorious sinner.
Someone you thought would never repent.
Someone who came to Jesus much later than you did.
And if you are both there through the saving work of Christ, the right response will not be to ask why they were welcomed.
It will be to worship the Savior who was merciful enough to welcome either of you.
Because heaven is not a competition between people who think they deserve to be there.
It is the home of those redeemed by Jesus Christ.
And when you finally understand how much grace it took to save you, you will stop being offended by how much grace God shows to someone else.
The greatest tragedy would not be arriving last at the vineyard—it would be standing inside it, surrounded by the Master's goodness, and never learning to rejoice in His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY AGREED TO EAT THEIR OWN CHILDREN. THEN ONE MOTHER BROKE HER PROMISE—AND A KING TORE HIS CLOTHES.
paragraphs: THEY AGREED TO EAT THEIR OWN CHILDREN. THEN ONE MOTHER BROKE HER PROMISE—AND A KING TORE HIS CLOTHES.
The horrifying agreement inside a starving city, the mother's cry that exposed a nation's collapse, and the God whose mercy reaches into places human beings can barely bear to remember.
Based on 2 Kings 6:24–7:20 | A Gospel Warrior Reflection on Judgment, Human Desperation, Repentance, and the Grace of Jesus Christ
There are stories in the Bible that comfort you.
Stories that remind you God is faithful. Stories that make you close your eyes, breathe deeply, and whisper, “Thank You, Lord.”
And then there are stories that make your stomach turn.
Stories so disturbing that you wonder why God allowed them to be written down.
This is one of them.
Two mothers.
Two children.
A starving city.
And an agreement so horrifying that even the king, a man accustomed to violence and suffering, tore his royal garments when he heard what had happened.
But before you turn away, understand something.

This story is not merely about what starvation can do to the human body. It is about what happens when a broken world reaches the limits of human strength—and why our deepest hope cannot rest in human power.
Because somewhere beneath the horror of this ancient account is a question that still reaches into our lives today.
What happens when desperation becomes so overwhelming that the unthinkable begins to look like the only way out?
And where is God when people are suffering beyond what words can describe?
Stay with this story.
Not because its darkness deserves your fascination.
But because the darkness makes the need for redemption impossible to ignore.
The city was Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.
Outside its walls stood the army of Ben-hadad, king of Aram, also called Syria in many English translations.
The enemy had surrounded the city.
Food supplies were running out.
The roads were blocked.
No ordinary family could simply walk into the countryside and gather grain.
And slowly, relentlessly, hunger began doing what armies sometimes could not.
It broke the people from within.
Second Kings 6:25 describes a famine so severe that a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver, while a small measure of what the Hebrew text calls dove's dung sold for five shekels.

Even the exact identification of that second commodity has been debated by interpreters. What is unmistakable is the point of the passage: things ordinarily regarded as undesirable had become extraordinarily expensive.
The economy had collapsed into desperation.
Imagine a mother searching her home for something—anything—to feed her child.
An empty container.
A cold cooking fire.
A little one asking when they would eat again.
And no answer she could honestly give.
The Bible does not tell us the private thoughts of the women in this account.
It does not describe their homes, their childhoods, or how long they had been hungry.
We should not pretend to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But it tells us enough to understand that this was no ordinary hardship.
This was a city approaching the edge of human endurance.
Then came the moment that made even the king stop.
He was walking along the wall of Samaria when a woman cried out to him.
In the Hebrew text, her appeal begins:
הוֹשִׁיעָה אֲדֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ
Hoshi'ah, adoni ha-melekh.
“Help, my lord, O king.”
—2 Kings 6:26
That first word comes from the Hebrew root associated with saving or delivering.
She was asking for rescue.
And the king's response was bitter.
“If the LORD do not help thee, whence shall I help thee?”
—2 Kings 6:27, KJV
He spoke of the threshing floor and the winepress—the very places from which food and drink might ordinarily come.
But there was nothing left to distribute.
No royal decree could make grain appear.
No crown could fill an empty stomach.
And no political authority, however powerful, could simply command the siege to end.
Then the king asked what troubled her.
Perhaps he expected another complaint about food.
Perhaps another plea for relief.
But what she said was far worse.
“This woman said unto me, Give thy son, that we may eat him to day, and we will eat my son to morrow.”
—2 Kings 6:28, KJV
Read those words again.
Not quickly.
Not as though they belong to a distant world that has nothing to say to ours.
Two women had made an agreement involving their own children.
The first woman's son was killed and eaten.
Then, when the next day came, the other woman hid her son.
And the first mother brought her complaint to the king.
The horror of the account is not simply that a terrible agreement was made.
It is that the woman presented the other mother's refusal to surrender her child as the injustice requiring royal intervention.
The moral world had become so distorted that a mother was asking the king to enforce an agreement that should never have existed.
The Bible records this without inviting us to enjoy the horror.
It does not ask us to admire either woman.
It does not give us permission to treat a murdered child as a mere illustration.
A real child, within the world of this narrative, had been destroyed.
And another child had been hidden.
We do not know whether the second mother's decision came from remorse, renewed maternal protection, fear, or some combination of motives.
The text does not tell us.
It simply tells us that she hid her son.
And sometimes the most responsible way to read Scripture is to let its silences remain silent.
But the king's response was visible to everyone.
When he heard the woman's words, he tore his clothes.
And beneath his royal garments, the people saw sackcloth.
In the ancient world, tearing one's garments was a recognized expression of grief, distress, or anguish.
Sackcloth was associated with mourning, humiliation, and sometimes repentance.
The king had already been wearing it beneath his clothes.
Something about the suffering of the city had affected him.
Yet there is an important distinction.
Being devastated by suffering is not the same thing as responding to God in faithful repentance.
Because what happened next reveals a king whose anguish turned toward blame.
In 2 Kings 6:31, he swore that Elisha the prophet would lose his head.
The narrative does not fully explain every motive behind his threat.
But it clearly shows his anger directed toward God's prophet.
Instead of giving us a simple portrait of a repentant ruler, Scripture presents a deeply troubled king whose response included violence.
And that should make us uncomfortable.
Because pain can bring people to their knees.
But pain can also make them search for someone to punish.
Some people become softer when life breaks them.
Others become harder.
Some cry out for mercy.
Others demand someone to blame.
And if we are willing to be honest, many of us have experienced both reactions within our own hearts.
Maybe you have never stood inside a besieged city.
Maybe you have never experienced hunger on anything approaching this scale.
But you know what it means to feel trapped.
To pray and wonder why the answer has not come.
To watch someone you love suffer while you feel powerless.
To become angry because the life you expected is not the life unfolding before you.
To ask God questions you are almost afraid to speak aloud.
“Lord, where are You?”
“Why has this happened?”
“How much longer?”
“Have You forgotten us?”
Those questions are not new.
They have echoed through generations of human suffering.
But there is something in this account that deserves our attention beyond the immediate tragedy.
Centuries before Samaria's siege, the covenant warnings given through Moses had described the terrible consequences that could accompany Israel's persistent rebellion.
Deuteronomy 28:53 warned that, under siege and extreme distress, people would eat the flesh of their own children.
Leviticus 26:29 contains a similarly horrifying warning.
These passages are not instructions.
They are not divine approval of cannibalism.
They are covenant warnings portraying the catastrophic consequences of judgment and siege.
Second Kings 6 depicts a tragedy that recalls those warnings with terrifying clarity.
This matters because the Bible is not presenting the event as an isolated example of human cruelty.
It belongs to a larger history of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness, national suffering, prophetic warning, and God's dealings with His people.
Yet we must also be careful.
Scripture does not authorize us to look at every starving family, every grieving parent, or every suffering child today and declare that their tragedy proves they personally sinned.
Jesus rejected that kind of simplistic judgment.
In Luke 13:1–5, He spoke about people who had suffered violent and sudden deaths. He did not teach that they were worse sinners than everyone else.
Instead, He called His hearers to examine their own need for repentance.
That is a crucial distinction.
The suffering of others is not an invitation for us to become their judges.
It is a reminder of the fragility of life, the seriousness of evil, and our desperate need for God.
And the child in Samaria must never disappear beneath our desire to draw a spiritual lesson.
That child's death was evil.
The mother's grief and guilt are not explained away by a sermon.
The king's torn clothes did not reverse what had happened.
And even the extraordinary deliverance that followed would not make that loss insignificant.
The Bible allows us to face that terrible reality.
But the story does not end on the city wall.
And this is where the account takes an astonishing turn.
While the king was threatening Elisha, the prophet announced a word from the LORD.
By the following day, food would be available at the gate of Samaria at dramatically reduced prices.
Read 2 Kings 7:1.
It was a promise that must have sounded almost impossible.
One day, famine.
The next, abundance.
One day, food beyond reach.
The next, ordinary provisions available again.
An officer who supported the king expressed disbelief.
Even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, he questioned whether such a thing could happen.
Elisha answered that the officer would see the promised provision but would not eat from it.
Then the narrative shifts away from the palace.
Away from the king.
Away from the powerful.
And toward four men with leprosy or a serious skin disease, sitting at the entrance of the city gate.
They were desperate too.
They reasoned that remaining where they were meant death.
Entering the starving city offered no hope.
So they decided to approach the Aramean camp.
And what they discovered was extraordinary.
The enemy had fled.
According to 2 Kings 7:6, the LORD had caused the Aramean army to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army.
Believing an overwhelming military force was approaching, they abandoned their camp.
Their tents remained.
Their supplies remained.
Their food remained.
The four men entered, ate, drank, and began collecting valuables.
Then something changed.
They realized that keeping the discovery to themselves while an entire city starved was wrong.
In the King James Version, their confession is unforgettable:
“We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.”
—2 Kings 7:9
This day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.
In Hebrew, the central expression is:
יוֹם־בְּשֹׂרָה הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה
Yom-besorah hayom hazzeh.
“This day is a day of good news.”
The word besorah refers to good news or a favorable report.
In its immediate context, it is news of deliverance from a military siege.
We should not pretend the verse was originally written as a direct prediction of the New Testament Gospel.
It was not.
But the language of good news creates a powerful biblical connection.
People facing death were told that deliverance had come.
People who believed they had no future discovered that the enemy had fled.
And those who found the provision recognized that the news was too important to keep to themselves.
Can you imagine?
Somewhere inside Samaria, parents were still looking at empty food containers.
Somewhere, people were wondering whether they would survive another day.
And outside the walls, food was waiting in an abandoned enemy camp.
They simply did not know it yet.
The four men carried the news back.
The king initially suspected a trap, but the report was investigated.
The abandoned camp was discovered.
And the people went out to obtain its provisions.
The word spoken through Elisha was fulfilled.
But the officer who had doubted the promise was trampled at the gate and died, just as the prophet had foretold.
Second Kings 7 does not end with a vague declaration that everything turned out perfectly for everyone.
It records provision, fulfilled prophecy, and judgment.
The starving city received relief.
Yet the murdered child did not return.
That is the tension we must not erase.
God's deliverance was real. So was the suffering that preceded it.
And now we come to the question that changes how a Christian reads this entire account.
Where is Jesus in a story like this?
We must answer carefully.
Jesus is not explicitly named in 2 Kings 6–7.
The passage is not secretly describing the crucifixion through every detail of the siege.
We should not turn the two mothers into invented symbols or force every character to represent someone in the New Testament.
But when we read the whole Bible as Christians, we see that this terrible account belongs to the larger story of humanity's need for redemption.
And that larger story leads us to Jesus Christ.
The siege reveals how deeply human life can be devastated by sin, violence, judgment, and desperation.
The king reveals the limits of earthly power.
The prophet's announcement reveals that deliverance ultimately came from the LORD.
And the four men reveal the moral urgency of sharing life-giving news.
Yet the Gospel announces something even greater than the lifting of an ancient siege.
It announces that Jesus Christ entered our fallen world to save sinners.
Not by pretending evil was harmless.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by declaring repentance unnecessary.
But by bearing our sins and accomplishing the redemption we could never achieve for ourselves.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
Notice those words.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired every mistake.
Not after we had made ourselves worthy.
Not after we had hidden every shameful chapter from view.
Christ died for sinners.
This does not mean every consequence of evil disappears in this life.
It does not mean victims must pretend their wounds never happened.
It does not mean forgiveness excuses abuse, cruelty, or injustice.
It means that the mercy of God in Christ is not reserved for people who can honestly claim they have never needed it.
And who among us could make that claim?
Some people reading this are carrying shame they have never confessed.
Not the horror of Samaria.
Perhaps something no one else knows.
A betrayal.
An addiction.
A relationship damaged by dishonesty.
A season of bitterness.
A choice that wounded someone.
Years spent resisting the voice of God.
You smile in public.
You answer messages.
You attend church.
You tell people you are doing fine.
But somewhere in the silence, you keep returning to the same question.
“Could God still forgive someone like me?”
Listen to the Gospel.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is not permission to continue in sin without repentance.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
And there is another truth we must remember.
Not everyone carrying pain is carrying guilt for what happened to them.
Some readers are not struggling because of something they did.
They are struggling because of something someone did to them.
If that is you, the Gospel does not demand that you accept blame for another person's wrongdoing.
Jesus sees the oppressed.
He cares for the wounded.
He calls His people to defend the vulnerable and practice justice.
And His grace is not limited to those who need forgiveness.
It is also hope for those who need healing.
Consider the difference between the king of Samaria and the King revealed in the Gospels.
The king of Samaria heard a woman's cry and was confronted by the limits of his power.
Jesus heard the cries of suffering people and responded with compassion.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the rejected.
He fed hungry crowds.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called sinners to repentance.
He gave dignity to people others had dismissed.
And when He saw the multitudes, Matthew 9:36 tells us He was moved with compassion because they were distressed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.
The Greek word used there is:
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη
Esplanchnisthē.
It expresses being deeply moved with compassion.
Not distant politeness.
Not empty religious language.
Deep compassion.
And this is the Jesus we proclaim.
A Savior who does not delight in human misery.
A Savior who does not overlook sin.
A Savior who entered suffering, bore the cross, rose from the dead, and offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Him in faith.
The cross was not a decorative symbol of religious optimism.
It was the place where the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And the resurrection was God's victorious declaration that death would not have the final word over Him.
This is why our hope is greater than the hope of Samaria.
Samaria needed food.
We need food too.
Hungry people must be fed, and Christians should never use spiritual language as an excuse to ignore physical suffering.
But humanity also needs reconciliation with God.
Jesus said:
“I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.”
—John 6:35, KJV
He was speaking of the life and satisfaction found in Him, not promising that His followers would never experience physical hunger.
His words invite us to recognize a need no earthly abundance can finally satisfy.
We need Him.
Not merely His blessings.
Not merely a solution to our immediate circumstances.
Not merely a religious identity that makes us look respectable.
We need Jesus Christ Himself.
And perhaps that is why this ancient account should disturb us so deeply.
Because it exposes the terrible things human beings can experience and do.
It strips away the illusion that civilization, wealth, authority, or religious appearance can save us from every form of evil.
It reminds us that earthly power has limits.
And it leaves us longing for a King whose righteousness cannot be corrupted and whose compassion cannot be exhausted.
That King is Jesus.
But there is something else in the story I cannot forget.
Those four men outside the city gate.
They found food.
They ate.
They discovered provision that could save lives.
Then they realized they could not remain silent.
“We do not well,” they said.
“This day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.”
How many people around us are starving for hope while we remain silent about Christ?
Not everyone who looks successful is at peace.
Not everyone laughing is happy.
Not everyone posting beautiful family pictures has a healthy home.
Not everyone sitting in a church pew has surrendered their life to Jesus.
And not everyone who has walked away from church has stopped longing for God.
Some are wounded.
Some are skeptical.
Some are ashamed.
Some have questions they are afraid Christians will judge them for asking.
Some have heard religion their entire lives but have never clearly understood the Gospel of grace.
They need more than an argument.
They need truth spoken with love.
They need Christians whose lives reflect the Savior they proclaim.
They need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is offered through Christ, and a new life can begin by His grace.
And sometimes that conversation begins with something as simple as sharing a message.
That is why I want to ask you something personal.
Who came to your mind while you were reading this?
A brother who has drifted from God?
A daughter who no longer prays?
A friend whose smile is hiding exhaustion?
A husband or wife who has become spiritually distant?
Someone who believes their past has disqualified them from ever coming back to Jesus?
Do not use this story to shame them.
Do not send it as a weapon.
Send it as an invitation.
Sometimes love knows when to speak publicly.
And sometimes love knows when to protect someone's dignity.
If this message exposed something in your own heart, you do not have to pretend.
You do not need to reveal private wounds or painful details to prove your sincerity.
God already knows what you are carrying.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes, wondering whether you can still come home to Him, remember the words of Jesus:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
—John 6:37, KJV
What an extraordinary promise.
Come to Him.
Not to an image of yourself that you are trying to maintain.
Not to the reputation you are afraid to lose.
Not to the religious performance you think might impress Him.
Come to Jesus.
Confess your sins.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Turn from the darkness that has been ruling your life.
And follow Him.
Grace does not mean sin was never serious.
Grace means Christ is a sufficient Savior.
And because He is alive, the past does not have to be the final author of your future.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because every earthly tragedy receives a happy ending before sunset.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as we desire.
Not because faith guarantees a life without grief.
But because Jesus Christ has accomplished a redemption that sin, shame, and death cannot ultimately overthrow.
That is why we continue proclaiming the Gospel.
That is why we continue creating Scripture-centered articles, devotionals, books, and discipleship resources.
Gospel Warrior is not simply trying to produce more content.
Our desire is to help more people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and discover the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our commitment to make biblical encouragement and Christian learning accessible to people who may not otherwise have the means to obtain them.
Not because a payment can purchase spiritual favor.
Not because anyone should feel guilty for being unable to give.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–18 shows how believers financially partnered with Paul in Gospel ministry.
It should not be confused with a required biblical tithe or presented as a substitute for giving to your local church.
Rather, it is an additional opportunity to participate in Christian ministry as God leads and as your circumstances allow.
It is the opportunity to help keep biblical teaching and Gospel encouragement available to people who need them.
And if you have reached this far, I want to leave you with one final question.
Are you merely surviving spiritually, or are you truly following Jesus?
Because there is a difference.
You can know religious language and still be far from God.
You can recognize Bible stories and still resist the truth they reveal.
You can speak about grace while refusing to repent.
You can be surrounded by Christian content and still neglect prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience.
But today, you can turn toward Christ.
Not tomorrow, when you think you will be more worthy.
Not someday, when your life finally looks presentable.
Today.
The God who brought deliverance to Samaria is the same God whose redemptive purposes find their fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
And the Gospel is not that we can somehow rescue ourselves if we become strong enough.
The Gospel is that Jesus came to save sinners.
So bring Him your guilt.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him the questions you cannot answer.
Bring Him the sins you need to confess.
Bring Him the brokenness you cannot repair by yourself.
And trust the Savior who died and rose again.
If you are ready to turn back to Him, you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I need You. I confess that I have sinned and cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You. Give me the courage to turn away from sin and walk in Your truth. Heal what is wounded, correct what is wrong, and make my life a testimony of Your grace. Amen.”
Prayer is not a formula that earns salvation. Our hope rests in Jesus Christ, received through faith, not in the perfection of our words.
And if you prayed sincerely, do not let this be the end of your response.
Open your Bible.
Seek fellowship in a faithful local church.
Learn from mature believers.
Walk in repentance.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
The story of Samaria began with a city surrounded by death.
It showed us a mother crying to a king who could not save her child.
It showed us a ruler tearing his garments in anguish.
It showed us four desperate men discovering that good news was too important to keep to themselves.
And it leaves us with a choice.
We can read the account, feel disturbed, and move on.
Or we can allow it to remind us how desperately this world needs the righteousness, mercy, and redemption found in Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest answer to human darkness is not pretending the darkness never existed.
It is turning toward the Savior who entered our broken world and overcame death.
The king of Samaria tore his clothes when he heard how far humanity had fallen. But the King of kings gave His life to redeem sinners who could never lift themselves back up.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BOOK THAT VANISHED… BUT THE SINS OF THE KINGS DID NOT
paragraphs: THE BOOK THAT VANISHED… BUT THE SINS OF THE KINGS DID NOT
What Were the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? — The Forgotten Royal Records of 1 Kings 14:29, the Terrifying Truth About What God Remembers, and the Grace That Can Rewrite Your Ending
Imagine discovering a book that contains everything your family tried to bury.

Every betrayal. Every secret compromise. Every decision that destroyed someone else's trust. Every moment when a person appeared righteous in public but lived an entirely different life behind closed doors.
Now imagine discovering that the book was written about a king.
A man who sat on a throne, commanded armies, inherited a sacred legacy, and ruled a nation that carried the name of the living God.
His name was Rehoboam.
And somewhere in the ancient history of Judah, there once existed a written account of his reign that we no longer possess.
The Bible mentions it almost casually.
But the question it leaves behind is anything but ordinary.
What happened to the chronicles of the kings of Judah? And why would Scripture point us toward a book that has disappeared?
Because hidden inside that question is something much more personal.
What happens when the world remembers your achievements, but God sees the condition of your heart?
What happens when your name survives in history, but your faithfulness does not?
And most importantly…
Can a life marked by failure still become a testimony of grace?

Stay with this, because a seemingly forgotten sentence in the Old Testament opens a window into the tragedy of a divided kingdom, the danger of inherited religion, and the extraordinary mercy of Jesus Christ.
And somewhere in this story, you may recognize yourself.
The Bible says:
"Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?"
— 1 Kings 14:29, KJV
Read that again.
"The rest of the acts."
"All that he did."
"Written in the book."
These words suggest that the biblical account was not intended to describe every political decision, military event, or administrative detail of Rehoboam's reign.
There were other records.
Other events.
Other stories.
But the Holy Spirit, working through the human authors of Scripture, preserved something more important than a complete royal diary.
The Bible gives us the history necessary to understand God's covenant dealings with His people.
And the story is devastating.
To understand the mysterious chronicles, we must first understand the king whose life led us to them.
Rehoboam was the son of Solomon and the grandson of David.
Think about that inheritance.
David had been called a man after God's own heart (1 Samuel 13:14; Acts 13:22).
Solomon had received extraordinary wisdom from God (1 Kings 3:12).
The temple in Jerusalem had been built during Solomon's reign.
The kingdom had experienced remarkable wealth, influence, and international recognition.
Rehoboam inherited a throne surrounded by sacred history.
But he also inherited a kingdom already weakened by spiritual compromise.
Solomon's later years had been marked by idolatry, and the Lord had announced that the kingdom would be torn from his dynasty, though a portion would remain for David's sake (1 Kings 11:9–13).
Then Rehoboam came to power.
The people approached him with a reasonable request.
Solomon's government had placed heavy burdens upon them. They asked Rehoboam to lighten their labor and taxation.
The older counselors advised him to serve the people and answer them kindly.
The younger men who had grown up with him urged him to demonstrate greater harshness.
And Rehoboam chose the voice that flattered his pride.
He answered the people with a threat of even heavier burdens.
The result was catastrophic.
The kingdom divided.
Ten northern tribes rejected the house of David and followed Jeroboam, while Rehoboam retained the southern kingdom centered in Judah, with Benjamin also associated with his rule.
One nation became two rival kingdoms.
One royal decision exposed the fragility of a kingdom already suffering from disobedience.
And an entire generation lived with the consequences.
There is something painfully familiar about that.
How many families have been divided because someone refused to listen?
How many marriages have been wounded because pride was louder than wisdom?
How many friendships have collapsed because one person cared more about being respected than being loving?
Sometimes the greatest damage does not begin with an obvious act of evil.
Sometimes it begins when a person is given the opportunity to humble themselves…
And refuses.
Rehoboam had a throne.
He had advisers.
He had an extraordinary family history.
But none of those things guaranteed that he would walk faithfully with God.
You can inherit a religious legacy without inheriting a surrendered heart.
That sentence should trouble every one of us who has ever confused familiarity with Christianity for genuine discipleship.
You can grow up hearing Scripture and still resist its authority.
You can know the language of prayer and still refuse repentance.
You can attend worship services while protecting sins you have no intention of abandoning.
You can carry the name of Christ publicly while privately resisting His lordship.
And eventually, the truth begins to show.
That is exactly what happened in Judah.
First Kings 14:22 records:
"And Judah did evil in the sight of the LORD, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins which they had committed, above all that their fathers had done."
— KJV
The text then describes idolatrous practices, high places, sacred pillars, Asherim, and grave moral and religious corruption (1 Kings 14:23–24).
This was not simply a political crisis.
It was a covenant crisis.
The people who had been called to worship the Lord were turning toward practices He had forbidden.
And the consequences did not remain invisible.
In the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign, Shishak king of Egypt came against Jerusalem.
He took away treasures from the house of the Lord and from the royal palace, including the gold shields Solomon had made (1 Kings 14:25–26).
Picture that moment.
The splendor of Solomon's kingdom was being carried away.
The symbols of royal glory were disappearing.
And Rehoboam responded by replacing the gold shields with shields of bronze.
Bronze.
Where gold had once stood.
The kingdom still had guards.
The palace still had ceremonies.
The king still occupied his throne.
But something precious had been lost.
And the replacement could not restore the original glory.
There is a warning here, although we must be careful not to turn every historical detail into an allegory.
The biblical account records an actual political and spiritual disaster. The bronze shields were real replacements for treasures taken by Egypt.
Yet the scene can still cause us to examine our own lives.
Have we ever tried to preserve the appearance of spiritual health after neglecting our relationship with God?
Have we ever substituted religious activity for repentance?
Have we ever learned to look strong while becoming spiritually exhausted?
The most dangerous kind of decline is not always the kind everybody notices.
Sometimes people continue applauding while the heart grows colder.
Sometimes the routine survives long after the devotion has faded.
Sometimes the outside still looks impressive.
And only God knows what has been lost.
But here is where the story becomes even more astonishing.
The mysterious book mentioned in 1 Kings 14:29 was not necessarily a book of Scripture that somehow fell out of the Bible.
It was a historical source referenced by the biblical writer.
The Hebrew expression behind "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah" is:
סֵפֶר דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים לְמַלְכֵי יְהוּדָה
Sefer divrei hayyamim lemalkei Yehudah.
Literally, the expression refers to a "book of the matters/events of the days concerning the kings of Judah," commonly rendered as the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
The word סֵפֶר (sefer) means a book, scroll, or written document.
The expression דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים (divrei hayyamim) refers to matters or events of the days—hence the idea of chronicles or historical records.
And יְהוּדָה (Yehudah) is Judah.
The wording points to written accounts associated with Judah's monarchy.
Such records may have contained details about royal administration, conflicts, political events, construction projects, and other affairs of the kings.
But Scripture does not give us the complete contents of this particular work.
We should not pretend to know what it said.
Nor can we establish with certainty whether the title referred to one continuous royal archive, a series of records, or a historical compilation.
What we can say is that Kings repeatedly refers to chronicles of the kings of Judah and, separately, chronicles of the kings of Israel.
These were distinct kingdoms, with distinct royal histories.
And the records referred to in Kings have not survived as identifiable, complete manuscripts available to us today.
There is another important distinction.
The lost royal chronicles of Judah should not simply be equated with the biblical books of 1 and 2 Chronicles.
The biblical books of Chronicles are preserved Scripture.
They retell and interpret significant portions of Israel's history, especially the history of David's dynasty, Jerusalem, the temple, and Judah.
They also draw upon historical traditions and mention other sources.
But the book cited in 1 Kings 14:29 cannot confidently be identified as our canonical books of Chronicles.
The similarity of the English titles can mislead modern readers.
And there is an especially interesting detail.
The biblical book of 2 Chronicles gives us additional information about Rehoboam that is not developed in the same way in 1 Kings.
Second Chronicles 12:1 says:
"And it came to pass, when Rehoboam had established the kingdom, and had strengthened himself, he forsook the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him."
— KJV
Did you notice the sequence?
He became established.
He became strong.
Then he forsook the law of the Lord.
That is a frightening pattern.
Not because strength itself is evil.
Not because success is automatically sinful.
But because prosperity can expose what a person has begun trusting more than God.
Some people seek the Lord desperately when everything is falling apart.
Then, when the crisis passes, prayer becomes less urgent.
Scripture becomes less important.
Worship becomes an obligation instead of a delight.
And the heart begins whispering, "I can manage from here."
Rehoboam's story confronts that temptation.
But the account does not end with nothing but rebellion.
When Shishak threatened Judah, the prophet Shemaiah confronted Rehoboam and the leaders with the Lord's message:
"Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak."
— 2 Chronicles 12:5, KJV
What happened next is easy to miss.
The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves.
They acknowledged:
"The LORD is righteous."
— 2 Chronicles 12:6, KJV
And when the Lord saw their humility, He declared that He would not destroy them completely.
There would still be consequences.
They would still experience subjection.
The lost treasures would not simply reappear.
But judgment was tempered with mercy.
Do not rush past that.
God's mercy did not mean that sin was harmless. It meant that destruction was not the only word spoken over them.
That is a truth many wounded believers desperately need to understand.
Repentance does not always erase every earthly consequence.
A broken trust may take years to rebuild.
A foolish decision may leave a financial burden.
A wounded relationship may require confession, patience, restitution, and time.
Some consequences may never be fully reversed in this life.
But genuine repentance matters.
Humility matters.
Turning back toward God matters.
And His mercy is not exhausted by the seriousness of our failures.
Yet Scripture refuses to romanticize Rehoboam's response.
Second Chronicles 12:14 gives a sobering summary:
"And he did evil, because he prepared not his heart to seek the LORD."
— KJV
The Hebrew behind "prepared" is related to כּוּן (kun), a verb associated with establishing, making firm, or directing something.
The verse describes a heart that was not firmly set toward seeking the Lord.
This helps us understand the tragedy.
Rehoboam experienced a moment of humility under judgment, but the overall biblical evaluation of his life remained negative.
His story warns us against confusing temporary fear with enduring faithfulness.
It is possible to feel remorse when consequences arrive without cultivating a heart devoted to God.
It is possible to cry because life has become painful while still refusing to surrender the sin that contributed to the pain.
And that raises a question far more important than the whereabouts of an ancient manuscript.
Is your heart actually set on seeking the Lord, or do you only reach for Him when everything else stops working?
That is not a question to answer for someone else.
It is a question to bring before God.
Because behind the historical curiosity of 1 Kings 14:29 lies an uncomfortable reminder.
Human history records kings.
God's Word evaluates their faithfulness.
A royal chronicle might preserve a king's battles, buildings, and political accomplishments.
But the biblical narrative repeatedly directs our attention to whether the king did what was right or evil in the sight of the Lord.
That difference matters.
People may remember your title.
God sees how you treated those who depended on you.
People may remember your achievements.
God knows whether you acted justly.
People may remember the image you carefully maintained.
God knows the truth of your inner life.
And Scripture teaches that human beings are accountable before Him.
Ecclesiastes 12:14 says:
"For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil."
— KJV
The New Testament reinforces this accountability.
Romans 2:16 speaks of the day when God will judge the secrets of humanity through Jesus Christ.
And Revelation 20:12 portrays the dead standing before God's throne as books are opened.
We should not claim that the lost chronicles of Judah are literally among those books.
Scripture does not say that.
The royal chronicles were historical documents, while Revelation uses the imagery of heavenly books in a vision of final judgment.
But the theological contrast is unmistakable.
Human records can disappear.
Human reputations can be manipulated.
Human applause can fade.
No human being can hide the truth from God.
Perhaps that thought makes you uncomfortable.
Maybe there is something in your past you have worked hard to forget.
A relationship you damaged.
A promise you broke.
A season of rebellion.
A secret habit.
A decision that still makes you ashamed.
Perhaps you are not afraid that people will discover what happened.
Perhaps you are afraid that God already knows.
He does.
And here is the Gospel truth you must not miss.
The God who knows the truth about your sin is the same God who sent His Son to save sinners.
This is where the story of Judah's kings leads us toward something infinitely greater than an ancient archive.
Because Rehoboam was not the final king in David's line.
The dynasty continued.
Through failures.
Through judgments.
Through exile.
Through generations of longing.
And ultimately, the New Testament announces Jesus Christ as the promised Son of David.
Matthew 1:7 even names Rehoboam in the genealogy leading to Jesus.
Think about that.
Rehoboam.
The king whose pride helped fracture a kingdom.
The king whose reign was marked by spiritual failure.
His name appears in the genealogy of the Messiah.
Not because his rebellion was good.
Not because God approved of his sin.
But because God's covenant purpose continued through a deeply flawed human history.
The genealogy of Jesus is not a celebration of human perfection.
It is a testimony to divine faithfulness.
And Jesus is not another Rehoboam.
Where Rehoboam answered the people with harshness, Jesus called the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28).
Where Rehoboam's pride contributed to division, Jesus humbled Himself and became obedient unto death (Philippians 2:5–8).
Where Judah's kings repeatedly failed to uphold covenant faithfulness, Jesus fulfilled the Father's will.
Where earthly kings could not rescue their people from the deepest bondage of sin, Christ came to save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).
And where royal power often demanded service, Jesus declared:
"For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."
— Mark 10:45, KJV
There is your true King.
Not merely a ruler who inherited a throne.
The Savior who went willingly to a cross.
Not a king who threatened the burdened.
The King who bore the burden of sin.
Not a king whose legacy depended upon gold shields and political strength.
The risen Lord whose kingdom will never end.
And this is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to the idea that Jesus simply helps us feel better about our mistakes.
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
God's holiness is real.
And forgiveness is not God pretending that evil never happened.
At the cross, Jesus Christ bore the penalty of sin for His people.
He died and rose again.
Salvation is offered by grace through faith in Him, not earned by religious achievements, family background, donations, or outward appearances.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
— KJV
And the next verse tells us that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not purchase permission to remain unchanged.
Grace brings us to the Savior who forgives and transforms.
This is why repentance is not an enemy of hope.
It is part of the response to the Gospel.
Jesus proclaimed:
"Repent ye, and believe the gospel."
— Mark 1:15, KJV
The Greek word translated "repent" is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), a command calling for repentance—a changed mind and orientation that turns away from sin toward God.
It is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered your wrongdoing.
It is not merely fearing punishment.
It is not promising to improve while refusing the lordship of Christ.
It is a real turning to God, inseparable from faith in the Savior.
And perhaps you need that invitation today.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you have cleaned up every visible part of your life.
Today.
Because there is something worse than having a painful past.
It is refusing the grace of God because you believe your past must have the final word.
Listen carefully.
You cannot rewrite history by pretending it never happened.
You cannot make sin holy by calling it a lesson.
You cannot save yourself through determination.
But Jesus Christ can forgive sinners, reconcile them to God, and make them new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
— KJV
That does not mean every consequence disappears overnight.
It means that belonging to Christ changes your standing before God and begins a new life under His grace.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to become your master.
Your failures may require honest confession.
They do not have to drive you away from the only Savior who can forgive them.
Your story may contain chapters you wish had never been written.
But through Christ, those chapters do not have to be the end.
Not by changing the facts of yesterday.
But by redeeming sinners and transforming what comes next.
And now return to the question that began this journey.
What were the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
They were historical records referenced by the biblical authors, apparently preserving additional accounts of Judah's monarchs beyond the selected events included in Scripture.
Their exact contents are unknown.
No complete surviving copy can be securely identified with the work cited in 1 Kings 14:29.
And although they may once have preserved details of royal lives, their disappearance has not prevented Scripture from communicating the essential theological lessons of those reigns.
The Bible does not give us every detail about Rehoboam.
It gives us enough to recognize the dangers of pride, the devastation of disobedience, the seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness, and the mercy of God toward those who humble themselves.
It also gives us enough to recognize that no ordinary king could become humanity's ultimate hope.
That hope belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
And maybe that is the most important discovery in this entire investigation.
We began searching for a missing book.
But we found a question about the direction of our own hearts.
If the story of your life were written today, what would it reveal about the God you claim to serve?
Not simply what you posted.
Not simply what you attended.
Not simply what you gave.
But how you loved.
How you repented.
How you forgave.
How you treated the powerless.
How you responded when Scripture confronted your desires.
And whether you truly trusted Jesus.
There is no need to perform for that question.
There is no need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
If you are struggling, tell the truth.
If you have drifted, return to Christ.
If you have sinned, confess it and seek His forgiveness.
If you have been hiding behind religious appearances, bring your real life into the light of His Word.
First John 1:9 promises:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
— KJV
What a promise.
Not that God will excuse rebellion.
Not that confession is a magical formula.
But that forgiveness and cleansing are found in the faithful and righteous God who has provided salvation through His Son.
And perhaps someone reading this has been waiting for a reason to come home to God.
This is your invitation.
Come to Jesus.
Not because you have finally become impressive.
Not because your record is clean.
But because He is merciful, and His sacrifice is sufficient.

If this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sins publicly. Bring them honestly before God, and seek wise, trustworthy pastoral support where needed.
Your story may encourage someone who believes change is impossible.
We are not gathering comments merely to create activity.
We want to make room for truth, prayer, encouragement, and people pointing one another back to Jesus.
Because the person quietly reading this may be carrying a battle no one else knows about.
And your words might remind them that they do not have to face it alone.
Not to shame them.
Not to expose them.
But to remind them that the Gospel is still good news for sinners.
Return to it when pride whispers that you do not need God.
Return to it when shame whispers that God could never receive you.
Return to it when you need to remember that the King who matters most is not Rehoboam, Solomon, or David.
It is Jesus Christ.
Our desire is to keep bringing people back to Scripture, the Gospel, repentance, grace, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
There is also something important we want to share with those who believe in this mission.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing another inspirational post.
We want to build a growing place of biblical learning, spiritual encouragement, discipleship, and resources that help people study God's Word beyond a single moment of inspiration.
And we want that work to continue expanding.
More resources.
More biblical teaching.
More opportunities to encourage struggling believers.
More ways to help people discover the truth of the Gospel.
For those who consider Gospel Warrior part of their regular spiritual nourishment, it may be one expression of generous Christian stewardship.
But we want to be completely clear about something that matters deeply to the Gospel.
Scripture teaches generous giving, but it also teaches that giving should be willing rather than compelled.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
— KJV
You do not have to pay to be loved by Jesus.

But if the teaching shared through Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, strengthened your faith, encouraged you to repent, or brought you back to the hope of the Gospel, we would be grateful if you prayerfully considered helping us continue that work.
These items are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
You can still help in meaningful ways.
Invite someone to read Scripture with you.
Pray for this ministry.
Tell someone what Jesus Christ has done.
And keep growing in the truth.
Because the goal has never been to build a community that merely admires religious content.
The goal is to point people toward the Savior who alone can forgive sin, reconcile us to God, and transform lives.
And now, one final thought.
The ancient chronicles of Judah have disappeared from our possession.
We cannot open their pages.
We cannot examine every sentence.
We cannot recover every forgotten detail of Rehoboam's reign.
But we have something far more precious than an ancient king's political record.
We have the testimony of Scripture concerning the King of kings.
We know that Jesus lived.
We know that He was crucified.
We know that He rose again, just as the Scriptures proclaim.
And we know that everyone who truly comes to Him in faith finds a Savior whose mercy is greater than the sinner's ability to save himself.
So do not spend your life trying to appear righteous while refusing the One who makes sinners right with God.
Do not let pride become your throne.
Do not let shame become your prison.
Do not let your past become your identity.
Come to Christ.
Trust His finished work.
Turn from sin.
Walk in His truth.
And remember that the most important question is not whether history will remember your name.
It is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Because when the applause is silent, when the earthly records are forgotten, and when every human kingdom has passed away, the Lord Jesus Christ will still reign.
The world may remember the scandal that marked your yesterday, but in Christ, your failure does not have to write the final sentence of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BY HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED… SO WHY ARE SOME FAITHFUL CHRISTIANS STILL DYING SICK?
paragraphs: BY HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED… SO WHY ARE SOME FAITHFUL CHRISTIANS STILL DYING SICK?

The heartbreaking truth about Isaiah 53:5 that challenges the prosperity gospel, confronts our deepest disappointments, and reveals a Savior whose wounds promise something even greater than the miracle we are begging Him to perform.
She prayed until her voice was almost gone.
The Bible lay open beside the hospital bed. Her husband's breathing had become shallow. Machines whispered and beeped in a room where every second felt like an eternity.
She had fasted. She had believed. She had asked the elders to pray. She had anointed him with oil. She had declared the promises of Scripture over his body.
And through tears she whispered the verse she had heard preached a thousand times.
“By His stripes we are healed.”
But the cancer kept spreading.
And one night, despite every prayer, every tear, every desperate declaration of faith…
Her husband died.
What happened to the promise?
Was her faith too weak?
Had she prayed incorrectly?
Was there some hidden sin that prevented the miracle?
Or had she misunderstood what God was promising in the first place?
Perhaps you have never stood beside a hospital bed like hers.

But maybe you have watched your mother suffer. Maybe your child has a diagnosis that makes you afraid to answer the telephone. Maybe your body has been fighting a disease for years while people keep telling you to believe harder.
And somewhere beneath your worship songs and your Sunday smiles, there is a question you are almost ashamed to ask.
If Jesus was wounded for my healing, why am I still hurting?
Please don't rush past that question.
Because the answer is not found in pretending that suffering isn't real.
And it certainly isn't found in accusing wounded Christians of lacking faith.
The answer begins at a cross, where the Son of God suffered wounds He did not deserve to accomplish a redemption we could never earn.
And understanding what those wounds actually purchased may change the way you pray, suffer, hope, and follow Jesus for the rest of your life.
The prophet Isaiah wrote approximately seven centuries before the earthly ministry of Jesus Christ:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” — Isaiah 53:5, KJV
These are among the most beautiful words ever written about the suffering Messiah.
But beautiful words can become dangerous when we separate them from their intended meaning.
The Hebrew phrase behind “and with his stripes we are healed” is:
וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא־לָנוּ
Uvaḥavurato nirpa lanu.
A careful translation is, “And by his wound, healing has come to us,” or, more traditionally, “And with his stripes we are healed.”
The Hebrew word חֲבֻרָה (ḥavurah) refers to a wound or stripe, particularly the injury produced by a blow.
The verb רָפָא (rapha) means “to heal.” It can describe physical healing, but Scripture also uses healing language for spiritual and covenant restoration.
That distinction matters enormously.
The Hebrew word itself does not automatically prove that Isaiah was promising immediate bodily recovery to every believer.
We must allow the surrounding passage to explain the kind of healing Isaiah is emphasizing.
And what surrounds this famous promise?
Transgressions.
Iniquities.
Punishment.
Peace.
Sin.
Isaiah 53:6 continues:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
The deepest wound addressed in this passage is humanity's rebellion against God.
The Servant suffers because we have sinned.
He is wounded because we have wandered.
He bears judgment so that guilty people can receive peace.
Isaiah is describing the astonishing exchange at the heart of the Gospel.
The righteous One suffers for the unrighteous.
The innocent One bears the burden of the guilty.
The Holy One makes a way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And the healing Isaiah celebrates is inseparable from that saving work.
This does not mean God is uninterested in your physical suffering.
It means we must not reduce the cross to a guarantee that Christians will never remain sick.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make dying people temporarily healthy.
He came to save sinners, conquer death, and bring His redeemed people into everlasting life.
And here is where the story becomes even more extraordinary.
Centuries after Isaiah wrote those words, the apostle Peter quoted the same prophecy.
But notice what he said immediately afterward.
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.” — 1 Peter 2:24, KJV
The Greek phrase is:
οὗ τῷ μώλωπι ἰάθητε
Hou tō mōlōpi iathēte.
Literally, “By whose wound you were healed.”
The word μώλωψ (mōlōps) refers to a bruise, welt, or wound.
The verb ἰάθητε (iathēte) means “you were healed.”
But Peter does something that should make every serious Bible reader stop.
He explains the purpose of Christ bearing our sins: that we might die to sins and live to righteousness.
Then he continues:
“For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.” — 1 Peter 2:25, KJV
Do you see it?
Peter does not say, “You were physically sick, but now none of you can remain sick.”
He says you were wandering sheep, but now you have returned to your Shepherd.
The healing in Peter's immediate explanation concerns our restoration from sin and estrangement from God.
The cross brings forgiveness, reconciliation, and a transformed life.
That is not a lesser miracle.
That is the miracle upon which every other Christian hope depends.
A healed body can still die.
A forgiven sinner who belongs to Jesus has eternal life.
And yet we must be careful not to swing into the opposite error.
Because the Bible does not teach that physical healing is irrelevant to Christ's mission.
Matthew 8:16–17 records Jesus casting out spirits and healing the sick, then explicitly connects those healings to Isaiah's prophecy:
“That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.” — Matthew 8:17, KJV
This is crucial.
Matthew shows that Jesus' healing ministry truly belongs to the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision.
His compassion was not symbolic.
Blind eyes opened.
Paralyzed people walked.
Lepers were cleansed.
People with genuine physical illnesses experienced genuine physical restoration.
Jesus cared about suffering bodies.
He still does.
So the biblical question is not whether Christ's redemptive mission includes physical healing.
It does.
The question is whether every believer is promised complete physical healing right now, in this present life, whenever healing is requested in faith.
And Scripture does not establish that guarantee.
The kingdom of God has already broken into history through Jesus Christ.
But its final consummation has not yet arrived.
Christ has risen.
Death has been defeated decisively.
Yet believers still experience weakness, disease, aging, grief, and physical death.
We live between the victory already accomplished and the restoration still awaiting its fullness.
Romans 8:23 says that believers, even though they have the firstfruits of the Spirit, still groan inwardly while awaiting “the redemption of our body.”
Read that again.
Believers who possess the Holy Spirit are still waiting for the redemption of their bodies.
Paul was not describing Christians who lacked sufficient faith.
He was describing the normal tension of Christian existence before the resurrection.
We have received salvation in Christ.
We are being sanctified by His Spirit.
And we await the day when our bodies will be raised imperishable.
That future is not uncertain.
But the timing matters.
The final, complete healing of God's people is guaranteed through Christ.
Complete freedom from every illness before death is not.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable evidence comes from a man who personally witnessed extraordinary miracles.
The apostle Paul.
Paul preached Christ.
Paul healed the sick by God's power.
Paul witnessed supernatural deliverance.
Yet Paul also carried an affliction he desperately wanted removed.
He called it a thorn in the flesh.
We are not told precisely what that thorn was, so we should not confidently diagnose it as a particular disease.
But we know it caused real distress.
Paul pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from him.
And God's answer was not the answer Paul requested.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Imagine that.
The apostle who preached the power of the risen Christ received an answer that did not involve the removal of his affliction.
Not because Christ lacked power.
Not because grace had failed.
Not because Paul needed to discover a more effective declaration.
But because God's sufficient grace and Christ's sustaining power were being displayed in weakness.
Sometimes God glorifies Himself by removing suffering.
Sometimes He glorifies Himself by sustaining His children through suffering.
Neither reality gives us permission to treat illness as proof of spiritual failure.
And Paul was not the only faithful believer who experienced bodily weakness.
In Philippians 2:25–27, Epaphroditus became gravely ill, nearly to the point of death.
Paul did not accuse him of unbelief.
He recognized that God had shown him mercy.
In 1 Timothy 5:23, Paul advised Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach and his frequent ailments.
He did not tell Timothy that recurring illness was impossible for a genuine Christian.
In 2 Timothy 4:20, Paul wrote that he had left Trophimus sick at Miletus.
These passages do not deny divine healing.
They dismantle the idea that faithful Christians are guaranteed uninterrupted physical health.
Even devoted servants of Christ experienced sickness.
And the Bible does not portray their suffering as evidence that Jesus had abandoned them.
Think about what that means for the woman beside the hospital bed.
Think about what it means for the father watching his child undergo another treatment.
Think about what it means for the believer whose prayers have not produced the miracle everyone expected.
Your illness is not a verdict on the strength of your faith.
Your unanswered request is not proof that Jesus has stopped loving you.
Your suffering does not automatically mean that you are being punished for a hidden sin.
Jesus directly challenged that assumption in John 9:1–3 when His disciples asked whether a man's blindness resulted from his sin or his parents' sin.
Christ rejected their proposed explanation.
Not every sickness can be traced to a particular personal wrongdoing.
Yes, Scripture teaches that sin and death entered the human story through the fall.
Yes, particular sins can sometimes have physical consequences.
But it is biblically irresponsible to assume that every sick Christian is sick because of unbelief, disobedience, or a secret offense.
And it is cruel to turn that assumption into a burden for people who are already suffering.
A mother who has buried her child does not need a preacher suggesting that she failed to believe hard enough.
A cancer patient does not need someone telling him that chemotherapy proves he has abandoned faith.
A disabled believer does not need to be treated as a defective testimony.
They need the truth.
They need compassion.
They need the presence of the body of Christ.
They need the Gospel.
And they need to know that the Savior who suffered on the cross understands suffering from the inside.
Jesus did not stand at a safe distance from human pain.
He entered it.
He wept at Lazarus's tomb.
He experienced exhaustion.
He endured betrayal.
He was beaten, mocked, scourged, and crucified.
He knows what it means to cry out in anguish.
And in Gethsemane, Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from Him, while surrendering Himself to the Father's will.
His prayer was not an expression of unbelief.
It was perfect trust expressed in the presence of terrible suffering.
This matters because some Christians have been taught that saying “Your will be done” is a confession of weak faith.
But Jesus Himself prayed in submission to the Father's will.
If surrender were unbelief, the sinless Son of God would have been guilty of it.
He was not.
Biblical faith does not mean commanding God to obey our preferred outcome.
Biblical faith means trusting God's character even when we cannot understand His providence.
We may pray boldly for healing.
We should pray boldly for healing.
James 5:14–16 encourages the sick to call for the elders of the church, to receive prayer and anointing with oil in the name of the Lord.
