The Greek includes the expressions τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα — tēn heautou gynaika, meaning "his own wife," and τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα — ton idion andra, meaning "her own husband."
The verse presents a reciprocal relationship of marital belonging and responsibility.
It does not contain a separate sentence explicitly stating, "Polygamy is adultery."
But its mutual language coheres with the monogamous pattern that characterizes New Testament teaching.
Paul continues in 1 Corinthians 7:3–4 by emphasizing the mutual marital responsibilities of husband and wife.
This was significant in a world where women could be treated as possessions or instruments of male advantage.
Christian marriage was not presented as a license for selfish power.
It was a relationship of mutual obligation before God.
Then in Ephesians 5, Paul describes marriage through the relationship between Christ and His church.
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (Ephesians 5:25, KJV)
Think about that command.
A husband is not told merely to exercise authority.
He is told to love sacrificially.
To give.
To serve.
To imitate the self-giving love of Jesus.
The chapter returns again to Genesis 2:24 and the one-flesh union.
And Paul says:
"This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." (Ephesians 5:32, KJV)
Marriage is not merely about satisfying desire.
It is meant to reflect covenantal faithfulness.
A love that does not abandon when sacrifice becomes costly.
A love that refuses to treat another person as disposable.
A love shaped by Christ.
The pastoral qualifications in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 also describe an overseer as the "husband of one wife."
The Greek expression is μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra, literally "a man of one woman" or "a husband of one wife."
Christians have debated whether this expression primarily excludes polygamy, emphasizes marital fidelity, addresses remarriage in particular circumstances, or combines several concerns.
It would be misleading to pretend that every interpreter agrees on all its implications.
But the language certainly reinforces the importance of marital faithfulness, and it fits the broader New Testament presentation of marriage.
So what can we responsibly conclude?
The Old Testament records and regulates polygyny.
It does not classify every polygynous union as the legal equivalent of adultery.
Yet the creation account, Jesus' appeal to that account, and the New Testament's portrayal of marital covenant establish the two-person union as the normative Christian pattern.

That is why the historic mainstream of Christian teaching has upheld monogamy, while recognizing that difficult pastoral questions can arise when people in existing polygamous households come to faith.
Those situations demand wisdom, truth, compassion, and careful attention to the responsibilities owed to spouses and children.
They should never be handled with simplistic commands that leave vulnerable people abandoned.
Biblical faithfulness is not measured by how quickly we can condemn someone else's household.
It is measured by whether we submit ourselves to the truth of God and act justly toward those affected by our decisions.
And there is another distinction we must make.
Jesus' teaching on adultery goes deeper than ancient legal definitions.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He exposes the sinful desire that can exist in the heart before an outward act is committed.
A person can have only one spouse and still be unfaithful in thought, intention, or action.
A marriage certificate does not automatically create purity.
A public reputation does not guarantee private faithfulness.
And winning a debate about polygamy does not make a person righteous.
Jesus is concerned with the heart.
The hidden motives.
The private compromises.
The desires we carefully protect from examination.
That is why this discussion must never become an excuse for anyone to justify sexual exploitation, betrayal, coercion, or selfishness.
Nor should it become an excuse to treat people living in complicated family circumstances as though they are beyond the reach of grace.
The Gospel is not an invitation to minimize sin.
It is an invitation to bring our whole lives into the transforming light of Jesus Christ.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because maybe you have never considered polygamy.
Maybe you are married to one person.
Maybe you are single.
Maybe you are divorced.
Maybe you are carrying wounds from a relationship that shattered your trust.
Maybe you were betrayed by someone who quoted Scripture beautifully but lived without integrity.
Maybe you have been the person who caused the wound.
And perhaps you came here expecting an argument about ancient marriage customs.
But now you are remembering a conversation.
A betrayal.
A promise you broke.
A person you hurt.
Or a wound you still cannot explain without your voice trembling.
Listen carefully.
The Bible does not expose human failure to convince us that redemption is impossible. It exposes our need for the Savior who makes redemption possible.
That is why we must eventually leave the arguments of kings and patriarchs and stand at the feet of Jesus.
In John 4, Jesus encounters a Samaritan woman at a well.
He tells her that she has had five husbands and that the man she now has is not her husband.
The passage does not tell us why her previous marriages ended.
It does not authorize us to invent a history of promiscuity, blame her for every broken relationship, or assume she was responsible for every loss.
But it does reveal that Jesus knew the truth of her circumstances.
And He still spoke to her.
He offered her living water.
He engaged her with dignity.
He revealed Himself to her.
And the woman who arrived at the well carrying her ordinary water jar became a witness who invited others to come and see Him.
This is the beauty of Christ.
He does not need to pretend that everything in our lives is right in order to approach us with grace.
He knows the truth.
And He calls us toward Himself.
That is what makes the Gospel different from mere moral instruction.
Moral instruction can tell you what you should have done.
The Gospel announces what Jesus Christ has done for sinners who cannot save themselves.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Not to use forgiveness as permission to continue in deliberate rebellion.
But to receive a new life in which grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that connection clear.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace trains.
Grace changes.
Grace calls us out of darkness and into a life that honors the Lord.
And that is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Abraham's family was complicated.
Jacob's household was wounded.
David fell terribly.
Solomon's heart wandered.
And still, through the history of deeply flawed human beings, God faithfully carried forward His promise of redemption.
Not because their sins were acceptable.
But because God's redemptive purpose was greater than their failures.
And at the center of that purpose stands Jesus Christ.
The Son of God.
The promised Messiah.
The descendant of Abraham and David.
The Savior who did not come to provide humanity with better excuses, but to rescue sinners and make them new.
So please do not leave this article merely asking whether you won an argument.
Ask whether you have surrendered your heart.
Ask whether your understanding of marriage is being shaped by the whole counsel of Scripture or only by passages that support what you already want.
Ask whether you are honoring the dignity of others.
Ask whether your relationships reflect truth, fidelity, justice, and sacrificial love.
And if the Holy Spirit is exposing something you have hidden, do not run from Him.
Run toward Christ.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is mercy for the broken.
There is hope for those who have failed.
And there is strength to walk in obedience, even when obedience costs something.
If this article confronted something you have struggled to understand, I would genuinely like to hear from you.

And if God has brought restoration into a relationship or healed something you thought would remain broken forever, consider sharing your testimony. Someone else may need to know that Christ is still at work.

Please keep the conversation gracious. Disagreement is not permission to humiliate another person. We can examine difficult biblical questions without forgetting that real people, real marriages, and real wounds exist behind them.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have grown distant from the faith, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ.
The goal is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to keep pointing people toward the Word of God and the Savior revealed in it.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture more clearly, encouraged you to repent, strengthened your faith, or reminded you of the grace of Jesus Christ, I want to invite you into something deeper.
For those who want to glorify God through their resources, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful expression of generosity.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers can participate in Gospel ministry through generous giving (Philippians 4:15–18).
But let us be clear about something important.
God loves a cheerful giver, not someone pressured by guilt (2 Corinthians 9:7).
These products are not the Gospel itself.
They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, spark conversations, and support the ongoing work.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
You do not need to purchase salvation.
Jesus has already accomplished what no amount of money could ever purchase.
Invite others to read Scripture for themselves.
Encourage honest, respectful conversations.
Pray that the Word of God will reach people who have never truly understood the Gospel.
It is whether people are being directed toward Jesus Christ, growing in biblical understanding, turning from sin, and learning to love God and their neighbors more faithfully.
And before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
Is polygamy the same as adultery?
Scripture requires a more careful answer than a simple slogan.
The two were not automatically identical offenses under ancient Israel's legal system.
Yet God's creation design, affirmed by Jesus and reflected in New Testament teaching, presents the faithful union of one husband and one wife as the normative pattern for Christian marriage.
The biblical record of polygamous households must neither be denied nor mistaken for an unrestricted endorsement of polygamy.
And above every argument stands a greater truth.
God's mercy toward imperfect people is not permission to disregard His will.
It is an invitation to return to Him.
So if you have been searching for a way to justify what God is calling you to surrender, may you find the courage to repent.
If you have been crushed by the failures of others, may you find comfort in the Savior who sees you.
If you have misunderstood Scripture, may you have the humility to learn.
And if you have wandered far from Christ, may you remember that His call to repentance is also a call to come home.
Because one day, the arguments will be over.
The comments will be forgotten.
The applause will fade.
The platforms we built will disappear.
But the truth of God will remain.
And the question that matters most will not be whether we successfully defended every opinion we held.
It will be whether we trusted and followed the Jesus whom Scripture reveals.
The most dangerous thing you can do with the Bible is use the failures God redeemed as excuses for the sins He is calling you to leave behind.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS KISSING BEFORE MARRIAGE REALLY A SIN? THE BIBLE'S ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING DEEPER THAN YOUR LIPS.
paragraphs: IS KISSING BEFORE MARRIAGE REALLY A SIN? THE BIBLE'S ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING DEEPER THAN YOUR LIPS.

Some Christians have been condemned for a kiss the Bible never explicitly forbids. Others have used that same silence to justify desires God never approved. But what if the real question isn't how far your lips can go—it's how much of your heart belongs to Jesus?
There was a moment when they stopped talking.
The conversation had been beautiful. They had laughed, shared stories, talked about their dreams, and even spoken about God.
He looked at her.
She looked back.
And suddenly, the distance between their faces felt smaller than the distance between what they wanted and what they believed.
He leaned closer.
She didn't move away.
Then came the kiss.
Nothing dramatic. No bedroom. No clothes coming off. No secret affair.
Just two people who cared about each other, sharing a moment of affection.
But later that night, she lay awake staring at the ceiling.
Did I just sin against God?
She had heard Christians say that kissing before marriage was sinful. She had heard others insist that anything short of sexual intercourse was perfectly acceptable.
One group made her afraid of affection.
The other made her wonder whether holiness had any boundaries at all.
And somewhere between those two voices, she desperately wanted to hear a third.
The voice of Jesus.
Because perhaps you've been there too.
Perhaps you've kissed someone you genuinely loved and wondered whether you had disappointed God.
Perhaps you've avoided even holding hands because someone convinced you that physical affection was automatically impure.
Or perhaps you've repeatedly crossed boundaries you knew were dangerous, comforting yourself with the argument that the Bible never specifically says, "Thou shalt not kiss before marriage."
Here's where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
The Bible does not explicitly command unmarried couples never to kiss.
But that doesn't mean every kiss is righteous.
And the Bible's silence about a particular physical action does not give us permission to ignore everything Scripture teaches about the heart behind it.
Before you defend your boundaries—or condemn someone else's—we need to open the Word of God.
Not church tradition pretending to be Scripture.
Not modern dating culture pretending to be freedom.
Not personal convictions elevated into universal commandments.
The Word of God.
Because Jesus did not die to replace one kind of bondage with another.
And He certainly did not save us so we could become experts at finding loopholes around holiness.
WHAT DOES THE BIBLE ACTUALLY SAY?
Let's begin with something that might surprise you.
The Bible speaks positively about certain kinds of kissing.
Romans 16:16 says:
"Greet one another with an holy kiss." (KJV)
In the original Greek, the expression is:
φιλήματι ἁγίῳ — philēmati hagiō
Literally, "with a holy kiss."
The word philēma means a kiss, while hagiō describes something holy or set apart.
Paul was referring to an appropriate expression of greeting and fellowship among believers in the cultural setting of the early church.
This was not permission for romantic intimacy without boundaries.
But it does establish something important.
A kiss is not inherently sinful simply because it is a kiss.
Scripture recognizes that physical expressions of affection can exist without sexual immorality.
We also see kisses expressing family affection, reconciliation, and friendship.
When the prodigal son returned home, broken by his rebellion and expecting rejection, his father ran toward him.
Luke 15:20 tells us that the father embraced him and kissed him.
The Greek verb used there is:
κατεφίλησεν — katephilēsen
It conveys an affectionate kiss, and the verb can express fervent or repeated kissing.
Picture that scene.
A son who had wasted his inheritance.
A son who had brought shame upon his family.
A son rehearsing an apology because he no longer believed he deserved to be called a son.
And a father who did not wait for him to finish proving his worth.
He ran.
He embraced him.
He kissed him.
Before the robe.
Before the ring.
Before the celebration.
There was the embrace of a father who loved his returning child.
That kiss was not sinful.
It was a beautiful expression of mercy.
But now we must make an important distinction.
The fact that Scripture approves of some kisses does not automatically mean every romantic kiss is appropriate.
Context matters.
Intent matters.
And the condition of the heart matters.
That brings us to the passage many people would rather avoid.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:27–28:
"Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." (KJV)
The Greek phrase translated "to lust after her" includes:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn
Here, Jesus is confronting the deliberate cultivation of lustful desire.
The Greek verb epithymeō can refer to desire or longing; context determines whether that desire is good or sinful.
In Matthew 5, Jesus is addressing lust in the context of the commandment against adultery.
He is not declaring that every experience of attraction is adultery.
He is exposing the danger of a heart that intentionally turns another person into an object of sinful desire.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because the issue is not merely whether your lips touched someone else's lips.
The issue is what you were choosing to nurture in your heart.
Were you expressing genuine affection with self-control?
Or were you deliberately awakening desires you had no intention of governing?
Were you honoring another person as someone made in the image of God?
Or were you using that person's body to satisfy something inside yourself?
Were you moving toward a relationship characterized by love, patience, and holiness?
Or were you searching for the closest possible experience to sexual intimacy while still claiming technical innocence?
Those questions cannot be answered by measuring the duration of a kiss.
A two-second kiss can be manipulative.
A longer kiss may be affectionate without being intended as a step toward sexual activity, though prolonged romantic intimacy can also become a powerful temptation.
The moral significance is not determined by a stopwatch.
And yet, neither can we pretend that physical affection has no effect on our desires.
THIS IS WHERE MANY CHRISTIANS CONFUSE WISDOM WITH COMMANDMENT.
Some believers choose not to kiss until marriage.
That can be a beautiful, thoughtful, God-honoring conviction.
They recognize their vulnerabilities. They want to protect their relationship. They believe abstaining from romantic kissing will help them practice self-control.
There is nothing wrong with that decision.
In fact, for some couples, it may be exceptionally wise.
But there is a difference between saying:
"We have prayerfully decided not to kiss before marriage."
And declaring:
"God says everyone who kisses before marriage is sinning."
The first is a personal boundary.
The second claims biblical authority.
And whenever we claim biblical authority, we must be able to demonstrate it from Scripture.
Jesus confronted religious leaders who elevated human traditions to the level of divine obligation.
In Mark 7:8, He said:
"For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men..." (KJV)
Now, this passage is not specifically about dating or kissing.
Its immediate context concerns religious traditions and ceremonial practices.
But it reveals a principle we must take seriously: human traditions must never be confused with God's commandments.
We must not forbid in God's name what God has not forbidden.
And we must not permit what God has actually condemned.
Both errors distort discipleship.
One can burden consciences with rules God never established.
The other can harden consciences against commands God has clearly given.
Christian maturity requires something more demanding than either extreme.
It requires discernment.
Romans 14 also helps us understand the importance of conscience in matters where believers may differ.
Paul was discussing disputed practices such as food and the observance of certain days, not romantic relationships.
Nevertheless, his teaching reminds us not to treat every personal conviction as a universal rule.
Romans 14:23 concludes:
"...for whatsoever is not of faith is sin." (KJV)
In context, Paul warns against acting contrary to one's conviction before God.
So if you sincerely believe a particular kind of physical affection would violate your conscience, do not force yourself to participate.
And if your boyfriend or girlfriend has established a boundary, love does not pressure them to abandon it.
Love respects conscience.
Love does not manipulate.
Love does not say, "If you really loved me, you would."
Love does not use Bible verses as weapons to demand physical access to another person's body.
A person who cannot respect your boundaries is not demonstrating biblical love by trying to cross them.
Read that again.
Because someone needs to hear it before making another excuse for a relationship that keeps wounding their conscience.
But there is another side to this conversation.
Some people have been taught to fear their own humanity.
They have been made to feel dirty for experiencing attraction.
They have been told that wanting to hold someone's hand, embrace someone they love, or share a simple kiss means their heart is already corrupt.
And slowly, their understanding of holiness becomes tangled with shame.
They begin to believe that God is disgusted by the very capacity for affection that He created.
But attraction itself is not automatically sin.
Desire is not always lust.
Affection is not always impurity.
And holiness is not the destruction of every human feeling.
Holiness is the surrender of our whole lives—including our desires—to the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
THE SONG OF SOLOMON REVEALS SOMETHING WE OFTEN FORGET.
The Song of Songs opens with a striking expression of romantic longing.
Song of Solomon 1:2 says:
"Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine." (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishshaqeni minneshiqot pihu
"Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth."
The Hebrew word neshiqot means "kisses."
The language is affectionate, poetic, and unmistakably romantic.
Scripture does not portray romantic affection itself as something filthy.
But we must be careful.
The Song of Songs is love poetry, and interpreters differ on the precise relationship and marital setting of particular scenes.
Therefore, this verse should not be used as a blanket permission slip for every kind of premarital physical intimacy.
What it does show is that romantic affection, rightly ordered, has a place within God's good design.
And that is important.
Because biblical purity is not the belief that the human body is evil.
God created the body.
God created marriage.
God created human beings with the capacity for affection and intimacy.
Genesis 1:31 says that God saw everything He had made, and it was very good.
Sin did not originate because human beings had bodies.
Sin entered through rebellion against God.
And redemption does not require us to hate our bodies.
It calls us to glorify God with them.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 that believers belong to God and are to glorify Him in their bodies.
The immediate context concerns sexual immorality and the believer's union with Christ.
The principle is profound.
Your body is not morally irrelevant.
What you do with it matters.
Not because your body is shameful.
But because it belongs to the Lord.
SO WHEN DOES KISSING BECOME SINFUL?
Here is where we must resist the temptation to give a simplistic answer.
Scripture does not provide a universal rule declaring every premarital romantic kiss sinful.
But Scripture does clearly condemn sexual immorality, lust, exploitation, deceit, and the deliberate pursuit of temptation.
First Thessalonians 4:3–5 says:
"For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication:
That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;
Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God:" (KJV)
The Greek word translated "fornication" is:
πορνείας — porneias
It refers to sexual immorality.
The passage calls believers to holiness and self-control rather than lustful passion.

Christians have differed on certain questions of how biblical sexual ethics apply to specific behaviors, but historic Christian teaching has consistently understood sexual intercourse as belonging within marriage.
A kiss is not automatically equivalent to sexual intercourse.
Nor does every romantic kiss automatically constitute porneia.
Yet kissing can become part of behavior that violates God's call to purity.
If a kiss is deliberately used to stimulate and escalate sexual activity that belongs within marriage, the couple cannot dismiss the moral concern merely because intercourse has not occurred.
If someone kisses another person without consent, that is not loving affection.
If someone uses kissing to manipulate, exploit, betray, or violate an existing commitment, the problem is not difficult to identify.
And if kissing repeatedly leads a couple into actions they believe dishonor God, wisdom calls them to reconsider their boundaries.
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 6:18:
"Flee fornication." (KJV)
Notice that word.
Flee.
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can stand before it becomes dangerous.
Not repeatedly invite temptation and then act surprised when self-control becomes difficult.
Flee.
But fleeing sexual immorality is not the same as declaring every form of romantic affection immoral.
That distinction matters because we are called to obey what Scripture actually teaches.
Not less.
Not more.
AND PERHAPS THE MOST REVEALING QUESTION ISN'T "CAN WE KISS?"
Perhaps it is:
"What happens to our relationship with God when we do?"
Does your physical affection remain consistent with mutual respect and self-control?
Can you stop without resentment?
Can you accept "no" without making the other person feel guilty?
Can you enjoy one another's company without continually pushing toward greater physical intimacy?
Can you pray together honestly, without using prayer as a way to excuse what your conscience is warning you about?
Can you speak openly about boundaries without one person becoming defensive, demanding, or controlling?
And when you disagree, can you honor the more cautious boundary rather than pressuring someone to surrender it?
These are not infallible tests of whether a particular kiss is sinful.
But they are meaningful questions for discerning whether a relationship is developing in wisdom, respect, and holiness.
Because Christian love is not simply about how strongly you feel.
It is also about how faithfully you act.
First Corinthians 13:4–5 reminds us that love is patient, kind, and not self-seeking.
Love does not treat another person's convictions as obstacles to overcome.
Love does not demand physical affection as proof of commitment.
And love does not need to cross a boundary to establish its sincerity.
Someone who truly loves you should care about your spiritual well-being even when that requires personal restraint.
BUT WHAT ABOUT THE PEOPLE WHO HAVE ALREADY GONE TOO FAR?
Maybe this article has stopped being theoretical for you.
Maybe you remember a relationship.
A night.
A decision.
A moment when you knew your conscience was troubled, but you kept going anyway.
Maybe the kiss became something more.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you would never cross.
And perhaps you have carried that memory for years.
You still worship.
You still pray.
You still read Scripture.
But somewhere inside, a quiet accusation follows you.
You ruined your purity.
You disappointed God.
You can never be the same again.
Listen carefully.
If you have sinned, Scripture does not invite you to pretend that nothing happened.
But neither does it tell you that your failure is more powerful than the grace of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not a message for people who have never fallen.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
All unrighteousness.
Not merely the sins that are socially acceptable.
Not merely the mistakes nobody discovered.
Not merely the failures that are easy to admit in church.
All.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
The Greek word commonly translated "repent" in the New Testament is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It refers to repentance, involving a change of mind and direction.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed after being caught.
It means turning from sin toward God.
It means refusing to make peace with what Christ calls us to leave behind.
It means receiving His mercy and learning to walk in obedience.
But repentance is not the purchase price of forgiveness.
Jesus Christ has accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
Through His death and resurrection, sinners are offered reconciliation with God.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not something we earn through our works.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus..." (KJV)
Think about that.
The enemy would love for your past to become your permanent identity.
But the Gospel announces something greater.
Your failure may be part of your story.
It does not have to be the final word.
And if you were pressured, coerced, or violated, do not confuse another person's wrongdoing against you with your own moral guilt.
You are not responsible for someone else's decision to disregard your consent.
God's grace is not an excuse for sin.
But God's grace is also not too weak to restore the repentant sinner.
This is why our message has always been:
Not because Jesus pretends sin is harmless.
Not because He changes His standards to accommodate our desires.
But because He forgives, restores, sanctifies, and transforms those who come to Him in faith.
The cross does not make holiness irrelevant.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the extraordinary mercy of God.
NOW LET ME SPEAK TO THE COUPLE WHO TRULY WANTS TO HONOR JESUS.
You do not need to prove your love by kissing.
And you do not need to prove your holiness by condemning every couple who chooses differently.
You need something deeper.
A relationship where Christ is not merely mentioned but obeyed.
Where boundaries are discussed before temptation becomes overwhelming.
Where affection is freely given, never demanded.
Where marriage is not treated as a magical solution to every struggle with lust.
Where you can confess weakness without being humiliated.
Where you can say, "We need to slow down," and hear, "I respect that."
Where you are more concerned about helping each other become faithful disciples of Jesus than about extracting every possible experience from the dating season.
If you choose to save your first kiss for your wedding day, do it joyfully and sincerely before God.
If you believe modest romantic kissing before marriage can be consistent with biblical holiness, do not use that conviction to dismiss the warnings Scripture gives about lust and sexual temptation.
And if you discover that kissing is repeatedly leading you into sinful behavior, have the humility to establish firmer boundaries.
You are not weak because you recognize your limits.
You are wise when you respond to them.
Second Timothy 2:22 says:
"Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart." (KJV)
Notice that Paul does not merely tell Timothy what to run away from.
He also tells him what to pursue.
Righteousness.
Faith.
Love.
Peace.
A pure heart.
Christian holiness is not merely the absence of forbidden actions.
It is the presence of a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
And that brings us to the truth underneath this entire debate.
YOU CAN AVOID EVERY KISS BEFORE MARRIAGE AND STILL HAVE A HEART FAR FROM GOD.
You can follow the strictest dating rules and still be proud, dishonest, cruel, or unloving.
You can boast about saving your first kiss while secretly looking down on believers whose convictions differ from yours.
And you can also claim freedom in Christ while knowingly feeding lust and refusing correction.
Neither legalism nor carelessness is the answer.
Jesus is.
He calls us away from self-righteousness.
He calls us away from sexual immorality.
He calls us away from the exhausting attempt to justify ourselves through perfect rule-keeping.
And He calls us into a life of grace-fueled obedience.
Not obedience that earns His love.
Obedience that grows from receiving it.
So before you ask whether God allows you to kiss someone before marriage, ask yourself something more searching.
Am I genuinely trying to honor Jesus, or am I simply trying to get permission for what I already want?
That question may expose something uncomfortable.
But sometimes the most loving thing God's Word can do is expose what we have been hiding.
And sometimes the most freeing thing it can do is remove a burden He never commanded us to carry.
Both require humility.
Both require surrender.
Both require us to stop making ourselves the final authority.
THE ANSWER IS NOT A LOOPHOLE. IT IS A LORD.
No, the Bible does not explicitly say that every kiss before marriage is a sin.
Yes, romantic kissing can become sinful when it involves lust, exploitation, unfaithfulness, or conduct contrary to God's commands.
And yes, choosing not to kiss before marriage can be a wise and honorable personal conviction without becoming a command imposed upon every Christian.
We must distinguish between what Scripture commands, what wisdom recommends, and what conscience may require of a particular believer.
But the greatest question is not simply what you are permitted to do.
It is whom you are becoming as you follow Christ.
Because one day, the question will not be whether you managed to win an argument about kissing.
What matters eternally is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
And belonging to Him changes the way you approach everything.
Your relationships.
Your desires.
Your boundaries.
Your forgiveness.
Your future.
Even the way you love.
If this article has confronted something in your heart, don't rush past it.
Maybe you have been carrying unnecessary guilt.
Maybe you have been excusing genuine sin.
Maybe you have pressured someone you claimed to love.
Maybe you have been judging others by a personal standard that Scripture never made universal.
Or maybe you are simply tired of trying to follow Jesus while being pulled between confusing voices.
Bring that honestly before the Lord.
You can also share a sincere question or testimony. You do not need to reveal private details or confess intimate experiences publicly to prove your faith.
Your honesty may help another believer realize they are not alone in their struggle.
Not merely to generate attention, but because a biblical conversation about love, purity, conscience, and grace may reach someone who would never think to ask these questions in church.
Because this ministry is not merely about winning debates.
It is about helping people know Jesus Christ, understand His Word, turn from sin, receive His grace, and grow in faithful obedience.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture more deeply, there is another meaningful way to stand with this mission.
But we want to be clear about something important.
God is not selling His favor.
And your financial circumstances do not determine how deeply He loves you.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not a promise that giving money will purchase blessings.
But joyful partnership in work you believe is worth supporting.
These resources and products are not what make the Gospel powerful.
Jesus Christ is.
But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, encourage meaningful conversations, and help support the continued work of this ministry.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for truth, whether they can contribute financially or not.
You can still help.
Pray for this ministry.
Read and apply the Scriptures.
And keep pointing people toward Jesus rather than toward personalities, platforms, or popularity.
Because our deepest desire is not simply to build an audience.
It is to see people transformed by the Gospel.
To see confused believers become grounded in Scripture.
To see wounded hearts discover the mercy of Christ.
To see young couples choose love that is patient, honorable, and self-controlled.
To see those trapped in shame understand that repentance and restoration are possible.
And to see those who have been living carelessly discover that grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The world does not need another generation that mistakes shame for holiness.
Neither does it need a generation that mistakes freedom for permission to sin.
It needs believers who know the difference between God's commands and human traditions.
Believers who are tender toward the wounded and uncompromising about truth.
Believers who can say, "The Bible does not explicitly forbid that," without abandoning wisdom.
And believers who can say, "This may be permissible," while still asking, "But will it help me honor Christ?"
Because at the end of everything, purity is not a trophy awarded to people with spotless romantic histories.
It is part of a life being made holy by the grace and power of God.
And the person who has never kissed anyone needs Jesus just as desperately as the person who has crossed every boundary and now longs to come home.
One cannot earn salvation through restraint.
The other is not beyond redemption because of failure.
Both must come to the same cross.
Both must depend upon the same Savior.
Both are invited to walk in the same transforming grace.
So whether your lips have never touched another person's, or your past contains memories you wish you could erase, hear this final truth:
Jesus is not asking you to build your identity around a kiss. He is calling you to surrender your entire life to Him.
And when your heart truly belongs to Christ, even the way you love another person begins to change.
Your past may remember the moment you fell, but in Christ, your future does not have to end where your failure began.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS TURNED WATER INTO WINE… SO WHY DOES THE BIBLE WARN US ABOUT DRINKING?
paragraphs: JESUS TURNED WATER INTO WINE… SO WHY DOES THE BIBLE WARN US ABOUT DRINKING?
The uncomfortable truth about alcohol, Christian freedom, hidden addictions, and the one question every believer must answer before taking another sip.
What if the greatest danger isn't the alcohol in your glass… but the thing you've slowly allowed to take control of your heart?
Somewhere tonight, a Christian is holding a glass of wine over dinner, grateful for the food, the company, and the goodness of God.
Somewhere else, another Christian is holding a bottle with trembling hands, promising himself this will be the last time.
And somewhere in between, a young believer is watching both of them, wondering why people who follow the same Jesus can reach such different conclusions about the same drink.
One says, "Jesus turned water into wine."
Another says, "The Bible warns us to stay sober."
One calls it Christian freedom.
Another calls it a dangerous compromise.
And both open their Bibles, convinced that Scripture supports their position.
But here's the question that ought to make every one of us uncomfortable:
Are we opening the Bible because we genuinely want to know what God says… or because we're hoping God will agree with what we've already decided to do?
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing we can do with Scripture is not reject it.
It's quote just enough of it to protect something we're unwilling to surrender.
And this conversation is far bigger than whether a Christian may drink a glass of wine.
It's about freedom.
Self-control.
Love.
Conscience.
The people watching our lives.
And the quiet difference between something being permissible and something being wise.
So before anyone rushes to defend their favorite position, we need to go somewhere uncomfortable.
We need to go to a wedding.
A wedding where Jesus Himself was present.
And where the wine ran out.
John 2:1–11 tells us that Jesus attended a wedding in Cana of Galilee with His mother and disciples.
During the celebration, a problem arose.
There was no more wine.
In that culture, a wedding feast was an important communal celebration. Running out of wine could bring serious embarrassment to the hosts.
Mary brought the situation to Jesus.
And Jesus instructed the servants to fill six stone water jars with water.
They obeyed.
When the liquid was drawn out and presented to the master of the feast, something extraordinary had happened.
The water had become wine.
Not ordinary water pretending to be wine.
Not merely a religious symbol that everyone misunderstood.
Wine.

The Greek word used in John 2:3 is οἶνος (oinos), the ordinary Greek term for wine. The word itself does not specify the precise alcoholic strength, but nothing in John's account requires us to reinterpret the miracle as the production of grape juice.
The master of the feast even remarked that the better wine had been kept until that moment.
And John tells us something profoundly important about the miracle.
"This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." (John 2:11, KJV)
Read that again.
The miracle was not primarily about alcohol.
It was about glory.
Jesus was revealing who He was.
The One who turned water into wine was showing His divine authority, His generosity, and the arrival of something greater than the old ceremonial order could provide.
And the disciples believed in Him.
That's where the story is pointing.
Not toward the bottle.
Toward the Savior.
But we must be careful here.
If Jesus provided wine at a wedding, we cannot honestly claim that Scripture universally forbids every Christian from consuming any amount of alcohol.
That conclusion would go beyond what the biblical text says.

Yet it would be equally careless to take this miracle and announce that Jesus therefore approves of every drinking habit, every social drinking environment, or every personal justification for alcohol.
John 2 does not teach that.
A miracle revealing Christ's glory is not a blank check for human indulgence.
And this is where the conversation becomes personal.
Because some people are not asking whether they may drink.
They're asking whether they can keep drinking without having to examine why.
There is a difference.
A man can hold a glass without being enslaved to it.
Another man can hold the same glass while quietly losing a battle nobody knows he's fighting.
The liquid may be the same.
The spiritual condition may be completely different.
And God sees what people around the table cannot.
Now listen to the apostle Paul.
"And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit." (Ephesians 5:18, KJV)
In the Greek text, the command begins:
καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ
Kai mē methyskesthe oinō.
"And do not get drunk with wine."
The verb μεθύσκεσθε (methyskesthe) concerns becoming intoxicated or drunk.
Paul's command is unmistakable.
Drunkenness is not a harmless Christian liberty.
It is something believers are commanded to avoid.
But notice what follows.
ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι
Alla plērousthe en pneumati.
"But be filled with the Spirit."
Paul places these commands in contrast.
One describes intoxication that undermines self-control.
The other calls believers to a life continually shaped by the Holy Spirit.
The command to be filled is expressed in a form that conveys ongoing Christian responsibility.
Paul is not merely telling Christians to avoid embarrassing behavior at parties.
He is calling them to a different way of living.
A life shaped by worship, gratitude, wisdom, and obedience.
And that raises a question worth asking in private.
When life becomes unbearable, what do you instinctively reach for?
When your marriage feels cold…
When your bills keep coming…
When your prayers seem unanswered…
When the grief returns after everyone else has gone home…
What do you reach for?
Some reach for prayer.
Some reach for Scripture.
Some call someone they trust.
Some reach for a drink.
And not every person who drinks is trying to escape reality. Scripture does not give us permission to assume that.
But if alcohol has become the thing you believe you cannot face life without, that deserves serious attention.
Because there is a difference between enjoying something and depending on it.
There is a difference between having freedom and needing to prove you have freedom.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:12:

Paul is not declaring every imaginable behavior morally acceptable. He is answering claims about freedom and insisting that what is permissible must still be evaluated by what is beneficial and what enslaves.
That last phrase should stay with us.
"I will not be brought under the power of any."
Not even something I can defend.
Not even something other Christians enjoy responsibly.
Not even something that seems harmless to everyone else.
Because Christian freedom was never meant to become another form of bondage.
And perhaps that's where this article has already begun touching a nerve.
You know the difference between wanting something and needing it.
You know when the second glass is no longer about taste.
You know when you start concealing how much you've consumed.
You know when your family notices a change before you admit one exists.
You know when the promise to stop tomorrow has become something you said yesterday.
And if any of that describes you, please hear this carefully.
You are not beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
But neither should you rename bondage as freedom simply because the Bible does not forbid every use of alcohol.
Christ does not call us to defend the chains He came to break.
He calls us to walk in truth.
And truth is sometimes painful before it becomes liberating.
The Bible itself refuses to give us a simplistic answer.
Psalm 104:14–15 describes God providing food and wine that gladdens the human heart.
Ecclesiastes 9:7 speaks of enjoying wine with a merry heart in the context of receiving life's gifts.
At the same time, Proverbs 20:1 warns:
"Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise." (KJV)
Proverbs 23:29–35 offers a vivid description of the misery, impaired perception, and repeated craving associated with excessive drinking.
And 1 Timothy 5:23 records Paul's advice to Timothy:
"Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities." (KJV)
Notice the precision.
"A little wine."
Paul was addressing Timothy's particular physical condition, not issuing a universal command that Christians must drink alcohol.
Yet the passage also makes it difficult to argue that every use of wine is inherently sinful.
Scripture acknowledges wine as something that can be received as a gift.
Scripture also warns that wine can become an instrument of foolishness, destruction, and enslavement.
Those truths are not contradictions.
They are part of the Bible's morally serious treatment of human life.
The same substance can be approached under very different circumstances, motives, and consequences.
And that is why the real question cannot stop at:
"Am I allowed?"
We must also ask:
"Is this wise?"
"Is this loving?"
"Is this helping me live faithfully before God?"
"Can I honestly exercise self-control?"
"And what happens to the people around me when I make this choice?"
Because the Bible does not merely call Christians to avoid crossing the line into obvious sin.
It calls us to walk in love.
And love changes the question.
Imagine a family dinner.
A Christian man sits at the table with a glass of wine.
He is not drunk.
He is not behaving recklessly.
He believes he has biblical freedom to drink moderately.
Across from him sits his younger brother.
Three months sober.
Three months since the shaking hands, the ruined relationships, the desperate prayers, and the decision to seek help.
The younger brother watches the glass.
He says nothing.
But the older brother knows his history.
Now the question is no longer merely whether the older brother has permission to drink.
The question is whether exercising that permission, in that moment, is an act of love.
Listen to Romans 14:21:
"It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak." (KJV)
The Greek begins:
καλὸν τὸ μὴ φαγεῖν κρέα μηδὲ πιεῖν οἶνον
Kalon to mē phagein krea mēde piein oinon.
"It is good not to eat meat or drink wine…"
The verse continues by connecting such restraint to the spiritual welfare of another person.
The context matters.
Romans 14 addresses disputes among believers about food, special days, conscience, and conduct before the Lord.
Paul does not teach that every objection raised by another person automatically creates a universal prohibition.
He is addressing the serious danger of using personal freedom in a way that contributes to another believer's spiritual stumbling.
His principle is not that Christians must surrender to every criticism.
His principle is that love must govern liberty.
And that is an extraordinary thing.
Because in the kingdom of God, maturity is not measured only by what you know you may do.
Sometimes maturity is revealed by what you are willing not to do.
Not because you're afraid.
Not because you're trying to earn salvation.
Not because abstinence automatically makes you holier than someone else.
But because another person's well-being matters more than proving a point.
Imagine the older brother quietly setting the glass aside.
No speech.
No self-congratulation.
No dramatic announcement.
Just love.
The younger brother may never even know why he did it.
But heaven sees the heart.
And perhaps that is one of the most beautiful forms of Christian freedom.
The freedom to say no.
Even when you could say yes.
Now we need to address something that can be deeply uncomfortable for both sides of this debate.
Some Christians have turned abstinence into a measure of salvation.
Others have turned moderation into a badge of spiritual sophistication.
Both can become forms of pride.
The Christian who abstains must not look down on a believer who drinks responsibly within biblical boundaries.
And the Christian who drinks must not ridicule the believer who abstains out of conscience, wisdom, personal history, or concern for others.
Romans 14:3 warns against despising and judging one another over disputed matters.
Romans 14:23 also teaches that acting against one's conscience is spiritually serious.
That means a believer who sincerely believes drinking would violate their conscience should not be pressured into it.
And a believer who chooses lifelong abstinence does not need to apologize for that decision.
There is nothing immature about refusing something that could become dangerous.
There is nothing legalistic about voluntarily giving up a liberty for the sake of love.
But we must also be honest enough not to call something a universal divine command when Scripture has not made it one.
God's Word deserves better than our exaggerations.
Biblical conviction must be anchored in what God has actually said, not merely in what we wish He had said.
And here is another detail that matters.
The Bible does record circumstances in which abstinence was specifically required or voluntarily embraced.
Priests were prohibited from drinking wine or strong drink when entering the tabernacle to perform their sacred duties (Leviticus 10:9).
Those under a Nazirite vow abstained from wine and other products of the grapevine during the period of their consecration (Numbers 6:1–4).
John the Baptist was instructed not to drink wine or strong drink (Luke 1:15).
These passages demonstrate that abstinence can have a meaningful place in devotion and obedience.
But they do not establish a universal command requiring every Christian to abstain throughout life.
Likewise, the fact that Jesus drank wine does not establish an obligation for Christians to drink.
Jesus was even accused by His critics of being "a winebibber" (Luke 7:34, KJV), but the accusation came from hostile observers and must not be treated as evidence of drunkenness.
Jesus was without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
The Bible's testimony is clear.
The Son of God did not need intoxication to experience joy.
He did not need a bottle to endure sorrow.
And He did not need human approval to remain faithful to His Father.
Which brings us to the question beneath all the other questions.
What is shaping your life more deeply: your appetite, your freedom, your fear of other people's opinions… or Jesus Christ?
Because you can abstain from every drop of alcohol and still have a heart filled with pride.
You can avoid every party and still be addicted to approval.
You can condemn drunkenness while secretly nurturing greed, bitterness, or lust.
And you can defend moderate drinking with accurate Bible verses while refusing to acknowledge that your own drinking has become destructive.
The Gospel confronts all of us.
Not merely the people whose sins are visible.
All of us.
Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
And Romans 5:8 tells us that God demonstrated His love toward us in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is the heart of Christianity.
Not a competition between drinkers and abstainers.
Not an argument about who is morally superior.
But the astonishing announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
People who have made terrible choices.
People who have hidden their pain.
People who have hurt their families.
People who have judged others harshly.
People who have promised to change and failed.
People who look respectable on Sunday while fighting battles no one sees.
People like us.
And this is where the story becomes more than a debate.
Because perhaps someone reading this remembers the night alcohol took something from them.
A relationship.
A job.
A friendship.
A sense of safety.
Maybe you remember a parent coming home drunk.
The sound of a door slamming.
The sudden silence at the dinner table.
The way everyone learned to read the room before saying anything.
Maybe you grew up promising yourself that you would never become the person who frightened you.
And now, years later, you're afraid of what you see happening in your own life.
Or perhaps you have never struggled with alcohol at all.
But you have loved someone who did.
You have watched a person you care about become someone you barely recognize.
You have heard apologies that sounded sincere.
You have wanted to believe every promise.
And you have prayed prayers that seemed to disappear into the ceiling.
If that is your story, the Bible does not require you to pretend the damage was small.
It does not require you to call addiction harmless.
It does not require you to remain in an unsafe situation.
And it does not require you to confuse forgiveness with the immediate restoration of trust.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical.
Repentance matters.
Accountability matters.
Safety matters.
And genuine change is ordinarily demonstrated over time.
Jesus offers grace, but grace does not demand that we deny reality.
For someone struggling with alcohol dependence, seeking medical treatment, professional counseling, and trustworthy Christian support can be a courageous part of pursuing recovery.
If a person is physically dependent on alcohol, suddenly stopping can cause dangerous withdrawal and may require medical supervision.
Prayer and appropriate treatment are not enemies.
God's people should never shame someone for seeking help.
And nobody should have to fight a life-threatening addiction alone.
Now, to the believer who enjoys an occasional drink without drunkenness or dependence, this article is not accusing you of a sin Scripture has not established.
But it is asking you to remain watchful.
Because wisdom never says, "I could never fall."
Wisdom says, "Lord, keep my heart."
First Corinthians 10:12 warns those who think they stand to take heed lest they fall.
And to the believer who has chosen total abstinence, this article is not telling you to loosen your convictions.
There may be excellent reasons to remain abstinent for the rest of your life.
Your history may make that wise.
Your conscience may require it.
Your responsibilities may call for it.
Your love for someone vulnerable may motivate it.
Or you may simply conclude that, for you, the potential risks outweigh any benefit.
That is a legitimate decision.
Indeed, abstinence is often the wiser choice when there is a history of addiction, impaired self-control, medical risk, a vulnerable person to protect, or a serious concern about spiritual stumbling.
And there is no biblical requirement that you take a drink to demonstrate your freedom in Christ.
But the greater issue is not whether your glass is full or empty.
The greater issue is whether your life is surrendered.
Because the Christian life is not merely about discovering the outer boundaries of what we can get away with.
It is about becoming more like Jesus.
And Jesus teaches us that love is not self-centered.
It gives.
It serves.
It sacrifices.
It considers the weak.
It protects the vulnerable.
It refuses to turn personal liberty into an excuse for harming others.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:31:
Whatever you do.
That includes drinking.
That includes abstaining.
That includes how you speak about Christians who make a different decision.
That includes what you do when someone confesses that alcohol is destroying their life.
That includes whether you respond with compassion or condemnation.
And that includes whether you are willing to surrender a preference when love requires it.
The question is not simply, "Can I drink this?"
It is, "Can I honestly do this to the glory of God?"
Sometimes the answer may be yes.
Sometimes the answer must be no.
And sometimes the wisest answer is, "Even if I could, I won't."
Not because the glass itself has magical power.
But because love has become more important than liberty.
And now consider one final contrast.
At Cana, Jesus turned water into wine.
At Calvary, Jesus poured out His own blood.
The first sign revealed His glory and led His disciples to believe.
The cross revealed the immeasurable cost of our redemption.
And at the Last Supper, Jesus spoke of the cup in connection with the new covenant in His blood (Luke 22:20).
Do not miss the difference.
The Gospel is not the story of a Savior who came merely to make our celebrations more enjoyable.
It is the story of a Savior who entered our broken world, bore our sins, died in our place, and rose again.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He came to bring forgiveness and new life.
He came to transform hearts that human effort alone could never make new.
And that is why the answer to this debate cannot end with a rule about beverages.
It must lead us to the Lordship of Christ.
Because if Jesus is Lord, nothing in our lives is beyond His authority.
Not our habits.
Not our desires.
Not our traditions.
Not our arguments.
Not our private compromises.
Not even the freedoms we have a legitimate right to exercise.
Everything belongs before Him.
And maybe the most important thing you can do after reading this is not announce your position on alcohol.
Maybe it is to get alone with God and ask:
"Lord, is there anything in my life that I keep defending because I'm afraid of what surrender would cost me?"
Then be quiet long enough to examine your heart in the light of Scripture.
You may discover that alcohol is not your struggle.
You may discover that pride is.
Or resentment.
Or fear.
Or the desperate need to control everything.
But perhaps you will discover that the drinking you have repeatedly minimized is beginning to control you.
If so, do not hide behind John 2.
And do not run away from Jesus because of Ephesians 5.
Run toward Him.
Confess what is true.
Ask for help.
Take the next faithful step.
Repentance is not pretending you were never wrong.
It is turning toward the God whose mercy is greater than your sin.
First John 1:9 promises that God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess their sins and cleanse them from unrighteousness.
And Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is not permission to continue in sin without concern.
It is the assurance that those who belong to Christ do not have to live forever under the sentence of their past.
You can stop hiding.
You can tell the truth.
You can begin again.
And if the road to recovery is long, you do not have to interpret every difficult day as proof that God has abandoned you.
Keep seeking Him.
Keep receiving appropriate help.
Keep walking in the light.
And remember that your identity is not ultimately determined by your worst night.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to win religious arguments while people silently fall apart.
Not to manufacture guilt or pressure people into pretending they are stronger than they are.
But to keep pointing wounded, searching, struggling people back to the truth of God's Word and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
If this article has challenged something in you, I would genuinely love to hear your perspective.

And if God has helped you overcome alcohol dependence, or if choosing abstinence has protected your life or family, consider sharing a testimony you feel safe making public. Your experience may encourage someone who has begun to lose hope.
Please don't turn the comments into a battlefield between Christians who drink moderately and Christians who abstain.
Let this be a place where Scripture is respected, truth is spoken, and people are treated with compassion.
Because a person asking for help is more important than winning an argument.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, perhaps this is worth sharing with them.
Because discipleship is not something we outgrow.
We all need to keep learning, repenting, and growing in Christ.
These resources are intended to help make biblical learning and spiritual encouragement more accessible, including to those who cannot afford paid materials.
But an important distinction deserves to be made.
God is not glorified by financial pressure disguised as devotion.
He is honored by sincere obedience, generous hearts, and faithful stewardship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, encourage someone, and make use of the free resources.
Every thoughtful share can help the message reach someone new.
Every respectful conversation can help someone examine Scripture more carefully.
And every voluntary contribution can help sustain the work of producing and distributing biblical resources.
Our hope is that people will not merely consume another Christian article.
We hope they will encounter biblical truth, turn toward Christ, and grow in a faith that changes how they live.
Because ultimately, this was never just about wine.
It was about what happens when Jesus becomes Lord over every part of our lives.
The glass we choose to lift.
The freedom we choose to surrender.
The person we choose to protect.
The truth we choose to confess.
The grace we choose to receive.
And the Savior we choose to follow.
So, does the Bible permit Christians to drink alcohol in moderation?
Yes. Scripture does not impose a universal prohibition on all moderate alcohol consumption.
Does the Bible condemn drunkenness?
Absolutely.
Can abstinence be the wiser, more loving, and more responsible choice?
Without question.

And for some people, particularly those recovering from alcohol dependence or unable to drink without losing control, abstinence is not merely a preference. It may be essential for their safety and recovery.
But the deepest question is not whether a Christian has a drink in hand.
It is whether that Christian is seeking to live under the gracious authority of Jesus Christ.
Because the Lord who turned water into wine is also the Lord who calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
He is worthy of more than our clever arguments.
He is worthy of our obedience.
Our honesty.
Our love.
Our freedom.
Our surrender.
And our whole lives.
One day, the question that matters most won't be whether you defended your glass successfully, but whether you surrendered your heart faithfully.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS WASN’T KNOCKING ON AN UNBELIEVER’S DOOR. HE WAS STANDING OUTSIDE HIS OWN CHURCH.
paragraphs: JESUS WASN’T KNOCKING ON AN UNBELIEVER’S DOOR. HE WAS STANDING OUTSIDE HIS OWN CHURCH.

The terrifying truth behind Revelation 3:20 that many Christians have never been told—and the breathtaking grace of a Savior who still knocks on the door of people who have learned to live without Him.
There is something deeply unsettling about a church filled with people singing about Jesus while Jesus Himself is standing outside.
Read that again.
Not outside a nightclub. Not outside a prison. Not outside the home of someone who has never opened a Bible.
Outside a church.
A congregation that knew His name. People who gathered for worship. People who probably believed they were doing just fine.
And Jesus was knocking.
We have heard Revelation 3:20 quoted so many times that its familiarity has almost robbed it of its power.
“Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.” — Revelation 3:20, KJV
For generations, this verse has appeared in evangelistic invitations, altar calls, sermons, and paintings depicting Jesus standing outside the door of the human heart.
And there is nothing inherently wrong with telling an unbeliever that Christ calls sinners to repentance and faith. The Gospel absolutely extends that invitation.
But something extraordinary happens when we return Revelation 3:20 to its original setting.
We discover that Jesus was not first speaking to people who had never heard of Him.
He was speaking to a church that had become dangerously comfortable without Him.
And suddenly, the verse becomes much more personal.
Because the most frightening spiritual condition is not always openly rejecting Jesus.
Sometimes it is becoming so accustomed to Christian activity that we no longer recognize how far our hearts have drifted from Christ Himself.
You can know the songs and still lose your wonder.
You can defend biblical truth and still resist its correction.
You can serve in ministry while secretly neglecting prayer.
You can be surrounded by Christian people and still feel spiritually empty.
You can speak passionately about the presence of God while privately living as though you no longer need Him.
And perhaps the most sobering possibility of all?
You can become so comfortable with that condition that you stop noticing anything is wrong.
That was the danger confronting Laodicea.
And it may be the warning some of us desperately need to hear today.
The book of Revelation begins with a vision of the risen and glorified Jesus Christ. In chapters 2 and 3, He addresses seven churches in the Roman province of Asia.
These are not imaginary congregations. They were real Christian communities facing real spiritual challenges.
To the church in Laodicea, Jesus introduces Himself as:
“These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of the creation of God.” — Revelation 3:14, KJV

That final expression does not mean Jesus was the first creature God made. The Greek word archē (ἀρχή) can refer to an origin, source, or beginning. In this context, it is understood by many interpreters as emphasizing Christ's relationship to creation as its source or ruler, consistent with the New Testament's wider testimony that all things were created through Him (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16–17).
The One speaking to Laodicea is no ordinary religious teacher.
He is the faithful and true Witness.
The One who sees what others cannot see.
And His diagnosis is devastating.

“I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.” — Revelation 3:15–16, KJV
Imagine hearing those words from Jesus.
Not from an angry critic.
Not from a disappointed pastor.
From the Lord of the Church.

We often hear lukewarm Christianity described as being halfway between passionate faith and outright unbelief. That interpretation captures the danger of spiritual compromise, but the imagery deserves careful attention.

Laodicea was a prosperous city in the Lycus Valley, near Hierapolis and Colossae. Hierapolis was associated with hot mineral springs, while Colossae was associated with refreshing water. Some scholars believe these regional water conditions illuminate Jesus' metaphor: hot water and cold water can both be useful, while unpleasant lukewarm water is fit for neither purpose.
The precise relationship between the local water supply and the metaphor remains debated, so we should not present that historical reconstruction as though Scripture explicitly explains it.
What the passage unmistakably condemns, however, is a self-satisfied spiritual condition that has become offensive to Christ.
And then Jesus reveals the illusion beneath it.
“Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.” — Revelation 3:17, KJV
There it is.
The sentence that should make every comfortable Christian examine their heart.
“I ... have need of nothing.”
Not necessarily spoken aloud.
Perhaps simply lived.
When prayer becomes an afterthought because we believe we can manage everything ourselves.
When repentance becomes rare because we have learned to justify almost anything.
When Scripture is opened only to prepare a message, defend an argument, or find a quotation for social media.
When worship becomes performance.
When ministry becomes reputation.
When financial stability quietly replaces dependence on God.
When our Christian identity remains visible, but our communion with Christ grows faint.
We may never say, “Jesus, I don't need You.”
Yet our habits can begin to communicate precisely that.
And the tragedy is that the Laodiceans apparently did not recognize their own poverty.
They thought they were rich.
Jesus said they were poor.
They thought they could see.
Jesus said they were blind.
They thought they were adequately clothed.
Jesus said they were naked.
There is a particular kind of spiritual danger that comes when our opinion of ourselves becomes more reassuring than the Word of God.
We begin measuring our relationship with Jesus by what other people can see.
Our church attendance.
Our religious vocabulary.
Our ministry involvement.
Our ability to quote Scripture.
Our reputation for being strong believers.
But Christ sees beyond all of it.
He sees the private life.
The neglected obedience.
The unforgiven offense we refuse to release.
The hidden compromise.
The pride dressed as discernment.
The prayerlessness disguised as busyness.
The wounded heart that has slowly replaced trust with resentment.
He sees the person beneath the Christian image.
And still, astonishingly, He speaks.
That is where this passage begins to reveal something even more beautiful than its warning.
Because Jesus does not simply expose Laodicea's condition and abandon the conversation.
He counsels them to receive from Him what they cannot provide for themselves.

“I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed ... and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.” — Revelation 3:18, KJV
The imagery would have carried particular force in a city known for prosperity and associated with textiles and medical activity.
But Jesus was not offering merchandise.
He was exposing the inadequacy of worldly resources to remedy spiritual poverty.
They needed true riches.
They needed covering for their shame.
They needed sight.
And all of it had to come from Him.
Do you see the mercy?
The One who exposes their poverty is also the One who offers what they lack.
The One who reveals their blindness is the One who can restore their sight.
The One who confronts their shame does not tell them to manufacture their own righteousness.
He calls them back to Himself.
That is the Gospel pattern.
We cannot purchase forgiveness with religious achievements.
We cannot heal our souls through outward success.
We cannot make ourselves righteous before God by becoming impressive enough.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ, who lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose again.
The One who calls us to repentance is the One through whom forgiveness and reconciliation with God are found.
And then comes a verse that changes the emotional atmosphere of the entire passage.
“As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.” — Revelation 3:19, KJV
As many as I love.
Not as many as I despise.
Not as many as I have decided are beyond recovery.
As many as I love.
The Greek text begins:
Ἐγὼ ὅσους ἐὰν φιλῶ, ἐλέγχω καὶ παιδεύω.
Egō hosous ean philō, elenchō kai paideuō.
A close translation is:
“Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline.”

The verb philō comes from phileō (φιλέω), a Greek verb expressing love or affection. The verb elenchō (ἐλέγχω) means to expose, convict, or reprove. Paideuō (παιδεύω) carries the sense of training or discipline.
This is not the language of a Savior who has stopped caring.
It is the language of loving correction.
The distinction matters.
Not every painful circumstance in a believer's life should be interpreted as direct punishment from God. Scripture itself rejects simplistic explanations of suffering.
But Revelation 3:19 makes clear that Christ's rebuke of Laodicea was not incompatible with His love.
It was an expression of it.
Sometimes the most merciful thing Jesus does is interrupt the illusion that everything is fine.
Sometimes His Word unsettles us because He refuses to leave us comfortable in something that is destroying our fellowship with Him.
Sometimes conviction is not the announcement that grace has disappeared.
It is a summons to return to the grace we have been neglecting.
And then we reach the famous verse.
The one printed on invitation cards.
The one quoted at evangelistic crusades.
The one many of us memorized as children.
“Behold, I stand at the door, and knock.”
But now we hear it differently.
Because we know whom Jesus is addressing.
A church.
A congregation that claimed to belong to Him.
A community that had become blind to its own spiritual need.
The original Greek of Revelation 3:20 reads:
Ἰδοὺ ἕστηκα ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν καὶ κρούω· ἐάν τις ἀκούσῃ τῆς φωνῆς μου καὶ ἀνοίξῃ τὴν θύραν, καὶ εἰσελεύσομαι πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ δειπνήσω μετ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὸς μετ’ ἐμοῦ.
A faithful translation is:
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with me.”
Notice the word ἕστηκα (hestēka).
It is a perfect-tense form of the verb meaning “to stand.” The wording portrays Jesus as standing at the door.
Then comes κρούω (krouō).
“I knock.”
The image is immediate.
Christ is standing at the door and knocking.

But we must be careful not to force more into the grammar than it actually says. The verse does not specify how long He has been standing there, and it does not describe a particular number of knocks.
The power is already in the picture Scripture gives us.
The risen Christ addresses a spiritually compromised church.
He confronts it.
He calls it to repentance.
And He offers restored fellowship.
Notice also the individual invitation within the corporate warning.
“If anyone hears my voice...”
The message is addressed to a church, but the response is personal.
A congregation may have grown complacent, yet each hearer is called to respond.
You cannot repent on behalf of someone else.
You cannot borrow another person's obedience.
You cannot substitute your family's Christian heritage for personal faith in Christ.
And you cannot assume that being surrounded by spiritual activity means your own heart is responding to His Word.
Jesus calls for a response.
Not merely admiration of the verse.
Not merely agreement that lukewarm Christianity is dangerous.
Repentance.
A turning away from self-sufficiency and sin.
A renewed dependence upon the Savior.
And what does He promise?
“I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.”
The Greek verb δειπνήσω (deipnēsō) means “I will dine” or “I will share a meal.”
In the ancient Mediterranean world, sharing a meal could express hospitality, friendship, welcome, and fellowship.
Jesus does not describe a brief, impersonal encounter.
He uses the intimate imagery of eating together.
The Lord who has just exposed the church's shame offers fellowship to the one who responds to His voice.
Think about that.
He could have ended the message with condemnation.
He could have left them staring at their spiritual poverty.
Instead, He offers communion.
And here is the part that can undo a heart that has been hiding for years.
Jesus already knows.
He knows what happened when nobody was watching.
He knows the promises you made and did not keep.
He knows how many times you said you would change.
He knows the bitterness you have carefully concealed beneath polite Christian language.
He knows how long it has been since you prayed with genuine openness.
He knows whether your service has become a substitute for intimacy with Him.
He knows your pride.
Your fear.
Your shame.
Your exhaustion.
He knows.
And His call to repentance still stands.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because obedience is optional.
Not because grace gives us permission to remain unchanged.
But because the mercy of Christ is greater than the illusion that we can save ourselves.
Perhaps you used to read your Bible with tears in your eyes.
Not because every page was easy to understand, but because you were hungry to know God.
Perhaps there was a season when prayer was not a duty you squeezed into your schedule.
It was where you went because you knew you could not carry life alone.
Perhaps you remember the first time the Gospel truly became personal.
When you realized that the cross was not merely a religious symbol.
That Jesus Christ had died for sinners.
That forgiveness was not something you could earn.
That the resurrection meant death did not have the final word.
That your past did not have to determine your future.
You remember the wonder.
And somewhere along the way, life became complicated.
You got hurt.
You became busy.
