To keep people from finding out?
Or to become clean before Him?
Because there is a kind of sorrow that hates the consequences of sin without truly hating the sin itself.
And there is godly sorrow that leads us to repentance.
The apostle Paul later wrote:
"For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death." (2 Corinthians 7:10, KJV)
Real repentance does not mean producing enough tears to persuade God.
It means turning toward Him in truth, acknowledging wrongdoing, and bearing fruit consistent with repentance.
It is not a performance.
It is not a public-relations strategy.
It is not a religious phrase used to escape accountability.
It is a turning of the heart toward the God whose mercy we desperately need.
And if this is exposing something you have been hiding behind your smile, you do not have to write your private sin in a public comment.
But perhaps you can honestly say, "Lord, give me a clean heart."
That prayer is more important than protecting the appearance that you already have one.
Now consider something else.
Saul and David were not the only kings in this story.
There was another King coming.
A King who would not use His authority to take what belonged to someone else.
A King who would not sacrifice an innocent man to protect His own reputation.
A King who would not hide His wrongdoing, because He had none.
A King who would willingly give His own life for guilty people.
And this is where the entire account becomes breathtaking.
David's family line would eventually lead to Jesus Christ.
When the angel Gabriel announced Jesus' birth to Mary, he said:
"The Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David: And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end." (Luke 1:32–33, KJV)
The covenant was never ultimately about preserving David's personal reputation.
It was about God's redemptive plan.
David was a deeply flawed king through whose lineage God would bring the sinless King.
And the difference between them could not be greater.
David arranged for a righteous soldier to be exposed to death to conceal his own sin.
Jesus, the truly righteous Son of God, willingly went to death to save sinners.
David took.
Jesus gave.
David concealed guilt.
Jesus bore the sins of others.
David's kingdom was stained by human wickedness.
Christ's kingdom is established in perfect righteousness.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus provides it.
This is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to a lesson about becoming a slightly better version of Saul or David.
We need more than improved behavior.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need new hearts.
We need a Savior.
And the Son of David came to accomplish what David could never accomplish for himself.
The apostle Peter declared that Jesus "did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth" (1 Peter 2:22, KJV).
Paul wrote:
"For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." (2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV)
This does not mean Jesus became personally sinful.
It means the sinless Christ bore our sin in His saving work, so that those who belong to Him may stand righteous before God.
At the cross, God's holiness and mercy were not enemies.
Sin was not dismissed as harmless.
The Savior gave Himself for sinners.
And through His resurrection, He conquered death.
That is the hope Saul needed.
That is the hope David needed.
And that is the hope you and I need.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret you have never confessed.
Maybe your life looks successful from the outside, but you know something inside has been drifting away from God.
Maybe you have been using ministry, church attendance, or religious activity to avoid confronting an area of disobedience.
Or maybe you have already confessed something terrible, and you wonder whether God could possibly receive someone with your history.
Listen carefully.
David's story does not tell you that serious sin is safe.
It tells you that God's mercy is real.
Saul's story does not tell you that one mistake automatically puts you beyond God's reach.
It warns you against rejecting God's word and allowing pride, fear, and self-preservation to rule your heart.
And Jesus' story tells you that forgiveness is not purchased by your performance.
It is received through faith in the crucified and risen Savior.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (1 John 1:9, KJV)
That promise is not permission to keep practicing evil.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
And sometimes coming into the light is painful.
It may require telling the truth.
Ending a relationship that dishonors God.
Confessing deception.
Seeking help.
Returning what was stolen.
Accepting consequences.
Asking forgiveness without demanding it.
Allowing someone you harmed the freedom to establish boundaries.
Walking through a long season of rebuilding what sin damaged.
But none of those difficult steps makes repentance less beautiful.
They make it real.
God is not asking you to manufacture an impressive religious appearance.
He is calling you to turn to Him.
And perhaps the most frightening spiritual condition is not the one in which you know you are broken.
Perhaps it is the one in which you have become so skilled at explaining away your disobedience that you no longer recognize your need for mercy.
Saul stood before Samuel with excuses.
David stood before Nathan with guilt.
Both were sinners.
Both were accountable.
Neither deserved to command God's favor.
Yet God's covenant promise continued through David, and the true Son of David came to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
That is the answer to the question.
Not favoritism.
Not the idea that adultery and murder were somehow less serious than disobedience.
Not a claim that repentance earns covenant blessings.
But the holiness of God, the reality of judgment, the necessity of repentance, and the astonishing faithfulness of a God whose promise pointed beyond David to Jesus Christ.
And now the question is no longer simply why Saul lost his kingdom while David's covenant continued.
The question is what we will do when God's word confronts us.
Will we defend the sin?
Or confess it?
Will we protect our image?
Or seek a clean heart?
Will we use grace as an excuse to remain unchanged?
Or will we come to Jesus Christ, whose grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for Him?
Because the Gospel does not merely offer a new ending to an old scandal.
It offers new life through a risen Savior.
And if you are wondering whether your past is too dark for Christ to redeem, remember this:
The genealogy of Jesus contains the history of a deeply fallen king.
Matthew 1:6 even remembers Solomon's mother as the wife of Uriah, refusing to let David's story be reduced to a polished royal romance.
The Bible does not need to erase the scandal to proclaim the grace.
God's redemption is not built on pretending the past never happened.
It is built on the saving work of Jesus Christ.
The wounds we have caused may require lifelong accountability.
The losses may not all be restored in this life.
The consequences may remain.
But the door of repentance is open, and Christ is able to save those who come to God through Him.
That is not cheap grace.
That is costly redemption.
Take a moment before God.
No performance.
No polished religious speech.
Just honesty.

"Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Forgive me. Teach me to stop defending what You are calling me to surrender. Give me a clean heart. Help me make right what I can, accept what I must, and follow You in truth. I trust in Your death and resurrection, and I need Your grace to transform my life. Amen."
And if you have a testimony of God's patient work in your life, consider sharing it. Your honest words may encourage someone who believes their failures have placed them beyond hope.
You do not need to expose private details to strangers. God already knows your story.
But there is something powerful about a community of believers who stop pretending to be flawless and begin pointing one another toward Christ.
And perhaps someone in your life needs this message today.
A father who thinks his mistakes have destroyed every possibility of change.
A mother carrying guilt that nobody sees.
A young believer secretly wrestling with temptation.
A church leader who needs to remember that public ministry never replaces private obedience.
A wounded person who needs to hear that God's forgiveness never excuses the wrong done against them.
Or someone who has walked away from Christianity because they mistakenly believed the Bible celebrates its heroes while hiding their crimes.
Because the world has enough voices teaching people how to protect their image.
We need more voices calling people back to Jesus.
Not out of guilt.
And certainly not because God's blessing can be purchased.
But voluntary generosity can be one meaningful way to glorify God by helping make Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
People who may never enter a church building.
People who have questions they are afraid to ask.
People who are struggling with shame, doubt, temptation, or spiritual exhaustion.
People who need someone to open the Scriptures and point them toward Jesus.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
The Gospel is the message.
And every act of service should point back to Him.
So before you leave this article, remember the two kings.
Remember Saul standing before Samuel, trying to defend what he had done.
Remember David standing before Nathan, confronted by the truth he had tried to bury.
Remember the covenant God made.
Remember the consequences David suffered.
And above all, remember the Son of David who came without sin, gave Himself for sinners, rose from the grave, and reigns forever.
Do not walk away thinking you are too righteous to fall.
Do not walk away thinking you are too sinful to repent.
Walk away knowing that God is holy, His word is true, His mercy is precious, and Jesus Christ is worthy of your complete surrender.
Because the greatest tragedy is not having a past that needs forgiveness—it is standing before the Savior who offers mercy and refusing to come into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE REFUSED TO KILL HIS ENEMY—BUT WAS HE DISOBEYING HIS COUNTRY OR OBEYING JESUS?
paragraphs: HE REFUSED TO KILL HIS ENEMY—BUT WAS HE DISOBEYING HIS COUNTRY OR OBEYING JESUS?
When the Government Demands a Weapon, but Christ Commands Love: The Christian Conscience, Military Service, and the Cost of Following Jesus
Imagine standing before a military officer.
Your country is calling you to serve. Your family expects you to be brave. Your neighbors believe that defending your nation is your sacred duty.
Then someone places a weapon in your hands.
You know what that weapon is designed to do.
And somewhere deep inside, a voice you cannot silence brings back the words of Jesus Christ:
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you.” — Matthew 5:44 (KJV)
Your hands begin to tremble.
Not necessarily because you are afraid to die.
But because you are afraid of taking a life that God created.
Now imagine the officer looking straight into your eyes and asking:
“Are you refusing to serve your country?”
And you answer:

“Sir, I am willing to suffer for my country. I am willing to carry the wounded. I am willing to risk my life to save another human being. But I cannot, in good conscience, take a life when I believe my Savior is calling me to love even my enemies.”
Silence.
Then comes the accusation.
“Coward.”
“Traitor.”
“Disobedient.”
“Fake patriot.”
Perhaps even the accusation that hurts most:
“You call yourself a Christian, but you refuse to defend the innocent?”
And suddenly, this is no longer a simple question about military service.
It is a question about the authority of Jesus Christ over the human conscience.
Can a Christian refuse military service because Jesus commanded His followers to love their enemies?
Yes, a Christian can sincerely refuse participation in military service, especially combat, because of a conscience shaped by Jesus' teachings.
But that is not the end of the biblical discussion.
Because Scripture also speaks about governing authorities, soldiers, justice, protecting others, and the moral responsibility to resist evil.
And faithful Christians have wrestled with these passages for centuries.
The deeper question is not whether we can find one Bible verse that supports our preferred position.

The deeper question is whether we are willing to let the whole counsel of God examine our hearts—even when it challenges our patriotism, our fear, our politics, or our understanding of what courage really means.
Because a person can refuse to carry a weapon for selfish reasons.
And another person can carry a weapon while sincerely believing he is protecting innocent lives.
The weapon alone does not reveal everything about the heart.
And the absence of a weapon does not automatically prove holiness.
Jesus sees deeper.
Much deeper.
The words that disturbed an empire
When Jesus delivered His Sermon on the Mount, He did not tell His disciples merely to avoid hating their enemies.
He commanded something far more radical.
In Matthew 5:44, the Greek text reads:
ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν
Agapate tous echthrous hymōn.
“Love your enemies.”
The word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is an imperative from agapaō, meaning to love. Here, Jesus commands His followers to love those who stand against them.
And ἐχθρούς (echthrous) refers to enemies.
Not merely people who irritate us.
Not merely people who disagree with our opinions.
Enemies.
People who oppose us.
People who may threaten us.
People whose actions make loving them painfully difficult.
Jesus continues in Matthew 5:45:
“That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
Think about that.
The God who has every right to judge wickedness still extends ordinary gifts of providence to people who reject Him.
And Jesus commands His followers to reflect the character of that Father.
This does not mean that evil is harmless.
It does not mean injustice should be ignored.
It does not mean victims must remain defenseless.
But it does mean that a Christian must never treat another human being as someone beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Even an enemy remains a person made in God's image.
Even an enemy may become a recipient of God's saving grace.
And this is where the Christian conscience begins to wrestle.
If Jesus commands me to love my enemy, can I deliberately take his life in battle?
Some Christians answer no.
Others believe that love for an enemy can coexist with the tragic necessity of using proportionate force to protect innocent people.
Both positions deserve careful examination against Scripture.
But neither position gives us permission to hate.
The moment Jesus refused the sword
Now travel in your imagination to the Garden of Gethsemane.
It is night.
Torches approach through the darkness.
Judas has betrayed the Son of God.
Armed men arrive to arrest the only truly innocent man who has ever lived.
Peter sees the danger.
He reaches for his sword.
Steel flashes.
A servant of the high priest loses his ear.
And Jesus says something Peter probably never expected.
“Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.” — Matthew 26:52 (KJV)
Luke 22:51 records that Jesus healed the wounded man's ear.
Consider the scene.
The man who had come with the arresting party was wounded.
Jesus did not celebrate his suffering.
He healed him.
The Savior was surrounded by hostility, yet His response revealed the extraordinary mercy of His kingdom.
But we must be careful not to make the passage say more—or less—than it says.
Jesus was preventing His disciples from violently resisting His arrest. He was willingly fulfilling the Father's redemptive purpose.
The passage does not explicitly declare that every soldier in every circumstance must abandon military service.
Nevertheless, Christian pacifists see in this moment a profound revelation of how disciples are called to respond to violence.
Jesus did not establish His kingdom through the sword.
He went to the cross.
And there, while suffering at the hands of His enemies, He prayed:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34 (KJV)
This is not weakness.
This is holiness.
This is not cowardice.
This is the Son of God refusing to abandon love even while enduring unimaginable injustice.
And anyone who claims to follow Him must take that example seriously.
But what about the soldiers in the Bible?
Here is where the discussion becomes more difficult.
Because the same Bible that records Jesus commanding love for enemies also records encounters with soldiers without always demanding that they leave their profession.
In Luke 3:14, soldiers asked John the Baptist what they should do.
John answered:
“Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.” (KJV)
The Greek expression translated “Do violence to no man” is:
Μηδένα διασείσητε
Mēdena diaseisēte.
The verb diaseiō can refer to intimidating, shaking down, or extorting someone through threats or force.
John was condemning the abuse of military authority.
He also warned against false accusations and greed.
Significantly, he did not explicitly command those soldiers to resign.
That observation matters.
However, it would also be a mistake to claim that John's silence settles every question about warfare or killing.
The passage directly addresses the conduct of soldiers, not every moral question about military service.
Then consider the Roman centurion in Matthew 8.
Jesus praised his faith.
He did not explicitly demand that he abandon his military position.
In Acts 10, Cornelius, another centurion, is described as devout and God-fearing. When the Gospel reached his household, Scripture does not record an order for him to resign from military service.
These accounts are significant for Christians who believe military service can be compatible with discipleship.
But again, silence is not the same as a comprehensive endorsement of every military action.
The Bible does not give us permission to turn a soldier's conversion into approval of unjust warfare.
Nor does it allow us to erase these soldiers from the biblical record because their existence complicates an argument for absolute pacifism.
We must let Scripture speak.
Even when it makes our conclusions harder.
What about Romans 13?
The apostle Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “sword” is μάχαιραν (machairan).
Paul recognizes that governing authorities exercise coercive power and bear responsibility for restraining wrongdoing.
For Christians who affirm the possibility of just military service, Romans 13 contributes to a broader biblical argument that legitimate authorities may sometimes use force to protect society.
But notice something crucial.
Romans 13 follows Romans 12.
And Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath.”
Then Romans 12:21 declares:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
Paul distinguishes personal vengeance from the governing authority's responsibility to administer justice.
Christians disagree about how these teachings apply to believers who personally serve as agents of the state.
Some believe Christians may participate in the state's legitimate protective functions without embracing hatred or revenge.
Others believe disciples must leave coercive violence to the governing authorities rather than personally participate in it.
That disagreement cannot be resolved by pretending either Romans 12 or Romans 13 does not exist.
And there is another important boundary.
Government authority is real.
But it is not absolute.
When the apostles were commanded to stop preaching Jesus, Peter and the others answered:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29 (KJV)
That principle is unmistakable.
No government possesses the authority to command a Christian to commit what God forbids.
But applying that principle to military service requires careful moral discernment.
It does not automatically prove that all military service is sinful.
Nor does it mean that obeying a military order excuses a Christian from moral responsibility.
An order to deliberately murder civilians, torture prisoners, or commit atrocities does not become righteous simply because a superior issued it.
A uniform cannot wash away sin.
A flag cannot replace the cross.
And loyalty to a nation must never become greater than loyalty to Jesus Christ.
The two Christian convictions that cannot simply be dismissed
Across Christian history, believers have developed two major approaches to this question.
One is often called Christian pacifism or Christian nonviolence.
It emphasizes Jesus' teachings about enemy-love, His refusal to defend His kingdom through violence, His willingness to suffer, and the apostolic instruction not to repay evil for evil.

Many Christians in historic peace-church traditions, including Mennonites, Quakers, and some Anabaptist communities, have understood these teachings as prohibiting their participation in killing during war.
For them, refusing combat is not necessarily refusing to love their country.
It can be an expression of obedience to Christ.
They may serve through medical care, disaster relief, humanitarian work, or other forms of noncombatant service.
The other major approach is often called just-war reasoning.
It recognizes the tragic possibility that force may sometimes be necessary to defend innocent people against aggression.

This tradition, developed extensively in Christian moral theology, argues that the use of force must be constrained by justice, legitimate authority, right intention, necessity, proportionality, and the protection of noncombatants.
It does not teach that every war is justified.
It does not teach that Christians should glorify violence.
And it certainly does not teach that hatred becomes holy when directed against an enemy nation.
Its central concern is that refusing to restrain violent aggression can sometimes leave vulnerable people exposed to terrible harm.
Imagine a soldier who sees armed attackers threatening helpless children.
He intervenes to protect them.
His purpose is not revenge.
His purpose is to save lives.

A Christian who follows just-war reasoning may believe that such protective action can be an expression of love for the victims, even while recognizing the terrible moral weight of using force against the attackers.
A Christian pacifist may respond that the follower of Jesus must seek protection through nonlethal means, courageous intervention, rescue, and sacrificial suffering rather than intentional killing.
These convictions differ profoundly.
But both must face difficult questions.
To the pacifist: How should Christians respond when the innocent face immediate, deadly violence?
To the Christian who accepts military force: How will you ensure that your willingness to fight never becomes hatred, revenge, blind nationalism, or participation in injustice?
Neither question should be treated lightly.
And neither person should assume that sincere disagreement automatically proves the other has abandoned Jesus.
The conscience that refuses to be bought
Now imagine a young Christian receiving an order to report for military service.
He has prayed.
He has studied Scripture.
He has spoken with mature believers.
He has wrestled with the Sermon on the Mount until the words seem engraved upon his soul.
He knows that people will misunderstand him.
He knows that refusing military service may bring legal consequences, depending on his country's laws.
He knows he may lose opportunities, face rejection, or be accused of cowardice.
Yet he cannot escape one conviction:
“I cannot personally participate in killing another human being without violating what I believe Jesus commands me.”
Is he automatically rebelling against God?
No.
A Christian may hold that conviction sincerely and seek conscientious-objector status or lawful noncombatant alternatives.
But sincerity alone does not make every interpretation correct. His conscience must remain open to Scripture, correction, prayer, and wise counsel.
Romans 14:23 says:
“For whatsoever is not of faith is sin.” (KJV)
In context, Paul is addressing disputes over matters such as eating and conscience, not directly discussing military service.
Nevertheless, the passage establishes an important principle: acting against one's sincere conviction before God is spiritually serious.
And Romans 14:12 reminds us:
“So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.”
We should not use these verses to suggest that personal conscience is infallible.
A conscience can be mistaken.
It can be poorly informed.
It can be hardened.
It must be shaped by God's Word.
But a Christian should not be pressured to violate a serious moral conviction simply because someone else finds that conviction inconvenient.

If you are facing compulsory service, seek reliable legal advice about the laws of your jurisdiction and any available conscientious-objector or alternative-service provisions. Christian conviction and legal exemption are related questions, but they are not identical.
And if you are a Christian already serving in the military, this discussion is not a declaration that God has abandoned you.
Your profession does not place you beyond the reach of grace.
Your calling is to examine every part of your life under the lordship of Christ.
The soldier who refuses to hate
Perhaps you are reading this while wearing a military uniform.
Perhaps you have served in combat.
Perhaps you have buried friends.
Perhaps you have witnessed things you still cannot describe without feeling something tighten inside your chest.
And perhaps a question has followed you home:
“Can Jesus still love someone like me?”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not a message that Christ saves only those whose past is clean.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we made ourselves worthy.
Not after we repaired every consequence of our failures.
Not after we found the words to explain everything we had done.
While we were yet sinners.
This does not erase moral responsibility.
It does not declare every action committed in war innocent.
Where there has been wrongdoing, repentance matters. Truth matters. Justice matters. Making amends where possible matters.
But neither does the Gospel declare that a person who has participated in war is beyond forgiveness.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The same Lord who called fishermen and tax collectors also received the faith of a Roman centurion.
The same Savior who rebuked Peter's sword also restored Peter after his devastating denial.
And the same Christ who prayed for His enemies on the cross still calls broken people to repentance and new life.
You are not required to pretend your wounds do not exist.
You are not required to call evil good.
You are invited to bring the truth into the presence of the One who died and rose again.
Because grace does not rewrite history by pretending the past never happened. Grace rewrites the future by bringing sinners into reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
That is the heart of our message.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The Christian who refuses to carry a weapon must still be willing to carry a cross
There is something that needs to be said to Christians who believe Jesus forbids them from participating in warfare.
Refusing military service does not automatically make a person courageous.
It may be courageous.
It may require extraordinary sacrifice.
But Christian nonviolence is more than refusing to shoot.
Jesus never commanded His followers merely to avoid certain weapons.
He commanded them to love.
And love demands action.
Will you help the wounded?
Will you shelter the displaced?
Will you feed those who have lost everything?
Will you care for the grieving family of someone who fought on the side you oppose?
Will you pray for people who mock your convictions?
Will you risk your comfort to protect vulnerable lives through peaceful means?
Will you serve your neighbors when there is no applause?
Because Christian nonviolence, if it is genuinely rooted in the Gospel, cannot be an excuse for indifference.
And Christian military service, if it is genuinely governed by biblical ethics, cannot become an excuse for cruelty.
Both must answer to Jesus.
The Christian who refuses to fight must not despise the soldier.
The Christian soldier must not despise the conscientious objector.
And neither may use religious language to escape the demands of sacrificial love.
Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” — Matthew 16:24 (KJV)
Notice what He did not say.
He did not promise that following Him would always make us popular.
He did not promise that everyone would understand our convictions.
He did not promise that obedience would never cost us something.
He called us to follow Him.
Even when the road is difficult.
But here is the question that reaches beyond the battlefield
What if the enemy Jesus is commanding you to love is not a soldier from another nation?
What if it is your father?
The friend who betrayed you?
The person who spread lies about your family?
The neighbor who humiliated you?
The relative whose words still hurt years later?
It is possible to argue passionately about whether Christians should participate in war while quietly nourishing hatred toward someone in our own home.
We can condemn violence on the battlefield while using our tongues to destroy people.
We can quote Matthew 5:44 and still refuse to forgive a brother.
We can preach peace to nations while refusing reconciliation across our own dinner tables.
And suddenly, the question becomes painfully personal.
If Jesus commands me to love an enemy carrying a weapon, what excuse do I have for refusing to love an enemy carrying only the memory of what they did to me?
That does not mean forgiveness removes accountability.
It does not mean an abused person must return to an unsafe relationship.
It does not mean trust is automatically restored.
Biblical love can coexist with boundaries, justice, and the protection of the vulnerable.
But hatred must not become the ruler of our hearts.
The cross confronts all of us.
The pacifist.
The soldier.
The politician.
The pastor.
The person who has never touched a weapon but has wounded others with words.
We all need mercy.
The cross is where our arguments must finally bow
At Calvary, Jesus was not dying because He had failed to resist Rome.
He was willingly giving His life according to the Father's saving purpose.
He bore our sins.
He fulfilled the Scriptures.
He accomplished what no military victory, political revolution, or human moral achievement could ever accomplish.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
Colossians 1:20 speaks of God making peace through the blood of Christ's cross.
The Greek phrase is:
εἰρηνοποιήσας διὰ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ σταυροῦ αὐτοῦ
Eirēnopoiēsas dia tou haimatos tou staurou autou.
“Having made peace through the blood of his cross.”
This is not merely a message about ending human conflicts.
In context, Paul is proclaiming the cosmic significance of Christ's reconciling work.
Sin has alienated humanity from God.
And peace with God comes through Jesus Christ.
The deepest problem in the human heart cannot be solved by military strength.
But neither can it be solved by merely refusing military service.
A person can be a pacifist and still need salvation.
A person can be a decorated soldier and still need salvation.
A person can possess a flawless public reputation and still need salvation.
Because our greatest need is not simply a new political position.
It is a new heart.
A heart humbled by repentance.
A heart rescued by grace.
A heart transformed through faith in the crucified and risen Savior.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than an argument.
It becomes an invitation.
Come to Christ.
Not to defend your image.
Not to prove you are morally superior.
Not to hide behind your uniform or your refusal to wear one.
Come as a sinner in need of mercy.
Confess what is true.
Turn away from sin.
Trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose from the dead.
And allow His Word to reshape the way you think about enemies, nations, justice, courage, forgiveness, and love.
So, can a Christian refuse military service because of Jesus' teaching on loving enemies?
Yes.

A Christian may conscientiously conclude that following Jesus requires refusing combat or military participation, and there are substantial biblical arguments and longstanding Christian traditions supporting that conviction.

But Scripture does not explicitly command every Christian soldier to resign, and other Christians, seeking to obey the same Lord, conclude that morally constrained military service may be permissible when directed toward the just protection of others.
The existence of sincere disagreement does not make every action morally acceptable.
Aggression, atrocities, revenge, cruelty, and the deliberate targeting of innocent people cannot be sanctified by patriotic language.
And neither position should be embraced merely because it is convenient.
The Christian must study Scripture faithfully, seek wisdom humbly, obey God above human authorities, and remain willing to bear the cost of conviction.
Above all, the Christian must refuse to surrender the command of Jesus to love.
Because whether you carry a weapon or refuse one, you cannot faithfully follow Christ while celebrating hatred.
And perhaps that is the question we should carry away from this discussion.
Not simply:
“Would I be willing to die for my country?”
But also:
“Am I willing to surrender my pride, my hatred, my revenge, and even my reputation in order to obey Jesus?”
That is where discipleship becomes real.
That is where faith stops being a slogan.
And that is where the cross exposes the difference between admiring Jesus and actually following Him.
If this message has unsettled something inside you, do not rush past it.
Bring that conviction before God.
Pray over the Scriptures.
Speak with mature believers who will help you seek truth rather than simply reinforce your opinions.

And if you believe Christians can disagree on this issue while remaining faithful to Christ, share your understanding respectfully. Let the conversation be governed by Scripture, humility, and love—not insults.
Someone reading your testimony may be carrying a question they have never dared to ask out loud.
Someone may need to know that struggling with a difficult moral question does not mean they must stop seeking Jesus.
And someone may need to hear that forgiveness is still possible.
We are not here to build a community that merely wins religious arguments.
We want to help people know Jesus Christ, understand His Word, repent of sin, receive His grace, and grow into mature disciples who live what they believe.
For those who have been praying about how to support Gospel-centered work, this can be one meaningful expression of generosity and partnership in the Gospel.
Scripture teaches that believers may support those who minister the Word, as reflected in Galatians 6:6 and 1 Corinthians 9:14. It also teaches that giving should be willing rather than coerced.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
God is glorified through faith in Christ, obedience, love, truth, worship, generosity, and faithful service.
These resources are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
Pray for this ministry.
Help another person open the Bible.
Speak about Jesus with someone who has lost hope.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by payments, purchases, or religious performance.
And that grace is exactly why we want the message to keep reaching people.
Because somewhere there may be a young believer staring at a military summons, frightened by the possibility of choosing between conscience and country.
Somewhere there may be a soldier who cannot sleep because of what he has seen.
Somewhere there may be a family praying for someone serving in a dangerous place.
Somewhere there may be a person who has spent years believing that what happened in war placed them beyond God's mercy.
And somewhere there may be a person who has never faced a battlefield but has spent a lifetime fighting a war of bitterness within their own heart.
All of them need more than an argument.
They need truth.
They need grace.
They need the Savior.
The final question is not whether you have always made the right decision.
None of us has.
The final question is whether you will bring your life, your conscience, your sins, your wounds, and your future under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Because the kingdom of God is not advanced by hatred.
And the peace that matters most cannot be manufactured by human power.
It was purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ.
You may never be called to lay down a weapon—but every follower of Jesus will be called to lay down something at the foot of the cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY BOTH LOVE JESUS. THEY BOTH BELIEVE THE BIBLE. SO WHY ARE THEY CALLING EACH OTHER UNFAITHFUL?
paragraphs: THEY BOTH LOVE JESUS. THEY BOTH BELIEVE THE BIBLE. SO WHY ARE THEY CALLING EACH OTHER UNFAITHFUL?

The painful debate over women serving as elders, the Greek words we cannot afford to ignore, and the dangerous moment when defending Scripture becomes an excuse to wound the very people Christ died to redeem.
She had served the church for twenty-three years.

She had prayed beside hospital beds. Taught children about Jesus. Comforted grieving mothers. Opened her home to struggling families. Shared the Gospel with people who had never stepped inside a church.
She knew Scripture. She loved Christ. Her life bore the unmistakable evidence of someone who had been walking with God through seasons nobody else knew about.
Then someone suggested she might be qualified to serve as an elder.
And suddenly, the conversations changed.
One person said, “God has clearly gifted her.”
Another responded, “But Scripture forbids it.”
Someone else whispered, “If you support women elders, you don't really believe the Bible.”
And before long, a woman who had spent decades serving Jesus found herself standing in the middle of a theological battlefield.
Not because she had denied the resurrection.
Not because she had rejected salvation by grace.
Not because she had abandoned the Gospel.
But because Christians who confessed the same Savior disagreed about how certain passages of Scripture should be understood.
Now imagine another believer.
A father. A faithful husband. A man who studies his Bible every morning before work. He sincerely believes God has reserved the governing office of elder for qualified men.
He doesn't hate women. He isn't trying to silence their testimonies. He believes women are equally created in God's image, equally redeemed by Christ, equally gifted by the Holy Spirit.
But he reads 1 Timothy 2 and 3 and believes obedience requires him to uphold a distinction between men and women in church leadership.
Then someone tells him, “Your position is hateful. You're standing against Jesus.”
And now he, too, is wounded.
Two believers.
Two consciences.
One Bible.
One Lord.
And a question that reaches much deeper than church leadership:
Can Christians disagree about whether women should serve as elders without questioning each other's faith?
Yes.
But that answer comes with a responsibility that neither side should escape.
We must take Scripture seriously enough to examine our interpretations, and we must take the Gospel seriously enough not to pronounce spiritual judgment where Christ has not authorized us to do so.
Because there is something profoundly troubling about a church that knows how to defend its position but has forgotten how to love its people.
And before anyone uses that sentence to dismiss doctrinal disagreement, hear this carefully.
Love does not make truth optional.
And truth does not make love disposable.
Jesus commands both.
The question is whether we are willing to obey Him when doing so costs us the satisfaction of winning an argument.
There is a reason this debate becomes so personal.
For some women, the question is not merely about a title. It touches years of feeling overlooked, dismissed, or treated as spiritually less capable.
For some men and women who hold the traditional position, the question is not about protecting privilege. It is about remaining faithful to what they sincerely believe God has commanded.
For others, the issue raises painful memories of church leaders who used biblical language to justify control, humiliation, or abuse.
And still others fear that cultural pressure is gradually persuading churches to abandon difficult biblical teachings.
These concerns are not identical.
They do not all lead to the same conclusions.
But they remind us that behind theological arguments are human beings carrying histories, convictions, fears, and wounds.
And Jesus sees every one of them.
So we cannot settle this debate by saying, “Everyone has their own truth.”
Christians do not have the freedom to manufacture truth according to preference.
Jesus prayed to the Father:
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” — John 17:17, KJV
The Greek text says:
ἁγίασον αὐτοὺς ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ· ὁ λόγος ὁ σὸς ἀλήθειά ἐστιν.
Hagiason autous en tē alētheia; ho logos ho sos alētheia estin.
“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.”
That is not a call to surrender biblical conviction.
It is a call to submit our convictions to God's Word, even when Scripture challenges our assumptions.
And that submission begins with a difficult admission.
Sincere Christians can agree that Scripture is authoritative while disagreeing about how particular passages should be interpreted and applied.
That does not make every interpretation equally correct.
It means we must distinguish the authority of God's Word from our own understanding of it.
Those are not always the same thing.
Consider the passage at the center of the debate.
In 1 Timothy 2:12, Paul writes:
The Greek reads:
διδάσκειν δὲ γυναικὶ οὐκ ἐπιτρέπω οὐδὲ αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρός, ἀλλ᾽ εἶναι ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ.
Didaskein de gynaiki ouk epitrepō oude authentein andros, all' einai en hēsychia.
A fairly direct rendering is:
“I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but to be in quietness.”
Now the difficulty begins.
The Greek verb αὐθεντεῖν (authentein) is unusually rare in surviving Greek literature, and scholars debate its precise nuance in this passage.
Some understand it as exercising authority in a relatively neutral sense.
Others argue that the context or usage suggests a more negative kind of authority, such as domineering or improperly assuming control.
The word itself does not settle the entire argument.
Neither does the English expression “usurp authority” in the King James Version settle the Greek meaning beyond dispute.
And ἡσυχία (hēsychia), commonly translated “quietness” or “silence,” can describe a quiet, peaceable disposition rather than necessarily absolute speechlessness in every setting.
That matters because Paul elsewhere acknowledges women praying and prophesying in 1 Corinthians 11:5.
We must read Scripture in conversation with Scripture.

Christians who hold the complementarian position generally understand 1 Timothy 2:12, especially in light of Paul's appeal to Adam and Eve in the following verses, as establishing a continuing restriction on women exercising the authoritative teaching and governing function associated with elders.

They also point to 1 Timothy 3:1–7 and Titus 1:5–9, where qualifications for overseers and elders include male-oriented descriptions, including the expression commonly translated “husband of one wife.”
They believe this pattern reflects God's ordering of the church rather than the spiritual inferiority of women.
That is a serious argument.
It deserves careful engagement.
It should not be dismissed as hatred simply because someone disagrees with it.
But Christians who hold the egalitarian position also bring biblical arguments that deserve honest consideration.
They point to women such as Priscilla, who participated with Aquila in explaining God's way more accurately to Apollos in Acts 18:26.
They point to Phoebe, whom Paul identifies in Romans 16:1 as a διάκονον (diakonon) of the church at Cenchreae.
The Greek term can refer to a servant, minister, or deacon, depending on context. Christians disagree about whether Phoebe held a formally recognized office.
They point to Junia in Romans 16:7, whom Paul mentions alongside Andronicus.

The Greek phrase ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις (episēmoi en tois apostolois) is disputed. Some understand it to mean that they were outstanding among the apostles; others understand it to mean they were well known to the apostles.
Even accepting the former interpretation would not, by itself, establish that Junia held the later church office of elder.
They also point to Galatians 3:28:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
The Greek concludes:
πάντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς εἷς ἐστε ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
Pantes gar hymeis heis este en Christō Iēsou.
“For you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

Egalitarian interpreters argue that the New Testament's witness to spiritual gifting, mutual participation, and unity in Christ supports women serving in all offices, including eldership, when properly qualified.

Complementarian interpreters respond that equality in Christ does not necessarily eliminate every distinction in church responsibilities, and that Galatians 3:28 primarily addresses equal standing in Christ rather than qualifications for ecclesiastical office.
Both sides must reckon with the full biblical evidence.
Neither side should pretend the other has no passages to explain.
And neither side should turn a contested interpretation into an automatic verdict on someone's salvation.
Here is where the conversation becomes painfully revealing.
A Christian may be wrong about women elders without being wrong about who Jesus Christ is.
That sentence does not make the question insignificant.
Church leadership matters. Sound doctrine matters. Obedience matters. The way a congregation orders its ministry matters.
A church cannot simply avoid making a decision about who may serve as elders.

But the question of whether someone has correctly interpreted an elder qualification is not identical to the question of whether that person has genuinely trusted in the crucified and risen Lord Jesus Christ.
Paul reminds the Corinthians of the Gospel he preached:
“Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.” — 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, KJV
This is the center of the Christian proclamation.
Jesus Christ, the Son of God, died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Salvation is found in Him.
We are not saved by possessing a flawless understanding of every disputed question in church governance.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8, KJV
This does not mean doctrine is unimportant or that genuine faith can be separated from the call to obey Christ.
It means that we must not add our preferred resolution of a disputed ecclesiastical question to the saving work of Jesus.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to repent.
Not necessarily of our position.
But of our pride.
Of the careless words we used.
Of the motives we assigned to people whose hearts we could not see.
Of the way we made fellow believers feel like enemies when they were trying, however imperfectly, to honor the same Lord.
Have you ever walked away from a theological discussion feeling strangely victorious and spiritually empty?
You proved your point.
You quoted the passage.
You exposed the weakness in someone's argument.
But somewhere along the way, you stopped seeing a brother or sister and started seeing an opponent to defeat.
And maybe the other person did the same to you.
That is not a small thing.
Paul warned:

“And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.” — 1 Corinthians 13:2, KJV
The word translated “charity” is ἀγάπη (agapē), love.
Not sentimental agreement.
Not indifference to holiness.
Not pretending that contradictory teachings can both be true in the same sense.
Love.
The kind of love that refuses to dehumanize someone even while firmly disagreeing.
The kind of love that can say, “I believe your interpretation is mistaken,” without saying, “Therefore, you cannot belong to Jesus.”
The kind of love that remembers the cross before reaching for another accusation.
And we must be equally clear about something else.
Not every disagreement is harmless.
Not every church practice is faithful.
Not every appeal to conscience excuses disobedience.
The New Testament commands believers to guard sound doctrine and correct serious error.
Paul's instructions about elders are not optional simply because modern Christians find them controversial.
The church must study, pray, interpret, and act.
But the seriousness of a disagreement does not automatically make it a test of saving faith.

There may be circumstances in which a person's broader attitude toward Scripture raises genuine concerns about their doctrine. Yet those concerns must be evaluated fairly, rather than assumed merely because someone reaches a different conclusion about women elders.
A believer who rejects biblical authority outright is making a different claim from a believer who submits to biblical authority but understands a passage differently.
We should not confuse those two situations.
And this is not merely a lesson for those who disagree about eldership.
It is a mirror for all of us.
Because the human heart has an astonishing ability to disguise arrogance as discernment.
Sometimes we call it defending truth when we are actually defending our ego.
Sometimes we call it protecting unity when we are actually avoiding uncomfortable Scripture.
Sometimes we call it standing for women when we have stopped listening to women who hold traditional convictions.
Sometimes we call it standing for biblical authority when we have stopped listening to women who are faithfully studying and teaching God's Word within their understanding of Scripture.
Jesus does not ask us to choose between courage and humility.
He calls us to both.
And there is a scene in the Gospels that should unsettle every Christian who has ever used religious certainty to humiliate another person.
In John 8, religious leaders bring before Jesus a woman accused of adultery.
They place her in public view.
Her sin becomes the center of a confrontation.
But the passage reveals that they are also testing Jesus.

The scene is complicated by an important textual fact: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and its original place in the Gospel of John is disputed. It should therefore not carry the weight of establishing a doctrine by itself.
Even so, the familiar account vividly illustrates a danger that the undisputed teachings of Jesus also condemn: the use of another person's vulnerability as a weapon of religious self-righteousness.
Jesus does not celebrate sin.
He calls the woman away from it.
But He also exposes the accusers.
And the story leaves us with a haunting question.
What happens when people become more interested in condemning someone than in seeing that person restored?
Now apply that question carefully to the church.
A woman who believes she is called to serve as an elder is not thereby comparable to someone caught in adultery.
A man who believes eldership is reserved for qualified men is not thereby comparable to a malicious accuser.
The situations are not morally equivalent.
But the warning about the human heart remains relevant.
We can take a legitimate concern for righteousness and corrupt it through pride.
We can take a legitimate concern for inclusion and corrupt it through contempt.
We can speak about Jesus while behaving in ways that make His people afraid to be honest.
And that should grieve us.
Because the church is not supposed to be a place where every theological question becomes a public execution of someone's character.
It is supposed to be a people who belong to the One who was crucified for sinners.
Perhaps the most challenging biblical instruction for this debate is found in Ephesians 4:15:
“But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ.”
The Greek expression is:
ἀληθεύοντες δὲ ἐν ἀγάπῃ
Alētheuontes de en agapē.
Often rendered “speaking the truth in love,” the participle can convey the broader idea of being truthful or practicing truth in love.
Truth and love are not rival commitments.
They belong together in Christian maturity.
And the verse tells us where that maturity is supposed to lead.
Into Christ.
Not into a personality cult.
Not into theological tribalism.
Not into the satisfaction of having the final word.
Into Christ.
That changes the way we disagree.

It means a complementarian Christian can say, “I believe Scripture reserves eldership for qualified men, and I cannot in good conscience affirm women elders,” while still recognizing an egalitarian Christian as a brother or sister in Christ.

It means an egalitarian Christian can say, “I believe Scripture permits qualified women to serve as elders, and I believe the church should recognize those gifts,” while still recognizing a complementarian Christian as a brother or sister in Christ.
It means neither person must surrender conviction to practice Christian charity.
It also means churches should be honest about their convictions.
If a congregation believes the office is reserved for men, it should not mislead women about its governing beliefs.
If a congregation believes qualified women may serve, it should explain its biblical reasoning rather than treating every question as evidence of prejudice.
If members cannot agree on the practice, they may need to serve in different congregations.
That can be painful.
But separation over a significant church-order disagreement need not become a declaration that the other person is outside the family of God.
Sometimes Christian maturity means acknowledging that we cannot serve under the same governance arrangement while refusing to turn that difference into hatred.
And when a church has genuinely mistreated someone, reconciliation must involve more than asking the wounded person to be quiet for the sake of unity.
There must be truth.
Accountability.
Repentance.
And, where possible, restoration.
Biblical unity is not maintained by concealing injustice.
Nor is biblical truth protected by treating every disagreement as abuse.
We need more discernment than that.
We need more humility than that.
We need Jesus.
Because at the foot of the cross, every one of us arrives empty-handed.
The scholar and the struggling new believer.
The woman who has preached the Gospel faithfully for decades.
The man who has guarded his congregation's doctrine with tears and prayer.
The person who believes women should serve as elders.
The person who believes Scripture restricts that office to men.
None of us stands righteous before God because our theological arguments are impressive.
Our hope is Christ.
Our righteousness is not self-manufactured.
Our forgiveness was purchased at a price we could never pay.
And when we remember that, the tone of the conversation begins to change.
We still open our Bibles.
We still examine Greek words.
We still consider context, grammar, history, and the whole counsel of God.
We still make decisions.
We still correct error.
But we stop acting as though the blood of Jesus belongs exclusively to the people who agree with us about every disputed interpretation.
Imagine what could happen if two believers sat across from each other and began with a different question.
Not, “How can I prove you wrong?”
But, “Help me understand how you reached that conclusion from Scripture.”
Imagine a woman who had felt dismissed finally being heard without someone immediately assuming she was rebelling against God.
Imagine a man who held a traditional interpretation being heard without someone immediately assuming he despised women.
Imagine both opening their Bibles, acknowledging difficult passages, and admitting where their own arguments required careful explanation.
They might still disagree when the conversation ends.
But perhaps they would leave with something they had almost lost.
Respect.
A clearer understanding.
A willingness to pray for one another.
And the realization that Christian fellowship is bigger than the need to win every argument.
This is not theological weakness.
It is an expression of spiritual maturity.
James 1:19 says:
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
Some of us have become swift to post, swift to accuse, and slow to understand.
We can recognize an opponent's weakest sentence from a mile away, but we cannot recognize the pain in their voice.
We have learned how to defend the faith online while forgetting how to treat fellow believers with gentleness.
And perhaps the Holy Spirit is confronting something deeper than our position on women elders.
Perhaps He is confronting the condition of our hearts.
Are we willing to be corrected by Scripture?
Are we willing to acknowledge when we have misrepresented another Christian?
Are we willing to apologize without adding excuses?
Are we willing to defend truth without enjoying someone's humiliation?
Are we willing to admit that knowing the right answer does not automatically mean we have responded in the right spirit?
That last question may be the one we remember long after this article is forgotten.
Because there will come a day when our arguments will no longer be performed before an audience.
There will be no comment section to applaud us.
No followers to congratulate us.
No screenshots to prove we won.
We will stand before Jesus Christ.
And the Lord who commanded us to love one another will not be impressed by cruelty disguised as courage.
That should humble every side of this debate.
It certainly humbles me.
If you have been wounded by this argument, I pray you will not allow the sins of people to persuade you that Christ Himself has abandoned you.
If you have wounded someone while defending your interpretation, I pray you will have the courage to seek forgiveness.
If you are uncertain what Scripture teaches about women serving as elders, do not be ashamed to keep studying.
Read 1 Timothy 2–3.
Read Titus 1.
Read Acts 18.
Read Romans 16.
Read 1 Corinthians 11 and 14.
Read Galatians 3 in its context.
Consider the strongest biblical arguments on both sides rather than only the weakest statements of those you oppose.
Seek wise counsel from mature believers and faithful teachers.
And pray for a heart that would rather obey Jesus than protect its own reputation.
Because this discussion is not ultimately about making everyone comfortable.
It is about becoming faithful.
Faithful in our interpretation.
Faithful in our conduct.
Faithful in our treatment of one another.
Faithful to the Gospel that saved us.
And if this article has exposed something in your own heart, don't rush past it.
Maybe you have been carrying resentment toward someone who disagreed with you.
Maybe you have been afraid to ask sincere questions because you feared being labeled rebellious or unbiblical.
Maybe you have spoken about other believers in ways you would be ashamed to repeat in the presence of Jesus.
Or maybe you are exhausted by watching Christians wound each other over issues that deserve serious, prayerful examination.
What Scripture most shapes your conviction?
You do not have to explain your entire story publicly to be worthy of prayer.
Let the comments become a place where people reason from Scripture, share testimony, ask honest questions, and practice the respect we are talking about.
Not every disagreement needs another battlefield.
Sometimes it needs a table, an open Bible, and two people willing to listen.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, consider sending the article to them.
Not as a weapon.
Not as a subtle accusation.
But as an invitation to remember what unites Christians even when important disagreements remain.
There is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Behind every article, biblical resource, and discipleship effort is a desire to reach people who may never enter a church building but are still searching for hope, forgiveness, and truth.
Some are struggling believers.
Some are questioning their faith.
Some have been hurt by religious communities.
Some are hearing about the grace of Jesus Christ for the first time.
We want to keep bringing Scripture into those places.
We want those resources to remain accessible and to keep expanding the reach of this work.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That matters.
You never need to purchase God's favor.
Grace is not for sale.
These are simple reminders of our gratitude, not the reason anyone should give.
The greater purpose is to help keep the message of Jesus Christ moving beyond our immediate circle.
Because this ministry is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
The One who forgives sinners.
The One who restores the broken.
The One who confronts our pride without abandoning us to despair.
The One who calls His church to holiness and love.
The One whose grace is greater than our failures.
And this brings us back to the woman who had served faithfully for twenty-three years.
And to the man who sincerely believed the office of elder was reserved for qualified men.
What if neither had to become the villain in the other's story?
What if the church could evaluate their convictions seriously, uphold its understanding of Scripture faithfully, and still refuse to destroy their dignity?
What if our theological conversations became places where biblical truth was honored and the character of Christ was visible?

What if the next person who disagreed with us did not walk away thinking, “Those Christians know how to fight,” but instead thought, “They really do take their Bible seriously, and they really do love one another”?
That would not settle every doctrinal question.
But it would bear witness to something the world desperately needs to see.
Jesus prayed that His people would be one, and He connected their unity to the world's recognition that the Father had sent Him (John 17:20–23).
That unity is not permission to abandon truth.
It is a summons to live under the truth of Christ together.
We may disagree about who should serve as an elder.
We may have to make different decisions about church leadership.
We may even worship in different congregations because our convictions cannot be reconciled in practice.
But where we share genuine faith in the biblical Christ and His Gospel, we should be very careful before declaring that the other person does not belong to Him.
Jesus knows His own.
And we should tremble at the thought of treating someone He has redeemed as though they were beyond His grace merely because they disagree with our interpretation of a disputed passage.
So defend Scripture.
Study diligently.
Stand by conscience.
Correct error with patience.
Protect the vulnerable.
Repent when you have sinned.
And love the people Christ has commanded you to love.
Not because doctrine doesn't matter.
But because Jesus matters more than our pride.
And the church belongs to Him.
One day, the argument will fall silent—but the way we treated the people Jesus died for will still matter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING WHO LOST HIS MIND BUT FOUND HIS GOD: WHEN HEAVEN BROKE NEBUCHADNEZZAR'S PRIDE
paragraphs: THE KING WHO LOST HIS MIND BUT FOUND HIS GOD: WHEN HEAVEN BROKE NEBUCHADNEZZAR'S PRIDE

He ruled an empire, commanded armies, and lived like a god among men. Then one sentence from heaven brought him to his knees. For seven appointed periods, the king who had everything lived like an animal. But the most terrifying part of his story isn't what happened to his mind. It's what God was exposing in his heart.
Imagine waking up one morning and discovering that everything you thought made you somebody was gone.
Your title. Your reputation. Your influence. Your wealth. Your ability to make decisions. Even your ability to think clearly.
Yesterday, people bowed when you entered a room.
Today, you are wandering through a field, soaked by the morning dew, eating grass like cattle.
No throne. No royal garments. No servants rushing to obey your commands.
Just a broken man beneath an open sky.
And somewhere beyond the palace walls, an empire continues without him.
This is not a fictional tragedy.
This is the astonishing account recorded in Daniel chapter 4.
But before you dismiss it as the strange punishment of an ancient king, there is something you need to understand.
Nebuchadnezzar's story is not merely about a man who lost his sanity.
It is about a man who became so consumed with his own greatness that he forgot the God who had allowed him to become great.
And if we're willing to be painfully honest, the same pride that destroyed his peace can quietly take root in ours.
You don't need a golden palace to have Nebuchadnezzar's problem.
Sometimes all it takes is a successful career, a growing bank account, a respected ministry, a comfortable life, or the belief that you no longer need anyone to tell you what to do.
Sometimes pride doesn't sound like rebellion.
Sometimes it sounds like, "I built this."
"I earned this."
"I deserve this."
"I don't need help."
And perhaps the most dangerous one of all:
"I can live without God."
Nebuchadnezzar learned the truth about that last statement in a way he would never forget.
And what happened when he finally lifted his eyes toward heaven changes how we should understand the entire story.
The king had already witnessed extraordinary demonstrations of God's power.
In Daniel 2, the Lord revealed the meaning of a troubling dream through Daniel, showing Nebuchadnezzar that earthly kingdoms rise and fall under divine sovereignty.
In Daniel 3, the king watched three faithful Hebrew men survive a blazing furnace after refusing to worship his golden image.
He had seen enough to recognize that Israel's God was unlike the gods of Babylon.
Yet witnessing God's power and surrendering to God's authority are not the same thing.
You can admire the truth without submitting to it.
You can speak respectfully about God while still insisting on being the ruler of your own life.
You can even recognize a miracle and return to the same pride that nearly destroyed you.
Then came another dream.
Nebuchadnezzar saw an enormous tree reaching toward heaven. Its branches stretched across the earth. Its leaves were beautiful, its fruit abundant, and creatures found shelter beneath it.
But suddenly, a holy watcher descended from heaven with a terrifying command.
The tree was to be cut down.
Its branches removed.
Its fruit scattered.
Only the stump and roots would remain, bound with iron and bronze.
Then the dream shifted from the image of a tree to the fate of a person.
Daniel 4:16 records the decree in Aramaic:
לִבְבֵהּ מִן־אֲנָשָׁא יְשַׁנּוֹן וּלְבַב חֵיוָה יִתְיְהִב לֵהּ
Libbeh min-anasha yeshannon, ulevav cheivah yityehev leh.
The sense is:
"Let his mind be changed from that of a man, and let the mind of a beast be given to him."
The word לְבַב (levav) means "heart," but in biblical Aramaic, as in biblical Hebrew, the heart can refer to the inner life, including understanding, thought, and disposition.
This was not simply a prophecy that the king would behave strangely.
His human understanding would be profoundly altered.
The dream also declared that seven עִדָּנִין (iddanin) would pass over him.
The word means "times" or "periods." Many interpreters understand these as seven years, but the Aramaic expression itself does not explicitly say "years."
And the purpose was unmistakable.
Daniel 4:17 explains that the living must know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of humanity and gives it to whomever He wills.
There it is.
The reason behind the judgment.
Not because Nebuchadnezzar had become too successful.
Not because wealth itself was the offense.
Not because God was threatened by the achievements of a human king.
The issue was that Nebuchadnezzar had begun treating borrowed authority as though it belonged to him absolutely.
He possessed a kingdom but had forgotten the King above every kingdom.
And then something remarkable happened.
God warned him.
Before the humiliation came, there was a dream.
Before the collapse, there was an interpretation.
Before the judgment fell, there was an opportunity to turn.
Daniel did not celebrate the terrible future awaiting Nebuchadnezzar. He was troubled by it.
And in Daniel 4:27, he pleaded with the king to break away from his sins by practicing righteousness and from his iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed.
Think about that.
The God who was about to humble this powerful ruler had already sent him a warning and a call to repentance.
That matters.
Because we often imagine divine judgment arriving without warning, while ignoring the many moments when Scripture calls us to turn from what is destroying us.
The uncomfortable conversation.
The passage of Scripture that exposes our motives.
The conviction we keep postponing.
The person who lovingly tells us the truth we don't want to hear.
Not every hardship is a punishment from God, and we must never assume that someone's mental illness or suffering proves hidden sin.
But Nebuchadnezzar's case is different because Scripture itself reveals the reason for his particular experience.
His humiliation was a specific divine judgment against his pride.
And the king had been told.
Twelve months passed.
Twelve months to consider the dream.
Twelve months to remember Daniel's warning.
Twelve months in which the king could have humbled himself.
Then one day, he was walking upon the royal palace of Babylon.
Perhaps the city stretched before him in breathtaking beauty. Babylon was famous for its monumental architecture and imperial power.
And the king spoke the words that exposed his heart.
Daniel 4:30 records:
"Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?"
Notice the language.
I have built.
My mighty power.
My majesty.
There was no acknowledgment of God's sovereignty.
No humility about the temporary nature of earthly power.
Only a man standing above his kingdom, admiring the reflection of himself in everything he could see.
And while the words were still in his mouth, a voice came from heaven.
The kingdom had departed from him.
He would be driven away from human society.
His dwelling would be with the beasts of the field.
He would eat grass like an ox.
And seven periods would pass over him until he knew that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men.
The judgment came immediately.
The man who had commanded armies could no longer command his own circumstances.
The man who had surrounded himself with royal luxury now lived exposed to the elements.
Daniel 4:33 describes his hair growing like eagles' feathers and his nails becoming like birds' claws.
It is a disturbing picture.
But we must be careful not to add things Scripture does not say.

Some have suggested that Nebuchadnezzar suffered from a condition resembling boanthropy, in which a person believes himself to be an ox or behaves like one. That is a modern comparison, not a diagnosis established by the biblical text.
Daniel does not provide a medical case report.
Nor does the chapter say Nebuchadnezzar physically transformed into an animal.
It describes a profound loss of human reason and dignity, expressed through animal-like behavior, as part of a divinely announced judgment.
The distinction matters because mental illness is not evidence that a person has been rejected by God.
People who experience psychiatric illness deserve compassion, appropriate care, and dignity. Nebuchadnezzar's unique experience must not become an excuse to shame those who suffer.
The theological focus of the passage is not that every loss of reason comes from pride.
It is that this particular king, in this particular judgment, was humbled so that he would recognize the sovereignty of God.
And there is another detail we cannot afford to miss.
The tree was cut down.
But the stump remained.
Why?
Because the judgment was not announced as the final destruction of Nebuchadnezzar.
There was still a future beyond the humiliation.
Daniel 4:26 explains that his kingdom would be restored once he acknowledged that heaven rules.
The stump was a sign that the story was not finished.
What a powerful image.
A tree stripped of everything that made it impressive.
Its towering height gone.
Its branches scattered.
Its beauty reduced to something almost unrecognizable.
Yet beneath the earth, roots remained.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what it feels like to become a stump.
You once had plans that seemed unstoppable.
Then something happened.
A relationship collapsed.
A business failed.
A hidden sin came into the light.
Your reputation suffered.
You discovered that the confidence you displayed publicly was covering fear, insecurity, or a desperate need to be admired.
And now you look at what remains and wonder whether anything good can grow again.
Nebuchadnezzar's stump was part of a specific prophetic promise. We should not turn it into a guarantee that every lost job, relationship, or earthly possession will be restored.
But it does remind us of something consistent with the wider witness of Scripture.
God is able to bring hope into circumstances that appear ruined.
And no human life is beyond His power to transform.
The turning point in Daniel 4 is breathtaking.
It does not begin with the king reclaiming his throne.
It does not begin with his servants finding him.
It does not begin with the palace gates opening.
It begins with a movement of his eyes.
Daniel 4:34 says:
"At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me."
Read that again.
I lifted my eyes to heaven.
For so long, he had looked down from the heights of his palace.
Down upon his subjects.
Down upon his achievements.
Down upon the empire he believed testified to his greatness.
But now, after being brought lower than he could ever have imagined, he looked up.
And his reason returned.
The Aramaic expression includes the word מַנְדְּעִי (mandei), meaning "my understanding" or "my reason."
The narrative connects the restoration of his understanding with his acknowledgment of the Most High.
He had to learn that possessing power did not make him the source of power.
He had to learn that ruling people did not mean he ruled history.
He had to learn that the throne of Babylon was never higher than the throne of heaven.
And when he finally acknowledged God, his words changed.
The king who once boasted about his own majesty began blessing the Most High.
He praised the One whose dominion is everlasting.
He confessed that God's kingdom endures from generation to generation.
And in Daniel 4:37, he declared that God's works are right, His ways are just, and He is able to humble those who walk in pride.
What a reversal.
The man who had glorified himself now glorified God.
The king who had claimed greatness as his own now acknowledged the One who truly reigns.
The man who had been brought low was restored to his kingdom.
But here is something important.

The chapter records Nebuchadnezzar's remarkable acknowledgment of God's sovereignty. It does not tell us everything about his later spiritual life or provide a complete account of his eternal destiny.
We should rejoice in the confession the text gives us without claiming more than Scripture reveals.
And still, the transformation in his testimony is impossible to ignore.
He went from "my majesty" to praising the King of heaven.
From self-exaltation to humility.
From boasting in his own power to confessing God's authority.
Now comes the question that makes this ancient story painfully personal.
What is the Babylon you keep taking credit for?
Is it your career?
Your family?
Your ministry?
Your intelligence?
Your influence?
Your reputation as the strong one who never falls apart?
Have you begun measuring your worth by how many people admire you?
Have you mistaken financial security for ultimate security?
Have you become so busy building a life that looks successful that you no longer have time to kneel before the God who gave you life?
Pride is not always loud.
Sometimes it wears the clothes of independence.
Sometimes it hides behind religious activity.
Sometimes it sounds like a prayer that asks God to bless our plans without ever asking whether those plans honor Him.
Sometimes pride is the refusal to apologize.
The inability to admit wrongdoing.
The resentment we feel when someone else receives recognition.
The secret belief that certain people are beneath us.
Or the conviction that we are too spiritually mature to need correction.
And that is why Nebuchadnezzar's story is not just a warning to kings.
It is a warning to anyone with a human heart.
Proverbs 16:18 teaches that pride goes before destruction and a haughty spirit before a fall.
James 4:6 tells us that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.
These are not merely warnings against arrogance in powerful people.
They are invitations to examine ourselves before God.
Because there is a terrible loneliness in always needing to be great.
You cannot receive correction without feeling attacked.
You cannot celebrate someone else's success without feeling diminished.
You cannot admit weakness without fearing that your entire identity will collapse.
You become a prisoner of the image you are desperately trying to maintain.
And the applause that once made you feel alive becomes something you cannot bear to lose.
But the Gospel offers something better than the exhausting pursuit of self-glory.
It offers freedom.
Not the freedom to pretend that sin doesn't matter.
Not the freedom to excuse pride.
But the freedom to stop pretending that we are our own saviors.
And this is where the story of Nebuchadnezzar leads us to something greater than the restoration of an earthly king.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
Because Daniel 4 shows us the danger of a ruler who exalted himself.
But Philippians 2 shows us the glory of the King who humbled Himself.
Nebuchadnezzar possessed earthly majesty and boasted about it.
Jesus, who truly shares in divine glory, did not cling to His privileges for selfish advantage.
Philippians 2:6–8 describes Christ's humility, His taking the form of a servant, and His obedience unto death, even death on a cross.
