Someone who has been hurt by ingratitude and needs to remember the mercy of Christ.
Someone who feels too ashamed to return to God.
Someone who thinks their past has placed them beyond redemption.
"Lord, let the right person encounter Your truth."
Someone whose faithfulness has encouraged you.
Someone who needs to know that their difficult season has not made them invisible to the Savior.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, curious seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along—not merely to increase an audience, but so that more people may encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
And before you leave this article, I want to ask you something more personal.
Not what the nine should have done.
Not what you think other Christians need to change.
But what is happening in your own heart.
Have you been asking Jesus for more while forgetting to thank Him for what He has already given?
Have you been so consumed by the next answered prayer that you have neglected the One who hears you?
Have you been following Him with your feet while your heart has slowly wandered elsewhere?
You don't have to answer publicly if your struggle is too personal.
But if this passage has awakened something in you, consider leaving a comment.
Or share a testimony of a time when God's mercy met you in a place where you thought hope had disappeared.
Your words may encourage another person to seek Christ.
Pray for them. Remind them of Scripture. Do not turn another person's vulnerability into an argument.
We are all dependent on mercy.
The ten lepers were.
The Samaritan was.
And so are we.
Now return with me one last time to that road between Samaria and Galilee.
Ten men stood far away.
Ten voices cried for mercy.
Ten men obeyed Jesus' instruction.
Ten were cleansed.
One turned back.
One glorified God with a loud voice.
One fell at the feet of Jesus and gave thanks.
And the Savior asked:
"Where are the nine?"
Two thousand years later, that question still reaches us.
Not because Jesus has stopped being merciful.
Not because we must earn His attention through perfect gratitude.
But because it is possible to become so fascinated with the gifts of God that we lose sight of the glory of God.
So tonight, before you ask Him for another thing, perhaps you can simply say:
"Lord Jesus, thank You."
Thank You for mercy I did not deserve.
Thank You for patience when I was stubborn.
Thank You for truth when I was deceiving myself.
Thank You for the cross where You bore the punishment for sin.
Thank You for the empty tomb and the hope of resurrection.
Thank You that repentance is still possible.
Thank You that forgiveness is found in Your name.
Thank You that my past does not have to be the final word over my future.
And Lord, if I have been walking away with blessings in my hands while neglecting You in my heart…
Teach me to return.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be having nothing left in your hands.
It would be having everything you once prayed for—and forgetting the Savior who is worth more than all of it.
Don't become so grateful for the miracle that you forget to fall at the feet of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD COMPARED HIS PEOPLE TO ANIMALS IN HEAT—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS IDOLATRY IS HARMLESS
paragraphs: GOD COMPARED HIS PEOPLE TO ANIMALS IN HEAT—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS IDOLATRY IS HARMLESS

Jeremiah 2:23–25 reveals a disturbing picture of spiritual unfaithfulness, the terrifying power of uncontrolled desire, and the relentless mercy of a God whose people kept running toward everything except Him.
There are things in the Bible that make you uncomfortable because they are difficult to understand.
And then there are things that make you uncomfortable because, once you understand them, you realize God may be describing you.
This is one of those passages.

God looked at His own covenant people—people who knew His name, remembered His miracles, possessed His commandments, and claimed to belong to Him—and compared their pursuit of false gods to animals driven by mating instincts.
Not lost sheep.
Not frightened lambs.
Animals in heat.
The language is startling. Almost embarrassing. Certainly not the kind of imagery most people expect to hear during a comfortable Sunday sermon.
But God did not choose those images accidentally.
He was exposing something that religious appearances could no longer conceal.
Something about desire.
Something about addiction.
Something about what happens when the human heart begins loving the things that are destroying it.
And before you decide this passage belongs only to ancient Israel, consider one uncomfortable question.
What if the idols you keep running toward are the very things you keep asking God to deliver you from?
Because the most frightening part of Jeremiah 2 is not the comparison to animals.
It is the response of people who had become so attached to their idols that they no longer wanted to stop.
Listen carefully.
The prophet Jeremiah records these words:

“How canst thou say, I am not polluted, I have not gone after Baalim? see thy way in the valley, know what thou hast done: thou art a swift dromedary traversing her ways; A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away? all they that seek her will not weary themselves; in her month they shall find her. Withhold thy foot from being unshod, and thy throat from thirst: but thou saidst, There is no hope: no; for I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.”
— Jeremiah 2:23–25, King James Version
Read those final words again.
“For I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.”
Not merely, “I made a mistake.”
Not, “I fell into temptation.”
Not even, “I did not realize what I was doing.”
But, in effect:
I love what is pulling me away from God.
And I intend to keep pursuing it.
That is where the passage becomes devastating.
Because God was not simply confronting sinful behavior.
He was confronting a heart that had begun defending its captivity.
And there is a difference.
A person can stumble into sin and grieve over it.
A person can struggle against temptation and desperately desire freedom.
But something more dangerous happens when the heart starts calling its chains a choice.
When compromise becomes an identity.
When the thing that once produced conviction begins producing excuses.
When someone no longer asks, “Lord, how do I escape this?”
But quietly decides, “I cannot imagine living without it.”
That is the spiritual condition Jeremiah was exposing.
And the original Hebrew makes the picture even more disturbing.
In Jeremiah 2:23, the people are compared to a young female camel, described with the Hebrew expression בִּכְרָה קַלָּה (bikhrāh qallāh).
The picture is of a swift young camel moving restlessly along her paths.
The Hebrew text portrays uncontrolled, wandering movement. The animal imagery communicates agitation and pursuit rather than settled direction.
Then Jeremiah intensifies the comparison.
He describes a wild female donkey accustomed to the wilderness, sniffing the wind in her desire.
The Hebrew phrase בְּאַוַּת נַפְשָׁהּ (be'avvat nafshāh) expresses the desire or craving of her being.
The passage describes the animal during its mating season, when its reproductive urge makes it readily discoverable by those seeking it.
God uses that startling picture to expose the intensity of Judah's pursuit of other gods.
The point is not that sexual desire itself is sinful.
God created sexuality, and Scripture honors its proper expression within marriage.
The point is that desire becomes destructive when it escapes its rightful boundaries and begins ruling the one who should be governing it.
Israel was not merely being tempted by idolatry.
The people were actively pursuing it.
They were not simply being dragged away.
They were running.
And that changes how we understand the passage.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to our spiritual lives is not something we hate.
It is something we love too much.
Think about that.
A person may hate the consequences of a sin while still loving the sin itself.
They may hate the guilt afterward.
Hate the secrecy.
Hate the damage to their relationships.
Hate the distance they feel from God.
Yet still return to the very thing that wounded them.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until the cycle becomes painfully familiar.
The promise.
The surrender.
The temporary satisfaction.
The emptiness.
The regret.
The prayer.
And then the return.
Not every repeated struggle means a person has hardened their heart. Genuine believers can fight long and painful battles against sin.
But Jeremiah warns us about something beyond the struggle itself.
He warns us about the moment we stop resisting and begin justifying.
The moment we stop grieving and begin celebrating what God has called us to leave behind.
The moment our hearts say what Judah said:
“I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.”
And here is what makes the entire chapter even more heartbreaking.
God was not speaking as an indifferent observer.
He was speaking as the covenant Lord whose people had betrayed Him.
Earlier, in Jeremiah 2:2, God remembers Israel's early devotion, using the language of bridal love.
He recalls the relationship that once characterized His people.
Then, in Jeremiah 2:5, He asks a question that should make every believer stop:
“What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain?”
What wrong had they found in Him?
What failure?
What unfaithfulness?
Had He abandoned them in Egypt?
Had He forgotten them in the wilderness?
Had He refused to provide?
Had He broken His covenant promises?
No.
The tragedy was not that God had proven unworthy of their devotion.
The tragedy was that they had exchanged the worthy God for worthless substitutes.
And Jeremiah 2:13 exposes the exchange:
“For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.”
There it is.
The anatomy of idolatry.
They abandoned a fountain.
And dug broken containers.
They turned away from the source of life.
And exhausted themselves trying to manufacture satisfaction.
Imagine someone standing beside a flowing spring of clean, refreshing water.
The water is freely available.
The supply is abundant.
Yet that person turns away, picks up a tool, and begins digging into dry ground.
Their hands blister.
Their strength fades.
They finally finish their cistern.
But it is cracked.
Every drop leaks away.
So they dig another.
And another.
And another.
Still thirsty.
Still desperate.
Still convinced that the next broken container will finally satisfy them.
That is the picture God gives of idolatry.
And it is painfully recognizable.
Some people dig their cisterns in money.
They tell themselves that once they earn enough, they will finally feel secure.
But the number keeps changing.
Some dig in human approval.
They cannot rest unless someone notices them, praises them, desires them, or validates their existence.
Some dig in sexual pleasure.
Some in status.
Some in control.
Some in resentment.
Some in the need to win every argument.
Some in a relationship they know is pulling them away from obedience to Christ.
And some even dig their cisterns inside religious activity.
They love being recognized as spiritual.
They love the platform.
The attention.
The reputation.
The appearance of holiness.
But somewhere along the way, they begin loving what ministry gives them more than the Savior whom ministry is supposed to glorify.
That possibility should sober every Christian, including anyone who writes, teaches, preaches, or leads in Jesus' name.
Because an idol is not always an obviously wicked object.
Sometimes it is a good thing elevated into the place that belongs to God alone.
Work can be good.
Marriage can be good.
Family can be good.
Achievement can be good.
Even ministry can be good.
But none of these things can carry the weight of being our ultimate source of identity, security, righteousness, or hope.
Only God can occupy that place.
And when we demand from created things what only the Creator can provide, we place impossible expectations upon them.
Then we become angry when they fail us.
We become anxious when they are threatened.
We become desperate when they disappear.
Not necessarily because those things are evil.
But because we have asked them to become gods.
And false gods cannot save.
They cannot forgive sin.
They cannot reconcile us to the Father.
They cannot conquer death.
They cannot give eternal life.
They cannot carry the full weight of a human soul.
Only Jesus Christ can.
But there is another detail in Jeremiah 2:25 that deserves our attention.
God says:
“Withhold thy foot from being unshod, and thy throat from thirst.”
The imagery suggests the exhausting consequences of pursuing false gods.
Feet worn by restless wandering.
A throat parched by thirst.
A life spent chasing something that never truly satisfies.
And what is the people's response?
“There is no hope.”
The Hebrew word נוֹאָשׁ (nō'āsh) conveys despair or the sense that the situation is beyond remedy.
But notice what follows.
“For I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.”
Their statement of hopelessness becomes entangled with their determination to continue.
It is as though they are saying:
There is no point trying to stop.
I love these other gods.
I will keep following them.
How many people have said something similar without realizing it?
“I've always been this way.”
“I've tried changing before.”
“God knows my heart.”
“Everybody struggles with something.”
“I can't help what I feel.”
“This is just who I am.”
Some of those statements may arise from genuine pain, exhaustion, or confusion. They are not automatically proof of rebellion.
But they become spiritually dangerous when we use them to declare that repentance is impossible or obedience is unnecessary.
Because the Gospel never teaches that sin is harmless.
And it never teaches that sinners are beyond the reach of grace.
Both truths matter.
You are not permitted to make peace with what Christ died to redeem you from.
But neither are you required to believe that your failures are stronger than His saving power.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying a struggle nobody knows about.
You have prayed.
You have cried.
You have made promises you could not keep.
You have looked at yourself afterward and wondered whether your repentance was ever real.
Perhaps you have become so ashamed that even opening your Bible feels difficult.
You assume every verse is another accusation.
Every sermon another reminder.
Every prayer another opportunity to disappoint God.
And perhaps you have started avoiding Him because you are afraid of what His holiness will expose.
But listen carefully.
The God who exposes idolatry is also the God who calls sinners to return.
His warnings are not invitations to despair.
They are summonses to repentance.
Jeremiah's message was severe because Judah's rebellion was severe.
The chapter must not be reduced to a motivational speech about personal habits. It concerns covenant unfaithfulness, false worship, moral corruption, and a nation refusing to acknowledge its sin.
Yet the wider prophetic witness also reveals God's promise to restore His people.
In Jeremiah 3:12, the Lord calls His faithless people to return and declares His mercy.
And in Jeremiah 3:22, we hear this extraordinary invitation:
“Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings.”
Not merely expose them.
Not merely condemn them.
Heal them.
Do you see the difference?
The same God who refuses to flatter our sin is willing to receive those who turn back to Him.
He does not heal by pretending the disease is harmless.
He heals by confronting what is destroying us.
And that brings us to the center of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ.
Because if Jeremiah 2 reveals the unfaithfulness of God's people, the New Testament reveals the astonishing faithfulness of the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
The Gospel is not the story of humanity finally becoming good enough to deserve God.
It is the story of God acting in grace to save people who could never save themselves.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully repaired our lives.
Not after every temptation disappeared.
Not after we had proved ourselves worthy.
Christ died for sinners.
But His grace is not permission to continue worshiping idols.
It is the power and invitation to turn from them.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires.
Grace does not simply comfort us while leaving our idols untouched.
Grace teaches us to say no to what is destroying us.
And yes to the Lord who gave Himself for us.
Consider the encounter between Jesus and the Samaritan woman in John 4.
She came to a well.
She needed water.
Jesus spoke to her about living water.
He also exposed the painful truth about her relationships.
He knew what was hidden.
He knew what had happened.
He knew the history she carried.
And yet He continued speaking with her.
He offered her something greater than the water she had come to draw.
He offered living water.
Do not miss the connection.
In Jeremiah, God's people forsook the fountain of living waters.
In John, Jesus offers living water to a woman whose life carried deep personal and spiritual complications.
The passages have their own historical contexts, but together they illuminate a glorious biblical truth:
The satisfaction humanity cannot manufacture is found in the life God gives through His Son.
Jesus did not tell the woman that truth no longer mattered.
He did not ignore her circumstances.
But neither did He treat her as someone unworthy of hearing the truth about eternal life.
And what happened?
She went back to her community.
She began telling people about Jesus.
The woman who had come to draw water became a witness to the One who offered living water.
That is what grace can do.
It can take the very life you thought had been reduced to shame and make it a testimony to the mercy of Christ.
Not because the past becomes good.
Not because sin stops being serious.
But because Jesus is greater than the sin He came to forgive.
And there is something else you need to understand.
The answer to idolatry is not merely stronger self-discipline.
Self-control matters. Scripture commands it, and the Holy Spirit produces it in believers.
Practical boundaries matter.
Accountability matters.
Confession matters.
Sometimes pastoral support, counseling, or specialized help may also be necessary, particularly where destructive patterns have become deeply entrenched.
But none of these things can replace the deepest need of the human heart.
A new relationship with God through Jesus Christ.
A changed heart.
A new allegiance.
A life increasingly shaped by the Holy Spirit.
Ezekiel 36:26 records God's promise:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”
That is more than behavior management.
It is transformation.
And it helps us understand why the Gospel is so much greater than simply telling people to try harder.
Jesus did not come merely to make sinners more respectable.
He came to save them.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died for sins.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
The Christian life then becomes a lifelong journey of learning to reject what once mastered us and to love the Savior who has redeemed us.
That journey may include painful battles.
There may be tears.
There may be moments when the old temptations feel frighteningly familiar.
But the presence of a battle does not mean that Christ has abandoned His people.
And the reality of grace does not mean we should surrender to sin.
Romans 6:12 says:
“Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof.”
Notice the language.
Do not let sin reign.
Sin wants a throne.
It wants authority.
It wants obedience.
It wants to become the voice that determines what you do, where you go, what you hide, and whom you serve.
But the throne of a redeemed life belongs to Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the question this passage has been leading us toward all along.
What has been sitting on the throne of your heart while you have been calling Jesus your Lord?
Is it a relationship?
A secret habit?
Your reputation?
Your money?
Your bitterness?
Your fear of being alone?
Your need to be admired?
Your refusal to forgive?
Or something so deeply woven into your daily routine that you have stopped recognizing it as a rival to God?
You do not have to answer publicly.
But you do need to answer truthfully before the Lord.
Because God already knows.
And hiding from the One who sees everything does not produce freedom.
It only deepens the exhaustion.
Remember Judah's worn feet.
Remember the parched throat.
Remember the restless animal chasing desire.
That is what the passage wants us to see.
Not merely the ugliness of idolatry.
But its futility.
All that running.
All that longing.
All that chasing.
And still no rest.
Still no living water.
Still no salvation.
And here is the heartbreaking irony.
The people were running away from the very God who could satisfy their deepest need.
Maybe you have been doing the same.
Running from prayer because you feel ashamed.
Running from Scripture because you fear conviction.
Running from Christian fellowship because you do not want anyone asking difficult questions.
Running toward distractions because silence makes you confront what is happening inside.
Running toward temporary comforts because surrender feels frightening.
And all the while, the invitation of Christ remains.
Come to Me.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
He is not inviting people to continue carrying their idols as masters.
He is calling the weary to Himself.
To trust Him.
To learn from Him.
To find rest in Him.
And that invitation is still precious today.
Not because repentance is easy.
But because the Savior is worthy.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because His mercy is extraordinary.
Not because we can rescue ourselves.
But because Christ is mighty to save.
There is a difference between being exposed and being abandoned.
Jeremiah exposes.
The Gospel reveals the Savior.
The Holy Spirit convicts.
And the grace of God calls sinners to repent and believe.
So if this passage has uncovered something in your life, do not waste the moment by simply feeling guilty.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it to God.
Stop defending what He is calling you to surrender.
Seek the help you need.
Turn toward Christ.
And take the next faithful step of obedience.
You may not be able to undo every consequence of yesterday.
You may need to rebuild trust.
You may need to apologize.
You may need to end a compromising relationship, remove access to a recurring temptation, seek wise counsel, or admit something you have been hiding.
Grace does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
But it does promise something greater than a spotless reputation.
Forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
A restored relationship with God.
And the hope of a life being transformed by His Spirit.
That is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because rebellion is romantic.
Not because every story ends with instant earthly restoration.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem sinners whose pasts cannot be rewritten by human effort.
He does not change the historical facts of what happened.
He changes what becomes possible through His saving grace.
The cross tells us sin is serious enough to require the death of the Son of God.
The resurrection tells us death itself did not have the final word.
And the Gospel tells us that the person you have been does not have to determine the person you will remain.
Perhaps that is why this message needs to travel beyond the people who already agree with it.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be smiling in public while privately losing a battle with temptation.
Someone in your family may have quietly concluded that God could never welcome them back.
Someone you know may be trapped between loving an idol and hating what that idol has done to their life.
They may never tell you.
But they may read what you share.
Not to advertise your spirituality.
Not to shame someone else.
But because biblical truth deserves to be heard, and someone may need the reminder that repentance and forgiveness are still possible through Jesus.
Not because every sentence is easy to receive.
But because there may come another day when your heart begins negotiating with something God has already told you to surrender.
On that day, return to Jeremiah 2.
Remember the broken cisterns.
Remember the exhausted pursuit.
Remember the fountain of living waters.
And remember the Savior who calls the weary to Himself.
I also want to invite you into something deeper than reading one article and moving on.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep placing Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, conviction, and discipleship resources before people who want to grow in their knowledge of Jesus Christ.
These resources are offered to help believers study the Bible, strengthen their faith, understand the Gospel, and continue growing in Christ.
For Christians who choose to give in this way, that support can be an expression of generosity and stewardship offered in gratitude to God.
But I want to be clear about something important.
Our salvation is God's gift through Christ, not something purchased through religious payments.
And Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Writing.
Research.
Publishing.
Resource development.
Outreach.
And the continuing effort to make biblical encouragement accessible to people who need it.
Those products can be useful reminders of Scripture and encouraging gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to help keep Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources reaching people.
Inviting a friend to read Scripture costs nothing.
Encouraging someone to return to Jesus costs nothing.
Following Gospel Warrior and sharing biblical resources can help others discover the teaching and encouragement they have been searching for.
Not about merchandise.
Not even about the number of people who might see this article.
About your heart.
When Jeremiah confronted God's people, the most devastating part of their response was not that they had fallen.
It was that they insisted on continuing.
“I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.”
What if today becomes the day you stop saying that?
What if today you stop defending the thing that has been draining your peace?
What if you stop calling your chains comfort?
What if you finally admit that the thing you keep chasing cannot give you the life you are asking it to provide?
What if you stop running?
Not because you have suddenly become strong enough.
But because you have finally recognized that Jesus is worthy of your surrender.
Not as a public performance.
Not as a substitute for genuine repentance.
But as a simple acknowledgment that you want to walk in the light.
Your words may encourage someone who believes their story is beyond redemption.
There is no magic in a comment.
No salvation in a phrase.
No spiritual reward earned by public engagement.
But there can be real encouragement when believers speak truthfully about God's mercy and point one another back to Jesus Christ.
So be honest with yourself.
And be honest before God.
What have you been chasing?
What has it cost you?
What has it promised that it never delivered?
And what would repentance look like in your life today?
Do not rush past those questions.
Because Jeremiah 2:23–25 was never intended to be a strange biblical curiosity.
It was a mirror held before a people who had forgotten the God who loved and delivered them.
And sometimes, when Scripture holds up a mirror, the most merciful thing we can do is stop looking away.
There is still a fountain.
There is still a Savior.
There is still forgiveness for the sinner who turns to Christ.
There is still grace sufficient to call us out of darkness and teach us to walk in the light.
So bring your restless heart to Jesus.
Bring your hidden failures.
Bring your excuses.
Bring your thirst.
Bring the desires you have allowed to rule you.
And ask Him to teach you to love what is holy, to hate what destroys, and to walk in the freedom of obedience to His Word.
Because the deepest tragedy is not simply that you once chased something that could never satisfy you.
It is that you could spend your whole life running from the Fountain while dying of thirst beside it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A WOMAN PRAYED SO DESPERATELY THAT A PRIEST THOUGHT SHE WAS DRUNK. BUT GOD HEARD EVERY WORD SHE NEVER SPOKE.
paragraphs: A WOMAN PRAYED SO DESPERATELY THAT A PRIEST THOUGHT SHE WAS DRUNK. BUT GOD HEARD EVERY WORD SHE NEVER SPOKE.
They judged her by what they could see. God listened to what they could not hear. And what happened next would change more than one woman's life. — 1 Samuel 1:12–16
There is a kind of pain that makes you cry.
And then there is a kind of pain that takes away your ability to explain why you are crying.
You still get out of bed. You still answer messages. You still show up for people. You still smile when somebody asks how you're doing.
But somewhere behind that smile, something is breaking.
And the hardest part?
Sometimes the people who are supposed to understand your pain are the very people who misunderstand it.
Imagine walking into the house of God with the last little bit of strength you have left, desperately needing mercy, only to be accused of something you never did.
Imagine being so broken that your lips are moving in prayer, but no sound is coming out.
And imagine a priest looking at you and deciding that you must be drunk.
That is not a fictional scene.
That is what happened to a woman named Hannah.
And if you have ever been misunderstood while fighting a battle nobody could see, her story may reach somewhere in your heart that you have kept locked for years.
But there is something even more important about Hannah's story.
It is not merely about a woman who desperately wanted a child.

It is about the God who hears the afflicted, the danger of judging what we do not understand, the surrender of our deepest desires, and the astonishing way God's redemptive purposes can unfold through ordinary human suffering.
And ultimately, it points us toward Jesus Christ, the greater gift of God, who came to redeem people whose tears could never save them.
Because sometimes the most important thing happening in a room is something nobody else can hear.
Hannah had been carrying a sorrow that would not leave.
The opening chapter of 1 Samuel introduces her as one of Elkanah's two wives. The other wife, Peninnah, had children. Hannah had none.
The biblical writer repeats this painful contrast because it is central to the story.
In the social world of ancient Israel, childlessness could carry profound grief and social vulnerability. But Scripture does not teach that a woman's worth depends upon motherhood.
Hannah's dignity was never determined by her ability to bear a child.
Yet her longing was real.
And her suffering was intensified by someone who knew exactly where she was hurting.
Peninnah provoked her severely, year after year.
Not once.
Not accidentally.
Year after year.
According to 1 Samuel 1:6–7, this provocation happened repeatedly, especially when the family went up to worship the Lord.
Think about that.
The place associated with worship had also become a place where Hannah's private grief was exposed.
She came to worship, and somebody reminded her of what she did not have.
She came to seek God, and somebody found another way to wound her.
She came carrying disappointment, and somebody made sure she felt it.
Have you ever experienced that?
You are already fighting to keep your faith alive, and somebody makes a careless remark.
You are grieving a loss, and somebody tells you to move on.
You are waiting for an answer, and somebody casually announces the very blessing you have been praying for.
You are trying to heal, and somebody treats your wound like a weakness.
And because you do not want to appear bitter, you swallow the hurt.
Again.
And again.
Until the pain becomes part of your daily life.
Hannah knew something about that kind of suffering.
Scripture says she wept and would not eat.
Her husband loved her. He even tried to comfort her.
In 1 Samuel 1:8, Elkanah asked why she was weeping and whether he was not more to her than ten sons.
His affection was genuine.
But his words could not erase her longing.
And there is a lesson here that many people desperately need to understand.
Someone can truly love you and still fail to understand the depth of what you are carrying.
That does not always make them cruel.
It makes them human.
But it also means that even the people closest to us cannot become what only God can be.
There are burdens a husband cannot remove.
There are wounds a wife cannot heal.
There are questions a parent cannot answer.
There are nights when even the most compassionate friend cannot reach the deepest part of your sorrow.
And that is where Hannah's story becomes painfully familiar.
Because one day, after eating and drinking at Shiloh, Hannah rose.
The Bible does not describe every thought that crossed her mind.
It does not tell us how long she had been rehearsing this prayer.
It does not say whether she had reached some dramatic emotional breaking point.
But it tells us what she did.
She went before the Lord.
Not because her life had become easier.
Not because Peninnah had stopped provoking her.
Not because she had received a promise that everything would turn out as she hoped.
She prayed while the problem was still there.
And that matters.
Because biblical faith is not pretending that suffering does not hurt.
Faith brings suffering into the presence of God.
Then came the prayer that a priest completely misunderstood.
First Samuel 1:10 describes Hannah as deeply distressed, praying to the Lord and weeping bitterly.
The Hebrew expression translated as bitter of soul is מָרַת נָפֶשׁ — marat nefesh.
It conveys profound inward anguish.
This was not a casual prayer offered between ordinary activities.
This was a wounded woman bringing the weight of her heart before God.
She asked the Lord to remember her and grant her a son. She also vowed that if God gave her a son, she would give him to the Lord for his lifetime (1 Samuel 1:11).
Her prayer was intensely personal.
But it was also an act of surrender.
She was asking for something she deeply desired while pledging to dedicate the gift to God's service.
And then Scripture records an extraordinary detail.
“Now Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard.” — 1 Samuel 1:13, KJV
Read that again.
She spoke in her heart.
Her lips moved.
But her voice was not heard.
In Hebrew, the phrase is:
רַק שְׂפָתֶיהָ נָּעוֹת וְקוֹלָהּ לֹא יִשָּׁמֵעַ
Raq sefatéha na'ot, veqolah lo yishaméa.
The sense is straightforward: only her lips were moving, and her voice was not being heard.
There is no need to invent a mysterious hidden meaning.
The plain meaning is already powerful.
Hannah was praying silently.
And the Lord did not need an audible voice to know what she was saying.
Somebody needs to hear that.
You do not have to manufacture impressive words to be heard by God.
You do not have to sound strong when you are weak.
You do not have to turn every prayer into a beautiful speech.
Sometimes your prayer is interrupted by tears.
Sometimes you cannot get beyond, “Lord, help me.”
Sometimes you sit in silence because you are afraid that if you begin speaking, everything you have been holding together will fall apart.
God is not limited by the weakness of your vocabulary.
Psalm 139:4 teaches that the Lord knows our words before they are spoken.
Romans 8:26–27 teaches that the Spirit helps believers in their weakness when they do not know what to pray as they ought.
Those passages do not promise that every request will be granted.
They reveal something far more foundational.
God's knowledge of His children is not dependent upon their ability to express themselves perfectly.
Your prayer does not become invisible because your pain has made you quiet.
But Eli, the priest, was watching Hannah.
And he reached the wrong conclusion.
He assumed she was drunk.
First Samuel 1:14 records his accusation:
“How long wilt thou be drunken? put away thy wine from thee.” — KJV
Imagine the weight of that moment.
Hannah had been humiliated by her rival.
She had been grieving over her childlessness.
She had come before God in tears.
And now, at the very place where she sought refuge, a religious leader accused her of drunkenness.
He saw her lips.
He did not hear her prayer.
And he interpreted what he saw through an assumption that was wrong.
How many people have experienced something painfully similar?
Someone sees you becoming quiet and calls you arrogant.
Someone sees you crying and calls you unstable.
Someone sees you setting boundaries and calls you rebellious.
Someone sees you struggling spiritually and assumes you have abandoned God.
Someone notices the outward expression of your pain and invents an explanation without ever asking what happened.
That is why Hannah's story is not only about prayer.
It is also a warning against careless spiritual judgment.
Religious authority does not make a person's assumptions infallible.
Eli held a sacred office.
But in this moment, he misread a suffering woman.
And Scripture preserves his mistake.
That should humble anyone who leads, counsels, teaches, or speaks in God's name.
Not every tear is evidence of unbelief.
Not every silence is rebellion.
Not every exhausted believer needs a rebuke.
Sometimes the person sitting quietly in the back of the church is fighting harder to hold on to faith than anybody realizes.
Sometimes the person who has stopped volunteering is overwhelmed.
Sometimes the woman who cannot stop crying needs compassion before correction.
Sometimes the man who seems distant is carrying a grief he does not know how to explain.
We must not confuse discernment with suspicion.
Jesus taught His followers to judge rightly rather than merely by outward appearance (John 7:24).
And the Lord reminded Samuel later in this same biblical book that human beings look at outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
What a striking connection.
In the opening chapter, Eli misjudged Hannah by what he could see.
Later, God would teach Samuel himself not to make the same mistake.
And Samuel was the very son Hannah would bear.
But before that promise unfolded, Hannah had to answer an accusation.
Her response deserves our attention.
She did not pretend the priest was right.
She did not accept a false label merely because it came from someone with religious authority.
She answered respectfully, but truthfully.
“No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 1:15, KJV
There it is.
One of the most moving descriptions of prayer in the Old Testament.
“I have poured out my soul before the LORD.”
The Hebrew expression is:
וָאֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת־נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי יְהוָה
Va'eshpokh et-nafshi lifnei Adonai.

Literally, the language speaks of pouring out one's nefesh—one's soul, life, or inner self—before the Lord. Adonai is used here in reading aloud the divine name represented by the four Hebrew letters YHWH.
Hannah was not describing a special prayer technique.
She was describing wholehearted honesty before God.
She brought her grief.
Her longing.
Her humiliation.
Her unanswered questions.
Her hope.
She did not have to disguise any of it.
And perhaps that is where this story meets you today.
Because you have been trying to pray like someone who has everything together.
You have been editing your emotions before bringing them to God.
You have been saying, “I'm fine, Lord,” when you are not fine.
You have been afraid that admitting your disappointment would make you ungrateful.
Afraid that confessing your exhaustion would make you faithless.
Afraid that acknowledging your questions would make you a bad Christian.
But Hannah did not hide her anguish.
She poured it out.
And Scripture does not condemn her for doing so.
The Psalms repeatedly show God's people bringing lament, fear, confusion, and sorrow into His presence.
God does not command His children to become emotionally dishonest in order to approach Him.
He calls them to trust Him.
And trust can speak through tears.
But here is the part of Hannah's story that we must not turn into a false promise.
Hannah eventually received the son she requested.
His name was Samuel.
But that does not mean every believer who prays intensely for a child will conceive.
It does not mean every illness will be healed in this life.
It does not mean every broken marriage will be restored.
It does not mean every financial crisis will disappear.
And it certainly does not mean that someone whose prayer remains unanswered simply did not have enough faith.
That would be a cruel misuse of Scripture.
Hannah's story records a particular act of God's providence within the unfolding history of Israel.
It is not a universal formula guaranteeing that intense prayer produces the outcome we desire.
The apostle Paul pleaded with the Lord about his thorn in the flesh, yet the Lord answered by declaring the sufficiency of His grace (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane that the cup might pass from Him, while submitting to the Father's will (Luke 22:42).
And Hebrews 11 remembers both those who experienced astonishing deliverance and those who endured suffering without receiving the fullness of what they hoped for in their earthly lives.
Biblical faith is not measured by whether we receive the outcome we requested.
It is anchored in the character of the God to whom we pray.
And that is why what happens next in Hannah's story is so beautiful.
After Hannah explained herself, Eli answered her with a blessing of peace and expressed the hope that the God of Israel would grant her petition.
Then 1 Samuel 1:18 says she went her way, ate, and her face was no longer sad.
Notice the timing.
She had not yet conceived.
Samuel had not yet been born.
The circumstances had not yet visibly changed.
And yet something had shifted.
The text does not explain every detail of Hannah's inward experience, so we should not pretend to know more than Scripture reveals.
But it does show a woman who rose from prayer and resumed eating before the answer became visible.
There is something deeply moving about that.
Not because her suffering had been imaginary.
Not because she had received a guarantee that all her desires would be fulfilled.
But because her story reminds us that we can entrust our burdens to God even while the future remains unknown.
Some of you are waiting for a miracle.
Others are waiting for the courage to survive another ordinary day.
Some are praying for children.
Some are praying for reconciliation.
Some are praying for freedom from a sin that has kept them ashamed.
Some are asking God to help them forgive someone who never apologized.
Some are grieving people who will never walk through the door again.
And some have stopped asking for a particular outcome because disappointment has become too painful.
Wherever you are, hear this carefully.
You are not required to pretend that the waiting does not hurt in order to trust the Lord while you wait.
And if you are struggling to trust Him at all, you can tell Him that too.
He already knows.
Eventually, Scripture says the Lord remembered Hannah.
That phrase does not mean God had previously forgotten she existed.
In biblical language, God's remembering often signals His faithful action toward someone within His covenant purposes.
Hannah conceived and bore a son.
She named him Samuel, connecting his birth with her request to the Lord.
And when the child was weaned, Hannah brought him to the house of the Lord at Shiloh.
There, she spoke words that complete the earlier scene.
She identified herself to Eli as the woman who had stood near him praying.
Then she declared:
“For this child I prayed; and the LORD hath given me my petition which I asked of him.” — 1 Samuel 1:27, KJV
Imagine Eli hearing those words.
The woman he had mistaken for a drunkard was now standing before him with the child for whom she had prayed.
The biblical text does not tell us Eli's private reaction.
It does not record an apology.
It does not describe a dramatic public vindication.
And we should not invent those details.
But the contrast is unmistakable.
He had misunderstood her silent prayer.
God had heard her petition.
And Hannah did not keep the child as though the blessing belonged to her independently of the Giver.
She fulfilled her vow and dedicated Samuel to the Lord's service.
That surrender is crucial.
Because the heart of this story is not simply, “Hannah prayed until God gave her what she wanted.”
It is also that Hannah recognized the gift as belonging to the Lord.
Her answered prayer became an occasion for worship and dedication.
And Samuel's life would matter far beyond Hannah's household.
He would become a prophet and judge in Israel, and he would play a significant role in the transition to the monarchy, including the anointing of David.
From David's royal line, according to the New Testament, Jesus Christ would come.
That does not mean Hannah understood the full scope of the future when she prayed.
It means that within the biblical narrative, her personal suffering and God's larger redemptive purposes intersected in a remarkable way.
But even Samuel was not the ultimate answer to humanity's deepest need.
Jesus is.
And this is where Hannah's story must lead us if we are going to read it as Christians.
Because our greatest problem is not that life has denied us something we desperately want.
Our greatest problem is that sin has separated humanity from the holy God who created us.
We need more than relief.
We need redemption.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And that Savior did not come merely to teach hurting people how to cope.
He came to rescue sinners through His life, death, and resurrection.
Jesus knows what it means to be misunderstood.
He was falsely accused.
He was rejected.
He was mocked.
He endured injustice.
He wept.
And in Gethsemane, He experienced such profound anguish that Luke describes Him praying earnestly as He approached the cross.
But Jesus was not simply another misunderstood sufferer.
He was the sinless Son of God, willingly giving Himself for sinners.
“Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.” — 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, KJV
This is the center of the Gospel.
Not that God will always give us the life we imagined.
But that Jesus Christ gave His life to reconcile us to God.
Not that our tears earn salvation.
But that Christ's blood secures redemption for those who belong to Him.
Not that our prayers make us righteous.
But that sinners are justified by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
The New Testament word often translated grace is χάρις — charis.
It speaks of favor or gift, and in the context of salvation, God's grace is undeserved.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes clear that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our works.
That means the person with a beautiful testimony needs grace.
The person with a shameful past needs grace.
The person who has been faithful for decades needs grace.
The person who has just fallen into sin needs grace.
The person who can barely whisper a prayer needs grace.
And the person who has been pretending to be spiritually strong while secretly falling apart needs grace too.
But grace does not leave us unchanged.
It calls us to repentance, faith, and a transformed life in Christ.
That is why our message is not simply about turning painful experiences into inspirational stories.
It is about a crucified and risen Savior who redeems sinners.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by promising that every consequence disappears.
But by forgiving repentant sinners, restoring fellowship with God, and making all things new according to His redemptive purposes.
Think about Hannah again.
She entered the house of the Lord with a sorrow others could not understand.
Her lips moved.
Her voice was not heard.
A priest misjudged her.
But her suffering was not hidden from God.
Now think about your own life.
What have you been carrying that nobody knows?
What prayer have you been afraid to pray again?
What disappointment have you covered with a smile?
What sin have you been hiding because you are terrified of what people would think if they knew?
What wound have you allowed to harden into resentment?
What part of your life have you quietly decided is beyond redemption?
Perhaps today is not the day you receive the answer you have been waiting for.
Perhaps today is the day you stop pretending before God.
The day you confess what needs to be confessed.
The day you release the bitterness you have been feeding.
The day you ask someone trustworthy to pray with you.
The day you return to Christ after months or years of wandering.
The day you acknowledge that you cannot save yourself.
And if you have never truly entrusted your life to Jesus Christ, do not mistake religious activity for reconciliation with God.
You can attend church and still need repentance.
You can know Bible verses and still need forgiveness.
You can admire Jesus and still need to surrender to Him as Lord.
The invitation of the Gospel is not to become impressive enough for God to accept you.
It is to turn from sin and trust in the Savior who died and rose again.
And if you are already His, come to Him with your burdens.
Not because He promises an easy life.
But because He is faithful.
Because He is merciful.
Because His grace is sufficient even when the answer is not what you hoped.
And because the final chapter of the believer's story is not written by grief, accusation, or death.
It belongs to the risen Christ.
I wonder how many people reading this have been carrying a Hannah-like sorrow in silence.
How many are still attending church while grieving privately?
How many are faithfully serving others while secretly exhausted?
How many have been misjudged because somebody saw their behavior but never understood their battle?
If that is you, I want to invite you to do something simple, but meaningful.
You do not have to expose private details or tell strangers everything you are going through.
Someone who is barely holding on may need to hear that Christ remained faithful to you.
Not because your story guarantees their outcome.
But because your testimony may remind them where to place their hope.
And if this article brought someone to your mind, please do not ignore that thought.
Send it privately to someone who has been struggling.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who have grown weary, those who have drifted from their faith, and even those who are still searching for truth.
Not to build a following around a personality.
But to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe in the mission of Gospel Warrior.
Every article, every biblical reflection, every discipleship resource, and every message of encouragement is part of an effort to help people encounter the truth of God's Word.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, you have an opportunity to help that work continue and expand.
Some believers may prayerfully choose to make this part of their regular Christian giving.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not driven by pressure or guilt (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your prayers matter.
Your sharing matters.
Your faithful witness matters.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in their understanding of Scripture, strengthen their walk with Christ, and become better equipped to live out the Gospel.
Because we do not want you merely to feel moved by an article for a few minutes.
We want to see people opening their Bibles.
Learning to pray.
Repenting of sin.
Growing in holiness.
Loving their families.
Serving their churches.
Discerning truth.
And becoming more deeply rooted in Jesus Christ.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
Jesus Christ is.
A ministry may publish thousands of words, but only God can give spiritual life.
A message may reach millions of screens, but the Holy Spirit is the One who convicts hearts through the truth.
It would be one more person turning from sin and trusting Jesus Christ.
One more weary believer finding renewed strength in His Word.
One more wounded soul learning to bring honest prayers before the Lord.
One more life transformed by the Gospel.
A woman is praying.
Her lips are moving.
Her voice cannot be heard.
A priest is watching.
He thinks he understands.
He does not.
And the God of Israel knows exactly what is happening.
That is where this story began.
But it is not where the Bible leaves us.
Years later, Hannah's son Samuel would serve the Lord.
Generations later, the promised Son of David would come.
And through His cross and resurrection, Jesus Christ would accomplish something infinitely greater than the removal of one woman's sorrow.
He would open the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
So bring Him your grief.
Bring Him your confession.
Bring Him your questions.
Bring Him the burdens you cannot explain.
And above all, entrust yourself to Jesus Christ.
Because you may spend your whole life being misunderstood by people.
But the Lord who knows your heart is not confused about what is happening inside it.
The world may never hear the prayer that breaks your heart, but God does not need your voice to hear your soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD CALLED HER HIS BRIDE. THEN HE EXPOSED WHAT SHE WAS DOING BEHIND HIS BACK.
paragraphs: GOD CALLED HER HIS BRIDE. THEN HE EXPOSED WHAT SHE WAS DOING BEHIND HIS BACK.

The Bible’s Most Disturbing Marriage Imagery Was Never About Romance. It Was About Idolatry, Spiritual Betrayal, and the Terrifying Possibility of Belonging to God While Giving Your Heart to Something Else.
There are chapters in the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that strengthen you.
And then there are chapters that make you uncomfortable enough to wonder whether God is exposing something you have spent years trying to hide.
Ezekiel 16 and 23 belong to that last category.
They contain some of the most graphic, disturbing, and emotionally devastating marriage imagery in all of Scripture.
God speaks about a bride He rescued, clothed, loved, and entered into covenant with.
Then He describes her betrayal.
Not with the gentle language we might expect from a devotional.
But with shocking accusations of adultery, prostitution, lust, exposure, bloodshed, and judgment.
And here is what makes these chapters especially difficult.
The betrayed Husband is God Himself.
The unfaithful bride represents His covenant people.
And the other lovers?
They represent the false gods, political powers, and misplaced dependencies that His people pursued while turning away from Him.
But before you dismiss these chapters as ancient history, consider one uncomfortable question.
What if the most frightening part of Ezekiel's prophecy is not what Israel did thousands of years ago?
What if it is how easily we recognize the same divided heart in ourselves?
Because some people have never bowed before a carved idol.
Yet they have sacrificed their peace, integrity, families, and obedience to things they cannot imagine living without.
Some have never entered a pagan temple.
Yet their hearts have become altars to approval, money, pleasure, power, resentment, or the desperate need to be loved.
And some still attend church every Sunday.
Still sing worship songs.
Still post Bible verses.
Still call Jesus Lord.
While quietly protecting the very thing He has been asking them to surrender.
That is where this story becomes painfully personal.
But to understand its warning, we must first understand its original meaning.

Ezekiel was not writing a modern romance or offering a casual comparison between marital infidelity and ordinary human weakness. He was a prophet addressing Judah and Jerusalem in the devastating context of covenant rebellion, approaching judgment, and exile.

The imagery is deliberately severe. These chapters describe sexualized violence, exploitation, and judgment in ways that can be deeply distressing, particularly for survivors of abuse. Their prophetic accusations must not be turned into permission for human cruelty, victim-blaming, or the mistreatment of women.
God is exposing covenant treachery through a shocking ancient prophetic metaphor.
And the story begins somewhere you might not expect.
Not with adultery.
Not with rebellion.
But with an abandoned child.
In Ezekiel 16, Jerusalem is portrayed as an unwanted newborn, left exposed, unwashed, and helpless.
Nobody comes to rescue her.
Nobody covers her.
Nobody treats her as precious.
Then God passes by.
And speaks.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:6 contains the striking command:
בְּדָמַיִךְ חֲיִי
Be-damayikh chayi.
Literally, “In your blood, live!”
The command is repeated in the verse.
“Live!”
Not because the child had earned survival.
Not because she had proven her worth.
Not because she could offer anything in return.
She was helpless.
And God intervened.
That is where the prophetic story begins.
With undeserved mercy.
With a life preserved by the One who had every power to pass by but chose to give life instead.
Perhaps that is the first thing some of us need to remember.
Before your testimony became impressive, you needed mercy.
Before you learned the language of worship, you needed mercy.
Before you knew how to explain grace, you needed grace.
And before you could do anything for God, your life already depended upon Him.
The child grows.
God describes covering her, entering into covenant with her, washing her, clothing her, and adorning her.
In Ezekiel 16:8, the Hebrew expression is:
וָאָבוֹא בִבְרִית אֹתָךְ
Va-avo bivrit otakh.
Meaning, “And I entered into a covenant with you.”
Then comes the extraordinary declaration:
וַתִּהְיִי לִי
Va-tihyi li.
“And you became Mine.”
This is covenant language.
Not merely an emotional attachment.
Not a passing attraction.
Not a relationship maintained only while everything feels pleasant.
God had bound Himself to His people in covenant faithfulness.
The Hebrew word berit (בְּרִית) means covenant: a binding relationship involving commitments and obligations.
Israel's life, calling, and blessings were gifts of divine grace, and the covenant called for faithful allegiance to the Lord.
Then something terrible happened.
The bride began to trust in her beauty.
Ezekiel 16:15 says, in the King James Version:
“But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown.”
Read that slowly.
She did not simply forget the One who rescued her.
She began trusting in what His generosity had given her.
The blessings became the foundation of her self-confidence.
The gifts became more important than the Giver.
The beauty that should have testified to divine mercy became an occasion for pride and unfaithfulness.
And suddenly, the story is no longer safely distant.
Because how often do we pray desperately when we have nothing, only to become spiritually careless when God provides?
We beg for employment.
Then our career becomes more important than obedience.
We pray for financial provision.
Then money becomes the thing that determines whether we feel secure.
We ask God for a relationship.
Then we become willing to compromise His Word because we are terrified of losing that person.
We pray for influence.
Then begin measuring our worth by applause.
We ask Him to open doors.
Then refuse to walk away when those doors lead us toward sin.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment in our spiritual lives is not always when everything falls apart.
Sometimes it is when everything finally seems to be going well.
Because prosperity can reveal what suffering sometimes conceals.
You can receive blessings from God and gradually begin living as though you no longer need Him.
That is the betrayal Ezekiel exposes.
But the prophet does not stop at pride.
He describes Jerusalem using God's gifts in the service of false worship.
The clothing, gold, silver, oil, and food associated with divine generosity are redirected toward idols.
Even more horrifying, Ezekiel 16:20–21 condemns the sacrifice of children.
This was not merely an emotional preference for something other than God.
It involved actual religious corruption, covenant violation, injustice, and bloodshed.
The prophetic marriage metaphor therefore cannot be reduced to a vague lesson about being distracted by modern technology or having an unhealthy hobby.
Those may become idols, but Ezekiel's accusations concern concrete historical sins and their devastating consequences.
And here is the detail that should make every reader tremble.
The people were not simply choosing different religious practices.
They were treating the God who had given them life as though His faithfulness could be exchanged for whatever promised immediate advantage.
They sought security through foreign alliances.
They pursued the worship of other gods.
They placed their confidence in powers that could neither save them nor remain faithful to them.
They wanted the benefits of belonging to God without the demands of covenant loyalty.
Does that sound familiar?
We want forgiveness without confession.
Comfort without surrender.
Blessing without obedience.
A Savior who rescues us from consequences, but not necessarily a Lord who confronts our desires.
We want Jesus near enough to help us.
But sometimes not near enough to challenge what we have decided to keep.
And if that sentence stings, do not rush past it.
Sit with it.
Because the purpose of biblical conviction is not to entertain our shame.
It is to bring what is hidden into the light.
Ezekiel 16:32 uses a particularly direct expression.
הָאִשָּׁה הַמְּנָאָפֶת
Ha-ishah ha-mena'afet.
“The adulterous wife.”
The accusation is not subtle.
The covenant relationship has been betrayed.
Yet one of the most heartbreaking verses appears earlier.
Ezekiel 16:22 declares:
“And in all thine abominations and thy whoredoms thou hast not remembered the days of thy youth.” (KJV)
She forgot.
She forgot the helplessness.
She forgot the rescue.
She forgot the One who said, “Live.”
And perhaps forgetting is where many spiritual disasters begin.
Not always with a dramatic declaration that we no longer believe.
Sometimes with prayer becoming optional.
With Scripture becoming unfamiliar.
With sin becoming explainable.
With conviction becoming inconvenient.
With worship becoming performance.
With the quiet assumption that because God has been patient, He must not be concerned.
Until one day, the things we once resisted become the things we defend.
And the voice we once followed becomes the voice we keep trying to silence.
Have you ever been there?
Have you ever felt the Holy Spirit confronting something, only to find yourself making excuses?
Have you ever asked God for forgiveness while secretly planning to return to the same compromise?
Have you ever looked spiritually healthy in public while knowing your private life was moving in another direction?
There is a kind of exhaustion that comes from trying to appear surrendered while remaining inwardly divided.
You can fool the people around you.
You may even become skilled at explaining yourself to yourself.
But you cannot hide your heart from God.
Then Ezekiel 23 intensifies the warning.
Two sisters appear in the prophetic vision.
Their names are Oholah and Oholibah.
In Hebrew:
אָהֳלָה — Oholah
אָהֳלִיבָה — Oholibah
Their names are commonly understood as “her tent” and “my tent is in her,” respectively, with the second name suggesting God's dwelling presence.
Ezekiel 23:4 identifies them directly.
Oholah represents Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.
Oholibah represents Jerusalem, the capital of Judah.
These are not two ordinary women whose private relationships are being exposed for public entertainment.
They are personifications of two covenant communities.
The prophet uses their imagined sexual conduct to portray the kingdoms' idolatry, political entanglements, and faithlessness.
Oholah's pursuit of Assyria represents the northern kingdom's destructive entanglement with foreign power and false worship.
Oholibah's conduct exposes Jerusalem's pursuit of Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt, alongside her religious and moral corruption.
The historical warning is severe.
The northern kingdom had already suffered catastrophe.
Judah had witnessed it.
Yet Judah continued in rebellion.
That is one of the most unsettling dimensions of Ezekiel 23.
It is possible to witness another person's downfall, understand the warning, and still refuse to change.
We see what addiction did to a family.
Yet insist our private habit is under control.
We see what dishonesty did to a ministry.
Yet excuse our own small deceptions.
We see what pride did to a leader.
Yet quietly cultivate the same hunger for recognition.
We see what bitterness did to a marriage.
Yet continue feeding resentment.
We see people lose what matters most.
And somehow convince ourselves that the same choices will lead us somewhere different.
The human heart can be astonishingly skilled at making exceptions for itself.

Ezekiel 23 also contains explicit sexual descriptions intended to shock its original audience. They should be read in their literary and historical context, not sensationalized or used to suggest that sexuality itself is shameful.
The underlying charge is covenant betrayal.
And the resulting judgment is terrifying.
These chapters describe the devastation of communities that persistently reject God's commands, participate in injustice, and place their trust in powers that ultimately destroy them.
But we must be careful here.
The violence portrayed in these prophecies is not a model for how husbands should treat wives, how churches should discipline people, or how anyone should respond to betrayal.
The Bible's prophetic imagery must never become an excuse for domestic abuse, sexual humiliation, or coercion.
God's holiness cannot be used to justify human cruelty.
And Ezekiel's warnings must not be turned into the claim that every person experiencing suffering is being punished for some hidden sin.
The prophets were addressing specific covenant communities in specific historical circumstances.
Their words still teach us about God's holiness, idolatry, justice, and mercy.
But faithful interpretation begins by respecting what the text actually says.
And then comes a turn that is almost impossible to forget.
After the exposure.
After the accusations.
After the warnings of judgment.
God speaks of remembering His covenant.
Ezekiel 16:60 declares:
“Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with thee in the days of thy youth, and I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant.” (KJV)
Nevertheless.
What a word.
It does not erase the seriousness of sin.
It does not pretend that rebellion caused no damage.
It does not mean that judgment was imaginary.
But it reveals that God's covenant purposes are not exhausted by His people's unfaithfulness.
The Hebrew begins:
וְזָכַרְתִּי אֲנִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי
Ve-zakharti ani et-beriti.
“Yet I will remember My covenant.”
In biblical covenant language, remembering is not merely recalling forgotten information.
It can express acting faithfully in accordance with a commitment.
And in Ezekiel 16, that divine remembrance opens the promise of restoration.
Ezekiel 16:63 ends with God speaking of making atonement for all that His people had done.
The Hebrew verb used there is related to kaphar (כָּפַר), meaning to make atonement or effect reconciliation in the appropriate context.
That matters.
Because the story does not end with the bride successfully repairing her own reputation.
It ends with God announcing His purpose to deal with her guilt.
The one who was rescued by mercy would need mercy again.
And now the story begins to point us toward something even greater.
Not because Ezekiel 16 and 23 are secretly simple predictions of Jesus in every detail.
They are not.
Their first meaning concerns Israel, Judah, Jerusalem, covenant violation, judgment, and promised restoration.
But within the wider witness of Scripture, the themes of covenant faithfulness, forgiveness, atonement, and God's commitment to restore His people find their ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The God who exposed His people's unfaithfulness did not abandon His purpose to redeem.
Through the prophets, He promised a new covenant.
In Ezekiel 36:26, He declares:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.” (KJV)
Notice what He promises.
Not merely improved circumstances.
Not simply a better public reputation.
A new heart.
Because our deepest problem is not that we need to become better at hiding our sins.
Our deepest problem is that we need to be changed.
We need forgiveness for what we have done.
And transformation in what we love.
We need more than religious appearance.
We need life from God.
That is why Jesus Christ is not merely an inspirational ending attached to an uncomfortable Old Testament story.
He is the center of the Gospel's answer to human sin.
He came into a world filled with people who had loved the wrong things, trusted the wrong powers, and broken God's commands.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He proclaimed the kingdom of God.
He called sinners to repentance.
He welcomed the broken without pretending their sin was harmless.
He went to the cross.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are proclaimed to all who repent and believe in Him.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired every consequence.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we learned how to sound spiritual.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
And Ephesians 5:25 tells husbands to love their wives:
“Even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
There is the astonishing contrast.
In Ezekiel, the covenant marriage metaphor exposes the horror of unfaithfulness.
In Ephesians, Christ's self-giving love becomes the model of sacrificial faithfulness.
Jesus does not teach His followers to imitate the violence described in Ezekiel's judgment imagery.
He commands a love shaped by His own self-giving.
He gave Himself for His people.
And Revelation 19:7 celebrates the marriage of the Lamb, using wedding imagery to portray the joy of God's redeemed people belonging to Christ.
The Bible's marriage imagery, read across its different contexts, carries both warning and hope.
God does not treat covenant faithfulness as meaningless.
And the Gospel does not treat sinners as beyond redemption.
The same Scriptures that expose the ugliness of idolatry also reveal the beauty of grace.
But grace must never be confused with permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus did not die so that we could make peace with the very sins that enslave us.
He came to save us from sin and reconcile us to God.
Repentance is not buying forgiveness through enough tears.
It is turning from sin toward God in response to His truth and mercy.
Faith is not simply admitting that Jesus exists.
It is trusting Him as Savior and acknowledging Him as Lord.
And transformation is not something we manufacture by sheer determination.
It is the work of God's grace and Spirit, producing a new direction of life.
That does not mean every struggle disappears overnight.
Some battles are long.
Some wounds require patient healing.
Some patterns need confession, accountability, wise pastoral care, and practical help.
But the believer does not have to call darkness light in order to survive.
We can bring our sins into the light because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Perhaps you have been carrying something nobody knows about.
Perhaps you have become attached to a relationship that repeatedly pulls you away from obedience.
Perhaps money has become your refuge.
Perhaps success has become your identity.
Perhaps bitterness has become so familiar that forgiveness feels like losing part of yourself.
Perhaps your idol is not something obviously wicked.
Perhaps it is something good that has become ultimate.
A person.
A dream.
A ministry.
A reputation.
Even the need to be seen as a faithful Christian.
And perhaps the hardest prayer you could pray tonight is not, “Lord, bless what I am building.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, show me what I have allowed to take Your place.”
Because idols are not always recognizable by their appearance.
Sometimes they are revealed by the sacrifices we are willing to make to keep them.
What are you willing to disobey God to protect?
What controls your sense of worth?
What loss would make you believe life is no longer worth living?
What desire consistently overrides your conscience?
What have you defended long after Scripture began confronting it?
These questions are not meant to crush the wounded.
They are meant to expose false refuges.
And if your heart is stirring right now, do not mistake conviction for an invitation to despair.
The proper response to God's truth is not to run farther into hiding.
It is to come to Christ.
First John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Not because confession makes us worthy.
But because forgiveness rests upon the faithfulness of God and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
That is the hope Ezekiel's dark imagery should ultimately drive us to seek.
Not the illusion that we were never unfaithful.
Not the comfort of comparing ourselves to people whose sins appear worse.
But the mercy of God that exposes evil truthfully and offers reconciliation through Christ.
And here is something worth remembering.
The greatest tragedy is not that God knows what you have hidden. It is that you might keep hiding from the One who calls you to repentance and offers you mercy.
You do not need to turn your confession into a public spectacle.
You do not need to expose private trauma to strangers.
You do not need to perform your pain to prove that you are sincere.
But you can stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
You can confess.
You can seek help.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can turn away from destructive patterns.
You can begin again in obedience, not by denying the past, but by trusting the Savior who redeems sinners.
And perhaps someone reading this has quietly believed that their past disqualifies them from ever being useful to God.
You remember the relationship.
The lie.
The betrayal.
The addiction.
The compromise.
The years you wasted.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The person you became when nobody was watching.
You look at the ruins and wonder whether there is anything left worth restoring.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not guarantee that every broken relationship will be repaired or that every opportunity will return.
But it does proclaim something infinitely greater.
Through Jesus Christ, guilty people can be forgiven.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The ashamed can approach God through a Savior.
The enslaved can begin walking in freedom.
And those who once lived for idols can learn to worship the living God.
That is not a small improvement.
That is redemption.
That is why we keep proclaiming the Gospel.
That is why we keep opening difficult passages rather than avoiding them.
Because there are people who have heard a thousand comforting messages and still do not understand what Jesus came to save them from.
There are believers who need more than another inspirational sentence.
They need Scripture.
They need sound teaching.
They need discipleship.
They need a community where truth and compassion belong together.
They need to hear that holiness matters and that mercy is real.
And if this message has exposed something in your own heart, I want to invite you to respond—not to impress anyone, but to acknowledge what God may be bringing to your attention.
You do not owe the internet the details of your struggle.
Your honesty may encourage someone else who thought they were fighting alone.
If this article reminded you of someone who is drifting from faith, consider sharing it with them privately, with kindness rather than accusation.
A single share may help someone encounter a biblical message they would never have searched for themselves.
Not because an algorithm saves souls.
Only Jesus saves.
But God can use ordinary acts of encouragement, testimony, and communication to bring His Word before people who need to hear it.
Return to Ezekiel 16 and 23 with your Bible open.
Read the entire chapters, including the uncomfortable sections and the historical context.
Compare them with Ezekiel 36, Jeremiah 31, Romans 5, Ephesians 5, and Revelation 19.
Do not simply remember the emotional force of this article.
Remember the Scriptures that give it meaning.

We want this community to be a place where the Bible is taken seriously, Jesus Christ is proclaimed faithfully, repentance is never separated from grace, and hurting people are invited toward truth rather than performance.
That mission is also why I want to speak openly about something practical.
Creating and sharing Christian teaching, maintaining resources, and expanding outreach require time, work, and financial support.
For those who regard regular financial giving as part of their worship, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one expression of generosity and stewardship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That principle matters deeply to us.

Nor should it be confused with an obligatory tithe to a local church. Christians hold different convictions about tithing under the new covenant, and their responsibilities to their families and local congregations deserve thoughtful consideration.
You are not purchasing grace.
You are helping sustain a ministry that seeks to proclaim it.
These resources are intended to help believers go deeper in Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, and continue growing in Jesus Christ.
The Word of God is not for sale.
The invitation to repent and believe in Jesus Christ is not behind a payment wall.
But if you are in a position to help, your generosity can make a meaningful difference in sustaining and expanding this work.
