That is the human heartbreak we must not overlook when we open Deuteronomy 24:1–4.
Because behind the ancient legal language were real women. Real households. Real consequences.
And when we read this passage carefully, something surprising emerges.
God was not celebrating divorce.
He was addressing a broken human reality.
But there is an even deeper revelation waiting for us.
A certificate could acknowledge the end of a marriage.
It could not determine the end of a woman's worth.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ would confront the very hardness of heart that made such laws necessary.
Stay with this story.
Because the difference between what Moses regulated and what Jesus revealed may change the way you understand marriage, rejection, repentance, and grace.
Deuteronomy 24 begins with a situation that was painfully familiar in the ancient world.
A man marries a woman. Later, he finds something about her that displeases him, described in Hebrew as עֶרְוַת דָּבָר (ʿervat davar).
The expression is difficult to translate precisely.
עֶרְוָה (ʿervah) can refer to nakedness, shame, or indecency. דָּבָר (davar) means a matter, thing, or word.
Together, the phrase is often translated as “some indecency” or “something indecent.”
But Scripture does not define the precise offense in this passage.
That matters.
Because we must never pretend the Bible gives details it does not give.
The Hebrew text continues by describing the husband writing a סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת (sefer keritut).
Literally, this is a “document of cutting off,” commonly translated as a certificate of divorce.
The verb behind keritut carries the idea of cutting or severing.
Think about that.
A marriage that had joined two lives was now being formally severed.
The document was given into the woman's hand, and she was sent out of the man's house.
The text does not describe her tears.
It does not tell us whether she begged him to reconsider.
It does not reveal whether she felt relieved, terrified, angry, or ashamed.
We should not invent those details as historical facts.
But we can recognize what the law meant in a society where marriage was deeply connected to household security, family relationships, and economic survival.
For some women, divorce could bring profound vulnerability.
For others, being released from a marriage might provide an opportunity to begin again.
And that is where the certificate becomes important.
It was not merely a piece of paper saying, “You are unwanted.”
It formally documented the dissolution of the marriage.
The woman was not simply being abandoned while her marital status remained unresolved.
The certificate recognized that the marriage had been severed, and the passage explicitly contemplates her becoming another man's wife.
It did not guarantee her financial security, erase social stigma, or ensure that she would remarry.
But it did have legal significance.
The certificate could close one marriage without necessarily closing every possibility of another.
There is something important here that many readers miss.
Deuteronomy 24:1–4 is not structured as a command requiring men to divorce their wives.
In the Hebrew, the passage presents a sequence of circumstances.
A man marries a woman.
He divorces her.
She leaves and becomes another man's wife.
That second marriage ends through another divorce or the second husband's death.
Then, finally, the actual prohibition appears.
Her first husband must not take her back as his wife after she has become another man's wife.
The central legal command concerns that attempted return.
The passage regulates a situation involving divorce and remarriage; it does not present divorce as God's ideal.
That distinction is essential.
Because when we confuse regulation with approval, we can make God appear to endorse the very brokenness He is addressing.
Consider how different that is from the way people sometimes speak about the Bible.
Someone says, “Moses allowed divorce, so God must have wanted it.”
But permission in a fallen world is not necessarily a declaration of divine delight.
And Jesus Himself would make that distinction unmistakably clear.
Before we reach His words, however, we need to understand what the prohibition meant.
Imagine that the woman has rebuilt her life.
She has entered another marriage.
Perhaps she has found stability. Perhaps she has experienced another season of sorrow.
The passage tells us that the second marriage eventually ends.
Now her first husband wants her back.
But Deuteronomy 24:4 forbids that remarriage.
The Hebrew calls the proposed return a תּוֹעֵבָה (toʿevah), commonly translated “an abomination” or “a detestable thing.”
This is strong moral language.
It shows that the law was not treating marriage as something people could dissolve, rearrange, and reverse without serious consequences.
The passage does not explain every reason behind the prohibition, and interpreters have proposed different explanations.
Some understand it as guarding against the manipulation of marriage and divorce.
Others emphasize the sanctity of marital relationships and the seriousness of the intervening marriage.
Whatever additional rationale one considers, the prohibition itself is clear.
The first husband could not simply reclaim his former wife after her subsequent marriage.
And we must be careful here.
The text does not say that the woman had become worthless.
It does not say that she had lost her humanity.
It does not say that every divorced woman was morally corrupt.
It establishes a specific prohibition concerning remarriage to the first husband after an intervening marriage.
There is a tremendous difference between those statements.
A law restricting a particular marital arrangement is not a declaration that a woman has no future.
And yet, throughout history, people have sometimes turned painful circumstances into permanent identities.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Abandoned.
Unwanted.
Damaged.
As though one word could explain an entire human being.
As though a broken relationship could erase every good thing God created in a person.
As though someone's worst season should become their permanent name.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Perhaps your story does not involve divorce at all.
Perhaps someone promised to stay and walked away.
Perhaps you trusted a person who betrayed you.
Perhaps you were the one who made destructive decisions, and you still carry the consequences.
Perhaps your marriage is intact, but the tenderness disappeared years ago.
You share an address, a table, maybe even a bed.
But somewhere along the way, you stopped sharing your hearts.
Or perhaps you have been wounded by religious people who knew how to quote Scripture but never learned how to treat hurting people with compassion.
And the question beneath your pain is still the same.
Can God write anything beautiful after something this painful?
The answer begins with understanding what Jesus said when religious leaders questioned Him about divorce.
In Matthew 19, the Pharisees approached Jesus and asked whether a man could divorce his wife for any cause.
That question did not arise in a vacuum.
Jewish interpreters had debated the meaning of Deuteronomy 24:1, particularly the expression ʿervat davar.
Some interpreted permissible grounds for divorce narrowly, while others understood them more broadly.
The question was therefore both theological and deeply practical.
How easily could a husband dismiss his wife?
What reasons were sufficient?
What did Moses really mean?
But Jesus did something extraordinary.
He did not begin by debating how far human beings could stretch the divorce provision.
He went back to creation.
He pointed to Genesis.
To the beginning.
To God's intention before sin fractured human relationships.
Jesus declared:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
— Matthew 19:6, KJV
Then the Pharisees asked why Moses had permitted a certificate of divorce.
And Jesus answered with words that expose the entire issue.
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
— Matthew 19:8, KJV
Read that again.
Because of the hardness of your hearts.
In the Greek text, Jesus uses the expression σκληροκαρδία (sklērokardia).
It refers to hardness of heart.
A stubbornness.
A resistance to God's will.
A heart that has become unwilling to respond rightly.
Jesus was not saying that marriage was disposable.
He was saying that the Mosaic concession addressed human hardness, not the original beauty of God's design.
The law dealt with the reality of broken relationships.
Jesus called His listeners back to the Creator's intention.
And suddenly the discussion becomes far more uncomfortable.
Because the deepest issue is no longer merely what a person can legally do.
It is what has happened inside the human heart.
A person can know the rules and still be cruel.
A person can follow a procedure and still refuse to love.
A person can defend a legal right while ignoring the spiritual condition that makes the action so destructive.
And that truth should make every one of us examine ourselves.
Not just divorced people.
Not just married people.
All of us.
Because hardness of heart can appear in many forms.
It can be the husband who refuses to listen.
The wife who weaponizes contempt.
The parent who will not apologize.
The believer who enjoys condemning others.
The church member who uses biblical language to hide pride.
The person who demands grace for personal failures but refuses to extend mercy to anyone else.
It is possible to hold a Bible in your hands while refusing to let its truth soften your heart.
And that should frighten us more than the opinion of people who know our past.
Because Jesus did not come merely to improve our religious vocabulary.
He came to save sinners and transform hearts.
There is another scene in the Gospels that makes this truth painfully personal.
In John 4, Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well.
She has come for water.
He begins a conversation that crosses social and religious boundaries.
Eventually, Jesus reveals that He knows her marital history.
She has had five husbands, and the man she currently has is not her husband.
We are not told the circumstances of all five marriages.
We are not told whether they ended through divorce, death, or a combination of circumstances.
We should not assume that every broken relationship was her fault.
But we do know that Jesus understood her situation with complete accuracy.
And He did not reduce her to a scandal.
He spoke to her about living water.
He revealed profound truth about worship.
And He identified Himself to her as the Messiah.
Imagine that.
A woman with a complicated marital history encounters the One who knows her story better than anyone.
And the conversation becomes a doorway to revelation.
She eventually leaves her water jar and goes to tell others about Jesus.
John 4:29 records her invitation:
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?”
— John 4:29, KJV
She did not suddenly acquire a spotless past.
She encountered the Savior.
And many Samaritans believed because of her testimony, as John 4:39 tells us.
That is grace.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not declaring every relationship righteous.
Not erasing the truth.
But revealing that a person's history does not place them beyond the reach of Christ.
Some of you have spent years believing that the worst thing that happened to you is the most important thing about you.
You were divorced, and people stopped seeing your faith.
You were betrayed, and you stopped believing you could be loved.
You committed adultery, repented, and still wonder whether forgiveness can truly reach that far.
You survived a destructive relationship, but every time someone speaks about marriage, you feel as though you are standing in a courtroom.
Please hear this carefully.
Jesus does not excuse sin, but neither does He turn away every wounded sinner who comes to Him.
His grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
His grace is the power and mercy by which sinners are forgiven and called into a new life.
And the Gospel does not require us to pretend that all suffering has the same cause.
Some people need to repent for the harm they have done.
Others need to stop carrying blame for harm inflicted upon them.
Some need to seek reconciliation where it is safe, appropriate, and consistent with biblical truth.
Others need protection from abuse and coercion.
Forgiveness does not require a person to remain in danger.
And no one should use Deuteronomy 24 or Jesus' teaching about marriage to pressure someone into enduring violence or to prevent them from seeking safety.
Faithfulness to Scripture demands that we take both holiness and human suffering seriously.
The Bible's teaching on divorce and remarriage also deserves careful study beyond this single passage.
Matthew 5:31–32 and Matthew 19:3–9 record Jesus' teaching, including Matthew's reference to sexual immorality.
Mark 10:2–12 emphasizes the seriousness of divorcing a spouse and marrying another.
First Corinthians 7 addresses marriage, separation, and situations involving an unbelieving spouse who departs.
Christians have differed over how these passages apply to particular circumstances, especially remarriage.
Those disagreements should never become an excuse for careless interpretation or harsh treatment of wounded people.
What is beyond dispute is that Jesus upheld the seriousness of marriage, exposed hardness of heart, and called His followers to faithfulness.
And His own life demonstrated compassion toward people whose lives were complicated by sin and suffering.
But there is something even more astonishing.
The Bible does not merely describe a God who speaks about broken relationships from a distance.
It uses the language of marriage, unfaithfulness, and restoration to reveal the tragedy of His people's covenant rebellion.
In Jeremiah 3:8, the Lord describes His judgment on faithless Israel using the image of a certificate of divorce.
The Hebrew phrase סֵפֶר כְּרִיתוּת (sefer keritut) appears there as well.
It is the same kind of divorce-document language found in Deuteronomy 24.
The prophetic image is severe.
Israel has turned toward other gods.
Covenant unfaithfulness has brought judgment.
Yet Jeremiah 3 also contains astonishing calls to return.
In Jeremiah 3:12, God calls faithless Israel to return and declares His mercy.
The point is not that the Lord is casually disregarding the prohibition of Deuteronomy 24:4.
Prophetic marriage imagery should not be flattened into an ordinary human divorce case.
The point is that Israel's covenant unfaithfulness was real, God's judgment was righteous, and His call to repentance revealed extraordinary mercy.
The prophets repeatedly show that God does not treat spiritual adultery as harmless.
But neither is His mercy exhausted by the depth of human rebellion.
And then we come to the New Testament.
To the One who calls Himself the bridegroom.
To Jesus Christ.
The One who loved His people even when they did not deserve His love.
The One who entered a world filled with betrayal, broken promises, and hardened hearts.
The One who would be rejected by those He came to save.
Think about the cross.
Jesus was not handed a certificate of divorce.
He was handed over to be crucified.
He was mocked.
He was rejected.
He was wounded.
And there, in the place of shame, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
The Gospel is not simply that God understands rejection.
It is that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
His sacrifice accomplishes what no human document can accomplish.
A certificate can establish a legal change in marital status.
It cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
It cannot remove sin.
It cannot reconcile a sinner to God.
But through Jesus Christ, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
— Ephesians 5:25, KJV
What a contrast.
Human beings can turn marriage into a place of selfishness, domination, abandonment, or betrayal.
But Christ's love is self-giving.
Holy.
Faithful.
Sacrificial.
He does not love His church because she has earned salvation through flawless performance.
He gives Himself to redeem and sanctify His people.
And that is why the story of a divorced woman holding an ancient certificate ultimately points us toward a much larger question.
Not merely, “Will someone marry me again?”
But, “Can I be made right with God?”
Not merely, “Can I recover what I lost?”
But, “Can Jesus make me new?”
Not merely, “Will people stop talking about my past?”
But, “What does the risen Savior say to those who come to Him?”
Listen to the promise of John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
— John 6:37, KJV
Those words are not a guarantee that every earthly marriage will be restored.
They are not a promise that every former spouse will return.
They are not permission to ignore biblical teaching about covenant faithfulness.
They are something deeper.
They are the promise of Christ's welcome to those who come to Him.
And perhaps that is the promise you need tonight.
Because maybe you have been asking God to restore a relationship when the first thing He is calling you to do is surrender your heart.
Maybe you have been waiting for another person to admit what they did before you will believe your life can move forward.
Maybe you have confused repentance with endless self-punishment.
Maybe you believe that because you failed once, you are permanently disqualified from being useful in God's kingdom.
But listen.
Your past must be faced truthfully.
Your sins must be confessed.
The consequences of your choices may still require humility, restitution, accountability, and patient obedience.
And some losses may never be reversed in this life.
Yet none of that means Christ is powerless to transform the person who comes to Him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
— 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
Notice what it says.
In Christ.
Not merely in a new relationship.
Not in a new house.
Not in a better reputation.
Not in the approval of the people who once rejected you.
In Christ.
That is where the deepest new beginning is found.
And perhaps this is where your own story becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to be the wounded person and still need repentance.
It is possible to have been wronged and still allow bitterness to consume your heart.
It is possible to have made a terrible mistake and then spend years refusing to believe that God's grace is greater than your guilt.
The Gospel does not invite us to deny reality.
It invites us to bring reality into the light of Jesus Christ.
Your tears.
Your anger.
Your regret.
Your questions.
Your broken vows.
Your wounded trust.
Your fear of being rejected again.
Bring them to Him.
Not because every painful situation has an easy answer.
But because the Savior who died and rose again is worthy of your trust even when the future remains uncertain.
And if this message has uncovered something you have been hiding, you do not have to pretend before God.
You can pray right now.

“Lord Jesus, You know my whole story. You know where I have sinned, where I have been wounded, and where my heart has grown hard. Forgive me for what I have done against You. Heal what is broken in me. Give me courage to face the truth, wisdom to obey Your Word, and grace to walk forward without surrendering to shame. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to live as someone who belongs to You. Amen.”
Perhaps that prayer feels difficult.
Perhaps your heart is not ready to say every word.
Then begin with the truth you can speak.
“Jesus, help me.”
He is not confused by your tears.
He is not surprised by your history.
And He does not need you to manufacture a perfect appearance before you seek His mercy.
If this article has reached a place in your heart you have struggled to explain, I would love to hear from you.
You do not have to reveal private details to be honest about needing prayer.
Your story may encourage someone who currently cannot imagine a future beyond their pain.
There may be a person on your Facebook friends list who has been quietly living with the shame of a broken marriage.
Someone who has stopped attending church because they fear the judgment of others.
Someone who thinks that because their family fell apart, God must have abandoned them.
Someone who needs to hear that Scripture speaks seriously about marriage without declaring that wounded people are beyond the reach of mercy.
Not to win an argument.
Not to expose someone else's failures.
But to put a message of biblical truth and Gospel hope where a hurting person might encounter it.
There may come a day when you need to return to Deuteronomy 24, Matthew 19, John 4, and the promise of new life in Christ.
We want to keep opening the Bible together.
Not merely collecting inspirational phrases.
But learning what God actually says, allowing His Word to correct us, comfort us, and lead us closer to Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, pursue spiritual maturity, and remain rooted in biblical truth.
It is a voluntary act of partnership in the work of producing and sharing biblical teaching, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered encouragement.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
You do not have to pay to receive His grace.

But if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, find encouragement, or grow in your relationship with Christ, you may wish to help make that same opportunity available to others.
It is the opportunity to participate in the work of sharing the Gospel and encouraging discipleship.
Your presence matters.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share sound biblical teaching matters.
We want Gospel Warrior to remain a place where people are pointed toward Christ, not pressured into giving what they cannot afford.
Because the purpose of this ministry is not to build a community around a payment.
It is to help build a community around the truth of Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave, I want you to return to the woman at the beginning of this story.
The woman holding a certificate.
The woman whose marriage has ended.
The woman facing a future she did not expect.
Deuteronomy 24 does not tell us her name.
It does not tell us how her life ended.
It does not give us permission to invent a happy ending for her.
But it does reveal something important.
The law recognized that a dissolved marriage had consequences and that the woman's subsequent marital life could not simply be treated as though it never happened.
And when Jesus addressed this passage, He called people beyond legal arguments to the deeper question of God's intention and the condition of the human heart.
That is where this ancient text meets us today.
Because some of us are desperate for a document that says we are free.
Others are desperate for an apology that may never come.
Some are praying for a marriage to be healed.
Others are grieving a marriage that has already ended.
Some are facing the consequences of their own unfaithfulness.
Others are carrying wounds they never chose.
But every one of us needs something no certificate can provide.
We need a Savior.
A Savior who tells the truth about sin.
A Savior who honors what God has established.
A Savior who calls hard hearts to repentance.
A Savior who receives those who come to Him in faith.
A Savior who died and rose again so that forgiveness and new life could be offered to sinners.
And when we stand before Him, the greatest question is not whether our earthly story unfolded the way we hoped.
It is whether we have entrusted ourselves to the One who can redeem us.
So do not confuse a broken chapter with the final word over your life.
Do not confuse another person's rejection with God's judgment.
Do not confuse God's mercy with permission to continue in sin.
And do not confuse the consequences of your past with the limits of Christ's power to transform your future.
If you have sinned, repent and come to Jesus.
If you have been wounded, bring your pain to Jesus.
If your heart has hardened, ask Him to soften it.
If your future frightens you, seek His wisdom for the next faithful step.
And if you are standing in the ruins of something you once believed would last forever, remember this:
A human signature may have ended a chapter of your life, but it does not have the authority to write the final sentence of your soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU RAISED YOUR CHILD TO LOVE GOD… SO WHY DID THEY WALK AWAY?
paragraphs: YOU RAISED YOUR CHILD TO LOVE GOD… SO WHY DID THEY WALK AWAY?

Is Proverbs 22:6 a guaranteed promise from God—or have we misunderstood a Scripture that has left countless Christian parents drowning in guilt? The truth may break your heart before it finally sets you free.
There is a kind of heartbreak that doesn't come with a funeral.
Your child is still alive.
You can still see their pictures. You might even hear their voice. They may still sit across from you at the dinner table.
But the little boy who once folded his hands beside your bed and whispered, “Dear Jesus…” now tells you he doesn't believe in God.
The little girl who once sang worship songs in the back seat of your car now wants nothing to do with church.
And somewhere between the sleepless nights, unanswered messages, and conversations that ended in tears, a Bible verse begins haunting you.
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.” — Proverbs 22:6 (KJV)
You remember reading it when they were small.
You believed it.
You built your parenting around it.
You prayed over their beds. You taught them Scripture. You brought them to Sunday school. You corrected them when they were wrong. You tried to make your home a place where Jesus was honored.
You weren't a perfect parent.
But you tried.
And now?
Now you stare at that verse and wonder something you are almost afraid to say aloud.
“God, did Your promise fail… or did I fail my child?”
Before you answer that question, there is something you need to understand.
Something about the original Hebrew.
Something about the nature of biblical wisdom.
And something about Jesus Christ that may completely change the way you carry the burden of your child's spiritual journey.
Because Proverbs 22:6 is not as simple as many of us were taught.
And misunderstanding it can turn a beautiful biblical instruction into a weapon of condemnation against the very parents it was meant to guide.
The Hebrew text reads:
חֲנֹךְ לַנַּעַר עַל־פִּי דַרְכּוֹ גַּם כִּי־יַזְקִין לֹא־יָסוּר מִמֶּנָּה
Chanokh la-na'ar al-pi darko, gam ki-yazqin lo-yasur mimmennah.
A fairly literal rendering is:
“Train a young person according to his way; even when he grows old, he will not turn aside from it.”
Notice something important.
The Hebrew does not explicitly say, “Teach your child Christianity, and God guarantees that child will remain a Christian.”
It doesn't even explicitly contain the word “should” in the phrase traditionally translated “the way he should go.”
That wording reflects an interpretive decision by translators.
The expression עַל־פִּי דַרְכּוֹ (al-pi darko) literally conveys the idea of “according to his way.”
And this is where the conversation becomes far more serious than a familiar Sunday school quotation.
Some interpreters understand the phrase as directing parents to train children in the proper way of life, consistent with the moral wisdom taught throughout Proverbs.
Others understand it as emphasizing instruction suited to the child's particular circumstances, development, or disposition.
Still others suggest the proverb may contain a warning: allow a young person to become established in his own uncorrected way, and those habits may remain with him into old age.
These interpretations are not equally accepted by every scholar, and the Hebrew alone does not settle the debate.
But they reveal something we must not ignore.
Proverbs 22:6 is about the enduring influence of early formation. It is not an explicit guarantee that faithful parenting will inevitably produce saving faith.
That distinction matters.
Especially when a mother is crying herself to sleep.
Especially when a father believes his child's rebellion proves he has failed God.
Especially when an adult son or daughter has walked away from the faith, and an entire family is quietly asking who deserves the blame.
We need to remember what kind of book Proverbs is.
Proverbs belongs to the Bible's wisdom literature.
Its sayings generally describe how life ordinarily works under God's moral order. They teach wisdom, discernment, discipline, and the consequences of human choices.
They are divinely inspired and trustworthy.
But not every proverb is intended to function as an unconditional promise that overrides every other factor in human life.
Consider Proverbs 15:1:
“A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.” (KJV)
That is profound wisdom.
A gentle answer often calms an angry situation.
But have you ever answered someone gently, only to watch them become even angrier?
Of course.
The proverb was not false.
It was never intended to guarantee that every angry person would respond peacefully to every gentle answer.
Or consider Proverbs 10:27:
“The fear of the LORD prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened.” (KJV)
Yet Scripture itself acknowledges that righteous people sometimes die young while wicked people sometimes live long lives.
Ecclesiastes 7:15 openly recognizes that troubling reality.
Biblical wisdom teaches us how to live faithfully in a complicated, fallen world.
It does not promise that faithful behavior gives us complete control over every outcome.
And that brings us to a painful truth.
You can teach your child the way of Christ without possessing the power to make your child love Christ.
Read that again.
You can teach.
You can pray.
You can model repentance.
You can open Scripture at the dinner table.
You can apologize when you lose your temper.
You can show your children what forgiveness looks like.
You can demonstrate that following Jesus is more than attending a church service.
But you cannot regenerate a human heart.
You cannot manufacture saving faith.
You cannot repent on behalf of another person.
And you cannot become the Holy Spirit for your son or daughter.
Jesus Himself said:
“Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” — John 3:3 (KJV)
Spiritual rebirth is not something parents can produce through perfect technique.
Salvation is God's gracious work, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not something we can boast of accomplishing.
That truth applies to our children too.
And perhaps this is where some parents need to stop carrying a burden that was never theirs to carry alone.
Because somewhere along the way, we began treating Proverbs 22:6 like a spiritual contract.
“I will do everything correctly, Lord, and You will guarantee the result I want.”
But children are not spiritual machines.
They are human beings.
They have minds, desires, weaknesses, influences, questions, and moral responsibilities of their own.
They live in a world filled with competing voices.
And as they grow, they make decisions their parents cannot always prevent.
This does not mean parenting is unimportant.
Far from it.
Deuteronomy 6:6–7 calls God's people to teach His words diligently to their children, speaking of them throughout ordinary daily life.
Ephesians 6:4 instructs fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
Parents are commanded to teach, nurture, correct, and demonstrate godliness.
These responsibilities are real.
And where parents have been harsh, neglectful, hypocritical, abusive, or spiritually careless, the biblical response is not to excuse the harm.
It is to repent.
To acknowledge what happened.
To seek forgiveness.
To make appropriate amends.
To pursue change.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
But neither does responsibility mean parents possess absolute control over their children's souls.
And Scripture gives us a striking reminder.
Think about Adam and Eve.
They lived in a world God had declared very good.
They had access to God's instruction.
They were not raised in a broken household by sinful human parents.
Yet they disobeyed.
Their rebellion was their own responsibility.
Now consider the prophet Samuel.
He served the Lord faithfully, yet 1 Samuel 8:3 tells us his sons did not walk in his ways. They pursued dishonest gain, accepted bribes, and perverted justice.
The passage does not give us enough information to declare Samuel a perfect father.
Nor does it authorize us to conclude that his sons' corruption must have been caused by his parenting.
It does show that a father's faithfulness in public ministry does not automatically guarantee that his children will follow his example.
And then there is the account of the prodigal son.
Luke 15 tells us of a younger son who demanded his inheritance, left his father, and squandered his possessions in reckless living.
Imagine the pain of that father.
He had a son who wanted his wealth but not his presence.
A son who wanted the gifts without the relationship.
A son who walked away while his father remained behind.
Some parents reading this know exactly what that feels like.
Your child may not have demanded an inheritance.
Perhaps they demanded distance.
Perhaps they said, “Stop talking to me about Jesus.”
Perhaps they told you that everything you taught them was wrong.
Perhaps they left home carrying bitterness you never knew existed.
And now you are trying to understand how the child you once carried in your arms could become someone you barely recognize.
But notice something about the father in Luke 15.
Jesus does not portray him chasing his son into the distant country and forcibly dragging him home.
The father allows the son to leave.
The son experiences the consequences of his decisions.
And when he finally comes to himself, he returns.
Luke 15:20 says:
“But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” (KJV)
What a picture.
A father who had been wounded by his son's departure now running toward him with compassion.
Not because the son's rebellion was harmless.
Not because sin no longer mattered.
But because repentance and restoration had become possible.
And Jesus told this story to reveal something even greater than parental love.
He was revealing the joy of heaven over sinners who repent.
The father in the parable points us toward the mercy of God.
And the returning son reminds us that a person who has wandered far is not beyond the reach of grace.
But we must be careful.
The parable does not guarantee that every wandering child will eventually return.
Jesus was not giving parents a formula for predicting their children's futures.
He was revealing the Father's compassion toward repentant sinners.
That is a hope worth holding.
But it is not a prediction we have authority to make about every individual.
Some children return to faith after years of wandering.
Some struggle for decades.
Some remain resistant.
And Scripture does not authorize us to promise an outcome God has not specifically promised.
That may be difficult to hear.
Especially when someone you love is far from Christ.
But biblical hope does not require us to invent guarantees.
Biblical hope rests in the character of God.
And His character is enough to keep us praying, loving, and speaking truth even when we cannot see the ending.
Maybe you are the parent who wonders whether one angry outburst ruined everything.
Maybe you remember the day you shouted instead of listening.
The night you were too exhausted to pray with your child.
The season when work consumed your attention.
The arguments that made your home feel more like a battlefield than a refuge.
Maybe you know there are things you should have done differently.
Then hear this carefully.
If you sinned against your child, confess it.
If you wounded them, don't hide behind your authority.
If you used Scripture to humiliate them, acknowledge the damage.
If you demanded outward religious performance while failing to demonstrate Christlike love, repent.
Do not use Proverbs 22:6 to avoid examining your own heart.
But do not use it to sentence yourself to lifelong condemnation either.
There is a difference between godly conviction and crushing despair.
Godly conviction calls us toward repentance and restoration.
Despair tells us there is no hope left.
The Gospel tells a different story.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
That is not permission to dismiss sin.
It is the glorious announcement that Jesus Christ has borne the condemnation of those who belong to Him.
Your parenting failures are serious enough to require grace.
But they are not greater than the grace found in Christ.
And your child's spiritual future is not secured by your perfection.
It rests ultimately with the God who saves.
Now perhaps you are reading this from the other side.
You are not the parent.
You are the child who walked away.
Maybe your parents loved Jesus, but you became angry with God.
Maybe church became associated with judgment, hypocrisy, or pain.
Maybe you watched people preach holiness publicly while practicing cruelty privately.
Maybe you were told never to ask questions, and eventually you stopped asking them because you stopped believing anyone would listen.
Or perhaps you simply wanted a life where nobody could tell you what to do.
Whatever your story, do not confuse the failures of Christians with the character of Christ.
Jesus did not come to defend hypocrisy.
He confronted it.
He did not excuse religious pride.
He exposed it.
He did not teach that outward religious performance could substitute for a transformed heart.
He called people to repentance and genuine faith.
And He did not reserve His mercy for people with respectable histories.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He forgave the guilty.
He restored the broken.
He called the lost to come home.
But He also told the truth about sin.
Because the grace of Jesus is not merely the permission to remain unchanged.
It is the mercy that calls us out of darkness and into new life.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
This is why our message has always been:
Not because Jesus guarantees that every painful family story will end exactly as we want.
Not because every broken relationship will be repaired before this life ends.
Not because the Gospel eliminates every consequence of our decisions.
But because Jesus Christ truly redeems sinners.
He forgives those who repent and believe.
He changes hearts.
He brings the spiritually dead to life.
He gives eternal hope to people who could never save themselves.
And He is worthy of our trust even when the chapters of our family stories remain unfinished.
There is another truth we must face.
Some parents have used Proverbs 22:6 to justify controlling their children long after childhood.
They quote the verse as though spiritual formation means eliminating every question, disagreement, or independent decision.
But biblical training is not the same as domination.
The Hebrew verb חָנַךְ (chanakh), from which the opening command in Proverbs 22:6 comes, carries the sense of initiating, dedicating, or training.
The same Hebrew root is used in other biblical contexts for dedication, including the dedication of a house.
In Proverbs 22:6, the context points toward initiating a young person into a formative path of life.
It does not give parents unlimited authority to manipulate, threaten, or coerce their children into outward conformity.
And it certainly does not teach that forced religious behavior is equivalent to genuine faith.
A child may memorize Bible verses while secretly resenting the Bible.
A teenager may attend church while feeling completely unknown.
An adult may repeat Christian language without trusting Christ.
External conformity can be encouraged, demanded, or imitated.
But genuine conversion cannot be manufactured.
That is why our goal must be greater than raising children who merely know how to behave in church.

We should long to raise children who understand who Jesus is, why sin matters, what grace means, why the resurrection changes everything, and how to bring their questions into the light of God's Word.
Children need truth.
They need boundaries.
They need correction.
They also need to witness humility, repentance, patience, integrity, and sacrificial love.
They need to see that the Gospel their parents preach is also the Gospel their parents desperately need.
Imagine the power of a father saying:
“I was wrong. I sinned against you. Please forgive me.”
Imagine a mother saying:
“I don't know the answer to that question yet, but we can search the Scriptures together.”
Imagine a child learning that Christian authority is not a license for cruelty, and that repentance is not only something adults demand from children.
That is not weak parenting.
That is parenting shaped by the cross.
And it matters because the way we live can either reinforce or undermine the words we teach.
Still, even the most faithful example cannot guarantee another person's response.
That is why we must refuse two dangerous extremes.
One says, “If your child walks away, you must have failed as a parent.”
The other says, “If your child walks away, your parenting had nothing to do with it.”
Neither statement can be universally defended from Scripture.
Sometimes parental sin has deeply contributed to a child's spiritual wounds.
Sometimes children reject the faith despite sincere and loving instruction.
Often, human stories are more complicated than outsiders realize.
We should not assign blame where Scripture has not given us enough information.
And we should not pretend that every family can be explained by a single verse.
Proverbs 22:6 calls us to take spiritual formation seriously.
It does not appoint us judges over every struggling family.
So what should you do if your child has walked away?
Keep loving them without pretending that truth no longer matters.
Listen before assuming you understand their reasons.
Where you have sinned, repent without attaching excuses to your apology.
Pray for them without treating prayer like a mechanism for controlling God's timing.
Speak of Jesus with sincerity rather than panic.
Keep your door open where it is safe and appropriate.
And remember that loving someone does not require enabling destructive behavior or abandoning necessary boundaries.
Most importantly, do not let your child's spiritual condition become the measure of your standing before God.
Your identity as a Christian is not ultimately “the parent whose child turned out right.”
Your identity is found in Jesus Christ.
If you belong to Him, you are His by grace.
Not because your children are perfect.
Not because your family looks impressive.
Not because every prayer has received the answer you hoped for.
But because Christ is a sufficient Savior.
And to the parent who has been quietly asking, “Is it too late?”
I cannot promise you that your child will return to the faith.
No honest teacher of Scripture should make that promise on the basis of Proverbs 22:6.
But I can tell you this.
You have not been commanded to stop praying.
You have not been commanded to stop loving.
You have not been commanded to stop trusting the Lord.
And as long as your child lives, you do not know every chapter that remains to be written.
The God who confronted Saul of Tarsus on the road to Damascus is not powerless before human rebellion.
The Savior who received a repentant criminal at the cross is not limited by a person's history.
The Lord who called Lazarus from the grave has power beyond anything human effort can produce.
Those accounts do not guarantee the conversion of a particular child.
But they remind us that no sinner is saved by human ability.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
So keep your hope where it belongs.
Not in a misinterpreted guarantee.
Not in your flawless performance as a parent.
Not in the illusion that you can control every outcome.
But in the mercy, truth, wisdom, and sovereign power of Jesus Christ.
And if you are a son or daughter who has been running from Him, perhaps this is the moment to stop making your parents' failures the final word about your relationship with God.
Your wounds may be real.
Your questions may be difficult.
Your history may be complicated.
But Jesus Christ deserves to be considered on the truth of who He is.
He lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls people everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
Not because your parents were perfect.
But because He is the Savior you need.
There is one final detail in Proverbs 22:6 that deserves our attention.
The verse speaks about the lasting influence of the path established in youth.
Whether we emphasize wise instruction or the warning against entrenched habits, the passage confronts us with the seriousness of formation.
What children repeatedly learn, practice, observe, and love can shape them for years.
That should move us to faithful action today.
Not fear-driven control.
Not the pursuit of a flawless family image.
Not desperate attempts to earn a guaranteed outcome.
But steady, humble, Christ-centered discipleship.
Teach them the Word.
Let them see you pray.
Let them see you repent.
Tell them about the cross.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them that grace is not cheap and that forgiveness is not imaginary.
Let them know that Jesus is not merely a family tradition.
He is Lord.
And when they grow old enough to make decisions you cannot make for them, entrust them to the God whose wisdom exceeds yours.
Because your assignment was never to become their savior.
Your assignment was to point them to the Savior.
Perhaps that is the sentence a grieving parent needed to hear today.
And perhaps that is the sentence a proud parent needed to remember before taking credit for a child's faith.
Whether your children are walking faithfully with Christ or wandering far from Him, the glory belongs to God.
We plant.
We water.
But God gives the increase.
As Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 3:6:

Paul was speaking specifically about the work of Gospel ministry, not offering a parenting formula. Yet the principle reminds us of something essential: human labor is real, but spiritual growth ultimately depends upon God.
That truth should make us diligent.
And humble.
And prayerful.
And merciful toward other families whose stories we do not fully understand.
Because somewhere tonight, a mother will open her Bible to Proverbs 22:6 and cry.
A father will wonder whether he lost his chance.
A young adult will wrestle with memories of a faith he once professed.
And someone who has spent years pretending everything is fine will finally admit that their family is hurting.
If that person is you, you don't have to pretend here.
You do not owe strangers the details of your pain.
But sometimes honest conversation opens the door to prayer, encouragement, and a community willing to walk with you.
And if this article helped you understand Proverbs 22:6 more faithfully, please don't let it end with you.
Not merely to spread a post, but because there may be a parent in your circle who has been silently blaming themselves for years.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually cold, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
We want to be a place where difficult questions are not buried beneath religious slogans, but examined in the light of God's Word.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, I want to invite you to something deeper.
Not because a monthly payment can earn His favor.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
It should not automatically be described as your biblical tithe or as a substitute for giving to your local church.
But it can be a meaningful expression of generosity and partnership in spreading the Gospel.
Our desire is to keep making biblical nourishment accessible while expanding the reach of these resources.
That benefit is simply an expression of appreciation.
It is not the reason we proclaim Christ.
And it is not the measure of anyone's devotion to Him.
The greater invitation is to participate in a community committed to biblical understanding, spiritual growth, accountability, encouragement, and the continuing work of sharing the Gospel.
We are not trying to sell the Gospel.
The Gospel is not for sale.
We are seeking support for the work of making its message known.
And that distinction matters.
Because everything we do must ultimately point away from ourselves and toward Jesus Christ.
Not our platform.
Not our popularity.
Jesus.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who restores the broken.
The One who speaks truth to the wandering.
The One who gives grace to the undeserving.
And the One whose saving power is not limited by the mistakes, fears, or failures of human parents.
So tonight, if your child is far from God, you may still cry.
You may still pray with trembling hands.
You may still wish you could go back and change a thousand things.
But when you open your Bible to Proverbs 22:6 again, I pray you will no longer hear a voice saying, “Your child wandered, therefore you failed.”
Instead, hear the call to faithful instruction, humble repentance, persevering love, and trust in the Lord.
You were never promised control over another human soul.
You were called to faithfulness before God.
And when your faithfulness has been imperfect, there is forgiveness in Christ.
When your strength is exhausted, there is grace in Christ.
When you cannot see the future, there is hope in Christ.
When the story is painful and unfinished, there is still a Savior who is worthy of your trust.
You may have spent years blaming yourself for the road your child chose, but the cross reminds you that you were never meant to be their redeemer—only to point them toward the One who is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS TOLD HIM TO SELL EVERYTHING… SO WHY DID HE LET OTHER RICH PEOPLE KEEP THEIR WEALTH?
paragraphs: JESUS TOLD HIM TO SELL EVERYTHING… SO WHY DID HE LET OTHER RICH PEOPLE KEEP THEIR WEALTH?

One wealthy man walked away from Jesus grieving. Another wealthy man welcomed Him with joy. Both encountered the same Savior. But what Jesus revealed about their money exposes something far more frightening than the size of a bank account.
There is a question most Christians would rather not ask.
What if Jesus walked into your life today, looked at everything you have worked so hard to build, and asked you to surrender the one thing you cannot imagine living without?
Would you still follow Him?
Not the Jesus we comfortably quote on Sunday mornings.
Not the Jesus we thank when the bills are paid, the business succeeds, the family is healthy, and life finally seems to be going our way.
The real Jesus.
The One who looked at a wealthy young man, loved him, and then spoke words that shattered his entire understanding of what it meant to be blessed.
“Go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me.” — Mark 10:21, KJV
Imagine standing there.

You have done everything respectable people told you to do. You have built something. You have protected your reputation. You have tried to live morally. You believe in God. You respect His commandments.
And now you are standing before the Son of God, asking the most important question a human being can ever ask.
What must I do to inherit eternal life?
You expect an answer that confirms you are on the right path.
Instead, Jesus touches the one place in your heart you have spent your entire life protecting.
Your wealth.
Your security.
Your control.
And suddenly, following God is no longer an inspiring religious idea.
It is a decision that could cost you everything.
But here is where the story becomes even more disturbing.
Jesus did not tell every wealthy person He encountered to sell everything.
He did not give Zacchaeus that exact command.
He did not give Joseph of Arimathea that exact command.
And when wealthy women supported His ministry from their resources, the Gospels did not record Jesus demanding that they first become penniless.
So what was happening?
Was Jesus applying different standards to different people?
Was the rich young ruler being punished for succeeding?
Or was Jesus revealing something about the human heart that we are still desperately trying to avoid?
Because the answer is not simply about money.
It is about what happens when something God has given us becomes something we cannot surrender back to Him.
And if we are willing to be honest, the rich young ruler may be far more familiar than we want to admit.
He might be sitting in our church.
He might be leading a ministry.
He might be the person everyone admires for being disciplined, successful, generous, and religious.
He might be looking back at us from the mirror.
The Gospel of Mark tells us something extraordinary about this encounter.
Before Jesus gave the devastating instruction, Mark recorded:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him.” — Mark 10:21, KJV
Read that again.
Jesus loved him.
The Greek text says:
ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν
emblepsas autō ēgapēsen auton
Looking intently at him, He loved him.
The verb ἐμβλέπω (emblepō) conveys a focused, attentive look. The verb ἀγαπάω (agapaō) expresses love.
Jesus did not look at this man with contempt.
He did not despise him because he had money.
He did not resent his success.
He saw him. And He loved him.
Then He confronted him.
That sequence matters.
Because sometimes the most loving thing Jesus can do is expose the very thing we have been using to avoid depending on Him.
The young man had asked about eternal life. Jesus directed him toward the commandments. The man replied that he had observed them from his youth.
Matthew records him asking, “What lack I yet?” (Matthew 19:20, KJV).
He sensed that something was still missing.
Think about the tragedy of that moment.
A man could have money, morality, social standing, religious discipline, and a respectable reputation—and still know that something inside him remained unresolved.
He had possessions.
But did his possessions have him?
Jesus answered with a command that went straight to the heart of the matter.
Sell what you have.
Give to the poor.
Have treasure in heaven.
Come.
And Mark tells us the man went away grieving because he had great possessions.
He came running toward Jesus.
He walked away sorrowful.
He came asking about eternal life.
He left because he could not release the life he already had.
That is one of the most heartbreaking scenes in the Gospels.
He was standing before the One who could give him eternal life, yet his earthly treasures had become too precious to surrender.
He wanted Jesus.
But he also wanted to remain in control.
And when those two desires collided, his sorrow revealed which one had the stronger hold.
The Greek word used to describe his reaction is στυγνάσας (stygnasas), conveying a darkened or dismayed expression.
This was not the casual disappointment of a man who had received inconvenient advice.
He was deeply distressed.
The cost of discipleship had become personal.
And perhaps that is why this account still unsettles us two thousand years later.
Because many of us love the idea of surrender until Jesus names something specific.
We sing, “I surrender all,” while quietly reserving the right to decide what “all” includes.
We pray for God's will, provided it does not threaten our plans.
We ask Him to bless our future, but become frightened when obedience might redirect it.
We want Jesus to be Savior.
But sometimes we resist Him as Lord.
And yet the story does not teach that every Christian must immediately liquidate every possession.
That would ignore the broader testimony of Scripture.
Consider another wealthy man.
His name was Zacchaeus.
He was a chief tax collector, and Luke explicitly describes him as rich (Luke 19:2).
Tax collectors in that setting were widely despised because of their association with Roman taxation and the opportunities the system created for exploitation.
Zacchaeus had wealth.
He had status within a corrupt and resented profession.
He had also become a man his community did not want to associate with.
Then Jesus came to Jericho.
And everything changed.
Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree because he wanted to see Jesus.
Imagine the scene.
A wealthy, influential man perched among branches like a child, desperate for a glimpse of someone he had never met.
Then Jesus stopped beneath the tree.
He looked up.
He called Zacchaeus by name.
And He invited Himself into his house.
The crowd complained.
Of course they did.
Why would a holy teacher enter the home of a man known as a sinner?
But Jesus was not confused about Zacchaeus's reputation.
He had come precisely because sinners needed saving.
And something remarkable happened.
Zacchaeus stood and declared:
“Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.” — Luke 19:8, KJV
Half.
Not everything.
Half of his possessions to the poor, along with a promise of fourfold restitution for those he had wronged.
And Jesus responded:
“This day is salvation come to this house.” — Luke 19:9, KJV
Do you see the difference?
The rich young ruler was explicitly commanded to sell his possessions and follow Jesus.
Zacchaeus was not recorded receiving that same instruction.
Yet Zacchaeus responded to Jesus with extraordinary generosity and repentance.
One wealthy man went away sorrowful.
Another wealthy man received Jesus joyfully and began putting his repentance into action.
Why?
Because the central issue was never whether a person could produce the correct percentage.
It was whether the heart had truly turned toward Christ.
Zacchaeus's generosity did not purchase his salvation.
His restitution did not bribe God into forgiving him.
His actions revealed a transformed response to the Savior who had come to seek him.
Jesus Himself explained His mission in Luke 19:10:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
That is the Gospel.
Not a wealthy man buying redemption through donations.
Not a sinner earning forgiveness through financial sacrifice.
But Jesus seeking the lost—and grace producing a new way of living.
The rich young ruler was being confronted with the treasure he could not release.
Zacchaeus demonstrated a willingness to release wealth and repair the damage his sin had caused.
The same Savior encountered both men.
But the condition of their hearts was revealed in different ways.
Now consider Joseph of Arimathea.
Matthew 27:57 identifies him as a rich man who had become a disciple of Jesus.
After the crucifixion, Joseph approached Pilate to request the body of Christ. He wrapped Jesus' body in clean linen and placed it in his own new tomb (Matthew 27:57–60).
His resources became part of an extraordinary act of devotion and burial.
Scripture does not tell us that Joseph sold everything before becoming a disciple.
Neither does it tell us the full history of his wealth.
What it does show is that a wealthy disciple used something valuable he possessed to honor Jesus.
Then there were the women who supported Christ's earthly ministry.
Luke 8:1–3 names Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, and others who provided for Jesus and His disciples from their resources.
They were not presented as spiritually inferior because they had material means to contribute.
Their resources were being used in service to Christ.
This does not make wealth automatically righteous.
It does not mean every wealthy believer is faithful.
And it certainly does not mean financial generosity can substitute for repentance.
But it does establish something important.
The New Testament does not give every disciple an identical command to dispose of all property.
It gives every disciple an uncompromising call to belong to Jesus.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Jesus was not merely asking the rich young ruler to become poor.
He was calling him to follow the Son of God.
And the man's wealth stood directly in the way.
The final words of Jesus' invitation were not simply “sell” and “give.”
They were “follow me.”
ἀκολούθει μοι
akolouthei moi
The command was personal.
The invitation was relational.
The goal was not poverty for its own sake.
The goal was discipleship.
And that brings us to the question many of us have avoided.
What is your “great possession”?
Perhaps you are not wealthy.
Perhaps you are barely surviving financially.
Perhaps you are working two jobs, raising children, caring for aging parents, or trying to make enough money to keep food on the table.
This passage is not permission for anyone to shame you for struggling.
Nor is it permission for religious leaders to demand that you surrender your family's necessities to prove your faith.
But the question of surrender still reaches every one of us.
Because money is not the only thing that can become an idol.
For some, it is a relationship they know is leading them away from obedience.
For others, it is pride.
A hidden addiction.
An image they have worked desperately to maintain.
A bitterness they refuse to release.
A reputation that matters more than truth.
A dream they have elevated above God's will.
A secret sin they have learned to excuse.
Or a sense of control so deeply rooted that trusting God feels terrifying.
We may never be asked to sell everything we own.
But every follower of Christ is called to surrender everything to His lordship.
Jesus said in Luke 14:33 that anyone who does not forsake all that he has cannot be His disciple.
The Greek expression ἀποτάσσεται πᾶσιν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ ὑπάρχουσιν (apotassetai pasin tois heautou hyparchousin) communicates renouncing or taking leave of all one's possessions.
That is a sweeping demand of allegiance.
It does not erase the different ways discipleship is lived out across the New Testament. It does mean that no possession can be treated as untouchable when Christ calls us to obey.
Everything we possess remains under His authority.
And the unsettling truth is that sometimes we discover what we worship only when obedience threatens to take it away.
You can say God is first in your life.
But what happens when His Word contradicts your desires?
You can say you trust His provision.
But what happens when generosity costs something?
You can say Jesus is enough.
But what happens when following Him threatens the approval of people whose opinions you treasure?
Faith becomes painfully real at the point where obedience becomes expensive.
And please understand this.
The Bible does not teach that money itself is the root of every evil.
First Timothy 6:10 says:
“For the love of money is the root of all evil...” — KJV
The Greek wording begins:
ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία
rhiza gar pantōn tōn kakōn estin hē philargyria
A careful rendering is, “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils.”
The key word is φιλαργυρία (philargyria), meaning love of money.
Not money itself.
The love of money.
That difference is crucial.
Money can purchase medicine for a sick child.
It can feed a hungry family.
But money can also become a false savior.
It can promise security while creating fear.
It can offer comfort while nurturing greed.
It can become a master that demands endless sacrifice but never grants lasting peace.
That is why Jesus warned in Matthew 6:24:
“Ye cannot serve God and mammon.”
The Greek term μαμωνᾷ (mamōna), from a Semitic term associated with wealth or possessions, points to riches functioning as a rival master.
Jesus did not say you cannot possess money.
He said you cannot serve both God and wealth.
And there is an enormous difference between possessing something and serving it.
A person may have little money and still worship it.
Another person may have substantial resources and hold them with genuine humility and generosity.
The amount alone does not reveal the heart.
God sees what numbers cannot measure.
But before anyone uses that truth to excuse greed, listen carefully to what Jesus said after the rich young ruler departed.
He told His disciples how difficult it is for the wealthy to enter the kingdom of God.
Then He gave an unforgettable picture.
It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter God's kingdom (Mark 10:25).
This was a deliberately shocking image of impossibility, not a lesson about a camel squeezing through some conveniently narrow city gate.
The disciples were astonished.
They asked:
“Who then can be saved?” — Mark 10:26, KJV
And Jesus answered:
“With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible.” — Mark 10:27, KJV
There it is.
The moment the entire story turns.
The rich young ruler could not save himself through moral achievement.
He could not purchase eternal life.
He could not earn salvation through religious discipline.
And neither can we.
The disciples asked who could be saved.
Jesus did not respond with a better financial strategy.
He pointed them to the power of God.
Salvation is not something the human heart can manufacture.
It is the work of divine grace.
And that is why this story must never be reduced to a fundraising sermon.
The rich young ruler was not being invited to purchase eternal life with the proceeds of a property sale.
He was being summoned to abandon his false security and follow the One in whom eternal life is found.
Jesus Christ.
The One who would soon be betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crowned with thorns.
And nailed to a Roman cross.
The One who had nowhere to lay His head would give His life for sinners who could never afford their own redemption.
Second Corinthians 8:9 declares:
“For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.”
Paul was speaking of the grace of Christ and the spiritual riches His saving work brings—not promising that every believer would become financially prosperous.
Think about that contrast.
A wealthy young man could not release his possessions to follow Jesus.
Yet Jesus willingly humbled Himself for the salvation of sinners.
He did not cling to earthly privilege.
He gave Himself.
And at Calvary, grace accomplished what human wealth never could.
The forgiveness of sin.
The reconciliation of sinners to God.
The hope of eternal life.
The resurrection confirmed that death would not have the final word.
And suddenly, the question is no longer merely, “How much should I give?”
It becomes:
“How can I keep treating temporary things as ultimate when Christ has given Himself for me?”
That is where generosity begins to change.
Not with guilt.
Not with manipulation.
Not with fear that God will reject us if we fail to donate.
But with a heart increasingly captivated by the grace of Jesus.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
The Greek word ἱλαρόν (hilaron) describes a cheerful or glad disposition.
And the phrase μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης (mē ex anankēs) means not from compulsion or necessity.
That matters profoundly.
Christian giving must never be turned into a transaction in which someone purchases God's approval.
A donation does not erase sin.
A monthly payment does not prove that a person loves Jesus more than someone who cannot afford to give.
And no ministry should claim that a financial contribution is required in order to glorify God.
Scripture teaches that believers glorify God through faith, obedience, worship, love, good works, and generous stewardship according to their means and calling.
Financial support can be one beautiful expression of that worship.
But it is never the price of belonging to Christ.
In fact, the New Testament gives a deeply moving picture of generosity in the widow who offered two small coins.
Jesus noticed her.
Not because her gift was impressive by worldly standards.
But because He saw the costly devotion behind it (Mark 12:41–44).

And the same Lord who noticed that widow also sees the exhausted parent who has nothing extra to give, the struggling believer quietly serving others, and the faithful disciple whose prayers are offered in secret.
He is not impressed by public appearances.
He sees the heart.
That is the kind of Gospel we want to keep proclaiming through Gospel Warrior.
A Gospel that refuses to flatter sin.
A Gospel that does not sell forgiveness.
A Gospel that does not confuse prosperity with holiness or poverty with spiritual failure.
A Gospel that tells the broken there is hope, the proud there is a need for repentance, the ashamed there is mercy, and the wandering that Jesus Christ still calls sinners to Himself.
And this is where your participation can become part of something meaningful.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, confront a hidden struggle, return to prayer, or remember that the grace of Christ is greater than your past, we invite you to help us continue and expand that work.
These are simply ways to express appreciation for those who help sustain the ministry—not spiritual rewards and never a measure of anyone's faithfulness.
But because someone scrolling through their feed may be quietly wrestling with the very question this story raises.
Perhaps it is a businessman who has built an empire but lost his peace.
Perhaps it is a young woman who has spent years chasing approval.
Perhaps it is a churchgoer who knows all the right religious language but has never surrendered to Christ.
Perhaps it is someone who has been taught that money can purchase divine favor.
Or perhaps it is a person who has never heard that salvation is a gift of grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
You may never know who reads what you share.
But you can offer them the opportunity to encounter the truth of Scripture.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, spiritually curious seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along and examine the claims of the Gospel for themselves.
The rich young ruler went away grieving.
And the Gospel account does not tell us what ultimately happened to him.
Did he spend the rest of his life defending his decision?
Did he convince himself that Jesus had asked too much?
Did he later remember the love in Christ's eyes and reconsider?
We are not told.
And we must not pretend to know.
Scripture leaves his later story unrecorded.
But perhaps that unresolved ending is part of what makes the encounter so piercing.
Because now the question moves from his life into ours.
Jesus still calls people to repent and believe the Gospel.
He still calls disciples to take up their cross.
He still warns against storing up treasures while neglecting the things of God.
He still exposes idols.
And He still offers grace to sinners who come to Him.
What will we do with that invitation?
Maybe your struggle is not money.
Maybe it is the guilt you have carried for years.
Maybe you have convinced yourself that you are too far gone to be forgiven.
Maybe you have been performing Christianity while hiding a heart that feels spiritually empty.
Maybe you know exactly what God has been confronting through His Word, and you have spent months trying to avoid it.
Then hear this.
Jesus did not come merely to make respectable people more respectable.
He came to save sinners.
He came for the lost.
He came for the broken.
He came for people whose pasts are filled with decisions they wish they could undo.
And the answer is not to purchase your way back into His favor.
The answer is to repent, believe in Christ, and trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Grace.
Not a financial achievement.
Not a religious performance.
Not a lifetime of trying to convince God you are worth saving.
Grace.
And the grace that saves us also begins transforming how we live.
It teaches us to turn away from sin.
To love what God loves.
To care for the poor.
To handle money with integrity.
To make restitution where we have wronged others.
To become generous rather than possessive.
To use what we have for good.
And to hold every earthly treasure with open hands.
Perhaps that is the real question beneath the story of the wealthy young ruler.
Not, “Does Jesus want me to become poor?”
But, “Is there anything I would rather keep than follow Jesus?”
That question deserves more than a quick religious answer.
It deserves prayer.
It deserves honesty.
It deserves the courage to let Scripture examine the motives we usually hide from everyone else.
So I want to invite you into the conversation.
And if you are struggling, you do not have to pretend to be stronger than you are.

If you have experienced God's grace changing your relationship with money, success, control, or some other deeply rooted attachment, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Your story may encourage someone who believes change is impossible.
No pressure to disclose anything private.
Just an honest conversation about what it means to follow Jesus.
Because somewhere in the middle of all our discussions about wealth, success, giving, and sacrifice, we must not lose sight of the greatest treasure of all.
Christ Himself.
The rich young ruler was offered the opportunity to follow Him.
Zacchaeus welcomed Him with joy.
Joseph of Arimathea honored Him with what he possessed.
The women in Luke 8 supported His ministry from their resources.
Different lives.
Different circumstances.
Different expressions of devotion.
But one Savior.
And one unchanging truth.
Jesus Christ is worthy of our trust, our obedience, our worship, and our entire lives.
Not because surrender purchases salvation.
But because the One who saves us is worthy of everything.
If this message has reached a place in your heart you have been afraid to confront, do not rush past it.
Pray.
Open the Scriptures.
Ask the Lord to expose what needs to change.
And remember that the same Jesus who confronted the wealthy young ruler also looked at him with love.
His truth was not cruelty.
His call was not hatred.
His invitation was to something infinitely greater than the wealth that man could not release.
Treasure in heaven.
Life with Christ.
A hope that death itself cannot destroy.
And if you have wandered far from God, the Gospel still announces that forgiveness and reconciliation are found in Jesus Christ.
Your past does not have to be the final chapter.
Your failures do not have to become your identity.
Your possessions do not have to become your master.
And your shame does not have to have the last word.
Because Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose again, and calls us to a new life through faith in Him.
That is why we keep proclaiming His Word.
Not to glorify a platform.
Not to build an empire around a personality.
But to keep pointing people toward the Savior who alone deserves the glory.
And when everything else fades, may we be found holding tightly not to the treasures that could never save us, but to Jesus Christ, who gave Himself to save us.
The greatest tragedy is not having something to lose—it is standing before the One who can give you eternal life and choosing what you cannot keep.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING WHO STOLE A MAN’S INHERITANCE… THEN TREMBLED WHEN GOD SPOKE
paragraphs: THE KING WHO STOLE A MAN’S INHERITANCE… THEN TREMBLED WHEN GOD SPOKE

He was one of Israel’s most wicked kings. He had power, wealth, and blood on his hands. But when judgment reached his ears, he did something nobody expected—and God saw what happened when the crown could no longer hide the man.
“And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly.” — 1 Kings 21:27 (KJV)
There is something terrifying about the moment a person realizes that God has seen everything.
Not just the sins people discovered.
Not just the mistakes that ruined relationships.
Not just the decisions that left visible damage.
Everything.
The private conversations. The secret compromises. The innocent people wounded by selfish ambition. The opportunities to do what was right that were deliberately ignored.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that life can continue looking perfectly normal while judgment is approaching.
You can still sleep in a comfortable bed.
Still wear expensive clothes.
Still have people calling you successful.
Still have an impressive title.
And still be standing on the edge of a divine reckoning.
King Ahab knew what it meant to possess almost everything a man could desire.
He ruled Israel. He lived in a palace. He commanded armies. His words carried political authority.
But there was something he wanted that did not belong to him.
A vineyard.
A seemingly insignificant piece of land beside his palace.
And that vineyard would expose something far more dangerous than greed.
It would expose what happens when a human heart begins treating its desires as more important than God's commandments.
The vineyard belonged to a man named Naboth.
To Ahab, it was convenient property. He wanted to turn it into a vegetable garden because it was near his house.
He offered Naboth money or another vineyard in exchange.
On the surface, the offer might have sounded reasonable.
But Naboth understood something Ahab was willing to overlook.
The land was his ancestral inheritance.

In Israel, inherited land carried covenant significance. The Law of Moses protected the inheritance of Israelite families and placed limits on its permanent transfer (Leviticus 25:23–28; Numbers 36:7).
Naboth answered:
“The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.” — 1 Kings 21:3 (KJV)
Those words were not merely the refusal of a stubborn landowner.
They were the conviction of a man who feared God more than he feared disappointing a king.
Naboth was saying, in effect, that some things were not his to surrender simply because someone powerful wanted them.
And Ahab could not bear hearing no.
The Bible describes him returning home resentful and displeased. He lay on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat.
Imagine that.
A king with an entire kingdom at his disposal was miserable because one faithful man would not surrender his inheritance.
Sometimes the clearest evidence that something has become an idol is how angry we become when God does not permit us to possess it.
Ahab wanted the vineyard.
