And 1 Timothy 5:17–18 recognizes the legitimacy of honoring and materially supporting faithful elders, particularly those laboring in preaching and teaching.
So let us be biblically honest.
A pastor receiving a salary is not sin. A pastor having financial stability is not sin. A pastor becoming widely known is not automatically sin.
The danger arises when wealth becomes an idol, ministry becomes a business of exploitation, and people are manipulated into financing the personal ambitions of a leader.
The Bible does not give us a universal price limit for a pastor's house, clothing, vehicle, or watch.
We should not invent commandments God has not given.
But neither should we ignore the commandments He has given.
Contentment.
Generosity.
Integrity.
Self-control.
Freedom from the love of money.
Faithfulness with what belongs to God.
A willingness to care for the vulnerable.
And an unmistakable commitment to the glory of Jesus Christ.
These are not optional qualities.
They are central to biblical leadership.
In 1 Timothy 3:3, an overseer is required to be “not greedy of filthy lucre” and “not covetous.”
Titus 1:7 likewise teaches that an overseer must not be greedy for dishonest gain.
A minister's character matters more than his public image.
And no amount of charisma can substitute for holiness.
But there is another side of this conversation that many believers would rather avoid.
Sometimes celebrity Christianity does not begin with the pastor.
Sometimes it begins with the congregation.
We want leaders who make us feel important.
We want churches that look successful.
We want spiritual experiences that impress our friends.
We want sermons that make us feel victorious without confronting the sin we have been protecting.
We want a Christianity that looks beautiful on camera but does not interfere too much with our private lives.
And when someone arrives with extraordinary speaking ability, expensive production, a powerful personality, and promises of an easier life, we can become fascinated.
Not necessarily because the person is evil.
But because our hearts are vulnerable to confusing outward success with spiritual authority.
Paul warned Timothy about people who would seek teachers who suited their desires rather than endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:3–4).
That warning should make us examine ourselves before we point at someone else.
Because it is possible to condemn a pastor's love of attention while secretly living for the approval of others.
It is possible to criticize a minister's expensive possessions while being consumed by envy.
It is possible to denounce a preacher's pride while refusing to repent of our own.
But Jesus did not call us to become professional accusers.
He called us to become disciples.
Disciples who love truth.
Disciples who practice discernment.
Disciples who refuse spiritual manipulation.
Disciples who also examine their own hearts.
The celebrity spirit is not confined to the pulpit. Sometimes it is sitting in the pew, waiting for its own opportunity to be applauded.
And that is where this conversation becomes deeply personal.
Because the gospel does not merely expose corrupt leadership.
It exposes every human heart that wants glory without surrender.
Now consider what Jesus said about religious leaders who loved public recognition.
In Matthew 23:5–7, He describes people who performed religious acts to be noticed, loved prominent places, and enjoyed respectful public greetings.
Then, in Matthew 23:12, He declares:
“And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.” — KJV
Jesus was not condemning every public act of religious devotion.
He was confronting the desire to turn spiritual life into a performance for human admiration.
And this warning has not expired.
Today, the prominent seats may look different.
The greetings may arrive through social media.
The public admiration may come through millions of views, television appearances, or carefully cultivated personal brands.
But the temptation remains the same.
Look at me.
Admire me.
Recognize me.
Make me important.
And the tragedy is that a person can become so occupied with being seen as a servant of God that he gradually forgets to serve God.
That is a frightening possibility.
Not only for pastors.
For Christian content creators.
For worship leaders.
For ministry founders.
For anyone who uses the name of Jesus publicly.
Including us at Gospel Warrior.
We must never imagine that pointing out the failures of others somehow makes us immune to the same temptations.
We also need humility.
We also need correction.
We also need accountability.
We also need to remember that the message belongs to Jesus, not to the messenger.
Because the moment a ministry becomes more concerned with protecting its reputation than obeying Scripture, something precious is already being lost.
And yet, we must be careful.
A large platform is not proof of compromise.
Jesus Himself drew enormous crowds.
The apostles preached publicly.
Paul's ministry reached cities and regions far beyond his birthplace.
The gospel is meant to be proclaimed.
There is nothing inherently wrong with using modern technology, publishing books, building facilities, or reaching millions of people.
A camera is not an idol.
A microphone is not a sin.
A successful ministry is not automatically a corrupt ministry.
The issue is not whether a preacher has a platform. The issue is what that platform is teaching people to worship.
Does the message lead people toward repentance and faith in Christ?
Does it explain Scripture faithfully?
Does it proclaim the crucified and risen Savior?
Does it encourage generosity without coercion?
Does it protect vulnerable people?
Does it allow meaningful accountability?
Does it acknowledge that spiritual leaders are fallible human beings?
Does it equip believers to follow Jesus even when their favorite preacher is absent?
Or does everything revolve around one personality?
One name.
One image.
One voice.
One untouchable leader.
That distinction matters.
Because spiritual abuse can flourish where unquestioning loyalty is mistaken for biblical faithfulness.
No pastor is the Savior.
No preacher is beyond correction.
No ministry founder owns the people of God.
And no Christian should be pressured to surrender biblical discernment as proof of loyalty.
Paul's words in 2 Corinthians 4:5 are particularly powerful:
“For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.” — KJV
Read that again.
We preach not ourselves.
The Greek text begins:
οὐ γὰρ ἑαυτοὺς κηρύσσομεν ἀλλὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν κύριον
Ou gar heautous kēryssomen alla Christon Iēsoun kyrion.
A close translation is:
“For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord.”
That is the heartbeat of Christian ministry.
Not ourselves.
Christ.
Not our greatness.
His lordship.
Not our fame.
His gospel.
The original Greek reinforces the contrast between the messengers and the One they proclaim.
Paul was not trying to build a congregation obsessed with Paul.
He wanted people to know Jesus.
And that raises an unforgettable question.
If a pastor disappeared from the spotlight tomorrow, would the congregation still know how to follow Christ?
Would they still open their Bibles?
Would they still pray?
Would they still worship?
Would they still love their neighbors?
Would they still trust the gospel?
Or has their faith become so dependent on a personality that losing the personality feels like losing God?
A healthy shepherd teaches the sheep to recognize the voice of the true Shepherd.
He does not train them to believe that his own voice is indispensable.
Jesus said:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27, KJV
They follow Him.
Not a brand.
Not a celebrity.
Not an institution.
Jesus.
And perhaps that is the most important truth in this entire discussion.
Because one day, the applause will stop.
The cameras will be turned off.
The expensive clothes will wear out.
The buildings will eventually need repair.
The social media numbers will become irrelevant.
And every Christian leader, like every other human being, will stand accountable before God.
Not for how impressive the ministry appeared.
But for faithfulness to the Lord who sees the heart.
James 3:1 warns that teachers will receive stricter judgment.
That should produce humility, not terror-driven manipulation.
It should encourage careful teaching, integrity, repentance, and dependence upon God's grace.
Because a pulpit is not a throne.
It is a place of responsibility.
And the church is not a personal empire.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
There is a scene in Acts 20 that gives us a glimpse of pastoral love.
Paul is preparing to leave the Ephesian elders.
He reminds them of his service, his tears, his teaching, and his willingness to endure hardship.
He warns them to care for the church of God.
And then, as they part, the people weep.
They embrace him.
They grieve because they love him.
There is no need for manufactured celebrity.
No desperate effort to impress.
Just the profound bond between a faithful servant and people whose lives have been touched by the gospel.
That is beautiful.
And it reminds us that biblical ministry is not cold, mechanical, or impersonal.
It is deeply human.
It involves sacrifice.
It involves exhaustion.
It involves showing up when people are hurting.
It involves preaching truth even when truth is unpopular.
It involves protecting the weak.
It involves confronting sin with gentleness and courage.
It involves loving people who may never be able to repay you.
And sometimes it involves doing work that nobody will ever applaud.
The late-night hospital visit.
The quiet prayer with a grieving parent.
The careful counseling of a struggling believer.
The faithful exposition of Scripture to a congregation of thirty.
The pastor who refuses dishonest financial gain.
The leader who admits a mistake and seeks forgiveness.
The minister who chooses integrity when compromise would be profitable.
Heaven sees what the cameras never capture.
And those quiet acts of faithfulness are not inferior to the work of someone preaching to thousands.
But what about pastors who have already fallen into pride, greed, or celebrity worship?
Is there hope for them?
Yes.
Because the gospel is not merely a warning to the proud.
It is an invitation to repent.
Remember Peter.
The same Peter who later instructed elders to shepherd God's flock had once denied knowing Jesus.
Three times.
His failure was real.
His shame was real.
But his story did not end beside the fire where he denied his Lord.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep (John 21:15–17).
Notice the beauty of that moment.
Jesus did not invite Peter to build a personal empire.
He called him to love Him and care for His people.
“Feed my sheep.”
Not your sheep.
My sheep.
Those two words should remain in the heart of every pastor.
The people belong to Jesus.
Their faith is precious.
Their wounds matter.
Their offerings must be handled responsibly.
Their trust must never be exploited.
And their spiritual growth must never be sacrificed for a leader's personal prestige.
A fallen leader who truly repents can find forgiveness in Christ.
But forgiveness does not automatically erase consequences, restore a leadership position, or remove the need for accountability and restitution.
Grace is not permission to continue exploiting people.
Grace teaches us to turn away from sin.
That is why this message is not ultimately about humiliating pastors.
It is about calling the entire church back to Jesus.
The wealthy pastor needs Him.
The struggling pastor needs Him.
The wounded church member needs Him.
The person who has become cynical about Christianity needs Him.
The believer who has confused financial prosperity with God's approval needs Him.
And the Christian who has become proud of exposing other people's failures needs Him too.
We all need the same Savior.
Because the ground at the foot of the cross is not divided into celebrities and ordinary people.
It is occupied by sinners who need mercy.
And the astonishing news of the gospel is that Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose from the dead, and offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
No amount of wealth can purchase that forgiveness.
No number of followers can earn it.
No church position can guarantee it.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the grace that saves us also calls us into a transformed life.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior will always return to one truth.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because wrongdoing should be hidden.
Not because accountability is unnecessary.
But because Jesus can bring repentance where there was pride, integrity where there was corruption, healing where there was spiritual injury, and new obedience where there was rebellion.
He does not rewrite the past by pretending it never happened.
He redeems people by bringing them into the truth.
And perhaps, as you read this, you are remembering a church that hurt you.
A pastor who disappointed you.
A ministry you once trusted.
Maybe you gave sacrificially because you believed you were helping people, only to discover that your generosity had been misused.
Maybe you were taught that questioning a leader meant questioning God.
Maybe you watched someone you loved lose faith after witnessing hypocrisy.
And now you are wondering whether you can trust anything associated with Christianity again.
Please hear this.
The failure of someone who claimed to represent Jesus does not mean Jesus has failed you.
You do not have to pretend the damage was insignificant.
You do not have to excuse manipulation.
You do not have to return to an unsafe spiritual environment to prove that you have forgiven someone.
But you also do not have to let a fallen human being become the final authority on who Jesus Christ is.
Look at Him.
Read the Gospels.
Listen to His words.
Watch how He treated the overlooked, the grieving, the ashamed, and the broken.
See how He confronted religious hypocrisy while extending mercy to repentant sinners.
See Him carrying the cross.
See the empty tomb.
And remember that Christianity rests upon the person and work of Jesus Christ, not the perfection of those who preach about Him.
If this message has touched an old wound, you do not need to reveal private details publicly.
And if you are a pastor, ministry worker, or Christian leader who feels the weight of this message, perhaps your prayer today is simpler.
Lord, keep my heart humble. Never let me love the spotlight more than the people You have called me to serve.
Not to prove anything to strangers.
But because sometimes speaking a sincere prayer helps us remember the commitment we want to live.
And to those who love their pastors, do not turn this article into permission to become suspicious of every faithful shepherd.
Encourage good leaders.
Pray for them.
Support them appropriately.
Protect their families from unreasonable expectations.
Remember that pastors are human beings who need rest, friendship, correction, and grace.
And when leadership is faithful, let your gratitude be sincere.
The church does not need a culture of constant accusation.
It needs a culture of truth, love, transparency, accountability, and Christ-centered service.
Now, there is something else I want to say, especially to those who believe Christian teaching and discipleship resources should continue reaching people who may never be able to pay for them.
At Gospel Warrior, our desire is to make Scripture-centered encouragement and learning resources accessible to more people.
These resources are offered to help people read, learn, reflect, and become better grounded in the faith.
But maintaining and expanding a ministry takes time, effort, and practical resources.
And if this work has helped you, you can become part of sustaining it.
Think of it as a recurring act of generosity toward a mission you believe is worth supporting.
But I want to make something unmistakably clear.
You do not have to pay us to prove your faith.

Biblical tithes and offerings are matters that deserve careful teaching and sincere stewardship. Christians differ on how Old Testament tithing applies under the new covenant, while the New Testament clearly encourages willing, generous, and cheerful giving.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
From generosity, not guilt.
From a desire to help, not a fear of missing God's blessing.
Those products can be useful reminders of faith, thoughtful gifts, and tools for reflection. But they are not the heart of this mission.
Jesus is.
You can pray.
You can encourage someone.
You can share a free resource.
You can tell a friend about a Scripture passage that helped you.
That simple act may reach a struggling believer, a discouraged pastor, a wounded church member, or someone who has been hesitant to return to Jesus.
What is one quality you believe every pastor should demonstrate before asking people to follow his spiritual leadership?
Is it humility?
Integrity?
Compassion?
Sound doctrine?
Accountability?
A willingness to serve?
Tell us why.
Your response may encourage someone who is trying to discern what healthy Christian leadership should look like.
Because the purpose of this conversation is not to create another online argument.
It is to help us recognize the character of Christ.
And now we return to the question that began everything.
Would Jesus approve of pastors living like celebrities?
Scripture does not give us grounds to condemn a pastor simply for being well-known, financially comfortable, or publicly influential.
But Jesus unmistakably rejects prideful self-exaltation, greed, hypocrisy, and leadership that seeks to be served rather than to serve.
He calls His shepherds to humility.
He calls His people to discernment.
He calls every one of us to repentance.
And He calls His church to remember who the true Head is.
Not the pastor with the largest audience.
Not the preacher with the most expensive possessions.
Not the personality whose name fills the building.
Jesus Christ.
The One who washed feet.
The One who welcomed the overlooked.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who carried our sins to the cross.
The One who rose again.
The One who is worthy of every crown, every honor, every song, and every act of worship.
And when the church finally understands that, we will stop asking merely how famous our leaders have become.
We will start asking whether their lives help us see Jesus more clearly.
Because at the end of everything, the greatest achievement of a Christian shepherd is not to make the world remember his name.
It is to help people know the name above every name.
And perhaps the most beautiful legacy any pastor could leave is a congregation that continues to love, obey, and worship Jesus long after the pastor's own voice has fallen silent.
The shepherd was never meant to become the star. His calling was to lead wounded sheep to the Savior whose scars still tell the greatest story of love.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD YOU CONFESS YOUR SINS TO A PRIEST, A PASTOR, OR DIRECTLY TO GOD? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE THE WAY YOU SEEK FORGIVENESS FOREVER
paragraphs: SHOULD YOU CONFESS YOUR SINS TO A PRIEST, A PASTOR, OR DIRECTLY TO GOD? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE THE WAY YOU SEEK FORGIVENESS FOREVER

What if the greatest obstacle between you and God's forgiveness isn't the absence of a priest, the silence of a pastor, or the weight of your past—but the fear that Jesus will reject you if He knows everything? Three powerful passages of Scripture reveal who forgives sin, why confession matters, and how a broken sinner can finally come home.
There is a confession you have been carrying that nobody has ever heard.
Perhaps it happened years ago.
Perhaps it happened last night.
Perhaps it is something you have already asked God to forgive a hundred times, yet every time you close your eyes to pray, the memory returns like a witness determined to testify against you.
You smile at church.
You sing the worship songs.
You tell people you are blessed.
But somewhere beneath the carefully maintained appearance of a faithful Christian, there is a question you are almost afraid to ask.
If people knew what I have done, would they still believe I belong to Jesus?
And then comes another question, quieter but even more terrifying.
Does God really forgive someone like me?
Maybe someone told you that you must confess your sins to a priest.
Someone else insisted that you should confess only to God.
Another Christian quoted James 5:16 and said believers must confess their sins to one another.
And suddenly, something as precious as forgiveness became surrounded by arguments, denominational disagreements, religious expectations, and confusion.
You are not looking for another theological fight.
You want to know whether you can approach God tonight, with your shame, your failures, your secrets, and your trembling faith—and genuinely receive His forgiveness.
You want to know what the Bible actually says.
Not merely what your denomination has always taught.
Not merely what your favorite preacher believes.
Not merely what makes you feel comfortable.
What does Jesus Christ, our crucified and risen Savior, actually make possible?
Because if we misunderstand confession, we may spend years hiding from the very One who came to save us.
And if we misunderstand forgiveness, we may either carry guilt Christ has already paid for or treat sin so lightly that we never experience the transforming power of repentance.
The truth begins with a remarkable promise.
The apostle John wrote:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
—1 John 1:9, King James Version (KJV)
Read those words again.
Not quickly.
Not as a religious slogan.
Read them as someone who has spent years wondering whether God is still willing to receive them.
"If we confess our sins..."
The Greek word translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), a form of homologeō, meaning to acknowledge, admit, or confess.
In this context, it means honestly acknowledging our sins rather than denying or concealing them.
Confession is not a performance designed to persuade God that we deserve another chance.
It is bringing our sin into the light before the God who already knows the truth.
You cannot inform an all-knowing God of something He has overlooked.
He saw the decision before you made it.
He heard the words before anyone else did.
He knows the thoughts you never spoke aloud.
Yet He still calls you to confess.
Why?
Because confession is not about giving God information.
It is about abandoning the lie that we can hide from Him.
Notice something equally important.
John does not say, "If we confess our sins, God might forgive us if we have suffered enough."
He does not say, "If we confess our sins, God will forgive us only after we prove that we will never fail again."
He says God is faithful and just to forgive.
The Greek expression πιστός ἐστιν καὶ δίκαιος (pistos estin kai dikaios) means "He is faithful and righteous" or "faithful and just."
This is extraordinary.
John connects forgiveness not merely with God's kindness but with His faithfulness and righteousness.
Why?
Because Christian forgiveness is not God pretending sin does not matter.
It rests on what Jesus Christ has accomplished.
Just two verses earlier, John declares that "the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin" (1 John 1:7, KJV).
And immediately afterward, he reminds believers that if anyone sins, "we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous" (1 John 2:1, KJV).
That changes everything.
The foundation of forgiveness is not the intensity of your tears.
It is not the eloquence of your confession.
It is not how convincingly you promise to become a better person.
The foundation of forgiveness is Jesus Christ—His sacrifice, His righteousness, and His finished work.
Your tears may be sincere.
Your sorrow may be deep.
Your repentance must be real.
But your tears are not your Savior.
Jesus is.
And that brings us to the question that has divided Christians for centuries.
If Christ is the One who saves us, must we confess our sins to a priest or pastor before God will forgive us?
The apostle Paul wrote:
"For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."
—1 Timothy 2:5, KJV
In the original Greek, the central phrase reads:
εἷς καὶ μεσίτης θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἄνθρωπος Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς
Heis kai mesitēs theou kai anthrōpōn, anthrōpos Christos Iēsous.
"One mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus."
The word μεσίτης (mesitēs) means "mediator," someone who stands between parties to bring about reconciliation or represent a covenantal relationship.
Paul's declaration is unmistakably Christ-centered.
Jesus is the unique mediator between God and humanity.
No pastor can die for your sins.
No priest can replace the sacrifice of Calvary.
No spiritual leader can become a second Savior.
Only Jesus Christ, truly human and truly divine, gave Himself as the ransom that reconciles sinners to God.
And because of Him, Scripture invites believers to approach God with confidence.
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."
—Hebrews 4:16, KJV
Think about that.
The throne you approach is called a throne of grace.
Not a throne where you must first convince God that your past is acceptable.
Not a throne reserved only for people whose lives have never been scandalous.
A throne of grace.
You can come to God through Jesus Christ.
Directly.
Personally.
Honestly.
You do not need to wait until a particular pastor is available before you can cry out for mercy.
You do not need to find the perfect religious vocabulary.
You can kneel beside your bed, sit in your parked car, stand in your kitchen, or weep on the floor where nobody sees you.
And pray:

"Father, I have sinned. I have no excuse. I cannot undo what I have done. But I believe Jesus died for sinners, and I am coming to You through Him. Forgive me. Cleanse me. Change my heart. Teach me to walk in Your truth."
That prayer is not powerful because the wording is magical.
It is meaningful because it expresses faith in Christ and honest repentance before God.
But there is another side to this conversation that we must not ignore.
Because someone reading this right now may be thinking:
"Then why do some Christians confess their sins to priests?"
That deserves a careful and respectful answer.

Roman Catholic Christians understand sacramental confession as an encounter with Christ's forgiveness through the ministry of an ordained priest. Their teaching appeals especially to John 20:22–23, where the risen Jesus speaks to His apostles about forgiving and retaining sins, and to the Church's understanding of apostolic ministry.
Eastern Orthodox Christians also practice sacramental confession, understanding the priest as a witness and minister within the Church's life of repentance and reconciliation.

Many Protestant Christians interpret these passages differently. They emphasize that forgiveness comes through Christ alone and that believers may confess directly to God without priestly sacramental absolution, while still recognizing the value of pastoral counsel, mutual confession, and church discipline.
These are genuine theological differences, not differences that should be dismissed through caricature.

Catholic and Orthodox teaching does not ordinarily claim that a priest replaces Jesus as the one mediator. Rather, those traditions understand ordained ministry as participating in or serving Christ's reconciling work.
Protestant traditions generally question whether the New Testament requires sacramental confession to an ordained priest as the ordinary means of receiving forgiveness.
The important distinction is this:
The Bible clearly teaches that God forgives sinners through Jesus Christ. Christians disagree about the precise role ordained ministers have in the Church's administration of that forgiveness.
We should not pretend that 1 Timothy 2:5, by itself, settles every historical disagreement about sacramental confession.
But neither should we allow denominational debates to obscure the truth every Christian desperately needs to hear.
Jesus Christ is indispensable.
His grace cannot be purchased.
His sacrifice cannot be replaced.
And no human being possesses independent power to forgive sins against God apart from God's authority.
Now consider the passage that makes this discussion even more personal.
"Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed."
—James 5:16, KJV
The Greek begins:
ἐξομολογεῖσθε οὖν ἀλλήλοις τὰς ἁμαρτίας
Exomologeisthe oun allēlois tas hamartias.
"Therefore, confess your sins to one another."
The Greek word ἁμαρτίας (hamartias) means "sins." Although the KJV uses "faults," the original wording directly concerns sins.
And the word ἀλλήλοις (allēlois) means "to one another."
This is important.
James does not describe confession merely as a private transaction between an isolated individual and God.
He teaches mutual confession and prayer within the believing community.
The immediate context also mentions calling the elders of the church to pray over someone who is sick (James 5:14–15).
But verse 16 broadens the language to "one another."
That means we must not reduce the entire passage either to confession exclusively before ordained ministers or to the idea that other believers have no meaningful role in our spiritual healing.
James is showing us something beautiful and uncomfortable.
The Christian life was never meant to be lived entirely behind locked emotional doors.
There are sins we need to confess to God.
There are wrongs we need to acknowledge to people we have hurt.
And there are struggles we may need to bring into the light with trustworthy, mature believers who can pray for us, encourage us, confront us when necessary, and help us pursue restoration.
Not every private sin needs to be publicly announced.
Not every person is safe to receive sensitive information.
Confession should never become gossip, humiliation, spiritual manipulation, or an opportunity for someone to exercise abusive control.
But secrecy can also become a prison.
Imagine a man who has spent years trapped in pornography.
Every Sunday he sings about holiness.
Every Monday he promises himself he will stop.
Every Friday he falls again.
He prays.
He cries.
He deletes his browsing history.
He makes another promise.
And slowly, shame begins whispering that he is the only Christian in the world who struggles like this.
Then one evening he finally tells a trusted, spiritually mature brother:
"I need help. I keep falling, and I don't want to live this way anymore."
Nothing magical happens because the words are spoken aloud.
But something important changes.
The struggle is no longer completely hidden.
Someone can pray with him.
Someone can ask difficult questions.
Someone can help him establish wise boundaries, pursue accountability, and seek professional support if needed.
And most importantly, he can be reminded that his hope rests in Jesus Christ, not in his ability to maintain an impressive religious appearance.
Or imagine a woman who wounded someone deeply with her words.
She has prayed privately for forgiveness.
But she knows the person she hurt is still carrying the consequences.
Should she simply say, "God has forgiven me," and refuse to acknowledge the damage?
No.
Biblical repentance takes responsibility.
Jesus taught His followers to pursue reconciliation when they recognize that a brother or sister has something against them (Matthew 5:23–24).
Where possible and appropriate, repentance may involve confession to the person harmed, an honest apology, restitution, and changed behavior.
Forgiveness from God does not erase our responsibility to make things right where we can.
And where wrongdoing involves abuse, exploitation, or criminal conduct, repentance does not replace protection of victims, reporting where appropriate, or lawful accountability.
Grace is not permission to avoid consequences.
Grace teaches us to stop hiding behind excuses and begin walking in the light.
This is why the answer to our original question cannot be reduced to a careless slogan.
Should Christians confess directly to God?
Yes. Scripture explicitly teaches believers to confess their sins and approach the Father through Jesus Christ.
Should Christians confess sins to one another?
Yes. James 5:16 teaches mutual confession and prayer, and other passages call believers to seek reconciliation and restoration.
Can pastors and spiritual leaders help?
Certainly. Faithful pastors, elders, and mature Christians can offer biblical counsel, prayer, accountability, and encouragement.
Must every Christian confess to an ordained priest as a necessary sacramental practice?

Christian traditions disagree. Catholic and Orthodox churches affirm sacramental confession within their theological understanding of the Church, while most Protestant traditions do not regard confession to a priest as necessary for receiving God's forgiveness.
But here is the question that reaches beneath every denominational argument.
Have you actually repented—or have you simply become skilled at feeling guilty?
Because guilt and repentance are not the same thing.
A person can feel terrible after being caught and still have no intention of changing.
A person can cry during worship and return to deliberate wrongdoing without any willingness to confront it.
A person can confess the same sin repeatedly while refusing the practical steps that genuine repentance requires.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death."
—2 Corinthians 7:10, KJV
Godly sorrow does not merely grieve the consequences of sin.
It turns toward God.
It begins to hate what destroys fellowship, truth, and love.
It seeks mercy and welcomes transformation.
This does not mean a repentant Christian will never struggle again.
John himself wrote, "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves" (1 John 1:8, KJV).
And he followed his teaching about confession with the reassurance that believers have an advocate in Jesus Christ when they sin (1 John 2:1).
The Christian life is not sinless perfection achieved through human willpower.
It is a life of continuing repentance, faith, obedience, and growth through God's grace.
The difference between struggling against sin and making peace with sin matters.
One cries out, "Lord, deliver me."
The other says, "Lord, leave this part of my life untouched."
And perhaps that is where the Holy Spirit is confronting someone reading these words.
You want forgiveness.
But do you want freedom?
You want the shame removed.
But are you willing to surrender the sin?
You want Jesus to comfort your wounded heart.
But will you allow Him to challenge the habits, relationships, pride, bitterness, and hidden compromises that keep wounding it?
Christ does not merely offer to make your old life more comfortable.
He calls you into new life.
And sometimes the most beautiful evidence of grace is not that you never fall.
It is that you stop defending the darkness and begin returning to the Light.
There is an ancient biblical picture of confession that brings this truth into focus.
King David knew what it meant to carry hidden guilt.
After his sin involving Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, David was confronted by the prophet Nathan (2 Samuel 11–12).
David's position as king did not make him innocent.
His public reputation could not erase his private guilt.
And when the truth was brought into the light, David said:
"I have sinned against the LORD."
—2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
In Hebrew:
חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה
Chatati la-YHWH.
"I have sinned against the LORD."
Those words are painfully simple.
No elaborate defense.
No attempt to blame Bathsheba.
No appeal to his royal achievements.
No suggestion that his previous victories made his wrongdoing less serious.
"I have sinned against the LORD."
David's confession was met with the announcement that the LORD had put away his sin, although serious consequences remained.
That distinction is essential.
Divine forgiveness is real.
So are the consequences of wrongdoing.
Later, in Psalm 32, David reflected on the burden of concealed sin:
"When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long."
—Psalm 32:3, KJV
Then he declared:
"I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid."
—Psalm 32:5, KJV
The Hebrew verb behind "I acknowledged" is אוֹדִיעֲךָ (odiakha), from the root ידע (yada), meaning "to know" or "to make known."
David was no longer concealing his guilt before God.
He was acknowledging it.
And in the same verse, he testified that the LORD forgave the guilt of his sin.
But do not romanticize David's story.
His actions caused devastating harm.
His confession did not make the suffering of others imaginary.
The Bible refuses to treat repentance as a convenient escape from responsibility.
Yet David's story also refuses to declare that even grievous sin places a repentant person beyond God's mercy.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin is small.
But that God's mercy is greater than the sinner's ability to rescue himself.
And nowhere is that mercy revealed more clearly than at the cross.
Picture Calvary.
Jesus is crucified between criminals.
One of them turns to Him and says:
"Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom."
—Luke 23:42, KJV
This man has no opportunity to rebuild his reputation.
He cannot travel back through time and undo his crimes.
He cannot begin a lifetime of religious accomplishments.
He cannot step down from the cross and prove himself through decades of visible service.
He turns to the crucified King.
And Jesus answers:
"Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise."
—Luke 23:43, KJV
Do not miss what this scene reveals.
The criminal's hope was not in a ritual he could perform.
It was not in a spiritual leader he could summon.
It was not in the moral achievements he could present.
His hope was in Jesus.
The passage does not exist to settle every later debate about church sacraments. But it powerfully demonstrates the sufficiency of Christ to save a sinner who turns to Him in faith.
The dying criminal had nothing to offer Jesus except his need—and Jesus was enough.
Perhaps you have spent years believing you must somehow become worthy before you can return to God.
Perhaps you are waiting until you have gone thirty days without failing.
Perhaps you think you need to feel more sorrow before your confession will count.
Perhaps you are terrified that your past is too ugly to bring into prayer.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
And the gospel does not begin with your ability to clean yourself.
It begins with the Savior who came to rescue sinners.
Paul wrote:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
—Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after our reputation was repaired.
Not after we mastered every temptation.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is not an invitation to remain unchanged.
It is the foundation of the transformation we could never accomplish by ourselves.
The same grace that forgives also teaches us to deny ungodliness and live differently (Titus 2:11–12).
And that brings us to the heart of this entire conversation.

Whether you come from a Catholic family, an Orthodox tradition, a Protestant church, or a background where you have never understood confession at all, do not allow an argument about religious practice to distract you from the person of Jesus Christ.
Study the Scriptures.
Understand what your church actually teaches.
Ask thoughtful questions.
Seek wise pastoral guidance.
Do not confuse honest theological disagreement with hatred for other Christians.
But above all, do not make peace with unconfessed sin.
Do not use grace as an excuse to continue harming others.
Do not allow shame to convince you that repentance is pointless.
And do not imagine that your spiritual future depends on a human being becoming your substitute Savior.
Jesus Christ is the one mediator.
He is the righteous advocate.
He is the crucified Redeemer.
He is the risen Lord.
He is the One who receives repentant sinners.
And He is the One who changes lives.
Maybe tonight you need to confess something to God.
Maybe tomorrow you need to apologize to someone you wounded.
Maybe you need to sit with a trustworthy pastor, priest, elder, counselor, or mature Christian and finally speak about the struggle you have been hiding.
Maybe you need to stop treating confession as a repeated emotional release and begin taking the difficult steps that repentance requires.
Whatever your situation, remember this:
Confession is not a way to earn the love of God. It is a truthful response to the God whose grace calls us out of darkness.
And the cross is the reason you can come without pretending.
There is a beautiful image in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son.
The younger son has wasted his inheritance.
He has brought shame upon himself.
He has rehearsed what he will say to his father.
He knows he is unworthy of the position he once enjoyed.
And while he is still far away, his father sees him.
The father runs.
He embraces him.
He welcomes him home.
The son confesses:
"Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son."
—Luke 15:21, KJV
The father does not pretend the rebellion never happened.
But he celebrates the son's return.
The parable reveals the extraordinary mercy of God toward the repentant.
And perhaps that is the picture your exhausted soul needs today.
Not a God who is unaware of your sin.
Not a God who calls evil good.
But a Father whose mercy is greater than you imagined, revealed to us through Jesus Christ.
You may have wandered far.
You may have disgraced yourself.
You may have broken promises that once seemed sacred.
You may have convinced yourself that your story is beyond repair.
But your past does not have the authority to declare what the grace of Jesus Christ cannot redeem.
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Turn away from sin.
Trust the Savior.
And begin walking with Him.
And if you have experienced God's forgiveness and want to encourage someone who believes their past has disqualified them, share a testimony of what Christ has done in your life.
Someone reading the comments may be silently wondering whether there is still hope for them.
Your words may help point them back to Jesus.
Return to the Scriptures when shame begins speaking louder than truth.

This ministry exists to proclaim Jesus Christ, encourage repentance, teach biblical truth, strengthen struggling believers, and remind wounded people that their story does not have to end where their sin began.
Our desire is not simply to attract readers.
It is to help people become disciples.
People who open their Bibles.
People who learn to pray.
People who confront sin honestly.
People who extend forgiveness.
People who grow in wisdom, humility, holiness, and love.
People whose lives increasingly reflect the Lord Jesus Christ.
These products are simply additional resources and expressions of appreciation. The greatest value of discipleship will never be merchandise.
It will always be knowing Jesus Christ more deeply.
And whether or not you can give financially, you can still participate in this mission.
Pray for the ministry.
Help someone discover the free resources.
Encourage someone who is close to giving up.
And never underestimate what God can do through a simple act of faithfulness.
Because at the end of the day, this is not about building a platform around a personality.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who calls us to repentance.
The One who makes all things new.
So before you leave this article, I want you to imagine one final scene.
A room.
A closed door.
A person sitting alone.
No congregation.
No applause.
No carefully chosen religious language.
Only someone who has finally grown tired of hiding.
Their hands are trembling.
Their eyes are filled with tears.
And for the first time in a long time, they whisper:
"Jesus, I have sinned. I need Your mercy. I cannot save myself. Please forgive me and change me."
There is no performance.
No bargaining.
No attempt to impress heaven.
Only a sinner coming to God through the Savior.
And Scripture gives that person a promise far stronger than any passing emotion:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
—1 John 1:9, KJV
That promise is not built upon the sinner's perfection.
It is grounded in the faithfulness of God and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
So do not wait until you feel worthy to seek Him.
Do not let your shame become your hiding place.
Do not confuse the voice of condemnation with the call of repentance.
Come to Christ.
Tell the truth.
Receive His mercy through faith.
And follow Him into a life that no longer belongs to the darkness.
Because the sin you are terrified to bring into the light is not greater than the Savior who died to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A PASTOR CURSE YOU FOR NOT GIVING AN OFFERING? THE TERRIFYING LIE THAT HAS KEPT TOO MANY CHRISTIANS AFRAID OF GOD
paragraphs: CAN A PASTOR CURSE YOU FOR NOT GIVING AN OFFERING? THE TERRIFYING LIE THAT HAS KEPT TOO MANY CHRISTIANS AFRAID OF GOD

When the pulpit becomes a place of financial threats, the offering plate becomes a weapon, and believers begin confusing a pastor's anger with God's judgment, one question must finally be answered: Does Jesus really punish people who cannot afford to give?
She had only enough money left to buy food for her children.
The bills were overdue. Her refrigerator was nearly empty. She had prayed all week for God to provide, and somehow, despite everything, she still found the strength to attend church that Sunday.
She wasn't there looking for a miracle wrapped in money.
She just needed to hear that God had not forgotten her.
But then the offering began.
The pastor stood behind the pulpit, his voice rising as he spoke about blessings, obedience, and financial sacrifice.
Then came the words that made her stomach tighten.
"If you refuse to give to God's work, don't complain when your finances collapse. You cannot expect God's protection while withholding what belongs to Him."
She looked down at the few bills folded inside her purse.
That money was supposed to feed her children.
And suddenly, she felt trapped between two fears.
If she gave it, what would her children eat?
If she kept it, would God punish her?
Her hands trembled.
Her eyes filled with tears.
And in that moment, something heartbreaking happened.
A woman who had come to church seeking the comfort of her heavenly Father began to fear that the same Father might harm her family because she could not afford an offering.
Now imagine Jesus standing beside that woman.
Would He threaten her?
Would He shame her?
Would He tell her that her children's hunger was the price of refusing to finance a ministry?
Or would He confront the religious system that had placed such a crushing burden on her shoulders?
Because before this article ends, we need to confront a question that reaches far beyond money.
When someone uses God's name to frighten you into giving, whose voice are you actually hearing?
The answer matters more than many Christians realize.
And it begins with something Scripture never teaches: that a pastor possesses personal authority to place a divine curse on a believer for refusing to give an offering.

A pastor may preach about generosity. He may teach biblical stewardship. He may encourage believers to support legitimate ministry needs. He may even warn against greed, dishonesty, and the spiritual dangers of loving money.
But he cannot manufacture a curse from God because you did not meet his financial expectations.
God's authority is not a weapon that belongs to the preacher.
And the Holy Spirit is not a debt collector.
Listen carefully to what the apostle Paul actually wrote.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, the Greek text says:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης· ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.
A faithful translation is:
"Each one should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver."
Two expressions deserve our attention.
The phrase ἐξ ἀνάγκης (ex anankēs) means "under compulsion" or "out of necessity or constraint."
And ἱλαρὸν δότην (hilaron dotēn) means "a cheerful giver."
Paul is not describing a congregation terrified into surrendering its last coins.
He is describing generosity that comes from a willing heart.
The surrounding context is a collection for believers in need. Paul encourages preparation, generosity, and integrity, but explicitly rejects coerced giving.
Think about that.
If a pastor tells you that God will destroy your finances unless you give him money, what has happened to the freedom Paul describes?
If you give because you are afraid of being cursed, are you giving cheerfully—or attempting to purchase safety?
And if the offering is obtained through spiritual intimidation, can the preacher simply call that pressure "faith"?
The Bible does not permit us to redefine coercion as worship.
But perhaps you have heard someone quote Malachi.
Perhaps the words still echo in your memory.
"You are cursed with a curse!"
That is Malachi 3:9, and it is one of the passages most frequently brought into discussions about tithing.
But what did God actually say, and to whom was He speaking?
In Malachi 3:9, the Hebrew text includes:
בַּמְּאֵרָה אַתֶּם נֵאָרִים
Bamme'erah attem ne'arim.
"You are cursed with a curse."
The Hebrew is serious. It refers to being under a curse, not merely experiencing disappointment or missing a financial opportunity.
But context changes everything.

Malachi was addressing the covenant unfaithfulness of Israel under the Mosaic covenant. The passage concerns tithes and contributions connected to Israel's worship, priestly provision, and covenant responsibilities.
In Malachi 3:10, God calls the people to bring the full tithe into the storehouse so there will be food in His house.
The text must be understood within Israel's covenant arrangement, including the agricultural and community responsibilities established in the Law.
It is not a blank check authorizing every modern pastor to threaten individual Christians with divine punishment whenever an offering falls short.
And it certainly does not establish that money placed into a particular preacher's hands determines whether God will protect your children.

The Old Testament law included tithes, offerings, provisions for Levites, and care for vulnerable people. Those arrangements cannot simply be transferred into the New Testament church without considering the work of Christ and the teaching of His apostles.
Christians differ over whether a ten-percent tithe remains a binding standard today or serves as a useful pattern for giving.
But regardless of that disagreement, no pastor receives biblical permission to extort offerings through personal threats.
Now consider the words of Paul in Galatians 3:13.
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
"Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law."
The Greek verb ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen) carries the sense of redeeming or buying out.

Paul is speaking about Christ's redemptive work in relation to the law's curse. His message is not that Christians will never experience suffering, poverty, hardship, discipline, or consequences for sin.
It is that Jesus Christ has accomplished what human religious performance could never accomplish.
Our standing before God rests upon Christ's saving work, received through faith, not upon our ability to satisfy a minister's financial demands.
Read that again.
The blood of Jesus is not less powerful than an unpaid offering.
The cross did not secure redemption only for those who can afford a monthly contribution.
And no human being can reverse Christ's saving work by announcing a curse from a pulpit.
There is a difference between God's sovereign judgment, which Scripture takes seriously, and a preacher claiming the power to impose that judgment because someone did not give him money.
That distinction is essential.
Because the same Bible that encourages generosity also exposes religious leaders who exploit the vulnerable.
Jesus warned in Mark 12:40 about religious figures who "devour widows' houses" while maintaining an appearance of devotion.
And immediately afterward, Mark records the account of a poor widow who placed two small coins into the temple treasury.
Jesus saw her.
He noticed what everyone else could easily overlook.
He knew that she had given out of her poverty.
But look carefully at the setting.
The widow's offering appears in the context of Jesus' warning about religious exploitation and His coming judgment on the temple establishment.
Christ commends the significance of her sacrifice, yet the passage does not command church leaders to demand the last resources of impoverished people.
It certainly does not authorize anyone to threaten widows, struggling parents, or vulnerable believers until they surrender what they need to survive.
Jesus saw the widow's sacrifice.
He also condemned those who devoured widows' houses.
We must never use one part of His teaching to silence the other.
And there is another passage that deserves to be heard in churches where offerings have become a source of fear.
In 2 Corinthians 8:12, Paul writes:
According to what a person has. Not according to what he does not have.
Imagine how many tears might have been prevented if those words had been preached as faithfully as Malachi 3:10.
Paul continues in 2 Corinthians 8:13 that his intention is not for others to be relieved while the Corinthians are burdened.
His concern is fairness, generosity, and the mutual care of God's people.
That does not mean generosity never involves sacrifice.
Sometimes love gives at real personal cost.
But sacrifice offered freely is not the same thing as sacrifice extracted through intimidation.
A believer may choose to give generously in hardship.
A pastor must not exploit that hardship.
A believer may trust God while giving sacrificially.
A preacher must not promise guaranteed wealth in exchange for a donation.
But it must not pretend that God has delegated to its leaders the authority to sell His favor.
Perhaps this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you have sat through a service where the pastor announced that anyone who did not give was blocking their own breakthrough.
Maybe you were told your business would fail.
That your children would suffer.
That sickness might enter your home.
That the enemy would gain access to your family because you had withheld an offering.
Maybe you gave money you did not have.
And afterward, instead of feeling joyful, you felt afraid.
You wondered whether the amount was enough.
Whether God was satisfied.
Whether the next unexpected expense was evidence that you had somehow failed Him.
And perhaps the most devastating part was that you stopped seeing God as a Father and began seeing Him as someone waiting for a payment.
If that happened to you, hear what Scripture says about the character of God.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
That is not permission to become selfish.
It is not an excuse to ignore genuine responsibilities.
It is the announcement that condemnation is not the believer's relationship to God in Christ.
Romans 8:33 asks, "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect?"
And Romans 8:34 points to Christ, who died, was raised, and intercedes for His people.
Your ultimate security is not in a preacher's approval.
It is in Jesus Christ.
The New Testament also tells believers to test spiritual claims.
First John 4:1 says not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits to see whether they are from God.
A preacher's confidence does not prove his interpretation.
A microphone does not create divine authority.
A title does not make every warning biblical.
And an emotional atmosphere does not transform a financial demand into a command from heaven.
In Acts 17:11, the Bereans are commended for examining the Scriptures to see whether the things they were being taught were true.
They did not treat the preacher's words as beyond examination.
Neither should we.
But now we must confront the other side of this question.
Because it would be just as wrong to use the reality of spiritual abuse as an excuse to dismiss biblical generosity altogether.
The answer to manipulative giving is not a hardened heart.
The answer is redeemed giving.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:21:
"For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."
Our relationship with money reveals something about our loves, priorities, fears, and trust.
Some believers genuinely struggle with greed.
Some possess the means to help others but refuse because they have made comfort their highest priority.
Some benefit from faithful ministry while never considering how to support its legitimate needs.
Scripture challenges those attitudes.
First Timothy 6:17–19 instructs the wealthy not to place their hope in uncertain riches, but to be generous and ready to share.
Galatians 6:6 teaches that those instructed in the word should share good things with those who teach.
First Corinthians 9:14 affirms that those who proclaim the gospel may receive their living from the gospel.
And 1 Timothy 5:17–18 recognizes appropriate support for elders who labor faithfully in preaching and teaching.
Supporting sound ministry is biblical.
Helping churches care for the needy is biblical.
Giving to advance the proclamation of the gospel is biblical.
But the reason matters.
We do not give to purchase God's love.
We give because His love has already reached us in Christ.
We do not give to prevent a pastor from cursing us.
We give because grace is transforming us into people who love God and our neighbors.
We do not give to earn salvation.
We give as people who have been saved by grace through faith.
And that difference changes everything.
In Acts 8, Simon attempted to obtain spiritual power through money.
Peter rebuked him severely.
The lesson is unmistakable: the gifts and authority of God are not commodities for sale.
The gospel is not a spiritual marketplace.
Forgiveness is not a product.
The Holy Spirit cannot be purchased.
In Matthew 10:8, Jesus told His disciples, "You received without paying; give without pay."
That statement does not prohibit the legitimate financial support of ministers, which other passages clearly affirm.
But it does remind us that God's grace must never be marketed as though it were available only to paying customers.
Consider also what Peter wrote to church elders.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, he instructs them to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for shameful gain, and not domineering over those entrusted to their care, but by being examples.
The Greek expression μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες (mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes) warns against domineering over others.
A shepherd is not supposed to rule through intimidation.
A shepherd is supposed to care for the flock.
A pastor who teaches generosity from Scripture is carrying out a legitimate responsibility.
A pastor who threatens the vulnerable to obtain their money is acting contrary to the pastoral example Peter commands.
And this is where every pastor, every ministry leader, and every Christian organization must examine itself.
Including ministries that ask for financial support.
Including ours.
Because the truth must apply equally to the person preaching it.
That would betray the very gospel we claim to defend.
So let me speak plainly about Gospel Warrior.

If these messages have helped you understand Scripture, strengthened your faith, challenged you to repent, or reminded you of the mercy of Jesus Christ, you are welcome to help this ministry continue and expand.
It is a voluntary act of support.
If you are already practicing faithful financial stewardship and have the means to help, we would be grateful for your partnership.
If you cannot afford it, please do not feel condemned.
Do not take money away from your children's necessities because you fear that God will be disappointed with you.
You can pray for this ministry.
You can share the truth.
You can encourage someone who is struggling.
You can help another believer understand the Scriptures.
These products are simply additional resources and expressions of support. They do not make anyone more spiritual, more forgiven, or more acceptable to God.
But please understand the difference between an invitation and a threat.
Not because you are afraid of what will happen if you refuse.
Not because your salvation depends on it.
Not because you must pay to prove that you love Jesus.
Because Christ has already taught us that genuine generosity is an expression of grace, not a response to extortion.
And this ministry must be willing to live under that same truth.
There is also something important that many people overlook.
You do not need money to help the gospel reach another person.
Sometimes one sincere act of sharing can put Scripture in front of someone who would never walk into a church.
Perhaps there is a friend who has quietly stopped attending services because of spiritual abuse.
Perhaps a family member has been living under fear because a religious leader told them that their poverty was proof of God's displeasure.
Perhaps someone you know still loves Jesus but no longer knows whom to trust.
Not to shame every pastor.
Not to stir up hatred toward the church.
Not to convince people that giving is unnecessary.
There may come another Sunday when a frightening statement is made from a pulpit, and you will need to return to the Scriptures rather than surrender to panic.
And now I want to ask you something more personal than whether you give ten percent, twenty percent, or any particular amount.
When you think about giving to God, what do you feel first?
Love?
Gratitude?
Trust?
Or fear?
Are you afraid that something terrible will happen if you cannot give?
Have you ever felt that your pastor's disappointment meant God had rejected you?
Have you ever sacrificed something essential because you believed you were buying protection from a curse?
Or perhaps you have been wounded so deeply by financial manipulation that you now struggle to trust any church at all.
And if you have a testimony of finding freedom through the truth of Scripture, consider sharing it.
Your story may help another person recognize that they are not alone.
You do not need to disclose private financial information or identify anyone publicly. A few honest words may be enough to encourage someone who is still suffering in silence.
Because the purpose of this conversation is not to create a crowd that despises pastors.
It is to help believers love truth, honor faithful shepherds, reject spiritual abuse, and return to Jesus.
There are many faithful pastors who serve sacrificially, preach with integrity, care for the poor, and refuse to exploit the people entrusted to them.
Thank God for those shepherds.
Pray for them.
Support them appropriately.
And when leaders misuse Scripture, respond with truth, wisdom, and accountability rather than hatred.
A church should be a place where the poor are loved, not financially cornered.
Where the wealthy are taught generosity, not promised a profitable return on every donation.
Where offerings are handled responsibly.
Where leaders are accountable.
And where Jesus Christ, not money, remains the center of worship.
Remember what happened when Jesus entered the temple and confronted those who had turned a place of worship into a marketplace.
In Mark 11:17, He spoke of God's house as a house of prayer for all nations and condemned its transformation into a den of robbers.
His anger was not directed at people who were too poor to give.
It was directed against corruption surrounding worship.
That should make every church leader tremble—not because they must fear the anger of their congregation, but because they are accountable to the Lord whose name they proclaim.
And perhaps it should comfort the struggling believer who has spent years trembling for the wrong reason.
You were afraid that God was angry because you could not afford to give.
But the Gospels reveal a Savior who confronted those who exploited the vulnerable.
You were afraid that your poverty made you worthless.
But James 2 warns Christians against showing favoritism to the wealthy while dishonoring the poor.
You were afraid that you had nothing acceptable to bring to God.
But Psalm 51:17 speaks of a broken and contrite heart that God will not despise.
You were afraid that your inability to give meant you could never be loved.
But Romans 5:8 says that God demonstrated His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
He did not wait for us to become financially useful.
He came to save sinners.
And that brings us to the deepest truth in this entire discussion.
The greatest problem in our lives is not that we have failed to put enough money into an offering plate.
It is that we have sinned against a holy God and cannot save ourselves.
No donation can erase our guilt.
No religious performance can purchase forgiveness.
No pastor can sell us eternal life.
But Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness is proclaimed.
Through Him, sinners are called to repentance and faith.
Through Him, broken lives can be restored.
Through Him, those who have been deceived can learn to walk in truth.
And through Him, even those who have misused religious authority can find mercy if they genuinely repent.
That is the gospel.
Not "Give me your money or God will destroy you."
But "Repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave Himself to save sinners."
The apostle Paul describes the heart of Christian generosity in 2 Corinthians 8:9:
"For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich."
In context, Paul uses Christ's self-giving grace to encourage generosity among believers.
The richness he describes must not be reduced to a promise that every Christian donor will become financially wealthy.
The riches of Christ's saving grace are greater than any bank account.
He gave Himself.
Not because we paid enough.
Not because we deserved it.
Not because we satisfied a preacher's financial target.
But because of grace.
And when grace truly captures the human heart, it changes the way we live.
We become more generous.
More compassionate.
More willing to support good works.
More attentive to the needs of others.
More faithful with whatever God has entrusted to us.
Not because we are being threatened.
But because we are being transformed.
That is the difference between fear-driven religion and Christ-centered discipleship.
One asks, "How much must I pay to keep God from hurting me?"
The other asks, "Lord Jesus, in view of Your mercy, how can I faithfully use what You have given me?"
One keeps people enslaved to anxiety.
The other teaches them to walk in obedience through love.
And perhaps, after everything you have read, you are finally ready to stop measuring God's love by the amount of money in your hand.
You can be poor and deeply loved by God.
You can be wealthy and desperately in need of repentance.
You can give generously and still need to examine your motives.
You can be unable to give financially and still honor Christ through prayer, service, honesty, compassion, and faithfulness.
The issue has never been whether money matters.
It does.
The issue is whether money has become a false measure of your worth before God.
And the cross answers that question forever.
Your worth is not established by the size of your offering.
Your access to God's mercy is not controlled by a pastor.
Jesus Christ is the only mediator between God and humanity, as 1 Timothy 2:5 declares.
So if someone stands before you and claims that God will curse you simply because you cannot afford to give an offering, do not answer with hatred.
Answer with Scripture.
Ask for the passage.
Read its context.
Seek counsel from mature, trustworthy believers.
Distinguish faithful teaching about generosity from threats designed to control you.
And remember that genuine spiritual authority serves under the Word of God; it does not stand above it.
If you have been using the fear of curses to pressure others into giving, there is a call for you too.
Repent.
Stop treating the vulnerable as sources of revenue.
Restore what you have wrongfully taken where possible.
Embrace accountability.
And return to the example of the Good Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.
Because this message is not only for wounded church members.
It is for all of us.
The giver.
The pastor.
The ministry leader.
The person who has money.
The person who has none.
Every one of us must come to the same cross.
Every one of us needs the same grace.
And every one of us must learn that the kingdom of God cannot be built faithfully through methods that contradict the character of Christ.
So tonight, if you are sitting alone, wondering whether God is disappointed because you had nothing to place in the offering plate, remember the woman from the beginning of this story.
The mother who came to church needing hope.
The mother who looked at the last money in her purse.
The mother who was made to believe she had to choose between feeding her children and escaping God's anger.
Now imagine her opening her Bible at home.
Her eyes fall on 2 Corinthians 9:7.
"Not reluctantly or under compulsion."
Then 2 Corinthians 8:12.
"According to what a person has, not according to what he does not have."
Then Romans 8:1.
"No condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
And slowly, for the first time in a long time, she begins to understand.
She does not have to purchase the mercy of God.
She does not have to fear that a pastor's financial disappointment has canceled the work of Christ.
She can care for her children, seek wisdom, give willingly when she is able, and continue trusting the Savior who knows her needs.
Perhaps she begins to cry again.
But this time, the tears are different.
Not because every problem has disappeared.
Not because someone promised her a miraculous financial return.
But because the gospel has begun to untangle the fear that religious pressure wrapped around her heart.
And perhaps that is what Jesus wants to do in your heart today.
Not make you careless about generosity.
Not make you bitter toward the church.
Not teach you to despise those who faithfully serve in ministry.
But free you to obey Him without being enslaved to human intimidation.
Save these Scriptures.
Because the gospel is too precious to be sold through fear.
The church is too important to be surrendered to exploitation.
And Jesus Christ is too glorious to be reduced to a financial transaction.
The Savior who gave His life to redeem you will never need a preacher's permission to love you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SIN SO DISTURBING GOD NAMED IT IN THE BIBLE—AND THE WARNING MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER UNDERSTOOD
paragraphs: THE SIN SO DISTURBING GOD NAMED IT IN THE BIBLE—AND THE WARNING MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER UNDERSTOOD

Leviticus 18:23 reveals something far deeper than a forbidden act: why God established boundaries for Israel, what happens when humanity rejects His created order, and how Jesus Christ offers redemption without ever calling evil good.
There are verses in the Bible that comfort us.
Verses we underline when life becomes unbearable. Verses we whisper through tears. Verses we send to someone who is losing hope.
And then there are verses that make us uncomfortable.
Verses we would rather skip.
Verses that confront the things human beings are capable of doing when desire is separated from holiness.
Leviticus 18:23 is one of them.
God gave Israel a command so disturbing that many Christians today have never heard it explained from the pulpit.
He explicitly prohibited sexual relations between human beings and animals.
And before you close this article because the subject feels too shocking, consider something.
Why would a holy God need to say something that should have been unthinkable in the first place?
Why did He include this prohibition among the laws that would distinguish Israel from the nations surrounding them?
And what does a command written thousands of years ago reveal about the human heart sitting behind a smartphone screen today?
Because the deeper question is not simply why God forbade one horrifying act.
The deeper question is what happens when human beings decide that their desires should determine their boundaries.
And if we follow this passage carefully, something extraordinary happens.
A disturbing prohibition begins to reveal the holiness of God.
The holiness of God exposes the rebellion of humanity.
And that rebellion brings us face-to-face with the desperate need for Jesus Christ.
But we must begin where Scripture begins.
Not with outrage.
Not with speculation.
Not with an attempt to make an ancient passage say something it never said.
With the Word of God itself.
Leviticus 18:23 declares in the King James Version:
“Neither shalt thou lie with any beast to defile thyself therewith: neither shall any woman stand before a beast to lie down thereto: it is confusion.”
That final word deserves our attention.
Confusion.
The original Hebrew uses the word תֶּבֶל (tevel).
It is a rare word that, in this context, describes a grave violation of proper boundaries—something perverse or a wrongful mixing of categories that should remain distinct.
The Hebrew does not merely describe an unusual preference or an alternative expression of desire.
It identifies conduct that violates God's established moral order.
Modern translations commonly render the concluding expression as “perversion.”
That distinction matters.
The biblical text is not primarily discussing psychological confusion or claiming that every kind of uncertainty is sinful.
It is condemning a particular sexual act as morally disordered.
And the context makes that unmistakable.
God was establishing boundaries for a people He had redeemed from slavery and called to live differently.
Israel had been brought out of Egypt.
They were not supposed to carry every practice of Egypt into their new life.
Nor were they supposed to imitate every practice of the land of Canaan.
Listen to what God said earlier in the chapter:

“After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do: and after the doings of the land of Canaan, whither I bring you, shall ye not do: neither shall ye walk in their ordinances.” — Leviticus 18:3, KJV
Notice the pattern.
God did not simply tell Israel what to avoid.
He told them whose ways they must not imitate.
Their identity was no longer supposed to be determined by the cultures surrounding them.
Their identity was rooted in the God who had delivered them.
And then, in Leviticus 18:4–5, He called them to walk in His judgments and statutes.
The message was unmistakable.
Redemption was supposed to change how they lived.
That is where this ancient passage begins to become painfully personal.
Because it is possible to leave Egypt geographically while still carrying Egypt in your heart.
It is possible to escape a place of bondage while continuing to love the habits that once enslaved you.
It is possible to say that God has rescued you while resisting the boundaries He establishes for your good.
Israel's challenge was not merely to cross a wilderness.
It was to learn what holiness looked like after deliverance.
And that challenge did not disappear when the wilderness journey ended.
But we need to understand something else.
Leviticus 18 is not a random collection of strange restrictions.
The chapter addresses forbidden sexual relationships, including incestuous relationships, adultery, and other prohibited acts.
The prohibition involving animals appears within that broader moral context.
God was drawing distinctions between legitimate and illegitimate sexual conduct.
He was teaching Israel that human sexuality was not morally unrestricted.
And the prohibition in verse 23 protects a boundary between human beings and animals that Scripture does not permit sexual desire to cross.
Animals are living creatures entrusted to human stewardship, not partners capable of entering the human covenant of marriage.
Genesis 1:26–28 presents humanity as uniquely made in God's image and entrusted with responsibility over other living creatures.
Genesis 2:18–24 presents human companionship and the marriage union within the relationship between man and woman.
These passages provide important creation context for understanding why Scripture distinguishes human sexual relationships from humanity's relationship with animals.
The Bible's prohibition is therefore not merely about social embarrassment or cultural preference.
It belongs to a moral vision in which created distinctions matter and human beings are accountable to their Creator.
And here we must resist the temptation to exaggerate the historical evidence.
Leviticus 18:24–30 connects the chapter's prohibited practices with the defilement of the nations that inhabited the land before Israel.
That is what Scripture says.
But the text does not provide a detailed historical account proving how frequently every individual prohibition was practiced in every neighboring society.
We should not invent sensational stories about ancient rituals or claim that every surrounding nation routinely practiced this particular offense.
The biblical warning is serious enough without embellishment.
God declared these practices defiling.
He warned Israel not to participate in them.
And He connected persistent moral corruption with judgment.
Leviticus 18:25 uses striking language about the land being defiled and expelling its inhabitants.
The imagery is severe.
Sin was not being presented as a harmless private matter.
The covenant people were being warned that rebellion had consequences beyond an individual's immediate desires.
Yet something even more revealing appears in the chapter.
God did not give Israel permission to assume that they were morally superior simply because they belonged to Israel.
They, too, were warned.
They, too, could defile the land.
They, too, could face judgment.
The warning was not, “Those people are terrible, but you are automatically righteous.”
It was, in effect, “You belong to Me. Do not walk in the same rebellion.”
And perhaps that is the part modern believers most urgently need to hear.
Because religious identity is not a substitute for obedience.
A Bible in your home does not automatically mean Scripture governs your decisions.
A Christian name in your social media biography does not automatically mean Christ rules your heart.
