A worship song playing in the background does not make hidden rebellion holy.
And knowing the language of grace does not give us permission to make peace with sin.
But before we turn this passage into an accusation against everyone else, we need to be careful.
Leviticus 18:23 condemns a specific act.
It does not authorize us to accuse people without evidence.
It does not justify cruelty, harassment, or the public humiliation of someone who has sinned.
And it certainly does not mean that people who struggle with disturbing thoughts, unwanted impulses, or a painful past are beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Scripture calls evil what it is.
But Scripture also reveals a Savior who came to rescue sinners.
Both truths matter.
Imagine, for a moment, someone sitting alone late at night.
Their phone is in their hand.
Their family believes everything is fine.
Their friends know the version of them that smiles in photographs.
Their church knows the version that says, “I'm blessed.”
But hidden beneath that familiar face is a struggle they are terrified to admit.
Perhaps it is pornography.
Perhaps an affair.
Perhaps a habit that has become a prison.
Perhaps memories of something they did and desperately wish they could undo.
Perhaps something done to them that they never chose and have carried in silence for years.
Those situations are not morally identical.
Someone harmed by another person's abuse is not guilty merely because they were victimized.
And an unwanted thought is not the same thing as a deliberate action.
But the human suffering behind secrecy, shame, temptation, and fear is real.
Some people hide because they are protecting sin.
Others hide because they are afraid no one will understand their pain.
And sometimes the same person is carrying both guilt that needs repentance and wounds that need healing.
This is why we cannot preach holiness without compassion.
And we cannot preach compassion by pretending holiness no longer matters.
The Gospel calls us to something deeper than either condemnation without hope or acceptance without transformation.
It calls us to the truth.
And the truth begins with a God who has the authority to establish boundaries.
Consider how often our culture treats boundaries as enemies of freedom.
If a desire feels powerful, we are tempted to believe it must be legitimate.
If a behavior is consensual between humans, some assume that settles every moral question.
If something is private, we may conclude that no one—including God—has the right to speak about it.
But Scripture does not define righteousness by the intensity of desire.
Nor does it teach that every impulse should be obeyed.
The strength of a desire does not determine its moral legitimacy.
And God's authority does not disappear when His commands become unpopular.
A boundary can be an expression of love.
A parent who keeps a child away from a dangerous road is not declaring war on the child's freedom.
The parent is protecting the child's life.
Of course, that illustration does not mean every human restriction is righteous or that every person claiming divine authority is trustworthy.
Human beings can misuse rules to control and abuse others.
That is why our standard must be God's revealed character and Word, not the arbitrary demands of religious personalities.
The God who establishes moral boundaries is also the God who commands justice, condemns oppression, and cares for the vulnerable.
His holiness is not permission for human cruelty.
And His mercy is not permission for human rebellion.
Now return to the language of Leviticus.
Throughout this chapter, the repeated concern is defilement.
The Hebrew verb טָמֵא (tameʾ) means to become unclean or defiled, depending on context.
In Leviticus 18, the concern is moral defilement associated with prohibited sexual conduct.
This is important because the Bible uses purity language in different ways.
Not every form of ritual uncleanness in the Old Testament was itself a personal sin.
Childbirth, bodily discharges, and contact with the dead could involve ritual impurity under Israel's ceremonial system.
But the forbidden acts in Leviticus 18 are presented as moral violations, not merely temporary ceremonial conditions.
Understanding that distinction protects us from careless interpretation.
It also helps us see why the New Testament's teaching about holiness remains significant.
Christians do not live under the Mosaic covenant as ancient Israel did.
The New Testament teaches that believers are not justified by keeping the Law of Moses.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Yet grace does not erase the moral seriousness of sexual sin.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3, Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “fornication” is πορνεία (porneia), a broad term for sexual immorality.
Paul was not teaching that salvation could be earned through flawless behavior.
He was teaching that those who belong to Christ are called to holiness.
The New Testament does not repeat every individual prohibition from Leviticus 18 in identical language.
But it consistently rejects sexual immorality and calls believers to honor God with their bodies.
And that brings us to a question that is more uncomfortable than the original headline.
What good is it to be shocked by a sin you have never committed while refusing to repent of the sins you practice every day?
It is easy to read Leviticus 18:23 and say, “I would never do that.”
But have you ever used another human being for your own gratification?
Have you ever betrayed someone's trust?
Have you ever fed a secret appetite while telling yourself it was harmless?
Have you ever treated another person as an object rather than someone made in the image of God?
Have you ever defended something simply because surrendering it would cost you?
These questions do not make every sin equally severe.
Scripture recognizes distinctions in conduct, responsibility, and judgment.
But they do expose something we would rather ignore.
We can condemn the sins that disgust us while excusing the sins that comfort us.
We can be deeply offended by someone else's darkness while carefully protecting our own.
And Jesus confronted that kind of hypocrisy.
In Matthew 7:3–5, He warned against noticing the speck in another person's eye while ignoring the beam in our own.
He was not forbidding all moral discernment.
He was confronting self-righteous judgment.
The kind that sees another person's failure clearly but refuses to examine its own heart.
And now the story takes a turn.
Because if Leviticus only showed us what God forbids, we might leave this passage with fear and nothing more.
We might see the seriousness of sin but never understand the possibility of redemption.
We might recognize our guilt without discovering where forgiveness can be found.
But the Bible does not end in Leviticus.
And the story of humanity does not end with our rebellion.
It moves toward a cross.
Toward a Savior.
Toward the One who never compromised holiness and never stopped calling sinners to repentance.
Jesus Christ did not come to announce that sin was imaginary.
He came because sin was real.
He did not suffer because humanity merely needed better self-esteem.
He suffered because humanity needed reconciliation with God.
The cross tells us something that our pride desperately resists.
Our sin is serious enough that we cannot save ourselves.
But God's love is so great that He gave His Son.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
Read that again.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had become respectable.
Not after we had successfully hidden every shameful chapter.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated “repentance.”
It refers to a change of mind or heart that, in the biblical call to repentance, involves turning away from sin and toward God.
Repentance is more than embarrassment over being exposed.
It is more than regret over consequences.
It is a genuine turning toward the Lord.
And faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting Him as Savior and Lord.
That is why the Gospel is not simply a message about escaping punishment.
It is a message about being reconciled to God and transformed by His grace.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:11:
Those words follow a serious warning about unrighteous conduct.
But notice what Paul says to the believers.
“Such were some of you.”
Not because their past never happened.
Not because their sins were insignificant.
But because their identity in Christ was no longer defined solely by what they had once been.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
What extraordinary words for people who knew the weight of their former lives.
And what extraordinary hope for someone reading this who believes their worst chapter has already determined their ending.
Maybe you have never committed the particular offense condemned in Leviticus 18:23.
Maybe you cannot imagine doing so.
But perhaps you know what it means to carry something you are ashamed to confess.
Perhaps you have promised God a hundred times that you would stop a destructive habit.
Perhaps you have wondered whether you have crossed a line beyond which forgiveness is impossible.
Hear what Scripture actually promises.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
That promise is not a license to continue deliberately in sin.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
And if your struggle involves conduct that harms another person or animal, repentance must include stopping that harm and taking responsible steps to protect the vulnerable.
Seeking appropriate professional help, accountability, and pastoral care can be part of that response.
If you have been abused, however, you do not need to repent for the abuse someone inflicted on you.
You deserve safety, support, and care.
The Gospel does not confuse the guilt of the perpetrator with the suffering of the victim.
That distinction is not a concession to modern culture.
It is an expression of biblical justice.
God sees what people do.
And He sees what has been done to people.
He is not indifferent to either.
This is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because consequences magically disappear when someone says a prayer.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem lives that human beings would have written off as hopeless.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the past never happened.
Grace rewrites the future by bringing forgiven sinners into a new relationship with God.
And sometimes the evidence of that transformation is not dramatic.
Sometimes it is a person finally confessing the truth.
Sometimes it is deleting what has been feeding a destructive habit.
Sometimes it is asking for help instead of hiding.
Sometimes it is accepting responsibility without making excuses.
Sometimes it is learning to live faithfully one ordinary day at a time.
Sometimes it is someone who has suffered abuse finally understanding that the shame belongs to the wrongdoer, not the victim.
And sometimes it is a believer discovering that holiness is not the enemy of joy.
It is part of what it means to belong to the God who made us.
There is another Hebrew expression that brings the heart of Leviticus into focus.
In Leviticus 19:2, God commands Israel to be holy because He is holy.
The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh) means “holy,” carrying the idea of being set apart and belonging to what is sacred.
Holiness involves separation from what defiles, but biblical holiness is more than avoidance.
It is belonging to God.
And that changes how we understand His boundaries.
God was not merely building fences around Israel's behavior.
He was forming a people whose lives would reflect their relationship with Him.
A people called to distinguish righteousness from wickedness.
A people commanded to treat life, bodies, relationships, and worship with reverence.
A people who would learn that being redeemed meant they could no longer simply imitate the world around them.
And Christians today should recognize the spiritual principle.
We do not become holy by pretending we have no weaknesses.
We pursue holiness because we belong to Christ.
We confess when we fail.
We receive His forgiveness.
We depend on the Holy Spirit.
And we learn to obey.
Not to purchase salvation.
But because salvation is a gift that changes the direction of our lives.
So what does Leviticus 18:23 ultimately reveal?
It reveals that God's moral boundaries extend even to actions human beings may consider too shocking to discuss.
It reveals that Israel was called to reject practices God identified as defiling.
It reveals that sexuality was never presented in Scripture as an unlimited field for human experimentation.
It reveals that being God's people required more than possessing a religious identity.
And when read within the whole biblical story, it reminds us why humanity needs a Redeemer.
Because the problem of sin cannot be solved by public outrage alone.
Outrage may identify wrongdoing.
But outrage cannot cleanse the conscience.
Public shame cannot regenerate the heart.
And pretending that every desire is good cannot reconcile humanity to a holy God.
Only Jesus Christ can save.
Only His sacrifice is sufficient for our reconciliation with the Father.
Only His grace can forgive and transform sinners who come to Him in faith.
And now I want to ask you something personally.
Not as someone reading an article.
Not as someone scrolling through another controversial subject.
But as a human being standing before God.
Is there a boundary God has established that you have been trying to negotiate instead of obey?
You do not have to tell the internet your private history.
You do not have to expose trauma or confess intimate details in a public comment section.
But you can be honest with God.
If Christ has brought you out of a season of darkness, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness without revealing details that would compromise your safety or another person's privacy.
Someone else may need to know that repentance is possible.
Someone else may need to know that grace is real.
Someone else may need to know that their story is not finished.
And perhaps this is also the right moment to think about what you are helping spread through your own social media presence.
Every day, millions of people share things that entertain, provoke, distract, or divide.
But imagine what could happen if more believers deliberately shared Scripture, thoughtful biblical teaching, and the hope of the Gospel.
Not to win arguments.
Not to embarrass sinners.
Not to build a reputation for religious superiority.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of being proclaimed.
Someone who has questions about Christianity.
Someone struggling with shame.
Someone who has become spiritually indifferent.
Someone who needs to encounter both the seriousness of sin and the extraordinary mercy of Christ.
The goal is not merely to increase an audience.
The goal is to keep pointing people toward the Word of God and the Savior revealed through it.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and expand, there is a deeper way to participate.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical teaching and discipleship resources accessible to people who are hungry to grow in their relationship with Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of a continuing effort to encourage biblical literacy, spiritual growth, repentance, and faithful Christian living.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry requires time, work, resources, and the generosity of people who believe in its mission.

It is a voluntary act of support that can help sustain the creation and distribution of Christ-centered teaching, expand the ministry's reach, and strengthen the availability of discipleship resources.
For believers who prayerfully choose to include this support in their monthly giving, it can be an expression of generosity and an offering toward Gospel ministry.
But we want to be biblically clear.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You glorify Him through faith, obedience, love, generosity, and a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
But the greatest value of supporting Gospel ministry is not a product or a discount.
It is the opportunity to participate in work that points people toward Jesus.
Because the mission belongs to Christ.
And the glory belongs to God.
Now, before you leave, return with me to the verse that started this entire conversation.
Leviticus 18:23.
A difficult command.
A disturbing subject.
An ancient warning about boundaries that human beings were never authorized to erase.
At first, it may have seemed like a passage with little relevance to your life.
But look where it has taken us.
From God's holiness to human rebellion.
From the danger of unchecked desire to the responsibility of obedience.
From the shame of hidden sin to the hope of repentance.
From the boundaries established in the Law to the mercy revealed in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the greatest surprise is this:
The passage did not simply invite us to examine a sin that most people would find horrifying.
It invited us to examine whether we truly believe that God has the right to tell us how to live.
That question reaches every heart.
Including mine.
Including yours.
The answer is not found in pretending we are better than everyone else.
It is found in surrendering to the One who is holy.
Jesus Christ did not come to make rebellion respectable.
He came to save rebels and make them new.
He did not die so that we could rename darkness as light.
He died and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and brought into the light.
So do not walk away from this passage merely feeling disgust toward someone else's sin.
Walk away with reverence for God.
With compassion for the wounded.
With a renewed commitment to protect the vulnerable.
With courage to confess what needs to be confessed.
With faith in the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
And with the determination to follow Jesus even when His Word challenges what the world has taught you to accept.
Because one day, the opinions of the crowd will no longer matter.
The applause will fade.
The arguments will end.
The screen will go dark.
And what will matter is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
The most frightening thing is not discovering how far sin can take a person—it is discovering how long we can resist the Savior who is calling us home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF JESUS PAID FOR ALL YOUR SINS, WHY DOES THE BIBLE STILL WARN YOU ABOUT JUDGMENT?
paragraphs: IF JESUS PAID FOR ALL YOUR SINS, WHY DOES THE BIBLE STILL WARN YOU ABOUT JUDGMENT?

The terrifying warning in Hebrews, the breathtaking promise in Romans, and the day every Christian will stand before Christ. What if the answer is neither “You can lose your salvation every time you sin” nor “You can live however you want because Jesus already paid”?
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.
Not the Jesus in a painting. Not the Jesus you heard about in a Sunday sermon. Not the Jesus people casually mention when life becomes difficult.
The real Jesus.

The One whose hands still bear the marks of crucifixion. The One who knows every secret you buried, every prayer you whispered, every temptation you entertained, every person you wounded, and every moment you chose obedience when nobody was watching.
There are no crowds to impress.
No reputation to protect.
No carefully edited testimony.
Just you.
And Him.
Now imagine hearing these words:
“For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.” — 2 Corinthians 5:10, KJV
Your heart stops for a moment.
Because you remember another verse.
One you held on to during the darkest nights of your life.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
Wait.
No condemnation?
But everyone must appear before Christ's judgment seat?
And then you remember the passage that made you uncomfortable enough to close your Bible.
Hebrews 10:26–27 warns that if we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment.
Suddenly, the question becomes painfully personal.
If Jesus already paid for all my sins, what exactly am I going to be judged for?
And perhaps an even more frightening question follows.
What if I have been calling something “grace” that Jesus has been calling me to repent of?
Don't rush past that.
Because the answer could change the way you understand the cross, your salvation, your secret struggles, and the eternity waiting beyond your final heartbeat.
But it may also bring extraordinary peace to a heart that has spent years being terrified of God.
Here is where we must begin.
Jesus did not die to make sin harmless.
He died because sin was so serious that nothing less than His own blood could accomplish our redemption.
And He did not rise from the dead merely to make guilty people feel better about remaining unchanged.
He rose to give dead sinners new life.
The same Gospel that removes condemnation also calls us out of darkness.
And unless we understand both truths, we risk turning the greatest announcement in human history into either a prison of fear or a permission slip for rebellion.
Consider the man who keeps falling into the same sin.
He hates what he is doing. He confesses. He prays. He tries again.
Some nights he wonders whether God has finally become tired of forgiving him.
Then consider another man.
He knows what Scripture says. He understands that his behavior is sinful. But he has decided that repentance is unnecessary.
After all, he tells himself, Jesus already paid for everything.
Both men may quote Romans 8:1.
Both may say they believe in grace.
But their relationship to sin is profoundly different.
One is fighting a battle he desperately wants to win.
The other has made peace with the enemy.
And the New Testament does not treat those two postures as spiritually identical.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
Paul's declaration in Romans 8:1 is astonishing.
In the original Greek, the opening reads:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
Ouden ara nyn katakrima tois en Christō Iēsou.
A faithful translation is:
“Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Notice the word katakrima (κατάκριμα).
It refers to condemnation, a judicial verdict of guilt and its penal consequences.
Paul is not merely saying that Christians should feel less ashamed.
He is declaring that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict that their sins deserve.
And notice something else.
The Greek text does not say, “There is less condemnation.”
It does not say, “There is no condemnation until your next failure.”
It says there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
This is not because God has forgotten what we did.
It is because Jesus has accomplished what we never could.

Paul explains the foundation in Romans 8:3–4: God condemned sin in the flesh through His Son, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in those who walk according to the Spirit.
The condemnation believers escape is not something God simply pretends never existed.
Sin was judged.
Christ bore our sins.
The cross was not divine indifference toward evil.
It was the place where God's justice and mercy met in the saving work of His Son.
Isaiah had already announced the suffering Servant centuries earlier:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” — Isaiah 53:5, KJV
The Hebrew expression translated “for our transgressions” includes the phrase:
מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ — mippeshaʿenu
It communicates that His suffering was because of our transgressions.
The Servant suffers on account of the rebellion of others.
And Peter connects that saving reality directly to Jesus:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness.” — 1 Peter 2:24, KJV
Read the second half again.
That we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness.
Jesus bore our sins not only to rescue us from their penalty, but also to bring us into a new way of life.
Forgiveness and transformation are not competing purposes of the cross.
They belong together.
And that brings us to the passage that makes so many Christians tremble.
Second Corinthians 5:10.
Paul writes:
The Greek expression translated “judgment seat” is:
βῆμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ — bēma tou Christou
The word bēma refers to a raised platform or tribunal from which judgment could be administered.
It was not a word that automatically meant a ceremony for handing out rewards.
It was a genuine place of evaluation and judgment.
Paul is telling believers that our earthly lives matter to the Lord who saved us.
Our choices matter.
Our motives matter.
Our stewardship matters.
How we treated people matters.
What we did with the opportunities God entrusted to us matters.
Even what nobody else saw matters.
But here is the crucial distinction.
Being evaluated by Christ is not the same thing as being condemned for sins that Christ has forgiven.
For those who are in Him, the final judgment cannot overturn the saving sufficiency of His sacrifice.
Paul has already said that there is no condemnation in Christ.
He is not contradicting himself three chapters later in a different letter.
He is teaching us that salvation by grace does not make our lives meaningless.
First Corinthians 3:12–15 offers an important illustration.
Paul describes believers' works being tested by fire. Some work endures and receives a reward. Other work is burned up, bringing loss.
Yet he says of the person whose work is burned:
“But he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.” — 1 Corinthians 3:15, KJV

That passage concerns the testing of work built upon the foundation of Jesus Christ. It does not teach that every person who professes Christianity will be saved regardless of whether their faith is genuine.
But it clearly demonstrates that loss at judgment and the loss of salvation are not automatically the same thing.
A believer's works can be exposed as worthless without the saving work of Jesus becoming worthless.
Imagine the difference between standing before a judge as a condemned criminal and standing before your Lord as someone He has redeemed, whose life He now evaluates in perfect truth.
Both encounters are serious.
But they are not the same verdict.
The Christian's confidence is not that Christ will discover nothing wrong.
Our confidence is that He already knows everything wrong and has provided a sufficient Savior.
And still, we should not become careless.
Because Paul says something immediately after speaking about Christ's judgment seat.
“Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men.” — 2 Corinthians 5:11, KJV
A more contemporary rendering of the Greek expression is “knowing the fear of the Lord.”
Paul does not respond to judgment by shrugging his shoulders.
He responds with reverence, accountability, and urgency.
Grace has not made him indifferent.
Grace has made him faithful.
Now we must face Hebrews.
Not soften it.
Not explain it away.
Not pretend the warning was written for somebody else simply because it makes us uncomfortable.
Hebrews 10:26 begins:
“For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.” — KJV
In Greek, the central expression is:
Ἑκουσίως γὰρ ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν
Hekousiōs gar hamartanontōn hēmōn.
It refers to our sinning deliberately or willfully.

The participle hamartanontōn is present in form, which fits the warning's portrayal of a continuing sinful posture. But grammar alone does not prove that the passage refers exclusively to repeated behavior rather than a particular deliberate act.
We must let the whole passage explain the danger.
And the surrounding verses are devastating.
Hebrews 10:29 describes someone who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, treated the blood of the covenant as unholy, and insulted the Spirit of grace.
This is not a casual description of a Christian who fell into temptation and returned to God in tears.
It portrays profound contempt for Christ and His saving sacrifice.
The broader context of Hebrews repeatedly warns against abandoning Christ, hardening the heart, and turning away from the only Savior.
The message is not that Christ's sacrifice becomes insufficient whenever a believer commits a deliberate sin.
The message is that there is no alternative sacrifice that can save someone who rejects Christ Himself.
There is no second Messiah waiting behind Jesus.
No greater blood beyond His blood.
No safer refuge outside the One who died and rose again.
Hebrews 10:26–31 therefore carries a warning we have no right to dismiss.
And faithful Christians have differed over precisely how that warning relates to the possibility of apostasy.
Some understand it as warning genuine believers against a real danger of falling away.
Others understand it as exposing those who have received substantial knowledge of the Gospel and participated in the covenant community without possessing persevering, saving faith.
These interpretations differ on an important theological question.
But neither responsible reading permits us to say that deliberate rejection of Christ is spiritually harmless.
The warning is real.
The Savior is sufficient.
And the proper response is not speculation about how close we can live to rebellion without crossing some invisible line.
It is to draw near to Christ in faith.
Perhaps someone reading this has a terrible secret.
You have sinned deliberately.
Not accidentally.
Not because you were unaware.
You knew.
You understood.
And you did it anyway.
Now you are afraid Hebrews 10 has permanently closed the door of mercy.
Listen carefully.
The passage is not an instruction to despair over every remembered act of willful sin.
If you are convicted, do not run away from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Do not excuse what happened.
Confess it.
Do not treat repentance as a performance designed to purchase forgiveness.
Come to the Savior whose blood alone can cleanse you.
Hebrews itself invites believers to approach God's throne of grace for mercy and help in time of need (Hebrews 4:14–16).
And just a few verses before the severe warning, Hebrews 10:22 urges us to draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith.
The same biblical book that warns against rejecting Christ also calls us to approach Him.
That is not a contradiction.
That is the urgency of the Gospel.
But perhaps your struggle is different.
You are not terrified of losing salvation.
You have become comfortable using salvation as an excuse.
You keep telling yourself that because Jesus paid for your sins, you no longer need to take your choices seriously.
You can mistreat people and never apologize.
You can nurture bitterness and call it discernment.
You can live a double life and call it privacy.
You can knowingly continue in sin and dismiss every warning as legalism.
And whenever conviction begins to rise, you silence it with the same sentence.
“I'm under grace.”
But Paul anticipated that argument.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
The Greek answer is emphatic:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito
It conveys something like:
Absolutely not! May it never be!
Paul does not merely discourage the idea.
He rejects it forcefully.
Why?
Because those united to Christ have died to sin and are called to walk in newness of life.
Grace is not the freedom to remain enslaved.
Grace is the gift that brings us out of slavery.
Titus 2:11–12 says that God's grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly lives.
Notice that.
Grace teaches.
Grace corrects.
Grace trains.
Grace changes us.
The grace that forgives the sinner also confronts the sin that is destroying the sinner.
And if the only thing our understanding of grace ever does is make us less concerned about holiness, we need to examine whether we have understood biblical grace at all.
Now imagine a father whose daughter has been rescued from a burning house.
He does not embrace her, weeping with gratitude, only to say, “Now go back inside. The fire doesn't matter anymore.”
He carries her away from the flames.
Because he loves her.
And that is an imperfect but helpful picture of what Jesus does.
He does not merely declare forgiveness while encouraging us to remain in the destruction from which He came to save us.
He calls us to follow Him.
Sometimes that calling will cost us.
A relationship we know is pulling us away from obedience.
A dishonest source of income.
A hidden addiction.
An apology we have postponed for years.
A habit we keep defending because surrender would be painful.
An identity we have built around something Christ is asking us to leave behind.
And this is where theology becomes painfully practical.
It is easy to discuss eternal security when nothing in our lives is being challenged.
It is harder when the truth reaches into our private decisions.
When Jesus says, “Follow Me,” He is not merely asking us to agree with an argument about salvation.
He is calling us to Himself.
Not because obedience earns His love.
But because the One who loved us and gave Himself for us is worthy of our trust.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together beautifully.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that nobody can boast.
And yet we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in.
Works are not the price of salvation.
They are part of the life for which salvation prepares us.
The root is grace.
The fruit is a transformed life.
And fruit matters because living faith does not remain forever untouched by the One in whom it trusts.
James 2:17 warns that faith without works is dead.
James is not teaching that we can purchase justification by collecting enough acts of obedience.
He is confronting the emptiness of a claimed faith that produces no corresponding life.
There is a difference between imperfect fruit and no concern for fruit at all.
A difference between stumbling on the road and deciding that the road no longer matters.
A difference between struggling against sin and celebrating it.
And no, Christians do not become sinlessly perfect in this life.
First John 1:8 says that if we claim to have no sin, we deceive ourselves.
But the very next verse offers a promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
That promise was written to a community of believers.
God did not place it in Scripture to encourage endless despair.
He placed it there because Christians still need confession, forgiveness, and cleansing.
We must not confuse the ongoing struggle with sin with the settled decision to reject the authority and mercy of Christ.
And we must not confuse a tender conscience with the absence of saving faith.
Some of the people most frightened by judgment are the very people who desperately want to honor Jesus.
They examine every thought.
Replay every failure.
Wonder whether their repentance was sincere enough.
Ask whether their faith was strong enough.
Fear that one unconfessed sin could somehow erase everything Christ accomplished.
If that describes you, hear this.
Your salvation does not rest upon the perfection of your repentance, but upon the perfection of your Savior.
Genuine repentance matters.
But repentance is not another Savior standing beside Jesus.
Faith matters.
But the strength of faith is not greater than the One in whom faith rests.
Christ is sufficient.
Hebrews 10:14 says:
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.” — KJV
The Greek text reads:
μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους.
Mia gar prosphora teteteleiōken eis to diēnekes tous hagiazomenous.
The sense is:
“For by one offering He has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.”
This is extraordinary.
One offering.
Not an endless succession of sacrifices.
Not a Savior who must be crucified again every time His people fail.
One sufficient offering.
And notice how the verse brings together an accomplished reality and an ongoing work.
Those who are being sanctified are described as perfected through Christ's offering.
His sacrifice is complete.
His sanctifying work continues in His people.
We must not turn the ongoing process of transformation into a denial of His finished sacrifice.
And we must not turn His finished sacrifice into a denial of the ongoing need for transformation.
Both truths belong to the same Gospel.
Now return to that scene.
You are standing before Jesus.
Everything is known.
Every hidden thing is brought into the light.
There is no possibility of deceiving Him.
But if you belong to Christ, you are not standing before a stranger whose mercy you must somehow persuade Him to give.
You are standing before the One who loved you and gave Himself for you.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who declared in John 10:27–28 that His sheep hear His voice, follow Him, and receive eternal life.
The One who said that nobody can snatch them out of His hand.
The One whose love Paul celebrates at the end of Romans 8.
Neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor any other created thing can separate those in Christ from the love of God in Him.
This does not make the warnings meaningless.
It makes the Savior precious.
The New Testament never tells us to choose between the promises and the warnings.
It calls us to hear both.
The promises assure us that Christ is able to save.
The warnings summon us to persevere in faith rather than turn away from Him.
The judgment passages remind us that our lives are lived before the holy God who sees all.
And the cross reminds us that our only hope before that holy God is Jesus Christ.
So what should we do with this truth?
Not panic.
Not pretend.
Not bargain with God.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Bring your secret struggles into His light.
Seek help from mature believers when you need accountability.
Make restitution where possible when you have wronged someone.
Forgive as you have been forgiven.
Return to Scripture.
Pray even when the words come slowly.
Keep following Jesus when obedience becomes costly.
And when you stumble, do not build a home in your failure.
Confess your sin and return to Him.
Because the answer to the Christian life is not less dependence upon Christ.
It is deeper dependence upon Christ.
Perhaps this article has confronted something you were trying not to face.
Maybe you have been treating God's patience as permission.
Maybe you have been living under condemnation that Christ never intended you to carry.
Maybe you are somewhere between the two, exhausted from the fight, longing to be holy, yet painfully aware of how much you still need His grace.
Whatever your situation, do not allow this moment to become another passing emotion.
Let it become an occasion for honest prayer.
You do not need impressive words.
You can simply pray:

“Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know what I have hidden, what I have excused, and what I have feared. Thank You for Your sacrifice. Forgive my sins. Teach me to hate what destroys my fellowship with You and to love what honors You. Where I have been careless, awaken me. Where I have been afraid, reassure me through Your Word. Where I have been resisting Your truth, lead me to repentance. Give me grace to persevere in faith and to walk in the life You have called me to live. I trust in Your mercy, not my own righteousness. Amen.”
And if that prayer expresses what is happening in your heart, I would love to hear from you.
You do not have to disclose private details publicly.
Sometimes a few honest words can open the door for another believer to pray with you.
And perhaps your testimony will help someone who has quietly believed that their struggle means God has abandoned them.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who desperately needs to understand this distinction between condemnation, accountability, and grace.
Someone who stopped attending church because they thought God could never forgive them.
Someone who has misunderstood the Gospel as permission to remain unchanged.
Someone who has spent years trying to earn a salvation Jesus offers by grace.
Not merely because it may reach more people, but because biblical truth is worth passing on.
There is something else I want to share with those who believe this ministry is worth helping to sustain.
Behind every article, devotional, biblical resource, and opportunity to encourage someone in the faith is an ongoing need for time, effort, and practical support.
Gospel Warrior exists to point people toward Jesus Christ, not toward a personality, a brand, or a substitute for the local church.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, you can become part of helping it continue and grow.
It can be an expression of Christian generosity and partnership in ministry.
But I want to be especially clear about something.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, sincere, and free from compulsion.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Your giving to your local church and your responsibilities to your family should not be neglected.
What matters is that any support you offer comes freely, with a clear conscience and a sincere desire to help the Gospel reach others.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as practical reminders of biblical truth and as ways to encourage others.
The library is part of our desire to make Christian learning and spiritual encouragement accessible, including to those who are not in a position to give financially.
You can glorify God without ever spending money here.
What matters most is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that people are encouraged to trust and obey Him.
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
And grace will never be something we can put a price on.
Now, before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
If Jesus paid for all our sins, why does the New Testament still warn believers about judgment?
Because the cross removes condemnation for those in Christ, but it does not remove our accountability to Christ.
Because the sacrifice that saves us also calls us to holiness.
Because biblical warnings are meant to be heard, not silenced.
Because a profession of faith should never become an excuse to reject the Savior we profess.
And because the Jesus who welcomes repentant sinners is the same Jesus before whom every knee will bow.
The answer is not to live terrified that His blood is insufficient.
Nor is it to live carelessly as though His blood were cheap.
The answer is to live by faith in the One who loved us enough to die for us, rose again, and now calls us to follow Him.
One day, the arguments will end.
The excuses will end.
The carefully maintained appearances will end.
The applause of people will fall silent.
And what will matter is not whether we successfully convinced everyone around us that we were righteous.
What will matter is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
So do not spend your life trying to make yourself appear worthy of the cross.
Come to the cross because you know you are not worthy.
And do not use the cross as an excuse to keep embracing what nailed your Savior there.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Rest in His finished work.
And follow Him with the life His grace is transforming.
The scars in His hands are not permission to keep running toward sin; they are the everlasting testimony of the love that calls you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID MARRIED ABIGAIL AFTER HER HUSBAND DIED… BUT THE BIBLE REVEALS SOMETHING ABOUT HIS OTHER WIFE THAT MOST PEOPLE NEVER NOTICE.
paragraphs: DAVID MARRIED ABIGAIL AFTER HER HUSBAND DIED… BUT THE BIBLE REVEALS SOMETHING ABOUT HIS OTHER WIFE THAT MOST PEOPLE NEVER NOTICE.

She was a wise woman trapped in a disastrous marriage. He was God's anointed king who nearly became a murderer. And when their lives collided, God exposed a dangerous truth about anger, marriage, mercy, and the difference between being chosen by God and actually obeying Him.
What if the most important part of Abigail's story isn't that she married David… but that she stopped him from becoming the kind of man he would later regret being?
There is something unsettling about the way the Bible tells the truth.
It doesn't always give us the beautiful ending we expect.
Sometimes it tells us that a woman escaped one painful marriage, only to enter a household where she would have to share her husband with another woman.
Sometimes it shows us a man deeply loved by God, yet dangerously close to committing a terrible sin.
And sometimes the person who saves that man from himself isn't a prophet, a priest, or a mighty warrior.
Sometimes it's a woman carrying bread, wine, roasted grain, and enough courage to confront an angry future king.
Her name was Abigail.

And if you've ever been married to someone difficult, carried the consequences of another person's foolishness, tried to keep peace in a home filled with tension, or wondered why God allowed your life to become so complicated…
You need to hear her story.
But don't rush toward the wedding.
Because before Abigail became David's wife, she became the voice that stopped bloodshed.
And what happened after the wedding reveals something just as important.
A marriage can change your circumstances without automatically healing everything in your life.
The story begins in 1 Samuel 25.
David had already been anointed to become king, but he was not yet sitting on Israel's throne. Saul still ruled, and David was living as a fugitive, surrounded by men who depended on his leadership.
Meanwhile, in the region of Carmel, there lived a wealthy man named Nabal.
He owned three thousand sheep and one thousand goats.
He had possessions, influence, and the appearance of success.
But Scripture introduces his character with devastating clarity.
He was harsh and badly behaved.
His wife, however, was different.
The Bible describes Abigail as discerning and beautiful (1 Samuel 25:3).
Notice that.
Before Scripture draws attention to her appearance, it recognizes her understanding.
Her wisdom mattered.
Her judgment mattered.
Her character mattered.
And she was about to need every bit of it.
David and his men had been in the wilderness near Nabal's shepherds. According to the servants' testimony, David's men had treated them well, protected them, and taken nothing from them.
When sheep-shearing season arrived, a time often associated with feasting and generosity, David sent messengers requesting provisions.
But Nabal responded with contempt.
He questioned David's identity and refused to share his food.
David was furious.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because David wasn't merely offended.
He was ready to kill.
He ordered his men to strap on their swords.
Four hundred armed men followed him.
His intention, as the narrative reveals, was to destroy the males belonging to Nabal's household.
Think about that.
The future king of Israel, the man who had refused to kill Saul when given the opportunity, was now preparing to spill blood over an insult.
He had shown extraordinary restraint toward a king who wanted him dead.
Yet he was about to lose that restraint because a wealthy fool humiliated him.
Isn't that frighteningly human?
Sometimes we survive the greatest battles of our lives, only to stumble over something smaller.
We forgive an enemy, then explode at someone in our own household.
We endure years of hardship, then lose control because somebody disrespects us.
We pray for patience, then justify our anger because we believe we have been treated unfairly.
David was God's anointed.
But being anointed did not make every impulse of his heart righteous.
And that distinction matters.
God's calling on your life is never permission to ignore God's commands.
Somebody needed to stop David.
And that somebody was Abigail.
When one of Nabal's servants learned what was coming, he went to Abigail.
He explained how David's men had protected them and how Nabal had insulted the messengers.
Then he warned her that disaster was approaching.
Abigail acted immediately.
She gathered two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five prepared sheep, roasted grain, raisins, and fig cakes.
She loaded the provisions onto donkeys.
And without informing Nabal, she went to meet David.
Try to imagine that moment.
The sound of hooves against the rocky path.
The dust rising from the wilderness.
The knowledge that armed men were approaching.
The terrible possibility that her household could be destroyed before the day was over.
Abigail wasn't walking into a comfortable conversation.
She was moving toward a man whose anger had become dangerous.
And she was carrying something stronger than a sword.
Wisdom.
When she saw David, she quickly dismounted and bowed before him.
She spoke with humility, but not with cowardice.
She acknowledged Nabal's foolishness.
She offered the provisions.
Then she confronted the moral danger David was facing.
Her words in 1 Samuel 25:31 are remarkable.
She urged him not to burden his conscience with needless bloodshed or with taking vengeance into his own hands.
Abigail was not merely trying to save her husband's property.
She was trying to save lives.
And she was trying to protect David from the consequences of his own rage.
There is a powerful Hebrew expression in her appeal.
In 1 Samuel 25:31, Abigail speaks of bloodshed without cause using the phrase:
וְלִשְׁפָּךְ־דָּם חִנָּם
Ve-lishpokh dam ḥinnam.
The expression communicates the shedding of blood without just cause.
This was not simply a dispute about wounded pride.
It was a question of guilt before God.
Abigail understood that David could win the confrontation and still lose something precious.
He could silence Nabal and carry the stain of innocent blood.
He could defeat the household and wound his own conscience.
He could satisfy his anger today and regret his actions for years.
And isn't that exactly how sin often works?
It promises relief in the moment.
Then sends the consequences afterward.
One message sent in anger.
One betrayal justified by loneliness.
One decision made because pride refuses to surrender.
One cruel sentence spoken to someone who trusted us.
One moment of revenge that becomes a lifetime of regret.
Abigail was asking David to consider the man he would become after his anger had passed.
And David listened.
In 1 Samuel 25:32–33, David blessed the LORD for sending Abigail to meet him and praised her discernment for keeping him from bloodguilt and from avenging himself.
That response deserves attention.
David did not say, "How dare a woman correct me?"
He did not insist that his authority made his anger acceptable.
He recognized the mercy of God in the correction he received.
Sometimes God's rescue doesn't arrive as an open door. Sometimes it arrives as someone brave enough to tell you that you're wrong.
Perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
Not every person who challenges you is your enemy.
Not every warning is rejection.
Not every interruption is spiritual warfare.
Sometimes the very thing you are calling an obstacle is God's mercy standing between you and a decision you cannot undo.
David turned back.
The bloodshed was prevented.
And Abigail returned home.
But the story was not finished.
Nabal was holding a feast, drinking heavily, and behaving like a king.
Abigail waited until morning to tell him what had happened.
When she did, Scripture says his heart died within him and he became like stone.
The text does not provide a modern medical diagnosis, and we should not pretend that it does.
Ten days later, Nabal died.
The Bible explicitly attributes his judgment to the LORD.
David heard about Nabal's death and praised God for defending his cause and restraining him from wrongdoing.
Then David sent messengers to ask Abigail to become his wife.
And Abigail accepted.
For someone reading quickly, this can feel like the perfect ending.
A foolish husband dies.
A courageous woman survives.
A future king recognizes her worth.
Marriage follows.
The story closes.
Except it doesn't.
Because Scripture includes a detail that changes how we understand the entire ending.
David married Abigail. But Abigail was not his only wife.
In 1 Samuel 25:42–43, the narrative records Abigail becoming David's wife and then adds that David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel.
The Hebrew of verse 43 begins:
וְאֶת־אֲחִינֹעַם לָקַח דָּוִד
Ve'et-Aḥino'am laqaḥ David.
Literally, the wording communicates that David had taken Ahinoam in marriage.
The verse continues by identifying her as a woman from Jezreel and stating that both women were his wives.
The Hebrew concluding expression is:
וַתִּהְיֶיןָ גַּם־שְׁתֵּיהֶן לֹו לְנָשִׁים
Vattihyeyna gam-shteihen lo lenashim.
In context, it means that both of them were wives to him.
This is not a modern assumption inserted into an ancient story.
It is what the biblical text reports.
And then verse 44 reveals another complication.
Saul had given Michal, David's earlier wife, to Palti son of Laish.
Later, in 2 Samuel 3:13–16, David would demand Michal's return, resulting in a painful scene in which she was taken from the man who had been living with her as his wife.
David's household was already complicated.
And it would become more complicated still.
Abigail did not enter the simple, exclusive marriage that many modern retellings quietly imagine.
She entered the household of a man who practiced polygamy.
That is not a minor detail.
It is part of the truth.
But we must be careful about what we do with that truth.
The Bible records David's multiple marriages.
It does not follow that God was endorsing every marriage decision David made.
There is a difference between Scripture describing human behavior and Scripture prescribing that behavior for God's people.
The biblical story begins with a foundational vision of marriage.
Genesis 2:24 describes a man leaving his father and mother, holding fast to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
Basar eḥad.
"One flesh."
When Jesus was questioned about marriage, He returned to this creation account.
In Matthew 19:4–6, He pointed to God's original design and declared that what God has joined together, humanity must not separate.
Jesus did not build His teaching about marriage around the accumulation of spouses by powerful kings.
He pointed back to the beginning.
And the history of Israel's kings repeatedly demonstrates how multiplied marriages could become entangled with rivalry, divided loyalties, and spiritual compromise.
Deuteronomy 17:17 specifically warned Israel's future king against multiplying wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
We should not invent a private conversation between David and Abigail or claim to know exactly how she felt about sharing her husband.
Scripture does not tell us.
It does not reveal whether she struggled with jealousy, felt neglected, or privately mourned the complexity of her new marriage.
Those possibilities may be emotionally imaginable, but they are not established biblical facts.
What Scripture does tell us is enough.
Abigail was wise.
David was restrained from bloodshed through her intervention.
Nabal died.
David married Abigail.
And David had another wife.
Later biblical history would reveal serious moral failures within David's household.
His story would contain betrayal, sexual sin, violence, grief, and consequences that no crown could erase.
This is why we must resist turning Abigail's marriage into a simplistic promise that every painful relationship will be replaced with a perfect one.
God never promised that.
And the Gospel is deeper than that.
Maybe you're reading this while carrying disappointment you never expected.
You thought the new relationship would heal the wounds of the old one.
You thought the promotion would finally make you feel secure.
You thought the ministry position would silence your insecurity.
You thought that after surviving one season of suffering, the next chapter would be free of complications.
But here you are.
Still praying.
Still learning.
Still discovering that changed circumstances do not automatically produce a changed heart.
And perhaps Abigail's story is speaking to you in a way you didn't expect.
Because the greatest miracle in this chapter is not a woman becoming the wife of a future king.
It is a man turning away from sin before innocent blood is spilled.
It is wisdom overcoming fury.
It is mercy interrupting revenge.
It is God preserving a deeply imperfect servant from doing something terrible.
And that brings us to Jesus Christ.
Because David, for all his greatness, was never meant to be the final answer.
He was an anointed king who still needed correction.
A courageous warrior who could still be ruled by anger.
A man who wrote beautiful words about God and later committed grievous sins against other people.
David needed grace.
Just like you.
Just like me.
And unlike David, Jesus Christ is the perfectly righteous King.
He does not need someone to restrain Him from sinful vengeance.
He does not abuse His authority.
He does not betray the people entrusted to His care.
He does not use His power to satisfy selfish desire.
He is the King who laid down His life for His people.
Abigail risked herself to prevent bloodshed.
Jesus willingly shed His own blood to redeem sinners.
Abigail stepped between an angry man and a vulnerable household.
Jesus, our great High Priest and mediator, gave Himself to reconcile sinners to God.
The comparison is not that Abigail was sinless or that her actions were identical to Christ's saving work.
They were not.
The beauty is that her courageous intervention can remind us of our desperate need for a greater Mediator.
One who doesn't merely prevent one terrible afternoon.
One who deals with the deeper problem of sin itself.
The apostle Paul writes in 1 Timothy 2:5 that there is one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus.
And in Romans 5:8, he declares that God demonstrated His love for us while we were still sinners: Christ died for us.
Do you understand what that means?
Jesus did not wait until your story became respectable before offering grace.
He did not wait until every mistake was corrected.
He did not wait until your past became something you could comfortably explain in church.
He came for sinners.
For the angry.
For the ashamed.
For the betrayed.
For the proud.
For the people who have wounded others.
For the people who have been wounded.
For those who need forgiveness.
And for those who need the courage to forgive.
But grace is not permission to continue in sin.
The same Savior who receives repentant sinners calls them to turn away from evil and follow Him.
David's willingness to listen to Abigail is a reminder that repentance can begin with a surrendered decision.
A sword put away.
A cruel word left unspoken.
A sinful plan abandoned.
A heart that finally says, "Lord, I was wrong."
And perhaps that is where this story meets your life today.
Maybe you are David.
Not because you are a king.
But because your anger has been speaking louder than your faith.
You have been rehearsing what someone did to you.
Planning how to make them regret it.
Convincing yourself that revenge would feel like justice.
And God is calling you to put down the sword.
Maybe you are Abigail.
You have spent years navigating another person's difficult behavior.
You know what it feels like to recognize danger before everyone else does.
You know the exhaustion of trying to prevent a crisis you did not create.
But hear this carefully.
Abigail's courage does not mean God requires you to remain in an abusive or dangerous situation.
Her story is not a command to absorb mistreatment, conceal violence, or risk your safety to keep someone else comfortable.
Seeking protection, involving trustworthy people, and asking for appropriate help are not failures of faith.
Wisdom is not the same as silently enduring harm.
Or maybe you recognize something of Nabal.
You have resources, opportunities, and blessings, but gratitude has slowly disappeared.
Your pride has become louder than your compassion.
You have treated people as though their dignity depended on their usefulness to you.
And today, before another relationship is damaged, God is calling you to humility.
The question is not which biblical character you can most easily criticize.
The question is what the Word of God is revealing about your own heart.
Because the Bible was never given merely to entertain us with the failures of people who lived thousands of years ago.
It was given to teach us, warn us, and point us toward the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
And here's something I cannot stop thinking about.
Abigail's intervention spared David from a terrible act.
Yet David would later commit other terrible sins.
He would eventually take Bathsheba, another man's wife, and arrange the death of her husband, Uriah, as recorded in 2 Samuel 11.
The man who once listened to Abigail's warning against bloodguilt would later become guilty of bloodshed himself.
That is heartbreaking.
And it should humble every one of us.
Because yesterday's obedience does not make us immune to tomorrow's temptation.
A powerful spiritual experience is not a substitute for daily surrender.
Knowing Scripture is not the same as obeying Scripture.
Having a calling is not the same as having an obedient heart.
And a reputation for loving God cannot excuse the people we hurt when we stop listening to Him.
David's later repentance, expressed with extraordinary anguish in Psalm 51, reminds us that even grievous sinners must come before God without excuses.
He cried for mercy.
He acknowledged his sin.
He asked God to create in him a clean heart.
The Hebrew of Psalm 51:10, numbered verse 12 in the Hebrew text, contains this plea:
לֵב טָהֹור בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God."
That is the prayer of someone who has stopped pretending.
And perhaps it needs to become ours.
Not "Lord, make everyone understand why I behaved that way."
Not "Lord, expose the people who made me angry."
Not "Lord, bless me so nobody remembers my mistakes."
But…
"Create in me a clean heart."
"Teach me to obey You when my pride is wounded."
"Help me stop using my pain as permission to hurt others."
"Forgive the sins I have hidden behind religious language."
"Make me more like Jesus."
This is where scandal begins to meet grace.
Not when we pretend the scandal never happened.
Not when we rewrite the facts to protect our reputation.
Not when we turn biblical characters into flawless heroes.
But when we bring the truth into the presence of a merciful Savior.
Jesus does not need us to falsify our stories in order to redeem them.
He knows the whole truth.
And He is still mighty to save.
Perhaps you have been afraid that your life is too complicated for God to use.
Your family has fractures.
Your marriage has scars.
Your past contains decisions you would never make again.
Your faith has survived seasons you barely know how to describe.
But look at the family history through which God ultimately brought the promised Messiah into the world.
Matthew 1 does not present a spotless human genealogy.
It includes broken people, painful histories, and surprising acts of grace.
And Matthew identifies Jesus Christ as the son of David.
The greater Son of David came into a world filled with human failure.
Yet He was without sin.
He came not to celebrate our wrongdoing, but to save us from it.
He came not to make repentance unnecessary, but to call us into repentance and faith.
He came not merely to improve our circumstances, but to reconcile us to God and make us new.
That is why our message is not simply that broken people can get another chance.
Our message is that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
His resurrection is the foundation of our hope.
And His grace is powerful enough to forgive, restore, and transform those who turn to Him.
Abigail's story may have started with a disastrous marriage.
But the most important truth it leaves us with is not that she married a king.
It is that God's mercy was working in the middle of human weakness.
And maybe, even now, His mercy is confronting something in you.
An anger you need to surrender.
A sin you need to confess.
An apology you need to make.
A boundary you need to establish.
A wound you need to bring before Christ.
A relationship in which you need wisdom rather than revenge.
Or a false image of yourself that you need to stop protecting.
Don't close this article and simply say, "What an interesting Bible story."
Let the Word examine you.
Because it is possible to admire Abigail's wisdom while refusing wise correction.
It is possible to condemn David's polygamy while excusing our own unfaithfulness.
It is possible to criticize Nabal's pride while being too proud to repent.
And it is possible to speak beautifully about grace while refusing to receive it.
Today, come to Jesus.
Not with a polished version of your life.
With the truth.
With the failure.
With the exhaustion.
With the sin you have been hiding.
With the tears you have been swallowing.
With the prayer you have been afraid to pray.
He is not asking you to save yourself.
He is calling you to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
And if you have already trusted in Christ, keep following.
Keep returning to His Word.
Keep allowing His truth to correct you.
Keep growing in holiness.
Keep receiving His mercy with gratitude.
Because being forgiven is not the end of discipleship.
It is the beginning of a life transformed by grace.
And if this story has exposed something you need to surrender, don't let that conviction disappear into another scroll.
Take a moment and pray.

"Lord Jesus, You know every part of my story. You know where I have been wounded and where I have wounded others. Forgive my sins. Cleanse my heart. Teach me to receive correction, reject revenge, and walk in Your truth. Help me trust Your grace without using it as an excuse for disobedience. Make my life a testimony of Your mercy. Amen."
You do not have to reveal private details to be honest before God.
Sometimes the beginning of healing is simply admitting that you need His help.
And perhaps someone reading the comments will discover that they are not the only person still learning to surrender.

If this message reminded you of someone who is battling anger, struggling through a painful relationship, carrying shame, or wondering whether God can still work through a complicated life, consider sharing it with them.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
It doesn't.
But because one faithful act of encouragement may place Scripture in front of someone who desperately needs it.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, people who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still searching for truth.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, honest repentance, Christian encouragement, and the transforming Gospel of Jesus Christ.
But there is another invitation I want to make.
An invitation not built on guilt, but on shared purpose.
Gospel Warrior exists because we believe the Word of God deserves to be proclaimed faithfully, clearly, and courageously.
Every article, devotional, Bible study, and discipleship resource is part of a larger mission: helping people know Jesus Christ, understand Scripture, and grow in their walk with Him.
And that work requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But it can be one meaningful way to participate in the work of sharing biblical truth.
It is an opportunity to help make more Gospel-centered resources available to others.
We want these resources to be useful reminders of Scripture, encouragement, and Christian discipleship in everyday life.
If this mission resonates with you, and you are financially able to participate, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
You can become a monthly supporter here:
The center of our mission is not a platform.
It is not a product.
It is Jesus Christ.
The One who sees the truth about us and still calls us to repentance.
The One who offers forgiveness through His cross.
The One whose resurrection gives sinners a living hope.
The One who can take a life marked by regret and transform it into a testimony of grace.
David married Abigail after Nabal died.
But Abigail was not his only wife.
That uncomfortable detail reminds us that even the great heroes of Scripture lived complicated and deeply imperfect lives.
And the deeper lesson is not that God approves of every decision His people make.
It is that God's redemptive purpose is greater than the failures of the people He calls.
So don't put your ultimate hope in David.
Don't put it in Abigail.
Don't put it in a better marriage, a new beginning, or the approval of other people.
Put your hope in Jesus Christ.
Because a human king may need someone to stop him from destroying others.
But the King of kings came to save those who could never save themselves.
And when He redeems a sinner, the past no longer has to be the final word.
The scandal may be part of your story, but through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, it does not have to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD FOR A SIGN… BUT WHAT IF HE’S ALREADY GIVEN YOU A COMMAND YOU’VE BEEN IGNORING?
paragraphs: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD FOR A SIGN… BUT WHAT IF HE’S ALREADY GIVEN YOU A COMMAND YOU’VE BEEN IGNORING?

What if the silence you're calling God's absence is actually the space between what He has already told you and what you're still unwilling to surrender? This may be the hardest answer to prayer you've ever had to face.
There is a prayer that sounds holy.
It sounds humble. It sounds patient. It even sounds like faith.
“Lord, just give me a sign.”
You've whispered it with tears in your eyes.
You've prayed it before making decisions. Before leaving relationships. Before forgiving someone who shattered your trust. Before walking away from something you knew was slowly destroying your soul.
“God, if this is really You, show me.”
And sometimes, asking God for guidance is exactly what we should do.
But there is another possibility.
One we rarely want to consider.
What if you aren't waiting because God hasn't spoken?
What if you're waiting because you don't like what He already said?
Read that again.
Because somewhere between your unanswered prayers and your unfinished obedience, there may be a truth you've been trying desperately not to confront.
Not every season of waiting is rebellion.
Not every unanswered question means you've ignored God.
But sometimes the greatest obstacle to our spiritual growth isn't that we cannot hear God's voice.
It's that we already understand His Word—and we're hoping He will eventually tell us something different.
And the frightening part?
We can become so comfortable asking for another sign that we forget the command we've already received.
There was a man in Scripture who came to Jesus with a question that sounded sincere.
He wanted eternal life.
He wanted to know what he needed to do.
He had kept commandments. He had lived a respectable life. From the outside, he appeared to be exactly the kind of person religious people would admire.
But Jesus saw what nobody else could see.
Mark 10:21 tells us:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him.”
Don't rush past those words.
Jesus loved him.
Before Jesus confronted him, He loved him.
Before Jesus exposed what was holding his heart captive, He loved him.
And then Jesus told him to sell what he possessed, give to the poor, and follow Him.
The man's response was devastating.
He went away sorrowful.
Why?
Because he had great possessions.
He had come asking Jesus about life, but when Jesus called him to surrender what ruled his heart, he walked away.
The tragedy wasn't that Jesus had refused to answer him.
The tragedy was that Jesus had answered him—and the answer revealed what he loved more.
Notice something else.
Jesus didn't chase him down and offer an easier version of discipleship.
He didn't say, “Never mind. Keep everything. Just follow Me when you're comfortable.”
The call remained.
And the man walked away grieving.
Perhaps that is where this story begins to feel uncomfortably familiar.
Because we, too, can approach Jesus asking for direction while quietly protecting the very thing His Word is confronting.
We ask God to restore our peace while refusing to release bitterness.
We ask Him to bless a relationship while ignoring what Scripture teaches about holiness and faithfulness.
We ask Him to change our hearts while continuing to feed the habits that harden them.
We ask Him to show us our purpose while overlooking the ordinary opportunities to love, serve, forgive, and speak truth already in front of us.
And sometimes we ask Him to open a door because we cannot bear the thought of closing one ourselves.
But here is what makes the Gospel so beautiful.
The Jesus who confronts you is the same Jesus who loves you.
His commands are not a cruel attempt to deprive you of life.
They are the words of the Savior who knows where life is found.
In John 14:15, Jesus says:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.”
The Greek text reads:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
Ean agapate me, tas entolas tas emas tērēsete.
A faithful rendering is:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.”
The verb τηρήσετε (tērēsete) comes from τηρέω (tēreō), meaning to keep, observe, or guard.
Jesus is not describing a transaction where we purchase His love through flawless performance.
He is describing the relationship between genuine love and obedience.
Obedience does not earn salvation.
It is a fitting response to the Savior who saves by grace.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because if you believe God will only love you after you obey perfectly, you'll spend your life terrified of failure.
But if you understand that Christ loved sinners enough to die for them, you'll begin to see obedience not merely as an obligation—but as a response of love.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
Not the other way around.
But somewhere along the way, many of us have confused seeking God's guidance with negotiating His authority.
We say, “Lord, lead me.”
But quietly add, “As long as You lead me somewhere I already want to go.”
We say, “Lord, use me.”
But add, “Just don't ask me to give up what makes me comfortable.”
We say, “Lord, change me.”
But hope He will leave our favorite sins untouched.
And then we wonder why our spiritual lives feel divided.
There is a moment in the Gospel of Luke that should make every person who claims to follow Jesus examine their heart.
Jesus asks in Luke 6:46:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
Imagine hearing that question directly from Christ.
Not from an angry preacher.
Not from someone trying to shame you.
From Jesus.
The One who healed the sick.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who wept at a tomb.
The One who would stretch out His arms on a Roman cross for people who could never save themselves.
“Why do you call Me Lord, but refuse to do what I say?”
What would you answer?
Would you tell Him you were waiting for confirmation?
Would you tell Him you needed more time?
Would you tell Him you were afraid?
Or would you finally tell Him the truth?
“Lord, I know what Your Word says. I'm just struggling to surrender.”
And perhaps that is the most honest prayer you've prayed in years.
Because spiritual maturity doesn't begin when we become experts at sounding faithful.
It grows when we stop pretending before the God who already knows us completely.
There is another scene in Scripture.
A wedding.
A celebration.
And suddenly, a problem.
The wine has run out.
Mary brings the need to Jesus.
Then she turns to the servants and speaks words that have echoed through centuries.
John 2:5:
“Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.”
Simple.
Uncomfortable.
Powerful.
Whatever He tells you, do it.
Not whatever feels convenient.
Not whatever everyone else approves.
Not whatever guarantees you won't be misunderstood.
Whatever He tells you.
Jesus instructs the servants to fill the waterpots with water.
And they do.
They fill them to the brim.
The water becomes wine through the power of Christ.
The servants did not manufacture the miracle through obedience.
Jesus performed the miracle.
But they obeyed the instruction they had received.
And that distinction matters.
Your obedience cannot create God's power. But your disobedience should never be disguised as waiting for His guidance.
You cannot force a miracle by doing enough religious things.
You cannot guarantee that God will give you the outcome you want by following a formula.
The Lord is sovereign.
His wisdom is greater than ours.
But when His Word is clear, the faithful response is not to demand an extraordinary sign before doing what He has already commanded.
It is to trust Him.
Even when obedience costs something.
Especially then.
Maybe you've been waiting for God to give you a sign that it's time to forgive.
But Ephesians 4:32 already calls believers to forgive one another as God in Christ has forgiven them.
That doesn't mean pretending the harm never happened.
It doesn't mean returning to an abusive relationship or removing necessary boundaries.
It means refusing to make vengeance the master of your heart.
Maybe you've been asking God whether you should confess the truth.
But 1 John 1:9 already assures us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Maybe you're asking if you should stop hiding a destructive pattern.
But Proverbs 28:13 warns against concealing sin and points toward mercy for those who confess and forsake it.
Maybe you've been waiting for permission to love someone who cannot repay you.
But Jesus has already called His followers to love even their enemies.
Maybe you're asking God whether your life matters.
But Scripture already declares that human beings are made in God's image, and the Gospel announces that Christ came to seek and save the lost.
And maybe the thing you most need to hear today is not a new revelation.
Maybe it is the Word you've been avoiding because you know it will change how you live.
But be careful here.
Because there is a danger in turning this message into another weapon against wounded people.
Some of you are not resisting a clear command.
You are exhausted.
You are grieving.
