You are trying to make a difficult decision where Scripture gives principles but does not name the exact choice.
You are wondering which job to accept, whether to move, how to care for someone you love, or what the next season of life should look like.
And you desperately want wisdom.
There is no shame in that.
James 1:5 invites those who lack wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.
Seeking wise counsel, praying patiently, examining Scripture, and waiting for clarity can all be acts of faith.
God has not promised that every major life decision will arrive with a supernatural sign.
Nor should every coincidence, emotion, dream, or open door be treated as a divine command.
We must test what we believe against Scripture.
We must seek wisdom.
We must refuse to use supposed private revelations to contradict God's revealed truth.
And we must remember that waiting on God can be faithful obedience too.
The question is not whether you have ever asked for a sign.
The question is whether you're using the desire for a sign to avoid something God has already made clear.
There is an ancient Hebrew word that brings this into sharper focus.
שְׁמַע — Shema.
It appears at the beginning of Deuteronomy 6:4:
“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.”
The Hebrew verb שָׁמַע (shama) means to hear or listen and, depending on context, can carry the sense of heeding or obeying.
That connection matters.
Biblical listening is not always merely receiving information.
It often calls for a response.
A person can hear the words of God without allowing those words to govern their life.
James later makes the same distinction with startling clarity.
James 1:22 says:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.”
Deceiving yourselves.
Not merely misunderstanding.
Not merely forgetting.
Deceiving.
That is what makes this so serious.
We can accumulate sermons, devotionals, Bible studies, Christian videos, and inspirational quotes while remaining unwilling to obey the very truths we keep consuming.
We can know the language of surrender without surrendering.
We can know the vocabulary of repentance without turning from sin.
We can post about trusting God while secretly insisting on controlling every outcome.
And we can become skilled at recognizing truth without letting truth confront us.
But the purpose of Scripture is not to make us impressive religious spectators.
It is to lead us to Christ and equip us for a life shaped by His truth.
And that brings us to a man who once stood on the wrong side of God's will while believing he was defending it.
Saul.
A man zealous for religion.
A man convinced he was right.
A man persecuting followers of Jesus.
Then, on the road to Damascus, everything changed.
The risen Christ confronted him.
Saul's certainty collapsed.
The man who had been moving with violent confidence suddenly found himself blind and dependent on others.
Acts 9 records the encounter.
And what followed was not merely a change of opinion.
It was the beginning of a transformed life.
The persecutor became a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The man who had tried to destroy the church became a servant of the Gospel.
But notice what made his story extraordinary.
It wasn't simply that Saul received a dramatic encounter.
It was that the risen Jesus Christ changed the direction of his life.
And that is the difference between chasing spiritual experiences and following the Savior.
A powerful moment may get your attention.
But discipleship involves trusting Christ with the life that follows.
Saul, later known as Paul, would eventually write about being crucified with Christ and living by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave Himself for him.
Not merely impressed by Jesus.
Not merely interested in Jesus.
Belonging to Jesus.
And maybe that's where this message is becoming personal.
Because you don't need another emotional experience if what you are avoiding is the ordinary, costly obedience of following Christ.
You may need to apologize.
You may need to tell the truth.
You may need to stop excusing a sin you've repeatedly renamed as a weakness.
You may need to seek help for something you cannot overcome alone.
You may need to make restitution where possible.
You may need to reconcile where reconciliation is safe and appropriate.
You may need to stop measuring God's faithfulness by whether He gives you the answer you prefer.
Or maybe you need to return to the simple things you've neglected.
Prayer.
Scripture.
Fellowship.
Service.
Love.
Faithfulness when nobody is watching.
Because not every act of obedience is dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like putting down the phone and finally praying honestly.
Sometimes it looks like telling your spouse the truth.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to join in cruelty when everyone else is laughing.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible after months of spiritual distance.
Sometimes it looks like reaching out to a trusted pastor or mature believer and admitting, “I need help.”
Sometimes it looks like saying, “Jesus, I cannot change myself. Please teach me to follow You.”
And sometimes the bravest spiritual decision of your life happens in a room where nobody applauds.
No audience.
No dramatic music.
No visible miracle.
Just a trembling heart choosing to obey the Lord.
But there is something even deeper you must understand.
God is not asking you to save yourself through obedience.
If that were possible, there would have been no need for the cross.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to give humanity a better list of instructions.
He came to redeem sinners.
To bear sin.
To reconcile us to God.
To accomplish what our righteousness could never accomplish.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we finally obeyed everything.
Not after we cleaned up every scandal.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy of grace.
While we were sinners.
He died for us.
And He rose again.
That is the Gospel.
Not that you can climb your way into God's acceptance by performing enough good deeds.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Savior, died for our sins and was raised from the dead, and that forgiveness and new life are found in Him.
Repentance is not a payment for mercy.
Faith is not a spiritual performance.
We come to Christ empty-handed.
And the grace that receives us also begins transforming us.
Titus 2:11–12 describes the grace of God as teaching us to turn away from ungodliness and live godly lives.
Think about that.
Grace doesn't merely forgive your past.
Grace trains you for a different future.
Not perfectly overnight.
Not without struggle.
Not without tears.
But genuinely.
And this is where the theme of scandal and grace becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Because some of you know what it means to have a past you wish you could erase.
You know the shame of making promises to God and breaking them.
You know what it feels like to return to a habit you swore you would abandon.
You know the humiliation of realizing that the person you presented to the world was not the person you were becoming in secret.
You know what it's like to stand in church and sing about surrender while silently holding on to something that is destroying you.
And perhaps you have wondered whether God is tired of hearing your voice.
Whether you've exhausted His patience.
Whether your failures have finally made you unreachable.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to minimize your sin.
The answer is to look at your Savior.
Remember Peter.
The disciple who declared his loyalty.
The disciple who promised he would never abandon Jesus.
The disciple who denied Him three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of the warning.
The terrible realization of what he had done.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
His confidence had collapsed.
His courage had failed.
His denial was real.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter's restoration did not mean his denial was harmless.
It meant the grace of Christ was greater than Peter's failure.
The same man who once denied knowing Jesus would later boldly proclaim Him.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
But because Jesus is mighty to save.
Not because obedience is optional.
But because forgiveness restores us to a life of following Him.
Not because our past disappears from history.
But because our past does not have to remain the master of our future.
And perhaps, today, the command you've been avoiding is the simplest and most important one of all.
Repent.
Turn to Christ.
Stop running.
Stop hiding behind religious language.
Stop waiting until you feel worthy enough to come home.
Jesus proclaimed in Mark 1:15:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
In Greek, the words include:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
The word μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) calls for repentance—a change of mind and heart that turns away from sin toward God.
The word πιστεύετε (pisteuete) calls for faith, for believing the good news.
Both are present-tense imperatives in this passage, expressing the call to repent and believe.
This is not merely an invitation to feel bad about your mistakes.
It is a summons to turn toward the Savior.
And it is not merely an invitation to agree that Jesus exists.
It is a call to trust Him.
The Lord who commands repentance is the Lord who offers forgiveness.
The Lord who calls us to follow Him is the Lord who gave His life for sinners.
And the Lord who exposes what is hidden is the Lord who can cleanse what we cannot repair.
So perhaps the prayer that needs to change today is not, “God, give me another sign.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, show me where I have been resisting Your Word.”
“Give me wisdom where I genuinely do not know what to do.”
“Give me courage where I already know what is right.”
“Forgive me for confusing delay with discernment.”
“Teach me to obey You out of love, not fear.”
“Help me trust Your goodness even when following You costs me something.”
And above all:
“Jesus, I belong to You. Lead me.”
You may not receive the extraordinary confirmation you've been hoping for.
You may not see every outcome in advance.
You may not understand why obedience must be difficult.
But you have something greater than a passing sign.
You have the testimony of Scripture.
You have the promises of God.
You have the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And for those who belong to Him, you have the Holy Spirit, who leads believers in truth and produces fruit in lives surrendered to Christ.
Don't mistake the absence of a spectacular experience for the absence of God's guidance.
And don't mistake a difficult command for a lack of His love.
The cross has already settled how far Christ was willing to go to rescue sinners.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word.
What is the one thing you already know God's Word is calling you to do, but you've been postponing?
Not the thing someone is pressuring you to do.
Not the thing fear is screaming at you to do.
Not a private impression that contradicts Scripture.
The thing you can honestly recognize as consistent with the teachings of Jesus.
What would obedience look like today?
Not next year.
Not when every circumstance becomes convenient.
Today.
Maybe you cannot fix everything immediately.
Maybe you need counsel, support, and time.
Maybe the first step is small.
But a small step of genuine faith is not insignificant.
And if you've fallen, don't make despair your permanent home.
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Receive His mercy.
Rise and follow Him again.
The Gospel is not a story about flawless people who never stumble.
It is the good news of a perfect Savior who rescues sinners and teaches them to walk in newness of life.
“Lord, give me courage to obey.”

And if Jesus has already brought you through a season when surrender felt impossible, share a little of your testimony. Someone reading the comments may be one step away from giving up, and your words may encourage them to turn back to Christ.
Don't underestimate the power of a truthful testimony.
There are people who will never enter a church this week but may read a Gospel message on their phone tonight.
Someone may be carrying shame that only the grace of Jesus can answer.
Someone may be searching for a reason to believe that restoration is still possible.
Not because following a page saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because daily Scripture, biblical teaching, encouragement, and honest conversations about repentance, forgiveness, healing, and discipleship can help keep our attention on the One who does.
These resources are meant to help believers return to Scripture, understand the Gospel, and grow in faithful discipleship.
And there is another way you can become part of this mission.

Scripture encourages generosity in supporting Gospel ministry. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from a willing heart, not compulsion.
That is why I want to be clear about something important.
You do not have to pay for God's love, blessing, forgiveness, or approval.
It can help make this mission sustainable.
It can help us continue reaching people who may never have heard the Gospel explained with clarity, compassion, and conviction.
And it can help keep free discipleship resources available to those who cannot afford to pay.
It is a voluntary partnership in the work.
These products are simply expressions of the ministry and reminders of biblical truth. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
Jesus is the reason.
You are still welcome here.
Read the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
Keep growing in the Word.
The mission is not to build a community where people feel they must pay to belong.
It is to point people to Jesus Christ—the Savior whose grace cannot be bought.
Because the greatest gift you could ever receive was already purchased at a cost none of us could afford.
Not with silver.
Not with gold.
But through the precious blood of Christ.
And now, before you leave this message, return to that question you came here carrying.
“God, will You give me a sign?”
Perhaps He will guide you through circumstances.
Perhaps He will give you wisdom through Scripture, prayer, and godly counsel.
Perhaps the answer will require patient waiting.
But if He has already spoken clearly through His Word, don't demand another sign as a condition of obedience.
Remember the rich young ruler.
Remember the servants at Cana.
Remember Saul on the Damascus road.
Remember Peter after his denial.
And most of all, remember Jesus.
The One who loved the rich young ruler even as He confronted his misplaced treasure.
The One whose power transformed water into wine.
The risen Lord who turned a persecutor into a witness.
The Savior who restored a disciple broken by his own denial.
The crucified and risen King who still calls sinners to repent, believe, and follow Him.
The question is no longer merely whether you will receive another sign.
The question is whether you will trust the Savior who has already spoken.
And if you've been running, today can be the day you turn around.
Not because you finally became worthy.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
Not because you can rewrite your own history.
But because His grace can redeem what sin has broken and transform the life you place in His hands.
One day, you may realize that the answer you kept begging heaven to send was already waiting in the words of Jesus you were afraid to obey.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE… BUT JESUS SAID SOMETHING FIRST THAT MOST PEOPLE KEEP SKIPPING
paragraphs: THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE… BUT JESUS SAID SOMETHING FIRST THAT MOST PEOPLE KEEP SKIPPING

Everyone wants the freedom Jesus promised in John 8:32. But the words immediately before that promise reveal why so many people know the truth, quote the truth, defend the truth… and still live like prisoners.
There is a kind of prison you can walk out of every morning without anyone noticing.
You can go to work from it. Raise children in it. Lead worship in it. Preach sermons in it. Post Bible verses from it. Smile for photographs while its invisible walls are closing in around your soul.
And the frightening thing?
You can become so accustomed to those walls that you eventually stop calling them a prison.
You call them your personality.
Your past.
Your weakness.
Your circumstances.
You tell yourself, "This is just who I am."
But what if the thing you have learned to live with is the very thing Jesus came to set you free from?
What if you have been quoting the promise of freedom while quietly ignoring the invitation that comes before it?
Because Jesus never simply said, "The truth will set you free," as though truth were some inspirational statement you could hang on your wall and forget by Monday morning.
He said something first.
Something that changes everything.
And once you see it, you may never read John 8:32 the same way again.
In John 8:31–32, Jesus spoke these words to Jews who had believed Him:
"If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." (John 8:31–32, KJV)
Read that again.
Not just the beautiful ending.
The beginning.
"If ye continue in my word…"
There is an invitation before the promise.
There is discipleship before the declaration of freedom.
There is a relationship with Christ that cannot be reduced to agreeing with a few religious statements.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us want Jesus to remove the chains while we keep holding on to the things that helped forge them.
We want peace without surrender.
Forgiveness without confession.
Transformation without repentance.
Freedom without allowing His Word to confront what is destroying us.
We want the comfort of His promises while resisting the authority of His voice.
And somehow, when the same wounds keep reopening and the same sins keep returning, we wonder why the truth we have heard so many times has not changed the way we live.
But Jesus was not offering a motivational slogan.
He was calling people to become His disciples.
And His words were far more searching than we sometimes realize.
In the original Greek, John 8:31 reads:
Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ, ἀληθῶς μαθηταί μού ἐστε.
Ean hymeis meinēte en tō logō tō emō, alēthōs mathētai mou este.
"If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples."
The word μείνητε (meinēte) comes from the Greek verb μένω (menō), meaning to remain, stay, continue, or abide.
Jesus was not describing a passing emotional experience.
He was describing a continuing relationship with His teaching.
Not a moment of inspiration followed by a lifetime of indifference.
Not one Sunday of conviction followed by six days of deliberately silencing His voice.
Not perfect performance, either.
Because abiding is not the same as never stumbling.
It is continuing with Christ rather than abandoning Him.
It is returning to His Word when your feelings want to lead you elsewhere.
It is allowing His teaching to correct you when correction is uncomfortable.
It is staying near enough to hear Him even when what He says exposes something you would rather hide.
And perhaps that is the part that hurts.
Because we love the Jesus who comforts us.
But do we love Him enough to listen when He corrects us?
We love hearing that He forgives.
But will we listen when He tells us to forgive?
We love hearing that He is faithful.
But will we trust Him when obedience becomes costly?
We love proclaiming that He is Lord.
But what happens when His Word contradicts the life we have been defending?
That is where the question becomes unavoidable.
Are we following Jesus?
Or have we become comfortable following our own preferences while asking Jesus to bless the journey?
There is a difference.
And that difference matters eternally.
Notice something else in the passage.
Jesus was speaking to people who had believed Him.
Yet, as the conversation continues, some of His hearers resist His words with increasing hostility. By John 8:59, the scene has become deeply confrontational.
That context matters.
Jesus was exposing the difference between an initial favorable response to His message and the genuine discipleship that continues in His Word.
He was not teaching that we purchase salvation through religious effort.
Scripture is clear:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV)
Salvation is God's gift.
We cannot earn it by reading enough chapters, attending enough services, donating enough money, or collecting enough good deeds.
But the grace that saves us does not leave us content to remain enslaved to the very sins from which Christ came to redeem us.
Jesus does not demand that we clean ourselves up before we come to Him.
He calls us to come to Him, and His grace begins changing us.
That is the difference between trying to earn His love and learning to live in His love.
One produces exhausted religious performance.
The other produces grateful obedience.
And if you have ever been exhausted from trying to appear spiritually strong while secretly falling apart, you need to hear this.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend that you are free. He is calling you to bring your chains into His light.
Maybe your prison is bitterness.
Someone hurt you years ago, and although the conversation ended, the argument has continued inside your mind ever since.
You replay what they said.
You imagine what you should have said.
You carry their offense into relationships with people who never wounded you.
And whenever the Holy Spirit brings forgiveness to your attention, you remember how much they hurt you.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending evil was acceptable. It does not require returning to an unsafe relationship or abandoning wise boundaries.
But it does mean refusing to make revenge the ruler of your heart.
Maybe your prison is a secret sin.
You have promised God so many times that you would stop.
You meant it every time.
You cried.
You prayed.
You deleted things.
You made new rules.
And then, in a moment of loneliness, anger, exhaustion, or temptation, you returned to what you swore you were leaving behind.
Now you are afraid to pray because you feel like a hypocrite.
You wonder whether God is tired of hearing your apologies.
You wonder whether someone like you can really change.
Or perhaps your prison is not something outwardly scandalous at all.
Maybe it is pride.
The kind that never admits wrongdoing.
The kind that can explain everyone else's sins but refuses to examine its own.
The kind that uses Bible verses to win arguments while avoiding the verses that expose the heart.
Maybe it is fear.
Maybe it is the need to be admired.
Maybe it is the belief that your worth depends on being needed, noticed, attractive, successful, or spiritually impressive.
Maybe you are not running toward some obvious temptation.
Maybe you are running from silence because silence forces you to face the condition of your soul.
And Jesus sees it.
Not merely the polished version people applaud.
Not merely the photographs, testimonies, ministry activities, and religious vocabulary.
He sees the exhausted person behind all of it.
The one who knows exactly what to say when someone asks, "How are you?"
"I'm blessed."
"I'm okay."
"God is good."
And God is good.
But sometimes you are not okay.
Sometimes you are wounded.
Sometimes you are hiding.
Sometimes you are carrying something that needs to be confessed, confronted, grieved, or surrendered.
And the tragedy is not that Jesus knows.
The tragedy is that you may be afraid to let Him deal with what He already sees.
Listen carefully to the next words of Jesus.
In John 8:32, the Greek says:
καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς.
Kai gnōsesthe tēn alētheian, kai hē alētheia eleutherōsei hymas.
"And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
The Greek word ἀλήθεια (alētheia) means truth.
The verb ἐλευθερώσει (eleutherōsei) means "will set free" or "will liberate."
But here is something we cannot afford to miss.
Jesus does not leave the meaning of this freedom to our imagination.
His hearers respond by appealing to their descent from Abraham and questioning why they would need to be made free.
Jesus answers in John 8:34:
"Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin." (KJV)
The Greek expression is even more revealing:
δοῦλός ἐστιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας
Doulos estin tēs hamartias.
"He is a slave of sin."
The word doulos refers to a slave, someone under another's mastery.
Jesus was speaking about bondage to sin.
Not merely difficult circumstances.
Not simply the freedom to express ourselves.
Not the modern idea that freedom means doing whatever we want without anyone telling us otherwise.
Because sometimes doing whatever we want is exactly how our bondage reveals itself.
We say, "Nobody controls me."
But anger controls our reactions.
Lust controls our attention.
Pride controls our apologies.
Envy controls our contentment.
Fear controls our decisions.
And the approval of other people controls the version of ourselves we allow the world to see.
We call it independence.
Jesus calls us to recognize the slavery underneath.
And then comes one of the most beautiful declarations in the entire chapter.
"If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed." (John 8:36, KJV)
There it is.
The center of everything.
Not simply truth as an abstract principle.
Not biblical knowledge detached from the Savior.
Not self-improvement disguised as Christianity.
The Son.
Jesus Christ.
The One who does not merely describe freedom but has the authority to give it.
This is why we must never separate John 8:32 from John 8:36.
The truth that sets us free is inseparable from the Son who sets us free.
Later, Jesus declares:
"I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." (John 14:6, KJV)
The One who calls us to abide in His Word is Himself the truth.
And that changes the entire picture.
Christian freedom is not merely learning enough information to become a better person.
It is being brought into a saving relationship with Jesus Christ, who delivers sinners from the dominion of sin and calls them into a new life.
Think about that.
The Savior who knows everything about you is the same Savior who willingly went to the cross for sinners.
He knew what humanity would do.
He knew betrayal.
He knew denial.
He knew hatred.
He knew the depth of human rebellion.
And still, He went to Calvary.
Not because sin was small.
But because His love was great.
At the cross, God's holiness was not ignored.
Sin was not excused.
Justice was not dismissed.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for our sins.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares, so that we might die to sins and live unto righteousness.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we were good enough to deserve rescue.
But that Christ came to save sinners.
Not that our past was imaginary.
But that His grace is greater than our guilt.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that His mercy makes repentance a doorway back to the God we have sinned against.
And now the invitation becomes personal.
Because the same Jesus who spoke in John 8 is not asking you to admire freedom from a distance.
He is calling you to follow Him.
To remain in His Word.
To trust Him.
To turn from sin.
To stop making peace with what is destroying your soul.
To stop treating conviction as an enemy when it may be the very mercy that brings you back to Him.
And no, that does not mean the Christian life becomes instantly painless.
Some habits require sustained struggle.
Some wounds require time, wise counsel, and healing.
Some relationships need boundaries.
Some consequences remain even after forgiveness.
And believers still face temptation and must continue depending on God's grace.
But freedom in Christ means sin no longer has the rightful claim to rule those who belong to Him.
Romans 6:14 says:
"For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace."
That is not permission to continue sinning without concern.
Paul immediately rejects that misunderstanding.
It is a declaration that grace brings us under a new Master.
And His name is Jesus.
Perhaps you have fallen again.
Perhaps this week you said something cruel.
Perhaps you returned to a habit you had been fighting.
Perhaps you have been living a double life, outwardly devoted but inwardly distant.
Perhaps you have been angry at God because life has not unfolded the way you prayed it would.
And now, reading these words, you feel that familiar heaviness.
Shame.
Regret.
Fear.
The thought that whispers, "You have failed too many times."
But hear what Scripture says.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (1 John 1:9, KJV)
Not because confession magically earns forgiveness.
But because God is faithful, and the cleansing He provides rests upon the saving work of Jesus Christ.
You do not need to defend your sin before the One who died to save you from it.
You do not need to pretend the wound is healed before asking Him for help.
You do not need to manufacture spiritual strength to make yourself worthy of His mercy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting Christ.
And keep coming to His Word.
Even when it corrects you.
Especially when it corrects you.
Because the Word of God is not merely something to consult when life falls apart.
It is the truth by which we learn to live.
When bitterness rises, return to His Word.
When temptation whispers, return to His Word.
When the enemy accuses, remember what His Word says about the finished work of Christ.
When pride makes you unwilling to apologize, return to His Word.
When fear tells you that obedience will cost too much, remember the Savior who gave everything to redeem you.
Not as a religious ritual to earn His approval.
But as a disciple learning to remain in the voice of the Shepherd.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing." (KJV)
There is that language again.
Abiding.
Remaining.
Continuing.
Life flowing from a relationship with Christ.
A branch does not produce fruit by pretending to be alive.
It bears fruit because it remains connected to the vine.
And perhaps this is what your soul has been missing.
Not another emotional high.
Not another inspirational quote.
Not another temporary promise to become better through willpower alone.
But a deeper, daily dependence upon Jesus Christ.
His Word shaping your thoughts.
His grace teaching you to say no to ungodliness.
His Spirit producing fruit that your own strength could never manufacture.
His forgiveness lifting the burden of confessed sin.
His truth confronting the lies you have believed for years.
This is where freedom begins to become visible in ordinary life.
When you finally admit you were wrong instead of protecting your pride.
When you refuse to feed a secret temptation.
When you seek help instead of hiding.
When you forgive without pretending the wound never happened.
When you open Scripture even though your emotions feel numb.
When you choose obedience while your feelings are still catching up.
When you stop asking, "How close can I get to sin without falling?"
And begin asking, "Lord Jesus, how can I walk closer to You?"
Not perfection overnight.
But real repentance.
Real faith.
Real growth.
Real grace.
And a real Savior who does not abandon His people.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always been so much more than an inspirational phrase.
Consider Peter.
He confidently declared that he was ready to die with Jesus.
Then, in the courtyard, fear overtook his courage.
Three times he denied knowing his Lord.
And the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered His words.
Then he went out and wept bitterly.
Can you imagine that moment?
The sound of the rooster.
The weight of what he had done.
The realization that the mouth which had promised loyalty had spoken denial.
For Peter, it was not an abstract theological discussion.
It was personal failure.
Public weakness.
A terrible collapse at the very moment he wanted to be brave.
But that was not the end of his story.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the care of His sheep, as recorded in John 21.
Peter's denial was real.
His tears were real.
His restoration was real.
And the grace of Christ was greater than his failure.
That is not permission to treat sin lightly.
It is reason never to treat the mercy of Jesus as though it were too small to redeem a repentant sinner.
Perhaps you see yourself in Peter.
You promised loyalty.
Then pressure came.
Fear came.
Temptation came.
And you discovered how weak you could be.
But your failure does not have to become the final chapter of your story.
Jesus Christ is still the Savior of sinners.
And if you belong to Him, His Word is not calling you into hopeless condemnation.
It is calling you back to the truth.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
Back to the One who alone can make you free.
I want to ask you something now.
Not as a test of how religious you are.
Not to embarrass you.
But because some questions deserve more than a quick answer.
What is the one area of your life where you keep asking God for freedom while resisting what His Word has already told you?
You do not have to announce every private struggle publicly.
Some confessions belong in prayer, and some need to be shared with a trustworthy pastor, mature believer, counselor, or person who can help you walk toward healing and accountability.
But do not let secrecy become your hiding place.
If Christ has already brought you through a season of bondage, consider sharing a testimony of His grace. Your story may help another believer realize that repentance and restoration are possible.
And if you are not ready to share anything publicly, that is okay too.
The most important response is not the comment people see.
It is the honest response you make before God.
Not because saving a post makes you more spiritual.

But because there may come a night when temptation feels louder than conviction, when shame tells you to hide, or when you need to remember the difference between knowing a Bible verse and abiding in the Savior who spoke it.
Return to John 8:31–36.
Read it slowly.
Read the whole conversation.
Let Jesus define the freedom He promises.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Maybe a family member who has grown distant from faith.
A friend quietly struggling with addiction or shame.
A believer exhausted from trying to maintain appearances.
Someone who knows the language of Christianity but has lost the joy of walking with Christ.
Not everyone who needs the Gospel will walk into a church this week.
Some may encounter a biblical truth while scrolling through their phone after a difficult day.
Some may begin asking questions they have avoided for years.
And some may be reminded that the door of repentance is not closed to those who turn to Christ.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Jesus through Scripture, biblical conviction, encouragement, repentance, forgiveness, healing, and discipleship.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another way to walk alongside this mission.
These resources are part of our commitment to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who may not have the means to purchase books or other learning materials.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry like this requires real work, time, and resources.
Writing, preparing, organizing, and distributing discipleship materials takes continued effort.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It does not make you more loved by Jesus.
And it should never replace the responsibilities you already have to your family, your local church, or those in genuine need.
It is a voluntary act of generosity that helps support the ongoing work of this ministry.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that generosity should be willing rather than pressured.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we extend this invitation.
If you choose to direct part of your voluntary ministry-giving budget toward Gospel Warrior, we would be grateful for that support.
Not because God needs your money.
But because ministries use earthly resources to carry out real work, and willing supporters can help make that work possible.
These items are simply resources and expressions of encouragement. They are not spiritual necessities, and purchasing them does not bring anyone closer to salvation.
The greatest gift we can ever point you toward is not something we sell.
It is the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
You can still read, pray, learn, share, invite others, and make use of our free discipleship resources.
A sincere prayer matters.
A thoughtful conversation matters.
A shared Scripture can matter.
And no financial circumstance can diminish your worth before God.
What matters most is that Jesus Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that people are encouraged to know Him, trust Him, and follow His Word.
Because this was never supposed to be about building a platform that points people toward us.
It is about serving a mission that points people toward Him.
And that brings us back to the words we began with.
"If ye continue in my word…"
Perhaps you came here because you wanted to feel encouraged.
Perhaps you expected another familiar reminder that the truth would set you free.
But now you have heard the invitation that comes before the promise.
Remain.
Continue.
Abide.
Not in your own righteousness.
Not in your religious reputation.
Not in the illusion that you can save yourself through determination.
Abide in the Word of Jesus Christ.
When you are strong, remain.
When you are weak, remain.
When you understand, remain.
When you are confused, keep bringing your questions to Him.
When you fall, repent and return.
When the world offers you a thousand different versions of freedom, remember the One who said that everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.
And remember what He said next.
"If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."
There is no greater freedom than being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
No deeper cleansing than the forgiveness He provides.
No more enduring hope than the resurrection of the Savior who conquered death.
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every word.
You cannot erase every consequence.
You cannot make your history disappear.
But by God's grace, your history does not have to remain the master of your future.
The same Christ who restored Peter still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The same Christ who died for the ungodly still offers forgiveness through His finished work.
The same Christ who declared that the truth would set His disciples free still calls people to remain in His Word.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, open your Bible.
Begin with John 8.
Read beyond the verse you already know.
And ask Him, sincerely:

"Lord Jesus, show me where I have been hearing Your Word without obeying it. Expose what I have been hiding. Forgive what I have been defending. Teach me to trust Your grace, turn from my sin, and remain in Your truth. I cannot save myself. I need You. Lead me into the freedom that only You can give. Amen."
And when you close your Bible, do not leave His words behind.
Carry them into the apology you need to make.
The temptation you need to resist.
The help you need to seek.
The person you need to forgive.
The truth you need to believe.
The ordinary, unseen decisions in which discipleship becomes more than something you say.
Because the promise was never that a beautiful quotation would break every chain.
The promise was spoken by a living Savior who calls us to abide in His Word.
And the Son is able to make us free indeed.
The prison may have taught you how to survive in chains, but Jesus did not give His life so you would mistake those chains for home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD CALL CERTAIN SEXUAL RELATIONSHIPS AN ABOMINATION? THE HEBREW WORD THAT STILL SHAKES THE CHURCH TODAY
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD CALL CERTAIN SEXUAL RELATIONSHIPS AN ABOMINATION? THE HEBREW WORD THAT STILL SHAKES THE CHURCH TODAY

Leviticus 18:22–30 | What the ancient Hebrew actually says, why God gave this command, what Christians must understand about the law, and how Jesus Christ meets sinners with truth, mercy, and transforming grace.
There is a word in the Bible that can make an entire room go silent.
Abomination.
Some people hear it and immediately feel justified in condemning others.
Some hear it and remember the day someone used Scripture to humiliate them.
Some avoid the word altogether because they are afraid of what it might mean for someone they love.
And some quietly wonder whether there is still a place for them in the presence of God.
Maybe you have a son who recently told you something you never expected to hear.
Maybe you have a daughter who stopped attending church because she no longer felt welcome.
Maybe you are a Christian who believes the Bible but struggles to understand why God would prohibit certain sexual relationships.
Or maybe the struggle is much closer than anyone realizes.
You love Jesus. You want to obey Him. But there is a conflict inside you that you have never been brave enough to describe out loud.
And every time someone quotes Leviticus 18:22, something inside you tightens.
Before we go any further, there is something we need to understand.
We cannot faithfully defend a Scripture we have not carefully understood. And we cannot faithfully represent Jesus while treating the people He came to save as enemies.
The question is not whether we should take God's Word seriously.
We absolutely should.
The question is whether we are willing to understand what God actually said, why He said it, to whom He said it, and how that passage fits within the whole story of redemption.
Because a Bible verse pulled away from its context can become a weapon in human hands.
But Scripture rightly understood is meant to lead us toward the God who is holy, just, merciful, and true.
And the story does not end in Leviticus.
It leads us all the way to the cross.
THE WORD THAT CHANGES HOW WE READ THE PASSAGE
Listen carefully to the wording of Leviticus 18:22 in the King James Version:
"Thou shalt not lie with mankind, as with womankind: it is abomination."
The Hebrew reads:
וְאֶת־זָכָר לֹא תִשְׁכַּב מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה תּוֹעֵבָה הִוא
Ve'et-zakhar lo tishkav mishkevei ishah; to'evah hi.
A close English rendering is:
"You shall not lie with a male as the lyings of a woman; it is an abomination."
Notice something important.
The Hebrew word זָכָר (zakhar) means "male."
The verb תִשְׁכַּב (tishkav) comes from shakhav, meaning "to lie down," a verb that can refer to sexual intercourse depending on context.
The expression מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה (mishkevei ishah) literally concerns the "lyings of a woman," an idiomatic expression referring to sexual relations.
And then comes the word that has generated centuries of argument:
תּוֹעֵבָה (to'evah).
Commonly translated "abomination" or "detestable thing."
But what does it mean?
It describes something regarded as deeply objectionable or detestable within the moral and religious framework of the text.
The word appears elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible in connection with idolatry, dishonest practices, and other prohibited conduct.
For example, Proverbs 11:1 calls dishonest scales a to'evah to the LORD.
Deuteronomy 7:25–26 uses related language concerning idols and their associated objects.
This matters because the Hebrew word does not mean that a particular human being is inherently disgusting or beyond God's mercy.
Leviticus 18:22 identifies a prohibited act. It does not authorize Christians to declare that an entire class of human beings is worthless, unlovable, or beyond redemption.
That distinction is not a modern attempt to soften Scripture.
It is a necessary distinction between what the passage actually says and what people sometimes make it say.
But neither should we pretend that understanding the Hebrew automatically removes the prohibition.
It does not.
The text itself is direct.
The difficult questions concern its scope, historical setting, relationship to other biblical laws, and application to Christians today.
And to understand those questions, we have to enter the world in which these words were first spoken.
GOD WAS SPEAKING TO A PEOPLE HE HAD JUST RESCUED
Imagine Israel standing on the other side of Egypt.
For generations, they had lived under oppression.
They knew what it meant to be controlled by a powerful nation.
They knew what it meant to have their identity shaped by a culture that did not worship the LORD.
Then God delivered them.
Not because they had earned His love.
Not because they had proven themselves morally superior.
But because He remembered His covenant.
Now the rescued people had to learn how to live as God's covenant people.
And this is where Leviticus 18 becomes essential.
Before the chapter lists prohibited sexual relationships, God declares:
"After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do: and after the doings of the land of Canaan, whither I bring you, shall ye not do." — Leviticus 18:3, KJV
Then He says:
"Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the LORD." — Leviticus 18:5, KJV
God was calling Israel to be distinct from the surrounding nations.
Their worship, family life, justice, sexuality, and treatment of others were to reflect their covenant relationship with Him.
And the chapter was not merely about one sexual act.
Read the entire passage.
Leviticus 18 addresses incestuous relationships, adultery, the offering of children to Molech, male same-sex intercourse, and sexual relations with animals.
It describes a range of practices that Israel was forbidden to adopt.
Verses 24–30 then warn that such practices defile the land and that Israel must not imitate them.
The repeated declaration is unmistakable:
"I am the LORD."
God was not presenting holiness as a popularity contest.
He was grounding Israel's conduct in His authority and covenant.
But there is another detail we must not overlook.
The passage does not provide a detailed explanation of why every prohibited act is wrong.
It gives commands, describes defilement, and places those commands within Israel's calling to holiness.
Some interpreters emphasize creation order and sexual boundaries. Others examine ancient kinship structures, ritual categories, and Israel's distinction from neighboring cultures.
Scholars also debate how these ancient prohibitions relate to modern categories of sexual orientation and committed same-sex relationships.
Those modern categories are not explicitly discussed in Leviticus 18.
We should not claim that the Hebrew text settles every contemporary question simply because we have learned to pronounce to'evah.
Knowing the original language is not permission to pretend we know more than the passage reveals.
And that is where biblical humility begins.
BUT WHY DO CHRISTIANS FOLLOW SOME OLD TESTAMENT COMMANDS AND NOT OTHERS?
This is the question many believers are afraid to ask.
And many people outside the church have been asking it for years.
"If Christians appeal to Leviticus concerning sexuality, why don't they follow all the other laws in Leviticus?"
It is a fair question.
Leviticus contains regulations concerning sacrifices, ritual purity, food, priesthood, and the life of ancient Israel.
Christians generally do not offer animal sacrifices.
They do not ordinarily observe Israel's ceremonial purity system.
They do not live under the civil institutions of ancient Israel.
So why does this passage still matter?
The answer cannot simply be, "Because it is in the Bible."
Every command in Scripture deserves serious attention, but faithful interpretation also requires understanding its covenantal setting and how the New Testament relates to it.
Christians believe Jesus Christ fulfilled the law and the prophets.
In Matthew 5:17, Jesus says:
"Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."
And the New Testament teaches that believers are not under the Mosaic covenant in the same manner as ancient Israel.
Acts 15 is especially important.
When Gentiles began turning to Christ, the early church faced a major question.
Did Gentile believers have to become observant Jews and keep the Mosaic law to belong to God's people?
The apostles did not impose the entire Mosaic law upon them.
Yet Acts 15:20 and 15:29 specifically instructed Gentile believers to abstain from sexual immorality, alongside other requirements.
The Greek word used is πορνεία (porneia), a broad term referring to illicit sexual conduct.
The precise range of behaviors included under this term must be interpreted from its context and the wider biblical witness.
Traditional Christian interpreters understand New Testament sexual ethics as maintaining the male-female marital framework while no longer requiring Israel's ceremonial and national laws.
Other Christian interpreters question whether ancient prohibitions address all forms of same-sex relationships understood today.
That disagreement is real.
And pretending it does not exist will not strengthen anyone's faith.
But neither does disagreement mean that Scripture says nothing meaningful.
It means we must read carefully, reason faithfully, and refuse to substitute slogans for serious biblical understanding.
The historic Christian understanding of marriage draws heavily from Genesis 1–2 and Jesus' teaching in Matthew 19:4–6, where He speaks of male and female becoming one flesh in marriage.
Romans 1:26–27 and 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 are also central to the discussion.
In 1 Corinthians 6:9, Paul uses the Greek terms μαλακοί (malakoi) and ἀρσενοκοῖται (arsenokoitai).
The first literally means "soft" and has different uses in ancient Greek. The second is a rare compound formed from words meaning "male" and "bed."
Many scholars see arsenokoitai as echoing the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13.
The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, uses the terms ἄρσενος (arsenos) and κοίτην (koitēn) in Leviticus 18:22.
That verbal connection is significant.
It is one reason many Christians understand Paul's teaching as continuing the sexual prohibition found in Leviticus.
However, scholars debate the precise scope of Paul's terms, especially how they should be related to ancient exploitative practices and modern consensual relationships.
A responsible Christian article should acknowledge that debate rather than disguise an interpretive conclusion as a universally uncontested translation.
For Gospel Warrior, the historic Christian sexual ethic can be taught with conviction.
But conviction does not require caricaturing those who disagree.
And it certainly does not give us permission to despise those who struggle.
Because the New Testament does something extraordinary.
After speaking about sin, Paul turns toward the transforming work of Christ.
And what he says next should make every self-righteous heart tremble.
"AND SUCH WERE SOME OF YOU."
Read 1 Corinthians 6:11 slowly.
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."
Do you see it?
Paul does not build a community around the idea that some sinners are too contaminated to approach Jesus.
He describes people whose lives have been touched by the saving grace of God.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Three words that reveal something no human condemnation can accomplish.
Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Not people who merely made a few harmless mistakes.
Real sinners.
People with painful histories.
People who have wounded others.
People carrying secret shame.
People who have built their identity around desires, achievements, relationships, or habits that cannot save them.
People who desperately need mercy.
And here is something the church must never forget.
The passage does not give us permission to single out one group while excusing everyone else.
Paul's surrounding list includes multiple kinds of wrongdoing.
Sexual immorality.
Adultery.
Greed.
Theft.
Drunkenness.
Verbal abuse.
Fraud.
And then he says:
"And such were some of you."
The ground beneath the cross is level.
Not because every sin is identical in its consequences.
Not because every person's story is the same.
But because no sinner can earn salvation through personal righteousness.
Every one of us needs grace.
The married man secretly watching pornography cannot use Leviticus to make himself morally superior to his unmarried neighbor.
The church leader committing adultery cannot preach holiness while hiding his betrayal.
The Christian who humiliates someone struggling with sexuality cannot pretend cruelty becomes righteous simply because it is wrapped in biblical vocabulary.
And the person who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy must not be told that the hypocrisy represents the heart of Jesus.
God's holiness exposes all of us. God's grace invites all of us to come to Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Not selective outrage.
Not spiritual superiority.
Not permission to continue knowingly in sin.
But repentance and faith in the Savior who died and rose again.
THE DANGER OF CALLING PEOPLE WHAT GOD CALLED AN ACT
Imagine someone walking into church for the first time in years.
They have rehearsed the decision all morning.
They almost turned around in the parking lot.
They have heard enough angry sermons online to expect rejection.
But something inside them still longs for God.
They sit near the back.
They listen.
And then someone speaks about abomination.
Not with careful explanation.
Not with tears.
Not with the humility of a fellow sinner.
But with visible disgust.
The person hears a message that sounds like this:
"You are the kind of person God cannot stand."
And before anyone has the opportunity to speak with them, they leave.
Now consider the tragedy.
The Bible teaches that every human being is made in the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 establishes human dignity in creation.
That dignity does not disappear because of someone's desires, history, beliefs, or moral failures.
We can believe that a particular action violates God's will without denying the humanity of the person involved.
We can maintain biblical convictions without mockery.
We can call people to repentance without humiliation.
And we can welcome someone into a church community without pretending that every theological disagreement has disappeared.
Jesus Himself was described as receiving sinners and eating with them.
In Luke 5:31–32, He explains that He came to call sinners to repentance.
Notice both truths.
He welcomed sinners.
And He called sinners to repentance.
Neither truth cancels the other.
A church that refuses to welcome people has forgotten the mercy of Christ.
A church that refuses to speak about repentance has forgotten the message of Christ.
But a church that speaks about repentance without love has also forgotten something essential.
Jesus did not tell His disciples to make people feel worthless.
He commanded them to love one another.
And He warned against hypocritical judgment.
Before you confront someone else's life, ask whether you have brought your own life honestly before God.
Because the Word of God is not a stone we throw from a safe distance.
It is a light under which we must first stand ourselves.
WHAT IF THE PERSON STRUGGLING IS SOMEONE YOU LOVE?
This is where the conversation stops being theoretical.
A mother sits at the kitchen table.
Her son has just shared something deeply personal.
His hands are shaking.
He has spent years wondering whether telling the truth will cost him his family.
His mother believes Scripture.
She also loves her son more deeply than words can express.
Now she faces a moment she never prepared for.
What should she say?
Perhaps the most important first words are not an argument.
Perhaps they are:
"I love you. Thank you for trusting me enough to tell me."
That is not a denial of biblical conviction.
It is an acknowledgment of a relationship that should not be destroyed by panic.
A parent can listen without immediately resolving every theological question.
A pastor can show compassion without abandoning his beliefs.
A Christian friend can disagree respectfully without turning someone's vulnerability into public gossip.
And a person experiencing same-sex attraction should not be automatically accused of choosing every feeling they experience.
Within traditional Christian theology, a distinction is often made between experiencing an attraction and deliberately acting upon it.
Christians also differ in how they understand temptation, desire, and moral responsibility.
But whatever one's theological position, no one should be pressured into shame, coercion, or the belief that God's love must be purchased through pretending.
The Christian call to discipleship is demanding for everyone.
Jesus calls all His followers to deny themselves and follow Him.
For some, obedience involves resisting sexual temptation.
For others, it involves ending an adulterous relationship.
For others, it means confronting pornography, greed, pride, dishonesty, or bitterness.
For all of us, it means learning to surrender our lives to Christ.
And surrender is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it is a quiet prayer spoken through tears.
"Lord, I do not understand everything. But I want to know You. Teach me to walk in truth."
God is not intimidated by an honest prayer.
HOLINESS WITHOUT LOVE BECOMES CRUELTY. LOVE WITHOUT TRUTH BECOMES SENTIMENTALITY. BUT IN JESUS CHRIST, GRACE AND TRUTH MEET.
John 1:14 describes Jesus as full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And that is what makes Christ different from the religious performances we sometimes mistake for Christianity.
He does not need us to dilute His teaching.
He does not need us to exaggerate His teaching.
He calls us to follow Him faithfully.
That means refusing to make a single sexual issue the entire definition of Christianity.
It also means refusing to act as though sexual ethics are irrelevant to Christian discipleship.
Our bodies matter.
Our relationships matter.
Our choices matter.
And our treatment of other people matters.
In fact, Jesus identified love for God and love for neighbor as the greatest commandments.
That means the Christian who speaks accurately about sexual morality but treats others with contempt has not fulfilled the whole calling of Christ.
And the Christian who wants to love others must still wrestle honestly with what God has revealed.
This is not an easy tension.
It was never meant to be solved by cruelty or denial.
It calls for biblical conviction, patient teaching, humility, repentance, and love.
And sometimes, it requires the courage to admit that we have spoken with more certainty than our understanding justified.
THE CROSS IS WHERE EVERY ONE OF US LOSES THE RIGHT TO BOAST
Now picture Calvary.
Not as a decorative cross hanging on a church wall.
But as the place where the Son of God suffered for sinners.
The crowd mocks Him.
The soldiers divide His garments.
His disciples have scattered.
And Jesus is crucified.
The One who had no sin bears the suffering of the cross.
This is where the Christian message reaches its center.
Not in the ability to identify someone else's failures.
Not in winning an argument about a Hebrew word.
Not in proving that our moral record is cleaner than our neighbor's.
But in Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had fixed ourselves.
Not after we had resolved every internal struggle.
Not after we had learned enough theology to impress anyone.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection announces that sin and death do not have the final word.
The Gospel is not a promise that following Jesus will remove every difficult feeling or settle every painful question immediately.
It is the good news that forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life are found in Jesus Christ.
Repentance matters.
Faith matters.
Obedience matters.
But none of these gives us grounds to boast over another human being.
Our salvation rests on Christ.
And if we truly believe that, our conversations about sexuality should sound different from the cruelty of the world.
There should be conviction.
There should be compassion.
There should be courage.
There should be patience.
And there should always be room for someone to hear the invitation of Jesus.
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." — Matthew 11:28, KJV
SO WHY DID LEVITICUS CALL IT AN ABOMINATION?
Because within the covenant law given to Israel, the sexual act described in Leviticus 18:22 was prohibited and classified as to'evah—something detestable under that law.
The surrounding chapter places the prohibition among practices Israel was commanded to avoid as part of its distinct covenant life.
The passage is concerned with conduct, holiness, defilement, and obedience to the LORD.
It does not explicitly discuss modern sexual orientation as a psychological category.
It does not provide a comprehensive account of every modern relationship.
And it does not authorize hatred, harassment, or dehumanization.
Historic Christian interpretation generally understands the prohibition as consistent with the Bible's wider sexual ethic, including the New Testament's teaching on sexual morality.
Other Christian interpreters disagree about its application to contemporary same-sex relationships.
The disagreement deserves serious engagement with Scripture, language, history, and theology.
But one truth must remain nonnegotiable for Christians on every side of the discussion:
No one is saved by being heterosexual. No one is saved by being married. No one is saved by winning a theological argument. Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And no one has earned the right to mistreat another person in His name.
That should humble every one of us.
Especially those of us who preach.
Especially those of us who teach.
Especially those of us who have used biblical truth more eagerly to expose someone else's sin than to confess our own.
Maybe the most uncomfortable question raised by this passage is not simply, "Why did God call this act an abomination?"
Maybe it is also:
"Have I allowed my confidence about someone else's sin to blind me to the sins in my own heart?"
Because it is possible to defend a biblical command while violating the biblical command to love your neighbor.
And it is possible to speak about holiness while refusing to practice humility.
If this article has exposed pride, hidden compromise, fear, or a wound you have been carrying, do not run from God.
Come to Him.
If you need forgiveness, ask Him for it.
If you need wisdom, seek it.
If you have mistreated someone, make it right.
If you are struggling with questions about your sexuality and your faith, do not assume that you must face them alone.
Seek mature, compassionate Christians who will listen carefully, handle Scripture responsibly, respect your dignity, and walk with you patiently.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony for anyone.
You do not have to pretend the struggle is easy.
And you do not have to abandon honest questions to begin seeking Jesus.
BEFORE YOU CLOSE THIS ARTICLE, THERE IS ONE MORE PERSON I WANT YOU TO THINK ABOUT.
Someone you know is silently struggling.
Perhaps they are ashamed of their past.
Perhaps they have been wounded by a church.
Perhaps they have been using the Bible to condemn everyone except themselves.
Perhaps they believe Jesus would never welcome them.
They might never tell you.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create an audience addicted to outrage.
Not to turn people's pain into religious entertainment.
But to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
Add a few words about what challenged you.
Not because sharing makes you more righteous.
But because someone in your circle may need to encounter a more faithful and compassionate explanation of God's Word.
But I also want to ask you something more personal.
What did this passage confront in your own heart?
Was it pride?
Was it fear?
Was it the way you have treated someone who struggles differently from you?
Was it your own need for repentance?
Or was it the realization that you have been afraid to approach Jesus because of something in your life?
You do not have to disclose private details or expose another person's story.
The goal is not public confession for its own sake.
The goal is to help one another turn toward Jesus.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical encouragement, Christian teaching, and discipleship resources accessible to people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
These resources are part of a mission worth sustaining and expanding.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, not coerced.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
You do not have to give money to earn His favor.
And your spiritual standing before Jesus is not determined by a monthly payment.
But if this ministry has helped you, and you have the means and desire to help it serve others, your partnership can be a meaningful act of generosity.
These are simply gifts of appreciation for those helping sustain the work.
The greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is making biblical truth more accessible.
It is encouraging weary believers.
It is helping families encounter Scripture.
It is reminding people that their story does not have to end where their deepest shame began.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep asking difficult questions.
Keep showing mercy.
Keep refusing to turn people into enemies.
Keep pointing people to Jesus.
Because when the world hears the word abomination, it may expect another argument filled with anger.
But when people encounter Christians shaped by the crucified and risen Christ, they should also encounter humility, compassion, holiness, and hope.
The law reveals the seriousness of sin.
The Gospel reveals the greatness of the Savior.
And grace does not mean sin was never serious.
It means God's mercy is greater than any sinner's ability to save themselves.
The person you were ready to condemn may be the very person Jesus is calling you to love—and the heart He wants to confront first may be your own.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY BROUGHT HER TO JESUS TO BE STONED. HE SENT HER AWAY WITH A COMMAND THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR LIFE.
paragraphs: THEY BROUGHT HER TO JESUS TO BE STONED. HE SENT HER AWAY WITH A COMMAND THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR LIFE.
Why did Jesus tell the woman caught in adultery, “Go, and sin no more”? The answer is far more confronting—and far more beautiful—than simply being forgiven.
She was caught in a sin she could not deny.
There was no time to prepare an explanation. No opportunity to repair her reputation. No chance to make herself look innocent.
And now she was standing in front of Jesus.
Not because she had come looking for forgiveness.
But because other people had brought her there to be condemned.
Imagine the humiliation.
People staring. Religious leaders accusing. Her most shameful moment exposed in public.
And somewhere in that crowd, perhaps, were people who had secrets of their own.
She had broken God's law.
That much was serious.
But the men standing around her were about to discover something equally serious.
Knowing someone else's sin does not make you innocent of your own.
And what Jesus did next would reveal a truth that every wounded sinner, struggling believer, religious hypocrite, and person hiding behind a respectable reputation desperately needs to understand.
Because the most astonishing part of this encounter was not merely that Jesus refused to condemn her.
It was what He told her after her accusers walked away.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Five words in the familiar English wording of the King James Version.
Five words that have been misunderstood, softened, weaponized, and sometimes almost forgotten.
But if you understand why Jesus said them, you may never look at grace the same way again.
And before we reach the end, there is a question you will have to answer.
Not about the woman.
About yourself.
The account appears in John 7:53–8:11, traditionally known as the woman caught in adultery.

One important detail deserves honesty before we go further. This passage, often called the Pericope Adulterae, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel and appears in different locations in certain manuscript traditions. Most modern Bible translations acknowledge this textual question. Christians differ on its textual status, and we should not pretend the evidence is simpler than it is.

Nevertheless, the account has a long history in the Christian tradition, and its central themes can be examined alongside teachings firmly established throughout the New Testament: the seriousness of sin, the danger of hypocritical judgment, the mercy of Christ, and His call to repentance.
We do not need to conceal difficult questions about Scripture to honor the God of truth.
Now picture the scene.
Jesus is teaching in the temple.
Suddenly, the scribes and Pharisees bring a woman before Him.
They say she has been caught committing adultery.
Then comes their challenge:
“Now Moses in the law commanded us, that such should be stoned: but what sayest thou?” (John 8:5, KJV)
They are not simply asking for pastoral counsel.
John 8:6 explicitly tells us that they were testing Jesus, seeking grounds to accuse Him.
The woman is standing there with her sin exposed, while her accusers are using her case as a weapon against someone else.
And there is something deeply disturbing about the scene.
Where is the man?
Adultery does not happen with only one participant.
Leviticus 20:10 assigns responsibility to both the adulterer and the adulteress. Deuteronomy 22:22 likewise speaks of both parties in a case of adultery involving a married woman.
Yet only the woman is brought before Jesus.
The passage does not explain where the man was, whether he escaped, or why he was absent. We must not invent details Scripture does not provide.
But the omission should make us cautious about assuming the accusers were pursuing justice with clean hands.
Their own stated purpose was to trap Jesus.
And that is where this story begins to move uncomfortably close to home.
Because religious people can sometimes become more passionate about exposing another person's failure than confronting their own.
We can become experts at identifying someone else's adultery while ignoring our own dishonesty.
We can condemn another person's sexual immorality while secretly entertaining lust.
We can criticize someone for falling into temptation while feeding the bitterness, pride, greed, or unforgiveness that has quietly taken root in our own hearts.
We can defend biblical truth in public while resisting biblical correction in private.
And sometimes the most frightening spiritual condition is not being caught in a scandal.
It is becoming so comfortable with our hidden sins that we no longer recognize our need for mercy.
Then Jesus does something unexpected.
He bends down and writes on the ground.
The crowd is waiting for an answer.
The accusers continue questioning Him.
But Jesus does not respond according to their timetable.
What did He write?
We do not know.
Some have suggested He wrote the sins of the accusers. Others have connected His action with Old Testament imagery.
Those possibilities may provoke reflection, but the passage never identifies the words He wrote.
And we must be careful not to preach speculation as revelation.
What Scripture does tell us is that Jesus eventually stands and says:
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” (John 8:7, KJV)
Read that again.
Jesus did not say adultery was acceptable.
He did not declare that God's moral law had suddenly become meaningless.
He did not teach that wrongdoing should never be confronted or that justice should never be pursued.
He challenged these accusers in this particular situation.
Under Deuteronomy 17:6–7, witnesses had a serious responsibility in capital cases, including taking the lead in carrying out the sentence.
Jesus' words exposed the moral seriousness of what they were demanding.
They wanted to stand as judges.
Jesus forced them to confront themselves.
And one by one, they departed.
The older ones first, according to John 8:9.
The text does not tell us everything happening inside their hearts.
But it tells us enough to see that their attempt to trap Jesus had failed.
Now the woman is standing before Him.
The accusing crowd has disappeared.
And the One who remains is the very One who has the authority to judge with perfect righteousness.
Imagine that moment.
She had been dragged into the open.
Her sin had been announced.
Her future had become uncertain.
And now she hears Jesus ask:
“Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?” (John 8:10, KJV)
She answers:
“No man, Lord.”
Then Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
There it is.
The sentence that changes everything.
Not because Jesus pretended she was innocent.
Not because adultery had become harmless.
Not because the holiness of God had been compromised.
But because Jesus' response held together two truths we are constantly tempted to separate.
Mercy is real. And sin is still serious.
Some people want a Jesus who offers forgiveness without calling anyone to change.
Others present a Jesus who demands change without offering tenderness to the broken.
But the Jesus revealed in Scripture cannot be reduced to either caricature.
He is full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
He welcomes sinners to repentance.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He exposes darkness.
He forgives.
He restores.
And He never teaches that the freedom He gives is permission to remain enslaved to sin.
To understand His command, look closely at the Greek.
John 8:11 reads, in part:
πορεύου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
Poreuou, kai apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
A natural English translation is:
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
The word πορεύου (poreuou) means “go” or “depart.”
The phrase ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν (apo tou nyn) means “from now on.”
The word μηκέτι (mēketi) means “no longer” or “no more.”
And ἁμάρτανε (hamartane) comes from the verb hamartanō, meaning “to sin.”
This is not merely a suggestion to feel less guilty.
It is a command to leave sinful conduct behind.

The Greek present imperative with the negative mēketi communicates a prohibition against sinning from this point forward. It does not, by itself, establish that the woman had a lifelong habit of adultery, nor does it prove that Jesus was promising she would never commit another sin.
It is a genuine call to a changed direction.
And notice the order.
Jesus first says, “Neither do I condemn thee.”
Then He says, “Go, and sin no more.”
He does not say, “Become morally perfect, and then I might show you mercy.”
Neither does He say, “I have shown you mercy, so your future choices no longer matter.”
He refuses to condemn her in that encounter and calls her away from sin.
That order matters.
Because genuine grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace gives sinners a reason to turn toward holiness rather than run from God in despair.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Maybe your scandal was never exposed in public.
Maybe nobody ever dragged you before a crowd.
Maybe your family still thinks you have everything together.
Maybe your church knows the version of you that smiles, worships, serves, and says all the right things.
But there is another version of your life that only God sees.
The conversations you delete.
The images you keep returning to.
The lies you have learned to tell without hesitation.
The bitterness you keep justifying.
The secret relationship.
The pornography.
The envy.
The pride.
The unforgiveness.
The compromises you promised would happen only once.
Or perhaps your struggle is not a particular outward scandal but a spiritual numbness that has slowly made obedience feel optional.
You still believe in Jesus.
You still know the songs.
You still recognize the Bible verses.
But somewhere along the way, you began treating the mercy of God as though it were an agreement that you would never have to change.
And now a question confronts you.
Have you been asking Jesus to forgive what you are still determined to protect?
That question is not intended to crush a repentant believer who is struggling.
There is a profound difference between a person who hates their sin and keeps turning back to Christ, and a person who has decided to make peace with sin while claiming grace as protection.
Christians can experience real struggles, repeated temptations, painful setbacks, and the slow work of spiritual growth.
First John 1:8 warns against claiming to be without sin.
First John 1:9 also promises that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
The Christian life is not a performance of flawless perfection.
But neither is repentance an empty word.
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), associated with a change of mind or understanding that, in biblical teaching, belongs with turning toward God.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered your wrongdoing.
It is not crying because your reputation has been damaged.
It is not making another emotional promise while secretly planning your next compromise.
True repentance involves acknowledging sin before God, turning from it, and seeking to walk in obedience through His grace.
That does not mean every deeply rooted struggle disappears overnight.
It means you stop calling darkness your home.
You stop defending what Christ calls you to leave.
You stop pretending that forgiveness and transformation are enemies.
And when you fall, you do not build an altar to your failure.
You return to the Savior.
This is why Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic:
“God forbid.”
Grace is not a loophole in God's holiness.
