And this is why the Gospel must remain at the center of our understanding.
The greatest fulfillment of God's faithfulness is not that every Christian will eventually receive the earthly outcome they desire.
It is that God has given His Son.
Jesus Christ lived in perfect obedience, died for our sins, and rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness is offered to sinners.
Through Him, the guilty can be justified.
Through Him, those who trust in Him are adopted into God's family.
Through Him, we receive an inheritance that death itself cannot destroy.
Peter describes it as an inheritance “incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4, KJV).
And perhaps that is the most extraordinary contrast in this entire story.
Eliezer was a possible heir to Abraham's earthly estate.
But in Christ, believers are made heirs of something infinitely greater than livestock, silver, land, or household possessions.
Romans 8:17 calls believers “heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ,” while also reminding us that following Christ involves suffering as well as future glory.
This inheritance cannot be purchased.
It cannot be earned by charitable donations.
It is received by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that truth must never be compromised.
Because if there is one thing the Church must guard, it is the difference between supporting Gospel ministry and buying God's favor.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot pay for forgiveness.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And His finished work is sufficient.
Yet when His grace truly takes hold of our hearts, it changes how we live.
We begin to care about the spiritual condition of others.
We become concerned for the people who have never heard the Gospel clearly.
We want the discouraged believer to find strength in Scripture.
We want the wandering Christian to return to Christ.
We want families to discover the Word of God together.
And we begin to understand that supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of love and stewardship.
Not a payment for grace.
But a response to grace.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to replace the faithful shepherding of pastors.
Not to make disciples dependent upon a personality or platform.
But to point people back to Scripture, back to repentance, back to the cross, and back to the living Jesus Christ.
And we want those resources to continue reaching people.
The person reading alone at two in the morning.
The father who wants to lead his family spiritually but does not know where to begin.
The young believer trying to understand the Bible.
The Christian who has fallen into sin and desperately needs to hear the truth about repentance and restoration.
The seeker who is quietly wondering whether Jesus really is who Scripture says He is.
This work requires time, resources, and faithful support.

It can be part of your personal generosity and support for Gospel outreach. But it should not be presented as a required tithe, a substitute for your responsibilities to your local church, or a condition for glorifying God.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from coercion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
If you are able and willing to partner with this mission, we would be grateful.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage believers, share biblical messages, and help sustain the work.
You are no less welcome here.
The Gospel is not reserved for those who can afford to give.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, encourage others, and grow in the truth of Scripture.
And there is another way you can help this message travel farther.
Not because every post must go viral.
Not because numbers are more important than people.
But because someone among your family, friends, or acquaintances may be quietly struggling with the same kind of disappointment Abraham carried.
Someone may need to be reminded that God's faithfulness is not measured by the speed of an answered prayer.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is still possible.
Someone may need to know that Jesus Christ receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
There may come a day when you need to return to Genesis 15 and remember that Abraham's unanswered questions did not prevent him from bringing his heart before the Lord.
And if this message has touched something you have been struggling to explain, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
You do not have to reveal private details.
You do not have to pretend that everything is fine.
Or, if you are going through a particularly difficult season:
“Pray for me. I'm still waiting.”
And if the Holy Spirit has brought conviction about something you have been hiding, perhaps your prayer today is simply:
“Lord Jesus, lead me to repentance.”
These are not magical phrases.
Typing them does not save you.
But honest words can open a conversation, encourage another believer, and remind someone that they are not the only person struggling to hold on to faith.
Your story may encourage someone who is finding it difficult to hope.
Now, before we leave Abraham beneath that ancient sky, there is one final detail worth remembering.
We know that Isaac was born.
We know that God's covenant promise continued through him.
But what happened to Eliezer of Damascus?
Scripture does not tell us.
The man Abraham once expected to inherit his estate disappears from the explicit narrative after Genesis 15.
We do not know how he reacted when Abraham received God's answer.
We do not know whether he felt relief, disappointment, joy, or nothing of the sort.
We do not know how long he lived or what became of him.
And perhaps the most faithful thing we can do is leave those unanswered questions where Scripture leaves them.
Not every person mentioned in the Bible receives a complete biography.
Not every mystery is explained.
Not every silence needs to be filled with speculation.
But the brief mention of Eliezer still serves a remarkable purpose.
It shows us how real Abraham's childlessness was.
And it prepares us to understand why God's declaration about a son mattered so profoundly.
Eliezer reminds us of what Abraham thought his future might look like.
Isaac reminds us of what God had specifically promised.
And Jesus Christ reveals the ultimate saving purpose toward which God's promise to Abraham was moving.
So perhaps the question is not simply, “Who was Eliezer of Damascus?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
What are you trusting to give your life security when the future remains uncertain?
Your savings?
Your achievements?
Your reputation?
Your plans?
Your ability to keep everything under control?
These things may have legitimate places in your life.
But none can bear the weight of being your savior.
Only Jesus Christ can do that.

And if you have spent years trying to build a life that no disappointment can shake, perhaps today is the day to remember that your deepest hope was never meant to rest upon a perfect earthly outcome.
It was meant to rest upon the Lord.
The same Lord who spoke to Abraham.
The same Lord who fulfilled His covenant purposes through generations.
The same Lord who sent His Son into a broken world.
The same Lord who raised Jesus from the dead.
And the same Lord who calls sinners everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
If you have never truly surrendered your life to Christ, do not confuse knowing biblical stories with knowing the Savior.
Come to Him.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive His forgiveness by faith.
And begin following Him, not because life will suddenly become easy, but because He alone is worthy of your trust.
If you already belong to Christ but have become weary, bring that weariness to Him.
You do not have to pretend that waiting is painless.
Abraham did not.
You do not have to invent certainty about outcomes God has not promised.
You can entrust those uncertainties to the One whose character has been revealed in Jesus Christ.
And you do not have to measure God's love by how closely your life resembles the future you once imagined.
Look to the cross.
Look to the empty tomb.
Look to the promises God has actually given in His Word.
Because the greatest hope of the Christian is not that every chapter will unfold as expected.
It is that Jesus Christ has overcome sin and death, and that everyone who belongs to Him has a future secured by His grace.
That is the beauty of redemption.
That is the wonder of the Gospel.
That is why our story can move from scandal to grace.
Not because our failures were harmless.
Not because our waiting was imaginary.
Not because our wounds never mattered.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem sinners, restore lives, and give an eternal hope that no earthly disappointment can finally destroy.

And perhaps one day, when you look back over the chapters you once feared would break you, you will see that even in seasons when you could not understand what God was doing, His Word was still worthy of your trust.
The most important thing about your unfinished story is not what you are still waiting to receive, but the Savior who has already given Himself for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE PAINTED HER EYES BEFORE THEY THREW HER TO HER DEATH. BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF JEZEBEL’S STORY WASN’T HOW SHE DIED.
paragraphs: SHE PAINTED HER EYES BEFORE THEY THREW HER TO HER DEATH. BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF JEZEBEL’S STORY WASN’T HOW SHE DIED.

She was a queen who commanded kings, silenced prophets, and terrified a nation. Yet when death finally arrived at her doorstep, she reached for her makeup. The story of Jezebel is not merely about a wicked woman’s downfall. It is a terrifying warning about the heart that refuses to repent—and a breathtaking reminder of the grace we must never take for granted.
“And when Jehu was come to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it; and she painted her face, and tired her head, and looked out at a window.” — 2 Kings 9:30, KJV
There is something deeply unsettling about a woman preparing her appearance while the footsteps of death are approaching.
Outside, a man is coming to end her reign.
Inside, a queen is standing before what may have been the final mirror of her life.
She knows the kingdom is collapsing.
Her son is dead.
The dynasty she helped build is falling apart.
The man approaching her palace has already killed the king.
And what does she do?
She paints her eyes.
She arranges her hair.
She positions herself at the window.
Not to escape.
Not to plead for mercy.
Not, as far as Scripture records, to repent.
She prepares to face the man who will order her death.
Her name is Jezebel.
And before you decide this is simply another story about a wicked queen who finally received what she deserved, there is something you need to understand.
The most dangerous thing about Jezebel was not the paint around her eyes. It was the rebellion she had allowed to rule her heart.
And that is where this ancient story begins to get painfully personal.
Because you do not have to wear a crown to become hardened.
You do not have to command a kingdom to become proud.
And you do not have to bow before a carved idol to discover that something other than God has taken His rightful place in your life.
Sometimes rebellion wears royal clothing.
Sometimes it wears Sunday clothes.
Sometimes it sits on a throne.
Sometimes it sits in a church pew.
And sometimes the person most desperately in need of repentance is the person who has become exceptionally skilled at looking as though everything is fine.
But to understand that final moment at the window, we need to understand the woman who stood behind it.
Jezebel was not an insignificant figure who happened to marry a powerful man.
According to 1 Kings 16:31, she was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and became the wife of Ahab, king of Israel.
Her arrival in Israel was connected to a devastating period of religious corruption.
Ahab served Baal and worshiped him. He erected an altar for Baal in Samaria and made an Asherah.
And Jezebel was not merely watching these things happen.
She actively promoted the worship of Baal and opposed the prophets of the LORD.
In 1 Kings 18:4, Scripture records that Jezebel was killing the prophets of the LORD, while Obadiah secretly hid a hundred prophets and supplied them with bread and water.
Think about that.
Men who spoke the truth about God were being hunted.
Faithfulness had become dangerous.
And the queen had turned her royal influence against the worship of the living God.
But her cruelty did not stop with religious persecution.
There was a man named Naboth.
He owned a vineyard beside Ahab's palace.
Ahab wanted it.
Naboth refused to surrender his ancestral inheritance, explaining that the LORD forbade him to give away the inheritance of his fathers.
Ahab returned home resentful, lay on his bed, turned away, and refused to eat.
Then Jezebel intervened.
She wrote letters in Ahab's name, sealed them with his seal, and arranged for false witnesses to accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king.
Naboth was taken outside the city.
And stoned to death.
An innocent man lost his life because someone powerful wanted what belonged to him.
Then Jezebel told Ahab to take possession of the vineyard.
Read 1 Kings 21 carefully.
This was not simply a woman with a strong personality.
This was calculated injustice.
Religious language was used to disguise murder.
Royal authority was used to steal property.
And an innocent man's blood was treated as an inconvenience.
Yet there was something Jezebel could not control.
She could manipulate witnesses, but she could not silence the God who had witnessed everything.
The LORD sent Elijah to confront Ahab.
Judgment was announced against Ahab's house, and Elijah declared that dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.
Years passed.
The prophecy did not disappear.
And this is where the story becomes especially sobering.
We often mistake delayed consequences for divine approval.
We keep doing what we know is wrong because nothing terrible has happened yet.
We tell ourselves that perhaps God is not concerned.
Perhaps He has overlooked it.
Perhaps we can continue living the same way.
But God's patience must never be mistaken for His permission.
The New Testament asks a searching question:
“Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?” — Romans 2:4, KJV
God's kindness is not an invitation to become more comfortable in sin.
It is an invitation to come home.
And sometimes the most frightening spiritual condition is not when a person feels convicted.
It is when a person has practiced ignoring conviction for so long that the warning no longer seems urgent.
Then came the day recorded in 2 Kings 9.
Jehu had been anointed to carry out judgment against the house of Ahab.
He drove toward Jezreel.
King Joram, the son of Ahab and Jezebel, went out to meet him.
When Joram asked whether Jehu came in peace, Jehu answered by referring to the idolatry and sorceries associated with Jezebel.
Joram attempted to flee.
Jehu drew his bow and struck him.
The king died.
Then the news reached Jezebel.
Her son was dead.
Jehu was approaching.
And she knew that the political world she had occupied for years was being violently overturned.
Now listen to how the original Hebrew describes what happened next.
The Hebrew text of 2 Kings 9:30 includes the words:
וַתָּשֶׂם בַּפּוּךְ עֵינֶיהָ
Vattāśem bappūkh ʿênêhā.
The expression describes her applying pūkh to her eyes—an eye cosmetic or pigment used for darkening or adorning them.
The verse continues:
וַתֵּיטֶב אֶת־רֹאשָׁהּ
Vattêṭev ʾet-rōʾšāh.
She attended to or arranged her head, commonly understood as preparing her hair or headdress.
The King James Version describes this as painting her face and tiring, or adorning, her head.
The Hebrew is more specific about her eyes.
But notice what the text does not tell us.
It does not explicitly say that Jezebel was trying to seduce Jehu.
It does not tell us she believed cosmetics could save her.
It does not reveal whether her appearance was intended as royal defiance, political theater, an attempt to maintain dignity, or something else.
Those are possible interpretations, not stated facts.
What Scripture does show is a queen deliberately preparing her appearance before confronting the man who had brought judgment upon her house.
And that image is unforgettable.
A collapsing kingdom.
A palace window.
A queen dressed for confrontation.
And a judgment she could no longer command away.
When Jehu entered the gate, Jezebel called out:
“Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?” — 2 Kings 9:31, KJV
That sentence was no ordinary greeting.
Zimri was a previous Israelite ruler who had assassinated his master and seized the throne, only to reign for seven days before his own downfall.
Jezebel's words were a pointed reference to that bloody history.
She was confronting Jehu with the example of a violent usurper whose reign ended in disaster.
Even in this final confrontation, she spoke as someone who understood the language of power.
But Jehu did not stop to negotiate.
He looked up toward the window and cried:
“Who is on my side? who?” — 2 Kings 9:32, KJV
Two or three eunuchs looked out.
Jehu commanded them to throw her down.
And they did.
The biblical account is brutal.
Her blood struck the wall and the horses.
Jehu trampled her underfoot.
Later, when he ordered that she be buried because she was a king's daughter, those sent to retrieve her found only her skull, feet, and palms.
The rest had been consumed.
The judgment foretold through Elijah had come to pass.
The queen who had once exercised terrifying influence over Israel was gone.
And the account closes with the fulfillment of the prophetic word.
No royal funeral restored her dignity.
No palace wall protected her.
No title reversed the judgment.
But please understand something essential.
The Bible is not teaching that wearing makeup is sinful, that beautiful women are dangerous, or that women who exercise influence deserve suspicion.
Jezebel was judged for her idolatry, persecution, injustice, and participation in the evil of Ahab's house.
Not for wearing eye cosmetics.
And the violence in this account is a specific episode of judgment within Israel's history—not permission for believers to threaten, humiliate, or harm people whom they consider sinful.
Christians are not called to imitate Jehu's violence.
We are called to follow Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because when we turn Jezebel's story into a shallow warning about lipstick, clothing, or feminine appearance, we can miss the far more serious warning Scripture is placing before us.
The question is not whether your eyes are painted.
The question is whether your heart is surrendered.
And that question belongs to every one of us.
The successful businessman who has built an empire but lost his integrity.
The church leader who knows how to preach repentance but struggles to confess his own wrongdoing.
The husband who can quote Scripture publicly while speaking cruelly to his wife privately.
The wife who appears gracious to everyone else but carries resentment she refuses to confront.
The young person who has learned how to look spiritually alive online while feeling increasingly distant from God.
The believer who has not prayed honestly in months but still knows exactly what to say when someone asks, “How are you doing spiritually?”
Perhaps you have become very good at arranging the outside while something inside is falling apart.
You still smile.
You still post encouraging verses.
You still attend worship.
You still tell people that God is good.
And He is.
But somewhere beneath the appearance, there is a wound you have been hiding.
A habit you have been defending.
A compromise you have been explaining away.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from obedience.
A bitterness you have allowed to become part of your identity.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is not the sin itself.
It is the constant effort required to pretend that nothing is wrong.
Jezebel's final appearance at the window should make us ask a difficult question.
What am I still trying to make look beautiful when God is asking me to make it right?
That question is not meant to condemn the brokenhearted.
It is meant to awaken the heart that has stopped listening.
Because there is an enormous difference between someone struggling against sin and someone who has decided to make peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and refusing to rise.
Between confessing weakness and celebrating rebellion.
Between crying out, “Lord, help me,” and insisting, “Lord, leave this part of my life alone.”
And here is where the story takes a turn that every wounded soul needs to hear.
Jezebel's story shows us the terrible reality of judgment.
But it is not the only story Scripture tells.
There is another woman in the Bible whose life was marked by shame and moral failure.
A woman who had lived through broken relationships.
A woman who came to a well at noon and encountered a Jewish man who knew more about her life than she expected.
Jesus.
In John 4, He spoke with a Samaritan woman who had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband.
Jesus did not pretend her circumstances were different from what they were.
He told the truth.
But He did not treat her as disposable.
He offered her living water.
And the woman who came to draw ordinary water left speaking to others about the One who knew her life.
Her encounter became a witness that drew people toward Christ.
Now be careful not to force these two women into an artificial comparison.
Jezebel and the Samaritan woman lived in very different circumstances, and Scripture does not present them as direct opposites.
But their stories help us see two truths that must remain together.
God takes sin seriously.
And Jesus offers grace to sinners.
That is not a contradiction.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Because if all we hear from Jezebel's story is that wicked people deserve judgment, we have not yet arrived at the good news.
The good news begins to shine when we realize that none of us can stand before a holy God on the strength of our own righteousness.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Not merely notorious queens.
Not merely corrupt rulers.
Not merely the people whose sins have become public scandals.
All.
The religious.
The respectable.
The ashamed.
The successful.
The broken.
The person who appears to have everything together.
And the person reading this with tears forming because something in these words has exposed a battle no one else knows about.
But the Gospel does not leave us standing beneath the weight of our guilt.
Jesus Christ entered our world.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed the broken without approving their sin.
He confronted hypocrisy without abandoning compassion.
He bore our sins in His body on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The cross reveals the seriousness of sin and the astonishing depth of God's love.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse evil.
He gave Himself as the sacrifice through which sinners can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
And this is why the Gospel is so much greater than a motivational message about starting over.
It is not merely about becoming a better version of yourself.
It is about being reconciled to the God from whom sin has separated you.
It is about receiving mercy you could never purchase.
Forgiveness you could never earn.
A new life you could never manufacture through appearances.
The Greek New Testament uses a beautiful word in Ephesians 2:8:
χάριτί — chariti
It is a form of χάρις — charis, meaning grace.
The verse declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8, KJV
Grace.
Not royal influence.
Not public admiration.
Not religious performance.
Not the number of people who applaud you.
Not how beautifully you can conceal your failures.
Grace.
Not one.
We support Gospel ministry because Christ has shown us mercy—not because we can purchase His favor.
That distinction must never be lost.
There is another Greek word that brings this message even closer to home.
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite
It is the command to repent, found in Mark 1:15.
Jesus proclaimed:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered your wrongdoing.
It is not simply crying because your choices have become painful.
It is a turning of the heart and life toward God, involving a change of mind that bears fruit in changed conduct.
It is abandoning the lie that sin can give us what only God can provide.
It is bringing into the light what we have spent years trying to hide.
And it is trusting Jesus Christ rather than our own righteousness.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some of us are not standing at Jezebel's window, but we are standing at the edge of decisions that could change our lives.
We know we need to forgive.
But pride keeps whispering, “Not yet.”
We know we need to confess.
But fear says, “What will people think?”
We know we need to leave the sin behind.
But desire says, “Just one more time.”
We know we need to return to prayer.
But shame says, “After everything you've done, how could God welcome you?”
Listen carefully.
Shame is not the voice you must obey.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance, and His invitation is real.
In John 6:37, He says:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
Read that again.
The One who knows your hidden failures is the One who invites you to come.
Not after you have made yourself impressive.
Not after you have convinced everyone that your life is perfect.
Come to Him.
With the truth.
With the tears.
With the consequences you cannot undo.
With the memories you wish you could erase.
With the sins you need to confess and forsake.
Come in repentance and faith.
And do not confuse coming to Jesus with escaping every earthly consequence.
Forgiveness does not erase the responsibility to make restitution where possible, seek reconciliation where appropriate, or accept accountability for harm done.
But the grace of Christ reaches deeper than your reputation.
And the power of His resurrection is greater than the life you have ruined through your own choices.
That is why 2 Corinthians 5:17 is so precious:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
Notice those words.
In Christ.
Not merely in a better environment.
Not merely in a new relationship.
Not merely in a religious community.
In Christ.
The transformation begins with belonging to Him.
And that is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because sin is imaginary.
Not because judgment is unimportant.
Not because every earthly story receives a comfortable ending.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem sinners, forgive the repentant, restore the fallen, and make all things new in those who belong to Him.
We must also remember that Scripture never records Jezebel repenting in her final moments.
We should not invent a hidden prayer or a secret conversion the biblical text does not reveal.
Her account ends in judgment.
And that makes the warning all the more serious.
The invitation to repent is precious precisely because we are not promised tomorrow.
You may have years ahead of you.
Or you may have far less time than you imagine.
None of us knows.
But you are reading these words now.
And while you have breath, do not treat the call of Christ as something that can safely be postponed forever.
There is no need to make yourself presentable before coming to the Savior.
He already knows.
He knows what happened when no one was watching.
He knows the promises you broke.
He knows the prayers you stopped praying.
He knows the people you hurt.
He knows the grief you carry.
He knows the difference between the image you present and the person you are when the room is empty.
And still the Gospel calls you to repent and believe.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to protect a reputation that is slowly suffocating your soul.
Perhaps you have been so busy defending yourself that you have forgotten how to humble yourself.
Perhaps you are exhausted from living two lives.
One for the world.
One behind closed doors.
And deep down, you are longing to stop pretending.
You do not need another mask.
You need the mercy of Jesus.
You do not need another carefully arranged appearance.
You need a heart surrendered to Christ.
You do not need to become famous for your faith.
You need to become faithful to the One who gave His life for you.
And if this story has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.
If God has already begun restoring something you thought was beyond repair, share a little of your testimony.
Someone else may need to know that they are not the only person learning how to return to Jesus.

And if your struggle is too private for a public comment, you do not need to expose intimate details to strangers. Bring it before God, and consider speaking with a trustworthy, mature Christian who can walk with you.
Faith is not a performance for an audience.
It is a life lived before the Lord.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with shocking Bible stories and then leave them spiritually hungry.
Not to build an audience around fear.
But to keep pointing people back to Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
There are people who will never walk into a church building this week but may encounter a biblical message while scrolling through Facebook.
A father silently battling guilt.
A mother wondering whether God still hears her prayers.
A young person questioning whether life has any meaning.
A believer who has grown spiritually cold.
A wounded soul who has begun to believe that their past has disqualified them from ever being loved again.
One article cannot replace the church, pastoral care, or a personal relationship with Christ.
But it can point someone toward the Savior.
And that is why sharing this message matters.
Not merely to increase its reach.
But because someone among your friends may be carrying a question they have never dared to ask.
Someone may need the reminder that judgment is real, repentance matters, and grace is still available through Jesus Christ.
We also want to invite you into something deeper than reading an occasional article.
These resources are intended to help you study Scripture, strengthen your prayer life, understand the Gospel, and keep growing when the emotional impact of a single article has faded.
Because lasting discipleship requires more than one powerful moment.
It requires truth that is revisited.
Prayer that becomes a habit.
Repentance that bears fruit.
Fellowship that provides encouragement and accountability.
And daily dependence upon Jesus.
Think of it as an opportunity for regular Christian generosity—an expression of gratitude and partnership in spreading biblical truth.
Some believers may choose to give from the portion of their budget they set aside for Christian ministry, while others may regard it as an additional offering.
And it is certainly not a payment for God's blessing.
You can glorify Him through obedience, prayer, generosity, service, faithfulness, and love.
These products are not the reason to give.
They are simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who choose to stand with the ministry.
The greater purpose is to help people encounter biblical truth and continue growing in Christ.
You are not less valuable to this community.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your faithful sharing of Scripture matters.
Your commitment to Jesus matters.
No one should ever feel pressured to give money they need for essential responsibilities or believe that God's love depends on a financial contribution.
We are saved by grace through faith.
And we serve because we have been loved.
Before you leave this article, I want to bring you back to that window in Jezreel.
The queen.
The painted eyes.
The approaching chariot.
The royal chamber that could no longer protect her.
For years, Jezebel had wielded power over other people's lives.
But there came a moment when power could no longer protect her from judgment.
And somewhere in that terrible account is a warning for every human heart.
Do not wait until everything is falling apart before you begin to take God's Word seriously.
Do not spend your whole life protecting an appearance while neglecting your soul.
Do not mistake the silence of delayed judgment for the absence of a holy God.
And do not imagine that the sins you have hidden from other people are hidden from Him.
But neither should you believe that your past is more powerful than the cross of Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not merely a warning that sinners will face judgment.
It is the announcement that the Son of God has died and risen so that sinners who repent and believe may receive forgiveness and eternal life.
Jezebel's story ends with a fallen queen.
But your story does not have to end with an unrepentant heart.
You can turn to Christ today.
You can tell the truth today.
You can confess what you have concealed.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can begin making right what you have made wrong.
You can stop treating your spiritual life as something to decorate and begin surrendering it to the Lord who sees beneath every surface.
Not because you are strong enough to save yourself.
But because Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior.
If the Lord exposed everything I have been hiding, would I run toward Him in repentance—or would I reach for another mask?
Take that question into prayer.
Let it search you.
Let it humble you.
And let it lead you to the cross.
Because the greatest tragedy is not having a past filled with scandal.
The greatest tragedy is refusing the grace that calls you to repentance and offers you a new life in Jesus Christ.
Jezebel prepared her eyes to face the man approaching her palace. Today, let your heart be prepared to meet the Savior who calls you to come into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “EVERYONE DID WHAT WAS RIGHT IN HIS OWN EYES”—THE BIBLE’S CIVIL WAR THAT ENDED WITH A SENTENCE MORE TERRIFYING THAN THE BLOODSHED
paragraphs: “EVERYONE DID WHAT WAS RIGHT IN HIS OWN EYES”—THE BIBLE’S CIVIL WAR THAT ENDED WITH A SENTENCE MORE TERRIFYING THAN THE BLOODSHED
When an entire nation called its own desires righteousness, the innocent paid the price. And the final verse of Judges exposes a danger that still lives inside the human heart today.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Not because it describes a demon.
Not because it announces a plague.
Not even because it speaks of an invading army.
But because it describes ordinary people who had become so convinced of their own righteousness that they could no longer recognize how far they had wandered from God.

And by the time that sentence appeared, a woman had been brutally abused and killed, a nation had descended into civil war, tens of thousands had died, cities had been destroyed, and hundreds of women had been treated as possessions to solve a political crisis.
The people responsible were not strangers to the name of God.
They were Israel.
The covenant people.
The people who had witnessed divine deliverance, received God's commandments, and inherited a land they could never have conquered without His mercy.
And yet the book of Judges closes with these chilling words:
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.” — Judges 21:25, KJV
Read that again.
Not everyone did what they knew was evil.
Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
That is what makes this verse so frightening.
Because the most dangerous spiritual blindness is not always the person who knows he is rebelling against God.
Sometimes it is the person who has convinced himself that God agrees with him.
And before we condemn ancient Israel, there is a question we must be brave enough to ask.
What if the same sentence could be written about us?
What if we have become so accustomed to defending our choices, excusing our compromises, and protecting our reputations that we have forgotten how to tremble before the Word of God?
What if the greatest danger to our souls is not that we have stopped believing in God, but that we have started believing our own opinions are as authoritative as His voice?
Stay with this story.
Because its ending is not merely about a nation that lost its way.
It is about the kind of Savior a lost world desperately needs.
And perhaps, somewhere in the ruins of this ancient tragedy, you will recognize something you have been trying not to see in yourself.
The Hebrew of Judges 21:25 reads:
בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
Bayyamim hahem ein melekh beYisra'el; ish hayyashar be'enav ya'aseh.
A close translation is:
“In those days there was no king in Israel; each person would do what was right in his own eyes.”
The word הַיָּשָׁר (hayyashar) comes from a Hebrew root associated with what is straight, upright, or right.
The expression בְּעֵינָיו (be'enav) means “in his eyes.”
And the closing verb, יַעֲשֶׂה (ya'aseh), expresses the action of doing.
Notice the contrast.
The issue is not simply that people acted.
It is that their own perception had become the standard by which their actions were judged.
Their eyes had become their courtroom.
Their desires had become their witnesses.
Their opinions had become their verdict.
But Scripture had already warned Israel against this very condition.
Deuteronomy 12:8 says:
“Ye shall not do after all the things that we do here this day, every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes.”
The tragedy of Judges is that Israel eventually became the very people God had warned them not to become.
And it did not happen overnight.
Spiritual collapse rarely does.
It happens when one compromise becomes acceptable.
When one act of disobedience is explained away.
When one generation stops teaching the next generation why God's commands matter.
When worship becomes a cultural identity instead of a surrendered life.
When people still speak God's name but increasingly refuse His authority.
Judges 2:10 describes a generation that arose after Joshua, one that did not know the LORD or the works He had done for Israel.
That does not necessarily mean every person had never heard God's name.
It reveals a devastating failure of covenant faithfulness and spiritual continuity.
The stories of God's mighty works had not produced a faithful generation.
And by the closing chapters of Judges, the consequences were horrifying.
In Judges 19, a Levite traveled with his concubine, a woman whose status in that ancient society left her especially vulnerable.
They arrived in Gibeah, a town belonging to Benjamin, one of Israel's own tribes.
What happened that night should never be softened into a comfortable religious illustration.
A mob surrounded the house where they were staying and demanded that the male guest be brought outside for sexual abuse.
The host proposed offering women instead.
Eventually, the Levite sent his concubine outside.
She was sexually assaulted through the night.
At daybreak, she collapsed at the doorway.
The text then describes the Levite finding her, placing her on his donkey, and taking her home. He subsequently dismembered her body into twelve pieces and sent them throughout Israel.
Judges 19 does not explicitly establish the precise moment of her death, but the account presents an appalling sequence of violence, betrayal, and dehumanization.
And here is something that must not be overlooked.
The Bible records what happened.
It does not command us to admire what happened.
The narrative exposes the moral disintegration of Israel. It does not present the Levite, the host, or the attackers as models of godly conduct.
The woman had almost no voice in the story.
Men made decisions.
Men defended their honor.
Men invoked the outrage of the nation.
And a woman bore the consequences of their wickedness.
That should trouble us.
Because whenever human beings become more concerned about preserving their image than protecting the vulnerable, something has gone terribly wrong.
And whenever religion is used to excuse cruelty, we are not witnessing holiness.
We are witnessing the corruption of something sacred.
The Levite's gruesome message stirred the tribes of Israel.
They assembled and demanded justice.
Benjamin refused to surrender the guilty men of Gibeah.
And what began as a demand for accountability became a civil war.
Brother fought brother.
Israelite fought Israelite.
The nation that should have stood united in covenant faithfulness turned its weapons against itself.

Judges 20 records catastrophic losses. Tens of thousands of fighting men died, including approximately forty thousand Israelites in the first two days of battle and twenty-five thousand Benjamite warriors in the subsequent defeat.
The victorious Israelites then attacked Benjamite towns, killing inhabitants and livestock and burning cities.
Only six hundred Benjamite men escaped to the rock of Rimmon.
Imagine the silence afterward.
Homes without fathers.
Families without sons.
Cities reduced to ashes.
A people who had sought to confront wickedness now standing amid the devastation of their own nation.
And then came another tragedy.
Israel realized that Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes, was facing near extinction.
But the Israelites had previously sworn not to give their daughters in marriage to Benjamite men.
Instead of humbly confronting the disastrous consequences of their decisions, they searched for a way around their oath.
They attacked Jabesh-gilead because its inhabitants had not attended the national assembly, and they brought back four hundred young women for the surviving Benjamites.
When that was not enough, they instructed the remaining men to seize young women during a festival at Shiloh.
Read Judges 21:10–23 for yourself.
It is disturbing.
And it is meant to be disturbing.
The chapter shows a community so entangled in violence, rash vows, and moral confusion that its proposed solutions perpetuated the suffering of innocent people.
The narrative does not portray the seizure of women as God's ideal for marriage.
It reveals how deeply the nation's judgment had deteriorated.
And after all of it—after the abuse, the murder, the civil war, the slaughter, and the abductions—the book ends.
No triumphant celebration.
No comforting declaration that everything had finally been repaired.
Just that terrible diagnosis.
“Every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
The sentence lands like a door closing on a darkened room.
And now comes the uncomfortable part.
Because we cannot read Judges faithfully if we only point at the ancient Israelites and say, “How could they?”
We must also ask, “Lord, where have I begun to resemble them?”
Perhaps you have never committed the terrible acts described in these chapters.
But have you ever defended something simply because admitting you were wrong would cost you your pride?
Have you ever hurt someone and spent more time explaining your intentions than acknowledging their pain?
Have you ever called something a blessing because you wanted it badly, even while knowing it required disobedience?
Have you ever used a Bible verse to win an argument while refusing to let that same Bible correct your heart?
Have you ever asked God to approve a decision you had already made?
That last question may be the one that hurts.
Because sometimes we do not actually want God's guidance.
We want His endorsement.
We want heaven to sign beneath choices our flesh has already approved.
And when Scripture challenges us, we become defensive.
When a faithful friend corrects us, we become offended.
When conviction interrupts our plans, we call it negativity.
We begin to confuse peace with comfort, freedom with self-rule, and grace with permission.
But grace was never given to make rebellion feel safe.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains believers to reject ungodliness and live righteous, godly lives.
Real grace does not merely comfort us while we remain enslaved to sin.
It teaches us to turn away from what is destroying us.
This is why the repeated statement about Israel having no king matters so much.
Judges 17:6, 18:1, 19:1, and 21:25 all draw attention to the absence of a king.
In its historical and literary setting, this refrain points toward Israel's need for righteous leadership and prepares readers for the monarchy that follows in the biblical story.
But we must be careful.
The Bible does not teach that simply placing a human king on a throne would cure the human heart.
Israel would eventually have kings.
Some would lead faithfully.
Many would lead the people into even greater wickedness.
And in 1 Samuel 8:7, when Israel demanded a king like the surrounding nations, the LORD told Samuel that the people had rejected Him from reigning over them.
So the deepest problem was never merely the absence of a political ruler.
It was the absence of faithful submission to the LORD.
And that is where this dark story begins pointing us toward something greater.
Someone greater.
A King who would not exploit the vulnerable.
A King who would not preserve His reputation by sacrificing the innocent.
A King who would not demand that others bleed to protect His pride.
A King who would come into a broken world and willingly shed His own blood to redeem sinners.
Jesus Christ.
Think about the contrast.
In Judges 19, a vulnerable woman is handed over to violent men while those responsible for her protection fail her.
In the Gospel, Jesus willingly gives Himself for His people.
The first is a horrifying act of human betrayal.
The second is the voluntary, saving sacrifice of the sinless Son of God.
They are not morally equivalent events.
And Scripture does not explicitly identify the woman in Judges 19 as a prophetic symbol of Christ.
But reading these passages together reveals a profound moral contrast between sinful human leadership and the self-giving love of the true King.
Jesus says in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
Human sin abandons the vulnerable.
The Good Shepherd lays down His life.
Human pride sacrifices others to preserve itself.
Christ humbles Himself in obedience to the Father, even unto death on the cross.
Human kingdoms are stained by the failures of their rulers.
Christ's kingdom rests upon the righteousness of a King who never sinned.
And suddenly the question becomes more personal than political.
Who is ruling your heart?
Not whose name appears in your social media biography.
Not what denomination you attend.
Who actually has the final authority when God's Word contradicts what you want?
Because it is possible to call Jesus “Lord” while resisting His lordship.
Jesus Himself asked in Luke 6:46:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
That question has not lost its power.
It still reaches into our marriages.
Our private conversations.
Our finances.
Our sexual choices.
Our resentments.
Our hidden habits.
Our treatment of people who cannot repay us.
Our willingness to tell the truth when lying would be easier.
Our response when someone exposes our wrongdoing.
And perhaps the most revealing place of all: the secret life no one sees.
Because the real test of surrender is often what we choose when nobody is watching.
You may have spent years building a Christian appearance while quietly protecting something Christ has been calling you to surrender.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from obedience.
A bitterness you have rehearsed so often that it now feels like justice.
A secret habit you keep promising to abandon tomorrow.
An apology you refuse to make because you believe the other person should apologize first.
A pattern of dishonesty you have renamed survival.
A form of pride you have mistaken for strength.
And maybe this article is uncomfortable because you recognize the pattern.
Not the atrocities of Judges.
But the instinct beneath them.
The instinct to place ourselves at the center of moral authority.
To say, “I know what God says, but in my situation…”
And then finish the sentence with whatever we have already decided to do.
Friend, that is a dangerous place to live.
Not because Jesus is unwilling to forgive you.
But because self-deception can make a person unwilling to seek forgiveness.
The greatest danger is not discovering that you have sinned.
The greatest danger is becoming so committed to defending your sin that you no longer want to be rescued from it.
Yet this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus did not enter the world to save people who had successfully made themselves righteous.
He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we cleaned up every hidden failure.
Not after we repaired every damaged relationship.
Not after we finally became impressive enough for heaven.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death and sin do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
But do not misunderstand this mercy.
Forgiveness is not a license to continue destroying yourself and others.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad because you were exposed.
It is turning toward God, acknowledging sin for what it is, and entrusting yourself to Jesus Christ.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, a term associated with a change of mind and, in biblical context, a turning toward God that bears fruit in life.
It is not merely emotional regret.
It is a reorientation of the person before God.
And the Greek word χάρις (charis), commonly translated “grace,” reminds us that salvation is God's undeserved favor, not a reward we purchase through religious performance.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
That is why your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Not because your sin was small.
Not because your excuses were convincing.
Not because your good deeds outweighed your failures.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
And there is a beautiful contrast between the final verse of Judges and the message of the Gospel.
Judges ends with everyone doing what was right in their own eyes.
Jesus calls His disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him.
The first way enthrones the self.
The second submits the self to Christ.
The first asks, “What seems right to me?”
The second asks, “Lord, what would You have me do?”
The first protects pride.
The second learns humility.
The first can leave wounded people behind while claiming righteousness.
The second calls us to love our neighbors, seek justice, show mercy, and walk faithfully before God.
And none of that means Christians become perfect overnight.
We still struggle.
We still need correction.
We still confess.
We still depend upon mercy.
But the direction of our lives changes because the One who saved us is also the One who leads us.
Perhaps you are reading this after making a decision you deeply regret.
Perhaps someone trusted you, and you betrayed that trust.
Perhaps you have been hiding behind spiritual language while knowing that something in your life is terribly wrong.
Perhaps you are not the person who caused the harm.
Perhaps you are the one who was harmed.
Then hear this carefully.
The atrocities recorded in Judges do not mean God approves of abuse, coercion, or the destruction of vulnerable people.
And if someone has used religion to pressure you into silence about abuse, that misuse of Scripture does not represent the heart of Jesus Christ.
Seeking safety, telling the truth, and obtaining appropriate help are not betrayals of faith.
The God who sees what human beings conceal is not fooled by religious appearances.
And the Gospel never requires victims to pretend that evil was good.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
He also calls His people to defend the vulnerable and practice justice.
Isaiah 1:17 says:
“Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.”
Biblical holiness is not measured by how loudly we condemn the world while ignoring the wounded at our doorstep.
It is revealed in obedience to God, including how we treat people who have no power to defend themselves.
That is one of the reasons this ancient story still matters.
It forces us to confront the possibility that religious communities can become deeply corrupted when loyalty to a group replaces loyalty to truth.
When protecting an institution matters more than protecting people.
When a leader's reputation becomes more important than repentance.
When a community calls accountability persecution.
When we condemn the sins of outsiders while making excuses for the sins of our own.
And when we begin to believe that being on the right side of an argument automatically means our hearts are right before God.
Judges refuses to let us become comfortable with that illusion.
It shows us a nation where people could recognize wickedness in others while repeatedly failing to confront the disorder within themselves.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
Maybe the verse that closes Judges is not merely describing ancient Israel.
Maybe it is holding up a mirror.
And perhaps the most merciful thing God can do for us today is allow that mirror to expose what we would rather keep hidden.
Because what is exposed can be confessed.
What is confessed can be brought before Christ.
And what is surrendered to Him can become the beginning of a changed life.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That does not erase earthly consequences or remove our responsibility to make things right where possible.
But it means guilt does not have to become your permanent identity.
Shame does not have to become your master.
Your past does not have to become the throne from which your future is ruled.
Jesus Christ is a better King.
And He does not merely offer better advice.
He offers redemption.
So perhaps tonight you need to stop explaining.
Stop rehearsing the reasons.
Stop comparing your sin to someone else's.
Stop saying, “At least I am not as bad as…”
And simply come before God.
No performance.
No religious mask.
No carefully edited testimony.
Just the truth.

“Lord Jesus, I have been doing what was right in my own eyes. I have defended what You were calling me to surrender. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. I cannot save myself. I trust in Your death and resurrection. Be Lord over the parts of my life I have tried to keep for myself. Amen.”
You do not need to make that prayer impressive.
You need to mean what you say.
And if you have already trusted Christ but have wandered into compromise, return to Him.
Do not let yesterday's failure become tomorrow's excuse.
Repentance is not the enemy of joy.
It is the path back toward fellowship with the God whose mercy you need.
There is one more thing I want you to consider.
Someone in your life may be living through a spiritual civil war right now.
Outwardly, they look fine.
They go to work.
They laugh in photographs.
They answer messages.
They post Scripture.
But inside, they are exhausted from trying to rule a life they were never meant to rule apart from God.
They know something is wrong.
They just do not know how to come home.
Perhaps this article could become the beginning of a conversation they have been afraid to start.
Not because it is comfortable.
But because there may come a day when you need to read Judges 21:25 again and remember that sincerity alone does not make a choice righteous.
God's Word must correct our eyes.
Where has God been teaching you to surrender your own understanding and trust His Word?
Maybe your answer is “I am still fighting.”
Maybe it is “Pray for me.”
Maybe it is “Jesus, forgive me.”
Or perhaps you have a testimony of how Christ brought you out of a season when you insisted on doing everything your own way.
You do not have to disclose private wounds or details you are not ready to share.
But your honest words may encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
Not as a formula for receiving salvation.
Not as a public performance.
But as a simple expression of the surrender you desire to live.
Because the Christian life was never meant to be sustained by one emotional moment.
We need the Word.
We need prayer.
We need sound teaching.
We need fellowship and accountability.
We need to keep returning to the cross and remembering whose righteousness saves us.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not merely producing content people will read today and forget tomorrow, but helping people encounter biblical truth that calls them toward lasting discipleship in Jesus Christ.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life of loving obedience—not by purchasing access to a ministry.
Those resources and products are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
There is no price attached to the grace of God.
Jesus has already paid the cost of our redemption through His finished work.
Our desire is simply to make Him known.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the final scene of Judges.
The smoke has settled.
The armies are gone.
Families have been shattered.
The vulnerable have suffered.
The nation has survived, but it is deeply wounded.
And the writer leaves us with that haunting sentence:
“Every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
For generations, humanity has repeated that tragedy in countless forms.
We have called pride strength.
We have called selfishness freedom.
We have called compromise wisdom.
We have called revenge justice.
We have called our preferences truth.
And we have sometimes called Jesus Lord while refusing to let Him rule.
But the Bible does not end in Judges.
The story moves forward.
Through the failures of kings.
Through the warnings of prophets.
Through exile, sorrow, and promises of restoration.
Until, in the fullness of time, a Child is born.
A Son is given.
And the King we could never produce through our own righteousness enters the world.
He touches the unclean.
He welcomes repentant sinners.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He defends the truth.
He goes to the cross.
He rises from the dead.
And He calls us to follow Him.
Not because we have always done what was right.
But because He alone is righteous.
Not because we deserve His kingdom.
But because His grace opens the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
The final word over the believer is not self-rule.
It is the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that is the hope we carry.
Not that human beings will finally become wise enough to save themselves.
But that the crucified and risen King is able to redeem those who turn to Him in faith.
So when you close this article, do not merely ask whether the ancient Israelites were wrong.
Ask whether Jesus truly has your heart.
Because you can win every argument, protect every excuse, and get everything you wanted—and still lose your way.
The most frightening place to be is not at the end of your strength, but at the center of your own throne, never realizing that the King who could save you is the One you keep refusing to obey.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE SENT EVERYONE OUT OF THE ROOM… THEN TURNED TOWARD A DEAD WOMAN AND SPOKE SIX WORDS THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING.
paragraphs: HE SENT EVERYONE OUT OF THE ROOM… THEN TURNED TOWARD A DEAD WOMAN AND SPOKE SIX WORDS THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING.

Why did Peter remove the mourners before raising Tabitha from the dead? The answer in Acts 9:36–42 reveals something extraordinary about prayer, the authority of Jesus Christ, the people the world overlooks, and the God who still sees you when everyone else thinks your story is over.
There was a dead woman upstairs.

Her friends were crying. Her body had already been washed and prepared. The people who loved her were holding the clothes she had made, as though touching something her hands had touched might somehow make losing her less unbearable.
And then Peter arrived.
He walked into a room filled with grief, saw the evidence of a beautiful life that had suddenly ended, and did something that must have seemed almost unthinkable.
He sent everyone outside.
Not just the loud ones. Not just the doubters. Not just those who could not stop crying.
Everyone.
Then he knelt down.
And prayed.
What happened next would shake an entire city.
But before we reach the miracle, there is something about this story that might reach into a place in your own heart you have been trying desperately to keep hidden.
Because sometimes the most painful part of your story is not what happened to you.
It is the fear that what happened has become the final word about you.

The marriage that collapsed. The child who walked away from God. The diagnosis that changed everything. The ministry that fell apart. The prayer you whispered until you grew tired of hearing your own voice.
And somewhere along the way, you began to wonder whether heaven had gone silent.
If you have ever stood beside something you loved and wondered whether it was too late, stay with this story.
But we must understand it as Scripture actually tells it, not as we might wish it to be.
Because the real miracle is already powerful enough.
In Acts 9:36, Luke introduces a disciple living in Joppa.
Her name was Tabitha.
In Greek, she was called Dorcas.
The name Tabitha comes from the Aramaic טביתא (Ṭabīṯā), meaning gazelle. The Greek Δορκάς (Dorkás) carries the same meaning.
Two names. Two languages. One extraordinary woman.
But Luke does not introduce her by mentioning her beauty, wealth, popularity, or influence.
He introduces her by describing how she lived.
The Greek text says:
αὕτη ἦν πλήρης ἔργων ἀγαθῶν καὶ ἐλεημοσυνῶν
Hautē ēn plērēs ergōn agathōn kai eleēmosynōn.
She was “full of good works and acts of charity” (Acts 9:36, ESV).
Notice that word.
Full.
Not occasionally kind when it was convenient.
Not generous only when someone important was watching.
Her life overflowed with practical expressions of compassion.
Tabitha made garments. She helped people in need. She used what she had to serve others.
And Scripture calls her a disciple.
The Greek word is μαθήτρια (mathētria), the feminine form of disciple. This is the only occurrence of this feminine noun in the New Testament.
Before Luke tells us about the extraordinary miracle that happened to Tabitha, he tells us about the ordinary faithfulness that characterized her life.
There is something beautiful about that.
She was not introduced as a woman who preached to thousands.
She was a woman whose faith could be seen in the things she made for people who needed them.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that.
You may never stand behind a pulpit.
You may never have a famous name.
You may spend your days cooking meals, working long hours, raising children, caring for aging parents, giving quietly, or encouraging people who never tell anyone what you did for them.
But a life surrendered to Jesus Christ is not insignificant simply because the world does not applaud it.
The kingdom of God has never measured faithfulness by the size of an audience.
Jesus said that even giving a cup of cold water in His name would not go unnoticed (Matthew 10:42).
And Tabitha's story reminds us that the Lord sees what the world overlooks.
Then, without warning, the story changes.
Acts 9:37 tells us that she became ill and died.
There is no explanation of the disease.
No account of her final conversation.
No suggestion that her death resulted from some hidden sin.
Only the devastating reality that a faithful disciple of Jesus became sick and died.
Being faithful to Christ did not make Tabitha immune to suffering.
Please do not miss that.
Some believers have been wounded by the suggestion that enough faith will prevent tragedy, illness, disappointment, or loss.
But the Bible never promises that genuine discipleship will remove every sorrow from our earthly lives.
Tabitha was full of good works.
And Tabitha died.
Those two truths appear in the same passage.
Faithfulness is not a guarantee that we will never enter the valley.
It is a reason to trust the Shepherd who walks with His people through it.
The believers washed her body and laid her in an upper room.
And then the widows gathered.
Can you imagine that room?
The silence between the sobs.
The trembling hands.
The unbearable sight of someone who had always been there, now lying motionless.
When Peter arrived, the widows stood around him weeping.
And they showed him the tunics and other garments Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Those clothes were more than fabric.
They were evidence of love.
A sleeve stitched for someone who could not afford a new garment.
A piece of clothing that had offered warmth and dignity.
A reminder that someone had noticed their need.
The widows were not merely telling Peter that Tabitha had been a good person.
They were showing him what her absence meant.
And suddenly, the story becomes painfully personal.
Because almost everyone knows what it means to hold something that reminds them of someone they miss.
A photograph.
An old message.
A favorite shirt.
A handwritten note.
A Bible with familiar handwriting in the margins.
Ordinary things become precious when the person connected to them is gone.
And sometimes we discover how deeply someone loved us only when we begin counting all the quiet ways they showed it.
But here is where the passage takes its remarkable turn.
Acts 9:40 says:
ἐκβαλὼν δὲ ἔξω πάντας ὁ Πέτρος
Ekbalōn de exō pantas ho Petros.
“But Peter put them all outside” (ESV).
Why?
Why would Peter send grieving people out of the room when they had already suffered so much?
Was he offended by their tears?
Was their grief somehow preventing the miracle?
Were they lacking enough faith?
The text does not say any of those things.
And we must be careful not to turn an assumption into a doctrine.
Luke does not explicitly tell us Peter's reason for removing everyone.
But Scripture gives us an important connection.
Years earlier, Peter had watched Jesus enter another room where a young girl lay dead.
The girl's name is not recorded, but her father was Jairus.
In Mark 5:35–43, Jesus arrived at Jairus's house amid weeping and commotion.
He put the crowd outside, took the girl's parents and three disciples with Him, and entered the place where she lay.
Then Jesus took her by the hand and said:
Ταλιθὰ κούμ
Talitha koum.
Mark preserves these words in Aramaic and explains their meaning:
“Little girl, I say to you, arise” (Mark 5:41, ESV).
And the girl got up.
Now consider what Peter does in Acts 9.
He removes the people from the room.
He turns toward the body.
And he says:
Ταβιθά, ἀνάστηθι
Tabitha, anastēthi.
“Tabitha, arise” (Acts 9:40, ESV).
Do you see the extraordinary resemblance?
Jesus said, “Talitha koum.”
Peter said, “Tabitha, arise.”

The words are not identical, and the New Testament records Peter's command in Greek rather than preserving an Aramaic command. We should not claim that Peter spoke a particular Aramaic phrase when Luke does not tell us that.
But the resemblance between these two resurrection accounts is unmistakable.
Peter had witnessed Jesus raise Jairus's daughter.
Now Peter stands in a room where another beloved person lies dead.
And his actions closely resemble what he had seen his Master do.
Yet there is one crucial difference.
Peter kneels down and prays.
Read that again.
Peter does not walk into the room behaving as though resurrection power belongs to him.
He does not command the mourners to create a certain atmosphere.
He does not announce that his spiritual greatness will produce a miracle.
He kneels.
And he prays.
Before he speaks to Tabitha, he speaks to God.
Before he gives a command, he depends upon the Lord.
This is the detail that changes how we understand the entire scene.
Peter was an apostle, but he was not the source of life.
Jesus Christ was.
The same Peter who had once denied knowing Jesus was now being used by the risen Lord to bear witness to His power.
The same Peter who had wept bitterly after his failure was now standing in a place where death itself would be confronted by the power of Christ.
And perhaps that is the deeper scandal of grace.
God was using a man whose past included one of the most painful failures recorded in the Gospels.
Remember Peter's denial?
Three times he denied knowing Jesus.
Three times he distanced himself from the One he had promised never to abandon.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Peter wept bitterly (Luke 22:54–62).
Imagine carrying that memory.
The sound of your own voice saying you did not know the Lord you loved.
The look of Jesus.
The shame.
The regret.
The terrible realization that you had done the very thing you insisted you would never do.
Yet Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
The risen Christ appeared to His disciples, and in John 21, Jesus graciously restored Peter to a life of love and service.
Jesus did not pretend the denial had never happened.
He addressed Peter's love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Grace did not make Peter's sin insignificant.
Grace meant his sin would not have the final word.
And now, in Acts 9, the man who once crumbled under the pressure of a servant girl's question was kneeling before God in a room where everyone else saw only death.
If you have ever wondered whether God can still use someone who has failed Him, look at Peter.
Not because failure is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ is a Savior who restores repentant sinners.
Peter's authority did not come from having a spotless past.
It came from the risen Christ who had called him, forgiven him, and commissioned him.
And that matters for us.
Because some of us have spent years allowing our worst moment to become our permanent identity.
You remember the betrayal.
The addiction.
The compromise.
The secret sin.
The season when you walked away from God.
The people you hurt.
The promises you broke.
And although you may believe Jesus forgives sinners, you struggle to believe His mercy can reach all the way into your own history.
But the Gospel does not announce that we can save ourselves by becoming better people.
It announces that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Our hope is not that we have never fallen.
Our hope is that Christ has risen.
And those who turn to Him in repentance and faith find forgiveness and new life in His name.
That is why Peter's prayer matters so much.
Because this miracle is not a monument to Peter.
It is a testimony to Jesus.
And we need to understand something else about the room.
Peter's decision to send everyone outside was not necessarily a declaration that grieving people were spiritually dangerous.
In fact, Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35).
Tears are not enemies of faith.
Grief is not automatically unbelief.
And suffering Christians should never be made to feel that their sorrow disqualifies them from God's compassion.
The passage does not establish a rule that we must remove certain people from our lives before God can work.
Nor does it teach that the presence of mourners limits divine power.
God is not weakened by human tears.
The connection with Jairus's daughter suggests that Peter may have been following the pattern he had witnessed in Jesus' ministry.
The private setting also allowed him to pray without turning the moment into a public spectacle.
But Luke's emphasis is on what Peter actually did.
He prayed.
Then he turned toward the body and spoke.
“Tabitha, arise.”
And she opened her eyes.
Imagine that moment.
The stillness.
The face that had been motionless.
The eyes that had been closed.
Then movement.
Breath.
Life.
Acts 9:40 tells us that when she saw Peter, she sat up.
Peter gave her his hand and raised her.
Then he called the believers and the widows and presented her alive.
The same widows who had stood there holding the clothes she had made were now looking at the woman who made them.
The same room that had held the terrible weight of death now held the astonishment of restored life.
Can you imagine the tears?
The embraces?
The voices calling her name?
The overwhelming realization that the woman they had prepared for burial was standing before them alive?
And yet, even here, Scripture directs our attention beyond the emotional wonder.
Acts 9:42 says:
καὶ ἐπίστευσαν πολλοὶ ἐπὶ τὸν κύριον
Kai episteusan polloi epi ton kyrion.
“And many believed in the Lord” (ESV).
There it is.
The purpose toward which the miracle points.
Not Peter's popularity.
Not Tabitha becoming a celebrity.
Not the establishment of a formula for raising the dead.
Many believed in the Lord.
The miracle became a witness to Jesus Christ.
This is why the account must never be reduced to a motivational message about removing negative people from your circle.
That might sound appealing.
It might even attract attention.
But it would miss the central testimony of Acts 9.
The risen Jesus was continuing His work through His apostles, and the result was that people turned to the Lord.
Earlier in the same chapter, Peter healed a paralyzed man named Aeneas.
And Peter explicitly declared:
“Jesus Christ heals you” (Acts 9:34, ESV).
That statement helps us understand the raising of Tabitha.
The power belonged to Jesus.
Peter was His servant.
And the glory belonged to the Lord.
Now perhaps you are wondering what this means for your own situation.
Does it mean the person you lost will return to life tomorrow?
Does it mean every illness will be healed if someone prays correctly?
Does it mean your marriage, finances, or circumstances must be restored exactly as you desire?
No.
The Bible does not give us permission to make those promises.
Tabitha's resurrection was an extraordinary act of God, not a guarantee that every Christian will experience the same miracle in this present life.
Even Tabitha, after being restored to earthly life, would eventually face physical death again.
Her resurrection was not yet the final resurrection promised to all who belong to Christ.
It was a sign pointing toward something greater.
Because Jesus Himself said:
“I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25, ESV).
And the Gospel promises a future resurrection in which death will finally be defeated.
The apostle Paul wrote that the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26).
And Revelation 21:4 looks forward to the day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is the Christian hope.
Not that every tragedy will be reversed immediately.
But that the risen Christ has conquered death and will bring His redeemed people into everlasting life.
And until that day, we pray.
We grieve.
We serve.
We persevere.
We trust.
Sometimes God answers in ways that leave us astonished.
Sometimes He sustains us through suffering we would never have chosen.
But His faithfulness is not measured solely by whether our circumstances change.
It is revealed most decisively in Jesus Christ, who loved us and gave Himself for us.
And there is another truth hidden in plain sight within Tabitha's story.
Before the miracle, her life had already been preaching.
Not through spectacular signs.
Through garments.
Through charity.
Through the needs of widows.
Through quiet, consistent acts of love.
What if we have spent so much time asking God to do something extraordinary through us that we have overlooked the ordinary obedience He has placed directly in front of us?
What if someone needs a meal more than they need another impressive speech?
What if someone needs to be visited?
Forgiven?
Encouraged?
Helped?
What if the most powerful evidence of your discipleship this week is not something you post, but something you do when no one is watching?
Tabitha's works did not purchase her salvation.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace saves us.
And grace transforms how we live.
The hands that once served selfish ambition can begin serving others.
The mouth that once spoke bitterness can begin speaking truth with love.
The heart that once resisted God can learn to surrender.
That is the beauty of redemption.
Jesus does not merely offer us a religious label.
He gives us new life.
And new life bears fruit.
Perhaps the most haunting question in this passage is not simply why Peter sent everyone outside.
Perhaps it is this:
If the people around you were asked to describe the evidence of Christ's love in your life, what would they hold up?
The widows held up garments.
Not trophies.
Not titles.
Not evidence of Tabitha's influence.
They held up things that reminded them they had been loved.
What would people remember about us?
Would they remember our arguments more than our compassion?
Our opinions more than our kindness?
Our religious language more than our willingness to help?
Would the people closest to us say that following Jesus made us more loving, more truthful, more humble, more generous?
This is not a question meant to crush a struggling believer.
It is an invitation to examine our hearts before the Lord.
Because repentance is not merely feeling bad about yesterday.
It is turning toward Christ today.
And there is still grace for the person who recognizes how far they have drifted.
Peter knew what it meant to need that grace.
Tabitha showed what a life shaped by that grace could look like.
And Jesus is the reason both stories matter.
If this passage has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Perhaps you have been serving everyone while quietly growing exhausted.
Perhaps you have been attending church while carrying a secret compromise.
Perhaps you have become so discouraged by unanswered prayers that you barely know how to pray anymore.
Or perhaps you have been measuring your worth by how visible, successful, or appreciated you are.
Bring it to Jesus.
Not to perform.
Not to pretend.
Not to impress Him with spiritual language.
Come honestly.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Ask forgiveness where you have sinned.
Ask for strength where you are weak.
Ask for wisdom where you are confused.
And remember that the Savior who restored Peter is not indifferent to broken people who come to Him.
Someone reading silently may need the encouragement that comes from hearing how Christ has sustained another believer.
But please remember this.
The miracle in Joppa did not end with everyone talking about Peter.
