Today, you can take one faithful step.
Not to earn the love of Jesus.
But because His love has reached you in the middle of your need.
And if you have been faithfully sowing through tears, this message is for you too.
Do not assume your obedience is meaningless simply because the results are not visible.
Do not assume God has forgotten your prayers.
Do not measure His faithfulness by the speed of your circumstances changing.
Remember what the psalmist wrote:
"They that sow in tears shall reap in joy."
— Psalm 126:5, KJV
In its original setting, Psalm 126 celebrates the Lord's restoration and expresses hope amid His people's continuing need.
It is not a guarantee that every earthly sorrow will end on our preferred timetable.
It is a testimony to the God who restores, the God whose people can hope in Him even while they weep.
The Hebrew expression הַזֹּרְעִים בְּדִמְעָה — hazzorʿim bedimʿah means "those who sow in tears."
What a picture.
Hands still working.
Eyes still weeping.
Faith still reaching toward God.
Perhaps that is you.
You are exhausted, but you keep praying.
You are grieving, but you keep trusting.
You have been disappointed, but you keep returning to Scripture.
You do not understand the season, but you refuse to abandon the Savior.
Keep your eyes on Christ.
Your tears are not proof that your faith has failed.
And your suffering is not proof that God has stopped loving you.
Now I want to ask you to do something that requires a little courage.
Leave one because it expresses something true.
And if you have experienced the restoring mercy of Christ, consider sharing a brief testimony of what He has done in your life.
You do not need to reveal private details or publicly confess anything that would be wiser to address with a trusted pastor, counselor, or the people directly affected.
But your honest words may encourage another person who feels alone.
Someone may see your testimony and find courage to seek help.
Someone may be reminded that the mercy of Jesus is not a distant theological idea.
It is the hope of real sinners who need a real Savior.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Not to chase attention.
But because someone in your circle may desperately need to understand that their choices matter—and that their failures do not have to be the end of their story.
Do not use this message to embarrass someone or publicly expose their struggles.
But before you go, there is one final picture I want you to carry.
Imagine standing in a field at sunset.
Behind you are the places where you planted pride, fear, selfishness, and regret.
You can see the damage.
You cannot pretend it is not there.
And perhaps, for a moment, you feel the crushing weight of everything you wish you had done differently.
Then you remember the cross.
The empty tomb.
The risen Christ who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His name.
You realize that you cannot undo the past.
You cannot guarantee tomorrow.
You cannot force every broken thing to become whole in this life.
But you can entrust yourself to the One who died for sinners and rose again.
You can turn from the darkness.
You can walk in the light.
You can begin to cultivate what is good.
And you can trust the Lord with the harvest.
Because the greatest hope of the Christian life is not that we have finally learned how to plant perfectly.
It is that Jesus Christ is merciful to imperfect people who turn to Him.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Persevere where obedience is difficult.
Give generously without trying to purchase God's blessing.
Love sincerely without demanding repayment.
And never mistake a painful chapter for the final authority over a life surrendered to Christ.
You cannot unplant yesterday's seeds, but in Christ, yesterday's harvest does not have to be the final word over your eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF JESUS IS REALLY GOD, WHY DID HE SAY, “THE FATHER IS GREATER THAN I”?
paragraphs: IF JESUS IS REALLY GOD, WHY DID HE SAY, “THE FATHER IS GREATER THAN I”?
The One Sentence That Seems to Contradict Christ’s Divinity—Until You Discover What Jesus Gave Up, What He Never Stopped Being, and Why He Went to the Cross for You.
There is a question that has shaken the faith of some Christians, fueled centuries of theological arguments, and left countless people wondering whether they have misunderstood Jesus all along.
And the unsettling part?
The question comes from Jesus’ own mouth.
“If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father: for my Father is greater than I.” — John 14:28, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
“My Father is greater than I.”
Greater?
But haven't Christians been taught that Jesus is God?
Doesn't the Bible say that the Word was God?
If Jesus is fully divine, why would He describe the Father as greater than Himself?
Was Jesus admitting that He was somehow less than God? Was He merely a powerful messenger? A created being? Someone beneath the Father in His very nature?
Or is there something extraordinary happening in this passage that we cannot see until we understand what Jesus was doing when He spoke those words?
Because this is not merely an argument about ancient Greek vocabulary.

This question takes us straight into the mystery of the incarnation, the humility of the Son of God, the agony of Calvary, and the astonishing truth that the One who possesses divine glory willingly entered our suffering.
And somewhere in that truth is a message for the person who has spent years believing that being important means never having to humble yourself.
Stay with this.
Because before we finish, the words “the Father is greater than I” may no longer sound like a threat to your faith.
They may become one of the most beautiful reminders of what Jesus willingly endured to save you.
Imagine the upper room.
The atmosphere is heavy.
Jesus knows that betrayal is approaching. He knows that His disciples will scatter. He knows the cross is waiting.
The men around Him do not fully understand what is coming.
They have left their livelihoods to follow Him. They have watched Him open blind eyes, command storms, forgive sins, and call the dead back to life.
They believe in Him.
But now He is talking about leaving.
And their hearts are troubled.
Jesus tells them:
“Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.” — John 14:1, KJV
Notice that.
Jesus does not tell His disciples to trust God instead of trusting Him.
He calls them to trust in God and in Himself.
Then He promises to prepare a place for them. He speaks of going to the Father. He promises the coming of the Holy Spirit.
And in the middle of comforting frightened disciples, He says something that people would later isolate from the conversation and use as an argument against His deity.
“The Father is greater than I.”
But here is where we must be careful.
A verse removed from its context can appear to say something the passage itself never intended.
Jesus was not delivering a lecture about being a lesser god.
He was comforting His disciples about His departure.
He was speaking as the eternal Son who had entered the world in genuine human flesh, taken the form of a servant, and was preparing to return to the glory of the Father.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
And to understand why, we need to go somewhere unexpected.
Not first to the manger.
Not even to the cross.
We need to go back before Bethlehem existed.
Before Abraham.
Before the first sunrise.
Before creation itself.
John opens his Gospel with these astonishing words:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” — John 1:1, KJV
The original Greek reads:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
Transliteration:
En archē ēn ho logos, kai ho logos ēn pros ton theon, kai theos ēn ho logos.
The final phrase is crucial:
καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος
Kai theos ēn ho logos.
“And the Word was God.”
John is making two truths clear simultaneously.
The Word was with God, indicating personal distinction.
And the Word was God, affirming His deity.
The Word is not identical to the Father as a person, yet He truly possesses the divine nature.
Some object that the Greek word theos in the final clause lacks the definite article and therefore should mean “a god.”
But Greek grammar does not work that simply.

The absence of the article does not automatically make a noun indefinite. In this construction, theos stands before the verb and describes what the Word is by nature. The wording distinguishes the Word from the person identified as ton theon while affirming His deity.
John's meaning is reinforced by what he writes next:
Think about the force of those words.
Everything that came into existence came into existence through the Word.
And apart from Him, nothing that was made was made.
John does not place the Word among the things created.
He places Him on the Creator's side of the distinction between Creator and creation.
Then, in verse 14, comes the sentence that changes everything:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us...” — John 1:14, KJV
The Greek says:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Not that the Word stopped being divine.
Not that God transformed into a mere human and ceased to be God.
The eternal Word became truly human.
This is the incarnation.
And it is impossible to understand John 14:28 properly without understanding John 1:14.
The One who became flesh did not cease to be what He eternally was. He took on what He had not previously possessed: a genuine human nature.
He entered a world of hunger, exhaustion, rejection, grief, temptation, suffering, and death.
The Creator entered His creation.
The eternal Son experienced human life.
The One through whom all things were made allowed Himself to be carried in human arms.
And eventually, He allowed human hands to nail Him to a cross.
Not because He had lost His deity.
But because He had come to redeem sinners.
Now listen carefully, because this is where another passage opens the mystery even further.
The apostle Paul writes:
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men.” — Philippians 2:5–7, KJV
The original Greek contains a phrase that deserves serious attention:
ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων
En morphē theou hyparchōn.
“Existing in the form of God.”
The word morphē refers here to a form or condition expressive of what someone truly is. Paul's parallel between the “form of God” and the “form of a servant” is essential to his argument.
Jesus did not merely appear divine.
Paul begins with Christ's divine status and then describes His astonishing humiliation.
But the next phrase has sometimes been misunderstood:
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν
Heauton ekenōsen.
Literally, “He emptied Himself.”
This is where the Greek verb kenoō gives us the theological term kenosis, meaning emptying.
And this raises a critical question.
What exactly did Jesus empty Himself of?
Did He surrender His deity?
Did He cease to be omnipotent?
Did He stop being God?
No.
Paul does not say that Jesus emptied Himself of His divine nature.
He explains the emptying through what follows: Christ took the form of a servant and entered genuine human existence.
His emptying was not the abandonment of deity but the astonishing humility of taking the servant's place.
He did not become less than divine in His nature.
He became truly human without ceasing to be divine.
He did not stop being the eternal Son.
He willingly embraced the lowliness and suffering of human life.
And that is why the language of “greater” in John 14:28 must be understood carefully.
The Greek word Jesus uses is:
μείζων
Meizōn.
It means “greater.”
It is a comparative word that can refer to greatness in different respects, including position, status, or authority.
The word by itself does not tell us that one person possesses a superior divine nature.
Context determines what kind of greatness is being discussed.
Within John's Gospel, Jesus speaks as the Son sent by the Father, carrying out the Father's will, and moving toward His return to the Father's glory.
The Father is greater in relation to the Son's incarnate mission and humbled condition. The Son is not thereby declared inferior in divine essence.

There is also a real distinction between the Father and the Son, including the Son's relationship to the Father and His willing obedience in the work of redemption. Christian theology must not erase that distinction.
Yet distinction of persons and order in the saving mission do not require inequality of divine nature.
This is why historic Trinitarian Christianity confesses one God in three distinct persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Not three gods.
Not one person wearing three different masks.
And not a supreme God who created a lesser divine being named Jesus.
The Father is God.
The Son is God.
The Holy Spirit is God.
They are personally distinct, yet share the one undivided divine being.
The mystery is profound, but the confession is not built upon John 1:1 alone.
Listen to Jesus elsewhere in John's Gospel:
“I and my Father are one.” — John 10:30, KJV
The Greek reads:
ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν
Egō kai ho patēr hen esmen.
The word hen, meaning “one,” is neuter, not masculine.
Jesus is not saying that He and the Father are the same person.
The plural verb “we are” preserves their personal distinction.

In context, Jesus speaks of His power to preserve His sheep and the Father's power to preserve them. The declaration of oneness is therefore bound to their unity in divine action, and John's broader Gospel supports the confession of their shared deity.
Notice what happens immediately afterward.
His opponents pick up stones.
They understand His words as making a claim that, in their judgment, constitutes blasphemy.
And Jesus does not respond by declaring Himself merely a created angel.
Instead, He continues speaking of His unique relationship with the Father.
Elsewhere He says:
“Before Abraham was, I am.” — John 8:58, KJV
The Greek is striking:
πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί
Prin Abraam genesthai egō eimi.
Before Abraham came into existence, Jesus says, “I am.”
The wording contrasts Abraham's coming into being with Jesus' extraordinary claim about Himself.
In the context of John's Gospel, it contributes to the revelation of His preexistence and divine identity.

There is also a meaningful connection with the divine self-revelation in Exodus, though we should not pretend that every Greek occurrence of egō eimi automatically carries the full meaning of God's name.
Sound interpretation respects both the words and their setting.
And John does not leave us guessing about where his Gospel is leading.
After the resurrection, Thomas sees the risen Jesus and cries:
“My Lord and my God.” — John 20:28, KJV
The Greek says:
Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου
Ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou.
“My Lord and my God.”
Thomas addresses Jesus directly.
And Jesus does not rebuke him for calling Him God.
Instead, He speaks of the blessedness of those who will believe without seeing.
That matters.
Because the same Gospel that records Jesus saying “the Father is greater than I” also records Thomas calling Jesus “my God.”
If we allow John to interpret John, we cannot casually discard one passage to preserve another.
We must hold both truths together.
Jesus is truly God.
Jesus is truly man.
The Son is distinct from the Father.
And in His earthly mission, the incarnate Son willingly obeyed the Father.
This is not a contradiction.
It is the heart of the incarnation.
But there is another detail in John 14:28 that is often overlooked.
Jesus says:
“If ye loved me, ye would rejoice...”
Why would His disciples rejoice that He was going to the Father?
Because His departure was not a defeat.
His humiliation was moving toward its appointed completion.
His death and resurrection would accomplish redemption, and His return to the Father would mean the glorification of the incarnate Son.
Earlier, Jesus had prayed:
“And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.” — John 17:5, KJV
Before the world was.
Before creation.
Before Bethlehem.
Jesus speaks of glory He already shared with the Father.
He is not asking to become divine for the first time.
He is speaking of the glory that was His before the world existed, now to be manifested in the completion of His saving mission.
The Father is greater than the Son in the Son's humbled earthly condition, but the Son's eternal divine identity has not disappeared.
And the story does not end with humiliation.
Paul continues:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:
That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth;
And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” — Philippians 2:8–11, KJV
There is something breathtaking here.
The One who stooped to the lowest place is exalted.
The One who accepted the servant's condition is confessed as Lord.
And Paul is drawing upon language from Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD declares that every knee will bow and every tongue will swear allegiance.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, Isaiah's declaration belongs to the one true God.
The Hebrew includes the words:
כִּי־לִי תִּכְרַע כָּל־בֶּרֶךְ
Ki li tikhra kol berekh.
“To me every knee shall bow.”
Paul applies this universal confession to Jesus Christ, while explicitly declaring that it brings glory to God the Father.
This is not a picture of a rival deity stealing the Father's honor.
It is a picture of the Father being glorified through the universal acknowledgment of the Son.
And now we have reached the point where this theological question becomes painfully personal.
Because Philippians 2 was not originally written merely to settle arguments about Christology.
Paul begins with a command:
“Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.”
He is speaking to believers about humility.
About selfish ambition.
About pride.
About considering others.
About the kind of heart that should exist among people who belong to Jesus.
And then he points to the Son of God.
Think about the contrast.
We are often desperate to be recognized.
Jesus willingly embraced humiliation.
We want people to notice our importance.
Jesus washed His disciples' feet.
We struggle to apologize because admitting wrong feels like losing.
Jesus, who committed no sin, accepted shame He did not deserve.
We want to defend our reputation at any cost.
Jesus endured mockery, false accusation, and crucifixion to accomplish the Father's saving purpose.
And perhaps that is where this passage begins to confront us.
Not because we have misunderstood a Greek verb.
But because we have misunderstood greatness.
We have spent so much of our lives believing that greatness means being above other people.
Being untouchable.
Being admired.
Being the one who never has to bend.
Yet the eternal Son, who had every right to divine glory, took the form of a servant.
The One who had nothing to prove humbled Himself for people who had nothing to boast about.
And some of us still cannot bring ourselves to say, “I was wrong.”
Some of us would rather lose a relationship than surrender our pride.
Some of us know how to defend the doctrine of Christ's deity while refusing to imitate the humility of Christ's heart.
We can explain the Trinity and still treat people cruelly.
We can quote Philippians 2 and still hunger for applause.
We can win an argument about Jesus and walk away behaving nothing like Him.
That should disturb us.
Because biblical truth is not given merely to make us better debaters.
It is given to lead us into worship, repentance, faith, and transformed living.
And before anyone misunderstands, humility does not mean pretending evil is good, remaining in abuse, or refusing to speak truth.
Jesus was humble without being dishonest.
He was gentle without surrendering righteousness.
He served without ceasing to be Lord.
His humility was holy strength directed toward the Father's will.
And that is what makes the cross so overwhelming.
Jesus was not a helpless victim trapped by circumstances beyond His control.
He willingly laid down His life.
He said:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” — John 10:18, KJV
He knew what was coming.
He knew the betrayal.
He knew the abandonment.
He knew the agony.
And He went forward.
For sinners.
For the proud.
For the ashamed.
For those who have tried to cover their guilt with religious appearances.
For people who know what it means to smile in public while privately wondering whether God could still forgive them.
Perhaps that is you.
Perhaps you have been reading about Greek grammar while carrying something much heavier than a theological question.
A failure you have never confessed.
A habit you keep returning to.
A relationship damaged by your pride.
A secret that makes you afraid of being fully known.
And somewhere beneath all your religious language is a question you have not dared to say aloud:
“If Jesus really knew everything about me, would He still want me?”
Here is what the Gospel declares.
He does know the truth about sinners.
And He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we earned a second chance.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve mercy.
While we were still sinners.
The eternal Son entered our humanity, lived in perfect obedience, bore our sins at the cross, and rose from the dead.
His sacrifice is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
It is the foundation of forgiveness and the call to a new life.
Grace does not tell us that sin is harmless.
Grace tells us that sin is so serious that Christ died to save us from it—and that God's mercy is so great that sinners can be forgiven through Him.
This is where scandal meets grace.
The scandal of our rebellion.
The scandal of our hypocrisy.
The scandal of our desperate attempts to save ourselves.
And then the grace of Jesus Christ.
Not a grace that denies the truth.
A grace that confronts our sin, offers forgiveness, and transforms those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending our past never happened.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.
But by giving repentant sinners a new standing before God and a new life in Christ.
And perhaps the most astonishing thing about this whole discussion is that the question began with the word “greater.”
We wanted to know who was greater.
We wanted to understand status, authority, and divine identity.
And Scripture led us to the cross.
To the place where the eternal Son humbled Himself.
To the place where the innocent suffered for the guilty.
To the place where our pride is exposed and God's mercy is displayed.
So when someone asks you, “If Jesus is God, why did He say the Father is greater than He is?” you do not need to panic.
You can open the Scriptures.
You can explain that John 1:1 affirms the deity of the eternal Word.
You can show that John 1:14 reveals the Word becoming flesh.
You can explain that Philippians 2 describes Christ's voluntary humiliation, not the loss of His divine nature.
You can read John 14:28 in its setting, where Jesus comforts His disciples as He prepares to return to the Father.
And you can show that the Father and Son are personally distinct without treating the Son as a created or inferior god.
But do not stop at explaining the doctrine.
Let the doctrine lead you to worship.
Because the question is not only whether you can defend the deity of Jesus.
The question is whether you have bowed before Him as Lord.
Have you trusted the Savior you claim to understand?
Have you repented of the sins you keep excusing?
Have you allowed His humility to confront your pride?
Have you received the forgiveness you cannot earn?
The Gospel does not invite you merely to admire Jesus from a distance.
It calls you to turn from sin and trust Him.
And if you have wandered, it calls you to return.
Not because you can repair your soul through religious effort.
But because the crucified and risen Christ is sufficient to save.
If these words have challenged something hidden in your heart, you do not have to pretend.
You can begin with a simple prayer:

“Lord Jesus, You are more glorious than I have understood and more merciful than I deserve. Forgive my pride, my unbelief, and my sin. Teach me to trust Your Word, surrender to Your lordship, and walk in the humility You have shown. Thank You for the cross and the hope of Your resurrection. Change my heart, and help me live for Your glory. Amen.”
And if this article has helped you understand something you once struggled to believe, I would genuinely love to hear from you.
Or tell us which verse changed the way you understand this question.
Perhaps you still have questions. You are welcome to ask them respectfully. Serious questions about Scripture deserve careful, patient answers, not ridicule.
And if you are carrying a spiritual struggle you have been afraid to admit, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
There are seasons when even those who love Jesus need encouragement from the family of faith.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win an argument at their expense.
But to help them encounter the full witness of Scripture.
If you believe Gospel-centered teaching like this should continue reaching more people, I also want to invite you into something beyond a single article.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter Jesus Christ through Scripture, understand the Gospel more deeply, grow in discipleship, and find encouragement to remain faithful.
We want these resources to remain accessible, including to people who may never be able to afford Christian books or paid study materials.

Following Gospel Warrior helps you stay connected to ongoing biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources. Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, curious seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along and examine the Scriptures for themselves.
But I want to be biblically clear about something important.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
God's favor is not for sale.
And supporting an online ministry should never replace your responsibilities to your local church, your family, or those in genuine need.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV

The New Testament encourages believers to support those who faithfully teach the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), but it also calls for generosity that is willing, sincere, and free from coercion.
Think of it as a recurring ministry contribution rather than a compulsory tithe. You may choose to include it in your personal giving as your convictions and circumstances allow.
You are still welcome here.
Read the free resources.
Grow in the Word.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Your worth before God is not measured by your ability to contribute financially.
What matters most is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that people are directed toward Him.
Because the goal has never been to build a community that simply admires Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to help build up disciples who know, love, worship, and follow Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who was with God in the beginning.
The same Jesus who is God.
The same Jesus who became flesh.
The same Jesus who took the form of a servant.
The same Jesus who humbled Himself to death on a cross.
The same Jesus whom the Father highly exalted.
The same Jesus before whom every knee will one day bow.
And the same Jesus who still calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His finished work.
So the next time you hear someone say, “Jesus cannot be God because He said the Father is greater,” remember the whole story.
Remember the upper room.
Remember the incarnation.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the glory He shared with the Father before the world existed.
And remember that His humility did not make Him less worthy of worship.
It revealed the astonishing depth of His love.
He did not have to stop being God to come down to us. He came down because we could never save ourselves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN JESUS CALLED “JEZEBEL”: THE SIN A CHURCH LEARNED TO TOLERATE—UNTIL CHRIST HIMSELF CONFRONTED IT
paragraphs: THE WOMAN JESUS CALLED “JEZEBEL”: THE SIN A CHURCH LEARNED TO TOLERATE—UNTIL CHRIST HIMSELF CONFRONTED IT

She was accused of leading believers into sexual immorality and idolatry. But the most terrifying part of Revelation 2:20–23 isn't what this woman was doing. It's what Jesus saw happening inside a church that still thought it belonged to Him.
Imagine walking into a church where the worship is beautiful.
The songs are moving. The people know Scripture. Someone is praying with tears streaming down their face. The congregation speaks passionately about love, acceptance, and spiritual freedom.
Everything looks alive.
But somewhere beneath the worship, something is dying.

A compromise has become a habit. A habit has become a teaching. And a teaching has become so familiar that people no longer recognize the difference between the voice of Jesus and the voice of someone using His name.
Then comes a message.
Not from an angry outsider.
Not from someone trying to destroy the church.
But from Jesus Christ Himself.
And His words are devastating.
“But I have this against you…”
Imagine hearing those words from the Savior who died for you.
Not because He has stopped loving you.
But because He loves you too much to pretend that what is destroying you is harmless.
This is the frightening, heartbreaking, and ultimately hope-filled story behind the woman called “Jezebel” in Revelation 2:20–23.
And before you decide this story is about somebody else's sin, somebody else's church, or somebody else's scandal, consider something.
The woman is not the only person Jesus confronts.
He also confronts those who have learned to tolerate what He calls them to reject.
And that brings this ancient warning dangerously close to our own hearts.
The setting is Thyatira, a city in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Türkiye.

The risen Christ addresses a real Christian congregation there. This is not a fictional courtroom scene or a story invented to frighten believers. It is part of the message recorded in Revelation, written to seven churches facing spiritual pressures, temptations, suffering, and compromise.
Before confronting Thyatira's sin, Jesus acknowledges something beautiful.
“I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first.” (Revelation 2:19, KJV)
Think about that.
This church was not described as completely inactive or devoid of faith.
There was love.
There was service.
There was perseverance.
There was evidence of growth.
Yet spiritual activity had not eliminated spiritual danger.
A congregation can be busy serving Jesus while failing to confront something that dishonors Him.
A person can appear spiritually mature in one area while quietly surrendering another area of life to sin.
And then Jesus identifies the problem.

“Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.” (Revelation 2:20, KJV)
Read that again.
Jesus did not merely condemn a woman's private behavior.
He confronted teaching that was leading His servants into sin.
And He confronted the church for allowing it.
The word translated “sufferest” in the King James Version means allow or tolerate in this context.
The underlying Greek verb is ἀφεῖς (apheis), from aphiēmi, which can mean to permit or allow.
Jesus was saying, in effect, that the congregation was allowing a destructive influence to continue among His people.
And the name He used carried a terrible history.
Jezebel.
To understand why that name mattered, we must return centuries earlier to the Old Testament.
In 1 Kings 16–21, Jezebel was the wife of King Ahab of Israel. She promoted Baal worship, opposed the prophets of the LORD, and played a central role in the injustice that resulted in Naboth's death.
Her story became a lasting biblical picture of idolatry, corrupt influence, and hostility toward God's truth.
But here is an important distinction.
Revelation does not tell us that the woman in Thyatira was literally the same Jezebel from the Old Testament. Centuries separated them.
Nor can we establish with certainty whether “Jezebel” was her actual name or a symbolic designation used to describe her resemblance to the infamous queen.
What Scripture does tell us is that this woman claimed prophetic authority and was influencing believers toward sexual immorality and participation in food associated with idol worship.
We must not invent her biography.
We do not know her appearance, her family history, the precise words of her teachings, or every method she used to gain influence.
But we know enough to understand the warning.
Someone claiming to speak with spiritual authority was teaching people to embrace behavior Jesus condemned.
And some believers were listening.
Perhaps that is what makes the passage so uncomfortable.
False teaching does not always arrive announcing itself as rebellion against God.
Sometimes it arrives wrapped in religious vocabulary.
Sometimes it offers permission where Scripture calls for repentance.
Sometimes it tells people that obedience is unnecessary, that compromise is harmless, or that spiritual maturity means moving beyond inconvenient commands.
It may sound compassionate.
It may sound sophisticated.
It may even sound liberating.
But any message that teaches people to make peace with sin is not freedom in Christ.
It is another form of bondage.
And bondage does not become holy simply because someone attaches God's name to it.
The Greek text of Revelation 2:20 uses two especially revealing expressions.
διδάσκει καὶ πλανᾷ — didaskei kai plana.
They mean “she teaches and leads astray.”
This is important.
The passage describes more than a person struggling privately with temptation.
It describes a corrupting influence that was being taught and spread.
There is a profound difference between a believer who falls into sin and grieves over it, and a teacher who persuades others that they need not repent of it.
Both need the mercy of Christ.
But the second can lead many others into destruction.
The passage also names the sins involved.
πορνεῦσαι (porneusai) refers to committing sexual immorality.
εἰδωλόθυτα (eidōlothyta) refers to things sacrificed to idols.
These are not vague accusations that we are free to redefine according to personal preference.
They concern sexual wrongdoing and idolatrous compromise.

In the ancient world, religious, economic, and social activities could overlap. Thyatira was associated with commercial trades and guilds, and scholars have suggested that pressures surrounding communal meals and pagan practices may help explain the temptation facing believers there.
That historical possibility is worth considering.
But Revelation does not specify the exact gatherings or circumstances involved, so we should not pretend to know more than the text reveals.
What is clear is that Christians were being drawn toward practices incompatible with their allegiance to Christ.
And Jesus was not indifferent.
Now imagine the personal cost of obedience.
What if refusing to participate meant losing opportunities?
What if remaining faithful made you unpopular?
What if the people around you insisted that you were taking Christianity too seriously?
What if compromise offered an easier path?
Suddenly this ancient church begins to look remarkably familiar.
Because temptation rarely presents itself as a request to destroy your life.
It often asks for one small exception.
Just this once.
Just this relationship.
Just this secret.
Just this compromise.
Just this thing everybody else is doing.
And then another.
Until the heart becomes comfortable with what once troubled the conscience.
Perhaps someone reading this knows that progression intimately.
You remember when a particular sin used to grieve you.
You remember when conviction came quickly.
You remember when you could not sleep without praying about it.
But after repeating it, excusing it, and hiding it, something changed.
The sin did not become less serious.
Your resistance became weaker.
And somewhere along the way, you began calling your surrender peace.
That is a dangerous place to live.
Not because Jesus has become unwilling to forgive.
But because we can become increasingly unwilling to admit that we need forgiveness.
Yet the next words of Jesus reveal something astonishing.
Something that should make every struggling sinner stop reading for a moment.
“And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not.” (Revelation 2:21, KJV)
Do you see it?
Before the announced judgment, there was an opportunity to repent.
Before the warning reached its most terrifying point, Jesus revealed that time had been given.
The Greek expression is ἔδωκα αὐτῇ χρόνον ἵνα μετανοήσῃ — edōka autē chronon hina metanoēsē.
It means, “I gave her time so that she might repent.”
The verb metanoeō refers to repentance—a change of mind and direction, turning away from sin toward God.
This is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what you did.
It is not regretting the consequences while secretly protecting the behavior.
Biblical repentance involves recognizing sin for what it is and turning toward the Lord in faith and obedience.
And Jesus gave her time.
Let those words reach the places you have been trying to hide.
Jesus gave her time.
The One whose eyes are described in Revelation 2:18 as being like a flame of fire was not ignorant of her actions.
He saw.
He knew.
He confronted.
And still, there was an opportunity to turn.
What a revelation of both His holiness and His patience.
The Lord who refuses to call evil good is also the Lord who calls sinners to repentance.
But the verse ends with a heartbreaking statement.
“And she repented not.”
Not because the passage says repentance was impossible.
Not because Jesus offered no warning.
But because she refused to turn.
There is something especially tragic about a person becoming so committed to defending a sin that even an opportunity for repentance is rejected.
And perhaps this is where the story stops being merely about Jezebel.
Because many of us know what it feels like to argue with conviction.
We know what it is to defend something we would once have confessed.
We know how to explain away a compromise.
We know how to appear spiritually strong while carrying a private contradiction.
A married person may be feeding an emotional relationship that is slowly becoming unfaithfulness.
A young believer may be hiding a pattern of sexual behavior that contradicts the faith they profess.
A church leader may be protecting a reputation instead of acknowledging wrongdoing.
A Christian may be placing money, approval, pleasure, or personal ambition above obedience to God.
And someone may be using the language of grace to avoid the call to repentance.
These are not identical situations, and we must not accuse everyone who struggles of being like the false teacher in Thyatira.
But every one of us needs to examine what we are allowing to rule our hearts.
Because grace was never intended to become permission to remain enslaved.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic: “God forbid.”
Grace does not make sin harmless.
Grace brings us to the Savior who breaks sin's claim over us.
And now the message to Thyatira grows more severe.
“Behold, I will cast her into a bed, and them that commit adultery with her into great tribulation, except they repent of their deeds.” (Revelation 2:22, KJV)
The language is deliberately forceful.
The bed associated with wrongdoing becomes part of an image of judgment.
The warning is not a license for readers to identify suffering people as recipients of divine punishment.
It is Christ's specific prophetic warning to those involved in the wrongdoing described in this passage.
Notice, however, that even here the words “except they repent” appear.
The warning still contains a call to turn.
Then comes one of the most difficult statements in the passage.

“And I will kill her children with death; and all the churches shall know that I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts: and I will give unto every one of you according to your works.” (Revelation 2:23, KJV)
We should not soften this verse until it loses its seriousness.
Neither should we use it recklessly.

The expression translated “her children” may refer to those who follow or belong to her corrupt teaching. Interpreters differ about whether the language is figurative or refers to literal offspring. The passage does not give us enough information to identify them with certainty.
What is unmistakable is the gravity of Christ's warning.
He will judge evil.
And He knows the truth beneath outward appearances.
The Greek says:
ἐραυνῶν νεφροὺς καὶ καρδίας — eraunōn nephrous kai kardias.
Literally, “searching kidneys and hearts.”
That may sound strange to modern ears.
But in ancient biblical imagery, the kidneys, or inward parts, could represent the deepest inner life, while the heart represented the center of thought, desire, and intention.
The meaning is profound.
Jesus searches what is hidden within us.
He sees beyond reputation.
Beyond performance.
Beyond carefully chosen words.
Beyond the version of ourselves we present to others.
He knows the motives we conceal and the desires we struggle to admit.
And that truth should humble every person who claims to belong to Him.
Because you can hide a conversation from your spouse.
You can hide a browser history from your family.
You can hide dishonesty from your employer.
You can hide a secret habit from your church.
You can even convince people that everything is fine.
But you cannot hide your heart from Jesus Christ.
And here is the part that should bring us to our knees.
The One who sees everything is also the One who went to the cross to save sinners.
He does not need our deception.
He calls us into the light.
And the light is not the enemy of a repentant heart.
It is where healing begins.
Think of the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers wanted to use her sin as a weapon.
Jesus exposed their hypocrisy and refused to join their condemnation.
But He did not tell her that sin no longer mattered.
He told her to go and sin no more.

The passage has a well-known textual history and is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John's Gospel, so it should not carry the entire weight of our understanding of grace and repentance.
Yet its portrayal of mercy joined with a call to holiness is consistent with the wider New Testament.
Think also of Peter.
He denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had promised loyalty collapsed under fear.
And after the rooster crowed, Peter wept bitterly.
His failure was real.
His grief was real.
But his story did not end in the courtyard of denial.
In John 21, the risen Jesus restored Peter to a life of service.
The man who had denied Christ was called again to shepherd His sheep.
That is what makes the Gospel so extraordinary.
Jesus does not pretend that sin never happened.
He redeems people who could never erase it themselves.
And consider the apostle Paul.
Before becoming a preacher of Christ, he persecuted the church.
He carried a history that could not be undone by a better public image.
Yet he testified that he had received mercy.
The grace of God did not make Paul's former violence acceptable.
It transformed the direction of his life.
That is the difference between excusing sin and being redeemed from it.
One asks God to leave us unchanged.
The other surrenders to the Savior who makes us new.
And perhaps you have been afraid to surrender because you believe that if everything hidden were exposed, nobody would love you anymore.
Maybe you have been carrying guilt for years.
Maybe your marriage has been wounded by betrayal.
Maybe pornography has become a secret prison.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending that your relationship with God is healthy when you know your heart has drifted.
Maybe you have been hurt by a spiritual leader who used authority to excuse wrongdoing.
Maybe you were taught that asking honest questions was rebellion.
Maybe someone used the word “Jezebel” to humiliate you, silence you, or dismiss you simply because you were a woman who spoke up.
If that happened, understand this clearly.
Revelation 2 does not authorize Christians to label women “Jezebel” merely because they are outspoken, influential, disagree with a leader, or challenge wrongdoing.
The passage concerns identifiable false teaching and conduct that led believers into sin.
It is not a weapon for controlling women or silencing legitimate concerns.
A church that condemns sexual immorality while protecting sexual abuse has not understood the holiness of Christ.
A leader who invokes Scripture to escape accountability has not earned the right to silence the wounded.
Jesus is not honored when His Word is used to conceal evil.
He is honored when truth is spoken, the vulnerable are protected, wrongdoers are held accountable, and repentance bears genuine fruit.
And for anyone who has been wounded by spiritual manipulation, the answer is not to return blindly to an unsafe situation.
You can seek safety, wise counsel, and appropriate help while continuing to seek Christ.
Because the voice of the Good Shepherd is not the voice of an abuser.
He does not need manipulation to establish His authority.
He is the truth.
Now return to Thyatira.
There is another detail many people overlook.
Jesus does not treat every believer in the church as though they are equally guilty.
In Revelation 2:24–25, He addresses those who have not accepted the corrupt teaching and urges them to hold fast to what they have until He comes.
That matters.
Because the message is not simply, “Everything is corrupt, and everyone is condemned.”
It is also a call for faithful believers to endure.
Not everyone had surrendered.
Not everyone had believed the deception.
And even in a compromised congregation, Christ knew those who remained faithful.
He knew their struggle.
He knew their perseverance.
He knew their refusal to bow.
Just as He knows yours.
Perhaps you are fighting a temptation nobody else understands.
Perhaps you are choosing integrity while watching dishonesty get rewarded.
Perhaps you are remaining sexually faithful in a culture that treats commitment as disposable.
Perhaps you are refusing to join in wrongdoing even though it costs you friendships, influence, or opportunity.
Jesus sees that too.
He does not only search hidden sins.
He also knows hidden faithfulness.
And the message to Thyatira ultimately points beyond its scandal to the authority and victory of Jesus Christ.
Revelation 22:16 identifies Jesus Himself as “the bright and morning star.”
The final hope of the Christian is not merely escaping a scandal.
It is belonging to Christ.
Knowing Him.
Being made new by Him.
And sharing in the life He gives.
That is why this story cannot end with Jezebel.
It must end with Jesus.
Because Jezebel represents the deadly seriousness of corrupting compromise.
But Jesus reveals the holy mercy that calls sinners to turn before judgment.
And the cross shows us how costly that mercy truly is.
At Calvary, Jesus did not negotiate with sin.
He bore its consequences on behalf of sinners.
He, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for us.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is not cheap forgiveness.
It is blood-bought grace.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not something we earn by our works.
And Ephesians 2:10 immediately reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the beautiful balance?
We are not saved because we become good enough.
We are saved by God's grace, and that grace begins transforming the way we live.
Repentance does not purchase forgiveness.
Christ has paid the price.
Repentance is part of turning to the One who forgives and restores.
And this is why we must be careful never to turn spiritual giving into another kind of bondage.
Your salvation cannot be purchased with a donation.
Your place in God's family is not determined by how much money you give to a ministry.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
Not a payment.
Not a platform.
Not a religious organization.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
Giving that honors God is not extracted through fear or guilt.
It flows from a willing heart.
Some are battling temptation.
Some are recovering from spiritual wounds.
Some are trying to understand the Bible for the first time.
Some have almost given up on their faith.
And some are one honest encounter with the Gospel away from beginning a new journey with Christ.
It can be one practical expression of your desire to glorify God by helping make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources more accessible.
This is not a replacement for every believer's responsibility to support their local church, nor should it automatically be treated as the biblical tithe.
It is an opportunity to give willingly toward a ministry you believe is serving Christ faithfully.
It is participating in work intended to point people back to Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not reserved for those who can afford to give.
We want people to have access to biblical nourishment whether they are able to contribute financially or not.
And there is another way to help that costs nothing.
Not because every post needs to go viral.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
But because someone in your circle may need to hear that compromise is dangerous, repentance is possible, and Jesus has not stopped calling sinners to Himself.
Maybe a friend needs this reminder.
Maybe a family member has quietly drifted from faith.
Maybe someone you know has been hurt by a church and needs to hear that Jesus is not the same as the people who misrepresented Him.
There is room to ask questions.
Room to learn.
Room to wrestle honestly with Scripture.
And always, the invitation to turn toward Jesus.
But before you leave, I want to ask you something more personal.
Not as a public performance.
Not to force you to reveal a private sin.
Not to make you feel ashamed in front of strangers.
Just an honest question between your conscience and the Lord.
What have you been calling harmless that Jesus has been calling you to surrender?
Maybe you already know.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has been convicting you for a long time.
Maybe you have been postponing a difficult confession.
Maybe you need to end a relationship that is leading you away from Christ.
Maybe you need to seek help for a destructive habit.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you have harmed.
Maybe you need to stop defending what Scripture has clearly confronted.
Or maybe your next step is simply to fall on your knees and pray the prayer you have been avoiding.
“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot justify it anymore. Please forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to walk in Your truth.”
You do not need an impressive speech.
You need an honest heart turned toward the Savior.
You can simply write “Christ is still healing me.”
Or “Pray for me.”
Or share a testimony of how Jesus brought you out of compromise and into a renewed walk with Him.
You do not have to disclose details that should remain private.
Your honest words may encourage someone else who thought they were the only person still struggling.
Because the church should never become a place where everyone pretends to be perfect.
It should be a people who confess that Jesus Christ is perfect, that His grace is sufficient, and that His truth calls us into a transformed life.
And perhaps that is the greatest lesson of Thyatira.
The danger was not simply that a woman taught what was false.
It was that people could become comfortable with falsehood while still surrounded by the language and activity of faith.
But the hope was not found in pretending the problem did not exist.
It was found in the voice of the risen Christ.
The same Lord who said, “I have this against you,” also called His people to repentance and faithfulness.
He did not abandon His holiness to show mercy.
And He did not abandon His mercy to defend holiness.
Both meet perfectly in Him.
So if you have wandered, come back.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have been deceived, return to Scripture.
If you have been wounded, seek healing in truth.
If you have remained faithful through costly trials, hold fast.
And if you think your past is too scandalous for the grace of God, look again at the cross.
The cross does not tell you that your sin was insignificant.
It tells you that the Savior's love was greater than the cost He willingly bore to redeem sinners.
The empty tomb tells you that death did not defeat Him.
And His living Word still calls people out of darkness into His marvelous light.
The woman called Jezebel was given time to repent.
The passage tells us she refused.
But you are reading this message now.
And the invitation of the Gospel is still before you.
Do not confuse God's patience with His approval of sin.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
And do not mistake the temporary comfort of compromise for the lasting freedom found in Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that Jesus knows the truth about your life.
The greatest tragedy would be hearing His call and choosing to remain hidden.
The Savior who sees the sin you cannot hide is the same Savior whose nail-scarred hands are sufficient to receive the sinner who finally comes into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS KNELT TO WASH FEET. SO WHY DO SOME CHRISTIAN LEADERS DEMAND A THRONE?
paragraphs: JESUS KNELT TO WASH FEET. SO WHY DO SOME CHRISTIAN LEADERS DEMAND A THRONE?
The King of Heaven Wrapped a Towel Around His Waist—And Exposed Everything Wrong With Leadership That Wants to Be Worshiped Instead of Serving.
What if one of the most uncomfortable questions Jesus could ask the modern Church is this: “Why are you demanding the treatment I willingly gave up?”

Imagine walking into a church where the pastor's arrival causes everyone to stand. Someone rushes to carry his Bible. Another makes sure his special chair is ready. People carefully choose their words because questioning him might be interpreted as questioning God.
He is surrounded by people who call him anointed.
But some of those same people are afraid to tell him the truth.

A struggling widow sits quietly in the back, wondering how she will feed her children tomorrow. A young believer is wrestling with sin but is terrified of being judged. A volunteer who has served faithfully for years is exhausted, overlooked, and afraid that saying no will make them seem spiritually rebellious.
And somewhere in the middle of all that religious activity, a disturbing question begins to rise.
When did following the Servant King become an excuse to build a kingdom around the servant?

Before anyone becomes defensive, this is not an attack on pastors. There are faithful shepherds who pray when nobody sees, sacrifice without recognition, visit hospital rooms, comfort grieving families, and carry burdens their congregations will never fully understand.
Scripture commands believers to respect faithful spiritual leaders, recognize their labor, and support those who teach God's Word (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).
But Scripture never commands believers to treat a pastor as though he were Jesus.
And there is a difference between honoring a shepherd and placing him on a throne.
To understand that difference, we must enter one of the most breathtaking scenes in the Gospel of John.
Not a cathedral.
Not a palace.
Not a conference filled with applause.
An upper room.
A table.
Twelve disciples.
And a basin of water.
The night before the crucifixion, Jesus knew exactly what was coming.
He knew the betrayal was already taking shape. He knew Peter would deny Him. He knew the disciples would scatter when fear overwhelmed their promises.
And He knew something else.
John 13:3 tells us that Jesus knew the Father had given all things into His hands, that He had come from God, and that He was returning to God.
Do not rush past that.
Jesus knew He possessed supreme authority. And what did He do with that authority?
He got up from supper.
He laid aside His outer garments.
He took a towel.
He wrapped it around Himself.
He poured water into a basin.
Then the Lord of glory knelt before His disciples and began washing their feet.
The hands that formed creation were now cleaning the dirt from human skin.
The One whom angels worshiped was performing the work of a servant.
The One who had every right to receive honor was demonstrating what holy authority looks like when it is governed by love.
And perhaps the most devastating detail is this:
Jesus knew Judas was going to betray Him. Yet the passage presents the foot-washing as extending to His disciples without recording Judas as an exception.
Think about that.
Jesus did not need to be ignorant of someone's betrayal to love him.
He did not surrender His holiness by serving a sinner.
He did not become less divine by stooping low.
He revealed the character of divine love.
John introduces this scene with a remarkable statement:
“Having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.” — John 13:1, KJV
The Greek phrase is εἰς τέλος (eis telos).
It can carry the sense of loving to the end, and in this context it also communicates the fullness of Christ's persevering love.
Jesus was not performing a public relations gesture.
He was loving His own as the hour of His suffering approached.
He was showing them the kind of love that would soon take Him to the cross.
And suddenly the towel becomes more than a towel.
It becomes a visible rebuke to every form of spiritual pride that uses authority to demand admiration while refusing humble service.
Because the King who deserved everything chose to serve.
And some of us who deserve nothing have become offended when nobody treats us as important.
That should trouble every Christian.
Not only pastors.
All of us.
The worship leader who becomes angry when someone else receives an opportunity.
The ministry worker who serves faithfully until nobody notices.
The Bible teacher who cannot accept correction.
The church member who demands recognition because of years of giving.
The believer who quotes Scripture about humility while secretly craving a position above others.
Pride does not always wear expensive clothing.
Sometimes it wears a ministry badge.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it stands behind a pulpit.
And sometimes it sits in the congregation, silently judging everyone else.
The frightening thing about spiritual pride is that it can make us feel close to God while making us increasingly unlike Christ.
Then Peter speaks.
When Jesus approaches him, Peter cannot understand what is happening.
“Lord, dost thou wash my feet?” — John 13:6, KJV
His response is understandable.
This is his Master.
His Teacher.
His Lord.
And now that Lord is kneeling before him.
Peter protests.
“Thou shalt never wash my feet.” — John 13:8, KJV
But Jesus answers:
“If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.” — John 13:8, KJV
There is something deeper here than an example of good leadership.
Jesus is teaching Peter that discipleship begins with receiving what only Christ can give.
Peter cannot cleanse himself into fellowship with Jesus.
He must allow the Savior to serve him.
The washing of feet becomes a profound picture of the cleansing and fellowship that come through Christ, even as the immediate scene also prepares the disciples to serve one another.
And this is where the Gospel confronts our pride from another direction.
Some people are too proud to serve.
Others are too proud to be served.
Some refuse to kneel because they believe they are above everyone else.
Others refuse to admit their need because they cannot bear to appear weak.
But the Gospel humbles both.
Before you can faithfully carry Christ's towel, you must acknowledge your need for Christ's cleansing.
You are not saved because you volunteered in church.
You are not forgiven because you gave money.
You are not justified because you respected your pastor.
You are not accepted by God because you served until your body was exhausted.
You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection accomplish what our religious performance never could (Ephesians 2:8–10; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And when that grace truly reaches the heart, it changes how we treat people.
Especially people who cannot offer us anything in return.
That brings us to the words every Christian leader should read slowly.
After Jesus finishes washing their feet, He puts His garments back on, returns to His place, and asks:
“Know ye what I have done to you?” — John 13:12, KJV
Imagine the silence.
Imagine the disciples looking at one another.
Imagine the embarrassment of realizing that the One they called Lord had just done something they themselves might have considered beneath them.
Then Jesus explains:
“Ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am.” — John 13:13, KJV
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not deny His authority.
He does not pretend that every role in the community is identical.
He does not suggest that leadership, teaching, or spiritual responsibility are unnecessary.
He affirms that He is their Teacher and Lord.
But then He reveals what His authority means for their behavior.
“If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.” — John 13:14, KJV
In the Greek text, the phrase ὀφείλετε ἀλλήλων νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας (opheilete allēlōn niptein tous podas) communicates an obligation to wash one another's feet.
The word ὀφείλετε (opheilete) expresses what is owed or required.
Jesus is not merely recommending humility as an attractive personality trait.
He is placing His followers under an obligation to love and serve one another.
The Lord who washed their feet has established the pattern.
And nobody who claims to represent Him has the authority to reverse that pattern.
Christian leadership is not permission to rise above the people Christ calls us to love. It is a responsibility to care for them in His name.
That does not mean a pastor must literally wash everyone's feet every Sunday.

Some Christian traditions practice foot-washing as an ordinance or meaningful expression of obedience. Others understand Jesus' instruction primarily as a command to practice humble, practical service.
Faithful Christians differ on that application.
But the central meaning is unmistakable.
The disciple is not greater than the Master.
And the servant does not become too important to serve.
Jesus makes that explicit:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord; neither he that is sent greater than he that sent him.” — John 13:16, KJV
The Greek word δοῦλος (doulos) refers to a servant or slave.
In this saying, Jesus confronts the absurdity of a disciple imagining himself above the Lord whose example he is commanded to follow.
If Jesus did not consider humble service beneath Him, how can His followers consider it beneath them?
That question should echo through every church office.
Every leadership conference.
Every ministry boardroom.
Every Christian household.
And every heart that has ever confused spiritual responsibility with personal superiority.
Because there is a particular danger when religious authority becomes wrapped in the language of God's approval.
A leader can begin believing that disagreement is rebellion.
That correction is persecution.
That financial questions are attacks against the anointing.
That accountability is disrespect.
That ordinary people should sacrifice endlessly while leaders remain beyond scrutiny.
But the New Testament does not present church leadership as unquestionable royalty.
Peter himself later writes to the elders:
The Greek expression μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες (mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes) warns against domineering leadership.
It is the language of exercising mastery over others, not shepherding them through godly example.
And that distinction matters enormously.
A shepherd protects the sheep.
A tyrant protects his position.
A shepherd teaches the truth.
A tyrant punishes uncomfortable questions.
A shepherd welcomes appropriate accountability.
A tyrant makes accountability seem sinful.
A shepherd cares about wounded people.
A tyrant cares primarily about whether those people remain useful.
Yet even here, we must be careful.
Not every wealthy pastor is corrupt.
Not every leader who receives an honorarium is greedy.
Not every church that provides transportation, housing, security, or administrative assistance to its ministers is practicing unbiblical favoritism.
Scripture explicitly teaches that those who labor in preaching and teaching may receive material support (1 Timothy 5:17–18; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
The issue is not whether a minister receives help.
The issue is whether that minister has begun treating God's people as instruments of personal privilege.
Biblical honor supports faithful service. Spiritual idolatry makes a human leader untouchable.
And the difference becomes painfully clear when someone gets hurt.
Consider the church member who approaches a leader privately about a serious concern.
She is trembling.
She has prayed for weeks.
She has struggled to find the courage to speak.
She does not want to destroy the church.
She loves the church.
That is precisely why she came.
But instead of receiving a patient hearing, she is told that questioning leadership is questioning God.
Now she leaves carrying two wounds.
The original concern.
And the fear that seeking truth has made her disloyal to Jesus.
If that has ever happened to you, hear this carefully.
Respecting spiritual authority does not require surrendering biblical discernment.

Scripture calls believers to test teaching (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1), address sin responsibly (Matthew 18:15–17), and handle accusations against elders with both fairness and seriousness (1 Timothy 5:19–20).
A faithful leader should not be condemned by rumors.
But neither should a leader be protected from legitimate examination merely because he occupies a pulpit.
God's Word protects truth, justice, and the flock.
Not the reputation of a powerful person at any cost.
And if you are a pastor reading this, please do not hear only accusation.
Hear an invitation.
The Lord who called you to shepherd His people has not asked you to become their savior.
You are allowed to be human.
You are allowed to be tired.
You are allowed to need encouragement.
You are allowed to receive support.
You are allowed to admit when you are wrong.
In fact, your willingness to repent may teach your congregation more about grace than a hundred sermons designed to make you appear flawless.
Your people do not need a pastor who never needs mercy.
They need a shepherd who knows where mercy is found.
And if you have been wounded by a leader, do not confuse the failures of that leader with the character of Jesus.
A pastor may have used authority to silence you.
Jesus used His authority to serve.
A religious institution may have treated you as disposable.
Jesus demonstrated a love that went all the way to the cross.
A leader may have demanded loyalty while refusing accountability.
Jesus, though sinless, willingly humbled Himself for the salvation of sinners.
Human representatives can misrepresent Christ.
But their failures do not change who Christ is.
The hands that some leaders use to point at their own importance are not the hands that saved you. The hands that saved you were pierced.
There is another scene in the Gospels that makes the contrast even sharper.
In Mark 10, James and John seek prominent places in Jesus' glory.
They want honor.
Recognition.
Positions of distinction.
And Jesus tells His disciples that worldly rulers exercise power over others, but His followers must not imitate that model.
“Whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister.” — Mark 10:43, KJV
The Greek word translated “minister” is διάκονος (diakonos), meaning servant or one who ministers.
Then Jesus reveals the foundation beneath His command:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45, KJV
This is the heart of everything.
Jesus did not merely come to demonstrate an admirable leadership technique.
He came to give His life as a ransom.
His humility was not a performance.
His service was not a branding strategy.
His sacrifice was not a way to attract followers who would finance His comfort.
He came to accomplish redemption.
The cross is not simply the greatest example of selflessness.
It is the place where the sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners.
And that changes everything.
Because the problem with the human heart runs deeper than leadership style.
We want to be important.
We want to be admired.
We want our sacrifices noticed.
We want our opinions treated as unquestionable.
We want the benefits of Christ's kingdom without always accepting the humility of its King.
Even when we condemn pride in others, we can secretly nourish the same pride within ourselves.
That is why the Gospel does not simply tell arrogant people to behave better.
It calls sinners to repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
It announces forgiveness through His blood.
It promises new life through His resurrection.
It teaches us to die to selfish ambition and walk by the Spirit.
And it reminds us that genuine transformation is not accomplished by shame alone, but by the grace and power of God.
Paul writes:
The passage continues by describing Christ's humility, obedience, and death on the cross.
One of its central Greek expressions is ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτόν (etapeinōsen heauton).
“He humbled himself.” — Philippians 2:8, KJV
Jesus did not lose His divine identity when He humbled Himself.
He willingly took the position of a servant and became obedient unto death.
And the Father highly exalted Him.
This is not a promise that humble Christians will become celebrities.
It is a revelation of Christ's unique obedience and exaltation, and a call for believers to adopt His self-giving mind.
The Christian life does not revolve around manufacturing our own greatness.
It revolves around belonging to the One who is truly great.
So perhaps the question is no longer simply why some Christian leaders expect royal treatment.
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Why do so many of us still want a crown before we are willing to carry a towel?
What happens when nobody applauds your generosity?
When someone else receives the position you wanted?
When you are asked to serve people who cannot advance your reputation?
When a struggling believer needs your patience more than your advice?
When your spouse needs an apology instead of another explanation?
When your children need your presence more than your public image?
When a fellow Christian corrects you using Scripture?
When repentance would cost you the admiration of people who think you can do no wrong?
Those are not glamorous moments.
Nobody may photograph them.
Nobody may invite you onto a stage to talk about them.
But they are precisely the kinds of moments in which Christlike humility becomes visible.
And here is something worth remembering:
The towel is not a prop for proving how humble you are. It is a reminder that love must become action.
You can post about servant leadership and still mistreat the people closest to you.
You can preach John 13 and still refuse to apologize.
You can wash someone's feet in a public ceremony and still humiliate them behind closed doors.
You can speak beautifully about sacrifice while expecting others to make every sacrifice for you.
Jesus did not say His disciples would be blessed merely because they understood His teaching.
He said:
“If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them.” — John 13:17, KJV
The Greek word translated “happy” is μακάριοί (makarioi), commonly rendered “blessed.”
The blessing Jesus speaks of is connected to actually doing what He has taught.
Knowing is not the same as obeying.
Admiring humility is not the same as practicing it.
Quoting Jesus is not the same as following Jesus.
And the Church desperately needs that distinction.
We do not need less biblical respect for pastors.
We need more biblical respect for Christ.
We do not need to despise spiritual leadership.
We need leaders whose authority is exercised under the authority of Scripture.
We do not need congregations that treat every pastor with suspicion.
We need congregations that practice discernment without abandoning love.
We do not need to replace one personality cult with another.
We need to return to the crucified and risen Savior who alone deserves our worship.
And perhaps, somewhere tonight, a pastor is reading this while sitting alone after a difficult Sunday.
He remembers when ministry was simpler.
When he first preached, he was overwhelmed that God would use someone like him.
He did not dream about status.
He dreamed about seeing people come to Christ.
He wanted to teach the Bible faithfully.
He wanted to care for souls.
But slowly, ministry became tangled with expectations, comparison, influence, money, pressure, and the fear of losing respect.
He began protecting his image.
He stopped listening to correction.
He became irritated by ordinary people with ordinary problems.
And somewhere along the way, the towel disappeared.
If that is you, the invitation is not to despair.
It is to repent.
Christ is not calling you to manufacture a perfect public image.
He is calling you back to Himself.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Seek accountability.
Listen to those you have hurt.
Return to the Word.
Remember the wonder of the Gospel that first brought you to your knees.
The Savior who washed His disciples' feet still calls His people to humble obedience.
And His grace is not too small to transform a proud heart.
Perhaps another reader is remembering a church where they once felt safe.
You trusted the people there.
You served.
You gave.
You prayed.
You defended the leadership when others raised concerns.
Then something happened that shattered your confidence.
Now even hearing the word “church” makes your chest tighten.
You still believe in Jesus, but you struggle to trust anyone who claims to speak for Him.
Your pain deserves to be taken seriously.
And healing does not require pretending the wrong was acceptable.
Forgiveness does not automatically mean restoring someone to a position of trust.
Reconciliation, where possible, requires truth and genuine repentance.
Accountability is not the enemy of grace.
Sometimes it is one of the ways truth and love begin repairing what sin has damaged.
But please remember this.
The Jesus of John 13 is not standing over you demanding that you protect an institution at the expense of truth.
He is the Lord who knelt.
The Lord who served.
The Lord who loved His own to the end.
And the Lord who went to the cross.
Do not allow a human being's misuse of His name to become the final word about His character.
Let Jesus Himself show you who He is.
This is why the message of Gospel Warrior matters so deeply to us.
Not because we have built a perfect ministry.
Not because our voices deserve unquestioning loyalty.
But because the Word of God must remain greater than the personalities who proclaim it.
We want to keep pointing people back to Scripture, to repentance, to grace, to forgiveness, and above all, to Jesus Christ.
If this article has helped you examine your heart, understand Scripture more clearly, or find the courage to return to Christ, consider helping this message reach someone else.
Not to shame every pastor.
Not to provoke unnecessary division.
But because someone you know may be confusing loyalty to a leader with loyalty to Jesus.
Someone may need the courage to practice humble leadership.
Someone may need to know that spiritual abuse is not the character of Christ.
Someone may need to remember that even after religious disappointment, the Gospel is still good news.
Maybe your response is a testimony of a pastor who served your family in secret.
Maybe it is a confession that you have wanted recognition more than obedience.
Maybe it is a quiet request for prayer because you are still healing from church hurt.
There is no need to expose private wounds publicly. But your honest reflection may encourage someone who thought they were struggling alone.
And if you believe this ministry is helping people encounter the truth of God's Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from pressure.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
You do not have to give money to prove your love for Jesus.
And you do not have to purchase access to His grace.
Those free resources are part of the mission: helping people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and become more firmly rooted in Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The Word of God must never become a tool for manipulating people's generosity.
And a ministry that teaches servant leadership must be willing to practice it in the way it asks for support.
That is part of what makes John 13 so powerful.
It does not allow us to preach humility to others while exempting ourselves.
It calls the preacher and the congregation.
The giver and the receiver.
The leader and the follower.
The wounded and the one who must repent.
All of us.
Back to Jesus.
Back to the basin.
Back to the towel.
Back to the cross.
Because the final answer to spiritual pride is not finding a more impressive religious personality.
It is beholding the Savior who had all authority and still chose to kneel.
The world may measure greatness by how many people stand when you enter a room.
Jesus showed His disciples a different kind of greatness.
One that bends down.
One that loves sacrificially.
One that tells the truth.
One that refuses to use people as stepping stones toward personal glory.
And one that ultimately leads us to the cross, where the sinless Son of God gave His life for sinners.
So before we ask why some Christian leaders expect to be treated like royalty, let every one of us ask a more personal question.
If Jesus walked into my life today carrying a towel, would He find me serving others—or demanding that others serve me?
That question is not meant to leave us hopeless.
It is meant to bring us to repentance.
Because the same Jesus who exposes our pride also offers forgiveness.
The same Jesus who commands us to serve also supplies grace for transformed living.
