And the same Jesus who knelt before His disciples is now the risen and exalted Lord, worthy of every knee bowing before Him (Philippians 2:9–11).
His humility never diminished His glory.
It revealed the depth of His love.
And His glory never made Him indifferent to our need.
That is the King we follow.
Not a king who demands that wounded sinners build his reputation.
But the King who gave Himself to redeem them.
The most dangerous throne in the Church may be the one we have quietly built inside our own hearts—and the only King who can save us from it is the One who first knelt with a towel.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD SENT A LYING SPIRIT… BUT WHY? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT KING AHAB THAT EVERY CHRISTIAN NEEDS TO HEAR
paragraphs: GOD SENT A LYING SPIRIT… BUT WHY? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT KING AHAB THAT EVERY CHRISTIAN NEEDS TO HEAR

What if the most frightening judgment of God isn't that He stops speaking to you—but that He allows you to keep hearing exactly what you desperately want to believe? The disturbing vision in 1 Kings 22:19–23 reveals what happens when a heart repeatedly rejects the truth. And hidden within this ancient royal scandal is a warning about deception, repentance, and the mercy of Jesus Christ that may be closer to your own life than you realize.
There were four hundred prophets telling a king exactly what he wanted to hear.
Four hundred voices.
One message.
Victory.
Success.
Everything was going to be fine.
And then there was one man standing against them.
One prophet who refused to change God's message just because the king didn't like it.
His name was Micaiah.
And what he revealed about the unseen world was so disturbing that people are still asking the same question thousands of years later.
Why would a holy God send a lying spirit into the mouths of prophets?
Read that question again.
Because this isn't a story about Satan deceiving someone while God helplessly watches.
The Bible actually describes a heavenly scene in which the LORD announces judgment, a spirit offers to deceive Ahab's prophets, and the LORD authorizes the mission.
It sounds unsettling.
Almost scandalous.

And if you've ever wondered whether God could allow someone to believe a lie, whether spiritual deception can become judgment, or whether the voices you trust are actually telling you the truth, you need to understand what happened in that throne room.
But there's something even more heartbreaking buried in this passage.
Ahab was warned about the deception before it destroyed him.
He heard the truth.
He recognized the prophet who spoke it.
And he still marched toward his own destruction.
That is where this story stops being merely about an ancient king.
And starts asking questions about us.
The story begins in 1 Kings 22.
King Ahab of Israel wanted to reclaim Ramoth-gilead from Syria. He invited King Jehoshaphat of Judah to join him in battle.
Jehoshaphat agreed to cooperate, but first requested something that every believer should take seriously.
“Enquire, I pray thee, at the word of the LORD to day.” (1 Kings 22:5, KJV)
Before the battle.
Before the strategy.
Before the armies moved.
Seek the LORD.
Ahab gathered approximately four hundred prophets, and their answer was overwhelmingly positive.
Go to battle.
You will succeed.
The Lord will deliver the city into your hands.
Imagine standing in that royal court.
The confidence.
The excitement.
The religious declarations.
The atmosphere of certainty.
Everybody seemed to agree.
And when everybody agrees with what you already want, questioning the message can feel unnecessary.
But Jehoshaphat sensed something was missing.
He asked whether there was another prophet of the LORD.
Ahab reluctantly admitted that there was one.
Micaiah, son of Imlah.
Then he said something that exposes the spiritual condition of his heart.
“I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.” (1 Kings 22:8, KJV)
There it is.
Not because Micaiah had been proven false.
Not because he was corrupt.
Not because he worshiped another god.
Ahab hated him because his messages were unpleasant.
The king had already decided what kind of truth he was willing to receive.
And that is where deception becomes dangerous.
Not simply when someone tells you a lie.
But when your heart begins treating correction as an enemy.
Some of us know what that feels like.
We want God to bless the relationship, but we don't want Him confronting the compromise.
We want Him to prosper the decision, but we don't want Him questioning the motives.
We want a sermon that comforts us, but not one that exposes what we've been hiding.
We want the promise without the repentance.
The crown without the cross.
The peace without surrender.
And sometimes, without realizing it, we begin surrounding ourselves with voices that agree with us instead of voices that lead us closer to Christ.
But the most dangerous voice in your life may not be the one that openly opposes God.
It may be the one that uses God's name to reassure you while you're walking away from His Word.
When Micaiah finally appeared, he initially echoed the favorable prediction, apparently in a manner Ahab recognized as insincere.
The king demanded the truth.
And Micaiah gave it.
He described Israel scattered upon the hills like sheep without a shepherd, indicating that the coming battle would leave the nation without its king.
Then he revealed an extraordinary vision.
“I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.” (1 Kings 22:19, KJV)
Stop there for a moment.
The earthly king was seated on his throne, surrounded by powerful people who told him what he wanted.
But Micaiah was shown another throne.
A greater throne.
A throne Ahab could not control.
The throne of the LORD.
The Hebrew text begins with the words:
רָאִיתִי אֶת־יְהוָה יֹשֵׁב עַל־כִּסְאוֹ
Ra'iti et-YHWH yoshev al-kis'o.
“I saw the LORD sitting on His throne.”
That detail matters.
Before the lying spirit is mentioned, Scripture establishes who reigns.
Not Ahab.
Not the prophets.
Not the spirit.
The LORD.
The Hebrew verb yoshev, meaning “sitting” or “seated,” presents God as enthroned.
This vision does not portray heaven in panic.
It portrays divine sovereignty.
The outcome is not beyond God's knowledge or authority.
And then comes the question that has troubled readers for centuries.
The LORD asks who will persuade Ahab to go up to Ramoth-gilead and fall there.
Different proposals are described.
Then a spirit comes forward.
The spirit says:
“I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” (1 Kings 22:22, KJV)
In Hebrew, the crucial phrase is:
רוּחַ שֶׁקֶר
Ruach sheqer.
A spirit of falsehood.
A lying spirit.
The word ruach can mean spirit, wind, or breath depending on context.
The word sheqer means falsehood, deception, or a lie.
There is no need to soften what the passage says.
The spirit proposes to deceive.
And the LORD responds:
“Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so.” (1 Kings 22:22, KJV)
Then Micaiah announces:
“Now therefore, behold, the LORD hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets, and the LORD hath spoken evil concerning thee.” (1 Kings 22:23, KJV)
How can that be?
Does God lie?
Does He approve of dishonesty?
Does He tempt people into evil?
And if He is perfectly holy, why would He authorize a spirit of deception?
These questions deserve more than a shallow religious answer.
Because the Bible is equally clear about another truth.
“God, that cannot lie.” (Titus 1:2, KJV)
And Hebrews 6:18 declares that it is impossible for God to lie.
James 1:13 teaches that God does not tempt anyone with evil.
So we cannot interpret 1 Kings 22 as though God suddenly became dishonest or morally corrupt.
God's holiness does not disappear when His judgment becomes difficult for us to understand.
The distinction lies in what the passage actually describes.
God is not presented as speaking a false prophecy Himself.
The spirit proposes deception.
God authorizes the spirit's activity as part of His judgment upon Ahab.
And most importantly, God sends Micaiah to expose the deception openly.
That last detail changes everything.
Ahab is not left without warning.
The king hears the entire account.
He is told that the prophets' message is deceptive.
He is told that disaster has been decreed.
He is given the opportunity to hear the truth before entering battle.
The narrative is not an invitation to believe that every misfortune proves God has deceived someone.
Nor does it authorize believers to accuse every mistaken teacher of being controlled by a lying spirit.
It is a specific prophetic account of judgment against a particular king whose rebellion had been repeatedly confronted.
And to understand why judgment had reached this point, we need to remember who Ahab was.
This was not a spiritually innocent man who had spent his life desperately searching for God's will.
Ahab had an extensive history of rebellion.
He promoted Baal worship in Israel.
He married Jezebel, whose influence intensified idolatry.
He tolerated and participated in a royal system that persecuted faithful servants of the LORD.
And in 1 Kings 21, he benefited from the judicial murder of Naboth, whose vineyard he desired.
Naboth had refused to surrender his ancestral inheritance.
Jezebel arranged for false witnesses to accuse him.
Naboth was executed.
And Ahab took possession of the vineyard.
Think about that.
A man died because a king wanted something that did not belong to him.
False testimony was used to destroy an innocent man.
And now, in 1 Kings 22, false prophetic testimony becomes part of the judgment against the king.
The narrative does not explicitly say this is a one-for-one punishment for Naboth's death.
But the moral irony is difficult to miss.
Ahab's kingdom had been corrupted by lies.
And now lies surrounded his throne.
Yet even before this, God had shown Ahab extraordinary mercy.
After Elijah pronounced judgment upon him in 1 Kings 21, Ahab humbled himself, tore his clothes, wore sackcloth, and fasted.
And God noticed.
The LORD told Elijah that because Ahab had humbled himself, the announced disaster upon his house would be delayed (1 Kings 21:27–29).
Let that settle into your heart.
Even Ahab.
Even this wicked king.
Even a man associated with idolatry, injustice, and bloodshed.
God took notice when he humbled himself.
The text does not portray Ahab's temporary humiliation as the complete transformation of his heart.
His later actions reveal that his resistance to God's Word remained.
But it does reveal something astonishing about the character of God.
The LORD is not indifferent to humility, even in someone with a terrible history.
And that makes the tragedy of 1 Kings 22 even heavier.
Ahab had experienced warning.
He had witnessed mercy.
He had heard prophetic truth.
But he continued resisting the Word of the LORD.
This brings us to the most frightening possibility in the entire account.
What if one of God's judgments upon persistent rebellion is allowing a person to experience the consequences of the falsehood they insist on embracing?
Scripture presents a related principle in Romans 1.
Three times in that chapter, Paul describes God giving people over to the consequences of their sinful desires and distorted thinking (Romans 1:24, 26, 28).
Notice the progression.
People exchange the truth of God for a lie.
They reject the Creator's rightful place.
And God gives them over.
Not because their choices are morally good.
Not because He has ceased to be holy.
But because divine judgment can include allowing human rebellion to bear its bitter fruit.
Second Thessalonians 2:10–12 also speaks of those who refuse to love the truth and are consequently subjected to powerful delusion in a context of final judgment.
These passages do not describe precisely identical events, and we should not force every detail into the same category.
But together they reveal a sobering biblical pattern.
Persistent rejection of truth is spiritually dangerous.
A lie does not become true because it is comforting.
A wrong direction does not become safe because many people recommend it.
And the approval of a crowd does not overturn the Word of God.
Somebody reading this has been asking God for confirmation about something He has already confronted through Scripture.
You have heard the warning.
You have felt the conviction.
You know what obedience would require.
But the cost frightens you.
So you keep looking for another voice.
Another opinion.
Another interpretation.
Another person who will tell you that what you are doing is acceptable.
Please understand something.
Not every disagreement is rebellion.
Not every difficult decision has an obvious answer.
Faithful Christians can sincerely differ over matters where Scripture does not speak directly.
And a believer should never surrender discernment merely because someone claims to speak for God.
But where Scripture clearly exposes sin, collecting reassurance cannot make disobedience holy.
And where Christ calls us to repent, no amount of religious approval can replace surrender.
This is why the New Testament commands believers to test the spirits (1 John 4:1).
This is why the Bereans were commended for examining the Scriptures to see whether what they heard was true (Acts 17:11).
This is why Paul warned that people would gather teachers to satisfy their own desires rather than endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:3–4).
The danger is not simply that false teachers exist.
The danger is that our own desires can make their messages attractive.
And now look again at Ahab.
He had four hundred voices offering reassurance.
He had one prophet warning of disaster.
But the number of voices did not determine which message was true.
God's Word did.
And the story becomes even more tragic when Ahab decides to enter the battle anyway.
He tries to protect himself by disguising his identity.
He tells Jehoshaphat to wear his royal robes while he enters the battle in disguise.
Perhaps he thought he could avoid being targeted.
Perhaps he believed he could escape the consequences of the prophecy.
But the biblical account describes an archer drawing his bow at random and striking Ahab between the joints of his armor.
The king was mortally wounded.
By evening, he was dead.
The prophecy had been fulfilled.
And the man who had rejected the truth could not outmaneuver the judgment God had announced.
Ahab could disguise his clothing.
But he could not disguise his heart before God.
He could conceal his identity from the enemy.
But he could not hide from the LORD who sees all things.
He could surround himself with prophets.
But he could not silence the truth by surrounding it with applause.
Are we asking God to guide our lives, or are we asking Him to approve the lives we have already decided to live?
That question reaches beyond kings and battlefields.
It enters homes.
Churches.
Relationships.
Businesses.
Private conversations.
Secret habits.
It reaches the person who knows they need to apologize but keeps defending their pride.
The husband who knows he has wounded his wife but keeps looking for excuses.
The wife who is carrying bitterness and quietly allowing resentment to become her identity.
The young believer who knows a relationship is pulling them away from Christ but fears being alone.
The church leader who has become more concerned about reputation than repentance.
The person who appears spiritually strong in public while secretly becoming exhausted from pretending.
And perhaps the person who has been reading this with a quiet ache in their chest.
Because you recognize yourself.
Not in every detail of Ahab's wickedness.
But in the painful familiarity of resisting something you know God is asking you to confront.
There is something deeply human about wanting the truth to be less costly than it is.
We want forgiveness without confession.
Healing without vulnerability.
Restoration without accountability.
Transformation without surrender.
But Jesus never offered a counterfeit peace.
He offered something infinitely better.
The truth that sets people free.
Jesus said:
“And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.” (John 8:32, KJV)
In the Greek text, the central phrase reads:
ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς
hē alētheia eleutherōsei hymas.
“The truth will set you free.”
The word alētheia means truth.
And eleutherōsei means “will free” or “will liberate.”
But Jesus was not speaking about truth as a vague inspirational concept.
In John 8:31–32, He connected this freedom with abiding in His Word and becoming His disciples.
Later, in John 8:34–36, He explained the bondage of sin and declared that the Son Himself gives genuine freedom.
And in John 14:6, Jesus identified Himself as the way, the truth, and the life.
This is where the story of Ahab leads us toward the heart of the Gospel.
Ahab surrounded himself with voices that promised victory while concealing destruction.
Jesus came as the Truth who exposes our sin so that we might receive life.
Ahab hated a prophet who spoke what he did not want to hear.
Jesus was rejected by sinners, yet willingly gave His life to save sinners.
Ahab attempted to escape judgment through disguise.
Jesus willingly endured the cross, bearing the judgment deserved by His people.
Ahab's story ends with the death of a king who resisted God's Word.
The Gospel announces the death and resurrection of the King who perfectly obeyed His Father and conquered sin and death.
The contrast is staggering.
And the grace is greater still.
Because the same Jesus who exposes our darkness does not invite repentant sinners to remain trapped in shame.
He calls us into the light.
He does not promise that repentance will be painless.
He promises that those who come to Him will not be cast out (John 6:37).
He does not excuse sin.
He forgives and transforms those who turn to Him in faith.
He does not call evil good.
He gives sinners a new life through His death and resurrection.
That is why the Gospel is not merely good advice for becoming a better person.
It is good news about what God has accomplished through Jesus Christ for people who could never save themselves.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” (Ephesians 2:8, KJV)
Grace.
Not a religious performance.
Not a carefully managed reputation.
Not a lifetime of pretending we never struggled.
Grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And grace never means that truth no longer matters.
It means that the truth about our sin no longer has to be the end of our story.
The cross tells us how seriously God takes sin.
The empty tomb tells us how completely Christ has triumphed.
And the call to repentance tells us that mercy is not permission to keep embracing the darkness.
Maybe that is what someone needs to hear today.
You have been afraid that if you finally tell the truth about your life, everything will fall apart.
You have spent years protecting an image.
You have learned how to smile while carrying guilt.
You have learned how to say “I'm blessed” when your soul feels far from God.
You have learned how to sound spiritual while avoiding the one conversation you know you need to have.
And perhaps you have begun believing that God would rather hear a polished prayer than an honest confession.
But listen to the promise of Scripture.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9, KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not an invitation to treat sin lightly.
It is an invitation to bring sin into the light before the God whose forgiveness rests upon the finished work of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to negotiate with your darkness.
You do not have to keep defending what is destroying you.
You do not have to wait until you feel worthy to come to Christ.
Come in repentance.
Come in faith.
Come honestly.
And when you fall, do not make hiding your home.
Return to the Savior.
This is what makes the story of Ahab so heartbreaking.
The king heard the warning, but refused to turn.
Yet you are reading that warning now.
And you are still able to respond.
We should never presume to know exactly how much time another person has, or declare that every hardship is a particular act of divine judgment.
But Scripture repeatedly calls us not to harden our hearts when we hear God's voice (Hebrews 3:15).
Today is an opportunity to listen.
To examine what we believe.
To test what we are being taught.
To repent where God's Word exposes sin.
To stop confusing popularity with truth.
And to follow Jesus even when obedience is costly.
Perhaps the deepest question in this entire account is not simply why God authorized a lying spirit in Ahab's judgment.
Perhaps it is why Ahab, after being told that his prophets were deceiving him, still chose to believe the message that would destroy him.
Because that is the warning we cannot afford to miss.
The most dangerous lie is often the one that gives us permission to keep living exactly as we please.
And the most loving truth may be the one that interrupts us before we ruin what God has entrusted to us.
If this has exposed something in your heart, don't rush to defend yourself.
Talk to Jesus.
You can begin with a prayer as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, I have not always loved the truth. Sometimes I have searched for approval when I needed correction. Sometimes I have defended what You were calling me to surrender. Forgive me. Expose every lie I have embraced. Give me a heart that loves Your Word more than my comfort, Your holiness more than my reputation, and Your presence more than the approval of people. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to follow You in truth. Restore what sin has damaged, and make my life a testimony of Your grace. Amen.”
And if that prayer describes where you are, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.

You do not need to disclose private sins or painful details publicly. God already knows your heart, and there is wisdom in seeking personal help from a trustworthy, biblically grounded Christian when you need it.
But sometimes a simple confession of dependence upon Christ becomes the beginning of a much-needed conversation.
And perhaps somebody else reading the comments will realize they are not the only one fighting to remain faithful.
Please don't let this message end with you.
Someone may be surrounded by people who tell them what they want to hear.
Someone may be drifting from Jesus while believing everything is fine.
Someone may be carrying a burden of shame and needs to discover that Christ still receives repentant sinners.
It is about becoming more faithful to the Word of God.
Because the Christian life was never meant to be sustained by one emotional moment.
We need God's Word continually.
We need prayer.
We need sound teaching.
We need fellow believers who love us enough to encourage us and, when necessary, correct us.
Not as a test of whether you truly love God.
Not because anyone can purchase His favor.
Not because giving money earns forgiveness or makes someone a more valuable Christian.
But because when believers freely and prayerfully support faithful Gospel work, their generosity can help that work continue and reach others.
Every article takes effort.
Every biblical resource has a purpose.
Every opportunity to encourage a struggling believer or help someone understand the Gospel matters.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
Not out of guilt.
Not out of pressure.
But out of gratitude for what Christ has done and a desire to serve others.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, encouragement, and opportunities to begin meaningful conversations about Jesus.
And beyond any product or discount, the greater purpose is discipleship.
Pray for this ministry.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Open your Bible with someone who has questions.
Your faithful witness matters, and God's grace is not measured by the amount you can give.
Because ultimately, Gospel Warrior is not about building an audience around a personality.
It is about pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
The One who speaks truth when the world offers deception.
The One who calls sinners to repentance without abandoning the promise of mercy.
The One who died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The One who can take a life stained by compromise, pride, failure, and regret and transform it through His grace.
And as we return one final time to that ancient battlefield, there is something we must not forget.
Ahab had a crown.
He had an army.
He had influence.
He had hundreds of prophets telling him victory was certain.
But none of those things could save him from the consequences of rejecting God's Word.
And here we are, centuries later, with more access to Scripture than many generations could ever have imagined.
Bibles on our phones.
Sermons available in seconds.
Devotionals, commentaries, and Christian teaching within reach.
Yet the central question remains painfully unchanged.
Will we love the truth enough to obey it?
Will we listen when Scripture corrects us?
Will we choose Christ when following Him costs us something?
Will we surrender the lie that comforts us for the Savior who can actually set us free?
The answer does not begin with being perfect.
It begins with coming honestly to Jesus.
Because the Gospel does not say that people with scandalous histories are beyond redemption.
It says that Christ came to save sinners.
And no sinner who truly turns to Him in faith needs to believe that their past must have the final word.
That is the hope we proclaim.
That is the grace we celebrate.
That is the truth worth sharing.
Ahab died clinging to a lie that promised him victory. You do not have to keep clinging to the lie that is stealing your life—Jesus Christ is still calling you into the truth that sets you free.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN EVERYONE CALLED A SINNER… AND THE FEET JESUS REFUSED TO PULL AWAY
paragraphs: THE WOMAN EVERYONE CALLED A SINNER… AND THE FEET JESUS REFUSED TO PULL AWAY

She walked into a room where nobody wanted her, carrying a past everybody remembered. But when her tears touched the feet of Jesus, something happened that exposed the hearts of the religious, shattered the power of shame, and revealed a Savior who sees what the world refuses to see.
There is something deeply unsettling about this story.
A woman entered a house where she was not welcome.
She was known for her sins. Her reputation had apparently arrived long before she did. The people in that room did not need an introduction. They already had an opinion.
And she knew it.
Imagine walking into a room where people know the worst things about your life.
Not your kindness. Not your private battles. Not the nights you cried because you hated what you had become.
Only your failures.
Imagine knowing that every glance might be another accusation.
Every whisper might be another reminder.
Every uncomfortable silence might be another judgment.
Now imagine walking into that room anyway.
Not because you had finally become respectable.
Not because you had convinced everyone you had changed.
But because Jesus was there.
And somehow, being near Him mattered more than being humiliated by everyone else.
That is where this story begins.
But what happened next reveals something far greater than a woman crying at the feet of Christ.
It reveals the terrifying possibility that a person can sit at the same table as Jesus, know religious language, maintain a respectable reputation, and still completely misunderstand His heart.
And it reveals something equally astonishing.
The person everyone considered spiritually unworthy might be the one who understands grace most deeply.
In Luke 7:36–50, Jesus accepted an invitation to eat at the home of a Pharisee named Simon.
Simon belonged to a religious movement known for its concern with obedience to God's law and traditions of religious purity.
He had invited Jesus into his home.
There would have been food, conversation, and the social expectations surrounding a meal in that culture.
Then something unexpected happened.
Luke writes:
— Luke 7:37, KJV
Notice what Scripture does not tell us.
It does not give her name.
It does not identify the specific sins for which she was known.
It does not say she was a prostitute, although that assumption has frequently appeared in retellings of this passage.
It does not identify her as Mary Magdalene.
And it does not identify her as Mary of Bethany, whose anointing of Jesus is recorded in another setting.
Luke simply calls her a woman who was known as a sinner.
That description was enough for Simon.
But it was not the whole story for Jesus.
Because people often remember the chapter of your life you are most desperate to leave behind.
They remember what you did.
They remember who you were.
They remember the scandal.
But they cannot always see what God is doing inside you now.
And perhaps that is why this story still hurts.
Because somewhere, someone reading this has spent years trying to escape a reputation that other people refuse to let die.
Maybe it was an affair.
Maybe an addiction.
Maybe a betrayal.
Maybe years of hypocrisy, secret compromises, or decisions that damaged people you genuinely loved.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is not what others remember.
It is what you cannot seem to forgive yourself for.
You have asked God for mercy, but the memory still returns.
You have tried to move forward, but shame keeps dragging yesterday into today.
You have smiled in church while silently wondering whether the people sitting beside you would still embrace you if they knew everything.
And beneath all those thoughts lies one question you are almost afraid to ask.
Would Jesus still let someone like me come close?
The woman in Luke 7 gives us a remarkable picture of the answer.
She approached Jesus from behind as He reclined at the table.
Then the tears began.
Luke 7:38 says:
"And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment."
Read that slowly.
She did not arrive with a prepared speech recorded for us.
She did not stand before the guests and explain her circumstances.
She did not attempt to defend her reputation.
She wept.
And the tears fell upon the feet of Jesus.
In the Greek text, Luke uses the word βρέχειν (brechein), meaning to wet or moisten, describing what her tears did to His feet.
The picture is intimate and deeply human.
Her tears were so abundant that they wet His feet.
She then wiped them with her hair, kissed them repeatedly, and anointed them with perfume.
The Greek verb κατεφίλει (katephilei) conveys affectionate kissing, and its form in this passage presents the action as continuing.
This was not a quick ceremonial gesture.
It was an extraordinary expression of love and humility.
And Jesus allowed it.
He did not pull His feet away.
He did not publicly shame her.
He did not demand that she first explain herself to the people watching.
He did not tell her that her reputation made her unfit to approach Him.
He received her act of devotion.
But we must understand something important.
Jesus was not approving her sins.
He was receiving a repentant sinner.
There is a world of difference.
The Gospel never teaches that sin is harmless.
Sin separates us from the holiness of God. It corrupts our desires, wounds relationships, and leads toward death.
Romans 6:23 declares that the wages of sin is death.
Jesus did not come to convince sinners that repentance was unnecessary.
He came to save sinners.
And salvation is far greater than being told that our wrongdoing does not matter.
It means that the Son of God takes sin so seriously that He willingly goes to the cross to deal with it.
Grace is not God pretending that evil is good.
Grace is God providing redemption for the guilty through Jesus Christ.
And the woman at His feet was about to discover how publicly and personally Jesus would speak of forgiveness.
But before Jesus addressed her, another heart was being exposed.
Simon was watching.
And what he thought reveals the danger of religious pride.
Luke 7:39 records his private judgment:
"This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman this is that toucheth him: for she is a sinner."
Simon thought he understood the situation.
He saw a sinful woman touching a religious teacher.
And he concluded that Jesus must lack spiritual discernment.
Surely, Simon reasoned, a true prophet would know what kind of woman this was.
But here is the extraordinary irony.
Jesus knew.
He knew enough to recognize the woman's condition.
And He also knew what Simon was thinking.
The Pharisee believed Jesus was failing to recognize sin.
In reality, Simon was failing to recognize mercy.
One man saw a scandal.
Jesus saw a woman whose love revealed a heart responding to grace.
And the Savior was about to show Simon that his greatest problem was not the woman standing near the table.
It was the pride sitting comfortably inside his own heart.
Jesus turned toward Simon and said that He had something to tell him.
Then He described two debtors.
One owed five hundred denarii.
The other owed fifty.
A denarius was commonly associated with a day's wage for a laborer, making both debts significant, although one was ten times larger than the other.
Neither debtor could repay what he owed.
That detail matters.
The smaller debtor was not capable of saving himself simply because his debt was smaller.
Both were helpless before the creditor.
Then the creditor freely forgave both debts.
Jesus asked Simon which debtor would love the creditor more.
Simon answered that it would be the one forgiven more.
Jesus affirmed his answer.
And suddenly the story was no longer merely about money.
It was about forgiveness.
About love.
About the human tendency to measure ourselves against other sinners instead of recognizing our own need for mercy.
The Greek verb used for the creditor's gracious cancellation of the debts is ἐχαρίσατο (echarisato), from χαρίζομαι (charizomai), a verb associated with freely giving or graciously granting.
The debtors did not purchase their release.
They received it.
That is essential to understanding what happened at Jesus' feet.
The woman was not buying forgiveness with perfume.
She was not purchasing salvation through tears.
She was not earning God's acceptance by demonstrating enough emotion.
Her love was evidence of her response to grace, not the price she paid for it.
Jesus then turned toward the woman while continuing to speak to Simon.
And what He said must have made that room profoundly uncomfortable.
"Seest thou this woman?"
— Luke 7:44, KJV
What a question.
Simon had been looking at her the entire time.
But Jesus asked whether he actually saw her.
Because there is a difference between looking at someone and seeing them.
Simon saw her reputation.
Jesus drew attention to her devotion.
Simon saw a category.
Jesus saw a person.
Simon saw the sin associated with her past.
Jesus recognized the love being expressed before Him.
And perhaps that question should disturb us more than we want to admit.
Do you see this woman?
Do you see the single mother whose history has become church gossip?
Do you see the young man struggling with pornography who is terrified to ask for help?
Do you see the former addict who fears that one mistake will convince everyone that he has never changed?
Do you see the believer who fell into sin, repented, and now wonders whether there is still a place for them among God's people?
Do you see the person who has hurt others and must still take responsibility, but desperately needs to know that repentance and restoration are possible?
Or do you only see what they did?
This is not a call to ignore wrongdoing, silence victims, or remove accountability.
Biblical mercy does not erase the need for truth, justice, restitution, or changed behavior.
But neither does biblical holiness authorize us to treat repentant sinners as permanently beyond the reach of God's grace.
Jesus never confused compassion with moral compromise.
And He never needed cruelty to demonstrate holiness.
Then He confronted Simon with three failures of hospitality.
Simon had provided no water for Jesus' feet.
The woman had wet His feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
Simon had given Him no kiss of greeting.
The woman had continued kissing His feet.
Simon had not anointed His head with oil.
The woman had anointed His feet with perfume.
These gestures carried meaning in the social world of the passage, although not every omission necessarily constituted a formal violation of hospitality.
Jesus' point was unmistakable.
The woman whom Simon despised had demonstrated an extraordinary love that Simon himself had failed to show.
Simon had welcomed Jesus into his house.
But the woman had approached Him with a heart overflowing in devotion.
And here lies a warning that every Christian, including the person writing these words, needs to hear.
It is possible to become familiar with religious activity while losing our tenderness toward Christ.
We can learn the vocabulary of grace without being humbled by it.
We can defend biblical truth while forgetting that the truth reveals our own desperate need for a Savior.
We can recognize sin in someone else's life while quietly excusing the pride, bitterness, envy, and lovelessness growing inside our own.
We can attend worship and still withhold our hearts.
We can become more concerned with looking righteous than with being reconciled to God.
Simon was close enough to Jesus to share a meal.
Yet he was in danger of missing the significance of the mercy unfolding before his eyes.
The woman had no impressive religious standing in the narrative.
Yet her actions displayed a love that Jesus publicly acknowledged.
Then came one of the most important statements in the entire account.
Jesus said:
"Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little."
— Luke 7:47, KJV
This verse must be read carefully.
At first glance, someone might assume Jesus meant that her love earned forgiveness.
But the parable immediately preceding it establishes the opposite order.
The creditor forgave the debts, and that forgiveness produced love.
The woman's extraordinary love demonstrated the reality of forgiveness, rather than purchasing it.
The Greek word ἀφέωνται (apheōntai), translated "are forgiven," is a perfect passive form of ἀφίημι (aphiēmi).
It presents her sins as having been forgiven, with the resulting state continuing.
Jesus was not teaching that enough tears can remove guilt.
He was revealing the gracious forgiveness that lay behind her love.
This is why we must resist turning her story into a message that says, "Cry hard enough, worship passionately enough, give enough money, and God will finally accept you."
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel is that sinners who cannot rescue themselves are called to repent and believe in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection provide the foundation of forgiveness and new life.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
The woman did not save herself by washing Jesus' feet.
Her tears were not a second Savior.
Her perfume was not a substitute for the cross.
And her public humiliation was not payment for her sins.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
Her actions expressed the love of someone who recognized how much mercy she needed.
And this changes the way we read the entire encounter.
Because the greatest miracle in that room was not that Jesus tolerated an embarrassing interruption.
It was that the Holy One of God could receive a sinner without becoming sinful Himself.
The religious instinct of Simon's judgment was to create distance from someone he regarded as morally contaminated.
But Jesus was not made unholy by the woman's touch.
His holiness was not fragile.
His mercy was not weakness.
His authority was not threatened by her past.
He was the Savior who came to seek and save the lost.
And the road that would eventually lead Him to Calvary was already revealing the depth of His mission.
Think about it.
The woman brought perfume.
Jesus would ultimately give His life.
The woman came carrying the shame of her sins.
Jesus would bear sin's judgment in His saving work upon the cross.
The woman knelt at His feet.
And those feet would one day be pierced in the crucifixion.
Luke does not explicitly connect these particular details in this scene, so we should not pretend they are hidden predictions.
But as we read this encounter in the light of the completed Gospel, the contrast is overwhelming.
She brought what she could.
Christ would accomplish what she never could.
She could express love.
Only He could provide salvation.
And that is why this story is not ultimately about the greatness of a woman's tears.
It is about the greatness of the Savior who received her.
There is another detail we cannot overlook.
Jesus did not merely defend her before Simon.
He spoke directly to her.
"And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven."
— Luke 7:48, KJV
Imagine what those words meant.
For a woman whose public identity was bound to sin, Jesus spoke a declaration of forgiveness.
The people at the table began asking among themselves who this man was who even forgave sins.
Their question was theologically significant.
In Scripture, forgiveness of sins ultimately belongs to God.
Jesus was exercising an authority that demanded an answer about His identity.
He was not merely offering emotional reassurance.
He was speaking with divine authority.
And then came the final words recorded to the woman.
"Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace."
— Luke 7:50, KJV
Not, "Your perfume has saved you."
Not, "Your tears have saved you."
Not, "Your public display has saved you."
Your faith has saved you.
The Greek reads:
Ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην.
Hē pistis sou sesōken se; poreuou eis eirēnēn.
"Your faith has saved you; go in peace."
The verb σέσωκέν (sesōken), from σῴζω (sōzō), is a perfect active form meaning "has saved," emphasizing a saving action with an enduring result.
And the final word, εἰρήνη (eirēnē), means peace.
This is more than a casual goodbye.
In the context of Jesus' declaration of forgiveness and salvation, it is a beautiful dismissal into the peace associated with God's saving mercy.
She entered a room where her sin was publicly remembered.
She left having heard Jesus declare forgiveness and salvation.
Luke does not tell us what happened to her afterward.
We do not know where she went, what conversations followed, or how her life unfolded.
Scripture leaves those details unwritten.
And perhaps that restraint is important.
We do not need to invent a dramatic future for her to recognize the extraordinary grace of what Jesus actually said.
Her story is already powerful enough.
But now the question turns toward us.
What if the thing keeping you away from Jesus is the very thing you most urgently need to bring before Him?
What if you have mistaken shame for repentance?
What if you believe that hating yourself is somehow proof that you are becoming holy?
What if you have spent years punishing yourself for sins that you should be confessing to God and turning away from in faith?
There is a difference between godly sorrow and hopeless condemnation.
Second Corinthians 7:10 teaches that godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, while worldly sorrow produces death.
True repentance does not merely say, "I feel terrible about what I did."
It turns toward God.
It acknowledges sin without excuses.
It seeks mercy through Christ.
And where our actions have harmed others, it bears fruit through changed conduct, responsibility, and appropriate efforts to make things right.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
It is refusing to let the past remain your master.
And faith is not confidence that you have finally become good enough.
It is trust in the Savior who is sufficient.
Perhaps you have been waiting to feel clean before approaching Jesus.
But sinners do not make themselves clean and then earn the right to come to Him.
They come to Him for cleansing.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice that Scripture does not say God forgives because we have successfully hidden the evidence.
It calls us to confession.
To truth.
To the light.
And to the mercy of God.
This does not mean that forgiveness eliminates every earthly consequence.
A broken marriage may require years of rebuilding trust.
A damaged relationship may not be restored immediately.
A criminal act may still carry legal consequences.
A person who has been harmed is not obligated to abandon wise boundaries simply because an offender says they have repented.
But none of those realities cancels the promise that genuine forgiveness and transformation are available through Jesus Christ.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying your life.
Grace is the beginning of a new way of living.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live godly lives.
The same grace that welcomes sinners also teaches them to leave sin behind.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not that your past was harmless.
It is that your past does not have to have the final word.
Not by rewriting history.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing the need for repentance.
But by redeeming sinners, giving new life, and transforming those who belong to Him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone in Christ is a new creature.
That is not a motivational slogan.
It is a declaration of what God's saving work makes possible.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this today.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because people know your worst chapter.
You are not too stained to repent.
You are not too far away to call upon His name.
You are not disqualified from seeking mercy because you once lived in rebellion.
But do not confuse the availability of grace with a guarantee that tomorrow will be yours.
The call of the Gospel is urgent.
Turn to Christ.
Not when you have successfully repaired your reputation.
Not when everybody has forgiven you.
Not when you can finally speak about your past without crying.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Today.
Because the same Jesus who received the woman in Simon's house is the risen Lord who calls sinners to Himself.
And He is worthy of more than our admiration.
He is worthy of our trust, worship, obedience, and entire lives.
If this story has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your sin for strangers to examine.
But you can take a small, sincere step toward the light.
And if you have experienced the forgiveness of Christ, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage someone who believes their life is already beyond redemption.
You never know who is silently reading.
The person who looks confident online may be carrying unbearable guilt.
The friend who never misses church may be struggling with secret sin.
The family member who seems distant from God may be longing for a reason to believe that forgiveness is still possible.
That is why sharing this message matters.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page, but because the truth of Christ deserves to be heard beyond the walls of our familiar circles.
We also want to speak openly about something important.
Producing and sharing Christ-centered teaching requires time, effort, resources, and continued support.
Our desire is to keep reaching people who are searching for truth, believers who need strengthening, and wounded hearts that need to hear the message of Jesus Christ.
It can be part of your personal Christian generosity and stewardship, offered with a grateful heart before God.
But we want to be clear about something Scripture makes essential.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that money can purchase spiritual reward.
But willing partnership in a mission that seeks to make Christ known.
These products are simply additional resources and expressions of encouragement. They are not measures of spiritual maturity, and purchasing them is never a requirement for discipleship.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share sound biblical teaching matters.
There is also a growing resource available to help you continue studying Scripture.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, strengthen their prayer lives, develop spiritual discernment, and deepen their walk with Jesus Christ.
Because the ultimate goal of this ministry is not to make people dependent on a Facebook page.
It is to point them toward Jesus Christ, His Word, and faithful life within His Church.
Because the woman in Luke 7 did not encounter a Savior who needed her perfume.
She encountered a Savior whose grace she desperately needed.
And that is where we must return before this story ends.
To the room.
To the table.
To Simon.
To the woman.
To Jesus.
Picture that final moment.
The religious guests were questioning His authority to forgive sins.
The woman had heard the words that mattered most.
"Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace."
We do not know whether she walked out still crying.
We do not know whether Simon's opinion changed.
We do not know whether the other guests treated her differently afterward.
But we know what Jesus said.
And that is enough.
Because the final authority over her standing before God did not belong to Simon.
It belonged to Christ.
And the same truth confronts us today.
People may remember your scandal.
Some may never understand your repentance.
Others may refuse to believe that you have changed.
And when you have harmed someone, their pain deserves to be taken seriously, even as you seek to walk in newness of life.
But no human reputation can replace the judgment of God.
And no human approval can accomplish the salvation that only Jesus gives.
So stop trying to purchase peace through endless self-punishment.
Stop mistaking religious appearance for a surrendered heart.
Stop believing that hiding your sin will somehow heal it.
Bring your guilt to Christ.
Confess what is true.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Trust the One who died for sinners and rose again.
And learn to walk in the peace that His Gospel provides.
The woman came to Jesus with tears.
But the deepest truth of the story is not that she cried.
It is that Jesus forgave.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
That is the beauty of grace.
And that is why no scandal is greater than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
The world may keep calling you by the name of your worst mistake, but when Christ forgives you, your sin no longer has the authority to write the ending of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU SIN SO MUCH THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT FINALLY LEAVES YOU?
paragraphs: CAN YOU SIN SO MUCH THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT FINALLY LEAVES YOU?
The Terrifying Silence After Repeated Sin, the Promise God Sealed Upon Your Soul, and the Grace That Still Calls You Home
There is a kind of silence that only a struggling Christian understands.
It comes after you have done the very thing you promised God you would never do again.
After another secret compromise. Another surrender to temptation. Another deleted conversation. Another night when conviction whispered, “Don't go there,” and you went anyway.
You knew the Scripture. You knew the consequences. You even felt that familiar warning in your conscience.
But you did it.
And now you're sitting alone, wondering whether something inside you has changed forever.
You try to pray, but the words feel empty.
You open your Bible, but the verses that once comforted you now seem to accuse you.
You remember how close God once felt. How freely you worshiped. How easily tears came when you heard the name of Jesus.
And suddenly, a question rises from somewhere deep inside your exhausted soul.
“What if I've sinned so many times that the Holy Spirit has finally left me?”
Not because you stopped believing in God.
But because you are terrified that God has stopped wanting anything to do with you.
If you've ever asked that question, please keep reading.
Because Scripture gives us an answer that is more comforting than our shame wants us to believe—and more serious than our flesh wants us to hear.
And somewhere between those two truths, we will find a Savior who does not treat sin lightly, yet still receives sinners who come to Him in repentance.
Before we go any further, we need to understand something.
Feeling far from God is not the same thing as being abandoned by God.
And feeling comfortable in sin is not the same thing as being secure in Christ.
Those two distinctions could change the way you understand your entire spiritual life.
The apostle Paul wrote something extraordinary to the Christians in Ephesus.

“In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory.” (Ephesians 1:13–14, KJV)
Read those words carefully.
Paul did not say believers were merely visited by the Holy Spirit.
He said they were sealed.
The Greek word translated “sealed” is ἐσφραγίσθητε (esphragisthēte), from the verb σφραγίζω (sphragizō).
It carries the idea of marking with a seal—identifying, authenticating, and indicating ownership or protection, depending on the context.
In the ancient world, seals could identify something as belonging to an authority or authenticate a document.
Paul uses this imagery to communicate something magnificent about salvation.
When you heard the Gospel and believed in Jesus Christ, God marked you as belonging to Him through the promised Holy Spirit.
Not because you had finally become flawless.
Not because you had conquered every temptation.
Not because you would never struggle again.
But because salvation rests upon the finished work of Jesus Christ, received through faith.
And Paul goes even further.
He calls the Holy Spirit the ἀρραβών (arrabōn) of our inheritance.
The word refers to a pledge, deposit, or guarantee—a first installment that assures what is to come.
The Spirit is not presented as a temporary emotional reward for Christians who manage to have a perfect week.
He is God's pledge of the inheritance promised to those who belong to Christ.
That is astonishing.
But now comes the question that makes this subject so difficult.
If believers are sealed by the Holy Spirit, why does Paul later warn those same believers not to grieve Him?
“And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.” (Ephesians 4:30, KJV)
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, or He will immediately abandon you.”
He says, in effect, do not grieve the very Spirit by whom you have been sealed for the day of redemption.
The Greek word translated “grieve” is λυπεῖτε (lypeite), from λυπέω (lypeō), meaning to cause sorrow, distress, or grief.
This is deeply personal language.
The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal spiritual force.
He is not a religious feeling that disappears whenever your emotions change.
He is the divine Person who dwells in God's people.
And Scripture says He can be grieved.
Think about that.
Your bitterness matters.
Your dishonesty matters.
Your sexual immorality matters.
Your unforgiveness matters.
The words you speak when nobody from church is listening matter.
The private decisions you excuse because nobody knows about them matter.
Not because God is looking for an excuse to stop loving His children.
But because the God who has drawn near to us is holy.
And the Spirit who indwells believers is not indifferent to the sin that Jesus died to save us from.
Look at the context of Ephesians 4.
Paul warns against falsehood, corrupt speech, sinful anger, stealing, bitterness, wrath, and malice. He then calls believers to kindness, tenderheartedness, and forgiveness.
This means grieving the Spirit is not merely about an isolated dramatic failure.
It can happen in ordinary moments when we choose what contradicts the character of Christ.
That grudge you've been feeding.
That lie you've been maintaining.
That person you've been destroying with your words.
That secret habit you've learned to defend.
The Spirit does not approve of these things simply because we continue attending church.
Grace does not make sin harmless. Grace makes transformation possible.
And this is where we must confront a dangerous misunderstanding.
Some Christians imagine the Holy Spirit leaves and returns repeatedly according to their latest spiritual performance.
They sin, so He leaves.
They confess, so He returns.
They stumble again, so He leaves again.
Their entire relationship with God becomes a revolving door of fear.
But Ephesians 1:13–14 and 4:30 do not describe the Spirit's sealing in that way.
Paul grounds Christian hope in God's saving promise, not in the believer's ability to maintain an uninterrupted record of obedience.
Yet another dangerous misunderstanding exists on the opposite side.
Some hear that believers are sealed and conclude that persistent, deliberate, unrepentant sin cannot possibly endanger their spiritual condition.
They begin treating grace as permission.
They say, “I'm saved anyway.”
They use the promises of God to silence the warnings of God.
And that is not biblical assurance.
That is presumption.
Scripture never teaches that we can embrace rebellion against Christ while remaining unconcerned about repentance.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts this directly.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Paul's answer is unmistakable.
The grace that saves us is not a license to continue making peace with the sin that enslaved us.
And this brings us to a man whose story should make every struggling believer stop and listen.
David.
The shepherd boy who became king.
The worshiper who wrote psalms.
The man who knew what it meant to experience God's favor.
And the man who committed adultery with Bathsheba, then arranged circumstances that led to the death of her husband, Uriah.
David was not ignorant of God's commandments.
He knew.
And still, he sinned.
Then he tried to cover it.
For a time, he continued living behind the appearance of royal authority while carrying the reality of hidden guilt.
But God saw everything.
When the prophet Nathan confronted him, the truth could no longer remain buried.
And out of that devastating confrontation came one of the most painful prayers in Scripture.
“Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.” (Psalm 51:11, KJV)
Those words have frightened generations of Christians.
Because if David feared losing the Holy Spirit, shouldn't we?
We must handle this passage carefully.
David lived under the old covenant, before the death, resurrection, and exaltation of Jesus Christ and before the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost.
In the Old Testament, the Spirit's empowering presence could be given for particular assignments, including kingship.
And David knew the story of Saul.
First Samuel 16:14 says that the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul.
David had seen what happened to a king who rebelled against God and lost the Spirit's empowering presence associated with his calling.
So when David cried, “Take not thy holy spirit from me,” his prayer carried real historical weight.
He was not casually expressing religious emotion.
He was a fallen king begging God not to cast him away.
But we must not automatically equate David's old-covenant experience with the new-covenant sealing described in Ephesians.
Jesus promised His disciples that the Father would give them another Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who would abide with them forever (John 14:16–17).
That promise matters.
The work of the Holy Spirit after Christ's glorification must be understood through the fuller revelation of the New Testament.
Psalm 51:11 is therefore not sufficient proof that a genuinely regenerated Christian loses the indwelling Spirit every time he falls into sin.
But neither should David's prayer be dismissed.
Because beneath it lies a truth every generation desperately needs.
A person who truly understands the holiness of God will never consider sin a small thing.
David did not say, “Well, everybody makes mistakes.”
He did not blame Bathsheba.
He did not blame the pressures of leadership.
He did not claim that his spiritual history excused his present rebellion.
He cried for mercy.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
The Hebrew word translated “create” is בְּרָא (berāʾ), from the verb בָּרָא (bārāʾ), a word used for God's creative activity.
David was not merely asking for improved behavior.
He was pleading for an inward work that only God could accomplish.
A clean heart.
A renewed spirit.
A life restored through divine mercy.
And here is something we often overlook.
David's hope was not that his sin had been insignificant.
His hope was that God's mercy was greater than his guilt.
That is the difference between repentance and religious performance.
Religious performance says, “I'll make myself worthy enough to return.”
Repentance says, “Lord, I have no excuse. Have mercy on me.”
And now we must face the central question.
Can a believer lose the Holy Spirit through persistent sin?
Christians who take Scripture seriously have reached different conclusions about whether a truly regenerated person can ultimately fall away from salvation.

Many Christians in the Reformed tradition understand the Spirit's seal as part of God's preserving grace. They believe those genuinely born again will ultimately persevere in faith because God keeps them, although true believers may fall into serious sin and require painful correction.

Many Christians in Wesleyan, Arminian, and other traditions affirm the Spirit's sealing while also understanding the New Testament's warnings about apostasy as describing a genuine danger of ultimately abandoning saving faith through persistent, willful rejection of Christ.
Both perspectives recognize that sin is serious, repentance is necessary, and salvation is found only in Jesus Christ.
Neither position should be reduced to a slogan that ignores the passages emphasized by the other.
Ephesians 1:13–14 strongly emphasizes God's pledge and the believer's inheritance.
Ephesians 4:30 warns believers against grieving the Spirit while reaffirming that they are sealed for the day of redemption.
Psalm 51:11 reveals David's desperate plea for God's continuing presence within his old-covenant setting.
These passages do not, by themselves, settle every question surrounding final apostasy.
Hebrews 3:12–14 warns against an evil heart of unbelief that departs from the living God and urges believers to exhort one another so they are not hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Hebrews 10:26–29 contains a severe warning about deliberate, continuing sin in the context of rejecting Christ's sacrifice.
First John 2:19 speaks of people whose departure revealed that they did not truly belong to the apostolic fellowship.
John 10:27–29, meanwhile, contains Jesus' magnificent assurance that His sheep hear His voice, follow Him, and will never perish or be snatched from His hand.
These passages deserve to be read together rather than selectively.
And here is what we can say without pretending that every Christian tradition agrees on every theological detail.

Persistent sin is spiritually dangerous. The Holy Spirit must not be grieved. Christ's promises are trustworthy. And no one should use either fear or false assurance as a substitute for repentance and faith.
The more urgent question is not whether you can identify the precise moment at which a person might lose the Spirit.
The more urgent question is what you are doing with the voice of God today.
Are you fighting the sin you hate?
Or have you started defending the sin you once confessed?
Are you returning to Christ after falling?
Or are you slowly teaching your conscience to stop listening?
There is a difference between a believer who struggles against sin and someone who has decided to make peace with rebellion.
That difference is not that one person has never fallen.
It is the direction of the heart toward Jesus Christ.
A struggling believer may stumble terribly.
Peter did.
On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him three times.
The man who had promised unwavering loyalty broke under fear.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering the sound of your own voice saying you did not know the One who had loved you.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Peter remembered Jesus' words and wept bitterly.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in a deeply personal encounter recorded in John 21.
Three times Jesus asked Peter about his love.
And the fallen disciple was entrusted with a renewed commission to care for Christ's sheep.
Peter's denial was real.
His tears were real.
His restoration was real.
And none of it happened because Peter deserved another chance.
It happened because Jesus is merciful.
But do not misunderstand Peter's story.
Restoration was not permission to deny Christ again.
Grace brought Peter back into faithful discipleship.
That is what the Gospel does.
It does not simply relieve guilt while leaving the heart unchanged.
It calls us out of darkness and into the transforming life of Christ.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying a secret.
Something you have not told your spouse.
Something you have hidden from your family.
Something you would never want displayed on the church screen.
Perhaps you have fallen into pornography again.
Perhaps bitterness has consumed you for years.
Perhaps you've been dishonest with money.
Perhaps you've allowed an emotional attachment to become an affair.
Perhaps you're living two lives—one in public, another in private.
Or perhaps your struggle is quieter.
Pride.
Envy.
Resentment.
A refusal to forgive.
A prayer life abandoned not because you no longer believe, but because shame has made approaching God feel unbearable.
And now you wonder whether the Spirit has left you.
Listen carefully.
Your feelings cannot reliably measure whether the Holy Spirit is present.
Spiritual dryness can have many causes. It is not automatic evidence of divine abandonment.
Likewise, emotional excitement during worship is not automatic proof that everything in your spiritual life is healthy.
The question is not merely whether you feel something.
The question is whether you will listen to what God has revealed and respond to Him.
If the Word exposes your sin, do not run from it.
If your conscience convicts you, do not drown it in distractions.
If you need to confess wrongdoing, stop postponing honesty.
If you need to end a sinful relationship, seek the strength and accountability necessary to end it.
If you have harmed someone, take responsibility and pursue appropriate restitution where possible.
If your struggle has become deeply entrenched, seek mature pastoral care and trustworthy support rather than fighting alone.
And if you have fallen again, do not confuse repentance with merely feeling terrible.
Repentance is more than emotional devastation.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance—a change of mind and heart that turns away from sin and toward God.
True repentance bears fruit.
It does not purchase forgiveness.
It responds to the mercy of the God who forgives.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice the foundation.
He is faithful.
He is just.
Our hope is not that we have cried enough tears.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And First John 2:1 says:
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”
Do you see both sides?
“That ye sin not.”
God does not excuse sin.
“And if any man sin.”
God has not left repentant sinners without an Advocate.
Jesus Christ the righteous.
Not Jesus Christ the reluctant.
Not Jesus Christ the exhausted.
Not Jesus Christ who must be persuaded to care.
Jesus Christ the righteous, whose saving work is sufficient and whose mercy never requires us to pretend that evil is good.
At the cross, Jesus bore the judgment our sins deserved.
At the resurrection, He demonstrated His victory over death.
And through the Holy Spirit, He calls His people into a life that increasingly reflects His holiness.
This is why the Gospel is not simply a story about escaping punishment.
It is a story about belonging to Christ.
Being forgiven.
Being made new.
Learning to walk in the Spirit.
And being transformed into the likeness of the Savior who loved us and gave Himself for us.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
And Romans 8:13 warns that living according to the flesh leads to death, while putting to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit leads to life.
The same chapter gives us assurance and summons us to holiness.
We need both.
Because assurance without holiness becomes distorted.
And holiness without grace becomes despair.
Somebody reading this has spent years swinging between those two extremes.
One week you feel saved.
The next week you feel condemned.
One day you believe God loves you.
The next day you wonder whether you have exhausted His patience.
Your entire spiritual identity has become a record of your latest victory or failure.
But the Christian life was never meant to be built upon your ability to save yourself.
It is built upon Jesus Christ.
He is the Savior.
You are not.
He is the Redeemer.
You are not.
He is the One who died and rose again.
And the same Lord who commands you to turn from sin also invites the weary and burdened to come to Him.
So come.
Not with excuses.
Not with a carefully edited version of your story.
Not with religious language designed to conceal what is actually happening.
Come with the truth.
“Lord, I have sinned.”
“Lord, I have resisted Your Word.”
“Lord, I have loved things that are destroying me.”
“Lord, I have been afraid to come back because I know I have failed You.”
“Lord Jesus, forgive me, cleanse me, and teach me to walk in obedience.”
There is no magic formula in those words.
What matters is genuine repentance and faith in the living Christ.
And if you are wondering whether you should wait until you feel worthy enough to pray, remember the tax collector in Luke 18:13.
He could not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He simply cried:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.”
Jesus said that man went home justified rather than the self-righteous Pharisee.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that God pretends sinners are innocent.
But that the righteous God justifies the ungodly through faith in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:23–26; 4:5).
The blood of Christ does not make sin acceptable.
It makes forgiveness possible without compromising God's justice.
And the grace that forgives also trains us to deny ungodliness and live differently (Titus 2:11–14).
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not merely about religious inspiration.
It is about the Gospel that confronts, rescues, restores, and transforms.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by erasing the truth of what happened.
Not by declaring that consequences no longer matter.
Not by promising that every damaged relationship will immediately be repaired.
But by redeeming people who could never redeem themselves.
David's story did not end with Bathsheba and Uriah, though his sin brought devastating consequences.
Peter's story did not end in the courtyard of denial.
And the story of every person who comes to Christ in genuine repentance does not have to be defined by the worst thing they have done.
That is not a promise of an easy life.
It is a testimony to the power of a gracious Savior.
Maybe the most important thing you can do tonight is stop asking whether you have failed too many times and start responding to the Lord who calls you to repentance.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more compromise.
Not when the guilt becomes unbearable.
Today.
If your heart has become hard, ask God to soften it.
If you've been hiding, bring your sin into the light.
If you've been resisting the truth, surrender to it.
If you need help, reach out to a trustworthy, biblically grounded believer who can walk beside you.
And if you've been clinging to Christ through tears, struggling against the same temptation, wondering whether there is still hope for someone like you, remember this:
The Savior who receives repentant sinners is not surprised by the depth of human weakness.
He knows what is in man.
And He is mighty to save.
There is something else I want to ask of you.
Don't let this message end with you.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who still attends church but privately believes God is finished with them.
Somewhere is a young believer who has fallen into sin and is too ashamed to ask for help.
Somewhere is a father carrying hidden guilt, a mother exhausted by spiritual battles, a teenager confused about salvation, or a friend who has quietly stopped praying.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
But because somebody may need to hear the Gospel through a message they would never have searched for themselves.
Not because the article itself has power, but because the Scriptures within it deserve to be revisited when fear, temptation, or shame tries to distort what God has said.
Our mission is to help people move beyond momentary inspiration into a growing understanding of God's Word.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, grow in prayer, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing and cheerful, not pressured or coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
You glorify Him through faith, obedience, love, generosity, and a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Think of the believer who might encounter a Scripture-centered article before making another destructive decision.
The person who might discover a free devotional while struggling with despair.
The family member who might begin reading the Bible because someone shared a message at the right moment.
But together, we can help make sound biblical resources more accessible.
It is the opportunity to participate in spreading the message of Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not for the sake of appearing spiritual.
Not because commenting can earn God's favor.
But because sometimes putting an honest response into words is a meaningful first step toward seeking prayer and encouragement.
What is the hardest part of your struggle right now: the temptation you keep returning to, the guilt you cannot seem to release, or the fear that God has stopped loving you?

And if God has already carried you through a season of serious spiritual struggle, consider sharing a testimony of His mercy. Your experience may encourage someone who currently believes restoration is impossible.
Please treat one another's stories with compassion. This is not a place to shame people for their struggles, diagnose the state of their souls, or turn another person's confession into gossip.
We all need the truth.
And we all need grace.
Because at the end of this conversation, the greatest question is not simply whether the Holy Spirit can be lost through persistent sin.
It is whether we will hear the Word of God and respond to Jesus Christ.
The Spirit's sealing is a magnificent promise.
The Spirit's grief is a serious warning.
David's repentance is a sobering example.
Peter's restoration is a beautiful testimony.
And the cross of Jesus Christ remains the only sufficient foundation for our forgiveness and hope.
Do not turn God's promises into permission to sin.
Do not turn God's warnings into a reason to despair.
Turn to Jesus.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls His people to follow Him.
The One whose grace does not merely comfort us in our darkness, but leads us into His marvelous light.
And if you have been wondering whether your story is already over, remember this:
The pages you stained with sin are not beyond the reach of the Savior who writes redemption in grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY THREATENED TO SILENCE THE APOSTLES. BUT ONE ANSWER SHOOK THE VERY AUTHORITIES WHO CONDEMNED JESUS.
paragraphs: THEY THREATENED TO SILENCE THE APOSTLES. BUT ONE ANSWER SHOOK THE VERY AUTHORITIES WHO CONDEMNED JESUS.

Why would ordinary men risk prison, public humiliation, brutal beatings, and even death for a message they could have stopped preaching? The answer in Acts 4:18–20 and 5:27–29 reveals something terrifying about human fear, something beautiful about God's grace, and a truth every Christian must confront before the moment comes when following Jesus costs them something.
There is a kind of silence that feels like peace.
You don't argue. You don't offend anyone. You don't risk losing friends. You don't speak about Jesus when the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
You tell yourself you're being wise.
You're protecting your relationships.
You're waiting for the right moment.
And sometimes, you genuinely are.
But sometimes...
The silence isn't wisdom.
It's fear wearing the clothes of wisdom.
Now imagine standing before the very religious authorities who had recently demanded the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.
You know what they are capable of.
You remember what happened to your Master.
You know that the men questioning you possess the influence to make your life miserable.
And they offer you a way out.
Not a complicated bargain.
Not an impossible demand.
Just stop talking about Jesus.
You can go home. You can live quietly. You can avoid the confrontation.
All you have to do is keep your mouth shut.
But Peter and John gave an answer that has echoed through nearly two thousand years of Christian history.
"For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." — Acts 4:20, KJV
Read that again.
We cannot but speak.
Not because they enjoyed conflict.
Not because they wanted attention.
Not because they were trying to build a religious movement around their own personalities.
They had encountered the risen Jesus Christ.
And once they understood who He was, what He had done, and what His resurrection meant, silence could no longer be their answer.
But there is something extraordinary about this story that many believers overlook.
