If someone possesses the resources needed for life, sees a fellow believer in need, and closes their heart against that person, how can God's love remain in them?
The Greek expression κλείσῃ τὰ σπλάγχνα (kleisē ta splanchna) is especially striking.
It conveys the act of shutting one's inward compassion.
The word splanchna refers literally to inward parts and figuratively to deep affection or compassion.
John is not simply describing someone who lacks spare money.
He is confronting someone who sees another person's need and deliberately closes the door of compassion.
Think about that.
The tragedy is not only that the needy person remains hungry.
It is that the person with the opportunity to love has begun shutting down something that should be alive within a follower of Jesus.
And John continues:
“Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.” (1 John 3:18, ESV)
Not merely in beautiful captions.
Not merely in emotional worship.
Not merely in the language of Christianity.
In deed.
In truth.
In love that becomes visible.
Now imagine a mother standing in a grocery store.
She has counted her money three times.
Rice. Eggs. Milk.
She cannot afford all three.
Her little boy points toward a small packet of biscuits.
“Mommy, can we get this?”
She smiles.
“Maybe next time.”
He doesn't know that she has already decided not to eat dinner.
He doesn't know that the smile on her face is holding back tears.
He doesn't know that she prayed that morning, asking God to help her make it through another day.
And perhaps, just a few steps away, another Christian is choosing between two things they don't really need.
This is not an accusation against everyone who has more.
Having resources is not itself a sin.
The Bible includes faithful people who possessed wealth and used it for good.
The question is not whether God has allowed something into our hands.
The question is whether His love has reached our hearts.
Because sometimes the answer to someone's prayer begins with a believer who notices.
A bag of groceries.
A warm meal.
A discreet payment for medicine.
An offer to help someone find work.
A phone call that says, “I heard things have been difficult. How can I help?”
Not every act of love requires money.
But genuine love rarely remains content with doing nothing when meaningful help is possible.
James confronts this with almost unbearable clarity.

“If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, be warmed and filled,’ without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?” (James 2:15–16, ESV)
Imagine looking into the eyes of someone who hasn't eaten and saying, “God bless you.”
Then walking away when you could have helped.
James is not attacking prayer.
Prayer is essential.
He is exposing the emptiness of religious words when we use them as substitutes for obedience.
Sometimes the most faithful thing you can do after praying for someone's daily bread is to share the bread God has already placed in your hands.
And here is where the story becomes even more personal.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to be the hungry person.
Perhaps you have stood in a grocery aisle pretending to compare prices when the truth was that you couldn't afford anything.
Perhaps you have watched your children eat while telling them you weren't hungry.
Perhaps you have borrowed money with trembling hands.
Perhaps you have prayed for provision and wondered why heaven seemed silent.
Perhaps someone once looked at your suffering and decided you weren't worth the inconvenience.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Your poverty does not make you less valuable to God.
Your empty wallet does not mean your faith has failed.
Your struggle is not proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
And needing help does not make you a burden unworthy of love.
The Gospel does not belong exclusively to people whose lives are comfortable.
Jesus Himself knew hunger.
After forty days of fasting in the wilderness, Matthew 4:2 tells us that He was hungry.
He knew exhaustion.
He knew rejection.
He knew what it meant to be misunderstood, betrayed, and abandoned.
And at the cross, the Son of God entered the deepest suffering to accomplish our redemption.
He did not come to save only the respectable, the successful, or the financially secure.
He came to seek and save the lost.
And the grace that rescues sinners also begins transforming the way rescued sinners treat one another.
That is why the early church's generosity was so remarkable.
Acts 2:44–45 describes believers sharing their possessions and distributing resources according to people's needs.
Acts 4:34–35 likewise portrays believers making provision so that needs within their community were addressed.
Their generosity was not a method of purchasing salvation.
It was the fruit of a community transformed by the risen Christ.
People who had received extraordinary mercy began extending mercy to others.
People who had been welcomed by grace began opening their lives.
People who knew that Jesus had given Himself for them began asking what they could give for the good of others.
And this is where we must be very careful.
Because even an article about generosity can become spiritually dangerous if it turns the grace of God into a financial transaction.
You cannot buy God's love.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot give enough money to erase a single sin.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9, ESV)
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
His perfect life.
His sacrificial death.
His victorious resurrection.
His mercy toward sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And yet Ephesians does not stop at verse 9.
Verse 10 tells us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Not saved by good works.
Saved for a life in which good works become the evidence of His transforming grace.
That distinction changes everything.
We do not feed the hungry to convince Jesus to love us.
We feed the hungry because we have encountered the love of Jesus.
We do not give to earn the cross.
We give because the cross has revealed a generosity beyond anything we could ever repay.
And we do not show compassion to make ourselves look holy.
We show compassion because Christ is teaching us to see people through His eyes.
There is a beautiful Hebrew word that helps us understand the character of the God we worship.
חֶסֶד — ḥesed.
It is often translated as steadfast love, lovingkindness, mercy, or covenant faithfulness, depending on the context.
In Micah 6:8, God calls His people to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with Him.
The Hebrew phrase וְאַהֲבַת חֶסֶד (we’ahavat ḥesed) expresses the call to love steadfast kindness or mercy.
Notice that God does not merely command outward religious performance.
He calls His people to love what reflects His character.
To love mercy.
Not reluctantly tolerate it.
Not perform it for applause.
Love it.
Because mercy is not an embarrassing interruption to Christian living.
Mercy belongs at its very heart.
And yet we need to confront another painful truth.
Sometimes we are more comfortable funding the appearance of ministry than participating in the costly work of love.
We love impressive stages.
Beautiful graphics.
Powerful music.
Large gatherings.
Inspirational messages.
There is nothing inherently wrong with these things.
They can serve worthy purposes.
But none of them can replace obedience.
A church can have excellent production and still need to examine how it cares for the vulnerable.
A Christian page can have thousands of followers and still need to remember that the people behind the screens are human beings, not numbers.
A ministry can grow in visibility while needing to grow equally in humility, integrity, accountability, and compassion.
And a person can share a thousand Bible verses without allowing a single one to challenge their selfishness.
Jesus did not command us to build an impressive image of Christianity.
He commanded us to love.
“By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:35, ESV)
That love is not sentimental decoration.
It is evidence.
It is costly.
It makes room.
It notices.
It serves.
It sometimes inconveniences us.
And it refuses to reduce another person's suffering to background noise.
Now picture the church gate again.
The worship service has ended.
The hungry man is still sitting outside.
But this time, someone stops.
Not a wealthy person.
Not a famous preacher.
Just an ordinary believer carrying a small bag of food.
“Have you eaten today?”
The man shakes his head.
“Not yet.”
The believer sits beside him.
Not standing over him like a superior person.
Not turning the moment into a public performance.
Not pulling out a camera to collect praise.
Just sitting beside him.
They share a meal.
They talk.
The stranger finally smiles.
And for a moment, something beautiful happens.
The person who was invisible becomes seen.
The person who was dismissed becomes heard.
The person who had been treated like an inconvenience is reminded that he has dignity.
That meal may not solve every problem in his life.
He may still need shelter, medical care, employment, friendship, or long-term support.
But love has taken its first step.
And sometimes the first step is the one that breaks the power of indifference.
There is a reason Jesus told the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke 10:25–37.
A wounded man lay beside the road.
Religious figures passed him.
But a Samaritan, someone whom Jesus' original audience might not have expected to be the hero, stopped and showed mercy.
He approached the wounded man.
He treated his injuries.
He transported him to safety.
He paid for his care.
Jesus then asked which person had proved to be a neighbor.
The answer was the one who showed mercy.
And Jesus said:
“You go, and do likewise.” (Luke 10:37, ESV)
That command still confronts us.
Because the question is not simply, “Who deserves to be my neighbor?”
The question becomes, “Am I willing to become a neighbor to the person who needs mercy?”
Even when they look different.
Even when their life is complicated.
Even when they cannot repay us.
Even when nobody will applaud.
Especially then.
Maybe you're reading this with a strange heaviness in your chest.
You remember someone.
A face.
A voice.
A moment when you could have helped but chose not to.
Maybe you were afraid.
Maybe you were distracted.
Maybe you were tired.
Maybe you simply didn't want to be bothered.
And now that memory is returning.
Do not mistake conviction for hopelessness.
The purpose of biblical conviction is not to convince you that you are beyond God's mercy.
It is to call you out of sin and back toward the Savior.
There is forgiveness for selfishness.
There is forgiveness for indifference.
There is forgiveness for religious pride.
There is forgiveness for the moments when we loved our comfort more than our neighbor.
But forgiveness is not an invitation to remain unchanged.
It is an invitation to repent and walk in a new direction.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind and turning away from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling guilty for a few minutes.
It is a response to God's truth that bears fruit in a changed life.
Remember Zacchaeus?
He was a wealthy tax collector, despised by many because of the abuses associated with his profession.
When Jesus came into his life, something changed.
In Luke 19:8, Zacchaeus declared that he would give half his possessions to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
Jesus did not teach that Zacchaeus purchased salvation through a generous donation.
His changed relationship with money was a visible expression of the transformation taking place in his life.
The man who had been known for taking began to give.
The man associated with exploitation began to pursue restitution.
The man whose story seemed defined by scandal encountered the grace of Jesus Christ.
And grace began rewriting his story.
Not because his past suddenly became acceptable.
Not because his wrongs no longer mattered.
But because the mercy of Christ was powerful enough to bring repentance, restoration, and a new direction.
And perhaps that is the miracle some of us need today.
Not another emotional moment that disappears by tomorrow.
Not another promise to become more compassionate someday.
But a real turning.
A decision.
A phone call.
A meal shared.
A family remembered.
A neighbor visited.
A heart reopened.
Maybe you cannot feed a hundred people.
Feed one if you can.
Maybe you cannot solve poverty in your city.
Help one person take a meaningful step toward stability.
Maybe you have no money to give.
Offer your time, your skills, your encouragement, your advocacy, your prayer, or your willingness to connect someone with trustworthy assistance.
Maybe you are the one struggling financially.
Then receive help without shame when it is offered in love.
The kingdom of God is not a competition over who can give the most.
And Christian generosity should never become a spectacle where people with little are pressured to sacrifice necessities while people with much receive applause for giving what costs them nothing.
Paul writes:
God does not ask you to pretend you possess resources you do not have.
And in 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul teaches that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That matters.
Especially when ministries invite financial support.

Because supporting Gospel-centered work can be a meaningful expression of stewardship, but it must never be presented as a payment for God's favor or a compulsory test of whether someone truly loves Him.
Your giving should be informed.
Prayerful.
Voluntary.
Responsible.
Rooted in love rather than fear.
There is an invitation to participate in a mission.
And if you choose to participate financially, do so freely, with a clear conscience, and with the desire to glorify Christ rather than impress people.
These products are not instruments of salvation, nor can any purchase bring you closer to God by itself.
They are simply resources and expressions of encouragement that may serve your walk with Christ.
That library is part of a larger conviction: biblical nourishment should not be reserved only for people who can afford to pay.
If you are not, you are still welcome.
The invitation to grow in Christ remains.
And there is another way to help that costs nothing.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because someone in your circle may need this reminder today.
Perhaps a believer has become comfortable with a faith that never leaves the church building.
Perhaps someone has been wounded by religious hypocrisy and needs to see that Jesus Himself condemned empty religious performance.
Perhaps a struggling parent needs to know that being poor does not make them forgotten by God.
Perhaps a person who has been blessed with abundance needs encouragement to use that blessing with wisdom and mercy.
You don't have to disclose private details or explain your suffering to strangers.
Sometimes a few words are enough to remind a community that there are real people behind the screens.
Someone else may need to hear that compassion is still alive.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to make people dependent on a page.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
And that brings us back to the question we began with.
Can you claim to love God while ignoring the hungry person outside your door?
The apostle John gives us a searching warning:
“Whoever loves God must also love his brother.” (1 John 4:21, ESV)
And 1 John 4:20 warns against claiming to love God while hating a brother.
John's immediate concern is love within the family of believers, but Scripture's broader witness also calls us to love our neighbors, show hospitality, practice mercy, and care for those in distress.
We must not pretend that one missed opportunity proves a person has never known Christ.
We are finite.
We cannot meet every need.
Sometimes we lack resources, sometimes we must establish boundaries, and sometimes the wisest response is to help through reliable people or organizations.
But a settled, unrepentant indifference toward human suffering is incompatible with the love that Christ commands His followers to cultivate.
The question is not whether you have ever failed to help.
We all have sinned and fallen short of God's glory.
The question is what you will do when God's Word exposes the condition of your heart.
Will you defend your indifference?
Or will you bring it to Jesus?
Will you keep searching for excuses?
Or will you ask Him to teach you compassion?
Will you remain satisfied with appearing religious?
Or will you surrender to the Savior who makes dead hearts alive?
Because Christianity is not merely a collection of correct statements about God.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ, producing a life increasingly shaped by His truth and love.
The hungry person outside your door is not a prop in your spiritual journey.
They are a human being made in the image of God.
They have a name.
A history.
A story.
Fears you may never understand.
Dreams that poverty may have interrupted.
And dignity that no circumstance can erase.
They do not exist merely to test your generosity.
They deserve to be treated with compassion because they are human.
And the Lord who commands us to love our neighbors is the same Lord who loved us when we were helpless to save ourselves.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (ESV)
There is the center of everything.
Not our generosity.
His.
Not our goodness.
His.
Not our ability to earn acceptance.
His finished work on the cross.
Jesus did not wait for us to become worthy before extending mercy.
He came into our brokenness.
He bore our sin.
He died.
He rose again.
And now He calls sinners everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
When that grace truly takes hold of a life, it does not leave our hands, priorities, and relationships untouched.
It teaches us to love because we have first been loved.
It teaches us to forgive because we have been forgiven.
It teaches us to give because we have received more mercy than we could ever deserve.
And it teaches us to see people whom the world has learned to ignore.
So tonight, before you go to sleep, ask yourself one question.
Not, “Did people think I was a good Christian today?”
Not, “How many people liked my Bible post?”
Not, “Did I sound spiritual enough?”
Ask this:
“Lord Jesus, whose suffering have I become too comfortable walking past?”
Then listen to what Scripture has already made clear.
And when an opportunity comes, respond with the wisdom, humility, and compassion Christ is growing in you.
Because somewhere tonight, a child is going to bed hungry.
Somewhere, an elderly person is eating alone.
Somewhere, a father is wondering how to provide for his family.
Somewhere, a mother is praying through tears.
Somewhere, a stranger is hoping someone will notice.
You cannot reach them all.
But you may be able to reach someone.
And that someone is not insignificant to God.
One day, our beautiful buildings, impressive achievements, public recognition, and carefully constructed reputations will no longer matter the way they do now.
What will matter is whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
And a life belonging to Him is called to bear the fruit of His love.
Not perfectly.
Not for applause.
Not to earn salvation.
But because grace changes people.
So don't allow this to become just another article that made you emotional for a moment.
Let it move you toward Christ.
Let it lead you to repentance where repentance is needed.
Let it remind you of the mercy you have received.
And let that mercy become visible in the way you treat the next person who needs your help.
The hungry stranger at the gate may never know your name.
The struggling mother may never be able to repay you.
The lonely neighbor may never tell anyone what you did.
But love does not need an audience to be real.
And the God who sees what is done in secret is never blind to genuine mercy.
Because the most heartbreaking tragedy is not that someone was hungry outside your door—it is that your heart could become so accustomed to their hunger that you no longer heard them knocking.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE CALLED HERSELF A PROPHETESS. JESUS CALLED HER JEZEBEL. AND THE MOST TERRIFYING PART WASN’T HER SIN—IT WAS THE CHURCH THAT ALLOWED IT.
paragraphs: SHE CALLED HERSELF A PROPHETESS. JESUS CALLED HER JEZEBEL. AND THE MOST TERRIFYING PART WASN’T HER SIN—IT WAS THE CHURCH THAT ALLOWED IT.

She spoke with spiritual authority. She influenced believers. She made compromise sound like revelation. But when Jesus addressed the church in Thyatira, He exposed something far more dangerous than a woman’s deception: a congregation learning to tolerate what was destroying its soul. — Revelation 2:18–29
Imagine sitting in a church where the worship is beautiful, the people are generous, the ministry is growing, and everyone seems to love Jesus.
The prayers sound sincere.
The sermons sound spiritual.
People are serving. Families are attending. The church has a reputation for love, faith, and perseverance.
But somewhere inside that congregation, something is happening that Jesus refuses to ignore.
Someone is teaching believers that they can belong to Christ while deliberately embracing what Christ has forbidden.
And instead of confronting the deception, the church has learned to live with it.
Then a message arrives.
Not from a visiting preacher.
Not from a denominational leader.
Not from an angry former member.
From Jesus Christ Himself.
And His words are terrifying.

“Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.” — Revelation 2:20, KJV
Read that again.
Jesus did not say the church had stopped believing in Him.
He did not say everyone had abandoned worship.
He said they were tolerating something that was corrupting His servants.
And perhaps that is where this ancient letter becomes painfully personal.
Because some of the most dangerous spiritual compromises do not begin when people openly reject Jesus.
They begin when people still profess to love Him but slowly stop taking His words seriously.
And before we examine the woman called Jezebel, we need to confront an uncomfortable possibility.
What if the greatest danger to your faith is not the temptation you recognize, but the compromise you have learned to defend?
The church in Thyatira was not a congregation without good works.
In fact, Jesus began by acknowledging what was beautiful about them.
“I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first.” — Revelation 2:19, KJV
Their love was real enough to be recognized.
Their service mattered.
Their perseverance had not gone unnoticed.
Their later works exceeded their earlier ones.
Yet none of those commendable qualities erased the seriousness of what Jesus was about to confront.
This is something modern Christianity desperately needs to remember.
A church can be active without being healthy in every area.
A ministry can accomplish meaningful good while still needing correction.
A believer can genuinely love Jesus and still be dangerously mistaken about what obedience requires.
Spiritual activity is not permission to ignore spiritual compromise.
And the One speaking to Thyatira was not merely another religious critic.
Revelation 2:18 introduces Him as the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like fine bronze.
The imagery is deliberate.
His eyes communicate penetrating knowledge. Nothing is hidden from His sight.
His feet convey strength and authority.
The Christ who speaks to His church is not confused by appearances.
He sees the worship.
He sees the service.
He sees the hidden teaching.
He sees what people applaud publicly and what they excuse privately.
And He sees the hearts beneath it all.
That should comfort the wounded believer who feels unseen.
But it should also sober anyone who has mistaken God's patience for His approval.
Then comes the name.
Jezebel.
A name so infamous that even people who have never studied the Bible have heard it used as an accusation.
But we must be careful here.
The original Jezebel was a queen in the Old Testament, married to King Ahab. Her story appears especially in 1 Kings 16–21 and 2 Kings 9.
She promoted Baal worship, opposed the prophets of the Lord, and was implicated in the judicial murder of Naboth.
Her influence was associated with idolatry, injustice, and hostility toward covenant faithfulness.
Centuries later, Jesus addressed a woman in Thyatira using that same name.
The Greek text of Revelation 2:20 reads, in part:
τὴν γυναῖκα Ἰεζάβελ, ἡ λέγουσα ἑαυτὴν προφῆτιν
Transliterated: tēn gynaika Iezabel, hē legousa heautēn prophētin.
The sense is: “the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess.”
The word προφῆτιν (prophētin) means “prophetess,” a female prophet.
And that detail matters.
Jesus was not condemning women simply for speaking about God or exercising spiritual gifts.
Scripture recognizes faithful women who prophesied, including Philip's four daughters in Acts 21:9. Acts 2:17–18 also speaks of sons and daughters prophesying through the outpouring of the Spirit.
The issue in Thyatira was not that the accused teacher was female.
The issue was that she claimed spiritual authority while leading Christ's servants toward conduct contrary to His will.
We should also acknowledge something important about the historical text.
Revelation does not give us enough information to establish whether “Jezebel” was her actual personal name or a symbolic designation comparing her influence to the Old Testament queen.
Many interpreters understand it as a symbolic name.
We are not told her complete biography, her appearance, her family background, or precisely how she gained influence.
And we must not invent those details.
But the accusation recorded in Revelation is unmistakable.
She was teaching and misleading Christ's servants into sexual immorality and participation in food associated with idol sacrifices.
The Greek verb translated “to seduce” in the King James Version comes from πλανάω (planaō), meaning to lead astray, mislead, or deceive.
This was not merely a disagreement about personal preference.
Jesus identified teaching that was leading believers away from covenant faithfulness.
And the setting makes the warning even more striking.
Thyatira was a city in the Roman province of Asia, known for commercial activity and trade associations.
Scholars have explored how participation in the city's social and economic life may have created pressure for Christians to attend gatherings involving pagan religious practices.
That historical context may help explain the temptation to compromise, although Revelation does not tell us exactly how the woman's teaching operated.
We should not pretend to know more than Scripture reveals.
But we can recognize the spiritual conflict.
Believers were living in a society where loyalty to Jesus could carry social consequences.
Compromise may have appeared convenient.
Accommodation may have seemed practical.
And someone claiming spiritual insight was apparently providing a way to make disobedience feel acceptable.
Does that sound completely foreign to our generation?
Think about how often people today are encouraged to redefine obedience around whatever feels easiest.
A relationship becomes more important than holiness.
Approval becomes more important than truth.
Personal desire becomes the final authority.
And the moment Scripture challenges our choices, we begin searching for someone who will tell us that God does not really mind.
Not every difficult situation has a simple answer.
Not every struggling Christian is deliberately rebellious.
Not every disagreement about biblical interpretation is deception.
But there is a real difference between a person wrestling honestly with God's Word and a teacher encouraging people to disregard it.
One is a struggle that calls for patient discipleship.
The other can become a spiritual trap.
And Jesus loved His church too much to remain silent.
What happens next is one of the most astonishing details in the entire passage.
“And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not.” — Revelation 2:21, KJV
Do not rush past that sentence.
Jesus gave her time.
Time to reconsider.
Time to turn away.
Time to repent.
The One whose eyes are like fire did not immediately announce judgment without an opportunity for repentance.
He had given her space to turn.
That is grace.
Not the cheap imitation of grace that tells us sin does not matter.
Not the distorted version of grace that promises forgiveness while treating repentance as unnecessary.
But the astonishing mercy of a holy Savior who calls sinners away from destruction.
The Greek word translated “repent” is related to μετανοέω (metanoeō), which speaks of repentance—a change of mind and direction, a turning away from sin.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what happened.
It is more than crying because the consequences became painful.
It is turning toward God with an honest willingness to abandon what dishonors Him.
And here is the heartbreaking part.
She was given time.
But according to the text, she did not repent.
How many people mistake delayed consequences for divine permission?
How many assume that because their hidden choices have not yet been exposed, heaven must be indifferent?
How many interpret another ordinary morning as proof that nothing needs to change?
But the patience of Jesus is not indifference.
Romans 2:4 reminds us that God's goodness is meant to lead us to repentance.
The open door of mercy is an invitation, not an endorsement of the sin we are being called to leave.
And if you are reading this while carrying something you know needs to change, please hear the difference.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend that your struggle never happened.
He is calling you to stop making peace with what is harming your relationship with Him.
Maybe it is a relationship you keep justifying.
Maybe it is an addiction you have hidden behind a convincing smile.
Maybe it is a pattern of dishonesty that has become so familiar you barely notice it anymore.
Maybe it is a spiritual leader whose words make you feel comfortable while quietly drawing you away from Scripture.
Or perhaps you have been wounded by religious people who used accusations of impurity to control, shame, or silence you.
If so, this passage must never be used as a weapon against you.
Being tempted is not the same as teaching others to sin.
Experiencing sexual abuse is not sexual immorality on the victim's part.
And being a woman with a strong voice, leadership ability, or spiritual gifts does not make someone a “Jezebel.”
That accusation has too often been thrown carelessly at women whom others simply dislike or cannot control.
The name Jezebel is not a biblical license for misogyny, humiliation, or spiritual abuse.
Jesus' rebuke concerns specific destructive teaching and unrepentant wrongdoing.
We must honor that distinction.
Otherwise, we risk committing injustice while claiming to defend holiness.
But we cannot soften the next part of the passage either.
Revelation 2:22–23 contains severe language of judgment.
Jesus warns of a bed of suffering, great tribulation for those participating in the wrongdoing unless they repent, and judgment upon those described as her children.
The imagery is sobering.
The text does not authorize us to identify modern people as objects of this judgment or to celebrate anyone's suffering.
Nor should we confidently assign a precise medical or historical mechanism to the threatened punishment when Scripture does not provide one.
The central warning is clear enough.
Christ does not treat the corruption of His people as a trivial matter.
He declares that the churches will know He is the One who searches hearts and minds and gives to each according to their works.
In the Greek text of Revelation 2:23, Jesus says:
ἐραυνῶν νεφροὺς καὶ καρδίας
Transliterated: eraunōn nephrous kai kardias.
The expression refers to searching the inward depths of a person.
Literally, the language speaks of “kidneys and hearts,” an ancient way of referring to the deepest inner life, including thoughts, motives, and desires.
That is why translations often communicate the sense as searching minds and hearts.
Jesus is not impressed by the spiritual image we manufacture.
He knows the motives beneath our decisions.
He knows when we are confused.
He knows when we are frightened.
He knows when we have been deceived.
And He knows when we are deliberately defending what His Word has already confronted.
Yet there is another detail that changes the emotional weight of this entire passage.
Jesus does not address every believer in Thyatira as though all are equally guilty.
He speaks separately to those who have not embraced the destructive teaching.
To them, He says:
“But that which ye have already hold fast till I come.” — Revelation 2:25, KJV
Hold fast.
Two words that can feel like oxygen to a weary Christian.
Perhaps you are exhausted from trying to remain faithful in an environment where compromise is celebrated.
Perhaps you have lost friendships because you refused to abandon your convictions.
Perhaps you are trying to rebuild your life after years of spiritual confusion.
Perhaps you have fallen, repented, and are learning how to walk with Jesus again.
Hear His invitation.
Hold fast.
Not to your pride.
Not to your reputation.
Not to the illusion that you are stronger than everyone else.
Hold fast to Christ.
Because the Christian life is not a competition to prove who has never struggled.
It is a life of faith, repentance, perseverance, and dependence on the Savior who has conquered sin and death.
And this is where the story of Thyatira points us toward the heart of the Gospel.
The Jesus who confronted Jezebel is the same Jesus who spoke with the Samaritan woman at the well in John 4.
He knew the truth about her complicated life.
Yet He did not treat her as disposable.
He offered living water.
The same Jesus who warned Thyatira about sexual immorality is the Jesus who forgave sinners and called them into a new life.
In John 8:11, in the traditional account of the woman caught in adultery, Jesus says, “Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
That account has a well-known textual history and is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John, so it should be approached with appropriate textual awareness.
Nevertheless, the combination of mercy and the call to holiness is firmly established throughout the New Testament.
Jesus does not offer forgiveness because sin is harmless.
He offers forgiveness because sinners need rescue.
He does not call us to repentance because He enjoys exposing our shame.
He calls us to repentance because He came to save us from sin.
And at the cross, we see just how seriously God takes both justice and mercy.
Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.
The cross does not make holiness unnecessary.
It makes transformation possible.
The resurrection does not simply promise that our story can have a better ending someday.
It announces that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
That is the difference between condemnation without hope and conviction that leads to life.
Conviction says, “This cannot remain as it is.”
Grace says, “Come to Christ. Forgiveness and a new beginning are possible.”
And genuine faith does not pit those truths against each other.
It receives both.
Perhaps that is why the phrase From Scandal to Grace matters so deeply.
Because scandal is not always what other people discovered about us.
Sometimes scandal is what we finally admit about ourselves.
The jealousy we concealed.
The compromise we justified.
The secret we protected.
The bitterness we baptized as discernment.
The desire we allowed to become our master.
The truth we kept avoiding because obedience would cost us something.
And then, somehow, through the mercy of God, the heart begins to soften.
The excuses become confession.
The hiding becomes honesty.
The pride gives way to surrender.
And the person who once defended the darkness begins longing for the light.
Not because they have become their own savior.
But because Jesus Christ is changing them.
This is why we must be careful about turning Revelation 2 into a story about one wicked woman while ignoring the church that tolerated her teaching.
The text addresses both the deceiving influence and the responsibility of those who allowed it to continue.
It asks uncomfortable questions of leaders.
Are we protecting people with truth, or protecting reputations with silence?
Are we teaching Scripture faithfully, or reshaping it to avoid difficult conversations?
Are we creating communities where sinners can confess and receive loving correction, or environments where everyone feels compelled to hide?
And it asks equally uncomfortable questions of individual believers.
Who is shaping your understanding of God?
Whose approval has become more important than obedience?
When someone corrects you with Scripture, do you examine the Word honestly, or immediately search for a reason to dismiss the correction?
Are you following Jesus, or merely following voices that make Christianity easier to accommodate to your desires?
Those questions are not meant to produce panic.
They are meant to invite examination.
Because discernment is not paranoia.
Holiness is not self-righteousness.
And love is not the refusal to tell the truth.
In fact, biblical love and truth belong together.
Jesus Himself commended the love of Thyatira before confronting its tolerance of destructive teaching.
He did not ask the church to become less loving.
He called it to become faithful.
That distinction could heal many Christian communities today.
We do not need more people casually labeling others as Jezebel.
We need more believers who know Scripture well enough to recognize deception, humble themselves enough to receive correction, and love people enough to pursue restoration.
We need pastors who refuse to exploit their authority.
We need teachers who can say, “I was wrong,” when Scripture corrects them.
We need churches where sexual sin is neither celebrated nor handled through cruelty, secrecy, or favoritism.
We need communities where those harmed by abuse are protected and where allegations are handled responsibly, rather than being buried beneath appeals to forgiveness.
We need Christians who understand that forgiveness does not eliminate accountability and that repentance is not a shortcut around consequences.
Above all, we need Jesus Christ at the center.
Not celebrity personalities.
Not fear-driven accusations.
Not religious performance.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One whose Word searches us.
The One whose mercy invites us.
The One whose grace changes us.
And there is something beautiful about how the letter to Thyatira ends.
After the rebuke, the warning, and the call to hold fast, Jesus gives a promise to the one who overcomes and keeps His works to the end.
Then, in Revelation 2:28, He says:
“And I will give him the morning star.” — KJV
The promise is rich with hope.
And later, in Revelation 22:16, Jesus identifies Himself as “the bright and morning star.”

Christians have therefore long understood the imagery as deeply connected with Christ Himself and the hope of His victorious reign, though interpreters discuss the precise relationship between these passages.
Consider the movement of the message.
It begins with a church facing deception and compromise.
It confronts the reality of sin.
It announces judgment and calls for repentance.
It urges the faithful to persevere.
And it ends with a promise filled with the hope of Christ.
That is not a message of despair.
It is a message calling the church back to its Lord.
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs tonight.
Not another religious argument.
Not another reason to despise themselves.
Not another accusation from someone who knows nothing about their private battles.
But a moment of truth before Jesus.
A moment to say:
“Lord, I have been compromising.”
“Lord, I have been listening to voices that pull me away from You.”
“Lord, I have confused Your patience with permission.”
“Lord, I have been afraid to surrender because I do not know what obedience will cost.”
“Lord, I need Your mercy.”
If those words describe you, do not turn them into another performance.
Bring them honestly to God.
Confess your sin.
Seek His forgiveness.
Receive the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And take the next faithful step, even if it is small.
If you need to end a destructive pattern, seek wise support.
If you need to confess wrongdoing, do so responsibly.
If you have been deceived, return to Scripture.
If you have harmed someone, pursue genuine repentance and appropriate accountability.
If you have been spiritually abused, seek safety and trustworthy help. You do not have to return to an unsafe environment to prove that you forgive.
And if you have spent years believing that your past has placed you beyond the reach of God's mercy, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue in deliberate sin.
It is an invitation to come into the light through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most important question now is not whether you can identify a Jezebel somewhere in the modern church.
Perhaps it is whether you are willing to let the Word of Christ examine your own heart.
Because it is possible to spend an entire lifetime exposing the sins of others while refusing to confront our own.
And it is possible to become so consumed with identifying darkness that we forget to walk in the light.
Jesus did not give Revelation to His church so that believers could become professional accusers.
He gave His Word to reveal truth, call His people to faithfulness, and direct their hope toward His ultimate victory.
So before you leave this article, consider one question.
What have you been calling acceptable that Jesus is calling you to surrender?
You do not need to publish your private sins.
You do not need to expose intimate details to strangers.
But if this message has stirred something in your heart, I would love to hear a simple, sincere response.
Your story does not need to be dramatic to matter.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony is simply this:
“I was drifting. Jesus called me back.”
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message, not as a public rebuke, but as a reminder that truth and mercy still meet in Jesus Christ.
You can also invite believers who are struggling, Christians who have grown spiritually weary, and friends who are still exploring faith to follow along.
The goal is not to win an argument.
It is to help people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
That is also why Gospel Warrior continues building resources for people who want to grow deeper in their understanding of the Bible.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their faith, understand the Gospel, and continue growing in Christ beyond a single article.
Not because a payment earns His favor.
But voluntary, prayerful generosity can still be a meaningful expression of Christian stewardship and partnership in Gospel work.
Philippians 4:15–18 describes believers sharing in the support of Paul's ministry, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled.
It can help support the continued creation of Scripture-centered articles, the development of discipleship resources, and the effort to reach more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
It is helping make resources available to others.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
The Gospel is.
But they can serve as everyday reminders of faith, encouragement, and the biblical truth we want to carry into our homes and communities.
A thoughtful comment may encourage another believer to keep going.
A personal invitation may help a friend rediscover the beauty of God's Word.
Because the point of Gospel Warrior has never been to make people dependent on a ministry.
It is to keep pointing people toward Jesus.
And that brings us back to the church in Thyatira.
A church that had love.
A church that had service.
A church that had faith.
A church that had perseverance.
But also a church that needed correction.
Jesus did not ignore its good works.
And He did not ignore its sin.
He loved His people enough to tell them the truth.
Perhaps that is the lesson we most need to carry away.
Christ does not ask us to choose between grace and holiness.
He calls us to receive His grace and walk in the new life that grace produces.
The scandal of our past does not have to become the identity of our future.
The deception we once believed does not have to remain the truth we follow.
The sin we once defended does not have to remain the master we obey.
Because Jesus Christ still calls people out of darkness.
He still forgives repentant sinners.
He still restores the broken.
He still strengthens the weary.
And He still says to His people:
Hold fast.
So when the world tells you that surrender is weakness, remember the cross.
When temptation tells you that compromise is freedom, remember the One who died to set you free.
When shame tells you that your story is finished, remember the empty tomb.
And when you wonder whether there is still hope for someone who has wandered so far, remember that the Savior who warned Thyatira also gave time to repent.
Do not waste the mercy of that invitation.
Come to Christ.
Hold fast to His Word.
Walk in His light.
And let His grace transform the story you thought could never change.
The most heartbreaking tragedy is not that Jesus sees the darkness we hide, but that we sometimes keep hiding from the very Savior who came to bring us into His light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY TURNED THEIR BACKS ON GOD… WHILE STANDING INSIDE HIS TEMPLE
paragraphs: THEY TURNED THEIR BACKS ON GOD… WHILE STANDING INSIDE HIS TEMPLE

Ezekiel saw twenty-five men bowing toward the rising sun. Their bodies were in God's sanctuary, but their worship belonged to something else. And the most terrifying part of this ancient vision is how easily we can recognize ourselves in it.

“And, behold, at the door of the temple of the LORD, between the porch and the altar, were about five and twenty men, with their backs toward the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east; and they worshipped the sun toward the east.” — Ezekiel 8:16, KJV
Imagine standing in the house of God.
The altar is nearby. The place where sacrifices were offered. The place where Israel was supposed to remember that sin is serious, mercy is precious, and the Lord alone is worthy of worship.
Everything around you speaks of holiness.
But then you see something that makes your stomach turn.
Twenty-five men.
Standing in the sacred courts.
Their backs turned toward the temple.
Their faces lifted toward the rising sun.
And they are bowing.
Not before the God who delivered Israel from Egypt.
Not before the One who parted the Red Sea.
Not before the Lord who gave His people a covenant, a land, and a place where His name would dwell.
They are worshiping something God created.
While turning their backs on the One who created it.
And perhaps the most disturbing thing about this scene is that they did not have to leave the temple to betray Him.
They did it right there.
In the place that should have reminded them of His presence.
Now read that again, slowly.
They were standing in a holy place while giving their devotion to something other than God.
And suddenly, this is no longer just a disturbing story about ancient Jerusalem.
It becomes a mirror.
Because a person can sit in church every Sunday and still spend the rest of the week bowing before something else.
A person can sing about surrender while quietly protecting the one sin they refuse to surrender.
A person can raise both hands in worship while allowing pride, bitterness, lust, greed, resentment, or the approval of others to rule the heart.
And sometimes the greatest spiritual danger is not that we have stopped speaking about God.
It is that we have learned how to speak about Him while living as though something else is more important.
But before we point at those twenty-five men, we need to understand what Ezekiel actually saw.
Because the truth of this passage is far more devastating than a simple warning against worshiping the sun.
And the grace revealed through Jesus Christ is far more beautiful than we deserve.
Ezekiel was a priest and prophet living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. Jerusalem had not yet experienced its final destruction, but the spiritual corruption of Judah was already deep.
In Ezekiel chapter 8, the prophet receives a vision in which the Lord shows him abominations being committed in Jerusalem.
First, Ezekiel sees an idolatrous image associated with jealousy near the entrance of the temple precincts.
Then he is shown seventy elders participating in forbidden worship, surrounded by images of creeping things and detestable creatures.
These elders are not simply making a mistake because they lack information.
They are hiding their practices and saying, according to Ezekiel 8:12, that the Lord does not see them.
Think about that.
They believe their darkness is hidden from the God whose eyes see everything.
Then Ezekiel sees women weeping for Tammuz, associated with a foreign religious practice.
And finally, the vision reaches the scene that should make every generation of believers tremble.
Twenty-five men worshiping the sun.
Inside the temple courts.
With their backs toward the sanctuary of the Lord.
The Hebrew text of Ezekiel 8:16 describes them with these words:
וַאֲחֹרֵיהֶם אֶל־הֵיכַל יְהוָה וּפְנֵיהֶם קֵדְמָה
Va'achoreihem el-heikhal Adonai, u'fneihem qedmah.
A faithful rendering is:
“Their backs were toward the temple of the LORD, and their faces were toward the east.”

The written Hebrew contains the divine name יהוה, commonly represented in English Bibles as LORD. Adonai in the transliteration reflects the traditional Jewish practice of saying “Lord” when reading that name aloud.
The Hebrew word אֲחֹרֵיהֶם (achoreihem) means “their backs” or “their backsides.”
And פְנֵיהֶם (peneihem) means “their faces.”
This is not merely poetic language.
The prophet describes an actual posture within his vision.
Their backs are turned toward the temple.
Their faces are turned eastward.
The Hebrew continues:
וְהֵמָּה מִשְׁתַּחֲוִיתֶם קֵדְמָה לַשָּׁמֶשׁ
Vehemmah mishtachavitem qedmah lashemesh.
Meaning:
“And they were bowing down toward the east to the sun.”
The word שֶׁמֶשׁ (shemesh) means “sun.”
And the verb describes an act of bowing or prostration.
These men were not simply admiring a sunrise.
They were engaged in forbidden worship.
That distinction matters.
Scripture does not condemn the beauty of the sunrise. Psalm 19 celebrates the heavens declaring the glory of God.
The problem was never the sun itself.
The problem was giving worship to the sun rather than to its Creator.
Deuteronomy 4:19 had already warned Israel against being drawn away to bow down to the sun, moon, and stars.
They had been warned.
They had been taught.
They had been given God's covenant.
Yet here they were.
Bowing.
And the location makes their rebellion even more shocking.
Ezekiel says they were between the porch and the altar, an especially significant area of the temple's inner court.
Their exact identities are not established by the passage, although their presence in that location suggests an especially serious corruption of worship.
The number twenty-five is explicit.
Their names are not.
And perhaps that absence of names should make us uncomfortable.
Because the passage does not allow us to dismiss the scene as merely the failure of a few recognizable villains.
It forces us to examine the nature of misplaced worship itself.
The sun rises every morning.
It gives light.
It provides warmth.
It helps sustain life on earth.
But it cannot forgive a single sin.
It cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
It cannot redeem a broken soul.
It cannot raise the spiritually dead.
It is a gift.
Not a god.
And one of the oldest tragedies of the human heart is that we can become so captivated by God's gifts that we begin to neglect the Giver.
Sometimes the gift is money.
Sometimes it is success.
Sometimes it is a relationship.
Sometimes it is the dream of becoming somebody important.
Sometimes it is the attention we receive.
Sometimes it is our own image.
And sometimes it is even the religious reputation we have carefully built.
We may never kneel before a golden statue.
We may never bow toward the sunrise.

But when something becomes the controlling love of our lives, something we trust more than God, obey against His Word, or refuse to surrender to Him, we are confronting the same fundamental problem of idolatry.
The Apostle Paul describes this exchange in Romans 1:25:
“Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.” — KJV
There it is.
The exchange.
The created thing takes the place of the Creator.
And that exchange can happen quietly.
It does not always begin with a dramatic announcement that we no longer believe in God.
Sometimes it begins with a small compromise.
A private conversation we know we should end.
A dishonest decision we justify because we need the money.
A grudge we keep feeding because forgiveness feels too costly.
A secret habit we defend because nobody else knows.
A relationship we refuse to bring under the authority of Christ.
And slowly, what once troubled our conscience begins to feel normal.
We still pray.
We still attend worship.
We still know the songs.
But there is a part of our lives where we have stopped listening.
A part of our hearts where God's Word is no longer welcome.
And we tell ourselves that everything is fine because we have not abandoned religion.
Yet the men in Ezekiel's vision had not abandoned the temple either.
That was precisely what made the scene so horrifying.
They were physically near the place of worship while spiritually engaged in rebellion.
And before we go any further, there is something important we must understand.
This passage is not permission to accuse every struggling Christian of secretly worshiping idols.
A believer who is grieving, exhausted, wrestling with temptation, or fighting to overcome sin is not automatically the same as someone deliberately defending rebellion against God.
Scripture distinguishes between the person who stumbles and seeks mercy and the person who hardens the heart and refuses correction.
That distinction matters because conviction is meant to lead us toward repentance, not hopelessness.
And perhaps you are reading this while carrying a struggle nobody knows about.
You love Jesus.
But you are tired.
You have prayed about the same weakness so many times that you are embarrassed to pray about it again.
You have promised God that things would change.
Then you failed.
Again.
And now you wonder whether the Lord is tired of hearing your voice.
Listen carefully.
The warning in Ezekiel is real.
God is holy.
Sin is not harmless.
Idolatry is not something to excuse.
But the answer to your failure is not to run farther from Jesus.
It is to stop hiding and return to Him.
Because the God who exposes sin is also the God who calls sinners to repentance.
And this is where the story becomes even more serious.
In Ezekiel 8:17, the Lord asks whether the abominations committed in Judah are a trivial matter. He also speaks of violence filling the land and repeated provocation against Him.
The corruption was not limited to private religious preferences.
False worship was connected with moral rebellion and injustice.
And in verse 18, the Lord announces judgment.
“Therefore will I also deal in fury: mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity: and though they cry in mine ears with a loud voice, yet will I not hear them.” — Ezekiel 8:18, KJV
Those words are terrifying.
They should be.
But we must not remove them from their historical setting or use them to claim that God refuses to hear every repentant sinner who has fallen into sin.
The Lord is addressing persistent covenant rebellion in Judah within Ezekiel's prophetic vision of impending judgment.
He is not declaring that a brokenhearted person who turns to Him in genuine repentance is beyond His mercy.
In fact, later in the same book, God says:
“For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye.” — Ezekiel 18:32, KJV
Do you hear the difference?
The warning is not an invitation to despair.
It is a summons to turn.
To live.
To stop treating mercy as permission to remain unchanged.
And the tragedy of Jerusalem's rebellion becomes even more heartbreaking as Ezekiel's vision continues.
In Ezekiel chapters 10 and 11, the glory of the Lord departs from the temple and the city.
The people had treated God's presence as though it were something they could presume upon while refusing His authority.
And eventually, Jerusalem would experience devastating judgment.
But Ezekiel's message does not end with destruction.
That is one of the most beautiful truths in the entire book.
The same prophet who saw the corruption of the temple also received promises of restoration.
The same book that exposes the stubbornness of the human heart contains one of Scripture's most breathtaking promises about what God Himself would do for His people.
Listen to Ezekiel 36:26:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” — KJV
A new heart.
Not a polished religious performance.
Not a better disguise.
Not merely stronger willpower.
A new heart.
And in verse 27, God promises to put His Spirit within His people and cause them to walk in His statutes.
The answer to humanity's deepest problem is not simply more religious activity.
We need God to transform us from within.
We need forgiveness.
We need cleansing.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need a Savior.
And that brings us to Jesus Christ.
Centuries after Ezekiel's vision, the Son of God entered the world.
He did not come as another created object demanding attention.
He came as the eternal Word made flesh.
John 1:3 says:
“All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.” — KJV
Think about what that means.
The sun that those men worshiped was itself part of creation.
And Jesus Christ, the eternal Son, is the One through whom all things were made.
The sun was never worthy of divine worship.
Christ is.
And when Jesus walked among us, He did not merely expose the darkness.
He came to rescue sinners from it.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called people to repentance.
He welcomed the broken who came to Him in faith.
He exposed false religion that honored God with the lips while keeping the heart far away.
And then He did something no idol, no religious system, and no human effort could ever accomplish.
He went to the cross.
The sinless Son of God bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
Not because our sin was small.
But because His grace is greater than our guilt.
Not because God decided holiness no longer mattered.
But because Jesus accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Justice was not ignored.
Mercy was not cheap.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing love of God.
And suddenly, the contrast becomes overwhelming.
In Ezekiel's vision, men turned their backs on the place associated with God's presence.
At Calvary, Jesus gave Himself to reconcile sinners to God.
In Ezekiel's vision, people bowed before something that could not save them.
At the cross, the Savior gave His life for people who could not save themselves.
In Ezekiel's vision, hearts had become hardened against the Lord.
Through the Gospel, God calls us to repentance and gives new life through His Son.
This is not merely a story about twenty-five men facing east.
It is a story that exposes the human need for redemption.
And it points us toward the only Savior who can truly change a heart.
The Greek New Testament uses a powerful word connected with repentance:
μετάνοια — metanoia.
It means repentance, a change of mind and orientation that involves turning away from sin and toward God.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus announces:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — KJV
The Greek command μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) means “repent.”
Jesus was not merely asking people to experience a moment of sadness.
He was calling them to a transformed response to God.
Repentance is not buying forgiveness through tears.
It is not earning salvation by becoming perfect.
It is turning from sin toward the God whose grace is received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And genuine repentance bears fruit in a changed life.
That is why the Gospel is both comforting and confronting.
Jesus loves sinners.
But His love does not make sin safe.
He forgives.
And He transforms.
He receives those who come to Him.
And He calls them to follow Him.
Maybe that is what you need to hear today.
Not another message telling you how impressive you are.
Not another comforting sentence that leaves your hidden compromises untouched.
But a loving, serious invitation to bring your entire life before Jesus.
The part everybody sees.
And the part you keep locked away.
The public testimony.
And the private struggle.
The prayers you speak aloud.
And the thoughts you are ashamed to admit.
Because Jesus does not need you to maintain a flawless image before you come to Him.
He calls you to come truthfully.
And perhaps the most important question you can ask yourself today is not, “Do I still believe in God?”
It is this:
“Is there anything in my life that I am treating as more worthy of my trust, love, or obedience than Jesus Christ?”
Do not rush past that question.
Maybe you have made financial security your refuge.
Maybe you have allowed the fear of losing someone to become stronger than your desire to obey God.
Maybe you have been chasing the admiration of strangers while neglecting the people God has entrusted to your care.
Maybe you have been so busy defending your reputation that you have forgotten what genuine humility looks like.
Maybe you have become skilled at discussing Scripture but slow to obey it.
Or perhaps you have been carrying guilt for years and have started to believe that your scandal is too great for grace.
If that is you, listen to the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Faithful.
Just.
To forgive.
And to cleanse.
Not because confession purchases salvation.
But because the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient, and God's promise is trustworthy.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to determine your future.
Your failure may have consequences.
Grace does not always erase those consequences.
But in Christ, guilt does not have to remain your identity.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is real.
Restoration is possible.
And transformation is not a fantasy.
There may be relationships you need to repair.
There may be habits you need to abandon.
There may be someone you need to forgive.
There may be a confession you need to make.
There may be accountability you need to seek.
There may be a painful but necessary decision you have postponed for months.
Whatever obedience requires, do not confuse the discomfort of surrender with the absence of God's love.
Sometimes the truth that wounds our pride is the very truth God uses to bring us back to life.
And here is something worth remembering.
The goal of this passage is not to make you suspicious of every other Christian.
It is to make you honest before God.
We can become so fascinated with identifying the idols of our generation that we fail to recognize the idols we have allowed into our own hearts.
We condemn the world for its darkness.
Then excuse the darkness we secretly enjoy.
We demand holiness from others.
Then negotiate exceptions for ourselves.
We speak passionately about biblical truth.
Then grow angry when that truth confronts our own choices.
And the Lord sees beyond every carefully constructed appearance.
But that should not make the repentant believer run away.
It should make us grateful that we can stop pretending.
There is freedom in finally telling the truth before God.
Freedom in admitting that we need help.
Freedom in saying, “Lord, I have allowed something to occupy a place in my heart that belongs to You.”
And freedom in discovering that the Savior we have sinned against is the very Savior who invites us to return.
Your story of God's mercy may encourage someone who believes they are beyond redemption.
Not every wound needs to be displayed publicly.
But nobody should have to believe they are the only person still fighting.
We need a community that speaks the truth.
A community that prays.
A community that restores gently.
A community that refuses to celebrate sin but also refuses to abandon the repentant.
Galatians 6:1 calls spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in a fault with gentleness, while watching themselves.
That is the spirit we need.
Truth without cruelty.
Grace without compromise.
Conviction without humiliation.
And hope anchored in Jesus Christ.
Not merely because a message needs more views, but because someone in your circle may be sitting in a church pew, carrying a silent battle, and wondering whether God still wants them.
Someone may be one honest prayer away from beginning the journey back.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is not the end of their story.
Someone may need to know that Jesus Christ still saves.
Because the Gospel is not a message we are meant to keep to ourselves.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, confront sin, or draw closer to Jesus, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Not because a monthly payment can replace your devotion to the Lord.
And not because supporting any particular ministry is a biblical requirement for proving that you love Jesus.
It is not.
But because the work of sharing biblical truth, creating discipleship resources, encouraging wounded believers, and reaching more people with the Gospel requires real effort, time, and resources.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That is the heart behind this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that money will purchase blessings.
A willing partnership in making Christ known.
Those free resources matter because access to biblical encouragement should not depend on someone's ability to pay.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, tools for reflection, and opportunities to begin meaningful conversations about Jesus.
It is participating in a ministry that seeks to keep pointing people back to the Word of God.
Pray that we never become more concerned with attention than with truth.
Pray that we never confuse popularity with faithfulness.
Pray that every article, resource, and message will direct people toward Jesus rather than toward the people producing the content.
Pray that Gospel Warrior will remain accountable to Scripture, faithful to the Gospel, and compassionate toward those who are hurting.
Because even a Christian ministry can become distracted.
Even a person who teaches about God must continually examine the heart.
Even those who call others to repentance must remain humble before the Lord.
And that brings us back to the temple.
Back to Ezekiel.
Back to those twenty-five men.
The prophet saw them with their backs turned toward the sanctuary and their faces toward the sun.
But Scripture does not tell us the individual names of those men, nor does it tell us that each one eventually repented.
We should not invent an ending the text does not provide.
What Scripture does give us is something greater than speculation about their personal futures.
It gives us the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
The invitation to turn from idols to the living God.
The promise of forgiveness through Christ.
The hope of a new heart.
And the certainty that the risen Savior is worthy of our entire lives.
So perhaps tonight, before you go to sleep, you need to have a conversation with God that you have been avoiding.
Not a polished religious speech.
Not a performance.
Just the truth.

“Lord Jesus, show me what has taken Your rightful place in my heart. Forgive me for the ways I have trusted, loved, or obeyed created things more than You. I cannot cleanse myself. I need Your mercy. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to turn away from sin, trust Your Word, and follow You with an undivided heart. Give me courage to obey, humility to repent, and strength through Your Spirit to walk in truth. Amen.”
And when you finish praying, do not leave repentance as merely an emotional moment.
Take the next faithful step.
Open your Bible.
Seek godly counsel if you need it.
Make things right where you can.
Turn away from what is leading you into sin.
Return to fellowship with believers who will help you follow Christ.
And remember that the Christian life is not sustained by the intensity of one emotional experience.
It is sustained by the grace of God as we continue trusting and following Jesus.
The sun those men worshiped would eventually set.
It always does.
Every earthly source of power, beauty, pleasure, status, and security has limits.
But Jesus Christ is not a temporary light.
He is the Light of the world.
And John 8:12 records His promise:
“I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.” — KJV
So stop chasing a light that cannot save you.
Stop protecting the idols that are slowly consuming your peace.
Stop assuming that being near holy things is the same as belonging wholeheartedly to the Holy One.
Turn to Jesus.
Not because your story is already clean.
But because He is the Savior who cleanses sinners.
Not because you have never fallen.
But because His grace calls you to rise and follow Him.
Not because you can rewrite your past.
But because redemption through Christ can give your life a future your past could never have produced.
And if there is one truth I want you to carry long after you close this article, it is this:
The most heartbreaking thing about those twenty-five men was not that they could see the sunrise—it was that they turned away from the God who made the sun.
Do not spend your life bowing before what was created while neglecting the One who gave His life to redeem you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID HE DIDN’T COME TO BRING PEACE—BUT A SWORD. WHAT IF THE PEACE YOU’RE PROTECTING IS THE VERY THING KEEPING YOU FROM GOD?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID HE DIDN’T COME TO BRING PEACE—BUT A SWORD. WHAT IF THE PEACE YOU’RE PROTECTING IS THE VERY THING KEEPING YOU FROM GOD?

One of the most misunderstood statements Jesus ever made reveals a terrifying possibility: you can keep everyone around you happy, avoid every uncomfortable confrontation, and still be quietly walking away from the One who died to save you.
There is a kind of peace that can cost you your soul.
Not because peace is evil.
Not because God wants your family divided.
Not because Jesus enjoys watching relationships fall apart.
But because sometimes what we call peace is really fear wearing respectable clothes.
Sometimes it is the silence you maintain because you are afraid of losing someone's approval.
Sometimes it is the compromise you keep making because obedience would change everything.
And sometimes it is sitting in church on Sunday, singing about surrender, while spending the rest of the week negotiating with the very sins Jesus died to free you from.
You smile. You agree. You avoid the difficult conversation.
Everyone thinks you are doing fine.
But somewhere deep inside, you know something is wrong.
Then you open your Bible and discover words that almost seem impossible to reconcile with the Jesus you thought you knew.
“Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword.” — Matthew 10:34 (KJV)
Wait.
A sword?
From Jesus?
The One whose birth was announced with peace?
The One who told His followers to love their enemies?
The One who rebuked Peter for drawing a weapon?
The One who willingly allowed Himself to be arrested, beaten, humiliated, and crucified rather than establish His kingdom through violence?
How could that same Jesus say He came not to bring peace, but a sword?
And perhaps the more unsettling question is this:
What if He was warning us about a kind of discipleship that looks peaceful on the outside but has already surrendered the truth on the inside?
Because once you understand what Jesus actually meant, you may never read this passage the same way again.
And you may never look at your own compromises the same way either.
Jesus did not speak those words in the middle of a military campaign.
He spoke them while preparing His disciples for the cost of following Him.

In Matthew chapter 10, Jesus sends His twelve apostles into the world. He gives them authority to minister, commands them to proclaim the kingdom, and warns them that following Him will not always bring applause.
They will encounter rejection.
They will face persecution.
They may be betrayed.
Even members of their own households may turn against them.
Then, in the middle of those warnings, He says something extraordinary.
The Greek text of Matthew 10:34 reads:
Μὴ νομίσητε ὅτι ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰρήνην ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν· οὐκ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰρήνην ἀλλὰ μάχαιραν.
Transliteration:
Mē nomisēte hoti ēlthon balein eirēnēn epi tēn gēn; ouk ēlthon balein eirēnēn alla machairan.
A close English rendering is:
“Do not think that I came to bring peace upon the earth; I did not come to bring peace, but a sword.”
The word translated peace is εἰρήνη (eirēnē).

It can describe peace, harmony, or the absence of conflict. In biblical usage, it can also express the deeper idea of well-being and reconciliation associated with the Hebrew concept שָׁלוֹם (shalom).
And the word translated sword is μάχαιρα (machaira), a word referring to a blade or sword.
Jesus deliberately uses a shocking contrast.
Peace.
Sword.
Harmony.
Division.
But here is where context becomes absolutely essential.
Jesus was not commanding His followers to take up weapons against people who disagreed with them.
He was explaining that His coming would force a decision so significant that even the closest human relationships could be affected.
How do we know?
Because He immediately explains Himself.
“For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law.” — Matthew 10:35 (KJV)
Then He adds:
“And a man's foes shall be they of his own household.” — Matthew 10:36 (KJV)
Jesus is drawing upon the language of Micah 7:6, a passage describing the breakdown of trust within families.
He is warning that allegiance to Him can expose divisions even where love, loyalty, and belonging should have been strongest.
This is not a command to hate your family.
It is not permission to insult your parents, abandon your responsibilities, or become cruel toward people who do not share your faith.
It is a warning that following Jesus may cost you the approval of people whose approval once meant everything to you.
And that is where this passage becomes painfully personal.
Imagine a young woman who has finally surrendered her life to Christ.
For years, she has been living in ways she knows are contrary to Scripture.
Her family considers those choices normal.
Her friends encourage them.
Nobody questions anything.
Then something changes.
She begins reading the Bible seriously.
She starts praying when nobody is watching.
She confesses sins she used to defend.
She begins setting boundaries she once believed were unnecessary.
And suddenly, people notice.
“Why are you acting so different?”
“Do you think you're better than us now?”
“Are you becoming one of those religious people?”
She tries to explain.
Not with arrogance.
Not with condemnation.
Just with the trembling honesty of someone who has encountered the mercy of Jesus and cannot pretend nothing happened.
But the room grows cold.
The invitations become fewer.
The jokes become sharper.
The people who once celebrated her choices now resent her convictions.
And she wonders whether following Jesus is worth the loneliness.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Maybe you are the only Christian in your household.
Maybe you have been mocked for refusing to participate in something you believe dishonors God.
Maybe you are trying to rebuild your marriage according to Scripture, but your spouse does not understand why you have changed.
Maybe your old friends keep asking where the person they used to know has gone.
Or perhaps your struggle is quieter.
You are not being persecuted.
Nobody is threatening you.
You simply know that telling the truth, confessing your sin, ending a dishonest arrangement, or refusing an unhealthy compromise could disrupt the comfortable life you have built.
So you keep postponing obedience.
Just one more week.
One more conversation avoided.
One more secret protected.
One more promise that you will surrender everything to God when the timing is better.
But the timing never seems to become better.
And gradually, you discover how easy it is to call something wisdom when it is actually fear.
How easy it is to call something patience when it is actually disobedience.
How easy it is to call something keeping the peace when it is really keeping a secret.
Not every quiet life is a surrendered life.
That is part of what makes Jesus' words so piercing.
But we must be careful.
Not every disagreement proves that you are suffering for righteousness.
Not everyone who criticizes you is persecuting you.
Sometimes people resist our behavior because we have been harsh, self-righteous, insensitive, or unwilling to listen.
Jesus never authorized Christians to manufacture conflict and then congratulate themselves for being rejected.
In fact, Scripture commands the opposite.
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” — Romans 12:18 (KJV)
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
As much as lieth in you.
Christians are called to pursue peace sincerely, humbly, and consistently.
But peace with others cannot always be maintained without compromising obedience to Christ.
That is the tension.
We must never create unnecessary division.
Yet we must never make human approval the price of faithfulness.
