But because the crucified and risen Savior can redeem people whose stories seemed ruined beyond repair.
Think of Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
The man who insisted he would remain faithful even unto death collapsed under the pressure of fear.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter remembered.
Luke 22:62 says he went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine those tears.
The unbearable knowledge that he had denied the very Lord he loved.
The memory of his own confident promises.
The humiliation.
The regret.
The terrible realization that he was not as strong as he believed.
But Peter's story did not end beside that fire of denial.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter and restored him to service, as John 21 records.
The Lord did not pretend the denial had never happened.
He confronted Peter with the question of love and commissioned him to care for His sheep.
The man who had failed was not beyond the reach of Christ's restoring mercy.
And maybe that is the sentence you have been waiting to hear.
Your failure does not have to be the final chapter.
If you are still breathing, do not mistake the invitation to repent for permission to delay repentance.
Come to Christ today.
Not when you have made yourself worthy.
Not when you have repaired your image.
Not when you have convinced everyone that you are spiritually strong.
Come with the truth.
Come with the guilt.
Come with the tears.
Come with the things you have been afraid to confess.
Come to the Savior who said:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." — John 6:37, KJV
And when He saves you, do not return to living as though your worth depends upon the applause of the world.
Your appearance will change.
Your achievements will eventually fade.
Your possessions will pass into other hands.
Even the people who praise you today may forget your name tomorrow.
But what is done in faithful obedience to Christ is not meaningless.
That is one of the enduring lessons we can draw from the women who gave their mirrors.
Their offering was not the foundation of their salvation.
Their gift did not make God indebted to them.
But their willing generosity became part of the work God had commanded.
And today, believers have opportunities to serve Christ through their own resources.
Sometimes that means helping a hungry family.
Sometimes it means supporting a faithful local church.
Sometimes it means providing Bibles, Christian teaching, or discipleship materials to people who cannot afford them.
Sometimes it means giving quietly to someone who has no way to repay you.
But we must keep the order right.
We do not give so that God will love us. We give because He has already shown His love in Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that each person should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That verse protects the beauty of Christian generosity.
Giving must not become a spiritual threat.
But voluntary support of sound gospel work can be a meaningful expression of generosity.
Paul thanked believers who partnered with him in the gospel and supported his ministry, as Philippians 1:5 and 4:15–18 show.
Their gifts were not payments for salvation.
They were expressions of fellowship and love in the work of Christ.
Not out of guilt.
Not because you owe us your money.
But because, if the Lord has used this ministry to encourage you, strengthen your faith, or lead you deeper into Scripture, you may desire to help make that same encouragement available to others.
Every article that points a weary soul back to Jesus matters.
Every biblical resource that helps someone understand the gospel matters.
Every testimony that reminds a struggling believer of Christ's mercy matters.
And if you believe this work should continue and expand, you can become part of sustaining it.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The gospel is.
And the greatest gift we could ever point you toward is not something you can purchase from a store.
It is the salvation God freely gives through His Son.
Not simply to increase a number.
Not merely to make a page more visible.
Someone may be sitting alone tonight, wondering whether God could ever forgive what they have done.
Someone may be slowly drifting away from the faith.
Someone may be smiling through a marriage that is falling apart.
Someone may be carrying a secret addiction.
Someone may have spent years believing their shame was stronger than the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps a passage of Scripture shared at the right moment will move that person to open a Bible, pray honestly, seek godly counsel, or return to Christ.
You cannot know every burden hidden behind the faces on your screen.
But you can choose to share the truth.
The purpose is not to collect religious information while leaving the heart unchanged.
It is to encourage people to open the Scriptures, know Christ more deeply, grow in sound doctrine, and live in faithful obedience to Him.
Because biblical knowledge should lead us toward worship, humility, love, and holiness.
And before you leave this article, I want to ask you something personal.
Not about your money.
Not about your appearance.
Not about how many people admire you.
What is your mirror?
What has become so important to your identity that the thought of surrendering it to God makes you afraid?
Is it your reputation?
Your need for approval?
Your desire to control every outcome?
Your bitterness toward someone who hurt you?
Your pride in being seen as the strong one?
Your habit of pretending that everything is fine?
Or perhaps it is the reflection of a person you used to be, a reflection you cannot seem to forgive.
Bring it into the light of God's Word.
You do not have to publish your private sins for strangers to read.
You do not have to expose another person's wounds to prove that you are sincere.
But you do need to be honest before God.
And where repentance is necessary, do not settle for emotional words without a changed direction.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust in Jesus Christ.
Seek reconciliation where it is right and possible.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Walk with mature believers who can encourage you in truth.
And remember that genuine spiritual transformation is the work of God's grace, not a performance designed to impress an audience.
You can write "Christ is still healing me" if you are learning to trust His grace through a difficult season.
You can write "No more hiding" if you are ready to walk honestly before God.
You do not have to share details you are not ready to share.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not walking alone.
And if God has brought you through a season of failure into repentance and restoration, consider sharing a testimony that gives glory to Jesus rather than to yourself.
Someone may need to hear that the Savior who restored Peter is still merciful to sinners today.
Now return with me, one final time, to the wilderness.
To the women.
To the mirrors.
To the bronze basin.
There is no recorded speech from those women in Exodus 38:8.
No dramatic farewell to their possessions.
No explanation of how they felt.
No names engraved upon the basin.
Just a brief statement that their mirrors were used in its construction.
And perhaps that is part of what makes their contribution so moving.
They did not need to become the center of the story.
Their gifts became part of something greater than themselves.
The basin stood in the tabernacle where priests washed in obedience to God's command.
And the whole tabernacle system, in its place within redemptive history, directs our attention toward the greater priesthood and finished sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
We should not claim that the women knew every future meaning Christians would later recognize in the tabernacle.
Scripture does not tell us that.
But we can stand on this side of the cross and see how the story of God's dwelling among His people reaches its fulfillment in Christ.
John 1:14 declares:
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
The Greek verb translated "dwelt" is ἐσκήνωσεν — eskēnōsen, meaning that He dwelt or pitched His tent among us.
The language resonates beautifully with the biblical theme of God's presence among His people.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He bore the judgment sinners deserved.
He died.
He rose again.
And through Him, those who believe are brought near to God.
That is the glory toward which the entire story moves.
Not the bronze.
Not the mirrors.
Not the basin.
Jesus Christ.
The One who sees beyond every outward reflection.
The One before whom every hidden thing is known.
The One who does not excuse sin but offers forgiveness through His own blood.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and gives new life by grace.
The One who can take a life marked by shame and make it a testimony to His mercy.
And maybe tonight, for the first time in a long time, you can stop staring at the person you wish you had been.
You can stop trying to manufacture a spotless image.
You can stop believing that if people discovered your weakness, there would be no hope left for you.
You can turn your eyes toward Jesus Christ.
Not because the mirror has suddenly become beautiful.
But because the Savior is beautiful beyond comparison.
And because His grace is greater than the reflection that has been tormenting you.
The women of Exodus gave their mirrors for the tabernacle.
What will you surrender in obedience to the Lord who gave Himself for you?
Do not answer quickly.
Let the question reach the places where your pride has built walls.
Let Scripture examine what you have been protecting.
Let the gospel remind you that surrender to Christ is not the destruction of your true hope.
It is the beginning of a life no longer ruled by the things that cannot save you.
And when you finally understand that, you may discover something extraordinary.
The most important thing about your life was never the face you saw in the mirror, but the Savior who loved sinners enough to go to the cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU WANT JESUS AS YOUR SAVIOR… BUT DO YOU REALLY WANT HIM AS YOUR LORD?
paragraphs: YOU WANT JESUS AS YOUR SAVIOR… BUT DO YOU REALLY WANT HIM AS YOUR LORD?

You want His blood to cover your sins. You want His grace to rescue your soul. You want His promises over your future. But what happens when the same Jesus who offers you forgiveness asks you to surrender the very thing you refuse to let go?
There is a frightening possibility that many churchgoing people rarely consider.
You can know the worship songs. You can quote the Bible. You can raise your hands when the music reaches its highest point.
And still spend most of your life resisting His authority.
Not because you have never heard His name.
But because you have learned how to speak about surrender without actually surrendering.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
The Jesus you call upon to save you is the same Jesus who calls you to follow Him.
You cannot rewrite His invitation to make room for the sins you have already decided to protect.
Read that again.

Because somewhere between wanting heaven and avoiding hell, between Sunday worship and Monday compromise, between asking God for blessings and resisting His correction, we may have forgotten something Jesus never concealed.
He did not simply say, “Admire Me.”
He said, “Follow Me.”
And following Him changes everything.
Imagine standing before Jesus.
Not before a preacher. Not before a congregation. Not before the people who know your Christian reputation.
Before Jesus Himself.

The One who saw every private decision. Every secret conversation. Every compromise you justified. Every conviction you silenced. Every opportunity to repent that you postponed because you thought there would always be another tomorrow.
You begin to speak.
“Lord, I believed in You.”
“Lord, I went to church.”
“Lord, I shared Your Word.”
“Lord, I did things in Your name.”
Then you remember something He once said.
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” — Matthew 7:21, KJV
Jesus continues in Matthew 7:22–23 by describing people who appeal to impressive religious works, only to hear Him declare that He never knew them.
Those words should disturb anyone who has mistaken religious activity for a living relationship with Christ.
But notice what Jesus is exposing.
He is not condemning a struggling believer who hates their sin and keeps returning to Him in repentance.
He is exposing the terrifying emptiness of a religious profession that exists without genuine allegiance to God.
The issue is not whether you have ever stumbled.
The issue is whether you have made peace with living apart from the One you call Lord.
There is a difference between falling into sin and building a home inside it.
A difference between struggling against temptation and defending it.
A difference between crying out for mercy and demanding that God approve what He has forbidden.
And that difference matters.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel better about remaining unchanged.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile us to the Father.
To give us new life.
And yes, to transform the hearts that once resisted Him.
In Luke 6:46, Jesus asks a question that cuts through centuries of religious performance:
“Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — KJV
The original Greek is even more striking:
Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;
Ti de me kaleite, Kyrie kyrie, kai ou poieite ha legō?
The sense is direct: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
The Greek word Κύριε (Kyrie) is the form of address from κύριος (kyrios), meaning “lord” or “master,” and, depending on context, a title of divine authority.
Jesus is confronting a contradiction between what people call Him and how they respond to His words.
He is not asking for a more emotional worship service.
He is asking why the lips acknowledge an authority the life refuses to obey.
And suddenly, the question becomes painfully personal.
What if the biggest obstacle in your walk with God is not that you do not know what He wants?
What if you know…
But you do not want to give it up?
That relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ.
That bitterness you have rehearsed so often that forgiveness now feels like betrayal.
That private habit you keep promising to abandon.
That dishonest business decision you excuse because everyone else does it.
That pride that would rather lose a relationship than admit wrongdoing.
That secret life you carefully separate from your public testimony.
You love hearing that Jesus forgives.
But when He confronts what is destroying you, something inside begins negotiating.
“Lord, anything but this.”
“I will serve You, but please do not touch that relationship.”
“I will follow You, but let me keep this one habit.”
“I will obey You, but not if it costs my reputation.”
“I will surrender, but not yet.”
And perhaps this is where the deepest spiritual battle begins.
Not between you and the world.
But between your will and the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
There is a man in Scripture whose story should make every comfortable Christian uncomfortable.
He came to Jesus with an extraordinary question.
“What shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?” — Mark 10:17, KJV
He was serious enough to approach Jesus. Morally respectable enough to speak of keeping the commandments. Wealthy enough to possess much.
By ordinary standards, he seemed like someone who had everything going for him.
But Jesus saw what no one else could see.
Mark 10:21 says:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him…”
Do not miss those words.
Jesus loved him.
Before Jesus exposed his attachment, He loved him.
Before He called him to a costly decision, He loved him.
Before the man walked away grieving, Jesus loved him.
Then Jesus told him to sell what he possessed, give to the poor, and follow Him.
This was not a universal command that every Christian must sell every possession to be saved. It was a specific confrontation with the attachment that ruled this man's heart.
Jesus placed His finger on the very thing the man could not imagine surrendering.
And the man went away sorrowful.
He wanted eternal life.
But when following Jesus threatened the treasure he loved most, he walked away.
That is the tragedy.
He stood before the greatest Treasure in the universe…
And chose what he could not bear to lose.
Now ask yourself something.
If Jesus confronted the one thing you are most afraid to surrender, what would it be?
Your money?
Your image?
Your independence?
Your relationship?
Your secret pleasure?
Your need to control everything?
Your right to remain angry?
What would make you walk away sorrowful?
Be careful before answering.
Because sometimes our idols are not the things we openly worship.
They are the things we quietly refuse to surrender.
And yet, even here, the Gospel shines.
Jesus did not expose that man's attachment because He enjoyed humiliating him.
Scripture tells us Jesus loved him.
The call to surrender was not cruelty.
It was an invitation to freedom.
The same is true when the Word of God exposes us today.
Christ does not reveal sin so that we will despair of His mercy.
He reveals the truth so that we will stop trusting what cannot save us.
And there is something else we must understand.
You are not saved because you have surrendered perfectly. You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
The original Greek uses the word χάριτί (chariti), from χάρις (charis), meaning grace.
Grace is not a wage you earn after becoming obedient enough.
It is God's undeserved favor.
Salvation is His gift.
You cannot purchase it through good deeds.
You cannot achieve it through religious performance.
You cannot make yourself worthy by collecting enough victories over temptation.
Jesus Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves through His sinless life, sacrificial death, and victorious resurrection.
But the passage does not end at verse nine.
Ephesians 2:10 says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God prepared for us to walk in.
Do you see the beautiful order?
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for a life that bears their fruit.
Obedience is not the price of salvation.
It is a fitting response to the Savior who has redeemed us.
And this is where many people misunderstand the Lordship of Christ.
They hear the call to obedience and immediately imagine a cruel master waiting to reject them after their next failure.
But that is not the Jesus revealed in the Gospel.
He is holy, yes.
He commands repentance, yes.
He calls His disciples to deny themselves, yes.
But He is also the Savior who welcomed sinners, touched the unclean, restored the broken, and gave His life for people who could never save themselves.
Consider Peter.
Peter loved Jesus.
Peter boldly promised loyalty.
He was convinced that even if others fell away, he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denial.
Three times, Peter denied knowing the Lord he had promised never to abandon.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine the weight of that moment.
Peter had not merely broken a rule.
He had denied his Lord.
The man who had walked on water at Jesus' invitation now stood drowning in shame.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of shame.
You promised God you would never go back.
And you went back.
You cried at the altar.
Then returned to the same compromise.
You said you were finished with the old life.
But somehow the old life found its way into your decisions again.
And now you wonder whether Jesus is tired of hearing your apologies.
But Peter's story did not end in the courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, beside the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus questioned Peter's love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The disciple who had denied Him was not beyond restoration.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
But Christ's mercy was real too.
And restoration did not mean Peter could simply return to life as though Jesus had no claim over him.
Jesus called him to love, serve, and follow.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved to the past.
Powerful mercy that brings us back to the One who makes us new.
There is another Greek word worth understanding.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus announces:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — KJV
The word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), from μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It calls for a change of mind and heart, a turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed because you were caught.
More than crying because your choices finally brought consequences.
More than saying “sorry” while secretly planning to continue.
Repentance means coming into agreement with God about sin and turning toward Him.
It does not mean that every temptation instantly disappears.
It does not mean that every wounded habit is healed overnight.
It does not mean a Christian will never fall again.
But it does mean we stop calling darkness light simply because darkness has become familiar.
It means we stop demanding that Jesus bless the very things from which He is calling us to turn.
And it means that when we fall, we do not have to hide from the Savior who calls us back.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is hope for the person who is tired of pretending.
Hope for the believer who has grown spiritually cold.
Hope for the person who has been living two lives.
Hope for the one who is ashamed to admit how far they have wandered.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Maybe you are reading this with tears forming in your eyes.
Maybe you are thinking about the person you have become behind closed doors.
Maybe you remember when prayer was not a routine but a lifeline.
When opening the Bible was not another obligation but a hunger.
When worship was not something you performed for other people but an honest response to the goodness of God.
And somewhere along the way, you became busy.
Distracted.
Comfortable.
Compromised.
You still believed in Jesus.
But you slowly stopped listening to Him.
And now these words are reaching places in your heart that you have kept locked for years.
Please hear this carefully.
Conviction is not the same as condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Those who belong to Christ are not living under the final sentence of condemnation.
Yet the same chapter speaks of putting to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit (Romans 8:13).
Grace does not eliminate the seriousness of sin.
Grace brings us into a new relationship with God, in which the Holy Spirit works to transform us.
The enemy would love for you to confuse conviction with hopelessness.
To believe that because you have failed, you might as well stop fighting.
To believe that because you have fallen repeatedly, returning to Christ is pointless.
But the Gospel calls you to neither denial nor despair.
It calls you to Jesus.
Not to a carefully edited version of yourself.
Not to a performance of spiritual perfection.
To Jesus.
With your sin confessed.
Your pride laid down.
Your excuses abandoned.
Your empty hands open.
There is a sentence from Jesus that may be one of the most challenging invitations ever spoken.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
The Greek word translated “daily” is καθ’ ἡμέραν (kath' hēmeran).
Daily.
Not once during an emotional worship service.
Not only when life becomes unbearable.
Not only when you need a miracle.
Daily.
When the alarm rings and nobody is watching.
When you have an opportunity to retaliate.
When telling the truth could cost you something.
When temptation offers relief without obedience.
When forgiveness feels impossible.
When following Jesus makes you unpopular.
When doing what is right means losing what you wanted.
The cross was not a fashionable religious accessory to Jesus' first hearers.
It was an instrument of execution, associated with suffering, shame, and death.
So when Jesus called people to take up their cross, He was not promising a comfortable life with occasional religious inconvenience.
He was calling them to costly discipleship.
A life no longer centered on self-rule.
But do not misunderstand the invitation.
Jesus is not asking you to suffer in order to prove that His sacrifice was insufficient.
His sacrifice is sufficient.
He calls you to follow because He is worthy, because His way is true, and because the life He gives is greater than the false promises of sin.
The question is not whether following Jesus will cost you something.
It will.
The question is whether you believe He is worth more than what you must leave behind.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
She stood accused, publicly exposed, surrounded by people ready to condemn her.
Jesus confronted the hypocrisy of her accusers, and they departed.
Then He said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Notice the two truths held together.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy and holiness.
Compassion and truth.
Grace and transformation.
Jesus did not join the crowd in condemning her.
But neither did He declare that sin no longer mattered.
He extended mercy and called her away from the life that had brought her there.
That is the heart of the Gospel we must never distort.
We must not turn Jesus into a merciless judge who refuses to receive repentant sinners.
And we must not reduce Him to a comforting religious figure who never challenges our desires.
He is Savior and Lord.
The Lamb of God who takes away sin.
The risen King to whom all authority belongs.
Philippians 2:9–11 declares that God highly exalted Jesus, and that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
The word κύριος (kyrios) appears again.
Lord.
Not merely an adviser.
Not a spiritual accessory.
Not someone we consult only after our plans fall apart.
Lord.
And one day, every knee will bow.
But today, the invitation is to bow willingly in faith, repentance, and love.
Not because we can earn His acceptance through surrender.
But because the crucified and risen Christ is worthy of our whole lives.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to make Christianity fit around your preferences.
You want peace without repentance.
Blessing without obedience.
Forgiveness without confession.
A crown without a cross.
A Savior who rescues you from judgment, but not a Lord who challenges the throne of your heart.
And yet, there is no greater freedom than belonging to Jesus Christ.
The world tells you freedom means doing whatever you want.
Jesus teaches that sin itself can become slavery.
John 8:34 says:
“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
And John 8:36 declares:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
What if the very thing you are afraid to surrender is the thing that has been holding you captive?
What if obedience is not the loss of your freedom but the beginning of freedom you have never truly known?
What if the Lordship of Jesus is not the end of your joy but the beginning of a joy no temporary pleasure could ever provide?
You do not need a weaker Jesus who approves everything you do.
You need the real Jesus who loves you enough to tell you the truth.
The Jesus who died for sinners.
The Jesus who rose from the grave.
The Jesus who welcomes the weary.
The Jesus who calls the proud to humility.
The Jesus who forgives the repentant.
The Jesus who restores the fallen.
The Jesus who transforms lives through His Spirit.
The Jesus who says, “Follow Me.”
And maybe, right now, you are finally ready to answer.
Not with another promise you intend to forget.
Not with another emotional moment that ends when you close your phone.
But with a genuine turning of your heart toward Christ.
You may not know how to repair everything you have damaged.
You may not know how to break every sinful pattern overnight.
You may not know how to face the consequences of the choices you have made.
But you can begin with the truth.

“Lord Jesus, I have called You my Savior while resisting Your authority in places I did not want You to touch. I have justified things Your Word calls sin. I have confused Your patience with permission. I have wanted Your blessings more than Your presence.
“Forgive me.
“I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I cannot save myself. I need Your mercy, Your righteousness, and Your transforming grace.

“Teach me to follow You. Give me a heart that loves what You love and turns away from what dishonors You. When I fall, draw me back to repentance instead of hiding. When obedience is costly, remind me that You are worthy.
“Jesus, I do not want to merely speak Your name. I want to belong to You.
“Be Lord over every part of my life.
“Amen.”
If those words express the honest desire of your heart, do not treat this moment as the finish line.
Let it be a beginning.
Open your Bible.
Return to prayer.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek forgiveness where you have wronged someone.
Find a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and where you can grow with other believers.
If you are struggling with a destructive pattern, seek trustworthy pastoral guidance and practical accountability.
And when you fail, do not run from Christ.
Run to Him.
Because the Christian life is not sustained by pretending we are strong.
It is sustained by the grace of the Savior who is faithful.
What is the hardest area of your life to surrender to Jesus right now?
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss publicly.
But if this message has brought something into the light, do not immediately bury that conviction beneath another distraction.
You may discover that you are not the only person fighting a battle behind a smile.
Sometimes the first honest words we speak are the beginning of a much-needed conversation about grace, repentance, and healing.
And please, think about someone you know who needs to read this.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to attack with Scripture.
Someone you genuinely love.
A family member who has drifted from faith.
A friend who is secretly struggling.
A believer who knows all the right words but has grown spiritually numb.
Someone who thinks they have wandered too far for Jesus to welcome them back.
One thoughtful share can begin a conversation you never expected.
Because discipleship should not end when an article ends.
It should continue when the phone is put down and the real decisions begin.
We want the person who cannot afford a Christian book to have access to biblical nourishment.
We want the struggling believer to find resources that help them return to Scripture.
We want families, new Christians, and longtime disciples to have opportunities to grow in their understanding of God's Word.
And keeping that mission growing takes time, work, resources, and people who believe it is worth supporting.
It is a voluntary way to partner with the ongoing work of Gospel-centered encouragement, Christian education, and discipleship.

For those who view financial giving as part of their worship, supporting Gospel ministry can be one meaningful expression of generosity. Scripture encourages willing, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7), and the support of those who labor in Gospel ministry (Galatians 6:6).
Those gifts cannot be bought.
Our salvation was purchased by Christ, not by our donations.
You are still welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep growing in the Word.
Use the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
And above all, keep following Jesus.
It will be lives directed toward Christ, believers strengthened by Scripture, sinners hearing the Gospel, and people learning to walk in the truth.
Your shares can help others discover it.
But only Jesus can save a soul.
And that is why everything must lead back to Him.
Now, before you leave, return to the question that brought you here.
You want Jesus as your Savior.
But do you really want Him as your Lord?
Not the version of Jesus who never interrupts your plans.
Not the version who agrees with everything you already believe.
Not the version who exists merely to make your life easier.
The real Jesus.
The One who told the truth even when people walked away.
The One who washed His disciples' feet.
The One who forgave sinners and confronted hypocrisy.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who rose victorious over death.
The One who is worthy of your trust, obedience, worship, and love.
Will you follow Him when His Word confronts your desires?
Will you trust Him when surrender feels frightening?
Will you come back when you stumble?
Will you let His grace transform you instead of using His grace as an excuse to remain unchanged?
You do not have to pretend that surrender is easy.
You do not have to claim that every battle is already won.
But you do have to reckon with the question Jesus Himself asked:
“Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?”
The question is not meant to leave you staring hopelessly at your failures.
It is meant to direct your eyes toward the Savior who calls you to follow Him.
And there is still mercy for the person who hears His voice today.
Remember Peter.
Remember the rich young ruler.
Remember the woman who stood accused.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
And remember that no amount of religious appearance can replace the life that comes through faith in Jesus Christ.
Your past may be scandalous.
Your failures may be painful.
Your compromises may be difficult to admit.
But your story does not have to end where your sin left you.
In Christ there is forgiveness.
In Christ there is redemption.
In Christ there is new life.
And through the work of His Spirit, there is genuine transformation.

The greatest tragedy would not be discovering that Jesus wanted more than your religious words, but spending your whole life calling Him “Lord” while refusing the grace that was calling you to follow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE WORSHIP GAVE YOU GOOSEBUMPS… BUT GOD NEVER GOT YOUR HEART?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE WORSHIP GAVE YOU GOOSEBUMPS… BUT GOD NEVER GOT YOUR HEART?
The Dangerous Difference Between Feeling God's Presence and Truly Following Jesus — And Why the Most Powerful Moment of Worship May Begin When the Music Stops.
The lights dimmed. The first chord filled the room. Thousands of hands slowly rose toward heaven.
Someone began to cry.
Someone fell to their knees.
Someone whispered, “Lord, I can feel You.”

And somewhere in that same crowd stood a person who had been secretly living in sin all week, arguing with their spouse that morning, ignoring God's conviction for months, and refusing to forgive someone who had wounded them years ago.
But when the chorus reached its highest note, tears streamed down their face.
For a few beautiful minutes, everything felt holy.
Then the music stopped.
The lights came back on.
The congregation went home.
And nothing changed.
Not the bitterness.
Not the hidden compromise.
Not the pride.
Not the private conversations that dishonored Christ.
Not the sin they had promised God they would surrender the last time the music made them cry.
And that raises a question many Christians are uncomfortable asking.
What if some of us have become addicted to the feeling of worship while slowly losing our hunger for the God we claim to worship?
Before you become defensive, understand something.
This is not an attack on worship music, emotional expressions, lifted hands, tears, or powerful church gatherings.
Scripture celebrates singing, shouting, instruments, reverence, and joyful praise. The Psalms are filled with them.
And genuine encounters with God's truth can move a person to tears.
But tears alone cannot tell us whether a heart has surrendered.
A powerful atmosphere is not the same thing as spiritual maturity.
And feeling overwhelmed during a song is not necessarily the same thing as being transformed by Jesus Christ.
There is something far more dangerous than a church without beautiful music.
It is a heart that knows how to respond to beautiful music but has forgotten how to respond to God's Word.
And perhaps the most unsettling part is this:
You can love the atmosphere surrounding Jesus while resisting the authority of Jesus.
You can sing about surrender while secretly negotiating the conditions of your obedience.
You can lift your hands on Sunday while refusing to release the resentment you carry into Monday.
You can weep when someone sings about the cross while continuing to excuse the very sins Christ died to save you from.
Not because every emotional worshiper is a hypocrite.
But because human emotions can be stirred without the human will being surrendered.
And Jesus never asked us merely to admire Him.
He called us to follow Him.
There is a scene in Scripture that should make every modern worshiper examine their heart.
In John 6, a crowd followed Jesus after witnessing His miraculous provision of bread.
They had seen something extraordinary.
They had experienced something unforgettable.
They wanted more.
But Jesus confronted the reason they were seeking Him.
In John 6:26, He told them they were looking for Him not because they had understood the signs, but because they had eaten the loaves and been satisfied.
Think about that.
They were following the right Person for the wrong reason.
They wanted what Jesus could provide.
But when He began teaching truths that challenged their expectations, many could no longer bear His words.
John 6:66 records the devastating outcome:
“From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.” — John 6:66, KJV
They had enjoyed the miracle.
But they would not remain for the message.
They loved receiving bread.
But they struggled to receive the Bread of Life.
And suddenly this ancient passage feels uncomfortably modern.
What happens when Jesus no longer gives you the emotional experience you expected?
What happens when the worship team does not sing your favorite song?
When the preacher stops offering comforting words and begins preaching repentance?
When the sermon confronts your relationships, your secret habits, your dishonesty, your unforgiveness, or your love of money?
When God seems silent, even though you have been praying faithfully?
Will you still follow Jesus?
If the goosebumps disappear, does your devotion disappear with them?
Because the Jesus who feeds the hungry crowd is the same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance.
The Jesus who comforts the brokenhearted is the same Jesus who commands His followers to deny themselves and take up their cross.
And the Jesus who receives our songs also sees the lives we live when nobody is watching.
That is where worship becomes more than music.
That is where discipleship begins to cost us something.
In John 4, Jesus spoke to a Samaritan woman whose life carried wounds, complicated relationships, and deep spiritual questions.
She wanted to discuss the proper location for worship.
Jesus redirected her toward something far deeper.
He declared:
“God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” — John 4:24, KJV
The Greek text reads:
πνεῦμα ὁ θεός, καὶ τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας αὐτὸν ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ δεῖ προσκυνεῖν.
Pneuma ho Theos, kai tous proskynountas auton en pneumati kai alētheia dei proskynein.
A close translation is:
“God is spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say that true worship requires a particular musical style.
He did not say that the loudest room contains the holiest people.
He did not say that the strongest emotional reaction proves the deepest relationship with God.
He spoke about worship in spirit and truth.
The Greek word προσκυνέω (proskyneō) means to bow down, prostrate oneself, or offer reverent homage.
In John's Gospel, the meaning of worship is inseparable from the One being worshiped.
And the word ἀλήθεια (alētheia) means truth.

In the context of John's Gospel, truth is not merely religious sincerity. It is bound to God's revelation, supremely revealed in Jesus Christ, who later declares Himself to be “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).
Jesus was not teaching that emotions are forbidden.
He was revealing that worship cannot be reduced to a sacred location, external performance, or religious atmosphere.
True worship must be directed toward God as He has revealed Himself.
It must be genuine.
It must be shaped by truth.
And it must not be separated from the Christ who makes access to the Father possible.
This is why a person can stand quietly in the back of a church, unable to sing because grief has stolen their voice, and still worship God sincerely.
This is why a mother whispering Scripture while washing dishes may be honoring Christ.
This is why a man sitting alone in his car, finally confessing a sin he has hidden for years, may be responding to God more faithfully than he did during the loudest song of the service.
And this is why the believer who obeys Christ when obedience is painful should never be considered spiritually inferior to someone whose worship is visibly emotional.
God is not measuring the volume of our voices.
He sees the heart.
But there is another passage that makes this conversation even more serious.
Centuries before the birth of Christ, the prophet Amos delivered a message to a people who maintained religious ceremonies while tolerating injustice.
God spoke through the prophet:
“Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols.” — Amos 5:23, KJV
And then came the command:
“But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.” — Amos 5:24, KJV
The Hebrew of that final verse reads:
וְיִגַּל כַּמַּיִם מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה כְּנַחַל אֵיתָן
Veyiggal kammayim mishpat, utsedaqah kenachal eitan.
A close rendering is:
“But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.”
The Hebrew word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat) concerns justice and right judgment.
The word צְדָקָה (tsedaqah) speaks of righteousness, including conduct consistent with what is right.
God was not condemning music itself.
He was confronting the contradiction between religious celebration and unrighteous living.
Their songs continued.
Their ceremonies continued.
Their religious identity remained visible.
But their treatment of others exposed something deeply wrong.
Imagine hearing that message today.
Imagine a congregation singing beautifully about God's holiness while its members excuse dishonesty, exploit vulnerable people, or refuse to make right the harm they have caused.
Imagine someone singing, “Lord, have Your way,” while refusing to let God's Word challenge a cherished sin.
Imagine praying for revival while refusing to repent.
The problem is not that the music is too beautiful.
The problem is that beauty can become a substitute for obedience.
And when religious excitement becomes more precious to us than righteousness, we have begun to confuse the gift with the Giver.
But please hear this carefully.
The answer is not to become suspicious of every tear, every raised hand, or every joyful expression of praise.
David danced before the Lord.
The Psalms command God's people to sing joyfully.
Paul and Silas sang hymns while imprisoned.
The early church knew both reverence and rejoicing.
The Bible does not teach emotionless Christianity.
It teaches worship that belongs to God.
There is a difference between being emotionally moved by the truth and making emotional intensity the test of whether God is present.
Sometimes genuine worship produces overwhelming joy.
Sometimes it produces grief over sin.
Sometimes it produces peace.
And sometimes it looks like trembling hands opening a Bible after a terrible day and whispering:
“Lord, I do not feel strong. I do not even feel close to You. But I still believe Your Word.”
That, too, can be worship.
Perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
You remember when worship seemed effortless.
The songs reached somewhere deep inside you.
Prayer felt alive.
Scripture seemed to leap from the page.
You could hardly wait to gather with other believers.
Then something happened.
A prayer seemed unanswered.
A relationship collapsed.
Someone in the church disappointed you.
A loved one died.
Your finances fell apart.
Depression, exhaustion, or grief made it difficult to feel anything.
You continued attending church, but the emotional warmth you remembered was gone.
And somewhere in the silence, you began asking yourself:
“Has God left me?”
“Am I doing something wrong?”
“Why can everyone else seem to feel His presence when I cannot?”
Listen.
The absence of a powerful feeling is not proof of the absence of God.
Your emotions are real, and they matter.
But they are not infallible instruments for measuring God's faithfulness.
The cross did not become less powerful on the days you felt spiritually empty.
The resurrection did not become less true because your prayers felt difficult.
And the promises of Christ do not expire when your heart is exhausted.
Jesus said:
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” — Hebrews 13:5, KJV
That promise is not dependent on the quality of a worship service.
It rests on the faithfulness of God.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying an unnecessary burden for years.
You thought you were spiritually failing because you did not cry when everyone else cried.
You thought your faith was weak because you did not tremble when someone prayed over you.
You thought God was distant because the music no longer moved you the way it once did.
But Christian faith is not a competition to see who can experience the strongest emotions.
It is trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
And sometimes trust becomes most visible when the feelings are absent.
Consider Jesus in Gethsemane.
There were no instruments.
No stage lights.
No congregation singing in harmony.
There was anguish.
There was prayer.
There was surrender.
Jesus prayed:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
That moment was not a display of emotional comfort.
It was the sinless Son's obedient submission to the Father as He approached the suffering of the cross.
And we must be careful not to turn His unique redemptive obedience into merely another example of human determination.
Jesus was accomplishing what no sinner could accomplish.
He was moving toward the cross where He would give His life for our salvation.
Yet His prayer also exposes the shallowness of a faith that only wants God's will when God's will feels pleasant.
Real surrender does not always feel victorious.
Sometimes it feels like tears.
Sometimes it feels like trembling.
Sometimes it feels like choosing faithfulness when everything inside you wishes the road were easier.
And here is where this conversation becomes deeply personal.
What if the most important thing God is confronting in your life is not your worship playlist but your unwillingness to forgive?
What if you have been asking Him for another powerful encounter while avoiding the confession you know you need to make?
What if you have been longing for revival in your church while resisting repentance in your home?
What if you have become so accustomed to singing about grace that you have forgotten grace also teaches us to renounce ungodliness?
Titus 2:11–12 tells us that God's saving grace trains us to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live upright, godly lives.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is God's undeserved favor that saves us through Christ and begins transforming how we live.
But this is where another danger appears.
Some Christians hear a message about obedience and immediately begin believing they must earn God's acceptance through perfect behavior.
That is not the Gospel.
You cannot sing beautifully enough to purchase salvation.
You cannot repent perfectly enough to deserve the cross.
You cannot accumulate enough good deeds to place God in your debt.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of our works.
And the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because we have transformed ourselves.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ, and that grace produces a new direction for our lives.
Obedience is not the price of salvation.
It is the fruit of a living faith.
And when we stumble, we do not need to hide behind another worship experience.
We need to return to Jesus.
The same Jesus who exposed sin also welcomed repentant sinners.
Think about Peter.
He had walked with Christ.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had made bold promises.
He had insisted that even if others fell away, he would remain faithful.
And then, in the courtyard, fear overcame his courage.
Three times he denied knowing Jesus.
Luke 22:61 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went outside and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
No music.
No congregation.
No beautiful atmosphere.
Just a broken man confronting the terrible reality of what he had done.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus was not beyond the reach of Jesus' restoring grace.
That does not make Peter's denial insignificant.
It makes Christ's mercy astonishing.
And perhaps that is the word someone needs tonight.
You do not need to manufacture a spiritual high to convince Jesus to receive you.
You need to come to Him truthfully.
Bring the pride.
Bring the secret compromise.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the exhausted faith.
Bring the shame you have tried to bury beneath religious activity.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive our confessed sins and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Not because our tears are impressive.
Not because our promises are flawless.
But because Jesus Christ is our righteous Advocate, and His sacrifice is sufficient.
That is the scandal of grace.
The holy Son of God willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The crucified Savior rose from the dead.
And those who could never save themselves are invited to receive forgiveness and new life through Him.
Not through a perfect performance.
Not through an unforgettable concert.
Not through the approval of a religious crowd.
Through Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But His grace does not merely give us a better feeling about our old lives.
It calls us into a new life with Him.
Romans 12:1 urges believers, in view of God's mercies, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, describing this as their spiritual or reasonable worship.
The Greek phrase λογικὴν λατρείαν (logikēn latreian) is translated in different English versions as “reasonable service” or “spiritual worship.”
Paul is describing a response to God's mercy that involves the offering of our whole selves.
Not just our voices.
Not just our Sunday mornings.
Our bodies.
Our choices.
Our relationships.
Our daily lives.
This does not mean every ordinary action automatically becomes worship regardless of motive.
It means the mercy of God should reshape the way we live before Him.
Worship continues when you close your Bible and refuse to participate in a dishonest transaction.
Worship continues when you speak gently to someone who has tested your patience.
Worship continues when you reject temptation even though nobody would know.
Worship continues when you admit you were wrong and ask forgiveness without defending your pride.
Worship continues when you serve someone who cannot repay you.
Worship continues when you open Scripture because you want to know God, not merely because you want to feel something extraordinary.
And worship continues when you love the truth enough to obey it.
There is a sobering warning in Matthew 7:21.
Jesus says:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” — KJV
In the surrounding passage, Jesus warns that impressive religious claims and even extraordinary works are not reliable substitutes for truly belonging to Him.
These are serious words.
They should move us toward humble self-examination, not toward declaring that every expressive worshiper is spiritually lost.
Only God knows every heart.
But we should not ignore what Jesus is teaching.
Religious language cannot replace a genuine relationship with Him.
And outward displays cannot make disobedience harmless.
The question is not whether you have ever raised your hands in worship.
The question is whether those hands belong to a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
Not without the ongoing need for grace.
But sincerely.
Because a genuine disciple may stumble terribly and still return in repentance.
The difference is not that true believers never fight sin.
It is that they are called to stop making peace with it.
And that brings us to the question beneath all the other questions.
If Jesus never gave you another emotionally overwhelming worship experience, would He still be enough for you?
If the music became quiet...
If the crowds disappeared...
If nobody noticed your faithfulness...
If your prayers required patient waiting...
If following Him cost you approval, comfort, or convenience...
Would you still say, “Lord, You are worthy”?
Would you still open His Word?
Would you still seek His kingdom?
Would you still trust His goodness?
Would you still follow the One who loved you and gave Himself for you?
There is a moment in John 6 that answers the question beautifully.
After many turned away, Jesus asked the Twelve whether they also wanted to leave.
Peter answered:
“Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.” — John 6:68, KJV
Not, “Lord, You always make us feel wonderful.”
Not, “Lord, Your gatherings are always exciting.”
Not, “Lord, following You is always comfortable.”
But:
“To whom shall we go?”
Peter recognized something the departing crowd had missed.
Jesus Himself was the treasure.
His words were the words of eternal life.
And there is nowhere else to find what only He can give.
Maybe this article has unsettled you.
Maybe you recognized yourself in the person who loves worship gatherings but struggles with private obedience.
Maybe you realized you have been measuring your relationship with God by how strongly you feel Him rather than by the truth of His Word.
Or maybe you are the weary believer who needed to hear that a quiet season does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
Wherever you are, do not turn this into another moment of temporary emotion.
Respond to God.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to forgive, begin seeking the grace to forgive.
If you need to make something right, take the next faithful step.
If you need to return to Scripture, open it.
If you need to ask for prayer, ask.
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ as Savior and Lord, do not confuse religious familiarity with saving faith.
Turn to Him.
Believe the Gospel.
The Son of God died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
He is worthy of more than our applause.
He is worthy of our trust, our love, and our lives.
And He is merciful toward those who come to Him.
I want to invite you to do something that may require more courage than raising your hands in a crowded room.
Be honest.
Not for an audience.
Not to prove how spiritual you are.
But because sometimes bringing our struggle into the light is the beginning of seeking help, prayer, and accountability.
If you are struggling through a season when God feels distant, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to disclose private details or confess sensitive struggles publicly. God hears the prayers you cannot put into words, too.
Someone may be quietly reading who desperately needs to know that faith can endure through spiritual dryness.
Your testimony may help them take another step toward Christ.
And please do not let this message end with you.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who has been attending church faithfully but is secretly exhausted from trying to feel spiritual enough.
Someone who believes their tears have dried up because God has stopped loving them.
Someone who has learned the language of worship but has never clearly understood the Gospel.
Someone who needs to be reminded that Jesus is greater than any experience we can have in His name.
Not to shame anyone.
Not to win a religious argument.
But to make the truth of Christ visible to someone who might otherwise never encounter this message.
Because our mission is not to create people who depend on powerful posts.
It is to point people toward the living Christ and help them grow in His Word.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into consistent biblical learning, prayer, spiritual maturity, and a deeper understanding of Jesus Christ.
And certainly not because the Gospel is for sale.
But Scripture does teach the value of freely and willingly supporting faithful Gospel ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–17 shows how believers participated in Paul's ministry through their material support.
What matters is that any support comes freely, prayerfully, and with a sincere desire to serve Christ.

It can help sustain the work behind the articles, devotionals, books, and free resources that encourage believers who may never have the opportunity to attend a Bible school or purchase an extensive Christian library.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
The deeper purpose is making sound biblical teaching more accessible.
The deeper purpose is helping people know the Savior, not merely recognize His name.
Your spiritual worth is never measured by what you can give to a ministry.
Christ is the Savior.
We are simply servants seeking to make Him known.
Beyond the music.
Beyond the emotions.
Beyond the excitement of another spiritual moment.
Back to Jesus.
Because one day the final song of your earthly life will end.
The applause will fade.
The crowds will disappear.
Every stage light will go dark.
And what will matter eternally is not how many times you felt overwhelmed in a worship service, but whether you truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who saves by grace.
The One who calls His people to follow Him.
So sing with all your heart.
Lift your hands if you wish.
Weep when the truth of God's mercy moves you.
Rejoice when the congregation praises His name.
But when the final chord fades, do not leave your devotion behind with the music.
Carry your faith into the ordinary places where obedience becomes difficult and love becomes costly.
Into your home.
Into your workplace.
Into your private decisions.
Into the moments nobody applauds.
Because worship was never meant to end when the music stopped.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking thing would be to spend your life chasing the feeling of being near Jesus while refusing to surrender to the Jesus who was reaching for your heart all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WAS USED, MISTREATED, AND LEFT IN THE WILDERNESS… BUT GOD CALLED HER BY NAME.
paragraphs: SHE WAS USED, MISTREATED, AND LEFT IN THE WILDERNESS… BUT GOD CALLED HER BY NAME.
The heartbreaking story of Hagar reveals a God who sees the tears nobody notices, hears the cries nobody answers, and meets the forgotten in places where everyone else has abandoned them.
What if the place where you felt most abandoned becomes the very place where you discover that God has never taken His eyes off you?
There is a kind of pain that doesn't come from losing someone.
It comes from realizing that someone you trusted never truly valued you.
You were useful when they needed you. Important when you could give them something. Welcome when your presence served their purposes.
But when you became inconvenient…
Everything changed.
Suddenly, the people who once needed you began treating you like a burden.
Your sacrifices were forgotten. Your loyalty meant nothing. Your tears became an irritation.
And somewhere between trying to remain strong and wondering what you did wrong, a terrible question began forming inside your heart.
Does anybody actually see what I'm going through?
Not the smile you wear in public.
Not the carefully arranged photographs.
Not the familiar answer, "I'm okay," when someone asks how you're doing.
But the real you.
The exhausted you.
The wounded you.
The person who sometimes cries after everyone else has fallen asleep.
The person who keeps praying even though heaven seems painfully quiet.
The person who has been holding everything together while quietly falling apart.
If you've ever felt that way, there is a woman in Scripture you need to meet.
Her name was Hagar.
And before her story was over, she would give us one of the most intimate descriptions of God recorded in the Old Testament.
El Roi.
The God who sees me.
But what makes her story so extraordinary is not simply that God saw her.
It's where He found her.
And what He said when He did.
Hagar was an Egyptian servant in the household of Abram and Sarai, whose names God would later change to Abraham and Sarah.
She was not the woman to whom God had originally given the promise of a son.
She was not the central figure in the covenant narrative.
She was a foreigner, a servant, and a woman living within a household where other people held tremendous power over her future.
Genesis 16 introduces her almost casually.
But there was nothing casual about what happened next.
God had promised Abram descendants. Yet Sarai remained unable to bear children, and the years were passing.
Waiting had become painful.
Hope had become difficult.
And Sarai decided to take matters into her own hands.
She gave Hagar to Abram as a wife so that she might obtain children through her.
Read that slowly.
Hagar's body became part of someone else's attempt to solve a problem.
Scripture does not record Hagar being asked whether she wanted this arrangement.
We should not pretend to know every thought she had. But we must not overlook the enormous imbalance of power surrounding her.
She was a servant.
They were her masters.
And decisions that would alter the course of her life were being made above her.
Sometimes the deepest wounds begin when someone with power forgets that the person beneath them is still a human being.
Hagar conceived.
And immediately, the household began to fracture.
Genesis 16:4 tells us that after Hagar became pregnant, her mistress became despised in her eyes.
The Bible does not present Hagar as morally flawless. Her attitude toward Sarai contributed to the conflict.
But neither does it excuse what happened to her afterward.
Sarai blamed Abram.
Abram placed Hagar back under Sarai's authority.
And then Scripture records a devastating sentence.
"So Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her."
— Genesis 16:6, ESV
The Hebrew word translated "dealt harshly" comes from the verb עָנָה (ʿanah), which can describe afflicting, humbling, or oppressing someone, depending on its context.
The text does not give us every detail of Sarai's treatment.
But it gives us enough to know that Hagar was suffering.
Enough that she ran.
Pregnant.
Vulnerable.
Away from the only household in which she had been living.
Toward the wilderness.
Can you imagine that journey?
No comfortable bed waiting at the end of the road.
No guarantee of food.
No certainty about where she would deliver her child.
And perhaps the most crushing thought of all…
The people who should have protected her had become the people she was trying to escape.
Some of you understand that kind of heartbreak.
Not because your circumstances are identical to Hagar's, but because you know what it feels like to be wounded by someone you expected to care for you.
A parent whose words still echo years later.
A spouse whose betrayal changed the way you trust.
A church community where you expected compassion but encountered humiliation.
A friend who disappeared when your life became complicated.
A family that remembers your mistakes more readily than your sacrifices.
And when you finally reached the point where you couldn't take another step, you wondered whether God had noticed any of it.
Hagar was somewhere in the wilderness when the story took a turn she could never have anticipated.
God came looking for her.
Genesis 16:7 says:
"The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur."
That word matters.
Found.
Hagar had fled from human cruelty.
But she had not escaped divine attention.
She was outside the household.
Outside the protection she needed.
Outside the plans other people had made for her.
But she was not outside the reach of God.
And then came a question.
"Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?"
— Genesis 16:8, ESV
Notice something beautiful.
He called her Hagar.
By name.
In the previous events, she had been treated as someone whose life could be arranged around the desires of others.
But here, in the wilderness, she was personally addressed.
The God of Abraham knew the name of the Egyptian servant.
He knew where she had come from.
He knew what had happened.
And He invited her to speak.
Her answer was painfully simple.
"I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai."
She did not pretend everything was fine.
She did not disguise the situation with religious language.
She told the truth.
And the God who met her in the wilderness did not need her to manufacture a stronger version of herself before speaking to her.
Perhaps that is something you need to hear today.
You do not have to pretend your marriage is healthy when it is breaking your heart.
You do not have to call betrayal a blessing.
You do not have to deny grief to demonstrate faith.
You do not have to hide your exhaustion behind a Bible verse.
The Lord already knows.
And because He knows, you can come to Him truthfully.
But Hagar's story contains a difficult detail that responsible Bible readers must not ignore.
The angel of the LORD instructed her to return to Sarai and submit to her authority.
That command can be deeply troubling, especially to someone who has experienced abuse.
We must handle it carefully.
Genesis 16 is not a blanket command for abused people to return to dangerous situations.

It records a particular divine instruction given to Hagar within a specific historical narrative. It does not authorize mistreatment, remove accountability from oppressors, or require victims to remain in danger.
Scripture repeatedly condemns oppression and calls God's people to protect the vulnerable.
If you are being abused, seeking safety, protection, and trustworthy help is not a failure of faith.
And notice that God's message to Hagar did not end with the instruction to return.
He also gave her a promise.
Her descendants would become too numerous to count.
And He told her something about the son growing within her.
"Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction."
— Genesis 16:11, ESV
Ishmael.
In Hebrew, יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yishmaʿel) means "God hears" or "God has heard."
Imagine that.
Before the child was born, God gave his mother a name that would continually remind her that her suffering had not gone unnoticed.
Every time she called her son…
Ishmael.
Every time she heard someone speak his name…
Ishmael.
She would be reminded of the God who heard her affliction.
And then Hagar did something remarkable.
She spoke a name for the LORD who had spoken to her.
Genesis 16:13 records the Hebrew expression:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Ro'i.
Often rendered:
"You are a God of seeing."
Or, in the familiar devotional expression:
"The God who sees me."
The Hebrew wording is compact and has generated some discussion about its precise nuance. But its central testimony is unmistakable.
Hagar had encountered the God who saw her in her distress.
And that changed the wilderness.
Not because the wilderness suddenly became a palace.
Not because every painful circumstance immediately disappeared.
But because she discovered that she was not invisible to the LORD.
Think about the astonishing reversal.
The woman who had been treated as an instrument in someone else's plan became the woman who testified personally about the God who saw her.
The servant who had fled into the wilderness became a witness to divine compassion.
And the place that looked like the end of her story became the setting of an encounter remembered for generations.
People may overlook you without God ever losing sight of you.
But the story doesn't end there.
And this is where Hagar's experience becomes even more heartbreaking.
Years passed.
Ishmael was born.
God fulfilled His promise to Sarah, and Isaac entered the household.
Then another conflict erupted.
Genesis 21 tells us that Sarah saw Ishmael laughing, in a context that led her to demand that Hagar and her son be sent away.
The apostle Paul later describes Ishmael's conduct toward Isaac as persecution in Galatians 4:29.
The biblical account does not invite us to erase that conflict.
But neither does it erase Hagar's humanity.
Abraham was distressed because Ishmael was his son.
God assured Abraham that He would also make a nation of Ishmael, while confirming that the covenant line would continue through Isaac.
Then Abraham gave Hagar bread and water and sent her away.
And once again…
Hagar entered the wilderness.
Only this time, she was not alone.
Her son was with her.
The water eventually ran out.
There was no visible solution.
No reserve supply.
No promise from another human being that help was on its way.
And the mother who had once fled while carrying her unborn child now faced the possibility of watching that child die.
Genesis 21:16 records her anguish:
"Let me not look on the death of the child."
She sat at a distance.
And she wept.
Try to imagine the unbearable helplessness of that moment.
A mother who could not provide what her child desperately needed.
A mother whose love was greater than her resources.
A mother who could not bear to watch the suffering unfolding before her.
There are parents reading this who know something of that terror.
You have stared at medical bills you could not afford.
You have worried about how to feed your children.
You have sat beside a hospital bed, pleading with God for one more chance.
You have smiled in front of your family while privately wondering how much longer you could keep going.
You have prayed prayers so desperate that they barely sounded like words.
And perhaps you have asked the question Hagar's circumstances seem to raise.
Lord, You saw me before. Do You still see me now?
Then Scripture says something extraordinary.
"And God heard the voice of the boy."
— Genesis 21:17, ESV
There it is again.
The meaning of Ishmael's name.
God hears.
Years earlier, God had said He heard Hagar's affliction.
Now, in the wilderness, God heard her son.
The promise had not vanished simply because the circumstances had become terrifying.
And the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven.
"What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is."
— Genesis 21:17, ESV
Where he is.
Not where someone thought he should be.
Not where his family wished he were.
Not where his circumstances might have been easier.
Where he is.
And then came the command to lift up the boy and hold him, accompanied by God's renewed promise to make him a great nation.
Genesis 21:19 says:
"Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water."
Read that again.
God opened her eyes.
And she saw a well.
The text does not explicitly tell us whether the well had already been there or whether God had newly provided it.
What it does tell us is that God enabled Hagar to see the provision she needed.
And she gave her son water.
The child lived.
God was with the boy as he grew.
The wilderness had not defeated the promise of God.
Now, be careful not to turn that moment into a guarantee Scripture never makes.
It does not mean every desperate situation will end exactly as we want.
It does not mean every illness will be healed immediately.
It does not mean every financial crisis will disappear overnight.
It does not mean the suffering of God's people is imaginary.
The Bible is far too honest about grief, persecution, and loss to permit those conclusions.
But Hagar's story does reveal something enduring about the character of God.
He is not indifferent to the afflicted.
He is not unaware of those pushed to the margins.
He is not limited by the failure of human beings to show compassion.
And He is faithful to His promises.
There is another truth here that we must not miss.
God's compassion toward Hagar did not mean that Ishmael replaced Isaac as the child of the covenant promise.
Genesis is clear that God's covenant with Abraham would be established through Isaac.
Yet God also promised to bless Ishmael, multiply his descendants, and remain with him.
The distinction matters.
God's covenant purposes and His compassion toward the vulnerable are not enemies.
His faithfulness to His redemptive plan did not require Him to ignore Hagar's suffering.
And that brings us to Jesus Christ.
Because Hagar's story is not simply an ancient account of a woman who survived the wilderness.
It reveals something about the God whose saving purposes unfold throughout Scripture and find their fulfillment in Christ.
We should not claim that every detail of Hagar's experience is a direct prediction of Jesus.
Nor should we pretend that Hagar and Sarah are interchangeable figures in the biblical story.
In Galatians 4:21–31, Paul uses Hagar and Sarah in an allegorical argument about slavery, freedom, law, and promise.
That passage has its own theological purpose, and it must be respected.
But when we read the whole Bible, we discover that the God who saw Hagar is the same God whose mercy is revealed decisively in His Son.
And look at the people Jesus noticed.
A woman suffering from bleeding for twelve years, whose desperate touch did not escape His attention.
A Samaritan woman at a well, whose complicated history did not prevent Him from speaking to her about living water.
A blind beggar crying out while others tried to silence him.
A tax collector despised by his community.
A thief dying beside Him.
A grieving mother walking behind the body of her only son.
Jesus did not merely notice the impressive, the powerful, or the religiously respectable.
He stopped for people others hurried past.
He spoke to people others avoided.
He welcomed repentant sinners whom self-righteous observers preferred to condemn.
And He did something infinitely greater than simply acknowledging human pain.
He came to save sinners.
Matthew 1:21 says of Jesus:
"You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."
The Greek name Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous) corresponds to the Hebrew name Yeshua, associated with the meaning "the LORD saves."
And that is the heart of the Gospel.
The God who sees our suffering also sees our sin.
He sees the wounds inflicted upon us.
And He sees the wrongs we ourselves have committed.
He knows when we have been betrayed.
And He knows when we have betrayed others.
He knows the injustice we have endured.
And He knows the selfishness, pride, bitterness, dishonesty, and disobedience we would rather conceal.
Nothing is hidden from Him.
Yet the astonishing news of Christianity is that God did not leave humanity without hope.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered our broken world.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He loved the unlovely.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He welcomed the repentant.
He bore our sins on the cross.
And He rose bodily from the dead.
His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
We are not saved because our suffering makes us righteous.
We are not forgiven because we have endured enough hardship.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
As Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches, salvation is God's gift, not something we earn through our works.
And this is where Hagar's story becomes personally searching.
Perhaps you came here because you feel forgotten.
But what if the God who sees you is also calling you to stop hiding from Him?
Not merely to ask Him to change your circumstances.
But to surrender your life.
To confess what you have been protecting.
To repent of what has been destroying you.
To release the bitterness you have been feeding.
To trust Christ with the parts of your story you have never allowed anyone else to touch.
Because the deepest hope of the Gospel is not simply that Jesus will make every difficult chapter comfortable.
It is that Jesus can redeem sinners, reconcile them to God, and begin transforming lives that once seemed beyond restoration.
He does not excuse sin.
He forgives repentant sinners.
He does not call evil good.
He overcomes evil with His goodness.
He does not promise that following Him means never entering another wilderness.
He promises His people something far more enduring.
His presence.
His grace.
His faithfulness.
And ultimately, resurrection life in a world where death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is more than a beautiful phrase.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because every consequence disappears.
Not because the scars are always removed.
But because the grace of Jesus Christ can give a redeemed future to people whose past seemed to have written their ending.
Hagar's story was not erased.
It was remembered in Scripture.
Her tears were not meaningless.
Her son was not forgotten.
Her wilderness was not beyond God's reach.
And neither is yours.
Maybe you have spent years believing that because someone abandoned you, you must be unworthy of love.
Maybe you have confused another person's cruelty with God's opinion of you.
Maybe you have carried shame for choices you made while desperately trying to survive.
Maybe you have wandered so far spiritually that returning to prayer feels almost impossible.
Or maybe you are the person who appears spiritually strong while secretly running on empty.
You still attend church.
You still share Scripture.
You still encourage other people.
But when the room becomes quiet, you wonder whether God remembers you.
Hear this carefully.
Your pain is not proof that God has forgotten you.
