There are sins we must never rename as marital rights.
And there are women who have spent years believing that honoring God means surrendering their right to bodily safety.
It is time to open the Scriptures carefully.
Not to make the Bible say what our culture wants.
Not to erase the beauty of marriage.
But to confront what happens when God's Word is twisted into permission to harm someone He created in His image.
And before we go any further, remember this:
A wedding vow is not permission for sexual violence. A marriage covenant does not cancel a person's humanity. And a husband's desire does not turn his wife's refusal into sin.
The Bible begins its understanding of marriage long before it speaks about marital responsibilities.
Genesis 1:27 declares:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים (be-tselem Elohim) means "in the image of God."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say the man bears God's image while the woman merely exists to satisfy him.
Both are created in God's image.
Both possess dignity that marriage does not erase.
Both are morally accountable before the Lord.
When Genesis 2:24 describes the man and woman becoming בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad), "one flesh," it reveals the profound union of marriage.
But becoming one flesh does not mean one person ceases to be a person.
Unity is not ownership.
Intimacy is not domination.
And covenant faithfulness is not permission to disregard another person's fear, pain, or refusal.
Somebody needs to hear that, especially the woman who has been told that because she said yes at the altar, she lost the right to say no in the bedroom.
You did not stop being made in God's image when you became someone's wife.
And no human being acquires unlimited authority over another person's body through marriage.
But what about 1 Corinthians 7?
This is where the conversation becomes difficult.
And this is where we must refuse to become careless with Scripture.
The apostle Paul writes:
Some have taken the first half of that verse and used it like a weapon.
They quote the wife's obligation.
Then they conveniently forget the husband's.
They emphasize authority.
Then they ignore reciprocity.
They speak of marital intimacy as though the husband possesses a divine entitlement to sexual access, regardless of his wife's condition or willingness.
But read the entire verse.
Paul deliberately speaks in both directions.
The Greek expression ἐξουσιάζει (exousiazei) conveys exercising authority or having authority over.
And the same verb is applied to both spouses.
Paul's instruction challenges unilateral control rather than establishing it.
The surrounding passage, 1 Corinthians 7:3–5, teaches mutual marital responsibility, consideration, and agreement. Verse 5 specifically recognizes mutual consent regarding periods of abstinence.
This passage affirms that sexual intimacy matters within marriage.
It does not authorize rape.
It does not instruct a husband to ignore his wife's resistance.
It does not grant permission to use intimidation, threats, restraint, or physical force.
And it certainly does not suggest that one spouse may commit violence to enforce what they believe the other owes them.
The text addresses marital obligations within a relationship of mutual responsibility. It is not a procedure for compelling sexual activity.
A spouse can neglect marital intimacy in ways that deserve honest conversation, counseling, and spiritual care.
But neglect, disagreement, or refusal never gives the other spouse permission to commit sexual violence.
A marital responsibility is not a license to force its fulfillment.
Imagine how differently some marriages might look if we taught the entire passage instead of using half a verse to silence half the marriage.
And then consider Ephesians 5.
The passage many people associate with wives submitting to husbands also gives husbands a command that should make every abusive man tremble at the seriousness of his responsibility.
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (Ephesians 5:25, KJV)
The Greek word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is the command to love.
But Paul does not leave the meaning of that love to the husband's imagination.
He gives its pattern.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who gave Himself.
The Lord who served.
The Bridegroom whose love was sacrificial rather than exploitative.
Think about that.
Christ did not demonstrate His love by exploiting the vulnerability of His people.
He laid down His life for them.
And a husband who claims Christ as his model cannot justify treating his wife's vulnerability as an opportunity to overpower her.
Ephesians 5:28–29 continues by calling husbands to love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them.
The Greek word ἐκτρέφει (ektrephei) conveys nourishing or caring for.
Θάλπει (thalpei) carries the sense of cherishing or tenderly caring for.
These are not words describing cruelty.
They describe care.
A man cannot credibly claim to cherish his wife's body while deliberately using it against her will.
He cannot invoke Christlike love while making her afraid of what happens when he is displeased.
And he cannot transform sexual violence into righteousness simply by attaching the word "marriage" to it.
Colossians 3:19 makes the command unmistakable:
"Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them." (KJV)
The Greek μὴ πικραίνεσθε (mē pikrainesthe) prohibits becoming bitter or harsh toward them.
The precise context concerns marital conduct, not a modern legal definition of sexual assault. But the moral direction is clear: Christian husbands are commanded toward love, not cruelty.
If harshness is forbidden, how could sexual brutality be defended as holy?
If husbands are commanded to cherish, how could deliberate violation be excused as obedience?
And if Jesus is our model, why would we defend conduct that contradicts His character?
There is another passage that deserves attention.
First Peter 3:7 instructs husbands to dwell with their wives according to knowledge, giving honor to them as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
The Greek word τιμή (timē) refers to honor or value.
Not possession.
Honor.
The passage even warns husbands that their prayers may be hindered when they fail in their responsibilities.
Think about the seriousness of that warning.
A man can appear religious.
He can attend church.
He can speak eloquently about Scripture.
He can lead prayers in public.
But his treatment of his wife still matters before God.
His private behavior is not hidden from the Lord simply because the congregation admires his public ministry.
And this is where the Church must confront something painful.
Sometimes the person asking for help is told to pray harder, submit more, become more affectionate, dress differently, or stop provoking her husband.
Sometimes a woman discloses sexual coercion and receives a lecture about her marital duties instead of concern for her safety.
Sometimes church leaders fear the scandal of exposing abuse more than the injustice of allowing it to continue.
Sometimes the language of forgiveness becomes a demand for silence.
And sometimes the very community that should help carry the wounded toward Christ becomes another place where they are afraid to speak.
That must never become normal.
A church does not protect the sanctity of marriage by protecting sexual violence.
It does not honor the Gospel by pressuring victims to remain silent.
And it does not preserve Christian testimony by hiding wrongdoing behind the reputation of a respected husband, ministry leader, or family.
A church that protects an abuser's reputation at the expense of a victim's safety has confused institutional image with biblical righteousness.
Consider what the prophet Isaiah declared:
"Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow." (Isaiah 1:17, KJV)
The Hebrew command דִּרְשׁוּ מִשְׁפָּט (dirshu mishpat) means "seek justice."
The call to justice is not an optional decoration of biblical faith.
It is part of God's demand that His people practice righteousness.
Psalm 82:3–4 likewise commands the defense of the vulnerable and their deliverance from the hand of the wicked.
These passages do not specifically address marital sexual assault. Their broader moral principles, however, forbid treating the vulnerable as disposable.
The Church must apply those principles faithfully.
We must also remember the difference between forgiveness and the removal of consequences.
Forgiveness is central to the Gospel.
But forgiveness is not a command to pretend that evil never happened.
Repentance does not mean avoiding accountability.
Reconciliation is not the same as forgiveness, and reconciliation cannot be demanded where safety, truth, and genuine change are absent.
A woman can pursue healing in Christ without immediately trusting someone who harmed her.
She can seek protection without betraying her faith.
She can report a crime without rejecting the Gospel.
She can establish boundaries without becoming an enemy of marriage.
And she should never be pressured to prove her forgiveness by accepting further sexual access or returning to danger.
Romans 13:1–4 recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in restraining and addressing wrongdoing.
The Church must not act as though spiritual counseling replaces the responsibility of civil authorities where crimes may have occurred.
Laws differ by jurisdiction, but marriage does not automatically remove criminal responsibility for sexual assault. The specific legal definitions and remedies depend on the applicable law.
The Church must never promise confidentiality in ways that obstruct legally required reporting or prevent appropriate protection.
Pastoral care should be compassionate, trauma-informed, and attentive to safety.
Where coercion or violence is alleged, couples counseling should not be imposed as the first solution, because it can expose the harmed spouse to further intimidation or retaliation.
Safety comes first.
Truth matters.
Accountability matters.
And so does the spiritual condition of the person who committed the harm.
Because the Gospel is not only a message of comfort to the wounded.
It is also a summons to repentance for the one who wounds.
To the husband who has used threats, pressure, fear, physical force, or religious language to obtain sexual access from his wife:
Do not hide behind your wedding vows.
Do not quote 1 Corinthians 7 while ignoring Ephesians 5.
Do not confuse your sexual desire with divine authority.
And do not assume that because your wife stopped resisting, she freely agreed.
Fear can silence a person.
Exhaustion can silence a person.
The knowledge that resistance will lead to punishment can silence a person.
Silence is not necessarily consent.
A marriage certificate is not consent.
Previous sexual intimacy is not consent to every future encounter.
And compliance under threats or force is not freely given agreement.
You may have convinced yourself that you were exercising a husband's rights.
But if you used coercion or violence, you must face the seriousness of what you did.
Stop the harmful behavior.
Respect your wife's boundaries and safety.
Do not pressure her to forgive, reconcile, withdraw a report, or conceal what happened.
Seek appropriate professional help and submit to lawful accountability.
And repent.
Not merely because you fear exposure.
Not because you want to save your reputation.
Not because you want your wife to return to the way things were.
Repent because sin is an offense against the God who made her.
Second Corinthians 7:10–11 describes godly sorrow as producing repentance and earnestness.
Real repentance is more than tears after being confronted.
It is a turning away from evil.
It does not demand instant trust as payment for an apology.
It does not blame the victim for the offender's actions.
And it does not treat consequences as persecution.
God's grace is real.
Forgiveness through Jesus Christ is real.
But grace must never be twisted into permission to continue harming another person.
The cross is not a hiding place for unrepentant cruelty.
It is where the seriousness of sin and the mercy of God meet.
And to the wife who recognizes herself somewhere in these words:
Perhaps you have been carrying a kind of shame you cannot explain.
Perhaps you have wondered whether you were selfish.
Perhaps someone told you that refusing sex made you a disobedient Christian wife.
Perhaps you have learned to avoid conflict by giving in, even when you feel frightened or distressed.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that the pain you experienced was simply part of marriage.
Please hear this carefully.
What someone did to you is not made righteous because that person is your spouse.
You are not required to call violence love.
You are not required to call coercion submission.
You are not required to call fear peace.
And you are not required to sacrifice your safety to preserve someone else's appearance of godliness.
Jesus knows what it means to be betrayed.
He knows what it means to suffer injustice.
He knows what it means for powerful people to misuse their authority.
And He does not ask us to pretend evil is good.
In Luke 4:18, Jesus announces good news to the poor and liberty to the oppressed, drawing from Isaiah's prophetic language.
This does not mean every painful circumstance will immediately disappear.
Nor does it mean a particular marriage will necessarily be restored.
It means the mission of Christ cannot honestly be used to celebrate oppression.
The Gospel announces redemption, truth, mercy, and the coming reign of God's righteousness.
Jesus is not indifferent to the wounded.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." (KJV)
You may not feel close to God right now.
You may struggle to pray.
You may be angry that people who spoke in His name failed to protect you.
You may even find it difficult to enter a church building.
Your pain deserves to be taken seriously.
You do not have to perform spiritual strength to receive compassionate help.

If you are currently unsafe, prioritize getting to a safer place when possible and contacting emergency services, a trusted person, a qualified domestic-violence service, or appropriate local authorities. If your communications are monitored, seek help through a safer device or trusted contact when you can.
You do not need to wait for a church committee to decide whether your suffering is serious enough to deserve protection.
And if you are a pastor, elder, counselor, ministry leader, or Christian friend reading this, there is a question you must confront.
What happens when a woman trusts you enough to tell you what happened?
Will you listen?
Will you believe that her disclosure deserves a serious, compassionate response without assuming you already know every fact?
Will you resist the temptation to protect the reputation of someone influential?
Will you avoid turning the first conversation into a debate about submission?
Will you help her access qualified support and appropriate reporting channels?
Will you remember that safeguarding a vulnerable person is not an attack on biblical marriage?
Or will you send her back into danger with a Bible verse she has already heard used against her?
James 1:27 speaks of pure religion as caring for vulnerable people in their affliction and keeping oneself unspotted from the world.
That is a demanding picture of faith.
Not merely preaching compassion.
Practicing it.
Not merely defending marriage as an institution.
Protecting the people within it.
Not merely condemning sexual sin outside marriage.
Having the courage to confront sexual violence inside marriage.
Because sexual violence does not become less serious when the perpetrator wears a wedding ring.
And the suffering of a wife does not become less important when the person responsible is her husband.
This is not a rejection of Christian marriage.
It is a defense of what marriage was meant to be.
A covenant marked by faithfulness.
A relationship in which love seeks the other's good.
A union in which intimacy is not obtained through terror.
A home where strength is used to protect rather than dominate.
A marriage where both husband and wife can speak honestly without fearing retaliation.
A place where the teaching of Christ is not merely displayed on the wall but reflected in the way two people treat each other when nobody else is watching.
And perhaps that is the question we have avoided for too long.
What does a Christian home actually look like when the church doors are closed?
When there is no pastor watching?
When there is no congregation to impress?
When a wife says, "I'm not comfortable"?
When she is tired?
When she is sick?
When she is afraid?
Does her husband remember that she is his fellow image-bearer, worthy of tenderness and honor?
Or does he believe that his vows entitle him to take what she has not freely agreed to give?
The answer reveals something important about his understanding of love.
Because the Gospel never teaches that power makes a person righteous.
Jesus taught His followers that greatness is expressed through service, not domination (Mark 10:42–45).
And the husband who wants to lead like Christ must first learn to love like Christ.
Not selectively.
Not only in public.
Not only when his wife agrees.
But especially when his desires and her well-being seem to come into conflict.
That is where character is revealed.
And that is where the Church must stop excusing what Scripture never commanded.
There may be someone reading this who has never told another person what happened.
Someone who has carried the secret for ten years.
Someone who still sleeps beside the person who hurt her.
Someone who has left but continues to struggle with guilt.
Someone who fears that telling the truth will destroy the family.
Someone who wonders whether God will be disappointed if she seeks protection.
I cannot promise that speaking will be easy.
I cannot promise that every church leader will respond wisely.
I cannot promise that the people you love will understand immediately.
But I can tell you this:
God's Word does not require you to rename sexual violence as marital obedience.
And seeking safety does not mean you have abandoned Jesus.
There is hope beyond what happened to you.
Healing may take time.
It may involve trusted friends, skilled counselors, medical care, legal protection, and the difficult work of rebuilding a sense of safety.
Your journey may not look like anyone else's.
And you do not owe the public your story.
But what happened does not have to become the final definition of your life.
That is why we keep returning to the Gospel.
Because the Gospel is not the promise that every earthly relationship will be repaired.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ entered our broken world, bore sin, conquered death, and offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
His resurrection declares that evil and death do not have the final word.
And His coming kingdom promises a justice no human institution can perfectly provide.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of the day when God will wipe away every tear and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise does not excuse delaying justice today.
It gives us reason to pursue righteousness while waiting for the fullness of God's restoration.
This is what we mean at Gospel Warrior when we speak about the journey from scandal to grace.
Not hiding the scandal.
Not minimizing the wound.
Not forcing a victim to reconcile.
Not offering an offender cheap absolution.
But bringing what is hidden into the light of God's truth.
Calling sin what it is.
Calling the guilty to genuine repentance.
Standing beside those who have been harmed.
And pointing every broken heart toward the Savior who alone can ultimately redeem what sin has devastated.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
But by offering a future that is not finally ruled by it.
If this article has opened your eyes to something the Church needs to confront, please don't let the conversation end here.
Someone may finally realize that marriage does not erase their dignity.
Someone may reconsider a teaching they have repeated without examining the whole counsel of Scripture.
Someone may be encouraged to seek help.
And someone who has misused biblical authority may be confronted with the need to repent.
You don't need to reveal personal details or describe any trauma.
Or write, "Lord, teach Your Church to protect the wounded."
If you need prayer, you may say, "Please pray for me," without explaining why.
And if you have a testimony of healing, wisdom, or restoration that you freely wish to share, your words may encourage someone who feels completely alone.
Let the comments become a place of biblical truth, compassion, and prayer, never a courtroom where survivors are pressured to prove their pain.
And if this ministry has helped you grow in your understanding of God's Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to creating Christ-centered articles, biblical teaching, devotionals, and discipleship resources that encourage believers to move beyond surface-level faith.
We want these resources to continue reaching people who are hungry for biblical truth, including those who cannot afford to pay for them.
That work takes time, resources, consistency, and people willing to help sustain it.
Scripture calls believers to generosity that is willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
But if you are able and genuinely desire to partner with us, your monthly contribution can become one practical expression of generosity toward a ministry whose mission you believe in.
These products are simply another way to encourage faith, reflection, and meaningful conversations about Jesus. They are not the reason we preach the Gospel.
Christ is.
Praying for this ministry matters.
Speaking the truth in love matters.
Protecting the vulnerable matters.
Before you leave, I want you to remember the woman from the beginning of this article.
The one sitting beside her husband in church.
The one who heard him singing while she fought back tears.
The one who wondered whether God expected her to endure what frightened and wounded her.
Maybe she is someone you know.
Maybe she is someone you will meet.
Maybe she has been reading every word of this article with trembling hands.
Or maybe, for the first time, she is beginning to understand that the voice of the man who hurt her is not the voice of God.
If that woman is you, I pray you find safe people who will listen, qualified help that will protect you, and a clearer understanding of the Lord who created you with dignity.
Your life matters beyond your marriage.
Your safety matters beyond another person's reputation.
Your voice matters even when others would rather you remain silent.
And Jesus Christ is worthy of a Church that tells the truth, protects the vulnerable, confronts wrongdoing, and refuses to turn His holy Word into an instrument of cruelty.
Because the question was never whether a husband can claim authority over his wife.
The question is whether we will recognize that no human authority is permitted to make evil holy.
And if the Church truly belongs to Jesus, it must never ask a wounded woman to carry the shame of the person who harmed her.
The ring on her finger was supposed to remind her of a promise of love, not become the reason she was afraid to say no.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LORD, LORD!”—THE TWO WORDS THAT MAY STILL LEAVE YOU OUTSIDE HEAVEN
paragraphs: “LORD, LORD!”—THE TWO WORDS THAT MAY STILL LEAVE YOU OUTSIDE HEAVEN

They preached in His name. They performed miracles in His name. They were convinced they belonged to Him. But when they finally stood before Jesus, they heard five devastating words: “I never knew you.” What did they miss—and could we be missing the same thing?
Imagine spending your entire life believing you were going to heaven.
You prayed when life became unbearable. You sang worship songs with tears in your eyes. You shared Bible verses on Facebook. You attended church. You told people that Jesus was Lord.
Maybe you even served in ministry. Maybe people admired your faith. Maybe someone came to Christ because of something you said.
And then comes the day when everything earthly disappears.
No more Sunday services.
No more religious titles.
No more carefully maintained reputation.
No more opportunity to hide behind the version of yourself everyone else believed.
You stand before Jesus Christ.
And you are certain He will welcome you.
But then you hear something so terrifying that it makes every earthly rejection seem insignificant.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Not, “I used to know you.”
Not, “You were once Mine, but I forgot you.”
“I never knew you.”
How could someone spend years speaking about Jesus and still be a stranger to Him?
How could someone perform extraordinary works in His name and still be rejected?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all...
What if the greatest danger facing some professing Christians is not that they have rejected Jesus openly, but that they have mistaken religious activity for truly belonging to Him?
This is not a story invented to frighten people into religion.
These are the words of Jesus Himself.
And He spoke them while teaching people how to enter the kingdom of heaven.
In Matthew 7:21–23, Jesus declares:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
“And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Notice something that should stop us in our tracks.
These people were not denying that Jesus was Lord.
They were calling Him Lord.
Twice.
They were not claiming to have served another god.
They were appealing to what they had done in Jesus' name.
They were not presenting themselves as enemies of Christianity.
They were presenting themselves as His servants.
And yet Jesus rejected their claim to belong to Him.
Why?
Because the issue was never simply whether they knew His name.
The issue was whether they truly belonged to Him.
There is something important hidden in the original Greek that English readers can easily overlook.
When Jesus says, “Lord, Lord,” Matthew records the expression:
Κύριε κύριε — Kyrie, Kyrie.
Kyrie is the vocative form of kyrios, meaning “Lord,” “master,” or one who possesses authority.
The repetition creates a forceful, urgent address. These people are not casually mentioning Jesus. They are appealing to Him directly and emphatically.
But repetition does not make a confession genuine.
A person can speak the right words without surrendering to the One those words identify.
And that is precisely the contradiction Jesus exposes.
He asks elsewhere:
“Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46, KJV)
There it is.
The contradiction between confession and conduct.
Between the mouth and the heart.
Between claiming Christ's authority and refusing to submit to it.
Imagine someone standing before a king, repeatedly declaring, “Your Majesty! Your Majesty!” while deliberately rebelling against everything the king commands.
The words may acknowledge his title.
But the rebellion exposes the person's allegiance.
And Jesus is not merely an earthly king.
He is the risen Lord before whom every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9–11).
Calling Him Lord is not a magical formula that guarantees salvation.
The question is whether our confession is the expression of genuine faith or a substitute for it.
But we must be careful here.
Because this passage has sometimes been used to terrify sincere Christians who are already struggling under the weight of guilt.
Some read these verses and immediately begin examining every failure, every temptation, every moment of weakness.
They wonder whether one more sin will cause Jesus to turn them away.
That is not the conclusion Jesus is teaching.
He is not declaring that only sinlessly perfect people enter heaven.
If that were true, nobody would enter.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
And 1 John 1:8 warns that claiming to have no sin is self-deception.
The gospel does not announce that Jesus came to save people who never needed forgiveness.
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
So what separates a struggling believer from the people Jesus describes?
The answer becomes clearer when we examine what these people say in their defense.
They do not cry out for mercy.
They do not appeal to Christ's sacrifice.
They do not confess their need for grace.
Instead, they present their religious achievements.
“Have we not prophesied in thy name?”
“Have we not ... cast out devils?”
“Have we not ... done many wonderful works?”
Their repeated argument is striking.
Look at what we did.
Now, the passage does not tell us everything about their inner motives. We should not pretend to know details Jesus did not reveal.
But it does show us the foundation of their appeal.
They point to extraordinary religious works as evidence that Jesus must receive them.
And Jesus exposes the fatal inadequacy of that claim.
Religious achievements, even astonishing ones, cannot establish that a person truly belongs to Christ.
A person may be publicly associated with God's work without being inwardly reconciled to God.
A person may know Christian language without possessing Christian faith.
A person may impress an audience without being approved by the Lord.
And spiritual experiences, however dramatic, must never replace the truth of God's Word as the measure of genuine discipleship.
Jesus had already warned about false prophets who appear harmless but are inwardly dangerous (Matthew 7:15–20).
He said they would be recognized by their fruits.
Then He warned that not everyone calling Him Lord would enter the kingdom.
Immediately afterward, He described two builders: one whose house stood because it rested on rock, and another whose house collapsed because it rested on sand (Matthew 7:24–27).
These teachings belong together.
The issue is not religious appearance.
It is whether a person's life rests upon Christ's words and responds to them in genuine faith.
And that brings us to another phrase in Matthew 7 that deserves our attention.
Jesus says that the one who enters the kingdom is the one who does the will of His Father.
In Greek, Matthew 7:21 uses:
ὁ ποιῶν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός μου
ho poiōn to thelēma tou patros mou
Meaning, “the one doing the will of My Father.”
Does that mean we earn heaven by obeying enough commandments?
No.
Scripture does not permit that conclusion.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not something we earn through works.
But the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10).
Do you see the difference?
Good works are not the price we pay to purchase salvation. They are the fruit that genuine saving faith produces.
Obedience does not make the cross sufficient.
The cross is sufficient because Jesus is sufficient.
But when His grace truly takes hold of a life, that grace does not leave the person content to make peace with sin.
Titus 2:11–14 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace also transforms.
And Jesus Himself explains the Father's will in a way that guards us against turning salvation into a religious performance.
In John 6:40, He says:
“And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.” (KJV)
The Father's will is not separated from faith in His Son.
It begins with receiving Jesus Christ, trusting Him, and responding to His truth.
A living faith produces obedience—not perfect obedience, but a real, Spirit-enabled turning toward God.
James 2:17 tells us that faith without works is dead.
Not because works replace faith.
But because a faith that never bears fruit gives us reason to question whether it is alive.
This is where the warning becomes deeply personal.
You can attend church and still refuse to forgive someone.
You can post Scripture while privately cultivating cruelty.
You can sing about holiness while defending a secret life you have no intention of surrendering.
You can speak beautifully about God's love while repeatedly exploiting people who trust you.
You can tell the world that Jesus is Lord while treating His commands as optional whenever obedience becomes inconvenient.
And perhaps nobody notices.
Your friends may not notice.
Your pastor may not notice.
Your followers may not notice.
But Jesus sees what human applause cannot reveal.
Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that nothing in creation is hidden from God's sight.
That truth should humble every one of us.
Not so that we become obsessed with appearing spiritually impressive.
But so that we stop confusing appearance with reality.
And then comes the phrase that cuts even deeper.
“I never knew you.”
The Greek reads:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
oudepote egnōn hymas
Literally, “I never knew you.”
Oudepote means “never,” or “not ever.”
Egnōn is a past-tense form of the verb ginōskō, meaning “to know.”
Of course, Jesus is not saying He lacked information about these people.
He is not an uninformed judge who failed to recognize their faces.
Throughout Scripture, God's knowledge of His people can describe something deeper than awareness of their existence.
It speaks of recognition, belonging, and relationship.
Consider 2 Timothy 2:19:
“The Lord knoweth them that are his.” (KJV)
Or John 10:14, where Jesus says:
“I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.” (KJV)
The terrifying reality in Matthew 7 is not that these people failed to make themselves famous enough for Jesus to recognize.
It is that they claimed a relationship with Him that He did not acknowledge as real.
And that changes everything.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about building a religious résumé.
It is about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Not merely knowing facts about Him.
Not merely knowing the songs.
Not merely knowing the vocabulary.
Not merely knowing how to sound like a believer.
But belonging to the Savior who died and rose again.
Think about Judas Iscariot.
He walked with Jesus.
He heard the teaching.
He witnessed miracles.
He was numbered among the twelve.
And yet outward proximity to Jesus did not mean his heart was faithful to Jesus.
John 12:4–6 reveals his dishonesty, and the Gospels record his betrayal.
That should make us cautious about assuming that closeness to Christian activity automatically means closeness to Christ.
But there is another disciple we must remember.
Peter.
Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ.
Peter promised loyalty.
Peter insisted he would remain faithful.
And then, on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering your own voice denying the Savior you loved.
Imagine hearing the rooster and realizing that your courage had collapsed exactly as Jesus predicted.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
And yet Peter's story did not end in rejection.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the care of His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Why is that so important?
Because there is a difference between falling into sin and embracing sin as your master.
There is a difference between a heart broken over failure and a heart determined to justify rebellion.
There is a difference between someone who needs restoration and someone who wants religious recognition without repentance.
Peter did not save himself by crying hard enough.
His tears were not payment for forgiveness.
His hope rested in the Savior who had prayed for him, died for sinners, risen from the grave, and graciously restored him.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
Maybe you have failed Jesus.
Maybe you have been hiding a habit you are ashamed to name.
Maybe you have promised God you would change, only to find yourself fighting the same temptation again.
Maybe your faith feels weak.
Maybe your prayers have become painfully honest because you no longer have the strength to pretend.
Do not mistake the warning of Matthew 7 for a declaration that every struggling Christian is beyond hope.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV)
Those words matter.
The same Jesus who warns against false assurance promises to receive those who truly come to Him.
He does not turn away repentant sinners because their past is ugly.
He does not require you to clean yourself into worthiness before receiving His grace.
He calls you to come.
To believe.
To repent.
To follow Him.
And when you fall, to return to Him rather than making peace with the darkness.
First John 1:9 promises forgiveness and cleansing to those who confess their sins.
And Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
The answer to false assurance is not endless self-torment. It is genuine faith in the genuine Savior.
Still, there is one final Greek expression in Jesus' warning that we cannot ignore.
When He says, “Depart from me, ye that work iniquity,” Matthew records:
οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν
hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian
Meaning, “you who practice lawlessness.”
The word anomia carries the sense of lawlessness, wrongdoing, or disregard for God's law.
This is not simply a description of people who have ever sinned.
That would describe all humanity.
Jesus identifies them as practitioners of lawlessness—people whose religious claims coexist with a life characterized by disregard for God's will.
Their profession and their practice contradict one another.
And that contradiction exposes the emptiness of their claim.
Notice also that Jesus does not say, “You did not perform enough miracles.”
He does not say, “You failed to become influential enough.”
He does not say, “Your ministry was too small.”
He does not demand a larger audience, a more impressive title, or a more successful religious career.
He exposes lawlessness and denies that they truly belonged to Him.

Which means someone serving quietly, loving faithfully, repenting sincerely, and trusting Christ may possess something infinitely more valuable than the most admired religious personality in the world.
The approval of Jesus is worth more than the applause of millions.
And now we need to ask a question that modern Christianity cannot afford to avoid.
What happens when we turn following Jesus into a performance?
When we measure spiritual success only by views, followers, donations, applause, or public recognition?
When being seen as holy becomes more important than actually pursuing holiness?
When defending our reputation becomes more urgent than confessing our sin?
When we are more concerned about losing an audience than grieving the heart of God?
We may build something impressive in the eyes of people while neglecting what matters most before Christ.
And those of us involved in Christian ministry must take this warning seriously.
No platform is a substitute for prayer.
No viral message is a substitute for obedience.
No ministry income is proof of God's approval.
Even sharing the gospel publicly cannot replace personally trusting the gospel we proclaim.
This warning belongs to the preacher as much as the listener.
To the writer as much as the reader.
To the person behind the microphone as much as the person sitting in the last pew.
It belongs to all of us.
And perhaps that is why Jesus spoke it so plainly.
Not to entertain our curiosity about who might be rejected.
But to confront our tendency to build confidence on everything except Him.
There is a danger in reading Matthew 7 and immediately thinking of someone else.
That hypocritical pastor.
That judgmental relative.
That Christian who hurt you.
That person who posts Bible verses but treats others terribly.
Perhaps some of those concerns are legitimate.
But Jesus did not give us this warning so that we could spend the rest of our lives confidently assigning other people to hell.
Only God knows the heart perfectly.
The warning calls us first to examine ourselves.
Second Corinthians 13:5 says:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” (KJV)
So perhaps the question today is not, “Which Christian do I think Jesus will reject?”
Perhaps it is...
“Lord, have I mistaken familiarity with Christianity for surrender to You?”
“Have I been using Your name while resisting Your Word?”
“Have I been defending a sin that You are calling me to confess?”
“Have I been trusting my religious accomplishments more than Your finished work?”
“Am I following You because I love You, or merely because I want what You can give me?”
Those questions are uncomfortable.
But discomfort can become mercy when it leads us toward repentance.
The worst response to Jesus' warning would be to hear it, feel briefly frightened, and then return unchanged to the very life He is calling us to leave.
The better response is to bring our hearts into the light.
Not with theatrical promises.
Not with a performance designed to impress others.
But with honesty before God.
“Lord Jesus, I cannot save myself.
I have sinned against You.
I have sometimes loved the appearance of faith more than the cost of following You.
Forgive me.
Expose what I have hidden.
Teach me to trust You, obey You, and love what You love.
Do not let me settle for a religious reputation while neglecting a real relationship with You.
Change my heart by Your grace.
I belong to You, not because I am worthy, but because You are the Savior of sinners.”
If that prayer expresses your heart, remember that the power is not in repeating a particular set of words.
The power belongs to Jesus Christ, who saves those who come to Him in faith.
And that leads us to the greatest hope in this entire passage.
The warning is terrifying.
But the gospel is glorious.
Because the same Jesus who will one day judge the world is the Jesus who willingly went to the cross to rescue sinners.
He did not merely tell us to become better people.
He bore our sins.
He suffered for the unrighteous.
He died and rose again.
First Peter 3:18 declares:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” (KJV)
Think about those final words.
That He might bring us to God.
Not merely bring us into a religious organization.
Not merely bring us into a social circle.
Not merely bring us into a lifestyle that looks respectable.
Bring us to God.
The very relationship sin had broken is what Christ came to restore.
The separation we could never overcome by our own goodness is what His sacrifice addresses.
The judgment we deserve is why His grace is so astonishing.
And the resurrection assures us that the crucified Savior is alive.
That is why the answer to Matthew 7 is not to work frantically until we feel worthy of heaven.
It is to abandon every false refuge and trust the One who alone can save.
True faith is not opposed to obedience.
True faith leads us into obedience.
True grace is not permission to cherish sin.
True grace teaches us to turn from it.
True discipleship is not pretending we never stumble.
It is following Jesus with a heart that continually returns to Him in repentance and faith.
And when we understand that, something beautiful happens.
We stop asking only, “How much can I do for Jesus so He will accept me?”
And begin asking, “Because Jesus has shown such mercy to me, how can I live for His glory?”
That is where generosity finds its proper place.
That is where service becomes worship rather than self-promotion.
That is where sharing the gospel becomes an act of love rather than a quest for attention.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a platform that replaces your local church.
Not to sell salvation.
But to keep pointing wounded, wandering, searching, and growing people back to Jesus Christ and the truth of Scripture.
If this message has helped you confront something you were avoiding, consider what might happen if it reaches someone who has quietly confused church attendance with salvation.
Someone who has spent years pretending.
Someone who believes their past is too shameful for forgiveness.
Someone who is slowly walking away from Christ because they have mistaken human hypocrisy for the character of Jesus.
Not merely because it might reach thousands.
But because it might reach the one person who needs it.
And if this message has exposed something in your own heart, you do not have to pretend otherwise.
If God has been restoring you after a season of wandering, share your testimony if you feel comfortable.
Your honesty may encourage another believer who thought they were the only one struggling.
There is room here for serious questions, honest struggles, biblical encouragement, and a deeper pursuit of Christ.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual encouragement more accessible.
And if this ministry has become a meaningful part of your spiritual growth, I want to invite you into something more personal.
For some, a message like this may be the beginning of a difficult but life-changing conversation with God.
For others, it may be a reminder to return to the Savior they have neglected.
For still others, it may be the encouragement they need to keep walking faithfully.
It is an opportunity to give generously toward a ministry you believe is serving Christ faithfully.
You are no less welcome.
You are no less valuable.
And your ability to give money has absolutely nothing to do with whether Jesus loves you or receives you.
Every act of genuine service matters when it is offered to God in faith and love.
Because one day, Gospel Warrior will not be the name that matters most.
Our books will not matter most.
Our most widely shared articles will not matter most.
The question will not be whether you followed a Christian page.
It will not be whether you purchased a Christian product.
It will not be whether you supported a ministry financially.
The question raised by Matthew 7 is far more searching.
Do you truly belong to Jesus Christ?
Have you trusted Him as Savior and acknowledged Him as Lord?
Is your life being shaped by His grace, His truth, and His call to repentance?
And here is the hope that should never be lost beneath the weight of this warning.
Jesus did not speak these words so that we would admire the danger from a distance.
He spoke them while people could still hear, repent, believe, and build their lives upon His words.
Today, you are hearing His warning.
Today, the invitation of the gospel is still being proclaimed.
Today, you can turn from empty religious confidence and come to the Savior who receives sinners.
You do not need a spotless history to come to Jesus.
You need the Savior whose blood cleanses sinners.
You do not need to manufacture an impressive spiritual résumé.
You need to trust the crucified and risen Lord.
You do not need to pretend your wounds, failures, and sins never happened.
You need to bring them into the light of His grace.
That is the heart of our message.
From rebellion to repentance.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From spiritual death to new life in Christ.
Not because we rewrote our own stories.
But because Jesus is the Redeemer who changes everything.
And when you finally stand before Him, may your confidence never be the number of things you accomplished while saying His name.
May your confidence be Jesus Christ Himself—the Savior who died for sinners, rose victorious, and knows those who are His.
Because the most frightening possibility is not that the world might forget your name.
It is that you could spend your life making the name of Jesus part of your public identity while never truly surrendering your heart to Him.
And the most beautiful possibility?
That the very Savior who warns you today is also the Savior who invites you to come to Him and live.
Do not settle for being recognized as someone who speaks about Jesus when His grace is inviting you to become someone who truly belongs to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR WIFE HASN’T WANTED SEX IN MONTHS. ARE YOU WRONG FOR FEELING REJECTED?
paragraphs: YOUR WIFE HASN’T WANTED SEX IN MONTHS. ARE YOU WRONG FOR FEELING REJECTED?

When the woman you love no longer reaches for you, the silence can break something inside you. But before rejection becomes resentment, there is a truth about marriage, intimacy, and the love of Jesus Christ that both husbands and wives desperately need to hear.
There is a kind of loneliness that only a married person can understand.
It is lying in bed beside someone you promised to love for the rest of your life… and feeling like you are sleeping a thousand miles apart.
Her back is turned.
The lights are off.
The house is quiet.
You reach toward her, hoping for something small. A touch. A kiss. Maybe just the reassurance that she still wants to be close to you.
But she moves away.
“I'm tired.”
And you tell her it's okay.
Because you love her.
Because you don't want to pressure her.
Because you know marriage is supposed to be about more than sex.
But what she doesn't hear is the conversation that begins inside your head after she falls asleep.
Does she still find me attractive?
Did I do something wrong?
Is there someone else?
Am I asking for too much?
Why do I feel so unwanted by the one person who promised to love me?
And perhaps the question that hurts most…
Am I a bad Christian husband for feeling this way?
Brother, I want you to hear something before you read another sentence.
Your desire to be wanted by your wife does not make you selfish. But what you do with the pain of feeling unwanted will reveal something important about the condition of your heart.
And wife, if you're reading this, please don't leave.
This is not an article written to accuse you.
It is not another message telling you that your body belongs to somebody else regardless of what you are carrying emotionally, physically, or spiritually.
This is about both of you.
Two people who may still love each other deeply but have forgotten how to reach each other without causing pain.
And somewhere between his silent rejection and her silent exhaustion, a marriage that once felt alive has begun to feel like a place where both people are merely surviving.
The tragedy is that sometimes neither spouse is the enemy.
They are both wounded.
They just don't know how to tell each other where it hurts.
And if that describes your marriage, please keep reading.
Because what Scripture actually teaches about intimacy is more beautiful, more demanding, and more compassionate than the arguments people often use to defend themselves.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the expression for “one flesh” is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
Basar means flesh.
Echad means one.
Two people becoming one flesh.
Not one person consuming the other.
Not one person's needs erasing the other's humanity.
One flesh.
A covenant union so profound that what happens to one spouse inevitably affects the other.
Sexual intimacy is one expression of that union, but the biblical vision of marriage reaches beyond the bedroom into companionship, faithfulness, tenderness, responsibility, and shared life.
That is why months without physical intimacy can hurt so deeply.
For some husbands, sex is not merely about physical release.
It is one of the ways they experience closeness, acceptance, affection, and the reassurance that their marriage is still alive.
When that connection disappears, the absence can feel personal even when the reason isn't personal at all.
But here is where the story becomes more complicated.
Your wife may not be rejecting you, even when you genuinely feel rejected.
Read that again.
Because those two realities can exist at the same time.
Your pain can be real.
And your interpretation of her pain can still be incomplete.
Perhaps she has been carrying exhaustion that sleep never seems to fix.
Perhaps childbirth changed her body in ways she still struggles to understand.
Perhaps menopause, hormonal changes, chronic pain, medication, depression, anxiety, or another medical concern has affected her desire.
Perhaps physical intimacy has become uncomfortable or painful, and she is embarrassed to tell you.
Perhaps she spends every day caring for children, managing responsibilities, meeting expectations, and trying to remain emotionally available to everyone until she has almost nothing left.
Or perhaps something happened between the two of you.
Something neither of you has fully addressed.
A harsh word.
A betrayal.
A pattern of criticism.
Years of feeling unheard.
An apology that was spoken but never followed by change.
And now, when you reach for her body, she remembers the distance she feels in her heart.
Not every marriage has these problems. Not every woman experiences desire the same way. And not every period without sex means something is broken.
But sometimes what looks like sexual rejection is the visible symptom of a much deeper wound.
And sometimes a husband has been hurting so long that he has stopped asking questions and started making accusations.
He says, “You never want me anymore.”
She hears, “You're failing me again.”
She says, “All you ever think about is sex.”
He hears, “Your need for closeness disgusts me.”
Then both retreat.
He becomes quieter.
She becomes more guarded.
He stops reaching.
She feels relieved that the pressure has stopped, but frightened by the growing distance.
And neither realizes how much love is being buried beneath conversations they are too afraid to have.
This is where many Christian marriages need more than another sermon about marital duty.
They need the truth of God's Word understood in its proper context.
First Corinthians 7:3–4 says:
“Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.
The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.” (KJV)
Some people read those verses and immediately conclude that a wife is obligated to have sex whenever her husband desires it.
But notice what Paul actually says.
“And likewise also.”
The Greek text of verse 4 includes the words ὁμοίως δὲ καί — homoiōs de kai, expressing the reciprocal nature of Paul's instruction: “and likewise also.”
Paul does not give the husband unilateral authority while denying the wife equal consideration.
He speaks of mutuality.
The husband is not presented as the sole owner of marital intimacy.
The wife is not presented as someone whose physical or emotional well-being can be disregarded.
Both spouses are called to care for one another.
In verse 5, Paul continues:
“Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again…” (KJV)
The Greek expression ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou means “by agreement” or “by mutual consent.”
That matters.
Paul treats sexual intimacy as an important part of marriage and encourages spouses not to neglect one another. Yet his teaching is framed by reciprocity and agreement, not intimidation or force.
These verses must never become weapons for demanding sex, overriding a spouse's refusal, or excusing coercion.
A biblical understanding of marital intimacy calls both husband and wife toward loving, willing, considerate participation.
It does not turn either person's body into a tool for satisfying the other at any cost.
And if someone has used Scripture to frighten, pressure, or force you into sexual activity, that misuse of Scripture does not reflect Christlike love.
Marriage does not eliminate the need for consent.
Love does not become righteous simply because it quotes a Bible verse.
Now, husband, I need to ask you something that may be uncomfortable.
When was the last time you touched your wife without hoping it would lead somewhere?
When was the last time you held her without turning the embrace into an invitation?
When was the last time you asked how she was doing and stayed long enough to hear the answer she was afraid to give?
Not because you were trying to earn intimacy later.
But because she is your wife.
A human being.
A daughter made in the image of God.
Someone whose heart matters even on the nights when her body cannot give you what you desire.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
The Greek verb translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate, from agapaō.
Paul commands husbands to love their wives according to the pattern of Christ's self-giving love.
And look at the example.
Jesus gave Himself.
He did not exploit the weakness of those He loved.
He did not use His authority to serve His own comfort.
He sacrificed Himself for their good.
That is the standard Christian husbands are called toward.
Not perfection.
Not pretending they have no needs.
But a love that refuses to make another person's vulnerability an opportunity for selfishness.
Husband, your loneliness deserves to be heard.
But your loneliness does not give you permission to punish your wife.
Not through threats.
Not through humiliation.
Not through comparisons with other women.
Not through pornography, an affair, or emotional withdrawal designed to make her suffer.
And not by using the Bible to make her feel guilty until she gives in.
You can be deeply disappointed without becoming cruel.
You can express your needs without demanding compliance.
You can say, “I miss being close to you,” without saying, “You owe me.”
That difference can change the entire atmosphere of a marriage.
But wife, there is something important for you to hear as well.
Your husband's longing for intimacy is not automatically evidence that he is shallow, lustful, or spiritually immature.
Sometimes he is trying to tell you something he doesn't know how to put into words.
I miss us.
I miss feeling chosen.
I miss knowing that you want to be close to me.
And if you have been turning away because you are exhausted, hurting, afraid, or emotionally disconnected, your experience deserves compassion.
You should never have to endure unwanted sexual activity to prove that you are a faithful wife.
But when it is safe to do so, your husband also deserves an honest conversation rather than endless uncertainty.
Not an obligation to give him sex.
An invitation to help him understand what has changed.
Perhaps the conversation begins with something as simple as:
“I love you. But something has been happening inside me, and I don't fully understand it either.”
Or:
“I want us to be close again, but I need you to understand why intimacy has become difficult.”
And perhaps his response needs to be:
“Thank you for telling me. I don't want you to feel pressured. I want to understand what you're going through, because I miss you, not just sex.”
Can you imagine what might happen if those words replaced months of blame?
Not every wound would disappear overnight.
Some problems require medical care, counseling, repentance, rebuilding trust, or patient changes in daily life.
And some marriages have serious issues of abuse or coercion that require protection and specialized support rather than simply more communication.
But in a marriage where both people are willing and safe, honesty can open a door that resentment has kept closed.
James 1:19 says:
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.” (KJV)
Sometimes the most spiritual thing a husband can do is stop preparing his defense long enough to understand his wife.
Sometimes the most loving thing a wife can do is stop assuming her husband's pain is merely a complaint about sex and listen to the loneliness underneath it.
And sometimes the most courageous thing both can do is admit:
“We have been hurting each other, and we need help.”
There is no shame in seeking help.

A qualified marriage counselor can help couples communicate about resentment, desire, and emotional distance. A healthcare professional can evaluate pain, hormonal concerns, medication effects, or other possible contributors to changes in sexual desire.
Prayer matters.
So does wise, practical care.
Faith and appropriate treatment are not enemies.
But I want to take you somewhere deeper now.
Because there is a danger in making your spouse's desire the final verdict on your worth.
Husband, if your wife has not wanted sex for months, you may begin to believe that you are no longer desirable, masculine, valuable, or loved.
And if that belief takes root, it can poison more than your marriage.
You may start looking for validation elsewhere.
A compliment from another woman suddenly feels unusually powerful.
A private message becomes tempting.
Pornography begins to look like an escape from rejection.
You tell yourself that you are only trying to feel wanted.
But sin has a way of offering temporary relief while deepening the very loneliness we are trying to escape.
And if you are standing at that crossroads right now, please hear this.
Do not let a season of unmet desire become the doorway to a lifetime of regret.
Your pain matters.
But pain does not make betrayal righteous.
Jesus speaks directly to the heart in Matthew 5:28, warning against looking at another person with lustful intent.
He does not treat private desire as morally insignificant simply because no one else can see it.
That is uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we want God to confront our spouse's failures while leaving our own secret compromises untouched.
We want Him to fix what hurts us without exposing what is corrupting us.
But Christ loves us too much to leave us hiding.
He calls us to repentance.
Not because His grace is small.
Because His grace is powerful enough to lead us out of the darkness.
And this is where the Gospel changes everything.
Jesus did not come merely to make unhappy husbands feel better or exhausted wives feel less guilty.
He came to save sinners.
People whose hearts are capable of selfishness, pride, bitterness, dishonesty, and unfaithfulness.
People who need more than relationship advice.
People who need redemption.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Notice the timing.
While we were still sinners.
Before we had repaired everything.
Before we had learned to love perfectly.
Before we had become the people we should have been.
Christ died for us.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who turn to Him in faith.
That is not permission to continue hurting others.
It is the very reason we can stop pretending, confess our sins, and begin walking in a new direction.
The husband who has been feeding bitterness can repent.
The wife who has been concealing painful truths may find the courage to speak.
The spouse who has betrayed trust can stop hiding and accept responsibility.
The couple who has forgotten how to pray together can begin again.
And the person whose marriage cannot be repaired by their efforts alone can still discover that Christ has not abandoned them.
Because the Gospel is not the promise that every marriage will be restored exactly as we want.
It is the promise that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save, forgive, sustain, and transform those who belong to Him.
Sometimes grace brings reconciliation.
Sometimes it brings the courage to confront destructive patterns.
Sometimes it brings protection, truth, and necessary boundaries.
But grace never requires someone to pretend that harm is love.
And grace never tells a wounded person that their value depends on another human being's sexual desire.
Brother, you were made in God's image before you became somebody's husband.
Sister, you were made in God's image before you became somebody's wife.
Your dignity did not begin on your wedding day.
And it does not disappear in a season of sexual difficulty.
That truth should humble both of you.
Because the person lying beside you is not merely someone who can meet your needs.
That person bears the image of the Creator.
Think about that the next time you are tempted to reduce your spouse to a disappointment.
Think about that the next time you are tempted to dismiss a pain you don't understand.
Think about that when you want to win the argument more than you want to understand the person.
Colossians 3:13 calls believers to forgive one another, just as Christ has forgiven them.
But forgiveness does not erase the need for truth, repentance, safety, or changed behavior.
And reconciliation cannot be manufactured by one spouse while the other refuses accountability.
Christian love is not the denial of reality.
It is the courage to face reality under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
So what do you do tonight?
Maybe your wife is already asleep.
Maybe you have not been intimate in three months.
Six months.
A year.
Maybe you have stopped counting because every passing week feels like another reminder of how far apart you have become.
You don't need to solve everything before sunrise.
You don't need a perfect speech.
But perhaps tomorrow, at a calm moment when neither of you feels pressured, you can say something different.
Not, “Why don't you ever want me?”
But:
“I've been feeling lonely, and I haven't known how to talk about it without making you feel blamed. I miss being close to you. I want to understand what you've been experiencing. Can we talk?”
And then listen.
Really listen.
Even if the answer is difficult.
Even if she says something you didn't expect.
Even if you discover that the problem is not simply a lack of desire, but a wound that needs attention.
And wife, if your husband approaches you with genuine humility, consider meeting that honesty with honesty of your own, if you feel safe.
You do not have to promise sex.
You do not have to manufacture desire.
You can begin with the truth.
“I've been struggling too.”
“I've been afraid to talk about this.”
“I need us to rebuild something.”
Maybe the first step toward intimacy will not be sex.
Maybe it will be a conversation without accusations.
A medical appointment.
A counseling session.
An apology that names the actual harm.
A practical change in how responsibilities are shared.
A hug that carries no hidden expectation.
A prayer spoken through tears.
And perhaps, over time, you will discover that genuine intimacy is not simply the moment two bodies come together.
It is the growing trust that allows two people to be honest, vulnerable, and lovingly present with one another.
The Song of Songs celebrates marital desire as something beautiful, not shameful.
In Song of Solomon 7:10, the bride says:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.” (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated “desire” is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah.
It speaks of longing or desire.
In this poetic context, the bride rejoices in her beloved's desire for her.
There is tenderness in that.
Mutual delight.
The joy of being loved and wanted.
God has not made sexual desire inherently dirty.
But He has also not made sexual desire an excuse to disregard love.
The beauty of marital intimacy is not found in one person winning access to another person's body.
It is found in affection and desire expressed within faithful, loving, mutually willing union.
And that is worth protecting.
Not just the frequency of sex.
The heart of the marriage.
Because a couple can have sex regularly and still be emotionally distant.
And a couple can experience a difficult season without sex while continuing to show extraordinary tenderness, loyalty, and love.
The question is not simply, “How do we get back to having sex?”
It is also, “How do we love each other faithfully in the situation we are facing?”
That question takes us closer to Christ.

And maybe, just maybe, the greatest breakthrough in your marriage will begin when you stop seeing your spouse as the obstacle to your happiness and begin seeing each other as people who need God's grace.
Husband, you are not wrong for feeling rejected.
Feelings of rejection can be painful, even when rejection was not intended.
But do not allow that feeling to become the authority over everything you believe about your wife.
Wife, you are not wrong for experiencing low desire, exhaustion, or difficulty with intimacy.
But when possible and safe, do not let silence become the only language your husband receives.
Neither of you has to pretend.
Neither of you has to surrender your dignity.
Both of you can bring your struggles into the light.
And both of you need Jesus.
Not a Jesus who simply takes your side against your spouse.
The real Jesus.
The One who exposes sin without abandoning the repentant.
The One who welcomes the weary.
The One who teaches us to love with humility and truth.
The One who died for our sins and rose again.
The One who can transform hearts that human effort alone cannot change.
If this article has exposed something in you, don't rush past it.
Maybe you are a husband who has been quietly drowning in rejection.
Maybe you are a wife who feels exhausted by expectations nobody seems to understand.
Maybe you are both.

Or, if you are comfortable sharing, tell us what you wish husbands and wives understood about emotional and physical intimacy. You do not need to disclose private details, and you never have to expose your spouse publicly to receive prayer.
Your words may help another person realize they are not alone.
Not to use as evidence against your spouse.
You may never know which husband is silently questioning his worth or which wife is crying because she cannot explain what has changed inside her.
Because the world is already full of voices teaching people how to defend themselves.
We need more voices reminding people how to follow Jesus.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to glorify a page.
Not to build a personality.
But to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
But I want to be careful here because the Word of God deserves honesty.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the heart of this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not the suggestion that you must pay to prove your love for Jesus.
But an opportunity to participate in work you believe is faithfully serving Him.
And beyond the products, the deeper invitation is to stay connected to biblical nourishment, spiritual encouragement, accountability, and discipleship that continually points back to Christ.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your value before God.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And no one should ever be made to feel that Christ's love must be purchased.
Before you leave, I want to speak one last time to the husband who began reading this article with a wounded heart.
You may still be lying beside your wife tonight without the physical affection you have been longing for.
The conversation may not happen immediately.
The answers may be more complicated than you hoped.
And the road toward healing may require patience, courage, outside help, and difficult changes from both of you.
But please don't let disappointment turn you into someone you never wanted to become.
Don't surrender your integrity because you feel unseen.
Don't confuse your wife's present lack of sexual desire with a final judgment on your worth.
Don't make your marriage an altar where your spouse must continually prove that you matter.
You matter because God made you.
And the cross of Jesus Christ reveals a love far greater than any human relationship can provide.
To the wife who has been carrying a burden she cannot explain, you are seen too.
Your exhaustion matters.
Your pain matters.
Your voice matters.
You are not simply a body that must perform to preserve somebody else's confidence.
You are a person worthy of dignity, tenderness, and truth.
And to both of you…
Perhaps tonight you can begin with a simple prayer.

“Lord Jesus, forgive us for the ways we have allowed fear, selfishness, bitterness, or silence to shape our marriage. Help us see each other with compassion. Give us courage to speak honestly, humility to listen, wisdom to seek help where needed, and strength to repent wherever we have sinned. Protect us from temptation and teach us to love in ways that honor You. Whether healing comes quickly or slowly, keep our hearts anchored in Your truth. In Your name, amen.”
Your marriage may be in a painful chapter.
But your story is not beyond the reach of God's grace.
And even if the outcome is different from what you prayed for, your life is still held by the risen Savior.
Because sometimes the deepest wound in a marriage is not that two people have stopped touching.
It is that two hearts have been crying out to be loved, while neither has known how to hear the other.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD ALLOW EZEKIEL TO USE LANGUAGE SO SHOCKING THAT MANY CHURCHES WON’T EVEN READ IT ALOUD?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD ALLOW EZEKIEL TO USE LANGUAGE SO SHOCKING THAT MANY CHURCHES WON’T EVEN READ IT ALOUD?

Ezekiel 23 is one of the Bible’s most disturbing chapters. But beneath its graphic language lies a terrifying revelation about spiritual betrayal, the patience of God, and the devastating cost of giving your heart to everything except the One who loves you.
There are chapters in the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that strengthen you.
And then there are chapters that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and wonder...
“Did God really say that?”
Ezekiel 23 is one of those chapters.
It contains language so sexually explicit, accusations so humiliating, and images so disturbing that many Christians have never heard the entire chapter read from a pulpit.
Some believers encounter it for the first time and feel genuinely shocked.
Others wonder why such language belongs in a holy book.
And some quietly ask a question they are almost afraid to say aloud.
“Why would God speak about His own people like this?”
But perhaps the most important question is not why the chapter makes us uncomfortable.
Perhaps it is why the sins being exposed had become so comfortable to the people committing them.
Because Ezekiel 23 was never written to entertain an audience with scandal.
It was a prophetic indictment of a people who had repeatedly exchanged covenant faithfulness for idolatry, political dependence, and spiritual rebellion.
And when you understand what was happening behind those shocking words, something changes.
You stop reading merely as a spectator of ancient Israel's failure.
You begin examining the things competing for your own heart.
And that is where this chapter becomes painfully personal.
Imagine someone who has loved you faithfully.
Someone who rescued you when you had nothing.
Someone who provided for you, protected you, and remained patient through repeated betrayal.
Now imagine that instead of responding with gratitude, you continually turn toward those who exploit you.
You pursue them.
You trust their promises.
You surrender your loyalty.
And when everything collapses, you return to the one who loved you, not necessarily because you have changed, but because you need rescuing again.
Then, once you recover, you repeat the betrayal.
How long could such a relationship continue without a reckoning?
That question helps us understand the emotional and covenantal background of Ezekiel 23.
But we must be careful.

This chapter is not permission to humiliate an unfaithful spouse, degrade women, or justify abuse. Its disturbing sexual imagery belongs to a specific prophetic literary form addressing nations, kingdoms, and their covenant violations.
The prophet is not offering ordinary marriage counseling.
He is announcing divine judgment against entrenched national unfaithfulness.
And the language is deliberately difficult.
The chapter begins:
“Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother.” — Ezekiel 23:2, KJV
These two symbolic sisters are named Oholah and Oholibah.
Their names are not incidental.
In the Hebrew text, the first is אָהֳלָה (Oholah), commonly understood as “her tent.”
The second is אָהֳלִיבָה (Oholibah), commonly understood as “my tent is in her.”
The Hebrew word אֹהֶל (ohel) means “tent,” a word that can carry associations with dwelling and, in biblical worship, the tabernacle.
These names are part of the prophecy's message.
Ezekiel identifies Oholah with Samaria, representing the northern kingdom of Israel, and Oholibah with Jerusalem, representing the southern kingdom of Judah.
“My tent is in her” is especially significant in connection with Jerusalem, the city where God's temple stood.
Jerusalem possessed extraordinary religious privilege.
The temple.
The priesthood.
The sacrifices.
The covenant history.
The memory of God's mighty acts.
Yet the presence of sacred institutions did not guarantee a faithful heart.
You can be surrounded by the things of God and still give your deepest allegiance to something else.
That was Jerusalem's tragedy.
And it remains a warning for religious people today.
A person can attend worship every week and still live under the control of greed.
A person can quote Scripture and still cultivate cruelty.
A person can speak passionately about holiness while hiding patterns of dishonesty.
A person can defend the reputation of a church while refusing to confront injustice within it.
The appearance of devotion is not the same as devotion itself.
But Ezekiel's accusation was even more specific.
Israel and Judah were not simply failing to maintain a private religious feeling.
They were turning toward foreign powers, adopting idolatrous practices, participating in corrupt worship, and trusting political alliances in ways that contradicted their covenant obligations.
The prophet describes their conduct through an extended metaphor of sexual infidelity.
The Hebrew word זָנָה (zanah) is important here.
Its basic sense concerns prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness. In prophetic literature, it is frequently used figuratively for idolatry and covenant betrayal.
That distinction matters.
Ezekiel is not claiming that every sexual image in the chapter represents a literal sexual act committed by the entire population.
He is using sexual betrayal as a metaphor for religious and political infidelity.
The shocking imagery is designed to expose how seriously Judah's conduct violated its covenant relationship with God.
Oholah, the northern kingdom, became entangled with Assyria.
Historically, Samaria fell to Assyria in 722/721 BC.
Her destruction was not a theoretical warning.
It had already happened.
