Judah had witnessed the collapse of its northern sister.
Jerusalem knew the history.
Jerusalem had seen the consequences.
And still, according to Ezekiel, she repeated and intensified the pattern.
Think about that.
It is one thing to stumble because you do not understand the danger.
It is another to watch someone else fall into a destructive pattern, recognize the consequences, and still convince yourself that your own outcome will somehow be different.
That is not merely ancient history.
That is human nature.
We watch pride destroy relationships, yet defend our own arrogance.
We watch greed consume families, yet tell ourselves one more compromise will finally make us secure.
We watch bitterness poison someone else's life, yet quietly feed our own resentment.
We watch spiritual neglect hollow out a person's faith, yet keep postponing prayer, repentance, and obedience.
We see the warning.
We understand the danger.
And somehow we still believe we are the exception.
Jerusalem did.
Then Ezekiel's language becomes even more disturbing.
In verse 20, the prophet uses an explicit comparison involving the sexual anatomy and emissions of animals.
The Hebrew text is graphic. Responsible translations should not pretend otherwise.
The passage uses sexual excess as an image of Jerusalem's consuming desire for foreign powers, particularly Egypt.
Its purpose is not to provide erotic detail for the reader's enjoyment.
It is to portray Judah's disordered loyalties in deliberately repellent terms.
The imagery is meant to shock.
But shock is not the same thing as understanding.
And it is possible to recognize the prophet's purpose without pretending the imagery is easy, or that every modern reader will experience it in the same way.
Some readers, especially survivors of sexual violence or humiliation, may find the chapter deeply distressing.
That reaction should not be dismissed.
Faithful interpretation requires both honesty about the text and compassion toward the people reading it.
The chapter's violent descriptions of judgment must never be turned into permission for believers to shame, threaten, or abuse anyone.
Ezekiel is describing divine judgment through an ancient prophetic allegory.
He is not instructing Christians to imitate its violence.
Yet underneath the unsettling language is a devastating theological accusation.
God's people were seeking security, satisfaction, and identity from powers that could not save them.
They had become fascinated with what would ultimately destroy them.
And that is one of sin's oldest strategies.
Sin rarely introduces itself as destruction. It usually arrives disguised as something you cannot live without.
It promises freedom.
Then it demands obedience.
It promises comfort.
Then it becomes a dependency.
It promises belonging.
Then it pressures you to compromise your convictions.
It promises control.
Then it begins controlling you.
And eventually, the thing you once pursued for security becomes the very thing you fear losing.
This does not mean every painful dependency, trauma response, or personal struggle is equivalent to Judah's deliberate national rebellion.
Scripture does not flatten every human wound into the same moral category.
But the chapter does invite us to examine where our trust and allegiance have gone.
What do you turn to when you feel empty?
What receives the loyalty that belongs to God?
What compromise have you begun calling normal because confronting it would require change?
What truth have you avoided because you already know what obedience would cost?
These are uncomfortable questions.
But they are not asked to drive you into despair.
They are asked because repentance begins when we stop defending what is destroying us.
And then comes one of the most haunting statements in the chapter.
Ezekiel 23:35 declares:
“Because thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back, therefore bear thou also thy lewdness and thy whoredoms.” — KJV
Listen carefully to the central accusation.
“Thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back.”
The Hebrew phrase וַתַּשְׁלִיכִי אוֹתִי אַחֲרֵי גַוֵּךְ (vattashlikhi oti acharei gavvekh) communicates the idea of casting God behind one's back.
This is more than a momentary lapse of memory.
It describes treating God as someone who no longer deserves attention or allegiance.
The issue was not that Judah had forgotten God's name.
The people still possessed their religious identity.
The temple still stood for much of the period being condemned.
Religious language had not disappeared.
But their conduct revealed a catastrophic displacement of loyalty.
They had pushed God behind them.
And that should make every religious heart tremble.
Because it is possible to remember the vocabulary of faith while losing the posture of surrender.
It is possible to know the songs without listening to the Lord.
It is possible to defend Christian traditions while resisting Christ's commands.
It is possible to say “God comes first” while organizing your entire life around something else.
Jesus would later confront a similar disconnect between religious appearance and inward devotion.
In Matthew 15:8, He says:
“This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.” — KJV
Jesus was citing Isaiah's prophetic warning.
Different historical circumstances.
The same devastating possibility.
Lips that honor God.
Hearts that wander from Him.
And here is where we must resist an easy mistake.
It would be convenient to read Ezekiel 23 and say, “Those people were terrible.”
It would be comfortable to turn their failures into a lesson about someone else's hypocrisy.
But Scripture was not preserved merely so that later generations could congratulate themselves for being better than their ancestors.
Romans 15:4 reminds us that what was written before was written for our learning.
The point is not to pretend every detail of Judah's history directly describes your life.
The point is to receive the warning rather than stand above it.
Because the human heart still knows how to manufacture substitutes for God.
Some substitutes look obviously sinful.
Others look respectable.
Success can become an idol.
Approval can become an idol.
Money can become an idol.
Religious influence can become an idol.
Even ministry can become an idol when the work of God becomes more important to us than obedience to God.
A person can spend years building a platform about Jesus while quietly neglecting prayer, integrity, compassion, and the people entrusted to their care.
A church can become so concerned with maintaining an image of spiritual success that it begins hiding the very sins it should be confronting.
And a believer can become so practiced at explaining away compromise that repentance starts feeling unnecessary.
That is a frightening place to live.
Not because God's grace has become weak.
But because self-deception can make us resistant to the grace we desperately need.
Now consider the historical weight of Ezekiel's warning.
The prophet ministered during the crisis surrounding Jerusalem's final years and the Babylonian exile.
Judah's leaders had repeatedly looked toward political alliances and foreign powers for security.
Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BC would expose the catastrophic failure of that confidence.
The temple would be burned.
The city would be devastated.
Many people would suffer death, displacement, and exile.
Ezekiel's prophecy belongs to that terrifying historical setting.
It should never be reduced to a vague motivational slogan.
Real people suffered.
Real communities collapsed.
And the biblical narrative places these events within the larger story of covenant judgment.
But the story of Ezekiel does not end in chapter 23.
And this is where the Gospel begins to illuminate the darkness without erasing the seriousness of the warning.
Because if all we hear is judgment, we have not yet listened to the whole prophetic book.
After announcing the consequences of Judah's rebellion, Ezekiel also records astonishing promises of restoration.
In Ezekiel 36:26, God declares:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” — KJV
Read that again.
“A new heart also will I give you.”
Not merely better appearances.
Not simply improved religious performance.
Not a more convincing public reputation.
A new heart.
The Hebrew phrase לֵב חָדָשׁ (lev chadash) means “a new heart.”
In biblical thought, the heart is not merely the seat of emotions. It is deeply associated with thought, desire, intention, and moral direction.
God was promising a transformation that went deeper than outward conformity.
He would renew His people from within.
And Ezekiel 36:27 goes further:
“And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes...” — KJV
Do you see the movement?
Ezekiel 23 exposes the betrayal.
Ezekiel 36 promises renewal.
The same prophetic book that refuses to minimize sin also refuses to leave restoration out of view.
God's holiness is not compromised by His mercy.
And His mercy is not evidence that sin was harmless.
The promise of a new heart is meaningful precisely because the old heart's condition was so serious.
But how would that promise find its fullest meaning?
The New Testament directs our attention to Jesus Christ.
Not because Ezekiel 23 is secretly a coded prediction of every detail of Jesus' earthly ministry.
It is not.
Its immediate subject is the covenant infidelity and judgment of Samaria and Jerusalem.
But within the wider biblical story, Ezekiel's promise of cleansing, renewed hearts, and God's Spirit prepares us to understand the salvation accomplished through Christ.
Jesus came into a world that had not solved the problem of sin.
Religious knowledge had not solved it.
Political strength had not solved it.
Human determination had not solved it.
And no amount of outward respectability could cleanse the conscience or reconcile sinners to God.
Jesus came not merely to expose our need.
He came to save.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
He did not become morally guilty.
He bore our sins in His sacrificial death.
He endured the cross, rose from the dead, and opened the way for forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
The apostle Paul writes:
And Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not wait for sinners to make themselves worthy of rescue.
He came because sinners could not rescue themselves.
And yet His grace does not teach us to remain comfortably enslaved to the very sins from which He came to deliver us.
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace trains us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace produces a changed life.
That is why repentance matters.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated “repentance.”
It conveys a change of mind or understanding that, in its biblical setting, involves a decisive turning toward God and away from sin.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what you were hiding.
It is not just being frightened by consequences.
It is turning to God in truth, trusting His mercy, and beginning to walk in obedience.
And no, genuine repentance does not mean you will never struggle again.
Christians still face temptation.
They still need confession.
They still need correction, growth, and the sustaining grace of God.
But there is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and deciding you no longer need to get up.
There is a difference between crying out for mercy and using the language of mercy to excuse deliberate rebellion.
Perhaps you know that difference more personally than you want to admit.
Perhaps there is something in your life you have been minimizing.
A habit you keep defending.
A relationship built on deception.
A resentment you refuse to surrender.
A secret compromise that has slowly reshaped your conscience.
Or perhaps your struggle is not a scandal visible to anyone else.
Perhaps you have simply grown cold.
You still believe the right things.
You still know the verses.
You still recognize the songs.
But somewhere along the way, prayer became rare, worship became mechanical, and the presence of God became less important to you than the approval of people.
You cannot remember the exact day it happened.
You only know you are not as close to Him as you once were.
And maybe that realization hurts.
If it does, do not turn that pain into another reason to hide.
Bring it to Christ.
Not because you can purchase His forgiveness through tears.
Not because your shame makes you worthy.
But because His mercy is sufficient, and His invitation to repent is real.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
There is no need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
There is no need to expose private wounds to strangers.
You can come to God truthfully, even if the only words you can manage are:
“Lord, I have been drifting. Have mercy on me.”
He already knows what you are afraid to confess.
And the Gospel tells us that those who come to Christ in faith are not turned away.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What an astonishing promise.
Ezekiel 23 shows the horror of covenant betrayal.
But Jesus reveals the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
And that is why we must not confuse the shocking language of judgment with the final word of the biblical story.
The final word for those who belong to Christ is not condemnation. It is redemption.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus...” — KJV
That is not a license to embrace sin.
It is the assurance that Christ has accomplished what guilty people could never accomplish for themselves.
The cross does not make sin insignificant.
The cross reveals both the gravity of sin and the greatness of divine love.
And the resurrection announces that death itself does not have the final victory.
So why did Ezekiel use language so shocking that many churches avoid reading it aloud?
Because the prophet was communicating the seriousness of Judah's covenant betrayal through a deliberately graphic allegory.
Because the people had repeatedly ignored warnings.
Because idolatry was not harmless religious experimentation.
Because their pursuit of foreign powers and false worship was leading toward national disaster.
Because religious privilege had not produced covenant faithfulness.
And because a people who had normalized their rebellion needed to hear an accusation they could not easily domesticate.
Yet we should not assume that the most graphic possible presentation is always the most faithful way to teach Scripture.
Pastors and teachers can address Ezekiel 23 honestly while exercising pastoral sensitivity, especially in mixed-age congregations and among people who have experienced sexual trauma.
Reverence for Scripture does not require sensationalism.
Sometimes faithfulness means explaining a difficult passage carefully rather than using its disturbing imagery to attract attention.
The goal is understanding, repentance, and renewed trust in God.
Not shock for its own sake.
And perhaps that is the challenge for us now.
Will we approach this chapter looking only for something scandalous?
Or will we allow its warning to confront our misplaced loyalties?
Will we use it to condemn people whose struggles are different from ours?
Or will we examine our own hearts before God?
Will we read its judgment and conclude that mercy has disappeared?
Or will we continue through Ezekiel until we hear God's promise to cleanse, renew, and restore?
Because the God who says, “I will give you a new heart,” is not asking us to repair our souls through religious performance.
He is calling us to receive the renewal that only He can give.
And through Jesus Christ, forgiveness and new life are not merely distant religious concepts.
They are the living hope of the Gospel.
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior.
Not a fascination with scandal.
Not a ministry built on humiliating the broken.
Not the idea that people must become impressive before they can approach God.
But a conviction that Scripture must be handled faithfully, Christ must remain central, and people must hear the truth about sin and the greater truth about the Savior who redeems sinners.
If this article made you examine something you have been avoiding, do not let the moment pass without bringing it before the Lord.
You might simply write, “Jesus, give me a new heart.”
Or “I’m still fighting. Pray for me.”
You do not have to disclose anything deeply personal. You can also share how Ezekiel 23 changed your understanding of idolatry, judgment, and grace.
Your honest reflection may encourage another believer who has been quietly struggling.
And think about someone you know who needs this message.
Someone who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has drifted away from faith.
Someone who is spiritually exhausted.
Someone who has been wounded by religion and needs to hear the Gospel presented with both truth and compassion.
That simple act can help sound biblical teaching reach people who might never enter a church building or open a Bible on their own.
Not because every difficult question has been answered here, but because Ezekiel 23 deserves more than a passing reaction.
Return to the chapter.
Read it in context.
Continue into Ezekiel 36 and 37.
Compare the prophetic warnings with the promises of restoration.
And keep asking how the whole counsel of Scripture directs us toward the holiness, justice, mercy, and saving work of God.
There is room here for serious questions, biblical learning, spiritual encouragement, and honest conversations about repentance and grace.
These resources are intended to make biblical learning more accessible, especially for people who want to grow but may not have the means to purchase a large collection of Christian books.
And if this ministry has helped you grow spiritually, I want to extend a personal invitation.
For believers who are able and willing to give, financial support can be one expression of generosity and stewardship.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It does not purchase God's favor.
And it should never replace your responsibilities to your family, local church, or people in genuine need.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That matters deeply.
Supporting Gospel ministry should come from willing generosity, not guilt or fear.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, tools for personal reflection, or thoughtful gifts for people you love.
It is helping make more Christ-centered teaching, biblical encouragement, and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
It is to follow Jesus.
Because the Gospel is bigger than a ministry.
The Gospel is the good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures.
It is the announcement that forgiveness is available through Him.
It is the call to repent, believe, and walk in the new life He gives.
And if you have spent years hiding behind appearances, perhaps today is the day to stop pretending.
If you have been chasing things that cannot satisfy your soul, perhaps today is the day to turn back.
If you have been using your past as evidence that God could never receive you, look again at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the Savior who receives sinners and transforms lives.
Ezekiel 23 is disturbing because betrayal is serious.
Ezekiel 36 is beautiful because renewal is possible.
And the Gospel is glorious because Jesus Christ has accomplished the salvation that we could never earn.
The question is no longer merely why Ezekiel used such shocking language.
The question is what we will do with the truth it reveals.
Will we continue pushing God behind our backs?
Or will we turn toward the One who calls us to repentance and offers us life?
The most heartbreaking thing would not be discovering how far your heart has wandered, but hearing Christ call you home and deciding you would rather keep hiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE NEVER CALLED HER A PROSTITUTE. SO WHY HAVE WE BEEN CALLING HER ONE FOR CENTURIES?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE NEVER CALLED HER A PROSTITUTE. SO WHY HAVE WE BEEN CALLING HER ONE FOR CENTURIES?

Jesus knew about her five husbands. He knew about the man she was living with. But what happened at that well was not the public humiliation of an immoral woman. It was a divine encounter that exposes how easily religious people can confuse someone's painful history with their identity—and how radically Jesus sees the people we have already judged.
There is something deeply disturbing about the way we have told her story.

For generations, she has stood in sermons, Bible studies, Christian books, and church conversations as the woman with five husbands. The immoral woman. The promiscuous woman. The woman who supposedly went from man to man because she could not control her desires.
Some have even called her a prostitute.
And perhaps you have heard that description so many times that you assumed it was written somewhere in your Bible.
But open John chapter 4.
Read it carefully.
Read what Jesus actually said.
Then read what He did not say.
Because there is one word that generations of people have attached to this woman that the Gospel of John never uses.
Prostitute.
Not once.
And that absence matters more than we might realize.
Not because sexual sin is unimportant. Not because repentance is optional. Not because Jesus overlooks the truth about our lives.
But because the Savior who knows everything about a person does not give us permission to invent what Scripture has not revealed.
And somewhere in this story is a person who has spent years carrying a name that God never gave them.
Maybe that person is you.
The encounter begins with a tired Jesus sitting beside Jacob's well near the Samaritan town of Sychar.
John tells us that it was about the sixth hour. On the usual Jewish reckoning, that would place the encounter around noon.
Jesus was weary from His journey.
That detail alone is astonishing.
The eternal Word who became flesh, the One through whom all things were made, was genuinely tired.
He sat beside a well.
And a Samaritan woman came to draw water.
Jesus asked her for a drink.
That sounds ordinary until we understand the world surrounding the conversation.
Jews and Samaritans had a long history of religious and ethnic hostility. Their disagreements involved ancestry, sacred history, worship, and the proper place to approach God.
And in that culture, a Jewish man initiating this kind of conversation with an unfamiliar Samaritan woman was unusual enough that even His disciples would later marvel.
Yet Jesus spoke first.
Not with an accusation.
Not with a warning.
Not with a lecture about her reputation.
He asked for water.
Sometimes the most extraordinary moments of grace begin with something painfully ordinary.
A conversation.
A question.
An unexpected kindness from someone who had every social reason to walk away.
The woman was surprised.
John 4:9 records her asking why a Jewish man would request a drink from a Samaritan woman.
But Jesus had come for more than water.
He began speaking about the gift of God and the living water He could give.
In the Greek text of John 4:10, the expression is ὕδωρ ζῶν (hydōr zōn)—literally, "living water."
In ordinary usage, living water could describe fresh, flowing water rather than stagnant water.
But Jesus was drawing her toward something far greater than a better source of drinking water.
He was speaking of the life God gives, a reality John later connects with the Holy Spirit in John 7:37–39.
The woman initially understood Him in terms of physical water.
She saw a deep well.
She saw a man without a bucket.
She saw an impossible offer.
But Jesus saw a thirst that no earthly well could satisfy.
He told her that ordinary water would leave a person thirsty again, but the water He gives would become a spring welling up to eternal life.
Imagine hearing that promise while carrying a life full of unanswered questions.
Imagine standing before someone who speaks as though the emptiness you have learned to live with does not have to be permanent.
She asked Him for that water.
And then the conversation took a turn that has been misunderstood by countless readers.
Jesus said:
"Go, call thy husband, and come hither." — John 4:16, KJV
She answered:
"I have no husband." — John 4:17, KJV
Jesus responded:
"Thou hast well said, I have no husband: For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly." — John 4:17–18, KJV
And there it is.
The passage that has become the foundation for so many assumptions about this woman.
Five husbands.
A sixth man who was not her husband.
And suddenly, in the imagination of many readers, an entire biography appears.
She must have been sexually reckless.
She must have seduced men.
She must have destroyed marriages.
She must have been a prostitute.
But stop.
Where does the passage actually say those things?
It doesn't.
The Greek of John 4:18 includes these words:
πέντε γὰρ ἄνδρας ἔσχες (pente gar andras esches)
"For you have had five husbands."
The word ἄνδρας (andras) can mean men or husbands depending on context. Here, the surrounding conversation clearly concerns husbands.
Jesus then says:
καὶ νῦν ὃν ἔχεις οὐκ ἔστιν σου ἀνήρ (kai nyn hon echeis ouk estin sou anēr)
"And the one you now have is not your husband."
Notice what Jesus reveals.
He knows her marital history.
He knows her present relationship does not constitute a marriage.
He knows she has spoken truthfully about having no husband.
But He does not explain why those five marriages ended.
He does not say whether she was widowed.
He does not say whether she was divorced.
He does not tell us whether she was abandoned, mistreated, or responsible for the breakdown of any of those relationships.
He does not identify the nature of her present arrangement beyond saying that the man she now has is not her husband.
Those missing details are not invitations for us to manufacture certainty.
They are boundaries around what we can responsibly claim.
In the ancient world, women could be profoundly vulnerable to decisions made by men.
Widowhood could bring financial insecurity.
Divorce could leave a woman socially and economically exposed.
A woman might have endured repeated losses or rejection with very little power to determine what happened next.
Does that prove the Samaritan woman was an innocent victim of five tragedies?
No.
And we must be just as careful not to invent a tragic biography as we are not to invent a scandalous one.
The truth is that Scripture does not tell us why she had five husbands.
We simply do not know.
And that is precisely the point.
There is a difference between recognizing a morally complicated situation and claiming to know every motive, action, and failure that produced it.
Jesus knew.
We don't.
Yet sometimes we speak as though we were standing beside that well with a complete record of her private life.
There is another detail that deserves attention.
John never uses the Greek word πόρνη (pornē)—a word meaning prostitute—to describe this woman.
Nor does he explicitly accuse her of adultery.
That does not mean her present relationship was necessarily righteous. Jesus plainly identifies a distinction between the man she has and a husband.
The passage is not a declaration that every relationship is acceptable.
But neither is it evidence that she sold sex or habitually pursued men.
Those are different claims.
And biblical faithfulness requires us to keep them different.
Why does this matter?
Because we can become so comfortable condemning sins that we begin condemning people for sins we cannot even establish.
We turn suspicion into certainty.
We turn speculation into doctrine.
We turn someone's incomplete story into a public warning.
And then we call it discernment.
But discernment is not the ability to imagine the worst about someone.
It is the responsibility to judge truthfully, humbly, and according to what God has actually revealed.
Jesus Himself said in John 7:24:
"Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment."
That command does not prohibit moral judgment.
It demands that our judgment be righteous.
And righteous judgment cannot be built on invented evidence.
Perhaps this is where the story begins to hurt.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like to have others tell a version of their lives that leaves out the truth.
They know what it is to be reduced to a divorce.
A pregnancy.
A failed relationship.
A broken family.
A past addiction.
A public mistake.
A season of rebellion.
Something they did.
Something done to them.
Or something people simply assumed.
They know what it feels like to enter a room and wonder whether everyone already believes a story they never had the chance to explain.
And the painful thing is that sometimes the harshest voices belong to people who know the language of grace but have forgotten how to practice it.
Yet this passage is not merely a warning against judgmental religion.
It is a revelation of Jesus Christ.
Watch what happens after Jesus exposes His knowledge of the woman's life.
She says:
"Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet." — John 4:19, KJV
Then she raises the dispute between Samaritan and Jewish worship.
Some readers treat this as an obvious attempt to change the subject.
Perhaps it was.
But John does not tell us her motive.
She may also have been responding to the discovery that she was speaking with someone who possessed prophetic knowledge.
What matters is how Jesus responds.
He does not refuse to discuss theology with her.
He does not say that her personal history makes her unworthy of spiritual understanding.
He engages her question about worship.
And then He reveals something that reaches far beyond her individual circumstances.
In John 4:23, Jesus declares that true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth.
The Greek expression is:
ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ (en pneumati kai alētheia)
"In spirit and truth."
Not merely at the correct mountain.
Not merely through inherited religious arguments.
But through the worship made possible by God's saving work, in accordance with His truth.
Jesus is not offering spirituality without repentance or worship without obedience.
He is announcing the coming reality of worship centered on the revelation and saving work of the Messiah.
And then the woman speaks of the Messiah who is coming.
Jesus answers in John 4:26:
"Ἐγώ εἰμι, ὁ λαλῶν σοι."
"I am he, the one speaking to you."

The Greek words ἐγώ εἰμι (egō eimi) mean "I am." In this sentence, Jesus is directly identifying Himself as the Messiah she expects. John's Gospel also uses this expression in other passages with profound theological significance.
Consider the wonder of that moment.
A Samaritan woman stands beside a well.
She has a history Jesus knows in full.
She belongs to a community divided from the Jews by generations of hostility.
And Jesus openly identifies Himself to her as the promised Messiah.
Not because her history is irrelevant.
Not because truth no longer matters.
But because God's saving grace reaches people whose lives are far more complicated than religious labels can explain.
This is what makes the Gospel so astonishing.
Jesus does not need to falsify our innocence in order to offer us mercy.
And He does not need to exaggerate our guilt in order to demonstrate His holiness.
He already knows the truth.
All of it.
The things others misunderstood.
The things we have concealed.
The wounds we did not cause.
The wrongs we did commit.
The sins we have tried to justify.
The regrets that still visit us in the quiet.
He sees without distortion.
And His call is not to remain hidden but to come into the light.
There is another popular claim about this woman that deserves examination.
People often say she came to the well at noon because the other women rejected her and she wanted to avoid their judgment.
It is possible.
But John never explicitly says that.
The unusual hour may invite questions, but it does not establish her social reputation.
We should not present an imaginative reconstruction as though it were a recorded fact.
And when we move from what Scripture says to what Scripture might allow, humility should govern our language.
That humility makes the actual story even more beautiful.
Because we do not need to invent a hostile village to appreciate the miracle that follows.
John tells us that the woman left her water jar and went into the town.
She began speaking to the people.
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" — John 4:29, KJV
Read that again.
Come, see.
She does not deliver a polished sermon.
She does not claim to understand every mystery of the faith.
She does not pretend that her life has always been righteous.
She points people toward Jesus.
And notice the way she speaks about His knowledge of her.
She does not say, "Come see the man who humiliated me."
She does not say, "Come see the man who publicly destroyed my reputation."
She tells them about someone who knew her life.
Her words are a personal testimony, not a transcript of every event that ever happened to her.
And that testimony mattered.
John 4:39 says:
"And many of the Samaritans of that city believed on him for the saying of the woman, which testified, He told me all that ever I did."
Many believed because of her testimony.
Then others came to Jesus, heard Him for themselves, and confessed that He was indeed the Savior of the world.
The woman was not the Savior.
Her testimony was not the foundation of salvation.
Jesus was.
And that is what makes her witness powerful.
A person does not have to possess a spotless history to tell the truth about a spotless Savior.
But there is something else we must not miss.
The Gospel of John does not explicitly record this woman's later life.
It does not give us a detailed account of her repentance, her subsequent relationships, or how she lived in the years that followed.
We should not manufacture those details either.
Her encounter with Jesus and her witness to the town are enough to show what John wants us to see.
Christ crossed barriers.
Christ revealed truth.
Christ offered living water.
Christ disclosed His identity.
And people came to believe in Him.
This is not a story about how the world was wrong to call a woman sinful because she was secretly perfect.
It is a story about how the world's categories are too small to contain the mercy, knowledge, and saving purpose of Jesus Christ.
And it forces us to ask an uncomfortable question.
How many people have we stopped listening to because we thought we already knew their story?
How many have we treated as permanently disqualified because of something in their past?
How many times have we been more interested in discovering someone's scandal than in helping them encounter the Savior?
And how many times have we used the truth of God's holiness as an excuse for our own cruelty?
We must not swing to the opposite extreme.
The Gospel is not permission to excuse sin.
Jesus never taught that repentance was unnecessary.
He began His public ministry announcing the kingdom of God and calling people to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
He warned people against remaining in sin.
He taught that evil comes from the human heart.
He called sinners to follow Him.
And at the cross, He bore the judgment our sins deserve.
Grace is not God pretending evil does not matter.
Grace is God acting in Christ to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Not while we were already impressive.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had earned the right to be loved.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to all who turn to Him in faith.
That is the heart of this story.
Not the five husbands.
Not the mystery of the sixth man.
Not the scandal we have imagined.
Jesus.
The One who sat beside the well.
The One who knew the truth.
The One who offered living water.
The One who revealed Himself as Messiah.
The One who would eventually go to the cross and rise from the grave.
The One who still calls thirsty souls to Himself.
And perhaps the most searching question in this passage is not what kind of woman she was.
Perhaps it is what kind of people we become when we read about her.
Do we become more careful with the truth?
More compassionate toward the wounded?
More serious about sin without becoming reckless with accusations?
More eager to introduce people to Christ than to expose them to public contempt?
Or do we read the passage, identify someone else's supposed failures, and walk away feeling superior?
The woman at the well is not an invitation to celebrate moral confusion.
She is not an excuse to erase biblical standards.
But neither is she a blank page on which we may write every sexual accusation we can imagine.
She is a real person in the Gospel narrative.
And Jesus treated her as someone worthy of a serious conversation about eternal life.
That should change the way we speak about people.
It should change the way we preach.
It should change the way we respond when someone confesses a complicated past.
It should even change the way we tell our own stories.
Because some of us have spent so long identifying ourselves by our worst chapter that we have forgotten the Gospel announces a new identity in Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
That promise does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean all broken relationships are automatically repaired.
It does not mean repentance is painless or that healing happens overnight.
It means that union with Jesus Christ brings a genuinely new life.
The past is no longer the final authority over the believer's identity.
Christ is.
And perhaps that is why this encounter has endured for nearly two thousand years.
Because every generation contains people who are thirsty.
Some are thirsty beneath religious appearances.
Some are thirsty beneath achievements and applause.
Some are thirsty after years of destructive choices.
Some are thirsty because others wounded them.
Some are thirsty while sitting in church every Sunday, singing songs about grace but secretly wondering whether grace could ever reach the truth about their lives.
And Jesus still speaks about living water.
He still tells the truth.
He still calls people to believe.
He still receives sinners who come to Him.
He still transforms lives through the Gospel.
You may have been called a failure.
A disgrace.
A hypocrite.
Unworthy.
Too far gone.
Perhaps some of those words came from people who should have helped you find your way back to God.
But listen carefully.
The answer is not to declare yourself innocent of everything.
The answer is to bring your entire life before the Savior who knows the difference between what happened to you and what you have done.
Confess what is truly sin.
Refuse to carry guilt for accusations that are not true.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Receive the mercy offered through Jesus Christ.
And begin walking in the truth.
You do not have to defend every chapter of your past to come to Jesus.
But you do have to come to Him.
Not merely to admire His kindness.
Not merely to find relief from shame.
But to trust Him as Savior and follow Him as Lord.
That is where grace leads.
Not into hiding.
Into the light.
And there is something extraordinary about what happened in Samaria.
The woman's invitation was simple.
"Come, see."
She pointed beyond herself.
And others encountered Christ.
That is still the calling of every faithful Christian witness.
Not to build our own fame.
Not to create a following around our personalities.
Not to turn people's wounds into entertainment.
But to make Jesus known.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Because there are people scrolling through their phones right now who have not opened a Bible in years.
People who are silently struggling with sin.
People who have been wounded by careless religion.
People who need sound biblical teaching instead of another shallow motivational message.
People who need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and Jesus Christ is sufficient.
And sometimes one article, shared at the right moment, becomes the beginning of a conversation that leads someone back to Scripture.
So if this message made you reconsider how you have spoken about someone's past, do not let that conviction disappear when you close this page.
Not to prove that you are more compassionate than someone else.
Not to start another argument.
But because someone in your circle may desperately need to know that Jesus sees them more truthfully than the world does.
And if you have been quietly carrying shame, or if this passage has exposed a judgmental attitude in your own heart, there is room for an honest response.
You do not have to disclose private details to strangers to prove that your response is sincere.
God already knows what is in your heart.
And if you need prayer, you can simply say, "Pray for me."
We want Gospel Warrior to be more than a place where people briefly feel inspired.
We want it to be a place where believers are continually drawn back to Scripture, challenged to repent, encouraged to persevere, and reminded that Jesus Christ is the center of everything.
There is also a deeper way to help this mission continue.
It is not a requirement for faithful Christian living.
And it is not a replacement for supporting your local church or fulfilling the responsibilities of Christian generosity.
Biblically, giving must never be presented as a way to purchase forgiveness, spiritual blessing, or salvation.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should be voluntary and cheerful, not forced by pressure or guilt.
But supporting trustworthy Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity.
They are simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who help sustain the work.
The deeper reason is the mission.
More Scripture.
More faithful teaching.
More encouragement for struggling believers.
More opportunities to point people away from despair and toward Jesus Christ.
Pray for it.
Share the Gospel.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures for themselves.
Help someone who has been wounded by condemnation discover the difference between human accusation and the conviction of the Holy Spirit.
Because genuine conviction leads us toward repentance and Christ.
Cruel condemnation often leaves people staring only at themselves.
And the world does not need another generation of Christians who know how to expose a scandal but have forgotten how to proclaim redemption.
It needs believers who love truth enough not to distort it.
Who love holiness enough to practice it.
Who love people enough to speak honestly.
And who love Jesus enough to make Him—not human failure—the center of the story.
The Samaritan woman came to a well for water.
She encountered the Messiah.
She went into her town and pointed others toward Him.
And many came to believe.
We do not know everything about her past.
We do not know everything about her future.
But we know whom she met.
And that is the part of her story John wants us to remember.
So the next time someone calls her a prostitute, open the Bible.
Ask where the text says that.
Then keep reading.
Read about the living water.
Read about worship in spirit and truth.
Read about the Messiah who revealed Himself.
Read about the townspeople who believed.
Read until the center of the story is no longer a woman's alleged scandal but the glory of Jesus Christ.
And when you close your Bible, remember that the same Savior who knew the truth about that woman knows the truth about you.
He knows the things you regret.
He knows the things others falsely believe.
He knows the sins you must confess.
He knows the wounds that still need healing.
He knows the fears you cannot explain.
And He is not asking you to rewrite your history to make yourself acceptable.
He calls you to repent, believe the Gospel, and receive the new life that only He can give.
Because the greatest miracle at Jacob's well was not that Jesus knew about five husbands.
It was that the Messiah stood before a thirsty human being and offered the gift of God.
The world may remember the history it thinks it knows about you. But Jesus knows the whole truth—and His grace can write a future your past could never have promised.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: NOT EVERY MIRACLE STORY COMES FROM GOD: THE DANGEROUS MISTAKE EVEN SINCERE CHRISTIANS MAKE
paragraphs: NOT EVERY MIRACLE STORY COMES FROM GOD: THE DANGEROUS MISTAKE EVEN SINCERE CHRISTIANS MAKE

When someone says, “God told me,” are you allowed to question them? What Jesus, the apostles, and the original Greek Scriptures reveal about miracles, deception, discernment, and the faith that refuses to be fooled.
A woman stood in a crowded church, trembling as tears rolled down her face.
She had been sick for years.
The doctors had tried. The medications had failed. The hospital bills had swallowed almost everything her family had saved.
Then someone prayed for her.
And that Sunday, standing before hundreds of people, she declared that God had healed her.
The congregation erupted.
People cried. Hands went up. Someone shouted, “Hallelujah!”
Her testimony spread across Facebook. Thousands watched. Hundreds shared it. People who had almost given up on God began believing again.
But several weeks later, her symptoms returned.
She was back in the hospital.
And suddenly, the same woman who had once been celebrated as living proof of God's healing power was lying in a hospital bed wondering something that nearly destroyed her faith.
“Did God fail me? Or did I misunderstand what happened?”
Now imagine something even more painful.
What if someone told her the sickness returned because she didn't have enough faith?
What if the people who celebrated her healing stopped calling when she became sick again?
What if her greatest spiritual wound came not from the disease itself, but from the Christians who made promises God had never made?
This is an illustrative story, not a documented testimony about a particular person. But the questions it raises are painfully real.
Because somewhere tonight, a mother is watching a miracle testimony while praying for her dying child.
A father is listening to a preacher promise financial breakthrough while wondering how he will feed his family.
A cancer patient is being told that if she believes hard enough, she will never need another treatment.
And someone who genuinely loves Jesus is afraid to ask whether any of these claims are true.
Because they have been taught that questioning a miracle testimony is the same as questioning God.
But what if refusing to examine a miracle claim is not a demonstration of faith at all?
What if Scripture actually commands us to do the opposite?
And what if the greatest danger is not that Christians will stop believing in miracles, but that they will start believing every extraordinary story without testing whether it is true?
Listen carefully.
You can believe that God performs miracles without believing every person who claims to have witnessed one.
Those are not contradictory convictions.
They are biblical convictions.
And understanding the difference may protect your faith from a kind of spiritual deception that often arrives wearing the language of Christianity.
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.” — 1 John 4:1, KJV
In the original Greek, the instruction begins with:
μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε
Mē panti pneumati pisteuete.
“Do not believe every spirit.”
John continues with:
ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα
Alla dokimazete ta pneumata.
“But test the spirits.”
That word δοκιμάζετε (dokimazete) comes from the verb dokimazō, meaning to test, examine, or evaluate in order to determine genuineness.
This is not an invitation to become cruel, cynical, or suspicious of everyone.
It is a command to exercise spiritual discernment.

John was specifically warning believers about false spiritual claims and teachers, especially those who denied the truth about Jesus Christ. The passage is not a technical manual for investigating every reported healing. But its governing principle is unmistakable: a spiritual claim does not become trustworthy merely because someone presents it as spiritual.
And that distinction matters.
Because not everything that makes you cry is true.
Not everything that gives you goosebumps comes from the Holy Spirit.
Not everyone who says “God told me” has actually heard from God.
And not every extraordinary event proves that the person interpreting it understands its source or meaning.
Jesus Himself warned us.
“For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.” — Matthew 24:24, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say deception would always look obviously evil.
He warned that false messiahs and prophets would use impressive signs and wonders to deceive.
The original Greek expression includes:
σημεῖα μεγάλα καὶ τέρατα
Sēmeia megala kai terata.
“Great signs and wonders.”
The words describe extraordinary signs and astonishing phenomena.

In context, Jesus was warning His disciples about deception surrounding His coming and the events He described in Matthew 24. We must not carelessly apply every detail of that prophecy to every modern testimony.
But we cannot ignore its warning.
An astonishing sign, by itself, is not sufficient proof that a messenger speaks for God.
That should change the way we listen.
Because some Christians have been taught to measure spiritual authority by how extraordinary a story sounds.
The more dramatic the testimony, the more anointed the speaker must be.
The louder the crowd, the stronger the presence of God.
The greater the emotional reaction, the more certain everyone becomes that heaven has spoken.
But Scripture never teaches that emotional intensity establishes divine authority.
In fact, the Bible gives us an even more unsettling example.
In Deuteronomy 13:1–3, Moses warned Israel about a prophet or dreamer who announced a sign or wonder.
And then he described something startling.
The sign could actually come to pass.
Yet if the prophet used that sign to lead Israel after other gods, the people were commanded not to listen.
Read that again.
The sign could happen, and the messenger could still be leading people away from God.
The Hebrew word for sign is אוֹת (ʾot), and the word for wonder is מוֹפֵת (mofet).
These terms can describe remarkable signs or wonders, but the passage establishes a crucial principle: an impressive event does not override God's already-revealed truth.
For Israel, the immediate issue was covenant loyalty to the LORD rather than following other gods.
For Christians reading the whole canon of Scripture, the principle remains deeply relevant.
A claim of supernatural power must never become an excuse to abandon the truth God has revealed.
If someone claims to perform miracles but teaches a different gospel, the miracle claim cannot rescue the teaching.
If someone claims divine authority but uses it to manipulate, exploit, or control people, we must not surrender our discernment.
If someone says God has given them power and then demands unquestioning obedience, that demand itself deserves examination.
Because the God who calls His people to trust Him has never commanded them to believe every human being who claims to represent Him.
But here is where the conversation becomes more personal.
What about genuine miracles?
Should Christians still believe God heals?
Absolutely, Christians have strong biblical grounds for believing that God has power to heal and act beyond ordinary human ability.
Jesus healed the sick.
He opened blind eyes.
He cleansed lepers.
He raised the dead.
The Gospels do not present His miracles merely as impressive performances. They reveal His compassion, His authority, and the arrival of God's kingdom.
In John 20:30–31, the apostle explains that the signs recorded in his Gospel serve a particular purpose: that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life through His name.
The miracles point beyond themselves.
They point to Jesus.
And that is one of the most important tests we can apply to modern miracle testimonies.
Does this testimony ultimately magnify Jesus Christ, or does it make a human personality the center of attention?
Does it encourage humble gratitude to God?
Or does it pressure people to idolize the supposed miracle worker?
Does it strengthen confidence in the gospel?
Or does it suggest that access to God's power depends on purchasing something, joining an exclusive group, or paying a particular preacher?
Does it lead people toward truth, repentance, and love?
Or does it demand that they silence their questions and surrender their judgment?
The answers matter.
But we must be careful here too.
A testimony mentioning Jesus does not automatically prove that every detail is accurate.
A person can sincerely praise God while misunderstanding what happened medically.
Someone may recover unexpectedly without knowing the full cause.
Someone may experience a genuine improvement and later discover that the original diagnosis was mistaken.
And yes, someone may deliberately fabricate a story.
Those possibilities are not identical.
We should never treat a mistaken person as automatically dishonest.
Nor should we treat a sincere person as automatically correct.
Sincerity tells us something about a person's intentions. It does not, by itself, establish the truth of a claim.
And if you have ever been disappointed by a miracle testimony, you need to hear this.
You are not required to choose between loving the person and examining the story.
You can do both.
You can say, “Thank God for what you have experienced,” while also asking, “What exactly happened?”
You can celebrate improvement while waiting for medical confirmation.
You can pray with someone while encouraging them to continue appropriate treatment.
You can acknowledge that God is able to heal without declaring a healing medically verified when it has not been verified.
That is not unbelief.
That is truthfulness.
And truthfulness matters because real people can be harmed when we confuse hope with certainty.
Think about the mother who stops her child's treatment because someone promises a guaranteed supernatural cure.
Think about the man who gives away money he cannot afford to lose because a preacher tells him a miracle will follow his donation.
Think about the young Christian who begins to believe God hates him because his illness remains after everyone prayed.
These are not small consequences.
A testimony can strengthen faith.
But an exaggerated or false testimony can also devastate someone who desperately needed honest hope.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part is that some believers have learned to protect a miracle story more fiercely than they protect the suffering person who believed it.
That is not the heart of Jesus.
When a desperate father approached Christ about his afflicted son, he cried:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.” — Mark 9:24, KJV
The Greek records his plea:
Πιστεύω· βοήθει μου τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ.
Pisteuō; boēthei mou tē apistia.
“I believe; help my unbelief.”
What an extraordinary confession.
Not polished.
Not impressive.
Not pretending to possess perfect confidence.
Just a hurting father standing before Jesus with the faith he had and the weakness he could not hide.
And Jesus did not demand that the father manufacture a spectacular testimony before receiving compassion.
The account goes on to describe Jesus delivering the boy.
There is something beautiful here.
The father brought his imperfect faith to the perfect Savior.
He did not have to pretend.
And neither do you.
If you are praying for healing and still hurting, you do not need to invent a victory story to make God look powerful.
If you are struggling financially, you do not need to claim a breakthrough that has not happened.
If you are battling depression, grief, addiction, or overwhelming fear, you do not need to announce that every struggle has disappeared just to prove you love Jesus.
You can tell the truth.
You can say, “I am still waiting.”
You can say, “I am still hurting.”
You can say, “I don't understand what God is doing.”
You can even say, “Lord, I believe. Help my unbelief.”
And your honesty does not disqualify you from His grace.
There is another passage that many believers overlook.
Paul wrote:
“Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” — 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21, KJV
Notice the balance.
Do not despise.
But test.
Do not automatically reject.
But do not automatically accept.
The Greek phrase πάντα δὲ δοκιμάζετε (panta de dokimazete) carries the command to test everything in that context.
Paul was addressing the Thessalonian church's treatment of prophetic utterances. His words should not be flattened into a claim that every testimony is prophecy.
Nevertheless, they reveal a healthy biblical posture toward claims made within the believing community.
Neither gullibility nor blanket dismissal.
Neither blind enthusiasm nor contempt.
Open hearts. Open Bibles. Careful judgment.
And this is where discernment becomes an act of love.
Because the person who asks careful questions may be protecting the very people a sensational story could harm.
The person who refuses to spread an unverified healing claim may be protecting someone else's hope from unnecessary devastation.
The pastor who tells a congregation, “We are grateful for this report, but we are still confirming the details,” is not necessarily lacking faith.
He may be demonstrating integrity.
And integrity should never be treated as an enemy of the Holy Spirit.
The book of Acts gives us a powerful example.
When Paul and Silas preached in Berea, the people received the message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether the things they heard were so (Acts 17:11).
The Greek verb associated with their examination is ἀνακρίνοντες (anakrinontes), from anakrinō, meaning to examine or investigate carefully.
They did not reject the message simply because it was unfamiliar.
But neither did they abandon examination because the speakers were persuasive.
They searched the Scriptures.
And Luke commended them.
Imagine what would change if Christians approached extraordinary testimonies with that same combination of eagerness and care.
We would still pray.
We would still celebrate genuine answers to prayer.
We would still rejoice when someone recovers unexpectedly.
But we would stop treating questions as spiritual rebellion.
We would stop pressuring suffering believers to claim healing before it happened.
We would stop allowing emotional videos to replace biblical understanding.
And we would stop confusing a person's popularity with God's approval.
Because here is a truth that may be uncomfortable.
A miracle story can go viral without being verified.
A video can receive millions of views without becoming reliable evidence.
A preacher can have thousands of followers without teaching sound doctrine.
A testimony can make an entire congregation weep and still contain mistaken conclusions.
Popularity measures attention.
It does not establish truth.
And sometimes the stories that deserve the greatest scrutiny are precisely the ones people are most afraid to question.
But do not misunderstand the warning.
We must not swing to the opposite extreme and assume that every testimony is fraudulent.
That would be unjust.
When someone says God answered a prayer, listen with respect.
When someone describes a remarkable recovery, rejoice in their well-being.
When someone believes they have experienced divine intervention, allow them to share their experience without immediate ridicule.
Then distinguish carefully between what they experienced, what can be independently established, and what they believe the experience means.
Those are three related but different questions.
For a medical healing claim, details such as the diagnosis, treatment history, clinical records, objective findings, and follow-up may help establish what actually happened.
Even an unexpected recovery does not automatically establish its supernatural cause.
And the absence of a complete medical explanation does not, by itself, prove a miracle.
We can acknowledge the limits of our knowledge without pretending that uncertainty proves either divine intervention or deception.
Christians disagree about whether certain miraculous gifts continue in the church today. Faithful believers have debated those questions by appealing to Scripture.
But across those differences, we should agree that lying, exploiting the vulnerable, and teaching a false gospel are not acceptable ways to glorify God.
The standard must never become, “Was the story exciting enough?”

The deeper questions are whether the account is truthful, whether its interpretation is warranted, whether its message agrees with Scripture, and whether the people involved are being treated with love.
And now we must face the most important question of all.
What happens when the miracle you begged God for never comes?
What happens when the cancer does not disappear?
When the marriage is not restored?
When the child does not recover?
When the financial rescue never arrives?
When you have prayed until your voice is gone, and the hospital room is still painfully quiet?
Does that mean Jesus has abandoned you?
No.
And Scripture gives us a reason deeper than a motivational slogan.
The apostle Paul pleaded with the Lord three times concerning the thorn in his flesh.
The Lord's response was:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Paul was not told that every painful circumstance would immediately disappear.
He was assured of sustaining grace.
We should not assume Paul's thorn was identical to every modern illness. Scripture does not identify it with that level of certainty.
But the passage does show that a faithful servant of Christ may continue to experience severe weakness without being abandoned by God.
And consider Hebrews 11.
Some believers experienced extraordinary deliverance.
Others endured imprisonment, suffering, persecution, and death.
The same chapter honors them for faith.
The outcomes were different.
Their God was not.
That destroys the cruel assumption that every unanswered healing prayer proves a lack of faith.
Sometimes God grants the deliverance we long for.
Sometimes He sustains His people through suffering they never would have chosen.
And the final Christian hope is not that every believer will escape sickness and death in this present age.
It is the resurrection through Jesus Christ.
The gospel does not promise that Christians will never enter a grave.
It announces that the crucified and risen Savior has conquered death and will raise His people.
That is a hope no misleading testimony can improve upon.
And no unanswered prayer can erase.
Now look at the cross.
The Son of God was mocked.
His enemies challenged Him to save Himself.
His body was wounded.
His followers scattered.
And to those watching, the scene looked like defeat.
If God's favor could be measured only by immediate rescue from suffering, Calvary would have been impossible to understand.
Yet the New Testament proclaims that through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, God accomplished redemption.
The greatest display of God's saving power did not look like the kind of triumph the crowd demanded.
It looked like a suffering Savior.
And then came the empty tomb.
This is why our faith must rest on Christ rather than on the latest extraordinary story circulating online.
Paul summarized the gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.

The Christian proclamation of the resurrection is not merely a generic claim that something inexplicable happened. It is a specific historical and theological claim at the center of apostolic preaching.
Paul even discussed witnesses to the risen Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:5–8.
Christian faith is not strengthened by pretending evidence and truth do not matter.
It is strengthened by remembering whom we trust and why.
And perhaps this is where someone reading needs to stop for a moment.
Because maybe you have believed a miracle testimony that later fell apart.
Maybe you shared it with your family.
Maybe you defended the preacher.
Maybe you donated money because you thought doing so would unlock a blessing.
Maybe you even convinced someone else to believe it.
And now you feel ashamed.
Please hear this.
You do not have to defend a false claim to defend Jesus.
You do not have to protect a dishonest ministry to protect the gospel.
You do not have to pretend you were never mistaken.
Repentance is not the enemy of faith.
It is one of the ways we return to truth.

The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind or turning of heart. In the New Testament's call to repentance, this involves turning from sin toward God, not merely feeling embarrassed about a mistake.
And sometimes repentance includes admitting that we gave a human voice more authority than Scripture.
Sometimes it means apologizing to someone we pressured.
Sometimes it means correcting a testimony we shared before verifying it.
Sometimes it means refusing to participate in a system that profits from people's desperation.
And sometimes it simply means whispering:
“Jesus, forgive me. I wanted something spectacular so badly that I stopped asking whether it was true.”
There is grace for that confession.
Because Jesus did not come merely to improve our religious excitement.
He came to save sinners.
He came to call us out of darkness into His light.
He came to redeem people who have been deceived, people who have deceived others, people who have wandered, and people who are exhausted from trying to appear spiritually strong.
But His grace never requires us to celebrate falsehood.
Grace leads us toward truth.
And truth leads us back to Him.
Not because a comment earns God's attention.
Not because a public confession is required for forgiveness.
But because there may be another believer reading who needs to know they are not alone in learning how to trust Jesus without trusting every religious claim.
You do not owe strangers the details of your suffering.
But you deserve to know that your pain matters.
And you are not spiritually inferior because you still need prayer.
Before you believe or share the next miracle testimony, remember this.
Ask what actually happened.
Ask whether the claim can be verified.
Ask whether the interpretation goes beyond the evidence.
Ask whether the teaching agrees with Scripture.
Ask whether the people involved are being treated with compassion and honesty.
And above all, ask whether the testimony is directing attention toward Jesus Christ or making someone else appear indispensable.
If the story is true, honest examination does not make it less true.
If the story is mistaken, correction can prevent harm.
If the story is deliberately fabricated, refusing to spread it is an act of integrity.
And if the facts remain uncertain, it is perfectly acceptable to say:
“I don't know.”
Those three words are not a confession of spiritual failure.
Sometimes they are the most truthful words a Christian can speak.
We can live with unanswered questions because our salvation does not depend on having an explanation for every extraordinary event.
It depends on Jesus Christ.
And that brings us to something deeply personal about the mission of Gospel Warrior.
We do not want to build a community that simply chases the next emotional story.
We want to help build a community that knows the Scriptures, loves Jesus Christ, recognizes deception, practices repentance, receives grace, and grows into spiritual maturity.
A community where the wounded are not shamed.
Where sincere questions are not silenced.
Where the gospel matters more than religious performance.
Where truth is not sacrificed for attention.
And where discipleship continues long after someone finishes reading a Facebook post.
You are voluntarily helping sustain and expand a Christian teaching and discipleship ministry.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, not coerced.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That matters to us.
Because we believe spiritual nourishment should not be reserved only for people who can afford to pay.
The free resources are there to serve.
Not merely to increase views.
Someone may be blaming themselves for a healing that never happened.
Someone may be giving money they cannot afford because a religious personality promised supernatural results.
Someone may be close to abandoning Christianity because they confused the failure of a human testimony with the failure of Jesus Christ.
But before you leave, I want to ask you one final question.
And I hope you will answer it with honesty rather than with the answer you think a Christian is supposed to give.
Have you ever believed a miracle testimony that later made you question your faith, or have you experienced an answer to prayer that deepened your trust in Jesus?
Your testimony does not have to be dramatic.
Your story does not have to end with instant healing.
And you do not have to reveal anything private to prove your faith.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony is simply this:
“I was confused. I was wounded. I was almost deceived. But Jesus brought me back to His Word.”
Because the greatest Christian testimony is not that we have seen something spectacular.
It is that Jesus Christ has shown mercy to sinners, reconciled us to God through His death and resurrection, and is transforming those who belong to Him.
Miracles may astonish us.
But the gospel saves us.
A sensational story may capture our attention for a moment.
But the crucified and risen Christ is worthy of our trust forever.
And when the crowd goes silent, when the testimony is questioned, when the healing has not come, and when every human promise has failed, the believer still has somewhere to turn.
Not to a stage.
Not to a celebrity preacher.
Not to a viral video.
But to Jesus.
Because even when the miracle you hoped for never happens, the Savior who died and rose again has not ceased to be worthy of your faith.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING WHO ROTTED FROM WITHIN: HE HAD A THRONE, A CROWN, AND EVERYTHING MONEY COULD BUY—BUT WHEN HE DIED, NOBODY MOURNED HIM.
paragraphs: THE KING WHO ROTTED FROM WITHIN: HE HAD A THRONE, A CROWN, AND EVERYTHING MONEY COULD BUY—BUT WHEN HE DIED, NOBODY MOURNED HIM.

He ruled a nation, murdered his own brothers, abandoned the God of his fathers, and died from a horrifying disease. But the most terrifying part of his story wasn't how he died. It was what Scripture said about the life he left behind. And somewhere in his tragedy is a warning every Christian needs to hear before it's too late.
“And he departed without being desired.” — 2 Chronicles 21:20, KJV
Imagine living your entire life chasing power, recognition, security, and respect…
Only to reach your final breath and discover that the very people you spent your life ruling were not grieving your departure.
Imagine possessing everything the world calls success, yet leaving behind a legacy so painful that your death brings no recorded national sorrow.
No royal celebration of your life.
No funeral fire honoring your reign.
No burial among the honored kings.
Just a crown that could no longer protect you.
A throne that could no longer comfort you.
And a name remembered in Scripture as a warning.
His name was Jehoram.
He was the king of Judah.
And his story is one of the most disturbing accounts in the Old Testament.
But before you distance yourself from this man because of his terrible sins, consider something.
Nobody begins life planning to become a warning to future generations.
Nobody wakes up as a child dreaming of becoming someone whose heart is so hardened that even the blessings surrounding him cannot turn him toward God.
And almost nobody recognizes the moment when small compromises begin becoming a way of life.
That's what makes this story frightening.
Not because every person will commit Jehoram's crimes.
But because the human heart is capable of becoming comfortable with things it once knew were wrong.
And because a person can be surrounded by the evidence of God's goodness while slowly refusing the God who gave it.
Jehoram inherited something extraordinary.
He was the son of Jehoshaphat, a king who, despite his failures, had sought the Lord and worked to strengthen true worship in Judah.
Jehoram did not grow up without access to the truth.
He inherited a kingdom shaped by the spiritual history of David's house.
He had brothers.
He had wealth.
He had authority.
He had opportunities that countless others would never experience.
But the Bible tells us that when his father died and Jehoram established himself upon the throne, he did something almost unimaginable.
He killed his own brothers.
Not strangers.
Not foreign invaders.
His brothers.
Men who had shared his family history.
Men who had received gifts and fortified cities from their father.
Men whose existence apparently threatened the security of his power.
Second Chronicles 21:4 records that Jehoram killed his brothers with the sword, along with some of the princes of Israel.
Think about the darkness of that decision.
The throne was already his.
He had already inherited the kingdom.
Yet possessing authority was not enough.
He wanted to eliminate anyone he perceived as a threat.
And here is where the story begins reaching beyond an ancient palace.
Because sin does not always begin with a sword.
Sometimes it begins with jealousy that nobody confronts.
Bitterness that nobody surrenders.
Pride that refuses correction.
An obsession with control.
A private compromise that slowly becomes a public disaster.
Perhaps you have never harmed someone physically.
But have you allowed resentment to poison the way you speak about another person?
Have you sacrificed a relationship because your pride mattered more than reconciliation?
Have you become so determined to protect your reputation that admitting wrongdoing feels unbearable?
Jehoram's sins were extraordinarily severe. We must never minimize them or pretend our ordinary struggles are identical to murder.
Yet his life exposes something Scripture repeatedly warns about: when the heart turns away from God, sin can become increasingly destructive.
James 1:15 says:
“Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “lust” is ἐπιθυμία (epithymia), meaning desire or longing. In James's warning, it refers to desire that draws a person toward sin.
The passage does not teach that every desire is evil.
It teaches that sinful desire, when embraced and allowed to develop, produces sin, and that sin ultimately leads toward death.
Jehoram's story shows how terrifying that progression can become.
He did not merely abuse his political power.
He led Judah into spiritual unfaithfulness.
Second Chronicles 21:6 tells us that he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, following the corrupt example associated with Ahab's house, and that he did evil in the sight of the Lord.
He had married a daughter of Ahab's family.
The influence surrounding his reign helped lead Judah further into idolatry.
And the king who should have been responsible for governing God's people faithfully became an instrument of their spiritual corruption.
But here is something remarkable.
God did not immediately destroy the royal house.
Second Chronicles 21:7 says:
“Howbeit the LORD would not destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and as he promised to give a light to him and to his sons for ever.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Jehoram was unfaithful.
But God remained faithful to His covenant promise.
That distinction matters enormously.
God's faithfulness did not mean Jehoram's wickedness was acceptable.
It did not mean there would be no judgment.
It meant that God's covenant purposes were greater than the rebellion of one corrupt king.
And that promise would eventually find its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the promised Son of David whose kingdom would never end.
Jehoram had a royal inheritance.
But he did not possess a faithful heart.
And there is a difference.
You can inherit a Christian family history without personally trusting Christ.
You can grow up hearing Scripture without obeying it.
You can know the language of worship without living a life of repentance.
You can stand in a church, lift your hands, and still be hiding something that desperately needs to be brought into the light.
A Christian upbringing is a blessing.
But it cannot repent on your behalf.
Your parents' faith cannot replace your own response to Jesus.
Your church attendance cannot purchase forgiveness.
Your religious reputation cannot make an unrepentant heart righteous before God.
And the throne Jehoram inherited could not save him from the consequences of his rebellion.
As his reign continued, his kingdom began to unravel.
Edom revolted against Judah's rule.
Libnah also rebelled.
The Chronicler explicitly connects these troubles to Jehoram's abandonment of the Lord, the God of his fathers.
Then came a warning.
A writing from Elijah the prophet.
Second Chronicles 21:12–15 records the message of divine judgment against Jehoram.
It confronted his idolatry.
It confronted his corruption of Judah.
It confronted the murder of his brothers, whom the message described as better than he was.
And it announced devastating consequences for his household, his possessions, and his own body.
The warning was specific.
A severe disease of his intestines would come upon him.
And the disease would progress until his bowels came out because of the sickness.
This is not a detail invented to make the story more dramatic.
It is what the biblical text actually records.
And it is horrifying.
But notice something important.
God's warning did not come without moral explanation.
Jehoram was not portrayed as an innocent man randomly selected for suffering.
The passage explicitly presents his judgment in connection with his extraordinary wickedness.
