They remind us that Scripture is not a collection of imaginary perfect people.
It is the record of God's dealings with real humanity.
People who lived.
People who died.
People who married.
People who sinned.
People who suffered.
People whose names were remembered long after the world forgot their voices.
Yet we should be careful not to make the genealogy say more than it says.
First Chronicles 2:18–24 does not tell us that Caleb repented of a particular sin.
It does not describe Azubah's private grief.
It does not reveal Jerioth's feelings.
It does not tell us that every member of the family experienced spiritual transformation.
And it does not teach that complicated relationships are automatically blessed because they appear in the biblical record.
What it does show is that these lives and family connections were preserved within the history of Judah.
When read alongside the wider testimony of Scripture, that history reminds us that God's saving purposes unfold in a world marked by human frailty, suffering, and sin.
The fullest revelation of His grace is not found in our speculation about ancient families.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
And now, perhaps, the question is no longer about Caleb.
Perhaps the question is about you.
What have you allowed your family history to tell you about your worth?
What secret have you mistaken for your permanent identity?
What failure have you treated as though it were stronger than the blood of Christ?
What relationship have you refused to bring before God because you fear what obedience might require?
And what would happen if, instead of trying to rewrite the past yourself, you surrendered your future to the One who makes all things new?
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That promise is not a guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears the moment someone believes.
Scars may remain.
Grief may continue.
Trust may require time to rebuild.
Some relationships may never be restored in this life.
But union with Christ means that the believer's standing before God and direction of life have been fundamentally changed.
The past is no longer the final verdict.
Sin is no longer the rightful master.
Condemnation is no longer the destiny of those who belong to Christ.
And that is a hope worth holding onto when your emotions have not yet caught up with what God has promised.
Maybe you are reading this while sitting alone.
Maybe your marriage is struggling.
Maybe you are a father who knows he has failed his children and wants to begin making things right.
Maybe you are a mother who has spent years carrying shame that was never hers to carry.
Maybe you are a son or daughter still trying to understand why the adults in your childhood made the choices they did.
Maybe you have been attending church for years, but you know there is a part of your life you have never truly surrendered to Jesus.
This is not an invitation to pretend your pain is small.
It is an invitation to bring your whole life to a Savior who is greater than your pain and your sin.
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ, do not confuse knowing Christian language with knowing Him.
Turn to Him.
Confess your sin.
Believe that He died for sinners and rose again.
Receive His mercy by faith.
And begin following Him—not because your life is already perfect, but because He is Lord.
If you have wandered from Him, return.
If you have sinned against someone, take responsibility.
If you need help, seek it.
If you are wounded, do not be ashamed to ask for prayer and wise support.
If you are exhausted, remember that Christ's invitation is not reserved for people who have everything together.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
That invitation still stands.
Not for the sake of appearances.
Not because you owe strangers an explanation of your pain.
But because sometimes a simple, honest response becomes the beginning of a meaningful conversation.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus has helped you turn away from sin, endure suffering, or begin rebuilding what was broken, consider sharing it.
Your testimony will not replace the Gospel.
But it may help another person recognize that they are not alone in needing the Savior.
Think about someone you know.
Someone who feels ashamed of their family.
Someone who believes their mistakes have disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has stopped opening the Bible because they feel unworthy.
Someone who smiles in public while quietly wondering whether God could still welcome them.
Because one article may encourage someone for a day.
But a life rooted in God's Word needs nourishment again and again.
That is why Gospel Warrior continues developing resources for people who want more than passing inspiration.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, there is another meaningful way you can participate.
Not because a payment earns God's favor.
Not because salvation, grace, or spiritual maturity can be purchased.
They cannot.
But because supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a genuine expression of Christian generosity and partnership.
Philippians 1:5 speaks of partnership in the Gospel, and Philippians 4:15–18 shows how believers materially supported Paul's ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 also reminds us that giving should be willing and cheerful, not compelled.
But voluntary, faithful support can help make more teaching, more discipleship resources, and more Gospel-centered content possible.
Think about the difference between reading something that encourages you and helping make that same encouragement available to someone else.
A believer struggling with temptation.
A parent looking for biblical guidance.
A young person trying to understand the Gospel.
We cannot promise how many people will respond.
Only God knows the full fruit of any ministry.
But we can faithfully sow the Word and trust Him with the outcome.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of Scripture and opportunities to encourage others, but they are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
The Gospel is.
The mission is to make Jesus known, help believers grow in His Word, and continue pointing people toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, and transformation.
Christ has already paid the price of our redemption.
Our response is gratitude, worship, obedience, and love.
That brings us back to where we began.
An ancient father.
A genealogy.
Women whose names survived the centuries.
Children whose family circumstances were recorded without the explanations modern readers might want.
Death.
Remarriage.
A concubine in the wider family record.
And a descendant named Bezalel, whom God equipped for sacred work.
It would be easy to leave this passage thinking only about the complications of an ancient household.
But perhaps the greater lesson is that the Bible invites us to look at human history without pretending that human beings are flawless.
And then it directs our attention to the only One who truly is.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who entered real human history.
The Holy One who never sinned.
The Lamb of God who bore the sins of His people.
The risen Lord who offers forgiveness and new life.
Your story may contain chapters you would never have chosen.
Some may have been written through the sins of others.
Some may be chapters for which you must personally repent.
Some may still bring tears when you remember them.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, none of those chapters has greater authority than His finished work.
You do not have to deny the past.
You do not have to glorify the scandal.
You do not have to call evil good.
You can tell the truth.
You can repent where repentance is needed.
You can seek healing where wounds remain.
You can forgive without pretending that justice does not matter.
And you can trust the Savior who is able to bring redemption into the most complicated human stories.
Because the greatest miracle is not that God can make an embarrassing family history sound respectable.
It is that God can take guilty sinners, forgive them through Jesus Christ, and make them His own.
And when the world tries to tell you that your beginning has already decided your ending, remember the cross.
The pages behind you may still carry the scars, but in Christ, the final word belongs to grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE… BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISUNDERSTANDING WHAT JESUS MEANT ALL ALONG?
paragraphs: THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE… BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISUNDERSTANDING WHAT JESUS MEANT ALL ALONG?

You can know the Bible, recognize the truth, defend your faith, and still be imprisoned by something you refuse to surrender. Jesus never promised freedom through information alone. What He revealed was far more personal, more confronting, and more beautiful than most people realize.
There is a kind of prison that doesn't have bars.
You can go to work inside it. Raise children inside it. Sing worship songs inside it. Post Bible verses on Facebook inside it.
You can even stand in church, lift your hands, whisper “Hallelujah,” and go home to the same invisible chains you've been dragging for years.
Nobody notices.
Because you've learned how to smile while you're struggling.
You've learned how to say “God is good” while secretly wondering why your heart still feels so heavy.
You've learned enough Scripture to encourage everyone else, yet there are nights when you cannot seem to believe those promises apply to you.
And perhaps the most painful part?
You know what's right. You know what's wrong. You know what the Bible says. But knowing hasn't always stopped you from returning to the very thing that's destroying your peace.
So when Jesus says, “The truth shall make you free,” something inside you wants to ask a question you might never say aloud.
Lord, if I know the truth… why am I still struggling?
That question deserves more than another inspirational quote.
It deserves an encounter with what Jesus actually said.
Because one of the most quoted promises in Christianity has also become one of the most misunderstood.
And when we return to its original setting, something extraordinary happens.
The words become more than a slogan.
They become a confrontation.
An invitation.
And for those willing to follow Jesus, a promise of freedom that reaches deeper than anything mere information could accomplish.
In John 8:32, Jesus declares:
“And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.” — John 8:32, KJV
Beautiful words.
But here is what we often overlook.
Jesus wasn't speaking to people who had never heard about God.
He was speaking to people who had religious knowledge, spiritual heritage, and confidence in what they believed.
And He was about to expose a slavery they didn't even recognize.
That should make every one of us pay attention.
Because sometimes the most dangerous prison is the one we've convinced ourselves doesn't exist.
To understand the promise, we have to read the sentence immediately before it.
Jesus says in John 8:31:
“If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed.” — KJV
Then comes the promise about knowing the truth.
Notice the order.
First, continuing in His word.
Then, knowing the truth.
Then, freedom.
Jesus does not present freedom as the automatic reward for collecting enough religious facts.
He connects it to remaining in His teaching as His disciples.
The original Greek makes this even more striking.
The phrase translated “If ye continue in my word” contains the verb μείνητε (meinēte), from μένω (menō), meaning to remain, abide, or continue.
It carries the idea of staying.
Not visiting Jesus when life falls apart.
Not borrowing His words when they support our preferences.
Not treating Scripture like an emergency exit while refusing to let Christ become Lord over our daily lives.
Remaining.
Staying with Him.
Continuing in what He has said.
Even when His words expose something we'd rather protect.
Even when obedience costs us comfort.
Even when the truth challenges the version of ourselves we've spent years defending.
And then Jesus says:
καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς.
Kai gnōsesthe tēn alētheian, kai hē alētheia eleutherōsei hymas.
“And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” — John 8:32, translated from the Greek.
The word ἀλήθεια (alētheia) means truth.
The verb γνώσεσθε (gnōsesthe) means “you will know.”
And ἐλευθερώσει (eleutherōsei) means “will set free.”
These are not mysterious secret codes. Their significance comes from the sentence and the larger conversation.
Jesus is not condemning factual knowledge. Christianity is grounded in real truth about what God has done in history.
But in this passage, the freedom He promises is not simply intellectual enlightenment.
The very next verses reveal why.
When Jesus speaks of freedom, His listeners respond:
“We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man.” — John 8:33, KJV.
Think about that response.
They appeal to their ancestry.
Their identity.
Their religious inheritance.
And they resist the implication that they need liberation.
Yet Jesus answers with words that strip away every comfortable illusion:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.” — John 8:34, KJV
There it is.
The prison Jesus is addressing.
Sin.
Not merely ignorance.
Not simply a lack of education.
Not an unfortunate shortage of motivational thinking.
Sin.
The power that makes human beings choose what wounds them, defend what corrupts them, and hide what desperately needs to be brought into the light.
And suddenly, this conversation is no longer about people standing in Jerusalem two thousand years ago.
It's about us.
It's about the husband who knows that harsh words can wound his wife, yet keeps allowing anger to rule his tongue.
It's about the woman who knows that bitterness is poisoning her heart, yet replays the same betrayal every night because forgiveness feels like surrendering justice.
It's about the believer who knows what Scripture teaches about purity, yet returns to a private habit that leaves them ashamed.
It's about the person who knows that lying is wrong but has built an entire public image around pretending.
It's about the churchgoer who knows the language of grace but cannot stop measuring other people by their worst mistakes.
And perhaps it's about someone reading this right now.
Someone who loves Jesus.
Someone who genuinely wants to change.
Someone who has promised God, more than once, that this would be the last time.
But the struggle returned.
And with it came the whisper:
Maybe I'm not really His.
Listen carefully.
The presence of a struggle does not automatically mean your faith is counterfeit.
But neither should we mistake the desire to change for the act of repentance.
Jesus calls us beyond hiding, beyond excuses, and beyond surrendering to sin as though it owns us.
And the good news is that He does not merely stand outside our prison telling us to try harder.
He came to accomplish the freedom we could never purchase through our own righteousness.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because John 8 doesn't end with Jesus exposing slavery.
In verse 36, He declares:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.” — John 8:36, KJV
Read that again.
Not “If you become intelligent enough.”
Not “If you memorize enough verses.”
Not “If you successfully conceal every failure.”
Not even “If you manage to repair yourself.”
If the Son makes you free.
The freedom is His to give.
And the One offering it is not merely another religious teacher.
He is the Son.
The very One who says in John 14:6:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — KJV
Do you see the connection?
The truth Jesus teaches is inseparable from who He is.
He is not saying that facts don't matter.
He is revealing that the saving truth of God finds its fullest expression in Him.
Truth has a face.
Truth entered our broken world.
Truth walked among sinners.
Truth confronted hypocrisy without becoming hypocritical.
Truth touched the unclean.
Truth welcomed the repentant.
Truth stood before human injustice, was condemned, and went to the cross.
And the One who is Truth rose again.
That changes everything.
Because the deepest answer to our bondage is not merely learning another religious principle.
It is being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Picture a man sitting alone in his car outside a church.
The service has ended.
Families are driving home.
The parking lot is almost empty.
But he cannot bring himself to turn the key.
He heard the sermon.
He sang the songs.
He greeted people who asked how he was doing.
“I'm blessed,” he told them.
And perhaps he meant it.
But his phone is beside him.
And on that phone are conversations he knows he should never have started.
There are messages he has hidden.
Choices he has rationalized.
Promises he has broken.
He remembers his wife trusting him.
He remembers the man he once wanted to become.
And now he is staring through the windshield, wondering how someone who knows so much about God could have wandered so far from obedience.
He doesn't need another excuse.
He doesn't need someone to tell him that his choices don't matter.
He needs the truth.
But he is terrified of what telling the truth will cost him.
Perhaps that is where you are.
Not necessarily in a parked car.
Maybe in your bedroom.
Maybe at work.
Maybe sitting beside someone who has no idea how much you're hurting.
Maybe carrying a secret that has become heavier every year.
And this is where the enemy's deception becomes especially cruel.
Sin tempts us with the promise of freedom.
Do what you want.
You deserve this.
Nobody has to know.
You can stop whenever you choose.
Then, after we fall, shame begins making its own demands.
Hide.
Pretend.
Don't tell anyone.
God must be tired of you.
The very thing that promised freedom becomes a source of captivity.
But Jesus tells the truth about sin precisely because He came to save sinners.
His confrontation is not an invitation to despair.
It is a call to repentance.
And repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what we've done.
The New Testament word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance—a change of mind and direction involving a genuine turning from sin toward God.
It is not a magical word that erases consequences.
It is not a performance designed to earn forgiveness.
It is a response to God's grace, involving honest acknowledgment of sin and a turning toward the Savior.
There may be apologies to make.
Relationships to repair.
Secrets to confess appropriately.
Temptations to flee.
Boundaries to establish.
Trusted spiritual leaders or counselors to approach.
And some consequences may remain even after genuine forgiveness.
But none of those realities cancel the mercy available in Christ.
First John 1:9 tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the sacrifice of Jesus is sufficient.
At the cross, God's holiness and mercy are not competing stories.
Christ bears sin, and through Him forgiveness is offered.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we successfully repaired our reputations.
Not after we made ourselves worthy.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain in rebellion.
Not a religious excuse to continue harming people.
Grace saves, forgives, and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
Grace doesn't make holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes a new life possible.
And perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
You are not beyond the reach of Jesus because your story has ugly chapters.
You are not required to pretend those chapters were beautiful.
You are not asked to rename darkness as light.
You are invited to bring the truth into the presence of the One who saves.
Look at Peter.
He knew Jesus personally.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard teachings that transformed lives.
He even declared that he was ready to die with his Lord.
Yet when fear pressed against him, he denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61–62 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The terrible realization.
The memory of his promises.
The sound of his own denial still echoing.
The unbearable knowledge that he had failed the One he loved.
Peter didn't need more information about whether denying Jesus was wrong.
He already knew.
He needed mercy.
He needed restoration.
And after the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, the risen Christ questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with caring for His sheep.
Jesus did not pretend the denial never happened.
But Peter's failure did not become the final word over his life.
That is not cheap grace.
That is resurrection grace.
The kind that confronts the truth and still opens a future.
The kind that refuses to let sin have the last word over someone who turns back to Christ.
The kind that transforms a broken disciple into a witness of the risen Lord.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing the historical facts.
Peter really denied Him.
The tears were real.
The failure was real.
But so was the resurrection.
So was the restoration.
And so was the calling that followed.
This matters because sometimes we think freedom means never remembering what happened.
Sometimes we imagine that being forgiven means never feeling grief over what we did.
Sometimes we assume that if Jesus has truly changed us, every temptation, emotional wound, and painful consequence must disappear immediately.
But Scripture gives us a more substantial hope.
Romans 6 teaches that believers united with Christ are no longer to live as slaves to sin.
That doesn't mean Christians become incapable of temptation or failure.
It means sin is no longer their rightful master.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a declaration that sin is harmless.
It is the glorious announcement that those who belong to Jesus are no longer under sin's condemning verdict.
And sanctification—the lifelong work of growing in holiness—continues as we walk by the Spirit.
There may still be battles.
There may still be tears.
There may be days when obedience feels costly.
But freedom in Christ is deeper than the absence of difficulty.
It means you no longer have to call darkness your home.
You can confess instead of conceal.
You can repent instead of rationalize.
You can seek help instead of pretending to be invincible.
You can forgive without claiming that injustice was acceptable.
You can tell the truth even when lies once seemed safer.
You can obey Christ because His grace is at work in you.
And when you stumble, you can return to Him rather than running farther into the darkness.
Not because you are strong enough to save yourself.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Now return to the words that began this entire conversation.
“You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
What if we've been quoting that verse while overlooking the very next confrontation?
What if we've celebrated the language of freedom while resisting the Lordship of the One who gives it?
What if we have spent years asking God to remove the consequences of our choices while refusing to surrender the choices themselves?
These questions are uncomfortable.
They should be.
But they are not meant to push you away from Christ.
They are meant to bring you nearer.
Because the truth that exposes our sin also points us toward the Savior.
And this is where we must make a distinction.
There is a difference between being informed about Jesus and trusting Jesus.
A person can study the historical evidence for Christianity and still reject Christ.
A person can explain the doctrine of grace and still refuse to repent.
A person can quote verses about forgiveness while withholding mercy from others.
Even the religious leaders in John 8 were familiar with Scripture and confident in their spiritual heritage.
Yet Jesus challenged them to recognize their need for Him.
Knowledge matters deeply.
Sound doctrine matters.
Understanding Scripture in context matters.
But biblical knowledge is meant to lead us into faithful trust, worship, obedience, and love.
It was never meant to become a hiding place for spiritual pride.
Jesus says in John 8:31 that His true disciples continue in His word.
Not merely admire it.
Continue in it.
And that means the truth we claim to believe must eventually confront the life we actually live.
Perhaps you have been reading this with a particular name in mind.
Someone who hurt you.
Someone who betrayed you.
Someone whose choices caused wounds you still carry.
Or perhaps the name is your own.
Maybe you are remembering a version of yourself that you desperately wish you could erase.
An affair.
An addiction.
A lie.
An abortion.
A betrayal.
A season of unbelief.
A relationship you damaged.
A child you neglected.
A moment when you chose fear over faithfulness.
Whatever the story, please hear this carefully.
Your sin must not be minimized.
The people you hurt must not be forgotten.
Repentance does not eliminate the need for accountability or restitution where appropriate.
But the Gospel declares that no repentant sinner must remain defined forever by the worst thing they have done.
Christ offers forgiveness and a new identity to those who come to Him in faith.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
That does not mean your memories instantly disappear.
It means that in Christ, a new creation has begun.
Your past may explain part of your story.
It does not have to rule your future.
Your failure may have consequences.
It does not have to become your master.
Your shame may be loud.
It is not greater than the Gospel.
And the Savior who called Peter back from bitter tears still calls sinners to repentance and faith today.
Maybe this is the moment to stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Maybe this is the moment to stop calling a secret sin a private weakness when you know it is becoming a master.
Maybe this is the moment to tell God the truth you've been afraid to say aloud.

Lord, I know the verses. I know the right answers. But there are places in my life where I have resisted You. I need more than information. I need Your mercy. I need Your power to change. Teach me to remain in Your word. Lead me into genuine repentance. Forgive me through Jesus Christ. Help me walk in the freedom You have purchased.
There is no magic in the wording of that prayer.
The hope is not in the eloquence of your confession.
The hope is in Jesus Christ—crucified, risen, and able to save.
And if you're reading this while feeling completely exhausted from fighting the same battle, please don't confuse the call to repentance with a demand to heal alone.
Reach out to a trustworthy pastor, mature believer, or qualified counselor where needed.
Bring what is hidden into appropriate, safe accountability.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray even when your words are trembling.
Take the next obedient step.
And keep looking to Christ.
Not to your own perfection as the foundation of your salvation.
To Christ.
Because freedom begins with His saving work, and a life of discipleship learns to walk in what His grace has made possible.
I wonder how many people on your Facebook friends list are quietly fighting battles like these.
The father who provides for everyone but privately feels he has failed his family.
The young woman who smiles in photographs but cries when nobody is watching.
The teenager who has started believing that one terrible mistake has ruined their future.
The believer who has stopped praying because shame keeps whispering that God doesn't want to hear their voice.
The person who has never understood Christianity beyond rules and religious traditions.
And the friend who thinks Jesus came only to condemn people like them.
Perhaps they have heard the phrase “The truth will set you free” a thousand times.
But perhaps nobody has ever shown them the Savior at the center of that promise.
That's why sharing biblical truth matters.
Not because a Facebook post can save a soul.
Only Jesus saves.
But God can use His Word, faithfully communicated by ordinary people, to awaken questions, encourage repentance, strengthen believers, and point hurting hearts toward Christ.
Not as a performance of faith.
Not to prove that you're more spiritual than anyone else.
But because someone who follows you may need to encounter these Scriptures today.
And if a particular person is struggling privately, consider sending it to them personally with gentleness rather than exposing their pain publicly.
Sometimes one thoughtful message can begin a conversation that someone has been afraid to start.
And I want to invite you to do something else.
Not for appearances.
Not because you owe strangers the details of your wounds.
But because there is something powerful about refusing to let shame convince you that you are the only one still learning to surrender.
You do not have to disclose a private sin or painful experience publicly.
And if God has brought you through a season of repentance and restoration, consider sharing a brief testimony of His grace.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not alone in their struggle—and that hope is still possible in Jesus Christ.
And invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have drifted from church, and even those who are still questioning Christianity to follow along.
The Gospel is too precious to keep locked inside our comfortable circles.
There is also something important I want to share about the mission behind Gospel Warrior.
Every article, devotional, and biblical resource we create is part of a larger desire: to help people encounter the truth of Scripture and grow in their understanding of Jesus Christ.
We want that library to keep growing.
We want more people to have access to resources that help them study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and understand the Gospel.
And that kind of work takes time, effort, resources, and the faithful support of people who believe in the mission.
It cannot purchase forgiveness, blessing, or spiritual standing.
Those things are not for sale.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by financial contributions.
The greater purpose remains discipleship.
Helping people open their Bibles.
Helping struggling believers return to Christ.
Helping families encounter biblical truth.
Helping people understand that the Gospel is not about pretending to be righteous, but about coming to the righteous Savior who redeems sinners.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
And faithfully living out the Gospel in your own home, workplace, church, and community is an extraordinary way to glorify God.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
The same Jesus who looked at religious people who thought they were already free and told them the truth about their bondage.
The same Jesus who refused to flatter sinners but willingly died to save them.
The same Jesus who restored Peter.
The same Jesus who declared that if the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
And that brings us back to the question we began with.
Is “The truth will set you free” about knowing facts?
Yes, truth involves what is real, and knowing the truth of God's revelation matters.
But in John 8, Jesus is speaking about something far deeper than acquiring information.
He is calling people to continue in His word, become His genuine disciples, recognize their slavery to sin, and receive the freedom only the Son can give.
The truth is not an impersonal technique for improving your life.
It is God's revelation leading us to Jesus Christ.
And Jesus is not merely interested in making you better informed.
He came to redeem you.
So the next time you hear someone quote John 8:32, remember John 8:36.
Remember the Son.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember Peter's tears and his restoration.
Remember that grace never requires you to lie about your sin.
It invites you to confess it and turn toward the Savior.
And tonight, when the noise quiets down and you're alone with the thoughts you've been avoiding, perhaps you will remember this:
You can spend your entire life learning how to describe the prison—or you can come to the Son who alone can set you free.
The door to salvation is not opened by your ability to impress God.
It is opened through the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Remain in His Word.
Walk in His truth.
And when your past tries to convince you that nothing can ever change, remember that the risen Christ is still in the business of redeeming lives.
The chains you learned to live with were never meant to become the name you answer to—Jesus calls you to belong to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF JESUS ALREADY DIED FOR YOUR SINS, WHY IS HE STILL PLEADING FOR YOU IN HEAVEN?
paragraphs: IF JESUS ALREADY DIED FOR YOUR SINS, WHY IS HE STILL PLEADING FOR YOU IN HEAVEN?

The Cross Was Enough. The Tomb Is Empty. Your Debt Has Been Paid. So Why Does Scripture Say Jesus Is Still Interceding for You? The Answer May Change the Way You Face Your Guilt, Your Failures, and the God You Are Afraid to Approach.
There is something happening in heaven right now that most Christians rarely think about.
And once you understand it, you may never look at your relationship with Jesus the same way again.
Somewhere tonight, a believer is crying over a sin they promised God they would never commit again.
Someone is sitting on the edge of their bed, Bible unopened, convinced that heaven must be tired of hearing their apologies.
A father is ashamed of the words he spoke to his children.
A mother is quietly wondering whether her prayers still reach God.
A young Christian has fallen back into an addiction they thought they had conquered.
And somewhere, someone who used to worship with tears in their eyes can barely whisper the name of Jesus anymore.
Not because they stopped believing.
But because they cannot understand why God would still want them.
Maybe that someone is you.
You remember the promises you made. You remember the night you surrendered. You remember how sincere your repentance felt.
And you remember what happened afterward.
The compromise.
The temptation.
The failure.
The shame.
That terrible moment when you looked at yourself and wondered, How can I still be struggling with this after everything Jesus has done for me?
But what if I told you that the most astonishing part of your salvation is not merely that Jesus died for you two thousand years ago?
It is that the Jesus who died for you is alive forevermore.
And Scripture reveals that He continues to intercede for those who belong to Him.
Not because Calvary failed.
Not because His blood was insufficient.
Not because the Father is reluctant to forgive you.
But because the Savior who accomplished your redemption has never abandoned His people.
And the difference between those two ideas changes everything.
Listen carefully to what Hebrews 7:25 declares:
“Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.” — Hebrews 7:25, KJV
Read those last words again.
He ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Not merely He once lived.
Not He occasionally remembers them.
Not He intercedes only when they have performed well enough.
He ever lives.
And He intercedes.
The original Greek makes this even more remarkable.
The phrase translated “to the uttermost” is εἰς τὸ παντελές (eis to panteles).

It carries the sense of completeness or entirety. In this context, it emphasizes Christ's ability to save completely, with the surrounding emphasis on His permanent priesthood supporting the assurance that His saving work will not fail.
This is not a promise that every person is automatically saved regardless of faith or repentance.
Hebrews identifies the beneficiaries as those who draw near to God through Jesus Christ.
But for those who belong to Him, the promise is breathtaking.
Your salvation does not rest on the strength of a temporary human priest.
It rests on the eternal life and permanent priesthood of the risen Son of God.
The Greek expression πάντοτε ζῶν (pantote zōn) means “always living,” and ἐντυγχάνειν (entynchanein) describes His interceding on their behalf.
Jesus is not a dead religious founder whose followers must somehow keep His legacy alive.
He is the living High Priest.
The One who carried your sins to the Cross is the One who represents His people before the Father.
And that raises a question we cannot afford to misunderstand.
If Jesus cried, “It is finished,” why does He still intercede?
Because His finished sacrifice and His continuing intercession are not competing works.
They are inseparable dimensions of His one perfect priestly ministry.
When Jesus declared, “It is finished” in John 19:30, the Greek word recorded is τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
It comes from a verb meaning to complete, accomplish, or bring to fulfillment.

The word is sometimes popularly described as meaning “paid in full.” That image can help illustrate the completed work of Christ, but it is important to understand that John does not present the word as a technical financial receipt.
Its immediate meaning is that Jesus had accomplished the work appointed to Him.
The sacrifice was not almost sufficient.
It was sufficient.
Hebrews 10:14 says:
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.”
One offering.
Not a sacrifice that must be repeated every time you fall.
Not another crucifixion whenever you confess your sins.
Not another payment whenever your conscience begins accusing you.
One offering.
And yet the same New Testament that proclaims His completed sacrifice also announces His continuing intercession.
Why?
Because the sacrifice that secured redemption is the foundation of the intercession through which our living Savior represents His people.
Jesus does not keep dying for believers.
He lives forever as the victorious High Priest whose once-for-all sacrifice remains sufficient.
His intercession is not an attempt to persuade an unwilling Father to become merciful.
The Father Himself loved the world and sent the Son (John 3:16–17).
The Son willingly gave His life.
The Holy Spirit applies the blessings of Christ's redemption to those who believe.
There is no division of love within the Trinity.
The Father is not looking for an excuse to destroy you while Jesus desperately tries to hold Him back.
That picture may sound dramatic.
But it is not the Gospel.
The Gospel reveals the united saving purpose of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
And perhaps that is where some of us need to begin healing.
Because we have spent years imagining God as someone who tolerates us only because Jesus keeps pleading with Him.
But Jesus Himself said:
“For the Father himself loveth you, because ye have loved me, and have believed that I came out from God.” — John 16:27, KJV
The Father loves those who belong to Christ.
The Son intercedes for them.
And the Spirit helps them in their weakness.
This is not divine reluctance.
This is divine grace.
Now imagine a courtroom.
You are standing before the Judge.
Every secret is known.
Every hidden motive is exposed.
Every excuse has collapsed.
You cannot claim that you have always obeyed.
You cannot pretend that your intentions have always been pure.
You cannot erase your past by promising a better future.
And then you remember the words of Romans 8:33–34:

“Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.”
Do you see what Paul is saying?
The believer's confidence is not that there are no sins to confess.
It is that God justifies those who are in Christ, and no accusation can overturn the saving verdict secured through Him.
The One who died has risen.
The One who rose is at God's right hand.
And the One at God's right hand intercedes for His people.
This is not a courtroom where Jesus argues that your sins never happened.
He does not defend you by pretending evil is harmless.
He is your righteous Advocate because He has already dealt with sin through His own sacrifice.
John writes:
Notice the tenderness.
My little children.
John does not begin by encouraging sin.
He writes so that believers will not sin.
But he also knows that believers still stumble.
And when they do, he does not tell them that their only hope is to find a new Savior.
He points them back to Jesus Christ the righteous.
The Greek word translated “advocate” is παράκλητος (paraklētos).
In this setting, it refers to one who comes to another's aid, an advocate who represents someone.
And John does not call Jesus merely an advocate.
He calls Him Jesus Christ the righteous.
That matters.
Because the One representing you before the Father is not compromised by the very sin from which He saves you.
He is righteous.
His sacrifice is sufficient.
His priesthood is permanent.
And His advocacy never depends on pretending that your disobedience was acceptable.
Grace does not excuse sin.
Grace brings sinners to the Savior who forgives, cleanses, and transforms them.
But there is another scene in Scripture that makes this truth almost painfully personal.
A night filled with betrayal.
A table surrounded by disciples.
A man named Simon Peter, confident that his loyalty could survive anything.
Peter loved Jesus.
He was sincere.
He was passionate.
He was convinced that even if others fell away, he would remain faithful.
Then Jesus said something that must have shaken him.

“Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.” — Luke 22:31–32, KJV
Pause there.
Jesus knew Peter was about to deny Him.
He knew the fear that would overwhelm him.
He knew the moment Peter would insist that he did not know the very Savior he had promised to follow.
And before Peter's failure unfolded, Jesus told him:
I have prayed for thee.
There is an important detail in the original Greek.
In verse 31, the word translated “you” is plural. Satan's desire to sift extended to the disciples.
But in verse 32, Jesus turns specifically to Peter.
ἐγὼ δὲ ἐδεήθην περὶ σοῦ (egō de edeēthēn peri sou).
“But I have prayed for you.”
The “you” here is singular.
Personal.
Direct.
Jesus knew exactly whom He was addressing.
He was not surprised by Peter's coming failure.
And He was not indifferent to Peter's future.
Notice what Jesus prayed.
Not that Peter would never experience a moment of collapse.
But that his faith would not ultimately fail.
And Jesus spoke of Peter's return and future ministry.
Later that night, Peter denied Him three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that look.
The One Peter loved.
The One he had followed.
The One he had just denied.
Scripture does not describe every emotion contained in that moment, so we should not invent what Jesus' expression looked like.
But we know what followed.
Peter wept.
And Peter's story did not end there.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
Beside the Sea of Galilee, the risen Lord asked Peter three times whether he loved Him.
And three times, Peter was given a commission to care for Christ's sheep (John 21:15–17).
The man who had denied Jesus was restored to serve Him.
Not because denial was insignificant.
Not because Peter deserved another opportunity.
But because the grace of Christ was greater than Peter's failure.
Maybe you know what it means to hear the rooster crow in your own life.
Not literally.
But that moment when the Holy Spirit brings conviction and every excuse suddenly sounds empty.
When the screen goes dark.
When the argument ends.
When the secret is exposed.
When the person you hurt walks away.
When you finally admit that you have become someone you never intended to be.
And the question rises from somewhere deep inside:
Can Jesus still receive me after this?
If you are in Christ, do not confuse the pain of conviction with a declaration that you have been abandoned.
Run toward the Savior, not away from Him.
Confess what is wrong.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Ask for help if the battle has become more than you can face alone.
And remember that the risen Jesus is not surprised by the weakness of the people He came to redeem.
Hebrews 4:15–16 declares:

“For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.”
The Greek word συμπαθῆσαι (sympathēsai) speaks of sympathizing or sharing in another's suffering.
Jesus understands the reality of human weakness.
He experienced genuine temptation.
He endured suffering.
He knows grief, exhaustion, rejection, betrayal, and anguish.
Yet He remained without sin.
That is why His compassion is not sentimental permission to continue in darkness.
It is holy compassion from the Savior who can truly help us.
The throne we approach through Christ is called the throne of grace.
Not because God has abandoned His holiness.
But because through Jesus Christ, sinners who belong to Him can receive mercy and timely help.
And here is something worth remembering when shame tells you to stay away from prayer.
Your greatest need for grace is not a reason to hide from Jesus. It is a reason to draw near to Him.
The enemy would love for you to believe that your only options are perfection or despair.
But the Gospel calls you to something different.
Repentance.
Faith.
Confession.
Dependence.
Obedience empowered by grace.
A lifelong walk with the Savior who is both your righteousness and your High Priest.
And this brings us to a question that has quietly tormented countless Christians.
If Jesus intercedes for believers, does that mean I can keep sinning without concern?
Absolutely not.
Romans 6:1–2 answers:
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?”
The grace that assures you of Christ's intercession is the same grace that calls you out of slavery to sin.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become comfortable with what destroys your soul.
He came to save His people from their sins.
Not merely to make them feel better while they remain chained to them.
The person who truly understands Christ's intercession does not say, “Now I can sin as much as I want.”
They begin to say, “How can I keep treating lightly what cost my Savior so much?”
Not from terror that every stumble automatically cancels salvation.
But from growing love for the One who gave Himself for them.
And if you are living in deliberate, unrepentant rebellion while assuming that a religious label guarantees your safety, Scripture calls you to examine yourself and return to Christ.
His intercession is not a license for hypocrisy.
It is a glorious assurance for those who draw near to God through Him.
There is another distinction we must understand.
Jesus is our unique mediator before God.
First Timothy 2:5 declares:
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
The original Greek word μεσίτης (mesitēs) means mediator.
No human being can purchase access to Christ's intercession.
No donation can improve the sufficiency of His blood.
No financial contribution can make God more willing to forgive you.
Jesus alone is the mediator.
And salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith, not something earned by works or purchased with money (Ephesians 2:8–9).
This is why the message of the Gospel must never be confused with a transaction.
You do not give money to make Jesus love you.
You do not purchase spiritual protection.
You come to God through Jesus Christ.
And that access is grounded in His finished work, not your financial capacity.
Yet there is a beautiful response that grace can produce.
Generosity.
When Christ captures the heart, people often begin asking how they can help others hear the same Gospel that changed their lives.
Not because generosity purchases redemption.
But because gratitude can become an expression of worship.
The apostle Paul spoke of believers supporting Gospel ministry, while also insisting that giving should be willing rather than pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That verse matters deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
And if you choose to partner with this ministry, we want that decision to come from faith, conviction, and a genuine desire to help the message of Jesus reach more people.
Think about the person who has not yet heard what you are reading.
The believer sitting alone in a dark room, wondering whether God is finished with them.
The young man fighting a secret addiction.
The woman whose shame has silenced her prayers.
The father who desperately wants to lead his family back to Christ but does not know where to begin.
The person who has never opened a Bible because they assume Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
What if one article reaches them at the right moment?
What if one Scripture opens their eyes?
What if one Gospel message becomes the beginning of repentance, healing, discipleship, and a changed life?
The message has power because it points to Christ.
And when believers freely support faithful Gospel work, they help create opportunities for that message to be shared.
That is part of the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
We want to continue writing, teaching, sharing Scripture, and making biblical discipleship resources accessible to people who need them.
Resources for people who want to understand Scripture more deeply.
Resources for believers who are learning to pray again.
Resources for those wrestling with temptation, spiritual exhaustion, doubt, family struggles, forgiveness, and the daily call to follow Jesus.
And resources for those who have realized that Sunday inspiration is not enough.
They want to grow.
They want to understand.
They want to become rooted in the Word.
It is the mission.
And it is the opportunity to receive ongoing spiritual encouragement and discipleship while helping others receive it too.
You are no less welcome.
Your value before God is not measured by your ability to give.
You can still pray for this ministry, read the free resources, grow in Scripture, and share the Gospel with others.
You never know who is silently struggling behind a smiling profile picture.
Someone in your family.
Someone from your church.
Someone who has stopped attending worship.
Someone who has been hiding a battle for years.
But before you move on, I want to ask you something personal.
Not as a performance.
Not because you owe strangers an explanation of your pain.
But because sometimes an honest response can become the first step toward asking for help and encouraging another struggling believer.
When was the last time you truly believed that Jesus still cared about you in the middle of your weakness?
Not when you were worshiping confidently.
Not when everything was going well.
Not when you felt spiritually strong.
But when you were ashamed.
When you were tired.
When you had nothing impressive to offer.
When all you could pray was, “Lord, help me.”
You do not need to reveal private details to prove that your struggle is real.
There is room here for honest faith.
For testimony.
For confession to God.
For believers to encourage one another toward Jesus.
Not because following a page makes anyone a disciple.
But because the truth of God's Word is worth hearing, studying, testing against Scripture, and carrying into everyday life.
Now, before this article ends, I want to take you somewhere else.
Not to a courtroom.
Not to Peter beside the fire.
But to a garden.
Jesus is praying.
His disciples are nearby.
The Cross is approaching.
And in John 17, we hear the Son speaking to the Father.
This is not the same as the heavenly intercession described in Hebrews 7:25, but it gives us a remarkable glimpse into Jesus' concern for His people.
He prays for those the Father has given Him.
He prays that they will be kept.
He prays that they will be sanctified in the truth.
And then He says something extraordinary.
“Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word.” — John 17:20, KJV
He was not praying only for the disciples standing nearest to Him.
He was praying for those who would later believe through their message.
Generations not yet born.
Believers not yet gathered.
People who would one day hear the apostolic Gospel and trust in Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
Before you ever knew how to pronounce the word intercession, Jesus had already prayed for those who would believe in Him.
Before you knew the weight of your own failures, He knew the mission He had come to accomplish.
Before you learned how desperately you needed grace, He was moving toward the Cross where that grace would be revealed at immeasurable cost.
And after His resurrection and ascension, Scripture tells us that He continues to intercede.
Not as a helpless victim.
Not as a Savior whose work remains unfinished.
But as the victorious Son of God.
Hebrews 9:24 says that Christ entered heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us.
And Hebrews 7:25 tells us He always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through Him.
This is the answer to the question we began with.
Why does Jesus still intercede for believers if His sacrifice was already enough?
Because His intercession is the ongoing ministry of the risen High Priest who has accomplished a complete and sufficient redemption.
He does not need to offer Himself again.
He does not need to improve His sacrifice.
He does not need to overcome the Father's unwillingness.
He lives forever, representing His people on the basis of the saving work He has already accomplished.
His continuing intercession does not reveal a deficiency in the Cross.
It reveals the permanence of His priesthood.
The Cross was sufficient.
The resurrection was victorious.
The Savior is alive.
And His people are not left to preserve themselves through their own strength.
That does not mean the Christian life will be painless.
It does not mean every struggle disappears immediately.
It does not mean believers never face discipline, suffering, or painful consequences.
And it certainly does not mean repentance is optional.
But it does mean that the believer's hope rests on someone infinitely greater than their own spiritual performance.
Jesus Christ.
The righteous Advocate.
The merciful High Priest.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One who saves completely those who draw near to God through Him.
So tonight, if your conscience is heavy, do not answer it with another empty promise that you will somehow become good enough on your own.
Answer it by coming to Christ.
Confess your sins.
Trust His mercy.
Turn away from what you know is wrong.
Receive the help He provides through His Word, His Spirit, and the fellowship of His people.
If you have not yet trusted Jesus Christ, the invitation is not to become a better version of yourself before approaching Him.
It is to repent and believe the Gospel.
Jesus died for sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Forgiveness and new life are found in Him.
And if you already belong to Him but have been living as though every failure means you must begin your salvation all over again, remember what Hebrews actually says.
He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him.
Because He always lives.
And He intercedes.
You may have forgotten your last prayer.
You may have lost count of the tears.
You may not remember the last time you felt spiritually strong.
But the hope of the Christian is not built on how firmly we can hold ourselves together.
It is built on the living Christ who holds His people fast.
And one day, when every earthly struggle is over, the redeemed will not stand before God boasting about how flawlessly they maintained their own salvation.
Their hope will be the Lamb who was slain.
Their worship will belong to the One who redeemed them.
Their confidence will be in Jesus.
The same Jesus who received Peter after his denial.
The same Jesus who welcomed repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who bore our sins in His body on the tree.
The same Jesus who rose from the dead.
The same Jesus who now lives forever.
And perhaps that is the truth your exhausted soul needed tonight.
Not another message telling you to pretend you are strong.
Not another voice insisting that your wounds make you worthless.
But the Gospel reminding you that your Savior is alive, His sacrifice is sufficient, and His grace calls you to come home.
Your failure may be part of your story.
But through repentance and faith in Christ, it does not have to be the final word.
The sin that brought you to tears does not have to be the chapter that buries your hope, because the Savior who carried your sin to the Cross is still alive to bring His people home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JOB MADE A COVENANT WITH HIS EYES… BUT WHAT ABOUT THE THINGS YOU LOOK AT WHEN NOBODY IS WATCHING?
paragraphs: JOB MADE A COVENANT WITH HIS EYES… BUT WHAT ABOUT THE THINGS YOU LOOK AT WHEN NOBODY IS WATCHING?

He lost his wealth, his children, his health, and almost everything that made life bearable. But long before suffering tested Job's faith, he had already made a private decision about purity. And what he said thousands of years ago may expose one of the most dangerous battles Christians are fighting today.
There is something terrifying about a sin that knows how to stay quiet.
It doesn't always announce itself with a scandal.
Sometimes it begins with a glance.
A picture.
A video.
A conversation that becomes a little too personal.
A message you would never want your spouse to read.
A search history you would be ashamed to show your children.
And sometimes, it begins with something so ordinary that you convince yourself nothing is wrong.
You looked.
You lingered.
You imagined.
Then you told yourself it didn't matter because nobody knew.
But what if the greatest danger wasn't that somebody might eventually discover what you were looking at?
What if the greater danger was what those secret moments were slowly doing to your heart?
And what if the battle you keep losing in private is the very battle Jesus is calling you to bring into His light?
There is a verse buried inside one of the Bible's most heartbreaking stories that deserves far more attention than it usually receives.
In the King James Version, Job declares:
"I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?"
Read that again.
Not a covenant with his hands.
Not merely a promise about what he would never physically do.
A covenant with his eyes.
Before there was an affair to regret, Job wanted to confront the gaze that could begin one.
Before there was a secret relationship, he wanted to guard the thoughts that could make betrayal seem desirable.
Before temptation could become a practiced habit, he had already decided that his eyes would not be allowed to lead his heart wherever desire demanded.
And here is what makes that declaration even more remarkable.
Job was not making it from a comfortable life untouched by tragedy.
He was speaking from the wreckage.
His children were dead.
His possessions were gone.
His body was afflicted.
His friends had questioned his integrity.
And in the middle of defending himself against their accusations, Job began describing the kind of life he had sought to live before God.
One of the first things he mentioned was his eyes.
Why?
Because Job understood something our generation desperately needs to recover.
A person's integrity is not measured only by what they refuse to do in public. It is also revealed by what they choose not to entertain in private.
The original Hebrew makes his declaration especially powerful.
Job 31:1 begins:
בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי
Berit karati le'enay.
Literally, the words mean:
"A covenant I have made with my eyes."
The Hebrew word berit (בְּרִית) means covenant, a binding commitment or solemn agreement.
The verb karati comes from karat (כָּרַת), meaning "to cut." In biblical Hebrew, "cutting a covenant" is an established expression for making a solemn commitment.
Job was not describing a passing resolution made during an emotional moment.
He was describing a deliberate commitment.
He had determined that his eyes would be governed by moral conviction rather than uncontrolled appetite.
The remainder of the Hebrew verse reads:
וּמָה אֶתְבּוֹנֵן עַל־בְּתוּלָה
Umah etbonen al-betulah.
A close rendering is:
"How then could I gaze attentively upon a young woman?"
The word betulah (בְּתוּלָה) commonly refers to a virgin or unmarried young woman.
The verb etbonen comes from a root associated with considering, observing, or paying careful attention.
This matters because Job was not teaching that merely seeing a woman is sinful.
He was describing the deliberate, morally compromising gaze that turns another human being into an object of desire.
The surrounding passage confirms that his concern involved sexual integrity. In Job 31:9–12, he explicitly rejects being enticed toward another man's wife and committing adultery.
Job's words are therefore not a command to fear women, despise beauty, or pretend sexual attraction does not exist.
They are a declaration that desire must never be allowed to overrule faithfulness.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because noticing beauty is not the same as deliberately cultivating lust.
Experiencing temptation is not the same as surrendering to it.
An unwanted thought is not the same as choosing to entertain it.
But when the heart begins willingly feeding what God has called us to resist, something dangerous is taking place.
And Jesus addressed that danger with words even more searching than Job's.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus said:

"Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart."
Notice where Jesus directed His attention.
The heart.
Not because physical adultery is unimportant.
Not because thoughts and actions carry identical consequences.
But because the commandment against adultery reaches deeper than outward behavior.
Jesus exposes the inward desire that can precede outward betrayal.
The Greek wording is revealing.
Matthew 5:28 includes:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
Pros to epithymēsai autēn.
In this context, the phrase communicates looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her.

The verb epithymeō can mean to desire or long for something. Desire itself is not automatically sinful in every biblical context. Here, however, Jesus is addressing desire directed toward what is morally forbidden.
He is confronting the intentional cultivation of lust.
And suddenly, Job's ancient covenant feels painfully modern.
Because we live in a world where temptation no longer waits outside the door.
It travels in our pockets.
It glows beside our beds.
It appears while we are tired, lonely, disappointed, angry, or spiritually exhausted.
It knows how to disguise itself as entertainment.
It knows how to turn curiosity into habit.
And habit into secrecy.
And secrecy into shame.
A person can spend the morning singing worship songs and the evening feeding desires they are too embarrassed to confess.
A husband can sit beside his wife while giving his imagination to women he has never met.
A wife can become emotionally attached to someone who offers the attention she has been missing at home.
A young believer can genuinely love Jesus and still feel trapped in a pattern of pornography that seems impossible to break.
A single Christian can convince themselves that because they are not physically involved with anyone, whatever happens on their screen is harmless.
And someone who has served in church for twenty years can quietly become a stranger to the convictions they once defended.
Not everyone struggles in the same way.
Not every temptation becomes an addiction.
Not every person who falls is living a double life.
But the danger is real.
And the silence surrounding it can be devastating.
Because there is a particular kind of loneliness that comes from knowing people admire the version of you they see in public while you are ashamed of the person you become when the door closes.
You begin to wonder whether your prayers still mean anything.
Whether your worship is sincere.
Whether God is tired of hearing the same confession.
Whether you have failed too many times to be restored.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you really do want to change.
You hate the cycle.
You hate the secrecy.
You hate the way your conscience becomes heavy afterward.
Yet when temptation returns, you find yourself standing at the same crossroads.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until eventually you begin believing the most dangerous lie of all.
"This is just who I am."
No.
Your struggle may be real.
Your choices may have been sinful.
The consequences may be serious.
But your sin does not have the authority to declare that redemption is impossible.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not people who successfully convinced everyone they were already righteous.
Sinners.
People with histories.
People with regrets.
People who have betrayed trust.
People who have made promises and broken them.
People who know what it means to cry over something they once willingly pursued.
But before we rush toward comfort, we need to understand something.
Grace does not make lust harmless.
Forgiveness does not make betrayal insignificant.
And the promise of restoration is not permission to continue feeding the very thing that is destroying us.
The Gospel does not invite us to become comfortable in darkness.
It calls us into the light.
Job understood that private conduct mattered before God.
Immediately after declaring his covenant with his eyes, he asked in Job 31:4:
"Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?"
That question should stop us.
Because there is a difference between behaving because people might catch you and pursuing holiness because you belong to God.
One depends on surveillance.
The other grows out of reverence.
Job was not saying that he could earn salvation through perfect self-control.
He was defending the integrity of his life against accusations that his suffering must have been punishment for hidden wickedness.
And the larger book of Job makes something essential clear: suffering is not reliable proof that someone has committed a particular sin.
Job's friends repeatedly misunderstood this.
Job himself did not possess complete understanding of everything God was doing.
But he knew that his relationship with God mattered even when nobody else could see his decisions.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Imagine your phone lying on the table.

Imagine every image you deliberately revisited, every inappropriate conversation you encouraged, every secret fantasy you knowingly entertained, and every moment you chose to cross a boundary being brought into the light.
Not to entertain an audience.
Not to humiliate you.
But to reveal the truth.
Would you recognize the person those choices describe?
Would your private life agree with the faith you publicly profess?
Would the people who trust you feel safe with the decisions you make when they are absent?
Those are uncomfortable questions.
They should be.
Scripture was never given merely to make us feel affirmed.
Second Timothy 3:16 teaches that Scripture is profitable for doctrine, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness.
Sometimes the Word of God comforts us.
Sometimes it confronts us.
And sometimes the very passage that wounds our pride becomes the instrument God uses to rescue us from a much deeper wound.
But here is something I do not want you to miss.
The answer to lust is not learning to hate yourself. It is learning to surrender yourself to Christ.
Self-hatred cannot produce holiness.
Shame alone cannot transform desire.
Fear of exposure may restrain behavior for a season, but it cannot give a dead heart new life.
Only Christ can save.
Only His grace can reconcile us to God.
And through the Holy Spirit, believers are called and empowered to put sinful desires to death and walk in newness of life.
Romans 8:13 says:
"For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live."
Notice those words.
Through the Spirit.
Not through pretending temptation does not exist.
Not through boasting about personal discipline.
Not through hiding behind religious activity.
Through the Spirit.
This is why the Gospel is so much more than an instruction to try harder.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our outward reputation.
He came to reconcile us to God, forgive our sins, and transform us from the inside out.
And the One who calls us to purity is not a Savior who is ignorant of temptation.
Hebrews 4:15 declares:
"For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin."
Jesus knows what temptation is.
Yet He never sinned.
He understands human weakness without excusing disobedience.
And He offers mercy without surrendering holiness.
That means you do not need to hide your struggle from Him.
He already knows.
You can stop pretending.
You can confess what happened.
You can acknowledge the damage.
You can take responsibility without making excuses.
And you can ask for the grace to begin walking differently.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Not because sin is small.
But because the saving work of Jesus Christ is sufficient.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds in Him a Savior who is able to forgive and restore.
That is the heart of our message.
Not because the scandal never happened.
Not because consequences automatically disappear.
Not because repentance erases the pain another person has suffered.
But because our worst chapter does not have to be the final chapter when Christ becomes the Lord of our lives.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She stood publicly accused of adultery.
Her shame had become a spectacle.
The people surrounding her were prepared to condemn her.
And Jesus confronted the hypocrisy of her accusers.
When they departed, He spoke words that have echoed through generations.
John 8:11:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."
Do not separate those two statements.
"Neither do I condemn thee."
"Go, and sin no more."
Mercy and a call to holiness.
Compassion and transformation.
Jesus did not celebrate her sin.
Neither did He join the crowd in destroying her.
He confronted the moment with a righteousness and mercy that her accusers had failed to understand.

And while this passage has a well-known textual history—its earliest surviving Greek manuscripts do not include John 7:53–8:11—the account's call to mercy and repentance agrees with truths clearly taught elsewhere in the New Testament.
The invitation remains unmistakable.
Christ does not call us to remain enslaved to what He came to save us from.
And perhaps this is the moment when you need to stop negotiating with something that has been quietly stealing your peace.
Delete the material you keep returning to.
End the inappropriate conversation.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Set boundaries around the situations where you repeatedly fall.
Find a mature, trustworthy believer who can pray with you and hold you accountable.
If compulsive sexual behavior has become difficult to control, seek qualified professional help alongside pastoral care.
And if your choices have wounded another person, do not use forgiveness as a way to avoid honesty, responsibility, or the patient work of rebuilding trust.
Real repentance is more than feeling terrible after getting caught.
It involves turning toward God and away from sin.
And sometimes that turning requires difficult, practical decisions.
Jesus used startling language in Matthew 5:29 about removing an eye that causes one to sin.
He was not instructing His followers to injure themselves.
He was emphasizing the seriousness of dealing decisively with whatever draws us into sin.
If an app repeatedly becomes the doorway to temptation, remove it.
If isolation makes you vulnerable, change your routine.
If secrecy is feeding the struggle, bring it into appropriate, trustworthy accountability.
Not because those actions can purchase salvation.
But because grace teaches us to reject ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says:

"For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world."
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace also teaches.
And sometimes the first lesson is learning to say no to something you have been calling harmless for far too long.
Maybe you are reading this as someone who has already lost something because of lust.
A marriage.
A relationship.
A ministry position.
The trust of someone you love.
Or perhaps nothing has collapsed publicly.
Yet.
And you know there is a private compromise that needs to end before it grows into something far more destructive.
Listen carefully.
Do not wait for your life to fall apart before you take God's warning seriously.
Job made a covenant with his eyes.
What would it look like for you to make a serious commitment to purity today?
Not a dramatic promise built on temporary emotion.
Not another vow that depends entirely on willpower.
But a humble, practical surrender to Jesus Christ.
"Lord, my eyes belong to You."
"My body belongs to You."
"My imagination belongs to You."
"My relationships must honor You."
"Teach me to see people as human beings made in Your image, not objects for my selfish pleasure."
"Give me the courage to flee what I once entertained."
"And when I am weak, remind me to run toward Your mercy instead of hiding in shame."
That prayer will not automatically erase every temptation.
Spiritual growth is not always instant.
There may be painful conversations.
There may be habits that take time to change.
There may be consequences that must be faced with humility.
But no sincere step toward Christ is meaningless.
And one of the most beautiful promises in Scripture is found in 1 Corinthians 10:13:

"There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it."
God is faithful.
Those three words matter.
When your resolve feels fragile, God is faithful.
When temptation feels overwhelming, God is faithful.
When you have to confess another failure and return to the difficult work of repentance, God remains faithful.
His faithfulness does not mean we can become careless.
It means we are not abandoned to fight temptation without His help.
And there is another truth that deserves to be spoken, especially to anyone carrying shame from the past.
You are not required to pretend that you never sinned in order to testify that Jesus Christ has changed your life.
A redeemed testimony does not glorify the sin.
It glorifies the Savior.
You can acknowledge the darkness without celebrating it.
You can speak about failure without making failure your identity.
You can admit that your choices hurt people while remaining committed to restitution, healing, and faithfulness.
And you can tell the next generation that purity is not an outdated religious obsession.
It is part of learning to love God and other people with integrity.
Because the person on the other side of the screen is not an object.
The person who trusts you is not disposable.
The vows you made are not meaningless.
And the body God has given you is not spiritually irrelevant.
First Corinthians 6:19–20 reminds believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that they are called to glorify God in their bodies.
That is not a message of disgust toward the human body.
It is a declaration of its dignity and sacred responsibility.
You were not created merely to obey every appetite.
You were created to know God.
To love Him.
To honor Him.
And through Jesus Christ, to live in a way that reflects His transforming grace.
Perhaps you have spent years thinking purity means simply avoiding one particular sin.
But biblical purity reaches deeper.
It changes the way you look at people.
It teaches you to honor rather than consume.
To protect rather than exploit.
To remain faithful rather than seek secret alternatives.
To tell the truth rather than construct a respectable image around hidden compromise.
And it reminds you that the greatest goal of holiness is not being admired as a good Christian.
It is belonging wholeheartedly to Jesus.
That is why this message matters beyond a single article.
Every day, someone is losing a private battle.
Someone is afraid to confess.
Someone is beginning to believe that compromise is normal.
Someone is wondering whether they can ever change.
And someone who appears strong in public is silently desperate for a reminder that repentance and restoration are still possible through Christ.
If that person is you, please do not leave this moment with nothing more than another feeling of guilt.
Respond to what God has shown you.
Open your Bible.
Pray.
Confess.
Seek help where needed.
Take the next faithful step.
"No more hiding. Jesus, make my heart clean."
You do not need to reveal intimate details publicly. God knows what you are carrying, and you can seek deeper accountability privately with someone trustworthy.
Your words may remind another believer that surrender is possible and that their struggle does not have to end in despair.
And please do not keep this message only to yourself.
But because someone among them may be one honest encounter with Scripture away from taking their first step toward repentance.

We want this community to be a place where people encounter Scripture, hear the Gospel of Jesus Christ, receive biblical encouragement, confront sin with honesty, and discover that genuine hope is found in the crucified and risen Savior.
