The Bible does not contain a verse that specifically mentions internet pornography or married couples watching sexually explicit videos together. It would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.
But Scripture does speak extensively about lust, sexual holiness, marital intimacy, the dignity of human beings, and the difference between freedom and spiritual bondage.
Those teachings give Christians serious reasons to reject pornography as a tool for strengthening marriage.
Not because sexual pleasure within marriage is dirty.
Quite the opposite.
Because biblical marital intimacy is far more beautiful than pornography can adequately represent.
Go back to the beginning.

Before shame entered the human story, before betrayal, before broken marriages, before anyone learned to hide their pain behind a smile, Scripture describes the first marriage with an astonishing sentence.
Genesis 2:24 says:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the expression translated "one flesh" is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
Basar means flesh.
Echad means one.
The phrase speaks of a profound marital union. It includes bodily intimacy, but its significance is not exhausted by the physical act of sex.
Marriage is not simply two people sharing a bed.
It is two lives joined in covenant.
Two vulnerable human beings learning to belong to one another faithfully.

Two people who do not need to perform for an audience because they have promised to love one another even when age, exhaustion, illness, disappointment, and ordinary human weakness change their bodies and circumstances.
And immediately after that declaration, Genesis 2:25 gives us another extraordinary picture:
"And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed." (KJV)
Read that again.
Naked.
And not ashamed.
Not because they were physically perfect.
Not because they had mastered techniques.
Not because they were comparing themselves with other bodies.
They were together without the need to hide.
That is the kind of intimacy pornography cannot manufacture.
Pornography may present nakedness, but nakedness is not the same as vulnerability.
It may portray sexual activity, but activity is not the same as covenant love.
It may create excitement, but excitement is not necessarily evidence of spiritual or relational health.
And this distinction matters because something can produce an immediate pleasurable response without necessarily contributing to long-term trust, emotional safety, or marital flourishing.

Some couples report that watching pornography together increases arousal or sexual communication. Research on pornography and relationships is mixed and depends on factors such as frequency, individual attitudes, secrecy, relationship quality, and whether partners use it together or separately.
It would be inaccurate to claim that every couple who watches pornography experiences measurable relationship deterioration.
But it would be equally inaccurate to conclude that a pleasurable experience or a positive short-term report proves pornography strengthens a marriage in the biblical sense.
Scientific studies can examine satisfaction, behavior, and relationship outcomes.
They cannot determine whether a practice is holy before God.
For Christians, that question must also be examined through Scripture.
And Scripture asks us to look beyond what feels good.
Jesus said something in Matthew 5:28 that still challenges the way we understand sexual desire:
"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." (KJV)
The original Greek includes the expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn.
In this context, it refers to looking at a woman with lustful intent.

The Greek verb epithymeō can express desire or longing, and its moral significance depends on the context. Here, Jesus is confronting a sexually covetous gaze that violates the faithfulness God desires.
He is not declaring that noticing beauty is automatically sinful.
He is not condemning the ordinary experience of sexual attraction.
And He is certainly not teaching married people to be ashamed of desiring their own spouses.
He is exposing the moral significance of deliberately cultivating lust toward someone outside the marriage.
That is where the question about pornography becomes deeply uncomfortable.
When a married couple watches sexually explicit material, the images usually involve other human beings presented for sexual observation and stimulation.
Even when both spouses agree to watch, their mutual agreement does not erase the moral questions surrounding what they are intentionally viewing and how they are responding to it.
A husband cannot make lust toward another person holy simply because his wife is sitting beside him.
A wife cannot make the deliberate sexual consumption of other people spiritually harmless simply because her husband approves.
Marriage sanctifies sexual union between husband and wife. It does not automatically sanctify every sexual practice they might mutually choose.
And that truth is not an attack on marriage.
It is a defense of its sacredness.
Consider the words of Hebrews 13:4:
"Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "undefiled" is ἀμίαντος — amiantos.
It means undefiled, unstained, or unpolluted.
The verse honors marriage and calls for sexual faithfulness. It does not provide an exhaustive list of every permissible or impermissible marital activity.
But it certainly does not teach that anything becomes morally acceptable simply because it occurs between married people.
Christian freedom is never freedom from the character of Christ.
And there is another issue that often remains unspoken.
What if one spouse does not actually want to watch pornography?
What if they agree because they are afraid of disappointing their husband or wife?
What if the words "I'm okay with it" really mean "I'm afraid you'll stop wanting me if I say no"?
What if the wife laughs along while secretly wondering whether her body is enough?
What if the husband agrees because he is terrified of appearing sexually inadequate?
What if both are pretending to be comfortable because neither knows how to admit that something feels wrong?
Not every couple experiences these fears.
But where they exist, they deserve to be heard rather than dismissed.
Because consent matters, but genuine intimacy requires more than the absence of an objection.
It requires honesty.
Safety.
Mutual consideration.
The freedom to speak without fear of punishment, ridicule, withdrawal, or retaliation.
First Corinthians 13:5 teaches that love "seeketh not her own." (KJV)
Biblical love does not merely ask, "Can I persuade you to do this with me?"
It also asks, "Will this honor you? Will this protect our trust? Can you tell me the truth without being afraid of losing my affection?"
And perhaps one of the most Christlike things a husband or wife can say is:
"I love you more than I love this experience. If this troubles your conscience, I want to understand why."
That is not weakness.
That is love learning to resemble Jesus.
There is also something we should never forget about the people appearing in pornography.
They are not merely images.
They are human beings made in the image of God.
Their lives have histories we may never know.
Their circumstances may involve willing participation, commercial pressures, exploitation, coercion, or other realities invisible to viewers.
We cannot responsibly assume that every performer is coerced.
But neither can viewers reliably know from a video alone that everyone involved has been treated with dignity and genuine freedom.
A Christian ethic of love cannot be concerned only with what a husband and wife experience while watching.
It must also care about the humanity of the people being watched.
Because the people on the screen are not disposable instruments for somebody else's pleasure.
They are neighbors.
And Jesus commanded us to love our neighbors.
Now, someone may be thinking:
"But what if watching pornography together really did improve our sex life?"
That experience should not simply be dismissed.
Perhaps it helped you and your spouse begin discussing desires you had been too embarrassed to mention.
Perhaps it exposed how little you had communicated about intimacy.
Perhaps it revealed that both of you were longing for greater affection, novelty, or emotional connection.
Those discoveries may be real.
But consider this carefully.
What if the valuable part was not the pornography, but the conversation it finally forced you to have?
What if you could keep the honesty and leave the pornography behind?
What if you could talk about desire without bringing strangers into the center of your sexual imagination?
What if you could rediscover affection without measuring yourselves against performances created for an audience?
What if you could pursue excitement without making your marriage dependent on explicit images?
The Bible does not present married sexual intimacy as something Christians should merely tolerate.
Read the Song of Songs.
Its poetry celebrates attraction, delight, longing, and mutual affection within the biblical vision of love.
Read Proverbs 5:18–19.
A husband is encouraged to rejoice in his wife and delight in her love.
Read 1 Corinthians 7:3–5.
Paul teaches mutual marital responsibility and warns against using sexual abstinence carelessly, while emphasizing mutual agreement.
These passages do not portray marriage as a cold arrangement in which desire must be suppressed.
They show that sexual affection has a legitimate, honored place in married life.
Christian holiness is not the death of marital passion.
It is the call to express that passion in ways consistent with faithfulness, love, and reverence for God.
And perhaps that is where some marriages need healing.
Not because the couple has too much desire.
But because they have forgotten how to cultivate desire for each other without relying on outside stimulation.
There may be years of unspoken disappointment.
Unresolved arguments.
Exhaustion from raising children.
The quiet grief of aging.
Changes in sexual functioning.
Medical concerns.
Past trauma.
A spouse who no longer feels attractive.
Another who feels constantly rejected.
Sometimes pornography becomes part of an attempted solution to pain that neither person knows how to name.
And removing pornography, by itself, will not automatically resolve every one of those deeper struggles.
Some couples need patient conversations.
Some need medical care.
Some need counseling from a qualified professional who respects their faith.
Some need to rebuild trust after secrecy or betrayal.
Some need to learn how to offer affection without making every embrace an expectation of sex.
And some need to admit something that sounds painfully simple:
"I miss you."
Not just your body.
Not just what we used to do.
I miss laughing with you.
I miss feeling safe enough to tell you what hurts.
I miss being able to look into your eyes without wondering whether I am disappointing you.
I miss us.
If those words describe your marriage, hear this.
You do not need to pretend everything is fine to be a faithful Christian.
You do not need to defend every decision you have made.
And you do not need to turn your spouse into an enemy in order to take holiness seriously.
The Gospel calls us to repentance, but repentance is not the same as humiliation.
The Greek noun commonly translated "repentance" is μετάνοια — metanoia.

It speaks of a change of mind or heart that turns a person toward a different way of living. In the New Testament, repentance involves a genuine turning toward God, not merely feeling embarrassed about wrongdoing.
That distinction is life-changing.
Because shame says, "You are disgusting. Hide."
But the Gospel calls sinners to come into the light, confess their sins, receive God's mercy, and walk in newness of life.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus..." (KJV)
This promise does not mean sin is harmless.
It means condemnation does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
Jesus does not minimize what needs to change.
He offers grace powerful enough to make change possible.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was exposed before a crowd.
Her accusers wanted judgment.
Jesus confronted their hypocrisy, refused to join their condemnation, and told her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)
Notice both truths.
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin behind.
Grace did not require Jesus to pretend that sin was good.
Holiness did not require Him to abandon the sinner.
That is the Savior Christian marriages desperately need.
Not a Savior who simply approves whatever makes us feel comfortable.
Not a Savior who crushes us under the weight of our failures.
But the Savior who tells the truth and offers forgiveness.
Perhaps you are reading this with your spouse.
Perhaps one of you has already become uncomfortable.
Perhaps the other is feeling defensive.
Perhaps you have used pornography together for years and never seriously questioned it.
Or perhaps you have already stopped, but the memories, comparisons, or unresolved arguments remain.
Whatever your story, resist the temptation to turn this article into a weapon.
Do not shove it in your spouse's face and say, "See? I told you."
Do not use Scripture to humiliate someone you promised to love.
Instead, consider asking one another a question that requires courage from both sides.
"Are we truly growing closer, or have we been avoiding something we need to talk about?"
And then listen.
Without interrupting.
Without preparing a defense.
Without turning vulnerability into evidence for the next argument.
Because the goal is not for one spouse to win.
The goal is for both to walk more faithfully with Christ.
Ephesians 5:25 tells husbands:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
That is a staggering standard.
Christlike love is not built on entitlement.
It gives itself for the good of the beloved.
And Ephesians 5:21 calls believers to submit to one another in the fear of God.
Within marriage, love must never become an excuse for coercion, manipulation, or disregard for conscience.
If your spouse says no to pornography, love listens.
If your spouse admits discomfort, love makes room for honesty.
If your spouse confesses a struggle, love responds with truth and compassion.
And if both of you realize that something you once considered harmless has been shaping your desires in ways inconsistent with your faith, you can choose a different direction together.
Not because your marriage is hopeless.
But because your marriage is worth nurturing.
You can begin with a simple prayer.

"Lord Jesus, we have not always understood how to love each other well. Forgive us where we have allowed lust, selfishness, fear, or dishonesty to shape our intimacy. Teach us to see each other with tenderness and dignity. Heal what we have hidden. Give us courage to speak truthfully, humility to listen, and wisdom to honor You with our bodies and our marriage. Amen."
That prayer is not a magical solution.
There may still be difficult conversations.
There may be habits that take time to change.
There may be emotional wounds that require careful attention.
But spiritual transformation rarely begins with having every answer.
Sometimes it begins with surrendering the excuses that have kept us from asking better questions.
And this is where the question in the title finally finds its answer.
Can watching pornography together make a Christian couple feel more sexually excited or connected in the moment?
For some couples, yes.
Can that experience, by itself, establish that pornography is strengthening their marriage?
No.
And can Christians confidently claim that mutual marital consent makes the deliberate consumption of pornography consistent with Jesus' teaching about lust, holiness, and covenant faithfulness?
Scripture gives us compelling reasons to answer no.
Not because marriage should be devoid of pleasure.
But because pleasure is not the highest authority over a Christian marriage.
Jesus is.
First Corinthians 6:12 says:
"All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any." (KJV)
Paul is not declaring every behavior morally permissible. He is challenging the misuse of freedom and rejecting enslavement to bodily appetites.
The question is not merely whether a couple can experience pleasure through pornography.
It is whether the practice is beneficial, whether it cultivates faithfulness, and whether it helps them honor Christ.
And sometimes the most liberating words in a marriage are not "We can do whatever we want."
Sometimes they are:
"We don't need this anymore."
We can choose each other.
We can tell the truth.
We can learn.
We can heal.
We can be patient.
We can pursue intimacy that does not require us to compare ourselves with strangers.
We can allow Jesus to reshape what we desire, not merely forgive what we regret.
And if we stumble, we can return to Him rather than disappear into secrecy.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
The cross is not simply God's declaration that our past can be forgiven.
It is also the foundation of a new life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
This does not promise that every marital wound disappears instantly.
But it declares that union with Christ changes the deepest reality of a believer's life.
Your history does not have to dictate your future.
Your worst choices do not have to become your permanent identity.
And a marriage that has experienced confusion, compromise, or betrayal is not necessarily beyond restoration.
Restoration may require accountability, professional help, changed behavior, and the slow rebuilding of trust.
It cannot be demanded from a wounded spouse.
But it can be pursued with humility, wisdom, and grace.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain Christians with religious language while leaving their hearts untouched.
But to keep bringing difficult, deeply human questions into the light of Scripture.
To speak about what families often hide.
To encourage repentance without cruelty.
To proclaim grace without excusing sin.
To help believers grow beyond surface-level Christianity into a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
If this article has challenged something you believed, don't let that conviction disappear beneath the next notification.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read the passages in their full context.
Pray over them with an open heart.
And if you are married, consider sharing this article privately with your spouse as an invitation to a gentle, honest conversation—not as an accusation.
There may be a husband quietly struggling with lust who needs to know that surrender is possible.
There may be a wife wondering whether she is allowed to express discomfort.
There may be a couple trying desperately to rebuild intimacy without knowing where to begin.
Never use a public tag to expose someone's personal struggle.
Now I want to ask you something, and I hope you will answer with sincerity.
What do you believe Christian couples most often confuse with genuine intimacy: sexual excitement, emotional closeness, or spiritual unity?
Not to condemn other marriages.
Not to compete over who is more righteous.
But because honest conversations can help believers grow.
If this article has exposed something you need to surrender, you may comment, "Jesus, teach me to love with a pure heart."
If your marriage is in a difficult season, you can simply comment, "Pray for our marriage."
You do not need to disclose intimate details publicly. God hears even the prayers you are not ready to explain.
And if you have experienced Christ's restoration in your marriage, your testimony may give another couple hope.
There is also a meaningful way to help this ministry continue.

It is voluntary financial support that helps sustain the work of creating, researching, writing, and sharing Christ-centered resources. As support grows, it can also help us expand our reach and serve more people.
For those who want to honor God through their giving, supporting faithful Christian teaching can be one meaningful expression of generosity.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and it commends willing, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But let's be clear about something important.
What matters is that any gift comes freely, responsibly, and from a heart that desires to serve Christ.
These resources can be reminders of biblical truth in everyday life, gifts for loved ones, and practical encouragement along the journey of discipleship.
The free resources remain an invitation to learn and grow.
If this mission reflects what God has placed on your heart, prayerfully consider joining the community of monthly supporters.
But never forget the greater purpose.
We are seeking to point people to a Savior.
A Savior who sees what is hidden.
Who knows the difference between genuine intimacy and temporary escape.
Who understands the loneliness that can exist inside a marriage.
Who calls His people to holiness without abandoning them in their weakness.
Who died for sinners, rose again, and offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Him in faith.
Maybe you began reading this article hoping to find permission.
Maybe you began reading it expecting condemnation.
But perhaps what you needed most was an invitation.
An invitation to stop confusing pleasure with peace.
An invitation to stop hiding behind mutual agreement when your conscience is troubled.
An invitation to love your spouse not merely as someone who satisfies your desires, but as someone entrusted to your care.
An invitation to believe that the same Jesus who forgives sin can teach you how to love differently.
Because the greatest intimacy in a Christian marriage is not found in how much two people are willing to watch together.

It is found in how truthfully they can stand before one another, how faithfully they can love one another, and how willingly they can bring their entire relationship under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
One day, the screen will go dark.
The excitement will fade.
Bodies will age.
Life will change.
And what remains will matter far more than what once stimulated you.
Will there be trust?
Will there be tenderness?
Will there be faithfulness?
Will there be two imperfect people who kept returning to Christ and learning to love each other with greater honesty?
That is worth fighting for.
That is worth praying for.
That is worth surrendering lesser things to pursue.

Because the deepest tragedy is not that two people might lose their passion—it is that they might spend years sharing a bed while never discovering how beautiful it is to be truly known, faithfully loved, and together surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BOAZ TOLD HIS YOUNG MEN NOT TO TOUCH RUTH—WHAT DANGER WAS HE PROTECTING HER FROM?
paragraphs: BOAZ TOLD HIS YOUNG MEN NOT TO TOUCH RUTH—WHAT DANGER WAS HE PROTECTING HER FROM?

She was a poor widow, a foreigner, and a woman working alone in a field where nobody owed her kindness. Then one man gave an order that revealed how dangerous her situation really was. But what happened in that field was more than a story about protection. It was a glimpse of the Redeemer who would one day come through her bloodline.
There is something deeply unsettling about the fact that Boaz had to say it.
“Have I not charged the young men that they shall not touch thee?” — Ruth 2:9, KJV
Read that again.
Not touch her.
Why would a wealthy landowner need to tell his workers something that should never have needed saying?
What kind of danger could be waiting for a woman whose only crime was being hungry, widowed, foreign, and desperate enough to gather leftover grain?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all...
How many people today are walking through their own fields of desperation, hoping nobody takes advantage of how vulnerable they have become?
Before we answer what Boaz was protecting Ruth from, we need to understand something about the woman standing in that field.
Because Ruth did not arrive in Bethlehem looking for romance.
She arrived carrying grief.
She had buried her husband. Her mother-in-law, Naomi, had lost her husband and both her sons. Their household had been shattered by death, and the future offered no obvious security.

Ruth was a Moabite woman living among Israelites. She was an outsider in a society where family ties, land ownership, and community standing could make the difference between survival and destitution.
She had no husband to provide for her. No guarantee that strangers would welcome her. No certainty that tomorrow would bring enough food.
Yet she had already made one extraordinary decision.
When Naomi urged her to return to her own people, Ruth refused to abandon her.
She declared:
“Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” — Ruth 1:16, KJV
Those words were not spoken from a place of comfort.
They were spoken while her future remained uncertain.
Ruth was choosing loyalty without a guarantee of prosperity. She was entrusting herself to the God of Israel without knowing how her next meal would arrive.
And sometimes that is what faith looks like.
Not a person standing on a platform announcing how blessed they are.
But someone waking up after another sleepless night, wiping away tears nobody saw, and choosing to do the next faithful thing.
Perhaps you know that feeling.
You have prayed, but the bills are still waiting.
You have trusted God, but the person you loved is still gone.
You have tried to live faithfully, but life has not suddenly become easier.
And the temptation whispers, If God really sees me, why am I still struggling?
Ruth's story does not answer that question with an easy promise.
It answers by showing us a God who is at work even when His providence is not yet visible.
When Ruth went out to glean, she was not asking to become wealthy. She was trying to survive.
Under Israel's law, landowners were commanded to leave portions of their harvest for the poor, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19–22 reveal something beautiful about God's character: He did not want the vulnerable to be forgotten in the pursuit of prosperity.
The field was supposed to become a place where the poor could find food without being stripped of their dignity.
But a righteous law did not automatically mean every person would act righteously.
A woman could have a legal right to glean and still face mistreatment from the people around her.
And Ruth was especially vulnerable.
She was a foreign widow with little social protection, gathering food among workers who had more power than she did.
Then Scripture tells us something extraordinary.
“And her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz.” — Ruth 2:3, KJV
Her hap.
From Ruth's limited perspective, she had simply arrived at a particular field.

The Hebrew expression uses the language of chance or happenstance. The narrator describes how the encounter appeared from the human point of view, while the larger story invites us to recognize God's providential care.
Ruth did not know that the owner was a relative of Naomi's deceased husband.
She did not know that this field would become central to her future.
She did not know that her ordinary decision to gather grain would lead to one of the Bible's most beautiful accounts of redemption.
She only knew she needed food.
And sometimes the moment God uses to change a life begins with something as ordinary as getting through another day.
Then Boaz arrived.
He noticed Ruth and asked his overseer who she was.
The overseer identified her as the young Moabite woman who had returned with Naomi.
Her reputation for loyalty had reached the community before she had ever spoken personally with Boaz.
And when Boaz approached her, he did something significant.
He did not treat her as an inconvenience.
He did not dismiss her because she was a foreigner.
He did not use her poverty as an opportunity to demand something from her.
Instead, he spoke directly to her.
“Go not to glean in another field, neither go from hence, but abide here fast by my maidens.” — Ruth 2:8, KJV
Then came the command that should make every reader pay attention.
“Have I not charged the young men that they shall not touch thee?” — Ruth 2:9, KJV
In the original Hebrew, the expression is:
לְבִלְתִּי נָגְעֵךְ
Levilti nog‘ekh.
It means, in context, “not to touch you.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root נגע (naga‘), meaning “to touch,” “to reach,” or, in certain contexts, “to strike” or “afflict.”
The word itself does not prove that anyone had already assaulted Ruth, nor does it establish that sexual assault was specifically being planned.
That distinction matters.
We must never manufacture an event Scripture does not report simply to make a biblical story more dramatic.
But the context makes the concern unmistakable.
Boaz was placing a protective boundary around a vulnerable woman.
His command was not merely about personal space. It belonged to a broader effort to ensure that Ruth could work without being mistreated.
And later, when Ruth told Naomi about Boaz's kindness, Naomi responded:
“It is good, my daughter, that thou go out with his maidens, that they meet thee not in any other field.” — Ruth 2:22, KJV
Naomi understood that remaining among trusted workers mattered.
Her concern reinforces the reality that Ruth's safety could not be taken for granted.
And there is another detail many readers overlook.
In Ruth 2:15, Boaz ordered his young men not to reproach or humiliate Ruth.
In Ruth 2:16, he instructed them not to rebuke her.
The Hebrew terms in these verses point toward shame, insult, or harsh treatment.
Boaz was not simply preventing physical interference.
He was protecting her from degrading treatment as well.
Think about that.
He did not merely say, Do not hurt her.
He made room for her to work.
He told her where she could safely gather grain.
He gave her access to water that his workers had drawn.
He invited her to eat with the harvesters.
He instructed his men to leave extra grain for her.
He did not make her beg for every ounce of dignity.
And this is where the story begins to expose something in us.
Because some people know exactly what it feels like to need help from someone who has the power to humiliate them.
The employee who cannot afford to lose a job and silently endures inappropriate behavior.
The single mother who has to ask for assistance and fears being judged.
The widow who discovers that some people become less compassionate when they realize she has no one to defend her.
The struggling believer who approaches a church hoping for mercy but worries that their pain will become somebody else's gossip.
The person who has been treated as though their desperation gives others permission to disrespect them.
If any of that sounds familiar, Ruth's story deserves your attention.
Because the God who commanded Israel to care for widows and foreigners was not indifferent to their vulnerability.
And Boaz, though imperfect and human, was acting in a way that reflected God's concern for justice, mercy, and the dignity of those who lacked power.
But notice something else.
Boaz did not protect Ruth because she belonged to him.
At this point in the story, they were not married.
She had not promised him a relationship.
She owed him no romantic affection in exchange for his kindness.
He was not entitled to her body, her gratitude, or her future.
He simply had the ability to protect someone vulnerable, and he used that ability for good.
That is a powerful lesson in a world where generosity is sometimes offered with hidden conditions.
True kindness does not turn another person's need into leverage.
True protection does not demand ownership.
And godly character is not measured merely by how someone treats people who can reward them.
It is revealed by how they treat people who cannot repay them.
Then Ruth asked a question that reveals how deeply Boaz's kindness affected her.
“Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?” — Ruth 2:10, KJV
Why me?
Why would you notice someone like me?
Why would you show kindness to a foreign woman who has so little?
The Hebrew word translated “grace” in this verse is חֵן (chen), meaning favor or gracious acceptance.
Ruth was astonished that she had received such favor.
And perhaps that question sounds familiar too.
Why would God care about me after everything I have done?
Why would Jesus receive someone who has made so many mistakes?
Why would grace reach into a life that seems permanently stained by regret?
Here is where we must be careful not to confuse Ruth's story with the Gospel itself.
Boaz was not Jesus.
He was a real Israelite landowner, a man who feared God and acted generously toward a vulnerable widow.
Yet his role within the larger biblical story helps us see themes that reach their fulfillment in Christ.
Boaz later becomes a family redeemer, often described using the Hebrew word גֹּאֵל (go’el).
A go’el was a family member who could fulfill certain responsibilities to protect or restore the interests of relatives, including matters involving land and family inheritance.
In Ruth's story, Boaz's actions are connected with preserving the family line and restoring hope to Naomi and Ruth.
But Jesus accomplishes a redemption infinitely greater than the restoration of land or the continuation of a family name.
Jesus redeems sinners from the guilt and bondage of sin through His death and resurrection.
As 1 Peter 1:18–19 declares, believers are redeemed not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
Boaz could provide food and security in a dangerous season.
Christ provides forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
Boaz could act as a faithful family redeemer within Israel's covenant life.
Christ is the Savior who gave Himself for people who could never purchase their own salvation.
And that difference matters.
Because the greatest danger facing humanity is not merely the cruelty of other people.
It is the reality of sin, judgment, and separation from the holy God who created us.
We need more than someone to improve our circumstances.
We need a Redeemer who can forgive our sins and make us new.
And that is exactly why Jesus came.
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” — Luke 19:10, KJV
Not the impressive.
Not the people who have successfully hidden every failure.
Not those who have earned their way into God's favor.
The lost.
The guilty.
The broken.
The spiritually exhausted.
Those who know that beneath the polished photographs and carefully chosen words, something inside them desperately needs mercy.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners calls them to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
His forgiveness is not an excuse to cherish the sins that wounded us and dishonored God.
It is an invitation to leave them behind.
And sometimes the first step toward healing is admitting what we have been trying so hard to conceal.
Perhaps you have spent years pretending you are fine.
Perhaps you have grown accustomed to surviving without ever feeling safe.
Perhaps you have made choices you regret, and now you wonder whether your story can ever become something beautiful again.
Look at Ruth.
Her story did not begin in a palace.
It began in bereavement, poverty, and uncertainty.
But her suffering was not the final chapter.
And neither does your past have to be the final word about your future.
That does not mean every widow will remarry.
It does not mean every financial hardship will end with unexpected wealth.
It does not mean every person who mistreats you will suddenly become compassionate.
The book of Ruth is not a formula guaranteeing that faithful people will receive the same earthly outcome.
It is a testimony to God's faithfulness working through ordinary obedience, courageous loyalty, and the kindness of people who take His commands seriously.
And then comes one of the most tender moments in the entire account.
Boaz tells Ruth:
“The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.” — Ruth 2:12, KJV
Under whose wings.
The Hebrew expression is:
תַּחַת־כְּנָפָיו
Tachat-kenafav.
Literally, “under His wings.”
The imagery speaks of refuge, shelter, and protective care.
Ruth had left her homeland and entrusted herself to the God of Israel.
And Boaz recognized her faith.
But there is a beautiful development later in the story.
In Ruth 3:9, Ruth asks Boaz to spread his garment over her.
The Hebrew word כָּנָף (kanaf) can mean “wing” or the edge of a garment, depending on the context.
The literary connection is striking.
In chapter two, Boaz speaks of Ruth seeking refuge beneath God's wings.
In chapter three, Ruth asks Boaz to extend his garment over her as a family redeemer.
The man who prayed for God's protection over Ruth would become one of the means through which God provided for her.
Sometimes God's answer to a prayer for protection includes calling someone to become an instrument of that protection.
Not everyone is called to play Boaz's particular role.
But every follower of Christ is called to love their neighbor.
To refuse exploitation.
To defend the vulnerable.
To practice generosity without manipulation.
To make our homes, churches, workplaces, and communities places where people are treated with dignity.
And perhaps this is the part of Ruth's story that some Christians need to hear most.
We love talking about being blessed like Ruth.
But are we willing to act with integrity like Boaz?
We pray for God to send help when we are struggling.
But when we are the ones holding the resources, the influence, the opportunity, or the authority, do we use them to serve others?
Or do we become another reason vulnerable people are afraid?
A church cannot claim to honor the God of Ruth while humiliating the poor.
A Christian cannot celebrate Boaz's protection while excusing harassment or coercion.
A believer cannot praise the generosity of Scripture while using another person's desperation for personal advantage.
James 1:27 reminds us that pure religion includes caring for orphans and widows in their affliction and remaining unstained by the world.
That is not an optional decoration added to the Christian life.
It is part of what genuine faith looks like when it becomes visible.
And if this story has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past that conviction.
Perhaps you need to repent for how you have treated someone weaker than yourself.
Perhaps you need to ask forgiveness from someone you embarrassed when they came to you for help.
Perhaps you need to stop confusing control with protection.
Or perhaps you are the one who has been hurt.
Perhaps you need to hear that another person's abuse of power does not erase your dignity before God.

And if you are facing harassment, exploitation, or threats today, please understand that biblical faith does not require you to remain in danger. Seek safety and trustworthy help. Godly protection never demands that you silently endure abuse.
Now return to the field.
Imagine Ruth at the beginning of that morning.
Her hands are empty.
Her future is uncertain.
Her heart carries losses she cannot undo.
She does not know that a man named Boaz will notice her.
She does not know that the landowner will tell his workers to leave her alone.
She does not know that she will receive food, kindness, and an unexpected measure of security.
And she certainly does not know the extraordinary place her family will occupy in the history of redemption.
Because the story does not end with a full basket of grain.
It does not even end with a wedding.
Ruth and Boaz eventually marry, and Ruth gives birth to a son named Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And generations later, the Messiah comes through David's royal line.
Matthew 1:5 names Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Let that settle in your heart.
The foreign widow gathering leftover grain became an ancestor of the Savior of the world.
The woman who had so little was woven into a story far greater than she could have imagined.
And it was not because she had earned a place in God's redemptive plan through flawless performance.
It was because God was faithfully carrying forward His purposes through real people, real suffering, real obedience, and real grace.
From Moab to Bethlehem.
From bereavement to belonging.
From an uncertain harvest to a family line that would lead to Jesus.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But even here, we need to understand that beautiful statement correctly.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending sin never happened.
He does not call evil good.
He does not erase the seriousness of wrongdoing or dismiss the wounds of those who have suffered.
He redeems.
He forgives repentant sinners.
He restores fellowship with God.
He transforms those who belong to Him.
And He promises a final restoration in which sin, death, and suffering will no longer have the last word.
The cross is the greatest evidence that God does not need to deny the darkness in order to overcome it.
At Calvary, human evil was unmistakably real.
The sinless Son of God was rejected, mocked, and crucified.
Yet through His sacrificial death and victorious resurrection, God accomplished salvation for all who trust in Christ.
That is not a sentimental ending.
That is the Gospel.
And it means that no amount of religious performance can purchase the forgiveness that Jesus freely offers through faith.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot donate enough money to erase your sins.
You cannot earn redemption by sharing a Christian article.
Salvation is the gift of God, received by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for religious activity. (Ephesians 2:8–9)
But when grace takes hold of a person's life, it changes what they love.
It changes how they give.
It changes how they serve.
It changes what they are willing to do for the sake of others.
And this is where Ruth's story becomes more than something we admire.
It becomes something we are called to live.
Somewhere today, another Ruth is trying to survive.
Perhaps she is a widow wondering how to feed her children.
Perhaps he is a father carrying a burden nobody knows about.
Perhaps it is a young believer trying to remain faithful in a hostile environment.
Perhaps it is someone who has walked away from church after being wounded by people who claimed to represent Jesus.
Perhaps it is the person reading these words right now.
And perhaps God will use one act of kindness, one biblical truth, one prayer, or one faithful Christian to remind that person they have not been forgotten.
This is why Gospel-centered discipleship matters.
Not because a ministry can replace the local church.
Not because a social media page can become anyone's savior.
But because biblical teaching, encouragement, and Christian community can help direct weary hearts back to the One who truly saves.
That is the mission behind Gospel Warrior.
To keep proclaiming Jesus Christ.
To speak biblical truth without hiding the seriousness of sin.
To remind the broken that grace is real.
To encourage repentance without abandoning compassion.
To point struggling believers toward Scripture, prayer, fellowship, and spiritual maturity.
And to help people discover that their darkest chapter does not have to become their final identity.
A simple share may place Scripture before someone who would never have searched for it.
And please do not leave without joining the conversation.
You do not need to reveal details you are not ready to share.
Sometimes a few sincere words can become the beginning of prayer, encouragement, and Christian fellowship.
And if this article has challenged how you treat others, perhaps your response is simply:
“Lord, teach me to protect, not exploit.”
Because the question is not only whether God will send someone to help us.
Sometimes the question is whether we will become the kind of people through whom He helps someone else.
What matters is that your giving comes from a willing heart.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not a pressured giver.
Not someone made to feel that God's approval depends on a payment.
But someone whose generosity flows from gratitude for what God has done.
These products and benefits are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
And the greatest reason to support any Christian ministry is not merchandise or recognition, but a sincere desire to help make the truth of Christ known.
A person who cannot give financially is not less valuable to God.
A person who never purchases anything is not excluded from the grace of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
But those who have freely received His grace can freely choose to serve, give, and help others hear the same good news.
And now, before you leave, I want you to think about Ruth one final time.
Think about the woman walking into a field with no certainty about what awaited her.
Think about the grief she carried.
The hunger she faced.
The courage it took to keep going.
Think about Boaz, a man who could have ignored her but instead chose to treat her with honor.
Think about the command he gave his workers.
Do not touch her.
Do not shame her.
Do not rebuke her.
Let her gather.
Let her drink.
Let her eat.
And then think about Jesus.
The One who did not merely provide grain for the hungry but declared Himself the Bread of Life.
The One who did not merely defend the vulnerable but laid down His life for sinners.
The One who did not merely extend temporary kindness but opened the way to eternal reconciliation with God.
The One whose grace calls us out of sin and into new life.
Perhaps your life does not look like Ruth's.
Perhaps you are not a widow.
Perhaps you have never gathered grain in a field.
But you know what it means to feel uncertain.
You know what it means to need mercy.
You know what it means to wonder whether there is anything beautiful left in a story that has already contained so much pain.
Then hear this.
Your suffering is real, but it is not proof that God has abandoned you.
Your past is real, but through Christ it does not have to rule your future.
Your sins are real, but the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior is greater than the guilt of everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
And your life, however ordinary it may appear, can still be lived for the glory of God.
So come to Jesus.
Not because you have become strong enough.
Not because you have finally made yourself worthy.
Not because you can promise that you will never stumble again.
Come because He is merciful.
Repent. Believe. Follow Him.
And when His grace begins transforming your life, let it become visible in how you treat the next vulnerable person who crosses your path.
Because somewhere, someone is standing in a field they never wanted to enter.
And the kindness you choose to show may become one of the ways they encounter the love of Christ.
Ruth walked into that field looking for enough grain to survive, never knowing that God was weaving her name into the earthly family line of the Bread of Life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “YOUR NAVEL IS A ROUNDED BOWL”—WAIT… WHY IS THE BIBLE TALKING ABOUT THE HUMAN BODY LIKE THIS?
paragraphs: “YOUR NAVEL IS A ROUNDED BOWL”—WAIT… WHY IS THE BIBLE TALKING ABOUT THE HUMAN BODY LIKE THIS?

The shocking intimacy of Song of Songs 7:1–3, the Hebrew poetry most Christians have never understood, and the beautiful truth about desire, dignity, shame, and the God who created the human body without embarrassment.
There are verses in the Bible that make you close your eyes and worship.
There are verses that make you fall to your knees and repent.
And then there are verses that make you stop reading, look at the page again, and whisper…
“Wait. Did God really allow THAT to be written in Scripture?”
This is one of them.
“Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies.”
— Song of Solomon 7:2, KJV
Your navel?
A rounded goblet?
Your belly like a heap of wheat?
And just a verse later, the poet describes a woman's breasts as two young gazelles.
In the Bible.
The same Bible that commands holiness. The same Bible that warns against sexual immorality. The same Bible that calls believers to flee lust and glorify God with their bodies.
So what is happening here?
Is this a contradiction?
Is the Bible being provocative?
Or have generations of Christians become so uncomfortable with the human body that we have forgotten something profoundly beautiful about the God who created it?
Stay with me, because the answer reaches much deeper than ancient romantic poetry.
It reaches into the shame some people carry when they look in the mirror.
Into marriages where affection has slowly disappeared.
Into the hearts of believers who have confused holiness with embarrassment.
And into one of the earliest scenes in Scripture, where two human beings stood before God without clothing, without shame, and without fear.
But to understand why this passage matters, we must first allow the Bible to speak in its own language, within its own context, without forcing it to say something it never intended.
Because Scripture does not need us to make it less human to make it holy.
And the truth waiting inside this passage might change the way you see your body, your marriage, your struggles, and even the grace of Jesus Christ.
The Hebrew text of Song of Songs 7:2, corresponding to 7:3 in the Hebrew verse numbering, begins with these words:
שָׁרְרֵךְ אַגַּן הַסַּהַר אַל־יֶחְסַר הַמָּזֶג
Shorerekh aggan hassahar, al-yechsar hammazeg.
A close translation is:
“Your navel is a rounded bowl; may the mixed wine never be lacking.”
The Hebrew word שָׁרְרֵךְ (shorerekh) is traditionally understood as “your navel,” although some interpreters suggest that the image may refer more broadly to the woman's lower abdomen.
אַגַּן (aggan) means a basin or bowl.
הַסַּהַר (hassahar) describes its rounded form.
And הַמָּזֶג (hammazeg) refers to mixed wine.
The King James Version's phrase “which wanteth not liquor” uses older English in which “liquor” can mean a liquid or drink. The Hebrew specifically points to mixed wine.
Notice what the poet is doing.
He is not writing an anatomy textbook.
He is not delivering medical information.
And he is certainly not providing permission to treat a woman's body as an object for public consumption.
He is using the language of abundance, beauty, delight, and intimate admiration.
The imagery is deliberately sensual.
That is important to acknowledge.
We do not honor Scripture by pretending that sensual language is not sensual.
The Song of Songs is love poetry, and its celebration of physical attraction is part of its meaning.
But sensuality and sin are not identical.
That distinction matters more than many Christians realize.
Because somewhere along the way, some believers absorbed the idea that the human body itself was something suspicious.
That attraction was automatically dirty.
That married couples should be embarrassed by their own affection.
That the safest way to be spiritual was to become uncomfortable with anything physical.
But the Bible begins somewhere very different.
Genesis 1:27 tells us that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
And after surveying His creation, including embodied human life, God declared it “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
The Hebrew expression is:
טוֹב מְאֹד (tov me'od)
“Very good.”
Not merely tolerable.
Not an unfortunate physical shell imprisoning a supposedly more important soul.
Very good.
Then Genesis 2:25 records something extraordinary:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Read that again.
Before the fall, there was nakedness.
But there was no shame.
There was embodiment.
But no humiliation.
There was marital union.
But no exploitation.
The human body did not become evil when humanity sinned.
What changed was the human relationship with God, with one another, and with ourselves.
After disobedience, Adam and Eve became aware of their nakedness in a new way, covered themselves, and hid from God (Genesis 3:7–10).
Shame entered the story.
Fear entered the story.
Hiding entered the story.
And humanity has been hiding ever since.
Some people hide behind expensive clothes.
Some behind carefully edited photographs.
Some behind religious language.
Some behind a marriage that looks beautiful in public but has grown painfully distant in private.
Some hide because another person taught them to despise their bodies.
And some carry shame because they have used their bodies in ways they now deeply regret.
Perhaps that is why this ancient poem can feel so unsettling.
It speaks openly about physical beauty in a world where bodies have become battlegrounds.
But we must be careful.
Song of Songs 7 is not a command for everyone to look a certain way.
It is not God's universal beauty standard.
It is not a checklist for evaluating a woman's worth.
It is the language of a particular lover delighting in a particular beloved.
And that makes the context essential.
The passage begins:
“How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince's daughter! the joints of thy thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a cunning workman.”
— Song of Solomon 7:1, KJV
The Hebrew begins:
מַה־יָּפוּ פְעָמַיִךְ בַּנְּעָלִים בַּת־נָדִיב
Mah-yafu fe'amayikh banne'alim, bat-nadiv.
“How beautiful are your steps in sandals, O noble daughter!”
The expression translated “prince's daughter” or “noble daughter” is poetic language of honor.
The speaker is not beginning with contempt.
He is not humiliating the woman.
He is celebrating her.
Then comes the description of her body, moving through images of crafted jewels, a rounded bowl, wheat, lilies, and young gazelles.
In Hebrew poetic tradition, this kind of descriptive praise is often called a wasf, a poem celebrating the beloved's beauty through a sequence of images.
Its metaphors are not intended to be read as literal comparisons of physical measurements.
A belly is not literally a pile of grain.
Breasts are not literally animals.
A navel is not literally a wine vessel.
The images evoke beauty, vitality, softness, abundance, elegance, and delight.

When Song of Songs 7:2 describes the belly as wheat surrounded by lilies, the poet is drawing upon images of fertility, nourishment, and loveliness from the agricultural world familiar to his audience.
And when verse 3 says:
“Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins.”
— Song of Solomon 7:3, KJV
The imagery suggests graceful symmetry and tenderness.
This is the vocabulary of ancient love poetry.
And yes, it is intimate.
But here is something worth noticing.
The woman in Song of Songs is not merely a silent body being described.
Throughout the book, she speaks.
She desires.
She remembers.
She invites.
She expresses longing.
She celebrates her beloved.
In Song of Songs 7:10, she declares:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
This is not a picture of one person possessing another like property.
The Song portrays mutual attraction, affection, and delight.
And that mutuality is part of what makes the book so remarkable.
In a world where human bodies are frequently reduced to commodities, Scripture gives us a poetic portrait in which love involves personal recognition and reciprocal desire.
The beloved is not merely a body.
She is a person.
And the body being celebrated belongs to someone who has a voice.
That is a distinction our generation desperately needs to recover.
Because there is a difference between being admired and being consumed.
There is a difference between being cherished and being used.
There is a difference between desire that honors another person and desire that treats another person as disposable.
Jesus makes that moral distinction unmistakably clear.
In Matthew 5:28, He warns against looking at another person with lustful intent.
The Greek expression includes:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
Pros to epithymēsai autēn.
“To desire her,” within the context of Jesus' warning about an adulterous intention of the heart.
The verb ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō) can refer to desire or longing; context determines whether that desire is sinful.
Jesus is not declaring that every recognition of beauty is adultery.
He is confronting the deliberate cultivation of wrongful sexual desire.
The Song celebrates intimate delight.
Jesus condemns lustful intent.
These teachings are not enemies.
They address different moral realities.
The Bible can celebrate marital love while condemning adultery, exploitation, and sexual immorality.
In fact, it must do both to remain faithful to its own teaching.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
The same God who commands sexual purity also honors marriage.
The same God who forbids adultery also permits and celebrates faithful marital intimacy.
Holiness is not hatred of the body.
Holiness is the consecration of our entire lives, including our bodies, to God.
And perhaps this is where the passage becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because the question is no longer simply, “Why would the Bible describe a woman's navel?”
The question becomes:
What has happened to our understanding of the body that makes us more comfortable with shame than with God's original declaration of goodness?
Think about the person who avoids mirrors because years of criticism have convinced them they are unattractive.
The wife who wonders whether her husband still sees her after years of childbirth, exhaustion, and changing seasons.
The husband who has quietly come to believe that his worth is measured only by performance, strength, or physical appearance.
The young believer who wants to honor Christ but has never been taught how to distinguish healthy attraction from sinful lust.
The person who was violated, exploited, or shamed and now struggles to believe that their body still deserves dignity.
Song of Songs does not solve all these wounds.
And we should never pretend that one poetic passage can erase the consequences of trauma, betrayal, or abuse.
But it challenges the lie that the human body is inherently disgraceful.
Your body is not worthless because it has changed.
Your dignity is not erased because someone mistreated you.
Your value is not determined by whether another human being finds you attractive.
And your worth before God is not measured by how closely you resemble the woman described in an ancient love poem.
That woman is being celebrated within a particular relationship.
She is not being established as the standard by which all women must be judged.
The Christian understanding of human dignity begins much deeper than appearance.
It begins with creation in God's image.
And it finds its fullest redemptive hope in Jesus Christ.
But there is another danger we must avoid.
We must not turn Song of Songs into something it is not.
Throughout Christian history, some interpreters have read the Song allegorically as portraying God's love for Israel or Christ's love for the Church.
Those readings have influenced centuries of Christian devotion.
And Scripture certainly uses marriage imagery elsewhere to describe God's covenant relationship with His people.
Ephesians 5:25, for example, commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church and gave Himself for her.
But Song of Songs 7:1–3 does not explicitly identify the woman's navel, belly, or breasts as symbols of particular spiritual doctrines.
We should not invent hidden meanings and present them as though the Hebrew text demands them.
The poem's immediate literary subject is human love.
That is not a problem to be solved.
It is part of the Bible's witness to God's good creation.
And within the wider Christian canon, this celebration of faithful love can lead us to reflect on the God who designed humanity for covenantal relationships, dignity, and holiness.
But the passage does not need to become a secret code about Jesus to have a rightful place in Christian Scripture.
Its beauty belongs to the story of creation.
And creation belongs to the God revealed through Jesus Christ.
Now consider something even more astonishing.
When the eternal Son of God entered our world, He did not merely appear to be human.
He became flesh.
John 1:14 declares:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
The Greek reads:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
The word σάρξ (sarx) means “flesh.”
Its meaning varies with context, but here John is making an extraordinary declaration about the incarnation.
The eternal Word truly entered human existence.
Jesus Christ took on genuine humanity.
He experienced hunger.
He experienced weariness.
He wept.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died.
And He rose bodily from the grave.
Christianity is not a religion that teaches us to escape the physical world because matter is inherently evil.
It proclaims that the Creator entered His creation to redeem sinners.
And the bodily resurrection of Jesus is central to that proclamation.
This is why the human body cannot simply be dismissed as something unworthy of God's concern.
First Corinthians 6:19–20 calls believers to honor God with their bodies.
Paul writes:
Notice the direction of the command.
Not despise your body.
Not worship your body.
Not use your body however you please.
Glorify God in your body.
That means our physical lives matter morally and spiritually.
How we treat others matters.
How we handle desire matters.
How we practice fidelity matters.
How we respond to temptation matters.
How we care for those whose bodies have been wounded matters.
And how we speak about ourselves matters, too.
There is a terrible irony in condemning the very body God created while simultaneously claiming to honor its Creator.
But there is an equally dangerous error in using God's good creation as an excuse for sinful behavior.
The Gospel rejects both extremes.
We do not need to be ashamed that God made us embodied creatures.
And we do not have permission to turn bodily desire into our god.
Jesus calls us to something better.
A life where grace does not excuse sin but transforms sinners.
A life where holiness is not merely a performance for religious people.
A life where repentance is possible because mercy is real.
A life where our bodies are not instruments of exploitation but are offered to God in worship.
Romans 12:1 urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.
That is an extraordinary invitation.
The same body you may have spent years criticizing can become an instrument of obedience.
The same hands that once participated in wrongdoing can now serve others.
The same lips that once spoke cruelty can now speak truth and encouragement.
The same life that once seemed dominated by shame can now become a testimony to grace.
Not because your past was harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
And His grace is powerful enough to change the direction of a human life.
Perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that means.
You have made choices you regret.
You have crossed boundaries you knew were wrong.
You have allowed lust to distort the way you look at people.
Or perhaps you were the one treated as an object, and someone else's sin left wounds you never deserved.
Those experiences are not morally identical.
The person who sinned needs repentance and forgiveness.
The person who was harmed needs safety, justice, compassionate care, and the assurance that another person's wrongdoing did not make them guilty.
But both need to know that Jesus Christ does not abandon people to darkness.
His mercy is not an invitation to continue in sin.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
And Romans 8:1 announces that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is not cheap reassurance.
That is Gospel truth.
Christ does not tell us that sin never mattered.
He went to the cross precisely because sin matters.
But He also declares that sin and shame do not have to write the final chapter for those who belong to Him.
That is not merely a beautiful phrase.
It is the story of what happens when human brokenness encounters the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The scandal of our rebellion.
The scandal of betrayal.
The scandal of hypocrisy.
The scandal of a world that can celebrate bodies while destroying the people who inhabit them.
And then, astonishingly, grace.
Grace that calls sinners to repentance.
Grace that restores what sin has disfigured.
Grace that teaches us to love without exploiting.
Grace that teaches us to honor without idolizing.
Grace that teaches us to live in our bodies without being enslaved by our desires.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
But by giving forgiven sinners a new future in Him.
And now, return to that opening verse.
“Thy navel is like a round goblet…”
Does it still sound strange?
Perhaps.
Ancient Hebrew poetry does not always resemble modern romantic language.
But perhaps it no longer sounds scandalous in the same way.
Because we can recognize what the poet is celebrating.
A beloved person.
Physical beauty.
Intimate affection.
The delight of love expressed through images of abundance and life.
And we can also recognize what the passage does not authorize.
It does not authorize lust.
It does not excuse infidelity.
It does not endorse objectification.
It does not make physical attractiveness the measure of human value.
And it does not promise that every person must marry or experience romantic desire to live a complete life.
Jesus Himself lived a fully human, holy, unmarried life.
And Paul honors singleness as a meaningful calling in 1 Corinthians 7.
So whether you are married, single, widowed, divorced, or walking through a difficult season, your dignity is not dependent upon romantic attention.
Your ultimate identity is not found in being someone's beloved.
For the Christian, the deepest security is found in belonging to Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because human admiration can fade.
Physical beauty changes with age.
Relationships can disappoint.
Even the most devoted spouse cannot carry the weight of being another person's savior.
But Jesus Christ remains faithful.
He does not love His people because they have perfect bodies.
He does not save them because they are attractive.
He does not forgive them because they have successfully hidden every embarrassing part of their lives.
He saves by grace through faith.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
Salvation is God's gift, not something we earn through moral achievement, physical appearance, religious performance, or financial generosity.
And that is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
You cannot purchase the mercy of Jesus.
You cannot give enough money to make God owe you forgiveness.
Christ has already accomplished what no human payment could accomplish.
The question is whether you will turn to Him in repentance and faith.
And if you already belong to Him, whether you will allow His Word to reshape the way you think, love, speak, and live.
Maybe today that begins with repentance for the way you have looked at other people.
Maybe it begins with asking forgiveness from your spouse for years of emotional neglect.
Maybe it begins with refusing to keep measuring your worth against unrealistic standards.
Maybe it begins with seeking help for wounds you have carried in silence.
Or maybe it begins with opening your Bible again, this time without embarrassment, and allowing God to teach you what holiness actually means.
Because the Bible is not afraid of the human condition.
It speaks about love and longing.
Beauty and betrayal.
Marriage and singleness.
Desire and discipline.
Sin and forgiveness.
Death and resurrection.
And at the center of its redemptive message stands Jesus Christ.
Not a distant religious idea.
Not a motivational slogan.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who calls sinners out of darkness.
The One who receives the repentant.
The One who makes all things new.
Sit with the Scriptures.
Read Song of Songs 7 in its wider context.
Read Genesis 1–3.
Read Matthew 5.
Read 1 Corinthians 6.
Read John 1.
Ask yourself whether your understanding of holiness comes from God's Word or from fear, cultural assumptions, and teachings you have never examined.
And then, if you are willing, join this conversation.
Or perhaps your prayer is more personal.
You do not need to disclose private experiences publicly to participate.
A simple prayer or a verse that has encouraged you may be enough to strengthen someone else.
Someone may be quietly reading who needs to know that change is possible.
Someone may have spent years believing that being holy means hating themselves.
Someone may be trapped in lust and desperately needs to hear that repentance and freedom are possible through Christ.
Someone may be carrying shame for harm they never chose.
Your words, offered with wisdom and compassion, might point that person toward hope.
Not merely because the subject is surprising.
Not because an unusual Bible verse might attract attention.
Because people need to know that Scripture celebrates God's good creation without celebrating sin.
Because our generation needs something deeper than body worship on one side and body shame on the other.
We need Jesus Christ.

If someone comes to mind as you read this, consider tagging them respectfully, especially a friend who loves studying Scripture or someone who would appreciate a thoughtful discussion about faith and human dignity.
There may come a day when you need to revisit these passages, examine the Hebrew again, or remind yourself that God's Word is more beautiful and more challenging than the assumptions we bring to it.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have grown distant from their faith, and even seekers who are still asking difficult questions.
We are not here to pretend that following Jesus is easy.
We are here to keep pointing one another toward the Savior who is worthy of our lives.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and grow, there is another meaningful opportunity.
Scripture teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
These products can serve as everyday reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share encouragement with others.
It is participating in a ministry effort that seeks to keep Scripture accessible, Christ central, and discipleship meaningful.
Read the Scriptures.
Use the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
And continue growing in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
And the worth of a soul is never measured by a monthly payment.
What matters is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully, people are encouraged to examine God's Word, and lives are transformed by His grace.
Now, before you leave, remember where this entire conversation began.
With a verse that seemed almost too intimate to belong in the Bible.
A navel described as a rounded bowl.
A belly compared to wheat surrounded by lilies.
A woman's beauty celebrated through the imagery of ancient love poetry.
What first appeared shocking became an invitation to examine something much deeper.
The goodness of creation.
The dignity of the human person.
The holiness of covenant love.
The danger of lust.
The tragedy of shame.
The necessity of repentance.
And the redeeming grace of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps the greatest surprise is not that the Bible speaks so openly about the human body.
Perhaps the greater surprise is that we have sometimes forgotten how deeply God cares about the whole human person.
He created us.
He knows our frailty.
He sees our sin.
He knows our wounds.
And He calls us to Himself through Jesus Christ.
Not so we can continue hiding.
But so we can walk in truth.
Not so we can excuse our darkness.
But so we can repent and receive His mercy.
Not so we can worship the body.
But so we can glorify the One who made us.
And if the Gospel has taught us anything, it is this:

The body you were taught to despise was created with dignity, the sin you were tempted to hide can be brought into the light, and the life you thought was beyond redemption can still be transformed by Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WALKED INTO THE KING’S PALACE WITH A LIE… AND EXPOSED A TRUTH DAVID DIDN’T WANT TO FACE
paragraphs: SHE WALKED INTO THE KING’S PALACE WITH A LIE… AND EXPOSED A TRUTH DAVID DIDN’T WANT TO FACE
The Woman from Tekoa, the Son Who Could Not Come Home, and the Uncomfortable Truth About Mercy, Justice, and the God Who Makes a Way for the Banished — 2 Samuel 14:1–20
She was not really a widow.
Her sons had not fought each other.
No grieving family was demanding the death of her only surviving child.
The tears, the mourning clothes, the heartbreaking story… all of it was part of a carefully arranged performance.
And somehow, this unnamed woman from Tekoa was about to make one of Israel’s most powerful kings confront a contradiction in his own heart.
But here is what makes this story unsettling.
The king she confronted was David. The man after God’s own heart. The worshiper who wrote psalms. The sinner who knew what it meant to receive mercy he did not deserve.
And yet there was someone in his own family whom he could not bring himself to welcome home.
Have you ever found it easier to believe that God could forgive you than to forgive someone who wounded you?
Have you ever prayed for reconciliation while secretly hoping the other person would suffer a little longer?
Or perhaps you have been the one standing outside the door.
Waiting for a phone call.
Waiting for someone to say, “Come home.”
Waiting for a relationship to become something other than a graveyard of things nobody wants to discuss.
Then stay with this story.
Because beneath the royal robes, the political maneuvering, and the woman's invented tragedy lies a question that still reaches into Christian homes today.
What happens when someone knows the language of mercy but struggles to live it?
And even more importantly, what happens when our desire for reconciliation moves faster than our willingness to face the truth?
The answer is more complicated, more painful, and ultimately more revealing than many people realize.
David’s household was already bleeding.
His son Amnon had sexually violated his half-sister Tamar. When David learned what had happened, he became furious, but the biblical account does not describe him administering justice against Amnon.
Tamar’s brother Absalom took her into his house.
And there she remained, devastated.
Two years passed.
Two years of silence.
Two years in which a sister carried the consequences of a terrible wrong while the man who committed it remained alive.
Then Absalom arranged for Amnon to be killed.
He fled to Geshur, where he remained for three years.
The royal family was fractured. One son was dead. Another was in exile. Tamar’s suffering had not been undone.
And David was left with grief that could not be neatly separated from his failures as a father and king.
This matters because the story of the woman from Tekoa does not begin with a simple misunderstanding between two relatives.
It begins with sexual violence, murder, unresolved injustice, and a family whose wounds were never properly addressed.
We must not romanticize that suffering just to make a beautiful lesson about forgiveness.
Tamar was a real victim within the biblical narrative.
Amnon’s actions were evil.
Absalom’s revenge was murder.
And David’s anguish did not erase his responsibility to govern justly.
Then, in 2 Samuel 14:1, we read that Joab, the son of Zeruiah, perceived that the king’s heart was occupied with Absalom.
Joab was a military commander who understood David’s family and the political consequences of Absalom’s exile.
He wanted to influence the king.
But instead of confronting David directly, he devised a plan.
He sent to Tekoa and brought back a wise woman.
Scripture does not give us her name.
No genealogy.
No record of her husband.
No explanation of her life before this moment.
Only the description of a woman whose intelligence would become the instrument of a carefully staged appeal.
Joab instructed her to pretend to be a mourner.
She was to wear mourning clothes, avoid anointing herself with oil, and appear as someone who had been grieving for a long time.
He even supplied the words she was to speak.
Imagine that moment.
A woman preparing to enter the presence of the king, dressed as though death had emptied her home.
Every detail was designed to make her suffering believable.
And when she finally stood before David, she fell on her face and cried for help.
David asked what troubled her.
She told him she was a widow.
She claimed that her two sons had fought in a field, where nobody had intervened, and one had killed the other.
Now, she said, the whole family was demanding that she surrender the surviving son so he could be executed.
If that happened, she would lose both children.
Her husband's name and inheritance would disappear.
Her family line would be extinguished.
It was a devastating picture.
One son already dead.
Another facing death.
A mother standing between the grave and the last surviving remnant of her household.
And David listened.
At first, he told her to return home and promised to issue instructions concerning her case.
But she pressed further.
She wanted more than a vague promise.
She wanted the king’s protection.
Eventually, David swore that not one hair of her son would fall to the ground.
The woman had obtained exactly what Joab needed.
A royal declaration of mercy.
A commitment made before David understood how the story would be turned against him.
Then came the moment that changed everything.
She asked permission to speak one more word.
David agreed.
And the grieving widow disappeared from the conversation.
Not physically.
But in the meaning of her words.
She was no longer merely pleading for her imaginary son.
She was confronting the king about his real one.
In 2 Samuel 14:13, she challenged David for speaking in a way that seemed to make him guilty concerning God's people, because he had not brought back his banished son.
The king had shown compassion in the case presented to him.
But what about Absalom?
What about the son still living far from Jerusalem?
What about the conflict David had left unresolved?
