You do not need to surrender your conscience to demonstrate Christian love.
And you do not need to become cruel in order to become courageous.
But now I want to speak to the person who has quietly carried the consequences of someone else's misuse of Scripture.
The one who still loves Jesus but struggles to enter a church building.
The one who hears the word “submission” and remembers being threatened.
The one who once volunteered with joy but now feels exhausted whenever somebody asks for another sacrifice.
The one who was told that speaking about harm would damage God's reputation.
The one who began to believe that silence was the price of belonging.
Please hear this.
Jesus Christ is not the same as the person who misrepresented Him to you.
The failure of a spiritual leader does not make the Gospel false.
The misuse of a Bible verse does not make the Bible untrustworthy.
The hypocrisy of a religious person does not erase the holiness of God.
And the wounds you carry do not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
He knows the difference between a shepherd and someone who exploits the sheep.
In John 10, Jesus identifies Himself as the Good Shepherd.
He says:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” — John 10:11, KJV
Notice the direction of the sacrifice.
The Good Shepherd gives His life for the sheep.
He does not treat the sheep as expendable instruments for protecting His reputation.
He does not demand that the wounded pretend they are unharmed.
He lays down His life.
And this is where the entire story turns.
Because the greatest scandal in human history was not that a corrupt religious leader escaped accountability.
It was that the sinless Son of God was condemned while guilty sinners stood in need of mercy.
Jesus was falsely accused.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Struck.
And crucified.
Yet He did not remain in the grave.
He rose again.
And through His death and resurrection, God offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life to all who repent and believe in Him.
The Gospel does not teach that sin should be hidden.
It declares that sin is so serious that Christ gave Himself to save us from it.
Grace is not permission to continue in darkness.
Grace calls us into the light.
Forgiveness is not pretending evil never happened.
Forgiveness rests upon the mercy of a Savior who knows exactly how devastating evil is.
And repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because somebody discovered the truth.
It is turning from sin toward God.
That invitation is for everyone.
The wounded believer.
The bitter critic.
The frightened witness.
The fallen pastor.
The person who abused authority.
The person who remained silent when courage was needed.
The person who has been hiding behind religious language.
And the person who has almost given up on faith altogether.
Nobody comes to the cross with a reputation impressive enough to save them.
We come as sinners who need mercy.
And the ground is level at the foot of the cross.
But mercy must never be confused with the absence of earthly consequences.
A repentant leader may receive God's forgiveness and still need to step down from leadership.
A person who has committed a crime may repent and still be answerable to civil authorities.
A relationship may experience forgiveness without immediately regaining trust.
Reconciliation, where possible and safe, requires truth, repentance, and meaningful change.
The Gospel offers redemption.
It does not require victims to deny reality.
And perhaps that is the truth someone has been waiting years to hear.
You can love Jesus and still acknowledge what happened.
You can believe in grace and still seek justice.
You can pray for someone's repentance without placing yourself back under their control.
You can leave an unsafe situation without leaving Christ.
And you can begin healing even before everyone involved admits the truth.
There is one final detail about David that deserves to remain in our hearts.
He had an opportunity to take Saul's life.
Instead, he left judgment in God's hands.
But he also refused to call darkness light.
That is the balance we desperately need today.
A church where leaders are honored but never idolized.
Where accusations are examined fairly rather than accepted blindly.
Where wrongdoing is confronted rather than concealed.
Where wounded people are heard rather than threatened.
Where faithful pastors are supported rather than constantly attacked.
Where repentance matters more than reputation.
Where truth is not treated as an enemy of unity.
And where Jesus Christ remains the only unquestionable Lord of His Church.
Because the Church does not belong to the loudest preacher.
It does not belong to the wealthiest donor.
It does not belong to the most influential ministry founder.
It was purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ.
And He has not surrendered His authority to anyone.
If this message has exposed something you have been carrying, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
Not a public accusation against someone whose situation we do not know.
Not a place to spread names, rumors, or unverified allegations.
But a place where truth and grace can meet.
You do not have to share private details to be worthy of prayer.
And if you have a testimony of how God restored your trust in Him after spiritual disappointment, your words may encourage someone who is barely holding on.
Maybe this article reminded you of someone.
A friend who quietly stopped attending church.
A family member who was hurt by religious hypocrisy.
A believer who thinks asking questions means losing faith.
A pastor who genuinely wants to lead with humility and integrity.
Or someone who has never trusted Christianity because of what they witnessed among Christians.
Not to create hostility against the Church, but to help people distinguish the character of Jesus from the failures of human beings.
Because our calling is not to build an audience that blindly agrees with us.
It is to point people toward the Savior who calls every one of us to truth, repentance, faith, and love.
That is also why I want to speak openly about something that helps this ministry continue.
Not because you owe this ministry your loyalty.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering from the resources God has entrusted to you.
Scripture teaches generosity that is willing rather than pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
It is a voluntary way to help sustain and expand this particular ministry.
The greater purpose is the ministry we can help sustain together.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible.
We want the Gospel to be shared because it is true, not because someone paid to hear it.
Read.
Pray.
Encourage someone.
A thoughtful Facebook share may reach a person we could never have reached ourselves.
A personal tag may bring this message to someone who has been silently struggling.
A sincere comment may remind another wounded believer that they are not alone.
And your prayers matter.
The mission is not about proving loyalty to Gospel Warrior.
It is about making much of Jesus Christ.
Because one day, every earthly title will lose its power to impress.
Every platform will fall silent.
Every hidden thing will stand before the righteous judgment of God.
And the question will not be how successfully we protected our image.
It will be whether we belonged to Christ.
Whether we trusted His mercy.
Whether we obeyed His truth.
Whether we loved the people He entrusted to our care.
Whether we were willing to repent when His Word exposed our sin.
So let us honor faithful shepherds.
Let us pray for pastors and spiritual leaders.
Let us refuse reckless accusations and malicious gossip.
Let us protect the vulnerable.
Let us pursue truth with humility.
Let us reject revenge.
Let us welcome genuine repentance.

And above all, let us keep our eyes on Jesus Christ, the Shepherd who never abuses His sheep, the King who never corrupts justice, and the Savior whose grace is powerful enough to transform even the hardest heart.
David would not raise his sword against Saul.
But he would not bury the truth to protect Saul's reputation either.
And maybe the lesson we have needed all along is not that anointed people must never be questioned.
Maybe it is that we must never use another person's sin as permission to abandon our own obedience to God.
Because truth without love can become cruelty.
Love without truth can become complicity.
But in Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
And there is room at His cross for both the wounded person who needs healing and the guilty person who truly repents.
The hands that were nailed to the cross will never demand that you hide another person's sin to prove your love for Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A DIVORCED CHRISTIAN REMARRY? THE WORDS OF JESUS THAT HAVE DIVIDED FAITHFUL BELIEVERS—AND THE TRUTH TOO MANY BROKEN HEARTS NEVER HEAR
paragraphs: CAN A DIVORCED CHRISTIAN REMARRY? THE WORDS OF JESUS THAT HAVE DIVIDED FAITHFUL BELIEVERS—AND THE TRUTH TOO MANY BROKEN HEARTS NEVER HEAR

Jesus spoke about divorce with unmistakable seriousness. Paul addressed abandonment. And one small Greek phrase has become the center of a centuries-old disagreement. But behind every theological argument is a human soul wondering: “Does God still have a future for me?”
There is a kind of silence that happens when someone asks a question in church and suddenly realizes everyone has an opinion about their life.
“Can I get married again?”
Five words.

But behind them might be fifteen years of marriage. Children who cried themselves to sleep. A spouse who walked away. An affair that destroyed trust. A home that became unsafe. A divorce certificate that arrived after years of desperate prayers.
Or perhaps something even more complicated.
Perhaps you were the one who sinned.

You betrayed someone. You broke your vows. You made decisions you cannot undo. And now, years later, you have genuinely repented, surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, and begun wondering whether the possibility of marriage is forever closed to you.
One Christian tells you, “God forgives. You can start again.”
Another opens the Bible and says, “Jesus called remarriage adultery.”
Both claim to love Scripture.
Both may sincerely fear misrepresenting God.
And suddenly, the question is no longer simply whether you can remarry.
It becomes something much more frightening.
“If I get this wrong, will I be disobeying the Lord I love?”
If that question has ever kept you awake at night, please stay with me.
Because we are going to examine words that cannot be ignored, exceptions that cannot be casually dismissed, and disagreements that deserve more honesty than they usually receive.
And before this is over, we need to confront something that can be even more dangerous than getting the interpretation wrong.
We need to confront what happens when people use God's holiness to crush wounded souls—or use God's grace to excuse what He calls sin.
Both errors can lead people away from Jesus.
And neither one is acceptable.
When the Pharisees approached Jesus about divorce in Matthew 19, they were not simply seeking compassionate guidance for struggling marriages.
They were testing Him.
“Is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?” (Matthew 19:3, ESV).

The question emerged within a Jewish world where interpretations of Deuteronomy 24:1 differed. Some teachers understood the grounds for divorce narrowly, particularly in relation to sexual misconduct. Others permitted divorce for a much wider range of offenses.
Jesus refused to begin where they wanted Him to begin.
Instead of debating how easily a marriage could be dissolved, He took them back to why marriage existed.
“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female...?” (Matthew 19:4, ESV).
Then He declared:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” (Matthew 19:6, ESV).
In Greek, the central command reads:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν, ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω.
Ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō.
The meaning is clear:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Notice the force of Jesus' answer.
He did not describe marriage as merely a private agreement that could be terminated whenever two people stopped feeling fulfilled.
He pointed to God's creative design.
Marriage is a covenantal union, not a disposable arrangement.
And that matters because our culture often asks whether marriage still makes us happy before asking whether we are being faithful.
But there is another danger.
Some Christians hear Jesus' command to preserve marriage and conclude that a person must remain physically present in a dangerous household no matter what happens.
That is not what this passage says.
Jesus' defense of marriage must never become an excuse for violence, coercion, intimidation, or abuse.
A marriage covenant does not grant one spouse ownership over the other's body, conscience, or safety.
And no one should be pressured to remain in immediate danger while church leaders debate the technicalities of divorce.
Yet the seriousness of Jesus' words remains.
Marriage matters to God.
Faithfulness matters to God.
And what God joins together must never be treated as something we can casually tear apart.
Then comes the sentence that changes the entire conversation.
In Matthew 19:9, Jesus says:
“And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery.” (ESV).
Read that again.
Slowly.
Jesus explicitly condemns a particular pattern of divorce followed by remarriage.
But He also includes a phrase that has generated enormous theological disagreement.
μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ
Mē epi porneia.
Commonly translated, “except for sexual immorality.”
The word porneia refers broadly to sexual immorality. Its precise scope depends on context, and it should not simply be equated with every possible kind of marital unhappiness.
Here is where the disagreement begins.

Many Protestant interpreters understand Jesus to be identifying a genuine exception: when a spouse commits serious sexual immorality, the innocent spouse may have legitimate grounds for divorce and, in their interpretation, may also be free to remarry.
Their reasoning is that the exception modifies Jesus' condemnation of divorce and remarriage, not merely the divorce itself.
They argue that Jesus would not introduce an exception without allowing it to carry meaningful consequences.
But other faithful Christians disagree.
Some understand the exception as permitting separation or divorce in certain circumstances without necessarily granting permission for another marriage while the original spouse remains alive.
Others understand porneia more narrowly in this context, including interpretations involving unlawful unions or particular sexual violations.
These positions are not identical, and they should not be carelessly combined.

The Roman Catholic Church, for example, teaches that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by divorce. A declaration of nullity is not permission to dissolve such a marriage; it is a judgment that a valid marriage bond was not established in the first place.

Eastern Orthodox churches have historically approached some tragic marital breakdowns through a different pastoral and ecclesial framework, sometimes permitting remarriage under penitential conditions.
And among Protestants, substantial disagreement remains.
Some allow remarriage following adultery or abandonment.
Others maintain that remarriage is ordinarily prohibited while a former spouse lives.
Still others recognize additional circumstances involving severe covenant-breaking, though they differ about how such conclusions are established biblically.
These are not minor disagreements.
They affect consciences, families, children, church membership, pastoral care, and the future of people who desperately want to obey Jesus.
But we must be careful.
The existence of disagreement does not mean Jesus' words are unclear about everything.
He is unmistakably opposed to treating marriage as disposable.
He is unmistakably opposed to using divorce as a convenient pathway to another relationship.
And He is unmistakably calling His followers to a higher standard of covenant faithfulness.
The disputed question is how His exception applies to the possibility of remarriage.
That distinction matters.
Because a person can acknowledge genuine interpretive disagreement without pretending every interpretation is equally persuasive.
And a person can hold a firm conviction without accusing every Christian who disagrees of deliberately rejecting Scripture.
Then Paul enters the conversation.
And the question becomes even more difficult.
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul addresses marriages involving believers and unbelievers.
He tells a Christian spouse not to divorce an unbelieving spouse who is willing to remain in the marriage.
But then he describes a different situation.
What if the unbelieving spouse leaves?
Paul writes:
The Greek phrase is:
οὐ δεδούλωται ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἡ ἀδελφὴ
Ou dedoulōtai ho adelphos ē hē adelphē.
Literally, the brother or sister “has not been enslaved” or “is not enslaved.”
Those words are profoundly important.
Paul does not command the abandoned believer to force an unwilling spouse to stay.
He recognizes the reality of abandonment.
He speaks of peace.
But does “not enslaved” mean the abandoned Christian is also free to remarry?
That is precisely where interpreters disagree.

Some argue that release from the marriage obligation includes freedom to enter another marriage. They see abandonment as a genuine dissolution of the marital relationship and consider Paul's language sufficiently broad to include remarriage.
Others point out that Paul does not explicitly say “free to remarry” in this verse.
They also observe that the Greek verb translated “enslaved” here is different from the verb used elsewhere to describe being bound in marriage.
In 1 Corinthians 7:39, for example, Paul states that a wife is bound to her husband while he lives, but is free to marry after his death.
For interpreters who prohibit remarriage while a former spouse lives, that difference in language is significant.
For interpreters who permit remarriage after abandonment, it is not decisive.
And there is another layer.
In 1 Corinthians 7:10–11, Paul instructs a separated wife to remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband, and he tells the husband not to divorce his wife.
Some Christians regard that instruction as establishing the ordinary rule even after divorce.
Others understand Paul's later discussion of abandonment as introducing an additional circumstance that must be considered separately.
Here is the crucial point.
We must not pretend Paul explicitly answers a question he leaves open to interpretation.
He explicitly addresses separation, abandonment, reconciliation, and peace.
Whether his words authorize remarriage in the abandonment case is a conclusion interpreters draw from the passage and its relationship to the rest of Scripture.
That conclusion deserves careful examination, not confident oversimplification.
And now we arrive at the part of this conversation that may hurt.
Because perhaps you are reading this while remembering the day your spouse confessed an affair.
Perhaps you remember the trembling hands.
The messages on the phone.
The explanations that kept changing.
The horrible realization that the person you trusted had been living another life.
Or perhaps you remember the day your husband or wife simply stopped coming home.
You prayed.
You waited.
You tried counseling.
You asked God to soften a heart that seemed determined to leave.
And eventually, the marriage ended.
Now someone has told you that if you ever marry again, you will be living in adultery.
Another person has told you that God wants you to move on.
And you do not know whom to believe.
Please hear this.
Your suffering does not make every decision permissible. But neither does your divorce make you untouchable, worthless, or beyond the mercy of Christ.
Jesus did not come to build a community where wounded people must hide their stories to be treated with dignity.
He came to call sinners to repentance and to save those who cannot save themselves.
And that includes people whose marriages have collapsed.
It includes people who were betrayed.
It includes people who abandoned their vows.
It includes people whose sin contributed to the destruction of a family.
It includes people who are ashamed of what they have done.
But grace must never be confused with automatic permission.
Forgiveness and permission are not the same thing.
A Christian may be completely forgiven for past sin while still needing to ask whether a particular future action is consistent with God's Word.
That is why this subject cannot be resolved simply by saying, “God wants you happy.”
Nor can it be resolved by saying, “You are divorced, therefore your life is permanently ruined.”
Both statements fall short of the Gospel.
Consider another passage.
In Romans 7:2–3, Paul uses marriage as an illustration while explaining the relationship between believers and the law.
He describes a married woman as bound to her husband while he lives and says that if she belongs to another man while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress.
Those who oppose remarriage after divorce often appeal to this passage, along with Luke 16:18 and Mark 10:11–12.
They emphasize that Jesus' teaching in Mark and Luke contains no stated exception.
And their concern deserves to be heard.
They fear that modern Christianity has become so eager to affirm second marriages that it has softened the radical demands of Jesus.
That concern should not be mocked.

But other interpreters respond that Romans 7 is using the ordinary permanence of marriage to illustrate another theological point, not presenting a comprehensive treatment of every possible exception.
They also argue that Matthew's exception clause must be taken seriously when interpreting the parallel Gospel accounts.
Their concern is that a blanket prohibition may fail to recognize situations Jesus and Paul specifically address.
That concern should not be mocked either.
This is what responsible biblical interpretation requires.
Not selecting the verse that confirms what we already want.
Not pretending a difficult passage does not exist.
Not allowing our personal experience to become the final authority.
But reading Scripture alongside Scripture, respecting context, recognizing literary purpose, and asking what the biblical authors actually intended to communicate.
And there is one more painful reality we cannot ignore.
What about abuse?
What about a spouse who repeatedly threatens violence?
What about someone who uses Scripture to control, humiliate, isolate, or terrorize another person?
What about children who are afraid to go home?
Christians differ over whether particular patterns of severe abuse constitute grounds for divorce and whether they permit remarriage.
Some understand persistent, severe abuse as a form of covenant abandonment, even when the abusive spouse has not physically left.
Others believe Scripture permits necessary separation for protection without necessarily dissolving the marriage bond or authorizing remarriage.
Still others approach these circumstances through church discipline, civil protection, and pastoral discernment.
These differences must be acknowledged.
But the immediate duty to protect people from harm must not be delayed until every remarriage question is settled.
If you are being abused, seek safety and appropriate help from trusted people, qualified professionals, and relevant authorities.
A church should never make a person's physical safety dependent on winning a theological argument.
God's commands are not weapons for abusers.
And protecting a person from violence is not an attack on the sanctity of marriage.
Now consider something that makes this entire discussion even more personal.
What if the divorce happened before you became a Christian?
What if you were already remarried when you came to faith?
What if you and your current spouse have children together?
What if your first marriage ended decades ago?
What does repentance require now?
These are serious pastoral questions.
Christians disagree about how to apply the biblical passages to existing remarriages, especially when another family has already been established.
Some believe a remarriage entered contrary to Scripture begins in sin but should not automatically be dissolved after it has become an actual marriage.
Others believe that if a present relationship is biblically adulterous, repentance may require separation.
There are also differences concerning whether a prior marriage was valid, whether reconciliation remains possible, and how obligations to children and former spouses should be honored.
No responsible article can settle every one of those cases with a single sentence.
And no pastor should treat a complicated human history as though it were a theological puzzle without real people inside it.

If this describes your situation, seek careful counsel from spiritually mature church leaders who will open Scripture with you, listen to the facts, take your safety seriously, and explain their conclusions without manipulation.
Do not rush into another marriage merely because someone tells you that grace makes every choice acceptable.
But do not accept a lifelong sentence of shame merely because someone speaks with certainty.
The loudest voice in the room is not necessarily the voice most faithful to Scripture.
And the person who sounds the strictest is not automatically the holiest.
Jesus reserved some of His strongest rebukes for religious leaders who placed heavy burdens on others while failing to show the justice, mercy, and faithfulness that God's law required.
That does not mean biblical commands can be discarded whenever they become painful.
It means biblical truth must be handled truthfully, humbly, and with the character of Christ.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was accused of adultery.
Her accusers were eager to condemn her.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of those who stood ready to stone her.
And when they departed, He spoke words that every wounded sinner needs to understand.
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” (John 8:11, ESV).
Notice what Jesus did not do.
He did not pretend sin was harmless.
He did not redefine adultery to make everyone comfortable.
He did not tell her that repentance was unnecessary.
But neither did He treat her as though her failure had erased her humanity.
Mercy and holiness stood together in the same Savior.

We should also remember that the account of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is marked accordingly in many modern Bible translations. Christians differ about its textual status. Its portrayal of mercy joined to a call away from sin is consistent with teachings securely attested elsewhere in the New Testament, but we should be transparent about that manuscript question.
And that brings us to the heart of this article.
The Gospel is not the announcement that divorce does not matter.
It is not the announcement that remarriage is always permissible.
It is not the announcement that every person who remarries is necessarily living in unrepentant sin.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and that everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness and new life.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:11, after naming serious patterns of sin:
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” (ESV).
What a sentence.
“And such were some of you.”
Not because their past never happened.
Not because their actions never wounded anyone.
Not because holiness no longer mattered.
But because the saving grace of Jesus Christ was powerful enough to transform people whose lives had been marked by sin.
Maybe that is what you need to hear.
Your past is real.
The damage may be real.
The consequences may remain.
And some doors may not be open simply because you wish they were.
But your story is not beyond the reach of the Redeemer.
A divorce decree cannot erase the image of God in you.
An affair does not make repentance impossible.
A failed marriage does not place a person outside the reach of the cross.
And obedience to Christ is never wasted, even when it costs you something you deeply desire.
For one person, faithfulness may mean pursuing reconciliation where it is safe, appropriate, and genuinely possible.
For another, it may mean accepting that reconciliation cannot be forced.
For another, it may mean remaining single because of a sincere conviction about Scripture.
For another, it may mean entering a new marriage only after careful biblical examination of the grounds for divorce.
For someone already remarried, it may mean seeking wise counsel about repentance, present covenant responsibilities, and how to honor Christ faithfully now.
These are not interchangeable circumstances.
And none should be approached with a casual heart.
But here is what every one of those people needs equally.
Jesus.
Not merely a ruling.
Not merely an exception.
Not merely a church's permission.
Jesus Christ Himself.
Because marriage is not the Savior.
Singleness is not the Savior.
A second wedding is not the Savior.
Even a perfect record of marital faithfulness cannot justify a sinner before God.
Only Christ can save.
And His grace does not make obedience unnecessary.
His grace teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God brings salvation and trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
That means genuine grace is never an invitation to stop caring what God commands.
It is the power that draws us back to Him.
So can a divorced Christian remarry?

The most responsible answer is that Christians agree divorce and remarriage must be governed by Scripture, but they disagree about whether—and under which circumstances—the Bible permits remarriage while a former spouse is still alive.
Many understand sexual immorality in Matthew 19:9 and abandonment in 1 Corinthians 7:15 as possible biblical grounds for remarriage.
Others believe those passages do not remove the continuing marriage bond in a way that permits remarriage.
The disagreement is real.
The consequences are serious.
And the answer in an individual case requires more than a slogan.
But the question beneath the question may be even more important.
Are you seeking God's permission to do what you already want, or are you genuinely willing to obey Him even if His answer is difficult?
That question is not only for divorced people.
It is for the married Christian who has begun entertaining an emotional affair.
It is for the spouse who is looking for an excuse to abandon a marriage because the excitement has faded.
It is for the church leader who wants a simple rule more than a truthful understanding of a complicated situation.
It is for the Christian who uses grace to justify disobedience.
And it is for the Christian who uses truth as an excuse to withhold compassion.
All of us must come before the same Lord.
All of us must surrender our preferences.
All of us need mercy.
Perhaps tonight you will close this article without having every question answered.
Perhaps you will still need to sit with your pastor.
Perhaps you will need to study Matthew 5, Matthew 19, Mark 10, Luke 16, Romans 7, and 1 Corinthians 7 more carefully.
Perhaps you will need to confess something.
Perhaps you will need to forgive someone.
Perhaps you will need to stop pursuing a relationship until you have honestly examined whether it honors Christ.
Perhaps you will need to stop condemning someone whose full story you do not know.
But whatever happens next, do not run from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Bring Him the confusion.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the memories you cannot erase.
Bring Him the sin you have been defending.
Bring Him the fear that you may never be loved again.
And ask Him for something greater than the answer you were hoping to hear.
Ask Him for a heart that loves the truth.
Ask Him for courage to obey.
Ask Him for humility to recognize where sincere Christians differ.
Ask Him for the strength to walk in holiness without surrendering to despair.
And ask Him to teach His Church how to speak about broken marriages without breaking wounded people further.
Because from scandal to grace does not mean from sin to permission.
It means from sin and shame to the transforming mercy of Jesus Christ.
It means the cross is powerful enough to forgive what we cannot undo.
It means resurrection hope reaches places where human hope has died.
And it means the Author of redemption is still at work, even when the next chapter looks nothing like the one we planned.
If this article has touched a place you rarely talk about, I want to invite you into a conversation that requires courage.

You do not have to disclose private details to strangers. A few honest words are enough. And if you have experienced God's grace through a painful marital season, your testimony may encourage someone who believes their life is already over.
We want this community to be a place where difficult questions are not hidden, where repentance is not mocked, where grace is never cheapened, and where Jesus Christ remains at the center.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment available to people who may not otherwise have access to it.
But if you believe this work is worth sustaining, your partnership can make a meaningful difference.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.
You are still welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep studying.
Keep praying.
Keep sharing the truth.
Above all, keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because someday, the deepest question will not be whether you managed to convince everyone that your marital history was acceptable.
It will be whether you knew Christ, trusted His mercy, and sought to walk faithfully in His truth.
The Savior who met sinners with both compassion and a call to repentance has not changed.
His holiness has not diminished.
His mercy has not run dry.
His cross is still sufficient.
His resurrection is still our hope.
And the broken places of your life are not hidden from His sight.
Your marriage may have ended, but the mercy of Jesus has not—and the chapter you wish you could erase does not have to be the final word over your soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE DIDN’T JUST STEAL HIS FATHER’S THRONE. HE TOOK HIS FATHER’S WOMEN—AND MADE ALL ISRAEL WATCH.
paragraphs: HE DIDN’T JUST STEAL HIS FATHER’S THRONE. HE TOOK HIS FATHER’S WOMEN—AND MADE ALL ISRAEL WATCH.

Why did Absalom’s adviser command something so shocking? The disturbing truth behind 2 Samuel 16:20–22 reveals how sexual humiliation became a weapon of political power—and why the story ultimately points us to a King who conquers not by disgracing others, but by bearing our disgrace Himself.
There are sins committed in darkness.
And then there are sins deliberately dragged into the sunlight because someone wants the whole world to see.
What happened on the rooftop of King David’s palace was not a secret affair. It was not a moment of uncontrollable passion. It was not even primarily about sexual desire.
It was a calculated political act.
A son wanted his father's kingdom.
An adviser knew exactly how to make reconciliation almost impossible.
And ten women, whose names Scripture does not even record, were caught in the middle of a brutal struggle for power.
But here is what makes this story even more disturbing.
Years earlier, another man had stood on a rooftop in Jerusalem, looked upon a woman, and used royal power to take what was not his.
That man was David.
Now David's own son was standing at the center of a public sexual scandal in the very palace his father had abandoned.
Coincidence?
Not according to the biblical narrative.
And before we finish, you may discover that the most frightening thing about this story is not simply what Absalom did to his father.
It is what happens when human beings become so desperate for control that they stop seeing other people as people.
Because the moment power becomes your god, someone else usually becomes your sacrifice.
And that is where this story begins.
Absalom was not an ordinary rebellious son.
He was handsome, charismatic, politically gifted, and deeply wounded by the dysfunction of his father's household.

His sister Tamar had been sexually violated by their half brother Amnon. David became angry, but the biblical account records no corresponding punishment of Amnon. Absalom eventually murdered Amnon and fled.
Years passed.
The family never truly healed.
And resentment became something far more dangerous.
A political ambition.

Absalom began cultivating public loyalty. He positioned himself near the city gate, listened to people's grievances, questioned whether they would receive justice, and presented himself as the leader who would finally care about them.
Second Samuel 15:6 describes the result:
“So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” (KJV)
Notice the language.
He did not begin by taking the throne.
He began by taking hearts.
That is often how destructive leadership works.

It offers understanding before demanding allegiance. It presents itself as the answer to every disappointment. It convinces wounded people that their pain can be healed by putting someone new in power.
And sometimes, by the time people recognize the manipulation, they have already surrendered their judgment.
Eventually, Absalom declared himself king.
David fled Jerusalem.
The father who once defeated Goliath was now running from his own son.
Imagine that journey.
The king leaving his city.
The palace behind him.
The sound of weeping.
The humiliation of watching his own household collapse.
David had conquered enemies on battlefields, but he could not command his broken family to become whole.
Then Absalom entered Jerusalem.
And he turned to a man named Ahithophel.
Ahithophel was no ordinary political adviser.
Second Samuel 16:23 says that his counsel was regarded in those days with extraordinary authority, as though someone had consulted the word of God.
That description explains his influence. It does not mean that his advice was morally approved by God.
A person can possess remarkable intelligence and still use it for devastating evil.
A person can understand politics and completely misunderstand righteousness.
A person can give advice that works and still lead someone toward destruction.
Absalom asked:
“Give counsel among you what we shall do.” (2 Samuel 16:20, KJV)
Ahithophel's response was chilling.

“Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.” (2 Samuel 16:21, KJV)
Read that carefully.
Ahithophel was not recommending romance.
He was recommending a public act of sexual domination.
He wanted Absalom to take the women associated with David's royal household, making a visible declaration that David's authority had been replaced.
In the ancient royal world, access to a king's women could carry political significance because the royal household was closely associated with the king's position.
We see this connection elsewhere in Scripture.
When Reuben slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine, Genesis 35:22 recorded the offense, and Genesis 49:3–4 later connected Reuben's sexual misconduct with the loss of his preeminence.

In 1 Kings 2:13–25, Adonijah's request to marry Abishag, who had attended David in his old age, was interpreted by Solomon as a threat connected to the kingdom, even though 1 Kings 1:4 explicitly states that David had not had sexual relations with her.
These passages do not make every case identical.
But they reveal a recurring political reality.
A king's household was not treated as an entirely private sphere.
Claims involving women associated with the royal household could be interpreted as claims involving royal succession.
Ahithophel understood this.
And he wanted Absalom's rebellion to become unmistakable.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 16:21 makes his reasoning particularly revealing.
וְשָׁמַע כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל כִּי־נִבְאַשְׁתָּ אֶת־אָבִיךָ
Ve-shama kol-Yisra'el ki-niv'ashta et-avikha.
A close rendering is:
“And all Israel will hear that you have become odious to your father.”
The Hebrew verb translated “become odious” conveys the idea of becoming offensive, detestable, or repugnant.
Ahithophel wanted the nation to know that Absalom had crossed a line so grievous that ordinary father-son reconciliation would appear impossible.
Why?
Because rebellion becomes unstable when followers suspect their leader might negotiate peace and abandon them.
Ahithophel wanted to remove that uncertainty.
He wanted Absalom's supporters to believe there was no turning back.
The final words of his counsel explain the political objective:
“Then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.”
Strengthened hands meant strengthened resolve.
His supporters would become more confident that Absalom was committed to overthrowing David.
In other words, Ahithophel was saying:
Make your rebellion so public, so offensive, and so irreversible that everyone knows you have chosen the throne over your father.
And Absalom listened.
Second Samuel 16:22 records:
“So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.” (KJV)
A tent.
A rooftop.
A public announcement through an act of sexual possession.

The text does not require us to imagine the entire population literally watching the sexual acts themselves. The tent and the phrase “in the sight of all Israel” emphasize the public, notorious character of what Absalom did.
It was meant to be known.
It was meant to humiliate David.
It was meant to announce a transfer of power.
But we must not miss the people whom political readings often leave behind.
The women.
David had left ten concubines to keep the palace when he fled, according to 2 Samuel 15:16.
These women did not design Absalom's rebellion.
They did not appoint Ahithophel.
They did not choose the political struggle consuming Jerusalem.
Yet their bodies became the instruments through which powerful men communicated dominance.
Scripture does not tell us their private thoughts or describe their individual responses. We should not invent details about what each woman experienced.
But neither should we romanticize their situation.
The narrative presents them within a severe imbalance of power, subjected to an act orchestrated for political humiliation.
They were not merely symbols in a royal dispute.
They were human beings.
And the tragedy did not end on the rooftop.

After David returned to Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 20:3 tells us that he placed these ten women in a guarded house, provided for them, and did not resume marital relations with them. They lived in confinement until their deaths, described as living in widowhood.
The rebellion ended.
But their lives were never restored to what they had been.
That detail should trouble us.
Because sometimes history remembers the names of kings while barely acknowledging the suffering of those crushed beneath their decisions.
And sometimes people who never started a conflict carry its consequences for the rest of their lives.
Perhaps that is the part of this story you recognize.
Not the throne.
Not the palace.
But the feeling of being caught in somebody else's war.
A family dispute you did not create.
A betrayal you did not deserve.
A relationship where someone treated your dignity as expendable.
A powerful person making decisions while you were left to live with the damage.
The Bible does not call such cruelty good simply because it appears in the story of Israel's kings.
Describing evil is not endorsing evil.
And the God who inspired Scripture does not require us to pretend that the suffering of vulnerable people is insignificant.
But there is another layer to this passage.
One that takes us back to David's own sin.
Years earlier, in 2 Samuel 11, David had been on the roof of his palace when he saw Bathsheba bathing.
He sent messengers.
He took her.
And after she became pregnant, he attempted to conceal what had happened.
When his schemes failed, David arranged for her husband Uriah to be placed in deadly battle conditions.
Uriah died.
David then took Bathsheba as his wife.
For a time, the king appeared to have successfully managed the scandal.
But 2 Samuel 11:27 ends with a devastating judgment:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” (KJV)
What the palace could conceal, God could see.
What political power could excuse, God condemned.
The prophet Nathan confronted David.
And in 2 Samuel 12:11–12, Nathan announced that calamity would arise against David from his own household and that his wives would be taken in public view.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 is striking:
כִּי אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ בַסָּתֶר וַאֲנִי אֶעֱשֶׂה אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנֶגֶד הַשָּׁמֶשׁ
Ki attah asita va-sater, va-ani e'eseh et-ha-davar hazzeh neged kol-Yisra'el ve-neged ha-shamesh.
A close translation is:
“For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.”
Secretly.
Before all Israel.
Before the sun.
The contrast is deliberate.
David's abuse of power had been concealed.
The humiliation that entered his household would become public.
The rooftop scene in 2 Samuel 16 is therefore not merely a random political scandal.
It is a narrative fulfillment of Nathan's prophetic warning.
But we must handle that truth carefully.
God's announcement of judgment does not mean that Absalom's actions were morally righteous, that Ahithophel's counsel was holy, or that the women deserved what happened to them.
The Bible can describe God sovereignly bringing judgment through human events while still holding the human participants accountable for their evil.
Absalom remained responsible for his rebellion.
Ahithophel remained responsible for his counsel.
And the women must never be blamed for David's earlier sin.
This distinction matters because careless interpretations can turn Scripture into a weapon against victims.
The prophetic warning explains the theological significance of the event.
It does not justify the abuse.
And here is the painful lesson.
David had been forgiven, but forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence of what he had done.
When David confessed, “I have sinned against the LORD,” Nathan answered in 2 Samuel 12:13:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die.” (KJV)
That was real mercy.
Real forgiveness.
But the chapter also records continuing judgment and grief.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending nothing happened.
Grace does not require victims to deny their wounds.
Repentance does not guarantee that broken trust immediately returns.
And a forgiven sinner may still need to face consequences, repair what can be repaired, and accept responsibility for damage that cannot simply be undone.
That is not the absence of grace.
It is the seriousness of sin.
Perhaps you have prayed for forgiveness over something that still haunts you.
Perhaps God has been merciful, yet the consequences remain.
A relationship has changed.
A child no longer trusts you.
A marriage is struggling.
A decision made years ago continues to affect your family.
And you wonder whether the presence of consequences means the absence of God's mercy.
David's story says otherwise.
But it also refuses to make repentance cheap.
The grace of God is not permission to keep harming people.
It is the mercy that calls us to turn from sin and walk in truth.
Now look again at Absalom.
He wanted the kingdom.
He wanted recognition.
He wanted the people to believe he was the rightful answer to David's failures.
And his adviser offered him a shortcut.
Do something shocking.
Make it public.
Force everyone to choose sides.
Make yourself impossible to ignore.
Does that sound entirely ancient?
We live in a world where public humiliation can become a form of influence.
Where people expose private wounds to win an argument.
Where families use secrets as weapons.
Where leaders confuse fear with respect.
Where someone may destroy another person's reputation simply to prove that they have power.
And where even religious people can become so obsessed with winning that they forget whom they are called to love.
Ahithophel's strategy was effective in its immediate political purpose.
But effectiveness is not righteousness.
Not every open door is from God.
Not every successful strategy has God's approval.
Not every influential voice deserves your obedience.
And not every adviser who knows how to strengthen your position knows how to protect your soul.
You can gain an audience and lose your integrity.
You can win a conflict and destroy your family.
You can appear powerful while becoming a prisoner of the very sin you used to obtain power.
Absalom entered Jerusalem as a conqueror.
But he was not free.
His ambition had become his master.
And before long, the rebellion would collapse.
In 2 Samuel 18, Absalom died during the conflict with David's forces.
When David heard the news, he cried:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!” (2 Samuel 18:33, KJV)
Stop there.
The son who publicly humiliated his father was dead.
The father whose kingdom had been threatened was weeping.
There was no celebration in David's cry.
Only grief.
A father mourning a son he could no longer reach.
A family devastated by sins that had multiplied across generations.
And a throne that could not bring back the dead.
That is the tragedy of Absalom.
He wanted his father's kingdom so desperately that he helped destroy the possibility of peace with his father.
And in the end, the kingdom he wanted could not save him.
But the Bible does not leave us with Absalom.
It leads us toward a greater King.
And this is where the story becomes more than a warning about political power.
Because centuries later, another Son of David would enter Jerusalem.
Not to seize a throne through sexual humiliation.
Not to strengthen His followers by making reconciliation impossible.
Not to sacrifice vulnerable people for His own advancement.
He came to give Himself.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The King whose kingdom is not established by exploiting others.
Listen to His own words:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45, KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Absalom used other people's humiliation to advance his claim to power.
Jesus willingly endured humiliation to save sinners.
Absalom sought to make himself king by taking.
Jesus revealed His kingship through sacrificial giving.
Absalom's rebellion fractured a household.
Christ came to reconcile sinners to God.
And on another day of public shame, the true King was stripped, mocked, and crucified.
He did not commit the sins for which He suffered.
He bore the judgment sinners deserve.
The cross was not another act of selfish royal ambition.
It was the place where the sinless Savior voluntarily laid down His life.
Philippians 2:8 declares:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” (KJV)
The world says power is proved by how many people you can make suffer for you.
Jesus reveals a kingdom in which the King suffers to redeem His people.
That is not weakness.
That is holy love.
And when Jesus rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin, shame, and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This does not mean every earthly wound instantly disappears.
It does not mean every family relationship will be restored in this life.
It does not mean that victims must return to unsafe situations or that repentance removes the need for justice.
It means something deeper.
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Mercy is real.
And the crucified and risen Christ offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Him in faith.
Maybe you see yourself in David.
You have done things you wish you could undo.
You have hidden failures behind a respectable appearance.
You have asked God to forgive you, but you still struggle to face the truth about what happened.
Do not confuse concealment with healing.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Seek to make right what you can.
And trust the mercy of Jesus Christ, who receives repentant sinners.
Maybe you recognize something of Absalom in your own heart.
You have allowed pain to become bitterness.
You have justified cruelty because someone once treated you cruelly.
You have wanted revenge so badly that you stopped caring who would be hurt.
Your wounds matter.
But they do not give you permission to wound others.
Jesus calls you away from revenge and toward repentance.
Or perhaps you recognize the ten women.
You were not the person who started the conflict.
You were the person who suffered because of it.
You were treated like a possession.
Your voice was ignored.
Your dignity was sacrificed for someone else's ambition.
Hear this clearly.
What someone did to you does not determine your worth before God.
You are not merely the worst thing that happened to you.
And the Gospel never asks you to call evil good.
Christ sees the afflicted, welcomes the burdened, and calls His people to protect the vulnerable and practice justice.
The same Savior who calls sinners to repentance also calls His followers to love their neighbors rather than exploit them.
That is why we must never read this passage only as a lesson about kings and thrones.
It is a warning about what happens when power is divorced from righteousness.
When ambition silences conscience.
When clever counsel replaces godly wisdom.
When a person's desire to win becomes greater than their willingness to obey God.
And when the people caught in the middle are forgotten.
The question is no longer simply, “Why did Ahithophel tell Absalom to sleep with his father's concubines?”
We know why.
He wanted a public demonstration of royal power.
He wanted to make Absalom's break with David unmistakable.
He wanted to strengthen the rebels by convincing them that reconciliation was no longer a realistic possibility.
The harder question is this:
What are you willing to sacrifice to get what your heart has decided it must have?
Your integrity?
Your marriage?
Your children?
Your conscience?
Your relationship with God?
Because the thing you are willing to sin to obtain can become the very thing that destroys you.
And no earthly throne is worth the loss of your soul.
Jesus asks in Mark 8:36:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (KJV)
Absalom gained Jerusalem for a moment.
But he lost far more than he understood.
Jesus offers something no stolen throne can provide.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new heart.
A new direction.
An eternal kingdom that cannot be overthrown.
And the invitation is not reserved for people whose stories are clean.
David's story was stained by adultery, abuse of power, deception, and bloodshed.
Yet Scripture also records his confession and God's mercy.
The point is not that sin becomes insignificant when God forgives.
The point is that God's grace is greater than the sinner's ability to save himself.
That is why we keep returning to the Gospel.
Not because scandal is entertaining.
Not because brokenness makes a compelling headline.
But because Jesus Christ is the only Savior who can redeem sinners without denying the seriousness of their sin.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying shame for years.
You smile in church.
You encourage everyone else.
You know how to quote Scripture.
But there is something you have never brought honestly before God.
Or perhaps you are exhausted from trying to forgive someone who has never acknowledged the harm they caused.
You do not need to manufacture a testimony for an audience.
You need the truth.
You need the grace of Christ.
You need wise, faithful people who will help you walk in that truth.
And if your life has become a place of hidden sin, today is a good day to stop hiding.
Not because public exposure saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But because repentance begins with turning away from the lie that you can heal while continuing to protect what is destroying you.
And if God has been teaching you to release bitterness without excusing injustice, share what He has been showing you. Your testimony may help someone who feels alone.
We are not here to collect perfect religious answers.
We are here to point one another toward Jesus.
And that is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish dramatic Bible stories.
Not merely to attract attention.
But to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, recognize sin, discover the mercy of Christ, and grow into mature disciples who love God and love their neighbors.
Return to the Scriptures for yourself. Read 2 Samuel 11–20 and consider the whole narrative, not merely the scandal on the rooftop.
There is also a deeper way to stand alongside this ministry.
For Christians, generosity can be an expression of worship and gratitude to God. But it must always be willing, never pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
You can honor Christ through faithful stewardship, serving others, sharing biblical truth, supporting gospel work, and giving freely according to your ability and conviction.
That benefit is simply an expression of appreciation. The greater purpose is to strengthen biblical discipleship and make Christ-centered resources more accessible.
You are welcome to learn, grow, and share the truth whether or not you become a paying supporter.
Somebody is still trapped in shame.
Somebody is confusing religious performance with repentance.
Somebody has been wounded by a person who claimed to represent God.
Somebody thinks their past is too dark for forgiveness.
Somebody has never heard that the Son of David came not to exploit sinners, but to redeem them.
And somebody may encounter the Gospel because you chose to pass along the truth.
But never forget the center of the message.
It is not Absalom.
It is not Ahithophel.
It is not even David.
It is Jesus Christ.
The King who did not need to steal a throne.
The Savior who refused to use people as instruments of selfish ambition.
The Son of David who carried the cross, conquered the grave, and now calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
So do not leave this story merely horrified by an ancient scandal.
Leave it asking whether your own heart is being ruled by Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy would be to recognize Absalom's ambition, condemn Ahithophel's counsel, grieve David's failures, and never surrender your own sin to the Savior.
The rooftop in Jerusalem reminds us how far sinful people will go to seize a kingdom.
The cross outside Jerusalem reveals how far the love of Christ went to redeem His people.
And there is one truth I hope stays with you long after you close this article:
Absalom tried to become king by making others bear his shame. Jesus proved Himself the true King by willingly bearing the shame of sinners to bring them home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “SUCH WERE SOME OF YOU”—THE FIVE WORDS SATAN NEVER WANTED YOU TO READ AFTER PAUL’S LIST OF SEXUAL SINS
paragraphs: “SUCH WERE SOME OF YOU”—THE FIVE WORDS SATAN NEVER WANTED YOU TO READ AFTER PAUL’S LIST OF SEXUAL SINS
First came the sins nobody wanted exposed. Then came a sentence nobody expected. And hidden between those two realities is the Gospel that can turn your deepest scandal into a testimony of grace.
There is a terrifying way to read the Bible.
You can read just enough to feel condemned… and stop one verse before discovering what Jesus Christ has done for sinners.
Imagine someone sitting alone at two in the morning.
The room is dark. The phone is still glowing. The search history has already been erased.
Another promise has been broken.
Another temptation has won.
Another prayer sounds painfully familiar.
“Lord, I'm sorry. I said I wouldn't do this again.”
Maybe it was pornography.
Maybe an affair.
Maybe a sexual relationship that crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
Maybe a secret addiction, a pattern of lust, or a relationship that has slowly pulled your heart away from obedience to Christ.

Or perhaps your struggle has nothing to do with sex. Perhaps it is greed, drunkenness, deception, bitterness, or the quiet pride that makes you feel morally superior to people whose sins are more visible than yours.
Whatever the struggle, you know the feeling.
That terrible distance between the person you appear to be and the person you fear you have become.
You still know the worship songs.
You still know how to say “God bless you.”
You might even serve in church.
But somewhere inside, a question keeps returning.
If people knew everything about me, would they still believe I belong to Jesus?
And then you open your Bible to 1 Corinthians 6.
Paul begins naming sins.
Sexual immorality.
Idolatry.
Adultery.
Men who engage in same-sex sexual acts.
Theft.
Greed.
Drunkenness.
Verbal abuse.
Swindling.
And suddenly, the passage no longer feels like something written to an ancient church.
It feels painfully close.
Paul warns that those characterized by such unrighteousness will not inherit the kingdom of God.
He does not soften the warning.
He does not call darkness light.
He does not suggest that God's grace makes repentance unnecessary.
And for a moment, the weight of those words is almost unbearable.
But please…
Do not close your Bible at verse 10.
Because verse 11 contains one of the most astonishing declarations ever written to people with sinful pasts.
“And such were some of you.”
Five words in the familiar English phrasing.
A lifetime of shame confronted by the power of the Gospel.
And a truth that changes everything.
The apostle Paul was writing to real believers in Corinth, a city shaped by the religious, commercial, and sexual practices of the Greco-Roman world.
These were not imaginary people in a theological illustration.
They were men and women with histories.
Some had worshiped idols.
Some had exploited others.
Some had committed sexual sins.
Some had been controlled by destructive desires.
Some had lived in patterns of behavior that contradicted the holiness of God.
And yet Paul addressed the Corinthian congregation as people called to belong to Jesus Christ.
How?
Not because their sins had never happened.
Not because their past was suddenly harmless.
Not because God had decided holiness no longer mattered.
But because something greater than their past had entered their lives.
Jesus Christ had saved them.
Listen to the passage in its original Greek.
“Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε· ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:11
A careful English rendering is:
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Notice the first part.
Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε — Kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
The Greek verb ἦτε (ēte) is an imperfect form of the verb “to be,” referring here to what some of them formerly were.
Paul was not saying that their sins had been imaginary.
He was not denying their history.
He was acknowledging it.
Some of you really lived this way.
Some of you really practiced these things.
Some of you really were caught in those patterns.
But then comes a word that changes the direction of the sentence.
ἀλλά — alla.
BUT.
It is a small Greek word carrying an enormous contrast.
You were this.
But.
You lived that way.
But.
You were guilty.
But.
You were not beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ.
That little word does not erase God's judgment against sin.
It announces that God's saving grace has intervened.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that distinction.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It may explain why trust is difficult.
It may explain the consequences you still carry.
It may even explain why certain temptations remain painfully familiar.
But for those who belong to Christ, the past does not possess the final authority to define their standing before God.
Jesus does.
Now consider what Paul says next.
“But you were washed.”
The Greek word is ἀπελούσασθε (apelousasthe), from a verb meaning to wash off or wash away.

Its form is middle voice, so it should not be treated as though the Greek grammar alone proves a simple passive statement. Nevertheless, within Paul's sentence, the cleansing is inseparable from the saving work of Christ and the Spirit of God.
Paul is describing something far deeper than improving one's reputation.
He is speaking of cleansing from sin.
Think about that.
There are stains no amount of public success can remove.
You can move to another city.
Change your phone number.
Delete old conversations.
Start a new relationship.
Build a new career.
Become admired by people who know nothing about your history.
And still carry guilt that follows you into every quiet room.
Because the deepest problem of sin is not merely that someone might discover it.
The deepest problem is that sin is committed before a holy God.
And no amount of hiding can cleanse the conscience.
That is why the Gospel is such extraordinary news.
The blood of Jesus Christ accomplishes what our self-improvement never could.
First John 1:7 declares that the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
Jesus did not come merely to teach guilty people how to appear respectable.
He came to save sinners.
He lived the righteous life we failed to live.
He died for sins He did not commit.
He bore the judgment sinners deserve.
And He rose from the dead, victorious over sin and death.
That is why forgiveness is not God pretending evil never happened.
Forgiveness is mercy grounded in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the person who needs to hear that most is the person who has been trying to punish themselves long after confessing their sin.
You replay the memory.
You hate what you did.
You wonder whether God is tired of hearing your prayers.
But self-condemnation cannot accomplish what only Christ can accomplish.
There is a difference between godly sorrow that leads to repentance and hopeless shame that tells you there is no way home.
Second Corinthians 7:10 speaks of godly grief producing repentance that leads to salvation.
The Holy Spirit convicts us of sin so that we turn toward God.
Despair tells us to remain hidden.
Grace calls us into the light.
And then Paul continues.
“But you were sanctified.”
The Greek is ἡγιάσθητε (hēgiasthēte).
It means “you were sanctified,” or set apart as holy.
This is not merely a promise that one day, after years of effort, God might finally consider you His.
Paul is describing a decisive work of God in those who have come to Christ.
They have been set apart for Him.
And this new belonging carries a new calling.
Because grace does not simply forgive the sinner while leaving sin enthroned.
Grace brings us into a new relationship with God, in which we are called to grow in holiness.
This matters especially when discussing sexual sin.
The Bible does not teach that sexual desire itself makes a person filthy.
Nor does it teach that a person who experiences temptation has automatically committed every sin they are tempted to commit.
Scripture distinguishes temptation from sinful action, and calls believers to resist temptation through the power and grace of God.
But Scripture also refuses to treat sexual conduct as morally meaningless.
Paul's warning in 1 Corinthians 6 is serious because our bodies matter to God.
A few verses later, he tells believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that they have been bought with a price.
Therefore, they are to glorify God in their bodies.
That means following Jesus involves more than claiming a Christian identity while deliberately protecting a lifestyle of disobedience.
It means surrendering our desires, choices, relationships, and bodies to the Lord who redeemed us.
And surrender can be costly.
Sometimes it means ending a relationship that continually leads you into sin.
Sometimes it means confessing deception.
Sometimes it means seeking pastoral care, accountability, or professional help for compulsive behavior.
Sometimes it means making restitution.
Sometimes it means accepting consequences instead of demanding that forgiveness erase them.
And sometimes it means waking up the next morning and choosing obedience again, even though yesterday's temptation has not magically disappeared.
Sanctification does not mean a believer never struggles. It means sin is no longer something we are called to defend as our master.
Romans 6 teaches that those united with Christ are no longer to let sin reign in their mortal bodies.
This does not promise instant freedom from every temptation.
But it does proclaim a new allegiance.
You do not have to make peace with the very thing Christ calls you to forsake.
And you do not have to believe that a difficult struggle makes obedience impossible.
The same Lord who commands holiness also gives grace to help His people pursue it.
Then comes Paul's third declaration.
“But you were justified.”
The Greek word is ἐδικαιώθητε (edikaiōthēte).
It means “you were justified.”
This is courtroom language.
It concerns being declared righteous before God.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost too beautiful for a guilty conscience to comprehend.
Imagine standing before a judge who knows everything.
Every hidden motive.
Every private betrayal.
Every secret compromise.
Every lie you convinced yourself was necessary.
Every moment when you knew what was right and deliberately chose otherwise.
There is no missing evidence.
No technical loophole.
No successful performance.
You cannot argue that your good deeds have somehow canceled your guilt.
And then the Gospel announces that righteousness before God is received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Not earned by moral achievement.
Not purchased by religious donations.
Not secured by a spotless personal history.
Christ Himself is the Savior.
Romans 3:23–24 declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, and that justification is by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That includes the sexually immoral person who repents.
The greedy person who repents.
The proud person who repents.
The religious hypocrite who repents.
And the person who spent years believing that everyone else was too sinful to deserve the mercy they themselves desperately needed.
At the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast.
The person with a publicly scandalous past cannot save themselves.
And the person with a respectable reputation cannot save themselves either.
We are not rescued because our sins were small. We are rescued because our Savior is great.
But there is something else we must understand about Paul's list.
It is often read as though Paul were only interested in condemning sexual sin.
He was not.
Sexual immorality and adultery are there.
The Greek terms μαλακοί (malakoi) and ἀρσενοκοῖται (arsenokoitai) also appear in verse 9.
These terms deserve careful treatment.

Malakoi literally means “soft ones,” and its meaning depends on context. In this vice list, it is often understood as referring to males associated with certain sexual practices, though its precise scope is debated.

Arsenokoitai is a rare compound built from words meaning “male” and “bed,” and is widely understood by traditional Christian interpreters as referring to male same-sex sexual activity. Scholars continue to debate its exact historical scope and the best English rendering.
It would be irresponsible to pretend these translation questions do not exist.
It would also be irresponsible to erase Paul's moral argument simply because parts of the vocabulary are difficult.

The larger passage places sexual conduct under the lordship of Christ, and traditional Christian interpretation understands Paul's teaching in continuity with the biblical sexual ethic expressed elsewhere in Scripture.
But notice something essential.
Paul does not isolate one group of sinners and declare everyone else morally superior.
He includes thieves.
Greedy people.
Drunkards.
Those who verbally abuse others.
Those who defraud others.
And elsewhere in Scripture, pride, hatred, envy, hypocrisy, and countless other sins are condemned.
This passage gives nobody permission to mock, harass, dehumanize, or mistreat another person.
Every human being bears God's image and deserves dignity.
And every human being needs God's mercy.
The church must never become a place where certain sins are publicly condemned while other sins are privately celebrated.
The businessman who cheats people cannot hide behind his respectable suit.
The church leader who manipulates others cannot hide behind his microphone.
The married person committing adultery cannot hide behind a wedding ring.
The person filled with contempt cannot hide behind theological vocabulary.
And the believer who condemns everyone else's failures while refusing to repent of their own has not understood the warning.
Paul begins verse 9 with a command that should make all of us examine ourselves.
“Do not be deceived.”
The warning is not an invitation to obsess over someone else's sins.
It is an invitation to stop lying to ourselves about our own.
And still, the passage does not end with the warning.
It ends with grace.
That is the extraordinary thing.
Paul could have written a letter that simply reminded the Corinthians how terrible their former lives had been.
Instead, he reminded them what Christ had done.
“Such were some of you.”
Not “such were all of you,” because Paul was not claiming every Corinthian believer had committed every listed sin.
Not “such are you forever,” because he was addressing people whose lives had been changed through Christ.
And not “such were some of you, therefore you can never be tempted again.”
The Corinthians still needed correction.
The very existence of this letter proves that believers can struggle with serious sin and need serious rebuke.
But their failures were not a reason to abandon the Gospel.
They were a reason to return to its truth.
That distinction may save someone from two equally destructive lies.
The first lie says, “God is gracious, so my sin does not matter.”
The second says, “My sin is terrible, so God's grace cannot reach me.”
Both misunderstand the cross.
The cross reveals how serious sin really is.
And the cross reveals how astonishing God's mercy really is.
Jesus did not die so that we could comfortably remain enslaved to the sins that destroy us.
He died and rose so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and brought into new life.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Because there is a difference between believing that Jesus forgives sinners and believing that Jesus can forgive you.
You can preach grace to everyone else while secretly believing that your own history is the exception.
You can tell a struggling friend that God is merciful, then spend the night wondering whether you have exhausted that mercy.
You can sing about the blood of Jesus while still living as though your shame is more powerful than His sacrifice.
But hear the Gospel.
Christ did not wait for sinners to become clean before coming to save them.
Romans 5:8 says God demonstrated His love for us in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
And when Jesus called people to follow Him, He did not invite them to continue unchanged.
He called them to repentance and faith.
Think of the woman caught in adultery in John 8, a passage whose manuscript history is disputed and which is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts.
In the familiar account, Jesus refuses to join the crowd in condemning her, yet also tells her to leave her life of sin.
Mercy and holiness are not enemies.
Or think of the Samaritan woman in John 4.
Jesus knew her complicated relational history.
He did not need her to manufacture a respectable story before speaking to her about living water.
And the conversation led her to tell others about Him.
Or think of the apostle Paul himself.
Before becoming a messenger of the Gospel, he persecuted the church.
Later, he called himself the foremost of sinners in 1 Timothy 1:15–16, pointing to Christ's mercy as an example of His patience.
The man who wrote “such were some of you” knew something about a past that could not be undone.
He had memories.
He had a history.
He had reasons to be humbled.
But he also had a Savior.
And that is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus makes the past disappear.
Not because repentance cancels every earthly consequence.
Not because faith guarantees that every damaged relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But because Jesus can redeem a life that sin has wounded.
He can forgive what you cannot undo.
He can transform what you thought would always control you.
He can teach you to walk in truth after years of hiding.
He can give you a new purpose even when your old mistakes still cast shadows.
And He can turn the testimony of a forgiven sinner into an invitation for someone else to come home.
That is not a promise that every Christian story will be easy.
Some believers still face painful consequences from former choices.
Some still battle temptations.
Some carry wounds caused by other people's sins.
And some need years of wise counsel, healing, accountability, and patient discipleship.
The Gospel does not require us to pretend those realities are simple.
It gives us hope in the middle of them.
Because our confidence is not in the speed of our recovery.
Our confidence is in the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
Maybe you are reading this while hiding something.
Maybe your marriage is strained because of a betrayal.
Maybe you are exhausted by a habit you keep promising to stop.
Maybe you are afraid to ask for help because you have built an image of spiritual strength that nobody is allowed to question.
Maybe you have been wounded by people who used Scripture as a weapon rather than speaking truth with love.
Or maybe you are the person who has spent years pointing at the sins of others because you are terrified to confront your own.
Wherever you are, the invitation is not to manufacture another religious performance.
It is to come honestly before Christ.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Believe the Gospel.
Seek the help you need.
Make what amends you can without demanding that others immediately trust you.
And continue following Jesus, one obedient step at a time.
First John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
And Romans 8:1 declares that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Those promises are not excuses for deliberate rebellion.
