But hidden from the queen was the child who would eventually be revealed as king.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because many of us know what it feels like to live through a season in which God's promises seem hidden.
You pray, but nothing seems to change.
You try to do what is right, but someone dishonest appears to prosper.
You choose faithfulness, but your circumstances become more difficult.
You watch people who hurt others gain influence while people who quietly do good seem forgotten.
And somewhere inside you, a painful question begins to form.
“Lord, where are You?”
That question does not make you the first believer to struggle.
The Psalms are filled with the cries of people who trusted God and still wrestled with His apparent silence.
“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” — Psalm 13:1, KJV
David knew that feeling.
And perhaps you do too.
But the story of Joash teaches us to distinguish between what we can see and what God has actually promised.
Athaliah was visible.
Joash was hidden.
Athaliah wore the crown.
Joash carried the surviving royal claim.
Athaliah controlled the palace.
But she did not control God's covenant.
And those six years did not mean that the LORD had abandoned His word.
They meant the story was not finished.
That is not permission to promise ourselves that every painful situation will end exactly as we want.
God never promised that faithful people would escape every tragedy in this fallen world.
But He has promised that His redemptive purposes will not fail.
And that truth becomes even more powerful when we follow the story beyond its opening verses.
In the seventh year, Jehoiada the priest organized the protection and public presentation of Joash.
Second Kings 11:12 records that the child was brought forth, crowned, and anointed.
The people clapped their hands and cried:
“God save the king.”
The boy who had been hidden was now standing before the nation.
Athaliah heard the commotion.
She entered the temple area and saw the young king standing in the place appointed for the royal ceremony.
And she cried:
“Treason, Treason.” — 2 Kings 11:14, KJV
There is a terrible irony in that moment.
The woman who had seized power after the destruction of the royal heirs accused the rightful heir's supporters of treason.
The one who had tried to eliminate the dynasty was now confronting the survival of that dynasty.
Athaliah was subsequently taken outside the temple precincts and executed by order of Jehoiada, as recorded in 2 Kings 11:15–16.
The biblical narrative does not invite us to celebrate violence for its own sake.
It records the judgment of a violent usurper and the restoration of Judah's royal succession.
And then something else happened.
Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD, the king, and the people, that they should be the LORD's people.
The temple of Baal was torn down.
The people turned again toward covenant faithfulness.
The story was not simply about replacing one ruler with another.
It was about restoring the rightful order of worship and allegiance.
Because Judah's deepest problem was never merely political.
It was spiritual.
And that is where this ancient account reaches into our own lives.
We can remove an Athaliah from a throne without removing the idols from our hearts.
We can change our circumstances without surrendering our sin.
We can condemn the wickedness of someone else while protecting the pride, bitterness, dishonesty, or hidden rebellion within ourselves.
It is possible to recognize evil in the palace and still refuse to confront evil in the mirror.
That is why the Gospel does more than tell us that God will eventually judge wicked rulers.
It tells us that every one of us needs a Savior.
Not because every person has committed Athaliah's crimes.
But because all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Romans 3:23 leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
And Romans 3:24 immediately points us toward the astonishing hope of being justified freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
This is the difference between moral outrage and Gospel transformation.
Moral outrage says, “Look how wicked she was.”
The Gospel asks, “What sin in my own heart must I bring into the light of Christ?”
Moral outrage wants the villain exposed.
The Gospel wants sinners redeemed.
And while Scripture never promises that every unrepentant person will be restored, it proclaims that no repentant sinner is beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ.
Even a person whose past is filled with terrible choices must not be told that God's mercy is unavailable if they truly turn to Him.
That does not erase justice.
It does not remove the consequences of wrongdoing.
It does not require victims to deny their suffering or place themselves back into danger.
But it does mean the cross of Christ is sufficient for all who repent and believe.
Now consider something even more remarkable.
Joash was a descendant of David.
His preservation kept the royal line from being extinguished in this crisis.
And through the long, complicated history of that dynasty, Scripture directs our attention toward a greater King.
Jesus Christ.
Matthew opens with these words:
“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” — Matthew 1:1, KJV
Jesus is the fulfillment toward which the Davidic covenant points.
Not because Joash was perfect.
He was not.
In fact, the later chapters of his life are deeply sobering.

Second Chronicles 24 tells us that after Jehoiada died, Joash turned away from the LORD, listened to corrupt influences, and even ordered the killing of Zechariah, Jehoiada's son, who confronted Judah's unfaithfulness.
Think of the tragedy.
The boy whose life had been protected through Jehoiada's household eventually became a king who persecuted the faithful witness of that same household.
This is one of the reasons we must not turn Joash into a simplistic hero.
His rescue was extraordinary.
His later failures were real.
His story demonstrates the faithfulness of God, but it also exposes the limitations of human kings.
Judah did not merely need another descendant of David on the throne.
Judah needed the righteous Son of David.
A King whose obedience would not collapse when faithful advisers died.
A King who would not betray the Father.
A King who would not use innocent blood to preserve His power.
A King who would willingly shed His own blood to save sinners.
And that King is Jesus.
Athaliah sought to preserve her throne through the destruction of others.
Jesus, the rightful King, humbled Himself and gave His life for others.
Athaliah grasped for power.
Jesus, though truly divine, took the form of a servant and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, as Philippians 2:5–8 declares.
Athaliah's story is marked by a royal household threatened by death.
Jesus entered death itself and rose victorious.
The contrast is breathtaking.
One ruler was willing to kill to keep a crown.
The King of kings accepted a crown of thorns to redeem His people.
And on the cross, something happened that no earthly ruler could accomplish.
Jesus bore the penalty of sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose again on the third day.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to all who repent and believe.
The Greek New Testament uses the word χάρις (charis) for “grace.”
It speaks of God's favor and gift, not a reward that sinners can purchase or earn.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — KJV
That means your past is not stronger than Christ's ability to forgive.
Your shame is not more powerful than His mercy.
Your failure does not have the final authority over your life.
And your salvation does not depend on becoming impressive enough to deserve God's attention.
It depends on the Savior who died and rose again.
But grace is not permission to continue living in rebellion.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners calls them to repentance.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a change of mind and direction—a turning from sin toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad because we were exposed.
It is not crying for a moment and returning comfortably to the same cherished sin.
It is turning toward the Lord with genuine faith, acknowledging our wrongdoing, and seeking to walk in obedience through His transforming grace.
Perhaps that is where this story finds you.
Maybe you have been wounded by someone who should have protected you.
Maybe a parent, relative, leader, or trusted person used their position to control or harm you.
Athaliah's story reminds us that a person's title does not make their actions righteous.
Family authority does not excuse cruelty.
Religious language does not sanctify abuse.
And seeking safety, wise counsel, and appropriate protection is not a betrayal of faith.
Or perhaps you recognize something different.
Not Athaliah's violence, but her hunger for control.
You have been trying to hold everything together by force.
You cannot bear being corrected.
You are afraid of losing your influence, your reputation, your position, or the approval of people.
And in trying to protect what you have, you have begun to wound the people God has placed around you.
If that is you, do not look away.
The Lord's call to repentance is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
You do not have to defend the sin that is destroying you.
You can confess it.
You can turn from it.
You can seek forgiveness and make appropriate restitution where possible.
And you can ask Jesus to transform the parts of your heart that you have been afraid to surrender.
But there is another person in this story you may recognize.
Jehosheba.
The person who did the right thing when doing the right thing was dangerous.
The person whose courage did not make her famous in the way kings and queens become famous.
The person who acted without knowing how the next six years would unfold.
Maybe that is you.
You have been protecting someone vulnerable.
You have been standing for truth in a family that prefers silence.
You have been trying to remain faithful while everyone around you seems willing to compromise.
And sometimes you wonder whether your quiet obedience matters.
Jehosheba's story says that faithful courage matters deeply.
Not because we can always predict the outcome.
But because obedience to God is never meaningless.
You may never stand before a cheering crowd.
You may never receive public recognition.
But faithfulness is not measured by applause.
The Lord sees what people overlook.
And the smallest act of courage can become part of a story much larger than we understand.
Still, there is one more truth we cannot afford to miss.
The child hidden in the temple was not the final answer.
Joash eventually died.
His kingdom did not last forever.
And even the restoration of Judah's throne did not cure the human heart.
The final answer was always greater than Joash.
It was Jesus Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The righteous King.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who does not merely rescue us from earthly enemies but delivers repentant sinners from the dominion of darkness and brings them into His kingdom.

Colossians 1:13–14 speaks of God delivering us from the power of darkness and translating us into the kingdom of His dear Son, in whom we have redemption through His blood, even the forgiveness of sins.
And that is why the message of Athaliah cannot end with a dead queen and a rescued child.
It must lead us to the living Christ.
Because the most important question is not simply whether Athaliah lost her throne.
It is whether Jesus reigns in your heart.
Have you trusted Him?
Have you confessed the sin you keep trying to excuse?
Have you surrendered the control you keep trying to maintain?
Have you received His grace by faith rather than trying to earn your way into God's favor?
Have you allowed the truth of the Gospel to confront you as well as comfort you?
You may have read this story expecting to discover the identity of a ruthless queen.
But perhaps the Lord is using it to uncover something much closer to home.
A wound that needs His healing.
A sin that needs confession.
A relationship that needs truth.
A fear that needs surrender.
A heart that needs Christ.
And if you are exhausted from pretending everything is fine, you do not have to perform spiritual strength in front of God.
He already knows.
You can pray:

“Lord Jesus, You know the things I have hidden, the ways I have been wounded, and the ways I have sinned. Forgive me. Teach me to repent sincerely. Heal what has been damaged, give me courage to obey You, and help me trust Your Word when I cannot understand my circumstances. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I place my hope in Your mercy, not in my own goodness. Be Lord of my life. Amen.”
Sometimes the comment section becomes more than a place for reactions.
It becomes a place where someone discovers that they are not the only person struggling, repenting, grieving, or learning to trust God again.
And perhaps someone reading your testimony will find the courage to turn toward Christ.
That is also why I want to ask something personal.
Not because every person who sees it will agree with it.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
But because someone in your family, among your friends, or quietly following your life may need to hear that the promises of God are not defeated by the wickedness of human beings.
Or send this privately to someone who is struggling with betrayal, fear, or the feeling that God has forgotten them.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep bringing biblical truth into places where confusion, discouragement, and spiritual hunger are real.
Writing, researching, preparing, and sharing faithful Christian content requires time, resources, and continued support.

For those who wish to express their worship through financial generosity, supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one meaningful way to give. Scripture encourages willing, cheerful generosity in 2 Corinthians 9:7 and teaches believers to support those who labor in teaching the Word in Galatians 6:6.
We want people to do more than consume inspiring words.
We want them to open their Bibles.
To test what they hear against Scripture.
To grow in prayer.
To turn from sin.
To know Jesus more deeply.
To become disciples who are rooted in truth rather than carried by every emotional trend.
Because this ministry is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And our greatest hope is not that people become loyal to a page.
It is that they become faithful followers of Christ.
Now return with me, one final time, to that ancient palace.
Athaliah believed she had eliminated the royal heirs.
A little boy remained hidden.
For six long years, the throne appeared to belong to the woman who had seized it.
But the story did not end where she expected.
And generations later, the true Son of David came into the world.
He was rejected.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
For a moment, His enemies may have believed the story was over.
But on the third day, the tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ had risen.
And unlike Joash, He reigns forever.
So when you read about Athaliah, do not merely remember the grandmother who tried to destroy Judah's royal heirs.
Remember the God who remained faithful to His covenant.
Remember the courageous woman who protected a child.
Remember the limits of every human king.
And above all, remember the Savior who came through David's line to accomplish what no earthly throne could ever accomplish.
The redemption of sinners.
The forgiveness of the guilty.
The restoration of those who turn to Him.
The gift of eternal life.
Because the throne Athaliah tried to steal could never compare to the throne Jesus will never lose.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE SENT AWAY TWO WIVES… THEN THE BIBLE RECORDED THE CHILDREN HE HAD WITH ANOTHER WOMAN.
paragraphs: HE SENT AWAY TWO WIVES… THEN THE BIBLE RECORDED THE CHILDREN HE HAD WITH ANOTHER WOMAN.

Buried in a genealogy most Christians skip is the unsettling story of Shaharaim—a man with a complicated household, two women sent away, and a family history Scripture refuses to erase. But what does this ancient record actually reveal about marriage, brokenness, consequences, and the grace of Jesus Christ?
“And Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives.” — 1 Chronicles 8:8 (KJV)
There are some Bible verses that make you stop reading.
Not because they contain a spectacular miracle.
Not because an angel appeared, a sea opened, or fire fell from heaven.
But because they sound painfully familiar.
A man. Two wives. A separation. Another woman. More children.
And somewhere behind those few ancient words, a household whose full story we will never know.
Imagine being one of the people whose entire family history was reduced to a sentence.
No explanation of what went wrong.
No account of who cried.
No record of who left willingly, who felt abandoned, or what the children understood.
Just names.
And a sentence that has survived thousands of years.
He sent them away.
Before we go any further, there is something important we must understand.
The Bible does not tell us that Shaharaim was a hero for doing this.
It does not tell us that God commanded him to send those women away.
It does not tell us that his later children were a divine reward for his decisions.
And it certainly does not give anyone permission to discard a spouse when marriage becomes difficult.
Scripture records what happened without necessarily approving what happened.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing we can do with the Bible is take a man's behavior and call it God's blessing simply because his story appears in a sacred book.
And sometimes the most beautiful thing we can discover is that God allowed a deeply complicated human history to remain in His Word without pretending it was simple.
The man's name was Shaharaim.
His story appears in 1 Chronicles 8, in the genealogy of Benjamin.
Not in a dramatic chapter filled with dialogue.
Not in a story where we hear God's voice explaining every decision.
In a genealogy.
The kind of passage many of us hurry through because the names are difficult to pronounce and the details seem distant from our lives.
But slow down.
Because there is something unsettling here.
The Hebrew of 1 Chronicles 8:8 includes the phrase:
אַחֲרֵי שִׁלְחוֹ אֹתָם
ʾaḥărê shilləḥô ʾōtām
Meaning, in context, “after he had sent them away.”
The Hebrew verb comes from the root שׁלח (š-l-ḥ), meaning “to send” or “to send away.”
The text uses language of sending away, but it does not explain every legal or personal circumstance surrounding the separation.
That is important.

Some English translations, including the King James Version, identify Hushim and Baara as Shaharaim's wives in this verse. Other translations reflect the difficulty of the Hebrew wording and its relationship to the surrounding genealogy.
The passage is ancient, compressed, and not without interpretive challenges.
We should not pretend to know what the Holy Spirit has not revealed.
We cannot confidently reconstruct the conversations inside Shaharaim's household.
We cannot prove why the women were sent away.
We cannot say whether either woman was mistreated, whether there were legal divorces, or what motives governed Shaharaim's decisions.
But we can say this:
The biblical record preserves a complicated family history without giving us permission to romanticize it.
And perhaps that is exactly where some of us need to begin.
Because there are people reading this who know what it means to have a family story they would rather not explain.
Maybe you grew up in a house where one parent disappeared.
Maybe you watched a marriage collapse while everyone outside the home thought everything was fine.
Maybe you were the child from the second relationship.
The person introduced with an awkward pause.
The one who learned too early that adults can make decisions children must spend years trying to understand.
Or perhaps you are the person who made those decisions.
You hurt someone.
You walked away when you should have stayed and sought help.
You made promises you did not keep.
And now, years later, the consequences still have names, birthdays, memories, and faces.
There is a kind of pain that does not disappear just because life continues.
And that is why this little genealogy deserves our attention.
Because life continued for Shaharaim, too.
First Chronicles 8:9–10 records children associated with Hodesh, another woman named in his household:
Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Shachia, and Mirma.
The Hebrew of verse 9 begins:
וַיּוֹלֶד מִן־חֹדֶשׁ אִשְׁתּוֹ
wayyôled min-Ḥōdeš ʾištô
That is, “And he fathered [children] by Hodesh his wife.”
The genealogy then continues, mentioning additional sons connected with Hushim in verse 11.
Notice something.
Hushim has not simply vanished from the record.
Even after the language about sending away, her name remains connected with Shaharaim's family history.
The exact chronology and relationships are not fully explained, and verse 11 is another reason to read the passage carefully rather than invent a tidy narrative.
These are not merely decorative details.
They remind us that a genealogy can preserve relationships whose complexity we do not completely understand.
And here is where the story begins to reach beyond the ancient world.
A new chapter in someone's life does not automatically erase the responsibilities of the previous one.
A new marriage does not make past children irrelevant.
A new relationship does not cancel old wounds.
A new beginning is not the same thing as repentance.
And having more children is not, by itself, proof that God approves of every decision that came before them.
Some people confuse continued life with divine endorsement.
But the Bible never teaches that every person who prospers is righteous, or that every person who suffers has sinned.
Jesus directly challenged simplistic assumptions about suffering and guilt in John 9:1–3.
The presence of children is a gift of life, not a certificate declaring every parental decision holy.
And this is especially important when we talk about families.
Because children are never the scandal.
A child born into a complicated family is not a mistake.
A child conceived outside God's design for marriage does not inherit the moral guilt of the circumstances surrounding conception.
Every human being bears the dignity of being made in God's image (Genesis 1:26–27).
No one should have to spend their life apologizing for the circumstances of their birth.
Read that again if you need to.
You are not responsible for the decisions adults made before you could speak.
You may carry consequences you never chose.
You may have questions no one has answered.
You may still feel the ache of being overlooked, compared, abandoned, or treated as though you belonged to the wrong chapter of somebody else's life.
But your worth was never determined by the neatness of your family tree.
And the Gospel gives us an even deeper reason to hope.
Because Jesus Christ entered a world full of complicated family histories.
Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy.
And that genealogy does not hide every uncomfortable detail.
Judah and Tamar appear in the story behind Matthew 1:3.
Rahab is named in Matthew 1:5.
Ruth, a Moabite woman whose loyalty and faith became part of Israel's story, is named there too.
And in Matthew 1:6, Solomon's mother is identified through the painful history of David and Uriah.
These accounts are not identical to Shaharaim's story.
We should never flatten their differences.
But together they reveal something remarkable about the biblical witness.
God does not need a sanitized human history to accomplish His redemptive purposes.
He does not call betrayal faithfulness.
He does not rename adultery righteousness.
He does not excuse injustice because a powerful man committed it.
Yet human sin does not have the power to overthrow God's purposes.
Think about David.
The king who wrote beautiful psalms also committed grievous sins.
He took Bathsheba, another man's wife, and arranged for Uriah's death (2 Samuel 11).
The prophet Nathan confronted him.
David was not told that his royal position made him innocent.
He was not told that because God had chosen him, his actions no longer mattered.
He heard the words:
“Thou art the man.” — 2 Samuel 12:7 (KJV)
And suddenly, the king could no longer hide behind his throne.
That is one of the hardest mercies God can give us.
To expose what we have been defending.
To confront what we have been excusing.
To reveal that we cannot heal what we insist on hiding.
David eventually confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13 (KJV)
That confession did not remove every earthly consequence.
Forgiveness was real.
Consequences were real.
Both truths stood together.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
Grace is not permission to repeat the wound.
Forgiveness is not an instruction to pretend nothing happened.
Repentance is not simply feeling emotional because you were caught.
Biblical repentance involves turning toward God and away from sin, with a transformed direction of life.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance.”
It speaks of a change of mind and orientation, not merely temporary regret.
When Peter called people to repent in Acts 3:19, he was calling them to turn toward God.
And when John the Baptist spoke about repentance, he demanded fruit consistent with it (Matthew 3:8).
That means a person who has harmed a family cannot simply say, “God forgave me,” while refusing to take responsibility for the damage.
Where possible and appropriate, repentance seeks to tell the truth, make restitution, fulfill obligations, and pursue reconciliation without demanding that wounded people immediately trust again.
Sometimes that includes financial responsibility.
Sometimes it means acknowledging children who were neglected.
Sometimes it means ending deception.
Sometimes it means respecting boundaries and allowing the people you hurt to heal without controlling their process.
And sometimes repentance means accepting that forgiveness does not guarantee the restoration of a particular relationship.
God's mercy is not a weapon to force someone back into an unsafe situation.
That is not grace.
That is spiritual manipulation.
Jesus never taught us to use holy language to cover unholy behavior.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce, He took them back to God's design for marriage.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus pointed to creation, to the union of husband and wife, and to the seriousness of what God joins together.
He also explained that Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart (Matthew 19:8).
Jesus did not treat marriage as something disposable.
He did not teach that a person's desire for a new beginning automatically justified abandoning an existing covenant.
His teaching confronts the human tendency to make our own desires the final authority.
At the same time, biblical teaching on marriage must never be twisted into a demand that victims remain exposed to violence, coercion, or abuse.
The seriousness of marriage does not make cruelty holy.
Protecting the vulnerable is not rebellion against God.
And seeking safety is not the same thing as treating marriage lightly.
We must handle these passages with reverence, compassion, and care.
Because somewhere reading this is a person who has already been crushed by careless religious advice.
Someone who was told to endure what should have been confronted.
Someone whose suffering was dismissed because the person causing it knew how to quote Scripture.
And somewhere else is a person who needs to stop calling selfishness freedom.
Both need truth.
Both need the Gospel.
But they do not need the same confrontation.
Jesus knows the difference.
Remember the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus told her that she had had five husbands and that the man she was then living with was not her husband.
We are not given enough information to know all the reasons behind those earlier marriages.
We should not invent a history of promiscuity or blame where Scripture does not provide it.
But we do know that Jesus knew the truth about her circumstances.
And He still spoke with her.
He did not flatter her with a lie.
He did not reduce her to her relationship history.
He offered her living water.
He spoke of worship in spirit and truth.
And He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
There is something breathtaking about that encounter.
The One who knew her life most completely was the One who could offer her what no human relationship could provide.
Not another temporary escape.
Not another person expected to carry the weight of her deepest thirst.
Living water.
The gift of God.
And she went back to her town with a testimony that invited others to come and see Jesus.
Her story was no longer simply something to conceal.
It became an occasion to point people toward Christ.
That is not because the past stopped mattering.
It is because Jesus was greater than the past.
And this is where Shaharaim's brief genealogy becomes a mirror.
Not because we know enough to condemn every decision he made.
We do not.
Not because we can prove that his household followed the same pattern as every broken modern family.
We cannot.
But because the passage reminds us that Scripture does not erase the complicated reality of human relationships.
And when we read that reality in the light of the whole Bible, we are confronted with questions we cannot easily escape.
What have we called normal that God is calling us to examine?
Whose pain have we ignored because our own life became more comfortable?
Have we confused being forgiven with being free from responsibility?
Have we allowed bitterness to become our identity?
Have we started believing that the circumstances of our birth determine the value of our lives?
Have we treated someone's past as though Jesus could never redeem them?
And perhaps the hardest question of all:
Are we asking God to heal our story while refusing to surrender the part of it we still want to control?
That question is not only for divorced people.
It is not only for parents.
It is not only for those who have experienced betrayal.
It is for all of us.
Because every human heart knows something about wanting mercy without exposure.
We want Jesus to forgive the sin we are still protecting.
We want peace without confession.
We want restoration without humility.
We want a beautiful testimony without the painful honesty that often comes before it.
But Jesus did not go to the cross merely to make us feel better about remaining unchanged.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to free us from the dominion of sin.
He came to make us new.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
Notice where that promise is found.
In Christ.
Not in a new relationship.
Not in a different city.
Not in a better public image.
Not in pretending the past never happened.
In Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because the deepest human problem is not merely that our families are complicated.
It is that sin has separated humanity from the holy God who made us.
Romans 3:23 tells us that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
Romans 6:23 tells us that the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
And Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners, through Christ's death for us.
The Gospel is not the announcement that our actions have no consequences.

It is the announcement that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sinners and rose again, so that those who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
He does not merely edit the public version of our story.
He transforms the person at its center.
And sometimes that transformation begins with a sentence we have been afraid to say.
“I was wrong.”
“I need forgiveness.”
“I hurt people.”
“I cannot keep living like this.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
Or perhaps:
“Lord, I have spent years believing that what happened to me made me unworthy of love.”
And in the presence of Christ, that lie begins to lose its grip.
Because your family's history may explain some of your wounds.
But it does not have the authority to define your eternal worth.
Your father may have left.
Your mother may have struggled.
Your marriage may have ended.
Your children may be carrying pain you deeply regret.
Your life may contain chapters you wish you could rewrite.
But no human failure can make the saving power of Jesus insufficient.
And no amount of religious performance can replace the need for His grace.
That is why we must be careful with the phrase “From Scandal to Grace.”
It does not mean scandal is good.
It does not mean every broken relationship should be celebrated as a stepping stone toward something better.
It does not mean every painful decision was secretly God's command.
It means that even where sin, shame, sorrow, and brokenness have entered the human story, the grace of Jesus Christ is sufficient to forgive, restore, and transform those who come to Him.
The cross does not excuse the scandal.
The cross reveals how seriously God takes sin—and how astonishingly far His love went to save sinners.
And the resurrection declares that death and sin do not have the final victory over those who belong to Christ.
That is the hope.
Not that every earthly relationship will be repaired exactly as we wish.
Not that every person we hurt will return.
Not that every painful memory will disappear overnight.
But that Jesus is alive.
That repentance is possible.
That forgiveness is available through Him.
That healing can begin.
And that the future of a redeemed person is not imprisoned by the worst chapter of the past.
Perhaps you have been reading this with a particular name in your mind.
A father.
A mother.
An ex-spouse.
A child.
Someone who left.
Someone you abandoned.
Someone you still cannot forgive.
Or perhaps the name is your own.
Not to pretend everything is simple.
Not to manufacture an emotion.
But to ask Jesus to lead you in truth.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to seek help, seek help.
If you need to make something right, begin where you can.
If you need to grieve, do not mistake grief for a lack of faith.
And if you have been carrying guilt for decisions that were never yours, ask the Lord to help you lay down that burden.
You do not need to confess somebody else's sin as though it were your own.
You need the Savior who knows your story completely.
There may be someone reading this who has never genuinely surrendered to Jesus Christ.
You know Christian language.
You know how to appear strong.
You may even know how to encourage other people.
But when you are alone, you know there are places in your heart you have never opened to Him.
Today, you can come honestly.
You do not have to make yourself worthy before approaching Christ.
You come because you need His mercy.
Confess your sin.
Turn to Him.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Follow Him as Lord.
And remember His promise:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
There is room to come to Christ.
Not room to cherish sin forever.
But room to be forgiven, cleansed, and changed by the Savior.
And for the believer who has grown weary, this is your reminder:
God has not called you to manufacture a perfect-looking life.
He has called you to walk in the light.
To love truth.
To practice mercy.
To pursue holiness.
To carry your responsibilities faithfully.
To forgive as you have been forgiven.
And to keep your eyes on Jesus.
The same Christ who confronted sin also welcomed repentant sinners.
The same Christ who defended the vulnerable also challenged the proud.
The same Christ who spoke with the woman at the well went willingly to the cross.
And the same Christ who rose from the grave remains the hope of every broken human story.
If this article has touched a part of your life you rarely talk about, I want to invite you into something more meaningful than simply reacting to another post.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to reveal private details or expose anyone else's pain.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And please, think about the person who might need this message.
The friend who still blames themselves for their parents' separation.
The single mother who wonders whether her family can ever find peace.
The father trying to rebuild trust after years of regret.
The young adult who believes their birth circumstances made them less valuable.
The believer who has confused grace with permission to avoid repentance.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are growing weary, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who do not yet believe.
Not because we are building a following around ourselves.
But because the Word of God deserves to be heard, understood, and lived.
There is a real difference between enjoying Christian content when it appears on your feed and intentionally helping make ongoing biblical discipleship resources available to more people.
For some supporters, this may be part of their broader Christian giving—a voluntary offering of gratitude and partnership in Gospel work.
But I want to be clear about something important.
God is not selling grace.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
If you cannot, you are still welcome here.
You can still pray, learn, grow, share the Word, and encourage others.
Because the mission is bigger than a transaction.
It is about Christ being proclaimed and people being strengthened in the truth.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, and opportunities to begin meaningful conversations about faith.
One thoughtful comment might encourage someone to seek prayer.
One invitation might help a friend begin reading the Bible again.
We cannot promise what God will do through any single post.
But we can be faithful with the opportunities He places before us.
And faithfulness matters.
Now, before we finish, return with me to that little genealogy.
Shaharaim.
Hushim.
Baara.
Hodesh.
The children whose names were written down.
The relationships we cannot fully reconstruct.
The questions Scripture leaves unanswered.
We began with a man who sent women away.
We end with the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
And that contrast should move us.
Because Shaharaim's record is not a hidden promise that every complicated family will have a perfect earthly ending.
It is a reminder that the Bible speaks about real people, not polished characters designed to make us comfortable.
And when we bring our own complicated histories to the whole counsel of Scripture, we discover a truth more beautiful than pretending everything was fine.
Jesus Christ came into a world that was not fine.
He came among sinners.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He rose again.
And He calls us out of darkness into His marvelous light.
You may not be able to change the names in your family history.
You may not be able to undo every decision.
You may not be able to recover every lost year.
But in Christ, you can stop running from the truth.
You can receive forgiveness.
You can begin walking in obedience.
You can seek healing without denying the wound.
You can take responsibility without surrendering to despair.
And you can trust the Lord with the chapters you cannot repair by your own strength.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but only Jesus Christ has the authority to write the final verdict over your redeemed life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SON OF A FOREIGN KING’S DAUGHTER WHO NEARLY STOLE HIS FATHER’S THRONE
paragraphs: THE SON OF A FOREIGN KING’S DAUGHTER WHO NEARLY STOLE HIS FATHER’S THRONE

Absalom was born into royalty, raised in privilege, and loved by a king. But behind his beautiful face was a wounded heart—and behind his rebellion was a family tragedy that still speaks to broken homes, betrayed children, and Christians who have learned to hide their pain behind a smile.
“And his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur.” — 2 Samuel 3:3 (KJV)
There is something terrifying about a person who has everything the world admires… yet is slowly dying on the inside.
A beautiful face.
A powerful family.
A promising future.
A name people recognize.
And a wound nobody wants to talk about.
That was Absalom.

But before he became the son who rebelled against his father, before he gathered an army, before his hair became entangled in the branches of a great tree, before King David cried out in unbearable grief…
He was somebody's little boy.
And the Bible tells us something about his beginning that most people read without stopping.
His mother was Maacah.
His grandfather was Talmai, king of Geshur.
His father was David, the future king of a united Israel.
Absalom was born into a royal family with connections on both sides of his bloodline.
Yet royal blood could not protect him from a broken home.
And a father's crown could not heal what was happening inside his son's heart.
Perhaps that is why this story feels so painfully familiar.
Because some people grow up in houses where everything looks respectable from the outside, while inside, everyone is learning how to survive what nobody will acknowledge.
Some families have photographs full of smiles but conversations full of silence.
Some children have everything they need financially and almost nothing they need emotionally.
And some fathers are admired by the entire community while their own children are quietly wondering why they cannot reach their hearts.
If you have ever lived inside that kind of contradiction, stay with this story.
Because Absalom's life contains a warning we cannot afford to ignore.
And David's tears reveal something that success, reputation, and even royal authority cannot replace.
The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 3:3 identifies Absalom as:
וְהַשְּׁלִשִׁי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בֶּן־מַעֲכָה בַּת־תַּלְמַי מֶלֶךְ גְּשׁוּר
Veha-shelishi Avshalom ben-Ma'akhah bat-Talmai melekh Geshur.
“And the third, Absalom, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.”
Notice what Scripture actually says.
Maacah was the daughter of a foreign king. Geshur was a kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee, outside Israel's central tribal territory.
But the text does not tell us that Maacah was personally wicked, that her foreign ancestry caused Absalom's rebellion, or that she raised him to betray his father.
Those accusations would go beyond what God has revealed.
The Bible gives us his family connection, not permission to invent his mother's motives.
And that distinction matters.
Because the tragedy of Absalom was not that foreign blood flowed through his veins.
His tragedy was what happened when family sin, injustice, grief, vengeance, ambition, and pride collided.
Even his name carries an aching irony.
אַבְשָׁלוֹם — Avshalom.
A name commonly understood to mean “father of peace” or “my father is peace,” drawing on the Hebrew words associated with father and peace.
Peace.
Imagine that.
A boy whose name spoke of peace would become one of the most heartbreaking symbols of conflict in David's household.
Sometimes the greatest contradiction in a person's life is the distance between the name they carry and the pain they live with.
And Absalom's story was about to become much darker.
His sister Tamar was violated by their half-brother Amnon.
Second Samuel 13 records one of the most disturbing episodes in David's family.
Tamar pleaded with Amnon not to commit such wickedness. He refused to listen. After assaulting her, he rejected her and sent her away.
The young woman who had entered his room in innocence left devastated.
And when Absalom learned what had happened, he took Tamar into his household.
The Bible says she remained there desolate.
That word should stop us.
Desolate.
Not merely embarrassed.
Not simply disappointed.
Desolate.
A young woman's life had been shattered by someone within her own family.
And the people who should have protected her had failed.
David heard about what happened and became very angry.
But the biblical narrative does not record him bringing Amnon to justice.
We should not pretend to know everything David did privately. Scripture does not give us every conversation.
Yet the silence surrounding any recorded judicial response is devastating.
Tamar's suffering remained.
Amnon's crime remained.
And Absalom's anger remained.
For two years, Absalom waited.
Two years of watching.
Two years of remembering.
Two years in which Scripture records that he spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad.
Then Absalom arranged for Amnon to be killed.
What began with a terrible injustice became another terrible injustice.
Absalom's outrage over his sister's suffering was understandable.
His decision to murder his brother was not righteous.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
You can be genuinely wounded and still become responsible for the wounds you inflict on others.
Pain can explain why a person is angry.
It cannot automatically justify what that person does with the anger.
Some people reading this know exactly what it means to have been wronged.
You were betrayed by someone you trusted.
You were neglected by someone who should have protected you.
You watched injustice happen while people with authority looked the other way.
And somewhere inside, you made a promise.
“I will never let anyone hurt me like that again.”
But slowly, protection became suspicion.
Suspicion became resentment.
Resentment became a desire to make someone pay.
And without realizing it, you began carrying the very darkness you once hated.
That is one of the most frightening possibilities in the human heart.
Not that suffering always makes us cruel.
It does not.
Many wounded people become extraordinarily compassionate.
But when bitterness is cherished and vengeance is treated as justice, suffering can become the soil in which further evil grows.
Absalom fled after Amnon's death.
And where did he go?
To Geshur.
To the kingdom of his maternal grandfather, Talmai.
Second Samuel 13:37 tells us he fled to Talmai, son of Ammihud, king of Geshur.
The detail from 2 Samuel 3:3 suddenly becomes important.
The foreign royal family introduced at Absalom's birth later becomes the place of his exile.
His mother's family connection provided a destination when his relationship with his father's house had collapsed.
He remained there three years.
Three years away from Jerusalem.
Three years separated from David.
And Scripture tells us David mourned for his son.
Think about that.
A father grieving.
A son in exile.
A daughter whose suffering had helped ignite the tragedy.
A murdered brother.
A family carrying wounds that power could not erase.
Eventually, through Joab's intervention, Absalom returned to Jerusalem.
But even then, reconciliation was incomplete.
For two years, he lived in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face.
Then David finally summoned him.
Absalom bowed before his father.
And David kissed him.
For a moment, perhaps someone watching would have believed the family was finally healing.
The estranged son had returned.
The king had embraced him.
The separation appeared to be over.
But a kiss is not necessarily the same as restored trust.
And an outward reunion does not prove that every wound has been addressed.
Scripture does not tell us everything spoken between David and Absalom.
It does, however, show what happened next.
Absalom began building his public image.
He acquired a chariot, horses, and fifty men to run before him.
He positioned himself near the city gate, where people came seeking judgment.
He listened to their complaints.
He sympathized with their frustrations.
He suggested that the king's administration was failing them.
Then he presented himself as the answer.
Second Samuel 15:4 records his words:
“Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!” (KJV)
It sounded compassionate.
It sounded courageous.
It sounded like someone finally cared about ordinary people.
But Scripture exposes what was happening beneath the performance.
“So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” — 2 Samuel 15:6 (KJV)
Stole.
Not merely won.
Stole.
The Hebrew verb is וַיְגַנֵּב — vaygannēv, from a root meaning “to steal.”
The narrator deliberately describes Absalom's political maneuvering as a theft of hearts.
He used personal attention, promises of justice, and public affection to build loyalty to himself.
And this is where his ancient story becomes disturbingly modern.
Not everyone who speaks tenderly to you is trying to lead you toward truth.
Not everyone who recognizes your pain is qualified to guide your healing.
Not everyone who promises justice is acting from righteous motives.
Sometimes people learn to use the language of compassion while quietly feeding their own hunger for power.
And sometimes we do it ourselves.
We want to be seen as the misunderstood one.
The righteous one.
The one who would do everything better if only someone would give us the opportunity.
We rehearse every failure of the people who hurt us.
We gather supporters.
We turn private bitterness into a public identity.
And slowly, our desire to be vindicated becomes more important than our willingness to be transformed.
Absalom did not merely want his father's attention anymore.
He wanted his father's throne.
He launched a rebellion.
David fled Jerusalem.
The king who had once faced Goliath now had to flee from his own son.
The warrior who had defeated enemies on battlefields was facing devastation within his family.
And the consequences of David's own earlier sins hung heavily over this entire story.
We cannot tell Absalom's story faithfully without remembering 2 Samuel 11 and 12.
David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged the death of Uriah.
When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13 (KJV)
Nathan announced God's forgiveness, but also warned that the sword would not depart from David's house.
Forgiveness did not mean every earthly consequence would disappear.
David was a man who had experienced extraordinary mercy.
He was also a father whose family would experience extraordinary suffering.
This does not mean Tamar deserved what happened, or that the individual sins of David's children were somehow excused.
It means the biblical narrative refuses to separate the spiritual and moral condition of a household from the devastating consequences that can unfold within it.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something difficult.
You can love God and still make choices that wound the people closest to you.
You can repent sincerely and still need to take responsibility for consequences.
You can be gifted, respected, successful, and spiritually influential while areas of your private life desperately need correction.
David's crown did not make him immune to sin.
And his relationship with God did not make family responsibility optional.
Then came the battle.
David's forces confronted Absalom's army in the forest of Ephraim.
Before they departed, David gave his commanders an extraordinary instruction.
“Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom.” — 2 Samuel 18:5 (KJV)
The young man.
After everything Absalom had done.
After the rebellion.
After the betrayal.
After the attempt to take his father's kingdom.
David still spoke of him as the young man.
His son.
His child.
The one he wanted spared.
And then came the moment that would turn a political rebellion into one of Scripture's most heartbreaking scenes.
Absalom was riding on a mule when he passed beneath a great oak.
His head became caught in the branches, and he was left suspended as the mule continued on.
Second Samuel 18:9 describes his head being caught. Although the earlier narrative emphasizes his remarkable hair, this verse does not explicitly say his hair caused the entanglement.
Joab and his men killed him despite David's command to deal gently with him.
The rebellion was broken.
The kingdom was preserved.
The threat to David's throne was over.
From a military standpoint, David's forces had prevailed.
But when the news reached the king, he did not celebrate.
He trembled.
He went up to the chamber over the gate.
And he wept.
Listen to the words Scripture preserves.
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!” — 2 Samuel 18:33 (KJV; 19:1 in some Hebrew verse numberings)
Read that again.
Not as an ancient quotation.
Hear it as a father's cry.
“My son.”
“My son.”
“My son Absalom.”
The king who had lost so much was now mourning the son who had tried to destroy him.
David could survive a rebellion.
But the death of Absalom broke his heart.
And those words contain a grief that no royal victory could silence.
“Would God I had died for thee.”
I wish I could have died instead of you.
How many parents have whispered something similar over a hospital bed?
How many fathers have stared at a photograph, wishing they could go back and say the words they never said?
How many mothers have carried the unbearable ache of a child they could not save?
How many families have discovered too late that winning an argument is not the same as preserving a relationship?
And how many sons and daughters are still alive, still reachable, still waiting for someone to stop defending their pride long enough to tell the truth?
Perhaps that is where this story meets you.
Maybe you are not Absalom plotting rebellion.
Maybe you are the child who never felt heard.
Maybe you are Tamar, carrying pain that people around you minimized or ignored.
Maybe you are David, realizing that your public achievements have not repaired the damage in your private relationships.
Maybe you are a parent whose child no longer answers your calls.
Or a son who has spent years pretending he no longer cares whether his father reaches out.
Or a daughter who keeps smiling at family gatherings while remembering what happened behind closed doors.
Please hear this carefully.
Reconciliation is good, but it must never be used to pressure someone into returning to abuse or danger.
Forgiveness does not erase accountability.
Grace does not require pretending that evil was harmless.
And peace is not the same as silence.
The God of Scripture does not ask us to call injustice righteousness.
But He does call us away from allowing hatred to become our master.
And this is where Absalom's story points us beyond David's broken household toward the greater hope of the Gospel.
David cried, “Would God I had died for thee.”
But David could not exchange his life for Absalom's.
He could not undo the murder.
He could not reverse the rebellion.
He could not bring his son back from death.
His love was real.
His grief was real.
But his power was limited.
Now consider Jesus Christ.
The promised Son of David.
Not merely another king born into David's dynasty, but the Messiah whose kingdom would never end.
Luke 1:32–33 declares that God would give Jesus the throne of His father David and that His kingdom would have no end.
David was a flawed king whose family was fractured by sin.
Jesus is the righteous King who came to rescue sinners.
David wished he could die in his son's place.
Jesus willingly gave His life for sinners.
This is not a claim that Absalom's death was itself a prophecy of the crucifixion. Scripture does not say that.
It is a contrast that helps us recognize the extraordinary difference between the helpless grief of an earthly father and the saving work of the Son of God.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had cleaned up every secret.
Not after we had repaired every relationship.
Not after we had proven ourselves worthy.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
And the Greek of Romans 5:8 makes that reality especially striking:
ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν
Eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn.
“While we were still sinners.”
That is grace.
Not God declaring our sin harmless.
Not God overlooking the suffering we have caused.
Not God telling victims that their wounds do not matter.
Grace means that through Jesus Christ, forgiveness and transformation become possible for people who could never save themselves.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing depth of divine love.
And unlike Absalom's story, the story of Jesus does not end with a dead son and a grieving father.
Jesus rose from the dead.
The grave did not have the final word.
Sin did not defeat Him.
Death did not hold Him.
And through His resurrection, everyone who trusts in Him has a living hope.
This is why the Gospel is not simply a message about becoming a nicer person.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
It is the call to repent and believe in Him.
It is the promise that forgiveness is available through His name.
And it is the power of God to begin making people new.
Maybe you have spent years being the angry son.
Maybe you have become the distant father.
Maybe your greatest struggle is not with another person but with the person you see in the mirror.
You know what happened.
You know what you did.
You know what you should have done differently.
And you keep wondering whether your story has gone too far to be redeemed.
Listen.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot make every consequence disappear.
You cannot force another person to forgive you or rebuild trust.
But you can come to Jesus Christ today.
You can confess what is true.
You can stop protecting the sin that is destroying you.
You can seek help.
You can pursue justice where harm has occurred.
You can make restitution where possible.
You can begin walking in repentance, humility, and obedience.
And where reconciliation is safe and appropriate, you can take the first honest step without demanding that the other person immediately meet you halfway.
The Gospel does not promise that every broken earthly relationship will be restored in this lifetime.
But it does promise that those who belong to Christ are not abandoned to the hopelessness of their past.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
That is not a promise that your history never happened.
It is the declaration that your history no longer has the authority to define your identity apart from Christ.
And perhaps the most important question in this entire story is not why Absalom rebelled.
It is what you are doing with the pain you carry today.
Are you allowing it to drive you toward God?
Or are you allowing it to become the excuse for the very sins you once condemned?
Are you seeking healing?
Or have you become so attached to your anger that you no longer know who you would be without it?
Are you asking God to transform your heart?
Or only asking Him to prove that everyone who hurt you was wrong?
There is a difference.
And eternity is too serious to ignore it.
If this story has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Talk to God about it.
Not with a polished religious performance.
With the truth.

“Lord Jesus, I have been hurt. And I have also sinned. I cannot heal myself by hiding, retaliating, or pretending. Forgive me. Teach me to repent where I am wrong, seek help where I am wounded, and trust You with the things I cannot control. Change my heart. Lead me in Your truth. Amen.”
You do not have to explain your private story publicly.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not alone in the struggle.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you out of bitterness, pride, or rebellion, consider sharing it. Your testimony may encourage someone who is standing where you once stood.
There is also someone in your life who may need this message.
A father who has become distant.
A son who feels forgotten.
A mother carrying silent grief.
A believer who has confused forgiveness with pretending nothing happened.
A friend who is slowly allowing resentment to consume their life.
Sometimes sharing the truth is one small way of serving someone we may never know is struggling.
Because there may come a day when you need to remember that being wounded does not give you permission to wound others—and that Jesus offers a better way than revenge.
Our desire is not simply to publish words that stir emotions for a moment.
It is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, biblical truth, and faithful discipleship.
For those who choose to give, it can be an intentional expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
But let us be biblically clear about something important.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These resources are intended to help you keep reading, learning, reflecting, and growing in your walk with the Lord.
If this ministry has helped you understand Scripture more clearly, confront a difficult truth, or return your attention to Christ, consider helping us continue that work.
Not because you owe us something.
But because freely chosen generosity can help make faithful biblical encouragement available to more people.
You can become a monthly supporter here:
Because the goal has never been merely to grow an audience.
The goal is to glorify Christ.
To proclaim His Gospel.
To call sinners to repentance.
To encourage the wounded with truth.
To remind the weary that the grace of God is not exhausted.
And to help people discover that genuine transformation is possible through the One who died and rose again.
Now return with me, one last time, to the chamber above the gate.
David is weeping.
His son is dead.
The kingdom has survived.
But the father is broken.
“O my son Absalom…”
He cannot call his son back.
He cannot recover the lost years.
He cannot undo what has happened.
And Scripture leaves us with the unbearable weight of that grief.
But it does not leave the whole Bible there.
Centuries later, another Son of David would enter Jerusalem.
He would be rejected.
He would be betrayed.
He would wear a crown of thorns rather than seize a crown through rebellion.
He would give His life, not to preserve an earthly throne, but to accomplish redemption.
And He would rise again.
Absalom's story warns us what sin, vengeance, and pride can destroy.
Jesus Christ reveals what grace, truth, and sacrificial love can redeem.
Do not wait until grief is standing over a grave before you recognize the cost of cherished bitterness.
Do not mistake a public smile for a healed heart.
Do not confuse religious reputation with genuine repentance.
And do not believe that your worst chapter must become the final verdict over your life.
Come to Christ while there is still time.
Tell Him the truth.
Receive His mercy through faith.
And follow Him into the life of repentance and transformation to which He calls you.
Because the most tragic thing about Absalom was not that he was born the grandson of a foreign king.
It was that a man whose name spoke of peace pursued a throne through rebellion and died before he could enjoy the peace his name proclaimed.
And the most beautiful truth of the Gospel is that the true Son of David did not come to steal hearts for His own selfish ambition.
He came to save sinners through His own blood.
Do not spend your life fighting for a throne when the King of grace is calling you to surrender your heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “EVERYTHING IS PERMISSIBLE”—THE BIBLE VERSE THAT COULD BE DESTROYING YOUR SOUL IF YOU READ IT WRONG
paragraphs: “EVERYTHING IS PERMISSIBLE”—THE BIBLE VERSE THAT COULD BE DESTROYING YOUR SOUL IF YOU READ IT WRONG
Paul never gave Christians permission to live however they wanted. He exposed a dangerous kind of freedom—one that can leave you smiling in public while quietly becoming a prisoner in private.
There is a frightening possibility that deserves your attention.
You can be doing something that isn't explicitly forbidden in Scripture… and still be allowing it to slowly destroy the person God is calling you to become.
Read that again.
Because some of the most dangerous things in your spiritual life don't arrive looking like sin.
They arrive looking like freedom.

A harmless conversation. An innocent attraction. Another hour scrolling. A private habit nobody knows about. A relationship you keep defending. A form of entertainment that gradually makes darkness feel normal.
And somewhere in the middle of it all, you whisper the words that have become the favorite defense of countless Christians:
“But I'm free in Christ.”
Yes. You are.
But free to do what?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
What if the thing you keep defending as your freedom is the very thing that has begun to master you?
Nearly two thousand years ago, the apostle Paul confronted this dangerous confusion in a church that looked surprisingly familiar.
The believers in Corinth lived in a wealthy, influential, morally complicated city. They were surrounded by competing philosophies, religious practices, social pressures, and sexual immorality.
And the church was struggling.

They possessed spiritual gifts, but they were divided. They celebrated knowledge, but sometimes lacked love. They understood that Christ had brought freedom, yet some were apparently using that freedom to justify behavior that contradicted their new identity in Him.
Then Paul wrote words that would confront generations of believers:
“Everything is permissible for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything.
— 1 Corinthians 6:12, translated from the Greek
Those words sound simple.
Until you realize Paul was not merely asking whether Christians were allowed to do something.
He was asking whether that something was beginning to own them.
And the difference could change your entire life.
In the original Greek, the statement translated “Everything is permissible for me” reads:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν — Panta moi exestin.
Literally, “All things are lawful for me,” or “All things are permitted to me.”
But here is a detail many readers miss.

Paul repeats the phrase and immediately qualifies it. Many biblical scholars understand “All things are lawful for me” as a slogan circulating among the Corinthians, which Paul quotes in order to challenge its misuse.

The Greek manuscripts do not contain our modern quotation marks, so interpreters must recognize the possible slogan from the context. Either way, Paul's argument is unmistakable: Christian freedom cannot be separated from what is beneficial, what builds up others, and what honors the Lord.
Paul continues:
ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει — all’ ou panta sympherei.
“But not all things are beneficial.”
The verb sympherei carries the sense of being advantageous, profitable, or helpful.
Paul was challenging believers to think beyond the question of permission.
Something may be permitted without being spiritually helpful.
Something may be enjoyable without being wise.
Something may be socially acceptable without being worthy of your devotion.
And something may begin as a choice but eventually become a chain.
Then comes Paul's devastating declaration:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος — all’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos.
“But I will not be mastered by anything.”
Notice the relationship between the words.
The Greek verb exestin concerns what is permitted or authorized. The verb exousiasthēsomai concerns being brought under someone's or something's authority.
Paul is making a striking contrast.
You may claim authority to choose something.
But what happens when that thing begins exercising authority over you?
You say you can stop whenever you want.
But can you?
You say the relationship isn't affecting your walk with God.
But why are you hiding parts of it?
You say the entertainment is harmless.
But why does your heart feel increasingly comfortable with what once troubled your conscience?
You say you are simply enjoying your freedom.
But why does surrendering that pleasure feel almost unbearable?
This is where Paul's words stop being a theological discussion and become a mirror.
Because there is a difference between having access to something and having freedom from it.
And sometimes the clearest evidence that something has gained too much power over your heart is how fiercely you defend your right to keep it.
Think about that.
You might not be addicted to a substance.
You might be addicted to approval.
You might not be trapped in an obviously destructive relationship.
You might be trapped in the fear of being alone.
You might not be worshiping a carved idol.
You might be giving your identity, peace, and emotional stability to money, recognition, success, attention, or the opinion of someone who barely thinks about you.
Not every strong desire is an addiction. Not every enjoyment is idolatry. Scripture does not condemn every ordinary pleasure.
But even good things can become disordered when they occupy a place in our hearts that belongs to God.
And Paul is asking us to examine that possibility.
Not so we can become terrified of every decision.
But so we can stop confusing freedom with the absence of restraint.
Because biblical freedom is something far more beautiful than simply getting to do whatever we want.
It is the freedom to belong to Jesus without being enslaved by lesser masters.
And that brings us to the part of the passage that changes everything.
Paul does not leave his argument hanging in the air.
He brings it directly to the human body, sexual immorality, and our union with Christ.
In 1 Corinthians 6:13–20, Paul reminds believers that the body is not meant for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
He points to the resurrection of Jesus.
He reminds Christians that their bodies are members of Christ.
And then he makes an astonishing declaration:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV
Stop there.
You are not your own.
In a world constantly telling you that ultimate freedom means belonging to nobody but yourself, Scripture announces something radically different.
You belong to the One who loved you enough to redeem you.
Not because God sees you as an object to control.
Not because Jesus came to steal your joy.
But because sin had already shown what cruel mastery looks like.
And Christ came to rescue you.
The price Paul speaks of points to the saving work of Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for sinners.
Your body matters because Christ has redeemed you.
Your choices matter because your life belongs to Him.
Your freedom matters because it was purchased through His sacrifice.
Christian obedience, then, is not an attempt to purchase God's love.
It is a response to the love that has already been revealed in Jesus.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come to make sin more convenient.
He came to save sinners.
He did not shed His blood so we could rename bondage as freedom.
He gave Himself to bring us out of bondage and into a new life.
And He did not rise from the dead merely to improve our public image.
He rose so that those who belong to Him might walk in newness of life.
But perhaps you are reading this while carrying something you have never told another person.
A struggle that keeps returning.
A temptation you promised God you would resist.
A secret that makes you feel like two different people.
The believer everyone sees.
And the exhausted person you meet when the door closes.
You love Jesus.
You know what Scripture says.
You have prayed.
You have cried.
You have made promises.
And somehow, you keep finding yourself back in the same place.
Afterward comes the silence.
The shame.
The familiar thought:
“Maybe I'm not really changing.”
Perhaps you've even begun avoiding prayer because you cannot bear to approach God with another confession.
Listen carefully.
The fact that you need repentance does not mean you are beyond redemption.
But neither does God's mercy mean your sin is harmless.
Both truths matter.
Jesus does not call us to pretend that darkness is light.
And He does not tell repentant sinners that darkness has the final word.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
The religious leaders placed her in the middle of a public confrontation over adultery. Her wrongdoing had become the center of a spectacle.
Jesus refused to participate in their self-righteous cruelty.
After her accusers departed, He said:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
— John 8:11, ESV
Do you see it?
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin behind.
Jesus did not say adultery was acceptable.
He did not say her past defined her forever.
He did not excuse her sin, and He did not join her accusers in using her humiliation as entertainment.
He called her toward a different future.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes a new beginning possible.
And this is why Paul's words about freedom are not an attack on joy.
They are a rescue mission.
Because sin has a way of making promises it cannot keep.
It promises relief and leaves you restless.
It promises intimacy and sometimes leaves you more isolated.
It promises control and gradually demands more.
It promises freedom while quietly building a prison around your desires.
Not every struggle follows the same pattern, and not every painful consequence can be traced to personal sin. But when a desire begins to rule us, Paul's warning becomes painfully relevant.
“I will not be mastered by anything.”
Those words should make us examine the things we have stopped questioning.
And perhaps the question is not merely whether you are allowed to watch it, buy it, pursue it, post it, or participate in it.
Perhaps the question is what it is doing to your heart.
Is it helping you love God more faithfully?
Is it strengthening or weakening your self-control?
Is it shaping you toward truth or making deception easier?
Is it building up the people around you?
Can you receive it with gratitude and walk away from it freely?
Or has it begun demanding a place in your life that you are unwilling to surrender?
Paul returns to the same principle in 1 Corinthians 10:23:
“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up.
— ESV
Then, in the following verse, he turns our attention toward others:
“Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.”
— 1 Corinthians 10:24, ESV
Now the picture becomes even clearer.
Christian freedom is not only about what a choice does to you.
It is also about what your choices do to others.
In the immediate context of 1 Corinthians 10, Paul is discussing food associated with idols, matters of conscience, and the importance of not causing unnecessary harm to others.
He is not teaching that every personal preference must become a universal law.
He is teaching believers to exercise their freedom with wisdom and love.
That distinction matters.
Some Christians have used passages like this to impose human rules where Scripture has not established them.
They have treated personal convictions as though they were commandments from God.
They have made other believers feel guilty for enjoying legitimate gifts.
But Paul was not replacing freedom in Christ with a new system of man-made bondage.
Romans 14 reminds us that believers must not despise or condemn one another over genuinely disputable matters.
At the same time, freedom must never become an excuse for what Scripture clearly identifies as sin.
Paul makes that plain in Galatians 5:13:
“For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.”
— ESV
There it is.
Freedom that serves.
Freedom that loves.
Freedom that refuses to make self-indulgence the center of everything.
Freedom that is strong enough to say no.
And sometimes, saying no is not the loss of freedom.
It is the evidence that freedom is beginning to grow.
Imagine someone who once could not go a day without returning to a destructive habit.
Then, through prayer, repentance, honest accountability, wise support, and the transforming work of God, that person begins to experience change.
The struggle may not disappear overnight.
There may be setbacks.
There may be tears.
There may be difficult conversations and decisions that cost something.
But little by little, the old master loses its unquestioned authority.
That is not merely behavior modification.
For the Christian, genuine transformation is rooted in a deeper reality: belonging to Jesus Christ and learning to walk by His Spirit.
Romans 6:14 declares:
“For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.”
— ESV
Paul is not promising that Christians will never experience temptation again.
Nor is he suggesting that believers can reach a state where they no longer need confession, humility, or dependence on God.
He is announcing that sin is no longer the rightful ruler of those who belong to Christ.
The power of sin has been decisively challenged through the death and resurrection of Jesus.
And that truth changes how we fight.
We do not fight for God's acceptance as though Christ has done nothing.
We fight from the grace we have received.
We do not repent to convince Jesus to begin loving us.
We repent because His mercy calls us out of what destroys us.
We do not pursue holiness to make ourselves superior to other people.
We pursue holiness because the Savior who rescued us is holy.
And sometimes the first step toward freedom is the confession we have been avoiding.
“Lord, this has more power over me than I wanted to admit.”
“Lord, I have been defending what I should have surrendered.”
“Lord, I have confused Your patience with Your approval.”
“Lord, I want You more than I want this sin, but I need Your help.”
There is no need to make those words impressive.
God is not waiting for a beautifully written speech.
He calls us to come truthfully.
First John 1:9 gives believers this assurance:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— ESV
Notice where the confidence rests.
Not in the perfection of our confession.
Not in the intensity of our emotions.
Not in how long we have managed to avoid failure.
Our confidence rests in God's faithfulness and justice, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
That is why shame does not have to write the final chapter.
Your past may be real.
