The text says they burned them, then buried their bones.
The passage does not explicitly explain why they burned the bodies, and interpreters have suggested different possibilities.
But what is unmistakable is that these men acted courageously to recover and honor the dead.
The narrative does not condemn them for this treatment of the bodies.
We should also remember that the account describes burning followed by the burial of bones, not necessarily modern cremation as practiced today.
It therefore cannot settle every question about contemporary funeral choices.
Nevertheless, it challenges the simplistic claim that every biblical instance of burning human remains is automatically portrayed as wicked.
The Bible requires more careful reading than that.
And there is another passage that speaks powerfully to the limits of human decay.
Ecclesiastes 12:7 declares:
"Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." (KJV)
The verse reminds us that our lives are ultimately held by God.
It does not establish cremation as preferable to burial, nor does it prescribe a funeral procedure.
It points us toward the Creator who gave life in the first place.
And this brings us to the question beneath the question.
Are we trusting in the power of God?
Or have we unknowingly placed our confidence in the preservation of the body?
Because if resurrection required an undamaged corpse, then the hope of countless faithful believers throughout history would be in doubt.
Christians who died in persecution.
Christians who were burned for their faith.
Christians whose bodies were never recovered.
Christians who disappeared in wars, disasters, and shipwrecks.
Would their suffering somehow disqualify them from the resurrection?
Absolutely not.
Jesus said in John 6:40:
"And I will raise him up at the last day." (KJV)
Notice who makes that promise.
Jesus.
And notice who performs the action.
Jesus.
The believer's resurrection is not secured by the funeral director.
It is not secured by the cemetery.
It is not secured by the condition of the casket.
It is secured by the Savior who conquered death.
But someone reading this may still be struggling.
Perhaps you have always believed that cremation is wrong.
Perhaps your church strongly prefers burial.
Perhaps your parents taught you that a Christian should never choose cremation.
Should you simply abandon those convictions?
Not necessarily.
Romans 14 teaches believers to take conscience seriously in matters where Christians may reach different conclusions before the Lord.

Although Romans 14 does not specifically discuss cremation, its principles of sincere conviction, accountability to God, and avoiding contempt toward fellow believers are relevant when addressing matters not explicitly settled by a universal command.
If you believe burial is the most fitting way to honor the body and testify to the resurrection, you may choose burial with a clear conscience.
That can be a beautiful expression of Christian hope.

But if another believer chooses cremation respectfully, without denying the resurrection or treating the body with contempt, we should be cautious about declaring that person guilty of a sin Scripture has not explicitly identified.
There are also important differences among Christian traditions.
Some churches strongly favor burial because of its symbolism and historical place in Christian practice.

The Roman Catholic Church permits cremation for legitimate reasons while retaining a preference for burial and requiring reverent treatment of cremated remains. It also rejects cremation chosen as an expression of denial of Christian teaching about resurrection.
Many Protestant churches likewise permit cremation, though individual denominations and congregations may differ in their guidance.
Other Christian communities discourage or prohibit it as a matter of their ecclesiastical discipline and theological tradition.
These differences deserve respectful discussion.
We do not honor Scripture by pretending every Christian tradition interprets funeral practices identically.
And we do not honor Christ by treating grieving believers with cruelty.
There is also a practical reality that should not be ignored.
Funerals can be expensive.
Some families face devastating financial decisions while they are already emotionally exhausted.
A grieving widow may have very little money.
Children may be struggling to provide a dignified farewell for their parents.
A family may choose cremation because of cost, transportation, local regulations, or the deceased person's wishes.
These circumstances do not automatically make every decision wise or spiritually appropriate.
But neither should we assume that a family choosing cremation is rejecting God.
Poverty is not proof of irreverence. And an expensive funeral is not proof of holiness.
The dignity of a person is not measured by the price of a coffin.
The depth of Christian love is not measured by the size of a tombstone.
And the promise of resurrection cannot be purchased through funeral arrangements.
Yet Christians should still ask thoughtful questions.
Are we treating the body with respect?
Are we making this decision in faith rather than in contempt for Christian teaching?
Are we considering the conscience of the family and the testimony of our church?
Are we honoring the deceased without placing ourselves under an unnecessary burden of fear?
Are we remembering that the body matters to God?
Because the Christian faith does not teach that the body is worthless.
In 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, Paul reminds believers that their bodies belong to God and that they are to glorify Him in their bodies.
The immediate context concerns how Christians live, particularly their bodily holiness, rather than prescribing what must happen after death.
Still, the passage reinforces an essential Christian conviction.
Our bodies matter.
We are not disposable souls trapped in meaningless flesh.
God created human beings as embodied persons.
The Son of God truly took on human flesh.
Jesus truly died bodily.
Jesus truly rose bodily.
And the Christian hope is not simply that our souls will escape the physical world forever.
It is that God will redeem His creation and raise His people to new life.
This is why the resurrection matters so much.
In 1 Corinthians 15:14, Paul writes:
Everything stands or falls on the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Not on whether a believer was buried.
Not on whether a believer was cremated.
But on whether Jesus truly defeated death.
And the New Testament declares that He did.
Here is the moment when this discussion becomes deeply personal.
One day, unless Christ returns first, someone will have to decide what happens to your earthly remains.
Someone may choose your clothes.
Someone may select a photograph.
Someone may stand before a congregation and struggle to speak your name without crying.
Someone may hold your Bible.
Someone may discover the prayers you wrote in the margins.
Someone may remember the last conversation they had with you and wish they had said one more thing.
And in that moment, the most important question will not be whether your body is placed beneath the earth or respectfully cremated.
The most important question will be whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Because a beautifully preserved body cannot save a soul.
A magnificent funeral cannot forgive sin.
A marble tomb cannot produce eternal life.
And no burial tradition can accomplish what only the crucified and risen Savior can do.
Jesus said:
"I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." (John 14:6, KJV)
The Gospel does not invite us to place our confidence in the way we will die.
It calls us to place our faith in the One who died and rose again.
We have sinned against a holy God.
We cannot earn our way into His kingdom.
We cannot undo our guilt through religious performance.
But Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, bore our sins on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
His resurrection is the foundation of our hope.
Through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
Not because they have arranged their funeral correctly.
But because Christ has accomplished what they could never accomplish for themselves.
This is grace.
Undeserved.
Unpurchased.
Greater than our failures.
Stronger than our shame.
And more powerful than death.
Perhaps your life has become a scandal.
Perhaps there are things in your past you would never want spoken aloud at your funeral.
Perhaps you have lived for years carrying regret, addiction, betrayal, bitterness, or secret sin.
Perhaps everyone sees a respectable Christian on Sunday, but God knows the battles you fight when nobody is watching.
Listen carefully.
The greatest danger is not that your body might become ashes. It is that you might spend your life avoiding the Savior who offers you forgiveness and eternal life.
The answer is not despair.
It is repentance.
Turn to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust His mercy.
Follow Him.
The One who raises the dead is also able to transform the living.
And that is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes more than a slogan.
He rewrites the story of the guilty through forgiveness.
He rewrites the story of the broken through restoration.
He rewrites the story of the lost through redemption.
And for those who belong to Him, He will one day replace the humiliation of death with the glory of resurrection.
Not because our bodies never became dust.
But because Jesus Christ is Lord over the dust.
Maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes because someone you loved was cremated.
Maybe a relative told you that your mother could never rise again.
Maybe you have carried that fear silently for years.
Hear what Scripture actually gives you permission to believe.
Cremation itself is not identified in the Bible as an act that prevents the resurrection of a believer.
The condition of a person's remains does not overpower the promise of Christ.
We cannot pronounce the eternal destiny of a particular individual merely because of their funeral arrangements.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
And we can entrust those we love to His perfect justice, wisdom, and mercy.
You do not need to invent a promise Scripture never made.
You do not need to pretend that every person who dies automatically enters heaven.
But neither must you carry a terror Scripture does not require you to carry.
God has not asked you to believe that ashes are stronger than His Son.
And if you are making a funeral decision today, seek wisdom prayerfully.
Read Scripture.
Speak with your pastor.
Consider the teachings of your church.
Honor your family's legitimate concerns.
Treat the remains of the deceased with dignity.
And remember that a Christian funeral should ultimately direct attention toward the hope of Jesus Christ.
Not toward superstition.
Not toward financial pressure.
Not toward the condemnation of grieving people.
But toward the Gospel.
Because the Christian's final hope is not an untouched grave.
It is an empty tomb.
The tomb of Jesus Christ.
And that changes everything.
Revelation 21:4 gives us a picture of the future God promises His redeemed people:
"And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away." (KJV)
Imagine that.
No more funeral calls.
No more hospital corridors filled with desperate prayers.
No more standing beside a grave wishing you could hear one more familiar laugh.
No more children asking why their father is never coming home.
No more spouses reaching across an empty bed.
No more death.
Not because humanity finally discovered how to preserve the body forever.
But because Jesus Christ will bring death's reign to an end.
That is the hope worth defending.
That is the truth worth sharing.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to frighten people into religious performance.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell salvation or God's favor.
But to keep pointing wounded, searching, struggling people back to the Scriptures and to Jesus Christ.
If this article corrected something you believed, comforted you about someone you lost, or challenged you to examine your own relationship with Christ, don't keep that moment to yourself.
Has this question affected your family? Or are you still wrestling with what Scripture teaches?
Your experience may help someone else who has been too afraid to ask.
You do not have to share details you are not ready to share. But you may discover that others are carrying the same questions and sorrow.
There is also a deeper way to stand with this ministry.
Scripture reminds us in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that God loves a cheerful giver. Christian generosity should arise from love, faith, and willingness, not pressure or fear.
Your prayers matter.
Your comments matter.
Your sharing matters.
Your encouragement matters.
There is no price attached to the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
You can explore the resources, keep learning, and help others discover them.
Because this is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about making the Savior known.
And before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
Can Christians practice cremation without violating biblical teaching?

Yes, cremation can be consistent with biblical teaching when it is chosen for reasons that do not reject Christian faith, when human remains are treated respectfully, and when the decision is made with appropriate regard for conscience and church teaching. Scripture honors burial as a significant and longstanding practice, but it does not establish a universal prohibition of cremation or teach that cremation prevents bodily resurrection.
That conclusion does not make burial meaningless.
It makes Christ supreme.
And if there is one truth I pray you never forget, it is this:
Your resurrection hope is not in how faithfully your body is preserved after death, but in how faithfully Jesus Christ keeps His promise to raise those who belong to Him.
One day, the dust will no longer be silent.
The graves will surrender their dead.
And every promise of the risen Savior will prove stronger than the power of death.
Ashes cannot silence the voice of the Savior who calls His people home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A CHRISTIAN WOMAN TOUCH HER OWN BODY WITHOUT BETRAYING GOD?
paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN WOMAN TOUCH HER OWN BODY WITHOUT BETRAYING GOD?
The Question Millions of Women Are Afraid to Ask: What the Bible Actually Says About Masturbation, Sexual Desire, Secret Shame, and the Grace of Jesus Christ.
There is a question some Christian women would rather carry to their graves than whisper inside a church.
Not because they don't love Jesus.
Not because they've abandoned their faith.
But because they are terrified of what the answer might reveal about them.
She reads her Bible. She prays. She worships on Sundays. She genuinely wants to honor God with her life.
But sometimes, late at night, when the house is quiet and nobody is watching, she experiences sexual desire.
And sometimes, she responds to that desire by touching her own body.
Then comes the question.
Did I just betray Jesus?
Perhaps she asks God for forgiveness immediately afterward. Perhaps she promises never to do it again. Perhaps she feels nothing afterward, and that frightens her even more.
Because somewhere along the way, she learned to associate sexual pleasure with spiritual danger.
Now she wonders whether her own body has become an enemy of her faith.
But what if the question isn't nearly as simple as the answers she's been given?
What if some Christians have spoken with absolute certainty about something Scripture never explicitly names?
And what if, at the same time, other voices have dismissed biblical warnings about lust, self-control, and holiness simply because masturbation is not directly mentioned?
We need to talk about both.
Because the woman asking this question doesn't need another person shouting condemnation at her.
Neither does she need someone twisting Scripture to make every desire automatically acceptable.
She needs the truth. And she needs to encounter that truth in the presence of Jesus Christ.
Before we go any further, understand something important.
This article is not permission to abandon holiness.
It is not an invitation to indulge every sexual impulse.
And it is certainly not a declaration that everything we do privately is morally irrelevant.
It is an invitation to examine what God has actually revealed, distinguish Scripture from human assumptions, and discover how grace and holiness belong together.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel better about their sin.
He came to save sinners, forgive them, and transform their lives.
And transformation begins with truth.
Consider the first uncomfortable fact.
The Bible does not explicitly mention female masturbation, nor does it contain a direct command declaring masturbation itself sinful.
Read that carefully.
This does not automatically establish that every instance of masturbation is morally right. Scripture also gives principles that govern actions it does not name individually.
But it does mean that Christians should be careful about declaring, "God explicitly forbids this," when no such explicit prohibition exists.
That distinction matters.
Especially when a woman's conscience is already burdened by fear.
One passage frequently brought into this conversation is Genesis 38, the account of Onan.
For generations, people have connected Onan's wrongdoing with masturbation.
But look at what the passage actually describes.

Onan was obligated under the family circumstances of his time to provide offspring for his deceased brother's household. Instead, he deliberately prevented conception while engaging in intercourse with his brother's widow.
Genesis 38:9 explains that Onan knew the offspring would not be considered his.
His wrongdoing involved his refusal to fulfill his responsibility, along with his exploitation of the situation.
The passage is not describing a woman stimulating herself, nor does it establish a general biblical prohibition against masturbation.
We cannot responsibly turn a passage about Onan's actions into a command that the text itself never gives.
And yet, that is not the end of the conversation.
Because Jesus speaks directly about the moral significance of what happens inside the human heart.
In Matthew 5:28, He says:
"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." — Matthew 5:28, KJV
The Greek expression translated "to lust after her" includes the words:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn
The verb epithymeō means to desire or long for something. Depending on its context, that desire may be good or sinful.
In Matthew 5:28, Jesus is condemning a deliberately lustful way of looking at another person.
He is confronting the heart that turns another human being into an object of covetous sexual desire.
Notice what Jesus is doing.
He is not teaching that merely recognizing someone as attractive is adultery.
He is not saying that every involuntary sexual feeling is a deliberate sin.
And He is not specifically discussing masturbation.
He is exposing the moral condition of a heart that chooses to cultivate lust.
That raises an important question.
When a Christian woman masturbates, what is happening in her heart?
Is she intentionally entertaining sexual fantasies that violate her marriage vows or objectify another person?
Is pornography shaping her desires?
Is she repeatedly using sexual stimulation to escape emotional pain, loneliness, anxiety, or despair?
Is the behavior becoming difficult to control, interfering with her responsibilities, or weakening her relationships?
Or is she experiencing bodily sexual desire without pornography, without deliberately lusting after another person, and without the behavior controlling her life?
Those situations are not necessarily morally identical.
And pretending they are does not produce better biblical understanding.
It produces confusion.
Paul gives us another important principle in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
"All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any." — KJV
Paul is not giving Christians unlimited permission to do whatever they want. He is challenging the idea that freedom means surrendering ourselves to whatever appetite demands satisfaction.
The Greek phrase:
οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος — ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos
communicates Paul's refusal to be mastered or brought under the authority of anything.
That is a powerful principle for sexual ethics.
Because a Christian should be concerned not only with whether an act is explicitly prohibited, but also with whether it is gaining destructive power over her.
Can she choose not to engage in it?
Can she face loneliness without always needing sexual release?
Can she respond to temptation without feeling helpless?
Is she growing in self-control?
Or is something increasingly governing her behavior?
These questions are worth asking.
But we must be equally careful not to assume that every experience of sexual pleasure is evidence of addiction, spiritual bondage, or rebellion.
Frequency alone does not establish compulsive behavior.
And shame alone does not prove that an action is sinful.
A conscience can be troubled because it recognizes genuine wrongdoing.
But a conscience can also be burdened by misinformation, fear, or teachings that go beyond Scripture.
That is why the conscience needs formation through biblical truth, not merely stronger feelings of guilt.
Now consider something that many women have never been encouraged to think about.
Your body is not inherently dirty because it is capable of sexual pleasure.
Genesis 1:27 tells us that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
And Genesis 1:31 declares that what God had made was very good.
The Hebrew expression is:
טוֹב מְאֹד — tov me'od
"Very good."
This does not mean that every possible use of the body is morally good.
The fall affected human desires, relationships, and actions.
But it does mean that being embodied is not a spiritual defect.
A woman's body is not a mistake.
Her capacity for sexual feeling does not make her less worthy of dignity.
Her biological responses do not automatically establish that she has sinned.
Christian holiness does not require pretending the body does not exist.
In fact, Scripture speaks positively about sexual delight within marriage.
Proverbs 5:18–19 celebrates marital affection and satisfaction.
The Song of Songs portrays desire and mutual delight between lovers.
The Bible is not embarrassed to acknowledge that sexuality is part of human life.
Yet these passages celebrate sexual love in a relational context. They do not directly answer the question of solitary sexual stimulation.
That distinction is important.
We should not use the goodness of created sexuality to justify every expression of sexual desire.
But neither should we treat sexual desire itself as proof that something is wrong with a woman.
Perhaps this is where some readers need to stop and consider what they have believed about themselves.
Have you confused temptation with surrender?
Have you confused a physical response with a deliberate moral decision?
Have you been apologizing to God simply for possessing a body?
Or have you been using the absence of an explicit prohibition to avoid examining desires that are genuinely drawing you away from Him?
Those are different spiritual problems.
And they require different kinds of honesty.
Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5 that God's will includes sanctification, abstaining from sexual immorality, and learning to live in holiness and honor rather than uncontrolled passion.
The Greek word translated "sanctification" is:
ἁγιασμός — hagiasmos
It refers to holiness or consecration.
God's desire is not merely that Christians avoid certain outward behaviors.
He calls them into lives increasingly set apart for Him.
But we must read Paul's words in context.
The passage clearly teaches sexual holiness and self-control. It does not specifically define masturbation as sexual immorality.
Christians disagree about how its broader principles apply to masturbation.
Some conclude that masturbation is inherently inconsistent with God's design for sexuality because sexual expression properly belongs within marital intimacy.

Others conclude that masturbation is not necessarily sinful in itself, while recognizing that lust, pornography, compulsive behavior, violation of conscience, and other circumstances can make particular instances morally wrong.
Both positions attempt to reason from broader biblical principles, because neither can point to a verse explicitly addressing masturbation itself.
That does not mean every argument on either side is equally persuasive.
It means intellectual and spiritual honesty require us to acknowledge where interpretation is involved.
A Christian woman seeking to honor God should examine these arguments carefully, in prayer, with Scripture open.
She should not be pressured into pretending the Bible says something it does not say.
Nor should she be encouraged to dismiss holiness because a direct command is absent.
And there is another passage that deserves attention.
Romans 14:23 concludes:
"For whatsoever is not of faith is sin." — KJV
Paul's immediate discussion concerns disputed practices, food, and the conscience.
His point is that a person should not knowingly act against a conscience that remains unconvinced before God.
This principle can help us think about disputed moral questions, although Romans 14 is not itself a teaching about masturbation.
If you believe an action would be disobedient to God, do not force yourself past that conviction simply because someone online tells you to relax.
Seek understanding first.
Study.
Pray.
Ask whether your conviction is rooted in Scripture, thoughtful application, or fear.
And remember that a conscience can become more accurately informed.
You do not honor God by deliberately violating your conscience.
But neither do you honor Him by refusing to examine whether your conscience has been taught correctly.
Now imagine a woman sitting on the edge of her bed after another night of wrestling with this question.
She is not looking for an excuse to abandon Jesus.
She is afraid He is disappointed in her.
She remembers every sermon about purity.
Every warning about hidden sin.
Every statement suggesting that a truly godly woman should never experience certain desires.
And she whispers:
"Lord, do You still love me?"
Here is where the Gospel must become more than a religious slogan.
Because the answer to that question is not found in whether she managed to maintain a perfect record of sexual behavior.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — KJV
Christ did not wait for human beings to become morally flawless before demonstrating His love.
He came precisely because we needed redemption.
This does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.

The account appears in John 7:53–8:11, a passage whose placement in the earliest textual tradition is disputed. Many modern Bibles note that the earliest surviving manuscripts do not include it at this location. It should therefore be handled with appropriate textual care.
Nevertheless, the narrative portrays a powerful picture consistent with Jesus' wider ministry.
A woman is publicly exposed.
Her accusers are ready to condemn her.
And Jesus confronts the hypocrisy surrounding her accusation.
In John 8:11, the familiar account records His words:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — KJV
Notice the two movements.
Mercy.
And a call to change.
Jesus does not treat sin as meaningless.
But neither does He reduce the woman to her worst moment.
This is the balance we desperately need.
Grace is not the denial of holiness.
And holiness is not the denial of grace.
At the cross, the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's mercy meet.
And if you are a woman struggling with sexual shame, you need to understand this.
Jesus is not asking you to purchase His love with a spotless record.
Salvation is not earned through sexual restraint, charitable giving, religious activity, or any other human achievement.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
But the very next verse, Ephesians 2:10, teaches that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave us unchanged.
It creates the foundation for a new life.
So what should a Christian woman actually do when she faces this question?
She should begin with honesty rather than panic.
She can acknowledge her sexual feelings without automatically condemning herself for having them.
She can examine whether lust, pornography, compulsive patterns, emotional avoidance, or disregard for her commitments are involved.
She can consider the different Christian interpretations of masturbation and evaluate their biblical reasoning.
She can choose abstinence while her conscience remains uncertain.
She can seek wise pastoral guidance from someone who understands Scripture and will not shame her.
And if the behavior is causing significant distress or feels genuinely uncontrollable, she can also seek qualified mental-health support without treating professional care as a failure of faith.
She should not confuse a biological urge with a command that must be obeyed.
And she should not confuse every uncomfortable emotion with the voice of the Holy Spirit.
God's Word, rightly understood, must guide her.
This is especially important for women who are single, widowed, divorced, or living apart from their spouses.
Christian communities sometimes discuss sexual ethics as though only married people experience sexual desire.
But singleness does not erase the body.
Widowhood does not eliminate longing.
Divorce does not automatically silence sexual feelings.
And a woman who has chosen celibacy does not stop being human.
The church should be able to discuss these realities with compassion, seriousness, and biblical integrity.
Without ridicule.
Without sensationalism.
Without treating women as spiritually inferior for asking questions.
And without offering simplistic answers to deeply personal situations.
There is a reason James 1:5 invites believers who lack wisdom to ask God.
We need wisdom precisely because not every question can be resolved by repeating a slogan.
Sometimes spiritual maturity means admitting that Scripture gives a clear principle without explicitly naming every possible application.
Sometimes it means choosing restraint.
Sometimes it means correcting a mistaken belief.
Sometimes it means confessing genuine sin.
And sometimes it means releasing shame that God never commanded us to carry.
The Christian life requires discernment.
Not merely fear.
Now I want to speak to the woman who has been quietly reading this while wondering whether she should even have opened the article.
Perhaps you are afraid someone will judge you for being curious.
Perhaps you have struggled for years.
Perhaps you have never masturbated, but you experience sexual desire and feel guilty simply because it exists.
Perhaps you disagree with some of what you've read.
You are welcome to examine every claim against Scripture.
Please do.
Your relationship with Jesus is too important to build on the unquestioned authority of an article, a preacher, or a social media page.
Acts 17:11 commends those who examined the Scriptures to evaluate what they were being taught.
That is the kind of discipleship we want to encourage.
Not blind agreement.
Not emotional dependence on a ministry.
But deeper faithfulness to Christ.
And there is one more truth we cannot afford to miss.
The greatest question in your spiritual life is not simply, "Have I ever masturbated?"
It is, "Am I trusting Jesus Christ, submitting my life to His Word, and allowing His grace to transform me?"
Sexual ethics matter.
Obedience matters.
Repentance matters.
But Christianity is not merely a system of behavior management.
It is reconciliation with God through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
It is the forgiveness of sins.
It is the gift of the Holy Spirit.
It is learning to walk in the light.
It is becoming more like the Savior who loved us and gave Himself for us.
And this is why Romans 8:1 is so precious:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." — KJV
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα — Ouden ara nyn katakrima
"So then, there is now no condemnation."
The word katakrima refers to condemnation or an adverse judicial sentence.
Paul is proclaiming the believer's standing in Christ, not claiming that Christians never sin or never need correction.
Read the rest of Romans 8.
The chapter speaks about the Spirit, putting sinful deeds to death, adoption as God's children, suffering, hope, and the inseparable love of God in Christ.
No condemnation is not permission to remain enslaved.
It is the foundation of a transformed life.
And perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
If you have sinned, you can repent and receive forgiveness through Christ.
If you have been falsely condemned by human traditions, you can seek freedom through biblical truth.
If you are confused, you can keep studying without pretending to have answers you do not yet possess.
If you are exhausted from hiding, you can seek trustworthy Christian community.
You do not need to manufacture certainty.
You need to remain faithful to the One who is truth.
And please, do not mistake the tenderness of this message for a declaration that sin does not matter.
It matters so deeply that Christ gave His life to redeem sinners.
But do not mistake the seriousness of sin for proof that Jesus is unwilling to receive those who come to Him.
John 6:37 records His promise:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." — KJV
That promise is worth holding onto.
Even when your questions are difficult.
Even when your conscience is troubled.
Even when you are still learning what faithful obedience requires.
Because the Savior who calls you to holiness is also the Savior who invites you to come to Him.
And if this conversation has touched something you have never been able to say aloud, you are not required to disclose intimate details publicly.
But you are invited to participate in a conversation that the church too often avoids.
You might comment, "Lord, teach me Your truth," if you want to pursue biblical understanding without fear.
Or comment, "Christ is still healing me," if you are learning to bring shame, confusion, or hidden struggles into the light of His grace.
We need conversations where Scripture matters more than embarrassment, and where people can disagree without humiliating one another.
And if someone you know is silently wrestling with sexual shame, consider sharing this article with them privately.
Not because every person needs to reveal their private struggles, but because thoughtful, compassionate, Scripture-centered discussions deserve to reach beyond the walls of a church building.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have drifted from faith, and even those who do not yet believe to encounter the Gospel through thoughtful, Christ-centered teaching.
Because the goal is not to win arguments about difficult subjects.
The goal is to help people know Jesus Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior has become a meaningful part of your spiritual journey, there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
These resources are intended to help people open their Bibles, grow in understanding, and strengthen their walk with the Lord.
And the more sustainable this ministry becomes, the more opportunities we have to continue and expand that work.
Scripture teaches that believers may voluntarily support Gospel ministry.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly, or of necessity.
Giving should never be coerced.
And financial support should never be presented as the price of God's favor, forgiveness, or blessing.
It is not a substitute for repentance.

And it should not automatically be equated with the biblical tithe owed to a local church. Christians hold different convictions about tithing, but support for an independent ministry is best understood as a voluntary offering or gift, given according to one's conscience and circumstances.
If you already support your local church, care for your family, or have other important financial responsibilities, please honor those commitments.
But if you believe Gospel Warrior is faithfully serving others, and you have the means to participate, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
Not because God needs your money.
Not because you owe this ministry anything.
But because sharing biblical truth requires time, effort, resources, and people who believe the work is worth sustaining.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, opportunities for encouragement, and meaningful gifts for people you love.
It will always be the people we hope to reach with the message of Jesus Christ.
Financial support is one way to participate.
Prayer, encouragement, and sharing biblical truth are meaningful ways too.
Because this ministry does not exist to make people dependent on Gospel Warrior.
It exists to point them toward Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the woman who began this story.
The one sitting alone in the darkness.
The one asking whether touching her own body means she has betrayed God.
Perhaps she came looking for a simple yes or no.
But she deserves something more faithful than a confident answer Scripture itself does not explicitly provide.
She deserves to know that sexual desire is not automatically sin.
That masturbation is not directly addressed in the biblical text.
That lust, self-control, holiness, and conscience are genuinely important.
That Christians disagree about how these principles apply.
That she should not violate her conscience or ignore what she believes God is teaching her.
And that no question about her sexuality is beyond the reach of honest prayer, careful biblical study, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Above all, she deserves to know that the Gospel is not the story of a perfect woman who never struggled.
It is the story of a perfect Savior who came to redeem imperfect people.
A Savior who tells the truth.
A Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
A Savior who offers forgiveness.
A Savior who transforms those who belong to Him.
So if you are reading this with tears in your eyes, do not allow shame to be the final voice speaking over your life.
Open your Bible.
Bring your questions to God.
Seek wise counsel.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where grace is offered.
And keep following Jesus.
Because the Christian life is not about pretending that your body, your questions, or your struggles do not exist.
It is about bringing your whole life under the gracious lordship of Christ.
And one day, when you look back at the questions that once terrified you, perhaps you will discover that the most important change was not simply that you found an answer about masturbation.
It was that you learned to seek God without hiding behind fear.

The deepest freedom is not found in having every desire satisfied or every struggle instantly silenced, but in discovering that your most difficult questions do not have to drive you away from the Savior who calls you into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD GAVE HER A CERTIFICATE OF DIVORCE… THEN CRIED, “COME BACK TO ME.”
paragraphs: GOD GAVE HER A CERTIFICATE OF DIVORCE… THEN CRIED, “COME BACK TO ME.”

Why did God use the image of a divorced wife to expose His people's unfaithfulness? The heartbreaking truth of Jeremiah 3:6–14 reveals the terrifying seriousness of sin, the astonishing patience of God, and the grace that still calls wandering hearts home.
What kind of love looks at someone who has betrayed it, walked away from it, and publicly embraced another… and still says, “Return to Me”?
Not because the betrayal was harmless.
Not because the wounds were imaginary.
Not because faithfulness no longer mattered.
But because mercy was speaking where judgment had every right to speak.
God describes a wife who has been unfaithful. He speaks of a certificate of divorce. He exposes the shame of a broken covenant. And then, almost unbelievably, He calls the unfaithful to return.
This is not a romantic story about a husband tolerating abuse. It is not permission for anyone to remain in a dangerous marriage. And it is certainly not God minimizing betrayal.
It is something infinitely more searching.
It is the holy God of Israel confronting the people He had redeemed, sustained, warned, and loved—people who had repeatedly exchanged His glory for idols that could neither save nor satisfy them.
And beneath the judgment, there is a question that still reaches into our lives today:
What happens when the God you have abandoned is the very One calling you home?
Jeremiah 3:6–14 takes us into one of the most emotionally devastating confrontations in the Old Testament.
During the reign of King Josiah, God told Jeremiah to look at what had happened to the northern kingdom of Israel.
Israel had turned from the Lord toward other gods. The prophets repeatedly described this covenant betrayal through the language of marital unfaithfulness.
God said:
“Have you seen that which backsliding Israel hath done? she is gone up upon every high mountain and under every green tree, and there hath played the harlot.” — Jeremiah 3:6, KJV
The high mountains and green trees were not innocent details in this accusation. They pointed toward places associated with idolatrous worship.
Israel had not merely forgotten a religious tradition.
She had turned away from the living God.
The Hebrew word used in this passage for the unfaithful Israel is מְשֻׁבָה (meshūvāh), from the root שׁוּב (shuv), meaning “to turn” or “to return.”
In this context, the word describes one who has turned away—faithless, backsliding, persistently wandering.
That matters.
Because the same Hebrew root will become central to God's invitation to return.
The tragedy is not simply that Israel made mistakes.
The tragedy is that she kept turning away from the One who had called her to Himself.
And before we point our fingers at ancient Israel, perhaps we should examine the things that quietly compete for the throne of our own hearts.
We may never bow before a carved idol.
But we can build an entire life around money and call it security.
We can crave human approval more than God's approval and call it belonging.
We can nurture bitterness and call it self-protection.
We can secretly feed lust and call it a private struggle we will deal with someday.
We can chase success, attention, comfort, pleasure, or control until obedience to Christ becomes negotiable.
Not every desire is an idol.
But even a good thing can become an idol when we give it the trust, devotion, and ultimate allegiance that belong to God alone.
Sometimes the most dangerous distance from God is not the distance everyone can see.
It is the distance hidden beneath a convincing Christian appearance.
You still know the songs.
You still recognize the verses.
You may even know exactly when to say “Amen.”
But somewhere along the way, your heart has begun to drift.
And perhaps no one knows.
Except God.
Then comes one of the most sobering statements in the passage.
God says:
“And I saw, when for all the causes whereby backsliding Israel committed adultery I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce…” — Jeremiah 3:8, KJV
Read that carefully.
God says He gave faithless Israel a certificate of divorce.
The Hebrew expression includes סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת (sefer keritut), literally a written document of cutting off, commonly understood as a certificate of divorce.
This is covenant language.
And it is deliberately shocking.

The Lord is not describing an ordinary human marriage. He is using the recognizable legal and relational imagery of divorce to explain the seriousness of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness and the judgment that followed.

The northern kingdom had been conquered by Assyria, and many of its inhabitants had been carried into exile. That historical catastrophe, recorded in 2 Kings 17, provides the essential background for Jeremiah's imagery.
The covenant people had repeatedly rejected God's warnings. Judgment was not an empty threat.
The image of divorce communicated a devastating truth: Israel could not continually violate the covenant and presume that there would never be consequences.
God's love was never indifference toward evil.
His patience was never approval of rebellion.
His holiness was never negotiable.
And that is where this passage begins to confront us personally.
We sometimes confuse God's patience with His permission.
Because judgment does not immediately fall, we imagine our compromises are harmless.
Because our hidden sins have not been exposed, we begin to think they are unseen.
Because we can still pray, worship, and speak Christian language, we assume our hearts must be close to God.
But the Lord sees what public appearances conceal.
He sees the resentment we keep feeding.
The dishonesty we keep defending.
The secret habits we keep excusing.
The obedience we keep postponing.
And yet, this is what makes Jeremiah's message so astonishing.
The God who exposes covenant betrayal is also the God who calls the betrayer to return.
Before we reach that invitation, however, Scripture reveals another painful detail.
Judah had watched what happened to Israel.
The southern kingdom had seen the consequences of idolatry and unfaithfulness.
Judah had been given a warning written into the history of her own sister nation.
And still, she refused to learn.
Jeremiah 3:10 says:
“And yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah hath not turned unto me with her whole heart, but feignedly, saith the LORD.” — KJV
Feignedly.
In other words, not sincerely.
Judah's return was outward, not wholehearted.
This is particularly striking because the passage is set during the reign of Josiah, a king associated with significant religious reforms.
Outward reform could take place while hearts remained divided.
The Hebrew phrase בְּשֶׁקֶר (besheqer) carries the sense of falsehood or deceit.
God was confronting a people whose outward religious behavior did not correspond to genuine inward repentance.
And suddenly the passage becomes painfully contemporary.
Because there is a difference between looking changed and being changed.
There is a difference between feeling guilty because you were caught and grieving because you have sinned against God.
There is a difference between managing your reputation and surrendering your heart.
You can remove an idol from your surroundings while secretly keeping it enthroned in your desires.
You can speak about holiness while refusing to release the sin you have grown comfortable protecting.
You can appear spiritually alive while privately becoming indifferent to the voice of God.
And perhaps that is why this passage is so unsettling.
It does not merely ask whether we attend church.
It asks whether we belong to God with an undivided heart.
It does not merely ask whether we know the right answers.
It asks whether we are willing to obey the One who gave them.
It does not merely ask whether we have changed our behavior.
It asks whether we have truly returned.
And here is something we must understand about repentance.
Biblical repentance is not a performance designed to convince God that we deserve another chance.
It is a genuine turning from sin toward the Lord, with a changed heart that bears fruit in a changed life.
It does not purchase grace.
It responds to grace.
It does not mean we become sinlessly perfect overnight.
It means we stop making peace with the rebellion that is destroying us.
And then, in Jeremiah 3:11, God delivers a startling verdict.
Faithless Israel, He says, has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.
Not because Israel was innocent.
Not because Israel's idolatry was acceptable.
But because Judah had witnessed Israel's judgment and still persisted in hypocrisy.
Greater knowledge had brought greater responsibility.
The people who had seen the warning had no excuse to treat it as irrelevant.
That should sober those of us who have heard the Gospel repeatedly.
We have access to Scripture.
We have heard sermons.
We have been warned about the deceitfulness of sin.
We know that Jesus calls His followers to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him.
And yet knowing the truth does not automatically mean we are living in it.
Sometimes familiarity with holy things makes us dangerously comfortable around truths that should bring us to our knees.
But then the atmosphere changes.
The God who has exposed Israel's unfaithfulness commands Jeremiah to proclaim a message toward the north.
And what follows is one of the most breathtaking invitations in the entire passage.
“Return, thou backsliding Israel, saith the LORD; and I will not cause mine anger to fall upon you: for I am merciful, saith the LORD, and I will not keep anger for ever.” — Jeremiah 3:12, KJV
Return.
There it is.
The word Israel had resisted.
The word Judah had imitated outwardly but not embraced wholeheartedly.
The word that reveals what God is calling His people to do.
In Hebrew, the command is שׁוּבָה (shuvah).
Return.
Turn back.
Come home.
Notice the profound wordplay.
The people are described as turning away, and God calls them to turn back.
Their unfaithfulness is real.
Their guilt is real.
The consequences are real.
But so is God's invitation.
He identifies Himself as merciful.
The Hebrew word חָסִיד (chasid) in Jeremiah 3:12 describes God's gracious, faithful character. It is related to the language of covenant loyalty and steadfast devotion.
God is not saying that sin does not matter.
He is revealing that His mercy is not exhausted by the seriousness of the sin He has just condemned.
But do not miss what comes next.
God does not invite Israel to pretend nothing happened.
He does not ask her to invent excuses.
He does not say that repentance means blaming someone else for her decisions.
Instead, He says:
“Only acknowledge thine iniquity, that thou hast transgressed against the LORD thy God…” — Jeremiah 3:13, KJV
Only acknowledge your iniquity.
There is no elaborate religious performance demanded here.
No elaborate explanation capable of making betrayal sound innocent.
No carefully polished testimony designed to preserve appearances.
God calls His people to tell the truth about their sin.
That does not make confession a payment for forgiveness. It means genuine repentance stops arguing with God's verdict.
And perhaps this is the sentence some of us have been avoiding.
“Lord, I sinned.”
Not merely, “I was going through something.”
Not merely, “People pushed me too far.”
Not merely, “Everybody struggles with this.”
Those circumstances may be real. Pain, temptation, wounds, and weakness can help explain how we reached a particular place.
But they do not turn disobedience into righteousness.
There is healing in bringing the truth into God's light.
There is freedom in no longer having to defend what God is calling us to surrender.
And there is hope for the person who has finally grown tired of pretending.
Maybe you are reading this with a burden nobody else knows about.
Maybe you have been fighting a habit that keeps pulling you back into shame.
Maybe your prayers have become mechanical.
Maybe you once burned with love for Jesus, but now you struggle even to open your Bible.
Maybe you have hurt people you love.
Maybe you have been more concerned about appearing spiritual than actually walking with God.
Or maybe you have never truly trusted Christ at all, despite being surrounded by Christian language your entire life.
Hear the invitation of Scripture.
Return.
Not because your sin was insignificant.
But because God's mercy is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
And then comes Jeremiah 3:14.
A verse so tender that, after everything we have read, it almost seems impossible.
“Turn, O backsliding children, saith the LORD; for I am married unto you…” — KJV
The Hebrew reads:
שׁוּבוּ בָנִים שׁוֹבָבִים נְאֻם־יְהוָה כִּי אָנֹכִי בָּעַלְתִּי בָכֶם
Shuvu vanim shovavim, ne'um-YHWH, ki anokhi ba'alti vakhem.
A careful rendering is:
“Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD, for I am your master [or husband].”
The Hebrew verb בָּעַלְתִּי (ba'alti) is related to a term that can convey the idea of being a husband, master, or lord.
That is why English translations differ. The KJV reads “I am married unto you,” while some modern translations render the expression in terms of God's lordship or mastery.
The underlying point is covenantal: God is asserting His rightful relationship and authority over the people He calls to return.
And that brings us to the question at the heart of this entire passage.
How can God speak of giving Israel a certificate of divorce in verse 8 and then speak of His continuing covenant claim in verse 14?
Because Jeremiah is using prophetic covenant imagery, not providing a simple legal account of an ordinary marriage.
The divorce image communicates the reality of judgment and covenant rupture brought about by Israel's persistent idolatry.
The call to return reveals that judgment has not silenced God's merciful purposes or erased His sovereign right to summon His people back.
The imagery is meant to make us feel both truths.
The betrayal was serious enough to bring devastating consequences.
And the Lord was merciful enough to call the unfaithful to repentance.
We should not flatten either side.
If we speak only about judgment, we can miss the astonishing invitation.
If we speak only about mercy, we can minimize the holiness of the One extending it.
Scripture refuses both distortions.
God is holy.
God is just.
God is merciful.
And His invitation to return is not an invitation to continue unchanged.
It is a call to abandon false gods and come back to Him.
There is also an important distinction here for anyone whose own marriage has been marked by betrayal, abandonment, coercion, or abuse.
This prophetic image must never be used to pressure an injured spouse to remain in danger, excuse repeated mistreatment, or treat reconciliation as automatic.
God's covenant relationship with Israel is not interchangeable with the responsibilities and safety considerations of a human marriage.
The passage reveals God's character and confronts idolatry. It does not erase the biblical seriousness of wrongdoing or the need for protection, justice, accountability, and genuine repentance.
And now we must look beyond Jeremiah.
Because the story of covenant unfaithfulness does not end with Israel's exile.
The prophets looked forward to a greater work of restoration.
Jeremiah himself would later announce God's promise of a new covenant.
In Jeremiah 31:31–34, the Lord promises a covenant marked by His law written upon hearts, a true knowledge of Him, and the forgiveness of sins.
The answer to humanity's deepest problem would require more than improved outward behavior.
We needed hearts made new.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed reconciliation with God.
And that is where the story leads us to Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not tell us that God simply decided to overlook evil.
It tells us that the Son of God came into our broken world, lived in perfect obedience, died for sinners, and rose again.
At the cross, God's holiness and mercy are not enemies.
Jesus bears sin and opens the way for guilty people to be reconciled to God.
As Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
Not after we had made ourselves worthy.
Not after we had successfully hidden every failure.
Not after we had built a religious reputation impressive enough to impress heaven.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And the risen Jesus calls people everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
This is the difference between merely feeling bad about sin and coming to Christ for salvation.
Shame says, “Hide yourself.”
Pride says, “Justify yourself.”
Self-righteousness says, “Repair yourself until you deserve acceptance.”
But the Gospel says, “Come to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.”
He is not a Savior for people who have never fallen.
He is the Savior of sinners.
He does not redeem us so we can remain enslaved to what destroys us.
He redeems us to make us His own.
And in the New Testament, the imagery of covenant love reaches another breathtaking expression.
Christ is presented as the Bridegroom, and His redeemed people as His bride.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — KJV
Think about that.
Jeremiah shows us the heartbreaking seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness.
The Gospel shows us the astonishing cost of Christ's redeeming love.
We cannot simply equate every detail of Israel's prophetic marriage imagery with the church. These passages have distinct historical settings and covenant contexts.
But together, within the unfolding story of Scripture, they reveal the seriousness of human unfaithfulness and the greatness of God's saving purpose in Christ.
The God who calls sinners to return has provided the Savior through whom forgiveness and reconciliation are offered.
And perhaps that is the part of this story you most need to hear.
Your sin is not something to celebrate.
Your rebellion is not something to excuse.
Your hidden compromises are not harmless.
But your past does not have to be the final word over your future.
Because Jesus Christ is able to forgive, cleanse, and transform those who come to Him.
Not every consequence disappears immediately.
Not every broken relationship is automatically restored.
Not every wound heals overnight.
But forgiveness in Christ is real.
New life in Christ is real.
And the transforming work of the Holy Spirit is real.
You may have wasted years.
You may have ignored warnings.
You may have become skilled at hiding your spiritual emptiness.
You may have carried guilt so long that you have started to mistake it for your identity.
But guilt does not have to become your permanent home.
Bring it into the light of Christ.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn away from what is destroying your fellowship with God.
Seek help and accountability where they are needed.
Make restitution where it is possible and right.
And stop confusing the invitation to return with a demand that you somehow save yourself.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His grace can reconcile sinners to God.
And the grace that forgives also teaches us to walk in holiness.
That is why this message cannot end as merely an interesting study of ancient Hebrew words.
The Hebrew matters because it helps us hear the text accurately.
The history matters because it prevents us from inventing meanings the passage never intended.
The covenant context matters because it reveals the gravity of Israel's rebellion.
But the truth of Scripture must also reach our hearts.
What are you holding on to that God is calling you to surrender?
What have you been defending that you already know is disobedience?
Where have you learned to look faithful while secretly drifting?
And what would genuine repentance look like in your life today?
Not next month.
Not when circumstances become easier.
Not after one more season of compromise.
Today.
Perhaps it begins with a prayer that is not polished at all.

“Lord Jesus, I have wandered. I have made excuses. I have allowed things into my heart that do not belong there. I cannot cleanse myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive my sins. Teach me to hate what is evil and love what is good. Give me a heart that obeys You, not merely a mouth that speaks about You. I surrender myself to You. Lead me in Your truth. Amen.”
If that prayer reflects the genuine cry of your heart, do not stop at emotion.
Open the Scriptures.
Seek a faithful local church.
Walk with mature believers who will speak truth with love.
Confess your struggles to trustworthy Christians who can pray with you and help you pursue holiness.
And when you stumble, do not make your stumbling an excuse to abandon Christ.
Return to Him.
Again and again, not to exploit His mercy, but because you are learning to live by His grace.
And if this message exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sins publicly.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to prove your salvation through a comment.
But because sometimes the first honest words we speak become the beginning of a much-needed conversation with fellow believers who will stand with us in prayer.
Your experience does not replace Scripture, but it may encourage someone who feels too ashamed to seek help.
Someone reading this may believe they have wandered too far.
Your words might remind them that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may need this message more than you realize.
A friend who has quietly stopped attending church.
A family member who has been wounded and is struggling to trust God.
A believer who looks strong in public but feels spiritually exhausted in private.
A person who has never understood why Christians speak so passionately about grace.
This is also why we are building something deeper than a collection of inspirational posts.
We want the person who cannot afford a book to have access to biblical encouragement.
We want the struggling believer to have resources that point back to Scripture.
We want families, new Christians, longtime believers, and those searching for truth to find materials that help them study, pray, and grow.
And we want this work to continue expanding.
We also want to be clear about something important.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully, not under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your tithe and offerings are matters of biblical stewardship and conscience before God, and no one should be made to feel that supporting this particular ministry is necessary to glorify Him.
It helps turn a shared burden for discipleship into sustained work.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus Christ is.
Pray for the people encountering these messages.
Your generosity matters.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to speak truth in love matters.
It is to make Jesus Christ known.
Because the point of Jeremiah 3 is not that unfaithfulness is beautiful.
It is that God is holy, sin is devastating, repentance is necessary, and His mercy is astonishing.
And the point of the Gospel is not that we can rescue ourselves through religious effort.
It is that Jesus Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He died.
He rose again.
And He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
So perhaps the question you should carry away from this article is not simply, “Why did God use the image of a divorced wife?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Where have I been unfaithful to God, and what is keeping me from returning to Him?”
Because the most heartbreaking part of Jeremiah's message is not only that Israel wandered.
It is that she was being called to return, yet had repeatedly refused.
Do not let familiarity with God's invitation become another excuse to delay your response.
Do not mistake religious appearance for genuine surrender.
Do not allow shame to convince you that you must hide from the Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
Come to Christ.
Not with excuses.
Not with a performance.
But with faith.
With confession.
With a heart willing to be changed.
And remember this when the enemy tempts you to believe that your story can never become anything more than a record of your failures:
The sin you once tried so desperately to hide can become the very place where you finally stop running and discover how desperately you need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FIRST MAN IN THE BIBLE TO TAKE TWO WIVES ALSO BRAGGED ABOUT KILLING A MAN—AND HIS WORDS EXPOSE SOMETHING TERRIFYING ABOUT THE HUMAN HEART
paragraphs: THE FIRST MAN IN THE BIBLE TO TAKE TWO WIVES ALSO BRAGGED ABOUT KILLING A MAN—AND HIS WORDS EXPOSE SOMETHING TERRIFYING ABOUT THE HUMAN HEART

Before the flood, before the Ten Commandments, and long before humanity learned to celebrate its own rebellion, one man gathered his two wives and delivered a chilling speech. What he said reveals how sin can turn a wounded heart into a dangerous one—and why the world still desperately needs Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply disturbing about a man who can speak of taking another human life without a trace of remorse.
But perhaps even more disturbing is a man who turns that violence into poetry.
He doesn't whisper his confession.
He doesn't fall to his knees.
He doesn't ask God for mercy.
He calls his wives together.
And he tells them to listen.
His name was Lamech.
And buried in the fourth chapter of Genesis is one of the earliest recorded human speeches after the fall—a speech so dark that thousands of years later, it still sounds frighteningly familiar.
Because Lamech wasn't merely talking about violence.
He was revealing what happens when a human being begins to treat his own pride as more important than another person's life.
And before you decide this ancient man has nothing to do with you, consider something.
Have you ever been hurt so deeply that you secretly wanted someone else to hurt just as badly?
Have you ever rehearsed an argument in your head, imagining the perfect words that would finally make someone regret what they did to you?
Have you ever called something justice when, somewhere deep inside, you knew it was revenge?
Stay with me.
Because this story begins with two wives and a disturbing declaration.
But it leads us to a question that reaches into our marriages, our families, our churches, our hidden resentments, and the places in our hearts we rarely allow anyone to see.
What happens when a wounded person decides that revenge is more important than mercy?
And what happens when that person is us?
Genesis 4:19 tells us:
"And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah." — Genesis 4:19, KJV
At first glance, it might seem like a simple family record.
One man.
Two women.
A household.
But Genesis is not giving us this information without context.
The Bible has already introduced God's design for marriage.
In Genesis 2:24, a man leaves his father and mother, cleaves to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
One man.
One woman.
One covenant union.
Then, only two chapters later, Scripture introduces Lamech, the first man explicitly recorded as taking two wives.
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים
Vayyiqqaḥ-lo Lemekh shtei nashim.
Literally, in context:
"And Lamech took for himself two wives."
Notice the expression shtei nashim.
Two wives.

The text does not tell us what Adah and Zillah felt about this arrangement. It does not describe their marriage as a romantic success, nor does it explicitly record God condemning Lamech in that verse.
But placed against the marriage pattern established in Genesis 2, this is a significant development.
Humanity is already moving away from the beginning God declared good.
And the narrator is about to show us something even darker.
Because Lamech's household was not without accomplishments.
His descendants are associated with livestock keeping, musical instruments, and metalworking.
Genesis 4:20–22 introduces Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-cain.
There is cultural development here.
Skill.
Creativity.
Industry.
The ability to cultivate the world and produce things of beauty and usefulness.
And that detail matters.
Because the Bible is showing us something we still struggle to understand.
A civilization can become more sophisticated without becoming more righteous.
A person can become extraordinarily talented without becoming humble.
A family can become financially successful without becoming spiritually healthy.
A society can develop remarkable technology while remaining morally broken.
And a man can build an impressive life while his heart is being consumed by pride.
We see versions of this everywhere.
People who can manage companies but cannot manage their anger.
People who know how to influence thousands but do not know how to apologize to one person.
People who can explain Scripture beautifully yet refuse to forgive someone who offended them.
People whose public lives look impressive while their private relationships are falling apart.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that we can become so occupied with what we are building that we stop noticing what we are becoming.
Then Lamech opens his mouth.
And the story changes.
"And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt." — Genesis 4:23, KJV
Read that again.
He is addressing the two women closest to him.
Adah.
Zillah.
Listen to me.
Hear what I have to say.
And then comes the declaration.
"I have slain a man."
The Hebrew reads:
כִּי אִישׁ הָרַגְתִּי לְפִצְעִי וְיֶלֶד לְחַבֻּרָתִי
Ki ish haragti lefits'i, veyeled leḥabburati.
The Hebrew expresses Lamech's claim that he has killed a man in connection with his wound and a young man in connection with his injury or bruise.
The exact circumstances are not given.

Some interpreters understand the two descriptions as referring poetically to one victim. Others see the possibility of two victims. The Hebrew parallelism makes the one-victim reading plausible, but the text does not settle every detail.

We also cannot establish whether the killing happened in self-defense, retaliation, or another circumstance. The wording associates the killing with an injury Lamech received, but it does not give us a complete account of the event.
What we can see is the posture of his speech.
There is no recorded confession of wrongdoing.
No appeal for God's forgiveness.
No expression of sorrow over a life lost.
Instead, his words move toward an extraordinary declaration about vengeance.
"If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold." — Genesis 4:24, KJV
There it is.
The chilling climax.
But to understand why this is so disturbing, we must remember who Cain was.
Cain had murdered his brother Abel.
The first recorded human murder arose within a family.
Not between strangers.
Not on a battlefield.
Between brothers.
And when God confronted Cain, Cain was judged.
Yet even after Cain's terrible sin, God placed a mark upon him and warned that anyone who killed him would face sevenfold vengeance.
That protection was God's declaration.
It was not Cain giving himself permission to murder again.
It was not an invitation for human beings to establish their own systems of unlimited retaliation.
It was God's prerogative to judge and restrain further bloodshed.
Now listen to Lamech.
Cain was promised sevenfold vengeance.
Lamech announces seventy-sevenfold.
The Hebrew says:
כִּי שִׁבְעָתַיִם יֻקַּם־קָיִן וְלֶמֶךְ שִׁבְעִים וְשִׁבְעָה
Ki shiv'atayim yuqqam-Qayin, veLemekh shiv'im veshiv'ah.
In context:
"If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold."
The numbers function within a poetic declaration of intensified vengeance. They should not be treated as a mathematical formula establishing exactly how much punishment anyone deserved.
And we should not pretend that Lamech had received the same divine promise given to Cain.
Genesis records no such promise to Lamech.
What we hear is a man invoking Cain's protection and escalating the language of vengeance around himself.
A man speaking as though his injuries justify an extraordinary response.
A man whose words make his own wounded pride sound terrifyingly powerful.
And this is where the ancient story begins to walk into our homes.
Because most of us will never stand before our families and boast that we have killed someone.
But revenge does not always begin with bloodshed.
Sometimes it begins with a sentence.
"I'll make sure they regret what they did."
Sometimes it begins with silence.
"I'll never speak to them again, and I want them to suffer because of it."
Sometimes it begins with a social media post designed to humiliate someone without naming them.
Sometimes it begins with a parent who uses cruel words against a child because the parent feels disrespected.
Sometimes it begins with a husband or wife who keeps bringing up an old failure, not to resolve the wound, but to maintain power over the other person.
Sometimes it begins inside a church.
A disagreement becomes an offense.
An offense becomes resentment.
Resentment becomes a campaign to destroy someone's reputation.
And somehow, the person seeking revenge convinces themselves that God must be on their side.
That is the danger.
Not every desire for justice is sinful. Scripture repeatedly calls God's people to protect the vulnerable, confront evil, and pursue what is right.
Abuse must not be excused. Crimes should be addressed through appropriate authorities. Forgiveness does not require someone to remain in danger or abandon wise boundaries.
But there is a difference between seeking justice and worshiping revenge.
Justice asks what is right.
Revenge can become obsessed with making another person suffer.
Justice recognizes moral boundaries.
Revenge is tempted to cross them.
Justice can entrust final judgment to God.
Revenge wants to sit on the throne itself.
And sometimes the hardest spiritual truth to accept is this:
The fact that someone genuinely hurt you does not mean every response you desire is righteous.
Perhaps someone betrayed your trust.
Perhaps someone spread lies about you.
Perhaps someone abandoned you when you needed them most.
Perhaps you are still carrying words spoken years ago by a person who has never apologized.
Your pain may be real.
Your grief may be justified.
The injustice may have been serious.
God does not require you to pretend otherwise.
But pain can become dangerous when it begins demanding permission to become cruel.
That is why Lamech's speech matters.
It exposes how easily the human heart can turn a wound into a weapon.
And then Scripture gives us a contrast so beautiful that it is almost impossible to miss once you see it.
Centuries later, Peter approached Jesus with a question about forgiveness.
"Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" — Matthew 18:21, KJV
Peter probably thought he was being generous.
Seven times.
Surely that was enough.
But Jesus answered:
"I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." — Matthew 18:22, KJV
Now look carefully.
Lamech speaks of vengeance seventy-sevenfold.
Jesus speaks of forgiveness using language of overwhelming abundance.
In Greek, Matthew 18:22 includes the expression:
ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά
Heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta.

This expression is traditionally translated "seventy times seven," as in the King James Version. It is also understood by many scholars as "seventy-seven times," reflecting the Greek rendering of Genesis 4:24 in the Septuagint.
The precise numerical rendering is debated, but Jesus' meaning in context is clear.
He is not giving Peter a forgiveness counter.
He is confronting the desire to calculate the point at which mercy may finally be exhausted.
And the literary connection to Lamech's words is striking.
Where Lamech's speech magnifies vengeance, Jesus teaches His disciples to practice forgiveness beyond petty calculation.
Where the ancient boast centers on the wounded self, Jesus calls His followers toward a mercy shaped by the kingdom of heaven.
Think about that.
One man says, in effect, "My injury deserves multiplied vengeance."
Jesus teaches His disciples to forgive again and again.
One voice represents the escalation of human retaliation.
The other calls sinners into the radically different life of God's kingdom.
But Jesus did not merely deliver beautiful teaching about forgiveness.
He walked toward a cross.
And there, the contrast becomes almost unbearable.
Imagine the scene.
The Son of God has been betrayed.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Struck.
Scourged.
Crowned with thorns.
Nailed to wood.
He is not suffering because He committed some hidden crime.
He is the righteous One suffering at the hands of sinners.
And while the people around Him are committing an unspeakable injustice, Luke records these words:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." — Luke 23:34, KJV

Some early manuscripts omit this sentence, a textual question noted in modern Bible editions. Nevertheless, the prayer is deeply consistent with Jesus' teaching on loving enemies and with the wider New Testament witness to His mercy.
Consider the contrast.
Lamech calls his wives to hear about his vengeance.
Jesus, suffering on the cross, prays for His persecutors.
Lamech's words center on the injury done to him.
Jesus' words reveal mercy even in the face of terrible injustice.
Lamech speaks of multiplied vengeance.
Jesus bears the judgment our sins deserve so that guilty people may receive forgiveness through Him.
And this is where we must be careful not to reduce Christianity to a simple lesson about being nicer to people.
The Gospel is far greater than anger management.
Jesus did not come merely to teach violent people to become peaceful or bitter people to become pleasant.
He came to save sinners.
People like Cain.
People like Lamech.
People like Peter, who would later deny Him.
People like the thief dying beside Him.
People like you.
People like me.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had fixed everything.
Not after we had made ourselves worthy.
Not after we had learned how to hide our worst failures behind a respectable appearance.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
But grace is not permission to continue embracing evil.
It is God's undeserved favor calling us away from sin and into new life through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this is realizing that the deepest problem in their life is not merely what another person did to them.
It is what their own heart has become while carrying that wound.
Maybe bitterness has become your daily companion.
Maybe you have grown comfortable wishing disaster on someone.
Maybe you have been justifying words you know were cruel.
Maybe you have been hiding behind the sentence, "But you don't understand what they did to me."
And perhaps nobody does understand the full weight of what happened.
But Jesus does not need to misunderstand your suffering in order to challenge your response to it.
He knows what betrayal feels like.
He knows what false accusation looks like.
He knows what it means to be abandoned by people who promised to remain faithful.
And He is not asking you to call evil good.
He is calling you to refuse to let evil become your master.
Romans 12:19 says:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."
Those words do not mean that wrongdoing should go unchallenged or that victims must remain silent.
