“And she said, The glory is departed from Israel: for the ark of God is taken.” — 1 Samuel 4:22, KJV
In Hebrew, the child's name is written אִי־כָבוֹד, commonly transliterated ʾÎ-kāḇôḏ — Ichabod.
The key word is כָּבוֹד (kāvôḏ), meaning glory, honor, or weightiness.

The name Ichabod is traditionally understood in the context of this passage as “no glory” or “where is the glory?” The mother's own words give its meaning within the narrative: Israel's glory has departed.
The verb translated “is departed” comes from the Hebrew root גלה (g-l-h), which can express departure, removal, or exile.
The Hebrew wording conveys the dreadful reality she was lamenting: glory had gone away from Israel.
But we need to be careful here.
The Bible does not say that God had ceased to exist.
It does not say that the Philistines had defeated the LORD.
And it does not mean that God had become powerless because the ark was captured.
In fact, the very next chapter destroys that misunderstanding.
In 1 Samuel 5, the captured ark is brought into the temple of Dagon, the Philistine god.
And Dagon falls before the ark.
Then he falls again, this time with his head and hands broken off.
The LORD demonstrates His supremacy even in enemy territory.
Israel had lost the ark.
But God had not lost His throne.
Israel had suffered judgment.
But the LORD had not surrendered His sovereignty.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes we interpret the collapse of our circumstances as proof that God has been defeated.
We lose a relationship and assume God has abandoned us.
We bury someone we love and wonder whether heaven has gone silent.
We watch a ministry fall into scandal and ask whether the Gospel itself has failed.
But the failure of human beings does not invalidate the faithfulness of God.
The sins of priests do not make the LORD unholy.
The collapse of religious leadership does not make Jesus Christ untrustworthy.
And the loss of something precious does not mean that the God who holds eternity has lost control.
The ark was captured, but the LORD was never conquered.
And perhaps someone reading this needs that truth more than they realize.
Because you know what it feels like to live through an Ichabod moment.
A season when everything familiar seems to disappear.
When the prayers feel heavy.
When the house becomes quiet.
When the person who promised to stay leaves.
When you discover that someone you trusted was not who you believed them to be.
When you look at the wreckage of your decisions and wonder whether you have destroyed everything God once entrusted to you.
And perhaps your greatest fear is not that you lost something.
Perhaps your greatest fear is that you have gone so far that God no longer wants you.
But hear this carefully.
The story of Ichabod is a warning about sin and the seriousness of God's holiness.
It is not permission to declare that every suffering person has been abandoned by God.
Phinehas's wife was not identified as guilty of her husband's sins.
Her suffering should never be used to blame grieving mothers, widows, or anyone enduring tragedy.
And your pain is not automatic evidence of God's punishment.
Jesus Himself rejected the assumption that every tragedy can be traced to the personal sin of its victims (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3).
There are consequences of sin.
There is divine discipline.
There is judgment.
But there is also suffering in a fallen world, and there are tears that faithful people shed while still belonging to God.
So do not let someone weaponize Ichabod against your wounded heart.
Instead, allow this story to ask the question it was meant to ask.
Have we mistaken religious appearances for a genuine relationship with the living God?
Because there is something even more heartbreaking than losing the things we love.
It is becoming so comfortable with sin that we stop caring whether our lives honor the Lord.
And here is where this ancient tragedy leads us toward the hope of the Gospel.
Centuries after the birth of Ichabod, another child was born into Israel.
Not in a palace.
Not surrounded by earthly power.
But in humble circumstances.
His mother was Mary.
His name was Jesus.
And unlike the corrupt priests who dishonored God, this Son would live in perfect obedience to His Father.
Unlike the leaders who exploited sacred responsibilities, this Son would give Himself for the people He came to save.
Unlike the priests whose sin brought disgrace, this Son would become our great High Priest, holy and without sin.
And when the apostle John described Him, he used language that answers the deepest ache of Ichabod.
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.” — John 1:14, KJV
In the Greek New Testament, the word translated “dwelt” is ἐσκήνωσεν (eskēnōsen), from a verb meaning to pitch a tent or dwell.
It recalls the language of God's dwelling among His people.
And the word translated “glory” is δόξα (doxa).
John is telling us that the eternal Word became flesh and lived among us, revealing divine glory.
Do you see the beauty of this?
In 1 Samuel 4, a dying woman cried out that glory had departed from Israel.
In John 1, the apostle announces that the glory of the eternal Son has been revealed among us.
This is not a claim that John was directly quoting the story of Ichabod.
It is a profound biblical contrast.
Human sin brings shame and judgment.
But God's redemptive purpose reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The answer to humanity's deepest spiritual crisis is not a sacred object carried into battle.
It is the Savior who came into the world.
Not a religious performance.
Not a public reputation.
Not a perfect-looking Christian life.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Son of God.
And what He did at Calvary changes everything.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make religious people feel better about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
He came to call us to repentance.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins in His body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
He came to do what no priest, no ritual, no human achievement, and no religious symbol could ever accomplish.
He came to redeem us.
And consider the darkness of the cross.
The sky grew dark.
Jesus suffered.
He cried out, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46, KJV), invoking Psalm 22.
And then He died.
To those watching, it may have looked as though evil had won.
As though hope had been buried.
As though the story had reached its final, unbearable sentence.
But three days later, the tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And the resurrection announced what no human failure, no empire, no grave, and no power of darkness could overturn.
The Savior had conquered sin and death.
The cross was not the defeat of God's redemptive plan.
It was central to its fulfillment.
And the resurrection was God's triumphant vindication of His Son.
This is why our theme is more than a beautiful phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends sin never happened.
Not because grace makes repentance unnecessary.
Not because following Christ guarantees that every earthly tragedy will be reversed.
But because Jesus can redeem people who could never redeem themselves.
He forgives the repentant.
He restores the broken.
He transforms the surrendered.
He gives eternal life to those who believe in Him.
And He promises His people a future that even death cannot steal.
Maybe your story has chapters you wish you could tear out.
Maybe there are decisions you still regret.
Maybe your children have seen the worst of you.
Maybe your marriage carries wounds nobody else knows about.
Maybe you once served God with passion, but somewhere along the way you became spiritually cold.
You still know the right words.
You still know how to look okay.
But when the room becomes quiet, you know something is wrong.
You have been trying to survive on memories of a relationship with God that you are no longer nurturing.
And perhaps the most frightening thing is how normal that distance has started to feel.
If that is you, please don't keep hiding behind your religious reputation.
Come to Jesus.
Not with excuses.
Not with a performance.
Not with promises that you will make yourself worthy first.
Come in repentance and faith.
Confess your sins.
Turn toward the One who died and rose again.
Because Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
And Jesus Himself promised:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
That promise is not fragile.
It does not depend on whether your past is impressive.
It rests on the faithfulness of Christ.
The woman in 1 Samuel 4 died with the words of departed glory on her lips.
We are not told what became of her child.
We are not told how Ichabod grew up.
We are not given a sentimental ending to her personal story.
And we should not invent one.
Sometimes Scripture allows tragedy to remain tragic.
Sometimes the mother dies.
Sometimes the child grows up without the parent.
Sometimes the earthly story does not end the way we desperately wish it would.
But the Bible does not end in 1 Samuel 4.
And for those who belong to Jesus Christ, death and sorrow will not have the final word.
Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear from His people's eyes, and that death, mourning, crying, and pain will pass away.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
Not a guarantee that this world will never break your heart.
But the promise that Jesus Christ is making all things new.
And if this story has touched a wound you have never spoken about, you do not have to pretend to be strong here.
Maybe your honest prayer tonight is only a few words.
“Lord, I have been drifting.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Father, I am exhausted.”
“Lord, teach me to come home.”
You can begin there.
You do not need to expose private details publicly. God knows the story even when you cannot find the words.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that God's grace is still at work in broken lives.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who looks completely fine.
Their profile picture is smiling.
Their posts seem normal.
Their family photographs look happy.
But you have no idea what happened after they put their phone down last night.
Maybe they are grieving.
Maybe they are struggling with temptation.
Maybe they have stopped praying because they feel ashamed.
Maybe they have been hurt by a religious leader and are struggling to trust anyone who speaks about God.
Maybe they are one difficult night away from giving up on the faith they once cherished.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because biblical truth and the hope of Christ are worth passing on.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually lukewarm, those who are searching, and even those who do not yet believe.
Not because we are building a following around ourselves.
But because we want more people to encounter the truth of God's Word and the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Your local church, your family responsibilities, and your ability to give wisely matter.
God is not honored by pressure disguised as devotion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And that is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not a payment for God's blessing.
Not a purchase of spiritual favor.
Not a replacement for belonging to a faithful local church.
But a voluntary way to help Gospel-centered teaching reach more people.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and support the ongoing work.
Because grace is not merchandise.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And the invitation to follow Jesus is freely proclaimed.
You can pray for the ministry.
You can invite someone to read the Scriptures.
Every act of faithful encouragement matters, even when it never appears on a financial statement.
Because the mission has never been to make Gospel Warrior the center of anyone's faith.
The mission is to point people to Jesus Christ.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who transforms.
The One whose glory does not depend on the reputation of a ministry, the success of a platform, or the applause of a crowd.
Now, before you leave, I want you to return with me to that room in ancient Israel.
A woman is dying.
A newborn son has entered the world.
Her husband is gone.
Her father-in-law is gone.
The ark has been captured.
And a name is spoken through unimaginable grief.
Ichabod.
The glory is departed.
It is one of the saddest birth announcements in Scripture.
But imagine what that story teaches us when we read it in the light of the whole Bible.
The people of Israel could not preserve God's blessing through outward religion while despising His holiness.
Their priests could not save them.
Their religious excitement could not save them.
Their possession of a sacred object could not save them.
They needed the living God.
And so do we.
We need more than inspiration.
More than a religious identity.
More than an emotional moment that disappears by morning.
We need forgiveness.
We need a new heart.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the question this story leaves with every one of us.
If everything you use to look spiritual were stripped away…
If the titles disappeared…
If the audience stopped applauding…
If nobody knew how often you attended church…
If the only thing left was the truth of your heart before God…
Would you still be clinging to Jesus?
Not to your image.
Not to your achievements.
Not to your ability to impress others.
To Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that a person can lose everything this world offers.
The greatest tragedy is to spend an entire life surrounded by the things of God while refusing to know Him.
But there is hope for the sinner who turns to Christ.
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is forgiveness through His blood.
There is new life through His resurrection.
And there is a Savior who will never turn away the one who truly comes to Him.
So if you remember only one thing from this story, remember this:
You may not be able to rewrite the chapter that broke your heart, but Jesus Christ can redeem the life you surrender to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I AM DOING A NEW THING” — BUT WHAT IF THE FIRST THING GOD WANTS TO CHANGE IS YOU?
paragraphs: “I AM DOING A NEW THING” — BUT WHAT IF THE FIRST THING GOD WANTS TO CHANGE IS YOU?

Isaiah 43:19 was never simply a promise of a new job, a new relationship, or a better opportunity. It was spoken to people who had lost almost everything—and it reveals something far greater than the fresh start we keep asking God to give us.
There is something heartbreaking about a person who keeps asking God for a new beginning while secretly refusing to let Him touch the very thing that is destroying their life.
They want a new relationship, but they keep carrying the same unhealed bitterness.
They want a new job, but their identity still rises and falls with their paycheck.
They want a new season, but they are still negotiating with the sin that devastated the last one.
They want God to open another door.
But what if God is calling them to stop running through doors that lead them away from Him?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable possibility of all...
What if you have been praying for God to change your circumstances while He has been patiently calling you to surrender your heart?
Before you claim Isaiah 43:19 as your personal announcement of promotion, marriage, financial breakthrough, or sudden opportunity, you need to hear what God was actually saying.
Because this verse is more beautiful than the motivational captions we have built around it.
And far more confronting.
“Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.” — Isaiah 43:19 (KJV)
Beautiful, isn't it?
But do you know who first heard those words?
Not someone waiting for a promotion.
Not a single person hoping to meet the love of their life.
Not an entrepreneur waiting for a business breakthrough.
God was speaking to His covenant people, Israel, in a prophetic message of restoration from exile.
A people whose national life had been shattered.
A people facing the bitter consequences of rebellion, judgment, displacement, and loss.
A people who needed more than improved circumstances.
They needed the God they had repeatedly turned away from.
And this is where the verse begins to cut deeper than most people expect.
Because God was not simply promising to make their lives more comfortable.
He was announcing that their failure would not have the final word over His redemptive purposes.
Read that again.
Their failure would not have the final word over God's redemptive purposes.
That is the kind of new beginning Scripture is talking about.
And if you have ever looked at your life and wondered whether you have ruined too much to be restored, this message is for you.
Isaiah 43 does not begin with God pretending Israel had been faithful.
He knew their history.
He knew their idolatry.
He knew their disobedience.
He knew how often they had exchanged His glory for things that could never save them.
Yet listen to what He says earlier in the chapter:
“But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.” — Isaiah 43:1 (KJV)
Thou art mine.
Imagine hearing those words when everything around you seems to testify that your story is finished.
When the consequences of yesterday are still sitting beside you at breakfast.
When people remember the version of you that you desperately wish they would forget.
When you have apologized, repented, cried, tried to rebuild, and still cannot escape the memory of what happened.
When you wonder whether God sees anything in you beyond your worst decision.
And then, through His Word, you encounter the God who redeems.
Not a God who calls evil good.
Not a God who dismisses rebellion as harmless.
But the holy God who is able to restore people who could never rescue themselves.
That is the heart of this passage.
To understand it properly, we need to look at the words God actually inspired through the prophet Isaiah.
The Hebrew of Isaiah 43:19 begins:
הִנְנִי עֹשֶׂה חֲדָשָׁה
Hinnēnī ʿōśeh ḥădāšāh.
A faithful rendering is:
“Behold, I am doing a new thing.”
The word ḥădāšāh (חֲדָשָׁה) means something new.
The expression emphasizes God's own action.
Notice who is doing the work.
Not Israel.
Not the strength of their determination.
Not their ability to manufacture a breakthrough.
God Himself.
And that matters because the people receiving this promise were not being told to create their own salvation.
They were being called to recognize the saving action of the Lord.
The next words are equally powerful:
עַתָּה תִצְמָח
ʿAttāh tiṣmāḥ.
“Now it shall spring forth.”
The verb tiṣmāḥ comes from a Hebrew root associated with sprouting or growing.
It evokes the picture of something emerging into view.
Something God is bringing forth.
Something that may not yet be fully visible to those who desperately need it.
But do not turn that beautiful image into a guarantee that every private ambition is about to succeed.
The passage is not saying that every desire you have is a seed God has promised to grow.
It is saying that God is able to accomplish His saving purposes where human beings see no way forward.
And the historical context makes this extraordinary.
Earlier in the passage, Isaiah recalls the Lord who made a path through the sea, drawing attention to Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Isaiah 43:16–17).
Then God announces:
“Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old.” — Isaiah 43:18 (KJV)
Does that mean God's people were commanded to erase their memories?
Of course not.
Throughout Scripture, Israel was repeatedly instructed to remember God's mighty acts.
The point is not spiritual amnesia.
The point is that Israel must not imagine God's future deliverance is limited to the exact pattern of His past deliverance.
The God who once made a path through the sea could now make a path through the wilderness.
The God who once delivered His people from Egypt could bring His exiled people home.
God was not trapped in yesterday's miracle.
And neither should His people assume that yesterday's experience exhausted what He could do.
That is the original beauty of Isaiah 43:19.
The Lord was promising a new act of deliverance, not distributing blank checks for every dream His people might have.
And that distinction may save someone from years of unnecessary disappointment.
Because perhaps you have been told that if you believe hard enough, God must give you the relationship.
If you declare Isaiah 43:19 often enough, the money must arrive.
If you post the verse, claim the verse, repeat the verse, and refuse to entertain doubt, the opportunity must come.
But what happens when the opportunity does not come?
What happens when the person you prayed would stay decides to leave?
What happens when the business closes?
When the test results are not what you hoped?
When you lose the job instead of receiving the promotion?
When you are still waiting after everyone else seems to have moved forward?
Does that mean God has failed?
Does that mean you did not have enough faith?
No.
It means Isaiah 43:19 was never a divine obligation to fulfill every earthly expectation.
God's faithfulness is not measured by how closely His decisions resemble your plans.
Sometimes His providence includes a door opening.
Sometimes it includes a door closing.
Sometimes His kindness is experienced through unexpected provision.
Sometimes His sustaining grace carries us through suffering that does not immediately disappear.
And sometimes the deepest work God is doing cannot be photographed, announced, or celebrated in a social media testimony.
Because nobody can see repentance happening inside a heart.
Nobody can measure the moment pride finally begins to surrender.
Nobody knows how much courage it takes for someone to delete a secret conversation, confess a hidden sin, ask forgiveness, or choose obedience when nobody is watching.
But heaven is not indifferent to what happens in secret.
Jesus taught that the Father sees what is done in secret (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18).
And perhaps the new thing you need most is not something the world will applaud.
Perhaps it is the grace to become truthful again.
Perhaps it is the strength to forgive.
Perhaps it is the humility to admit you were wrong.
Perhaps it is the willingness to stop calling something a blessing when it keeps leading you into disobedience.
Perhaps it is learning that your value was never determined by whether somebody chose to stay.
Perhaps it is discovering that Jesus is enough even when the answer you wanted never comes.
That does not mean every painful experience is a punishment from God.
Scripture refuses that simplistic conclusion.
In John 9:1–3, Jesus challenged the assumption that a man's blindness must have resulted from a particular personal or parental sin.
Not every wilderness is the consequence of rebellion.
Some suffering comes because we live in a fallen world.
Some comes through the wrongdoing of others.
Some accompanies faithful obedience.
And sometimes we simply do not know why a particular sorrow has entered our lives.
But whatever the cause, the wilderness does not place us beyond the reach of God's mercy.
That is one of the most astonishing truths running through Isaiah.
The Lord does not abandon His redemptive purposes because His people are powerless.
He acts.
He rescues.
He restores.
And as the book of Isaiah unfolds, the promise of restoration points beyond the immediate return from exile toward the greater saving work God will accomplish through His Servant.
Isaiah 53 presents the suffering Servant who bears the sins of many.
The New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of this suffering and saving mission (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:24).
And now we begin to see the deeper beauty of the story.
Because the greatest new thing God has accomplished is not merely the restoration of earthly circumstances.
It is the redemption He has brought through Jesus Christ.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed sinners without celebrating their sin.
He exposed hypocrisy without abandoning compassion.
He called people to repentance while offering mercy to those who knew they needed it.
And then He went to the cross.
Not because human beings had finally become worthy.
But because sinners needed a Savior.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8 (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully repaired our reputation.
Not after we had proven that we would never fail again.
Not after we had cleaned up every part of our history.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It reveals how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's grace truly is.
The cross tells us that forgiveness is not cheap.
And the resurrection tells us that sin and death do not have the final victory.
This is where the message becomes painfully personal.
Because you can get a new job and still be enslaved to greed.
You can enter a new relationship and still be ruled by jealousy.
You can move to a new city and carry the same secret addictions.
You can build a new public image while remaining spiritually exhausted behind closed doors.
You can even become more active in church while quietly drifting away from genuine intimacy with Christ.
A new environment does not automatically create a new heart.
A new opportunity does not erase guilt.
A new relationship cannot accomplish what only reconciliation with God can accomplish.
And that is why the New Testament gives us a declaration far greater than any motivational slogan:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
The original Greek begins:
ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις
Hōste ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ—a new creation.”
The expression kainē ktisis means “new creation.”
This is not merely the idea of rearranging an old life until it looks more attractive.
Paul is speaking about the reality of belonging to Christ and participating in the new-creation work God has begun through Him.
Notice the condition.
In Christ.
Not merely inspired by Christ.
Not merely familiar with Christian language.
Not merely someone who shares Bible verses when life becomes difficult.
In Christ.
United to Him by faith.
Reconciled to God through Him.
Called into a life shaped by His grace and lordship.
And that changes the entire conversation about new beginnings.
Because the greatest question is no longer, “God, when will You give me something new?”
It becomes, “Lord Jesus, am I truly Yours?”
That question may be uncomfortable.
But it is far too important to avoid.
You can know every popular promise about breakthrough and still fail to understand the Gospel.
You can be excited about God's blessings while remaining resistant to His commands.
You can want the benefits of Christianity without wanting the Christ who calls you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him (Luke 9:23).
And there is a tragedy in wanting Jesus to transform everything around you while refusing to surrender anything within you.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8?
Her shame had become public.
Her accusers wanted condemnation.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of those who stood ready to stone her.
And when her accusers had departed, He told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11 (KJV)
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Compassion.
And a summons to a different life.
Jesus did not tell her that her sin was beautiful.
He did not say that repentance was unnecessary.
He did not reduce her entire identity to her worst moment either.
He offered mercy while calling her away from sin.
That is the grace we desperately need.
Not a counterfeit grace that leaves us comfortable in destruction.
Not a crushing religion that convinces us our past makes redemption impossible.
But the grace of Jesus Christ that forgives, restores, and transforms.
And perhaps that is what you have been missing.
You thought you needed another chance to prove yourself.
But what you truly needed was to come to the Savior who already knows everything about you.
The things you admit.
The things you hide.
The things you regret.
The things you still defend.
The moments you wish you could relive.
The words you cannot take back.
The people you hurt.
The wounds others left in you.
The compromises you once promised you would never make.
He knows.
And still, the Gospel announces that everyone who turns to Christ in repentance and faith may receive forgiveness and new life.
Not because their sin was harmless.
But because His sacrifice is sufficient.
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.” — Ephesians 1:7 (KJV)
Think about that.
Your history may contain a scandal.
Your conscience may carry regret.
Your reputation may have suffered.
Your consequences may still be real.
And not every broken earthly relationship will necessarily be restored.
But your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Because Jesus Christ is able to save.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not that Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not that consequences disappear automatically.
Not that every person we hurt must immediately trust us again.
But that our sin does not have to remain our identity, our condemnation does not have to remain our destiny, and our brokenness does not have to be the end of our story.
In Christ, forgiveness is real.
Repentance matters.
Restoration is possible.
And transformation begins with the grace of God, not with the performance of a perfect person.
Maybe you are reading this while waiting for something.
A job offer.
A medical answer.
A reconciliation.
A financial breakthrough.
A husband.
A wife.
A child.
A chance to rebuild after a humiliating failure.
There is nothing wrong with bringing those desires before the Lord.
Scripture invites believers to pray about their needs (Philippians 4:6–7).
Ask Him.
Trust Him.
Seek His wisdom.
But do not reduce His goodness to the outcome you prefer.
And do not mistake a delayed answer for an absent Savior.
The same Jesus who conquered the grave is worthy of your trust when the road ahead remains unclear.
You may not receive every new thing you desire.
But everyone who belongs to Christ has something infinitely greater than a guarantee of earthly success.
They have a living Savior.
They have forgiveness.
They have the Holy Spirit.
They have the promise that God will complete the good work He has begun in them (Philippians 1:6).
And they have a future resurrection hope that no disappointment in this present age can destroy.
One day, the new creation will be fully revealed.
Revelation 21:5 records the words of the One seated upon the throne:
“Behold, I make all things new.”
Not merely a new opportunity.
Not merely a better season.
Not merely a temporary escape from pain.
All things new.
A new heaven and a new earth.
The end of death, mourning, crying, and pain.
The full and final triumph of God's redemptive purposes through Jesus Christ.
That is where the Christian hope is ultimately headed.
And suddenly Isaiah 43:19 becomes more than a verse to post when life is going well.
It becomes a testimony to the character of the God who saves.
The God who makes a way where His people cannot make one.
The God whose faithfulness outlasts human failure.
The God whose promises find their ultimate “Yes” in Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).
So when you read, “I am doing a new thing,” do not rush past the One who is speaking.
Do not become so fascinated with the gift that you overlook the Giver.
Do not become so consumed with your next season that you neglect your eternal soul.
And please...
Do not spend your whole life asking God to change your story while resisting the Savior who came to redeem it.
Maybe the most important prayer you can offer today is not, “Lord, give me something new.”
Maybe it is this:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent so much time asking You to change what is happening around me that I have neglected what needs to change within me. Forgive my sins. Expose what I have hidden. Heal what is wounded. Teach me to repent where I have rebelled. Give me the courage to obey even when obedience costs me something. Help me trust Your wisdom when Your answer is different from my desires. I do not merely want a better life. I need You. Make me more like You. Amen.”
And if that prayer expresses what is happening in your heart, do not rush away from this moment.
You do not have to pretend that you have everything figured out.
You do not have to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
You can simply be truthful.
You do not need to reveal private details. Even a few honest words can open the door for another believer to encourage you in prayer.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that repentance, forgiveness, and a changed life are not merely religious ideas.
They are realities of God's grace.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message.
Someone who has been interpreting every closed door as proof that God has abandoned them.
Someone who believes their past disqualifies them from ever coming home to Christ.
Someone who has been chasing one breakthrough after another while their soul is starving for the Gospel.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
Not because an algorithm determines spiritual faithfulness.
But because the truth of Jesus Christ deserves to be made known, and a simple act of sharing may place biblical encouragement before someone who would never have searched for it.
Because faith was never meant to survive on occasional inspiration alone.
We need the Word of God.
We need prayer.
We need the fellowship and accountability of the local church.
We need faithful teaching that points us back to Jesus when our emotions are pulling us in a hundred different directions.
And that is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the church.
Not to sell God's blessings.
Not to turn the Gospel into a transaction.
But to help make Christ-centered biblical encouragement and discipleship resources accessible to more people.
These resources are offered freely because we believe biblical nourishment should not be reserved only for people who can afford to pay.
But keeping resources accessible, creating thoughtful biblical content, and reaching more people requires ongoing support.
For Christians who are able to give, supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a genuine expression of generosity and worship.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly, or of necessity.
Biblical giving is not supposed to be extracted through fear, guilt, or emotional pressure.
It does not guarantee a financial breakthrough.
And it is not a substitute for the giving, stewardship, and responsibilities you prayerfully practice through your local church.
It can be part of how you steward what God has entrusted to you for the benefit of others.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The resources, the articles, the books, the community, and the ongoing work are meant to serve something greater: helping people encounter biblical truth and grow as disciples of Christ.
You are still welcome.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Pointing even one person toward the truth of Jesus Christ is worthwhile.
Because the goal is not to build a community impressed by our name.
The goal is to help people know His Name.
And before you leave, return with me to that opening question.
What if the first thing God wants to change is you?
Not because every problem in your life is your fault.
Not because God is withholding His love until you improve yourself.
But because the greatest gift He can give you is not an easier life separated from Him.
It is reconciliation with Himself through Jesus Christ.
The God who promised a way through the wilderness has revealed the fullness of His saving grace in the Savior who declared:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6 (KJV)
There it is.
The answer beneath all our searching.
The hope beyond every closed door.
The Savior greater than every new opportunity.
You may still be waiting for the job.
You may still be grieving the relationship.
You may still be rebuilding after the scandal.
You may still be walking through a wilderness with questions you cannot answer.
But the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Repent and believe.
Receive the forgiveness only He can give.
Follow Him, even when the path is difficult.
And remember that the God who began His saving work will not fail to accomplish His eternal purposes.
Because sometimes the miracle is not that God gives you the life you once imagined.
Sometimes the miracle is that, through Jesus Christ, He gives you a new life you could never have created for yourself.
You were begging God for a new chapter, while Jesus was offering you something far greater—a new creation.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY PREACHED GRACE TO THE WORLD… THEN COULDN’T AGREE WITH EACH OTHER: The Painful Separation of Paul and Barnabas
paragraphs: THEY PREACHED GRACE TO THE WORLD… THEN COULDN’T AGREE WITH EACH OTHER: The Painful Separation of Paul and Barnabas

One man believed John Mark deserved another chance. The other believed the mission was too important to risk another failure. Both loved Jesus. Both had served God faithfully. Yet their disagreement became so sharp that they walked away from each other. What happened next reveals a truth every wounded Christian, divided family, and struggling church needs to hear.
What do you do when the person you disagree with is someone who genuinely loves Jesus?
Not someone trying to destroy your faith.
Not an enemy of the Gospel.
Someone who has prayed beside you. Suffered beside you. Served beside you.
Someone who has seen God move in your life, and you have seen God move in theirs.
And then one day, you reach a disagreement neither of you seems willing to surrender.
The conversations become uncomfortable.
The silence becomes heavier.
And suddenly, the person you once called your partner in ministry is walking in a different direction.
If you have ever experienced that kind of heartbreak, there is a story in Scripture you need to hear.
Because two of the most influential missionaries in the early church experienced something painfully similar.
Their names were Paul and Barnabas.
And the disagreement that separated them began with a young man named John Mark.
But here is what makes this story so extraordinary.
The man Paul once refused to take on a missionary journey would eventually become someone Paul specifically requested at his side.
Don't miss that.
A relationship that appeared damaged beyond repair was not necessarily beyond the reach of God's grace.
And somewhere inside that uncomfortable truth is a message for the person you have stopped believing can change.
Maybe even the person staring back at you in the mirror.
The story begins before the argument.
Barnabas was not simply Paul's coworker. He was one of the people who had believed in Paul when others were afraid of him.
After Paul's conversion, the disciples in Jerusalem were understandably suspicious. This was the man who had persecuted believers.
But Acts 9:27 tells us that Barnabas took Paul and brought him to the apostles, explaining how Paul had encountered the Lord.
Imagine that.
Before Paul became widely known as a missionary and apostle, Barnabas had been willing to stand beside a man whose past frightened the church.
Later, when the church in Antioch was growing, Barnabas went to Tarsus to find Saul, brought him to Antioch, and ministered alongside him (Acts 11:25–26).
Barnabas had seen something in Paul that others initially struggled to see.
The possibility of a transformed life.
The power of grace.
The reality that a person's past does not have to determine their future.
And perhaps that helps explain why Barnabas would later be unwilling to give up on John Mark.
But before we decide Barnabas was right and Paul was wrong, we need to understand what actually happened.
During their first missionary journey, Paul and Barnabas had taken John Mark with them as a helper.
Acts 13:5 records his presence.
But when they reached Perga in Pamphylia, something happened.
Acts 13:13 says that John left them and returned to Jerusalem.
Scripture does not tell us exactly why.
Was he frightened?
Was he homesick?
Was he overwhelmed by the demands of missionary life?
Did he disagree with the direction of the journey?
We simply do not know.
And that matters.
Because sometimes Christians are so eager to explain someone's failure that we begin inventing motives God never revealed.
What Scripture does reveal is that Paul regarded Mark's departure as serious enough to question his reliability for another journey.
And the next time Mark's name came up, everything changed.
Acts 15:36 records Paul proposing that he and Barnabas return to visit the believers in the cities where they had proclaimed the word of the Lord.
It was a beautiful idea.
They wanted to strengthen the churches.
They wanted to see how the believers were doing.
They wanted to continue the work Christ had entrusted to them.
Then Barnabas wanted to bring John Mark.
Paul disagreed.
And suddenly, two men united by the same Gospel could not agree about the same person.
The Greek text of Acts 15:37 says:
Βαρναβᾶς δὲ ἐβούλετο συμπαραλαβεῖν καὶ τὸν Ἰωάννην τὸν καλούμενον Μᾶρκον.
Barnabas wanted to take along John, the one called Mark.
But Acts 15:38 explains Paul's objection.
He did not consider it right to take along the man who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work.
Notice the difference.
Barnabas wanted to take Mark.
Paul believed Mark's previous withdrawal made that decision unwise.
Both men were looking at the same history.
But they were weighing its implications differently.
Barnabas saw someone he wanted to bring along again.
Paul saw a previous departure that raised a serious concern about the mission.
And here is where the story becomes painfully human.
Sometimes the disagreement is not about whether grace matters. It is about what grace should look like in a particular decision.
One believer says, "Give him another chance."
Another says, "We need to know he is ready."
One says, "People can change."
Another says, "The consequences of failure are real."
One sees potential.
Another sees responsibility.
And sometimes both are recognizing concerns that deserve to be taken seriously.
Grace does not mean pretending that trust has never been broken.
Wisdom does not mean declaring that a person who failed once can never be useful again.
Forgiveness and restored responsibility are related, but they are not identical.
You can forgive someone without immediately placing them back into the same position.
And you can acknowledge someone's past failure without condemning them to remain defined by it forever.
The challenge is learning to distinguish biblical wisdom from fear, genuine accountability from punishment, and patient restoration from careless trust.
Then Luke describes the disagreement in words that should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Acts 15:39 says:
ἐγένετο δὲ παροξυσμὸς ὥστε ἀποχωρισθῆναι αὐτοὺς ἀπ’ ἀλλήλων.
And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from one another.
The Greek word παροξυσμός (paroxysmos) describes a sharp contention or intense disagreement.
Luke does not present this as a minor difference of opinion.
It was serious enough to end their missionary partnership.
Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus.
Paul chose Silas and departed, commended by the believers to the grace of the Lord.
Two different directions.
Two different traveling companions.
One deeply uncomfortable moment in the history of the early church.
And perhaps the most surprising detail is what Scripture does not say.
It does not explicitly declare Barnabas the winner.
It does not explicitly declare Paul the winner.
It does not tell us that every word spoken in their disagreement was righteous.
Nor does it tell us that either man abandoned Christ.
Luke reports the conflict without giving us permission to invent a complete moral verdict.
That should humble us.
Because Christians can be remarkably quick to choose sides in situations where God has not given us all the facts.
We hear one account.
We see one emotional post.
We listen to one wounded person.
And before the whole story is known, we have already decided who deserves our sympathy and who deserves our condemnation.
But Proverbs 18:17 reminds us that the first person to present a case can appear right until another comes forward and examines it.
How many relationships have been destroyed because someone chose a side before seeking the truth?
How many church conflicts have grown because people defended personalities instead of pursuing righteousness?
How many believers have confused loyalty to a friend with loyalty to Christ?
Paul and Barnabas force us to confront something we would rather avoid.
Being committed to the same Savior does not guarantee that we will always reach the same judgment.
Christians are still human.
We bring different experiences, fears, responsibilities, strengths, and weaknesses into our decisions.
And even sincere believers can handle disagreement imperfectly.
But the existence of disagreement does not excuse bitterness.
It does not justify slander.
It does not give us permission to destroy another believer's reputation.
And it certainly does not make our personal opinion equal to the authority of Scripture.
Jesus taught His followers to pursue reconciliation (Matthew 5:23–24).
Paul later instructed believers, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (Romans 12:18, KJV).
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
As much as lieth in you.
Biblical peacemaking requires genuine effort, but it does not promise that every relationship will continue in the same form.
Sometimes reconciliation is possible while a particular partnership remains unwise.
Sometimes two believers can continue serving Christ faithfully without continuing to serve together.
And sometimes the most important question is no longer, "How do I prove I was right?"
It becomes, "How do I honor Jesus in what happens next?"
Because winning an argument is a poor victory if we lose our love for the people Christ died to redeem.
Yet this story has another layer.
Barnabas was known for encouragement.
Acts 4:36 explains that the apostles gave Joseph the name Barnabas, meaning "son of encouragement" or "son of consolation."
He was also related to Mark. Colossians 4:10 identifies Mark as Barnabas's cousin.
That family connection may have influenced his concern for Mark, although Scripture does not explicitly tell us his motives.
What we can say is that Barnabas was willing to take Mark with him.
He did not allow the young man's earlier withdrawal to become the final recorded chapter of their work together.
And if you have ever been the person who failed, that detail matters.
Maybe you abandoned something God had called you to do.
Maybe fear overtook your faith.
Maybe you made a promise you did not keep.
Maybe people who once trusted you now hesitate when your name is mentioned.
You know the terrible feeling of walking into a room and wondering whether everyone remembers your worst decision.
You know what it means to wish you could explain yourself.
You know what it feels like when your past seems louder than your repentance.
John Mark's story reminds us that an earlier failure does not necessarily mean a person has no future usefulness in God's service.
But the story does not end with Barnabas taking Mark to Cyprus.
Years later, something remarkable appears in Paul's letters.
In Colossians 4:10, Paul mentions Mark and instructs the church to welcome him if he comes.
In Philemon 24, Mark is named among Paul's fellow workers.
Then comes one of the most moving statements in the entire story.
In 2 Timothy 4:11, Paul writes:
Read that again.
The man Paul once did not consider suitable to accompany them on the journey was now someone Paul considered useful for ministry.
The Greek says:
ἔστιν γάρ μοι εὔχρηστος εἰς διακονίαν.
For he is useful to me for ministry.
The word εὔχρηστος (euchrēstos) means useful, serviceable, or beneficial.
What a remarkable change in how Mark is described.
Once, Paul refused to take him.
Later, Paul specifically requested him.
Scripture does not explain every conversation, every apology, or every step that led to this later relationship.
We should not invent a dramatic reconciliation scene the Bible never records.
But the evidence is clear that Mark eventually became a valued coworker of Paul.
And that is enough to make the heart tremble.
Because the same Paul who once objected to Mark's participation later testified to his usefulness.
The earlier conflict did not have the final word.
And perhaps the person you have permanently labeled by one painful season is still capable of becoming someone you cannot yet imagine.
That does not mean every broken relationship will be restored.
It does not mean every person who hurt you will repent.
It does not mean you should ignore manipulation, abuse, or repeated untrustworthiness.
Christian forgiveness is not a command to abandon discernment or personal safety.
But it does mean we should be careful about declaring that God's transforming grace has reached its limit in another person's life.
Think about Peter.
He denied knowing Jesus three times.
Yet the risen Christ restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Think about Paul himself.
He had persecuted the church.
Yet Jesus called him, transformed him, and sent him to proclaim the very Gospel he once opposed.
And think about John Mark.
His departure from a missionary journey became the center of a painful disagreement.
Yet he later served alongside Paul.
The Gospel does not teach that failure is harmless.
It teaches that failure does not have to be final.
But there is something even deeper here.
The greatest story of restoration is not ultimately about Paul, Barnabas, or Mark.
It is about Jesus Christ.
Because before we ask whether someone deserves another chance from us, we need to remember the mercy we ourselves have received.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Jesus did not wait until we had a flawless record.
He came for sinners.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
The cross does not minimize sin.
It reveals how serious sin truly is.
And the resurrection reveals that sin and death do not have the final victory over those who belong to Christ.
That is why Christian reconciliation must begin with humility.
We are not perfect people graciously tolerating the existence of other imperfect people.
We are sinners who desperately need the mercy of God.
So before you condemn someone for failing you, remember how patiently Christ has dealt with you.
Before you demand that everyone understand your perspective, ask whether you have truly listened to theirs.
Before you call someone spiritually immature because they disagree with you, examine whether pride has entered your own heart.
And before you insist that a broken relationship is beyond hope, remember that the risen Jesus is still transforming lives.
Perhaps you are the Paul in someone's story.
You have been entrusted with serious responsibilities.
You have watched someone's choices damage trust.
You are afraid that giving another opportunity too soon will endanger the work.
Your concern may be legitimate.
But do not let discernment become a permanent sentence against a repentant person.
Perhaps you are the Barnabas.
You see potential where others see failure.
You are willing to encourage someone who has disappointed people.
That compassion may be a beautiful gift.
But remember that encouragement should not require ignoring legitimate concerns or dismissing the responsibilities others carry.
Perhaps you are John Mark.
You left when you should have stayed.
You were not ready for something you thought you could handle.
And now you wonder whether your usefulness to God has ended.
Hear this carefully.
Your past must be faced honestly.
Repentance matters.
Growth matters.
Faithfulness matters.
But your worst moment does not have authority to overrule the grace of Jesus Christ.
You are not saved by proving that you have never failed. You are saved by the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–10 reminds us that salvation is God's gift, not the result of our works, and that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not merely comfort us in our failures.
It teaches us to leave sin behind and walk in newness of life.
And perhaps that is the most important truth in this entire account.
Paul and Barnabas separated.
But Jesus remained Lord.
The mission continued.
The Gospel was still proclaimed.
And Mark's later usefulness reminds us that God was not finished working in the life of the person at the center of the dispute.
We should not romanticize the separation as though conflict itself were God's preferred method of multiplying ministry.
The Bible does not say their disagreement was necessary or that the sharpness of their conflict was good.
But neither should we imagine that human conflict can somehow defeat the purposes of the risen Christ.
God is sovereign even when His servants are painfully imperfect.
And that should bring us to our knees.
Because maybe the real issue in your life right now is not a disagreement about ministry.
Maybe it is the brother you no longer speak to.
The sister whose message you refuse to open.
The friend you once prayed with but now avoid.
The church leader whose decision wounded you.
The person you trusted who disappointed you.
Or the apology you know you should offer but keep postponing because your pride wants to be vindicated first.
You keep replaying the conversation.
You remember what they said.
You remember how it made you feel.
And somewhere along the way, the wound became part of your identity.
But what if Jesus is calling you to something deeper than being proven right?
What if He is calling you to speak truth without cruelty?
To forgive without pretending?
To establish wise boundaries without nurturing hatred?
To pursue peace without compromising righteousness?
To admit your own mistakes without excusing someone else's?
To recognize that another believer can genuinely love Jesus and still disagree with your judgment?
And perhaps, when repentance and changed conduct make it possible, to open a door you thought would remain closed forever?
Colossians 3:13 calls believers to bear with one another and forgive one another, remembering how the Lord has forgiven them.
This is not sentimental religion.
It is costly obedience.
It is the kind of obedience that forces us to surrender the satisfaction of revenge.
The kind that makes us confess, "Lord, I have been more interested in defending my pride than reflecting Your character."
The kind that changes the way we speak about people who are not present to defend themselves.
The kind that makes us stop treating a fellow Christian as an enemy simply because we cannot agree.
And the kind that remembers we all stand in need of the same Savior.
If Paul could later recognize Mark as useful for ministry, is there someone whose growth you have refused to recognize because you are still holding on to who they used to be?
And if you are the one who failed, have you allowed shame to convince you that repentance, growth, and renewed faithfulness are pointless?
Do not confuse the consequences of yesterday with the impossibility of tomorrow.
Do not demand instant trust from people you have wounded.
But do not abandon the work of becoming faithful simply because restoration takes time.
And do not let someone else's inability to recognize your growth become an excuse to stop following Jesus.
The One who calls you to repentance is also the One who gives grace to walk in obedience.
Maybe today you need to make a phone call.
Maybe you need to apologize without adding an excuse.
Maybe you need to stop spreading a story that makes another believer look worse than the facts justify.
Maybe you need to forgive someone while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
Maybe you need to admit that your judgment, however sincerely held, is not infallible.
Or maybe you need to return to Jesus after a season of running away.
Whatever the situation, bring it into the light.
Because healing rarely begins while pride is still pretending there is nothing to heal.
If this story has exposed something in your heart, I want to invite you to do more than simply react to it.
You do not have to publish the details of your pain.
You do not have to expose someone else's private struggle.
But you can let your response become a small, sincere confession that you need the Lord's wisdom.
Someone who has lost hope may need to hear that restoration is possible, even when it is difficult.
Because the world does not need more Christians who know how to win religious arguments while forgetting how to love.
It needs believers who speak truth, practice repentance, pursue holiness, and demonstrate the mercy they have received in Christ.
Not to build a personality around a ministry.
Not to turn faith into merchandise.
Not to replace the local church or the responsibility of believers to support their own congregations.
But to keep pointing wounded, searching, struggling people toward the living Word of God and the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
And if these messages have helped you draw closer to the Lord, I want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and Christian learning more accessible to people who are hungry for truth.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry takes real work and real resources.

It can be part of your personal Christian giving, offered with gratitude to God. But it is not a substitute for your responsibility to give faithfully according to your convictions and commitments to your local church, nor is it a payment that earns God's favor.
Scripture is clear in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
You glorify God through faith, obedience, love, generosity, and a life surrendered to Christ.
But the deeper invitation is not about a discount.
It is about helping make biblical truth available to another person who may be one Scripture away from asking the questions that lead them to Jesus.
Another struggling believer who needs encouragement.
Another family longing for spiritual renewal.
Another person who has been told their past makes them worthless.
Another John Mark who needs to discover that a painful failure does not necessarily end their usefulness in God's hands.
Every thoughtful share can open a conversation.
Every sincere comment can encourage another believer.
Every invitation to read Scripture can point someone toward the truth.
We cannot control how another person will respond.
But we can faithfully offer what God has entrusted to us.
And ultimately, the purpose of all of this is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
It is to make Jesus Christ known.
Because Paul was not the Savior.
Barnabas was not the Savior.
John Mark was not the Savior.
And neither are we.
Jesus is.
He is the One who reconciles sinners to God.
He is the One who calls His people to repentance.
He is the One who teaches us to forgive.
He is the One who transforms lives.
And He is the One whose grace is greater than the shame of those who come to Him in faith.
So when you remember Paul and Barnabas, do not remember only the argument.
Remember the warning against pride.
Remember the need for wisdom.
Remember the difference between forgiveness and restored trust.
Remember that Scripture does not give us permission to invent motives or assign blame beyond what God has revealed.
Remember that sincere Christians can disagree without ceasing to belong to Christ.
And remember the extraordinary words Paul later wrote about Mark.
"Bring him."
"He is useful to me."
What a testimony to the possibility of change.
Not because every relationship receives the ending we want.
Not because every wound disappears.
But because our present understanding of someone's life is not the same thing as God's final verdict.
And above all, remember the Savior who died and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, redeemed, and made new.
The person remembered for walking away may yet become the person remembered for faithfully returning—and the grace of Jesus is greater than either chapter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE COULD DEFEND EVERY VERSE… BUT COULDN’T DEFEND THE WAY HE TREATED PEOPLE.
paragraphs: HE COULD DEFEND EVERY VERSE… BUT COULDN’T DEFEND THE WAY HE TREATED PEOPLE.
He was quick to correct everyone's theology—until one uncomfortable question exposed the difference between knowing the Word of God and allowing the Word of God to change him.
He knew the Scriptures.
He knew the Greek.
He knew the Hebrew.
He could explain why your favorite preacher was wrong, why your interpretation was questionable, and why your understanding of grace needed correction.
He could dismantle a theological argument in minutes.
But one evening, someone asked him a question that no seminary lecture, commentary, or theological debate had prepared him to answer.
“If you know Jesus so well… why is it so difficult to see Jesus in the way you treat people?”
Silence.
Not because he couldn't find a verse.
He had hundreds.
Not because he couldn't construct an argument.
He had spent years learning how.
But because, for the first time in a very long time, someone wasn't questioning what he believed.
They were questioning what his beliefs had made of him.
And the most frightening possibility was beginning to settle into his heart.
What if he had become exceptionally skilled at defending the truth while quietly resisting the very truth he defended?
Stay with this.
Because somewhere between the next few paragraphs and the final Scripture, you may discover that this story isn't really about him.
It might be about you.
And if we're willing to be painfully honest, it might be about me too.
He wasn't a villain.
That's what made the story so uncomfortable.
He loved studying the Bible. He genuinely cared about sound doctrine. He believed false teaching could damage souls, and he wasn't wrong.
Scripture itself commands believers to hold firmly to faithful teaching and refute what contradicts it (Titus 1:9).
Truth matters.
Doctrine matters.
What we believe about Jesus matters eternally.
But somewhere along the way, something subtle had happened.
His love for truth had begun to mingle with his love for being right.
At first, nobody noticed.
He simply wanted people to understand Scripture accurately.
Then he started enjoying the feeling of catching mistakes.
A poorly worded sermon became an opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge.
A struggling believer asking an imperfect question became another theological problem to correct.
A new Christian sharing an awkward testimony became someone whose language needed immediate refinement.
And every time he won an argument, something inside him whispered that he had defended God's honor.
Sometimes he had.
But sometimes he had merely defended his own pride using God's name.
That distinction is terrifying.
Because pride doesn't always walk into church wearing expensive clothes and demanding applause.
Sometimes pride carries a Bible.
Sometimes it quotes Scripture accurately.
Sometimes it speaks confidently about holiness while refusing to apologize to the people it has wounded.
And sometimes it mistakes the satisfaction of winning an argument for the fruit of the Holy Spirit.
He could recognize heresy from a distance.
But he couldn't recognize contempt in his own voice.
He could explain biblical reconciliation.
But he hadn't spoken to a family member in months because neither wanted to admit being wrong.
He could teach about the patience of God.
But his children were becoming afraid to ask him questions.
He could preach about the gentleness of Christ.
But his wife had learned to choose her words carefully around him.
And when someone confronted him about the contradiction, he reached for the one weapon that had never failed him.
Another Bible verse.
Only this time, the verse wasn't enough to silence the question.
Because the question was not whether Scripture was true.
The question was whether he was obeying it.
There is a moment in the Gospel of John that should disturb anyone who has ever mistaken biblical knowledge for spiritual maturity.
Jesus speaks to religious leaders who diligently searched the Scriptures.
They were not ignorant men.
They took the sacred writings seriously.
Yet Jesus told them:

“You search the scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.” — John 5:39–40, World English Bible
The Greek phrase in verse 40 is devastating:
καὶ οὐ θέλετε ἐλθεῖν πρός με
Kai ou thelete elthein pros me.
“And you are unwilling to come to me.”
Notice what Jesus exposed.
Their problem was not a lack of access to Scripture.
Their problem was an unwillingness to come to the One to whom Scripture pointed.
They were studying the testimony while resisting its central Person.
They were examining the words while rejecting the living Word standing before them.
And suddenly, the danger becomes personal.
You can know the biblical languages and still need to repent.
You can explain justification and still struggle to extend forgiveness.
You can understand sanctification and still resist the Spirit's correction.
You can accurately describe the humility of Christ while refusing to humble yourself before the people you've hurt.
None of this makes theology unnecessary.
It makes genuine theology more necessary than ever.
Because sound doctrine should lead us toward the living Christ, not merely toward greater confidence in ourselves.
Paul understood this.
He was no enemy of theological precision. His letters contain some of the deepest doctrinal teaching in Scripture.
Yet he also wrote:
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” — 1 Corinthians 8:1, WEB
The Greek is remarkably vivid.
ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ, ἡ δὲ ἀγάπη οἰκοδομεῖ
Hē gnōsis physioi, hē de agapē oikodomei.
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”
The verb physioi carries the image of being inflated or puffed up.
The verb oikodomei speaks of building up.
One swells the ego.
The other strengthens another person.
Paul's immediate concern was knowledge used without loving consideration for others in the controversy over food offered to idols. He was not condemning biblical knowledge itself.
He was exposing what happens when knowledge becomes detached from love.
And that distinction reaches into our churches, our homes, our comment sections, and our private conversations.
When you correct someone, are you trying to build them up?
Or are you trying to prove that you're above them?
When you respond to a theological mistake, do you care about the person making it?
Or have they become nothing more than an opponent to defeat?
When someone disagrees with you, do you still see a human being made in God's image?
Or do you immediately see a target?
These are not small questions.
Because it is possible to speak true words with a heart that desperately needs correction.
And then comes the Scripture that leaves almost no room for excuses.
“The Lord's servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him.” — 2 Timothy 2:24–25, WEB
Read that again.
The Lord's servant must be able to teach.
Yes.
But also gentle.
Patient.
Willing to correct without becoming quarrelsome.
Biblical correction is not forbidden.
It is commanded in the appropriate circumstances.
But the manner of correction is not irrelevant to the God whose truth we claim to represent.
The Greek word translated “gentle” in verse 24 is:
ἤπιον — ēpion
It describes gentleness, not weakness.
And verse 25 speaks of correcting opponents with:
πραΰτητι — prautēti
Gentleness or meekness.
This is not permission to compromise the Gospel.
It is a command to refuse the arrogance that can disguise itself as courage.
Jesus Himself confronted hypocrisy, rebuked false teaching, and spoke with extraordinary authority.
But He also welcomed the weary, restored the broken, showed compassion to sinners, and humbled Himself in obedience to the Father.
We cannot take His boldness while rejecting His humility and claim to be imitating Him faithfully.
That evening, the man finally stopped talking.
The person who had challenged him was not trying to humiliate him.
They were exhausted.
Exhausted from being corrected but rarely heard.
Exhausted from watching biblical discussions become contests.
Exhausted from hearing beautiful explanations of Christian love that seemed to disappear whenever someone disagreed.
Then came another question.
Softer this time.
Almost trembling.
“When was the last time you admitted you were wrong without explaining why you were still mostly right?”
He looked away.
He remembered the arguments.
The messages.
The conversations he had replayed in his mind, congratulating himself for the responses he should have given.
He remembered people who had stopped opening up to him.
He had assumed they were unwilling to receive truth.
Perhaps some were.
But had he ever considered that others might have been afraid of how he would respond?
And then another memory surfaced.
His child, standing in the doorway.
Trying to explain a mistake.
He remembered interrupting.
Correcting.
Lecturing.
He remembered how quickly the child's eyes dropped toward the floor.
He had called it discipline.
But had he listened?
Had he been patient?
Had he made room for confession without crushing the person confessing?
For the first time, he wasn't searching his memory for examples of other people's theological failures.
He was remembering his own.
And it hurt.
Because conviction often begins where our favorite explanations finally run out.
Not every criticism is accurate. Not every accusation should be accepted without examination.
But neither should every criticism be dismissed simply because it threatens our self-image.
Sometimes God uses an uncomfortable conversation to bring us back to something we have been avoiding.
The man had spent years learning how to interpret difficult passages.
Now he needed to let a clear passage interpret his behavior.
James 1:22 says:
“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” — WEB
There it was.
The danger.
Not ignorance.
Self-deception.
He could hear the Word.
Explain the Word.
Defend the Word.
And still deceive himself if he refused to obey it.
And perhaps the most painful realization was this:
He had sometimes demanded repentance from others while treating repentance in his own life as an unnecessary interruption.
But the Gospel was never meant to make us experts at identifying everybody else's sin while remaining comfortable with our own.
Jesus asked:
“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but don't consider the beam that is in your own eye?” — Matthew 7:3, WEB
Jesus did not command us to abandon discernment.
In the verses that follow, He teaches that the beam must first be removed so that we can see clearly to help our brother.
The order matters.
Humility before correction.
Self-examination before accusation.
Repentance before self-righteous superiority.
And here is where the story becomes even more uncomfortable.
Because you may not be a Bible teacher.
You may not know Greek.
You may never have entered a formal theological debate.
But perhaps you know what it feels like to be right about someone's mistake and wrong about how you treated them.
Perhaps you have used silence to punish someone.
Perhaps you have withheld an apology because you believed the other person sinned first.
Perhaps you have shared powerful sermons about forgiveness while keeping a private list of people you refuse to forgive.
Perhaps you have defended Christian values publicly while neglecting Christian kindness privately.
Perhaps the people who know your theology best are the people who experience your patience least.
And perhaps, even now, part of you wants to think of someone else who needs to read this.
I understand.
It's easier to recognize pride when it belongs to another person.
But what if the Holy Spirit is inviting us to stop looking across the room and start looking into our own hearts?
Not to condemn us without hope.
But to lead us into repentance.
Because the most beautiful part of this story is not that the man was exposed.
It is that exposure did not have to be the end of his story.
He could have doubled down.
He could have defended himself.
He could have called the conversation an attack on biblical truth.
He could have walked away, convinced that nobody appreciated his faithfulness.
Instead, after a long silence, he whispered something he hadn't said sincerely in far too long.
“I think I've been proud.”
No speech.
No qualifications.
No carefully constructed defense.
Just the beginning of confession.
And then:
“I've hurt people while telling myself I was helping them.”
The words were difficult.
But for the first time that evening, he wasn't trying to win.
He was beginning to surrender.
That did not erase the damage.
It did not automatically restore every relationship.
It did not mean the people he had wounded were required to trust him immediately.
Repentance would need to become visible through changed behavior, patient listening, honest apologies, and consistent love.
But something had begun.
Not the abandonment of truth.
The abandonment of pride.
And that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to make arrogant sinners feel embarrassed about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
Including religious sinners.
Including self-righteous sinners.
Including people who have used the right words with the wrong hearts.
Including people who have confused spiritual authority with personal superiority.
Including you.
Including me.
The apostle Paul knew what it meant to be religiously zealous and profoundly wrong.
Before his conversion, he persecuted the church.
He later described himself as having been a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man, yet one who received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13).
The same man who once persecuted followers of Christ became a servant of the Christ he had opposed.
Not because his former actions were harmless.
Not because sincerity made persecution acceptable.
But because the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than the sins of those who truly turn to Him.
Paul wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15, WEB
That is the Gospel.
Not that your theological knowledge can save you.
Not that your religious reputation can cleanse you.
Not that enough correct arguments can compensate for an unrepentant heart.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
At the cross, our pride finds no reason to boast.
Our sin is exposed.
God's justice is not ignored.
And His mercy is revealed through the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our accomplishments (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And that same grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and live differently (Titus 2:11–12).
Grace does not tell the proud person that pride is harmless.
Grace calls the proud person to come to Christ.
Grace does not excuse cruelty because the theology was technically correct.
Grace teaches us to repent and walk in love.
Grace does not require us to pretend that broken relationships have instantly healed.
Grace gives us the courage to confess, seek reconciliation where possible, and persevere in changed behavior.
And if you have spent years becoming someone who always has an answer but rarely offers an apology, hear this carefully.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life being the person your pride has made you.
In Christ, there is forgiveness.
In Christ, there is hope.
In Christ, there is a new way to live.
Ezekiel 36:26 contains God's promise to His people:
“I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” — WEB
The Hebrew phrase for “a new heart” is:
לֵב חָדָשׁ — lev chadash
A new heart.
In its original context, this promise concerns God's restoration and renewal of His people. It is not a guarantee that every stubborn personality will change overnight.
But it reveals something essential about God's saving work.
God is concerned with more than outward religious performance.
He transforms people from within.
And through the new covenant established by Jesus Christ, believers are called to live by the Spirit rather than merely maintain the appearance of righteousness.
That is why the fruit of the Spirit includes love, patience, kindness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).
Not merely impressive knowledge.
Not merely public confidence.
Not merely the ability to recognize someone else's error.
The Spirit produces a transformed life.
A life that increasingly reflects the character of Christ.
So imagine the man returning home after that conversation.
Imagine him standing outside his child's bedroom.
For once, he isn't rehearsing a lecture.
He isn't preparing a defense.
He knocks.
His child looks up.
And he says:
“I owe you an apology.”
The child waits.
“I've been harsh with you. I've interrupted you when you were trying to explain. I've acted like being your father means I never have to admit when I'm wrong.”
A pause.
“I was wrong. Will you forgive me?”
Perhaps the child cries.
Perhaps the child says nothing.
Perhaps trust takes time to rebuild.
But the father has finally begun to practice something he once knew only how to explain.
Humility.
Now imagine him speaking to his wife.
Listening without immediately correcting her description of the problem.
Acknowledging specific failures without adding the word “but.”
Accepting that an apology is not a transaction that purchases instant reconciliation.
Then imagine him opening his Bible the next morning.
The same Bible.
The same sacred words.
