The man who had spent years making other kings helpless was about to discover what helplessness felt like.
And what he said afterward is one of the most chilling confessions in the Old Testament.
But before you distance yourself from this ancient king, before you decide that this story has nothing to do with your life, consider something.
You do not need a crown to become cruel.
You do not need a throne to worship power.
And you do not need to cut off someone's fingers to leave wounds that follow them for years.
Sometimes the most dangerous throne is the one we build inside our hearts.
And sometimes the person sitting on it is us.
The Bible introduces this king in Judges 1:4–7.
His name was Adoni-bezek.
The name אֲדֹנִי־בֶזֶק (ʾAdonî-Bezeq) is commonly understood to mean “lord of Bezek,” identifying him by his authority or association with Bezek.
The setting is important.
Joshua had died, and the book of Judges opens with Israel seeking the LORD's direction concerning the battles ahead. Judah was instructed to go first, and Simeon joined Judah in the campaign.
Judges 1:4–5 records that Judah went up, the LORD delivered the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hand, and they encountered Adoni-bezek at Bezek.
Then came the terrible reversal.
The King James Version records:

“And they found Adonibezek in Bezek: and they fought against him, and they slew the Canaanites and the Perizzites. But Adonibezek fled; and they pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes.” — Judges 1:5–6
Pause there.
He fled.
The man who had made others run for their lives was now running for his own.
He was caught.
The man who had held others captive was now in captivity.
And the same mutilation he had imposed upon defeated kings was inflicted upon him.
Scripture does not invite us to enjoy this violence. It records a brutal event in Israel's ancient history and then allows the defeated king's own words to expose the significance he saw in it.
Listen carefully to his confession.

“And Adonibezek said, Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me. And they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.” — Judges 1:7 (KJV)
“As I have done, so God hath requited me.”
There is an entire sermon inside that sentence.
And perhaps an entire lifetime of regret.
In the Hebrew text, the confession ends:
כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתִי כֵּן שִׁלַּם־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Ka'asher asiti, ken shillam-li Elohim.
A close translation is:
“As I have done, so God has repaid me.”
The Hebrew verb שִׁלַּם (shillam) comes from a verb that can express paying, repaying, or making recompense.
The king himself interpreted what happened to him as divine repayment.
Notice that distinction.
The text records his confession. It does not provide us with permission to declare that every person who suffers is being punished for something they have done.
Jesus explicitly challenged that kind of simplistic judgment in Luke 13:1–5 and John 9:1–3.
But in this particular account, Adoni-bezek recognized a devastating correspondence between his own cruelty and what had happened to him.
He had stripped others of their dignity.
Now his dignity was stripped away.
He had treated kings like animals beneath his table.
Now he was no longer sitting above anyone.
And the throne that once made him feel untouchable could not save him.
Can you imagine the silence that followed his confession?
No boasting.
No royal decree.
No army rushing to rescue him.
Just a defeated man confronting the reality of what he had done.
The text does not tell us everything he thought or felt. We cannot know whether his words expressed genuine repentance or simply an acknowledgment that judgment had caught up with him.
But we know what he said.
“As I have done...”
Four words that reveal a terrible moment of recognition.
And there is something deeply unsettling about those words.
Because sometimes the consequences of our actions do not arrive immediately.
Sometimes pride is rewarded for a season.
Sometimes cruelty looks like strength.
Sometimes deception produces temporary success.
Sometimes a person can hurt others, move on, build a comfortable life, and convince themselves that nothing will ever come of it.
But a delayed consequence is not proof that God is indifferent.
Ecclesiastes 8:11 warns that when judgment against evil is not carried out speedily, the human heart can become emboldened to do wrong.
That is a frightening possibility.
Not because God is impatient.
But because human beings can mistake His patience for permission.
Think about that person you humiliated when you had the advantage.
That family member whose weakness you used against them.
That friend whose trust you betrayed.
That employee you treated as though their dignity depended on your approval.
That spouse who kept asking to be heard while you kept insisting on being right.
Or perhaps you were the one sitting beneath someone else's table.
The one who was mocked.
The one who was manipulated.
The one whose pain became somebody else's entertainment.
The one who learned to remain silent because speaking only made things worse.
This story speaks to both sides of that suffering.
To the person who has abused power, it says that power does not erase accountability.
To the person who has been wounded by someone powerful, it says that the person who harmed you is not beyond God's sight.
But there is something else we must understand.
God's justice is real. Yet God's justice is not an invitation for us to become cruel in return.
That distinction matters.
The book of Judges describes many violent and morally disturbing events. Not everything recorded in its pages is presented as an example for Christians to imitate.
The mutilation of Adoni-bezek is part of the narrative, not a command for believers to punish their enemies in the same way.
Jesus calls His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44).
Paul writes:
That does not mean injustice should be ignored.
It does not mean victims must remain in dangerous situations.
It does not mean abusers should escape accountability.
Seeking protection, establishing boundaries, telling the truth, and pursuing lawful justice can all be consistent with Christian faithfulness.
It means that revenge must not become the god of our hearts.
Because when we allow another person's cruelty to transform us into someone equally cruel, their sin has begun shaping our character.
And Jesus calls us to something greater.
But now comes the question that changes the direction of this entire story.
What happens when you are not simply the person who has been hurt?
What happens when you realize you have also hurt others?
What happens when you cannot honestly say you were always the victim?
What happens when you remember the lies you told, the people you used, the promises you broke, and the opportunities you had to do right but deliberately chose wrong?
What happens when your conscience begins whispering...
“As I have done...”
Perhaps you have never been a king.
But you know what it means to regret something.
You know what it means to replay a conversation in your mind and wish you could take your words back.
You know what it means to look at an old photograph and remember a version of yourself you are ashamed of.
You know what it means to lie awake wondering whether you have gone too far.
And perhaps the hardest part is this:
You cannot go backward.
You cannot unsay the words.
You cannot recover every opportunity.
You cannot erase every consequence.
You cannot make every wounded person trust you again.
So what do you do when the past is real, the damage is real, and your guilt is real?
This is where the story of a defeated king leads us to something far greater than the story itself.
It leads us to the Gospel.
Not because Judges 1:4–7 secretly describes the crucifixion. It does not.
Not because Adoni-bezek is presented as a direct prophecy of Jesus. He is not.
But because this account raises a question the Gospel answers with breathtaking clarity.
How can guilty people stand before a holy and just God?
Adoni-bezek could recognize that he had received a consequence resembling the cruelty he had inflicted.
But recognition alone is not the same as redemption.
A person can admit wrongdoing and still remain unchanged.
A person can fear consequences without loving righteousness.
A person can regret being caught without grieving the evil they committed.
True repentance goes deeper.
It means turning toward God, acknowledging sin without excuses, and seeking the transformation that only His grace can accomplish.
And here is the glorious difference between merely facing the consequences of sin and receiving salvation in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not say that sin is harmless. It says that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Not just ancient tyrants.
Not just violent rulers.
Not just people whose failures became public scandals.
All of us.
The respectable person.
The religious person.
The person who looks faithful on Sunday but secretly struggles through the week.
The person who knows the right Bible verses but has not surrendered the hidden parts of their life.
The person who has been harmed.
And the person who has done harm.
All of us need grace.
And the wonder of Christianity is not that God pretends our sins never happened.
It is that God has acted in history through His Son to reconcile sinners to Himself.
At the cross, Jesus did not excuse evil.
He bore sin.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
Centuries later, the apostle Peter applied the suffering of Christ to our salvation.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God...” — 1 Peter 3:18 (KJV)
Read that again.
The just for the unjust.
The innocent for the guilty.
The righteous One suffering to bring sinners to God.
Adoni-bezek's story shows a man who recognized the return of his own cruelty.
The cross shows us the sinless Savior who willingly suffered for sins He never committed.
That is not a small distinction.
That is the heart of redemption.
Jesus Christ was not another fallen king being punished for His own wrongdoing.
He was the holy Son of God who gave Himself for sinners.
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is why the Gospel is more than a message about becoming a better person.
It is the announcement of what God has done through Jesus Christ.
It is the call to repent and believe.
It is the promise that forgiveness is available through Him.
It is the beginning of a transformed life.
The Greek word often translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It refers to a change of mind or understanding and, in biblical calls to repentance, carries the demand to turn away from sin toward God.
When Jesus proclaimed, “Repent ye, and believe the gospel” in Mark 1:15, He was not merely inviting people to feel sorry.
He was calling them to respond to the arrival of God's kingdom.
To turn.
To believe.
To surrender.
To follow.
And perhaps that is the word someone reading this needs today.
Turn.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret compromise.
Not after you have convinced everyone you are fine.
Turn to Jesus Christ.
You do not have to invent a better past before coming to Him.
You cannot.
But you can come honestly.
You can confess what you have done.
You can stop defending what God calls sin.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can begin making restitution where appropriate and possible.
You can ask the Holy Spirit to transform the habits that have harmed you and others.
And you can trust that the grace of Christ is greater than the power of sin to define your eternal destiny.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
A forgiven person may still need to rebuild trust.
A repentant person may still need to face legal consequences.
A restored believer may still carry painful memories.
Grace is not a way to escape responsibility.
Grace is the gift that makes a new life possible without denying the truth about the old one.
Consider the apostle Paul.
Before he became one of the most influential witnesses to Jesus Christ, he persecuted the church.
He approved of Stephen's death and sought to imprison believers.
He later described himself as a former blasphemer, persecutor, and injurious man.
Yet he wrote:
“And the grace of our Lord was exceeding abundant with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 1:14 (KJV)
Paul never needed to pretend that his past was innocent.
He testified that Christ had shown him mercy.
And that mercy changed the direction of his life.
The persecutor became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The man who once sought to silence Christians became a witness willing to suffer for Christ.
That is transformation.
Not a rewritten historical record.
A redeemed life.
And that is what we mean when we say:
Jesus does not rewrite history by making yesterday's evil good.
He rewrites the story of a redeemed life by giving the forgiven sinner a new identity, a new direction, and an eternal hope.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It may explain some of your fears.
It may explain why certain memories still bring tears to your eyes.
But through Jesus Christ, your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
Notice the words.
In Christ.
Not simply religious.
Not merely inspired.
Not just emotionally moved by a powerful story.
In Christ.
United to Him by faith.
Forgiven through His sacrifice.
Made new by His grace.
This is why I do not want you to finish this article merely thinking about a king who lost his thumbs and big toes.
I want you to think about the King who bore the wounds of crucifixion.
The King who did not use His authority to exploit the helpless.
The King who washed His disciples' feet.
The King who welcomed repentant sinners.
The King who spoke forgiveness even while suffering.
The King who conquered death.
The King whose throne will never collapse.
Jesus Christ.
Adoni-bezek used power to bring other kings beneath his table.
Jesus used His authority to serve, and through His death and resurrection He opens the way for sinners to come to God.
One king made weakness an object of humiliation.
The true King of kings displayed His love through sacrificial suffering.
One king's confession was, “As I have done, so God hath requited me.”
But the song of the redeemed is different.
Not because we deserve better.
But because Christ has shown mercy.
And if that truth is beginning to break through the walls you have built around your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you have been living with hidden guilt.
Maybe you have been asking God why your life feels so empty despite everything you have achieved.
Maybe you have been carrying anger toward someone who treated you as though you were worthless.
Maybe you have been trying to punish yourself for sins Jesus calls you to confess and forsake.
Or maybe you have been using your own pain as permission to wound other people.
Whatever brought you here, the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Not with a performance.
Not with a polished explanation.
Not with a list of reasons why your sin was understandable.
Come in truth.
Come in repentance.
Come in faith.
And receive the mercy He freely offers.
If you need words to express that surrender, you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have tried to justify things I should have confessed. I have carried guilt, pride, bitterness, and wounds that I cannot heal by myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to repent sincerely, to make right what I can, to forgive as You command, and to walk in obedience to Your Word. I surrender my life to You. Change my heart and make me more like You. In Your name, amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula. Our hope rests in Jesus Christ Himself, not in the mere repetition of words.
And if you have prayed sincerely, do not treat this as the end of your journey.
Open your Bible.
Seek a faithful local church.
Grow in prayer.
Learn to obey Christ.
Walk with believers who will encourage you, correct you when necessary, and remind you of the Gospel when your strength feels small.
Because following Jesus is not about experiencing one emotional moment and returning unchanged to the life you were living.
It is about belonging to Him.
Day after day.
Even when nobody is watching.
Even when obedience is costly.
Even when the old habits call your name.
Even when healing takes longer than you expected.
And perhaps this is where your own story can become an encouragement to someone else.
And please, do not let this message stop with you.
Not because a social media post makes anyone more righteous.
But because someone among your family, friends, or followers may be carrying a burden they have never told anyone about.
Someone may be living with regret.
Someone may have stopped believing that forgiveness is possible.
Someone may be standing at the edge of giving up on faith.
Your simple act of sharing could place the truth of Scripture before someone who desperately needs to hear it.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe this ministry is worth helping to sustain.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep pointing people toward the Lord Jesus Christ through biblical content, Gospel-centered storytelling, Christian books, devotionals, and discipleship resources.
Behind every article is a continuing mission to reach people, encourage believers, and make resources available to those who want to grow deeper in their understanding of Scripture.
We want that work to continue.
And, by God's grace, we want it to reach even more people.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Those words matter to us.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
These are small, tangible ways we want to express our appreciation to those who help this ministry continue.
The greater purpose, however, is not merchandise.
It is helping people open their Bibles again.
It is encouraging believers to stand firm when life becomes difficult.
It is reaching the person who feels too ashamed to enter a church.
It is pointing the wounded toward Christ, the proud toward repentance, the weary toward His promises, and the lost toward the Savior.
If that is a mission you believe is worth supporting, I warmly invite you to become part of it.
The Gospel must never be placed behind a price tag.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
His grace cannot be purchased.
And your value before God is not measured by a monthly contribution.
What matters eternally is whether you belong to Christ.
That brings us back to the king at Bezek.
The king who once believed he could do anything he wanted.
The king who made seventy other kings gather scraps beneath his table.
The king who fled when his own power collapsed.
The king whose final recorded words confronted the cruelty of his past.
“As I have done, so God hath requited me.”
His story ends with his death in Jerusalem.
There is no recorded restoration.
No recorded conversion.
No recorded second chance.
Scripture does not tell us his eternal destiny, and we should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But Scripture has revealed something wonderful about Jesus Christ.
He receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
He calls the proud to humble themselves.
He calls the guilty to repent.
He calls the wounded to trust His justice rather than surrender their hearts to revenge.
He calls His people to live differently because His grace has changed them.
And He promises:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
That promise is worth remembering when shame tells you not to pray.
When regret tells you that you are beyond forgiveness.
When pride tells you that you do not need forgiveness.
When fear tells you that your past is stronger than the cross.
The king at Bezek could not return to the moment before he committed his cruelties.
Neither can you return to yesterday.
But today, while you still have breath, you can turn to the living Christ.
You can tell the truth.
You can repent.
You can believe.
You can begin walking in the newness of life that His grace makes possible.
And years from now, when someone asks what happened to the person you used to be, may your answer not be a story about how you made yourself righteous.
May it be a testimony about the Savior who showed you mercy.
Because the most devastating thing about your past is not that you cannot change what happened—it is the tragedy of refusing the Savior who can change what happens next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES GOD STILL GIVE APOSTLES TODAY? THE TRUTH THAT COULD SAVE THE CHURCH FROM DECEPTION—AND BRING US BACK TO JESUS
paragraphs: DOES GOD STILL GIVE APOSTLES TODAY? THE TRUTH THAT COULD SAVE THE CHURCH FROM DECEPTION—AND BRING US BACK TO JESUS

Some say the age of apostles ended. Others insist God is raising up new apostles today. But beneath the titles, miracles, controversies, and competing voices lies a question far more serious: Are we following the apostles of Jesus Christ—or following people who have learned how to use His name?
Imagine standing inside a church where the atmosphere is electric.
The worship is powerful. People are crying. Hands are raised. Someone approaches the pulpit, and the entire congregation stands.
They call him an apostle.
He speaks with authority. He declares that God has given him a special anointing. He says questioning his leadership is questioning God's appointed servant.
Then something happens.

A struggling mother is told that her breakthrough depends on sowing a financial seed. A young believer is warned not to question the apostle's revelations. A faithful church member discovers that disagreeing with leadership can mean being accused of rebellion against the Holy Spirit.
And somewhere in that congregation sits a person who genuinely loves Jesus but is beginning to wonder...
Is this what Christ intended when He gave apostles to His Church?
Now imagine another church.
There is no impressive stage. No expensive clothing. No one demanding special treatment.

An older missionary sits beside a young believer, explaining the Scriptures. He has spent decades planting churches, enduring persecution, preaching Christ, and caring for people who could never repay him.
He has never called himself an apostle.
Yet his life resembles the sacrificial ministry we read about in the New Testament.
So who is closer to the biblical picture?
The person carrying the title?
Or the person carrying the cross?
Before answering, we need to confront something uncomfortable.
Not everyone who calls himself an apostle has been sent by Jesus.
But neither does every claim that God continues to send people necessarily mean someone is trying to replace the Twelve.
The truth requires more than suspicion, tradition, or emotional experiences.
It requires Scripture.
And Scripture has something to say that may challenge people on both sides of this debate.
When Jesus walked the shores of Galilee, He did not establish His Church through celebrity personalities or religious empires.
He called ordinary people.
Fishermen. A tax collector. Men with weaknesses, fears, ambitions, and misunderstandings.
Luke 6:13 records that Jesus chose twelve disciples and named them apostles.
The Greek word is ἀπόστολος (apostolos), meaning someone sent as a messenger, envoy, or commissioned representative.
That word matters.
An apostle is not simply someone who possesses impressive spiritual influence. The term concerns being sent with a commission.
But here is where careful Bible reading becomes essential.
The New Testament does not use the word apostle in exactly the same way in every passage.
And overlooking that distinction can lead us into serious confusion.
The Twelve occupied a unique place in the history of redemption.
Jesus personally chose them during His earthly ministry. They witnessed His resurrection, proclaimed His teaching, and served as foundational witnesses to the Gospel.
After Judas betrayed Jesus, Peter explained the qualifications involved in replacing him.
Acts 1:21–22 describes someone who had accompanied Jesus' followers throughout His public ministry and could become a witness of His resurrection.
Matthias was chosen to take Judas's place.
Later, Paul would also identify himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ, not through ordinary human appointment but through the calling of the risen Lord.
In Galatians 1:1, Paul writes:
And in 1 Corinthians 9:1, he asks:
“Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?”
Paul's calling was extraordinary.
He was not simply a gifted preacher promoted into a higher church office.
He encountered the risen Christ and received a commission to proclaim the Gospel, particularly among the Gentiles.
The foundation was being laid.
And foundations are not laid repeatedly every time another generation builds upon them.
Ephesians 2:20 describes God's household as:
“And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;”
The Greek expression for cornerstone is ἀκρογωνιαῖος (akrogōniaios).
Jesus Christ is the decisive cornerstone, the One who determines the alignment and integrity of the whole structure.
The apostles and prophets are described as foundational, but Jesus remains the supreme reference point.
That means no apostle, ancient or modern, has the authority to replace Christ, contradict His Gospel, or become the ultimate object of the Church's loyalty.
And this brings us to a distinction that every Christian should understand.
The foundational apostolic witness is unique. The Church's mission to proclaim that witness continues.
Christians who believe the foundational office of apostle has ceased are not necessarily denying that God still sends missionaries, evangelists, church planters, and courageous Gospel workers.
They are saying that the original apostolic foundation cannot be reproduced.
Christians who believe some form of apostolic ministry continues often point to the wider New Testament usage of the term and to Ephesians 4.
Both positions deserve careful biblical examination rather than careless accusations.
Because Ephesians 4:11 says something important.
“And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;”
The Greek text begins:
Καὶ αὐτὸς ἔδωκεν τοὺς μὲν ἀποστόλους
Kai autos edōken tous men apostolous.
“And He Himself gave some as apostles.”
The verb ἔδωκεν (edōken) comes from didōmi, meaning “to give.”
Paul presents these ministries as gifts from the exalted Christ to His Church.
And why did Christ give them?
Not to create spiritual celebrities.
Not to establish untouchable religious authorities.
Not to build financial empires.
Ephesians 4:12 explains their purpose:
“For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:”
The goal is the maturity and strengthening of God's people.
Not their permanent dependence on one powerful personality.
Not their fear of questioning a leader.
Not their inability to approach God without a supposedly superior spiritual intermediary.
Jesus gives ministry gifts so that His people may grow into maturity in Him.
Ephesians 4:13 continues by describing the goal of unity in the faith and knowledge of the Son of God.
Notice where the passage directs our attention.
Not toward the greatness of apostles.
Toward the fullness of Christ.
That is the test every ministry must face.
Does this ministry make people more dependent on Jesus—or more dependent on the minister?
But there is another detail we cannot ignore.
The New Testament uses apostolos beyond the Twelve and Paul.
Acts 14:14 refers to Barnabas and Paul as apostles.

Romans 16:7 describes Andronicus and Junia as notable in relation to the apostles, although scholars debate whether the Greek phrase means they were outstanding among the apostles or well known to them.
Philippians 2:25 calls Epaphroditus a messenger of the Philippian church, using the Greek word apostolos.
Second Corinthians 8:23 likewise speaks of messengers of the churches using the plural apostoloi.
These passages demonstrate that the word could refer to commissioned messengers in a broader sense.
But they do not automatically prove that every such messenger possessed the same authority as the Twelve or Paul.
That distinction is essential.
A church-sent messenger is not necessarily a foundational apostle of Jesus Christ.
And the fact that the New Testament uses the same Greek noun in different contexts does not erase the differences between those contexts.
This is where the debate becomes more complex than many sermons admit.
Some Christians argue that because Ephesians 4 includes apostles among Christ's gifts for building up the Church, apostolic ministry must continue until the Church reaches full maturity.
Others argue that the apostles continue to build up the Church through their authoritative testimony preserved in Scripture, while other ministries carry that teaching forward.
The passage does not explicitly settle every question about the continuation of the office.
Faithful Christians therefore disagree.
But there is something Scripture makes unmistakably clear.
No person today may claim an authority that places his words above the Gospel delivered through Christ's apostles.
Galatians 1:8 contains one of the strongest warnings in the New Testament:
“But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.”
Read that again.
Paul does not exempt himself from the standard.
Even if he were to preach a different Gospel, that message would deserve rejection.
Think about what that means.
If the apostle Paul himself refused to place his personal status above the Gospel, what gives any modern religious leader the right to demand unquestioning obedience?
Not a title.
Not a prophecy.
Not a vision.
Not a testimony about visiting heaven.
Not a crowd of thousands.
Not a collection of impressive miracles.
The Gospel remains the standard.
And Jesus Christ remains Lord.
Perhaps you have been hurt by someone who claimed extraordinary spiritual authority.
Perhaps you were told that your doubts were rebellion.
Perhaps you gave money you could barely afford because someone promised that God would release a miracle if you sacrificed enough.
Perhaps you remained silent while something inside you whispered that this could not be right.
Listen carefully.
You do not have to reject Jesus to reject spiritual manipulation.
You do not have to abandon the Church to recognize that some leaders have abused their authority.
You do not have to silence your conscience to prove your loyalty to God.
In Acts 17:11, the Bereans were commended for examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether Paul's message was true.
Think about that.
They examined the teaching of Paul.
A genuine apostle.
And Scripture presents their examination as noble.
If the Bereans could test Paul's preaching against Scripture, Christians today should not be afraid to test the claims of anyone who calls himself an apostle.
This is not rebellion against biblical authority.
It is submission to the truth of God.
And then comes a warning that should sober every person who claims apostolic status.
In Revelation 2:2, Jesus commends the church in Ephesus for testing those who claimed to be apostles and discovering that they were false.
False apostles were not merely a modern problem.
They existed in the earliest generations of Christianity.
Second Corinthians 11:13 warns:
“For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ.”
Paul continues by explaining that deception can appear attractive and righteous.
That should make us cautious.
Not cynical toward every pastor.
Not suspicious of every missionary.
Not hostile toward every supernatural claim.
But discerning.
Because deception does not always announce itself with obvious evil.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it speaks with tears.
Sometimes it uses the language of anointing, revival, breakthrough, and spiritual covering.
Sometimes it promises access to God while quietly making people dependent on a human leader.
And sometimes the warning sign is not what a leader teaches about Jesus.
It is how the leader treats people who ask questions.
Jesus told His disciples in Mark 10:42–45 that rulers of the Gentiles exercise authority over others, but His followers must not imitate that pattern of domination.
Instead, greatness among His people is expressed through service.
The Son of Man Himself came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.
That changes everything.
Because the clearest model of Christian leadership is not a throne surrounded by admirers.
It is Jesus kneeling with a towel.
Washing feet.
Serving people who would misunderstand Him.
Loving disciples who would fail Him.
And ultimately going to the cross for sinners who could never earn His mercy.
What kind of apostolic ministry could possibly be faithful to that Christ while demanding the opposite spirit?
A leader may have a genuine calling.
A leader may be used powerfully by God.
A leader may establish churches, train disciples, and reach thousands.
But spiritual fruit is not measured by the number of people who bow to that leader's authority.
It is measured by faithfulness to Christ, sound teaching, holiness, love, and the building up of His people.
Paul's own life makes this painfully clear.
In 1 Corinthians 4:9–13, he describes the apostles enduring humiliation, hardship, persecution, and mistreatment.
In 2 Corinthians 11, he recounts beatings, imprisonments, dangers, exhaustion, hunger, and anxiety for the churches.
His apostolic ministry was marked by suffering and sacrificial service.
Not a guarantee of earthly luxury.
Not immunity from correction.
Not the right to exploit vulnerable believers.
This does not mean every faithful Christian leader must live in poverty or that receiving financial support is wrong.
Scripture teaches that Gospel workers may receive appropriate material support.
First Corinthians 9:14 says that the Lord ordained that those who preach the Gospel should live from the Gospel.
First Timothy 5:17–18 likewise affirms the legitimacy of supporting worthy elders.
But financial support is not permission for coercion, greed, or promises of blessings that God has not made.
And this matters deeply when we discuss modern apostles.
Because some believers are not really asking whether apostles exist today.
They are asking something much more personal.
Can I trust spiritual authority again after what happened to me?
Maybe you once admired a leader so deeply that you stopped questioning anything he said.
Maybe you defended him when others raised concerns.
Maybe you thought leaving his ministry meant leaving God's protection.
And when the truth finally came out, you felt ashamed.
You wondered how you could have missed the signs.
You wondered whether your faith had been foolish.
You wondered whether God had abandoned you.
But the failure of a religious leader does not mean the failure of Jesus Christ.
Judas walked among the Twelve.
He heard Jesus teach.
He witnessed extraordinary things.
Yet he betrayed the Lord.
His betrayal did not make Jesus false.
And the corruption of a modern religious leader does not make the Gospel false.
Christ remains holy when His representatives fail.
Christ remains faithful when His servants become unfaithful.
Christ remains the Good Shepherd when human shepherds wound the sheep.
And this is where the story turns from scandal toward grace.
Because Jesus did not come merely to expose false authority.
He came to rescue sinners.
Including proud leaders who need repentance.
Including wounded believers who need healing.
Including confused Christians who need discernment.
Including those of us who have sometimes followed personalities more passionately than we followed Scripture.
We all need grace.
And none of us can purchase it.
The Gospel is not that Jesus came to give us impressive titles.
The Gospel is that the sinless Son of God died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures.
That is Paul's summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The risen Christ is not waiting for us to discover a modern apostle who can unlock salvation.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Salvation is found in Him.
Acts 4:12 declares that there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.
Not the name of a denomination.
Not the name of a prophet.
Not the name of an apostle.
The name of Jesus Christ.
And if a ministry is truly apostolic in its faithfulness to the Gospel, that is where it must continually lead people.
Back to Jesus.
Back to His Word.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
Back to the cross.
Back to the empty tomb.
Now we can answer the question more carefully.
Does God still give apostles to the Church today?
It depends on what we mean by “apostles.”

If we mean the unique, foundational apostles who were commissioned as authoritative witnesses of the risen Christ and whose testimony forms part of the Church's foundation, Scripture gives us no clear reason to expect that foundational role to be continually recreated.
The Church does not need a new foundation.
It already has Christ as its cornerstone and the apostolic witness preserved in Scripture.
If we mean people sent by churches to proclaim the Gospel, establish congregations, strengthen believers, and carry Christ's mission into new places, that sending work certainly continues.
The Church still needs missionaries.
It still needs church planters.
It still needs evangelists.
It still needs faithful teachers and shepherds.
And it still needs courageous believers willing to suffer so that others may hear about Jesus.
Whether such workers should be called apostles today remains a matter of disagreement among Bible-believing Christians.
Some reserve the title for the foundational apostles.
Others use it for contemporary missionary or church-planting ministries, while distinguishing their authority from that of the original apostles.
Still others believe the office itself continues in some form.
Those positions should be evaluated according to their biblical arguments, not merely their labels.
But no contemporary claim to apostleship can legitimately establish new Scripture, replace the apostolic Gospel, or demand the unquestioning allegiance that belongs to Christ alone.
That is the boundary we must not surrender.
And perhaps the most revealing question is not whether someone has the right to put Apostle before his name.
Perhaps it is whether his life reflects the Lord whose name he claims to represent.
Does he preach Christ crucified and risen?
Does he teach Scripture faithfully?
Does he welcome responsible examination of his teaching?
Does he demonstrate humility and accountability?
Does he protect the vulnerable?
Does he equip believers to grow into maturity rather than keeping them spiritually dependent on himself?
Does he handle money with integrity?
Does he point people toward Jesus even when doing so costs him personal recognition?
These questions matter far more than an impressive title.
Because the Church's greatest need is not a new generation of untouchable religious celebrities.
It is a generation of disciples who know the voice of their Shepherd.
People who can distinguish truth from manipulation.
People who love Scripture enough to examine what they hear.
People who refuse to exchange the freedom of the Gospel for spiritual intimidation.
People who understand that Christian leadership is a sacred responsibility, not a license to dominate.
And people who remember that even the most gifted servant is still only a servant.
There is something especially beautiful about the way John the Baptist expressed the heart of faithful ministry.
John 3:30 says:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
John was not one of the Twelve apostles, but his words express an attitude every Christian minister should embrace.
More of Jesus.
Less of self.
More of His truth.
Less of personal glory.
More disciples who know Christ.
Fewer people trapped in the orbit of a religious personality.
Imagine what would happen if that became the heartbeat of our churches.
Imagine leaders who were more concerned about people's salvation than their own reputation.
Imagine ministries where questions were answered with Scripture rather than threats.
Imagine churches where wounded believers were treated with compassion instead of being told to remain silent.
Imagine Christians who were so grounded in the Gospel that no title, prophecy, or impressive performance could easily pull them away from Christ.
That kind of spiritual maturity is worth praying for.
Worth teaching.
Worth sacrificing for.
Worth supporting.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality cult.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to claim authority over your conscience.
But to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, recognize the beauty of the Gospel, grow in discernment, and walk more faithfully with Jesus Christ.
Our heart is to reach the person who is questioning everything.
The believer who is spiritually exhausted.
The Christian who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
The family member who has drifted from faith.
The seeker who wants to know whether Jesus is truly different from the people who have misrepresented Him.
And the disciple who knows that spiritual growth requires more than an occasional inspirational message.
It requires consistent nourishment in God's Word.
We want biblical resources to remain accessible to people who need them.
Including those who cannot afford to pay.
But reaching more people, preparing resources, sustaining ministry efforts, and expanding this work requires practical support.
Instead, consider it a voluntary ministry offering—an opportunity to support additional Gospel-centered discipleship and outreach.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You do not have to give money to earn His blessing.
These products are not the Gospel.
They cannot replace Scripture, prayer, Christian fellowship, or a living relationship with Jesus.
They are simply additional resources and reminders that can accompany a life of faith.
But because someone may be struggling with the very questions we have discussed.
Someone may be trapped under manipulative spiritual authority.
Someone may have been taught that questioning a leader means questioning God.
Someone may be walking away from Christianity because they have confused the failures of human beings with the character of Jesus.
But before you leave, I want to ask you something.
And I hope you will answer from the heart.
Do you believe God still appoints apostles today, or do you believe the foundational apostolic office ended with the first generation of Christ's witnesses?
More importantly, what biblical passage has shaped your conviction?
Not to attack another believer.
Not to win an argument.
But to help one another search the Scriptures with humility and courage.
Let the conversation become a place where truth is pursued, wounded people are treated with compassion, and Jesus is honored above every human reputation.
Because someday, every ministry title will lose its earthly significance.
Every platform will become silent.
Every applause-filled auditorium will empty.
Every earthly reputation will face the judgment of God.
And what will matter is not how many people called us powerful.
It will be whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
Whether we trusted His grace.
Whether we remained faithful to His truth.
Whether our lives bore witness to the Savior who died and rose again.
The apostle Paul understood this.
He did not end his life asking the Church to worship his legacy.
He pointed believers toward the Lord he had served.
And that is where this conversation must end.
Not with the glory of apostles.
Not with fear of false apostles.
Not with endless arguments about titles.
But with the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
The One who called sinners.
The One who restored Peter after his denial.
The One who confronted Saul on the road to Damascus and transformed a persecutor into a preacher of the Gospel.
The One who still calls people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The One who can restore your faith even after someone misused His name.
The One who can forgive your pride, heal your wounds, correct your errors, and teach you to follow Him again.
Perhaps you have spent years looking for someone with enough spiritual authority to make you feel safe.
But your ultimate security was never meant to rest in a human title.
It rests in the Savior who laid down His life for His sheep.
So test the teachings.
Examine the Scriptures.
Honor faithful leaders without idolizing them.
Reject manipulation without rejecting Christ.
Remain teachable.
Remain humble.
Remain anchored in the Gospel.
And above all, follow Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that someone falsely claimed to be an apostle.
It would be spending your life defending the authority of a human messenger while missing the voice of the Savior who came to rescue you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS MASTURBATION REALLY A SIN… OR HAVE CHRISTIANS BEEN CONDEMNING SOMETHING THE BIBLE NEVER ACTUALLY FORBIDS?
paragraphs: IS MASTURBATION REALLY A SIN… OR HAVE CHRISTIANS BEEN CONDEMNING SOMETHING THE BIBLE NEVER ACTUALLY FORBIDS?
The uncomfortable truth about sexual desire, secret habits, lust, shame, and the grace of Jesus Christ—because sometimes the greatest spiritual battle is the one nobody knows you're fighting.
There is a question millions of Christians have whispered in prayer but would never dare ask in church.
A question that has followed some believers from adolescence into adulthood. From their bedrooms into their marriages. From moments of temptation into moments of worship.
“God… is masturbation actually a sin?”
And perhaps the more frightening question is this:
“If I keep doing it, does that mean something is wrong with my relationship with You?”
Some people have cried after doing it.
Some have promised God they would never do it again, only to find themselves struggling days later.
Others have stopped feeling guilty altogether and wonder whether that means they have found freedom—or simply stopped listening to their conscience.
And then there are those who have searched their Bibles, looking for one unmistakable verse that says masturbation is sinful.
They couldn't find it.
Because here is something every Christian deserves to know:
The Bible never directly names masturbation or explicitly declares the physical act itself sinful.
That statement may surprise you.
It may even make you uncomfortable.
But if we are going to honor Scripture, we must be honest about what God has revealed—and equally honest about what He has not explicitly said.
We cannot manufacture a commandment and call it holiness.
But neither can we assume that everything Scripture does not specifically name is automatically pleasing to God.
And somewhere between those two dangerous extremes is a conversation that desperately needs to happen.
Not in the language of humiliation.
Not through fear disguised as discipleship.
But beneath the searching light of God's Word, where truth and grace meet.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make ashamed people feel more ashamed.
He came to save sinners, expose darkness, forgive transgression, and transform hearts.
And if this subject has been a secret battlefield in your life, please keep reading.
There is more at stake here than a private physical habit.
There is also more grace available than you may have imagined.
Let's begin with a man whose story has been used for generations to condemn masturbation.
His name was Onan.
In Genesis 38:8–10, Onan was commanded to fulfill his family responsibility toward his deceased brother's widow, Tamar, in the ancient context of preserving his brother's family line.
Instead, he deliberately prevented conception while having intercourse with her.
God judged his conduct.
For centuries, some Christians have pointed to this account as proof that masturbation is sinful.
But there is a serious problem with that interpretation.
Onan was not masturbating.
The text describes intercourse and deliberate withdrawal. His wrongdoing occurred in a context of refusing his familial obligation while exploiting the sexual relationship.
Genesis 38 does not teach that masturbation itself is the sin for which Onan was judged.
To claim otherwise is to make the passage say something it does not say.
And God's Word deserves better than that.
But before anyone celebrates and declares the entire question settled, we need to listen to something Jesus said.
Something far more penetrating than a discussion about outward behavior.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus teaches:
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Notice what Jesus does.
He moves the conversation from the visible act to the invisible intention.
From what people can observe to what God already sees.
The Greek expression in Matthew 5:28 includes the words:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn
In this context, the phrase communicates looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her.
The verb epithymeō can refer broadly to desire. Desire itself is not always sinful; context determines its moral character.
Here, Jesus is confronting sexually covetous desire directed toward another person.
He is not teaching that every involuntary attraction is adultery.
He is exposing the deliberate cultivation of lust.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because sexual attraction is not automatically sin.
Experiencing arousal is not automatically sin.
Having a sexual body is not evidence that something is spiritually defective about you.
God created human beings as embodied creatures.
Genesis 1:27 declares that humanity was created in God's image, and Genesis 1:31 describes God's creation as very good.
Sexuality is not an embarrassing accident God forgot to remove from humanity.
But like every good aspect of human life, sexual desire can become distorted.
A person can move from experiencing attraction to deliberately feeding lust.
From recognizing beauty to mentally possessing another human being.
From experiencing a physical urge to building an inner world of sexual fantasy that treats people as objects rather than neighbors made in God's image.
And this is where the question becomes painfully personal.
When you masturbate, what is happening in your heart?
Are you intentionally entertaining sexual fantasies that violate the love, faithfulness, and purity Scripture calls you to pursue?
Are you using pornography?
Are you imagining someone else's spouse?
Are you feeding desires that make it harder to honor real people?
Are you using sexual stimulation as your only refuge whenever loneliness, anxiety, rejection, or sadness becomes overwhelming?
Or are you dealing with a physical experience that does not involve pornography, deliberate lust, or an obviously harmful pattern?
Those situations should not be carelessly treated as identical.
Scripture clearly condemns lustful intent and sexual immorality. It does not directly settle every possible circumstance involving masturbation.
Faithfulness requires us to preserve that distinction.

Some Christians conclude that masturbation should always be avoided because they believe it cannot be separated from lust, self-focused sexual gratification, or sexuality outside God's intended covenant of marriage.
Others believe the act itself is not necessarily sinful when separated from lust, pornography, compulsive behavior, and violations of conscience.
These positions differ, and sincere believers have reached different conclusions.
The Bible gives us important moral principles, but it does not provide a direct verse resolving every part of this debate.
So we should be cautious about declaring every Christian who disagrees with us rebellious against God.
Yet we should be just as cautious about using biblical silence to excuse something that is damaging our spiritual life.
Because Paul wrote something that should make every believer examine the habits that quietly govern them.
In 1 Corinthians 6:12, he says:
“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.
The Greek expression behind “I will not be dominated” is:
οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος
ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos
The language concerns being brought under another's power or authority.
Paul is addressing Christian freedom and the danger of being mastered by something.
And that raises an uncomfortable question.
Even when you believe you are free to do something, has that thing begun to control you?
Can you choose not to engage in it?
Can you face stress without automatically reaching for it?
Can you experience loneliness without needing immediate sexual relief?
Can you put away pornography if it has become part of your routine?
Can you recognize when a habit is damaging your sleep, responsibilities, relationships, or spiritual attention?
These are not questions designed to humiliate you.
They are questions about freedom.
And freedom is not simply the ability to satisfy every desire.
Sometimes freedom is the ability to say no to something you strongly want.
But hear this carefully.
A recurring sexual urge is not, by itself, proof of addiction.
Neither does every repeated behavior demonstrate that someone is enslaved.
Human sexuality is complicated. Habits, emotional needs, physical development, stress, and personal convictions can all influence behavior.
Christians should avoid labeling themselves spiritually ruined or clinically addicted simply because they experience sexual desire.
At the same time, when a pattern becomes difficult to control and causes significant distress or harm, seeking wise pastoral support or qualified professional help can be an act of courage.
Not defeat.
And there is another verse we need to handle carefully.
First Thessalonians 4:3–5 says that God's will includes sanctification, abstaining from sexual immorality, and learning to live in holiness and honor rather than uncontrolled passion.
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is:
πορνεία — porneia
In the New Testament, porneia refers broadly to prohibited sexual conduct.
But we must not pretend the word automatically names every sexual behavior we personally disapprove of.
The passage calls believers to holiness and sexual integrity. It does not specifically mention masturbation.
What it does establish is that our sexual lives matter to God.
Our bodies are not spiritually irrelevant.
Our desires are not exempt from discipleship.
And Christian holiness is not simply a matter of asking, “How much can I get away with?”
A better question is:
“Lord, how can I honor You with my body, my thoughts, my relationships, and the desires I don't fully understand?”
That question changes the conversation.
Because now we are no longer searching for a technical loophole.
We are seeking Christ.
And perhaps that is where this subject becomes most difficult.
Because for some people, masturbation is not merely about sexual desire.
Sometimes it is about loneliness.
Sometimes it begins after another rejection.
Sometimes it happens when the house is quiet and the person who smiles at everyone during the day finally has to face the emptiness waiting at night.
Sometimes it becomes a familiar response to stress.
A temporary escape from anxiety.
A momentary distraction from grief.
A substitute for comfort when genuine emotional connection feels impossibly far away.
And sometimes it is simply connected to sexual arousal, without the deeper emotional meaning people assume must be present.
We need enough compassion to recognize the difference.
Imagine a young man sitting on the edge of his bed after another difficult night.
His phone is beside him.
His Bible is across the room.
He has prayed the same prayer so many times that the words almost feel worn out.
“Jesus, I'm sorry.”
He remembers the sermon about purity.
He remembers the promise he made last Sunday.
He remembers how sincere he felt during worship.
And now, in the silence, a terrible thought enters his mind.
“Maybe I'm not a real Christian.”
That thought is more destructive than many people realize.
Because shame has a way of turning a struggle into an identity.
Instead of saying, “I have done something I believe was wrong,” a person begins saying, “I am disgusting.”
Instead of seeking God, they hide from Him.
Instead of confessing honestly, they perform spiritual confidence in public while quietly collapsing in private.
But the Gospel does not teach that your worth is measured by the absence of sexual temptation.
Nor does it teach that one failure places you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
Ouden ara nyn katakrima
The word katakrima refers to condemnation, a judicial verdict against someone.
Paul's declaration is not that sin has suddenly become harmless.
It is that those who belong to Christ are no longer under condemnation because of His saving work.
That is breathtaking.
Because Christianity does not offer salvation through flawless sexual performance.
It offers salvation through Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who bore sin.
The One who calls people to repentance.
The One whose grace does not merely cover our past but begins transforming how we live.
And we must never confuse grace with permission to cultivate sin.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts that misunderstanding directly.
Paul asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may increase.
His answer is emphatic.
Absolutely not.
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes a new life possible.
But neither should we confuse holiness with constant self-hatred.
Conviction draws us toward repentance. Crushing shame often tempts us to run away from the very Savior we need.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers wanted to make her sin the final word over her life.
Jesus refused to participate in their merciless spectacle.
Yet He did not celebrate her wrongdoing.
His words held both mercy and moral seriousness:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
There is an important textual note here: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, so its textual history is disputed.
We should acknowledge that honestly rather than build an entire doctrine on a disputed passage.
Nevertheless, the combination of Christ's mercy and His call to repentance is firmly established throughout the New Testament.
And it matters here.
Because Jesus does not require you to pretend sin is harmless in order to receive mercy.
And He does not require you to believe you are hopeless in order to take holiness seriously.
He invites you into the light.
Not so you can be destroyed by exposure.
But so you can stop living a double life.
Perhaps you have spent years asking, “Is masturbation always a sin?”
And perhaps the most faithful answer begins with admitting what Scripture does and does not say.
The physical act is not directly named or universally prohibited in an explicit biblical command.
However, the lust, pornography, sexual objectification, unfaithfulness, or loss of self-control that may accompany it can involve clear moral concerns.
Whether masturbation without those elements is itself sinful remains an area of disagreement among Christians.
A believer's conscience matters, too.
Romans 14:23 teaches that acting against one's faith is sinful, within Paul's discussion of disputed practices.
That does not mean every feeling of guilt proves that God has forbidden something.
Conscience can be informed by Scripture, but it can also be shaped by misinformation, fear, and unhealthy teaching.
A tender conscience needs biblical formation, not endless panic.
If you are convinced before God that a behavior is wrong, do not force yourself to violate that conviction.
But also allow Scripture, prayer, wise counsel, and careful reflection to help you distinguish genuine conviction from unsupported condemnation.
And if you believe the act is not inherently sinful, do not use that conclusion to dismiss the clear biblical commands concerning lust, faithfulness, holiness, and self-control.
Christian maturity is not measured by how quickly we can win an argument about sexual ethics.
It is revealed in how sincerely we submit our whole lives to Christ.
There is a beautiful prayer in Psalm 139:23–24:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!”
In Hebrew, the opening plea is:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
Choqreni El, veda levavi
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
That prayer is not an invitation to obsessive self-accusation.
It is a surrender to God's truthful and loving examination.
David is asking God to reveal what needs correction and to lead him into the everlasting way.
And maybe that is the prayer we need more than another argument.
“Lord, search me.”
“Show me where my desires have become disordered.”
“Show me where I have confused natural temptation with deliberate sin.”
“Show me where I have justified something harmful.”
“Show me where religious shame has taught me to fear You instead of trusting Your mercy.”
“Teach me to live with a clean conscience and a surrendered heart.”
That is not weakness.
That is discipleship.
And if pornography is part of your struggle, do not minimize its power to shape how you see people.
Repeatedly consuming sexually explicit material can reinforce habits of objectification and distorted expectations, and for some people it becomes a difficult pattern to change.
But recovery is not accomplished merely by promising harder.
Sometimes you need to change what you access.
Sometimes you need to remove sources of temptation.
Sometimes you need an accountability relationship with someone trustworthy and mature.
Sometimes you need counseling to address emotional patterns beneath the behavior.
And sometimes you need to stop interpreting every difficult day as proof that God has abandoned you.
Because spiritual growth is often a process.
Sanctification is real.
So is struggle.
Philippians 1:6 expresses Paul's confidence that God, who began a good work among the Philippian believers, would bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
That promise is not a guarantee that every habit will disappear immediately.
It is a reason to place our confidence in God's faithfulness rather than our own perfection.
You may have prayed sincerely and still struggled.
You may have experienced genuine progress and then encountered temptation again.
You may be married and still wrestle with sexual habits you don't understand.
You may be single and tired of being told that your desires make you spiritually inferior.
You may even be someone who has never struggled with this issue but has judged those who do.
Wherever you find yourself, the Gospel calls you to something deeper than either permissiveness or condemnation.
It calls you to truth spoken in love.
It calls you to humility.
It calls you to repentance wherever repentance is needed.
And it calls you to remember that no private sexual question should become greater than the Savior who came to redeem the whole person.
This is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because every action is acceptable.
Not because repentance no longer matters.
Not because Jesus came to make us comfortable with whatever controls us.
But because Jesus rewrites the stories that sin, shame, secrecy, and despair try to make permanent.
The cross tells us that sin is serious.
The empty tomb tells us that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And the grace of God teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live transformed lives, as Titus 2:11–14 explains.
This is not a Gospel of pretending.
It is a Gospel of redemption.
And perhaps someone reading this right now has been carrying years of unnecessary terror.
You were told that every sexual feeling was filthy.
That every physical response was rebellion.
That God was constantly disappointed in your existence.
And you believed it.
You learned to hide.
You learned to apologize for being human.
You learned to imagine God as someone waiting for another reason to reject you.
But the Bible does not ask you to hate the body God created.
It asks you to honor God with your body.
There is a profound difference.
And perhaps someone else reading this has been using biblical silence to avoid examining a pattern that is clearly harming them.
You know what pornography has been doing to your thoughts.
You know how often you have chosen fantasy over genuine connection.
You know when a desire has become an excuse to neglect responsibilities or violate commitments.
And you have been telling yourself that because the Bible does not mention masturbation by name, there is nothing to examine.
But Christian freedom is not a hiding place from the truth.
Jesus calls you to walk in the light.
Both readers need grace.
Both readers need honesty.
Both readers need Christ.
And neither needs another human being pretending to know more than Scripture reveals.
Before you leave this article, consider something.
If a struggling believer came to you tonight, ashamed and afraid to ask this very question, what kind of Christian would you be?
Would you immediately condemn them?
Would you dismiss every concern they raised?
Or would you open Scripture with them, tell the truth carefully, and help them move closer to Jesus?
Because the way we handle questions like this reveals something about our understanding of the Gospel.
Truth without love can become cruelty.
Love without truth can become permission to remain in bondage.
But truth spoken in love can become an instrument of restoration.
And restoration is what Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim.
If this article challenged something you believed, helped you understand Scripture more accurately, or gave you courage to seek God honestly, please don't let the conversation end in silence.
You do not need to disclose intimate details publicly.
Your dignity matters.

And if you have a testimony of God's grace helping you overcome shame, destructive habits, or spiritual confusion, consider sharing what you are comfortable sharing. Your experience may help another believer realize that they are not alone.
But there is something else I want to share with you.

Every article we publish, every biblical question we explore, every resource we prepare, and every soul we hope to encourage represents a continuing commitment to make the truth of Jesus Christ accessible.
The Gospel itself is not for sale.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
But generosity can be one meaningful expression of worship when it is freely offered, responsibly stewarded, and directed toward work that honors Christ.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctance or compulsion.
That principle matters deeply to us.
It helps make room for more biblical conversations that people are often afraid to have.
More truth.
More encouragement.
More opportunities to point wounded hearts toward Jesus.
Because we want this community to be more than an audience.
We want it to be a place where people grow in biblical understanding, encourage one another, and keep returning to the transforming truth of Christ.
You can still pray for the ministry.
You can still invite someone to read Scripture.
You can still encourage a struggling believer.
And you can still help carry the message of Christ into places we may never personally reach.
You are not saved by winning every battle against temptation.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us to turn from sin, grow in holiness, and walk in the light.
Do not let religious shame write a verdict Scripture never pronounced.
Do not let personal desire silence a command Scripture clearly gives.
Do not turn a disputed question into a weapon against other believers.
And do not allow this private struggle, whatever its circumstances, to become the entire definition of your spiritual life.
Your deepest identity is not found in a habit.
Not in an urge.
Not in a failure.
Not in a perfect record.
For those who belong to Jesus Christ, identity is rooted in the Savior who died and rose again.
So tonight, when the room becomes quiet and the questions return, you do not need to invent certainty where Scripture has not given it.
You can open your Bible.
You can pray honestly.
You can seek wise counsel.
You can turn away from what you know is sinful.
You can examine what remains uncertain with humility.
And you can approach the throne of grace with confidence in the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Because the most important question is not merely whether you have ever struggled with sexual desire.
It is whether you are willing to bring your whole life—including the parts you have hidden—under the loving lordship of Christ.
The secret you were afraid would make Jesus turn away may become the very place where you finally learn to stop hiding and walk in His light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY PUT BRACKETS AROUND HER STORY… BUT DID SOMEONE TRY TO REMOVE THE MERCY OF JESUS?
paragraphs: THEY PUT BRACKETS AROUND HER STORY… BUT DID SOMEONE TRY TO REMOVE THE MERCY OF JESUS?

Why John 7:53–8:11 is missing from some ancient manuscripts, why modern Bibles warn readers about it, and what the woman caught in adultery can teach us about truth, grace, repentance, and the Savior who refuses to leave sinners unchanged.
Imagine opening your Bible to one of the most unforgettable encounters ever associated with Jesus Christ.
A woman is standing in the middle of an angry crowd.
Her shame has become public entertainment.
Her accusers are holding the Law over her head.
Death is being discussed as though her life means nothing.
And Jesus is there.
Then you notice something strange.
There are brackets around the entire story.
Or perhaps a footnote beneath the passage says:
“The earliest manuscripts do not include John 7:53–8:11.”
Wait.
What?
One of the most beloved accounts of mercy in the Bible comes with a warning that it may not have been part of John's original Gospel?
Was something removed?
Did someone tamper with Scripture?
Are modern Bible translators trying to erase the compassion of Jesus?
Or is there something much deeper happening here—something every Christian who truly loves the Word of God needs to understand?
Because this is not merely a question about eleven verses.
It is a question about whether we love the Bible enough to examine its history honestly.
Whether our faith can withstand difficult evidence.
And whether we are willing to distinguish what we desperately want a passage to say from what the evidence actually allows us to claim.
But there is another question hiding beneath the controversy.
If you had been standing in that courtyard, watching a terrified woman surrounded by people ready to condemn her, whose face would you have recognized?
The woman's?
The accusers'?
Or perhaps both?
Stay with me.
Because before we reach the end, we are going to confront something far more personal than brackets on a printed page.
We are going to confront the frightening possibility that we can defend the Bible with our mouths while resisting the very grace and holiness it reveals.
And that should make every one of us examine our hearts.
The passage traditionally known as the woman caught in adultery is found in John 7:53–8:11. Scholars often call it the Pericope Adulterae, meaning the passage about the adulterous woman.
The story begins with Jesus teaching in the temple.
Religious leaders bring before Him a woman who has allegedly been caught committing adultery.
They place her in the center of the gathering.
Not privately.
Not gently.
In front of everyone.
Then they challenge Jesus.
The King James Version records their accusation:
“Now Moses in the law commanded us, that such should be stoned: but what sayest thou?” (John 8:5, KJV).
The text immediately explains that their question was a trap. They were seeking grounds to accuse Jesus.
And that detail matters.
Because the woman is not the only person being examined in this encounter.
Jesus Himself is being tested.
The accusers appear to be interested in justice, but the narrative exposes their ulterior motive.
They want to use this woman's situation against Him.
Notice something else.
Where is the man?
The Law of Moses addressed both parties involved in adultery. Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 make that clear.
Yet the account presents only the woman.
We are not told what happened to the man, whether he escaped, or why he was absent. We should not invent details Scripture does not provide.
But we can recognize the troubling imbalance in the scene.
One person stands exposed.
Others stand ready to condemn.
And Jesus refuses to be manipulated.
Then comes one of the most mysterious moments in the entire account.
Jesus bends down and writes on the ground.
What did He write?
The names of the accusers?
Their hidden sins?
A passage from the Law?
Perhaps a reference to Jeremiah 17:13, where those who forsake the Lord are associated with writing in the earth?
These interpretations have been suggested across Christian history.
But the passage does not tell us what Jesus wrote.
And sometimes faithfulness to Scripture means having the humility to say, “We do not know.”
The Greek verb used for His writing is κατέγραφεν (kategraphen), from katagraphō, meaning to write down or inscribe.
It does not reveal the content of His writing.
Whatever Jesus wrote, the narrative directs our attention toward what He said.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” (John 8:7, KJV).
The Greek reads:
Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτος ἐπ᾽ αὐτὴν βαλέτω λίθον.
Ho anamartētos hymōn prōtos ep’ autēn baletō lithon.
A close rendering is:
“Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”
Consider the force of that moment.
Jesus does not declare adultery righteous.
He does not pretend the Law is meaningless.
He exposes the moral seriousness of those who are eager to carry out judgment while standing under judgment themselves.
The passage should not be twisted into the claim that no human court may ever punish wrongdoing or that Christians must never exercise moral discernment.
Its setting is a hostile attempt to trap Jesus through a public accusation.
His response exposes the accusers and their motives.
And then the stones begin to lose their power.
One by one, the accusers leave.
The woman remains.
Jesus asks whether anyone has condemned her.
She answers that no one has.
And He says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV).
Read that again.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
But do not stop there.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy.
And a summons to holiness.
Compassion.
And a call to change.
This is why so many believers treasure this account.
Yet now we must face the difficult historical question.
Why do modern Bibles place brackets around it?
The answer is not that translators suddenly decided they disliked the story.
It is not evidence of a secret campaign to erase Jesus' mercy.
And it is not proof that modern Christianity has abandoned the Bible.
The brackets exist because of a genuine textual question.
The New Testament was originally written in Greek, and we do not possess the original handwritten manuscripts produced by its authors.
What we have are thousands of Greek manuscripts and additional ancient translations, quotations, and other witnesses.
These manuscripts were copied across centuries.
Most textual differences are small—spelling variations, word order, or other changes that do not substantially alter meaning.
Some differences, however, concern larger passages.
John 7:53–8:11 is one of the most important examples.

Two of the earliest substantial surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, both dating to the fourth century, do not contain this account in its familiar location.
Other early Greek witnesses also omit it.
The surviving manuscript evidence is not uniform, however.
The passage appears in many later Greek manuscripts and became deeply established in the Christian tradition.
And here is a particularly important detail.
In some manuscript traditions, this story appears in different locations.
Some witnesses place it elsewhere in John.
Others associate it with Luke, including a location after Luke 21:38.
That movement is significant.
When a passage appears in different positions across manuscript traditions, it can suggest that scribes were preserving a story whose placement in the Gospel text was uncertain.
This does not automatically tell us who first told the story.
It does not prove that the events never happened.
But it is important evidence when asking whether the passage originally stood where we now read it.

The earliest surviving Greek manuscript evidence and the passage's variable placement are major reasons why many textual scholars conclude that John 7:53–8:11 was probably not part of the original composition of the Fourth Gospel.
That is a serious conclusion.
And Christians should not be afraid to understand it.
Because loving Scripture does not require pretending that difficult manuscript evidence does not exist.
It requires handling that evidence truthfully.
Now consider another important witness.
The fourth-century Christian writer Didymus the Blind appears to refer to a story about a woman accused of sin before Jesus, although the details and textual relationship require caution.

And Augustine, writing in the late fourth and early fifth centuries, discussed the account and suggested that some people had removed it from their copies because they feared it might encourage adultery.
Augustine's observation is historically fascinating.
It shows that the passage was known and that its transmission was already being discussed in antiquity.
But we must be careful.
Augustine's explanation for why some copies lacked the story is not, by itself, proof that the passage originally belonged to John and was subsequently removed.
A historical explanation offered by an ancient writer is evidence of what that writer believed, not automatic confirmation of the events he proposed.
This distinction matters.
