We should not replace one unsupported conspiracy with another merely because the second sounds more favorable to our expectations.
The evidence is complex.
And faithfulness requires honesty.
So what about the famous story itself?
Could Jesus actually have encountered this woman?
Could the event preserve an authentic memory from His ministry, even if it was not originally written by John?
Some scholars consider that possible.
Others are more skeptical.
The surviving evidence does not allow us to establish the episode's historicity with certainty.
That is why we should distinguish two questions that are often confused.
Did this account originally belong in the Gospel of John?
And did the event described actually happen?
Those are not identical questions.
A story could preserve an early historical memory without having been written by the author of the Gospel in which it later appeared.
But possibility is not proof.
Christians do not honor Jesus by claiming more certainty than the evidence supports.
And here is something many people miss.
The mercy of Jesus does not depend on the authenticity of this one disputed passage.
Even if John 7:53–8:11 was not part of John's original Gospel, the compassion, forgiveness, and transforming authority of Christ remain firmly established in undisputed New Testament passages.
Look at Luke 7:36–50.
A woman known as a sinner approaches Jesus in tears.
Others look at her with contempt.
Jesus speaks of forgiveness and faith.
Look at Luke 15.
Jesus tells of a father who welcomes his repentant, lost son.
Look at Luke 19:1–10.
Zacchaeus, a tax collector despised by many, encounters Jesus and responds with a transformed life.
Look at Mark 2:15–17.
Jesus shares a table with tax collectors and sinners, explaining that He came to call sinners.
Look at John 3:17.
God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through Him might be saved.
And look at Romans 8:1.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV).
That truth does not hang on a disputed textual passage.
It stands on the Gospel itself.
But there is something even more important.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel better about remaining guilty.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins.
He died and rose again.
The cross is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross reveals how seriously God takes sin—and how astonishingly far His love goes to redeem sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that we were innocent.
Not that our choices never mattered.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that Jesus Christ came to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
Now return to the woman in the disputed passage.
Think about what makes this story so emotionally powerful.
She is standing in the center of a crowd.
Her failure is known.
Her future is uncertain.
The people surrounding her seem to know everything about her worst moment.
And nothing about her tears.
We are not told her name.
We are not told her family circumstances.
We are not told what happened to her afterward.
We are not even told whether she obeyed Jesus' final instruction.
And those silences should remain silences.
But perhaps the account unsettles us because we recognize something of ourselves in that courtyard.
Maybe your sin was never exposed publicly.
Maybe nobody gathered around you with stones.
Maybe your shame has never appeared on a screen, in a church meeting, or in a conversation behind your back.
But you know what it feels like to remember something you wish you could undo.
A relationship you damaged.
A betrayal you concealed.
A habit you promised God you would abandon.
A season when you knew the truth and still chose what was wrong.
Or perhaps you have been the person holding the stone.
You knew someone else's failure.
You repeated their story.
You enjoyed being right more than you desired their restoration.
You called it discernment.
But somewhere along the way, compassion disappeared.
And maybe the person who needs repentance today is not the one you have been judging.
Maybe it is you.
That is a hard thought.
I know.
Because it is easier to study a crowd from two thousand years ago than to recognize the crowd inside our own hearts.
It is easier to debate a textual footnote than to confess the bitterness we have been carrying.
It is easier to defend biblical authority online than to obey Christ when He tells us to forgive, repent, tell the truth, and love our enemies.
And that is where this discussion becomes painfully personal.
We can spend hours arguing about whether the woman caught in adultery belongs in John.
But what happens when the undisputed words of Jesus confront us?
What happens when He says, “Repent ye, and believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15)?
What happens when He tells us to forgive?
What happens when He calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him?
What happens when Scripture tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9)?
Do we obey?
Or do we prefer arguments that never require surrender?
Please do not misunderstand.
Textual criticism matters.
Manuscript history matters.
Accurate translation matters.
If we believe Scripture is God's Word, then we should care deeply about what its authors actually wrote.
That is precisely why honest Bible translations alert readers to significant textual questions.
A footnote is not necessarily an attack on faith.
Sometimes it is an act of transparency.
A translator who quietly hides meaningful manuscript uncertainty may leave readers less informed.
A translator who identifies the uncertainty gives readers the opportunity to investigate the evidence.
And that is not something Christians need to fear.
The Greek word ἀλήθεια (alētheia) means truth.
In John 17:17, Jesus prays:
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” (KJV).
The Greek phrase is:
ὁ λόγος ὁ σὸς ἀλήθειά ἐστιν
ho logos ho sos alētheia estin.
“Your word is truth.”
If we belong to the God of truth, we must not defend His Word with exaggerations, fabricated evidence, or claims we cannot substantiate.
Truth does not become more glorious when we decorate it with misinformation.
And faith does not become stronger by refusing to ask hard questions.
Some Christians will continue reading John 7:53–8:11 as part of their received biblical tradition.
Others will read it as an ancient account associated with Jesus while acknowledging that it probably was not part of John's original text.
Those differences deserve thoughtful discussion.
But neither position should become an excuse for contempt toward fellow believers.
The textual question is real.
The evidence should be examined.
And the undisputed Gospel of Jesus Christ remains worthy of our complete trust and obedience.
Now, there is another Greek expression worth remembering.
In John 8:11, the final command attributed to Jesus is:
μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
mēketi hamartane.
“Sin no more,” or “Do not continue sinning.”
The expression is not permission to imagine that believers can attain sinless perfection through their own strength.
Nor should it be softened into a meaningless suggestion.
It is a call to leave sin behind.
And that call is consistent with the wider New Testament.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live godly lives.
Grace does not merely forgive.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace brings us to Christ, and Christ changes the direction of our lives.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is not simply that Jesus can make your past feel less painful.
It is that Jesus Christ can redeem sinners and give them new life.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your shame is not beyond His mercy.
Your past is not a greater authority than the risen Savior.
But His grace is not an invitation to protect the very sin He came to save you from.
It is an invitation to repent.
To surrender.
To stop hiding.
To bring the truth into the light.
To trust the One who died for sinners and rose again.
Maybe you have been avoiding God because you believe He already knows too much about you.
He does know.
Psalm 139 reminds us that nothing about our lives is hidden from Him.
But the Gospel announces something astonishing.
The God who knows the truth about our sin has provided a Savior.
And you do not have to invent a better version of your past before coming to Christ.
You come confessing the truth.
You come with repentance and faith.
You come because Jesus saves sinners.
Not because you have finally become impressive enough to deserve Him.
If this article has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you have been more interested in proving someone wrong than helping them find Christ.
Maybe you have used religious knowledge to hide your own disobedience.
Maybe you have been quietly convinced that your past disqualifies you from ever being loved by God.
Or maybe you have been taught to fear every difficult question about the Bible, as though one manuscript footnote could destroy the risen Lord.
Hear this carefully.
Our confidence is not built on pretending every textual question has an easy answer.
Our confidence rests in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection are proclaimed throughout the New Testament.
And because He is worthy of our trust, we can pursue truth without panic.
We can acknowledge uncertainty without abandoning faith.
We can recognize the seriousness of sin without becoming cruel.
And we can proclaim grace without denying repentance.
That is the kind of discipleship Gospel Warrior exists to encourage.
Not shallow religious excitement that disappears tomorrow.
Not viral arguments that leave hearts unchanged.
But Scripture-centered growth that draws people closer to Jesus Christ.
If you have been searching for a Christian community that takes both biblical truth and personal transformation seriously, I want to invite you to walk with us.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word.
And there is a practical way you can help us continue and expand that mission.
It is a voluntary act of support for a ministry mission you believe is worth sustaining.
For those who choose to give from a heart of worship, that support may be understood as part of their Christian generosity and offering to God.
But let us keep this biblically clear.
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
But a meaningful opportunity to help sustain and expand Christian teaching and discipleship resources.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for reflection, or thoughtful gifts that encourage others in their walk with Christ.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter Scripture, hear the Gospel, and grow as disciples of Jesus.
If that mission matters to you, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
You never know who among your friends has been struggling with doubts about the Bible.
Someone may have encountered the brackets around John 7:53–8:11 and quietly wondered whether Scripture could still be trusted.
Someone may be carrying shame that has kept them away from prayer.
Someone may need to understand that God's grace does not excuse sin but calls us into a new life through Christ.
And someone may need to hear that difficult questions do not have to become the end of faith.
And please, do not leave without joining the conversation.
I want to ask you something personal.

When you read the story of the woman caught in adultery, do you identify more with the woman who needed mercy, the accusers who needed humility, or someone who is still struggling to understand how truth and grace belong together?
Comment honestly.
You can write, “Christ is still healing me,” if you know God is still working in your life.
Or comment, “I want to know His Word,” if this discussion has encouraged you to study Scripture more carefully.
If you need prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.” You do not have to share private details to be welcomed into prayer.

And if you disagree with any of the textual conclusions presented here, you are welcome to explain your reasoning respectfully. Let us be people who love the truth enough to examine evidence and love one another enough to remain gracious.
Because the purpose of studying Scripture is not to win arguments while losing the character of Christ.
It is to know the Lord, understand His Word, and respond in faith and obedience.
Before you close this article, I want you to remember the original question.
Why do some modern Bibles place brackets around the story of the woman caught in adultery?
Because significant ancient manuscript evidence raises serious doubt that John 7:53–8:11 was part of the Gospel's original text.
That is the historically responsible answer.
But here is the greater truth.
No brackets can remove the mercy of Jesus from the undisputed pages of Scripture.
No manuscript debate can erase the cross.
No textual footnote can undo the resurrection.
And no uncertainty about this particular passage changes the Gospel's invitation to repent, believe in Christ, receive forgiveness, and walk in newness of life.
The Bible is not asking you to build your hope on the uncertain placement of one ancient story.
It is calling you to place your hope in the crucified and risen Savior.
So study carefully.
Ask difficult questions.
Reject sensational claims.
Tell the truth about the evidence.
And above all, come to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest question is not whether a printer placed brackets around a passage.
It is whether you will allow the truth of God's Word to confront your sin and lead you to the Savior.
And perhaps the most haunting thing about this entire discussion is this:
You can spend your whole life arguing about the stones in someone else's hands while refusing to surrender the one you are holding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FORGOTTEN MAN WHO HELD THE PEN WHEN GOD GAVE THE WORLD ROMANS
paragraphs: THE FORGOTTEN MAN WHO HELD THE PEN WHEN GOD GAVE THE WORLD ROMANS

His name appears only once in Scripture. He wasn't the apostle. He wasn't the preacher. But hidden inside one of Christianity's most powerful letters is a man whose quiet service still speaks to every believer who has ever wondered, “Does what I do for God really matter?”
There is a man in your Bible whom millions of Christians have read past without ever noticing.
He wasn't one of the Twelve.
He didn't walk on water. He didn't raise the dead. Scripture records no sermon he preached, no miracle he performed, and no church he planted.
Yet his handwriting may have carried some of the most extraordinary words about sin, judgment, mercy, justification, and salvation ever written.
Words that would confront generations of sinners.
Words that would comfort the brokenhearted.
Words that would help shape centuries of Christian theology.
Words that would explain how a holy God can declare guilty people righteous without compromising His justice.
And near the end of that remarkable letter, almost as though someone briefly stepped out from behind the curtain, a man introduced himself.
“I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord.” — Romans 16:22 (KJV)
Read that again.
“I Tertius…”
Not Paul.
Tertius.
Wait.
If Paul wrote Romans, why does another man say he wrote it?
And why would God preserve the name of someone most Christians would never remember?
The answer is more beautiful than a historical curiosity.

Because somewhere in this forgotten man's story is a truth for the mother who serves without recognition, the father who works until his hands ache, the believer who quietly supports ministry, the volunteer nobody thanks, and the Christian who sometimes wonders whether heaven notices the little things.
But before we get to that, we need to understand what actually happened.
The Letter to the Romans is rightly attributed to the apostle Paul.
Romans 1:1 identifies him as its sender: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God.”
And yet Romans 16:22 reveals that Tertius was the one who physically wrote the letter.
There is no contradiction.
In the ancient world, writers commonly employed a secretary, sometimes called an amanuensis, to record correspondence.
Paul was the author of Romans. Tertius was its scribe.
Paul was responsible for the apostolic message. Tertius helped put that message into written form.
The distinction matters.
Tertius was not secretly the theological author of Romans. We have no evidence that he invented Paul's arguments, supplied the doctrine of justification, or independently composed the letter.
Nor does Scripture tell us precisely whether Paul dictated every word, worked from prepared material, or allowed his scribe some limited freedom in expression.
What we do know is enough.
Tertius served in the production of a letter that would outlive both men.
And he left behind one sentence that has survived nearly two thousand years.
The original Greek makes the moment even more striking.
Romans 16:22 reads:
Ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ Τέρτιος ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολὴν ἐν κυρίῳ.
Transliteration:
Aspazomai hymas egō Tertios ho grapsas tēn epistolēn en kyriō.
A close translation is:
“I, Tertius, the one who wrote the letter, greet you in the Lord.”
Notice the phrase ὁ γράψας τὴν ἐπιστολήν (ho grapsas tēn epistolēn).
It means “the one who wrote the letter.”
Here, the natural understanding is that Tertius performed the physical writing.
But something else deserves attention.
He did not merely say, “I wrote this.”
He said, “I greet you in the Lord.”
Those final words matter.
His greeting was not simply a professional signature from a hired secretary.
It was a greeting expressed within the Christian relationship believers shared through Jesus Christ.
Whether Tertius was paid for his work, volunteered his service, or held some other role is not disclosed.
But his greeting places him within the Christian fellowship surrounding Paul.
He wasn't merely a hand holding a pen.
He was a person whose name and greeting were welcomed into the letter.
And suddenly, a quiet man becomes visible.
Think about the setting.
Romans was most likely written in the mid-to-late 50s AD, during Paul's time in Greece, probably in Corinth or its vicinity.

Romans 16:1–2 commends Phoebe, who was associated with the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth. Romans 16:23 mentions Gaius and Erastus, names that also fit the broader Corinthian setting, although not every identification is certain.
Scholars generally understand the letter to have been written before Paul's journey to Jerusalem described in Romans 15:25–26.
We cannot reconstruct the exact room, the hour, or the appearance of Tertius.
Scripture does not tell us whether he was young or old, wealthy or poor, enslaved or free.
Some have speculated about his social standing because Tertius is a Latin name meaning “third,” and numbered names could be used among enslaved and formerly enslaved people.
But that does not prove his status.
We should never turn speculation into biblical biography.
Still, consider what we can reasonably picture.
A letter is being prepared.
Paul is communicating truths that have consumed his life since the risen Christ confronted him.
The message concerns the whole human race.
The guilt of humanity.
The holiness of God.
The righteousness revealed through faith.
The death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
The reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles.
The life of the Spirit.
The mercy of God.
And the transforming power of the Gospel.
Tertius is there, recording the words.
Perhaps he understood immediately how extraordinary the message was.
Perhaps some passages challenged him before they ever challenged Rome.
We don't know.
But imagine hearing this sentence as it was being committed to writing:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23 (KJV)
All.
Not merely the notorious sinner.
Not merely the corrupt official.
Not merely the violent criminal.
All.
The respected religious person.
The generous neighbor.
The person who smiles in public but carries bitterness in private.
The one who knows the language of worship but has quietly wandered away from God.
You.
Me.
Every human being who has ever needed mercy.
And then comes the breathtaking answer.
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 3:24 (KJV)
Freely.
By grace.
Through redemption.
In Christ Jesus.
Do you understand what that means?
God does not declare sinners righteous because they have finally become impressive enough to deserve His acceptance.
He justifies through the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.
The Greek word translated “freely” is δωρεάν (dōrean), carrying the sense of something given without payment by the recipient.
And χάρις (charis) means grace or favor.
This is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
Paul himself confronts that distortion in Romans 6:1–2.
Grace is not God's agreement to leave us unchanged.
Grace is His undeserved favor that brings us to Christ, where forgiveness and a new life are found.
Maybe that is where this story becomes personal.
Because some of us have spent years trying to earn what Christ came to give.
We serve because we are terrified of disappointing God.
We give because we are afraid He will abandon us if we stop.
We smile because we don't want anyone to discover how exhausted we really are.
We call ourselves Christians, yet deep inside, we still behave as though the cross was not enough.
And Romans interrupts that exhausting performance.
It tells the truth about our sin.
Then it points us to a Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
Ouden ara nyn katakrima.
Literally, in its opening thought: “Therefore, now, no condemnation.”
The word κατάκριμα (katakrima) refers to condemnation, a judicial sentence against someone.
Paul is announcing the astonishing security of those who belong to Christ.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because judgment is imaginary.
Not because God has forgotten His holiness.
But because Jesus Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And if you have been carrying the weight of yesterday's failures, hear this carefully.
Your past is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
Your shame is not more powerful than His resurrection.
Your history does not have the authority to overturn what God has accomplished through His Son.
But the promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a blanket declaration that repentance and faith are unnecessary.
The same letter calls people to believe, confess Jesus as Lord, and live in the newness of life that follows union with Him.
This is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement with religious vocabulary.
Not motivational optimism decorated with Bible verses.
Not a transaction in which we purchase God's approval through our religious performance.
It is salvation by God's grace through Jesus Christ, received by faith, producing a life increasingly transformed by the Holy Spirit.
And here is the astonishing part.
The man who physically wrote down these truths is remembered in Scripture for doing something extraordinarily ordinary.
He wrote.
He served.
He contributed to the work entrusted to him.
No dramatic testimony is recorded.
No extraordinary title accompanies his name.
Just Tertius.
The one who wrote the letter.
There is something deeply comforting about that.
Because we live in a world obsessed with being seen.
We measure significance through attention.
We mistake recognition for usefulness.
We sometimes assume that if our names are not announced, our work must not matter.
And even in Christian ministry, that temptation can creep in.
We admire the preacher holding the microphone but overlook the person preparing the room.
We celebrate the missionary traveling across oceans but forget the believers who faithfully pray and give.
We notice the person whose testimony moves thousands but miss the quiet Christian sitting beside a grieving friend.
Yet the body of Christ was never designed to function through one visible person.
Paul explains this beautifully in 1 Corinthians 12.
Different members.
Different functions.
One body.
And the members that appear weaker are indispensable.
That is not a license to romanticize exploitation or demand that faithful people remain invisible.
It is a reminder that usefulness in God's kingdom is not measured by public applause.
Maybe you are a Tertius in somebody else's story.
You helped someone return to church, but nobody knows.
You sent a message at the exact moment a friend was losing hope.
You prayed for a child who still seems far from God.
You gave what you could to support the spread of the Gospel.
You shared a Scripture that someone read silently at midnight.
You encouraged a struggling believer who never told you how much your words mattered.
And sometimes you wonder whether any of it made a difference.
Listen.
We cannot promise that every unseen act will produce a spectacular earthly outcome.
Scripture does not promise that.
But Scripture does assure believers that faithful labor in the Lord is not empty.
“Forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.” — 1 Corinthians 15:58 (KJV)
That promise rests on the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because what matters is not whether the world remembers your name.
What matters is whether your life is being offered faithfully to the Lord.
Tertius gives us a remarkable glimpse of this truth.
Yet we must be careful not to make him the hero of a letter whose great subject is Jesus Christ.
Romans does not exist to celebrate the greatness of its scribe.
It exists to proclaim the Gospel of God concerning His Son.
And the Gospel is far greater than the person holding the pen.
Paul writes:
Not the power of a famous preacher.
Not the power of a gifted writer.
Not the power of a religious organization.
The power of God.
That is why the message can move through imperfect human servants without depending upon their greatness.
The servant may be forgotten.
The Gospel remains.
The messenger may die.
Christ lives.
The ink may fade.
The truth of God's Word endures.
And perhaps this is the most humbling thing about Tertius.
He was close enough to the writing of Romans to leave his greeting in its final chapter.
Yet his name never becomes the center of the story.
It is as though his brief appearance reminds us that God uses real people in the transmission of His Word, and then directs our eyes back to the Savior.
And isn't that what faithful Christian service should do?
Not make people dependent upon our personalities.
Not turn ministry into a monument to ourselves.
Not persuade people that supporting a human organization is the same thing as purchasing God's blessing.
But point them beyond us.
To Christ.
Always to Christ.
There is another detail in Romans that makes this even more beautiful.
Paul did not write as a man who believed he had no need of other believers.
The final chapter is filled with greetings, names, relationships, gratitude, and evidence of shared labor.
Phoebe.
Priscilla and Aquila.
Urbanus.
Tryphena and Tryphosa.
Persis.
Gaius.
Tertius.
These were not interchangeable decorations around Paul's ministry.
They were real people in the network of Christian fellowship and service.
Some labored at great personal cost.
Some opened their homes.
Some carried responsibilities we can only partly reconstruct.
And together, their presence reminds us that the spread of the Gospel has always involved more than the person standing at the front.
God works through His people.
Through voices.
Through hands.
Through hospitality.
Through generosity.
Through teaching.
Through encouragement.
Through writing.
Through sacrificial service.
And yes, through the ordinary believer who decides that the message of Jesus Christ is worth helping others hear.
That brings us to a question more important than whether your name will ever be remembered.
What are you doing with the Gospel that has been entrusted to you?
Not everyone is called to preach publicly.
Not everyone has the resources to finance a large ministry.
Not everyone can travel.
Not everyone can write.
Not everyone can teach.
But every Christian is called to belong to Christ and to live faithfully before Him.
Perhaps your contribution today is repentance.
Perhaps it is forgiving someone.
Perhaps it is returning to prayer after months of spiritual dryness.
Perhaps it is opening your Bible again.
Perhaps it is speaking honestly about the struggle you have hidden behind a carefully maintained smile.
Perhaps it is sharing the Gospel with someone you love.
And perhaps, for some, it is helping sustain a ministry that is committed to making biblical teaching and discipleship resources accessible to more people.
But before we talk about giving, we must remember something essential.
You cannot buy God's favor.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot replace repentance with financial support.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price of redemption.
Romans 3:24 calls justification a gift of grace.
Romans 5:8 reminds us that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Romans 10:9–13 points us toward faith in the risen Lord.
Our giving, therefore, must never be presented as the price of God's acceptance.
It can, however, become a sincere expression of gratitude and partnership in the Gospel.
Paul's teaching in 2 Corinthians 9:7 is clear:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
The same verse teaches that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion.
Not because heaven can be purchased.
Not because God needs your money.
But because the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be proclaimed faithfully, and those who have the means and desire can participate in that work.
Gospel Warrior exists to point people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
Our theme is not simply a memorable phrase.
That is the story of the Gospel.
Sin is real.
Shame is real.
Consequences are real.
But so is the mercy of God.
The cross does not pretend the scandal of human rebellion never happened.
It reveals how seriously God takes sin and how astonishingly He has acted to save sinners through His Son.
The resurrection declares that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And the Holy Spirit transforms believers into people who increasingly reflect their Savior.
That is the message we want more people to encounter.
The exhausted mother scrolling through Facebook after everyone else is asleep.
The father wondering whether his family can ever recover from the damage he caused.
The young person trapped between religious expectations and private temptation.
The believer who knows the language of worship but has forgotten the joy of walking with Jesus.
The person who has avoided church because they are ashamed of what others might discover.
The skeptic who has heard plenty about Christianity but very little about Christ Himself.
They do not need another performance.
They need the truth.
They need the Scriptures opened faithfully.
They need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is found in Jesus, and no one becomes too broken for the Gospel to call them home.
This is why your partnership can matter.
Supporting an online ministry should not replace responsibilities to your family, your local church, or others who depend on you.
Give wisely.
Give freely.
Give because you believe in the work.
And if you are unable to give financially, please understand this without any ambiguity:
You are no less welcome, no less valued, and no less loved by God.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your presence in a community seeking to grow in Christ matters.
These are simply thank-you benefits, not spiritual rewards or promises of divine favor.
More Scripture.
More Christ-centered encouragement.
More biblical discipleship.
More opportunities to help people understand the Gospel.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into deeper study, prayer, obedience, and spiritual maturity.
Because the goal is not merely to make someone feel something for thirty seconds.
The goal is to help people know Jesus Christ, understand His Word, and walk with Him when the emotions of the moment have passed.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen.
Someone may be convinced that their small acts of faithfulness are meaningless.
Someone may be serving quietly while fighting discouragement.
Someone may be struggling with guilt and desperately need to encounter the truth of Romans 8:1.
Someone may need to learn that salvation is not earned by religious performance but found through Jesus Christ.
And someone may discover this message because you chose to place it where they could read it.
For the day you wonder whether your prayers matter.
For the day you begin comparing your calling with someone else's platform.
Come back and remember the man who held the pen.
And I want to ask you something personal.
Not a question designed to make you look spiritual.
A question that invites honesty.
Have you ever felt like a Tertius—doing your best to serve God, yet wondering whether anyone notices?
Maybe you're still fighting.
Maybe you're exhausted.
Maybe you've been faithful in public while quietly falling apart in private.
Maybe you need someone to pray with you.
And if this story has reminded you that Christ can use ordinary people for His purposes, tell us about someone whose quiet faithfulness helped shape your life.
Your testimony might encourage another believer to keep going.
But please don't leave this article thinking the central lesson is simply that you should work harder for God.
That would miss the heart of Romans.
The heart of Romans is not that ordinary people can become extraordinary by trying harder.
The heart of Romans is that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
And from that reconciliation flows a transformed life.
Paul's letter eventually brings us to a magnificent appeal:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” — Romans 12:1 (KJV)
Notice the order.
By the mercies of God.
Before the appeal to surrender comes the announcement of mercy.
Before the call to offer our lives comes the revelation of what God has done through Christ.
We do not surrender to make God merciful.
We surrender because His mercy has reached us.
We do not serve to purchase redemption.
We serve because redemption has changed us.
We do not give to earn salvation.
We give, when able and willing, as one expression of love and gratitude.
And we do not seek recognition as the ultimate reward of faithfulness.
We seek to honor the Lord who first loved us.
Tertius wrote down the letter.
Paul delivered the apostolic message.
But the Savior proclaimed throughout Romans is Jesus Christ.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One in whom there is no condemnation for those who belong to Him.
The One who calls us to repentance, faith, and a new life.
And perhaps, when you open your Bible tonight and read Romans again, you will notice something you missed before.
At the end of a letter that has transformed countless lives, a man briefly introduces himself.
“I Tertius…”
Then he steps back into history.
We are not told what happened to him afterward.
We do not know how long he lived.
We do not know whether he ever imagined that believers nearly two thousand years later would still be reading his name.
And we should not pretend to know what Scripture has left unsaid.
But we do know that his service became part of the history of a letter through which generations have encountered the Gospel.
That is enough to make us grateful.
Not because Tertius was the redeemer.
But because his quiet contribution directs our attention toward the Redeemer.
So tonight, if you feel forgotten, remember that your worth is not determined by the number of people who know your name.
If you feel ashamed, turn to the Christ who receives repentant sinners.
If you feel exhausted, remember that God's grace is not a wage paid to the impressive.
If you feel unqualified, remember that the church is a body of many members, each called to serve according to the gifts and opportunities God provides.
And if you have spent your life trying to prove that you deserve to be loved by God, stop looking to your achievements for the assurance only Christ can give.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Let His Word expose what needs to change.
Let His grace lead you away from sin.
Let His mercy humble you.
Let His resurrection give you hope.
And let your life, whether public or hidden, become an offering of gratitude to the One who saved you.
Because the greatest miracle in the story of Romans is not that a forgotten man held the pen.
It is that the God who is perfectly holy made a way for guilty sinners to be forgiven and brought near through Jesus Christ.
And the greatest thing about your story will never be how many people remember you.
It will be whether your life points them toward Him.
The world may never remember the hands that carried the message—but heaven's greatest treasure is the Savior that message reveals.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU KEEP POSTING ABOUT JESUS… BUT WHEN WAS THE LAST TIME YOU ACTUALLY SAT ALONE WITH HIM?
paragraphs: YOU KEEP POSTING ABOUT JESUS… BUT WHEN WAS THE LAST TIME YOU ACTUALLY SAT ALONE WITH HIM?

Your timeline is full of Scripture. Your stories are full of worship. Your captions tell everyone how much you love God. But there's a question your followers cannot answer—and perhaps you've been afraid to answer it yourself: Does Jesus still have your attention when nobody is watching?
You posted about Jesus this morning.
Maybe it was a Bible verse. Maybe a worship song. Maybe a powerful reminder that God is faithful, that prayer changes things, that Jesus is coming again.
People reacted. Someone commented, “Amen.” Another person shared your post. Perhaps someone even messaged you to say your words were exactly what they needed.
And that matters. Don't misunderstand me.
God can use a simple post to reach a heart you may never meet.
But something happened after you put your phone down.
Or perhaps something didn't happen.

You had time to check who liked your post. Time to see who viewed your story. Time to scroll through someone else's life. Time to answer messages, watch videos, read comments, and return to your notifications more times than you can remember.
But somewhere in the middle of all that activity, there was Someone you never stopped to talk to.
The very Jesus you spent the morning telling everyone about.
And here is the question that might make you uncomfortable enough to keep reading:
What if you've become so busy talking about Jesus that you've slowly stopped talking to Jesus?
Not because you stopped believing.
Not because you deliberately walked away.
But because somewhere along the way, your public expression of faith became more consistent than your private communion with the One who saved you.
And the frightening part?
You can go a long time without noticing the difference.
Because religious activity can make spiritual distance look like spiritual maturity.
You can know how to encourage people while secretly feeling empty.
You can post about peace while your own heart is restless.
You can tell strangers to trust God while quietly carrying burdens you haven't brought before Him.
You can write about prayer without remembering the last time you prayed without rushing.
And you can become very good at describing a relationship that you've stopped intentionally nurturing.
That is not an accusation against every Christian who posts online.
It is an invitation to examine something only God and your own heart can truly see.
And before you assume this message is for somebody else, consider one more question.
If your phone stopped working tonight, would your relationship with Jesus still feel alive tomorrow morning?
Because there is a difference between having Christian content around you and having communion with Christ within your daily life.
One can fill your screen.
Only the other draws you into the presence of the living God.
And Jesus once walked into a home where that difference became painfully clear.
Martha was busy.
Not busy doing something sinful. Not wasting her time on meaningless distractions. She was serving. Preparing. Making sure things were ready.
And Jesus was in her house.
Imagine that.
The Son of God was physically present, and Martha was working hard to honor Him.
Meanwhile, her sister Mary sat at His feet, listening.
Eventually, Martha became frustrated.
She asked Jesus to tell Mary to help her.
And His response remains one of the most tender and confronting moments in Scripture.
“Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.” — Luke 10:41–42, KJV
In the Greek text, Luke describes Martha as περιεσπᾶτο (periespato) in verse 40, a word conveying the idea of being distracted or pulled away by her many preparations.
Then Jesus speaks of the ἀγαθὴν μερίδα (agathēn merida)—the good portion Mary had chosen.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say serving was worthless.
He did not say hospitality was sinful.
He did not condemn Martha for caring about practical responsibilities.
He lovingly corrected a situation in which many concerns had distracted her from what mattered most at that moment: receiving His words.
Martha was serving Jesus.
Mary was listening to Jesus.
And in that moment, Martha needed to remember that being occupied with things for the Lord must never replace attentiveness to the Lord Himself.
Now bring that story into our world.
Your kitchen may not be filled with preparations for an honored guest.
But your phone is filled with notifications.
Your schedule is filled with responsibilities.
Your mind is filled with unfinished conversations, financial worries, family concerns, deadlines, disappointments, and things you cannot control.
And perhaps your social media is filled with Jesus.
Yet your soul is starving for the quiet attention you haven't given Him.
You can be Martha with a smartphone.
Busy defending the faith. Busy posting Scripture. Busy encouraging others. Busy answering questions. Busy maintaining a Christian presence online.
All while the most important relationship in your life receives whatever attention is left over.
And sometimes there is nothing left.
But here is what makes this so personal.
You didn't necessarily intend for it to happen.
You remember when prayer felt different.
When you opened your Bible because you wanted to know God, not because you needed a caption.
When a passage of Scripture confronted you so deeply that you had to stop reading.
When you could sit quietly before the Lord without needing music playing, a camera recording, or someone else knowing what you were doing.
When repentance was more important than appearing spiritually strong.
When worship wasn't something you performed.
It was the response of a heart overwhelmed by grace.
Maybe you remember those days.
Maybe you miss them more than you admit.
Or maybe you have never experienced that kind of personal devotion and have quietly wondered whether your faith is supposed to be more than what you've known.
Either way, this invitation is for you.
Because Jesus did not save you merely to turn you into someone who produces religious content.
He saved you to reconcile you to God.
The apostle Peter describes Christ's suffering with these words:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God…” — 1 Peter 3:18, KJV
Read that final phrase again.
That He might bring us to God.
Not merely to a religious identity.
Not merely to a collection of Christian habits.
Not merely to a platform where we can speak about Him.
To God.
Through His death and resurrection, Jesus opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to the Father.
And sometimes we become so absorbed in the visible activities surrounding Christianity that we neglect the very fellowship with God that Christ died to make possible.
That should stop us in our tracks.
Because the cross was not a marketing strategy.
The empty tomb was not a content opportunity.
The blood of Jesus was not shed so that we could look spiritually impressive before other people.
He gave Himself to redeem sinners, forgive the guilty, reconcile the estranged, and make us His own.
And the Savior who calls us to follow Him also calls us to abide in Him.
In John 15:4, Jesus says:
“Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.” — KJV
The Greek verb is μείνατε (meinate), from μένω (menō), meaning to remain, stay, or abide.
Jesus is not describing an occasional religious performance.
He is describing continuing dependence upon Him.
A branch does not manufacture life by looking productive.
Its fruitfulness depends on remaining connected to the vine.
And this is where the question becomes impossible to ignore.
Are you remaining in Christ—or merely maintaining an image of someone who does?
Because those are not the same thing.
You can build an audience around Jesus without making your audience the measure of your faithfulness to Jesus.
You can receive hundreds of encouraging comments and still need to confess a sin nobody knows about.
You can have a beautifully organized collection of Bible verses and still struggle to obey the passage you read yesterday.
You can know how to sound spiritually mature while privately resisting the Lord's correction.
And yet, please hear this carefully.
The answer is not to abandon every public expression of faith.
The answer is to refuse to let public expression replace private devotion.
There is nothing wrong with sharing Scripture.
There is nothing wrong with Christian pages, ministries, videos, testimonies, or online discipleship.
There is nothing wrong with using technology to proclaim the Gospel.
The apostle Paul rejoiced when Christ was proclaimed, even while recognizing that some preached with deeply flawed motives (Philippians 1:15–18).
The message matters.
And so does the heart of the messenger.
But what happens when the messenger becomes more concerned about being seen as faithful than actually walking faithfully?
Jesus addressed the danger of religious performance directly.
In Matthew 6:5–6, He warned against praying in order to be seen by others. Then He instructed His disciples to pray privately to their Father.
The Greek word ταμεῖόν (tameion) in Matthew 6:6 refers to an inner room or private chamber.
The point was not that God can only be encountered in a particular physical room.
Nor was Jesus forbidding public prayer. Scripture itself contains faithful examples of believers praying together.
He was confronting the desire to use prayer as a performance for human approval.
The same principle reaches into our digital lives.
When you post a Bible verse, is your heart genuinely seeking to honor God?
When you share a testimony, are you grateful for His grace—or secretly dependent on people's reactions to feel spiritually significant?
When you write about holiness, are you also allowing Scripture to confront the hidden areas of your own life?
When you tell others to surrender, what are you still refusing to surrender?
Those questions are uncomfortable.
But they are worth asking.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not open rebellion.
It is becoming comfortable with religious appearances while resisting personal examination.
And there is a passage that should make every person who publicly speaks about Jesus approach that responsibility with humility.
In Matthew 7:22–23, Jesus warns that some will appeal to impressive religious works while lacking a genuine relationship with Him.
His words are sobering:
“And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
This passage does not teach that an exhausted Christian who struggles to maintain a devotional routine has automatically lost salvation.
Nor does it mean that missing prayer on a difficult day proves someone never belonged to Christ.
Jesus is warning against false confidence in religious works apart from genuine allegiance to Him.
That distinction matters.
Because the purpose of this message is not to terrify a struggling believer into thinking salvation depends on perfect daily performance.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
But saving grace does not leave us indifferent to the Savior.
It teaches us to turn away from sin and grow in godliness (Titus 2:11–14).
And genuine faith is not content forever with an appearance of devotion that refuses the reality of obedience.
Perhaps that is why this message hurts.
Not because you don't love Jesus.
But because deep down, you know you have allowed other things to occupy the place your heart once reserved for Him.
You keep telling yourself you'll pray later.
After the work is finished.
After the children are asleep.
After the next video.
After one more message.
After one more scroll.
After life becomes less complicated.
But life keeps moving.
And later keeps becoming tomorrow.
Then tomorrow becomes another week.
And eventually you realize something heartbreaking.
You have spent more time watching other people talk about God than you have spent personally seeking Him.
You know what your favorite preacher said last Sunday.
You know which Christian post went viral.
You know which worship song everyone is sharing.
But you cannot remember the last time you opened the Bible without a notification interrupting you.
And suddenly the question is no longer about social media.
It is about your heart.
What have you been feeding it?
What have you been neglecting?
What have you allowed to become normal?
And what would change if you began giving Jesus the attention you so freely give to everything else?
Maybe the answer begins with a small, painfully honest prayer.
“Lord, I have been distracted.”
Not impressive.
Not eloquent.
Not something you need to post.
Just true.
“Lord, I've been telling others to trust You while struggling to bring my own fears before You.”
“Lord, I've been encouraging people to read their Bibles while neglecting Your Word myself.”
“Lord, I have become more concerned with looking like a strong Christian than admitting how desperately I need Your grace.”
“Lord, forgive me.”
And there, in that place of honesty, something beautiful can begin.
Not because your confession earns forgiveness.
But because the Gospel announces forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
The apostle John writes:
This promise is not permission to treat sin lightly.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and return to the truth.
The Christian life is not sustained by pretending we never drift, never struggle, and never need correction.
It is lived through continuing dependence upon the mercy and faithfulness of God.
And maybe someone reading this needs to hear something very specific.
Jesus is not asking you to manufacture a perfect devotional record before you come to Him.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting in His finished work rather than your religious achievements.
If you have wandered, don't turn your wandering into another excuse to stay away.
If your prayers have become rare, begin praying again.
If Scripture has remained unopened, open it.
If you have been hiding a sin beneath an impressive Christian image, bring it into the light and seek the help you need.
If you have become spiritually exhausted, remember that Christ's invitation is not reserved for people who have everything together.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
Jesus does not promise a life without hardship.
He calls the burdened to Himself.
And there is something profoundly comforting about the fact that the One who knows our hearts completely is also the One who welcomes repentant sinners.
Think about Peter.
He was outspoken.
Confident.
Ready to declare his loyalty to Jesus.
He insisted he would never deny Him.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing the Lord three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memories.
The terrible contrast between what he had publicly promised and what he had privately done.
Peter knew what it meant for his words about Jesus to exceed the faithfulness of his actions.
But that was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter by the Sea of Tiberias.
In John 21, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
The conversation was painful, personal, and restorative.
Peter's failure was not excused.
But neither was it allowed to be the final word over his life.
Grace met him there.
And the same Christ who restored Peter remains the hope of believers who have failed Him.
Not because our failures are harmless.
But because His mercy is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
From denial to restoration.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From spiritual pretense to honest surrender.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending our sin never happened.
Not by declaring repentance unnecessary.
Not by teaching that grace makes obedience optional.
But by saving sinners through His death and resurrection and transforming those who belong to Him.
Perhaps you will simply put your phone down.
Find a quiet place.
Open your Bible.
And say, “Jesus, I want to know You more deeply.”
No audience.
No camera.
No perfectly arranged coffee cup beside an open Bible.
No inspirational caption.
No need to prove anything to anyone.
Just you, coming before the Father through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you will read Psalm 51 and let David's confession teach you how to repent.
Maybe you will read John 15 and consider what it means to abide in Christ.
Maybe you will sit with Luke 10 and recognize yourself in Martha's distractions.
Maybe you will read Romans 8 and remember that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Maybe you will pray for five honest minutes.
Maybe longer.
The number of minutes is not the point.
This is not a competition to see who can spend the most time praying.
And private devotion is not a transaction in which we purchase God's love with our attention.
It is the response of a redeemed heart to the God who loved us first.
The goal is not to build another religious performance behind a closed door.
The goal is to know Christ, hear His Word, trust His promises, confess our sins, and follow Him in ordinary life.
Because a private prayer that nobody applauds can be an expression of genuine faith.
A quiet act of obedience that nobody sees can honor God.
An apology you finally offer.
A temptation you resist.
A person you forgive.
A burden you surrender.
A passage of Scripture you obey even when it costs you something.
These things may never go viral.
But they matter deeply.
And when the time comes to speak about Jesus publicly, your words can flow from a life increasingly shaped by His truth.
You don't have to stop posting about Jesus.
Just don't let posting about Him become a substitute for walking with Him.
Let the Bible verse you share be a verse you are willing to obey.
Let the prayer you post remind you to actually pray.
Let the testimony you tell remain rooted in gratitude rather than a hunger for attention.
Let your platform be a place of service, not a place where you measure your spiritual worth.
And remember that you do not need an audience to be loved by God.
You already have access to the Father through Christ.
That is a privilege no algorithm can give you and no decline in engagement can take away.
And if this article has exposed something in your heart, don't rush past it.
You do not need to write a long public confession or reveal private struggles to strangers.
But perhaps you can take one small, honest step.
And if God has been restoring your relationship with Him, consider sharing a testimony. Your words might encourage another believer who thinks they are the only one struggling.
Not every meaningful spiritual response needs to be public. Some things belong in prayer, trusted Christian fellowship, or pastoral care.
But a sincere word of encouragement can remind someone that they are not walking alone.
And perhaps there is someone in your family, a friend, a discouraged believer, a person drifting from the faith, or even someone who doesn't yet know Christ who needs to read this.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Not because the Gospel needs an algorithm to remain powerful.
But because a simple act of sharing can place biblical encouragement in front of someone who might never have searched for it.
Because the aim of this ministry is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to point people to the Savior.
And that is also why I want to speak openly about something important.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter biblical truth, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and find encouragement in their walk with Jesus.
Behind every article, devotional, teaching resource, and ministry effort is a desire to make the truth of Scripture accessible to more people.
These resources are part of our commitment to making Christian learning and spiritual encouragement available beyond the people who can afford to pay.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding a ministry requires time, resources, and faithful support.
And if Gospel Warrior has genuinely encouraged your walk with Christ, I want to invite you to become part of helping that work continue.
Some Christians may prayerfully choose to include support for a ministry like this within their regular charitable giving or offerings.
But let us be biblically clear.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing rather than pressured.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
In the Greek, ἱλαρὸν δότην (hilaron dotēn) means a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite support.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
And certainly not by claiming that financial support purchases His blessing.
Christ has already accomplished what no amount of money could ever accomplish for us.
Our salvation is His gift.
These products are not substitutes for Scripture or spiritual growth. They are simply additional resources and reminders that can accompany everyday Christian life.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, and grow.
You can still benefit from the free resources we make available.
And your encouragement, prayers, thoughtful comments, and willingness to share sound biblical teaching can also help this work reach others.
It is that you come to know Jesus Christ and continue growing in Him.
Because one day, every notification will fall silent.
The posts you spent hours perfecting will become yesterday's content.
The comments will stop arriving.
The numbers will lose their importance.
The platforms themselves may change beyond recognition.
But Jesus Christ remains the same.
And when you stand before Him, your confidence must not rest in how many people liked your Christian posts, how many articles you shared, or how publicly religious you appeared.
Your hope must rest in the crucified and risen Savior.
The One who bore sin.
The One who conquered death.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The One who forgives, restores, and transforms.
So tonight, before you post another verse telling the world how wonderful Jesus is, perhaps spend a little time alone with Him.
Tell Him what you've been afraid to say.
Confess what you've been trying to hide.
Thank Him for mercy you could never deserve.
Read His Word without trying to turn every insight into content.
Pray for the people who need Him.
And ask Him to make your private life increasingly consistent with the faith you publicly proclaim.
Then, when you return to your screen, share the truth with a heart that remembers why it matters.
Not to impress people.
Not to prove you are holy.
Not to win an argument.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy to be known, loved, obeyed, and proclaimed.
And because someone on the other side of your screen may be longing for the very hope you have found in Him.
Don't become so busy telling the world that Jesus is worth knowing that you forget to spend your own life knowing Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE MARRIED INTO A KINGDOM… AND HER MARRIAGE HELPED TURN HER HUSBAND AGAINST GOD
paragraphs: SHE MARRIED INTO A KINGDOM… AND HER MARRIAGE HELPED TURN HER HUSBAND AGAINST GOD

One royal wedding. Two powerful families. A deadly compromise that spread through generations. And a warning every Christian family needs to hear before the people they love become the people who lead them away from God.
“Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab.” — 2 Chronicles 18:1 (KJV)
The wedding probably looked beautiful.
Two royal families. Two powerful kingdoms. A marriage that promised influence, security, and a future filled with political possibilities.
There may have been celebrations in the palace. Congratulations from important people. Smiles from those who believed this union would make both kingdoms stronger.
But behind the celebration was something far more dangerous than anyone may have wanted to acknowledge.
A family that knew the God of Israel was joining itself to a royal house notorious for rebellion against Him.
And the consequences would eventually reach into the bedrooms of a palace, the graves of murdered brothers, the streets of Jerusalem, and the future of David's royal family.
The bride was Athaliah.
The groom was Jehoram, son of King Jehoshaphat of Judah.
And what began as a royal marriage became part of one of the darkest chapters in Judah's history.
But there is something even more disturbing about this story.
Jehoram did not begin as an outsider who had never heard about God.
He was raised in the royal family of Judah, where the worship of the LORD was part of the kingdom's identity.
His father, Jehoshaphat, had sought the LORD, removed forms of idolatry, and sent teachers throughout Judah to instruct the people in God's Law (2 Chronicles 17:3–9).
Jehoram had inherited a spiritual legacy many people would have considered a blessing.
Yet when he became king, he turned toward the wicked practices of Ahab's house.
And Scripture gives us a chilling explanation.
“For he had the daughter of Ahab to wife.” — 2 Chronicles 21:6 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not because the Bible is saying every man's sin is his wife's fault.
Jehoram was responsible for his own choices. Scripture makes that unmistakably clear.
But because this marriage became one of the channels through which a deeply corrupt royal influence entered Judah's throne.
A marriage meant to strengthen a kingdom helped weaken its faithfulness to God.
And before we judge that ancient king too quickly, perhaps we should ask ourselves a question we would rather avoid.
Have you ever welcomed something into your life because it looked like a blessing, only to discover that it was slowly pulling your heart away from Jesus?
Not everything that opens a door is sent by God.
Not every relationship that promises security will protect your soul.
And not every opportunity that makes your life bigger will make your faith stronger.
Sometimes the most dangerous compromise does not arrive looking like rebellion.
Sometimes it arrives looking like the answer to your prayers.
Jehoshaphat was not a man without faith.
That is what makes this account so painful.
The Bible describes him as a king who sought the LORD and encouraged Judah to walk in God's ways. Yet this same king formed an alliance with Ahab, the king of Israel.
Ahab was no ordinary political partner.
Under his reign, Israel had been led deeper into Baal worship, and his wife Jezebel had supported the persecution of the LORD's prophets (1 Kings 16:30–33; 18:4).
Jehoshaphat should have understood the spiritual danger.
But somewhere between political calculation and royal ambition, he joined himself to Ahab's house.
The Hebrew wording of 2 Chronicles 18:1 is revealing:
וַיִּתְחַתֵּן לְאַחְאָב
Vayyitḥattēn le-Aḥ'av.
It means, in context, that Jehoshaphat formed a marriage alliance with Ahab.
The verb comes from the Hebrew root חתן (ḥ-t-n), associated with marriage and relationships by marriage.
This was more than a diplomatic handshake.
Their royal families were being joined.
The biblical account does not tell us every conversation that led to the marriage, nor does it reveal Jehoshaphat's private motives. We should not invent what Scripture leaves unspoken.
But it does reveal the spiritual danger of his alliance.
When Jehoshaphat later joined Ahab in a military campaign, the prophet Jehu confronted him with a question that still pierces the conscience:
“Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD?” — 2 Chronicles 19:2 (KJV)
That rebuke was spoken about Jehoshaphat's support of Ahab.
It should not be carelessly turned into a command to hate unbelievers. Jesus commands us to love even our enemies.
The issue was not ordinary kindness, friendship, or compassion toward people outside the faith.
The issue was an alliance that gave strength and legitimacy to a ruler whose rebellion against God was already unmistakable.
And that distinction matters.
Christians are called to love people without surrendering their allegiance to Christ.
We can show kindness without approving evil.
We can build bridges without abandoning truth.
We can pursue peace without placing our conscience on the altar of acceptance.
But Jehoshaphat's story shows how even a person with a genuine history of seeking God can make decisions that carry painful consequences beyond his own lifetime.
His son Jehoram would eventually inherit Judah's throne.
And then the darkness became impossible to ignore.
When Jehoram established himself as king, he killed his own brothers with the sword, along with some of Judah's princes (2 Chronicles 21:4).
His brothers were not described as enemies attacking him in battle.
They were members of his own family.
Men who shared his blood.
Men whose lives stood in the way of his control.
The Bible does not tell us that Athaliah ordered these murders, and we must not accuse her of actions Scripture does not specifically attribute to her.
But it does connect Jehoram's evil reign with his marriage into Ahab's family.
Listen to the full warning:

“And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, like as did the house of Ahab: for he had the daughter of Ahab to wife: and he wrought that which was evil in the eyes of the LORD.” — 2 Chronicles 21:6 (KJV)
Jehoram did not merely inherit a throne.
He embraced a pattern of rebellion.
The tragedy is not that he lacked access to truth.
The tragedy is that he turned away from the truth available to him.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story begins to sound painfully familiar.
There are people who grew up hearing Scripture, praying with their families, and attending worship services.
They knew the songs.
They knew the language of faith.
They knew how to say, “God is good.”
Then something entered their lives that gradually became more important than obeying Him.
A relationship they were afraid to lose.
A promotion they wanted too badly.
A circle of friends whose approval felt necessary.
A secret habit they kept defending.
A compromise they promised would happen only once.
And slowly, the things that once troubled their conscience stopped troubling them.
They did not necessarily wake up one morning declaring war against God.
They simply kept choosing what they wanted until obedience began to feel inconvenient.
That is one of sin's most frightening characteristics.
It can become familiar long before its consequences become visible.
And by the time the damage is undeniable, other people may already be suffering from choices they never made.
But there is an important truth here for anyone who has been wounded by another person's influence.
Being surrounded by ungodliness does not remove your responsibility to choose what is right.
And being married to someone who sins does not automatically make you guilty of that person's sins.
Jehoram could not stand before God and make Athaliah responsible for everything he had done.
He was accountable for his own wickedness.
In the same way, you are not called to carry the guilt of another person's deliberate disobedience.
If you are living in a difficult marriage, this passage is not a command to remain in abuse or to blame yourself for your spouse's behavior. Seek safety and trustworthy help when needed.
The warning is about spiritual allegiance, moral responsibility, and the danger of embracing influences that normalize rebellion against God.
And Jehoram's rebellion did not remain confined to his personal life.
He made high places in Judah's mountains and led Jerusalem and Judah into spiritual unfaithfulness (2 Chronicles 21:11).
The king who should have guarded the nation's worship helped lead the nation away from the LORD.
What began in the royal household spread into the kingdom.
And that is another uncomfortable truth.
Our private compromises are not always private in their consequences.
A parent's unrepented bitterness can shape the atmosphere of a home.
A leader's hidden dishonesty can injure people who trusted him.
A believer's willingness to excuse evil can teach the next generation that conviction is negotiable.
Sin rarely respects the boundaries we try to place around it.
But God's response to Jehoram's wickedness also reveals something extraordinary.
Judah had become deeply corrupt under its king.
Jehoram had committed terrible evil.
Yet Scripture declares:
“Howbeit the LORD would not destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David.” — 2 Chronicles 21:7 (KJV)
Do not miss those words.
The LORD would not destroy the house of David.
Not because Jehoram deserved protection.
Not because Judah's rebellion was insignificant.
Not because God had stopped caring about holiness.
But because God had made a covenant with David.
The Hebrew expression behind the LORD's refusal to destroy David's house is:
וְלֹא־אָבָה יְהוָה לְהַשְׁחִית אֶת־בֵּית דָּוִיד
Velo-avah Adonai lehashḥit et-beit David.
A close rendering is:
“And the LORD was not willing to destroy the house of David.”
The word לְהַשְׁחִית (lehashḥit) carries the sense of destroying or ruining.
This was not an announcement that Jehoram would escape judgment.
He would not.
It was a declaration that the LORD would remain faithful to His covenant despite the wickedness of this particular king.
Jehoram would face devastating consequences.
His kingdom would suffer invasion and loss.
His sons and wives would be taken captive, except for his youngest son, Jehoahaz, also called Ahaziah (2 Chronicles 21:16–17; 22:1).
And Jehoram himself would suffer a severe disease before dying after an eight-year reign.
Scripture records that he departed without being desired and was not buried in the royal sepulchers (2 Chronicles 21:18–20).
A man who inherited privilege, power, and a godly family legacy left behind a story of violence, rebellion, and disgrace.
But the consequences did not end with his death.
His son Ahaziah became king.
And Athaliah, his mother, continued to exert a destructive influence.
Second Chronicles 22:3 says of Ahaziah:
“For his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly.”
There it is.
A mother's influence, explicitly described by Scripture as counsel toward evil.
Not every mother counsels her children toward righteousness.
Not every royal family protects its heirs.
Not every voice that says, “I only want what is best for you,” is leading you toward what is good.
That is why we must learn to measure counsel by God's truth rather than by the closeness of the person giving it.
Someone can love having influence over your life without loving the direction God wants your life to take.
And someone can be deeply important to you without being a trustworthy guide for your soul.
Ahaziah followed the wicked ways of Ahab's house and eventually died during the judgment that came upon that royal family (2 Chronicles 22:7–9).
Then the story became even darker.
When Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she attempted to destroy the royal offspring of Judah and seized power (2 Chronicles 22:10).
A grandmother turned against the royal family that included her own descendants.
The dynasty through which God's covenant promise to David was being carried appeared to be in mortal danger.
Imagine the palace.
The fear.
The violence.
The uncertainty.
The possibility that David's royal line might be extinguished.
But while Athaliah was trying to secure a throne through bloodshed, God had not forgotten His promise.
A woman named Jehoshabeath, also called Jehosheba, rescued the infant Joash, son of Ahaziah, from among the royal children facing death.
She and those helping her hid the child, and he remained concealed in the house of God for six years while Athaliah ruled (2 Chronicles 22:11–12).
Six years.
A murderous queen occupied the throne.
A little boy remained hidden.
And the covenant promise of God had not failed.
Picture that child growing up without understanding the full weight of the danger surrounding his life.
He did not know every political decision that had brought his family to this point.
He had not arranged Jehoshaphat's marriage alliance.
He had not chosen Jehoram's wickedness.
He had not advised Ahaziah to follow evil.
Yet he was living in the shadow of generations of destructive choices.
And still, God preserved him.
There is something deeply moving about that.
Because some of you reading this know what it feels like to inherit a situation you did not create.
You grew up in a home where anger was normal.
You learned fear before you learned peace.
You watched people who were supposed to protect you become the reason you needed protection.
You have spent years trying to escape patterns that began before you were born.
And sometimes you wonder whether your family's history has already decided your future.
But listen carefully.
Your family's history is not your final identity in Christ.
The sins of previous generations may have real consequences. The wounds can be deep. Healing may require time, support, wise counsel, and painful honesty.
But you are not condemned to repeat every destructive pattern you inherited.
Through Jesus Christ, repentance and new life are possible.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
The Greek phrase is:
καινὴ κτίσις
Kainē ktisis.
“A new creation.”
Not merely a person trying harder to preserve an old identity.
A new creation in Christ.
This does not mean every consequence of the past disappears overnight.
It means that union with Christ brings a genuinely new standing and a new life that is no longer defined by the dominion of sin.
And that is why the story of Judah's royal family matters far beyond the politics of ancient Israel.
Because the preserved line of David points us toward a greater King.
A King who would not merely inherit a throne.
A King who would save sinners.
Centuries after these events, Matthew opened his Gospel by identifying Jesus Christ as the son of David and the son of Abraham (Matthew 1:1).
The genealogy in Matthew 1 traces the royal line through Jehoram, Uzziah, and the generations that followed, ultimately presenting Jesus as the promised Messiah.

Matthew's genealogy is selective, as ancient genealogies sometimes were, and does not name every intervening king. But its theological purpose is clear: Jesus stands in the line of David's royal promise.
The preservation of David's house in Chronicles was part of the unfolding history through which God's covenant purposes continued.
And those purposes find their fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
But Jesus was not another Jehoram.
He did not use power to murder His brothers.
He did not turn His throne into an instrument of selfish ambition.
He did not lead His people into idolatry.
He came as the righteous Son of David.
Where earthly kings failed, He remained faithful.
Where sinners pursued power at the expense of others, He humbled Himself and gave His life for others.
Where Jehoram's reign brought death and destruction, Jesus came to bring reconciliation and eternal life.
The cross exposes the full seriousness of human sin.
The resurrection declares the victory of the Savior.
And the Gospel announces that even people with terrible histories can be forgiven and transformed through repentance and faith in Him.
That is why this account must not end with Athaliah's violence or Jehoram's disgrace.
It must lead us to Christ.
Because without Jesus, we might read this story merely as a warning about choosing the wrong spouse or making the wrong alliance.
But with Jesus at the center, we see something greater.
We see the holiness of God, the destructiveness of sin, the faithfulness of His covenant promises, and the desperate need every generation has for a Savior.
And perhaps the most important question is no longer what Jehoshaphat did centuries ago.
Perhaps it is what you are allowing into your heart today.
What have you been calling harmless that Scripture calls dangerous?
What relationship, ambition, habit, or compromise has slowly gained authority over your obedience to Christ?
What have you been defending simply because you are afraid of what repentance might cost you?
You may still be attending church.
Still sharing Bible verses.
Still telling people you believe in God.
But deep inside, you know there is an area of your life you have been refusing to surrender.
And maybe nobody else knows.
Maybe the people closest to you think everything is fine.
Maybe you have become so skilled at looking spiritually strong that you no longer know how to admit you are struggling.
But Jesus knows.
He sees beyond appearances.
He knows the things you have concealed.
And His call to repentance is not an invitation to pretend that sin does not matter.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to dress up your confession.
No need to convince God that your choices were less serious than they were.
No need to compare yourself with someone whose sins appear worse.
Come honestly.
Come humbly.
Come trusting the finished work of Jesus Christ.
If you have been compromising, repent.
