If you have been using your influence to lead others into sin, repent and seek to make things right.
If you have been ignoring godly counsel, return to the truth.
If you have been wounded by someone else's wickedness, do not confuse their sin with your worth.
And if you are frightened by the damage already done, remember that the Gospel does not promise to erase history, but it does proclaim a Savior who redeems sinners and makes new life possible.
The story of Jehoram warns us that a godly inheritance does not guarantee a godly life.
The story of Athaliah warns us that unchecked ambition and wicked influence can devastate a family.
The story of Jehoshabeath reminds us that courageous faithfulness matters even when evil appears to be winning.
And the preservation of Joash reminds us that God's promises are not defeated by the schemes of earthly rulers.
But above every one of those lessons stands Jesus Christ.
The true King.
The faithful Son of David.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who can take a person whose life has been marked by shame and bring them into the grace of God.
This is why we say:
Not because Jesus makes sin acceptable.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because faith removes every earthly consequence.
But because the grace of God in Christ is powerful enough to forgive the repentant sinner, restore fellowship with God, and begin a transformation that human effort alone could never accomplish.
Maybe this article reached you while you were questioning a relationship.
Maybe you have been wrestling with a decision that looks beneficial but troubles your conscience.
Maybe you are a parent afraid that your choices have affected your children.
Maybe you are the child who has spent years trying to recover from those choices.
Or maybe you are simply exhausted from pretending that everything is spiritually fine.
You do not need to announce your deepest private struggles to the entire world.
But you do need to be honest before God.
And if you need prayer, there is room for that honesty here.
If you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you out of compromise, you are welcome to share what is appropriate. Your story may encourage someone who has almost given up hope.
And if this account made you think of someone you love, consider tagging them with kindness, not accusation.
Do not use this message as a weapon against a spouse, a child, or a friend.
Use it as an invitation to return to Christ together.
Not simply because it might receive attention, but because there may be someone in your circle who has never seriously considered how one compromise can influence an entire family.
A friend who needs courage to make a difficult decision.
A parent praying for a wandering child.
A young believer learning the difference between love and spiritual compromise.
A person who has lived under the weight of family shame and needs to hear that Jesus offers a new beginning.
We want biblical truth to remain accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word, including those who cannot afford to pay for resources.
But we want to be clear about something important.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not pressured or manipulated (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And if your present circumstances do not allow you to give financially, you are no less loved by God and no less welcome in this community.
Your prayers, your encouragement, your thoughtful comments, and your willingness to share biblical truth are valuable ways to participate.
We want to see you growing in Scripture.
Learning to discern truth from error.
Finding strength to resist compromise.
Becoming more deeply rooted in Christ.
And helping others encounter the Gospel that has changed your life.
It is the grace of God offered through Jesus Christ.
A grace that cannot be earned by a donation.
A forgiveness that cannot be bought through a membership.
A salvation received by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8–9).
That is the message worth protecting.
That is the truth worth sharing.
That is the Savior worth following.
And now, before you leave this story, return for one final moment to the palace in Jerusalem.
A king who inherited a godly legacy chose wickedness.
A royal marriage became entangled with spiritual corruption.
Brothers died.
A kingdom suffered.
A queen seized power through violence.
And a child was hidden while the throne seemed lost.
Yet God's covenant promise endured.
The darkness was real.
The consequences were devastating.
But the darkness did not have the final word.
And for everyone who belongs to Jesus Christ, that truth reaches far beyond ancient Judah.
Your past may explain some of your wounds, but it does not have the authority to cancel the promises of God.
Your family may have handed you a painful history, but Jesus offers you a new identity.
Your mistakes may have consequences you must face, but repentance can mark the beginning of a different direction.
Do not wait until compromise has taken more than you ever intended to surrender.
Turn to Christ while you can hear His call.
And never forget:
One generation's compromise can leave scars on a family, but one sinner who turns to Jesus can begin a legacy of repentance, faith, and grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS NEVER SAID, “COME CLOSE AND KEEP YOUR SIN.”
paragraphs: JESUS NEVER SAID, “COME CLOSE AND KEEP YOUR SIN.”
The Terrifyingly Beautiful Truth Hidden in James 4:8 — Why God Calls Us to Clean Hands, Pure Hearts, and a Repentance That Changes Everything
There is a kind of Christianity that wants God's presence without God's correction.
It wants the comfort of being forgiven without the discomfort of confessing what needs forgiveness.
It wants heaven without holiness. Blessings without surrender. A Savior who rescues, but never confronts.
And perhaps the most frightening thing about it is how easily we can recognize it in everyone except ourselves.
We know the worship songs. We know when to raise our hands. We know how to say, “God is good,” even when something inside us has been quietly drifting away from Him.
We can share Bible verses in the morning and entertain bitterness at night.
We can encourage someone to trust God while secretly refusing to obey what He has already made clear to us.
We can look spiritually alive in public while becoming dangerously comfortable with sin in private.
And still, we tell ourselves everything is fine.
But what if the very Scripture we quote for comfort contains a command we have been avoiding?
What if the invitation we love — “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” — was never intended to be separated from the words that immediately follow it?
Because James did not stop there.
And neither should we.
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.” — James 4:8, KJV
Read that again.
Slowly.
The same verse that promises God's nearness also commands cleansing and purity.
Not because God hates the sinner.
Not because His mercy is insufficient.
But because the God who welcomes us into His presence loves us too deeply to pretend that the sin destroying us is harmless.
And that changes everything.
Somewhere along the way, many of us learned to repeat the invitation while forgetting the repentance.
We loved the first sentence because it made us feel wanted.
We avoided the second because it made us feel exposed.
But James was not writing a sentimental promise about experiencing a peaceful moment during worship.
He was confronting spiritual compromise.

In James 4:1–3, he exposes the desires, quarrels, and selfish passions causing conflict among believers. In verse 4, he uses the shocking language of spiritual adultery to describe friendship with the world that becomes hostility toward God.
Then comes the turning point.
“But he giveth more grace.” — James 4:6, KJV
More grace.
Two words that should make the exhausted sinner stop breathing for a moment.
Because after exposing their divided loyalties, James does not announce that God has run out of mercy.
He announces that God gives more grace.
But notice what follows.

God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. James calls believers to submit themselves to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, grieve over sin, and humble themselves before the Lord.
This is not a collection of disconnected religious slogans.
It is one urgent appeal to return to God.
And when James says, “Cleanse your hands,” the original Greek is unmistakably direct.
καθαρίσατε χεῖρας, ἁμαρτωλοί
Katharisate cheiras, hamartōloi.
“Cleanse your hands, sinners.”
The verb καθαρίσατε (katharisate) is an imperative — a command to cleanse.
The hands represent more than physical dirt. In the biblical imagery James draws upon, they point to conduct, actions, and moral responsibility.
What have you been doing?
What have your hands participated in?
What have you been excusing because nobody else knows?
Then James goes deeper.
ἁγνίσατε καρδίας, δίψυχοι
Hagnisate kardias, dipsychoi.
“Purify your hearts, you double-minded.”
The verb ἁγνίσατε (hagnisate) calls for purification.
And δίψυχοι (dipsychoi) describes those who are double-minded, divided in their loyalties.
The word is built from elements associated with “two” and “soul” or “life.” Its force in this passage is not a clinical diagnosis of ordinary uncertainty. James is confronting divided allegiance.
A heart trying to belong to God while remaining attached to what opposes Him.
A life that wants to follow Jesus without surrendering the rival desires competing for its devotion.
James is not merely saying, “Improve your behavior.”
He is confronting both the visible actions and the hidden loyalties from which those actions grow.
Clean hands without a surrendered heart can become religious performance. A claim to a pure heart without changed conduct can become spiritual self-deception.
God is concerned with both.
And long before James wrote these words, the same truth was already woven into the Hebrew Scriptures.
Psalm 24:3–4 asks:
“Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart...” (KJV)
In Hebrew, the expressions are:
נְקִי כַפַּיִם וּבַר־לֵבָב
Neqi khappayim uvar-levav.
“Clean hands and a pure heart.”
The connection is striking.
God's holiness is not satisfied by an impressive outward appearance while the inward life remains deliberately corrupt.
And yet this raises a painful question.
Who among us can honestly say our hands have always been clean?
Who can stand before the searching holiness of God and claim that every motive has been pure?
Not the person who has never missed church.
Not the person who knows the most Scripture.
Not the person whose family believes they are spiritually strong.
Not the person writing these words.
Not you.
Not me.
Scripture declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory (Romans 3:23).
And this is where the Gospel becomes more beautiful than the shallow comfort we sometimes substitute for it.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to tell dirty hands to become clean.
He came to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He bore our sins in His body on the cross (1 Peter 2:24).
He died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
His blood cleanses from sin (1 John 1:7).
And through Him, forgiveness is offered to those who turn to God in faith.
The command to repent is not an announcement that you must earn the right to be loved by God.
It is a call to stop clinging to what Christ died to save you from.
There is a difference.
A life transformed by grace is not a life that purchased grace through transformation.
Repentance is not the price we pay to make Christ merciful. It is the turning of a heart that desperately needs His mercy.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She stood publicly accused of adultery.
Imagine the shame.
The watching faces.
The knowledge that her sin had become the subject of a crowd's judgment.
She was no longer being treated as a person with a future.
She had become a scandal.
And Jesus, confronted by her accusers, exposed the hypocrisy of those eager to condemn her.
One by one, they departed.
Then Jesus spoke words of extraordinary mercy.
“Neither do I condemn thee...” (John 8:11, KJV)
But He did not stop there.
“...go, and sin no more.”
There it is again.
Mercy and holiness.
Grace and repentance.
Compassion without permission to continue in sin.
Jesus did not deny the seriousness of her wrongdoing.
He refused to make condemnation the final word over her life.
The account does not tell us everything that happened to that woman afterward. We should not invent a biography Scripture does not provide.
But the words Jesus spoke are enough to reveal His heart.
He offered mercy while calling her away from sin.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to understand that same truth.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
But neither should you make peace with the very thing Christ calls you to leave behind.
You may be reading this with a secret nobody knows.
A relationship you keep defending, even though you know it is pulling you away from obedience.
A habit you repeatedly promise to surrender.
A resentment you have carried for so long that it feels like part of your personality.
A hidden pattern of dishonesty.
A private addiction.
A carefully maintained image of spiritual strength covering a life that is quietly falling apart.
Or perhaps your struggle is less visible.
You are not living in some dramatic public scandal.
You are simply growing cold.
Prayer has become occasional.
Scripture has become optional.
Worship has become routine.
Conviction has become an inconvenience.
And slowly, without any single dramatic decision, you have begun to treat distance from God as normal.
You still believe in Jesus.
But you have stopped listening closely to Him.
And maybe the hardest thing to admit is that you miss the tenderness you once knew in your walk with God.
You miss praying without pretending.
You miss opening Scripture with a heart willing to obey.
You miss the freedom of not having to hide.
Listen carefully.
James 4:8 is not telling you that you must become perfect before you can approach God.
If that were the message, none of us could come.
It is telling you to come to God with a heart willing to turn from sin rather than defend it.
Come honestly.
Come humbly.
Come without rehearsing excuses.
Because the One who commands repentance is also the One who gives grace.
And there is a profound difference between a believer struggling against sin and a person determined to make sin comfortable.
The struggling believer may fall and weep.
The unrepentant heart increasingly learns to fall and justify it.
One cries out for rescue.
The other begins to resent the call to change.
This does not mean that every difficult season, every intrusive thought, every unanswered question, or every battle with temptation proves that someone is spiritually double-minded.
Temptation itself is not the same as surrendering to sin.
Spiritual growth can be slow.
Recovery from destructive patterns can involve repeated struggle, wise accountability, and patient perseverance.
But grace never asks us to rename darkness as light.
It teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live in a way that honors God (Titus 2:11–12).
And perhaps that is the question we most need to face.
Have I been asking God to remove the consequences of something I am still unwilling to surrender?
That question is uncomfortable.
It should be.
Not because discomfort saves anyone.
But because truth can expose the places where self-deception has been growing.
James continues:
“Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness.” (James 4:9, KJV)
These are startling words.
Especially in a world where nearly everything tells us to avoid uncomfortable feelings.
But James is not commanding believers to live permanently without joy.
He is calling people who have become careless about sin to recognize its seriousness.
There is a time to stop laughing at what is destroying your soul.
A time to stop calling compromise a harmless weakness.
A time to stop treating repentance as an embarrassing religious word.
The Greek word translated “mourn” in James 4:9 is πενθήσατε (penthēsate), a command to grieve or mourn.
This is the sorrow appropriate to recognizing our rebellion against a holy God.
But biblical sorrow is not intended to become an endless prison of self-hatred.
Paul explains in 2 Corinthians 7:10 that godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, while worldly sorrow produces death.
The difference matters.
Worldly sorrow may grieve being exposed.
Godly sorrow grieves the sin itself and turns toward God.
Worldly sorrow can collapse into despair.
Godly sorrow, responding to God's grace, moves toward repentance and life.
And if you have ever cried alone after realizing how far you have wandered, you may understand something about this.
Not every tear is evidence of repentance.
But genuine repentance may begin with the painful honesty of finally refusing to lie to yourself.
Think of Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed His power.
He had boldly declared his loyalty.
And then, when fear closed around him, he denied knowing the Lord.
Three times.
When the rooster crowed and Peter remembered Jesus' words, he went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).
Imagine the weight of that moment.
The man who had promised faithfulness had denied his Master.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus met His disciples again.
And in John 21, the risen Christ spoke directly to Peter, asking him about his love and entrusting him with the care of His sheep.
The disciple who had fallen so painfully was not beyond the reach of restoring grace.
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never denied Him.
Yet He did not leave Peter forever defined by that denial.
That is the Gospel's transforming power.
Not that sin never mattered.
But that sin and failure do not have the final word when Christ restores a repentant sinner.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now perhaps you can see why James 4:8 is so precious.
It does not invite us to a shallow religious experience.
It calls us into an honest relationship with the living God.
It confronts what is divided.
It exposes what is unclean.
It summons us to humility.
And it places that summons beside one of the most tender promises in Scripture:
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.”
Not because our repentance forces God to act.
Not because our tears purchase forgiveness.
Not because we have finally become impressive enough to deserve His attention.
But because the gracious God who calls sinners to return is faithful to His promises.
Listen to the cry of David after his sin was exposed.
In Psalm 51:10, he prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The word בְּרָא (bera) comes from the Hebrew verb bara, “to create.”
David was not merely asking for better appearances.
He was pleading for inward renewal that only God could provide.
And that prayer points us toward the deeper promise of the new covenant.
In Ezekiel 36:26–27, God promises His people a new heart, a new spirit, and the work of His Spirit within them.
The transformation God requires is also the transformation He graciously works in His people.
That is why Christian repentance must never be separated from Christ.
We do not cleanse ourselves into salvation through moral determination.
We come to the Savior who cleanses, forgives, and renews.
We confess our sins because He is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us (1 John 1:9).
We turn from sin because His grace has given us a new direction.
And we continue walking with Him because sanctification is not merely a dramatic moment at an altar.
It is the ongoing work of God in the life of someone who belongs to Jesus.
Some days that walk will feel full of joy.
Other days it will involve painful honesty.
There may be apologies you need to make.
Truths you need to confess.
Boundaries you need to establish.
Relationships you need to reconsider.
Forgiveness you need to extend.
Accountability you need to seek.

And when you have seriously harmed someone, repentance may require taking responsibility and making appropriate restitution where possible, without demanding that the person you hurt immediately trust you again.
Real repentance is more than feeling emotional during a sermon.
It bears fruit.
Not perfectly.
Not instantly in every area.
But genuinely.
And sometimes the first visible fruit is simply this:
You stop defending what you once refused to surrender.
You stop hiding behind the phrase “God knows my heart” as though His knowledge of your heart makes obedience unnecessary.
Of course He knows your heart.
That is precisely why you can bring it to Him honestly.
He knows the wounds.
He knows the fears.
He knows the desires you struggle to understand.
He knows the sin you have tried to excuse.
And none of it surprises Him.
But He calls you to repentance because He is holy, and because His grace is powerful enough to change the direction of a human life.
Maybe tonight your prayer does not need to be eloquent.
Maybe it needs to be honest.

“Lord Jesus, I have been trying to hold on to You while refusing to release things that dishonor You. I have called compromise weakness when I needed to call it sin. I have asked for peace while resisting Your correction. Please forgive me. Cleanse me through Your grace. Give me a heart that loves what You love and turns away from what grieves You. Teach me to obey You, not to earn Your love, but because You first loved me. I cannot save myself. I need You. Amen.”
If that prayer reflects what is happening inside you, do not rush past this moment.
Open your Bible to James 4:6–10.
Read the entire passage.
Not only the promise you love.
Read the commands that surround it.
Read the words about humility.
Read the call to submit to God.
Read the warning about divided loyalties.
And then read verse 10.
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.” (KJV)
What an ending to such a piercing passage.
God does not call the proud to congratulate themselves.
He calls the humble to come before Him.
And He promises to lift them up.
The path downward in humility is not the end of the story.
God's grace meets the repentant heart.
Perhaps that is why the enemy of our souls would prefer us to remain trapped between two lies.
The first says, “Your sin is not serious. You do not need to change.”
The second says, “Your sin is too serious. You can never be forgiven.”
The Gospel exposes both.
Sin is serious enough that Christ died for our sins.
Grace is glorious enough that Christ rose again.
And the risen Savior calls sinners to repentance and faith.
Not to perform holiness for an audience.
Not to build a religious reputation.
Not to pretend that transformation happens without struggle.
But to belong to Him.
Fully.
Honestly.
Without making a secret agreement with the darkness.
Someone reading it may need to know that restoration through Christ is possible.
There is room here for honesty.
There is room for those who are still learning to walk faithfully.
There is room for the person who knows Scripture but needs to return to obedience.
And there is room for the person who has never truly surrendered to Jesus Christ and is beginning to understand the difference between religious familiarity and saving faith.
The most important response is the one you make before God.
But do not underestimate how a truthful testimony can encourage someone who feels alone.
And if one person's face came to mind while reading this, consider sharing this article with them.
Not as an accusation.
Not as a weapon.
Not as a way of announcing that you think they are a sinner.
Not because the article itself has spiritual power, but because the Scriptures within it deserve to be revisited.
There may come a day when compromise feels easier than obedience.
When shame tempts you to hide.
When pride tempts you to justify yourself.
When spiritual exhaustion makes you forget the beauty of returning to God.
On that day, remember James 4:8.
And remember that the call to cleanse your hands and purify your heart is not an invitation to manufacture your own salvation.
It is a call to turn toward the Savior whose grace alone can cleanse and transform.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to produce inspirational words that people read once and forget.
But to keep placing biblical truth before people who are hungry for Jesus Christ, including those who are struggling, questioning, returning, and learning to follow Him faithfully.
These resources are part of a larger mission to make biblical encouragement and discipleship more accessible.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life of love and obedience, not by purchasing access to a ministry.
But when believers freely support trustworthy Gospel-centered work, their generosity can help that work continue reaching others.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that Christian giving should be willing rather than reluctant or compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is the spirit of this invitation.
No pressure.
No promise that financial giving will purchase God's favor.
No suggestion that someone with limited resources is less faithful.
Just an opportunity for those who believe in this mission and are able to help sustain it.
These items are not substitutes for Scripture, discipleship, or the fellowship of a local church. They are simply additional resources and expressions of encouragement connected to the ministry.
Because the mission is bigger than a page.
Bigger than a book or a product.
The mission is to point people to Jesus Christ.

And if every article, every shared Scripture, every free resource, and every act of generosity ultimately directs attention away from ourselves and toward the crucified and risen Savior, then the work is serving its proper purpose.
But before you leave, there is one final question.
Not for the person you wish would read this.
Not for the friend whose choices concern you.
Not for the church member whose hypocrisy has frustrated you.
For you.
What are you still holding on to that Jesus is calling you to surrender?
Do not answer too quickly.
Sit with that question.
Bring it before God.
Ask Him to search your heart, as David prayed in Psalm 139:23–24.
And when His Word exposes something that needs to change, do not run from Him.
Run toward Him.
The same Lord who calls you to repentance is the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
The same Gospel that exposes your need also announces His sufficient grace.
The same Jesus who died on the cross rose from the grave, and His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final victory.
You may have spent years hiding behind an image.
You may have wasted opportunities.
You may have wounded people.
You may have fallen more times than you can count.
Repentance will not erase every earthly consequence, and restoration may require time, responsibility, and difficult obedience.
But through Jesus Christ, forgiveness is real.
New life is real.
And the transforming grace of God is real.
So cleanse your hands.
Purify your heart.
Humble yourself before the Lord.
Not by trusting your own goodness.
But by turning to Christ, trusting His mercy, and walking in the new life His grace makes possible.
Because the most tragic thing would not be discovering that your hands are dirty.
It would be hearing the Savior call you to come near — and choosing to keep hiding from the One who can make you clean.
Your sin may explain where you have been, but only Jesus Christ can give you the new life you could never create for yourself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WIPED HER MOUTH AND SAID, “I HAVE DONE NOTHING WRONG.” — THE TERRIFYING BIBLE VERSE ABOUT SIN THAT NO LONGER FEELS LIKE SIN
paragraphs: SHE WIPED HER MOUTH AND SAID, “I HAVE DONE NOTHING WRONG.” — THE TERRIFYING BIBLE VERSE ABOUT SIN THAT NO LONGER FEELS LIKE SIN

Proverbs 30:18–20 exposes something more frightening than adultery itself: a heart that has learned to sin without trembling, hide without shame, and convince itself that God sees nothing. But what happens when Jesus confronts the secrets we have become comfortable keeping?
There is a kind of sin that makes a person fall to their knees and cry.
And then there is a kind of sin that makes a person look in the mirror, straighten their clothes, smile at their family, open their Bible, and continue living as though absolutely nothing happened.
The second should frighten us.
Not because it is necessarily more visible.
But because it has become invisible to the person committing it.
Imagine this.
A woman returns home.
Her husband may be waiting. Her children may be sleeping. The house is quiet. Everything looks ordinary.
She washes her face. Checks her reflection. Perhaps answers a message. Perhaps prepares for tomorrow.
Nothing about her appearance suggests that something sacred has been betrayed.
And if someone asks whether anything is wrong, she has already rehearsed her answer.
“Nothing.”
Not a trembling confession.
Not a desperate plea for forgiveness.
Just one word.
Nothing.
The Bible describes a disturbing picture of this kind of moral indifference in Proverbs 30.
And the most frightening part of this passage is not merely what the woman did.
It is what she said afterward.
“I have done nothing wrong.”
Read that again.
Because somewhere between the sin and the denial, something terrible has happened inside the human heart.
And before you decide this article is about someone else's marriage, someone else's secret affair, or someone else's hypocrisy, understand something.
The Bible may be about to expose a place in your own heart that you have carefully avoided.
In Proverbs 30:18–20, Agur, the speaker in this section of Proverbs, says:
“There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not:
The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid.
Such is the way of an adulterous woman; she eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have done no wickedness.”
— Proverbs 30:18–20, King James Version
These are not random illustrations.
Agur begins with four mysterious ways: an eagle moving through the sky, a serpent crossing a rock, a ship navigating the sea, and a man with a young woman.
The Hebrew word translated “way” is דֶּרֶךְ (derekh).
It can mean a road, path, manner, or course of conduct.
In this passage, Agur is contemplating movements and relationships whose ways are difficult for him to comprehend or trace.
Then comes the unsettling comparison.
“Such is the way of an adulterous woman.”
The Hebrew reads:
כֵּן דֶּרֶךְ אִשָּׁה מְנָאָפֶת
Ken derekh ishah mena'afet.
Literally, “So is the way of an adulterous woman.”
The word מְנָאָפֶת (mena'afet) comes from the Hebrew root נאף (na'af), meaning to commit adultery.
Scripture is not describing an innocent misunderstanding or a harmless attraction.
It is describing a violation of marital faithfulness.
Then comes the devastating image:
אָכְלָה וּמָחֲתָה פִיהָ וְאָמְרָה לֹא־פָעַלְתִּי אָוֶן
Akhlah u-machatah fiha ve-amerah, lo fa'alti aven.
“She eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done no wickedness.’”
The word אָוֶן (aven) can refer to wickedness, wrongdoing, or moral evil.
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say that she confessed.
It does not say she was overwhelmed with remorse.
It does not say she recognized the devastation of betrayal.
It pictures someone behaving as though the wrongdoing were no more consequential than finishing a meal and wiping away the evidence.
That is the force of the imagery.
The text does not give us her name, her marriage history, her motives, or her eventual fate. Nor does it explicitly say that she had stopped feeling guilt altogether.
But it does show a chilling declaration of innocence where there has been wrongdoing.
And that is enough to confront us.
Because the greatest danger is not simply that people can commit sin.
It is that people can become skilled at explaining it away.
At first, there was hesitation.
At first, the conscience protested.
At first, the heart knew something was wrong.
Then came the explanations.
“I deserve to be happy.”
“My spouse doesn't understand me.”
“It's only a conversation.”
“Nothing physical happened.”
“God knows how lonely I am.”
“Everybody has secrets.”
“It's not hurting anyone.”
And eventually, what once required an excuse no longer seems to require an explanation.
But sin does not become righteous because we have become comfortable with it.
And silence is not the same as innocence.
A person can silence a conscience without obtaining forgiveness.
A person can erase messages without erasing accountability.
A person can convince friends that everything is fine while standing before a God who knows the truth.
And a person can become so practiced at pretending that even genuine repentance begins to feel unnecessary.
That is why Proverbs 30:20 deserves more than a quick reading.
It deserves an examination of the heart.
But we must be careful here.
This passage is not permission to condemn women while excusing men.
The seventh commandment says:
“Thou shalt not commit adultery.”
— Exodus 20:14, KJV
It does not say that adultery is wicked only when committed by a woman.
The same biblical standard applies to husbands and wives.
A man who betrays his wife and justifies himself is not morally superior to the woman in Proverbs.
A woman who betrays her husband and conceals it is not exempt from God's truth.
And a person who has never physically committed adultery should not assume that the subject has nothing to do with them.
Because Jesus took the conversation deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He said:
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Jesus was not saying that lust and physical adultery produce identical earthly consequences.
He was exposing the fact that sin is not merely a matter of outward behavior.
The heart matters.
What we entertain matters.
What we deliberately cultivate matters.
What we do when nobody is watching matters.
And suddenly, the woman wiping her mouth is no longer a distant figure from an ancient proverb.
Her denial becomes a mirror for every person who has ever said:
“It wasn't really lying.”
“I only looked.”
“I was just venting.”
“I didn't mean anything by it.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“I'll repent later.”
Perhaps your secret is not adultery.
Perhaps it is bitterness you have been feeding for years.
Perhaps it is a private addiction that has slowly taken control of your thoughts.
Perhaps it is an emotional attachment you know is crossing boundaries.
Perhaps it is dishonesty hidden behind a respectable reputation.
Perhaps it is the resentment you nurture while publicly speaking about forgiveness.
Or perhaps you have become so accustomed to religious activity that you no longer notice how far your private life has drifted from the Jesus you publicly proclaim.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say amen.
You know how to encourage someone else with Scripture.
You know how to post about God's goodness.
But there is a room inside your heart where you do not want the light turned on.
And you keep telling yourself:
“It's nothing.”
Yet the Holy Spirit may be confronting you with a question you cannot easily dismiss.
If it is nothing, why are you so determined to keep it hidden?
Not every private struggle is a secret sin. Privacy itself is not wrongdoing. And not every feeling of shame is evidence of guilt.
But when we knowingly protect what God has called us to forsake, we should not mistake concealment for peace.
Proverbs 28:13 says:
“He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.”
Notice both parts.
Confession.
And forsaking.
God does not invite us merely to become better at describing our failures.
He calls us to turn from them.
The biblical language of repentance helps us understand this.

The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a change of mind and disposition. In the New Testament, genuine repentance is inseparable from turning toward God, as Acts 3:19 makes clear:
“Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out.”
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered the truth.
It is not crying because consequences arrived.
It is not apologizing while secretly planning to repeat the betrayal.
True repentance means acknowledging sin before God, turning away from it, and seeking to walk in obedience.
It does not mean a person instantly becomes perfect.
It means that instead of defending the darkness, the person begins walking toward the light.
And sometimes that is where the deepest struggle begins.
Because confession can be costly.
Truth may expose a carefully protected reputation.
A betrayed spouse may need time, boundaries, and honest answers.
Trust may not return quickly.
Consequences may remain even after forgiveness is sought.
And for some, telling the truth may mean finally admitting that the life everyone admires is not the life they have actually been living.
But hear this.
The grace of Jesus Christ is not permission to keep hiding. It is the invitation to stop hiding.
And there is another scene in Scripture that makes this truth almost unbearable in its beauty.
A woman is brought before Jesus.
She has been caught in adultery.
Her accusers stand around her.
Her sin is public.
Her humiliation is complete.
There is no carefully maintained image left to protect.
In John 8:3–11, a passage traditionally included in Christian Bibles, the scribes and Pharisees bring this woman to Jesus.
They want to trap Him.
They invoke the Law of Moses.
They ask what should happen to her.
And Jesus answers:
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.”
— John 8:7, KJV
One by one, her accusers depart.
Then Jesus asks:
“Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?”
She answers:
“No man, Lord.”
And Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:10–11, KJV

There is an important textual detail worth knowing. John 7:53–8:11 is absent from several of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, and modern Bible editions often identify this textual question. Christians have long treasured the account, but we should be transparent about its manuscript history rather than pretending there is no discussion.
Its portrayal of mercy joined to a call away from sin is consistent with truths firmly taught elsewhere in Scripture.
And what a picture it gives us.
The woman in Proverbs says, “I have done no wickedness.”
The woman brought before Jesus has no such defense recorded.
One picture shows wrongdoing being denied.
The other shows a sinner standing before the One who speaks both mercy and truth.
We must not assume these are the same woman, or that Scripture is intentionally presenting them as paired historical figures.
They are not.
But read together, these passages confront us with two radically different responses to sin.
Denial says, “I have done nothing wrong.”
Repentance says, “Lord, I need Your mercy.”
And the Gospel announces that mercy is available because of Jesus Christ.
Not because adultery is harmless.
Not because betrayal is insignificant.
Not because God has lowered His standard.
But because Jesus came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we became impressive Christians.
Not after we finally found a way to make our past look acceptable.
Christ died for sinners.
And that includes the adulterer who genuinely repents.
The liar who turns toward the truth.
The hypocrite who finally stops pretending.
The broken believer who has fallen and cries out for mercy.
The person who is terrified that God could never forgive what they have done.
The Cross does not declare that sin never mattered.
The Cross reveals just how seriously God takes sin—and how extraordinary His love is toward sinners.
Jesus did not suffer so that we could continue living comfortably in rebellion.
He died and rose again so that sinners could be reconciled to God and receive new life through Him.
That is why grace is so much more than a comforting religious word.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) is commonly translated “grace.”
In the context of salvation, it speaks of God's undeserved favor.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
You cannot purchase this grace.
You cannot earn it through public religious performance.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
But the grace that saves us also begins transforming us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace instructs us to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live godly lives.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace teaches.
Grace restores.
Grace changes the direction of a life.
And perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
Because there are two people reading this article.
One is hiding sin.
The other is still bleeding from someone else's sin.
To the one who is hiding:
You may have convinced everyone around you.
You may have learned how to delete the evidence, redirect the conversation, and silence uncomfortable questions.
You may even have convinced yourself that your choices are justified.
But God already knows.
Psalm 139:1 says:
“O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me.”
There is no secret He needs you to explain before He can see it.
And yet He calls you to repentance.
Not because He enjoys your humiliation.
But because sin destroys, and His mercy calls you away from destruction.
Stop calling darkness light.
Stop using pain as permission to wound someone else.
Stop confusing God's patience with His approval.
And stop assuming that because judgment has not arrived, accountability never will.
Today, you can begin telling the truth.
Today, you can confess your sin to God.
Today, you can seek wise pastoral counsel, end an adulterous relationship, establish necessary boundaries, and take responsible steps toward honesty and restoration.
If your situation involves abuse, coercion, or danger, seek qualified support and a safe plan rather than confronting someone in a way that puts you at risk.
Repentance requires truth.
But it does not require recklessness.
And to the person who has been betrayed:
Please hear this carefully.
Someone else's adultery is not proof that you were inadequate.
Their deception is not evidence that you were unworthy of faithfulness.
You may be questioning every memory.
Every affectionate word.
Every ordinary evening that now feels contaminated by what you did not know.
You may find yourself wondering whether you were foolish to trust.
You were not wrong to value faithfulness.
And you are not required to pretend the betrayal was small simply because you are a Christian.
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
It does not automatically restore trust.
It does not eliminate the need for accountability.
And it does not require remaining in an unsafe situation.
Jesus cares about truth, justice, mercy, and the wounded.
You can seek healing without denying what happened.
You can pray for someone without immediately trusting them again.
You can place your broken heart before Christ even when you have no idea what restoration will look like.
And you can remember that the Savior who calls sinners to repentance is also near to those who are crushed.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the repentant sinner.
And there is room for the wounded person who can barely find words to pray.
That is the astonishing beauty of the Gospel.
It does not flatten every story into the same experience.
It does not erase the difference between wrongdoing and suffering.
But it offers hope in the presence of both.
Not about the woman in Proverbs.
Not about someone who betrayed you.
Not about the scandal everyone in your community still whispers about.
About you.
What have you been calling “nothing” that God has been asking you to surrender?
Perhaps you already know.
Perhaps the question brought a name to mind.
A habit.
A conversation.
A compromise.
A resentment.
A lie.
Perhaps your heart has been fighting conviction for months.
You still attend church.
You still believe in God.
You still love the idea of Jesus.
But you have been resisting His authority over one particular part of your life.
And you are exhausted.
Exhausted from maintaining appearances.
Exhausted from explaining things away.
Exhausted from being one person in public and another person in private.
What if today is the day you stop running?
What if the most important sentence you speak is not, “I have done nothing wrong,” but:
“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. Please forgive me. Change my heart.”
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not because confession makes sin insignificant.
But because the forgiveness of God rests on the saving work of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to defend what Jesus calls you to surrender.
You do not have to make your darkness look respectable.
You do not have to become worthy of grace before asking for it.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Bring the truth.
Bring the shame.
Bring the broken promises.
Bring the parts of your story you wish you could erase.
And trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose victorious over death.
There is no biblical promise that every damaged marriage will be restored.
There is no guarantee that every relationship will return to what it was.
And genuine repentance does not erase every earthly consequence.
But there is a real promise of forgiveness and new life for those who turn to Jesus Christ in faith.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That is not a promise that your past never happened.
It is the announcement that your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because the wounds were shallow.
Not because the consequences disappeared.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He can take a life ruled by deception and teach it to walk in truth.
He can take a heart hardened by compromise and awaken it to repentance.
He can take someone who believed forgiveness was impossible and show them the immeasurable riches of His mercy.
And He can take a person who has spent years saying, “I have done nothing wrong,” and bring them to the liberating confession:
“Lord, I was wrong. And I need You.”
That is not the end of hope.
It may be the beginning of transformation.
We want these words to become invitations to prayer, encouragement, and honest Christian community—not public pressure to disclose what should remain private.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person struggling to find their way back to God.
And perhaps your testimony, shared wisely and freely, will remind another person that repentance is possible and grace is real.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to expose someone's private failures.
But because somebody scrolling through Facebook tonight may be standing at the very edge of a decision that could change their life.
Someone may be about to destroy a marriage.
Someone may be trapped in a cycle of secret compromise.
Someone may believe they are beyond forgiveness.
And someone may desperately need to remember that Jesus Christ still calls sinners to repentance and offers them mercy.
Not because every sentence will be easy to read again.
But because there may come a day when you need to remember the difference between guilt that drives you into hiding and godly sorrow that leads you toward repentance.
We are here to proclaim Jesus Christ, encourage repentance, teach biblical truth, strengthen struggling believers, and point wounded hearts toward the grace of God.
Our mission is not to entertain people with religious controversy.
It is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and grow as disciples of Jesus Christ.

You may choose to treat that support as part of your personal Christian giving, according to your convictions and commitments. It is a voluntary ministry contribution, not a biblical replacement for every believer's responsibility to prayerfully consider giving to their local church and other needs.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
We want it to come from a willing heart that values the proclamation of the Gospel.
These products can be reminders of biblical truth in everyday life, but they are not the heart of our ministry.
Jesus is.
We want the Word of God to reach people, regardless of their ability to give.
Pray for the people who will read it.
Speak about Jesus with someone who needs hope.
And live the truth you proclaim.
Because the greatest evidence of the Gospel's power is not how loudly we announce it.
It is how deeply Christ transforms our lives.
Before you leave, return with me to that unsettling picture in Proverbs.
A woman eats.
She wipes her mouth.
She says she has done no wickedness.
The verse ends there.
We are not told whether she ever repented.
We are not told whether she ever confessed.
We are not told whether she ever stopped pretending.
But your story is still being written.
You still have an opportunity to respond to God's truth.
You can continue defending the darkness.
Or you can come into the light.
You can keep saying, “I have done nothing wrong.”
Or you can bow before the Savior and say, “Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And that difference matters more than your reputation, your public image, your religious accomplishments, or the applause of people who do not know your heart.
Because one day, the question will not be how successfully you concealed your sin from other people.
The question will be whether you have truly come to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
And for the person who does, there is mercy.
There is forgiveness.
There is new life.
There is grace.
The most tragic ending is not that your sin was discovered. It is that mercy was offered, and you chose to keep pretending you needed none.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN TRYING TO REPENT BEFORE YOU EVEN KNOW HOW TO BELIEVE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN TRYING TO REPENT BEFORE YOU EVEN KNOW HOW TO BELIEVE?
Does repentance come before faith, or does faith in Jesus Christ produce repentance? The answer could change everything about how you understand salvation, grace, and the God who is calling you home.
There is a man sitting alone in his car outside a church.
The service has already started.

He can hear the worship through the walls. He knows some of the songs. He even remembers singing them years ago, back when following Jesus seemed simpler, back when he hadn't made so many decisions he now wishes he could erase.
But tonight, he cannot bring himself to open the door.
Because he has a question.
Not the kind of question people usually ask during Bible study.
The kind that keeps you awake at two in the morning.
“Do I have to change my life before I can come back to Jesus… or do I come to Jesus because I cannot change my life?”
He wants to repent.
He really does.
But he has promised God he would change before.
He has cried after committing the same sin. Deleted the same contacts. Made the same commitments. Prayed the same desperate prayers.
And somehow, he keeps ending up here.
Ashamed.
Exhausted.
Wondering whether his repentance was ever real.
Perhaps that man is closer to your story than you would like to admit.
Perhaps you have never sat outside a church, but you have sat at the edge of your bed, staring at the floor, wondering why you still struggle with something you thought you surrendered years ago.
And somewhere along the way, you began believing that Jesus would receive you once you became sufficiently repentant.
But what if the very way you have been thinking about repentance has been keeping you from understanding the grace that makes repentance possible?
What if you have been trying to produce, through your own strength, something Scripture describes as a gift God grants?
And what if the answer is not as simple as choosing whether repentance or faith comes first?
Because three passages of Scripture bring us face-to-face with a truth that is both deeply humbling and extraordinarily hopeful.
And we need to hear all three.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus begins His public proclamation with words that confront every human heart:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
In the original Greek, the command reads:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Two commands.
One Savior.
One urgent response to the arrival of God's kingdom.
The word μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) comes from μετανοέω (metanoeō), meaning to repent, to change one's mind or understanding in a way that involves a genuine turning of one's life.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling bad about what happened.
It is not simply being embarrassed because somebody discovered your sin.
It is not promising to behave better so that God will finally approve of you.
Repentance involves a real turning away from sin and toward God.
And the word πιστεύετε (pisteuete) comes from πιστεύω (pisteuō), meaning to believe, trust, or place faith in.
In the context of the Gospel, believing is more than agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting the good news God has revealed in His Son.
Both verbs in Mark 1:15 are present imperatives, calling for a response that is not merely a passing religious moment.
But notice something important.
Jesus does not say, “Make yourself righteous, prove that your repentance is good enough, and afterward you may believe.”
Neither does He say, “Claim to believe in Me while remaining comfortably committed to the sins from which I call you.”
He commands repentance and faith together.
And this is where we must be careful.
The order in which two commands appear in a sentence does not, by itself, establish a universal chronological sequence for how salvation happens in every human heart.
Jesus is announcing that the kingdom of God has drawn near.
The proper response is to turn from sin and trust the good news.
Repentance and faith are distinguishable, but they are inseparably connected in a genuine response to Christ.
You cannot meaningfully turn toward Jesus as Savior while deliberately insisting that the sin He came to save you from must remain your master.
And you cannot practice Christian repentance apart from turning toward the God whose mercy makes salvation possible.
But there is another passage that makes this question even more profound.
Acts 11:18 records the response of Jewish believers after hearing how God had welcomed Gentiles into the fellowship of salvation.
They glorified God and declared:
“Then hath God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life.” — Acts 11:18, KJV
Read that again.
God granted repentance.
The Greek expression is:
τὴν μετάνοιαν εἰς ζωὴν ἔδωκεν
Tēn metanoian eis zōēn edōken.
“He gave repentance leading to life.”
The word ἔδωκεν (edōken) means “gave” or “granted.”
And μετάνοιαν (metanoian) refers to repentance.
This is not a minor detail.
The believers did not praise the Gentiles for somehow manufacturing enough moral determination to deserve entrance into God's family.
They glorified God because He had opened the way of life to people whom many had previously regarded as outsiders.
The wider context matters.
Peter had been explaining how the Holy Spirit came upon the Gentiles as they received the Gospel. God's saving welcome was not restricted by ethnic background or by humanly imposed barriers.
And the believers recognized the divine grace behind what had happened.
Repentance unto life was something God had granted.
That does not mean human beings never genuinely repent.
They do.
God's gracious work does not make the human response imaginary.
It means that repentance is never a reason for sinners to boast as though they had independently earned salvation.
Think about that.
The very turning toward God that exposes your need for mercy is itself something Scripture connects to His gracious initiative.
You may have spent years treating repentance like an admission fee you must pay before approaching Christ.
But repentance is not the purchase price of salvation.
Jesus Christ has already accomplished what no sinner could accomplish through His sinless life, sacrificial death, and resurrection.
We are not saved because our sorrow is deep enough.
We are not justified because our tears are numerous enough.
We are not forgiven because our promises are finally impressive enough.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 leaves no room for boasting in ourselves.
And yet grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace brings sinners to the Savior who calls them to repent.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because there is a kind of preaching that makes people afraid to approach Jesus until they have already repaired themselves.
And there is another kind of preaching that tells people they can receive Jesus without ever confronting the sin that is destroying them.
Neither should be confused with the full biblical message.
The Gospel is not “Clean yourself up, and then Christ will consider saving you.”
But neither is it “Keep worshiping your sin, and call that faith.”
The Gospel announces a crucified and risen Savior who receives sinners by grace and transforms those who belong to Him.
Now consider the third passage.
Paul writes to Timothy about correcting those who oppose the truth, instructing the Lord's servant to do so with gentleness:
“If God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth.” — 2 Timothy 2:25, KJV
The Greek includes the remarkable expression:
μήποτε δώῃ αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς μετάνοιαν
Mēpote dōē autois ho theos metanoian.
“Perhaps God may grant them repentance.”
Again, repentance is something God grants.
And notice the setting.
Paul is not describing a preacher humiliating sinners into submission.
He is instructing a servant of the Lord to correct opponents gently, patiently, and without quarrelsomeness.
Why?
Because the deepest change in the human heart cannot be forced through anger, intimidation, or religious performance.
Truth must be proclaimed.
Error must be corrected.
People are responsible for their response.
But God is the one upon whom the servant ultimately depends for the gift of repentance.
That should change the way we speak to struggling believers.
It should change the way parents pray for wandering children.
It should change the way churches respond to people trapped in destructive patterns.
And it should change the way you approach God when your own heart feels stubborn, cold, or spiritually exhausted.
You can pray:

“Lord, I know I need to repent. But even my heart feels resistant. Please open my eyes to the truth. Help me hate what is destroying me. Help me love what is pleasing to You. Turn my heart toward Christ.”
That is not an excuse for remaining in sin.
It is an acknowledgment that genuine spiritual transformation requires God's grace.
But now we must return to the original question.
Does repentance come before faith, or does faith in Christ produce repentance?
The biblical answer requires more care than a simple slogan.
Mark 1:15 commands both repentance and faith as the appropriate response to the Gospel.
Acts 11:18 and 2 Timothy 2:25 teach that repentance is granted by God.
Other passages illuminate their relationship.
Acts 20:21 speaks of “repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Acts 26:20 calls people to repent, turn to God, and demonstrate repentance through their deeds.
In Acts 16:31, Paul tells the Philippian jailer:
“Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved.”
John's Gospel repeatedly emphasizes believing in Jesus for eternal life.
And 1 Thessalonians 1:9 describes believers turning to God from idols to serve the living and true God.
Taken together, these passages do not establish a stopwatch-like sequence in which every person must first complete one spiritual action before beginning the other.
Christians across different theological traditions have explained the relationship somewhat differently.
Some emphasize repentance and faith as two inseparable aspects of conversion: turning away from sin and turning toward Christ.
Others emphasize that God first renews the sinner's heart, enabling both repentance and faith.
Still others emphasize God's preceding grace, which enables a genuine human response without eliminating the possibility of resisting that grace.
These are meaningful theological differences, and Scripture should not be made to say more than a particular passage actually says.
Yet the central Gospel truth remains clear.
No sinner earns salvation by repenting well enough, and no genuine saving faith treats Christ's call to repentance as irrelevant.
Repentance is not a competing Savior.
Faith is not a license to continue in rebellion.
And Jesus is not waiting at the finish line for you to achieve moral perfection before He will receive you.
He is the Savior to whom sinners are called to come.
There is a difference between a repentant person who still struggles with sin and an unrepentant person who has made peace with it.
One may fall and grieve because the sin contradicts the Lord they love.
The other may defend, celebrate, or excuse the sin while refusing Christ's authority.
But even here, we must be humble.
We cannot always measure another person's spiritual condition by looking at one isolated moment of failure.
Nor should we reassure ourselves merely because we occasionally feel guilty.
The question is not whether you have ever fallen after professing faith.
The question is whether you are turning toward Christ in trust and surrender, or deliberately turning away from Him.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
Then, under pressure, he denied knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine the weight of that failure.
The voice of his own denial.
The memory of his confidence.
The unbearable realization that he had done exactly what he insisted he would never do.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Peter remembered the Lord's words and wept bitterly.
But Peter's tears were not the price of his restoration.
The risen Jesus came to His disciples.
And in John 21, He dealt personally with Peter, calling him again to love and service.
Peter's story does not make denial harmless.
It makes the mercy of Christ magnificent.
The Savior Peter denied was the Savior who restored him.
Now think about the younger son in Luke 15.
He demanded his inheritance, left his father's house, and wasted what he had received.
Eventually, he found himself in humiliation and hunger.
Then Scripture says something extraordinary.
“And when he came to himself…” — Luke 15:17, KJV
He recognized what he had done.
He resolved to return.
He confessed his sin.
But before he could finish the speech he had prepared, his father received him with compassion.
The son did not return with an impressive record of reform.
He returned acknowledging his guilt and depending upon mercy.
And the father did not celebrate the rebellion.
He celebrated the return.
This parable is not a technical explanation of the precise logical order of regeneration, faith, and repentance.
It is a picture of the astonishing mercy of God toward the lost who return.
And perhaps that is the picture someone reading this desperately needs.
Because somewhere, someone is convinced they have gone too far.
A husband who has hidden an addiction from his family.
A woman carrying the shame of decisions she cannot undo.
A young believer who keeps falling into the same temptation.
A church leader who looks spiritually strong in public but knows how much darkness has been tolerated in private.
A person who grew up hearing about Jesus but has never truly surrendered to Him.
Perhaps someone has even begun to wonder whether God is tired of hearing their prayers.
Listen carefully.
The cross does not minimize your sin.
It reveals how serious sin truly is.
But the cross also reveals how far the love of God went to redeem sinners.
Jesus did not die because humanity needed a little encouragement.
He died because we needed a Savior.
And He rose again because death would not have the final word.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Not after we conquered every temptation.
Christ died for sinners.
But do not misunderstand this grace.
The Christ who receives sinners also calls them to follow Him.
He does not promise that discipleship will be effortless.
He does not pretend that obedience is optional.
And He does not teach us to rename darkness as light.
His grace forgives.
His truth confronts.
His Spirit sanctifies.
His love disciplines.
His mercy restores.
And His Gospel creates a new direction for those who belong to Him.
This is why repentance cannot be reduced to a single emotional experience.
There is an initial turning to God in conversion, and there is also an ongoing life of repentance as believers confess sin, reject it, and grow in holiness.
Even mature Christians continue to need the mercy of God.
First John 1:9 reminds believers of God's faithfulness and righteousness in forgiving and cleansing those who confess their sins.
And 2 Corinthians 7:10 distinguishes godly sorrow, which produces repentance, from worldly sorrow, which produces death.
Feeling terrible is not automatically the same thing as repenting.
Some people feel terrible because they were exposed.
Some feel terrible because they lost something.
Some feel terrible because their self-image has been shattered.
But godly sorrow directs us toward God.
It does not merely say, “I hate what happened to my reputation.”
It says, “Lord, I have sinned against You.”
And true repentance begins to bear fruit.
It may involve confession.
Restitution where appropriate.
Ending a destructive relationship.
Seeking accountability.
Making an apology without demanding immediate forgiveness.
Rejecting a habit that has been defended for years.
Accepting consequences rather than using religious language to escape responsibility.
But these actions are not payments that purchase justification.
They are fitting expressions of a heart turning toward God.
We are not saved by the fruit of repentance. But genuine repentance is not content to remain forever fruitless.
And what about the believer who is still struggling?
What about the person who has sincerely confessed sin, yet continues to fight powerful habits?
Do not confuse the presence of a battle with proof that God has abandoned you.
At the same time, do not confuse the existence of a battle with permission to stop resisting.
Bring your struggle into the light.
Seek wise pastoral help.
Find trustworthy Christian accountability.
Where addiction, trauma, or other serious difficulties are involved, appropriate professional care may also be an important part of seeking help.
And above all, keep looking to Christ.
Not because your struggle is insignificant.
But because your Savior is sufficient.
Philippians 1:6 expresses Paul's confidence that God would complete the good work He had begun among the Philippian believers.
Christian hope is not confidence in our own flawless determination.
It is confidence in the faithfulness of God.
And now I want to return to that man sitting outside the church.
The one who could not bring himself to open the door.
Imagine he finally walks inside.
He sits in the back, hoping nobody notices.
The preacher speaks about repentance.
For a moment, his heart sinks.
Here it comes, he thinks.
Another reminder of everything I have failed to become.
But then he hears the Gospel.
Not a message that excuses his sin.
Not a message that tells him to stop caring about holiness.
A message about Jesus Christ, crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
A message about grace that cannot be earned.
A message about repentance that God grants.
A message about faith that rests upon the Savior rather than the sinner's ability to save himself.
And suddenly, the question begins to change.
Instead of asking, “Have I made myself worthy enough to come to Christ?”
He begins asking, “Why have I been running from the only One who can save me?”
He realizes that he does not need to manufacture a perfect spiritual performance before coming to Jesus.
He needs Jesus.
He needs to turn from sin.
He needs to trust the Savior.
He needs the mercy he cannot earn and the transformation he cannot accomplish apart from God's grace.
And perhaps, for the first time in years, his prayer becomes painfully simple.

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Teach me to repent. Help me trust You. Change what I cannot change by my own strength. I surrender myself to You.”
Not a magic formula.
Not words that guarantee salvation merely because they are repeated.
But an honest expression of the repentance and faith to which the Gospel calls us.
And perhaps that is where you are right now.
Not outside a church.
But at the doorway of surrender.
You have spent so long debating whether you have repented enough that you have forgotten the One to whom repentance points.
You have examined your emotions.
Measured your tears.
Counted your failures.
Compared your spiritual progress with somebody else's.
And somewhere in that exhausting process, you have begun looking more at yourself than at Christ.
But your hope was never meant to rest on the perfection of your repentance.
Your hope rests in the perfection of your Redeemer.
Repentance does not make Jesus willing to save. Jesus is the Savior whose grace calls sinners to repentance and faith.
That is the difference between trying to purchase mercy and receiving mercy through Christ.
So does repentance come before faith?
In Mark 1:15, Jesus names repentance before believing, but the verse does not settle every theological question about their precise order.
Does faith in Christ produce repentance?

Faith and repentance are deeply interconnected, and genuine trust in Christ leads to a life of turning from sin. Yet Scripture also explicitly teaches that God grants repentance, so we should not portray it merely as a human achievement produced independently of divine grace.
The safest biblical conclusion is this:

God graciously calls sinners through the Gospel to repent and believe in Jesus Christ. Repentance and saving faith belong together, and the Christian life continues in trusting Christ and turning from sin.
You do not need to solve every theological debate before responding to the Gospel.
You need the Savior whom the Gospel proclaims.

And if you are already His, you need to keep returning to His Word, confessing your sins, trusting His promises, and walking in the grace that teaches us to deny ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending they have never failed.
But to keep pointing broken, struggling, growing, and searching people toward the truth of Jesus Christ.
From hiding to confession.
From self-righteousness to dependence upon Christ.
From spiritual confusion to biblical understanding.
From the weight of sin to the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior.
And if this message has exposed something in your own heart, please do not let it become another article you read, feel, and forget.
You do not have to publish the details of your struggle. God already knows them.
And if you have experienced Christ's restoring mercy, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage someone who thinks restoration is impossible.
Because a world overflowing with spiritual noise desperately needs the truth of God's Word.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow in your understanding of Christ, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not extracted through guilt or pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
These items are not the reason we preach Christ. They are simply another way to encourage faith, spark conversations, and express our appreciation to those helping the ministry continue.
Those free resources matter to us.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is losing hope.
Speak the truth of Christ with love.
Because the Gospel does not belong to those who can afford to fund its proclamation.
It is good news for sinners who desperately need a Savior.
And before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
Does repentance come before faith, or does faith produce repentance?
Perhaps the most important thing you can do today is stop treating that question as a reason to delay coming to Christ.
Hear His command.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask God for the grace to turn from what is destroying you.
Trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
And walk with Him in the newness of life that His grace makes possible.
Because the greatest scandal is not that sinners have fallen so terribly.
It is that the sinless Son of God willingly bore the shame and judgment sinners deserved, so that those who trust in Him might be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
And the greatest grace is not that God pretends our sins never mattered.
It is that Jesus Christ paid the price we could never pay.
You may have spent years trying to become worthy enough to return to Jesus, when the whole time your only hope was the mercy of the Jesus you needed to return to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE HID A CHILD WHILE A QUEEN MURDERED THE ROYAL FAMILY—AND FOR SIX YEARS, THE ENEMY NEVER KNEW A KING WAS STILL ALIVE
paragraphs: SHE HID A CHILD WHILE A QUEEN MURDERED THE ROYAL FAMILY—AND FOR SIX YEARS, THE ENEMY NEVER KNEW A KING WAS STILL ALIVE

Her name was Jehosheba. She never sat on a throne, never commanded an army, and never received a crown. But one courageous act helped preserve the royal line through which Jesus Christ would eventually come. This is the extraordinary biblical account of the woman who stood between a murderous queen and a child God had not forgotten.
There was a little boy somewhere inside the palace who was supposed to be dead.
His grandmother wanted him dead.
The people who could have protected him were being slaughtered.
And the kingdom of Judah was about to discover what happens when someone becomes so desperate for power that even innocent children are considered enemies.
But in the middle of that bloodshed, one woman made a decision that would change the course of biblical history.
She did not announce it.
She did not gather an army.
She did not wait until the danger passed.
She took a child who was marked for death and hid him.
And for six long years, while a murderous queen occupied the throne, the future king of Judah remained alive because someone had the courage to protect him.
Her name was Jehosheba.
And if you have ever wondered whether the quiet things you do for God really matter, you need to know her story.
Because sometimes the person God uses to preserve something extraordinary is the person almost nobody notices.
And sometimes the most important victory happens long before anyone knows there was a battle.
The kingdom was drowning in blood.
The story begins in 2 Kings 11, following the death of King Ahaziah of Judah.
His mother, Athaliah, saw an opportunity.
Rather than allowing the legitimate royal succession to continue, she seized power through violence.
Scripture records the horror with devastating simplicity:
"When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal." — 2 Kings 11:1, KJV
Read that again.
She destroyed the royal offspring.
These were not foreign invaders threatening her kingdom.
They were members of the royal family.
Her own descendants were among those endangered by her ambition.
Imagine the terror inside that palace.
The footsteps in the corridors.
The sudden realization that royal blood no longer meant protection.
The children who could not understand why they were in danger.
And somewhere in that nightmare was Joash, an infant son of the dead king.
He was part of the family Athaliah intended to eliminate.
He had no army.
No political influence.
No ability to defend himself.
He was simply a child whose existence stood in the way of someone else's desire for control.
And then Jehosheba entered the story.

"But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain." — 2 Kings 11:2, KJV
There is something almost unbearable about the contrast.
Athaliah was destroying lives to secure a throne.
Jehosheba was risking her safety to preserve one.
One woman saw a child as an obstacle.
The other saw a life worth saving.
And the difference between them was not their access to power.
It was what they chose to do with the power they had.
Jehosheba's name deserves to be remembered.
In Hebrew, her name appears as יְהוֹשֶׁבַע (Yehoshevaʿ), commonly understood to carry the meaning "Yahweh has sworn" or "Yahweh is an oath."
Her name is especially meaningful when we remember the promise God had made concerning David's royal house.
In 2 Samuel 7:12–16, the Lord promised David an enduring dynasty. That promise would ultimately find its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the Son of David whose kingdom has no end.
But here, in the days of Athaliah, the Davidic royal line faced a terrifying threat.
A murderous ruler was trying to wipe out the royal descendants.
And the survival of one child became extraordinarily significant.

We must be careful not to claim more than Scripture says. The Bible does not record Jehosheba receiving a special vision or hearing an audible command from God. It does not tell us everything she thought or felt.
What it does tell us is enough.
She acted.
She rescued Joash.
She hid him and his nurse.
And the child survived.
Sometimes we want to know every detail of a biblical hero's heart.
But God has given us something more concrete.
