Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it once was.
But because through His death and resurrection, He can forgive, cleanse, reconcile sinners to God, and begin a transformation that human effort alone cannot accomplish.
He rewrites the direction of a surrendered life.
He gives a future to people who thought they had destroyed every possibility of one.
And He teaches us that our deepest identity need not remain chained to our worst decision.
Maybe you needed to hear that today.
Maybe you have been hiding behind the words, “It's complicated.”
Maybe it really is complicated.
But complexity does not remove our responsibility to obey God.
Maybe you have been saying, “Nobody understands what I'm going through.”
Perhaps they don't.
But Jesus does.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our great High Priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
He understands temptation without surrendering to it.
He understands suffering without becoming unjust.
And because He is merciful, we are invited to approach the throne of grace for mercy and help in our time of need.
So bring Him the truth.
Not the edited version.
Not the version that makes you look innocent.
Not the version designed to win an argument.
The truth.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you need to end an immoral relationship, seek the strength and appropriate support to do so.
If you have harmed someone, stop the harm and take responsibility.
If you have been abused, seek safety and trustworthy help; you are not required to place yourself back in danger to prove forgiveness.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you are exhausted from fighting temptation, do not mistake your exhaustion for defeat.
And if you have fallen, do not make your fall a permanent home.
Return to Christ.
Because the same Lord who says, “Repent,” is the Lord who gave His life so that repentant sinners might be forgiven.
And that is where this ancient command finally brings us.
Not merely to a forbidden marriage.
Not merely to a scandalous church.
Not merely to a discussion of Hebrew law.
But to the question every human heart must eventually face.
Will I allow God's Word to correct me, even when obedience costs me something I desperately want?
That is a question for the married and the unmarried.
For the pastor and the person in the back pew.
For the young believer discovering the faith and the Christian who has spent decades inside the church.
For the person who has sinned publicly and the person whose private life remains hidden.
And for those who have never thought of themselves as particularly sinful.
Because we all need more than religious information.
We need a Redeemer.
We need the cleansing mercy of Christ.
We need the Holy Spirit to reshape our desires.
We need the truth of Scripture to confront the lies we tell ourselves.
And we need a community that loves us enough to speak honestly and patiently walk with us toward maturity.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn painful Bible passages into sensational entertainment.
Not to use the failures of others as an opportunity to feel superior.
But to open the Scriptures, confront difficult truths, proclaim the Gospel, encourage repentance, and help people grow in a living relationship with Jesus Christ.

If this article has exposed something you have been avoiding, I want to invite you to respond—not to impress strangers, and not to disclose details that should remain private, but to take one honest step toward God.
You do not have to explain your private circumstances publicly.
God already knows.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not walking alone.
And if this message brought someone to your mind—a family member, a close friend, a struggling believer, or someone who has quietly drifted away from Christ—consider sharing it with them.
Not as an accusation.
As an invitation.
Because one shared message may become the beginning of a conversation someone has been afraid to start.
And one honest conversation may lead someone back to the Word of God.
There is another way you can help us continue this work.
It is not a condition for receiving His grace.
And it is not a substitute for supporting your local church or fulfilling other responsibilities God has entrusted to you.

But it can be a voluntary act of generosity—a ministry offering that helps sustain and expand the work of sharing biblical teaching, Gospel-centered articles, discipleship materials, and Christian encouragement with more people.
Scripture reminds us in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But an opportunity to participate in work you believe is helping people encounter His truth.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
More people reading Scripture.
More families having honest conversations about faith.
More believers learning to distinguish genuine grace from dangerous compromise.
More wounded hearts being pointed toward the compassion and truth of Jesus.
More people discovering that the Gospel is not merely a religious message to admire, but the good news of a Savior who calls us to follow Him.
The precious blood of Christ is infinitely more significant than anything we could ever contribute.
And that brings us back to where we began.
A man was forbidden to take his father's wife.
Even though she was not his mother.
Why?
Because God's boundaries were not determined merely by what a person could justify.
They were rooted in His holy design.
And when that same sin appeared in Corinth, the church was called not to celebrate it, but to mourn, confront it, and seek the offender's ultimate salvation.
That truth still matters.
We cannot call something holy simply because we desire it.
We cannot make disobedience righteous by finding someone who agrees with us.
We cannot use the word grace to silence the voice of repentance.
But neither should we imagine that a scandal places a repentant sinner beyond the mercy of Christ.
That would be another lie.
Jesus Christ is not powerless before our darkest chapters.
He is the crucified and risen Savior.
He is able to forgive.
He is able to cleanse.
He is able to restore fellowship with God.
He is able to teach a once-rebellious heart to love righteousness.
And He is worthy of our surrender.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, ask yourself one question before you close this article.
Am I asking Jesus to transform my life, or am I asking Him to approve the life I refuse to surrender?
Do not rush past that question.
Take it into prayer.
Open the Scriptures.
Tell God the truth.
And remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to manufacture a beautiful confession.
There is no need to pretend you are stronger than you are.
Come to Christ with a repentant heart.
Trust in His finished work.
And follow Him into the light.
Because the most devastating thing about sin is not simply that it can destroy what we love.
It is that it can persuade us to defend the very thing destroying us.
And the most beautiful thing about Jesus is that He loves sinners enough not to leave them enslaved to what is killing them.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter—but you must stop asking the darkness to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD FORBADE HIM FROM TOUCHING HIS OWN SISTER—EVEN WHEN THEY HAD DIFFERENT MOTHERS. BUT THE REASON GOES DEEPER THAN YOU THINK.
paragraphs: GOD FORBADE HIM FROM TOUCHING HIS OWN SISTER—EVEN WHEN THEY HAD DIFFERENT MOTHERS. BUT THE REASON GOES DEEPER THAN YOU THINK.

Leviticus 18:9 reveals a disturbing truth about forbidden intimacy, the sacredness of family, the danger of hidden desire, and the grace of Jesus Christ that can redeem even the most shame-filled past.
There are sins people commit in public.
And there are sins that survive because everyone involved has agreed to remain silent.

Some secrets are buried beneath family photographs. Some hide behind respectable reputations. Some have followed people from childhood into adulthood, leaving wounds they have never found the courage to describe.
And some begin with a terrifying confusion between love and desire.
Imagine growing up in a household where someone who should have protected your innocence became the person who violated it.
Imagine being told that what happened was normal.
That nobody needed to know.
That because you had different mothers, perhaps it wasn't really wrong.
Now imagine opening the Bible and discovering that thousands of years ago, God had already spoken directly against that very excuse.
Not vaguely.
Not reluctantly.
Not with some convenient loophole for complicated families.
He addressed it explicitly.
And what makes this passage so powerful is not merely what God prohibited.
It is what His prohibition reveals about the value of human beings, the responsibility of families, the holiness of our bodies, and the God who refuses to call exploitation love.
But there is another question waiting beneath this ancient command.
If God draws such a firm boundary around sexual sin, what happens to the person who has already crossed it?
Stay with that question.
Because the answer leads us from the terrifying seriousness of sin to the breathtaking mercy of Jesus Christ.
Leviticus 18:9 declares:
“The nakedness of thy sister, the daughter of thy father, or daughter of thy mother, whether she be born at home, or born abroad, even their nakedness thou shalt not uncover.” — Leviticus 18:9, KJV
Read that again.
The daughter of your father.
Or the daughter of your mother.
God did not say that the prohibition applied only when a brother and sister shared both parents.
He explicitly included siblings connected through either parent.
A half-sister was not an exception.
A different mother did not erase the family relationship.
A different household did not turn a forbidden sexual relationship into an acceptable one.
And this was not a minor detail accidentally inserted into ancient legislation.
It was part of God's deliberate instruction to Israel concerning sexual holiness.
To understand the weight of those words, we need to enter the Hebrew text.
The verse begins:
עֶרְוַת אֲחוֹתְךָ בַת־אָבִיךָ אוֹ בַת־אִמֶּךָ
ʿErvat ʾachotekha, bat-ʾavikha ʾo vat-ʾimmekha.
Literally, the opening identifies “the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father or the daughter of your mother.”

The Hebrew word עֶרְוָה (ʿervah) means nakedness or exposed private parts. In the legal language of Leviticus 18, the expression “uncover nakedness” functions as a sexual euphemism, referring to prohibited sexual intimacy.
The Hebrew אָחוֹת (ʾachot) means sister.
בַּת־אָבִיךָ (bat-ʾavikha) means daughter of your father.
בַּת־אִמֶּךָ (bat-ʾimmekha) means daughter of your mother.
These distinctions matter.
They demonstrate that the command was not restricted to full siblings. It deliberately covered a sister related through the father or through the mother.
The verse also includes language traditionally translated “born at home or born abroad,” indicating that differences in household circumstances did not remove the prohibition.
The text does not invite readers to search for technicalities.
It closes them.
And this is where an ancient command confronts a modern temptation.
Human beings are remarkably skilled at creating explanations for things they already want to do.
“We're not fully related.”
“We didn't grow up together.”
“Nobody will find out.”
“We both have feelings.”
“It doesn't hurt anyone.”
But Scripture does not determine holiness by the cleverness of our excuses.
God's moral boundaries are not invitations to negotiate.
They are commands to be understood and obeyed.
Yet before we go any further, we must be careful about something essential.
Leviticus 18:9 prohibits sexual relations between siblings. It does not prohibit ordinary, appropriate family affection, nor does it suggest that every sibling relationship is suspicious.
The subject is sexual intimacy, not innocent closeness.

And although the verse directly addresses a male Israelite, the moral concern is not that only men can sin sexually. The surrounding biblical teaching establishes sexual boundaries that protect the integrity of family relationships.
Leviticus 18:6 introduces the wider principle:
“None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.” — KJV
Notice how God concludes the command.
I am the LORD.
He does not appeal merely to public embarrassment.
He does not make the prohibition dependent upon whether the community discovers the relationship.
He grounds it in His own authority.
That matters because human desire can become an unreliable moral compass.
Not everything we strongly desire is good for us.
Not everything that feels intimate is holy.
Not every relationship that calls itself love reflects the character of God.
And not every secret deserves to remain hidden.
God established family relationships with responsibilities that must not be confused with sexual entitlement.
A sister is not a sexual possibility.
A brother is not entitled to his sister's body.
Family membership never grants someone permission to cross another person's bodily boundaries.
And where there is coercion, manipulation, intimidation, grooming, or abuse, the wrong becomes even more devastating.
No family member has the right to demand sexual access.
Not because they are older.
Not because they provide financial support.
Not because they claim affection.
Not because they invoke religion.
And certainly not because they insist that silence will protect the family's reputation.
A family secret does not become holy simply because exposing it would be painful.
Someone reading this may already be feeling uncomfortable.
Perhaps because this passage raises a question you have never considered.
Perhaps because it reminds you of something you witnessed.
Or perhaps because it touches a memory you have spent years trying to forget.
If someone sexually violated you, especially when you were a child or unable to give meaningful consent, the responsibility belongs to the person who violated you.
You were not responsible for preventing another person's wrongdoing.
You do not need to confess another person's abuse as though it were your own sin.
And forgiveness never requires you to return to danger, abandon appropriate boundaries, or conceal an ongoing crime.
God's holiness must never be weaponized against the wounded.
That distinction is not a modern attempt to soften Scripture.
It is consistent with Scripture's concern for justice, truth, and those who are vulnerable.
Psalm 82:3 calls for justice on behalf of the afflicted and needy.
And Jesus issued a grave warning against causing vulnerable little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
The God who commands sexual holiness is not indifferent to sexual harm.
But another difficult question remains.
If this boundary is so important, why do we encounter troubling family relationships in the Bible itself?
Consider Abraham and Sarah.
In Genesis 20:12, Abraham describes Sarah as the daughter of his father but not of his mother.
That makes their marriage especially challenging for readers who later encounter Leviticus 18:9.
The biblical account does not hide the complication.
Abraham lived centuries before the giving of the Mosaic Law at Sinai, and Genesis records the relationship without presenting that passage as a universal authorization for half-sibling marriage.
This distinction is crucial.
The Bible's record of an event is not automatically God's endorsement of that event.
Scripture frequently tells us what human beings did without instructing us to imitate everything they did.
The lives of the patriarchs include faith, obedience, deception, conflict, fear, and deeply complicated family histories.
Their stories reveal the need for God's grace, not the perfection of every human decision.
And when God later gave Israel explicit sexual boundaries, the command concerning siblings was unmistakable.

Leviticus 20:17 reinforces the seriousness of the matter by addressing a man who has sexual relations with his sister, whether she is his father's daughter or his mother's daughter, and prescribing a severe covenantal penalty.
These passages belong to Israel's ancient legal setting. Christians must not treat their civil penalties as permission to inflict private violence or punishment today.
Nevertheless, the prohibition itself is consistent with the broader biblical vision of sexual holiness.
And the New Testament makes that continuity especially significant.
In 1 Corinthians 5, the apostle Paul confronts a situation involving a man in a sexual relationship with his father's wife.
The Greek text of 1 Corinthians 5:1 includes the expression:
γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν
Gynaika tina tou patros echein.
The expression describes someone having his father's wife.
Paul does not celebrate this as personal freedom.
He confronts it as serious sexual immorality within the church.

The relationship in 1 Corinthians 5 is not identical to the half-sibling relationship prohibited in Leviticus 18:9. But Paul's response demonstrates that the coming of Christ did not make every previously forbidden family relationship sexually permissible.
Grace does not turn exploitation into righteousness.
Forgiveness does not redefine sexual immorality as holiness.
And Christian freedom is never permission to treat another person's body as an object for gratification.
Yet the gospel also refuses to leave us with condemnation as the final word.
Because if we are willing to examine our lives under God's holiness, we eventually encounter a truth that reaches beyond this particular prohibition.
We have all needed mercy.
Perhaps your struggle has never involved a forbidden family relationship.
Perhaps yours is pornography.
An affair.
A hidden addiction.
A pattern of manipulation.
A secret relationship you know you should end.
Or perhaps the sin that troubles your conscience is something entirely different.
The point is not that all sins cause identical harm or carry identical consequences.
They do not.
The point is that none of us can make ourselves righteous before God through denial, self-justification, or a carefully managed public image.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — KJV
Those words dismantle our superiority.
But they do not erase moral responsibility.
The person who deliberately harms another must not hide behind the statement that everyone sins.
Repentance requires truth.
Where abuse has occurred, repentance includes ending the abuse, refusing excuses, accepting appropriate accountability, and respecting the safety and autonomy of the harmed person.
Where a crime has been committed, spiritual language must never be used to obstruct lawful reporting or justice.
And where someone is trapped in an abusive situation, seeking protection and trustworthy assistance is not a failure of faith.
It can be an act of courage.
Now consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She stood in the middle of a public accusation.
The religious leaders wanted judgment.
The crowd was watching.
Her disgrace had become a spectacle.
And Jesus responded in a way that exposed the consciences of her accusers.
Eventually, the accusers departed.
Then Jesus spoke words that have echoed through centuries:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
There is an important textual detail here. John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and modern Bibles commonly identify its disputed textual status.
The account has been treasured in Christian tradition, but it should not be treated as though its manuscript history were beyond question.
Even so, the truths of mercy and repentance are clearly taught throughout the undisputed New Testament.
And notice the two truths expressed in the familiar account.
Jesus does not encourage sin.
And He does not portray mercy as something a sinner can never receive.
Go, and sin no more.
Not, “Your actions never mattered.”
Not, “Continue as you were.”
Not, “There is no such thing as wrongdoing.”
His mercy calls for a changed life.
That is the difference between grace and permission.
Permission says, “Stay exactly as you are, regardless of the harm.”
Grace says, “Come to Christ, receive mercy, and walk in a new direction.”
And nowhere is that invitation clearer than in the message of the cross.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity needed a more sophisticated way to defend its failures.
He came because sin is real, judgment is serious, and sinners cannot save themselves.
He lived without sin.
He gave Himself for our sins.
He died and rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed.
First Corinthians 6:9–11 speaks directly about people whose former lives were marked by serious sin, including sexual immorality.
After naming patterns of unrighteousness, Paul writes:
Such were some of you.
What extraordinary words.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because consequences magically disappeared.
Not because those who had been harmed were obligated to trust the people who harmed them again.
But because the saving work of Christ can change a person's standing before God and begin a genuinely transformed life.
The Greek text begins with a phrase of remarkable significance:
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε
Kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
The verb ἦτε (ēte) means “you were.”
Paul is speaking about the former condition of some believers in Corinth.
He is not promising that every consequence of their past will disappear.
He is proclaiming that their past sins do not have to remain the defining reality of their relationship with God.
This is the heart of redemption.
And this is why the message of Gospel Warrior is not merely a slogan.
The scandal may have been real.
The betrayal may have been real.
The guilt may have been real.
The wounds may still be real.
But Jesus Christ is not powerless in the presence of a ruined story.
He does not rewrite history by pretending evil never occurred.
He rewrites lives through truth, repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and the transforming work of His Spirit.
Sometimes that transformation includes confession.
Sometimes it requires ending a relationship.
Sometimes it means entering counseling, accepting legal consequences, or making restitution where appropriate.
Sometimes it means finally telling someone trustworthy what happened.
Sometimes it means learning that you are allowed to establish boundaries even with people who share your blood.
And sometimes it means admitting that the shame you have carried was never yours to carry.
That is why we must never confuse the person who was harmed with the person who caused the harm.
One may need protection, healing, and reassurance.
The other must face responsibility, repentance, and accountability.
Both need truth.
But their situations are not morally interchangeable.
And the gospel must never be distorted to make them so.
Perhaps you are reading this as someone who has deliberately crossed a sexual boundary.
Do not turn this article into another opportunity to explain away your choices.
Stop the wrongdoing.
Do not pressure anyone into silence.
Seek appropriate pastoral and professional help.
Accept accountability.
If someone has been harmed, prioritize their safety rather than your reputation.
Do not demand forgiveness as proof that they have healed.
And do not confuse being forgiven by God with being automatically entitled to renewed access to another person's life.
True repentance produces fruit.
It does not merely produce emotional speeches.
But perhaps you are reading as someone who was betrayed.
Someone who was manipulated into believing that affection required surrendering your boundaries.
Someone who has spent years wondering why you froze, why you stayed silent, or why you could not stop what happened.
Hear this carefully.
Another person's sin against you does not make you spiritually contaminated.
Your worth is not determined by what someone did to your body.
Your dignity has not been erased.
You do not have to expose your story publicly to prove that you are healing.
And you do not have to rush forgiveness or reconciliation to satisfy someone else's expectations.
Christ's compassion is not reserved for people whose lives look untouched by tragedy.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” — KJV
Sometimes the most courageous prayer is not eloquent.
It is simply:
“Jesus, help me.”
Three words.
Spoken through tears.
Spoken after years of silence.
Spoken by someone who no longer knows how to explain what hurts.
And sometimes that prayer becomes the beginning of a journey toward healing.
This is why Leviticus 18:9 deserves more than a quick reading or a sensational headline.
It reminds us that God's boundaries are not arbitrary inconveniences.
They reveal that sexual intimacy carries moral responsibilities.
They teach us that family relationships must not be exploited.
They confront our habit of manufacturing exceptions for forbidden desires.
And they lead us to recognize how desperately humanity needs the holiness, wisdom, mercy, and saving grace of God.
The passage is not an invitation to become fascinated with another family's scandal.
It is an invitation to examine our own hearts.
Are we honoring God's boundaries?
Are we protecting the vulnerable?
Are we making excuses for behavior Scripture calls wrong?
Are we using religious language to conceal wrongdoing?
Are we extending compassion to people who have been wounded?
And most importantly, are we allowing Jesus Christ to transform the way we live?
There is a world of difference between knowing a Bible verse and surrendering to the Lord who gave it.
You can quote Leviticus and still mistreat people.
You can defend biblical morality and still conceal injustice.
You can appear righteous in public while refusing repentance in private.
Jesus warned against religious hypocrisy for precisely this reason.
Holiness is not a costume.
It is not a social media identity.
It is not a weapon for humiliating those whose struggles differ from ours.
It is a life increasingly shaped by obedience to God, love for our neighbors, and the transforming grace of Christ.
And that transformation is not something we manufacture through willpower alone.
It is the work of God in those who belong to Jesus Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
A new creation.
Not a flawless person who will never struggle again.
Not someone whose past has been erased from every human memory.
But someone whose life has been brought under the saving lordship of Jesus Christ.
Someone who can begin walking in truth.
Someone who no longer needs to defend sin as though it were a permanent identity.
Someone who can pursue holiness without pretending to be beyond the need for grace.
And perhaps that is the message you needed today.
Not another excuse.
Not another accusation.
Not another reason to hide.
But a reminder that Jesus Christ calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
You do not need to reveal private details, identify anyone who harmed you, or make a public confession to strangers.
Your dignity and safety matter.

And if you have witnessed Christ bring genuine transformation into your life, consider sharing a testimony of His goodness. Someone who feels beyond redemption may need to hear that God's grace is not exhausted.
There is also someone in your circle who may need this message.
A friend who has mistaken secrecy for safety.
A believer wrestling with temptation.
A parent who needs to understand why protecting children matters more than protecting appearances.
A person whose past has convinced them that God could never welcome them.
Or someone who has never understood why biblical holiness and divine compassion belong together.
It is about knowing Jesus Christ and being transformed by His grace.
If these messages have helped you grow, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people encounter biblical truth, grow in discipleship, and discover the hope of the gospel beyond a single social media post.
We want these resources to keep reaching people who are hungry for Scripture, including those who may not have the means to purchase Christian books or discipleship materials.
Scripture teaches us that generosity should arise from a willing heart.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
Not because someone has frightened you into believing that God will be disappointed if you do not pay.
But willingly.
Prayerfully.
Joyfully.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, tools for reflection, or thoughtful gifts for people you love.
But the greatest reason to join is not merchandise.
It is the opportunity to participate in sharing biblical truth and helping more people encounter the message of Jesus Christ.
Invite someone to read Scripture.
Pray for a person who is struggling.
Encourage someone to seek help.
Speak the truth without cruelty.
Show compassion without compromising righteousness.
Glorifying God is not confined to financial support. It is reflected in a life of faith, obedience, generosity, justice, love, and worship.
The gospel is not for sale.
It is proclaimed freely to everyone who will hear.
So as we return one final time to Leviticus 18:9, remember what this ancient command teaches.
A different mother does not make a sister sexually available.
A shared father does not make forbidden intimacy acceptable.
A hidden relationship does not become righteous because it escapes public attention.
And a sincere feeling does not override the moral boundaries God has revealed.
But remember something else.
The God who exposes sin also calls sinners to repentance.
The God who commands justice cares for those who have been harmed.
And the Savior who died for our sins and rose again offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
Perhaps you came to this article curious about an unusual Old Testament prohibition.
Perhaps you stayed because the words became uncomfortably personal.
Perhaps you discovered a truth you needed to confront.
Or perhaps you found language for a wound you had never been able to name.
Wherever you find yourself, do not leave with only a shocking fact about ancient Israel.
Leave with a clearer vision of God's holiness.
A deeper respect for human dignity.
A stronger commitment to protecting the vulnerable.
A more serious understanding of repentance.
And a greater appreciation for the grace revealed in Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest message of Scripture is not that human beings have never fallen into terrible sin.
It is that God, in His holiness and mercy, has acted through Jesus Christ to save sinners and call them into newness of life.
The cross does not make evil insignificant.
It reveals how seriously God takes sin—and how extraordinary His saving love truly is.
The past may explain the scars you carry, but it does not have the authority to write the final sentence of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD NEVER PROMISED TO GIVE YOU EVERYTHING YOU WANT. SO WHAT DID HE REALLY MEAN?
paragraphs: GOD NEVER PROMISED TO GIVE YOU EVERYTHING YOU WANT. SO WHAT DID HE REALLY MEAN?

“Delight yourself in the Lord, and He will give you the desires of your heart.” — Psalm 37:4. One of the most beautiful promises in Scripture has also become one of the most misunderstood. And what it actually means might break your heart before it sets you free.
What if the Bible verse you've been holding on to for years doesn't mean what you thought it meant?
What if you've been praying, waiting, believing, crying, and wondering why God hasn't given you the very thing you thought He promised?
And what if the answer isn't that God has forgotten you?
What if He's been loving you too deeply to give you something that would eventually destroy you?

Stay with me. Because somewhere between the promise you memorized and the disappointment you've been carrying, there is a truth about God's heart that could change the way you pray for the rest of your life.
And it begins with a question most of us are afraid to ask.
Do you really want God? Or do you want what you believe God can give you?
That question hurts.
Especially when you've been faithful.
Especially when you've prayed the same prayer for years.
Especially when you've watched someone else receive the very blessing you've been begging God for.
You attended church. You worshiped when you didn't feel like worshiping. You gave when you had little. You served when you were exhausted. You tried to obey even when obedience cost you something.
And somewhere along the way, you held on to Psalm 37:4 like a signed agreement from heaven.
“Delight yourself in the Lord, and He will give you the desires of your heart.”
So you delighted.
Or at least you tried.
You prayed for that marriage.
That baby.
That healing.
That job.
That financial breakthrough.
That restored relationship.
That one opportunity that could finally change everything.
But the months became years.
The door stayed closed.
The diagnosis didn't change.
The person you loved walked away.
The promotion went to somebody else.
And the prayer you once whispered with confidence eventually became a question you barely had the strength to speak.
“Lord, what happened to Your promise?”
Perhaps you never said it aloud because you were afraid it would sound like unbelief.
But God already knows.
He knows the disappointment behind your smile.
He knows how difficult it has become to celebrate other people's blessings while you're still waiting for your own.
He knows the prayers you stopped praying because hoping again felt more painful than accepting defeat.
And He is not threatened by your honest questions.
But He loves you too much to leave you with a misunderstanding of His Word.
Because Psalm 37:4 is not a blank check.
It is an invitation into something infinitely greater.
And to understand it, we need to return to what God actually said.
The original Hebrew of Psalm 37:4 reads:
וְהִתְעַנַּג עַל־יְהוָה וְיִתֶּן־לְךָ מִשְׁאֲלֹת לִבֶּךָ
Ve-hit'annag 'al-YHWH, ve-yitten lekha mish'alot libbekha.
A close English rendering is:
“Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the requests of your heart.”
The Hebrew verb הִתְעַנַּג (hit'annag) comes from a root associated with delight, pleasure, and enjoyment.
It does not mean merely performing religious activities so God will reward you.
It speaks of finding your delight in the LORD Himself.
Not merely in His blessings.
Not merely in His provision.
Not merely in His answers.
In Him.
The expression מִשְׁאֲלֹת לִבֶּךָ (mish'alot libbekha) refers to the requests or desires of your heart.
And this is important.
The verse genuinely promises that God gives the desires of the heart. We should not rewrite it as though it simply says, “God will change all your desires and never grant any requests.”
But neither should we tear the promise away from its context and turn it into a guarantee that God will fulfill every personal ambition.
Psalm 37 tells us what kind of life surrounds this promise.
“Trust in the LORD, and do good” (verse 3).
“Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him” (verse 5).
“Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him” (verse 7).
The psalm was written in a world where wicked people sometimes prospered while those seeking righteousness suffered.
Sound familiar?
David wasn't teaching people how to use God to acquire everything they wanted.
He was teaching them how to trust God when life seemed unfair.
How to remain faithful when evil appeared successful.
How to wait when righteousness seemed unrewarded.
How to find security in the LORD instead of becoming consumed by what other people possessed.
And suddenly the promise begins to look different.
Delighting in God is not a technique for getting your way. It is learning to treasure God above your way.
That doesn't mean your dreams are automatically sinful.
Wanting to marry isn't sinful.
Wanting children isn't sinful.
Wanting financial stability isn't sinful.
Wanting healing isn't sinful.
Wanting to build something meaningful, provide for your family, or escape a painful situation isn't sinful.
God is not offended by every human longing.
Jesus Himself taught us to ask our Father for daily bread (Matthew 6:11).
But there is a difference between bringing your desires to God and making your desires the condition of your devotion.
There is a difference between praying, “Father, I would love to have this,” and quietly deciding, “Father, if You don't give me this, I don't know whether I can trust You anymore.”
And that is where this verse becomes deeply personal.
Because sometimes what we call faith is actually an attempt to control the outcome.
We pray.
We fast.
We give.
We serve.
And without realizing it, we begin treating obedience like a payment toward the future we want.
We never say it directly.
But somewhere in our hearts, the agreement becomes:
“God, I'll do my part. Now You do Yours.”
Then disappointment arrives.
And suddenly our relationship with God feels like a transaction that went wrong.
But Jesus did not die on the cross to become the manager of our wish lists.
He died to reconcile sinners to the Father.
To forgive us.
To rescue us from sin.
To give us a new heart.
To bring us into eternal life with God.
The Gospel is not that Jesus guarantees every earthly dream.
The Gospel is that Jesus gives Himself to people who could never earn Him.
And there is no greater gift.
But perhaps you're thinking, “That sounds beautiful. Yet what about the desire I still carry? What about the prayer that hasn't been answered?”
I want you to remember a garden.
Not the Garden of Eden.
Another garden.
Gethsemane.
There, under the crushing weight of what lay ahead, Jesus prayed.
Luke 22:42 records His words:
“Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
In Greek, that final surrender is expressed:
πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω.
Plēn mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō.
“Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
Think about that.
The sinless Son of God expressed a genuine desire to the Father.
He did not pretend the suffering ahead was pleasant.
He did not deny the anguish.
He prayed honestly.
And then He surrendered.
Not because His Father was cruel.
Not because prayer was meaningless.
But because the Father's saving purpose would be accomplished through the cross.
The cup was not removed.
Jesus went to Calvary.
And through His suffering, sinners can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
Now consider what that means for the way we understand answered prayer.
If even Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane did not result in the removal of suffering, how could we conclude that Psalm 37:4 guarantees every believer a life in which every desired outcome must happen?
Our Savior showed us that faithful prayer can include both honest longing and complete surrender.
And sometimes the deepest expression of trust is not, “God, I know You will give me exactly what I asked.”
Sometimes it is:
“Father, You know what I want. You know why I want it. You know how much it hurts. But I trust Your wisdom more than my understanding.”
That is not weak faith.
That is faith learning to kneel.
And perhaps this is where your heart needs to hear something important.
A prayer that receives a different answer is not necessarily a prayer that was ignored.
The apostle Paul knew this.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7–10, Paul describes a painful affliction he calls a thorn in the flesh.
Three times he pleaded with the Lord for it to leave him.
Three times.
This was not someone unfamiliar with faith.
This was Paul.
A man who preached Christ, suffered for the Gospel, and witnessed extraordinary works of God.
Yet the affliction remained.
And the Lord answered:
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”
Paul wanted the thorn removed.
God gave him sustaining grace.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Paul lacked faith.
It does not say he failed to claim the promise correctly.
It does not say he needed to give more money, repeat a declaration, or prove his devotion.
Instead, the Lord taught him to depend on divine strength in human weakness.
That matters.
Because someone reading this has been quietly blaming themselves for an unanswered prayer.
Maybe you thought your mother died because you didn't pray hard enough.
Maybe you thought your marriage ended because your faith wasn't strong enough.
Maybe you believed that if you had fasted longer, given more, or spoken more positively, everything would have turned out differently.
Please hear what Scripture actually teaches.
God invites us to pray in faith, but faith is not a supernatural mechanism that forces Him to fulfill our preferred outcome.
And suffering is not automatic proof that you have failed Him.
Sometimes faithful believers suffer deeply.
Sometimes righteous people wait for years.
Sometimes Christians die without seeing a particular earthly desire fulfilled.

Hebrews 11 celebrates people who experienced remarkable deliverance, but it also remembers faithful people who endured persecution, deprivation, and death without receiving everything promised during their earthly lives.
Their faith was not worthless.
Their hope reached beyond this present world.
And so does ours.
But there is another side to this truth.
God does answer prayers.
He does provide.
He does heal according to His will.
He does open doors.
He does restore relationships.
He does give good gifts.
James 1:17 reminds us that every good and perfect gift comes from above.
We do not need to become suspicious of blessings to avoid misunderstanding Psalm 37:4.
We simply need to remember that blessings are gifts, not proof that God loves one person more than another.
And an unanswered request is not proof that God loves someone less.
The cross has already settled the question of whether God loves His people.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when we finally became successful.
Not when our marriages became perfect.
Not when our bank accounts recovered.
Not when our prayers were answered exactly as expected.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is grace.
And grace changes everything.
But there is still something about Psalm 37:4 that many of us miss.
When God becomes the delight of your heart, your relationship with your own desires begins to change.
Not always instantly.
Not without struggle.
Not through pretending you no longer want what you want.
But as you walk with Christ, His Word begins to confront what is sinful, refine what is good, and reshape what matters most.
The desire for revenge may become a longing for justice without hatred.
The hunger for recognition may become a desire to serve faithfully even when nobody applauds.
The obsession with wealth may become a longing for provision, generosity, and contentment.
The desperate need to be chosen by another person may become a growing confidence that your worth is not determined by human rejection.
This is part of spiritual transformation.
Romans 12:2 speaks of being transformed by the renewal of the mind.
Philippians 2:13 teaches that God works in His people both to will and to work for His good pleasure.
That doesn't mean every longing disappears.
It means our desires are no longer meant to rule us.
Christ becomes Lord over them.
And sometimes He grants the very thing we have requested.
Sometimes He calls us to wait.
Sometimes He redirects our path.
Sometimes He gives us strength to endure what we desperately wanted to escape.
And sometimes we do not understand His providence in this life.
We must be careful not to pretend we know God's secret reasons for every disappointment.
Not every closed door can be confidently explained as protection.
Not every tragedy should be described as a hidden blessing.
And not every painful loss will make sense before eternity.
Scripture does not give us permission to invent explanations for another person's suffering.
It gives us something more trustworthy.
A crucified and risen Savior who is worthy of our trust even when we cannot explain our circumstances.
And maybe that is what you need tonight.
Not another person telling you that your breakthrough is guaranteed next week.
Not another promise that if you perform one more religious act, heaven will finally release what you want.
Not another message that makes you feel guilty for being disappointed.
Maybe you need permission to come before God without pretending.
To tell Him that you're tired.
That you're confused.
That you still want the thing you've been asking for.
That you're struggling to trust Him.
And then, by His grace, to say:
“Lord, even here, teach me to delight in You.”
Because the greatest tragedy would not be reaching the end of your life without receiving every earthly thing you desired.
The greater tragedy would be receiving everything you ever wanted and never coming to know the Savior your soul truly needs.
Jesus asked in Mark 8:36:
“For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?”
Imagine gaining the career.
The house.
The money.
The recognition.
The relationship.
The admiration.
Imagine finally having everything that once kept you awake at night.
And still being separated from God.
What would any of it be worth?
This is why Jesus must remain at the center of our understanding of blessing.
He is not merely the One who helps us build the life we have imagined.
He is the Savior who calls us to repent, believe the Gospel, deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
He is the One who forgives sins.
The One who welcomes the repentant.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who gives eternal life to those who trust in Him.
And the One who will one day make all things new.
Psalm 37:4 ultimately belongs within that greater story of trusting the LORD, receiving His goodness, and resting in His righteous purposes.
It is not permission to turn God into a servant of our ambitions.
It is an invitation to discover that God Himself is worthy of our deepest affection.
And here is the beautiful paradox.
When Christ becomes your greatest treasure, you can still pray boldly for the things you desire.
You can still ask for healing.
You can still ask for a spouse.
You can still ask for children.
You can still ask for provision.
You can still ask for reconciliation.
You can still ask for an opportunity that seems impossible.
You do not have to kill every dream to prove you love God.
But you can place every dream into the hands of the One who loved you enough to bear your sins on the cross.
You can ask without demanding.
Hope without presuming.
Wait without pretending.
Grieve without abandoning faith.
And rejoice without making earthly blessings your god.
That is a freedom the world cannot manufacture.
Because if your peace depends on getting everything you want, your peace will always be vulnerable to losing it.
But if your deepest hope rests in Jesus Christ, even your unanswered prayers cannot separate you from His love.
Romans 8:38–39 assures believers that neither death nor life, nor anything else in all creation, can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Not the diagnosis.
Not the rejection.
Not the financial struggle.
Not the years of waiting.
Not the unanswered question.
Your circumstances may change.
Your plans may collapse.
Your strength may fail.
But the risen Christ remains faithful.
And perhaps, after all these years, you can finally read Psalm 37:4 without treating it as a contract for your preferred future.
You can read it as a call to love the LORD Himself.
To trust His character.
To commit your way to Him.
To pray honestly.
To surrender humbly.
To receive His gifts gratefully.
And to remember that your greatest inheritance is not something you can purchase, achieve, or lose to another person.
It is life in Jesus Christ.
Maybe you came into this article hoping to find out how to get God to give you what you want.
And somewhere along the way, you discovered a harder, holier question.
What if the greatest answer to your prayer is not that God gives you everything you desire, but that through Christ, He teaches your heart to desire Him above everything?
If that question has exposed something in you, don't run from it.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you've been using prayer to bargain with God, repent and return to Him.
If you've been carrying disappointment, tell Him.
If you've allowed bitterness to grow, confess it.
If you've been seeking His gifts more than His presence, ask Him to renew your love.
There is forgiveness for the repentant sinner.
There is mercy for the weary believer.
There is grace for the person who has wandered.
There is hope for the heart that has forgotten how to trust.
Not because we have finally prayed perfectly.
But because Jesus Christ is a perfect Savior.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Him, today you can turn from sin and place your trust in the crucified and risen Lord.
You don't need to manufacture a flawless spiritual performance.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
You can pray honestly:

“Lord Jesus, I confess that I have often wanted Your blessings more than I have wanted You. Forgive me for treating Your promises as guarantees of my own plans. Forgive my pride, my unbelief, and the ways I have allowed disappointment to harden my heart. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to trust You, to treasure You, and to follow You even when I don't understand what You're doing. Change the desires that lead me away from You. Strengthen the desires that honor You. And when my prayers are not answered the way I hoped, remind me that Your grace is still sufficient. In Your name, Jesus, amen.”
If you prayed that sincerely, don't keep your struggle hidden behind a religious smile.
You don't need to share private details. But sometimes an honest sentence becomes the beginning of encouragement for someone else who thought they were struggling alone.

And if God has already taught you something through a season of waiting, share your testimony. Not to suggest that everyone's story will end the same way, but to remind another believer that God's grace is real even in the waiting.
There is someone on your Facebook friends list who is silently questioning God's goodness because a prayer hasn't been answered.
Someone who still goes to church but has begun to lose hope.
Someone who thinks God has abandoned them because life didn't turn out the way they expected.
Not merely to help a page grow.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, receive encouragement, face honest conviction, and keep returning to the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
And if you've been blessed by this ministry, there is another meaningful way you can help us continue.
Scripture teaches us that giving should be willing, not pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver and that giving is not to be done reluctantly or under compulsion.
Christ has already accomplished what money could never purchase.

But if you believe in this mission, if the Lord has given you the ability to support it, and if you want to help more people encounter the truth of the Gospel, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside us.
These are simply tokens of appreciation. The true purpose of this ministry is not merchandise.
It is helping people grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
Because this has never been about buying God's favor.
It has always been about proclaiming His grace.
And that brings us back to the promise that started everything.
“Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart.”
Maybe the desire you've been praying about will be granted.
Maybe the answer will come after years of waiting.
Maybe God will lead you somewhere you never expected.
Maybe some questions will remain unanswered this side of eternity.
But you do not have to wait for every desire to be fulfilled before you begin delighting in Him.
You can begin today.
Right here.
With the life you actually have.
With the wounds you're still carrying.
With the prayers that still make you cry.
With the dreams that haven't happened.
With the sins you need to confess.
With the grace you desperately need.
Come to Christ.
Not because He has promised to give you everything you ever wanted.
But because He is worthy of your heart even when everything else is uncertain.
And when you finally understand that, Psalm 37:4 stops being a verse you use to demand your preferred outcome.
It becomes an invitation to discover the One your soul was created to know.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners, forgave the guilty, restored the broken, and rose victorious over death is still calling people to Himself.
Your disappointment does not have to become the end of your faith.
Your past does not have to become the final word over your future.
Your sin does not have to remain your master.
In Christ there is forgiveness, redemption, and new life.
Because the story God is writing through His grace is greater than the story you once thought you needed.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing you will ever discover is this:
You may not receive everything your heart once wanted, but in Jesus Christ, you can receive the Savior your heart has always needed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LET HIM KISS ME WITH THE KISSES OF HIS MOUTH.” — YES, THAT IS IN YOUR BIBLE. BUT HAVE YOU EVER ASKED WHY GOD PUT IT THERE?
paragraphs: “LET HIM KISS ME WITH THE KISSES OF HIS MOUTH.” — YES, THAT IS IN YOUR BIBLE. BUT HAVE YOU EVER ASKED WHY GOD PUT IT THERE?

Before you blush, skip the verse, or turn it into something purely spiritual, understand this: God was never embarrassed by the love He created. And hidden within this ancient love poem is a truth about desire, intimacy, faithfulness, and the kind of love our wounded world is desperately trying to find.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.” — Song of Solomon 1:2 (KJV)
Yes. You read that correctly.
Not from a romance novel.
Not from a forbidden manuscript.
Not from some scandalous love letter discovered beneath the ruins of an ancient palace.
From the Bible.
The same Bible that declares, “Be ye holy; for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16).
The same Bible that warns against sexual immorality.
The same Bible that tells us to flee youthful lusts.
And there, almost startlingly, in the middle of Holy Scripture, a woman speaks with breathtaking honesty about her desire to be kissed.
Not merely noticed.
Not admired from a distance.
Kissed.
And the Holy Spirit, who inspired Scripture, did not erase her words.
Think about that.
Somewhere along the way, many Christians became so uncomfortable discussing romantic desire that we began treating the subject as though holiness required pretending it did not exist.
We taught people how to avoid temptation, but sometimes forgot to teach them how to understand love.
We warned young people about lust without always explaining the beauty of faithful intimacy.
We spoke about marriage as a responsibility while rarely celebrating the affection God intended to flourish within it.
And when people encountered verses like Song of Songs 1:2, they sometimes laughed nervously, changed the subject, or hurried toward a spiritual interpretation that made the human romance disappear.
But what if we have been rushing past something beautiful?
What if the scandal is not that God allowed these words into Scripture?
What if the scandal is that we have sometimes been more embarrassed by God's good creation than God Himself?

Stay with me, because this ancient poem has something to say to the person who longs to be loved, the spouse who feels forgotten, the believer struggling with shame, and the wounded soul wondering whether love can ever feel safe again.
And to understand it, we must begin where the text begins.
With a woman who is not afraid to speak.
In the original Hebrew, Song of Songs 1:2 opens:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
The verb yishaqeni expresses the woman's wish that her beloved would kiss her.
The word neshiqot means “kisses.”
And pihu means “his mouth.”
There is no need to invent a secret meaning to make the sentence acceptable.
It is romantic language.
Personal language.
The language of longing.
The next Hebrew phrase is equally revealing:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Ki-tovim dodekha miyyayin.
Literally, “For your loves are better than wine.”
Here, dodekha refers to expressions of romantic love or affection. English translations commonly render the expression as “your love” or “your caresses.”
The Hebrew word yayin means wine, an image associated in biblical poetry with celebration, pleasure, and gladness.
She is saying that the affection of her beloved is more delightful than one of life's most celebrated pleasures.
Notice something remarkable.
The woman begins by speaking about her beloved in the third person: “Let him kiss me.”
Then she turns toward him directly: “For your love is better than wine.”
It is as though longing suddenly becomes an encounter.
The beloved is no longer merely someone she thinks about.
He is someone she addresses.
That is the intimacy of poetry.
And that is how the Song begins.
Not with an argument.
Not with a command.
Not with a theological lecture.
With desire.
But here is where careful reading matters.
The Song of Songs is ancient Hebrew love poetry. It celebrates the beauty of mutual affection, attraction, longing, delight, and committed love between a man and a woman.
Its language is sometimes tender, sometimes playful, sometimes intensely passionate.
And yes, sometimes startlingly physical.
That does not make it unholy.
It makes it a testimony to the goodness of embodied human love within God's created order.
Genesis tells us that God made humanity male and female and called His creation very good (Genesis 1:27, 31).
Before sin entered the world, Adam and Eve were naked and unashamed (Genesis 2:25).
Shame, exploitation, betrayal, and distorted desire belong to the tragedy of the Fall.
The human body itself is not the enemy.
Nor is faithful marital affection.
The enemy is sin, which takes what God made good and twists it away from His purposes.
And perhaps that is where this verse begins touching wounds we do not usually discuss in church.
Because not everyone reading these words has experienced love as something beautiful.
Some people hear the word kiss and remember tenderness.
Others remember betrayal.
Some remember their wedding day.
Others remember the person who promised forever and left.
Some know the comfort of being held by someone faithful.
Others know what it feels like to lie beside a spouse and still feel painfully alone.
And some carry memories they never asked for, where affection was used as a disguise for manipulation, coercion, or abuse.
If that is your story, please hear this.
What happened to you does not define your worth, and someone else's misuse of intimacy does not make you unclean.
God does not call exploitation love.
He does not call coercion romance.
He does not ask victims to pretend that betrayal was beautiful.
Biblical love cannot be separated from truth, faithfulness, dignity, and care.
The Song's celebration of mutual desire must never be twisted into permission to demand physical affection from another person.
Love does not erase another person's freedom or safety.
And the fact that Scripture celebrates romantic intimacy does not mean every believer must marry, experience sexual desire, or enter a romantic relationship to live a complete life.
Jesus Himself lived a fully holy human life without marrying.
The apostle Paul honored singleness as a genuine gift and calling (1 Corinthians 7:7–8).
Marriage is good.
Singleness can also be good.
Neither determines a person's value before God.
Our deepest worth is not established by whether another human being wants to kiss us.
It is established by the God who made us and, through Christ, calls us to Himself.
But we must not rush past the human beauty of the Song.
Because its poetry also confronts a painful misunderstanding that has wounded generations of believers.
Holiness is not the absence of affection.
And passion is not automatically the presence of sin.
The question is not merely whether desire exists.
The question is what desire loves, what it seeks, how it treats another person, and whether it submits to the wisdom and holiness of God.
A husband who cherishes his wife is not becoming less spiritual by expressing tenderness.
A wife who delights in her husband is not becoming less godly by expressing romantic affection.
Marriage was never intended to be merely two exhausted people sharing bills, responsibilities, and a roof while affection slowly disappears.
Scripture calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25).
That is not a command to dominate.
It is a call to sacrificial, self-giving love.
And the Song reminds us that marital love can include delight, admiration, pursuit, tenderness, and joy.
But there is another danger we must avoid.
We must not turn this poem into a promise that every relationship will feel like poetry every day.
Real love sometimes looks less like a passionate embrace and more like a tired husband washing dishes while his wife rests.
Sometimes it looks like an honest apology after a painful argument.
Sometimes it looks like staying beside someone through sickness.
Sometimes it looks like listening instead of defending yourself.
Sometimes it looks like rebuilding trust, slowly and truthfully, after damage has been done.
Romance can be beautiful.
But covenant faithfulness is not measured only by romantic intensity.
The love celebrated in Scripture is never meant to excuse selfishness simply because the emotions feel powerful.
And that brings us to a line later in the Song that deserves to be heard alongside its opening invitation.
“...love is strong as death...” — Song of Solomon 8:6 (KJV)
A few words later, the poet declares:
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it...” — Song of Solomon 8:7 (KJV)
The book that begins with a longing for kisses eventually speaks of a love so enduring that even overwhelming waters cannot extinguish it.
Do you see the movement?
Attraction matters.
Affection matters.
But enduring love must become more than a moment of desire.
It must have depth.
Faithfulness.
A strength that does not disappear when life becomes difficult.
And this is where the Song begins opening a window toward an even greater biblical story.
We need to be careful here.
Song of Songs 1:2 does not explicitly say that the kiss represents Jesus, salvation, the Holy Spirit, or a particular spiritual experience.
Its immediate meaning concerns the longing of a woman for her beloved.
We should honor that meaning rather than forcing every romantic image into a hidden Christian code.
Yet the Bible also uses marriage and bridegroom imagery to reveal the covenant relationship between God and His people.
The prophets speak of the Lord's covenant love for Israel (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19–20).
John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the bridegroom (John 3:29).
Paul uses marriage to illuminate the relationship between Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32).
And Revelation celebrates the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9).
These passages do not erase the human romance of Song of Songs.
They help Christians see that faithful human love belongs within a much larger biblical vision of covenant love.
A vision that reaches its greatest revelation in Jesus Christ.
And here, the story becomes personal.
Because some of us have spent years chasing the feeling of being wanted.
We wanted someone to choose us.
Someone to see us.
Someone to stay.
Someone to look at our scars and not turn away.
Maybe you tried to find that assurance in a relationship.
Maybe you kept forgiving promises that were never followed by change.
Maybe you confused being pursued with being cherished.
Maybe you accepted attention because you were starving for affection.
And maybe the hardest truth is that even after someone loved you, the emptiness remained.
Not because their love meant nothing.
But because no finite human being can carry the weight of being your savior.
No spouse can forgive your sins.
No romantic partner can conquer death.
No human kiss can reconcile you to God.
No relationship, however beautiful, can become the foundation of your eternal hope.
That place belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
And this is why the Gospel is not simply another love story.
It is the announcement that the holy God we have sinned against has acted in grace to save sinners through His Son.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Read those words again.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we made ourselves attractive to God.
Not after we finally overcame every temptation.
Not after our past became presentable.
Not after we learned to sound holy in public.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
The love of God in the Gospel is not sentimental approval of everything we do.
It is holy, costly, redeeming love.
Jesus did not come to tell us that sin does not matter.
He came because sin matters so profoundly that only His saving work could accomplish our reconciliation with God.
At the cross, divine justice and mercy are not treated as enemies.
Christ bears sin's judgment on behalf of His people, and forgiveness is offered through Him.
His resurrection declares that death does not have the final word.
And those who repent and believe in Him receive forgiveness and new life.
That is love beyond romantic poetry.
Not because romantic love is worthless.
But because the Gospel answers a deeper need.
The need to be reconciled to the God who created us.
Now think about another kiss recorded in Scripture.
Not the kiss of a lover.
The kiss of a betrayer.
In the garden of Gethsemane, Judas approached Jesus and identified Him with a kiss.
Luke 22:48 records Jesus asking:
“Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?”
What a terrible contrast.
In Song of Songs, a kiss expresses desired affection.
In Gethsemane, a kiss becomes the instrument of betrayal.
The same human gesture.
Two radically different meanings.
One associated with love.
The other with treachery.
And Jesus knew.
He knew who Judas was.
He knew what the kiss meant.
He knew the suffering that awaited Him.
Yet He continued toward the cross.
Not because betrayal was good.
Not because evil was harmless.
But because the Son of God had come to fulfill the Father's saving purpose.
And suddenly the distance between the beauty of Song of Songs and the agony of Gethsemane reveals something about our fallen world.
We were created for truthful love.
Yet sin has taught us to disguise betrayal as affection.
We were created for faithfulness.
Yet we have learned how easily promises can be broken.
We were created to love God and our neighbors.
Yet we have often loved ourselves at their expense.
And every one of us needs grace.
Not merely the person who betrayed us.
Not merely the person who hurt us.
Us.
We may not all have committed the same sins.
But all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23).
And none of us can rescue ourselves by pretending otherwise.
Perhaps you have never betrayed anyone with a kiss.
But have you ever said, “I love You, Lord,” while deliberately holding on to something He calls you to surrender?
Have you ever worshiped with your lips while your heart remained distant?
Have you ever wanted God's comfort while resisting His correction?
Have you ever asked Him to bless a relationship you knew was leading you away from obedience?
These are not questions meant to crush a wounded conscience.
They are invitations to honest repentance.
Because grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace brings sinners into the light.
And Jesus Christ is not afraid of what the light reveals.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memory of his own words.
The realization that fear had exposed the weakness beneath his confidence.
But after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
And Christ's mercy was greater than Peter's failure.
That is not cheap grace.
That is restoration.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to understand that distinction tonight.
You cannot undo every consequence of yesterday.
You cannot demand that every person you hurt trust you again.
You cannot erase another person's pain simply by saying you have changed.
But you can repent.
You can confess what is true.
You can turn from sin.
You can seek to make things right where possible.
You can receive the forgiveness offered through Jesus Christ.
And by His grace, you can begin walking in a different direction.
Your past may explain some of your scars, but it does not have the authority to write the final chapter of a life surrendered to Christ.
This is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing every earthly consequence.
But by forgiving sinners, making them new, and teaching them to live in the truth.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
What a promise.
Not a new image.
Not merely a better reputation.
A new creation in Christ.
And now return to that woman in Song of Songs.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
Her words remind us that human beings were made with the capacity to desire, to delight, to love, and to be loved.
But the Gospel reminds us that even our deepest human desires must find their rightful place beneath the lordship of Jesus.
Romantic affection is a gift.
It is not a god.
Marriage can reflect something beautiful about covenant faithfulness.
It cannot replace our covenant Lord.
A kiss can communicate tenderness.
It cannot save a soul.
And if you are single, widowed, divorced, abandoned, or grieving a love you thought would last, you are not excluded from the deepest hope of Scripture.
The invitation of Jesus is not reserved for people whose love lives are beautiful.
It is for the weary.
The repentant.
The brokenhearted.
The guilty who need forgiveness.
The lonely who need the presence of God.
The proud who need humbling.
The ashamed who need to know that forgiveness is possible.
Christ calls people to Himself.
And the love He gives is not fragile like human approval.
Romans 8:38–39 teaches that neither death nor life, nor any other created thing, can separate those who are in Christ Jesus from the love of God.
That is the assurance no romantic relationship can ultimately provide.
Maybe your marriage needs renewed tenderness.
Maybe your relationship needs honest boundaries.
Maybe your heart needs healing before you pursue another person.
Maybe you need to stop calling something love when it is destroying your obedience to God.
Maybe you need to ask forgiveness from someone you have hurt.
Or maybe you have been trying to earn God's love through religious performance, forgetting that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Wherever this finds you, do not merely admire the beauty of biblical love.
Allow Scripture to examine the condition of your own heart.
And if something has been exposed, do not hide it behind a religious smile.
Bring it to Jesus.
You can pray honestly:

“Lord Jesus, I have confused love with things that cannot save me. I have carried wounds, desires, fears, and sins that I cannot heal or overcome by my own strength. Forgive me. Teach me to love what is good, reject what is evil, and honor You with my heart, my body, and my relationships. Help me receive Your grace and walk in repentance and truth. Where I have been wounded, lead me toward healing. Where I have wounded others, teach me humility and responsibility. Make my life a testimony to Your redeeming love. Amen.”
And if this article uncovered something you have been afraid to admit, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
Not a performance of spirituality.
Not a competition over who sounds the holiest.
Just honesty before God.
You do not have to reveal private wounds publicly. Even a simple “Pray for me” is enough to invite your brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you.
And please, do not keep this message to yourself if someone you love needs to hear it.
Someone needs to discover what Scripture actually says.
Someone needs to know that biblical purity is not contempt for the body.
Someone needs to understand that desire requires wisdom, not denial of its existence.
Someone needs to hear that Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from God, and even people who do not yet believe to follow along.
Because the goal is not simply to make people feel something for a moment.
It is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior has become a source of biblical encouragement in your life, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Not because giving money makes someone more saved, more holy, or more loved by Jesus.
That would be contrary to the Gospel of grace.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives shaped by love and obedience. Generosity can be one beautiful expression of that worship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
But beyond any product or discount, our prayer is that you grow deeper in Christ.
If you are able and willing to help us continue and expand that work, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
Because ministry is not sustained by money alone.
It is sustained through God's grace and the faithful service of His people.
Some give.
Some write.
Some teach.
Some pray.
Some share.
And through ordinary acts of faithfulness, the truth of Christ continues reaching human hearts.
So before you leave, remember where we began.
A woman, thousands of years ago, expressing the beautiful longing to be kissed by the one she loves.
An ancient Hebrew poem that refuses to treat faithful human affection as something inherently dirty.
A Bible that celebrates love while calling us to holiness.
A Gospel that tells us human love, however beautiful, cannot save us.
And a Savior who entered our broken world, endured betrayal, carried our sins to the cross, and rose again so that all who trust in Him might have eternal life.
Perhaps the most important question is no longer whether the Bible really says, “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
It does.
The deeper question is whether we will allow the God who gave us the capacity to love to teach us what love is for.
Not worshiping desire.
Not despising it.
But bringing our whole lives under the gracious and holy lordship of Jesus Christ.
Because the most beautiful love story is not the one in which two imperfect people finally discover that they cannot live without each other.
It is the true story of the sinless Savior who gave Himself to redeem people who could never save themselves.
And that love does not merely make the heart race.
It calls the sinner to repentance.
It makes forgiveness possible.
It transforms the life.
It gives hope beyond the grave.
The kiss you longed for might have made you feel wanted for a moment, but the cross reveals a Savior whose redeeming love can change your eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SEVEN WOMEN WILL BEG ONE MAN TO GIVE THEM HIS NAME—BUT THE REASON IS MORE TERRIFYING THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: SEVEN WOMEN WILL BEG ONE MAN TO GIVE THEM HIS NAME—BUT THE REASON IS MORE TERRIFYING THAN YOU THINK

Isaiah 4:1 reveals a desperate scene of shame, judgment, and survival. But what happens when we follow the prophecy into the next verses reveals something far greater: the difference between desperately wanting a name to cover our disgrace and receiving the grace of the One who can truly wash it away.
Imagine a world where seven women approach one man.
Not because he is wealthy.
Not because he is handsome.
Not because they have fallen in love with him.
But because they are desperate for something he possesses.
His name.
They are willing to feed themselves. Clothe themselves. Carry their own expenses. They are not even asking him to provide for them.
They just want him to take away their disgrace.
And the most unsettling part?
God Himself revealed this scene through the prophet Isaiah.
Listen carefully to the words:
“And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach.” — Isaiah 4:1, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
“Only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach.”
They are not pleading for affection.
They are pleading for acceptance.
And perhaps that is where this ancient prophecy begins to touch something painfully familiar in the human heart.
Because sometimes, the thing we desperately want from another person is not even love.
It is the assurance that we are no longer someone to be ashamed of.
But before we turn this prophecy into a message about our own lives, we must understand what God was actually saying.
Because Isaiah 4:1 is not a romantic prophecy about seven women marrying one extraordinary man.
It is not a secret prediction that seven women will literally marry Jesus.
And it is not permission to turn a passage about judgment into a sensational teaching about marriage.
The truth is far more sobering.
And when understood in its proper context, far more powerful.
Isaiah was speaking to Judah and Jerusalem during a time of spiritual rebellion, social injustice, arrogance, and coming judgment.
The people had become confident in their outward appearance while their inward condition was collapsing.
Their society had learned how to display prosperity without practicing righteousness.
They knew how to look impressive.
But they were forgetting how to walk humbly before God.
Isaiah 3 describes corrupt leadership, oppression, pride, and the devastating consequences of covenant unfaithfulness.
Then comes a terrifying warning.
“Thy men shall fall by the sword, and thy mighty in the war.” — Isaiah 3:25, KJV
Suddenly, Isaiah 4:1 begins to make sense.
