She was an Egyptian servant under Sarai's authority.
The text does not record her consent to this arrangement.
That silence matters.

Because too often, when we read Genesis 16, we talk about Abram's faith, Sarai's impatience, and the birth of Ishmael while barely noticing the woman whose body became the place where their decision unfolded.
Her name was Hagar.
She was not merely a plot device in someone else's spiritual journey.
She was a human being.
And God knew her name.
Then came the pregnancy.
Genesis 16:4 tells us that Abram went in to Hagar, she conceived, and afterward Sarai became despised in Hagar's eyes.
The Hebrew expression is especially revealing.
וַתֵּקַל גְּבִרְתָּהּ בְּעֵינֶיהָ
Vattēqal gevirtāh be‘ênêhā.
Literally, the sense is that her mistress became light, or diminished, in her eyes.
The Hebrew verb is related to קָלַל (qalal), which can carry the idea of being light, insignificant, or treated with contempt.
This is why translations speak of Sarai being despised or looked upon with contempt.
It describes a deterioration in Hagar's regard for Sarai.
But notice what the passage does not tell us.
It does not disclose every thought in Hagar's mind.
It does not explain all the emotions behind her changed attitude.
It does not authorize us to invent conversations or motives that Scripture never records.
Perhaps her pregnancy altered how she viewed her position. Perhaps the household's power dynamics intensified existing tensions.
We can recognize those possibilities without presenting them as established facts.
What we know is enough.
The relationship became bitter.
And bitterness rarely remains confined to the heart.
Sarai saw what was happening.
And she was angry.
Genesis 16:5 records her complaint to Abram:
“My wrong be upon thee.”
She had proposed the arrangement.
Abram had agreed.
Hagar had conceived.
Now Sarai held Abram responsible for the humiliation she experienced.
And suddenly the promise they had been waiting for had become entangled with resentment.
Have you ever watched something you thought would solve a problem create a deeper one?
A decision made because you were tired of waiting.
A relationship entered because you were afraid of being alone.
A compromise justified because the outcome looked promising.
A door forced open because heaven seemed silent.
Then the consequences arrived.
And you discovered that getting what you wanted was not the same as receiving peace.
There is a warning here, but it must be handled carefully.
The problem was not that Sarai longed for a child. The problem was the human harm bound up in the way the household pursued that longing.
Desire is not automatically sin.
Waiting is not automatically unbelief.
And suffering is not proof that someone has failed God.
But desperation can tempt us to treat people as instruments for reaching our desired future.
That is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because we may never have stood inside Abram's household.
But many of us know what it means to be caught inside someone else's decisions.
A parent makes a choice, and the child carries the wound.
A leader protects a reputation, and the vulnerable person bears the consequences.
A spouse refuses accountability, and the family absorbs the damage.
Someone with power creates a crisis, then demands that someone with less power quietly endure it.
Hagar's story forces us to ask a question we might prefer to avoid.
When our plans hurt another person, are we willing to recognize their suffering, or do we become angry when they no longer see us the same way?
Then Abram spoke.
Genesis 16:6 records his response to Sarai:
“Behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee.”
Read that again.
He was the father of the child Hagar carried.
He was the man whose household had brought her into this situation.
And when the conflict became unbearable, he placed her back under Sarai's authority.
There is no recorded defense of Hagar in his response.
No recorded intervention to protect her from what followed.
Instead, the text says Sarai dealt harshly with her.
The Hebrew is:
וַתְּעַנֶּהָ שָׂרַי
Vatte‘annehā Saray.
The verb comes from עָנָה (‘anah), which in this context means to afflict, oppress, or treat harshly.
It is not a mild description of an uncomfortable disagreement.
The same Hebrew root is used elsewhere for serious affliction, including Israel's oppression in Egypt in Exodus 1:11–12.
Genesis does not describe every act Sarai committed against Hagar, so we should not invent specific forms of abuse.
But the biblical description is unmistakably serious.
Hagar was afflicted.
And she fled.
A pregnant woman.
An Egyptian servant.
Leaving a household with resources and protection, heading into the uncertainty of the wilderness.
We do not know every fear that accompanied her departure.
But we know she was running from harsh treatment.
And this is where the story changes.
Because the people who should have protected her had failed her.
But God had not lost sight of her.
Genesis 16:7 says:
“And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness.”
Found her.
What a remarkable phrase.
Hagar was fleeing.
Yet the biblical narrative does not portray her as invisible.
The messenger of the LORD encountered her beside a spring on the road to Shur.
And then came a question.
“Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?” — Genesis 16:8 (KJV)
God's messenger addressed her by name.
Hagar.
Not merely by her usefulness.
Not merely by her pregnancy.
Not merely as the woman at the center of Abram and Sarai's conflict.
Hagar.
Her answer was painfully direct.
“I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai.”
No elaborate explanation.
No carefully polished testimony.
Just the truth.
She was running.
There are moments when spiritual honesty begins with words that simple.
I am hurting.
I am afraid.
I do not know what to do.
I cannot pretend anymore.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to sound stronger than you feel.
You tell people you are fine because explaining your pain is exhausting.
You serve in church while carrying grief nobody notices.
You encourage others while privately wondering whether anyone would recognize your own exhaustion.
You believe God sees everything.
But sometimes you still wonder whether He sees you.
Hagar's encounter speaks directly into that question.
Yet we must not rush past the difficult part.
The messenger instructed Hagar to return to Sarai and submit to her authority.
That command belongs to this specific biblical encounter. It must never be turned into a blanket instruction that abused people should return to dangerous situations or remain under oppression.
Scripture records a particular divine direction to Hagar; it does not give modern abusers permission to demand submission or silence.
If you are experiencing abuse, seeking safety, protection, and trustworthy help is not a betrayal of faith.
And we should remember that Genesis does not describe Hagar's suffering as good.
God's attention to her does not excuse the people who harmed her.
The encounter also contained a promise.
Genesis 16:10 records the messenger declaring that Hagar's descendants would be multiplied beyond counting.
Then came the announcement of her son's name.
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma‘el.
Ishmael.
A name connected to the Hebrew words for hearing and God.
The explanation is given in Genesis 16:11:
“Because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.”
The Hebrew name communicates the truth:
God hears.
Not because Hagar had escaped every consequence.
Not because her circumstances had suddenly become easy.
Not because every relationship in her life had been restored.
But because her suffering had not escaped divine attention.
And then Hagar spoke words that would echo across generations.
Genesis 16:13 says:
“Thou God seest me.”
The Hebrew expression is:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro’i.
Often understood as “You are a God who sees me.”
The passage's Hebrew wording and the surrounding explanation have interpretive complexities, but its central testimony is clear: Hagar recognized the extraordinary reality of being seen by God.
Think about the contrast.
In Abram's household, she was identified by her position.
In the wilderness, she was addressed by her name.
In the household, her pregnancy intensified conflict.
In the wilderness, her unborn child received a name carrying the testimony that God had heard her affliction.
The woman who fled human cruelty encountered divine attention.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this has needed for years.
Being overlooked by people does not mean you have been overlooked by God.
But Hagar's story does not end in Genesis 16.
Years later, another crisis would come.
Genesis 21 records Hagar and Ishmael being sent away after Isaac's birth.
This time, their water ran out in the wilderness.
Hagar placed her child under a shrub and moved away because she could not bear to watch him die.
The text records her weeping.
And then Genesis 21:17 says:
“And God heard the voice of the lad.”
There it is again.
God heard.
The name Ishmael was not an empty religious slogan.
The God who had heard Hagar's affliction had not become deaf to the cries of her son.
God opened Hagar's eyes, and she saw a well of water.
The narrative does not say that God magically erased every hardship in her future.
But it shows that He had not abandoned them in that moment of desperate need.
And now we must ask the question that brings this ancient story into the center of the Gospel.
What does Hagar's story reveal about Jesus Christ?
We should not pretend that Genesis 16 explicitly names Jesus or that every detail of Hagar's experience is a hidden prediction of the cross.
It does not.
But when we read Scripture as a whole, we encounter the same divine character revealed with breathtaking fullness in Jesus Christ.
The God who saw an afflicted servant in the wilderness is the God whose Son entered a world of suffering.
Jesus did not build His ministry around flattering the powerful.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the rejected.
He spoke with people whose reputations made others uncomfortable.
He noticed those who were easily ignored.
In Luke 7:13, when Jesus encountered a widow grieving her only son, Scripture says He had compassion on her.
In John 4, He spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well and revealed knowledge of her life without treating her as disposable.
In Luke 19:10, Jesus declared that the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.
And at the cross, the sinless Savior bore the sins of others.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” — 1 Peter 3:18 (KJV)
This is where the Gospel goes beyond the comfort of knowing that God sees our pain.
Jesus came not only to comfort sinners in their brokenness, but to rescue them from sin and reconcile them to God.
Because if we read Hagar's story carefully, we cannot divide humanity into a simple world of innocent sufferers and wicked offenders.
We encounter real oppression.
We encounter resentment.
We encounter failures of responsibility.
We encounter wounded people whose responses may also be complicated.
And if we are honest, we may recognize ourselves in more than one place.
Sometimes we have been Hagar, wounded by decisions we never controlled.
Sometimes we have acted like Sarai, allowing frustration to turn into harshness toward another person.
Sometimes we have acted like Abram, avoiding responsibility when intervention would have required courage.
That recognition should not erase the profound differences in power and responsibility between these individuals.
It should lead us to examine our own hearts without blaming the oppressed for their oppression.
Because the Gospel is not merely an invitation to identify the wrongs committed against us.
It is also a summons to acknowledge the sins within us.
Have we used our influence to protect ourselves at another person's expense?
Have we allowed jealousy to become cruelty?
Have we watched someone suffer and chosen silence because speaking would be inconvenient?
Have we mistaken religious activity for genuine obedience?
Have we asked God to bless our plans while ignoring the people those plans might harm?
These are not comfortable questions.
But conviction can become a doorway to repentance.
And repentance, through Jesus Christ, is not the end of hope.
It is the beginning of returning to the One who gives grace.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
Notice what this promise does not say.
It does not say we are forgiven because we have suffered enough.
It does not say our good works can purchase mercy.
It does not say we can undo every consequence of our actions through religious effort.
Forgiveness rests on the faithfulness and justice of God, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And genuine repentance bears fruit in changed lives.
If we have wounded someone, repentance may require confession, accountability, restitution where possible, and a willingness to stop repeating the harm.
If we have been wounded, grace does not require us to deny what happened.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending abuse was acceptable.
Reconciliation, where possible, requires truth and cannot be demanded at the expense of someone's safety.
Jesus does not redeem people by teaching them to call evil good.
He brings us into the light.
And the light exposes what darkness has tried to hide.
Maybe that is why Hagar's story still unsettles us.
Because it reminds us that a household can speak about God's promises while still treating someone unjustly.
A person can know the language of faith and still need to repent.
A family can carry a sacred calling and still experience devastating dysfunction.
But human failure does not make God's character unfaithful.
Abram and Sarai's story would continue.
God would fulfill His promise concerning Isaac.
Hagar and Ishmael would not disappear from His concern.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ would come as the promised offspring through whom God's blessing reaches the nations, as the New Testament explains in Galatians 3:16.
That is the larger story.
Not that every painful decision becomes righteous because God can work beyond it.
Not that every wounded relationship will be repaired exactly as we hope.
Not that believers will be spared wilderness seasons.
But that God remains faithful to His purposes, even when human beings act with weakness, fear, and sin.
And in Jesus Christ, the invitation to receive mercy reaches people who have nothing to boast about.
The wounded can come.
The ashamed can come.
The repentant sinner can come.
The exhausted believer can come.
The person who has spent years hiding behind a respectable appearance can come.
Jesus said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
Not because every burden is imaginary.
Not because every wound disappears overnight.
But because the Savior is worthy of our trust.
And perhaps today, the most courageous prayer you can offer is not a beautiful prayer.
Perhaps it is simply:
Lord Jesus, You see what happened.
You see what I have done.
You see what I have carried.
You know the bitterness I have allowed to grow.
You know the wounds I have hidden.
Forgive my sins. Heal what is broken in me. Give me courage to obey Your truth. Teach me to trust You without harming others or surrendering to despair.
I cannot rewrite yesterday.
But I believe You can redeem a life surrendered to You.
Amen.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be living through a season that feels painfully similar to Hagar's wilderness.
They may be carrying a burden nobody knows about.
They may be questioning whether God notices their suffering.
They may be surrounded by religious words but starving for genuine compassion.
Not because an algorithm determines the value of a soul.
But because Scripture has a way of reaching people at moments when human encouragement is not enough.
I also want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not have to publish the details of your wounds to be worthy of prayer.
There may be someone reading your words who recognizes their own struggle and realizes they are not alone.
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish articles.
Not merely to gather reactions.
But to keep bringing people back to the Scriptures, to the person of Jesus Christ, and to the transforming truth of the Gospel.
We want this to be a place where people can encounter biblical truth, thoughtful encouragement, conviction that leads to repentance, and hope rooted in Christ rather than empty promises.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and expand, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Scripture teaches:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
And that same verse teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion.
So this invitation is not a demand.
You cannot purchase God's favor through a monthly payment.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 declares.
These products are not the reason to support the Gospel.
They are simply one way we hope to express appreciation to those who help make the ministry's work possible.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in their understanding of Scripture, strengthen their walk with Jesus, and continue learning beyond a single article.
Jesus Christ must remain the center.
Not a platform.
Not merchandise.
Not the person writing the article.
Jesus.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who receives those who come to Him in faith.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who transforms lives through His grace.
And as you leave this story, remember Hagar.
Remember the bitterness inside that household.
Remember the failures of those who held power.
Remember the pregnant woman fleeing into the wilderness.
Remember the spring.
Remember the question.
Remember the name.
Hagar.
And remember the testimony she carried from that encounter.
You are a God who sees me.
The wilderness did not erase her identity.
The cruelty she experienced did not make her invisible to God.
And the failures of human beings did not cancel His compassion.
Now carry that truth into your own life.
If you have sinned, turn to Jesus in repentance.
If you have been wounded, bring your pain before Him and seek the help and protection you need.
If you have power over others, use it with humility and justice.
If you have been silent while someone suffered, ask God for courage to act rightly.
And if you have spent years believing that your life is too damaged to matter, remember that the Gospel is not the announcement that good people have earned a second chance.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The cross reveals the seriousness of our sin.
The resurrection declares the victory of our Savior.
And grace calls us not merely to feel better about yesterday, but to become new in Christ.
The people who wounded Hagar may have treated her as though she were invisible, but the God who found her in the wilderness knew her name before she ever cried out to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD FORBADE A MAN FROM SLEEPING WITH A WOMAN AND HER DAUGHTER—BUT THE REASON GOES DEEPER THAN SEX
paragraphs: GOD FORBADE A MAN FROM SLEEPING WITH A WOMAN AND HER DAUGHTER—BUT THE REASON GOES DEEPER THAN SEX

Leviticus 18:17 reveals a disturbing truth about lust, family betrayal, and the sacred boundaries God established to protect human dignity. And when we follow this uncomfortable Scripture all the way to Jesus Christ, we discover something even more powerful: the God who exposes sin is also the God who offers redemption.
There are sins that destroy a marriage.
There are sins that destroy a family.
And then there are sins that make a daughter look at her own mother and wonder whether she was ever truly safe.
Imagine a woman discovering that the man she trusted, the man who shared her bed, her secrets, and perhaps her home, had also pursued her daughter.
Imagine the silence at the dinner table.
The unbearable questions.
The daughter wondering whether she had somehow caused it. The mother struggling between heartbreak and disbelief. The family relationships that may never feel the same again.
Now imagine opening the Bible and discovering that thousands of years ago, God had already spoken directly against this kind of sexual wrongdoing.
Not because He hated intimacy.
Not because He considered sexuality dirty.
But because He knew that human desire, when separated from holiness and love, could become an instrument of devastating betrayal.
And the most astonishing part?
The Hebrew text contains a word that exposes the seriousness of this sin with remarkable force.
Listen carefully to what God actually said.
Leviticus 18:17 declares in the King James Version:

“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness.”
That final word deserves our attention.
Because God was not merely establishing an ancient social custom.
He was identifying a violation of family boundaries so serious that His covenant people were forbidden to normalize it.
And to understand why, we must enter the world of the text rather than force the text into the world of our assumptions.
The original Hebrew begins:
עֶרְוַת אִשָּׁה וּבִתָּהּ לֹא תְגַלֵּה
ʿErvat ʾishshah u-vittah lo tegalleh.
Literally, the phrase means:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter.”
The expression “uncover nakedness” is not simply about seeing someone without clothing. Within Leviticus 18, it is a Hebrew expression referring to prohibited sexual relations.
The verb תְגַלֵּה (tegalleh) comes from the root גלה (galah), meaning to uncover or reveal.
The noun עֶרְוָה (ʿervah) refers to nakedness and, in this legal context, sexual exposure.
God was not discussing an accidental glance.
He was prohibiting sexual involvement that crossed forbidden family boundaries.

The verse also extends the prohibition to a woman's granddaughter through either her son or her daughter. The issue is therefore broader than one specific mother-daughter relationship. It concerns sexual relationships involving closely connected generations of the same family.
Then comes the explanation:
שַׁאֲרָה הֵנָּה
Sheʾarah hennah.
“They are her close relatives.”
The Hebrew emphasizes their familial connection.
These women are not unrelated individuals whose relationships can be considered in isolation. They belong to an interconnected family structure.
A sexual relationship with one cannot be morally separated from the consequences of involving another in that same forbidden union.
And then Scripture delivers its verdict:
זִמָּה הִוא
Zimmah hi.
“It is wickedness.”
The Hebrew noun זִמָּה (zimmah) can describe wickedness, depravity, or an evil sexual scheme, depending on context.
Here, it condemns the prohibited relationship as a serious moral wrong.
Notice something important.

The Hebrew text does not explicitly say that the prohibition was given because the daughter would become jealous, because the mother would be emotionally devastated, or because the family would suffer psychological trauma.
Those consequences may be very real.
But we must distinguish what Scripture explicitly teaches from the reasonable moral implications we draw from it.
The stated reason in Leviticus 18:17 is the close family relationship, and the act is condemned as wickedness.
That distinction matters.
Because we do not honor God's Word by making it say more than it says.
We honor His Word by listening carefully enough to hear what He actually revealed.
And what He revealed is already serious enough.
The God of Israel did not permit sexual desire to erase the boundaries of kinship.
A man could not simply claim that because he desired someone, he had a right to pursue her.
Desire was never meant to become the final authority over righteousness.
And that truth is just as relevant today.
We live in a world where people sometimes defend destructive relationships with phrases that sound compassionate.
“We love each other.”
“Nobody understands our connection.”
“We never intended to hurt anyone.”
“It's complicated.”
But sincerity does not automatically make a relationship holy.
Strong feelings do not turn a forbidden act into an acceptable one.
And secrecy does not make betrayal disappear.
Some relationships are wrong not because the emotions involved are necessarily imaginary, but because the actions violate obligations and boundaries that love itself should respect.
That is part of the moral force of Leviticus 18.
God does not ask merely whether something is desired.
He asks whether it is righteous.
And the difference between those questions can change an entire life.
Consider the setting.
Leviticus 18 was given to Israel as part of God's covenant instruction after the exodus from Egypt.
The chapter opens with a command that establishes the larger issue.
God tells Israel not to imitate the practices of Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going.
Instead, they were to walk according to His statutes.
Then comes Leviticus 18:5:
“Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the LORD.”
This chapter is not an isolated collection of strange ancient restrictions.
It belongs to a larger biblical vision of holiness.
God was forming a people who were to be different from the nations around them.
Their worship mattered.
Their treatment of others mattered.
Their sexual conduct mattered.
Their family relationships mattered.
Holiness was never meant to exist only inside a place of worship while injustice and exploitation flourished behind closed doors.
And that should trouble anyone who has learned to appear righteous in public while concealing destructive behavior in private.
Because the God who said, “I am the LORD,” was claiming authority over the whole life of His people.
Not merely their ceremonies.
Not merely their sacrifices.
Not merely the words they spoke when others were listening.
Their lives.
Their bodies.
Their relationships.
Their conduct when no human witness was present.
And perhaps that is where this passage begins to feel uncomfortably personal.
Because although most readers may never have committed the specific act prohibited in Leviticus 18:17, many understand the temptation to excuse something they know is wrong.
The private conversation that should have ended.
The flirtation that crossed a boundary.
The hidden messages.
The emotional attachment that became more important than a marriage covenant.
The secret someone keeps protecting because admitting the truth would require repentance.
Not every temptation is the same as the offense described in Leviticus.
And we must never pretend that all sexual sins have identical consequences.
But there is a common spiritual danger.
When desire becomes our master, we begin negotiating with boundaries that once seemed obvious.
We stop asking, “What does God say?”
And start asking, “How far can I go without anyone finding out?”
That is a dangerous question.
Because a hidden sin can become a public wound long before it becomes a public scandal.
And God cares about the people who are wounded.
Think about the daughter.

In situations involving coercion, manipulation, or abuse, especially when the daughter is a minor or the man occupies a position of parental authority, the wrongdoing can include a profound betrayal of trust and responsibility.
A child cannot be held responsible for an adult's sexual exploitation.
A person who is coerced or abused is not guilty merely because someone violated them.
This distinction is essential.
Leviticus 18:17 identifies a prohibited sexual relationship. It must never be twisted into a weapon for blaming victims or silencing those who have been harmed.
Scripture consistently calls God's people to oppose injustice and protect the vulnerable.
Psalm 82:3–4 commands:
“Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.”
God's concern for holiness does not cancel His concern for the wounded.
It includes it.
And if someone has used religious language to pressure you into silence about abuse, that pressure should not be confused with biblical faithfulness.
Truth matters.
Safety matters.
Justice matters.
And forgiveness does not require a victim to return to danger, conceal a crime, or pretend that trust has already been restored.
That is not rebellion against grace.
That is taking evil seriously.
But there is another question that must be answered.
Why would God prohibit sexual relationships involving a woman and her daughter when the Bible itself records troubling family arrangements among people in earlier generations?
For example, Jacob married both Leah and Rachel, who were sisters, as recorded in Genesis 29.
Later, Leviticus 18:18 specifically prohibited taking a wife's sister as a rival wife while the first wife was living.
The Bible also records instances of polygamy and other deeply complicated family arrangements.
Does that mean God changed His mind about holiness?
Not necessarily.
We must distinguish between Scripture describing what people did and Scripture approving what they did.
A historical account is not automatically a moral endorsement.
Genesis often shows the painful consequences of human choices without interrupting every narrative to provide a formal legal judgment.
Jacob's household, for example, was marked by rivalry, jealousy, and deep family conflict.
The existence of a practice in biblical history does not prove that the practice represents God's ideal.
And when Jesus was questioned about marriage and divorce, He directed His listeners back to God's creation design.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus referred to the creation of male and female and the union in which husband and wife become one flesh.
He did not present marriage as an arrangement where human appetite could override covenant faithfulness.
He called attention to what God had joined together.
That is where the larger biblical story begins to come into focus.
The Bible does not treat sexuality as meaningless.
It treats it as powerful.
Powerful enough to create life.
Powerful enough to express covenant intimacy.
Powerful enough, when misused, to inflict lasting harm.
The answer to destructive sexuality is not to despise the human body.
The answer is to recover the holiness of love.
Love does not ask how many boundaries it can cross.
Love asks how faithfully it can honor God and protect another person's dignity.
And this is where the story takes a turn that some readers may not expect.
Because the Bible does not end with Leviticus.
And the God who exposes wickedness does not leave repentant sinners without hope.
Centuries after Moses, Jesus Christ stood before a world filled with broken families, hidden shame, sexual wrongdoing, hypocrisy, and wounded people.
He did not come to declare that sin was harmless.
He came to save sinners.
John 1:14 tells us that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And we see that combination powerfully in John 4.
Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well.
He knows the painful complexity of her relationship history.
He tells her that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband.
Yet He does not reduce her entire identity to her history.
He speaks with her.
He reveals Himself to her.
He offers living water.
And she becomes a witness to others, inviting her community to come and see the One who knew her life.
We should be careful not to invent details about this woman that Scripture does not provide.
The text does not tell us why each marriage ended, whether she was responsible for those endings, or whether she had been abandoned or mistreated.
What it does show is extraordinary.
Jesus knew the truth about her life.
And He still engaged her with dignity.
He did not need to deny reality in order to offer hope.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Christ does not save us by pretending sin is not sin.
He saves by confronting the reality of our condition and offering the grace we could never earn.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had perfected our image.
Not after everyone had forgotten our failures.
Not after we had finally become impressive enough to deserve His attention.
Christ died for sinners.
But grace is not permission to continue harming others.
The same Gospel that offers forgiveness also calls us to repentance.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It means to repent, involving a change of mind and direction.
In biblical usage, repentance is more than temporary regret or embarrassment over being caught.
It is a turning toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Jesus said in Mark 1:15:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Repent.
Believe.
Not conceal.
Not rationalize.
Not blame the wounded.
Not demand immediate forgiveness from people who are still struggling to recover from what happened.
Repentance takes responsibility.

And where serious harm has occurred, genuine repentance may involve confession, ending the wrongdoing, accepting appropriate consequences, making restitution where possible, and respecting the safety and boundaries of those affected.
Forgiveness before God is not a license to escape earthly accountability.
Grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant abuse.
It is God's invitation to leave darkness and walk in the light.
Perhaps someone reading this has been living with a secret.
Perhaps it is not the specific sin named in Leviticus 18:17.
Perhaps it is a betrayal that has been eating away at your conscience.
Perhaps you have spent years defending something God has been asking you to surrender.
You can convince other people that everything is fine.
You can create a convincing explanation.
You can even become skilled at quoting Scripture while avoiding the one passage that confronts your behavior.
But you cannot heal a wound by insisting it does not exist.
And you cannot build a transformed life while remaining determined to protect the very thing that is destroying it.
There is hope.
Not because the wrongdoing was small.
But because the mercy of Jesus Christ is great.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice that the promise does not require us to call darkness light.
It invites us to confess.
To stop defending what God condemns.
To stop treating our desires as unquestionable authorities.
To come into the light.
And to trust the Savior whose blood was shed for sinners.
But perhaps you are not the person who committed the betrayal.
Perhaps you are the person who suffered because of it.
Perhaps someone who should have protected you crossed a boundary that should never have been crossed.
Perhaps your family demanded silence to preserve its reputation.
Perhaps you were told that speaking about what happened would dishonor God.
Hear this carefully.
The shame of another person's wrongdoing does not belong to you.
You do not have to carry the moral guilt of someone who exploited, manipulated, or violated you.
And you do not have to call something acceptable simply because it happened inside a religious household.
The Lord sees what people conceal.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
God's nearness does not mean every wound disappears overnight.
Healing can take time.
It can involve grief, trustworthy support, professional care, difficult boundaries, and the slow rebuilding of a sense of safety.
But your suffering does not make you invisible to Him.
And the cross of Jesus Christ is not a demand that you deny what happened.
It is the revelation of a Savior who entered a world of evil and suffering to overcome sin and death.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the repentant sinner.
And there is room at the feet of Jesus for the wounded person who is still learning how to breathe again.
These are not identical situations.
They should never be treated as though they are.
But both reveal how desperately humanity needs a Savior.
That brings us back to the question that began this entire conversation.
Why did the Old Testament forbid sexual relations with a woman and her daughter?
Because God established boundaries around close family relationships and explicitly condemned this kind of sexual union as wickedness.
Because holiness includes what people do with their bodies, not merely what they profess with their lips.
Because sexual desire does not have the authority to overturn God's moral instruction.
And because, when we read this command within the whole counsel of Scripture, we recognize that God calls His people to faithfulness, self-control, justice, and love that refuses to exploit others.

The specific prohibition was given within Israel's covenant law, but Christians do not need to pretend that every provision of the Mosaic law functions identically under the new covenant in order to recognize its moral seriousness.
The New Testament continues to condemn sexual immorality and calls believers to honor God with their bodies.
First Corinthians 6:18–20 speaks of fleeing sexual immorality and remembering that believers belong to God.
The Christian response, therefore, is not simply to memorize an ancient prohibition.
It is to surrender the whole life to Jesus Christ.
To allow His truth to confront our excuses.
To allow His grace to break the power of shame.
To allow His Spirit to cultivate holiness, faithfulness, and self-control.
And to remember that the purpose of the Gospel is not merely to produce people who look respectable.
It is to reconcile sinners to God through Christ and transform them into people who increasingly reflect His character.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior will never be that your scandal is greater than the cross.
But neither will we tell you that the cross makes your sin insignificant.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable with the darkness.
He gave Himself to redeem us.
Titus 2:14 says that Christ “gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.”
Redeem.
Purify.
Transform.
That is the Gospel's direction.
From bondage toward freedom.
From deception toward truth.
From rebellion toward repentance.
From shame toward the grace of God.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by erasing the reality of the past.
Not by declaring every consequence canceled.
But by making a genuinely new life possible through His death and resurrection.
And perhaps that is why you needed to encounter this difficult passage today.
Not to satisfy curiosity about an ancient sexual prohibition.
But to remember that God cares about what happens behind closed doors.
He cares about the vulnerable.
He cares about truth.
He cares about the person whose conscience has been warning them to turn back.
And He cares about the person who has been carrying a wound no one else seems willing to acknowledge.
If this article has confronted something in your life, I invite you to respond with sincerity rather than performance.
You do not need to disclose intimate details, name anyone involved, or expose private trauma in a public comment.
God already knows the parts of your story that you are not ready to tell the world.
And if you have a testimony of how Christ has brought you from darkness into a changed life, your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that transformation is impossible.

Not because every person needs to know your private struggles, but because someone in your circle may be wrestling with the difference between love and lust, between guilt and repentance, or between religious appearances and genuine holiness.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, people who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still searching for faith to follow along.
Because God's Word deserves to be studied carefully, not merely quoted dramatically.
And because the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be heard beyond the walls of a church building.
Some believers prayerfully include support for Gospel-centered ministries as part of their regular giving. If you choose to do that here, we receive it with gratitude as a ministry offering.
But I want to be clear about something important.
You do not have to pay for God's forgiveness.
You do not have to give money to prove your faith.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, not something purchased through religious support.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible, including to those who cannot afford to contribute financially.
Not everyone can give financially.
But everyone who belongs to Christ has opportunities to bear witness to Him.
And that is what matters most.
Not our popularity.
Jesus Christ.
His truth.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His grace.
His power to redeem and transform.
Because one day, the arguments we used to justify our sin will no longer matter.
The reputation we worked so hard to preserve will no longer save us.
The secrets we kept will not become righteous simply because they remained undiscovered.
What matters eternally is whether we have turned to the Savior who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Leviticus 18:17 reminds us that God does not overlook evil simply because it happens inside a family.
The Gospel reminds us that evil does not have to be the final word over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And that is a truth worth remembering.
Worth living.
Worth sharing.
The most powerful ending to a scandal is not when the world finally stops talking about it, but when a life truly surrendered to Jesus begins telling a different story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FRIEND WHO HELPED DESTROY A PRINCESS: WHEN THE WRONG VOICE TURNS SECRET SIN INTO SOMEONE ELSE’S NIGHTMARE
paragraphs: THE FRIEND WHO HELPED DESTROY A PRINCESS: WHEN THE WRONG VOICE TURNS SECRET SIN INTO SOMEONE ELSE’S NIGHTMARE

Amnon had a wicked desire. Jonadab had a clever plan. Tamar paid a devastating price. And buried inside 2 Samuel 13 is a warning every parent, every young person, every believer, and every person who has ever trusted the wrong friend needs to hear.
“But Amnon had a friend.” — 2 Samuel 13:3 (KJV)
Six words.
Because sometimes the most dangerous person in your life is not the one who openly hates you.
Sometimes it is the person who sits beside you, laughs at your jokes, knows your secrets, understands your weaknesses, and knows exactly what to say when your conscience is trying to stop you.
His name was Jonadab.
He was not an invading enemy. He was not a stranger hiding outside the palace gates.
He was family.
He was a friend.
And when Amnon was wrestling with a desire that should never have been entertained, Jonadab did not tell him to repent.
He taught him how to arrange the opportunity.
What followed was not a harmless mistake. It was sexual violence, betrayal, humiliation, and a family tragedy whose consequences would echo through the house of David.
But before we walk into that terrible room, there is something we must understand.
Not everyone who helps you get what you want is helping you become who God created you to be.
Some people will help you satisfy a desire while remaining completely indifferent to the person that desire may destroy.
And the frightening part?
They may call themselves your friends.
The story begins in 2 Samuel 13.
Amnon was a son of King David. Tamar was his beautiful half-sister, the full sister of Absalom.
Scripture tells us Amnon became consumed with desire for Tamar. He was distressed, frustrated, and increasingly troubled because he could not have what he wanted.
The biblical narrator uses the language of love to describe Amnon's feelings, but what happens next exposes how profoundly corrupted those feelings had become.
Love does not require another person to surrender their dignity.
Love does not manipulate.
Love does not force.
Love does not destroy someone and then discard them.
What Amnon called love became an obsession that refused to recognize Tamar's humanity.
And that is where Jonadab entered the story.
The King James Version says:
“But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother: and Jonadab was a very subtil man.” — 2 Samuel 13:3
Notice how Scripture introduces him.
Not as an enemy.
Not as a criminal.
As a friend.
The Hebrew text describes Jonadab as אִישׁ חָכָם מְאֹד — ish chakham me'od, meaning a very wise, clever, or shrewd man.
The Hebrew word chakam (חָכָם) can describe wisdom or skill. But the context determines how that intelligence is being used.
Jonadab was clever.
He could read people.
He could recognize weakness.
He could develop a strategy.
But intelligence without righteousness can become a weapon.
A person can be brilliant at solving problems and still be dangerously foolish about what is right.
Jonadab noticed Amnon's condition.
He asked why the king's son looked so troubled morning after morning.
Amnon confessed his desire for Tamar.
Now imagine that moment.
Imagine what a godly friend could have said.
“Amnon, she is your sister. You need to stop feeding this desire.”
“Do not confuse your feelings with permission.”
“You are about to hurt someone who trusts this family.”
“Let me help you turn away before you destroy your life and hers.”
That would have been friendship.
That would have been courage.
That would have been love.
Instead, Jonadab offered a plan.
In 2 Samuel 13:5, he told Amnon to lie down, pretend to be sick, wait for King David to visit, and ask that Tamar be sent to prepare food in his presence.
Read that again.
Jonadab did not merely encourage a sinful thought.
He supplied the deception that would help Amnon isolate Tamar.
He understood the palace.
He understood the father's concern for his son.
He understood how Tamar's kindness and family duty could be exploited.
He took something innocent—a sister caring for a supposedly sick brother—and turned it into the setting for a terrible betrayal.
There is a chilling lesson here.
The wrong friend does not always create the evil in your heart. Sometimes the wrong friend simply gives it a plan.
And that is why Proverbs 13:20 matters:
“He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.” (KJV)
Friendship is never spiritually neutral.
The people closest to us can strengthen our conscience or teach us to silence it.
They can help us confess what is wrong or teach us how to conceal it.
They can point us toward Jesus or convince us that getting what we want matters more than obeying Him.
Think about your own life.
Who do you call when temptation becomes overwhelming?
Who hears the thoughts you are ashamed to admit publicly?
Who has access to the version of you that nobody else sees?
And when you confess something dangerous, do they help you resist it?
Or do they help you justify it?
Because the person who laughs while you compromise may not be the person who stands beside you when the consequences arrive.
Amnon followed Jonadab's counsel.
He pretended to be sick.
David visited him.
Amnon asked for Tamar.
And David sent her.
There is something especially painful about this part of the story.
Tamar was not sneaking into a forbidden place.
She was obeying a request from her father, the king.
She entered her brother's house to perform an act of care.
She prepared food.
She approached someone who claimed to need help.
And the trust that brought her into that room was used against her.
Amnon then ordered the others to leave and demanded that Tamar come closer.
When he seized her and demanded sex, Tamar resisted.
Her words in 2 Samuel 13:12 are devastating:
“Nay, my brother, do not force me; for no such thing ought to be done in Israel: do not thou this folly.” (KJV)
She said no.
She identified the act as wrong.
She pleaded with him.
She spoke about the disgrace and harm that would follow.
She tried to reason with a man who had already decided that his desire mattered more than her voice.
And Scripture tells us:
“Howbeit he would not hearken unto her voice: but, being stronger than she, forced her, and lay with her.” — 2 Samuel 13:14 (KJV)
Those words should never be softened.
Amnon raped Tamar.
She did not consent.
She did not cause it.
She did not deserve it.
Her kindness was not an invitation. Her presence was not permission. Her relationship to Amnon did not make the violation less serious.
And no amount of spiritual language should ever transfer the blame from the perpetrator to the person he harmed.
Tamar was sinned against.
Amnon was responsible for his actions.
Jonadab's counsel helped arrange the opportunity.
And the adults and family structures around Tamar failed to give her the protection and justice she needed.
Then came another cruelty.
After assaulting Tamar, Amnon's feelings turned to hatred.
The man who claimed to love her ordered her away.
The one who had demanded her presence now demanded her removal.
Tamar protested again, recognizing the additional harm of being cast out.
But Amnon refused to listen.
He called his servant and ordered Tamar out, and the door was bolted behind her.
Can you imagine that sound?
A door closing.
A bolt sliding into place.
And a young woman standing outside, carrying trauma she never chose.
Second Samuel 13:19 describes Tamar placing ashes on her head, tearing the distinctive robe she wore as a virgin daughter of the king, and going away crying aloud.
Her grief was visible.
Her devastation was public.
And yet the chapter does not record the justice or restoration she deserved.
Instead, verse 20 describes her living desolate in her brother Absalom's house.
The Hebrew word שֹׁמֵמָה — shomemah carries the sense of desolation or devastation.
Scripture does not invite us to treat Tamar as a disposable character in Amnon's story.
Her suffering matters.
Her voice matters.
Her future matters.
And if you have ever been betrayed by someone you trusted, hear this carefully:
What someone did to you does not define your worth before God.
You are not dirty because another person sinned against you.
You are not responsible for another person's violence.
You are not beyond God's compassion because your story contains something painful.
And you do not owe your abuser access, silence, or reconciliation without repentance, safety, and accountability.
Jesus Christ never asks us to rename evil as good.
He is full of grace and truth.
Both matter.
Perhaps one of the most heartbreaking details is that Tamar's suffering was not the end of the tragedy.
David became angry when he heard what had happened, but the chapter records no effective action from him against Amnon.
Absalom carried hatred toward Amnon.
Two years passed.
Then Absalom arranged Amnon's death.
The violence did not heal Tamar.
Revenge did not restore what had been taken.
And the royal family continued descending into conflict.
This is what unchecked sin can do.
It does not remain neatly confined to the person who first entertained it.
It spreads into relationships.
It damages families.
It produces grief that others must carry.
But we must be careful about one thing.
The lesson is not that every survivor's suffering inevitably produces further destruction.
Nor is it that Tamar somehow brought judgment upon her family.
The moral responsibility remains with those who chose evil, enabled it, or failed to confront it.
And Jonadab's role deserves serious attention.
Later in the chapter, when news of Amnon's death reached David, Jonadab appeared again.
He explained that Absalom had been determined to kill Amnon because of what Amnon had done to Tamar.
Jonadab knew the background of the tragedy.
The same man who had once supplied Amnon with a plan now spoke as someone who understood the consequences.
Scripture does not tell us everything Jonadab thought or felt.
It does not explicitly describe his private motives or record his repentance.
We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But what Scripture does reveal is enough to warn us.
Jonadab's cleverness helped Amnon reach Tamar. It did not help Amnon become righteous.
And there is a difference between a friend who helps you escape discomfort and a friend who helps you escape sin.
One tells you what you want to hear.
The other loves you enough to tell you what you need to hear.
One protects your appetite.
The other cares about your soul and the people your choices may hurt.
One says, “Here is how you can get away with it.”
The other says, “You need to stop before somebody gets hurt.”
That second kind of friend may make you uncomfortable.
They may challenge your excuses.
They may refuse to participate in your deception.
They may insist that you seek help, confess wrongdoing, and accept accountability.
But Proverbs 27:6 says:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.” (KJV)
Sometimes the friend who refuses to help you sin is the friend who loves you most.
And sometimes the person who constantly agrees with you is not protecting your peace.
They are protecting your rebellion from being challenged.
There is also another warning hidden in this story.
Be careful whose suffering becomes invisible when you are discussing somebody else's desires.
People often talk about Amnon's lust.
They discuss Jonadab's manipulation.
They analyze David's failures.
They examine Absalom's revenge.
But Tamar must not disappear behind the men who shaped the tragedy.
She was not merely the consequence of their bad decisions.
She was a person with a voice, dignity, and a life.
And she was the one who pleaded for righteousness when the men around her failed to practice it.
That should convict the Church.
When somebody comes forward with an account of abuse, our first concern must not be how to protect the reputation of the powerful.
It must not be how to avoid embarrassment.
It must not be how to make the story disappear.
We must take harm seriously, protect those at risk, respond with compassion, and pursue appropriate accountability.
Romans 12:9 tells believers:
“Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.” (KJV)
We cannot claim to hate evil while protecting the systems that allow it to continue.
And we cannot call it biblical forgiveness when we pressure the wounded to remain silent.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending nothing happened.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
Repentance is not a public performance designed to avoid consequences.
True repentance turns away from sin and bears fruit consistent with that change.
Now here is where this ancient story becomes painfully personal.
Perhaps you have never known a Jonadab by that name.
But you may have known someone who told you to lie because the truth would cost too much.
Someone who encouraged you to pursue a married person because you deserved happiness.
Someone who laughed at your conscience when you were trying to leave pornography behind.
Someone who helped you hide an addiction, betray a spouse, manipulate a relationship, or exploit another person's trust.
Someone who kept saying, “Everybody does it.”
Or, “Nobody will ever know.”
Or, “You only live once.”
Or, “God will forgive you anyway.”
Listen carefully.
God's mercy is not permission to make plans for the sin you already know you should abandon.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether we should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic: God forbid.
Grace is not a hiding place for deliberate cruelty.
Grace is God's invitation to come out of darkness and walk in newness of life.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because if this story only teaches us to avoid bad friends, we have not yet reached the deepest need of the human heart.
We need more than better company.
We need a Savior.
We need the One who can expose what we have concealed, forgive what we have confessed, and transform the desires that have ruled us.
We need the One who does not use the vulnerable for His own gratification but gives Himself in sacrificial love.
The contrast is extraordinary.
Amnon used his strength to overpower someone weaker.
Jesus, though possessing all authority, humbled Himself and gave His life for sinners.
Amnon exploited another person's trust.
Jesus is faithful and true.
Amnon's distorted desire brought devastation.
Christ's self-giving love opens the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
In the Greek New Testament, Ephesians 5:2 says:
“καὶ περιπατεῖτε ἐν ἀγάπῃ” — kai peripateite en agapē.
“Walk in love.”
Paul then points to Christ, who loved us and gave Himself up for us.
The word ἀγάπῃ — agapē refers here to the love believers are commanded to practice, a love defined in this passage by Christ's sacrificial example.
That is not the love Amnon demonstrated.
Christlike love does not ask, “How much can I take from this person?”
It asks, “How can I honor God in the way I treat this person?”
It does not turn another human being into an object.
It recognizes that every person bears dignity as one made in God's image.
And for the person reading this who has committed serious wrong, the Gospel does not offer cheap excuses.
It calls you to repentance.
Stop blaming temptation.
Stop blaming the people you harmed.
Stop hiding behind religious language.
Confess the truth.
Turn from the behavior.
Accept appropriate consequences.
Seek qualified help where needed.
Make restitution where possible without pressuring the person you harmed.
And come to Jesus with genuine repentance.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
That promise is glorious.
But it is not a license to continue abusing, deceiving, or exploiting others.
The grace that forgives also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
And to the person carrying wounds from someone else's sin, the invitation is different.
You do not need to confess guilt for what was done against you.
You need compassion, safety, truth, and support.
You may need people who will listen without minimizing your experience.
You may need professional care and the protection of appropriate authorities.
And you may need time.
Healing is not a competition.
You do not have to pretend you are fine to prove that you trust God.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” (KJV)
That verse does not promise that every wound disappears immediately.
It reveals something precious about the character of God.
He does not despise the brokenhearted.
He draws near.
And this is where the message of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a slogan.
Not because every scandal ends happily on earth.
Not because every victim receives justice immediately.
Not because every family becomes whole again.
And certainly not because the past can be erased by pretending it never happened.
But because sin and suffering do not have the final authority over those who belong to Christ.
The cross declares that God takes evil seriously.
The resurrection declares that death and darkness will not have the final word.
And the Gospel declares that repentant sinners can be redeemed and wounded people are never beyond the reach of God's compassionate care.
Jesus does not rewrite history by denying what happened.
He changes our eternal future through His death and resurrection, and He calls us to walk in His truth today.
Perhaps the most important question now is not simply, “Who was Jonadab?”
It is this:
Who has been advising your heart lately?
Whose voice are you trusting when you are tempted?
Who tells you the truth when you are wrong?
And whose voice are you becoming in somebody else's life?
Are you helping a friend repent?
Or helping them conceal their sin?
Are you protecting the vulnerable?
Or protecting the reputation of the person who hurt them?
Are you using your intelligence to serve righteousness?
Or to make disobedience easier?
Because you may never stand in a royal palace.
You may never counsel a king's son.
But one day somebody may come to you carrying a dangerous desire, a secret compromise, or a decision that could wound another person.
And what you say next may matter more than you realize.
Do not be Jonadab.
Be the friend who tells the truth.
Be the parent who teaches children that love never excuses coercion.
Be the believer who protects those who are vulnerable.
Be the Christian who refuses to confuse loyalty with covering up evil.
Be the person who chooses righteousness even when righteousness costs you a friendship.
And if you recognize yourself in the person who has been taking the wrong advice, do not wait until another life is damaged before you change direction.
Turn to Christ today.
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is hope for the broken.
There is a better way to live.
And there is a Savior whose truth is stronger than the lies we have learned to believe.
Before you leave this article, I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Have you ever had someone encourage you to do something you knew was wrong?
Or have you ever been the person who needed the courage to tell a friend, “No. I will not help you do this”?
And if you have experienced betrayal or abuse, please know that you do not owe anyone your story in a public comment. Your safety and dignity matter more than engagement on a post.
If this ministry has helped you grow, I also want to invite you to become part of what we are building.
Gospel Warrior is committed to sharing biblical truth, Gospel-centered encouragement, and discipleship resources with people who are hungry to know Christ more deeply.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and remain rooted in biblical truth.
But making resources available, developing new materials, and expanding the ministry takes time, effort, and financial support.
And God's grace, forgiveness, and blessing cannot be purchased.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through shared commitment to making the truth of Christ known.
These products can serve as reminders of faith and encouragement, but the heart of the ministry will always be Jesus Christ and His Word.
Now, before we close, let us pray.
Heavenly Father,
Search our hearts.
Show us the voices we have allowed to influence our decisions.
Forgive us for the times we have mistaken cleverness for wisdom, approval for friendship, and personal desire for love.
Give us courage to resist evil even when it is disguised as good advice.
Teach us to be friends who speak truth with humility and compassion.
Protect our children, our families, and the vulnerable among us from those who would exploit their trust.
Lord, we remember those who, like Tamar, have suffered betrayal, abuse, and injustice.
Draw near to them.
Surround them with people who will listen, believe them without rushing to judgment, take their safety seriously, and help them receive the support and justice they need.
Let no wounded person believe that another's sin has made them worthless in Your sight.
And for those who have done wrong, bring genuine conviction, honest confession, repentance, and accountability.
Break the power of deception.
Destroy the excuses that keep people enslaved to sin.
Lead us all to the cross, where Your holiness and mercy meet.
Lord Jesus, teach us to love as You loved.
Not selfishly.
Not possessively.
Not with hidden agendas.
But with truth, purity, sacrifice, and grace.
May our homes be places of safety.
May our churches be places where evil is confronted and the wounded are cared for.
May our friendships lead us closer to You.
And may our lives testify that Your Gospel truly transforms hearts.
In the mighty name of Jesus Christ,
Amen.
And remember this, long after you close this page:
The wrong friend may help you open a door that destroys a life. The right friend will love you enough to stop you before you reach for the handle.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOTHER WHO FOUGHT THE SKY FOR HER DEAD SONS—AND THE GOD WHO DID NOT FORGET HER
paragraphs: THE MOTHER WHO FOUGHT THE SKY FOR HER DEAD SONS—AND THE GOD WHO DID NOT FORGET HER

Seven bodies. One grieving mother. A lonely hill where the birds came for the dead. And a heartbreaking act of love that finally reached the throne of a king. The story of Rizpah is not just about a mother's grief. It is about the terrible cost of injustice, the courage of those who refuse to look away, and the God who sees what the world would rather forget.
There are some kinds of pain that make people scream.
And there are others that leave them so shattered they can barely make a sound.
But imagine a mother standing beneath an open sky, staring at the bodies of her sons.
No funeral.
No final embrace.
No quiet grave where she could kneel and whisper goodbye.
Only their lifeless bodies exposed to the heat of the day, the cold of the night, and the hungry creatures circling overhead.
And a mother who refused to leave.
Her name was Rizpah.
And if you have ever loved someone you could not save, prayed for something that never happened, or wondered whether God could possibly see your suffering, you need to stay with this story.
Because the most devastating part is not what happened to her sons.
It is what their mother did afterward.
And what happened when the king finally heard.

The Bible introduces Rizpah as a concubine of King Saul and the daughter of Aiah (2 Samuel 3:7). She was a woman whose life was tied to the royal household, but whose own voice is never recorded in Scripture.
We do not hear her prayers.
We do not know what she said when her sons were taken.
We do not know whether she begged, protested, collapsed, or stood in stunned silence.
Scripture does not tell us.
But it tells us what she did when almost everything that mattered to her had been taken away.
And sometimes an action speaks so powerfully that centuries cannot silence it.
The tragedy unfolds in 2 Samuel 21, during the reign of David.
Israel had suffered a famine for three consecutive years. When David sought the LORD, he was told that bloodguilt rested upon Saul and his household because Saul had put the Gibeonites to death.
This matters.
The Gibeonites were a people to whom Israel had sworn protection generations earlier (Joshua 9:15–20). Whatever Saul believed justified his actions, his violence had violated a solemn covenant.
The famine was therefore connected, in the biblical account, to an unresolved national wrong.
David approached the Gibeonites and asked what would make atonement for the offense.
They did not request money.
They did not ask for land.
They demanded seven male descendants of Saul to be handed over for execution.
David agreed, while protecting Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, because of his own oath to Jonathan.
Among those handed over were Rizpah's two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth—the latter being a different Mephibosheth from Jonathan's son.
Five other men, descendants of Saul's household through Merab, were also handed over.
Seven men.
Seven lives.
Seven bodies.
And somewhere within this national reckoning was a mother who would have to endure something almost impossible to comprehend.
The men were executed at the beginning of the barley harvest.
And then came the verse that turns this ancient account into one of Scripture's most haunting portraits of maternal grief.

“And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.” — 2 Samuel 21:10, KJV
Read that again.
She would not let the birds settle upon them by day.
She would not let the wild animals approach them by night.
Her sons were dead.
She could not reverse the execution.
She could not restore their breathing.
She could not carry them back into the days when they were little boys running toward her voice.
But there was still one thing she could do.
She could remain.
And she did.
The Hebrew text contains a detail that makes this vigil even more piercing.
In 2 Samuel 21:10, the phrase וַתַּטֵּהוּ לָהּ אֶל־הַצּוּר (vattattēhû lāh ʾel-hatstsûr) describes Rizpah spreading the sackcloth for herself upon the rock.
The Hebrew word שַׂק (saq) means sackcloth, a coarse fabric associated with mourning, humiliation, and distress.
She did not spread a royal canopy.
She did not prepare a comfortable bed.
She took the fabric of grief and made her place upon the rock.
And the text says she stayed from the beginning of harvest until rain fell from heaven.
Scripture does not give the exact number of days. The interval suggests a prolonged vigil, potentially lasting months, but we should not pretend to know its precise duration.
What we do know is enough.
She remained through the passing days and nights.
When the sun rose, she faced the birds.
When darkness came, she faced the animals.
When exhaustion pressed upon her, the biblical narrative still presents her guarding the dead.
Imagine the sound of wings breaking the silence.
Imagine a shadow passing over the rock.
Imagine a mother rising again, her body weary, her heart shattered, because she knows what is coming.
And imagine having to do it again.
And again.
And again.
The world might have considered those men nothing more than condemned bodies.
But she knew their names.
She remembered their childhoods.
She remembered the faces that had once looked toward her for comfort.
She knew the difference between the judgment pronounced over them and the love she still carried for them.
Death had taken their lives.
It had not taken away her motherhood.
And there is something deeply human here that many grieving people will understand.
Sometimes love continues long after the person we love can no longer receive it.
A mother still prepares a meal for a child who will never come home.
A husband reaches across an empty bed before remembering.
A daughter keeps her father's old messages because deleting them feels like losing him twice.
Someone walks past a familiar chair and feels the entire weight of absence.
Grief does not always look like crying.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to throw away a shirt.
Sometimes it looks like sitting beside a hospital bed long after there is nothing left to say.
Sometimes it looks like a woman on a rock, driving away birds.
And perhaps that is why Rizpah's story still hurts.
Because the circumstances are ancient.
But the love is painfully familiar.
Yet we must not turn her suffering into a beautiful metaphor so quickly that we forget the terrible questions surrounding it.
Seven men were executed because of the bloodguilt associated with Saul's household.

The passage reports that David surrendered them to the Gibeonites. It does not give us the personal guilt or innocence of each man, nor does it record a direct divine command instructing David to execute these seven individuals.
That distinction matters.
Elsewhere, Scripture teaches that children are not to be put to death for the sins of their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20).
The Bible does not ask us to ignore these tensions.
It asks us to read carefully.

The historical narrative describes a grave act of covenantal reckoning in ancient Israel. It does not establish a universal Christian command to punish descendants for the wrongdoing of their ancestors.
Nor should anyone use this passage to claim that every famine, disaster, or personal tragedy is God's punishment for a particular sin.
Jesus Himself rejected simplistic explanations that automatically equated suffering with personal guilt (John 9:1–3; Luke 13:1–5).
Rizpah's story is not permission to blame the grieving.
It is an invitation to recognize suffering that power and public decisions can leave behind.
And in this story, the woman whose words are never recorded becomes the person whose actions can no longer be ignored.
Because eventually, somebody tells the king.
“And it was told David what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done.” — 2 Samuel 21:11, KJV
What a sentence.
She had no recorded speech before the throne.
No army.
No royal decree.
No authority to command the nation.
But her vigil became known to David.
And what David did next is essential to understanding the story.
He went to recover the bones of Saul and Jonathan, which had been taken by the men of Jabesh-gilead after their deaths. He also gathered the remains of the seven men who had been executed.
Then he arranged for Saul, Jonathan, and the seven descendants to be buried in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father, in Benjamin.
The account concludes:
“And after that God was intreated for the land.” — 2 Samuel 21:14, KJV
In other words, after these events, God responded to the plea concerning the land.
Notice the movement of the narrative.
A national wrong is confronted.
Seven descendants are executed.
A mother guards their exposed bodies.
The king learns what she has done.
The remains are gathered and buried.
And the account closes with God responding concerning the land.
Scripture does not explicitly say that Rizpah's vigil alone caused the famine to end. Nor does it tell us that she spoke directly to David or that the king publicly apologized.
But it unmistakably places her extraordinary devotion at the turning point before the burial.
Her refusal to abandon the dead became part of the story that moved the king to act.
There is a Hebrew expression near the end of verse 14 worth remembering: וַיֵּעָתֵר אֱלֹהִים לָאָרֶץ (vayyēʿātēr ʾĕlōhîm lāʾārets).
It conveys that God was entreated on behalf of the land, or responded to the supplication concerning it.
The Hebrew does not say that Rizpah earned God's mercy by suffering enough.
It does not teach that human endurance purchases divine favor.
It tells us that this painful history reached a conclusion in which the dead received burial and God responded concerning the land.
And here is where the story begins to confront us personally.
How many people are suffering in plain sight while everyone else continues with ordinary life?
How many mothers are carrying grief that no one has bothered to ask about?
How many fathers have learned to cry only when the house is empty?
How many believers are still attending church, still smiling, still serving, while something inside them is quietly collapsing?
We may not see bodies exposed upon a hill.
But we see people abandoned to shame.
We see families crushed by loss.
We see the wounded treated as inconveniences.
We see people whose stories are reduced to rumors, mistakes, scandals, and labels.
And sometimes the most Christlike thing we can do is refuse to look away.
Not because we can solve every tragedy.
Not because our presence makes suffering disappear.
But because human beings made in God's image must never become disposable.
Rizpah's vigil does not make her the Savior of the story.
It reveals the fierce devotion of a grieving mother.
And for Christians reading this account in the light of the whole Bible, it also creates a profound contrast that leads us toward Jesus Christ.
Rizpah guarded the bodies of those who could no longer defend themselves.
Centuries later, the Son of God would be publicly exposed to humiliation and death.
Jesus was mocked, stripped of His garments, crucified, and placed under a sentence of condemnation.
Yet unlike the seven descendants of Saul, Christ was personally sinless.
He did not die because He had inherited moral guilt from His earthly family.
He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
The apostle Peter wrote:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree...” — 1 Peter 2:24, KJV
And Paul declared:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us...” — Galatians 3:13, KJV
The Greek of Galatians 3:13 says Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν (Christos hēmas exēgorasen), meaning “Christ redeemed us.”
The verb ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen) carries the idea of redeeming or buying out of a condition of bondage or obligation.
This is not a claim that Rizpah's sons were direct prophetic substitutes for Jesus.
Their deaths are not presented in Scripture as a model of Christian atonement.
Rather, the contrast helps us see the uniqueness of Christ.
Rizpah could guard the dead.
She could not conquer death.
David could order a burial.
He could not resurrect the buried.
But Jesus entered death and rose again.
That is the difference between even the deepest human devotion and the saving power of the Son of God.
Rizpah remained near the bodies of her sons because she loved them.
Jesus laid down His own life to redeem those who had sinned against Him.
And when He rose from the grave, death did not have the final word.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that faithful people never suffer.
Not that every grieving mother gets the miracle she begged for.
Not that every injustice is repaired before sunset.
But that Jesus Christ entered a world of sin, cruelty, shame, and death, and through His death and resurrection opened the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and everlasting life.
The risen Christ does not ask the grieving to pretend their losses are small.
He Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35).
He knew sorrow.
He knew betrayal.
He knew what it meant to be abandoned.
And the resurrection assures us that the grave is not the final horizon for those who belong to Him.
This does not erase Rizpah's pain.
It gives Christian readers a hope beyond what Rizpah's story itself reveals.
And maybe today you are not standing over the body of someone you love.
Maybe you are standing over the ruins of a life you barely recognize.
A marriage that collapsed.
A child who has wandered far from God.
A family torn apart by betrayal.
A reputation destroyed by a scandal.
A secret sin that has consumed years of your peace.
A season of grief that has made you wonder whether you will ever feel alive again.
Perhaps you are tired of being the strong one.
Tired of hearing that everything happens for a reason.
Tired of people quoting verses at you without ever sitting long enough to hear you cry.
Hear this carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to deny your wounds.
It calls you to bring your wounded heart to Jesus.
And repentance is not the same as pretending that nothing happened.
If you have sinned, Christ calls you to turn from that sin and trust His mercy.
If you have been sinned against, His invitation is not to excuse abuse or remain in danger.
If you are grieving, He does not demand that you manufacture happiness to prove your faith.
The same Lord who calls sinners to repentance also welcomes the weary and heavy laden.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
Perhaps the most important words you can pray today are not impressive.
Perhaps they are simply:
“Jesus, I am tired.”
