Not because the people who hurt you finally apologized.
Not because your circumstances suddenly became safe.
Not because you managed to prove your worth.
But because the God who rules heaven and earth has never needed human permission to notice someone else's suffering.
Her name was Hagar.
And if you have ever felt invisible, there is something in her story you need to hear.
Because the first person Scripture explicitly records giving God a name in response to a divine encounter was not a king, a priest, or a celebrated patriarch.
It was an Egyptian enslaved woman who had been mistreated and was fleeing through the wilderness.
And the name she spoke still reaches into the darkest places of human experience.
“You are the God who sees me.”
But to understand how extraordinary those words are, we have to understand what happened before the angel appeared.
God had promised Abram descendants.
Yet years passed, and Sarai remained childless.
In Genesis 16, Sarai proposed that Abram have a child through Hagar, her Egyptian enslaved servant.

The ancient world sometimes treated enslaved women's reproductive lives as something their owners could control. The biblical account records this arrangement without presenting it as God's command or moral approval.
And that distinction matters.
Because something being described in Scripture does not automatically mean God endorses it.
Hagar was not introduced as a woman freely choosing the future she wanted.
She was a servant under another woman's authority, drawn into a household's desperate attempt to secure the fulfillment of a divine promise.
Genesis 16:3 says Sarai gave Hagar to Abram as a wife.
But the text also continues to identify Hagar as Sarai's servant.
Her vulnerable status did not disappear.
And when Hagar conceived, the household began to fracture.
Genesis 16:4 tells us that after she became pregnant, her mistress was diminished in her eyes.
The text does not tell us everything Hagar was thinking. We should not pretend to know every motive hidden in her heart.
But we do know what followed.
Sarai blamed Abram for the conflict.
Abram answered by placing Hagar back under Sarai's authority.
And then came the sentence that should make every reader uncomfortable.
“And when Sarai dealt harshly with her, she fled from her.” — Genesis 16:6, ESV
The Hebrew word translated “dealt harshly” comes from the verb עָנָה (ʿanah), which in this context conveys affliction, humiliation, or harsh treatment.
Scripture does not invite us to romanticize what happened.
Hagar was afflicted.
And she ran.
Maybe you have never crossed a literal desert.
But you know what it feels like to reach the point where staying seems unbearable and leaving seems terrifying.
You know what it means to be exhausted by a situation you did not create alone.
You know what it is to wonder whether anyone understands the cost of what you've been carrying.
Hagar fled into the wilderness.
And then Genesis 16:7 records a moment that is easy to read too quickly.
“The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur.” — Genesis 16:7, ESV
Read that word again.
Found.
The Hebrew verb is מָצָא (matsaʾ).
He found her.
The text does not say Hagar discovered a secret spiritual formula.
It does not say she performed an extraordinary act of worship to attract heaven's attention.
It does not even record her praying before this encounter.
It says the angel of the LORD found her.
She was not beyond God's reach.
And neither is anyone else who has been pushed to the margins of human concern.
There is something profoundly beautiful about where this encounter happened.
Not inside a palace.
Not at a religious festival.
Not before an audience of influential people.
Beside a spring in the wilderness.
A place where a desperate traveler might stop because water meant the possibility of another day.
And there, in the middle of her uncertain future, the angel spoke.
“Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?” — Genesis 16:8, ESV
He called her Hagar.
By name.
In a story where powerful people had treated her life as something they could arrange, heaven addressed her as a person.
And the question was deeply personal.
Where have you come from?
Where are you going?
God was not asking because He lacked information.
The question invited Hagar to speak about her situation.
And she answered with painful simplicity.
“I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai.”
There was no polished testimony.
No carefully rehearsed religious language.
Just the truth.
She was running from the woman who had mistreated her.
Sometimes the beginning of spiritual honesty is not a beautiful prayer.
Sometimes it is finally telling the truth about what happened.
“I am hurting.”
“I am afraid.”
“I don't know what to do.”
“I am tired of pretending.”
And the God revealed in Scripture is not threatened by truthful lament.
But then the story takes a difficult turn.
The angel tells Hagar to return to her mistress and submit to her authority.
We must not rush past that command.
Nor should we turn it into a weapon against people suffering abuse today.

Genesis 16:9 records a specific instruction given to Hagar in a particular historical encounter. It is not a universal command requiring abused spouses, trafficked people, or endangered individuals to remain in harmful situations.
The same Scriptures that record this command also reveal God's concern for the oppressed, His condemnation of injustice, and His call to protect the vulnerable.
A person facing abuse today deserves protection, wise counsel, and practical safety—not pressure to endure violence in silence.
And Genesis itself does not pretend that Hagar's difficulties were permanently resolved by this encounter.
Years later, in Genesis 21, Hagar and her son would again find themselves in the wilderness.
Yet here in Genesis 16, the angel's message included a promise.
God would multiply her offspring beyond counting.
Then came an announcement that must have sounded astonishing to a woman whose suffering had been so easily dismissed.
“Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction.” — Genesis 16:11, ESV
Ishmael.
In Hebrew, יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yishmaʿel).
The name means “God hears” or “God will hear.”
Think about that.
The child Hagar was carrying would bear a name that testified to God's attention to her suffering.
The promise did not erase every consequence of the broken household.
It did not make the injustice acceptable.
It did not mean Ishmael's future would be free of conflict.
Indeed, Genesis 16:12 foretells a difficult, contentious future for him.
But God had heard Hagar's affliction.
The Hebrew word עֳנִי (ʿoni) speaks of affliction, misery, or distress.
And the Lord's response was not indifference.
The God who saw her was also the God who heard her.
Somebody reading this has been carrying a prayer so long that silence has started to feel like rejection.
You have asked God why the doors remain closed.
Why the healing has taken so long.
Why the people who hurt you appear to be moving forward while you are still trying to recover.
Why obedience has sometimes felt harder than you expected.
And perhaps you have begun to wonder whether your tears have become invisible.
Hagar's story does not promise that every painful situation will be resolved immediately.
But it does confront the lie that suffering makes you unworthy of God's attention.
Then comes one of the most unforgettable verses in Genesis.
“So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, ‘You are a God of seeing.’” — Genesis 16:13, ESV
The Hebrew expression is:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro'i.
“You are a God of seeing.”
Often expressed devotionally as:
“You are the God who sees me.”
The Hebrew is rich and the verse's following words are difficult to translate precisely. But its central revelation is unmistakable.
Hagar recognized that the living God had seen her.
The one treated as disposable had been personally addressed by heaven.
The woman whose suffering had been overlooked had received divine attention.
The outsider had encountered the Lord.
And the astonishing thing is that Hagar did not give God this name from a place of worldly triumph.
She was still in the wilderness.
She still faced an uncertain road.
But she now knew something about God that changed how she understood her own existence.
She was seen.
There is a difference between having every question answered and discovering that you have not been abandoned.
And sometimes the second truth is what gives you the strength to face the questions that remain.
But Hagar's story becomes even more powerful when we read it within the whole story of Scripture.
Because Genesis is not ultimately a collection of isolated inspirational moments.
It is part of the unfolding revelation of God's redemptive purpose.
The promise to Abram would continue through Isaac, the son later born to Sarah, as Genesis 17 and 21 make clear.
Ishmael was not the child through whom that particular covenant line would continue.
Yet God did not disregard Ishmael.
He promised to bless him and make him into a great nation.
That matters.
Because God's covenant purposes never meant that people outside the chosen family were invisible to Him.
And as the biblical story unfolds, God's promise to bless all the families of the earth through Abraham reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The Savior born from Abraham's line did not come merely to admire the respectable.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He touched people others avoided.
He spoke with those others dismissed.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He defended the dignity of the vulnerable.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
And He showed a world obsessed with status that God's kingdom operates according to a radically different measure of greatness.
Consider the woman at the well in John 4.
Another woman.
Another encounter near water.
Another life carrying complicated history.
And once again, a woman found herself speaking with someone who knew more about her circumstances than she expected.
Jesus did not ignore the truth about her life.
But neither did He reduce her to the worst or most complicated parts of her story.
He offered living water.
He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
And the woman who had come to draw water went back to her community speaking about the One she had encountered.
There are meaningful echoes between these wilderness and wellside encounters, even though they are distinct events with different circumstances.
Both remind us that God is not confined to the places where religious people expect to find Him.
And both direct our attention toward a truth that becomes gloriously clear in Christ.
The God who sees human suffering has acted decisively to redeem sinners through His Son.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than an emotional comfort.
Because our deepest problem is not only that other people have sinned against us.
It is also that we ourselves have sinned before a holy God.
We have wounded others.
We have hidden things.
We have chosen pride when humility was required.
We have sought control when trust was needed.
We have sometimes behaved more like Abram and Sarai at their worst than we would ever want to admit.
And Scripture will not let us divide humanity neatly into innocent sufferers and guilty offenders.
We may be deeply wounded by another person's sin while still needing forgiveness for our own.
That is why Jesus did not come merely to tell hurting people that they matter.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God bore our sins.
He suffered injustice without becoming unjust.
He endured rejection without surrendering His obedience to the Father.
He died for our sins and rose again, defeating death and opening the way to reconciliation with God.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, ESV
Notice what the verse does not say.
Christ died for us once we became impressive.
Once we repaired our reputation.
Once we stopped struggling.
Once we proved that we deserved mercy.
No.
While we were still sinners.
This is grace.
Not permission to continue in sin without repentance.
Not a denial of the harm sin causes.
Not a promise that following Jesus will remove every earthly hardship.
Grace is God's undeserved favor, given through Jesus Christ, calling us out of darkness and into a transformed life.
And repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can forgive and renew us.
Maybe that is what makes Hagar's story so unsettling.
Because when we read about her suffering, we naturally want God to confront the people who harmed her.
And rightly so. Injustice matters.
But when the Gospel turns its light toward our own hearts, we must also ask:
Whom have I overlooked?
Whose pain have I minimized?
Have I used my position, my influence, my words, or even my religion to make someone else feel small?
Have I demanded grace for myself while withholding mercy from others?
Have I become so concerned about God's promises for my future that I have forgotten His commands concerning how I treat people today?
These are uncomfortable questions.
But sometimes the truth that heals us must first expose us.
The Gospel does not only comfort the wounded.
It also calls the proud to repentance.
And it brings both to the feet of Jesus.
If this story has uncovered something in your heart, don't rush past it.
Maybe you need to forgive someone, while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
Maybe you need to seek forgiveness from someone you have harmed.
Maybe you need to stop hiding behind religious appearances and tell God the truth.
Maybe you need to ask for help because your situation has become unsafe.
Or maybe you have spent years believing that what happened to you has permanently defined you.
Listen carefully.
What happened to Hagar was real.
Her suffering was not imaginary.
The injustice did not become good simply because God met her in the wilderness.
And your suffering does not have to be minimized for God's grace to be magnificent.
Redemption does not require us to call evil good. It means evil does not have the final authority over those who belong to Christ.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is so deeply rooted in the Gospel.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
Not because the consequences of sin magically disappear.
But because Jesus Christ can forgive sinners, restore the repentant, heal wounded hearts, and make new what sin has devastated.
He is not a cosmetic improvement to an old life.
He is the risen Savior who gives new life.
And there is something else we should remember about Hagar.
Her encounter with God was not the end of her story.
In Genesis 21, after Isaac's birth, Hagar and Ishmael were sent away.
Once again, she found herself in the wilderness.
Once again, the future looked terrifying.
And when the water was gone, she placed her child beneath a bush and sat at a distance because she could not bear to watch him die.
Can you imagine?
A mother who had once received a promise now facing a moment when everything appeared lost.
She wept.
And Genesis 21:17 says God heard the voice of the boy.
Then God opened Hagar's eyes, and she saw a well of water.
The God who had heard her affliction in Genesis 16 had not forgotten His promise in Genesis 21.
But notice something important.
The story does not say that remembering God's promise prevented Hagar from experiencing fear, exhaustion, or grief.
Faithful people can still experience overwhelming sorrow.
People who have encountered God can still face another wilderness.
And the presence of suffering does not automatically mean the absence of faith.
Sometimes we imagine that once God has met us, we should never struggle again.
But Scripture tells a more truthful story.
The God who met Hagar beside one spring was still faithful when she faced another desert.
And the Christ who saves us does not abandon His people when their journey becomes difficult.
His resurrection is the guarantee of a hope greater than our present circumstances.
His grace sustains us.
His Word corrects us.
His Spirit strengthens His people.
And His promise of final restoration reaches beyond anything this broken world can offer.
Perhaps that is why this ancient account continues to speak so powerfully.
Because somewhere tonight, a mother is crying quietly after putting her children to sleep.
A father is staring at bills he does not know how to pay.
A young believer is ashamed of a sin they keep returning to.
Someone who used to pray confidently now struggles to find words.
A person wounded by a church community is wondering whether they can trust anyone again.
Someone is smiling in public while privately fighting despair.
And someone else is reading this with tears in their eyes because, for the first time in a long time, they feel as though the Bible is speaking directly into the place they have been trying to hide.
If that is you, hear what this passage actually gives us.
Not a guarantee of immediate rescue from every difficult circumstance.
Not permission to ignore wise counsel or practical help.
Not a promise that everyone who hurt you will repent.
But a revelation of God's character.
He sees.
He hears.
He knows.
And through Jesus Christ, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal hope to everyone who turns to Him in faith.
You do not need to pretend that your wilderness is beautiful.
You do not need to call your wounds blessings.
You do not need to prove your worth by carrying pain silently.
You can bring your honest heart before the Lord.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, there is no better time to turn to Him than now.
Confess your sins.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive His grace by faith.
Follow Him in repentance and obedience.
Not because your story is already clean.
But because the Savior is holy, merciful, and mighty to save.
And if you already belong to Christ but have grown weary, come back to His Word.
Come back to prayer.
Come back to the fellowship of believers who will help you walk in truth.
Come back to the cross, where human sin was exposed and divine mercy was displayed.
You may be in the wilderness.
But the wilderness does not have to become your identity.
Jesus Christ is greater than the darkest chapter of your story.
And that is why we continue sharing these messages through Gospel Warrior.
Not simply to collect reactions on a screen.
Not to build a following around human personalities.
But to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to reveal private details to be part of a community that prays.

And if this passage convicted you about the way you have treated someone, perhaps your next response should be more than a comment. Perhaps it should be a sincere apology, a changed decision, or an act of justice and mercy.
Because God's Word was never meant merely to move our emotions.
It was meant to shape our lives.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make sound Christian teaching accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word.
But we want to be biblically clear about something important.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, not pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
The purpose of everything we create is to keep drawing attention back to His Word, His finished work, and the life-changing truth of His Gospel.
No donation can earn salvation.
No ministry can replace the local church or the Lord Jesus Christ.
We are servants pointing toward the Savior.
And the Savior is the One who changes lives.
Before you leave, I want you to return to that desert spring one more time.
Picture Hagar standing there.
Dust on her feet.
A child growing inside her.
An uncertain road ahead.
She had been mistreated by people who possessed far more power than she did.
She had no guarantee that tomorrow would be easy.
But she had encountered the living God.
And she gave Him a name that generations would remember.
El Ro'i.
The God who sees.
Thousands of years later, we know something Hagar could not yet have seen in its fullness.
The promised Redeemer has come.
Jesus Christ has died for sinners.
The tomb is empty.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness and eternal life.
That is the hope we carry.
Not that every scandal will become a success story in the eyes of the world.
But that through the grace of Jesus Christ, sin does not have to have the last word.
Shame does not have to have the last word.
Your worst decision does not have to have the last word.
And the cruelty of someone who hurt you does not possess the authority to determine your eternal worth.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And His mercy is greater than the darkness we bring to Him.
So if you have been hiding, come into His light.
If you have sinned, repent and trust His forgiveness.
If you have been wounded, seek His healing and the help you need.
If you have grown weary, return to His promises.
Someone else may need to hear how His faithfulness sustained you.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Hagar's wilderness was not how far she had run—it was that even there, she was never beyond the sight of God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD FORBID A MAN FROM “UNCOVERING A WOMAN’S NAKEDNESS”? THE DISTURBING TRUTH HIDDEN IN LEVITICUS 18:6
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD FORBID A MAN FROM “UNCOVERING A WOMAN’S NAKEDNESS”? THE DISTURBING TRUTH HIDDEN IN LEVITICUS 18:6
One ancient Hebrew expression. One command that modern readers often misunderstand. And one uncomfortable truth about sex, family, secrecy, and the holiness of God that still confronts us today.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
There are Bible verses that strengthen you.
And then there are Bible verses that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and whisper, “Lord… what exactly are You saying?”
Leviticus 18:6 is one of them.
Because when God told Israel not to approach someone to “uncover nakedness,” He was not simply giving instructions about clothing.
He was addressing something far more intimate.
Something that could destroy families.
Something that could turn trust into betrayal, affection into exploitation, and what should have been a place of safety into a lifetime of wounds.
And here is what makes this passage so important.
If you misunderstand the expression, you may misunderstand the command. But if you understand the Hebrew, you begin to see why God spoke so seriously about sexual boundaries.
The verse says:
“None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.”
— Leviticus 18:6, KJV
Read those final words again.
“I am the LORD.”
Not merely, “This is socially unacceptable.”
Not merely, “This is how your ancestors behaved.”
God placed His own authority behind the command.
But why?
What does “uncover nakedness” actually mean?
And why does a passage written thousands of years ago still matter to people struggling with sexual temptation, hidden shame, family wounds, and the longing to be made clean?
The answer begins in the Hebrew.
And it may challenge some things you have heard preached about this verse.
In the original Hebrew, the central expression is:
לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה
Legal·lōth ʿerwāh — “to uncover nakedness.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root גלה (g-l-h), meaning “to uncover,” “to reveal,” or “to expose.”
The noun עֶרְוָה (ʿerwāh) refers to nakedness, particularly intimate or sexual nakedness, and can carry the sense of shameful exposure depending on the context.
But here is the critical distinction.
In Leviticus 18, this is not merely a description of someone accidentally seeing another person without clothes.
It is a sexual expression used within a series of prohibitions against unlawful sexual relations.
And we know this because the surrounding verses explain what the expression means in context.
Leviticus 18:7 forbids uncovering the nakedness of one's father or mother, then specifically identifies the mother's nakedness.
Leviticus 18:8 prohibits uncovering the nakedness of one's father's wife, explaining that her nakedness is connected to the father's.
Leviticus 18:14 speaks of an uncle's nakedness and immediately clarifies the prohibition by referring to approaching his wife.
Leviticus 18:20 then speaks explicitly of sexual intercourse with a neighbor's wife.
The chapter is not a random collection of rules about looking at bodies.
It is addressing sexual relationships that God forbade.
The wording in Leviticus 18:6 is even more revealing when we examine its opening phrase:
אִישׁ אִישׁ אֶל־כָּל־שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה
A close rendering is:
“None of you shall approach anyone who is a close relative to uncover nakedness.”
The expression שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ (she'er besaro) refers to someone of one's own flesh, a close relative.
And לֹא תִקְרְבוּ (lo tiqrevu) means “you shall not approach” in this construction.
The command concerns approaching a close relative for a prohibited sexual purpose.

This matters because the verse is sometimes quoted as though God were forbidding all physical closeness between men and women, or as though every instance of seeing someone's nakedness automatically constituted the specific offense described here.
That goes beyond what this passage actually says.
The biblical context identifies the issue as forbidden sexual intimacy, especially within relationships of close kinship.

And the original wording of verse 6 does not simply say “a woman.” Its prohibition is expressed broadly in relation to close relatives, with the following verses specifying the forbidden relationships.
That is why careful interpretation matters.
We do not honor Scripture by making it say more than it says.
We honor Scripture by listening carefully to what God actually revealed.
And when we do, something powerful emerges.
God was placing boundaries around relationships in which trust, family responsibility, and sexual conduct could become dangerously entangled.
Imagine a home where the people who should protect you are the very people you fear.
Imagine growing up around someone whose affection comes with an expectation you never agreed to.
Imagine carrying a secret for years because speaking the truth might divide the family.
Imagine being told to remain silent to preserve a reputation while your own heart quietly falls apart.
For some people, those words are not hypothetical.
They describe childhood.
They describe family gatherings.
They describe memories they have spent years trying to bury.
And this is where we must handle the passage with both conviction and compassion.
God's prohibition of sexual wrongdoing must never be twisted into condemnation of the person who was violated.
A child who has been abused has not become guilty of the abuser's sin.
A person who was coerced has not forfeited their worth before God.
Someone who was assaulted does not become spiritually dirty because another person committed evil against them.

Scripture itself recognizes the moral distinction between wrongdoing and victimization. Deuteronomy 22:25–27, in its discussion of sexual violence, explicitly places guilt upon the attacker rather than the victim in the case it describes.
That distinction matters.
Because some people have been carrying shame that belongs to someone else's actions.
Some have been told to forgive without being allowed to speak.
Some have been pressured to protect an abuser in the name of family unity.
Some have even been made to believe that exposing wrongdoing dishonors God.
But hiding abuse is not holiness.
Protecting a reputation at the expense of the vulnerable is not righteousness.
And forgiveness does not require silence, continued access to an abuser, or the abandonment of justice.
The God who commands holiness is also the God who loves justice.
Psalm 82:3–4 calls for justice for the weak and the fatherless and for the deliverance of the afflicted and needy.
And the Lord Jesus spoke with extraordinary seriousness about causing vulnerable little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
So when we read Leviticus 18, we must not reduce its commands to a cold list of forbidden acts.
We must recognize the moral seriousness of the relationships involved.
The family was never meant to become a hiding place for sexual exploitation.
The home was never meant to become a sanctuary for predators.
And the authority entrusted to a parent, guardian, or relative was never permission to take what God had forbidden.
But there is another side to this passage that we cannot ignore.
Because not every sexual sin begins with violence.
Some begin with a secret conversation.
An inappropriate attachment.
A boundary deliberately crossed.
A desire entertained until the conscience grows quieter.
Someone says, “We didn't mean for it to happen.”
Someone else says, “Nobody will ever know.”
And sometimes those words become the doorway to betrayal.
The Bible does not teach that every desire is itself the same as a completed act. But Jesus warns that deliberately cultivating lust is a serious matter of the heart (Matthew 5:27–28).
Sin can begin long before it becomes publicly visible.
That is why God's boundaries are not merely concerned with what other people can discover.
They are concerned with what we are becoming when nobody is watching.
And perhaps that is the uncomfortable question this passage leaves with us.
Not simply, “What did ancient Israel do?”
But, “What am I allowing in my life that I already know I should surrender?”
Maybe it is a relationship you keep defending even though you know its intimacy has crossed a moral boundary.
Maybe it is pornography that has slowly reshaped the way you see other people.
Maybe it is an emotional affair you have renamed “friendship” because admitting the truth would demand change.
Maybe it is a secret that has survived only because you have become skilled at hiding it.
Or perhaps you are reading this from the opposite side of the wound.
You did not choose what happened.
You did not invite the betrayal.
And you have spent years wondering whether God sees you differently because of it.
Please hear this.
Your suffering is not proof that God has rejected you.
The Lord sees what people conceal.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
— KJV
That promise does not mean every wound disappears immediately.
It does not mean trauma is healed by pretending nothing happened.
And it does not mean a person must avoid professional care, trusted support, or lawful protection.
But it does mean that suffering does not place you beyond the reach of God's compassion.
Now consider something else.
Why did God give Israel these commands in the first place?
Leviticus 18:3 provides part of the answer.
Israel was warned not to imitate the practices of Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going.
God was forming a people whose lives would reflect His character rather than simply mirror the surrounding cultures.
Then comes the repeated declaration:
“I am the LORD.”
That statement appears throughout the chapter.
It is the foundation of the command.
Israel's sexual conduct was not supposed to be governed merely by appetite, opportunity, custom, or convenience.
It was to be governed by the God who had delivered them.
And notice the order.
God had already brought Israel out of Egypt before giving these instructions at Sinai.
Obedience was not the price they paid to make God their Redeemer.
It was part of how a redeemed people were called to live.
That distinction prepares us to understand the Gospel.
Because the Bible's story does not end with humanity being commanded to be holy.
It moves toward the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
And that brings us to Jesus Christ.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was accused of adultery.
She stood surrounded by people ready to condemn her.
Her wrongdoing had become public spectacle.
And Jesus refused to participate in their trap.
He confronted the accusers and then spoke directly to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:11, KJV
Those words must be understood together.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy did not become permission to continue in sin.
And the call to change did not erase the mercy being offered.
Jesus did not announce that adultery was suddenly righteous.
He also refused to treat the woman as though her failure were the entirety of her identity.
This is one of the breathtaking realities of the Gospel.
Jesus does not need to pretend sin is harmless in order to show mercy to sinners.
He is full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
He calls people out of darkness because He loves them, not because He delights in humiliating them.
And the cross reveals just how seriously God takes both sin and redemption.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
— KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had perfected ourselves.
Not after every secret had been resolved.
Not after we had become worthy of salvation through our own efforts.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
But that grace is never presented as a license to keep doing evil.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic.
“God forbid.”
Grace does not merely offer relief from guilt.
It calls us into a new life.
And this is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because forgiveness makes accountability unnecessary.
But because the finished work of Jesus Christ makes repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life possible.
The Gospel does not erase historical facts.
It changes what sin and shame are allowed to say about a person who belongs to Christ.
Consider the Apostle Paul.
Before his conversion, he persecuted the church.
He later acknowledged the seriousness of his former life.
Yet the grace of God transformed him into a servant of the very Christ he had opposed (1 Timothy 1:12–16).
His past remained part of his testimony.
But it was no longer the final word.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to understand.
If you have sinned sexually, do not excuse it.
Do not call evil love.
Do not blame another person for choices that were yours.
Do not use God's forgiveness as a reason to avoid confession, restitution, or accountability.
If you have harmed someone, genuine repentance includes stopping the harm, respecting their safety and boundaries, and accepting appropriate consequences.
But do not imagine that your sin is more powerful than the blood of Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— KJV
The promise is not that confession makes wrongdoing insignificant.
The promise is that God is faithful to forgive and cleanse those who come to Him.
And if you are the person who was harmed, you are not required to describe yourself as the guilty one in order to receive God's care.
You may need healing rather than repentance for the harm done against you.
You may need protection rather than another demand to remain quiet.
You may need people who will listen, believe you, help you find safety, and walk beside you patiently.
Jesus does not ask the wounded to call evil good.
He is the light of the world (John 8:12).
And light reveals what darkness tries to hide.
There is another Hebrew expression worth understanding.
In Genesis 2:24, the Bible says that a man shall leave his father and mother, hold fast to his wife, and that they shall become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad) — “one flesh.”
This is not the same expression used in Leviticus 18:6.
But the relationship between the passages is illuminating.
Genesis presents marriage as a covenantal union in which two become one flesh.
Leviticus establishes boundaries against sexual unions that violate God's commands.
And Jesus Himself returns to Genesis 2:24 when teaching about marriage in Matthew 19:4–6.
He does not treat the body as meaningless.
He does not treat sexual intimacy as a trivial appetite.
He places marriage within the purposes of the Creator.
This does not mean every person must marry to live a faithful Christian life. Jesus and Paul both affirm the dignity of unmarried life (Matthew 19:10–12; 1 Corinthians 7).
It means that our bodies and relationships matter to God.
And for believers, that truth becomes even more personal.
First Corinthians 6:19–20 teaches that the believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and calls Christians to glorify God in their bodies.
Your body is not spiritually irrelevant.
The way you treat other people is not spiritually irrelevant.
What you do in secret is not spiritually irrelevant.
And neither is the dignity of the person standing before you.
That person is not an object to consume.
Not a secret to exploit.
Not a body without a soul.
Not an opportunity to satisfy desire without responsibility.
They are a human being made in the image of God.
This is why sexual holiness cannot be reduced to avoiding a list of forbidden acts.

It also involves learning to love without exploiting, exercising self-control, honoring commitments, respecting boundaries, and refusing to treat another person's vulnerability as an invitation to sin.
And if that sounds impossible because of the life you have lived, remember what the Apostle Paul wrote to believers in Corinth.
After describing serious sins from which people needed to turn, he said:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
“Such were some of you.”
There is hope in those words.
Not because the sins were imaginary.
But because the grace of God had begun a real transformation.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not through human achievement.
But in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of God.
That is what makes Christianity different from a message of mere self-improvement.
The Gospel does not simply say, “Try harder to become a better person.”
It announces what God has done through Jesus Christ to reconcile sinners to Himself and calls those who believe to walk in the new life His grace provides.
And now, after everything we have seen in Leviticus 18:6, perhaps the question has changed.
We began by asking why God forbade someone from approaching a close relative to uncover nakedness.
We discovered that the Hebrew describes prohibited sexual intimacy, not merely the accidental sight of an unclothed body.
We saw how the surrounding chapter establishes boundaries around family relationships and sexual conduct.
We saw that God's commands must never be used to shame victims or conceal abuse.
And we saw that the holiness revealed in the Law points us toward our need for the grace and redemption found in Jesus Christ.
But now the question becomes personal.
What will you do with the truth?
Will you keep defending what Scripture calls sin?
Will you continue hiding something that needs to be brought into the light?
Will you keep allowing shame to tell you that Christ cannot receive a repentant sinner?
Will you keep carrying blame for something another person did to you?
Or will you begin bringing the truth before the Lord?
Not with a rehearsed religious performance.
Not with impressive words.
But with honesty.
“Lord Jesus, I need You.”
Sometimes those five words are where a life begins to change.
Maybe you need to confess.
Maybe you need to seek help.
Maybe you need to end a sinful relationship.
Maybe you need to establish a boundary that should have existed years ago.
Maybe you need to tell a trusted person about the harm you have endured.
Maybe you need to believe that the Savior who died and rose again is able to receive you even after everything you have done.
Whatever the next faithful step looks like, do not confuse hiding with healing.
And do not confuse religious appearance with genuine transformation.
Jesus came to save sinners.
And He is worthy of more than the version of ourselves we allow other people to see.
You do not owe strangers the details of your pain. A few sincere words can still open the door to encouragement, prayer, and Christian fellowship.
And perhaps there is someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message.
Someone who has misunderstood this passage.
Someone struggling with sexual temptation.
Someone who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has been hurt by people who were supposed to protect them.
You may never know whose private prayer is answered when biblical truth reaches them at the right moment.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people move beyond inspirational quotations into meaningful engagement with Scripture, repentance, spiritual growth, and a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning accessible to people who are hungry for the Word, including those who may not have the means to purchase Christian books.
And that work needs people who believe it is worth sustaining.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for financial contributions (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But if you believe this ministry is faithfully serving the Gospel and you have the ability to support it, your voluntary generosity can be one meaningful expression of stewardship.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver, not someone pressured into giving.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through a shared desire to help more people encounter the truth of Scripture.
These products are simply an additional way to express gratitude. They are not the reason anyone should give.
The greater purpose is to help sustain the ministry and encourage continued growth in Christ.
And if you cannot contribute financially, you are still welcome here.
The free biblical resources remain part of our mission, because the Gospel is not merchandise and the love of Christ is not for sale.
Before you leave, remember where this journey began.
One ancient command.
One Hebrew expression.
One warning about forbidden intimacy.
But behind that command was the holiness of a God who cares about what human beings do with their bodies, their relationships, their responsibilities, and the trust placed in their hands.
And beyond the Law, we see the Savior who came not to abolish God's righteousness but to fulfill the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 5:17).
The same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance offers forgiveness through His death and resurrection.
The same Jesus who exposes darkness offers light.
The same Jesus who tells us to turn away from sin also invites the weary and burdened to come to Him (Matthew 11:28).
So do not leave this article merely knowing what an ancient Hebrew phrase means.
Leave knowing that God's Word deserves to be understood in context.
Leave remembering that holiness and compassion belong together.
Leave refusing to excuse abuse, exploit another person's vulnerability, or make peace with hidden sin.
And above all, leave looking to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest hope of the Gospel is not that we can rewrite our own history.
It is that Jesus Christ can redeem people whose histories they cannot change.
The past may still carry your fingerprints, your tears, or your scars—but it does not have the authority to write the final sentence over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHRISTIAN COUPLES USE SEX TOYS WITHOUT SINNING? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING DEEPER THAN WHAT HAPPENS IN YOUR BEDROOM.
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIAN COUPLES USE SEX TOYS WITHOUT SINNING? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING DEEPER THAN WHAT HAPPENS IN YOUR BEDROOM.
What Scripture actually says, what it never says, and the uncomfortable question every Christian husband and wife must answer before bringing anything new into their marriage.
There are questions Christians whisper because they are afraid someone will hear them.
Questions they would never ask during Sunday fellowship.
Questions that make a husband hesitate, a wife blush, and a married couple wonder whether even discussing them means something is wrong with their faith.
And somewhere tonight, behind a closed bedroom door, two people who genuinely love Jesus may be struggling with one of those questions.
“Is this allowed?”
Not because they want to rebel against God.
Not because they have stopped believing in holiness.
But because they love each other, desire intimacy, and desperately want to know where marital freedom ends and sin begins.
Perhaps one spouse suggested introducing a sex toy into their private intimacy.
Perhaps the other immediately felt uncomfortable.
Perhaps both were curious but afraid.
Or perhaps one silently agreed, not because they wanted to, but because they feared disappointing the person they married.
And suddenly, what should have been a conversation between two people who promised to love each other became a battlefield of desire, guilt, expectations, and spiritual uncertainty.
Here is where this conversation becomes more serious than many people realize.
Not everything that happens between married people automatically honors God. But not everything that makes religious people uncomfortable is automatically condemned by God either.
Read that again.
Because the difference matters.
And before anyone declares, “Of course it is sinful,” or confidently announces, “Anything is acceptable because we are married,” we need to open Scripture.
Not our assumptions.
Not internet opinions.
Not the loudest voice in a Christian comment section.
The Word of God.
Because the real question is not simply whether a Christian couple may use a particular object.
The deeper question is whether their choices reflect the love, holiness, mutual honor, and self-giving character of Jesus Christ.
And the answer requires more than a convenient Bible verse.
It requires honesty.
Especially when that honesty makes us uncomfortable.
The first thing we must acknowledge is something many religious discussions conveniently overlook.
The Bible does not explicitly mention modern sex toys.
There is no verse that specifically names them, categorically approves them, or categorically prohibits them.
That does not mean Scripture has nothing to say about marital intimacy.
It means we must be careful not to place words in God's mouth.
Deuteronomy 4:2 warns God's people against adding to or subtracting from His commandments.
That principle should make every Christian teacher cautious about turning personal convictions into universal divine laws.
If Scripture does not explicitly prohibit something, we should not pretend that it does.
But if Scripture does not explicitly mention something, we should not automatically assume it is wise, loving, or morally acceptable either.
Biblical discernment requires us to examine the principles God has revealed.
And one of the most important passages begins with a truth that our culture has almost forgotten.
Marriage is not supposed to be a place where one person owns the other's body.
It is supposed to be a covenant of mutual belonging, responsibility, and love.
Listen to the apostle Paul.

In 1 Corinthians 7:3–4, he teaches that husbands and wives have reciprocal marital responsibilities and that neither spouse should treat their body as though the other has no legitimate place in their shared intimate life.
The Greek text contains a remarkable expression:
ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει
Hē gynē tou idiou sōmatos ouk exousiazei.
Literally, in context: “The wife does not exercise authority over her own body.”
But Paul does not stop there.
He applies the same principle to the husband.
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει
Homoiōs de kai ho anēr tou idiou sōmatos ouk exousiazei.
“Likewise, the husband does not exercise authority over his own body.”
The Greek verb exousiazō concerns exercising authority or control.
Notice the astonishing symmetry.
Paul does not give the husband unlimited authority over his wife.
He does not portray the wife as an instrument for satisfying her husband's desires.
He describes reciprocal marital obligations.
And the surrounding passage matters.
In verse 5, Paul instructs spouses not to deprive one another except by mutual agreement for a time, in the context of prayer.
The phrase translated “by agreement” is:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou
It expresses mutual consent or agreement.
This passage is not a license for sexual coercion. It must be read alongside the Bible's commands to love, honor, and care for one another.
Marriage does not erase a person's dignity.
A wedding ring does not transform pressure into love.
And a marriage vow does not make someone's discomfort irrelevant.
Husbands, hear this carefully.
If your wife feels frightened, humiliated, pressured, or spiritually troubled by something you want to introduce into your intimacy, her concerns are not obstacles you must overcome.
They are feelings you must take seriously.
Wives, the same truth applies to your husbands.
A husband is not less masculine because he has boundaries.
A wife is not less loving because she says no.
Mutual intimacy should never require one spouse to betray their conscience to satisfy the other.
That is not the spirit of Christlike love.
And it leads us to another passage that many Christians rarely hear discussed honestly.
The Song of Songs.
Yes, that book.
The one some people read with embarrassment because its language is unmistakably romantic, affectionate, and sensual.
The book celebrates desire within a relationship of committed love.
In Song of Songs 4:7, the beloved is praised as altogether beautiful.
In Song of Songs 7, the poetry openly celebrates physical attraction.
And in Song of Songs 8:6, love is described in Hebrew with extraordinary intensity:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki-ʿazzāh khammāwet ʾahăvāh.
“For love is strong as death.”
The Hebrew word ʾahăvāh means love, and the passage portrays its extraordinary strength.
Scripture is not embarrassed by marital affection.
God did not create human bodies and then discover that married people might desire one another.
He designed humanity as embodied beings.
Genesis 2:24 describes a husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
“One flesh.”
This describes the profound union of marriage, involving more than a moment of physical intimacy.
It includes covenantal belonging, shared life, and bodily union.
But here is the distinction we cannot afford to miss.
The goodness of marital sexuality does not mean every possible sexual practice is automatically good.
A husband and wife can be legally married and still behave selfishly.
They can be sexually active and emotionally disconnected.
They can share a bed while hiding resentment, insecurity, and loneliness.
They can even agree to something outwardly while one spouse inwardly feels trapped.
So the question must go deeper than, “Are we married?”
It must become, “Are we loving one another in a way that honors the God who created marriage?”
This is where Romans 14 becomes especially relevant.
Paul is addressing disputes about food and religious observances, not sexual practices. We should not pretend otherwise.
But his teaching offers important principles about conscience and disputed matters.
Romans 14:23 concludes with these Greek words:
πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν
Pan de ho ouk ek pisteōs hamartia estin.
“And whatever is not from faith is sin.”
The immediate context concerns acting against one's convictions before God.
It does not mean that every uneasy feeling automatically establishes a universal moral prohibition.
Nor does it mean a sincere conscience can make something God forbids acceptable.
But it does mean that conscience matters.
Imagine a wife who has been taught her entire life that every form of sexual pleasure is shameful.
She marries a man who loves her.
He wants their intimacy to be joyful.
Yet every time she experiences desire, she feels guilty.
She wonders whether enjoying her husband's affection makes her impure.
She may need compassionate biblical teaching, patient conversation, and perhaps counseling to untangle shame from genuine conviction.
Now imagine another wife whose husband repeatedly pressures her to participate in something she finds distressing.
He tells her, “We're married. The Bible says your body belongs to me.”
Those are not the same situations.
One may involve unnecessary shame that needs healing.
The other involves pressure that must stop.
And both require something far more spiritually mature than a simplistic yes-or-no answer.
They require love that listens.
Love that refuses to manipulate.
Love that cares more about the person than the experience.
This is why Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 10:23 deserve attention.
“All things are lawful,” Paul quotes, before explaining that not everything is beneficial or builds others up.
He is not giving unlimited permission for every behavior.
He is challenging the idea that permissibility alone determines wisdom.
And in verse 24, he directs believers to seek the good of others rather than merely their own advantage.
Apply that principle carefully to marriage.
Even when a practice is not explicitly forbidden, is it beneficial?
Does it strengthen affection?
Does it respect both spouses?
Does it encourage tenderness and honest communication?
Or does it create anxiety, resentment, comparison, or dependence on something that is damaging the relationship?
Those questions matter.
And we need to address something else that often gets ignored.
Pornography.
Because some couples encounter the idea of sex toys through pornographic content, and that can introduce another serious issue.
Jesus teaches in Matthew 5:28 that deliberately looking at another person with lustful intent violates the purity of the heart.
The Greek word used for lustful desire in that verse is:
ἐπιθυμῆσαι — epithymēsai
It refers there to desiring someone lustfully.
Not every form of desire is sinful; the moral character of desire depends on its object and context.
But pornography can encourage the sexual objectification of others, distorted expectations, secrecy, and relational harm.
And a married couple cannot make those problems disappear simply by saying, “We are doing this together.”
Marriage is not a spiritual exemption from the call to holiness.
At the same time, it would be inaccurate to claim that every sex toy is inherently connected to pornography or that its use necessarily involves lust toward someone outside the marriage.
Those are different questions.
A particular object is not morally identical to the circumstances in which someone first encountered it.
We must examine actual conduct, motives, effects, and biblical principles rather than relying on guilt by association.
This brings us to the central question.
Can Christian married couples use sex toys without violating their convictions?

Some Christians conclude that limited, mutually agreed use within marriage may be permissible when it involves no pornography, coercion, degradation, adultery, or other violation of biblical teaching.
Other Christians believe such practices are inconsistent with their understanding of God's design for marital sexuality, even when both spouses consent.
These differences reflect genuine disagreements about how biblical principles apply to a modern practice Scripture does not directly address.
We should not falsely suggest that all faithful Christians have reached the same conclusion.
Nor should we manufacture a divine command where Scripture gives no explicit one.
The responsible biblical answer is that couples must exercise prayerful discernment, informed conscience, mutual agreement, and serious attention to the character of their relationship.
Consent is necessary, but consent alone does not settle every moral question.
A couple must also consider whether the practice is loving, wise, consistent with their commitments, and spiritually healthy.
And if either spouse cannot participate with a clear conscience, the loving response is not to pressure them until they surrender.
It is to honor that boundary.
There is no biblical requirement that a Christian marriage include sex toys.
There is no need to introduce them to prove sexual maturity, love, or marital devotion.
And there is no biblical basis for declaring every couple sinful merely because they have considered a practice Scripture does not specifically name.
But perhaps the most uncomfortable truth is still ahead.
Because sometimes the greatest danger in a Christian bedroom is not an object.
It is selfishness.
It is a husband who cares more about gratification than his wife's emotional well-being.
It is a wife who dismisses her husband's vulnerability because she assumes men should never struggle.
It is a couple who can discuss physical techniques but cannot discuss forgiveness.
It is two people who know how to touch each other's bodies but have forgotten how to care for each other's hearts.
And that is where the Gospel confronts us.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
In Greek, the central command begins:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
The verb agapate is a command to love.
And Paul's model is not domination.
It is Christ's self-giving sacrifice.
Jesus did not demonstrate love by demanding that others exist for His comfort.
He gave Himself for the good of those He loved.
That changes the entire conversation.
A husband who follows Jesus should ask, “How can I love my wife so that she feels cherished, respected, and safe?”
A wife who follows Jesus should ask, “How can I love my husband with honesty, tenderness, and genuine care?”
And both should be willing to ask, “Are we seeking something that builds our marriage, or are we avoiding a deeper problem we are afraid to confront?”
Because no object can repair a marriage built on dishonesty.
No novelty can substitute for repentance.
No sexual experience can heal the wound of betrayal without truth, accountability, and restoration.
And no amount of physical closeness can replace spiritual intimacy with God.
Some of you reading this are not actually struggling with the question in the title.
You are struggling with what happened after you tried to answer it.
Perhaps you said yes when you wanted to say no.
Perhaps you introduced something into your marriage and later felt troubled by it.
Perhaps you accused your spouse of being spiritually weak because they disagreed with you.
Perhaps you have carried shame about your body for years, and you are only now discovering that God did not create marital affection to be an enemy of holiness.
Or perhaps your marriage has become so distant that even discussing intimacy feels impossible.
And somewhere beneath all those arguments is a quiet prayer.
“Lord, how did we get here?”
That is the moment I want you to remember something.
Jesus Christ is not frightened by the conversations you are afraid to have.
He knows the motives you hide.
He sees the pain you cannot explain.
He knows when your conscience is troubled.
He knows when you have been selfish.
And He knows when religious shame has made you afraid of something God has not forbidden.
He calls us neither to careless indulgence nor to invented rules.
He calls us to truth.
To repentance where we have sinned.
To wisdom where Scripture requires discernment.
To grace where shame has overwhelmed us.
To love that protects rather than exploits.
And to holiness that transforms more than outward behavior.
In John 8, Jesus encounters a woman publicly accused of adultery.
The account is traditionally included in John 7:53–8:11, although its earliest manuscript history is disputed, and many modern Bibles note that textual issue.
The story portrays a powerful combination of mercy and moral seriousness.
Jesus refuses to join the crowd's condemnation, yet His words also call the woman away from sin.
That combination matters.
Grace is not permission to ignore God's will.
And holiness is not permission to humiliate people.
The Gospel does not tell us to pretend that sin is harmless.
It tells us that sinners can find forgiveness and transformation through Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
Romans 8:1 announces that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
And 2 Corinthians 5:17 describes the transforming reality of belonging to Christ as a new creation.
Those promises are not limited to the respectable parts of your life.
They reach into your private struggles.
Your marriage.
Your shame.
Your hidden fears.
Your failures.
Your desperate need to begin again.
And perhaps this is the most important thing a Christian couple can hear today:
You do not need to win an argument about sex toys to begin honoring Jesus in your marriage.
You can begin tonight.
By telling the truth.
By apologizing for pressure.
By listening without defensiveness.
By acknowledging a boundary.
By confessing selfishness.
By seeking trustworthy pastoral guidance when your convictions differ.
By getting professional help when coercion, trauma, or persistent conflict has damaged intimacy.
By praying together without using prayer to manipulate one another.
And by remembering that your spouse is not your possession.
Your spouse is a person made in the image of God.
Someone you promised to love.
Someone whose dignity matters to Jesus.

If you are unmarried, this discussion is not an invitation to dismiss the Bible's sexual ethic. Scripture consistently places sexual union within the covenant of marriage and calls all believers to holiness.
If you are married, your covenant is not an excuse to abandon discernment.
And if you are wounded, ashamed, or spiritually confused, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine.
Bring the truth into the light.
Not to entertain strangers with your private life.
But to begin healing in the presence of God and, where appropriate, with trustworthy people who can help.
The Christian life was never meant to be a performance of perfection.
It is a life of following the One who saves sinners and teaches them to walk in truth.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create another place where struggling Christians are publicly shamed.
Not to manufacture controversy simply to collect attention.
But to bring difficult questions into the light of Scripture and keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
Not the intimate details of your marriage. Those deserve privacy.
But the spiritual truth you are taking away.
You do not have to explain your situation publicly.
Sometimes a simple request for prayer is enough.
A thoughtful share could help that person encounter truth without humiliation.
Not because you must agree with every conclusion, but because careful biblical reflection deserves more than a few seconds of reaction.
And if you believe this ministry is helping people encounter Christ and grow in His Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, prayer, repentance, spiritual maturity, and a closer walk with Jesus Christ.
They are free because we believe biblical nourishment should be accessible to people who need it.
But producing, organizing, maintaining, and expanding a ministry also involves real work and real expenses.
That is where your voluntary support can make a difference.
You can view that monthly contribution as an offering of support for a ministry you believe in.
What Scripture clearly teaches is the importance of sincere, willing generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia.
“Each one as he has decided in his heart.”
Paul continues by teaching that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which I want to invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
Not by suggesting that your standing before God depends on a payment.
But through a sincere opportunity to participate in a ministry that seeks to glorify Christ.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter biblical truth.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read.
Still learn.
Still pray.
Still share.
Still grow.
Still invite others.
The grace of God is not for sale.
And no monthly payment can purchase the forgiveness Jesus secured through His death and resurrection.
That salvation is received by grace through faith, not earned through giving.
Jesus alone saves souls.
Never confuse the two.
As we come back to the question that started this conversation, I want to leave you with something far more important than an argument about what belongs in a Christian bedroom.
One day, the greatest question about your marriage will not be whether you owned a particular object.
It will be whether you learned to love one another faithfully before God.
Whether you told the truth when deception was easier.
Whether you respected boundaries when selfishness demanded more.
Whether you sought forgiveness when pride told you to remain silent.
Whether your marriage reflected the sacrificial love of Jesus Christ.
And whether you allowed the Gospel to change the parts of your heart that nobody else could see.
Because the deepest transformation Christ brings is not merely a change in what we permit or prohibit.
It is a change in who we are becoming.
People who love truth.
People who practice mercy.
People who reject exploitation.
People who honor their commitments.
People who repent when they fail.
People who refuse to make shame their permanent identity.
People who know that holiness and grace are not enemies.
They meet in Jesus Christ.
So if you are a Christian husband or wife wrestling with this issue, do not let fear make the decision for you.
Do not let curiosity make the decision for you.
Do not let social media make the decision for you.
And do not let a preacher's personal preference replace careful biblical discernment.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Listen to one another.
Honor your conscience without weaponizing it against your spouse.
Seek wise counsel where needed.
And pursue a marriage in which both people can say, with sincerity, “We want Jesus to be Lord here, too.”
Because He is not merely Lord of your Sunday worship.
He is Lord of your Monday decisions.
Your private conversations.
Your desires.
Your fears.
Your relationships.
Your marriage.
And every place where truth and grace are desperately needed.
The most sacred change in your marriage may begin not when you discover what you are allowed to do, but when you finally learn how to love as Christ has loved you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD SAW A CRIME WHERE EVERYONE ELSE SAW COLLATERAL — THE FORGOTTEN COMMAND THAT REVEALS THE HEART OF JESUS
paragraphs: GOD SAW A CRIME WHERE EVERYONE ELSE SAW COLLATERAL — THE FORGOTTEN COMMAND THAT REVEALS THE HEART OF JESUS

Why did God forbid Israel from taking a millstone as security for a loan? Because what looked like an ordinary financial transaction could become an assault on a family's survival. And buried in Deuteronomy 24:6 is a truth that could change how you see poverty, power, mercy, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
Imagine owing someone money.
Not because you were reckless. Not because you were lazy. Not because you wanted a lifestyle you couldn't afford.
Your child became sick. The harvest failed. Work disappeared. The little you had was no longer enough.
You borrowed because you were desperate to keep your family alive.
Then one morning, the person you owed came to your door.
He didn't ask for your jewelry. You had none.
He didn't ask for your savings. They were gone.
He wanted something sitting in the corner of your home.
Two stones.
Ordinary, heavy, worn from years of use.
The stones you used to grind grain into flour.
The stones that helped turn the day's grain into bread for your children.
And now, because you couldn't repay your debt, he wanted to take them.
You stood there looking at the very thing your family depended on, realizing that if he carried those stones away, tomorrow's meal might become impossible.
You were already struggling to survive.
Now the price of borrowing was threatening your ability to survive at all.
And then, thousands of years ago, God spoke into that exact kind of situation.
“No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge.” — Deuteronomy 24:6 (KJV)
Read those last words again.
He taketh a man's life to pledge.
God didn't merely say it was an unfair business practice.
He described the taking of a family's essential means of preparing food as taking a life in pledge.
And suddenly, two ordinary stones became a window into the heart of God.
Because there are things you can legally possess that you have no moral right to take.
And there are people whose desperation must never become your opportunity for profit.
But the story becomes even more powerful when we look at what the Hebrew actually says.
The original Hebrew of Deuteronomy 24:6 reads:
לֹא־יַחֲבֹל רֵחַיִם וָרָכֶב כִּי־נֶפֶשׁ הוּא חֹבֵל
Lo-yachavol rechayim va-rachev, ki-nefesh hu chovel.
A close translation is:
“No one shall take a handmill or an upper millstone as a pledge, because he is taking a life as a pledge.”
The Hebrew word רֵחַיִם (rechayim) refers to a mill or millstones used for grinding grain.
The word רָכֶב (rachev) identifies the upper millstone, the movable stone used in the grinding process.
And the word that makes this command especially striking is נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh).
It is frequently translated as “soul,” but its meaning in biblical Hebrew is broader than the modern idea of an invisible spiritual component of a person.
Depending on context, nefesh can refer to life, a living being, a person, or one's very existence.
Here, the context concerns the necessities of human survival.
God was not saying the stones possessed a human soul.
He was declaring that taking the equipment necessary to prepare a family's food was, in a profoundly serious sense, taking their life as collateral.
The lender might see a valuable object.
The borrower saw the means of feeding a household.
God saw the human life that depended on it.
And that difference matters.
Because God has never evaluated human suffering merely by what appears on a financial statement.
He sees the person behind the debt.
The family behind the missed payment.
The hunger behind the empty cupboard.
The fear behind the exhausted smile.
And the dignity that remains even when someone has nothing left to offer.
Think about what that meant in ancient Israel.
Grain was a major part of everyday life. Families depended on milling grain into flour for preparing bread and other foods.
A household mill was not simply a convenient kitchen accessory.
It was essential equipment for daily living.
Removing it could seriously interfere with a family's ability to prepare food.
And in a society without modern welfare systems, refrigeration, or the conveniences many people now take for granted, the consequences could be devastating.
The creditor might have had a legitimate claim to repayment.
But God placed a boundary around how that claim could be enforced.
A debt did not give one person unlimited authority over another person's life.
That is the extraordinary moral force of this command.
God did not abolish lending in this passage.
He did not declare every borrower innocent or every lender wicked.
He did not teach that financial obligations were meaningless.
Instead, He established a limit.
The creditor's right to security could not override the borrower's basic means of survival.
And if you think this was an isolated command, listen to the surrounding laws.
In Deuteronomy 24:10–11, God instructed creditors not to enter a borrower's house to seize a pledge. They were to remain outside while the borrower brought the pledge out.
In verses 12–13, if the borrower was poor and gave a garment as security, the creditor was to return it by sunset so the person could sleep in it.
Imagine that.
The creditor might be thinking about recovering his money.
God was thinking about whether a poor man would be warm enough to sleep.
And in Deuteronomy 24:14–15, God prohibited withholding the wages of a poor and needy hired worker, because that worker depended upon those wages.
The pattern is unmistakable.
God was establishing a community where economic power carried moral responsibility.
Where vulnerability was not an invitation to exploitation.
Where the poor were not stripped of their dignity simply because they lacked resources.
And where obedience to God included the way people treated one another when money was involved.
That should make every one of us uncomfortable in the right way.
Because it is possible to be financially successful and spiritually careless.
It is possible to know the language of worship while ignoring the cries of people who cannot afford to eat.
It is possible to speak about God's blessings while treating struggling people as though their suffering makes them less worthy of respect.
And it is possible to demand every cent someone owes us while forgetting the mercy we ourselves have received.
Jesus exposed that very contradiction in the parable of the unforgiving servant in Matthew 18:21–35.
A servant was forgiven an enormous debt by his master.
But after receiving mercy, he went out and demanded payment from a fellow servant who owed him a much smaller amount.
When that fellow servant pleaded for patience, the forgiven man refused.
He had experienced compassion.
Yet he would not extend it.
He had been released from a crushing obligation.
Yet he was willing to crush someone else.
Jesus' warning was severe.
Receiving mercy should transform the way we treat others.
And here is where the ancient millstone begins to feel uncomfortably modern.
Because perhaps we have never taken someone's grinding stones.
But have we ever taken advantage of someone who had no other choice?
Have we ever used another person's desperation to secure a better deal?
Have we ever humiliated someone because they couldn't repay us?
Have we ever withheld compassion because we believed their mistakes disqualified them from receiving it?
Have we ever looked at a struggling person and assumed we knew the entire story?
Or perhaps you are the one who has been standing on the other side of the door.
The one who owes.
The one who cannot sleep.
The one who keeps checking the balance, hoping the numbers will somehow change.
The parent who says, “I'm not hungry,” because there is only enough food for the children.
The worker who smiles in public but goes home terrified of another unpaid bill.
The believer who still attends church but feels ashamed because life has not turned out the way everyone expected.
You love God.
You pray.
You work.
You try.
And yet, sometimes, it still isn't enough.
If that is you, please hear what this passage actually reveals.
Your financial situation does not erase your humanity.
Your poverty does not remove your dignity.
Your debt does not make you less worthy of just treatment.
And your struggle does not mean God has stopped seeing you.
The God who cared whether an Israelite family could grind grain for tomorrow's bread has not become indifferent to the suffering of people today.
That does not mean He promises immediate financial relief to everyone who believes.
Scripture does not give us permission to make that promise.
Faithful Christians can experience poverty, injustice, sickness, and prolonged hardship.
But the character of God revealed in this command gives us something deeper than a guarantee of instant prosperity.
It reveals that human need matters to Him.
That justice matters to Him.
That the powerful are accountable to Him.
And that the vulnerable are not invisible before Him.
Now consider something even more extraordinary.
The command in Deuteronomy was given to Israel centuries before Jesus walked the earth.
But when Jesus came, He did not reveal a different God with an unrelated heart.
He revealed the Father.
In Luke 4:18–19, Jesus announced His mission using the language of Isaiah:
“He hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised.” — Luke 4:18 (KJV)
Jesus was not merely interested in appearing compassionate.
He entered a world filled with actual human suffering.
He touched lepers whom others avoided.
He noticed people whom crowds overlooked.
He fed the hungry.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He challenged religious hypocrisy.
He confronted those who used religion to burden others without extending mercy.
And He taught that the way we treat the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, and the vulnerable matters deeply to God.
In Matthew 25:35, Jesus said:
“For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in.”
The same divine concern for human dignity that appears in Deuteronomy finds a profound expression in the ministry of Christ.
But we must go further.
Because Christianity is not merely a message about being kinder to people in financial difficulty.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to rescue sinners through His life, death, and resurrection.
And that brings us to a different kind of debt.
A debt no amount of money could settle.
Scripture teaches that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23).
Our greatest problem is not merely that we have suffered injustice.
It is also that we ourselves have sinned against a holy God.
We have loved selfishly.
We have judged harshly.
We have failed to do good when we knew what was right.
We have chosen pride when humility was required.
We have wounded others with words, actions, and indifference.
And no amount of religious performance can purchase our justification before God.
Then comes the astonishing announcement of grace.
Colossians 2:13–14 describes what God has done for believers through Christ:

“And you, being dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, hath he quickened together with him, having forgiven you all trespasses; Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross.” (KJV)
Paul uses the image of a written record standing against us.
The Greek expression χειρόγραφον (cheirographon) refers to a handwritten document or record and could be used in contexts involving obligations or indebtedness.
In Colossians 2:14, it describes the record associated with the decrees standing against us.
Paul's point is not that ordinary bank loans automatically disappear when someone becomes a Christian.
Nor is he claiming that the millstone law was secretly a prediction about modern financial contracts.
He is announcing something far greater.
