The chapter ultimately points toward God's own shepherding care, a promise Christians understand in light of Jesus, the Good Shepherd.
What a contrast.
Human shepherds may fail.
But the Good Shepherd does not abandon His calling.
Human leaders may misuse authority.
But Jesus never needs to manipulate people to remain Lord.
Human institutions may disappoint us.
But Christ remains faithful.
And maybe, just maybe, that is the truth your heart has been longing to hear.
You can honor a pastor without surrendering your conscience to him.
You can love a church without pretending it is perfect.
You can receive correction without accepting intimidation.
You can leave a congregation without leaving the body of Christ.
And you can walk into another faithful church without believing that God's mercy has been left behind in the building you departed.
Some of you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you have carried this fear for years.
You left.
Then something painful happened.
Someone became sick.
A business failed.
A relationship ended.
And you remembered the warning.
"See? This is what happens when you leave."
So you blamed yourself.
You wondered whether your children were suffering because of your decision.
You wondered whether God had turned His face away.
Please do not interpret every tragedy through the threats of a religious leader.
Scripture does not give us permission to make those accusations.
The Lord is sovereign, wise, holy, and loving.
We do not always know why suffering comes.
But we do know that Jesus is not a weapon for pastors to use against people who disappoint them.
And if you are still frightened, hear this promise:
"The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." — Psalm 23:1, KJV
The Hebrew begins:
יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר
Adonai ro‘i, lo eḥsar.
"The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not lack."
The divine name in the Hebrew text is represented by the four letters יהוה, traditionally read aloud as Adonai in Jewish practice.
And the word רֹעִי (ro‘i) means "my shepherd."
Not merely the shepherd of your congregation.
Not merely the shepherd of your pastor.
My Shepherd.
David's confidence rested in the Lord.
And Christians see the fullness of God's shepherding care revealed in Jesus Christ, who said, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11).
He knows His sheep.
He calls them.
He lays down His life for them.
And He is worthy of their trust.
Maybe your next step is to remain and work toward reconciliation.
Maybe your next step is to seek accountability for serious wrongdoing.
Maybe your next step is to leave a spiritually harmful environment and join a healthy church.
Those decisions require prayerful wisdom, careful discernment, and attention to the actual circumstances.
But whichever path you take, do not make fear of a human being your final authority.
Let Scripture guide you.
Let truth govern you.
Let love shape you.
And let Jesus Christ be Lord.
Because the Gospel is not the story of a frightened person desperately trying to remain inside the boundaries of one pastor's approval.
It is the story of sinners rescued by grace, reconciled to the Father, and transformed through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
The scandal of religious power being used to control.
The grace of discovering that Christ's authority is greater.
The scandal of shame, confusion, and spiritual wounds.
The grace of repentance, healing, forgiveness, and renewed faith.
The scandal of believing that your future belongs to the person who threatened you.
The grace of remembering that your life belongs to Jesus.
And perhaps your testimony will one day become the encouragement another frightened believer needs.
Not a testimony of hatred toward the Church.
Not a testimony of rejecting all spiritual authority.
But a testimony of learning to distinguish the voice of the Good Shepherd from the voices of people who sometimes misrepresent Him.
And if Christ has helped you find healing after a painful church experience, consider sharing a testimony that honors Him without unnecessarily exposing or attacking others.
Your story might remind someone that there is still hope.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, seekers, and even those who have grown distant from faith to walk with us as we continue opening God's Word together.
There is also a deeper way to participate in this mission.

At Gospel Warrior, we believe that biblical truth should be shared generously, that wounded believers deserve compassionate guidance, and that discipleship must always point people toward Jesus rather than toward dependence on a personality or platform.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
"God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
But more important than any discount is the opportunity to help make Scripture-centered encouragement available to people who may be searching for hope in the middle of spiritual confusion.
You are welcome to keep reading, learning, sharing, and growing with us.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The love of Christ cannot be purchased.
Our prayer is that every person who encounters Gospel Warrior will be pointed beyond our platform and toward the Savior who alone deserves our worship.
It is seeing another soul understand the Gospel, repent, trust in Jesus, and grow in the freedom of belonging to Him.
So tonight, if you are still sitting on that bed, afraid of what might happen if you leave a church...
Open your Bible.
Read John 10.
Read Romans 8.
Read 1 Peter 5.
And remember whose hands hold His sheep.
Not the hands that threaten.
Not the hands that manipulate.
Not the hands that demand unquestioning loyalty.
The nail-pierced hands of Jesus Christ.
You may have walked out of a church building with tears in your eyes, but that does not mean you walked out of the hands of your Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PHARAOH ORDERED HER TO KILL THE BABIES. SHE CHOSE TO FEAR GOD INSTEAD.
paragraphs: PHARAOH ORDERED HER TO KILL THE BABIES. SHE CHOSE TO FEAR GOD INSTEAD.
Her name was Shiphrah. She had no throne, no army, and no earthly power. But one decision in a delivery room exposed the limits of an empire—and revealed the kind of courage God never forgets.
There was a moment in ancient Egypt when a woman's hands were expected to become instruments of murder.
Those hands had spent years helping mothers bring children into the world. They had touched tiny fingers, wiped newborn faces, and witnessed the trembling relief of women who had survived childbirth.
But now the king wanted those same hands stained with innocent blood.
And the terrifying part?
The command came from the most powerful man in the nation.
Disobey him, and she could lose everything.
Obey him, and innocent children would die.
Her name was Shiphrah.
And before you dismiss her story as something that happened thousands of years ago, consider this:
What happens when doing what is right threatens everything you've worked to protect?
What happens when obedience to God could cost you your position, your security, your reputation, or even your life?
What happens when the world demands something your conscience knows is evil?
Because somewhere between Pharaoh's command and the cries of newborn children, Shiphrah faced a decision that still confronts believers today.
Will you fear the person who can threaten your future, or will you trust the God who holds eternity?
And there is something extraordinary buried in this account.
Scripture remembers the name of the woman who refused to obey Pharaoh.
But the Pharaoh who gave the command?
In this passage, he remains unnamed.
Don't miss what that means.
The ruler had the throne.
The midwife had a name.
And thousands of years later, we are still speaking hers.
Exodus 1 opens with a nation growing under oppression.

The descendants of Israel had multiplied in Egypt. What began with the family of Jacob had become a numerous people. But a new king arose who did not know Joseph, and instead of seeing Israel's growth as something to be respected, he saw it as a threat.
Fear became policy.
Policy became oppression.
Oppression became brutality.
The Egyptians forced the Israelites into hard labor, but the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied.
Then Pharaoh escalated his cruelty.
He summoned two Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, and commanded them to kill the male Hebrew babies during childbirth while allowing the girls to live.
The Hebrew text of Exodus 1:16 contains the chilling instruction:
אִם־בֵּן הוּא וַהֲמִתֶּן אֹתוֹ
Im-ben hu, vahamitten oto.
A close translation is:
“If it is a son, you shall put him to death.”
No ambiguity.
No misunderstanding.
This was not ordinary government administration. It was an order to murder defenseless children because of their identity.
Imagine being summoned before the king and hearing those words.
Imagine returning to your work knowing that every birth could now become a test of your loyalty.
Imagine a mother looking into your eyes, trusting you with the most vulnerable moment of her life.
And knowing that the government had ordered you to betray that trust.
The Bible does not describe Shiphrah's private thoughts. It does not tell us whether her hands trembled, whether she struggled to sleep, or whether she feared punishment.
We must not invent those details as history.
But we know the decision she and Puah made.
And the words of Scripture are astonishing.
“But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.” — Exodus 1:17, KJV
Read that again.
They feared God.
And they let the boys live.
Not because Pharaoh had become merciful.
Not because the law had changed.
Not because obedience was convenient.
They refused because a higher moral authority stood above the throne of Egypt.
The Hebrew expression is:
וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
Vattirena hamyalledot et-ha'Elohim.
“The midwives feared God.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root יָרֵא (yare), associated with fear, reverence, and awe.
In this context, fearing God was not merely an inward religious feeling.
It became an outward act of costly obedience.
They recognized that Pharaoh's authority was not ultimate.
God's authority was.
And that changes how we understand courage.
Courage is not always the absence of fear.
Sometimes courage is knowing exactly what obedience might cost—and refusing to surrender your conscience anyway.
Some of you reading this know what that feels like.
Maybe nobody has ordered you to commit the evil Pharaoh commanded. Your circumstances may be entirely different.
But you know what it means to face pressure.
The pressure to falsify something at work because everyone else does it.
The pressure to remain silent when someone vulnerable is being mistreated.
The pressure to compromise your convictions to keep a relationship.
The pressure to pretend that something sinful is acceptable because telling the truth might make you unpopular.
And sometimes the hardest battle is not against a cruel ruler.
Sometimes it is against the desperate voice inside you whispering:
Just do what they want. You cannot afford to lose anything else.
Shiphrah's story confronts that voice.
Not with a promise that obedience will always be safe.
But with the truth that God is worthy of obedience even when obedience is costly.
Yet there is another woman we must not overlook.
Puah.
Her name appears beside Shiphrah's because Scripture presents their courage together.
They were not competing for recognition.
They stood against the same evil.
They protected the same vulnerable lives.
And their names were preserved together.
There is something beautiful about that.
Sometimes God strengthens your faith through someone who refuses to let you stand alone.
A friend who tells you the truth when everyone else flatters you.
A brother or sister in Christ who prays with you when compromise seems easier.
A believer who quietly says, “We cannot do that. We belong to Jesus.”
Not every act of faithfulness happens on a platform.
Not every courageous believer becomes famous.
Sometimes the kingdom of God is served through two people who agree that they will not participate in evil.
And heaven does not need an audience to recognize faithfulness.
But the story becomes even more intense.
Pharaoh discovers that the male children are still living.
He summons the midwives again.
“Why have ye done this thing, and have saved the men children alive?” — Exodus 1:18, KJV
Imagine the weight of that question.
The king knew his command had not been carried out.
The women now stood accountable before the very authority they had disobeyed.
Their response, recorded in Exodus 1:19, was that the Hebrew women were vigorous and gave birth before the midwives arrived.
This part of the story deserves careful handling.

The passage does not provide enough information for us to determine every circumstance behind their explanation. Christians have differed over whether it was entirely factual, strategically incomplete, or deceptive.
We should not use the account to make dishonesty a virtue.
What the text explicitly commends is their fear of God and their refusal to kill the children.
And what happens next is remarkable.
“Therefore God dealt well with the midwives: and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty.” — Exodus 1:20, KJV
God dealt well with them.
The Hebrew reads:
וַיֵּיטֶב אֱלֹהִים לַמְיַלְּדֹת
Vayyetav Elohim lamyalledot.
A close rendering is:
“And God did good to the midwives.”
Then Exodus 1:21 explains:
“And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses.” — KJV
The Hebrew expression וַיַּעַשׂ לָהֶם בָּתִּים (vayya'as lahem batim) literally speaks of making “houses” for them.
In this context, many interpreters understand it to refer to God establishing households or families for the midwives, rather than simply constructing physical buildings.
Scripture does not tell us all the details of that blessing.
But it does tell us why God dealt favorably with them.
They feared Him.
Now be careful here.
This is not a formula promising that every courageous Christian will receive financial prosperity, a comfortable home, or protection from suffering.
The Bible itself shows faithful people who endure imprisonment, rejection, persecution, and death.
Hebrews 11 celebrates believers who experienced extraordinary deliverance alongside others who suffered terribly while remaining faithful.
Shiphrah's story is not proof that obedience purchases an easy life.
It is evidence that God sees faithfulness that earthly powers overlook.
And perhaps that is what someone needs to hear today.
You have been trying to do the right thing, but nobody seems to notice.
You refused a dishonest opportunity, and someone else got ahead.
You walked away from a sinful relationship, and now the loneliness hurts.
You chose forgiveness when bitterness felt justified.
You told the truth, and it cost you something.
You prayed.
You obeyed.
You tried to remain faithful.
And somewhere along the way, you began wondering whether God had forgotten.
But Shiphrah's name still stands in Scripture.
Not because she controlled the outcome.
Not because she possessed worldly greatness.
But because she feared God when a powerful man demanded evil.
The world may never applaud your obedience. That does not mean God has overlooked it.
And now comes a detail that makes the story even more significant.
Pharaoh's command failed.
The boys continued to live.
The people continued to multiply.
And the ruler who attempted to suppress Israel could not stop God's purposes.
But Pharaoh did not surrender.
Exodus 1:22 records that he escalated the violence, commanding his people to cast every Hebrew son into the Nile.
The threat became even more widespread.
This is important because it prevents us from romanticizing the story.
Shiphrah and Puah's courage did not instantly end oppression.
Their obedience was real.
God's favor was real.
And the suffering of Israel was still real.
Sometimes faithfulness changes a life without immediately changing an entire system.
Sometimes a righteous decision saves someone today while the wider battle continues tomorrow.
That does not make the decision meaningless.
It makes it necessary.
And then, in the very next chapter, a child is born.
A Hebrew boy.
His mother hides him for three months.
When she can no longer conceal him, she places him in a basket among the reeds by the river.
That child is Moses.
Scripture does not say Shiphrah or Puah personally delivered Moses or saved him. We must not claim that they did.
But their story belongs to the same unfolding account of God's preservation of His people.
Pharaoh tried to destroy Israel's sons.
Yet God would raise up a son of Israel to confront Pharaoh.
The king who commanded babies to be thrown into the river would eventually face a man who had been rescued from that very river.
What a reversal.
And still, Moses was not the ultimate Savior.
He was a servant through whom God delivered Israel from Egyptian bondage.
The greater deliverance would come through Jesus Christ.
And this is where Shiphrah's story becomes more than an inspiring account of human courage.
It leads us toward the heart of the Gospel.
Because centuries later, another ruler would feel threatened by the birth of a child.
Matthew 2 records that Herod, seeking to destroy the young Jesus, ordered the killing of boys in Bethlehem and its surrounding region who were two years old and under.
Once again, a ruler responded to perceived danger with violence against children.
Once again, the innocent were threatened by the powerful.
And once again, the purposes of God were not defeated.
Joseph was warned in a dream and took Mary and Jesus to Egypt.
Think about that.
The land once associated with Pharaoh's oppression became a place of refuge for the child who would save His people from their sins.
Matthew presents Jesus' return from Egypt in connection with Hosea 11:1:
“Out of Egypt have I called my son.” — Matthew 2:15, KJV
The biblical story is not a collection of disconnected moral lessons.
It is the unfolding revelation of God's redemptive purposes, culminating in Christ.
And Jesus came to accomplish something no human midwife, prophet, or deliverer could accomplish.
He came to rescue sinners from the judgment and bondage of sin.
Shiphrah refused to become an instrument of death.
Jesus willingly entered a world ruled by sin and death so that, through His own death and resurrection, He could bring eternal life to those who believe.
Shiphrah's obedience preserved vulnerable lives.
Christ's perfect obedience secured salvation for His people.
Romans 5:19 teaches that through the obedience of the One, many will be made righteous.
And Philippians 2:8 declares that Jesus humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
There is our hope.
Not that we can become brave enough to earn God's acceptance.
Not that our good deeds can erase our guilt.
Not that our sacrifices can purchase salvation.
Our hope is Jesus Christ, who obeyed perfectly where we have failed and gave Himself for sinners who could never save themselves.
And perhaps this is the moment the story stops being about Shiphrah.
And starts being about you.
Because you may admire her courage while secretly remembering the moments when you did not have it.
The moment you knew the truth but remained silent.
The moment you chose approval over obedience.
The moment you compromised because you were afraid of losing someone.
The moment you followed the crowd even though your conscience was troubled.
Maybe you have carried the memory for years.
Maybe you have convinced everyone around you that you are spiritually strong.
You know the worship songs.
You know the right words.
You know how to smile at church.
But there are decisions in your past that still haunt you.
And the question you are afraid to ask is not, “Could I have been like Shiphrah?”
It is:
“Can God still receive someone who has failed to be faithful?”
Listen carefully.
Yes.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because grace gives us permission to continue in rebellion.
But because Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Peter denied knowing Jesus three times.
And after the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The thief on the cross had no opportunity to rebuild his reputation or perform a lifetime of religious works.
Yet when he turned to Jesus in faith, Christ promised him paradise (Luke 23:39–43).
And the apostle Paul, who had persecuted the church, later testified that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).
Do you see it?
The Gospel is not merely an invitation to admire brave people.
It is an invitation to come to the Savior who forgives cowards, restores the fallen, cleanses the guilty, and transforms those who surrender to Him.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
That does not mean He erases the historical consequences of every choice.
It means your sin does not have to be the final word over your life.
The cross declares that sin is serious enough to require the death of the Son of God.
The resurrection declares that death itself could not hold Him.
And the Gospel calls you to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Maybe your next act of courage is not confronting a Pharaoh.
Maybe it is confessing a sin you have hidden.
Maybe it is apologizing to someone you wounded.
Maybe it is refusing to participate in wrongdoing even if it costs you.
Maybe it is protecting someone who has no power to protect themselves.
Maybe it is finally admitting that your religious appearance has been hiding a heart that desperately needs Christ.
Whatever it is, do not confuse conviction with hopeless condemnation.
The Holy Spirit does not expose sin merely to leave repentant sinners drowning in shame.
He points us to Christ, in whom forgiveness and new life are found.
First John 1:9 reminds us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
That is not permission to live carelessly.
It is freedom to stop hiding.
Freedom to repent.
Freedom to begin walking in obedience—not to purchase salvation, but because grace has brought you to the Savior.
Shiphrah feared God more than Pharaoh.
And perhaps today you need to ask yourself:
Whose approval has become more important to me than the Lord's?
What have I been calling “necessary” that Scripture calls sin?
What truth have I been avoiding because obedience might change my life?
And where is Jesus calling me to trust Him rather than surrender to fear?
Do not rush past those questions.
Some of the most important spiritual battles happen when nobody else is watching.
There may be no audience.
No applause.
No public recognition.
Only a decision between what is convenient and what is right.
But that decision matters.
You can simply write “I'm still fighting.”
Not as a declaration that your strength is enough.
But as a confession that you still need the grace of Jesus Christ and the prayers of His people.

And if Christ has already brought you through a season when you thought your faith would collapse, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading may need to know that repentance, restoration, and renewed obedience are possible through Him.
There is no shame in asking your brothers and sisters to pray.
There is no spiritual prize for pretending you never struggle.
And there is no substitute for bringing your heart honestly before God.
Shiphrah's courage was not the source of Israel's salvation.
God was.
And your courage will never be the source of your salvation either.
Jesus is.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around human personalities.
Not to replace the local church, pastoral care, or the fellowship of believers.
But to keep pointing people back to the Scriptures, back to repentance, back to the cross, and back to the risen Savior.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who have not opened a Bible in months.
People who feel disqualified by their past.
People quietly wrestling with unbelief.
People who know how to appear happy while their homes are falling apart.
People who need more than another inspirational quote.
They need the truth of Jesus Christ.
That is why I want to ask something personal.
Not merely because you enjoyed reading it.
But because someone among your friends may be facing a decision that requires courage, or carrying guilt that only the Gospel can address.
It is not a replacement for repentance, faith, or obedience.
And it should never be treated as a requirement for glorifying God.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, including how we steward the resources He entrusts to us.
It is distinct from giving to your local church and should not be presented as a required biblical tithe.
But it can be a sincere expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
It is the opportunity to help biblical truth reach another person.
Another struggling believer.
Another discouraged parent.
Another young person questioning whether following Jesus is worth the cost.
Another wounded soul who needs to hear that forgiveness is found in Christ.
Read the Word.
Pray.
Serve faithfully in your church.
Love your neighbor.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone.
Every act of obedience offered to God matters, whether or not money is involved.
The goal is to make much of Jesus.
And now, before you leave, I want you to picture the story one final time.
An Egyptian throne.
A royal command.
Two Hebrew midwives.
And newborn children who could not defend themselves.
Pharaoh possessed the machinery of an empire.
Shiphrah and Puah possessed no comparable political power.
Yet the king could command them to do evil, and they could refuse.
They could not control everything that happened next.
They could not guarantee their own safety.
They could not end all the suffering of their people.
But they could fear God.
And they did.
Centuries passed.
The empire changed.
Its rulers died.
Its monuments weathered.
But the names Shiphrah and Puah remained in the Word of God.
And now their testimony has reached you.
Not so you can admire them for a moment and return unchanged to whatever compromise has been ruling your heart.
But so you can remember that obedience matters, even when it is unseen.
That innocent lives matter.
That human authority is never greater than God's moral law.
That faithfulness may be costly.
And that the Savior who calls you to follow Him is also the Savior whose grace is sufficient for repentant sinners who have failed.
So when fear whispers, “You cannot afford to obey,” remember Shiphrah.
When shame whispers, “You have failed too badly to return,” remember Peter—and the risen Christ who restored him.
And when the world whispers, “Your life is too small to matter,” remember the two women whose names outlived the king who threatened them.
But above all, remember Jesus.
The One who was obedient unto death.
The One who bore our sins on the cross.
The One who rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through faith in Him.
The One who does not merely inspire better behavior, but gives new life.
So be honest before God today.
What is the one thing you need to surrender to Jesus?
Let it be more than words on a screen.
Let it become a prayer you carry into your next difficult decision.
Because in the end, the greatest miracle of this story is not that a king's command was resisted.
It is that the God who saw two faithful women in Egypt is the same God who has made Himself known to us through Jesus Christ.
And in Him, there is forgiveness for your yesterday, grace for your today, and hope for your tomorrow.
Pharaoh had the power to threaten their lives—but he never had the power to make God forget their names.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SIN WAS SHOCKING. BUT WHAT THE CHURCH DID ABOUT IT WAS EVEN WORSE.
paragraphs: THE SIN WAS SHOCKING. BUT WHAT THE CHURCH DID ABOUT IT WAS EVEN WORSE.

He was sleeping with his father’s wife. The congregation knew. And instead of mourning, they were proud. Nearly 2,000 years later, Paul's warning still confronts every church that has confused the love of Jesus with permission to keep living in sin.
“It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife.” — 1 Corinthians 5:1 (KJV)
Imagine walking into church on a Sunday morning.
The worship is beautiful. The congregation is singing. People are raising their hands, quoting Scripture, greeting one another with smiles.
Everything looks holy.
But somewhere among the worshipers sits a man involved in a sexual relationship with his own father's wife.
And people know.
The leaders know. The congregation knows. The scandal is no longer a secret.
Yet somehow, the church has learned to live with it.
The music continues. The gatherings continue. The religious conversations continue.
And nobody seems willing to confront what God has already condemned.
Then a letter arrives from the apostle Paul.
And within a few sentences, the atmosphere changes.
Because Paul does not congratulate the church for being accepting.
He asks why they are not grieving.
“And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned.” — 1 Corinthians 5:2 (KJV)
Read that again.
The scandal was not merely what one man was doing.
The scandal was what an entire congregation had become comfortable tolerating.
And before we point our fingers at Corinth, there is a question we cannot escape.
What happens when the people who are supposed to represent Jesus become more afraid of confronting sin than of grieving the heart of God?
This is not simply an ancient story about sexual immorality.
It is a mirror.
And sometimes the most uncomfortable thing about Scripture is discovering that the person standing inside the mirror looks disturbingly familiar.
Long before Paul wrote to Corinth, God had already spoken clearly about this kind of relationship.
Leviticus 18:8 declares:
“The nakedness of thy father's wife shalt thou not uncover: it is thy father's nakedness.” (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the command begins:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה
ʿErvat ʾeshet-ʾavikha lo tegalleh.
Literally, the expression means, “The nakedness of your father's wife you shall not uncover.”
The Hebrew expression “uncover nakedness” is a recognized biblical idiom for prohibited sexual relations in this legal context.
This was not merely a warning against embarrassing one's family.
It was a direct prohibition against sexual intimacy with a father's wife.
The expression includes a stepmother, not only a biological mother. Scripture distinguishes this prohibition from the separate prohibition concerning one's mother in Leviticus 18:7.
The moral boundary was clear.
The relationship violated God's revealed command and dishonored the family relationship that the law was protecting.
Centuries later, the church in Corinth was facing precisely this kind of offense.
Paul wrote in Greek:
Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia.
The sense is, “Sexual immorality is actually being reported among you.”
The word πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to sexual immorality. Its precise application is determined by the context.
Here, Paul immediately identifies the offense:
ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν
Hōste gynaika tina tou patros echein.
The phrase describes a man having his father's wife.
Paul does not specify whether the father was still alive, whether the woman was legally married to him at that moment, or how the relationship began.
We should not invent details Scripture does not provide.
But we do know this.
The man was involved in a relationship that violated a clear biblical sexual boundary, and the church was failing to respond appropriately.
Paul was astonished that such immorality existed among people who confessed the name of Christ.
But his next words are especially revealing.
He did not simply say, “How could this man do such a thing?”
He said, in effect, “How can you be proud when you should be mourning?”
The Greek word translated “puffed up” is πεφυσιωμένοι (pephysiōmenoi), from a verb associated with being inflated or arrogant.
The church was exhibiting pride when the situation demanded grief and humility.
We are not told exactly what the Corinthians were proud of. Perhaps they imagined themselves spiritually mature. Perhaps their broader divisions and arrogance had blinded them.
But we must be careful not to claim that they were celebrating the immoral relationship itself. Paul does not explicitly say that.
What he does say is devastating enough.
They were proud when they should have been brokenhearted.
And this is where the story stops feeling ancient.
Because we know what it is like to protect appearances.
We know what it means to smile in public while something is rotting in private.
We know how easily people learn to excuse what they once would have confessed.
A compromise begins quietly.
A message that should never have been sent.
A relationship that should never have developed.
A secret that requires another secret to survive.
A conscience that once trembled before God slowly becomes accustomed to the very thing that used to bring conviction.
And then comes the most dangerous sentence a person can speak to himself:
“It's not that serious anymore.”
But sin does not become holy because we have become familiar with it.
And a church does not become more Christlike by pretending that God's commandments no longer matter.
There is a difference between welcoming a sinner to hear the Gospel and affirming a believer's decision to remain unrepentant.
Jesus welcomed sinners.
He ate with tax collectors. He spoke with the morally disgraced. He extended mercy to people religious society had written off.
But His mercy was never an invitation to make peace with darkness.
In John 8:11, Jesus tells the woman brought before Him:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (KJV)
Mercy and a call to holiness were not enemies in the ministry of Jesus.
They belonged together.
He did not demand that sinners repair themselves before approaching Him.
He came to save sinners.
But He also came to transform them.

And if our version of Christianity offers forgiveness without repentance, comfort without truth, and belonging without any call to discipleship, we must ask whether we are faithfully representing the Jesus revealed in Scripture.
Because the Gospel is not permission to remain enslaved.
It is the announcement that through Jesus Christ, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
Paul understood this.
That is why his response in 1 Corinthians 5 was so serious.
He instructed the congregation to remove the unrepentant man from its fellowship.
The language is severe. Paul even speaks of delivering the man to Satan.
But we cannot ignore the purpose Paul gives.
“That the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” — 1 Corinthians 5:5 (KJV)
The objective was not entertainment.
Not humiliation.
Not revenge.
Not the satisfaction of watching a fallen person suffer.
The stated objective was ultimately redemptive.
The church was to take sin seriously because the man's spiritual condition mattered.
And the holiness of the congregation mattered.
Paul continued with an image his readers would understand:
“Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?” — 1 Corinthians 5:6 (KJV)
A small amount of leaven works through an entire batch of dough.
His warning was that tolerated, unrepentant sin could corrupt the life of the community.
Not because every struggling Christian must be expelled.
Not because the church should become a gathering of people who pretend to be perfect.
But because openly persistent, serious sin among those professing faith cannot simply be treated as spiritually harmless.
There is an enormous difference between a believer who is fighting temptation, confessing failure, and seeking restoration, and someone who insists that repentance is unnecessary.
The first needs encouragement, patient discipleship, and grace.
The second needs loving, truthful confrontation.
Both need Jesus.
And both must be treated with dignity.
Biblical church discipline is never a license for spiritual abuse, public spectacle, coercion, or protecting powerful people while punishing the vulnerable.
Where abuse, exploitation, or criminal wrongdoing is involved, safeguarding people and reporting to appropriate authorities must not be replaced by an internal religious process.
The woman in Corinth is not described as a church member, and Paul does not explain her circumstances. We should not presume her motives, consent, or responsibility beyond what the passage tells us.
His direct instructions concern the man and the congregation's responsibility toward a professing insider.
And that distinction matters.
Because Paul explicitly refuses to make the church responsible for policing every person outside its fellowship.
He writes:
The church must not demand that unbelievers live as though they have already surrendered to Christ.
Its responsibility is to proclaim the Gospel, practice holiness, and exercise appropriate accountability within its own community.
That should make every Christian think.
We can spend hours condemning the darkness outside the church while refusing to address the darkness we have allowed inside our own hearts.
We can debate the sins of society while refusing to confess the sins we hide behind religious language.
We can become experts at identifying what is wrong with everyone else.
And strangers to repentance ourselves.
Maybe the Corinthian man is not the person in this story who most resembles us.
Maybe it is the congregation.
The people who knew.
The people who continued.
The people who had grown accustomed to something that should have moved them to tears.
And if that possibility makes you uncomfortable, perhaps it is worth sitting with the discomfort instead of rushing past it.
Because conviction is not always an enemy.
Sometimes it is mercy interrupting the slow destruction of a soul.
Consider Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
He believed he would stand firm.
Yet when fear came, he denied knowing the Lord three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of his own confident promises.
The terrible realization that he had done exactly what Jesus said he would do.
And then the eyes of the Savior.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep, as John 21:15–19 records.
The same disciple who had publicly denied Jesus was graciously restored to serve Him.
That is not cheap grace.
That is the astonishing mercy of a risen Savior.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what Peter's tears feel like.
You remember when prayer came naturally.
When opening your Bible felt like meeting someone you loved.
When your conscience was tender.
When you could not imagine becoming comfortable with the thing you are now struggling to surrender.
But something happened.
You became tired.
You became lonely.
You were wounded.
You made a compromise.
Then another.
And somewhere along the way, shame convinced you that returning to God would be harder than continuing to hide.
So you learned to perform Christianity.
You know the songs.
You know when to say amen.
You know how to post encouraging verses.
You know how to look spiritually strong.
But there are nights when the room becomes quiet and you wonder whether God still wants anything to do with you.
Listen carefully.
The blood of Jesus is not weaker than the sin you are ashamed to confess.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise does not make sin harmless.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
You do not need to pretend that evil was good.
You do not need to rewrite God's Word to make your choices comfortable.
You do not need to convince yourself that the Holy Spirit has stopped caring about your life.
You can come into the light.
You can confess.
You can turn.
You can seek help.
You can begin taking the difficult, practical steps that repentance sometimes requires.
And you can trust the Savior who died and rose again to receive those who come to Him in faith.
But there is another detail in Paul's letter that we must not miss.
After addressing the sin in Corinth, Paul points the church toward Passover.
“For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.” — 1 Corinthians 5:7 (KJV)
There it is.
The center of the entire confrontation.
Jesus Christ.
Not moral superiority.
Not religious reputation.
Not the pleasure of exposing someone else's disgrace.
Christ, our Passover Lamb.
The One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One whose sacrifice makes forgiveness possible.
The One whose resurrection announces that sin and death do not have the final word.
Paul's command to remove the old leaven is grounded in what Christ has already accomplished.
Holiness is not the price by which we purchase salvation.
It is the fitting response of those who belong to the Savior.
We do not repent to make the cross sufficient.
We repent because the crucified and risen Christ is sufficient, and His grace calls us out of the darkness.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace also trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not merely pardon for yesterday.
It is also God's transforming work in us today.
And this is where the Corinthian story becomes even more moving.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul speaks of someone who has been disciplined by the majority and now needs forgiveness, comfort, and reaffirmed love.
Many interpreters have connected that individual with the man from 1 Corinthians 5.
Others caution that the identification is uncertain because Paul does not explicitly name him or identify the offense.
We should respect that uncertainty.
But regardless of whether the passages concern the same person, the principle is unmistakable.
Paul did not believe church discipline should become permanent rejection when repentance and restoration were appropriate.
He warned that excessive sorrow could overwhelm a person.
He called believers to reaffirm love.
Do you see the beauty of that?
The same apostle who insisted that the church must not ignore serious sin also insisted that the church must not withhold comfort and forgiveness from someone who needed restoration.
Truth without love becomes cruelty.
Love without truth becomes compromise.
But truth and love, faithfully held together under the lordship of Jesus Christ, can become instruments of healing.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not excusing what God has forbidden.
Not reducing a person forever to the worst thing he has done.
But proclaiming that repentance and forgiveness are possible because Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose from the dead.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because the Savior is greater.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret.
Maybe your marriage is suffering because of choices you have refused to confront.
Maybe you have been involved in a relationship you know you need to leave.
Maybe pornography has become a private prison.
Maybe bitterness has lived in your heart for so long that you now call it discernment.
Maybe your struggle has nothing to do with sexual sin.
Maybe it is dishonesty, pride, envy, greed, unforgiveness, or the exhausting need to appear spiritually superior.
Or perhaps you have been deeply wounded by the hypocrisy of Christians who preached holiness while concealing wrongdoing.
Your wounds matter.
And no one should use this passage to silence victims, conceal abuse, or demand that wounded people return to unsafe situations.
Jesus is not honored by protecting a religious institution at the expense of the vulnerable.
He is honored when His people walk in truth, justice, humility, repentance, and love.
Whatever brought you here, the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Not with a carefully edited version of your life.
Not with a religious performance.
Not with an argument explaining why your particular sin should be exempt from God's Word.
Come with the truth.
Come with the grief.
Come with the exhaustion.
Come with the confession you have been afraid to speak.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
What a promise.
The One who knows the truth about you is the very One who invites you to come.
And if you are already a believer, remember that repentance is not something you graduate from.
It remains part of the Christian life.
The mature Christian is not the person who has learned to conceal every weakness.
It is the person who continues to bring his life into the light of God's Word and depend upon the grace of Christ.
That includes churches.
A congregation can have excellent preaching, beautiful worship, active ministries, and impressive attendance while still needing to repent.
No church is above correction.
No pastor is above accountability.
No ministry is too important to be truthful.
No reputation is worth sacrificing the integrity of the Gospel.
And no sinner who genuinely turns to Christ should be treated as though redemption is impossible.
Perhaps that is why this ancient letter still feels so painfully current.
It forces us to ask whether we love Jesus enough to receive His correction, not merely His comfort.
Whether we care about souls enough to speak truth with gentleness.
Whether we believe in grace enough to welcome genuine repentance.
And whether we are willing to let the Word of God examine us before we use it to examine everybody else.
If this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain your private struggle publicly.
And if Christ has restored you after a season of failure, consider sharing a testimony of His mercy. Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that change is impossible.
Do not underestimate what an honest testimony can do.
Somewhere, someone is reading Scripture with a heart full of shame.
Someone is wondering whether it is too late to come home.
Someone has mistaken conviction for rejection.
Someone needs to hear that Jesus does not call us to hide our sin, but to bring it into the light where His grace can meet us.
If a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider sending this article privately with kindness rather than using it as a public accusation.
Because faith needs more than a moment of emotion.
It needs roots.
It needs the Word.
It needs prayer, fellowship, accountability, and continued growth in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
Those free resources matter deeply to our mission.
But sustaining and expanding that work also requires practical support.
And you cannot purchase His favor.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not through financial contributions, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
But Scripture also honors willing generosity in support of Gospel work.
Paul wrote:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
That is the kind of support we want.
Not pressured.
Not purchased through guilt.
Not offered out of fear that God will be disappointed if you cannot afford it.
But freely given, from a grateful heart, by those who believe in the mission and have the means to help.
It is helping make more Scripture-centered content and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
You can still read, pray, share, comment, invite others, and make use of the free resources.
Your spiritual worth is not measured by your ability to give money.
We are grateful for every sincere way people participate in spreading the Gospel.
Because the mission is not to build a community around a payment.
It is to point people toward a Person.
Jesus Christ.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The One who calls sinners to repentance, offers forgiveness through His blood, and transforms lives by His grace.
And that brings us back to Corinth.
Back to the congregation.
Back to the man whose conduct could no longer be ignored.
Back to Paul's painful question.
Why were they proud when they should have mourned?
The answer is not given in full.
But the warning remains.
When a church loses its capacity to grieve over sin, it is in danger of losing its capacity to understand grace.
Because grace only becomes astonishing when we understand what we have been forgiven.
The cross does not tell us that sin was harmless.
It tells us that sin was so serious that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
And the resurrection tells us that the story does not have to end in shame.
So do not walk away from this article merely thinking about the sins of another person.
Ask the harder question.
“Lord, where have I become comfortable with what You are calling me to surrender?”
Then listen.
Open His Word.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek wise, trustworthy help where it is needed.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Not because repentance earns His love.
But because His grace is too precious to treat as permission to remain in chains.
The church in Corinth needed correction.
Peter needed restoration.
And every one of us needs the mercy of Christ.
Some of us need to stop hiding.
Some need to stop pretending.
Some need to stop condemning people whom God is calling us to help restore.
And some need to remember that the Savior who calls us to holiness is also the Savior who welcomes the repentant home.
If there is one sentence I hope remains with you long after you close this article, it is this:
The sin you keep defending may be the very prison Jesus is calling you to leave—and the grace you are afraid to receive may be the beginning of your freedom.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID HAD SIX SONS BY SIX DIFFERENT WOMEN BEFORE HE RULED ALL ISRAEL—AND THE BIBLE DIDN’T HIDE A SINGLE NAME
paragraphs: DAVID HAD SIX SONS BY SIX DIFFERENT WOMEN BEFORE HE RULED ALL ISRAEL—AND THE BIBLE DIDN’T HIDE A SINGLE NAME

Before the crown united a nation, David’s household was already divided among multiple wives. But beneath the royal marriages, complicated family history, and painful consequences lies a Gospel truth we cannot afford to miss: God can use a deeply flawed person without approving everything that person does.
“And unto David were sons born in Hebron.” — 2 Samuel 3:2, KJV
There is something unsettling about reading the Bible carefully.
Not because Scripture is unreliable.
But because it is so painfully honest.

We love hearing about David standing before Goliath with nothing but a sling and a stone. We love the shepherd boy who trusted God when an entire army trembled. We love the worshiper who poured out his heart in the Psalms, the warrior who refused to kill Saul, and the king described as a man after God's own heart.
But there is another David.
A David whose household was more complicated than many Sunday sermons ever mention.
A David who had multiple wives before he became king over all Israel.
A David whose family would eventually become a place of jealousy, sexual violence, murder, rebellion, and unimaginable grief.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of the story is this:
God knew everything about David before He chose him.
Every weakness. Every compromise. Every future failure.
Yet God did not erase the uncomfortable chapters to make His servant look more respectable.
He preserved them.
Because the Bible was never written to convince us that God's people were perfect.
It was written to reveal the faithfulness of a holy God who works amid human brokenness—and ultimately to lead us to the only King who never sinned.
And if you have ever wondered whether the mistakes in your own history have made you impossible for God to redeem, David's story deserves more than a passing glance.
But we must begin where Scripture begins.
Not with excuses.
With the truth.
Second Samuel 3:2–5 records six sons born to David during his reign in Hebron. David had already been anointed king over Judah, but he had not yet become king over the united nation of Israel.
The King James Version records:
“And unto David were sons born in Hebron: and his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess;
“And his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite;
“And the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;
“And the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith;
“And the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital;
“And the sixth, Ithream, by Eglah David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.”
— 2 Samuel 3:2–5, KJV
Six sons.
Six named mothers.
One future king over all Israel.
And a family story that was already far more complicated than the heroic paintings suggest.
The Hebrew text begins with the words:
וַיִּוָּלְדוּ לְדָוִד בָּנִים בְּחֶבְרוֹן
Vayyivvaledu leDavid banim beChevron.
Literally, in natural English:
“And sons were born to David in Hebron.”
The Hebrew does not soften the family record. It simply introduces the sons and identifies their mothers.
This matters because biblical accuracy requires us to distinguish what the passage actually says from what we might assume it says.

The passage identifies six women as mothers of David's sons. Other passages explicitly identify several of these women as David's wives, and 2 Samuel 3:5 calls Eglah his wife. Taken together, the biblical record establishes that David had a plural household during his Hebron years.
It does not establish that these were his only wives, nor that he had no other children during that period.
In fact, David's marital history was already complicated before Hebron.

First Samuel 18 describes his marriage to Michal, Saul's daughter. First Samuel 25 describes his marriages to Abigail and Ahinoam. And 2 Samuel 3:13–16 later recounts Michal being returned to David after Saul had given her to another man.
This was not a simple family portrait.
And we should not pretend it was.
But here is where the story becomes even more important.
The fact that God recorded David's multiple marriages does not mean God commanded or endorsed them.
That distinction changes everything.
In Genesis 2:24, the foundational marriage text describes a man leaving his father and mother, holding fast to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
Basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Jesus Himself returned to this creation pattern in Matthew 19:4–6, emphasizing the union of husband and wife and declaring that what God has joined together, humanity must not separate.
And long before David occupied the throne, Deuteronomy 17:17 had already warned Israel's future kings:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.” — KJV
The Hebrew phrase is especially revealing:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים
Velo yarbeh-lo nashim.
“And he shall not multiply wives for himself.”
That was not a warning written after David's family troubles.
It was part of God's instruction for Israel's kings.
Scripture records polygamous households throughout Israel's history, but recording a practice is not the same as presenting it as God's ideal.
And here is the question that should trouble every believer who has ever tried to justify a personal compromise by pointing to a biblical character:
If God could use David while David was making choices that departed from His design, does that mean those choices were acceptable?
No.
It means God's power is not limited by human perfection.
But His grace must never be mistaken for permission to ignore His Word.
Some of us need to hear that.
Because we have become remarkably skilled at finding biblical examples that appear to excuse what we already want to do.
We point to David's marriages while ignoring God's design for marriage.
We point to Samson's strength while ignoring his recklessness.
We point to Solomon's wisdom while overlooking the warning that his many wives turned his heart away from the Lord.
And sometimes, without realizing it, we stop asking, “What does God desire?”
We start asking, “What can I get away with and still call myself blessed?”
That is a dangerous place for the human heart to live.
Because being used by God is not the same as being approved by God in everything we do.
David was genuinely chosen.
David genuinely loved the Lord.
David also genuinely sinned.
All three truths belong in the same Bible.
And if we remove any one of them, we distort the story.
Consider what eventually happened within his household.
Amnon, David's firstborn son, sexually violated his half-sister Tamar in 2 Samuel 13.
Tamar's suffering was devastating.
Her brother Absalom eventually arranged Amnon's murder.
Absalom later rebelled against David, attempted to seize the throne, and died during the conflict.
Adonijah, another of David's sons, would later attempt to establish himself as king while David was still alive.
These were not minor family disagreements.
They were tragedies involving real people, wounded relationships, abused power, and irreversible loss.
We should be careful not to claim that every one of these events was directly caused by David's polygamy. Scripture does not make that simple causal statement.
The biblical narrative does, however, show the dangers of unchecked desire, rivalry, violence, failed accountability, and the misuse of royal privilege.
And it forces us to confront something we would rather avoid.
You can have a calling from God and still make decisions that damage people around you.
You can be gifted and still need correction.
You can worship sincerely and still have blind spots that must be brought into the light.
You can be admired publicly while your private life desperately needs repentance.

David's family story is not permission to look down on complicated households today. Children are never guilty merely because of the circumstances of their birth, and people who have experienced divorce, abandonment, abuse, or family division should not be treated as spiritually inferior.
The point is not to shame broken families.
The point is to take sin seriously without denying the possibility of grace.
And there is another chapter in David's life that makes this truth impossible to ignore.
Bathsheba.
By the time we reach 2 Samuel 11, David is no longer simply the king of Judah.
He is king over Israel.
He possesses authority, wealth, military power, and a royal household.
Yet the man who once refused to seize Saul's throne through violence now uses his position in a devastating abuse of power.
He takes Bathsheba, a married woman.
When she becomes pregnant, David attempts to conceal what happened.
And when concealment fails, he arranges circumstances that lead to the death of her husband, Uriah.
This is not a romantic love story.
It is a story of royal wrongdoing, betrayal, and bloodshed.
And God does not excuse it.
The prophet Nathan confronts David.
“You are the man,” Nathan declares in 2 Samuel 12:7.
Imagine that moment.
The powerful king.
The decorated warrior.
The beloved psalmist.
The man whose name would be remembered for generations.
Standing exposed before the Word of God.
No army could defend him from that truth.
No crown could make him innocent.
No reputation could erase what he had done.
And then David speaks words that every proud human heart eventually needs to learn:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
In Hebrew:
חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה
Chatati laYHWH.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
There is no lengthy explanation in that confession.
No attempt to shift responsibility onto Bathsheba.
No speech about the pressures of leadership.
No claim that his good deeds outweighed his wrongdoing.
He confesses.
And Nathan responds:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die.” — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
Grace.
But not cheap grace.
Not grace that pretends Uriah is alive.
Not grace that erases Bathsheba's suffering.
Not grace that removes every consequence.
David is forgiven, yet painful consequences continue to unfold in his household.
That is one of the most sobering truths in Scripture.
Forgiveness removes the guilt of sin before God, but it does not always remove every earthly consequence of sin.
A relationship may still need rebuilding.
Trust may still need to be earned.
A victim may still need protection and justice.
A family may still need years of healing.
A person may be truly forgiven and still have to take responsibility for what they damaged.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace calls sinners to repentance and offers what they could never earn.
And perhaps this is where David's story begins to feel uncomfortably personal.
Because you may not have six wives.
You may never have worn a crown.
You may never have commanded an army or occupied a palace.
But you know what it means to carry contradictions inside yourself.
You know what it means to love God and still struggle with temptation.
To pray sincerely and then lose your temper.
To sing about surrender while secretly holding on to something God has told you to release.
To appear strong in front of other people while feeling spiritually exhausted when nobody is watching.
Maybe there is a relationship you mishandled.
A child you failed to listen to.
A marriage you neglected.
A person you hurt and never properly apologized to.
Maybe there is a secret you keep hoping will disappear if you never speak about it.
And perhaps you have spent so much time protecting the version of yourself other people admire that you have forgotten what it feels like to stand honestly before God.
David's story comes close enough to whisper something we desperately need to understand.
You do not have to hide from the God who already knows.
But neither can you heal by pretending your sin is harmless.
The same Lord who sees your wounds also sees the wounds you may have caused.
He is merciful enough to receive a repentant sinner.
And holy enough to call that sinner into a different way of living.
That is why Psalm 51 is so powerful.
Its superscription connects it to Nathan's confrontation of David after his sin involving Bathsheba.
David cries:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
The Hebrew begins:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The verb bara, translated “create,” is also used in Genesis 1:1 when God creates the heavens and the earth.
That does not mean the two passages describe the same kind of creation.
But the shared verb gives David's prayer extraordinary force.
He is not merely asking God to improve his public image.
He is asking for inward renewal that only God can accomplish.
Not a better disguise.
A clean heart.
Not another excuse.
A renewed spirit.
Not the appearance of holiness.
The reality of transformation.
And maybe that is the prayer you have been avoiding.
Because it is easier to ask God to change your circumstances than to ask Him to expose what needs changing inside you.
It is easier to pray for the people who hurt you than to admit where you have hurt others.
It is easier to share a verse about forgiveness than to seek forgiveness from someone you wronged.
But repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
It is the turning of a sinner toward the God who gives life.
And here is the beautiful thing about David's story.
It does not end with David.
If it did, we would be left with a complicated king, a troubled household, and the lingering question of whether any human ruler could ever truly be trusted.
But Scripture carries us forward.
Through generations.
Through promises.
Through failures.
Through exile and longing.
Until another Son is born into David's royal line.
Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:1 introduces Him as:
“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” — KJV
And Matthew's genealogy does something astonishing.
It does not sanitize the family history.
Matthew 1:6 refers to Solomon's mother through her connection to Uriah, keeping the memory of that painful history within the account of Jesus' ancestry.
The Gospel does not require the past to be rewritten into something respectable before Christ can enter the story.
Instead, the genealogy points us to the Savior who enters a real human history marked by sin, sorrow, and God's faithfulness.
But we must be clear.
Jesus did not inherit David's moral failures.
He came from David's royal line, yet He is the sinless Messiah.
Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted as we are, yet without sin.
David took what was not his.
Jesus gave Himself for others.
David sometimes used royal power to serve his own desires.
Jesus, though truly Lord, humbled Himself and became obedient unto death.
David's household knew betrayal, violence, and grief.
Jesus entered a world of betrayal, violence, and grief—and bore our sins at the cross.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus came to provide forgiveness.
That is the difference between a flawed king and the perfect King.
And it is why the Gospel is not merely an inspirational message about overcoming mistakes.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
We are not saved because our personal stories eventually become impressive.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ, not by works we can boast about (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the grace that saves us also calls us into a transformed life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
In the Greek text, the phrase is:
καινὴ κτίσις
Kainē ktisis.
“New creation.”
Not merely a person who has learned to hide the past more effectively.
A person brought into a new reality through union with Christ.
This does not mean every wound disappears overnight or that spiritual growth happens without struggle.
It means that in Christ, sin no longer has the final claim over your identity and future.
And that is why we say:
Not because Jesus changes historical facts.
He does not make David's sins disappear from Scripture.
He does not pretend that victims were never harmed.
He does not ask wounded people to call injustice acceptable.
Jesus rewrites everything because He brings redemption where sin once appeared to have the final word.
He gives forgiveness to the repentant.
He gives hope to the ashamed.
He gives a new beginning to those who turn to Him.
He teaches us to confess rather than conceal, to restore rather than exploit, to love rather than consume, and to serve rather than dominate.
He does not merely help us tell a better story about ourselves.
He makes us new.
And if this article has stirred something in you, do not rush past it.
Perhaps you need to pray the prayer David prayed.
Perhaps you need to stop defending a compromise.
Perhaps you need to apologize without demanding immediate forgiveness.
Perhaps you need to seek wise pastoral care, professional support, or accountability for a situation you cannot resolve alone.
Perhaps you have been carrying shame for something someone else did to you, and you need to hear clearly that their sin was not your guilt.
Or perhaps you have been so disappointed by the failures of Christian leaders that you have started wondering whether Jesus Himself can be trusted.
Remember this:
David was never meant to be your perfect Savior.
Neither was any pastor, preacher, ministry founder, or Christian influencer.
Only Jesus is worthy of that place.
And if your faith has been shaken by the failure of someone you admired, you do not have to pretend that failure was small.
You can grieve it honestly while holding fast to the One who never fails.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality cult.
Not to sell the illusion that Christians never struggle.
Not to place another human being on a pedestal.
But to keep pointing wounded, wandering, searching, and growing souls toward the truth of Jesus Christ.
Toward Scripture that can be examined.
Toward repentance that is real.
Toward grace that does not compromise holiness.
Toward discipleship that continues long after the emotional moment of reading an article has passed.
And we want you to be part of that mission.
And please, do not leave without joining the conversation.
You never know who might find courage through what God has done in your life.
You do not need to reveal private details to participate. A sincere prayer or a simple word of encouragement can strengthen someone else.
These resources are offered to encourage deeper study, stronger faith, and a more Scripture-rooted walk with the Lord.
But there is also something important we want to share with those who believe in this mission.
Producing biblical articles, developing discipleship resources, maintaining a growing library, and expanding our reach require time, effort, and ongoing support.

Scripture encourages generosity toward the work of the Gospel. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not from pressure or compulsion.
That is the spirit in which we make this invitation.
Please continue honoring your family responsibilities, your local church commitments, and the convictions you hold before God.
There is no spiritual price tag on grace.
These products are not the reason to give.
They are simply one way of expressing appreciation to those who voluntarily stand with this mission.
You can still pray for the ministry.
You can still invite someone to study the Scriptures.
You can still encourage another believer.
You can still make a meaningful difference.
It is about the Gospel reaching people.
It is about the Word of God being understood rather than twisted.
It is about people finding the courage to repent, the strength to persevere, and the hope that comes from knowing Jesus Christ.
Six sons.
Six mothers.
A future king.
A family history filled with complexities that would later become even more painful.
God could have given us a polished biography that concealed every embarrassing detail.
But He did not.
He allowed the truth to remain.
Because the hope of Scripture is not that God's servants were always admirable.
The hope of Scripture is that God's promises remained faithful even when His servants were not.
David's story teaches us that being chosen is never an excuse for disobedience.
His repentance teaches us that confession matters more than reputation.
His family's suffering teaches us that sin has consequences beyond the sinner.

And his royal line ultimately directs our eyes to Jesus, the Son of David, whose kingdom is not built upon exploitation, whose righteousness never fails, and whose mercy is sufficient for all who come to Him in faith.
So perhaps the question today is not simply how many wives David had.
Perhaps the deeper question is what you are doing with the truth God has already shown you about your own heart.
Will you defend what needs to be surrendered?
Will you hide what needs to be confessed?
Will you continue carrying shame that Christ invites you to bring to His cross?
Or will you come to Him?
Not as someone pretending to be perfect.
But as someone who knows exactly how much a Savior is needed.
Because the most powerful part of David's story was never the number of people in his household.
It was the faithfulness of the God who refused to let human failure destroy His redemptive promise.
And that promise finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but only Jesus Christ can give you a new heart—and your darkest chapter does not have to become your final one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY WERE CRYING FOR A FALSE GOD… WHILE STANDING AT THE DOOR OF THE TRUE ONE
paragraphs: THEY WERE CRYING FOR A FALSE GOD… WHILE STANDING AT THE DOOR OF THE TRUE ONE

The disturbing vision of women weeping for Tammuz in Ezekiel 8 reveals a terrifying possibility: You can stand near the presence of God, carry the appearance of devotion, and still give your deepest love to something that cannot save you.
There is something deeply unsettling about the sound of someone crying outside a door.
Especially when the One behind that door has the power to heal everything they are crying about.
Imagine standing at the entrance of God's Temple in Jerusalem.

The walls have witnessed generations of prayers. The sacred courts have heard the cries of repentant sinners. This is the place associated with the name of the LORD, the God who delivered Israel from slavery, sustained them in the wilderness, and repeatedly called His people back when they wandered.
But something is terribly wrong.
Women are sitting near the entrance.
They are weeping.
Their tears are real. Their grief is visible. Their devotion is unmistakable.
But their tears are not being offered to the LORD.
They are weeping for Tammuz.
And the God whose Temple they have approached is showing His prophet something horrifying.
Not every tear is an act of worship.
Not every spiritual experience is evidence of surrender.
And not everything that makes your heart tremble is worthy of your heart.
Before you dismiss this as an ancient story about people who worshiped strange gods, consider something.
What if the most frightening part of Ezekiel's vision is not how different those worshipers were from us?
What if it is how painfully familiar their misplaced devotion can become?
Because sometimes the thing standing between us and God is not something we openly hate.
Sometimes it is something we love more than Him.
And that is where this story begins to reach into places we would rather keep hidden.
The prophet Ezekiel was living among the Judean exiles in Babylon when the LORD gave him an extraordinary vision.

According to Ezekiel 8:1, it was the sixth year of the exile, in the sixth month, on the fifth day. Ezekiel was sitting in his house with the elders of Judah before him when the hand of the Sovereign LORD came upon him.
In the vision, the Spirit lifted him and brought him to Jerusalem.
What he was about to see would expose the spiritual corruption that had taken root among God's covenant people.
This was not a casual tour of the Temple.
It was a revelation of covenant betrayal.

Ezekiel first saw an idolatrous image provoking jealousy. Then he was shown elders burning incense before images of creeping things and detestable idols. Later, he would see men turning their backs toward the Temple of the LORD and bowing toward the rising sun.
And between these scenes came one of the strangest and most haunting statements in the entire book.
Ezekiel 8:14 records:
"וְהִנֵּה־שָׁם הַנָּשִׁים יֹשְׁבוֹת מְבַכּוֹת אֶת־הַתַּמּוּז"
Ve-hinneh sham ha-nashim yoshvot mevakkot et-ha-Tammuz.
A close translation of the Hebrew is:
"And behold, there the women were sitting, weeping for Tammuz."
The Hebrew word מְבַכּוֹת (mevakkot) comes from the verb בכה (bakhah), meaning "to weep" or "to cry."
The form describes the women as engaged in weeping.
And the name תַּמּוּז (Tammuz) identifies the object of their lament.
That matters.
The text does not say these women were crying out to the LORD in repentance.
It does not say they were grieving over the sins of Jerusalem.
It says they were weeping for Tammuz.
Then the LORD said to Ezekiel:
"Have you seen this, O son of man? You will see still greater abominations than these." — Ezekiel 8:15, ESV
Imagine hearing those words.
God was not impressed by the intensity of their religious emotion.
He was exposing the object of their worship.
And that distinction can change the way we examine our own hearts.

Tammuz was associated with Dumuzi, a deity known from ancient Mesopotamian religious traditions. In those traditions, Dumuzi was connected with fertility, vegetation, shepherding, and seasonal cycles. Ancient laments mourned his loss or descent into the realm of the dead.

The precise ritual being practiced by the women in Ezekiel's vision is not explained in detail by Scripture. Scholars generally understand the scene as reflecting a mourning practice associated with this deity.
We should not invent details the Bible does not give us.
Scripture does not tell us the women's names, their personal histories, or the private thoughts behind their tears.
But it tells us enough to understand the offense.
A practice associated with another deity had entered the sacred precincts of the LORD's Temple.
The place that should have testified to the exclusive worship of Israel's God had become a setting for religious compromise.
And here is the tragedy.
They were near the Temple.
But nearness to a holy place did not make their worship holy.
They were expressing deep emotion.
But the depth of their emotion did not make its direction right.
They were participating in a religious practice.
But religious activity could not transform an idol into the living God.
That is a warning we desperately need.
Because we live in a world that often treats sincerity as the highest form of truth.
"If it feels right, follow it."
"If it makes you happy, it must be good."
"If your heart is deeply moved, surely God must be pleased."
But Scripture challenges that assumption.
You can sincerely believe something false.
You can passionately pursue something destructive.
You can cry over something that is quietly becoming your master.
And you can mistake the strength of your feelings for the approval of God.
That does not mean tears are wrong.
Jesus Himself wept.
John 11:35 gives us those two extraordinary words:
"Jesus wept."
Our Savior was not ashamed of human grief.
He entered it.
He understood it.
He carried it.
The problem in Ezekiel 8 was not that women were crying. Nor was it that women, rather than men, were uniquely guilty. The surrounding vision condemns the idolatry of both male and female worshipers.
The problem was the worship of a false god within the place devoted to the LORD.
And the same danger can confront any human heart.
You may never have heard of Tammuz before today.
You may never have bowed before a carved image.
You may never have participated in an ancient mourning ritual.
But have you ever given something created the kind of ultimate trust, devotion, or obedience that belongs to the Creator?
Have you ever been more terrified of losing someone's approval than of disobeying God?
Have you ever protected a sinful relationship because you could not imagine living without it?
Have you ever compromised your convictions to preserve your reputation?
Have you ever pursued money so desperately that your peace disappeared whenever your bank account changed?
Have you ever known that God was calling you to surrender something, but kept negotiating with Him because you were not ready to let it go?
This is where the ancient Temple begins to feel uncomfortably close.
Because an idol does not always announce itself as an idol.
Sometimes it arrives as a dream.
Sometimes as romance.
Sometimes as ambition.
Sometimes as comfort.
Sometimes as the desperate need to be admired.
Sometimes even as a religious platform that becomes more important to us than the Christ we claim to proclaim.
A good gift becomes spiritually dangerous when we begin demanding from it what only God can give.
