A relationship can be a blessing without becoming our savior.
Work can be meaningful without becoming our identity.
Money can be useful without becoming our security.
Ministry can be fruitful without becoming our god.
And this is the question Ezekiel's vision forces upon us:
What are you giving your deepest devotion to while telling yourself that God still has first place?
That question hurts because many of us know how to maintain an appearance.
We know how to say, "God is good," while privately resisting His correction.
We know how to post Bible verses while carrying bitterness we refuse to release.
We know how to lift our hands during worship while holding tightly to something Christ has commanded us to surrender.
We know how to speak about faith while secretly building our entire sense of worth on human applause.
And perhaps the most painful truth is this:
Sometimes we are not unaware of the compromise.
We are simply exhausted from trying to justify it.
We tell ourselves it is not that serious.
We compare ourselves with someone whose sin looks worse.
We promise God we will change later.
We call conviction "guilt" and try to silence it.
We ask for peace while refusing to abandon the very thing disturbing our souls.
But God loves His people too much to pretend that divided worship is harmless.
The LORD's jealousy in Scripture is not petty insecurity. It is His holy opposition to covenant unfaithfulness and to the false worship that destroys His people.
In Exodus 20:3, He commands:
"You shall have no other gods before me."
Not because He is one option competing for our attention.
But because He alone is God.
And nothing else can bear the weight of our worship.
Think about the idols people build their lives around.
They promise fulfillment but demand endless sacrifice.
They promise acceptance but make us terrified of rejection.
They promise control but leave us anxious about everything we cannot control.
They promise identity but collapse the moment circumstances change.
They promise freedom but slowly teach us to obey our appetites.
And when they fail us, we often run back to them, hoping they will finally give what they have never been able to provide.
That is the cruelty of idolatry.
It asks for the devotion of a god while possessing none of God's power to save.
But Ezekiel's vision does not end with the women weeping.
And the story of God's people does not end with the exposure of their sin.
This is where the Gospel begins to shine against a very dark background.
Because the same prophetic book that reveals the corruption of the human heart also announces God's promise to transform it.
Later, in Ezekiel 36:26, the LORD declares:
"And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you." — ESV
In Hebrew, the promise begins:
"וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ"
Ve-natatti lakhem lev chadash.
"And I will give you a new heart."
Notice what God promises.
Not merely improved religious behavior.
Not merely a more convincing outward appearance.
Not merely stronger emotions during worship.
A new heart.
A transformed inner life.
A work of grace reaching deeper than performance.
Ezekiel 36:27 continues with God's promise to put His Spirit within His people and move them to walk in His statutes.
That is the difference between merely hiding an idol and receiving a heart that increasingly loves the living God.
And Christians recognize the fulfillment of God's saving promises through Jesus Christ and the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Jesus did not come merely to make religious people more religious.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He came to bear the judgment that sin deserves and bring forgiveness through His death and resurrection.
He came to do what idols never could.
He came to give life.
And perhaps you need to hear this more than anything else today.
The God who exposes your idols is also the God who calls you to return.
His Word may uncover something you have spent years hiding.
His truth may challenge a relationship you have defended.
His holiness may confront the secret compromises you have learned to tolerate.
But the invitation of the Gospel is not to despair.
It is to repent and believe.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible about what we have done.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, a turning of mind and life toward God.
Biblical repentance involves acknowledging sin, turning away from it, and returning to the LORD in faith.
It is not purchasing forgiveness through tears.
It is not earning grace through self-punishment.
It is not promising to become perfect before approaching Christ.
It is coming to the Savior because we cannot save ourselves.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — ESV
Read that again.
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the sacrifice of Jesus Christ is sufficient.
This is what makes the Gospel so astonishing.
The idols we serve demand that we give ourselves to them.
But Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
The idols we trust cannot forgive our rebellion.
But Jesus shed His blood for the forgiveness of sins.
The idols we chase cannot conquer death.
But Jesus rose from the grave.
The idols we cling to eventually fail.
But Christ remains faithful.
And there is another detail in Ezekiel that should leave us trembling.
In Ezekiel 8, the people were corrupting the Temple associated with God's dwelling among His covenant people.
But in John 2:19–21, Jesus speaks of the Temple in a way His disciples later understand as referring to His own body.
He says:
"Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." — John 2:19, ESV
John explains that Jesus was speaking about the Temple of His body.
Do you see the extraordinary movement of the biblical story?
Ezekiel reveals the horror of idolatry in God's Temple.
The Gospel reveals the Son of God giving His own body to death and rising again so sinners can be reconciled to God.
This does not mean the women weeping for Tammuz were secretly reenacting the death and resurrection of Christ. Scripture does not teach that, and we should not force such a connection.
The contrast is far more powerful when we allow the text to speak truthfully.
Tammuz belonged to the religious traditions of the ancient world.
Jesus Christ entered real human history, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and was proclaimed risen by His witnesses.
Christian faith does not rest on a seasonal fertility ritual.
It rests on the saving work of the crucified and risen Lord.
And He is not asking you to manufacture religious emotion to impress Him.
He calls you to trust Him.
To follow Him.
To surrender the throne of your heart.
Because the greatest tragedy is not simply that human beings sometimes worship false gods.
It is that we can become so attached to those false gods that we resist the mercy of the true One.
Maybe your idol is not obvious to anyone else.
Maybe it is the person you cannot stop chasing even though the relationship keeps pulling you away from obedience.
Maybe it is the success you have sacrificed your integrity to obtain.
Maybe it is the resentment you have carried for so long that forgiveness now feels like surrendering your identity.
Maybe it is the secret habit that keeps promising relief while leaving you ashamed.
Maybe it is your own image.
The version of yourself you desperately need everyone to admire.
The version that never struggles.
Never doubts.
Never confesses.
Never needs help.
And perhaps you have become so skilled at appearing strong that you have forgotten how to be honest before God.
But listen.
Jesus already knows.
He knows the thought you would never post.
He knows the compromise you keep explaining away.
He knows the prayer you stopped praying because you were afraid of what obedience might cost.
He knows the disappointment that hardened into anger.
He knows the wound you keep covering with spiritual language.
And still, His Gospel calls sinners to come.
Not because He approves of the darkness.
But because He alone can bring us out of it.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
"Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." — ESV
Not come to the idol that keeps exhausting you.
Not come to the applause that disappears tomorrow.
Not come to the relationship that has become your entire reason for living.
Come to Me.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
It is the exhaustion of living divided.
Trying to serve Christ while protecting the thing that competes with Him.
Trying to experience peace while resisting the truth.
Trying to look whole while privately falling apart.
And sometimes the beginning of healing is a painfully simple confession:
"Lord, I have loved something more than I have loved You."
No excuses.
No performance.
No bargaining.
Just truth.
And a willingness to turn toward Jesus.
Perhaps your prayer tonight needs to be this:

"Father, show me what has taken Your rightful place in my heart. Expose what I have defended. Forgive what I have hidden. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. I cannot change my own heart by sheer determination. I need Your mercy. I need Your Spirit. I need Jesus. Lead me into genuine repentance and faithful obedience. In Christ's name, amen."
There is no shame in bringing your sin into the light of Christ.
The danger is insisting that darkness is where you belong.
And if this article has uncovered something in your life, please do not rush past that moment.
You do not need to share every private struggle publicly. Some matters are best brought to God and to a trusted, mature believer who can walk with you.
But you do not have to keep pretending that the battle does not exist.
Someone reading silently may need to know that genuine change through Christ is possible.
Your story may not be finished.
But God's grace is not exhausted.
There may also be someone in your family, your church, or your circle of friends who needs this message.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Not because you have appointed yourself their judge.
But because you love them enough to remind them that Jesus is better than anything that competes for their soul.
Because a message like this should not end with a moment of emotion.
It should lead us back to the Word of God.
Back to prayer.
Back to obedience.
Back to the local church.
Back to the cross.
Back to Jesus.
And if Gospel Warrior has been a source of biblical encouragement in your life, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.
Not as a payment for God's favor.
Not as proof that your faith is genuine.
But voluntary support can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity when it is given freely, wisely, and for the right reasons.
The apostle Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
That is the spirit in which we invite you.

Some believers may prayerfully choose to make that support part of their planned Christian giving. Others may rightly prioritize their local church, family responsibilities, and other needs. Traditional tithes and offerings should not be confused with a required payment to an online ministry.
What matters is not pressure.
It is faithful stewardship and a willing heart.
The products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The resources are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is already the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, as Romans 1:16 declares.
But your generosity can help carry that message farther.
Imagine someone scrolling through Facebook late at night.
Someone exhausted from pretending.
Someone quietly trapped in a sin they are afraid to confess.
Someone convinced they have gone too far to return.
Someone whose faith has become little more than an outward routine.
And then they see an article you shared.
They read about women weeping for Tammuz at the entrance to God's Temple.
They begin examining the misplaced devotion in their own heart.
They remember that Christ died for sinners.
They open their Bible.
They pray honestly for the first time in months.
They seek help.
They begin to turn toward Jesus.
You may never know that happened.
But it is one reason sharing truth with compassion matters.
I want you to think about the entrance to that Temple.
The women sitting there.
The tears falling.
The religious devotion directed toward a god who could not save.
And I want you to remember that the living God was not blind to what was happening.
He saw.
He spoke.
He exposed.
And through the unfolding testimony of Scripture, He revealed His saving mercy in Jesus Christ.
Now imagine your own heart standing in the light of that truth.
No religious performance.
No carefully edited image.
No excuses.
Just you before the God who knows everything.
What would He find occupying the place that belongs to Him?
And what would happen if, today, you finally surrendered it?
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic moment.
You do not need to prove the sincerity of your repentance through public emotion.
You need the Savior.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who calls sinners to repent and believe.
The One who forgives.
The One who transforms.
The One who is worthy of everything.
Because the true tragedy of Ezekiel 8 is not that people were weeping.
It is that they were giving their devotion to something that was not God.
And the hope of the Gospel is that our story does not have to end there.
You can turn.
You can confess.
You can come to Christ.
And by His grace, you can learn to love Him above everything else.
The most heartbreaking thing is not to be found weeping at the door of God's house, but to spend your life clinging to what cannot save you while the Savior calls you to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE CAME TO EXPOSE A KING WITH QUESTIONS—BUT WHAT SHE DISCOVERED LEFT HER SPEECHLESS
paragraphs: SHE CAME TO EXPOSE A KING WITH QUESTIONS—BUT WHAT SHE DISCOVERED LEFT HER SPEECHLESS

The Queen of Sheba traveled across dangerous distances to test Solomon’s wisdom. She expected extraordinary answers. What she encountered was something far greater—and 3,000 years later, her story still confronts everyone searching for truth, carrying unanswered questions, or wondering whether God is really who He says He is.
“And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions.” — 1 Kings 10:1 (KJV)
She did not travel all that distance because she was easily impressed.
She was a queen.
She had wealth. Influence. Authority. Resources. People who answered when she called. Servants who attended to her needs. An entire kingdom accustomed to her commands.
But there was something she did not possess.
An answer to every question.
And somewhere beyond the borders of her kingdom, a rumor had reached her ears.
There was a king in Jerusalem whose wisdom was unlike anything the world had seen.
Not merely a man who could speak beautifully.
Not simply a ruler surrounded by gold.
A king whose understanding had become so extraordinary that his reputation was connected to the name of the LORD.
And the queen wanted to know whether the stories were true.
So she prepared a journey.
Camels carrying spices. Precious stones. Gold. An impressive royal procession crossing the ancient world.
But the most important thing she carried was invisible.
Questions.
Questions difficult enough to test a king.
Questions that wealth could not answer.
Questions that required something deeper than intelligence.
And perhaps that is where her story begins to sound strangely familiar.
Because you may not have a crown.
You may not command an army.
You may not own gold or precious stones.
But you know what it means to carry questions that refuse to leave you alone.
Why did God allow that loss?
Why did the person you trusted betray you?
Why does obedience sometimes feel harder than rebellion?
Why do people who ignore God appear to prosper while those trying to follow Him struggle?
Why does heaven sometimes seem silent when your heart is screaming?
And perhaps the question you have been afraid to say aloud:
“Lord, if You are really with me, why does my life look like this?”
The Queen of Sheba came with hard questions.
And Scripture tells us something remarkable.
Solomon did not dismiss them.
He did not shame her for asking.
He did not demand that she pretend to understand.
First Kings 10:2 says she came to Solomon and communed with him of all that was in her heart.
Read that again.
All that was in her heart.
The Hebrew expression is כָּל־אֲשֶׁר הָיָה עִם־לְבָבָהּ (kol-asher hayah im-levavah), expressing everything that was in her heart.
This was more than a ceremonial exchange between rulers.
She brought what she had been carrying within.
And Solomon listened.
There is something deeply moving about that.
Because many people have spent years sitting in churches while secretly believing their questions make them unworthy of belonging there.
They smile during worship.
They say amen.
They post Bible verses.
But beneath the surface, their faith is wrestling with things they are terrified to confess.
They fear that asking difficult questions means they are doubting God.
Yet the Bible does not hide the struggles of people who sought Him.
David cried out in anguish.
Job wrestled with suffering.
Habakkuk questioned the violence and injustice around him.
Thomas struggled to believe the resurrection testimony.
And the father of a suffering child cried to Jesus:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.” — Mark 9:24 (KJV)
God's Word does not teach us to celebrate unbelief.
But it does show us that honest questions can become the beginning of a deeper search for truth.
The danger is not always that you have questions.
Sometimes the danger is that you have stopped bringing them to God.
You have allowed disappointment to become distance.
You have allowed pain to become suspicion.
You have allowed unanswered prayers to become a reason to abandon the One who alone can give eternal life.
And slowly, without realizing it, you have begun treating your wounds as greater authorities than His Word.
But the Queen of Sheba did something many people never do.
She went searching.
She refused to settle for secondhand reports.
She wanted to see whether what she had heard was true.
And when she arrived in Jerusalem, the answers were only the beginning.
First Kings 10:3 declares:
“And Solomon told her all her questions: there was not any thing hid from the king, which he told her not.” (KJV)
Every question she presented received an answer.
But then something happened that no amount of preparation could have anticipated.
She looked around.
She saw Solomon's wisdom.
She saw the house he had built.
She saw the food at his table.
She saw the organization of his servants, the attendance of his ministers, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up to the house of the LORD.
And Scripture records an extraordinary reaction.
“There was no more spirit in her.” — 1 Kings 10:5 (KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
וְלֹא־הָיָה בָהּ עוֹד רוּחַ
Ve-lo hayah vah od ruach.
Literally, there was no more breath or spirit in her.
The expression communicates overwhelming astonishment.
She was left breathless.
Not because she had seen something imaginary.
Not because someone had manipulated her emotions.
But because the reality before her exceeded the reports she had received.
She had heard about Solomon's wisdom.
Now she had witnessed it.
She had heard about the greatness of his kingdom.
Now she stood inside it.
And what she saw surpassed what she had believed.
Listen to her own words:
“Behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard.” — 1 Kings 10:7 (KJV)
The half was not told me.
Imagine the weight of that confession.
A powerful queen who had traveled from afar suddenly realized that everything she had heard had been an understatement.
But the most important moment of this story is not her amazement at Solomon.
It is what she said next.

“Blessed be the LORD thy God, which delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel: because the LORD loved Israel for ever, therefore made he thee king, to do judgment and justice.” — 1 Kings 10:9 (KJV)
She recognized that Solomon's wisdom and royal position were connected to the LORD's favor and purpose for Israel.
Notice where her praise went.
Beyond the gold.
Beyond the palace.
Beyond the impressive servants.
Beyond the king himself.
To the LORD.
That is the moment this story becomes far more than a historical account of royal splendor.
Because genuine God-given wisdom should never terminate in admiration of the person who possesses it.
It should direct attention toward the God who gives it.
And here is where we must be careful.
Solomon's kingdom was magnificent, but Solomon was not the Savior.
His wisdom was a gift, but he was not the source of all wisdom.
His reign displayed extraordinary blessing, but his heart would later be led astray.
First Kings 11 records a devastating turn.
The same Solomon who once asked God for wisdom eventually allowed his many foreign wives to turn his heart after other gods.
The king whose wisdom astonished a queen failed to remain wholly devoted to the LORD.
Think about that.
A man can possess extraordinary wisdom and still make devastatingly foolish choices when he stops obeying God.
A person can know Scripture and still resist surrender.
A person can teach truth and still tolerate hidden compromise.
A person can impress a crowd while quietly drifting away from the God he claims to serve.
That should sober every one of us.
Because the tragedy of Solomon's later years reminds us that knowledge alone cannot save a human soul.
Religious reputation cannot save us.
Public success cannot save us.
Even extraordinary spiritual privileges cannot replace faithful obedience.
And this is where the story begins to turn toward Someone greater.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ spoke about the Queen of Sheba.
He did not treat her journey as a meaningless legend.
He used her response to confront a generation that was demanding signs while refusing to recognize the truth standing before them.
In Matthew 12:42, Jesus said:

“The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” (KJV)
A GREATER THAN SOLOMON IS HERE.
Do you understand the weight of those words?
The Queen of Sheba traveled an extraordinary distance to hear the wisdom of a human king.
But the people standing before Jesus were encountering One greater than that king.
Solomon received wisdom from God.
Jesus is the eternal Son of God, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).
Solomon ruled an earthly kingdom.
Jesus is the promised Messiah whose kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:32–33).
Solomon's obedience eventually failed.
Jesus obeyed the Father perfectly, even unto death (Philippians 2:8).
Solomon could answer difficult questions.
Jesus came to deal with humanity's deepest problem.
Sin.
The Queen of Sheba was astonished by the greatness of Solomon.
But the Gospel reveals a King whose greatness is displayed not merely through royal splendor, but through humility, sacrifice, resurrection, and saving grace.
The King of kings entered a broken world.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He showed compassion to the weary.
He spoke truth that exposed hidden hearts.
He endured rejection, betrayal, mockery, and crucifixion.
And He did not go to the cross because humanity had become worthy of His sacrifice.
He went because sinners desperately needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we stopped struggling.
Not after we finally became impressive enough to approach Him.
While we were sinners.
That is grace.
And it changes everything.
Because perhaps you have been approaching God the way the Queen of Sheba approached Solomon.
You have heard the reports.
You have heard people testify about forgiveness.
You have watched others speak about peace.
You have seen lives transformed.
But deep inside, you are still wondering whether what you have heard could ever become real for you.
Could Jesus forgive what you did?
Could He receive someone who has fallen so many times?
Could He restore a person who has wasted years?
Could He save someone who has spent most of life running from Him?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that you are good enough to climb your way to God. It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says salvation is by grace through faith, not of works.
And the invitation of Christ remains:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
Not everyone who comes to Christ receives an immediate explanation for every painful event.
The Bible does not promise that.
Some questions remain unanswered in this life.
Some grief must be carried through seasons of patient trust.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
But Jesus offers something greater than the illusion of controlling every outcome.
He offers Himself.
His forgiveness.
His presence.
His truth.
His eternal life.
And His promise that those who come to Him in faith will not be cast out (John 6:37).
That is why this account should confront both the skeptic and the believer.
To the skeptic, it asks:
You have heard things about Jesus. But have you seriously examined who He claimed to be, what He taught, and what His death and resurrection mean?
To the believer, it asks something equally searching:
You already know the name of Jesus. But are you actually following Him?
Because there is a frightening difference between being familiar with Christ and being surrendered to Christ.
You can know the language of Christianity while refusing the Lordship of Jesus.
You can admire His teachings while resisting His commands.
You can share Scripture publicly while privately making peace with sin.
You can spend years near Christian things without cultivating a life of repentance, prayer, obedience, and love.
And sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not open rebellion.
It is comfortable familiarity.
You hear another sermon.
Another Bible verse.
Another warning.
Another invitation to return.
And you tell yourself there will be time tomorrow.
But tomorrow is not promised.
The Queen of Sheba responded to what she had heard by making the journey.
And Jesus, the greater King, calls us not merely to admire His wisdom but to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in Mark 1:15 is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite).
It calls for repentance—a genuine turning of mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because your sin was discovered.
It is not merely crying because your choices have consequences.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And true faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting Him as Savior and Lord.
That does not mean Christians become instantly flawless.
It means grace does not leave us content to remain enslaved to what Christ came to deliver us from.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live in a way that honors Him.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
And this is why our message has always carried such weight:
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because every damaged relationship is automatically restored.
But because Jesus can redeem a life that sin has devastated.
He can forgive the guilty.
He can humble the proud.
He can restore hope to the ashamed.
He can give a new identity to those who have been defined by their worst decisions.
And He can turn a testimony of rebellion into a testimony of mercy.
Perhaps the scandal in your life is something other people know about.
Or perhaps it is something nobody has ever discovered.
The secret addiction.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The dishonesty that has become normal.
The relationship you know is drawing you away from God.
The spiritual pride that allows you to condemn others while excusing yourself.
The quiet refusal to forgive.
The faith you display in public but neglect in private.
Whatever it is, hiding it does not heal it.
Jesus already knows the truth.
And His call is not to continue pretending.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not permission to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to stop defending what is destroying you.
You do not have to manufacture a flawless testimony before coming to Christ.
You come because you need His mercy.
And maybe that is the hardest question of all.
Not whether God can forgive you.
But whether you are willing to stop running from the forgiveness He offers.
The Queen of Sheba came to test Solomon with hard questions.
But now the greater King confronts us with a question no amount of wealth, influence, intelligence, or religious activity can answer for us.
What will you do with Jesus Christ?
Will you keep Him at a comfortable distance?
Will you admire Him without obeying Him?
Will you continue postponing the repentance you know is necessary?
Or will you surrender?
Maybe your prayer today does not need to be eloquent.
Maybe it needs to be honest.

“Lord Jesus, I have heard so much about You, but there are places in my heart I have kept closed. I have questions, wounds, fears, and sins I can no longer pretend are harmless. Forgive me. Teach me to trust Your Word. Turn my heart away from what dishonors You. Help me follow You, not merely speak about You. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I need Your grace. Change me from the inside out. Amen.”
These words are not a formula that earns salvation.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith.
But if that prayer expresses the sincere turning of your heart toward Him, do not let this moment disappear beneath the distractions of another ordinary day.
Open your Bible.
Read Matthew 12.
Read 1 Kings 10 and 11 together.
Notice both the splendor of Solomon's reign and the warning of his later compromise.
Then read the Gospels and behold the greater King.
And as you do, remember this:
The Queen of Sheba was willing to travel far to investigate the wisdom she had heard about.
You have the testimony of Jesus Christ preserved in Scripture within reach.
Do not allow familiarity to make you careless with such a gift.
And please, do not walk through this conviction alone.
You do not need to reveal private details to strangers. But sometimes an honest response becomes the beginning of encouragement, prayer, and genuine Christian fellowship.
And if this message brought someone to mind, do not ignore that person.
Perhaps it is a family member who has slowly drifted from church.
A friend who has become bitter toward God.
A believer who is quietly struggling.
A young person who knows Christian language but has never seriously examined the Gospel.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus came.
And if you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, consider joining this growing community of people who want more than occasional religious inspiration.
We want to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, discipleship, and a living relationship with Jesus Christ.
Because one of the greatest things we can offer another human being is not another argument to win.
It is an invitation to encounter the truth about Jesus.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another way to walk alongside this mission.
These resources are intended to nourish faith, encourage spiritual maturity, strengthen biblical understanding, and equip people to share the Gospel faithfully.
We believe the message of salvation must never be treated as something that can be purchased.
The grace of God is not for sale.
Prayer is not for sale.
Forgiveness is not for sale.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry of biblical teaching, free resources, and ongoing discipleship does require people who are willing and able to help.
Scripture teaches that believers may generously support those who labor in Gospel ministry (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14; 2 Corinthians 9:7).
But Scripture also teaches that giving should never be driven by guilt, compulsion, or the promise that God's favor can be bought.
If you have been looking for a practical way to help extend biblical encouragement beyond your own circle, this is one way to do it.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for reflection, and opportunities to encourage meaningful conversations about faith.
It is the people who may be reached.
The person who opens a devotional while struggling with despair.
The believer who returns to Scripture after years of spiritual neglect.
The family member who shares a Gospel message with someone who has stopped attending church.
The reader who discovers that Christianity is not about pretending to be righteous but about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
We cannot promise that every article will change a life.
Only God can bring spiritual life and lasting transformation.
But we can remain faithful in planting and watering, trusting Him for the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).
And perhaps your partnership can help place another faithful message within reach of someone who needs to hear it.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
And your love for Jesus cannot be measured by a monthly payment.
What matters is that Christ is honored, His Word is handled faithfully, and His Gospel is proclaimed.
Because this was never meant to be about building a platform greater than the message.
It is about using every opportunity entrusted to us to point beyond ourselves to the Savior.
Just as the Queen of Sheba looked beyond Solomon's splendor and blessed the LORD, may everything we do direct attention beyond Gospel Warrior to Jesus Christ.
The One who is greater than Solomon.
The One whose wisdom cannot fail.
The One whose righteousness is perfect.
The One who gave His life for sinners.
The One who rose victorious over death.
The One who calls the weary to Himself.
And the One who is worthy of our trust, our obedience, our worship, and our lives.
The Queen of Sheba came searching for answers and left astonished by the wisdom of a king.
But you are being invited to something greater than astonishment.
You are being called to faith.
To repentance.
To grace.
To a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And one day, when every earthly crown has lost its shine, every palace has turned to dust, and every human achievement has passed away, the glory of Jesus Christ will remain.
So do not spend your whole life admiring the wisdom of a lesser king while ignoring the Savior who stands above them all.
She traveled across kingdoms to hear a king's wisdom. The greater King came into our broken world to save sinners—and the question now is whether you will receive Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS SEXUAL FANTASY ALWAYS LUST? THE QUESTION MATTHEW 5 FORCES US TO EXAMINE.
paragraphs: IS SEXUAL FANTASY ALWAYS LUST? THE QUESTION MATTHEW 5 FORCES US TO EXAMINE.

Jesus never said that every sexual thought makes you guilty. But what He actually said about the desires we secretly entertain may expose something far deeper than most of us are prepared to confront.
There is a kind of battle nobody sees.
It doesn't happen in a bedroom with another person. It doesn't leave evidence on your phone. It doesn't necessarily involve pornography, physical contact, or an affair.
Sometimes it happens while you're lying awake at 2:00 in the morning, staring into the darkness.
A memory returns. An image forms. A possibility crosses your mind.
And suddenly, you're standing at a crossroads nobody else knows exists.
Do you dismiss the thought? Do you entertain it? Do you deliberately return to it because of the pleasure it promises?
Or do you wake up the next morning feeling guilty about something you never physically did?
Here is the question that has troubled countless Christians, including people who genuinely love Jesus:
If something sexual happens only in my imagination, have I already sinned against God?
Some believers have been taught that the slightest sexual thought is lust. Others have convinced themselves that anything is permissible as long as nothing happens physically.
But what if both answers are too shallow?
What if Jesus was not merely counting sexual thoughts, but exposing what the human heart chooses to desire?
And what if understanding that difference could free some people from unnecessary shame while calling others to a repentance they have been avoiding for years?
Because there is something extraordinary hidden in the original Greek of Matthew 5:28.
And once you understand it, you may never read that verse quite the same way again.
Jesus was speaking to people who understood the commandment against adultery.
They knew the boundary.
Don't cross it. Don't commit the act. Don't betray the marriage covenant.
But Jesus went deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He declared:
"You have heard that it was said, You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart." (ESV)
Now pay attention.
Jesus did not simply say that noticing an attractive person is adultery.
He did not say that every involuntary sexual image passing through the mind is adultery.
He addressed a particular kind of looking, one connected to deliberate, covetous desire.
The Greek text contains these words:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn
The phrase expresses looking at a woman with a view to desiring or coveting her.
The verb epithymeō means to desire, long for, or covet. Importantly, the word itself does not always describe sinful desire. Its moral meaning depends on what is desired and the context.
For example, in Luke 22:15, Jesus uses the related expression epithymia epethymēsa to describe His earnest desire to eat the Passover with His disciples.
Desire, therefore, is not automatically evil simply because it is intense.
But in Matthew 5:28, the context is adultery.
Jesus is confronting sexual desire that violates the moral boundaries of faithfulness.
The Greek wording emphasizes looking with the purpose or result of lustful desire. It does not provide a mechanical test for precisely how many seconds a thought must remain before it becomes sinful.
And that distinction matters.
Because there is a difference between a thought entering your mind and your heart deliberately making room for it.
There is a difference between recognizing beauty and mentally possessing someone who does not belong to you.
There is a difference between experiencing temptation and willingly nurturing it.
Not every thought that enters your mind reveals what you have chosen. But what you repeatedly welcome, cultivate, and pursue can reveal what your heart is learning to love.
Think about that.
A Christian man walks through a crowded place and notices an attractive woman.
He recognizes her beauty.
Then he continues walking.
Has he necessarily committed adultery in his heart?
No. Matthew 5 does not justify that conclusion.
Now imagine that same man deliberately returns his gaze, begins imagining sexual intimacy with her, and repeatedly cultivates those images for his own gratification.
The external circumstances may appear identical.
But something inward has changed.
The issue is no longer merely that he noticed someone.
He is now intentionally entertaining a desire that Jesus calls him to confront.
And women are not exempt from this examination. Although Jesus uses a man looking at a woman in this passage, the moral concern about covetous sexual desire applies to both sexes.
This is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we ask, "Is this technically a sin?" when the question we are avoiding is, "Why am I so determined to keep this fantasy?"
We want to know where the line is.
Jesus wants to know what is happening in our hearts.
And those are not always the same conversation.
But before we go further, we need to correct something that has wounded far too many sincere believers.
Temptation is not automatically the same as sin.
Hebrews 4:15 teaches that Jesus was tempted as we are, yet without sin.
That truth is essential.
Christ experienced genuine temptation without surrendering to evil.
James 1:14–15 explains how desire can entice a person and, when it is conceived, give birth to sin.
These passages require us to distinguish between encountering temptation and consenting to it.
An unwanted sexual thought is not necessarily an act of chosen lust.
An intrusive image is not automatically a moral decision.
An involuntary bodily response does not, by itself, establish sinful intent.
And a believer who experiences unwanted thoughts does not need to interpret every mental interruption as evidence of spiritual failure.
Some Christians have spent years trapped in a cycle of fear.
A thought appears.
They panic.
They ask God for forgiveness.
They inspect their feelings to determine whether they secretly enjoyed it.
Then they become afraid that even the act of remembering the thought means they have sinned again.
Their spiritual life becomes an endless courtroom.
Every thought is evidence.
Every sensation is suspicious.
Every moment of uncertainty feels like condemnation.
If that describes you, hear this carefully.
Jesus did not come to make His people prisoners of obsessive self-accusation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." (ESV)
That is not permission to embrace sin.
It is a promise that those who belong to Christ are not left under its condemning sentence.
The Holy Spirit convicts us toward repentance and life.
He does not require us to achieve perfect certainty about every passing thought before we can trust the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice.
But now we must face the other side.
Because grace is not a hiding place for desires we have decided to protect.
And the person who says, "It's only happening in my imagination," may need to hear something very different.
Imagine a married man who never physically cheats on his wife.
He attends church.
He serves faithfully.
He tells everyone he loves his family.
But every night, he deliberately fantasizes about another woman.
He mentally constructs a relationship he knows would betray his marriage if it became real.
He looks forward to those private moments.
He cultivates them.
He returns to them.
And when his conscience begins to trouble him, he reassures himself:
"At least I haven't actually done anything."
But has he really done nothing?
Jesus challenges precisely that kind of reasoning.
The heart is not morally irrelevant simply because nobody else can see it.
God's concern reaches beyond outward behavior.
The commandment against adultery is not merely a prohibition against physical betrayal. Jesus reveals that covenant faithfulness also has an inward dimension.
This connects directly to the tenth commandment.
In Exodus 20:17, God prohibits coveting what belongs to one's neighbor, including the neighbor's wife.
The Hebrew word translated "covet" is:
תַחְמֹד
taḥmōd
It comes from the Hebrew root ḥ-m-d, which can describe desiring or finding something desirable. In the commandment's context, it refers to wrongful coveting.
The commandment addresses a desire directed toward what one has no right to claim.
And this is why Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5 is not a random new restriction.
He is exposing the depth of God's moral concern, a concern already present in the Law.
The problem is not that human beings possess the capacity for sexual desire.
God created human beings as embodied creatures.
Genesis 1:27 describes humanity as created male and female in God's image.
Genesis 2:24 celebrates the one-flesh union of husband and wife.
And the Song of Songs includes joyful, poetic expressions of romantic and physical longing within its celebration of love.
Scripture does not teach that sexuality is inherently filthy.
It teaches that sexuality is morally significant.
It matters how we desire, whom we desire, what we do with desire, and whether our desires honor God and other people.
So now we arrive at the question that cannot be answered responsibly with a careless yes or no.
Is sexual fantasy always lust?
Not every sexual thought or imaginative experience is necessarily sinful lust.
But neither is every sexual fantasy morally innocent.
A married person imagining loving intimacy with their own spouse is not automatically violating Matthew 5:28.
Such imagination can exist within the context of covenant love and mutual faithfulness.
Likewise, someone who experiences an uninvited sexual image, a dream, or a passing attraction has not necessarily chosen to covet another person.
But deliberately cultivating sexual fantasies about someone outside the marriage covenant raises serious questions about lust, coveting, and faithfulness.

For unmarried believers, the same principle calls for discernment. The question is not simply whether a person is legally married, but whether the desire being cultivated honors God's design for sexuality and treats others with dignity rather than reducing them to objects of gratification.
Scripture does not provide an exhaustive catalog of every possible fantasy.
It gives us moral principles that require honest application.
And Christians may differ over particular situations not explicitly addressed in the biblical text.
But we must not turn that uncertainty into an excuse to ignore what Scripture clearly teaches.
Jesus calls His followers to purity of heart.
Paul tells believers in 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5 to abstain from sexual immorality and to live in holiness and honor rather than uncontrolled lustful passion.
And Philippians 4:8 calls Christians to direct their thoughts toward what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and commendable.
These passages do not mean that every imperfect thought makes someone spiritually hopeless.
They mean that our inner lives matter to God.
And here is where this becomes painfully personal.
Sometimes sexual fantasy is not merely about sex.
Sometimes it is about loneliness.
Sometimes it is about wanting to feel desired.
Sometimes it is about escaping a marriage that has become emotionally distant.
Sometimes it is about trying to numb rejection, grief, stress, or disappointment.
Sometimes it is about imagining an intimacy that real life has not provided.
And sometimes it is simply about the pleasure of indulging a desire we know we should not feed.
These motives are not morally identical, and none automatically makes a particular fantasy permissible.
But understanding what drives a recurring pattern can help us confront it truthfully.
Perhaps you have been praying for freedom while refusing to examine the wound beneath the behavior.
Perhaps the fantasy has become your private refuge.
Nobody can reject you there.
Nobody can disappoint you there.
Nobody can see how desperately you want to be loved.
For a few moments, you feel wanted.
Then the fantasy ends.
And the emptiness returns.
So you go back.
Again.
And again.
Until the place you escape to begins to feel like the place you cannot escape from.
And somewhere in that cycle, you begin to wonder whether God is disgusted with you.
But consider how Jesus responded to people whose sexual histories were tangled with shame.
In John 4, Jesus encountered a Samaritan woman whose relational history was complicated.
He knew the truth about her life.
He did not pretend it was irrelevant.
Yet He spoke to her about living water.
He revealed Himself to her in a conversation that transformed her understanding of who stood before her.
She eventually went back to her community and told people about Him.
The woman who had come to draw water became a witness pointing others toward Christ.
That is extraordinary.
Jesus did not need ignorance of her past to offer her the truth.
He knew.
And He still engaged her.
Now remember another encounter.
In Luke 7:36–50, a woman known in her community as a sinner approached Jesus while He was dining in a Pharisee's house.
She wept at His feet.
Her tears fell.
Her hair became a towel.
Her costly perfume became an offering of love.
The religious host saw her reputation.
Jesus saw her faith and love.
And He declared that her sins were forgiven.
He did not call evil good.
He revealed the astonishing mercy of God toward a repentant sinner.
This is the Gospel.
Not that sin is imaginary.
Not that our private choices are meaningless.
Not that holiness is optional.
But that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
People whose outward lives look respectable while their inner lives are in ruins.
People who have made promises they repeatedly broke.
People who are exhausted from pretending.
People who have confused shame with repentance.
People who have hidden behind religious activity because they are terrified of being truly known.
And people who have begun to believe that their worst private thoughts are the truest thing about them.
Listen carefully.
Your struggle may describe a battle you are facing, but it does not have to become the identity that defines your future in Christ.
The cross is not proof that sin doesn't matter.
The cross is proof that sin matters so profoundly that our redemption required the self-giving sacrifice of the Son of God.
First Peter 2:24 says that Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.
Notice both movements.
Forgiveness.
And transformation.
Mercy.
And a new way of living.
Jesus does not merely offer to make us feel better about remaining enslaved.
He calls us into freedom.
But freedom is not always instantaneous.
Sometimes it begins with an honest confession.
"Lord, I have been feeding something I should have surrendered."
Sometimes it begins with a different confession.
"Lord, I have been condemning myself for thoughts I never chose, and I need to learn to trust Your grace."
Sometimes it means turning away from pornography, cutting off sources of temptation, establishing healthy boundaries, or seeking accountability from a mature and trustworthy Christian.
Sometimes it means repairing neglected intimacy in marriage through honest communication, patience, and mutual care.
Sometimes it means receiving professional help for compulsive behavior, trauma, or persistent intrusive thoughts.
And sometimes it means learning that you do not have to fight every unwanted thought by staring at it until you are certain it is gone.
You can redirect your attention without treating the thought as a verdict on your soul.
Jesus' words in Matthew 5:29–30 about tearing out an eye or cutting off a hand communicate the seriousness of dealing with sin. They are not instructions to physically injure yourself.
His language is deliberately forceful.
Sin is not something to casually nurture.
But neither is holiness achieved through self-hatred.
Real repentance is a turning toward God, not merely a collapse into disgust with ourselves.
And this brings us to a question more searching than the one in the title.
What do you do when nobody is watching?
Not because God is waiting to humiliate you.
But because the unseen life is still part of the life He is redeeming.
Would you willingly surrender a fantasy if you became convinced it was drawing your heart away from Christ?
Would you allow Scripture to correct you even when the correction costs you a source of pleasure?
Would you also allow Scripture to comfort you when your conscience is accusing you of something you did not choose?
Because both require humility.
One requires surrendering a cherished indulgence.
The other requires surrendering a cherished accusation against yourself.
And sometimes the second is harder than the first.
There are people reading this who need to stop making peace with deliberate lust.
And there are people reading this who need to stop treating every unwanted thought as proof that God has abandoned them.
Both need Jesus.
Both need truth.
Both need grace.
Both need the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.
And neither needs another religious performance designed to conceal the condition of the heart.
David understood something about this.
After his devastating sin involving Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, he cried out to God in Psalm 51.
In verse 10, the Hebrew reads:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God." (ESV)
The word bara, translated "create," is used in Scripture for divine creative activity.
David was not merely asking God to improve his public image.
He was pleading for inward renewal.
He knew that the deepest problem could not be solved by appearing righteous before other people.
He needed God to work within him.
And perhaps that is the prayer you have been avoiding.
Not simply, "God, make these thoughts disappear."
But, "Lord, show me what I am choosing, what I am fearing, what I am craving, and what I need to surrender."
"Teach me to distinguish temptation from consent."
"Teach me to love what is holy without despising the body You created."
"Teach me to seek intimacy without turning another person into an object."
"Teach me to receive forgiveness without using grace as permission to continue in sin."
"Create in me a clean heart."
Not a heart that has never experienced temptation.
A heart being made new by God.
And if you have fallen repeatedly, remember this:
First John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
That promise is not a license for deliberate disobedience.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic emotional breakdown to make your repentance genuine.
You do not need to tell strangers the intimate details of your struggles.
You do not need to prove your sincerity by hating yourself.
You need to turn to Christ in faith, confess what is truly sinful, and walk in the grace that trains us to live differently.
And when you stumble, return to Him.
Not because sin is harmless.
But because His mercy is greater than the lie that says there is no way back.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious words while their souls remain untouched.
Not to turn private pain into public spectacle.
But to keep pointing wounded, wandering, struggling, and growing people toward the truth of Jesus Christ.

If this article helped you understand the difference between temptation and chosen lust, consider saving it. There may come a night when shame becomes loud again, and you need to remember what Scripture actually says.
You do not owe the internet your private history. You can ask for prayer without revealing details.
And if this challenged something you previously believed about Matthew 5, share what you are learning. Your question or testimony may help another believer approach Scripture with greater humility.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry to grow in Christ.
Scripture teaches the importance of supporting Gospel work. In Philippians 4:15–18, Paul gratefully acknowledges the financial partnership of believers who helped sustain his ministry.
And in 2 Corinthians 9:7, he reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That matters here.
You do not have to pay to receive His grace.
Think of it as a willing ministry offering, not a mandatory biblical tithe or a payment for spiritual favor.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
More Scripture-centered teaching.
More resources for spiritual growth.
More opportunities to encourage believers who are struggling in silence.
More ways to point people toward Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The forgiveness of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
We invite support because the work matters, not because your salvation depends on it.
And perhaps that is the most important distinction of all.
Because the same Jesus who confronts lust is the Jesus who welcomes repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who exposes what is hidden is the Jesus who offers forgiveness.
The same Jesus who calls us to holiness is the Jesus who supplies grace for the journey.
So tonight, when the room becomes quiet and the battle in your mind begins again, remember what Matthew 5 actually calls you to examine.
Not merely whether a thought appeared.
But what your heart is choosing to cherish.
Not merely whether anyone else knows.
But whether you are willing to bring your inner life into the light of Christ.
And not merely how many times you have struggled.
But whether you are still willing to turn toward the Savior who died and rose again to redeem sinners.
Because Jesus is not interested in teaching you to become better at hiding.
He calls you to walk in truth.
And the Gospel offers something infinitely better than the exhausting performance of appearing pure while secretly drowning.
It offers forgiveness for real sin.
Grace for real weakness.
Truth for real confusion.
And hope for real transformation.
The thought you never invited does not have to become your condemnation, and the sin you finally surrender does not have to become your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY ARE SOME CHURCHES MORE CONCERNED ABOUT WHAT WOMEN WEAR THAN HOW MEN TREAT THEM?
paragraphs: WHY ARE SOME CHURCHES MORE CONCERNED ABOUT WHAT WOMEN WEAR THAN HOW MEN TREAT THEM?
When a Woman’s Clothing Becomes a Bigger Scandal Than a Man’s Sin, Something Has Gone Terribly Wrong in the House of God.
She walked into church hoping to find Jesus.
She didn't know that before anyone asked how her soul was doing, someone would have an opinion about her clothes.
Her skirt was too short. Her neckline was too low. Her dress was too tight. Her appearance was apparently distracting someone from worship.
But nobody noticed how tightly she was holding her Bible.
Nobody noticed that she had cried herself to sleep the night before.
Nobody knew she had almost stayed home because the last time she opened up about what a man had done to her, someone asked what she had been wearing.
And the most heartbreaking part?
She had come to church because she thought it was the one place where she wouldn't have to defend her dignity.
What happens when a church becomes better at inspecting a woman's clothing than confronting a man's cruelty?
That question is uncomfortable.
It should be.

Because somewhere between our sermons about holiness and our conversations about modesty, some Christian communities have developed a dangerous habit of scrutinizing women while excusing, minimizing, or overlooking the behavior of men.
Not every church. Not every pastor. Not every Christian.
But it happens often enough that we cannot dismiss the question simply because it makes us uncomfortable.
And before anyone misunderstands, this is not an argument against biblical modesty. Scripture speaks about modesty, self-control, purity, and honoring God with our bodies.
This is about something deeper.
When we preach modesty without confronting mistreatment, we risk teaching women to manage men's behavior while allowing men to avoid responsibility for their own sin.
And that is not the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Picture another woman.

She has been married for years. She serves in ministry, attends Bible studies, gives faithfully, smiles at church, and knows exactly how to say, "God is good," even when her home feels anything but good.
Her husband is respected.
He knows Scripture. He prays beautifully in public. He shakes hands with the pastor. People admire his leadership.
But behind closed doors, he humiliates her, controls her, threatens her, and makes her afraid.
One Sunday, she finally finds the courage to tell someone.
Instead of asking whether she is safe, they ask whether she has been submitting enough.
Instead of confronting his behavior, they ask whether she has been respecting him.
Instead of recognizing the danger, they tell her to pray harder.
Prayer is essential.
But prayer was never intended to become an excuse for refusing to protect someone who is being harmed.
And submission was never a biblical permission slip for abuse.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Think about that.
Jesus did not terrorize His bride.
He sacrificed Himself for her.
He did not use His authority to crush her.
He laid down His life.
Any man who invokes Christ's authority to justify cruelty has misunderstood the very Lord whose name he is using.
And any church that protects a man's reputation at the expense of a woman's safety has confused institutional preservation with biblical faithfulness.
This is where we need to open our Bibles instead of merely defending our traditions.
Because Jesus Himself confronted a religious culture that sometimes placed burdens on people while neglecting the weightier matters of God's law.
In Matthew 23:23, Jesus rebuked religious leaders for carefully attending to tithing while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
In the original Greek, three words stand out:
κρίσις — krisis — justice or righteous judgment.
ἔλεος — eleos — mercy.
πίστις — pistis — faithfulness.
Jesus was not saying that obedience in smaller matters was meaningless. In fact, He said the leaders should have practiced the weightier matters without neglecting the others.
His rebuke was against distorted priorities.
And that distinction matters.

Because when a church can quickly identify a woman's supposedly inappropriate clothing but struggles to confront sexual harassment, coercion, intimidation, or abuse, it needs to examine whether its priorities reflect the heart of Christ.
A dress can be discussed in minutes.
But confronting a respected leader may cost influence, donations, relationships, or reputation.
And sometimes that is where the real test of holiness begins.
Not in what we are willing to criticize.
But in what we are willing to confront, even when confronting it costs us something.
Now consider the words of Jesus in Matthew 5:28.
He taught that a man who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
The Greek expression includes πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn, describing looking at a woman with the purpose of desiring her lustfully.
Notice where Jesus directs responsibility.
To the person doing the looking.
To the heart choosing to cultivate lust.
To the individual who must repent.
Jesus did not tell men that their obedience depended on women successfully preventing temptation.
He confronted the sinful intention of the person looking.
That does not mean clothing choices are morally irrelevant or that Christians should ignore modesty.
It means a man's responsibility for his thoughts and actions cannot be transferred onto a woman's body.
Men are not helpless creatures controlled by fabric.
They are moral beings accountable before God.
And women are not responsible for carrying the burden of every man's self-control.
This becomes even more striking when we consider 1 Timothy 2:9–10, where Paul encourages women to dress modestly, with propriety and self-control, and to be known for good works.
The Greek word αἰδώς — aidōs, translated in this context as modesty or propriety, carries the idea of a respectful sense of what is fitting.
And σωφροσύνη — sōphrosynē points toward sound judgment, self-restraint, or self-control.

Paul's instruction is not merely about the amount of skin covered. The passage also addresses elaborate hairstyles, gold, pearls, and costly clothing, challenging ostentatious displays of wealth and status.
His emphasis is on godly character rather than making outward appearance the measure of spiritual worth.
Modesty matters.
But so do humility, integrity, justice, compassion, and the way we treat other people.
A woman can dress modestly and still be mistreated.
A woman can make an unwise clothing choice and still deserve respect.
A woman can struggle spiritually and still deserve protection.
Her dignity does not begin at the hemline of her skirt.
It begins with the God who created her in His image.
Genesis 1:27 declares that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
The Hebrew expression בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — b'tselem Elohim means "in the image of God."
Not in the image of cultural expectations.
Not in the image of a church's preferred dress code.
Not in the image of what makes other people comfortable.
In the image of God.
That truth gives every human being a dignity that must not be treated as disposable.
And if a church teaches women to honor God with their appearance while failing to teach men to honor God through their treatment of women, something essential is missing.
But there is another scene in Scripture that should make every Christian think deeply.
John chapter 8 describes a woman brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery.
The religious leaders placed her in the middle of the crowd.
They publicly exposed her sin.
They demanded judgment.
And they attempted to use her situation to trap Jesus.
But there is a troubling detail.
Adultery involves more than one person.
Where was the man?
The passage does not tell us.
We should not invent details the Bible does not provide. We do not know why the man was absent or what happened to him.
But the scene undeniably places one accused woman in the center of public condemnation while the man involved is nowhere in the account.
And Jesus refuses to let the crowd use her as an instrument of their religious agenda.
He says in John 8:7, as rendered in the King James Version:
"He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her."
One by one, the accusers leave.
Then Jesus speaks to the woman.
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11, KJV.
Two truths stand together.
Jesus refused to participate in her public destruction.
Jesus also refused to pretend sin did not matter.
Grace and repentance.
Mercy and holiness.
Compassion and truth.
This is the beauty of Christ.
He does not need to humiliate people to call them to transformation.

A textual note is important here: John 7:53–8:11, the passage traditionally known as the woman caught in adultery, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and appears in different locations in portions of the manuscript tradition. Many modern Bibles mark this passage accordingly. Christians should understand that textual history rather than conceal it. The account's themes of mercy, repentance, and opposition to hypocritical judgment are also taught in undisputed passages throughout the New Testament.
And those themes are desperately needed today.
Because there are women who have stopped attending church, not because they rejected Jesus, but because they became exhausted by the way people claiming His name treated them.
There are women who were told their clothing caused a man's inappropriate behavior.
Women who were pressured to remain silent to protect a ministry.
Women who were encouraged to preserve a marriage's appearance while their safety was ignored.
Women who were taught to forgive without being given room to grieve, seek protection, or pursue justice.
And there are men who have been harmed by religious hypocrisy too.
This is not about declaring women innocent of every sin or men guilty of every wrongdoing.
Men and women alike need repentance.
Men and women alike need grace.
Men and women alike are accountable to the same holy God.
The issue is whether we apply biblical truth consistently, especially when someone vulnerable is being harmed by someone powerful.
James 2:1 warns believers against showing favoritism.
And James 2:13 reminds us that mercy triumphs over judgment.
Imagine what would change if our churches took those commands seriously.
Imagine a young woman entering a sanctuary and being welcomed as a person rather than evaluated as a potential distraction.
Imagine a teenage boy being taught that sexual purity means taking responsibility for his own thoughts, choices, and behavior, rather than blaming girls for his temptation.

Imagine a pastor hearing an allegation against a respected church member and responding with seriousness, fairness, concern for safety, and appropriate reporting to civil authorities rather than reflexively defending the accused.
Imagine church leaders understanding that biblical forgiveness does not eliminate consequences, accountability, or the need for protection.
Imagine modesty being taught as part of a larger Christian vision of humility and godliness rather than as a tool for shame.
Imagine men being called to Christlike love with the same seriousness that women are called to modesty.
That would not weaken the church.
It would strengthen its witness.
Because the world does not need a church that is skilled at appearing holy while hiding what is wrong.
It needs Christians who are willing to walk in the light.
First John 1:7 speaks of walking in the light as God is in the light.
And Ephesians 5:11 calls believers not to participate in the unfruitful works of darkness but to expose them.
That includes wrongdoing that happens behind respectable appearances.
That includes misconduct by people who know how to quote Scripture.
That includes injustice that becomes inconvenient to confront.
And this is where the conversation becomes personal.
Because perhaps you are not the woman who was judged.
Perhaps you are the person who made the comment.
Perhaps you have looked at someone's appearance and decided something about their character without knowing their story.
Perhaps you have repeated the phrase, "She was asking for it," without realizing how deeply that contradicts personal responsibility.
Perhaps you have remained silent when someone was being mistreated because the person responsible was influential, generous, or well-liked.
Perhaps you have defended a ministry's reputation more fiercely than you defended someone who was hurting.
If that is you, this is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to repent.
The Gospel is not merely good news for people who have been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
It is also good news for those who have participated in it and are willing to turn from their sin.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Not for people who successfully maintained an appearance of righteousness.
Not for people who could convince everyone else they were spiritually superior.
For sinners.
Romans 5:8 tells us that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners, through Christ's death for us.
And 1 John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
That promise is not permission to continue doing harm.
It is an invitation to genuine transformation.
Repentance is more than feeling embarrassed after being confronted.
It means turning away from sin.
For someone who has mistreated another person, that includes stopping the harm, accepting accountability, respecting boundaries, and making appropriate restitution where possible.

For a church that has failed someone, repentance may require acknowledging wrongdoing, correcting harmful teaching, cooperating with authorities where appropriate, establishing safeguards, and accepting that trust cannot be demanded.
And for the person who has been hurt, please hear this carefully.
You do not have to remain in danger to prove that you have forgiven someone.
Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation.
Reconciliation requires truth, repentance, and the rebuilding of trust. In situations involving abuse, reconciliation may be unsafe or inappropriate.
Seeking help, reporting a crime, obtaining protection, or establishing boundaries is not a rejection of Jesus.
God does not ask you to pretend that evil is good.
Psalm 34:18 says the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
That is a promise worth remembering when religious people have made you feel invisible.
But there is something else we must not overlook.
Jesus never reduced women to their appearance.
Consider the woman at the well in John 4.
She came to draw water.
Jesus engaged her in a serious conversation about worship, truth, and living water.
He knew the painful and complicated realities of her life.
Yet He did not treat her as unworthy of hearing profound spiritual truth.
She became a witness to her community, inviting others to encounter Him.
Consider Mary of Bethany in Luke 10:38–42.
She sat at Jesus' feet listening to His teaching, taking the posture of a disciple.
When Martha questioned the situation, Jesus defended Mary's choice to listen to Him.
Consider the women who followed Jesus and supported His ministry, described in Luke 8:1–3.
And consider the resurrection accounts, where women were among the first witnesses to the empty tomb and the risen Christ.
These accounts do not erase the distinctions and responsibilities discussed elsewhere in Scripture.
But they unmistakably show that women were not peripheral to the ministry of Jesus.
They were seen.
They were taught.
They were entrusted with meaningful participation in His work.
And if Jesus treated women as people worthy of truth, dignity, and spiritual attention, why should His church settle for treating them as walking dress-code violations?
That question is not an attack on holiness.
It is a call to a more complete holiness.
A holiness that reaches the heart.
A holiness that confronts exploitation.
A holiness that refuses favoritism.
A holiness that values truth over appearances.
A holiness that protects the vulnerable without abandoning fairness or due process.
A holiness that calls every believer, male and female, to become more like Jesus.
Because the answer to distorted teaching is not to discard Scripture.
It is to return to Scripture faithfully.
The answer to legalism is not lawlessness.
It is grace that teaches us to live godly lives, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
The answer to hypocrisy is not silence.
It is repentance.
And the answer to a wounded church is not a prettier religious performance.
It is Christ Himself.
Maybe that is why this conversation hurts.
Because so many people were taught that church was supposed to be a hospital for the broken.
Then they arrived carrying wounds and discovered that some people were more interested in inspecting their clothing than helping them heal.
Some were corrected before they were understood.
Some were shamed before they were heard.
Some were told to be quiet when they desperately needed someone to listen.
And some eventually walked away believing that Jesus must be as harsh as the people who claimed to represent Him.
But human hypocrisy is not the character of Christ.
Please do not confuse the failures of His followers with the faithfulness of the Savior.
Jesus is not intimidated by your questions.
He is not threatened by the truth about what happened to you.
He is not honored when someone uses His name to conceal wrongdoing.
And He is not glorified by a church that demands outward respectability while tolerating inward corruption.
His grace is powerful enough to forgive sinners.
His truth is powerful enough to expose sin.
And His resurrection is powerful enough to give hope where shame once seemed to have the final word.
That is why we keep returning to the message at the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem lives that sin, shame, betrayal, and suffering have deeply affected.
He can restore a person's relationship with God.
He can teach the proud to become humble.
He can lead the cruel toward repentance.
He can give the wounded courage to seek truth and healing.
He can transform people who once defended hypocrisy into people who now stand for righteousness.
And He can build communities where holiness is not measured merely by what people wear on Sunday, but also by how they love, speak, serve, protect, and act throughout the week.
So here is a question worth asking before we leave this conversation.
When a woman walks through the doors of your church, what does she encounter first?
A suspicious glance?
A whispered criticism?
An unspoken demand to prove she belongs?
Or a community committed to the truth and love of Jesus Christ?
And when a man mistreats a woman, what happens next?
Does someone ask what she did to provoke him?
Or do we hold him responsible for his own conduct while responding to everyone involved with truth, justice, and appropriate care?
Because a church's commitment to holiness is revealed not only in the standards it announces, but also in the integrity with which it applies them.
If this article exposed something you have witnessed, experienced, or perhaps even participated in, I would genuinely like to hear your thoughts.
You do not have to share painful details publicly to deserve compassion.
We want this ministry to be more than a page people visit when a message moves them.
We want it to be a place where people continually return to the Word of God and are challenged to grow in the knowledge and grace of Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who may not have the means to purchase Christian books or discipleship materials.
Not out of guilt.
And certainly not because anyone must pay to prove that they love or glorify God.
But Scripture also teaches the beauty of voluntary generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
What matters is that your giving is sincere, responsible, and offered freely before the Lord.
Those products are reminders of the message we share, but the heart of this ministry is not merchandise.
It is the Gospel.
It is the Word of God.
It is people growing in Christ.
It is reaching the person who feels too ashamed to pray, too wounded to trust, or too far gone to believe that grace is still possible.
Because the church does not need more people who know how to look holy while treating others carelessly.
It needs men who resemble Jesus in their character.
Women who are valued as image-bearers of God.
Leaders who refuse to protect wrongdoing.
Believers who choose repentance over appearances.
And communities where grace never becomes an excuse for sin, and holiness never becomes an excuse for cruelty.
So the next time a woman walks into church, remember that you may know what she is wearing, but you do not know what she has survived.
You may notice her appearance, but you cannot see the prayers she whispered through tears.
You may know the rules you want her to follow, but you do not yet know the burdens she has carried.
Before you reduce her to a judgment, remember the Savior who sees the heart.
Before you defend a powerful person's reputation, remember the Lord who loves justice.
And before you mistake religious appearances for righteousness, remember the cross.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die to create a community skilled at hiding sin behind respectable clothing.
