These free resources are part of the heart behind the ministry: making Christian teaching and spiritual nourishment more accessible, not putting the Gospel behind a paywall.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite people to study Scripture.
Encourage someone to seek Christ.
A simple act of sharing may place biblical truth before someone who would never have searched for it on their own.
Our mission is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to keep pointing people back to Jesus.
Back to His Word.
Back to the cross.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
Back to the Savior who alone has the power to make sinners new.
And now, before you leave, remember the two names that began this story.
Ahab.
Zedekiah.
Men who spoke in God's name while betraying His commands.
Their names remain in Scripture as a warning.
Not because God wanted His people to become obsessed with scandal, but because truth matters, holiness matters, and no claim to spiritual authority places anyone beyond accountability.
Yet there is another name greater than theirs.
A name above every name.
Jesus Christ.
The One who never lied in the Father's name.
The One who never betrayed His calling.
The One who was tempted yet without sin.
The One who bore our sins on the cross and rose victorious from the grave.
The One who can forgive the guilty without calling evil good.
The One who can comfort the wounded without minimizing what happened to them.
The One who can take a life fractured by sin and begin the patient, holy work of restoration.
So do not finish this article merely asking, "How could those two prophets do something so terrible?"
Ask something deeper.
"Lord, is there anything in my life that I am still afraid to surrender to You?"
And when He brings the truth into the light, do not run farther into darkness.
Run to Christ.
Because the God who knows every hidden thing is also the God who, through Jesus Christ, calls repentant sinners out of hiding and into the freedom of His grace.
The secret you are terrified to bring into the light may be the very place where your surrender to Jesus finally begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF JESUS IS GOD, WHY DID HE SAY HE DIDN’T KNOW WHEN HE WOULD RETURN?
paragraphs: IF JESUS IS GOD, WHY DID HE SAY HE DIDN’T KNOW WHEN HE WOULD RETURN?
One Sentence That Seems to Contradict His Divinity—Until You Discover What Happened When the Eternal Son Stepped Into Human Flesh.

There is a question that has shaken the faith of sincere Christians, fueled countless debates, and given skeptics what they believe is one of their strongest arguments against the divinity of Jesus Christ.
And the unsettling part?
The question comes from the mouth of Jesus Himself.
Not from an atheist. Not from a false teacher. Not from someone trying to discredit Christianity.
From Jesus.
He was sitting on the Mount of Olives, speaking about the future, the coming judgment, and the day when the Son of Man would come in power and glory.
Then He said something extraordinary.
“But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father.” — Mark 13:32 (KJV)
Read those last words again.
Neither the Son.
Wait.
If Jesus is truly God, and God knows everything, how could Jesus say He did not know the day or hour of His return?
Was He admitting that He was not God?
Was He somehow less divine than the Father?
Or is there something about the incarnation that many Christians have never fully understood?

Because buried inside this difficult question is a truth so breathtaking that it takes us from the throne of heaven to the dust of Bethlehem, from the glory of eternity to the humiliation of the cross, and from our deepest human weakness to the astonishing grace of God.
And when you begin to understand it, you may never read Philippians 2 the same way again.
But first, we must do something many people avoid.
We must allow the difficult words of Jesus to remain difficult.
We must not twist Scripture to protect a doctrine.
The truth of Jesus Christ does not need protection from the words of Jesus Christ.
It needs careful understanding.
And the journey begins with a single Greek sentence.
In Mark 13:32, the original Greek includes these words:
οὐδὲ ὁ υἱός, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
Oude ho huios, ei mē ho patēr.
A faithful translation is:
“Nor the Son, except the Father.”
The Greek expression οὐδὲ ὁ υἱός really does mean “nor the Son.”
There is no hidden grammatical trick that makes the statement disappear.
Jesus truly said it.
And that matters.
Because biblical faith is not built by pretending uncomfortable verses do not exist.
It is built by listening to everything God has revealed.
John tells us that the Word was with God and that the Word was God (John 1:1). He then declares that this same Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).
Thomas looked upon the risen Jesus and cried, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28).
Paul describes Christ as the One in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9).
And Hebrews speaks of the Son in language of divine glory, creation, and eternal sovereignty (Hebrews 1:2–3, 8–12).
Yet Mark records Jesus saying that the Son did not know the hour.
These passages are not competing voices that we are free to silence whenever one becomes inconvenient.
They are all part of the testimony of Scripture.
So how do we hold them together?
We begin by understanding something Christianity has confessed for centuries.
Jesus Christ is not half God and half man. He is truly God and truly man.
Not two separate persons.
Not a divine being merely pretending to be human.
Not an ordinary man who eventually became God.
He is the eternal Son of God who assumed a complete human nature without ceasing to be divine.
One Person, two natures.
Fully divine.
Fully human.
And suddenly, the question becomes much deeper than whether Jesus possessed divine knowledge.
It becomes a question about what it meant for the eternal Son to enter our human condition.
Imagine the scene.
The One through whom all things were made entered the world as a baby.
The One who sustains creation was carried in His mother's arms.
The One who gives life experienced hunger.
The One who created the seas became thirsty.
The One whom angels worship grew tired enough to sleep in a boat.
And the One who is life itself willingly submitted to death.
This is not a contradiction of His divinity.
This is the staggering mystery of His incarnation.
Luke tells us that Jesus grew in wisdom and stature (Luke 2:52).
Think about that.
He grew in wisdom.
That is not how we would describe a merely disguised deity pretending to experience childhood.
That is how Scripture describes a real human life.
Jesus did not simply wear humanity like a costume.
He truly became man.
He knew what it was to grow, learn, suffer, become weary, and live in dependence upon the Father.
And this is where Philippians 2 becomes essential.
Paul writes:
The Greek is remarkable.
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν
Heauton ekenōsen.
Literally:
“He emptied Himself.”
That word, ekenōsen, comes from the Greek verb kenoō, meaning to empty or make empty.
But what exactly did Jesus empty Himself of?
His divinity?
His eternal existence?
His divine nature?
No.
And here is where we must be extremely careful.
Philippians 2 does not say Jesus stopped being God.
It does not say He discarded His divine attributes or became a lesser deity.
The passage explains His self-emptying through what follows: He took the form of a servant and was born in human likeness.
The eternal Son humbled Himself, not by abandoning deity, but by assuming genuine humanity and entering the lowliness of servanthood.
He did not cease to be what He eternally was.
He became what He had not previously been.
Human.
The One who was equal with God did not cling to the privileges of His exalted position for selfish advantage.
Instead, He entered a world of pain, rejection, temptation, suffering, and death.
Not because He had lost His divine identity.
But because He had come to save people who could never save themselves.
And perhaps the most astonishing part is this:
He did not come merely to experience humanity.
He came to redeem it.
Now return to Mark 13:32.
When Jesus said that the Son did not know the day or hour, He was speaking during His earthly ministry, in the reality of His incarnate human life.
In historic Christian theology, His human nature included a genuinely human mind and human experience.
And a genuinely human mind is not automatically identical to the infinite divine knowledge belonging to the divine nature.
This distinction is important.
The eternal Son remains omniscient in His deity.
Yet in His earthly human life, Scripture presents Him as growing in wisdom and, in Mark 13:32, acknowledging that He did not know the appointed hour.
That is not the same as saying His divine nature became ignorant.
Nor does it mean Jesus was two persons, one knowing and another speaking.
It means the one divine Person truly lived a human life.
Christians have expressed the relationship between Christ's divine knowledge and human knowledge in different ways, and Scripture does not explain every detail of that mystery.
Some emphasize that Jesus did not exercise or communicate divine knowledge independently during His earthly mission. Others emphasize the genuine limitations of His human knowledge.
What we must not do is claim that the Greek word for “know” secretly means “reveal” in Mark 13:32.
That interpretation is sometimes suggested, but it is not the ordinary meaning of the text and should not be presented as a proven solution.
Jesus said He did not know.
Our responsibility is to take His words seriously while also taking seriously the full biblical testimony to His deity.
And there is another detail worth noticing.
In the same chapter, Jesus describes the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory (Mark 13:26).
He speaks of gathering His elect (Mark 13:27).
He warns His disciples to remain watchful.
The point of His teaching is not to provide a mathematical formula for the end of history.
It is to call His people to faithful readiness.
Jesus is not inviting His followers to become obsessed with discovering a date He did not disclose.
He is commanding them to live in such a way that they are ready whenever He comes.
And that brings us to something deeply personal.
Because many of us have spent more time asking when Jesus will return than asking whether our lives reflect the Jesus who is returning.
We want to understand prophecy.
But do we obey His commands?
We want to identify the signs.
But have we repented of the sins we keep excusing?
We want to know what happens at the end of the world.
But what is happening inside our hearts right now?
We can debate the Greek text, study the chronology, compare interpretations, and defend the doctrine of the incarnation.
Those are worthwhile things when done faithfully.
But knowledge about Christ must never become a substitute for knowing Christ.
And sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not ignorance.
It is the ability to explain sacred truths while resisting the Lord those truths reveal.
You can defend the deity of Jesus in a comment section and still refuse to surrender your bitterness to Him.
You can argue passionately about the Second Coming while neglecting the people He has commanded you to love.
You can know the theological meaning of kenosis and still be unwilling to humble yourself before God.
And if that stings, perhaps it is because this question is no longer merely about Mark 13:32.
Perhaps it has become a question about us.
What are we doing with the Jesus we claim to believe in?
Because the One who humbled Himself did not call us merely to admire His humility.
He called us to follow Him.
Paul introduces the teaching of Philippians 2 with a command:
“Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.” — Philippians 2:5 (KJV)
Do you see it?
Paul did not write these words merely to satisfy intellectual curiosity about the incarnation.
He was urging believers to abandon selfish ambition, embrace humility, and care for one another.
The theology was meant to transform the way they lived.
The eternal Son humbled Himself.
And we struggle to apologize.
He took the form of a servant.
And we fight to be recognized.
He endured rejection.
And we sometimes abandon obedience the moment following Him becomes uncomfortable.
He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
And we hesitate to surrender the very sins from which He came to deliver us.
This is not written to crush the struggling believer.
It is written to awaken us to the beauty and seriousness of the Gospel.
Because the story does not end with our failures.
It never did.
The cross is where our rebellion meets the mercy of God.
Listen to the rest of Paul's words:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” — Philippians 2:8 (KJV)
There it is.
The destination of His humiliation.
Not merely Bethlehem.
Not merely the carpenter's workshop.
Not merely the dusty roads of Galilee.
Calvary.
The eternal Son entered our humanity to accomplish what fallen humanity could never accomplish for itself.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He suffered without sin.
He offered Himself for sinners.
And He rose again in victory.
His humanity was not a weakness that ruined God's plan.
It was essential to the saving mission He willingly undertook.

Hebrews tells us that because the children share in flesh and blood, Christ likewise partook of the same, so that through death He might defeat the one who held the power of death and deliver those enslaved by fear (Hebrews 2:14–15).
And Hebrews 4:15 reminds us that our High Priest can sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
Think about what that means for the person reading this who feels completely exhausted.
The person whose prayers have become whispers.
The person who smiles in church but cries alone at night.
The person who has failed again and wonders whether God has finally become tired of forgiving them.
The person who knows all the right Christian language but feels spiritually empty.
Jesus is not a distant Savior who merely observed human suffering from heaven.
He entered our world.
He knew hunger.
He knew weariness.
He knew sorrow.
He knew betrayal.
He knew the agony of suffering.
And He remained perfectly faithful.
That does not mean He experienced every particular hardship you have faced.
It means He is a genuinely human, sinless, compassionate High Priest who is able to help those who come to Him.
You do not have to pretend your weakness is invisible to Him.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect spiritual performance before approaching His throne.
You are invited to come boldly to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this tonight:
The Jesus who entered human weakness is not ashamed to receive a broken sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
He does not excuse the darkness.
He brings us out of it.
He does not call evil good.
He forgives, cleanses, and transforms those who turn to Him.
He does not merely rewrite our public reputation.
He changes our relationship with God.
This is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not because our past never happened.
Not because the consequences of sin always disappear.
Not because grace gives us permission to continue in rebellion.
But because Jesus Christ died and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
And now, consider one final detail about the day and hour.
After His resurrection, the disciples asked Jesus about the restoration of the kingdom to Israel.
He answered:
“It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.” — Acts 1:7 (KJV)
Notice the emphasis.
He did not give them a date.
He redirected their attention to their calling.
In the very next verse, He promised that they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon them and that they would be His witnesses (Acts 1:8).
The disciples wanted a timetable.
Jesus gave them a mission.
And perhaps we need that correction too.
We do not know when He will return.
We do know that He has called us to repent, believe the Gospel, love one another, make disciples, and bear witness to His truth.
We do not know the appointed hour.
We do know that every hour is an opportunity to walk faithfully with Him.
We do not know how many more opportunities we will have to speak to someone we love about Jesus.
But we know the message entrusted to us.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And salvation is found in Him.
That is why the question, “If Jesus is God, why did He say He did not know the day or hour?” should not drive us away from Christ.
It should drive us deeper into the mystery and wonder of who He is.
The eternal Son did not stop being God when He became man.
He truly entered our humanity.
And in that humanity, He humbled Himself all the way to the cross.
But the cross was not the end.
Paul continues:
“Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name.” — Philippians 2:9 (KJV)
The One who humbled Himself has been exalted.
The One who was crucified is risen.
The One who was rejected will be confessed as Lord.
And the One who promised to return will fulfill His promise.
We cannot calculate the day.
We cannot command the hour.
We cannot force the mysteries of the incarnation into a simple slogan that answers every philosophical question.
But we can worship the One whom Scripture reveals.
We can trust His saving work.
We can obey His Word.
And we can live ready.
Maybe you began reading this article looking for an argument to settle a theological debate.
But perhaps, somewhere along the way, another question began stirring inside you.
If Jesus humbled Himself so completely to save sinners, why am I still holding back the part of my life I know He is calling me to surrender?
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe it is a secret habit.
Maybe it is unforgiveness.
Maybe it is the exhausting effort of appearing spiritually strong when you are barely holding on.
Whatever it is, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The call to repentance is not an announcement that grace is unavailable.
It is an invitation to stop running from the Savior who is able to forgive and restore.
Turn to Him.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Trust what He accomplished through His death and resurrection.
And ask Him to teach you to walk in the newness of life He gives.

You do not have to disclose your private struggles publicly. A sincere prayer request is enough. And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from shame into forgiveness and a changed life, your words may encourage someone who believes their story is beyond redemption.
Not to win an argument.
Not to embarrass someone with questions.

But because there may be a struggling believer, a skeptical friend, a family member, or someone quietly walking away from Christianity who has never heard this passage explained with both biblical honesty and compassion.

We want this community to be a place where difficult questions are not silenced, biblical truth is not compromised, repentance is not forgotten, and the grace of Jesus Christ is never reduced to an empty religious slogan.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who may not be able to afford paid materials.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, there is another way you can participate in its mission.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful rather than forced or pressured (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That distinction matters deeply to us.
These are small expressions of thanks.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
We want to see people reading their Bibles again.
Families praying together again.
Wounded believers finding their way back to faithful Christian community.
People who once hid in shame discovering the forgiveness of Christ.
And Christians growing beyond inspirational words into genuine spiritual maturity.
The Gospel must never become something people feel they have to purchase.
Christ has already paid the price for our redemption.
Our calling is to proclaim Him faithfully.
So before you leave, return once more to that mountain outside Jerusalem.
Picture Jesus speaking to His disciples about the future.
The disciples are listening.
The world is moving toward events they cannot fully comprehend.
And Jesus says that no one knows the day or hour—not even the Son, but the Father.
For some, those words will remain a difficult theological question.
For others, they will become an invitation to study the incarnation more carefully.
But for the believer who has begun to see the whole picture, they can also become a reminder of the extraordinary humility of the Savior.
The eternal Son truly entered human life.
He did not abandon His deity.
He did not pretend to be human.
He humbled Himself.
He obeyed.
He suffered.
He died.
And He rose again.
One day He will return.
Until then, we are not called to manufacture certainty about the date.
We are called to faithfulness to the Person.
So let the scholars study.
Let the sincere questions be asked.
Let Scripture speak.
And let every discovery lead us back to the One who stands at the center of it all.
Jesus Christ.
Truly God.
Truly man.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen in glory.
Coming again.
And worthy of our trust today.
The most important thing is not whether you know the hour He is coming, but whether you know the Savior who came to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE HAD TWO WIVES. THE BIBLE NAMED THEM BOTH. BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT SCRIPTURE DOESN’T TELL US.
paragraphs: HE HAD TWO WIVES. THE BIBLE NAMED THEM BOTH. BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT SCRIPTURE DOESN’T TELL US.
Helah and Naarah. Two women. Two family lines. Three verses buried in a genealogy—and a powerful reminder that being mentioned in history is not the same as having your whole story understood.
There are people whose names are remembered, but whose pain is never recorded.
People who lived, loved, carried responsibilities, raised children, endured difficult seasons, and eventually disappeared from the earth—leaving behind only a few words about their existence.
And sometimes, when you open your Bible, you meet them.
Not in a dramatic confrontation.
Not beside a burning bush.
Not standing before a king.
But hidden inside a genealogy most readers hurry past.
A man had two wives.
Their names were Helah and Naarah.
And Scripture carefully preserved the children associated with each woman.
That is almost everything we are told.
But before you turn the page, consider something.
What if one of the most important lessons in this passage begins with refusing to pretend we know what God has not revealed?
Because sometimes we are so eager to find a scandal that we invent one.
So eager to find a victim that we assign suffering without evidence.
So eager to make Scripture speak to our circumstances that we stop listening to what Scripture actually says.
And that is where this little family record begins to challenge us.
First Chronicles 4:5–7 reads in the King James Version:
“And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.
And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.
And the sons of Helah were, Zereth, and Jezoar, and Ethnan.”
Read those words again.
Ashur.
Helah.
Naarah.
Four sons associated with Naarah.
Three sons associated with Helah.
Seven names of sons preserved across two maternal lines.
No explanation of how the marriages began.
No statement about which woman married first.
No description of jealousy, favoritism, abuse, or household rivalry.
No recorded conversation between the women.
No divine approval or condemnation of Ashur's particular marriages in these verses.
Just a family record.
And yet there is something deeply human about it.
Because every family has a history.
And almost every family has details that never make it into the official record.
The Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles 4:5 includes these words:
וּלְאַשְׁחוּר אֲבִי תְקוֹעַ הָיוּ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים חֶלְאָה וְנַעֲרָה
Ule'ashchur avi Teqoa hayu shtei nashim, Chel'ah veNa'arah.
In context, this means:
“And Ashhur, the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah.”
The Hebrew expression שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים (shtei nashim) means “two women” or, in this marital context, “two wives.”
The text is straightforward.
It does not hide the existence of the two marriages.
It does not turn the women into one anonymous group.
It identifies them separately.
And then it distinguishes their descendants.
The names matter because the Chronicler is preserving family identity, ancestry, and the continuity of the people of Judah.
This is not primarily a romance story.
It is not a courtroom verdict about marriage.
It is not an invitation to speculate about which wife was loved more.
It is a genealogy.
But that does not make it meaningless.
Sometimes the most faithful way to honor a biblical person is to stop inventing the parts of their life that God chose not to disclose.
Think about how easily we do the opposite in our own families.
Someone hears that a marriage ended, and immediately assumes somebody was unfaithful.
Someone discovers that a father had children from different relationships, and immediately assigns blame.
Someone sees two siblings living very different lives, and decides one must have been favored.
Someone learns a little about a family's past, and suddenly believes they understand everything that happened behind closed doors.
But knowing a fact is not the same as knowing a heart.
And knowing a family tree is not the same as knowing a family's wounds.
Perhaps you understand that more personally than you want to admit.
Maybe people know your name but not your struggle.
They know you are married, but not what you have prayed through.
They know you have children, but not the nights you have stayed awake worrying about them.
They know you attend church, but not how desperately you have fought to keep believing.
They know the version of your life that can be summarized in a sentence.
They do not know the chapters you have cried through.
And sometimes, what hurts most is not that people misunderstand you.
It is that they speak with absolute confidence about a life they have never lived.
Helah and Naarah remind us to be careful with the stories of others.
But their record also raises a larger biblical question.
What should Christians understand when Scripture describes a man having more than one wife?
The answer requires more than an emotional reaction.
It requires the whole counsel of Scripture.
The Bible records polygamous households in the Old Testament.
Abraham's household included Sarah and Hagar, although Hagar's situation also involved servitude and serious injustice.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel, along with Bilhah and Zilpah.
Elkanah had Hannah and Peninnah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon multiplied wives and eventually turned his heart toward other gods.
These accounts are not identical, and they should not be treated as though every marriage produced the same circumstances.
But they establish an important interpretive principle.
The Bible's description of human behavior is not automatically God's endorsement of that behavior.
Genesis 2:24 establishes the foundational marriage pattern:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew phrase בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad) means “one flesh.”
It speaks of a profound marital union, not merely a household arrangement or reproductive partnership.
And when Jesus addressed marriage in Matthew 19:4–6, He returned to the creation account.
He did not build His teaching around the complicated marriages of the patriarchs.
He pointed back to God's design in the beginning.
Jesus said:
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
That matters.
Because Christians must never confuse what God permitted or regulated within fallen human societies with the original pattern Jesus Himself affirmed.
At the same time, we must not falsely claim that 1 Chronicles 4:5–7 explicitly condemns Ashur or describes his household as miserable.
It does neither.
The passage tells us he had two wives and records their descendants.
The wider biblical witness gives us the framework for understanding marriage.
And the Gospel teaches us what to do when human lives fall short of God's design.
Not to celebrate sin.
Not to manufacture accusations.
Not to deny consequences.
But to bring the truth into the light of Christ.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is much easier to examine Ashur's family than to examine our own hearts.
We can discuss ancient polygamy for hours while refusing to confront modern unfaithfulness.
We can debate the marriages of Old Testament men while ignoring the promises we have broken.
We can criticize biblical households while quietly tolerating bitterness, lust, deception, pride, or emotional cruelty inside our own.
We can point at somebody else's family history while refusing to repent of what is happening in our own home today.
And Jesus will not allow us to hide behind that kind of religion.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He reaches beyond outward behavior and confronts the lustful intentions of the heart.
In Matthew 7:3–5, He warns against obsessing over another person's fault while ignoring our own.
The problem is not that we should stop discerning right from wrong.
The problem is that we often prefer judgment over self-examination.
And if you have been using somebody else's scandal to avoid confronting your own sin, this may be the moment to stop.
Not because God has abandoned you.
But because He is calling you into the light.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction exposes what needs repentance and directs us toward Christ.
Condemnation leaves us believing there is no hope.
The Gospel does not invite us to remain comfortable in sin.
It invites us to come to the Savior who died for sinners.
And that includes the sins nobody else knows about.
The hidden resentment.
The secret compromise.
The dishonesty you have justified.
The apology you refuse to make.
The relationship you know needs boundaries.
The wound you have allowed to become an excuse for wounding someone else.
The public appearance of holiness that conceals a private life you are afraid to surrender.
You may be able to manage what people know.
But you cannot hide your heart from God.
Hebrews 4:13 says:
“Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.”
That verse can feel terrifying.
Until you remember who Jesus is.
Because the One who knows the truth about you is also the One who came to save sinners.
The One who sees what you have done is the One who shed His blood for the forgiveness of sins.
The One who calls you to repentance is not calling you to manufacture your own redemption.
He is calling you to Himself.
And there is another beautiful detail worth noticing in this genealogy.
The Chronicler did not merely record Ashur and then move on.
Helah and Naarah were named.
Their sons were associated with them individually.
Their identities were not entirely swallowed by the identity of their husband.
We should not exaggerate what that means.
The text does not tell us that these women were especially honored, unusually powerful, or personally righteous.
But it does preserve their names and their distinct places in the family record.
And that is worth observing.
Especially in a world where people are so often reduced to the relationships, mistakes, labels, and circumstances surrounding them.
You may be known as someone's former spouse.
Someone's difficult child.
Someone's disappointing parent.
The person whose marriage failed.
The person who became pregnant before marriage.
The person who struggled with addiction.
The person who walked away from church.
The person whose family history everybody whispers about.
But those descriptions are not the whole of who you are.
Your history matters.
Your choices matter.
Your responsibilities matter.
And where you have sinned, repentance matters.
But your past does not have the authority to decide whether the grace of Jesus Christ can reach you.
That authority belongs to God.
And He has already demonstrated His mercy at the cross.
Consider the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1.
Matthew does not present a spotless parade of human achievement.
He includes Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
And the wife of Uriah, whom we know from the Old Testament as Bathsheba.
Their stories differ profoundly.
Tamar's story involves serious family injustice.
Rahab's history includes prostitution and her remarkable confession of faith in Israel's God.
Ruth was a Moabite widow whose loyalty and faith became part of Israel's story.
Bathsheba's inclusion recalls David's grave abuse of power, adultery, and the killing of Uriah. We must not shift David's responsibility onto her.
These women should not be flattened into a collection of scandals.
They were real people whose circumstances, choices, vulnerabilities, and experiences deserve careful reading.
And yet their presence in the Messiah's genealogy reveals something extraordinary.
God's redemptive purpose was not defeated by human brokenness.
Jesus entered a real human history.
A history marked by suffering, sin, outsiders, failures, and unexpected mercy.
And He came not merely to become another name in that history.
He came to redeem sinners.
Matthew 1:21 declares:
“And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
There it is.
The center of everything.
Not Ashur.
Not Helah.
Not Naarah.
Not our curiosity about an ancient household.
Jesus Christ, who saves His people from their sins.
The Bible does not tell us whether Helah or Naarah experienced jealousy, loneliness, affection, peace, or rivalry.
We must leave those questions unanswered.
But the Bible does tell us what kind of Savior Jesus is.
He welcomed sinners who came to Him.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He showed compassion to the vulnerable.
He called people to repentance.
He gave His life as a ransom for many.
And He rose from the dead.
That is not speculation.
That is the Gospel proclaimed in Scripture.
And perhaps that is the truth you needed more than another dramatic theory about somebody else's life.
You do not need to know every hidden detail of Helah's story to know that God sees you.
You do not need to invent Naarah's emotions to acknowledge your own.
You do not need to turn Ashur into a villain the passage never explicitly describes in order to recognize that humanity needs redemption.
You need to look at Jesus.
Because when you stand before God, your greatest hope will not be that your family history was respectable.
It will not be that nobody discovered your mistakes.
It will not be that your reputation survived.
It will be the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The apostle Paul wrote in Romans 5:8:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we perfected our image.
Not after we erased every consequence.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve salvation.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not mean repentance is optional.
It means repentance is possible because God's grace has met us in Jesus Christ.
And that grace is not permission to keep living in darkness.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God instructs believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly lives.
Real grace changes the direction of a life.
Sometimes gradually.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes through confession, accountability, restitution, and rebuilding trust.
But always with Christ as the source of our hope.
Maybe your family history is complicated.
Maybe there are children from different relationships.
Maybe there is an estranged parent.
Maybe there is a marriage you wish you could repair.
Maybe you have been carrying shame for decisions you cannot undo.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove that your life is more than the worst thing people remember about you.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not promise to rewrite history by pretending nothing happened.
He does something greater.
He forgives repentant sinners, gives them new life, and teaches them to walk in truth.
The consequences of yesterday may still require responsibility today.
Some relationships may need time.
Some trust may have to be rebuilt.
Some wrongs may require confession and restitution.
Some situations may require protection, boundaries, and wise pastoral or professional help.
Grace does not erase justice.
Forgiveness does not make abuse acceptable.
Reconciliation does not mean remaining in danger.
And redemption does not depend on pretending that pain was harmless.
But the cross declares that sin and shame do not have to be the final word over a person who belongs to Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That is not a promise that every earthly consequence instantly disappears.
It is a declaration of new creation in Christ.
A new identity.
A new allegiance.
A new life shaped by the One who died and rose again.
And now, perhaps, the most searching question is not what happened between Helah and Naarah.
It is what you will do with the truth God has placed before you.
Will you keep hiding behind your reputation?
Will you keep treating your past as a permanent prison?
Will you keep using somebody else's failures to excuse your own?
Or will you finally bring your whole life to Jesus?
Not the polished version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version that knows how to say all the right Christian words.
The real you.
The exhausted you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The person who still believes but is struggling.
The person who has prayed for forgiveness and still finds it difficult to accept that forgiveness is possible.
Come to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn away from what needs abandoning.
Ask forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Seek help where you cannot safely or wisely walk alone.
And trust the Savior whose blood is sufficient to cleanse sinners.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not because confession earns salvation.
But because the God who saves us is faithful to His promise.
And if this article has brought something painful into the light, you do not have to disclose your private wounds publicly to prove your faith.
But perhaps you can encourage someone else with a simple, sincere response.
Your story may encourage someone who believes their own situation is beyond redemption.
Not every testimony needs dramatic details.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony is simply this:
“I was running from God. And by His grace, I came home.”
If someone came to mind while you were reading, do not ignore that moment.
Perhaps it is a friend carrying family shame.
A parent who feels like a failure.
A believer who has quietly drifted away.
A person who thinks church is only for people with clean histories.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, and even those who are still searching for faith to walk with us through God's Word.
Because this mission is not about making a page famous.
It is about making Christ known.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or encouraged you to return to Jesus, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand its ministry of biblical teaching, Christian encouragement, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered content.
These resources are intended to help people open their Bibles, understand their faith, develop spiritual discipline, and grow in their relationship with the Lord.
But creating, maintaining, and expanding a ministry requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
Giving is not supposed to be extracted through fear or spiritual pressure.
It should arise from a willing heart.
You do not need to give money to earn His favor.
These items are simply an expression of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards or a measure of anyone's faith.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
More biblical nourishment.
More resources for people hungry for God's Word.
More encouragement for believers who feel forgotten.
More opportunities to point someone away from despair and toward Jesus Christ.
Pass along the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
Open your Bible.
Live what you learn.
Because the greatest evidence that the Gospel has reached your heart is not that you clicked a button.
It is that Jesus Christ is changing how you live.
And now we return to those three quiet verses in First Chronicles.
Ashur had two wives.
Helah and Naarah.
Their children were recorded.
Their names survived.
And the details of their private lives remain largely unknown.
Perhaps that is where we should leave their story.
Not with invented tears.
Not with imaginary arguments.
Not with accusations Scripture never makes.
But with reverence for what God has revealed and humility about what He has not.
And with gratitude that the Bible does not end in a genealogy.
It leads us through the history of God's redemptive promises to Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who entered human history.
The sinless Savior who bore our sins.
The risen Lord who calls us to repentance and faith.
The One whose grace is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
Your family history may be complicated.
Your name may have been dragged through conversations you never heard.
Your past may contain decisions you would give anything to change.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your life is not merely a record of what went wrong.
It is a testimony of what His grace can make new.
People may remember the chapter that broke you. But in Christ, that chapter does not have to be the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM HAD SIX MORE SONS AFTER SARAH DIED—BUT THE BIBLE CALLS THEIR MOTHER BOTH HIS WIFE AND HIS CONCUBINE. WHY?
paragraphs: ABRAHAM HAD SIX MORE SONS AFTER SARAH DIED—BUT THE BIBLE CALLS THEIR MOTHER BOTH HIS WIFE AND HIS CONCUBINE. WHY?

The forgotten story of Keturah reveals a surprising distinction between marriage, inheritance, and God's covenant—and a powerful truth about the grace that reaches beyond the family everyone remembers.
What if one of the most overlooked women in Abraham's story exposes something we have misunderstood about God's promises?
Most Christians know Sarah.
They know about the years of waiting. The impossible pregnancy. The laughter that came when God fulfilled what human biology said could never happen.
They know Isaac, the promised son.
Some remember Hagar, the Egyptian servant whose suffering God saw in the wilderness.
But there is another woman.
Her name was Keturah.
And when you finally notice her, a question rises from the pages of Scripture that is far more complicated than it first appears.
Was she Abraham's wife?
Or was she his concubine?
Because Genesis calls her one thing.
And Chronicles calls her another.
And if you read too quickly, you might miss the remarkable truth hiding between those two descriptions.
But before we answer that question, imagine something.
An elderly man standing near the closing chapters of his life.

He has buried the woman who walked beside him through decades of uncertainty. The woman who left home with him. The woman who endured infertility, family conflict, disappointment, and the staggering fulfillment of a divine promise.
Sarah is gone.
Genesis 23:1 records that she lived 127 years.
Abraham mourned her.
He purchased a burial place in Machpelah and laid her to rest.
The Bible does not tell us every private thought that passed through his heart.
But anyone who has buried someone deeply loved understands something about the silence that follows.
There are places in a home where memories remain long after a person is gone.
And then, almost unexpectedly, Scripture introduces another woman.
Genesis 25:1 says in the King James Version:
"Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah."
Wait.
A wife?
Yes.
The Hebrew text reads:
וַיֹּסֶף אַבְרָהָם וַיִּקַּח אִשָּׁה וּשְׁמָהּ קְטוּרָה
Vayyosef Avraham vayyiqqach ishah, ushemah Qeturah.
In context, this means that Abraham took a wife named Keturah.
The important Hebrew word is אִשָּׁה (ishah), which can mean "woman" or "wife," depending on context.
Here, the construction "took a wife" clearly presents Keturah as Abraham's wife.
Not merely an unnamed servant.
Not simply a passing relationship.
Scripture identifies her as a wife.
And then comes something even more surprising.
Genesis 25:2 records that she bore Abraham six sons.
Zimran.
Jokshan.
Medan.
Midian.
Ishbak.
Shuah.
Six sons.
After the extraordinary story of Isaac's birth, Abraham's household becomes the source of still more descendants.
But then you turn to another passage.
And suddenly the question becomes unavoidable.
First Chronicles 1:32 says:
"Now the sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bare Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah."
Read that carefully.
The same woman.
The same six sons.
The same Abraham.
But now the description is different.
Abraham's concubine.
The Hebrew word used here is פִּילֶגֶשׁ (pilegesh).
It refers to a concubine, a woman recognized in an ancient household as a secondary partner or wife, generally without the same status and inheritance standing as a principal wife.
That distinction matters.
Because our modern understanding of the word "concubine" can lead us to imagine something that does not fully reflect the ancient social setting.
In the patriarchal world, a concubine was not necessarily a secret lover or an unrecognized sexual partner.
She could belong to a recognized household relationship while occupying a lower legal or social position than the primary wife.
The Bible describes such arrangements, although describing an ancient practice is not the same as commanding or approving it for every generation.
So was Keturah a wife or a concubine?
The most careful biblical answer is that Scripture calls her both.
Genesis 25:1 identifies her as a wife.
First Chronicles 1:32 identifies her as a concubine.
These descriptions need not contradict each other if Keturah was a wife whose standing in Abraham's household was secondary, especially in relation to the inheritance reserved for Isaac.
And there is a crucial detail that makes this explanation especially compelling.
Genesis 25:5–6 says:
"And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.
But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country."
There it is.
The distinction was not merely about what Keturah was called.
It had consequences for inheritance.
Abraham gave Isaac the principal inheritance.
The other sons received gifts and were sent eastward.
They were not presented as heirs of the particular covenant promise that God had established through Isaac.
And this brings us to the deeper question.
Why?
Why would a man have several sons, yet the biblical narrative place such extraordinary emphasis on only one?
Was God showing favoritism?
Were the other children worthless?
Did their lives matter less?
No.
And if we confuse covenant election with human worth, we will misunderstand one of the central themes of Genesis.
Long before Keturah's sons were born, God had already made His covenant purpose clear.
In Genesis 17:19, God told Abraham:
"Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son indeed; and thou shalt call his name Isaac: and I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him."
Notice the order.
God did not wait to see which child would be the strongest.
He did not hold a competition among Abraham's descendants.
He identified Isaac before Isaac was even born.
The covenant line would come through Sarah's promised son.
And that promise was not erased when Abraham later fathered more children.
Genesis 21:12 reinforces it:
"For in Isaac shall thy seed be called."
This did not mean that Ishmael, Keturah's sons, or their descendants had no value before God.
In fact, Genesis 17:20 records God's promise to bless Ishmael and make him fruitful.
The distinction was about the specific line through which God's covenant purposes would unfold.
Being outside Isaac's particular covenant line did not mean being outside God's knowledge, concern, or providence.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that distinction.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to be the child who was not chosen.
The person who received less.
The one who watched somebody else inherit the family business, the approval, the opportunity, or the attention.
Maybe you have spent years wondering why someone else seemed to receive what you prayed for.
You watched their doors open.
You watched their prayers answered.
You watched them celebrated.
And somewhere inside, a question formed that you were almost ashamed to ask.
"God, did You forget me?"
Keturah's story does not promise that everyone will receive the same earthly inheritance.
It does not teach that every disappointment will be reversed in this life.
But it does remind us that God's covenant purposes are not determined by human comparisons.
And the full revelation of the Gospel gives us something even greater to hold on to.
In Jesus Christ, people from every nation are invited to receive the blessing promised through Abraham.
But before we reach that beautiful conclusion, there is another mystery worth confronting.
Was Keturah actually Hagar?
Some readers may be surprised to discover that this question has been discussed for centuries.
In Jewish interpretive tradition, particularly in Genesis Rabbah 61:4 and in Rashi's commentary on Genesis 25:1, Keturah is identified with Hagar.
According to that interpretation, Abraham reunited with Hagar after Sarah's death.
It is a striking possibility.
Imagine the woman who had once been sent into the wilderness returning to Abraham's household.
Imagine the emotional complexity.
The history.
The wounds.
The questions.
But there is a difference between an ancient interpretive tradition and something the biblical text explicitly establishes.
Genesis does not directly identify Keturah as Hagar.
The narrative introduces Keturah by her own name, and First Chronicles also calls her Keturah.
Some interpreters therefore understand her to be a distinct woman.
Others preserve the traditional identification with Hagar.
Scripture itself does not settle the question conclusively.
And that matters.
Because faithfulness to God's Word sometimes means having the courage to say, "We are not told."
We do not honor Scripture by pretending to know what God has not revealed.
We honor it by refusing to turn speculation into certainty.
The same caution applies to another question.
Did Abraham marry Keturah only after Sarah died?
Genesis places the account of Keturah after Sarah's death and after Isaac's marriage to Rebekah.
That narrative sequence naturally suggests a later marriage.
But Genesis sometimes arranges material thematically rather than providing a strict chronological timeline.
Therefore, while marriage after Sarah's death is a reasonable reading, the text does not explicitly date the beginning of Abraham's relationship with Keturah.
Nor does it tell us Keturah's age, the exact dates of her sons' births, or the private circumstances of their relationship.
We must not invent details merely because they would make a more dramatic story.
The truth is already powerful enough.
And there is one more detail that deserves attention.
Abraham lived 175 years, according to Genesis 25:7.
Sarah died when Abraham was approximately 137, based on the ages given in Genesis.
That leaves about 38 years between Sarah's death and Abraham's death.
If Keturah's children were born during those years, their births would have occurred during Abraham's advanced age.
But Scripture does not explicitly say that God performed a second reproductive miracle for Keturah comparable to Isaac's promised birth.
We should not claim one.
Isaac's birth occupies a unique place in the biblical narrative because God specifically promised him to Abraham and Sarah when they were beyond the ordinary expectation of childbearing.
Keturah's sons are real descendants of Abraham.
But Isaac remains the son through whom the covenant promise is traced.
And here the story becomes far bigger than an ancient question about marriage.
Because generations later, the apostle Paul would return to Abraham's family history to explain something extraordinary about Jesus Christ.
Galatians 3:16 says:
"Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ."
Paul is not denying that Abraham had many biological descendants.
He is explaining the ultimate fulfillment of the promise in Christ.
The Greek word he emphasizes is σπέρμα (sperma), meaning "seed" or "offspring."
Like the Hebrew זֶרַע (zeraʿ), it can function collectively, referring to descendants, while Paul draws attention to its singular form in his Christ-centered argument.
His point is not that Abraham had only one child.
His point is that the promised blessing reaches its fulfillment in one Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
And then Paul says something that changes the way we understand belonging.
Galatians 3:29:
"And if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise."
Read that again.
If you belong to Christ, you are Abraham's offspring and an heir according to the promise.
Not because you can prove your bloodline.
Not because your family has a religious reputation.
Not because you were born into the right nation or raised in the right household.
But because you belong to Jesus Christ through faith.
That is the breathtaking beauty of the Gospel.
The covenant story that began with one man and one promised son becomes part of God's unfolding purpose to bless the nations through the Messiah.
And the door of salvation is not opened by ancestry.
It is opened through Christ.
Think about the people Jesus welcomed.
The tax collector who had betrayed his neighbors for money.
The woman whose reputation had become the subject of public shame.
The thief dying beside Him, with no opportunity to rebuild his earthly life.
The sinner who had nothing left to offer except a desperate cry for mercy.
Jesus did not tell them that their past was harmless.
He did not pretend sin was righteousness.
He called people to repentance.
He forgave sinners.
He restored the broken.
He brought the undeserving near through grace.
And that is where the story of Abraham's household becomes personally confronting.
Because some of us are still living as though our greatest problem is that somebody else was chosen first.
But the Gospel tells us our deepest problem is sin—and our greatest need is reconciliation with God.
You can spend your whole life fighting for recognition and still never find peace.
You can inherit money, property, influence, and a respected family name, yet remain spiritually lost.
You can win every argument about your place in the family and still refuse the Savior who calls you to surrender.
The greatest inheritance is not the one Abraham left to Isaac.
It is the eternal life God gives through His Son.
First Peter 1:3–4 describes believers as having a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ and an inheritance that cannot perish, spoil, or fade.
That inheritance is not secured by your performance.
It is secured by Christ's redeeming work.
His sinless life.
His sacrificial death.
His victorious resurrection.
And His promise to receive those who come to Him in faith.
Maybe you opened this article because you were curious about Keturah.
Maybe you wanted to settle a biblical disagreement.
Maybe you simply wondered how one woman could be called both a wife and a concubine.
But perhaps somewhere along the way, a more personal question began pressing against your heart.
Not, "What was Keturah's status?"
But, "Where do I stand before God?"
Because there is a difference between knowing Abraham's family tree and belonging to Abraham's promised Savior.
There is a difference between debating Scripture and allowing Scripture to expose your heart.
And there is a difference between admiring Jesus and surrendering your life to Him.
You may know every detail of Genesis 25 and still be carrying a secret that is slowly destroying you.
A bitterness you refuse to release.
A sin you have learned to excuse.
A wound you keep hiding behind a smile.
A relationship with God that has become nothing more than religious appearance.
And perhaps the hardest words you could say tonight are the simplest.
"Lord Jesus, I need Your mercy."
But those words do not have to be the end of your story.
They can mark the beginning of repentance, healing, and a transformed life.
Because the Gospel is not about pretending the scandal never happened.
It is about the holy Savior who entered a world ruined by sin, bore the judgment sinners deserve, and rose again so that forgiveness and new life could be offered through Him.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus is sufficient.
Not because every consequence disappears.
But because condemnation does not have the final word over those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not because the past can be rewritten as though it never happened.
But because the risen Christ can give a sinner a new future.
And maybe that is the truth you have been resisting.
You have spent years trying to prove that you deserve a place.
Jesus calls you to stop trusting in your own righteousness and come to Him in faith.
You have spent years believing your family history determines your destiny.
Jesus calls you to become part of God's family through Him.
You have spent years comparing your blessings with somebody else's.
Jesus calls you to seek first His kingdom.

And if the story of Keturah teaches us anything about reading the Bible faithfully, it is that we must learn to distinguish what Scripture says, what history helps us understand, and what we are tempted to assume.
Keturah was called Abraham's wife.
She was also called his concubine.
She bore six sons.
Those sons received gifts, while Isaac received Abraham's principal inheritance and remained the covenant heir.
The biblical text does not definitively tell us whether she was Hagar or exactly when her relationship with Abraham began.
Those are the boundaries of what we can responsibly claim.
But the larger story does not end with a dispute over ancient household status.
It leads us toward the promised Seed.
Jesus Christ.
And through Him, the blessing of Abraham reaches people who could never have claimed it through genealogy alone.
Galatians 3:14 says that the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ, so that believers might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
That is grace.
Not a prize for being born in the right household.
Not a reward for being more impressive than someone else.
A gift received through faith in the Savior.
And perhaps this is the moment to stop treating that gift as something you can postpone forever.
You do not know how many tomorrows you have.
Neither did Abraham.
His story eventually ended with a burial.
Genesis 25:8 says he died "in a good old age, an old man, and full of years."
And Genesis 25:9 records something deeply moving.
Isaac and Ishmael buried their father.
Two sons whose family history included painful division stood in the same account at their father's burial.
Scripture does not tell us whether all their wounds were healed.
It does not describe a reconciliation conversation.
We should not invent one.
But the image remains sobering.
Whatever earthly distinctions once separated them, Abraham's life had reached its end.
His possessions could be distributed.
His body could be buried.
His years could be counted.
But God's promise continued.
And the fulfillment of that promise would ultimately be found in Christ.
That is the difference between what passes away and what endures.
Your possessions will not last forever.
Your reputation will not last forever.
The arguments you spent years trying to win will eventually grow silent.
But what you do with Jesus Christ matters eternally.
Have you been fighting harder for an earthly place than you have been seeking the Lord who offers eternal life?
Have you been so occupied with other people's blessings that you have neglected the mercy God is extending to you?
Have you been hiding behind religious knowledge while avoiding personal repentance?
You do not need to perform holiness for the people watching you.
You need the Savior who already knows the truth about you.
Come to Him.
Confess your sins.
Trust His death and resurrection.
Receive His forgiveness.
And follow Him.
Not to prove your faith to strangers.
Not because typing a sentence earns God's favor.
But because sometimes an honest testimony encourages another person who thought they were suffering alone.

If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with care, or sending this article privately. It might be a friend struggling with rejection, a family member wrestling with faith, or someone who has confused their past with their permanent identity.
Return to the passages. Read Genesis 25 and Galatians 3 for yourself. Test what you have read against God's Word.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible to people who cannot afford expensive resources.
And we want to continue reaching more people with the message of Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from the heart, not from pressure or compulsion.
God is glorified through faith, obedience, worship, generosity, and love—not through a payment transaction.
Our purpose is not simply to build an audience.
It is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, turn from sin, and walk more faithfully with Jesus Christ.
Because somewhere there is a person who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Somewhere there is a believer who has nearly given up.
Somewhere there is a family carrying generations of shame.
And somewhere there is a soul that needs to hear that salvation is found not in family status, personal achievement, or religious performance, but in the crucified and risen Savior.
Keturah's story began for us as a question about a woman's place in Abraham's household.
But the Gospel brings us to a greater question.
Do you belong to Jesus Christ?
Because when this life is over, the inheritance that matters most will not be what somebody left in your hands.
It will be whether, by grace through faith, you have been brought into the family of God through His Son.
And here is the truth I hope stays with you long after you close this article:
The world may spend your whole life arguing over where you belong, but Jesus Christ is the only Savior who can give you a home that death itself cannot take away.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU DON’T WATCH PORN. YOU JUST READ EXPLICIT STORIES EVERY NIGHT. BUT DOES GOD SEE A DIFFERENCE?
paragraphs: YOU DON’T WATCH PORN. YOU JUST READ EXPLICIT STORIES EVERY NIGHT. BUT DOES GOD SEE A DIFFERENCE?

You never opened a pornographic video. You never visited those websites. You told yourself it was only fiction, only romance, only words on a screen. But what if the real question isn't what your eyes have watched, but what your heart has learned to desire?
There is a kind of temptation that doesn't arrive looking like temptation.
Sometimes it arrives as a beautiful love story.
A lonely woman. A mysterious stranger. A forbidden attraction. Two people who understand each other in ways nobody else ever has.
You tell yourself you're only reading because the story is good.
And perhaps, at first, that's genuinely why you started.
But somewhere between the innocent conversations and the increasingly intimate chapters, something changes.
You begin anticipating certain scenes.
You skim past ordinary dialogue to reach the moments that stir something inside you.
You promise yourself you'll stop after one more chapter.
Then midnight becomes one in the morning.
One becomes two.
And when the screen finally goes dark, the story doesn't always end.
It follows you into your imagination.
Into your expectations.
Sometimes even into the way you look at your spouse, your relationships, or the life you wish you had.
And the next evening, you return.
Not necessarily because you love the characters anymore.
But because you remember how the story made you feel.
Here is the uncomfortable question few people want to ask:
If pornography can awaken and feed lust through images, can sexually explicit fiction do something similar through words?
And if it can, does calling it literature make the spiritual danger disappear?
Before you defend yourself, before you close this article, before you assume another Christian is about to condemn you for something nobody understands, please hear this.
Jesus did not come to destroy people who struggle.
He came to rescue sinners.
And sometimes His rescue begins with a question we have spent years avoiding.
Perhaps that question is waiting for you tonight.
Because the issue is not simply what you have been reading.
It is what you have been allowing to shape your heart.
Jesus said something in Matthew 5:28 that should make every Christian examine the private life nobody else can see.
In the original Greek, His words include:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
Pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn.
The phrase speaks of someone looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her.
Jesus continues by saying that such a person has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
Notice something important.
Jesus was not saying that noticing someone's beauty is automatically adultery.
He was not condemning every involuntary thought, every experience of attraction, or the ordinary human capacity for sexual desire.
He was exposing the deliberate cultivation of lust.
The Greek verb ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō) means to desire or long for something. Depending on context, that desire can be good or sinful.
In Matthew 5:28, the context is a desire directed toward sexual unfaithfulness.
Jesus was teaching that obedience to God cannot be reduced to outward behavior while the heart deliberately entertains what contradicts His will.
And that brings us to something deeply personal.
You may never have watched an explicit video.
You may never have touched another person.
You may have remained physically faithful to your spouse.
But have you repeatedly invited sexual fantasies into your imagination, knowing that their purpose is to excite desires outside God's design?
Have you found yourself emotionally investing in fictional intimacy while withdrawing from the real relationships God has placed in your life?
Have you been feeding an appetite that grows stronger every time you promise yourself it will be the last chapter?
These questions are not meant to declare that every romance novel is pornography.
They are meant to help us distinguish between appreciating a story and deliberately using a story to cultivate lust.
Because the medium is not the ultimate moral test. The content, the intention, and the response of the heart matter.
A photograph can portray genuine beauty without being pornographic.
A novel can describe marital affection without being sinful.
The Bible itself contains poetry celebrating marital love.
And the Song of Songs is a powerful reminder that God did not create human sexuality as something inherently filthy.
He created it good.
In Genesis 2:24, marriage is described as a covenantal union in which husband and wife become one flesh.
Sexual intimacy, rightly understood, is not an embarrassment to God's holiness.
It is part of His good creation.
But a good gift can be distorted when desire becomes detached from love, faithfulness, and obedience.
That is where discernment becomes necessary.
And that is where the uncomfortable difference between reading and watching begins to narrow.
Consider the woman who closes her romance novel, turns toward her sleeping husband, and feels disappointed.
He is a good man.
He works hard.
He has flaws, of course.
He forgets things. He gets tired. He doesn't always know the perfect words to say.
But the fictional man she has spent hours imagining never seems to suffer from those limitations.
He always knows what she needs.
He speaks with impossible precision.
He anticipates every emotional longing.
His affection is dramatic. His desire is relentless. His devotion seems effortless.
The husband beside her is real.
The man in her imagination is carefully written to be irresistible.
And slowly, without intending to, she may begin comparing a real human being with a fantasy that was never required to survive ordinary life.
Now consider the single believer who feels profoundly lonely.
They are not reading because they hate God.
They are reading because they want to feel wanted.
They want to experience the tenderness they have prayed for.
They want someone to choose them.
And for a few hours, fiction gives them the sensation of being loved without the possibility of rejection.
There is genuine pain beneath that habit.
Pain that deserves compassion, not ridicule.
But even understandable pain can lead us toward unhealthy forms of comfort.
A substitute can temporarily soothe loneliness without healing it.
A fantasy can imitate intimacy without offering the mutual responsibility, vulnerability, and faithfulness that real love requires.
And sometimes the greatest danger is not that we stop believing in God.
It is that we quietly begin asking something else to comfort us in ways that increasingly pull us away from Him.
James 1:14–15 describes the progression of temptation.
In Greek, the passage uses the expression:
ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας
Hypo tēs idias epithymias.
It means "by one's own desire."
James describes a person being drawn away and enticed by desire, then explains how desire, when it conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin, when fully grown, brings forth death.
This does not mean every desire is sinful.
Nor does it mean that being tempted makes you guilty.
Temptation and deliberate consent are not identical.
Even Jesus was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
But James warns us not to treat desire as spiritually harmless simply because it has not yet produced an outward action.
What we repeatedly entertain can influence what we eventually pursue.
That is why the question is not merely, "Did I watch pornography?"
It may also be, "Am I intentionally returning to material because it stimulates lust?"
If the answer is yes, then changing the format from video to written fiction does not automatically change the moral character of what is happening.
There are meaningful differences between visual pornography and written sexual material. They differ in presentation, production, and sometimes in the exploitation involved.
It would be inaccurate to claim that every explicit novel has the same ethical circumstances or effects as every pornographic video.
But Scripture gives us no reason to assume that deliberately cultivated lust becomes righteous simply because the stimulus is textual.
Words can awaken imagination.
Imagination can become a place where desire is deliberately rehearsed.
And repeated choices can become habits.
Yet this is not the end of the story.
Because there is another person we need to talk about.
The Christian who already knows.
The one who has felt convicted before.
The one who has deleted the reading app, only to reinstall it weeks later.
The one who has prayed, "Lord, I don't want to keep doing this."
The one who genuinely loves Jesus but feels ashamed of what happens in private.
Perhaps you know that person very well.
Perhaps that person is you.
And perhaps the hardest part is not the habit itself.
Perhaps it is the fear that God must be tired of hearing you apologize.
You promised last time.
You meant it.
You cried.
You prayed.
You felt free for a while.
Then came another difficult evening.
Another disappointment.
Another lonely night.
And the familiar temptation returned.
Now you wonder whether your repentance was ever real.
Listen carefully.
A repeated struggle does not prove that God's mercy has run out. But God's mercy is never an invitation to make peace with what is harming your soul.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
That is the King James Version.
Not a sentimental slogan.
Not permission to continue sinning without concern.
A declaration rooted in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
The same apostle who proclaimed freedom from condemnation also taught believers to put sinful practices to death through the Spirit, as Romans 8:13 explains.
Grace does not tell you that sin is harmless.
Grace tells you that sin does not have to be your master.
And repentance is more than feeling terrible after the final chapter.
The New Testament frequently uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance.
It speaks of a change of mind, a turning that bears fruit in the direction of one's life.
Real repentance does not mean achieving flawless performance overnight.
It means turning toward God in truth, no longer defending what He is calling you to surrender.
Sometimes that begins with a very ordinary decision.
Not opening the app tonight.
Not purchasing the next installment.
Not pretending you can repeatedly expose yourself to something that stirs lust and remain unaffected.
Not keeping a secret habit protected by the excuse that it is technically different from pornography.
And perhaps, most importantly, not treating the behavior as the only problem while ignoring the ache underneath it.
Because some people need to repent of deliberately indulging lust.
Some also need help addressing loneliness, grief, anxiety, emotional neglect, or unhealthy coping patterns.
Often, both realities exist together.
A believer can need spiritual accountability and compassionate emotional support.
There is no contradiction between the two.
The Gospel does not require us to pretend our wounds are imaginary.
But neither does it require us to let those wounds govern our obedience.
And now I want you to remember a scene from John chapter 8.
A woman stands before Jesus after being accused of adultery.
Her accusers want judgment.
They want her exposed.
They want the law used as a weapon against her.
Jesus confronts the hypocrisy of the accusers, and one by one they leave.
Then He speaks to the woman.
In John 8:11, the Greek text records:
Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου, ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.
Oude egō se katakrinō; poreuou, apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
A faithful rendering is:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
There is a textual detail worth knowing: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, so modern Bible editions often mark the passage as textually disputed.
We should be honest about that rather than conceal it.
Yet the scene's central themes of mercy and the call to holiness are firmly taught elsewhere in undisputed New Testament passages, including Romans 8:1, Titus 2:11–12, and 1 John 1:9.
And the message is striking.
Jesus does not celebrate adultery.
He does not tell the woman that her actions were morally insignificant.
But neither does He join the crowd in destroying her.
Mercy and holiness meet.
Compassion and truth stand together.
And that is what makes the Gospel so different from both condemnation and compromise.
Condemnation says, "You have sinned, therefore there is no hope for you."
Compromise says, "There is nothing you need to change."
Jesus calls sinners to Himself, offers forgiveness, and summons them into a transformed life.
That is the difference between being exposed for humiliation and being brought into the light for healing.
And perhaps that is why this subject feels so uncomfortable.
Because nobody wants to discover that something they considered harmless has slowly become a hiding place.
Nobody wants to admit that a story has sometimes become more appealing than prayer.
Nobody wants to confess that imaginary intimacy has become easier than real vulnerability.
But God already knows what happens when the lights go out.
Psalm 139:1–4 teaches that the Lord knows our thoughts and words.
And still, the Gospel announces that Christ came to save sinners.
Not impressive people who have successfully concealed every weakness.
Sinners.
People who need forgiveness.
People who need new hearts.
People who cannot rescue themselves through discipline alone.
That includes the person struggling with pornography.
It includes the person struggling with sexually explicit fiction.
It includes the person whose outward religious reputation looks spotless while their private life is unraveling.
And it includes the person who has been using shame as another excuse to stay away from God.
You do not have to wait until you have become spiritually impressive to come to Jesus.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come willing to surrender what you have been defending.
The cross was not necessary because our sins were small.
The cross was necessary because our need was great.
And Jesus Christ did not merely die to improve our reputation.
He died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 declares.
He offers forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
He gives His people the Holy Spirit.
He calls them into a life of growing holiness.
And He does not abandon them the moment obedience becomes difficult.
Maybe tonight, your next act of faith will not look dramatic.
Maybe it will look like putting your phone on the other side of the room.
Maybe it will look like telling a trusted, mature Christian that you have been struggling.
Maybe it will mean choosing a different book, rebuilding intimacy with your spouse, addressing the loneliness you have avoided, or seeking wise counseling when the habit feels difficult to control.
Maybe it will mean praying the simplest prayer you have prayed in years.
"Lord Jesus, I have been looking for comfort in places that cannot save me. Forgive me. Teach me to desire what is good. Help me stop hiding. Change my heart."
Not because those words are a magical formula.
But because honest confession is a beginning.
