Jesus entered the true heavenly sanctuary through His own blood, securing eternal redemption, as Hebrews 9:11–12 teaches.
Eli could not faithfully preserve the holiness entrusted to his household.
Jesus is the holy, innocent, undefiled High Priest described in Hebrews 7:26.
And while Eli's story ends with the collapse of a priestly family, the Gospel announces a Savior whose priesthood will never pass away.
Hebrews 7:25 declares that Christ is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them.
Do you see the difference?
Our hope is not that we will never fail like Eli.
Our hope is that Jesus has succeeded where sinful human beings have failed.
And because He is faithful, we are not condemned to remain the people we have been.
The father who regrets years of silence can repent.
The mother who confused love with enabling can ask God for wisdom and courage.
The pastor who failed to confront wrongdoing can acknowledge the truth, take appropriate action, and seek to make things right.
The believer who has protected a secret at the expense of someone else's well-being can stop hiding and begin walking in the light.
Repentance does not erase every consequence.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore someone to a position of trust.
And grace never requires wounded people to pretend they were not wounded.
But in Christ, repentance is not a hopeless journey into shame.
It is a return to the God who receives sinners through the finished work of His Son.
The Greek word commonly translated "repent" in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It means to repent, to undergo a change of mind or purpose. In biblical context, genuine repentance is more than a passing emotion; it involves turning toward God in a way that bears fruit in life.
Jesus declares in Mark 1:15:
"The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel."
The message is not simply, "Feel terrible about what you have done."
It is, "Turn to God. Believe the good news. Do not remain where sin has kept you."
And that is the invitation waiting on the other side of Eli's tragedy.
Maybe you have been silent when you should have spoken.
Maybe you have spoken when you should also have acted.
Maybe you have confused loyalty with righteousness.
Maybe you have watched something destructive continue because you were terrified of what confrontation might cost.
Or perhaps you are the one who has been harmed by people who should have protected you.
You do not need to carry responsibility for another person's wrongdoing.
God sees what others minimize.
And the Gospel does not demand that you surrender your safety in order to prove that you have forgiven someone.
Jesus is not asking you to call darkness light.
He is calling us into the truth.
And truth can be painful before it becomes freeing.
Some of us need to confess what we have done.
Some need to acknowledge what we have allowed.
Some need to seek help.
Some need to establish boundaries that should have existed years ago.
Some need to stop defending a person merely because that person shares their blood, their surname, their ministry, or their church.
And all of us need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Because without Him, even our strongest convictions cannot save us.
But through Him, sinners can be forgiven, hearts can be changed, and lives can be redirected toward righteousness.
Remember what the Lord said in 1 Samuel 2:30:
"for them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed."
Those words should sober us.
God's honor must never become secondary to our comfort, our family name, our popularity, or our religious position.
And yet the One who calls us to honor Him is also the One who has opened the way for our forgiveness through the cross.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse sin.
He bore its judgment.
He did not pretend evil was harmless.
He gave His life to redeem sinners.
And He rose again, proving that death and sin would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same life-changing truth:
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because every broken relationship is instantly restored.
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
But because Jesus can give a repentant sinner a future that is no longer ruled by the past.
And perhaps, right now, the Holy Spirit is bringing one specific situation to your mind.
A conversation you have postponed.
A wrong you have excused.
A truth you have been afraid to face.
A wound you have hidden behind a smile.
Do not turn this moment into another warning that never becomes obedience.
Bring it to Jesus.
Ask Him for wisdom.
Ask Him for courage.
Ask Him for a heart that loves people enough to tell the truth and honors God enough to act rightly.

You do not have to reveal private details or publicly expose someone else's sins. Your honesty can begin with a simple prayer, and your next step can happen in the safety of wise, trustworthy counsel.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, repentance is never separated from grace, and wounded people are reminded that Jesus Christ remains the only Savior.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, not merely to those who can afford it, but also to people who may have very little and still hunger for God's Word.

For believers who set aside part of their giving to support Christian teaching and outreach, this can be one meaningful expression of generosity alongside their responsibilities to their local church, family, and those in need.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, Christian giving should come from a willing heart, not pressure or compulsion.
These are simply ways to say thank you for helping us keep the work going.
Pray for the ministry.
Help someone discover the free resources.
Speak of Christ to someone who needs hope.
It is to point people to Jesus.
And if even one person reads the story of Eli, stops making excuses for sin, turns toward Christ, and begins walking in truth, that is a reason to give thanks to God.
Before you leave, remember the question that began this story.
Why did Eli fail to restrain his sons even after hearing the reports?
Because knowing something is wrong is not the same as faithfully responding to it.
Because words can be sincere and still fall short of the responsibility entrusted to us.
Because love, when separated from obedience to God, can become an excuse for allowing harm to continue.
And because honoring those we love above the Lord can lead us into decisions that wound the very people we hoped to protect.
But Eli's failure does not have to become your pattern.
Today, you can choose truth over denial.
Courage over avoidance.
Repentance over excuses.
Christ over every competing loyalty.
You can love people deeply without approving of their sin.
You can show grace without abandoning accountability.
You can forgive without pretending that trust requires no rebuilding.
And you can begin again, not because you are strong enough to rewrite your own story, but because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
So tonight, when the noise fades and you are alone with God, ask yourself one question.
Not simply, "Have I spoken against what is wrong?"
But, "Have I been faithful with the responsibility God has actually given me?"
And then listen.
Because the most dangerous silence is not always the silence of someone who never knew the truth.
Sometimes it is the silence that remains after the truth has already been heard.
May we never become so afraid of losing someone's approval that we forget what it means to be faithful to the God who loves us enough to call us into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SEVEN DEMONS COULDN’T KEEP HER FROM JESUS—AND DEATH COULDN’T STOP HIM FROM CALLING HER NAME
paragraphs: SEVEN DEMONS COULDN’T KEEP HER FROM JESUS—AND DEATH COULDN’T STOP HIM FROM CALLING HER NAME

Mary Magdalene had a past that could have swallowed her future. But the woman Jesus delivered became one of the faithful witnesses to His resurrection. And somewhere between her darkest captivity and that empty tomb is a truth every wounded soul needs to hear.
“And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils.” — Luke 8:2 (KJV)
There is something almost unbearable about the thought of Mary Magdalene standing outside an empty tomb, crying.
Because before she ever wept over the death of Jesus, she had already known what it meant to live in a darkness she could not free herself from.
Seven demons.
Not seven mistakes. Not seven embarrassing chapters. Not seven rumors whispered by people who thought they knew her.
Scripture says seven demons had come out of her.
And yet, when the Gospel tells us what happened on the morning of the resurrection, this same woman was standing near the tomb of the One who had changed her life.
She had known deliverance.
She had known devotion.
Now she was standing in grief, believing the One who had rescued her was gone.
And then something happened that turned her mourning into a message the world would never forget.
Jesus spoke her name.
But to understand why that moment matters so much, we have to go back to the woman she was before that morning.
Not the woman religious imagination invented.
Not the woman centuries of speculation have portrayed.
The woman Scripture actually reveals.

Luke introduces her in a remarkably brief statement: Mary, called Magdalene, was among the women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, and seven demons had gone out from her (Luke 8:1–2).
In the Greek text, the phrase is ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει (aph’ hēs daimonia hepta exelēlythei).
It means, in context, “from whom seven demons had gone out.”
The verb describes something that had already happened, with the resulting reality still significant to the story.
Mary was no longer being introduced as someone awaiting deliverance.
She was a woman who had been delivered.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because the Gospel does not begin Mary's story by telling us how impressive she was.
It tells us how desperately she had needed freedom.
We are not told exactly how those demons affected her daily life. We are not told what she said, what she suffered physically, how long the oppression lasted, or how others treated her.
And we must be careful not to turn those silences into invented facts.

The Bible does not say Mary Magdalene was a prostitute. It does not identify her as the unnamed sinful woman in Luke 7. It does not say her seven demons were seven particular sins. Nor should her experience be used to suggest that mental illness is necessarily demonic oppression.
Those are distinctions worth protecting.
Because Mary's actual testimony is powerful enough without adding anything to it.
She was afflicted. Jesus delivered her. And her life became a testimony to His grace.
Perhaps that is where her story begins touching yours.
Because not every prison has visible bars.
Some people are sitting in church with a smile while carrying grief they have never spoken aloud.
Some are raising children while silently fighting despair.
Some are serving in ministry while exhausted from battles nobody sees.
Some have spent years trying to outrun shame, addictions, destructive habits, bitterness, secret compromises, or memories they wish they could erase.
And some have become so accustomed to their wounds that they no longer remember what it feels like to hope.
Mary's affliction was specifically described as demonic. Yours may be something entirely different.
But the Gospel offers a hope deeper than the particular form of our suffering.
Jesus Christ is not powerless before the things that overwhelm us.
He is not surprised by human brokenness.
He does not need a polished testimony before He can extend mercy.
And He does not wait for sinners to become their own saviors.
He came because we could not save ourselves.
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” — Luke 19:10 (KJV)
Think about that.
The Son of God did not enter this world merely to congratulate the righteous.
He came seeking the lost.
He came calling sinners to repentance.
He came to bear sin, conquer death, and reconcile people to God through His cross.
And Mary Magdalene became a living witness that His authority was not merely something He preached about.
It was something that had transformed her life.
Yet there is another detail in Luke's account that is easy to overlook.
After naming Mary and other women who had been healed, Luke tells us that these women supported Jesus and His disciples from their own resources (Luke 8:3).
Mary was not merely mentioned as someone who had received help.
She was named among those who followed and helped sustain the ministry.
The Gospel does not tell us precisely how much she contributed or what sacrifices she made. But it places her among women whose gratitude took practical form.
That is beautiful.
Because grace does not purchase our devotion like a transaction.
Grace awakens love.
We do not serve Jesus to make Him owe us something.
We serve because He has already shown us mercy beyond anything we could earn.
And if you have ever been rescued from a place you thought would destroy you, you understand something about that kind of gratitude.
Sometimes you cannot explain it.
You simply know you do not want to return to the life from which Christ has called you.
But Mary's story did not stop with deliverance.
It moved toward a cross.
And the cross would test everything.
John 19:25 tells us that Mary Magdalene stood near the cross of Jesus, alongside His mother and other women.
Imagine what that meant.
The One who had delivered her was now suffering.
The One whose presence had changed her life was being crucified.
The hands through which others had received healing were pierced.
The voice that had spoken with divine authority was heard in agony.
And the woman who had known the freedom of His power now had to witness the suffering of His love.
We cannot know every thought that passed through Mary's mind.
But we know she was there.
She did not possess the full understanding of the resurrection that Christians now confess.
She could not yet see how this terrible Friday would lead to the triumph of Sunday.
She saw her Lord dying.
And sometimes faithfulness looks less like having all the answers and more like refusing to turn away from Jesus when you do not understand what is happening.
There are people reading this who know that feeling.
You prayed for someone, and they still died.
You tried to do what was right, and your life still fell apart.
You trusted God, and the door you desperately wanted to open remained closed.
You believed the Lord was leading you, and suddenly the road became darker than you expected.
And the question rose inside you:
“Jesus, where are You in all of this?”
Mary's story does not offer a shallow promise that faithful people will never grieve.
It shows something much greater.
The resurrection was already coming, even while Mary was still crying.
That is not a guarantee that every earthly loss will be reversed in the way we desire.
It is the declaration that Christ's victory over death gives His people a hope that suffering cannot ultimately destroy.
Jesus truly died.
He was truly buried.
And on the third day, He truly rose again.
This is not merely a metaphor for beginning again.
It is the historical and theological claim at the heart of Christianity.
And Mary Magdalene was about to become one of its named eyewitnesses.
John 20 opens with Mary coming to the tomb early, while it was still dark.
She discovered that the stone had been taken away.
Her immediate conclusion was not that Jesus had risen.
She thought His body had been removed.
She ran to Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved.
Later, after they had gone away, Mary remained outside the tomb weeping.
Read that carefully.
She was standing near the greatest victory in human history.
And she was crying because she did not yet understand what had happened.
There is something deeply human about that.
Sometimes we are standing in the middle of a chapter whose meaning we cannot yet see.
Sometimes our grief is real, even when our understanding is incomplete.
And sometimes we need more than an explanation.
We need the Lord Himself.
Mary looked into the tomb and saw two angels.
They asked why she was weeping.
She answered that her Lord had been taken away, and she did not know where He had been laid.
Then she turned and saw Jesus.
But she did not recognize Him.
He asked her why she was weeping and whom she was seeking.
Thinking He was the gardener, she asked where the body had been taken.
And then comes one of the most tender moments in all four Gospels.
“Jesus saith unto her, Mary.” — John 20:16 (KJV)
Just one word.
Her name.
In the Greek text of John 20:16, Jesus says:
Μαριάμ — Mariam.
Mary responds:
Ῥαββουνί — Rabbouni.
John explains the meaning as “Master,” a respectful form of address for a teacher. The word reflects a Semitic expression preserved within the Greek Gospel narrative.
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not describe a long sermon.
It does not record Jesus listing everything Mary had done right since her deliverance.
It does not portray Him demanding that she prove her worth before recognizing Him.
He called her by name.
And she recognized her Lord.
The woman from whom seven demons had gone out was now speaking with the risen Christ.
The tomb was empty.
Death had not defeated Him.
Her grief had not been the final chapter.
The voice she thought had been silenced forever was calling her name again.
Perhaps that is the sentence you need to sit with.
Not because you should imagine yourself as Mary in every detail.
Not because Scripture promises that Jesus will audibly speak your name in the same way.
But because the risen Christ is the same Savior who calls His sheep, knows them, and gives them eternal life (John 10:27–28).
He is not a distant religious symbol.
He is the living Lord.
And through the Gospel, He still calls sinners to repent, believe, and follow Him.
You may have been called many things in your life.
A failure.
A disappointment.
A hypocrite.
An embarrassment.
A lost cause.
You may have called yourself even worse.
But the verdict that ultimately matters is not the cruelest label someone attached to you.
It is what God declares concerning those who belong to Jesus Christ.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because our past never had consequences.
But because Jesus bore the judgment sinners deserved, and those united to Him by faith receive forgiveness and new life.
This is why grace is so astonishing.
It does not pretend the darkness was never there.
It announces that darkness does not have the authority to defeat the Savior.
And Mary's encounter at the tomb did not end with private comfort.
Jesus gave her a message.
“Go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God.” — John 20:17 (KJV)
And John 20:18 records that Mary Magdalene went and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord.
Think about the movement of her story.
A woman once described in connection with terrible spiritual affliction was now entrusted with the announcement of the risen Christ to His disciples.
Not because she had become the center of the Gospel.
But because Jesus was the center of her testimony.
Her message was not, “Look how remarkable I have become.”
It was, in essence, “I have seen the Lord.”
And that is the heart of every genuine Christian testimony.
Not how strong we were.
Not how clean our record looked.
Not how successfully we rebuilt ourselves.
But what Jesus Christ has done.
The Gospel never asks us to deny the seriousness of our sins or minimize the suffering we have endured.
It calls us to bring the truth into the light.
To repent where we have sinned.
To seek help where we are wounded.
To forgive as we have been forgiven.
To pursue holiness through the power of the Holy Spirit.
And to trust that the Savior who died and rose again is able to make us new.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
That promise does not mean every consequence disappears overnight.
It does not mean a Christian never struggles again.
It does not mean healing always happens instantly.
It means our identity and destiny are fundamentally changed in Christ.
The past may still need to be confronted.
Relationships may need to be repaired.
Patterns may need to be broken through repentance, discipleship, accountability, and patient obedience.
But for the believer, the past no longer has the final word.
Jesus does.
And that brings us to a question that is more personal than Mary's history.
What are you still allowing to define you that Christ is calling you to surrender?
Maybe it is something you did years ago.
Maybe it is something done to you that you have mistakenly carried as shame.
Maybe it is a secret sin you have been protecting while publicly pretending everything is fine.
Maybe you are spiritually exhausted, and the thought of returning to God feels almost impossible.
Or perhaps you have been around Christianity long enough to know the right words, but you have never truly surrendered your life to Christ.
Listen carefully.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic story like Mary's to need a Savior.
You do not need seven demons in your past to understand your need for grace.
Every human being has sinned and fallen short of God's glory (Romans 3:23).
And every person who is saved is saved by grace through faith, not by personal achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Mary's deliverance was extraordinary.
But the Savior she followed is the hope of every sinner who comes to Him.
That is why this story is not ultimately about demons.
It is about Jesus.
It is about His authority.
His compassion.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His grace.
And His power to change the direction of a human life.
If this has touched something you have been carrying silently, you do not have to pretend in this moment.
You can pray right where you are.

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have hidden, what I regret, what has wounded me, and where I have wandered from You. I confess my sins and turn to You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising from the dead. Forgive me, cleanse me, teach me to follow You, and lead me into the truth. Help me stop building my identity around my failures and begin living in obedience to Your Word. I place my hope in Your mercy. Amen.”
You do not have to reveal private details or explain wounds you are not ready to share.
Sometimes a few sincere words can become the beginning of a meaningful conversation, an encouragement to another believer, or an opportunity for someone to pray with you.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and following Jesus is worth it.
Because the world is full of people who know how to hide their pain.
What it desperately needs is the truth of a Savior who is able to redeem sinners.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around human suffering.
Not to sell the illusion of instant transformation.
Not to replace the local church, faithful pastors, or the personal study of Scripture.
But to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ through biblical teaching, Gospel-centered encouragement, repentance, discipleship, and the hope of redemption.
Every article shared may reach someone who would never walk into a church on their own.
Every Scripture reflection may become an invitation to open the Bible again.
Every honest conversation may encourage someone to seek prayer, return to Christian fellowship, or take another step toward Christ.
Not simply to increase its visibility.
The truth of the Gospel is worth returning to.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and encouragement accessible to more people.
You may choose to regard that support as part of your Christian giving, while remembering that Scripture also teaches believers to care for the needs of their local churches and communities.
God is glorified through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and countless acts of faithful service.
But when you freely support sound biblical ministry, your generosity can become one practical expression of that love.
Paul wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not the suggestion that God's approval can be purchased.
But a willing partnership in helping the message of Jesus Christ reach more hearts.
It is the opportunity to participate in sustaining and expanding a ministry devoted to pointing people toward Christ.
Because the goal is not merely to gather an audience.
The goal is to make much of Jesus.
And now, before you leave this story, return with me one last time to the garden outside the tomb.
Mary is weeping.
She does not yet understand.
She thinks everything has been taken away.
And then Jesus says her name.
That moment did not erase the reality of the cross.
It revealed the victory that came through it.
The Savior she had watched die was alive.
And the woman who came looking for His body left with a message of resurrection.
There is no need to exaggerate that story.
It is already extraordinary.
And its central truth remains unchanged more than two thousand years later.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sins, buried, and raised from the dead, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The risen Lord is worthy of your trust.
His grace is sufficient to forgive the repentant sinner.
His resurrection is the foundation of Christian hope.
And His call to follow Him is not an invitation to keep living comfortably in darkness, but to walk in the light.
Mary Magdalene's story reminds us that a person's worst affliction need not be the last thing said about their life.
And the Gospel tells us something greater still.
The final word over those who belong to Christ is not condemnation.
It is redemption.
So do not worship your past.
Do not excuse your sin.
Do not surrender your hope to despair.
Turn to Jesus.
Follow Him.
And when the opportunity comes, tell someone what He has done.
Because the most unforgettable part of Mary's story was never the number of demons that came out of her.
It was the risen Savior who called her by name—and the life that became a witness to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF GOD NEVER TOLD YOU THAT?
paragraphs: WHAT IF GOD NEVER TOLD YOU THAT?
“The Heart Is Deceitful” — The dangerous difference between hearing the voice of God and hearing your own desires dressed in spiritual language.
Perhaps one of the most dangerous things a Christian can say is not, “I don't believe in God.”
It is, “God told me.”
Especially when He didn't.
Because once we attach God's name to something we desperately want, we can become almost impossible to correct.

Suddenly, advice becomes opposition. Biblical correction becomes persecution. Accountability becomes a lack of faith. Anyone who questions our decision becomes someone who supposedly doesn't understand what God is doing in our lives.
And without realizing it, we may have stopped following God and started asking God to endorse the life we already wanted.
Read that again.
Have you ever prayed about something while secretly hoping God would give you only one particular answer?
Have you ever wanted a relationship so badly that you interpreted every coincidence as divine confirmation?
Have you ever made a decision out of anger, loneliness, ambition, desperation, or emotional exhaustion, and then convinced yourself that God had placed it on your heart?
Perhaps you weren't intentionally lying.
Perhaps you genuinely believed it.
But sincerity is not the same as spiritual accuracy. A person can sincerely believe something and still be sincerely mistaken.
This is precisely why Scripture gives us a warning that should make every believer examine themselves.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9 (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the passage reads:
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿĀqōḇ hallēḇ mikkōl, wəʾānuš hûʾ; mî yēḏāʿennû.
A close translation would be:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and incurably sick; who can understand it?”

The Hebrew word עָקֹב (ʿāqōḇ) carries the sense of deceitfulness or crookedness. The word לֵב (lēḇ), translated as “heart,” refers to much more than emotions. In biblical Hebrew, the heart encompasses the inner person, including thoughts, desires, intentions, understanding, and will.
The word אָנֻשׁ (ʾānuš) describes a condition that is desperately sick or incurable.
Jeremiah is exposing something far deeper than emotional instability.
He is exposing humanity's capacity for self-deception.

The heart can manufacture explanations that protect our pride. It can disguise selfishness as self-care, bitterness as discernment, revenge as justice, ambition as calling, lust as love, and disobedience as freedom.
And perhaps most dangerously, it can disguise personal desire as divine direction.

In its immediate context, Jeremiah 17 contrasts the person who places ultimate trust in human strength with the person who trusts in the Lord. The problem is not simply that human beings experience emotions. The problem is misplaced trust and a sinful heart capable of turning away from God.
But notice what God says immediately afterward:
“I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.” — Jeremiah 17:10 (KJV)
God knows what we cannot always recognize within ourselves.
He sees the motive beneath the prayer.
The insecurity beneath the ambition.
The resentment beneath the silence.
The loneliness beneath the attachment.
The pride beneath the spiritual vocabulary.
He knows whether we are genuinely seeking His will or merely seeking His permission.
And that should humble every one of us.
Imagine someone sitting alone at midnight, staring at a message they know they probably shouldn't answer.
They have prayed. They have cried. They have promised themselves they would walk away from a relationship that repeatedly pulls them toward compromise.
But tonight, loneliness feels unbearable.
Then the message arrives.
“I miss you.”
Their heart races.
Suddenly, they remember a sermon about forgiveness. A worship song plays at precisely the right moment. A familiar Bible verse appears on their Facebook feed.
And before long, they whisper:
“Maybe God is telling me to give this another chance.”
But what if those circumstances are not divine instructions?
What if they are interpreting everything through the lens of what they desperately want?

Forgiveness is biblical. Reconciliation can be beautiful. But forgiveness does not automatically require returning to an unsafe relationship, ignoring destructive patterns, or abandoning godly boundaries.
Sometimes, what we call confirmation is simply our desire finding something it can agree with.
Psychology calls a related tendency confirmation bias: our inclination to favor information that supports what we already believe or want to believe.
Scripture has long confronted the spiritual danger of self-deception.
“Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts.” — Proverbs 21:2 (KJV)
We are remarkably skilled at explaining ourselves to ourselves.
That is why a feeling, however powerful, cannot become the final authority over a Christian's life.
You can feel peaceful about something that is wrong.
You can feel uncomfortable about something that is right.
You can feel attracted to something destructive.
You can feel terrified while walking in obedience.
Jesus Himself demonstrated that obedience does not always feel emotionally comfortable.
In Gethsemane, facing the suffering of the cross, He prayed:
“Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42 (KJV)
The original Greek contains these extraordinary words:
πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω.
Plēn mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō.
“Nevertheless, let not my will, but Yours, be done.”
The Greek word θέλημα (thelēma) means will, desire, or intention.
Here we see the sinless Son of God experiencing genuine human anguish without allowing that anguish to turn Him away from perfect obedience to the Father.
Jesus did not pretend the suffering was easy.
He did not deny the weight of what lay before Him.
Yet He surrendered.
And here we encounter one of the most uncomfortable questions of Christian discipleship:
When was the last time you surrendered something you genuinely wanted because you knew it was contrary to God's revealed will?
Not something you had already grown tired of.
Not something that had stopped benefiting you.
Something you still wanted.
Something your emotions were still defending.
Something your flesh was still begging you to keep.
Because following Jesus is not merely inviting Him into our plans. It is surrendering our lives to His lordship.
We live in a culture that constantly tells us to follow our hearts, trust our feelings, protect our happiness, and live our personal truth.
But Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23 (KJV)
The Gospel does not teach us to worship our inner voice.
It teaches us to follow Christ.

That does not mean every desire is sinful, every emotion is unreliable, or every inner impression should be dismissed. God created us with the capacity to feel, love, grieve, rejoice, and desire. Scripture also teaches that God works within His people.
Philippians 2:13 declares that God works in believers both to will and to do according to His good pleasure.
But there is an enormous difference between acknowledging that God can work within our hearts and assuming that everything arising within our hearts comes from God.
The Holy Spirit is God.
Our emotions are not.
Our impressions are not.
Our preferences are not.
And our interpretations are not infallible.
This is why the apostle John wrote:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.” — 1 John 4:1 (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα
Dokimazete ta pneumata.
“Test the spirits.”
The verb δοκιμάζω (dokimazō) means to examine, test, or evaluate something to determine its genuineness.
In context, John is particularly addressing false prophets and the necessity of testing their confession concerning Jesus Christ.
The principle is clear: spiritual claims must not be accepted merely because they sound spiritual.
Likewise, Paul instructs believers in 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21 not to despise prophecies but to test everything and hold firmly to what is good.
Biblical discernment is not unbelief.
It is obedience.
You do not dishonor God by carefully examining whether an impression truly comes from Him. You honor His truth by refusing to casually attach His name to your assumptions.
The Bereans were commended in Acts 17:11 because they examined the Scriptures daily to determine whether the things they were being taught were true.
If even apostolic preaching was examined against Scripture, why should our private feelings be exempt from examination?
No dream, impression, prophecy, coincidence, personal conviction, or emotional experience possesses the authority to overturn what God has revealed in Scripture.
God will not lead you into adultery and call it destiny.
He will not instruct you to deceive someone and call it provision.
He will not authorize bitterness and call it discernment.
He will not encourage spiritual manipulation and call it leadership.
He will not justify exploitation and call it ministry.
He will not contradict His own character to accommodate your desires.
Second Timothy 3:16–17 teaches that Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, correction, reproof, and training in righteousness.
The Greek word θεόπνευστος (theopneustos) means “God-breathed.”
Our feelings must be examined in light of Scripture, not Scripture manipulated to accommodate our feelings.
Yet sometimes we do exactly that.
We search for a verse that agrees with our decision instead of allowing the whole counsel of Scripture to examine our decision.
We collect encouraging passages while avoiding corrective ones.
We listen to sermons that affirm us while rejecting those that confront us.
We surround ourselves with people who tell us what we want to hear and call their agreement confirmation.
And when someone finally challenges us, we say:
“You don't know what God put on my heart.”
But what if the correction you are resisting is something God is using to protect you?
What if the person you have labeled negative is actually demonstrating the courage to love you truthfully?
What if your greatest spiritual breakthrough is not receiving another confirmation, but finally becoming willing to be corrected?
Proverbs 12:15 reminds us that the way of a fool seems right in his own eyes, but a wise person listens to counsel.
Godly counsel is not infallible either. It must also be examined against Scripture. But a heart that refuses every form of correction should be deeply concerned about its own condition.
Pride often becomes most dangerous when it learns to speak Christian.
It knows how to quote verses.
It knows how to pray publicly.
It knows how to say “God's timing,” “my season,” “my calling,” and “the Lord revealed it to me.”
But beneath all that vocabulary, it may still be refusing to surrender.
And perhaps this article is touching something you have been avoiding.
A decision.
A relationship.
A financial pursuit.
A ministry ambition.
A grudge.
A secret compromise.
Something you have repeatedly defended by saying that God placed it on your heart.
You do not have to publicly disclose the details. But you can become honest before the One who already knows them.
Not as an empty religious expression. Not because commenting earns God's favor. Let it be a simple declaration of your willingness to be corrected, healed, and transformed.
David understood the need for this kind of honesty.
After everything he had experienced, including the devastating consequences of his own sin, he knew that human beings needed more than confidence in themselves.
He prayed:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” — Psalm 139:23–24 (KJV)
The Hebrew opening is:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
Ḥoqrēnî ʾēl, wəḏaʿ ləḇāḇî.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
David was not asking God to confirm that everything inside him was right.
He was inviting God to expose whatever was wrong.
That is a prayer of spiritual maturity.

“Lord, show me where my desires are deceiving me. Reveal where my wounds are influencing my judgment. Expose where my pride has disguised itself as conviction. And if I am wrong, give me the humility to admit it.”
Imagine how many unnecessary wounds could be avoided if we prayed like that before making life-changing decisions.
Imagine how many relationships, churches, families, and ministries could be protected if we stopped treating personal impressions as unquestionable revelations.
Before declaring, “God put this on my heart,” ask yourself whether the desire agrees with Scripture in its proper context.
Ask whether it reflects the character of Jesus Christ.
Ask whether you are willing to receive correction from mature, trustworthy believers.
Ask whether you would still obey God if His answer disappointed you.
Examine whether your desire is producing the fruit of the Spirit described in Galatians 5:22–23 or feeding the works of the flesh described immediately before it.
And when Scripture does not provide a specific answer about a particular decision, seek wisdom through prayer, sound judgment, godly counsel, and humility.
You do not need to claim a direct revelation for every decision you make.
Sometimes the most spiritually mature thing you can say is:
“I have prayed about this, and I believe this may be the right decision, but I could be mistaken. I am willing for God to correct me.”
There is no shame in acknowledging the limits of your understanding.
The danger is pretending those limits do not exist.
But Jeremiah 17:9 is not the end of the story.
If it were, we would be left with nothing but despair.
The same God who exposes the sickness of the human heart also promises renewal.
In Ezekiel 36:26, speaking of His covenant restoration of Israel, God declares:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.” — Ezekiel 36:26 (KJV)
The Hebrew expression לֵב חָדָשׁ (lēḇ ḥāḏāš) means “a new heart.”
This promise points toward the profound work of divine renewal that Christians understand in light of the new covenant and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
God does not merely expose our brokenness.
He provides redemption.
Jesus did not come simply to teach deceitful hearts how to behave better. He came to save sinners, reconcile us to God, and bring us into new life through His death and resurrection.
At the cross, Christ bore the judgment our sins deserved.
Through His resurrection, He conquered death.
Through faith in Him, we receive forgiveness and are called into a life of repentance, renewal, and obedience.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
Yet spiritual renewal does not mean believers instantly become incapable of error. Christians still need sanctification, correction, discernment, and the ongoing renewal of their minds.
Romans 12:2 tells us to be transformed by the renewing of our minds so that we may discern the will of God.
The Greek word translated as transformed is μεταμορφοῦσθε (metamorphousthe).
It speaks of transformation rather than merely maintaining an outward religious appearance.
The Gospel is not about decorating the old life with Christian vocabulary.
It is about becoming a new person in Christ.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Perhaps you have already made decisions that you claimed were God's will.
Perhaps you used His name to defend something that eventually wounded you or someone else.
Perhaps you manipulated people spiritually without recognizing what you were doing.
Perhaps you are now looking at the consequences of a decision you once celebrated as divine confirmation.
And the shame is overwhelming.
You wonder how you could have been so wrong.
You wonder whether God could ever trust you with anything again.
You wonder whether your failure has permanently disqualified you from a meaningful life of faith.
Hear the Gospel.
Being wrong does not place you beyond the reach of grace. But grace invites you to stop defending what needs to be confessed.
First John 1:9 assures believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
You can repent.
You can acknowledge the truth.
You can seek forgiveness from those you have wounded.
You can accept correction.
You can begin walking in a different direction.

Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence, and restoration does not always mean returning to the position or relationship you once had. But your failures do not have to have the final word over your life.
Jesus Christ is greater than the worst chapter of your story.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create a community of people who pretend to have perfect hearts, but to point imperfect people toward a perfect Savior.
Not to manufacture emotional experiences, but to encourage genuine biblical discipleship.
Not to build faith around personalities, but to continually bring people back to the authority of Scripture and the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
There may come a day when your emotions are louder than your discernment, and you will need to remember these truths.
Your simple act of sharing could place biblical encouragement in front of someone who is wrestling with a decision they have not told anyone about.

Scripture recognizes the importance of supporting those who labor in Gospel ministry. Galatians 6:6 encourages those receiving instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach them, while 1 Corinthians 9:14 affirms the legitimacy of material support for Gospel workers.
If you desire to glorify God through your financial stewardship, supporting faithful Gospel-centered work can be one meaningful expression of that desire.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, God loves a cheerful giver, not someone giving under compulsion.
Salvation is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
And before you leave, wherever you are right now, consider making this your prayer:
“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I confused my desires with Your direction. Forgive me for using Your name to defend my pride, my fears, my ambitions, and my disobedience.
Search the places within me that I have been afraid to examine. Correct what needs correction. Heal what needs healing. Remove what keeps drawing me away from You.
Give me a heart that loves truth more than affirmation, obedience more than comfort, and Your presence more than the fulfillment of my personal desires.
Teach me to examine everything in the light of Your Word. Give me wisdom through Your Holy Spirit, humility to receive correction, and courage to repent when I am wrong.
Even when Your will is different from mine, help me trust Your goodness.
Let my life belong to You.
Not my will, Lord, but Yours be done.
In Jesus' name, Amen.”
Never forget that the goal of Christianity is not to become so confident in your own heart that you never question it.
It is to become so devoted to Jesus Christ that you are willing to let Him transform it.
The next time you feel something powerful rising within you, resist the temptation to immediately declare, “God told me.”
Pray.
Examine Scripture.
Seek wisdom.
Remain teachable.
And remember that the God who loves you enough to comfort you also loves you enough to correct you.
Sometimes His mercy looks like a closed door.
Sometimes His wisdom reaches you through an uncomfortable conversation.
Sometimes His grace exposes the very thing you have spent years protecting.
And sometimes the greatest evidence of spiritual growth is not that you finally received what your heart wanted, but that you became willing to surrender it to Christ.
The heart may write a beautiful story to justify its rebellion, but only Jesus can rewrite that story into redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE TOUCHED HIS ROBE, BUT HE TOUCHED HER IDENTITY: WHY JESUS CALLED A BLEEDING WOMAN “DAUGHTER”
paragraphs: SHE TOUCHED HIS ROBE, BUT HE TOUCHED HER IDENTITY: WHY JESUS CALLED A BLEEDING WOMAN “DAUGHTER”
For twelve years, her body had been bleeding. In one encounter, Jesus gave her something even deeper than physical healing—and perhaps it is exactly what your wounded soul has been searching for.
Imagine suffering for so long that you can barely remember who you were before the pain began.
Imagine waking up every morning hoping something would change, only to discover that yesterday's suffering had followed you into another day.
You prayed.
You waited.
You exhausted your resources.
You watched other people receive the very things you had been begging God for.
And somewhere between your unanswered questions and your silent tears, you began wondering whether God still saw you.
Whether He still cared.
Whether you still belonged.
There was a woman in Scripture who understood that kind of suffering.
We do not know her name. We do not know what her voice sounded like, what dreams she once carried, or how many nights she cried herself to sleep.
But we know what had happened to her.
And more importantly, we know what Jesus called her.
Daughter.
One word.
Two thousand years later, that word still carries enough tenderness to confront the shame of a wounded soul.
Mark 5:25–26 tells us:
“And a certain woman, which had an issue of blood twelve years, and had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse.”
Twelve years.
Approximately 4,383 days of living with a condition she could not overcome.
This was not simply an inconvenience. It was a prolonged physical affliction with financial, religious, and potentially devastating social consequences.
According to Leviticus 15:25–27, a woman experiencing an abnormal discharge of blood was considered ceremonially unclean for the duration of that discharge.
The Hebrew word associated with this condition is טָמֵא — tamé, meaning ritually or ceremonially unclean.
But we must understand something important.
Ceremonial uncleanness was not automatically evidence of personal sin, moral corruption, or divine punishment.
This woman was suffering from a bodily condition. Scripture does not accuse her of wickedness.
Yet the requirements surrounding ritual purity could profoundly affect ordinary human contact, religious participation, and daily life.
Imagine having to navigate those restrictions for twelve years.
Imagine the exhaustion of constantly being aware of your condition.
Imagine the possibility of people becoming more conscious of what was happening to your body than of what was happening inside your heart.
The Bible does not tell us precisely how her community treated her. But the burden described in the text is already heartbreaking enough without inventing details.
She had spent everything.
She had endured many treatments.
And instead of recovering, she had grown worse.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
Not necessarily because you have the same illness, but because you have been fighting something that seems determined to outlast you.
A marriage that is falling apart.
A sickness that keeps returning.
An addiction you are ashamed to admit.
A financial crisis that has swallowed your peace.
A childhood wound that still influences your adult relationships.
A private battle with sin that nobody knows about.
A depression that makes even getting out of bed feel like an achievement.
You have become skilled at smiling while suffering.
You tell people you are fine because explaining what is happening inside you feels more exhausting than pretending.
And sometimes the most painful part is not the suffering itself.
It is the fear that suffering has become your identity.
But then, this woman heard about Jesus.
Mark 5:27–28 says:
“When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole.”
She did not have an impressive introduction.
She did not arrive with wealth, influence, or religious credentials.
She came through the crowd carrying twelve years of suffering and a desperate confidence that Jesus could do what no one else had been able to do.
She reached for His garment.
And immediately, something happened.
Mark 5:29 records that the flow of blood stopped, and she knew in her body that she had been healed of her affliction.
She had come seeking healing.
She could have disappeared into the crowd.
But Jesus stopped.
“Who touched my clothes?” — Mark 5:30
The disciples were bewildered. People were pressing against Him from every direction.
Yet Jesus continued looking around.
The woman, frightened and trembling, came forward, fell before Him, and told Him the whole truth.
The whole truth.
Not a carefully edited testimony.
Not a version designed to protect her reputation.
Not merely the beautiful ending.
She told Him the truth.
There is something deeply moving about that moment.
For twelve years, her condition had shaped her life. Now she was standing before the One who had the authority to heal her.
And what would He say?
Would He rebuke her?
Would He embarrass her?
Would He treat her as an interruption?
Jesus was already on His way to the house of Jairus, whose daughter was desperately ill.
There was another emergency waiting.
Another family crying.
Another life in danger.
Yet Jesus made room for this suffering woman.
He did not treat her as an inconvenience.
And then He spoke the words that have echoed through generations.
“Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.” — Mark 5:34
The original Greek reads:
Θυγάτηρ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην, καὶ ἴσθι ὑγιὴς ἀπὸ τῆς μάστιγός σου.
Thygatēr, hē pistis sou sesōken se; hypage eis eirēnēn, kai isthi hygiēs apo tēs mastigos sou.
A close English rendering is:
“Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace, and be healthy, free from your affliction.”
The first word is extraordinary.
Θυγάτηρ — Thygatēr.
Daughter.
A word of familial relationship, used here as a tender and reassuring form of address.
In the recorded Gospel accounts, this is the only individual woman whom Jesus directly addresses with this particular word.
He could have simply confirmed her healing.
He could have told her that she was free to leave.
Instead, He addressed her with tenderness before sending her away in peace.
The woman who had approached Him trembling was not dismissed as a stranger who had inconvenienced Him.
She was called daughter.
Jesus did not merely acknowledge what had happened to her body.
His words communicated personal care, dignity, and reassurance.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to reach into the deepest places of our own lives.
Because sometimes, what we need most is not merely for something painful to stop.
We need to know that we are still loved while we are hurting.
We need to know that our worst experiences have not made us invisible to God.
We need to know that our wounds do not have the final authority to determine who we are.
Perhaps someone abandoned you and made you feel unwanted.
Perhaps your own failures have made you believe you are beyond forgiveness.
Perhaps people remember your scandal more clearly than they remember your humanity.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to prove that you deserve to be loved.
But the Gospel is not the story of human beings earning their way into God's family.
It is the story of Jesus Christ making redemption possible for people who could never save themselves.
John 1:12 declares:
“But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.”
Through faith in Christ, believers receive the privilege of becoming children of God.
Romans 8:15 speaks of the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father.”
The Aramaic word אַבָּא — Abba means Father, expressing a genuine familial relationship of trust and belonging.
The Gospel does not merely offer a better public image.
It offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a new identity in Christ.
That is why your past does not have to become your permanent address.
But notice something else in Jesus' words to the woman.
Σέσωκέν σε — Sesōken se.
This expression comes from the Greek verb σῴζω — sōzō, which can mean to save, rescue, deliver, or heal, depending on the context.
Here, the immediate context clearly includes physical healing. The perfect-tense form also presents the saving or healing action as accomplished, with a resulting state.
Jesus was confirming what had happened to her.
However, we must not misunderstand His statement about faith.
Her faith was not a magical force.
The fabric of His garment was not a supernatural formula.
She was not healed because she had mastered a spiritual technique.
Her faith was directed toward Jesus.
The power belonged to Christ, not to the woman.
And that distinction matters because there are wounded believers who have been made to feel guilty for remaining sick.
They have been told that if they possessed enough faith, their cancer would disappear.
If they prayed correctly, their depression would end.
If they believed harder, their disability would vanish.
But Scripture does not give us permission to make those promises.
Paul experienced an affliction that God did not remove despite repeated prayer (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).
Timothy experienced recurring physical ailments (1 Timothy 5:23).
Trophimus was left sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20).
Faithfulness to Christ does not guarantee immediate physical healing in this present life.
God can heal miraculously. He can also work through medicine, treatment, counseling, and the care of others. And sometimes, His sustaining grace meets us in suffering that remains.
The ultimate promise of complete restoration belongs to the resurrection and the coming renewal of all things (Revelation 21:4).
So please hear this.
If you are still suffering, your suffering is not automatic proof that your faith is defective.
If your prayers have not been answered in the way you hoped, that does not mean Jesus has stopped caring.
You can belong to Christ while your body is still weak.
You can trust Him while your eyes are still filled with tears.
You can be deeply loved by God while walking through circumstances you do not understand.
You do not owe the internet the private details of your pain. But perhaps those words can become a simple prayer and an encouragement to someone else who feels alone.
There is another remarkable detail hidden in the structure of Mark's account.
The suffering woman had been bleeding for twelve years.
Jairus's daughter was twelve years old.
For as long as one girl had been alive, another woman had been suffering.
One was identified through the name and position of her father, a synagogue leader.
The other remains unnamed in Scripture.
Yet Jesus showed compassion to both.
Mark places their stories together in Mark 5:21–43, inviting us to witness Christ's authority over disease and death.
While Jesus was speaking to the woman, news arrived that Jairus's daughter had died.
But Jesus was not defeated by the apparent delay.
He went to the house, took the girl by the hand, and spoke words that Mark preserves in Aramaic:
Ταλιθὰ κούμ — Talitha koum.
“Little girl, I say to you, arise.” — Mark 5:41
And she rose.
Consider the beauty of these intertwined encounters.
A suffering woman reaches out and touches Jesus.
Jesus reaches out and takes the hand of a dead child.
Under the ceremonial laws of the Old Testament, abnormal bodily discharges and contact with the dead were associated with ritual uncleanness (Leviticus 15:25–27; Numbers 19:11).
Yet in these encounters, suffering and death do not overcome Jesus.
His healing authority overcomes them.
The woman is healed.
The child is raised.
The One standing before them is not merely another religious teacher offering comforting words.
He is the Lord who possesses authority over what humanity cannot conquer.
And this points us toward something greater.
The cross.
Because the same Jesus who stopped for a bleeding woman would eventually shed His own blood.
The same Jesus who spoke peace to a trembling sufferer would endure the agony of crucifixion.
The same Jesus who restored a little girl to life would Himself enter death and rise victorious on the third day.
He did not come merely to improve our circumstances.
He came to save sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
Christ bore our sins so that through Him we might be reconciled to God.
First Peter 2:24 connects His wounds with our deliverance from sin and our calling to live in righteousness.
The deepest human problem is not simply that we suffer.
It is that sin has separated us from God.
And the greatest miracle is not merely that a bleeding body can be healed.
It is that a guilty sinner can be forgiven, a rebellious heart can be transformed, and a person spiritually dead in sin can receive new life through Jesus Christ.
That is grace.
Grace does not pretend that sin is harmless.
Grace does not erase our responsibility to repent.
Grace does not give us permission to return comfortably to the very things from which Christ calls us to turn.
Grace meets us in the truth of our condition and offers what we could never purchase for ourselves.
Forgiveness.
Redemption.
Reconciliation.
New life.
The woman had spent everything she possessed seeking relief from her condition.
But the mercy she received from Jesus was not something she purchased.
And neither is your salvation.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9
You cannot buy your way into God's family.
You cannot donate your way into forgiveness.
You cannot earn eternal life through religious activity.
You come to Christ through repentance and faith, trusting in what He has accomplished through His death and resurrection.
And when you truly understand the grace you have received, generosity becomes a response to love rather than an attempt to purchase it.
Now return for a moment to that woman standing before Jesus.
Her body had been healed.
She had told Him the whole truth.
And He said:
“Go in peace.”
The Greek expression is ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην — hypage eis eirēnēn, literally, “go into peace.”
The word εἰρήνη — eirēnē means peace and carries rich biblical associations with the Hebrew concept of שָׁלוֹם — shalom, which encompasses peace, well-being, and wholeness.
Jesus sent her away with reassurance rather than condemnation.
She did not have to leave trembling in fear of His response.
And perhaps you have spent too many years trembling before an image of God that you constructed out of human rejection.
You think He must be as impatient as the people who abandoned you.
As unforgiving as the people who constantly remind you of your past.
As disappointed as the voices that tell you that you will never change.
But look at Jesus.
Look at how He receives this frightened woman.
Look at how He makes time for her.
Look at how He speaks.
The holiness of Christ does not make Him indifferent to human suffering.
His compassion does not make Him indifferent to sin.
In Him, perfect holiness and perfect mercy meet.
You do not need to pretend before Him.
You do not need to conceal the things He already knows.
Bring Him your grief.
Confess your sin.
Bring Him your questions.
Bring Him the broken pieces of the life you thought you had ruined beyond repair.
Hebrews 4:16 invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
And remember, the purpose of coming to Jesus is not merely to receive something from His hands.
It is to receive Him.
To know Him.
To follow Him.
To surrender to Him.
To discover that even when your circumstances remain difficult, Christ Himself is a treasure that suffering cannot take away.
Maybe you arrived at this article looking for an explanation of a single word in Scripture.
But perhaps that word has confronted something much deeper inside you.
You have been calling yourself a failure.
A disappointment.
A lost cause.
A burden.
Someone too damaged to be useful.
Someone too sinful to be forgiven.
Yet the authority to define your identity does not belong to your shame.
For those who are in Christ, Scripture declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
That does not mean there are no consequences for our actions.
It means condemnation no longer has the final word over those who belong to Christ.
There is room for repentance.
There is hope for transformation.
There is mercy for the person who returns to God.
Your scandal may explain where you have been, but it does not have the authority to determine where the grace of Jesus can take you.
We want to create a place where biblical truth is not diluted, repentance is not avoided, grace is not cheapened, and wounded people are continually pointed toward Jesus Christ.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), while also reminding us that giving must come willingly from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is an opportunity to participate in sustaining a ministry committed to pointing people toward Christ.
If you believe in what we are building and are able to help, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside us as a monthly supporter.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Grace is not for sale.
Jesus remains the center of everything we do.
Before you leave, remember that unnamed woman.
She approached Jesus from behind, carrying twelve years of suffering.
She reached for His garment.
She fell before Him trembling.
She told Him the whole truth.
And the Savior who knew her condition did not reduce her to it.
He called her daughter.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that if people knew the whole truth about you, they would walk away.
But Jesus already knows.
He knows the sins that need forgiving.
The wounds that need tending.
The pride that needs surrendering.
The tears that nobody has witnessed.
The parts of your story that you wish you could erase.
And still, He calls sinners to repentance, invites the weary to come to Him, and promises never to cast out those who come to Him in faith (Matthew 11:28; John 6:37).
Do not let shame keep you hiding from the One who alone can redeem you.
Come to Jesus.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
But because He is merciful.
Not because you have successfully rewritten your past.
But because through His cross and resurrection, He offers a future that your past could never purchase.
The world may remember what happened to you.
People may remember what you did.
But in Christ, neither suffering nor forgiven sin gets to write the final chapter.

She came hoping Jesus would stop her bleeding. She left knowing that the One who held authority over her suffering had not forgotten her humanity. And the voice that called her daughter was louder than twelve years of pain.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “MY SHEEP HEAR MY VOICE” — BUT WHAT IF THE VOICE YOU’VE BEEN FOLLOWING ISN’T JESUS?
paragraphs: “MY SHEEP HEAR MY VOICE” — BUT WHAT IF THE VOICE YOU’VE BEEN FOLLOWING ISN’T JESUS?

One of the most quoted promises in John 10:27 may also be one of the most misunderstood. What Jesus actually meant could change the way you understand faith, discernment, obedience, and your relationship with God forever.
What if the most dangerous voice in your life is not the one telling you to abandon God, but the one convincing you that you are following Him when you are actually following yourself?
Think about that for a moment.
How many times have we said, “God told me,” when what we really meant was, “This is what I wanted”?
How many relationships have we entered because we believed God sent someone, only to discover that loneliness was doing the talking?
How many decisions have we justified with spiritual language because admitting that we were wrong would have wounded our pride?
How many times have we mistaken emotional excitement for divine confirmation, personal ambition for God's calling, and the silence of our conscience for the peace of the Holy Spirit?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all:
Have we become so familiar with talking about Jesus that we have forgotten what it means to actually follow Him?
Jesus said something in John 10:27 that should bring extraordinary comfort to the believer, but also profound conviction to anyone who claims to belong to Him.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27, KJV
Many Christians quote the first part of that verse.
Far fewer seriously examine the last.
We want to hear His voice.
We want supernatural confirmation.
We want direction, reassurance, prophetic words, answered prayers, and unmistakable signs that God is moving in our lives.
But Jesus did not merely say that His sheep hear Him.
He said they follow Him.
And there is an enormous difference between wanting to hear what God has to say and being willing to obey what He has already said.
To understand the depth of this statement, we need to examine the Greek text in which the Gospel of John was preserved:
Τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι.
Ta probata ta ema tēs phōnēs mou akouousin, kagō ginōskō auta, kai akolouthousin moi.
A close English translation reads:
“The sheep that are mine hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”

Jesus likely spoke Aramaic in many of His earthly conversations, but the canonical Gospel of John comes to us in Koine Greek. Therefore, the Greek text is the appropriate foundation for examining the wording of this passage rather than claiming certainty about an unrecoverable original Aramaic utterance.
The Greek word translated as “hear” is ἀκούουσιν (akouousin), from ἀκούω (akouō), meaning to hear or listen.

The word itself does not automatically mean obedience in every context. However, Jesus connects hearing with following, making it clear that He is describing something deeper than merely receiving audible information.
The sheep recognize and respond to their Shepherd.
They do not simply hear a sound.
They respond to a Person.
This echoes an important biblical pattern found in the Hebrew Scriptures.
In Deuteronomy 6:4, Israel is called to listen:
שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai Echad.
“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.” — Deuteronomy 6:4, KJV
The Hebrew word שָׁמַע (shama) can mean hearing, listening, heeding, or obeying, depending on its context.
Throughout Scripture, truly listening to God is frequently connected with responding faithfully to Him.
The issue is not whether sound reaches our ears.
The issue is whether God's truth reaches our hearts and changes the direction of our lives.
Imagine a man sitting alone in his car after another argument with his wife.
His hands are gripping the steering wheel. His eyes are exhausted. He knows the words he said were cruel, but he keeps replaying everything she did wrong.
He opens his phone, scrolls through Christian videos, and eventually finds a message about how God removes people who disturb your peace.
Suddenly, he feels justified.
Maybe God is telling him to walk away.
Maybe his wife is the problem.
Maybe he deserves better.
But somewhere beneath all the noise, Scripture confronts him with something he does not want to hear.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
He wanted confirmation.
Scripture confronted him with responsibility.
He wanted permission to protect his pride.
Christ called him toward humility, love, and repentance.
Which message was more comfortable?
And which was more consistent with the Shepherd?

This does not mean someone must remain in an abusive or dangerous situation. Seeking safety and appropriate help is not a failure of Christian faith. But in ordinary conflicts, we must be careful not to use spiritual language to escape the accountability Scripture places upon us.
Sometimes the truth we least want to hear is the very truth we most desperately need.
The context of John 10 makes Jesus' words even more powerful.
He was not giving His disciples a technique for receiving secret messages from heaven.
He was revealing His identity as the Good Shepherd.

The conversation follows the events of John 9, where Jesus healed a man who had been blind from birth. Instead of celebrating God's work, certain religious authorities interrogated the man and eventually cast him out.
Imagine being rejected by the very people you expected to represent God.
Imagine receiving a miracle and losing your community.
Imagine finally being able to see the world around you, only to discover how spiritually blind some of the people around you had become.
But John 9:35 records something beautiful.
Jesus heard that the man had been cast out.
And Jesus found him.
The religious authorities had rejected him.
The Shepherd went looking for him.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
That is the difference between spiritual leadership that protects its own power and the Shepherd who gives Himself for His sheep.

It also echoes Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's unfaithful shepherds for feeding themselves while neglecting the flock. God promises to seek the lost, care for the injured, and shepherd His people, including through the promised Davidic shepherd.
When Jesus declares Himself the Good Shepherd in John 10, He stands within this extraordinary biblical promise.
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” — John 10:11, KJV
He is not merely another religious teacher offering advice.
He is the Shepherd who lays down His life to save His flock.
Later, during the Feast of Dedication, Jesus is confronted by people demanding that He tell them plainly whether He is the Christ.
Jesus points to His works and addresses their unbelief in John 10:24–26.
Then comes the declaration:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
The immediate context is about recognizing Jesus, believing in Him, belonging to Him, and receiving eternal life through Him.
It is not primarily a promise that every Christian will receive an audible voice, a private revelation, a dream, or supernatural instructions concerning every decision.
That distinction matters.
Because somewhere tonight, a sincere believer may be lying awake wondering why God never speaks to them the way other Christians claim He speaks to them.
They have prayed.
They have cried.
They have fasted.
They have waited.
They have watched people announce, “God told me this,” and “God showed me that,” until they began wondering whether something was wrong with their own faith.
Maybe that person is you.
You love Jesus, but you do not always feel His presence.
You read your Bible, but sometimes the words seem difficult to understand.
You pray, but the room remains quiet.
You wonder whether the Shepherd has forgotten your name.
Please understand what Jesus actually promised.
The absence of an extraordinary spiritual experience is not evidence that you do not belong to Christ.
Scripture records occasions when God communicated through dreams, visions, and extraordinary revelations. But John 10:27 does not establish such experiences as the required evidence of salvation.

Christians differ on how certain spiritual gifts and forms of divine guidance operate today. Nevertheless, every claim of divine guidance must be tested, and no subjective impression possesses authority to overturn God's revealed truth.
The apostle Paul reminds us in 2 Timothy 3:16–17 that Scripture is God-breathed and equips God's people for every good work.
Hebrews 1:1–2 declares that God has spoken climactically through His Son.
And 1 John 4:1 warns believers not to believe every spirit but to test them.
You do not need to manufacture a supernatural experience to prove that Jesus loves you.
You do not need to compete with someone else's testimony.
You do not need to hear an audible whisper before trusting the promises He has already given.
Your feelings may fluctuate.
His faithfulness does not.
Your emotions may become exhausted.
His Word remains true.
Your prayers may sometimes feel painfully unanswered.
But your emotional experience is not the final authority on whether Christ has abandoned you.
Notice the next expression in John 10:27.
κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά — kagō ginōskō auta.
“And I know them.”
The Greek verb γινώσκω (ginōskō) means to know, recognize, or understand. In this context, Jesus is describing His personal relationship with those who belong to Him.
He does not merely know that they exist.
They are His sheep.
The Shepherd knows His flock.
He knows the battles you cannot explain.
He knows the prayers you could barely finish.
He knows the shame you carry behind your carefully maintained appearance.
He knows the history you are afraid someone will discover.
He knows the moments when your faith felt strong and the nights when you wondered whether you had any faith left.
And the wonder of the Gospel is not that you successfully concealed your brokenness from Jesus.
It is that He knew the truth about sinners and willingly went to the cross to redeem them.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became respectable.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we finally learned how to appear spiritual.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
But grace must never be confused with permission to continue embracing the sin from which Christ came to redeem us.
Jesus completes His statement with these words:
καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι — kai akolouthousin moi.
“And they follow me.”
The Greek verb ἀκολουθέω (akoloutheō) means to follow, accompany, or go after someone. In the Gospels, it frequently describes discipleship.
The verbs for hearing, knowing, and following in this passage are in the present tense, presenting these realities as characteristic of the relationship between the Shepherd and His sheep.
Jesus is describing a life oriented toward Him.
Not sinless perfection.
Not uninterrupted spiritual success.
Not salvation earned through religious performance.
But genuine discipleship.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 makes unmistakably clear. Yet the very next verse explains that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Obedience is not the purchase price of salvation.
It is the fruit of a life being transformed by grace.
A sheep can stumble.
A believer can struggle.
A disciple can experience fear, confusion, temptation, and even devastating failure.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
The same Peter who had confidently declared his loyalty eventually found himself weeping bitterly over his own betrayal.
His failure was public enough to become part of the biblical record.
Imagine carrying that memory.
Imagine knowing that when your Savior was suffering, you insisted you did not even know Him.
Yet the resurrected Jesus restored Peter in John 21.
And what did Jesus say to him?
The scandal of Peter's failure was not the final chapter of his story.
Jesus called him forward.
That is why the Gospel is not merely a message for people who have never fallen.
It is good news for people who have fallen and discovered that their only hope is the mercy of Christ.
From denial to restoration.
From shame to renewed discipleship.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But we must also confront an uncomfortable reality.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and deliberately using grace to defend it.
There is a difference between falling while following Christ and refusing to follow Him because we prefer our own direction.
There is a difference between confessing our weakness and celebrating our rebellion.
When Jesus calls us to forgive, we cannot automatically declare our bitterness a divine instruction.
When Scripture calls us toward sexual holiness, we cannot assume that the intensity of our desires makes them God's approval.
