The story moves from forbidden intimacy to holy covenant, from human rebellion to divine redemption, from the devastating consequences of unfaithfulness to the glorious fulfillment of Christ's saving purpose.
Not because the scandal was insignificant.
But because Jesus is greater.
Imagine the person who once believed they were permanently disqualified discovering that Christ's righteousness—not their ability to rewrite history—is the foundation of their hope.
Imagine the wounded believer discovering that what was done against them does not determine their eternal worth.
Imagine the repentant sinner finally abandoning the exhausting performance of pretending to be innocent and discovering the freedom of being forgiven.
This is the Gospel.
Not humanity climbing toward God through moral perfection.
But God reaching toward fallen humanity through Jesus Christ, calling people to repentance, faith, and new life.
And this message deserves to travel beyond the boundaries of your screen.
Somebody on your Facebook friends list is secretly drowning in shame.
Somebody is fighting temptation while smiling through every photograph.
Somebody has been betrayed and cannot imagine trusting again.
Somebody believes Christianity has nothing to offer except condemnation.
There is something beautiful about receiving spiritual nourishment and then willingly helping make that nourishment available to someone else.
You may choose to include this support as part of your personal Christian giving and offerings, according to your convictions, responsibilities, and what you have prayerfully determined before God.
Scripture reminds us:

“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Giving is an opportunity to glorify God through willing generosity—not a transaction that purchases His favor.
You cannot buy salvation.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
Jesus has already accomplished what no amount of money could accomplish.
But you can help support the proclamation of that truth.

Your generosity can help sustain the work that places Scripture before another struggling soul, another broken family, another searching heart, and another person who desperately needs to hear that redemption is possible.
These are practical ways we seek to thank those who stand alongside this ministry while continuing to encourage deeper biblical learning and Christian discipleship.
Because the mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Jesus Christ known.
One day, the things humanity once celebrated in darkness will be exposed before the righteous Judge.
One day, every counterfeit pleasure will reveal its emptiness.
One day, the redeemed will rejoice at the marriage supper of the Lamb.
Revelation 19:9 declares:
“Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb.”
What a destination for people who once wandered so far from God.
What a future for those who thought their past had destroyed every possibility of hope.
What a Savior.
So do not mistake the patience of God for permission to continue in rebellion.
Do not mistake conviction for rejection.
Do not mistake your scars for your identity.
Come to Christ.
Bring the truth you have been avoiding.
Bring the sin you have been excusing.
Bring the wounds you have been concealing.
Bring the exhausted heart that has forgotten what spiritual freedom feels like.
Repent. Believe. Surrender. Walk in the light.
The Bridegroom is worthy of more than your Sunday worship and your carefully curated public image.
He is worthy of your whole life.
And when the accusations of your past whisper that you will never become anything more than the worst chapter of your history, remember the journey from Leviticus to Revelation.
Remember the cross standing between humanity's rebellion and the redeemed bride's celebration.
Remember the blood of the Lamb.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the Savior who makes all things new.
The blood of Jesus does not pretend that your darkest chapter never happened. It declares that, in Christ, your darkest chapter does not have the authority to write your final one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD CLOSED THE WOMBS OF AN ENTIRE ROYAL HOUSEHOLD BECAUSE A KING HAD TAKEN ANOTHER MAN’S WIFE.
paragraphs: GOD CLOSED THE WOMBS OF AN ENTIRE ROYAL HOUSEHOLD BECAUSE A KING HAD TAKEN ANOTHER MAN’S WIFE.
But the most shocking part of this biblical scandal is that God confronted a king, protected a woman, corrected a prophet, and demonstrated a mercy that none of them could afford to take for granted.
Imagine going to sleep as a powerful king, believing everything in your kingdom is under control, only to hear God Himself tell you in a dream:
“Behold, thou art but a dead man.”
— Genesis 20:3, KJV
No invading army.
No assassination plot.
No rebellion threatening your throne.
Just God confronting you over a woman you had brought into your household.
And what makes this story even more disturbing is that the king did not initially know the woman was married.
He had been deceived.
The man responsible for that deception was not some godless criminal or notorious enemy of Israel.
It was Abraham.
The father of faith.
The man who had received extraordinary promises from God.
The man whose descendants would eventually become a great nation.
Yes, even a man who walked with God could become so consumed by fear that he compromised the truth and endangered someone he was supposed to protect.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story begins to feel uncomfortably personal.
Because sometimes the greatest scandals do not begin with hatred, lust, or rebellion.
Sometimes they begin with fear.
Fear of losing someone.
Fear of being rejected.
Fear of suffering.
Fear of losing control.
Fear that makes us manipulate circumstances instead of trusting the God we claim to believe in.
Abraham had journeyed into Gerar, where Abimelech ruled as king. Concerned that he might be killed because of Sarah, Abraham introduced her as his sister.
There was an element of truth in his statement. According to Genesis 20:12, Sarah was his half-sister.
But she was also his wife.
And Abraham deliberately concealed the truth that mattered most.
A half-truth becomes deception when it is used to make someone believe a lie.
How many relationships have been destroyed that way?
How many marriages have suffered because someone insisted they technically did not lie?
How many Christians have justified dishonesty because telling the whole truth would cost them something?
We reveal enough information to appear innocent while hiding enough information to escape accountability.
We call it protecting ourselves.
Sometimes, Scripture calls it deception.
Abimelech took Sarah into his household, unaware that she belonged to an existing marriage covenant.
But before he could touch her, God intervened.
Genesis 20:3 records God's warning:
“Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man's wife.”
The original Hebrew describes Sarah as:
בְּעֻלַת בָּעַל — be'ulat ba'al
An expression meaning a married woman, a woman who has a husband.
The issue was not simply that Abimelech had taken a woman whom Abraham loved. Sarah was already bound within a marriage covenant.
God recognized that covenant even when Abraham's deception had concealed it from everyone else.
The king's authority did not give him permission to violate it.
His wealth could not purchase an exemption.
His ignorance did not make the situation something God would simply overlook.
But what happens next reveals something extraordinary about God's justice.
Abimelech responded:
“Lord, wilt thou slay also a righteous nation?”
— Genesis 20:4, KJV
He explained that Abraham had called Sarah his sister and that Sarah had also identified Abraham as her brother.
Then he appealed to the integrity of his heart and the innocence of his hands.
And God acknowledged his integrity.
Genesis 20:6 contains one of the most revealing statements about divine restraint in the entire narrative:
וָאֶחְשֹׂךְ גַּם־אָנֹכִי אוֹתְךָ מֵחֲטוֹ־לִי
Va'echsokh gam-anokhi otekha mechatō-li.
Meaning, “I also restrained you from sinning against Me.”
Read that again.
God did not merely expose a dangerous situation after the damage had been done.
He prevented Abimelech from committing the offense.
There was a sin the king might have committed, a covenant he might have violated, and consequences he might have brought upon himself.
But God restrained him.
Sometimes mercy does not arrive looking like an open door.
Sometimes mercy is the door that refuses to open.
Sometimes it is the opportunity that disappears, the temptation that gets interrupted, or the truth that comes out before the damage becomes irreversible.
Not every disappointment is divine intervention, and Scripture does not authorize us to interpret every closed door as a direct message from heaven.
But Genesis 20 reminds us that God is capable of protecting us even from dangers we do not yet understand.
How many times have we thanked God for the blessings we received but forgotten to thank Him for the sins His grace helped us avoid?
How many things would we have destroyed if every selfish desire had been granted?
How many times have we mistaken unrestricted freedom for blessing when what we desperately needed was restraint?
Abimelech had power.
But power without restraint can become destruction.
And God loved righteousness too much to allow this situation to continue unchallenged.
Then comes the part of the story that many people overlook.
Genesis 20:17–18 says:
“So Abraham prayed unto God: and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children.
For the LORD had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham's wife.”
The Hebrew wording is particularly emphatic:
כִּי־עָצֹר עָצַר יְהוָה בְּעַד כָּל־רֶחֶם
Ki-atsor atsar YHWH be'ad kol-rechem.
The expression atsor atsar combines the Hebrew infinitive absolute with a finite verb from the same root, intensifying the action.
It communicates that the LORD had indeed, or completely, closed every womb within Abimelech's household.
This was not presented as an ordinary medical occurrence.
Within this particular biblical narrative, Scripture explicitly identifies God's intervention and connects it to the situation involving Sarah.
An entire royal household experienced the consequences of a crisis that began with deception and the taking of another man's wife.
What began as Abraham's attempt to protect himself became a crisis involving people far beyond himself.
Sin rarely respects the boundaries of the person who commits it.
A father's dishonesty can wound his children.
A mother's bitterness can poison relationships.
A husband's unfaithfulness can devastate an entire family.
A leader's secret compromise can shake a whole congregation.
One person's decisions can leave other people carrying pain they never chose.
That does not mean everyone who suffers is personally guilty of the sin that caused their suffering.
And this distinction matters deeply.
If you are struggling with infertility, please do not read Genesis 20 as a declaration that God is punishing you for hidden sin.
Scripture gives us no authority to make that accusation.
Elizabeth and Zechariah were described as righteous before God, yet they experienced childlessness for many years (Luke 1:6–7).
Jesus Himself rejected the simplistic assumption that every physical affliction must be traced to a particular person's sin (John 9:1–3).
Your empty nursery is not evidence that God has rejected you.
Your unanswered prayers are not proof that your faith is defective.
Your tears are not a confession of guilt.
Genesis 20 describes a specific act of divine judgment and intervention. It is not a universal explanation for infertility.
Never weaponize a passage of Scripture against someone whose heart is already breaking.
But there is another uncomfortable truth in this story.
Abimelech, the foreign king, confronted Abraham, the prophet of God, about his dishonesty.
“What hast thou done unto us?”
— Genesis 20:9, KJV
Imagine the humiliation.
The man who knew God's promises was being questioned about his moral conduct by the man he had deceived.
Abraham had assumed that there was no fear of God in Gerar.
Yet Abimelech demonstrated a moral concern that exposed Abraham's own compromise.
The believer had misjudged the outsider.
The prophet had acted out of fear.
The man with the covenant promises had failed to trust the One who made them.
Does that sound familiar?
Sometimes we are so busy identifying the darkness in the world that we refuse to confront the darkness in ourselves.
We condemn unbelievers for dishonesty while making excuses for our own.
We demand repentance from strangers while protecting our favorite sins.
We quote Scripture publicly while privately violating the principles we preach.
We know how to look spiritual.
But looking spiritual and living surrendered are not the same thing.
A Bible verse in your biography cannot substitute for integrity in your relationships.
A ministry title cannot sanctify manipulation.
Years of serving God do not make you incapable of falling into sin.
Abraham's story is not permission to compromise.
It is a warning against spiritual pride.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years pretending that everything is fine.
You know what people would think if they discovered the whole truth.
You know which conversations you have avoided.
You know which apologies you owe.
You know which secrets you have protected.
You know the difference between the person people celebrate and the person you become when nobody is watching.
And you are exhausted.
Exhausted from managing appearances.
Exhausted from defending decisions you know were wrong.
Exhausted from asking God to bless a life you are unwilling to surrender.
You do not have to disclose your private struggles publicly. But you do need to bring them honestly before Christ.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
But as a sincere expression of your desire to stop hiding and begin walking in truth.
Because the most beautiful part of Genesis 20 is not that God closed the wombs.
It is that God restored what had been afflicted.
God instructed Abimelech to return Sarah to Abraham.
Abimelech obeyed.
He returned her, gave gifts, and publicly addressed the situation.
Abraham then prayed for him.
And God healed the household.
The same God who confronted the scandal made restoration possible.
But notice something astonishing.
God still identified Abraham as a prophet in Genesis 20:7, despite Abraham's failure.
That did not mean God approved of his deception.
It meant Abraham's failure had not erased God's covenant purposes.
God's grace is not an endorsement of everything His people do.
It is His undeserved kindness toward people who could never establish their own righteousness before Him.
Abraham was not the hero because he never failed.
God was faithful even when Abraham failed to demonstrate the faithfulness he should have.
And this is where the story begins to point us toward something greater.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Centuries later, through the very covenant line God had promised to Abraham, the Savior would enter human history.
Matthew 1:1 introduces Jesus as the son of David and the son of Abraham.
The Messiah came through a family history containing deception, brokenness, moral failure, suffering, and scandal.
Yet Jesus Himself was without sin.
Where human beings compromised, Christ remained faithful.
Where we concealed the truth, Christ embodied the truth.
Where we attempted to save ourselves at the expense of others, Jesus willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
Abraham endangered another person because he feared for his own life.
Jesus laid down His own life for the salvation of others.
What a breathtaking contrast.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek word used for sinners is ἁμαρτωλῶν — hamartōlōn, referring to those who are sinful.
Christ did not wait for us to become morally impressive before demonstrating His love.
He came for sinners.
He died for sinners.
He rose again, defeating death and opening the way to reconciliation with God for those who trust in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not that our sins are insignificant.
But that Christ is sufficient.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that forgiveness is available.
Not that consequences automatically disappear.
But that condemnation does not have the final word for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).
Grace does not teach us how to hide our scandals more effectively.
Grace teaches us how to stop living in them.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
The grace that forgives is also the grace that teaches us to change.
So if you have taken something that was never yours, return it where possible.
If you have deceived someone, tell the truth.
If you have wounded someone, acknowledge the damage.
If you have violated a covenant, repent sincerely and seek appropriate accountability.
If you have been using God's forgiveness as an excuse to continue harming others, remember that biblical repentance is more than feeling sorry when you are caught.
It involves a genuine turning toward God.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia expresses repentance, a change of mind and heart that, in its biblical context, calls us toward a changed direction in life.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot demand that everyone immediately trust you again.
You cannot guarantee that every broken relationship will be restored.
But through Jesus Christ, your past does not have to determine the spiritual direction of your future.
And if you are the person who was wounded by someone else's deception, remember that forgiveness does not require you to abandon wisdom, safety, accountability, or healthy boundaries.
God sees the person who was harmed, too.
Sarah was not forgotten in this story.
God knew her situation even when Abraham's actions placed her in danger.
There are moments when the people who should protect us fail us.
There are moments when the people who speak about God wound us.
But their failure does not define the character of Jesus.
Do not confuse the imperfections of His followers with the perfection of the Savior.
Perhaps this is the message someone on your Facebook timeline desperately needs today.
Someone is hiding behind a respectable reputation.
Someone is carrying the consequences of another person's decisions.
Someone believes their past has disqualified them from ever being loved by God.
Someone is silently wondering whether there is still a way home.
Let your social media become more than a collection of photographs, arguments, entertainment, and temporary distractions.
Let it become a place where someone might encounter biblical truth when they need it most.

Ministry requires more than good intentions. Creating biblical resources, expanding discipleship initiatives, and consistently bringing Scripture-centered encouragement to people requires time, labor, and practical support.

Paul recognized the importance of supporting those who labor in proclaiming the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that Christian giving should come willingly from the heart, not through compulsion.
It is not a payment for salvation.
It is not a purchase of God's favor.
It is not a substitute for your responsibilities to your local church, family, or those in need.
Helping biblical truth reach more people.
Helping believers grow deeper roots.
Helping those wounded by life discover that the Gospel speaks to their brokenness.
Helping someone who thinks they are beyond redemption encounter the message of Jesus Christ.
And if you cannot contribute financially right now, never believe that your prayers, encouragement, or willingness to share the Gospel are insignificant.

The Gospel is for the wealthy and the poor, the respected and the rejected, the strong and the exhausted, the person who has walked with God for decades and the person who is taking their first trembling steps toward Him.
Before you leave, ask yourself one question.
What part of your life are you still trying to protect through fear, deception, or control instead of surrendering it to Jesus?
Abraham had promises, yet he struggled with fear.
Abimelech had authority, yet he needed divine restraint.
An entire household experienced affliction, yet God brought healing.
And through it all, God's faithfulness remained greater than human failure.
That is why your story does not have to end at the chapter you are most ashamed of.
There is still a Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
There is still mercy for those who come to Him.
There is still forgiveness through His blood.
There is still hope beyond the wreckage of human failure.
Come out of hiding.
Bring the truth into the light.
Surrender what you have been desperately trying to control.
Let Jesus confront what needs confronting, forgive what needs forgiving, and transform what needs transforming.
Because the greatest miracle is not merely that God can restore what sin has damaged.
It is that He can transform the very heart that once caused the damage.
Your scandal may explain the tears on yesterday's pages, but it does not have the authority to write the final chapter of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE DIED NAMING HIM AFTER HER PAIN. HIS FATHER REFUSED TO LET THAT BE HIS IDENTITY.
paragraphs: SHE DIED NAMING HIM AFTER HER PAIN. HIS FATHER REFUSED TO LET THAT BE HIS IDENTITY.

She called him the son of her sorrow. His father called him the son of his right hand. What happened on that road thousands of years ago may change the way you see your wounds, your identity, and the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
Imagine carrying a child for months, dreaming about the life you would give him, only to realize that bringing him into this world would mean leaving it yourself.
No opportunity to watch him grow.
No opportunity to hear him call you Mother.
No opportunity to hold his hand through the difficult seasons of his life.
Just enough strength to give him a name before taking your final breath.
That is what makes one of the most heartbreaking moments in Genesis so difficult to read.
And perhaps what makes it even more personal is that some of us are still living under names given to us during somebody else's season of pain.
Names we never chose.
Identities we never deserved.
Labels that followed us long after the people who gave them to us were gone.
But what if your pain was never supposed to have the final authority over who you are?
Genesis 35:16–19 records the devastating final moments of Rachel, the beloved wife of Jacob.
They were traveling from Bethel toward Ephrath, later identified as Bethlehem, when Rachel went into extremely difficult labor.
This was the woman who had once cried out in desperation, “Give me children, or else I die” (Genesis 30:1, KJV).
Now, in a heartbreaking turn of events, she was dying while bringing her second son into the world.
The midwife attempted to comfort her.
“Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.” — Genesis 35:17 (KJV)
But Rachel would not survive.
And in the final moments of her life, Scripture records something extraordinary.
“And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin.” — Genesis 35:18 (KJV)
The original Hebrew reads:
וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ בֶּן־אוֹנִי וְאָבִיו קָרָא־לוֹ בִנְיָמִין
Vattiqra shemo Ben-Oni, ve'aviv qara-lo Vinyamin.
“She called his name Ben-Oni, but his father called him Benjamin.”
Ben-Oni (בֶּן־אוֹנִי) is traditionally understood in this context as “son of my sorrow” or “son of my suffering.”
Benjamin (בִּנְיָמִין) is traditionally understood as “son of the right hand.”
In biblical imagery, the right hand frequently represents strength, honor, authority, and favor (Psalm 110:1; Psalm 118:16).
The Hebrew word translated as “sorrow” has other possible nuances in different contexts, but Rachel's dying circumstances strongly support the traditional understanding of her son's name.
One child.
Two names.
One devastating moment.
Two profoundly different ways of identifying the life that would continue after it.
Rachel named him from within her suffering.
Jacob gave him another name.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us what Jacob was thinking when he changed the child's name. We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But the contrast between those two names is undeniable.
And there is something deeply moving about it.
The circumstances surrounding Benjamin's birth were tragic, but tragedy did not remain his name.
Jacob could not reverse what had happened.
He could not bring Rachel back.
He could not erase the grief of that road.
Changing the child's name did not change the circumstances of his birth.
Rachel was still buried near Bethlehem. Jacob even erected a pillar over her grave, according to Genesis 35:20.
The sorrow was real.
The loss was permanent in this earthly life.
Yet the child would carry a different name.
Perhaps that is where this ancient story begins to collide with your own.
Maybe nobody literally named you Ben-Oni.
But life found other ways of calling you the child of sorrow.
The unwanted child.
The disappointing son.
The difficult daughter.
The abandoned spouse.
The failed parent.
The addict.
The adulterer.
The hypocrite.
The family embarrassment.
The Christian who fell again.
The person everyone remembers for the worst thing they ever did.
Perhaps someone wounded you so deeply that their words became the voice inside your head.
Perhaps your parents were carrying unresolved pain, and you grew up absorbing the consequences of wounds you did not create.
Perhaps you were born into poverty, rejection, broken relationships, or a household where love always seemed conditional.
Or perhaps the name you carry today came from something you actually did.
Something you cannot blame on your childhood.
Something you cannot excuse by pointing toward somebody else's behavior.
Something you would give almost anything to undo.
And now, whenever you try to pray, whenever you try to worship, whenever you try to believe that God could still use your life, a familiar accusation rises within you.
“Remember what you did.”
“Remember who you hurt.”
“Remember how many times you promised to change.”
“Remember what everybody knows about you.”
You may have spent years answering to a name that your heavenly Father never intended to define your entire existence.
But here is where we must understand the Gospel correctly.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve your self-esteem.
He did not come to tell you that your sins were insignificant, that your choices had no consequences, or that every uncomfortable accusation against you was false.
Some accusations may be true.
Some wounds were inflicted by you.
Some relationships were damaged because of your decisions.
Biblical grace does not require us to rewrite history dishonestly.
It calls us to bring the truth into the light.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that you were never guilty.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save the guilty.
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” — Luke 19:10 (KJV)
The beauty of redemption is not that God pretends the scandal never happened.
The beauty of redemption is that the scandal does not have to become the final chapter of a life surrendered to Christ.
The apostle Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:17:
The original Greek contains the expression:
καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis
Meaning “new creation.”
Notice that Paul does not merely describe a new reputation, a new public image, or a more respectable version of your former self.
He speaks of new creation.
And the foundation of that transformation is found in two words:
In Christ.
Not in your ability to impress religious people.
Not in your perfect attendance at church.
Not in your ability to hide your struggles.
Not in the money you give.
Not in how successfully you convince the world that you have changed.
In Christ.
Through His death and resurrection, sinners who repent and believe receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
This is not positive thinking.
This is redemption.
This is why the same apostle who once persecuted the Church could later proclaim the Gospel he had previously attempted to destroy.
This is why Peter's denial of Jesus did not have to be the end of his discipleship.
This is why the thief on the cross could receive Christ's promise of paradise even when he had no remaining lifetime in which to rebuild his earthly reputation.
Grace did not make their pasts imaginary.
Grace demonstrated that Jesus was greater than their pasts.
And there is another remarkable detail in Rachel's story that deserves our attention.
She died on the way to Bethlehem.
Generations later, according to Matthew 2:1, Jesus Christ would be born in Bethlehem.

We must be careful here. Genesis does not explicitly present Benjamin's renaming as a direct prophecy about Jesus. But when we read these events within the wider biblical story, the geographical connection offers a deeply moving reflection.
Near Bethlehem, a mother died while bringing her son into the world.
In Bethlehem, centuries later, the Son of God entered the world, taking on human flesh, and would eventually give His life to redeem sinners.
The One born in Bethlehem would Himself become intimately acquainted with sorrow.
Isaiah 53:3 describes the suffering servant as:
“A man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
The Hebrew expression is:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת — ish makh'ovot
Literally, “a man of pains” or “a man of sorrows.”
The Christian understanding of Isaiah 53 finds its fulfillment in the suffering of Jesus Christ, as reflected in Acts 8:32–35 and 1 Peter 2:24.
Jesus did not remain distant from the suffering of humanity.
He entered it.
He experienced rejection.
He experienced betrayal.
He experienced grief.
He bore our sins upon the cross.
And after His resurrection, Scripture declares that He is seated at the right hand of God (Hebrews 1:3; Romans 8:34).
The One acquainted with sorrow is now exalted at the right hand of the Father.
And because of Him, those who belong to Christ are no longer defined solely by their former bondage to sin.
Romans 8:15 introduces another beautiful Greek word:
υἱοθεσία — huiothesia
Meaning “adoption” or “adoption as sons.”
It describes the believer's gracious reception into God's family through Christ.
You are not simply a criminal whose record has been forgiven.
Through Christ, you are welcomed into the family of God.
You are given a relationship you could never purchase, earn, or manufacture through religious performance.
And perhaps that is the truth somebody reading this desperately needs today.
You have been trying to earn a place at a table where Christ invites you through grace.
You have been punishing yourself for sins you have already sincerely confessed.
You have been confusing repentance with endless self-hatred.
But genuine repentance is not spending the rest of your life despising yourself.
It is turning away from sin and turning toward God.
It involves humility, confession, obedience, and a willingness to make restitution where possible.
It does not demand that you remain spiritually imprisoned forever.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
That does not mean there will never be correction.
It does not mean consequences will disappear.
It does not mean healing will happen overnight.
It means that condemnation no longer has the final word over those who are in Christ.
There is a difference between the conviction that calls you out of darkness and the despair that tells you there is no reason to leave it.
Godly sorrow leads toward repentance, as Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 7:10.
The Gospel gives you a reason to get up, confess the truth, seek forgiveness, pursue holiness, and begin walking faithfully again.
Even when your voice shakes.
Even when people remember.
Even when rebuilding takes years.
Even when the consequences of yesterday are still waiting for you tomorrow morning.
Benjamin's new name did not erase Rachel's grave.
And your redemption may not erase every earthly consequence of your past.
But your past does not possess greater authority than Jesus Christ.
Please remember that.
Especially on the nights when you cannot sleep.
Especially when you see the people you disappointed.
Especially when an old memory returns and makes you feel unworthy of praying.
Especially when the enemy of your soul would rather have you hiding from God than running toward Him.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent of what needs to be abandoned.
Seek reconciliation where it is appropriate and possible.
Accept accountability.
And trust the Savior whose blood is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in faith.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
Perhaps you are not the person who caused the wound.
Perhaps you are the person who inherited it.
You are still grieving a mother, a father, a child, a marriage, or a childhood you never truly had.
Please do not read Rachel's story as though sorrow itself were something shameful.
Jesus wept.
The Psalms are filled with lament.
Grief is not necessarily evidence of unbelief.
You can love God deeply and still cry over what you have lost.
You can trust His promises and still need time to heal.
You can belong to Jesus and still have difficult days.
Christian hope does not demand that you pretend the grave is empty when someone you love has died.
Christian hope rests in the truth that Christ Himself rose from the grave, and that death will not have the ultimate victory over those who belong to Him.
Your tears are not an embarrassment to God.
And your suffering is not the entirety of your identity.
If these words have reached a place in your heart that you rarely allow anyone to see, perhaps today is the day to stop carrying everything in silence.
You do not owe the internet the private details of your wounds. Sometimes a simple request for prayer is enough.
And if you see someone else asking for prayer, take a moment to pray for them.
Let this become more than a comment section.
Let it become a place where wounded people are reminded of the truth, where repentance is encouraged, where grace is not cheapened, and where Jesus Christ receives the glory.
You may never know who reads it.
You may never see the tears behind their screen.
But you can make the truth of the Gospel available to someone who desperately needs to hear it.
That is one meaningful way to participate in the work of encouraging others toward Christ.
Our desire is not merely to fill your newsfeed with religious content.
It is to help bring biblical truth into the ordinary, painful, complicated realities of human life.
To reach the believer who is exhausted.
The Christian who has become spiritually complacent.
The seeker who has questions.
The person who has walked away from church.
And the sinner who wonders whether there is still a way home.
It also teaches that giving should come from a willing heart.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
It is not a mandatory tithe, a replacement for your responsibilities to your local church, or a payment for God's favor.
Salvation is freely given through the grace of Jesus Christ.
These benefits are our way of thanking those who choose to stand alongside this ministry.
But the greater purpose is helping the message of Scripture reach beyond the people who are already reading it.
If you believe this work is worth continuing, and you have the means and willingness to support it, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Now, before you leave, return for a moment to that road outside Bethlehem.
A mother was dying.
A father was grieving.
A newborn child entered a world he could not yet understand.
Rachel's final words gave him a name connected to her suffering.
But the name by which Scripture would remember him was Benjamin.
The sorrow remained part of his story.
It did not remain his name.
And while Genesis does not promise that every earthly tragedy will be reversed, the Gospel gives us something greater than the promise of an easier life.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Redeemer who brings forgiveness to the guilty.
The risen Lord who gives eternal hope to the grieving.
The One who can transform a life without pretending its darkest chapters never existed.
So stop believing that your worst chapter has already determined the ending.
Bring your sorrow to Jesus.
Bring your scandal to Jesus.
Bring the sin you are ashamed to confess, the grief you cannot explain, and the broken pieces you do not know how to put together.
He is not asking you to manufacture a spotless history before coming to Him.
He is calling you to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Your scars may remain.
Your memories may remain.
Your earthly circumstances may take time to change.
But in Christ, your standing before God is no longer determined by the darkest chapter of your former life.
The grave beside the road was real, but it was not the end of Benjamin's story. And the darkest chapter of your life does not have to be the final word over yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS CALLED IT THE CHILDREN’S BREAD. SHE ASKED FOR THE CRUMBS. HE CALLED HER FAITH GREAT.
paragraphs: JESUS CALLED IT THE CHILDREN’S BREAD. SHE ASKED FOR THE CRUMBS. HE CALLED HER FAITH GREAT.

She was a foreigner, a desperate mother, and a woman standing on the other side of centuries of division. What happened when Jesus finally answered her reveals something extraordinary about faith, humility, grace, and the heart of God.
What do you do when the only One who can change your situation seems unwilling to answer you?
When you have prayed until your words become tears?
When heaven seems silent, people grow tired of your struggles, and the very God you are running toward appears to be the One standing between you and your miracle?
Would you still worship Him?
Would you still believe He is good?
Would you still call Him Lord?
There was a mother in Scripture who faced something remarkably similar.

We do not know her name. We do not know how many nights she had spent crying beside her daughter. Scripture does not tell us how long she had carried the unbearable pain of watching someone she loved suffer while being powerless to rescue her.
But we know that her daughter was grievously tormented by a demon.
And we know that when this mother heard that Jesus was near, she went after Him.
Not for money.
Not for recognition.
Not for herself.
She came because someone she loved was suffering, and she believed Jesus possessed the authority to do something about it.
Perhaps you understand that kind of desperation.
Perhaps you have a child who has walked away from God. A spouse whose heart has grown cold. A family member trapped in addiction. Someone you love who is fighting a battle you cannot fight for them.
You would carry their suffering yourself if you could.
But you cannot.
And sometimes the most painful part of loving someone is discovering that your love alone cannot save them.
Matthew records that Jesus withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. There, a Canaanite woman came crying out:
“Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.” — Matthew 15:22, KJV
There is something extraordinary hidden in her opening words.
In the original Greek, she cried:
Ἐλέησόν με, κύριε, υἱὸς Δαυίδ.
Eleēson me, kyrie, huios Dauid.
“Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.”
The word ἐλέησόν (eleēson) comes from eleeō, meaning to show mercy or compassion.
She was not demanding payment for her goodness. She was not presenting her religious achievements. She was not negotiating with God on the basis of what she believed she deserved.
She was pleading for mercy.
And she called Jesus the Son of David — a title deeply connected to Israel's messianic hope and God's covenant promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:12–16.
Matthew deliberately identifies her as a Canaanite. Mark's parallel account describes her as a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth (Mark 7:26).
She was a Gentile.
Historically, the name Canaanite carried memories of conflict, separation, and generations of hostility between peoples.
Yet here was this woman recognizing something about Israel's Messiah that many of His own people struggled to accept.
She had no recorded religious credentials.
But she knew where to run.
Then came the response that makes this passage so uncomfortable.
“But he answered her not a word.” — Matthew 15:23
Silence.
Not a promise.
Not an explanation.
Not even an immediate acknowledgment.
Imagine how difficult that moment must have been for a mother already carrying so much pain.
She had found Jesus.
She had called Him Lord.
She had asked for mercy.
And still, there was silence.
Have you ever been there?
You prayed faithfully, but the medical results did not change.
You begged God to restore your marriage, but the distance only grew.
You asked Him to bring your children home, yet they seemed to wander further away.
You worshipped with tears in your eyes while secretly wondering whether God had forgotten your address.
There is a particular kind of suffering that comes when you believe God can intervene, but you do not understand why He has not.
Scripture does not explicitly reveal everything Jesus intended through His initial silence. We should not invent motives the text does not give us.
But the conclusion of this encounter reveals something essential.
His silence was not the end of her story.
And silence, by itself, is not proof that God has abandoned yours.
The disciples then approached Jesus and urged Him to send her away because she kept crying after them.
The woman who needed mercy had become an interruption to those walking beside the Messiah.
What a sobering picture of how religious people can sometimes respond to human suffering.
We can know Scripture and still overlook the wounded.
We can sing about grace and become impatient with those who desperately need it.
We can defend Christianity so loudly that we forget to demonstrate the compassion of Christ.
May we never become so comfortable walking with Jesus that we become irritated by the cries of people trying to reach Him.
Jesus then said:
“I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” — Matthew 15:24
To understand this statement correctly, we must understand the biblical story.
Jesus' earthly ministry was directed primarily toward Israel, fulfilling God's covenant promises and the words of the prophets.
This was not a declaration that Gentiles were permanently excluded from salvation.
Long before this encounter, God had promised Abraham that through him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3).
Isaiah 49:6 spoke of God's servant becoming a light to the nations.
And after His resurrection, Jesus commanded His disciples to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19).
The Gospel would go to the Jew first and also to the Gentile, as Romans 1:16 explains.
There was an order in God's redemptive plan.
But that order was never intended to make His mercy the exclusive possession of one ethnicity.
And this desperate mother was about to experience a remarkable glimpse of that mercy.
Matthew tells us that she came closer and worshipped Him.
The Greek word used is προσεκύνει (prosekynei), from proskyneō, which can describe bowing down, paying homage, or worshipping.
She lowered herself before Jesus and spoke three simple words:
“Lord, help me.” — Matthew 15:25
Κύριε, βοήθει μοι.
Kyrie, boēthei moi.
Lord, help me.
No elaborate sermon.
No impressive theological vocabulary.
No carefully rehearsed prayer.
Just the cry of someone who had reached the end of her own strength.
Some of the most sincere prayers you will ever pray will not be beautiful enough to impress another human being.
They will come from bathroom floors, hospital corridors, sleepless bedrooms, empty kitchens, and trembling lips.
Sometimes all you have left is:
Lord, help me.
And those words can express genuine faith.
Then Jesus said something that has challenged readers for centuries.
“It is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it to dogs.” — Matthew 15:26
The original Greek reads:
Οὐκ ἔστιν καλὸν λαβεῖν τὸν ἄρτον τῶν τέκνων καὶ βαλεῖν τοῖς κυναρίοις.
“It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs.”
The word translated as dogs is κυναρίοις (kynariois), a diminutive form related to kyōn, the Greek word for dog.
It can refer to little dogs, and the imagery of a household meal suggests dogs associated with the home rather than necessarily wild dogs roaming the streets.
However, we must not soften the passage dishonestly.
The diminutive does not automatically make the comparison affectionate or remove its uncomfortable distinction.
Jesus' metaphor still distinguishes between the children receiving bread and the dogs beneath the table.
In the context of His preceding statement, the children represent Israel, and the bread represents the blessings associated with His messianic ministry.
Mark's parallel account adds an especially important word:
“Let the children first be filled.” — Mark 7:27
The Greek word πρῶτον (prōton) means “first.”
First does not mean only.
The distinction concerns priority within God's unfolding redemptive purpose, not a permanent denial of mercy to the nations.
Nevertheless, the woman's response is what makes this encounter unforgettable.
She could have walked away.
She could have become offended.
She could have allowed the disciples' impatience, the silence, and the difficult words to become reasons for abandoning her appeal.
Instead, she answered:
“Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table.” — Matthew 15:27
In Greek:
Ναί, κύριε, καὶ γὰρ τὰ κυνάρια ἐσθίει ἀπὸ τῶν ψιχίων τῶν πιπτόντων ἀπὸ τῆς τραπέζης τῶν κυρίων αὐτῶν.
“Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs falling from their masters' table.”
Notice the brilliance of her answer.
She did not deny the children's place.
She did not demand that their bread be taken away.
She did not argue that God owed her anything.
Instead, she found hope within the very image Jesus had given her.
The Greek word ψιχίων (psichiōn) refers to crumbs or small fragments of food.
Her argument was not that the children's bread should be withheld from them.
It was that their blessing did not have to exclude her daughter from receiving mercy.
What extraordinary faith.
She understood that the mercy of Jesus was not so limited that blessing one person required abandoning another.
She was asking for what seemed small within the metaphor, while trusting Jesus with something unimaginably precious to her.
Her daughter's freedom.
There is a profound difference between humility and believing you are worthless.
This woman was not declaring that she had no human dignity. She was acknowledging that she could not demand divine mercy as something owed to her.
Biblical humility is not self-hatred.
It is the surrender of self-righteousness.
And grace is not God's reward for convincing Him that we are sufficiently miserable.
Grace is His undeserved kindness.
How often do we approach God carrying an invisible list of reasons why He should answer us?
Lord, I have served You.
Lord, I have given money.
Lord, I have attended church.
Lord, I have tried to be a good person.
Why is this happening to me?
Obedience matters. Faithfulness matters. Generosity matters.
But none of them makes God our debtor.
Romans 11:35 asks who has first given to God that God should repay him.
The Gospel is not a transaction between our achievements and God's blessings.
It is the astonishing announcement that Jesus Christ came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And then, after everything this mother had endured, Jesus answered her:
“O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt.” — Matthew 15:28
Ὦ γύναι, μεγάλη σου ἡ πίστις.
Ō gynai, megalē sou hē pistis.
“O woman, great is your faith.”
The word μεγάλη (megalē) means great or remarkable.
Πίστις (pistis) means faith, trust, or belief.
Jesus publicly commended the faith of a Gentile woman.
The one who had been crying for mercy was now being recognized by the Messiah Himself.
The one the disciples wanted sent away became an enduring example of faith for generations of believers.
And Scripture concludes:
“And her daughter was made whole from that very hour.”
Jesus did not need to enter her house.
He did not need to stand beside her daughter.
Distance was no obstacle to His authority.
The mother had asked for mercy.
The daughter received deliverance.
And a woman whose name history does not record became someone whose faith the world would remember.
From an uncomfortable conversation to an extraordinary revelation of mercy.
From standing outside Israel's covenant privileges to receiving a blessing from Israel's Messiah.
From desperation to deliverance.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But please understand something before you turn this passage into a formula for getting everything you want from God.
This account does not promise that every sickness will immediately disappear, every marriage will be restored, or every earthly tragedy will be reversed if you simply pray hard enough.
Faith is not a technique for controlling God.
The apostle Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to be removed, yet the Lord answered that His grace was sufficient (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).
Even Jesus, in Gethsemane, prayed in submission to the Father's will (Matthew 26:39).
Some prayers receive the answer we desperately desire.
Others lead us through suffering we never would have chosen.
But Christian faith rests in the character of Christ, not merely in the outcome of our circumstances.
The greatest miracle Jesus came to accomplish was not simply the temporary removal of earthly suffering.
He came to save His people from their sins.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He came to defeat death through His death and resurrection.
And the cross reveals the ultimate depth of the mercy this mother sought.
Jesus bore our sins in His own body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
He died for our sins and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Through Him, those who were once far away have been brought near by His blood (Ephesians 2:13).
That is why the Gospel is such extraordinary news.

Through Christ, believing Jews and Gentiles are reconciled to God in one body. Ephesians 2:19 declares that believers are no longer strangers and foreigners but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household.
Think about that.
The Gospel does not leave redeemed sinners permanently beneath the table, surviving on whatever happens to fall.
Through faith in Jesus Christ, we receive adoption as God's children (Galatians 3:26; 4:4–7).
Not because we earned a place.
Not because we were born into the right family.
Not because our past was clean enough.
But because Jesus paid the price of our redemption.
Perhaps you have spent years believing your past disqualifies you from coming near to God.
Perhaps there are sins you have never confessed, wounds you have never spoken about, and failures that still make you ashamed to pray.
Do not confuse the seriousness of your sin with the limits of Christ's mercy.
Repent.
Turn away from what is destroying your soul.
Confess your sins before Him.
Trust in His finished work.
The same Gospel that exposes our rebellion also announces forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem your life.
And perhaps today, your prayer is no more complicated than the prayer of that desperate mother.
Lord, help me.
You do not need to reveal the private details of your suffering. Let those words become an opportunity for brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for one another, as James 5:16 encourages us.
Someone reading this may need the reminder that suffering is not the whole story.
Ministry requires more than words. It requires time, resources, faithful stewardship, and people willing to help carry the work forward.
If you prayerfully choose to allocate part of your giving toward this work, do so freely and responsibly, without neglecting your family, local church, or other biblical responsibilities.
As Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7
Christ's grace is not for sale.
Every act of service offered to God in faith matters.
And when you close this article, remember that unnamed mother.
Remember the silence.
Remember the difficult conversation.
Remember the three words she spoke when she had nothing impressive left to say.
Lord, help me.
Remember how Jesus commended her faith.
And above all, remember the Savior to whom she entrusted her daughter's life.
Your circumstances may still be uncertain.
Your prayers may still be unanswered.
Your heart may still be carrying wounds that nobody else understands.
But the crucified and risen Christ remains worthy of your trust.
Come to Him in repentance.
Come to Him in faith.
Come to Him without pretending that you have everything figured out.
She came asking for crumbs from the table. The Gospel reveals a Savior who, through His own blood, brings believing strangers into the household of God.
Never mistake your brokenness for a reason to stop coming to Jesus.
The hands you are reaching for are the very hands that were pierced to redeem sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DEAR JESUS, PLEASE DON'T LET GO OF MY GRANDCHILD. I'M TRYING TO BE STRONG, BUT MY HEART IS BREAKING. 💔🙏
paragraphs: DEAR JESUS, PLEASE DON'T LET GO OF MY GRANDCHILD. I'M TRYING TO BE STRONG, BUT MY HEART IS BREAKING. 💔🙏
An aching prayer from a grandparent standing between fear and faith, trusting the Savior who welcomed little children, hears our cries, and remains faithful even when tomorrow is uncertain.
There are photographs you take because you want to remember a beautiful moment.
And then there are photographs you never imagined you would have to take.
A little child lying on a hospital bed.
A white hospital gown. A pink blanket. A tiny arm surrounded by medical tubing. An oxygen mask covering a face that should be smiling, laughing, and asking questions about the world.
And somewhere behind that photograph is a grandparent whose heart is quietly breaking.
That grandparent is me.
I have prayed many prayers in my lifetime. Prayers of thanksgiving. Prayers for forgiveness. Prayers for protection over my family.
But there is something different about praying when your grandchild is lying in a hospital bed.
The words do not come as easily.
Sometimes all you can manage is a whisper.
"Lord Jesus, please..."
And then the tears finish the sentence.
I look at my grandchild, and I remember how small those hands once were. I remember the laughter, the ordinary days, the little things I never realized were such extraordinary gifts.
How quickly an ordinary day can become a day you will never forget.
One moment, life feels familiar.
The next, you are watching a machine, listening to medical instructions, waiting for another update, and silently asking God for more time, more strength, more mercy.
You discover that even the strongest person in the family can feel helpless.
Because there are some battles love cannot fight with its own hands.
You can hold a child.
You can comfort a child.
You can stay beside a child through the night.
But you cannot command sickness to leave.
And that is when you remember how desperately you need Jesus.
Lord, I cannot heal my grandchild. But I can bring my grandchild before You.
I keep thinking about the words of Jesus in Mark 10:14:
"Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these." (NIV)
In the original Greek, Jesus says:
Ἄφετε τὰ παιδία ἔρχεσθαι πρός με
Aphete ta paidia erchesthai pros me.
"Let the little children come to me."
These words were spoken when people were bringing children to Jesus and His disciples tried to stop them.
But Jesus did not consider those children an interruption.
He welcomed them.
He took them in His arms and blessed them.
And today, as I look at my grandchild in that hospital bed, I hold on to what this passage reveals about the heart of my Savior.
Children matter to Jesus.
Their lives matter.
Their suffering is not beneath His concern.
Their weakness does not make them less precious.
And although this passage is not a promise that every sick child will immediately recover, it reminds me that I am bringing my grandchild before a Savior whose compassion is real.
That truth gives me somewhere to place my trembling heart.
Because, Lord, I am afraid.
I am afraid of hearing words I do not want to hear.
Afraid of watching another painful procedure.
Afraid of seeing my grandchild struggle.
Afraid of what tomorrow might bring.
And sometimes I am afraid to admit how afraid I really am.
But Your Word does not tell me that faith means pretending I have no fear.
In Mark 9:24, a father desperate for his suffering child cried out to Jesus:
"I do believe; help me overcome my unbelief!" (NIV)
What an extraordinary confession.
Faith and struggle in the same sentence.
Belief and desperation in the same breath.
And Jesus did not reject that father for bringing Him an imperfect faith.
Today, I understand that father's cry in a way I never wanted to understand.
Lord, I believe. Please help the part of me that is trembling.
I believe You are powerful.
I believe You are compassionate.
I believe You are able to heal.
But I also know that I cannot see everything You see, and I cannot control what happens next.
So I am not coming to You with a demand disguised as a prayer.
I am coming as a grandparent who loves this child more deeply than words can express.
I am asking You for healing.
I am asking You for mercy.
I am asking You for another ordinary day when this hospital bed is only a memory.
Another morning when my grandchild can wake up without these frightening surroundings.
Another opportunity to hear that precious voice.
Another chance to hold that little hand without wondering what the next medical update will say.
Lord Jesus, please hear me.
Please place Your mercy over my grandchild.
Please strengthen this little body.
Ease every breath that feels difficult.
Calm every moment of distress.
Relieve pain and discomfort.
Give rest where there has been exhaustion.
Restore strength where sickness has brought weakness.
And if healing comes slowly, give us the patience to endure the waiting without losing hope.
Guide every doctor who examines my grandchild.
Give wisdom to every nurse.
Help the medical team recognize what needs attention, choose appropriate treatments, and respond quickly when something changes.
Bless the medicines, procedures, and care being provided.
Protect my grandchild from complications.
And give us the wisdom to listen carefully, ask the right questions, and make decisions with love and understanding.
Father, I thank You for the people who have dedicated their lives to caring for the sick.
Their work matters.
Their knowledge matters.
Their compassion matters.
And I pray that through their care, my grandchild will receive the help that is needed.
I remember the prayer of the early church in Acts 4:30:
"Stretch out your hand to heal and perform signs and wonders through the name of your holy servant Jesus." (NIV)
They prayed boldly because they knew the power belonged to God.
So I, too, will pray boldly.
Not because my words can force Your hand.
Not because I have earned a miracle.
Not because I can promise what You have not promised.
But because You invite Your children to bring their needs before You.
Jesus, if it is Your will, please grant my grandchild healing and recovery.
Let this little body grow stronger.
Let breathing become easier.
Let the treatments work.
Let the doctors see encouraging progress.
Let the day come when we hear those beautiful words:
"You can take your grandchild home."
Lord, I long for that day.
I long to see this child playing again.
Laughing again.
Sleeping peacefully without the sounds of hospital equipment nearby.
I long for the ordinary things I once took for granted.
Because sickness has taught me something painful.
Sometimes the blessings we overlook are the very blessings we would give anything to experience one more time.
A peaceful night.
A healthy appetite.
A little smile.
A child's laughter filling the house.
What once seemed small now feels priceless.
And perhaps someone reading this understands.
Perhaps you are a grandmother who has cried silently so your family would not see you falling apart.
Perhaps you are a grandfather who keeps saying, "Everything will be okay," while privately asking God for strength.
Perhaps you are a mother or father sitting beside a hospital bed, trying to remain calm while your mind races through a thousand possibilities.
Or perhaps you have already walked through a hospital season that changed your life forever.
If that is you, I want you to know something.
You do not have to pretend before God.
You do not have to manufacture a smile.
You do not have to hide your tears to prove that you trust Him.
Psalm 34:18 says:
"The LORD is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit." (NIV)
In Hebrew, the opening words are:
קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב
Qarov Adonai lenishberei-lev.
"The LORD is near to the brokenhearted."
The Hebrew expression nishberei-lev speaks of those whose hearts are broken or crushed.
It does not describe people who have everything under control.
It describes people who have reached the limits of their own strength.
People like me, in this moment.
And perhaps people like you.
This verse does not say the brokenhearted will never suffer.
It tells us that God is near to them.
And sometimes, when you cannot understand what God is doing, the truth that He has not abandoned you becomes the anchor that keeps your soul from drifting into despair.
I also remember something even more astonishing.
Jesus Himself wept.
John 11:35 tells us:
"Jesus wept." (NIV)
The original Greek is just two words:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
"Jesus wept."
At the tomb of Lazarus, the Son of God did not stand untouched by the sorrow surrounding Him.
He wept.
The One who would call Lazarus out of the tomb entered the grief of those who mourned.
That means I do not pray to a Savior unfamiliar with human sorrow.
I pray to Jesus Christ, who knows what tears are.
Who knows what suffering is.
Who knows what it means to face death.
And who conquered the grave through His own death and resurrection.
That is why the Gospel is more than a promise that every painful circumstance will change exactly when we want it to.
The Gospel is the good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Through Him, sinners can receive forgiveness.
Through Him, broken people can be reconciled to God.
Through Him, death does not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
And through Him, even in the darkest valley, we have a hope that suffering cannot permanently destroy.
I do not know exactly how this hospital journey will unfold.
But I know who Jesus is.
And I know that my grandchild is precious to Him.
So tonight, or whenever you are reading this, I ask you to join me in prayer.
Heavenly Father,
I come before You in the mighty and merciful name of Jesus Christ.
You know my grandchild.
You know every detail of this little life, every need, every struggle, every fear, and every medical concern.
Nothing is hidden from You.
Father, please look upon my grandchild with compassion.
Bring healing where there is illness.
Bring strength where there is weakness.
Bring comfort where there is pain.
Bring peace where there is fear.
Protect this child through every treatment and every difficult hour.
Let the medical care be effective.
Let the body respond well.
Let each new day bring signs of recovery.
And Father, please watch over the heart of this child.
When the hospital feels frightening, bring reassurance.
When sleep is difficult, grant rest.
When pain comes, bring relief.
When familiar faces are needed, surround this child with love.
Lord, strengthen the parents and the entire family.
You know the exhaustion that cannot be explained.
The financial worries.
The unanswered questions.
The moments when everyone tries to be brave for everyone else.
Provide what is needed.
Send people who will help in practical ways.
Give us unity, patience, courage, and wisdom.
Keep us from blaming ourselves or one another when fear becomes overwhelming.
Teach us to carry each other's burdens.
And Lord, I pray for the grandparents who are watching their grandchildren suffer.
Some are sitting in hospital corridors.
Some are far away and unable to visit.
Some are praying beside a bed.
Some are waiting for a telephone call.
Some are carrying grief they cannot put into words.
Please draw near to them.
Remind them that their tears are seen.
Their prayers are heard.
Their love matters.
And their weakness does not disqualify them from coming to You.
Father, I surrender what I cannot control.
But surrender does not mean I have stopped asking.
I am still asking for healing.
Still asking for recovery.
Still asking for more years, more birthdays, more laughter, more memories.
Still asking to see my grandchild grow.
Yet above all, I ask that Your presence sustain us and Your grace keep us close to Jesus, whatever tomorrow holds.
Please do not let this suffering harden our hearts.
Let it deepen our compassion.
Teach us to treasure life.
Teach us to love more faithfully.
Teach us to pray more sincerely.
And draw our family nearer to the Savior who gave His life to redeem us.
In the precious name of Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior.
Amen.
There is one more thing I want to say.
I know this world is full of painful stories.
Children fighting illnesses.
Parents exhausted by hospital bills.
Grandparents trying to be strong.
Families praying for miracles.
And sometimes, after seeing so much suffering, people begin to wonder whether God still cares.
I understand the question.
But I cannot look at the cross of Jesus Christ and conclude that God is indifferent to human suffering.
At Calvary, Jesus entered the deepest reality of our broken world.
He bore our sins.
He suffered.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The cross does not mean every hospital story ends the way we desperately want it to.
But it means God's love has been revealed in Jesus Christ, and His resurrection gives us a hope greater than the grave.
This is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
The scandal of sin brought separation from God.
The grace of Christ offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life to everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
And although the Gospel does not promise a life without sickness, it assures believers that suffering cannot cancel the saving work of Jesus.
Romans 8:38–39 reminds us that neither death nor life, nor anything else in all creation, can separate God's people from His love in Christ Jesus.
That is the truth I am holding on to beside this hospital bed.
And that is the truth I want my grandchild to grow up knowing.
If this prayer touched something deep within you, please do not walk away silently.
I want the comments to become more than words beneath a post.
I want them to become a place where people encourage one another, where families discover they are not praying alone, and where believers remember that we are called to bear one another's burdens.
Not to demand a response.
But to remind them that someone cares.
Save this prayer for the difficult nights.
For the moments when medical updates are delayed.
For the mornings when courage feels hard to find.
I also want to invite you to help us continue this Gospel mission.
Gospel Warrior exists to share the truth of Jesus Christ with people who are hurting, searching, struggling, and longing to grow in faith.
Keeping these resources available, producing more Christ-centered teaching, and reaching more families requires ongoing support.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should come from the heart, not from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which I invite you.
Not from guilt.
Not from fear.
But because, if you believe in this mission, your willing support can help us continue and expand it.
And please remember: you do not have to purchase anything to receive the grace of God. Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, not something money can buy (Ephesians 2:8–9).
It is that people will come to know Jesus.
That wounded hearts will find hope in Him.
That sinners will repent and receive His forgiveness.
That struggling believers will return to His Word.
And that our families, even through suffering, will discover how precious His presence truly is.
As for me, I am still here.
Still praying.
Still trusting.
Still watching over my grandchild.
Still hoping for the day when this little one can leave the hospital and return home.
And if you remember only one thing from everything I have written, please remember this:
My grandchild may be lying in a hospital bed, but my hope is resting in the hands of the risen Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “GOD TOLD ME…” — BUT WHAT IF GOD NEVER SAID IT?
paragraphs: “GOD TOLD ME…” — BUT WHAT IF GOD NEVER SAID IT?
The most dangerous deception may not be the voice that tells you to abandon God, but the one that sounds spiritual enough to make you believe you are obeying Him.
Imagine spending years defending a decision God never asked you to make.
Imagine breaking someone's heart, walking away from a responsibility, entering the wrong relationship, or destroying a friendship because you were absolutely convinced that God had spoken.
And then, somewhere between the consequences and the tears, a terrifying question enters your mind.
Was that really God… or was that me?

Perhaps you wanted something so desperately that every coincidence became confirmation. Every emotional experience became revelation. Every open door became divine permission. Every person who questioned you became an obstacle the enemy had sent.
You prayed, but perhaps you were not genuinely asking God what He wanted.
You were asking Him to approve what you had already decided.
And that is where spiritual deception becomes dangerously personal.
Few statements carry as much weight among Christians as the words, “God told me.”

Those three words can comfort the broken, encourage the weary, and inspire courageous obedience when spoken truthfully. But when misused, they can manipulate people, silence accountability, justify sinful behavior, and attach the authority of heaven to the desires of a human heart.
Someone says, “God told me you are supposed to marry me.”
Another says, “God told me to leave my spouse.”
A preacher declares, “God told me that you must give this amount of money.”
Someone refuses correction because, supposedly, God has already confirmed everything.
But since when did claiming to hear God make someone incapable of being wrong?
The Bible never teaches us to abandon discernment simply because something sounds spiritual.
In fact, it commands the opposite.
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.” — 1 John 4:1, KJV
The original Greek reads:
Μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα εἰ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν.
Mē panti pneumati pisteuete, alla dokimazete ta pneumata ei ek tou theou estin.
A close translation is, “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to determine whether they are from God.”
The Greek word δοκιμάζετε (dokimazete) means to examine, test, or assess something to determine its genuineness.
John is not encouraging unbelief. In the immediate context, he is warning believers about false prophets and teachings that deny the truth concerning Jesus Christ.
Biblical faith is not gullibility.
Discernment is not rebellion.
Testing a spiritual claim is not an insult to God. It is obedience to His written Word.

Paul reinforces this in 1 Thessalonians 5:19–22. He tells believers not to quench the Spirit or despise prophecies, but also commands them to examine everything, hold firmly to what is good, and abstain from evil.
Notice the balance.
Do not reject everything.
Do not believe everything.
Test everything.
God's truth does not become less true when examined.
Perhaps one of the hardest realities to accept is that sincerity does not guarantee accuracy.
You can sincerely believe something and still be mistaken.
You can cry during worship, feel chills while praying, experience an extraordinary dream, and still misunderstand what those experiences mean.
Your emotions are real, but your interpretation of them may be wrong.
A powerful feeling is not automatically a prophetic revelation.
An inner voice is not automatically the Holy Spirit.
A coincidence is not automatically divine confirmation.
And peace is not always proof that you are making the right decision.
Sometimes obedience brings peace. Sometimes it brings trembling knees, sleepless nights, sacrifice, and tears.
Jesus Himself experienced profound anguish in Gethsemane.
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
In Greek:
Πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω.
Plēn mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō.
“Nevertheless, let not my will, but yours, be done.”
That is the posture of genuine surrender.
Jesus was not searching for emotional comfort as the final confirmation of the Father's will. He submitted to the Father even when obedience meant suffering.
Sometimes the clearest evidence of spiritual maturity is not how confidently you declare that God has spoken.
It is how willingly you surrender when His written Word contradicts what you desperately want.
Jeremiah 17:9 contains a sobering description of the human heart.
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿAqov hallev mikkol, ve'anush hu, mi yeda'ennu.
The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick; who can understand it?
The Hebrew word עָקֹב (ʿaqov) carries the sense of being deceitful or crooked.
The following verse reminds us that the Lord searches the heart and examines the inner person.
God understands motives we have not yet recognized in ourselves.
That is why our desires must be surrendered to Him rather than automatically treated as messages from Him.
Loneliness can influence what you believe God is saying about a relationship.
Anger can disguise itself as righteous indignation.
Ambition can masquerade as divine calling.
Fear can sound like spiritual caution.
Pride can convince you that you are too anointed to be corrected.
And bitterness can make revenge feel like divine justice.
Not every mistaken impression is demonic. Sometimes it is simply human weakness, misunderstanding, emotional exhaustion, or an unexamined desire.
That is precisely why we need grace, humility, Scripture, and accountability.
Think about the religious leaders in Jesus' day.
They possessed extensive knowledge of Scripture. They spoke about God. They maintained religious traditions. Yet many opposed the very Messiah to whom the Scriptures testified.
Jesus told them:
“Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.” — John 5:39–40, KJV
It is possible to speak constantly about God while resisting the truth He has revealed.
It is possible to use Scripture without submitting to its message.
Even Satan quoted Scripture when tempting Jesus in the wilderness.
In Matthew 4, the devil cited Psalm 91 while attempting to persuade Jesus to throw Himself from the temple.
Jesus answered with Scripture rightly applied.
“It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” — Matthew 4:7, KJV
The presence of a Bible verse did not make the temptation holy.
Context mattered.
Truth mattered.
The character and will of God mattered.
So when someone tells you that God has spoken, or when you believe you have received personal direction, begin with what God has already revealed in Scripture.
God will not contradict His own truth to accommodate your desires.
He will not authorize adultery because a relationship feels destined.
He will not command dishonesty because financial success appears to be waiting on the other side.
He will not give someone permission to manipulate another person's conscience in His name.
He will not redefine sin simply because obedience has become inconvenient.
Second Timothy 3:16 describes Scripture using the Greek word θεόπνευστος (theopneustos), meaning God-breathed.
Scripture possesses divine authority and equips believers for faithful living.
Our personal impressions must remain subject to that authority.
Not the other way around.
But what about decisions that Scripture does not address individually?
Which job should you accept? Whom should you marry? Should you move somewhere new? Should you begin a ministry?
Scripture may not provide a specific name, address, or employment contract, but it provides the moral boundaries, wisdom, priorities, and principles through which those decisions should be examined.
James 1:5 encourages believers to ask God for wisdom.
Proverbs 15:22 teaches the value of receiving counsel.
Romans 12:2 connects discernment with the transformation and renewal of the mind.
You do not need to manufacture a supernatural announcement for every decision.
Sometimes faithful decision-making involves prayer, biblical wisdom, careful consideration, trustworthy counsel, and the freedom to choose responsibly before God.
And sometimes the most spiritually responsible thing you can say is:
“I believe God may be leading me in this direction, but I am still praying, examining Scripture, and seeking wisdom.”
There is humility in those words.
There is room for correction.
There is an acknowledgment that God is infallible, but your understanding is not.
Examine also the fruit of what you believe you have heard.
James 3:17 describes wisdom from above as pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, and sincere.
The Greek word εὐπειθής (eupeithēs) conveys the idea of being willing to listen or open to persuasion.
Consider that carefully.
Heavenly wisdom is not characterized by an arrogant refusal to listen.
When every question makes you angry, every correction feels like persecution, and every disagreement becomes evidence that others lack spiritual discernment, something deserves examination.
That does not mean everyone who questions you is right. Jesus Himself faced unjust opposition.
But genuine spiritual conviction does not require you to declare yourself beyond accountability.
In 1 Corinthians 14:29, Paul instructs that prophets may speak and that others should weigh what is said.
Even within a congregation exercising prophetic gifts, discernment was expected.
